The article discusses Microsoft's acquisition of Nokia's cell phone business and licensing its patent portfolio, a move aimed at building a devices and services strategy. Microsoft has been evolving into a devices and services company for several years, with limited success, and the acquisition of Nokia is the latest acceleration of that strategy. The joint company won't take the same form as Apple, as Microsoft still needs to keep its manufacturers onside.

Microsoft's acquisition of Nokia is a response to the changing market, where the interest has shifted from the desktop to the tablet or smartphone. The company needs to retain its connection to the desktop, as owning the desktop (via Windows) and building additional services on top, like Office or search, has been vital for Microsoft's strategy until now. To be a winner in the business market, it also has to be a winner in the consumer market, something that wasn't the case a decade ago.

Nokia, which has struggled in the smartphone market, lashed itself to Microsoft's mast in the hope of reviving its fortunes. The acquisition is seen as inevitable, but analysts are split on what its biggest implications are. Microsoft's challenge remains how to unite the myriad services and brands — Windows, Nokia, Live, Surface, Xbox, Bing, and more — into a cohesive experience that will command and cement customer loyalty.

The acquisition carries risks for Microsoft, as its success has been built on being hardware agnostic, and already its move into the tablet market with Surface has unsettled its manufacturers. If Nokia's rumored tablet appears too, this will further complicate Microsoft's relations with these partners who are essential for the success of Windows 8 (as well as Office and other products).

On balance, Microsoft needed to make a bold move into mobile, as not doing so would mean certain terminal decline. The acquisition allows Microsoft to get deeper integration, the benefit of Nokia's patents, and removes any risk of Nokia either going Android or being acquired by someone else. The success against iOS and Android will depend on how the companies integrate.

The acquisition is a long journey, and in some countries, Windows Phone 8 market share is now above five percent and close to 10 percent. It thus still offers a limited reach for developers and marketers. Nokia is still massively popular in some emerging countries, but competition is very high with Far East manufacturers and low-cost Android devices. The success of the acquisition will depend on Microsoft's new strategy for emerging markets beyond just mobile phones.

The article also discusses the history of Nokia's decline, which started in 2008 when Apple disrupted the market with the iPhone. Nokia failed to respond, and by 2010, Apple had taken the leadership position in smartphone volumes. Microsoft's strategic rationale for the acquisition is to accelerate growth, with a goal of pulling in over $45 billion dollars in smartphone revenue by 2018 by securing just 15% of the projected global smartphone market. However, this goal is seen as unrealistic, as it is five years away, and the App Store only opened five years ago.

In conclusion, Microsoft's acquisition of Nokia is a bold move aimed at building a devices and services strategy, but the success of the acquisition will depend on how the companies integrate and Microsoft's new strategy for emerging markets beyond just mobile phones. The acquisition is a long journey, and the success will depend on Microsoft's ability to unite the myriad services and brands into a cohesive experience that will command and cement customer loyalty.

The new Supreme Court term, which commenced on Monday, is expected to see conservatives potentially securing victories on contentious issues such as public sector labor unions and affirmative action in universities. The court is also likely to consider cases related to abortion, contraception, and immigration.

One of the significant cases is Friedrichs v. California Teachers Association, which challenges the compulsory payment of union dues by government employees, arguing it violates their First Amendment rights. The case has the potential to weaken the power of labor unions, particularly if the conservative justices rule in favor of the plaintiffs.

Another case, Fisher v. University of Texas at Austin, concerns the constitutionality of affirmative action programs in public universities. The court will revisit this issue after an appeals court upheld the University of Texas's affirmative action program, which the plaintiff, Abigail Fisher, contends discriminated against her based on her race.

The court is also expected to rule on Evenwel v. Abbott, a case that questions whether state legislative districts should be apportioned based on eligible voters or all people, potentially shifting political power from urban areas to rural areas with more white voters.

Religious nonprofits are challenging the Obama administration's process for allowing them to opt out of providing contraception under Obamacare, with several petitions pending at the Supreme Court. The court has already heard a case allowing for-profit companies to seek religious exemptions from Obamacare’s coverage requirements.

Two abortion-related cases are also likely to land on the court's docket this term, involving requirements for doctors performing abortions to have admitting privileges at nearby hospitals and abortion clinics meeting hospital or surgical center standards. These cases could significantly impact abortion access, particularly in rural areas.

The cases' resolutions will have significant political implications, with potential ramifications for the 2016 presidential election and the court's ideological balance. The current court is the first in history split along partisan lines, with the party of the president who appointed each justice being a reliable predictor of judicial ideology. As several justices are nearing retirement age, the upcoming term will likely further shape constitutional and other law for potentially a generation or more.

Woodward found Colonial-era, hand-hewn and hand-planed joists and foundation walls in the basement, which he believes are remnants of the 1750s tavern. If confirmed, the building would be Manhattan's oldest and its preservation is being advocated by Woodward and historian David Freeland. The Iron Dome system, jointly funded with the United States, is designed to shoot down short-range rockets, not slow-flying aircraft.

The Israeli military targeted 25-year-old Mohammed Makawi, who they linked to a radical group involved in a recent Sinai border attack that resulted in an Israeli death. Hospital sources in Gaza confirmed Makawi's death. The armed wing of Hamas, which controls the Gaza Strip, and the smaller Islamic Jihad group were reported to have participated in the rocket attack.

Gaza has been under the control of Hamas since 2007, and the border between Gaza and Israel is tense, with frequent clashes. Over 470 rockets have been fired from Gaza this year, but this was the first time since June that Hamas had acknowledged launching rockets at Israel. The Israeli army said it targeted "Hamas terror activity sites and terrorist squads responsible for the rocket fire," but gave no details.

The latest rocket barrage from Gaza was a response to an Israeli air strike that killed one militant and wounded a second the previous day. Hamas spokesman Abu Ubaida stated that the rocket firing was a message to Israel that it would not accept "a formula of a one-sided aggression by the occupation on flimsy pretexts." He also indicated that Hamas had displayed a "high level of coordination" with Islamic Jihad in unleashing the latest rocket barrage.

The homemade weapons fired from Gaza are inaccurate but potentially lethal. An Israeli spokeswoman said some exploded harmlessly on Monday near the border with the Gaza Strip, but a kibbutz resident reported that children could have been killed. The incident involving the unmanned aircraft and the subsequent rocket attacks highlight the ongoing tension and conflict between Israel and Palestinian militant groups in the Gaza Strip.

The stolen Picasso painting "La Coiffeuse," worth millions of dollars, has been recovered in the United States after being smuggled from Belgium. The painting, which was reported missing from a Pompidou Centre storeroom in Paris in 2001, was shipped under false pretenses as a $37 "art craft."

U.S. Attorney Loretta Lynch filed a civil complaint to forfeit the Picasso and return it to France. The painting was discovered in a FedEx shipment from Belgium to Newark, and its shipping papers described it as a holiday-themed "art craft."

The oil painting is owned by the French government and was last exhibited in Munich in 1998. Officials at the Pompidou Centre thought it was safe and sound until they received a loan request for it in 2001, searched the storerooms, and could not find it. They declared the painting, then valued more than $2.5 million, stolen.

French museum officials came to New York last month to examine the painting in person alongside historical records and photographs, and they confirmed that it was "La Coiffeuse." Under federal law, imported merchandise can be seized by the government if it was stolen or smuggled.

The recovery of the Picasso painting comes at a time when the cultural world is reeling from the destruction of statues by the Islamic State in Iraq. The Pompidou Centre hopes to display the painting again publicly in May. U.S. and French authorities have not announced any arrests in the case.

A volcanic eruption in Tonga, located approximately 65 kilometers northwest of the capital, has created a new island. New Zealand volcanologist Nico Fournier, who visited the site, described the island as approximately 1.8 kilometers by 1.5 kilometers, rising about 100 meters above the sea. The island is made mainly of loose scoria and is expected to erode within a few months once the volcano stops erupting. The ocean around the island is likely fairly shallow, perhaps only about 100-200 meters deep. The new island has no name yet, with naming rights falling to Tonga's king. The volcano is erupting from two vents, one on the uninhabited island Hunga Ha'apai and the other underwater. The ash being emitted is wet and is primarily depositing close to the vent, building up the new island. Foliage near the volcano appears to be dying off due to ash and gases in the atmosphere. Tonga is situated on the Pacific 'Ring of Fire', an area known for frequent seismic activity.

The U.S. Census Bureau's latest report reveals that the number of children receiving food stamps in America has significantly increased since the Great Recession in 2007. In 2014, approximately 16 million children, or one out of every five, were on food stamps, which is a dramatic increase from 2007 when about one in eight children were receiving food stamps. This data is derived from the Census' 2014 survey on families.

The Census also reported that the rate of children living with married parents who receive food stamps has doubled since 2007. This finding has fueled debates, with some Republicans suggesting that the Obama administration aims to increase the number of people on government aid programs. In 2012, former House Speaker Newt Gingrich referred to President Barack Obama as the "food stamp president," a comment that was perceived as racist by some.

The debate over food stamps has led to a continuous argument between Republicans and Democrats. Republicans argue that the end of the recession should allow for a reduction in food stamp spending, while Democrats credit President Obama for a rebounding economy and argue that the program should not be cut yet, given the high number of people still relying on it.

The total number of people using food stamps has almost doubled since the start of the Great Recession, reaching nearly 48 million in 2013. Although the number dipped slightly in 2014, it remains high at about 46 million people.

Republicans have been attempting to cut food stamp spending since 2013 as part of a larger plan to balance the budget. In 2013, the House voted to cut $39 billion from food stamps over a decade, and in 2014, President Barack Obama signed a final deal that will cut $8.7 billion from the program over ten years. This cut is estimated to reduce food stamp benefits by about $90 per month for the hundreds of thousands of homes that use them.

Other findings of the survey show a rapidly changing America, with more children being raised in single-parent homes and more young people delaying marriage. In 2014, 27% of children under 18 were living in single-parent homes, compared to 9% in 1960. The number of marriages also dwindled, with less than half of households in America made up of married couples, compared to three-quarters in 1940. The median age for people first getting married in 2014 was 29 for men and 27 for women, up from 24 and 21 respectively in 1947.

This initiative by Starbucks is a significant step towards making services more accessible for people with disabilities, demonstrating the potential for technology to bridge communication gaps and foster inclusivity.

Conch shells hold cultural significance in Florida Keys, with native-born islanders known as Conchs, and the Keys being nicknamed the Conch Republic. Empty conch shells have been used as signaling devices in the Florida Keys for centuries. This incident serves as a reminder that it is illegal to take live conch shells from Florida beaches.

In a recent incident, eight out of 14 critically endangered black rhinos have died after being relocated to a reserve in southern Kenya. The Kenyan Ministry of Tourism and Wildlife suspects salt poisoning as the cause of death, as the rhinos tried to adapt to saltier water in their new home. This incident has been described as a "complete disaster" by Kenyan conservationist Paula Kahumbu of WildlifeDirect.

The black rhino population worldwide is estimated to be fewer than 5,500, all of them in Africa, with Kenya's black rhino population standing at 750, according to the World Wide Fund for Nature. The loss of these rhinos is significant, as it exceeds the number of rhino fatalities caused by poaching so far this year in Kenya.

Cathy Dean, chief executive of Save the Rhino, expressed shock and sadness over the incident and called for an external investigation into what went wrong. She suggested inviting vets and translocation specialists from countries like Namibia to conduct the investigation.

The black rhinos were moved from the Nairobi and Lake Nakuru national parks to a new sanctuary created in Tsavo East national park. The surviving rhinos are being closely monitored, and the ongoing move of other rhinos has been suspended.

This is not the first time black rhinos have been moved to Tsavo East, which originally had a population of nearly 2,000, according to Save the Rhino, but now has between 10 and 20. Kenya aims to increase its black rhino population to 2,000 by creating populations in areas that provide the right habitat for the animals to thrive.

Translocation of endangered animals, or moving them to new locations, carries risks and is not as common in Kenya as in other southern African countries. In Kenya, it is done every three to four years, whereas other countries are doing it every year.

The Kenyan government has invited an external expert from South Africa to join the investigation, and if negligence is found to be a contributory factor, disciplinary action will be taken. The investigation results will be made public as soon as they are received.

This incident serves as a reminder of the challenges faced in conserving endangered species and the need for careful planning and monitoring during translocation processes.

A North Korean soldier has defected to South Korea, marking the first such incident in nearly two-and-a-half years. The soldier, reportedly stationed near the heavily fortified Demilitarized Zone (DMZ), claimed to have shot and killed his platoon and squad commanders before crossing over. South Korean troops confirmed the soldier's desire to defect and escorted him to a guard post, where he is now undergoing interrogation.

The incident occurred along the western section of the DMZ on Saturday. Defections by North Koreans along the DMZ are rare, with the last known incident involving a soldier occurring in March 2010. The senior analyst in Seoul for the International Crisis Group, Daniel Pinkston, suggests that the defection may not indicate instability in North Korea, as soldiers posted to the border are typically loyal and vetted.

Following the incident, South Korea has increased surveillance along the DMZ and activated its crisis management facility. However, there is no sign of any unusual activity on the northern side. The DMZ is a legacy of the 1953 armistice that ended the three-year Korean War, but the two Koreas have never signed a peace treaty.

The summer gold rush in Northern California is expected to be the best in two decades, according to a gold mining expert. The heavy rain and subsequent flooding have washed out known gold digs, uprooted trees, and eroded the landscape, but have also brought more gold to the surface. The storms have churned the landscape, making it the optimum time for gold hunting. Officials from the Bureau of Land Management say the erosion concentrates the gold by removing the lighter rock and soil. Gold can be found using simple tools like a gold pan or more advanced equipment like a sluice box. One hot spot this year will be below the Oroville Dam, where the huge water releases from the spillway could reveal new pockets of gold. Gold mining is a popular hobby for many, providing a chance of a reward and a way to recharge after a stressful week at work. However, it's important to note that finding gold is not guaranteed and should not be a primary source of income.

The lawsuit also accuses the show's hosts, David Visentin and Hilary Farr, of prioritizing the television show over the homeowners' interests. The production company disputes the allegations and intends to defend itself vigorously in this matter. The couple's attorney stated that the company's incentive was to make decisions that favor the television show but not the homeowners. The lawsuit also questions the business model of Big Coat TV, as it is not licensed as a general contractor. The actual work done on the house was reportedly disastrous, leaving the home irreparably damaged with open duct work, low-grade industrial carpeting, unpainted surfaces, and windows painted shut. The couple also claims that the show never used a licensed architect to develop plans for their house and that they were never shown houses that were actually for sale in North Carolina. Maria Armstrong, Big Coat's CEO and the show's executive producer, says that the company intends to vigorously defend what it considers false allegations.

Anissa Weier, one of the two girls accused of stabbing a classmate in 2014 in an attempt to appease the fictional character Slender Man, plans to plead not guilty by reason of mental disease or defect in the upcoming hearing. This move follows her co-defendant, Morgan Geyser, who made a similar plea last month. A 90-year-old man, Anthony Aiello, has been arrested and charged with murdering his 67-year-old stepdaughter, Karen Navarra, after investigators used data from her Fitbit to piece together evidence. The incident occurred on September 8 at Navarra's home in San Jose, California.

Navarra, a pharmacy technician, was found dead on September 13 by a co-worker after failing to show up to work. Police found her slumped over in a chair, clutching a large kitchen knife with a gaping slit to her neck, and the scene appeared to be staged as a suicide. However, an autopsy revealed multiple deep and intrusive wounds to her head and facial area, which a doctor determined could not have been self-inflicted.

Aiello initially told police that he dropped by Navarra's home on September 8 to bring her pizza, but his account didn't match up with surveillance footage that showed his car at her home for at least 21 minutes that day. Aiello also claimed he saw Navarra driving by and honking with someone else in the passenger seat, but police determined that her car never left in the direction he described.

Navarra was wearing a Fitbit when she was found, and investigators consulted with the company to see if the device could offer any clues. The Fitbit data showed a significant spike in Navarra's heart rate at 3:20 p.m. on September 8, followed by a rapid slowing and the device stopping to register a heartbeat at 3:28 p.m. Aiello was confronted with this evidence during his initial interview, but he denied being present when Navarra was killed and suggested that someone else might have been in the house.

Police also found clothes in Aiello's hamper covered in blood splatter, and he told them he cuts himself frequently. Aiello is being held without bail and is due in court on October 4.

This is not the first time a Fitbit has been used as evidence in a murder case. In 2015, a Connecticut man was arrested after his wife's Fitbit data showed her last movements were more than an hour after her husband said she had been killed by intruders. In another case, a man's Fitbit acted as an alibi in Wisconsin.

A male student, identified as John Doe, from the University of Chicago has filed a lawsuit against the university, alleging that it has created a "gender-biased, hostile environment against males." The student claims that the university violated Title IX, a federal law that prohibits gender discrimination, by treating him unfairly in sexual assault investigations.

John Doe was twice investigated for sexual assault by the university, with the first allegation made by a female student, Jane Roe, in 2014. The university found him not guilty in that case. However, Jane Roe then launched a vendetta against him, placing his name on a list of students accused of sexual misconduct, and making defamatory statements about him on social media. The university did not take any steps to correct Roe's conduct, according to the lawsuit.

The second allegation was made by another female student, Jane Doe, this year, over an alleged instance of sexual assault in 2013. John Doe has also filed a Title IX complaint against Jane Doe, but the university took no action. The lawsuit seeks $175,000 in damages.

The lawsuit alleges that the university's handling of the complaints against John Doe was motivated by pro-female, anti-male bias, and that the university's policies and procedures for investigating sexual assault allegations are biased against men. The lawsuit also claims that the university's confidentiality policies prevented John Doe from personally refuting Roe's defamation within the university community.

The case is part of a recent trend of litigation by male students at American universities who claim to have been discriminated against in sexual assault investigations in violation of Title IX. So far, these claims have generally failed, though last month a federal appeals court ruled in favor of a similar suit against Columbia University.

The university and the female students involved in the lawsuit have declined to comment. The next hearing in the case is scheduled for September 14. The case will continue to be conducted using pseudonyms for the plaintiff and female defendants, as the plaintiff requested.

The article discusses the benefits of using hand grips, specifically the Motus grips, for preventing low back injuries, particularly during snow shoveling. The D-grip, mounted mid-way down the handle, provides lifting leverage to the forward hand, making it a first class lever, and allows for increased leverage, enabling the user to lift heavier loads with ease. The T-grip, mounted at the upper end of the handle, improves posture by allowing the user to stand taller with less back bend and provides a greater range of motion.

A case study assessment by Dean Kriellaars, Ph.D., from the University of Manitoba, found that the grips permit the wrist angle to remain in a near neutral position, which is beneficial to the structures in and about the wrist. The hand-grip also requires the forearm to be in a pronated position, resulting in a different muscle strategy during lifting tasks.

The change in wrist position and forearm pronation results in an increased shoulder abduction angle, a decrease in trunk flexion angle, and a reduction in the load borne by the implement. These changes reduce the potential for blister formation and are beneficial for the prevention and rehabilitation of low back injuries.

The Church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem, believed to be the tomb of Jesus Christ, has undergone archaeological tests that confirm its dating back to A.D. 325, the same era when the Romans first identified the site as holy. The tests, conducted by the National Technical University of Athens, used radioactive elements in architectural glue and ground-penetrating radar to date the Holy Edicule, a small structure enshrining the tomb. The results, reported by National Geographic, suggest that the tomb was constructed around the same time as it was identified by the Romans.

The tomb was opened for restoration work in October 2016, and the restoration took decades to settle due to disputes among the three Christian denominations sharing custody over the church. The same Greek team that restored the Acropolis in Athens was chosen to carry out the project. Archaeologists believe there may be more surprises to come at the site.

The tomb was discovered by the Romans and enshrined around 326 A.D., according to historical accounts. A long shelf, or "burial bed," within the tomb is believed to be where the body of Jesus Christ was laid out following crucifixion. A marble cladding covering the "burial bed" is believed to have been installed in 1555 at the latest, and most likely was present since the mid-1300s.

When the tomb was opened on the night of October 26, 2016, scientists were surprised to find an older, broken marble slab incised with a cross beneath the marble cladding. The lower slab was most likely mortared in place in the mid-fourth century under the orders of Emperor Constantine, according to new test results. These results provide evidence for the earliest shrine on the site and confirm the historical construction sequence of the Edicule.

The mortar samples were independently dated at two separate labs using optically stimulated luminescence (OSL), a technique that determines when quartz sediment was most recently exposed to light. The scientific results will be published by Moropoulou and her team in a forthcoming issue of the Journal of Archaeological Science: Reports. The Church of the Holy Sepulchre remains a significant site for Christianity, and the new test results provide further evidence for its historical significance.

Participants can try their local version of Resilience IPA, with every dollar spent on Resilience benefiting those impacted by the Camp Fire.

Untappd is also participating in the release of Resilience IPA, offering users a limited edition badge that can be earned by checking in to any Resilience IPA from any of the breweries that are officially participating.

Sierra Nevada is grateful to the brewing community, suppliers, wholesalers, and retailers for their support in rebuilding Butte County, one pint at a time.

In a recent development, Sam Patten, a former associate of Paul Manafort, pleaded guilty to failing to register as a foreign agent for his work lobbying on behalf of a Ukrainian political party. Patten's guilty plea was made in federal court in Washington, and he agreed to cooperate with the U.S., providing insights from a longtime international political operative.

Patten's cooperation may offer valuable information to prosecutors, as his Russian business partner has already been indicted in Special Counsel Robert Mueller's probe. Patten worked with Manafort and on Ukrainian campaigns, and reportedly worked on microtargeting operations with Cambridge Analytica.

The nature of Patten's cooperation isn't clear, but his plea agreement suggests that the Trump Inaugural Committee improperly accepted funds from a foreigner. Patten admitted to illegally helping a Ukrainian oligarch buy a ticket to Trump's swearing-in through a straw-man donor, though he wasn't charged as part of his cooperation agreement.

Patten's lobbying work for a Ukrainian oligarch and his political party from 2014 was performed through a company he co-owned with a Russian national, which received over $1 million for the work, according to the U.S. Patten's plea was heard before U.S. District Judge Amy Berman Jackson, who is also overseeing Manafort's money-laundering and obstruction of justice trial in Washington, scheduled to start next month.

Patten's work for Cambridge Analytica came during the 2014 election cycle, and it was later adopted by "at least one major U.S. presidential candidate," according to the Daily Beast. Patten formed a consulting firm in 2015 with Konstantin Kilimnik, who has been indicted alongside Manafort on obstruction of justice charges. Kilimnik has ties to Russian intelligence and has been identified in filings as having worked for the Russian military's intelligence service known as the GRU.

The Patten case was referred by Mueller's team to the U.S. attorney's office in Washington, which is handling it. Andrew Weissmann, one of the lead Mueller team attorneys in the Manafort prosecution, was seen at court ahead of Patten's appearance. It's unclear why Mueller referred the case, but previously, he referred information about Trump's former personal lawyer Michael Cohen to the U.S. attorney in Manhattan.

The Senate Intelligence Committee made a separate criminal referral to the Justice Department based on statements and documents provided by Patten. The nature and extent of Patten's cooperation with Mueller's investigation remain to be seen, but his plea could provide valuable insights into the ongoing probe into Manafort and potential ties between the Trump campaign and Russia.

The South Korean President Park Geun-hye is facing a political crisis as allegations of corruption and influence-peddling continue to mount against her. A recent twist in the scandal involves the discovery of Viagra in her offices, which authorities claim were purchased to combat altitude sickness during official trips. However, the pills were never used. The president is accused of allowing her friend, Choi Soon-sil, to influence her decisions. Choi, the daughter of a shadowy quasi-religious leader, is at the center of the scandal.

Meanwhile, South Korean authorities have raided the offices of Samsung and the national pension fund as part of a corruption investigation linked to the president. The investigation centers around allegations that Park pressured the fund to support a Samsung merger.

Samsung's offices had already been raided over related allegations. The raid on Wednesday was in relation to a merger last year between Samsung C&T and an affiliate firm, Cheil Industries.

For weeks, tens of thousands of protesters have gathered in Seoul demanding Park's resignation, a call she has resisted. The discovery of Viagra will likely add to the political pressure on her to step down, as many Koreans believe she is living in a "different world."

The Viagra was originally developed as a treatment for angina, a heart condition that constricts the vessels that supply the heart with blood. It failed in treating angina, but during drug trials, many volunteers reported an unusual side effect - lots of erections. Scientists ran more tests and discovered its effectiveness at treating erectile dysfunction. Because of biological similarities between the lungs and penis, scientists also discovered it could help protect against pulmonary hypertension, common in climbers.

The scandal surrounding Park Geun-hye has created a frenzy on the internet, with the president bracing for an impeachment push by opposition parties and some members of her own Saenuri party. The scandal is seen as undermining South Korea's democracy.

The search for Malaysia Airlines Flight MH370, which disappeared on March 8, has reached a critical stage as the batteries in the black box beacons are nearing the end of their 30-day expected life. A U.S. Navy "towed pinger locator" onboard Australia's Ocean Shield picked up two signals consistent with black box locator beacons over the weekend, but efforts to pick up the pings again have been unsuccessful. The signals represent the best lead in the search yet, and if no further transmissions are detected, the search for the black boxes will be challenging due to the large search area and the slow, painstaking work required. An autonomous underwater vehicle (AUV) named Bluefin-21 is onboard the Ocean Shield and could be sent to look for wreckage on the sea floor, but narrowing the search zone first is critical. The search will continue for debris on the ocean's surface, even after the black boxes are found, as investigators seek to understand why the plane went down. The search is taking place 1,400 miles northwest of the Australian west coast city of Perth, with up to 11 military planes, three civilian planes, and 14 ships participating in the search. So far, searchers have only turned up fishing gear and other detritus.

The resignation letter from Kate Downing, a member of the Palo Alto Planning and Transportation Commission, highlights the unaffordable housing crisis in Palo Alto and the Bay Area as a whole. Downing and her husband, both professionals, have decided to move to Santa Cruz due to the exorbitant cost of housing in Palo Alto. They currently rent a home for $6,200 a month, but if they were to buy the same home and share it with children, the monthly payment would be $12,177, which is an entire professional's income before taxes.

Downing criticizes the Palo Alto City Council for ignoring the majority of residents who have asked for affordable housing to be prioritized. She suggests several measures that could help alleviate the housing shortage, such as allowing two floors of housing instead of one in mixed-use developments, enforcing minimum density requirements, legalizing duplexes, easing restrictions on granny units, and allowing single-use areas like the Stanford shopping center to add housing.

Downing points out that the high cost of housing is affecting not just professionals like herself, but also teachers, first responders, and service workers. She notes that the city council's focus on office development and high-end housing is exacerbating the jobs-housing imbalance that is driving housing prices throughout the Bay Area to spiral out of control.

Downing's resignation letter has sparked a debate in Palo Alto about the need for affordable housing and the city's role in addressing the crisis. Several candidates running for City Council have vowed to make creation of more housing options a priority if elected. The letter also highlights the broader issue of housing affordability in the Bay Area, which has been a topic of concern for many residents and policymakers.

The AMC movie theater chain has decided to scrap its controversial plan to allow movie-goers to text during films, following a backlash from customers on social media. The proposal, which was aimed at attracting millennials, was met with overwhelmingly negative reactions on Twitter. AMC CEO Adam Aron said the idea has been relegated to the cutting room floor, and the company will focus on other plans to entice more consumers to go to the movies. Aron had suggested making some theaters friendlier to moviegoers who want to use their smartphones while watching a movie, saying that it would be difficult to tell a 22-year-old to turn off their cellphone. The harsh reaction to AMC's proposal falls in line with U.S. sentiment on when it's appropriate to use a smartphone, with 95% of Americans polled saying it's not OK to use a smartphone "at the movie theater or other places where others are usually quiet." Aron says the company will invest more than $1 billion to enhance theaters and their systems.

O.J. Simpson, the former NFL star and media personality, was granted parole after serving nine years of a nine-to-33-year sentence for an armed robbery and kidnapping in Las Vegas. The parole hearing was covered extensively by cable news networks, recalling the "trial of the century" that transfixed the nation over 20 years ago. Simpson apologized for his role in the crime and promised to have no conflicts if released. He is expected to be released as early as October and plans to move to his home in Florida.

The parole board voted unanimously to grant Simpson parole, citing his good behavior in prison, stable release plans, and lack of prior criminal convictions. Simpson's appearance before the board was marked by his energy and good humor, despite his age and time behind bars.

The case was revisited in recent years through the award-winning documentary "O.J.: Made in America" and the FX true-crime drama "The People v. O.J. Simpson." The themes of criminal justice, race, celebrity, and domestic violence explored in these works remain remarkably resonant in modern culture.

Simpson testified that he was misled during the robbery and that one of his associates, Tom Riccio, threw him under the bus to avoid punishment. Riccio, however, claimed that Simpson orchestrated the robbery and gathered men with guns. Simpson said he regretted taking Riccio's call and participating in the crime.

Simpson's legal team argued that the nine-to-33-year sentence did not match the crime and that it was a form of payback for his controversial acquittal in the deaths of his ex-wife Nicole Brown Simpson and her friend Ronald Goldman. Even one of the victims in the robbery, Bruce Fromong, agreed that the sentence was not about justice but about getting the man who was acquitted of murder in 1994.

Simpson has always denied killing Brown and Goldman, and their families won a wrongful death civil judgment against him in 1997. At a parole hearing in 2013, Simpson said he regretted the Las Vegas kidnapping and robbery.

The parole hearing featured testimony from Simpson's oldest daughter, Arnelle, who described him as her best friend and rock. Simpson also testified that he had taken two "Alternative to Violence" classes and had been a model prisoner at Lovelock Correctional Center, a medium-security prison in the Nevada desert.

The case was marked by colorful characters, secret recordings, and a Las Vegas heist, and was described as a low-budget parody of "Ocean's Eleven" by CNN. Simpson's legal team argued that the nine-to-33-year sentence was excessive and that Simpson was being punished for his acquittal in the murder trial.

Simpson's release is expected to be a significant event, as an entire generation has come of age since he was an almost inescapable public figure. The case remains a controversial and fascinating chapter in American history, with themes that continue to resonate in modern culture.

Jim Jordan, a powerful Republican congressman from Ohio, is facing allegations from former wrestlers he coached at Ohio State University in the 1990s that he was aware of, but did not respond to, sexual misconduct by the team doctor, Dr. Richard Strauss. The university is investigating Strauss, who died in 2005, for allegedly abusing students during his tenure as team doctor from the mid-1970s to late 1990s. Jordan, who was assistant wrestling coach at the university from 1986 to 1994, has repeatedly denied knowing about the abuse.

Three former wrestlers told NBC News that it was common knowledge that Strauss showered regularly with students and inappropriately touched them during appointments, and that it would have been impossible for Jordan to be unaware. One wrestler said he told Jordan directly about the abuse. Former head coach Russ Hellickson, Jordan's mentor, said in a recent video that he had told Strauss that he was being too "hands on" with students.

DiSabato, whose allegations against Strauss prompted Ohio State to open its investigation, called Jordan a "liar." DiSabato said he reached out to Jordan this year to tell him he planned to go public with his allegations, but Jordan asked him not to get him involved. Yetts, another former wrestler, said he and others told Jordan about Strauss.

Jordan has denied any knowledge of the abuse and has not responded to requests to be interviewed by investigators. Ohio State has interviewed more than 150 former students and witnesses as part of its investigation. Former athletes from 14 Ohio State sports have reported abuse by Strauss, according to the university.

Jordan has received support from President Donald Trump, who said he believes Jordan and that he is an "outstanding man." Jordan has also received threatening emails from DiSabato, which he forwarded to the U.S. Capitol Police.

Dailey, another former wrestler, said he has spoken twice with investigators from Perkins Coie, the law firm overseeing the probe for the university. Dailey said he was too embarrassed to report the abuse directly to Jordan at the time, but he said Jordan took part in conversations where Strauss' abuse of many other team members came up.

Dailey said he is a Republican and that he contributed to Jordan's first political campaign for state representative in 1994. "What happened drove me out of the sport," said Dailey, a married father of two who works as a fundraiser for an Ohio college. "So I was surprised to hear Jim say that he knew nothing about it."

Coleman, another former wrestler and a former UFC world champion, told The Wall Street Journal that Jordan was aware of the abuse and had not taken action. "There's no way unless he's got dementia or something that he's got no recollection of what was going on at Ohio State," said Coleman, who said he was Jordan's roommate on several wrestling trips.

Jordan, via spokesman Ian Fury, has denied any knowledge of the abuse. On Wednesday, Jordan, a founder of the arch-conservative House Freedom Caucus, who has been floated to succeed retiring House Speaker Paul Ryan, repeated the denial in an interview with Politico. Fury did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Thursday after Dailey's remarks.

Strauss died of suicide in 2005. The university opened an investigation into the abuse in April after former Ohio State wrestler Mike DiSabato came forward with allegations. The Perkins Coie investigators are in possession of a video made by DiSabato in which Hellickson said he had told Strauss that he was being too "hands on" with students.

In Johnston County, North Carolina, a 911 dispatcher named Tim Medlin is being hailed as a hero for his quick thinking that potentially saved a woman's life. On January 14, the woman called 911, stating she was locked in the trunk of a moving car by her jealous boyfriend. The call was hard to understand, and when it disconnected, Medlin was unable to reach her.

Medlin then had the idea to text the woman from the office's emergency cellphone. She responded, providing crucial information about the make and color of the vehicle and her belief that she was headed to Fayetteville. Medlin contacted the Cumberland County Sheriff's office, who then contacted Verizon Wireless to locate the phone.

The woman also gave authorities the name of her boyfriend, Nicholas Mattevi. Once they had a location, Fayetteville police spotted the car, rescued the woman, and arrested Mattevi. Jason Barbour, Johnston County's 911 director, praised Medlin's actions, stating that this incident highlights the need for 911 centers to be updated so they can initiate texts from their systems.

Mattevi was charged with false imprisonment and released on a $10,000 bond. The incident underscores the importance of quick thinking and innovative solutions in emergency situations.

The article discusses the transition of credit cards in the U.S. to chip-enabled cards as a response to the increasing card fraud over the past 15 years. The new cards, which have a microchip on the front, will require insertion into a reader instead of swiping at checkout terminals. The microchip contains a user's payment information and generates a unique code for each purchase, making it more difficult for criminals to reproduce counterfeit cards.

The new system promises increased security, with Visa's Stephanie Erickson stating that countries which adopted the technology saw counterfeit fraud reduce by 60 to 70 percent. However, the chip-based cards take longer to process, which could lead to longer lines at checkout, especially during high-traffic periods such as Black Friday.

On October 1, merchants who have not upgraded their payment terminals will be liable for fraudulent transactions. Consumers will not be affected as federal law requires banks to reimburse consumers for fraud. Not all consumers will receive chip-enabled cards by the deadline, with some banks waiting until existing cards expire or are close to expiring.

The article also emphasizes the importance of using the chip device instead of the swipe device for increased security. Ed Mierzwinski, the consumer program director of U.S. PIRG, encourages the use of the chip device for added security. The transition to chip-enabled cards is part of an effort to make credit card transactions more secure and reduce fraud in the U.S.
