Hurricane Irene, a Category 3 storm with 115 mph winds, is approaching the Eastern Seaboard, prompting states of emergency in seven states from North Carolina to Connecticut. The hurricane is expected to make landfall along North Carolina's Outer Banks on Saturday, potentially causing widespread damage and flooding.

In response, officials have ordered the evacuation of nursing homes and hospitals in low-lying coastal areas, and New York City may suspend all mass transit beginning Saturday. The Martin Luther King Jr. National Memorial dedication has been postponed indefinitely.

The hurricane center warns of tidal surges 5 to 10 feet high in North Carolina, accompanied by destructive and life-threatening waves. Projections show Irene making landfall between Morehead City, NC, and Cape Hatteras before pushing north. Up to 200,000 tourists and residents are affected by evacuation orders in North Carolina alone.

The storm could inundate the state's coastal areas with 6 to 10 inches of rain, and up to 15 inches in some locations. Forecasters predict Irene will diminish to a Category 2 storm after pummeling North Carolina, with sustained winds up to 110 mph as it plows into Virginia, Maryland, and Delaware.

States are rushing to prepare their own evacuation plans, and the Federal Emergency Management Agency has established emergency supply depots at Ft. Bragg, N.C., McGuire Air Force Base in New Jersey, and Westover Air Reserve Base in Massachusetts. Cars loaded with coolers and surfboards are fleeing the Outer Banks, and up to 200,000 tourists and residents are affected by evacuation orders in North Carolina alone.

Officials urge people to take the storm seriously, as Irene is so big and powerful that severe road flooding and widespread electrical outages are likely, especially in the Northeast, where the ground is saturated from recent rains. If Irene follows its current projected path, it will be the first hurricane to hit the U.S. mainland since Ike devastated the Texas coast in 2008.

Researchers have developed a new alcoholic beverage using recycled coffee grounds, potentially offering a unique twist to the spirits industry. The process involves collecting and drying used coffee grounds from a Portuguese coffee roasting company, heating the powder in water to extract liquid, adding sugar, and fermenting the mixture with yeast cells. The resulting "Spent Coffee Ground spirit" contains 40% ethanol, comparable to other hard liquors such as vodka and tequila.

Eight trained taste testers evaluated the product, describing it as having a coffee aroma and a bitter, pungent taste. The scientists noted that the taste could improve with age. Unlike caffeine-alcohol mixes that are known for their potentially dangerous effects, most of the caffeine is said to disappear during the brewing process.

While coffee-flavored beers and caffeine-liquor mixes are not new, this new spirit offers a distinct coffee aroma and taste. The development of this beverage could cater to the significant demand for coffee and alcohol in the United States, where Americans are the dominant consumers of hard liquor and coffee. Further information about this study can be found in the September issue of LWT - Food Science and Technology.

Pope Francis has expressed deep sadness and shock over the murder of four Catholic nuns and 12 other people at a home for the elderly in Aden, Yemen. The attack, which occurred on Friday, was reportedly carried out by gunmen who handcuffed the victims and shot them in the head. The nuns were part of the Missionaries of Charity congregation, founded by Mother Teresa.

No group has claimed responsibility for the attack, but Yemeni officials have blamed Islamic State. The victims included nuns from Rwanda, India, and Kenya, and they were serving breakfast to the home's 80 residents when the attack occurred.

Pope Francis described the attack as an "act of senseless and diabolical violence" and called for an end to the ongoing violence in Yemen. In a message signed by Vatican Secretary of State, Cardinal Pietro Parolin, the Pope expressed his prayers for the dead and his spiritual closeness to their families and all affected by the attack. He also appealed for all parties in the Yemen conflict to renounce violence and renew their commitment to the people of Yemen, particularly those most in need.

The attack comes amid a brutal civil war in Yemen between Iran-backed Zaidi Shia Houthi rebels in the north and the Saudi-Arabia backed government in the south. Islamic State and Al-Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula (AQAP) have both taken advantage of the war to gain ground in the country. More than 6,000 people have been killed and 2.4 million people displaced in Yemen's war, according to the UN. Forces loyal to the government and southern militias regained control of Aden in July, aided by Saudi-led coalition air strikes and troops.

A Santa Rosa woman, Delia Garcia-Bratcher, has been arrested and charged with felony child abuse after allegedly grabbing a 12-year-old boy by the throat at Olivet Charter Elementary School in Santa Rosa, California. The incident occurred on Friday, and Garcia-Bratcher was released on $30,000 bail on Saturday. The mother reportedly came to the school to confront the boy about bullying her daughter, but investigators have not found any evidence linking the boy to the bullying allegations. School district officials are also investigating the bullying claims. Sonoma County prosecutors are still awaiting the sheriff's report before deciding on any charges. The school district has policies requiring visitors to sign in at the office and wear a badge, and a letter about the incident will be emailed to parents. Garcia-Bratcher has asserted on a Facebook page that she was hurt by the accusation and that "the truth will be told." Lt. Mark Essick of the sheriff's department stated that even if bullying was occurring, Garcia-Bratcher had no business confronting the boy directly.

In a study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, researchers found that African elephants can differentiate between human languages and respond accordingly. The study, conducted at Amboseli National Park in Kenya, played recordings of human voices for elephants, some of which were from local Maasai men, a group that often comes into conflict with elephants, and others from Kamba men, who are less of a threat. The elephants tended to gather together and move cautiously away when they heard the adult male Maasai voices, but showed no concern when they heard females, boys, or adult male Kamba speakers. The study suggests that elephants can discriminate between different languages, although it does not mean they understand the words. The elephants' ability to differentiate between human voices is considered an advanced thinking skill that other animals have not shown. The study also found that older elephants with matriarchs in their group were better at assessing the threat from different speakers. The study's authors believe that the elephants are using their famed powers of memory to build up knowledge of the humans they share their habitat with. The study indicates that the conflict between humans and elephants is growing, as the elephants are able to differentiate between threatening and non-threatening humans.

Russell Crowe, known for his prickly reputation, walked out on a BBC Radio 4 interview after being accused of giving Robin Hood an Irish accent during the discussion about his new film, Robin Hood. The incident occurred during an interview with Mark Lawson on the Front Row program. Lawson suggested there were hints of Irish in Crowe's accent, but Crowe vehemently denied it, stating, "You've got dead ears, mate, you've seriously got dead ears if you think that's an Irish accent." The exchange became testy, with Crowe refusing to answer questions about his accent and his portrayal of Robin Hood. Crowe's bad temper has led to a number of run-ins over the years, including a 2005 charge of second-degree assault in New York. The incident has sparked controversy, with some critics claiming Crowe's accent sounds like an Australian doing an impression of Jim Bowen from Bullseye, while others have suggested he had 15 different accents.

A rookie NYPD officer, Peter Liang, was indicted for manslaughter and other charges in the November shooting death of an unarmed man, Akai Gurley, in a darkened stairwell of a housing project in Brooklyn. The grand jury indictment came after a secret panel heard evidence for a few days. Liang is accused of acting recklessly when he discharged his gun, striking Gurley in the chest. He was also charged with reckless endangerment, second-degree assault, and official misconduct.

The shooting sparked protests and calls for reform, with many comparing it to the deaths of Michael Brown and Eric Garner, unarmed black men killed by police officers in Missouri and Staten Island, respectively. In contrast to those cases, the grand jury in this case only heard evidence for a few days, and Liang did not testify.

Liang's lawyer decided not to allow him to testify before the grand jury, and it is unclear why. Gurley's girlfriend, who was with him at the time of the shooting, said the officers never identified themselves before shooting him. Liang declined to comment when reached on his cellphone.

This is the second NYPD officer to be indicted in a week. Officer Joel Edouard was indicted on charges of assault and official misconduct for stomping a marijuana suspect's head.

Mayor Bill de Blasio released a subdued message, urging everyone to respect the judicial process as it unfolds. The indictment was first reported by NY1. The case is expected to be a closely watched test of the city's efforts to improve police-community relations.

On August 5, the bodies of Ron Tarnowski, 82, and Mary Tarnowski, 78, an elderly couple from Duluth, Minnesota, were found in a remote swampy area after they had been missing for eight days. The couple was last seen on surveillance video at a Country Corner store near Brookston, Minnesota, on July 29. Ron had early-stage dementia, and Mary had right-sided paralysis, making it difficult for her to speak.

The U.S. Border Patrol Helicopter found their vehicle in a rural area about 150 yards off of Highway 2 in the Brookston area. It appears that the couple drove off the road onto a swampy trail that was likely only used as a snowmobile trail during the winter. Mary Tarnowski was found in the car, which was stuck on the trail, and Ron Tarnowski was found closer to the highway. It is suspected that Ron went to get help after the car became stuck, but he did not make it back.

Autopsy results are pending, but it is likely that the couple died of exposure. A post on the Find Ron and Mary Tarnowski Facebook page stated that the couple had been found deceased in a remote area about a mile from their hunting camp. The couple had been married for 59 years.

Ron Tarnowski served in the Air Force and was a retired captain for the local fire department. He and Mary spent most of their days confined to their home in Dulth, where Mary suffered from a stroke that left her paralyzed on the right side of her body. Ron served as her caretaker for more than 35 years, assisting her with daily tasks and rarely leaving her side.

In recent years, Ron began showing signs of early-stage dementia, making it difficult for him to take care of Mary. Getting around became even more difficult for the couple, and they rarely left their home. Occasionally, Mary would ask her husband to go for a drive, but they never stayed away for very long and always returned home before nightfall.

On the evening of July 29, the couple's son, Karl Tarnowski, and his wife found the elderly couple's home empty and their Chevy Tahoe gone. They called the police to report them missing, and a week-long search effort ensued, involving the family, law enforcement, and hundreds of community members in Duluth.

Relatives and local authorities posted fliers all over the surrounding area and posted updates on a Facebook group called “Find Ron and Mary Tarnowski,” which was followed by more than 7,000 people across Minnesota and the United States. Retired Duluth firefighters joined the search for one of their own. Duluth residents tied purple ribbons around trees and on businesses, in honor of the Alzheimer’s Association. They held news conferences outside the Tarnowskis’ home attended by the Duluth police chief and about 100 community members.

Despite the extensive search efforts, the couple was not found until eight days later. The autopsy results are pending, but it is likely that the couple died of exposure. The family has expressed their gratitude for the support and efforts of the community during the search.

In Pakistan, a controversial game show hosted by Aamir Liaquat Hussain, a popular talk show host, is giving away abandoned babies during live broadcasts as part of a ratings battle during the Islamic holy month of Ramadan. The babies are rescued by the Chhipa Welfare Association, an NGO that receives up to 15 abandoned babies a month. Hussain claims the giveaway is to make people happy and reward them during Ramadan, and to show an alternative to street kids being used for suicide bombing attacks.

The show's host, Hussain, is known for his mix of religion and entertainment, often followed by controversy. He cooks, interviews clerics and celebrities, entertains children, and hosts game shows. He usually gives prizes like motorbikes, mobile phones, and land deeds to audience members who answer questions about Islam. During the Ramadan run, he gave away two infant girls and plans to give away a baby boy.

The couple who received the baby girls were unsuspecting and did not know they would be handed a newborn during the show. Adoption is not officially recognized in Pakistan, and the couple will have to apply for guardianship at a family court. Some viewers praised the show's baby giveaway, while others declared it a publicity stunt.

The show has been extremely popular, breaking ratings records and may be extended beyond its Ramadan run. Hussain plans another program where the audience will be from the minority Hindu, Sikh, and Christian communities. He believes his show is unifying a fractured nation, plagued by sectarian violence, religious intolerance, and terrorism.

However, critics argue that the show is a publicity stunt and that babies are not trophies to be handed to just anyone. There are concerns about the vetting process and the legal implications for the couples receiving the babies. The show's producers did not return calls seeking comment, and it is unclear if poor families wishing to keep their children will also be helped. The Pakistani media, which has flourished over the past decade, often fights for audiences and advertising by seeing who is most outrageous.

The document details the ongoing court-martial of U.S. Army Sergeant Adam Holcomb, who is accused of hazing and hounding Private Danny Chen, a Chinese American soldier, to the point of suicide. The incident took place at a combat outpost in Afghanistan in October 2011.

In the court-martial, several former members of Holcomb's platoon testified that Holcomb subjected Chen to racial slurs and physical abuse, including dragging him across rocky ground for disobeying a platoon rule. Pvt. Marcus Merritt, an African American soldier, testified that Holcomb addressed him with a racial slur and threatened to kill him. Merritt also stated that he became suicidal due to the punishment and humiliation he endured from Holcomb.

Holcomb faces charges of negligent homicide, assault, reckless endangerment, and other counts. He is the first of eight soldiers, including an officer, to face court-martial in connection with Chen's death. The other seven soldiers' courts-martial are scheduled for later this year.

Holcomb's immediate superior, Staff Sgt. Darren Holt, testified that he confronted Holcomb after the sergeant physically abused Chen. Holt reported the incident to superiors, stating that physically abusing a soldier was wrong.

Chen's death outraged some Chinese American activists in New York City's Chinatown, where Chen grew up with his immigrant parents. Several activists are attending the court-martial, along with journalists from China.

Holcomb's military lawyers have argued that Chen killed himself because his parents had disowned him for joining the Army instead of attending college. They have also portrayed Chen as an incompetent soldier who required constant discipline for violations such as sleeping on guard duty or reporting for his guard post without his helmet.

Defense lawyers have claimed that nicknames, even those with racially tinged overtones, were common "terms of endearment" in the small, tight-knit platoon. One African American platoon member, they said, encouraged soldiers to call him "Black Mamba."

Under cross-examination, former members of the platoon conceded that most discipline meted out by Holcomb was justified by Chen's failure to follow orders or regulations. Several soldiers testified that Chen never gave any overt indication that he was contemplating suicide.

Instagram, a popular photo-sharing app owned by Facebook, faced backlash after updating its privacy policy and terms of service earlier this week. Users expressed concerns about the potential use of their photos in advertising and the sharing of personal data. In response, Instagram's co-founder, Kevin Systrom, announced on Thursday that the company would revert to its previous terms of service, effective immediately. Systrom also clarified that Instagram has no intention of selling users' photos and that the company values user privacy. The controversy led to an increase in users on rival photo-sharing apps such as Pheed and Flickr. Instagram did not disclose any significant number of account deletions or concerns about losing ground in the photo-sharing market.

A controversial new bill in New Jersey aims to reduce distracted driving by imposing hefty fines and potential license suspensions for activities such as eating, drinking, grooming, reading, or using electronic devices while driving. The bill, sponsored by Assemblyman John Wisniewski, does not specifically mention coffee or eating, but has sparked concerns about overreach and enforcement.

The proposed fines for violators range from $200 to $400 for the first offense, $400 to $600 for a second offense, and up to $800 for a third or subsequent offense, along with a possible 90-day license suspension and motor vehicle points. The bill is modeled after a law in Maine and is intended to educate, not punish, drivers.

Supporters of the bill argue that it is necessary to discourage distracted driving, which is a leading cause of accidents. According to the latest figures from the federal government, in 2014 there were some 400,000 accidents involving distracted drivers, and 3,000 of those resulted in death.

Critics, however, question how the bill can be enforced and whether it goes too far in restricting common behaviors such as changing the radio station or adjusting the volume. Some argue that the bill is an overreach and that existing laws, such as those banning the use of hand-held cell phones and texting while driving, are sufficient.

Despite the controversy, supporters of the bill argue that it could have a similar effect as seat belt laws, which have increased seat belt use in the state, even without fines. The more widespread the message of eliminating distractions becomes, the more likely it is to be ingrained in everyday behavior, similar to seat belt usage. The bill is currently making its way through the legislature and has yet to be voted on.

North Korea's figure skaters Ryom Tae-Ok and Kim Ju-Sik have secured a spot at the 2018 Winter Olympics in Pyeongchang, South Korea, becoming the first North Korean athletes to qualify for the event. The pair's qualification is seen as a positive development amid escalating tensions on the Korean peninsula. The International Olympic Committee has been supporting several North Korean athletes in their efforts to qualify, and speed skaters and Nordic skiers could join the figure skaters with their own qualifiers coming up. The final decision regarding their Olympic participation rests with the North Korean Olympic committee.

The qualification of Ryom and Kim will be welcome news to South Korea's President Moon Jae-in, who believes North Korean participation in Pyeongchang will provide a good opportunity for inter-Korean peace and reconciliation. The two nations have been on convivial sporting terms this year, with North Korea sending its women’s hockey team and a taekwondo team to compete in the South. However, the Olympics have never gone forward free of geopolitics, and North Korea boycotted the 1988 Summer Olympics held in Seoul.

The skaters' coach, Kim Hyon-son, stated that the decision to participate in the Olympics is up to the North Korean Olympic Committee. The skaters appeared relaxed and open but requested that no questions be asked about the Olympics, likely due to the decision being out of their hands. The outcome was important to North Korea, as it has invested considerable time and money to make the skaters eligible for the Winter Games and respected at the international level. The skaters trained over the summer in Montreal with French coach Bruno Marcotte, whose wife is a two-time world pairs champion.

Adrianne Haslet-Davis, who lost her left leg in the 2013 Boston Marathon bombing, has announced her participation in this year's 120th Boston Marathon. Haslet-Davis, a professional ballroom dancer, aims to raise funds for the Oklahoma City-based Limbs for Life Foundation through her team, "#AdrianneStrong." After vowing to dance and run the marathon following the bombing, Haslet-Davis has been training and is now up to 10 miles. She plans to run the April 18 race, dedicating her race to supporters and other survivors. Haslet-Davis returned to the marathon finish line last year to dance, symbolizing her inspiring comeback.

The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) has issued guidance on Made in USA claims, requiring that products advertised as such must meet the "all or virtually all" standard. This means that all significant parts and processing must be of U.S. origin. Manufacturers and marketers must have a reasonable basis to support their Made in USA claims and should look back far enough in the manufacturing process to ensure that any significant foreign content has been included in their assessment of foreign costs. Qualified Made in USA claims are also allowed, but should only be used when a product includes U.S. content or processing but does not meet the criteria for an unqualified claim. The FTC also has jurisdiction over foreign origin claims in advertising and other promotional materials, and requires that imported products be marked with a foreign country of origin. The report from Truth in Advertising found over 100 products labeled as Made in USA on Walmart's website to be false, and the company has since removed the labels from the website.

The death of Julia Roberts' half-sister Nancy Motes, who was found dead at 37 in an apparent suicide via overdose, has caused a stir, with a suicide note allegedly containing dark secrets about Roberts. Motes' fiancé John Dilbeck, who found her body, has claimed that Roberts inflicted "pure cruelty" on her sister, and that the suicide was a desperate attempt to expose the alleged treatment. A source close to the situation has revealed that Dilbeck plans to assert his right to be a beneficiary of Motes' estate and keep control of her possessions, including gifts and intimate family photos given by Roberts. The sisters had a complex relationship, with Roberts trying unsuccessfully for years to get Motes to enter rehab. Motes' family and Dilbeck are reportedly in conflict, with fears that Dilbeck could be holding Motes' personal items hostage and potentially selling them to the highest bidder if they contain damaging information about Roberts. If you or anyone you know is struggling with thoughts of suicide, help is available at the national Suicide Prevention Lifeline.

The article discusses the financial disclosure of Anthony Scaramucci, the newly appointed White House communications director. According to the disclosure, Scaramucci earned $4.9 million from his ownership stake in SkyBridge Capital in addition to more than $5 million in salary between January 2016 and June 2017. The disclosure also highlights Scaramucci's extensive wealth and potential conflicts of interest due to his investments.

Scaramucci's financial filing values SkyBridge Capital at more than $50 million and states that he owns nearly 44 percent of the firm. The sale of the company, which is expected to close in the third quarter of this year, will result in Scaramucci receiving the agreed-upon purchase price for his share of the sale proceeds.

The sale of SkyBridge Capital is being scrutinized by regulators, including the interagency Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States, to ensure that it carries no risk to national security. The panel's review can be overruled by President Donald Trump.

Scaramucci's appointment to the White House was delayed in part because of the complicated nature of the SkyBridge sale. He joined Ex-Im Bank in June as a temporary move, but has since been on unpaid leave from the bank.

Scaramucci responded angrily to a leak of his financial disclosure information, threatening to contact the FBI and the Department of Justice. He did not specify what information was leaked, but the article cites the incoming communications director's required financial disclosure in reporting the earnings from SkyBridge.

The article also mentions Scaramucci's other assets, including a minority stake in the New York Mets worth as much as $5 million, investments in real estate, and a stake in Juice Press, a chain of snack and smoothie shops in the Northeast. Scaramucci earned $88,000 as a contributor to Fox News, and has three mortgages with U.S. Bank for a total liability of $2.5 million to $7 million.

Hillary Clinton has decided against choosing Bernie Sanders as her running mate for the upcoming presidential election, according to a source familiar with the decision. Sanders, who has yet to officially concede the Democratic primary to Clinton, was not expecting to be considered for the vice presidential position and does not view Clinton's decision as a slight.

Sanders remains focused on transforming the Democratic Party and has no intention of becoming Clinton's partner. The Vermont senator's loyal supporters might perceive him as a sell-out if he were to join the Clinton ticket, another person close to Sanders stated on Wednesday.

During their private meeting on Tuesday night, which lasted approximately 90 minutes, Sanders did not bring up the issue of being Clinton's running mate. Since 1996, Alexa Internet has been donating their crawl data to the Internet Archive, with the data being added to the Wayback Machine after an embargo period. This practice continues to the present day, with the data flowing in daily.

The study conducted by Dr. Samantha Hendren and her team at the University of Michigan reveals that one in seven colorectal cancer patients in the U.S. is younger than 50, challenging the common perception that colorectal cancer primarily affects older men. The study, published in the journal Cancer, analyzed data from patients diagnosed between 1998 and 2011 from the Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results (SEER) Program of the National Cancer Institute.

Younger patients were more likely to be diagnosed with advanced-stage colorectal cancer, with 30% more likelihood of having tumors that had spread to the lymph nodes and 50% more likelihood of having cancer that had advanced to other organs. Despite this, younger patients lived slightly longer without a cancer recurrence, with a five-year survival rate of 95.1% for localized disease, 76% for regional disease, and 21.3% for distant disease compared to older patients.

Younger patients were also more likely to undergo surgery and radiation therapy than older patients. The study suggests that the findings indicate the need for improved risk assessment and screening decisions for younger adults. The study authors believe their work is a wake-up call to the medical community to look for signs of colorectal cancer in patients younger than 50.

The study highlights the need for further research to determine whether changing preventive screening guidelines to start at a younger age would ultimately prevent more cancer deaths. The study's limitations include a lack of data on family history and other risk factors for colorectal cancers, and the possibility of treatment choices and overall survival being influenced by selection bias.

The study underscores the importance of early detection and aggressive treatment for colorectal cancer in younger patients. Doctors should be on the lookout for warning signs of colorectal cancer, such as anemia, bowel bleeding, and a blockage in the colon. People with a family history of colorectal cancer and others who are at higher risk should begin screening earlier than the age of 50. The study calls for the cancer community to prepare for the increasing number of very young colorectal cancer survivors who will need long-term support to cope with the physical and psychological consequences of their disease and treatments.

In Madison, Wisconsin, the Air National Guard is conducting nighttime training flights with F-16 fighter jets until Thursday, potentially causing noise disturbances until 10 PM. Residents may hear jets taking off or landing during this period. The training flights are part of the pilots' and maintenance personnel's readiness training, and flight paths have been designed to minimize noise.

Meanwhile, a rare geological event called a "frostquake" or cryoseism occurred in southern Wisconsin on Tuesday night. This event happens when water that drains into the ground freezes, expands, and causes the ground to fracture. The frostquake was reported in areas from Columbus to Fox Lake and Johnson Creek to Oconomowoc, causing a loud boom that shook houses. Although no damage was reported, the phenomenon is relatively rare but not unheard of in Wisconsin.

The nuclear crisis in Japan following the earthquake and tsunami has escalated, with the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) describing the situation as "very serious." The Fukushima Dai-ichi nuclear plant, located in northeastern Japan, has experienced multiple reactor meltdowns and rising temperatures in spent fuel pools, posing a significant risk of a large-scale radiation release.

Emergency workers have been trying various methods to cool the reactors, including using helicopters, fire trucks, and water cannons. However, the situation remains critical, and it could take days or even weeks to regain control of the plant. The IAEA has expressed concern over the low water levels in spent fuel pools, particularly in Unit 3, where the rods are not fully submerged.

The crisis has prompted international concern, with the U.S. recommending a 50-mile evacuation zone for its citizens, a wider radius than the 30-mile band Japan has ordered. The U.S. has also offered assistance to Japan, including the use of intelligence-collection aircraft to monitor the situation.

The humanitarian aftermath of the earthquake and tsunami has also been devastating, with nearly 7,000 people confirmed dead, over 10,000 missing, and hundreds of thousands left homeless. Many are battling near-freezing temperatures in shelters, and supplies of food, water, medicine, and heating fuel are in short supply.

Despite the ongoing nuclear crisis and humanitarian disaster, the Japanese workers at the plant have been praised for their efforts to avert a larger-scale radiation release. The crisis has also stirred memories of Japan's past nuclear nightmare, the atomic bombs dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki in 1945.

In addition to the nuclear and humanitarian crises, the crisis has also had a significant impact on global financial markets and manufacturing, with power shortages forcing factories to close and sending shockwaves through trade. The Japanese yen has also soared, leading to a rare concerted intervention by the Group of Seven (G7) rich nations to restrain its rise.

Overall, the situation in Japan remains critical, with the nuclear crisis posing a significant risk of a large-scale radiation release, and the humanitarian aftermath of the earthquake and tsunami causing widespread suffering and hardship.

In this summary, a Tennessee man named Eugene Bowen was sentenced to 20 months in prison for his role in a money order fraud scheme involving a former South Jersey U.S. Postal Service (USPS) employee, Marc Saunders. Bowen admitted to cashing stolen money orders provided by Saunders, who had given him the task of recruiting others to cash the orders. Three accomplices, including Bowen, have been sentenced for their involvement in the scheme. The scheme's organizer, Saunders, received a five-year probationary sentence with eight months of home confinement, and was ordered to pay restitution of nearly $100,000. The investigation was led by special agents of the USPS Office of the Inspector General. The scheme began when a postmaster failed to return a money order printing machine and neglected to destroy loose money orders, which were later stolen and used in the fraud. The stolen money orders were cashed at various post offices across the United States, with some being cashed in Knoxville, Tennessee, and York, Pennsylvania. The investigation linked the cellphones and social media accounts of the participants to identify those involved in the scheme.

The article discusses the concept of a "sober January," a popular trend of abstaining from alcohol for the month of January following excessive drinking during the holiday season. The author, a former alcoholic, argues that this practice can be harmful and misleading for individuals with alcohol dependency issues. They explain that a sober January can give the false impression that one does not have a problem with alcohol, and can even be used as a tool for denial.

The author shares their personal experience of participating in multiple sober Januaries and how it contributed to their denial about their alcoholism. They also criticize Alcohol Concern, a UK alcohol charity, for promoting the dry January challenge, as it may attract individuals with alcohol dependency problems.

The author suggests that instead of attempting to abstain from alcohol for a month, individuals concerned about their drinking habits should assess whether they have a problem and seek help if necessary. They reference Bill Wilson, the co-founder of Alcoholics Anonymous, who believed that alcoholics have an "allergic reaction" to alcohol and that controlled drinking can exacerbate the craving for more alcohol.

The author concludes by suggesting that if one's sole aim is to save money, they should try having a pint every night but just one, to prove they don't have a problem. They acknowledge that January can be a difficult month, and it's important for non-alcoholics to have help getting through it.

The University of Winnipeg Library, in collaboration with various institutions, has initiated an ongoing web-archiving project focused on Manitoba's involvement with the Truth and Reconciliation Commission. The collection encompasses a wide array of topics, including survivors' stories, apologies, cultural events, and more. The project has received financial support from Manitoba Tourism, Culture, Heritage, Sport and Consumer Protection, and the Government of Canada.

Meanwhile, a rare Enigma machine used by Nazi Germany during World War II was sold at auction in Bucharest, Romania, for 45,000 euros ($51,500). The machine, which was in almost perfect condition, was initially purchased at a flea market for just 100 euros by a collector who recognized its significance as a vital tool for Nazi war efforts. The Enigma machine was used by the German military to encrypt messages, but the codes were eventually cracked by a team of cryptologists at Bletchley Park in England, a breakthrough that is widely credited with shortening the war by at least two years.

Last month, another Enigma machine was sold at Christie's New York Books for a world auction record of $547,500. Romania, which was an ally of Nazi Germany until 1944, may host other cryptographic machines yet to be discovered, according to historians.

Scientists at Oregon Health & Science University have successfully recovered stem cells from cloned human embryos, a significant milestone in the field of medicine. This achievement could potentially lead to new treatments for diseases such as Parkinson's and diabetes, as stem cells can transform into any cell type in the body. The process involves creating tissue from stem cells that match the patient's DNA, reducing the risk of rejection during transplants.

The researchers used a technique called therapeutic cloning, which involves fusing a donor cell with an unfertilized egg, reprogramming the DNA to an embryonic state, and harvesting the stem cells once the embryo reaches the blastocyst stage. This method has been met with ethical concerns due to the destruction of human embryos during the process.

The team, led by Shoukhrat Mitalipov, revised a series of steps in the process to achieve success, which took six years after similar success with monkey embryos. Mitalipov also believes that human embryos created with this technique could not develop into cloned babies, and he has no interest in pursuing that.

The new work was financed by the university and the Leducq Foundation in Paris. Dr. George Daley, a stem cell expert who didn't participate in the work, called the results "one landmark step in a very long journey" towards creating DNA-matched transplant tissue.

However, Daley also noted that scientists must compare the embryo-cloning approach with another technology that reprograms blood or skin cells directly into substitutes for embryonic stem cells. This reprogramming approach is technically simpler and doesn't involve embryos or require the donation of human eggs. It was widely acclaimed when it was reported in 2007, and its developer shared a Nobel Prize last year.

The new results mean "we have another tool," said Daley. "We have to learn more about this tool." Daley believes scientists will prefer using the reprogramming approach unless it can be proven "beyond a shadow of a doubt" that embryo cloning produces better cells for treating patients.

The Rev. Tad Pacholczyk, director of education for National Catholic Bioethics Center, reiterated his opposition to embryo cloning, calling the approach unethical. Marcy Darnovsky, executive director of the Center for Genetics and Society, was glad that Mitalipov doubted the embryos could be used to clone babies. She said the report still provides a good opportunity for the federal government to ban the use of cloning for reproduction.

In a daring heist reminiscent of the movie "Mission: Impossible," a gang of thieves stole over £2 million worth of rare books from a warehouse near Heathrow airport. The theft, which took place on January 29, involved the thieves climbing onto the roof, cutting holes through reinforced skylights, and abseiling down into the building. The books, which included works by Galileo, Isaac Newton, and Leonardo da Vinci, were being stored temporarily as they were due to be flown to the California Book Fair. The most valuable book stolen was a 1566 edition of "De Revolutionibus Orbium Coelestium" by Copernicus, worth an estimated £215,000. The International League of Antiquarian Booksellers has published two lists detailing every book believed to have been stolen, including a 1656 Galileo book titled "Opere di Galileo Galilei" and a 1506 edition of Dante's "Divine Comedy." The police are investigating the theft and have appealed for information. The booksellers affected by the theft have been left devastated and are asking anyone with information to contact the police.
