After the woman left, Salerno noticed a missing necklace, which was later recovered by police at a South Yarmouth pawn shop. When Salerno reported the theft to the police, he was charged with soliciting a prostitute. His response, as reported by the Cape Cod Times, was, "I don't give a (expletive). I'm 90 years old." Both the woman, Karen Proia, and Salerno pleaded not guilty during their arraignments on Tuesday.

Michael Schumacher's medical files, which contain details of his surgical procedures, have been stolen and are being offered for sale to the media, according to his manager, Sabine Kehm. The files are believed to have been taken from the hospital in Grenoble where Schumacher, the seven-time Formula One champion, was being treated after sustaining life-threatening injuries in a skiing accident six months ago. Schumacher was moved from Grenoble to University Hospital Lausanne in Switzerland last week following an announcement that he was no longer in a coma. Kehm stated that the stolen documents and data have been offered for sale for several days, and that the authorities are involved in the investigation. She emphasized that the contents of any medical files are private and confidential and must not be made public. Schumacher, aged 45, has been in hospital for nearly six months following his accident at the French Alpine resort of Meribel in December. The Grenoble hospital's media office has reportedly sued for 'theft and breach of medical confidentiality' to initiate an investigation. A spokesman for the German newspaper Bild confirmed that the tabloid was among several media outlets offered Schumacher's alleged medical records, but they rejected the offer. The French prosecutor investigating the accident concluded that speed was not a factor in Schumacher's fall.

The study, published in the Journal of the American Medical Association, found that getting a flu shot may lower the risk of heart problems, including heart attacks and strokes. The researchers analyzed data from 6,735 participants in 5 published and 1 unpublished randomized clinical trials. They found that 3% of those who received a flu shot went on to have a heart problem within a year, compared to about 5% of those in the placebo groups. The reduction was more dramatic for those with recent heart disease, with about 10% of participants with a recent heart problem going on to have another heart problem after receiving the flu shot, compared to about 23% in the placebo groups. The study suggests that getting a flu shot may be particularly beneficial for those with recent heart disease. The researchers note that the findings cannot definitively prove that the flu shot prevents heart problems, but they add to the evidence supporting the recommendation for flu vaccination for those with heart disease.

In a tragic incident, at least nine people have died and over 100 undocumented immigrants are believed to have been severely injured in a tractor-trailer in Texas. The discovery was made after a Walmart employee called authorities following a request for water from one of the victims. The trailer, which may have been carrying more than 100 individuals, reportedly had no working air conditioning system.

The San Antonio Police Department is investigating the incident as a human trafficking case. The driver, James Matthew Bradley Jr., has been held in connection with the incident, and federal prosecutors plan to file a criminal complaint against him on Monday.

The high temperature in San Antonio on Saturday was 100 degrees Fahrenheit (38 degrees Celsius), and the lack of air conditioning and the crowded conditions inside the trailer likely contributed to the severe injuries and deaths. Two of the survivors are 15 years old.

The US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) will take over the case once the victims undergo treatment. ICE acting Director Thomas Homan has deplored the incident as a major case of human smuggling.

Authorities are still investigating the origin of the trailer and how long it was parked at the Walmart. The incident has sparked calls for immigration system reform and increased efforts to combat human trafficking. Texas Governor Greg Abbott has highlighted a bill he signed in May that provides information to the trucking industry about how to spot and report signs of human trafficking.

Walmart has declined to release any details about the incident, citing the ongoing investigation. The store did capture some of the incident on camera, but the footage has not been released to the media.

The KFC Double Down Chicken Sandwich, a highly anticipated new menu item, has been released. The sandwich consists of two boneless Original Recipe Filets, two strips of bacon, two slices of Monterey Jack and pepperjack cheese, and a special Colonel's Sauce. The sandwich is not for the health-conscious, with 540 calories, 32 grams of fat, and 1380 milligrams of sodium. The reviewers found the chicken to be moist and the bacon to be legit, but the cheese and sauce often blended together, making it difficult to distinguish the individual flavors. The sandwich is filling and could potentially become a popular "hangover food." However, the reviewers rated it a 2 out of 5, finding it to be a disappointing and overly salty meal. Despite its flaws, the sandwich is not the most expensive $5 meal in town.

The International Criminal Court (ICC) has initiated a preliminary investigation into allegations of crimes against humanity committed by Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte and other officials in relation to the government's deadly crackdown on drugs. The investigation will focus on events since July 1, 2016, in the context of the "war on drugs" campaign.

The ICC's prosecutor, Fatou Bensouda, stated that her office would analyze crimes allegedly committed during this period. The inquiry will be the ICC's first preliminary examination in a southeast Asian nation. The investigation was prompted by a report submitted last year that accused Duterte of extrajudicial executions and mass murder over three decades, dating back to his time as mayor of Davao.

According to official statistics, 4,000 people have been killed by the police in anti-drug operations since Duterte became president. However, a 77-page report submitted by a Philippine lawyer, Jude Sabio, alleged the death toll was over 8,000.

Gary Alejano, an opposition politician who tried to get Duterte impeached last year, welcomed the move, stating it offered "a ray of hope for the victims of his war on drugs." He believes they have a "strong case" if given the opportunity to be heard.

Duterte's spokesperson, Harry Roque, described the inquiry as a "waste of the court's time and resources," stating that many of the allegations predated the Philippines signing up to the ICC in 2011. However, Bensouda specifically referenced killings since 1 July 2016 in her statement.

Roque also alleged that "domestic enemies" were behind the complaint and said Duterte was prepared to go on trial and defend his actions. He maintains that the thousands who died were suspects who resisted arrest, but human rights groups and political opponents allege that many murders have been carried out and covered up.

Since securing a landslide victory in the 2016 elections on a pledge to kill tens of thousands of criminals and eradicate drugs in Philippine society, Duterte has authorized police to violently crack down on illegal drug use, urging them to kill suspects and promising to protect them from prosecution. His abrasive tongue and brutal methods have kept him popular in the Philippines, where he enjoys high approval ratings and legislative support.

Human Rights Watch has welcomed the ICC's move, calling for an independent international investigation into Duterte's war on drugs. Phil Robertson, a deputy director in its Asia division, said the ICC "absolutely should initiate a full investigation into these alleged crimes because to date there has been no serious attempt to investigate them by the Philippines police or prosecutors, much less take suspected killers to court."

On December 19, a 51-year-old man set himself on fire in St. Peter's Square, Vatican City. The man doused himself with gasoline and ignited the flames. Initial attempts to extinguish the blaze were made by a Jesuit priest who used his jacket, followed by two police officers who used a fire extinguisher. The man is currently in critical condition, and the motives for his actions remain unknown. A piece of paper with his daughter's phone number was found at the scene. The incident brought back memories of a similar case 15 years ago when Alfredo Ormando, a gay man, set himself ablaze to protest the Church's stance on homosexuality. The Vatican police have since restricted access to the square following the incident.

Orexigen Therapeutics Inc.'s shares nearly doubled after winning a U.S. panel recommendation for their prescription diet pill, Contrave. The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) advisers stated that the weight-loss benefits of Contrave outweigh the risks of elevated pulse and blood pressure, and a large study on cardiovascular risk can wait until after approval. The FDA delayed competing treatments from Arena Pharmaceuticals Inc. and Vivus Inc. in October due to safety concerns.

The FDA's support for Contrave eases concerns that had caused Orexigen shares to drop more than a third this year. Orexigen gained from watching the FDA's safety focus and saw that a commitment to minimize risks and conduct more studies would be needed for approval.

Orexigen and partner Takeda Pharmaceutical Co. are scheduled to receive a decision from the FDA by Jan. 31. Approval may be delayed while the company and the agency work out details of the prescribing information and the new study.

Contrave, Orexigen's first product, is a combination of two approved drugs that target different parts of the brain that influence appetite and cravings. The pill contains bupropion, an antidepressant also used to quit smoking, and naltrexone, a treatment for alcohol and painkiller addiction.

In clinical trials, patients on Contrave lost more weight than those in the placebo group, but the drug missed the FDA's second standard of effectiveness in failing to show at least a 5% benefit over placebo. Patients on the drug also had higher pulse and blood pressure than patients on placebo, even after losing weight.

The FDA advisory committee voted 13-7 that the modest weight-loss benefits of Contrave outweigh the drug's blood pressure risk. The FDA will make an approval decision by Jan. 31. The agency does not have to follow the advice of its advisory committees, but it often does.

Vivus, based in Mountain View, California, said it plans to respond within six weeks to the FDA’s request for more information about heart risks and birth defects linked to Qnexa. This would trigger a new two- to six-month review. Arena's Lorcaserin is also under review by the FDA.

The three companies and their partners have been in a race to introduce the first prescription weight-loss pill in more than a decade. Basel, Switzerland-based Roche Holding AG’s Xenical, approved in 1999, is the only long-term medicine for weight loss since Abbott Park, Illinois-based Abbott Laboratories’ Meridia was pulled off the market in October because of heart risks.

In a heartwarming display of human kindness, two Delta pilots delayed their flight to allow an Arizona family to attend the funeral of their loved one, Jay W. Short, who passed away from lung cancer at the age of 56. The family faced a 90-minute delay in their flight from Phoenix, leaving them with only 7 minutes to make a connecting flight in Minneapolis. The funeral was scheduled for the following morning. Despite the door to the jetway being closed and the plane taxiing towards the runway, the pilots, Capt. Adam Cohen and his first officer, saw the family's distress and turned the plane back to allow them to board. The family expressed their gratitude, calling it a "gift that no one else could give." Delta Airlines praised Cohen's decision, stating it was a reflection of the human touch they aim to provide customers. However, airline analysts noted that Cohen risked censure from his company for his actions.

The Berkshire Hathaway board has concluded that former executive David Sokol deliberately misled Warren Buffett when pitching an investment, potentially facing legal action and SEC probe. The board found that Sokol violated company policies by purchasing $10 million worth of Lubrizol stock while facilitating Buffett's deal to buy the company, a move that could result in a recovery of Sokol's trading profits. The report paints a picture of Buffett being deceived by Sokol, but also aims to exonerate Buffett from wrongdoing. Sokol's attorney disputes the board's report, stating that Sokol's Lubrizol investments were allowed by his employment agreement and that he had disclosed his stake to Buffett twice. The report may alleviate pressure on Buffett during the company's annual meeting this weekend.

The Human Rights Foundation has criticized Oscar-winning actress Hilary Swank and other celebrities for attending a lavish birthday party for Chechen leader Ramzan Kadyrov, who has been accused of human rights abuses. The event, which also featured Jean-Claude Van Damme and British violinist Vanessa-Mae, was a multimillion-dollar bash attended by several celebrities, including Kevin Costner who declined due to his production schedule. The Human Rights Watch has called on the stars who attended the party to reimburse any money they were paid to participate, stating that their attendance bolsters Kadyrov's image and legitimizes a brutal leader. The Human Rights Foundation president, Thor Halvorssen, described the celebrities' attendance as "disheartening and shameful." The artists' representatives were not immediately available for comment. The event was held to celebrate the 193rd anniversary of the founding of Grozny, Chechnya's capital, which was pushed to coincide with Kadyrov's birthday. Kadyrov, who was uncertain about who paid for the party, stated that the funds came from Allah. The Human Rights Foundation has raised concerns about Swank's attendance, as her manager had initially stated that she had no plans to attend the party in Chechnya.

The article discusses the controversy surrounding Republican Congresswoman Michele Bachmann's accusations against two prominent Muslims, Huma Abedin and Keith Ellison, of having ties to the Muslim Brotherhood. The accusations were met with widespread criticism from both Democrats and Republicans, who viewed them as a conspiracy theory. However, Bachmann's supporters in her district, particularly in the exurbs north of the Twin Cities, have rallied around her, viewing her as the only one telling the truth.

The article also mentions that Bachmann's political star has risen once again on the far right, despite her campaign for the presidential nomination falling apart and her being a source of annoyance for House Republican leaders. The left is again targeting her for defeat, with Democrats focusing on Jim Graves, a wealthy Minneapolis businessman, as the moderate alternative to Bachmann.

Additionally, the article mentions a report that Bachmann cited in her attack on Abedin, which claims that anti-tax crusader Grover Norquist helped the Muslim Brotherhood infiltrate the U.S. government. The report was produced by the Center for Security Policy and accused Norquist of using various organizations to promote Islamist agendas.

Overall, the article highlights the ongoing controversy surrounding Bachmann's accusations against Abedin and the differing reactions to them from her supporters and critics. It also touches on the broader political context of Bachmann's political career and the upcoming election in her district.

The Las Vegas shooting on Sunday night resulted in 59 fatalities and 527 injuries, making it the deadliest mass shooting in modern U.S. history. Stephen Paddock, the alleged shooter, fired from a Mandalay Bay hotel room, targeting a music festival crowd. The shooter's position overhead provided a vantage point that put concertgoers at risk, as inaccurate shots could still reach huddled areas.

Audio recordings suggest that at least one of Paddock's weapons fired automatically, discharging multiple bullets with a single trigger press. Weapons capable of burst fire, which harness recoil for rapid fire, have been federally regulated in the U.S., but it's unclear if Paddock possessed such weapons or used altered semiautomatic ones.

Authorities recovered at least 16 rifles and a handgun from Paddock's hotel room, including AR-15-style rifles. Paddock had purchased some guns in Arizona. The shooting has been described as the 273rd mass shooting this year, prompting discussions about gun control and human reactions in such situations.

A particularly jarring video shows a man standing and taunting the shooter amidst the chaos and fear, highlighting the wide range of human reactions during mass shootings. The death toll has been updated to reflect the latest information.

Lou Ferrigno, the actor known for his role as The Incredible Hulk, was hospitalized after a pneumonia vaccination went wrong. Ferrigno shared the news on his social media accounts, stating that he ended up in the hospital due to fluid in his bicep after the vaccination. He advised his followers to be cautious when receiving shots, suggesting they ensure the person administering the shot swabs the spot correctly and watches the needle come out of the package. It is unclear what specific shot was given to Ferrigno, but the Center for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) reports that both PCV13 and PPSV23 are recommended for adults 65 and older to avoid contracting pneumococcal diseases. Despite the incident, Ferrigno is expected to recover and has several acting projects lined up for 2019. He is also known for his career in bodybuilding and co-founded his family's fitness program, Ferrigno Fit.

In a conversation with The Daily Beast, former Reagan budget director David Stockman urged Republicans to shut down the government to force through $60 billion in budget cuts. Stockman believes that the Obama administration is weak and will fold under pressure, and that a temporary government shutdown would have minimal impact on the economy. He described the ongoing budget negotiations in Washington as a "wakeup call" and criticized the elected officials for their inability to address the nation's debt and stalled economy. Stockman also criticized House Budget Committee Chairman Paul Ryan for offering discredited ideology over practical solutions and predicted a long and agonizing epoch in which incomes will fall and the economy will stall. He described the Tea Party's demand for a government shutdown as necessary to force action on the budget, and criticized the inclusion of polarizing policy riders in the budget proposal. Stockman also criticized Ryan's budget plan for not addressing the country's entitlement costs and tax reform. He also predicted that interest rates on the national debt will rise in the coming years, increasing federal spending by half a trillion dollars. Overall, Stockman's comments paint a grim picture of the country's fiscal future and call for bold action to address the nation's debt and stalled economy.

The provided text appears to be a combination of two different documents. The first part is a list of various criminal offenses and their associated punishments according to Iranian law, as outlined in the Islamic Penal Code. The second part is a report by Amnesty International titled "Growing Up on Death Row: The Death Penalty and Juvenile Offenders in Iran."

The crimes mentioned in articles 692 and 693, if committed during the night, result in the maximum punishment. Article 696 outlines the process for enforcing judgments, including the sale of the offender's belongings or detaining them until they pay debts.

Articles 697 through 700 deal with various forms of libel, insult, and dishonoring, and the associated punishments.

Articles 701 through 713 cover traffic crimes, including public consumption of alcoholic beverages, gambling, and tramping, and the associated punishments.

The final part of the text is a report by Amnesty International on the use of the death penalty against juvenile offenders in Iran. The report states that Iran continues to execute juvenile offenders in violation of international law, and highlights the cases of several juvenile offenders who have spent years on death row. The report also criticizes piecemeal reforms in Iran's penal code as failing to deliver justice for juvenile offenders.

A group of 31 senior scientists and clinicians from various universities in the UK and Imperial College have published an editorial in the Journal of Alzheimer's Disease, suggesting that viruses and bacteria, particularly the herpes virus, chlamydia bacteria, and spirochaete, are major causes of Alzheimer's disease. They argue that these microbes trigger the build-up of sticky amyloid plaques and misfolded tau proteins in the brain, leading to memory loss and cognitive decline. The team calls for urgent investigation and clinical trials of antimicrobial drugs to halt dementia.

The herpes virus, which causes cold sores, is known to damage the central nervous system, and the limbic system in the brain, which regulates mood and instinct, is associated with mental decline and personality changes. The authors point out that a gene mutation, APOEe4, which makes one in five people more susceptible to Alzheimer's disease, also raises their susceptibility to infectious disease.

Currently, most scientists are focusing on finding treatments that prevent the build-up of amyloid plaques and misfolded tau proteins in the brain. However, the editorial suggests that it is a viral or bacterial infection that triggers the plaque build-up in the first place.

The team's call for action is based on substantial published evidence into Alzheimer's, but their work has been largely ignored or dismissed as controversial. They argue that opposition to their concepts resembles the fierce resistance to studies some years ago which showed that viruses cause certain types of cancer and that a bacterium causes stomach ulcers, which were ultimately proved valid.

The editorial has received mixed reactions from the research community. Some researchers agree with the team's findings, while others are skeptical. Dementia charities have noticed that viruses and bacteria are more common in people with Alzheimer's disease, but they emphasize that there is currently insufficient evidence to tell us that microbes are responsible for causing Alzheimer's disease in the vast majority of cases.

The team's research could have implications for the future treatment of Parkinson's disease and other progressive neurological conditions. They propose that further research on the role of infectious agents in Alzheimer's disease causation, including prospective trials of antimicrobial therapy, is now justified.

The Chinese authorities have confirmed a case of forced abortion on a woman named Feng Jianmei, who was seven months pregnant, after images of her baby's corpse were posted online. The incident occurred in Shaanxi province, where Feng was forced to abort her pregnancy due to failing to pay a fine for violating China's strict "one-child" population control policy.

The Shaanxi provincial government has launched an investigation and has recommended action against the perpetrators, stating that this is a serious violation of the National Population and Family Planning Commission's policies. The government has not identified the perpetrators but has vowed to prevent such incidents in the future.

Internet users in China have reacted with anger, comparing the incident to acts perpetrated by "Japanese devils and Nazis." Feng's relative told AFP that she and her husband had opposed the termination.

China's one-child policy, implemented since the late 1970s, aims to control a population that has grown to 1.3 billion people. Under the policy, urban families are generally allowed to have one child, while rural families can give birth to two children if the first is a girl. They have to pay a fine if they contravene the rules.

Rights groups claim that as a result of the policy, thousands of women have been forced by authorities to terminate their pregnancies. Blind activist Chen Guangcheng, who recently left China for the United States after fleeing house arrest, was once jailed after angering local officials for bringing to light hundreds of forced abortions.

The US has expressed opposition to China's one-child policy, stating that it strongly opposes all aspects of China's coercive birth limitation policies, including forced abortion and sterilization.

The document summarized is a plan for the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) brought by Kansas Secretary of State Kris Kobach to his meeting with President-elect Donald Trump on November 20, 2016. The plan, titled "Department of Homeland Security Kobach Strategic Plan for First 365 Days," proposes several changes for the DHS, including the update and reintroduction of the National Security Entry-Exit Registration System (NSEERS). This system, originally implemented in the wake of the September 11 attacks, required certain immigrants, including men and boys from 25 mostly Muslim nations, to register with the federal government upon their arrival. The plan also suggests adding "extreme vetting questions" for high-risk foreigners, including questions about support for Sharia law, jihad, and the U.S. Constitution. The plan also proposes ending the flow of Syrian refugees into the United States. Kobach, who has been mentioned as a potential pick for a position within the Trump administration, did not immediately respond to requests for comment. The plan was visible in a photograph from The Associated Press.

The French satirical magazine Charlie Hebdo has published nude cartoons of Prophet Mohammad, which could further escalate tensions following violent protests in the Muslim world over an anti-Islam film. The cover of the magazine shows a Muslim in a wheelchair being pushed by an Orthodox Jew, referencing a popular French film. Another cartoon depicts a naked Mohammad exposing his posterior to a film director. This is not the first time Charlie Hebdo has caused controversy over issues related to Islam; last year, it published an edition "guest-edited" by Prophet Mohammad, resulting in its offices being firebombed.

French Prime Minister Jean-Marc Ayrault has defended the newspaper's right to publish caricatures of the prophet while urging calm in the country with the largest Muslim population in western Europe. He emphasized France's tradition of free speech but also stated that anyone offended by the cartoons could take legal action. Ayrault also refused a request to hold a demonstration in Paris against the controversial US-made anti-Islam film "Innocence of Muslims," which has sparked violent protests across the Muslim world.

The publication of the cartoons was met with immediate calls for media responsibility and appeals for calm from political and religious leaders. Charlie Hebdo's editor denied being deliberately provocative at a sensitive time. The tensions around the film in France have sparked debate about the limits of free speech.

In response to the tensions, France has decided to temporarily close its embassies and schools in 20 countries on Friday as a precautionary measure. French Foreign Minister Laurent Fabius has criticized the move as a provocation and ordered security to be beefed up at French diplomatic offices in the Muslim world. The government has also called for restraint over the cartoons, restating the principles of free speech in France and urging those shocked by the images to take action through the courts.

The latest Charlie Hebdo caricatures have been criticized by Muslim leaders as another Western insult to their faith, and there are concerns that they could exacerbate tensions and provoke reactions. The French leadership is emphasizing the importance of free speech while urging calm and responsibility in the face of the controversy.

Country music star Carrie Underwood made a young fan's dream come true during her concert in Louisville, Kentucky, by giving him a kiss on the lips on stage. The 12-year-old fan, named Chase, had a sign that read "Carrie be my first kiss." After warning the boy that her husband, NFL player Mike Fisher, was in the audience, Underwood obliged and shared a lip-to-lip kiss with the brave fan. The singer later posted a picture of the moment on Twitter and thanked Chase for the memorable experience. Underwood's "Blown Away Tour" will include home state shows in Oklahoma City and Tulsa in October and November.

Catherine Zeta-Jones, a renowned actress and mother, has checked into a mental health facility for a brief stay to treat her Bipolar II Disorder. The decision was made due to the stress of the past year, which included her husband Michael Douglas' cancer treatment, legal battles, and personal struggles. Zeta-Jones' publicist confirmed that she is feeling great and looking forward to starting work on her two upcoming films. Bipolar II Disorder, also known as manic-depressive illness, is characterized by unusual shifts in mood and energy. While it is common for the disorder to develop in late teens or early adulthood, it can also develop later in life. Zeta-Jones, 41, has been open about her struggles, particularly during Douglas' cancer diagnosis in 2010. The couple, who married in 2000 and have two children together, have reportedly grown closer as a result of these challenges.

In Cornwall, three surfers have tragically died after getting into difficulties in the sea off Mawgan Porth beach near Newquay. The incident occurred around 1.30pm on Sunday, with onlookers spotting a group of seven, including four children, in trouble in the water. An air and sea rescue mission was launched, and the three adults were recovered unconscious from the water but later pronounced dead. The four children were rescued and were safe, police said.

The woman and one of the men who died were in their 40s and from Cornwall. The second man was in his 50s and was from outside the police force’s area. A spokesman said his family has been contacted.

Local authorities are investigating the full circumstances of the incident, with police expressing their condolences to the families involved. The rough seas on Sunday afternoon may have contributed to the incident, but it is unclear whether the water was being watched by lifeguards at the time.

Mawgan Porth is a popular spot for surfers and walkers, with its Atlantic breakers and idyllic coastal path. The tragedy serves as a reminder of the dangers that can lurk in the sea, particularly for inexperienced surfers who may exhaust themselves swimming against the flow or panic in a rip current.

Vanderbilt University has announced its decision to remove the name "Confederate" from Confederate Memorial Hall, a dormitory on its campus, by repaying an 83-year-old donation of $1.2 million to the United Daughters of the Confederacy. The university has been referring to the building as Memorial Hall since 2005, but was previously blocked from changing the name due to the original donation and naming rights.

The decision to remove the name comes after a 14-year effort by the university to address the symbolism of the building, which has been a source of debate due to its location in the heart of the university's freshman commons and its association with the Confederacy. Chancellor Nicholas S. Zeppos, who has been in favor of changing the building's name since he arrived on campus in 1987, called the name "deeply offensive and painful" for many people.

The United Daughters of the Confederacy originally donated $50,000 in 1933 toward the building’s construction and naming rights in order to honor Confederate soldiers who died during the Civil War. In 2002, Vanderbilt attempted to rename the building Memorial Hall, but the Tennessee Division of the United Daughters of the Confederacy sued to keep the original name. A Tennessee appeals court ruled in 2005 that Vanderbilt could remove “Confederate” from the inscription only after it had returned the donation at its current value.

Anonymous donors recently provided the university with the $1.2 million needed for the purpose of repaying the donation. The Vanderbilt Board of Trust authorized the move this summer. Doug Jones, the Nashville attorney who represented the Daughters of the Confederacy against Vanderbilt, called the move "a real slam on the history of our country."

Universities across the country have faced similar decisions as they re-evaluated the implications of their buildings' names. Students and officials at Middle Tennessee State University in Murfreesboro have spent months pushing to remove the name of Nathan Bedford Forrest, a founder of the Ku Klux Klan, from a campus building. MTSU and the Tennessee Board of Regents approved the change, which now goes before a state panel.

Zeppos flatly rebuffed the criticism that changing the name of a residence hall would compromise the university's approach to its long and complicated history. "We are not saying this is not part of Vanderbilt's history," he said. "I think we teach history by how we talk about these events."

The longstanding effort to rename the residence hall took on renewed urgency over the past couple of years, as universities across Tennessee and the country grappled with the shadow of racism and slavery on their campuses. At Vanderbilt, founded in 1873 just eight years after the Civil War ended, the name change follows a series of changes made over the past year to address diversity, including the addition of a chief diversity officer to the university's leadership team.

The university's decision to remove the mention of the Confederacy from the building has been praised by students and officials, who see it as a positive step towards addressing diversity and inclusivity on campus. Ariana Fowler, president of Vanderbilt Student Government, said the decision demonstrates the administration's attentiveness to student needs and concerns, and sets a great precedent for advocating on behalf of those who may feel marginalized on campus.

Crews were already working to cover the name over the building’s entrance as of Monday night. The move comes as the Southern Baptist Convention has also voted to urge its congregations to stop displaying Confederate flags. The church is by far the largest in the South.

The estate of the late artist Dash Snow is taking legal action against McDonald's for using Snow's graffiti tag, "SACE," without permission in the decoration of several restaurants worldwide. The lawsuit, filed by Snow's former girlfriend and estate manager, Jade Berreau, alleges copyright infringement, trademark infringement, unfair competition, falsification of copyright management information, and negligence.

Snow, who died in 2009 at the age of 27, was a renowned street artist who began his career in the 1990s as part of the graffiti crew IRAK. He took an anti-commercial stance and would never have aligned himself with a brand like McDonald's, according to the lawsuit.

The lawsuit claims that the appropriated "SACE" tag is prominently placed in the McDonald's restaurants and that media coverage implied that Snow authorized the use of his work on the walls of the corporate chain. The plaintiff argues that the fast food chain's use of Snow's designs could harm the value of his original artworks, which have sold for hundreds of thousands at auction houses like Sotheby's.

In June 2016, Berreau asked McDonald's to remove Snow's recognizable graffiti tag from the restaurants, to no avail. The lawsuit claims that McDonald's has arrogantly refused to comply with the request.

The controversy arose in March 2016 when a refurbished McDonald's in the gentrifying district of Brixton, South London, generated controversy for its questionable graffiti-covered décor. Locals took to Twitter to vent their frustration about the "edgy" designs, with one Twitter user, @bernehxoxo, replying to a tweet from the Evening Standard, "stoked about the sace throw! Rip".

The lawsuit, filed in a federal court in Los Angeles, seeks damages and an injunction to stop McDonald's from using Snow's artwork without permission. The estate argues that McDonald's is attempting to trade on Snow's name and reputation.

The fiscal cliff negotiations between Congressional leaders, President Barack Obama, and House Speaker John Boehner have reached a stalemate, with Boehner's Plan B collapsing on Thursday night. The breakdown in talks comes after a week of public acrimony and failed attempts to reach a compromise on deficit reduction and tax increases for upper-income Americans.

The negotiations began in earnest on Monday, with Boehner proposing a deal that would let tax rates rise for upper-income people in exchange for new revenue through a tax overhaul in 2013. However, Boehner faced opposition from his own party, with House Ways and Means Chairman Dave Camp and Budget Chairman Paul Ryan expressing concerns about the level of new tax revenue called for in the broader plan.

On Friday, both Obama and Senate Democratic leader Harry Reid spoke with Boehner in a bid to resurrect a deal, but it remains unclear whether a compromise can be reached before the year-end fiscal cliff deadline. The breakdown in negotiations offers little evidence that the election of Obama and House Republicans has brought the two sides any closer together, and has further poisoned an already distrustful relationship.

Boehner could soon face a decision whether to call for a vote on some sort of plan that could avert the cliff's spending cuts and tax increases, but might imperil his position if he had to rely on Democrats to pass it. The negotiations offer little evidence that a long-term solution to the budget woes will be reached before the new year, with both sides expecting a small package doing little to tackle the long-term budget problems and deferring the battle until next year.

A professor at Leipzig University, Annette G Beck-Sickinger, has apologized for denying an internship to an Indian student due to the "rape problem in India." The incident came to light after emails exchanged between the professor and the student were posted on Quora by a colleague of the student. The professor also refused a PhD application from another student in March 2014 for similar reasons. The matter emerged amidst a renewed debate on Germany's poor record in women's safety, especially after the controversy generated by the banned documentary, India's Daughter.

In her apology, Beck-Sickinger admitted to making a mistake and expressed regret for any hurt feelings. She claimed the issue was a misunderstanding and the outcome of an unpleasant discussion with the Indian student. Beck-Sickinger, a professor of biochemistry and bio-organic chemistry, did not deny the email exchange with the Indian student who initially accused her.

The professor's rationale for refusing Indian male students for internships and higher education was criticized for being illogical, unbecoming of someone of her station, and showing a false consensus bias. However, in her apology, she insists that she rejected the applications because the positions were full, and the talk on rape was a spin-off, after he kept pestering her.

German ambassador Michael Steiner strongly condemned the professor's denial of internship and endorsed India's efforts to deal with violence against women. He emphasized that India is not a country of rapists and encouraged Beck-Sickinger to learn more about India and its people.

Leipzig University, founded in 1409, is one of Germany's oldest universities and is known for its interdisciplinary, international comprehensive approach. Last week, the Indian government barred the screening of India's Daughter, a documentary on the brutal gang-rape of a young student in December 2012, which has sparked a fresh debate on rape and steps to counter violence against women in India.

In a groundbreaking medical procedure, doctors in Toronto performed in-utero surgery on a two-month-old baby boy named Sebastian Havill, who was diagnosed with a severe congenital heart defect known as complete transposition of the great arteries (TGA). The surgery, believed to be the world's first balloon atrial septoplasty in utero to treat TGA, was performed on May 18, 2023, at The Hospital for Sick Children and Mount Sinai Hospital.

Sebastian's parents, Kristine Barry and Christopher Havill, were informed of the procedure when they learned of their baby's condition during an anatomy scan at 20 weeks. The couple was assured by doctors that the surgery could fix the problem, which would require switching the arteries within a week of birth due to the closed walls in Sebastian's heart, preventing blood from getting oxygen after his birth.

On the day of the surgery, about 30 medical staff were present, including surgeons, cardiologists, and a person with an incubator. With ultrasound guidance, doctors inserted a needle into Barry's uterus and into Sebastian's heart to blow up a tiny balloon, making a hole about 3.5 millimetres wide in his atrial septum. This allowed the blood and oxygen to circulate properly, a temporary fix until they could perform surgery after birth.

The surgery was a success, and just 20 minutes later, the room erupted in applause. Five days after the surgery, Barry was induced into labor and gave birth to Sebastian only 10 minutes in. Sebastian successfully underwent the open-heart surgery that babies with congenital TGA must have, and he was sent home the week after.

About three babies a year in Ontario have the same extreme case of congenital heart defect that Sebastian has. His parents will take him to a neuro-development program at Sick Kids to make sure he's hitting all his milestones at 6, 12, 18, 24, and 36 months old. Sebastian may run into issues at any stage in his development, but in general, he is expected to lead a normal life.

Barry and Havill express their gratitude to the medical teams at the two hospitals for saving their baby's life. Sebastian's parents say he is a healthy, normal baby at home in Barrie, Ont., fussing on his mother's lap as his dad smiles and soothes him. The doctors have told the couple that Sebastian's scar from his open-heart surgery will eventually fade, and will be barely visible by adulthood.

Baltimore Ravens cornerback Tray Walker, 23, has tragically passed away from injuries sustained in a motorcycle accident in Florida on Thursday night. The crash occurred at NW 21 Avenue and NW 75 Street in Miami, where Walker collided with a Ford Escape while not wearing a helmet and riding a bike without lights. Police do not suspect alcohol or drugs as factors in the crash, and neither do they believe Walker was racing. The Ravens selected Walker in the fourth round of the 2015 NFL Draft and he played in eight games for the team last season, primarily on special teams.

Upon learning of Walker's accident, head coach John Harbaugh penned a letter to the players expressing his condolences and offering words of encouragement. Team members have expressed their grief and shared memories of Walker, who was known for his good heart, energy, and promise. His teammates, coaches, and family are mourning his loss and offering support to his family during this difficult time.

A man named Grim LeRogue, formerly known as Joe Rogan, stormed the field at Yankee Stadium on Monday night with aspirations of confronting Alex Rodriguez over his relationship with Cameron Diaz. Police sources revealed that LeRogue was carrying five pictures, one of which was of Rodriguez with an X over his face and a gun pointed at his head, accompanied by a message stating that Rodriguez had ruined too many "white queens." LeRogue also had a picture of Diaz with the message "We will be together soon."

LeRogue, who has a history of assault and burglary charges, did not have any weapons on him during the incident. He is known to have a soft spot for Osama bin Laden, as one of the pictures he carried depicted the al-Qaeda leader with the inscription "I will serve you," and described him as his "master." LeRogue also carried pictures of Whitney Houston and her ex-husband Bobby Brown.

On Houston's picture, LeRogue captioned her as "Whitney Bin Laden," and wrote "You will soon be my master's wife." On Brown's photo, he wrote "You need to be terminated." LeRogue was charged with assault and interfering with a sporting event and was taken to Lincoln Hospital in the Bronx for a psychiatric evaluation.

LeRogue's mother, Cathy, expressed shock over her son's actions, stating that he has a history of drinking and is not the saintly kid he is being portrayed as. LeRogue, who is also a known graffiti vandal, is set to self-publish a 700-page novel about a ninja or something next month. LeRogue reportedly admitted to the police that he wanted publicity for his book.

In an interview on CNN's "Piers Morgan Tonight," New Jersey Governor Chris Christie expressed his frustration with billionaire Warren Buffett, who has been advocating for the "Buffet Rule" that suggests millionaires pay at least the same tax rate as middle-class households. Christie stated, "He should just write a check and shut up," and added, "Just contribute... If he wants to give the government more money, he’s got the ability to write a check — go ahead and write it." Christie further clarified that his job as governor is to be responsible for all New Jerseyans, and he is not in favor of class warfare. The interview also touched upon Christie's views on same-sex marriage and his advice for GOP candidate Mitt Romney.

The San Francisco home featured in the 1993 movie "Mrs. Doubtfire" was targeted in a suspected arson attack on Monday night. Authorities were called to the home on Broadway and Steiner Street after someone attempted to set fire to the garage door and front door, possibly using an accelerant such as gasoline. The home is currently owned by a plastic surgeon who suspects a former client may be responsible for the incident. The home gained notoriety last August following the death of Robin Williams, who starred in the film, with fans leaving flowers and notes as a memorial. Police are investigating the incident and no suspects have been identified. The home has previously been a site of remembrance for Williams, who took his own life last year.

The National Portrait Gallery in Washington D.C. unveiled portraits of former President Barack Obama and former First Lady Michelle Obama on Monday. Barack Obama's portrait was painted by Kehinde Wiley, an artist known for his vibrant depictions of African-Americans, while Michelle Obama's portrait was commissioned to Baltimore-based artist Amy Sherald.

The portraits were unveiled as part of a rite of passage for most former presidents, with their portraits hanging in the museum. Barack Obama's choice of Wiley makes him the first African-American artist to execute an official presidential portrait for the National Portrait Gallery.

Obama's portrait depicts him sitting against a backdrop of green foliage, with Wiley taking thousands of photographs to create the painting. The former president joked about his appearance in the portrait, saying he tried to negotiate for less gray hair and smaller ears, but Wiley's artistic integrity would not allow it.

Michelle Obama's portrait was painted by Amy Sherald, who is known for her unique style and her portraits that underscore themes of social justice. Sherald painted Michelle Obama in a flowing, patterned dress with a halter neckline, and her expression is thoughtful.

The Obamas looked at the portfolios of over two dozen artists before deciding on Wiley and Sherald. Obama's portrait will hang in the hall of presidents, while Michelle Obama's portrait will be placed in another gallery. Both portraits will be open to public viewing on Tuesday.

The unveiling of the portraits marks the former first couple's re-emergence on the public stage, only this time for an event that has nothing to do with politics. The Obamas expressed their gratitude to the artists and spoke about the impact their portraits will have on future generations, particularly on girls and girls of color.

Richard Carpenter, the surviving member of the iconic duo The Carpenters, has filed a lawsuit against Universal Music Group (UMG) and A&M Records, alleging that they have been underpaying him and the estate of his late sister, Karen, in digital royalties for their music. The lawsuit, filed in Los Angeles Superior Court, claims that the record labels have been misclassifying digital downloads as sales of records, resulting in lower royalty rates. The Carpenters' estate is seeking compensatory damages of at least $2 million.

The lawsuit also alleges that the defendants undercounted digital downloads and applied an incorrect base price to the sales of CDs. The case is similar to a previous lawsuit involving the recordings of Eminem, where the defendants were several affiliates of UMG. The 9th Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that digital downloads were a licensing of master recordings rather than a sale of records.

Richard Carpenter expressed regret that he was unable to resolve the royalty dispute amicably and stated that the Carpenters' recordings, which are among the best-sellers in the history of popular music, continue to contribute significantly to UMG/A&M's annual profits. The lawsuit claims breach of contract and breach of the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing.

The Carpenters, who recorded 11 albums and released 31 singles during their career, won three Grammys. Karen Carpenter passed away in 1983. A spokeswoman for UMG did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The Carpenters are represented by Larry Iser and Greg Gabriel at Kinsella Weitzman Iser Kump & Aldisert.

Dominique Strauss-Kahn, the 62-year-old managing director of the International Monetary Fund (IMF), was charged with attempting to rape a New York hotel maid in a scandal that has potentially derailed his presidential aspirations in France. The incident occurred in Strauss-Kahn's $3,000-a-night suite at the Sofitel hotel in New York's Times Square on Saturday. The maid, 32, claimed that Strauss-Kahn emerged naked from the bathroom and sexually assaulted her. He was expected to appear in court later on Sunday.

Strauss-Kahn has been a prominent figure in global finance, leading the IMF through the 2007-09 global financial crisis and playing a key role in Europe's debt crisis. He was a French finance minister from 1997-1999 and is a possible candidate in next year's presidential vote. However, he has a reputation for being a womanizer, and in 2008, he apologized for an affair with a female IMF economist who was his subordinate.

The scandal has thrown the IMF into a leadership crisis and has turned France's presidential election campaign upside down. Strauss-Kahn was a clear front-runner in the polls, but his presidential ambitions appear to be dead in the water unless the case against him quickly unravels and he is shown to be innocent.

The IMF has named John Lipsky as acting managing director to fill the leadership vacuum, but the charges against Strauss-Kahn are a huge embarrassment for the institution. The allegations have also raised questions about the IMF's response to Strauss-Kahn's previous improper conduct.

Strauss-Kahn's wife, Anne Sinclair, has jumped to his defense, stating that she does not believe the accusations against him. He has hired New York lawyer Benjamin Brafman, a seasoned defense attorney who has defended pop stars and football players in the past.

The contrast between Strauss-Kahn's luxurious hotel suite and his subsequent arrest and detention in a bare holding cell in New York's Harlem neighborhood could not have been more dramatic. The charges against him carry a potential prison sentence of 15-20 years if proven. The IMF has collected DNA evidence from the hotel suite, and Strauss-Kahn is expected to go before a state court later on Sunday.

The International AIDS Conference, due to begin in Melbourne on Sunday, has been hit by a tragedy as several attendees were among the victims of the Malaysia Airlines MH17 crash over Ukraine. The International AIDS Society (IAS) confirmed that a number of colleagues and friends en route to the conference were on board the flight that was shot down, killing all 298 people on board. Many medical researchers have expressed sympathy online upon hearing that both World Health Organisation (WHO) staff and well-known HIV researchers had died in the crash. Friends and colleagues of Dutch HIV researcher Dr Joep Lange took to social media to express shock that he was among the victims. Glenn Thomas, a WHO media adviser, is also believed to be among the victims. UNAIDS executive director Michel Sidibe and the president-elect of the International AIDS Society, Chris Beyrer, have expressed their condolences. The passenger plane had been flying from Amsterdam to Kuala Lumpur when it was shot down. The Australian government has confirmed that 27 Australians were among the victims. The International AIDS Conference is now in its 20th year and has attracted major speakers, including former US president Bill Clinton, Sir Bob Geldof, and Indonesian Health Minister Nafsiam Mboi. The conference organizers have not released numbers, but did confirm that expected attendees were among the dead. The crash has also affected the AIDS research community, with many researchers and activists en route to the conference. The IAS has expressed its sincere sadness at the loss of colleagues and friends and has offered condolences to the loved ones of those who have been lost to this tragedy. The IAS has also heard reports that among the passengers was a former IAS president Joep Lange and if that is the case then the HIV/AIDS movement has truly lost a giant. The Australian government has offered to cooperate with DFAT to provide assistance to any delegates who require support. Emails sent to several WHO staff prompted out-of-office replies stating they were en route to Melbourne for the AIDS conference. Representatives from WHO could not be immediately contacted. Mark Gettleson, a London-based campaigner, tweeted that AIDS activists were also heading from Europe to Melbourne. "Several on #MH17 flight were @STOPAIDS activists en route to #AIDS2014 conference in Melbourne, fighting to save lives. Tragic," he wrote. The International AIDS Conference is now in its 20th year and has attracted major speakers, including former US president Bill Clinton, Sir Bob Geldof, and Indonesian Health Minister Nafsiam Mboi.

The U.S. Federal Air Marshals have been secretly observing American travelers on domestic flights under a previously undisclosed program called "Quiet Skies." Thousands of unsuspecting passengers have been subjected to targeted airport and inflight surveillance since the program began in March 2010. The Transportation Security Administration (TSA) acknowledged the Quiet Skies program, stating it has been around in one form or another since 2010, but declined to specify how passengers are targeted or if any arrests have resulted from the initiative. Air marshals follow about 35 Quiet Skies targets a day, observing their behavior such as fidgeting, using electronics, sweating heavily, or sleeping. TSA spokesman James Gregory insists the TSA does not single out travelers based on race, religion, or nationality, but privacy advocates are concerned about the constitutional questions raised by the program.

In a separate news article, Egyptian archaeologists have opened a 30-tonne black granite sarcophagus to find three decomposed mummies after sewage water apparently leaked inside. The tomb was found buried five meters beneath the surface and was believed to contain the remains of a prominent figure, with some considering the possibility that it could contain the corpse of Alexander the Great. However, the mummies found inside were not in the best condition and only the bones remain. The skulls of the three mummies will now be analyzed to identify their ages and cause of death. Experts believe the trio were probably soldiers, with one of the skulls displaying evidence of arrow blows. The sarcophagus, almost three meters across and two meters high, is believed to date from the early Ptolemaic period, which began following the death of Alexander in 323 BC.

In a recent incident, a customer was refused service at Chinatown Coffee Co. in Washington D.C., after ordering espresso over ice. The barista argued that the drink would ruin the quality of the espresso. This controversy is not new, as a similar incident occurred in 2008 at Murky Coffee in Arlington, where a customer was also refused the same drink. The customer in the Chinatown incident, in response, wrote a detailed Yelp review and the incident gained attention online. In 2008, the incident at Murky Coffee went viral, sparking a national debate. Murky Coffee later detailed their house rules in an open letter to the customer. The incident has been described as a "tempest in a teapot" by The Washington Post. The question remains, do customers have the right to order drinks as they please, even if it goes against a coffee shop's policy?

A global e-mail virus, named "Here you have," spread on Thursday, causing disruptions in various multinational businesses such as NASA, Comcast, Disney, and Wells Fargo. The virus, initially thought to be a worm, is actually a Trojan that spreads when users click on a malicious link in an e-mail. The virus attempts to stop and delete security services and can propagate through e-mail contacts and shared drives.

The virus's origin is unknown, but it may be linked to a cyber-jihad organization called "Brigades of Tariq ibn Ziyad." The virus is similar to the "Anna Kournikova" virus from 2001, which also used the subject "Here you have."

The Department of Homeland Security is investigating the virus, and the U.S. Computer Emergency Readiness Team and DHS National Cyber Security Division are expected to issue a bulletin. Adobe Systems advised computer security experts of vulnerabilities in Adobe reader software, which could explain the virus's .pdf format.

To avoid falling victim to the virus, users are advised not to click links in e-mail messages from unknown people or even from friends, as the source of the message might be a virus. Keeping a computer protected with an antivirus or a security suite can provide additional protection.

The virus has caused disruptions in work, with some employees forced to go without e-mail altogether. While the virus hasn't had a major impact on operations, it has caused annoyance and frustration for employees trying to get work done.

The 2006 letter from Cardinal Leonardo Sandri, a top Vatican official, confirms that the Holy See received information in 2000 about the sexual misconduct of then-Cardinal Theodore McCarrick, a U.S. prelate who resigned in July 2018. The letter, addressed to Father Boniface Ramsay, a New York priest who had made the initial allegation, was published by the Catholic News Service on September 7, 2018.

Ramsay had informed the Vatican in a November 2000 letter about McCarrick's misconduct with seminarians from Seton Hall University's Immaculate Conception Seminary. Ramsay, who in 2000 was on the faculty at the seminary, had sent the letter at the request of the then-Vatican ambassador because he had heard so many complaints from seminarians that McCarrick would invite them to his beach house and into his bed.

Sandri, who was the No. 3 in the Vatican's secretariat of state at the time, wrote Ramsay on Oct. 11, 2006, seeking his recommendation for a former seminarian for a Vatican job. In it, he referred to Ramsay's 2000 letter, confirming that the Vatican had received information about McCarrick's misconduct.

Archbishop Carlo Maria Vigano, at the center of a storm rocking Pope Francis' papacy, cited Ramsay's 2000 letter in his own expose of a cover-up about the McCarrick affair. He named Sandri among a long list of Vatican officials who knew about McCarrick's penchant for seminarians. Vigano also accused Francis of knowing in 2013 of McCarrick's misconduct but of rehabilitating him from sanctions purportedly imposed by Pope Benedict XVI.

Sandri's letter is significant because it corroborates Ramsay's story as well as Vigano's claims. It shows the Vatican knew about allegations against McCarrick in 2000, a year before St. John Paul II made him a cardinal. And it further implicates the Benedict's papacy for failing to take action against McCarrick for years even as more allegations against him arrived.

Vigano says Benedict eventually imposed some form of sanction on McCarrick in 2009 or 2010, nearly a decade after Ramsay's letter arrived. The fact that Sandri cited it so readily suggests it wasn't lost in a pile of unread mail somewhere, but was relevant even for a simple job reference.

Significantly, Sandri appeared more concerned about the sexual purity of the seminarian-candidate than that McCarrick might have sexually abused or harassed him, or abused his power over him.

McCarrick resigned as a cardinal in July after a U.S. church investigation determined an accusation that he groped a teen-age altar boy in the 1970s was credible. Since then several seminarians have come forward to say he routinely bedded them, or harassed them when they refused.

His lawyer has said the accusations are serious and that McCarrick looks forward to invoking his right to due process at the right time.

On Wednesday night, a shooting outside Frederick High School in Maryland left two students injured during a junior varsity basketball game. The shooting occurred around 8:10 p.m., and the shooter or shooters are still at large. The victims, who are teenagers, were flown to a Baltimore hospital for non-life-threatening injuries. Their identities and ages have not been released.

Police are investigating the motive behind the shooting, with some students reporting that it may be gang-related or connected to rival teams. Witnesses reported seeing four to five males dressed in big coats and with their hands in their pockets enter the gymnasium during the game and leave shortly before the shooting.

Frederick High School and nearby West Frederick Middle School were closed to students on Thursday, but school staff reported to work at their normal hours. All other Frederick County schools remained open. The schools will reopen on Friday.

The shooting caused panic among parents, who rushed to the scene to check on their children. Students were taken to the Terrace Lanes Bowling Alley parking lot, where they were picked up by their parents.

The Frederick County Public Schools announced the incident on Twitter, stating that the two injured students are receiving care. They also confirmed that all other staff and students at Frederick High are safe and accounted for.

The school system will have a crisis team available to students and staff, and arrangements are being made to return personal items left at the school. Anyone with information on the shooting is asked to call the police.

The shooting is rare in the area, and police believe the victims were targeted. The investigation is ongoing, and police are searching the school grounds for any evidence that will help generate new leads. As of Thursday afternoon, no arrests have been made.

Steven Spielberg's "Bridge of Spies" is a complex Cold War drama that challenges the audience to trust its narrative. The film, written by Matt Charman, Joel Coen, and Ethan Coen, stars Tom Hanks as James Donovan, a Brooklyn lawyer who becomes embroiled in the center of the Cold War when the CIA sends him to negotiate the release of a captured American U-2 pilot. The story is based on a true event and follows Donovan's journey as he negotiates the release of a Soviet spy, Rudolf Abel, played by Mark Rylance.

The film is a slow burn that requires patience from the audience, as it pieces together details in a way that makes sense only in the third act. Hanks delivers a nuanced performance as Donovan, a real person with doubts and a runny nose, while Rylance steals the show as Abel, a sympathetic and docile Soviet spy.

"Bridge of Spies" is a moral drama driven by an insurance lawyer, a departure from typical spy thrillers. The film's spiky, subversive wit often works at cross-purposes with traditional themes of patriotism and American exceptionalism. The Coen brothers are credited with taking a whetstone to the original script, and their influence is evident in the film's complex narrative and character development.

The film opens with the FBI's real-time pursuit and arrest of Abel, setting the tone for the Cold War-era fears that pervade the film. Donovan fights for Abel despite the scorn of the public, the indifference of the legal system, and the danger to his family. When he goes to Berlin to negotiate the exchange of Abel for a detained U-2 pilot, Donovan decides to defy the CIA and try to release another imprisoned American as well.

"Bridge of Spies" is a muddle that has been handcrafted by experts, a spy thriller that insists on kindness, and an ensemble piece that knows enough to acknowledge a natural screen presence whenever Rylance is in view. The film is a testament to Spielberg's ability to execute ambitious plans and entertain audiences while defying their skeptical movie expectations.

The Gilmore Girls follow-up movies have been officially greenlit for production, with six original cast members, including stars Alexis Bledel and Lauren Graham, set to reprise their roles. The quartet of Scott Patterson, Kelly Bishop, Sean Gunn, and Keiko Agena will also return. The four 90-minute movies, treated as a farewell season, are being written and directed by Amy Sherman-Palladino and her husband Daniel Palladino. Set in present day, the films will unfold over a calendar year, with each covering a different season. The revival is produced by Dorothy Parker Drank Here Productions in association with Warner Bros. Television.

The original series, which aired from 2000-2007, followed Lorelai Gilmore, her daughter Rory, and the residents of Stars Hollow. The revival will see creator Amy Sherman-Palladino returning as executive producer, joined by her husband Daniel Palladino. Notable absences from the returning cast include Liza Weil, Yanic Truesdale, and Luke's baseball cap. The exact title and premiere date for the revival are yet to be announced.

Lauren Graham, who played Lorelai Gilmore, tweeted about the revival, confirming that they have just completed a table read for the first film. The revival will likely address the issue of Rory's exes, as the original series left fans wanting closure on this front. The revival is set to premiere on Netflix.

Two suspected drug-smuggling tunnels linking warehouses in Tijuana and San Diego have been discovered by U.S. and Mexican authorities. The first tunnel, found on Tuesday, was approximately 600 yards long, secured with wooden trusses, and equipped with lighting and a crude rail system. The second tunnel, discovered on Thursday, was more sophisticated, featuring ventilation and a multi-tiered electrical rail system. No drugs or other contraband were found in either tunnel or the warehouses on either side of the border. A 73-year-old California woman, Glennys Rodriguez, was arrested on suspicion of overseeing the operation of the first tunnel. Rodriguez is the only person facing charges so far, but several other individuals are believed to be related to the tunnels. These latest discoveries mark the sixth and seventh cross-border passages found since 2010, with over 80 tunnels discovered in California and Arizona since 2006. The quantity of drugs that may have been successfully channeled through these tunnels is unknown. The busts are said to have eliminated a multi-million dollar drug smuggling venture.

At the G20 summit in Toronto, world leaders agreed on a timetable for cutting deficits and halting the growth of their debt, while acknowledging the need to move carefully to avoid setting back the fragile global recovery. President Obama and Treasury Secretary Timothy F. Geithner advocated a measured approach to debt reduction, but the United States, along with other countries, endorsed a goal of cutting government deficits in half by 2013 and stabilizing the ratio of public debt to GDP by 2016. The timetable was couched as an expectation, rather than a firm deadline, and Japan, which is heavily dependent on domestic borrowing, was not expected to meet the targets.

The leaders also discussed banking regulations, but could not agree on a proposal for a global bank tax. The G20 reaffirmed a deadline for agreeing on new capital standards for banks, but signaled that several countries might not implement the standards by 2012, as initially planned.

President Obama arrived in Canada with three victories under his belt, including European leaders agreeing to conduct stress tests on their big banks, China announcing that it would allow a gradual appreciation of its currency, and Congressional negotiators agreeing on a far-reaching overhaul of financial regulations. However, the mood at the summit was far from cheery, with leaders facing challenges of lagging growth, heavy debts, and anxious voters.

The G20 statement called for rebalancing the world economy to be less reliant on debt-financed spending by North American and Western European consumers, and appealed to China to increase spending on infrastructure, let its currency fluctuate, and strengthen social protections. However, China did not make any new commitments, and removed a proposed clause from the joint statement that would have praised China for agreeing to greater exchange-rate flexibility.

Overall, the G20 outcome was a victory for Chancellor Angela Merkel of Germany, who argued that without actions to rein in spending, investors would drive up governments’ borrowing costs, as they did in Greece. President Obama said that the communiqué reflected his policies and that "we can't all rush to the exits at the same time." However, some economists view the pledge on deficits as imperiling the prospects for growth, and argue that the risks of a new downturn are minimal.

Ivanka Trump, the daughter of President Donald Trump, used a personal email account to send hundreds of messages discussing official White House business last year, according to sources familiar with a White House examination of her correspondence. The emails were reportedly sent before she was briefed on the rules regarding the use of personal emails for official business.

The discovery of Ivanka Trump's email use alarmed some advisers to President Trump, who feared that her practices bore similarities to the personal email use of Hillary Clinton, an issue that Trump's father had made a focus of his 2016 campaign. Ivanka Trump's emails contained mostly logistical and personal information, but some may have been in violation of federal records rules.

Austin Evers, from the group American Oversight, which submitted the freedom of information request that led to the discovery of Ivanka Trump's use of personal email, said the "president's family is not above the law." He called for Congress to investigate the matter, raising questions about whether Ivanka Trump turned over all of her emails for preservation as required by law and whether she was sending classified information over a private system.

Peter Mirijanian, a spokesman for Ivanka Trump's counsel Abbe Lowell, said in a statement that Ivanka Trump sometimes used her private account, almost always for logistical and scheduling concerning her family. He added that Ivanka Trump did not create a private server and never transmitted any classified information.

The use of personal emails for government business could violate the Presidential Records Act, which requires that all official White House communications and records be preserved as a permanent archive of each administration. It can also increase the risk that sensitive government information could be mishandled or hacked, revealing government secrets and risking harm to diplomatic relations and secret operations.

The Clinton email saga involved Hillary Clinton's use of a private email server while she was secretary of state. An FBI investigation concluded that Clinton should not face charges, but said she and her aides had been "extremely careless" in their handling of classified information. It is not illegal for White House officials to use personal email accounts for government business, but under the Presidential Records Act and Federal Records Act, government officials must forward any official correspondence to a work account within 20 days for preservation. There are also rules against sharing classified or privileged information on personal email accounts.

In a significant development, Allen Weisselberg, the long-time Chief Financial Officer of the Trump Organization, was granted immunity by federal prosecutors in New York during the course of the Michael Cohen investigation. This information was first reported by The Wall Street Journal. Weisselberg is identified as "Executive 1" in the criminal information filed by prosecutors in the Michael Cohen case.

According to prosecutors, Cohen, then Trump's attorney, sent an invoice to Weisselberg for a payment that was actually meant to reimburse Cohen for a payment to Stormy Daniels. Weisselberg then directed another Trump Organization executive to pay the invoice from the Trust, describing it as a retainer for January and February 2017.

Weisselberg, who began working for the Trump Organization in the 1970s, was also treasurer of the Donald J. Trump Foundation, which has been sued by the New York attorney general for alleged violations of state law.

Cohen mentioned Weisselberg's name in a recorded phone conversation with Trump about a payment to kill a story about Trump's alleged relationship with Playboy model Karen McDougal. The tape was seized during the FBI's April raid on Cohen's residence and office.

On the tape, recorded two months before the 2016 presidential election, Cohen mentions that he has spoken to Weisselberg about setting up a corporation to process the payment. "David", apparently David Pecker, a Trump friend who is the chairman and CEO of American Media and publisher of the National Enquirer, was involved in the agreement to purchase McDougal's story.

This development marks the third longtime confidant of President Trump known to have provided information in the illegal hush-money investigation that has implicated the president. President Trump’s former personal attorney Michael Cohen pleaded guilty to eight criminal charges on Tuesday.

In response to the passing of King Bhumibol Adulyadej, who died on Thursday after 70 years on the throne, Thai authorities have taken measures to prevent traders from exploiting the surge in demand for black mourning attire. The Commerce Ministry has deployed teams to inspect markets and ensure that prices of black clothing remain fair and reasonable. Traders have been asked to clearly label their prices and not to hoard goods, with violators facing severe penalties.

The government has declared a year of mourning and requested that everyone wear black or white for the first 30 days. As a result, there has been a significant increase in the demand for black clothing, with many people in Bangkok wearing black since the king's death. Shoppers have been flooding to markets to purchase new clothes, and traders have reported brisk business.

Despite the increased demand, traders have denied raising prices unreasonably. Songkhan Tansonan, a street vendor, reported selling 200 black shirts by midday on Saturday and 400 the previous day, purchasing them for 90 baht from wholesalers and selling them for 120 or 130 baht.
