In the aftermath of the San Bernardino shootings on December 2, 2015, an officer identified Syed Rizwan Farook, a co-worker of most of the victims, as a possible suspect. Farook and his wife, Tashfeen Malik, carried out the attack that killed 14 people and wounded 21 others at the Inland Regional Center, a social services agency. The couple, who the FBI said had become radicalized, died in a firefight with officers in San Bernardino, an hour east of Los Angeles, about four hours later.

The shooting occurred during an annual meeting of the county Department of Public Health, which was renting the auditorium. Trudy Raymundo, director of the department, was preparing to make a presentation when she heard gunfire outside. A gunman in a black ski mask and dressed all in black then burst through the door and started shooting. Raymundo dropped to the floor and huddled under a table with other colleagues as bullets sprayed the room that had been decked out with a Christmas tree, ornaments, and other seasonal decor.

County health employees had trained for an active-shooter scenario a year earlier in the same room. "Everyone was trying to be quiet and not draw attention to themselves as they were trained to do, to try to find as much protection as you can," said Corwin Porter, assistant director of the department. "Unfortunately the room just didn't provide a whole lot of protection."

Family members of witnesses said the initial gunfire lasted about 30 seconds and then the shooters reloaded and fired again before fleeing without saying a word. Dispatch recordings reveal the back-and-forth from officers in the field and calm-talking dispatchers, including some of the confusion and misinformation that was relayed as they tried to figure out how many suspects were involved and whether they were still at the Inland Regional Center.

Investigators believe Farook may have been plotting an earlier attack in California with someone else, two U.S. officials said. One of the officials said the two conspired in 2012 and a specific target was considered. Neither of the officials could say how serious the plotting got. San Bernardino shooters: What we do and don't know about their radicalization. One official said the two decided not to go through with the earlier attack after a round of terror-related arrests in the area. "They got spooked," the official said.

Investigators are examining a $28,500 deposit made to Farook’s bank account in the weeks before the Dec. 2 rampage. A U.S. counterterrorism official said that he didn’t have details on the transfer, but that it “would be consistent with them making preparations for grandma and the kid.” “They had purposely thought through that problem,” said the official. “There were other indications of preparations.” Reuters reported that the loan to Farook was made by the online lender Prosper. In a statement, Prosper said that the company is "prohibited by law from disclosing any non-public, personally identifiable information regarding any loan originated through our platform." "All loans originated through the Prosper platform are subject to all identity verification and screening procedures required by law, including U.S. anti-terrorism and anti-money laundering laws," the spokesperson said. "Like all Americans, Prosper is shocked and saddened by recent events in San Bernardino."

A senior law enforcement official told NBC News Tuesday that FBI investigators have been told that Farook discussed staging an attack in California as early as 2012. The official said investigators don’t yet know what to make of the claim, although they say it may bolster their growing suspicion that Farook was radicalized long before he returned from Saudi Arabia last year with his wife. The latest revelations come after NBC News reported Monday that federal investigators are interviewing a neighbor of Farook and Malik who bought two of the four guns that were used in the massacre.

The research study, published in Computers in Human Behavior, investigates the influence of media (email and voicemail) and task type (romantic and utilitarian) on emotional responses and message content. The study found that individuals sending romantic emails were more emotionally aroused and used stronger, more thoughtful language than those leaving voicemails. This is believed to be the first research study on how people respond to email using physiological measures.

The study, conducted by Indiana University and California State University-Sacramento, found that email induced more arousing psychophysiological responses than voicemail, regardless of whether the message was utilitarian or romantic. Gender was not found to be a factor in the study.

The researchers also found that the medium used can shape the content of the message. Senders of utilitarian messages sent less positive emails than voicemails for the same communication task. However, when composing romantic messages, senders included the most positive and most arousing emotional content in emails and the least positive and least arousing emotional content in voicemails.

The study's findings run counter to media naturalness theory, suggesting that email and other text communications may not be as unnatural a medium as previously thought, particularly among millennials who have grown up with email and text messaging. The study warns managers against misinterpreting the findings to suggest that face-to-face meetings, personal phone calls, and other direct forms of communication aren't as useful, as they are best for clarifying complex or unclear information.

The study was conducted by placing skin sensors on the subjects' faces to measure muscle movement associated with positive and negative emotion, and on their feet to measure arousal. Subjects were randomly chosen to do voicemail or email first and produce a utilitarian or a romantic message first. Taylor M. Wells, the study's co-author, conducted the research while she was a doctoral candidate at the Kelley School of Business at Indiana University.

However, family photos offer anecdotal support for the DNA's scientific conclusion. Linda, the redhead, is pictured growing up in a family of blondes, while Denice, the blonde, is surrounded by brunettes and redheads in pictures with her siblings and cousins.

For 72 years, Denice and Linda have unknowingly walked in each other's footsteps. Denice, who lacked stamina and coordination, found herself in a family of athletes, while Linda, the only athlete in her family, would have fit in quite nicely with Denice's family.

Since finding each other in April, Denice and Linda have met several times and have even been visiting Marianne Mayer, the woman who raised Denice, and Rochelle Nielsen, the woman who gave birth to Linda. The women have found comfort in each other's company and have begun meeting the families to which they should have belonged.

Despite the shock of the discovery, both women agree that it was better to find out about the mistake than to remain in the dark. In a statement released on March 30, Tesla provided updates on the investigation into the fatal crash of a Tesla Model X on March 23, which resulted in the death of the driver, 38-year-old Walter Huang, an Apple engineer. The accident occurred on the 101 Highway near Mountain View, California, while the vehicle was on autopilot.

According to Tesla, in the moments before the collision, the autopilot was engaged with the adaptive cruise control follow-distance set to minimum. The driver had received several visual and one audible hands-on warning earlier in the drive, but the driver’s hands were not detected on the wheel for six seconds prior to the collision. The vehicle logs show that no action was taken by the driver despite having about five seconds and 150 meters of unobstructed view of the concrete divider with the crushed crash attenuator.

Tesla also revealed that the crash attenuator, a highway safety barrier which is designed to reduce the impact into a concrete lane divider, had been crushed in a prior accident without being replaced. This is the level of damage Tesla has never seen in any other crash involving a Model X.

Walter Huang's brother, Will, told San Francisco ABC station KGO that Walter had complained "seven to 10 times the car would swivel toward that same exact barrier during auto-pilot." However, Tesla stated that they were unable to duplicate the issue when the vehicle was taken to the dealership.

The California Department of Transportation (CalTrans), which is responsible for maintaining the barriers, released a statement to KGO saying "replacement work was scheduled." The previous accident that damaged the barrier took place 11 days before Huang's fatal crash.

Tesla emphasized that the safety of their customers is their top priority and they are working closely with investigators to understand what happened and what they can do to prevent similar accidents in the future. They also stated that their autopilot "unequivocally makes the world safer for the vehicle occupants, pedestrians and cyclists."

The investigation into the fatal crash is still ongoing with the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB). Autopilot and autonomous vehicles have come under increased scrutiny recently after a woman was killed by one of Uber's autonomous vehicles in Tempe, Arizona. Arizona's governor suspended Uber's license to test autonomous vehicles on public roads last week.

The discovery of Fort Caroline, the oldest fortified settlement in North America, was announced at an international conference on France at Florida State University. Historian Fletcher Crowe, a Florida State University alumnus, and co-author Anita Spring, a professor emeritus of anthropology at the University of Florida, claim that the fort is located on an island at the mouth of the Altamaha River, two miles southeast of the city of Darien, Georgia, rather than near Jacksonville, Florida, as previously believed. The fort was built by the French in 1564 and predates St. Augustine, the Lost Colony of Virginia, Jamestown, and the landing of the Pilgrims in Massachusetts.

Researchers have been searching for actual remains of Fort Caroline for over 150 years, but Crowe and Spring say they have found evidence to support their claim. They found a number of 16th-century maps that pinpointed the location of Fort Caroline, some of which were in French, Latin, Spanish, and English. They also matched French maps from the 16th to 18th centuries of what is today the southeastern coast of the United States with coastal charts of the United States published by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, and with maps published by the U.S. Geological Survey.

One reason scholars claimed that Fort Caroline was located near Jacksonville is because they believed the local Indian tribes speaking the Timucuan language were living near the fort. However, Crowe and Spring proved that the Native Americans living near the fort spoke a language called Guale. The fort appears to be situated in an impoundment used for duck hunting in the fall, and thankfully, the site is protected by the Georgia Department of Natural Resources.

If Crowe and Spring's findings are correct, it would fundamentally redefine the term "French Florida," which has been thought to mean Northeast Florida, including Jacksonville, Lake City, and Gainesville. Instead, French Florida forms a great oval extending from the Santee River of South Carolina, down to the St. Marys River, which serves today as the border between Georgia and Florida. French Florida extends from Darien on the coast, up to Milledgeville, east of Macon.

The discovery of Fort Caroline is expected to have significant implications for the history of early colonization in North America. The site has not yet been excavated by archaeologists, but Crowe and Spring expect to begin digging within a few months. They have a special-use permit from the state of Georgia to search where they believe Fort Caroline is, and they are getting additional funding for their research.

Owen Hanson, a 35-year-old Californian who had sent the vicious DVD to Cipriani and his wife, was sentenced to 21 years and three months in prison last Friday. By the time of his arrest in September, 2015, Hanson had smuggled hundreds of kilograms of cocaine into Australia through connections in Mexico and Peru. Hanson, a former University of Southern California football player, was able to sell a kilogram of cocaine for $230,000 in Australia, compared to $20,000 in Los Angeles.

RJ Cipriani, who also goes by the name Robin Hood 702, and his wife Greice Santo were terrorized by Hanson's henchman for years. The actress was sent packages and received continous abusive and threatening phone calls. Hanson's threats against Cipriani and his wife were so severe that Cipriani went to the FBI and became a confidential source, codenamed Jackpot.

During Hanson's sentencing last week, Cipriani delivered an emotional victim impact statement, detailing the threats made against his wife and the long-lasting impact they had left. The Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR) is a significant milestone in the history of human rights, proclaimed by the United Nations General Assembly on December 10, 1948. Drafted by representatives from various legal and cultural backgrounds, the Declaration sets out fundamental human rights to be universally protected. It has been translated into over 500 languages and serves as a common standard for all nations.

The Declaration begins with a preamble emphasizing the importance of inherent dignity, equal rights, and the promotion of social progress. It consists of 30 articles that outline various human rights, including the right to life, liberty, and security; freedom from slavery and torture; the right to privacy, family, and property; and the right to freedom of thought, expression, assembly, and religion.

Article 1 asserts that all human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights, while Article 2 ensures that everyone is entitled to all the rights and freedoms set forth in the Declaration without discrimination. Article 3 guarantees the right to life, liberty, and security of person, and Article 4 prohibits slavery and servitude.

Article 5 forbids torture and cruel, inhuman, or degrading treatment or punishment, and Article 6 ensures the right to recognition as a person before the law. Article 7 mandates equality before the law and equal protection against discrimination. Article 8 grants the right to an effective remedy by the competent national tribunals for acts violating fundamental rights.

Article 9 prohibits arbitrary arrest, detention, or exile, and Article 10 guarantees the right to a fair and public hearing by an independent and impartial tribunal. Article 11 asserts the presumption of innocence until proven guilty, and Article 12 protects against arbitrary interference with privacy, family, home, or correspondence.

Article 13 guarantees freedom of movement and residence within the borders of each state, and Article 14 grants the right to seek and enjoy asylum from persecution. Article 15 affirms the right to a nationality, and Article 16 guarantees the right to marry and found a family, with equal rights during marriage and at its dissolution.

Article 17 grants the right to own property, and Article 18 guarantees freedom of thought, conscience, and religion, including the freedom to change one's religion or belief. Article 19 ensures the right to freedom of opinion and expression, and Article 20 grants the right to freedom of peaceful assembly and association.

Article 21 asserts the right to participate in government, and Article 22 guarantees the right to social security and the realization of economic, social, and cultural rights. Article 23 ensures the right to work, free choice of employment, just and favorable conditions of work, and protection against unemployment.

Article 24 grants the right to rest and leisure, including reasonable limitation of working hours and periodic holidays with pay. Article 25 asserts the right to a standard of living adequate for health and well-being, including food, clothing, housing, and medical care.

Article 26 guarantees the right to education, with education being free, compulsory, and generally available, and higher education being equally accessible to all on the basis of merit. Article 27 ensures the right to participate in the cultural life of the community, and Article 28 asserts the right to a social and international order in which the rights and freedoms set forth in the Declaration can be fully realized.

Article 29 mandates duties to the community, with limitations on rights and freedoms solely for the purpose of securing due recognition and respect for the rights and freedoms of others and of meeting the just requirements of morality, public order, and the general welfare in a democratic society. Article 30 states that nothing in the Declaration may be interpreted as implying any right to engage in any activity or perform any act aimed at the destruction of any of the rights and freedoms set forth in the Declaration.

However, it is unclear whether these measures will be enough to stop North Korea from continuing to develop its nuclear weapons program.

Former U.S. Representative Corrine Brown, a Florida Democrat, has been found guilty of 18 counts of conspiracy, wire/mail fraud, and tax fraud in a case involving a sham charity, One Door for Education. The charity, which was supposed to award scholarships to disadvantaged students, bilked donors out of $833,000, with only $1,200 actually reaching the students' education. The charges against Brown include seven counts of wire fraud, five of mail fraud, one of conspiracy, and three of falsifying tax returns. She was found not guilty on two mail fraud and two wire fraud charges.

Prosecutors argued that Brown inflated her charitable giving to receive larger tax refunds and failed to disclose tens of thousands of dollars in income from One Door and other sources. They presented evidence such as bank records, checks, emails, and hundreds of other documents to make their case that Brown directed the deposit of $37,000 of One Door cash into her account and was instrumental in planning events that cost the charity $330,000.

Brown's defense hinged on the argument that her chief of staff, Ronnie Simmons, was the real mastermind behind the fraud. Her attorney, James Smith, stated that Brown relied heavily on Simmons and other staff to help keep her personal life in order. Brown maintained her innocence and refused to answer questions after the verdict was rendered.

Smith plans to file a motion for a new trial, and Judge Timothy Corrigan has at least three months to sentence Brown if he rejects the motion. Corrigan will also decide the fate of two Brown associates, former chief of staff Ronnie Simmons and One Door for Education President Carla Wiley, who both testified against her. Simmons told the court he's hoping for leniency in exchange for his cooperation.

The sentencing phase could take 90 days or longer for Brown, who left office earlier this year after losing her re-election bid in the district she had represented for nearly a quarter-century. The Justice Department issued tough words for Brown, stating that she violated the public trust and the integrity of the American system of government.

A Casselberry mother, Sarah Anne Markham, was arrested on charges of child neglect for refusing to take her dehydrated newborn to a hospital due to her vegan beliefs. The baby was diagnosed as dehydrated and losing weight by a pediatrician, who advised Markham to admit the child to Florida Hospital South for treatment. However, Markham did not comply and was uncooperative with police when they tried to interview her. Markham stated that she wanted a second opinion from a "natural" or "vegan" doctor but could not provide any information about the doctor. Markham also said she purchased organic soy formula from Whole Foods Market and believed it was safe for her newborn, despite not confirming with a doctor if it was appropriate. Markham was arrested and later bonded out of jail. The baby was taken to Florida Hospital South for treatment and placed into state custody. A judge later granted Markham custody of her son, Caleb, with the condition that she provides a nutritionist's report within 10 days. Markham's attorney expects the criminal case against her to be dismissed.

In a tragic incident at the T-Bois Blues Festival in Larose, Louisiana, a 28-year-old woman named Jacqui Stavis was killed and two other women were injured when lightning struck their tent on Friday, March 18. Stavis, a massage therapist from New Orleans, was found unresponsive and later pronounced dead at a Lafourche Parish hospital. The two other women, aged 30 and 24, were hospitalized, with the 24-year-old being transported to University Medical Center in New Orleans. A large Labrador dog in the tent was also killed.

The three women had sought shelter in a small personal tent during a thunderstorm near the festival grounds. Following the lightning strike, Stavis was unresponsive, and her two friends had injuries associated with electric shock.

The T-Bois Blues Festival, headlined by guitarist Anders Osborne, ran from March 16 to 18. Organizers did not allow new tents to be set up on Saturday. The festival is known as the "Cajun Burning Man" and is staged at an alligator farm.

Jacqui Stavis was described by friends as a joyful, petite sprite who loved music, art, and New Orleans. She had moved to New Orleans with her boyfriend, musician Jake Gold, after graduating from Wesleyan University in Connecticut.

The incident has left the New Orleans community in shock, with many expressing their grief on social media. Stavis' brother, Erick Yingling, said that she had created a broad, de facto family that went beyond actual kin to include "musicians and misfits, entrepreneurs and artists, community activists and attorneys."

The low-key, three-day T-Bois event offers home-cooked Cajun food, catfish, crawfish, beer, and camping for all ticket-holders. It is held on an alligator and crawfish farm and features two small stages mostly featuring acts who play some variation on the blues. The festival is closed out each year by New Orleans guitarist Anders Osborne.

Investigations into the incident are ongoing.

The story revolves around a 17-year-old boy named Mohammed Islam from Queens, who was reported to have earned $72 million from stock market investments. The story was first published by New York Magazine and quickly went viral. However, it was later revealed that the story was a fabrication created by Islam and his friend Damir Tulemaganbetov.

The boys admitted to the New York Observer that they had made up the story, and their public relations firm, 5W Public Relations, confirmed the inaccuracy of the story. The boys claimed they were swept up in media attention and didn't realize the consequences of their actions.

The story was published in New York Magazine's annual "Reasons to Love New York" issue, and it was later amended to back away from the $72 million figure. The magazine apologized for the inadequate fact-checking process and took full responsibility for the error.

The story highlights the importance of fact-checking in journalism and the potential consequences of fabricating stories. It also raises questions about the credibility of media sources and the impact of such stories on individuals and their families. The boys expressed regret for their actions and apologized to their parents and friends for the embarrassment caused by the fabricated story.

In Fargo, North Dakota, 22-year-old Savanna Greywind, who was eight months pregnant, was found dead in the Red River on Sunday, with a preliminary autopsy revealing her cause of death as homicidal violence. The police found Greywind's newborn daughter in an apartment in the same building where she lived, and charged the man and woman who lived there, Brooke Crews and William Hoehn, with conspiracy to commit murder. The child is now under the care of social services.

According to court documents, Crews admitted to taking advantage of Greywind to obtain her child, while Hoehn claimed to have found Crews cleaning up blood in their bathroom and presenting him with the newborn. Both suspects are also charged with conspiracy to commit kidnapping and giving false information to police. They did not enter pleas during a court hearing on Monday, with bond set at $2 million for each suspect.

The two suspects were neighbors of Greywind, who was a member of the Turtle Mountain Band of Chippewa. A memorial was started on the steps of the apartment building where Greywind lived with her parents, and included flowers, candles, stuffed animals, and a portrait of a young Native American woman.

At the same time Greywind's body was found, a farmstead on the Minnesota side of the river was being searched, with suspicious items found that led authorities to believe it might be a crime scene. The autopsy of Greywind's body is ongoing in Minnesota's Ramsey County.

Family members declined to comment outside the courtroom, with one member, Amanda Vivier, expressing anger and struggle to process the situation. The case has sparked outrage and calls for justice in the community.

The remains of Brazilian football legend Garrincha, who won two World Cups with Brazil in 1958 and 1962, have gone missing, according to his family and local authorities. Garrincha, who was known as the greatest dribbler of all time, died in 1983 and was buried in Mage's Raiz da Serra Cemetery. However, on Tuesday, the city government and Garrincha's relatives confirmed that his remains could not be found, with cemetery officials theorizing they were lost during an exhumation.

There are two grave sites with the name Garrincha at the Raiz da Serra Cemetery. One is at the lower part of the ground, where Garrincha was originally buried. The other is some 200 meters away, on higher ground. If the exhumation theory is true, Garrincha's body would have been removed around 10 years ago from its original burial site.

Garrincha's daughter, Rosangela Santos, expressed her upset over the situation, saying, "My father doesn't deserve this." According to Garrincha's cousin, Joao Rogoginsky, another family member needed to be buried at the original site, and Joao was told at the time Garrincha's bones were taken and placed in a drawer. However, Joao did not accompany the exhumation, and the family did not receive any documentation.

The mayor of Mage, Rafael Tubarao, wants to honor the former Selecao legend in October, on the occasion of his 84th birthday, and vowed to find the remains with the family's blessing. Tubarao plans to conduct an exhumation of the graves and a DNA test to determine if one of the bodies is Garrincha's.

Garrincha, who was born on October 28, 1933, in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, overcame a series of physical defects to become one of his country's greatest soccer players. He starred for the 1958 World Cup–winning team, and was named the best player of the tournament when Brazil repeated as champions four years later. However, his career was blighted by drink problems, and he died of cirrhosis of the liver at the age of 49.

NASA has suspended most of its activities with Russia due to the ongoing violation of Ukraine's sovereignty by Russia. The International Space Station (ISS) is exempt from this suspension, as it is a symbol of international cooperation in space. The US relies on Russia for transporting crew members to and from the ISS, as it is the only country capable of doing so since the end of the US space shuttle program in 2010. NASA's move comes as no surprise, as Congress has banned NASA from working with China due to concerns about technology transfers and human rights. The US is working on developing launch systems that can carry humans, but these systems are not yet operational. The suspension of activities with Russia is expected to intensify the debate in Congress over restoring NASA's ability to launch astronauts from US soil.

In addition, the article discusses the potential impact of the suspension on global space partnership and Russia's space program. Ivan Moiseyev, Director of the Space Policy Institute, warns that the suspension will have a "rather significant" impact on space exploration projects globally. However, he also notes that Russia will adjust its projects to the new reality and that the impact on its space program is unlikely to be catastrophic.

The article also mentions the ongoing diplomatic pressure on Russia following its re-unification with the Russian-majority Crimea peninsula, which was taken over by Ukraine after the Soviet fall. Measures include sanctions against Russian and Crimean officials and businesses, who had their foreign assets seized. In a recent development, NATO member states suspended cooperation with Moscow allegedly until Russia changes its stand on the Ukrainian crisis, prompting the Russian Foreign Office to accuse the allies of trying to manhandle the country into accepting their viewpoint.

On October 22, 2015, a knife-wielding masked man attacked a school in Trollhattan, Sweden, killing a teacher and a student before being shot dead by police. The attack took place in the morning at the Kronan primary and middle school, which has around 400 students ranging from pre-school to high school.

The attacker, a 21-year-old resident of Trollhattan, knocked on the doors to two classrooms and stabbed those who opened them. One male teacher, aged 20, died following the incident, along with a pupil, whose age was confirmed by police in the evening as 17. Two male students aged 11 and 15, and another male teacher were also seriously wounded.

Police arrived at the scene and fired two shots, one of which hit the attacker. The attacker died later at the hospital, and the second victim was a student, but the police did not disclose which one. The three wounded were taken to the hospital, where they underwent surgery. One student and the attacker died later at the hospital.

The attacker had "sharp stabbing weapons," which another police official told the AP may have included a sword. Police searched the attacker's home and found "interesting" things, without elaborating.

Swedish Prime Minister Stefan Lofven described the day as a "black day" and said his thoughts were with the victims and their families, the students and staff, and the whole community affected by the attack. King Carl XVI Gustaf said Sweden was "in shock" following the attack.

Some pupils have described how they initially thought the man's appearance was a prank. Eyewitnesses described chaos at the school, with hundreds of students fleeing from the building screaming.

Police are investigating possible links to right-wing groups, but have not released any details. Local media have reported that the suspect's accounts on Facebook and YouTube suggest an interest in Hitler and Nazi Germany.

The school held a meeting on Thursday morning to discuss teachers' fears that they could not control access to the school. The Dagens Nyheter newspaper said students must go through a public cafe to reach the school's cafeteria and other parts of the building.

The attack is rare in Sweden, where school attacks are uncommon. The last recorded school shooting in Sweden occurred 20 years ago, in which one pupil was shot dead.

A former Marine, Itzcoatl Ocampo, who was awaiting trial for the murders of six people, including four homeless men, died in his jail cell on Thursday. Ocampo, 25, was found ill in his single-man cell at Central Jail in Santa Ana on Wednesday and was later pronounced dead at a hospital. The Orange County district attorney's office is investigating the death, and an autopsy will be performed in the coming days.

Ocampo was accused of a "serial thrill-kill" rampage in Orange County, California, in late 2011 and early 2012. Prosecutors alleged that he stabbed four homeless men in a spree that targeted vulnerable victims and was motivated by his belief that the homeless were a blight on the community. He was charged with four counts of murder, with special allegations of multiple murders, lying in wait, and use of a deadly weapon.

Ocampo's defense attorney, Michael Molfetta, suggested that the jail deputies may not have been adequately supervising Ocampo, who had mental health issues. Molfetta stated that if spent just three minutes with Ocampo, it was clear that he had severe mental issues.

The victims' families are disappointed that Ocampo will not face trial, as the district attorney's office was seeking the death penalty against him. Ocampo's parents separated in 2010, and his father became homeless after losing his job. During the killing rampage, Ocampo visited his father on the streets and warned him about the dangers of being homeless.

Ocampo's family and friends were shocked by the accusations against him, as they described him as generous to the homeless and someone who frequently gave food and money to panhandlers. However, prosecutors said Ocampo selected homeless men and stalked them, setting a personal goal of 16 slayings. Ocampo told police after his arrest that he targeted the homeless because they were "available and vulnerable" and that he believed he was performing a public service by eliminating a blight on the community.

A federal judge in California has granted a three-month delay in the lawsuit brought by Stormy Daniels, a pornographic film star, against President Trump and his personal attorney, Michael Cohen. The delay is due to the ongoing criminal investigation into Cohen in New York, where he is being examined for his role in suppressing embarrassing stories about Trump during the 2016 campaign.

Cohen invoked his Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination in the Daniels lawsuit, citing the ongoing investigation. FBI agents raided Cohen's home, office, and hotel room earlier this month in search of documents related to the Daniels nondisclosure agreement.

Daniels, who claims to have had an affair with Trump over a decade ago, is seeking to void a deal she reached with Cohen days before the election, under which she was paid $130,000 in exchange for her silence. Cohen has admitted to facilitating the payment using his own money from a home-equity line of credit.

Trump, who previously denied any knowledge of the payment arranged by Cohen, acknowledged Cohen's involvement in the deal for the first time in a recent interview. The Daniels' suit, filed last month, named the president and Essential Consultants, a limited liability company Cohen created as a vehicle for the payment, as defendants. Daniels later added Cohen as a defendant.

It is not uncommon for defendants facing both civil liability and criminal prosecution to request a pause in civil proceedings to avoid giving sworn testimony and producing documents that could prove incriminating. The delay in the Daniels' lawsuit allows Cohen to avoid incriminating himself in the criminal investigation.

In New York, Judge Kimba Wood refused to let Trump's attorneys review Cohen's seized documents to see if they should be returned because they are secret under attorney-client privilege. Wood appointed a "special master" to review which of the material will be available to prosecutors, and which will be withheld.

The delay in the Daniels' lawsuit has been met with disagreement by Daniels' attorney, Michael Avenatti, who plans to file an appeal early next week. Avenatti tweeted, "While we certainly respect Judge Otero’s 90-day stay order based on Mr. Cohen’s pleading of the 5th, we do not agree with it. We will likely be filing an immediate appeal to the Ninth Circuit early next week. Justice delayed is justice denied. # basta."

Cohen's attorney, Brent Blakely, did not respond to a message seeking comment. The delay in the Daniels' lawsuit marks a significant development in the ongoing legal saga surrounding Trump, Cohen, and the nondisclosure agreement with Daniels.

Google, now operating under its new parent company Alphabet, has encountered an issue with German automaker BMW over the use of the name Alphabet. BMW owns a fleet services company with the same name and the domain Alphabet.com, which Google has not been able to acquire. BMW has stated that it is not planning on selling its domain, and Alphabet has not yet taken any legal action.

The restructuring of Google into Alphabet was announced in August, with the new company launching abc.xyz as its domain name. Alphabet, led by Google founders Larry Page and Sergey Brin, is now the parent company of Google, with the aim of separating the core products (search, Gmail, Android, etc.) from its more far-reaching projects (Fiber, Calico, X, self-driving cars).

The move to Alphabet has caused some confusion, as more than 100 companies have trademark registrations in the U.S. that incorporate the word alphabet in some capacity. For example, Alphabet, Inc. is an Ohio company that manufactures electrical components for the auto industry. The @Alphabet Twitter handle is also already owned by a man named Chris Andrikanich.

In the days leading up to Google's announcement, Y Combinator founder Paul Graham wrote a blog post stating that it is an absolute must for companies to own the .com domain for their names, as not owning the .com domain "signals weakness." However, Google founder Page said Alphabet wouldn't be introducing products under its own name, so it wouldn't be a public-facing name like Google.

It is an interesting turn of events for Google, as the company has encountered the same problem many face when trying to purchase a domain for their own website. Despite the issues with domain names, Alphabet is excited about the new chapter in the life of Google and the opportunities it presents for the company.

The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has revealed that most dark chocolate bars contain milk, even those labeled as dairy-free, vegan, or lactose-free. This can pose a risk for individuals with severe milk allergies, as even a small amount of milk can trigger a dangerous reaction.

In a study, the FDA found milk in 61% of the 100 dark chocolate bars tested, with only six bars listing milk as an ingredient. The remaining 88 bars did not list milk as an ingredient, but 51 of them contained milk. This is because milk can inadvertently wind up in dark chocolate due to shared equipment used in the production of milk chocolate.

The FDA suggests that consumers read "may" as "likely" when it comes to advisory statements on dark chocolate products. Three out of every four dark chocolate products with an advisory statement for milk were found to contain milk proteins. Confusingly, some products may have both dairy-free or vegan statements and advisory statements for milk.

The chocolate industry is working to understand the needs of allergic consumers and communicate potential milk allergens in dark chocolate through advisory labeling. The FDA is also considering options for addressing the issues identified in the study, and the Preventive Controls for Human Food rule, scheduled to become final this fall, will require food manufacturers to implement a food safety plan that identifies safeguards to prevent or significantly reduce hazards, including food allergens.

Consumers who are sensitive or allergic to milk should check the ingredients list and avoid dark chocolate products with an advisory statement for milk, even if they also have dairy-free or vegan statements. They should view products with dairy-free claims or without any mention of milk with caution, unless the manufacturer is a trusted source and/or uses dedicated equipment for making milk-free chocolate products.

President Donald Trump played a full round of golf on Sunday, a habit he previously criticized in former President Barack Obama. The White House initially stated that Trump had only played a few holes, but later admitted that he played 18 holes after professional golfer Rory McIlroy posted about it on his website. This weekend marks Trump's third straight visit to his Mar-a-Lago resort in Florida, which he has nicknamed the "Winter White House."

Trump has been playing golf more frequently than his predecessors, having waited just two weeks to play his first round. He recently golfed with Japanese Prime Minister Shinzo Abe and is expected to engage in more golf diplomacy.

On Sunday, Trump played golf with McIlroy, Clear Sports CEO Garry Singer, former Yankees right fielder Paul O'Neill, and Trump friend Rich Levine. McIlroy revealed that Trump scored around 80. McIlroy had been delaying his return to golf due to a rib injury, but could not turn down Trump's invitation.

McIlroy's decision to play golf with Trump sparked a social media backlash, with many criticizing him for associating with a divisive figure like Trump. However, some, including golf columnist Lawrence Donegan and Piers Morgan, defended McIlroy, arguing that it was unfair to judge him for playing golf with the President.

Trump has also played golf with Tiger Woods, "The Big Easy" Ernie Els, and LPGA tour star Lexi Thompson. Trump's golfing has become a part of his diplomatic efforts, with golf diplomacy expected to continue.

In a private meeting last week, President Trump proposed to House Speaker Paul Ryan that the U.S. military could fund the construction of the border wall with Mexico, as he was disappointed with the $1.6 billion allocated in the recent $1.3 trillion spending bill. Trump has suggested that the Pentagon could fund the wall due to a perceived national security risk, but this idea is unlikely to be realized due to the need for congressional approval and potential opposition from military officials and Democrats.

The border wall was a key campaign promise for Trump, who repeatedly stated that Mexico would pay for it. However, Mexico has refused to contribute, and the administration has been unable to secure the $25 billion in long-term funding for the wall in recent negotiations with Democrats. The urgency to strike a deal reflects the growing belief that the spending bill represents the last chance for the Trump administration to secure substantial wall funding during his first term, as top Republicans anticipate that Democrats will gain House seats in the upcoming midterm elections.

The spending bill only earmarks $641 million for new primary fencing in areas with no barriers, and most of the money can only be spent on designs that were deployed as of last May. This means that the prototype designs the Trump administration is exploring cannot be built, except along a stretch of the border near San Diego where a barrier is already in place.

The idea of using military funds for the border wall is Trump's latest attempt to find a way to build the wall, as he continues to face criticism for his handling of the issue. The move would likely face steep hurdles with appropriators in Congress, and it is unclear how serious Trump is about pursuing this option.

The University of Virginia student, Hannah Graham, has been missing since September 13, and the police are urging property owners in Charlottesville and Albemarle County to look for any signs of her. The police chief, Timothy J. Longo, stated during a news conference that searchers have combed through most of Charlottesville and are now moving south into surrounding farms and woodland. He also urged real estate agents and others to look in and around vacant homes and buildings.

Longo said that Hannah Graham had an iPhone 5S with a pink case that has not been found, and he asked people to report anything unusual on their properties, including unexpected tire tracks, clothing, or other evidence that might help the police find her. Longo said that they have no idea where she is, and he expressed hope that they will find her soon.

The police are also asking for help in identifying spots that Jesse L. “LJ” Matthew Jr., the man charged with abducting Graham, frequents. The police asked for help finding places where Matthew likes to fish, for example. A reward of $100,000 is being offered for information leading to the safe return of the 18-year-old U-Va. sophomore from Fairfax County.

Jesse L. Matthew Jr. was arrested in Galveston, Texas, on Wednesday afternoon and appeared in court on Thursday. The police will not approach Matthew about the case because he has invoked his right to consult with an attorney. Local authorities said they would try to speak with him late Thursday or early Friday, and they were searching his car for evidence.

Matthew is the last person known to have seen Graham, and he has been charged with abduction with intent to sexually assault her. The police have not detailed what evidence they have against him. Matthew was taken into custody without incident.

The owner of the restaurant where Graham was last seen said that Graham never entered the establishment with her alleged abductor, instead waiting outside for him while he purchased drinks. The account differs from what the police have said about Graham's interactions with Matthew at Tempo. Longo said that his investigators “have at least one witness statement that puts Hannah Graham inside the bar with Mr. Matthew. You’re always evaluating witness statements in an ongoing investigation, and we will be talking to folks again, but we have that statement.”

An extensive search has turned up almost no trace of Graham after she was seen at Tempo. The police have collected evidence from Matthew's car and apartment, and Longo said that prosecutors decided to press charges against Matthew after reviewing evidence from experts at the crime lab in Richmond. The charge against Matthew suggests that the police believe Matthew took Graham against her will or while she was in a state that left her unable to consent.

Those close to Matthew, who is 6-foot-2 and weighs 270 pounds, have said they know him as a “gentle giant” who prayed at a local church, worked at the U-Va. hospital caring for patients, and volunteered at the private Covenant School as a football coach.

The article discusses Chelsea Clinton's role as Vice Chair of the Clinton Foundation, a philanthropic organization founded by her father, former President Bill Clinton. The foundation has faced criticism for past bureaucratic ineptitude and conflicts of interest, but Chelsea is working to modernize it using data to track results, get younger people involved, and help raise a $250 million endowment. She is also helping promote her mother's projects, such as a partnership to save the African elephant and a data-driven initiative analyzing rights for women globally. Chelsea is also tackling big causes such as delivering affordable treatments against diarrhea, getting more people involved in public service, and pushing for equal LGBT rights globally. The article also discusses Chelsea's personal life, including her marriage to Marc Mezvinsky and her efforts to find a balance between her public and private life. The article concludes by discussing Chelsea's plans for the future, including finishing her PhD dissertation, doing more softball interviews for NBC, finding the best coffee shop in every city, tweeting more or less daily, and potentially running for Congress someday. The article also mentions the foundation's complicated nature, with eight CEOs and a confusing structure of divisions and initiatives. The foundation is also described as a unique construction designed to generate real good, with Bill Clinton's ability to bring together corporations, NGOs, not-for-profits, and governments to partner and commit to solving specific global problems. The article also mentions the impact of Chelsea's celebrity and political heritage on her role within the foundation, and the challenges of working within a Clinton enterprise without being solely defined by her parents. The article also mentions the potential for Chelsea to play a larger role in her mother's political campaigns in the future.

A Los Angeles entertainment executive, identified as Jane Doe, filed a lawsuit against Match.com on Wednesday, seeking to compel the popular dating site to screen its members for sexual predators. The lawsuit was filed after Jane Doe alleges she was sexually assaulted by a man she met on the platform last year. Mark L. Webb, the attorney representing Jane Doe, plans to request a temporary injunction to halt Match.com from signing up new members until the site implements safety measures.

Webb described his client as an Ivy League graduate working in film and television. The incident occurred at Urth Cafe in West Hollywood, where the alleged assailant seemed charming, and Jane Doe agreed to see him again. However, after the second date, he is said to have followed her home and forced himself upon her.

The woman learned that the man had been previously convicted of several counts of sexual battery after the incident. Charges are pending in the Match.com case, according to Webb. The attorney stated that his client wants Match.com to check members' names against public sex offender registries, arguing that it's better than no safety measures at all.

In addition to the lawsuit, other news items include the arrest of a man in connection with his wife's death, which occurred 30 years ago, and the lifting of the admissions suspension for UCLA's Islamic studies program.

The 24-day Israeli military operation in the Gaza Strip, known as Operation Protective Edge, continues with a focus on destroying Hamas' tunnel network. An Israeli delegation traveled to Cairo for ceasefire talks. Three Israeli soldiers were killed and 12 wounded in the Khan Yunis area of south Gaza, bringing the death toll in the military to 56. Three Israeli civilians have been killed in the current conflict. The death toll in the Gaza Strip has reached 1,442 according to Palestinian health officials, with over 8,295 wounded. Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas has declared Gaza a "humanitarian disaster area" and accused Israel of committing war crimes. A 72-hour ceasefire has been agreed upon by Israel and Hamas, starting on Friday, August 1st. The ceasefire will begin at 8 a.m. local time and will be followed by negotiations with the Egyptian government to reach a durable ceasefire.

The article discusses two separate incidents of grizzly bear attacks in Yellowstone National Park. In the first incident, a grizzly bear mauled and killed a hiker named Brian Matayoshi on July 7. The park officials initially chose not to euthanize the bear as it was reacting naturally to protect its cubs. In a subsequent incident, a hiker named John Wallace was killed by a bear in August, and DNA evidence linked the bear to the scene of both deaths. The bear, a female, was euthanized to protect park visitors and staff.

The investigation into the second incident remains open, and it is unclear if the same bear was responsible for both deaths. The bear's two cubs were captured and relocated to the Grizzly and Wolf Discovery Center in West Yellowstone.

The article also mentions that there were no witnesses to Wallace's killing, and he was hiking alone in a backcountry area frequented by bears. The bear was found at the scene through DNA analysis of hair and scat samples.

The article also notes that there have been increasing conflicts between humans and grizzlies in the Yellowstone area, with 295 conflicts recorded last year. The majority of these conflicts involved bears killing livestock or damaging property to get food.

The article concludes by stating that an estimated 600 grizzlies live in the greater Yellowstone area, which includes parts of Wyoming, Montana, and Idaho. The Center for Grizzly Studies and the Wolf Discovery Center in West Yellowstone aim to educate the public about these animals and their importance to the environment. The author of the TripAdvisor review recommends visiting the Center as a great experience for all age groups.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has postponed a scheduled teaching session on the public health response to a nuclear blast, which was set to take place on Tuesday. The session, titled "Preparing for the Unthinkable," was part of the CDC's regular series of monthly webinars, Public Health Grand Rounds. The CDC's decision to change the topic came after a surge of media interest due to escalating tensions between President Trump and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.

The CDC initially announced the session with a photograph of a nuclear blast mushroom cloud, but on Friday, they changed the topic to influenza and removed the announcement about nuclear blast preparedness. The CDC stated that the change was due to the current high volume of flu cases across the country, which is causing strain on health systems.

The CDC's Tuesday session will now focus on guidance for health professionals on reducing the spread of the flu and addressing shortages of antiviral medicines in affected areas. The original session on nuclear attack preparedness will be rescheduled for a future Grand Rounds.

The CDC's Public Health Grand Rounds aim to provide the most up-to-date, scientifically accurate information to clinicians, researchers, and other public health professionals. The initial announcement for the nuclear blast preparedness session highlighted the devastating effects of a nuclear detonation and the crucial role of public health in responding.

Additionally, the CDC has reported that the flu is currently widespread across the country and is not expected to subside soon. The agency has also been involved in efforts to combat the deadly monkeypox virus in Africa. President Trump has also been involved in a war of words with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un over the size of their respective nuclear arsenals.

The tax reform bill passed by the U.S. House and Senate, if enacted, would significantly reduce or eliminate the federal estate tax, a move that would be a victory for Iowa's Republican congressional delegation who have long opposed the tax. However, evidence shows that family farmers and small business owners represent a tiny share of estate tax payers, and the taxes they owe rarely force them to sell land or quit farming.

The estate tax is a 40% tax on wealth assessed when a person dies, and currently is applied to assets above $5.5 million for individuals and $11 million for couples. The House and Senate bills double those exemptions to $11 million and $22 million, and the House version abolishes the tax completely in 2024.

U.S. Sen. Chuck Grassley, a member of the tax-writing Finance Committee in the Senate, has long presented the estate tax as a potentially ruinous burden on farmers and small business owners. Despite this evidence, Grassley has argued that the estate tax creates financial hardship for family businesses to survive and thrive. He also argued that it forces family members to liquidate to pay the death tax. However, experts say that the taxes farmers and small business owners owe rarely force them to sell land or quit farming.

The changes to the estate tax in the tax reform bill would save billions for the richest Americans, with 72% of estate tax payments coming from the top 1% of U.S. taxpayers, and 42% coming from the top 0.1%. However, the number of farmers and small businesses affected by the estate tax is small, with only a few dozen potentially affected each year.

In conclusion, the tax reform bill would significantly reduce or eliminate the federal estate tax, a move that would be a victory for Iowa's Republican congressional delegation who have long opposed the tax. However, evidence shows that family farmers and small business owners represent a tiny share of estate tax payers, and the taxes they owe rarely force them to sell land or quit farming. The changes to the estate tax in the tax reform bill would save billions for the richest Americans, but the number of farmers and small businesses affected by the estate tax is small.

The Conservative Party has narrowed down its leadership contest to two candidates, Theresa May and Andrea Leadsom, following the elimination of Michael Gove. May received 199 votes, Leadsom 84, and Gove 46 in the second round of voting by MPs. The final decision will be made by the Conservative Party's 150,000 members, with the result due on 9 September. Both candidates are women, marking the first time since Margaret Thatcher's resignation in 1990 that a female will become the UK's prime minister.

The winning candidate will replace David Cameron, who resigned after the UK voted to leave the EU in the referendum. The contest's electorate represents a "very distinctive slice of Britain," according to polling expert Professor John Curtice, being mostly over 50, disproportionately male, and "overwhelmingly middle class." The spending limit for the contest is £135,000, and hustings will be organized across the UK. Voting will close at noon on 9 September, with votes counted electronically.

A particularly dangerous superbug, known as the "phantom menace," is on the rise in the United States, according to a report by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). This superbug belongs to the family of bacteria known as CRE, which are difficult to treat due to their resistance to most antibiotics. They are often deadly, with some instances killing up to 50% of patients who become infected. The new type of CRE, which is the focus of the report, carries a plasmid, a mobile piece of DNA, with an enzyme that breaks down antibiotics. This makes them even more dangerous as they can transfer this antibiotic resistance to normal bacteria present in our bodies.

Bacteria develop antibiotic resistance in two ways. Some can evolve their own genome in ways that deactivate antibiotics, although this ability can't be shared with pathogens outside their own family. Others rely on a shortcut: they get infected with a plasmid carrying the resistance gene. This makes them more dangerous because plasmids can make copies of themselves and transfer within a family of bugs and as well as jump to other families of bacteria, which can then "catch" the resistance directly without having to develop it through evolution.

In a related development, a dangerous new superbug gene discovered in China two weeks ago has been found in bacteria infecting one person in Denmark. This gene makes the bacteria resistant to colistin, the antibiotic of last resort. Similar to the 'phantom menace' type of CRE, the gene is contained in a plasmid.

Experts have warned that the latest development is frightening. "History shows that these mobile resistance genes can spread around the world quickly, silently riding in people, animals and food," said Lance Price, director of the Antibiotic Resistance Action Center at George Washington University's Milken Institute of Public Health, in a statement. He said the news that the superbug gene first found in China has now turned up in Denmark "suggests that this scenario is playing out in real time."

CDC received reports counting at least 43 patients in 19 states with this type of CRE superbug between June 2010 and August 2015. Most U.S. clinical laboratories that test for CRE organisms wouldn't identify this particular type of bacteria because it's not part of standard testing. CDC changed its definition of the organism in January to help increase detection.

The report highlights the urgent need to combat antibiotic resistance and the importance of improved detection methods for these dangerous bacteria. The CDC continues to monitor the emergence of carbapenemases and is working to limit their spread. The agency recommends identifying patients carrying carbapenemase-producing CRE and instituting transmission-based precautions and enhanced environmental cleaning to prevent transmission.

Royalty Exchange, a company specializing in music royalty auctions, has signed a letter of intent to purchase at least 15% of an income stream from Eminem's music. The deal is part of a larger plan to acquire other musical assets and take the company public. The new company, Royalty Flow, aims to raise between $11 million and $50 million via a Regulation A+ crowdfunding effort and potentially list on NASDAQ.

The initial deal involves brothers Jeff and Mark Bass, who invested in Eminem's catalog early in his career. They have agreed to sell up to 25% of their interest to Royalty Flow, with the possibility of receiving $18.8 million if they sell the full 25%. The earnings from the brothers' Eminem holdings grew 43% to $5.07 million last year.

However, Eminem himself is not involved in the deal, as confirmed by his representative. The rapper's label, Interscope, also issued a statement stating that he was not consulted about the sale of his royalties.

The deal allows fans and smaller investors to invest directly in Eminem's business, potentially setting a new model for future endeavors. Joel Martin, a business partner of the Bass brothers, said, "If you’re a fan and wanna bet on that artist, you’ve got some skin in the game. It takes the average investor and puts them in a position they wouldn’t be in before."

Royalty Flow plans to acquire and hold royalties from music catalogs of the world's biggest music artists, with the intention of paying dividends to investors once listed on NASDAQ. The minimum investment for the initial offering is $2,250 for 150 shares, which works out to $15 a share.

The Regulation A+ filing to allow for crowdsourced funding was created by the JumpStart Our Business Start-up (JOBS) Act, signed into law by then-President Barack Obama in 2012. While Royalty Flow will use a broker dealer for compliance, the offering will not have an underwriting investment bank.

Beyond the Eminem investments, Royalty Flow will consider investments in publishing catalogs but expects to remain a passive investor, without control of the assets. The company aims to acquire and hold royalties from music catalogs of the world's biggest music artists, potentially creating a new business model for other superstar artists.

Royalty Flow will be run separately from Royalty Exchange, as they are two different business models. Royalty Exchange is an auction platform that allows investors to bid and buy an asset with one winning bid in the end, while Royalty Flow allows for multiple investors to own a piece of the assets. Since its inception, Royalty Exchange’s auctions have sold songwriter royalties for music recorded by various artists, including Rick Ross, Kevin Gates, Dr. Dre, George Clinton, Britney Spears, Kacey Musgraves, and the Bee Gees.

The deal comes at a time when streaming revenues are expected to boom over the next few years, potentially making investments in music assets substantial. Royalty Exchange has already sold shares of Wiz Khalifa's "See You Again," Chris Brown's "Drunk Texting," and the Ariana Grande-Lil Wayne track "Let Me Love You" as part of investment packages, some for as much as $71,000. The portion of "See You Again" generated $11,372 before it went on sale through Royalty Exchange, and Eminem has far more revenue potential.

Some music industry experts argue that tearing apart an artist's catalog and selling it piecemeal, without involving the artist, is disrespectful. However, Joel Martin, FBT's manager, argues that it's just another way for publishers and record labels to profit off artists' work. The Eminem catalog auction is expected to take place in October as part of Royalty Flow.

The eldest son of the late Cuban revolutionary leader Fidel Castro, Fidel Castro Diaz-Balart, also known as "Fidelito" or Little Fidel, committed suicide on Thursday at the age of 68 after being treated for months for depression, according to Cuban state-run media. Born in 1949, Fidelito was the product of his father's brief marriage to Mirta Diaz-Balart, the daughter of a prominent pre-revolution politician. His parents divorced, and he spent some of his early years in the US before his father brought him back to Cuba.

Fidelito was a nuclear physicist, trained by the former Soviet Union, and served as head of Cuba's national nuclear program from 1980 to 1992. He was also a scientific advisor for the Cuban Council of State and vice president of Cuba's Academy of Sciences at the time of his death. Fidelito's ideas for developing renewable energy on the island were not incorporated into state policy, an academic colleague, Jonathan Benjamin-Alvarado, told Reuters.

Fidelito's death came just over a year after that of his father, Fidel Castro, who died aged 90 in 2016. His funeral will be planned by his family, but no further details have been given. Fidelito's personal life was generally kept away from the public eye, and his mental health issues were not widely known before his death. His parents' divorce and his history of living in his father's shadow may have contributed to his depression. Fidelito's death has shocked ordinary Cubans, but the unexpected circumstances of his death have come as a surprise.

In a rare interview, Jerry Sandusky, the former Penn State assistant football coach, discussed his work with children and the sexual abuse charges against him. He described his relationships with children as "precious times" and said the physical aspect of the relationships "just happened that way."

Sandusky confirmed some details of the events that prosecutors have cited in charging him with 40 counts of molesting young boys. The study published in The BMJ suggests that women who consume more potatoes before pregnancy may have a higher risk of developing gestational diabetes during pregnancy. The researchers tracked over 21,000 pregnancies and found that women who typically ate two to four servings of potatoes a week had a 27% increased risk of gestational diabetes, while those who ate more than five portions had a 50% increased risk. The study also found that substituting potatoes with other vegetables, legumes, or whole grains at least twice a week could lower the risk of gestational diabetes by 9-12%. The study highlights the importance of moderation in potato consumption and emphasizes the benefits of a diet rich in vegetables and whole grains. However, UK experts stressed that more research is needed to confirm the findings and that women should not avoid eating potatoes altogether. The study was conducted by researchers from the National Institutes of Health's Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute of Child Health and Human Development and Harvard University.

The "Gospel of Jesus's Wife," a papyrus fragment discovered in 2012 and claimed to contain a reference to Jesus being married, is increasingly being questioned for its authenticity. The papyrus was purchased in 1999 and allegedly obtained in 1963 by Hans-Ulrich Laukamp, a co-owner of ACMB-American Corporation for Milling and Boreworks. However, recent investigations have cast doubt on Laukamp's ownership and the papyrus' origins, as representatives of Laukamp's estate and co-owners have denied his ownership, and antiquities officials in Berlin have no record of its exportation.

Additionally, a second papyrus, which includes text from the Gospel of John and has similar handwriting and ink to the "Gospel of Jesus's Wife," has been found to be a fake, with identical line breaks to a 1924 papyrus. Christian Askeland, a research associate, argues that the similarities suggest that the "Gospel of Jesus's Wife" is also likely a forgery.

Egyptologists who have examined the "Gospel of Jesus's Wife" firsthand have expressed a need for more time to analyze the new findings before commenting. Biblical scholars have also expressed skepticism, with some arguing that the papyrus' unusual and suspicious features suggest it is a forgery.

Harvard University, which announced the discovery, has remained silent on the new developments, not responding to requests for comment. The reasons for Harvard's silence are unclear, with unconfirmed reports of divisions within the Harvard Divinity faculty over the authenticity of the papyrus.

The Smithsonian Channel is still planning to premiere a documentary on the "Gospel of Jesus's Wife" on Monday evening.

In a hearing with the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence, the director of the National Security Agency (NSA), Keith Alexander, stated that since the September 11 attacks, more than 50 potential terrorist events have been thwarted with the help of NSA surveillance programs. Four of these incidents were detailed at the hearing, including thwarted plots to bomb the New York subway system and the New York Stock Exchange by linking known suspects in Pakistan and Yemen to contacts in the United States. The NSA also disclosed that counterterrorism officials targeted fewer than 300 phone numbers or other "identifiers" last year in the massive call-tracking database secretly assembled by the U.S. government.

Alexander said the programs were subject to "extraordinary oversight" and that 90% of the potential terrorist incidents were disrupted by the Web traffic program known as PRISM. He was less clear about how many incidents the call-tracking effort had helped to avert. Deputy FBI Director Sean Joyce said the Web traffic program had contributed to arrests averting a plot to bomb the New York Stock Exchange that resulted in criminal charges in 2008. Joyce also indicated that the PRISM program was essential to disrupting a plot to bomb the New York City subways in 2009.

At the hearing, Alexander detailed the scope and safeguards of the programs, while Deputy Attorney General James Cole laid out the legal basis for the surveillance. Cole said that because of the leaks, the government runs the risk of losing its capability to operate the collection programs. He did not say why but said they won't know for several months how the leaks affected the agency's surveillance abilities.

There is a debate within the intelligence community about what can be revealed to prove these programs work versus what should stay classified for fear of burning sources and methods. The NSA is set to disclose information about the other cases in a private session with lawmakers on Wednesday.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) reported that the number of pregnant women in the United States and its territories with Zika virus infections has tripled, reaching 279. The CDC is also reporting pregnant women who have tested positive for the virus, even if they don't show symptoms, to provide a more comprehensive understanding of the virus's impact. United Parcel Service (UPS) reported a decline in fourth-quarter profit due to increased costs during the holiday season. The company, the world's largest package delivery company, had anticipated a surge in holiday packages but failed to materialize. As a result, UPS will implement surcharges for residential packages over several years as contracts with major customers are renegotiated. UPS CEO David Abney stated that these pricing strategies are designed to ensure the company is properly compensated for the value it provides.

In 2014, UPS averaged more than 30 million deliveries a day during the holiday season, about six million more a day than in 2012 and 75% more than its average. However, the company's domestic ground package unit experienced a more than 60% drop in operating profit due to the increased costs.

UPS spent $500 million last year on network improvements and worked closely with retail customers to prevent a repeat of the miscues in late 2013. However, the rising popularity of e-commerce made forecasting volumes a moving target.

For the full-year 2015, UPS forecast earnings in a range of $5.05 to $5.30 per share, lower than analysts' estimates of $5.15 a share this year. UPS reported fourth-quarter net profit of $1.15 billion, down nearly 2% from $1.17 billion a year earlier. Earnings per share came in at $1.25, unchanged from a year earlier and matching the expectations of analysts.

Quarterly revenue rose 6% to $15.9 billion from $15 billion a year earlier, including a 7.5% increase in revenue from its domestic ground package business. Operating expenses jumped more than 20% to $9.2 billion from $7.65 billion, primarily affecting the domestic ground package unit.

UPS shares were up 1.2% in early trading following the earnings report. The company plans to offset the added expenses of keeping up with increased holiday loads by implementing surcharges for residential deliveries.

A Utah State Prison inmate, Ramon Estrada, died on Sunday due to an apparent heart attack related to renal failure. The cause of death is under investigation by the Utah State Medical Examiner's office. Estrada was scheduled for kidney dialysis on Friday, but a technician from South Valley Dialysis Center, the contracted treatment provider, did not show up on both Friday and Saturday. As a result, Estrada missed his dialysis treatments for two days.

Six other inmates who also missed their treatments were taken to University Hospital for evaluation. Four were treated and returned to prison, while one remains hospitalized. The corrections department's clinical services director has been placed on leave while an internal investigation is underway to review the response of prison staff, the contract provider, and communication procedures to prevent a similar incident from happening again.

The University of Utah Health Care, which operates the dialysis center, has expressed concern about the scheduling error and plans to conduct a thorough review of the circumstances that led to Estrada's death. The corrections department is taking immediate steps to ensure that prison staff have contact numbers for technicians and that they receive post-treatment reports and make better chart notes about the inmates' condition.

Estrada was set to be paroled in less than three weeks and had been in prison since August 2005 on a rape conviction. The master sommelier examination, often referred to as the hardest test you've never heard of, has been marred by a cheating scandal. As a result, 23 of the 24 newly anointed sommeliers, including four from the Bay Area, have had their titles revoked. The offending master sommelier has been barred from CMS events and is facing termination of membership. The CMS will offer the 23 candidates two chances to re-take the tasting portion of the exam, one later in 2018 and another in spring or summer 2019, and will refund all fees for these exams. The master sommelier exam is a grueling test that involves years of preparation and is the crowning achievement for wine service professionals. This year, 24 people passed the test, earning the right to add the coveted "MS" suffix to their names. The information breach pertains only to the tasting portion of this year's exam, which is a 25-minute blind tasting where candidates must identify each wine's grape variety, region of origin, and vintage. The CMS goes to great lengths to prevent opportunities for cheating, including sequestering candidates before and after the exam and never revealing the identities of the wines. The success of the "Somm" documentary series has added to the MS exam's aura, and credentials like those administered by the CMS are becoming increasingly popular among sommeliers who want to advance their careers. Passing the final test can mean a significant material difference in a somm's life, with an advanced sommelier in the U.S. earning an average salary of $87,000, while a master earns an average of $164,000. The news of the cheating scandal has sent shockwaves throughout the sommelier community, which tends to regard its examinations with an air of religiosity. The CMS claims that about 25 to 30 percent of test takers pass the Advanced exam, and only about 10 percent pass the theory portion of the Master exam. The cost to take each examination is $995.
