Title: Feeling Younger May Lower Mortality Risk, According to New Research

A recent study published in JAMA Internal Medicine suggests that feeling younger than one's actual age could have health benefits, including a lower death rate. The research, conducted by the University College London, found that older adults who felt 3 or more years younger than their actual age had a lower mortality rate compared to those who felt their age or older.

The study involved 6,489 participants from the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing, with an average chronological age of 65.8 years and an average self-perceived age of 56.8 years. Participants were divided into three groups: those whose self-perceived age was close to their actual age, those who felt more than 1 year older, and those who felt 3 or more years younger.

The researchers found that the mortality rate was 14.3% among adults who felt younger than their actual age, 18% among those with a self-perceived age close to their actual age, and 24.6% among those who felt older than their actual age. The association between self-perceived age and death caused by cardiovascular disease was strong, although not between self-perceived age and cancer death.

The authors suggest that greater resilience, sense of empowerment, and will to live, as well as specific health behaviors such as adhering to medical advice, could explain the lower mortality rates in people feeling younger than their actual age. They also propose that interventions may be possible to target individuals who feel older than their actual age with health messages promoting positive health behaviors and attitudes toward aging.

The study's findings have implications for healthcare professionals, as they suggest that self-perceived age has the potential to change and could be a useful indicator of health and mortality risk. The authors call for further research to validate these findings and investigate the mechanisms underlying the associations.

Recently, Medical News Today reported on a separate study suggesting that running for exercise could slow the aging process. Senior citizens who run several times a week expend the same amount of energy as a typical 20-year-old when walking. The study adds to the growing body of evidence suggesting that maintaining physical activity and a positive mindset can contribute to a longer, healthier life.

The cost of gifts mentioned in the traditional Christmas carol "The Twelve Days of Christmas" has increased by 6.1% this year, according to the annual Christmas Price Index (CPI) by PNC Wealth Management. The total cost for all 364 items listed throughout the song amounts to $107,300. The rise in prices is larger than expected considering the modest economic growth. Six items in the song haven't seen a price increase, including maids-a-milking, ladies dancing, lords-a-leaping, calling birds, turtle doves, and the partridge.

However, some items have seen significant price hikes. Seven swans a-swimming have increased by 11%, setting you back $7,000, while six geese a-laying have risen by 29.6%. Five gold rings have jumped 16.3% to $750, and three French hens are now $165. The price of a pear tree has risen by 11.8% to $189.99.

Last-minute shoppers will pay a bit more for the gifts online, with the cost of a set of core items in each verse costing $40,440 online compared to $24,431 in traditional stores. The difference is due to the extra expense of shipping live birds and a 1.5% increase in internet costs.

PNC Financial Services Group Inc. compiles the list by checking jewelry stores, dance companies, pet stores, and other sources. Some of its sources this year include the National Aviary in Pittsburgh and the Pennsylvania Ballet Company. The partridge remains the cheapest item at $15, while swans are the most expensive, costing $1,000 each.

He hopes by going public with the diagnosis, it will help dispel the stigma of HIV and inspire others to come forward. The global goal to provide HIV treatment to 15 million people by the end of 2015 has been met, according to a report released by UNAIDS this week. The report highlights enormous progress made in achieving one of the U.N.'s Millennium Development Goals, with nearly 37 million people around the world living with HIV. However, new infections in Eastern Europe, Central Asia, the Middle East, and North Africa have increased by 25 percent since 2000. The bigger goal now is making sure that 90 percent of those living with HIV are diagnosed and can begin receiving treatment, according to the U.N. The ultimate milestone: End the AIDS epidemic by 2030. However, progress will also have to address cultural and legal roadblocks, including the criminalization of sex work, drug use, and same-sex sexual relationships in some countries. Charlie Sheen could face legal problems in California for having unprotected sex while knowing he is infected with HIV, which is a crime punishable by up to 8 years in prison. No one has come forward yet complaining that Sheen exposed them to HIV.

The death of Max Spiers, a British conspiracy theorist and UFO researcher, has sparked online speculation among conspiracy theorists, with some suggesting he may have been murdered due to his investigations. Spiers, who was in good health according to his family, died in Warsaw, Poland, on July 16th, 2016, and was found dead on a sofa in a Warsaw apartment. Polish authorities attributed his death to natural causes, but no post-mortem examination was carried out at the time.

Spiers' mother, Vanessa Bates, believes that her son may have been targeted due to his investigations into UFOs, government cover-ups, and politicians, business people, and celebrities. She said that he had recently moved on to investigating these areas and that he had been "digging in some dark places." Bates also said that her son had suffered from migraines in the days before he died and was taking antibiotics when she last spoke to him on July 14th. He also complained on social media of being "way too tired" around this time and cancelled an interview because of his health.

The Foreign Commonwealth Office (FCO) said it was not investigating the death as it happened abroad. A spokesperson told The Independent that the FCO provided assistance to the family of a British national following his death, but explained that the UK had no jurisdiction to investigate the death of British nationals overseas. They said investigations into Spiers' death were the responsibility of the Polish government.

Despite the lack of official investigation, many of Spiers' online followers believe he may have been murdered because of his investigations. On one website, Project Camelot, a blogger wrote: "The entire circumstances are suspicious and I urge everyone to encourage the release of details about what really happened and call for an autopsy." Another, Craig Hewlett, added: "If it wasn't true what he talks about then why would they kill him? Healthy people don't just get sick and die, they get poisoned."

Spiers was buried in Canterbury cemetery after his mother arranged to have his body flown home a week after his death. Because Spiers' body was repatriated, a UK coroner's investigation could be initiated and a post-mortem examination was carried out by a pathologist in Kent. However, Bates said she still did not know the result more than two months later, or whether there would be an inquest. She said: "Apparently, he had not suffered any obvious physical injuries but he could have been slowly poisoned, which is why the results of toxicology tests from his post-mortem are so important."

Spiers was known for his beliefs in UFOs, extraterrestrials, and the New World Order. He claimed that Zionists and Nazis had the same agenda and that extraterrestrials were helping humanity. He also believed that information was being downloaded through sex to control people in high positions. Spiers' death has sparked a wave of speculation and conspiracy theories, with some believing that he was targeted for his investigations. However, the official investigation into his death is still ongoing.

The Iranian President, Hassan Rouhani, has responded to a letter from U.S. President Barack Obama, expressing a desire for face-to-face talks instead of the more bureaucratic negotiations with the group of five major world powers. This shift in strategy is a significant step towards a potential diplomatic breakthrough, as Iran seeks to restore its economy and improve relations with the world.

The correspondence between the two leaders has sparked hope, but the differing interpretations of the letter highlight the political hurdles and mistrust that both sides must overcome. While Obama's letter was seen as a pledge to resolve issues and move forward by the Iranians, the Americans viewed it as a general congratulatory message with no immediate relief from sanctions.

The overtures to the United States are part of a broader shift in Iran's strategy, which includes domestic liberalizations and a return of the military to the barracks. These changes, along with the changed diplomatic tone, have led some experts to believe that the changes are more than cosmetic.

Rouhani will present Iran's new face to the world next week with speeches at the United Nations General Assembly, the Council on Foreign Relations, and the Asia Society, as well as television interviews with Charlie Rose and CNN. In an opinion essay published in The Washington Post, Rouhani urged world leaders to seize the opportunity presented by Iran's recent election and respond genuinely to his government's efforts to engage in constructive dialogue.

Skeptics have pointed out that Obama has reached out to Iran before, but his previous attempts at dialogue were unsuccessful. However, this time, Obama's letter found a receptive audience, including Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, the supreme leader of Iran, for the first time.

Iran is hoping that the White House will lift some sanctions as a gesture to show its seriousness about the talks, particularly the ban on Iranian money transfers through the Swift system. The leadership is desperate to escape the financial sanctions imposed in recent years, as they can live without oil sales but not without the ability to transfer money.

The world must know that time is not unlimited for solving the nuclear problem, Rouhani said. The leadership is convinced that the next six months, before campaigning begins for parliamentary elections in March, represent the best opportunity to reach a nuclear agreement in over a decade.

At the White House, officials share the sense that this time may be different, as Rouhani is sending signals that he wants to end the sanctions and knows he does not have a lot of time to deliver. Dennis B. Ross, a former adviser to Obama on Iran, said Rouhani is committed to fulfilling his promises to his people, including his pledge to engage in constructive interaction with the world.

In Sicily, a team of divers recovered nearly 40 ingots from the sea floor, originating from a ship that sank 2,600 years ago. The ship, believed to have been en route to Gela from Greece or Asia Minor, may have been caught in a storm and sunk just before reaching the port. The ingots are made of an alloy called orichalcum, a brass-like material that was considered a mysterious and valuable metal in ancient times.

According to the ancient Greeks, orichalcum was invented by Cadmus, a Greek-Phoenician mythological character. The fourth century B.C. Greek philosopher Plato mentioned orichalcum in his Critias dialogue, describing it as a legendary metal used in Atlantis. Plato wrote that the metal, second only in value to gold, was mined in Atlantis and used to cover the interior walls, columns, and floors of Poseidon's temple.

Analyzed with X-ray fluorescence, the 39 ingots turned out to be an alloy made with 75-80 percent copper, 15-20 percent zinc, and small percentages of nickel, lead, and iron. The discovery confirms that Gela, founded in 689 B.C., grew to become a wealthy city with artisan workshops specialized in the production of prized artifacts. The ingots were indeed destined for these workshops and were used in high-quality decorations.

However, some scholars, such as Enrico Mattievich, a retired professor of physics, argue that the ingots are not properly made from orichalcum. Mattievich believes that orichalcum has its roots in the Peruvian Andes and in the Chavín civilization that developed there from 1200 B.C. to 200 B.C. Mattievich claims that ancient Greeks discovered America and that a metallic alloy similar to Plato's description was found in a set of metallic jaguars of Chavin style, which turned out to be made of 9 percent copper, 76 percent gold, and 15 percent silver.

Regardless of its origins, the shipwreck and its cargo are expected to provide valuable information on Sicily's most ancient economic history. The team plans to excavate the shipwreck to uncover the entire cargo.

The UPS cargo jet that crashed short of a runway at Birmingham's airport on August 14, 2013, received warnings about its rate of descent seconds before impact, according to investigators. The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) and FBI are investigating the crash, which occurred less than a mile from the end of Runway 18 at Birmingham's airport before dawn. The twin-engine Airbus A300 aircraft was being flown by Captain Cerea Beal, Jr., who had 8,600 hours of flight experience, including 3,200 hours in an A300.

Investigators have not determined the actual cause of the crash, but a recorder captured the first of two audible warnings in the cockpit 16 seconds before impact, indicating the A300 was descending at a rate outside normal parameters given its altitude. The plane was at the end of a 45-minute flight from Louisville, Ky., to Birmingham when it went down.

The shorter Runway 18, which lacks electronics for a full instrument landing, is located near rough terrain and has been a concern for some pilots. Veteran commercial pilot Ross Aimer, a retired United Airlines captain, said he had landed on Runway 18 about a half-dozen times, including on some flights as a cargo pilot. However, he noted that he would choose another runway if given the option.

The longer runway was closed for maintenance work on its lights early Wednesday, leaving the shorter runway as the only path to the ground. The NTSB previously said a preliminary investigation didn't reveal any evidence of engine failure before the plane struck trees about one mile away from the end of the runway.

The crash resulted in significant damage, with pieces of the aircraft and large pieces of limbs crashing onto two homes. Witnesses reported seeing the plane on fire before it hit the ground. The investigation into the cause of the crash is ongoing, with a key task being determining why the UPS jet was low enough to hit trees.

The transcript of a conversation between US President Donald Trump and Australian Prime Minister Malcolm Turnbull, obtained by the Washington Post, reveals Trump's lack of understanding and mental limitations. The conversation revolves around a deal to settle 1,250 refugees who have been detained by Australia in the United States.

Australia has a policy of refusing to accept refugees who arrive by boat due to concerns about smuggling and unsafe passage with a high risk of deaths at sea. The United States government agreed under President Obama to vet 1,250 of these refugees and accept as many as deemed safe.

In the conversation, Trump fails to understand the facts and reasons behind Australia's policy. He calls the refugees "prisoners" and repeatedly brings up the Cuban boatlift, a situation in which Castro dumped criminals onto Florida. Trump is unable to absorb Turnbull's explanation that the refugees are economic refugees, not from conflict zones, and that the United States has the ability to turn away any it deems dangerous.

Trump also fails to understand the number of refugees in the agreement, stating that it is 2,000 or even 5,000, when the given number is 1,250. He expresses his displeasure at having to accept the refugees, stating that it will make him look bad and harm his image among his supporters.

The conversation also reveals Trump's narcissistic tendencies, as he boasts about his crowd sizes and compares himself favorably to other world leaders, including Vladimir Putin. Trump also expresses his frustration with deals in general, stating that he is being "killed" on the refugee deal.

The leak of the conversation transcript may be a cry for help from within the administration, as it reveals Trump's incoherence and lack of understanding in private negotiations, potentially making high-level diplomacy and crisis resolution more difficult. The transcripts also confirm that the administration has deliberately misled the public about the conversations.

In the aftermath of a devastating 7.0 magnitude earthquake that struck Haiti on Tuesday, January 13, 2010, the capital city of Port-au-Prince was left in ruins. The disaster flattened government buildings such as the president's palace and the cathedral, as well as hospitals and other vital infrastructure.

In the chaos that followed, Haitians scrambled to save the injured using makeshift stretchers and ambulances. As international aid began to arrive, an Air China plane carrying a Chinese search-and-rescue team, medics, food, and medicine landed in Port-au-Prince, along with three French planes carrying aid and a mobile hospital. A British relief team arrived in neighboring Dominican Republic.

The United States and other nations pledged to send food, water, and medical supplies to assist Haiti, which is the Western Hemisphere's poorest nation. The International Red Cross estimated that 3 million people, or a third of the population, may need emergency relief.

In the streets of Port-au-Prince, survivors set up camps amid piles of salvaged goods, including food scavenged from the rubble. Doctors and medical teams worked tirelessly to treat the injured at makeshift clinics and hospitals that withstood the quake. Cuba, which already had hundreds of doctors in Haiti, treated injured in field hospitals.

President Barack Obama promised an all-out rescue and humanitarian effort, including the military and civilian emergency teams from across the U.S. The aircraft carrier USS Carl Vinson was expected to arrive off the coast on Thursday, and the Navy said the amphibious assault ship USS Bataan had been ordered to sail as soon as possible with a 2,000-member Marine unit.

Survivors used sledgehammers and their bare hands to try to find victims in the rubble. Bodies lay everywhere in Port-au-Prince, with no estimate on how many people were killed. Haitian President Rene Preval said the toll could be in the thousands, while leading Sen. Youri Latortue estimated the number could be 500,000, although nobody really knew.

Calls from victims seeking help from emergency services weren't getting through because systems that connect different phone networks were not working. About 3,000 police and international peacekeepers cleared debris, directed traffic, and maintained security in the capital, but law enforcement was stretched thin even before the quake and would be ill-equipped to deal with major unrest.

Looting began immediately after the quake, with people seen carrying food from collapsed buildings. Inmates were reported to have escaped from the damaged main prison in Port au Prince. It was unclear whether the U.S. ground troops heading to Haiti would be used for security operations as well as humanitarian efforts.

The disaster affected both the poor and the prominent, with the body of Archbishop Joseph Serge Miot found in the ruins of his office, and Haitian Senate President Kelly Bastien rescued from the collapsed Parliament building and taken to a hospital in the neighboring Dominican Republic.

The International Committee of the Red Cross launched a website to help Haitians find loved ones missing in the quake. As dusk fell on Wednesday, thousands of people gathered outside the crumpled presidential palace, including hundreds of women who waved their hands and sang hymns in a joyful, even defiant tone.

In a significant shift in the fast casual Mexican restaurant industry, Moe's Southwest Grill has dethroned Chipotle Mexican Grill as America's favorite chain, according to a recent Harris Poll. Chipotle, which had held the top spot for the past three years, did not even make it into the top four this year.

The decline for Chipotle comes amidst a series of food-borne illness outbreaks, including norovirus, salmonella, and e. coli incidents that sickened hundreds of customers. These incidents led to a 30% drop in sales and a 33% dip in the company's share price.

On the other hand, Moe's Southwest Grill, which has over 600 locations, secured the first place finish in the Harris Poll for the first time. The chain showed the largest increase in brand equity (13%) among all restaurants measured, demonstrating a significant movement in brand perception.

The poll results also revealed that Taco Bell finished second, Qdoba Mexican Grill came in third, and Baja Fresh Mexican Grill took fourth place, further indicating Chipotle's fall from grace.

The Harris Poll surveyed over 97,000 US consumers aged 15 and over. Moe's was praised for its responsiveness to customer feedback and needs. Bruce Schroder, Moe's president, had previously stated, "We really view the competition as share of stomach."

Moe's is part of Focus Brands Inc., which operates other chains such as Carvel, Cinnabon, and Auntie Anne's Pretzels. The company saw a 5% increase in foot traffic thanks in part to Chipotle's struggles, according to a Placed survey.

Despite Moe's success, Chipotle still has some loyalists, such as the Washington man who is working towards his goal of eating a meal from the chain 366 days in a row. However, the company is facing criticism for not doing enough to reassure customers about the safety of its food, despite adopting new food safety protocols.

The fast casual restaurant landscape has become more competitive, with chains offering healthier food and new menu options to attract customers. Qdoba rolled out a new taco menu last year, Taco Bell has gained prominence for its breakfast menu and started selling alcohol in some restaurants, and Moe's is known for a wide selection of ingredients for build-your-own tacos, quesadillas, and burrito bowls.

In conclusion, Moe's Southwest Grill has seized the opportunity presented by Chipotle's food safety issues to become America's favorite Mexican-inspired fast casual restaurant chain. However, Chipotle still has a larger market share and sales, and there is potential for Moe's to attract more customers and close the visitation gap with Chipotle.

The dispute over Kurt Cobain's iconic guitar, played during Nirvana's 1993 MTV Unplugged concert, is escalating into a costly court battle. Kurt Cobain's daughter, Frances Bean Cobain, is attempting to reclaim the guitar from her estranged husband, Isaiah Silva, who claims it was a wedding gift from Frances in 2014. The Martin D-18E guitar, once insured for $1 million, is now believed to be worth significantly more. Frances Bean denies gifting the guitar to Silva, and Courtney Love, Cobain's widow, has stated that it is a family heirloom.

Tensions have escalated, with reports of threatening messages sent by Love's manager to Silva's ex-girlfriend. Despite months of negotiation, Silva is reportedly holding out, leading to a potential court battle. In September, a judge ordered Frances Bean to pay Silva $15,000 a month in temporary spousal support.

In a separate development, Silva is seeking spousal support from Frances Bean, claiming he left a steady job when they married and that she had promised to cover his expenses. Silva is requesting $25,000 a month, stating that Frances has substantial funds from her father's estate. However, Frances has stated in her divorce documents that the Cobain estate money is hers alone and not Silva's.

Both parties have yet to comment publicly on the ongoing disputes.

Scarlett Johansson and Ryan Reynolds, known for their private nature, have shocked fans with their sudden split. Despite keeping their marriage private, they released a statement expressing their decision to end their relationship with love and kindness. The couple rarely spoke about their relationship in the press, with Reynolds admitting to being more guarded since their marriage. To avoid personal questions during the promotional tour for Reynolds' upcoming film, 'Green Lantern', insiders reveal that any press member asking such questions will be asked to leave. The couple's friends express their surprise at the split, noting that they will likely never discuss the details of their failed relationship.

A Delaware family of four, including the head of a private middle school and a dentist, has been hospitalized for several weeks after falling ill during a vacation at a resort in the U.S. Virgin Islands. The family, who became seriously ill on March 20, was staying at the Sirenusa Condominium Resort in Cruz Bay, St. John. Preliminary tests by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) have found the presence of the pesticide methyl bromide in the unit where the family stayed. Methyl bromide is a potent neurotoxin that is prohibited for residential use due to health concerns. The EPA is investigating the use of the pesticide at the resort and is contacting people, including resort employees, to determine how many others might have been exposed. The Justice Department is also investigating the company responsible for the application of the pesticide. The family's two teenage sons are in critical condition, while the father has regained consciousness and the mother has been treated and released. The EPA has confirmed that the problem is indeed methyl bromide and has said that the chemical can cause convulsions, coma, cognitive deficits, inflammation of the lungs, and other serious health effects. The EPA banned the chemical for residential use in 1984, and that ban extends to U.S. territories, including the Virgin Islands. The EPA is continuing to test and monitor the property and is investigating the details of the family's exposure to make sure it never happens again. The rental company that manages the property has terminated its contract with the pest control company responsible for the application of the pesticide. The family's attorney has said that many questions remain about how the pesticide was manufactured, distributed, and applied in a residential area, and that the family is confident that the responsible parties will be brought to justice and held accountable.

The 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals has upheld key parts of Texas's strict anti-abortion law, potentially leaving as few as seven abortion clinics in Texas. The decision upholds requirements that abortion clinics meet hospital-level operating standards, which small clinic owners say demand millions of dollars in upgrades they cannot afford.

The court's ruling upholds provisions that mandate hospital-like structural requirements for Texas abortion clinics, including specific room and doorway sizes, air sterilization systems, backup generators, and blood supplies on hand. Abortion providers argue these requirements are unnecessary and will not enhance the safety of the procedure.

Before the law passed in 2013, there were 40 abortion clinics in Texas. Now, there are 17, with only seven meeting the building standards upheld by the court. Each of the remaining clinics is located within the Austin, Houston, Dallas, Fort Worth, and San Antonio metropolitan areas.

The court made an exception for Whole Woman’s Health in McAllen, which will not be required to meet all building requirements or gain admitting privileges for one doctor. The court earlier upheld provisions requiring doctors at abortion clinics to obtain admitting privileges at nearby hospitals and regulations that mandate where and when a woman can take abortion-causing pills.

Abortion-rights supporters argue that the law is a thinly veiled attempt to block access to abortions in Texas and have promised to appeal to the U.S. Supreme Court, which temporarily sidelined the law last year. The ruling will allow Texas to start enforcing the restrictions in about three weeks unless the Supreme Court steps in and temporarily halts the decision.

The ruling is the 5th Circuit's latest decision in a lawsuit challenging some of the toughest abortion restrictions in the country. The New Orleans-based court, considered one of the most conservative in the nation, allowed Texas to enforce the restrictions when abortion providers first sued in 2013, but the U.S. Supreme Court put the law on hold last year and ordered the 5th Circuit to reconsider.

Under the new restrictions, the only remaining abortion facilities in Texas would be in major cities. One exception would be in McAllen, near the Texas-Mexico border, which the 5th Circuit exempted from some restrictions, but attorneys for the center argue that even those exemptions are so limited that it may not be practical to keep that McAllen clinic open.

For women in El Paso, the closest abortion provider in Texas would require a 1,200-mile round trip to San Antonio, or they would have to cross the border into New Mexico. The appeals court found that option suitable, noting that a clinic was just across the border in Santa Teresa, New Mexico. The court also said abortion clinics failed to show that most women would be unconstitutionally burdened by the law.

Attorneys for the state dismissed opponents' arguments about women being burdened by fewer abortion facilities, saying that nearly 9 in 10 women in Texas would still live within 150 miles of a provider. A new slate of conservative leaders in Texas has vowed to continue stifling abortion-rights efforts.

Russia has appointed actor Steven Seagal as a "special representative" for US-Russian humanitarian ties. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs announced this on its official Facebook page, stating that Seagal's role will be to promote US-Russia relations in the humanitarian sphere, including collaboration in the spheres of culture, public, and youth exchanges. Seagal, who became a Russian citizen in 2016, is a close friend of Russian President Vladimir Putin and has been an ardent supporter of Putin, defending his government against allegations of election meddling in the United States.

In a separate development, Tunisian Prime Minister Youssef Chahed met with Russian officials to discuss plans for increasing trade, economic, and scientific cooperation between the two countries. The Russian Federation proposed a program for trade, economic, and scientific cooperation between the two countries for the years 2019-2021, which the Tunisian Prime Minister agreed to expedite for approval at a forthcoming meeting. Both parties also agreed to accelerate the ratification of a previously signed agreement on nuclear energy cooperation and the signing of several other projects and documents related to visa facilitation, automobile transport, and environmental protection.

The Tunisian side also informed the Russians about their plans for infrastructure development, expressing interest in involving Russian companies, particularly those specializing in automobile and railway construction, in relevant tenders. The Russians expressed support for their economic operators to respond to such offers. The meeting acknowledged the development of cooperation between Tunisia and Russian regions, particularly between Tunisia and Tatarstan, with the President of Tatarstan visiting Tunisia last October for a business forum with Tunisian businessmen. Both parties agreed to encourage such contacts in the future. The overall discussion was concrete and helpful in understanding how to move forward in the development of their cooperation in all areas.

A 59-year-old man named James Zordel from Russell, Kansas, died after colliding with a black cow on a blacktopped road on Friday night. The accident occurred around 6.5 miles south of Interstate 70 near Russell, according to Kansas Highway Patrol crash logs. Zordel was driving a 1992 Suzuki motorcycle northbound on 189th street when the collision happened. The incident occurred in the dark, and there were no witnesses. It is unclear if the cow suddenly appeared from the side of the road or if Zordel was speeding. Tragically, Zordel was not wearing a helmet and died at the scene. The Kansas Highway Patrol is investigating the accident, but the exact cause may remain unknown due to the dark conditions.

Bill and Kris Bresnan, a couple from Toms River, New Jersey, have been married for nearly 40 years and have a unique love story. Every day since they met in 1974, Bill has written a love letter to Kris, totaling over 10,000 letters. The letters, which are filled with endless 'I love yous,' began as notes scribbled on napkins and small pieces of paper during their daily commuting routine.

The couple calls their collection of letters a 'love diary' and organizes them chronologically in 25 boxes at their home. Bill continues to write the letters to this day, signing them with an infinity sign and the phrase 'I love you, my darling.' The letters document their daily activities, such as restaurants they ate at or movies they saw, and serve as a reminder of their perfect match.

The couple has never had a major fight and never goes to bed angry, starting each morning with a clean slate. They are now screening the letters, deciding which are appropriate to be saved for their four children someday, and gently disposing of notes meant for their eyes only.

Bill's biggest fear is forgetting to give Kris a card, but he remains sharp and continues to write them daily. One of his favorites out of the 10,000-plus letters were a series of 50 cards, one for each of the 50 days before her 50th birthday.

The daily expressions of love are part of Bill's recipe for making a relationship last, among other things, such as never going to bed mad and talking about everything. The couple continues to keep the romance alive through little things they do together in their daily routine, such as playing 'Boggle' over breakfast and having candlelit dinners with wine.

Bill also goes big once in a while, such as reenacting the Katherine Hepburn movie 'Summertime' by taking Kirsten to Italy and doing everything in the movie together. He also gave her a friendship ring featuring hieroglyphics he saw during a trip to Egypt that were an expression of a pharaoh's eternal love for his son.

Despite the countless good times, the couple has weathered many storms together, such as when Bill was diagnosed with cancer a few years ago, and Kirsten was by his side. Bill hopes that their love story will inspire younger couples who seem to be more in love with their gadgets.

Though Bill has already sent his wife plenty of Valentine's Day cards before the date, they will still do something simple to celebrate, such as having a nice dinner, a special bottle of wine, and a piece of chocolate. They are past the craving for jewelry and expensive nonsense and simply enjoy being together.

Former Miss Delaware Amanda Longacre has filed a lawsuit against the Miss Delaware Scholarship Organization and the Miss America Organization, seeking to be reinstated as Miss Delaware and to compete in the Miss America pageant. The lawsuit, filed in Delaware's Court of Chancery, alleges that Longacre was disqualified for being too old, despite repeatedly submitting her birth certificate, driver's license, and resume to prove her eligibility. The lawsuit seeks $3 million in damages, including $2.5 million for other contestants who were recruited and then disqualified, and $500,000 for Longacre herself. The lawsuit also seeks the restoration of Longacre's titles as Miss Pike Creek and Miss Delaware, as well as a waiver to allow her to compete for Miss America in September. The Miss America Organization has stated that the lawsuit has no merit and they will defend it vigorously. The Miss Delaware Scholarship Organization has not yet commented on the lawsuit. Longacre was initially disqualified two weeks into her reign in June, and was replaced by first runner-up Brittany Lewis. Longacre claims that she lost potential career enhancements and had to spend over $4,500 on expenses such as a voice coach, clothing, hair and makeup as a result of her disqualification. The lawsuit also seeks to require the pageants to make age requirements clear on their websites and to all potential contestants.

The Arcade Fire's interactive music project, "The Wilderness Downtown," offers a unique and personalized experience for viewers. By entering a childhood address, users can create a customized music video for the song "We Used to Wait." The video incorporates Google Maps data and various windows displaying videos, animations, and satellite shots of the entered location. The project, directed by Chris Milk, combines elements of video, interactive art, and web technology, and is optimized for Chrome and Safari. The experience evokes strong feelings of nostalgia, making it a compelling addition to the Arcade Fire's latest album, The Suburbs. The project showcases the potential for music videos to transition from traditional television to the web, offering a more immersive and personalized experience for viewers.

In rural Ohio, the investigation into the killings of eight family members entered its fifth day. The victims, all members of the Rhoden family, were found dead at four crime scenes, with seven of them having been shot multiple times and some showing signs of soft tissue bruising, indicating a struggle. The autopsy report also revealed that one victim was shot nine times.

The hunt for the perpetrator(s) expanded, with more than 200 law enforcement officials involved. Ohio Attorney General Mike DeWine has described the slayings as a "carefully planned and sophisticated operation."

Investigators have found marijuana-growing operations at three of the crime scenes, although it's unclear if this is related to the murders. DeWine has said there were over 300 tips received and 79 pieces of evidence sent for testing and analysis, including for DNA and fingerprints.

The victims were identified as 40-year-old Christopher Rhoden Sr., his ex-wife, 37-year-old Dana Rhoden, their three children, 16-year-old Christopher Rhoden Jr., 19-year-old Hanna Rhoden, and 20-year-old Clarence "Frankie" Rhoden, Christopher Rhoden Sr.'s brother, 44-year-old Kenneth Rhoden, their cousin, 38-year-old Gary Rhoden, and 20-year-old Hannah Gilley, whose 6-month-old son with Frankie was unharmed. Two other children, a 6-month-old and a 3-year-old, were also unharmed.

Authorities have not suggested a motive or named any suspects. Leonard Manley, father of Dana Rhoden, expressed his disbelief that his daughter could have been involved in anything illegal, stating that the assailant knew the family well. A Cincinnati-area businessman offered a $25,000 reward for information leading to those responsible.

Google has ventured into the realm of wedding planning, launching a dedicated platform that allows couples to create wedding websites, edit photos, and plan their big day using templates in Google Sites, Google Docs, and Picnik. The service, announced on Google's official blog, features wedding-specific templates in collaboration with renowned wedding planner Michelle Rago, who also provides planning tips.

To promote the new offering, Google is hosting a wedding sweepstakes, offering a $25,000 prize and the opportunity to have Rago plan the winning couple's wedding. This move marks Google's latest attempt to integrate itself into consumers' lifestyles, following the launch of Google Health in 2008, which allows users to manage their health information. However, concerns about privacy have arisen in the past, such as when Google Health partnered with CVS to provide online access to prescription drug history, raising questions about the company's access to sensitive personal information.

Michelle Rago, the collaboration partner for this project, is a globally recognized wedding planner and destination expert. She shares her tips for planning the perfect wedding, whether it takes place on the beaches of Bali or in a backyard. Rago's background includes extensive travel and work with Google for Education.

MasterCard has announced plans to introduce biometric security checks, allowing customers to verify their identity for online payments using selfies and fingerprints, instead of passwords. The decision was made at the Mobile World Congress in Barcelona, with trials already conducted in the US and Netherlands. MasterCard's head of international markets, Ann Cairns, stated that biometric checks would enhance security and reduce fraud.

The new system, which will be launched in the UK soon, requires users to download an application to their devices. When making an online purchase, users will still need to provide their credit card details. However, if further authentication is required, they will be asked to look at their phone's camera or use its fingerprint sensor. If opting for a selfie, users will have to blink into the camera to prove they are not just holding up a photo.

MasterCard's safety and security division chief, Ajay Bhalla, stated that consumers dislike passwords due to their insecurity and the fact that people often use the same password for multiple sites. He believes biometric authentication is a more secure and convenient solution, given that everyone has a mobile phone and internet connectivity is widespread.

MasterCard is not the only company experimenting with facial scans as an authentication tool. China's e-commerce giant Alibaba and tech giants Microsoft and Google already use biometric tests for device unlocking. However, security researchers have raised concerns about the potential for facial scans and fingerprint sensors to be compromised. MasterCard insists its other security mechanisms can prevent or detect suspicious behavior, and that the facial scan and fingerprint data will not be transmittable in a form that could be intercepted, stolen, or used by scammers.

The introduction of biometric checks is expected to decrease fraud levels, potentially leading to savings that could be passed back to merchants and consumers. The rollout is set to begin this summer in several countries, including the US, Canada, and several European countries.

In a controversial incident, Republican presidential candidate Donald Trump failed to correct a questioner at a town hall event who claimed President Obama is Muslim and suggested getting rid of Muslims. The questioner's remarks were denounced by Democrats, including Hillary Clinton, Bernie Sanders, and Martin O'Mally, as well as the Democratic National Committee Chairwoman Debbie Wasserman Schultz, who called Trump a racist. Trump's campaign manager later claimed that Trump did not hear the question about Obama being a Muslim. This incident recalls Trump's 2011 quest to challenge Obama's birthplace, which ended with Obama releasing his long-form birth certificate. The incident follows a debate performance that garnered mixed reviews for Trump. Trump announced he would cancel his trip to South Carolina, citing a significant business transaction. New Jersey Governor Chris Christie said he would not lecture Trump on how to respond to such comments, but emphasized that leaders have an obligation to correct voters on certain issues. The incident has brought attention to ongoing falsehoods about Obama's background, with a recent CNN/ORC poll finding that 29% of Americans believe Obama is a Muslim, including 43% of Republicans.

In the 73rd annual Golden Globes, Ricky Gervais returned as the host and did not disappoint in his bluntly sarcastic and offensive monologue. He mocked numerous celebrities, including Sean Penn, Caitlyn Jenner, Roman Polanski, Jennifer Lawrence, Jeffrey Tambor, Ben Affleck, and Mel Gibson.

Gervais' jokes ranged from mocking the Hollywood Foreign Press for deeming The Martian a comedy, to joking about his own Golden Globe awards, to making personal jabs at celebrities like Robert Downey Jr. and Mel Gibson. He also made several jokes about the upcoming presidential election, including joking about deporting Eva Longoria and America Ferrera.

One of the most controversial moments of the night came when Gervais introduced Mel Gibson, who was infamously taken down by Gervais during the Globes in 2010. Gervais asked Gibson, "What the f--k does 'sugar t-ts' even mean?" which was entirely bleeped by NBC.

Before the ceremony, Gervais tweeted a shirtless photo of himself with a profane message warning that he would offend Hollywood on Sunday night. During the red carpet, Gervais confirmed to Matt Lauer that his Globes bosses gave him free reign to say whatever he wanted.

Ricky Gervais has hosted the Golden Globes the most times, with four appearances. He is known for his dark sense of humor and controversial jokes that often involve celebrities in the audience. He has won a Golden Globe himself for his role in The Office.

Mel Gibson has been involved in several controversies, including allegations of anti-Semitism and misogyny. During the 2006 DUI arrest, he was recorded making several offensive comments, including using the N-word and ranting against "wetbacks." In 2010, Gervais made several jokes about Gibson during the Golden Globes, which led to a heated exchange between the two.

The incident occurred in Pembroke Pines, Florida, where a police officer was allegedly denied service at an Arby's restaurant due to her profession. The officer, identified as Sgt. Jennifer Martin, claimed that the shift manager stepped in for an employee and said, "He doesn't want to serve you because you are a police officer."

The manager, Angel Mirabal, later explained that it was a misinterpreted attempt at humor. Despite employees claiming to be unaware of the incident, a group of police officers' wives held a protest outside the restaurant, expressing their disapproval.

The CEO of Arby's, Paul Brown, contacted the police chief and apologized on behalf of the organization, assuring that the employee's behavior was "unacceptable and not representative of the company's values." The police chief accepted the apology, considering the matter closed.

However, the Broward County Police Benevolent Association is calling for a public apology to every law enforcement officer instead of just the chief of the Pembroke Pines Police Department. Arby's has offered free meals to uniformed cops in South Florida as a gesture of goodwill, but so far, no officers have accepted the offer at the Pembroke Pines shop where the incident took place.

The incident triggered an outpouring of support from competitors, with McDonald's, Whole Foods, and local residents delivering food and donuts to the Pembroke Pines Police Department. The police union has asked that the employee who refused to serve the officer be fired, while the officer's grandfather maintains that the employee was just making a joke.

Speaker John Boehner has reiterated his stance that President Barack Obama must accept entitlement cuts and no tax increases to secure a debt-ceiling increase from Congress. This statement was made ahead of a White House meeting with congressional leaders to discuss averting a U.S. debt default. Boehner's comments follow Obama's praise for Boehner's openness to a "grand bargain" that would involve spending cuts on programs like Medicare, Medicaid, and Social Security in exchange for up to $1 trillion in new revenue.

Boehner withdrew from one-on-one discussions with Obama over the weekend due to criticism from conservative lawmakers and activists, including House Majority Leader Eric Cantor. Boehner emphasized that the disagreements are about policy, not personalities or process.

Boehner insists that the House will not pass a bill with tax increases, but only one with spending cuts exceeding the debt limit increase, and real spending restraints. He also called for the passage of a balanced-budget amendment, which will be taken up by the House next week.

Boehner prefers tax reform that simplifies and reduces rates, promoting economic growth and more federal revenue, but opposition from Cantor and Senate Republicans has forced him to abandon such an agreement. Boehner and Obama are at odds over tax increases and the extent of entitlement reform needed to solve the problem. The deadline for a deal on spending cuts and the borrowing limit is August 2nd.

During a hearing of the House Committee on Science, Space, and Technology, Republican Mo Brooks of Alabama questioned the notion that global warming is causing sea levels to rise. Instead, he proposed that silt deposition and erosion could be contributing factors. Brooks argued that silt and mud washed by rivers into the ocean could cause water levels to rise as it settles on the sea floor, and that erosion on the California coastline and England's White Cliffs of Dover could also displace water and force it to rise. However, Philip Duffy, president of the Woods Hole Research Center, disagreed, stating that on human timescales, these effects are minuscule. Brooks also claimed that Antarctic ice is growing, not shrinking, a statement that was challenged by Duffy who cited NASA as a source. Brooks insisted that his NASA base in his district was telling him something different. Brooks' claims have been met with criticism and skepticism from scientists and climate experts.

The document discusses the ongoing negotiations between Senate Republican Leader Mitch McConnell, the White House, and Democratic leaders regarding a debt ceiling deal. The negotiations were prompted by the Senate's failure to pass a bill by Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid to raise the debt ceiling by $2.2 trillion. The biggest two outstanding issues are the Republicans' insistence on deficit reductions without new tax revenues and the enforcement mechanism for a new joint House-Senate committee to achieve estimated $1.6 trillion in savings by the end of the year.

The negotiations have shown progress, with McConnell and Vice President Biden engaging in multiple back-and-forth phone calls. However, House Speaker John A. Boehner (R-Ohio) has not yet signed off on the agreement, causing a potential hang-up. Defense cuts, which are likely to be part of the deal, could be problematic for many Republican lawmakers. The negotiations are expected to continue, with both sides aiming to find a compromise before the Treasury's deadline to pay all the nation's bills, which is three days away. The mood on Capitol Hill is one of relief, with Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) describing it as a significant step away from the possibility of default.

The article discusses the potential for a significant increase in the cost of cigarettes in New Zealand, with the Health Ministry suggesting that a packet could cost up to $100 by 2020 as part of efforts to make the country smoke-free by 2025. The proposed increase, which includes a shock rise of 30-60% followed by annual increases of 30%, is described as "probably unrealistic" but is considered the most effective method to reduce smoking prevalence. The government is also considering other measures such as regulating tobacco as a highly toxic substance, banning smoking in cars with children, and increasing anti-smoking media campaigns. However, concerns have been raised about the potential for a black market to emerge due to the high prices. The discussion paper is an internal policy document and does not yet represent government policy.

The document provides information on controlling Giant Hogweed, an invasive plant that can cause severe health hazards and environmental damage. The plant can be controlled manually, mechanically, and with herbicides. Manual control methods include root cutting, flower head/seed head removal, cutting and mowing, and cut and cover. Mechanical control will not cause immediate death of the plant and may require multiple treatments per year for several years. Herbicide control involves the use of systemic herbicides such as glyphosate and triclopyr.

To be successful in eradicating Giant Hogweed, control methods will have to be repeated for a few years, in order to kill the plants missed the prior year as well as the plants emerging from the seed bank. It is important to prevent the introduction of new seeds into the area, and to control new, smaller infestations first before the seed bank has a chance to establish.

The document also includes safety instructions for controlling Giant Hogweed, as the plant's sap can cause severe skin burns and blindness if it comes into contact with the skin and eyes. It is recommended to wear protective gear, including long waterproof gloves, long sleeves, pants, boots, and eye protection, and to prevent UV sunlight from reaching the skin.

Recently, Giant Hogweed was found for the first time in Virginia, and officials are warning residents to be on the lookout for potential sightings. The plant can grow up to 14 feet and can inhibit the growth of native species. If you want to remove the plant, it is recommended to do so by physical removal or using herbicides such as glyphosate or triclopyr. It is important to note that hogweed seeds can remain viable in the soil for 15 years, so long-term monitoring is important.

The document also includes a link to a more extensive PDF format of the Giant Hogweed Control Methods document, as well as a link to The Best Management Practice Manual for the control of this invasive plant.

The PricewaterhouseCoopers (PwC) has taken full responsibility for the mix-up at the 89th Academy Awards, where La La Land was initially announced as the Best Picture winner instead of Moonlight. PwC partner Brian Cullinan, responsible for handing out the winners' envelopes, accidentally handed Warren Beatty and Faye Dunaway the envelope containing the winner of Best Actress, which was La La Land's Emma Stone.

In a statement, PwC apologized for the error and the way they handled the situation, stating that protocols for correcting the mistake were not followed quickly enough by Cullinan or his partner. The company expressed remorse for those involved, including Beatty, Dunaway, host Jimmy Kimmel, and the casts of La La Land and Moonlight.

Cullinan had earlier boasted about PwC's long-standing relationship with the Academy and their expertise in handling the Oscars balloting. However, this relationship could be in jeopardy following the mix-up.

Investigations are ongoing, and potential changes being considered include stationing two auditors at each stage entrance as a fail-safe measure and reviewing the Emma Stone tweet posted by Cullinan just before the error occurred. The Academy is reviewing the entire incident and has not yet announced any next steps. Cullinan has not commented publicly since the blunder.

A music enthusiast named Craig Mandell has launched a crowdfunding campaign titled "Don't Let Nickel Back" to prevent the Canadian band from performing in London. The campaign is inspired by a recent successful Tilt campaign that brought the Foo Fighters to Charlottesville, VA. Mandell aims to discourage Nickelback from playing in London by sending emails to the band's management, with the severity of the message depending on the amount donated. For every dollar donated, Mandell will send one email, while a $5 donation will result in a slightly more forceful email, and a $50 contribution will include an attached mp3 of Nickelback's music. The campaign aims to prevent Nickelback from performing in London, with Mandell stating that all proceeds will go to charity or therapy for those affected by the band.

Meanwhile, a separate crowdfunding campaign to bring the Foo Fighters to Cornwall has reached its target of £150,000 in just two days, but the organizers must now convince the band to agree to play a show in the English county. The original version of this story misidentified the crowd-funding platform as GoFundMe, but it was actually Tilt.

The film "True Grit," directed by the Coen brothers, is a Western drama based on Charles Portis' 1968 novel of the same name. The story revolves around a 14-year-old girl named Mattie Ross, played by Hailee Steinfeld in her film debut, who hires a one-eyed marshal named Rooster Cogburn, portrayed by Jeff Bridges, to find her father's killer. Mattie, who is determined to avenge her father's death, accompanies Rooster and a Texas Ranger named La Boeuf, played by Matt Damon, on their journey through Indian territory. The film is a reboot of the 1969 original, which starred John Wayne as Rooster Cogburn. The Coen brothers' adaptation is praised for its beautiful cinematography, character development, and performances, particularly Bridges' portrayal of Rooster Cogburn. The film was released in theaters in December 2010.

Rhonda Thill, a St. Paul woman, lost her husband Randy Thill in a motorcycle accident three weeks ago. The gold wedding ring he wore every day for nearly 19 years was also thought to be lost, but Rhonda couldn't bear to lose it as well. Despite efforts by friends and family to find the ring, it was not found until a group of bikers from the Los Valientes and Sober Soldiers motorcycle clubs, led by Tim Allen and Jay Stevens, searched the accident site on July 12. Jay Stevens found the ring pushed into the soil behind a weed in the median where Randy died. The group returned the ring to Rhonda, who was overwhelmed with gratitude for the kindness and effort shown by strangers. A benefit ride and poker run, "Riding with Randy," is being held on September 5 at the St. Paul Saloon to raise funds for Rhonda and her children.

The Bracamonte family, residing in Upland, California, has been involved in a prolonged dispute with their live-in nanny, Diane Stretton, who refused to leave their home after being fired. The family hired Stretton via Craigslist in March to care for their three children in exchange for room and board. However, after a few weeks, Stretton stopped working and refused to leave her room. The family terminated her employment on June 6, but she refused to vacate the premises.

Stretton has been spotted driving past the house and her belongings remain in her room. She has communicated that she will move out by July 4, but under certain conditions. The Bracamontes are skeptical about her intentions, fearing she might try to lock them out of their home while they are out of town for a family wedding on July 2.

The Bracamontes initially were pleased with Stretton's work, but things deteriorated over time. They claim they did a criminal background check before hiring her, but did not do a credit check. The employment agreement included a place to live, so the family must go through the proper legal channels to evict her. The eviction process can take months to complete, and if the tenant refuses to leave, they could face arrest for trespassing and/or violation of a court order.

Stretton's litigious past has come to light, with more than a dozen cases in three Southern California counties dating back to 2002. She is a plaintiff in 7 cases and a defendant in 6 more, involving nonpayment, property damage, negligence, and abuse of the legal system. Stretton has refused to speak to the media, hiding under window screens in her car outside a police station at one point during the standoff. The Bracamontes have plans to be away for July 4, but intend to keep their house attended by family members.

The Legal Aid Society has obtained a temporary stay for Pablo Villavicencio, an Ecuadorean restaurant worker, preventing his deportation to Ecuador. Villavicencio was arrested on June 1 while making a delivery to a Brooklyn Army base, after a routine background check revealed an active warrant for his arrest for immigration law violations. The 35-year-old father of two young girls was ordered to leave the United States in 2010 but failed to do so.

The stay was granted by Federal Judge Alison Nathan and will last until July 20. Villavicencio will remain in Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) custody in New Jersey until his case goes to court. New York Governor Andrew Cuomo had asked federal homeland security officials to look into the case, expressing concerns about recent detentions and their legal implications.

In a letter to the ICE office in New York, Cuomo said Villavicencio's "expedited removal serves no legitimate public safety purpose and the circumstances leading to his arrest and detention raise serious legal and policy concerns." Villavicencio's wife, Sandra Chica, is an American citizen, and their daughters, ages 2 and 3, were born in the U.S.

When he arrived at Fort Hamilton, guards requested identification, and he produced a city identification card. A background check showed that Villavicencio had been ordered to leave the United States in 2010, but he stayed. Redmond Haskins, a spokesman for The Legal Aid Society, said Villavicencio has no criminal record.

The attorneys said they will work with Villavicencio to help him secure valid immigration status. The case has sparked outrage from Villavicencio's family and local officials, with Cuomo calling for an investigation into ICE conduct. The attorneys said the emergency stay was based on a habeas corpus petition filed Saturday morning, and that the stay will allow him to pursue relief from removal.

The new Showtime series "The Big C" stars Laura Linney as Cathy, a high school teacher diagnosed with Stage IV melanoma. The show is framed as a comedy, with Cathy's imminent death sentence unleashing a freer side of her. She decides not to tell anyone about her cancer, including her husband, son, and brother. Instead, Cathy tells people off, flirts with her doctor, and lives each day as if it were her last. The show is at its best when it is sardonic and subdued, with some black humor that is reminiscent of the kind of impolitic truth-telling found in movies like "Liar, Liar" and "The Invention of Lying." However, the show takes some easy shortcuts in casting other characters, with Oliver Platt, Phyllis Somerville, and Gabourey Sidibe playing roles that are similar to ones they have played in the past. The show has a strong and believable script, and Linney delivers a powerful performance, but it struggles to balance comedy and drama effectively.

In Meigs County, Tennessee, a shootout occurred early Wednesday morning at a mobile home on Moore Cemetery Road, resulting in the death of Timothy Dewayne Johnson, 52, and the hospitalization of his nephew, Larry Eugene Johnson Jr., 28. The incident appears to have been over a prized pet fighting rooster named "Bubba," which was found tied to a chair outside the trailer. Timothy Johnson had accused Larry of stealing the rooster, leading to a confrontation that ended in gunfire. Larry Johnson, who was armed with a semi-automatic handgun, was reportedly shot in the chest under his left arm, and in self-defense, he fired multiple times. Both families claim the two men had a good relationship, and the case is under investigation by the Meigs County Sheriff's Office, the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation, and the 9th Judicial District Attorney General's office. The district attorney's office will await the conclusion of the autopsy, toxicology results, and completion of an investigative file before presenting the case to the Meigs County grand jury in November.

The death of 17-year-old Kendrick Johnson, a three-sport athlete, has raised questions and doubts about the official findings of an accidental death. Johnson was found dead in a rolled-up gym mat at Lowndes County High School in January. State medical examiners concluded that he suffocated after getting stuck while reaching for a sneaker. However, his parents never accepted this explanation and commissioned a second autopsy in June.

During the second autopsy, it was discovered that the teen's internal organs were missing, and his body was stuffed with newspaper before burial. The private pathologist who conducted the second autopsy, Dr. Bill Anderson, found a blow to the right side of Johnson's neck that was "consistent with inflicted injury." Challenging the state autopsy's finding of positional asphyxiation, he concluded the teen died as the result of "unexplained, apparent non-accidental, blunt force trauma."

The funeral home that handled Johnson's embalming and burial, Harrington Funeral Home, claimed they never received the teen's organs. The Georgia Bureau of Investigation (GBI), which conducted the first autopsy, stated that the organs were placed back in the body after the autopsy and released to the funeral home. However, the GBI spokeswoman could not explain the missing organs.

A former FBI agent, Harold Copus, who reviewed the death scene imagery, questioned how Johnson died and stated that he believes the teen met with foul play. The U.S. Justice Department announced in September that it wouldn't open a civil rights investigation into the case. However, federal prosecutors in south Georgia are reviewing the imagery to determine whether a separate investigation is necessary.

Johnson's parents have come to believe their son's death was no accident, and the macabre discovery about their son's body has only deepened that belief. The family is pushing for a thorough investigation into their son's death.

President Barack Obama, frustrated by the lack of progress in budget negotiations, called for daily meetings with House Speaker John Boehner and Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid to prevent a government shutdown. The President expressed his readiness to meet for as long as necessary to resolve the issue. Boehner and Reid were scheduled to meet later on Tuesday, but if no agreement was reached, Obama threatened to summon both men to the White House the following day and continue the meetings daily. The President's call for action came after a failed meeting between the White House team and Boehner. The House Speaker is under pressure from newly elected House members, many aligned with the ultraconservative tea party, to slash spending and lower taxes. Boehner has proposed a one-week extension to keep the government running, with an additional $12 billion in spending cuts. However, the President has only agreed to a short-term extension of two or three days to push for a longer-term deal. As a government shutdown appears imminent, both sides have been advising government agencies on the proper steps in preparation. The House Budget Committee Chairman, Paul Ryan, unveiled a Republican budget blueprint that includes controversial proposals to convert Medicare into a system operated by private insurers and to sharply cut Medicaid spending. Despite the ongoing negotiations, there is no visible movement on the impasse over Republican policy riders attacking Obama's health care and financial reform laws, cutting taxpayer funds to Planned Parenthood, and reversing environmental policies.

In a tweet on September 15, 2017, President Donald Trump criticized the response of Scotland Yard to a terrorist attack that occurred in the London subway, stating that the individuals responsible were "in the sights of Scotland Yard" and that law enforcement should have been more proactive. British officials, including Prime Minister Theresa May, rebuked Trump for his comments, stating that it is not helpful to speculate on an ongoing investigation. The diplomatic row between the U.S. and U.K. threatened to undermine the special relationship and intelligence sharing arrangements between the two countries. Trump later claimed that the U.S. had made more progress against ISIS in the past nine months than the Obama administration had in eight years and called for a more proactive and "nasty" approach to fighting terrorism. The incident marked the latest in a series of instances where Trump's comments on terrorism and foreign policy have caused controversy and strained relations with U.K. officials.

The Great Recession has significantly impacted the retirement plans of many Americans, with approximately 40% of people aged 45 and over who were not yet retired pushing back their retirement plans. This can have far-reaching effects on various aspects of American society, including Social Security, financial markets, and future workforce demographics.

The report also reveals that 54% of those with incomes under $25,000 have no retirement savings or pension, contrasting with only 10% of those earning $100,000 or more. Among those aged 55 to 64 who had not yet retired, only 18% plan to follow the traditional retirement model, with many expecting to keep working as long as possible or taking on part-time jobs.

The survey also found that one-fourth of all respondents, including 14% of those aged 45 or more, are clueless about their retirement plans, which is a significant concern. The lack of preparedness is not solely due to a lack of planning but also due to limited financial resources and poor awareness.

The report also highlights the uneven nature of the recovery, with over two-thirds of respondents reporting being the same or worse off financially compared to 2008. The survey found that Americans' biggest financial concerns centered on retirement, education, and jobs.

Other findings from the Fed survey include:
- A third of households who had applied for credit in the previous 12 months reported being turned down or getting less than they asked for.
- 10% of households said their income fluctuates significantly from month to month.
- Wage growth has been soft throughout the recovery, straining household budgets and dampening consumer spending.

In conclusion, the report underscores the need for Americans to save more for retirement and increase their financial literacy. The shift from defined-benefit to defined-contribution plans places significant responsibilities on individuals to plan for their own retirement, but only about one-fourth appear to be actively doing so.

Ariel Winter, the 19-year-old star of Modern Family, is known for her bold and confident attitude on social media, often posting scantily clad photos without caring about criticism. However, her appearance on Conan O'Brien's show was met with criticism for her use of a baby voice, which many found cringeworthy and disturbing. In an interview with Elite Daily, Winter spoke about her social media presence and her decision to post provocative photos, stating that she doesn't care about trolls and haters and encourages others to express themselves freely. Recently, Winter also faced backlash for her choice of attire at a Modern Family event, with some commenters implying that she was overdressed and making offensive comments. In response, Winter took to Instagram to defend herself, stating that people should let others feel good about themselves and wear what they want. The controversy surrounding Winter's appearance and behavior highlights the ongoing issue of body-shaming and the pressure on women to conform to certain standards of beauty and dress.

Japanese author Haruki Murakami, a renowned surrealist and global bestseller, will be answering questions from readers on his own website from January 15 to 31, 2021. The website, named "Murakami-san no tokoro" or "Mr. Murakami’s place," will solicit problems from fans of the author, whose novels are published in dozens of languages around the world. Murakami will pen answers to queries, offering his opinions and advice on how to tackle all manner of difficulties, said Shinchosha Publishing. The publicity-shy writer will answer questions written in a variety of languages and will also answer fans’ questions on his likes and dislikes, including his favorite animal, cats, and the Yakult Swallows, the Japanese baseball team he supports. Problems and queries will be accepted until the end of January, and Murakami’s answers will be published over the following two months. This scheme echoes a similar project in 2006, and offers a rare chance for Murakami’s legions of fans to communicate directly with a writer who spends much of his time hiding from the glare of the media.

Haruki Murakami is one of Japan’s best known writers and has repeatedly been tipped as a future Nobel Literature laureate. The 65-year-old, who reportedly spends much of his time in the United States, has a cult following for his intricately-crafted tales of the absurdity and loneliness of modern life, and peppers his work with references to pop culture.

The article also includes a poem by Clive James titled "Fred" which discusses the desire to be like Fred Astaire, and a poem by Isobel Dixon titled "The Glen." The poem by Kathryn Maris titled "The Adulteress" is also included, which discusses the woman's self-deprecating joke name for herself and her struggle with being labeled as an adulteress. Lastly, a poem by Patrick Daly titled "Words" is included, which discusses the author's longing to learn the language of trees and the struggle to make out the words of.

The article ends with the mention of a poem by Benjamin Myers titled "On Approaching Pendle Hill" which features in his collection Heathcliff Adrift. The poem discusses the history of witches burned or branded on Pendle Hill and the always being the women being blamed for misfortunes.

In his recent address to the nation, President Obama announced plans to use force against the Islamic State (IS) in Syria, following swift and brutal actions by the terrorist group in Iraq. On Monday, the U.S. launched airstrikes in Syria, targeting not only IS but also the Khorasan Group, an Al Qaeda offshoot. This offensive, carried out with a few Arab allies, raises questions about the potential for a prolonged air campaign in Syria, as the country's leadership did not invite intervention.

Until recently, Obama had resisted American involvement in Syria's civil war due to its complex nature, with President Bashar Assad, a secular dictator, facing a multitude of opponents, some of whom are extremist. However, the rapid advance of IS in Iraq, the terrorization of minorities, and the beheadings of two American journalists led Obama to promise a long-term campaign to "degrade and ultimately destroy" IS.

The airstrikes in Syria represent a significant shift in Obama's policy, as he had previously been cautious about intervention in Syria. The threat posed by IS justifies this change, but there are concerns about the potential for an escalating role for the U.S. military in Syria and Iraq. The U.S. must clarify its strategy and objectives before committing to a long-term campaign.

The airstrikes in Syria are a welcome offensive against IS, a group that threatens U.S. interests and the rights of those in the Middle East. However, it remains to be seen whether the threat is serious enough to justify a prolonged military involvement. The U.S. must carefully consider its actions to ensure a clear strategy and achievable aims.

The Supreme Court declined to intervene in a death penalty case involving Ronald Mikos, a foot doctor convicted of murdering a former patient in 2005. Mikos did not testify during his trial, and his lawyers argued that prosecutors misused his silence as a lack of remorse. The 7th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in Chicago upheld the sentence.

In a separate case, federal prosecutors announced they will seek the death penalty for Brendt Christensen, a former University of Illinois graduate student accused of kidnapping, torturing, and killing a visiting scholar from China, Yingying Zhang, in June 2017. The decision to seek the death penalty requires the approval of U.S. Attorney General Jeff Sessions, which means the trial will likely be delayed for months.

Christensen is accused of choking and sexually assaulting another victim in 2013 in central Illinois and has claimed additional victims. Prosecutors allege he expressed a desire to be known as a killer. Christensen, who is being held without bond, was tentatively set to go to trial on February 27, 2018, on a charge of kidnapping resulting in a death.

The last person to be sentenced to death in a federal courtroom in Illinois was Dr. Ronald Mikos in 2005. Mikos, who is still awaiting execution in federal prison in Terre Haute, Ind., had his appeal to the U.S. Supreme Court denied nearly a decade ago.

The announcement in Christensen’s case marks at least the third time in recent weeks that Sessions has opted to push for the death penalty. Earlier this month, prosecutors will seek the death penalty against Billy Arnold, an alleged gang member accused of killing two rivals in Michigan. In December, Sessions greenlighted pursuit of the death penalty against Jarvis Wayne Madison, a Florida man who allegedly kidnapped and killed his estranged wife.

In their five-page motion, prosecutors said the death penalty was warranted because Christensen “is likely to commit criminal acts of violence in the future that would constitute a continuing and serious threat to the lives and safety of others.” No details of the alleged 2013 sexual assault by Christensen were provided other than the initials of the victim, “M.D.” The alleged assault occurred the year Christensen was admitted to the university’s highly competitive physics graduate program.

The investigation focused on Christensen after police concluded his Saturn was the car seen in surveillance video from a nearby parking garage. Christensen initially told the FBI he was home all day playing video games on the day Zhang disappeared, but he later changed his story. Police searched Christensen’s car and found visits to a sadomasochism fetish website with discussion threads on kidnapping fantasies.

On June 29, Christensen attended a campus rally for Zhang with a girlfriend, who unbeknownst to him was wearing an FBI wire. He was captured on audio recordings describing his "ideal victim" as he pointed out people in the crowd, prosecutors have previously said. Other recordings made that day captured Christensen admitting to having kidnapped Zhang and describing how she fought back as he held her against her will, according to prosecutors.

A few hours before Zhang’s kidnapping, a female U. of I. graduate student reported to police that a man wearing aviator sunglasses had pulled up to her in a black sedan and flashed a badge. She refused to get in the car and he drove off. A few days later, the woman picked out Christensen’s photo from among six shown her by the FBI, but Christensen’s lawyers are seeking to block the testimony, saying she couldn’t be certain because of the sunglasses.

The U.S. Foreign Corrupt Practices Act, which prohibits companies from paying foreign officials to gain business, is under scrutiny by lobbyists, including an arm of the U.S. Chamber of Commerce with ties to Wal-Mart. An investigation by The New York Times found that Wal-Mart de Mexico, the company's largest foreign subsidiary, paid over $24 million in bribes to secure construction permits. When a whistleblower alerted top executives in 2005, an investigation was launched but later shut down without any information being reported to law enforcement.

The allegations threaten Wal-Mart's cleaned-up image, which was established after facing criticism for low wages and putting small businesses out of business.
