Two Wal-Mart executives, Jeff Gearhart and Thomas Hyde, who were involved in the 2005 investigation, are board members of the U.S. Chamber Institute for Legal Reform, an arm of the U.S. Chamber of Commerce that has been critical of the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act.

Wal-Mart's shares dropped nearly 5% on Monday, and the company faced questions about how much it knew about the corruption and why it did not inform authorities. Representatives Elijah E. Cummings (D-Md.) and Henry A. Waxman (D-Calif.) have requested an in-person meeting with Wal-Mart's CEO to discuss the bribery allegations.

The U.S. Justice Department is investigating potential criminal charges under the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act, and the company is conducting its own review of the allegations. The investigations may lead to executive departures, U.S. penalties, and slowed expansion in Mexico and other markets. The penalties for settling such investigations have grown significantly larger in recent years, and Wal-Mart could face penalties of up to $4.5 billion, depending on the facts uncovered.

The bribery allegations were first described in an April 21 New York Times story. In a December 2011 U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission filing, Wal-Mart said it was examining whether it was in compliance with the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act, without specifying the region or time period in question.

Wal-Mart de Mexico, which operates about 20% of Wal-Mart's stores worldwide, fell 12% on Monday, and the parent company's shares dropped 4.7%. The investigations may slow Wal-Mart's growth in Mexico if authorities feel pressure to show more scrutiny of its permits.

Wal-Mart executives, including then-CEO Lee Scott and current CEO Mike Duke, were made aware of the bribery allegations in 2005. Two top Democrats on congressional panels have moved to start a probe and request a meeting with Wal-Mart executives. Shareholders will pressure the company to take action against any executives who did not act on the bribery allegations sooner.

In Sparks, Nevada, a standoff at an apartment ended tragically with the deaths of Mark and Debby Constantino, a couple known for their appearances on the Travel Channel's reality show "Ghost Adventures." The couple was found dead on Tuesday following an hours-long standoff between police and Mark Constantino, who had shot at officers but did not injure them. The incident began with a call about a man found dead at a home in northwest Reno, where Debby Constantino had been living. She was reported missing, and her estranged husband, Mark Constantino, was suspected of the death.

Debby Constantino had obtained a restraining order against her husband last week, and the two were scheduled to appear in court in December regarding their pending divorce. The Constantinos were paranormal investigators who lectured at conferences and maintained a website.

The incident led to the evacuation and lockdown of the Courtside Gardens Apartment complex near Sparks High School. The high school was put on lockdown as a precaution but was eventually released at the normal time. Police did not release the cause of death for the couple and are still investigating the case.

The couple's deaths come amidst a broader discussion about domestic abuse and its prevalence among celebrities. Charlie Sheen, Emmy award winner and star of Two and a Half Men, tops the list of famous people charged with domestic abuse, with multiple incidents in 1996 and 2009. Other celebrities who have been charged with domestic abuse include Mel Gibson, Josh Brolin, Mickey Rourke, Steven Seagal, James Brown, Madonna, and Sean Penn. Famous ladies such as Carmen Electra and Emma Roberts have also been charged with domestic abuse. The discussion around this issue invites thoughts on the role of drugs and alcohol in celebrity domestic abuse cases and the value of celebrity relationships despite abusive partners.

The film "Sparkle," a remake of a 1976 musical, serves as a bittersweet farewell to Whitney Houston, who passed away during production. Houston delivers a powerful performance in a church scene, which is the film's highlight, but the movie as a whole is criticized for being a flat and unremarkable entry in the star-is-born genre. The story follows three sisters, Sparkle, Sister, and Dolores, who try to make it as a girl group in Detroit during the Motown era. The film features cameos by Cee Lo Green and Mike Epps, and Houston plays the girls' churchgoing single mother, Emma, who warns her daughters about the dangers of the entertainment industry. The movie is criticized for its formulaic plot and cardboard dialogue, but Houston's performance is praised for its emotional depth. The film is a mixed bag, with Houston's final on-screen performance being the standout moment.

U.S. Supreme Court Justice Antonin Scalia, a conservative legal icon and the longest-serving justice on the current court, died on February 13, 2016, at the age of 79. He was found dead at a luxury resort in West Texas, where he had been attending a private party with about 40 people. There was no evidence of foul play, and it appeared that he died of natural causes.

Scalia was nominated by President Ronald Reagan in 1986 and was confirmed without a nomination fight. He was the first Italian-American justice on the court and was known for his sharp intellect, barbed wit, and zeal for verbal combat. He was a fierce opponent of abortion, affirmative action, and what he termed the "so-called homosexual agenda."

Scalia's death has far-reaching implications for the Supreme Court, as he was a key vote on a number of important cases. His replacement will likely be President Obama's third Supreme Court nomination, but it is unclear whether the Republican-controlled Senate will confirm a nominee before the end of Obama's term.

Scalia's death immediately became a political issue, with some Republicans calling for the vacancy to be filled after the next president takes office, while Democrats argued that the Senate has a constitutional responsibility to fill the vacancy.

Scalia's body was transported from El Paso to an airport and will be flown back to Washington, D.C. He will be succeeded by his wife Maureen and their nine children.

Scalia's legacy is significant, as he was a leading advocate of originalism, the idea that judges should interpret the Constitution according to what he believed the original authors intended. He was also known for his wit and passion for intellectual battle, and his dissents were often as influential as his majority opinions.

In his dissent in the landmark same-sex marriage case Obergefell v. Hodges, Scalia wrote, "The Court's decision is a threat to American democracy." He believed that marriage should be decided by the people, not the courts.

Scalia's death is a loss for the court and the country, and his replacement will be a key factor in shaping the direction of the court for years to come.

The collections curated by Mark Graham, available to the public via the Internet Archive's Archive-IT service, include web captures of ISKME.org and IGC.org sites. In a notable incident, a Catholic priest in the Philippines was suspended for using a hoverboard during Christmas Eve Mass. The priest, who remained unidentified, drew criticism after cell phone footage of him riding the hoverboard and singing during the service went viral. The diocese of San Pablo deemed the act inappropriate, stating that the Mass is not a personal celebration for introducing novel elements. The priest has since apologized for his actions, acknowledging that they were not appropriate, and has been removed from his church to reflect on the incident. The suspension comes amidst the popularity of hoverboards as a Christmas gift, despite their associated risks.

On Saturday night at Six Flags Amusement Park in Queensbury, New York, a 14-year-old girl from Greenwood, Delaware, fell from a stopped gondola ride, the "Sky Ride." The girl, who was riding with a child relative, fell approximately 25 feet from a stationary two-person car. The ride was promptly stopped by an operator after receiving word of a rider in distress. The girl struck a tree before landing in the crowd below. She was treated by park emergency medical staff and subsequently transferred to Albany Medical Center, where she is reported to be in stable condition with no serious injuries.

An unidentified 47-year-old man from Schenectady, New York, who was a guest at the park, sustained a back injury while attempting to catch the falling girl. He was treated and released from a hospital.

Authorities inspected the ride and confirmed it was in proper working order. The park has closed the attraction for a thorough review. Officials stated that there does not appear to be any malfunction of the ride. The park emphasized that the safety of its guests is a top priority. No further information was immediately available. This incident is part of an ongoing effort to archive pages and fix broken links on the web.

In this article, Republican presidential candidate Mitt Romney released his U.S. tax returns for 2010 and estimates for 2011, revealing a lower effective tax rate compared to many top wage-earners. Romney's income primarily comes from investment profits, dividends, and interest, while the majority of Americans rely on paychecks. The returns show that Romney and his wife Ann paid a total of $6.2 million in taxes on an income of $42.5 million in 2010, equating to an effective tax rate of 13.9%. For 2011, they expect to pay $3.2 million, resulting in a 15.4% effective tax rate.

These rates are lower than the top income tax rate on wages, which is 35%, due to the U.S. tax code favoring investment income over wage income. President Barack Obama, in his State of the Union speech, will focus on making the tax code fairer as part of his reelection campaign. He will renew his appeal for the "Buffett rule," which aims to ensure the ultra-wealthy pay their "fair share" of taxes.

Romney did not release tax returns from the years 1984-1999, during which he made his fortune as a private equity financier with Bain Capital. However, he received approximately $13 million in income over the past two years from "carried interest," a form of earnings taxed at the 15-percent investment income tax rate, not the higher wage income rate.

The article also discusses the upcoming Republican state primary contest in Florida on January 31, where candidates are fighting for the nomination to face Obama in the November 6 general election. The release of Romney's tax returns was intended to counter attacks from his chief rival, Newt Gingrich, who questioned Romney's financial transparency and portrayed him as out of touch with most Americans.

Romney's tax returns show that he and his wife contributed $7 million to charity over the two years covered, with much of it going to the Mormon church. The returns also reveal holdings in funds based in the Cayman Islands and other overseas entities, but advisers stated these were not vehicles to avoid taxes.

The article concludes by mentioning that Romney had not been audited by the Internal Revenue Service in the last 10 years and that he paid all taxes that were legally required. The tax issue may have contributed to Romney's loss to Gingrich in the South Carolina primary last Saturday, as Romney's fuzzy answers on releasing his records aggravated the problem. However, Romney is looking to regain momentum in Florida to defeat Gingrich in the upcoming primary.

SpaceX successfully launched a classified U.S. spy agency mission, NROL-76, on May 1, 2017, from Kennedy Space Center, Florida. The mission was initially scheduled for Sunday but was delayed due to a sensor issue. High-altitude winds nearly halted the launch, but SpaceX proceeded with the Falcon 9 rocket launch at Launch Complex 39A. The first-stage booster made a successful return to a soft landing at Launch Complex 39A. This was SpaceX's first dedicated mission for the National Reconnaissance Office, the intelligence agency responsible for satellites. The satellite launch marked the start of what some consider a new era of rocket launches, with SpaceX competing with United Launch Alliance for government contracts. This was SpaceX's fifth launch of the year, continuing its rebound from a launch pad rocket explosion last summer that grounded the company for the last four months of 2016. Another Falcon 9 is being prepared to launch a commercial satellite from Kennedy Space Center as soon as May 15.

In a series of exclusive reports, it has been revealed that Josh Duggar, a former reality star from the show 19 Kids and Counting, is facing a lawsuit for allegedly using a random man's image on his dating profiles, including Ashley Madison. The man, Matthew McCarthy, claims that his image was used without his consent, causing him embarrassment and harassment. The profile in question was found on OkCupid, with the username joesmithsonnwa, which is also Duggar's alleged Ashley Madison email handle. The profile was later taken down, but screenshots suggest it was active around the same time Duggar's reported credit card stopped paying for his Ashley Madison account. The profile listed Duggar's occupation as "politics," which matches Duggar's role as the executive director of the Family Research Council. However, there is no definitive evidence linking the profile to Duggar, and he has yet to respond to these allegations. The Internet continues to search for signs of infidelity, but so far, no concrete evidence has been found.

The Internet Archive is implementing crawls to archive web pages as they are created, aiming to preserve the original intended content of pages even if they are changed or removed from the web. This initiative aims to fix broken links on the web by replacing them with links to the archived versions of the pages.

Meanwhile, UC Irvine faced controversy this year due to the withdrawal of over 500 admission offers. The university took a stricter approach in processing admissions, which led to the revocation of offers for 499 students, 299 of whom had issues with their transcripts, and 209 with grade-related concerns. As of Friday, 63 students who appealed have been reinstated.

The university's Vice Chancellor for Student Affairs, Thomas Parham, apologized for any mistreatment or ignored feelings of the affected students. The apology came after the student government association sent a letter and a petition demanding an apology, reimbursement for students whose admission status was revoked, and a guarantee of admission for students who complete two years at a community college.

UCI received over 104,000 applications for the 2017-18 academic year, offering admission to 31,103 freshmen, of whom about 7,100 accepted. However, the university had planned a freshman class of approximately 6,250 students. The over-enrollment and subsequent revocation of offers led to student complaints on social media.

Students who had their offers revoked claimed that either the university or their high school made mistakes, causing them anxiety. Some students, like Johnny Wang and Simran Chopra, have appealed the decisions, while others, like Julia Kim, have already found alternative universities.

UCI has increased the number of people reviewing appeals and expects to complete them by the end of next week. The university emphasizes that all students who meet the terms and conditions of the admissions offer will be welcomed into the Anteater family, and no acceptance will be withdrawn due to over-enrollment.

The U.S. Defense Secretary, Leon Panetta, has put on hold the confirmation of Marine Gen. John Allen as commander of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) due to an FBI investigation into his alleged inappropriate communications with Jill Kelley, a Tampa socialite who triggered the investigation. The investigation began when Kelley complained to the FBI about receiving harassing emails that were later traced to Paula Broadwell, David Petraeus's biographer and alleged mistress.

Gen. Allen, the current U.S. commander in Afghanistan, exchanged numerous emails with Kelley, and at one point, she tried to get the FBI to drop the matter due to concerns about personal information being provided to investigators. However, it was later discovered that Allen had been in communication with Kelley since 2010, and the FBI has turned over emails between the two to Pentagon investigators.

Investigators have not found any sensitive or classified material in the emails, but they are still reviewing the material. Allen has denied having an affair with Kelley or sharing any classified information with her. He also told officials that he never had been in a room alone with Kelley and that there had been no affair or sex.

The White House Press Secretary, Jay Carney, said that President Obama remains supportive of Gen. Allen. A defense official urged against prejudging, saying that Gen. Allen's nomination as NATO commander may yet go forward.

Jill Kelley is an "honorary consul" of South Korea, a diplomatic position that she assumed last August. She has been friendly with many top military commanders in Tampa, home of the U.S. Central Command, which Gen. Petraeus once ran. However, her emails, sent to Gen. Allen and other senior officials, may appear flirtatious in nature, but this does not necessarily mean she engaged in any adulterous relationships.

The investigation into the Petraeus scandal has also revealed that Kelley's sister, Natalie Kwaham, invoked Allen and Petraeus's names in her custody battle. Spokesmen for Senators John Kerry and Sheldon Whitehouse both said the senators had met Kwaham through Kwaham's boyfriend Gerald Harrington, a Democratic Party fundraiser.

The FBI conducted a consensual search at Broadwell's home in Charlotte, North Carolina, on Monday, though it is unclear why. The FBI does not believe Petraeus committed any crimes, but they are still examining Broadwell's conduct.

In summary, the FBI investigation into David Petraeus's communications has led to the discovery of inappropriate emails between Marine Gen. John Allen and Jill Kelley, a Tampa socialite. The investigation has caused the delay of Allen's nomination as commander of NATO, and he has denied having an affair with Kelley or sharing any classified information with her. The investigation into the Petraeus scandal is ongoing, and Kelley's sister has invoked Allen and Petraeus's names in a custody battle.

Hollywood legend Tony Curtis, known for his roles in Spartacus and Some Like it Hot, disinherited his five children, including actress Jamie Lee Curtis, in his last will and testament. The will, obtained by Inside Edition, states that Curtis intentionally chose not to provide for his children, instead leaving his estate to his fifth wife, Jill Vandenberg Curtis. One of his children attempted to contest the will, but the attempt was unsuccessful. Curtis, who passed away from cardiac arrest at the age of 85, had children with three of his wives and had a long and successful career spanning over 60 years. His daughter Jamie Lee Curtis, from his marriage to actress Janet Leigh, paid tribute to him at his funeral. Following his death, Jill Curtis stated that Tony's last will and testament and his passing wishes were private family matters.

The families of four American hostages who were killed by the Islamic State have issued a joint letter to President Obama, urging him to take action to find and return Austin Tice, the last unaccounted-for American reporter in the Syrian civil war who was captured in August 2012. Tice's parents have been advocating for increased search efforts, as the Obama administration's term comes to an end. State Department spokesman John Kirby confirmed that U.S. officials are working through the Czech government to find information on Tice's welfare and whereabouts. The families of the slain hostages, including journalists James Foley and Steven Sotloff, and humanitarian aid workers Abdul-Rahman Peter Kassig and Kayla Mueller, have expressed their support for the Tice family and urged the Obama administration to use all appropriate means to bring Tice home safely. The families have not specified any particular steps that the administration could take, but have urged officials not to hesitate in leveraging all available resources. The Tices have been advocating for changes in hostage policy, and were at the White House together a year ago when President Obama announced a revamped process based on the families' recommendations. Austin Tice, now 34, is a U.S. Marine-turned-journalist who reported for outlets including McClatchy and The Washington Post. He vanished in Syria in mid-August 2012, and is believed to have been seized by loyalists of the Syrian regime, not by the Islamic State. The Syrian government denies any knowledge of his whereabouts. This August will mark his fourth year in apparent detention. The families of the slain hostages have recognized the Tice family's anguish and expressed their support, acknowledging that maintaining hope during the crisis requires mountain-moving faith.

A video game titled "Active Shooter," developed by Revived Games and published by ACID, was set to be released on Steam, a popular PC gaming platform. The game, which allowed players to simulate a school shooting, drew intense criticism from survivors of the Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School shooting in Parkland, Florida, and other anti-gun activists. The game's developer marketed it as a "dynamic SWAT simulator" and offered players the option to play as either the shooter or a SWAT team member.

After receiving widespread backlash, Valve Corporation, the owner of Steam, announced that it had removed the game from its online storefront. The company stated that the developer and publisher, Ata Berdiyev, had a history of customer abuse, copyright infringement, and user review manipulation. Berdiyev had previously been removed from Steam last fall under different business names.

Many critics argued that the game glorified violence and was in poor taste, especially in the wake of the Parkland shooting. Sen. Bill Nelson (D-FL) called the game "inexcusable," and Emma Gonzalez, a Parkland activist, tweeted, "Valve Corp shut down this shovelware immediately please."

This isn't the first time a video game has caused controversy for its depiction of school shootings. In 2011, another game, "School Shooter," was pulled after public outcry. The removal of "Active Shooter" from Steam follows Valve's announcement that it will soon address the broader conversation about its content policies.

In a discussion at the Harvard Kennedy School's Institute of Politics, House Minority Leader Nancy Pelosi stated that she will not trade anything for President Donald Trump's border wall, referring to it as a "manhood issue" for the President. Pelosi emphasized that Democrats support border security but prefer to focus on strengthening existing measures as part of a comprehensive immigration overhaul.

Trump is pushing for a fight over border wall funding in the upcoming December appropriations negotiations, with GOP leaders prepared to push for the wall. Seven of the 12 annual appropriations bills, including the Department of Homeland Security spending bill where any wall funding would be appropriated, are operating under a continuing resolution that expires on December 7.

Pelosi's stance on the wall is unlikely to matter much in the House, where Republicans during the lame duck session should have enough votes to pass the $5 billion Trump requested for the wall for fiscal 2019. However, Senate Democrats will be the real obstacle to Trump securing wall funding during the lame duck.

If the appropriations negotiations get deferred into the next Congress, Pelosi could have more leverage if Democrats win the House majority in November. Pelosi expressed confidence about being elected speaker if Democrats win the majority but said that's the furthest issue from her mind at the moment.

Pelosi also discussed Democrats' top priorities for next year if they're in the majority, such as lowering health care costs, increasing paychecks, and improving the nation's green infrastructure. The specifics of the agenda will be built out by the consensus of the Democratic members, but Pelosi noted that there seems to be agreement among incumbents and candidates about what the first bill should be: campaign finance reform.

Other legislative issues Pelosi mentioned that Democrats plan to act quickly on are gun control and protecting Dreamers, young undocumented immigrants brought to the U.S. as children. Regarding the House's oversight responsibilities, Pelosi reiterated her view that impeachment is divisive but made clear that Democrats will take seriously their responsibility to hold Trump and his administration accountable.

In the 2014 All-Star Game, National League pitcher Adam Wainwright showed respect to Derek Jeter by letting him have a moment at the plate, but his post-game comments about intentionally giving Jeter a "pipe shot" caused controversy and backlash. Wainwright's comments were seen as disrespectful to Jeter, who was playing in his final All-Star Game. The incident highlights the problems with the current All-Star Game format, which awards home-field advantage in the World Series to the winning league. The system has become too complex, with fans, players, and managers involved in the process, leading to confusion and a lack of focus on the game itself. The incident also raises questions about whether players like Jeter, who may not be at their peak performance, should still be playing in the All-Star Game. Overall, Wainwright's experience at the 2014 All-Star Game highlights the need for MLB to reevaluate the event and its format.

On June 14, 2016, a Chinese tourist was fined $1,000 and a $30 court processing fee for walking off the boardwalk in the Mammoth Hot Springs thermal area at Yellowstone National Park. The visitor reported seeing the individual break through the fragile travertine crust and collect thermal water, which the tourist admitted to doing for medicinal purposes. The incident came a week after an Oregon man died after falling into one of Yellowstone's hot springs. The Chinese tourist was issued a federal violation notice and was required to appear in the Yellowstone Justice Center Court. Park officials emphasized the importance of staying on designated trails and boardwalks in thermal areas for visitor safety and the protection of the park's natural resources. Earlier this month, another tourist incident occurred at Yellowstone when a bison was loaded into a vehicle by visitors who believed it was cold. The bison later had to be euthanized when it could not be reunited with its herd.

The article discusses the dangerous health effects of betel nut, a popular psychoactive substance in Asia, particularly in Taiwan. Betel nut is a seed from the Areca palm, often chewed after being wrapped in leaves of the Piper betle vine and coated with lime. It is estimated that around 600 million people worldwide use betel nut, making it the fourth most popular psychoactive substance after nicotine, alcohol, and caffeine.

The article highlights the link between betel nut use and oral cancer, with 80 to 90 percent of the 5,400 men diagnosed with oral cancer or lesions in Taiwan admitting to chewing betel nuts. The Taiwanese government is taking action to reduce the prevalence of betel nut use by providing free programs aimed at convincing people to quit and offering incentives to betel nut farmers to cut down their trees and grow other crops.

The article also mentions that betel nut has a long history in South and Southeast Asia and the Pacific Basin, and is considered an important cultural and social tradition in many countries. However, growing evidence points to serious health effects from regular use, including oral cancer, oral submucous fibrosis, gum irritation, tooth decay, and cardiovascular disease.

The World Health Organization classifies betel nut as a carcinogen, and many studies have shown a convincing link between betel nut use and cancer of the mouth and esophagus. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration does not consider betel nut safe for chewing or eating and has placed it on its Poisonous Plants Database.

The article concludes by mentioning that health organizations and governments are taking steps to increase awareness of betel nut risks, with Taiwan declaring an annual "Betel Nut Prevention Day" and city officials in Taipei fining anyone seen spitting betel nut juice and requiring them to attend withdrawal classes. The World Health Organization has also released an action plan to reduce betel nut use in the Western Pacific.

U.S. Secretary of State Hillary Clinton has ruled out running for president in 2012 or 2016, stating that she is content with her current role as Secretary of State. During an interview in New Zealand, Clinton clarified that she has no plans to run again, despite speculation following the Democrats' losses in the midterm elections. Clinton also defended President Barack Obama and put the Democrats' losses into perspective, acknowledging that they were significant but not out of the ordinary for midterm elections. In a separate incident, New Zealand Prime Minister John Phillip Key accidentally referred to Clinton as "President Clinton" during a speech, causing laughter and applause.

The Treasury Department has released emails that suggest the Obama administration may have disregarded warnings and potentially brushed aside a conflict of interest while pushing for a government loan to solar-panel maker Solyndra LLC. Solyndra received a $535 million Department of Energy loan guarantee in September 2009, with the loan itself coming from a part of the Treasury Department.

The emails show that Steven J. Spinner, a senior Energy Department official and a 2008 Obama fund-raiser, pushed for the loan's approval despite his wife's law firm representing Solyndra. Spinner communicated frequently with Solyndra officials and urged the White House budget office to move more quickly on approving the loan. He also inquired about the progress of the loan, referring to the office of the vice president and the White House.

The emails offer further evidence of high-level cheerleading on behalf of Solyndra, a company that declared bankruptcy last month and laid off 1,100 workers. Despite promoting Solyndra as a model of new technology, administration officials were raising concerns about its viability, the legality of a later restructuring, and whether the government was sufficiently protected should the business fail.

The company was the first recipient of a federally guaranteed loan for alternative energy projects, but now is being investigated by the Justice Department over whether it provided misleading financial information to federal authorities. Congressional investigators are also looking at whether the Obama administration adequately oversaw the granting of the loan.

The latest emails also show that senior White House and Treasury Department officials voiced concerns at several stages of the ill-fated loan guarantee. At one point, they show that the White House considered making a bigger public event than previously known of the formal approval of the company’s financing package.

Top officials, including Rahm Emanuel, then the White House chief of staff, weighed whether President Obama would visit the company to formally announce the loan guarantee, which occurred in September 2009. Ultimately, Mr. Obama did not participate in the event. Vice President Joseph R. Biden Jr. did by video teleconference and Energy Secretary Steven Chu attended. Earlier, Carol Browner, the White House coordinator for energy and climate change policy, met with an investor in the company.

The emails reveal that some White House officials were concerned about the company’s health and the haste with which the loan guarantees were moving, while others were eager to hurry it along to make a public relations splash. They also show that days before the Obama administration gave conditional approval to the loan guarantee, a major investor behind the deal met with Ms. Browner.

The controversy surrounding Solyndra has escalated with each new release of documents to a Republican-led House energy subcommittee investigating the matter. President Obama defended the Energy Department in a news conference, saying its decisions were made by career professionals. Also, the head of the embattled loan program announced that he would step down, although Energy Department officials said he was not doing so because of the Solyndra matter.

The emails show that Energy Department officials moved ahead with a new deal that would repay company investors before taxpayers if the company defaulted. The emails, which were reviewed by The Washington Post, show for the first time concerns within the administration about the legality of the Energy Department’s extraordinary efforts to help Solyndra. The FBI raided Solyndra last month, shortly after it closed its doors.

The documents offer new evidence of wide disagreement between officials at the Energy Department and officials at the Treasury Department and Office of Management and Budget, where questions were raised about the carefulness of the loan vetting process used to select Solyndra and the special help it was given as its finances deteriorated. Energy Department officials continued to make loan payments to the company even after it had defaulted on the terms of its loan.

The Solyndra controversy has become a political issue, with Republicans accusing the Obama administration of favoritism and potential illegal actions in the loan approval process. The administration has defended its actions, stating that the loan was made by career professionals and that the restructuring of the loan was legal. The investigation into Solyndra is ongoing.

The article discusses the reactions of key Democrats to President Obama's speech on Afghanistan. The speech outlined his plan for withdrawing troops from Afghanistan, but the logic of the withdrawal date and the focus on national self-interest and realism were criticized. The speech was compared to Henry Kissinger's focus on national self-interest, and the lack of Wilsonian-Bushian flourishes about democracy and women's rights. The article also discusses a separate piece by Derek Thompson on the "doom loop" of Western liberalism, which argues that low birth rates and immigration policies could lead to stagnation and authoritarianism. The article concludes by expressing disappointment with President Obama's decision to escalate the war in Afghanistan, but acknowledges that he is facing difficult choices due to the incompetence of the Bush-Cheney administration. The article also notes that Obama's speech was well-written and spoken with conviction, but expresses doubt that the plan will be successful. The article ends by stating that Obama has shown that it is possible to urge a nation to war using reason and logic, rather than patriotic fibs.

Alvin Cross Jr., a man from Albany, Georgia, found himself back in prison after accidentally texting his probation officer asking for drugs. Cross was on probation for an unknown offense when he sent a text message asking, "You have some weed?" to his probation officer. Upon receiving the message, the probation officer contacted the police who then raided Cross's home and discovered a bag of cocaine. Cross pleaded guilty on Monday to cocaine possession and was given one year in prison and another year for violating his probation. This incident serves as a reminder of the potential consequences of careless texting, especially when on probation.

The Commission on Wartime Contracting in Iraq and Afghanistan released a report highlighting significant waste, fraud, and abuse in the $117 billion spent on contractors since 2002 in Iraq and Afghanistan. The report criticizes the federal government for over-relying on contractors for various purposes, including monitoring other contractors, and for poor planning and oversight. The commission calls for major reforms to the government's contracting programs, including the creation of special teams of federal workers to monitor projects, restricting the use of contractors for security, and improving the government's contractor oversight database. The report also notes the high risks faced by contractors, with over 2,200 deaths and 49,800 injuries between September 2001 and December 2010. The commission is urging Congress and the Department of Defense to take action on the report's recommendations.

Lucinda Smith, a 43-year-old mother of two from Billericay, Essex, passed away due to sepsis, a form of blood poisoning, following a minor hand scrape while gardening. According to her mother, Shirley, Smith initially visited her GP with a pain in her shoulder, but was diagnosed with a trapped nerve and prescribed anti-depressants. Three days later, her condition worsened, with her arm and hand becoming swollen and blotchy, and she was vomiting. She was then admitted to Basildon Hospital, where a blood test revealed sepsis. Despite immediate treatment with intravenous antibiotics and transfer to a critical care unit, Smith suffered organ failure and died.

Shirley believes that if her daughter had received the correct medical treatment when she first complained of feeling unwell, she could have been saved. Sepsis is a potentially life-threatening complication of an infection that occurs when chemicals released into the bloodstream to fight the infection trigger inflammatory responses throughout the body, leading to organ damage and failure.

Sepsis can begin outside of the hospital and is more common in seniors and people with weaker immune systems. Early treatment, usually with antibiotics and large amounts of intravenous fluids, improves chances for survival. People should be aware of the signs of sepsis, including shivering, fever or very cold, extreme pain or discomfort, clammy or sweaty skin, confusion or disorientation, shortness of breath, high heart rate, and seek medical care immediately if they notice these symptoms after developing an infection.

A 60-year-old man from Leonora, Australia, was found dead on Wednesday near Wiluna, approximately 1000 kilometers north-east of Perth, after his vehicle broke down. The man had abandoned his vehicle and walked more than 40 kilometers in search of help with only a small container of water. A woman who left the same vehicle about 24 hours after the man was found on the road by people from Wongawol Station and was taken to Windidda Station, where the man had been heading. The man's body was found by the road only two kilometers from Windidda Station. Police have reported no suspicious circumstances, and a report will be prepared for the coroner.

The incident has highlighted the importance of safety measures for travelers in remote locations. People who travel through remote areas have been urged to stay with their vehicle if they become lost or incapacitated, as searchers can more easily spot a vehicle from the air than a person. Travelers should carry a three-day supply of food and water for each person, ensure their vehicle is in good condition and suitable for the road conditions, and have sufficient fuel between refueling points. Travelers should also let people at their destination know their plans and estimated time of arrival.

The incident occurred during the summer months, with Wiluna, the biggest population center in the region, having a forecast maximum temperature of 39 degrees Celsius (102 Fahrenheit) on Thursday. The man's death serves as a reminder of the dangers of traveling in remote areas without proper precautions, and authorities are urging travelers to take necessary safety measures.

In a significant crackdown on dissent, an Egyptian court handed down heavy prison sentences to nearly two dozen Islamist women and girls, some as young as 15, for protesting against the military-backed government. The sentences came a day after police brutally dispersed protests by secular activists under a new anti-protest law. The harsh sentences and the scenes of police violence the previous day are seen as signs of the government's increasing boldness in silencing dissent, with tactics reminiscent of the Hosni Mubarak era.

The crackdown is rearranging Egypt's political landscape after months of focusing on crippling the Muslim Brotherhood and other Islamist groups. This week, security forces have targeted secular youth activists opposed to the military and police. Some government supporters fear that the government's actions could widen the base of the opposition, potentially bringing together supporters of ousted President Mohammed Morsi and secular activists, despite their bitter opposition to the Islamists.

The crisis is fragmenting the loose coalition of liberal and secular groups that supported the military in its removal of Morsi. In a Mediterranean city courtroom, the 21 young female defendants, aged 15 to 22, were sentenced to prison terms ranging from 11 years to being held until they turn 18. The Muslim Brotherhood's political arm, the Freedom and Justice Party, condemned the sentences as a "deterrent" for their opposition to the military.

Meanwhile, hundreds of secular youth activists protested in downtown Cairo against the government's clampdown on dissent. The center of the crisis is a new law banning any protests or public political gatherings of more than 10 people without a prior police permit, imposing stiff fines and jail terms for violators.

Prominent activists, including Alaa Abdel-Fattah and Ahmed Maher, have been arrested for allegedly inciting others to break the protest law. In a sign of the Islamists' eagerness to find a common cause with secular activists, the Brotherhood-led coalition supporting Morsi reached out to them, but their overtures were rejected by the youth activists.

In a separate development, the head of the defense team for the jailed protesters was arrested, raising concerns about the freedom of lawyers to defend those accused under the new law. The arrest of Ahmed El-Hamrawy, who has defended freedoms since the military removed Morsi, is seen as punishment for his opposition to the government.

The crackdown comes ahead of an election season that will include a referendum on amendments to the Islamist-drafted, Morsi-era constitution. The new constitution, which gives wider powers to the military and the president, is opposed by secular activists, while the Brotherhood rejects the entire amendment process and the new government in general. The crisis is deepening, with the potential for increased violence and further fragmentation of the political landscape.

A seven-story building under construction illegally in Thane, a suburb of Mumbai, India, collapsed on Thursday evening, resulting in at least 45 deaths, including 15 children, and over 70 injuries. The building, which was already occupied by residents, was found to have been built using substandard materials and without the necessary permits. The collapse is believed to be due to the use of poor construction practices, a common issue in India. The authorities are investigating the incident and searching for the builders to arrest them. This tragedy highlights the issue of illegal construction in India, where unscrupulous builders often pay bribes to authorities to turn a blind eye to illegal structures. Building collapses are not uncommon in India, with numerous similar incidents occurring in recent years.

In a dramatic turn of events in Southern California, a 12-year-old girl narrowly avoided becoming a suicide statistic, thanks to a rookie police officer, Officer Chris Perez, who had been on the South Pasadena Police force for only a year. On a routine patrol, Perez found the girl on a 6-inch ledge of York Bridge, ready to jump. With the potential for a fatal misstep, Perez approached her calmly, engaging in a careful conversation to build trust. The girl revealed she was running away from a group home due to poor treatment.

After a back-and-forth exchange, Perez managed to rescue the girl by bear-hugging her and pulling her to safety. The girl, initially sad and distraught, was found to have no other family apart from an aunt, whom she wished to live with. The girl is currently in protective police custody, awaiting further evaluation.

Officer Perez, who was only an hour into his shift when he encountered the girl, expressed his discomfort with being labeled a hero but was glad his parents, especially his father who is also an officer, took notice of his actions. This incident serves as a poignant reminder of the importance of empathy, patience, and quick thinking in critical situations.

Camp John Waters, a three-day summer camp event scheduled for September 2017, invites fans of the cult filmmaker to immerse themselves in a weekend of debauchery and campy delights in Kent, Connecticut. The event, held at Camp Getaway, offers a variety of activities including ziplining, canoeing, screenings of Waters' films, 'Blood Mary Bingo', Hairspray karaoke, burlesque lessons, a 'Scotch and Cigars' session, a costume contest, and a Q&A with Waters. He will also perform a one-man show and read from his new book, "Make Trouble".

"Make Trouble", adapted from his speech to the Rhode Island School of Design class of 2015, is a book that has received high praise for its witty and inspirational content. It is illustrated by Eric Hanson and has been described as a great read that inspires all outsiders who strive to change society. The book is a reflection of Waters' manifesto and has been praised for its timelessness and relevance in today's social climate.

The Camp John Waters event promises to be a unique experience for fans, offering a chance to interact with the filmmaker and enjoy a weekend of filthy fun. The book, "Make Trouble", is a must-read for anyone seeking inspiration and a dose of Waters' signature well-intentioned belligerence.

In Youngstown, Ohio, a tragic fire occurred on December 10, 2018, claiming the lives of five children, including 1-year-old twins, and leaving their mother injured. The fire started on the first floor of a two-story wood home, built over 90 years ago. The only survivor was the children's mother, who jumped out of a second-story window. The other three children who died were ages 9, 3, and 2.

Firefighters arrived to find flames throughout the home's first floor. They were able to pull out three of the children, but they died at a hospital. The mother was taken to a hospital and is being treated for injuries. One firefighter was treated at the scene, and another was taken to a hospital for treatment and released.

The cause of the fire is still under investigation by state and local authorities. So far, there's nothing that indicates the fire was suspicious. A memorial to the children is growing outside the home.

The family had just moved into the house about six months ago. The community has shown compassion, with people dropping off stuffed animals in honor of the children. Rev. Lewis Macklin, a police chaplain, plans to meet with city councilwoman Anita Davis to discuss ways to raise funds for the family.

This fire is the most deadly in Youngstown since a 2008 arson that claimed the lives of two adults and four children. The cause of the current fire is believed to be accidental at this point. The house's owners are Lindsey Maggie and Lindsey Henry of Campbell. The house's value was $7,930, according to Zillow.com.

Officials have confirmed the identities of the five children killed: Aleysha Rosario (9), Charles Gunn (3), Ly'Asia Gunn (2), and Brianna and Arianna Negron (1). Their mother, 26-year-old America Negron Acevedo, is receiving medical treatment at MetroHealth's Burn Center in Cleveland. She is in "stable but critical" condition.

In a special event held by Microsoft, the company officially unveiled Kinect, the new motion-control system for Xbox 360, which was previously known as Project Natal. The event took place during a Cirque du Soleil performance in Los Angeles, where Microsoft demonstrated various ways Kinect can be used, such as playing games, exercising, and even controlling the Xbox dashboard. The potential of Kinect was highlighted, but it was noted that it has not yet been fully realized. Microsoft is aiming to compete with Nintendo's Wii and its Balance Board, Wii Fit, and Wii Sports, and plans to reveal more details about Kinect, including pricing and availability, at its E3 press conference on Monday. The event was a mix of a religious revival and a Las Vegas show, with audience members wearing white ponchos and being led through mock living rooms to see the Kinect system in action.

Lawyers for Boston Marathon bomber Dzhokhar Tsarnaev have appealed his conviction and death sentence, arguing that publicity made it impossible for him to receive a fair trial in Boston due to widespread outrage over the 2013 bombing. The defense claims that the trial should have been held elsewhere due to continuous and unrelenting publicity about the bombings, the defendant, and his family, as well as wrenching survivor stories. The appeal also argues that the death penalty is unconstitutional, citing a recent dissent by U.S. Supreme Court Justice Stephen Breyer. Tsarnaev was sentenced to death in June for his role in the bombings that killed three people and injured over 260. Despite the dramatic news, Tsarnaev's fate will take years to reach its conclusion, as only three of 340 prisoners sentenced to federal death row have been executed in the last 50 years. The defense has indicated two strong lines of likely appeal: that the trial should never have been held in Boston, and that the defense was given insufficient time to mount a full argument in mitigation.

Democratic presidential candidate Sen. Bernie Sanders is set to introduce a bill on Capitol Hill on Thursday, aiming to ban privately run prisons. Known as the "Justice Is Not For Sale" Act, the bill would prohibit federal, state, and local governments from using private prisons within three years. The bill also seeks to reduce high fees for prisoner services, reinstate a federal parole system, and reduce the number of immigrants held in detention centers.

Sanders accuses the private prison industry of creating a "perverse incentive" to keep jails filled, and he calls the industry "disgraceful" and "morally repugnant." The bill is co-sponsored by Rep. Raul Manuel Grijalva (D) of Ariz., and it comes as Sanders seeks to broaden his appeal among African-American and Latino voters.

The bill may help Sanders make inroads with voting demographics he has struggled to reach as an Independent senator from a small, nearly entirely white state. Hillary Clinton, who enjoys far more recognition and support from African-American voters, has also criticized mass incarceration but has yet to propose a specific reform plan.

The bill faces an uphill battle in Congress, but other bipartisan prison reform bills are likely to pass this fall, as both parties recognize new research casting doubt on the assumption that tough sentencing laws result in lower crime rates. The release of Sanders’s plan comes as he seeks to address the issue of privately run prisons and detention facilities, which has emerged as a hot-button issue among key constituencies in the Democratic nominating process.

Sanders is scheduled to appear at a news conference on Thursday to unveil the bill. The bill also includes provisions aimed at lowering the prison population, such as reinstating the federal parole system and ending the requirement that Immigration and Customs Enforcement maintain a minimum of 34,000 detainees a day.

The bill is part of Sanders's broader agenda to address mass incarceration and criminal justice reform. Sanders frequently describes the "international disgrace" that more people are incarcerated in the United States than any other country in the world. Sanders plans to continue his practice of using his position as a senator to highlight his agenda as a presidential candidate.

Arturo Carvajal, a doctor from Hollywood, Florida, has filed a lawsuit against Houston's Restaurant in Miami, alleging negligence for failing to advise him on the proper way to eat an artichoke. In May 2009, Carvajal ordered a grilled-artichoke special at the restaurant, which he had never encountered before. Believing it was a food he might have eaten in his native Cuba, he consumed the entire artichoke, unaware that the outside leaves are tough and indigestible.

Carvajal claims that as a result, he suffered severe abdominal pain and was hospitalized, where an exploratory laparotomy revealed artichoke leaves lodged within his bowel. The lawsuit seeks unspecified damages for bodily injury, pain and suffering, disability, disfigurement, aggravation of pre-existing conditions, and medical expenses.

Scientists from the U.S. and Denmark are embarking on a groundbreaking study to map the underground hydrothermal features of Yellowstone National Park, using an electromagnetic system suspended from a helicopter. The research aims to shed light on the plumbing system responsible for geysers like Old Faithful and hydrothermal explosions.

The electromagnetic system, developed in Denmark, acts like an X-ray to determine the flow paths of hot water beneath the surface. The data collected will help scientists distinguish between water, rocks, and solid earth, providing insights into the infrequent but sometimes massive hydrothermal explosions that have occurred in the park.

One such explosion, believed to be the largest in the world, occurred approximately 13,800 years ago, leaving a crater beneath Yellowstone Lake that measures 1-1/2 miles across.

The study, a collaboration between the U.S. Geological Survey, Yellowstone National Park, the University of Wyoming, and Denmark's Aarhus University, will fill in the gaps of knowledge about the underground water system that feeds thermal features in the park.

The survey will take at least four weeks to complete, with the helicopter flying along the Mammoth-Norris corridor. The goal is to locate unstable ground and provide information that could help the park in future development, ensuring tourists can enjoy the park's features without causing damage or putting themselves in harm's way.

Carol Finn, one of the scientists on the surveying team, expressed her excitement about the project, calling it a "last frontier" in Yellowstone's geology. The survey can visualize the geology and water down to about 500 meters, or 1500 feet. The findings could potentially reveal hazards from volcanoes, similar to previous work elsewhere in the U.S.

The article tells the story of the lost city of the Pharaoh, a massive Hollywood set built for the 1923 film The Ten Commandments, directed by Cecil B. DeMille. The set, which required over 1,500 carpenters and used more than 25,000 pounds of nails, was built on 22,000 acres of sand dunes near Guadalupe, California. DeMille nearly bankrupted himself and his studio to build the set, and when filming wrapped, he supposedly dynamited the structures and buried them in the sands to prevent other directors from benefiting from his vision.

 Thirty-three years later, a filmmaker named Peter Brosnan heard a story about the buried remains of the set and became determined to find and excavate it. He spent several years searching for clues and finally discovered the set's location in 1983. The discovery made headlines around the world, and Brosnan received funding and support from various organizations to excavate the set and make a documentary about it. However, he faced constant challenges with funding and permitting, and by the mid-1990s, he had given up the dig.

 In 2010, a woman offered to fund the project, and Brosnan was able to excavate most of a sphinx in 2011. He has since put together a rough cut of the documentary and is looking for distributors and considering the film festival circuit. The Dunes Center in Guadalupe, which is responsible for the conservation of the dunes where the set is buried, is currently displaying parts of one of the large plaster sphinxes and smaller relics that have been successfully pulled from the sand. However, the ruins may not survive another 92 years, as powerful storms have shifted the sands and exposed more of the set to the elements. The Dunes Center needs $100,000 to unearth another sphinx before it's too late.

 In recent years, a sphinx statue was unearthed in the dunes, and a company called Applied Earthworks is now using aerial photography to help the Dunes Center find more artifacts buried in the sands. The goal is to align historical photographs of the camp with current features on the ground to relocate the location of the set. The studio had a contract to return the area to its natural state once filming was complete, but evidence shows that it did not happen. The search for more artifacts is ongoing.

The owner of the Deepwater Horizon drilling rig, involved in the largest oil spill in U.S. history, criticized the six-month ban on deepwater drilling imposed by the U.S. government. Transocean Ltd. President Steven Newman stated that there were measures the Obama administration could implement immediately to allow the industry to resume work without the arbitrary six-month time limit.

The criticism came as a federal judge in New Orleans began to consider lifting the moratorium, which was imposed after the disaster began. The judge is expected to decide by Wednesday whether to overturn the ban. During a two-hour hearing, plaintiffs' attorney Carl Rosenblum argued that the six-month suspension of drilling work could prove more economically devastating than the spill itself.

On the sidelines of an oil conference in London, BP PLC, which owns the Deepwater Horizon rig, pledged to speed up the payment of claims from the $20 billion fund set up to compensate oil spill victims. Meanwhile, Kenneth Feinberg, who has been tapped by the White House to run the fund, said many people are in desperate financial straits and need immediate relief.

BP said it has spent $2 billion fighting the spill for the last two months and compensating victims, with no end in sight. It's likely to be at least August before crews finish two relief wells that are the best chance of stopping the flow of oil. The British oil giant released its latest tally of response costs, including $105 million paid out so far to 32,000 claimants.

The government sent BP a $51.4 million bill for the response effort. BP has already paid two other bills totaling $70.9 million. Shares of BP, which have lost about half their value since the April 20 oil rig disaster that killed 11 workers, fell nearly 3 percent Monday in New York trading to $30.86.

BP chief executive Tony Hayward canceled a scheduled Tuesday appearance at the London oil conference, citing his commitment to the Gulf relief effort. The last-minute pullout followed stinging criticism of Hayward's attendance at a yacht race on the Isle of Wight off the coast of southern England on Saturday.

Obama's administration has been struggling to show it is responding forcefully to the spill, which has gushed anywhere from 68 million to 126 million gallons of oil into the Gulf. As part of that effort, the Interior Department halted the approval of any new permits for deepwater drilling and suspended drilling at 33 existing exploratory wells in the Gulf.

However, a lawsuit filed by Hornbeck Offshore Services of Covington, La., claims the government arbitrarily imposed the moratorium without any proof that the operations posed a threat. Hornbeck says the moratorium could cost Louisiana thousands of jobs and millions of dollars in lost wages. During Monday's hearing, U.S. District Judge Martin Feldman asked a government lawyer why the Interior Department decided to suspend deepwater drilling after the rig explosion when it didn't bar oil tankers from Alaskan waters after the Exxon Valdez spill in 1989 or take similar actions in the wake of other industrial accidents.

The judge is expected to rule on whether to overturn the ban by Wednesday. If the ban is lifted, it remains to be seen whether the industry will be able to resume operations without further incidents.

The Jefferson Memorial in Washington D.C., a prominent landmark, has been affected by a colony of microscopic organisms known as biofilm, causing the once gleaming white rotunda to darken. The biofilm, a combination of algae, bacteria, and fungi, is proving challenging for the National Park Service (NPS) as they investigate treatment methods.

The blackened appearance of the memorial is not unique; biofilm can be found on various monuments worldwide, including the Lincoln Memorial, Congressional Cemetery, and even on monuments in Egypt. The presence of nutrients and a suitable environment for growth, such as stone, is a common factor in the existence of many biofilms. In the case of the Jefferson Memorial, the erosion of marble through natural weathering may have contributed to its development.

The NPS has formed a multi-disciplinary team of conservators, architects, and molecular biologists to study the growth on the Jefferson Memorial and test potential treatment options. Treatment of biofilm is difficult due to the lack of a permanent removal method and the need to avoid further damage to the soft marble of the memorial or encouraging further growth.

Recently, the NPS began testing ten different chemical biocides on small patches affected by biofilm at the base of the Jefferson Memorial. They are also exploring non-traditional treatment options, such as ozonated water and irradiation with lasers. No timeline for treatment has been set, and the chosen treatment method will determine the cost and timeline for restoration.

The National Mall and Memorial Parks, managed by the NPS, preserves, protects, and interprets civic spaces and commemorative works in the heart of Washington D.C., including the Washington Monument, Lincoln Memorial, and Martin Luther King Jr. Memorial. The Jefferson Memorial, dedicated in 1943, has been affected by biofilm since less than a decade ago, possibly due to decreased air pollution or a unique microclimate near the memorial. The NPS is continuing to study the biofilm and research treatment methods to restore the dome to its original luster while ensuring its long-term preservation.

Talia Jane, a 25-year-old former customer service representative at Eat24, a food-ordering app owned by Yelp, was fired two hours after she publicly admitted on Twitter that she couldn't afford groceries. Jane moved to San Francisco in August to work for the company, but struggled to make ends meet due to the high cost of living in the city. She earned $12.25 an hour, or $8.15 after tax, and had to factor in more than $200 per month in transportation fees. Jane had also planned to find a co-worker to room with her, but discovered many of them were either living at home or unable to afford the rent.

Jane's struggles were detailed in a Medium post entitled "An Open Letter To My CEO," which went into detail about her struggles making ends meet. The post has been shared across the tech world on Twitter and has been viewed more than 85,000 times. In the post, Jane criticized Yelp for its low pay and high turnover rate of employees in her position.

After publishing the post, Jane said her company email account stopped working two hours later, and she was told by her manager and HR that the letter and what she wrote violated Yelp's terms of conduct. Yelp CEO Jeremy Stoppelman took to Twitter to address the post, signaling that the company would like to make the issue around housing costs, rather than Yelp.

In a statement to BuzzFeed News, a Yelp spokesperson said, "We do not comment on personnel issues. However, we did agree with many of the points in Ms. Jane’s post and we viewed it as her real, personal narrative about what it’s like to live in the Bay Area. Most importantly, it’s an important example of freedom of speech." The spokesperson also confirmed that the company is expanding its Eat24 customer support team into its Phoenix office, where it will pay the same wage.

Jane's story has sparked a conversation about the high cost of living in the Bay Area and the struggles of low-wage workers in the tech industry. It has also been criticized by some as an example of an entitled millennial complaining about a job they didn't want in the first place. However, many have praised Jane for speaking out about her experiences and drawing attention to the issue of affordable housing in the Bay Area.

On May 21, 2014, a fatal bus accident occurred on the I-10 near the California-Arizona border, killing four passengers and injuring several others. Images from the scene showed the large metal pipes that likely caused the accident. The California Highway Patrol reported that three passengers were airlifted, four others were transported in ambulances to hospitals, and fourteen others were transported by bus to a hospital for evaluation of minor injuries. The truck that scattered the pipes was operated by VG Transport, based in Rialto, east of Los Angeles. Federal safety records show that VG Transport has not been involved in any crashes reported to state officials over the past two years, but the driver of the truck was found to have driven eight hours without a break and operated a truck without undergoing periodic inspections during a random inspection in October 2013.

The bus was operated by El Paso-Los Angeles Limousine Express Inc., which received a "satisfactory" safety rating as of its last review in February. The company's 55 vehicles have been involved in five crashes since June 2012, one of which involved a single death.

The accident occurred around 2:15 a.m. just west of Blythe, near the Arizona border, where the eastbound truck's spilled cargo obstructed both lanes in each direction. The article discusses two separate but interconnected topics: the disappearance of two sisters in the U.S. and the preservation of Jeddah's Al-Balad heritage site using modern technology.

Regarding the missing sisters, they moved to the U.S. in mid-2015, and their mother reported them missing to the police in August. The family sought asylum in the U.S., and the Saudi government allegedly ordered them to return home. The investigation is ongoing.

Moving on to the preservation of Al-Balad, the ancient port center of Jeddah, it has been a UNESCO Cultural Heritage Site since 2014. Despite its historical significance, many of its buildings have been lost due to fire and disrepair. A Saudi-based company, FalconViz, is using state-of-the-art drone technology and Autodesk software to document and register these historical buildings for future generations.

Founded in the 7th century C.E., Al-Balad once served as the center of trade and commerce for Jeddah. Over time, many of its ancient walls and souq were torn down due to weathering and the construction of modern buildings. What remains are unique remnants of ancient building styles seldom seen elsewhere in Saudi Arabia.

Preserving these ancient buildings comes with challenges, particularly due to the tight spaces between buildings. Traditional methods would be time-consuming, labor-intensive, and inaccurate. However, with the advent of laser-scanning technology and photogrammetry, the process has become more efficient. FalconViz, with its expertise in drone technology, can now document previously inaccessible areas of Al-Balad for more accurate preservation.

Each drone sweep produces dozens of images of a building, creating a complex point cloud of data. This data is then imported into Autodesk software to create detailed 3D models that preserve even the minutest structural details. These models can be used for various purposes, including running stress tests, planning emergency responses, and generating accurate as-built plans.

The preservation of Al-Balad's historical buildings is crucial as they serve as a cultural symbol and a reminder of Saudi Arabia before the oil era. FalconViz's mission is to "digitally document the world" and assist in the preservation of cultural treasures. The same technology used for preservation is also used for the development of modern urban infrastructure, planning, and construction. This diverse dual use of technology is helping to preserve these ancient structures and restore them to their former glory.

Henri Bendel, a 123-year-old luxury retailer, is closing its doors in January 2019 due to declining sales. The decision was made by parent company L Brands, which acquired Bendel in 1985. The closure includes the iconic Fifth Avenue store in New York, as well as the brand's e-commerce business and all 23 brick-and-mortar stores. Bendel, known for its designer purses and shoes, was an early pioneer in the American fashion industry and introduced Coco Chanel's designs to the U.S. in 1913. The brand was founded in 1895 by Henri Bendel and became one of the first luxury retailers to open a flagship store on Fifth Avenue in 1912. L Brands, which also owns Victoria's Secret and Bath & Body Works, said the closure is to improve company profitability and focus on its larger brands with greater growth potential. The decision comes amid a difficult year for L Brands due to increased retail competition.

The death of Kayla Mueller, an American aid worker who was held captive by the Islamic State (ISIS) for over two years, was confirmed on Tuesday, February 10, 2015. The news came after her family received photographs of her corpse from ISIS, which showed her with bruises but did not provide clear evidence of how she died.

Mueller was kidnapped in August 2013 while leaving a hospital operated by Doctors Without Borders in Aleppo, Syria. During her captivity, she was believed to have been given to a commander in ISIS and was sometimes in the company of an ISIS leader who was being tracked by U.S. intelligence. However, there were no ground-level intelligence sources or American spies in Syria, so the U.S. relied on airborne collection platforms like satellites and drones to gather information.

Mueller's family received a proof of life last year, but there was no indication of her whereabouts since then. ISIS claimed that she was killed in a coalition airstrike launched by Jordan, but U.S. officials have not been able to confirm this account. The U.S. government has not shared details about Mueller's time in ISIS captivity out of respect for her family, but has not corroborated any theories about her conditions throughout her captivity.

Mueller's family released a letter she wrote from her cell last year, in which she said she was "in a safe location, completely unharmed [and] healthy." She also wrote that she was "treated with the utmost respect [and] kindness." Mueller's friends and family expressed their grief and praised her empathy and compassion.

President Obama called Mueller "an outstanding young woman and a great spirit" and said that her spirit would live on. He also said that the U.S. government had done everything it could to rescue Mueller and other hostages. The family of another American aid worker who was captured by ISIS and murdered by the group, Abdul-Rahman Kassig, offered their condolences to the Mueller family.

Mueller's death has raised awareness about Syrian refugees, with her family and friends expressing hope that her death would achieve what she had worked for before her kidnapping. The White House released a statement of condolence from President Obama, in which he said that the country shared in the Mueller family's grief. Mueller's family also released letters she wrote to her family, including one on her father’s birthday in 2011, in which she wrote, "I find God in suffering. I’ve known for some time what my life’s work is, using my hands as tools to relieve suffering."

North Korea attempted to launch an intermediate-range missile on April 15, the birthday of the country's "eternal president," Kim Il Sung, but the attempt failed. The missile, believed to be a Musudan, was launched from the east coast of North Korea at around 5:30 a.m. local time, but it deviated from a normal trajectory and is presumed to have failed. South Korea's military remains on high alert, as North Korea has been making claims about technological advances and is believed to be working towards the goal of sending a nuclear-tipped missile to the U.S. mainland. The failed test is seen as a setback for North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, and it has drawn criticism from major ally China. The U.S. Defense Department called the test a "fiery, catastrophic" failure, and further tests are expected. The failed test heightens the possibility that North Korea will conduct a fifth nuclear test within weeks. The U.S.-based 38 North website has seen activity at North Korea's nuclear site based on satellite imagery, and the possibility of a fifth nuclear test "cannot be ruled out." North Korea is banned by U.N. Security Council resolutions from launching ballistic missiles or carrying out nuclear tests, but it continues to do so. The international community has responded to North Korea's latest provocations with tough sanctions aimed at cutting off the state's ability to procure parts and finance its weapons-of-mass-destruction program. The failed missile test comes amid heightened tensions, as North Korea prepares for two key events: the anniversary of Kim Il Sung's birth and the first congress of the communist Workers' Party in 36 years. Kim Jong Un is expected to use the congress to bolster his legitimacy.

The photograph of a 9-year-old Indian boy named Lakhan Kale, who is disabled and tied to a bus stop in Mumbai, has sparked outrage due to the lack of resources for the disabled in India. Lakhan, who suffers from cerebral palsy, epilepsy, and is deaf and mute, was tethered to the bus stop by his grandmother, Sakkubai Kale, when she worked selling toys and flower garlands. The boy's father died several years ago, and his mother abandoned the family.

Concerns among charities and the police led to Lakhan being taken into care at a government-run institution. Activists say his plight on the streets comes as little surprise in India, where those with disabilities face daily stigma and discrimination and a lack of facilities to assist them. Lakhan's grandmother, who raised him on the street, said she tied him up to keep him safe while she worked.

Social worker Meena Mutha has since managed to place Lakhan in a state-run south Mumbai home, which takes in a range of needy children from the disabled to the destitute. However, activists and charities argue that there is a need for the government to provide more residential centers for children like Lakhan. Across India, the 40 to 60 million people with disabilities often face similar struggles to get the help they need.

A long-awaited bill was introduced into the Indian parliament in February aiming to give disabled people equal rights, but it has yet to be passed. Lawyer Rajive Raturi, who handled disability cases at the Human Rights Law Network, said he hoped the new parliament, dominated by the Bharatiya Janata Party, would listen to the stakeholders and make a decision. The bill, if passed, could change attitudes towards people with disabilities and provide them with equal rights, including access to education, employment, and legal redress against discrimination.

The article discusses allegations of sexual misconduct against celebrity chef Mario Batali, who has stepped away from his business empire following accusations from nine women. The article focuses on incidents that occurred at The Spotted Pig, a New York City restaurant that Batali frequently visited and was an investor in.

Trish Nelson, a former waitress at The Spotted Pig, describes Batali as a "monster" and recounts multiple instances of inappropriate behavior, including groping and attempting to kiss her. Other employees, including Jamie Seet and Natalie Saibel, also describe similar experiences with Batali.

The article also discusses the workplace culture at The Spotted Pig, with employees describing a lack of boundaries, emotional abuse, and intimidation. Ken Friedman, co-owner of The Spotted Pig, is accused of sexual assault by former employee Erin Fein, who says he assaulted her in his car outside the restaurant in 2014.

The article also discusses the ongoing criminal investigation into Batali by the New York Police Department, and the impact that these allegations are having on the restaurant industry as a whole. Trish Nelson and other women who have spoken out about their experiences at The Spotted Pig say they are doing so in an effort to give a voice to women in the industry and to prevent similar incidents from happening in the future.
