The investigation into the e-mail exchanges between General John R. Allen, the top NATO commander in Afghanistan, and Jill Kelley, a Tampa socialite, is ongoing at the Pentagon. The inquiry was initiated after the FBI discovered the e-mails in the course of an investigation into anonymous e-mails sent to Kelley warning her to stay away from David H. Petraeus, then the C.I.A. director. The e-mails between Allen and Kelley, which cover a period of two and a half years starting in 2010, are potentially "inappropriate" and number in the hundreds. The investigation is being conducted by 15 investigators working seven days a week, and they have narrowed their focus to 60 to 70 e-mails that "bear a fair amount of scrutiny."

The investigation is delaying and could derail General Allen's appointment to be the NATO supreme allied commander in Europe. The defense official did not disclose the content of the e-mails, but they could potentially violate Defense Department policy, government regulations, or military law. The violations could range from inappropriate language on a government computer to adultery, prohibited under military law; more than an incidental use of government property for personal matters; and security breaches. However, there is no evidence so far that there have been security violations.

General Allen, who is married and the father of two, is cooperating with the investigation and has said through associates that he did not commit adultery. The inquiry does not appear to have progressed to interviews with General Allen or Ms. Kelley, 37, the wife of a cancer surgeon and the mother of three. The defense official said investigators were trying to determine whether the e-mails violated Defense Department policy, government regulations, or military law.

The investigation has caused delays in General Allen's appointment to be the NATO supreme allied commander in Europe, and it is unclear what he will do when he returns to the United States at the end of the year. Gen. Joseph F. Dunford Jr., who has been nominated to succeed General Allen as part of a regular military rotation, is expected to be confirmed by the Senate before the end of the year and to be in Kabul by February.

Jill Kelley has hired a top Washington attorney and is trying to change the narrative about her friendship with top military brass. Kelley became the focus of national media attention earlier this month, and she and her husband befriended Petraeus and General Allen when the generals served at U.S. Central Command, which is headquartered at Tampa's MacDill Air Force Base. Kelley became an unofficial social ambassador for the base and was well known around Tampa's social scene.

There have been conflicting accounts of the nature of the e-mails between Kelley and General Allen. Some have called a few of the emails between the two "flirtatious," but sources close to Kelley say they were not. The scandal this week cost Kelley her appointment as an honorary consul for the South Korean government, which she had gotten because of her friendship with Petraeus. The Koreans said she had misused the title in her personal business dealings.

Kelley's attorney has accused Tampa attorney Barry Cohen of breaking attorney-client privilege by publicly speaking about conversations he had with Kelley in 2009 while representing her in a dispute she had with a tenant. In those conversations, they discussed her friendships with various military personnel. Cohen said Tuesday evening that he had not seen Lowell's complaint letter and that Kelley had "lost the battle in the court of public opinion."

A woman, suspected of impersonating a Target employee, is being sought by Fairfax County police in Virginia for stealing over $40,000 worth of iPhones from a Richmond Highway store on March 15. The suspect, who was familiar with store procedures and the location of iPhones in the stockroom, managed to gain access to the stockroom, take the iPhones, and leave the store with them. Surveillance footage shows the woman leaving the store in a Volvo station wagon. Anyone with information about the case can contact Fairfax County police at 703-691-2131. The police have released surveillance footage of the suspect leaving the store for public assistance in identifying her.

The iPad made its debut during the 2010 Oscars, with an ad showcasing its features and Steve Jobs' presence on the red carpet. The ad, while following Apple's creative style, has sparked buzz and speculation about potential new features as the April 3 release approaches. Jobs, a board member at Disney, was at the event as Disney produced the Oscar-winning animation "Up." The ad has sparked discussions about the iPad's appeal and potential ownership.

In the aftermath of Hurricane Sandy, voting faced numerous challenges in New York and New Jersey on Tuesday, with long lines, lack of electricity, and confusion plaguing polling sites. Despite efforts to help storm victims vote, such as shuttle buses, combined voting locations, and an executive order allowing storm victims to vote outside of their district, problems arose at many locations.

At the Scholars’ Academy on Beach 104th St. in Rockaway Park, several voting locations were consolidated into one tent-covered polling site, but poll workers arrived to find that generators, heaters, and lights were missing. Marie Howley of Rockaway Park, who had driven in from Rockville Centre on Long Island, was the only complainant, citing a lack of sufficient light in the tents.

In hard-hit Hoboken, various issues caused long waits for voters to cast ballots at a combined polling location for two districts on Grand Street. The doors of the Multi Service Center of Hoboken weren’t open at 6 a.m., poll workers struggled to find a key to open the operational voting machines, and voters were told they might have to cast paper ballots.

In Park Slope, voters who usually cast their ballots at John Jay High School, now serving as a shelter for storm evacuees, were directed to PS 282, more than a half a mile away. Some residents had received fliers passed out on Monday by Assemblyman James F. Brennan redirecting them to the new site. Lines stretched outside the school and around the block, but displaced voters got a break and were directed to a separate entrance where lines were shorter.

At the Jacqueline Kennedy Onassis High School in midtown Manhattan, polling workers ran out of affidavit ballot envelopes needed for voters who weren’t registered at the polling site. Voters were instructed to try other polling places in midtown.

Despite these issues, voting was going smoothly at some sites. Voters have no wait time to use a polling booth at one Teterboro site that is accepting votes from displaced Moonachie residents.

New Jersey residents who chose to vote electronically were facing confusion and uncertainty whether their votes would be counted. Kate Supple, a 29-year-old Jersey City resident who was displaced by Sandy and staying in Manhattan, emailed her application to the Hudson County clerk Monday but has yet to receive her ballot and was worried that her vote wouldn’t be counted.

President Obama thanked his supporters, spoke about unity, and said he wants to work with Republicans and Democrats to move the country forward. He also said he plans to meet with Mitt Romney to discuss how they can work together.

Massachusetts voters flocked to the polls today, drawn by the chance to vote in sharply contested races for president and US Senate. Many precincts reported long lines and steady turnout. In Waltham, where voters began arriving at 6:30 a.m., turnout was strong. Jilda Diorio, 67, voted Republican, saying it was “time for a change as far as the presidency goes,” and she liked how US Senator Scott Brown, who is being challenged by Democrat Elizabeth Warren, “worked across the aisle.” Terry Goodridge, on the other hand, voted Democratic, saying Obama had “accomplished a lot,” and as for Romney, “we’ve had our fill of him.” In Copley Square around noon, the line to vote stretched out of the Boston Public Library and onto the sidewalk. Jim Riordan, 55, said he had waited in line two hours to cast his ballot. Riordan, an independent, said he voted for Obama, who by his reckoning “did a good job,” and Warren. Sarah Godfrey, 33, said she planned to split her ticket by voting for Romney for president and Warren for Senate. “I’m just not happy with the situation right now, and if things aren’t going well, it doesn’t make sense to vote for the incumbent,” said Godfrey, who voted for Obama in 2008. “I’m not saying it’s necessarily Obama’s fault, but maybe we can give somebody else a shot this time.” As of 3 p.m., 148,133 people had cast their vote in Boston, representing 38.26 percent of registered voters, according to the city. Turnout is slightly lower than during the last presidential election. In Belmont, a cheer went up outside the Beech Street Center after Romney, a former Massachusetts governor, and his wife, Ann, cast their votes in their hometown. Brown voted in Wrentham around 7:30 a.m. and said he expected the election, which is considered to be extremely close by experts, will have a clear winner by 10 p.m. tonight. Some 200 people were already in line waiting to vote when Brown arrived. “I’ve never seen it this crowded before,’’ Brown said. “And I’ve been here for 25 years.’’ In Cambridge, Warren cast her vote around 7:45 a.m., and went to the polling place accompanied by her husband and granddaughter. “This campaign was never about me,” Warren told reporters after voting. “This campaign was about all of us, about all the people who invested in it, all the people who truly believed that if you got out there and worked together you can make a difference.”

In the document, Senator John McCain expressed concerns about the Republican Party's chances in the upcoming Senate elections, predicting that the results might not be clear until after election night due to close races in California and Washington. McCain, a co-sponsor of campaign finance legislation, expressed concerns about the large amounts of money being spent in the midterm elections, particularly from anonymous sources and unions.

On the issue of the Bush era tax cuts, McCain suggested extending them for a couple of years before addressing the issue again. He also expressed support for former Alaska Governor Sarah Palin, calling her an "outstanding candidate" for the Republican presidential nomination in 2012, but stopped short of endorsing her. McCain stated that it was too early to pick winners and losers in the political race.

The U.S. Supreme Court heard arguments in a case challenging the redistricting plan passed by Wisconsin's Republican-controlled legislature in 2011, which was found to violate the Constitution by the lower court due to partisan gerrymandering. The case, Gill v. Whitford, could have far-reaching national implications, as a ruling in favor of the Democrats could require states to follow new rules when drawing congressional and legislative districts, limiting their abilities to give edges to either party. The case is closely divided, with liberal justices expressing openness to the idea that courts should intervene when lawmakers draw election maps that greatly favor their party, while conservatives are skeptical that judges can come up with a way to determine whether and when legislators have gone too far. The stakes are high for Wisconsin's Democrats, who have been out of power for seven years, and the case could have a broad national impact if Wisconsin's maps are thrown out. The Supreme Court is expected to rule by summer.

In the Rio Olympics of 2016, two little-known middle distance runners, Nikki Hamblin from New Zealand and Abbey D'Agostino from the USA, displayed extraordinary sportsmanship during a 5000m heat. After a collision, D'Agostino helped Hamblin back on her feet despite suffering an anterior cruciate ligament injury. Both athletes completed the race together, embodying the Olympic spirit of excellence, friendship, and respect. Their act of kindness and selflessness earned them the Pierre de Coubertin medal, reserved for those who demonstrate the Olympic spirit.

In a separate incident, the Norwegian men's handball team was also honored for their sportsmanship. Despite losing their Olympic dream due to an illegal player on the German team during a European championship match, they chose not to protest, allowing Germany to qualify instead.

These acts of fair play and human spirit underscore the importance of sportsmanship beyond the medals and records set during the Olympic Games. The International Olympic Committee and the International Fair Play Committee recognized these champions of sportsmanship, celebrating their inspiring moments of fair play.

Sheila Mullowney, a blogger, is embarking on a cross-country bicycle journey to prove her love, regain her health, and lose weight. The journey is documented on her website, FatGuyAcrossAmerica, and email notifications are available for updates. The journey has been challenging due to medical issues and a bent rim on her bicycle, but she is currently in Rhode Island receiving support from Newport Bicycle. Eric Hites, a 560-pound man from Danville, is also on a similar journey across the United States to lose weight and save his marriage. He started two weeks ago in Falmouth, Massachusetts, and has already lost 60 pounds, but a bent rim on his bicycle has kept him in Tiverton, Rhode Island since late last week. Newport Bicycle is outfitting him with a new bike that can withstand his weight so he can continue his journey. Hites hopes to lose hundreds of pounds and get down to 300 pounds, and he has a website called Fat Guy Across America where people can follow his journey. Hites' journey began when he was dropped off by his dad on the side of the road in Massachusetts with his $170 bike last month, but he has since lost 60 pounds and gained national attention. He is determined to complete his journey and has received support from various individuals and organizations along the way. Both Sheila Mullowney and Eric Hites are using their journeys to inspire others and raise awareness about health and weight loss.

In a controversial turn of events during an NFL game between the Kansas City Chiefs and the New England Patriots, Chiefs safety Husain Abdullah, a devout Muslim, was penalized for unsportsmanlike conduct after he dropped to his knees in prayer following an interception. The league's rule book prohibits players from celebrating while on the ground, but the NFL later acknowledged that the penalty was unwarranted, stating that the "officiating mechanic in this situation is not to flag a player who goes to the ground as part of religious expression."

Abdullah, who took a year off from football to make a pilgrimage to Mecca, had promised himself that he would pray in the end zone if he ever scored a touchdown. The interception was the sixth of his career, and the football he intercepted from Tom Brady will be kept as a memento.

The Council on American-Islamic Relations (CAIR) issued a statement asking the NFL to clarify its policy on prayer to prevent the appearance of a double standard. Chiefs coach Andy Reid, who had two priests present at his postgame news conference, expressed support for Abdullah, stating that "when you go to Mecca, you should have the privilege to slide anywhere you want to slide."

The penalty sparked controversy on social media, with some expressing concern that the NFL might try to fine Abdullah for his celebration. Despite the penalty, Abdullah's interception was still a significant moment in the game, with the Chiefs ultimately emerging victorious with a score of 41-14.

Amanda Knox, the American college student who was convicted of murder in Italy in 2009, has returned to writing as a freelance journalist for the West Seattle Herald. Knox's roommate, Meredith Kercher, was found dead in 2007, and Knox and her boyfriend, Raffaele Sollecito, were arrested and charged with the murder. They were acquitted in 2011, but the conviction was upheld in 2014, and Knox has not been extradited to Italy while the case is appealed. Knox has been working as a freelance reporter for the West Seattle Herald for a few months, and the paper asked her to write for them because of her writing skills, not her notoriety. Knox is covering a variety of topics, including human-interest stories and local theater productions. The Herald is aware that Knox's celebrity status will generate outside attention, but they hired her because she is a resident of West Seattle and a qualified writer. Knox is currently covering a high-school production of Tom Stoppard's Rosencrantz and Guildenstern Are Dead for the paper. The play is a re-envisioning of the tragedy Hamlet from the perspective of two minor characters, and Finley, the literature and drama teacher, argues that high school is an appropriate setting for exploring the questioning of reality and identity. The performances are scheduled for November 6, 7, 8 and 12, 13, 14 at West Seattle High School's campus.

In a historic move, Oxford Dictionaries announced that their "Word of the Year" for 2015 is not a traditional word but an emoji, specifically the "Face With Tears of Joy" emoji. This decision reflects the growing popularity and cultural significance of emojis in digital communication. The emoji, also known as LOL Emoji or Laughing Emoji, was found to be the most commonly used in the U.S. and the U.K., where Oxford is based.

Oxford University Press, the publisher of Oxford English Dictionary and Oxford Dictionaries Online, partnered with SwiftKey to determine the most popular emoji of the year. The "Face With Tears of Joy" emoji accounted for nearly 20% of all emoji use in the U.S. and the U.K. The runner-up in the U.S. was the number symbol.

Caspar Grathwohl, the president of Oxford Dictionaries, explained that the choice of an emoji reflects the open and expressive nature of modern digital communication. He added that the emoji embodies the playfulness and intimacy that characterizes emoji-using culture.

Though this marks a significant recognition for emojis, Oxford has not yet added or defined any emoji in their actual databases. The word emoji has been in both the OED and Oxford Dictionaries Online since 2013.

Japanese telecommunications planner Shigetaka Kurita is credited with inventing emojis in 1999. The name for these alphanumeric images comes from combining the Japanese words for picture (e-) and character (moji).

The shortlist for Oxford's Word of the Year included terms like ad blocker, Brexit, Dark Web, lumbersexual, on fleek, refugee, sharing economy, and they (singular). However, the "Face With Tears of Joy" emoji won out as the 2015 "word" of the year for both the U.S. and the U.K.

This marks the 12th year that Oxford has selected an official word of the year, following words like vape and selfie in recent years. The selection process involves a team of lexicographers, consultants, and other staff members who discuss several options and select a word, expression, or in this case, emoji, that reflects the ethos, mood, or preoccupations of the year.

The Mets' owners, Fred Wilpon and Saul Katz, have settled a lawsuit with Irving Picard, the trustee for victims of Bernie Madoff's Ponzi scheme, for $162 million. The settlement, brokered by former New York governor Mario Cuomo, allows the Mets' owners to apply for reimbursement of $178 million in losses from certain funds, reducing their actual payment to Picard. The settlement talks were initiated due to concerns over a potential trial's impact on the owners' reputations. The lawsuit sought to recover $386 million, but the settlement amounts to a swap: Picard dropped claims that the men ignored Madoff warnings, while Wilpon and Katz agreed to pay back fictitious profits from net winner accounts from 2002 to '08. The actual payment to Picard will be a fraction of the settlement amount, as the Wilpons will be reimbursed for losses from their loser funds, and the settlement terms allow for deductions from the owed amount if Picard disburses funds to the Wilpons. The Mets still face significant financial trouble, with losses of $120 million over the past two years, payroll cuts, and a portion of the team up for sale.

In a forthcoming Marietta City Council meeting, the council will decide on a retired police officer's request to keep his K-9 partner, Ajax, who is currently considered city property under Ohio law and set for auction. Retired officer Matthew Hickey, who recently left the force due to an injury, initially believed he could keep Ajax by paying the working dog's value, estimated between $3,500 and $4,000. However, Ohio law mandates that police dogs be treated as city property and sold at auction if their handlers leave the force and a new handler is unavailable.

Hickey, who considers Ajax a family member, has been supported by a GoFundMe campaign that has raised over $70,000. The city council will consider options for Hickey and Ajax during a meeting on Thursday, and it has been announced that the council will offer Hickey an auxiliary officer position to enable him to keep Ajax. The GoFundMe page has been verified, ensuring the funds will be directly transferred to the intended recipient.

Chris Brown has spoken with New York Police Department detectives regarding a bar fight that left him with a gash on his chin. Sources claim Chris' lawyer, Mark Geragos, provided the NYPD with evidence implicating Drake and Meek Mill as the aggressors. Chris is considered a witness and a victim, not a suspect, while Drake is reportedly cooperating with authorities. The incident may have been instigated by someone in Chris' camp.

Separately, Rihanna is struggling with her busy schedule. The singer, who is working on her seventh album and has recently ventured into acting, has been hospitalized for fatigue. Despite concerns from fans, Rihanna attributes her health issues and weight loss to her demanding schedule, expressing a desire to regain her previous physique.

The town of Langley, located on Whidbey Island, is facing an unprecedented infestation of wild rabbits. The bunnies, believed to be the descendants of a few European hares that escaped from the fairgrounds decades ago, are causing significant damage to the community. The rabbits are burrowing holes in the middle school football field, destroying building foundations, and posing health risks to people and pets. The critters have found a safe haven in the city, away from predators, and some residents are feeding them, exacerbating the problem. The school district is considering spending $60,000 to fence the property off, and a community meeting is scheduled for October 7 to discuss solutions. The rabbits are adorable but are causing significant issues for the community, and some residents are advocating for more natural solutions, such as installing pavers and chicken wire around potential breeding grounds, rather than extermination. The city's mayor has decided not to hire a trapper or authorize the slaying of rabbits due to political concerns. Some residents are frustrated with the damage caused by the rabbits, while others are feeding and sheltering them. There are concerns about coyotes preying on the rabbits and eventually moving on to household pets, but there is little evidence to support this claim. Trapping and hunting rabbits is a complex issue with different rules for different species, and it is not a popular solution among some residents and the police.

Google reported a significant increase in profits for the third quarter of 2011, with net income surging to $2.73 billion on net revenue of $7.51 billion. This marks a 26% increase from the same period in 2010. The company's stock price has risen by more than 6% as a result, reaching $595.

Google's CEO, Larry Page, described the quarter as "great" and highlighted the growth of Google+, the company's new social networking service. There are now over 40 million users on Google+, with numbers growing rapidly.

The profits come amidst big changes at Google, including its plan to acquire Motorola Mobility. Despite these changes and moves into mobile technology, Google remains a search advertising-based business, with a 33% year-over-year revenue increase to $9.72 billion.

Google currently employs around 31,353 people worldwide, up from 28,768 at the end of June. The company, which employs about 1,000 people in the Seattle area, is expanding its real estate in the area.

However, the report also reveals that the U.S. Internal Revenue Service is auditing Google's tax practices, specifically its method of avoiding federal income taxes by shifting profits to offshore subsidiaries. The IRS is scrutinizing how Google valued software rights and other intellectual property it licensed abroad.

The audit is not public, but it is known that the IRS has requested information from Google about its offshore deals after three acquisitions, including its $1.65 billion purchase of YouTube. The transfer of these rights overseas has enabled Google to attribute earnings to foreign units that pay lower taxes.

Google has been using a pair of strategies called the “Double Irish” and “Dutch Sandwich” to cut its worldwide tax bill by about $1 billion a year. This involves moving profits through units in Ireland, the Netherlands, and Bermuda. Google reported an effective tax rate of 18.8% in the second quarter, less than half the average combined U.S. and state statutory rate of 39.2%.

The IRS is increasing its scrutiny of multinational companies' tax practices, with a focus on income shifting to offshore tax havens. In May, the IRS appointed its first transfer-pricing director, Samuel Maruca, and announced the assignment of additional agents and attorneys to examine a few large companies as part of a pilot program.

The French tax authority also began reviewing Google’s income shifting in December, examining transactions between the company’s French and Irish subsidiaries. The French inquiry was prompted by the October 2010 Bloomberg article on the company’s tax-cutting strategy.

Google's taxes have also drawn government scrutiny from the Securities and Exchange Commission. Last December, the SEC asked the company for "greater detail" about the profit it said it had earned in countries with lower tax rates and the impact on its effective tax rate. The SEC completed its review of Google’s filings in February, but it is unclear what action, if any, the agency took.

The International Space Station (ISS) experienced a cooling system malfunction on Wednesday, with one of its external loops shutting down due to a temperature limit. NASA stated that the crew and the station were never in any danger, but an emergency spacewalk may be necessary to fix the issue. The problem is suspected to be caused by a malfunctioning flow control valve for the station's ammonia coolant. Engineers are currently trying to determine whether a software fix can restore the valve's functionality or if a spacewalk will be required. The ISS's life support system remains operational, and non-critical systems have been turned off in certain modules as a precaution. The ISS's current mission, Expedition 38, is scheduled to end in March 2014, and the station is planned to operate through 2020, with potential extensions. The crew consists of six astronauts from the US, Russia, and Japan.

Shermain Miles, a 52-year-old woman from Chicago, was released from prison after serving a year for assaulting a City Council member. With 396 arrests since 1978, Miles has struggled with substance abuse and mental health issues, but she is determined to turn her life around. On her train journey home, Miles expressed hope for a new start, stating that she has given up drugs and alcohol permanently. She plans to move to a residential home for ex-inmates in Humboldt Park. Despite her past, Miles was well-behaved during her latest prison term, and there is optimism that she will succeed this time. However, some remain skeptical, fearing that Miles may return to her old habits.

The transcript of an interview between Nicholas Kristof and Iranian President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad discusses various topics, including the release of American hikers imprisoned in Iran, Iran's nuclear program, human rights abuses, and the political situation in Syria.

Ahmadinejad initially stated that the American hikers would be released soon, but their release did not happen as expected. He claimed that they had entered Iran illegally and would have faced punishment in any country.

Regarding Iran's nuclear program, Ahmadinejad repeated an offer made in a previous interview to stop all nuclear enrichment if the West would supply nuclear fuel enriched to a 20% level. He insisted that Iran would happily give up its enrichment processing if it could get this enriched uranium for "cancer treatment medication."

Ahmadinejad called for Syria to stop its violent crackdown on protesters, but when asked about the difference between his own harsh crackdown on dissidents in Iran, he claimed that many of the dead in Iran were members of security forces, suggesting that protesters were not deliberately targeted.

The interview became more confrontational, with Ahmadinejad denying Iran's involvement in the death of Neda Agha-Soltan, a young woman who was shot and killed during protests in Iran. He suggested that she had been murdered by his opponents, working with the BBC, as part of a bizarre snuff film.

The interview also touched on human rights issues, with Ahmadinejad claiming that Iran is more democratic than the United States and denying that his government had hidden anything related to its nuclear program.

Overall, the interview was characterized by Ahmadinejad's efforts to be friendly and conciliatory, but also by his resistance to tough questions and his tendency to deny or downplay allegations of human rights abuses and nuclear deceptions.

On Tuesday, a suspected car bomb explosion occurred in the Kizilay neighborhood of Ankara, Turkey, near government buildings. The blast, which was likely caused by a bomb in a vehicle, killed three people and injured 15, with five in critical condition. The explosion took place near a primary school and destroyed several parked vehicles. The Turkish Interior Minister, Naim Sahin, stated that it is highly probable that the attack was a terror attack. President Abdullah Gul condemned the attack as a terrorist act. The Kurdish separatists, leftists, and Islamist militants have carried out bomb attacks in Turkish cities in the past. The incident occurred while Prime Minister Tayyip Erdogan was in the United States for talks with President Barack Obama. The explosion comes at a time when Kurdish rebels have escalated their attacks on Turkish targets.

In a recent development, a Twin Cities couple is suing the Minnesota Department of Human Services, the Minnesota Attorney General, and a commissioner with the Mille Lacs Band of Ojibwe to allow the adoption of their child by a white couple. The couple, identified as John and Jane Doe, argue that the requirement to inform their tribes about the adoption violates their constitutional right to due process and equal protection.

The lawsuit challenges federal and state laws enacted in the 1970s and 1980s that aimed to keep Indian children in Indian families. The laws were implemented to address the historical practice of breaking up Indian families by sending their children into institutions or to non-Indian adoptive parents. The couple wants the court to throw out the state’s requirement to inform a tribe of an adoption.

Mark Fiddler, one of the couple's attorneys, stated that Indian parents are the only parents in the state that have the duty to notify about an adoption. He added that if the parents chose to have an abortion, they would not have to tell the tribe. Fiddler noted that if the parents or the adoption agency chose not to tell the tribe, they would open themselves to fraud charges and risk having the adoption voided if the truth were discovered.

Advocates for the law argue that the couple are putting their own interests above the rights of the child, who would be better served with an Indian family. They argue that a tribe plays a strong role as a parent to adopted Indian children, helping to connect them to their culture, which cannot be done by a white family, no matter how caring they are.

Patina Park, an attorney and the executive director of the Minnesota Indian Women’s Resource Center, stated that putting the baby with an Indian family would better serve the child. Sandy White Hawk, who has counseled hundreds of Indians who were adopted into white families, said the rates of suicide and depression among those Indians are high. She said the grief is loss of identity, and non-native homes cannot give an adopted Indian child their culture.

The health commissioner for the Mille Lacs Band of Ojibwe named in the suit, Samuel Moose, did not return a call requesting comment. A spokesman for the band said they have not yet been served with the lawsuit. A spokeswoman for Minnesota’s Department of Human Services declined to comment, saying the agency needed to review the lawsuit. A spokesman from the attorney general’s office declined to comment on the lawsuit, saying the office was improperly listed as a defendant.

The case highlights the ongoing debate over the Indian Child Welfare Act, which could make it difficult for non-Native American families to adopt Native American children. The Bureau of Indian Affairs is pushing for the enforcement, but some argue it's not what's best for the children. Legal documents refer to a little girl named S.A.W., who was almost removed from her foster home because she is 1/128 Native American. It took a battle in court for her to stay with her foster family. Some argue that tribes wait too long to intervene after children have stayed in a stable home for months, causing harm to the children. The Cherokee Nation has stated that rule changes to help enforce the Indian Child Welfare Act are long overdue and necessary to protect the best interest of Indian children and promote the stability and security of Indian tribes and families.

The article discusses New Zealand's ambitious plan to eradicate all invasive vertebrate predators, such as rats, brushtail possums, stoats, and more, from the country by 2050. The goal is to protect the country's rare endemic species and boost its reputation as a destination for unspoiled natural beauty.

The plan is not far-fetched, according to Josh Donlan, director of Advanced Conservation Strategies. Around the world, more than 1,000 islands have been cleared of invasive species through 'mega eradications.' New Zealand, with its leading experts in the field, has carried out more than 200 of them.

However, the size of the current target represents a tremendous leap, as New Zealand's total area is about 268,000 square kilometers, and the country's cities and towns complicate eradication efforts and provide countless places for animals to hide.

To succeed, the project will require public and political support and money. In a 2015 paper, the team estimated the entire cost at around NZ$9 billion (US$6 billion), arguing that the savings to pest-control programs, and the reduction in environmental damage and crop loss, would more than cover the outlay.

The article also discusses the history of invasive species in New Zealand, which has been a poster child for the havoc wreaked by invasive species. For millennia, it was an island of small lizards and flightless birds, such as the iconic kiwi. Since land mammals, including humans, first arrived some 750 years ago, the number of species of native vertebrate fauna has nearly halved — at least 51 species of bird have disappeared in that time.

The mammalian pests are a drain on New Zealand's economy. The government spends around NZ$70 million each year on pest-control programs for animals, and invasive predators cost the country an estimated NZ$3.3 billion a year in lost productivity. Most of the losses come from agriculture, but government officials also worry about the hit to the country's reputation as a destination for unspoiled natural beauty.

The article also highlights the story of Razza, a rat that nearly ended James Russell's scientific career 12 years ago. Russell was studying how rats take hold and become invasive, but Razza evaded capture and swam to a nearby island, causing Russell to hunt the animal for 18 weeks. This experience led to the development of new techniques for tracking and killing a single rodent, which is crucial in efforts to completely eradicate a species.

The article concludes with discussions on new technologies and genetic biocontrols that might be able to suppress invaders by introducing harmful traits. The powerful gene-editing tool CRISPR–Cas9 could be used to disrupt a gene that is vital for survival or reproduction or that makes an animal more susceptible to a certain poison. Then, using what is known as a gene drive, scientists could engineer that gene to spread through the population.

However, gene drives have only been used in the lab and mostly with insects, and there are concerns about reverse invasions and the danger of introducing harmful traits. Another genetic technique, being developed in New Zealand as part of Russell's project, could avoid some of these difficulties. The Trojan Female Technique targets mitochondria, the tiny power plants inside cells. Mutations in mitochondrial DNA can seriously impair the ability of sperm to swim. Because these mutations affect the fitness only of males, and because mitochondria are passed down only through the female line, these traits can survive natural selection. Females carrying the mutations would have sterile male offspring, but their daughters would be able to breed, producing yet more sterile males.

Overall, the article discusses the challenges and opportunities of eradicating invasive species from New Zealand, highlighting the country's unique position in terms of public support for conservation and the need for new technologies and genetic biocontrols to achieve the ambitious goal of being free of invasive vertebrate predators by 2050.

The article discusses the potential security challenges and concerns surrounding the upcoming Sochi Winter Olympics in Russia, particularly the logistical and diplomatic challenges of evacuating American athletes in case of a terrorist attack. The U.S. military has plans to use two warships in the Black Sea and planes on standby in Europe for evacuation, but any American rescue operation would heavily depend on the approval of Russian President Vladimir Putin, who sees the games as a matter of national pride. Experts warn that lone attackers also pose a significant threat to the Games, and fears of Olympic terror have grown in the countdown to the games, which formally open on February 7. The U.S. Olympic Committee has declined to discuss the details of security for the American athletes, but some teams are paying a private company, Global Rescue, for additional security. The article also mentions that the biathlon team has bought satellite phones for its coaches and is recommending that traveling families of its athletes purchase medical and evacuation insurance. Some American athletes have expressed concern about safety issues in Russia, with at least two members of the high-profile hockey team telling their families not to travel to Sochi to cheer them on. The article concludes by discussing the heightened security measures being taken by Russia for the games, with 40,000 police officers and 70,000 soldiers being used for security, as well as the confidence of some nations, such as Israel and Germany, in Russian security agencies to provide adequate protection for the Games.

In a groundbreaking study conducted by UBC's School of Health and Exercise Sciences, it has been revealed that women have greater muscle endurance than men during dynamic, everyday movements. The research, published in the June 2017 issue of Applied Physiology, Nutrition, and Metabolism, found that women can outlast men by a significant margin in foot exercises, which involve the calf muscles essential for standing and walking.

The study, led by Assistant Professor Brian Dalton, recruited 17 participants, eight men and nine women, who were at a similar level of physical fitness. Participants were asked to flex their foot against a suite of sensors as quickly as possible 200 times. The results showed that males were faster and more powerful at the outset but became more fatigued much faster than females.

Dalton believes that similar results would be observed for other muscle groups and that his findings are consistent with previous research. He suggests that this new understanding could inform the design of exercise programs and work environments to minimize work-related fatigue and improve overall productivity.

The study's findings challenge the traditional notion that men are physically stronger than women. However, it's important to note that this research only focused on one isolated muscle group.

Meanwhile, a separate discussion revolves around the lack of well-known milestones and traditions for female athletes. The four-minute mile is a widely recognized achievement for male runners, but its female equivalent remains unfamiliar to many. This disparity highlights the need for more focus on celebrating and documenting female athletic achievements to create a richer tradition and inspire future generations.

The UBC study was funded by the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada. For more information, contact Nathan Skolski, Associate Director, Public Affairs at the University of British Columbia's Okanagan campus.

The American Dream Miami, a retail and entertainment complex, has been approved by the Miami-Dade County Commission. The $4 billion project, developed by Triple Five Worldwide Group, is set to be the largest mall in the U.S., spanning 6.2 million square feet. The complex will feature a water park, indoor ice rink, artificial ski slope, numerous restaurants, and up to 1,200 stores.

Triple Five Group, known for the Mall of America in Minneapolis, anticipates that 30 million people will visit the property each year. However, the project has faced opposition from existing malls in Miami due to the city's saturated retail market. Concerns have also been raised about the development's potential water and energy use, and its impact on the city's stormwater system.

The American Dream Miami is part of a trend of "destination malls" or "super-regional malls," which focus on experiential attractions to subsidize regular retail shops. These malls often include attractions like movie theaters, bars, casinos, restaurants, and amusement park rides.

Triple Five is also working on another destination mall in New Jersey, called American Dream Meadowlands, which will include a Nickelodeon theme park. The Miami project is expected to open in the spring of 2024, while the New Jersey complex is scheduled to open in 2019.

The approval of the American Dream Miami comes at a time when store closures are accelerating, and many malls across the U.S. are struggling. The rise of online shopping and changing consumer habits have led to the closure of hundreds of malls and thousands of mall-based stores in the past two decades.

The American Dream Miami could provide a more viable model for struggling malls and malls of the future. By focusing on experiential attractions, the project aims to attract visitors from the entire region rather than just people who live nearby.

The emergence of entertainment as part of the shopping mall is becoming increasingly important, according to retail analysts. Destination malls can be more profitable to developers than traditional malls, as they keep people in the center longer and attract visitors who may not have initially intended to shop.

The American Dream Miami is expected to create jobs and boost the local tourist-based economy. However, critics argue that the project is unnecessary, given the oversaturation of retail spaces in the U.S. and the rise of online shopping. The project's impact on the environment and the city's stormwater system is also a concern for some locals and environmentalists.

In a dramatic turn of events, Jim Carrey is embroiled in a legal battle over the death of his former girlfriend, Cathriona White, who committed suicide in 2015. White's mother and estranged husband are suing Carrey, alleging he was responsible for her death, claiming she was distraught over getting herpes from him. However, Carrey denies these allegations, stating that White falsely accused him of giving her an STD as part of an extortion attempt.

According to Carrey, White had texted him in 2013 about bumps on her vagina, but he claims she actually got those bumps from a wax job. He further alleges that White, with her lawyer, falsely tried to extort several million dollars from him, using the bumps as evidence of herpes and trying to pin it on him. Carrey also claims that White had herpes before they even met.

The lawsuit alleges that Carrey provided White with illegal drugs, knowing her prior history of depression and suicide. Carrey's lawyer has previously denied his involvement, stating he had "nothing to do" with her death. After months of stalling, Carrey is scheduled to appear in a sworn deposition next week in Los Angeles Superior Court.

In a recent development, Carrey has claimed that White created an elaborate extortion scheme using fake medical records to make it seem she was clean before she met him. He alleges that White got her friend's medical records showing a clean bill of health and altered them to make it appear the records were hers. Carrey's legal team has made an ultimatum, stating either White's estate provides non-forged medical records or admits she had multiple STDs before she met the actor.

Michael Avenatti, attorney for Cathriona's estate, has called Carrey's new claim "complete and utter bullshit." He has threatened that if the truth comes out, Carrey and his advisers may face criminal prosecution. The case is set to unfold in the coming weeks.

A resident of Newman, a mining town in Western Australia, was surprised to see a plane parked outside the local pub, the Purple Pub, after its owner allegedly taxied it down the main street to get a drink. The incident occurred on October 31 at around 2:00 pm. The light aircraft, a Beechcraft two-seater prop-driven plane, had no wings and was being steered by foot pedals. The plane's owner, a 37-year-old man, does not hold a pilot's license and did not have a steering wheel. The man was charged with an act likely to endanger the life, health, or safety of a person and had his plane impounded. The incident was taken seriously by the police due to the presence of children walking home from school at the time. The man is due to appear in the Newman Magistrates Court on November 18. Witnesses have been asked to contact the police. The plane attracted a crowd, and there were people taking pictures of the incident.

Disney has been granted a patent for a proposed shoe recognition system designed to track guests' movements and gather information within its theme parks. The system, described in a patent filed in April 2015 and granted last week, involves a network of cameras and sensors that blend in with the surroundings.

Upon arrival, a robot at the entrance area will use a foot sensor to capture a detailed image of a guest's foot and a camera to capture its color. The devices are angled towards the ground and placed at a low level, making them easier to conceal from guests. Sensors around the park, out of guests' line of sight, will unobtrusively capture information about guests' movements.

The data collected from the system is expected to help improve park management and future planning. By tracking the most popular rides and common guest paths from ride to ride, the amusement park owners can tailor experiences for guests and optimize operations.

Disney argues that tracking shoes is more effective than current scanning methods, such as biometric scanning, which can be invasive, obtrusive, and inaccurate if guests are wearing certain accessories like sunglasses or hats. The shoe recognition system is less invasive and can use additional information like lower leg data, tread wear, and foot size to distinguish between guests.

Concerned with guest awareness of tracking, Disney has also rejected plans for overall clothing recognition as those systems require cameras that are visible to the person. Clothing recognition can also produce unreliable results as many guests have similar attire and will change their clothing throughout the day.

This new system could potentially help Disney improve its guest experience, driving new and repeat visitation that contributes significantly to Central Florida's $66 billion tourism and travel industry, attracting 60 million people annually to the region.

In Rocklin, California, a 13-year-old girl named Ashley Wood was found dead in her home on Monument Springs Drive on Tuesday morning. Her 14-year-old sibling, who lived in the same house, was picked up by police as the only suspect in the case. The community is in shock, with neighbors expressing their condolences and disbelief. Ashley was a dedicated athlete who trained in gymnastics and attended Sierra Elementary school before leaving the school system in 2013. The Department of Justice is involved in the investigation, and the home where Ashley was killed is co-owned by Jeffery Ronald Wood, who also works at the Placer County District Attorney’s Office. The boy's name has not been released due to his minor status. The Rocklin Police Department is being assisted by the California Department of Justice, and an autopsy is scheduled. The community is praying for the family coping with the loss of a daughter and the arrest of a teenage relative accused of killing her.

Reader's Digest, the 91-year-old publisher, filed for bankruptcy in February 2012 to shed $465 million in debt, as consumers shift towards electronic media. The company, which was founded by DeWitt and Lila Wallace, went public in 1990 and was later acquired by private-equity firm Ripplewood Holdings LLC in 2007 for $1.6 billion. The bankruptcy filing follows a drop in advertising and the debt incurred in its acquisition.

The company plans to restructure and transform its core businesses around its iconic brands, with the aim of reducing its debt by 80%. The bankruptcy is supported by Wells Fargo & Co., and $465 million of remaining senior notes will convert to equity.

Reader's Digest has been buffeted by economic downturns and the shift from traditional print media to digital media, which has severely hampered its ability to thrive. The company's flagship print magazine is read by more than 25 million people, and it publishes 75 magazines globally.

In 2010, the FTC started an investigation into the marketing of the Ab Circle Pro fitness product, sold by a Reader's Digest subsidiary. As part of a 2012 settlement, the company agreed to pay as much as $23.8 million.

The company has had some success in the sale of Allrecipes.com and Every Day with Rachel Ray to Meredith Corp. Last year. The company plans to focus its resources on its strong North American publishing brands, which have shown a new vitality as a result of its transformation efforts, particularly in the digital arena.

The international operations, including Canada, are not part of the filing. The case is In RDA Holding Co. Inc., 13-22233, U.S. Bankruptcy Court, Southern District of New York (White Plains).

In his Thanksgiving message, President Trump expressed gratitude for the nation's progress under his administration, highlighting achievements such as job creation, a strong economy, and military successes against the Islamic State group. He praised the U.S. military, particularly those serving in Afghanistan, and promised "big, fat, beautiful tax cuts." Trump also defended his role in securing the release of three college basketball players detained in China. He concluded his messages with a call for national unity and thanksgiving. Meanwhile, millions of Americans are preparing for travel during the holiday season, with potential delays expected due to increased traffic.

In a significant operation, authorities in New York announced the largest gun bust in the city's history, taking down two smuggling rings that were funneling illegal guns from the South for resale on the city's streets. A total of 19 individuals were arrested, and 254 firearms were recovered. The operation, named "Up on the Hill," targeted two gun runners, Walter Walker and Earl Campbell, who oversaw the loosely organized rings and sold their illicit goods through the same city dealer.

Walker, based in Brooklyn, used a rap studio at 1991 Atlantic Ave. as his home base in the city. Earl Campbell, concerned about NYPD's stop-and-frisk tactics, was caught on tape discussing his concerns about bringing the guns to New York.

Another perp, Mathew Best, an aspiring rapper from Brooklyn, was also involved in the operation. He posted several photos of guns and cash on Instagram and boasted about having more guns than the Air Force. Best helped Walker peddle the guns.

Walker made trips to New York City practically every week to sell guns, and the transactions between the men were swift and extremely profitable, with the guns selling for at least three times their original price. The thugs knew they could get a premium for the weapons given New York's strict gun laws. Nearly $160,000 was made on the sale of at least some of the weapons.

Mayor Bloomberg praised the operation, stating that the seizure of these guns had saved lives. The bust was due in part to the NYPD's pro-active policies such as its controversial stop-and-frisk. The Manhattan DA's office and federal Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives are involved in the ongoing investigation. The case is being handled primarily by the city's Office of the Special Narcotics Prosecutor.

Edward Snowden, the former CIA employee who leaked top-secret documents about U.S. surveillance programs, has faced difficulties in seeking asylum outside the United States. On Tuesday, it was reported that Snowden withdrew his asylum bid in Russia, and several European countries said such applications would not be considered if made from abroad.

Snowden is believed to have been in the transit area of Moscow's airport since his arrival from Hong Kong on June 23. He had sent asylum requests to 21 countries, including China, France, Ireland, and Venezuela, but eight European countries said the requests were invalid. Russia said Snowden later withdrew the application to Moscow as the Kremlin had set conditions.

Snowden accuses U.S. President Barack Obama of putting pressure on the countries to which he has applied for asylum. He is wanted by the U.S. on charges of leaking secrets. The U.S. has annulled Snowden's passport, and Ecuador, where he had initially hoped to get asylum, has been giving mixed signals about offering him shelter.

Snowden described himself as "a stateless person," accusing the U.S. government of stopping him from exercising the "basic right...to seek asylum." He said in a statement that the U.S. administration is using citizenship as a weapon.

In a statement, WikiLeaks said that most of the asylum requests, including to Russia itself, were handed to the Russian consulate at Sheremetyevo airport late on Sunday for delivery to the relevant embassies in Moscow. The requests were submitted by Sarah Harrison, a British member of the Wikileaks legal team acting as Snowden's representative, the statement added.

However, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov later said Snowden withdrew the application to Russia because Moscow had said he should give up "anti-American activity." Russian President Vladimir Putin had said that while Moscow "never hands over anybody anywhere," Snowden could only stay on condition that he stopped damaging Russia's "American partners" with his leaks.

The leaking of thousands of classified intelligence documents has led to revelations that the U.S. is systematically seizing vast amounts of phone and web data. The expanded requests for asylum come as the Obama administration contends with European allies angry about the release of documents that alleged U.S. eavesdropping on European Union diplomats. Obama said Monday that the U.S. would provide allies with information about new reports that the NSA had bugged EU offices in Washington, New York, and Brussels. But he also suggested such activity by governments would hardly be unusual.

The incident report details the death of Tawon Boyd, a 21-year-old man from Baltimore, who died after an altercation with county police officers. The incident occurred on Wednesday, following a 911 call for an ambulance. Initially, the police department stated that the call was placed by Boyd's girlfriend, Deona Styron, but later updated their account, stating that they believed the female yelling on the phone was the caller.

According to the police report, Boyd was under the influence of a narcotic and seemed confused and paranoid. He repeatedly asked officers to enter his home, claiming that his girlfriend had secretly recorded him while someone else was in the house. Boyd also asked a neighbor to call the police.

During the encounter, Boyd attempted to enter two police cars and ran to a neighbor's house, shouting for help. The report notes that Boyd seemed to scratch the author's neck and accidentally kick another officer, named Garland, while trying to stand. Boyd grabbed a third officer's face, and the officer, Bowman, "delivered two closed fist strikes to the suspect’s face with his right fist."

Boyd's family's attorney, Latoya Francis-Williams, stated that Boyd was attacked and choked by Officer Bowman. The autopsy results are yet to be released, but Francis-Williams said there was swelling on the brain and fluid on the brain, and Boyd's kidneys failed, leading to his heart stopping.

The Baltimore County police and fire departments are investigating the circumstances surrounding Boyd's death. The autopsy results will be crucial in determining whether the drug haloperidol, given to Boyd by medics to calm him down, contributed to his death. The police department has confirmed that the impact of the calming drug will be a key element in this case.

Boyd's family is planning a funeral instead of a wedding and baby shower. His mother, Martha Boyd, expressed her disappointment, stating that the police could have used non-lethal methods like tasers or pepper spray.

The incident report also states that Boyd told police there was someone in the house, and they needed to go inside and search. Francis-Williams stated that Boyd's mind was not right cognitively but not aggressive or angry. Boyd's girlfriend told police that he had been drinking and smoking pot, and when officers tried to take him to a hospital for an emergency evaluation, Boyd ran, screaming, and knocked on neighbors' doors, asking them to call the police.

The incident report ends with a redacted list of minor injuries sustained by the officers. The autopsy results are expected to take at least seven days to complete.

President-elect Donald Trump accused President Obama of putting "roadblocks" in his way during the transition process, a reversal of his earlier praise for Obama's efforts to ensure a smooth transition. Trump's tweets came after Obama cautioned against "the urge to turn inward" and stressed the need to "resist the urge to demonize those who are different," remarks some thought were aimed partly at Trump. Trump was also critical of a number of steps the Obama administration is taking in its final weeks related to Israel, including a speech by Secretary of State John F. Kerry on Middle East policy. Trump said the "beginning of the end" was the "horrible" Iran nuclear deal reached last year that was supported by a coalition of world powers but vigorously opposed by Israel. Trump was also highly critical of the Obama administration's refusal to veto a United Nations Security Council resolution condemning Israeli settlements in the West Bank and East Jerusalem. During a conference call with reporters, Trump's pick for White House press secretary, Sean Spicer, said Trump's tweets "speak for themselves." Trump and Obama had a "nice conversation" on Wednesday, according to Trump, but it is unclear what was discussed. Trump also said he will hold a press conference in early January. The White House has defended a decision by the Energy Department not to comply with a request from the Trump transition team to provide names of employees who worked on the Obama administration's climate policy efforts. Obama has repeatedly committed to a peaceful and smooth transition of power.

President Barack Obama has issued a new Executive Order (E.O.) under the national emergency with respect to Ukraine, finding that the actions and policies of the Russian government with respect to Ukraine, including the deployment of Russian military forces in Crimea, undermine democratic processes and institutions in Ukraine, threaten its peace, security, stability, sovereignty, and territorial integrity, and contribute to the misappropriation of its assets. This new authority expands upon E.O. 13660, which the President signed less than two weeks ago, by authorizing the Secretary of the Treasury, in consultation with the Secretary of State, to impose sanctions on named officials of the Russian government, any individual or entity that operates in the Russian arms industry, and any designated individual or entity that acts on behalf of, or that provides material or other support to, any senior Russian government official.

In response to the Russian government’s actions contributing to the crisis in Ukraine, this new E.O. lists seven Russian government officials who are being designated for sanctions. These individuals are Vladislav Surkov, Sergey Glazyev, Leonid Slutsky, Andrei Klishas, Valentina Matviyenko, Dmitry Rogozin, and Yelena Mizulina. The United States also will seek to hold accountable individuals who use their resources or influence to support or act on behalf of senior Russian government officials.

In addition to the new E.O., the Treasury Department today has imposed sanctions on four other individuals under E.O. 13660, issued on March 6, for their actions or policies that threaten the peace, security, stability, sovereignty, or territorial integrity of Ukraine and in undermining the Government of Ukraine. They are Crimea-based separatist leaders Sergey Aksyonov and Vladimir Konstantinov; former Ukrainian presidential chief of staff Viktor Medvedchuk; and former President of Ukraine Viktor Yanukovych.

Obama stressed that the government has the authority to go after officials in the Russian arms sector and those who support Russian cronies if the government doesn't pursue a diplomatic solution to the crisis in Ukraine. The sanctions focus on the individual personal assets, but not companies that the officials may manage on behalf of the Russian state. Any assets that the individuals have in U.S. jurisdiction have been frozen and Americans are prohibited from doing business with them.

The White House announcement came after the European Union announced on Monday travel bans and asset freezes on 21 people for their involvement in the Ukraine crisis. The EU is not expected to announce the individuals who are being cited until Tuesday, but Obama administration officials believe there is some overlap in the U.S. and EU lists. Vice President Biden will visit Poland and Lithuania next week, where he is to huddle with leaders in the region on the Ukraine crisis. Obama will travel to the Netherlands next week to take part in the biennial Nuclear Security Summit, but the situation in Ukraine will be the main focus on the sidelines of the summit.

In conclusion, President Obama has imposed new sanctions on seven Russian officials and four Ukrainians involved in the separatist effort in Ukraine, in response to the Russian government’s actions contributing to the crisis in Ukraine. The sanctions focus on the individual personal assets, but not companies that the officials may manage on behalf of the Russian state. Obama stands ready to use these authorities in a direct and targeted fashion as events warrant, and if Russia continues to interfere in Ukraine, the United States is prepared to take additional steps to impose further political and economic costs.

The article discusses the debate over warming up cars on cold days. Chris Lague, a service writer at Partner Tire & Service in Vermont, asserts that modern cars no longer require idling for more than 30 seconds to a minute before driving, as the oil takes that amount of time to reach the moving parts of the engine. This is due to the advancements in fuel injection and on-board computers.

Kristen McIntyre, a stay-at-home mom in Essex, Vermont, also supports the quick, idle-free getaway for environmental reasons. Vermont enacted a statute in 2014 that prohibits idling for more than 5 minutes out of any 60-minute period, with some exceptions.

However, not everyone agrees with Lague. Bill Brisson, 54, from Burlington, Vermont, warms his car up for 8 to 10 minutes on cold winter mornings, arguing that the engine oil is still like molasses at freezing temperatures.

The article also mentions a separate incident in Roseville, Michigan, where a man named Nick Taylor received a ticket for warming up his car in his own driveway. The ticket was issued due to the car being left unattended with the keys in the ignition, a public safety issue according to the police chief. The incident sparked outrage and discussions on social media.

The article concludes by emphasizing that modern cars warm up faster when driven than when idling, and that idling for more than 5 minutes in Vermont is against the law, with some exceptions.

Stanford University has implemented a new policy that bans hard alcohol, including shots and high-volume distilled liquor containers, at all undergraduate student parties, effective immediately. The policy aims to decrease the consumption of hard alcohol and is part of the school's efforts to change the campus culture around alcohol use. Undergraduate parties will now be limited to serving beer and wine only, and any group or residence that has undergraduate members is subject to the new policy. The policy change follows rumors of a ban that were met with campus-wide opposition in March, and a campus-wide referendum in April saw 91.46% of voters opt against a hard alcohol ban. The repercussions for policy violations remain unchanged, with students failing to comply facing referrals to Residence Deans and the Office of Alcohol Policy and Education. The policy was not directly related to the Brock Turner case, but came out of general concern about binge drinking and a social culture centered on alcohol consumption. Critics argue that the new rules are a tone-deaf response to growing concerns about sexual assault and may increase safety risks associated with drinking. Some fear that the ban may drive students to binge drink in dorm rooms, where perpetrators of sexual assault may be more likely to attack vulnerable victims. Others worry that students will drink more heavily before parties, increasing risks that someone might take advantage of them. Critics also argue that universities should be working to shift the culture around sexual assault, provide thorough education on consent, and hold perpetrators accountable in meaningful ways.

In a study published in the journal Neuropsychopharmacology, researchers found that the taste of beer, without its alcoholic effects, can trigger the release of dopamine, a brain chemical associated with pleasure. The study involved 49 male volunteers who were given a taste of their favorite beer, sports drink, or water. The participants' brains were scanned using Positron Emission Tomography (PET) to study the effect of beer's taste on dopamine receptors. The results showed higher increases in dopamine after the men tasted beer compared with tasting the sports drink or water, suggesting that the taste of alcohol is enough to prompt a pleasurable response in the brain. The men who had a family history of alcoholism showed an even greater spike in dopamine levels after tasting the beer, indicating that the dopamine response may be a heritable risk factor for alcoholism. The study's senior author, neuroscientist David Kareken of the Indiana University School of Medicine, stated that this is the first experiment in humans to show that the taste of an alcoholic drink alone can elicit dopamine activity in the brain's reward centers. The findings could potentially be useful in assessing predisposition to alcohol abuse. However, the effects of the alcohol itself on the brain could not be ruled out entirely.

In a dispute over arsenic contamination in wastewater, the Gardiner Water and Sewer Treatment District in Montana has filed a lawsuit against the National Park Service (NPS) over wastewater treatment issues related to Yellowstone National Park. The district claims that for the past few years, they have been trying to work with the NPS to resolve the matter, but with no response from the Park Service, they have been compelled to sue.

The issue began in February 2015 when high levels of arsenic were detected in sewage coming from the town of Mammoth, which is home to park employees and sits just inside Yellowstone's northern border. The arsenic was not coming from the park's wastewater, but appeared to be flowing into the system from manholes or holes in underground pipes. The district's engineer recommended that the district address this infiltration problem with the park prior to beginning any sludge removal project.

The district wrote letters to the Park Service in March 2015 and December 2015, asking the agency to locate and repair the areas of infiltration, but the Park Service did not respond. In August 2016, the district sent a third letter and received a written response from the Park Service confirming that the infiltration problems were accurate and ongoing, but that money for the project probably won't be available until 2020 at the earliest.

The lawsuit claims that the park breached an oral contract to help pay for the sludge pond replacement, and is trespassing since the damage caused by the arsenic is ongoing. The district also says Yellowstone National Park is creating a "danger to public safety" by not addressing the arsenic. In addition to breach of contract and trespass claims, the district is suing for public and private nuisance and negligence. The district is seeking a judge to order the park to address its arsenic problem, to monitor its sewer lines quarterly and provide the district with reports, and to help pay for the sludge removal project.

In Butler, Alabama, three inmates, Demarcus Woodard, Germayel Culbert, and Justin Terrell Gordon, escaped from a Choctaw County jail early Saturday. Woodard and Culbert are charged with murder, while Gordon is charged with armed robbery. The inmates attacked a guard, choked him, and stole his keys and cell phone before fleeing on foot. The guard was treated and released at a local hospital. Authorities, including the FBI and U.S. Marshals Service, are searching for the inmates, expanding the search to other areas. The inmates were held in one cell, and one of them was reportedly sick before the escape. The incident occurred in Choctaw County, a rural area with a population of fewer than 14,000, located in southwestern Alabama. The manhunt is ongoing, and updates will be provided as more information becomes available.

The film "Flight" directed by Robert Zemeckis revolves around the life of a troubled airline pilot, Whip Whitaker, played by Denzel Washington. The movie begins with a thrilling and suspenseful portrayal of a plane crash, where Whip's quick thinking and skills save most of the passengers. However, it is later revealed that Whip was under the influence of alcohol and cocaine at the time of the crash, raising questions about his heroism and raising concerns about his addiction.

The movie delves into Whip's personal life, his strained relationships with his family, and his struggle with alcoholism. Whip's addiction is further explored through his interactions with various characters, including his lawyer, his ex-wife, and a recovering addict named Nicole. The movie also features a hearing by the National Transportation Safety Board, where Whip's toxicology report is a key issue.

"Flight" is praised for Washington's powerful and nuanced performance, as well as Zemeckis' direction and the movie's emotional depth. However, some critics find the movie's script to be uneven and the storyline to be convoluted at times. Overall, "Flight" is a compelling drama that explores the complexities of addiction and the consequences of making poor choices.

In addition to the main storyline, the movie also features a subplot about a video game character named Ralph, voiced by John C. Reilly, who embarks on a journey to become a hero. This subplot is intended to be a light-hearted and humorous contrast to the main storyline, but some critics find it to be a distraction from the main narrative.

Overall, "Flight" is a thought-provoking and emotionally charged drama that offers a nuanced portrayal of addiction and the struggle to overcome it. Washington's performance is praised as one of his best, and the movie is a must-see for fans of the actor and the genre.

The University of Virginia has issued a four-year ban from its campus to Richard Spencer and nine other individuals associated with white-supremacist marches that took place on the school's grounds in August 2017. The ban was enforced due to the individuals' involvement in violent incidents, including a torchlight march and the Unite the Right rally that resulted in numerous injuries and the death of counterprotester Heather Heyer.

Richard Spencer, a U-Va. graduate, organized the torchlight march and gave a speech in which he took credit for "defeating" counterprotesters. The following day, Spencer and the others took part in the white-supremacist Unite the Right rally in Charlottesville.

The university's decision to ban the individuals was based on their violation of policies of conduct, not speech. The university stated that Spencer's role in organizing the torchlight march and his speech at the statue provided evidence of his involvement in a conspiracy to commit acts of violence.

In addition to Spencer, the banned individuals include Benjamin Daley, Antonio Foreman, Thomas Gillen, Elliott Kline, Michael Miselis, Vasillious Pistolis, Robert Ray, Wil Smith, and Cole White. Four of the banned individuals, Daley, Miselis, Gillen, and White, were recently arrested and charged with violating federal laws against rioting for their actions during the Unite the Right rally.

This decision follows a year-long investigation by the U-Va. Police Department in coordination with state and federal law enforcement agencies. A violation of the no-trespass order is a criminal trespass offense, and violators would be subject to arrest. The trespass warnings expire four years after the date they are served.

In response to the university's decision, Walter Heinecke, a U-Va. associate professor who helped injured students during the white supremacist march, called it "a highly appropriate move." Heinecke expressed gratitude that the university is taking action to address white supremacy on its campus.

The story highlights the discovery of three bodies on the property of Todd Kohlhepp, a South Carolina real estate agent who is accused of murder and kidnapping. The bodies were found on Monday, with the third one being close to the one recovered the day before. The official cause of death and gender of the bodies are yet to be determined.

The story also mentions that Kohlhepp was arrested last week after the rescue of Kala Brown, who was found chained by her neck and ankle in a metal shipping container on his property. Kohlhepp confessed to a series of killings, authorities said, and faces murder and kidnapping charges. He is also suspected of being connected to at least seven homicides.

Investigators are checking multiple properties Kohlhepp has owned inside and outside South Carolina. The search for human remains has now expanded to other properties he owns or used to own, including places outside of South Carolina.

Kohlhepp is charged with kidnapping Brown and more criminal counts are expected. He has chosen to represent himself and not hire an attorney. The judge denied bond for Kohlhepp on four murder charges for gunning down the motorcycle shop's owner, service manager, mechanic, and bookkeeper.

The story also mentions that Kohlhepp was a registered sex offender and was sentenced to 14 years in prison in Arizona for binding and raping a 14-year-old neighbor at gunpoint. He was released in 2001 and managed to obtain a real estate license in South Carolina in 2006.

The search for human remains is ongoing, and it is unclear how far and for how long it will continue. The investigation is widespread and no longer limited to South Carolina. The Associated Press is not naming the woman because the suspect is a sex offender, though authorities have not said whether she was sexually assaulted.

Title: Zack Snyder's Gritty Reboots and Controversial Style

Zack Snyder, a director known for his gritty reboots, has made a name for himself in Hollywood. When studio executives seek a darker, more muscular take on a superhero, Snyder is their go-to choice. His signature style involves stripping away the joy and light-heartedness from characters, replacing it with a brooding, muscular portrayal reminiscent of his work in "300."

Superman, traditionally a symbol of morality in a harsh world, is transformed under Snyder's direction. The Man of Steel becomes a brooding figure who shows little regard for collateral damage, even going as far as to destroy buildings without hesitation. This gritty approach has become synonymous with Snyder's work.

However, Snyder's style has not been without controversy. GQ's third annual list of individuals who have overstayed their welcome in the spotlight includes Snyder, citing his use of fame for questionable reasons. The list, which is usually limited to 25 individuals, included an additional mini-list of individuals whose influence has waned so significantly that they are being retired from the list permanently.

This summary suggests that Zack Snyder's gritty reboots, while popular among some audiences, have also been met with criticism for his treatment of superhero characters and his use of fame.
