The 1,500-year-old carved altar discovered at the La Corona archaeological site in northern Guatemala is providing insights into the political strategies of the Mayan dynasty known as the Kaanul, or the Snake Kings. The altar, which was found in a collapsed temple and took a year to excavate, depicts the Tikal ruler Chak Took Ich'aak conjuring two local gods from a shaft in the form of a double-headed snake. The same man appears 20 years later as a vassal of the Kaanul dynasty and the ruler of the nearby city of Peru-Waka.

Archaeologists believe that the Kaanul's eventual victory over Tikal was the result of decades of astute politicking and cultural appropriation, rather than just battles. Chak Took Ich'aak and his son are depicted on the altar praying to local gods to legitimize their rule, suggesting an attempt to appeal to local interests. The Kaanul dynasty had backing from a more powerful entity, similar to Cuba having the backing of the Soviet Union in defeating a more powerful opponent.

The enormous city-state of Tikal, known for its towering temples, battled for centuries for dominance of the Maya world with the Kaanul dynasty. Just a few decades after the altar was carved, Kaanul apparently defeated Tikal by amassing a string of allied cities that encircled and eventually strangled Tikal. The symbol of the Kaanul dynasty were stone masks carved in the form of grinning snakes.

The altar is on display at the National Museum of Archaeology and Ethnology in Guatemala City, and its broader significance is that it shows the behind-the-scenes machinations of the Snake Kings as they expanded their empire in the direction of Tikal. The discovery fills in the gaps and pieces together the puzzle of the Mayan culture's political relationships.

Excavating and investigating in the remote Mayan Biosphere Reserve where La Corona lies can be hazardous, with the region being threatened by looting, invasions, and incursions by criminal gangs, drug-traffickers, and illegal ranchers. The region is rich in archeological remains, and authorities are trying to counter encroachment by criminal groups besieging Peten.

The Mayan culture reached its apogee during the classical period from 250-900 before going into decline over the next 300 years. The discovery of the La Corona altar provides valuable insights into the political strategies of the Mayan dynasties during this period.

The decommissioning process of Japan's Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Station, which suffered meltdowns in 2011 following a devastating earthquake and tsunami, has entered a crucial phase. On Tuesday, operators began dismantling protective covers from one of the reactors, a necessary step before extracting the 292 spent fuel rods inside. The Tokyo Electric Power Company (TEPCO) aims to remove all covers by the end of next year and start fuel rod extraction in 2020.

In a related development, the Japanese government approved an increase in compensation payments for the Fukushima crisis to 7.07 trillion yen ($57.18 billion). TEPCO will receive an additional 950 billion yen in public funds. The disaster, which occurred in March 2011, resulted in the meltdown of three reactors, causing widespread destruction and displacement.

Tens of thousands of evacuees remain in temporary housing, and electricity bills for Japanese households have risen 25% since the catastrophe due to increased fossil fuel imports. The government plans to lift evacuation orders for most displaced people within two years as part of a plan to cap compensation payouts and speed up reconstruction.

Inside the plant, TEPCO has faced challenges in controlling the situation, and the cleanup is expected to cost tens of billions of dollars and take decades to complete. The government aims to make affected areas safe for habitation again, although some areas may remain off-limits for decades.

In this summary, Iran's President-elect Hassan Rouhani has called for an end to government and clergy interference in the private lives of Iranian citizens, advocating for a more open society and free Internet access. Rouhani's comments are part of his message of moderation at home and better relations abroad, which contributed to his surprise election victory last month.

Rouhani's vision of a more open society within the Islamic system will depend on the backing of Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, who sits at the top of Iran's complex hybrid system of clerical rule combined with elements of elected representation. Rouhani has also attacked Iran's state television, IRIB, for its lack of honesty, morality, and justice, and has called for freedom of expression to address domestic issues.

In conclusion, Rouhani's election victory has sparked hope for change in Iran, with the President-elect advocating for a more open society, free Internet access, and an end to government and clergy interference in private lives. However, Rouhani faces potential opposition from hardline conservatives and must navigate the complexities of Iran's hybrid system of clerical rule and elected representation to achieve his vision.

The article discusses the use of social media activism, specifically the #BringBackOurGirls campaign, in response to the kidnapping of over 200 Nigerian schoolgirls by Boko Haram. The author, D.A. Lovell, expresses concerns about the effectiveness of hashtag activism, particularly in relation to issues affecting the black community. Lovell argues that while social media campaigns can raise awareness and generate attention, they may not lead to tangible results and can give users a false sense of accomplishment.

Lovell points out that the #BringBackOurGirls campaign has been ongoing for weeks, but the girls remain in grave danger, and the focus of U.S. reporting on the plight of the girls has declined. Lovell suggests that social media activism might not be as powerful as many think it is when it comes to achieving tangible results, and that a more strategic approach is needed to push for accountability and justice.

The author also discusses the issue of media bias and the lack of coverage given to similar events in other parts of the world, such as the burning of 60 boys to death in a boarding school in Yobe, Nigeria, in February, which received no hashtag campaign. Lovell argues that the media gives its audience what they think they want, and that if readers don't suggest they are interested in an issue, there will be no primetime coverage.

Despite the criticisms, Lovell acknowledges that hashtag activism can be effective in bringing a campaign to people's attention and pressuring politicians and leaders to take action. However, Lovell emphasizes the need for a more strategic approach to social media activism, and the importance of personal research and accurate information in order to make a lasting difference.

Finally, the article discusses the potential impact of hashtag activism on terrorists, who are increasingly using social media to spread their message and recruit new members. Lovell suggests that widespread condemnation of terrorism on social media may serve as a foil to the terrorists' aims, but also acknowledges the potential for terrorists to employ social media editors to manage their online presence.

Overall, the article provides a nuanced perspective on the use of social media activism, highlighting both its potential benefits and limitations, and emphasizing the need for a more strategic approach to social media activism in order to achieve tangible results.

The European Space Agency's (ESA) Gravity field and steady-state Ocean Circulation Explorer (GOCE) satellite, nicknamed the "Ferrari of space" due to its sleek design, has re-entered Earth's atmosphere and burned up. The last contact with the satellite was on Sunday, 75 miles above Antarctica. US tracking data suggests any surviving debris fell into the South Atlantic, just off the tip of South America, south of the Falkland Islands.

GOCE was launched in 2009 to map variations in Earth's gravity. The satellite ran out of fuel on October 21 and had been steadily losing altitude since. The mission was operating in an extremely low orbit, and needed to constantly thrust an electric engine to stay aloft. Pre-return modeling had indicated that perhaps a fifth to a quarter of GOCE's one-tonne mass could have endured the fiery fall through the atmosphere.

The Inter-Agency Space Debris Coordination Committee chose GOCE as its special study project for 2013, activating a large number of tracking and surveillance facilities around the world to monitor the satellite's descent to Earth. GOCE's slender, fin-shaped construction, combined with its magnetic attitude-control system, maintained a stable orientation until very late in the descent.

This re-entry marks ESA's first uncontrolled re-entry in more than 25 years. The agency does, however, regularly manage controlled re-entries, such as its space station freighter, the Automated Transfer Vehicle, which can weigh some 13 tonnes when it comes back to Earth.

GOCE's data is a key reference in civil engineering for relating heights measured at widely separated locations, and for the computer models that need to understand how the oceans move to forecast future changes in climate.

The National Library of Medicine, a component of the National Institutes of Health, is archiving web content related to health, medicine, and the biomedical sciences to fulfill its mission. Albert Lin, a research scientist at the University of California, San Diego, is leading an expedition to find the tomb of Genghis Khan and other ancient Mongolian artifacts. Through a website called Field Expedition Mongolia, developed jointly with National Geographic, volunteers are helping sift through 85,000 high-resolution satellite images of Mongolia to locate ancient structures. The volunteers are amateurs working from their home computers, and they are instructed to tag images as "roads," "rivers," "modern structures," "ancient structures," or "other." Last summer, Lin and his colleagues inspected the places that had been tagged by the online volunteers, and they discovered 3,000-year-old Bronze Age tombs, remnants of large cities, and ancient monoliths hidden in the region's vast, grassy steppe. This project is an example of "citizen science," where new technology, when used effectively by large groups of people, can help speed up scientific developments, reduce costs, and increase efficiency.

Another example of citizen science is EteRNA, a project created by researchers at Carnegie Mellon and Stanford universities, which allows players to tinker with nucleotide bases and come up with synthetic RNA designs to speed up discoveries in biomedicine. Galaxy Zoo, an older project, allows volunteers to help classify images of galaxies taken by a robotic telescope to generate more than 20 academic papers by researchers around the world in astrophysics and astronomy journals. The U.S. Geological Survey is using crowdsourcing and technology to digitize a project called the Bird Phenology Program, which was started by an American ornithologist in 1881 to gather information on bird migration. The project was closed in 1970, but the cards containing the information remain in file cabinets, and volunteers can log on and enter the information into a central database.

These projects demonstrate the power of citizen science in advancing scientific research and making it more accessible to the public. Volunteers feel a sense of accomplishment and connection to the scientific process, and they are able to contribute to significant discoveries from the comfort of their own homes.

Regarding personality development, most psychologists believe that a person's fundamental personality traits, such as introversion or extroversion, remain consistent throughout life. However, changes in personality are often a response to external factors like career, marriage, or parenthood.

Research suggests that personalities become more stable as individuals move from their 20s to their 30s, 40s, and 50s, but this stability may decrease in old age. A study conducted in New Zealand recruited 4,000 participants aged 20 to 80, who completed a personality questionnaire twice, with a two-year gap between sessions. The survey measured five major personality traits: extraversion, agreeableness, conscientiousness, neuroticism, and openness to experience, as well as honesty-humility.

The study found that most people's personalities were generally stable, following a bell curve over time, with the highest stability observed at middle age and a subsequent decrease in old age. Interestingly, the oldest participants' stability in traits like conscientiousness, openness to experience, and honesty-humility matched that of the youngest participants.

The research also identified "domain-specific" variations, or traits that seemed to be linked to specific life stages. For instance, individuals in their 30s showed high levels of neuroticism, which decreased and was replaced by conscientiousness, openness, and honesty-humility by the time they reached their 50s.

The article discusses the ongoing legal battle surrounding the use of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA) Amendments Act in the case of Adel Daoud, a 19-year-old Chicago man accused of planning a bomb attack in downtown Chicago. The Act, which was passed in 2008, allows for the interception of foreign targets' emails and phone calls without an individual warrant, including when the foreigners are in communication with Americans or legal residents.

Daoud's lawyers have filed a motion claiming that the government is refusing to disclose whether evidence against Daoud was obtained under Section 702 of the FISA Amendments Act. If the government acknowledges this, Daoud would have the right to challenge the law's constitutionality. The government, however, has stated that the evidence was acquired through a traditional FISA court order, rather than under the expanded surveillance program authorized in 2008.

The lawyers argue that the government is being disingenuous and that the evidence likely came from Section 702. They claim that the government is trying to avoid a constitutional challenge to the law. The U.S. Supreme Court in February rejected a constitutional challenge to Section 702 by a group of journalists, lawyers, and human rights advocates, stating that they had no standing to sue because they had not proved that their communications had been intercepted.

The case has raised concerns about the government's use of secret surveillance programs and the potential infringement on individuals' constitutional rights. The lawyers for Daoud argue that the government should be required to abide by the original FISA statute, which requires the government to notify defendants when evidence being used against them is derived from surveillance authorized by the law.

The case is set to go to trial in February 2023. The outcome could have significant implications for the use of secret surveillance programs in criminal cases and the balance between national security and individual privacy.

The Peach Spring Tuff study provides insights into the behavior of pyroclastic flows from supervolcanoes, specifically the Silver Creek caldera that erupted 18.8 million years ago. The research combines recent laboratory experiments and field data from the 1980s to suggest that pyroclastic flows from the ancient eruption took the form of slow, dense currents, not fast-moving jets as previously thought.

The study found that pyroclastic flows from the Silver Creek caldera likely traveled at modest speeds of about 10 to 45 miles per hour, contrary to the assumption that they would have to start off with high speeds to cover such long distances. The findings could have implications for disaster preparedness efforts, as understanding the behavior of pyroclastic flows can help forecast their behavior during a volcanic eruption.

The research was conducted by Olivier Roche at Blaise Pascal University in France, David C. Buesch at the United States Geological Survey, and Greg A. Valentine at the University at Buffalo. It will be published on March 7, 2023, in Nature Communications. The study suggests that people living near a supervolcano might have a few hours to evacuate once the disaster starts, as the pyroclastic flows move at slower speeds than previously thought. However, it is important to note that the safest course of action is to evacuate before a flow starts.

A religious counselor in New York's ultra-orthodox Jewish community, Nechemya Weberman, was convicted on Monday of repeatedly sexually abusing a young girl who had sought his counsel. Hidekichi Miyazaki, a 105-year-old Japanese man, broke his own record as the oldest competitive sprinter on September 23, 2020, at the Kyoto Masters Athletics Autumn Competition in Kyoto, Japan. Miyazaki, affectionately known as the "Golden Bolt," finished the 100-meter sprint in 42.22 seconds, surpassing his previous record of 34.10 seconds set in 2013.

Born on September 22, 1910, Miyazaki celebrated his 105th birthday just a day before the competition. Despite his age, he shows no signs of slowing down and aims to race Usain Bolt, the world's fastest man, whom he admires and imitates with his signature "lightning" pose. Miyazaki, who stands at 1.53 meters and weighs 42 kilograms, trains by carrying a kilogram weight during daily walks around his local park.

Miyazaki took up running in his early 90s as a new hobby after many of his friends passed away. He has competed in several competitions, including the Asia Masters Athletics Championships in 2019, where he finished in 34.61 seconds. Miyazaki plans to continue competing and improving, with his next competition being the Japanese Masters Championships. His determination and resilience serve as an inspiration to many.

The Politico/Morning Consult poll reveals that Obamacare's popularity is increasing among voters, with 45% approving and 45% disapproving of the landmark health-care law. This shift in sentiment comes as President Donald Trump and the Republican-controlled Congress aim to repeal and replace the Affordable Care Act (ACA).

The poll indicates that a slight majority of voters would approve of either wholesale repeal or partial repeal of Obamacare, with 24% wanting a complete repeal and 27% favoring a partial repeal. On the other hand, 12% want to keep the law as is, and 26% want to see it expanded.

When voters were asked about nine separate provisions in the ACA, they wanted to keep eight of them. The only provision that voters want to get rid of is Obamacare's individual mandate, which requires nearly all Americans to have some form of health coverage or face a possible tax penalty.

The discussions among Congressional Republicans regarding the repeal of Obamacare are focused on resolving the issue of the millions of people in 31 states covered under the Medicaid expansion the law enabled. Four governors, including Wisconsin's Scott Walker and Ohio's John Kasich, are involved in these talks to help find a solution that accommodates the concerns of both conservatives and politicians from states that accepted federal dollars to expand coverage for low-income adults under Obamacare.

The stakes for Republicans are high, as they are facing vocal opposition at congressional town halls regarding possible rollbacks to Obamacare. The Republican-led repeal and replace plans are still under development, with key issues such as the extent of the repeal and the inclusion of tax credits and health savings accounts yet to be determined. The party is under a time constraint due to the use of fast-track budget rules that will allow them to avoid a filibuster in the Senate and pass a repeal bill on a party-line vote.

On May 30, 2014, Omotayo Adeoye, a 17-year-old student at the High School for Math, Science, and Engineering at City College in Harlem, committed suicide after being caught cheating on a German test. The incident occurred during class, when her teacher, Eva Malikova, noticed Adeoye using her cell phone. Malikova took away the device, and Adeoye reportedly apologized. However, she left the school and walked to the Hudson River at West 165th Street, where she placed her school ID on a rock and jumped into the water.

Adeoye did not know how to swim, and her father reported her missing to the police. Witnesses pleaded with her to come out of the water, but she disappeared. The police launched a search for her, but as of Saturday evening, they had not recovered a body.

Adeoye was described as a bright and talented student who played basketball and soccer. She had been selected for a research fellowship at City College’s Grove School of Engineering the previous summer. Her friends paid tribute to her on Facebook, describing her as intelligent, funny, and kind.

The Department of Education launched an investigation into the incident, and the schools chancellor promised a new look at student mental health awareness. The incident has raised concerns about the pressure and stress that students at competitive high schools face, and the need for schools to provide support for students struggling with mental health issues.

Edward Snowden, a former National Security Agency contractor and admitted leaker of U.S. state secrets, is currently in Russia and is expected to travel to Cuba and possibly Venezuela en route to possible asylum in Ecuador. The U.S. has called on Russia to hand Snowden over to Washington, but Russia has stated that they do not have any contact with Snowden. Snowden fled Hong Kong on Sunday to dodge U.S. efforts to extradite him on espionage charges, and Ecuador's Foreign Minister has said that Ecuador is considering Snowden's asylum request. The anti-secrecy group WikiLeaks has said it is helping Snowden. The U.S. is disappointed by Hong Kong's decision to allow Snowden to flee and has registered its strong objections to the Chinese government through diplomatic channels. The U.S. has revoked Snowden's passport and is in touch with countries that Snowden could travel through or to, reminding them that Snowden is wanted on criminal charges and reiterating Washington's position that Snowden should only be permitted to travel back to the U.S. Snowden is believed to have more than 200 sensitive documents, and it is unclear if he is finished disclosing highly classified information. The Chinese government was pleased that Snowden disclosed the extent of American surveillance of Internet and telephone conversations around the world, but in the longer term, China’s overall relationship with the U.S., which spans global economic, military and security issues, was more important than the feelings of the public in China and Hong Kong, who felt that the contractor should be protected from the reach of the U.S. Snowden's options are limited, as he needs a country that is willing to stand up to the U.S. and protect him from extradition. The U.S. is likely to have problems interrupting Snowden's passage, as the U.S. does not have an extradition treaty with Russia, but does with Cuba, Venezuela, and Ecuador. Even with an extradition agreement, any country could give Snowden a political exemption. The likelihood that any of these countries would stop Snowden from traveling on to Ecuador seems remote, as diplomatic tensions have thawed in recent years, but Cuba and the U.S. are hardly allies after a half-century of distrust, and another country that could see Snowden pass through, Venezuela, could also prove difficult, as relations between the two countries are strained.

The FBI is contemplating domestic terrorism charges against an individual accused of shooting a guard at the conservative Family Research Council. The FBI defines domestic terrorism as acts of violence committed by Americans against fellow Americans, motivated by extremist ideologies originating within the United States. Currently, the FBI is actively pursuing seven individuals who have been charged with such crimes, with five of them being women. This move by the FBI underscores their commitment to addressing domestic terrorism, a growing concern in the United States. The specific details of the case at the Family Research Council are yet to be fully disclosed, but it serves as a reminder of the ongoing efforts to combat extremist activities within the country.

In the World Cup host city Samara, Russian residents are being asked to shower in pairs to conserve water for visiting fans. The water system authorities have increased supplies to cater to the increased water use during the football tournament and a recent heat wave. Thousands of visitors, contributing to the increased water consumption, have led to this water-saving measure. The utility company, Samarskiye Kommunalniye Systemy, issued a press release on Wednesday, highlighting the need for water conservation.

The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints took a significant step towards transparency by releasing the first published pictures of a small sacred stone believed to have been used by founder Joseph Smith in translating the Book of Mormon. The stone, along with photos of the printer's manuscript of the Book of Mormon, were displayed at a news conference in Salt Lake City.

The religion's drive to be more transparent is aimed at filling a void on the internet for accurate information, as curiosity increased while church membership tripled to 15 million over the past three decades. The pictures of the stone and manuscript are part of a new book that also contains photos of the first printer's manuscript of the Book of Mormon.

The stone, which is dark brown with lighter brown swirls, is believed to have been stored in a weathered leather pouch made by one of Joseph Smith's wives, Emma Smith. The church has always possessed the stone, which was transported across the country during Mormon pioneers' trek from Illinois to Utah in the mid-1800s.

Mormons believe that 185 years ago, Smith found gold plates engraved with writing in ancient Egyptian in upstate New York. They say God helped him translate the text using the stone and other tools, and it became known as the Book of Mormon. The manuscript in the new book belongs to the Community of Christ, a faith that was created by early Mormons who stayed behind when most members of the religion moved west to Utah.

The church has been releasing books containing historical documents that shed light on how Smith formed the faith. It also has issued a series of in-depth articles that explain or clarify some of the more sensitive parts of the religion's history that it once sidestepped, such as its past ban on black men in the lay clergy and its early history of polygamy.

The church paid a price for its past decisions to stay silent on topics or keep key artifacts in the vault, said Richard Bushman, a Mormon historian and emeritus professor at Columbia University. "Their faithful members would stumble on information on the internet. Not having heard about them, they were shocked and disillusioned," Bushman said.

Today the church is taking a new approach by saying, "We can face up to the facts. We don't have to make the picture prettier than it is," he said. The pictures in the new book show different angles of the stone and the pouch in which it was stored. The stone will remain in the vault.

The church's campaign seems aimed at preventing current members from leaving and showing non-Mormons the faith has nothing to hide, said Terryl Givens, professor of literature and religion and the James Bostwick chair of English at the University of Richmond.

As an American-born religion much younger than most world religions, the origins of Mormonism have come under greater scrutiny and put pressure on the church to prove its stories, Givens said. "The other churches' origins are concealed by the mist of history," Givens said. "Mormonism is the first world religion in which the origins were exposed to public view, to documentation, to journalists and newspaper reporting."

The pictures in the new book are part of a larger effort by the church to be more transparent and to clarify sensitive tenets. The church has faced criticism for its secrecy and its handling of historical documents in the past. The release of the pictures of the stone and manuscript is a step towards addressing those criticisms.

The church's historian, Steven E. Snow, acknowledged the dynamic, saying: "The Internet brings both challenge and opportunities. We're grateful for the opportunity to share much of our collection through the use of the Internet."

A photo of a black Labrador Retriever named Mya being held upside down and forced to drink beer from a keg at a party off the College at Brockport: State University of New York campus went viral on social media, leading to the arrest of two students, Shane Oliver and Robert Yates. The incident occurred on March 8, 2014, at a house on Monroe Avenue in Brockport. Oliver is accused of holding the dog, while Yates is accused of taking the photo and posting it on the Twitter account @SUNYPartyStory. Both students have been charged with a misdemeanor under Agriculture and Marketing Law for torturing/injuring an animal. The College at Brockport has confirmed that Robert Yates is a student and plans to have a conversation with him. Mya's owner was not home when the photo was taken, and the dog has been taken by the local dog warden and is in good physical condition. The school has expressed concern over the incident and will investigate and take appropriate action. The event has sparked strong reactions on social media, with many expressing outrage over the treatment of the dog.

Dr. Conrad Murray, Michael Jackson's personal physician, was found guilty of involuntary manslaughter for causing Jackson's 2009 death by a powerful surgical anesthetic. The verdict was delivered after a jury of 12 deliberated for about nine hours over two days. Murray now faces jail time, a maximum sentence of four years in state prison, and the probable loss of his medical license.

The prosecution painted Murray as a deceptive and incompetent doctor who failed to provide proper care to Jackson, leading to his overdose death. Witnesses testified to numerous medical missteps, including giving propofol in an unmonitored setting, fumbling at basic resuscitation, and keeping no records.

Central to the government's case were the doctor's own words from a police interview two days after Jackson's death, in which he admitted to giving the singer the propofol and two other drugs earlier in the day. Dr. Steven Shafer, a renowned anesthesiologist and propofol expert, testified that the levels of the drug found during an autopsy showed Murray lied about how much propofol he administered.

Following the verdict, Murray was ordered to jail, and law enforcement has deemed him a "keep away inmate," meaning he will be assigned a single cell for his own protection and an escort to keep an eye on him at all times. He will not be allowed to mingle with the general inmate population, which will likely make him feel safer but also incredibly lonely.

Title: Injury Patterns and Risks in Collegiate Pole Vaulting

The study aimed to describe the injury incidence, patterns, and risks in collegiate pole vaulters. The research was conducted as a prospective cohort study over a single track-and-field season, involving 135 vaulters from 15 universities.

The study found that 41% of vaulters sustained an injury during the season, with a total of 70 injury events reported during 8823 exposures. This equated to 7.9 injuries per 1000 athlete-exposures.

The low back was the most common injury location, accounting for 16.7% of all injuries, followed by the hamstrings and lower leg, each accounting for 13.9%. A majority, 60%, of injuries were to the lower extremities, 21% to the upper extremities, and 18% to the back. No head or neck injuries were reported.

In terms of injury types, muscular strains accounted for 39.2% of all injuries, while overuse injuries accounted for 25.5%. Thirty percent of injuries, including 83% of low back injuries, occurred during the plant/takeoff phase of the vault.

One-third of lumbar injuries were spondylolysis, with 75% of these being season-ending. The odds of injury were 2.7 times greater in vaulters with multiple prior injuries.

In a separate study, the authors reviewed 32 catastrophic pole-vault injuries that occurred between 1982 and 1998. The majority of injuries were catastrophic head injuries (31) or a thoracic spine fracture resulting in paraplegia (1). Three common mechanisms of injury were identified: landing on the landing pad with the head on the surrounding hard ground (53%), landing in the vault box after being stranded at the height of the jump (25%), and completely missing the landing pad (16%).

The authors recommend increasing the minimum landing pad size and enforcing the rule requiring soft surfaces adjacent to the landing pads as primary measures to prevent injuries. Other potential preventive strategies include rule and equipment changes.

A Florida teenager, Austin Hatfield, is recovering at Tampa General Hospital after being bitten by a venomous water moccasin, also known as a cottonmouth, that he was illegally keeping in a pillowcase on his bed. The incident occurred on Saturday night, two days after Hatfield captured the snake in his girlfriend's yard in Wimauma. The snake escaped from the pillowcase and bit Hatfield when he tried to recapture it.

The bite caused massive swelling, and Hatfield was initially in critical condition but has since been upgraded to good condition. He reportedly needed several antivenin treatments. The snake was euthanized for identification and treatment of the bite.

Hatfield did not have a permit to possess the venomous reptile, and he captured the water moccasin illegally. The Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission is investigating, and Hatfield could face charges.

Water moccasins are heavy-bodied snakes with heads wider than their jaws and are known for their cotton-white interior mouths. They are pit vipers that can detect temperature differences as small as one degree from their surroundings, allowing them to strike their prey accurately. Those who come across them should give them a wide berth, as they will defend themselves if threatened.

In a controversial move, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has proposed a plan to relocate five apartment buildings in the Ulpana outpost in the West Bank, which were ordered to be demolished due to being built on privately owned Palestinian land. The plan involves transporting the three-story concrete structures to a nearby West Bank site, where they will be reassembled. However, construction specialists argue that this would be a costly and complex process, with each building requiring a week and $125,000 for sawing alone, and total costs potentially reaching $25 million. The Palestinians claim all of the West Bank, which Israel captured in the 1967 Mideast war, as part of a future state. In Israel, any talk of uprooting settlements is contentious. The Ulpana arrangement is an attempt by Netanyahu to avert the prospect of destroying a settlement and battling its residents. The evacuation of the settlers from the buildings began on Tuesday, with the settlers peacefully complying with the directive of a prominent rabbi at Beit El, who counseled them to avoid a violent confrontation. Netanyahu has promised to construct 300 more homes in Beit El to compensate for the evacuation. The government has requested an extension until mid-November to complete the relocation process, which cannot be completed by the court-set deadline of July 1. The Palestinian landowners are unlikely to gain access to their property anytime soon, as the area remains fenced off as part of the settlement.

The 2018 Gerber Spokesbaby, Lucas Warren, a 1-year-old from Dalton, Georgia, has made history as the first child with Down syndrome to win the title since the contest began in 2010. Lucas's contagious smile and outgoing personality captured the hearts of the Gerber team, who selected him from over 140,000 entries. The Warrens were awarded a $50,000 cash prize and Lucas's year will be documented on Gerber's social media platforms. The family hopes that Lucas's win will shed light on the special needs community and promote acceptance and inclusion. Katie Driscoll, founder and president of Changing the Face of Beauty, applauds Gerber's move towards more inclusive advertising.

In this article, Guy Scott, Zambia's new Vice President, discusses his unique position as the first white man to hold such a high office in independent Africa, his relationship with Robert Mugabe, and the complex relationship between Zambia and China. Scott, a Scottish-born economist, was appointed Vice President after the Patriotic Front party won the 2011 election, ending the former government's 20-year rule. He is the only white face in the Zambian national assembly and has been popular among the black electorate, leading to discussions about reconciliation with the colonial past.

Scott praises Mugabe's performance at a recent trade summit in Malawi and acknowledges the importance of Africa keeping hold of its own wealth, rather than losing out to foreign investors. However, he does not condone Mugabe's land seizures and mismanagement of Zimbabwe's economy. Scott's popularity among Zambians has been a surprise, as he is one of only 40,000 whites in a population of 13 million.

One of the biggest challenges facing Scott and President Michael Sata is Zambia's relationship with China. China has been a significant investor in Zambia since the 1960s, but local people struggle to compete against Chinese businesses and unskilled labor. Scott and Sata were elected on an anti-Chinese ticket, but Scott admits they have had to tone down the "China-bashing." He believes that the Chinese have something valuable to offer, but they need to improve their management and dealings with unions.

Scott is prepared to stand up to Chinese investors, but he acknowledges that the honeymoon period is not over, and people are still waving at him in the street. However, he knows that things could change quickly, and he is ready to face any challenges that come his way. The article also mentions that Scott was named acting leader following President Sata's death in October 2012, and presidential elections were held within 90 days to choose a permanent successor.

Kayla Mueller, an American hostage held by ISIS in Syria, was subjected to torture, verbal abuse, forced labor, and rape by the group's top leader. Despite her harrowing ordeal, Mueller's fellow hostages describe her as a courageous and selfless individual who never lost hope. Four former hostages who shared cells with Mueller spoke publicly for the first time about their shared ordeal for ABC News' "20/20" broadcast, "The Girl Left Behind."

Mueller was held captive for 18 months, during which she was subjected to various forms of abuse, including prolonged isolation, sensory deprivation, stress positions, forced labor, and sexual assault. However, she spent six weeks at an abandoned oil refinery in Syria with other Western hostages in 2014, where she was not subjected to the same level of abuse.

Former hostage Daniel Rye Ottosen recalled an instance where Mueller turned the tables on her captors. When one of the ISIS guards tried to claim that Mueller had converted to Islam, she corrected him, stating that she had not. Her fellow hostages were impressed by her courage and strength.

Mueller's spirit seemed to dim towards the end of her life, as her parents concluded after meeting a Yazidi girl who was imprisoned with Mueller in late 2014. However, Mueller was more optimistic about being freed when she briefly shared a cell with three women from Doctors Without Borders in early 2014.

The women from Doctors Without Borders entered Syria in November 2013, but a Doctors Without Borders official did not inform them that Mueller and three Doctors Without Borders workers had been abducted before their entry into Syria. This omission has been a source of controversy, with the executive director of Doctors Without Borders in the U.S. defending the decision as being made to keep Mueller's kidnapping quiet for her safety.

Mueller's fellow female hostages described their shared prison as a 12-foot-by-12-foot room with brick whitewashed walls, a blacked-out window, a single lightbulb hanging from the ceiling, and mattresses and blankets on the floor. They passed their time swapping stories, drawing, reading the Quran, and planning escapes. Mueller sometimes cracked them up doing impressions of guards, including one brute they called "Edges."

Mueller told the women about her previous six months of confinement, held mostly in isolation except for brief periods when she cared for a 14-year-old Shiite girl and another woman affiliated with Syrian President Bashar al-Assad's regime. All faced various forms of abuse by ISIS.

Mueller was more optimistic about being freed when she briefly shared a cell with the Doctors Without Borders women in early 2014. However, the Doctors Without Borders women were told by the ISIS captors to memorize an ISIS email address for the Mueller family to begin negotiations. This eventually led to extraordinary negotiations for her release, the former hostages and the Mueller family said in an ABC News investigation spanning more than two years.

Mueller was killed in captivity in February 2015, and ISIS claimed responsibility for her death. However, the White House denied that an airstrike killed her, confirming her death of unstated causes a few days after the ISIS claim. Mueller's proof of life video was released by ISIS in 2013, and her parents turned to the nongovernmental aid organizations for which their daughter worked for help, but found little assistance. Instead, they were told that her release was in the government's hands. The full proof of life video will be shown for the first time in an upcoming ABC News 20/20 special about Mueller's life and death in captivity.

In a series of tweets, author Zinzi Clemmons announced that she will no longer be writing for Lena Dunham and Jenni Konner's online feminist newsletter Lenny Letter. Clemmons' decision is due to what she calls Dunham's "well-known racism," which she experienced firsthand during their college years. Clemmons describes a strain of "hipster racism" among Dunham's circle, which uses sarcasm as a cover and often gaslights its victims.

Clemmons recalls a member of Dunham's circle using the N-word in conversation and justifying it as a joke. This incident, along with Dunham's initial support for Girls writer Murray Miller, who was accused of sexual assault by actress Aurora Perrineau, prompted Clemmons to leave Lenny Letter.

Clemmons' statement comes at a time when she is in Nigeria for a literary festival, where she is hearing stories from women facing dire conditions. She urges readers to consider the plight of the 26 Nigerian girls who drowned while being trafficked off the coast of Italy.

Clemmons' decision to leave Lenny Letter has been met with support from other writers, particularly women of color, who are calling for a divestment from Dunham. Clemmons' statement serves as a reminder of the importance of addressing and confronting racism, even within circles that claim to promote feminism and social justice.

The exhibition "Dreamful Slumbers: Drawings and Video" by James Fotopoulos is now on display at Microscope Gallery in New York, running from January 7 to February 6, 2012. The exhibit features over 80 charcoal drawings made between 2008 and 2011, as well as new video works. The title of the exhibition is inspired by a line from William Blake's "The Book of Urizen" and marks Fotopoulos' return to drawing, a practice he began in his youth.

Fotopoulos, who was featured at the Whitney Biennial and MoMA in the mid-2000s, created the works during a period of intense artistic introspection. He felt that if he couldn't succeed in harnessing his images and emotions using current technology, he should stop making work. This statement is significant given that Fotopoulos had already made over 100 films and videos.

The drawings in the exhibition contain imagery of animals, bodies, personal symbols from youth, and letters and words as personal codes of memories and dreams. The works trace the development of Fotopoulos' current works in charcoal, starting with simple black and white images, to a longer period of experimentation with reds, to a sudden focus on blue.

New video works on installation, such as "Wellness," bring to the forefront the discussion and connection between drawing and making moving images. A series of Fotopoulos' just completed works titled "Blue" completely bind the two, making a work in two parts: a drawing and a 15 to 20 second video.

In addition to the exhibition, Marni Kotak's performance art piece "The Birth of Baby X" is also on display at Microscope Gallery. Kotak is transforming the gallery into a home-birth center where she will give birth to her baby as a work of art. The exhibit is part of her long-term project "Raising Baby X," which will document her child's upbringing from birth through college. Kotak will be making the gallery her home as she waits for the contractions to start, with the baby due sometime during the next 5 or 6 weeks.

Fotopoulos was born in Chicago and currently lives and works in Philadelphia. His films and videos have been screened internationally, including at the Whitney Biennial, MoMA, and the Sundance Film Festival. Kotak's performance art works have been featured at various galleries and museums, including Anthology Film Archives, Momenta Art, and the Walker Art Center.

Pope Francis, the first Latin American pope, has a unique backstory that dates back to his childhood in Buenos Aires. At the age of 12, Jorge Mario Bergoglio was spurned by his childhood sweetheart, Amalia Damonte, which reportedly led him to pursue a religious career. Damonte, now 76, recalled that Bergoglio once said, "If I can't marry you, I'll become a priest," after she rejected him.

Damonte's parents kept them apart due to their disapproval of their relationship. She shared that Bergoglio had written her a letter, but she did not respond, which resulted in her father punishing her.

Meanwhile, Bergoglio's sister, María Elena Bergoglio, expressed concerns about her brother's new role as the 266th pontiff. She mentioned that he had initially expressed reluctance but was elected on Wednesday, replacing Pope Benedict who stepped down last month.

Bergoglio inherits a Catholic Church grappling with various challenges, including growing competition from evangelical churches in the Southern Hemisphere, a priest shortage, and a sexual abuse crisis. Despite these challenges, María Elena expressed pride in her brother's appointment, acknowledging his historical significance as the first pope from outside Europe and the first Latin American pope.

Anne Hathaway, who is a close friend of fashion designer Valentino, had planned to wear one of his designs to the Oscars, where she ultimately won her first Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress. However, she ended up wearing a controversial Prada column dress instead, due to a last-minute change caused by the similarity of her original choice to a dress worn by her Les Miserables costar Amanda Seyfried. Jennifer Aniston, who was also expected to wear a Valentino design, ended up in a bright red strapless gown instead, with speculation suggesting that Hathaway's camp may have influenced her decision to avoid a potential fashion clash. Hathaway later issued a statement expressing regret over the change, as she had long admired Valentino and had intended to wear one of his designs in honor of their relationship.

Taylor Swift made a significant impact by donating $50,000 to a GoFundMe campaign for a young girl named Naomi, who is battling cancer. The donation was so generous that it caused GoFundMe to increase its donation limit from $15,000 to $50,000. This is the largest donation in GoFundMe's history, and the company's CEO, Rob Solomon, stated that Swift's act of generosity could inspire future generations of giving.

Naomi's family, who are described as compassionate and loving, have been struggling with the unexpected diagnosis of Acute Myelogenous Leukemia (AML), a more aggressive type of leukemia that requires intensive therapy for 6-9 months. The family has been facing mounting medical expenses, and the GoFundMe campaign was started to help cover these costs.

Taylor Swift's donation came at a time when Naomi was unable to attend one of Swift's concerts due to her illness. Swift wrote a heartfelt message accompanying the donation, expressing her sympathy and offering support to Naomi and her family.

This isn't the first time Swift has used her influence to bring about change. Earlier this summer, she wrote an open letter to Apple, urging the company to pay artists during the free trial period of its streaming service. Apple complied with her demands, demonstrating the impact Swift can have on corporate policies.

The GoFundMe campaign for Naomi can be found at http://www.gofundme.com/teamnaomi. The family has expressed their gratitude for the outpouring of support they have received during this difficult time.

The article discusses the aftermath of the Democratic and Republican National Conventions, focusing on the polling data and strategies of both President Barack Obama and Mitt Romney's campaigns. The Romney campaign, while pleased with Obama's lackluster performance, admitted that the post-convention bounce they hoped for fell short of expectations, with state-by-state polling numbers, particularly in Ohio, favoring Obama. Both campaigns anticipate little movement in national polls before the first debate on October 3, which they consider the most important day of the campaign.

The article also highlights the differences in strategies between the two campaigns. Romney plans to run a one-size-fits-all campaign, focusing on the economy's poor state, blaming Obama, and emphasizing the need for a change of leadership. The Republican strategy relies heavily on negative ads and the support of Romney's billionaire backers. In contrast, the Obama campaign is concerned about the composition of undecided voters, who are mostly white, educated, economically stressed, and middle-aged.

Preliminary polling data suggests that Obama received a bounce in the polls from the Democratic Convention, with his lead over Romney increasing in several national tracking polls. However, the full impact of the bounce is yet to be seen, as the tracking polls only partially reflect the Democratic Convention data. The article suggests that Obama could potentially have an eight-point lead over Romney once the tracking polls fully roll over to post-convention data, making him a clear favorite as the campaign enters the final stretch.

The article also discusses the historical context of post-convention polling deficits and the challenges faced by Romney in winning over key voting blocks, such as the Reagan Democrats, Hispanic voters, security moms, and highly educated voters. The article concludes by acknowledging the risks of jumping to conclusions based on early polling data but suggests that the upside case for Romney is a quick cooling off of Obama's polling bounce, while the downside case is a stickier bounce that could make Romney a clear underdog.

The operation that killed Osama bin Laden, the leader of al-Qaida, revealed new details on Wednesday, contradicting the original claims made by the Obama administration. According to U.S. officials, four of the five people killed in the raid, including bin Laden himself, were unarmed and never fired a shot.

The operation took place on May 2, 2011, when a team of Navy SEALs stormed a compound in Abbottabad, Pakistan, where bin Laden was hiding. The SEALs initially took small-arms fire from the guest house in the compound, but the only time they were shot at was when they killed bin Laden's courier and his wife, who died in the crossfire.

As the SEALs moved through the compound, they found several stashes of weapons and barricades, suggesting that the residents were prepared for a violent and lengthy standoff. However, the operation was more of a precision operation, with the SEALs moving carefully through the compound, room to room, floor to floor.

The SEALs then encountered a man standing in the dark with one hand behind his back on the first floor of the main residence. Fearing he was hiding a weapon, the SEALs shot and killed the lone man, who turned out to be unarmed.

Bin Laden's 19-year-old son was also unarmed when he was shot and killed by the SEALs. Bin Laden himself was shot and killed when he peered over the railing from the floor above. He was wearing pajamas and was unarmed at the time.

The SEALs also found several young girls in the compound and carefully gathered up 22 women and children to ensure they were not harmed. Some of the women were put in plastic straps used to bind someone's hands at the wrists and left for Pakistani security forces to discover.

Despite the fact that only one of those killed was armed, everyone was considered a serious threat. Accounts of the operation had varied widely in the first few days after it was completed, with White House officials initially suggesting that bin Laden had been holding a gun and perhaps firing at U.S. forces. There was also a report that he used his wife as a human shield.

President Barack Obama ordered grisly photographs of bin Laden in death sealed from public view, stating that "We don't need to spike the football" in triumph after the raid. The decision was made to prevent the photographs from becoming a propaganda tool for bin Laden's adherents eager to incite violence.

The operation was a success, and the SEALs helicoptered out of the compound with computer files, flash drives, DVDs, and documents that intelligence officials are analyzing in hopes of degrading or destroying the network bin Laden left behind. The SEALs involved in the operation have returned to their home base outside Virginia Beach, Va., and have undergone extensive debriefing.

The operation was a significant victory in the war on terror, and it marked the end of a decade-long search for bin Laden. The disclosure that he was living in relative comfort inside Pakistan has raised questions about the Pakistani government's commitment to the search for the terrorist leader. The White House has announced that Obama will visit Fort Campbell, Ky., on Friday to greet troops returning from Afghanistan, which the United States attacked in 2001 after its leaders refused to turn over members of the al-Qaida leadership living there.

Pink, the singer-songwriter, graced the cover of People's 2018 Beautiful issue with her children, 15-month-old son Jameson Moon and 6½-year-old daughter Willow Sage. In an interview with Ellen DeGeneres, Pink joked about the cover, saying no one was allowed to look her directly in the eyes for the week the magazine was out. She also recalled laughing out loud upon learning about the title and expressed gratitude towards her children for securing the deal.

Pink's younger child, Jameson, is yet to understand the significance of his mother's cover, while Willow now has another example of what beautiful means. Willow, however, still feels self-conscious about her looks, as she told her mother during a conversation about Pink's viral August 2017 MTV VMAs speech about body image.

Pink discussed the meaning of beauty in the interview, stating that her 13-year-old self would not have listened to her current perspective. She expressed her appreciation for the changing perception of beauty and emphasized that it means different things to different people. Pink also highlighted her sense of humor as the best part of the experience.

The Beautiful Issue features numerous celebrities, including Pink, posing with their pets, best friends, and without makeup. The issue is on newsstands from Friday and can be found on PEOPLE.com. The singer also opened up about her parenting style, stating that she believes in giving affection and letting her children know they can count on her and her husband, motocross racer Carey Hart. She also emphasized the importance of fairness and justice in her household.

The U.S. Ambassador to Syria, Robert Ford, visited the embattled city of Hama on Thursday, marking a show of support for Syrians fighting for democracy. The visit came amidst ongoing violence and a general strike in Hama, which has been wracked with tension after a series of peaceful demonstrations. The city has been the site of violent crackdowns by security forces, resulting in numerous arrests and deaths.

President Bashar al-Assad fired the Hama provincial governor and security forces removed tanks from the city, indicating a possible easing of tensions. Ambassador Ford met with over a dozen Hama residents and visited a hospital treating those wounded in the security forces' crackdown.

The Syrian government accused Ford of going to Hama without obtaining prior permission, claiming it was evidence of U.S. involvement in Syria's internal affairs. However, U.S. officials stated that they had notified the Syrian government of the embassy team's travel to Hama.

The visit followed a massive protest in Hama last Friday, where over 500,000 people are reported to have participated, making it the single biggest protest yet against the Assad government. Reports suggest that at least 13 protesters were killed across the country during Friday's protests.

The city of Hama holds significant historical significance, as it was the site of a brutal military crackdown targeting Sunni Muslims by the Alawite-dominated government in 1982, resulting in thousands of deaths.

In another development, the Syrian ambassador was summoned by the U.S. for talks this week over reports that embassy staff had filmed U.S. protests against the crackdown in Syria. Additionally, an estimated 1,000 Syrians have fled Hama in fear of another military crackdown.

In a Twitter exchange, actor Mark Hamill, renowned for his role as Luke Skywalker in the Star Wars franchise, engaged in a debate with Republican Senator Ted Cruz over net neutrality. The discussion ensued after the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) voted to repeal rules that protected net neutrality, a move criticized for favoring big corporations. Hamill took issue with Senator Cruz's tweet, pointing out that Cruz had misspelled his name in the tweet. Hamill's tweet, in response, humorously suggested that Cruz might be distracted by watching porn at work.

The repeal of net neutrality rules, led by FCC chairman Ajit Pai, has been met with criticism from various quarters, including artists, actors, and musicians. Critics argue that the move will disadvantage smaller entities in the entertainment and creative industries. The debate between Hamill and Cruz occurred amidst the release of the latest Star Wars movie, The Last Jedi, which generated widespread excitement. Hamill, known for his active presence on Twitter, has previously expressed his disapproval of President Trump.

The exchange between Hamill and Cruz highlights the ongoing debate over net neutrality, with supporters arguing for its preservation as a means to ensure equal access to the internet for all. The incident also underscores the increasing use of social media platforms like Twitter as a platform for political discourse and public engagement.

The document provides detailed information about the costs and fees associated with attending Georgetown University, including tuition, one-time fees, student activities fee, course fees, materials fees, Yates Field House membership, student health insurance, payment plans, late registration and outstanding balance service charge, returned check fee, payment options, memo items, financial holds, delinquent accounts, dining plans, and housing rates.

Seth Owen, a high school valedictorian from Jacksonville, Florida, is facing financial challenges as he tries to attend Georgetown University. After discovering he was gay, Owen's parents sent him for conversion therapy and eventually told him to move out. Owen has been living with friends and has maintained a 4.16 GPA while homeless. Despite receiving a financial aid package from Georgetown, Owen still needs $22,000 for his first year of tuition. A GoFundMe page has been set up to help him raise the necessary funds.

The document also includes information about the tuition rates for the academic year 2018-2019, including the full-time rate for 12-20 credit hours and the part-time rate for more than 20 credit hours. Certain fees are charged to students once at the beginning of their studies, such as the orientation and transcript fees. The student activities fee funds various activities throughout the year, including Georgetown Day. Course fees are charged for lab courses and materials fees are charged for certain programs. The Yates Field House membership ensures access to the gym facilities and is mandatory for any student taking 12 or more credit hours. Georgetown University requires that all full-time students have health insurance, and students who are not already enrolled in an insurance program will be required to accept the plan offered by the university.

Students with an outstanding balance prior to the start of pre-registration for the next semester will have a financial hold placed on their account, which will prevent registration for future terms, prevent graduation, and prohibit the generation of an official transcript. Any student who becomes inactive and has an outstanding balance will be sent a final bill and, if the account is not settled in full within 30 days, the account will be assessed a final month's service charge and referred to a collection agency.

Dining plans at Georgetown include All Access plans, which entitle the student to an unlimited number of meals for the number of days indicated in the plan description, and Weekly plans, which entitle the student to the stated number of meals per week. Flex dollars are included in some dining plans and can be used at various on-campus dining facilities. Refunds and changes to dining plans are subject to a pro-rated charge.

Rates for housing at Georgetown are per semester and include residency halls, apartments, and townhouses. For more detailed information, please visit the website for Georgetown Student Living.

Jake Perry, a 85-year-old plumber from Austin, Texas, is widely known as a "cat man" due to his extensive collection and care for cats. Throughout his life, Perry has adopted and re-homed hundreds of cats, and has twice broken the Guinness World Record for the oldest cat, with Granpa Rexs Allen and Creme Puff living to ages 34 and 38 respectively. Perry believes that love, a special diet, and mental stimulation are the keys to his cats' unusually long lives.

Perry's cats are fed a diet of dry commercial cat food, home-cooked breakfasts of eggs, turkey bacon, broccoli, coffee with cream, and red wine every two days, and are shown nature documentaries in a home movie theater. Perry also believes that love and close personal relationships contribute to his cats' longevity, and remembers each of their birthdays.

The science behind Perry's longevity formula is shaky, with the American Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals regarding caffeine as toxic to cats, and a vet believing that the cats' coffee may help with their kidneys. However, it is widely accepted that sterilization of cats, which eliminates infectious disease risks and reduces roaming, contributes to increased life expectancy in cats.

Perry's cats have been celebrated and psychologically analyzed for their extreme dedication to their owner. Now, toward the end of his own life, Perry believes he has discovered the secret to feline longevity. The man who may have accidentally discovered feline semi-immortality has vanished, leaving many questions about his methods and impact on his neighbors unanswered.

In a speech at the inaugural conference of the China Aerospace Studies Initiative, Deputy Defense Secretary Robert Work highlighted China's rapid advancements in military technology, posing a significant challenge to the U.S.'s military superiority in air and space. China is reportedly developing radar-evading aircraft, advanced reconnaissance planes, sophisticated missiles, and top-notch electronic warfare equipment.

Work emphasized the need for the Pentagon to seek new technologies and systems to maintain its edge, citing the erosion of the U.S.'s long-held technological superiority. He mentioned the development of directed energy weapons as one potential solution, capable of shooting down missiles at a fraction of the cost.

The comments come amidst ongoing strategic and economic talks between the U.S. and China, with hundreds of Chinese officials in Washington for the three-day U.S.-China Strategic and Economic Dialogue. Xu Qiliang, a vice chairman of China's Central Military Commission, also called for accelerated innovation and development of China's national defense technology.

Both parties acknowledge the bilateral relationship as one with both cooperative and competitive aspects, with Work hoping that the cooperative aspects will outweigh the competitive ones over time. However, the Defense Department, as the 'hedge force,' is preparing for potential escalation in international competition.

The China Aerospace Studies Initiative is a partnership between the U.S. Air Force and the RAND Corporation, aimed at boosting U.S. research on China's aerospace ambitions. The initiative underscores growing concerns about China's military advancements and the need for the U.S. to adapt and respond accordingly.

China has suspended imports of shellfish from the west coast of the United States, affecting a $270 million Northwest industry and primarily targeting geoduck clams, oysters, and other two-shelled bivalves. The ban was imposed due to high levels of arsenic and a toxin causing paralytic shellfish poisoning found in recent shipments from Northwest waters. The restriction, which took effect last week and continues indefinitely, applies to waters of Washington, Oregon, Alaska, and Northern California. U.S. officials are awaiting more details from Chinese officials to identify the exact source of the contaminated clams.

The geoduck industry, particularly concentrated in Washington's Puget Sound, is experiencing significant consequences. Approximately 5 million pounds of wild geoduck are harvested annually, with an additional 2 million pounds from aquaculture. China, which accounted for nearly 90% of geoduck exports in 2012, is the primary market for these clams, which sell for retail prices of $100 to $150 per pound in China.

The ban has resulted in a significant loss of jobs for divers and harvesters, with thousands out of work. Local geoduck companies are adjusting by developing other markets in New York, California, and Seattle, while also exploring alternative solutions. The Suquamish Tribe, one of the largest geoduck providers, is idling its divers and seeking political intervention to overturn the ban.

The U.S. government is negotiating with the Chinese government to reopen shellfish trade, but the investigation and potential resolution could take months. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) stopped issuing certification for shellfish exports last Friday.

Tom Hiddleston received his first-ever Emmy nomination for Lead Actor in a Limited Series or Movie for his role in the six-part miniseries, The Night Manager, based on John le Carré's espionage novel of the same name. The series also received an Outstanding Limited Series nomination, and Hiddleston's costars Hugh Laurie and Olivia Colman, as well as director Susanne Bier, were also nominated. Hiddleston expressed his delight at the nomination, stating it was a huge undertaking and an enormous labor of love. The actor, known for his film and theater work, felt the switch to television was not unusual and was excited after reading the first script. Hiddleston is currently filming Thor: Ragnarok in Australia and confirmed his relationship with Taylor Swift, stating they are together and very happy.
