Martin explained that about two years ago, he was a mess because he couldn't enjoy the things that they were good at, and he couldn't appreciate the great things around him due to his personal issues. He took responsibility for the breakup, stating that he needed to make some changes and not blame anyone else.

The new album, Ghost Stories, allowed Martin to be honest and get to the root of his problems. He believes that everyone needs to be broken in some way and go through challenges, whether it's love, money, kids, or illness. He emphasized the importance of not running away from those challenges.

Martin also mentioned that he has taken up boxing to improve his physical condition and recently hired a personal trainer recommended by rapper Jay Z.

In addition to discussing his personal life and new album, Martin expressed his admiration for pop boyband One Direction and Kanye West, stating that he understands what they are talking about and appreciates their talent.

The full interview with Chris Martin will be broadcast on Monday night on Zane Lowe's BBC Radio 1 show. The band's lead single, Magic, was released in March, and they will be headlining the Saturday night at Radio 1's Big Weekend in Glasgow. Coldplay is also planning to reveal the lyrics for all nine songs from their upcoming Ghost Stories album by hiding Chris Martin's handwritten lyric sheets in libraries across the world. Clues to the exact locations of the lyrics will be posted on the band's Twitter account using the hashtag #lyricshunt. One of the hidden envelopes will contain a special golden ticket, giving the finder and a guest a free trip to London to see Coldplay perform at the Royal Albert Hall on 1 July.

The article discusses the issue of the US exporting most of its recyclable waste, particularly plastic, to China, which has been the primary buyer for over five years. However, China's Operation Green Fence, launched in 2013, is causing problems for American waste recycling companies as it forbids the import of certain types of solid waste, including unwashed plastics and other illegal waste mixed in with the good stuff. This is problematic for the US because China is the primary source of demand for its to-be-recycled plastic exports.

The US's reliance on China to buy up its plastic trash has meant that it's neglected to keep developing its own plastic recycling capacity. The drop-off in Chinese demand, and the lack of immediately accessible alternatives, could hit American cities hard, as they have made commitments to recycle but don't have a plan for what to do with the waste if it can't be exported to China.

Recycling companies across the US are struggling to find buyers for many of the plastics they have traditionally accepted, as China is no longer buying plastic items with the numbers 3, 6, or 7 on them, and inspectors are checking for and rejecting shipments of mixed plastics from overseas. This is causing problems for recycling depots, which are now having to sort plastic by specific resin instead of just one big bin, increasing costs for US cities.

Recycling companies in Portland, Oregon, are meeting with officials to find new buyers for the recyclable plastics China won't take. The new European data protection law requires users to consent to the use of cookies and data gathered from their use of the platform.

A South Carolina woman, Lana Clayton, was charged with murder and tampering with a drug product or food after allegedly poisoning her husband, Steven Clayton, by putting eye drops into his water for several days. The chemical tetrahydrozoline, found in over-the-counter eye drops such as Visine, was detected in Steven's body during an autopsy. The couple lived in a house valued at $822,000 on Lake Wylie, and Steven Clayton was known for his generosity and community involvement. Lana Clayton worked for the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs in Charlotte and had no prior criminal record in South Carolina. The motive for the alleged poisoning remains unknown, and Lana Clayton has not yet appeared before a magistrate or hired a lawyer. This is the second spousal arrest in a homicide involving a York County couple in less than a month.

In this news article, Joshua Vandiver and Henry Velandia, a same-sex couple, are fighting against the Defense of Marriage Act (DOMA) to prevent Velandia's deportation to Venezuela. Velandia, a salsa dancer and dance school founder, emigrated from Venezuela in 2002, while Vandiver is a Ph.D. candidate at Princeton University. They were married in Connecticut in 2010, but due to DOMA, Vandiver cannot sponsor Velandia's application for legal residency. Velandia is currently in deportation proceedings and will appear before an immigration judge in Newark, N.J., on Nov. 17. The couple is advocating for the repeal of DOMA and urging members of Congress to halt deportation hearings against foreign-born spouses of U.S. citizens. They have gained support through a Facebook group and a presentation at Whitman College. The couple hopes that the U.S. Supreme Court's ruling on DOMA, which was deemed unconstitutional by a lower court in July, will delay Velandia's deportation. Legal experts suggest that their chances are slim.

Rep. Darrell Issa has escalated the legal war over Fast and Furious, a failed ATF gun-walking program, by directly accusing President Barack Obama of either abusing his power or having his aides conspire with Justice Department officials to manage the aftermath of the program. In a letter to Obama, Issa accused the president of either being involved in the program or obstructing a congressional investigation by asserting executive privilege.

The White House has indicated it was not involved in the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives program, and Issa offered no evidence to back up his accusation. The letter is unlikely to force action by the president but is sure to grab headlines and build drama before the House votes on whether to hold Attorney General Eric Holder in contempt of Congress for refusing to turn over documents.

The House is expected to vote on the contempt motion on Thursday if the Department of Justice does not fork over documents they subpoenaed on the botched gun-tracking operation. Democrats are seeking to portray the Republican contempt motion against Holder as an assault on minority rights, with civil rights leaders scheduled to hold a press conference about the effect that placing Holder in contempt of Congress would have on his ability to protect the rights of black and Hispanic voters, homeowners, and immigrants.

Republicans have accused Holder and the Obama administration of stonewalling Congress, but Democrats are now trying to steer the "Fast and Furious" debate away from transparency and toward voter suppression. The contempt motion passed Issa's committee along strict party lines and is expected to pass the House, but securing Democratic support appears unlikely. Issa has noted that 31 Democrats sent a letter to President Obama expressing serious concerns about the administration's handling of Fast and Furious and the tragic fallout of having used the "gun-walking" tactics.

The Hill contacted all 31 Democrats for this article, but only four lawmakers said they were definitely not going to support the measure. The remaining 26 House Democrats did not respond to requests for comment. The contempt motion has proven to be divisive, with Democratic leaders calling it politically motivated. If the House finds Holder in contempt, it can refer the charge to the DOJ, but legal experts don't expect the DOJ to act on such charges, and the GOP-led House would then have to decide if it will file a legal challenge in federal court. Many Republicans have called for Holder to resign, expressing frustration with Fast and Furious as well as the administration's challenge of state election laws.

The Pi Kappa Alpha (Pike) fraternity chapter at Florida International University (FIU) has been suspended following the discovery of a private Facebook group where members posted about selling drugs, hazing, and engaging in sexist, homophobic, and body-shaming behavior. The group also discussed unsportsmanlike conduct during soccer games and a reputation for hazing. The university is investigating possible violations of its code of student conduct and the fraternity has been instructed to cease all meetings and events. This is not the first time Pike has faced discipline, as it has been found guilty of various offenses since 2006, including underage drinking, hazing, and vandalism. The suspension is the latest in a series of incidents involving Greek life at universities, with some raising concerns about the culture of these organizations and the potential for universities to turn a blind eye to their misbehavior due to their benefits in attracting new students, donations, and on-campus housing.

In a separate incident, a student at the University of Tennessee was hospitalized in critical condition after participating in a "butt-chugging" party at the UT Pike house, where students were inserting tubes into their rectums to funnel alcohol. This practice can be deadly. The university and the fraternity's international headquarters have since suspended the chapter for 30 days, pending an investigation into the allegations. The student's father is irate that news of his son's hospitalization has made headlines and has stated that there are significant errors that will be corrected. The university has released a 12-page police report detailing the incident.

In a tragic incident, one man is brain-dead, and five others are hospitalized with potential permanent brain damage after participating in a Phase I clinical trial for a Portuguese pharmaceutical company, Bial, in Rennes, France. The experimental drug, an FAAH inhibitor meant to act on the body's endocannabinoid system, was administered to 90 volunteers since July, with 65 receiving the drug and the rest a placebo. The trial was conducted by Biotrial, a French-based company known for carrying out thousands of trials since its establishment in 1989.

The adverse effects occurred on Thursday, with one volunteer admitted to the hospital on Monday, and the others on Wednesday and Thursday. The French health ministry has suspended all trials related to the drug, recalled all volunteers, and opened an investigation. The minister, Marisol Touraine, assured that no drug currently on the market is implicated in the failed trial.

Clinical trials are crucial for gathering data on new treatments for serious diseases like cancer, multiple sclerosis, and arthritis. Thousands of people participate in such trials annually, and incidents like this are rare. The study was a Phase I trial, in which healthy volunteers take the medication to evaluate its safety, tolerance, and pharmacological profile.

Standardized regulations for clinical trials are largely the same throughout Europe, but they minimize risk rather than abolish it, as there is an inherent risk in exposing people to any new compound. This incident serves as a reminder of the risks associated with experimental drugs and the importance of rigorous testing and safety measures in the development of new treatments.

The newsletter discusses two health-related topics: Placenta previa and a miraculous survival of a premature baby in China.

Placenta previa is a condition where the placenta partially or fully covers the cervix, leading to severe bleeding before or during delivery. The placenta provides oxygen, nutrients, and removes waste products from the baby. In most pregnancies, the placenta attaches to the top or side of the uterus, but in placenta previa, it attaches to the lower area of the uterus, potentially requiring a cesarean section for delivery.

In a remarkable story from China, a baby girl was born at just 23 weeks after doctors performed an emergency operation to correct a problem with her mother's cervix. The baby, now eight days old and weighing 660 grams, was born premature and faced a low survival rate. However, against all odds, she has survived and is currently receiving around-the-clock care in an incubator.

The baby's small size has earned her the nickname 'chopstick girl' by local media, as she is the same height as a chopstick. Due to her extreme prematurity, her organs and veins are not fully developed, causing complications in administering the correct medication and nutrients. Despite these challenges, the medical team is hopeful for her recovery.

In a study published in the journal PLOS One, researchers at the Max Planck Institute for Psycholinguistics in the Netherlands have found evidence that the word "Huh?" may be a universal word, appearing in similar forms and functions across languages scattered across five continents. The study, conducted by Mark Dingemanse, Francisco Torreira, and Nick Enfield, examined variations of the word in 10 languages, including Dutch, Icelandic, Mandarin Chinese, the West African Siwu, and the Australian aboriginal Murrinh-Patha. The researchers found that "Huh?" is a word that has to be learned in subtly different forms in each language, but it is much more similar across languages than words normally should be. The researchers propose that the similarity of "Huh?" across languages is due to the fact that it is found in a strongly similar environment in all these languages, namely the environment of other-initiated repair in conversations. The researchers suggest that this is an example of convergent evolution, where different species living in similar conditions can independently evolve similar traits. The study is part of a larger investigation of language and social interaction funded by the European Research Council. The researchers argue that "Huh?" is an indispensable tool in human communication, as it allows us to signal when we have problems with hearing or understanding what was said, and our conversations would be constantly derailed by communicative mishaps without words like this. The study found that all of the languages studied had a word with a near-identical sound and function as English 'Huh?' This is remarkable because usually, words in unrelated languages sound completely different. Compare, for example, these very different-sounding words for 'dog': inu in Japanese, chien in French, dog in English. One might object that this suggests that 'Huh?' is not a word at all. But in a careful phonetic comparison, Dingemanse and colleagues find that it is. Although 'Huh?' is much more similar across languages than words normally should be, it does differ across languages in systematic ways. 'Huh?' is not like those human sounds that happen to be universal because they are innate, such as sneezing or crying. It is a word that has to be learned in subtly different forms in each language. The researchers studied the specific context in which this word occurs and found that in human communication, when we are somehow unable to respond appropriately, we need an escape hatch: a way to quickly signal the problem. This signal has to be easy to produce in situations when you're literally at a loss to say something; and it has to be a questioning word to make clear that the first speaker must now speak again. Since these functional requirements are fundamentally the same across languages, they may cause spoken languages to converge on the same solution: a simple, minimal, quick-to-produce questioning syllable like English 'Huh?', Mandarin Chinese 'A?', Spanish 'E?', Lao 'A?', or Dutch 'He?'. The researchers also found that "Huh?" is a universal word not because it is innate but because it is shaped by selective pressures in an interactional environment that all languages share: that of other-initiated repair. The study enhances evolutionary models of language change by suggesting that conversational infrastructure can drive the convergent cultural evolution of linguistic items.

In an exclusive interview with Variety, Olivia Munn revealed that Fox initially did not respond after she reported "The Predator" actor Steven Wilder Striegel to the studio. Munn, who plays a biologist in the film, called Fox twice after learning that Striegel, a friend of director Shane Black's, had pleaded guilty in 2010 to two felonies related to attempting to lure a 14-year-old female into a sexual relationship through the internet. Striegel served six months in jail.

Fox later deleted the scene featuring Striegel's character hitting on Munn's character. Munn said she was happy that the scene was removed, as she felt it was important to stand behind the work they did in the movie.

Striegel had previously appeared in several of Black's films, including "Iron Man 3" and "The Nice Guys." Black later apologized for the error in judgment, but Munn said she was disappointed that he never reached out to her personally.

Munn also discussed the importance of Hollywood being aware of an actor's background, especially in light of the #MeToo movement. She said that it's important to remember that movies have a global reach and that having someone with a history of abusing children in a movie is not acceptable.

A spokesperson for Fox said that the studio was not aware of Striegel's history when casting the film, and that they removed his scene within 24 hours of learning the details. Black has since apologized for the error in judgment.

Munn's comments come as the #MeToo movement continues to bring attention to sexual misconduct in Hollywood and other industries. Munn has been a vocal advocate for the movement and has spoken out about her own experiences with harassment in the past.

Overall, Munn's interview highlights the importance of Hollywood being aware of an actor's background and taking action to protect victims of abuse. Munn's actions in reporting Striegel to Fox and advocating for the removal of his scene demonstrate her commitment to standing up for what is right.

Oyster, a subscription service for e-books, is shutting down after two years of operation. The company's founders announced the closure in a blog post on Monday, stating that they believe the phone will be the primary reading device globally over the next decade and that they are seeking new opportunities to fully realize their vision for e-books. Google has reportedly hired "a portion of the Oyster team," including CEO Eric Stromberg and co-founders Andrew Brown and Willem Van Lancker, to work at Google Play Books, but Google has not confirmed this.

Oyster took a novel approach to the e-book market by offering only a subscription book service for $9.95 a month. However, the service struggled to compete with traditional book sales and with Amazon's rival subscription service, Kindle Unlimited. Despite attracting the attention of publishers and amassing a library of over 1 million titles, Oyster was unable to gain significant traction with consumers.

In April, Oyster changed its model by expanding into online retail with an e-book store that sold individual books. However, this move came at an auspicious time for the book industry, as publishers have begun setting prices evenly across the e-book market. By expanding into online sales, Oyster was gunning for Amazon, which is estimated to control more than half the US e-book market and even more abroad.

Oyster users could only access the service through an app for smartphones, tablets, and computers, but not Amazon's popular Kindle e-reader. The company did have an app for the Amazon Fire tablet.

Update: Google has confirmed that it has hired "a portion of the Oyster team" to work at Google Play Books. The hiring includes Oyster's CEO and two co-founders. It is not clear if Google plans to launch its own version of Oyster's book subscription service.

The chemical spill in West Virginia's Elk River last week affected over 300,000 residents, causing a water crisis. The incident occurred in a state with a history of regulatory issues concerning the coal and chemical industries, which form the backbone of its economy. Critics argue that West Virginia's resistance to federal oversight and tight environmental controls puts its population and workers at risk.

The spill originated from a ruptured tank at a storage facility owned by Freedom Industries, which stores a chemical used for coal washing. No charges have been filed against the company, but an investigation is ongoing. The chemical, 4-methylcyclohexane methanol (MCHM), has contaminated the water supply, forcing schools and businesses to close, and necessitating the distribution of emergency water.

The state has been criticized for its lax regulations, with some states requiring inspections of chemical storage facilities, while West Virginia only inspects production facilities. The site of the spill has not been inspected since 1991. Gov. Earl Ray Tomblin has promised to work on tightening regulations of chemical storage facilities during the current legislative session.

The spill is not the first environmental emergency in West Virginia. In 2008, a chemical plant explosion killed two employees, and a subsequent investigation found that managers withheld information from emergency responders and misused a law intended to keep information from terrorists to hinder federal investigators. The state has also faced accusations of bureaucratic disorganization, a preference to let polluters escape punishment, and a revolving door of regulators moving to higher-paying jobs at the companies they once policed.

The spill has highlighted West Virginia's reliance on the coal and chemical industries, which have been major forces in the state's politics. Cleanup efforts are showing signs of improvement, with tests conducted at a water treatment plant downstream from the site of the leak showing little to no traces of contamination. Officials plan to lift the do-not-use ban by zones, starting with downtown Charleston and priority zones including hospitals and major water consumers.

Efforts to clean up the spill and tighten regulations are expected to continue, as the state grapples with the consequences of its history of regulatory issues concerning the coal and chemical industries.

Dominique Strauss-Kahn, the former head of the International Monetary Fund, gave his first interview since his arrest in May for sexual assault, maintaining that the encounter with a New York hotel maid was consensual and a moral failing on his part. In the interview, he also dismissed separate claims by a French writer that he tried to rape her in 2003 as imaginary. Strauss-Kahn faced criminal charges in the New York case, but they were dropped last month, and he is still facing a lawsuit brought by the maid. He said he would take time to reflect on his future in politics, but added that his life had been consecrated to being useful to the public good. The interview came off as somewhat scripted, with Strauss-Kahn looking unruffled and responding calmly to the questions. The former IMF chief reserved his harshest words for the US criminal justice system, saying he was afraid and humiliated by it. Strauss-Kahn was once considered a top contender in France's presidential race, but his political future remains uncertain.

Starbucks Corp. has partnered with Danone SA to expand its presence in the grocery market by selling Greek yogurt parfaits and other similar items. The yogurt products, co-branded as "Evolution Fresh, Inspired by Dannon," will first be sold in Starbucks cafes next spring, then in supermarkets in 2015. The move is part of Starbucks's strategy to diversify its traditional coffee business and tap into the fast-growing yogurt market, which is a $6 billion business in the U.S.

Starbucks acquired Evolution Fresh in November 2011 for $30 million and has since taken on other new ventures, including a line of energy drinks, a San Francisco Bay-area bakery, and its own single-serve coffee espresso brewer. Danone's Oikos brand Greek yogurt topped the list of best-selling food products launched in the U.S. last year, and the partnership will give Danone access to millions of consumers through Starbucks's cafes.

The financial terms of the deal were not disclosed, but Starbucks expects no additional capital expenses due to Danone handling the distribution. The partnership comes as Starbucks's grocery business has been expanding faster than its cafe sales, with revenue from selling items in supermarkets and other retailers jumping 50 percent to $1.29 billion in the year ended in September 2013.

Competition in the yogurt market will be tough, with leading maker Chobani Inc. recently coming out with 14 new items, including flavors like coconut, key lime, and orange vanilla. The hope is that Americans will start eating yogurt more often during the day, rather than just at breakfast.

Starbucks shares fell 1.2 percent to $68.19 at 12:02 p.m. in New York, having gained 29 percent this year through yesterday, compared with a 19 percent increase for the Standard & Poor's 500 Index. The partnership is seen as a "next big strategic step" in Starbucks's health and wellness evolution.

The document "Baby Name Report Card: Beneficial and Harmful Baby Names" by Albert Mehrabian, Ph.D., discusses the impact of baby names on personal, social, and work-related activities throughout a lifetime. The book provides a comprehensive analysis of desirable, attractive, and beneficial names versus undesirable, unattractive, and harmful ones.

The report categorizes names into several dimensions such as ethical-caring, popular-fun, successful, masculine-feminine, and overall attractiveness. It offers guidelines for selecting names that will impart positive and beneficial impressions, rather than negative and harmful ones. The book also includes useful information for adults who are dissatisfied with their first or last names and would like to assume new names.

The document also discusses the influence of family tradition and older relatives on the naming process. It mentions instances where grandparents or in-laws offer financial incentives or other rewards to have their names chosen for the baby. However, it also highlights the millennial trend of parents choosing unique and personal names for their children, often with the help of naming consultants.

The report concludes with creative solutions parents are coming up with to balance family tradition and personal preference, such as combining family names with something unique, choosing middle names, or using Hebrew names. The Hudocks, the example provided in the document, chose to honor a grandparent by naming their son after him.

In Murphy, North Carolina, the family of Cornelia June Rogers Miller is seeking the person responsible for writing a controversial obituary that portrayed Miller negatively, stating that her presence would not be missed by many. Miller, who lived in Florida and had a summer home in Murphy, passed away in February. The obituary, published by the Cherokee Scout, described Miller as having a love for drugs, making no contributions to society, and rarely sharing kind words or deeds.

The obituary has since gone viral, causing controversy within Miller's family and online. Miller's son, Robert, has accused his sisters of writing the obituary, although one sister denies this claim. The obituary has also been accused of plagiarizing sections from a 2008 obituary for Dolores Aguilar that appeared in the Vallejo Times Herald in California.

Robert Miller finds the obituary tragic and sad, and hopes that the memories his parents shared in Murphy will not be forgotten. He has sent a new obituary to the paper that will run next week, which he hopes will accurately reflect his mother's life as a loving, generous woman. The Cherokee Scout has stated that the family's will overrode the editor in publishing the original obituary.

The Bermuda Triangle, a region located between Miami, Puerto Rico, and Bermuda, is a controversial area where ships and planes are believed to mysteriously vanish without trace. First coined in a pulp magazine article in 1964, the Bermuda Triangle has been associated with various explanations, including aliens, the devil, and the lost city of Atlantis. However, researchers have recently suggested that methane bubbles from the sea floor could potentially sink ships and explain some of the odd disappearances.

Researchers at the Arctic University of Norway discovered huge underwater craters off the coast of Norway, which they believe could be a cause of enormous blowouts of gas. These craters, measuring up to 45m deep and 800m wide, could potentially create bubbles at the surface that could sink ships.

David May and Joseph Monaghan of Monash University in Australia demonstrated how a giant bubble from an undersea deposit of solid methane, known as gas hydrates, could swamp a ship. They found a sunken vessel within the center of one particularly large eruption site, now known as the Witches Hole, and proposed that the vessel's loss of buoyancy could be attributed to bubbles of methane gas released from an erupting underwater hydrate.

However, it is not yet clear whether gas blowouts happen in the Bermuda Triangle area, or how they would make planes vanish from the sky above. Additionally, several incidents attributed to the Bermuda Triangle may not be as mysterious as they seem, as some supposedly vanished boats were later found, and other vanishings, such as the disappearance of five Flight 19 training planes, can be explained by more mundane causes.

The Bermuda Triangle has been criticized as a phantom mystery, with some of the incidents attributed to it having simple explanations. However, the idea that methane release could sink ships holds some water, and further research is needed to determine its potential impact on shipping in the region.

During an extraordinary hearing, Supreme Court nominee Brett Kavanaugh and Christine Blasey Ford testified in front of the Senate Judiciary Committee. Meanwhile, U.S. Capitol Police announced the arrest of Jackson A. Cosko, a former Democratic staffer, for allegedly posting private information about Republican senators on the Wikipedia Internet website. Cosko, 27, faces five federal counts, including making public restricted personal information, making threats in interstate communications, identity theft, witness tampering, and unauthorized access of a government computer. He also faces District charges of second-degree burglary and unlawful entry.

Cosko, who most recently worked for Sen. Maggie Hassan (D-N.H.) as a "legislative correspondent/systems administrator," left Hassan’s office in May. He has been working as an intern in the office of Democratic Rep. Sheila Jackson Lee of Texas and has been fired. The arrest is tied to the investigation into the posting of personal information about Republican senators on the Wikipedia site during the hearing on sexual assault allegations against Kavanaugh.

The information posted purportedly included phone numbers and home addresses for three Republican members of the Senate Judiciary Committee: Sen. Lindsey O. Graham (S.C.), Sen. Mike Lee (Utah), and Sen. Orrin G. Hatch (Utah). The information was quickly removed after it was discovered, and aides contacted authorities.

Edits to the online encyclopedia were traced to IP addresses of computer devices assigned to the U.S. Capitol. It remains unclear whether the publication of such information was done to intimidate the senators following the dramatic hearings on Thursday. The investigation will continue, and additional charges may be forthcoming.

In the realm of political campaigns, a humorous twist was introduced by Republican presidential candidate Jon Huntsman, as he responded to Herman Cain's controversial "smoking man" ad with a parody featuring his three daughters. The daughters, dressed in horn-rimmed glasses and false mustaches, mimicked Cain's ad with a satirical twist, deadpanning lines about promoting Huntsman's candidacy and reviving the economy. The climax of the video showcases the daughters blowing soap bubbles in unison, replacing Cain's aide taking a drag on a cigarette. The video, titled "Jon2012Girls," was posted on YouTube on October 28, 2011, and added a light-hearted touch to the political landscape during a time when significant Supreme Court hearings and rulings were taking place regarding the Defense of Marriage Act (DOMA) and California's Proposition 8.

In a tragic incident on the Northeast Side of San Antonio, a jewelry store robbery at Rolling Oaks Mall resulted in one death and seven injuries. According to San Antonio Police Chief William McManus, two armed suspects attempted to rob a Kay Jewelers store. Two citizens, who were later referred to as "good Samaritans," tried to intervene. One of the citizens was shot dead by one of the suspects, and the other citizen, who had a concealed carry license, shot and wounded the other suspect. The second suspect then fled, shooting six people inside the mall. The mall was locked down, and police are questioning witnesses and conducting a sweep of the mall to ensure the second suspect is not still inside. The names of the individuals involved have not been released. The investigation is ongoing.

Audi is introducing an innovative system that allows drivers to know the exact time remaining before a traffic light changes from red to green. This industry-first feature uses wireless technology to link vehicles with traffic-management computers in select US cities, with five to seven cities expected to implement it by the end of the year. The system is available on the 2017 Q7 SUV and A4 sedan, but drivers must subscribe to Audi's Connect Prime service, which costs $199 for six months. The technology aims to make driving more enjoyable by reducing the stress associated with traffic lights. Over time, it could potentially turn off the car during stops, or suggest alternative routes based on traffic data. The system is part of Audi's broader strategy to enhance vehicle-to-infrastructure communication, which is crucial for the evolution of self-driving cars. Audi emphasizes that this service is built directly into the car, rather than being an app from Apple or Google.

Miley Cyrus, the former Disney star, is releasing her new album "Can't Be Tamed" and is embracing a more mature image, despite criticism for her provocative attire and music. In a recent interview, Cyrus defended her choices, stating that she is not trying to be provocative but rather consistent with her record's sound and her personal style. She admitted to being comfortable with her body and dressing in a way that makes her comfortable, which often includes revealing outfits. Cyrus is also set to shed her Disney persona, Hannah Montana, when the show ends this year, allowing her to fully embrace her solo stardom and sex appeal.

Separately, Heather Locklear is reportedly moving out of a psychiatric ward at a southern California hospital and into a long-term facility for ongoing mental health and substance abuse issues. Locklear was hospitalized a few days ago following a reported overdose scare. Sources close to her family have spoken with doctors, who believe that Locklear's problems require more significant long-term care than what can be provided at the hospital.

West Virginia Democratic Governor Jim Justice announced on Thursday that he will switch his party affiliation to the Republican Party, a move that reflects the state's rightward tilt and Trump's popularity in the state. Justice made the announcement at a rally with President Donald Trump in Huntington, West Virginia. Justice's flip is significant as it leaves the Democrats with control of just 15 governor mansions. The move blindsided his old party, with many West Virginia Democrats expressing disappointment and hurt feelings. The Democratic Governors Association had worked closely with Justice on his gubernatorial run, but the RGA spent millions of dollars trying to defeat him in 2016, attacking him for failing to pay taxes and fines related to his businesses. Justice's move is likely to make the coming months more complicated for Sen. Joe Manchin, who now stands as the state's most prominent Democrat ahead of a tough reelection challenge in 2018. The move also comes as Trump visits West Virginia, a state that he won by a landslide in 2016, and where his promises to renew American greatness, to "bring back jobs" and restore the coal industry have struck a chord. Trump's pro-mining rhetoric and policies have been popular in West Virginia, where the coal industry has seen a stark decline in recent years. The economic scene in West Virginia is almost as bleak, with the state having one of the country's lowest median household incomes, a labor force participation rate of just 53.1 percent, and a high rate of drug overdose deaths.

In the Los Angeles Dodgers' 5-0 win against the Tampa Bay Rays on August 10, 2013, Juan Uribe learned a valuable lesson the hard way. While on third base with one out in the fourth inning, Uribe stepped off the base, allowing the Rays to tag him out discreetly. Dodgers teammate Yasiel Puig shared a reminder on Twitter, using the phrase "El pie en la base" (Foot on the base) to prevent such mistakes in the future. The incident was captured on video and gained attention due to its embarrassing nature for Uribe.

The US has expressed concerns over potential massacres by the Syrian government in the town of al-Haffa in Latakia province, where UN military observers have been denied access. The UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon and peace envoy Kofi Annan have expressed grave concern about the violence in Haffa and Homs, where UN observers witnessed sustained shelling. The ceasefire brokered by Annan has largely collapsed, and Annan has appealed for access to Haffa due to concerning reports about regime plans.

Meanwhile, heavy fighting was reported in several Syrian cities, including Rastan, Talbisa, Idlib, and Deir al-Zour, where a car bomb exploded, killing 10 people. The Syrian government blames the violence on foreign-backed armed terrorist gangs, while the US emphasizes political and economic measures to pressure President Bashar al-Assad's government.

A UN report released Monday includes Syrian government forces and their allied "shabiha" militias for the first time on a list of 52 governments and armed groups that recruit, kill, or sexually attack children in armed conflicts. The report details numerous human rights violations against children in Syria, including killing, maiming, arbitrary arrest, detention, torture, and sexual violence.

Russia has called for Iran to take a role in ending the 15-month-old conflict, while the US Secretary of State Hillary Clinton rejected the idea of involving Iran. Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov will travel to Tehran on Wednesday to discuss the initiative.

The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau has announced plans to regulate large loan servicers in the $1.2 trillion student debt market, following reports that people with student debts are often tripped up by these servicers, particularly when seeking to change repayment terms. The Institute for College Access and Success reported that in 2011-12, 71% of students earning bachelor's degrees in the US had student loans, with an average debt of $29,400, up from $23,450 four years earlier. The report shows that rising tuition and stagnant family incomes are contributing to the need for students to borrow.

The average student debt load has risen to nearly $30,000, according to a new report from The Institute for College Access and Success. While colleges are raising tuition, family incomes are still suffering from the effects of the recession and remain flat. Many graduates are still having difficulty finding jobs that pay enough to cover student loan payments.

The report also shows that students from Delaware graduated with the highest average debt, while students in South Dakota were the most likely to graduate with debt. While most students take out federal loans, a fifth hold private loans, which are often more difficult for borrowers to manage and have less flexible repayment plans. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's annual student loan ombudsman report out in October reported that students with private student loans in particular have difficulty enrolling in alternative repayment plans, and private loan servicers often allocate payments to maximize late fees and pay off low-interest loans first rather than costlier high-interest loans.

The report also provides individual state and college data, with two private colleges, Anna Maria College and Wheelock College, both in Massachusetts, having more than 80% of graduates with student loans and the highest average debt per borrower, around $49,000, among colleges that provided figures. At two other private schools, Becker College in Massachusetts and Marylhurst University in Oregon, average debt was a few thousand dollars lower, but there were more borrowers — more than 90% of their graduates had debts. The report cautions that some colleges that did not take part in the survey might have been left off the roster, particularly for-profit schools, which award about 6% of bachelor's degrees and where students are much more likely to borrow money and borrow far more on average.

A 45-year-old man named Robin Lee was arrested by British Transport Police for charging his iPhone using a socket on a London Overground train on July 10th. The incident occurred at Camden Road station, and Lee was initially arrested for "abstracting electricity" under section 13 of the Theft Act 1968. He was later "de-arrested" for the first offence but was further arrested for unacceptable behavior after becoming aggressive towards a police community support officer (PCSO).

Sockets on London Overground trains are marked clearly as for use by cleaners only. Lee posted an image of his custody record on Twitter, with the reason for arrest stating "abstracting electricity phone charger on phone. Unacceptable behavior."

Lee later deleted his posts on Twitter, and photos of his custody record have also been deleted. The amount of electricity Lee abstracted is likely to be small, with the cost of keeping an iPhone fully-charged for a year being less than £1.

Online discussions on a London Underground forum suggest that the sockets are provided for cleaners to use when cleaning trains in depots and are not intended for public use. Some members have pointed out that the sockets may be energized all the time, which could pose a risk of power surge if electronic equipment is directly plugged into them.

Last week, a 19-year-old man named Nick Silvestri made headlines in New York after jumping on stage before a Broadway play in an attempt to charge his phone using a fake socket that was part of the set. He said his phone had 5% left as "girls were calling all day."

The document discusses the ongoing search for Hannah Graham, a second-year student at the University of Virginia who has been missing since late Friday/early Saturday morning. Police are seeking a person of interest, described as a black male in his late 20s or early 30s, with a close-shaved head, a goatee, and a slight "beer belly." Surveillance videos have been released showing an unidentified man following Graham on the night she disappeared. Police are canvassing the downtown Charlottesville area for more surveillance videos and have interviewed the man seen in the videos. Anyone with information about Graham's whereabouts or the person of interest can call a tip line. A reward of $50,000 is being offered for information about her disappearance.

The police have released a description of the man of interest, who was seen with Graham in the 3-500 blocks of E. Main St. on the Downtown Mall in the City of Charlottesville around 1-1:15 am on September 13th. The man is described as being in his late 20s-early 30s, 5'10"-5'11", 250-285 pounds, with a close-shaved head, goatee, and a slight "beer belly." He was wearing black jeans and a white T-shirt.

A community search is being organized for this coming Saturday and Sunday, and a candlelight vigil will be held for Graham at the UVA Amphitheater at 9 p.m Thursday. Graham is described as approximately 5'11" tall with a skinny build, with blue eyes, light brown hair and freckles. She was last seen wearing a black crop top with mesh cutouts. Graham is a second-year student at UVA who graduated from West Potomac High School last year. She's originally from the U.K., but her parents live in Alexandria in Fairfax County. Police still want to hear from anyone who may have seen Graham or from businesses who might have surveillance video. They urge anyone with information to call the tip line at 434-295-3851.

The U.S.-China Internet Industry Forum held at Microsoft's campus in Redmond, Washington, brought together top CEOs from various tech companies for a meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping. The gathering included notable figures such as Apple's Tim Cook, Microsoft's Satya Nadella, Amazon's Jeff Bezos, Facebook's Mark Zuckerberg, Alibaba's Jack Ma, and several other executives.

During the event, President Xi toured Microsoft's facilities, including technology demonstrations of products like the HoloLens and data visualization software. He later met with the CEOs, many of whom had already spoken with him at a roundtable meeting earlier in the day.

Mark Zuckerberg, who spoke with Xi in Mandarin, considered the encounter a personal milestone as it was his first time speaking with a world leader entirely in a foreign language. Zuckerberg's Facebook page featured a post about the meeting, which sparked debate among internet users over China's censorship.

The meeting between tech leaders and President Xi highlighted the significant influence and market control that China holds, as the event attracted the top 10 American technology companies, with a combined market value of approximately $2.5 trillion. The gathering served as a testament to the allure of being in Xi's orbit and the potential opportunities in the Chinese market.

The attendees included CEOs from various industries, such as Sugon, Didi-Kuaidi, Broadband Capital, CEC, Baidu, AME Cloud Ventures, Inspur, Airbnb, Sequoia Capital China, Sohu, AMD, Lenovo, Microsoft, Qualcomm, CETC, Intel, Qihoo 360, LinkedIn, SINA, Facebook, JD.com, Cisco, Alibaba, IBM, China Minister Lu Wei, and Apple.

The meeting between tech leaders and President Xi touched upon various topics, including cybersecurity, intellectual property theft, and the need for constructive dialogue on cyber issues to benefit both countries and the world. The event marked the 20th anniversary of cooperation between Microsoft and China, with President Xi expressing his admiration for Microsoft products and the Windows operating system.

The United States has announced a retaliatory measure against Russia, ordering the closure of a Russian consulate in San Francisco and scaling back its diplomatic presence in Washington and New York. This action is in response to Russia's earlier decision to reduce the U.S. diplomatic staff in Moscow, a move taken in retaliation for U.S. sanctions. The U.S. State Department claims this action brings both countries into "parity," with each having three consulates in the other country. The Russian offices affected by the U.S. order are required to close by September 2, including a "chancery annex" in Washington and a "consular annex" in New York. The U.S. has fully implemented the Russian decision to reduce its mission in Russia and hopes that this action will help avoid further escalation, aiming to improve relations between the two countries and increase cooperation on mutual concerns. The U.S. is prepared to take further action if necessary.

In a highly anticipated meeting on the sidelines of the G20 summit in Hamburg, US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin met for the first time. The meeting, which lasted over four times its scheduled half-hour length, was personalized and excluded key members of Trump's team who are more skeptical about Russia. The discussion focused on various topics, including Syria, Ukraine, and election hacking, but it is unclear if any substantial progress was made.

Russia's election hacking was raised during the meeting, but it did not seem to take top priority. US Secretary of State Rex Tillerson stated that Trump was focused on moving forward from the issue, while Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov claimed Trump had accepted Putin's denials of involvement. A working group on non-interference in future elections was agreed upon, but this is unlikely to reassure those in Washington concerned about Russia's actions.

The meeting's format and tone were a win for Putin, as it was held in a small room with only the respective foreign ministers and two translators present, reducing the chance of leaks. Putin looked impassive but was likely pleased, as he had been briefed that a disdain for supposed "fake news" would be a promising area of potential common ground with Trump.

The meeting comes amid ongoing investigations in the US into whether there was any collusion between Trump's presidential campaign and Russia. Some US senators have expressed concern about reports that the administration plans to discuss the return of diplomatic compounds in Maryland and New York to Russia, which were seized by the Obama administration last year in response to alleged Russian election meddling.

Trump is also grappling with a response to North Korea's successful test of an intercontinental ballistic missile, which analysts say had a long enough range to reach Alaska. Curbing Pyongyang's nuclear ambitions has been Trump's most pressing foreign policy priority. He met with leaders from Japan and South Korea on Thursday evening to discuss it and is also scheduled to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping at the G20. Some politicians, such as Representative Francis Rooney, suggest that this meeting could provide an opportunity to reset the Russia relationship in a positive manner.

Belinda Stuckey, a 35-year-old primary school teacher from Sydney, Australia, has gone on 136 dates in the past two years through the internet dating site eHarmony but has never had a second date with any of the men she met. Despite being one of the most contacted members on the site, receiving around 10 matches a day, and having matched with an astounding 4,700 men since joining in December 2013, Miss Stuckey remains single. She attributes her popularity to her honesty with her profile, stating that she does not see the point of putting out someone she is not. Despite her apparent bad luck in finding love, Miss Stuckey remains hopeful and is ready to keep going until she finds her perfect match. She says she has thick skin and takes rejections with a grain of salt, knowing that her ideal partner is still out there.

Warren Buffett, the CEO of Berkshire Hathaway Inc., is seeking new investment opportunities after spending over $26 billion on the company's biggest-ever deal last year. In his annual letter to shareholders, Buffett expressed the need for more large deals to supplement the earnings of Berkshire's numerous businesses, which span industries such as insurance, candy, utilities, and home manufacturing.

Buffett's letter, titled "God Bless the U.S.A.", emphasized the abundance of opportunities in America and Berkshire's commitment to investing domestically. The company spent over $5 billion last year on property and equipment in the United States, with plans for future investments primarily at home.

The letter also highlighted Berkshire's financial performance, with net income of $13 billion in 2010, a 61% increase from 2009, and a 13% rise in book value. Shares of Berkshire Hathaway closed at $127,550, up 29% in 2010, more than double the broader stock market's performance.

Buffett's letter provides insights into his investment philosophy and offers advice to investors. He discussed the importance of having the right chief executive, citing the difference in outcomes between Sears Roebuck's and Montgomery Ward's CEOs in the late 1960s and Sam Walton.

Regarding succession plans, Buffett praised his insurance business head, Ajit Jain, and new hire Todd Combs, but did not provide specific details about his future leadership. Buffett also took a swipe at the hedge fund industry, criticizing high payouts to general partners who walk away rich when results are poor.

Buffett addressed one of Berkshire's most closely watched holdings, the $5 billion investment in Goldman Sachs, explaining that Goldman has the right to repurchase his preferred shares.

Buffett attributed much of the year's success to the acquisition of Burlington Northern Santa Fe railroad, calling it the highlight of 2010. The $26 billion deal increased Berkshire's earnings power by more than 30%. Buffett also emphasized the environmental benefits of rail travel over trucking.

Buffett concluded the letter by teasing his shareholders, stating that he is on the hunt for "more major acquisitions" and that his "trigger finger is itchy." Despite the large cash reserves, Buffett has sworn off dividends and stock repurchases, indicating that the funds will be used for future investments.

The Solar Impulse 2, a solar-powered airplane, successfully completed a record-breaking 4,000-mile flight from Nagoya, Japan, to Hawaii, marking the longest and most dangerous leg of its around-the-world journey. Pilot André Borschberg landed the plane in Hawaii after nearly five days in the air, breaking the record for the longest solo flight by time. The flight was the eighth of 13 legs, with Borschberg and co-pilot Bertrand Piccard alternating the long solo flights aboard the plane.

During the journey, Borschberg had to endure temperatures close to 37C (100F) in the cockpit and was only able to rest in 20-minute intervals. He tweeted throughout the journey, sharing his experiences and the challenges he faced, including climbing the equivalent altitude of Mount Everest four times during the fourth day of the leg.

The Solar Impulse 2 must find clear skies during the day to receive as much solar energy as possible and conserve energy at night by descending to a lower altitude and slowing speed. The plane's mission is to raise awareness about climate change and showcase what can be done using only renewable energy.

The mission began on March 9 from Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, and will continue with the next leg to Phoenix, Arizona, as weather permits. The plane will then land at a location in the Midwest, New York City, and undertake two final flights over the Atlantic Ocean and the Mediterranean Sea before landing back at Abu Dhabi.

In Harford County, Maryland, a shooting incident occurred at a Rite Aid Distribution Center on Thursday morning, resulting in multiple fatalities and injuries. The shooting suspect, a woman, is in critical condition at a hospital. Authorities have not yet identified the suspect. The incident occurred at the 1500 block of Perryman Road, near Spesutia Road.

Law enforcement agencies, including the FBI, DEA, ATF, Maryland State Police, MDTA Police, Natural Resources Police, and local municipal departments of Aberdeen, Havre de Grace, and Bel Air, responded to the scene. The Harford County Sheriff's Office urged anyone still in the building to dial 911.

Four victims with gunshot wounds were taken to Johns Hopkins Bayview Medical Center, and one victim was taken to Christiana Hospital in Newark, Delaware. The families of the victims, all adults, are yet to be notified.

Sheriff Jeffrey Gahler confirmed that a single handgun was used in the incident, and no shots were fired by law enforcement at the scene. He also stated that there is no additional threat to the community.

Authorities are working to reunite displaced workers with their loved ones. A family reunification center has been set up at the Level Fire Company at 3633 Level Village Road in Havre de Grace. The Harford County Emergency Operations Center is partially activated due to the situation, and the Harford County Information Hotline at 410-838-5800 has been activated for people trying to get in touch with family and loved ones.

This is a developing story, and more information will be released as it becomes available. Our thoughts are with the victims and their families.

Kristine Bunch, a mother who was imprisoned for 22 years for the murder of her three-year-old son in an arson fire, was released from jail on Wednesday after new evidence was presented that led to a new trial. Bunch, who was 22 at the time of the fire, was sentenced to 60 years in prison but was granted a new trial in March by the Indiana Court of Appeals. The Center on Wrongful Convictions at Northwestern University School of Law took up Bunch's case in 2007 and presented new evidence to the appeals court based on technological advances in fire investigations. The new evidence showed that Bunch's son died of carbon monoxide poisoning, not burns, and that some test results provided by the state were incorrect. On Wednesday, Senior Circuit Judge W. Michael Wilke granted Bunch's release, pending her new trial. Bunch was initially in a state of shock upon being sentenced to 60 years, but upon her release, she expressed no bitterness and said she wanted to give back and help others who have been wrongfully convicted. Bunch has dreams of going to law school and focusing on criminal law. She also wants to reconnect with her family, especially her 16-year-old son, whom she has never lived with except for the first night of his life. Bunch was taken from the jail in a new dress and black patent leather shoes and was greeted by her mother, son, and other family members upon her release. The case has garnered attention and support from various organizations, including the Women's Project at Northwestern University School of Law. The Women's Project is an exoneration effort focused exclusively on freeing wrongly convicted women and has already agreed to represent six women in cases involving child head trauma and arson science. The project is led by Karen Daniel and Judy Royal, who have helped exonerate over two dozen people, most of whom are men. The Women's Project is also conducting an in-depth study of wrongful convictions of women accused of killing their children.

The 93-year-old President of Zimbabwe, Robert Mugabe, is reportedly having eye problems that make him sensitive to bright lights, according to his spokesman George Charamba. This explanation has been given for Mugabe's frequent appearances of closing his eyes during meetings, which has sparked speculation about his fitness to rule. Mugabe intends to stand in presidential elections next year. He is currently receiving specialized medical treatment for his eyes in Singapore. The spokesman compared Mugabe's condition to that of Nelson Mandela, who was also sensitive to bright lights due to his time spent in a limestone quarry while imprisoned. Photographic evidence shows Mugabe closing his eyes during conferences dating back over a decade. The recent health trips of Mugabe have been a source of concern in Zimbabwe, which is preparing for elections next year, with critics questioning Mugabe's fitness to rule, especially given the country's struggling economy. However, Mugabe refers to Zimbabwe as "one of the most highly developed countries in Africa."

The Internet Archive is working on a project to archive web pages as they are created and preserve links to the archived versions of pages that are referenced. This is aimed at fixing broken links on the web. The company Hyperloop Transportation Technologies has announced that it will use a passive magnetic levitation system for Elon Musk's proposed 700mph maglev train, which involves transporting people through low-pressure tubes at high speeds. The system will use magnetic fields in the tunnel to lift the pod before a thrust force is applied to accelerate it, and regenerative braking will be used to recharge the battery. Critics have questioned whether the Hyperloop will ever come to fruition due to cost and safety concerns.

Elon Musk's Hyperloop concept had its first public demo in the Nevada desert, testing only the propulsion mechanism. The demo focused on the propulsion technology rather than the speed, and Hyperloop One announced new funding and new partners in transportation and engineering, including Danish architect Bjarke Ingels. Hyperloop Transportation Technologies has licensed passive magnetic levitation technology to power its prototype system, which it plans to show off in the desert north of Las Vegas.

Competing teams are showing off their Hyperloop prototypes, with Hyperloop One testing its propulsion mechanism and Hyperloop Transportation Technologies planning to showcase the evolution of its technology to investors and media. Hyperloop technology offers the possibility of moving people and things at great speeds without using fossil fuels, but faces infrastructure and regulatory hurdles and a high price tag. The foundations of its tech are familiar, with the maglev principle already at work on high-speed trains in Europe and Japan. However, Hyperloop would face the same infrastructure and regulatory hurdles that vex high-speed rail projects and autonomous cars.

Critics have questioned whether Hyperloop will ever come to fruition, targeting cost and safety as potential major setbacks. Hyperloop Transportation Technologies is addressing safety concerns with a passive levitation system, which will eliminate the need for power stations along the Hyperloop track and keep construction costs low. The system has huge safety advantages, as levitation occurs purely through movement, and if any type of power failure occurs, Hyperloop pods would continue to levitate and only after reaching minimal speeds touch the ground. SpaceX, the rocket company founded by Tesla CEO Elon Musk, is also working on Hyperloop technology.

The article discusses the harrowing journey of a 30-year-old North Korean woman named Suh, who fled North Korea in 2008 and is now making her way from Laos to Thailand with her 18-month-old daughter, Ji-yeon. The journey is fraught with danger, as Suh and her companions must avoid detection by police to reach Thailand, where they hope to find a better life.

In North Korea, many women are sold to Chinese husbands and forced to live secretly in northern China. Some of these women are coerced into performing online sex work for men, often through smartphone apps, to earn money. Suh herself resorted to doing "video chatting" after her second child was born and her husband's meager construction earnings couldn't support the family.

Suh and two other women from her village in northeastern China fled over the summer, leaving her 5-year-old daughter behind with her Chinese husband. They traveled by bus and car down through China to the border with Laos, which they crossed illegally in the black of night, with Suh carrying Ji-yeon on her back.

The women were met by a Washington Post reporter in Vientiane, Laos, as they paused on their journey. The women talked for hours about their lives in North Korea and in China, but appeared to play down their experiences out of shame. The reporter was able to verify most of their stories with the pastor and broker who were helping them escape.

The women had a friend film them at work before they left, so they could prove what they had been doing. The videos showed the women — sometimes in brightly colored underwear, sometimes naked — sitting against a low bed covered with a purple Hello Kitty quilt in front of two computers on a low table. Men, sometimes visible, sometimes not, gave them instructions. Most of the men they "chatted" with online were in South Korea, but a few were in America and even Africa.

Safely out of China, the other two women, both called Kim, wanted to get to South Korea, but Suh had her heart set on a more ambitious destination: the United States, "the strongest country on Earth." Suh said, "I think my daughter is one lucky baby. All the suffering is worth it. Our destiny has changed."

The women faced many challenges and difficult decisions on their journey, including leaving Suh's 5-year-old daughter behind and crossing the Mekong River, which had swollen due to heavy rain and caused their boat to miss the drop point. They were discovered by local police and taken to a prison, but were eventually taken to Bangkok and are now being held at a detention center. Suh has applied for asylum in the United States, even though she speaks no English and knows she will receive little support, unlike in South Korea.

The article also discusses the broader issue of North Korean women being sold to Chinese husbands and forced into online sex work or other forms of exploitation. The Chinese government is making efforts to address trafficking, but the State Department's 2016 Trafficking in Persons Report noted that North Korean women and girls are still subjected to sexual slavery, forced prostitution, and forced labor in China. The article concludes by emphasizing the handicaps that North Koreans face, as Suh asks, "Why are our lives so different, just because of where we are born?"

The Taliban have claimed responsibility for the kidnapping of a British female aid worker in Afghanistan, demanding an exchange for the jailed Pakistani scientist Aafia Siddiqui. The woman, who is in her 30s and works for a U.S. charity, was travelling with three Afghan men when they were ambushed in Kunar Province. The Taliban commander Mohammed Osman stated that they would demand the release of Siddiqui, who was jailed for 86 years last week by a New York court for attempted murder of U.S. agents and soldiers. Siddiqui, a neuroscientist and mother of three, was arrested in Afghanistan in 2008 and has been accused of opening fire on FBI agents. The British embassy in Kabul is investigating the report, and an extensive search is being carried out for the unnamed Scottish woman. The motive for the kidnapping is not clear, but insurgent involvement is likely as the Taliban usually take foreigners alive. The group was attacked as they travelled from Kunar province to Jalalabad, a rugged region close to the border with Pakistan which is a known Taliban stronghold. The incident comes barely a month after the death of British doctor Dr Karen Woo, who was shot dead in an ambush. The Foreign Office confirmed last night that a British national is missing in Afghanistan. The Taliban have also claimed responsibility for Woo's death, saying she was preaching Christianity. The latest kidnapping and Woo's death have raised concerns about the safety of foreign aid workers in Afghanistan. Meanwhile, a top NATO commander in Afghanistan said there should be no rush to withdraw alliance forces in 2011, as it would be much harder to send them back if necessary. Lieutenant-General Nick Parker said the withdrawal of NATO forces from Afghanistan should not be rushed, and the significance of a July 2011 U.S. withdrawal date had been overemphasised. Almost 150,000 foreign troops, mostly American, are fighting a now nine-year NATO-led war against Taliban insurgents. This year has been the deadliest for foreign forces, and pressure in participating countries has mounted for troops to be withdrawn.

Rep. Gabrielle Giffords, who survived a gunshot wound to the head, is embarking on a challenging rehabilitation journey at a Houston center. Her progress has been impressive, but doctors warn that severe brain trauma patients often have to relearn basic tasks. Giffords will undergo intensive speech and occupational therapy for several hours daily. The bullet went through the left side of her brain, potentially affecting her vision, language, and memory. Medical risks remain, including seizures, weight loss, and depression. Doctors are optimistic about her recovery due to her young age, intelligence, and family support. She will have a helmet during therapy and will need to replace the portion of her skull removed after the shooting. The journey to Houston includes an escort by VFW motorcycle riders and an air ambulance flight. Her husband, astronaut Mark Kelly, is hopeful about her long-term recovery, predicting she will walk through the hospital's front door within two months.

The article discusses the upcoming addition of a leap second to Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) on December 31, 2016, to keep UTC synchronized with astronomical time. The extra second is necessary because Earth's rotation is not constant and is gradually slowing. Leap seconds have been added since 1972, approximately every 18 months, to keep the difference between UTC and astronomical time (UT1) to less than 0.9 seconds.

The addition of a leap second can cause problems for timekeeping computers, which are unable to conceive of a 61st second by the very nature of their coding. Google, which runs Network Time Protocol servers, has come up with a solution to this problem by running clocks 0.0014% slower across the ten hours before and ten hours after the leap second, and "smearing" the extra second across these twenty hours. This method, called "smeared time," was first proposed by Google in 2008 and has been used by other companies in similar positions.

Google is encouraging anyone running IT operations to use its NTP servers to help cope with the next leap second. The company will let anyone use its NTP servers free of charge, and has provided detailed instructions for synchronizing systems to its smeared time. Other cloud companies, such as Akamai and Amazon, are also using similar methods to smear the leap second over a 24-hour period around the event.

The article also provides background information on leap seconds, including the reasons they are necessary and the future of leap seconds. Leap seconds are added when needed, based on measurements, and are intended to keep UTC within one second of astronomical time. The International Earth Rotation and Reference Systems Service (IERS) measures Earth's rotation and publishes the difference between UT1 and UTC. Leap seconds have always occurred at the end of December or the end of June, on the last second of the UTC day.

The article concludes by noting that the addition of a leap second is a relatively rare event, but one that can cause problems for timekeeping computers. Google's solution of smearing the extra second across twenty hours is an elegant solution to this problem, and the company is encouraging other companies to adopt a standard noon-to-noon, 24-hour smear, with the leap second dead center, instead of on the end.

In the upcoming film "A Star is Born," Lady Gaga makes her feature film debut, marking her first collaboration with director and co-star Bradley Cooper. The movie is a remake of the 1976 film featuring Barbra Streisand and Kris Kristofferson. Gaga plays Ally, a struggling musician whose career takes off after meeting Cooper's character, Jackson Maine, a washed-up country singer. The film, set for release on October 5, also stars Andrew Dice Clay, Sam Elliott, and Dave Chappelle. Gaga and Cooper wrote original music for the film, which was recorded live during filming, including performances at Coachella in 2017. The film follows the tumultuous relationship between the two characters, with Gaga's character's career success leading to personal struggles. Cooper, who also sings live in the film, told Entertainment Weekly that the film's central theme is a "broken love story" expressed through music.

A newly discovered bug on iPhones causes the devices to become unusable when the system date is set to January 1, 1970. This bug is related to an old issue with Unix-based operating systems, similar to a previous glitch on Facebook. The bug appears to affect iPhone 5S, iPad Air, iPad Mini 2, and sixth-generation iPod Touch, or newer models of these devices. Changing the date to January 1, 1970, and attempting to restart the device results in the Apple logo screen getting stuck. The bug has been demonstrated in a video by tech website 9to5mac, and Apple has yet to respond to queries about the issue. The bug seems to have originated from an image posted on the anonymous forum 4Chan, and has since been spotted on Facebook and Reddit. Users who have fallen victim to the bug have reported their devices becoming 'bricked', with no success in restoring or updating them.

The US CEO of Volkswagen, Michael Horn, has admitted that the company was dishonest with US regulators and the public regarding emissions tests on their vehicles. The scandal, which involves the use of a defeat device to falsify emissions data, could result in fines of up to $18bn, criminal charges for executives, and legal action from customers and shareholders. The device recognizes when the car is being tested and immediately cuts emissions to a level much lower than normal and unsustainable under usual driving conditions.

Shares in Volkswagen fell by another 5% on Tuesday after losing almost a fifth of their value on Monday. In further developments, France's finance minister called for a Europe-wide investigation into diesel cars to "reassure" the public. South Korea also announced an investigation into emissions of Volkswagen cars, and if problems are found, the inquiry could be expanded to all German diesel imports.

The US Congress is also investigating the scandal, and the US Department of Justice could conduct a criminal investigation into Volkswagen. Horn, speaking at an event to launch a new version of the Passat sedan, said that Volkswagen had been dishonest with the EPA and the California air resources board and that the company had "totally screwed up." He added that the company would pay what it had to pay to make things right and restore trust.

One official involved in uncovering the alleged behavior has suggested that the emissions-fixing scandal could extend to other companies and countries. The US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) said on Friday that Volkswagen had installed illegal software to cheat emission tests, allowing its diesel cars to produce up to 40 times more pollution than allowed. The US government ordered Volkswagen to recall 482,000 VW and Audi cars produced since 2009.

Industry leaders in Britain claimed there was no evidence that manufacturers are cheating the system in Europe but admitted it needs to be reformed. The devices are thought to work by injecting more urea – an exhaust fluid – into the car when it is being tested. This limits nitrogen oxide emissions to a fraction of their usual level. The car detects it is being tested because devices such as the anti-collision systems have to be turned off when it is in the laboratory. The extra urea is not injected into the car when it is on the road because it would quickly run out.

The comments from Horn are the first in public by a senior VW executive since the scandal emerged, although the company apologized on Sunday. He left the event without taking questions. The US allegations involve a series of diesel cars produced by Volkswagen and the brands it owns, such as Audi. These include the Audi A3, VW Jetta, Beetle, Golf, and Passat models. Volkswagen has halted sales of these models.

In a Connecticut bankruptcy court filing, rapper 50 Cent (real name Curtis Jackson III) claims to have $25 million in assets but $33 million in liabilities, making him financially unstable. The filing was made after a New York City jury ordered him to pay $7 million to a woman who accused him of posting a sex tape featuring her online.

The rapper's assets include an $8 million Connecticut mansion, a $572,000 home in Valley Stream, LI, and an Atlanta home worth $464,000. His monthly income is approximately $185,000, primarily from royalties and investments. However, he spends $72,000 a month to maintain his suburban Hartford mansion and has additional expenses such as $5,000 for gardening, $5,745 for a Bentley car lease, and $12,000 in child support for two kids.

The rapper's debts include the $7 million judgment to Lastonia Leviston and an $18 million debt to electronics company Sleek Audio. He also owes money to his stylist, barber, and fitness coach. Despite his financial troubles, the filing claims he has $10 million in cash and $500,000 worth of cars.

Since April, 50 Cent has paid over $330,000 to American Express and another $52,000 to his stylist Erin McSherry. The rapper is due back in bankruptcy court on Wednesday. The filing is part of a larger effort to archive pages on the internet and fix broken links.

House Budget Committee Chairman Paul Ryan, in collaboration with Democratic Senator Ron Wyden, is set to unveil a new approach to Medicare on Thursday. This proposal aims to preserve the 46-year-old federal health program by offering traditional, government-run Medicare as an option for future retirees, alongside a variety of private plans. The plan allows for a government subsidy, known as premium support, to adjust based on the cost of the policies, providing more protection for seniors and potentially saving less in the budget compared to Ryan's previous plan.

Ryan's new approach marks a departure from his controversial plan to end traditional Medicare, which faced criticism from Democrats and was embraced by some Republicans. The new proposal could complicate election-year politics for both parties, as it combines elements from both parties' ideas on Medicare reform.

The plan would take effect for new retirees beginning in 2022 and would add catastrophic coverage with a cap on out-of-pocket costs. The subsidies would grow slightly faster than the overall economy, following the standard for Medicare spending set by President Obama's health legislation.

Ryan and Wyden's proposal aims to demonstrate an emerging consensus on preserving Medicare and move that consensus forward. The plan does not mention the Affordable Care Act, and the lawmakers have emphasized their commitment to providing government health coverage for people older than 65.

The new approach from Ryan and Wyden could potentially muddy Democrats' campaign message of preserving Medicare against privatization, as Wyden's involvement in the proposal could be seen as a bipartisan effort to find common ground on Medicare reform. The pair is scheduled to release their proposal at an event hosted by the Bipartisan Policy Center on Thursday.

The DNA evidence in the JonBenet Ramsey case, which was used to exonerate the Ramsey family in 2008, has been called into question by a joint investigation by the Daily Camera and 9NEWS. The investigation found that the DNA evidence does not support a key development in the case, former Boulder prosecutor Mary Lacy's conclusion that a DNA profile found on JonBenet's underpants and long johns necessarily belonged to the killer.

The investigation found that the DNA samples recovered from the long johns came from at least two people in addition to JonBenet, something Lacy's office was told but did not disclose in clearing the Ramseys. The presence of a third person's genetic markers has never before been publicly revealed.

Additionally, the independent experts raised the possibility that the original DNA sample recovered from JonBenet's underwear, which has been used to identify or exclude potential suspects, could be a composite and not that of a single individual.
