The investigation could have implications for the future direction of the investigation, as it could lead detectives to consider anew the possibility that someone in JonBenet's family was responsible for her death, or to take a new look at dozens of potential suspects who were ruled out because their DNA didn't match the profile known as Unknown Male 1.

The findings could also cut both ways, as they do not implicate or exonerate anyone in the family. Ramsey lawyer Lin Wood, who has not reviewed the evidence, said he has "absolute and total confidence" in Lacy's integrity.

The investigation was based on laboratory test results and reports on which Lacy based her decision to exonerate the Ramseys. The reporters sought a review of that evidence by independent experts.

The murder of JonBenet, a 6-year-old beauty pageant contestant, remains unsolved nearly 20 years later. The case exploded into the national consciousness within days of the discovery of her body on Dec. 26, 1996, in the family's home in Boulder, Colorado. The case has been marred by numerous missteps and controversies, including the high-profile arrest and subsequent release of John Mark Karr in 2006.

Lacy established herself as a supporter of the intruder theory in the Ramsey case, and her decision to exonerate the family in 2008 was widely criticized by some prosecutors and investigators. The investigation by the Daily Camera and 9NEWS raises questions about the evidence used to support Lacy's decision, and calls for renewed action on the case.

The discovery of Laci and Conner Peterson's bodies in April 2003 marked a significant moment in the investigation of Laci's husband, Scott Peterson, for their murders. Scott was arrested and convicted the following year, receiving a death sentence. However, there is a stark contrast between the authorities' account of Scott's reaction to the news and his own.

Retired Modesto detective Jon Buehler, who was involved in the case, recalls that Scott showed little emotion upon learning about the deaths of his wife and unborn son. Scott, on the other hand, claims he had a strong emotional reaction but chose to hide it from the detectives.

The contrast between their versions is highlighted in the ongoing A&E docuseries The Murder of Laci Peterson. In an exclusive clip from the third episode, both Buehler and Scott describe their reactions to the news.

Scott Peterson, who was once described as a "manipulator" by one of the jurors who put him to death, remembers his emotional response differently. In a call earlier this year from death row with his sister-in-law Janey Peterson, he claims he had a physical reaction but controlled it to avoid showing emotions to the detectives.

Despite a largely circumstantial argument by prosecutors that Scott murdered his pregnant wife while he was having an affair with unwitting lover Amber Frey, who later testified against him at trial, he and his family maintain his innocence. However, Laci's mother has stated that she is certain justice was served.

Scott's case is still being appealed. The Murder of Laci Peterson continues on A&E.

In a separate development, a new ABC documentary, Truth and Lies: The Murder of Laci Peterson, features interviews with investigators and those involved in the case, and airs on ABC on September 14. The documentary includes Laci's mother's recollection of her last memory with Laci, which took place just days before her disappearance.

Laci's mother describes sitting with Laci and Scott, watching TV, when Laci mentioned feeling her unborn son kick. Laci's mother put her hand on Laci's stomach, but didn't feel any movement. Laci then told her mother that Scott didn't like to touch her stomach. This detail troubled Laci's mother and was the last time she saw her daughter.

The ABC special also includes never-before-seen home video of Laci, excerpts from Scott's pre-arrest interview with Diane Sawyer, and Barbara Walters' pre-conviction interview with Scott's parents.

European Union foreign policy chief Catherine Ashton met with deposed Egyptian President Mohamed Morsi on Monday night, marking the first contact Morsi has had with an independent official since his removal from power almost a month ago. The meeting took place at an undisclosed location and was confirmed by Ashton's spokesman. Ashton found Morsi to be in good health and said he had access to television and newspapers.

The meeting between Ashton and Morsi comes amid ongoing political turmoil in Egypt, with clashes between security forces and Morsi supporters leaving about 80 dead over the past two days. Last week, prosecutors announced that Morsi was being investigated over allegations of espionage and murder, accusations that his supporters have dismissed as politically motivated.

Ashton's meeting with Morsi was part of a two-day visit to Egypt aimed at facilitating conversations that might lead to a political solution. During her visit, Ashton met with a wide range of Egyptian political figures, including the commander of the armed forces, liberal activists and politicians, and representatives of the Muslim Brotherhood.

After her meeting with Morsi, Ashton met with Egypt's interim vice president, Mohamed ElBaradei, who said that he thought Morsi had "failed" during his year in power but that his Muslim Brotherhood allies should be part of the new political "road map" going forward.

Ashton's visit appeared to have at least temporarily calmed the tense capital, with no violence reported after her meeting with Morsi. However, Morsi's supporters rallied in Cairo on Tuesday night and marched toward the military intelligence headquarters, although no violence had been reported by early Wednesday.

U.S. Defense Secretary Chuck Hagel spoke by telephone with Egypt's military commander, Abdel Fatah al-Sissi, on Tuesday, urging "restraint" in dealing with protesters and calling for "an inclusive reconciliation process."

Overall, Ashton's meeting with Morsi is seen as a potential step towards a political solution in Egypt, although the ongoing violence and political divisions suggest that a resolution may be some time away.

A seriously ill woman, identified as Beatriz, underwent a cesarean section in El Salvador to deliver a baby with little chance of survival due to the country's strict abortion laws. Beatriz, 22, who suffers from lupus and kidney failure, was 27 weeks pregnant and her baby was born without a brain. The Health Ministry announced that the operation was performed to save Beatriz's life and avoid breaking the law. The baby did not survive. The Supreme Court of El Salvador had previously denied Beatriz's request for a medical abortion, citing the country's constitution which protects life from the moment of conception. The Inter-American Court of Human Rights had issued a ruling calling on El Salvador to take action to save Beatriz's life, but it no longer applied in the case as the Health Ministry had already intervened. The case has drawn attention to abortion laws in El Salvador and predominantly Roman Catholic Latin America.

The Joint Sea exercise, a week-long naval drill involving Russia and China in the Baltic Sea, has a smaller-than-expected participation due to its symbolic nature, according to Maxim Shepovalenko, a former Russian navy captain and expert at the Moscow-based Center for the Analysis of Strategies and Technologies (CAST). The exercise includes anti-submarine, anti-aircraft, and anti-ship drills, as well as anti-piracy and search and rescue operations.

Meanwhile, concerns are rising in eastern Europe and Ukraine regarding Russia's planned war games in September, with U.S. Army Lieutenant General Ben Hodges, who heads U.S. Army forces in Europe, stating that these exercises could be a "Trojan horse" aimed at leaving military equipment in Belarus. NATO allies are particularly worried due to Russia's history of employing special forces training, longer-range missiles, and unmanned aerial vehicles in previous large-scale exercises, which were later used in Russia's annexation of Crimea, support for separatists in eastern Ukraine, and intervention in Syria.

Russia has invited observers for the exercise if it exceeds 13,000 forces, but some NATO allies believe the Russian exercise could number more than 100,000 troops and involve nuclear weapons training, the biggest such exercise since 2013. NATO will maintain normal rotations during the Russian war game, while carrying out previously scheduled exercises in Sweden, Poland, and Ukraine. The only additional action planned during that period is a six-week deployment of three companies of 120 paratroopers each to Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania for "low-level" exercises.

The Joint Sea exercise between Russia and China is seen as a response to joint drills by the United States and Beijing's two key Asian rivals - India and Japan – in the Indian Ocean earlier this month. China has been expanding its military reach by building up its naval forces and establishing its first overseas military base in Djibouti this year.

On July 18, 2018, Robert and Falon Griffin welcomed their daughter, Gracelyn Mae Violet Griffin, in an unexpected location - a bathroom stall at a Chick-fil-A restaurant in San Antonio, Texas. The couple was on their way to the hospital when Falon, who was 38 weeks pregnant, urgently needed to use the restroom. The Chick-fil-A was closed, but the staff allowed them inside. As Falon began to scream, it became clear that Gracelyn was about to be born.

Robert, who served as the attending physician, delivered their daughter with the umbilical cord wrapped around her neck twice. He was able to unwrap the cord before paramedics arrived. The entire process took just six minutes. Robert's Facebook post about the birth has since gone viral, receiving thousands of likes and shares.

Chick-fil-A has shown its appreciation for the family by gifting Gracelyn free Chick-fil-A for life and guaranteeing her a job when she turns 16. Plans for her first birthday party, which will be chicken-nugget-themed, are already in the works. The Griffins, who were already fans of Chick-fil-A, had bought Gracelyn a "Little Nugget" onesie prior to her birth.

The Chick-fil-A employees, who were young and off the clock, were praised for their quick thinking and calm demeanor during the unexpected delivery. The Griffins are grateful for their help and consider the employees their friends for life.

Anton Martynenko, a 32-year-old man from Eagan, Minnesota, was sentenced to 38 years in prison on Tuesday for using social media to obtain child pornography from over 155 high school boys in multiple states. This is the largest child pornography production case in Minnesota history.

Martynenko, who pleaded guilty in January, was accused of regularly scouring internet sites devoted to high school athletes to locate his targets. In many cases, he posed as a teenage girl to solicit nude photos from the boys, which he then posted on social media. Prosecutors say Martynenko not only collected child pornography but also "delighted in the humiliation, embarrassment, and potential negative consequences his actions caused his victims."

At least two of Martynenko’s victims committed suicide, but it is not known what role, if any, his scheme had in their deaths. Prosecutors are aware of three boys who engaged in sexual activity with Martynenko, which he claims were consensual encounters.

Martynenko was also involved in providing information to federal investigators on jail conversations he had with Danny Heinrich, the man who killed Jacob Wetterling. However, it was clarified that Martynenko did not help solve the Heinrich-Wetterling case.

One of Martynenko's victims spoke at the sentencing, stating, "It's very satisfying to see this man sit in prison for the rest of his life." Martynenko's mother, who also addressed the judge, expressed hope for a sentence heavier on treatment than it was on incarceration, stating, "He's my only child."

The investigation into Martynenko's activities began with a call from a Rosemount teenager to local police and eventually expanded to include the FBI. Martynenko was arrested in November 2015, minutes after sending his final Twitter message to a Minneapolis officer who was granted permission to operate a teen victim's account undercover.

Investigators unspooled detailed "target lists" of teenage boys that Martynenko sought to contact. The case highlighted the importance of using the internet safely, as one of the things that keeps U.S. Attorney Andrew Luger up at night are the actions of a man like Anton Martynenko. Luger stated, "This case highlighted how deeply disturbing the criminal obsession of a man like Martynenko can be. How not only does he steal the innocence of teenage boys but through extortion, threats, and physical acts he inflicted unspeakable psychological damage to his victims."

The Seelbach cocktail, a popular bourbon-champagne drink associated with the Seelbach Hilton Hotel in Louisville, KY, has been revealed as a fabrication by its creator, Adam Seger. Seger, who was the director of restaurants at the hotel in 1995, claimed to have discovered the recipe for the cocktail and revived it. However, he recently admitted to the New York Times that the entire story was a promotional move and that the cocktail is his creation.

Seger stated that he concocted the tale of its invention to promote the hotel and create a signature cocktail. The story was published in the Courier-Journal in 1997 and later included in books such as "New Classic Cocktails" and "Vintage Spirits and Forgotten Cocktails." The cocktail has been featured on menus worldwide and has been a part of Louisville lore.

Seger admitted to Gaz Regan, one of the authors of "New Classic Cocktails," that he fabricated the story. Regan said he had always suspected that Seger created the drink but was charmed by the story and needed recipes for the book.

The Seelbach Hilton is aware of Seger's transgression but has no plans to remove the cocktail from its menu. Matthew Willinger, the hotel’s director of public relations, said the cocktail "has certainly been a tradition of the hotel and will remain part of its future."

The Seelbach cocktail recipe includes Old Forester bourbon, triple sec, Angostura bitters, Peychaud bitters, chilled Korbel Brut, and an orange twist for garnish. The cocktail has been a part of the hotel's menu since Seger revived it in 1995. Despite the revelation of its fabricated history, the Seelbach cocktail continues to be a popular drink at the Seelbach Hilton.

The article discusses the benefits and availability of fast cash loans, specifically payday loans with no credit check, which can be obtained quickly and easily, often within an hour or two. These loans can help individuals address unexpected financial issues such as medical expenses, utility bills, credit card debts, and wedding expenses. The loans can be repaid through comfortable monthly installments over a period of one to four weeks, making them a practical solution for short-term financial needs.

To qualify for these loans, the applicant must be a permanent resident of the UK, over 18 years old, in regular employment earning at least £1000 per month, and have a bank account that is not more than three months old. The loans are available online, and the application process is straightforward, requiring the completion of an online form that can be filled out quickly.

While fast cash loans come at a price, with fees and interest charges, it is emphasized that planning ahead and saving for emergencies is a more cost-effective solution. Predatory lenders may try to convince borrowers to take on more debt, but it is important to remember that more loan money equals more interest charges.

In conclusion, fast cash loans can be a useful tool for addressing short-term financial needs, but it is important to understand the costs and to plan ahead for emergencies whenever possible.

In the article by Dennis Prager, published on December 24, 2013, the author, a Jewish religious figure, expresses his desire to wish fellow Americans a "Merry Christmas" rather than "Happy Holidays." He argues that Christmas is not only a Christian holy day but also an American national holiday, and that many famous Christmas songs were written by Jewish composers such as Irving Berlin, Johnny Marks, Jule Styne, Sammy Cahn, Jay Livingston, Ray Evans, and Mitchell Parish.

Prager criticizes the notion that non-Christians are excluded by public celebration of Christmas, stating that it is a destructive product of the 1960s and '70s leftist culture. He recalls his own family's tradition of watching the Christmas Mass from the Vatican every Christmas Eve and his brother singing Christmas songs as a member of the Columbia University Glee Club.

The author also addresses the attempts to remove Christmas from the public sphere, such as the substitution of "Happy Holidays" for "Merry Christmas" and the banning of Christmas trees and Christmas songs in public schools. He argues that these attempts are destructive to society because they exclude everyone, including Jews, from the goodness and joy that the Christmas season brings.

Prager also discusses the misconception that Jews are excluded from celebrating Christmas, stating that many Jews, including himself, celebrate Christmas in their own way. He concludes by criticizing the left's attempts to remove Christian references from society and the role of Jews, particularly non-religious Jews, in these attempts. He also criticizes the left's use of multiculturalism to divide Americans by religion, ethnicity, race, and national origins.

AirAsia Flight 8501, a passenger jet with 162 passengers and crew onboard, disappeared on Sunday while flying from Surabaya, Indonesia to Singapore. The plane vanished from radar about halfway through the flight. The cause of the disappearance is unknown, but possible factors include bad weather, pilot errors, metal fatigue, or terrorism. The last communication between the pilot and air traffic control was a request to avoid clouds and fly higher to 38,000 feet. This is the third Malaysian jet to crash this year, but there is no evidence of a connection between the incidents. The search-and-rescue operation is being conducted near Belitung island in the Java Sea, and investigators will try to recover the flight data and cockpit voice recorders to gather more information. The Airbus A320 is a safe and widely used jet, with a good safety record. AirAsia, the airline operating the flight, has a strong presence in Southeast Asia and a generally good safety record, but it operates in a region where air travel has expanded faster than the number of qualified pilots, mechanics, and air traffic controllers. The plane was flying through a thunderstorm at the time of the disappearance, but it is common for pilots to fly around thunderstorms if possible. The plane was certified to fly up to 39,000 feet, but it can experience problems as low as 37,000 feet, depending on temperature and weight. It is still unclear what traffic controllers saw on their screens when the plane disappeared from radar. The region's economy has grown rapidly, leading to an increase in airline traffic, with Indonesia being one of the world's five fastest-growing air travel markets.

The Reuters/Ipsos poll released on Wednesday indicates that more than half of U.S. citizens believe that most or all of the country's 11 million illegal immigrants should be deported. The poll highlights the difficulties facing lawmakers trying to reform the U.S. immigration system, as resistance to easing immigration laws persists despite the biggest push for reform in Congress since 2007.

Key senators are exploring an immigration bill that would require every U.S. worker, citizen or not, to carry a high-tech identity card that could use fingerprints or other personal markers to prove a person's legal eligibility to work. The idea has privacy advocates and others concerned that the law would create a national identity card that could track Americans at airports, hospitals, and through other facets of their lives.

Attitudes toward immigration are polarized by party, with 75% of Republicans thinking all or most immigrants should be deported, compared to 40% of Democrats. The poll results are in line with other polls in recent years, suggesting that people's views on immigration have not changed dramatically since the immigration debate reignited in Congress last month.

A group of eight U.S. senators are working on a bipartisan deal to enact immigration reform, the first major attempt since a similar overhaul died in Congress six years ago. The senators' proposal calls for a full path to citizenship for illegal immigrants once they pay back taxes and a fine and wait in line behind others applying to become Americans.

The Arizona lawmaker, John McCain, is a key part of the Republican side of the senators' bipartisan immigration effort. At a town hall meeting on Tuesday, residents of his state complained bitterly about the lack of security on the border with Mexico. One man asked why troops had not been deployed to the border, to which McCain responded that only a gun could stop them.

The Reuters/Ipsos poll was conducted Friday through Tuesday and surveyed 1,443 Americans over the age of 18. The precision of the poll is measured using a credibility interval of plus or minus 2.9 percentage points.

Morley Safer, a legendary CBS News correspondent and iconic figure on 60 Minutes for 46 years, died at the age of 84 in Manhattan. Safer was a familiar reporter to millions, joining 60 Minutes in 1970 after a successful career as a foreign correspondent. He was the first U.S. network newsman to film a report inside Communist China and earned peer praise and government condemnation for his controversial reporting in Vietnam.

Safer's piece from the Vietnamese hamlet of Cam Ne in 1965, showing U.S. Marines burning villagers' huts, was cited as one of the 20th century's best pieces of American journalism. His work on 60 Minutes included investigative pieces, cultural profiles, and offbeat stories that showcased his unique storytelling abilities and wit.

Safer won numerous awards throughout his career, including four duPont-Columbia University awards, three Peabody awards, and 12 Emmys. He is survived by his wife, one daughter, three grandchildren, a sister, and a brother. A memorial service will be announced at a later date.

In honor of Safer's retirement, a tribute was aired on 60 Minutes, featuring some of his most memorable stories, including his groundbreaking report from Cam Ne and his exoneration of Lenell Geter, a black man wrongly accused of armed robbery in Texas. Safer's work was known for its original voice, quality storytelling, and ability to link the written word with the visual image. He will be remembered as a charismatic and influential figure in the world of journalism.

The U.S. Department of Agriculture has approved Idaho-based J.R. Simplot Co.'s new genetically modified potato, known as the "Innate" potato. The potato has been altered to produce less acrylamide, a suspected human carcinogen, and to resist bruising. However, one of Simplot's oldest business partners, McDonald's, has stated that it does not use genetically modified potatoes and has no plans to change its sourcing practices.

Simplot is a major supplier of potato products for various restaurant chains, including McDonald's. The fast-food industry has previously shown resistance to genetically modified potatoes, as seen with Monsanto's bug-resistant "New Leaf" line of genetically modified potatoes, which were pulled from production due to lack of business over a decade ago.

Simplot spokesman Doug Cole did not address the company's plans to sell to the fast-food industry or the dehydrated potato industry, which has urged growers against planting GMO potatoes. However, Cole stated that the fresh potato market would embrace Innate. Consumers are expected to be receptive to the reduced sugars and potential carcinogens in the Innate potato.

Rupert potato grower Duane Grant, who has been told by buyers in the dehydrated potato industry not to plant the GMO potatoes, hopes to find willing buyers to plant the biotech potatoes and reap the higher yields that come with their reduced bruising. Consumers are more likely to accept Simplot's potato than Monsanto's due to its benefits for consumers, not just growers.

The key for Simplot and for growers will be convincing the food industry to trust the product, as the industry is concerned about potential consumer backlash. McDonald's decision not to use the Innate potato has been celebrated by consumer advocacy groups, with Food & Water Watch Executive Director Wenonah Hauter urging competing fast-food chains such as Burger King to follow McDonald's lead.

On July 14, 2017, a sinkhole, initially the size of a small swimming pool, rapidly expanded and swallowed a boat, destroyed two homes, and forced the evacuation of 10 other homes in Land O' Lakes, Florida. The sinkhole grew to 200 feet wide and 50 feet deep, causing the first home to collapse. Firefighters managed to rescue two dogs and retrieve some belongings before the home's collapse. The home next door was also destroyed by the sinkhole. No injuries were reported, but 100 homes lost power, and the American Red Cross is assisting displaced residents.

Property records show a sinkhole previously occurred on the property where the first house was swallowed in 2012, and it had been stabilized. The home last sold in 2015. Sinkholes in the area are typically stabilized by boring holes into the ground and injecting concrete.

Ten other homes in the neighborhood have been deemed unsafe, and their residents have been voluntarily evacuated. Officials are working to restore power and assist the displaced residents. The Associated Press, a global news network, reported on this event, emphasizing its commitment to independent, comprehensive journalism.

Hurricane Harvey, which made landfall in Texas in August, has claimed another victim. A 31-year-old man named Josue Zurita died last week after being diagnosed with a rare flesh-eating bacterial infection known as necrotizing fasciitis. Zurita was helping to repair homes damaged by the floods when he contracted the infection.

According to the Galveston County Health District, Zurita was admitted to the hospital on October 10 with a seriously infected wound on his upper left arm. He was diagnosed with necrotizing fasciitis and died six days later.

Zurita was a hard-working carpenter who moved to the United States from Mexico to help his family. He remained in the area to help with the rebuilding efforts after Hurricane Harvey. An obituary on the Galveston-based Carnes Brothers Funeral Home's website describes Zurita as a "loving father" who will be remembered for his smile and willingness to help his neighbors.

Dr. Philip Keiser, the Galveston County local health authority, said that the infection most likely occurred when bacteria from hurricane debris or floodwater entered Zurita's body through a wound or cut. This case was the only known instance of necrotizing fasciitis in Galveston County related to Hurricane Harvey.

Necrotizing fasciitis is a rare bacterial infection that kills soft tissue. It can spread quickly and can become lethal within a short amount of time. According to the National Institutes of Health, several types of bacteria can cause the infection. Proper wound care is key to preventing such deadly infections.

Zurita's death follows that of Nancy Reed, a 77-year-old Houston-area woman who died in September from necrotizing fasciitis related to Harvey floodwaters. J.R. Atkins, a former first responder, also contracted a flesh-eating bacterial infection but survived. He had been kayaking through floodwaters to check on neighbors affected by the hurricane.

To prevent such deadly infections, proper wound care is key. Keep open wounds covered with clean, dry bandages until they heal, especially if you are working in floodwaters, and avoid contact with natural bodies of water if you have an open wound. Don't delay treating minor, non-infected wounds, and wash hands often with soap and water. If you notice any redness or swelling of a wound, or if you have a fever, seek medical attention.

Ford has announced a $1 billion investment over five years into Argo AI, a previously unheard of artificial intelligence startup founded by Bryan Salesky, a multi-year veteran of Google’s self-driving team, and Peter Rander, who led autonomous efforts at Uber up until September 2016. The deal effectively means Ford is buying a majority stake in Argo AI, though it is framed as an investment instead of an acquisition. Argo AI will help Ford develop the autonomous system for a self-driving vehicle the car company plans to put on the road by 2021. The investment is part of Ford’s strategy to own the expertise of some of the robotics world’s brightest and most experienced self-driving experts, as it competes with Silicon Valley companies like Tesla, Alphabet Inc.’s Waymo, and Uber. Ford will operate Argo AI with substantial independence, and the startup will have offices in Michigan and California and expects to have 200 employees by the end of the year. The investment is part of Ford’s continuing investment strategy to transform into a mobility company, with a focus on ride-hailing, ride-sharing, and even bicycle rentals. The investment in Argo AI reflects a growing desire on the part of automakers and tech companies to combine forces in order to tackle the still daunting task of making autonomous driving an everyday reality.

In this news article, a family in Atlanta, the Fowlers, decided to donate their wedding reception to the homeless after their daughter's wedding was cancelled. The reception was held at the Villa Christina restaurant, complete with gold plates, crystal glasses, and a four-course meal. The Fowlers contacted Hosea Feed the Hungry, a local homeless organization, and partnered with them to provide the meal to 200 homeless individuals. The event was a success, with the homeless guests enjoying the meal and the Fowlers finding the experience rewarding. The Fowlers are considering making this an annual event and encouraging others to donate cancelled events to charities.

Mitt Romney, the former 2012 GOP presidential nominee and current U.S. Senate candidate, predicted that President Donald Trump will be reelected in 2020. Speaking at a gathering of major GOP donors, Romney cited an improving economy and the likelihood of Democrats nominating an outside-the-mainstream candidate as factors bolstering Trump's political fortunes. Romney has praised some of Trump's early actions as president while criticizing his bombastic style. Despite their past differences, the relationship between Trump and Romney has warmed somewhat, with Trump endorsing Romney for the Utah Senate seat after longtime Utah Sen. Orrin Hatch announced he wouldn't seek reelection. Romney also offered a bullish assessment of the GOP's 2018 midterm prospects, arguing that the party would retain control of both chambers of Congress. Romney is heavily favored to capture the Utah Senate seat, facing a June 26 runoff for the GOP nomination against Mike Kennedy, a conservative state representative.

Jason Garnett, a 23-year-old hotel worker from Harrogate, UK, experienced an embarrassing and unusual medical condition last Friday. He woke up with an erection that persisted for over 17 hours, despite his attempts to alleviate it with an ice bath and a jog. After eight hours, Garnett sought help from his roommate and was taken to a hospital, where he was diagnosed with priapism, a rare condition that can cause permanent damage to the penis if left untreated. Doctors drained over two pints of blood from Garnett's penis and injected it with medication 24 times to reduce the blood flow and alleviate the condition. Garnett described the pain as "ten out of ten" and said his penis now looks "black and blue." He is now recovering and reported that everything is back to normal.

The Kansas waterslide, Verrückt, at Schlitterbahn Waterparks and Resorts in Kansas City, Kansas, will be permanently removed following the conclusion of an ongoing investigation into the tragic accident that occurred last summer, in which a 10-year-old boy named Caleb Schwab was killed. The slide, billed as the world's tallest, has been closed since the incident.

Verrückt, which means "insane" in German, features multi-person rafts that drop from a height of 17 stories at speeds of up to 70 mph, followed by a hump and a 50-foot descent to a finishing pool. Riders were harnessed with two nylon seatbelt-like straps and held ropes inside the raft. Riders were required to be at least 54 inches tall, and each raft carried between 400 and 550 pounds.

The investigation into the accident is being conducted by attorneys for Caleb and the two women who were injured in the same raft. No charges or lawsuits have been filed as of Tuesday.

Schlitterbahn Waterparks and Resorts has expressed its deep sorrow over the tragedy and stated that the safety of its staff and guests is its top priority. The company has been cooperating with investigative teams and the families and attorneys affected by the accident.

Once the investigation is concluded and permission is granted by the court, Verrückt will be decommissioned and permanently removed from its tower. The company has not yet announced what will be built in its place.

The announcement comes as the criminal investigation into the tragedy is not yet complete. The Kansas City, Kansas Police Department has confirmed that criminal charges are unlikely but the case remains open.

The family of Caleb Schwab, represented by attorney Michael C. Rader, has been working with Schlitterbahn and their attorneys to permanently decommission the slide and ensure that it is eventually torn down. It is still unknown if the public will ever find out what went wrong on the day of the tragedy, as the case could be settled before going to court.

Independent investigations are ongoing, with a team of attorneys and experts for the Schwab family and the two female passengers inspecting the slide in September 2016. The investigation is expected to be thorough, testing every part of the slide and looking at every inch of what is being investigated.

A 36-year-old woman named Marie Joseph was found dead in a state-run pool in Fall River, Massachusetts on Tuesday night, apparently having been in the water since Sunday. The pool's staff has been placed on administrative leave while authorities investigate the incident. The pool was last used on Monday, as shown in a local newspaper's photo.

According to Fall River Police Lieutenant Roger LaFleur, officers were called to the Vietnam Veterans Memorial Swimming Pool at Lafayette Park at around 10 p.m. on Tuesday and pulled Joseph's body from the water. She was later pronounced dead at a hospital.

The state Department of Conservation and Recreation, which operates the pool, announced that all 30 of its deep-water pools will close for 24 to 48 hours while investigators review safety procedures. The pool's staff has been placed on administrative leave.

Fall River Police Chief Daniel Racine stated during a news conference that a 9-year-old boy who was with Joseph at the pool on Sunday told police that she had an accident on a water slide. The boy said that Joseph unexpectedly slid down the slide and landed on top of him, and he believed she went under the water and did not surface.

Bristol District Attorney C. Samuel Sutter, who was also at the press conference, said that the sequence of events after Joseph went underwater and did not resurface is unclear. He stated that "exactly who the boy spoke to and what that person did and what happened next, this is the beginning stages of the investigation."

The cause of death is unknown pending an autopsy by the state medical examiner. Phone numbers listed for Joseph were not in service, and numbers for her relatives could not be located.

Joseph D. Camara, a Fall River city councilor, stated that while many residents use the pool regularly, a temporary closure during the review makes sense. He also expressed sympathy for Joseph and her family, calling the situation tragic.

B.J. Fisher, director of health and safety at the American Lifeguard Association, stated that finding a body in a pool days after a drowning is unusual but not unprecedented. He noted that the turbidity of the water, meaning its lack of clarity, can make it difficult to see the bottom of the pool. He also stated that drownings are often silent and can happen in a matter of seconds.

In a two-year undercover operation, the FBI arrested 24 suspected hackers across 13 countries for involvement in computer fraud. The operation, named Operation Card Shop, targeted an online forum known as Carder Profit, which was a marketplace for stolen credit card numbers, hacking tips, and other illegal activities. The sting prevented potential losses of over $200 million and notified credit card providers of over 400,000 compromised credit and debit cards. The arrests were made in various countries, including the United States, Britain, Bosnia, Bulgaria, Norway, and Germany. The operation aimed to combat the growing sophistication of credit card fraud and dismantle a significant portion of the underground economy. The FBI created the Carder Profit forum in 2010 and monitored it until its closure in May 2012. Two individuals were arrested in the New York area, with one, Mir Islam, known as JoshTheGod, accused of trafficking in 50,000 stolen credit card numbers and admitting to helping the hacker group UgNazi. The other individual, Joshua Hicks, was charged with access device fraud. The FBI also filed a complaint against Wyndham Worldwide Corp for failing to keep customer data secure, resulting in the theft of hundreds of thousands of payment card numbers and $10.6 million in fraudulent charges.

The article details the execution of convicted killer Carey Dean Moore in Nebraska. The execution took place at the Nebraska State Penitentiary in Lincoln on Tuesday at 10 a.m. The execution was carried out by lethal injection, with a timeline of events provided. The first drug administered was diazepam, followed by fentanyl, cisatracurium besylate, and potassium chloride. Moore's body was later remanded to the Nebraska State Patrol for an autopsy. The article also includes a description of the execution chamber and the witnesses present, including Moore's family and spiritual adviser. The article concludes by stating that Moore was pronounced dead by Lancaster County Coroner Pat Condon, out of sight of witnesses.

House Majority Leader Eric Cantor (R-Va.) announced his resignation from House leadership on July 31, 2014, following his primary loss to tea party challenger David Brat. Cantor's decision came after a swift rise through the ranks of national politics and upended a leadership team that had run the House since the 2010 tea party wave election. House Republicans plan to hold new leadership elections on June 19, 2014, and several senior Republicans are mulling bids for top posts. Kevin McCarthy (R-Calif.), the next in line after Boehner and Cantor, is preparing to run for majority leader, but will face competition from more conservative colleagues such as Pete Sessions (R-Texas) and Jeb Hensarling (R-Texas). The large Texas Republican delegation, which represents 10 percent of the entire House Republican Conference, is expected to meet later to discuss potential leadership slots for Sessions or Hensarling. The fast-paced developments have left rank-and-file members stunned, and several conservatives have expressed a desire to see a southern conservative replace Cantor. Cantor's resignation as majority leader will be effective July 31, but he will remain in the House until his term ends in January. Cantor's defeat was historic, as he was assumed to be the next speaker of the House. Cantor's public appearance on Wednesday came after a closed-door speech to his colleagues earlier in which he said that it "doesn't have to be a bad day." He was the recipient of several standing ovations. Cantor endorsed California Rep. Kevin McCarthy to succeed him as majority leader.

President Donald Trump has announced that he will nominate Robert Wilkie, the current acting Veterans Affairs Secretary, to become the permanent leader of the department. The announcement comes after the nomination of Ronny Jackson, Trump's former personal physician, was withdrawn due to workplace conduct issues. Wilkie, a veteran GOP aide, has been serving as acting secretary since March and was confirmed by the Senate for a Pentagon post last year. His nomination is expected to face a smoother confirmation process than Jackson's.

The selection of Wilkie is the latest leadership development for the VA, which has been plagued by high-profile departures and ethics scandals. Jackson withdrew his bid to lead the VA in April amid allegations of a toxic work environment, drunken driving, and poor prescription records. In March, Trump ousted Jackson's predecessor, David Shulkin, due to growing tensions with the White House.

The announcement of Wilkie's nomination has been met with positive reactions from Senate Committee on Veterans’ Affairs Chairman Johnny Isakson and Rep. Phil Roe, chairman of the House panel on veterans' affairs. However, Wilkie's nomination could face a potential snag due to his involvement in the ongoing probe of Trump's ties to Russia.

The staffing shake-up at the VA comes as congressional lawmakers continue to debate the future of the agency, with Democrats expressing concerns about efforts to privatize the VA. The American Veterans non-partisan advocacy group has welcomed Wilkie's nomination, stating that he would provide "needed stability" for the VA.

In a series of interviews on Sunday, several political figures commented on various issues. Senators Susan Collins (R-Maine) and Carolyn Maloney (D-N.Y.) suggested that the Secret Service, which is only 11% female, could benefit from more gender diversity to prevent incidents like the recent prostitution scandal in Colombia. Marco Rubio, Florida Senator, stated he would respect Mitt Romney's process for selecting a vice president, after previously expressing opposition to the role. Rubio indicated his preference for Jeb Bush to take the position if asked. Senator Joe Lieberman (I-Conn.), who was Al Gore's vice presidential running mate in 2000, announced he would stay out of the 2012 presidential race. President Barack Obama was reported to be "apoplectic" about excessive spending at the GSA, following revelations of extravagant hotel suites and other expenses. Lastly, Conservative Senator Tom Coburn (R-Okla.) expressed support for the White House's response to the Secret Service scandal, stating it was an "aberration" and expressing faith in the director of the Secret Service, Mark Sullivan.

Hillary Clinton's campaign has clarified that her team individually read "every email" before deleting those deemed private, amidst controversy over her exclusive use of personal email while serving as Secretary of State. The clarification comes after it was revealed that while more than 30,000 work-related emails were turned over to the State Department, nearly 32,000 were deemed "private" and deleted.

Clinton's spokesman Nick Merrill made the clarification in a written statement to Fox News, stating that the team had assumed reading every single email was understood as the most important step in the process. However, the initial fact sheet did not clearly state that every email was read.

The admission of deleting thousands of messages and Clinton's insistence on keeping her personal server private has stirred the ire and curiosity of lawmakers who want greater access to her communications as secretary, as they complain much of it may be gone forever.

Republican House Speaker John Boehner is expected to announce a new investigation into Clinton's email practices this week, including her admission that more than 31,000 emails were destroyed because she determined them to be personal.

The clarification that "every email was read" does not necessarily ease concerns, as questions remain over who gets to decide what's personal and what's public, and whether Clinton's lawyers can be trusted to make the determination that the public is entitled to.

Clinton's team outlined a multi-step process for reviewing her emails, which included a search of all emails Clinton received from a .gov or state.gov account during her tenure, a search for names of 100 State Department and other U.S. government officials, organizing and reviewing emails by sender and recipient, and searching for terms such as "Benghazi" and "Libya."

The results of the search were that Clinton's attorneys found 30,490 work-related emails and 31,830 emails that were deemed "private and personal." Clinton said she deleted all of the personal emails because she felt she "had no reason to save them."

The revelation has only raised more questions about what was in those emails and why Clinton used a private account in the first place. Clinton said she did so out of "convenience," but acknowledged during a press conference it "would have been better" if she had used two separate phones and two email accounts.

Democratic strategist and Clinton ally James Carville suggested that Clinton may not have wanted Republican Rep. Louis Gohmert rifling through her emails, and that the controversy "amounts to nothing but a bunch of people flapping their jaws about nothing."

However, the State Department's loose record-keeping practices have raised concerns among historians and open government advocates, as many messages of historical importance may have been destroyed unless individual officials made a practice of saving their emails or printing out paper copies. The State Department has acknowledged that regular archiving of the work email in-boxes of senior officials besides the secretary did not begin until "February of this year."

On January 29, 2011, a suicide bomber riding a motorcycle packed with explosives targeted and killed Abdul Latif Ashna, the deputy governor of Afghanistan's southern Kandahar province. The attack occurred as Ashna was being driven to work in the provincial capital. The Taliban claimed responsibility for the attack, which also wounded three of Ashna's bodyguards. The attack was the highest-profile strike of its kind in months and raised concerns about a resurgence of assassinations of public officials in Kandahar, a traditional Taliban stronghold. The killing undermines efforts to improve governance and public services in the province, which is crucial to the overall war effort in Afghanistan. U.S. Ambassador Karl Eikenberry condemned the attack and called it a "vicious assassination." The Taliban have been weakened by targeted strikes, but the insurgency has made inroads in some previously calm areas of the country, and the movement's leaders have rebuffed efforts to bring them to the bargaining table. Elsewhere in Afghanistan, more than 200 demonstrators rallied at the Iranian Embassy to protest the execution of Afghans in Iran and call for the release of Afghan political prisoners. The Taliban also claimed responsibility for a bombing at a Kabul supermarket that killed a prominent Afghan family, including a young doctor at a military hospital and a political science professor at Kabul University. The Afghan government and international intelligence officials are investigating the bombing.

In a study led by the University of Toulouse's Young-Ho Eom, it was found that Frank Sinatra is the most important figure in the English-language Wikipedia, followed by Michael Jackson and Pope Pius XII. However, when considering all 24 major language editions of Wikipedia, Adolf Hitler emerged as the most important figure, with Michael Jackson in second place and Madonna in third.

The study aimed to determine if Wikipedia was biased in the attention it gives to various figures, either by gender, time, or location. The results showed that most important historical figures across Wikipedia language editions are male and born in western countries after the 17th century. The study used Google's PageRank algorithm to analyze Wikipedia pages and determine importance, but the results were odd due to a quirk of Wikipedia: the site contains an almost complete collection of named species, with Carl Linnaeus being linked from many of these pages.

To get around this issue, the researchers applied a second way of measuring importance called CheiRank. By combining PageRank and CheiRank, they arrived at the final measure, 2DRank, which led to Frank Sinatra taking the top spot in the final analysis. The study also highlighted the importance of archiving pages as they are created and archiving the pages they refer to, with the goal of fixing all broken links on the web.

The article discusses the political reactions to President Donald Trump's decision to launch missile attacks against the Syrian government on Thursday, April 6, 2017. The strikes were in response to a chemical weapon attack allegedly ordered by Syrian President Bashar al-Assad. The attacks divided Congress, with some lawmakers offering support while others raised constitutional concerns.

Top Democrats, including House Minority Leader Nancy Pelosi and Senate Democratic Whip Dick Durbin, supported the strikes but expressed concerns about escalation and the need for Congressional approval. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer also supported the strikes but called for a strategy and consultation with Congress.

Libertarian-minded Republicans, such as Sens. Mike Lee of Utah and Rand Paul of Kentucky, blasted Trump's decision to launch strikes without first getting approval by Congress. They were joined by liberal Democrats, including Sen. Brian Schatz of Hawaii and Rep. Ted Lieu of California, who also argued the use of force requires congressional approval under the Constitution.

On the other hand, Republican defense hawks, such as Sens. John McCain of Arizona and Lindsey Graham of South Carolina, offered full-throated praise for Trump’s decision. Other GOP members who praised Trump, such as Rep. Marsha Blackburn of Tennessee, had previously signed a letter warning against a unilateral attack without Congressional authorization.

The article also mentions criticism of MSNBC’s breaking news anchor and 11th Hour host Brian Williams for his seemingly euphoric reaction to the missile launch attack on a Syrian airbase. During his show, Williams said the images of the missiles launching were "beautiful pictures of fearsome armaments making a brief flight." Critics deemed the comments as insensitive or perhaps as a bit too cavalier given the circumstances. Williams defended his comments, stating that they were a quote of poetry.

Overall, the article highlights the political divisions and debates surrounding Trump's decision to launch missile attacks against the Syrian government and the criticism faced by MSNBC's Brian Williams for his reaction to the event.

The article "A Rape on Campus" published by Rolling Stone magazine describes a brutal gang rape of a woman named Jackie during a party at the University of Virginia (UVA) fraternity house, Phi Kappa Psi. The article generated worldwide headlines and caused much soul-searching at UVA. University president Teresa Sullivan promised a full investigation and to examine the way the school investigates sexual assault allegations.

Initially, the magazine honored Jackie's request not to contact the men who she claimed participated in the assault for fear of retaliation against her. However, in the face of new information reported by the Washington Post and other news outlets, there appear to be discrepancies in Jackie's account. The fraternity has issued a formal statement denying the assault and asserting that there was no "date function or formal event" on the night in question. Jackie herself is now unsure if the man she says orchestrated the attack, identified in the story as "Drew," was a Phi Kappa Psi brother. According to the Washington Post, "Drew" actually belongs to a different fraternity and when contacted by the paper, he denied knowing Jackie. Jackie told Rolling Stone that after she was assaulted, she ran into "Drew" at a UVA pool where they both worked as lifeguards. In its statement, Phi Kappa Psi says none of its members worked at the pool in the fall of 2012. A friend of Jackie’s (who we were told would not speak to Rolling Stone) told the Washington Post that he found Jackie that night a mile from the school's fraternities. She did not appear to be "physically injured at the time" but was shaken. She told him that that she had been forced to have oral sex with a group of men at a fraternity party, but he does not remember her identifying a specific house. Other friends of Jackie’s told the Washington Post that they now have doubts about her narrative, but Jackie told the Washington Post that she firmly stands by the account she gave to Erdely.

Rolling Stone published the article with the firm belief that it was accurate. Given all of these reports, however, they have come to the conclusion that they were mistaken in honoring Jackie's request to not contact the alleged assaulters to get their account. In trying to be sensitive to the unfair shame and humiliation many women feel after a sexual assault, they made a judgment – the kind of judgment reporters and editors make every day. They should have not made this agreement with Jackie and they should have worked harder to convince her that the truth would have been better served by getting the other side of the story. These mistakes are on Rolling Stone, not on Jackie. They apologize to anyone who was affected by the story and they will continue to investigate the events of that evening.

The article has caused a significant amount of controversy and has led to calls for the suspension of all fraternities at UVA. The university has since suspended all fraternities and sororities until January 9, 2015, and has launched an investigation into the allegations made in the article. The university has also encouraged anyone with information about the incident to come forward to the police. The Washington Post has reported that the Charlottesville police are investigating the incident and have interviewed several people, including Jackie and members of Phi Kappa Psi. The fraternity has also launched its own internal investigation into the allegations. The incident has sparked a larger conversation about sexual assault on college campuses and the need for universities to take action to address the issue.

In 2013, the television shows "Breaking Bad" and "Homeland" influenced baby name trends. The names Jesse and Skyler from "Breaking Bad" saw significant increases in popularity, with Jesse up by 13% and Skyler up by 70%. However, names like Skinny Pete, Combo, and Badger remained niche. "Homeland" inspired the names Brody, Carrie, and Dana.

Sophia and Jackson continued their reign as the top choices for girls and boys respectively, with Sophia celebrating its ninth consecutive year at the top and Jackson its sixth. Oliver and Layla entered the top 10, pushing out Logan and Zoe.

The list also highlighted some popular trends in baby names, including names with personal meaning, such as family names and names of inspiring role models. The names Korie, Silas, George, Giorgio, Georgia, North West, Kanye, West, Kimberly, Marnie, Shoshanna, Lena Dunham, and Hannah saw significant increases in popularity.

Celebrities with negative press, such as Reese Witherspoon, Paula Deen, and Lindsay Lohan, saw a decrease in name popularity. Among the TODAY anchors, Al, Hoda, and Willie saw gains in popularity, while Savannah, Carson, Matt, and Natalie saw a decrease. Kathie Lee and Tamron were not found in the database.

The list was based on the names of over 550,000 babies born in 2013 to moms registered on BabyCenter's website. The list combined names that sound the same but have multiple spellings, such as Sophia and Sofia, or Jackson and Jaxon.

On Tuesday, both New York and Los Angeles public school systems received bomb threats, but only Los Angeles closed schools, affecting over 640,000 students. The threats, sent via Cockmail, an email host affiliated with the controversial 8chan, were deemed non-credible due to various indicators such as the use of explicit domains and a lowercase spelling of "Allah."

The Los Angeles threat, which originated from an IP address in Frankfurt, Germany, was traced back to an email with pornographic content. The New York threat, while similar, was considered a hoax by the NYPD. The emails threatened a jihadi attack using bombs and nerve gas, but the details were so outlandish that New York Mayor Bill de Blasio deemed them not credible.

LAUSD officials initially characterized the threat as "credible" but later determined it was not after a 12-hour investigation involving the LAPD, LAUSD, Los Angeles County Sheriff's Department, and FBI. The schools will reopen Wednesday, and officials believe the threat was designed to disrupt large cities.

The decision to close schools in Los Angeles has been met with mixed reactions, with some parents supporting the decision due to safety concerns, while others criticized it as a hoax. The threat against New York City schools was also deemed a hoax, and both cities' schools will remain open.

The incident highlights the challenge of balancing safety concerns with potential hoaxes, and the importance of thorough investigation before making decisions that affect thousands of students and parents.

The Tennessee Virtual Academy, a for-profit online public school, is under scrutiny for allegedly manipulating student grades to improve its image. An email obtained by NewsChannel 5 Investigates suggests that school leaders instructed teachers to delete failing grades from the school's electronic grading system, a practice that some lawmakers and education officials consider as cheating.

The email, written by the Tennessee Virtual Academy's vice principal, suggests that teachers should delete students' failing grades from October and September to show only the November progress. This action is seen as a way to hide the students' poor performance from parents and the public.

State Representative Gloria Johnson, a Knoxville Democrat and career teacher, expressed her concern about the email, stating that it's unacceptable to delete grades from the computer system. K12 Inc., the company operating the school, has refused to answer questions regarding the issue.

The Tennessee Virtual Academy's principal, Josh Williams, defended the action, stating that the goal was to "more accurately recognize students' current progress." He compared the grade deletions to the "common practice in traditional schools" of allowing make-up tests, alternative assessments, and extra credit opportunities.

However, the internal email also suggests that Virtual Academy teachers had already attempted those sorts of efforts to boost student grades. The email also indicates that the school's success or failure will be judged based on the standardized tests that students take at the end of the year, not on individual grades.

Governor Bill Haslam has proposed legislation that would cap the number of students who could enroll at 5,000. A bill up in a House subcommittee aims to essentially shut down the Tennessee Virtual Academy.

The controversy surrounding the Tennessee Virtual Academy has led to a heated debate in the Tennessee legislature, with some lawmakers questioning the school's practices and the profits of its parent company, K12 Inc.

Houston Texans defensive end J.J. Watt has been ruled out for the season due to a tibial plateau fracture sustained in the team's game against the Kansas City Chiefs. Watt was unable to walk off the field under his own power and was taken to a hospital in an ambulance. The Texans also announced that outside linebacker Whitney Mercilus will miss the rest of the season with a torn pectoral muscle. Watt, who missed 13 games in the 2016 season due to a back injury, has been a dominant force in the NFL, earning three Associated Press Defensive Player of the Year awards, four Pro Bowl selections, and four first-team All-Pro selections. Watt has also used his platform to raise over $37 million for Hurricane Harvey relief efforts. The Texans will now rely on Brandon Dunn, Joel Heath, and Carlos Watkins to fill the void left by Watt and Mercilus.

The attempted murders of Russian double agent Sergei Skripal and his daughter Yulia Skripal are under investigation by British authorities, who believe they were poisoned with a nerve agent at the front door of Sergei's Salisbury home. The highest concentration of the nerve agent was found on the front door, and counter-terrorism detectives will continue to focus their inquiries on the home address for the coming weeks and possibly months. The Skripals were found unconscious on a park bench in Salisbury earlier this month. Yulia was visiting her father.

Local police have retaken control of The Maltings shopping center and London Road cemetery from counter-terrorism detectives, where officers focused their investigation into the nerve agent attack in previous weeks. More than 130 people could have been exposed to the chemical weapon in the aftermath of the poisoning in Salisbury, which the UK government believes was committed by the Russian state.

In response to the poisoning, more than 150 Russian officials have been expelled from more than 25 countries, and the UK government is considering further measures to punish Russia, including a ban on the City of London from selling Russian sovereign debt. Public health experts are still working to establish whether the nerve agent attack presents a long-term risk to Salisbury's residents, who will receive a £1m support package from central government to help recover.

Detective Sergeant Nick Bailey, who was also hospitalized, is thought to have become ill after going to the house and was one of the first on the scene. The disclosure will intensify the manhunt for the would-be assassins who had targeted Col Skripal, 66, and his 33-year-old daughter. It will also heap further pressure on the Kremlin, which is accused of being behind the attack.

About 250 counter-terrorism detectives continue to work around the clock on the investigation, supported by a full range of experts and partners. Officers continue to trawl through more than 5,000 hours of CCTV and examine more than 1,350 exhibits that have been seized. Approximately 500 witnesses have been identified and hundreds of statements taken. Traces of the nerve agent have been found at some of the other scenes detectives have been working at over the past few weeks, but at lower concentrations than that found at the home address.

Surveillance footage shows Sergei Skripal shopping at a convenience store days before he was poisoned. Diplomatic fallout has ensued, with the UK expelling 23 Russian diplomats over the poisoning, which it blames on Moscow. Russia denies it was involved and has suggested the UK could be behind it. In a show of support for Britain, more than 20 other countries have kicked out Russian diplomats. British Foreign Minister Boris Johnson has thanked the countries for standing with Britain and said they did it despite the risk of retaliation. Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov has accused the US of pressuring and blackmailing other countries to expel Russian diplomats. The Skripals may never fully recover, according to UK officials.

The document discusses various topics related to generational trends, employment, and education. The main focus is on the Millennial generation, which has surpassed Baby Boomers as the largest living generation in the United States. The Millennial generation, defined as those born between 1981 and 1998, is found to have a longer tenure with their employers compared to Generation X workers when they were the same age.

The U.S. Department of Labor collects data on job tenure every two years as part of the Current Population Survey. In January 2016, 63.4% of employed Millennials reported that they had worked for their current employer at least 13 months, compared to 59.9% of 18-35-year-olds in February 2000, most of whom are today’s Gen Xers. Among young workers with longer tenures, 22% of Millennial workers had been with their employer for at least five years, similar to the share of Gen X workers in 2000.

One factor contributing to Millennials staying with employers longer is their relatively high levels of education, which is typically associated with longer tenure. Among 25-35-year-old workers in 2016, 38% of Millennial men and 46% of Millennial women had completed at least a bachelor’s degree, compared to 31% of male and 34% of female 25-35-year-old workers in 2000.

The increasing job tenure of college-educated Millennials is consistent with a decline in employer switching among all working-age adults since the 1980s. The reasons for the decline are not well understood, but recent research indicates that the rise of dual-career households, the decline in middle-skill jobs, occupational licensing, and the need for employees to retain health insurance cannot account for much of the decline in job-switching.

The longer tenure of college-educated Millennials compared with that of Gen X workers does not necessarily translate into higher wages or more job security. They may be sticking with their current employers due to a dearth of opportunities to get a better job with a different employer. However, their reported tenure makes clear that the "job-hopping Millennial" characterization does not fit the broad Millennial workforce.

The trend is different among less-educated young adults. For example, among Millennials with a high school education, 70% of men and 69% of women had been with their employer at least 13 months, similar to their high-school-educated counterparts among today’s Gen Xers in 2000.

The document also mentions that Millennials have surpassed Baby Boomers as the nation’s largest living generation, with 75.4 million Millennials compared to 74.9 million Baby Boomers. The Millennial generation continues to grow as young immigrants expand its ranks, while the Boomer generation is older and their numbers are shrinking as the number of deaths among them exceeds the number of older immigrants arriving in the country.

The document was originally published in January 2015 and updated on April 25, 2016, to indicate that Millennials have officially surpassed Baby Boomers in population. The document also mentions a new study by the Bay Area Council that found the cost of living in the area may send millennials packing, leaving experts to fear the region's thriving tech industry will suffer. The document also mentions Hurricane Irma and its impact on South Florida.

Four individuals, including two men and two women, aged 18 and 24, have been arrested in Chicago for a brutal and racially charged attack on an 18-year-old man with special needs. The incident was broadcast live on Facebook, where the victim was tied up, kicked, beaten, and subjected to racial slurs and profanities about President-elect Donald Trump. The attackers also forced the victim to drink toilet water and cut into his scalp, leaving a visible bald patch.

The victim was reported missing by his parents on Monday and was found wandering a Chicago street in distress on Tuesday. The suspects are believed to have known the victim from school, and police are considering kidnapping charges in addition to hate crime charges.

The attack has sparked outrage and condemnation, with Chicago Police Supt. Eddie Johnson calling the actions "reprehensible" and "sickening." The victim's family has asked for privacy and prayers as they cope and heal.

Facebook confirmed that it removed the original video from the suspect's profile, stating that it does not allow people to celebrate or glorify crimes on the platform. However, the company also allows videos to be shared to condemn violence or raise awareness about it.

The incident comes at a time when Chicago is under intense scrutiny for its high homicide rate, with 762 homicides in 2016. Chicago police spokesman Anthony Guglielmi emphasized that the investigation has so far not revealed a racial or political motive for the attack.

The four suspects are expected to appear in bond court on Friday. The victim is expected to make a full recovery and is currently at home in Crystal Lake. The attack has also been addressed by President Barack Obama, who called it "horrific" and "terrible."

The study published in the American Journal of Men's Health reveals that men gain weight after becoming fathers for the first time, whether they live with their children or not. The average weight gain for a 6-foot-tall man who lives with his child is about 4.4 pounds, while a 6-foot-tall non-resident father gains about 3.3 pounds. This weight gain is in addition to the increase resulting from marriage.

The study, led by Dr. Craig Garfield of Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine, tracked the weight of over 10,000 men from adolescence to young adulthood. The study controlled for other factors that could contribute to weight gain such as age, race, education, income, daily activity, screen time, and marriage status.

The weight gain may be due to changes in lifestyle and eating habits, as new responsibilities and the availability of kid-friendly, high-calorie foods and snacks can affect a father's ability to find time to exercise and take care of themselves.

Pediatricians are in a good position to counsel new fathers about taking care of their health, as many new fathers don't have a personal physician. The study highlights the importance of addressing the unique health challenges faced by new fathers, as they are less likely to be seeing doctors regularly.

The study is titled "Longitudinal Study of Body Mass Index in Young Males and the Transition to Fatherhood." It was supported by grant K23HD060664 from the Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute of Child Health and Human Development of the National Institutes of Health.

The IRS report released on Tuesday, often compared to the Watergate probe, did not find any evidence of intentional partisan motive by the IRS. The report, however, did criticize the IRS for using inappropriate criteria to identify applications for tax-exempt status, particularly focusing on conservative groups with names like "Tea Party" or related terms. The report found that the criteria gave the appearance of bias, and that donor lists and details were an unnecessary and burdensome request in the vetting process.

The report did not directly accuse the IRS of bias, but rather of the appearance of impropriety. The report also did not address the issue of whether the IRS misled Congress regarding the targeting program after May 2012. This issue is likely to be addressed during the Ways and Means hearing this Friday.

The report found that the majority of applications flagged by the Cincinnati office had indications of significant violations of tax policy. The report also made clear that the IRS knew that it overstepped its bounds when it asked for donor records, and that they decided to destroy all donor lists that were sent in for potential political cases.

The report's title, "Inappropriate Criteria Were Used to Identify Tax-Exempt Applications for Review," is criticized for not accurately capturing the full story, which includes confusion, incompetence, and unacceptable delays in the IRS unit that manages questionable 501(c)(4) applications. There is no allegation of politicization in the report, but the delays and inappropriate requests for information are unacceptable.

The study published in the Journal of the American Medical Association reveals a significant increase in nonfatal self-inflicted injuries among U.S. youth, particularly girls, between 2001 and 2015. The data was collected from emergency room visits and analyzed by the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

The overall rate of self-inflicted injuries among youth showed no significant trend until 2008, but increased 5.7% annually thereafter. The increase was more pronounced among females, with rates among girls aged 10 to 14 years increasing 18.8% per year from 2009 to 2015, and rates among girls aged 15 to 19 years showing a 7.2% increase per year during 2008-2015. Rates among females aged 20 to 24 years exhibited a 2.0% increase per year throughout 2001-2015.

The most common method of self-inflicted injury for females was drug overdose or self-poisoning, followed by intentional cutting with sharp objects. The study did not include information on which methods were most common by age nor on how many injuries were severe or required hospitalization.

The study highlights the need for comprehensive suicide and self-harm prevention strategies, including strengthening access to and delivery of care for suicidal youth within health systems, creating protective environments, promoting youth connectedness, teaching coping and problem-solving skills, and identifying and supporting at-risk youth within communities.

The researchers noted that the findings underscore the need to focus on reducing self-harm, as it is a key risk factor for suicide. The study's results underestimate the problem since they don't include self-injuries treated in doctors' offices or elsewhere.

The study's findings parallel rising reports of teen depression and suicide, and some mental health experts suggest that cyberbullying, substance abuse, and economic stress from the recent recession might be contributing factors.

In Madison, Wisconsin, a peaceful protest took place following the fatal shooting of an unarmed black 19-year-old named Tony Robinson by a white police officer, identified as Officer Matt Kenny. The shooting occurred on March 6, 2015, after Kenny responded to a call about a disturbance and forced his way into Robinson's apartment. The incident sparked protests in the city, with demonstrators chanting "Black Lives Matter."

Madison Police Chief Mike Koval released the name of the officer involved in the shooting and assured the community that his department would defend the rights of protesters while urging restraint. Koval also stated that Kenny had been injured but did not provide details. It was unclear whether Robinson was alone at the time of the shooting.

Tony Robinson's death came days after the U.S. Justice Department announced that it would not issue civil rights charges against Darren Wilson, the white former Ferguson, Missouri, officer who fatally shot an unarmed black 18-year-old, Michael Brown, after a struggle in the street last August. The shooting of Robinson and other high-profile deaths of black suspects at the hands of police officers have prompted nationwide protests.

Koval struck a conciliatory tone while addressing the potential for more protests in Madison, saying he understood the community's distrust after "this tragic death." He also asked protesters to follow what he said was the lead of Robinson's family in asking for "nondestructive" demonstrations.

Robinson's family and friends gathered for a community meeting, where they read a statement prepared by Robinson's mother, Andrea Irwin. Irwin expressed her grief and disbelief over her son's death, stating, "I haven't even had a chance to see his body."

Kenny, a more than 12-year veteran of the Madison department, had been involved in a previous officer-involved shooting in 2007, but was cleared of wrongdoing because it was determined to be a "suicide by cop" situation. In that shooting, Kenny responded to a 911 call of a man with a gun and shot the man twice after police said he pointed the gun at officers. It turned out to be a pellet gun.

Kenny has been placed on administrative leave pending results of an investigation by the state's Division of Criminal Investigation. The shooting of Tony Robinson has raised questions about the integrity of investigations into officer-involved deaths, as a 2014 Wisconsin law requires police departments to have outside agencies investigate such incidents.

Madison, the state capital and home to the University of Wisconsin's flagship campus, has a population of about 243,000, with approximately 7 percent of residents being black. The shooting took place in a two-story gray house on Williamson Street, also known as Willy Street.

The Madison community is awaiting answers and transparency from the authorities regarding the circumstances surrounding Tony Robinson's death. The incident has once again brought attention to the issue of police violence against black individuals and the need for accountability and reform.

In a rally in Franklin, Tennessee on October 3, 2015, Republican presidential candidate Donald Trump discussed his views on gun control in response to the shooting at an Oregon community college that left nine dead. Trump, who holds a handgun carry permit in New York, argued that the shooting could have been limited if instructors or students had been armed. He criticized "gun-free zones" and emphasized the importance of self-defense. Trump also drew comparisons between himself and Charles Bronson's character in the film "Death Wish," stating that anyone who attacks him would be "shocked." Trump's comments on gun control have evolved significantly over the years, and he has previously supported the ban on assault weapons and longer waiting periods for gun purchases. This is the most extensive and emotionally charged discussion about firearms that Trump has had since launching his campaign in June.

The summary of the document provides a timeline of key events in the life of Anthony Weiner, a former Democratic U.S. Representative from New York, who pleaded guilty to criminal charges related to his online communications with a minor.

Weiner's political career began in 1998 when he was elected to Congress. In 2005, he came in second in a bid for the Democratic nomination for mayor of New York City. In 2010, he wed Huma Abedin, a close aide to then-Secretary of State Hillary Clinton.

In 2011, Weiner was embroiled in a sexting scandal when a lewd photograph was sent from his Twitter account. He initially lied about the incident, but eventually admitted to sending the lewd photo and resigned from Congress in 2011.

In 2013, Weiner launched a run for New York City mayor, but his campaign was derailed by another sexting scandal. In 2016, more sexting scandals emerged, including allegations of inappropriate communications with a 15-year-old girl, which led to a federal investigation.

On May 19, 2017, Weiner pleaded guilty to a single count of transmitting obscene material to a minor. He admitted to exchanging online messages with the girl beginning in January 2015 and "sharing explicit images and encouraging her to engage in sexually explicit conduct." Weiner could face up to 10 years in prison, but is likely to serve a much shorter term. His sentencing is scheduled for September 8, 2017.
