The investigation into Weiner's online communications with the 15-year-old girl also led to the discovery of emails on his laptop that were sent by his estranged wife, Huma Abedin, which prompted the FBI to reopen an investigation into Hillary Clinton's emails.

The document also mentions that Weiner's sexting scandals have been the subject of a documentary, and that he has been the subject of multiple late-night TV jokes and news headlines. The document concludes by stating that Weiner will likely go to prison for his crimes.

Arizona State University (ASU) permanently expelled the Tau Kappa Epsilon (TKE) fraternity for hosting a racially insensitive Martin Luther King Jr. holiday weekend party. The university's statement cited violations of the student code of conduct, including engaging in discriminatory activities, violating alcohol rules, violating terms of earlier disciplinary sanctions, and off-campus conduct that may present a risk or danger.

The party, which was unregistered and off-campus, involved students wearing stereotypical hip-hop clothes, posing with watermelon cups, and flashing gang signs. The images drew swift criticism from civil-rights leaders, who demanded the university expel the fraternity.

ASU had previously placed TKE on probation in 2012 due to a fight involving fraternity members. In 2012, the University of Arizona also stripped its local chapter of TKE of recognition after an investigation showed multiple instances of dangerous hazing.

The fraternity's national spokesman, Alex Baker, said they would release the results of their own investigation shortly. The local chapter was unavailable for comment. The incident has drawn national attention, with CNN's Anderson Cooper featuring it on his "Ridiculist" segment.

ASU President Michael Crow quoted Martin Luther King, saying, "We must remember that intelligence is not enough. Intelligence plus character – that is the goal of true education." Crow emphasized that these values are reflected in ASU's Student Code of Conduct, and any violations by students may result in disciplinary action.

In a controversial move, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) has arrested a Mexican immigrant, Daniel Ramirez Medina, who was previously granted protection under the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) program. The arrest, which occurred last week in Seattle, WA, has sparked concerns among immigrant rights groups and civil-rights attorneys, who argue that it could signal a broader crackdown on immigrants under the Trump administration.

Ramirez, a 23-year-old with no criminal history, was granted a permit to live and work legally in the U.S. under DACA, a program that protects children who were brought to the U.S. illegally by their undocumented parents. If Ramirez's detention was intentional, he would be the first DACA recipient arrested under the Trump administration, a move that could potentially lead to further arrests of immigrants previously considered legal residents of the U.S.

Ramirez's lawyers have filed a petition in federal court in Seattle seeking his release, arguing that the government violated his constitutional rights by arresting him after he had previously been granted permission to stay in the United States. In the lawsuit, Ramirez claims he had disclosed his DACA paperwork twice to ICE officers, once in his father's home and a second time while in a processing center. However, ICE has countered that Ramirez is a "self-admitted gang member" encountered during the arrest of a felon who had previously been deported.

The arrest has been met with criticism from politicians and advocacy groups. Sen. Maria Cantwell has pledged to look into the situation, while U.S. Rep. Pramila Jayapal has demanded Ramirez's immediate release. Seattle Mayor Ed Murray and Councilmember M. Lorena González have reaffirmed Seattle's status as a sanctuary city and called for clarification on the administration's stance on DACA recipients.

The lawsuit alleges that Ramirez has been in the United States since he was 7 years old. A hearing in the case is scheduled for Friday, and the judge has ordered the government to respond to the petition by Thursday. If Ramirez is found to have been unlawfully detained, it could set a precedent for future cases involving DACA recipients.

The Oregon Legislature is considering a new bill, House Bill 2875, that would impose a five-cent per pound tax on wholesale coffee to fund alternative education programs and primary school reading programs. The bill is sponsored by the Oregon House Committee on Revenue, but the chair of the Committee on Revenue stated that the bill is not going anywhere. If passed, the bill would go into effect on July 1, 2018, but an estimate of how much revenue this new tax would provide was not mentioned. The bill requires a three-fifths majority from both the Oregon House of Representatives and Senate to pass.

The funds raised from this new tax would go toward establishing the “Alternative Education Sustainability Fund.” Half of those funds would go toward the Oregon Military Department to be used in the Oregon National Guard Youth Challenge Program. The other half would fund grants for Oregon school districts that operate alternative high school programs, as well as primary schools. Schools that operate alternative high school programs and primary schools would be able to apply for those grants from the Oregon Department of Education. If awarded, the grant money could be used for “cost of operations and capital construction” of alternative high school programs and primary school reading programs.

The Oregon Legislature is set to convene on February 1 to decide how best to deal with the state’s $1.8 billion budget gap, whether to ditch the statewide ban on rent control, and other pressing issues. The budget framework for the 2017-2019 biennium was released on January 19 by the Co-Chairs of the Joint Ways and Means Committee, and it detailed how Oregon’s incoming revenue is 8% lower than what’s needed at current levels. The framework listed a number of spending categories where cuts would need to take place, including education and health care.

With rent prices in Portland continuing to climb, many in the Rose City are calling for quick action to protect renters. In response to these calls for action, House Speaker Tina Kotek filed House Bill 2001 to repeal Oregon’s ban on city and county ordinances regulating rents. Her bill also aims to allow cities and counties to adopt rent stabilization programs (with certain restrictions) and impose a temporary moratorium on rent increases greater than 5% for residential tenancies (with some exceptions). The House Speaker announced that she supported a state limit on rent increases and banning no-cause evictions at the state level back in September 2016. A similar bill, sponsored by multiple representatives, also seeks to allow cities and counties to create ordinances regulating rent. Both bills will face opposition from House Republicans.

House Republicans believe that high rent prices are a result of a “basic breakdown in the laws of supply and demand” and suggest relieving pressure by incentivizing the development and construction of affordable units, to increase supply and lower demand. They also want to prioritize rural Oregon during this legislative session by “forcing the majority party to be mindful of the impact of new laws on rural communities” and “advocating for policies that will help incentivize economic growth in rural Oregon.”

In addition, the legislature will also have a number of other important issues to tackle, including justice and ethics reforms, such as setting up data collection, policies, and training necessary to further cut down on profiling, reforms to how people are charged for certain drug offenses, how grand juries operate, and adequately fund public defense and increase support for legal assistance in civil cases. The legislature will also consider drafting legislation to limit the number of Salem employees that move from influential government positions to eventually turning into lobbyists that interact with the government, as well as the reverse.

Starbucks CEO Howard Schultz remains optimistic about the company's growth in China despite the country's slowing economy. The coffee giant plans to open more than one store per day in China for the next five years, aiming to have nearly 5,000 stores by 2021. Starbucks has already been successful in China, with the majority of its business now coming from Chinese customers instead of expats and tourists. Schultz expects China to eventually overtake the U.S. as Starbucks' largest market.

Starbucks' success in China stands in contrast to other American brands like Facebook, Netflix, Uber, and Google, which have faced challenges in the Chinese market. KFC and McDonald's, which have enjoyed success in China for years, are now facing difficulties and are looking for partners to take over their franchise operations. Schultz attributes Starbucks' success to its focus on coffee and avoidance of sensitive technology markets.

NASCAR has requested its fans to refrain from displaying the Confederate Flag at its races, following a statement signed by tracks that host the Sprint Cup, Xfinity, and Camping World Truck series. The decision comes after Daytona International Speedway announced a flag exchange program for Sunday's Coke Zero 400, allowing fans to voluntarily exchange Confederate flags for American flags. The request pertains to "overt displays" of the Confederate flag, and the program could be extended to other tracks. The move is a continuation of the theme started by NASCAR chairman Brian France, who expressed a desire to eliminate the flag from NASCAR events last week. The sport with strong southern roots has previously stated it does not sell any officially-licensed merchandise with the Confederate flag symbol and supports the effort to remove the flag from the South Carolina Capitol.

Three children in Salinas, California, were found in a state of neglect and abuse, with the oldest child being chained to prevent her from getting food. The children, aged 8, 5, and 3, were discovered on March 14 during a welfare check at their home. The mothers, Eraca Dawn Craig, 31, and Christian Jessica Deanda, 44, were arrested and charged with numerous child abuse offenses. The children were hospitalized and showed signs of physical and emotional abuse. The women, who are domestic partners, do not appear to have prior criminal records in Monterey County. The children have been placed in foster care, and the case is being described as particularly heinous. Both women are currently in Monterey County Jail.

A Canadian Federal Court Justice, Robin Camp, has resigned following a recommendation from the Canadian Judicial Council for his removal over his conduct during a 2014 rape trial. Camp's comments during the trial, including asking the complainant why she couldn't keep her "knees together," were deemed "so manifestly and profoundly destructive of the concept of impartiality, integrity, and independence of the judicial role" by the council.

Camp's resignation came after he fought hard to save his job, publicly apologizing, attending counselling and education sessions, and seeking an opportunity to explain his actions to the larger body of judicial council members. However, the council's ruling stated that the deep harm done to public confidence made his dismissal necessary.

The case has raised questions about the handling of sexual assault trials and the need for mandatory judicial training on gendered issues such as sexual assault, domestic violence, and sexual harassment. The incident is seen as a "watershed moment" in how courts treat sexual assault cases.

This is not the only recent case to raise questions about how judges handle sexual assault. In another case, a judge acquitted a taxi driver accused of sexually assaulting a passenger so intoxicated that she passed out, stating "clearly, a drunk can consent."

Camp's resignation follows two other cases where the council recommended Parliament remove a judge from the bench, with both men resigning almost immediately. The cost of Camp's legal battle has been paid for by taxpayers through the Commission for Federal Judicial Affairs.

Scientists in East Africa are planning to use trained rats to screen for tuberculosis (TB) in prisons in Tanzania and Mozambique. The rats, trained by the Belgian non-governmental organization APOPO, are known for their ability to detect TB and have a success rate of almost 100%. APOPO, with funding from the United States Agency for International Development (USAID), plans to recruit and train more rats to carry out prison screening, which is expected to be faster and more reliable than existing methods.

TB is the leading cause of death from an infectious disease, with around 9 million new cases and 2 million deaths worldwide each year, according to the World Health Organization. In Tanzania, many cases go undiagnosed due to a lack of awareness and resources for screening, creating a burden for health authorities. APOPO's TB detection rat technology is fast, cheap, and has the potential to greatly lower screening costs in poor countries.

The rats undergo a rigorous training process that begins when they are four weeks old. They learn to recognize the presence of TB in samples of sputum and are rewarded when they succeed. The testing process starts when a rat is presented with a row of 10 sputum samples, and when it detects TB, the rat hovers over the sample for 3 seconds.

APOPO's current programs have screened over 340,000 TB samples, halting over 36,000 further infections, and increased detection rates by over 40% in several partnered clinics. Khadija Abraham, an expert at Tanzania's National Leprosy and Tuberculosis Programme, said trained rats have a great ability to detect a wide range of strong-smelling molecules that could help track down undiagnosed TB cases, especially in rural areas.

APOPO plans to expand the program to all prisons, shantytowns, factories, and other settings in Tanzania, Mozambique, and other high TB-burden countries, as well as in high-risk groups such as those living with HIV/AIDS. This will improve and save lives all over the globe at a low cost.

On August 17, 2015, a Trigana Air Service passenger plane crashed into a mountain in Indonesia's Papua province, resulting in the death of all 54 people on board. The plane was flying from Jayapura to Oksibil, a journey that usually takes 42 minutes, when it lost contact with air traffic control. Relatives of the passengers were waiting at the airport when they received the news of the crash.

Rescuers faced difficulties reaching the crash site due to rugged terrain and bad weather. On Tuesday, more than 70 rescuers were able to reach the site and found the plane's wreckage at an altitude of 2,600 meters (about 8,500 feet). The flight data recorder and cockpit voice recorder, commonly known as the "black boxes," were found in good condition.

The data they contain could help explain what caused the crash. The National Search and Rescue Agency (BASARNAS) chief, Henry Bambang Soelistyo, stated that the plane was totally destroyed and all the bodies were burned and difficult to identify. All 54 bodies have been recovered and will be taken to Jayapura for identification.

The victims included four postal workers escorting four bags of cash totaling $468,750 in government aid for poor families to help offset a spike in fuel prices. The airline, Trigana Air Service, has had a history of incidents, with 19 serious incidents since 1992, resulting in the loss of eight aircraft and major damage to 11 others.

Indonesia has a patchy aviation record, with two other major crashes in the past year. In December 2014, an AirAsia flight went down in the Java Sea, killing all 162 on board. More than 100 people died in June 2015 in the crash of a military transport plane. Indonesia scored poorly on a 2014 safety audit by the U.N. aviation agency, largely because its Ministry of Transportation is understaffed.

The crash is the latest in a string of aviation disasters in Indonesia, a Southeast Asian archipelago nation of 250 million people and some 17,000 islands. The sprawling nation is one of Asia's most rapidly expanding airline markets, but it is struggling to provide enough qualified pilots, mechanics, air traffic controllers, and updated airport technology to ensure safety. From 2007 to 2009, the European Union barred Indonesian airlines from flying to Europe because of safety concerns.

The Democratic National Convention on Tuesday was marked by a surprising level of energy and enthusiasm, as noted by various journalists. David Gergen on CNN stated that the enthusiasm in the hall was more palpable than at the Republican Convention. POLITICO's Dylan Byers and Alexander Burns observed that there was more energy in the Democratic Convention than in the entire three days of the Republican Convention.

Michelle Obama's speech during the convention was particularly well-received, with 28,003 tweets-per-minute at its peak, nearly double the 14,289 mark reached by Mitt Romney's acceptance speech at the Republican Convention last week. The speech, which aimed to illustrate the differences between Obama and his Republican challenger, was filled with short, snackable lines that resonated on Twitter.

Overall, the Democratic Convention sparked more than 3 million tweets in its first night, nearing the 4 million point reached by the entirety of last week's Republican Convention. The convention was described as passionate, energetic, and confident, in contrast to the Republican Convention which was perceived as lacking in energy and enthusiasm. However, some critics, such as radio host Laura Ingraham, argued that the convention felt stale and lacked the youthful energy of the 2008 convention.

In the weekend box office, "The Angry Birds Movie" took the top spot with a debut of $39 million, marking the third-best animated debut of the year. The family comedy, based on the popular app game, features the voices of Jason Sudeikis, Sean Penn, Maya Rudolph, Danny McBride, and Josh Gad. Despite mixed reviews, audiences embraced the film, with 61% liking it. "Captain America: Civil War" fell to second place, earning $33.1 million in its third week, bringing its domestic total to $347.4 million and its worldwide total to over $1 billion. "Neighbors 2: Sorority Rising" debuted at No. 3 with $21.8 million, while "The Nice Guys" and "The Jungle Book" rounded out the top five. "The Nice Guys" performed better than expected with $11.3 million, and "The Jungle Book" has earned $327.5 million since its release.

The new iPad, announced by Apple, is the latest installment in their popular tablet series, set to go on sale on March 16. The device resembles the iPad 2, but features several improvements, including a more powerful processor, a higher resolution display, and the ability to access 4G wireless networks.

The new iPad's display is a major selling point, with Apple claiming it is the sharpest and most vibrant screen ever seen on a mobile device. The device also features an improved camera, dictation capabilities, and the ability to tap into 4G networks without sacrificing much battery life or jacking up prices. The iPad 2 will remain in the lineup and will be cheaper, with a 16GB model now fetching $399, a $100 drop from a week ago.

The new iPad's 4G capabilities are a significant upgrade, as it is the first iPad to access the 4G networks being deployed by AT&T and Verizon Wireless. The device was tested on Verizon's 4G LTE network and was found to be very fast, with download speeds often faster than home cable-modem service. However, the device's 4G capabilities are a battery hog, so Apple has implemented several power-saving measures to maintain the iPad's battery life.

The new iPad's display and 4G capabilities are impressive, but some features that were expected to be included, such as expanded storage options, a smaller-screen model, and Adobe Flash support, were left out. The device also does not feature Siri, the chatty personal assistant found on the iPhone 4S. Despite these omissions, analyst Piper Jaffray estimates that Apple will sell up to 60 million iPads this year, on top of the 55 million sold since the original iPad was introduced in 2010.

Overall, the new iPad is a significant upgrade from the iPad 2, with a stunning display, fast wireless capabilities, and improved camera optics. The device's strong battery life, app ecosystem, and lack of competition in the tablet market make it a strong choice for consumers, provided price is not a concern. The device is available starting at $499 for 16GB, with prices increasing for larger storage capacities and models with 4G wireless capabilities.

The Indian government has dismissed an official, A.K. Verma, from the Central Public Works Department (CPWD) for an unauthorized absence from duty that lasted 25 years. Verma, who joined CPWD in 1980, went on earned leave in December 1990 and did not return to work thereafter. An inquiry was initiated against him in 1992 for major penalty for wilful absence from duty, but no action was taken until recently. The dismissal was ordered by Urban Development Minister M. Venkaiah Naidu to streamline the functioning of CPWD and ensure accountability.

India's bureaucracy has a reputation for being notoriously work-shy, with civil servants often arriving late, taking long lunches, or spending parts of their day on the golf course. A 2012 survey by the Political and Economic Risk consultancy ranked India's bureaucracy as the worst among major Asian countries. Prime Minister Narendra Modi, who took office in May 2014, has been cracking down on absenteeism, including making New Delhi bureaucrats sign in at work using a fingerprint scanner, with the results publicly available online.

The dismissal of A.K. Verma is a significant step towards addressing the issue of absenteeism in India's bureaucracy, and it is expected to set a precedent for similar cases in the future. The government's action is part of a broader effort to improve the efficiency and accountability of the public sector in India.

In his annual New Year's Day speech, North Korean leader Kim Jong-un claimed to have a nuclear button on his desk and asserted that the entire United States is within range of North Korean nuclear weapons. Kim also vowed not to attack unless threatened, but emphasized the need to focus on mass-producing nuclear warheads and ballistic missiles for operational deployment in 2018.

Kim offered a potential olive branch to South Korea, suggesting he was open to dialogue and considering sending a delegation to the Winter Olympics in Pyeongchang, South Korea, in February. This gesture was welcomed by the president of the PyeongChang Games' organizing committee, who described it as a New Year's gift.

Kim's conciliatory tone towards South Korea was seen as a marked change from the norm, as North Korea usually ignores South Korea and maintains the position that it will deal with the US on its own. Some analysts suggest that Kim may be seeking to improve ties to offer some respite from the growing economic pressures from recent UN sanctions and to position his regime as moving towards its neighbours while the US is seeking to isolate it.

US President Donald Trump responded to Kim's latest threats with a non-committal "We'll see, we'll see". North Korea has come under increased criticism and sanctions over the past year due to its nuclear weapons programme and repeated testing of conventional missiles.

Experts say North Korea's nuclear capabilities do not yet match Kim's boasts, but there is little doubt its capabilities have advanced significantly in the past year. The idea of improving relations between the two Koreas is one that is frequently spoken about but seldom achieved, and Kim's warmer words could also be seen as an attempt to drive a wedge between Seoul and Washington.

Daryl Kimball, executive director of the Arms Control Association, stated that Kim's claims about his country's nuclear capability underscored that there was no viable "military solution" to denuclearizing North Korea and that sanctions alone would not persuade Pyongyang to halt or reverse its nuclear buildup. Kimball suggested that the upcoming Olympics provide an important opportunity to break the ice and to begin discussions with the North Koreans on mutual steps that reduce the chances of miscalculation and war.

The article discusses the water consumption involved in the production of bottled water, comparing it to other beverages. The International Bottled Water Association (IBWA) recently conducted a study to determine the amount of water used to produce one liter of bottled water, finding that for North American companies, it takes 1.39 liters of water. This is less than the water required for a liter of soda (2.02 liters), beer (4 liters), wine (4.74 liters), and hard alcohol (34.55 liters).

However, water activists argue that the IBWA study only considers water used in the actual production process and not the water used in the supply chain, including water used for packaging. Ertug Ercin from the Water Footprint Network suggests that a true water footprint should include all freshwater used in production, including water used for packaging, as well as water used in the supply chain.

Ercin states that three liters of water might be used to make a half-liter bottle, and that drilling for oil to make plastic and producing paper also uses substantial amounts of water. Despite this, bottled water packaging uses less water than soda, which requires extra water for growing sugar and making dyes.

Chris Hogan, spokesman for the IBWA, acknowledges that the study did not consider the entire water footprint but argues that it is challenging to know where to stop in terms of calculations. Hogan also notes that the bottled water industry is working to be as efficient as possible with water, as it is crucial to their operations. The article concludes by mentioning that Alexa Internet has been donating their crawl data to the Internet Archive since 1996, with the data being added to the Wayback Machine after an embargo period.

In this article, two separate news stories are presented. The first story focuses on Jennifer Westfeldt, an actress and writer, who will start performances of the new play "The Power of Duff" at Vassar's Powerhouse Theater in upstate Poughkeepsie. The theater has a summer-camp vibe, and Westfeldt, who was once kicked out of camp for taking her boyfriend out for pizza, joked about her longtime boyfriend Jon Hamm visiting the campus.

The second story discusses the controversy surrounding Madonna's upcoming gig in Warsaw, Poland, which falls on the city's annual World War Two remembrance day. Catholic youth activists are calling on local officials to cancel the concert, claiming it would be disrespectful to the estimated 200,000 people who perished during the 1944 Warsaw Uprising. The activists have launched an online petition and have criticized Madonna for her provocative stage shows, which they claim promote homosexuality, pornography, and attack the Catholic faith.

Madonna's latest tour, MDNA, has been controversial, with incidents such as flashing her breast in Turkey and France, exposing her bottom onstage in Rome, and incensing French politician Marine Le Pen by screening a video that juxtaposed a swastika over her head. Despite these controversies, Madonna's MDNA tour may end up being the highest-grossing concert run of all time.

In a separate story, Madonna has scrapped plans for her first Australian tour in 20 years. Her manager, Guy Oseary, reportedly told promoter Live Nation about Madonna's change of heart overnight. Live Nation Australia confirmed the cancellation, but had no further comment. Madonna was set to announce summer dates for Melbourne and Sydney on July 12, but postponed the announcement until after the London Olympics.

Finally, the article reports on Madonna's concert in London, where hundreds of fans walked out, branding it the worst gig ever. Fans blamed a 10.30pm curfew, poor sound quality, rain, and a failure to perform hits from Madonna's back catalog for the dismal concert. Despite the negative reviews, some fans still tweeted that Madonna was excellent. Madonna's press spokeswoman was unavailable for comment about the mass walk-out.

The United States has begun deploying the Terminal High-Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) system in South Korea, a move aimed at protecting against threats from North Korea. The decision to deploy THAAD comes a day after North Korea launched four ballistic missiles, breaking international sanctions. The move has angered China and Russia, who see the system's powerful radars as a security threat. South Korea's liberal presidential candidates have expressed concerns that the security benefits of having THAAD would be curtailed by worsened relations with neighbors China and Russia. China has threatened to take "necessary measures" to protect itself and has criticized the deployment, triggering protests against a South Korean retail giant, Lotte, which agreed to provide a site for THAAD. The Chinese government has also reportedly banned Chinese tour groups from visiting South Korea. The THAAD system is designed to intercept and destroy short and medium-range ballistic missiles during the last part of their flights. The North's latest missile launch is believed to be an improved version of a Scud missile, capable of hitting Japan, including U.S. military bases in Okinawa. The deployment of THAAD is controversial, with domestic opposition in South Korea and international concerns from China and Russia. The system's powerful X-band radars have raised concerns that they could be used to spot Chinese missile launches and feed the data to cue up other US defensive systems, potentially affecting China's deterrent capability. The deployment is likely to worsen tensions between South Korea and China, with reports of economic retaliation against South Korean businesses, including Lotte, which allowed THAAD to be installed on one of its sites. The UN Security Council is due to meet on Wednesday to discuss the latest missile launch by North Korea.

The study published in the Journal of the National Cancer Institute reveals that drinking alcohol before the first pregnancy increases the risk of both benign breast disease (BBD) and breast cancer, regardless of drinking after the first pregnancy. The research, led by Dr. Ying Liu from Washington University School of Medicine, analyzed data from over 91,000 women who took part in the Nurses' Health Study II.

The study found a dose-dependent relationship, meaning the more alcohol a woman drinks during the time between her first menstrual period and first pregnancy, the higher her risk of developing breast cancer. The link was observed regardless of drinking after the first pregnancy.

The researchers also found that longer intervals between the first menstrual period and first pregnancy showed stronger associations compared with shorter intervals. Drinking after the first pregnancy was associated with breast cancer risk but not BBD.

The study suggests that alcohol intake, particularly before the first pregnancy, may play a significant role in the development of breast cancer. The findings have potential implications for breast cancer prevention, with the researchers recommending that women reduce their alcohol consumption, especially before the first pregnancy, to reduce their breast cancer risk.

It is crucial to note that the 11% increased risk should be put into perspective, as a woman's lifetime risk of breast cancer is about one in eight, or 12%. The study did not provide a statistic for lifetime breast cancer risk for nondrinkers.

The American Cancer Society provides more information on risk factors for breast cancer. The study emphasizes the importance of moderation in alcohol consumption for breast cancer prevention.

In a rally in North Dakota, President Trump emphasized the importance of maintaining the Republican majority in the Senate, particularly in light of Supreme Court Justice Anthony Kennedy's retirement. Trump was campaigning for Republican Rep. Kevin Cramer, who is challenging Democratic Sen. Heidi Heitkamp in an election that could result in a Senate seat flip for the GOP. Trump argued that Cramer would support his agenda and court picks, while Heitkamp would not. Heitkamp, however, has previously voted in favor of one of Trump's Supreme Court nominees, Neil Gorsuch.

Heitkamp responded by stating that she would continue to be an independent voice in the Senate, regardless of the election. Trump continued to tie Heitkamp to the national Democratic party throughout the rally, mentioning her alleged alignment with Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, House Minority Leader Nancy Pelosi, and liberal California congresswoman Maxine Waters.

Justice Kennedy's retirement provides the Trump administration with an opportunity to shift the balance of the Supreme Court for decades. Trump has promised to nominate a judge who will serve for 40-45 years and has a list of 25 potential nominees. Kennedy, who was nominated by President Reagan and served for 30 years, was known for his centrist influence but sided with the court's liberal justices on issues such as abortion rights and same-sex marriage.

The Senate is currently split 51-49 for Republicans, but the margin for error is small due to the absence of Sen. John McCain, who has been battling brain cancer. Red state Democrats, including Heitkamp, Manchin, and Donnelly, will play a crucial role in determining the level of resistance a new Supreme Court nominee faces. Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell has indicated that a vote on Kennedy's replacement will take place as soon as this fall. Trump made it clear that Heitkamp's vote for a new nominee will not earn her a pass from him or Republicans ahead of the November elections.

The Democratic National Committee (DNC) recently experienced a suspected cyber attack on its voter database, prompting an investigation by the Federal Bureau of Investigation. The DNC believes this incident is a sophisticated attempt to gain access to sensitive voter information, which is considered the party's most valuable data.

This incident underscores the increased vulnerability of various systems in the cyber age, making elections susceptible to manipulation. The potential threats range from voter-registration systems in the 50 states to the inner workings of political parties.

Rob Joyce, the former White House cybersecurity coordinator, recently noted that the focus has shifted from using cyber realms to steal secrets to using them to impose national power.

In response to these threats, political groups and government organizations have been on high alert ahead of the midterm elections, with Microsoft revealing that hackers tied to Russian intelligence targeted the Senate and conservative think tanks in the U.S. This was followed by Facebook identifying a political influence campaign aimed at potentially disrupting the midterms.

However, in a recent update, the DNC announced that the suspected hacking attempt was actually an unauthorized "simulated phishing test." The DNC, a cloud service provider, and a security research firm worked together to thwart the potential attack by detecting and shutting down a fake login page designed to gather usernames and passwords. Despite this, the incident serves as a reminder of the ongoing threats and the need for vigilance in the cyber age.

On June 25, 2017, a tourist ferry named El Almirante, carrying approximately 170 passengers, capsized in a reservoir near Medellin, Colombia, resulting in nine deaths and 28 people missing. The incident occurred during a holiday weekend, making the reservoir a popular destination. The ferry, which was four stories high, appeared to be overloaded and no life vests were worn by passengers, according to survivors.

Rescue efforts were initiated immediately, involving local firefighters, air force pilots, and recreational boat owners. Dramatic videos circulating on social media showed passengers desperately crawling down from the fourth-floor roof as the boat began to sink.

Preliminary reports suggest that 99 people were rescued, while another 40 managed to reach the shore on their own. The disaster response agency in Antioquia state reported nine deaths and around 28 people still missing. The cause of the boat sinking remains unclear.

Daniel Giraldo, an Italian restaurant owner in Guatape, rushed to the scene after hearing the sound of ambulances. He saw a baby girl saved from the water but learned that her mother was missing. Authorities are urging passengers or their loved ones to report to a rescue center and are calling for scuba divers to assist with the search.

The reservoir, surrounding the rocky outcrop of El Penol, is a frequent weekend destination, located about an hour from Medellin. This incident has raised concerns about safety measures on tourist boats in the area. AP writers Christine Armario from Bogota, Colombia, and Joshua Goodman from Caracas, Venezuela, contributed to this report.

On November 3, 2011, a peaceful Occupy Wall Street protest in Oakland, California, turned violent after dark. Protesters, many wearing masks, shattered windows, set fires, and vandalized businesses with graffiti. Police responded with tear gas and flash-bang grenades, making dozens of arrests. The chaos occurred near the Occupy Oakland encampment in Frank Ogawa Plaza, which had been the center of a general strike earlier in the day. Thousands of people angry at economic inequality marched to the Port of Oakland, shutting it down.

The violence in Oakland followed a mostly peaceful day of protest, during which thousands of people participated in marches and rallies across the U.S. in solidarity with the Occupy Wall Street movement. The movement, which began in September, aims to challenge the world's economic systems and the distribution of wealth. The port shutdown was a significant victory for organizers in Oakland, but police said that about 7,000 people participated in demonstrations throughout the day, with a few incidents of vandalism at local banks and businesses.

Supporters of the Occupy Wall Street movement staged smaller-scale demonstrations in New York, Philadelphia, Los Angeles, and elsewhere. In New York, about 100 military veterans marched in uniform and stopped in front of the New York Stock Exchange. In Boston, college students and union workers marched on Bank of America offices, the Harvard Club, and the Statehouse to protest the nation's burgeoning student debt crisis.

The larger Occupy movement has yet to coalesce into an organized association, but organizers in Oakland view the strike and port shutdown as a significant victory. The movement has gained momentum in recent weeks, capturing the world's attention by shutting down one of the nation's busiest shipping ports. Port officials hoped to resume operations on Thursday, but continued missed shifts represent economic hardship for maritime workers, truckers, and their families, as well as lost jobs and lost tax revenue for the region.

Angel Gonzalez, a man who spent 20 years in prison for a rape and abduction conviction that was later overturned, was released on Tuesday after being cleared of a separate property damage charge. Gonzalez's conviction for the 1994 rape and abduction was dismissed on Monday, but he remained in prison due to the property damage charge. After the property charge was dismissed, Gonzalez was released and expressed gratitude to his supporters and attorneys.

Gonzalez's family was excited and relieved at his release, with his mother saying she was proud of him and his brother saying they were all happy and excited. Gonzalez's mother had been a strong supporter throughout his time in prison, and Gonzalez said he wanted to hug her and thank her for her support.

Gonzalez's conviction for the rape and abduction was overturned after new DNA testing showed that the evidence did not connect him to the crime. The Innocence Project found problems with the investigation and Gonzalez's conviction, leading to a re-examination of the case and the new DNA testing. Immigration and Customs Enforcement also canceled a detainer that would have required Gonzalez to be turned over to ICE custody after he finished serving his sentence.

Gonzalez used his time in prison to educate himself and learn skills. He is an artist and mentored other prisoners, particularly those who spoke Spanish. Gonzalez's brother said that he and Gonzalez often did things together before Gonzalez was imprisoned, and that he was looking forward to learning from his brother now that he is free.

It is not clear what Gonzalez's future immigration status will be, as he is a Mexican national who had obtained a visa but whose visa expired after his arrest. Attorneys are working to ensure that Gonzalez can remain in the country if he is freed. Deporting him upon his release would be a "huge travesty of justice," according to one of his attorneys, as Gonzalez had planned to seek citizenship before he was imprisoned.

Lake County prosecutors plan to exonerate Gonzalez, which would add to the list of criminal convictions in the county that have been wiped away by DNA evidence. The rape victim was distraught to learn of prosecutors' plan to clear Gonzalez, according to the state's attorney. It is not clear whether Gonzalez will be freed after his scheduled appearance in Lake County court.

The Russian man accused of the Salisbury poisoning, which occurred in March, is identified by investigative website Bellingcat as Colonel Anatoliy Chepiga, a military officer who received an honor from Vladimir Putin. The UK investigators identified one of the two suspects as Ruslan Boshirov, but President Putin claimed Boshirov was a civilian, and on Russian TV, he himself said he visited Salisbury as a tourist. However, Bellingcat says he is actually an intelligence officer.

Chepiga has served in Chechnya and Ukraine and was made a "Hero of the Russian Federation" in 2014. British officials have not commented, but the BBC understands there is no dispute over the identification. Dmitry Peskov, a spokesman for the Kremlin, insisted that the suspect is a civilian.

The Skripals, a former Russian spy and his daughter, were poisoned with Novichok on 4 March. Both survived, but Dawn Sturgess, a local woman not connected to the original attack, died in July after being exposed to the same substance. It is thought Chepiga travelled to the UK on a false passport, along with another Russian national who used the name Alexander Petrov.

Chepiga trained at one of Russia's elite academies and served with a special forces unit under the command of the GRU - Russia's military intelligence service. He earned more than 20 military awards for his service. He is believed to have transferred to Moscow in about 2009, where he was given a false identity as Ruslan Boshirov. He has been working undercover for the past nine years.

In December 2014, he was made a Hero of the Russian Federation. The medal, awarded in a secret ceremony, is typically handed out by the Russian president. It is only given to a handful of people each year. The timing suggests it was for operations in Ukraine.

Chepiga and Petrov flew in to Gatwick Airport from Moscow on 2 March 2018 and visited Salisbury on two consecutive days, including 4 March, the day of the poisoning. Both men returned to Moscow on the same day. European arrest warrants and Interpol red notices have subsequently been issued for the pair. Russia does not extradite its own nationals.

Chepiga is accused of the poisoning of Sergei Skripal, a former Russian spy, and his daughter Yulia in Salisbury. The attack was approved by the Russian state, according to the UK government. The event sparked a series of accusations and denials between the UK and Russian governments, culminating in diplomatic expulsions and international sanctions.

The Russian government has not commented on the allegations made by Bellingcat, but a pro-Kremlin tabloid published an online article listing "three reasons" why Chepiga was not involved in the Skripal poisoning, adding that he was not a Russian secret services operative.

The UK government has said there will be a "price to pay" for Russia's actions. Addressing world leaders at the United Nations, Theresa May criticised Russia for its "desperate fabrication" over the Salisbury spy poisoning. The prime minister accused Russia of "flagrantly breaching international norms" citing "the reckless use of chemical weapons on the streets of Britain by agents of the Russian GRU".

Bellingcat is an investigative website that uses open-source computer software and social media as part of its work. The claims about Chepiga were made following an investigation by Bellingcat. The firm says it then obtained extracts from the passport file of Anatoliy Vladimirovich Chepiga, which contained a photograph that strongly resembled a younger "Boshirov". A Bellingcat journalist, who writes under the pseudonym Moritz Rakuszizky, said he believed the firm was shortly going to be able to identify the second suspect in the Skripal case. "We believe based on the information we have gathered so far that he [Petrov] is a junior rank relative to Chepiga," he told BBC Two's Newsnight.

"The Fourth Kind" is a supernatural horror film starring Milla Jovovich, Elias Koteas, and Will Patton. Directed by Olatunde Osunsanmi, the film is a re-enactment of supposed real events documented by Alaska psychologist and hypnotherapist Dr. Abigail Tyler, who delved into her patients' experiences of mass sleeplessness and alien abductions. The film heavily borrows from The Blair Witch Project and Paranormal Activity, with Bulgaria standing in for Alaska. The film features interviews with hypnotized abductees and includes a few genuine scares. Milla Jovovich plays both herself and Dr. Tyler, with the latter character experiencing personal troubles, including the murder of her husband, her daughter going blind, and her son hating her. The film's title refers to the close encounters of the fourth kind, which is being kidnapped by off-world beings. The film received a mixed review, with critics praising Milla Jovovich's performance but criticizing the film's unbelievability and artifice. The film is now playing at Elgin Mills, Empire North York, and is rated 14A.

Heather McGill, the wife of Alabama State Senator Shadrack McGill, posted a fiery Facebook message on Monday night, addressing multiple women who have allegedly been sending private messages and explicit photos to her husband through Facebook. McGill claimed that these women have been soliciting her spouse, even when children are present, and threatened to publicly name and shame them. The post was a response to incidents during McGill's last legislative campaign, including an instance where two strippers showed up at his home in the middle of the night. Since taking office, McGill has experienced similar issues, with women sending him half-naked photos and claiming to have had a good time with him. McGill's wife's post has received support from over 300 people, and the senator himself thanked his wife for managing his Facebook account. The post has brought attention to the issue of inappropriate behavior towards politicians on social media platforms.

Ohio State football players Terrelle Pryor, Daniel Herron, DeVier Posey, Mike Adams, Solomon Thomas, and Jordan Whiting have been suspended for the first five games of the 2011 season due to NCAA violations. The violations include accepting discounted rates on tattoos and selling personal Ohio State memorabilia to a local tattoo parlor owner for thousands of dollars between 2009 and 2010.

Pryor, the team's star quarterback, must repay $2,500 to a charity for selling his 2008 Big Ten championship ring, a Fiesta Bowl sportsmanship award, and his 2008 gold pants. Herron, the leading rusher, must repay $1,150 to a charity for selling his football jersey, pants, and shoes for $1,000 and receiving discounted services worth $150. Posey must repay $1,250 to a charity for selling his 2008 Big Ten championship ring for $1,200 and receiving discounted services worth $50. Adams must repay $1,000 to a charity for selling his 2008 Big Ten championship ring. Thomas must repay $1,505 to a charity for selling his 2008 Big Ten championship ring for $1,000, his 2008 gold pants for $350, and receiving discounted services worth $155. Whiting must pay $150 to a charity for receiving discounted services.

The players will still be eligible to play in the Sugar Bowl on Jan. 4, 2011, against Arkansas. Ohio State athletic director Gene Smith said the school will appeal the suspensions, stating that while sanctions should be rendered, they are severe. The NCAA did not suspend the players for the Sugar Bowl because they did not receive adequate rules education during the time period the violations occurred. The subsequent investigation by the Ohio State compliance office led to interviews with the players and then the suspensions.

Coach Jim Tressel said, "We as coaches feel the buck stops here. We're the ones who need to make things even more crystal clear." The problems came to light as a result of a federal probe into the affairs of the tattoo parlor owner. If players miss the five games next year, they would sit out contests against Akron, Toledo, the University of Miami, Colorado, and the Big Ten opener against Michigan State.

Ariel Castro, a former school bus driver, was sentenced to life in prison plus 1,000 years for kidnapping and abusing three women in Cleveland, Ohio. The women, Amanda Berry, Gina DeJesus, and Michelle Knight, were held captive for over a decade in a house that Castro had transformed into a prison. Castro used his children's names to lure the women into his house, taking advantage of their trust. The women were subjected to sexual, physical, and emotional abuse, and were starved and beaten. Castro kept a diary that detailed the women's experiences, including forced sexual conduct, being locked in a dark room, and being treated like prisoners of war. The sentencing hearing included testimony from law enforcement officers and mental health experts, and a model of the house where the women were held was presented in court. The women have since made public appearances and released statements thanking the community for their support.

The article provides a detailed account of Osama bin Laden's nine-year hideout in Pakistan, as revealed by his youngest wife, Amal Ahmad Abdul Fateh, to Pakistani investigators. Bin Laden moved among five safe houses in various cities, fathering four children, at least two of whom were born in a government hospital in Pakistan. The family was assisted by two brothers named Ibrahim and Abrar, who are believed to be Abu Ahmed al-Kuwaiti, a Pakistani-born Pashtun known as "the courier" to American intelligence.

Bin Laden's three widows are currently under house arrest in Islamabad, and two of them have been uncooperative with investigators. However, Ms. Fateh, who was wounded during the raid that killed her husband, has spoken out. The report suggests that Bin Laden managed to evade detection despite the efforts of Pakistani security services, raising questions about their effectiveness. The wives are of interest because they hold valuable information about Bin Laden's movements and activities during this period. The wives and two adult children are expected to be charged with breaking Pakistani immigration laws. The report, while containing flaws, offers a unique insight into Bin Laden's life on the run in Pakistan.

The article discusses the significant weight gain among Americans over the past six decades, with both men and women experiencing substantial increases. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, the average American woman now weighs 166.2 pounds, which is almost identical to the average American man's weight in the 1960s. American men have gained nearly 30 pounds since then, with the average weight now at 195.5 pounds.

The data shows that both sexes have gained almost an inch in height since the 1960s, contributing to the overall weight gain. However, women have seen a slightly higher percentage increase in weight gain (18.5%) compared to men (17.6%). Today's American man weighs nearly as much as 1.5 American women from the 1960s.

The study attributes the weight gain to three main factors: consuming less healthy food, eating more overall, and decreased physical activity. The average American is now the third-heaviest person globally, behind only the Pacific island nations of Tonga and Micronesia. Compared to other countries, the average American is 33 pounds heavier than the average Frenchman, 40 pounds heavier than the average Japanese citizen, and a whopping 70 pounds heavier than the average citizen of Bangladesh.

The study suggests that addressing population weight gain could be crucial for world food security and ecological sustainability. The issue is particularly concerning in the U.S., where more than one-third of adults over 20 are considered obese, and over 69% are either overweight or obese. The problem also affects children, with more than 1-in-5 U.S. children between the ages of 12-19 being obese, and 17.7% of kids ages 6-11 weighing in at obesity levels.

The Pulaski County Sheriff's Office is continuing its investigation into the death of five-year-old Noah Thomas, whose body was found in a septic tank on his parents' property on Thursday. The autopsy has been completed, but the cause of death is pending. The sheriff's office is urging the public to come forward with any information or tips they may have, as no arrests have been made, no suspects have been identified, and no charges have been filed. Noah was last seen by his mother on Sunday morning, and his body was found shortly after 1 p.m. on Thursday. The FBI is providing forensic support to the investigation. A candlelight vigil is planned to remember Noah's life, and will be held on Friday at the Pearisburg Rec Center. The sheriff's office is encouraging people to continue coming forward with information about the boy's disappearance or death.

The iPhone 4S's voice-controlled personal assistant, Siri, has caused controversy after a 12-year-old boy, Charlie Le Quesne, heard an explicit response from Siri in a Tesco store in the UK. The conversation started when Charlie asked Siri how many people are in the world, to which Siri responded with a vulgar phrase. The store's managers suspect that Siri may have been tricked by pranksters into thinking the rude phrase was the name of its owner, which can be set during the phone's setup instructions. This incident has led to an investigation by Tesco and the phone being sent back to Apple for diagnosis.

Siri's explicit response is not entirely unexpected, as the A.I. has a known dark sense of humor, with a dedicated blog, S*** That Siri Says, showcasing its amusing answers to questions. However, this is the first time Siri has ventured into R-rated territory. Previously, Siri's responses have been snarky but mostly harmless, such as suggesting places to bury a body or listing types of soil when asked to "talk dirty to me."

In addition to this incident, Siri has been under scrutiny for showing a preference for pro-life pregnancy centers over clinics that provide abortions. Apple has acknowledged this issue and promised to improve Siri's responses in the coming weeks. The article also provides a step-by-step explanation of how Siri composes its answers on SmartPlanet.

In a significant political development in Iraq, the Shiite cleric Muqtada al-Sadr, who once led a militia against the American invasion, has positioned himself as a key player in the country's political deadlock. His party has thrown its support behind the embattled Prime Minister Nouri al-Maliki, a move that could potentially spook the United States. The hard-line Shiite group's support could help al-Maliki secure another term, despite opposition from the United States, which views al-Sadr as a threat to Iraq's security. The March elections failed to produce a clear winner, leaving the nation in turmoil. The final agreement on forming the new government could take weeks, if not months. The Sadrist support of al-Maliki marks a turnabout, as the group has previously demanded his replacement. The move has the potential to alarm Washington and could signal an increased influence of Iran in Iraq. The Sadrists are demanding key government positions, including deputy parliament speaker and several Cabinet-level ministry posts, which would allow them to hire supporters and boost political loyalty. The Obama administration opposes giving power to al-Sadr and his followers, viewing it as a "big win" for Iran. The development could complicate efforts to establish a thriving democracy in Iraq.

The European data protection law requires users to enable cookies on their web browsers to continue using websites. The cookies are used to customize user experience, perform analytics, and deliver personalized advertising. By agreeing, users consent to the use of cookies and data gathered from their use of the platforms.

In a separate news, President Donald Trump sent a $25,000 personal check to the family of Army Cpl. Dillon Baldridge, who was killed by an Afghan police officer in June. The check was sent after reports surfaced that Trump had promised the soldier's father a personal donation during a condolence call but never followed through.

The White House confirmed the donation, stating that it was a personal check from Trump. The timing of the donation raised questions, as it came after reports that the check had been sent. The White House spokesperson said the check had been "in the pipeline" since Trump's conversation with the father and that there was a substantial process involving multiple agencies when the President interacts with the public, especially when transmitting personal funds.

The donation comes amid ongoing controversy over how presidents handle condolence calls to families of those killed in action and Trump's feud with a Democratic congresswoman over his call with the widow of Sgt. La David Johnson, who was killed earlier this month in Niger. Trump has denied allegations that he said Johnson "knew what he signed up for, but I guess it still hurt."

The White House is also dealing with Trump's statements about President Barack Obama not calling all the families of those killed during his presidency and suggesting that reporters ask his chief of staff, retired Gen. John Kelly, whether Obama called him after his son died in Afghanistan. Kelly's son Robert died when he stepped on a landmine in Afghanistan in 2010.

A man named Michael Whalen is facing animal abuse charges in Virginia Beach, Virginia, after shooting and burying his 15-year-old dog, Allie, on the Oceanfront. Whalen claims that Allie had Cushing's disease, which caused her to have seizures, and that one night in February, during a particularly severe seizure, he shot her to end her suffering. Whalen buried Allie at the 85th street beach, but a resident found her, leading to the charges. Whalen's attorney, George Yates, argues that Whalen was acting as a responsible pet owner by taking care of his animal and euthanizing it when it was suffering. Whalen is speaking out to set the record straight and hopes his case will shed light on euthanasia rights. A local veterinarian has stated that a gunshot is not considered a form of euthanasia based on current guidelines and standards. Whalen is expected in court in June.

The documentary "The Hunting Ground" explores the issue of campus sexual assault, focusing on two specific cases: Kamilah Willingham's at Harvard Law School and Erica Kinsman's at Florida State University.

Kamilah Willingham's story involves an alleged sexual assault by Harvard Law student Brandon Winston in 2011. After reporting the incident to the Harvard Office of Sexual Assault and Responses, Willingham filed a complaint with the Administrative Board of Harvard Law School. An independent Fact Finder was appointed to investigate the claim, and the Fact Finder's report found that Winston was not credible and that Willingham did not give affirmative consent. The Administrative Board found Winston guilty of sexual misconduct, but he was later reinstated following an appeal process that violated Title IX guidelines.

Erica Kinsman's story involves an alleged rape by Florida State University quarterback Jameis Winston in 2012. Kinsman reported the incident to the police, but the investigation was delayed and incomplete. The case was eventually closed without charges being filed. Kinsman later sued Winston for sexual battery, and he counter-sued for tarnishing his image.

The documentary has faced criticism from some faculty members at Harvard Law School and from Winston's legal team, who claim that the film distorts the truth and omits exculpatory evidence. However, the filmmakers stand by their work and invite viewers to draw their own conclusions. The documentary aired on CNN despite legal threats from Winston's legal team.

Kyle Hunter, an experienced meteorologist with over 20 years of experience, is suing CBS Corporation and Los Angeles affiliates KCAL and KCBS for age and gender discrimination. Hunter claims that the stations are prioritizing young, attractive women over qualified male meteorologists, and that his repeated attempts to apply for two open weather broadcaster positions were ignored or rebuffed. The lawsuit alleges that CBS is seeking to attract more male viewers to their primetime news programs with sexy newscasters. Hunter is being represented by lawyer Gloria Allred, who states that this may be the first case of its kind where a man is claiming discrimination based on age and gender. The lawsuit seeks unspecified damages, punitive damages, and attorney's fees. Hunter claims that he was passed over for two jobs in favor of women with no meteorological qualifications, and that the stations had to drop their American Meteorological Society certification requirement in order to hire them. The case has received attention due to Hunter's high-profile attorney, Gloria Allred, who has represented clients in cases of sexual harassment and discrimination in the past. CBS has responded to the lawsuit by calling it frivolous and based on misstatements of fact, and has stated that they will vigorously defend themselves in court.

The Japanese Yamazaki Single Malt Sherry Cask 2013 has been named the best whisky in the world, according to the 2015 World Whisky Bible. This marks the first time a Japanese whisky has claimed the top spot, and the first year a Scottish malt has failed to make the top five. Whisky expert Jim Murray, who oversaw the review of over 4,500 whiskies, described the Yamazaki as a "drink of near incredible genius" and a "single malt which no Scotch can at the moment get anywhere near." Murray criticized Scottish distilleries for producing drab or mediocre malts and called for "a little dose of humility" to recognize the need for improvement. The winning whisky, with only 18,000 bottles produced, is available in a few hundred specialist shops in the UK for around £100. Additionally, the English tipple Chapter 14 Not Peated, from the English Whisky Company, was awarded the best European whisky of the year.

The film adaptation of Lois Lowry's 1993 young-adult novel, "The Giver," is set in a dystopian future where humans live in solitary communities with restrictive rules. The story follows Jonas, a teenager chosen to become the new Receiver, who learns about the world's history and experiences from the Giver, an elderly man who possesses all the world's collective memories. The film, directed by Philip Noyce, is set in a society that seems to have influenced other dystopian young-adult works such as "The Hunger Games," "Ender's Game," and "Divergent."

The film's cast includes Brenton Thwaites as Jonas, Jeff Bridges as the Giver, Meryl Streep as the Chief Elder, Katie Holmes as Jonas' mother, and Alexander Skarsgard as Jonas' father. The story revolves around Jonas's journey as he learns about the true nature of the world and makes choices that challenge the society's rules.

While the film's visuals and performances are laudable, the acting, particularly by Katie Holmes, is criticized for being too heavy-handed and reminiscent of her role in Scientology. The film is also criticized for being too predictable and lacking the subtlety and ambiguity of the original novel. Despite these criticisms, the film is not considered a terrible movie, but rather one that falls flat and lacks the impact of other young-adult films based on books.

In this summary, two suspicious packages were found at the Jacksonville International Airport on Tuesday, leading to a nearly five-hour shutdown and the evacuation of the terminal. One of the packages was deemed destructive and had to be deactivated offsite by a bomb squad. The airport reopened after the packages were handled, but the exact nature of the destructive package and any potential arrests were not confirmed. Passengers on incoming flights were bused to offsite hotels, and individual airlines are working to restart operations. The incident caused delays and inconvenience for passengers, but no major incidents were reported. The Associated Press reported this news, with additional contributions from David Fischer in Miami and Lisa J. Adams in Atlanta.
