In the Indian town of Sadiya, Upper Assam, an unidentified species of aggressive spiders, resembling tarantulas, have caused panic and two confirmed deaths. The spiders invaded the town on May 8, during a Hindu festival, biting residents and causing a mass panic. The victims described the spiders as leaping at people and latching onto them after biting.

Two people, Purnakanta Buragohain and an unidentified schoolboy, died after being bitten. Local hospitals were overwhelmed with people seeking treatment for spider bites. A team of scientists from Dibrugarh University and Gauhati University arrived on May 22 to investigate and find an antidote.

Dr. L R Saikia, head of the Department of Life Sciences, Dibrugarh University, stated that the spider could be a new species, but its venom needs to be tested before it can be definitively called a killer spider. British naturalist Dr Vejay Singh suggested that the swarming could be due to an environmental crisis, such as flooding.

Sadiya, known for its Maoist community, is now fearing a fresh onslaught of the "alien" spiders. The town's residents are seeking answers as to how the spiders arrived and what can be done to protect themselves. The truth about the mysterious spider attacks in Assam continues to be covered by a cobweb of uncertainty.

In this article, France launched air strikes against Islamist guerrillas in Mali, forcing them to flee towns in northern Mali. The Islamists retaliated by seizing the small western town of Diabaly from the Malian army, highlighting the challenging campaign ahead to restore order in the West African nation. French jets targeted Douentza, a town held by the Islamists since September, but the fighters had left before the air strikes arrived. In Timbuktu, where inhabitants have been subjected to brutal Islamic law, the Islamists fled in anticipation of an attack. In Gao, another northern city held by the Islamists, the jihadists were nowhere to be seen after bombing by Rafale warplanes. At least 60 insurgents were killed in Sunday's assault, according to residents and a security source. Mali's Foreign Minister Tieman Hubert Coulibaly said in Paris that more than 100 Islamists had been killed in the four days since France launched operations to stem a guerrilla advance towards Bamako. A spokesman for the Ansar Dine (Defenders of the Faith) group, Senda Ould Boumama, said the withdrawal was a "tactical retreat" to reduce civilian casualties, in comments published on Mauritanian news website Alakhbar. A leader of the Movement for Oneness and Jihad in West Africa (MUJAO), vowed revenge. "France has attacked Islam. We will strike at the heart of France," said Abou Dardar of the Al-Qaeda-linked group. France's Foreign Minister Laurent Fabius hailed the "quasi-unanimous" international backing for the offensive, strongly supported by Mali. A meeting of the 15-nation UN Security Council on Mali also expressed unanimous "understanding and support" for the military intervention. France and other council countries want to speed up the deployment of a UN-mandated 3,300-strong West African intervention force in Mali. Nigeria, which will lead the force, plans to have 600 troops on the ground "before next week," President Goodluck Jonathan said. Benin, Ghana, Niger, Senegal, Burkina Faso, and Togo have also pledged troops. Britain and Canada have offered military transporters to the French military and the United States said it will share intelligence and provide logistical support. "I commend France for taking the steps that it has," US Defense Secretary Leon Panetta said. Algeria said it had closed its 2,000 km (1,250 mile) desert border with northern Mali to stop Islamists crossing into the country. The Islamists seized upon the chaos of a military coup in Bamako in March to seize northern Mali, sparking widespread international fears that they could set up a terrorist safe haven. The UN Security Council had given approval for a military offensive that UN officials had said could not be launched until September. However, the Islamist offensive and France's military intervention has led to predictions by diplomats that the plans will be reviewed.

A newly discovered octopus, yet unnamed, is causing a stir due to its adorable appearance, resembling a cross between a Pac-Man ghost and a Pokemon creature. The small, squishy, pink-colored octopus, belonging to the Opisthoteuthis genus, has distinctive webbing between its tentacles that allows it to float like a parachute. Researchers at the Monterey Bay Aquarium Research Institute (MBARI) are working to classify and name this species, with one potential name being Opisthoteuthis adorabilis. The naming process is complex and lengthy, involving publishing papers, collecting specimens, and distributing them to museums. This octopus is known for its big round eyes, unusual for its size, and its unique swimming patterns. It swims by moving its fins, pulsing its webbed arms, pushing water through its funnel for jet propulsion, or a combination of all three. The octopus is found in the deep sea along the California coast and is being studied to understand its role in the greater ocean ecosystem.

In her acceptance speech at the Democratic National Convention, Hillary Clinton became the first female presidential nominee of a major party. She emphasized the importance of community and togetherness, contrasting her vision with Donald Trump's. Clinton criticized Trump for his business practices, immigration policies, and lack of specific policy suggestions. She also acknowledged the influence of Bernie Sanders' campaign on her platform. The speech was followed by emotional speeches from Khizr Khan, a Pakistani immigrant whose son died serving in Iraq, and other veterans. The convention aimed to build a broad coalition, reaching out to moderates, Independents, and Republicans who reject Trump. The night was marked by intense patriotism and nationalism, as well as a focus on social justice issues. The speech did not have the soaring rhetoric of some of Clinton's past speeches, but it served its purpose in setting out her vision and contrasting it with Trump's.

A 19-year-old man named Aftab M. Aslam, residing in Johns Creek, Georgia, was initially reported missing on April 27, with his family claiming he had been kidnapped. The Johns Creek Police, Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), and Georgia Bureau of Investigation (GBI) launched a search for Aslam, using the phone that sent the kidnapping text as evidence. However, Aslam returned home unharmed on Sunday evening, stating he had left for personal reasons. Investigators are verifying his account, and no charges have been filed yet. Anyone with information regarding Aslam's whereabouts is asked to contact Det. James Harris. The initial report of a kidnapping proved to be false, as Aslam returned home on his own.

The story highlights the ongoing search for Malaysia Airlines Flight 370, which disappeared on March 8, 2014, with 239 people on board. The Bluefin-21 submarine has scanned over 90% of the underwater search area set out by investigators, but has not found any sign of the Boeing 777 jetliner. A metal object that washed ashore on Australia's coast was initially considered an "object of interest" in the search, but was later determined not to be from the missing plane. The search efforts have been complicated by the fact that the ocean is full of garbage, and many promising leads have turned out to be false alarms. Despite the search coming up empty for over a month, Australian Prime Minister Tony Abbott has said that they will not rest until they have done everything they can to solve the mystery. The search strategy may be rethought if the current underwater search fails to turn up evidence of the plane, and a long-term strategy for the search is already being mapped out. If the flight data recorders are found, they would likely go to the Australian Transport Safety Board's accident investigation lab, but the investigation is officially Malaysian. The search for the missing plane continues, with up to 11 military aircraft and 11 ships set to search for the plane on Thursday.

The article discusses the discovery of Homo floresiensis, also known as "hobbits," a species of human relative that lived on the island of Flores in Indonesia thousands of years ago. The hobbits stood about 3.5 feet tall and weighed around 75 pounds. They made stone tools and may have coexisted with Komodo dragons. Initially, it was believed that the hobbits lived as recently as 12,000 years ago, which would have meant they outlived Neanderthals and potentially interacted with modern humans. However, a new analysis of the site where the fossils were found suggests that the hobbits vanished from the island much earlier, around 100,000 to 60,000 years ago. The new age estimates are based on five independent dating methods, including uranium decay rate in bone and luminescence in soil. The erosion of older deposits in certain sections of the cave may explain why earlier investigations underestimated the age of the hobbit remains. The article also discusses the ongoing debates about the hobbits' origins, their relationship with modern humans, and the possible causes of their extinction, including climate shifts, volcanoes, and hunting by pygmy elephants. The article concludes that further excavations of Liang Bua and other sites on Flores could offer more clues and answer essential questions about the development, lifestyle, and extinction of this mysterious species.

The NFL has announced that Super Bowl 50, scheduled for February 2016, will mark a departure from the traditional use of Roman numerals in its branding. Instead, the event will be graphically represented using Arabic numerals, specifically '50', due to the 'L' not being considered aesthetically pleasing. The decision was made after extensive design work, which included 73 different logo versions since April 2013. The logos for Super Bowl 50 feature the Lombardi Trophy, the Golden Gate Bridge, Coit Tower, and the Transamerica Pyramid, symbolizing the game's location in California, known as the "Golden State". The NFL will celebrate the 50th anniversary of the Super Bowl throughout the lead-up to the event, but will revert to using Roman numerals for Super Bowl LI in 2017. This change in numeral style is a first since Super Bowl IV in 1970.

Former Massachusetts state senator Brian Joyce was arrested and charged on Friday with over 100 counts, including racketeering, wire fraud, extortion, and money laundering. The indictment alleges that Joyce, who served as assistant majority leader, used his legislative seat for private gain by accepting bribes and kickbacks, including a free Jeep and hundreds of pounds of Dunkin' Donuts coffee, in exchange for official actions. Joyce pleaded not guilty and was released on bond. The indictment also accuses Joyce of creating a shell company to launder the proceeds from his bribery and kickback schemes, and of pressuring state and municipal officials to take official action on government matters. The arrest follows a tumultuous week for the State House, with Senate President Stan Rosenberg taking a leave of absence following allegations of sexual assault against his husband.

A lawsuit has been filed by Monica Thompson against Portland Adventist Medical Center, seeking $8.6 million in damages. The lawsuit alleges that the hospital's negligence led to the death of Thompson's ten-day-old son, Jacob, who was given to her while she was heavily medicated with painkillers and sleep aids. The incident occurred on August 6, 2012, when Thompson dozed off and accidentally smothered her son in her sleep.

The lawsuit claims that the hospital was at fault for medicating the breastfeeding mother, putting the infant in her bed without supervision, and not having clear policies or enforcement on the dangers that the combination could create. The suit also seeks relief for the emotional distress caused to Thompson due to the unintentional killing of her firstborn child.

The American Academy of Pediatrics has previously recommended against bed-sharing, citing the risk of suffocation. In 2014, a study in the Journal of Perinatology documented the deaths of 15 healthy infants while sharing beds with their mothers in U.S. maternity wards.

Jacob was the first child of Monica and Graham Thompson, born via Caesarean section on August 2, 2012. According to the lawsuit, Thompson was medicated with Ambien and Vicodin a few hours before a nurse walked into her room, gave her the baby, and left around 3 a.m. on Aug. 6, 2012. An hour later, Thompson realized her son wasn't moving and called for help.

Jacob was stabilized and transferred to Randall Children’s Hospital at Legacy Emanuel Medical Center, where he died on Aug. 12, 2012, after being taken off life support. The lawsuit seeks damages for the baby’s “desperation and anxiety” as he was suffocated and Thompson’s counseling expenses for depression and post-traumatic stress disorder. The suit was filed by Lake Oswego attorney Diego Conde.

The new study conducted by a team of researchers led by Psychologist Andrew Gallup of SUNY College at Oneonta challenges the common belief that yawning increases oxygen supply to the brain. Instead, the study suggests that yawning functions to regulate brain temperature for improved alertness and mental efficiency. The researchers found that contagious yawning is most frequent when the temperature is around 20°C, and diminishes when temperatures are either too hot or too cold. The study was conducted in Vienna, Austria, and Arizona, USA, comparing the frequency of yawning in both summer and winter months. The results showed that people in Vienna yawned more in summer than in winter, while people in Arizona yawned more in winter than in summer. The study adds to the growing body of research suggesting that the underlying mechanism for yawning, both spontaneous and contagious, is involved in regulating brain temperature. The cooling of the brain, in turn, functions to improve arousal and mental efficiency. The study's findings suggest that yawning is not functional when ambient temperatures are as hot as the body, and may not be necessary or may even have harmful consequences when it is freezing outside.

The Women's Convention, organized by the Women's March, is set to take place in Detroit later this month. The convention aims to bring together an unprecedented number of activists and leaders to share strategies and build on the momentum from the Women's March. Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) will address the crowd on the opening day of the three-day event, organizers announced on social media.

The announcement immediately drew backlash, with critics arguing that a man should not be the headliner at a women's convention. Tamika Mallory, one of the convention organizers, defended the Sanders decision, stating that he "knows how to mobilize a new generation of activists" and is "probably one of the most powerful U.S. senators ... on progressive issues, women’s issues…"

Organizers expect upward of 3,000 people to attend the convention, with over 60 speakers scheduled to speak, including actress and producer Piper Perabo, political commentator and community organizer Sally Kohn, The Young Turks reporter Nomiki Konst, co-executive director of the Indivisible Project Leah Greenberg, Michigan Democratic gubernatorial candidate Gretchen Whitmer, Michigan state Rep. Stephanie Chang, Georgia gubernatorial candidate Stacey Abrams, and others.

In addition to Sanders, only one other man, Rep. Maxine Waters (D-Calif.), is scheduled to speak at the convention. The event's theme is "Reclaiming Our Time," inspired by Waters' repeated phrase during a House Financial Services Committee hearing. Waters is also expected to address convention-goers, as will actress Amber Tamblyn and other politicians, activists, and celebrities.

The overall message of the convention is to empower voices in the face of sexual violence, harassment, domestic violence, police brutality, and other forms of mistreatment. The convention is pegged to be one of the largest of its kind, offering a variety of workshops and training sessions. Tickets for the convention are available online, with the cost for all three days being $295 for adults and $125 for students, or $125 for a single day.

Despite the backlash over Sanders, organizers maintain that the convention is led predominantly by women of color and that the decision to have him speak was not intended to diminish the importance of women's voices. They emphasize that the convention is about unity and the collective liberation of women of all races, ethnicities, ages, abilities, sexual identities, gender expressions, immigration statuses, religious faiths, and economic statuses.

On Tuesday morning in Fort Dodge, Iowa, Rachel Kohnen, a pregnant woman, was rushed to the hospital as she was in labor. Accompanied by her husband Ben, they were driving at 85 mph in a 55 mph zone, prompting a police chase. The Kohnens refused to pull over, leading to tire spikes being laid on the road to stop them. They were eventually held at gunpoint until police realized the urgency of the situation. Rachel Kohnen gave birth to their fourth child, a nearly 10-pound baby named Hazel, about an hour after being escorted to the hospital. The police followed standard protocol for a high-speed chase, assuming the driver was under the influence, but no charges have been filed against the couple. The incident occurred due to the couple's urgent need to reach the hospital, and they had attempted to call 911 for assistance, but the dispatcher could not understand them due to Rachel's contractions. The Manson Police Chief suggested that calling ahead for help could prevent such situations.

In St. Peter's Square, four women from the Ukrainian Femen group protested against the Vatican's opposition to gay marriage by going topless, revealing slogans "In Gay We Trust" and "Shut Up" on their bare backs. The pope was not visibly disturbed during his traditional prayer. The protest coincided with a large demonstration in Paris against the French president's plan to legalize gay marriage and allow gay couples to adopt children, which has been strongly opposed by French Catholic bishops and the Vatican. In response to an Italian court's rejection of an appeal by a father who feared his son would not have a balanced upbringing if he lived with his mother and her female partner, the Vatican's newspaper, L'Osservatore Romano, reaffirmed the Vatican's view that no one has the "right" to children and that the traditional family unit is the ideal place for children to grow. The Vatican has become increasingly vocal against homosexual marriage in recent months, with Pope Benedict XVI reiterating the Church's opposition to it in December.

The State Department faced criticism for a controversial tweet posted on its travel advisory account on March 30, 2016. The tweet, which was later deleted, read, "Not a '10' in the US? Then not a 10 overseas. Beware of being lured into buying expensive drinks or worse—being robbed. #springbreakingbadly." Many users on social media criticized the tweet as sexist and patronizing, with some calling it irresponsible and objectifying. The State Department initially defended the tweet, stating that it was intended as a warning for Americans traveling overseas, but later apologized and took down the post. The incident comes amidst a week when many colleges and universities are on spring break, and the State Department has faced scrutiny for its Twitter activity during this period. Additionally, a parody account was created in response to the original tweet, poking fun at the controversy.

Bangladesh's anti-terrorism unit has arrested the main suspect, Farabi Shafiur Rahman, in the murder of U.S. blogger Avijit Roy, who was hacked to death in Dhaka last week. Farabi, previously jailed for ties to the extremist Hizbut Tahrir Islamist group, was arrested at a bus stop in Dhaka and has confessed to threatening Roy. Roy, an engineer of Bangladeshi origin, was killed by machete-wielding assailants on Thursday while returning from a book fair. His wife, fellow blogger Rafida Ahmed, was injured and is still in hospital. Farabi was arrested in 2013 for social media comments supporting the murder of another blogger but was later released on bail. He allegedly posted photos of the crime scene and threats against Roy on Facebook. Roy's killing comes amid a crackdown on hardline Islamist groups in Bangladesh, where religious extremism has increased in recent years. Bangladesh ranks 146th out of 180 countries in press freedom.

The Obama administration is refining its use of offensive cyber operations to counter evolving threats of electronic assaults against the United States. A top-secret presidential directive, Presidential Policy Directive 20, issued in October 2012 but never published, outlines the government's plans for Offensive Cyber Effects Operations (OCEO). The directive states that OCEO can offer unique and unconventional capabilities to advance US national objectives around the world with little or no warning to the adversary or target and with potential effects ranging from subtle to severely damaging.

The directive authorizes the government to identify potential targets of national importance where OCEO can offer a favorable balance of effectiveness and risk as compared with other instruments of national power. It also contemplates the possible use of cyber actions inside the US, though it specifies that no such domestic operations can be conducted without the prior order of the president, except in cases of emergency.

The aim of the document was "to put in place tools and a framework to enable government to make decisions" on cyber actions. The administration published some declassified talking points from the directive in January 2013, but those did not mention the stepping up of America's offensive capability and the drawing up of a target list.

The revelation that the US is preparing a specific target list for offensive cyber-action is likely to reignite previously raised concerns of security researchers and academics, several of whom have warned that large-scale cyber operations could easily escalate into full-scale military conflict.

The directive's publication comes as the president plans to confront his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping at a summit in California on Friday over alleged Chinese attacks on western targets. Even before the publication of the directive, Beijing had hit back against US criticism, with a senior official claiming to have "mountains of data" on American cyber-attacks he claimed were every bit as serious as those China was accused of having carried out against the US.

The document includes caveats and precautions stating that all US cyber operations should conform to US and international law, and that any operations "reasonably likely to result in significant consequences require specific presidential approval". The document says that agencies should consider the consequences of any cyber-action, including the impact on intelligence-gathering; the risk of retaliation; the impact on the stability and security of the internet itself; the balance of political risks versus gains; and the establishment of unwelcome norms of international behavior.

Among the possible "significant consequences" are loss of life; responsive actions against the US; damage to property; serious adverse foreign policy or economic impacts. The US is understood to have already participated in at least one major cyber attack, the use of the Stuxnet computer worm targeted on Iranian uranium enrichment centrifuges, the legality of which has been the subject of controversy.

In the presidential directive, the criteria for offensive cyber operations is not limited to retaliatory action but vaguely framed as advancing "US national objectives around the world". In an exclusive interview with ABC News, President Barack Obama denied being tense during his airport tarmac encounter with Arizona Governor Jan Brewer, as she described. Obama joked about being accused of not being intense enough and being too relaxed. Brewer, in her 2011 book, accused Obama of being condescending and patronizing, and complained about being treated coldly by White House staffers.

During the interview, Obama also signaled an aggressive tact for his early re-election campaign, critiquing his Republican opponents by name and insisting he's ready to "fight with every fiber of my being" for a second term. He pushed back against what he called Republicans' "rhetorical flourishes," including Newt Gingrich's oft-repeated contention that Obama is the "food stamp president."

Obama also used the interview to single out three of his Republican rivals, jabbing Mitt Romney, Newt Gingrich, and Rick Santorum as adherents of a failed political philosophy. He argued that his alternative – higher taxes on the wealthy to bankroll new government spending – is a "recipe for a fair, sound approach to deficit reduction and rebuilding this country."

The president also discussed his family's readiness for the quickly escalating fight expected on the campaign trail in the days ahead, with Michelle Obama expressing enthusiasm for campaigning for the next nine months. Obama also addressed the tension between Israel and Iran over the country's alleged clandestine nuclear program, stating that he's keeping a watchful eye on the situation but would not discuss classified military information.

Actor Mark Wahlberg, now 43, has filed an application with the Massachusetts Board of Pardons to have his decades-old assault conviction erased. In 1988, at the age of 16, Wahlberg was convicted of assault after a violent attack that left another man blind in one eye. Since then, Wahlberg has expressed remorse for his actions and has dedicated himself to becoming a better person and citizen.

In his pardon application, Wahlberg outlines the events that led to his arrest. He attempted to steal two cases of alcohol from a man outside a convenience store in Dorchester, hitting him over the head with a wooden stick and then running away from police, where he punched another man in the face. Wahlberg was under the influence of alcohol and narcotics at the time of the incident.

Wahlberg has been open about his past actions and has spoken about them publicly for over 20 years. He has also been involved in various charities and has done good deeds to rebuild his life, including the Mark Wahlberg Youth Foundation, the Dorchester Boys and Girls Club, the renovation of the Boston-area Parish Gym, and attending church nearly every day.

Wahlberg wants a pardon in order to help with his restaurant businesses and to work with at-risk kids. He believes that receiving a pardon would be a formal recognition that he is not the same person he was on the night of April 8, 1988, and would serve as an example of how lives can be turned around and how people can be redeemed.

The process for Wahlberg to receive a pardon could take some time, as the Board of Pardons needs to investigate the petition and decide if it warrants a public hearing before it is recommended to the governor. If the governor approves, the pardon still needs the approval of the governor's council.

In a separate note, Wahlberg has also revealed that his wife is happy he's going bald for cancer charity One Mission, as she thinks he looks like "an old Harry Styles" from One Direction. Wahlberg is challenging other celebrities to join him in the Buzz For Kids campaign, which will benefit One Mission programs to help kids with cancer at Boston Children’s Hospital and other institutions.

In a significant development, the European Court of Justice has ruled against Nestle's attempt to trademark the shape of its four-finger KitKat bar in the UK. The court stated that Nestle must prove that the public relies solely on the shape to identify the snack, a requirement that becomes challenging when goods also display a brand name such as KitKat. This decision follows a long-standing legal battle between Nestle and Cadbury, with Cadbury arguing that the shape alone was not distinctive enough for consumers to associate it with the rival snack.

The ruling is a significant but not final victory for Cadbury, which has been battling to prevent Nestle from obtaining the trademark. The case will now return to the UK High Court for a final decision. Nestle had argued that in the 80 years since the chocolate bar was introduced, the four fingers have become almost completely associated with KitKats. However, the court's decision suggests otherwise.

Nestle has previously faced similar challenges in trademarking other aspects of its products. For instance, it took more than 40 years for it to register the slogan "Have a Break" as a trade mark, finally succeeding in 2006.

The Kit Kat name originates from a literary club that met at a pie shop in London in the late 17th century. The group was called the Kit Kat club and took its name from an abbreviated version of the owner's name.

The ruling may have implications for other confectionery producers, as a ruling in favor of Nestle would have potentially stopped them from making chocolate bars of the same shape or size. The case is: C-215/14, Societe de Produits Nestle SA v. Cadbury UK Ltd.

The Nuclear Security Summit was held in Washington on April 1, 2016, with over 50 world leaders in attendance, including U.S. President Barack Obama, Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau, Dutch Prime Minister Mark Rutte, Chinese President Xi Jinping, and French President Francois Hollande, among others. The summit aimed to address the threat of nuclear terrorism and to secure nuclear materials around the world.

Obama urged world leaders to do more to safeguard vulnerable nuclear facilities to prevent terrorist groups like Islamic State from obtaining atomic weapons or radioactive "dirty bombs." He stated that no group had succeeded in obtaining bomb materials but that al Qaeda had long sought them, and he cited actions by Islamic State militants behind recent attacks in Paris and Brussels that raised similar concerns.

The required 102 countries have now ratified an amendment to a nuclear security treaty that would tighten protections against nuclear theft and smuggling. The United States and Japan also announced they had completed the long-promised task of removing all highly enriched uranium and separated plutonium fuels from a Japanese research reactor.

Despite significant strides by Obama in persuading dozens of countries to rid themselves of bomb-making materials or reduce and safeguard stockpiles, much of the world's plutonium and enriched uranium remain vulnerable to theft. Obama convened a separate meeting of world powers to take stock of the landmark nuclear pact they negotiated with Iran last July, which is a critical component of his nuclear disarmament agenda and a major piece of his foreign policy legacy.

Obama also addressed the ongoing conflict in Syria and Ukraine, as well as the nuclear threat posed by North Korea. He criticized Republican presidential candidate Donald Trump for his suggestion that Japan and South Korea should be allowed to build their own nuclear arsenals, stating that such a move would be proof of foreign-policy ignorance and that Americans do not want anyone with such views to occupy the White House.

The summit also discussed the threat of a "dirty bomb," which would use conventional explosives to disperse radioactive material and sow panic. U.S. officials stated that they had no doubt that Islamic State, which controls swaths of Syria and Iraq, was interested in obtaining such materials, but authorities had no explicit evidence that the group had tried to do so.

In conclusion, the Nuclear Security Summit aimed to address the threat of nuclear terrorism and to secure nuclear materials around the world. Obama urged world leaders to do more to safeguard vulnerable nuclear facilities and to tighten protections against nuclear theft and smuggling. The summit also discussed the ongoing conflicts in Syria and Ukraine, the nuclear threat posed by North Korea, and the threat of a "dirty bomb." Obama also criticized Republican presidential candidate Donald Trump for his suggestion that Japan and South Korea should be allowed to build their own nuclear arsenals.

Katie Couric, a former co-host of the Today show, appeared on Watch What Happens Live with Andy Cohen on May 1, 2018, to discuss the sexual misconduct allegations against her former colleague Matt Lauer. During the interview, Couric clarified her previous comments about Lauer pinching her on the butt, stating that it was a joke that she now regrets making. Couric also spoke about the pain the scandal has caused for those who worked with Lauer and emphasized that she was always treated respectfully and appropriately during her time on the show.

Couric also addressed some of the reports about Lauer's behavior, stating that the full extent of what happened may not have been fully revealed and that some reports have been misconstrued. She specifically took issue with reports that Lauer had a button under his desk to lock his door, behind which inappropriate activity allegedly took place. Couric claimed that the button was simply a privacy feature and was not used for nefarious purposes.

Couric's appearance on Watch What Happens Live comes after she spoke about Lauer on The Wendy Williams Show, where she expressed sympathy for those who worked with Lauer and did not witness or experience any of the alleged misconduct. Couric also apologized for previously joking about Lauer's behavior on the show.

Watch What Happens: Live is a late-night, interactive talk show that features guests from the world of entertainment, politics, and pop culture. Past guests have included Sarah Jessica Parker, Tina Fey, Khloe Kardashian, Jennifer Lopez, and Lance Bass. The show airs on Bravo and can be streamed on the network's website and social media platforms.

"Pain & Gain," directed by Michael Bay, is a grisly true-crime drama that showcases excessive action, muscle-headed entertainment, and vulgarity, while maintaining a relatively modest structure compared to Bay's other works. The film, based on a series of articles by Pete Collins, follows Daniel Lugo (Mark Wahlberg), a personal trainer and bodybuilding enthusiast, who, after serving time for an investment scam, aspires for a South Florida lifestyle. He is motivated by a self-pitying sense of entitlement and sets out to kidnap Victor Kershaw (Tony Shalhoub), a wealthy blowhard, to gain access to his assets.

Daniel enlists the help of Adrian (Anthony Mackie) and Paul (Dwayne Johnson), fellow gym rats with their own dreams and aspirations. Adrian desires to overcome his steroid-related sexual problems and win the love of Robin (Rebel Wilson), a nurse specializing in such ailments. Paul, an ex-convict, grapples with his sense of righteousness despite backsliding. The story also involves a stripper named Sorina (Bar Paly) who believes Daniel and his partners are government agents on a secret mission.

The film, written by Christopher Markus and Stephen McFeely, is a violent, blood-filled, and vulgar journey that leaves viewers questioning whether they have witnessed a stupid or brilliant movie about the nature and consequences of stupidity. Despite compressing some events and characters, "Pain & Gain" stays true to the facts as presented in Collins's chronicle of idiotic criminality and sloppy police work.

In a shocking incident, a Japanese research academic was allegedly gang-raped and held captive for nearly three weeks by a group of five men in India. The incident occurred in Gaya district, Bihar, a town known for its Buddhist pilgrimage center. The woman, who had been studying life in rural India, was lured by a man posing as a tour guide to travel to the area. Upon arrival, two other men allegedly held her at gunpoint and raped her.

The police have arrested five men in connection with the case, with two of them being brothers. The woman managed to escape and reached Kolkata, where she filed a police complaint. The incident has sparked concern and outrage, given the increasing number of rape cases reported in India in recent years. The authorities have promised to strengthen their efforts to ensure the safety of foreign tourists in the country.

Colombia's famous drug-sniffing dog, Sombra, has a bounty on her head from the country's most powerful drug lord, Dairo Antonio Úsuga, also known as Otoniel. Sombra, a six-year-old German shepherd, has been deployed in ports on the Atlantic coast, including Turbo, where she has found nearly 10 tonnes of cocaine. The Urabeños, Colombia's most powerful criminal organization, have put a price of 200 million pesos ($70,000) on Sombra's head after she found almost 10 tonnes of their cocaine. Sombra has been with the counter-narcotics police force since she was a puppy and is credited with sniffing out drugs leading to the arrest of 245 suspects. Due to the bounty on her head, Sombra has been moved from her post in Turbo to Bogotá's El Dorado International Airport, outside the Urabeños' territory on the coast, for her safety. The Urabeños have offered a bounty on Sombra's head because of the financial losses her sensitive nose has caused them. Sombra's accomplishments have made her the cuddly face of Colombia's anti-drug effort, and she has been featured on local television and asked to pose for selfies with admirers. The narcotics police regularly post about her accomplishments on Twitter. The Urabeños, originally a paramilitary outfit, are now Colombia's largest criminal organization and control much of the drug trade. Otoniel remains at large and in control of the vast organization. In response to the bounty on Sombra's life, General Jorge Nieto, head of the national police, has ordered the dog transferred to Bogotá’s El Dorado International Airport, outside the Urabeños’ territory on the coast. Additional officers will now accompany Sombra on her rounds.

In Charlotte, North Carolina, a 9-year-old girl named Zianna Oliphant delivered a tearful and powerful speech at a City Council meeting, addressing the recent shooting of an African-American man, Keith Lamont Scott, by the police. The shooting, which sparked protests in the city, has raised questions about the use of deadly force by police against people of color.

Zianna, who expressed her feelings about the incident and the ongoing racial tensions, said she was inspired to speak at the meeting on a whim. She expressed her frustration and sadness, stating that "we are black people and we shouldn't have to feel like this." The girl's mother, Precious Oliphant, was proud of her daughter's courage and eloquence, but also shared her own concerns about discrimination and racism that her children might face growing up in Charlotte.

Despite her young age, Zianna demonstrated a mature understanding of the issues at hand and expressed a desire to become a doctor to help people. Her speech was met with applause and some chants of "no justice, no peace." The incident has brought attention to the ongoing tensions between the police and the black community in Charlotte, and has sparked calls for changes in the city's policing practices.

On the Fourth of July, Representative Beto O'Rourke joined Willie Nelson on stage during Nelson's annual Fourth of July Picnic, an event celebrating country music. O'Rourke, who was met with a mix of cheers and boos, used the opportunity to express his hope that Texans would help show the rest of the United States that there's no need to fear immigrants, Muslims, or anyone considered different.

After the event, Nelson announced that he would be headlining a rally and concert for O'Rourke on September 29th in Austin. This announcement sparked controversy, with some of Nelson's fans taking to social media to boycott and disown the country legend, accusing him of aligning with O'Rourke's "socialist" positions.

However, others were supportive of Nelson and questioned those skeptical of the country legend. Nelson's political activism goes back decades, with his support of the environment, same-sex marriage, and marijuana legalization. He has supported President Barack Obama, Sen. Bernie Sanders, and Hillary Clinton in recent years.

Nelson's new album, "My Way," featuring standards associated with the repertoire of Frank Sinatra, is set to be released on Legacy Recordings on the same day as the concert. The event, which will also feature Leon Bridges, Joe Ely, Carrie Rodriguez, Tameca Jones, and Nelson’s sons Lukas and Micah Nelson, is free but requires an RSVP via O'Rourke's website.

The controversy surrounding Nelson's support of O'Rourke comes as the two are entangled in a tight Senate race, with O'Rourke challenging incumbent Ted Cruz. The race has gained national attention in recent months.

Aung San Suu Kyi, the Nobel Peace Prize laureate from Myanmar, embarked on her first visit to Europe in nearly a quarter of a century, accepting the Nobel Peace Prize she received two decades ago. The trip was disrupted when she fell ill at a press conference in Bern, Switzerland. During her visit, Suu Kyi urged foreign governments not to form joint ventures with Myanmar's state-owned oil and gas company until it improves its business practices, citing a lack of transparency and accountability. She also expressed concerns about the lack of transparency in contracts with Chinese oil firm CNPC and praised Total as a responsible investor in Myanmar. The visit comes after months of cautious rapprochement with Myanmar's government, and follows the lifting of more than a decade-old restrictions on Myanmar by the International Labour Organization (ILO) in recognition of progress in the country. Suu Kyi emphasized the need for responsible investment to help Myanmar along the path to democracy after nearly 50 years of military rule.

A 54-year-old man named David Benes from Florida was arrested for physically restraining his 80-year-old girlfriend and attempting to perform an exorcism on her. The incident occurred on Monday night at their shared home outside Tampa, where they have been in a relationship for three years. According to the Pasco County Sheriff’s Office, Benes held the woman down and tried to exorcise the devil from her against her will. The woman called 911 the next day after Benes resumed his exorcism attempts. The woman had visible injuries, including bruises and scratches on her arms, and Benes had also removed batteries from the home's phones and taken her car keys. Benes, who appeared intoxicated, was arrested on Tuesday and charged with battery on a person 65 years or older, false imprisonment, and other offenses. He has a history of battery convictions in Pasco County. The woman was found sitting outside the home crying, and Benes was too drunk to remember the incident.

Arizona's new abortion law, set to take effect on Thursday, bans abortions starting at 20 weeks of pregnancy, making it one of the strictest abortion laws in the United States. The law, which was signed by Republican Governor Jan Brewer in April, is being challenged in court by the New York-based Center for Reproductive Rights and other groups.

Under the new law, abortions are banned except in cases of medical emergencies. This is a change from Arizona's current ban at viability, which is generally considered to be about 24 weeks. A normal pregnancy lasts about 40 weeks.

The law also requires doctors to offer information about perinatal hospice services to women considering abortion at any stage of their pregnancy because of a fatal fetal abnormality. The law defines gestational age as beginning on the first day of the woman's last period, meaning abortions are actually banned starting at 18 weeks of pregnancy.

Eight other states also ban abortions after 20 weeks, but Arizona is the only one with a law that actually pushes the ban back to 18 weeks into the pregnancy. According to state records, women in Arizona terminate about 100 pregnancies a year after 20 weeks, but it's unclear how many of those are because of a problem with the pregnancy.

The new law has raised concerns among some medical professionals and advocacy groups, who argue that it will force women to carry pregnancies to term even in cases where the fetus has a fatal defect and will die shortly after birth. The law has also sparked criticism from abortion-rights groups, who argue that it violates women's constitutional rights to make decisions about their own bodies.

The two organizations that offer perinatal hospice services in Arizona, MISS Foundation and Embrace, provide counseling and support to families who are facing the loss of a child due to a fatal fetal abnormality. The organizations help families develop birth plans, attend births, organize meals, create mementos, make funeral arrangements, and provide emotional support.

However, the organizations have expressed concern that they may be overwhelmed by the increased demand for their services once the law takes effect. The organizations scrape by with private donations and volunteer help, and they worry they won't have the resources to meet the needs of all the families who will be seeking their help.

The Arizona law is part of a broader trend of anti-abortion legislation being passed by Republican-led state legislatures across the country. The other laws include restrictions on clinic operations, mandates for specific disclosures, and a prohibition on a type of late-term abortion.

The Center for Reproductive Rights, which is challenging the Arizona law in court, argues that under Supreme Court decisions starting with the 1973 Roe vs. Wade ruling that legalized abortion, states can only regulate how abortions are performed, not ban them, before a fetus is viable.

The Center for Reproductive Rights has also filed a notice that it will be appealing the decision of U.S. District Judge James Teilborg, who ruled on Monday that the Arizona law is constitutional. The judge wrote that the state provided "substantial and well-documented" evidence that an unborn child has the capacity to feel pain during an abortion by at least 20 weeks.

The Arizona law is expected to face further legal challenges in the coming weeks and months.

The Bitcoin price surged above $9,000 on Tuesday following productive discussions on cryptocurrency at a G-20 meeting in Buenos Aires, Argentina. The discussions, held in a closed-door session, were deemed productive by the Central Bank of Argentina's governor, Federico Sturzenegger.

Meanwhile, a concerning report emerged regarding the underlying blockchain of Bitcoin. German researchers discovered that unknown persons are using Bitcoin's blockchain to store and link to child abuse imagery. This could potentially make the possession of the blockchain illegal in many countries, posing a significant threat to the cryptocurrency.

The blockchain, an open-source, distributed ledger that records every Bitcoin transaction, was found to contain around 1,600 files, eight of which were of sexual content. This includes one image of child abuse and two files containing 274 links to child abuse content.

The researchers warned that the mere possession of a blockchain could become illegal if it contains illegal content, potentially endangering the multi-billion dollar markets powering cryptocurrencies such as Bitcoin. Since mining is essential for the function of Bitcoin, having illegal content within the blockchain could cause significant issues for the currency.

Despite these concerns, the Bitcoin community seems unfazed, with the price rising due to positive news about the G-20's stance on cryptocurrencies. At the time of writing, Bitcoin's price stood at $9,097.

This is not the first time warnings over the ability to store non-financial data within the blockchain have been issued. In 2015, Interpol sent out an alert stating that the design of the blockchain means there is the possibility of malware being injected and permanently hosted with no methods currently available to wipe this data.

The issue of child sexual abuse material is particularly sensitive, but the Bitcoin community appears unconcerned about the potential impact of the latest news on the cryptocurrency's ecosystem. The researchers' findings highlight a potential legal and moral quandary around possession and the blockchain.

A fugitive, Lois Riess, is suspected of murdering a woman in Florida and stealing her identity to evade arrest. Riess, 56, is wanted for the murder of her husband, David Reiss, in Minnesota in March. She is believed to have targeted the Florida victim, Pamela Hutchinson, 59, because of their similar appearances. After killing Hutchinson, Riess allegedly stole her cash, credit cards, ID, and car, and is using her identity. Authorities are searching for Hutchinson's white 2005 Acura TL with Florida license plate Y37TAA. Riess is suspected to be hiding out in Texas. A warrant for her arrest has been issued for murder, grand theft auto, and grand theft of personal identification in Lee County, Florida, and second-degree murder charges are being prepared in Minnesota. Riess is accused of taking $10,000 from her husband's business account and forging his signature on checks worth $11,000. She is considered armed and dangerous and anyone who sees her is urged to call 911.

Al Gore, the former vice president and Democratic nominee, is not considering a run for the 2016 presidential race, according to his advisers. Despite speculation among Democrats due to Hillary Clinton's troubles, Gore is reportedly focused on addressing the climate crisis. The recent buzz about Gore running for president stemmed from conversations among his supporters and discussions about a potential path financially and politically. However, Gore has not made any formal or informal moves towards running, and there's been no official confirmation from him. The speculation may have arisen due to Clinton's ongoing email-related issues, flagging poll numbers, and the surge of Bernie Sanders' campaign. Gore won the popular vote in the 2000 election but lost the White House. Since then, he has focused on environmental campaigning and business ventures, but has largely stayed out of public view in recent years.

In a 15-year study conducted by researchers at the University of Dundee, it was found that women who have had their appendix or tonsils removed may have higher fertility rates. The study analyzed medical records from over half a million British women and found that for every 100 pregnancies in women who had not undergone any procedures, there were 134 pregnancies in women who had their appendix removed, 149 pregnancies in women who had their tonsils removed, and 143 pregnancies in women who had both removed.

The researchers suggest that the operations could directly affect fertility or there may be a "behavioral" explanation. One possibility is that regularly infected tonsils or appendixes raise levels of inflammation in the body, which affects the ovaries and womb. The Dundee team favor a behavioral explanation such as women enjoying more "liberal sexual activity," being both more likely to get pregnant and have pelvic inflammatory disease, which could lead to an appendix being removed.

The findings may lead to new treatments, but experts advise women not to have their tonsils and appendix taken out unnecessarily. The study challenges the previous belief that appendectomies can damage fertility by blocking the fallopian tubes. The researchers warn that many women who sought fertility help may have been wrongly told their failure to get pregnant was down to having their appendix removed.

The current research follows a report in 2012 that linked appendectomies to higher rates of pregnancy. The new study backs this previous insight on a wider scale but added the extra association with tonsillectomies and people who have undergone both surgeries. More research is needed to figure out the exact reasons behind the link.

Bryson DeChambeau won the Northern Trust golf tournament on August 26, 2018, in Paramus, N.J., securing a four-shot victory over Tony Finau. DeChambeau's victory was a significant step towards playing in both the Ryder Cup and the FedEx Cup. He is currently leading the FedEx Cup standings and is virtually assured of being one of the top five seeds at the Tour Championship, with a chance to win the $10 million bonus.

DeChambeau's only wild shot was on the 18th hole, but he still managed to make par and finish at 18-under 266. Finau also made a strong statement about a potential captain's pick for the Ryder Cup. Tiger Woods, who came in second at the PGA Championship, finished tied for 40th, 14 shots out of the lead.

In a separate event, Tiger Woods was asked about his relationship with President Donald Trump. Woods stated that he has known Trump for a number of years and has played golf with him, both before and during his presidency. When asked about some people being threatened by Trump's policies and Woods' seemingly friendly relationship with the president, Woods responded that "we all must respect the office." He also declined to comment further on the state and discourse of race relations. Trump later praised Woods' answers and recent play on Twitter.

Title: Obama Addresses the Impact of Ferguson and Eric Garner on Law Enforcement Awareness

In a recent development, former U.S. President Barack Obama has highlighted the significant influence of the events in Ferguson, Missouri, and the case of Eric Garner on the growing awareness about the application of law enforcement not being always in a "colorblind fashion."

Obama, in a conversation with the social media giant Twitter, emphasized the role of social media platforms in facilitating this awareness. He noted that users can now add their location to tweets, providing a more authentic and contextual understanding of events happening around the world.

The former president specifically referred to the incidents in Ferguson and the death of Eric Garner, both of which sparked widespread protests and conversations about racial bias in law enforcement. These events, according to Obama, have contributed to a growing awareness and conversation about the need for law enforcement to be applied without regard to race.

Obama also took the opportunity to address the option for users to delete their Tweet location history. This feature, he said, allows users to maintain their privacy while still engaging in discussions about local issues.

In conclusion, Obama's comments underscore the role of social media in facilitating discussions about race and law enforcement. The events in Ferguson and the death of Eric Garner have been instrumental in raising awareness about the need for law enforcement to be applied in a fair and unbiased manner. The ability to add location to tweets and the option to delete location history further emphasizes the importance of privacy in these discussions.

James Cameron, a renowned filmmaker known for his work on "Titanic" and "Avatar," successfully reached the deepest point on Earth, the Mariana Trench's Challenger Deep, over the weekend. The journey was fraught with potential dangers, including implosion due to material weakness or design flaws, freezing due to lack of heating resources, fire from electrical faults, melting of the sub's viewport due to hydrothermal vents, and entanglement in submarine communication cables. However, Cameron managed to return safely after a three-hour dive in his 12-ton sub, the Deepsea Challenger.

Upon reaching the bottom, Cameron described the scene as resembling the moon, with no signs of life other than a few shrimplike amphipods. He spent less time than planned due to a hydraulic fluid leak, which forced an early ascent. Cameron hinted at future dives and received congratulations from Arnold Schwarzenegger and the Deep Sea Challenge organizers. The adventure will be documented by National Geographic in 3D.

The Pentagon's official Twitter account erroneously retweeted a call for President Donald Trump's resignation, made by an activist account, on November 16, 2017. The Pentagon spokesperson, Col. Rob Manning, stated that an authorized operator of the account inadvertently shared content that was not endorsed by the Department of Defense. The tweet, which was quickly deleted, called for the resignation of President Trump, Alabama Senate candidate Roy Moore, and Senator Al Franken, all of whom have been accused of sexual misconduct. The Pentagon's official Twitter account, @DeptofDefense, does not have a disclaimer stating that retweets do not constitute an endorsement. The incident comes amidst renewed questions about the President's own behavior regarding sexual harassment allegations. White House press secretary Sarah Huckabee Sanders declined to comment further when asked if it is the White House's position that the women who have accused the President are lying.

Mary A. "Pink" Mullaney, a beloved 85-year-old woman from Milwaukee, passed away on September 1. Her family chose an extraordinary obituary to honor her life, filled with humorous and heartwarming anecdotes that reflect her kind and generous spirit. The obituary offers practical advice, such as reusing old pantyhose, helping possums, and sharing chicken sandwiches with the homeless. It also includes whimsical suggestions, like believing a hitchhiker named "Peat Moss" and feeding picky-eating children through a laundry chute. The full obituary can be found at http://www.feerickfuneralhome.com/notices.php?id=1036. The obituary serves as a tribute to a woman who lived a life devoted to others and will be remembered for her kindness and unique sense of humor. The family encourages others to follow in her footsteps and reach out to those in need. In memory of Pink, Newsline 9 is reviving their "Someone You Should Know" series, inviting readers to share stories of inspiring individuals in their community.

In Manchester, Connecticut, a husband and wife, Clifford Knight (45) and Latoya Knight (38), both of Windsor, were arrested on April 2nd following an altercation at the Royal Buffet. The incident began as a dispute over crab legs at the buffet line, which escalated into a physical fight. A 21-year-old man was punched in the face and suffered a cut lip and broken tooth. His mother intervened using pepper spray, which was deemed self-defense and she was not charged.

Clifford Knight was charged with third-degree assault and disorderly conduct, while Latoya Knight was charged with disorderly conduct and threatening. Both were released on bail and are expected in court on April 14th. The Manchester Fire Department responded to vent the restaurant due to the use of pepper spray, and the Health Department temporarily closed it to assess the air quality. The restaurant reopened the following day. The initial report stated the injured victim was a juvenile, but it has since been corrected to a young adult.

The article discusses the growing trend of "Snapchat dysmorphia," a phenomenon where people are requesting plastic surgery to look more like their filtered selfies. This trend is causing concern among experts due to its potential negative effects on self-esteem and its potential to trigger body dysmorphic disorder (BDD), a mental illness classified on the obsessive-compulsive spectrum. The article was published in JAMA Facial Plastic Surgery by researchers from Boston University School of Medicine's Department of Dermatology.

Snapchat and Instagram filters, as well as other editing apps like Facetune, allow people to easily edit away imperfections and present an unattainable look. While people most often use filters or editing software for minor fixes, traditional cosmetic procedures often can't reproduce the "instant fix" people see in their edited photos.

"Snapchat dysmorphia" is a form of BDD, a mental disorder that causes people to be extremely preoccupied with a perceived flaw in appearance that to others can't be seen or appears minor. People who have BDD tend to obsess over their appearance and body image, often checking the mirror, grooming or seeking reassurance for many hours a day. Treatments include cognitive behavioral therapy and medication.

The annual American Academy of Facial Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery survey found that selfies continue to be a driving force behind why people wish to get plastic surgery done. In 2017, the survey found that 55 percent of surgeons reported seeing patients who requested surgery to look better in selfies, a 13 percent increase from the previous year's results.

Being inundated by these edited images on a regular basis can take a toll on people, and looking at a photo of yourself and not seeing the same thing reflected in the mirror or an unedited photo can make people unhappy. In some cases, it can even lead to developing body dysmorphic disorder.

The article warns that it is unlikely that people will change their behavior in the near future, but encourages awareness and recognition of the difference between reality and fantasy. The authors emphasize the importance of seeking help if one is struggling with body image issues or body dysmorphic disorder.

The Baltic Sea is a significant location for shipwrecks, particularly from the two World Wars, with over 1,000 known objects in German waters alone. Thomas Dehling, a maritime expert, oversees the mapping and surveying of these shipwrecks, focusing on potential hazards to shipping. The Baltic Sea is also popular among recreational divers, but it's dangerous due to fishing nets and the need for expertise to navigate the area.

A recent discovery in the Baltic Sea involves a 170-year-old champagne shipment found in a sunken trade schooner off the coast of Finland. The champagne, produced by well-known brands like Veuve Clicquot Ponsardin, was analyzed by a team of scientists led by Philippe Jeandet. The chemical and sensory analysis revealed differences compared to modern champagne, suggesting less controlled winemaking practices in the 19th century.

The aged champagne contained lower alcohol content and higher sugar levels, which can be attributed to a colder climate, less efficient yeast, and the addition of sugar syrup during production. The champagne also had enhanced levels of iron, copper, sodium, and chlorine, indicating the use of metal and wood vessels and the addition of copper sulfate and salt during the manufacturing process.

The sugar content of the champagne provides an important clue about the destination of the trade schooner, suggesting it was likely destined for the Germanic Confederation, which preferred moderately sweetened champagne. The discovery has sparked interest in the potential for deep-sea aging as a technique to enhance or augment the taste of various wines. The champagne has been auctioned off for up to 100,000 euros each, and some bottles have been sent to museums or historical institutions.

The Boy Scouts of America (BSA) has proposed to lift the ban on gay youth members but maintain the exclusion of gays as adult leaders. The decision, which will be voted on by the National Council in May, comes after a survey of scouting community members showed support for the change. The proposal has received mixed reactions, with gay rights groups demanding a complete lifting of the ban and conservative groups wanting it maintained. The Mormon Church, the largest organization in scouts, is studying the proposal, leaving the outcome of the vote uncertain. In a controversial move, an Egyptian court has sentenced 528 supporters of ousted President Mohammed Morsi to death, a decision that has been widely condemned for its procedural irregularities and breach of international human rights law. The defendants were found guilty of charges relating to an attack on a police station in Minya in August, during which a police officer was killed. The trial, which lasted less than an hour, was described as "cursory" and "rife with procedural irregularities." The prosecution did not present evidence implicating any individual defendant, and defence lawyers were prevented from presenting their case or calling witnesses. Another 683 Morsi supporters, including the Muslim Brotherhood's general guide, Mohammed Badie, and the chairman of its Freedom and Justice Party, Saad al-Katatni, went on trial at the same court on Tuesday. The trial was adjourned until April 28, when a verdict will be given. The UN High Commissioner for Human Rights expressed concern over the mass imposition of the death penalty after a trial that was rife with procedural irregularities. Sixteen Egyptian rights groups also voiced concern, saying the trial constituted a "dangerous, unprecedented shift in the Egyptian judiciary's treatment of such cases" and represented "a grave violation of both the right to a fair trial and the right to life." The Egyptian interim government defended the court, insisting that the sentences had been handed down only "after careful study." The defendants may appeal the verdicts, and legal experts expect a higher court to order a retrial or reduce their sentences. The trials have raised deep concerns among human rights activists over the lack of due process as Egyptian authorities push swift and heavy prosecutions in their crackdown against Islamists and the Muslim Brotherhood. About 16,000 have been arrested in the crackdown since the military's ouster of President Mohammed Morsi last summer.

The Obama administration's prisoner swap with Iran in 2016, which was intended to be a humanitarian gesture, has been criticized for releasing or dropping charges against more Iranians than Americans, and some of the Iranians were accused of posing threats to national security. The seven men Obama described as "civilians" were convicted of or awaiting trial for sanctions-related offenses, but in reality, some were accused by the Obama administration's own Justice Department of posing threats to national security. Three were part of an illegal procurement network supplying Iran with U.S.-made microelectronics with applications in surface-to-air and cruise missiles, and another was serving an eight-year sentence for conspiring to supply Iran with satellite technology and hardware. As part of the deal, the U.S. dropped its demand for $10 million that a jury said the aerospace engineer illegally received from Tehran. The administration also dropped charges and international arrest warrants against 14 other men, all of them fugitives. The Obama administration did not disclose their names or what they were accused of doing, noting only that the U.S. "also removed any Interpol red notices and dismissed any charges against 14 Iranians for whom it was assessed that extradition requests were unlikely to be successful." The deal has been criticized for undermining the Obama administration's own non-proliferation efforts and American national security. The Trump administration has pledged to do a full review of the Iran deal and Iran's compliance with it, which could reveal the extent to which the Obama administration undermined its own non-proliferation efforts to get the deal. Former Obama administration officials deny that the men could still be prosecuted if they continue their illegal activity, but with their cases dropped, international arrest warrants dismissed, and investigative assets redirected, the men, especially the 14 fugitives, can now continue activities the U.S. considers to be serious threats to its national security. The Obama administration's decision to grant clemency to the seven men and drop charges against the 14 fugitives has been criticized for undermining strategic enforcement efforts against a broad array of Iranian procurement networks operating in the U.S. that have provided Tehran with a steady stream of critically important parts and technologies for its nuclear and ballistic missile programs and to maintain and expand its military and weapons systems.

Scientists have discovered a new species of dinosaur, named Caihong juji, in China that lived during the Jurassic period 161 million years ago. The dinosaur, which was crow-sized and bird-like, had colorful feathers that shimmered and shifted in the light, similar to those of hummingbirds. The discovery suggests a more colorful Jurassic World than previously imagined.

The dinosaur's feathers had pancake-shaped melanosomes, which are responsible for pigmentation and are similar to those found in hummingbirds with iridescent feathers. Much of its body had dark feathers, but its head, neck, and chest were covered in iridescent feathers. Caihong was a two-legged predator with a Velociraptor-like skull and sharp teeth, probably hunting small mammals and lizards.

Caihong had crests above its eyes that looked like bony eyebrows. It is the earliest-known creature with asymmetrical feathers, a trait used by birds to steer when flying. The feathers on its tail suggest that tail feathers, not arm feathers, were first utilized for aerodynamic locomotion.

Caihong is extremely similar to some early birds such as Archaeopteryx, which lived 150 million years ago. Its forelimbs were configured like wings, and it is not clear what function the feathers had, although it is possible that they helped the animal to get in the air.

The dinosaur's full scientific name, Caihong juji, means "rainbow with a big crest." The holotype specimen is an adult and is well-preserved, with most elements preserved in their original anatomical positions. The skull is long and shallow, with five major openings from lateral view. The maxilla has a relatively small and high anterior ramus and a slender subantorbital-fossa ramus. The nasal is a major element contributing to the roof of the snout. The lacrimal is tetra-radiated, with an anterior process, a posterior process, a descending process, and a fourth dorsolateral process. The frontal contributes to the dorsal border of the large orbit. The postorbital has an extremely long jugal process, which extends ventrally close to the ventral border of the orbit. The quadratojugal has an extremely long jugal process, which is considerably thickened mediolaterally. The dentary is a long and shallow bone, roughly triangular in lateral view.

Caihong had probably 10 cervical vertebrae, no more than 13 dorsal, 5 sacral, and 26 caudal vertebrae. The cervical centra appear to be weakly angled in lateral view. The dorsal centra are anteroposteriorly long and lack distinctive pneumatic fossae or foramina. The sacrum comprises five vertebrae, but little can be said about their morphology. A complete caudal series comprises 26 vertebrae and is proportionally much shorter than those of all other Yanliao taxa. The proportionally short bony tail is due to the relatively small size of each vertebra.

The scapula is slightly shorter than the humerus and the rectangular coracoid has a prominent coracoid tubercle and a relatively small postglenoid process. The furcula is relatively slender. Unlike oviraptorosaurs and dromaeosaurids, but as in troodontids, other Tiaojishan theropods, and some basal avialans, ossified sternum and uncinate processes are absent.

The forelimbs in Caihong measure only about 60% the hindlimb length, proportionally shorter than most other basal paravians. The humerus is nearly as robust as the femur in most basal paravians, but it is proportionally shorter than in other Tiaojishan theropods and many basal paravians. However, the ulna and radius are longer than the humerus, a feature so far known only in flighted avialan taxa among theropods. As in basal troodontids, other Tiaojishan theropods, and to a lesser degree, Archaeopteryx, the ulna is weakly bowed and the radius is only slightly thinner than the ulna. The manus resembles those of other Tiaojishan theropods and to a lesser degree basal troodontids: a relatively long metacarpal II, a straight and relatively robust metacarpal IV, a long phalanx II-1, a long phalanx III-2, and the combined lengths of the subequally long phalanx IV-1 and IV-2 considerably smaller than IV-3 length.

The pelvis closely resembles those of other Tiaojishan theropods and Archaeopteryx. The ilium has a preacetabular process considerably longer than the postacetabular process that is slightly downturned; the pubis is slightly curved posteriorly and it has a strongly hooked boot. The ischium is a strap-like element that is extremely short and broad anteroposteriorly, and most unusually, it has a large rectangular obturator process.

The hind limbs are highly elongated, measuring about 3.1 times the length of the dorsal series. The sub-arctometatarsalian pes has a hallux that is proportionally smaller than that of most other basal paravians and a moderately enlarged and hyperextensible second pedal digit.

Feathers are well preserved over the whole body, except for the anterior portion of the rostrum and unguals. Caihong's body contour feathers are proportionally longer than those of other known non-avialan theropods. Feathers attached to the skull and neck are either long and linear or short and sinuous in preserved aspect. Juan Salaz, a 37-year-old American citizen, has been captured in Mexico after 16 years on the run following his 1997 escape from a Texas prison. Salaz was serving a combined 105-year sentence for aggravated kidnapping and attempted capital murder of two Houston police officers. He escaped from the Garza East prison in Beeville by scaling over three 16-foot razor wire fences. In 1995, Salaz and another man abducted a man at gunpoint and opened fire on police during a ransom exchange, resulting in injuries to two officers. Salaz was seriously wounded but recovered and later pleaded guilty. Geronimo Soto Alvarado, his accomplice, is serving a life sentence. Salaz is awaiting extradition to Texas to complete his sentence, leaving Jose Fernando Bustos-Diaz as the only remaining Texas prison fugitive. Bustos-Diaz escaped in 2010 and is believed to be in Mexico.

A 25-year-old German man developed seizures after solving Sudoku puzzles, following an avalanche accident that caused oxygen deprivation to his brain. The man, a physical education student, was skiing with a friend in November 2008 when an avalanche occurred, burying him and causing him to lose consciousness. His friend, a paramedic, rescued him and started CPR immediately. The man suffered a ruptured spleen and hip fracture, and while buried under the snow, he experienced hypoxia, which led to the death of inhibitory fibers in his right centro-parietal region of the brain.

As a result, the man developed myoclonic jerks, which are sudden muscle twitches, and started having spontaneous tonic-clonic seizures in his left arm. The seizures were triggered by the man's intense three-dimensional imagination that activated when he solved Sudoku puzzles. The seizures did not occur when the man completed other types of math problems or while he was reading. The doctors prescribed anti-epileptic medication to keep the seizures under control, and the man was seizure-free for more than five years, thanks to taking the medication regularly and steering clear of Sudoku. The man's seizures were a rare case of reflex epilepsy, which is characterized by seizures induced by external stimuli such as reading, making calculations, or playing games.

The Dallas Morning News, a traditionally conservative newspaper, broke with 75 years of tradition on Wednesday by endorsing Hillary Clinton for president, marking the first time it has endorsed a Democrat since Franklin Delano Roosevelt in 1940. The newspaper criticized Donald Trump for playing on fear, exploiting xenophobia, racism, and misogyny, and for exhibiting a dangerous lack of judgment and impulse control. However, the study's findings may not be as true today due to the decline in newspaper circulation and the increasing polarization of American politics.

The Dallas Morning News' endorsement of Clinton is a sign of how much Trump's campaign has shaken even staunch bastions of Republicanism. However, it remains to be seen whether the endorsement will make a difference to voters, given the polarized state of American politics and the waning influence of newspapers.

The newspaper's endorsement of Clinton is a significant development in the 2016 presidential race, and it will be interesting to see whether it has an impact on voters in Texas, a must-win state for Trump.

Scientists have developed a drug that mimics sunlight to induce tanning in human skin samples, potentially offering protection against skin cancer. The drug, tested on mice with fair skin, triggers the production of melanin, the body's natural sunblock, without the harmful effects of UV radiation.

The drug works by bypassing the damage caused by UV light and directly activating the production of melanin. The team behind the study, led by Dr. David Fisher at Massachusetts General Hospital, hopes this discovery could prevent skin cancer and slow the aging process.

The drug is different from self-tanning lotions, sun beds, and pills that claim to boost melanin production but still require UV light. The researchers are not motivated by creating a new cosmetic, but rather by addressing the "very significant frustration" of the lack of progress in skin cancer, the most common type of cancer.

The drug has shown promising results in tests, with the melanin produced able to block harmful UV rays. The researchers plan to combine the drug with sunscreen to provide maximum protection from solar radiation.

The drug could potentially allow for a ginger tan, as it may work even on redheads, who normally burn rather than tan. However, it is not yet clear if the drug might affect red hair color.

The drug is not yet ready for commercial use, and the researchers plan to do more safety testing. They will likely want to give it a better name than an SIK-inhibitor. The British Association of Dermatologists has called the study a "novel approach" to preventing skin cancer, and welcomed any research into ways to prevent skin cancer.

The potential benefits of the drug extend beyond cancer prevention, as it could also slow the appearance of aging by preventing UV damage. Dr. Fisher sees this as a promising development, as "many people would say the obvious and most dramatic sign of aging is what skin looks like, and even casual UV damage over the years causes damage."

Clark's family, including his girlfriend Salena Manni and their children Aiden and Ciaro, are devastated by his death.

According to police, Clark was shot 20 times and was hit multiple times. Initially, police believed Clark was armed, but later clarified that he was only holding a cellphone. The object Clark was holding when he was shot was not the tool bar that deputies in a helicopter saw.

Clark's brother Stevante is trying to understand the encounter and believes there could have been another way for his brother to be apprehended without being killed. The family is demanding justice and have started a memorial fund.

The Sacramento Police Department has released body cam footage of the shooting, which shows Clark being shot near the 7:40 mark. The department plans to show the video to Clark’s family by the end of the week and make it publicly available within a week.

The shooting has sparked protests and vigils in the community, with activists calling for transparency and accountability from the police department.
