The Sacramento County District Attorney’s Office, city attorney’s office, and the city Office of Public Safety Accountability will investigate the shooting, as will SPD homicide detectives, internal affairs, and Crime Scene Investigation units.

Clark leaves behind two young sons, Cairo and Aiden, and was known for his love of sneakers, football, and video games. His family and friends are mourning his loss and are working to raise funds for his funeral expenses. The community is demanding justice for Clark and are calling for changes in police policies and procedures.

A massive winter storm hit the East Coast on January 2, 2014, causing widespread disruptions. The storm dumped 20 inches of snow in parts of New England and threatened to cripple much of the Midwest and Northeast. Sub-zero wind chills and blowing snow shut down interstates and airports, with John F. Kennedy Airport in New York and Boston's Logan International effectively shut down. Schools across the Northeast, including all public schools in New York City, were closed. The cold behind the snowstorm could be deadly, with parts of the Midwest expecting lows not seen since the mid-1980s. The high temperature in New York City was expected to be in the teens during the day and drop to between 5 and 8 degrees in the evening, with the wind chill making it feel well below zero. New York Governor Andrew Cuomo declared a state of emergency and closed several major roads. The storm affected air travel, with over 1,600 flights being canceled on Friday on top of about 2,000 on Thursday. The delays and cancellations in the Midwest and Northeast created a logjam in the rest of the country's flight schedules, with dozens of flights at LAX in Los Angeles being put on hold or scrapped. The cold weather was also affecting residents, with temperatures from upstate New York to Maine below zero and wind chills minus-30 in some spots. Across the Northeast, residents were fretting about the blast of bitter cold. The storm was expected to continue into Friday, with more snow and frigid temperatures expected.

In a shocking incident, a woman gave birth at her workplace, Ceva Logistics in Redford, Michigan, on April 1, 2015. The woman, a 26-year-old from Wyandotte, attempted to conceal the birth and the death of her newborn baby. The baby was found dead in the mother's bag under her desk in the cubicle.

The discovery was made when employees heard moaning coming from the women's restroom and found blood on the bathroom stall. The mother, who had blood on her, had returned to her cubicle and tried to resume work. The autopsy was performed on the baby, but the results are still pending.

The company, Ceva Logistics, informed its 150-plus employees and offered grief counseling. However, the logistics director, Ken L'Heureux, declined to comment on specifics of what happened, stating that it is under investigation. The family of the woman also declined comment.

The woman worked for a temp service, Level Professional Services, and had previously told people at Ceva that she wasn't pregnant. The temp agency, Level Professional Services, also offered counseling for affected employees.

Police are awaiting autopsy results to determine if the baby was born alive or if the death was a potential homicide. It has not yet been determined if the mother will face charges. The Wayne County Medical Examiner's Office conducted an autopsy on the newborn on April 1, and the results are expected in two weeks.

A charter school located north of downtown San Antonio, Great Hearts Monte Vista, is under fire after an eighth-grade American History class was assigned a worksheet titled "The Life of Slaves: A Balanced View." The assignment, which asked students to list the "positive aspects" and "negative aspects" of living life as a slave, has been widely condemned as insensitive and inappropriate.

The worksheet was posted on social media by an anonymous parent, who expressed concern and anger over the assignment. The post gained traction, with other parents at the school, local lawmakers, and even U.S. Representative Joaquin Castro voicing their disapproval.

In response, Great Hearts Texas Superintendent Aaron Kindel issued a statement, confirming that the assignment was only used at the school's Monte Vista North campus and was "very inappropriate and entirely inconsistent" with the school's "philosophy and culture." Kindel also stated that the teacher responsible for the assignment has been placed on leave while "all the facts" surrounding the issue are assessed.

The textbook for the course, "Prentice Hall Classics: A History of the United States," has been removed from use and will be audited. If deemed imprudent, the textbook will be permanently replaced with one that accurately reflects the school's values.

Headmasters and teachers at the Monte Vista North campus will meet with students who were assigned the worksheet to explain the mistake and engage them in lessons that are more thoughtful about this period of American History. Kindel also emphasized that the school intends to ensure such an incident does not happen again.

However, Pearson, the manufacturer of the textbook, has since denied any involvement in the worksheet, stating that it was not created, endorsed, or encouraged by their company. They strongly condemned the implication that there was any positive aspect to slavery.

This is not the first time Pearson has been accused of racial insensitivity. In 2017, a nursing student criticized the company for including stereotypical depictions of race in its book. Pearson leaders apologized and removed the content from its books.

The incident at Great Hearts Monte Vista has sparked a larger conversation about the need for sensitivity and cultural competency in educational materials, particularly when teaching about sensitive topics like slavery. The school has scheduled a follow-up communication on May 9, 2018, to update parents on the investigation's progress and any subsequent actions.

Dunkin' Donuts is rebranding itself as "Dunkin'" to emphasize its focus on coffee and other beverages, with doughnuts still on the menu. The name change will take effect in January, starting with US stores, and will eventually be adopted globally. The company aims to modernize its image and attract younger customers through simplified menus, dedicated mobile ordering lanes, and digital kiosks. The new logo retains the familiar rounded font and color scheme. The rebranding is part of Dunkin' Brands' strategy to position itself as a "beverage-led" company, with beverages, particularly coffee, accounting for 60% of US sales. The company plans to open 1,000 new US stores by the end of 2020.

Oracle Team USA, led by skipper James Spithill, pulled off one of the most remarkable comebacks in sports history to win the 34th America's Cup. Just a week ago, Emirates Team New Zealand led the competition 8-1 and needed one more win to secure the trophy. However, Oracle Team USA, facing stiff penalties, staged an incredible comeback, winning eight consecutive races to clinch the cup in a winner-take-all Race 19. The team's speed and strategy proved crucial in the thrilling competition, which was brought to the competition by Oracle CEO Larry Ellison, who skipped an Oracle conference to celebrate with his crew. The victory was akin to the Boston Red Sox sweeping the final four games of the 2004 ALCS over the New York Yankees and the Philadelphia Flyers overcoming a 0-3 deficit to beat the Boston Bruins in the 2010 NHL playoffs.

The Telegraph magazine's cover story "The mystery of Melania" contained false statements that should not have been published, as acknowledged following public backlash. In a new ad from Planned Parenthood, superstar singer Mary J. Blige expressed her support for President Obama's re-election, highlighting his stance on women's rights and healthcare. The ad features Blige, rapper Q-Tip, and actress Julianne Moore.

However, a controversial ad produced by Michael Moore and MoveOn.Org, claiming to represent the Greatest Generation, contained explicit and offensive language towards Republican candidate Mitt Romney and his supporters. The ad has been criticized for its inappropriate and divisive content, with the final speaker making threats and promises of violence. The full ad can be viewed online, but viewer discretion is advised.

In July 2010, Russian spy Anna Chapman, one of ten spies deported from the United States, posed in provocative photographs for the Russian edition of Maxim magazine. The photos, which will be featured in the next issue, show Chapman dressed in nylon and lace and holding a handgun. Maxim described Chapman as having ignited Russian patriotism more than the soccer team. The Kremlin has used the spy case, reminiscent of the Cold War, to boost the prestige of its intelligence services and counteract what was perceived as a major disgrace for Russia's Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR). Despite the media attention, the spy ring was reported to have failed to secure any significant intelligence before their arrests in the United States. Russian President Dmitry Medvedev awarded the group the country's highest state honors on Monday. The exchange of the ten Russians with four imprisoned Russians who were accused of trading secrets with the West was completed.

Tila Tequila, a former reality television star, has caused controversy by posting a photo on Facebook that appears to celebrate Nazism. The image, which was taken at Auschwitz, shows Tequila wearing a swastika armband and an SS hat, and has been widely criticized as anti-Semitic. Tequila has also posted a blog entry in which she defends Adolf Hitler and accuses Jewish people of controlling the world's banks and media. In addition, she has released a new song called "It's Going Down!" that contains anti-Semitic lyrics. Tequila's embrace of Nazi ideology has been met with backlash from both the public and white supremacists. She previously declared that she had converted to Judaism in 2011, but her recent actions suggest a change of heart. Tequila has a history of mental health issues, having entered rehab in 2012 after suffering a brain aneurysm caused by a drug overdose.

In Florida, the battle between plaintiffs' lawyers and Big Tobacco continues intensely, with over 7,000 lawsuits pending in state and federal courts. This legal landscape stems from a 2006 Florida Supreme Court ruling, known as the "Engle" ruling, which requires jurors in future smoking cases to acknowledge tobacco products as "defective" and "unreasonably dangerous."

The Engle ruling has significantly benefited smoking plaintiffs in Florida, resulting in over $250 million in damages from Engle progeny cases. The latest development comes from Bronson, Florida, where a jury awarded $80 million to the daughter of a two-pack-a-day smoker who died of lung cancer in 1996. The jury found that the defendant, R.J. Reynolds, was 90% at fault, while the deceased was 10% responsible.

The Horner verdict marks a shift in the tobacco industry's recent winning streak, which saw eight consecutive defense verdicts in Engle cases. The latest victory was on Friday, when a Miami jury sided with Philip Morris USA in a smoking trial. Plaintiffs' counsel David Sales stated, "People need to be reminded, again and again, of the true cost—in precious human life—that R.J. Reynolds has imposed and continues to impose on our society." The tobacco industry has yet to comment on the Horner verdict.

California has agreed to end its long-term isolation of imprisoned gang leaders, marking a significant shift in the state's controversial segregation policies. The agreement, which restricts the unlimited isolation of inmates, comes in response to a class-action federal lawsuit filed on behalf of nearly 3,000 California inmates held in segregation statewide.

The practice of isolating inmates for extended periods, often for a decade or longer, has been criticized for its harsh conditions and potential for cruel and unusual punishment. Inmates are typically confined to 80-square-foot cells for all but about 90 minutes each day, with limited contact with visitors, reading materials, and communication with the outside world.

The new policy will segregate only inmates who commit new crimes behind bars, moving away from the previous practice of locking gang members in soundproofed, windowless cells solely to prevent them from directing illegal activities. Corrections and Rehabilitation Secretary Jeffrey Beard stated that the changes will move California "more into the mainstream of what other states are doing."

The conditions in California's segregation units have triggered intermittent hunger strikes by tens of thousands of inmates in recent years. The practice has also drawn criticism from President Barack Obama and U.S. Supreme Court Justice Anthony Kennedy.

The lawsuit was initially filed in 2009 by two killers serving time in the security housing unit at Pelican Bay. By 2012, Todd Ashker and Danny Troxell were among 78 prisoners confined in Pelican Bay's isolation unit for more than 20 years. More than 500 had been in the unit for more than 10 years, though recent policy changes have reduced that number to 62 inmates isolated for a decade or longer as of late July.

The settlement will limit how long inmates can spend in isolation, while creating restrictive custody units for inmates who refuse to participate in rehabilitation programs or keep breaking prison rules. It will also house those who might be in danger if they live with other inmates, such as the 71-year-old Hugo Pinell, who was killed by fellow inmates in August just days after being released from isolation.

Jules Lobel, the inmates' lead attorney and president of the Center for Constitutional Rights, hailed the settlement as a "monumental victory for prisoners" and an important step towards ending solitary confinement in California and across the country. Marie Levin, sister of 57-year-old reputed gang leader Ronnie Dewberry, expressed her anticipation for the first time in 31 years that she will be able to hold and touch her brother.

The union representing most prison guards has expressed disappointment that they were not involved in the negotiations, but Corrections and Rehabilitation Secretary Jeffrey Beard has pledged to address their concerns regarding guard safety. The settlement expands on recent changes that have reduced the number of segregated inmates statewide from 4,153 in January 2012 to 2,858 currently.

Under the new policy, gang members and other inmates can be segregated for up to five years for crimes committed in prison, though gang members can receive an additional two years in segregation. The segregation system was adopted about 35 years ago in response to a series of slayings of inmates and guards, but was not reconsidered until recently due to other crises, including severe crowding.

In a discussion on Fox & Friends, Brian Kilmeade defended President Donald Trump's border policies, stating that they are necessary to ensure the safety of the United States by vetting individuals entering the country and deterring illegal immigration. Kilmeade argued that the President is enforcing the rule of law and dealing with a pressing issue that affects the country's security. He also emphasized that the immigrants in question are not American children, and while compassion should be shown, their needs should not be prioritized over those of American taxpayers.

On Wednesday, Trump signed an executive order aimed at ending the controversial policy of separating children from their parents at the U.S.-Mexico border, but the order also allows for the indefinite detention of children with their parents. The executive order has been met with criticism, and MSNBC's Stephanie Ruhle has spoken out against Kilmeade's remarks, pointing out the importance of treating all children with compassion, regardless of their nationality.

Kilmeade has since offered a clarification for his remarks, stating that he did not intend to minimize the importance of children, but rather to emphasize the need for the rule of law and the protection of American citizens. The discussion on Fox & Friends highlights the ongoing debate surrounding immigration policy in the United States and the differing perspectives on how to address the issue.

The United States has announced it will increase support for the Syrian opposition in their efforts to topple President Bashar al-Assad. This includes direct support in the form of medical and food supplies, as well as an additional $60 million in aid to help the opposition deliver basic governance and other services in rebel-controlled areas. The decision comes after a meeting of the Friends of Syria group in Rome, where Secretary of State John Kerry also promised to travel to Ankara to discuss the Syria crisis with top Turkish officials. The promise of direct, non-lethal aid to the rebels represents a shift in US policy on Syria, but falls short of providing the weapons and munitions that the rebels say they need to defeat government forces. The US decision is designed to increase the pressure on President Assad to step down and allow a democratic transition, as the US Secretary of State John Kerry stated that President Assad is "out of time and must be out of power." The $60m in aid to the opposition Syrian National Coalition (SNC) represents a doubling of US support, and is intended to help the opposition deliver governance and basic services in rebel-controlled areas. The signals are clear that diplomatic patience is running out, and the international calculus is slowly shifting. The debate on arming the Syrian opposition is not going away, and non-lethal military aid looks to be the next step for some governments. However, the arming debate is complex, as more weapons may up the contest but could also increase the bloodshed in the short term. The European Union has also announced changes to its arms embargo on Syria, allowing EU states to provide armoured vehicles, non-lethal military equipment and technical aid to the rebels, but not weapons. The Syrian rebels say weapons and ammunition are what they need most, and a meeting to select the prime minister of the SNC, scheduled for the weekend, was unexpectedly postponed on Thursday, and no new date has been set. Meanwhile, fighting in Syria continues and the humanitarian situation is worsening, with over one million Syrians having fled the conflict into neighbouring countries, and two million having been internally displaced. The World Health Organisation has warned of disease outbreaks and worsening medical services. After the meeting, the SNC leader, Moaz al-Khatib, called on President Assad to make "one wise decision in your life" and stand down "for the future of your country."

A federal judge, Peter J. Messitte, has ruled that the District of Columbia and Maryland can proceed with a lawsuit against President Trump, alleging that his business dealings have violated the Constitution's ban on receiving improper emoluments, or payments, from individual states and foreign governments. This is the first time such a lawsuit has cleared the initial legal hurdle, with the judge finding that the plaintiffs have legal standing to sue the president.

The lawsuit focuses on Trump's business at the Trump International Hotel in downtown Washington, where government clients, including Kuwait and Bahrain, have patronized the hotel, potentially to the detriment of competitors and taxpayers. The judge wrote that Maryland and the District had sufficiently argued that Trump's hotel "has had and almost certainly will continue to have an unlawful effect on competition."

The judge also rejected an argument that only Congress may decide whether the president has violated the emoluments clauses. He stated that in the absence of Congressional approval, the court could review the president's actions to determine if they comply with the law.

If the ruling stands, the District and Maryland may seek internal documents from the Trump Organization to determine how much money the Washington hotel has taken in from state and foreign governments. The judge narrowed the lawsuit's scope to the Washington hotel, stating that the District and Maryland had standing to sue because they could plausibly claim to have been injured by Trump's receipt of payments from foreign and state governments.

The case could allow the District and Maryland to seek the president's financial documents and tax returns. The Justice Department, which is representing the president in this case, did not immediately say whether it would appeal.

This case was filed last year, one of a raft of lawsuits in the months after Trump's inauguration, all of them alleging that he was violating the Constitution's emoluments clauses. The first step in all these cases has been an argument over what lawyers call "standing" — in essence, determining whether the plaintiff has a right to sue. In December, a federal judge threw out one of the emoluments lawsuits, brought by the nonprofit watchdog group Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, stating that the Constitution gave Congress — and only Congress — the right to enforce these rules.

The case involving the District and Maryland had a hearing earlier this year before Messitte at a federal court in Greenbelt, Md. In that hearing, the Justice Department, arguing on Trump's behalf, made a similar argument in an effort to throw out the attorney generals’ suit. However, in his ruling Wednesday, Messitte rejected that idea.

On June 30, 2013, tens of thousands of Egyptians gathered in Cairo's Tahrir Square and cities across the country to demand the resignation of President Mohammed Morsi, marking the one-year anniversary of his inauguration. The protests were organized by the youth activist group Tamarod, which claimed to have collected over 22 million signatures in a petition calling for Morsi's removal.

The demonstrations were met with opposition from Morsi's Islamist supporters, who vowed to defend him. Clashes between the two sides resulted in at least seven deaths and hundreds of injuries, with the majority of the violence occurring in Nile Delta cities and Alexandria.

The protests were a culmination of polarization and instability that have been building since Morsi's inauguration in June 2012. The past year has seen multiple political crises, bouts of bloody clashes, and a steadily worsening economy, with power outages, fuel shortages, rising prices, and persistent lawlessness and crime.

Morsi and his Islamist allies, including the Muslim Brotherhood and more hard-line groups, argue that street demonstrations cannot be allowed to remove a leader who won a legitimate election, and accuse Mubarak loyalists of being behind the campaign to oust him. They have also given the confrontation a sharply religious tone, denouncing Morsi's opponents as "enemies of God" and infidels.

On the other side is an array of secular and liberal Egyptians, moderate Muslims, Christians, and what the opposition claims is a broad sector of the general public that has turned against the Islamists. They argue that the Islamists have negated their election mandate by trying to monopolize power, infusing government with their supporters, forcing through a constitution they largely wrote, and giving religious extremists a free hand, all while failing to manage the country.

The opposition believes that with sheer numbers in the street, they can pressure Morsi to step down, perhaps with the added weight of the powerful military if it signals the president should go. Defense Minister Gen. Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi had given the president and his opponents a week to reach a compromise, warning that the military would intervene to prevent the nation from entering a "dark tunnel."

The protests on June 30, 2013, were unprecedented in size and scope, with up to 500,000 protesters in Cairo's Tahrir Square and similar rallies reported in dozens of other Egyptian cities. The scale of the protests was remarkable because they were a bottom-up, grassroots effort and not directed by political opposition leaders.

Morsi was defiant in the face of the dissent, telling The Guardian that he had no plans to meet the protesters' demand for an early presidential election. "If we changed someone in office who [was elected] according to constitutional legitimacy – well, there will be people opposing the new president too, and a week or a month later they will ask him to step down," Morsi said.

The Egyptian leader, however, said he did not know in advance of el-Sissi's comments last week, indicating a possible rift between the two. The military's role in the political crisis remains unclear, but army troops were deployed in some of Cairo's suburbs on June 30, with soldiers standing at traffic lights and major intersections. Army helicopters flew over Cairo on several occasions, adding to the day's sense of foreboding.

The outcome of the political crisis remains uncertain, with the possibility of further violence and instability in Egypt. The opposition's demand for Morsi's resignation and early presidential elections is likely to continue, while Morsi and his Islamist allies are likely to resist, citing their democratic mandate. The military's role in the crisis is a wildcard, with the possibility of a coup or intervention to prevent further violence and instability. The situation is being closely watched by the international community, with concerns about the stability of Egypt and the region as a whole.

In the recent political landscape of Maine, Leslie Gibson, a Republican candidate for a state House seat, has withdrawn from the race following backlash over his controversial comments about teenage survivors of the Florida school shooting. Gibson's derogatory remarks targeted Emma Gonzalez and David Hogg, two prominent activists advocating for stricter gun control laws in the wake of the Parkland, Florida shooting.

Gibson's comments, which included calling Gonzalez a "skinhead lesbian" and Hogg a "bald-faced liar," sparked outrage from both Democrats and Republicans. Gibson later apologized, but the damage was done, leading to increased support for other candidates to challenge him.

Thomas Martin Jr., another Republican contender, entered the race on Thursday, citing Gibson's comments as his motivation. Eryn Gilchrist, a 28-year-old Democrat, also joined the contest, stating she felt "horrified and embarrassed" at the prospect of Gibson representing her.

Gibson, who had been cruising towards an unopposed election, announced his decision to withdraw from the race on Friday, stating it was "the best thing for everybody." He expressed hope that his departure would bring things back to normal and allow him to find some peace and quiet after the turmoil of recent days.

The incident highlights the growing influence of the teenage survivors of the Florida school shooting, who have become vocal advocates for gun control reform. Their activism has led to increased scrutiny and criticism of those who oppose their views, as seen in the case of Leslie Gibson.

The Millennium Tower in San Francisco, known as the city's tallest residential building, has faced another setback as a large crack was reportedly found in a window on the 36th floor over the Labor Day weekend. The City and County of San Francisco Department of Building Inspection has issued a correction notice, requiring building engineers to evaluate the extent of repairs needed and investigate the condition of the glass panel and adjacent curtain wall system by September 7, 2018.

The crack was reported by a resident who heard a "creaking sound and then a large pop" before the crack appeared at 2:30 a.m. on Sunday. Supervisor Aaron Peskin confirmed the crack and stated that the window system, part of the "curtain wall," is designed to sustain hurricane force winds. Peskin has asked the Building Inspection Department to consider closing the sidewalks below the cracked window due to safety concerns.

The Millennium Tower has been sinking and tilting since construction began in 2005, with the building sinking some 17 inches and tilting about 14 inches. Residents paid anywhere from $1.6 million to $10 million for their units. The building has been the subject of numerous lawsuits, including one from the homeowners association seeking $200 million.

This incident adds to the existing concerns about the stability of the high-rise. City inspectors issued a notice of violation on Tuesday, giving the Millennium management 72 hours to report back on the extent of the problem and the soundness of the building’s façade in light of the failure. The Millennium management has acknowledged the incident and assured residents that a team of experts would assess the problem.

The failure of the 36th floor window could be evidence of strain on the steel lattice that forms the façade, raising concerns about the possibility of a fire spreading through gaps between floors. For now, a barrier has been placed along Mission Street until repairs are made. Peskin has emphasized the need for immediate action from the city Department of Building Inspection to ensure the safety of thousands of people who walk by the building every day.

In a significant development, ten volunteer firefighters from the Fairmont Rural Fire Department and the Orrum Fire Department have been arrested and accused of a two-year conspiracy to set numerous fires in woods and abandoned structures throughout Robeson County, North Carolina. The investigation, led by the Robeson County Sheriff’s Office, involves approximately 90 arson-related charges, with more expected.

The accused firefighters include Melquan Williams, Austin Seth Hunt, Ashley Marie Oxendine, John Austin Huggins, Jordan Scott, Kenny Caulder Jr., Willie Fuentes Strickland, Jordan Emmanuel Hunt, Shellia Huggins, and William Kendall Strickland. Charges range from felony arson to felony conspiracy, and bond for each individual was set between $100,000 and $200,000.

Sheriff Kenneth Sealey stated that the fires were not accidental and have cost taxpayers significantly due to the numerous calls to put them out. The investigation began following a tip, and more arrests are possible. Anyone with information regarding the case is asked to contact Lt. Kevin Graham of the Robeson County Sheriff’s Office at 910-671-3100.

The study conducted by researchers at the University of York has found that exposure to low concentrations of the antidepressant Prozac (fluoxetine) can disrupt the courtship behavior of wild starlings, potentially impacting their reproductive success. The researchers replicated the typical concentration of Prozac found in worms and insects at sewage treatment plants and fed them to starlings living in outdoor aviaries. During the breeding season, male starlings paired with females that had consumed Prozac-laced worms sang less and were more aggressive towards them. Female starlings, however, did not seem to be affected by the male's behavior and were inconsistent in their own behavior. The study suggests that exposure to antidepressants could reduce female attractiveness, adding to the growing evidence that environmental concentrations of pharmaceuticals can alter important traits related to individual fitness and population dynamics. The researchers emphasize that this does not mean that it's bad to take antidepressants, but there is a need for new technologies to clean out sewage to minimize the impact on wildlife. Further research is needed to determine if the same behavior is happening in the wild and to understand the broader implications of pharmaceuticals in the environment on wildlife populations.

The article discusses a study published in the journal Molecular Ecology that reveals a surprising finding about sperm whales' genetic makeup. Researchers found that the majority of sperm whales today can be traced back to a single female, referred to as an "Eve-like whale." This discovery was made by analyzing mitochondrial DNA from 1,633 whales and finding low genetic diversity, which is not unusual for large animals known as megafauna.

The study's lead author, Alana Alexander, expected to find low diversity but was surprised by the extent of it. The researchers found that the sperm whale's social structure, which is matrilineal, may be the reason for this low diversity. Sperm whales are known for their large size, weighing up to 45 tons, and having the largest brain of any creature on Earth.

The low diversity found in sperm whales makes them more susceptible to threats such as climate change, which can disturb their preferred habitats. This lack of diversity can also prevent the whales from straying too far from their region and mixing with other populations. The study suggests that today's sperm whale mothers need to get out more to ensure the survival of their species.

The study also highlights the interplay of natural selection, genetic drift, geographic isolation, mating systems, and population size in determining patterns of genetic diversity within species. The sperm whale provides an interesting example of a long-lived species with few geographic barriers to dispersal, but strong genetic structure due to both geographic and social philopatry. The study shows that sperm whales are a unique example of a worldwide population expansion followed by rapid assortment due to female social organization.

On October 12, the Peterson Air Force Base in Colorado Springs discharged approximately 150,000 gallons of water containing toxic perfluorinated compounds (PFCs) into the local sewer system. The chemicals, which are linked to various health issues, were held in a tank at a firefighter training area on the base. The spill was discovered during an inspection and notified Colorado Springs Utilities the following day.

The wastewater treatment plant was unable to remove the PFCs before they were discharged into Fountain Creek, which flows south towards Pueblo. The Colorado Springs Utilities have stated that they are working with the military to keep PFCs out of their system, aiming to protect both their customers and the system from this chemical.

The PFC-laced wastewater has already contaminated groundwater and public drinking water systems south of Colorado Springs, an area home to an estimated 80,000 people. Peterson AFB is suspected as one source of the contamination. The Air Force has contributed $4.3 million to help communities deal with the contamination.

The Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment has expressed concern about the spill and will coordinate with the Colorado Department of Public Health and the Environment to collect water samples along Fountain Creek, if necessary. The Air Force is investigating the cause of the discharge and plans to replace the firefighting foam at the base within two weeks.

The spill has left residents like Mary Fletcher, who has lived in the Widefield area for 30 years, feeling frustrated and concerned about the quality of their tap water. Fletcher, who has been diagnosed with an autoimmune disease, wonders whether the water caused it. The Air Force banned the use of the foam outside fire emergencies last year and announced a plan to replace the product at all of its bases around the globe.

Former President George W. Bush and Vice President Dick Cheney reunited for the groundbreaking of Bush's presidential library at Southern Methodist University in Dallas. This marked their first public appearance together since leaving office in 2009. Bush's memoir, "Decision Points," was recently released, and he has been promoting it in interviews. Cheney, who has been a vocal defender of the Bush administration, appeared frail due to a recent heart surgery. During the ceremony, Bush praised Cheney, stating that he was the right choice as his running mate in 2000 and a great vice president. Cheney, in turn, praised Bush for preventing another 9/11 attack and promised to share more thoughts about Bush's presidency at the library's grand opening. The library and affiliated policy institute are seen as vehicles for Bush to continue shaping his presidential legacy.

SkyMall, the in-flight shopping catalog known for its quirky and often humorous product offerings, has filed for bankruptcy protection. The parent company, Xhibit, cited in-flight Wi-Fi access and increased competition from online retailers like Amazon as major factors contributing to the decline in sales. Founded in 1990, SkyMall's catalogs were once a staple of airline travel, offering a wide range of products from pet toys to garden gnomes. However, with the rise of electronic devices and the convenience of online shopping, fewer passengers were browsing the SkyMall catalog. The company's bankruptcy filing comes after Delta and Southwest Airlines ended their contracts with SkyMall, leaving the company with a severe liquidity crisis. Despite the bankruptcy filing, Xhibit hopes to sell its main assets, including the SkyMall online retail business, in April through a court-supervised auction. The decline of SkyMall is a reflection of the broader struggles faced by the mail-order industry, which has seen a significant drop in revenues over the past decade due to increased competition from online retailers and a dwindling customer base.

The 12 boys and their football coach who had been trapped in a flooded cave in Thailand for 10 days have been found alive by rescuers. The group was discovered on Monday night by two British divers who had joined the search operation. They were found on a rock shelf about 4km from the mouth of the cave, and were seen by torchlight sitting on a ledge above water. The boys are believed to be aged between 11 and 16, and most of them cannot swim. Rescuers are now considering how best to bring the group to safety, with the governor of Chiang Rai stating that they will not rush to take the lads out of the cave and that those with zero risk will be evacuated first. Heavy rain could cause water levels to rise and threaten the air pocket where the group has taken refuge. The boys have received their first food and medical treatment since being found, and are being kept entertained by rescuers. The Thai authorities have appealed for donations of full-face scuba diving masks small enough to fit the boys, in order to reduce the risk of their breathing apparatus coming loose as they travel through flooded passageways. The boys and their coach went missing on 23 June, and it is believed they entered the cave when it was dry and became trapped by rising waters from heavy rainfall. Attempts are being made to reduce the risk of further flooding of the caves by pumping water from the underground system, and a phone line is being installed so the boys can talk to their families. The search for the group had gripped the nation as it was unclear where they were or whether they were even still alive. The discovery of the boys has been hailed as a heroic effort by Thai officials, with the Prime Minister stating that "everybody is a hero".

A new study published in the New England Journal of Medicine has found no direct link between the use of antidepressants during pregnancy, specifically selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), and one type of birth defect, heart malformations. The study contradicts previous research that suggested antidepressant use in pregnancy could be risky. The study was conducted over a seven-year period, from 2000 to 2007, using data from 46 states and Washington, D.C. The researchers focused on antidepressants, including SSRIs, tricyclic antidepressants, serotonin–norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs), bupropion, and other antidepressants. The study cohort consisted of nearly a million women who had given birth while on Medicaid without supplementary private insurance, between the ages of 12 and 55. The researchers excluded women who had been treated with drugs known to cause birth defects or who had infants diagnosed with a genetic abnormality. The study found no increased risk of heart defects in babies born to mothers who had taken antidepressants during the first three months of pregnancy. The study was approved by the institutional review board of Brigham and Women's Hospital, and the need for informed consent was waived. The researchers used logistic-regression analysis to estimate odds ratios for cardiac malformations and their corresponding 95% confidence intervals. The results are referred to as relative risks. The researchers performed prespecified subgroup and sensitivity analyses to evaluate the robustness of the primary results. The study findings run counter to two previous studies that caused the U.S. Food and Drug Administration to formally warn health care professionals that early prenatal exposure to paroxetine (Paxil) may increase the risk of heart malformations at birth. The current study's findings may provide reassurance to pregnant women who require antidepressants for the treatment of depression.

Howard Stern, a long-time friend of Donald Trump, expressed concerns about Trump's mental health and the impact of the presidency on him. Stern stated that Trump desires to be liked and loved, and the role of president may not provide him with the adoration he seeks. Stern believes that Trump's love for Hollywood and the press will be challenged by the negative sentiments directed towards him, which could be detrimental to his mental health.

Stern and Trump have a history of appearances on Stern's radio show, where Trump engaged in crude discussions about women and celebrities. During the campaign, Trump's demeaning comments about women on the show resurfaced in the media. Despite their friendship, Stern is opposed to Trump's politics, and he was surprised when Trump decided to run for president. Stern remembers a time when Trump supported Hillary Clinton and questions the sincerity of Trump's shift to the conservative side.

Stern also suggested that Trump ran for president to secure a better contract for "The Apprentice" from NBC. He added that Trump is still upset about losing the election and is investigating voter fraud to hand the presidency back to Clinton. Stern's concerns about Trump's mental health and the impact of the presidency on him are based on Trump's desire for approval and his history of enjoying the Hollywood and media scene.

The 3-year-old girl Sherin Mathews, who went missing in Richardson, Texas, on October 7, 2017, has not been found as of October 12, 2017. Her parents, Wesley and Sini Mathews, have hired attorneys and are no longer cooperating with the police investigation. The girl was last seen at 3 a.m. on Saturday by her father, who told investigators that he directed her to stand by a tree outside their home after she did not drink her milk. He reported her missing five hours later. Wesley Mathews was arrested on a child endangerment charge and was released on bond, while Sini Mathews has been described as "distraught" by her attorney. An FBI Evidence Response team has been processing the family's home, and the search for the girl has expanded beyond the immediate neighborhood. The girl's 4-year-old sister was removed from the family's custody by Child Protective Services. The Amber Alert for Sherin Mathews was discontinued on Monday, but could be reactivated in the future.

The Los Angeles City Council voted to raise the city's minimum wage to $15 an hour by July 2020, making it the largest city in the U.S. to adopt such a measure. The decision is part of a broader national effort to address poverty, led by labor unions and Democratic politicians seeking to address income inequality. The new wage will affect workers and businesses throughout the city, with the minimum wage increasing to $10.50 in July 2016, and incrementally every year until it reaches $15 in July 2020. For small businesses with 25 or fewer employees, the wage hike will come on a modified schedule, with the incremental increases starting in July 2017 and the minimum wage reaching $15 by July 2021.

The move toward a higher minimum wage has been met with criticism from business groups, who warn that the mandate will force employers to lay off workers or leave the city altogether. Ruben Gonzalez, the Los Angeles Area Chamber of Commerce's senior vice president for public policy and political affairs, predicted that many businesses would absorb their new labor costs by laying off employees, reducing work hours, or moving out of the city entirely. Councilman Mitchell Englander, the council's only Republican, cast the lone opposing vote, stating that the council action could "make it impossible for entire industries to do business" in Los Angeles.

The minimum wage increase follows months of public debate and lobbying, with the stakes for low-wage workers reflected in testimony from workers such as Juan Moran, a line cook in Little Tokyo, who stated that the current statewide minimum wage of $9 per hour isn't enough to live on. The campaign to raise the minimum wage has become a focus of Democrats seeking to revive their party's focus on income inequality, and once Los Angeles' wage hike is finalized, the city will join other West Coast cities that have enacted higher minimum wages in the last two years. New York City and Washington, D.C., are also weighing $15-an-hour minimum wage proposals.

The shift toward raising the minimum wage by local lawmakers comes at a time when the fight for $15 movement has swelled into the largest protest by low-wage workers in U.S. history. On 15 April, some 60,000 workers in more than 200 U.S. cities took part in the Fight for $15 demonstrations. Many of them were low-wage employees of companies like Walmart and McDonald’s, which have since pledged to increase their workers’ pay by $1-$2 an hour, a raise activists said is still not enough.

The federally mandated minimum wage has stayed at $7.25 since June 2009, while the unemployment rate has dropped to 5.4% – a seven-year low – and the number of jobless claims is at a 15-year low. President Barack Obama previously called on Congress to raise it to $10.10, and Democrats, led by Washington senator Patty Murray and Congressman Bobby Scott, have introduced a bill that would raise federal minimum wage to $12 an hour by 2020.

The article discusses the current state of the Indianapolis Colts and the future of quarterback Peyton Manning, who missed the entire 2011 season due to neck injuries. The Colts finished the season with the worst record in the NFL, securing the No. 1 pick in the draft next April. Manning, who is under contract with the Colts, is currently in the process of rehabilitating from his neck surgeries and is hopeful to return to the field next season. The team is expected to draft Stanford quarterback Andrew Luck with the No. 1 pick, which could potentially signal the end of Manning's time with the Colts. The article also mentions the New England Patriots, who clinched home-field advantage throughout the AFC playoffs with a 49-21 win over the Buffalo Bills, and the Saints, who set several NFL and club records in their 45-17 victory over the Panthers. The Jaguars also made headlines by clinching the NFL rushing title and breaking Fred Taylor's single-season franchise record, as well as securing the top pick in the draft for the Colts. The Titans, Texans, Dolphins, Packers, Bears, Eagles, and 49ers also had notable games during the final week of the NFL regular season.

On Monday, an avalanche struck a group of 52 students and 11 teachers from seven high schools during a three-day mountaineering expedition near the Nasu Onsen resort, 93 miles north of Tokyo. The incident resulted in the death of seven students and one teacher, and over 40 injuries, two of whom are in critical condition. The avalanche occurred around 8:30 a.m., as the group was training to walk in the accumulated snow, which had reached over 1 ft (30 cm) in the Nasu highlands between midnight and 9 a.m.

The police are investigating whether the deaths resulted from professional negligence given the extreme conditions at the time. The training took place about 500 meters from their hotel at an altitude of 1,300 meters. The avalanche occurred on the upper part of the slope. The incident follows heavy snowfall and avalanche warnings in the area.

Rescue efforts were hampered by bad weather and heavy snowfall, with the Japanese Self-Defense Force assisting in the disaster response. The prime minister, Shinzō Abe, said the government would ensure the rescue was a top priority. The Nasu Onsen family ski resort, which has two lifts and one rope-tow, ended its ski season on March 20.

In a separate incident in neighboring Fukushima prefecture, a 70-year-old man was found unconscious after an avalanche on Monday afternoon. He had been climbing Mount Adatara with a 64-year-old man who was unhurt, NHK reported. The region had experienced an increase in unusual snow in recent days despite it being late March, which combined with rising temperatures increased the avalanche risk.

The deputy director of the White House's Office of National Drug Control Policy, Michael Botticelli, admitted during a House Oversight Committee hearing that marijuana is less deadly than alcohol. However, he maintained that marijuana is not a benign drug. In response to questions from Rep. Gerry Connolly (D-VA), Botticelli acknowledged that the number of deaths from marijuana overdoses is very rare, contrasting this with the high number of deaths from prescription drugs and alcohol-related causes. Despite President Obama's recent comments supporting state-based efforts to legalize marijuana, the administration still opposes these efforts. The administration maintains that marijuana is a harmful drug under the Controlled Substances Act, and the Department of Justice's responsibility to enforce this act remains unchanged. The hearing highlighted the ongoing conflict between state and federal laws regarding marijuana, with 22 states and the District of Columbia having approved marijuana for medical or recreational use. The D.C. city council recently voted to decriminalize marijuana possession, putting Congress in a difficult position as they must decide whether to intervene or not. Some Democrats defended Obama's recent remarks, citing concerns about the disparate impact of federal marijuana enforcement policies on minorities.

Engineers at the University of Twente in the Netherlands have developed a sperm-like robot that can be controlled using magnets. The robot, named "MagnetoSperm," is inspired by the movement of sperm cells and is made from a flexible polymer with a metal-coated head. The team was able to make the robot "swim" forward and steer it towards a fixed point using a magnetic field no stronger than a fridge magnet. The researchers hope that this technology could be useful in medical and manufacturing applications, such as targeted drug delivery and in vitro fertilization. The study was published in the journal Applied Physics Letters. The robots, which are about six times longer than a human sperm, can move at up to 0.5 body lengths per second, but the researchers are working on making them smaller and faster. The researchers believe that the use of an external magnetic field to control the motion of the robots could be useful for assembling objects on the nanoscale and microscale. The study's first author, Dr Islam Khalil, said that "MagnetoSperm can be used to manipulate and assemble objects at these scales, using an external source of magnetic field to control its motion." Dr Matthew Baker, who studies molecular motors at the Victor Chang Cardiac Research Institute in Sydney, called the work "very cool," but noted that the tiny contraptions are not robots in the traditional sense, as the magnetic field is doing most of the work.

Liverpool manager Rafael Benitez has turned to a Serbian horse placenta healer, Marijana Kovacevic, to address the club's injury crisis, with Glen Johnson and Fabio Aurelio flying to Belgrade for treatment. The controversial healer has gained fame for her unorthodox methods, which involve using fluids derived from horse placentas and electrolysis. Johnson and Aurelio are doubtful for the key game against Manchester City, with Johnson carrying an injury since before the Champions League game against Lyons in November. Kovacevic charges €3,000 for three days of treatment and has treated several Premier League stars, including Robin van Persie of Arsenal. Liverpool's Yossi Benayoun and Albert Riera have also visited Kovacevic in the past few weeks, as well as three Manchester City players. Johnson is the first English player to be identified as a patient of Kovacevic, and there is no indication as to whether Steven Gerrard, who also has a groin problem, has visited her. The Serbian Football Federation has expressed concerns about Kovaceziv's methods and has made discreet enquiries about bringing her in-house. Liverpool have won only once in their last nine games.

In Kolkata, India, a Jet Airways plane undergoing routine cleaning revealed two hidden lunch boxes in the toilets containing 12 gold bars each, causing a bomb scare and subsequent smuggling investigation. The gold bars, estimated to be worth 73.68 million rupees ($1.18 million), were suspected to be from Dubai, where the plane usually operates between the gold trading hub and Mumbai, India's largest gold market. This incident is part of a growing trend of gold smuggling into India, due to the government's increased import duty and restrictions. Customs officials believe that they catch less than 10% of the smuggling activities, and a revenue intelligence officer stated that it is impossible to keep a check on the numerous operating groups. The finance minister acknowledged a slight increase in smuggling due to the new measures, but insisted that no one can carry more than 5 kg of gold undetected. Investigations are ongoing, with airline and airport staff being questioned, and crews are now on alert for passengers spending unusual amounts of time in the toilets.

The case of Shana Grice, a 19-year-old woman from Portslade, East Sussex, who was found dead in her home last August, is currently being heard at Lewes Crown Court. The prosecution alleges that Michael Lane, 27, murdered Grice after a history of stalking and harassment.

Grice had contacted the police several times over a period of months, reporting incidents such as being followed, receiving unwanted flowers, and finding a note on her new boyfriend's car. However, in March, she was given a fixed penalty notice for failing to disclose her past relationship with Lane and for wasting police time with a false report, while no further action was taken against Lane.

On July 9, Lane was cautioned and told to stay away from Grice after he let himself into her home to watch her sleep. The next day, Grice reported receiving several calls from a withheld number, including one with heavy breathing, but the case was left on file with no further inquiries. On July 12, Grice reported being followed by Lane, but the incident was treated as low risk.

On the day of Grice's death, Lane admitted to entering her home and having sex with her, but denied any involvement in her murder. He claimed to have found her body but went into shock and did not dial 999 or check whether she was still alive. He also admitted to leaving a note on Grice's boyfriend's car and fitting a tracker device to her car, but denied setting her bedroom on fire.

The trial is ongoing, with Lane denying the murder charge. The case highlights concerns about the police's handling of domestic abuse complaints and the potential for victims to be penalized for reporting incidents.

In the recent primary election held in Oklahoma, incumbent Representative Frank Lucas won with a significant margin of 82.8%, while his opponent, Timothy Ray Murray, received only 5.2% of the votes. However, Murray has announced plans to contest the election results, claiming that Lucas is deceased and has been replaced by a body double.

Murray's allegations, which are detailed on his campaign website, assert that Lucas was executed in Ukraine in 2011. Lucas, who has been in Congress for 20 years, has expressed surprise at these accusations, stating that he finds it shocking to read that he is not who he claims to be.

The Oklahoma State Election Board has confirmed that Murray has until 5 p.m. today to file a formal petition to challenge the election results. The deadline for challenging a candidate's qualifications was on April 15.

The unusual claims made by Murray echo the plot of the 1993 movie "Dave," where a man impersonates the president due to his striking resemblance. Murray, in his defense, asserts that he will never use a body double or artificial intelligence to represent him or his message.

This is not the first time such claims have been made in Oklahoma politics, with Keith Gaddie, a political scientist at the University of Oklahoma, describing it as the "stupidest" he's ever heard. The specifics of Murray's claim have been on his campaign website for some time but gained attention only after the primary.

Stacy Buck, a representative for Lucas, has confirmed that the congressman is alive and has never been to Ukraine. However, the office has chosen not to make further comments at this time.

The new Herman Cain campaign ad, titled "Now is the time for action!", has generated controversy due to its unusual content. The ad features Mark Block, Cain's chief of staff, delivering optimistic statements about the Cain candidacy before taking a drag from a cigarette and puffing out smoke. The smoking scene has sparked debate about its purpose, with theories ranging from a defiant response to past tobacco industry associations, a deliberate attempt to appeal to certain demographics, a viral marketing strategy, or simply an impulsive decision by Cain. However, Mark Block later clarified that there was no deeper meaning to the smoking scene and that it was intended to convey excitement about the campaign. The ad has added to the ongoing debate about Cain's seriousness and staying power as a national candidate, as well as his ability to handle the media spotlight.

In a significant development, two men, Larry Don Patterson and William Lloyd Harbour, aged 65, were arrested in connection with the shotgun slayings of two 13-year-old and 12-year-old girls, Doris Karen Derryberry and Valerie Janice Lane, in California, more than 40 years ago. The arrests were made on September 13, 2016, after DNA evidence found on one of the victims was matched with the suspects. Both men were living in Olivehurst, California, at the time of the crime.

The girls had gone missing on November 12, 1973, after visiting a shopping mall in nearby Linda and failing to return home. Their bodies were found the next day alongside a dirt road in a wooded area near Marysville, north of Sacramento, where they had been shot at close range with a shotgun. The case remained unsolved until March 2014, when an investigator decided to send DNA samples from the cold case for testing. Seven months later, state DOJ technicians reported that the DNA in the semen matched the genetic profiles of the suspects, who had their DNA samples collected due to their past criminal activities.

Both suspects have served prison sentences. Harbour was imprisoned for drug offenses in 1997 and 2003, while Patterson was arrested in 1976 for raping two adult women and again in 2006 for failing to register as a sex offender. The families of the victims, some of whom are now elderly, have endured decades of suffering and grief for not knowing who was responsible for the brutal murders of their loved ones. Both men will face murder charges.

The investigation took more time to reopen due to the age of the case, with several investigators and the pathologist who conducted the autopsy having since died. Patterson was arrested in Oklahoma's Creek County, southwest of Tulsa, while Harbour was arrested after a traffic stop near his home in Olivehurst. The families have requested privacy following the arrests.

The AllOut.org petition aimed at supporting EA, the game publisher, against anti-gay boycott groups, was temporarily taken down due to spam bot attacks. The spam bots added duplicate comments, most of which supported EA, to the petition. The petition had no contact with EA, and the goal of the campaign was to support EA's decision to include LGBT options in their games in the face of opposition. The spam attacks came from anonymous IP addresses, and it is unclear who was behind them. AllOut.org is continuing to investigate and update the campaign page with the correct signature count. The petition was launched as a response to the Family Research Council's bullying of companies and organizations that take a positive stance on gay rights or present positive, affirming images of LGBT people. The petition has received support from gamers all over the world. AllOut.org has also launched another campaign to fight for gay rights in Russia. There is no response from the boycott groups yet, and there is no evidence suggesting that any of the spam was orchestrated by EA or anyone else. The attacks came from anonymous IP addresses, and it is unclear who was behind them. The petition has received support from gamers all over the world.

Sarah Catherine Long, a 41-year-old woman from Davidson, North Carolina, was found dead on July 23 in her townhouse, with a single gunshot wound above her left ear. Initially, the police classified the death as a suicide, but inconsistencies soon emerged. The gun was found in Long's left hand, and she was right-handed. The medical examiner could not definitively determine whether Long died from the gunshot wound, and there was no blood on the hand that would have fired the gun.

Nearly four months later, the authorities are still investigating whether there was foul play in Long's death. The investigation has revealed that Long was having an affair with a married man, William Becker, who came forward after her death and produced documents showing that she had left him everything in her will, totaling nearly $1 million.

Becker was also the first to report Long's death to the police, and neighbors reported seeing him at Long's home on July 19, the last time she was seen alive. One neighbor reported hearing a loud bang.

The police interviewed Long's doctor, who said she only had abnormal cells on her cervix, a diagnosis she had dealt with before and could cure with a minor outpatient procedure. Becker's wife told the police that he may have tried to poison her with a smoothie on May 8.

The police have identified a person of interest in the case, but they cannot disclose any additional details. They have also seized Long's computer, router, and Yahoo Mail account in hopes of recreating the last days of her life. The authorities are awaiting forensic results to determine if Long was drugged and whether gunpowder residue was found on her hands.

In this article, Saudi media outlets Al-Hayat and Sabq mistakenly reported as fact a satirical article by US comedian Andy Borowitz, in which he joked that President Barack Obama would admit to Congress that he is Muslim as a compromise with Republicans. The joke, published on The Borowitz Report and Huffington Post, was intended as a humorous commentary on the ongoing debate over Obama's religious beliefs. Despite Obama's repeated assertions that he is Christian, some Muslims and Republicans in the US suspect him of being secretly Muslim. The Saudi media's serious reporting of the joke highlights the sensitivity and misunderstandings surrounding Obama's religious identity.

Title: Twitter Introduces Location Feature in Tweets and iOS 8 Microwave Charging Hoax Debunked

Twitter has introduced a new feature that allows users to add a location to their tweets. This location data can be turned on or off before each tweet and can be deleted from the user's history. Meanwhile, a recent hoax circulating on social media platforms like Twitter and Reddit has claimed that the newly released iOS 8 allows iPhones to be wirelessly charged in a microwave using a feature called "Wave."

However, Apple has confirmed that this is a hoax, and iPhones should not be microwaved under any circumstances. The fake "Wave" ads have been traced back to a 4chan thread, a platform known for its pranks and hoaxes. This isn't the first time 4chan has attempted such a hoax. Last year, a similar spoof attempted to convince Apple users that iOS 7 would make their phones waterproof.

It is unclear how many people fell for the Wave hoax, but several people tweeted about the feature and later posted photos of fried iPhones and burned microwaves. It is advised to exercise caution when encountering such hoaxes on the internet.

4chan is an online imageboard website where users can post anonymously. It is known for its diverse and often controversial content, ranging from humor and activism to explicit and disturbing content.

The World Health Organization (WHO) has declared Cuba as the first country in the world to stop the transmission of HIV and syphilis from mothers to their babies, marking a significant achievement in global public health. This accomplishment demonstrates the possibility of controlling epidemics of both infections. WHO Director-General Dr. Margaret Chan described this as one of the greatest public health achievements possible, signifying a major victory in the long fight against HIV and sexually transmitted infections.

The transmission of HIV can occur at birth or through breastfeeding if the mother is infected. However, if the mother receives HIV drugs before and after giving birth, and if the newborn is given drugs, the risk falls to less than 1 percent. The WHO estimates that 1.4 million women with HIV become pregnant every year, and without treatment, there's a 45 percent chance they will infect their newborns. In 2013, 67 percent of all pregnant women infected with HIV in low- and middle-income countries were able to get the necessary drugs to protect their babies.

Similarly, stopping syphilis transmission is achievable if women receive antibiotics to treat the infection. Nearly 1 million pregnant women worldwide are infected with syphilis annually, leading to 360,000 babies born dead or dying soon after birth, being born prematurely, or being born infected in 2012.

Cuba's success in eliminating mother-to-child transmission of HIV and syphilis is attributed to its universal access to healthcare, early access to prenatal care, HIV and syphilis testing, and treatment for mothers who test positive. The WHO and the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) started an effort to end congenital transmission of HIV and syphilis in Cuba and other countries in the Americas in 2010. Cuba's achievement should encourage donors and governments to redouble their efforts in the fight against AIDS.

A Minnesota doctor, Dr. Michael Todd Schulenberg, treated Prince twice in the month leading up to his death, including the day before he passed away, and prescribed him medication. The search warrant, which was initially left unsealed, was later sealed after authorities realized the error. The warrant authorized the search and seizure of Prince’s medical records at North Memorial Medical Center in Robbinsdale. Dr. Schulenberg, who no longer works with the health system, had given a statement to deputies, stating that he had treated Prince on April 7 and April 20, and had prescribed him medications to be filled at a Walgreens. The nature of the tests and the medications prescribed were not specified in the warrant.

Investigators returned to Paisley Park, Prince's estate outside Minneapolis, on Tuesday for more than five hours. The warrant also reveals that Kirk Anthony Johnson, a close associate of Prince’s who manages Paisley Park, was present when detectives arrived at the death scene. Johnson had stated that Prince had been treated in the Ridgeview health system for an undescribed illness in 2014 or 2015.

Prescription data is being investigated as authorities look into the means by which Prince received prescription opioids, which are subject to additional federal regulation. The Midwest Medical Examiner’s Office in Anoka is conducting the investigation to determine how Prince died. Results are pending, and neither foul play nor suicide is suspected.

The investigation also involves another doctor, Dr. Howard Kornfeld, who was contacted by Prince's representatives seeking help a day before the superstar was found dead on April 21. The Kornfelds' attorney, William Mauzy, has stated that Dr. Kornfeld sent his son to meet with Prince, but the meeting never took place. The second Minnesota physician, who has not been publicly identified, had cleared his morning calendar to evaluate Prince on the day his body was found, but the appointment never took place.

Dr. Schulenberg's attorney, Amy Conners, declined to comment, citing patient confidentiality. The warrant does not specify what medications were prescribed or whether Prince took them. The results of the investigation are still pending.

The Instant Pot, a Canadian-designed multi-functional cooker, is set to be the top-selling product on Amazon during the Black Friday sales event. The device, which combines the functions of a rice cooker, pressure cooker, steamer, and slow cooker, among others, has gained popularity due to its convenience and efficiency in preparing meals quickly. The inventor, Robert Wang, initially developed the Instant Pot in 2010 to solve the problem of busy families resorting to unhealthy fast food options for dinner. The device has received praise from food experts and has attracted over 750,000 members to its official Facebook group for sharing recipes. The Instant Pot has become a hit, with versions regularly ranking as top sellers in Amazon's rice cooker and electric pressure cooker categories. The device's success is attributed to its ability to make cooking easier and healthier, as well as its affordability and versatility. The Instant Pot has also been praised for its safety features, which prevent novice cooks from burning their food. The company, Double Insight, became profitable in 2012 and has seen significant growth in revenue since then. The Instant Pot has gained a cult-like following, with many users posting about their experiences and sharing recipes on social media. The device has also been used to help people in need during emergencies, such as hurricanes Harvey and Irma. The Instant Pot's success has led to other companies producing similar multi-cookers, with the market showing no signs of slowing down.

International authorities have arrested Orlando Tercero, a 22-year-old man, in connection with the murder of Haley Anderson, a nursing student from Long Island. Tercero, a former boyfriend of Anderson, was arrested in Nicaragua on Tuesday and is being transferred to the prison in El Chipote, about 40 miles southwest of Managua.

Anderson's body was found in a Binghamton off-campus home on Friday, and her death was ruled a homicide on Saturday. The circumstances surrounding her death have not been revealed, but police have stated that Anderson and Tercero had a previous domestic/romantic relationship.

Anderson was a nursing student at the State University of New York at Binghamton and lived about a mile away from the campus. She was last seen alive around 4 a.m. on Thursday and was with her roommates before she went missing.

Authorities suspect that Tercero fled to Nicaragua because he has family there. A warrant is being prepared for Tercero's arrest in the United States. The university has expressed condolences to Anderson's family and friends.

Anderson's death has been a tragic blow to her family in Westbury and her former coworkers at Ralphs Italian Ices. A wake and funeral for Anderson will be held this weekend in her hometown. The investigation is ongoing, and all evidence will be presented to a grand jury. If Tercero is indicted, the district attorney will push for a speedy extradition.

The Indian foreign ministry has lodged a complaint with Saudi Arabian authorities over an alleged brutal attack on a 58-year-old Indian woman, Kasturi Munirathinam, who was working as a domestic helper in Riyadh. According to reports, Munirathinam's right arm was chopped off by her employer when she tried to escape from their house last week. The family of Munirathinam, residing in the southern Indian city of Chennai, has claimed that she was being tortured by her employers and is seeking compensation and help with medical expenses. The Saudi authorities have not yet commented on the incident. Indian Foreign Minister Sushma Swaraj expressed her concern over the incident on Twitter, stating that India would seek justice for the victim and has taken up the matter with the Saudi Foreign Office. The family has also requested the Tamil Nadu state government's financial assistance and the Indian government's help in securing Munirathinam's return to India.

Thousands of men and women from India travel to Arab states every year to work as domestic servants and laborers. The poor treatment and abuse of maids in the Middle East is a familiar issue, as demonstrated by the disturbing story of a young Ethiopian woman who was treated like a slave while working as a domestic helper in Saudi Arabia. This incident comes amidst heightened tensions after a Saudi diplomat in New Delhi was accused of raping maids last month. The Indian government is urging for an independent probe into the incident and seeking severe punishment for the employer if found guilty.

In Dallas, electronic construction signs along Interstate 30 and other locations were hacked, displaying messages targeting the 2016 presidential candidates. The messages included "Donald Trump is a shape-shifting lizard!" and "Bernie for president," in support of Bernie Sanders. Another message read, "Work is canceled. Go back home." The signs, owned by the Texas Department of Transportation (TxDOT), were typically used to inform drivers about road construction. TxDOT stated that the hacked messages bumped warnings to motorists about nearby construction zones and considered it a serious issue that could potentially cause accidents. The signs have since been returned to their normal messages. This incident is not the first of its kind, as similar situations have been reported across the country, with the perpetrators gaining access to the electronic sign's control panel and changing the message it displays. Hacking these roadside signs is considered a third-degree felony, punishable by up to 10 years in prison. TxDOT encourages anyone noticing suspicious activity around portable signs to contact them or local police.

In Arlington, Washington, a massive mudslide occurred on March 23, 2014, leaving at least eight people dead and dozens missing. The slide, about one square mile wide, destroyed numerous homes and a mile-long stretch of Highway 530. Rescuers initially heard voices coming from the debris, but as of Sunday, they had not found any signs of life. The search continued through the night, but hopes of finding survivors dimmed. The slide also critically injured several people, including an infant, and caused significant damage to the surrounding area. Governor Jay Inslee described the scene as "a square mile of total devastation." The cause of the slide is believed to be ground made unstable by recent heavy rainfall. The search for the missing continued, with authorities expressing concern that some may have been unable to escape the slide as it happened. The National Weather Service issued a flash flood watch for the area through Monday afternoon.

On July 6, 2015, a hiker was killed and five others were injured when a section of the Big Four Ice Caves in Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest collapsed. The accident occurred due to the recent heat wave, which weakened the caves, making them extremely dangerous. The collapse was similar to an avalanche, with tons of ice and rock falling near the mouth of the popular caves.

Chloe Jakubowski, an 18-year-old visitor, was one of the people who sought refuge from the heat at the Big Four Ice Caves. She was with friends just inside the cave when they heard a loud crack, followed by ice and debris raining down. Jakubowski and others helped the injured as best they could before emergency services arrived.

Rescue efforts were delayed for nearly 45 minutes due to a lack of cellphone reception in the area. The body of the deceased, who was not identified, remained at the scene on Tuesday morning. Five people—three adults and two juveniles—were taken to area hospitals, with three of them being airlifted due to serious injuries.

The Snohomish County Sheriff's Office warned visitors in May to exercise extreme caution near the ice caves due to the warm weather causing sections of the caves to collapse. The office also stated that access to the caves hasn't been forbidden, as it's a United States Forest Service decision.

This tragic incident marks the first fatality at the ice caves since 2010, when 11-year-old Grace Tam was killed by a boulder of ice that came off the caves while her father was taking photographs. Tam's family sued the U.S. Forest Service, but the lawsuit was dismissed. However, a sign at the trail viewpoint now serves as a reminder of Grace's death.

Recovery efforts will continue, and the area around the Big Four ice caves will remain closed until search and rescue teams can assess the safety of the caves and recover the deceased victim of the collapse. Temperatures reached 80 degrees in the area of the caves on the day of the accident, contributing to the unstable conditions.

The document presents a campaign launched by students, staff, professors, and alumni from Point Loma Nazarene University (PLNU) to raise $40,000 for The Beauty for Ashes Fund at PLNU. The fund aims to provide college education to survivors of human trafficking, a growing issue both in the United States and worldwide. The campaign emphasizes the importance of education in the long-term rehabilitation of survivors and encourages donations to support tuition, room, and board for accepted students. The funds will also cover student vocational discernment and administrative support. The campaign has already started and survivors are in the process of applying. The funds raised, whether reaching the goal of $40,000 or not, will go to the Beauty for Ashes Fund at PLNU. The campaign is part of a broader movement to end modern-day slavery in America, with PLNU being an institution that has always focused on reaching the marginalized. The campaign has received media attention and offers various perks, such as handmade soap and artwork, for donors. The campaign encourages people to help by spreading the word, getting involved with PLNU, or contacting BeautyforAshes@pointloma.edu for more information.

The United States conducted airstrikes against Islamic State (ISIS) targets in northern Iraq on Friday, marking the first direct military action against the extremist group. The airstrikes targeted ISIS artillery units and convoys advancing on the Kurdish regional capital of Irbil, as well as a mortar position. The airstrikes were in response to ISIS's seizure of key infrastructure and towns, forcing hundreds of thousands to flee for their lives.
