The comparisons between Romney's trip and Obama's visit to Europe four years ago are stark, with Obama's successful wooing of a quarter of a million people in Berlin contrasting with Romney's missteps in London.

The Gulf of Mexico's low-oxygen "dead zone" this year covers an area of 5,052 square miles, approximately the size of Connecticut but smaller than the 2013 dead zone. The finding was made by a team of scientists led by Louisiana Universities Marine Consortium Director Nancy Rabalais. The dead zone is primarily caused by excessive nitrogen, mainly from Midwest agricultural runoff. The five-year average size of the low-oxygen area is 5,543 square miles, which is almost three times larger than the target set by a federal/state Mississippi River Gulf of Mexico Watershed Nutrient Task Force in 2001. The target was reconfirmed in 2008 but has never been met.

The Mississippi River discharge levels and associated nutrient data, supplied in May by the USGS, pointed to an average size hypoxia area based on the inputs that fuel mid-summer's dead zone algal growth. If heavy rains in the Upper Midwest in June and the record high nitrate concentration in the Mississippi River at Baton Rouge on July 18 had coincided with a later survey, the area would have been larger.

This is the 30th year that Rabalais' LUMCON team has measured the size of the Louisiana dead zone. Louisiana State University and Florida State University scientists participated in this year's cruise. The research was paid for by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, the Environmental Protection Agency's Gulf of Mexico Program, and the National Science Foundation.

The size of the low-oxygen area drew an immediate response from several environmental groups that have sued the Environmental Protection Agency in an attempt to get the agency to adopt regulations that would reduce nutrients flowing into the Mississippi by adopting numeric standards for the amount of nitrogen flowing in the river.

The Gulf dead zone, which fluctuates in size but measured 5,052 square miles this summer, is exceeded only by a similar zone in the Baltic Sea around Finland. The elongated Gulf zone typically hugs the Louisiana coastline from the Mississippi River Delta to the state's border with Texas, and some years extending offshore of Texas and Mississippi.

The scientists found that the discharge of water from the Mississippi this year was near the long-term average since 1935, and that there was a slightly lower nitrate concentration measured this year at Baton Rouge. However, the amount of water flowing out of the river just before the three-week measurement period was slightly above average, and the nitrate concentration had reached a near-record high. The late burst of nutrient loading and freshwater discharge generated lush conditions for phytoplankton growth off the Mississippi and Atchafalaya rivers. They added that the effects of that growth were exacerbated by recent wind and current directions that pushed Atchafalaya River water to the east, where it joined with Mississippi River water between the two river mouths.

The continuous flow of nutrients, year after year, also results in some of the nitrogen being stored in sediments, where it can be released in later years, adding to the nutrients causing algae blooms. Reducing the size of the hypoxic area requires changes in land use, and pilot projects and recent developments have demonstrated that this can be done for crops with benefits for farm communities, soil health, erosion reduction, and without compromising yields or profit.

The article discusses the aftermath of fatal accidents involving General Motors (GM) vehicles with faulty ignition switches, linked to at least 13 deaths. The families of the victims have settled with GM, although the exact terms of the settlements are confidential. Some families have expressed dissatisfaction with the process, claiming that their loved ones were unfairly blamed for the accidents.

In response to the accidents, GM has pointed to factors such as high speeds, failure to wear seatbelts, and alcohol use as potential causes. However, The New York Times found that alcohol was only a factor in four of the ten accidents identified.

GM has not yet announced a plan for compensating the families of the deceased or other potential victims. Federal safety regulators believe that more than 13 lives may have been lost due to the defect. Kenneth R. Feinberg, a victim-compensation expert hired by GM, is expected to unveil a plan for addressing the thousands of claims filed against the automaker in the coming weeks.

One of the victims was Mikale Erickson, who died in a 2004 accident in Texas while riding in a Saturn Ion. His fiancee, Candice Anderson, was driving and was charged with manslaughter. Anderson learned in late May that Mikale's death was one of the 13 linked to the faulty ignition switch. Mikale's mother, Rhonda Erickson, has not received any communication from GM and believes the company owes her an apology.

The article also highlights the emotional impact of the accidents on the families involved. Anderson, who was convicted of criminal negligent homicide, has carried the guilt for Mikale's death for many years. Both Anderson and Mikale's family are hoping to get more answers from GM's internal investigation.

In a recent incident, Comcast, a major cable provider, has come under fire for changing the billing name of a customer, Ricardo Brown, to "Asshole Brown" following a dispute with his wife, Lisa Brown, over canceling their cable service. The disagreement occurred when Lisa was referred to a retention specialist who apparently took offense to being told "no." Comcast has since apologized for the incident, confirming that the name change was unacceptable and inappropriate, and is conducting a thorough investigation to determine what happened. The company is also offering the Browns a full refund for the past two years of service. This is not the first time Comcast has been criticized for its customer service, as the company is known for making it difficult to cancel accounts and retaining an army of retention specialists whose job is to keep customers from signing off. In 2014, journalist Ryan Block recorded a Kafkaesque conversation he had with a Comcast retention specialist from hell, which has been listened to nearly 6 million times.

This summary discusses a new study comparing relational aggression in boys and girls, which is defined as harming others through damaging or manipulating peer relationships. The study, led by Pamela Orpinas, found that significantly more boys than girls exhibited a pattern of high relational aggression in the early years of the study, with 66.7% of students reporting high aggression being male.

Dr. Orpinas believes that this finding challenges the common perception that girls are more socially nasty than boys. She suggests that schools and parents need to recognize relational aggression isn't a single-gender phenomenon and should focus on prevention programs for both boys and girls.

Rosalind Wiseman, author of "Queen Bees and Wannabes" and "Masterminds and Wingmen," argues that boys' social lives and emotional well-being are often overlooked. She believes that adults should give boys a language for talking about their worries and experiences, and model positive behavior, including not being relationally aggressive themselves.

Both Dr. Orpinas and Ms. Wiseman emphasize the importance of making it cool to be positive and caring about other kids, and of emphasizing the positive behavior exhibited by children rather than focusing solely on aggression. They argue that this can help combat the problem of relational aggression and promote a more positive social environment for children.

The Los Angeles Times won the Pulitzer Prize for public service and feature photography in 2011. The public service award was given for the newspaper's investigation into the corruption in Bell, a city in Los Angeles County. The investigation revealed that Bell officials secretly enriched themselves with extravagant salaries and benefits while illegally raising taxes on residents. As a result, criminal charges were filed against former Bell City Manager Robert Rizzo, who received an $800,000 salary and hundreds of thousands of dollars more in perks. The Bell coverage also received the Selden Ring Award for investigative reporting, the American Society of News Editors' distinguished writing award for local accountability reporting, the Investigative Reporters and Editors' top honor, and the George Polk Award for local reporting.

Barbara Davidson, a photographer for the Los Angeles Times, won the feature photography award for her images of victims of violent crime in South Los Angeles, Compton, and Watts. Her work told an "intimate story of innocent victims trapped in the city's crossfire of deadly gang violence."

In addition to the Pulitzer Prize, the Los Angeles Times also won the Selden Ring Award for investigative reporting, the American Society of News Editors' distinguished writing award for local accountability reporting, the Investigative Reporters and Editors' top honor, and the George Polk Award for local reporting for their coverage of the Bell scandal.

The Pulitzer Prize for fiction was awarded to Jennifer Egan for "A Visit from the Goon Squad," and the prize for drama was awarded to Bruce Norris for "Clybourne Park." The prize for history was awarded to Eric Foner for "The Fiery Trial: Abraham Lincoln and American Slavery," and the prize for biography was awarded to Ron Chernow for "Washington: A Life." The prize for poetry was awarded to Kay Ryan for "The Best of It: New and Selected Poems," and the prize for general nonfiction was awarded to Siddhartha Mukherjee for "The Emperor of All Maladies: A Biography of Cancer." The prize for music was awarded to Zhou Long for "Madame White Snake."

The Washington Post won the prize for breaking news photography for its coverage of the Haiti earthquake, and the Wall Street Journal won the prize for editorial writing for Joseph Rago's editorials challenging President Obama's healthcare reform legislation. The Boston Globe's art critic, Sebastian Smee, won the criticism prize for his "vivid and exuberant writing about art." The nonprofit investigative news site ProPublica earned the national reporting prize for coverage of the nation's economic meltdown by reporters Jesse Eisinger and Jake Bernstein. It was the first Pulitzer given for reporting that appeared only online, not in print.

On a recent flight from Beijing to Melbourne, a passenger experienced a terrifying incident when her battery-operated headphones exploded mid-flight, causing burns to her face, hand, and singeing her hair. The Australian Transport Safety Bureau (ATSB) has issued a warning about the potential risks of using battery-powered devices during flights, citing the incident as a reminder of the dangers.

The woman, whose identity has been concealed by the ATSB, was listening to music on her personal headphones when she fell asleep about two hours into the flight. She woke up to a loud explosion and felt burning on her face. She grabbed her face, causing the headphones to go around her neck. The headphones continued to burn, sparking and producing small amounts of fire. Flight attendants quickly poured a bucket of water on the headphones, but the battery and cover were melted and stuck to the floor of the aircraft.

For the remainder of the flight, passengers endured the smell of melted plastic, burnt electronics, and burnt hair. The woman's hand was also burnt, and passengers coughed and choked throughout the rest of the flight.

The ATSB has assessed that the batteries in the device likely caught fire. The ATSB reminds passengers using battery-powered devices to keep them in an approved stowage, unless in use. Spare batteries must be in carry-on baggage, not checked baggage. If a passenger's smartphone or other device falls into the seat gap, they should locate their device before moving powered seats. If they cannot locate their device, they should refrain from moving their seat and immediately contact a cabin crew member.

This incident follows several other incidents involving battery-powered devices catching fire on planes, such as Samsung Galaxy phones and hoverboards. Samsung recalled their Galaxy Note 7s due to faulty batteries that were catching fire. In another incident, a phone battery caused a fire on a Qantas plane last year when the phone became stuck in a reclining chair and was crushed.

Lithium ion batteries, commonly used in phones and handheld electronics, use highly flammable liquid that can explode if a battery short circuits. Poorly constructed or older model lithium batteries are more likely to short circuit, but over-heating and over-charging can also potentially cause an explosion in a 'perfect' battery. The chance of a device exploding is "something like one in 10 million," according to Ken Boyce from American safety consulting and certification company UL.

The Civil Aviation and Safety Authority has more information about traveling safely with batteries and portable power packs. The ATSB is currently investigating the incident and will provide more information as it becomes available.

In a shocking turn of events, local photographer Muhammad Malik stumbled upon the aftermath of a deadly shooting near the Empire State Building this morning. He quickly shared a graphic image of one victim on Instagram, captioning it with a quote from rapper Nas. On Facebook, he posted "MAN DOWN! SHOTS FIRED!". As news organizations sought to use the image, Malik initially appeared to capitalize on the situation, posting on Twitter about receiving calls from various media outlets and using the hashtag "#chaching". However, when contacted by Daily Intel, Malik expressed remorse, stating that he was not seeking monetary gain and found the situation too overwhelming. He also asserted that his actions were not intended to be offensive. The incident serves as a reminder of the complex ethical considerations that arise in the wake of tragic events, particularly in the digital age.

Mickey Rooney's will, which leaves his estate to a stepson and nothing to his wife or other children, is being challenged by his widow, Jan Rooney, and his eight biological children. In a court filing, Jan Rooney's lawyer, Eugene Belous, claims that the will contains a "blatant misstatement" about agreements between her, the actor, and his conservator. The challenge argues that Rooney's rights as a surviving spouse were not waived in an agreement signed after the couple separated in 2012.

Rooney's stepson, Mark Rooney, who was the actor's caretaker during his final two years, is named as the sole heir to his estate in the will. The will was signed just weeks before Rooney's death at 93.

Rooney's court-appointed conservator, Michael Augustine, has stated that the challenge of the will is "totally without merit." Augustine also said that Rooney's widow, who was separated from her husband for the last two years of his life, is seeking public attention with the challenge.

Although Rooney disinherited his children, his wife, and all but one of her children in the will, court papers suggest there is not much in his estate to fight over. His personal property is valued at just $18,000 despite an unmatched 90-year film career.

A hearing is scheduled for Monday to start the process of probating the actor's will. An attorney for Mickey Rooney's children is also contesting the will, according to Belous. The will signed by Rooney on March 11, 2014, left the entire estate to stepson Mark Rooney.

In a controversial move, Kellyanne Conway, a senior advisor to President Donald Trump, promoted Ivanka Trump's clothing line on Fox News on February 9, 2017, urging viewers to "go buy Ivanka's stuff." This action appears to violate ethics rules that prohibit federal employees from using their public office to endorse products. The White House later stated that Conway had been "counseled" on the matter, but did not elaborate.

The promotion of Ivanka Trump's brand came after President Trump criticized Nordstrom for dropping his daughter's clothing line on Twitter. The hashtag #BuyIvanka began circulating on Twitter in response to Conway's comments.

Chris Lu, a former deputy secretary of Labor, tweeted a screenshot of the federal ethics law that he believes Conway broke with her comments. The law states that an employee shall not use his public office for his own private gain, for the endorsement of any product, service, or enterprise, or for the private gain of friends, relatives, or persons with whom the employee is affiliated in a nongovernmental capacity.

A bipartisan letter was sent to the Office of Government Ethics (OGE) on February 9, 2017, asking that office to determine whether Conway should receive a stronger disciplinary response, including suspension, demotion, or dismissal.

Conway appeared on Fox News again on February 9, 2017, and when asked about the uproar, said, "I'm not going to comment on that... I have nothing more to say about it." She said that the president "supports me 100%."

The OGE did not return a request for comment, but it said in a series of tweets that it was fielding an "extraordinary volume" of phone calls, emails, and web traffic from citizens in response to "recent events." The ethics office stressed that it does not have enforcement power, like Congress or the FBI. When it learns of possible ethics violations, it said, it contacts the relevant agency and provides guidance.

This report was updated at 10:06 a.m. on February 9, 2017.

The leaked photographs from Stephen Paddock's hotel room at the Mandalay Bay in Las Vegas reveal a jumble of high-powered weapons, dozens of scattered shell casings, a possible note, and Paddock's corpse. The images suggest that Paddock killed himself with a shot to the head before a police SWAT team stormed his room. The leaked images, some of which are too graphic to publish, provide a striking insight into the sheer number of weapons Paddock had amassed in the days before he opened fire.

Las Vegas investigators are concerned about the source of the leaks and have opened an internal investigation. In the past, leakers from police departments have faced disciplinary action, including job loss, without facing criminal prosecution. For instance, in 2009, a Los Angeles Police Department officer was fired for leaking photographs of pop star Rihanna during an ongoing investigation.

Police have recovered 23 guns from inside the hotel and believe Paddock used 10 suitcases to take them up to his room. The images also show shell casings and guns mounted on tripods. The leaked images also show Paddock's body, his legs dressed in dark trousers and slip-on shoes. On a table close to his feet, there appears to be a roll of electrical tape, along with what may be a sheet of paper and a pen. At this stage, police have not mentioned recovering any sort of note.

Las Vegas sheriff Joe Lombardo has said that Paddock may have been 'radicalized' and that his girlfriend, Marilou Danley, who returned to the US from a visit to Asia, may be able to provide some insights. Officials met her when she arrived in Los Angeles and whisked her out of a side door in a wheelchair. On Tuesday, Lombardo told reporters he hoped and expected she would provide information about Paddock that would be of help to them.

Investigators are urging patience as they work to process the room and identify a motive for Paddock's decision to open fire on a country music concert attended by 22,000 people.

The New Zealand government has been accused of implementing a mass metadata surveillance system in 2012 and 2013, despite public assurances to the contrary. Edward Snowden, a former NSA analyst and whistleblower, provided documents that show the government worked in secret to exploit a new internet surveillance law to initiate the program. The documents indicate that the GCSB, with ongoing NSA cooperation, implemented Phase I of the mass surveillance program called "Speargun" at some point in 2012 or early 2013. This phase involved the covert installation of "cable access" equipment, which appears to refer to surveillance of the country's main undersea cable link, the Southern Cross cable. The cable carries the vast majority of internet traffic between New Zealand and the rest of the world, and mass collection from it would mark the greatest expansion of GCSB spying activities in decades.

The documents also show that the GCSB provided mass surveillance data to the NSA and that Prime Minister John Key was aware of this fact. Key has since admitted that the GCSB did plan a program of mass surveillance aimed at its own citizens, but claims that he ultimately rejected the program before implementation. However, the documents indicate that Speargun was not just an idea that stalled at the discussion stage, but a system that the GCSB actively worked to implement.

The revelations have raised questions about the ethics and credibility of the Key government, as the new surveillance planning took place at high levels of the government and expressly intended to use the new surveillance law as its basis even as Key himself insisted that the law provided no such authority. The disclosure comes just days before New Zealand's national election, and the anti-surveillance Internet Party, which is predicted to win several seats in Parliament, has organized a "Moment of Truth" event to discuss the revelations. The documents are likely to further fuel controversy surrounding the Key government, which has been embroiled in a scandal involving illegal GCSB spying and allegations of dirty tricks against political opponents.

In Santa Monica, three women - Monica Kenyon, Sonia Ulrich, and Marla Saltzer - are being hailed as heroes after they prevented a man from drugging a woman at the FIG restaurant on Thursday. The women noticed the man acting suspiciously and saw him put an unknown substance in the woman's drink. They alerted the restaurant staff, who confirmed the women's story and notified the police. The man was arrested with multiple vials of a clear substance on him. The women's quick action and the restaurant's support were credited with saving the woman from being drugged. The incident has sparked a wave of gratitude and support from people who have shared their own stories of similar incidents. The women's Facebook post, which includes a "Charlie's Angels"-style photo, has already been shared over 70,000 times.

Two potential challengers, Nancy Mace and Lee Bright, have announced their intentions to run against U.S. Senator Lindsey Graham in South Carolina's Republican primary next year. Mace, a businesswoman and the first woman to graduate from The Citadel, and Bright, a truck company owner, aim to challenge Graham's third six-year term in the Senate. They join Richard Cash, who lost a 2010 Republican congressional runoff, in the race.

Political analysts suggest that a large field of libertarian opponents could help Graham by splitting Tea Party votes among his challengers. Graham's campaign has $6.3 million on hand, and he has started a super PAC to support his re-election bid. An anti-Graham political organization was also formed last month to defeat the senator.

Mace plans to announce her campaign at a GOP breakfast in Goose Creek on Saturday. She has been mulling a run against Graham for months, as he has been targeted by Tea Party followers for his willingness to compromise with Democrats on some issues. Bright, who has a voting record that reflects his commitment to limited government, plans to enter the race within the next few weeks.

Cash, another challenger, said the additional candidates will bring more interest into the race. He is not just running against Graham but wants to share his positive message of "hope and heritage." The Graham campaign declined comment until the candidates formally announce their runs.

Mace faces a tough challenge in going up against Graham, a seasoned politician. However, a good showing could propel her to another future office, such as the state Legislature. Bright will run a very aggressive campaign, experts said. However, a Bright candidacy could anger libertarians who prefer Mace, popular in some circles because she broke the gender barrier at South Carolina's previously all-male military college.

Graham's positions on some issues have grown more conservative as his 2014 re-election drew closer. For instance, he has launched several attacks against the Obama administration for its handling of the attack on the U.S. diplomatic mission in Benghazi, Libya. Some money could come from outside the state, such as from the Club for Growth, said Mark Tomkins, a University of South Carolina political scientist. "Do the Koch brothers come in?" Tomkins said of the influential Midwestern businessmen known for backing conservative candidates. "I'm not sure they are not pleased with Graham. There's a lot of money out there none of us know about."

Clare Bronfman, an heiress to the Seagram's liquor fortune, was arrested on racketeering charges in connection with the investigation of NXIVM, a self-improvement organization accused of branding some of its female followers and forcing them into unwanted sex. Bronfman, who appeared in court wearing flip-flops and a T-shirt, pledged a $100 million bond to ensure her return to court. U.S. District Judge Nicholas Garaufis set the high amount after hearing prosecutors label her a flight risk and learning she has a net worth of roughly $200 million. Bronfman is accused of taking a number of steps to help NXIVM's founder and leader, Keith Raniere, exercise control over members of the upstate New York group, including identity theft, interception of electronic communications, and money laundering. She was part of an "inner circle" of loyalists who "committed a broad range of serious crimes from identity theft and obstruction of justice to sex trafficking, all to promote and protect Raniere and NXIVM," U.S. Attorney Richard Donoghue said in a statement. Raniere was arrested in Mexico this year and was brought to the U.S. to face charges that he, along with an adherent, the TV actress Allison Mack, coerced followers into becoming slaves to senior members. In a statement, a lawyer for Bronfman, Susan Necheles, called the charges "the result of government overreaching and charging an individual with crimes just because the government disagrees with some beliefs taught by NXIVM and held by Clare." Also arrested Tuesday were Nancy Salzman, who was the organization's longtime president; her daughter, Lauren Salzman; and a former bookkeeper for the group, Kathy Russell. All three were released on bail without entering pleas. Despite criticism for years by ex-followers who called NXIVM a cult and a pyramid scheme, the organization's intense self-improvement classes had, at one point, earned it thousands of adherents, including some with Hollywood ties. They included Nicki Clyne, an actress who appeared on "Battlestar Galactica"; Bronfman's sister Sara Bronfman; a son of former Mexican president Carlos Salinas de Gortari; and India Oxenberg, a daughter of "Dynasty" actress Catherine Oxenberg. In an indictment, prosecutors say Mack helped Raniere recruit women to a secret sub-society within NXIVM whose members were branded by way of a surgical tool with a symbol that resembled his initials. Women were expected to be subservient to "masters," prosecutors said, including giving in to demands for sex. The arrest of Bronfman, who has long been affiliated with NXIVM, wasn't a surprise. At a court hearing in June, a judge rejected an attempt to get Raniere released on $10 million bail paid for by Bronfman after prosecutors labeled her a co-conspirator. In earlier court filings, the government detailed how Bronfman gave away tens of millions of dollars of her fortune to support Raniere and his group, including paying for private air travel at a cost of $65,000 a flight. It also said Bronfman has "paid for numerous lawyers to bring suits against Nxivm critics." Raniere, Mack, and some of the other defendants were expected to appear together at a pretrial hearing on Wednesday in Brooklyn.

The survey conducted by Nielsen and Sony Electronics ranked the most impactful television events of the past 50 years based on consumer recall, discussion, and location of viewing. The Sept. 11 terrorist attacks in 2001 were deemed the most memorable event, followed by Hurricane Katrina in 2005, the O.J. Simpson verdict in 1995, the Challenger space shuttle explosion in 1986, and the death of Osama bin Laden in 2011. Other notable events included Princess Diana’s funeral in 1997, the Oklahoma City bombing in 1995, Barack Obama's Election Night speech in 2008, and the John F. Kennedy assassination in 1963. The study found that television news events had a greater impact on viewers' lives compared to entertainment events, such as the final episode of "M-A-S-H" or the "Who shot J.R.?" episode of "Dallas." Men and women agreed on the three most impactful events, but had different rankings for other events, such as the death of Whitney Houston and the bombing of Baghdad. The study also revealed that the passage of time has diluted the impact of some events for younger generations, while age played a significant role in the ranking of events. The study was based on an online questionnaire of 1,077 adults and could serve as a baseline for future research on the impact of television on viewers.

Katie Couric has announced her departure from CBS Evening News, effective June 4, after a tenure of nearly five years. Couric is yet to reveal her future plans, stating that she is exploring a format for more diverse storytelling. There are reports that she is in talks with CBS about a daytime syndicated show and possibly continuing with the news division. However, ABC seems to be a strong contender for Couric's services, offering a talk show and wider exposure across its network news platforms, including the 2012 presidential election coverage and prime-time specials. NBC is no longer in the running. CBS is expected to announce Scott Pelley of 60 Minutes as Couric's successor. Couric's inability to move CBS Evening News out of third place in the ratings may have contributed to her decision to leave. The exact details of Couric's future are still being discussed.

The Internet Archive is working on a project to preserve web pages as they are created and archive pages that they refer to. This aims to fix broken links on the web by replacing them with links to the archived versions of the pages. The project is called "No More 404" and is currently being implemented on supported websites.

Meanwhile, Abby Wambach, a US soccer player, and Glennon Doyle Melton, a Christian author and blogger, have announced their engagement. Melton shared a photo of herself with Wambach on Facebook, captioning it with a message about their decision to hold hands forever. Wambach also shared the same photo on Instagram.

Melton announced her divorce from husband Craig Melton just three months ago, and Wambach announced her divorce from her wife of three years, Sarah Huffman, in April following an April DUI arrest that forced Wambach to confront her struggles with substance abuse.

Melton and Wambach have been regularly featured on each other's social media pages since their relationship was revealed. On Saturday, Wambach shared a smiling selfie with Melton, captioning it with a message about how she doesn't mind traveling when she's with her girlfriend. Melton also shared a heartfelt message to Wambach in honor of Valentine's Day earlier this week.

Melton has been an outspoken advocate for same-sex marriage and wrote about her stance on homosexuality in a 2013 post on her blog Momastery. She wrote that she hoped her coming out would help her children feel emboldened to be truthful with themselves and others.

The Internet Archive's project aims to preserve the entire web, including all its broken links, by archiving pages as they are created and archiving the pages that they refer to. This way, as the pages that are referenced are changed or taken from the web, a link to the version that was live when the page was written will be preserved. The goal is to fix all broken links on the web.

The December jobs report, released by the Labor Department, showed a significant decline in job growth with only 74,000 new jobs added, the lowest in three years. This disappointing figure ends 2013 on a weak note, following optimistic economic reports suggesting a strong finish. The unemployment rate dropped to 6.7%, the lowest since October 2008, but this decrease was due to more Americans leaving the workforce rather than finding new jobs.

The report also revealed revisions to previous months' employment gains, with November's increase revised upwards by 38,000 to 241,000, and October's remaining unchanged at 200,000. However, the December civilian labor force participation rate was weaker compared to the previous month and lower than in December 2012.

In December, the retail sector saw a rise of 55,000 jobs, while wholesale trade and professional and business services also experienced growth. Conversely, the construction sector lost 16,000 jobs, and the federal government's workforce shrank by 7,000. The average work week for private employees decreased slightly, while average hourly earnings rose by 2 cents to $24.17, with an annual increase of 42 cents.

The slow hiring in December, potentially influenced by colder weather, raises concerns about the momentum of the job market as it enters 2014.

A man named Xavier Jajuan Davis, 31, has been arrested and charged with three counts of criminal sexual conduct in Grand Rapids, Michigan. He is currently being held in the Kent County Jail on a $400,000 bond. The charges stem from two separate incidents, one on October 25th at DeVos Place and another on December 28th on Oak Park Drive. Details of both incidents have not been disclosed. Davis is also facing a lawsuit filed by him against the City of Grand Rapids and three members of the police department. The lawsuit alleges that Davis was targeted, arrested, and held in jail for 129 days before being cleared of sexual assault charges in January. The lawsuit claims that police had evidence, including cell phone and Uber records, that proved Davis was not at the scene of the crime, but they failed to release him. Davis was assaulted while in jail and lost his home, jobs, and had to spend time in a homeless shelter as a result of the false imprisonment. The city has not yet responded to the lawsuit. Davis has a criminal past, including a 2012 home invasion conviction and a 2015 window peeping charge.

In a press release on Tuesday, authorities announced that missing Georgia teen Aubrey Carroll, who went missing from Spalding High School in Griffin, Georgia in May 2016, has been found safe and unharmed. Aubrey, now 17, returned home to his mother on Monday and released a video on the Spalding County Sheriff's Office Facebook page, expressing his gratitude for the prayers and support from the community.

Investigators from the Spalding County Sheriff's Office (SCSO), FBI, and the Griffin Judicial Circuit District Attorney's Office met with Aubrey's parents on April 10, 2018 to brief them about the progress of the investigation. During this meeting, they shared with Aubrey's parents a Facebook page that he had launched under an assumed identity and informed them that he had had personal contacts with law enforcement agencies ranging from Alabama to Arizona.

Through the investigation, authorities learned that Aubrey had traveled extensively on the west coast and in the midwest, becoming a part of a group of people who lived by bartering, operating with cash only, and traveling from state to state. They described the group as looking like a group of people from the Woodstock era in their clothing and lifestyle.

Authorities and Aubrey's parents mutually decided not to reach out to the teen until he had another encounter with law enforcement for fear that Aubrey would disappear again. Since he is now 17 years old, and no longer a juvenile, there was no lawful way to force him to come back to Georgia.

One of Aubrey's family members decided to reach out to him anyway, and was able to convince him to call his mother. Aubrey called his mother and told her that he was ready to come home, but with certain conditions in place such as who he would talk to and where he would go when he got home.

Aubrey's mom contacted authorities on Monday night to say that Aubrey was safe and with her. Lt. Mike Morris and Sheriff Dix met with Aubrey the next morning to talk about his disappearance. Aubrey told them that he left on his own and had not been abducted, hurt, abused, exploited, or harmed in any way.

Investigators from the SCSO, FBI, and the Griffin Judicial Circuit District Attorney's Office worked together to find Aubrey, and the discovery was a joint effort with the Texas Rangers. Aubrey's story is "absolutely amazing" and both he and his mother want to send a message to those who are missing a loved one: "Keep praying, keep looking, and keep your faith. Miracles happen."

In a concerning turn of events, personal and sensitive information, including social security numbers, banking information, and police records, were found among confetti at the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade. The confetti strips, which appear to be shredded police documents, contain details about arrest records, incident reports, and even information about Mitt Romney's motorcade. Some of the identified detectives are undercover, and their highly sensitive personal information was also printed on the confetti strips. The Nassau County Police Department has expressed concern and will be investigating the matter, while Macy's, the parade's sponsor, assures that they use commercially manufactured confetti.

The reconstruction of shredded documents, as in this case, is possible with the aid of technology. Scanners and automated software programs can identify potential neighboring shreds and display them onscreen for confirmation. The ease of reconstruction depends on the size and direction of the shreds. In the past, documents have been reconstructed by hand, as during the 1979 Iranian Revolution when classified CIA documents found in the U.S. Embassy were reassembled by local carpet weavers. This incident at the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade raises questions about security measures and the potential misuse of sensitive information.

In the aftermath of the devastating 7.0 magnitude earthquake in Haiti, relief efforts are underway to deliver food, water, and medical care to the affected population. However, three days after the disaster, many cries for help remain unanswered due to a lack of search and rescue teams and emergency supplies. The United Nations has fed 8,000 people, but two to three million people remain in dire need. Patience is wearing thin, and reports of looting have increased as another day passes without power or fresh water.

Adolphe Reynald, a top aide to the mayor of Port-au-Prince, supervised a makeshift first aid center that was registering long lines of wounded people but had no medicine to treat them. The United Nations reported that 9,000 people had been buried in mass graves, and collecting bodies has become one of the few ways to earn money. Valencia Joseph, 32, said he had been paid $100 a day to pull bodies from the rubble, estimating that he and others had collected 2,000 bodies.

Secretary of State Hillary Clinton announced that she would visit Haiti on Saturday to show support for the victims of the earthquake. The Obama administration granted Haitians living in the United States protection from deportation for 18 months and permission to work. President Obama spoke with Haitian President René Préval and pledged the United States' full commitment in helping rebuild from the quake, which destroyed at least 30% of the capital and half the buildings in some neighborhoods.

The United States took firmer control of the emergency operation on Friday, with the Federal Aviation Administration managing air traffic into Haitian airspace. No planes from the United States, military or civilian, would be allowed to land without express permission from the agency. Exceptions to the new rule would be granted only to humanitarian aid planes, based on arrival times and on the availability of space at the airport. The F.A.A. warned pilots that fuel still was not available at the airport, and that any aircraft bound for Haiti would need to have enough fuel to circle in the air for at least an hour.

Admiral Mike Mullen, the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, said that 9,000 to 10,000 American troops were expected in Haiti by Monday, with about 5,000 ground troops providing security and logistical support, among other duties. The Pentagon was poised to send more troops and an aircraft carrier, the Carl Vinson, arrived off Haiti's shores with 19 helicopters aboard, serving as a staging area for relief flights, purified water, and other supplies.

Port-au-Prince remained relatively calm, but the United Nations reported that one of its food warehouses in the capital had been looted. Looting of houses and shops increased, and anger boiled over in unpredictable ways, with residents near the city's overfilled main cemetery stoning a group of ambulance workers seeking to drop off more bodies. Some people were bracing for the worst, fearing that hunger and desperation might prompt an explosion of violence.

Up to 100,000 people may have died in the Haiti earthquake, according to the Pan American Health Organisation. The UN launched an appeal for more than $550 million in aid, and former US President Bill Clinton announced plans to model a disaster assistance fund along the same lines he and former President George Bush Sr pursued for victims of the Asian tsunami. Barack Obama has asked Clinton, a UN special envoy to Haiti, to work with George Bush on a fundraising effort.

A Hungarian camerawoman working for N1TV, a nationalist television channel linked to the country's far-right Jobbik party, was filmed tripping a man carrying a child and kicking two refugee children at the border hotspot of Rőszke on Tuesday. The incident was captured on video by a German reporter and quickly went viral, leading to the creation of a Facebook group called "The Petra László Wall of Shame." László was subsequently fired by N1TV for her unacceptable behavior. The channel's editor in chief Szabolcs Kisberk said in a statement that the camerawoman's employment had been terminated with immediate effect.

The incident occurred as dozens of refugees tried to escape police officers at a Hungarian camp, with tensions having risen for days as refugees attempted to continue their journey to Germany and Austria but were stopped by local police. The camerawoman's actions were widely condemned on social media, with many calling for an apology from the TV station and some stating that the incident was evidence that most Hungarian journalists and media outlets are in line with Prime Minister Viktor Orban, who has taken a tough stance toward the influx of refugees.

Opposition parties Együtt-PM and the Democratic Coalition have said that they will initiate charges of violence against a member of the community against László, which is punishable by up to five years in prison. The incident has further highlighted the tensions and challenges faced by European countries as they deal with the ongoing refugee crisis.

The cast for Celebrity Big Brother has been announced, and reactions on Twitter are mixed. The lineup includes Omarosa Manigault, Brandi Glanville, Metta World Peace (Ron Artest), Marisa Jaret Winokur, Keisha Knight Pulliam, Chuck Liddell, Shannon Elizabeth, Ross Matthews, Mark McGrath, Adriana Gutierrez, and James Maslow. Celebrities such as Andy Cohen and Lance Bass have shared their opinions on the casting, with Cohen predicting that Brandi Glanville will dominate Omarosa, and Bass naming Ross Mathews, Shannon Elizabeth, and Marisa Winokur as his top picks to win. The announcement has sparked a range of reactions, with some expressing excitement for the potential drama between Omarosa and Brandi, while others have criticized the casting of a former White House aide. Some have even suggested that the show could have included Spencer Pratt instead. The announcement has generated a significant amount of buzz, with many eagerly anticipating the upcoming season.

Russian special forces successfully rescued 23 Russian sailors from the hijacked oil tanker, Moscow University, in a helicopter-backed operation on Thursday. The ship, carrying 86,000 tons of crude oil worth about $50 million, was taken over by Somali pirates the previous day. The special forces, aboard the Russian anti-submarine destroyer Marshal Shaposhnikov, boarded a helicopter and rappelled down to the Moscow University. Shots were fired during the raid but no one was injured. The pirates are being held aboard the tanker, and one pirate is reported to have died during the raid, although this is yet to be confirmed. The crew had locked themselves in a safe room when the pirates took over the ship. The successful rescue operation is in line with a trend by international military forces who are more aggressively combating piracy. Pirates currently hold more than 300 hostages taken from ships attacked off East Africa in the last several months. The international community has had problems formulating an accepted policy to try and jail pirate suspects. This operation will please the Kremlin, which has been seeking to revive Russia’s naval muscle despite limited resources.

The Jerusalem-based soccer club Beitar Jerusalem announced on Sunday that it would change its name to "Beitar Trump Jerusalem" in honor of US President Donald Trump's recognition of Jerusalem as Israel's capital and his decision to move the US embassy from Tel Aviv. The club praised Trump for his courage and love for Israel, stating that he had made history by recognizing Jerusalem as the eternal capital of Israel. The announcement comes a day before the official opening of the new US embassy in Jerusalem's Arnona neighborhood, which will be attended by US Deputy Secretary of State John J. Sullivan, Secretary of Treasury Steven Mnuchin, Senior Adviser Jared Kushner, Adviser Ivanka Trump, and Special Representative for International Negotiations Jason Greenblatt, among others.

Beitar Jerusalem, one of Israel's top soccer clubs, is currently in second place in the premier league. However, the club has a long history of anti-Arab and anti-Muslim sentiment, and is the only club in the Israeli league that has never had an Arab Muslim player. Officials on the team have indicated in the past that it is unofficial policy. Earlier this year, the club promised to crackdown on racist fans and close down the eastern section of its ground, which is infamous for housing the club's most rabid fans, including the ultra-nationalist "La-Familia" faction. Last year, 19 members of the group were charged with attempted murder, including of rival supporters.

Meanwhile, thousands of Palestinian protesters converged along the border with Israel on Monday, drawing Israeli fire that killed at least 16 people in the bloodiest day of weeks of demonstrations and casting a cloud over Israel's festive inauguration of the new US embassy in contested Jerusalem. With their anger fueled by the embassy opening, protesters set tires on fire, while the Israeli military said protesters assaulted the border fence. By midafternoon, at least 16 Palestinians, including a 14-year-old boy, were killed while over 500 were wounded by Israeli fire, Palestinian health officials said. In the West Bank, several thousand people gathered in the center of Ramallah, while hundreds marched to the Qalandiya crossing on the outskirts of Jerusalem, where protesters threw stones at Israeli troops.

The protest in Gaza was to be the biggest yet in a weekslong campaign against a decade-old blockade of the territory. The march was also directed at the inauguration of the US embassy in Jerusalem later Monday. The relocation of the embassy from Tel Aviv, a key campaign promise of President Donald Trump, has infuriated the Palestinians, who seek east Jerusalem as a future capital. "A great day for Israel," Trump tweeted early Monday. Monday marked the biggest showdown in recent weeks between Israel's military and Gaza's Hamas rulers along the volatile border. It is the culmination of a campaign, led by the Islamic militant Hamas and fueled by despair among Gaza's 2 million people, to break the decade-old border blockade of the territory by Israel and Egypt. Since weekly border marches began in late March, 58 Palestinian protesters have been killed and more than 2,300 wounded by Israeli army fire. Hamas leaders have suggested a border breach is possible Monday, while Israel has warned it would prevent protesters from breaking through the barrier at any cost.

The Gibson Guitar Corporation, a renowned manufacturer of musical instruments, was recently raided by the Justice Department due to allegations of trafficking in illegally obtained wood. The raid was enforced under the Lacey Act, a century-old endangered species law that was amended in 2008 to include plants. The government claims that Gibson's Madagascar ebony was contraband, citing emails that suggest the company maintained a supply chain connected to illegal timber harvests.

Gibson vigorously denies these allegations, stating that all of its purchases from Madagascar have complied with U.S. and Malagasy law. The company asserts that the seized wood was legally obtained from India and that it stopped importing wood from Madagascar in 2009.

The Lacey Act requires end users of endangered wood to certify the legality of their supply chain all the way to the trees. The Environmental Investigation Agency's (EIA) investigations have concluded that Gibson knowingly imported tainted wood. Andrea Johnson, director of forest programs for the EIA, states that Gibson was exploring the possibility of sourcing illegally from Madagascar.

The guitar industry is divided on the Lacey Act. Some, like Chris Martin, Chairman and CEO of the C.F. Martin Guitar Co., support it as a means to stop illegal logging. Others, such as attorney Ronald Bienstock, are concerned about its retroactive nature and the potential burden of proving the provenance of wood acquired decades ago.

The situation has impacted businesses like Nashville's George Gruhn, one of the world's top dealers of old guitars, banjos, and other rare stringed instruments. The law's requirements have made it challenging for him to continue his overseas business, which previously accounted for 40% of his sales.

The case against Gibson is ongoing, and its resolution may clarify what constitutes responsible sourcing under the Lacey Act. The government's enforcement of the act is intended to reduce illegal logging and promote responsible sourcing of wood.

Jonah Hill returned as the host of Saturday Night Live for the third time, delivering a solid performance but facing criticism for the show's overly large cast, making it difficult for viewers to get to know the members. The episode included a humorous monologue featuring Leonardo DiCaprio, a parody of Spike Jonze's "Her" with Hill falling in love with himself, and a Weekend Update segment featuring Kenan Thompson as the Miami police officer who arrested Justin Bieber. The sketch "Lamborghini" was praised for its humor, while "Inside SoCal," "Benihana," and "Ranch" received lower ratings. The average score for the episode was 5.73, placing it among other recent hosts such as Paul Rudd, Jimmy Fallon, and Bruce Willis.

Lady Gaga's latest album, 'Born This Way,' has been banned in Lebanon due to its alleged offensive content towards Christianity. The Lebanese government also previously banned Gaga's single 'Judas' from their radio stations. Malaysia has also banned the title track from their radio stations, citing concerns about promoting homosexuality. Gaga's album went platinum in its first week in the US, but its controversial themes have sparked debates about religious censorship and the impact of institutionalized religion on government. Gaga has expressed her views on religion's influence on government in a recent interview with The Guardian.

News Corp. announced the closure of its 168-year-old U.K. tabloid, News of the World, amidst a scandal involving the paper's controversial reporting tactics. The paper, known for its mix of investigative journalism, celebrity gossip, and right-wing politics, is accused of intercepting voice mails of everyday people, including a 13-year-old murder victim, and celebrities. The closure was initiated due to the "inhuman" allegations, with the final edition to be published this Sunday. The scandal has led to calls for the resignation of Rebekah Brooks, the CEO of News Corp.'s U.K. newspaper unit, and potential arrests of other executives. The closure may be a step towards addressing the ongoing phone-hacking scandal that has been ongoing since 2005.

Nine-year-old James Savage from Los Banos successfully completed a remarkable swim on June 14, 2016, as he swam across the San Francisco Bay to Alcatraz Island and back. The previous record for the youngest swimmer to achieve this feat was held by a 10-year-old. James' swim, which took approximately two hours, was not without challenges, as he encountered strong currents and waves that made him want to give up 30 minutes into the swim. However, with encouragement from his coach and his father, James persevered and completed the swim. The accomplishment has earned James recognition, and he is now aiming for his next goal: swimming the length of the Golden Gate Bridge, which is 8,981 feet (2,737.4 meters). James' coach, Josh Weinberger, and his father were confident in his abilities, having seen him undergo rigorous training to prepare for the challenge. A fleet of paddlers accompanied James during the swim to ensure his safety. The event was covered by NBC affiliate KSEE, and James was interviewed after the swim, expressing his determination and gratitude for the support he received.

The trial of former U.S. Senator John Edwards is underway, with key witness Andrew Young testifying about his role in covering up Edwards' affair with Rielle Hunter during Edwards' 2008 presidential campaign. Young revealed details about the use of a "bat phone" for Edwards to communicate with Hunter, the money used to cover up the relationship, and Edwards' request for Young to claim paternity of Hunter's child. Edwards is accused of violating campaign finance laws by using over $900,000 in illegal donations to hide his affair and maintain his presidential campaign. Young's testimony will continue today. The trial is being updated on Twitter (@newsandrecord) and Facebook (facebook.com/newsandrecord).

Andrew Young, a longtime aide to Edwards, testified about how in 2007 he found out Edwards' lover was pregnant and revealed details about living with Hunter, the money used to cover up the relationship, and a special "bat phone" that Edwards used for talking to her. Edwards is on trial for violating campaign finance laws. At issue is nearly $1 million in contributions from heiress Rachel "Bunny" Mellon and Texas trial lawyer Fred Baron that went to conceal his affair with Hunter, a campaign videographer. Edwards initially brushed off allegations he was the father of Hunter's baby, saying she was a "crazy slut" and there was a 1-in-3 chance it was his child. Young avoided looking at Edwards as he took the stand for his second day of testimony. Edwards sat with an occasional smile, calmly looking at Young. Young described Hunter as a difficult houseguest who refused to buy her own groceries, but had no problem shopping at places like Neiman Marcus. One night in December, Young discovered reporters outside his house who were trying to dig up information on Hunter's pregnancy. The next day, Edwards called him and launched into what Young described as a "campaign stump speech." Edwards wanted Young to claim paternity of Hunter's baby. A few days later, Young, his family, and Hunter went into hiding. They stayed at luxury hotels in Hollywood, Fla.; San Diego and Santa Barbara, Calif.; and Baron's mansion in Aspen, Colo. Young said he went along with the scheme because he was in "really deep," having already taken in Hunter, and because he believed in the causes Edwards represented. Young's testimony will continue today. The trial is being updated on Twitter (@newsandrecord) and Facebook (facebook.com/newsandrecord).

Justin Bieber, in an interview with Big Boy on Los Angeles' Power 106 station, announced that he is retiring from music after the release of his new album "Journals." However, sources have since stated that this is a joke, and Bieber is merely looking to change things up in his career and mature as an artist. "Journals" is a collection of previously released songs and unreleased tracks, videos, and the "Believe" theatrical release trailer, available on iTunes from Dec. 16 through Jan. 2, 2014. Bieber's "Believe" concert documentary will be released in theaters on Christmas Day.

The viral video on Steven Stubenraugh's Facebook page, which has garnered over 3.8 million views, depicts a man punching a kangaroo in Australia. The incident occurred during a wild pig-hunting trip organized for a young man named Kailem, who passed away from cancer last week. The man, known as "Goo," punched the kangaroo after it had a dog in a headlock. There has been debate over the authenticity of the footage and whether it's acceptable to punch an animal in self-defense. Kailem's friends filmed over an hour of video for a DVD as a memento for Kailem's family. The dog is reportedly unharmed due to wearing a breastplate to protect it from boar tusks. The man, who works as a zookeeper at Taronga Western Plains Zoo, has remained silent due to his government job. The dog and the man are reportedly fine, with the man's hand only being lightly injured. The incident further solidifies the perception of Australia as a wild and unusual place.

The New York Post is reporting that lawmakers are discussing Jamie Dimon, CEO of JPMorgan Chase, as a potential replacement for current Treasury Secretary Timothy Geithner. Despite Dimon's expressed interest in serving his country, it's unclear if he would be a natural fit in the Obama administration due to differences in policy on key issues such as consumer protection and handling too-big-to-fail banks. Dimon opposes the establishment of a consumer-protection agency and has defended big banks' right to exist, which contradicts White House policy. Geithner is still facing criticism in Congress over his handling of the government's financial bailout, the dollar's weakness, and high unemployment.

The U.S. speedskating team will revert to their previous Under Armour suits for the remainder of the Sochi Olympic Games, following a disastrous performance in the first six events. The team had been using a new suit, which was introduced last month and marketed as the fastest ever in the sport, but complaints about the suit's performance have led to a change. The skaters had struggled in Sochi, with no U.S. speedskater medaling, including the world's top-ranked skaters, Shani Davis and Heather Richardson. The suit became a leading suspect for the poor showing, with skaters attempting to modify their suits this week to no avail. The team had brought their old suits with them to Sochi, and many skaters have expressed a preference for the older suits. U.S. Speedskating executive director Ted Morris said the team is evaluating everything, from athletes' training to their diets, in addition to Under Armour's suits. The team is hoping for a change in results with the familiar suits, as they have performed well in the World Cup suits in the past. The last time the U.S. failed to medal in speedskating was at the 1984 Olympics in Sarajevo.

A 25-year-old NSA contractor named Reality Winner has been arrested and charged with leaking a classified document about Russian hacking of U.S. electoral systems to The Intercept. Winner, who served in the Air Force from 2010 until December 2016, was a Cryptologic Language Analyst for the Air Force and fluent in the languages of Afghanistan. She was arrested at her home on Saturday and faces one count of "gathering, transmitting or losing defense information."

The arrest highlights a cultural shift in the intelligence community, with a growing subset of employees leaking secrets to the public and the news media. This new class of rogue employees includes Chelsea Manning, Edward Snowden, and now Winner. The NSA is a military intelligence agency, and many of the people who work on the front lines of intelligence gathering are young enlisted personnel who need a very high security clearance to eavesdrop on terrorists and foreign officials.

Winner's social media presence shows her to be frequently critical of President Trump and concerned about environmental issues. Her Twitter account, under the username @Reezlie, follows accounts related to WikiLeaks, Anonymous, and alt government agency accounts that became popular after President Trump's inauguration. She also retweeted posts from these accounts and liked tweets about White House press secretary Sean Spicer's reported lax approach to his personal data security.

Winner's attorney, Titus Thomas Nichols, said she has yet to enter a plea, although a detention hearing is scheduled for Thursday. She remains jailed in Lincoln County. Her mother, Billie Winner-Davis, called her a "very passionate" person who was outspoken about her beliefs, but never active in politics. Winner's stepfather, Gary Davis, described her as a veteran and a patriot.

The lines are blurry between insider threats and the public's right to know, and the issue is getting worse, according to intelligence historian Matthew Aid. He said the arrest of Winner highlights a new kind of insider threat that the agency can't defend against. The Justice Department announced charges against Winner on Monday, and she is accused of leaking classified information used as the basis for an article published by The Intercept on Monday afternoon.

An American financial trader named Josh Sanchez-Maldonado, aged 24, from San Francisco, has gone missing in London after traveling there for a job interview. He was last seen leaving his hotel in Feltham, west London, on October 22. His family, who have flown to the UK to search for him, described him as a "very goal-oriented, very organized, detailed, kind, lovable, and respectful person." Sanchez-Maldonado had flown to London from Japan the day before his disappearance and was expected to return to San Francisco via Dublin the next day but did not catch the flight. He had been in touch with his father daily since his travels began, but last spoke on October 21. The nature of the job interview and the company he was supposed to meet are unknown. The family believes the job must have been related to finance, as Sanchez-Maldonado enjoys the London market. Police are growing increasingly concerned for his safety and wellbeing and have appealed for any information on his whereabouts. Described as white, about 5ft 8in tall, with a slim build and short, dark hair, Sanchez-Maldonado was last seen wearing a dark coloured flat cap, a brown/grey T-shirt, white shorts, and black trainers. He was believed to be interested in visiting London's financial districts, including the City and Canary Wharf. The family has pleaded with Londoners to take good care of him and has asked anyone with information to contact the police. The U.S. Embassy in London is also working closely with his family and British police.

Anne Hathaway, the Oscar-winning actress, has given birth to a baby boy named Jonathan Rosebanks Shulman on March 24. The news was first reported by E! News. Hathaway and her husband, Adam Shulman, who is an actor-producer, got engaged in November 2011 and married in September 2012. The couple had announced Hathaway's pregnancy last November, and she made her first public reference to it in a bikini Instagram photo in January. Fans have praised Hathaway for choosing a normal name for her son, as opposed to some celebrities who have given their children unusual names. The couple had a relaxed baby shower in March with close friends, including Matthew McConaughey's wife Camila Alves. The baby is reportedly doing well, and the family is surrounded by friends and family in Los Angeles. Hathaway has expressed her desire to have a family of a certain size, including naturally born and adopted children. She had previously stated that she wanted to have as many children as she could afford.

The Kenai City Council in Alaska is considering a proposal to introduce a cat leash law, similar to the one for dogs, due to an increase in complaints about roaming cats and the growing cat population at the Kenai Animal Shelter. The proposed ordinance, which was introduced by Mayor Pat Porter and council member Tim Navarre, would require cats to be restrained at all times by a leash, chain, fence, or building. The maximum penalty for violating this ordinance is a fine of up to $500 per violation.

The Kenai Animal Shelter has received an increased number of complaints about cats roaming at large, defecating on private property, invading plant beds, and disturbing property owners. The shelter's resources have been taxed due to the growing cat population. Kenai City Manager Rick Koch has recommended delaying the vote on the cat ordinance to research historical information and provide that information to council members.

Some residents are concerned about compliance and the potential impact on animal control resources. Former council member Ryan Marquis testified that the ordinance assumes compliance and could have an unexpected fiscal impact on the shelter. He suggested that the shelter's budget may need to be increased to support the new program.

The cat leash law will have a hearing and vote on October 5. If approved, it would make Kenai one of the few cities in Alaska with a cat leash law.

A rally was held outside the NFL's headquarters in New York on August 23, 2017, in support of unsigned quarterback Colin Kaepernick. Over 1,000 people attended, many wearing Kaepernick's jersey. Kaepernick, who was born to a black man and a white woman but was adopted by a white couple, opted out of his contract with the San Francisco 49ers in March and remains unsigned. Some critics argue that his lack of a job is due to his on-field performance, while supporters claim he is being blackballed for his advocacy against police brutality, which led him to refuse to stand for the national anthem during games.

Speakers at the rally included Women's March organizer Tamika Mallory, who urged football fans to turn off the TV if the league doesn't stand up for black lives. The Reverend Jamal Bryant criticized the NFL for valuing black players only when they are wearing a football uniform and not when they express their conscience. The NAACP called for a meeting with the NFL to discuss Kaepernick's situation, with interim president Derrick Johnson stating that it's "no sheer coincidence" that Kaepernick isn't on a roster.

The rally concluded after about an hour and a half of speeches, poems, and prayers. The NAACP's state president in New York, Hazel Dukes, said the league's actions imply to young black men that the league only values their lives when they are wearing a football uniform. Goodell has stated that the league isn't blackballing Kaepernick.

Other players have followed Kaepernick's actions, with some doing so in this year's preseason. On Monday, a group of Cleveland Browns players prayed in silent protest during the national anthem, earning the ire of an Ohio Supreme Court justice. The justice wrote on Facebook that he wouldn't attend any games at which "draft dodging millionaire athletes disrespect the veterans who earned them the right to be on that field."

The Gallup-Healthways Well-Being Index ranked Hawaii as the state with the highest resident well-being in 2015, a title it has held five times since 2008. Alaska followed closely in second place, while Montana, Colorado, and Wyoming rounded out the top five. The report, which is based on over 175,000 telephone interviews, measures residents' well-being across five dimensions: purpose, social, financial, community, and physical. Nationally, well-being remained statistically the same between 2014 and 2015, but there were some positive trends, such as a decline in the national uninsured rate, a decline in the overall smoking rate, and an increase in reported exercise. However, obesity continued to climb, reaching a new high mark in 2015. The South dominated the bottom of the list, while the West won out, claiming all but two of the top 10 spots. The report provides an overview of well-being trends within the United States and is available for download. Subscribing to the Well-Being Index will keep you updated on new reports and insights.

The article discusses the rise of the Joint Special Operations Command (JSOC), a secretive military unit within the United States that has grown significantly since the September 11 attacks in 2001. JSOC, which includes the Army's Delta Force, the Navy's SEAL Team 6, the Air Force's 24th Special Tactics Squadron, and the Army's 160th Special Operations Aviation Regiment and 75th Ranger Regiment, has become a powerful force in the U.S. counterterrorism efforts.

The unit has grown from 1,800 troops prior to 9/11 to as many as 25,000, and it has its own intelligence division, drones, reconnaissance planes, satellites, and cyberwarriors. JSOC has been involved in intelligence-gathering missions and lethal raids in various countries, including Iraq, Afghanistan, Yemen, Pakistan, Somalia, the Philippines, Nigeria, and Syria.

JSOC's operations are highly classified, and the unit has maintained a level of obscurity that even the CIA has not been able to achieve. The unit's leaders rarely speak in public and have no unclassified website. JSOC's troops often work in civilian government agencies or U.S. embassies abroad, where they dispense with uniforms and wear no name or rank identifiers.

JSOC has been given the rare authority to select individuals for its kill list and to kill them rather than capture them. Critics argue that this individual man-hunting mission amounts to assassination, which is prohibited by U.S. law. JSOC's kill list is not usually coordinated with the CIA, which maintains a similar but shorter roster of names.

JSOC's first overseas mission was Operation Eagle Claw, an attempted rescue of diplomats held hostage by Iranian students at the U.S. Embassy in Tehran in 1980. The unit's extreme secrecy made conventional military commanders distrustful, and as a consequence, it was rarely used during conflicts. However, JSOC's lethality was demonstrated in the December 2001 mountain battle at Tora Bora, where it killed many enemy forces.

JSOC has made mistakes, such as the "wedding party incident" in 2002, where a JSOC reconnaissance team hunting Taliban accidentally hit a wedding party, killing civilians. Nevertheless, JSOC's success in targeting the right homes, businesses, and individuals has been about 50 percent, according to two senior commanders.

The article also discusses JSOC's role in non-military assignments, such as tracing the flow of money from international banks to finance terrorist networks and psychological operations. JSOC has become deeply involved in these activities, which it renamed "military information operations" to sound less intimidating. JSOC routinely sends small teams in civilian clothes to U.S. embassies to help with what it calls media and messaging campaigns.

JSOC's new 30,000-square-foot office building turned command center is located across the highway from the Pentagon in suburban Virginia. The focus of Joint Special Operations Task Force-National Capital Region, which operates out of this building, is not the next terrorist network but the Washington bureaucracy. Some 50 battle-hardened JSOC warriors and a handful of other federal intelligence and law enforcement agencies work there. Mexico is at the top of its wish list, and JSOC's National Capital task force is creating targeting packages for U.S. domestic agencies that have sought its help, including the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency.

In Waukesha, Wisconsin, two middle school girls charged with attempting to kill a classmate to gain favor with the fictional character Slender Man were ruled competent to stand trial on Thursday. The girls, aged 12 and 13, were found in June and charged with attempted first-degree intentional homicide.

During a hearing, Waukesha County Circuit Judge Michael Bohren found Anissa Weier, 13, competent after a three-hour hearing, despite differing conclusions from mental health experts. Morgan Geyser, 12, had been set for a similar hearing, but her defense team dropped their objection to a state psychiatrist's finding that she had regained competency after being ruled incompetent in August.

Morgan Geyser was diagnosed with schizophrenia by the state psychiatrist, and her attorney requested that she continue to be held at the Winnebago Mental Health Institute for monitoring. The preliminary hearings, set for February, will determine if there is enough evidence to proceed to trial. If found guilty, the girls could face up to 60 years in prison as adults, or secure confinement until they're 25 as juveniles.

The long-awaited hearings come after the girls stabbed a classmate, Payton Leutner, in a Waukesha park in May, following a sleepover to celebrate Geyser's birthday. The pair told investigators they were trying to gain the favor of Slender Man, a fictional online character. Leutner survived her wounds and has since returned to school.

Attorneys for each girl have said they will try to have their cases moved to juvenile court. At Geyser's first competency hearing in August, mental health experts testified that she exhibited disturbing behavior and beliefs, including conversations with fictional characters and a belief in Slender Man, unicorns, and her own power of "Vulcan mind control."

The girls' attorneys argued that the psychologists had more experience working with juveniles and spent more time with the girls before reaching their conclusions. One psychologist was concerned that the older girl didn't have a meaningful understanding of time frames, including the fact she could go to prison far longer than she has been alive. The preliminary hearings will determine if there is enough evidence to proceed to trial, and if the case can be moved to juvenile court.

Shaniece Luke, a Harlem woman, has been presented with an $11.67 million medical bill from the state Office for People with Developmental Disabilities (OPWDD), which she believes is retaliation for filing a wrongful death lawsuit against the agency and the Queens developmental center where her mentally disabled brother, Rasheen Rose, died in 2012. Rose, who was born with severe autism and was never able to communicate verbally, died at the Bernard Fineson Developmental Center in Queens Village after being physically restrained by three staffers, including a 275-pound worker who sat on him for up to 30 minutes. The city medical examiner ruled the death a homicide in December 2012. Luke's attorneys claim that at least nine other staff members, including two doctors and two nurses, were in the room when Rose became unresponsive. The OPWDD declined comment, citing the pending litigation. This is not the first time such bills have been sent to families suing the state for abuse in care. Assemblyman Harvey Weisenberg, an advocate for the disabled, called it "retaliation" and "an outrage." The OPWDD stated that they were following federal Medicaid obligations in seeking reimbursement, as not doing so could put federal Medicaid funding at risk. Luke is seeking unspecified punitive and other damages in a federal lawsuit against the staff named in the lawsuit, who have denied any wrongdoing. The Cuomo administration announced plans to close four developmental centers over four years, including Fineson in 2017.

The Internet Archive is working on a project to preserve web pages and their references, aiming to fix broken links on the web. Simultaneously, Salma Hayek mourns the death of her beloved dog, Mozart, who was found fatally shot last week on her ranch. Hayek, who delivered Mozart herself, expressed her hope for justice from the Washington State authorities. The actress, known for her love for animals, often shares photos with them on Instagram, including a recent one with a canine co-star on the set of 'Drunk Parents'. Last July, Hayek was among several A-listers who expressed outrage over the killing of Cecil the Lion.

The Supreme Court confirmation hearing for Brett Kavanaugh, President Trump's nominee for the high court, took place on Tuesday, September 4, 2018. The hearing was marked by partisan quarreling and protests from both Democrats and Republicans. The hearing began with disputes over Kavanaugh's records withheld by the White House and the unusual vetting process by Republicans that failed to include documents from three years Kavanaugh worked in the Bush administration, and 100,000 more pages withheld by the Trump White House.

Democrats, including several senators poised for 2020 presidential bids, tried to block the proceedings and railed against the lack of access to important chunks of Kavanaugh's records. Republicans, in turn, accused the Democrats of turning the hearing into a circus. President Trump jumped into the fray, stating on Twitter that Democrats were "looking to inflict pain and embarrassment" on Kavanaugh.

In his statement at the end of more than seven hours of arguing, Kavanaugh spoke repeatedly about the importance of an independent judiciary and the need to keep the court above partisan politics. He called himself a judge with a straightforward judicial philosophy, stating that a judge must be independent and must interpret the law, not make the law. He also promised to be "a team player on the Team of Nine."

The Supreme Court is often thought of as nine separate judges, rather than a team. However, justices often say they seek consensus, and they like to focus on how frequently they reach unanimous decisions. Barring a major surprise over the next two days of questioning, the committee is expected to vote along party lines to send Kavanaugh's nomination to the full Senate. Majority Republicans can confirm Kavanaugh without any Democratic votes, though they'll have little margin for error.

Several dozen protesters, shouting one by one, disrupted the hearing at several points and were removed by police. Protesters argued that the Republicans were hiding something by withholding information and that installing Trump's second pick to the Supreme Court would irreparably end access to abortion and dismantle the Affordable Care Act.

The panel's top Democrat, Sen. Dianne Feinstein, described the hearing's "very unique circumstances."
