She stated that not only is the country deeply divided politically, but also that the Senate finds itself with a president who faces his own serious problems. Feinstein was referring to investigations surrounding Trump.

Sens. Susan Collins of Maine and Lisa Murkowski of Alaska are the only two Republicans even remotely open to voting against Kavanaugh, though neither has said she would do so. Abortion rights supporters are trying to appeal to those senators, who both favor abortion access.

Kavanaugh sat silently and impassively for most of the day, occasionally sipping water and taking notes on senators' points. Besides his family, he was accompanied by outgoing White House Counsel Don McGahn and Deputy Attorney General Rod Rosenstein.

The hearing was chaotic, with protesters repeatedly interrupting the session, and tempers flaring among senators. Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, denounced what he called the "mob rule." Struggling to speak over protesters, Sen. Orrin Hatch, R-Utah, said: "These people are so out of line they shouldn't be in the doggone room." Sen. Dick Durbin, D-Ill., told Kavanaugh the opposition being shown at the hearing reflected the concern many Americans have over Trump's "contempt of the rule of law" and the judge's own expansive views on executive power.

The hearing was a display of how mean, angry, and despicable the other side is, according to President Trump, who tweeted that Democrats were "looking to inflict pain and embarrassment" on Kavanaugh. The chairman's opening remarks were delayed for nearly an hour and a half as Democratic senators sought to cut off the hearings, raising an uproar over a last-minute document dump sent to the Judiciary Committee late Monday encompassing more than 42,000 pages from the nominee's tenure in the George W. Bush White House.

Democrats questioned Kavanaugh's judicial philosophy and even his honesty. Sen. Patrick J. Leahy, D-Vt., pointedly told Kavanaugh he would question him about that "when you are under oath." Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I., referred to the Republican-appointed conservatives on the court headed by Chief Justice John G. Roberts Jr. as the "Roberts Five" and said the justices were always looking for ways to benefit the "big fundraisers and influencers of the Republican Party."

Barring any major last-minute surprises, Kavanaugh appears to be on track to be confirmed by the end of the month. Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman Charles E. Grassley said a committee vote is likely to occur Sept. 20. That would allow Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., to tee up votes on the floor confirming Kavanaugh during the last week of September. The Supreme Court's new term begins Oct. 1.

The public fight over his nomination will be intense, according to Grassley, who said Tuesday's opening session indicated that the hearing would be "a bad start." Democratic senators repeatedly interrupted Grassley over the document issue, and by the end of the day more than 70 protesters had been arrested. Their theme: The Republicans are hiding something by withholding information.

Another focus of the hearing was Trump himself, who has frequently leveled attacks against the judiciary and law enforcement. Two Republican senators — Ben Sasse, Neb., and Jeff Flake, Ariz. — praised Kavanaugh personally and professionally, but raised questions about Trump's attacks on the Justice Department and how Kavanaugh would handle cases involving presidential power. In a tweet Monday, Trump criticized Attorney General Jeff Sessions for the recent indictments of two Republican members of Congress on corruption charges and for the timing, so close to the House midterm elections.

The BBC's political editor, Nick Robinson, was caught on camera violently stamping on an anti-war activist's placard during a live broadcast. The incident occurred when the activist repeatedly interrupted Robinson's report. In a blog post later that day, Robinson admitted to losing his temper and regretted his actions. Meanwhile, Ed Balls, the symbol of Labour's crushing electoral defeat, gave his first interview since the event. In the interview, Balls reflected on his political career, highlighting his achievements such as keeping Britain out of the euro, establishing an independent Bank of England, raising the education leaving age to 18, and implementing policies like Sure Start and the national minimum wage. He also expressed a sense of loss and personal defeat following Labour's electoral failure but emphasized the importance of reflecting on one's accomplishments rather than dwelling on what could have been done differently.

U.S. stocks fell on Tuesday due to disappointing earnings reports from companies like Microsoft and Caterpillar, which cited the strong U.S. dollar as a drag on earnings growth. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 234 points, or 1.3%, to 17,445, while the S&P 500 declined 19 points, or 0.9%, to 2,038, and the Nasdaq Composite lost 60 points, or 1.3%, to 4,711. The decline was partly due to Microsoft's forecast of lower-than-expected earnings and Caterpillar's disappointing 2015 outlook, which also reported fourth-quarter earnings that missed expectations. The strong U.S. dollar was cited as a major factor in the weak earnings outlook. The Russell 2000 index, a benchmark for small-cap U.S. companies, was down 0.2%. Concerns about a strong U.S. currency are driving some investors to small-cap stocks, as they are less exposed to the stronger dollar. The S&P 500 is on track to see earnings inch up 0.1% from a year earlier, which is the slowest quarterly pace of growth since the third quarter of 2012. The decline in oil prices and weak economic activity overseas are also contributing to low expectations for the current earnings season.

Steve Simoff, a 61-year-old janitor, commutes 35 miles from his home in Davis City, Missouri to his job at Lakeside Casino in Osceola, Iowa. Due to financial constraints, he often walks along Interstate Highway 35, hitchhiking rides when possible. Simoff's daily commute begins at 3:30 p.m. and can take up to four hours, depending on the number of rides he catches. His story mirrors that of James Robertson, a Detroit commuter who made national headlines for his 21-mile walk to work. Unlike Robertson, Simoff does have a car, but gas money is tight. The community often helps Simoff on his way, and he has cultivated a diverse group of road friends over the years. Simoff is dedicated to his job and considers himself a hero to his grandson. He remains humble, stating that he walks to work because he needs to support his family.

Michael Vaudreuil, a 54-year-old who worked as a custodian at Worcester Polytechnic Institute (WPI) while studying mechanical engineering, has been hired by aerospace firm Pratt & Whitney. Vaudreuil's story of perseverance in the face of adversity went viral after he graduated from WPI, and four employees from Pratt & Whitney reached out to him independently, expressing interest in hiring him. Vaudreuil will be working in the Hot Section Engineering division at Pratt & Whitney, which deals with jet engine combustion chambers, and turbine and exhaust systems. He is looking forward to the satisfaction and fulfillment that will come with the job, and feels like he has won the lottery. Vaudreuil's story has resonated with millions, and he hopes it will change the perception of older graduates and job candidates. He is grateful for the media attention and the outpouring of support from around the world. Vaudreuil will be moving to Connecticut with his wife, Joyce, and starting his new job on July 11. He is excited to have landed a job in his chosen field of aerospace, which brings his story full circle, as he earned an associate's degree in aeronautical technology decades ago but never pursued a career in the field.

Robert F. Kennedy Jr., the son of the late US Attorney General, announced a $100,000 challenge to prove the safety of vaccines, particularly those containing the mercury-based preservative thimerosal. Kennedy has been a longtime advocate of the debunked link between thimerosal and autism, a claim repeatedly denounced by medical organizations and physicians.

Kennedy claimed he has spoken with White House staff several times in the last month to discuss the creation of a Trump administration panel to examine vaccine safety. The panel would be led by Kennedy himself, as per discussions with President Trump in January. However, the Trump administration has yet to confirm these claims.

The issue of vaccine safety has been a topic of interest for President Trump, who has raised it several times, including during a recent conversation with Betsy DeVos. The American Academy of Pediatrics and 350 other medical organizations have expressed "unequivocal support" for the safety of vaccines in a letter to President Trump.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) clearly states that there is no link between vaccines and autism. Kennedy, however, accused the CDC of being a "cesspool of corruption" and a "vaccine company" that hides science from the public.

Actor Robert De Niro, who has a son with autism, supported Kennedy's claims during a panel discussion at the National Press Club. Kennedy announced the "World Mercury Project Challenge," offering $100,000 to anyone who could find a scientific study that demonstrated the safety of thimerosal-containing vaccines in children and pregnant women.

Scientists immediately denounced Kennedy's claims as incorrect and a dangerous ploy. Peter Hotez, president of the Sabin Vaccine Institute, stated that there is an abundance of evidence showing that vaccines are safe, and there's not even any plausibility of an association with autism.

The panel, which included De Niro, was held at the National Press Club in Washington D.C. Kennedy presented 240 studies, three charts, and several binders that he claimed proved certain vaccines were unsafe to a certain population of children. However, these claims have been widely disputed by the scientific community.

Kennedy's motivations for the challenge and his continued advocacy for the debunked link between vaccines and autism have been denounced by many as a dangerous ploy. Hotez stated that such press conferences become a distraction from the important work that needs to be done in the field of vaccine safety.

Aaron Schock, a Republican congressman from Illinois, is launching a health initiative called the Fit for Summer, Fit for Life challenge to help Americans improve their health. Schock is known for his commitment to fitness and health, and he believes that a good example is the best sermon. He is a self-made politician who won his first election at 19 and has been in politics for over a decade. He is focused on major issues that will affect his own generation the most, including energy and the environment, the budget deficit, spiraling health-care costs, and a growing obesity crisis. Schock is a deficit hawk who favors tax incentives to spur investment in alternative energy and infrastructure. He is also launching a workout routine for people with high-stress day jobs. Schock is known for his media-friendly profile and has received attention for his youthful appearance and polished demeanor. He is the first U.S. rep born in the 1980s and is often compared to the character Alex P. Keaton from the TV show Family Ties. Schock's approach to politics is unconventional, and he is focused on long-term strategic thinking and planning. He believes that success in politics, like success in the gym, requires a goal, a strategy, and discipline. Schock is also known for his optimism and believes that the problems facing America are not insurmountable. He is committed to helping his generation embrace health and fitness as a personal responsibility and is launching the Fit for Summer, Fit for Life challenge to help Americans take control of their health.

Three Hawaii-based Marines, identified as Sgt. Benjamin E. Johns, Lance Cpl. Jacob D. Jacoby, and Lance Cpl. Carlos Orozco III, are facing a court-martial for allegedly hazing a fellow Marine, Lance Cpl. Harry Lew, who later committed suicide in Afghanistan. The Marines are charged with wrongfully humiliating and demeaning Lew, and some face additional charges of assault, cruelty, and maltreatment. The trial date for the accused Marines has not been set, and they will face a general court-martial, the most serious charges in the military justice system.

Lew's suicide occurred on April 3, and he was a nephew of U.S. Rep. Judy Chu of California. The Marines' actions have been closely watched, with the case capturing attention from Silicon Valley to Washington, D.C. The Marines are presumed innocent until proven guilty, and no trial date has been set.

The alleged abuse began after Lew was transferred to a new unit 10 days before his death. Lew was described as an avid breakdancer and a happy young man who joined the military to "take care of the Taliban." The Marines' leaders tried various approaches to keep Lew awake, but on his last night, the efforts escalated into alleged acts of violence and humiliation, according to the charges heard.

The military justice system will hold a hearing to determine if there is enough evidence to proceed with the trial. If convicted, the Marines could face punishment, but it's unclear what that would be. The Marines have taken a hard stance against hazing, saying repeatedly that it "does not tolerate hazing of any kind."

Joan Rivers, a trailblazing comedienne, received a star-studded funeral on Sunday in New York City, as requested in her book. The service at Temple Emanu-El on Fifth Avenue was attended by numerous celebrities, including Kathy Griffin, Howard Stern, Sarah Jessica Parker, Whoopi Goldberg, and many more from the worlds of Hollywood, fashion, media, and finance.

Rivers' daughter, Melissa, read a heartfelt letter to her mother, and Hugh Jackman sang a tune from "The Boy from Oz." The service was filled with laughter and tears, reflecting Rivers' unique personality and career. Fans lined the block outside, some dressed in designer clothes to honor the late "Fashion Police" host.

Rivers, who died at 81 after a throat procedure, was a pioneer for comedians, particularly women. She was a TV talk show host, actress, fashion critic, and had a line of jewelry. The cause of her death is still being investigated. In lieu of flowers, donations can be made to God's Love, We Deliver; Guide Dogs for the Blind; or Our House. The service was a fitting tribute to a woman who lived life to the fullest and left an indelible mark on the entertainment industry.

In an interview, Seth Rogen humorously discussed the challenges of voice-over work for an airline, stating that announcements required speaking loudly over the engine's noise. He also reflected on his film, The Green Hornet, which he cowrote and starred in, describing it as the "perfect storm of bad shit happening." Evan Goldberg, his co-writer, added that they were making the film for both America and China, potentially contributing to its reception. Rogen jokingly suggested that they should avoid making expensive movies where they can't incorporate their signature humor, implying a focus on their strengths in future projects.

A young man named Kenneth Bachman from Sewell, New Jersey, recently took an extraordinary Uber ride that spanned over 300 miles across four states. The incident occurred after a night of partying at a fraternity event in Morgantown, West Virginia, where Bachman had been drinking heavily. He ordered an Uber to take him home, but his destination was actually his residence in Gloucester County, New Jersey, which is more than five hours away.

The Uber driver, who accepted the long journey for a hefty fee of $1,635.93, took Bachman home safely. However, Bachman suspects the ride would have cost around $800 had he ordered a standard Uber, but he unintentionally ordered the more expensive UberXL.

The journey consisted of a base fare of $3.94, a $2.35 booking fee, $696.95 for distance, and $115.90 for time. The high cost was due to surge pricing, which doubled every charge except the booking fee.

Bachman, who passed out during the ride, woke up to find himself in the car with the driver, who was unable to pay for tolls. Bachman had to stop at a CVS in Sewell to get cash for tolls on the way back. Despite the unusual circumstances, Bachman gave his driver five stars.

Uber confirmed that the ride did indeed occur and that the driver took the rider to the destination he requested. The company also resolved the matter with Bachman, who agreed to pay the fare. Bachman plans to return to West Virginia to pick up his belongings.

This incident marks one of the longest trips via a car-sharing service, although the record for the longest trip is yet to be confirmed. In the past, an Uber ride from the Dallas-Fort Worth area to Nashville, which is more than 650 miles, was reported, taking more than 11 hours.

This report has been updated to correct the make and model of the Uber car.

In a tragic incident in Queens, New York, an 11-year-old boy named Anthony Perez McClean died after he bravely jumped into a frozen pond to save his 12-year-old friend who had fallen through the ice. The accident occurred at Forest Park around 4 p.m. on Tuesday.

According to reports, Perez and his friend were playing near the pond when the older boy walked onto the ice and fell through. Perez immediately rushed to help and also fell through the ice. Rescuers, who had to wade through chest-high, frigid water, managed to pull Perez out but found him unconscious. Despite CPR efforts on the scene and during transportation to Jamaica Hospital, he was pronounced dead.

Perez's neighbors in Middle Village were shocked and saddened by the news but praised his heroic actions. Carmen Rivera, who lives downstairs from the Perez family, called him a hero, while Leonardo Coraci described him as a good and respectful kid.

The FDNY urged parents to warn their children about the dangers of playing on frozen bodies of water in the winter. FDNY Deputy Chief George Healy emphasized that the ice is not safe, especially when temperatures reach just above freezing, as was the case on Tuesday when New York City hit 35 degrees. He also reported that some of the rescuers fell through the ice themselves while trying to save Perez, and two firefighters were treated for hypothermia.

The incident has sparked a call for increased awareness about the dangers of frozen bodies of water in the city. The FDNY has emphasized the importance of parents warning their children about the risks and reminding them that the ice is not safe.

Ozzy Osbourne, the British rock legend, has expressed his disgust towards the Westboro Baptist Church in Kansas for using his song 'Crazy Train' during protests against gays in the military. The church, known for its anti-gay demonstrations at military funerals, used the song during a demonstration at the U.S. Supreme Court, where the court is reviewing a ruling that awarded $5 million to the family of Lance Cpl. Matthew Snyder, whose funeral was previously protested by the church. Ozzy, in a statement, said he was "sickened and disgusted" by the use of his song to promote hate and evil. The church's version of the song turned it into a hate-mongering chant, which contradicts the song's original message of tolerance and understanding.

The United States is currently experiencing a series of severe winter storms, causing widespread disruptions across multiple states. The latest storm has resulted in nearly 1 million homes and businesses losing power in four states, with over 2,700 flights canceled. The storm has brought snow, ice, and cold temperatures to various regions, from the Midwest to New England. In Boston, snow is falling heavily, causing trees to crack and power lines to come down. Governor Andrew Cuomo has declared an emergency in New York due to heavy snows taxing salt reserves, and transportation regulators have waived rest rules for salt-truck drivers. In Kansas, a third weather-related death has been announced. The storm has been particularly harsh in the High Plains, with temperatures as much as 40 degrees below normal in some places. The storm is expected to continue affecting millions of people over the next few days, with more snow and ice forecasted for the Northeast and cold temperatures for the midsection of the country.

In a recent interview with Charlie Rose, George Lucas, the creator of the "Star Wars" saga, expressed his feelings about Disney's handling of "Star Wars: The Force Awakens" and the sale of Lucasfilm to the Walt Disney Company in 2012. Lucas criticized Disney's approach to the sequel, stating that he was against making the new movie "for the fans" and felt he sold his company to "white slavers," referring to Disney. However, he later issued an apology for his remark.

Lucas sold Lucasfilm to Disney for $4.06 billion, and the studio developed "The Force Awakens" with J.J. Abrams and Kathleen Kennedy. In the interview, Lucas discussed his decision to stay out of the new installment, stating that Disney wanted to make something for the fans, while he just wanted to tell a story. He also mentioned that Disney didn't want him involved in the project, as he would only cause trouble.

Lucas has previously seemed supportive of "The Force Awakens," and it's even been said that he liked the movie and attended its premiere. However, it seems that the "remakequel" style of the movie wouldn't have been the path Lucas would have taken if he were still at the helm.

In the interview, Lucas also discussed other topics, including his early acting career, his Oscar nomination for "Gilbert Grape," and rumors about him testing for roles in "Batman Forever" and the "Star Wars" prequels.

Lucas has had a long and successful career in the entertainment industry, and his comments about Disney's handling of "Star Wars" have sparked a debate among fans and industry insiders. It remains to be seen how the franchise will continue to evolve under Disney's ownership.

Ohio State coach Urban Meyer has spoken out regarding accusations of enabling lawless behavior by former Florida player Aaron Hernandez, who is currently accused of murder. Meyer sent a text to The Dispatch to clarify that Hernandez was held to the same drug testing policy as every other player during his time at Florida. The text also stated that Meyer and his staff worked hard to mentor and guide Hernandez. The Rolling Stone magazine is set to release a detailed investigation into Hernandez's life, which alleges that he was a regular user of the hallucinogenic drug PCP and had become so paranoid that he carried a gun wherever he went. The magazine also alleges that Hernandez's college coach, Urban Meyer, may have helped cover up failed drug tests and violent incidents during his time at the University of Florida. Meyer has repeatedly denied these accusations.

Former Alaska Governor Sarah Palin obtained a 20-day protective order against an 18-year-old Pennsylvania man, Shawn R. Christy, who allegedly stalked and threatened her. The protective order was granted by Alaska Magistrate Judge Colleen Ray after Palin and her attorney presented evidence of implied threats through phone and written messages. Palin testified that Christy had made statements such as "watch your back," bought a one-way ticket to Alaska, and sent a gun purchase receipt. Palin claimed to fear for her life and her family's safety, stating that Christy had also contacted her daughter, Willow, and believed he had a relationship with her. Christy was ordered to have no contact with Palin's family and to stay a mile away from her home and from a Wasilla area high school. A hearing on a request for a long-term order is scheduled for October 13. Palin travels extensively around the country, giving speeches and supporting conservative candidates. The Mat-Su Valley Frontiersman newspaper first reported the case.

Alan Thicke's sons, Robin and Brennan, have filed a legal petition against their stepmother, Tanya Callau, alleging that she is attempting to obtain a larger share of Thicke's estate than what was intended in his will. The sons claim that Callau is threatening to challenge the prenuptial agreement signed in 2005 and is demanding more due to her alleged support of Thicke and his youngest son, Carter.

According to the petition, Thicke left each of his three children equal shares of a Carpinteria ranch, 75 percent of his personal effects, and 60 percent of his remaining estate. He left Callau the ranch's furnishings, 25 percent of his personal effects, a $500,000 life insurance policy, all of his death benefits from pensions and union memberships, and 40 percent of his remaining estate. He also provided that she could live at the ranch, as long as she paid for its expenses and maintained the property.

The sons claim that Callau is now insisting that the prenup is invalid, and they are seeking a court ruling on the extent to which the Trust's property is Thicke's separate property and whether Callau's challenge to the prenup is barred because she waived her community property rights when signing it.

Tanya Callau's attorney, Adam Streisand, has disputed the sons' claims, stating that Callau never threatened to take private family matters public and intends to handle the false statements privately.

The sons, who are co-trustees of Thicke's living trust, say they are taking legal action to honor their father's legacy and protect his intentions. Thicke died suddenly in December at the age of 69 after his aorta ruptured while playing hockey with his son Carter.

Amy Krouse Rosenthal, an author and filmmaker, passed away from ovarian cancer in March 2017, leaving behind her husband, Jason Rosenthal, and three children. In her final days, she wrote a heartbreaking dating profile for Jason, which was published in the New York Times. The essay, titled "You May Want to Marry My Husband," highlighted Jason's thoughtfulness, handiness, and kindness, and expressed her love for him and their children.

After Amy's death, Jason experienced despair and found it difficult to cope with the loss. Four months later, his father also passed away due to complications from Parkinson's disease. In a recent TED Talk, Jason opened up about his late wife's final days and his struggle to find joy again after losing his companion of more than 26 years. He shared that he tries to honor Amy by finding beauty and joy in simple moments and cherishes memories of their time together.

The essay about Jason prompted many women to reach out to him, including one who proposed marriage under the condition that he stop drinking. Jason also cherished a letter from a close family friend who remembered Amy's creativity, even in making cornbread croutons at a Shabbat dinner.

The Rosenthal family has set up a foundation in Amy's name to raise money for ovarian cancer research and children's literacy, causes that were near and dear to her heart. Jason, although still grieving, is learning to find joy and honor Amy's memory by seeking out beauty and simple pleasures in life. He shared that he is not sure if he will remarry in the future, but he is grateful for the love and support he has received from others.

President Trump's first budget proposal, titled "America First: A Budget Blueprint to Make America Great Again," was released on Thursday, March 16, 2017. The budget proposal aims to increase defense spending by $54 billion and offset this by stripping money from more than 18 other agencies. The proposal calls for significant cuts across much of the government, including the elimination of dozens of federal programs that assist the poor, fund scientific research, and aid America's allies abroad.

The budget proposal would result in a reduction of more than 20% at the Agriculture, Labor, and State departments, and more than 30% at the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA). The proposal also calls for the elimination of future federal support for the National Endowment for the Arts, the National Endowment for the Humanities, and the Corporation for Public Broadcasting. Within the EPA alone, 50 programs and 3,200 positions would be eliminated.

The proposed cuts could represent the widest swath of reductions in federal programs since the drawdown after World War II, potentially leading to a significant cutback in the federal non-military workforce. White House Office of Management and Budget Director Mick Mulvaney said, "You can't drain the swamp and leave all the people in it."

Many of Trump's budget proposals are likely to face stiff resistance from lawmakers on Capitol Hill, even from Republicans, whose support is crucial because they must vote to authorize government appropriations. Republicans have objected to the large cuts in foreign aid and diplomacy that Trump has foreshadowed, and his budget eliminates funding for a number of programs that serve low-income Americans and minorities, such as the Low-Income Home Energy Assistance Program and the Community Development Block Grant program.

The budget proposal would not take effect until the new fiscal year on October 1, but the president must still reach a separate agreement with Congress by the end of April, when a temporary funding bill expires. If they cannot reach an agreement, and if Trump's new budget plan widens fault lines, then the chances would increase for a partial government shutdown starting on April 29.

The president and Congress must also raise the debt ceiling, which has become a politically fraught ritual. Although the ceiling was extended until March 15, budget experts say the government should be able to continue borrowing money by suspending or stretching out payments through August or September.

White House budget proposals are often changed by lawmakers, but they serve as a marker for how the president plans to govern and as an opening bid on budget talks. Mulvaney said the White House was open to negotiation, but he was unapologetic about the size and scope of the reductions.

The 53-page budget plan offers the clearest snapshot yet of Trump's priorities. However, it is also far shorter and vaguer than White House budget plans normally are. One of the missing details is precisely where and how many jobs would be eliminated across the federal government.

Parts of the budget proposal appear to contradict Trump's agenda. For example, the budget proposes a $5.8 billion cut to the National Institutes of Health, despite Trump's recent address to Congress in which he spoke of finding "cures to the illnesses that have always plagued us." The proposal also eliminates a Transportation Department program that funds nearly $500 million in road projects. It does not include new funding amounts or a tax mechanism for Trump's infrastructure program, postponing those decisions.

The proposed budget extensively targets Obama programs and investments focused on climate change, seeking to eliminate payments to the United Nations’ Green Climate Fund — one key component of the U.S. commitment to the Paris climate agreement — and to slash research funding for climate, ocean, and earth science programs at agencies such as NASA and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. At the same time, clean-energy research, heavily privileged by the Obama administration, would suffer greatly under the budget with the elimination of the ARPA-E program (Advanced Research Projects Agency-Energy) at the Energy Department and an unspecified cut to the agency’s Office of Energy Efficiency and Renewable Energy.

Many Republicans have criticized these programs in the past as wasteful and ineffective, but supporters have said the programs are vital for communities in need. The proposed budget would not take effect until the new fiscal year on October 1, but the president must still reach a separate agreement with Congress by the end of April, when a temporary funding bill expires. If they cannot reach an agreement, and if Trump's new budget plan widens fault lines, then the chances would increase for a partial government shutdown starting on April 29.

The document is a news article about the death of a 61-year-old man named James M. Emswiller who fell from a balcony during the filming of a movie about Fred Rogers, titled "You Are My Friend." The incident occurred in Mt. Lebanon, Pennsylvania, and Emswiller was involved in the sound production of the movie. He was taken to UPMC Mercy in critical condition, but later died from his injuries. The cause of death was determined to be blunt impact injuries to the head and torso, and the manner of death was listed as an accident. The film, which stars Tom Hanks as Fred Rogers, was on hold following the incident. Emswiller had previously won an Emmy Award for his work on the TV movie "Bessie." The movie is inspired by a real-life friendship between Rogers and journalist Tom Junod.

In Chaoyang City, China, a 1-year-old boy named Hanhang endured a harrowing experience when a chopstick became lodged in his nose for 10 days, causing a brain infection. The incident occurred while Hanhang was eating chow mein with his parents. After tripping and falling, the chopstick was driven up his nose, and his parents removed the object, unaware that it had punctured his brain.

The family took Hanhang to the hospital for treatment, but doctors failed to notice the chopstick fragments in his brain. Hanhang's condition worsened at home, with repeated vomiting and lethargy, prompting a second hospital visit. An X-ray revealed the chopstick piece, and doctors immediately removed the remaining six centimeters. Although Hanhang has a brain infection, his condition improved significantly.

This incident serves as a reminder of the potential dangers associated with chopsticks and young children. In 2014, a 2-year-old Chinese boy had a chopstick penetrate three inches into his brain, and a 12-year-old boy underwent surgery after chopsticks he was carrying penetrated his neck during a fall on a playground. Parents are advised to keep chopsticks out of reach of children and only allow their use at the dinner table.

A volunteer for Ben Carson's presidential campaign, Braden Joplin, aged 25, died on Tuesday after a car accident in western Iowa. The accident also injured three other campaign workers who were treated at a hospital in Atlantic, Iowa, and later released. Joplin was a student at Texas Tech University and had been volunteering for Carson's campaign in Iowa since earlier this month. Carson, who was in South Carolina at the time of the crash, suspended his campaign events and flew to Nebraska to be with Joplin's family. Carson expressed his condolences and called Joplin an "amazing young man." Other presidential candidates, including Hillary Clinton, Ted Cruz, Marco Rubio, Bernie Sanders, and Jeb Bush, also offered their condolences. The Carson campaign will cover travel expenses for Joplin's family to Omaha, Nebraska.

The article is a personal narrative about a woman's experience with breast cancer diagnosis. The author, who remains anonymous, shares her journey from learning about the diagnosis to undergoing various medical tests and receiving the confirmation of cancer spread to one of her lymph nodes. Throughout the process, she uses humor and social media to cope with her fears and share her experiences with others. The author emphasizes the importance of acceptance, calmness, and love in dealing with the unknown and the gravity of the situation. The article ends with the author's determination to find her way back home, implying her resolve to fight the cancer and return to a normal life. The article also highlights the role of technology, particularly social media, in providing support and coping mechanisms during difficult times.

A British couple returned home from a Caribbean cruise with parasitic infections that caused itchy, red rashes on their backsides. The couple, aged 52, contracted cutaneous larva migrans, a skin condition caused by a hookworm infection, after sunbathing on a beach in Martinique. The most common culprit for the infection in the Caribbean is the hookworm Ancylostoma braziliense.

People can pick up the parasite after encountering hookworm larvae, which can be excreted in the feces of an infected animal, typically a dog or cat, onto sandy beaches or moist soil. A high percentage of dogs and cats are infected with hookworm, especially strays. Once a hookworm larva penetrates a person's skin, it can burrow around, leaving a trail-like rash of inflamed skin known as a "creeping eruption."

The couple sought help from the medical staff on the cruise ship, but their treatments did not help. When they returned home, they went to the hospital, where doctors diagnosed them with cutaneous larva migrans. The couple was given anti-parasitic medication, but five days later, the woman went to the emergency room because she was experiencing shortness of breath, a dry cough, and chest pain. A small percentage of people with cutaneous larva migrans may get symptoms in their lungs.

The couple was given a second dose of anti-parasitic medication, and the treatment quickly helped clear up their skin as well as their lungs. Caribbean beaches aren't the only places where hookworms can be found; some beaches along the Gulf Coast of the U.S. and the Atlantic seaboard may also be teaming with the parasites. To prevent infection, people should wear shoes and use protecting mats or other coverings to prevent direct skin contact with sand or soil.

The article discusses the claims made by the top U.S. general in Europe, Army Gen. Curtis Scaparrotti, who suggested that Russia might be supplying the Taliban in Afghanistan. Scaparrotti testified before the Senate Armed Services Committee that he had witnessed an increase in Russia's influence on the Taliban, including potential material support. He did not elaborate on the type of equipment or when the support was provided.

Russia's communications with the Taliban have been a point of contention, with U.S. officials and military officers expressing concern. Russia has justified its contacts with the Taliban by stating that the insurgent group is fighting the Islamic State in Afghanistan, not the U.S.-backed Afghan government. However, U.S. commander of NATO forces in Afghanistan, Gen. John Nicholson, has decried Russia's contact with the Taliban, stating that it has given cover to a group that has worked for years to undermine the United States and the government in Kabul.

The Taliban's influence in Afghanistan has been growing, as evidenced by their capture of the strategic district of Sangin in the south province of Helmand. This district was previously controlled by U.S. and British forces. The capture of Sangin has prompted calls for more troops to help train the Afghan military and reverse the "stalemate" in the country. Currently, about 5,000 NATO troops are in the country, in addition to the 8,400-strong American presence.

The article also mentions that Russia fought its own bloody war of attrition in Afghanistan in the 1980s, pulling out after suffering heavy losses from U.S.-supplied insurgents. However, Russia's renewed interest in the region seems to be growing, according to Scaparrotti.

The article concludes by stating that the stakes are high in Afghanistan, with more than 1,800 American troops having been killed in fighting since the war began in 2001. The U.S. and NATO must win in Afghanistan, according to Scaparrotti.

In response to these claims, the head of the Russian foreign ministry's department responsible for Afghanistan, Zamir Kabulov, denied the allegations, stating that they were designed to justify the failure of the U.S. military and politicians in the Afghan campaign. Kabulov also accused the U.S. of fabricating these claims.

The FCC has proposed to eliminate net neutrality rules, giving internet service providers (ISPs) the freedom to create fast and slow lanes, prioritize their own traffic, and block apps or services. The proposal removes the common carrier designation from internet providers, arguing that the 2015 net neutrality ruling was flawed and unnecessary. ISPs will still have to disclose when they engage in such practices, and the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) will have oversight.

Net neutrality supporters argue that these policies could unfairly advantage ISPs' own content, but the FCC believes that only the largest ISPs could potentially do so. The FCC also intends to prevent states from passing their own net neutrality laws, citing potential obstacles to broadband service delivery. The order is set to be voted on in December and is expected to pass. The proposal aims to facilitate investment and innovation by removing regulatory uncertainty and lowering compliance costs.

McDonald's has announced that it will replace plastic straws with paper ones in all its UK and Ireland restaurants, starting from September. This move is part of a global effort to reduce plastic waste and follows successful trials in selected restaurants earlier this year. The restaurant chain uses 1.8 million straws a day in the UK and aims to complete the transition to paper straws by 2019. The decision has been welcomed by Environment Secretary Michael Gove, who called it a "significant contribution" to helping the environment.

The move to paper straws is part of a broader trend among companies to reduce their use of single-use plastic products. In January, UK supermarket Iceland committed to eliminating plastic packaging from its own brand products by 2023, and bottled water brand Evian announced plans to produce all its plastic bottles from 100% recycled plastic by 2025.

The issue of plastic waste is a serious one, with Europeans producing 25 million tons of plastic waste per year, according to the European Commission. Less than 30% of this is collected for recycling. The use of plastic straws, which are made from plastics such as polypropylene and polystyrene, is a particular concern as they take hundreds of years to decompose if not recycled. Many end up in landfill and the oceans, causing harm to marine wildlife.

However, not everyone thinks total bans on plastic straws are the answer. Some argue that plastic straws are necessary for people with disabilities, children, and the elderly. Others have raised concerns about the safety and suitability of paper alternatives. Tetra Pak, a food packaging company, has also argued that plastic straws serve a "vital" function in cartons and should not be banned.

McDonald's has said that plastic straws will still be available "for those that require it," but they will be kept behind the counter. Transition to paper straws will also take place in selected restaurants in the US, France, Norway, and other countries. In some countries, straws are being offered on request only.

The move by McDonald's is part of a broader effort by the company to reduce its environmental impact. In 2018, McDonald's announced plans to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by 36% by 2030, and to source 100% of its beef from sustainable sources by 2020. The company has also committed to using 100% renewable energy in its restaurants and offices by 2025.

Overall, the move by McDonald's to replace plastic straws with paper ones is a positive step towards reducing plastic waste and protecting the environment. However, it is important to ensure that alternatives are safe and accessible for all, and that efforts to reduce plastic waste are part of a broader commitment to sustainability.

Chinese artist Ai Weiwei, a vocal critic of the government, was allowed his first family visit since his arrest over 40 days ago. Ai Weiwei, who is under investigation for suspected "economic crimes", met his wife Lu Qing at an unknown location on Sunday. The artist's wife was summoned to a police station and taken to another location where she was allowed a brief meeting with her husband.

Ai Weiwei is a maverick who has frequently clashed with authorities. In 2009, he was beaten up by police in Sichuan while trying to testify for a dissident. He is also known for his criticism of China's hosting of the 2008 Olympics and his frequently censored blog, which was read by 10,000 people a day until it was shut down by authorities.

The meeting between Ai Weiwei and his wife was very brief, and there were many other people present, some of them taking notes. Ai told his wife that those holding him were taking good care of him, he was healthy, and she should not worry. However, Lu Qing said she could see redness in her husband's eyes, and he seemed conflicted and upset.

The family were warned by police not to discuss the visit with the media as it could "be bad for Mr Ai's case". The Foreign Ministry has insisted that Ai's case has "nothing to do with human rights or freedom of expression".

Ai Weiwei's case has prompted an outcry in the art world and among officials in the US and EU who say his treatment is a sign of China's deteriorating human rights. The artist's influence has ranged far beyond that of the usual contemporary artist, turning him into a social activist and tapping into anger among many Chinese at official corruption and indifference. Since his disappearance, art museums, collectors, and artists have rallied behind him.

A Balch Springs woman, Mary Jane Lane, aged 50, was arrested on Tuesday in Dallas, Texas, for driving while intoxicated (DWI) after she ran over her husband, Randall Lane, when he tried to wake her up at a red light. According to the Dallas Police report, Lane passed out at a red light on Northwest Highway and Ferndale, and her husband got out of the SUV to unfasten her seat belt. However, Lane woke up and pressed the accelerator, causing her husband to be dragged and suffer injuries to his head and both legs.

Lane initially faced charges of intoxication assault and leaving the scene of an accident, but these were later downgraded to DWI. She is currently in the Dallas County Jail on a $20,000 bond, and the condition of her husband is not known. The incident occurred around 5 p.m. on Tuesday.

The Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) has recently released a collection of once-classified UFO documents, which primarily date from the 1940s and 1950s. The documents were declassified in 1978 and include reports of UFO sightings in various parts of the world, such as East Germany, Spain, North Africa, and the Belgian Congo.

The CIA has highlighted five documents that they believe X-Files character Agent Fox Mulder would find interesting, including reports of flying saucers over East Germany, Spain, and North Africa, as well as a survey of UFO reports from 1952. They have also highlighted five documents that they believe Agent Dana Scully, Mulder's skeptical partner, could use to prove that there is a scientific explanation for UFO sightings.

One of the most intriguing stories from the documents is about a massive flying pan-like object that was reportedly seen in West Germany in 1952. The object was described as having a diameter of about 15 meters and was reported to have landed in a forest clearing in Germany's Soviet Zone. The object was said to have two rows of holes, each about 12 inches in diameter, and a large, conical tower at the top.

Another interesting story is about two fiery discs that were spotted hovering over uranium mines in the Elisabethville district of the Belgian Congo in 1952. The discs were described as aluminum-colored metal, between 39 and 49 feet in diameter, and had a central knob that seemed to stay absolutely still as the outer disc rotated at tremendous speeds.

The documents also include reports of smoke trails and unusual objects emitting a pale green light over Barcelona, Spain, and Sousse, Tunisia. The CIA did not release documents to show exactly how all of those investigations were resolved, but other documents suggest that most seem to be hoaxes or misidentified objects.

The release of these documents comes as the new X-Files series airs on Fox, and the CIA has acknowledged the show's influence in their decision to highlight the documents. The documents can be found on the CIA's website, and the agency invites readers to explore them and decide for themselves whether they believe in the existence of extraterrestrial activity.

The ongoing government shutdown in the United States has significantly impacted various science and health agencies, affecting both ongoing research and patient care. The National Institutes of Health (NIH) has been particularly affected, with the NIH Clinical Center, the largest research hospital in the world, closing its doors to new patients. Many of the hospital's patients suffer from cancer, rare genetic diseases, or serious infections that have not been relieved elsewhere.

The shutdown has also affected ongoing clinical trials at the NIH Clinical Center. No new studies will be started, and no new patients will be enrolled in the 1,437 studies currently underway, including 255 studies looking at cancer treatments for adults and children. The hospital's reduced staff will continue to care for existing patients, but new patients will not be admitted unless the NIH Clinical Center's director deems it medically necessary.

Meanwhile, workers at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) will show up to feed and care for animals in NIH labs, but basic research conducted by NIH scientists there will stop. The CDC's activities will be significantly reduced during the shutdown, with only about 4,000 of the CDC's 13,000 staff members continuing to work. The CDC will not be conducting multi-state outbreak investigations, but will keep the emergency operation center working at a reduced capacity, which can be geared up quickly if a serious outbreak of illness is discovered.

PulseNet, the CDC's foodborne disease tracking program, is still up and running, but there will be no monitoring of seasonal flu activity across the U.S. Ongoing investigations, such as the one looking into several outbreaks of the brain-eating amoeba Naegleria, will continue, but surveillance of H7N9 (bird flu) and the coronavirus that causes MERS (Middle East Respiratory Syndrome) will be "much less robust," according to the CDC.

Roughly 45 percent of the workers at the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) have been furloughed, leaving the agency "unable to support the majority of its food safety, nutrition, and cosmetics activities." Some work, such as that related to some activities funded by user-fees in the Center for Tobacco Products, and "high-risk recalls, civil and criminal investigations, import entry reviews, and other critical public health issues," will continue.

Mission Control at NASA's Johnson's Space Center in Houston remains open for business, providing its usual support for the International Space Station. However, the rest of the center in Houston is closed, and most employees have been put on furlough. A NASA memo obtained by SpaceRef suggests most NASA employees weren't even allowed to turn on their computers. The Mars rover Curiosity is still making its rounds on the red planet (staffed by non-civil servants), but managers in charge of MAVEN, NASA's next mission to Mars, worry that even a brief shutdown could delay their project's Nov. 18 launch. If the orbiter misses its launch period, another window won't open again for 26 months, the mission managers say.

At the U.S. Geological Survey, only 43 of its 8,600 employees are deemed essential and working during the shutdown. Just before she was furloughed Tuesday, a USGS spokesperson told NPR's Richard Harris that there will be skeleton crews working at headquarters, at the earthquake center in Boulder, Colo., and at the volcano observatories, plus a couple of people are continuing to keep an eye on the data coming in from the two Landsat satellites. These spacecraft collect critical information about the earth's surface that's used by scientists and businesses. For now, the satellite data will only be archived, and analyzed and distributed as images later.

The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration is affected by the shutdown, but officials there told NPR's Jon Hamilton that the weather forecasting portions of the agency are deemed "necessary to protect lives and property," and will continue their work unabated. The National Weather Service also stayed open during the federal shutdown in the winter of 1996 — and successfully forecast a blizzard.

Nearly 95 percent of the Environmental Protection Agency's 16,000-member staff has been furloughed. This means there will be lots of delays in the programs that safeguard the nation's air, water, land, and food. Some cleanup activities are being postponed at more than 500 hazardous waste sites in nearly every state of the country. Some reviews of chemicals and pesticides are being stalled. But efforts to clean up leaking underground storage tanks will continue. EPA officials would also still respond to any environmental emergencies that arise, such as big chemical spills.

In a contingency plan released late last week, the U.S. Forest Service called for keeping 41 percent of its workforce on hand in case of a government shutdown. The agency said it needed about 13,000 workers to carry out essential activities such as fire suppression, law enforcement, protection of federal lands, and protection of research studies where a halt in activity could destroy or endanger study findings.

The Nuclear Regulatory Commission, which is responsible for overseeing the nation's nuclear reactors, has saved up enough money to continue full operations for another week. After that, it will focus on its core role policing safety at the nation's nuclear plants. NRC spokesman Eliot Brenner says "the NRC will continue to have on site, at all 100 nuclear reactors in this country, its resident inspectors." But most of the agency's nearly 4,000 employees will be sent home. In the unlikely event an accident occurs, Brenner says they could be recalled quickly.

During the shutdown, the panda cam at The Smithsonian's National Zoo has been turned off. Officials at Craters of the Moon National Monument are about to get more boots on the ground to search for a missing Boise woman. The monument has 19 employees and all but three were about to be placed on furlough due to the government shutdown. On Wednesday, however, officials there say the park has received permission to keep 10 workers under the "excepted" status during the search. The search effort had already been scaled back due to rescue agencies being called back to their respective headquarters and poor weather earlier in the week. Only three staff members are at the park monitoring infrastructure resources. Family members have called for experienced hikers to help

Finland's state-owned postal service, Posti, is expanding its services this summer by offering a weekly lawn-mowing service. Customers can choose between 30-minute or 60-minute sessions, which will be available on Tuesdays due to lower mail volumes on that day. The service will be performed using the customer's lawnmower and will cost 65 euros per month for the half-hour sessions.

The idea for the lawn-mowing service came from Posti's mail delivery employees as part of their efforts to find services that make people's lives easier. The service will be available nationwide between May and August.

Posti has also launched a trial with the South Karelia Social and Health Care District (Eksote) to provide home care and services for people with disabilities. Posti's employees will assist customers with eating and daily chores as part of meal or mail delivery. The aim is to improve the clients' ability to function and quality of life at home.

Posti is investing in developing its business in services related to care, security, housekeeping, and property management as traditional mail volumes decrease. The company has years of experience in cooperation with municipal home care in the form of meal deliveries and aims to extend its services to housekeeping and property management.

Posti's lawn-mowing service is tax-deductible for domestic costs and can be ordered via Posti's online shop. Orders for the service must be placed no later than one week before the start of the next calendar month. The service will be available for the last two weeks of May for half the monthly price.

However, the Real Estate Employers group, which represents property maintenance companies, has expressed concerns about the plan, stating that postal workers may not have the right skills to operate power-driven machinery and equipment.

Posti's network of professionals reaches both densely and sparsely populated areas every weekday, which helps municipalities to provide support in the client's home. Posti's task is to help clients with their daily chores during the visit, to talk to them, and to notify Eksote of any exceptions. Combining home services with Posti's other operations - meal deliveries or mail delivery - is a natural choice. Posti can arrange even short visits cost-effectively.

The Carolina Panthers have deactivated defensive end Greg Hardy for Sunday's home opener against the Detroit Lions due to his domestic violence conviction. The decision was made by the team on Sunday morning, following public outcry against the NFL for taking a light stance on domestic violence, particularly in the wake of the Ray Rice scandal. Hardy was found guilty in July of assaulting and threatening his ex-girlfriend, but the Panthers and the NFL initially chose not to punish him while he appealed the decision and pursued a jury trial. The team's decision to deactivate Hardy was made by coach Ron Rivera, who said it was in the best interest of the Carolina Panthers. The team's players have expressed support for Hardy's return to the lineup, but Rivera was vague about when that might happen. The Panthers' decision to deactivate Hardy comes after the Ravens released Ray Rice and the Vikings deactivated Adrian Peterson following their own domestic violence incidents. The decision has sparked debate about the NFL's handling of such cases and the role of team owners in supporting commissioner Roger Goodell.

In St. Charles, Missouri, a two-year-old child named Braydon Barnes died due to hyperthermia after being left alone in a room with a space heater for approximately 38 hours. The incident has turned into a criminal investigation, with the child's parents, Kathleen M. Peacock and Lucas R. Barnes, facing charges of child abuse, neglect, and manufacturing methamphetamine.

The tragedy occurred on December 20, when Peacock discovered her son dead and sought help from a neighbor. The child's room was reportedly extremely hot. An autopsy confirmed the cause of death as hyperthermia.

The police investigation revealed that the parents were engaged in methamphetamine production at the time of the incident. They allegedly ignored the child's cries while they were on a weekend drug binge at their home.

Relatives and neighbors express deep sorrow and shock over the incident. Some had distanced themselves from the couple due to their drug use, noting that the child appeared malnourished recently. Neighbors hope the parents receive the maximum punishment if convicted.

The space heater in question has no thermostat and does not turn off automatically. The incident has highlighted the need for awareness and use of services like the St. Louis Crisis Nursery to prevent similar tragedies. Relatives of the family hope to raise awareness about other children who might be in similar situations and in need of help.

The CNN report also mentions that the parents were home all weekend while Braydon was left unattended in his room. The investigation is ongoing.

The Zika virus, primarily transmitted by the Aedes aegypti mosquito, has been linked to severe birth defects, particularly microcephaly, in at least 1,300 children across eight countries. A new study by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) estimates that the risk of a fetus developing microcephaly due to Zika infection during the first trimester of pregnancy ranges from about 1% to 13%.

The study, published in The New England Journal of Medicine, is based on approximately 400 microcephaly cases in the Brazilian state of Bahia, diagnosed between July 2015 and February 2016. The researchers made calculations to account for different scenarios, including one where most people were infected and another where Zika infections were less common.

The study found that the risk of microcephaly decreases as an outbreak progresses, as more women become immune to the virus before getting pregnant. However, it's important to note that Zika can also cause other birth defects.

The CDC study is significant as it provides healthcare professionals with a risk estimate to counsel pregnant women about the potential risks to their babies. The findings also underscore the need for healthcare systems across the Americas to prepare for caring for babies with extensive disabilities.

The study suggests that it's possible the virus could have been capable of causing microcephaly in the past, but that earlier outbreaks were too small for relatively rare events such as microcephaly to be noticed.

In addition to microcephaly, researchers have found previously unreported eye problems possibly linked to the Zika virus that could result in severe visual impairment. In a case study, ophthalmology researchers from Brazil and Stanford University examined the eyes of three infant boys from Northern Brazil born in late 2015 with microcephaly. Among the findings, the researchers identified several types of ocular issues not previously observed in relation to Zika virus, some of which could cause visual impairment if untreated.

The CDC advises all babies with microcephaly in areas hit by Zika to be examined by an ophthalmologist. The study underscores the need for continued research and vigilance to understand the full impact of the Zika virus on human health, particularly during pregnancy.

A high school student, Chelsey Ramer, from Escambia Academy High School in Atmore, Alabama, was denied her diploma after wearing an eagle feather on her graduation cap. The feather is a symbol of her Native American heritage. The school had issued a contract that forbids any "extraneous items during graduation exercises," and students violating the contract would not receive their diplomas until appropriate disciplinary actions were taken and a $1,000 fine was paid. Ramer, a member of the Poarch Creek Band of Indians, had requested permission to wear the feather but was denied. The school's headmaster, Betty Warren, is no longer with the school, and it is unclear if this change is related to the graduation incident. The school has not responded to requests for comment. Ramer's diploma is still withheld, and the school's policy has been criticized as disrespectful and discriminatory towards Native American students.

The analysis provided by the Washington Times criticizes President Obama's American Jobs Act, claiming it is a lie and that the president knows it. The article argues that the bill, which aims to raise taxes on wealthier Americans and corporations, is not supported by both Democrats and Republicans as Obama claimed in his speech to Congress. Instead, the bill is facing opposition from Democrats due to the upcoming elections and the potential for increased taxes. The article also suggests that the president's strategy of blaming Congress for the country's economic problems may backfire, as Democrats are preparing to bail on him and save their own skins. The article concludes by stating that the jobs bill is dead and that it will be House Republicans who write a bill that can actually pass the Senate. The article also mentions that President Obama's populist reincarnation since Labor Day, with his attacks on tax-coddled millionaires, corporate-jet owners, and oil companies, emerged from a moment of reflection during a summer of discontent. The article suggests that the president's strategy may do little to break the political paralysis gripping Washington or solve the riddle of joblessness, but it has returned the president to a message and style that fits more comfortably than his long, and often awkward, courtship of corporate America and its Republican allies in Congress.

A tragic traffic accident occurred in Huludao, China, where a car struck a crowd of children outside a primary school, resulting in five fatalities and 18 injuries. The driver was apprehended, and the cause of the incident is currently under investigation. Security footage shows the car swerving into the crowd, but it's unclear whether this was a deliberate attack or an attempt to avoid obstacles. This incident follows a series of vehicle-related attacks in China, including one last month in Ningbo that killed two and injured 16. Previous attacks, such as those in 2010 that resulted in nearly 20 child deaths, have prompted increased school security measures. However, violence near schools persists; in June, a man killed two children with a kitchen knife in Shanghai, and last year, an explosion at a kindergarten gate in eastern China killed eight people. The attackers' motivations are often linked to mental illness or societal alienation.

The study by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has revealed significant differences in suicide rates across various occupations in the U.S. Farmers, lumberjacks, and fishermen have the highest suicide rate, while librarians and educators have the lowest. The highest rates were observed in manual laborers who work in isolation and face unsteady employment, including carpenters, miners, electricians, and those in construction. Dentists, doctors, and other healthcare professionals had an 80% lower suicide rate compared to farmers, fishermen, and lumberjacks.

The study, which analyzed data from 17 states, found that farmers, fishermen, and forestry workers had the highest suicide rate of 85 per 100,000. Carpenters, miners, electricians, and construction workers followed closely with 53, while mechanics and those in installation, maintenance, and repair had a rate of 48. Factory and production workers had a rate of 35, and architects and engineers had 32.

The highest female suicide rate was seen in the protective service occupations category, which includes police, firefighters, and corrections officers. The second highest rate for women was in the legal profession. The study is not comprehensive, as it only covers 17 states and could not calculate suicide rates for specific jobs.

Suicide is the 10th leading cause of death in the U.S., with the highest numbers and rates in middle-aged adults. The highest male suicide rates were in the farming, fishing, and forestry group, while the highest female rate was among protective service workers.

The CDC's occupational suicide list includes farmers, fishermen, and forestry workers at the top with a rate of 85 per 100,000. The list also includes carpenters, miners, electricians, and construction workers, mechanics, factory and production workers, architects and engineers, police, firefighters, and corrections workers, artists, designers, entertainers, athletes, media, computer programmers, mathematicians, statisticians, transportation workers, corporate executives and managers, lawyers and workers in the legal system, doctors, dentists, and other healthcare professionals, scientists and lab technicians, accountants, others in business and financial operations, nursing, medical assistants, health care support, clergy, social workers, real estate agents, telemarketers, sales, building and ground, cleaning, maintenance, cooks, food service workers, childcare workers, barbers, animal trainers, personal care and service, office workers, administrative support, education, training, and librarians.

The article discusses the movie "The Mummy," a reboot of the classic Universal Pictures monster film, which is the inaugural entry in a planned "Dark Universe" franchise. The movie, directed by Alex Kurtzman and written by David Koepp, Christopher McQuarrie, and Dylan Kussman, has received mixed reviews due to its numerous references to other horror and sci-fi movies, its old-school sexism, and its violent and controversial portrayal of the Middle East.

The movie's plot revolves around an explorer named Nick Morton (Tom Cruise), who disturbs the tomb of an ancient Egyptian princess, Ahmanet (Sofia Boutella). Once reanimated, she becomes the incarnation of all evil and seeks to take over the world. The movie also features Russell Crowe as Dr. Henry Jekyll, the head of an anti-evil agency, and Annabelle Wallis as Jenny, a faux-archeologist and Nick's love interest.

The article criticizes the movie for its lack of originality, its relentless borrowing from other movies, and its thematic confusion. The author finds the movie's sexism and violence towards the Middle East particularly problematic, and notes that the movie's attempts to establish Dr. Jekyll as a Banner/Hulk or Nick Fury-type character are unsuccessful. The author also criticizes the movie's special effects and action sequences, which they find murky and unimpressive.

Despite these criticisms, the author acknowledges that the movie has some charm and that Tom Cruise's charisma shines through. They also express curiosity about the future of the Dark Universe franchise, which is planned to include reboots of other classic Universal monster movies such as "The Bride of Frankenstein," "The Invisible Man," and "The Wolfman."

Overall, the article presents a negative review of "The Mummy," criticizing its lack of originality, its thematic confusion, and its problematic portrayal of the Middle East. However, the author acknowledges that the movie has some charm and expresses curiosity about the future of the Dark Universe franchise.

The California Supreme Court has approved a change in the legal oath for new lawyers, requiring them to swear to conduct themselves with dignity, courtesy, and integrity, in addition to supporting the Constitution and faithfully discharging their duties as attorneys. The change was urged by the American Board of Trial Advocates and the State Bar of California, with former State Bar President Patrick Kelly pushing for the new language based on his observation of increasing uncivil behavior among lawyers. The new oath is a general admonition and will not serve as a basis for discipline, unlike actions such as lying or stealing, which can lead to disbarment. The change is seen as a reminder of positive professional behavior and is being campaigned for by the American Board of Trial Advocates to be adopted by other states. Other news items include the LAPD mourning after three officers were killed in two months, Donald Sterling's plans to fight to keep the Clippers, and the Red Cross assisting homeless residents displaced after a shelter fire.

Actress Sally Struthers, known for her role in "All in the Family" and charity ads, was arrested in Maine on September 12 for drunk driving. She was charged with criminal operating under the influence and posted $160 bail. Struthers, currently performing in the musical "9 to 5" at the Ogunquit Playhouse, denies the charges against her. Her arraignment is scheduled for December 14.

The article discusses the fundraising strategies of various presidential candidates in the 2016 election. Bernie Sanders, a Democratic candidate, has refused to accept support from super PACs and instead relies on small donations from individuals, with an average donation of $31.30. This strategy has resulted in a campaign built on populist issues like income inequality and has drawn significant support from rank-and-file voters. Sanders has raised more money in gifts of $200 or less than any candidate, Democrat or Republican, and has received millions of dollars through ActBlue, an online site that facilitates contributions to Democrats. Despite this, Sanders still lags behind Hillary Clinton in fundraising, but he remains optimistic about his campaign's prospects.

David Duke, a former grand wizard of the Ku Klux Klan, has expressed support for Donald Trump, praising his stance on immigration and his ability to appeal to the American people. Trump has been criticized for his controversial comments towards journalists, including Univision reporter Jorge Ramos and Fox News anchor Megyn Kelly.

Joe Biden, who is considering a run for president, is grappling with personal tragedy and pressure from the presidential hype surrounding him. Biden is more subdued and introspective than usual, and is taking a more measured approach to his deliberations about running for president. He has been reaching out to Democratic operatives and would-be donors, but has not yet made a decision about whether to run.

The article also discusses the struggles of returning Republican candidates Rick Perry and Rick Santorum to keep their own donors interested in their campaigns. A majority of their 2012 donors have defected to other candidates, contributing to financial woes in both of their campaigns. Perry and Santorum are the only two members of a 17-person presidential field who competed in 2012, and should have strong, up-to-date fundraising bases, but many of their donors have turned to other candidates, with Texas Sen. Ted Cruz being the most popular alternative. Perry and Santorum have raised significantly less money than other candidates, with former Florida Gov. Jeb Bush raising $11.4 million in the initial two weeks of his campaign and Cruz raising $4.3 million in his opening week.

In a significant development, Indian authorities have arrested Abu Jindal, a key figure allegedly involved in the planning of the 2008 Mumbai attacks. Known as the handler of the 10 gunmen who carried out the deadly assault, Jindal was remanded to police custody. The attacks targeted luxury hotels, the main railway station, and a Jewish cultural center, resulting in 165 deaths and the death of nine gunmen. The sole surviving gunman, Mohammad Ajmal Amir Qasab, was convicted and given a death sentence in 2010. The 60-hour siege began on November 26, 2008, and strained relations between India and Pakistan. After initial denials, Pakistan acknowledged that the assault was partially planned on its territory, and Qasab was a Pakistani citizen. Abu Jindal, who hails from Maharashtra, was traced and arrested in India after three years of tracking. His arrest has identified the mysterious voice recorded during the conversation between the terrorists and their handlers in Pakistan. Jindal was operating out of terror camps in Karachi and Pakistan-occupied Kashmir and was a key figure in the terror group's plan to carry out strikes in India's hinterland.

The BrandZ Top 100 Most Valuable Global Brands report was released, showcasing a 8% increase in brand value year-on-year, reaching $3.6 trillion. The report highlighted technology brands as the main drivers of value growth, with Amazon and Alibaba experiencing significant increases. Retail, led by e-commerce, saw a 14% increase in category value growth.

The 2017 BrandZ Top 100 was dominated by technology brands, with Apple and Google maintaining the top two positions. Amazon entered the top 10 at No. 4, with a 41% increase in brand value. Technology brands comprised 54% of the Top 100 value, up from 37% in 2006.

US brands led the ranking, with 54 of the Top 100 based in the US, and US brands now comprising 71% of the Top 100 value. Chinese brands, however, showed significant growth, with 13 brands in the Top 100, up from only 1 brand 12 years ago. Chinese brands rose 937% in brand value over 12 years, and now comprise 11% of Top 100 value.

The average age of a Newcomer is 20, while the average age of a Top 100 brand is 67. Tencent, a Shenzhen-based tech firm, broke into the top 10 most valuable brands, making it the first Chinese firm to achieve this.

Google, Apple, Microsoft, Amazon, Facebook, AT&T, Visa, Tencent, IBM, and McDonald's were the top 10 most valuable brands, with Google maintaining the top spot. The report emphasized the growing influence of technology brands and the rise of Chinese brands in the global market.

Joan Lee, the wife of Marvel Comics legend Stan Lee, passed away on Thursday in Los Angeles at the age of 95. Lee had been hospitalized after suffering a stroke earlier in the week. The family confirmed the news in a statement, asking for privacy during this difficult time.

Joan and Stan were married on December 5, 1947, and were together for 69 years. They had two children, J.C. (Joan Celia) and Jan, who died three days after her birth in 1953. Joan was a former British hat model who met Stan when he was supposed to take her friend on a date.

Before marrying Stan, Joan impulsively married an American soldier during World War II, in what turned out to be an unhappy relationship. After a six-week stay in Reno, Nevada, a judge granted her divorce, and she married Stan in a room next door.

Stan cited Joan as inspiration for the burgeoning Fantastic Four project he co-created with Jack Kirby in 1961. The pair moved to California in 1981 so Stan could develop Marvel TV and film works. Joan did voice work on "Fantastic Four" as Miss Forbes and "Spider-Man" as Madame Web in the 1990's animated Marvel shows. She also had a role in 2016’s "X-Men: Apocalypse."

Joan authored a novel, "The Pleasure Palace," in 1987 about a man’s mission to create the world’s most luxurious ocean liner while simultaneously balancing three romances. She also had three unpublished but finished novels at home.

Marvel paid tribute to Joan in a statement, saying "We are so saddened to hear about the loss of Joan Lee. We lost a member of the Marvel family today and our thoughts and prayers go out to Stan and his daughter Joan in this difficult time."

Stan Lee's POW! Entertainment posted an update on his Twitter account, saying "On behalf of Stan, thanks for the heartfelt condolences. He is well and truly appreciates the outpouring of love for Joan." The post included a comic book drawing of the couple.

Amanda Knox, an American student convicted of the murder of her British roommate Meredith Kercher in Italy in 2007, has stated that she will become a fugitive if an Italian court upholds her conviction in a new appeal. Knox is currently facing the possibility of having her acquittal overturned and being sentenced to a hefty prison term. The trial is ongoing at the Florence appeals court, and a verdict is expected on January 30. If the court upholds the guilty verdicts, Italy could request Knox's extradition from the US, a move that her lawyers would challenge, at least in part on the US legal principle of double jeopardy. The case has been ongoing for over six years, and Knox has remained in Seattle during the proceedings. In an interview, Knox expressed optimism about the verdict but also approached it with trepidation, stating that she wants to talk directly to Kercher's family but is aware that such a move would not be welcome. If the court upholds the guilty verdicts, it will still have to be validated by Italy's supreme court before any extradition request can be made. Legal experts say the picture is not clear-cut, as the 2011 appeal verdict that quashed Knox and Sollecito's convictions was not confirmed by the supreme court, which ruled last year that the decision to acquit was flawed.
