Sollecito's defense lawyer argued that he was the innocent victim of a deeply flawed prosecution and should be allowed to walk free. Both defendants insist they are innocent.

Ted Haggard, the former New Life Church pastor who faced a sex and drug scandal in 2006, is set to appear on the celebrity version of ABC's reality show "Celebrity Wife Swap." Haggard will swap partners with actor Gary Busey, known for his appearances on "Celebrity Rehab" and "Celebrity Apprentice." The show, based on a British format, will film Thursday at the GLBT Pride Center in Colorado Springs. Haggard, who has been featured on numerous news reports and documentaries, has remained married to his wife, Gayle, despite the scandal that forced him to resign as senior pastor of New Life Church and as president of the National Association of Evangelicals. Busey and Haggard share some surprising parallels, as Busey is a born-again Christian and active minister with Promise Keepers, while Haggard has returned to the ministry as pastor of St. James, a nondenominational Christian church in Colorado Springs. Haggard has not commented on the show. The identity of Busey's "wife" participating in the show has not been confirmed.

A 150-year-old chestnut tree, known as the Anne Frank Tree, which provided comfort to Anne Frank while she was in hiding from the Nazis, collapsed on Monday due to heavy wind and rain. The tree, which was infected with fungus and had been scheduled for felling in 2007, fell across several gardens but missed the Anne Frank House museum, located nearby. No injuries were reported. The tree was one of the few signs of nature visible to Anne Frank from the concealed attic where she hid for over two years during World War II.

In 2007, the tree was granted a last-minute reprieve after a battle in court, and city workmen encased the trunk in a steel support system to prevent it from falling. However, the support system failed under windy weather on Monday. The Netherlands' Trees Institute, one of the most prominent supporters of the preservation project, said it was "unpleasantly surprised" by the news of the tree's fall.

Clones of the tree have been taken, including 11 planted at sites around the United States and 150 at a park in Amsterdam. It is not clear whether a new tree will replace the original one on the same spot, since it rests on property belonging to a neighbor. Anne Frank made several references to the tree in the diary she kept during her time in hiding, and her diary has become the most widely read document to emerge from the Holocaust.

Parts of the tree were later being offered for sale on Dutch auction website marktplaats.nl, with the highest offer reaching 10 million euros ($12.72 million). The Support Anne Frank Tree group, which fought to keep the tree alive, said there were no plans to plant a sapling on the site or preserve the tree’s remains.

Gilad Schalit, an Israeli soldier who was held captive by Hamas for over five years, has been released in a prisoner swap deal. Schalit's father said that his son will need time to recover from psychological and physical wounds. Schalit had been suffering from shrapnel wounds and had spent the last few years in isolation. The family of Schalit expressed hope that he would lead a normal life.

The prisoner exchange involved the release of over 1,000 Palestinian prisoners, with 477 being released on Tuesday. The majority of these prisoners will return to the Gaza Strip, while some will be deported to countries such as Jordan, Turkey, and Qatar. The deal is perceived as a political victory for Hamas, despite the fact that the organization was unable to include the release of prominent Palestinian Marwan Barghouti in the negotiations.

The deal sparked controversy in Israel, as the list of Palestinians who were released includes some convicted of killing Israelis in the past. Families of terror victims petitioned against the deal before the Israeli High Court on Monday, hoping to delay the prisoners' swap. However, Israeli President Shimon Peres said in a meeting with the victims' families that it was his duty to save Schalit's life.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu issued a warning to the freed Palestinian militants, stating that Israel would continue to fight terror and that any released prisoner who returned to violence would be held accountable. Concerns about the deal were underscored by comments from one of the freed prisoners, Hamas militant leader Yehia Sinwar, who called on the movement to kidnap more soldiers.

Thousands of people gathered to welcome Schalit's return, with celebrations taking place in both Israel and the Palestinian territories. In Gaza, tens of thousands of flag-waving Palestinians celebrated the homecoming of hundreds of prisoners, while in the West Bank, released prisoners were taken to the grave of iconic Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat. Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas addressed jubilant crowds, stating that the sacrifices of the prisoners were not in vain and that they would see the results of their sacrifices in an independent Palestinian state.

In this article, the demise of the New York City subway token is discussed, marking the end of its 53-year run as a means of payment for subway rides. The token, introduced in 1953, has become a symbol of New York City's identity due to its democratic nature and association with the subway system. However, the token's use has been dwindling, with only 8% of all rides using tokens by early 2023.

The token's demise was expected due to the introduction of fare cards in 1994. The blue and yellow MetroCards are cheaper to produce and can offer discounts and transfers, making them a more efficient payment method. The last version of the token, introduced in 1995, will no longer be valid for subway rides as of May 4, 2023.

The token's popularity has led to its use in various forms of memorabilia, including key rings, cuff links, and even dresses. The People's Hall of Fame presents inductees with an enormous replica of a token, and there are Frisbees shaped like giant tokens.

The article also discusses the challenges faced by the subway system, such as petty crime and speculation involving the tokens. As the tokens gained in value, criminals devised ways to steal them, and fare increases led to speculation by collectors. However, the value of the tokens is not expected to be significant, with the last version of the token selling on eBay for between $1.99 and $14.50.

The article concludes with a discussion about the future of the token booths, now rechristened as "station service booths." Subway riders have suggested various names for the booths, such as MetroCard sales booth, fare sales booth, and MetroCard Hut. However, people may still refer to them as token booths due to habit.

Bernie Sanders, a U.S. Senator, is quoted in the article discussing gun control measures. Sanders supports President Obama's agenda on gun control, which includes strengthening and expanding instant background checks, doing away with the gun show loophole, and addressing mental health capabilities to prevent gun violence. Sanders believes that while no solution can permanently solve the issue of gun violence, significant steps can be taken to prevent it.

On January 27, 2015, a luxury hotel in Tripoli, Libya, was attacked by an affiliate of the Islamic State group. The attack resulted in the deaths of 10 people, including an American and four Europeans. The group, known as "Islamic State in Tripoli Province," claimed responsibility for the attack, stating it was in retaliation for the death of Abu Anas al-Libi, a Libyan Qaeda operative who died in a New York hospital after being captured by U.S. commandos in 2013.

The Corinthia Hotel, a hub for foreign tourists and businesspeople, was targeted in the attack. The hotel also houses the offices of several foreign embassies, but most foreigners have fled Libya due to the country's descent into chaos and armed conflict since last summer. The attack began when five masked gunmen stormed the hotel, firing randomly at staff in the lobby. A car bomb explosion followed in the parking lot, killing at least five guards and damaging some windows in the hotel's facade.

The affiliate previously claimed responsibility for an attack on the Algerian Embassy and posted pictures of fighters touring markets and distributing pamphlets. The group identified the attackers as Abu Ibrahim al-Tunsi and Abu Suleiman al-Sudani, suggesting they were Tunisian and Sudanese.

Since the 2011 uprising that ousted longtime dictator Moammar Gadhafi, Libya has been awash in armed militias, including several Islamic extremist groups. A group of Islamist militias controls Tripoli, while the internationally recognized government convenes in the far east of the country. The attack on the Corinthia Hotel tested the leadership of the Libya Dawn coalition, which controls Tripoli, as it was forced to either denounce some of its militant allies or appear to countenance the violence.

The rival coalition, under the banner Operation Dignity, is based in the Eastern cities of Tobruk and Bayda and includes fighters from the Western city of Zintan, along with fighters and officers who were loyal to Colonel Qaddafi and those who renounced him. Its military effort is led by Gen. Khalifa Hifter, who tried last year to stage a military takeover, promising to rid Libya of Islamists.

The attack on the Corinthia Hotel underscores the ongoing chaos and violence in Libya, as the country struggles to build a coherent and functional government to replace the one led by Colonel Qaddafi. Regional and ideological militias continue to battle for power and territory, often competing to coerce or intimidate the feeble institutions of the transitional government.

On Monday, May 28, 2013, a fatal car accident occurred in Newport Beach, California, claiming the lives of five high school students. The victims, three girls and two boys, were students at two high schools in the Irvine Unified School District. The driver was identified as 17-year-old Abdulrahman Alyahyan, a senior at University High School.

Among the passengers were Robin Cabrera, a 17-year-old senior at Irvine High School, and her 16-year-old sister Aurora, a sophomore at the same school. Also killed were Cecilia Zamora and Nozad Al Hamawendi, both 17-year-old juniors at Irvine High School.

The crash occurred around 5:20 p.m. when the Infiniti sedan veered off the road, hit a tree, and caught fire. The impact was so severe that the car was split in half, and four of the students died immediately. The other victim was declared dead at a hospital.

Friends gathered outside Irvine High School to console each other and remember their friends. The Cabrera sisters were accomplished dancers in the school's dance program, and Zamora was also in the dance program.

Alyahyan, the driver, was known for his love of cars, and the passengers included his best friend, Nozad Al Hamawendi. The two were part of a larger group of about 10 close friends who were either first- or second-generation immigrants from various Middle Eastern countries.

The crash is being investigated, and speed is believed to have been a factor. The posted speed limit on Jamboree Road, where the accident occurred, is 55 mph.

The tragic accident has left the community in mourning, with counselors being sent to the schools to help students deal with the situation. Graduation ceremonies are approaching at both Irvine and University High Schools.

This accident is one of the worst car accidents in Newport Beach's recent memory, and even veteran police and firefighters were stunned by the death toll. The city has a history of high-profile car wrecks linked to speeding.

Bristol Palin, the oldest daughter of Sarah Palin and a single mother, releases her memoir titled "Not Afraid of Life." The book offers an intimate look into her life, from growing up in Alaska to coping with public scrutiny during her mother's political rise, becoming a single mother at seventeen, and her experiences on ABC-TV's Dancing with the Stars. Bristol discusses her religious faith, aspirations for the future, and her recent personal life developments, including a new boyfriend and relocation to Arizona. However, a sex talk event at Washington University was canceled due to student opposition. The memoir promises candid insights into Bristol's life and values.

Arizona Senator Jon Kyl, the second-ranking Republican in the Senate, announced his retirement from Congress on February 10, 2011, marking the end of his third term. He will not seek re-election in 2013. Kyl, who has served four terms in the House and one in the Senate, has been a key figure in finance and defense policy. His departure leaves a vacancy that could lead to an interesting fight for his replacement.

Several potential candidates have been mentioned, including Republican Rep. Jeff Flake, Homeland Security Secretary Janet Napolitano, and Democratic Representative Gabby Giffords, who is recovering from a recent shooting. Kyl expressed hope that his successor would share his conservative values, prioritize national security, and work diligently for the people of Arizona.

The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee sees Kyl's retirement as a potential opportunity to gain a Senate seat in Arizona, which hasn't elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1988. Kyl's decision makes him the fifth senator, and the second Republican, to announce their departure ahead of the 2012 cycle.

Google has altered its autocomplete suggestions on its search engine after being alerted to antisemitic, sexist, and racist entries. The autocomplete feature aims to suggest common searches after a user enters one or more words into the site's search box or address bar of its Chrome browser.

Typing the phrase "are Jews" into Google, the search engine suggested "evil", for "are women" it suggested "evil" again, and for "are Muslims" it suggested "bad". Google took action within hours of being notified on Friday of the autocomplete results but did not comment on its decision to alter some but not all of the results raised in the article.

Google said that its search results are a reflection of the content across the web, and that the autocomplete predictions are algorithmically generated based on users' search activity and interests. The company acknowledged that terms that appear in autocomplete may be unexpected or unpleasant and that it does its best to prevent offensive terms, like porn and hate speech, from appearing.

This is not the first time Google and others' autocomplete and search algorithms have caused offense. In July 2015, an auto-suggested photo tag within Google's Photos service labeled two black teenagers as "Gorillas". Google apologized and said it was working on "longer term fixes" around the recognition of dark-skinned faces as well as the linguistics of photo labels.

In May 2015, Google apologized when the White House was returned as a result for searches for "nigger house" and "nigger king" within Google Maps. Google declined to explain why the results occurred but a spokesperson said: "Some inappropriate results are surfacing in Google Maps that should not be, and we apologize for any offense this may have caused."

In April this year, Google apologized after a search for "unprofessional hairstyles for work" yielded image results showing predominantly black women with natural hair, while searching for "professional" ones returned pictures of coiffed, white women. In June, Google's image search also caused offense by returning criminal mugshots for searches of "three black teenagers" but not for "three white teenagers".

Google has also previously denied "conspiracy theories" accusing it of censoring its search results to please the Conservative party in exchange for a deal over its taxes.

Leading academics have said that Google must urgently review its search ranking system because of "compelling" evidence that it is being "manipulated and controlled" by right-wing propagandists. Cathy O'Neil, a data scientist and the author of Weapons of Math Destruction, said that unless Google acknowledges responsibility for the problem, it would be a "co-conspirator" with the propagandists.

Frank Pasquale, professor of law at Maryland University, found this "a very troubling and disturbing development". He said: "They’ve gone on in the fly and plugged the plug on certain search terms in response to your article, but this raises bigger and more difficult questions. Who did that? And how did they decide? Who’s in charge of these decisions? And what will they do in the future? This is clearly just being done in response to a story in the media, but it’s not accountable, and it’s not sustainable. I find it really troubling that they’ve taken this very quick and hasty response without any explanation of how and why they’ve done it."

Google has removed the lines suggesting that Jews and black people are evil and that blacks "commit more crimes", but it is still suggesting Muslims were "bad" and that Islam "should be destroyed". While Facebook has faced criticism in the wake of revelations about how the site had become a conduit for fake news, the problem facing Google is potentially even more intractable.

O'Neil said that she believed Google would ultimately have to hire human editors. She said: "There’s a growing list of social media empires that have been attempting with all their power and might to claim that they don’t have editorial responsibility, but they have been proven wrong. They have been proven wrong by this troll army, and quite clearly when it comes to the questions that require a subtle understanding of the truth versus lies, they are going to have to use human judgment. It is clearly very frightening what is going on here. Google has done a huge amount of work to avoid exactly this scenario. And yet the troll army has still managed to break through all its resources and defenses. It is very troubling and they are clearly very, very good at this, but it’s why Google has to own this problem. It is doing a terrible job here."

A rare, lost Jackson Pollock painting is set to be auctioned on June 20, 2017, at J. Levine Auction & Appraisal in Scottsdale, Arizona. The painting, an abstract gouache measuring 22 ½ x 32 inches, was discovered in a Sun City garage after the auction house was contacted to appraise a signed L.A. Lakers poster.

The painting's provenance is strong, having come from the estate of Jenifer Gordon (Cosgriff), a lifelong friend of Clement Greenberg, an influential visual art critic most closely associated with American Modern art of the mid-20th century, Hazel Guggenheim McKinley, a mid-20th century modern artist and sister of Peggy Guggenheim, and Jackson Pollock himself.

Josh Levine, owner and CEO of J. Levine Auction & Appraisal, spent nearly 18 months and tens of thousands of dollars researching and authenticating the painting. The forensic report states that the painting's dating to the mid-20th century is well established, and no pigments or binding media introduced in the late 1950s and 1960s have been detected.

Levine believes that the painting was one of Pollock's missing gouaches in his catalogue raisonné or from the period of 1945 to 1949. However, the Pollock-Krasner Foundation does not authenticate paintings, and there have been many high-profile disputes in the past regarding the authenticity of Pollock paintings.

The auction house is located at 10345 N. Scottsdale Rd., in Scottsdale, Arizona. Online bidding is available now, with live bidding slated to begin at 11 a.m. PT on June 20. Levine is confident that this is an original Pollock and is putting his reputation on the line by calling it a Jackson Pollock. He is excited about the auction and believes that the painting will sell for at least $10 million. The owner of the painting had no idea of its value until Levine told him about Pollock.

The world's first "three-parent baby" was born five months ago to Jordanian parents, who had sought help due to the mother carrying mitochondrial DNA mutations for Leigh syndrome, a fatal neurological disorder. The treatment, which was performed in Mexico, involved a new In vitro fertilization technique that incorporated DNA from three parents. The couple had already lost two children due to the same disorder, and for religious reasons, they rejected the traditional technique used in the UK that involves discarding an embryo. Instead, a different "three-parent" technique known as spindle nuclear transfer was used, which involves removing the nucleus from the mother's egg and inserting it into a donor's egg, after removing its own nucleus. The resulting egg was then fertilized with the father's sperm. The complete findings will be presented at the American Society for Reproductive Medicine's Scientific Congress in Salt Lake City in October.

The idea of three-parent babies has sparked criticism from some groups, who claim it could pave the way for "designer babies." However, England's chief medical officer Dame Sally Davies commented that the intention is to ensure that mothers who carry faulty mitochondria can have healthy children free from devastating and often deadly conditions caused by serious mitochondrial disease. Leigh syndrome can be caused by mutations in one of more than 75 different genes, most of which are found in nuclear DNA, while some are found in mitochondrial DNA.

The most common cause of Leigh syndrome is disruption of complex I, accounting for nearly one-third of cases. At least 25 genes involved in the formation of complex I, found in either nuclear or mitochondrial DNA, have been associated with Leigh syndrome. Disruption of complex IV, also called cytochrome c oxidase or COX, is also a common cause of Leigh syndrome, underlying approximately 15 percent of cases. One of the most frequently mutated genes in Leigh syndrome is SURF1, which is found in nuclear DNA and provides instructions for making a protein that helps assemble the COX protein complex. Mutations in the SURF1 gene typically lead to an abnormally short SURF1 protein that is broken down in cells, resulting in the absence of functional SURF1 protein. The loss of this protein reduces the formation of normal COX complexes, which impairs mitochondrial energy production.

The most common mtDNA mutation in Leigh syndrome affects the MT-ATP6 gene, which provides instructions for making a piece of complex V, also known as the ATP synthase complex. MT-ATP6 gene mutations, found in approximately 10 percent of people with Leigh syndrome, block the generation of ATP. Other mtDNA mutations associated with Leigh syndrome decrease the activity of other oxidative phosphorylation protein complexes or lead to reduced formation of mitochondrial proteins, all of which impair mitochondrial energy production.

Other gene mutations associated with Leigh syndrome decrease the activity of one or more oxidative phosphorylation protein complexes or affect additional steps related to energy production. For example, Leigh syndrome can be caused by mutations in genes that form the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex or coenzyme Q10, both of which are involved in mitochondrial energy production. Mutations in genes that direct the replication of mtDNA or the production of mitochondrial proteins can also disrupt mitochondrial energy production.

Although the exact mechanism is unclear, researchers believe that impaired oxidative phosphorylation can lead to cell death because of decreased energy available in the cell. Certain tissues that require large amounts of energy, such as the brain, muscles, and heart, seem especially sensitive to decreases in cellular energy. Cell death in the brain likely causes the characteristic lesions seen in Leigh syndrome, which contribute to the signs and symptoms of the condition. Cell death in other sensitive tissues may also contribute to the features of Leigh syndrome.

The prevalence of Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia has decreased significantly since 2000, according to a study published in the Journal of the American Medical Association. Researchers studied records from 21,000 people with an average age of 75 and found that the rate of dementia fell from 11.6% in 2000 to 8.8% in 2012. The study suggests that better education may be one reason for the decline, as the average amount of education increased from 11.8 years in 2000 to 12.7 years in 2012. The study also found that more intensive treatment for diabetes, hypertension, and high cholesterol levels may have contributed to the decline in dementia risk. The study's findings fit in with other recent reports that have shown a fall in dementia rates. However, the Alzheimer's Association notes that the total number of Americans with Alzheimer's and other dementias is expected to continue to increase dramatically. The study's authors suggest that increased physical activity, eating a heart-healthy diet, social engagement, and keeping the brain active with puzzles or games can help prevent Alzheimer's or at least delay it. A whole industry has arisen out of this research, with mixed success. The study's findings are welcome news in an aging world, as there is no cure for dementia and trials of various treatments have been far from successful.

The study published in the journal PLOS One found that men who exhibit sexist behavior in online gaming environments are often less skilled and performing worse than their peers. Researchers Michael Kasumovic and Jeffrey Kuznekoff observed 163 plays of the video game Halo 3 and found that men generally treated each other cordially, but men who were less skilled at the game made frequent, nasty comments to female gamers. The study suggests that this behavior is a result of low-status males trying to maintain their social rank in the face of a female disrupting the pre-existing male hierarchy. The researchers argue that video games provide a unique opportunity to study real-life behavior, as they remove signals of dominance, provide information on gender and individual performance, and have a biased sex-ratio towards men. The study does not offer solutions for online sexism, but suggests that online spaces such as Facebook and Pinterest, where women outnumber men, may be less problematic. The study provides a clearer picture of inter-sexual competition and highlights the importance of considering an evolutionary perspective when exploring the factors that affect male hostility towards women.

Data Privacy Day is observed globally on Friday, emphasizing the importance of personal data protection. Facebook has announced two new security features to enhance user protection. The first feature is the expansion of HTTPS usage, which encrypts communication between users and Facebook to keep data secure, especially when using public Wi-Fi. Users can enable this option in the "Account Security" section of the Account Settings page.

The second feature is Social Authentication, which uses social design to verify user identity. Instead of traditional captchas, Facebook may show users pictures of their friends and ask them to name the individuals in the photos. This method is more secure as hackers may know passwords but not who the user's friends are. Facebook will continue to test and gather feedback on these features.

Facebook encourages users to visit the Facebook Security Page for more information on keeping personal data safe on Facebook and across the internet. Despite the new features, concerns remain about the slow rollout and the lack of automatic HTTPS activation for all users.

In a heartwarming tale of heroism, Lisa Stephenson, a pregnant woman from Delaware, became a hero to two families in Maine after her keen instincts led to the discovery of their missing teenage daughters. On November 2, while working at the Blue Crab Grill in Newark, Stephenson found the girls' job applications suspicious as they appeared too young to be working, didn't include home addresses or phone numbers, and claimed their phones and money were stolen in New York.

Stephenson, who lives just over the state line in Elkton, Maryland, felt uneasy about the girls' safety, given their location near a questionable truck stop. Upon returning home, she conducted a Facebook search and found a missing persons notice about a 16-year-old girl from Brunswick, Maine, and her 14-year-old friend from Bath, Maine, who had vanished together on October 25.

Stephenson contacted the older girl's mother and enlisted the help of her cousins, police deputies in a nearby county, who tracked down the girls after they were seen panhandling in front of a clothing store on November 3. The girls had stolen one of their mother's cars and had driven through several states, potentially putting themselves in dangerous situations.

The girls returned to Maine and are now safe at home, albeit grounded and with the older girl banned from using social media. Stephenson, who doesn't consider herself a hero, hopes her actions inspire others to speak up when something seems off. The older girl's mother has praised Stephenson on Facebook, calling her a hero for her actions.

On November 27, 2017, it was announced that Prince Harry, fifth in line for the British throne, will marry American actress Meghan Markle in May 2018 at Windsor Castle's St. George's Chapel. The couple has been dating for about a year and a half. The wedding will be paid for by the royal family, and Queen Elizabeth II will attend. Meghan Markle will become a British citizen and be baptized in the Church of England, although this process will take some time. The exact date of the wedding has not been revealed. The engagement of Prince Harry and Markle has been met with enthusiasm in Britain, with newspapers hailing it as a breath of fresh air and symbol of a modernizing monarchy. The couple's first joint interview revealed that Harry proposed over a roast chicken dinner at his London home, and that Markle immediately fit in with his family, with the corgis taking to her straight away. The couple's first official joint engagement will take place in Nottingham on Friday. Meghan Markle will become the fourth patron of The Royal Foundation, a charitable organization set up by the Duke and Duchess of Cambridge and Prince Harry. The couple will live in Nottingham Cottage in the grounds of Kensington Palace, the official residence of the Duke and Duchess of Cambridge. One of Markle's two dogs, Guy, is already in the UK, while the other, Bogart, is with friends of Markle's in Canada. In choosing St George's Chapel at Windsor as the venue, the couple are following in royal tradition. Although Markle has been married before, that will not pose any obstacle to a church wedding as the Church of England permits divorcees to remarry. The last royal wedding involving a divorcee was a civil ceremony rather than a church marriage. Harry's father, Prince Charles, married Camilla Parker Bowles in 2005 in a town hall in Windsor. The Church of England nevertheless allows the remarriage of divorced people "in exceptional circumstances." Markle attended a Catholic school as a child, but is not a practicing Roman Catholic, so an Anglican wedding will not raise any denominational questions. The couple will wed in St George's Chapel at Windsor Castle. The news of the engagement has prompted hopes that Brits might be granted an extra day off on the day of the nuptials, but Downing Street has said that there are "no plans" for a special holiday to celebrate the wedding of Prince Harry and Markle. The couple opened up for the first time about their relationship in an interview with the BBC's Mishal Husain, revealing that they met for a blind date in July 2016 and that Harry proposed during a "cozy night" earlier this month at the couple's Nottingham Cottage at Kensington Palace. The ring features a stone from Botswana accompanied by two smaller diamonds from the jewelry collection of Harry's mother, the late Princess Diana.

In a heartbreaking yet inspiring tale, the story revolves around Kristina Chesterman, a 21-year-old nursing student who was killed by a suspected drunk driver in September 2013. Despite her untimely death, Kristina's legacy lives on through her organ donation, which has saved the lives of five individuals.

Kristina's bucket list, discovered by her mother after her death, included aspirations such as flying a plane, running through a poppy field, and saving a life. Though she was unable to accomplish many of these goals, her organs have enabled others to experience some of these dreams.

One of the recipients is Jayden Kirby, a 1-year-old boy who received a part of Kristina's liver and shares the same birthstone as her. Another recipient is Sakariah "Zak" Pappachan, a Fremont resident who received Kristina's kidney and is now advocating for organ donation.

The impact of Kristina's life extends beyond organ donation. Her friends and family have taken on her bucket list, with some accomplishing tasks such as skydiving and traveling. Her death has also led to the creation of the Chico State's Kristina Chesterman Memorial Nursing Scholarship and plans for a medical clinic to be built in her name in Nigeria.

Kristina's family and organ recipients have formed strong bonds, providing comfort and support during a difficult time. The story is a poignant reminder of the impact one life can have, even in the face of tragedy.

The summarized article discusses two heartwarming stories that highlight the power of family connections, especially in times of distance.

The first story revolves around Allegro, a Polish online auction website, which released a Christmas advertisement that has garnered over two and a half million views. The ad tells the story of a grandfather who learns English to communicate better with his family living abroad. The campaign aims to reflect the lives of millions of Polish people who have left the country but maintain ties with their families back home.

The second story features Ji Lee, a designer from New York, who shared a touching video about his 75-year-old Korean father who moved to Brazil. After his grandchildren moved back to Korea, the family was concerned about the grandfather's well-being. To bridge the gap, Lee encouraged his father to learn Instagram and draw pictures for his grandchildren. Initially resistant, the grandfather eventually began drawing daily, improving his skills over time. His Instagram page, initially with 1,000 followers, quickly gained popularity, reaching over 63,000 followers in just two days.

Both stories emphasize the importance of family connections, even in the face of distance, and the power of technology in bringing families together. The Allegro advertisement poses the question, "What are you looking for?" as the slogan of their campaign, encouraging viewers to reflect on their own lives. The story of Ji Lee's father, on the other hand, has inspired many to reconnect with their aging parents and awaken their inner passion and talent through technology.

President Obama called on Congress on Tuesday to find a temporary solution to delay the sequester, deep automatic spending cuts in domestic and defense spending scheduled to take effect on March 1. The sequester, worth $1.2 trillion over a decade, has caused anxiety among government workers and contractors. Obama did not outline a specific proposal but suggested that Congress should pass a small package of spending cuts and tax changes to postpone the sequester for a few months. To delay the sequester for several months, any plan passed by Congress would have to reduce borrowing by tens of billions of dollars through a combination of alternative spending cuts or tax increases. The White House will work with Congress on crafting the package.

The sequester is not the only looming deadline. A continuing resolution funding the government expires in late March, and the government will shut down without further action by Congress. There is another deadline to raise the federal debt limit in the summer. The Congressional Budget Office released its economic projections for the year ahead, showing that the federal budget deficit will come in under $1 trillion by the end of 2013, the first time in five years. The gap between taxes and spending is estimated to narrow to $845 billion in the fiscal year that ends in September.

Obama's push for a short-term solution received Democratic support in the Senate on Tuesday. "I agree with President Obama that if we can't agree now on a long-term solution, the best thing for families and the economy would be to pass a balanced short-term sequestration replacement while the House and Senate work on our budget resolutions," said Sen. Patty Murray (D-Wash.), chairwoman of the Senate Budget Committee.

The sequester was a mechanism that Congress and the White House designed in 2011 to force policymakers to generate significant deficit reduction over the next 10 years. While they have made progress on that front, they have not come to a broad agreement as many hoped. The sequester would slice $1.2 trillion in domestic and defense spending over 10 years, indiscriminately cutting most programs. Some programs, such as Medicaid and food stamps, are exempt. The "fiscal cliff" deal at the start of the year postponed the sequester for two months.

Obama favors a broader plan to permanently end the sequester and replace it with a series of reductions in health care and other mandatory spending as well as the elimination of tax breaks that benefit the wealthy and industries. Republicans favor deep cuts to spending without raising taxes any more. Speaker John Boehner is signaling he will not accept revenue increases that President Barack Obama is expected to propose to delay the automatic spending cuts that take hold at the beginning of March.

Martin Shkreli, the CEO of Turing Pharmaceuticals, has become the target of public outrage and death threats after his company raised the price of Daraprim, a drug used to treat a rare parasitic infection in immunocompromised patients, from $13.50 to $750 per pill. The more than 5,000% increase and Shkreli's brash defense of the decision have made him a pariah among patients-rights groups, politicians, and hundreds of Twitter users. Other drug companies have made similar moves, but few have been as publicly unapologetic about it. The backlash became so intense that Shkreli agreed to lower the price of Daraprim to an "affordable level."

Shkreli, the son of Albanian and Croatian immigrants, grew up in a working-class community in Brooklyn, New York. He began his first internship at Cramer Berkowitz & Co, a hedge fund founded by television personality Jim Cramer, at the age of 17. In 2006, he started his own hedge fund, Elea Capital Management, but it closed a year later after a $2.3 million lawsuit from Lehman Brothers. After Elea, Shkreli started MSMB Capital Management in 2008, which would be his launch pad for founding biotech firms including Turing.

Turing was not Shkreli's first foray into the pharmaceutical industry. In 2011, he founded biotech firm Retrophin, with the goal of focusing on medicines for rare diseases. He was ousted as head of the company in 2014 amidst allegations he improperly handled legal settlements. A year later the company filed a $65 million lawsuit that claimed Shkreli created Retrophin and took it public simply to pay off investors in his old hedge fund, MSMB when the fund went under. Shkreli has denied the accusations.

On August 4, 2017, a jury found Shkreli guilty of three of eight counts, including securities fraud, in a criminal case brought by US prosecutors. But they cleared him of allegations that he had looted Retrophin to make payments for the hedge funds. The civil suit brought by Retrophin remained pending as of 4 August.

Turing Pharmaceuticals was launched in February 2015 after Shkreli was forced out of Retrophin. The business claims its goal is to focus on treatments for serious diseases for which there are limited options. "We are dedicated to helping patients, who often have no effective treatment options," a statement on Turing's website said. The company only has two products on the market, Daraprim and Vecamyl, which treats hypertension.

Shkreli has argued the Daraprim price increase was warranted because the drug is highly specialized; he likened the Daraprim to an Aston Martin previously being sold at the price of a bicycle. The additional profits he said will be used to make improvements to the 62-year-old drug recipe.

The controversy over Daraprim has brought attention to the issue of skyrocketing costs of generic drugs, which has been a problem for some time. Other drugs have seen their prices increase by thousands of percent in the past year, and there isn't enough market demand for these generic drugs to motivate a new competitor to enter the field. The Daraprim scandal exploded this week for several reasons, including an odious pharma executive, Hillary Clinton's speech, and widespread media coverage. However, the hard part is achieving lasting reform, and no one agrees on how to do that. The most promising solution is probably pushing on regulators, such as the FDA, to speed up its process to encourage new generic manufacturers.

Sacha Baron Cohen, the actor behind the character Borat, has offered to pay fines for six Czech tourists who were arrested in Kazakhstan for wearing mankinis, a piece of beachwear made famous by Borat. The tourists were fined for "minor hooliganism" after posing for photos in the capital city of Astana. The incident has sparked mixed reactions on Kazakh social media, with some supporting the tourists and others criticizing them. The incident brings back memories of the 2006 film Borat, which earned Cohen a Golden Globe award but also attracted controversy. Kazakhstan banned the film and threatened to sue Cohen, but later thanked him for boosting tourism in the country. Mankinis have also been banned in Newquay, England, in an attempt to reduce crime and improve the town's image.

Texas Senator Ted Cruz is set to announce his presidential bid on Monday, making him the first high-profile Republican to officially enter the 2016 race. Cruz, a conservative and uncompromising politician, has been hinting at his intentions for months. He is known for his strong opposition to President Obama's health care law and his promise to abolish the Internal Revenue Service, scrap the Education Department, and curtail federal regulators. Cruz has considerable appeal among the Republican Party's base of conservative voters, and he plans to raise between $40 million and $50 million over the course of the primary campaign. However, he may face challenges in securing high-dollar donations, endorsements from the political establishment, and comparisons to President Obama. If he advances to a general election, Cruz trails likely Democratic nominee Hillary Clinton in early polls. Cruz's wife, Heidi, a managing director at Goldman Sachs, will join him on the campaign trail. Cruz was born in Canada but is eligible to run for president according to two lawyers who wrote in the Harvard Law Review. If he fails to win the presidency, he will retain his Senate seat through early 2019.

Greece is on the brink of passing unpopular austerity measures, including wage cuts, tax increases, and privatizations, in an attempt to avoid default. The measures must be approved by parliament before Greece can receive the next installment of aid from foreign lenders. Prime Minister George A. Papandreou has a five-vote parliamentary majority, but the measures are controversial within his own Socialist Party. Riot police clashed with protesters outside the Parliament building during the debate, and the nation's unions began a 48-hour general strike. The European Union, the European Central Bank, and the International Monetary Fund have said they will release $17 billion that Greece needs to pay its expenses through the summer if the measures are passed. The vote is scheduled for Wednesday, and at least one member of Parliament from the Socialist Party who had opposed the bill has changed his mind. The demonstration on Tuesday was one of the first in which labor unions joined with younger demonstrators who have gathered in downtown Athens every night for the past month. The protests turned violent as groups of youths threw rocks, firebombs, and firecrackers. The measures are intended to help Greece deal with its recession, but many Greeks believe the politicians are responsible for the crisis and are resisting the austerity measures.

The study published in the journal Current Biology on October 5, 2015, reveals that the Chernobyl disaster zone, once a site of a nuclear catastrophe, has become a thriving nature preserve teeming with elk, roe deer, red deer, wild boar, and wolves. The findings are a testament to the resilience of wildlife and may hold important lessons for understanding the long-term impact of the Fukushima disaster in Japan.

The study, led by Professor Jim Smith of the University of Portsmouth, shows that the mammal populations in the Chernobyl Exclusion Zone have bounced back after the initial radiation effects and pronounced reductions in wildlife populations following the accident in 1986. The researchers found that the relative abundance of elk, roe deer, red deer, and wild boar within the exclusion zone are now similar to those in four uncontaminated nature reserves in the region. The number of wolves living in and around the Chernobyl site is more than seven times greater than can be found in those nature reserves.

Helicopter survey data also reveal rising trends in the abundance of elk, roe deer, and wild boar from 1 to 10 years after the accident. A dip in the wild boar population at one point was traced to a disease outbreak unrelated to radiation exposure.

The researchers conclude that the Chernobyl Exclusion Zone supports an abundant mammal community after nearly three decades of chronic radiation exposure. These increases came at a time when elk and wild boar populations were declining in other parts of the former Soviet Union.

Tatiana Deryabina from the Polessye State Radioecological Reserve in Belarus, a few miles from the site of the Chernobyl accident, expressed her pleasure that their work is reaching an international scientific audience. Jim Beasley, a study co-author at the University of Georgia, noted that the unique data showing a wide range of animals thriving within miles of a major nuclear accident illustrate the resilience of wildlife populations when freed from the pressures of human habitation.

The study demonstrates that the mere presence of people is more damaging to wildlife than is radiation poisoning. The findings challenge the common perception that Chernobyl was a disaster for both people and wildlife. However, it's important to note that the study does not address the health effects of radiation on individual animals, which is a subject of ongoing research by other scientists.

In Mcallen, Texas, an elderly couple, William Steele (95) and Myrtle Steele (92), died, and their son, Richard Steele (67), was injured in a bee attack on their remote ranch near Hebbronville. The incident occurred on Monday while the family was cleaning a hunting cabin, where they exposed a hive of bees. Richard Steele was injured, and his parents died from hundreds of bee stings. Myrtle Steele was airlifted to a Corpus Christi hospital but died the following day. Richard was transported to a Laredo hospital and later released. The bees were likely Africanized honey bees, commonly known as "killer bees," which are aggressive and common in South Texas. The bees swarmed and attacked the family when they moved a wood stove, exposing the hive. The USDA advises against untrained individuals attempting to remove swarms, and if attacked, individuals should run away quickly without stopping to help others. This incident highlights the danger of Africanized honey bees, especially in rural areas.

Iris Zink, a nurse practitioner in Michigan, demonstrated extraordinary compassion by donating a kidney to one of her long-time patients, Ginny Holcomb. Research In Motion (RIM), the mobile company behind the BlackBerry, is expected to announce a net loss for its first fiscal quarter and may continue to struggle in the coming quarters. The company's earnings are projected to show a net loss of 3 cents per share on $3.1 billion in revenue, a significant decline from last year's profit of $1.33 per share on nearly $5 billion in revenue.

The bearish outlook for RIM's earnings has been echoed by analysts such as Jefferies analyst Peter Misek, who expects the earnings announcement to be "terrible" and predicts a challenging August. RIM's stock value has plummeted over the past year, losing 68% of its value and dropping its market capitalization to $4.8 billion.

RIM's troubles are attributed to a variety of factors, including plummeting device sales, a confused management team, and a seemingly outdated product line. Some analysts have suggested that RIM might try to sell its devices business to focus on services and leverage its intellectual property. However, Wedge Partners analyst Brian Blair has expressed skepticism about the value of RIM's assets.

RIM's CEOs, Mike Lazaridis and Jim Balsillie, were known for their split personality in the executive suite, according to former executives. Their offices were located a 10-minute drive apart, and meetings with both CEOs present were rare. This split leadership may have contributed to RIM's current decline, as both CEOs pursued different strategies without coordinating effectively.

Heins is slashing costs and has hired investment bankers to explore options, including the possibility of a sale of the company. RIM's proprietary email delivery technology and its ability to perform tasks that other smartphones cannot are seen as valuable assets. However, the company's manufacturing capability is not considered worth much by some analysts.

In Santa Fe, more than $1 million worth of jewelry was stolen from Diva Diamonds & Jewels during a crowded holiday lighting event on Friday. The thieves, a woman and two men, are believed to have scoped out the store for about two weeks before the heist. The jewelry was taken from an unlocked case while employees were busy with customers. The suspects were seen in the store in the weeks before the theft, asking questions about the jewelry. The Santa Fe Police Department is seeking help from the public to identify the suspects and have released images of them on their public information officer's Facebook page. Anyone with information is urged to contact detective Abe Maes at 505-231-6497 or detective Matthew Champlin at 505-469-5707. The incident has raised concerns among other merchants in the area, as there is a high density of jewelry stores in downtown Santa Fe.

North Carolina lawmakers have approved a bill expanding the rights of concealed handgun permit holders, which now heads to Governor Pat McCrory for his signature or veto. The bill allows permit holders to carry their weapons in bars and restaurants that serve alcohol, funeral processions, and in their vehicles parked on college or public school campuses.

The bill also removes information regarding those with concealed handgun permits from public view and strengthens penalties for firearm law violations. It also increases the amount of information, such as mental health problems, in the state's background check system.

The bill was met with opposition from some lawmakers, particularly those representing educational institutions. However, supporters argue that the college provision merely legalizes something that already happens, such as parents picking up students or business meetings with university executives.

The bill dropped a controversial provision that would have repealed the requirement for a background check and permit issued by county sheriffs for handgun purchases. Sheriffs will now have to keep records and show cause when rejecting a handgun permit application, but will no longer be able to restrict the number of permits an individual can obtain in a year.

The bill passed with a vote of 73-41 in the House and 32-14 in the Senate. The bill's supporters argue that those with concealed handgun permits have undergone extra training and background checks, making them less of a concern for public safety.

A 14-year-old boy, known as "El Ponchis," suspected of being a paid assassin for the South Pacific drug cartel, was arrested in Mexico while attempting to flee to California. The teen, who allegedly admitted to participating in at least four decapitations, was traveling with two of his sisters. Born in San Diego, he is a U.S. citizen and was arrested at an airport near Cuernavaca, Mexico, with plans to cross the border to San Diego.

The boy, who goes by the nickname "El Ponchis," claimed he was kidnapped at the age of 11 and forced to work for the Cartel of the South Pacific, a branch of the Beltran Leyva gang. He allegedly received $2,500 for each killing, while the minimum wage in Mexico is less than $5 a day. His sisters, who were also arrested, were reportedly accomplices, often acting as decoys to lure victims.

The arrest of "El Ponchis" and his sisters comes amidst a surge in drug-related violence in Mexico, with cartels battling each other and the army to gain access to the multibillion-dollar U.S. market. The bloodshed has increasingly moved south from the border region to previously quiet locations such as Cuernavaca and Monterrey.

The story of "El Ponchis" has sparked outrage, as many youths have been used by drug cartels in their violent conflicts. The federal government has acknowledged the recruitment of young people without hope or opportunities in the most violent areas of the country. Despite her ongoing health issues, Townsend is now considering getting back into modeling, a career she gave up on after she was fitted with the bags. Townsend's courage and bravery have inspired many, and she is now considering modeling for a lingerie label that designs for people with colostomy bags. Townsend's story is a testament to the power of self-acceptance and the importance of embracing one's differences. Townsend's story is a reminder that beauty comes in all shapes and sizes, and that everyone has something unique to offer.

Three astronauts safely returned to Earth on September 2nd, ending a record-breaking mission for NASA's Peggy Whitson. Whitson, who spent 288 days on the International Space Station (ISS), set a new record for the most cumulative time in space by an American with 665 days accrued. Her crewmates, NASA astronaut Jack Fischer and Russian cosmonaut Fyodor Yurchikhin, both spent 136 days aboard the orbiting laboratory.

The Soyuz MS-04 spacecraft undocked from the space station's Poisk module and landed on the steppes of Kazakhstan at 9:21 p.m. EDT (0121 Sept. 3 GMT). The landing was followed by a medical check-up and a traditional welcoming ceremony. Recovery teams watched the landing from helicopters nearby before descending to the landing site to help the space travelers out of their capsule.

Whitson, Fischer, and Yurchikhin arrived at the ISS in April with an empty seat in their Soyuz. Whitson filled that seat for the return flight after NASA and Russia's space agency Roscosmos agreed to extend her stay through Expedition 52. The Soyuz spacecraft tipped over onto its side upon landing, which is common for Soyuz crew landings.

NASA astronauts Peggy Whitson, Jack Fischer, and Russian cosmonaut Fyodor Yurchikhin pose for a photo after landing in Kazakhstan on Sept. 3, 2017 local time (late Sept. 2, EDT). Whitson spent 288 days on the space station during her flight, with Fischer and Yurchikhin spending 136 days on their mission.

The Expedition 52 crew will spend the next 45 days doing physical rehabilitation and undergoing a series of medical tests both for health reasons and scientific research. They will also debrief with ground teams about procedures that worked well, procedures that need improvement, and ideas for operational improvements.

Back at the space station, NASA astronaut Randy Bresnik, European Space Agency astronaut Paolo Nespoli, and Russian cosmonaut Sergey Ryazansky will be the only three crewmembers on board until Sept. 12, when the Expedition 52/53 crewmembers arrive. NASA astronauts Joe Acaba and Mark Vande Hei and Russian cosmonaut Alexander Misurkin will then dock at the ISS in their Soyuz MS-05 spacecraft and will spend the next six months in space.

Whitson, a biochemist, set a breakneck pace on all three of her space station expeditions, continually asking for more scientific research to do. She even experimented on food up there, trying to add some pizazz to the standard freeze-dried meals. Tortillas transformed into apple pies on her watch.

Whitson was supposed to fly back in June after a half-year in space. But when an extra seat opened up on this Soyuz, she jumped at the chance to stay in orbit an extra three months. Only one other American, yearlong spaceman Scott Kelly, has spent longer in space on a single mission.

Except for the past week, Whitson said her mission hurried by. She's hungry for pizza and can't wait to use a regular flush toilet again. She's also eager to reunite with her husband, Clarence Sams, a biochemist who also works at Johnson Space Center in Houston.

Because of the effects of Hurricane Harvey, NASA could not get its plane from Houston to Kazakhstan in time for the crew's landing. Instead, the European Space Agency offered to transport Whitson and Fischer to Cologne, Germany, where they will meet up with the NASA plane for the final leg of their journey. They should be back in Houston on Sunday night.
