They hope to use this bill to highlight the irony of marijuana remaining illegal while alcohol is not, and to emphasize the potential financial benefits of legalizing marijuana, which could generate between $20 million and $70 million in tax revenue annually, according to a Rand Corporation study. The lawmakers have also sponsored H.277, which proposes the legal sale and regulation of marijuana in Vermont, and Senate Bill 95, which would also legalize the drug. Despite the proposed alcohol ban, neither lawmaker supports the bill's passage, viewing it as a means to draw attention to their marijuana legalization efforts.

On Friday, supporters in Ferguson, Missouri, rebuilt a memorial dedicated to Michael Brown, who was fatally shot by a police officer in August, after it was intentionally destroyed overnight. The memorial, located near the Canfield Green apartment complex where Brown was shot, was filled with flowers, signs, and other mementos. Pictures of the destroyed memorial spread on social media, prompting supporters to gather and restore the makeshift shrine.

Ferguson Police Department's public relations officer, Timothy Zoll, initially stated that no crime had been reported in connection to the memorial's destruction. However, he was later placed on unpaid leave after admitting he referred to the memorial as "trash" and misleading his superiors about his interview with The Washington Post. The City of Ferguson initiated an internal investigation and stated that Zoll's negative remarks about the memorial did not reflect the feelings of the Ferguson Police Department.

The memorial was rebuilt by morning, and the Ferguson Police Department is focusing on creating a trusting relationship with the community and improving the department's effectiveness. The incident has once again brought attention to the racial tensions and police-community relations in Ferguson, which have been a subject of national discussion since Brown's death.

In this summary, we discuss two unusual animal-related news stories. The first story, from Weirdnews.about.com, involves a man being tickled by snakes in a video. The larger snakes focus on the belly or back, while the smaller ones explore other areas like the man's face. Despite the snakes being nonvenomous, the experience may not be soothing for most people.

The second story, from Doseng.org, highlights a unique practice in Thailand at the Maesa Elephant Camp in Chiang Mai. Tourists are offered a "stress-relieving" experience where an elephant places its foot on their back. However, there's a twist: sometimes, a baby elephant is initially presented, only for it to be replaced by an adult one at the last moment, potentially causing distress among the tourists. This practice, while intended to be humorous, raises concerns about the treatment of animals and the expectations set for tourists.

President Obama delivered a crucial speech on the Iran nuclear agreement on Wednesday, arguing that the congressional vote that could block the deal is "the most consequential foreign policy debate since the decision to go to war in Iraq." The White House has been instructed to make the president and other senior administration officials available to any skeptic with unanswered questions or concerns about the deal. Officials said that Mr. Obama's address would be followed by a series of news media interviews that would be shown next week. The administration plans to dispatch cabinet members, including Energy Secretary Ernest J. Moniz, to travel the country outlining the provisions of the deal.

Obama's speech was directed at congressional Democrats, as he framed the debate as a choice between diplomacy and war. He criticized Republicans who oppose the deal, stating that they are making "common cause" with Iranian hard-liners. Obama also compared the Iran deal to the nuclear test ban treaty with the Soviet Union proposed by President Kennedy in 1963.

The Iran deal, two years in the making, would relax sanctions against Iran in exchange for a promise not to develop nuclear weapons and inspections by the International Atomic Energy Agency. Critics, including every major Republican presidential candidate, say Iran cannot be trusted and that the economic benefits of the deal will only strengthen Iran's ability to threaten Israel and foment extremism throughout the Middle East.

The effort to build support for the deal gained momentum on Tuesday as three closely watched Democratic senators – Barbara Boxer of California, Tim Kaine of Virginia, and Bill Nelson of Florida – declared their backing, along with a handful of House Democrats. Obama's team is working with Representative Nancy Pelosi of California, the minority leader, to build support to potentially sustain a presidential veto of legislation rejecting the accord.

Obama made a special appeal to the Jewish community on Tuesday, meeting with about two-dozen leaders of Jewish groups that span the religious and ideological spectrum, including the conservative American Israel Public Affairs Committee, the liberal J Street, and leaders of reform and orthodox congregations. The president is trying to counter a determined lobbying campaign by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who continues his effort to scuttle the deal by appealing to American Jews in a webcast on Tuesday.

The Iran deal is a defining achievement for Obama amid an often rocky foreign policy record. He has been arguing forcefully that diplomacy can yield benefits, even as his administration continues to use targeted strikes by drones and struggles to deal with civil war in Syria, the rise of the Islamic State, and confrontation with Russia over Ukraine. Obama has been irked by ad campaigns against the deal, including one comparing him to Neville Chamberlain, the British prime minister leading up to World War II, who has been widely blamed for not standing up to Adolf Hitler.

Obama's speech at American University was drawn historical parallels, as it was the same place President Kennedy gave his 1963 speech proposing a nuclear test ban treaty with the Soviet Union at the apex of the Cold War. The White House seemed to be encouraging those comparisons – to a point. White House press secretary Josh Earnest said both Kennedy and Obama "entered into a diplomatic agreement with an adversary of the United States that did succeed in advancing the national security interests of the United States." However, unlike Kennedy, Earnest said, Obama did not have to make any concessions about its own defense. "There’s no impact from this nuclear agreement on the United States and either our nuclear programs or our military programs," Earnest said Tuesday.

In a two-hour White House meeting on Tuesday night with Jewish American groups, Obama seemed particularly bothered by a multimillion-dollar ad campaign aimed at stopping the deal. On Wednesday afternoon, the president used his Twitter account to say: “There’s no such thing as a ‘better deal.’ Walking away risks war.” As he nears the end of his tenure, Obama has been arguing forcefully that diplomacy can yield benefits, even as his administration continues to use targeted strikes by drones and struggles to deal with civil war in Syria, the rise of the Islamic State, and confrontation with Russia over Ukraine.

The new book "Mockingbird Songs: My Friendship with Harper Lee" by Wayne Flynt, a close friend of the late Pulitzer Prize-winning author, offers insights into the life and relationships of Harper Lee, best known for her novel "To Kill a Mockingbird." The book, set for release on May 2, sheds light on Lee's relationship with Truman Capote, her fear of obsessive fans, her nervousness before interviews, and her possible involvement in the publication of "Go Set a Watchman."

Lee, who was known as Nelle Harper Lee in her hometown of Monroeville, asked Flynt not to write about her while she was alive. However, Flynt feels the book allows Lee to speak beyond the grave without compromising her privacy. Lee called Capote a "compulsive liar" in a 2006 letter to Flynt, revealing a reason for their strained friendship. Capote, who was the inspiration for the character Dill in "To Kill a Mockingbird," became jealous of Lee's success.

Lee also expressed her fear of the media and fame's spotlight, having once had a stalker and being concerned about stalkers and assassination. Additionally, Lee was so nervous before interviews and speaking engagements that she would vomit. The book also touches upon Lee's possible lack of full participation in the decision to publish "Go Set a Watchman" due to her age and health issues, but at the time, she welcomed its publication.

The book promises to provide a detailed account of Lee's life and relationships, offering a unique perspective on the famously private author. Readers can learn more about Truman Capote's "compulsive lying" and other aspects of Lee's life when "Mockingbird Songs" is released on May 2.

Jamie Tull, a 33-year-old former public elementary school teacher from Riverbank, California, was found alive on August 4, 2017, after being missing for nearly three weeks. Tull had crashed her car and was last heard from on July 17. She was found emaciated, sunburned, and lying in tall grass less than a mile from the crash site near Le Grand, California.

Authorities said Tull had survived by eating a few bugs and drinking from a dirty cattle trough. She had also stopped taking her prescription medication for emotional issues. Tull told rescuers that she did not want to be found and only wanted food and water.

Tull's family and friends found her and confirmed the news to FOX40. She was flown to a hospital in Fresno for medical treatment and will be returned to her relatives for care. Tull's father said she has bipolar disorder and had not taken her medication for about six months due to advice from a pastor and his wife.

Search efforts for a missing man at San Francisco's Ocean Beach were suspended, and an Oregon woman had a life-or-death ordeal during a day hike. The search for Tull was suspended once she was found.

The surrounding landscape where Tull was found was described as desolate grazing land with homes visible in the distance. Merced County Sheriff Vern Warnke said that when he arrived, Tull only wanted food and water. He also mentioned that Tull was trying to get to Yosemite, which is more than 60 miles away from Le Grand.

A military veteran died on July 3, 2014, at the Raymond G. Murphy VA Medical Center in Albuquerque, New Mexico, after waiting for an ambulance to take him 500 yards to the emergency room. The veteran collapsed in the hospital cafeteria, which is next to the main hospital building. According to VA spokeswoman Sonja Brown, staff followed policy by calling 911 for a medical emergency that happened outside the main hospital. It took an ambulance about 11 minutes to be dispatched and arrive at the cafeteria, which is about a five-minute walk from the emergency room. The man's name has not been released, and his family is considering legal action.

The death comes as the Department of Veterans Affairs is under scrutiny for widespread reports of long delays for treatment and medical appointments and of veterans dying while on waiting lists. A review last week cited "significant and chronic system failures" in the nation's health system for veterans. The review also portrayed the struggling agency as one battling a corrosive culture of distrust, lacking in resources, and ill-prepared to deal with an influx of new and older veterans with a range of medical and mental health care needs.

The VA is currently reviewing its policy regarding medical emergencies that occur outside the main hospital. It is not clear if any vehicles owned by the VA could have transported the veteran, and national VA representatives did not respond to a request for comment. The man's death has sparked criticism and calls for reform of the VA, but some experts argue that it is unfair to attack the VA too harshly on this incident, as it appears to be an unusual case.

Ethan Couch, the Texas teen who famously used the "affluenza" defense in a deadly drunken-driving case, is currently in a legal battle in Mexico to avoid deportation. His attorney, Fernando Benitez, stated that the case is an international law matter and that they are focused on ensuring Couch is not mistreated according to the Mexican constitution. Benitez denied reports that Couch had a gun at the time of his detention.

Couch won a delay in his deportation based on a constitutional appeal in Mexico that could lead to a trial process lasting weeks or even months. Any flaw in the process of his detention by Mexican immigration authorities can be considered a violation of due process and of his human rights, legal analysts say.

Benitez argued that a fast-track deportation would expose Couch to a criminal procedure in the United States that may not be up to Mexican constitutional standards. He said Couch's Texas-based defense team asked him to intervene after the teen was caught in Mexico.

Couch was arrested in Mexico after a video surfaced that appears to show him at a party where people were drinking, which would be a violation of his probation. His mother, Tonya, was also arrested and has been charged with hindering an apprehension.

Couch was sentenced to 10 years' probation for driving drunk and crashing into a disabled SUV in 2013, killing four people and injuring several others. He pleaded guilty to four counts of intoxication manslaughter and two counts of intoxication assault causing serious bodily injury.

During his trial, a defense expert argued that Couch's wealthy parents had coddled him into a sense of irresponsibility, a condition termed "affluenza." The condition is not recognized as a medical diagnosis by the American Psychiatric Association, and its invocation drew ridicule.

Unless he files for asylum, Couch will not be able to stay in Mexico indefinitely. If he is deported, he could face up to 120 days in an adult jail, followed by 10 years of probation, and if he violates probation again, he could face up to 10 years in prison per death. A probation violation hearing is set for January 19.

The Daily Caller, a right-wing news site, has launched a unique promotion to attract email sign-ups: a weekly gun giveaway until Election Day. The gun, an FMK9C1, is engraved with the Bill of Rights and manufactured by FMK Firearms, whose founder, Jim Pontillo, has expressed extreme right-wing views on American politics and firearm ownership. The contest is open to legal US residents aged 21 and over, and the winner must pass a background check and comply with local firearm regulations. The Daily Caller's "Guns and Gear" section, sponsored by the NRA, primarily republishes content from NRA sources. Pontillo's controversial opinions, also expressed in columns for Human Events, include claims that progressive policies burden Americans, that separation of church and state is a perversion of the First Amendment, and that firearm ownership threatens liberal philosophies. The contest's official rules outline eligibility, winner selection, notification, and liability, as well as disqualification and liability clauses.

Clarissa Dickson Wright, a prominent British television cook and food historian, passed away at the age of 66 in Edinburgh. Known for her eccentricity and irreverence, she rose to fame as one half of the BBC's Two Fat Ladies duo with Jennifer Paterson. The pair, who toured the UK in a motorcycle-sidecar, were known for their high-fat recipes and sometimes controversial views.

Born into an affluent family, Dickson Wright became a barrister at 21 but struggled with alcoholism. She later quit law and turned to cooking, eventually becoming a guild butcher. She was discovered by producer Patricia Llewellyn and the Two Fat Ladies show debuted in 1996.

The show attracted criticism for its high-fat ingredients and off-color humor, but was also praised for its unique style and Dickson Wright's knowledge of food history. Following Paterson's death in 1999, Dickson Wright continued to appear on television, including in Clarissa and the Countryman with presenter John Scott.

Dickson Wright was also a champion of countryside pursuits and was convicted of attending an illegal hare coursing event in 2009. In more recent years, she suggested that badgers, which were being culled, should be eaten to solve the problem.

Dickson Wright's agents, Heather Holden-Brown and Elly James, said her fun, laughter, and intelligence would be missed. Television chef Jamie Oliver called her entertaining to watch and a passionate foodie, while The Observer's restaurant critic Jay Rayner described her as a truly fabulous woman.

Dickson Wright's autobiography, Spilling the Beans, details her well-documented battle with alcohol and her privileged upbringing, which was overshadowed by her surgeon father's drinking. She never married but had a long-term relationship with Clive, who died in 1982.

Clarissa Dickson Wright will be remembered as a great British eccentric, a commanding presence on television, and a champion of traditional British cooking and countryside pursuits.

A woman with an extremely drug-resistant form of tuberculosis (XDR-TB) is being treated at the National Institutes of Health (NIH) outside Washington, D.C. The woman traveled to at least three states before seeking treatment, and health officials are now tracking down hundreds of people who may have been in contact with her. XDR-TB is so dangerous that health officials will have to make a concerted effort to warn anyone who may be at risk. The patient was transferred to the NIH via special air and ground ambulances and is staying in an isolation room in the NIH Clinical Center specifically designed for handling patients with respiratory infections, including XDR-TB. The National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID), part of the NIH, is providing care and treatment for the patient in connection with an existing NIH clinical protocol for treating TB, including XDR forms.

The patient, who isn’t being identified in any way, may face months or even years of treatment. Ordinary TB is hard to treat and requires, at a minimum, weeks of antibiotics. XDR-TB resists the effects of almost all the known TB drugs. Sometimes patients have to have pockets of infection surgically removed. Only about a third to half of cases can even be cured.

The patient traveled from India to the United States through Chicago O'Hare airport in April and also spent time in Missouri and Tennessee. Seven weeks after arriving in the United States, the patient sought treatment for and was diagnosed with active TB. She was isolated in a suburban Chicago hospital before being sent to NIH. CDC and NIH are testing the patient to see what drugs may help her.

TB is not as easily spread as diseases like the flu or measles, but it is a dangerous illness, especially for people with weakened immune systems. Health officials are taking the situation seriously. Contact tracing is underway for people who had prolonged direct contact with the woman, including those who sat in the same row or near the woman on the flight.

TB is caused by bacteria spread from person to person through the air. It usually affects the lungs and can lead to symptoms such as chest pain and coughing up blood. TB has been declining in the United States, but globally, each year it sickens about 9 million people and is a cause of 1.5 million deaths.

In 2007, Andrew Speaker, an Atlanta lawyer with multi-drug-resistant tuberculosis, was arrested and forcibly isolated under federal order after he defied CDC advisories and flew out of the country to get married. XDR-TB is very rare in the U.S., with only about 63 cases reported between 1993 and 2011.

The average cost of treating multidrug-resistant TB is $134,000, compared to $17,000 for a normal case. That can shoot up to $430,000 for an extensively resistant case. It’s not clear who will pay for this patient's treatment.

The CDC advises that all travelers should avoid high-risk settings where there are no infection control measures in place. Documented places where transmission has occurred include crowded hospitals, prisons, homeless shelters, and other settings where susceptible persons come in contact with persons with TB disease. The TB vaccine (BCG) is not generally recommended in the United States because it has limited effectiveness for preventing the most common forms of TB and in preventing TB in adults. The effect of BCG against XDR TB would likely be similar to the effect on drug-susceptible TB.

If a person thinks they have been exposed to someone with XDR TB, they should contact their doctor or local health department about getting a TB skin test or blood test for TB infection. They should tell the doctor or nurse when they spent time with this person and also where the person with XDR TB is being treated. If their test for TB infection is positive, they will need special follow-up. It can take from 6 to 16 weeks to find out if someone has XDR TB.

The risk of acquiring XDR TB in the United States appears to be low because XDR TB is uncommon in the U.S. However, TB can spread easily. As long as XDR TB exists, the risk to people in the United States is not zero, and the U.S. public health system must address the threat.

The article discusses a controversy surrounding the U.S. military's order for thousands of soldiers, particularly those from the California National Guard, to repay signing bonuses they received for re-enlisting to fight in Iraq and Afghanistan. The bonuses, which were offered as incentives to maintain the military's ranks during the prolonged international conflicts, were reportedly given out too liberally, with the largest payments not limited to certain skill areas as the rules dictated.

Nearly 10,000 soldiers are now scrambling to pay back these bonuses, which range from cash for re-enlistment to student loan repayments. The military argues that the law requires them to reclaim the overpayments, but many soldiers feel betrayed as they had served their required terms.

The California National Guard, in response, has stated that it does not have the authority to unilaterally waive these debts but welcomes any law passed by Congress to do so. They also mentioned that their adjutant general, Maj. Gen. David S. Baldwin, created an assistance center that has helped some soldiers retain $37 million of their original bonus payments.

This issue is not limited to California, but the state has emerged as a focal point due to its large guard force and a history of overpayments. A scandal over the California National Guard's use of bonus money was first unearthed in 2010, leading to a prison sentence for former Master Sgt. Toni Jaffe for making $15 million in false claims.

The controversy has led to anger from service members, veterans, and the public, with many expressing their discontent on social media. One veteran, former Army Captain Christopher Van Meter, refinanced his mortgage to repay $46,000 in re-enlistment bonuses and student loan repayments. Another veteran, former Army Master Sgt. Susan Haley, is now sending the Pentagon $650 each month to repay $20,500 in bonuses.

The Department of Defense states that repayment will not be sought if the member's inability to fulfill the eligibility requirements is due to circumstances determined reasonably beyond the member's control. However, after dozens of auditors reviewed the system that had paid soldiers bonuses without determining their eligibility, the California National Guard's veterans started getting repayment notices.

Some veterans are working to repay the money, while others are filing appeals, engaging in what's likely to be a prolonged fight against the service to which they once belonged. California National Guard officials have stated they are helping veterans through the appeals process.

On Monday, August 29, 2016, an Alaska Airlines flight from JFK Airport in New York to Seattle was diverted to Minneapolis-St. Paul Airport after a passenger attempted to open a door mid-flight. The man, estimated to be in his 20s, was acting oddly during boarding and was reportedly taking pills. He became unruly and tried to open a door at the rear of the 737, but the crew managed to calm him and divert the flight to Minneapolis. The man was arrested upon landing and later taken to Fairview Southdale Hospital in Edina, Minnesota. The crew radioed to land in Minnesota, stating they needed someone to "greet this customer, [who was] having a difficult time working and playing well with others." Passengers were told it was a medical emergency. Alaska Airlines confirmed that it is physically impossible to open an aircraft door while the aircraft is pressurized and in flight. It remains unclear if the man will face any charges. The flight finally arrived at Sea-Tac around 1 p.m. PST. The incident was captured on video by a passenger on the flight.

The Lucas Museum of Narrative Art, a first-of-its-kind interactive museum housing George Lucas' collection of artwork and movie memorabilia, will be built in Chicago. The museum, valued at $1 billion, will be located on a 17-acre site between Soldier Field and McCormick Place on parking lots. The museum will open in 2018 and is completely self-funded by Lucas.

Chicago was chosen over Los Angeles and San Francisco due to its larger location, easy accessibility to public transportation, and central location in a city renowned for its love of art and architecture. The museum will create hundreds of jobs and economic opportunities, according to Mayor Rahm Emanuel.

Lucas, who is married to Chicago businesswoman/civic leader Mellody Hobson, originally wanted to build the museum in his hometown of San Francisco, but site proposals on the field were rejected. Emanuel moved fast in February and quickly became a front-runner to snag the project.

The museum will house a collection that includes valuable Norman Rockwell paintings, examples of the special effects Lucas pioneered at Industrial Light & Magic, and memorabilia such as the Darth Vader costume. The works are wrapped around the theme of storytelling.

The decision to select Chicago has drawn opposition from open-space advocates, such as Friends of the Parks, who are concerned about the museum's impact on the lakefront. Under Emanuel's plan, the two Chicago Park District-owned parking lots would be leased to the museum for $1, and the parking lots would be moved underground at Lucas' expense.

The museum will be a significant cultural and educational asset for Chicago, as well as an unparalleled draw for international tourists. It will partner education with neighborhood schools and create jobs throughout the city of Chicago. Lucas expressed his excitement about joining the museum community and creating the museum in a city that has a long tradition of embracing the arts and architecture.

Nathaniel Marston, a former star of the soap opera One Life to Live, passed away on November 10, 2015, following a car accident on October 30. Marston was 40 years old at the time of the accident. His mother, Elizabeth Jackson, shared updates about his condition on her Facebook page, initially reporting that he was on life support with broken and fractured neck, broken shoulder, broken ribs, and a collapsed lung.

On November 11, Jackson announced that Marston had passed away peacefully, surrounded by loved ones. The accident occurred when Marston allowed his truck to drift across the northbound travel lane and enter the east dirt shoulder, causing the vehicle to overturn multiple times. Police confirmed that Marston was sober at the time of the accident.

Throughout the two weeks following the accident, Jackson shared updates about Marston's condition, expressing hope for his recovery and sharing the doctor's prognosis that, if he survived, he would likely be paralyzed from the neck down and require a ventilator. However, on November 9, Jackson reported that Marston was able to communicate and was determined to fight for his life.

Marston appeared on One Life to Live from 2001 to 2007. Arrangements are being made for a memorial service in New York City, Kauai, HI, and Gerlach, NV. The outpouring of support, prayers, love, and kindness from friends and fans has been a source of strength for Marston's family during this difficult time.

The November 4th episode of Saturday Night Live featured a mixed bag of performances. Aidy Bryant's impression of Sarah Huckabee Sanders, particularly her musical number to Demi Lovato's "Confident," was a highlight, showcasing Bryant's comedic talent and the sketch's commitment to pushing boundaries in political satire. However, Larry David's monologue received criticism for a joke about women in concentration camps, with many viewers finding it distasteful and inappropriate.

In the episode, Donald Trump, played by Alec Baldwin, visited Paul Manafort, portrayed by Alex Moffat, after Manafort's recent legal troubles. The sketch took a bizarre turn when Trump, Manafort, Vice President Mike Pence (Beck Bennett), and Attorney General Jeff Sessions (Kate McKinnon) took a naked shower together. The episode ended with a humorous twist involving a presidential turkey pardon.

The episode's political skits, such as the Sanders sketch and the "Through Donald Trump’s Eyes" and "Kellywise" sketches mentioned, were praised for their innovative approach to satire, acknowledging the surreal nature of current events and using it to create humor. However, the concentration camp joke in Larry David's monologue was widely criticized as inappropriate and tone-deaf.

Title: Transformers: Age of Extinction (2014)

Transformers: Age of Extinction is a science fiction/action film directed by Michael Bay, released in the U.S. in 2014. The film runs for 2 hours and 45 minutes and is rated PG-13 for violence, profanity, and painful dialogue. The main cast includes Mark Wahlberg, Stanley Tucci, Kelsey Grammer, Nicola Peltz, Jack Reynor, and Peter Cullen (voice).

The film is criticized for its length, story, characters, and excessive use of CGI. Critics argue that the movie is soulless, with a dull story, bland characters, and action that goes on for nearly three hours. The film is described as a waste of time, with no redeeming qualities other than the impressive CGI effects.

The plot revolves around the misadventures of four surviving Autobots, who seek out Optimus Prime, revived by a Texas mechanic named Cade Yeager (Mark Wahlberg). The Autobots, along with Cade's daughter, Tessa (Nicola Peltz), and Tessa's boyfriend, Shane (Jack Reynor), seek to avoid capture or destruction by Lockdown, a Decepticon who has come to Earth in search of Optimus Prime.

Mark Wahlberg is praised for his performance, although it is noted that it hardly matters in the grand scheme of the film. Stanley Tucci is commended for rising above the material and delivering the best one-liner in the movie. However, Nicola Peltz's performance is criticized as annoying, incompetent, and irritating.

The film is criticized for its contempt for the audience, with the filmmakers seemingly only interested in providing mindless spectacle and cool special effects. Despite the negative reviews, the film is expected to make so much money that a Transformers 5 is a foregone conclusion.

In summary, Transformers: Age of Extinction is a long, loud, and flashy film that offers little in terms of story, characters, or charm. While the CGI effects are impressive, the film is criticized for its soullessness, dull action, and excessive length. The film is not recommended for those seeking a meaningful cinematic experience.

The United Nations Security Council unanimously voted to pass additional sanctions against North Korea on Tuesday, aiming to rein in the rogue nation's rapidly developing nuclear program. President Donald Trump, however, expressed skepticism about the effectiveness of the sanctions, stating they were "just another very small step, not a big deal."

The North Korean Foreign Ministry condemned the sanctions, calling them a "heinous provocation" and a violation of the country's right to self-defense. Meanwhile, lawmakers in the House expressed frustration that the US isn't exerting greater pressure on China to stop North Korea's nuclear ambitions.

During a meeting with Malaysian Prime Minister Najib Razak, Trump suggested that tougher measures would still be necessary to address the North Korean issue. State Department spokeswoman Heather Nauert said the UN resolution represented "the strongest set of sanctions" so far, but acknowledged that more could be done.

China, North Korea's closest diplomatic ally and largest trading partner, is seen as key to resolving the standoff with Pyongyang. Rep. Brad Sherman, a California Democrat, said the US isn't threatening China enough with country sanctions due to political considerations.

The administration is pushing China to act, with Marshall Billingslea, assistant secretary in the Treasury Department's Office of Terrorism and Financial Intelligence, stating that China is looking the other way as North Korea uses its banking system and front companies to do business. Russian companies, meanwhile, continue to provide support to Pyongyang.

Both Billingslea and Susan Thornton, the acting assistant secretary for the State Department's Bureau of East Asian and Pacific Affairs, said the US is ready to counter any threat from North Korea with force, even as it pushes for a diplomatic solution.

In response to the sanctions, North Korea has threatened to inflict "the greatest pain and suffering" upon the US. On August 28, North Korea launched a missile directly over Japan, endangering Japanese airspace, and on September 3, the country conducted its sixth test of a nuclear device, marking "an unacceptable provocation."

In light of these developments, South Korea is forming a hit squad called the Spartan 3000 to take out North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. The unit is central to a longstanding plan to fight North Korea if necessary, called "Korea Massive Punishment and Retaliation." South Korea's previous president, Park Geun-hye, planned to have the unit ready by 2019, but the current administration wants it ready much sooner.

The announcement of the Spartan 3000 seems to have the approval of former South Korean military leaders, with one stating, "The best deterrence we can have, next to having our own nukes, is to make Kim Jong Un fear for his life." The unit is officially recognized by the Moon government and is part of a series of military moves South Korea has made in recent days to stave off a North Korean attack.

In a significant shake-up, President Donald Trump replaced his Chief of Staff Reince Priebus with Homeland Security Secretary John Kelly on Friday. Priebus, who had a turbulent six-month tenure, resigned privately on Thursday but denied resigning throughout the day on Friday. The announcement was made on Twitter after Trump landed at Joint Base Andrews. Kelly, a Marine Corps general, is expected to start on Monday.

Priebus' departure follows months of speculation about his ousting due to his inability to stem leaks, impose order, and the White House's legislative stumbles, including the failure to pass a health care replacement bill. Infighting among Trump's staff escalated, culminating in a vulgar screed from incoming communications director Anthony Scaramucci. Priebus lacked strong support from key members of Trump's inner circle, including his family.

The move allows for a new direction in the White House, with Steve Bannon expected to stay for now. Priebus, who traveled with Trump to Long Island for an event on gang violence, was informed of his dismissal while on the tarmac. He told CNN he offered his resignation on Thursday and expressed confidence in Kelly's abilities.

Kelly, who has been a star at Homeland Security, is due to begin his tenure on Monday. He served in the military for nearly five decades and has experience in various positions, including chief of Southern Command and senior assistant to the secretary of defense. His son was killed in combat in Afghanistan in 2010.

Priebus' 189-day tenure as Chief of Staff is the shortest in modern presidential history. His appointment was controversial, as he was seen as embodying the Washington Republican establishment that Trump had defeated in the primaries. Despite the challenges, Priebus helped Trump bridge the divide with many establishment Republicans during the general election and into his presidency.

Trenton Lewis, a 21-year-old UPS worker in Little Rock, Arkansas, has been walking five miles to work every day for the past seven months due to a lack of transportation. Lewis, a new father, said he felt the need to work and support his daughter. Despite the long walks in rain or cold, Lewis never missed a shift or was late to work.

His co-workers, Patricia and Kenneth Bryant, learned about Lewis' daily trek and decided to help. They collected donations from other UPS workers and bought Lewis a Saturn, which cost just shy of $2,000. The group surprised Lewis with the keys to the car in the UPS facility parking lot, and he was overwhelmed by the gesture.

Lewis now leaves for work at 3:30 a.m., allowing him to sleep in and giving his legs a break. He expressed gratitude for his co-workers' kindness and said he knew things would get better if he kept coming to work. On April 13, 2017, two police officers in Gwinnett County, Georgia were fired after videos surfaced on social media showing them assaulting a man during an arrest. Sgt. Michael Bongiovanni was terminated after a video showed him punching the man in the face as the man stepped out of a car with his hands up. Earlier, Officer Robert McDonald was fired for kicking the man in the head while he was handcuffed on the ground.

The incident occurred around 4 p.m. on Wednesday, and one video, shot from across the street, shows the man getting out of a vehicle with his hands raised before being punched by the arresting officer. Another video, shot from a different angle, shows the officer struggling with the man as he gets out of the vehicle and raises his hands. Shortly after the man is subdued and handcuffed, a second officer arrives and kicks the man in the head.

The man, identified as 21-year-old Demetrius Bryan Hollins of Lawrenceville, Ga., was charged with multiple traffic citations, obstruction of a police officer, and possession of less than an ounce of marijuana. Hollins told NBC News that he was trying to get to the camera app on his own cellphone to record the encounter when one officer started "shoving him in his car and telling him that he was never going to have a video, that he was never going to make the phone call to his mom. When I had my hands up, that’s when he punched me in the face."

The police department released both officers' personnel files and said that McDonald was an excellent example of a team player with a strong work ethic. McDonald had received several commendations and recognitions, including sharing the officer of the month honor in November 2015. However, Bongiovanni's personnel file showed that he had filed three use-of-force reports explaining why he used his stun gun or physical force in the course of his duties.

The police chief said during a news conference that a plan is in place to outfit uniformed officers with body cameras by the end of the year. Asked what message the incident sends, the chief said, "We have standards, we have policies, and we’re going to hold ourselves to those standards and to those policies. And if you violate those, there will be a swift investigation. And if those complaints are found to be sustained, action will be taken."

The incident has sparked outrage from community groups such as Black Lives Matter of Greater Atlanta, who have demanded that the officers be prosecuted for their actions. Hollins' attorney, Justin Miller, told NBC News that without the videos, the officers may have been able to "paint him as the bad guy, arrested him, brushed it under the rug and probably did it to them again the next time they saw him."

The Open Edge Cloud, a new technology, is set to revolutionize content delivery by creating a powerful solution using standard compute and storage in service provider networks. This edge cloud, equipped with Open APIs for rapid resource allocation, aims to cater to the performance demands of next-generation applications. The deal for Google's acquisition of Twitch, a popular gaming-streaming company, for over $1 billion is imminent, making it the most significant acquisition in YouTube's history. Twitch, founded in 2011, has over 45 million monthly users and has raised about $35 million in funding. The acquisition is expected to face scrutiny from U.S. regulators due to YouTube's dominance in the online video market. Twitch and YouTube both offer gameplay videos, with Twitch also competing in the e-sports market. The acquisition could potentially consolidate Google's position in the gaming and streaming industry.

A 66-year-old woman in Thailand developed a large, calcified mass in her lower leg, 50 years after being bitten by a venomous Malayan pit viper. The mass was initially noticed 10 years prior and resembled an enlarged cavity wrapped in a tough, calcified membrane on X-ray. The mass grew so large that it broke through the woman's skin. The authors of the report, researchers at the Prince of Songkla University in Thailand, suggest that the woman may have developed compartment syndrome due to the snakebite, which was left untreated. Compartment syndrome occurs when muscles, nerves, and blood vessels are held together by a tough tissue called the fascia, and can result from trauma or injury, leading to compromised blood flow. The mass was surgically removed, and the wound healed within a month. Calcific myonecrosis, the formation of a calcified mass due to muscle tissue death after a crushing injury or disruption of blood supply, is usually found in the lower leg and can be mistaken for a tumor. A biopsy is not recommended due to the high risk of infection. Prevention involves early detection and treatment of compartment syndrome.

Pope Francis is set to release an encyclical, a major teaching letter, on Thursday, June 18, focusing on the environment and the poor. The document, titled "Laudato Sii" or "Praised Be," is expected to promote climate action as a moral imperative and could have a significant impact on global warming efforts. The encyclical is being treated as a milestone that could position the Roman Catholic Church at the forefront of a new coalition of religion and science.

The encyclical is anticipated to be more impactful than international negotiations this year aimed at limiting greenhouse gas emissions, according to climate scientists. Jeff Kiehl of the National Center for Atmospheric Research and Gavin Schmidt, a NASA climatologist, expressed excitement about the encyclical, with Kiehl stating, "I mean it's just unbelievable."

The pope's environmental concerns are not new; he studied chemistry and worked as a chemist before entering the seminary. In January, he stated that science is largely settled on the causes of climate change and that greater stewardship of God's creation is necessary.

However, the encyclical is expected to face pushback from conservative Catholic religious figures, such as Republican presidential candidate Rick Santorum, who has accused the pope of being alarmist. Despite this, scientists applaud the pope for urging moral choices in a discussion dominated by the recitation of facts.

Climate scientists have been frustrated by a lack of forceful action by policymakers, with many expressing anger or exhaustion. A website called "Is this how you feel?" contains dozens of letters from climate scientists expressing their feelings about the situation.

The encyclical is expected to be launched by three people: a Catholic cardinal, a Christian Orthodox church leader, and a climate scientist identified as an atheist. The pope has a history of environmental concern and has repeatedly stated that the environment is not only an economic or political issue but is also an anthropological and ethical matter.

The encyclical is timed to have maximum public impact ahead of the pope's meeting with Barack Obama and his address to the US Congress and the UN general assembly in September. It is also intended to improve the prospect of a strong new UN global agreement to cut climate emissions, by adding a moral dimension to the well-rehearsed scientific arguments and raising the ambition of countries above their own self-interest.

Madonna, at the Toronto International Film Festival, premiered her film "W.E." and faced criticism for her alleged behavior towards volunteers. However, her camp has issued a press release denying that she asked volunteers to turn away from her, stating that she publicly thanked them for their hard work and was impressed by them. Madonna defended her filmmaking abilities and said she expects to earn her reputation as a director, just as she did as a musician. She also discussed the use of a punk anthem by The Sex Pistols in the film's soundtrack and her connection to the film's protagonist, Wallis Simpson. Madonna has been promoting "W.E." as her first film as a director and has expressed her hope for Oscar recognition for the film.

The article discusses the life of Evie, a transgender woman who once worked as a nanny for Barack Obama in Indonesia. Evie, born a man but identifying as a woman, has faced a lifetime of discrimination and violence due to her identity. The turning point came when she found the body of a transgender friend in a sewage canal, which led her to give away all her female clothing and live as a man.

Indonesia's attitude towards transgenders is complex, with an estimated 7 million living in the country, making it one of the most populous nations with a significant transgender population. While there are occasional pageants and transgender individuals working as singers or at salons, societal disdain still runs deep, and transgenders are often the butt of jokes in TV comedies. They have taken a lower profile in recent years due to attacks by Muslim hard-liners and the country's highest Islamic body's decree that they must live as they were born.

Many transgenders turn to prostitution due to a lack of job opportunities and a desire to live according to their true gender, putting themselves at risk of contracting AIDS and other sexually transmitted diseases. Some, like Evie, choose to hide their feelings, while others are pushing back, such as a 50-year-old Indonesian transvestite who applied to be the next leader of the national human rights commission.

The threat of violence against transgenders is real, with Indonesia's National Commission for Human Rights receiving about 1,000 reports of abuses per year, ranging from murder and rape to the disruption of group activities. Worldwide, at least one person is killed every other day, according to the Trans Murder Monitoring Project.

Evie, now 66, lives in a small hovel in a Jakarta slum, earning money by collecting and scrubbing dirty laundry. She hopes that Obama, who named Amanda Simpson as the first openly transgender appointee in the Commerce Department in 2010, will use his power to fight for people like her. Despite her difficult life, Evie takes pride in her past as Obama's nanny and uses it to defend herself against those who call her "scum."

In Texas, a work group of teachers has revised the state's social studies curriculum for schoolchildren, sparking controversy over the inclusion and exclusion of certain historical figures. The revised curriculum, approved by the State Board of Education on Friday, removes Helen Keller from a lesson on citizenship and replaces San Jacinto Day with Constitution Day.

The work group graded hundreds of figures, including historical and contemporary Texans, using a rubric to simplify the learning process. Notable figures such as Barbara Jordan, Sam Houston, Stephen F. Austin, and Henry B. González received perfect scores. However, former President Bill Clinton and Helen Keller were not included in the final list, with the work group citing a desire to avoid offending anyone and a need to simplify the curriculum.

The decision to remove Helen Keller from the curriculum has been met with criticism from some, including House Democratic Caucus Chairman Chris Turner, who tweeted, "If Helen Keller was an important historical figure when I was in school (and she was), then she still is today." Turner also urged board members to add former President Bill Clinton back into the curriculum, noting that he was the first and only woman to be the presidential nominee of a major party in U.S. history.

The State Board of Education's process for revising classroom standards has always been a subject of debate and controversy. In the past, members have clashed over issues such as the teaching of evolution and the inclusion of Mexican-American studies. This time, the board's decision to remove descriptions of the nation's "Judeo-Christian" heritage drew criticism from conservative Christian political advocacy groups, while others criticized the board for removing Clinton and Keller from the curriculum.

The board's decision to replace San Jacinto Day with Constitution Day has also been met with some criticism, as the Battle of San Jacinto is taught in fourth-grade social studies and high school U.S. history. The board's decision to revise the social studies curriculum is part of an annual process that discusses and debates new standards for Texas' 5.4 million schoolchildren.

Sen. John Kerry's daughter, Alexandra Kerry, was arrested for a potential DUI in Los Angeles early Thursday morning. On Saturday, during the LOTOJA bike race, a tragic accident occurred that resulted in the death of Robert Verhaaren, a 42-year-old cyclist from Mesa, Arizona. The incident occurred approximately 8 miles south of Jackson, Wyoming, on Highway 89, near a bridge over the Snake River. According to the Teton County Sheriff, Verhaaren swerved to avoid a pothole, lost control of his bicycle, and fell over a guardrail, plummeting about 35 feet into the shallow river.

Verhaaren was airlifted to St. John's Hospital in Jackson, where he was later pronounced dead. The initial examination revealed a possible cervical fracture, but the exact cause of death is yet to be determined. The accident has sparked concerns about the road conditions in that stretch of the race, with some residents expressing dissatisfaction about the poor roads.

Verhaaren was an avid cyclist and held the position of Managing Director at Universal Equity Group Funds Arizona. He earned a Bachelor's degree in accounting from Brigham Young University and a law degree from the New York University School of Law. He is survived by his wife and three children.

This incident marks the first fatality in the 30-year history of LOTOJA, an annual 206-mile bike race from Logan, Utah, to Jackson Hole, Wyoming, sanctioned by USA Cycling. The race was also marred by other accidents, including two bicyclists being hospitalized and around 200 cyclists experiencing flat tires early on.

The cycling community has been deeply affected by this tragedy. Verhaaren's brother, Michael, is married to Olympic BMX cyclist Arielle Martin, who was injured in an Olympic practice run and was unable to compete this summer. Arielle posted on her Twitter account expressing her devastation.

The Wyoming Department of Transportation could not be reached for comment regarding the road conditions. The cycling community mourns the loss of Robert Verhaaren, a beloved figure in the sport.

A series of three earthquakes occurred in Arizona on Sunday night, with the epicenters located just north of Black Canyon City. The quakes generated no reports of notable damage, but left people swaying or stunned from Black Canyon City to Camp Verde and across metro Phoenix as far as Queen Creek. The causative fault line has not been identified yet. Michael Conway of the Arizona Geological Survey stated that scientists will have a hard time identifying the origin due to the small size of the earthquake and lack of ground rupture. Aftershocks are expected over the next few days, many of them too small to feel. The quakes were relatively small, with the largest one occurring at 6.5 kilometers beneath the surface. No injuries were immediately reported, and the department of Black Canyon City received numerous calls from panicked and curious residents. The earthquakes were not destructive but were unsettling for many.

Professor Robert Shambaugh is a renowned expert on contemporary China and international relations, with a focus on Asia, the European Union, and transatlantic issues. Recently, there has been a shift in Chinese propaganda efforts regarding the nickname "Big Daddy Xi" for President Xi Jinping. Chinese propaganda chiefs have reportedly ordered state-controlled media to refrain from using the nickname, following concerns about the portrayal of Xi as a Mao-like autocrat. The nickname has been at the center of an energetic push to portray Xi as an omnipotent people's president, with an entire genre of "Big Daddy Xi"-themed songs emerging. However, the nickname has not appeared on Xinhua's website since April 27, and it is unclear why Beijing's propaganda officials have decided to step back from the nickname.

Experts believe this move may hint at growing discomfort about how Xi is portrayed, both in and outside China. In recent weeks, Chinese officials have expressed discomfort over the perception that a cult of personality is growing around their leader. The website of The Economist was blocked in China after a cartoon on its front page showed Xi sporting a Mao-style Zhongshan suit beside the headline: "Beware the cult of Xi." Writing in the New York Review of Books, Columbia University's Prof Andrew J Nathan accused Xi of bringing back "many of the most dangerous features of Mao's rule: personal dictatorship, enforced ideological conformity, and arbitrary persecution."

Kerry Brown, the author of "CEO, China: The Rise of Xi Jinping," suggested that the apparent move to purge Xi's nickname from headlines could be a possible admission that China's portrayal of its leader has backfired. Roderick MacFarquhar, a Harvard University China expert, said the apparent abandonment of the nickname was unlikely to signal a change in direction for the authoritarian leader, who has suggested he is the country's most powerful since Mao. MacFarquhar admitted the inner workings of Chinese politics were so opaque it was hard to grasp the significance of the move. "I think there are all sorts of currents around Chinese leaders at the moment, and it is difficult to tell who is on whose side," he said.

In conclusion, Professor Shambaugh is a highly respected expert on China and international relations. Recent developments in Chinese propaganda efforts suggest growing discomfort about the portrayal of President Xi Jinping, with Chinese propaganda chiefs ordering state-controlled media to refrain from using the nickname "Big Daddy Xi." Experts believe this move may indicate a backlash against the portrayal of Xi as a Mao-like autocrat, with concerns about the growing cult of personality around the leader.

The Academy of Motion Pictures Arts & Sciences has rescinded Sacha Baron Cohen's tickets for the 84th Academy Awards, citing concerns about a potential publicity stunt involving Cohen attending the event in character from his upcoming film, "The Dictator." Cohen was invited to attend the Oscars as a member of the cast of the best picture nominee "Hugo." The Academy reportedly requested assurances from Cohen that he would not appear in costume or promote the movie on the red carpet. Cohen's plan was to attend the Oscars in character as The Dictator and then change into a tuxedo. The study published in PLOS ONE reveals that great apes, including chimpanzees, bonobos, and orangutans, have the ability to understand false beliefs in people, a capacity previously thought to be unique to humans. The research was conducted at the Leipzig Zoo in Germany, where 34 great apes participated in a test designed to determine if they could understand when a person held a false belief.

In the test, a person placed an object in one of two boxes, while a great ape observed. For some tests, the original person stepped away, and another person moved the object to the other box and locked both boxes. When the original person returned, they tried to open the box where they believed the object was, not realizing it had been moved. This was known as the "false-belief" portion of the study.

The apes chose the correct box significantly more often than chance in the false belief portion of the study, demonstrating their ability to understand the person's false belief. Furthermore, the apes were more likely to help the person find the object when they had a false belief about its location.

The study's findings challenge the long-held belief that great apes lack the capacity to understand the intentions of people. Researchers believe that this ability could be a key factor in great apes' advanced social cognition. The study's lead author, David Buttelmann, from the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology in Germany, stated, "Apes are able to use this understanding in their social interactions."

The study used a test developed for human infants, about 18 months of age, to determine if the apes could understand when a person held a false belief. The apes were housed socially at the Leipzig Zoo and were not food deprived for testing. The researchers plan to extend this work to other animals to track the development of social cognition and understand what makes humans unique.

In a tragic incident at Los Angeles International Airport (LAX) on November 1, a gunman opened fire, critically wounding Transportation Security Administration (TSA) officer Gerardo Hernandez. The shooting occurred in Terminal 3, with the gunman reportedly expressing a desire to target TSA employees and criticizing their searches as unconstitutional.

The gunman, identified as Paul Ciancia, was shot four times by airport police officers and remains in fair condition at a hospital. The shooting led to a chaotic scene, with travelers diving for cover and concerns about potential bombs and accomplices.

However, paramedics were delayed in reaching Hernandez due to police not declaring the terminal safe to enter. For 33 minutes, Hernandez lay bleeding, with no immediate medical attention, as he was about 20 feet from an exit. It is unclear whether immediate medical attention could have saved his life.

Authorities are investigating the incident, focusing on possible lack of coordination between police and fire officials that may have prevented speedy treatment for Hernandez and other victims. TSA workers at LAX have expressed concerns about the lack of coordination.

The incident has highlighted the need for improved coordination between law enforcement and emergency services, particularly in active shooter situations. It has also brought attention to the training of officers in first aid and CPR, with a recent audit revealing a zero percent compliance rate for refresher training in the Los Angeles Police Department.

On a positive note, the condition of the alleged gunman, Paul Ciancia, has been upgraded from critical to fair. A public memorial service was held for Hernandez on the same day the upgrade was announced, attended by hundreds of people. Ciancia is charged with killing Hernandez and wounding three others, and faces potential death sentence if convicted.

On August 24, 2016, Maverick County officials confirmed the death of Lucila Robles, a 69-year-old woman who worked at Laughlin Air Force Base in Del Rio, Texas. Robles was killed in an explosion of a truck and trailer loaded with airbag cartridges near Quemado, Texas, on Monday morning. The truck was traveling from Del Rio to the Takata plant in Eagle Pass, Texas.

The driver of the truck, identified as Mario Alberto Rodriguez, 20, was injured along with a passenger. An older couple traveling in a Toyota SUV was also injured during the explosion. All four injured victims were transported to a hospital in Eagle Pass, and later airlifted to San Antonio.

The blast damaged some 10 nearby homes, breaking windows and dislodging doors from their hinges. Pieces of rubble and truck parts were found almost 1 mile away from the place of the explosion. The blast cratered the ground and damaged the road, causing the closure of U.S. Hwy 277 for some 30 hours on and off.

Investigators called off the search for Robles after two days when they discovered her remains in the smoldering debris of her house. An internal document provided by a former Takata employee shows that Takata transports its explosive compound more than 2,000 miles across the United States, from its propellant-manufacturing plant in Moses Lake, Wash., to a distribution center just north of the Mexico border in Eagle Pass, Tex.

The Department of Transportation is investigating the crash and explosion, looking into the safety compliance of the motor carrier, the handling of the cargo by the shipper, its packaging, how the truck was placarded, as well as the truck’s routing, to determine whether there were violations of any U.S. Department of Transportation safety regulations. Takata said the truck was operated by a subcontractor, which it did not name. The supplier immediately sent personnel to the site and has been cooperating with local investigators. Takata has strict safety procedures relating to the transportation of its products that meet or exceed all regulatory requirements.

The controversial comedy film "The Interview," about a fictional plot to assassinate North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, was released in more than 300 theaters across the United States on Christmas Day. The film's release was initially canceled after major U.S. theater chains pulled out due to threats of violence by a computer hacking group called Guardians of Peace. The United States blamed the attacks on North Korea.

In China and South Korea, hundreds of thousands of people flocked to illegal video sharing sites to see the movie. In the United States, movie theater managers and patrons alike said they believed there was nothing to fear from the threats, and the initial screenings on Thursday were uneventful. However, one of the online outlets that distributed the film ahead of its theatrical release, Microsoft Corp's Xbox Live, reported that users were experiencing problems getting connected on Thursday. A hacking group called the Lizard Squad claimed it was behind disruptions at both Xbox and Sony Corp's PlayStation Networks, but neither company offered an explanation for the connectivity problems.

The film was also available to U.S. online viewers through Google Inc's Google Play and YouTube Movie, as well as on a Sony website, www.seetheinterview.com. It can be seen in Canada on the Sony site and Google Canada's website. A Sony spokeswoman on Thursday said she had no figures on the number of downloads so far, and the studio was not expected to have box office numbers from theaters before Friday morning.

The audience at the first screening of the film in New York City remained silent during a scene showing the death of Kim Jong Un in the downing of his helicopter. Matt Rosenzweig, 60, of Manhattan, said the moments that drew the most applause had to do with the idea of acting against censorship rather than animosity toward North Korea. RAUCOUS APPLAUSE

Although Cinema Village manager Lee Peterson said the New York Police Department planned to post officers outside the theater, there was no visible police presence outside or inside the venue for the first screening. An afternoon screening at the Van Nuys Regency Theatres in the city's San Fernando Valley was two-thirds full and drew a diverse crowd ranging from teens to senior citizens, who laughed loudly throughout at Rogen and Franco's antics.

The movie, which is playing in theaters in major metropolitan areas as well as in smaller cities ranging from Bangor, Maine, to Jasper, Indiana, features Rogen and Franco as journalists who are recruited by the CIA to assassinate the North Korean leader. In Asia, online audiences seemed to find the movie tedious. "There is no drama and not much fun," said a blogger in South Korea. "It's all about forced comedy that turns you off. Couldn't they have done a better job making this movie?"

Sony decided to release the film after U.S. President Barack Obama, as well as such Hollywood luminaries as George Clooney and Republicans and Democrats in Washington, raised concerns that Hollywood was setting a precedent of self-censorship. The audience in Manhattan exited the theater to a throng of network TV cameras and a crowd of people lined up for the next showing. "It was more serious, the satire, than I was expecting," said Simone Reynolds, who saw the film while visiting from London. "There's a message for America in there too about America's foreign policy."

North Korea has called the film an "act of war." Most fans simply called "The Interview" a funny movie. Ken Jacowitz, a 54-year-old librarian from the New York borough of Queens, called it "a funny film made by funny people." He had a message for North Korea and the hackers: "You have given this movie whole new lives."

In September 1977, a baby girl was found abandoned at Amarillo Terminal Airport, Texas. The blonde, brown-eyed infant, later known as Jane Doe 927, was about 16-18 months old and was described as healthy despite some bruises. After the abandonment was reported, she was taken to Northwest Texas Hospital for observation. The Amarillo police opened an investigation, and the baby was placed into the custody of Potter-Randall County Child Welfare.

The investigation faded a month later after a hopeful New Mexico couple decided Jane Doe 927 was not their missing daughter. Parental rights were terminated in January 1978, and the adoption process followed. Four years later, a woman named Rosalee Webster returned to her Long Beach, California home without her daughter Bonnie. Rosalee told varying stories about what happened to Bonnie, including that she had died or been taken by Child Protective Services. In 1998, Rosalee's sister posted on a genealogy forum searching for information on Bonnie's whereabouts.

In 2018, a genealogist named Ronda Randall stumbled upon the post while researching a serial killer and began helping the family in their search. They found a matching description and photo of Jane Doe 927 in Amarillo Globe-News files. The woman who identifies as Jane Doe 927, Shelley Schooley, was adopted by a family in Odessa, Texas, in 1977. Schooley has always known about her abandonment and has a large extended family and a strong mother-daughter bond. Schooley and the Websters have connected and conversed about the "what ifs" in each of their stories, but Schooley cannot justify spending money on a DNA test to determine whether she is Bonnie Lee Webster or not.

The United States has put Iran "on notice" following a recent ballistic missile test by Iran, which was deemed a violation of a UN Security Council resolution. In a dramatic turn of events during the trial of Markelus Carter for the 2009 murder of Kenneth Warrington, a fight broke out between Carter and a witness, Steven Upham, in a holding cell at the Allen County Justice Center. The incident occurred during an afternoon break when Carter was mistakenly placed in the same cell with Upham. Carter then bit Upham on the arm before corrections officers intervened.

Upham, a blockmate of Carter's at Allen Oakwood Correctional Institution, testified that Carter had shared details about the murder with him. During cross-examination, the defense questioned Upham about other ways he could have obtained information on the murder besides a direct conversation with Carter. Upham admitted spending a significant amount of time in prison trying to secure an early release but denied being promised any reduction in exchange for his testimony in this case.
