The fight between Carter and Upham has added an unexpected element to the trial, with Carter appearing visibly shaken and with apparent red marks on his face after the incident. An investigation has been initiated to determine the cause of the error that led to the two inmates being placed together in the holding cell.

The book "SEAL Target Geronimo" by Chuck Pfarrer, a former commander of US Navy SEAL Team Six, provides detailed insights into the raid that led to Osama bin Laden's death. Contrary to popular belief, the mission was not a "kill mission" from the start, and the SEALs had no explicit orders to kill bin Laden. Instead, they were prepared to capture him if possible.

The raid took place in a three-story home in Abbottabad, Pakistan, where bin Laden was hiding. The SEALs' stealthy helicopter was not detected until it hovered over the roof, and within 10 seconds, they had jumped onto the roof, forced their way into bin Laden's bedroom, and engaged in a brief firefight. Bin Laden was killed almost instantly, and his pistol now hangs in SEAL Team Six's Virginia base.

Pfarrer's book also sheds light on the decisions made by the White House regarding air support and the use of stealth helicopters, which could have complicated relations with Pakistan. The book could potentially complicate the 2012 presidential race by revealing these details.

Additionally, the book argues that bin Laden's long-time deputy, Ayman Zawahiri, may have inadvertently led the US to bin Laden by repeatedly sending a courier, whose cover had already been blown, in and out of the compound. The book has been delayed for several weeks while being cleared by government officials and is due to be released later this month. However, it has been met with criticism from US officials who claim it contains inaccuracies.

Kuki Gallmann, an Italian-born conservationist and author of the best-selling memoir "I Dreamed of Africa", was shot and injured in an ambush at her conservation park in central Kenya. The attack occurred while she was patrolling her property with rangers from the Kenya Wildlife Service, assessing damage done to her property by arsonists who burned down buildings at one of her tourism lodges. Gallmann, 73, owns the Laikipia Nature Conservancy and a luxury safari lodge, which was burned down last month by suspected cattle herders.

The herders have been invading private property in search of fresh grazing in the drought-stricken Laikipia region. Insecurity has risen sharply in recent months as the drought has led armed herders to seek out new pasture, pitting them against big landowners and smallholders. Tens of thousands of cattle are thought to have been driven on to private land and at least a dozen people have been killed.

The attack on Gallmann may have been in retaliation for a police operation that killed 100 cattle in the conservancy. The herders accused police of trying to force them off the land by shooting their livestock, while police say the livestock were killed in crossfire with the herders, who were using the animals as shields.

Gallmann moved to Kenya in 1972 with her husband and son who both later died in separate accidents. She later became a Kenyan citizen. "I Dreamed of Africa" was turned into a film starring Kim Basinger. The arson attack on Gallmann's Mukutan Retreat last month left it in ruins. There were no visitors staying at the time.

The land invasions started late last year. British national and ranch owner Tristan Voorspuy was killed last month when he went to inspect damage done by the herders on one of his lodges. Opposition leader and former Prime Minister Raila Odinga said ranch owners deserve protection under the law like all Kenyans.

Many of the ranches, some of which double as wildlife conservancies, were acquired during the period of British colonial rule, some as early as 1900, according to a government report. Others were purchased after Kenya became independent in 1963. Many of the farmers' association's members are in the tourism business.

The violence in Laikipia is politically motivated, according to Martin Evans, the chair of the Laikipia Farmers' Association. "It started a year ago," Evans said. "At the time it started, there was plenty of rain, it was nothing to do with lack of grass at that time so yes, I think it's definitely being pushed by politicians." Kenyan President Uhuru Kenyatta's office issued a statement warning politicians in the area not to inflame the situation with "reckless rhetoric."

In Cairo, Egypt, tens of thousands of supporters and opponents of President Mohamed Morsi clashed violently on Wednesday, resulting in over 125 injuries and at least five deaths. The conflict began when Islamist protesters, led by the Muslim Brotherhood, moved to disperse a demonstration by Morsi's non-Islamist opponents outside the presidential palace. The clashes continued into the night, with both sides accusing each other of using live ammunition. The Obama administration called for both sides to respect each other and refrain from violence. The conflict reflects the deepening divide between Egypt's secular and Islamist factions, with the opposition galvanized by Morsi's decree granting him nearly unrestricted powers and the hurried approval of a constitution that the opposition says is weighted with Islamic law. The government has set a referendum on the draft constitution for December 15. The Muslim Brotherhood has accused opposition leaders, including Mohamed ElBaradei, of inciting violence and conspiring with Zionists to overthrow Morsi's government. The Egyptian army has deployed tanks outside the presidential palace to secure the site. The crisis deepened on Thursday with three of Morsi's aides resigning in protest and the opposition calling for another protest outside the palace. The situation remains tense and volatile.

A life-sized, naked foam sculpture of Donald Trump, titled "The Emperor Has No Balls," created by the anonymous art collective Indecline, is set to be auctioned off by Julien's Auctions in Los Angeles on October 22. The statue, estimated to sell for between $10,000 and $20,000, is the only one remaining from a series that appeared in New York, San Francisco, Seattle, Cleveland, and Los Angeles earlier this month. A portion of the auction's proceeds will benefit the National Immigration Forum, an immigrant advocacy organization.

The statue, which depicts Trump with a massive belly, small fingers, and some missing genitals, has caused controversy in various locations, with some officials requesting it be obfuscated or moved. However, Matt Kennedy of La Luz de Jesus gallery, who rescued the statue, refused. The statue will be on display at Julien's Auctions Westside gallery from October 17-22 before being sold.

In addition to the "Naked Trump" statue, the auction will feature works by renowned artists such as Banksy, Keith Haring, Jean-Michel Basquiat, Andy Warhol, and Shepard Fairey. Another notable piece is American pop artist Knowledge Bennett’s “Hillary Clinton Cojones,” featuring the Democratic White House hopeful wearing a tuxedo, expected to fetch up to $15,000.

Trump, who has pledged to build a wall between the U.S. and Mexico to keep immigrants out and to deport millions of undocumented immigrants, is not the only politician represented in the auction. The auction aims to raise funds for immigrant support groups, reflecting the political climate of the ongoing presidential election cycle.

The University of California has announced it will cover medical expenses for students pepper-sprayed during an Occupy Davis protest last week. Authorities have dropped charges against 10 individuals arrested during the protest, and an advisory panel, led by Bill Bratton, former police chief of Los Angeles, Boston, and New York, will investigate the incident. Chancellor Linda P.B. Katehi insists that the school's police department defied her orders when they used force against students, and she has ordered police to remain ready to help campers if an emergency arises but to stay out of sight. The incident has sparked widespread criticism, calls for Katehi's resignation, and a systemwide review by UC officials, with the Legislature agreeing to hold hearings on the matter. Katehi believes that the policies used to respond to encampments need to be updated to better accommodate modern student needs and expectations.

In a tragic incident in Pittsburgh, 12-year-old Shamera Harris died after being dragged by a car driven by her father, Richard Benton, who was allegedly under the influence of alcohol. The incident occurred on Sunday night when Benton, despite being advised not to drink by his girlfriend Carla Harris, offered to drive to pick up their daughter and a friend from the Waterworks Mall.

Upon arrival at the friend's house, Benton asked their daughter to step out of the car so he could take a picture. In the process, he fiddled with the gearshift, causing the car to roll backward, dragging Shamera and slamming into a tree. Carla Harris tried to stop the car and perform CPR on her daughter, but she was pronounced dead at the scene.

Benton, who was released on nonmonetary bond on Monday, has been charged with driving under the influence. He refused a breath test and refused to comply with field sobriety tests at the scene. The Allegheny County medical examiner's office found that Shamera died of blunt force trauma and ruled her death an accident. The police investigation continues.

Shamera was a student at Pittsburgh Dilworth PreK-5 and Pittsburgh Obama 6-12, where she was known for her good behavior and academic achievements. The schools offered counseling services to students following the tragic incident.

Carla Harris stated that she would not have allowed her daughter to ride in the car if she had suspected Benton was drunk. The family is mourning the loss of Shamera, who they described as a gift from God. This is the second sudden death in the family, as Shawn Harris, Shamera's father, was found shot in Morningside's Joe Natoli Field two years ago.

The funeral arrangements for Shamera are yet to be finalized. The incident has brought grief to the family and the community, and Carla Harris expressed her inability to communicate with Benton at this time. The police have stated that if there is evidence implicating Benton in Shamera's death, charges will be filed.

The Internet Archive is working on a project to archive web pages as they are created and preserve links to the archived versions of pages that are changed or removed. This aims to fix broken links on the web and provide a way for people to see the original intended content of a page.

In a separate story, Matthew Hay-Chapman, a homeless man living in San Francisco's Golden Gate Park, is being hailed as a hero for helping police capture two Orange County jail escapees over the weekend. Hay-Chapman, who has a keen eye for current events, spotted the fugitives hanging out near a police station and alerted authorities, leading to their capture. He is in line to collect a $140,000 reward for his actions.

Hay-Chapman has had a difficult life, having been raised on military bases and working various jobs before suffering severe back pain that left him unable to work. He has a disabled daughter and a troubled son, and his family says he has trouble staying on a steady course but is sharp and up-to-date on current events.

The capture of the fugitives has given Hay-Chapman a chance to rebuild his life and help his family, and he plans to use the reward money to do so. The police chief praised Hay-Chapman for his courage and sharp observation skills, and the Orange County sheriff's department has promised to work with agencies offering rewards to ensure the money goes to him.

The White House has been linking President Obama's actions to the biographies of previous presidents on its website, highlighting his role in various historical moments. This practice, first noticed by the conservative Heritage Foundation and neoconservative magazine Commentary, has been met with a response from the Republican National Committee (RNC), who have humorously depicted Obama in world-changing events such as Christopher Columbus' landing in the New World, Napoleon's coronation, and guest-lecturing with Albert Einstein. The White House insists that the official biographies remain unaltered, with the added links providing additional information about Obama's contributions. The additions, particularly those related to fighting for Medicare and Social Security or expanding the rights of gays and veterans, highlight the White House's efforts it would like to be noted.

The article also provides a detailed biography of Calvin Coolidge, the 30th President of the United States, who served from 1923 to 1929. Coolidge was known for his frugality, dry wit, and isolationist foreign policy. He refused to use federal economic power to check the growing boom or to ameliorate the depressed condition of agriculture and certain industries. Despite his negative and remote demeanor, Coolidge was also known for his accessibility and kindness in permitting himself to be photographed in Indian war bonnets or cowboy dress, and in greeting a variety of delegations to the White House. Coolidge's biography is from "The Presidents of the United States of America," by Frank Freidel and Hugh Sidey.

The study published in Lancet Psychiatry reveals that violent psychopaths have abnormalities in the brain regions responsible for learning from punishment, as compared to non-psychopathic violent offenders and non-offenders. Using fMRI scans, researchers found that psychopathic individuals had difficulty adapting their behavior in response to feedback and had noticeable abnormalities in their white and gray matter, particularly in areas associated with emotions like guilt, embarrassment, and moral reasoning. These findings suggest that psychopaths may not grasp punishment in the same way as others, which could explain why rehabilitation efforts often fail for this group. The researchers hope that understanding these neurological underpinnings of psychopathy could lead to the development of interventions during childhood, when psychopathic behavior emerges. They believe that targeted interventions could potentially reduce the rate of violent crime. The study highlights the differences between psychopathic offenders and regular criminals, with psychopaths being less responsive to threats, cold, and premeditated in their aggressive behavior, while regular criminals are more quick-tempered and aggressive in response to threats.

The Australian newspaper, the Herald Sun, published a controversial cartoon on Monday, two days after the US Open final, which portrayed tennis champion Serena Williams as an angry baby. The cartoon was criticized for its racist and sexist depiction of Williams, who received three code violations during her straight-sets loss to Naomi Osaka on Saturday.

Williams was given the first violation for coaching, which she argued against, stating, "I don't cheat to win — I'd rather lose." She was later given a violation for smashing her racket, costing her a point, and her third violation, for calling the umpire Carlos Ramos a "thief," cost her a game. Williams repeatedly demanded an apology from Ramos, arguing that male players weren't punished for similar or worse actions.

The cartoon, drawn by Mark Knight, shows Williams with grotesque features, including an oversized nose and lips, and pictured jumping up and down with a broken racket and a pacifier nearby, insinuating that Williams acted like a baby having a temper tantrum during the final. The cartoon also pictures Osaka in the background, where the umpire tells her, "Can you just let her win?"

The cartoon provoked an angry response on Twitter, with some users commenting on how Osaka appears to be portrayed as a white, blond woman in the drawing. One Twitter user said, "Regardless of the rights and wrongs of Williams' behavior, I really don't like that cartoon at all. Why is Naomi Osaka suddenly transformed into a white, blonde player? Why is Carlos Ramos white too? And why are Serena Williams' facial features distorted like that?"

Another Twitter user said, "Thank you for this cartoon. I will be sure to use it when I write about how Black women are treated and characterized for speaking up for themselves. The way you have drawn both women speaks volumes about who you are and how you feel about Black women. Shame."

The decision to reprimand Williams polarized the tennis industry and wider sporting press, especially after Williams claimed she had been treated differently than a male tennis player would have been. Billie Jean King, a US tennis great, suggested Williams had indeed identified a double standard in tennis.

J.K. Rowling, the author of the Harry Potter series, blasted the cartoon, saying, "Well done on reducing one of the greatest sportswomen alive to racist and sexist tropes and turning a second great sportswoman into a faceless prop." ESPN's Jemele Hill noted the racism is "About as subtle as Fran Drescher’s voice."

The US Open final was a polarizing event, with Williams losing to Osaka in straight sets, 6-2, 6-4. Headlines did not focus on Osaka's first major win, instead fixating on Williams' hat trick of code violations. The cartoon, while controversial, has brought attention to the treatment of Black women in sports and media.

Syrian Vice-President Farouk al-Sharaa is not in exile or under the protection of armed opposition groups, but is instead under house arrest. Despite rumors to the contrary, he remains active within the Syrian regime, maintaining communication with President Bashar al-Assad and a few other officials. His residence and movements are under heavy security, and he keeps in touch with members of the opposition and figures outside the regime.

Al-Sharaa has expressed concerns about the country's situation and criticizes certain decisions and actions, but does not publicly air his views in the media. He is a veteran of the regime and has his own opinions, having lived through an intense experience with the late Syrian President Hafez al-Assad.

Al-Sharaa is aware of the magnitude of changes in the Arab world and is capable of conducting self-criticism of the Baath party and the regime. He does not act outside his mandate, go over the president's head, or play behind his back. He mocks the media for the talk about his defection.

In the Syrian crisis, al-Sharaa differentiates between two opposition mobilizations. He believes that the drop in the number of peaceful protesters led to the rise in militants, and that the state should provide security to its citizens, but not decide on a military solution to the crisis. He acknowledges that there were mistakes made by the Arab League and the Syrian state, which cannot be forgotten or stepped over.

Al-Sharaa believes that Syria's problems have become complicated and require a Syrian-Syrian solution, with a dialogue aimed at solving the crisis politically from the start. However, he warns that things are not going in this direction, as the crisis has been Arabized, and Syria's membership in the League of Arab States was suspended without justification.

Al-Sharaa does not aspire to head any transitional government, but is concerned about Syria's future. He is a friend of the Russian people, admires China's development, and acknowledges Iran's support for the resistance in Lebanon. He believes that Iran could have played a bigger role in reaching an early political solution to the Syrian crisis.

The road to Damascus is marked by military and security checkpoints, cement barricades, and unaffordable bread queues. Farouk al-Sharaa sits in his home, which is under heavy security, and gives an account of the Syrian landscape since the first day of the crisis. He speaks about the regime and the party and state leadership, describes what is happening on the ground, and discusses the roles played by foreign powers against Syria and its historical role in the region.

Despite the ongoing crisis, al-Sharaa remains determined to play a role and propose a way out for Syria from the deepening crisis. He is a veteran Baathist and diplomat, known for his integrity and wisdom.

The article discusses the film "Queen of Earth," directed by Alex Ross Perry, and its premiere at the BAMcinemaFest. The film, which stars Elisabeth Moss, is described as a psychological thriller that explores the complex relationship between two women, Catherine and Virginia, and their emotional breakdowns. The film is compared to works by Ingmar Bergman, Woody Allen, John Cassavetes, and Rainer Werner Fassbinder, and is praised for its tense atmosphere and Moss's powerful performance. The article also mentions other films shown at the festival, including "The Invitation," "Nasty Baby," "Uncle Kent 2," and "Tangerine," and discusses the importance of the festival in showcasing independent films. The article concludes by describing the film as a disturbing and unsettling exploration of emotional pain and self-destruction.

Christopher Hitchens, a renowned journalist, author, and public intellectual, passed away on Thursday at the age of 62. He was a regular columnist at Slate, where he wrote the "Fighting Words" column since 2002. His colleagues and friends have shared tributes to honor his life and work.

June Thomas, Hitchens' editor at Slate, described editing him as the easiest job in journalism, noting his punctuality and ability to make his work seem effortless. Julian Barnes, a novelist, recalled a time when Hitchens did not respond to his first novel, attributing it to his high standards and busy schedule.

Jacob Weisberg, the Slate Group chairman, highlighted Hitchens' generosity towards young people, often going out of his way to help them, regardless of the potential benefits for himself. James Fenton, a poet and critic, shared memories of their friendship that began in Oxford in 1969.

Annette Gordon-Reed, a Harvard law professor, reminisced about a road trip they took together to Thomas Jefferson's mountaintop home, Monticello. Jonathan Karp, a publisher, praised Hitchens' writing skills, noting that he didn't require much editing and often came up with ideas in the shower.

Andrew Sullivan, a blogger, expressed his grief over Hitchens' passing, while David Corn, Washington bureau chief for Mother Jones, shared a story about how he came to envy Hitchens during their early careers. Anne Applebaum, a journalist, remembered Hitchens' unique use of language, while Fred Kaplan, an author and Slate columnist, shared memories of their first meeting in the early 1980s.

Hussein Ibish, a writer, highlighted Hitchens' personal generosity, noting that despite his confrontational public persona, he was kind and supportive to his friends. Victor Navasky, a former editor and publisher of The Nation, shared how he first invited Hitchens to contribute to the magazine in the late 1970s.

David Wolpe, a rabbi, shared a humorous anecdote about Hitchens' reaction to a review of his book on faith. Peter Pringle, an author, recalled covering the bloodless Portuguese revolution with Hitchens in 1974, while Craig Raine, a writer and founding editor of Arté, shared a story about a debate Hitchens participated in at the Oxford Union.

Anna Wintour, editor of Vogue, remembered hosting a book party for Gully Wells, where Hitchens, Amis, and Fenton reunited. Lee Siegel, a writer, reflected on Hitchens' unique personality, comparing him to a 19th-century figure.

David Sessions, a writer, compiled a list of Hitchens' best longreads, while Stephen Fry, a writer and actor, shared memories of their shared love for P.G. Wodehouse. The Daily Beast dedicated a section to Hitchens, featuring his greatest hits, tributes, and a final memoir that will be published early next year.

Hitchens' death was mourned by many, with Andrew Sullivan dedicating a portion of his blog to celebrating Hitchens' life and memories of their friendship. Hitchens' final memoir, titled "Mortality," will be released early next year.

Hiroo Onoda, a Japanese army officer who remained in hiding on Lubang Island in the Philippines for 29 years after World War II, passed away at the age of 91 in Tokyo. Onoda was one of the last holdouts from the war, having believed that the emperor was a deity and the war a sacred mission. He survived by foraging for food and sometimes killing villagers he assumed were enemies.

Onoda's homecoming in 1974 was met with a hero's welcome in Japan, where his ordeal was seen as a reminder of the redemptive qualities of duty and perseverance. His last order, to stay and fight, was given to him in early 1945, and he remained behind on Lubang Island when Japanese forces withdrew in the face of an American invasion.

Thousands of Japanese soldiers were scattered across China, Southeast Asia, and the Western Pacific after the war, with many going into hiding rather than surrendering or committing suicide. Onoda was found by Norio Suzuki, a student searching for him, in 1974. He officially declared dead in 1959, and his surrender was formalized by a delegation including his brother and former commander in 1974.

Onoda's story evoked waves of nostalgia and melancholy in Japan, with many seeing him as a symbol of traditional values. After his homecoming, he was examined by doctors, found in amazingly good condition, and given a military pension. He signed a $160,000 contract for a ghostwritten memoir, "No Surrender: My-Thirty Year War."

In his later years, Onoda moved to a Japanese colony in São Paulo, Brazil, where he raised cattle and married Machie Onuku, a Japanese tea-ceremony teacher. The couple returned to Japan in 1984 and founded the Onoda Nature School, a survival-skills youth camp. Onoda revisited Lubang in 1996 and gave $10,000 to a school there.

Onoda was born in Kainan, Wakayama, in central Japan in 1922. He joined the Japanese Army in 1942 and was trained in guerrilla warfare, philosophy, history, martial arts, propaganda, and covert operations. He was sent to Lubang Island in December 1944 to sabotage harbor installations and an airstrip to disrupt a coming American invasion.

Onoda's former commander, Maj. Yoshimi Taniguchi, returned to Lubang in 1974 to fulfill his promise to come back for Onoda, and relieved him of duty. Onoda saluted and wept, marking the end of his 30-year war. Onoda's death was announced by the Japanese government, who praised his strong will to live and indomitable spirit.

In this article, it is reported that Donald Trump has handed in his personal Android phone and received a new, secure phone approved by the Secret Service ahead of his inauguration. The new phone has a new number known only to a limited number of people, and it is expected that Trump's Twitter account may still be operated from another phone. The phone's limitations include the inability to make phone calls, as they can be easily intercepted. This marks a change for Trump, who is known for frequently using his phone to communicate with friends, business contacts, reporters, foreign leaders, and politicians. The Secret Service declined to comment for the story.

The article also notes that Barack Obama was the first president to use a mobile device approved by security agencies due to hacking concerns. Obama initially used a heavily modified BlackBerry, and later switched to a phone with most features disabled. He was not known to use the phone for making or receiving calls, but it was one of few devices that had access to the @POTUS Twitter account. Trump has said that he will continue to use his existing Twitter account in addition to the @POTUS account.

The article also mentions that the Trump presidency may have implications for the tech industry, with some people saying it may not be as bad as some think, while others find his potential influence on the industry "alarming." The article also mentions a separate story about the challenges faced by the Trump transition team in filling key administration posts. The team was still scrambling to fill key positions when Trump arrived in Washington, and as of Thursday, only two of his 15 cabinet nominees had been approved by congressional committees. The article also notes that Trump has traded in his Android phone for a secure, encrypted device approved by the Secret Service with a new number that few people possess.

The renewed #OscarsSoWhite controversy erupted again this week as the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences' members nominated exclusively white actors in the top acting categories for a second consecutive year. In response, director John Singleton defended the Academy, stating that Oscar nominations are subjective honors and not necessarily a reflection of a film's quality. Singleton, who became the first African-American to earn a Best Director nomination for 1991's Boyz 'N The Hood, suggested that the nominations are like a lottery and that every year there are films that don't get nominated but are later elevated over time.

Cheryl Boone Isaacs, president of the Academy, issued a lengthy statement on the lack of diversity in this year's Oscar nominations, expressing her heartbreak and frustration over the exclusion of performers of color. Boone Isaacs announced that the Academy is taking dramatic steps to alter the makeup of its membership and is conducting a review of its membership recruitment to bring about much-needed diversity in the 2016 class and beyond.

Director Spike Lee and actress Jada Pinkett Smith have vowed to boycott the Oscars, with Lee writing on Instagram that "how is it possible for the [second] consecutive year all 20 contenders in the acting category are white?" Pinkett Smith, wife of "Concussion" actor Will Smith, said in a Facebook video that the academy has the right to acknowledge and invite whomever it chooses, but leaving black actors "begging for acknowledgment" diminishes the community.

Straight Outta Compton producer Will Packer called the lack of nominations for people of color a "complete embarrassment," while the Rev. Al Sharpton blasted Hollywood for perpetuating a "fraudulent image of of progressive liberal politics and policies." Despite defending the Academy, Singleton told Variety there was one film he hoped would earn a nomination that ultimately did not: Straight Outta Compton. He added that Jason Mitchell, who played Eazy-E in the NWA biopic, should have been nominated for Best Supporting Actor.

Boone Isaacs' statement promising "dramatic steps" to increase diversity was met with a range of reactions, from skepticism that the Academy could make real changes to enthusiasm over the idea of diversity as a true Oscars priority. Many members applauded Isaacs' comments, with some expressing the opinion that the problem lies in the makeup of the Academy and the broader Hollywood industry. Others were skeptical of the Academy's ability to truly change its biases, questioning whether an organization the size of the Academy could be significantly altered just through an influx of new members. Some suggested that any real Academy makeover would have to also include purging the voting rolls of older members who have not worked in the movie industry in years or even decades.

Ivanka Trump, the daughter of President Donald Trump, is setting up a formal role in the White House without being officially employed. She will work out of a West Wing office, have access to classified information, and receive government-issued communications devices. Her attorney, Jamie Gorelick, stated that Ivanka Trump will follow ethics rules that apply to government employees, despite not holding an official title. This move has raised questions about potential conflicts of interest, as Ivanka Trump still owns her fashion and jewelry brand. She has handed daily management to the company president and set up a trust to provide further oversight. The business cannot make deals with any foreign state, and the trustees will confer with Gorelick over any new agreements. Ivanka Trump will also be able to veto proposed new transactions. She has barred the business from using her image to promote the products in advertising or marketing. Ivanka Trump's role in the White House has come under scrutiny due to the lack of precedent for a family member with such influence. The arrangement has been signed off on by the White House counsel's office, and the conflict issues were "worked through" with the Office of Government Ethics. However, ethics watchdogs question whether Ivanka Trump is going far enough to eliminate conflicts of interest. The arrangement has raised questions about why Ivanka Trump can't simply join the administration as a government employee. Ivanka Trump will also be donating the royalties and net proceeds from her upcoming book, "Women Who Work," to charities that focus on women in the workforce.

A school teacher named Kristin Westra, who works on Chebeague Island, has been reported missing from North Yarmouth. The community is deeply affected by her disappearance as she is well-known and loved by many. Westra teaches third through fifth grades at the island's school, which is currently under renovation. The search for Westra has involved local authorities, including firefighters, and the community has come together to support each other during this difficult time. A body was found less than half a mile from Westra's home on Friday, and while the identity has not been confirmed, her husband posted on Facebook expressing his grief. It is believed that Westra was experiencing anxiety and stress before her disappearance, and she had planned to seek help and return to her usual activities. A candlelight vigil was planned for Westra at the Congregational Church in Cumberland, but its status is unclear as of Friday afternoon. Meanwhile, the Senate has confirmed Brett Kavanaugh as the next Supreme Court justice, despite protests and controversy during the confirmation process. The vote was not smooth, with protesters interrupting the vote and causing brief upsets. Kavanaugh was sworn in by retired Justice Anthony Kennedy and current Supreme Court Judge John Roberts. President Donald Trump congratulated the Senate and Kavanaugh on Twitter.

In Eloy, Arizona, two skydivers were killed and one was injured in a mid-air collision on Tuesday afternoon during a week-long event at Skydive Arizona. The collision occurred approximately 200 feet from the ground, causing the skydivers' parachutes to collapse. One person died at the scene, another at a nearby hospital, and the third was flown to Maricopa Medical Center in Phoenix for treatment. The identities of the deceased have not been disclosed. Witnesses reported that both skydivers had open canopies when they collided, and their parachutes collapsed thereafter. The cause of the collision is under investigation, and authorities are interviewing witnesses throughout the night. Skydive Arizona, located near Eloy Municipal Airport, is the largest drop zone in the world for skydivers of all skill levels. The facility was recently the site of an all-female mass-formation jump attempt. Further updates will be provided by ABC15.

On caucus night in Iowa, several key factors will determine the outcome of the Republican presidential race. Mitt Romney, the frontrunner, is expected to perform well, but a win or a close second place is crucial for him to dispel lingering doubts about his ability to win over the Republican base. Turnout will play a significant role, with Romney and Ron Paul having the resources to turn out their supporters, while Rick Santorum is relying on momentum and the 2008 Mike Huckabee coalition. The weather could also favor Paul, as his supporters are generally seen as more motivated. A high turnout is expected to favor Romney, while a lower turnout would benefit Paul and Santorum. The caucuses in 2008 saw a turnout of just under 120,000, and anything less than that bar will add to the sense of restlessness about the field. The race has been tight, with Santorum, Paul, and Romney in a dead heat, according to the latest polls. The candidates have been campaigning intensely in the final days before the caucuses, with Romney, Paul, Santorum, Michele Bachmann, Rick Perry, and Newt Gingrich making their final pitches to voters. The caucuses will take place in 1,774 precincts across the state, and each voter will cast their ballot after listening to speeches from fellow precinct members on behalf of their favored candidates. The results of the caucuses will provide the first indication of which candidates have the momentum to continue in the race for the Republican nomination.

A Wisconsin federal judge has granted a temporary restraining order preventing the enforcement of a new abortion law in the state. The law, signed by Governor Scott Walker on Friday, requires doctors performing abortions to have admitting privileges to hospitals within 30 minutes of their practice. Planned Parenthood of Wisconsin filed a lawsuit against the law, alleging it is unconstitutional and treats doctors who perform abortions differently from doctors who perform other types of medical procedures.

U.S. District Judge William Conley granted the hold on Monday, citing a "troubling lack of justification" for the law and stating that the U.S. Supreme Court places the burden upon states to show such laws are "reasonably directed to the preservation of maternal health." Conley added that the record to date strongly supports a finding that no medical purpose is served by the requirement.

On July 18, 2015, a tragic accident occurred in Cutchogue, New York, when an alleged drunken driver, Steven Romeo, plowed his pickup truck into a limousine, killing four young women and injuring several others. The victims, all aged 23-24, were residents of Smithtown and were celebrating a major event in one of their friend's lives.

The limo, hired from Ultimate Class Limousine, was making a U-turn on Route 48 and Depot Lane when Romeo's pickup truck broadsided its right side. The crash took the lives of Brittney Schulman, Lauren Baruch, Stephanie Belli, and Amy Grabina. Three of the victims died at the scene, and the fourth died at Peconic Bay Medical Center.

Four additional passengers – Joelle Dimonti, Melissa Crai, Alicia Arundel, and Olga Lipets – survived the crash, along with the limo driver, Carlos Pino. Pino was treated for non-life-threatening injuries at a Suffolk County hospital.

The crash scene was devastating, with witnesses describing bodies hanging out of the limousine. The intersection where the accident occurred has been a concern for residents due to the convergence of vineyard-bound limousines making U-turns amid oncoming traffic on the rural road.

Steven Romeo, co-owner of Romeo Dimon Marine Service in Southold, was charged with DWI, a misdemeanor, but ordered held on $500,000 cash bail or $1 million bond. He pleaded not guilty at his arraignment at Eastern Long Island Hospital in Greenport, where he was admitted after the wreck.

Additional charges are expected in the case, as investigators continue to look into the incident. The Southold businessman was previously involved in a fatal accident in January 2014 at a construction site in Mattituck, where a worker was killed by a bucket that fell off a skid-steer loader being operated by Romeo.

The victims were described as vibrant and accomplished. Amy Grabina was a "die-hard" Boston Red Sox fan. Stephanie Belli had studied business at Farmingdale State College. Lauren Baruch was "unafraid to be the only one on the dance floor." Brittney Schulman graduated from SUNY Cortland last year and wanted to work in public relations in the fashion industry.

The limo picked up the women at Baruch's home, her father said. Some of their cars remained at the home, Steven Baruch said. The crash was the second multi-fatal wreck on Long Island in a week. Three members of a Queens family died July 12 when their car was rear-ended by an alleged drunken driver on the Southern State Parkway at the exit for Robert Moses Causeway.

The Cutchogue intersection where the limousine crash occurred has long been a worry to residents because of the convergence of vineyard-bound limousines making U-turns amid oncoming traffic on the rural road. It was not known if the limo cut in front of the truck, Southold Police Chief Martin Flatley said.

Flower bouquets had been placed in the roadway median at the crash site Sunday. People who live near the intersection said it’s a frequent spot for crashes. Ruth Urwand, who lives on Depot Lane, said she believes a regular stoplight should replace the blinking light that’s currently there.

The crash has led to an outpouring of grief and support from friends and family of the victims on social media. The Southold businessman was previously involved in a fatal accident in January 2014 at a construction site in Mattituck, where a 30-year-old worker was struck in the head and killed by a bucket that fell off of a skid-steer loader being operated by Mr. Romeo. He was not charged in that incident, but the U.S. Department of Labor’s Occupational Safety and Health Administration issued citations and fined the business, in part because Mr. Romeo had not been trained to use the equipment he was operating. A wrongful death suit filed by the worker’s family against Romeo Dimon Marine and the owner of the construction site is pending in New York State Supreme Court.

In a significant archaeological discovery, skeletons unearthed during excavations for the Crossrail project in London have been identified as victims of the Black Death, a plague pandemic that occurred in the 14th century. The remains, dating back to 1348-1350, were found in Charterhouse Square near the Barbican, solving a 660-year-old mystery about the location of a mass grave for plague victims.

The discovery was confirmed through forensic tests revealing traces of the DNA of the plague bacterium Yersinia pestis in the teeth of at least four skeletons. Archaeologists plan to expand their search for more victims across Charterhouse Square, using ground-penetrating radar to detect signs of additional graves.

The Black Death, also known as the Great Pestilence, swept across Europe between 1347 and 1351, killing millions of people. It arrived in Britain in 1348 and is believed to have wiped out up to 60% of the population at the time. In London, two emergency burial grounds were dug outside the city walls, with one already found at East Smithfield and the other believed to be under Charterhouse Square.

The skeletons provide a rare opportunity to study the medieval population of London, offering insights into their lives, diet, health, and social structure. Preliminary analysis shows that many of the skeletons suffered from malnutrition, rickets, and back injuries indicative of heavy manual labor. The later skeletons from the 1400s had a high rate of upper body injuries, suggesting they were involved in violent altercations.

Further studies aim to sequence the ancient bacterial DNA found in the teeth to understand how the plague has evolved and spread over the centuries. The £14.8bn Crossrail project, which aims to establish a 118km-long rail link with 37 stations across London, is due to open in 2018. The excavations have already uncovered Roman skulls, a Bronze-Age transport route, and the largest piece of amber ever found in the UK.

The findings will be featured in a Channel 4 documentary, "Return of the Black Death: Secret History," airing on April 6, 2014. The discovery not only sheds light on the devastating impact of the Black Death but also offers valuable insights into the lives of medieval Londoners.

The World Health Organization and the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention are assisting in the response to the outbreak. The virus is highly infectious and can be spread through direct contact with bodily fluids. Symptoms can include fever, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, headache, a measles-like rash, red eyes, and bleeding from body openings. The first victim of the outbreak was a 3-month-old girl, and at least 11 of those who attended her funeral have since died. Funerals in Uganda are typically elaborate affairs that draw huge crowds, and the government has urged people to avoid unnecessary contact with each other and discouraged handshakes. The Ugandan Ministry of Health has declared the outbreak in Kibaale district and identified the disease as the Sudan strain of Ebola hemorrhagic fever.

Archaeologists from the University of Southampton have discovered what may be one of the largest medieval royal palaces ever found, buried under the ground inside a vast prehistoric fortress at Old Sarum in Wiltshire, England. The probable 12th century palace was discovered using geophysical ground-penetrating 'x-ray' technology to map a long-vanished medieval city which has lain under grass on the site for more than 700 years.

The Old Sarum geophysical survey revealed the buried foundations of dozens of ordinary houses and a vast mystery complex that is likely to have been a huge royal palace. The 170 metre long, 65 metre wide complex, arranged around a large courtyard, had walls up to 3 metres thick and included a 60 metre long probable great hall, what appears to have been a substantial tower, and multi-story buildings with upper floors almost certainly supported by substantial columns.

Dr Edward Impey, Director-General of the Royal Armouries, said the location, design, and size of the courtyarded complex strongly suggest that it was a palace, probably a royal one. The prime candidate for constructing it is perhaps Henry I sometime in the early 12th century.

This is a discovery of immense importance, as it reveals the monumental scale of building work taking place in the earlier 12th century. The city was largely abandoned up to 140 years after most of it had been built, and because it has remained a green field site ever since, it is giving academics a unique opportunity to study a Norman city.

The construction of the Norman city of Old Sarum, including a spectacular cathedral, was symbolic of a large-scale monumental building trend which was taking place around the country in the late 11th century. However, by the early 13th century, the political and diocesan centre at Old Sarum was proving too cramped and exposed to the elements and was therefore moved, lock, stock and barrel, to a totally new location, Salisbury, two and a half miles to the south.

The latest scanning techniques were used to uncover a network of buildings at the 11th Century Old Sarum near Salisbury, Wiltshire. The results include a series of large structures, possibly defences, with open areas of ground behind possibly for mustering resources or people. Old Sarum was the original site of Salisbury, which is two miles away.

The techniques used to survey the land included magnetometry, earth resistance, ground penetrating radar, and electric resistivity tomography, which uses electrodes to probe underground. These new approaches are "exciting and innovative," according to Neil Holbrook from Cotswold Archaeology, and "could be applied pretty much anywhere."

The survey adds a whole new dimension to our understanding of a site which we thought we knew. In fact, there is so much more to be found out," he added. The plan shows for the first time just how much other activity there was around the castle and cathedral which have long been known. It sets those monuments within the context of a bustling, vibrant town established shortly after the Norman conquest.
