Slaughter was the first woman to chair the House Rules Committee and served her 16th term in Congress. She was known for her work in securing infrastructure money for her district, fighting for the troops, and setting safety standards for military body armor. Slaughter was born in Kentucky and had a degree in microbiology. She entered politics in the 1970s and served in various roles before being elected to the House of Representatives in 1986. She was the longest-serving member of Congress from New York and was currently hospitalized after falling at her Washington, D.C., residence last week. Her office confirmed that she was in stable condition. Dr. James Maxwell, a neurosurgeon at St. Mary's and Rochester General hospitals, is seeking the Republican nomination to challenge Slaughter in November's race. House Democratic Leader Nancy Pelosi and other top Democrats expressed their condolences for Slaughter's passing. Slaughter's chief of staff, Liam Fitzsimmons, released a statement praising her as a "force of nature" and a "relentless advocate for Western New York."

China, which produces 95% of the world's rare earth minerals, has been under scrutiny for its tight export quotas that have caused global prices to soar. The embargo on shipments, which affected Japan more than the US or Europe, was lifted only hours before Secretary of State Hillary Clinton raised the issue during a news conference in Honolulu. The embargo, which was initially only on shipments with a rare earth content of about 50% or more, has created a big incentive for companies to move factories to China due to the high cost of quotas. The cost of neodymium, a rare earth used in technologies like wind turbines, gasoline-electric cars, and Apple iPhones, has doubled outside China due to the export restrictions. Japan, the biggest importer of raw rare earths, has been affected more by China's tightening quotas as it tends to process them into industrial materials. The embargo was one of several measures China took in response to Japan detaining a Chinese fishing trawler captain. The exact interaction between American policy decisions and Chinese customs enforcement actions is unclear.

The story, published in Forbes on December 12, 2017, discusses the controversy surrounding Wilbur Ross, the United States Secretary of Commerce, and his net worth. Ross, who was appointed by President Donald Trump, has been under scrutiny for his reportedly inflated net worth and questionable financial dealings.

In 2017, Forbes planned to remove Ross from their list of the 400 wealthiest Americans due to his inability to provide documentation for assets he claimed were worth over $2 billion. Ross initially claimed these assets were held in trust and were not required to be disclosed in his federal filings. However, when asked for documentation, he cited privacy issues and eventually agreed to be removed from the list if the reason was that the assets were in trust.

Ross's net worth has been a subject of controversy since 2004, with allegations that he has padded his ego and business opportunities by misleading Forbes. Ten former employees of Ross's private equity firm, WL Ross & Co., have confirmed parts of the same story line, stating that Ross's penchant for misleading extended to colleagues and investors, resulting in millions of dollars in fines, tens of millions refunded to backers, and numerous lawsuits.

Additionally, six U.S. senators have stated that Ross failed to initially mention 19 lawsuits in response to a questionnaire during his confirmation process. In response to questions sent nearly a week before the article's publication, Ross and his team at the Commerce Department stated that Ross had filed all required disclosures in accordance with the law.

The article also provides a detailed account of Ross's career, including his early years at Rothschild, his founding of WL Ross & Co., and his significant financial successes, particularly in the steel industry. The article suggests that Ross's tactics, including potentially misleading statements during his confirmation hearings, are not new and are consistent with his behavior over the past few decades.

The story also mentions Trump's defense of appointing a billionaire like Ross to promote economic growth and his comments on the wealth of his administration. Trump stated that he does not want poor people to hold economic roles in his administration and that Ross and White House economic adviser Gary Cohn "had to give up a lot to take these jobs." Trump added that Cohn "went from massive pay days to peanuts."

The article ends with a quote from Trump, stating, "If you insist, I’ll do it. But I like it better this way, right?" This quote is in reference to Ross's appointment as Secretary of Commerce, suggesting that Ross may have been appointed due to his wealth and influence rather than his qualifications for the position.

The three-part miniseries "Super Cats" premieres on PBS from October 24 to November 7, with each episode available to stream the following day on PBS.org and PBS apps. The series, narrated by F. Murray Abraham, explores the secret lives of big cats across the globe, using the latest camera technology and scientific research.

Filmed over 600 days in 14 countries, the series features 31 species of cat, including the solitary snow leopard in the Himalayas, the elusive swamp tiger of South Asia, and the Californian bobcat, which is blind in one eye. The miniseries uncovers the social sides, complex communication, devoted parental care, courtship rituals, hunting patterns, and more of these charismatic and misunderstood animals.

Advances in technology allowed for several on-camera firsts, such as the nocturnal pursuits of a black-footed cat in South Africa, which hunts more in one night than a leopard does in six months. Remote cameras capture intimate moments between a mother Pallas' cat and her kittens, and low-light technology exposes a rare puma preying on Magellanic penguins. A swamp tiger takes a bath in the sea, a phenomenon previously unseen on television.

The production team includes Gavin Boyland, Stuart Dunn, Zubin Sarosh, Simon Enderby, Sue Gibson, David Loughedo, José Luis Rouco Fernandez, Kalyan Varma, Visual Air Productions, Nick Allinson, Ellie Williams, Nick Carline, Gillian Taylor, Jack Roberts, Doghouse Post Production, Wounded Buffalo, BDH Creative, Jonny Crew, Ben Peace, Fred Tay, Michael Lansdell, Bleeding Fingers, Monica Sonand, Russell Emanuel, Alexander Sliwa, Luke Hunter, Tatjana Hubel, Sabah Parks Department, Le Parc des Felins, University of Muhammadiyah, Palangka Raya, Borneo Nature Foundation, Shanshui/Panthera/SLT/SEEF/GZC, Junta de Andalucía, Junta de Extremadura, Ministry of Environment and Forests, India, and many others.

Episode 3, titled "Science and Secrets," premieres on November 7 at 8 p.m. on PBS (check local listings). The miniseries aims to shed light on the diverse and successful predators that are often misunderstood, revealing their behaviors captured on film for the first time.

In the past 72 hours, there has been a significant increase in overdose cases on Chicago's West Side, with over 74 cases reported, more than double the rate from the same period last year. The Chicago Fire Department and Chicago Police Department are investigating the spike, suspecting that the illegal drug, possibly heroin, may be laced with the powerful painkiller fentanyl.

Authorities recovered a sample of heroin that may contain fentanyl from two West Side locations. The Chicago Department of Public Health reported more than 20 overdose cases in just 24 hours. Some of the overdose victims were found with needles still in their arms.

The overdose victims were treated with Narcan, a heroin antidote, but required additional doses upon arrival at hospitals. The Chicago Recovery Alliance, which helps drug users, urged caution and advised having Narcan on hand.

Fentanyl-laced heroin has been causing overdoses across the nation, leading to a nationwide health alert issued by the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) in March. The last major outbreak of fentanyl-related deaths occurred between 2005 and 2007, killing over 1,000 people across the country, including dozens in the Chicago area.

The Chicago Department of Public Health is working closely with area hospitals to ensure they have necessary medication supplies, including Narcan, and are tracking individuals affected by the overdoses. The DEA is also trying to trace the source of the potent heroin.

The increase in heroin overdose deaths has been on the rise statewide since 2011, with 633 heroin overdose deaths occurring in Illinois last year, up from 583 in 2013. A recent report found that the Chicago area is racking up more heroin-related emergency room visits than any other metro area in the country, compounded by a decrease in state-funded drug treatment.

Government officials have been paying increasing attention to Illinois' heroin crisis, with lawmakers proposing numerous measures aimed at addressing the problem. The Chicago Tribune and The Washington Post contributed to this report.

A California man, Rodney Harmon, has filed a federal class-action lawsuit against Hilton Hotels Corporation, alleging deceptive practices regarding a 75-cent charge for a newspaper he did not request during his stay at the Hilton Garden Inn Sonoma County Airport. Harmon claims that the charge was hidden in small print on the sleeve of his room key, and that the practice is wasteful and harmful to the environment. The lawsuit asserts that millions of guests have been affected by this alleged deception, and could have significant implications if it sets a precedent for similar lawsuits against other hotel chains. Hilton has not yet responded to the lawsuit. Harmon's attorney, Kirk J. Wolden, believes that the case exemplifies the ways in which companies take advantage of consumers every day. The lawsuit also notes the decline in newspaper readership and circulation, and the environmental impact of wasted papers.

This summary provides an account of two distinct but related stories. The first story revolves around Margot Wölk, a young woman who was forced to taste Adolf Hitler's food during World War II as part of a group of 15 young women. Wölk, who had fled from her bombed-out Berlin apartment to her mother-in-law's home in Gross-Partsch, Poland, was recruited by the SS to taste the food prepared for Hitler's Eastern Front headquarters, the Wolf's Lair. The food was good but the women could not enjoy it due to the fear of poisoning and the knowledge that Hitler was a man they despised. Wölk was trapped at the Wolf's Lair, rousted from bed each morning by the SS, and never saw Hitler.

The second story is about Hyde Park, a farm purchased by a Richmond department store owner during World War II to shelter Jews escaping Nazi Germany. The farm, which was devoted to dairy and poultry operations, served as a training farm for students who sought to escape Adolf Hitler's extermination of Jews. About 30 Jewish immigrants lived and worked at Hyde Farmlands from 1938 to 1941, many of whom later went on to fight for the U.S.

Both stories highlight the struggles and hardships faced by individuals during World War II, with the first story focusing on the personal experiences of Margot Wölk and the second story focusing on the efforts of a department store owner to provide a safe haven for Jewish immigrants.

The article discusses two main topics: deliberate forgetting and the 9/11 attacks investigation.

Regarding deliberate forgetting, the article explains that until recently, there was little scientific evidence that people could intentionally influence their rates of forgetting. However, recent studies have shown that under certain conditions, people can deliberately forget things. The study by Jeremy Manning and Kenneth Norman suggests that we forget things by discarding the mental context within which those memories were first learned. The brain that attempts to remember keeps active the mental context, while the brain that tries to forget discards that context, letting go of the mental scaffolding that supported the construction of those memories.

The article also discusses the implications of this research on our daily lives, such as how we now tend to photograph important moments instead of experiencing them first-hand, which can lead to thinner and less truthful recollections.

The second topic is the investigation into the 9/11 attacks. The leaders of the independent commission that investigated the 9/11 attacks, former Governor Tom Kean of New Jersey and former Representative Lee Hamilton of Indiana, have weighed in again as the Obama administration prepares to make public at least some of the 28 pages from a separate, earlier investigation by a congressional panel that examined possible Saudi government involvement in the attacks. The pages have been kept secret since 2002. The two men stress that the 28 pages were based mostly on raw, unvetted material from the F.B.I. and should be evaluated with caution. They also emphasized that their commission investigated all leads in the 28 pages and only one Saudi government employee was implicated in the plot.

In conclusion, the article discusses the ability to deliberately forget things and the implications of this research on our daily lives, as well as the investigation into the 9/11 attacks and the upcoming release of the 28 classified pages.

Congress has moved to block President Obama's plan to shift control of the U.S. drone campaign from the CIA to the Defense Department, inserting a secret provision in the massive government spending bill that preserves the spy agency's role in lethal counterterrorism operations. The provision, included in a classified annex to the $1.1 trillion federal budget plan, restricts the use of any funding to transfer unmanned aircraft or the authority to carry out drone strikes from the CIA to the Pentagon.

The move reflects lawmakers' lingering doubts about the U.S. military's ability to conduct strikes against al-Qaeda and its regional affiliates without hitting the wrong targets and killing civilians. These apprehensions were amplified after a U.S. military strike in Yemen last month killed a dozen people, including as many as six civilians, in an 11-vehicle convoy that tribal leaders said was part of a wedding procession. U.S. officials said that the strike was aimed at a senior al-Qaeda operative but that reviews of the operation have raised concern that it failed to comply with White House guidelines requiring "near certainty" that no civilians would be harmed.

Senior lawmakers have been vocal in expressing concern about the prospect of the CIA ceding responsibility for drone strikes to the military. Sen. Dianne Feinstein (D-Calif.), the chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee and a member of the Appropriations Committee, said last year that she had seen the CIA "exercise patience and discretion specifically to prevent collateral damage" and that she "would really have to be convinced that the military would carry it out that well."

The spending bill sets budgets for agencies across the federal government for the fiscal year that ends Sept. 30. The measure cleared the House late Wednesday and is expected to be approved by the Senate this week and delivered to President Obama for his signature as soon as Saturday. The move by Congress carries implications for the course of the U.S. efforts against al-Qaeda at a time when its affiliates in Yemen, Somalia, Iraq, and Syria have become more worrisome to American counterterrorism officials than the terrorist organization's traditional core.

The administration first signaled its intent to shift control of drone operations to the Pentagon last year, when Obama announced new guidelines for counterterrorism missions, including a pledge of greater transparency, during a speech at the National Defense University. The overall pace of strikes has diminished significantly in Pakistan and Yemen, and CIA Director John O. Brennan has held secret meetings with Pentagon officials in recent months to work out logistical challenges and other impediments to shifting control of drone operations. However, the CIA still carries out the majority of strikes, and the collateral damage that has accompanied some JSOC strikes has generated growing opposition to removing the agency from such operations anytime soon.

The Pentagon has refused to release any details on the Dec. 12 strike carried out by JSOC in Radaa, a district that has become a stronghold for al-Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula, or AQAP. Yemen initially insisted that only militants had been killed, but it later acknowledged civilian casualties. The government then delivered rifles and other compensation to victims' families, payments that a Yemeni official described as a "deposit" to encourage clan leaders to take part in tribal mediation and accept further compensation rather than seek retaliation against the Sanaa government.

AQAP is responsible for near-miss attacks on the United States, including the attempted bombing of a Detroit-bound airliner on Christmas Day in 2009. The terrorist group has been driven out of territory it had gained over the past two years but is still considered by U.S. officials to pose a serious threat to the United States. In a meeting with U.S., European, and Middle Eastern diplomats last week, Yemeni President Abed Rabbo Mansour Hadi described the security situation as unstable and warned specifically of indications that potential al-Qaeda recruits from European and other Western nations were seeking to enter the country.

The Pennsylvania State Employees' Retirement System (SERS) announced on Wednesday that it will revoke Jerry Sandusky's $59,000 annual pension, following his conviction and sentence for child sexual abuse. Sandusky, a former Penn State University assistant football coach, was sentenced to at least 30 years in prison for molesting 10 boys.

Sandusky's lawyer, Karl Rominger, contends that SERS has no legal grounds for revoking the pension and plans to fight any attempt to do so. The retirement system determined that two of the criminal charges Sandusky was convicted of, involuntary deviate sexual intercourse and indecent assault, fall under the forfeiture law.

The forfeiture statute permits an employee to keep their contributions without interest, minus any fees or restitution associated with their conviction. Employees subject to forfeiture can appeal to the board of the State Employees' Retirement System, then through the state court system.

Sandusky entered the State Employees' Retirement System when he began working as a Penn State football coach in 1969. He collected a $148,000 lump sum payment when he retired from the university in 1999 and began receiving a monthly annuity. Between 1999 and September 2012, Sandusky received a total of $900,000 in pension payments.

In letters to the judge who sentenced Sandusky, the Sanduskys portrayed themselves as virtuous victims of a vast conspiracy, blaming powerful, image-conscious forces at Penn State University, lying cops, ambitious prosecutors, and a scandal-hungry news media. However, their letters were widely criticized by legal observers as shifting the blame to others and belittling the victims or the court.

Sandusky's adopted son, Matt, also claimed that Sandusky had molested him, which contributed to Sandusky's conviction. Matt Sandusky did not testify for either side in the trial.

In response to an open-records request, SERS released a letter to Sandusky notifying him that his crimes triggered forfeiture of his pension, and informing his wife, Dottie, that she is no longer entitled to a survivor's benefit. Sandusky's lawyer, Karl Rominger, argued that since Sandusky wasn't convicted of molesting a Penn State student, the forfeiture law does not apply to him. However, Philadelphia attorney Alaine Williams, an expert on public employee labor law, said courts have broadly construed the forfeiture law.

In addition to the pension forfeiture, Sandusky is also facing civil lawsuits from several of his victims. The Sanduskys' letters to the judge who sentenced Sandusky were mentioned in court but not read aloud. The letters were later made public and criticized by legal observers for shifting the blame to others and belittling the victims or the court.

The Transportation Security Administration (TSA) is exploring the possibility of offering its expedited screening program, TSA PreCheck, at no cost to frequent flyers as a solution to its growing budget costs and long airport lines. A study by researchers at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign suggests that waiving the $85 enrollment fee for high-volume travelers would result in annual savings of $34 million for the TSA. The study found that if 25 million travelers taking at least six trips a year were to use the TSA PreCheck lines, the savings would total $459 million a year, thanks to lower staff expenses and equipment costs. The TSA has not yet commented on the study, but the lead author of the study, Sheldon H. Jacobson, said the TSA asked for a copy of the study on Monday. The benefits of offering TSA PreCheck at no cost to frequent fliers include reduced lines at the airport, increased security, and savings for the TSA. However, some bad feelings might arise among travelers who are not frequent fliers and are not offered the fee waiver, and frequent fliers who are now paying the $85 fee may be upset when TSA PreCheck is suddenly offered free to new passengers.

The death of 15-year-old Steven Rosenthal, a Crane High School basketball player, has sparked controversy and protests in Chicago. On August 19, 2018, Rosenthal died of a self-inflicted gunshot wound to the head, according to official accounts. However, his family and community members have expressed skepticism about the police's account of his death, claiming that he was shot by officers during a chase.

On Sunday, over 120 people gathered at Johnson School of Excellence to protest Rosenthal's death. The crowd marched to Mount Sinai Hospital and later to CPD's 10th district headquarters, chanting "justice for Steve" and demanding the release of any footage or evidence related to the incident. The family's lawyer, Andrew Stroth, called for an independent investigation and insisted that eyewitnesses saw Rosenthal's death play out differently.

Chicago police have stated that there is no evidence that any officer fired a weapon during the encounter with Rosenthal. They also said no footage had been found that depicts the moment Rosenthal was shot, and it's unclear if state law would allow the public release of the existing footage. Rosenthal died a half-hour later at Mount Sinai Hospital.

Alonzo Crowder, head coach of boys basketball at Crane Medical Prep High School, said Rosenthal's mother died of an illness shortly after the season ended in March. Rosenthal's father died when he was 6. Still, neighbors and friends say the authorities’ account of Rosenthal shooting himself while running from police was out of character.

The Chicago Police Department has called Rosenthal's death "an absolute tragedy" and expressed condolences to the family. However, the family and activists are demanding answers and a full, independent, and transparent investigation into Rosenthal's death. They have not been able to view his remains or the evidence related to the case. The shooting remains under investigation, and the department has not yet decided to release the body cam video.

The document discusses a study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, which investigates the effects of reading from electronic devices before bedtime on sleep patterns. The study, conducted at Brigham and Women's Hospital in Boston, involved 12 participants who read either an iPad or a book for four hours each night before sleep for five consecutive nights. The researchers found that participants using iPads displayed reduced levels of melatonin, a hormone that helps induce sleepiness, took longer to fall asleep, and spent less time in restorative REM sleep. Additionally, iPad readers reported being sleepier and less alert the following morning, even after eight hours of sleep, and displayed delayed circadian rhythms.

The study suggests that the blue light emitted by electronic devices could be causing more profound sleep disruptions than previously thought. The researchers noted that other products, such as tablets, smartphones, laptops, and LED monitors, also produce similar blue-light emissions. While the standard Kindle e-reader was an exception, as it doesn't emit light, it was more akin to a printed book.

The researchers expressed concern about the long-term health consequences of chronic sleep loss caused by electronic devices, as suppression of melatonin has been linked to increased risk of prostate, colorectal, and breast cancers, and a persistent lack of sleep has been associated with obesity and diabetes. The study highlights the need for rethinking the safety and efficacy of electronic devices, as they do not require health studies on their impact like drugs do.

The study also provides insights into the sleep-disrupting effects of electronic devices on older teens, who are more likely to use them at night than younger children, even when an early school morning looms. The National Sleep Foundation's poll earlier this year revealed that nearly 90 percent of adults and 75 percent of children reported having at least one electronic device in their bedrooms. The study's findings underscore the importance of limiting electronic device use before bedtime to improve sleep quality and potentially reduce long-term health risks.

A 15-year-old girl who had been missing for over two years was rescued from a home in Washington Park, Illinois, where she claimed she was held captive and repeatedly sexually assaulted. The girl reported that she was raped, became pregnant, and gave birth to a child. The girl managed to escape this week with the help of a relative and went to the police, who then raided the house and arrested a 24-year-old man and his mother. The man's mother is suspected of aiding in the crimes, but neither she nor the man have been officially charged. The girl told police that she was held against her will, beaten, and sexually assaulted almost every day, and that her captor chased her down each time she tried to escape at gunpoint. The girl and her child were taken to an ambulance, and the girl was listed as a missing or runaway juvenile by St. Louis, Missouri, police in April 2010. A neighbor reported never witnessing anything suspicious, despite seeing the girl outside the house on multiple occasions.

Detroit Tigers outfielder Delmon Young was arrested and charged with a hate crime in Manhattan early on May 1st, following an altercation outside the Hilton Hotel. Young, who is African-American, allegedly shouted anti-Semitic slurs at a group of four men, one of whom was Jewish, and physically assaulted one of them. The victim, Jason Shank, suffered minor injuries. Young was hospitalized due to his intoxication and later released on a $5,000 bond.

Young's attorney, Dan Ollen, claimed that the bail was "silly" and "ridiculous," stating that Young has no criminal record and that there is evidence showing that the other party was the instigator. Ollen also stated that a videotape of the incident exists but does not contain audio. Young issued a statement expressing regret for the incident and vowing to improve himself as a person and player.

The Tigers management issued a statement saying they would allow the legal process to take its course. Young's teammates declined to comment on the matter. The incident is the latest in a series of troubles for Young, who was suspended for 50 games in 2006 for chucking a bat at an umpire.

The altercation occurred outside the Hilton Hotel on Sixth Avenue at around 2:40 a.m. The incident began after the four men spoke with a panhandler wearing a yarmulke and Star of David outside the hotel. Words were exchanged between Young and the men, at which point Young allegedly said, "You bunch of (expletive) Jews." Young then pushed and shoved one of the men, before tackling him to the ground, causing minor injuries to the man's elbow.

It is not yet clear whether the man, who refused medical attention, is Jewish. The misdemeanor charge — aggravated harassment — is punishable by up to a year in jail. The charge was submitted as a hate crime "because of a belief and perception regarding … religion (and) religious practice," according to the court document filed tonight. The Tigers are in New York to play the Yankees, and Young was expected to play in the series opener, but his arrest has caused him to miss the game.

The report by the United Nations University's Solving the E-Waste Problem (StEP) Initiative predicts that by 2017, the global volume of discarded electronic waste will nearly double, weighing as much as 200 Empire State Buildings. The forecast is based on data gathered by various organizations, including the United Nations, governments, and nongovernment and science organizations. The StEP Initiative has created an interactive e-waste map, which shows data from 184 countries, including the U.S. and China, which produce the most e-waste. The map reveals that the average person on Earth generates about 43 lbs. (20 kg) of e-waste annually, with the U.S. generating the seventh highest amount per capita. The U.S. National Center for Electronics Recycling (NCER) and MIT have released a report on U.S. e-waste, stating that in 2010, the U.S. generated about 258.2 million units of used computers, monitors, TVs, and cellphones, with 171.4 million collected for recycling and 14.4 million exported. The U.S. is a major exporter of used electronics, exporting more CRT monitors by weight than any other product and more cellphones than any other electronics product in terms of numbers. However, export numbers could be an underestimate, as exporters often want to keep them quiet to bypass restrictions or bad press. In terms of recycling, the U.S. is behind countries in the European Union, which have had established e-waste recycling programs for more than 10 years, whereas only 25 U.S. states have started similar programs. The StEP Initiative forecasts that by 2017, the world will produce about 33 percent more e-waste, or 72 million tons (65 million metric tons). This amount weighs about 11 times as much as the Great Pyramid of Giza. The report calls for better recycling and safer disposal of e-waste to address the growing problem.

The article discusses the significant role sleep plays in learning and memory retention. Research suggests that sleep is not only essential for supporting learning but may also be directly responsible for it. This is supported by the discovery that sleep is important for long-term potentiation, a strengthening of signals between neurons that is widely regarded as a mechanism of learning and memory.

During sleep, certain memories acquired during the day are reactivated and "replayed" in the brain, which may help make them longer lasting. The amount of improvement that occurs on memory tasks positively correlates with the length of time spent in certain stages of sleep.

A recent study by Stéphanie Mazza and colleagues at the University of Lyon found that sleep supercharges relearning, enabling individuals to relearn twice as quickly and up to three times more effectively. In the study, participants learned a list of Swahili-French word pairs, slept, and then relearned the pairs. Those who slept between the learning and relearning sessions had significantly better long-term retention of the word pairs than those who did not sleep.

The study's results suggest that sleep "transforms" memories, making the effects of initial learning stronger and empowering subsequent relearning. The authors noted that total sleep time was positively correlated with recall and relearning performance, indicating that the longer participants slept, the better they tended to do on both.

The study also found that the combination of sleeping after initial learning, plus engaging in relearning itself, generated long-term memory benefits. Without relearning, subsequent recall performance was no better than the wake group.

The article concludes that sleeping between study sessions can be a particularly potent learning strategy, especially when learners take the time to repeatedly revisit and relearn in order to achieve a high level of performance. Scheduling study sessions to occur shortly before going to bed is also likely to improve future remembering and relearning. The study's findings add to the growing body of evidence supporting the importance of sleep for learning and memory retention.

In Asheville, North Carolina, two police officers responded to a noise complaint during a Fourth of July block party and found a makeshift water slide on the street. Instead of issuing citations, they determined the slide allowed cars to pass and decided to join in the fun, much to the delight of the neighborhood children. The incident, captured on video and shared by the police department, garnered national media attention, including a nod from Good Morning America. Resident Katlen Joyce Smith shared that a local dad had built the slide for the children. The police's unexpected participation in the festivities brought a unique twist to what could have been a routine call.

The FBI has arrested Hunter Moore, the operator of the notorious revenge porn website anyoneup.com, and Charles Evens, a hacker accused of stealing nude photos of hundreds of victims to populate the site. Moore and Evens are charged with conspiracy, computer intrusion, and identity theft. The site, which began as a platform for ex-partners to post explicit photos of each other, allegedly relied on Evens hacking into email accounts to obtain private photos, for which he was paid $200 a week by Moore. The two began discussing the arrangement in 2011 via email, with Evens seeking $250 for nude pictures of multiple individuals in December 2011. Moore has defended the site, blaming victims for taking the photos that were published. If convicted, Moore and Evens face up to five years in federal prison for the conspiracy and computer hacking charges, and a mandatory two-year sentence for aggravated identity theft. The case serves as a reminder for email users to be diligent with their passwords and security questions. Charlotte Laws, an activist whose daughter was a victim of photo hacking by the site, helped push through a California law banning revenge porn.

Miss Honduras 2014, Maria Jose Alvarado, and her sister Sofia Trinidad have gone missing four days before Alvarado was scheduled to fly to London for the Miss World competition. The women disappeared after attending a friend's birthday party near their hometown of Santa Barbara. Initially, the police did not treat the disappearance as a crime, but later four people, including Trinidad's boyfriend and the owner of the party venue, were arrested and are being questioned. The missing women were last seen getting into a vehicle as they left the party. Alvarado, 19, was crowned Miss Honduras in April and was expected to compete in the Miss World Pageant in London next month. The case has caused consternation in Honduras, a country known for its high levels of violence. The Miss World competition is due to start on Thursday, with 120 contestants competing for the crown. The grand finale takes place on December 14 at ExCeL London. The disappearance of Alvarado and her sister has caused concern among the contestants and organizers of the Miss World competition.

The article discusses the potential changes to the filibuster rules in the United States Senate, particularly focusing on the threat by Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid to invoke the "nuclear option" to change the Senate cloture rules by 51 votes, rather than the usual 67. This move is aimed at narrowly focusing on presidential nominees to the executive branch, but it raises questions about the future of the filibuster and its role as a check on majority rights.

The filibuster has been increasingly used as a tool to block, delay, and frustrate the will of the majority party, and its potential elimination could make the Senate look more like the House, where the majority always gets its way. The crisis could be averted if Republicans end their filibusters on pending Obama nominees, but if Reid moves to change the rules by 51 votes, it could lead to further weakening and potential elimination of the filibuster.

The fight centers around a handful of nominees Reid has been pushing to confirm, with Republicans poised to block some of them, including Richard Cordray to lead the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and nominees for the National Labor Relations Board. These nominees are at the center of an ongoing legal struggle over the legality of Obama's use of recess appointment power to place them at the agencies.

Senate Minority Leader Mitch McConnell is trying to head off the high-stakes fight, but it's expected that Vice President Joe Biden would vote with Democrats in case of a 50-50 tie. The crisis could still be averted if Republicans end their filibusters on pending Obama nominees, but senators in both parties agree that if Reid moves to change the rules by 51 votes, it would be used by the majority in the future to further weaken the filibuster, potentially eliminating it altogether.

While Democrats believe the GOP would go that route anyway when they get back in the majority, Republicans argue that Reid's move all but assures a continued weakening and eventual demolition of the filibuster. The potential changes to the filibuster rules have significant implications for the institution, with some senators warning that it could set a dangerous precedent.

Under Reid's proposal, the Senate would no longer need 60 votes to break a filibuster on executive branch positions, bringing down that threshold to 51 votes. Senators would face a 60-vote requirement to end filibusters on legislation and judicial nominees. The debate over the filibuster rules is ongoing, with both parties expressing their concerns and trying to find a compromise.

In Northampton, Massachusetts, a black student named Oumou Kanoute was eating her lunch in a common room at Smith College when campus police were called to investigate her presence. The college president, Kathleen McCartney, has apologized for the incident and announced that a third-party investigator will review the case, and every staff member will undergo mandatory anti-bias training.

Kanoute, a rising sophomore and teaching assistant, was reading in the dining hall of the Tyler House dorm when an employee called the police, reporting a suspicious black man. Kanoute recorded the encounter on her phone and posted about it on Facebook, expressing outrage that she couldn't eat her lunch in peace and stating, "All I did was be black."

In response to the incident, Smith College's president sent a statement apologizing and assuring the student that she belongs in all Smith spaces. The college administration has placed the employee who made the call on leave pending an investigation.

Kanoute has called for the identity of the caller to be released, a public apology from the caller, and for them to be fired from the school. However, privacy laws prevent the college from releasing the name. Kanoute has turned to social media to gather support for her requests.

The incident has sparked discussions about racism and bias on college campuses and the need for anti-bias training for staff and faculty. Smith College has committed to mandatory anti-bias training for all staff and faculty, and is also investigating potential policy changes and affinity housing options. The college is also reviewing the legacy of its former president, William Allan Neilson, who has been criticized for his views on race.

The external investigation into the incident concluded that the caller provided a legitimate, non-discriminatory reason for calling the police, but acknowledged that the student was put in fear when the officer approached her. The college has offered restorative justice mediation between the student and the caller, and the caller has agreed to mediation.

The incident has also sparked discussions about the need for transparency and accountability on college campuses, and the role of the ACLU in advocating for the rights of students of color. The ACLU has been providing counsel to the student and has been in communication with the college since late August.

Overall, the incident at Smith College highlights the ongoing issue of racism and bias on college campuses, and the need for institutions to take action to address these issues and create safe and inclusive environments for all students.

The Greenwich High School football team in Connecticut has been criticized for naming one of its plays "Hitler." The play's signal involves an index finger laid across the upper lip. A Trumbull mother, Debbie Levison, whose son played against Greenwich, was outraged as her grandparents, aunts, uncles, and cousins perished at the hands of Hitler during the Holocaust. The football team and coaches met with the Connecticut Anti-Defamation League to understand the offense. The ADL's executive director viewed the use of Hitler's name as a teaching moment, stating there was no intent to intimidate or display anti-Semitism. Headmaster Chris Winters issued an apology and stopped the practice, also reaching out to the local Jewish community to express regret. Rabbi Mitchell M. Hurvitz of Temple Sholom applauded Winters' proactive response. The incident was seen as a failure of the Athletic Code of Conduct, which sets appropriate behaviors for student athletes. Greenwich school officials are now working to educate students about the gravity of such words and events like the Holocaust.

The Internet Archive is working on a project to preserve web pages as they are created and to archive pages that are referenced, aiming to fix broken links on the web. Meanwhile, a New Jersey police officer, Richard Recine, is under investigation for making controversial remarks about President Barack Obama and the U.S. Constitution. The incident occurred during a verbal confrontation with resident Steve Wronko at the Helmetta municipal building, where Recine was called after Wronko was seen taking pictures. The British Academy Film Awards, also known as BAFTAs, announced their nominations early this week. Steven Spielberg's historical epic, "Lincoln," dominated with 10 nominations, including best film, best actor for Daniel Day-Lewis, and best supporting actors for Tommy Lee Jones and Sally Field. Tom Hooper's musical "Les Miserables" and Ang Lee's adventure "Life of Pi" received nine nominations each, while "Skyfall" earned eight.

Joining Day-Lewis in the lead actor category are Ben Affleck for "Argo," Bradley Cooper for "Silver Linings Playbook," Hugh Jackman for "Les Miserables," and Joaquin Phoenix for "The Master." The lead actress nominees are Emmanuelle Riva for "Amour," Helen Mirren for "Hitchcock," Jennifer Lawrence for "Silver Linings Playbook," Jessica Chastain for "Zero Dark Thirty," and Marion Cotillard for "Rust and Bone."

The DGA Award usually predicts the winner of the Academy Award for best director. The guild will announce its television and commercial nominees on Wednesday. The feature nominees and their respective directorial teams were also announced.

Airbus Group, the world's largest commercial helicopter manufacturer, plans to test a prototype for a self-piloted flying car by the end of 2017. The vehicle, which would function as a taxi, is part of Airbus' Urban Air Mobility division, formed to explore concepts such as a personal transportation vehicle and a helicopter-style vehicle for multiple riders. The aim is for people to book the vehicle using an app, similar to car-sharing schemes. Airbus CEO Tom Enders believes the technology could help avoid gridlock on city roads and reduce costs for city infrastructure planners. However, the Federal Aviation Administration would need to approve the vehicle, and the technology is still in the experimental phase. Airbus declined to disclose the amount it is investing in urban mobility. The flying car concept is not new, with several companies working on the technology, including Google co-founder Larry Page and German manufacturer e-volo. However, the primary challenge is developing sense-and-avoid technology to prevent the vehicles from crashing mid-flight.

In November 2012, Israeli attacks on journalists and media facilities in Gaza during the fighting between Israel and Hamas violated international humanitarian law by targeting civilians and civilian objects with no apparent contribution to military operations. The attacks resulted in the deaths of two Palestinian cameramen, injuries to at least 10 media workers, and damage to four media offices, as well as the offices of four private companies.

One of the attacks killed a two-year-old boy who lived across the street from a targeted building. The Israeli government asserted that each of the four attacks was on a legitimate military target but provided no specific information to support its claims. After examining the attack sites and interviewing witnesses, Human Rights Watch found no indications that these targets were valid military objectives.

The Israeli government sought to justify attacks on Palestinian media by saying the military had targeted individuals or facilities that "had relevance to" or were "linked with" a Palestinian armed group, or had "encouraged and lauded acts of terror against Israeli civilians." These justifications, suggesting that it is permissible to attack media because of their associations or opinions, rather than their direct participation in hostilities, violate the laws of war and place journalists at grave risk, Human Rights Watch said.

The four attacks struck a car containing two cameramen from al-Aqsa TV, an antenna tower on two buildings housing media, and two floors of a building housing media in which the Israeli military said it had "surgically targeted" a Hamas "intelligence and command center." The Israeli government provided no specific information to demonstrate that these targets were being used for military purposes.

Human Rights Watch stated that journalists and media workers are civilians and are immune from attack unless they are directly participating in hostilities. Television and radio stations are civilian objects protected from attack unless they are used to make an "effective contribution to military action" and their destruction in the specific circumstances offers "a definite military advantage." For example, a radio station that is used to transmit military orders would be a legitimate military target. Broadcasts intended to improve civilian morale or express support for attacks are not considered direct participation in hostilities.

The Israeli government's statements that reflect the military having adopted an unlawful basis for attacks are evidence of war crimes because they show intent. Under international humanitarian law, Israeli forces unlawfully attacked civilians and civilian objects because of their ties to Hamas and have not shown any involvement in military operations to justify the attacks. The Israeli government has said it is investigating the events mentioned in the report and will respond further once the inquiry is completed.

On March 18, 2015, gunmen stormed the National Bardo Museum in Tunisia's capital, killing 23 people, including 18 foreign tourists. The attack is the deadliest on civilians in Tunisia in 13 years and a significant blow to the country's tourism industry, which is a crucial sector of its economy. The gunmen were killed after holding tourists hostage for several hours at the museum.

Tunisian authorities have identified the dead as including at least three Tunisians, five Japanese, four Italians, two Colombians, two Spaniards, one national each from the UK, Australia, France, and Poland, and an unknown number of South African tourists. Two Spanish tourists, Juan Carlos Sanchez and Cristina Rubio, who were hiding in the museum all night after the attack, were found safe on Thursday.

The attack targeted one of the most popular tourist attractions in Tunisia and occurred as deputies in the neighboring parliament building were discussing anti-terrorism legislation. According to Tunisian Prime Minister Habib Essid, one of the gunmen was known to the authorities but was not aware of any links to known militant groups. Essid also said that security services had flagged up Yassine Laabidi, but were not aware of "anything specific."

Tunisia has been struggling to tackle the growing terrorist threat in the region and thousands of Tunisians have left to fight in Syria and Iraq, triggering worries that returning militants could carry out attacks at home. The attack immediately raised questions about the Islamist terrorist threat to Tunisia amid mounting anxiety that jihadi violence is spilling over the border from neighboring Libya, as well as Algeria.

In response to the attack, Tunisia's Culture Minister, Latifa Lakhdar, said the museum will re-open to the public early next week. The country's presidency also announced that four arrests have been made in connection with the attack, and the army will be deployed to increase security in Tunisia's major cities.

World leaders have condemned the attack and expressed their support for Tunisia's counter-terrorism efforts. The UN Security Council issued a statement saying no terrorist action could reverse Tunisia's path towards democracy. The statement offered condolences to those affected by the attack and called for the perpetrators to be brought to justice.

Many Tunisians took to the streets of central Tunis to protest against the attack, waving flags and lighting candles outside the museum. Protests were also held in other cities across the country.

The attack is a huge blow for Tunisia's tourism industry and its government, which only emerged at the end of a long political transition several months ago. Tourism is a key sector of Tunisia's economy, with large numbers of Europeans visiting the country's resorts. In 2002, 19 people, including 11 German tourists, were killed in a bomb blast at a synagogue in the resort of Djerba. Al-Qaeda said it had carried out that attack.

Concerns about security in Tunisia have increased in recent months as neighboring Libya has become increasingly unstable. A large number of Tunisians have also left to fight in Syria and Iraq, triggering worries that returning militants could carry out attacks at home.

The article discusses the analysis of four-digit passwords by the data analysis firm Data Genetics, revealing popular and predictable combinations that are commonly used. The researchers found that the most popular combinations, such as "1234," "1111," and "0000," account for nearly 20% of all four-digit passwords. They also discovered that passwords starting with "19" rank above the 80th percentile in popularity, with those in the late 1900s being the highest. The least popular combination, "8068," appears less than 0.001% of the time. The data was collected by analyzing a database of 3.4 million stolen passwords that have been made public over the years, with the researchers using this data as a proxy for ATM PINs. The article warns against choosing popular or predictable passwords, as they are easier to guess.

The Senate Banking Committee Chairman, Christopher Dodd, plans to introduce a revised version of a sweeping bank reform legislation on Monday, without Republican support. Dodd had been working with Senator Bob Corker, a Republican, to reach a bipartisan agreement, but the efforts have failed due to pressure from the White House to expedite bank reform to make way for health care legislation.

The bill, which includes provisions for a new consumer protection division, new liability for credit raters, and additional oversight for payday lenders, is expected to be voted on by the committee during the week of March 22. However, Corker criticized Dodd's plan to complete the review of the bill in one week, calling it a travesty.

Disagreements still abound, particularly over shareholder empowering provisions that Democrats have installed in the bill, which Republicans are trying to remove, arguing they empower labor unions and environmentalist investor groups at the expense of shareholder value. The bill is also expected to include provisions for derivatives legislation, which is still being crafted by Senators Jack Reed and Judd Gregg.

Dodd's decision to push ahead without Republican support raises the risk that Congress may not be able to pass a substantive regulatory overhaul, as the White House and some Senate Democrats now plan to challenge the GOP to a partisan fistfight.

U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) recently seized approximately $1.6 million worth of counterfeit hoverboards at the Port of Charleston, South Carolina. The CBP's seizure of these counterfeit hoverboards is part of a larger effort to combat the growing issue of counterfeit goods entering the United States, which threaten economic security and pose safety hazards to consumers. The American Academy of Pediatrics has released an updated policy statement on creating a safe sleeping environment for infants, aiming to decrease the risks of sleep-related deaths, including Sudden Infant Death Syndrome (SIDS). The recommendations advise infants to share their parents' bedroom for at least the first six months and, optimally, for the first year of life. The policy statement, published in the November 2016 issue of Pediatrics, includes new evidence that supports skin-to-skin care for newborn infants, addresses the use of bedside and in-bed sleepers, and adds to recommendations on how to create a safe sleep environment.

The policy statement emphasizes the importance of infants sleeping on a firm sleep surface such as a crib or bassinet with a tight-fitting sheet, avoiding soft bedding, including crib bumpers, blankets, pillows, and soft toys. Parents are advised to feed their baby on their bed, rather than a sofa or cushioned chair, if there's even the slightest possibility that they may fall asleep. The baby should then be moved to his or her separate sleeping space, preferably a crib or bassinet in the parents' bedroom.

The AAP also recommends against using home monitors or commercial devices, including wedges or positioners, marketed to reduce the risk of SIDS. Infants should receive all recommended vaccinations, and supervised, awake tummy time is recommended daily to facilitate development.

The policy statement comes after approximately 3,500 infants die annually in the United States from sleep-related deaths, including SIDS, ill-defined deaths, and accidental suffocation and strangulation. The number of infant deaths initially decreased in the 1990s after a national safe sleep campaign, but has plateaued in recent years.

The AAP encourages doctors to have open and nonjudgmental conversations with families about their sleep practices, and media outlets and advertisers may also play a role in educating parents by following safe sleep recommendations when presenting images and messages to the public.

In a tragic incident, Washington mom Jordan DeRosier lost her seven-month-old son Sloan after he got tangled in his crib blanket. DeRosier made Sloan's cause of death public in a Facebook post, urging parents to learn from her "world-shattering mistake" and not to put their babies to bed with a blanket. DeRosier's words serve as a warning, and both she and the Good Housekeeping Institute's Chief Technologist Rachel Rothman advise that nothing should be in the baby's crib except the baby and a tight-fitting firm mattress and fitted sheet. Soft objects, loose bedding, or any items that could cause entrapment, suffocation, or strangulation should be out of the baby's sleep area.

The University of Virginia (UVA) has implemented new safety rules for fraternities in response to allegations of sexual assault and a gang rape at a fraternity house. The rules require at least three "sober and lucid" members to monitor behavior at parties, prohibit pre-mixed alcoholic drinks, and implement guest lists to control entry to the houses during events. One of the sober party monitors must be posted at a staircase leading to bedrooms and have immediate key access to each room in the house to prevent situations that could lead to sexual assault.

The new rules were announced after a Rolling Stone magazine article in November detailed a gang rape at a fraternity house during a freshman's first year. The article unraveled last month as key elements of the rape allegation fell into doubt and the magazine's managing editor apologized for journalistic lapses.

University officials and leaders of Greek organizations, among others in the UVA community, pledged to continue a push to improve safety at UVA regardless. The university unveiled an addendum to its "fraternal organization agreement" with 31 chapters belonging to UVA's Inter-Fraternity Council. Of those, 28 have houses, which are often the scene of parties where alcohol is available.

At the same time, the university released another safety addendum for its agreements with sororities and fraternities that belong to other Greek councils. That document promises steps to promote "bystander intervention" – a method of preventing sexual violence – as well as educational programs on alcohol use and safe parties.

On Nov. 22, three days after the Rolling Stone article appeared, UVA President Teresa A. Sullivan announced a suspension of social activities for campus Greek organizations. On Tuesday, Sullivan said the suspension would be lifted immediately, on condition that each chapter agree to the new safety provisions by Jan. 16, the second day of fraternity spring rush.

"I believe the new safety measures recommended by the student leaders in the Greek community will help provide a safer environment for their members and guests," Sullivan said in a statement. "I would like to express my sincere appreciation to our student leaders who have worked so diligently in the past several weeks to bring forth substantive recommendations and improvements consistent with the ideals of our community of trust."

IFC President Tommy Reid credited numerous fraternity and sorority members, among others, for working "around the clock for the past month and a half to develop these improvements to our system." The council, he said, "is excited for the spring semester and looks forward to continuing to lead the advancement of student safety at the university."

It is unclear how the new rules for the IFC will change the party culture at Virginia's flagship public university. J. Marshall Pattie, an associate dean of students, said some of the provisions – such as sober party monitors – already have been customary.

Now there will be a standard protocol: At least three "sober brothers" on duty at all parties, with more required as needed. At least one monitor must be stationed wherever alcohol is distributed, and at least one must be at the staircase. The monitors also must wear something that identifies them – with the identification common for all chapters.

On alcohol, the rules say that beer can be served in unopened cans and that wine can be served if visibly poured by a sober fraternity member. Prohibited are "pre-mixed drinks, punches or any other common source of alcohol." That means no beer kegs. Hard liquor can be served at large events if a fraternity hires a bartender through a company with a state license, or at smaller events if bottles are placed at a bar overseen by a sober monitor.

The documents released Tuesday make scant mention of laws against serving alcohol to people under the age of 21. Underlying the rules there appears to be an assumption that college students will drink at parties, regardless of the law, and that the university should try to make those parties as safe as possible.

On guest lists, Pattie said fraternities often have had such controls but that enforcement has varied. Sometimes, he said, a fraternity member might have asked a brother to wave somebody into a party who was not on the list. The new rules will call for a hired security agent to be stationed at the door during large parties to check guest lists. At smaller parties, a fraternity member will check the list.

These provisions are described in a section of the rules headlined, "Eliminating discomfort and chaos: Entry management."

The Navy's regional commander has postponed a port call for a destroyer in Naples, Italy, keeping it near Syria during the ongoing crisis. The ship, equipped with Tomahawk cruise missiles, could potentially be used in any military action against Syria if ordered. Meanwhile, the Russian government has called on Syrian President Bashar al-Assad to allow UN investigators access to areas east of Damascus following a chemical attack. However, Russian officials' move does not indicate a shift in their support for Assad or resistance to punitive measures in the Security Council.

Russian officials accused the Syrian opposition of planning the attack and not cooperating with the UN investigation. This accusation may be based on a misunderstanding, as Russian officials seemed to confuse YouTube's time-stamping system, which shows California time instead of Syria's local time.

CBS News reported on Friday that American intelligence agencies detected activity at known chemical weapons sites before the attack, which they believe could have been preparations for the assault. The Syrian government has not commented on these reports. The Russian foreign ministry praised the Assad government for cooperating with UN investigators and accused the opposition of not doing so.

Ortega, who has been unable to speak since the rampage, underwent surgery and is now "talking a little." The Krim family, including the surviving daughter Nessie, 3 ½, are in seclusion. The tragedy has sparked an outpouring of sympathy from strangers and friends of the family. The children's parents, CNBC executive Kevin Krim and wife Marina Linskey Krim, have received messages of support on social media. A massive congealed lump of fat, wet wipes, and other non-degradable items, known as a "fatberg," has been discovered in Baltimore's sewer system. The fatberg, located between Baltimore Penn Station and the 1700 block of Charles Street, has caused two significant sewer overflows in the past two weeks, including one on September 21 that discharged approximately 1.2 million gallons of sewage into the Jones Falls.

The Baltimore Department of Public Works (DPW) discovered the fatberg while investigating the cause of multiple sewer overflows in the area. The fatberg has caked the walls of a 100-year-old, 24-inch wide pipe, with up to 85% of the pipe being clogged.

Similar fatbergs have been found in other cities, such as London, where a 140-ton fatberg was discovered and is expected to take weeks to remove. Baltimore's fatberg has been mostly scraped off and sent to a landfill.

The DPW has a program to prevent fats, oils, and grease (FOG) from entering the sewer system, targeting restaurants and food service establishments. FOG can congeal, harden, and attach to other non-degradable items, causing blockages in the sewer system.

Private residences are not subject to the same regulations as food service establishments but are encouraged to keep FOG and non-flushable items out of the sewer system to prevent costly overflows. Simple tips include not putting FOG down the drain, disposing of unused grease in a can and then in the trash, not flushing "flushable" wipes, and only flushing poo, pee, and toilet paper.

The DPW is repairing and replacing the city's sewers to avoid infiltration of stormwater and upgrading the city's sewer collection and treatment systems under a sewer system consent decree. Any repairs or replacement of the sewer pipe that crosses Charles Street at Lanvale Street will be determined once the fatberg has been entirely removed.

The Supreme Court heard oral arguments on Tuesday in the case ABC vs. Aereo, a streaming video service that allows users to watch, record, and stream local TV programs over the internet. The case centers around whether Aereo's service violates broadcasters' exclusive rights to transmit works to the public.

Aereo uses tiny antennas set up in cities to pick up local TV signals and send them to subscribers for a fee. The broadcasters argue that this constitutes a public performance and requires a license, while Aereo claims that because each antenna, recording, and stream is initiated and controlled by individual users, it is a private performance.

Justice Stephen G. Breyer questioned the distinction between Aereo's service and a cable TV system, stating that Aereo's antennas could potentially pick up every television signal in the world and send it to a person's computer. However, this is physically impossible due to the limitations of antennas and the fact that the world is not flat.

Justice Sonia Sotomayor asked why Aereo isn't simply a cable TV company, given that it has facilities that receive transmissions from broadcasters and send them to subscribers for a fee. Aereo's attorney, David C. Frederick, responded by explaining that Aereo doesn't collect TV programming and retransmit it in bulk to its subscribers, but instead rents equipment to its subscribers who use it to watch or record one show at a time.

The broadcasters argue that Aereo's service would destroy an important revenue stream and pressure them to abandon free over-the-air broadcasting if it is allowed to continue without obtaining licenses. The outcome of this case could have significant implications for the degree to which innovative companies will have to seek permission from copyright owners to enable people to do in the cloud what they can do for themselves at home.

The case raises questions about the legality of cloud-based services and the distinction between public and private performances. The Supreme Court's decision could have far-reaching effects on the future of online TV and the cloud computing industry.

In 1938, the family escaped from Nazi-occupied Austria and embarked on concert tours throughout Europe and America. They eventually settled in Vermont in the early 1940s and opened a ski lodge in Stowe.

At the lodge, Maria played the accordion and taught Austrian dance with her sister Rosmarie. Born in the Austrian Alps after her family fled fighting from World War I, Maria was surrounded by music growing up, with her father playing the violin, accordion, and mandolin, and her mother playing piano and violin.

Maria also worked as a lay missionary in Papua, New Guinea. The Trapp Family Lodge, located in Stowe, Vermont, offers Austrian-inspired architecture, European-style accommodations, and activities for all seasons. Rosmarie von Trapp, Johannes von Trapp, and Eleonore Von Trapp Campbell were also born to Georg von Trapp and Maria von Trapp.

Elliott Broidy, a top Republican National Committee (RNC) fundraiser and supporter of President Trump, resigned from his position on Friday following revelations that Trump lawyer Michael Cohen arranged a $1.6 million settlement with a former Playboy model whom Broidy had impregnated. Broidy admitted to having a consensual relationship with the woman, and retained Cohen after being informed by Cohen that he had been contacted by the woman's lawyer. RNC Chairwoman Ronna Romney McDaniel accepted Broidy's resignation, stating that he did not want to be a distraction.

The criminal investigation into Cohen's business dealings, which began months ago, deepens the scrutiny of the longtime Trump confidant. Federal prosecutors have empaneled a grand jury to probe Cohen's business dealings, and are also examining his efforts to suppress damaging stories about Trump during the 2016 campaign.

The settlement between Cohen and Broidy came after Cohen negotiated a deal in October 2016 to pay $130,000 to adult-film actress Stormy Daniels, who alleged that she had a sexual encounter with Trump a decade earlier. Keith Davidson, the lawyer who represented Daniels at the time, also represented the Playboy model with whom Broidy had an affair.

In his statement, Broidy apologized to his wife and family for the hurt he had caused. He stated that he had offered to help the woman financially during the difficult period after she elected to have an abortion, but they have not spoken since that time. The woman's attorney, Peter K. Stris, declined to comment.

The Broidy deal reveals new details about the relationship between Davidson and Cohen. In October 2016, Davidson negotiated a confidentiality agreement for Daniels with Cohen, who is Trump's hard-charging fixer in New York. Daniels, whose real name is Stephanie Clifford, has sued to break the agreement, arguing that it is invalid because Trump failed to sign it. Cohen and Trump are seeking to force the matter out of court and into private arbitration, where proceedings are confidential.

The case is the latest unexpected twist in a sprawling drama involving top Trump associates, and deepens the scrutiny of Cohen, whose residences and office were raided by the FBI earlier this week. Federal prosecutors revealed on Friday that Cohen has been under criminal investigation for months, and that they have empaneled a grand jury to probe his business dealings. Investigators are also examining Cohen's efforts to suppress damaging stories about Trump during the 2016 campaign.
