Ashley Judd, the daughter of Naomi Judd and sister to Wynonna, has responded to media speculation about her appearance, specifically her puffy face and weight gain, with an op-ed piece for The Daily Beast. Judd explains that her puffy face was a result of steroid treatment for a sinus infection and her larger frame the result of "a lazy six months of not exercising."

In her essay, Judd questions why there was a conversation about her appearance in the first place and encourages a new conversation about the objectification and degradation of women's bodies in society. She argues that the conversation about her face is emblematic of the constraints on girls and women and the encroachment on their right to be simply as they are, at any given moment.

Judd also discusses the internalized beliefs and fears about worthiness that perpetuate mean-spirited criticisms of women's appearances and the role that both women and men play in perpetuating patriarchy. She calls for individuals, families, and groups of friends to make adjustments that support shedding unconscious actions and beliefs that contribute to the objectification and degradation of women.

The essay has been well-received, with many praising Judd for her smart and bold feminist stance. However, some have criticized Judd for her profession as a Hollywood actress, arguing that she knowingly traded her right to be simply as she is in exchange for fame and fortune.

Overall, Ashley Judd's op-ed piece highlights the ongoing conversation about women's bodies and the objectification and degradation of women in society. It encourages a new conversation about the role that both women and men play in perpetuating patriarchy and the importance of shedding unconscious actions and beliefs that contribute to mean-spirited criticisms of women's appearances.

On October 9, 2014, a century-old time capsule hidden in the head of a lion statue atop the Old State House in Boston was opened, revealing a hardcover book among other expected items such as letters, newspaper clippings, and maps from 1901. The time capsule was sealed in the statue since 1901 and forgotten until recently when the statue was taken down for refurbishing. The contents of the book remain a mystery as it had no visible markings and was left untouched due to its fragile condition. The Bostonian Society, which manages the Old State House, was "absolutely delighted" with the condition of the items inside the box. The society plans to put a new time capsule in the lion's head, made of titanium, and is currently soliciting suggestions for what to include. The Old State House, one of Boston's most popular tourist attractions, has a storied history, including serving as the seat of English rule in the northern colonies and the site of the Boston Massacre in 1770. The plan is to put a new time capsule in the lion's head, this one made of titanium. The society is currently soliciting suggestions of what to put in it, but said one item will be a medal from the ill-fated 2013 Boston Marathon. The lion and another statue, of a unicorn, were removed for repairs last month. The society is asking the public to suggest what should be left inside a new time capsule using the hashtag #lionandunicorn on social media. Suggestions so far range from Fenway Park dirt, the new iPhone and a miniature version of the “Make Way for Ducklings” sculpture, to unpaid city parking tickets and Big Dig architectural renderings. Heidi Rogers Grundhauser, the great-great granddaughter of Samuel Rogers, who placed the time capsule in the lion's head, is hoping to attend the opening ceremony and is excited to see what her great-great grandfather contributed to the capsule. The contents of the time capsule will be studied and put on public display at a later date.

In Richmond, Virginia, a police officer who reported fellow officers for allegedly threatening President Barack Obama and First Lady Michelle Obama has been fired. The officer, who remained anonymous, made the initial report to CBS 6 in May 2012, stating that a 20-year department veteran made inappropriate comments about harming the President and First Lady during a phone conversation with an officer providing exterior security. The officer also claimed that another voice in the background suggested planting a bomb under the stage.

The Secret Service investigated the incident and found no criminal wrongdoing, but two officers were fired amidst the controversy. The fired officers have been fighting to get their jobs back, claiming the allegations against them were false or greatly embellished. The whistleblower was terminated from the Richmond Police Department on Tuesday for violating department policy by doing an interview with CBS 6.

Employment attorney Thomas Roberts, who is not associated with this case, expressed concern about the potential chilling effect this termination could have on other police officers who might be afraid to speak out about matters of public concern. The fired officer is reportedly considering legal options. The new Chief of the Richmond Police Department, described as a believer in transparency, may reconsider the termination of the officers and open the remaining grievance hearing to the public.

Lt. Gov. Brian Schatz of Hawaii has been appointed to succeed the late U.S. Sen. Daniel Inouye, following a decision made by Governor Neil Abercrombie. The appointment was made after Abercrombie received a list of three candidates from the state Democratic Party, which included U.S. Rep. Colleen Hanabusa, Esther Kiaaina, and Schatz. Inouye had expressed his wish for Hanabusa to succeed him, but Abercrombie chose Schatz instead.

Schatz, a former state representative and former chairman of the state Democratic Party, will serve until an election is held in 2014. He is expected to be sworn in as early as this week, making him Hawaii's senior senator heading into the new Congress. Schatz expressed his gratitude for the appointment and stated his intention to make serving in the Senate his life's work.

The appointment of Schatz means that U.S. Rep. Mazie Hirono, who was elected in November to replace the retiring U.S. Sen. Daniel Akaka, will be the junior senator. Schatz plans to run in 2014 and 2016 to complete the remainder of Inouye's six-year term.

The appointment of Schatz has been met with mixed reactions. Inouye's chief of staff, Jennifer Sabas, expressed disappointment that Inouye's "last wish" was not honored but wished Schatz luck. Hanabusa, who was also a candidate for the position, congratulated Schatz and stated her intention to continue serving the people of Hawaii and supporting the delegation's efforts.

Schatz is expected to travel to Washington aboard Air Force One tonight and will participate in Senate votes to avert a fiscal cliff of federal tax increases and spending cuts scheduled to take effect in January. President Barack Obama cut short his annual Oahu vacation to work on the budget and other issues when Congress returns Thursday, and he invited Schatz to join him on the flight.

The appointment of Schatz marks a new chapter in Hawaii's political landscape, and his youth and potential for building seniority over time have been highlighted as key factors in his selection. The appointment has also sparked discussions about the importance of seniority in the Senate and the challenges facing the new delegation in addressing critical issues facing the nation and Hawaii.

The latest New York Times/CBS News Poll reveals that a majority of Americans favor the installation of video surveillance cameras in public places, viewing it as a necessary trade-off for increased security against terrorist attacks. The poll was conducted a week after the Boston Marathon attack, which was aided by the release of video footage of the suspects.

The poll indicates that the public perceives terrorism as an ongoing threat in the United States, with 9 out of 10 people acknowledging the need for constant vigilance. However, there are lingering questions about the role of intelligence agencies before the attacks, with opinions divided about whether they had collected information that could have prevented them.

President Obama defended the performance of the Federal Bureau of Investigation and the Department of Homeland Security in a White House news conference, stating that they had done their job. The poll suggests that Americans are willing to tolerate further tough measures to prevent future attacks, with 66% saying information about how to make explosives should not be allowed on the Internet.

The poll also shows that only 20% of people believe the government has gone too far in restricting civil liberties in the fight against terrorism, while 26% say it has not gone far enough. This is a shift from 2011 when more people expressed concerns about losing civil liberties.

The Boston bombings have led to increased fears of another attack, with 66% of Americans now thinking another terrorist attack in the U.S. is at least somewhat likely in the next few months, up from 37% last year. Despite this, most Americans (72%) are not less likely to attend large public events due to terrorism.

The poll received responses from 965 adults and has a margin of sampling error of plus or minus three percentage points.

The title sequence for the popular TV show Game of Thrones features an astrolabe, a navigational tool used by sailors to determine time and location based on the position of the sun and stars. The astrolabe in the sequence is a close-up of the sun surrounded by several bands, each with relief details that tell the pre-history of Westeros, the fictional world of the show. The title sequence was created by Elastic, and the Creative Director of Elastic, Angus Wall, was inspired by the maps of Westeros that precede each novel in the series.

Meanwhile, a real-life astrolabe, believed to be the oldest known marine navigation tool, was recently discovered in a shipwreck off the coast of Oman. The astrolabe dates back to between 1495 and 1500 and was recovered from the Esmeralda, a Portuguese explorer ship that sank during a storm in the Indian Ocean in 1503. The instrument was used by mariners to measure the altitude of the sun during their voyages.

The astrolabe was discovered in 2014 by David Mearns, who led the excavation and is the author of The Shipwreck Hunter. The bronze disc measures 17.5cm in diameter and is less than 2mm thick. The excavation team believed the object was an astrolabe, but they could not see any navigational markings on it. However, a later analysis uncovered its hidden details. Laser scanning work carried out by scientists at the University of Warwick revealed etches around the edge of the disc, each separated by five degrees. These etches would have allowed mariners to measure the height of the sun above the horizon at noon to determine their location.

The discovery of the real-life astrolabe adds to the historical significance of the navigational tool used in the Game of Thrones title sequence. The show's creators were inspired by the maps of Westeros, and the astrolabe in the sequence tells the pre-history of the world in relief-sculpture form. The turning gears and cogs in the sequence were meant to be reminiscent of Leonardo da Vinci's inventions.

In summary, the title sequence for Game of Thrones features an astrolabe that tells the pre-history of Westeros, while a real-life astrolabe, believed to be the oldest known marine navigation tool, was recently discovered in a shipwreck off the coast of Oman. The astrolabe dates back to between 1495 and 1500 and was recovered from a Portuguese explorer ship that sank during a storm in the Indian Ocean in 1503. The discovery of the real-life astrolabe adds to the historical significance of the navigational tool used in the Game of Thrones title sequence.

George Zimmerman, a former neighborhood watch volunteer, was found not guilty in the shooting death of unarmed teenager Trayvon Martin last year in Sanford, Florida. The verdict sparked deep emotional reactions across the country, resurrecting an intense national debate about race and racism in America. The case has been politicized, with Republican House member Steve King stating that President Obama had turned it into a political issue. Obama has not commented on the verdict, but critics are calling on his Justice Department to pursue a civil rights case against Zimmerman. The NAACP and others argue that race was a factor in the case, while Zimmerman's attorneys maintain that race had little bearing on the initial confrontation or the outcome. The verdict did little to close the stark divisions the case opened up among Americans along racial lines. The White House issued a statement in which Obama characterized Martin's death as "a tragedy . . . not just for his family . . . but for America." The president urged citizens to remember that a jury had spoken and to work towards widening the circle of compassion and understanding in their communities. Protests and rallies were held across the country, with some calling for justice for Trayvon Martin and others celebrating Zimmerman's acquittal. The Justice Department is continuing its civil rights investigation of Martin's death. The case has brought attention to the issue of racial profiling and the "stand your ground" law that protected Zimmerman. The family of Trayvon Martin is mourning his death and considering filing a civil lawsuit. The case has also sparked a conversation about race and gun violence in America.

Senator Ted Cruz, a Republican presidential candidate, spoke against Loretta Lynch's nomination for Attorney General on the Senate floor, citing concerns over her support for President Obama's executive action on immigration and her perceived continuation of Eric Holder's lawlessness. Cruz missed the final vote on Lynch's nomination, which passed 56-43, with Cruz being the only senator not to vote. Cruz's absence was attributed to a Dallas fundraiser and a meeting of the Republican Jewish Coalition in Las Vegas. Cruz had previously voted against cloture, a procedural vote that ended up passing, clearing the way for Lynch's eventual confirmation. Flint, Michigan, is facing another water crisis as a boil-water advisory was issued due to a water main break on Tuesday. The advisory was issued after a large water transmission line adjacent to Dort Highway broke, causing a water main break on Dupont. The leak has been contained, but the advisory will remain in effect until bacteria testing is completed on Thursday. Residents are advised to boil all filtered water for one minute before using it.

The latest setback comes as Mayor Karen Weaver is asking Michigan Governor Rick Snyder for $55 million to remove lead pipes in the city. The governor's office is reviewing Weaver's proposal, and $195 million has been requested as part of the budget plan for the 2016-2017 fiscal year.

The city's water problems trace back to the city's switch to Flint River water in April 2014 for its source of drinking water and the state's failure to require corrosive controls. The state acknowledged the problem in October.

In addition to the water crisis, damage is showing up in the city's fire equipment, with one pump already replaced due to severe rust, and the fleet's newest fire truck showing signs of premature damage and wear. The Flint Fire Department is also worried that the water could be corroding the fire suppression systems around the city.

Residents are advised to call (810) 766-7202 for more information, and tips on dealing with microbes are available through 1-800-426-4791.

Google's new Photos app has come under fire for mislabeling a photo of two black people as "gorillas." The incident, which was brought to Google's attention by a New York-based software developer, has sparked criticism due to the racist connotations of the label. Google executive Yonatan Zunger acknowledged the error and said the company had already taken steps to avoid similar mistakes in the future. He also mentioned that Google is working on longer-term fixes, including improving the recognition of dark-skinned faces and being more careful with the words used in photos of people. This is not the first time Google Photos has mislabeled one species as another, as it was previously tagging pictures of dogs as horses. Google has apologized for the incident and is taking immediate action to prevent such results from appearing in the future. The company has also faced criticism in the past for racist tags in Google Maps, and other platforms are also working to improve their automatic image labeling.

The Shroud of Turin, a cloth revered by some Christians as the burial cloth of Jesus, has been called into question by a new forensic investigation. The study, published in the Journal of Forensic Sciences, is the first analysis of the controversial shroud using bloodstain pattern analysis. The researchers, Matteo Borrini of Liverpool John Moores University and Luigi Garlaschelli of the Italian Committee for the Investigation of Claims of the Pseudosciences, used real and synthetic blood samples to conduct seven different tests on different body parts depicted on the fabric.

The researchers found that the bloodstains on the shroud are inconsistent with any single pose, suggesting that a standing model was used to imprint the patterns. The forearm rivulets corresponded to an arm held straight out around 90 degrees to the side, while the hand marks matched an arm held out at about 45 degrees. Some hand bloodstains traced angles at odds with each other as well, off by as much as 10 degrees. A simulated spear wound in the chest ran in completely different patterns than the one on the shroud, whether standing or prone.

The researchers also found that the blood over the spear wound formed rivulets, rather than a solidly filled stain, and that the lower back stain could not be replicated at all. These findings suggest that the shroud is not consistent with the blood flow patterns that would be expected from a crucified or hanging person.

The researchers concluded that the linen appears patched with bloodstains from a standing model, not a crucified man or facedown corpse, adding to evidence that the shroud is a medieval fraud. However, the investigation does not definitively prove that the shroud is a fake, and further research may be needed to fully understand its origins.

The Shroud of Turin has been the subject of debate and study for many years, and it remains a controversial and fascinating artifact for many people. The new forensic investigation adds to the ongoing debate about the authenticity of the shroud and its significance in Christian history.

In a heartwarming and poignant turn of events, Jill Kindt and Jo Grant, a same-sex couple from Australia, were the first to legally marry following the nation's redefinition of marriage law in December 2017. Despite being together for eight years, their marriage was only 48 days long due to Jill's terminal illness with a rare form of cancer.

Their private wedding took place in their garden on the Sunshine Coast, surrounded by friends and family. The ceremony was expedited due to Jill's terminal illness, and officials went to "extraordinary lengths" to make it happen quickly. The marriage was revealed in Queensland's parliament by Attorney-General Yvette D'Ath, who praised the efforts of those involved.

Jill and Jo had held a commitment ceremony in 2013, but their 2017 wedding made their marriage legal. Jill expressed her gratitude for those who helped make their dream a reality, despite the tragic circumstances. She said, "I know there are other couples that were married that weekend, and for different reasons. They are among the first … and the reason we did is a tremendously sad one."

Attorney-General Yvette D'Ath called the story inspiring, stating, "It's a story of hope that reframes Queensland as a modern, trailblazing state which recognizes equal rights and the most fundamental principle—that love is love."

Australia's first same-sex weddings occurred from January 9, but some couples, like Jill and Jo, were eligible for exemptions allowing them to wed earlier. Another couple, Lauren Price and Amy Laker from Sydney, also exchanged vows on December 16 after they too obtained a waiver exempting them from the one-month waiting period because their families were traveling from Wales to be there.

Since the marriage equality laws were passed, 159 same-sex couples have been married in Queensland. This story serves as a reminder of the importance of love, equality, and the extraordinary efforts people are willing to make for those they care about.

In Greenwich Village, workers upgrading water mains under Washington Square Park unearthed two centuries-old burial vaults that are believed to be part of a Presbyterian church cemetery. The vaults, discovered on November 5, 2015, are approximately 15-by-18 feet in size and contain more than a dozen sets of remains.

One of the vaults has visible skeletons and skulls, while the other contains more than a dozen stacked wooden coffins. Archaeologists and anthropologists are working on the site to gather information, including identifying the buried individuals, if possible.

The vaults were likely built in the late 18th or early 19th century. The nearby Greenwich Village park was a Potter's Field for yellow fever victims in the early 1800s, which is why archaeologists were already on the site.

New York City policy is to leave burial grounds undisturbed if possible, so project engineers are planning a new route for the water main. The discovery is not the first time historical artifacts have been found during planned upkeep projects in the city. In 2005, 18th-century houses, wells, and Revolutionary War buttons were discovered during construction work in lower Manhattan's South Street Seaport area.

The discovery of the burial vaults has been described as a wonderful find by archaeologists. Access by vehicles and pedestrians near the area will be restricted during the excavation, which will continue south of the burial vault. The Department of Design and Construction and the Landmarks Preservation Commission are working together to evaluate the extent and significance of the vault and its contents.

The 14-year-old Pakistani schoolgirl, Malala Yousafzai, who campaigned for the right to education, showed signs of improvement on Saturday as she moved her limbs, according to the military. The shooting of Malala, which has been denounced worldwide, occurred on Tuesday when a gunman boarded her school bus and opened fire. The Pakistani authorities have offered a reward of over $100,000 for the capture of her attackers.

Malala's condition is stable, and a team of specialist doctors is providing constant care to her. The next 36 to 48 hours are critical for her recovery, and she may be moved abroad for further treatment. Two other girl students who were wounded with Malala are also being treated. The military has made some arrests in connection with the incident, but the number of people in custody is not disclosed.

The attack on Malala has sickened Pakistan, where she won international prominence with a blog for the BBC that highlighted atrocities under the Taliban. Activists view the shooting as a wake-up call to those who advocate appeasement with the Taliban, but analysts suspect there will be no seismic shift in a country that has sponsored radical Islam for decades.

Schools opened with prayers for Malala on Friday, and special prayers were held at mosques across the country for her speedy recovery. The Defence of Pakistan Council, an Islamist alliance, cautioned against the attack on Malala being used as a reason to launch fresh military offensives against militants.

The best friend of Malala, Shazia Ramzan, who was also hit in the attack, vowed to defy the Taliban and return to school with her. Shazia, who was hit in the shoulder and hand, said Malala had told classmates she might be a target but refused to hide from the Taliban.

Tens of thousands rallied in Pakistan's largest city, Karachi, in support of Malala, with many carrying her picture and banners praising her bravery. The leaders of Pakistan's main Islamic parties have criticized the shooting, but have also tried to redirect the conversation away from Taliban violence and toward civilian casualties from U.S. drone attacks.

The United Arab Emirates plans to send a specialized aircraft to serve as an ambulance for Malala in case doctors decide to send her abroad for treatment. No decision has yet been taken to send her abroad, but the air ambulance is part of the contingency plan. Afghan President Hamid Karzai has written letters to top political and religious leaders in Pakistan denouncing the attack on Yousufzai and asking them to help battle extremism in both countries.

Army Captain William D. Swenson, who received the Medal of Honor for his heroic actions during a battle against the Taliban in Afghanistan in 2009, has requested to return to active duty in the Army. On April 22, 2018, a fatal bus accident occurred in North Hwanghae province, South Korea, resulting in the death of 32 Chinese tourists and four North Koreans. In a daring heist reminiscent of the film 'Ocean's Eleven,' an international crime syndicate is suspected of stealing approximately $12.7 million from ATMs in Japan in just three hours. The thieves, believed to be around 100 in number, coordinated withdrawals at 1,400 convenience store ATMs across Tokyo and 16 other prefectures. They used forged credit cards containing account details illegally obtained from Standard Bank in South Africa, making a single withdrawal of 100,000 yen (US$913) in each of the 14,000 transactions.

The heist, which took place on May 15, started just after 5am and ended just before 8am. All the ATMs were located at 7-Eleven stores. No arrests have been made, and it's speculated that the thieves may have already left Japan.

Standard Bank, which estimates its losses at $19.25 million, described the heist as a "sophisticated, coordinated fraud incident" involving a "small number" of fake cards. The bank assured that its customers had not suffered any losses and that swift action was taken to contain the matter.

This incident marks the second time Japan has been a victim of a large-scale ATM heist using forged credit cards. In a spree spanning 2012 and 2013, thieves managed to withdraw $41 billion in 26 countries, including Japan. Police are currently examining CCTV footage to identify the suspects and have asked South African authorities to investigate the source of the credit card information.
