He has numerous other high-profile credits outside of the show, including directing the film "Rosewater" and starring in "The Larry Sanders Show." Stewart's departure from "The Daily Show" will mark the end of one of the most venerable and trusted careers in making a complete mockery of the news. The show will continue, with Comedy Central stating that it will "endure for years to come."

The article recounts an incident where the author, Ron Lieber, was kicked out of Restaurant Marc Forgione in TriBeCa, New York, for confronting the chef about his loud and aggressive behavior towards staff members. The incident occurred during dinner service, with Lieber and his party of four being seated and hearing the chef yelling at a staff member in the kitchen. Feeling uncomfortable, Lieber walked into the kitchen to address the chef about his behavior, leading to a heated exchange. The chef eventually asked Lieber and his party to leave, citing disrespectful behavior.

The article also discusses the challenges of working in the restaurant industry, particularly for servers, and offers tips for diners on how to behave respectfully and considerately towards staff. These tips include making eye contact, respecting the choreography of service, not making a mess, speaking up if something is not to one's liking, handling the check properly, tipping generously, and staying out of the kitchen.

The article concludes by criticizing Lieber's behavior and arguing that he was acting as a self-entitled and boorish customer. The author suggests that Lieber's actions were disrespectful and inappropriate, and that he should have handled the situation differently. The article also notes that the chef, Marc Forgione, has since given his perspective on the incident, stating that he would not have served Lieber and his party if he had known they would behave in such a manner. The article does not offer a clear conclusion on who was in the right or wrong in this incident.

The French architect, Patrick Henri Devillers, linked to China's political scandal involving Bo Xilai and his wife Gu Kailai, is not to be extradited to any country, as per Cambodian Foreign Minister Hor Namhong. Devillers, who has lived in Cambodia for at least five years, had close business ties with the Bo family. China has requested his arrest, but the reasons remain undisclosed. Devillers is currently in Cambodian custody for further investigation.

Gu Kailai, suspected of murdering British businessman Neil Heywood, has reportedly admitted her guilt to Chinese investigators. She is said to have confessed to funneling billions of dollars overseas and implicated Bo Xilai in the scandal. The Chinese authorities are investigating whether Bo was aware of his wife's actions and have detained several associates.

The status and location of Devillers are unclear, and the French embassy and Cambodian authorities have not provided details. The events leading up to his arrest are also unknown, but it is believed that he was arrested about two weeks ago. Devillers had been close to Gu Kailai in the past, and there are suspicions that he was involved in moving her money overseas.

The scandal has highlighted China's tight diplomatic relationship with Cambodia, where China is the largest political and economic ally. China has boosted its influence in Cambodia in recent years, providing hundreds of millions of dollars in aid, loans, and investment.

The document outlines the process for electing the President of the United States, as stated in the U.S. Constitution. The President serves a term of four years, and is elected alongside the Vice President. Each state appoints electors equal to their number of Senators and Representatives, and no one holding an office of trust or profit under the U.S. government can be an elector.

The electors meet in their respective states to vote for two candidates, with at least one not being an inhabitant of their own state. The votes are then counted by the President of the Senate, and if no candidate receives a majority, the House of Representatives chooses the President. In choosing the President, the votes are taken by states, with each state having one vote, and a quorum requires members from two-thirds of the states.

The Congress determines the time of choosing the electors and the day they give their votes. Only a natural born citizen or a citizen of the U.S. at the time of the Constitution's adoption is eligible to be President, and they must be at least 35 years old and have lived in the U.S. for at least 14 years.

In case of the President's removal, death, resignation, or inability to discharge the powers and duties of the office, the same duties devolve on the Vice President. The President receives a compensation for their services, which cannot be increased or diminished during their term, and they cannot receive any other emolument from the U.S. during that period.

Before entering office, the President takes an oath to faithfully execute the office of President and preserve, protect, and defend the Constitution. The President is the commander-in-chief of the Army and Navy, and can require the opinions of the principal officer in each executive department on any subject relating to their duties. The President has the power to grant reprieves and pardons for offenses against the U.S., except in cases of impeachment.

The President, Vice President, and all civil officers of the U.S. can be removed from office on impeachment for, and conviction of, treason, bribery, or other high crimes and misdemeanors.

The summary of the news article discusses the Trump administration's decision to freeze $125 million in funding for the United Nations Relief and Works Agency (UNRWA), which provides aid to Palestinian refugees. The funding was supposed to be transferred by January 1 but was withheld, and there are concerns that a big part of the U.S. funding could be cut, which would be catastrophic for the organization and have negative consequences for Palestinian refugee camps in Gaza, the West Bank, Jordan, and Lebanon. The Israeli security establishment and the Coordinator of Government Activities in the Territories are concerned about the potential escalation of the humanitarian crisis in Gaza. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is not enthusiastic about cutting U.S. funding to UNRWA but is politically pressed by conservative ministers in his cabinet and the fact he can't be more dovish on the Palestinian issue than President Trump. Officials in the prime minister's office have conveyed to diplomats from several western countries that Israel does not object to cutting U.S. funding to the Palestinian Authority but prefers that the U.S. doesn't cut funding to UNRWA due to the fact it also serves Israeli security interests.

The second part of the summary discusses the Articles of Impeachment adopted by the House Judiciary Committee on July 27, 1974, against President Richard Nixon. The articles of impeachment were passed only by the Committee on the Judiciary and were never voted on in the full House of Representatives. Nixon was not impeached. The articles accuse Nixon of obstructing justice by preventing, obstructing, and impeding the administration of justice, and of engaging in a course of conduct or plan designed to delay, impede, and obstruct the investigation of illegal activities, including the Watergate scandal. The articles also accuse Nixon of misusing the powers of his office, including making false or misleading statements, withholding relevant and material evidence, and interfering with investigations by the Department of Justice, the Federal Bureau of Investigation, and Congressional Committees. The articles allege that Nixon's conduct was subversive of constitutional government, to the great prejudice of the cause of law and justice and to the manifest injury of the people of the United States.

Rookie is an online magazine and book series aimed at teenagers, publishing articles, photography, and artwork based on a different editorial theme each month. The magazine was founded by high schooler Tavi Gevinson in 2011 and has gained popularity among teenagers, as well as celebrities such as Lady Gaga.

In an essay for the magazine, Gevinson discusses the condescending and insulting comments she often receives from adult men when they find out she writes for Rookie. These comments are based on the assumption that teenage girls have poor taste and need the approval of men to validate their cultural preferences. Gevinson argues that this attitude is rooted in the fact that men have more power and influence in society, and that they are raised to believe that their opinions are the most important.

Gevinson uses examples from her own experiences, as well as those of other young female artists and critics, to illustrate the problem. She also discusses the way that media representations of young women often reinforce these stereotypes, and the impact that this has on the self-esteem and confidence of teenage girls.

Gevinson concludes by encouraging adult men to listen to and respect the opinions and tastes of young women, rather than dismissing them as inferior or insignificant. She also encourages young women to speak up and assert themselves, and to not let the opinions of others define their worth or limit their potential.

Rookie is no longer publishing new content, but the archives and books are still available, and the community created by the magazine continues to thrive. The magazine was a groundbreaking and influential platform for young women, and its legacy continues to be felt in the world of media and culture.

Keith Olbermann, the former top-rated host on MSNBC, is set to host a prime-time program for Current TV, a low-rated cable channel co-founded by Al Gore. The one-hour program will begin in the spring, and Olbermann will also become the chief news officer for Current. This move comes after Olbermann's departure from MSNBC due to some stormy interactions with management, including a suspension for contributing to political candidates.

Current TV is a privately and independently owned channel that targets young people and subsists on YouTube-style submissions and video journalists. The channel needs help to boost its ratings, and Olbermann's addition could potentially put it on the cable map. However, Current TV is available in only about 60 million homes, compared to MSNBC's 85 million.

Olbermann's move to Current TV would provide him with a measure of independence, as the channel is not owned by a large media company like MSNBC. It is also possible that Olbermann will pursue other ventures, such as an Internet destination.

The addition of Olbermann to Current TV would surely elevate the channel, bringing it attention it has never before received. Olbermann's departure from MSNBC was abrupt, and he has been savoring the speculation about his next move, even posting a countdown clock for his announcement on Twitter.

Comcast, which owns a 10% stake in Current TV, has denied any involvement in Olbermann's departure from MSNBC. Olbermann's new show on Current TV will air weeknights in primetime later in 2011.

Emma Paulsen, a dog walker from Langley, British Columbia, has been charged with six animal cruelty-related offenses and one count of public mischief following the deaths of six dogs in her care last May. The dogs died from heatstroke while enclosed in Paulsen's vehicle, and she initially reported them stolen after leaving them unattended while using a public washroom at a dog park. The charges include killing or injuring an animal, causing unnecessary pain and suffering to an animal, failing to provide the necessities of life to an animal, and falsely reporting an offence. Additionally, Paulsen faces two counts of causing an animal to continue to be under distress under the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, a charge that is precedent-setting in British Columbia. The dogs' owners have expressed relief at the news of the charges, and Paulsen faces up to five years in jail, a fine of $75,000, and a lifetime ban on owning animals if convicted.

On May 13, an 18-year-old prison inmate named Ezekiel Stevenson, temporarily released for a hospital visit, attempted an unsuccessful carjacking in South Carolina. Stevenson, who was aiming for a GTA-style carjack, targeted a driver with a proximity key fob. When Stevenson dragged the driver out of the car, he inadvertently took the key fob, allowing the owner to remotely lock and unlock the vehicle during the ensuing standoff.

The owner repeatedly unlocked the doors, preventing Stevenson from locking them, until the police were able to enter the car. Stevenson then fled into the woods but was apprehended within an hour. This incident highlights the advantage of proximity keys, as the car's immobilization played a crucial role in the arrest. Despite his usual criticisms, the author admits that this incident warrants an apology for proximity keys.

Title: "If I Stay" - A Tear-Jerking Adaptation of Gayle Forman's Novel

"If I Stay," directed by R.J. Cutler, is a heart-wrenching adaptation of Gayle Forman's popular novel. The film, which shares similarities with "The Fault in Our Stars," tells the story of Mia Hall (Chloë Grace Moretz), a 17-year-old cello prodigy who survives a devastating car accident but finds herself in a coma, contemplating life and death.

Mia's life, before the accident, is portrayed as idyllic. She is surrounded by supportive parents, played by Mireille Enos and Joshua Leonard, and falls in love with a guitarist named Adam (Jamie Blackley). Their relationship, a classic case of opposites attracting, is filled with romantic moments, such as a Halloween party where Mia dresses as Debbie Harry and Adam comes as Beethoven.

The film toggles between Mia's coma-induced out-of-body experiences and flashbacks of her life before the accident. While the emotionalism is intense, the narrative can drag at times, particularly during Mia's prolonged vigil in the hospital. However, Cutler's direction smoothly navigates Mia's double-sided experience, albeit with a style reminiscent of his work on "Nashville" rather than the ethereal otherworldliness of films like "The Lovely Bones."

Moretz, known for her roles in "Kick-Ass" and "Let Me In," submerges her edgy, moody character traits in service to Mia, a character that is somewhat bland and edge-free. Blackley is more convincing as the frontman of a rising, pseudo-hard-rock band. The musical sequences, including an impromptu Smashing Pumpkins jam in Mia's backyard, bring welcome energy to the film's talky scenes.

Despite its emotional intensity, "If I Stay" delivers a generous dose of pleasure, making it a potential hit with young audiences. The film is rated PG-13 and is now playing in theaters. However, some viewers may find the supernatural elements, particularly Mia's out-of-body excursions, to be silly or gigglesome.

In comparison, "Spirited Away," an animated masterpiece by Hayao Miyazaki, also deals with themes of life, death, and the supernatural, but it is a coming-of-age story that is beloved by film lovers of all ages. The 10-year-old heroine, Chihiro, finds herself in a fantastical world of spirits after her parents turn into pigs at an abandoned restaurant.

In a New Year's address, North Korean leader Kim Jong-un announced that his country's development of long-range missiles, specifically an intercontinental ballistic missile (ICBM), is in its final stages. Kim stated that the preparation for the ICBM test launch is nearly complete. North Korea has been under UN sanctions since 2006 due to its nuclear and ballistic missile tests. In 2016, the country tested ballistic missiles at an unprecedented rate, although experts suggest it is still years away from developing an ICBM capable of reaching the United States.

Meanwhile, in South Korea, Prime Minister and Acting President Hwang Kyo-ahn has pledged to bolster the military, stating that Seoul will spend whatever it takes to support the armed forces. Hwang dismissed calls to reconsider the decision to deploy an advanced US missile defense system, the Terminal High-Altitude Area Defense (THAAD), despite opposition from North Korea and China.

In his speech, Kim Jong-un also apologized for failing to achieve certain goals in 2016 and pledged to reinforce North Korea's self-defense and preemptive strike capabilities. He emphasized the importance of nuclear weapons as a cornerstone of policy, as long as the United States and South Korea continue their nuclear threats and annual joint military drills.

Kim further criticized the South for driving inter-Korean relations to their worst phase and urged Seoul to come up with aggressive measures to ease military tensions on the Korean peninsula. He also slammed the South's political situation, describing candle vigils in the South calling for the impeached President Park to step down as "anti-government rallies."

On the economic front, Kim highlighted the successes North Korea achieved from its 70-day battle and 200-day battle, two major national campaigns that were underway for a large part of last year. He stressed the need to improve the state's scientific output, electric production, chemistry, metal industry, mechanics, farming, fishing, and coal production, with a particular emphasis on light industry.

The annual speeches of North Korean leaders are regularly scrutinized for signs of potential policy changes for the year ahead. This article was written by Dagyum Ji and JH Ahn and featured an image from Rodong Sinmun.

The article discusses the strategies of dedicated Black Friday shoppers, who view the day after Thanksgiving as a full-contact sport and a game of survival. Shoppers like Rosemary Rizzo from Ronkonkoma, L.I., and Matt Kane from Allentown, N.J., prepare for the holiday shopping rush by doing extensive research, mapping out their routes, and prioritizing their purchases.

Rizzo, who has been shopping on Black Friday for over a decade, leaves her house at 9:30 p.m. on Thanksgiving and continues shopping until 1:30 p.m. the next day. She travels light, shops alone, and uses sites like BlackFriday.info to stay informed about sales in advance. Kane, on the other hand, prepares for the day by doing days of research and casing each store to see where each product will be placed.

Organization is key for these shoppers, who bring specific flyers, lists of recipients, and organized wallets to the stores. Past prizes include walking away with almost-impossible-to-find Wii Fits in 2008 and scoring a $4,500 Coach bag for $99.

The article also emphasizes the importance of having a clear plan, prioritizing purchases, and bringing backup to help with the long lines and crowds. It advises shoppers to power up with snacks and coffee and to check their attitude to make the most of the intense shopping experience.

Black Friday isn't just a day of shopping for the frugal; for some, it's a game of "Survivor." Shoppers like Kane view it as a competition and strive for victory. The article concludes by asking readers if they plan to hit the sales on the day after Thanksgiving and invites Black Friday veterans to share their tips for surviving the busiest shopping day of the year.

Army Sergeant Bowe Bergdahl, who was held captive by the Taliban for five years, is expected to arrive in San Antonio, Texas, on Friday at a military medical center for continued rehabilitation. Bergdahl was released from Taliban captivity on May 31 and has been recuperating at Landstuhl Regional Medical Center in Germany since June 1. He was deployed in eastern Afghanistan when he disappeared in June 2009.

The Pentagon confirmed that Bergdahl is en route to the United States aboard a U.S. military aircraft, having departed Ramstein Air Base earlier this afternoon. The soldier's arrival in Texas will continue the reintegration process at Brooke Army Medical Center.

The swap that led to Bergdahl's release sparked controversy, touching on a range of volatile issues, including ending the Afghanistan war, releasing Guantanamo detainees, and accusations by members of Bergdahl's unit that he deserted. Defense Secretary Chuck Hagel has defended the deal, saying it was Bergdahl's last and best chance to get out. Critics have said the cost of the swap was too high, and that Congress should have been notified in advance.

Bergdahl's letters to his family while imprisoned by the Taliban, published by The Daily Beast, provide some insight into his experiences. In the letters, Bergdahl discusses his life and partially explains why he disappeared in 2009. He also had harsh words for Army leadership, stating that "leadership was lacking, if not non-existent."

As Bergdahl recovers, details are slowly emerging about the conditions he endured during his captivity. The New York Times has reported that Bergdahl told medical staff that the box he was kept in for weeks at a time was pitch black and like a shark cage. CNN has reported that Bergdahl has said he was kept in a small box after trying to escape, according to a senior U.S. official, who spoke on the condition of not being identified. The official also told CNN that Bergdahl suffers from psychological trauma caused by physical abuse.

The exact conditions of Bergdahl's captivity are not known, and he has not spoken publicly since his release. As he continues to recover, the U.S. military and Bergdahl's family will likely face questions about his experiences and the circumstances surrounding his disappearance and release.

The Ohio Democratic primary saw Hillary Clinton emerge victorious, securing a significant lead in the race for the Democratic nomination. The economy was the top issue for voters, with a majority favoring Clinton and expressing concerns about trade with other nations taking away American jobs. In Michigan, Bernie Sanders had captured the group by double digits.

Clinton celebrated her victory in West Palm Beach, Florida, after the first three states were called in her favor. She aimed her remarks at Donald Trump, the leading Republican candidate, criticizing his policies and calling on Americans to fight against "bluster and bigotry."

Sanders, speaking in Arizona, criticized Clinton for her reliance on large donations and her ties to Wall Street. He also repeated his opposition to global trade, particularly in the Midwest industrial belt.

In Ohio, Clinton and Sanders competed for the most coveted prize, a bellwether state that would bestow not only delegates but also a new political narrative. After her loss in Michigan and persistent criticism of her record on global trade, Clinton's aides expressed exasperation that her detailed policy positions to bring jobs back to the hard-hit Midwestern states were a harder sell than what they deemed as unrealistic promises offered by Sanders. They retooled her economic pitch to resonate better in Midwestern states.

Clinton addressed union members in Youngstown, reminding them of her work in New York to bring jobs back to depressed upstate areas. She dispatched former President Bill Clinton to Akron and Toledo, two predominantly white working-class cities, to campaign for her.

Clinton's victories in Florida and North Carolina were due in large part to minority voters, particularly black voters in both states and Hispanics in Florida. Sanders had been expecting to lose Florida, given that only Democrats could participate in the primary and he tends to perform better when independents are in the mix. However, Clinton was also broadly popular in the state, as reflected in exit polls by Edison Research.

In Ohio exit polls, Clinton was far ahead among black voters, but she and Sanders ran closely among white voters. As in Michigan, Sanders was drawing huge support from independents and voters under 30, while Clinton was popular with Democrats and voters over 45.

Both candidates viewed Tuesday's primary results as a turning point in the race. Clinton advisers noted that Sanders had reached the halfway mark without showing any progress at narrowing her sizable lead in delegates, leaving him only one way forward—to win a series of landslides through the June primaries and pick up significantly more delegates than Clinton. Clinton advisers were confident about holding the delegate lead and ready to focus toward the general election.

Sanders advisers, while acknowledging they were far behind in the delegate count, predicted success in states with large liberal populations, like Wisconsin and California, and those with caucuses, a format that rewards voter enthusiasm and turnout and has favored Sanders recently. They argued that Clinton's best states were behind her—the primaries across the South and in Texas where her popularity among blacks and Hispanics resulted in troves of delegates.

Looking ahead, Sanders advisers predicted success in New York, Clinton's home state, given the high numbers of progressive voters and working-class Democrats who share his disgust with Wall Street. However, Clinton's big win in Ohio likely catapulted her into history as the first female nominee of a major party.

Sanders' presidential dreams aren't quite dead, but his remarkable insurgency is a teetering Jenga pile of youth support, momentum, and access to online millions—and Clinton just plucked out the buttressing block. She won Ohio resoundingly and proved that she could capture a diverse and populous industrial Midwestern battleground a week after her shocking loss in Michigan.

Clinton's wins coupled with Ohio Gov. John Kasich's not-so-fast-fellas victory in his home state serve as a dual rebuke to Donald Trump, who has now become the singular focus of fire for every candidate left in the race. In fact, every podium utterance (save for Trump's) sounded as if it had come off of the same speechwriting assembly line: America needs a uniter, not a divider; feel free to shout at my rally, I won't beat you up; why can't we all just get along, yadda, yadda, yadda.

The results cast the parties on divergent political paths: The Democrats seem destined to unite after a few more contests, while Kasich's Ohio win, coupled with a possible victory by Ted Cruz in Missouri, makes it more likely than ever that the GOP is headed for a contested convention.

In Lancaster, Ohio, armed civilians who had been guarding a military recruitment center were ordered off the property after one of them accidentally discharged his AR-15 rifle on Thursday. No one was injured, but the incident led to the armed volunteers being evicted. The shopping-center owner, U.S. Properties Group Portfolio Four LLC, issued a statement saying it was for the safety of tenants, customers, and construction personnel working in the immediate vicinity of the Military Recruiting Center that the armed individuals were asked to leave. Christopher A. Reed, 28, of Lancaster, was charged with discharging a firearm in the city limits and was issued a summons to appear in Fairfield County Municipal Court on Tuesday. Reed told police that he was holding his rifle outside the recruitment center when someone asked if he could take a look at it. Reed agreed, and while he was trying to clear the ammunition from the weapon, he accidentally fired one shot into the asphalt pavement. The only damage was a hole in the pavement. The rifle was taken from Reed pending his appearance in court, the incident report says. Conviction on the fourth-degree misdemeanor is punishable by a maximum of 30 days in jail. Reed was convicted of the same offense in 2013, and was fined $50, court records show. Some armed civilians have been guarding military recruiting stations in Ohio and elsewhere after the fatal shootings of five service members at a military recruitment center in Tennessee. Reed downplayed what happened, saying, "It is what it is, nobody got hurt." A Marine recruiter at the center was not authorized to speak to reporters. Before their eviction, armed civilians discussed why they were there. None was present when the rifle discharged. Kenneth Casteel, a 67-year-old Marine Corps veteran who served in Vietnam and sat in a folding chair with his M-16 rifle propped against it, said, "Government ain't going to do it, They won't give these guys any weapons to carry or keep in a safe. If we don't do it, who is going to do it? It's a matter of safety." The incident in Lancaster follows similar incidents in other states, such as Washington, where armed civilians have been guarding military recruitment centers since the deadly attack on a military recruitment center in Tennessee. The Army has warned its recruiters to treat the gun-toting civilians gathering at centers across the country as a security threat and to avoid anyone standing outside the recruiting centers attempting to offer protection and report them to local law enforcement and the command if they feel threatened. Recruiters were ordered not to interact or acknowledge the armed civilians, who have been greeted by a mix of concern, indifference, and gratitude by the public.

BP has accused Texas lawyer Mikal C. Watts of fraudulently inflating the number of clients he represented in the 2010 Gulf Coast oil spill settlement, thereby driving up BP's costs. In a lawsuit filed in Federal District Court in New Orleans, BP claims that Watts' inflated client count, which constituted nearly 80% of the people projected to file claims under the seafood industry program, led BP to put $2.3 billion into the special compensation program. BP is seeking to stop payments and reclaim some of the unspent money, citing "brazen fraud."

Watts, a prominent Democratic fund-raiser and litigator, has said that his clients came through referrals from other lawyers. However, BP claims that out of the more than 40,000 deckhands claimed as clients by Watts, only 648 individual crew claims were filed through the seafood fund, with only eight found eligible for payment. BP also alleges that 40% of the claims used Social Security numbers that belonged to someone other than the person supposedly making the claim, and 5% of the numbers belonged to dead people.

BP has been fighting the administration of the settlement in court and in the media. The company has paid nearly $13 billion in claims to businesses, individuals, and the government so far, and has paid out $1 billion from the seafood fund. BP argues that the inflated size of the fund would mean an undeserved "windfall" to members of the class.

Lawyers for plaintiffs in the case argue that BP is using the Watts controversy as an excuse to stop payments on the much larger program that affects deserving claimants. They contend that just $130 million was allocated to deckhands, and that BP's attempt to halt payments is unfair to the hardworking men and women of the seafood industry whose livelihoods were destroyed by the spill.

BP has been battling with the Plaintiffs Steering Committee over a separate portion of the pollution settlement: a $9 billion pact intended to compensate businesses outside of the seafood industry. Watts resigned from the Plaintiffs Steering Committee overseeing the multifaceted spill litigation against BP earlier this year, following federal agents executing search warrants at Watts Guerra's offices in San Antonio. The oil company has been accused of paying out claims from people who had no actual losses related to the spill, and a federal judge has temporarily halted payments.

The search for Malaysia Airlines Flight 370 resumed in the southern Indian Ocean on Saturday, with ships and planes scouring a newly defined search area for debris. However, none of the objects found were confirmed to be from the missing plane. The search area was moved due to a new analysis of radar data, which showed that the plane was moving faster than initially estimated, burning fuel more quickly, and possibly falling into the ocean farther north than previously believed. The new search area is about 700 miles northeast of the previous search area and presents more favorable conditions for the search. The search is ongoing, and families of the passengers are seeking answers from Malaysian authorities. The recovery of debris from Flight 370 would provide final confirmation that the plane had crashed into the ocean and offer at least partial resolution to the families and friends of the passengers and crew. It might also help solve the mystery of what caused the plane to veer off course. The approaching winter in the Southern Hemisphere could present obstacles to the underwater search for the plane's black boxes.

In a shocking revelation, Star magazine claims that former Vice President Al Gore's split from his wife Tipper after 40 years of marriage was due to an affair he was having with Larry David's ex-wife, Laurie David. The magazine reports that the pair, who have been friends and environmental activists, have been involved for two years. However, Laurie David has denied the affair, and a Gore spokeswoman has stated that Gore would not comment on personal matters. The Gores' split has been the subject of various speculations in the media, with some suggesting that Al Gore is gay or that Tipper's jealousy was putting stress on their marriage. The Gores were high school sweethearts and were considered one of the most solid marriages in politics.

The article from The Arizona Republic discusses a controversial incident involving a kindergartner who was given a referral for sexual misconduct after pulling his pants down on the playground. The mother of the child argues that her son is too young to understand the infraction terminology and that he pulled down his pants out of fear, not for sexual intent. The Dysart Unified School District, however, defends its actions, stating that administrators followed policy and that the boy's signature was not an admission of guilt but an acknowledgment of due process.

The incident raises questions about the appropriateness of discipline for young children and the understanding of such terminology. Experts suggest that children at this age may not fully comprehend the implications of such labels. They argue that administrators should focus on the behavior and help the child understand that the action was wrong, without labeling them with adult terms.

The article also touches on the uniform discipline policies implemented by school districts, which help maintain consistency but allow flexibility to handle individual cases. These policies have been influenced by the rise of zero-tolerance policies in the 1990s, driven by fears of crime and child sexual abuse scandals.

The article concludes with a list of the top 10 most commonly reported behavior infractions statewide, with fighting being the most common. The data, however, are self-reported and may not be entirely accurate. The incident with the kindergartner serves as a reminder of the need for schools to consider the age and maturity of students when applying discipline labels.

The report by attorney Ted Wells, commissioned by the NFL to investigate allegations of bullying within the Miami Dolphins team, has concluded that three players, Richie Incognito, John Jerry, and Mike Pouncey, engaged in a pattern of harassment against teammate Jonathan Martin and another unnamed young offensive lineman, as well as an assistant trainer. The report details a series of racially derogatory and homophobic comments, physical touching, and sexually explicit remarks made against Martin, the assistant trainer, and the other offensive lineman.

Incognito, who was suspended for the final eight games of the 2013 season for conduct detrimental to the team, was identified as the main instigator of the harassment. The report also found that Incognito and his teammates may not have been aware they were crossing any lines, as the team's rules of workplace behavior were not fully understood.

The report also addressed Martin's mental health issues, which may have contributed to his heightened sensitivity to insults. However, it ultimately concluded that Martin was indeed harassed by Incognito and the other players. The report also found that another player and one of the team's trainers were also frequent targets of abuse.

Incognito's lawyer criticized the report, stating that it contained errors and that the facts did not support a conclusion that Martin's mental health, drug use, or on-field performance issues were related to the treatment by his teammates.

The Dolphins, the NFL, and the NFL Players Association have all stated that they will review the report and take appropriate action. The report includes graphic language and details of the harassment, and a full version can be found online. The report also notes that the language and behavior described in the report are "deeply disturbing" and that the team has consulted with experts to create initiatives and a policy paper examining the issue, which will be released next week.

In an exclusive interview with Barbara Walters, Mary Kay Letourneau Fualaau and Vili Fualaau, the couple infamous for their illicit relationship that began when he was 13 and she was 34, discuss their headline-making marriage on the eve of their 10th wedding anniversary. The couple, who have two teenage daughters, Audrey and Georgia, will share intimate details about their relationship, including Mary Kay's plans to teach again and her intentions to have her status as a registered sex offender lifted. Vili Fualaau will discuss his struggles with alcoholism and depression, and the couple will discuss the challenges they have faced in their unconventional relationship. The interview will air on ABC's "20/20" on Friday, April 10, 2015. Letourneau first spoke to Walters in 2004 after being released from prison, when she expressed her desire to marry her former student. The couple wed in 2005.

The final U.S. senator for the 116th Congress will be chosen in Mississippi on Tuesday, determining whether Republicans have 52 or 53 seats in the Senate. The special election is between incumbent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, a Republican, and Mike Espy, a Democrat. National Republicans have mobilized on behalf of Hyde-Smith, while Democrats have responded with their own efforts. Both candidates have baggage, with Republicans focusing on Espy's past indictment and lobbying work, and Hyde-Smith facing criticism for a series of controversies, including a comment about attending a public hanging. The race is heading to a runoff because no candidate got over 50% of the vote in the first round. Mississippi is a deeply red state, but Democrats are hoping for a surge in black turnout to give Espy a chance. Trump is holding two rallies for Hyde-Smith on Monday. In other news, Trump spent his time on stage in Tupelo and Biloxi on Monday boasting about his administration's accomplishments, exaggerating threats to the country, and bragging about the economy under his watch. However, a cloud hung over the positive picture as General Motors announced plans to cut its workforce by 15% and shutter five plants, potentially costing more than 14,000 workers their jobs. Trump did not mention GM during the rallies, but told The Wall Street Journal he had warned the CEO to open a new plant in Ohio, one of the states slated to lose hundreds of jobs under the company's plans. The most politically effective message Trump delivered in Mississippi was his pitch on immigration, a topic that still motivates his supporters more than practically any other.

In the lead-up to the 2016 U.S. Presidential Election, Hillary Clinton and Donald Trump published op-eds in USA Today to address voters. Clinton emphasized her plans for economic growth, immigration reform, political reform, and criminal justice reform. She highlighted her commitment to creating jobs, investing in infrastructure and renewable energy, and making it easier for small businesses to grow. Clinton also pledged to introduce comprehensive immigration reform, overturn Citizens United, and work on end-to-end criminal justice reform.

Trump's op-ed focused on his campaign's central theme of "draining the swamp" and fixing a "rigged system." He did not mention the recent decision by FBI Director James Comey to clear Clinton of wrongdoing in the ongoing investigation. Clinton, in her op-ed, criticized Trump for his divisive campaign, fear-mongering, and insults. She urged voters to decide who they are as a country, emphasizing the importance of unity and working together.

Clinton's op-ed also outlined her vision for America, stating that she wants to be president for all Americans, regardless of political affiliation or background. She emphasized that the election is not just about the candidates but about the issues that matter to the American people. Clinton concluded by expressing her love for the country and her belief in its potential for greatness if the people work together and invest in each other.

At a funeral service in Tweed Heads, eight-year-old Chloe-May Kabealo bid farewell to her mother, Stephanie King, and two siblings, Ella Jane and Jacob, who tragically drowned when their car plunged into a northern NSW river following heavy rains. Chloe miraculously escaped the submerged car after it slid off a muddy Tumbulgum road into the Tweed River. The family of four was on their way home from a shopping trip when the accident occurred.

Local pastor Rob Stuttle, who conducted the service, reported that the close-knit community was rallying together as the clean-up of the devastated area continued. Chloe and her father Matt Kabealo are "coping as best as they can." Police hailed Ms. King a hero, stating that she was trying to save one of her children when she passed away.

Former police officer Matt Grinham and his family tried to help after the accident, but could not locate the car. Chloe, who was the sole survivor, managed to escape from the river and run to a nearby property to raise the alarm. She was treated for multiple lacerations, abrasions, and neck pain at Tweed Heads District Hospital.

A fundraiser was held for the grieving family, which raised over $10,000. Chloe spoke at the event, describing her miraculous escape. She said, "I unbuckled my seatbelt and I tried to go up for air, and then I just kept floating up out of something and then I got out." Chloe-May said her family had been supported over the past three weeks, and her father, Matt Kabealo, expressed his grief, saying, "I'm shattered buddy, I'm not holding up. (I'm) just being strong for my daughter. We're just going to get through it the best we can."

Advice for escaping a sinking car includes getting out as fast as possible, opening the windows, getting the door open, undoing your seatbelt, and using a headrest to break a window if necessary. If underwater, push away from the car and swim in the direction of bubbles.

The Palin family was involved in a violent brawl at a party in Alaska last month, which was recorded by police. The incident occurred at a birthday party for twin brothers Matthew and Marc McKenna, and was also Todd Palin's birthday. The fight was triggered by an older woman who shoved Bristol Palin's younger sister, Willow. During the brawl, Bristol claimed that a man knocked her down and called her a "f**king c**t." In a recording obtained by TMZ, Bristol can be heard sobbing to the police about losing her shoes and being mentally hurt by the incident. Willow can be heard dropping F bombs during her conversation with the police. Sarah Palin can be heard imploring the police to catch "the bad guys." The Palin family has been silent in the aftermath of the brawl, but RadarOnline.com has obtained police audio of the family's conversation with the police in the immediate aftermath of the fight. In the recording, Bristol can be heard describing how she was attacked and calling the man who attacked her a "30-year-old guy" who pushed her down on the ground and called her a "sl*t." Other partygoers had a different story, claiming that Bristol was the one who started the fight by punching the man multiple times. The police ultimately filed a report stating that Bristol had been punching the man repeatedly and that he had grabbed her arm and held her back, pushing her down while holding her hand as she was attempting to strike him. No charges have been filed in the incident.

The petition initiated by a high school student on Change.org led to the removal of Brominated Vegetable Oil (BVO) from Gatorade drinks, following concerns about its health implications and its ban in Europe and Japan. BVO, a flame retardant chemical, has been linked to health issues such as impaired neurological development, reduced fertility, early onset of puberty, and altered thyroid hormones. The petition, which garnered over 200,000 signatures, prompted PepsiCo to remove BVO from Gatorade.

However, the petitioner discovered that Powerade, a competitor of Gatorade, still uses BVO in some of its drinks, including Powerade's red fruit punch, which is sold in schools. This raises concerns as Powerade markets itself as a healthy sports drink. The petitioner is now urging Powerade to follow Gatorade's lead and remove BVO from its drinks.

The decision by Coca-Cola to remove BVO from Powerade is the latest evidence of food manufacturers responding to pressure for natural ingredients. The petitioner targeted Gatorade and Powerade due to their focus on athletics and health-conscious consumers. As Americans cut back on soda, sports drinks have become increasingly important for companies like Coca-Cola and PepsiCo.

The petition is still active and encourages signatures and sharing to pressure Powerade to remove BVO from its drinks. The petitioner argues that it is illogical for a company to use a controversial ingredient in a product marketed towards health-conscious athletes.

In a series of events that have sparked controversy and outrage, two African lions have been involved in incidents that resulted in their deaths. On March 30, 2016, a male lion named Mohawk was shot dead by rangers in Kenya after straying from the Nairobi National Park and attacking a man. The circumstances surrounding Mohawk's death have been met with criticism, as many believe that tranquilizers could have been used instead of lethal force.

In another incident, a lion named Sylvester escaped from Karoo National Park in South Africa, prompting an outcry from animal rights activists who advocated for its relocation rather than killing it. The South African parks service is currently considering various options for Sylvester, including returning him to the park, improving its fencing, moving him to another park, donating him to a conservation group, or killing him if he causes significant damage or poses a direct threat to humans.

The deaths of Mohawk and Sylvester highlight the difficult balance between protecting people and conserving lions, whose numbers have declined dramatically over the past century due to unregulated hunting, loss of habitat, and growing conflict with livestock herders. The incidents also underscore the challenges faced by wildlife officials in making decisions about how to handle potentially dangerous predators, taking into account factors such as the training of wildlife experts, available resources, and the population density of the area where the lion is roaming.

In Kenya, the straying of lions from Nairobi National Park has become a growing problem, as the city expands and infrastructure projects generate noise that disturbs the lions and causes them to leave the park. The Kenya Wildlife Service is working to ensure that contractors maintain the integrity of the park and keep all animals safe.

The deaths of Mohawk and Sylvester have sparked outrage and calls for justice, with many expressing their disappointment and frustration on social media. The incidents also serve as a reminder of the importance of conservation efforts and the need to strike a balance between protecting wildlife and ensuring the safety of people.

The top organized crime investigator in Peru, Eusebio Felix, was put on leave after misleading the public about a gang of serial killers known as "Pishtacos." Felix claimed that four suspected murderers apprehended by police were Pishtacos, who were said to extract fat from victims in accordance with an ancient Andean legend. However, it was later revealed that the investigation had been botched, and there may have only been one murder victim. The police initially claimed that the gang murdered up to 60 victims and exported their fat for thousands of dollars a liter to Italian cosmetics makers, but this was later found to be false. The police have been heavily criticized for their handling of the case, and anthropologists believe they foolishly believed the Pishtacos legend when searching for a motive for the murder. Politicians have also criticized the police for scaring away tourists.

Gillian Bennett, an 83-year-old woman from British Columbia, took her own life on Monday after a three-year battle with dementia. In a letter posted to her blog, she expressed her desire to avoid losing her "self" to the disease and leaving behind an "empty husk." Bennett died at her home on Bowen Island, surrounded by her husband and family.

Bennett's blog post advocated for assisted suicide, stating that she wanted to end her life before losing her ability to act due to the rapid erosion of her mind by dementia. She criticized law, religion, and medicine for their approaches to assisted suicide and called for the medical profession to mandate the administration of a lethal dose to end the suffering of terminally ill patients in accordance with their Living Will.

Bennett also expressed her wish to avoid becoming a financial burden on the Canadian healthcare system and a chore for her loved ones. She argued that rising life expectancy and an aging population make the elderly a growing burden on society, and she did not want to contribute to that burden.

Bennett's husband and family were aware of her decision ahead of time, and they spent the weekend visiting with her before she died. Her son and daughter were shocked but not surprised when she called them to say that Monday would be her last day.

Bennett's blog post and death have sparked a conversation around assisted suicide and the need for changes in law, religion, and medicine. Her husband, Jonathan, said that Gillian wanted to face death as she faced the challenges of her life: with intellectual curiosity, courage, and grace.

Bennett is survived by her husband, two children, six grandchildren, and two great-grandchildren. She will be remembered as a lively and full-of-life person who opened doors for others. Her final wish was to start a conversation about assisted suicide and to help others avoid the indignity and suffering she experienced in her final years.

A driver, Matthew Apperson, accused George Zimmerman, the former Neighborhood Watch volunteer acquitted of second-degree murder in the shooting death of Trayvon Martin, of threatening to shoot him during a road-rage incident in Lake Mary, Florida. Apperson called the police on Tuesday, stating that Zimmerman made threats and almost hit his car. However, Apperson did not press charges, and Zimmerman was not arrested.

Two days later, Apperson reported that he believed Zimmerman had followed him and was watching his movements. Police investigated and found Zimmerman nearby, but he was not charged. Zimmerman has had several run-ins with the law since his acquittal, including a domestic dispute with his then-girlfriend and an incident with his estranged wife.

Zimmerman is currently on trial in Sanford, Florida, on charges of second-degree murder in the shooting death of Trayvon Martin. The trial is ongoing, and various items have been introduced as evidence. The incident with Apperson is not related to the trial.

In a series of protests in eastern Ukraine, pro-Russian activists seized state buildings in three cities, including Donetsk, Luhansk, and Kharkiv, triggering accusations from the Ukrainian government that President Vladimir Putin of Russia was orchestrating "separatist disorder." The protesters, who waved Russian flags and demanded a referendum on joining Russia, stormed regional government buildings and security service offices, with around 1,500 people protesting in Donetsk before breaking into the regional administration building. In Luhansk, protesters demanded the release of people detained by security services and a referendum on joining Russia. The Ukrainian government, led by Prime Minister Arseny Yatseniuk, accused Russia of being behind the unrest and seeking to sow instability as a pretext for dispatching troops across the border. The protesters' actions echoed the run-up to Russia's annexation of Crimea in March. The Ukrainian government has drawn up a plan to handle the crisis, with senior officials heading to the affected regions. The unrest has been met with condemnation from the international community, with the United States and the European Union calling for Russia to respect Ukraine's territorial integrity. The situation remains tense, with the potential for further escalation.

Researchers have discovered a new virus, named human hepegivirus-1 (HHpgV-1), that can be transmitted through blood transfusions and other blood-based products. The virus shares similarities with both the hepatitis C virus, which can cause permanent liver damage, and the harmless human pegivirus. The discovery was made by a team led by Dr. Ian Lipkin at Columbia University, who emphasized that the new virus is not as harmful as SARS, MERS, or HIV.

The team found the virus in two samples from 46 volunteers who received blood products to treat hemophilia between 1974 and 1980. They also found it in two more people from a different study. Both patients appear to have cleared the virus, with no evidence it caused any disease. The genetic sequence of the virus has been published, allowing other scientists to start looking for it.

The researchers are unsure of the prevalence of the virus and its potential impact on human health. They are currently developing an antibody test to determine who is infected with HHpgV-1 in a larger population. The main challenge now is to assess whether any links to disease exist.

It's worth noting that this is not the only new virus discovered in the study. The team also found a new virus related to hepatitis A virus in seals, which they named phopivirus. This finding suggests that the diversity and evolutionary history of these viruses might be far greater than previously thought and may provide insight into the origin and pathogenicity of hepatitis A.

The discovery of HHpgV-1 underscores the importance of surveillance for infectious agents in the blood supply to ensure the safety of this critical resource for medicine and public health. Despite the potential implications, there's no need for panic, as there's no evidence that the virus has caused anyone harm.

Yahoo has revealed that it could pay its new CEO, Marissa Mayer, a total of up to $100 million over the next five years, according to a regulatory filing. The compensation package includes a salary of $1 million, annual bonuses of up to 400% of the base salary, equity awards, stock options, and a retention award of $30 million. Mayer, who was Google's 20th employee, is expected to receive around $5.4 million for the remainder of this year and around $20 million annually, with some of the amount tied to performance targets. The enormous compensation package was debated by the board, with some directors raising concerns about her and paying such a large amount. However, others argued that Mayer's talent, strong decision-making skills, and product innovation make her the right person to turn around Yahoo, which has struggled to revive itself for many years. The appointment of Mayer has garnered a lot of attention for Yahoo, with media coverage focusing on her being a woman and currently pregnant.

In September 2009, the FBI, led by agent James Craig, made a significant breakthrough in the case against the cybercriminal group responsible for the Zeus network, a notorious malware used for online account takeovers and financial fraud. Craig identified a New York-based server that played a crucial role in the Zeus network and obtained a search warrant to access its data. The server contained tens of thousands of lines of instant message chat logs in Russian and Ukrainian, which revealed the entire digital operation of the gang.

The FBI and cybersecurity firm Mandiant worked together to decipher the logs, which contained references to hundreds of victims and their stolen credentials. The investigation led to the discovery of a money mule operation, where individuals, including students and newly arrived immigrants in Brighton Beach, were used to cash out the funds stolen by the gang.

The case expanded beyond the virtual world, with the FBI investigating a scheme in New York involving three young women from Kazakhstan who were used as "money mules." By the summer of 2010, the FBI had disrupted the network, making 39 arrests around the world and seizing nearly 20 terabytes of data.

However, crucial players such as the mastermind, known as Slavik, remained elusive. Despite seven years of investigation, Slavik's identity and whereabouts remain unknown. Evgeniy Mikhailovich Bogachev, using the online monikers "lucky12345" and "slavik," is wanted for his alleged involvement in the racketeering enterprise and scheme that installed the Zeus malware on victims' computers. Bogachev was indicted in the District of Nebraska and the Western District of Pennsylvania, and a criminal complaint was issued in the District of Nebraska, tying the nickname "lucky12345" to Bogachev. As of now, Bogachev remains at large.

In the Winter Olympics held in Krasnaya Polyana, Russia, Shaun White, a three-time Olympic gold medalist in the halfpipe snowboarding event, failed to defend his title. White, who is known for his commanding performances, had a disappointing run that resulted in a fourth-place finish. Iouri Podladtchikov of Switzerland won the gold medal, with Ayumu Hirano from Japan taking the silver and Taku Hiraoka from Japan earning the bronze. This marked the first time since the halfpipe was added to the Olympics in 1998 that there were no Americans on the podium.

White's fourth-place finish was seen as a gift from the judges by some competitors, including Danny Davis, who finished in 10th place. Davis believed that the result was good for the sport, as it showed that there are other talented snowboarders besides White.

The halfpipe competition was criticized by several snowboarders, who described the conditions as substandard. Some athletes suggested that the event be postponed due to poor conditions and a lack of practice time. Despite these concerns, the competition went ahead, with crews working overnight to improve the shape of the pipe.

White had initially planned to compete in both the halfpipe and slopestyle events, but he pulled out of the slopestyle competition due to concerns over the size and shapes of the jumps. The American Sage Kotsenburg won the slopestyle event.

In the halfpipe event, White struggled with his runs, making hard landings and gasp-inducing bobbles. He attributed his performance to the conditions of the pipe, which he described as disappointing. White, who has built an empire on his snowboarding skills, said that he was happy to take the fourth-place finish for what it was and move on.

Podladtchikov, who won the gold medal, performed a rare trick called the Yolo flip, which White did not master first. Podladtchikov landed the trick perfectly, scoring 94.75 out of 100 points. The cheering crowd waved Swiss and Russian flags as Podladtchikov, who grew up in Davos but competed for Russia at the 2006 Turin Games, expressed his joy at being in Russia and speaking Russian, his mother language.

The halfpipe event marked the end of an era for White, who had won gold in 2006, 2010, and 2014. Despite his disappointing finish, White said that he was proud of his career and looked forward to continuing to ride. The event also marked the beginning of a new era, with younger riders like Hirano and Hiraoka taking center stage.

The search for Malaysia Airlines Flight MH370, which disappeared on March 8 en route from Kuala Lumpur to Beijing, entered a new phase on Friday with the deployment of a towed pinger locator to find the black box. The plane is believed to have crashed in the southern Indian Ocean, but no confirmed debris has been found. The search is being coordinated from Perth, Australia, and involves 14 aircraft and 11 ships. Two ships with locator capabilities are searching a 240km path, but the battery-powered signal from the black box's pinger is fading after 30 days. The area being searched was chosen based on analysis of satellite data, and the search is considered a race against time. The focus is now on a search area of about 217,000 sq km, 1,700 km northwest of Perth. The search for surface wreckage will continue, as a find would be the most effective way to pinpoint a sub-sea hunt. The search has been ongoing for four weeks, and there has been criticism of the Malaysian authorities' handling of the search and their release of information. The investigation is focusing on the cabin crew and pilots as possible suspects.

A new study by Consumer Reports found that store brand products can save shoppers an average of 30% on groceries, with significant savings of up to 52% on some items. In a taste test, store brands won 14 out of 21 match-ups, with ties in the remaining instances. Despite the savings, some shoppers are still reluctant to try store-brand products due to perceived quality concerns. However, Consumer Reports found that store-brand products are often of similar quality to their name-brand counterparts, with some exceptions in taste and nutrition. The study also found that national brands are generally pricier due to the cost of developing the product and turning it into a household name. The full results of the study are available in the October issue of Consumer Reports.

In a tragic and bizarre incident, a Florida pest exterminator named Jorge Barahona has confessed to putting his dead daughter in the back of his truck before a failed suicide attempt that left him and his adopted son hospitalized in critical condition. Barahona is charged with aggravated child abuse for an alleged attack on his 10-year-old adopted son, Victor Vocter.

The incident came to light when a Florida Department of Transportation employee discovered Barahona's pickup truck parked on the side of I-95, not far from the Palm Beach Lakes Boulevard exit. Inside the truck, they found Victor, who was soaked in chemicals and suffering from respiratory distress. An unresponsive Barahona was found on the ground outside the truck.

Barahona told police he was distraught over the death of his daughter and intended to commit suicide. He allegedly poured gasoline over his head and planned to ignite himself, but had second thoughts because Victor's head was resting on his lap.

The police report does not detail how the girl died and does not mention whether Barahona discussed her death with police. The boy is being kept in a hyperbaric chamber. He has stopped urinating and doctors are having a difficult time treating him because they do not know what kind of chemical agent caused his injuries.

Child welfare officials are investigating Barahona and his wife, Carmen Barahona. The Barahonas married in 1996 and reportedly operated CJ's Pest Exterminator Inc. out of their home. Records obtained by The Palm Beach Post show neither had a criminal record in Florida. They reportedly adopted four children, ages 7 to 11, with special needs from foster care.

DCF has investigated the Barahonas on three other occasions in the past several years. The previous cases were closed with "some or no indicators of abuse or neglect," according to The Miami Herald. The most recent investigation began on Thursday, four days before Barahona was found on the side of the interstate.

Investigators tried to locate the children, but Carmen Barahona told them that she was separated from her husband and that he had custody of them. A report issued later, however, "implicated" Carmen Barahona in Nubia's disappearance. DCF took custody of the two other children on Tuesday. A hearing will be held sometime today to determine whether they will be sent to foster care.

This incident has sparked a short-lived child welfare investigation and an unfolding drama that culminated on Monday when Alessandra's grandfather, Jorge Barahona, was found inside a red pickup truck along Interstate 95 in West Palm Beach, with one dead child, a girl, doused in chemicals in the back of the truck and a boy, in the cab, near death next to him. The girl is believed to be Victor's twin, Nubia.

A reward of $69,000 is being offered for information leading to the arrest in connection to the vandalism of hundreds of gravestones at Mount Carmel Cemetery, a Jewish cemetery in Northeast Philadelphia. The damage was reported on Sunday, with an estimated 300 gravestones found toppled and vandalized. A team is working to put the gravestones back up, and a GoFundMe has been created to help raise money to fix the damage.

The vandalism brings up dark memories and fears of anti-Semitic acts, according to Naomi Adler, the CEO of the Jewish Federation of Greater Philadelphia. This comes less than two weeks after similar vandalism was reported at Holy Redeemer Cemetery in Philadelphia, and a week after a Jewish cemetery in suburban St. Louis reported over 150 headstones vandalized.

Mayor Jim Kenney released a statement, expressing his heartbreak for the families affected and stating that hate is not permissible in Philadelphia. Governor Tom Wolf also called the act reprehensible and has asked the Pennsylvania State Police and Office of Homeland Security to offer their full resources towards protecting Jewish institutions and finding those responsible.

The Mizel Family Foundation, the Anti-Defamation League, an anonymous donor, Councilman Allan Domb, Mayor Kenney's office, and the Fraternal Order of Police Lodge #5 have all offered monetary rewards for information leading to an arrest and conviction. The police are conducting a criminal mischief-institutional vandalism investigation.

During a town hall meeting in Decorah, Iowa, President Obama had a heated exchange with a Tea Party activist, Ryan Rhodes, over allegations that Vice President Biden called Tea Party members "terrorists" during the debt ceiling debate. Obama did not directly address the question but defended himself against criticism, stating that he has been subjected to similar rhetoric throughout his presidency. The incident stems from a private meeting Biden attended with House Democrats, where one lawmaker accused Tea Party Republicans of behaving like "terrorists." Some audience members in Iowa expressed disapproval of Rhodes' behavior, while he maintained that he stood by his actions.

Michelle Hurst, known for her role as Miss Claudette in Orange Is the New Black, has awakened from a medically induced coma following a serious car accident. James Howells, an IT worker from the United Kingdom, accidentally discarded a hard drive containing 7,500 bitcoins worth over $127 million at a landfill site in Newport, South Wales in 2013. The hard drive was lost during a home clean-out, and Howells has been unable to retrieve it due to the city council's refusal, citing environmental and financial concerns.

Howells began mining bitcoins on his personal laptop in 2009, before the need for specialized hardware. In 2013, he sold the laptop on eBay, but kept the hard drive as a precaution. With the value of bitcoin skyrocketing from $300 to $10,000, Howells' lost bitcoins are now worth $75 million.

The council has expressed concerns about the costs and environmental impact of digging up the landfill, which contains around 350,000 tonnes of waste, with 50,000 added annually. The drive would likely have suffered significant corrosion due to the presence of landfill leachates and gases.

Howells has attempted to negotiate with the council, but they have not granted him permission to search for the hard drive. He believes that the council's financial situation may change in the future, making it necessary for them to allow him to search for the drive.

Despite the loss of his fortune, Howells remains active in the bitcoin community and is interested in Bitcoin Cash, a result of a hard fork in August. He believes that the bitcoin price will eventually surpass $100,000, making his lost bitcoins worth $750 million.

The council has warned that any attempts to search for the drive would be considered a criminal offence and could be dangerous. Howells still has the public address for the hard drive, and if found, the data would be encrypted, requiring his assistance to access.

The sidewheel steamer Keystone State, one of the largest ships on the Great Lakes, was discovered in Lake Huron by shipwreck hunter David Trotter and his team in July 2019. The ship, launched in 1849, sank in November 1861 during the American Civil War, claiming the lives of 33 crew members. The ship's mysterious cargo, labeled as "iron implements" or farm machinery, has sparked rumors that it was actually military supplies destined for the battlefield. However, Trotter's team found an empty cargo hold upon discovery.

The Keystone State was bound for Milwaukee, Wisconsin, when it sank, and its sudden departure and the unusual cargo have fueled suspicions. Trotter believes that the ship's captain, Wilkes Travers, may have been reluctant to turn the ship towards land for fear of being capsized in heavy seas due to the ship's design. The wreck is surrounded by a large debris field, and while no gold has been found yet, the team is still exploring the area.

Trotter, a retired Ford Motor Co. executive, has been shipwreck hunting for over 35 years and has made several significant discoveries in the Great Lakes. The team is still trying to determine the extent of damage caused by the storm, the impact of the hull hitting the bottom, and changes that have occurred over the last 152 years. The water depth limits divers to about 15 to 20 minutes of exploration before they must decompress for over an hour on the way back up.

The discovery of the Keystone State adds to the many shipwreck mysteries in the Great Lakes. While fact-checkers have repeatedly debunked this claim, it remains a standard attack line for Romney. The charge that Obama took $716 billion from Medicare recipients to pay for "Obamacare" has several problems, including the fact that Romney's running mate, Paul Ryan, included the identical savings in his budget plans that House Republicans voted for in the past two years.

The study published in the International Journal of Epidemiology has found that daily consumption of nuts and peanuts, but not peanut butter, is linked to lower mortality rates. The research was conducted within the Netherlands Cohort Study, which includes over 120,000 Dutch men and women aged 55-69 years. The associations between nut and peanut intake and cardiovascular death confirmed earlier results from American and Asian studies, but this study also found that mortality due to cancer, diabetes, respiratory, and neurodegenerative diseases was lowered among users of peanuts and nuts.

The researchers analyzed the relationship between nut and peanut intake and overall and cause-specific mortality since 1986. Total nut intake was related to lower overall and cause-specific mortality in men and women. The multivariable hazard ratios for total mortality compared those consuming 0.1-<5, 5-<10, and 10+ g nuts/day with non-consumers, with the ratios being 0.88, 0.74, and 0.77, respectively. Cause-specific hazard ratios comparing 10+ vs 0 g/day varied from 0.56 for neurodegenerative to 0.83 for cardiovascular disease mortality.

The study found that peanuts and tree nuts were inversely related to mortality, whereas peanut butter was not. In meta-analyses, the summary hazard ratios for highest vs lowest nut consumption were 0.85 for cancer and 0.71 for respiratory mortality. The study concluded that nut intake was related to lower overall and cause-specific mortality, with evidence for nonlinear dose-response relationships.

The benefits of nuts and peanuts may come from various compounds such as monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fatty acids, various vitamins, fiber, antioxidants, and other bioactive compounds. In contrast, peanut butter contains added components like salt and vegetable oils, and in the past, it has been shown that peanut butter contains trans fatty acids, which have adverse health effects.

The study's findings suggest that replacing saturated fats with essential polyunsaturated fats found in nuts and peanuts can have significant health benefits, including lower mortality rates from various causes. It is essential to avoid trans fats and limit saturated fats in the diet.
