Administrators from both schools met with the TSSAA on Monday, with Smyrna principal Rick Powell stating that both he and Riverdale principal Tom Nolan asked to allow their teams to continue to play, but remove their respective coaches from the postseason. The referee reported that Riverdale intentionally missed 12-16 free throws, while Smyrna refused to get the ball across the half-court line to avoid a 10-second count or to make the referees call an over and back violation intentionally.

Tullahoma and Lawrence County advanced to the Region 4-AAA semifinals, as Riverdale and Smyrna were removed from the postseason. The decision has caused a significant uproar, with both principals expressing their disappointment and regret for the actions of the coaches. Riverdale principal Tom Nolan has suspended coach Cory Barrett for the first two games of the 2015-16 school year, while Smyrna principal Rick Powell has not yet decided on additional punishment for coach Shawn Middleton.

The TSSAA has stated that the decision to remove the teams stems from the players' actions on the court, as they intentionally played to lose the game. The student athletes were reportedly the ones asking to call three seconds, standing back over midcourt, and not attempting to shoot at the basket. The incident has raised concerns about the ethics and integrity of high school athletic programs, as they are meant to teach students sportsmanship, morals, and values.

The incident has caused a significant uproar, with both schools and the TSSAA expressing their disappointment and regret for the actions of the coaches. The decision to remove the teams from the postseason has left a number of players, especially the seniors, feeling devastated and disappointed. The incident serves as a reminder of the importance of sportsmanship, ethics, and integrity in high school athletics.

Lindsey Graham, a Republican senator from South Carolina, is offering a deal to President Obama regarding the trial locations for alleged 9/11 mastermind Khalid Sheik Mohammed and four accused henchmen. Graham proposes that if Obama agrees to try them in military tribunals, Graham will work to close the Guantanamo Bay prison. This offer comes as Attorney General Eric Holder Jr. plans to try the suspects in a civilian court in New York, a move that has faced criticism. Graham's proposal aims to address the ongoing issue of closing Guantanamo Bay, a promise Obama made when he took office, but has yet to fulfill due to pressure from both political sides. The American Civil Liberties Union has criticized Obama for not backing Holder's plan, arguing that it would continue the policies of the previous administration. Graham's offer is seen as a potential way for Obama to recover from self-inflicted wounds over Guantanamo Bay.

In Sigmund Freud's famous work, Sex in Dreams, he posits that dreams and sexuality are closely linked, with the majority of adult dreams expressing erotic wishes. A study by the Kinsey Institute supports this claim, revealing that 37% of women aged 45 have experienced orgasms from sex dreams, and 5% have had their first orgasm through a dream. For men, 83% have experienced nocturnal emissions, although the connection to dreams was not specified.

A study published in the journal Dreaming found that sleeping on the stomach with arms raised increases the likelihood of having erotic dreams. The study involved 670 students who self-reported their dreams and sleeping positions. Those who frequently slept on their stomachs were more likely to have dreams about sex, being tied up, being unable to move, and being locked up. The most common theme was "erotomania," or the belief of having a secret admirer.

Researchers suggest that the stomach sleeping position puts pressure on the genitals and allows external stimuli to be incorporated into dreams. Lead researcher Kai-Ching Yu stated that the brain during sleep is not entirely detached from the external world, and stimuli are often incorporated into dream content.

However, sleeping on the stomach is not recommended for good sleep posture as it can lead to lower back pain. Ultimately, the decision to sleep in a position that increases the likelihood of erotic dreams is a personal choice. The study was published in Sleep and Hypnosis: A Journal of Clinical Neuroscience and Psychopathology in 2019.

A Russian researcher named Sergey Savitsky has been charged with attempted murder after allegedly stabbing his colleague at the Bellingshausen station in Antarctica on October 9. The incident occurred at the station's dining room, and the victim, whose name has not been disclosed, was sent to a hospital in Chile. Savitsky is currently under house arrest until December 8 and is cooperating with the investigation. According to a source, the incident may have been caused by the prolonged close proximity of the two researchers, leading to Savitsky's emotional breakdown. The Bellingshausen station, established by the Soviet Union in 1968, is located on King George Island and is one of several research stations in the area. The Russian authorities have not yet commented on the attack. The incident highlights the challenges of investigating crimes in Antarctica, as the continent is not owned by any single nation and multiple countries maintain research teams there.

Global stocks started 2016 with a significant decline, led by a tumble in U.S. stocks, as concerns over slowing global growth and renewed worries about China's economy intensified. The S&P 500 posted its worst start to a new year in over a decade, with all sectors closing lower. Investors sold off risky assets like equities and bought safe-haven assets such as gold and Treasurys, following a rout in Chinese shares and heightened tensions between Iran and Saudi Arabia. The Dow Jones Industrial Average also recorded a triple-digit loss, while the Nasdaq Composite tumbled by 2.1%. The selloff was triggered by a 7% slide in China's Shanghai Composite Index, which activated a new circuit-breaker system for Chinese stocks, halting trading on the mainland for the rest of the day. European stocks also slumped. Additionally, oil prices briefly spiked due to tensions between Saudi Arabia and Iran but have since fallen. U.S. construction spending sank 0.4% in November, and the Institute for Supply Management's manufacturing index slipped to its lowest level since the last month of the Great Recession. Other market movers included declines in shares of Tesla Motors, Netflix, and Amazon.com, while Volkswagen faced a lawsuit over alleged emissions-defeat devices in some 600,000 vehicles.

In an interview with POLITICO, Piers Morgan discussed his contentious encounter with conservative radio host Alex Jones on CNN last night. Jones, known for his gun advocacy and conspiracy theories, launched into a tirade against Morgan, gun control legislation, and various government conspiracies during the interview. Morgan described the encounter as "a big, long rant" and stated that Jones's performance was "the best advertisement for gun control you could wish for." Jones, who started a petition to deport Morgan, continued his rant even during the commercial break. Morgan noted that while he anticipated such a performance, Jones's influence among conservatives was the reason for having him on CNN. Jones is the host of The Alex Jones Show and the creator of InfoWars.com and PrisonPlanet.com, websites that promote a worldview described as being "governed by logic-leaping deductions and heedless pronouncements" by the Southern Poverty Law Center. Moments after the interview, Jones expressed his fear that he would be harmed by the New York Police Department or members of the mafia hired by NYC Mayor Mike Bloomberg. Jones claimed that he was accosted by a member of the NYPD before entering CNN headquarters in New York City. He also accused CNN's producers of panicking during the interview and cancelling a planned third segment with Morgan. Jones went on to say that he feared for his life, stating that Bloomberg and the NYPD were "mafia." Jones released a video expressing these fears on YouTube.

Pippa Middleton, the younger sister of the Duchess of Cambridge, has signed a publishing deal worth £400,000 for her first book, a guide to being the perfect party hostess. The book, which will include recipes, anecdotes, and details on various types of events, is expected to be released late next autumn, after the Queen's Diamond Jubilee celebrations but in time for the Christmas market. The negotiating process involved delicate discussions about the book's timing to avoid appearing to cash in on her royal connections. The high six-figure advance secured by her agent, David Godwin, indicates that the industry expects high sales. Michael Joseph, an imprint of Penguin Books, will publish the book, joining other authors such as Jamie Oliver, Jeremy Clarkson, and Ant and Dec on its roster. Other publishers who were also keen on the book include Harper Collins and Cornerstone, a branch of Random House. Pippa Middleton has toured around different publishing houses pitching the book over the last few months, and book executives said that she went down a storm. However, the book's release has sparked controversy, with some criticizing Pippa for cashing in on her royal connections and questioning her expertise in party planning and etiquette.

A woman was tragically killed in Henderson, north suburban Denver, after being struck by a Union Pacific steam locomotive returning from Cheyenne Frontier Days in Wyoming. The accident occurred at a crossing in Henderson at around 7:45 pm on Saturday. The victim, whose name has not been disclosed, was among several people taking photographs of the train. Approximately 700 passengers were on the train, with no other injuries reported. The train, known as the 'Denver Post Special', was being pulled by Locomotive 844, a famous steam locomotive originally built for passenger service. Union Pacific is leading the investigation into the incident, with passengers being bused back to Denver. The train remained at the scene for several hours. Steam Engine 844, known for its role as an "ambassador of goodwill" by Union Pacific, attracts steam aficionados who often photograph or videotape its excursions.

The article discusses the ongoing investigation into potential collusion between the Trump campaign and Russia during the 2016 presidential election. U.S. investigators are re-examining conversations detected by intelligence agencies in spring 2015 that involved Russian government officials discussing associates of Donald Trump. This re-examination was prompted by revelations that Trump's eldest son, Donald Trump Jr., met with a Russian lawyer in June 2016.

The meeting with the Russian lawyer was arranged after Trump Jr. was promised damaging information about Democratic rival Hillary Clinton. Trump Jr. released emails related to the meeting on Tuesday. He stated that the meeting yielded no useful information about Clinton and instead turned into a discussion about a Russian-American diplomatic dispute.

In the White House interview, President Trump said he did not fault his son for meeting with the Russian lawyer and was unaware of the meeting until a few days ago. He also said he directly asked Russian President Vladimir Putin if Russia was involved in the election meddling, to which Putin denied any involvement. Trump equivocated on whether he felt he could trust Putin, stating that they both look out for their countries' interests.

The article also mentions that the meeting between Trump and Putin in Germany resulted in a ceasefire agreement in part of Syria, but their interests collide on other issues. Trump's U.S. military buildup and drive to increase U.S. energy production are in direct conflict with Putin, whose nation is dependent on energy exports.

The article concludes with Trump stating that there was no collusion between his campaign and Russia, and that Democrats have used the accusations to justify Clinton's loss in November. He also expressed his belief that the White House is functioning well despite the ongoing investigations.

Chris Brown has been ordered to serve a month in jail for violating his probation, following his arrest on Friday. The singer was kicked out of a Malibu rehab center for breaking three rules, including a specific rule requiring him to maintain a two-foot distance from women at the facility due to his history of domestic violence. Brown allegedly violated this rule by touching the elbows and hands of a woman, leaving the facility on an unauthorized outing, and initially refusing to take a random drug test upon his return. He also reportedly made harsh comments during a rehab group session. Brown was previously ordered to spend 90 days in a residential facility for anger-management issues, and has a history of legal troubles, including an assault case in Washington, D.C. He is due back in court on April 17.

The Internet Archive is working on a project to preserve web pages as they are created and archive the pages they reference, aiming to fix broken links on the web. Wisconsin Historical Society is archiving websites of state government agencies, interstate agencies, and major social media pages of Wisconsin's Governor, Lieutenant Governor, and First Lady. R.L. Stine, known as the Stephen King of children's literature, announced he will write a new scary story on Twitter this evening, marking his third such story on the platform. Stine will also take over Scholastic's Twitter feed for a Halloween-themed Q&A on Thursday.

A 2-year-old boy in Wichita, Kansas, is recovering in good condition after an octopus was found lodged in his throat. The incident occurred on Tuesday night, and the boy was initially brought to a hospital in critical condition. The boy's 21-year-old mother returned home from work to find her 36-year-old boyfriend performing CPR on the child, who was not breathing.

Upon arrival at the hospital, doctors found the octopus lodged in the boy's throat, which appeared to be intended for sushi. The boy also had facial injuries. The Wichita Police Department's Exploited and Missing Child Unit interviewed the mother's boyfriend, identified as Matthew Gallagher, who is now facing child abuse charges. The investigation is ongoing, and a detective specially trained to interview young children will visit the boy soon. The boy's condition is described as "a very delicate situation." The incident has garnered attention, with the Kansas City Zoo naming three baby otters after "Star Wars" characters in a light-hearted response to the serious event.

In 2018, numerous prominent companies experienced data breaches, with over 1.1 billion records compromised between 2005 and August 2018. The Identity Theft Resource Center reported 9,395 breaches during this period. To combat this issue, the Trump administration released a new cybersecurity plan, focusing on offensive measures against foreign cyberattacks. However, criminal strategies continue to evolve, leaving consumers vulnerable to identity theft and fraud.

To determine the states most susceptible to identity theft and fraud, WalletHub compared the 50 states and DC across ten key metrics, including identity-theft complaints per capita, average loss amount due to online identity theft, and fraud & other complaints per capita. Nevada ranked as the most vulnerable state, followed by Florida and New Jersey.

To protect against identity theft, individuals should emphasize email security, sign up for credit monitoring, leverage account alerts, use common sense online, and keep personal information updated. For more tips and expert advice, visit WalletHub's Identity Theft Guide.

A Chilean mother, Sindy Melany Ortiz, is facing restrictions from seeing her newborn daughter due to her admission of smoking marijuana before giving birth. Ortiz claims she used marijuana for medicinal purposes to alleviate pain in one arm, and she is only allowed to see her daughter for two hours a day and is not permitted to breastfeed her. Hospital officials in Talcahuano, where the incident occurred, say they followed protocol after tests revealed substances that could potentially harm the baby. The local court has ordered the baby to remain at the Las Higueras hospital until a decision is made during a hearing on Thursday.

Ortiz contends that her rights as a mother have been violated, stating that she only uses marijuana for pain relief and is not a regular user. She says hospital staff questioned her about drug use, and when her daughter was born, she was told the baby would stay with her but could not be breastfed due to her marijuana consumption.

Chile's Congress recently approved a bill that seeks to decriminalize personal use and cultivation of marijuana, allowing the possession of up to 10g of cannabis and the growing of up to six plants. The bill aims to stop the persecution of medicinal users and provide them with a legal means to access their medicine. The bill is currently in the legislative process and could take years to pass. Earlier this year, Santiago, Chile's capital, hosted Latin America's first medical marijuana farm.

The study presented at the American Heart Association's Scientific Sessions 2016 suggests that repeatedly losing and regaining weight, or yo-yo dieting, may increase the risk of death from heart disease among postmenopausal women who were of normal weight at the start of the study. The research classified self-reported weight history from 158,063 post-menopausal women into four categories: stable weight, steady gain, maintained weight loss, and weight cycling. During a follow-up of 11.4 years, they found that women who had a normal weight at the beginning of the study but then lost and regained weight had about three and a half times higher risk for sudden cardiac death than women whose weight remained stable. Weight cycling in the normal-weight women was also associated with a 66 percent increased risk for coronary heart disease deaths.

The study has several limitations, including being observational, relying on self-reports, and including only older women. More research is needed to establish a causal relationship and to clarify the risks of weight cycling for younger-aged women and men. The American Heart Association reminds us of the seven steps for reducing the risk of heart disease: manage blood pressure, control cholesterol, limit sugar intake, get active, eat a healthy diet, keep a normal weight, and stop smoking.

Mitt Romney, a former Massachusetts governor and a potential Republican presidential candidate, has announced that he will not participate in the December 27th debate moderated by Donald Trump. Romney made this decision to focus on campaigning in Iowa, New Hampshire, South Carolina, and Florida. He had a conversation with Trump earlier in the day, explaining that they cannot make the debate due to scheduling conflicts and campaign commitments. Romney's decision follows similar moves by Ron Paul and Jon Huntsman, while Newt Gingrich and Rick Santorum have confirmed their attendance. The news was shared on Fox News, with Romney stating that Trump understood his perspective and wished him well.

The hacker collective Anonymous has declared war on ISIS following the deadly attacks in Paris, and has begun posting alleged personal information of suspected ISIS extremists. Anonymous has been collecting lists of Twitter accounts and websites belonging to ISIS, and has already taken down some of these sites and accounts. The group has also leaked alleged personal information about suspected ISIS members, including physical addresses. Anonymous has been involved in taking down ISIS-related accounts and websites since January, following the attack on the satirical French magazine Charlie Hebdo. However, Anonymous has been criticized for wrongly identifying people in the past, so it's important to exercise caution when using this information. Anonymous operates primarily online and uses hacking and distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks to disrupt communications. The group has promised to launch the "biggest operation ever" against ISIS and has already taken down over 3,800 pro-ISIS Twitter accounts following the Paris attacks. However, some experts question whether Anonymous' efforts will have any significant impact on ISIS's digital networks, as the group is likely using encrypted chat technology to communicate and can easily reestablish new accounts. There is also concern that Anonymous' actions could disrupt ongoing investigations if they are not coordinated with counterterrorism practitioners from within government.

Former President Bill Clinton earned $10.7 million in speaking fees in 2010, bringing his total earnings from paid speeches to $75.6 million in the past decade. This was his most lucrative year on the speaking circuit, surpassing his previous high of $10.2 million in 2006. Clinton delivered 52 paid speeches in 2010, with almost half of his earnings coming from 18 speeches in 13 countries. The former president has delivered a total of 417 paid speeches since leaving office in 2001, earning an average of $181,000 per event. International engagements account for $44.9 million of his total earnings, with Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia, and Mexico being his most popular destinations outside the U.S. In the U.S., Clinton has delivered the most speeches in New York, California, Florida, and Las Vegas, Nevada. Clinton's earnings from speeches have varied from year to year, with a significant increase in 2010 due to two high-paying events in Moscow and the United Arab Emirates. In the decade since leaving office, Clinton has also earned a $15 million advance for his memoir "My Life" and more than doubled that in earnings from book sales. In contrast, former President George W. Bush has earned at least $15 million from about 140 paid speaking engagements since leaving office in early 2009.

A heartwarming tradition of sending Christmas cards to Queen Elizabeth II by a British man named Simes' grandfather spanned over six decades, from 1952 until his death in 2011. Simes, inspired by his late grandfather's kindness, continued the tradition after his passing. In 1972, the Queen met Simes' grandfather at a reception in Izmir, Turkey, and recognized him as the sender of the annual Christmas cards. The Queen even wrote to congratulate him on his 100th birthday.

After Simes' grandfather's passing, the Queen sent a condolence letter, expressing her sadness at his loss. Simes, touched by the Queen's kindness, continues the tradition of sending Christmas cards to her every year. This story serves as a reminder of the power of small acts of kindness and the potential impact they can have, even on royalty. It also emphasizes the importance of sending Christmas cards, as they have the potential to brighten someone's day.

In the past week, two 10-year-old boys have been bitten by sharks in Florida, with the latest incident occurring in Daytona Beach Shores on Wednesday. The boy, who was visiting from Georgia, suffered minor injuries on his calf and was treated on the scene. This is the fourth reported shark bite in Volusia County this year, which was labeled as the shark bite capital of the world earlier this year by the International Shark Attack File.

Despite the increase in reported attacks, experts attribute the rise to better reporting and an increase in the number of people involved in water activities, rather than an increase in shark aggressiveness. In 2014, there were 72 reported attacks on humans around the world, three fewer than in 2013.

In another incident, a 16-year-old boy from Colorado lost part of his arm and suffered a leg injury in a shark attack in Oak Island, North Carolina, last Sunday. This prompted the town to consider a temporary ban on shark fishing, a move already undertaken by several cities along the East Coast.

Fishing piers can attract sharks due to the live bait in the water and the refuge offered by the piers' pilings. Experts advise swimming farther away from piers, regardless of whether a shark fishing ban is in place.

In response to the attacks, some towns in Florida have considered bans on shark fishing, but it's unclear whether such bans are effective. The act of fishing attracts animals to the bait, and if fishing is taking place in an area where people are swimming, it could potentially increase the likelihood of an attack.

The International Shark Attack File report compiled by the Florida Museum of Natural History and the University of Florida shows that there were only five shark bites reported in South Carolina waters in 2014, and just four in North Carolina last year, part of a gradual increase in recent years.

Derek Jeter and Minka Kelly, a couple for over three years, have ended their relationship. The split was amicable, and they remain friends. Jeter is currently playing for the NY Yankees, while Kelly is filming the reboot of Charlie's Angels in Miami. Last month, a documentary about Jeter's achievement of 3,000 hits as a shortstop premiered. Both stars are expected to move on following the breakup.

Genevieve Kelley, a woman who was wanted for kidnapping her daughter and unlawful flight since 2004, turned herself in on Monday. The whereabouts of her now 18-year-old daughter are still unknown. Kelley and her husband, Scott Kelley, fled New Hampshire with Mary Nunes, who was 8 at the time, after allegations of mistreatment by Mark Nunes, Mary's father, who had full custody rights. The U.S. Marshals Service was involved in efforts to locate Mary Nunes and the Kelleys, spanning the United States, Canada, and Central and South America. Genevieve Kelley was featured as the U.S. Marshals Service "Fugitive of the Week" in New Hampshire, coinciding with the nationally televised story of Mary Nunes and her kidnappers aired on CNN's "The Hunt." After Genevieve Kelley surrendered, U.S. Marshal David Cargill Jr. stated, "I am happy that (she) is in custody and will face justice for these charges, but we will all be the happiest, when we know Mary Nunes is safe." Scott Kelley is still considered a fugitive and is being sought by the Marshals Service. The arrest of Genevieve Kelley came the same day authorities in Texas announced that remains found in September were confirmed to be those of another fugitive, Kevin Patrick Stoeser, also featured on CNN's "The Hunt." Stoeser was a U.S. soldier who was dishonorably discharged, pleaded guilty in 2003 to child sexual assault and child pornography charges, and was sentenced to 13 years behind bars. Remains of another suspect featured on the "The Hunt" were also found earlier this year, and another suspect who was profiled on the show was killed in a gun battle with authorities. In August, the remains of Shane Miller were found in California. Miller was the prime suspect in the deaths of his wife and two young daughters. Mark Nunes, Mary's father, fondly remembers the last days he spent with his daughter before she disappeared with her mother and stepfather in 2003.

A high school senior, identified as Jacqueline Gomez, was found dead in a hotel room in north Houston on the morning following MacArthur High School's prom. The incident occurred at the Hyatt Hotel off the North Sam Houston Parkway. Authorities are investigating the cause of death, with initial reports suggesting alcohol and prescription painkillers may have been involved. The prom seemed to be a normal affair for those attending, but things got out of hand at the after-party. The boyfriend of the deceased girl has been cooperative with the police and there is no suspicion that he contributed to her death. Another prom, for Aldine High School, was held at the same hotel the following night. The tragic event has made some students think twice about their post-prom activities. The deceased girl, Jacqueline Gomez, was a senior at MacArthur High School and had been looking forward to prom. She had struggled with school as a sophomore but had made it through her senior year and was planning to take classes to become a pharmacy technician. The autopsy results are still pending and the Aldine ISD officials could not be reached for comment.

On Tuesday, an envelope containing a substance that tested positive for the toxic substance ricin was intercepted at the U.S. Capitol's off-site mail facility. The envelope was addressed to Sen. Roger Wicker (R-Mississippi). Preliminary tests indicate the presence of ricin, but additional testing is needed for a full analysis. The Senate mail facility has been closed for further testing, and all mail bound for Capitol Hill is being directed through a U.S. House facility. The Capitol complex has not been affected. A suspect has been identified, but no one is in custody as of Tuesday night. Sen. Claire McCaskill (D-Mo.) said members were briefed about the incident, and state offices have been told what to look for if there are more letters containing the toxic substance. Ricin is a highly toxic substance derived from castor beans, and there is no specific test for exposure or antidote once exposed. The letter had a Memphis, Tennessee, postmark and no return address. This is not the first time ricin has been found in the Capitol; in 2004, tests identified a letter in a Senate mailroom that served then-Majority Leader Bill Frist's office. Wicker, who was first appointed to the U.S. Senate in 2007, has been assigned a protective detail. The FBI and Homeland Security are investigating the incident.

Norway's Prime Minister Erna Solberg has issued an official apology for the mistreatment of Norwegian women who had intimate relationships with German soldiers during World War II. Approximately 50,000 Norwegian women are believed to have had such relationships, encouraged by SS leader Heinrich Himmler as part of Nazi Germany's white supremacist agenda.

The women, known as the "German Girls," were subjected to reprisals after Norway's liberation in 1945, including job dismissals, detentions, expulsions, and removal of nationality. Many were expelled from the country with their children.

Solberg stated that the women were victims of undignified treatment and that Norwegian authorities violated the fundamental principle that no citizen can be punished without trial or sentenced without law. She acknowledged that for many, these relationships were just teenage love or the love of their lives with an enemy soldier, and that the treatment left a lasting impact on their lives.

The apology was based on a report about Norway's post-war actions published by the country's Centre for Holocaust and Minorities Studies. Historian Guri Hjeltnes presented the study, stating that the women's only crime was breaking unwritten rules.

Reidar Gabler, whose mother was expelled in 1945 along with her German husband, attended the event and expressed that the apology was important for history. He stated that while many of the women directly affected are no longer alive, the apology also touches their families and children.

Norway had previously apologized to the estimated 10,000 to 12,000 children born as a result of relationships between Norwegian mothers and German soldiers in 2000. These children faced reprisals, including being placed in host families or special institutions and later battling for compensation.

The apology comes 70 years after the UN's Universal Declaration of Human Rights and serves as a reminder of the lasting impact of World War II on individuals and families.

On Saturday afternoon in Brooklyn, an FBI agent was shot while conducting surveillance for a drug investigation. The incident occurred near the corner of E. 92nd Street and Avenue N in Canarsie. The agent was shot in the shoulder and managed to return fire before the suspects fled. One suspect was later arrested at Kingsbrook Jewish Medical Center, seeking treatment for at least one gunshot wound. The second suspect was captured outside a business nearby on Remsen Avenue. The agent was rushed to Kings County Hospital with injuries that aren't believed to be life-threatening. The investigation is ongoing, and it's unclear what sparked the shootout or what the agent was surveilling at the time. The suspect in custody is in surgery for a gunshot wound to the hand, while the acquaintance who drove him to the hospital is being held on a charge of driving with a suspended license. No outstanding suspects are at large, according to NYPD Chief of Department Terence Monahan. The agent is expected to make a speedy recovery.

A strong 6.0-magnitude earthquake struck Northern California on August 24, 2014, with the epicenter near Napa Valley's renowned wineries. The earthquake caused significant damage, including broken wine barrels and bottles of precious vintages. Over 170 people were injured, and 100 homes were declared uninhabitable by state officials.

In the aftermath, volunteers and workers from various communities, including Home Depot, offered their help in the cleanup efforts. Lori Lemieux, a resident whose home was damaged in the earthquake, was touched by the teamwork and kindness of strangers. Premysl Balaz, a 33-year-old engineer from the Czech Republic, was one of the volunteers who helped build a database of red-tagged homes.

Across town, Patricia Trimble, the owner of a vintage store, received help from Marc Liotta, a Walnut Creek contractor, who offered his services and transportation to help with the cleanup. Liotta, who is semi-retired and has a history of volunteering for Habitat for Humanity and assisting in disaster-stricken areas, was moved by the community's spirit of helping each other.

The cleanup efforts were coordinated at the Grace Church of Napa Valley, where congregants prayed and then offered their help to those in need. Tim and Ann Whitlock, a couple whose home was severely damaged, received assistance from fellow congregants who helped pack their belongings into boxes and containers. Across town, Patricia Trimble's vintage store was also helped by volunteers.

The earthquake was the largest to hit the Bay Area in a quarter-century, and aftershocks continued to occur. California Governor Jerry Brown declared a state of emergency, and cleanup efforts were underway. The USGS and state geologists were working to determine the exact fault that caused the earthquake, with the West Napa Fault being the leading suspect.

The earthquake brought forward-reaching technology into focus, as the University of California, Berkeley's Seismological Laboratory received a 10-second warning before the shaking started. The warning could have been improved with an upgrade to the ShakeAlert system, which would have boosted the response time of the slowest seismometer by 2.5 seconds. The state legislature approved a bill to expand the system statewide in 2013, but the Office of Emergency Services must find $80 million to pay for it.

The earthquake is likely to bring new focus to Napa Valley's earthquake hazard, and more researchers will likely begin studies analyzing the earthquake and its causes. The recovery will require time and money, but residents are grateful that the damage wasn't worse. The two people who were most seriously injured in the earthquake, including a 13-year-old Napa boy struck by a crumbling chimney, were said to be improving and were expected to survive.

The U.S. jobs report for March, released on April 1, 2016, showed a solid month of hiring with 215,000 jobs added. The increase in employment was driven by large gains in the construction, retail, and health care industries. Despite the unemployment rate ticking up to 5% from 4.9%, this increase was due to more Americans coming off the sidelines to look for work.

The report suggests that employers remain confident in their business prospects, even as overall growth has slowed since last winter. Wage growth, however, remains a weak spot in the economy, with pay rising a modest 2.3% from a year earlier to $25.43.

Construction firms added 37,000 jobs, while manufacturing and mining sectors experienced job losses. The manufacturing sector has been hit by slower growth overseas, and the mining sector, including oil and gas drilling, has lost 185,000 jobs since September 2014 due to low oil prices.

Steady hiring is contributing to higher pay, but the rate of wage growth is below the peak of 2.6% reached in December 2015. Sluggish wage growth has been a persistent issue since the Great Recession ended in 2009, with paychecks typically growing at a 3.5% pace in a strong economy.

Consumer spending, a critical source of growth, has faltered since last winter after healthy gains in 2015. Americans have been saving more of their savings from lower gas prices rather than spending it. Other economic data has been mixed, with manufacturers potentially stabilizing after a difficult 2015, but home-buying activity has slowed due to a lack of available supply.

In summary, the U.S. jobs report for March shows a solid month of hiring, but wage growth remains a concern. Consumer spending and home-buying activity have slowed, while manufacturers may be stabilizing after a difficult year.

The Pepsi advertisement featuring Kendall Jenner has been widely criticized for trivialized protests for social justice causes. The ad shows Jenner joining a crowd of protesters and handing a can of Pepsi to a police officer, which critics say evokes a photo of Black Lives Matter protester Ieshia Evans. Pepsi initially defended the ad, but later apologized and pulled it, stating that they "missed the mark." The ad was criticized on social media, with many calling it "gloriously tone-deaf." The company had previously described the spot as featuring "multiple lives, stories and emotional connections that show passion, joy, unbound and uninhibited moments."

The ad was also mocked by late-night comedians, with Stephen Colbert joking that the ad was for "Attractive Lives Matter" and that the signs held by the protesters were "the most corporate message ever." Colbert also pointed out the absurdity of Jenner doing a fashion shoot while ripping off her wig.

In Walnut Creek, a 21-year-old former Stanford University student named Scott Bertics is suspected of murdering his ex-girlfriend, Clare Orton, 19, and then taking his own life on July 21st. The murder-suicide occurred at Orton's family home. According to police, Bertics built the two untraceable "ghost guns" he used from parts he ordered online, making them at home. These guns, which contained no serial numbers, are often referred to as "ghost guns" because they can be assembled without a background check.

Orton was home for the summer from San Diego State University, where she was an honors student majoring in environmental engineering. Bertics, a 2012 graduate of Acalanes High School in Lafayette, had also studied at Stanford University, majoring in electrical engineering and computer sciences before taking a leave of absence after the fall 2014 semester.

Police said there was no evidence that the retailers sold Bertics the gun parts illegally. The homemade guns usually include unfinished lower receivers, the critical mechanism from which bullets are fired. Lower receivers normally require serial numbers, but incomplete ones can be bought as just simple pieces of metal.

In September 2014, Governor Jerry Brown vetoed a bill that would have tightened laws on unregistered guns built with parts purchased online and delivered through the mail. The bill, proposed by state Sen. Kevin de León, D-Los Angeles, would have banned the sale of gun parts unless they had serial numbers and required buyers to go through background checks. At the time, De León warned that criminals, gang members, and anyone else who wants to avoid background checks can get the parts through the mail and assemble their own guns. In his veto message, Brown said, “I appreciate the author’s concerns about gun violence, but I can’t see how adding a serial number to a homemade gun would significantly advance public safety.”

The motive behind Bertics' actions remains unknown, but police have not found any evidence suggesting anyone else was involved or had knowledge of his plans prior to the tragedy. The investigation is still ongoing.

The Boulder police and prosecutors are planning a new round of DNA tests on key evidence in the unsolved 1996 murder of 6-year-old JonBenet Ramsey, according to a joint investigation by 9NEWS and the Boulder Daily Camera.

The move comes in the wake of serious flaws in the interpretation of previous DNA testing on the panties and long johns the girl was wearing when she was killed late on Christmas night in 1996, or early the next morning.

Boulder County District Attorney Stan Garnett and Boulder Police Chief Greg Testa both confirmed Tuesday that they and members of their staffs recently discussed the issue with Colorado Bureau of Investigation administrators, who are on the verge of unveiling new, more sophisticated DNA tests than their lab has ever used before.

The meeting took place shortly before Thanksgiving, Testa said. "We did meet with CBI and the district attorney's office, and we had a general discussion about evidence in the Ramsey case, including new technology and DNA testing," Testa said. "And we are going to take a look at the new technology, and see how they may help us further this investigation."

Garnett said he saw no reason to use an outside lab. "I'm confident that CBI can do what needs to be done at this time," he said.

The testing would be conducted with new, more sensitive "kits" required of crime labs by the FBI's Combined DNA Index System, the database that includes genetic profiles from more than 15.1 million known offenders and arrestees and more than 738,000 unsolved cases.

The 9NEWS/Camera investigation found that DNA evidence in the case doesn't support the controversial decision by former District Attorney Mary Lacy to clear the girl's family members from all suspicion in her death.

The two news organizations obtained exclusive access to the test results, laboratory notes, reports and correspondence relating to testing conducted in 2008, at Lacy's request, by a forensic laboratory in Virginia then-known as Bode Technology.

Multiple forensic experts who examined that evidence on behalf of 9NEWS and the Camera disputed all of Lacy's conclusions with regard to the DNA.

For example, they determined that male DNA located in JonBenet's panties and in two spots on her long johns contained genetic material from at least two people in addition to the 6-year-old. As a result, they suggested that the "profile" entered into the FBI's CODIS database in 2003 — dubbed Unknown Male 1 by investigators in the case — may not be the profile of an individual at all, but a conglomeration of genetic material from multiple people.

At the same time, the experts disputed Lacy's conclusions that the genetic material in the long johns "matched" the DNA in the panties, that there was no innocent explanation for its presence on the girl's clothing, and that it therefore had to belong to the killer.

And 9Wants To Know and the Camera found that Lacy was told of the results' ambiguities before she issued her controversial letter on July 9, 2008, clearing JonBenet's parents, John and Patsy, and her brother Burke of any suspicion in her murder.

DNA data base standards to change

Experts who reviewed the DNA evidence and emails between Lacy's office and Bode Technology were concerned that Lacy's approach showed signs of a phenomenon known as confirmation bias — an investigation tainted by a desire to reach a hoped-for result.

Lacy established herself as a strong supporter of the theory that an intruder killed JonBenet, dating back to her time as a chief deputy in the district attorney's office immediately following the murder.

As one example, then-DA's investigator Andy Horita wrote to the lab on March 12, 2008, that his bosses were "very excited" and "pleased" about the results that were being reported, and that "we're happy with what has been done and don't see the need for additional testing" unless strongly recommended by the lab.

An email one month earlier from Horita had alluded to the lab's assignment as an exercise "to validate the existing CODIS profile by eliminating point-of-manufacture controversies."

This, independent experts have said, runs contrary to the spirit of "double-blind" standards to which such testing should adhere.

Lacy, who left office in 2009 after serving two terms as Boulder's top prosecutor, has not responded to multiple requests for comment.

Phillip Danielson, a professor of molecular biology at the University of Denver and science adviser to the National Law Enforcement and Corrections Technology Center, said that new testing makes sense.

In 2017, the CODIS lab is going to begin requiring more sophisticated DNA tests that identify at least 20 individual points of comparison — as opposed to the standard of 13 required since 1997. All accredited DNA labs, including the one operated by the CBI, will have to use the new testing kits.

The testing done at Bode in 2008 was undertaken using a DNA kit known as Identifiler, which has the capability of identifying genetic markers at as many as 16 separate spots, known as loci. Thirteen of these loci comprise the FBI's core requirement for inclusion in the CODIS database

The now-contested sample from the Ramsey case that was entered into CODIS in December 2003 had the bare minimum of 10 loci, or genetic markers.

Experts endorse further testing

Danielson, one of the experts consulted by 9NEWS and the Camera, reiterated his belief that JonBenet's long johns and panties should be subjected to DNA testing called Y-STR that identifies only male genetic material.

"I still think that the best thing they could probably do in the JonBenet case is figure how many males are on the long johns, and how many are in the underwear, 'cause that's sort of a key point," Danielson said. "And the way to do that is to focus on the Y chromosome and amplify that. If there's two males there, we'll see it. If there's one male there, we'll see it."

Another of the experts consulted by 9NEWS and the Camera, the University of Colorado's Christopher McKee, concurred.

The diplomatic Quartet, consisting of Hillary Clinton (US Secretary of State), Sergei Lavrov (Russian foreign minister), Ban Ki-moon (UN Secretary General), and Baroness Ashton (EU foreign affairs representative), will meet at the UN headquarters in New York for the first time in six months. Portland Police Chief Michael Reese announced the reopening of a 2009 investigation into sexual assault allegations against former Vice President Al Gore, citing "procedural issues" with the original investigation. The initial investigation was closed in 2009 due to insufficient evidence, but Reese stated that command-level supervisors should have reviewed the case and made the decision on whether the investigation should proceed when the complainant, Molly Hagerty, came forward last year.

In 2006, Hagerty, a Portland massage therapist, accused Gore of groping and kissing her during a late-night massage at the Hotel Lucia. However, the police never contacted Gore, and detectives failed to consult with the Multnomah County district attorney's office. The case was closed due to Hagerty's lack of cooperation.

The Svalbard Global Seed Vault, a facility designed to safeguard global food supplies by storing backup seeds for seed banks worldwide, recently experienced water leaks due to high temperatures and unusual rainfall in the Svalbard area last fall. The seeds and the vault were never at risk, and the leaks have since stopped. The seeds are stored in a vault built into the rock of the mountain, while the tunnel leading to the entrance is designed to allow for water intrusion during the spring melt, which has occurred every year since the vault's construction.

The vault, operated by the Crop Trust, holds backups of seeds from seed banks around the world, with the goal of preserving crop diversity in the face of changing climate, natural disasters, and human conflicts. It has more than 860,000 samples, from almost all nations.

In a separate development, Syria's civil war has prompted the first withdrawal of seeds from the Svalbard Global Seed Vault. The seeds, including samples of wheat, barley, and grasses suited to dry regions, have been requested by researchers elsewhere in the Middle East to replace seeds in a gene bank near the Syrian city of Aleppo that has been damaged by the war. The seeds will be sent once paperwork is completed, and it would be the first withdrawal from the vault.

The seeds from the Aleppo collection have traits resistant to drought, which could help breed crops to withstand climate change in dry areas from Australia to Africa. The vault is designed to protect crop seeds against the worst cataclysms of nuclear war or disease and has been operating for over nine years.

This document summarizes various outbreaks of Marburg virus disease, a rare and severe hemorrhagic fever, from 1967 to 2012. The first outbreak occurred in Germany and Yugoslavia, where it was traced back to laboratory monkeys imported from Uganda. Since then, there have been 12 recorded outbreaks, most involving only a single patient.

In 1975, an outbreak occurred in South Africa, infecting a man who had recently traveled to Zimbabwe. The infection spread to his traveling companion and a nurse at the hospital, but both women recovered after receiving vigorous supportive treatment.

In 1980, an outbreak occurred in Kenya, where a man died despite specialized care in Nairobi. A doctor who attempted resuscitation developed symptoms nine days later but recovered.

In 1987, an outbreak occurred in Kenya, resulting in the death of a 15-year-old Danish boy who had visited Kitum Cave in Mount Elgon National Park. No further cases were detected.

In 1990, an outbreak occurred in Russia due to laboratory contamination.

In 1998-2000, an outbreak occurred in the Democratic Republic of Congo, primarily affecting young male workers at a gold mine in Durba. Cases were subsequently detected in the neighboring village of Watsa.

In 2004-2005, an outbreak occurred in Angola, believed to have begun in Uige Province. Most cases detected in other provinces were linked directly to the outbreak in Uige.

In 2007, a small outbreak occurred in Uganda, with four cases in young males working in a mine. To date, there have been no additional cases identified.

In 2008, an outbreak occurred in the USA, ex Uganda, with a U.S traveler returning from Uganda developing the illness four days after returning. A Dutch woman also developed the illness after a recent history of travel to Uganda and died in the Netherlands.

In 2012, an outbreak occurred in Uganda, with 15 cases identified in the districts of Kabale, Ibanda, Mbarara, and Kampala over a 3-week time period.

Marburg virus causes symptoms similar to Ebola, beginning with fever and weakness and often leading to internal or external bleeding, organ failure, and death. The death rate runs as high as 80 percent, although it was significantly lower in the initial outbreak when patients were cared for in relatively modern, European hospitals.

The most recent outbreak, also in Uganda, in 2021, resulted in the death of a 30-year-old hospital technician. Health officials quarantined about 80 people who came into contact with the victim, one of whom developed the early symptoms of the disease. As of October 5, 2021, testing on 11 potential cases of Marburg came back negative, including that of the victim's brother. Those who still show symptoms similar to Marburg three days from now will be re-tested at that time.

There is no cure for the virus, and like Ebola, Marburg can have a high death rate for those infected. However, Uganda has previously successfully handled similar situations of health threats involving Hemorrhagic fevers. The country's prime minister, Dr. Ruhakana Rugunda, stated that Uganda has experience and adequate capacity to deal with this health threat and that World Health Organisation has been informed.

In a historic victory, the United States defeated Mexico in a friendly soccer match held in Mexico City on August 15, 2012. Michael Orozco Fiscal scored the only goal of the game in the 80th minute, marking his first international goal. The Americans dominated for most of the night, with key contributions from Brek Shea, Terrence Boyd, and goalkeeper Tim Howard, who made several crucial saves to preserve the lead. California has announced a change in its sex-offender residency rules, moving away from a blanket ban on living within 2,000 feet of a school or park. Instead, the restrictions will be applied on a case-by-case basis. This decision follows a state Supreme Court ruling in San Diego County, which found that the previous law, known as Jessica's Law, was unconstitutional and did not effectively protect the public.

The change is expected to ease restrictions for some offenders, while maintaining them for those who have sexually abused children. The review of thousands of sex-offender parolee cases is expected to take two months. High-risk sex offenders with a current or prior conviction for lewd acts on a child under 14 will still be prohibited from living within a half-mile of any K-12 school.

Critics of the previous law argued that the strict residency restrictions led many sex offenders to become transients, as they struggled to find housing more than 2,000 feet from schools and parks in urban counties. The change is likely to affect densely populated counties like San Francisco.

However, the decision to loosen the restrictions has drawn criticism from George Runner, a former Republican state senator and author of Jessica's Law. Runner believes that the changes go beyond what the court intended and contradict the will of the voters who supported the law.

California currently has 6,000 sex offender parolees living in communities across the state, all of whom are required to register for life with police and disclose their address on a publicly searchable database, established under "Megan's Law."

In explaining his decision to unseal the deposition, US District Judge Eduardo Robreno cited the "stark contrast" between "Bill Cosby, the public moralist," and "Bill Cosby, the subject of serious allegations."

In the deposition, Cosby said he had engaged in consensual sexual activity with Constand and that he had obtained Quaaludes in order to give them to women with whom he wanted to have sex. The unsealed deposition was central to Cosby's arrest in December 2015.

Cosby has no plans to testify. His public persona, the large number of accusers, and the lack of forensic evidence make the trial likely to hinge on a classic case of "he said, she said."

Cosby solidified his stardom as Dr. Cliff Huxtable in "The Cosby Show." Prosecutors had sought to include testimony from 13 other accusers, but Judge Steven O'Neill ruled that would be too prejudicial.

Cosby has said he does not plan to testify. His deposition from the civil suit will stand as his explanation of what happened, and the trial is likely to hinge on a classic case of "he said, she said."

A 1,000-year-old Chinese 'Ding' bowl, initially purchased for $3 at a garage sale in 2007, was sold for a staggering $2.2 million at Sotheby's. The bowl, which dates back to the 10th or 11th century, is one of only two known bowls of its kind, with the other being housed in the British Museum.

'Ding' bowls are renowned for their thin potting, fine white body, and ivory-colored glaze that tends to run down in 'tears'. The bowl's decoration features an incised lotus spray design on the interior and overlapping leaves on the exterior, showcasing a spontaneous and free style.

The kiln site for 'Ding' ware is located in Quyang, Ding county, Hebei province. Early 'Ding' wares were small and utilitarian, with ornamental bowls mimicking more elaborate gold and silver wares common in palaces. The bowl's name, 'Ding', is derived from the county where the kilns were housed.

The bowl's new owner, London art dealer Giuseppe Eskenazi, beat four other bidders for the piece. Eskenazi, who previously paid $23.5 million for a rare blue-and-white jar from the 14th century, is no stranger to high-value purchases. The bowl's previous owner, a family from New York state, kept the bowl on their mantle for years before deciding to sell it.

This incident follows another recent discovery in a Long Island garage, where a collection of abstract Impressionist art was appraised at $30 million. The art, by Armenian-American artist Arthur Pinajian, was later shown at the Antiquorum Gallery in Midtown.

Masaaki Osaka, a notorious fugitive and suspected murderer in Japan, has been arrested after more than 45 years of evading authorities. The 67-year-old is accused of murdering a police officer during a Tokyo street protest in 1971, allegedly setting the officer on fire using a Molotov Cocktail petrol bomb.

Osaka was initially arrested in May for an unrelated minor offense, but his identity was confirmed through DNA tests. He was found in a Hiroshima apartment belonging to the Japan Revolutionary Communist League (JRCL), a radical left-wing group.

The JRCL, established in the late 1950s, was known for staging violent street protests, particularly against the recognition of the US military presence in Japan. Osaka is alleged to have assaulted the police officer with a steel pipe before setting him alight during a left-wing riot in Tokyo's Shibuya Ward in 1971.

Japan has no statute of limitations for murder, and Osaka's case is the longest a suspected criminal has spent evading arrest. The 15-year time limit was abolished in 2010. Osaka has remained silent since his arrest and is currently being transported from Hiroshima to Tokyo for further questioning.

The arrest of Masaaki Osaka marks the end of a long-standing manhunt and brings closure to a tragic event that has been a part of Japan's history for more than four decades.

Playboy, the iconic men's magazine founded by Hugh Hefner in 1953, has announced a significant change in its content strategy. Playboy's logo, featuring a rabbit head wearing a bow tie, is one of the most recognizable in the world. The company makes most of its money from licensing its brand for products including toiletries, drinks, and jewelry. About 40% of merchandising income is generated in China, where the magazine itself is not available.

Playboy has a rich history of notable interviews, including conversations with Martin Luther King Jr, Malcolm X, Jimmy Carter, Miles Davis, Vladimir Nabokov, and John Lennon and Yoko Ono. The Library of Congress in Washington produces a Braille version of Playboy for the blind and visually-impaired.

In the past, Playboy has been known for its riffing off business stories, such as a "Women of Wall Street" series in 1989. The magazine's attempts at a younger audience may face challenges in balancing its traditional identity and attracting a new demographic.

Assembly Bill 1884, introduced by California Majority Leader Ian Calderon, proposes a legislation that would require sit-down restaurants to offer plastic straws only upon request, with potential penalties of up to six months in jail and/or a fine not exceeding $1,000. However, Calderon clarified that the tough penalties will be amended during the legislative process. The bill does not aim to ban plastic straws but is intended to reduce environmental damage from plastic waste and raise awareness about the environmental impact of straws.

Approximately 500 million straws are used daily in the U.S., with only 9% of all plastics being recycled, and straws being non-recyclable due to their small size and lack of a resin code. After use, non-biodegradable plastic straws often end up in oceans and waterways, where they break down into micro-size pieces that can harm marine life. An estimated 500 million straws are used in the United States every day, with straws and stirrers ranking as the 6th most common item collected during California's Coastal Cleanup Day between 1989 and 2014. AB 1884 is a step towards lowering these alarming figures and encouraging consumers to change their plastic use behavior.

In an emotional open letter, Hans de Borst, a grieving father who lost his daughter Elsemiek de Borst in the missile attack on Malaysia Airlines Flight 17, addressed Russian President Vladimir Putin. De Borst accused Putin and Russian-backed separatists of being responsible for the downing of the commercial passenger jet on July 17, 2014. The Boeing 777 was en route from Amsterdam to Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, carrying Elsemiek, her mother, stepfather, and little brother. Elsemiek, a 17-year-old student, was looking forward to studying engineering at the Delft technical university. In his letter, de Borst expressed his anger and sorrow, stating that the lives of his family were ruined due to the tragic event. The letter was published by the Hart Van Nederland newspaper on Monday. This incident is part of an ongoing investigation into the downing of MH17, with the Dutch Safety Board and the Joint Investigation Team continuing to gather evidence to determine responsibility.

Judge Mitchell Nance, a family court judge in Kentucky, has announced that he will no longer hear adoption cases involving gay parents, citing his personal beliefs as a matter of conscience. Nance's decision has sparked controversy, with some supporting his stance and others viewing it as discriminatory and a violation of his duty to uphold the law.

Nance issued an order on Thursday stating that he believes allowing a "practicing homosexual" to adopt would not promote the best interest of the child. He disqualified himself from any adoption cases involving gay couples, citing judicial ethics codes requiring judges to recuse themselves when they have a personal bias or prejudice.

The announcement has drawn criticism from some lawyers and judicial ethics experts who view Nance's blanket statement as discriminatory and a sign that he is not fit to fulfill his duties as a judge. Kentucky state law permits gay couples to adopt children, and the U.S. Supreme Court ruled in 2015 that all states must allow same-sex marriage.

Nance's recusal has been compared to the case of Rowan County Clerk Kim Davis, who was jailed after refusing to issue marriage licenses to same-sex couples in 2015. Nance told The Washington Post that he stands by his order, based on the law and his conscience. He declined to comment further on the order or calls for him to resign.

The judge of the other division in Nance's court, Judge John T. Alexander, has said that he will hear any adoption cases affected by Nance's recusal. Gay parents seeking to adopt a child in the affected counties should not expect a legal delay as a result of Nance's decision.

Charles Geyh, an Indiana University law school professor who specializes in judicial ethics, told the Louisville Courier-Journal that Nance could be violating his oath to uphold the law by issuing such an order. Geyh said that if Nance is unable to set his personal views aside and uphold the law, it raises questions about his ability to honor his oath.

Chris Hartman, director of the Kentucky Fairness Campaign, called Nance's decision not to hear adoption cases for gay parents "clear discrimination." Hartman said that if Nance cannot deliver impartiality, fairness, and justice to all families in his courtroom, then he should not be a judge.

Yet other groups, such as the Family Foundation, a Lexington-based group that promotes "family-first conservatism," have expressed their support of the judge's decision to recuse himself. The group's spokesman, Martin Cothran, said that if judges are going to write their personal biases and prejudices into law, then judges with different views should be allowed to recuse themselves from such cases.

Nance has performed marriages but has never been asked to marry a gay couple. If he were asked, Nance said he would decline. Nance told the Glasgow Daily Times that he could recall being assigned to two adoption cases involving gay parents, including one from which he recused himself several years ago. About two to three months ago, Nance was assigned to a case in Metcalfe County involving a same-sex couple seeking to adopt. Nance said he ruled in favor of the parents, but decided then he should take action to recuse himself permanently from hearing such cases.

The document discusses an upcoming community town hall in Dearborn, Michigan on April 29th, titled "Rejecting Islamophobia: A Community Stand Against Hate." The event aims to address the persistent issue of anti-Arab and anti-Muslim bias, which has been a problem in the community. The Arab American community in Michigan has faced various challenges, such as politicizing community festivals and visits from controversial figures like Terry Jones. The latest challenge is the "Jessica Mokdad Human Rights Conference" organized by Pamela Geller and Robert Spencer, which is being criticized for exploiting the tragedy of a young Arab American girl to promote a bigoted agenda.

The town hall, organized by the Arab American Institute, will feature AAI President Jim Zogby, Executive Director Maya Berry, and other community, interfaith, and religious leaders, as well as Michigan public officials. The goal is to challenge the narrative presented by the conference and have a community conversation about how to respond to these continued attacks. The event is a response to the Islamophobic conference and a stand against the politics of division and bigotry promoted by the Islamophobes.

The document also includes unrelated articles about the best places for ice fishing in the US, best backcountry skiing in North America, and America's best Christkindl markets.

Former President George W. Bush canceled a scheduled visit to Switzerland due to potential legal action and protests against him. Bush was invited to speak at a Jewish charity gala in Geneva on February 12, but leftist groups planned to protest his visit, and human rights organizations filed criminal complaints against him for alleged torture during his presidency. The complaints allege Bush ordered the use of waterboarding, a technique considered a form of torture by many human rights experts.

Swiss officials stated that Bush would be protected with diplomatic immunity as a former head of state, but a right-wing member of the Swiss parliament called for his arrest on war crimes allegations. Keren Hayesod, the group that invited Bush, stated that the court actions against him did not play a role in their decision to cancel his participation in the gala.

Human rights groups, including Human Rights Watch and the International Federation of Human Rights (FIDH), stated that Bush canceled his trip to avoid legal action. They plan to submit a 2,500-page complaint against Bush in Geneva on Monday for alleged mistreatment of suspected militants at Guantanamo Bay. The groups claim that Bush's cancellation shows that he is avoiding accountability for his actions.

Sami El Hadjj, a former Al Jazeera journalist and former detainee at Guantanamo, was due to speak at the news conference where the complaint will be released. Reed Brody, counsel for Human Rights Watch, stated that Bush's world is a small place at the moment and that he may enjoy some level of impunity in the United States, but other countries will not treat him so indulgently.

The article discusses the ongoing Syrian civil war and the resulting refugee crisis, which is described as the most challenging in a generation. The conflict, which began in March 2011, has led to the displacement of millions of people, with the United Nations predicting that the number of refugees could reach 3.5 million by the end of the year.

The article focuses on the experiences of one family, the Deebs, who fled their home in Syria due to fighting between Syrian rebels and government forces. The family traveled to Kilis, Turkey, in search of safety, but found themselves living in a gravel-strewn field across from a Turkish-run camp, with no access to basic amenities. The family, along with hundreds of other Syrians, are squatting in this makeshift camp, living under plastic sheets and struggling to survive.

The article also discusses the challenges faced by the host countries, including Turkey, Lebanon, Jordan, and Iraq, in accommodating the large number of refugees. The influx of refugees has put a strain on resources and has led to increased tensions in host communities.

The article also touches on the fears that the refugees may import the conflict into the host countries, and destabilize borders. The Turkish border, in particular, is described as porous and lawless, with criminal gangs thriving in the cross-border smuggling of goods.

The article concludes by noting that the fighting continues in Syria, with no end in sight, and that the refugee crisis is expected to last for years. The United Nations and other international organizations are working to provide aid to the refugees and support the host communities, but the situation remains dire. The article is accompanied by a series of photographs depicting the destruction and violence in Syria, as well as the struggles of the refugees in Turkey.

The Internet Archive is working on a project to archive web pages as they are created and preserve links to archived versions of pages that are changed or removed. This project aims to fix broken links on the web. Former Louisiana Governor Edwin Edwards, a controversial figure known for his prison sentence, reality TV show, and quotable quotes, announced his comeback bid for Congress on March 17, 2014. Edwards served four terms as governor and is pursuing the vacant 6th Congressional District seat being vacated by Republican Bill Cassidy, who is running for Senate. Edwards' candidacy is considered a longshot due to the district's Republican leanings, but he has already filed his candidacy papers and chosen a treasurer. Edwards' campaign focuses on improving accessibility to healthcare, criticizing Republican Governor Bobby Jindal for refusing to accept expanded Medicaid coverage under Obamacare. Edwards served three terms as a congressman before becoming governor in 1971 and has a long and divisive political career, including a conviction on 17 counts of bribery, extortion, and fraud charges in 2000. Edwards spent more than eight years in federal prison, where he met his third wife, Trina Scott, who was 50 years his junior. The couple starred in a reality TV show last year. Edwards' son, Eli, was born in August 2013. Edwards' campaign has been met with skepticism, with some calling it a publicity stunt, but Edwards has expressed confidence in his ability to win.

The article discusses the residency controversy surrounding Wisconsin Republican Frank Lasee, a state senator who is running for the vacant 8th District seat in the U.S. House of Representatives. Lasee is facing questions about his residency due to his advertising of a two-bedroom apartment in De Pere, Wisconsin, on Airbnb.com for rent, which raised suspicions as he also owns a house in Racine, in the district of House Speaker Paul D. Ryan.

Reporters at the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel tried to book Lasee's apartment for one day last month, prompting questions from Lasee's wife, Amy Joy Lasee, who denied the request. The listing was then removed from Airbnb. Lasee initially declined to explain why the listing was taken down, stating "Because we wanted to." He later said they didn't want "everyone in the world looking at it."

Lasee explained that he has a "crazy living arrangement," living most of the time at the apartment but occasionally staying at the Racine house. He also speculated that backers of his primary opponent were the ones bringing up the issue. Lasee has a history of residency issues, as Democrats had filed a complaint about his residence with the state Government Accountability Board during a previous election, which was dismissed after he produced a 2011 lease.

The article also mentions Lasee's fundraising event at the home of big-time GOP donor Michael Eisenga, who has a history of self-dealing and a failed pay-to-play effort for a state law change. The article ends with a comment from Scot Ross, head of the liberal group One Wisconsin Now, stating that Eisenga now has his sights set on federal law, and that Lasee, with his history of residency issues, is an ideal target.

Sant Gopaldas, a Ganga activist, was admitted to the All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS) in Rishikesh on October 13 after a 15-day fast against mining operations at the Ganga river bed. He is currently being treated at the endocrinology ward, with his sugar level reportedly at 65. Gopaldas had been fasting at Triveni and Bag ghats of the Ganga in Rishikesh since June 24. His condition has prompted the administration to give permission to AIIMS authorities to take necessary measures, including force-feeding, to save his life.

The death of another prominent environmental activist, G.D. Agarwal, on October 11, at the age of 86, after a 118-day hunger strike to protest against government inaction on cleaning up the Ganges, has sparked an outpouring of grief and tributes from activists. Agarwal demanded a law to protect the river and the scrapping of construction of hydroelectric projects along its banks. His death has been met with demands for an independent investigation.

The Ganges, India's largest river system and one of its most polluted, has been a subject of concern for many years. Prime Minister Narendra Modi came to power in 2014 with a pledge to clean up the 1,570-mile-long river, but critics say a flagship five-year project launched in 2015 has fallen flat. Results of a federal audit released in Dec. 2017 revealed lapses in planning and financial management of the scheme and said under a quarter of the funds for the programme had been spent in two years.

In August 2020, the bodies of four male sea otters, a federally protected species, were found washed up on beaches near Santa Cruz, California. The US Fish and Wildlife Service announced a $10,000 reward for information leading to the arrest and conviction of the person responsible for the shootings. A fifth otter carcass was discovered with a suspected gunshot wound. The sea otters, which are protected by the Marine Mammal Protection Act, California state law, and the Endangered Species Act, play a crucial role in the ecosystem as a keystone species. Killing a sea otter can result in fines up to $100,000 and imprisonment.

Sea otters were once widespread along the Pacific coast but were hunted almost to extinction during the 18th and 19th centuries. In 1977, California’s remaining sea otters were listed as "threatened" under the Endangered Species Act. Today, they are primarily threatened by oil spills and coastal tanker traffic. In September 2013, three dead otters were found near Asilomar state beach, an unsolved crime that is now considered a "cold case."

The otter carcasses have been transported to the US Fish and Wildlife forensic lab in Oregon for necropsies. Anyone with information on the shootings is asked to call the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service at (650) 876-9078. The loss of these sea otters not only represents a loss of life but also a loss of their beneficial impact on the ecosystem.

A South Carolina man, Todd Kohlhepp, has been charged with the murder of four people at Superbike Motorsports in Chesnee, a quadruple slaying that occurred 13 years ago. Kohlhepp, who was seen walking the property with investigators, has led authorities to where he said two other bodies are buried. The sheriff announced that Kohlhepp is now suspected in the deaths of as many as seven people. Earlier, a body found in a shallow grave on the property was identified as Charles David Carver, the boyfriend of the kidnapped woman who was found chained in a storage shed on the property. Kohlhepp has been charged with the woman's kidnapping and is being held without bond. The victim has told investigators that she saw Kohlhepp shoot Carver. The sheriff has refused to comment on Kohlhepp's appearance at the search scene. The mother of the missing man whose girlfriend was abducted and found chained inside a storage shed is refusing to give up hope she will one day see her son alive. The pair were reported missing in early September. The woman has told investigators that she saw Kohlhepp shoot Carver. The search for more bodies on the property is ongoing. Kohlhepp was released from prison in Arizona in 2001 after being convicted of raping a 14-year-old neighbor at gunpoint and threatening to kill her siblings if she called police. He had to register as a sex offender.

Sergio Marchionne, the former CEO of Fiat Chrysler Automobiles NV (FCA), passed away on Wednesday at the age of 66. The Swiss University Hospital Zurich, where he was treated, revealed that Marchionne had been receiving treatment for a serious illness for more than a year. FCA stated that due to medical privacy, they had no knowledge of Marchionne's health condition.

Questions have arisen regarding how long Marchionne was ill and how much the company knew before making the situation public. FCA confirmed that they were aware of Marchionne undergoing shoulder surgery but were only informed last week about a serious deterioration in his condition, which led to him being unable to return to work.

Marchionne is renowned for rescuing Fiat and Chrysler from bankruptcy and bringing the brands together under one roof. He was due to step down at FCA in April 2019. The hospital declined to comment on Marchionne's illness but expressed its condolences to his family.

FCA's annual report in February stated that Marchionne's ability to run the company was critical to its strategic direction and business plan. It's unusual for companies to require executives to disclose medical problems, but some companies may require their top brass to undergo annual health checks to protect their business interests. FCA declined to comment on its health policies related to its top executives.

The news of Marchionne's death drew tributes from rivals and tears from his closest colleagues. He was one of the auto industry's most tenacious and respected CEOs.

Workers at the Goodyear tyre factory in Amiens, Northern France, have detained two managers, Michel Dheilly (production director) and Bernard Glaser (human resources chief), in a dispute over plans to close the plant. The workers are pushing for a more generous redundancy plan. The union describes the situation as calm, with the managers reportedly having access to water and mobile phones. The incident is a revival of the once-common practice of "bossnapping" in France, which typically lasts from a few hours to a couple of days without prosecution. The Amiens plant has a contentious history, with previous attempts to close it being stalled by violent protests and prolonged layoff procedures. This incident is the latest in a series of protests by union members, who were accused by a US executive last year of doing little work. The managers are being held in a room with access controlled by union representatives and employees. The situation is being described as "animated, sometimes calm, but without any meanness" by one of the captive managers. Police usually avoid intervention to prevent escalation.
