Jodie Foster, the Oscar-winning actress, has married her girlfriend of almost a year, photographer Alexandra Hedison. The couple, who started dating last summer, got married over the weekend, according to E! News. Foster, 51, previously came out in a stirring speech at the Golden Globes in 2013, thanking her ex-partner Cydney Bernard, the mother of her two sons. The news of their nuptials was confirmed by Foster's representative.

YouTube's top trending content currently features a breakup video between two popular comedy vloggers, Liza Koshy and David Dobrik. The pair, who have a combined following of over 21 million subscribers, announced their six-month separation in a video uploaded yesterday. Despite their busy schedules and growing apart, they remain best friends and insist that the split is amicable. The video has gone viral due to the deep emotional connection between the two, as they joke, cry, and praise each other. The breakup may have little impact on their individual status or future earnings, according to branding expert Tassilo Labuzinski. Fans have reacted with shock, upset, and praise to the news, with some holding out hope for a potential reconciliation. The video serves as a reminder of the unique pressures and challenges faced by YouTube couples in maintaining their relationships and brands in the public eye.

The Australian study published in the journal Archives of Sexual Behaviour found that men with facial hair, regardless of length, are more likely to hold hostile sexist views compared to their clean-shaven peers. The researchers interviewed over 500 men aged 18 to 72, dividing them into facial hair categories. Men with facial hair were found to be more inclined to agree with derogatory and patriarchal statements, while only a third of the men interviewed did not express some form of sexist statement. The study suggests that men with sexist views may grow beards to reinforce their masculinity and dominance. The researchers also speculate that wearing facial hair may cause men to adopt sexist attitudes due to social perceptions of them as more masculine, mature, dominant, and aggressive. The study found that Indian men, who made up 86% of the participants with facial hair, scored higher on sexism than American men (65% of whom had facial hair). Higher levels of education were associated with more benevolent sexism but less hostile sexism. The study adds to the growing body of research suggesting a link between masculinity, facial hair, and sexist attitudes.

Mark Salling, a former "Glee" actor, was arrested on Tuesday, December 29, 2015, in Los Angeles for possession of child pornography. The Los Angeles Police Department's Internet Crimes Against Children Task Force Unit executed a search warrant at Salling's Sunland, California home, where they found "hundreds" of images on one of his personal devices. Salling's computer and other electronic devices were also seized after he refused to share his passwords with authorities. Salling was in custody at the LAPD Metropolitan Detention Center in downtown Los Angeles at the time of publication, with bail set at $20,000. This isn't Salling's first public scandal, as he was sued by an ex-girlfriend alleging sexual battery in 2013 and ordered to pay a $2.7 million settlement. The arrest was in response to a tip received by the LAPD, and Salling's representatives have not yet commented on the matter. An update on the story states that Salling was released on bail at 2:26 p.m. PT, with his first court appearance scheduled for January 22. Further details suggest that law enforcement sources have found more than a thousand images of "child sexual exploitation" on Salling's computer, and that he lives alone, making it hard to argue someone else put the images in the computer.

In Bennington, Vermont, several residents have reported being attacked by a squirrel over the past few weeks. One of the victims, Kevin McDonald, was shoveling snow when a gray squirrel jumped onto him, delivering scratches. Despite throwing the animal off, it jumped back onto him twice. Another resident, a woman, was bitten on the back of the neck and is undergoing a rabies vaccination series as a precaution. However, Vermont Public Health Veterinarian Robert Johnson assures that there's never been a case of a squirrel passing rabies to a human. Johnson speculates that the squirrel might have lost its fear of humans due to being raised as a pet or encountering humans it doesn't recognize. Local Game Warden Travis Buttle is aware of the incidents and advises anyone attacked by a squirrel or any animal to seek medical advice. The squirrel, if rabid, would likely have died by now, but it has disappeared quickly after the attacks, making it difficult to test for rabies.

The Indian Ministry of Ayush has released a booklet titled "Mother and Child Care" that offers recommendations for pregnant women, including abstaining from meat, eggs, and certain negative emotions such as desire, anger, attachment, hatred, and lust. The booklet also advises pregnant women to surround themselves with good people, hang beautiful pictures in their room, and engage in spiritual thoughts. However, the advice has been met with criticism from the medical community, who argue that the recommendations are unscientific and potentially dangerous, especially considering India's poor record in maternal health. Critics point out that protein-deficiency malnutrition and anemia are common health concerns for pregnant women in India, and that meat and eggs are important sources of protein and iron. The government has defended the booklet, stating that it contains "wisdom accumulated over many centuries" and does not specifically advise against sex. The controversy highlights the ongoing tension between traditional and alternative medicine practices and evidence-based medicine in India.

The document discusses the harmful effects of highly fluorinated chemicals (HFCs) and provides a guide for consumers to avoid exposure to these chemicals. HFCs are used in various consumer products such as cookware, clothing, outdoor apparel, carpeting, and food packaging to provide nonstick, oil- and water-resistant properties. They are also used in some cosmetics.

Exposure to HFCs can lead to several health problems, including testicular and kidney cancer, liver malfunction, hormonal changes, thyroid disruption, high cholesterol, obesity, ulcerative colitis, lower birth weight and size, and other suspected health problems. Because HFCs are resistant to breakdown, they can persist in the environment for millions of years, leading to accumulation and higher levels of exposure in future generations.

Scientists from all over the world have expressed concerns about HFCs and are asking for a limit to the production and use of these chemicals. To avoid exposure to HFCs, consumers are advised to avoid products that are oil repellant or stain resistant, only purchase waterproof gear when necessary, avoid cosmetics with PTFE or any word containing “perfluor” or “polyfluor” on their ingredients list, replace Teflon nonstick cookware with cast iron, glass, or ceramic, avoid microwave popcorn and greasy foods wrapped in paper, and tell retailers and manufacturers that they want products without fluorinated chemicals.

The document also discusses a new study that found ten chemicals suspected or known to harm human health are present in more than 90% of household dust samples. The study adds to a growing body of evidence showing the dangers posed by exposure to a slew of chemicals people in developed countries encounter on a day-to-day basis. The chemicals come from a variety of household goods that include toys, cosmetics, furniture, cookware, cleaning products, and more.

The study calls for manufacturers to replace the chemicals in their products with safe alternatives, but voluntary participation aside, the path to force companies to replace chemicals remains difficult. An overhaul to the Toxic Substances Control Act passed earlier this year will require the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) to sign off on new chemicals before they enter the open market, but thousands of chemicals on the market today remain untested.

The document also discusses a second study that raises new questions about air exposures we might encounter outside the home. The study suggests magnetite nanoparticles, typically found in the air, may travel farther than previously believed throughout the human body and ultimately lodge in human brain tissue. Such particles from air pollution have long been linked to respiratory disease, but the link to brain health is “newly being appreciated.”

The document provides resources for further reading and action, including links to articles, editorials, and responses from the chemical industry and environmental organizations. It also encourages consumers to drive change for healthy products by making informed choices and supporting companies committed to phasing out HFCs.

In a recent revelation, a former CIA operative, Donald Rickard, admitted his role in the arrest of Nelson Mandela in 1962, which led to Mandela's 27-year imprisonment. Mandla Mandela, the grandson and heir of the former South African president, condemned this action as a "betrayal of our nation" and called on US President Barack Obama to apologize and make a full disclosure of the events leading up to Mandela's arrest. Mandla further suggested that the US should face censure by the United Nations.

Donald Rickard, the former CIA agent, viewed Mandela as a "toy of the communists" and provided the apartheid police with information on Mandela's whereabouts. Rickard, who passed away in March, lived an adventurous life, serving as a diplomat with the US State Department in various countries before retiring in Pagosa Springs, Colorado.

The disclosure has sparked outrage and calls for transparency, with Mandla stating that it puts an end to decades of denial about the West's role in supporting the apartheid regime. Mandla, who is also an ANC MP and traditional chief in the family clan, called on "freedom loving people of the world" to condemn this betrayal.

This revelation sheds light on a significant event in South African history, where the actions of a former CIA operative played a role in the imprisonment of a future statesman and global icon. The demand for transparency and accountability continues, with calls for the CIA to disclose more details about its role in Mandela's arrest and imprisonment.

Nokia, the Finnish telecommunications company, has announced a significant restructuring plan that includes the reduction of its workforce by 10,000 and the closure of production and research sites. This is the second time this year that Nokia has reduced its earnings forecast, and it comes as a result of intense competition from Apple and Samsung in the smartphone market. The job cuts amount to almost a fifth of the total workforce, excluding a joint venture with Siemens AG. Nokia's stock has fallen 18 percent to its lowest level since 1996, pushing its market value below $10 billion.

Nokia's CEO, Stephen Elop, took over in 2010 and has been reorganizing the company in an attempt to recover from a slump in sales and four straight quarterly losses. The company risks going out of business in as little as two years unless it reduces expenses, according to analyst Alexander Peterc of Exane BNP Paribas. Nokia's second-quarter adjusted operating margin at the devices unit will be worse than a loss equivalent to 3 percent of revenue in the first quarter, the company said.

The cost of insuring Nokia bonds using credit-default swaps has risen to its highest since May 25, raising concerns about the company's financial stability. Nokia has lost more than 70 billion euros in market value since Apple introduced the iPhone in 2007, taking the lead in smartphone innovation. While Nokia's falling value brings it closer to becoming a takeover target, the company needs to stabilize its business to attract suitors, said Lars Soederfjell, an analyst with Bank of Aaland in Stockholm.

As part of the changes, sites in Finland, Germany, and Canada will be closed, and executives Niklas Savander, Mary McDowell, and Jerri DeVard will leave. Nokia will also sell its Vertu luxury-phone unit to Swedish private-equity firm EQT Partners AB. The company had a net cash of 4.9 billion euros as of March 31.

The job cuts and closures will result in expenses of about 1 billion euros, Nokia said. The biggest share of cuts will come in research and development, where Nokia is killing whole projects to preserve others that are more important. Sales is the second-biggest area affected, and general overhead is third. Nokia aims to bring annual expenses at its devices business to about 3 billion euros by the end of 2013. That's down from 5.35 billion euros in 2010.

Nokia's total handset shipments declined 24 percent in the first quarter, allowing Samsung to overtake the company as the world's biggest mobile-phone maker. Nokia's operating margin for mobile phones plunged to 3.7 percent last year from more than 20 percent before Apple introduced the iPhone in 2007. "We don't have Nokia returning to profitability in devices in the foreseeable future, not this year and not next," said Peterc.

The restructuring is aimed at accelerating Nokia's cost-reduction efforts. Nokia has lost more than 70 billion euros in market value since Apple introduced the iPhone in 2007, taking the lead in smartphone innovation. While Nokia's falling value brings it closer to becoming a takeover target, the company needs to stabilize its business to attract suitors, said Lars Soederfjell, an analyst with Bank of Aaland in Stockholm. "Would you buy into this, with these type of fundamentals?" he said. "There's too much uncertainty."

Liu Wen, a 21-year-old model from China, will make history as the first Asian model to walk the Victoria's Secret runway during the fashion show airing on CBS on Tuesday. Wen, who was discovered through a regular modeling contest, will join an elite group of Victoria's Secret Angels, including Heidi Klum, who will also appear in the show.

Born in Yongzhou, China, Wen's family encouraged her to pursue a career as a teacher, but she won a modeling contest and eventually moved to Beijing to pursue her newfound passion. She quickly rose to fame, appearing on the covers of Chinese editions of FHM, Marie Claire, and Vogue, and landing on the cover of Chinese Elle alongside fellow rising star Emma Pei.

Wen made her runway debut in Milan, Italy, in 2008, followed by Paris, France, and New York fashion weeks. Although this will be her first time walking for Victoria's Secret, she is part of a growing trend for Asian models worldwide.

The Victoria's Secret fashion show is known for its elaborate costumes and production, with models wearing $3 million bras, large wings, and barely there lingerie. The models undergo hours of makeup, hair, and nail preparation before hitting the runway, with an average of five people working on each of the 38 models.

Wen is excited to be a part of the show and has been in touch with her family daily while traveling. She plans to continue modeling for now but may eventually try her hand at acting. Despite her success, Wen remains grounded and appreciates the respect that comes with being a teacher, which she originally planned to become.

The Gallup daily tracking poll shows GOP presidential candidate Mitt Romney leading President Obama by 3 points among likely voters, with 50% support for Romney and 47% for Obama. However, Obama maintains a 1-point advantage over Romney among registered voters, with 48% to Romney's 47%. The poll, which is a rolling seven-day average through Oct. 24, shows Romney's lead among likely voters has decreased from a high of 7 points in the previous week. The RealClearPolitics average of national polls shows Romney leading Obama by less than 1 percentage point, while an Associated Press-GfK poll released Thursday shows Romney edging Obama, 47-45. Battleground polls show many states remain a toss-up, with the race in Ohio being particularly close. In Ohio, a key state for both campaigns, a Time poll released Wednesday showed Obama up 5, with a 49-44 advantage, while a SurveyUSA poll showed the president topping Romney by 3. A poll from conservative outlet Rasmussen put the two candidates tied in the Buckeye State, with 48% support apiece among likely voters. The Gallup daily tracking poll has a margin of error of 2 percentage points. The polling trend suggests that Romney may have lost some momentum after the second presidential debate, with Obama gaining ground in most of the polls released on Wednesday. The FiveThirtyEight model, which looks at a broader array of polls, shows a slightly favorable trend for Obama over the past 10 days, with his chances of winning the Electoral College increasing to 71% on Wednesday from 68.1% on Tuesday.

The article discusses a person's fascination with fortune cookies, despite being non-superstitious. The individual, who is also a data analyst, decided to investigate the mysteries within the cookies by analyzing a sample of 1,035 Panda brand fortune cookies.

The analysis revealed that there were 676 unique fortunes, with about 46% beginning with letters A-I and 8% with letters W-Y. The obverse side of the fortunes had 556 unique combinations of lucky numbers, and 173 individual Mandarin vocabulary words and phrases.

The author also explored the idea of whether the lucky numbers on the fortunes were actually lucky. To test this, they compared the lucky numbers to Powerball numbers from 1997 to 2017. The results showed that an individual who bought a Powerball ticket for every lucky number combination would have made $4.4 million on $4.2 million in ticket purchases, compared to $1.7 million using random numbers.

The article also discusses the language one could learn from the backs of fortunes, with 173 Mandarin words, primarily focusing on food, health, and exercise. The fortunes were found to be mostly about the individual, with about half mentioning "you," your character, your strengths, and your weaknesses.

The author also created a bot to generate new fortunes based on the analysis of the 676 unique fortunes. However, the bot-generated fortunes were not always wise or unique, and some were even considered terrible.

The article concludes with a quote from a particularly wise fortune: "You may be disappointed if you fail. But you are doomed if you don't try." The author also created a Twitter account, @FortuneBot538, to share the bot-generated fortunes.

The High Court in London has granted a death certificate to George Bingham, the son of Lord Lucan, an aristocrat who disappeared over 40 years ago following the murder of his children's nanny, Sandra Rivett. The ruling brings a form of closure to one of the most mysterious cases to captivate the British public. Lord Lucan, born Richard John Bingham, vanished in November 1974 at the age of 39 after Rivett was bludgeoned to death at his home in London. His car was found abandoned near the southern English coast, and he was declared Rivett’s killer by a jury at an inquest in 1975. Over the years, sightings of Lucan have been reported in various countries, but none have been verified.

The latest twist in the decades-old mystery surrounding the fate of Lord Lucan emerged days before a procedural hearing at the High Court to determine whether a death certificate should be issued for Lucan. A member of Lucan's gambling set has claimed that Lucan traveled to a private zoo in Kent owned by his close friend John Aspinall and was fed to a tiger named Zorra after shooting himself. This account raises questions, as the principal people involved are all dead.

Lord Lucan was declared dead by the High Court in 1999, but Bingham said it didn't prove death "for all purposes." His application for the death certificate was made under the Presumption of Death Act, which came into force in 2014. Rivett's son Neil Berriman had opposed the application, telling the Daily Mail that if Lucan was still alive, he should be prosecuted.

Speaking to Britain’s Press Association after the ruling, George Bingham said, "I am very happy with the judgment of the court in this matter. It has been a very long time coming." Berriman told the news agency after the judgement Wednesday, "I think he's (Lucan) dead. It is fantastic and I am very pleased for him (Bingham)."

The new ruling allows Bingham to inherit the family title as the Eighth Earl of Lucan. However, the mystery surrounding the fate of Lord Lucan remains unsolved, with various theories circulating about his disappearance and possible death.

Michael Jordan and his wife Yvette Prieto are expecting identical twin girls in April, making it the former NBA star's fourth child. The couple married in 2013 after five years of dating. Meanwhile, Bruce Willis and his wife Emma Heming are also expecting their second child together. The couple, who married in 2009, have a 20-month-old daughter named Mabel Ray. Willis is also father to three daughters from his previous marriage to Demi Moore. Both couples are excited about their upcoming additions.

A 20-year-old man named Chanel Lewis, from Brooklyn, has been arrested and charged with the murder of Karina Vetrano, a 30-year-old woman who was strangled while out jogging in Queens, New York, last summer. The arrest was made on Saturday, with Lewis expected to be arraigned later on Sunday. The charge carries a penalty of 25 years to life in prison if he is convicted. The DNA profile of the attacker was obtained from genetic material found under Vetrano's fingernails, on her phone, and on her neck. Police believe that Lewis made incriminating statements when he was arrested and that the encounter that led to Vetrano's death was a chance one. No information on an attorney for Lewis was available. Vetrano's body was found badly beaten in a secluded marsh by her father after she went for a run not far from her home on Aug. 2.

Gustavo Falcon, one of the infamous "Cocaine Cowboys" from South Florida, was arrested after 26 years on the run on April 12, 2017. Falcon, who is 55 years old, was apprehended while riding his bike in Kissimmee, Florida. The U.S. Marshals for the Southern District of Florida had been tracking Falcon, who was suspected of living in Mexico or Colombia, and finally caught up with him in a rental property in the Orlando-Kissimmee area. During the arrest, officers discovered fraudulent driver's licenses, some of which were for Falcon's wife and adult children, listed under Miami addresses. Falcon eventually confirmed his identity before being booked without resistance in the Orange County Jail. Falcon's older brother, Augusto "Willie" Falcon, and fellow drug kingpin Salvador "Sal" Magluta were indicted by a federal grand jury in 1991, and Gustavo Falcon had not been seen since. Gustavo Falcon agreed to be sent to South Florida to face charges of conspiracy to import cocaine into the U.S. at his initial court hearing in Orlando, and was ordered held without bond. Augusto Falcon and Magluta were acquitted of all charges at their trial in 1996, but were later convicted of drug-related money laundering and sentenced to long prison terms. Their mansions, boats, cars, planes, bank accounts, and other ill-gotten gains were seized and sold by the government.

The Houla massacre in Syria, which resulted in over 100 deaths, including women and children, has led to a coordinated protest by numerous countries, including Turkey and Japan, who have expelled Syrian diplomats. This action follows similar moves by the United States, Britain, Canada, Australia, France, Germany, Italy, Spain, and Bulgaria. The Syrian government denounced the expulsions as "unprecedented hysteria." The U.N.'s human rights office reported that most of the victims were shot execution-style, with fewer than 20 people cut down by regime shelling. The U.N. special envoy, Kofi Annan, met with Syrian President Bashar Assad to try to salvage his peace plan, which has failed to stop the violence on the ground. Meanwhile, Syrian troops continued to bombard rebel-held areas, with no immediate casualties reported. The U.N.'s top human rights body planned to hold a special session to address the massacre. The expulsions of Syrian diplomats were criticized by Russia, which has blocked two previous resolutions calling for tougher action on Damascus. In response to the diplomatic expulsions, Syria gave the Dutch charge d'affaires 72 hours to leave. The U.N. observer mission in Syria confirmed the killings of 13 people in the northeastern province of Deir el-Zour. The mission said U.N. monitors found the bodies late Tuesday, with some of the dead appearing to have been shot in the head from short range and all having their hands tied behind their backs. The U.S. Treasury announced it will freeze the assets of the Syrian International Islamic Bank to tighten economic pressure on the Syrian government.

The article discusses the eerie coincidence of late actors' final movies often having dark and intense themes, such as Brittany Murphy's latest film, "Abandoned," in which she plays a woman under psychiatric evaluation whose husband has vanished. Previous examples include Heath Ledger's "The Imaginarium of Doctor Parnassus," Aaliyah's "Queen of the Damned," Bruce Lee's "Game of Death," Brandon Lee's "The Crow," Brad Renfro's "The Informers," River Phoenix's "Dark Blood," and Judy Garland's "I Could Go On Singing."

In a separate news, Redbox, a DVD rental company, has removed the box art images for Brittany Murphy's latest film, "Deadline," from its kiosks nationwide due to her sudden death on Sunday. The cover art shows Murphy's character lying lifeless in a bathtub, which was deemed inappropriate following her death. The company aims to complete the removal of the artwork by January 1st and has also pulled it from their website.

In "Deadline," Murphy plays a screenwriter who travels to a haunted Victorian mansion to finish a script on deadline, only to stumble upon videos recorded by past residents that lead her to have a psychological breakdown. The film was released after her death.

In a controversial ruling, a federal judge in St. Louis has ordered Carl and Janice Duffner, who have severe grass allergies, to plant turf grass in their yard or face potential fines exceeding $200,000 and even imprisonment. The Duffners, who have lived in their St. Louis suburb home since 2002, have a lush flower garden instead of turf grass, which they maintain as an alternative ground cover.

The city of St. Peters passed an ordinance in the last decade requiring homeowners to cover at least 50% of their yard areas with turf grass. The Duffners, upon moving in, had planted a lush flower garden. In May 2014, they received a letter from the city stating their yard was not in compliance. They applied for a variance, which was granted in July 2014, but it still required them to plant at least 5% turf grass. The couple refused and filed a lawsuit in 2014.

The litigation took a long and tortuous route, with adverse rulings and appeals. In 2016, the Duffners filed in federal court. Yesterday, U.S. District Court Judge John A. Ross issued a ruling that was mostly in favor of the city, finding that the facts presented by the Duffners were not enough to win the case.

David Roland of the Freedom Center of Missouri, who is representing the Duffners, finds the ruling outrageous and plans to appeal. He suggests that this case could potentially reach the U.S. Supreme Court and may attract advocacy groups that care about property rights. Roland argues that the ordinance is dangerous because it forces homeowners to proactively plant certain types of plants, which could potentially require homeowners to install swimming pools or maintain other costly features on their property. He emphasizes that people have the right to use their personal property in a lawful, harmless way and have the right to exclude things from their property they don't want there.

The article discusses the upcoming court hearing for former Penn State football coach Jerry Sandusky, who is accused of sexual abuse by multiple victims. One of the victims, known as Victim 1, is expected to testify at the hearing, marking the first time he will publicly confront Sandusky. Victim 1 is represented by attorneys Michael Boni and Slade McLaughlin, who plan to file civil litigation against Sandusky, Penn State, and other individuals. The Second Mile charity, founded by Sandusky, is also named as a potential defendant. The charity has asked donors to direct contributions to the Pennsylvania Coalition Against Rape, and is considering options for continuing its programs or closing altogether. Sandusky has denied the charges against him, and his attorney has suggested that some of the victims may recant their allegations. The Second Mile is seeking to dismiss a lawsuit seeking an injunction to prevent it from transferring financial assets. The case has caused controversy and led to the firing of Penn State's president and legendary football coach Joe Paterno.

On January 25, 2015, a 13-year-old boy named Suhayb Jamal Hassan died in an accidental shooting at his home in Eagan, Minnesota. The incident occurred while the boys, aged 13 and 15, were home alone with their 11-year-old sister. The 15-year-old initially reported to emergency dispatchers that his brother had accidentally stabbed himself while running with a knife inside the house. However, upon further investigation, the 15-year-old admitted to accidentally shooting his brother with their father's 9mm handgun during a game of "cops and robbers."

The handgun was hidden in the house and was unloaded, but a loaded magazine was nearby. At some point, the gun was loaded, then thought to be unloaded. The 15-year-old pulled the trigger and unintentionally fired one round toward his brother, striking him in the chest. The 11-year-old sister was uninjured and did not witness the shooting.

The 13-year-old was an eighth-grader at Blackhawk Middle School in Eagan, and the school notified students of his death and provided additional counselors. The investigation is ongoing, and the results will be turned over to the Dakota County attorney's office. The 15-year-old who accidentally shot his brother is not in custody, and no arrests are expected.

The family lived in a split-level house in a cul-de-sac, and neighbors often saw the two boys walking to school in the morning. The parents also have a second daughter. The neighbor expressed sadness about the incident, stating, "It's so sad. You hear about this happening a lot... kids playing with guns."

The FDA has ordered a San Francisco man, Trent Arsenault, to shut down his one-man sperm bank due to improper procedures. Arsenault, a tech worker, gained attention for his efforts to help the 99% who cannot afford to visit a pricey sperm bank, but his personal sexual practices have come under scrutiny. Arsenault's attorneys have argued against government regulation of his personal activities, and his cause has been embraced by various political and cultural crusaders. However, it has been revealed that Arsenault posts explicit videos and pictures of his sperm donations on the web, which he considers part of his identity as a "donorsexual." Arsenault's website boasts his attendance at the U.S. Naval Academy, but he dropped out after about half a year in a controversial fashion. Some potential parents have expressed concern about Arsenault's x-rated activities, and it has been reported that not all couples who have become pregnant with his children are aware of his porn sites. The FDA's order to cease manufacturing is based on federal law and affects couples across the USA. Anderson Cooper's show features an interview with Arsenault and one of his biological children.

In response to a hepatitis A outbreak that has claimed 15 lives and hospitalized nearly 300 homeless individuals in San Diego over the past 10 months, city officials have initiated several measures to address the unsanitary conditions contributing to the spread. On Monday, crews from Clean Harbors began power-washing sidewalks and street areas with a bleach and chlorine solution in downtown San Diego, with cleanings continuing in other areas on Wednesday and Friday. The city also announced it will extend the hours of 14 restrooms in Balboa Park, which will be open 24 hours a day starting Tuesday.

In addition, the city plans to set up multiple large tents to provide temporary, immediate shelter relief for hundreds of homeless people, equipped with restrooms, hand-washing stations, and showers. These tents are expected to be operational by the end of this year, with at least two businessmen offering donations of $1.5 million to help expedite the opening.

The city has identified three downtown areas to be cleaned every other week, with the first round including sidewalks along Imperial Avenue below the Interstate 5 overpass and several blocks north of F Street and south of B Street between 10th Avenue and 17th Street.

In a separate development, the city also announced the opening of three new temporary shelters, with at least one expected to be operational by the end of December. The shelters will have more than 100 beds, restrooms, showers, meals, and 24-hour security. Service providers will also be on site at all three locations, offering alcohol and substance abuse counseling and job search training.

The homeless population in San Diego has been growing in recent years, with 5,619 transients counted in January, a 10% increase from last year. The city has partnered with individuals in the private sector to fund operation costs for the shelters, with the final price to be finalized in the coming weeks.

However, not everyone is supportive of the plan. Joel Rocco, owner of Undisputed Gym in the East Village, claims the large homeless encampments surrounding his gym have detracted new clients, hurting his business. He believes that temporary housing will not make a significant impact unless a permanent housing solution is found.

The mayor hopes to have at least one of the temporary shelters operational by the end of December, with a final version of the plan to be presented to the city council in the coming weeks. The county is also taking steps to address the outbreak and plans to expand its efforts to other cities in the region soon. County health officials have already provided hepatitis vaccinations to 19,000 people and plan to install more hand-washing stations in areas where the homeless often gather.

Alan Miller McCarty, a 36-year-old man from Milton, Santa Rosa County, was sentenced to 20 years in prison for threatening to kill Circuit Judge Stasia Warren, whom he believed had ruled against him in a custody case. The threats were made in phone calls on September 29, 2020.

During the trial, McCarty frequently disrupted the courtroom by shouting obscenities and insulting the judge, witnesses, and the entire judicial system. He was moved to a small room with one-way glass to prevent further disruptions. Despite being found guilty on all charges related to the threats, McCarty remained unusually quiet during the guilty verdicts.

McCarty faces up to 40 years in prison when he is sentenced by Circuit Judge Matt Foxman on October 12. Besides the threats against Judge Warren, McCarty also threatened a pair of dispatchers in the phone calls.

McCarty was on suicide watch at the Volusia County Branch Jail and refused to dress for his trial, instead wearing a jail-issued orange jumpsuit. He wore handcuffs in view of the jury, unlike a typical trial. McCarty's outbursts included inviting the judge to perform oral sex on him, which the judge politely declined.

State Attorney R.J. Larizza described McCarty's threats as "chilling and offensive," stating that threatening judges is an attack on the very heart of the Criminal Justice System. McCarty's public defender, Ryan Belanger, argued that McCarty was a "very squeaky wheel" and felt he had no other choice but to make the threats since he was losing his children.

Assistant State Attorney Ashley Terwilleger, who prosecuted the case, stated that McCarty's words mattered and that Judge Warren was fearful that McCarty would make good on his threats. Terwilleger also mentioned that McCarty's children had been in Texas since about 2007 and he had not seen them for two years before his arrest last year.

During the trial, McCarty claimed that his statements on the phone calls were just words and he didn't mean it. McCarty was also equipped with an electric belt under his jumpsuit that would allow a deputy to deliver a stunning zap if needed.

McCarty called dispatchers on September 29 and threatened Warren, who hears juvenile delinquency and dependency cases. Judge Warren testified that she had been frightened when she was told of the threats McCarty had made against her life. McCarty was in the small room during Warren's testimony and would occasionally shout out something, calling Warren an "expletive liar" at one point during the morning.

The judge, jurors, attorneys, and deputies remained patient and professional throughout the trial, despite McCarty's insults and outbursts. McCarty also faces more charges since he is also accused of calling Stewart-Marchman-Act Behavioral Healthcare and threatening staffers there.

Google's ambitious plan to digitize every book ever published and create the world's largest digital library and bookstore has been halted by a federal judge in New York. The judge rejected a $125 million legal settlement between Google, authors, and publishers, citing concerns about copyright, antitrust, and Google's potential monopoly. The decision leaves the future of one of Google's most significant projects uncertain, raising concerns about the company's growing power over information. The settlement would have allowed Google to make millions of out-of-print books widely available online and sell access to them, while providing authors and publishers with new ways to earn money from digital copies of their works. The decision is a setback for both Google and the authors and publisher groups that sued Google over its book-scanning project in 2005. The judge left open the possibility of a revised agreement, and both parties are now considering their next steps. The decision has been hailed by some longtime opponents of the settlement, who hope it will prompt Congress to tackle legislation that would make orphan works accessible.

Revolutionmuslim.com, a radical Islamic website based in the US, has been identified as one of the sources that radicalized Roshonara Choudhry, who was sentenced to life imprisonment for attempting to murder former Labour minister Stephen Timms. The site praises Choudhry as a "mujaahidah," or holy warrior, and published a list of MPs who voted for the Iraq war, encouraging Muslims to try to kill them. The site also published details of Timms' constituency surgery times and venues, and even a link to buy a knife similar to the one used by Choudhry from Tesco Direct.

The website appears to incite further attacks on Timms, and includes a prayer in Arabic to "destroy your enemy and the enemies of Islam" naming Timms and the judge in the Choudhry case, Jeremy Cooke. The site also lists the 139 Conservative MPs and 244 Labour MPs who voted for the war, and includes videos of terrorist cleric Anwar al-Awlaki, who has been singled out by the head of MI5 as a figure of concern to the security services.

The Home Office is attempting to pressure US authorities to remove the list of MPs from the website. Roshonara Choudhry directly cited "a website called revolutionmuslim" in her police interviews as one of several radical sites she looked at. Choudhry also downloaded over a hundred hours of sermons by Anwar al-Awlaki, and the website includes videos by other extremist figures associated with Choudhary. The website is hosted by Enom, based in Bellevue, Washington, but calls to the company were not answered. Choudhary could not be reached for comment.

The International Thermonuclear Experimental Reactor (ITER), a massive fusion reactor project, is under construction in an Alpine forest in France. Weighing over 23,000 tons and standing a hundred feet tall, ITER aims to create a self-sustaining synthetic star by harnessing the power of nuclear fusion. The reactor will generate intense heat, gamma rays, X-rays, and a torrential flux of fast-moving neutrons. To contain this superheated cloud, the machine will use the largest system of superconducting magnets in the world, cooled to 269 degrees below zero.

The project, which requires a conservative estimate of $20 billion, is the most expensive scientific instrument on Earth. If successful, ITER could revolutionize energy production by providing a virtually pollution-free, carbon-free, and scarcity-free energy source. The reactor would run on seawater and lithium, never melt down, and potentially last for 30 million years.

However, ITER is facing significant challenges. A recent assessment found serious problems with the project's leadership, management, and governance. The damning report, initially restricted to a small number of senior managers and council members, could lead to funding withdrawals if not addressed.

The ITER headquarters, a five-story building with a simple interior, overlooks the construction site, which will eventually house a small city of nearly forty buildings. The project, a collaboration of 35 countries representing over half the world's population, is a testament to international scientific cooperation. The main road to the construction site is the A51 highway, passing by various energy sources, including hydroelectric dams, solar panels, and a coal plant converted to burn biomass. The area is also home to a state-funded research organization, the Commissariat à l’Énergie Atomique et aux Énergies Alternatives, created in 1945 to advance nuclear power and renewable energy.

In October 1966, Roger Watson and Dave Brown, both from northwest Detroit, were drafted and went through basic Army training together at Fort Hood, Texas. They became close friends but lost contact after returning home before serving in Vietnam. For decades, Roger wondered about his Army friend, Dave, while Dave searched for Roger's name on the Vietnam Veterans Memorial in Washington.

In 2010, Roger befriended his neighbor Peggy Brown, who was married to Dave. Peggy noticed Roger's Purple Heart license plate and 9th Infantry cap, which led to a series of emails between them about bird watching. Eventually, Peggy discovered that Roger was Dave's Army buddy.

The two men, who had lived as neighbors for 18 years without knowing it, finally met in October 2015. They were amazed and delighted to reconnect after nearly half a century. Roger and Dave plan to share a beer and watch their grandchildren grow up, as they have decades of catching up to do, living just 150 feet apart.

During their reunion, Roger and Dave shared war stories and reminisced about their experiences, including Roger's injury in Vietnam. The men and their wives are grateful for Peggy's neighborly interest in birds, which led to the long-lost friendship's reclamation.

Angela Lansbury, the 92-year-old actress known for her roles in "Beauty and the Beast" and "Murder, She Wrote," has issued a statement clarifying her controversial remarks about sexual harassment. In an interview with the Radio Times, Lansbury suggested that women bear some responsibility for making themselves attractive and contributing to sexual harassment. However, she also stated that there is no excuse for men to harass women.

Lansbury's comments sparked widespread criticism, including from Rape Crisis England & Wales, which stated that victim-blaming attitudes are harmful to sexual assault victims. Actress Patricia Arquette also criticized Lansbury on Twitter, stating that rapists rape regardless of a woman's appearance.

In her statement, Lansbury expressed her support for women's rights and her disappointment at being misinterpreted. She stated, "There is no excuse whatsoever for men to harass women in an abusive sexual manner," and added that she was troubled by how her comments were taken out of context.

Lansbury's statement comes after similar remarks made by designer Donna Karan, who suggested that women were "asking for it" by how they dressed in the immediate aftermath of the Harvey Weinstein sexual misconduct scandal. Karan later apologized for her comments. Weinstein denies all allegations of non-consensual sex.

The video released by Rosemont police on Friday shows Kenneka Jenkins, a 19-year-old Chicago woman, staggering alone through a deserted hotel kitchen and disappearing around a corner, which is the last time she was seen alive. The video does not capture her entering the walk-in freezer where her body was found. However, a motion-activated camera shows that no one else entered that area until her body was found.

The video was released after days of speculation about Jenkins' death and pressure from community activists dissatisfied with the investigation. Attorneys Larry Rogers Jr. and Sam Adam Jr., who represent Jenkins' family, announced at a news conference that they will conduct their own investigation and possibly seek a second autopsy.

Jenkins had attended a party in a hotel room that stretched into the early hours of September 9. Her sister last spoke to her around 1:30 a.m., and her mother received a call about 4 a.m. that Jenkins had gone missing. A 911 recording shows that Martin asked the police to review surveillance footage from the hotel, expressing concern because her daughter, who had a light tolerance for alcohol, had been drinking and was not the type to disappear.

The police advised patience, saying it would take a while for detectives to get hold of the video. The family filed a missing persons report later that morning, and the hotel was notified about 1:15 p.m. The hotel looked in all public areas and the floor on which the party was held but did not find Jenkins. The family returned to the hotel at 6 p.m. and knocked on guest doors, trying to find witnesses. The hotel called the police, and Martin said the officers who responded reviewed surveillance video and saw Jenkins "staggering" through the hotel about 3:20 a.m.

A second search ensued, and Jenkins was found dead in the freezer. The medical examiner's office has yet to pronounce a cause or manner of death, and the case has been the subject of intense speculation on social media, with many suggesting that she was murdered. However, Rosemont police have consistently said they are conducting a death investigation, not a homicide probe.

At the news conference, Rogers suggested that Jenkins' life could have been saved, or at least that she would have been found more quickly, had hotel staff listened to her friends and mother when they came seeking help. Martin, sitting between her attorneys, thanked everyone for their love and support and expressed a desire to see the footage of Jenkins walking into the freezer and closing herself within it.

On June 23, 2014, the United States deployed 80 troops to Chad to aid in the search for the Nigerian schoolgirls kidnapped by Boko Haram. The troops will operate surveillance flights and drone aircraft but will not participate in ground searches. The Pentagon had previously dispatched a team of eight experts to Nigeria to assist in the search. U.S. surveillance drones have been searching for the girls since May 11, and the new unit in Chad will enable longer surveillance flights.

The deployment is significant as it marks a significant escalation of Washington's contribution to the crisis, which has created global concern. The force will remain in Chad until their support in resolving the kidnapping situation is no longer required. The deployment is not based on any new intelligence leads, and the troops will be involved in maintaining aircraft and analyzing data.

Meanwhile, Nigeria has asked the United Nations to designate Boko Haram as a terrorist organization, which would enable countries to impose arms embargoes, travel bans, and asset freezes. The United Nations al Qaeda committee is expected to decide on the matter on Thursday.

Boko Haram has escalated its attacks in Nigeria, with twin blasts killing at least 118 people in the central city of Jos on Tuesday. The group has not claimed responsibility for the attacks but has previously claimed responsibility for the abduction of more than 200 schoolgirls in Chibok last month. The insurgent group has been branded a terrorist group by the United States last year, providing greater access to its finances and more ability to limit its movements.

The sudden escalation of attacks and the failure to find the missing schoolgirls has spread concern about the government's inability to quash the insurgency. Protests have been held daily nationwide to express frustration over the lack of progress in rescuing the schoolgirls. The international community and regional leaders have made clear their determination to support Nigeria and defeat the scourge of terrorism. A new plan has been announced to share intelligence and border surveillance between Nigeria and four neighboring countries, including Chad, while Western nations will provide technical expertise and training in the fight against the extremists.

A woman named Rebekah Martinez, who was reported missing in Humboldt County, California in November 2017, was found to be a contestant on the reality TV show "The Bachelor." Martinez had gone to Humboldt County to work on a marijuana farm and had been included in a cover story featuring missing persons in the county. Her mother had last spoken to her on November 12, and had told authorities that Martinez would be unreachable for a week or so. On "The Bachelor," Martinez gained attention for her 14-year age difference with the lead, Arie Luyendyk Jr. She has been actively posting on social media since she was reported missing and often posts about appearing on the show. After her story was reported by media on February 2, she tweeted a message referring to the photo used in the missing person's report.

The high rate of missing persons reports in Humboldt County was also discussed in the article. According to the North Coast Journal, Humboldt County has the highest per-capita rate of missing persons reports in California. The article examined why Humboldt County has such a high rate of missing persons, and looked at the cases of several missing persons, including Jeff Joseph, who disappeared in June 2014 and whose case remains unsolved. The article also discussed the challenges faced by families of missing persons in trying to find their loved ones and keep their cases in the public eye.

In conclusion, Rebekah Martinez, who was reported missing in Humboldt County, was found to be a contestant on "The Bachelor." The high rate of missing persons reports in Humboldt County was also discussed, and the challenges faced by families of missing persons in trying to find their loved ones were highlighted.

The National Credit Union Administration (NCUA) has filed a lawsuit against JPMorgan Securities and Bear Stearns & Co for selling $3.6 billion in mortgage securities to credit unions, which later collapsed due to losses from the securities. This is the second lawsuit against JPMorgan by the NCUA, with the first one filed in 2011 over $1.4 billion in securities. The lawsuit alleges that Bear Stearns made misrepresentations in the sale of mortgage-backed securities to several federal credit unions. JPMorgan has declined to comment.

In a separate development, Morgan Stanley was fined $5 million by Massachusetts regulators for breaking a decade-old pledge to prevent investment bankers from influencing analysts. This stems from Morgan Stanley's handling of Facebook's initial public offering (IPO) in 2012, which cost investors billions of dollars. The regulators found that a senior Morgan Stanley banker wrote a script that Facebook's then-treasurer used to update research analysts on the company's revenue outlook before the IPO. The banker had rehearsed the conversations with the treasurer beforehand.

The Massachusetts consent order criticized Morgan Stanley for helping Facebook provide analysts with more detailed information than other investors received. The bank didn't admit or deny the claims in settling. This is not the first time Morgan Stanley has been under scrutiny for its role in the Facebook IPO. Citigroup was fined $2 million by Massachusetts in October 2012 for a junior analyst improperly disclosing confidential information before the IPO. The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission is also reportedly looking into the IPO.

In response to the settlement, Erik Gordon, a professor at the University of Michigan’s Stephen M. Ross School of Business, said, “Coming from Massachusetts, where they could’ve gotten hit a lot harder, if anything, this is not encouraging to attorneys general.” Morgan Stanley has stated that it is committed to robust compliance with all applicable regulations and laws.

The town of Barrett in Pennsylvania has canceled its annual Halloween parade, 5K Scarecrow Race, and trick-or-treating this year due to the ongoing manhunt for Eric Frein, the accused cop-killer. The manhunt, now in its fourth week, has residents on edge, with increased police presence and frequent roadblocks affecting tourism and businesses. The town's supervisor, Ralph Megliola, expressed concerns about Frein potentially using Halloween disguises to evade capture. As an alternative, a "Trunk-or-Treat" event has been organized at a Catholic school in a nearby township. The manhunt has reportedly cost the town about $40,000, not including lost business revenue. The search for Frein, who is believed to be hiding in nearby woods, has been focused on the border of Pike and Monroe counties since the shooting at the Blooming Grove police barracks on Sept 12, which resulted in the death of one officer and the injury of another.

The "Make the Breast Pump Not Suck" Hackathon was held at MIT on September 20-21, 2014, with the aim of improving the design and technology behind breast pumps to make the act of pumping less awkward for working mothers. The event brought together 150 engineers, designers, parents, public health researchers, and lactation consultants to brainstorm new innovations to address the current problems with breast pumps, such as the motor being loud, having too many parts, being hard to clean, and being embarrassing to use.

The hackathon was organized by a group of MIT Media Lab students and researchers who are also parents, including Alexandra Metral, Catherine D'Ignazio, Alexis Hope, Taylor Levy, and Alexandra Metral. The event was sponsored by Vecna Technologies, Pejman Mar Ventures, Medela, Naia Health, Lasinoh, Simple Wishes, Pumping Essentials, Moxxly, Mamajamas, Ameda, the MIT Center for Civic Media, the MIT Center for Bits and Atoms, and iKatun.

The hackathon produced several potential innovations, including Compress Express, a breast pump that mimics the natural art of hand expression instead of using vacuum technology; Second Nature, a breast pump that mimics the way a baby suckles with massage and compression; PumpIO, an open software and hardware platform to make breast pumping smarter, more data-rich, and less isolating; Helping Hands, a hands-free compression bra for manually expressing breastmilk; and Mighty Mom utility belt, a fashionable, discreet, hands-free wearable pump that automatically logs and analyzes personal data.

The hackathon was a success in seeding ideas, connections, and projects that aim to make the breast pump experience less awkward for working mothers. The event also served as a catalyst for innovation in maternal and pediatric health more generally. The winners of the hackathon received prizes of $3,000, $2,000, $1,000, and $500, as well as a trip for two team members to Silicon Valley to pitch their ideas to investors.

The hackathon is part of a larger movement to address the lack of innovation in breast pumps and maternal health more generally. As one of the midwives at the event said, "Maternal health lags behind other sectors for innovation." The event highlights the need for more creative solutions to support families and children, particularly low-income, working women who often face challenges in breastfeeding or pumping breastmilk for their babies.

A 24-year-old woman, Anna Fermanova, is under house arrest in Plano, Texas, after attempting to transport three high-tech night vision scopes to Russia without a license. The scopes, which are on the U.S. Munitions List, were confiscated by federal officials at New York’s JFK International Airport on March 1. Fermanova was arrested earlier this month when she returned to the United States to visit family. She is facing charges for "knowingly and intentionally" attempting to export "defense articles on the United States Munitions list."

The case has been compared to that of Anna Chapman, a suspected Russian spy who was arrested in New York and then returned to Russia under a "spy swap exchange" earlier this month. There is no evidence that the two women knew one another.

Fermanova's attorney, Scott Palmer, claims that the charges are false allegations and too sensitive to be discussed. He said that Fermanova bought the scopes legally online for her husband, who intended to resell them to hunters.

Fermanova, who was born in Latvia, is a U.S. citizen and a 2005 graduate of the Ogle School of Hair Skin and Nails. She holds a cosmetologist license in Texas and splits her time between Moscow and Dallas, Texas, where she teaches English.

The incident has sparked growing concern in America over the actions of "cold-war style" spies, several of whom were caught living apparently ordinary lives in suburban America earlier this month.

Geraldine Largay, a 66-year-old hiker from Tennessee, survived for nearly a month after getting lost on the Appalachian Trail in July 2013. Her remains were found more than two years later, and a journal documenting her final days was among the personal effects found by the Maine Warden Service. The journal entries and text messages she tried to send her husband paint a picture of a misadventure that turned tragic when a search-and-rescue effort scoured the vast area in vain.

Problems began for Largay when she got lost after leaving the trail for a bathroom break while heading north en route to the Spaulding lean-to on July 22, 2013. She tried to send a text to her husband for help, but there was no cell coverage in the area. The next day, she walked west through the dense woods seeking a higher elevation, but her text to her husband also went unanswered. At that point, Largay decided her best chance of survival would be staying put. She set up a tent and wrote in a journal every day for at least the next 18 days. A final entry was dated Aug. 18 – 26 days after she set up camp.

The warden service found Largay's remains and her campsite more than two years later, detailing the search-and-recovery effort in a report on Nov. 12, 2015. The warden service's case file, which was obtained by the Morning Sentinel, contains hundreds of pages of evidence photographs, witness interviews, and tips. Largay kept the journal and her cellphone in a bag that was recovered by the warden service after a forester came across her tent and skeletal remains and led wardens to the site on Oct. 15, 2015.

Though Largay's family and friends described her as an experienced hiker, the wardens' case file indicated she had a poor sense of direction, and when she made a mistake, she would become easily flustered. Largay's husband reported her missing on July 24, 2013, after she failed to show up at a prearranged meeting point on state Route 27 in Wyman Township. The search for Largay was one of the most lengthy and expensive in state history.

The forester who found Largay's remains worked on a contract for the U.S. Navy, which owns the land where Largay was found. Largay died from a lack of food and water and environmental exposure, according to a report from the chief medical examiner. The warden service had not previously disclosed that a journal had been found at the site.

The release of the warden service's case file is the latest chapter in the disappearance that has transfixed the region and the large community of hikers who traverse the Appalachian Trail. Largay, an experienced hiker whose trail moniker was "Inchworm," had started hiking the trail in April 2013 with her hiking partner, Jane Lee. Their plan was to hike from Harpers Ferry, W. Va., to Maine’s Mount Katahdin, the northern terminus of the trail. A family emergency forced Lee to leave the trail as the duo crossed into New Hampshire. Largay continued to hike solo. An old back injury prevented her from carrying a full backpack, so her husband would meet her along the way with fresh supplies. George Largay last saw his wife on the morning of Sunday, July 21. On that day, Geraldine Largay set out on what was to be a three-day hike beginning near Maine’s Saddleback Mountain and terminating just north of the Sugarloaf Ski Resort. She was due to meet her husband at a parking lot off Route 27 there. He arrived at the appointed time but was not able to locate Largay. Thinking that a severe rainstorm the day before might have waylaid her, he spent that night in their vehicle, hoping she would arrive. The next morning, he hailed a State Police officer driving by and reported her missing.

European political leaders have hailed a vote in Greece's parliament as a vital step towards managing the country's debt crisis, which has been a concern for several other eurozone countries. The vote, which took place on Wednesday, was for a package of austerity measures that include spending cuts, tax increases, and privatizations. The measures were demanded by international lenders as a condition for continuing to support Greece. The vote was passed by a simple majority, with all but one lawmaker from the Socialist Party voting in favor. The measures will at least on paper lead to the dismantling of a big part of the economy’s state-run sector, including the privatization of 50 billion euros in state assets. The measures do not, however, provide for changing the Greek Constitution, which states that public-sector workers on permanent contracts have lifetime tenure. The government faces challenges in implementing the measures, including modernizing the country’s confusing tax code and collecting the billions of dollars in tax revenue that analysts say is at the heart of the country’s solvency problems. The government is also running low on political capital, having failed to form a coalition government with the center-right opposition after a revolt in the Socialist Party. It is unclear if the government can hold onto power long enough to see the austerity plan through. The measures have been met with protests in Greece, with protesters setting up roadblocks and clashing with police outside parliament. The government has warned that a "no" vote would be suicidal for Greece.

The Republican-controlled Congress, with a majority in both the House and Senate, is set to begin dismantling eight years of President Barack Obama's Democratic policies. The 115th Congress, which will be sworn in on Tuesday, will prioritize repealing the Affordable Care Act, tax reform, and the reversal of environmental regulations. The only obstacle to the conservative agenda will be Senate Democrats, who hold the power to filibuster legislation, but even that has its limitations. Twenty-three Democrats are up for re-election in 2018, including 10 from states that voted for Donald Trump, and they could break ranks and side with the GOP.

The first order of business for Republicans will be to repeal and delay the health care law, expediting the process for scrapping Obama's major overhaul but holding off on some changes for up to four years. The tax code is also in the crosshairs, with conservatives aiming to scuttle rules on the environment and undo financial regulations created in the aftermath of the 2008 economic meltdown, arguing they are too onerous for businesses to thrive.

The only obstacle to the far-reaching conservative agenda will be Senate Democrats, who hold the power to filibuster legislation, but even that has its political limitations. Twenty-three Democrats are up for re-election in 2018, including 10 from states Trump won, and they could break ranks and side with the GOP.

The Senate will also consider Trump's cabinet picks, and Senate Democrats are already trying to slow the process. However, they cannot do much more than that, because when they were in charge, they changed the rules so that presidential nominees other than Supreme Court picks need only 51 votes to be confirmed.

Democrats have encouraged members to avoid meeting with Trump's nominees until they have turned over their tax returns and made other disclosures. Republicans have been particularly upset that Senator Jeff Sessions of Alabama, whom Trump picked quickly to be attorney general, has either not gotten meetings with Democrats on the Senate Judiciary Committee or had meetings canceled.

The first public hearing on the intelligence community's assessment that Russia interfered in the US election is scheduled for Thursday in the Senate Armed Services Committee, with James Clapper, the director of national intelligence, set to testify. Expect individual panels to investigate, but not a special, high-profile select committee. McConnell has rejected that bipartisan call.

In late December, the Obama administration rolled out a major new environmental regulation intended to rein in mountaintop-removal mining. That regulation, one of dozens that Trump is expected to reverse, is meant to go into effect one day before his inauguration. However, Congress is likely to block it, using the Congressional Review Act, which permits lawmakers to undo new regulations with only 51 Senate votes within the first 60 legislative days of the rules’ completion.

Given time constraints on the Senate floor, members will have to pick some priorities. They are expected to train their sights on a rule that requires oil and gas producers to reduce methane gases, another that requires mining and fossil fuel companies to disclose payments they have made to foreign governments to extract natural resources, and still others that restrict pesticide use.

Republicans will also move quickly to repeal the Affordable Care Act. They plan to pass a truncated budget resolution for the remainder of the fiscal year — already a quarter over — that includes special instructions ensuring that the final repeal legislation could circumvent any Democratic filibuster. However, Republican leaders have not settled on a health care plan to replace Mr. Obama's, and they may delay the repeal measure's effective date for years.

The Senate must also consider Mr. Trump's cabinet picks, and Senate Democrats are already trying to slow the process. However, they cannot do much more than that, because when they were in charge, they changed the rules so that presidential nominees other than Supreme Court picks need only 51 votes to be confirmed.

Democratic leaders have encouraged members to avoid meeting with Mr. Trump's nominees until they have turned over their tax returns and made other disclosures. Republicans have been particularly upset that Senator Jeff Sessions of Alabama, whom Trump picked quickly to be attorney general, has either not gotten meetings with Democrats on the Senate Judiciary Committee or had meetings canceled.

Senator Dianne Feinstein of California postponed her meeting with Mr. Sessions until January because, she said, her schedule got too busy. “The senator doesn’t want to rush,” said her spokesman, Tom Mentzer.

One reason that Democrats are in no hurry is their bitterness over McConnell's refusal last year to hold a hearing on the Supreme Court nomination of Judge Merrick B. Garland.

Lingering in the background is the specter of Russia. Democrats — and some Republicans, who are at odds with Trump on the issue and may at times be a brake on him — want a vigorous investigation of its efforts to disrupt the election. The Obama administration, which took sweeping steps last week to punish the Russians over election hacking, will release a report this month that is likely to serve as a turning point in those discussions.

While Republicans may have a rare chance to open the flow of legislation, the party's leaders are acutely aware of the punishment that Americans have historically delivered in midterm elections when things have not gone well.

“This is no time for hubris,” McConnell said. “You have to perform.”

The study published in the journal Circulation suggests that adhering to five healthy lifestyle factors can significantly extend life expectancy in US adults. The five factors are never smoking, maintaining a healthy body-mass index, keeping up moderate to vigorous exercise, moderate alcohol intake, and a high-quality diet.

The study, which used data from the Nurses' Health Study and the Health Professionals Follow-Up Study, found that adhering to all five lifestyle factors at age 50 was associated with 14 additional years of life expectancy among women and 12.2 additional years among men, compared to not adhering to any of them. Each of these factors is significantly associated with a reduced risk of dying from the top two killers in the United States, cardiovascular disease and cancer.

The study's authors noted that the overall projected life expectancy at age 50 was to live 33.3 more years for women and 29.8 more years for men. However, among adults who reported that they adopted all five healthy lifestyle factors, they lived 43.1 more years among women and 37.6 more years among men. In contrast, those who reported that they adhered to none of the five healthy lifestyle factors lived only 29 additional years among women and 25.5 additional years among men.

The study's findings highlight the significant impact that lifestyle factors can have on life expectancy and encourage people to adopt a healthier lifestyle. The study's authors noted that it's not too late to make changes, even beyond age 50.

The study had some limitations, including that the data on adherence to the five lifestyle factors were all self-reported, making outcome vulnerable to measurement errors. Additionally, the data analysis did not include measures of certain health conditions that are risk factors for a shorter life expectancy, such as diabetes or high blood pressure.

Despite these limitations, the study's findings are significant and highlight the importance of adopting a healthy lifestyle to extend life expectancy. The study's authors noted that the impact of these simple behaviors on life expectancy was more pronounced than they had anticipated.

San Francisco Supervisor Scott Wiener has become the first public figure to disclose that he takes Truvada, an antiviral pill used for HIV prevention, also known as pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP). This drug, approved by the FDA in 2012, can reduce the risk of HIV infection by up to 99 percent if taken daily.

Wiener's announcement aims to reduce the stigma associated with Truvada and encourage more men to consider taking it. The drug, primarily used by men who have sex with men, has been slow to gain acceptance due to stigma and lack of awareness.

San Francisco is pushing an initiative to make Truvada more accessible and distribute it to residents who need it, including a plan to help pay for the drug for those who can't afford it. The drug can cost up to $14,000 a year but is covered by most insurance plans, and the drugmaker will help with the cost for those who need financial assistance.

The slow acceptance of the drug has been due to stigma and doctors' reluctance to prescribe it, especially if they don't regularly treat HIV-positive patients. San Francisco aims to increase accessibility to the drug, and Thursday's city meeting is focused on ensuring the drug is easily available to anyone interested in it.

Wiener, who represents a district that includes the Castro, ground zero for the HIV epidemic, hopes his disclosure will elevate awareness about PrEP as an available and powerful prevention tool. He believes that people need to feel comfortable talking about these issues without fear of stigma or denigration.

Truvada, made by Gilead Sciences, is a single tablet that combines emtricitabine and tenofovir disoproxil fumarate. If taken daily, it can cut the risk of HIV infection by more than 90 percent. The drug appears to also be effective for women and transgender men and women, with most users reporting no side effects.

The slow acceptance of the drug has been a concern for public health and city officials, who believe it could be key to stopping or significantly slowing down the spread of HIV. They aim to speed up its adoption nationwide, as only about 2,000 people are currently taking PrEP.

Dan Van Gorder, executive director of Project Inform, an HIV patient treatment and information advocacy organization, emphasizes the need for health departments and community groups to speed up the adoption of the drug, as it could prevent a lot of infections.

The document discusses the initial steps taken for the construction of Elon Musk's Hyperloop project, a high-speed transportation system that aims to reduce travel time between cities significantly. The project received a building permit for preparatory and excavation work at a vacant lot in Washington, D.C., located at 53 New York Avenue NE. The permit is a small but significant step towards the realization of the Hyperloop project, which aims to connect New York, Philadelphia, Baltimore, and Washington D.C. in a tunnel network.

The Hyperloop system uses magnetic levitation technology to propel pods filled with people and vehicles at high speeds. The technology has been licensed to Hyperloop Transportation Technologies (HTT), one of the two companies leading the hyperloop race. The system works by using permanent magnets on the underside of the capsules, which repel a passive track, with the only input energy coming from the speed of the pod.

The permit received in Washington, D.C., is not the final approval required for the construction of the tunnel, but it marks the beginning of the project. The D.C. Mayor's office is currently in conversation with the Boring Company to understand the general vision for the Hyperloop project. The District's Department of Transportation is also figuring out what other permits the Boring Company would need to cut under city roads and other public spaces.

The Hyperloop project has received backing from the White House Office of American Innovation, led by President Trump's senior advisor and son-in-law, Jared Kushner, as well as Maryland Governor Larry Hogan. Maryland officials say the tunnel would run under Maryland Route 295, with the D.C.-Baltimore leg being the initial stretch in the East Coast system.

The stations for the Hyperloop would be relatively small and toned down compared to traditional stations like Union Station. There would be a main line running between the four cities, with smaller lines spurring out from the city's central station for other potential destinations.

The project, however, faces several challenges, including the technical feasibility of the digging part, the safety and orchestration of the underground system of multiple superfast pods, and concerns about the impact on traditional mass transit systems. Some transportation advocates worry that moving cars in the high-speed system would undercut the benefits of more traditional mass transit.

Overall, while the Hyperloop project is still in its early stages, it represents a significant step forward in the development of high-speed transportation systems. The project has received initial approval and is moving forward, although many challenges remain to be addressed.

In Connecticut, a malfunction at a festival swing ride named Zumur caused a mechanical failure, resulting in the ride coming to an abrupt halt. This incident injured 13 individuals, mostly children, during the Norwalk Oyster Festival. The ride, which spins swings tethered to metal arms in an elliptical motion, caused riders to collide with each other when it suddenly stopped. Twelve children and one adult were taken to hospitals, with an 8-year-old boy remaining hospitalized with non-life-threatening injuries.

Stewart Amusement, the ride's operator, stated that state officials inspected the ride two days before the accident. Richard Stewart, the company's president, confirmed it was a mechanical failure and expressed hope that such an incident wouldn't happen again. The festival temporarily shut down rides after the accident but reopened them later following inspections by fire investigators and the ride company.

Amusement park safety expert Ken Martin highlighted that portable rides have a good safety record, but inspections in Connecticut occur only once a year. Martin advocates for stricter regulations, as there is currently no federal oversight of fixed amusement parks.

The incident at the Norwalk Oyster Festival has raised concerns about the safety of amusement rides, particularly those that are portable and inspected less frequently. Between 1990 and 2010, over 92,000 children were injured in amusement ride-related incidents, according to a study by the Center for Injury Research and Policy at Nationwide Children's Hospital in Ohio.

In an unfortunate incident before Crystal Palace's crucial 1-0 victory over Middlesbrough in the Premier League, the team's own bus was vandalized, causing an estimated £40,000 in damages. The vandalism occurred at a hotel near Crystal Palace's Selhurst Park home, where the bus was parked overnight. The vandals mistakenly believed the bus belonged to Middlesbrough, as it had been loaned to Crystal Palace by the latter's manager, Aitor Karanka, after his squad flew down to London on Friday. The vandalism involved painting Crystal Palace's name and colors on one side of the coach. The club's spokesman confirmed the incident, stating that police have been informed. The vandalized bus was replaced, and the team traveled to the game using another bus. Crystal Palace's January signing, Patrick van Aanholt, scored the only goal of the match, helping the team move out of the relegation zone.

George Zimmerman, the neighborhood watchman who was acquitted of second-degree murder and manslaughter charges in the shooting death of Trayvon Martin seven months ago, maintains that he was a victim during the incident. Zimmerman claims he was beaten before he fatally shot the 17-year-old. Despite the controversy surrounding the verdict, Zimmerman remains unwavering in his belief that he acted in self-defense. He has faced legal troubles since his acquittal, including speeding charges, domestic disputes, and accusations of threatening his girlfriend with a shotgun. Zimmerman has also faced PR issues, using his notoriety to sell paintings and agreeing to become a prize fighter for charity, despite his claims during trial that he couldn't hold off a teenager.
