Zimmerman continues to receive death threats and claims that those who label him as a racist don't know that some of his family members are black. Zimmerman has distanced himself from current events, preferring to watch comedy and home improvement shows instead. When asked about a similar case involving Michael Dunn, Zimmerman admitted his lack of knowledge about the situation.

Major League Baseball (MLB) has announced a change to the intentional walk rule, allowing teams to signal the walk from the dugout instead of having the pitcher throw four balls. While the change aims to speed up games, some players and fans are disappointed as the four-pitch intentional walk has led to occasional humorous or exciting moments.

For instance, Jason Kipnis of the Indians has scored twice on errant pitches during intentional walks, and Miguel Cabrera has delivered a memorable moment with a single on an attempted intentional walk. Some argue that the rule change will have minimal impact, as intentional walks only took an estimated 35 seconds per game last season.

However, the change has sparked playful suggestions, such as requiring the center fielder to throw the intentional walk or having managers mimic the "Walk like an Egyptian" dance as the signal. Overall, the elimination of the four-pitch intentional walk may not significantly affect game length, but it will undoubtedly take away a small part of baseball history.

On October 26, 2018, authorities arrested Cesar Sayoc, a 56-year-old Florida resident, in connection with more than a dozen suspected mail-bomb devices sent to prominent Democrats and outspoken critics of President Trump. The arrest came after a fingerprint found on one of the packages led investigators to a white van parked in Plantation, Florida, which was plastered with images of Trump and Vice President Pence, as well as pictures of liberal figures in crosshairs.

Sayoc was charged with five federal crimes, including illegal mailing of explosives, threats against former presidents, and assaulting current and former federal officers. He faces up to 48 years in prison. The bombs were sent to prominent Democratic politicians, donors, and CNN offices in New York, and additional explosive devices or suspicious packages were identified in New York and California.

A total of 13 bombs were mailed around the country, and FBI Director Christopher Wray said there could be more packages not yet discovered. The packages were not hoax devices, Wray said. Sayoc was initially cooperative after arrest, telling investigators that the pipe bombs wouldn't have hurt anyone and that he didn't want to harm anyone.

Sayoc's social media accounts showed he was a fervent supporter of Trump and had posted criticism of CNN and other media outlets. Among the posts were threats to individual political figures and media outlets, including CNN and CNN employees. Trump told reporters that he had heard Sayoc was a supporter of his, but that didn't mean much to the President.

Investigators believe the packages were sent in a staggered manner, with the most recent packages not turning up until 48 hours ago. The packages were addressed to Sen. Cory Booker, former National Intelligence Director James Clapper, Sen. Kamala Harris, and major Democratic donor Tom Steyer, bringing the total number of known packages sent by Sayoc to 14. However, he's been charged with sending only 13 packages.

Sayoc has a criminal history in Florida, including an arrest for making a bomb threat in 2002, for which he pleaded guilty and was sentenced to one year of probation. He also has a history of arrests for grand theft, battery, fraud, drug possession, and multiple probation violations. In 2014, he was arrested after stealing copper pipes at a Home Depot, to which he plead guilty.

The adjudication of each of the arrests could not be immediately determined from the summary of offenses provided by the Florida Department of Law Enforcement. Sayoc appears to have pleaded no contest to some offenses, and prosecutors appear to have dropped charges in other matters. Sayoc also was arrested in North Carolina in 1999 on a stolen vehicle charge, which was later dismissed. Florida voting records show Sayoc is a registered Republican. He filed for bankruptcy in 2012.

The arrest of Sayoc comes amid a coast-to-coast manhunt for the person responsible for a series of explosive devices addressed to Democrats including former President Barack Obama, former Vice President Joe Biden, and Hillary Clinton. The common thread among the bomb targets was their critical words for Trump and his frequent, harsher criticism in return. Trump claimed that he was being blamed for the mail bombs, complaining in a tweet that the media was wrongly blaming him and his heated rhetoric.

The article discusses new research that suggests dinosaurs, such as the Tyrannosaurus rex, may have sounded quite different from how they are portrayed in movies like Jurassic Park. Instead of roaring, they may have made low, throaty whooshes of air, similar to the coo of a pigeon or the mumble of an ostrich. This is based on a study that analyzed the vocalizations of various archosaurs, including birds and crocodiles, and found that a quarter of the birds species analyzed emitted low, closed-mouth sounds. The researchers believe that large-bodied dinosaurs may have had similar vocal abilities.

The study suggests that dinosaur sounds may be what scientists call "closed-mouth vocalizations." Unlike the high-pitched chirps and tweets from the open beaks of songbirds, closed-mouth sounds are low, throaty whooshes of air. A flesh sac called an esophageal pouch enables birds with proportionally large bodies to produce the low murmurs.

The researchers collected vocal data on various archosaurs and divided the types of sounds into various groups, including the close-mouth noises. They found that small birds, like sparrows and finches, did not make the closed-mouth noises, but birds with proportionally larger body types, like doves, ostriches, and the giant New Zealand cassowary, did. This suggests that large-bodied dinosaurs may have had similar vocal abilities.

The researchers were handicapped in their study because vocal organs, made of soft tissue, do not fossilize the way dinosaur bones do. However, there are a few other hints about what dinosaurs may have sounded like. Based on what scientists know about birds, dinosaurs likely did not have vocal cords, but instead had air sacs, and it is possible that they had a bird-like syrinx, too.

The study was published in the journal Evolution. The researchers believe that their findings could help us better understand the vocalizations of extinct early avian species and potentially their dinosaur ancestors. This could offer clues about what dinosaurs sounded like, making for a very different Jurassic world. Not only were dinosaurs feathered, but they may have had bulging necks and made booming, closed-mouth sounds.

The Red Hot Chili Peppers, set to perform at the Super Bowl halftime show alongside Bruno Mars, have been accused of miming during their performance of "Give It Away." Guitarist Vernon Reid noticed the absence of a cable connecting Flea's bass guitar to an amplifying device, and forensic photographic analysis on Twitter confirmed his observation. Flea later issued a statement on the band's website, explaining that they decided not to plug in their instruments to avoid pretending and to bring the spirit of who they are to the performance. Flea expressed gratitude to the NFL for having them and to Bruno Mars for inviting them, stating that he would do it all the same way again. The controversy over the Chili Peppers' performance has sparked discussions about the importance of authenticity in music, particularly in high-profile events like the Super Bowl halftime show.

The Republican field for the 2016 presidential election is growing rapidly, with a dozen candidates currently in the race, including five former or current U.S. Senators and four current or former governors. This is the largest field of candidates since 1860, when Abraham Lincoln was elected. The size of the field and its closely competitive rankings are causing a scramble among candidates to gain national attention and improve poll numbers, as only the top 10 GOP candidates in the polls will be allowed into televised debates.

Governor Chris Christie of New Jersey is expected to join the race in the coming weeks, but his well-known rhetorical skills may not be enough to secure a spot in the debates. In a Washington Post/ABC News poll, Christie was in eighth place, just five percentage points behind the first place candidates, U.S. Senator Rand Paul of Kentucky and Wisconsin Governor Scott Walker.

To gain traction in the media and improve poll numbers, Christie and his rivals will likely start playing nastier and faster than ever. Experts say that the large field of candidates makes it tougher to gain attention, and the summer months could complicate matters as TV audiences are about 10 percent less than in the winter months.

Christie has already begun employing a plan of attack, taking aim at 2016 contender Rand Paul for allowing parts of the Patriot Act to expire and chiding Jeb Bush for being "late to the party" with his economic plan. Christie has also proposed detailed plans for reforms to federal entitlement programs, immigration policy, taxes, and education, which could give him an advantage in such an unusually large field.

The 2016 campaign could last longer than any in recent memory due to the 2012 Citizens United U.S. Supreme Court ruling, which allows unlimited amounts of cash to back presidential candidates. This could result in a prolonged nominating process and potentially a brokered convention, as no candidate is expected to reach the 1,100 delegates needed to secure the nomination.

Christie's launch rally at his high school in New Jersey on Tuesday will include friends who remember his years as class president, but no teleprompter, in an effort to live up to his campaign slogan, "Telling it like it is." Christie will spend five straight days in New Hampshire, plunging into hand-to-hand campaigning and offering himself as a pragmatic, results-oriented conservative. He will signal his willingness to take on tough issues, such as entitlements, and highlight his ability to win and govern in a blue state. Christie's wife, Mary Pat, and the rest of his family, along with longtime supporters and friends, will attend the rally.

The study published in the journal Science reveals a significant shift in understanding about dinosaurs, suggesting that they were likely covered in feathers or had the potential to grow them. The discovery of the 150-million-year-old fossil Kulindadromeus zabaikalicus in Siberia, a plant-eating dinosaur from the ornithischian group, showcases feather-like structures, challenging the previous belief that feathers were exclusive to the theropod group. This discovery indicates that feathers were more widespread among dinosaurs than initially thought, dating the origin of feathers millions of years further back.

The dinosaur, about 1m long, had a short snout, long hind legs, short arms, and five strong fingers, with teeth adapted for chewing plants. The discovery of these feather-like structures outside theropods suggests that they may have been present in the earliest dinosaurs, challenging the traditional view of dinosaurs as dry, scaly creatures.

While the discovery does not imply that all dinosaurs had feathers, it confirms the long-held idea that dinosaurs were initially feathered and warm-blooded. The feathers were likely used for insulation and signaling, with flight adaptation coming later. However, some experts have expressed doubts about the feather-like structures found in Kulindadromeus, as they resemble streamers rather than the branching structure of bird feathers.

The discovery has significantly changed our understanding of dinosaurs, suggesting a more diverse and fluffy appearance than previously thought. However, further research is needed to confirm the exact nature of these feather-like structures and their evolutionary significance.

The 12-year-old Arkansas girl, Kali Hardig, who was diagnosed with a rare and often fatal infection caused by the brain-eating amoeba Naegleria fowleri, is now able to say a few words after undergoing experimental treatment and early detection. Kali contracted the infection after a trip to a now-shuttered Arkansas water park that featured a sandy-bottomed lake. The amoeba is typically found in warm freshwater bodies and enters the body through the nose while swimming or diving.

Kali's mother, Traci Hardig, reported that Kali can now say "yes" and "no," as well as "Hi mama," "daddy," and "nanny." Doctors believe Kali's success is due to the experimental treatment and early detection and diagnosis. Kali was brought to Arkansas Children's Hospital with a high fever on July 19, and doctors cooled her body down to reduce swelling and treated her with a breast-cancer drug. Tests now show no sign of the parasite in her system.

However, doctors warn that Kali may have long-term deficits and may need months of therapy. Kali will likely remain at the hospital for at least a few more weeks. The family has set up a Facebook page, "Prayers for Kali Le-Ann," to update supporters on her progress.

In a tragic turn of events, a 12-year-old South Florida boy, Zachary Reyna, who was also battling the same infection at Miami Children's Hospital, has been declared brain dead and will be taken off life support on Sunday night. Reyna contracted the infection while knee-boarding in ditch water in Glades County. Although antibiotics had successfully fought off the infection, Reyna suffered extensive brain damage. The family has indicated that Reyna has already "passed" after showing negative brain activity for days, but he will be kept on a ventilator until Sunday night so that his organs can be donated.

The family and doctors are urging people to take precautions to avoid contracting the infection, such as limiting water contact with the nose, avoiding water-related activities in warm freshwater during periods of high water temperatures and low water levels, and avoiding stirring up bottom sediment in shallow, warm freshwater areas. There have also been cases from the use of Neti pots, in which contaminated water is used to irrigate the nose.

The New York State Attorney General, Eric Schneiderman, is investigating whether energy-drink manufacturers are deceiving consumers by making misleading statements about the ingredients and health benefits of their products. Farhad Manjoo, a technology columnist for the Wall Street Journal, proposed last year that Twitter increase its character limit from 140 to 280 to accommodate the platform's evolving uses, such as news, jokes, conversations, and arguments. However, the idea was met with skepticism, with critics arguing that it would inconvenience SMS users and lead to lengthy, unreadable tweets.

Recently, Twitter announced the creation of "expanded tweets," which allow for "interactive experiences" within text-laden posts. Although tweets can still only be 140 characters long, select organizations, including the New York Times, the Wall Street Journal, BuzzFeed, TMZ, and the WWE, can append additional content to tweets that reference their content. This expanded content can include headlines, author bylines, Twitter handles, photos, and article snippets, amounting to a total of 410 characters.

Expanded tweets are seen as a positive development for Twitter, as they add depth to the service while still maintaining its abridged roots. They make Twitter feel less disjointed, allowing users to see what's behind links before clicking on them and following their favorite writers directly from tweets. However, critics argue that expanded tweets only benefit a select few organizations, and there are concerns that Twitter is moving towards becoming a more feature-rich social network, potentially losing its simplicity and focus.

Twitter has stated that the preferential treatment given to select organizations is temporary and part of a slow rollout of the complex technical change. Over time, it is expected that more and more sites will be allowed to automatically expand into summaries within tweets. This means that in the near future, users will be able to see more content, such as images and videos, directly within tweets, making Twitter a more engaging destination.

Kelly started her show on Wednesday by apologizing for her comments, but disappointment within NBC News runs deep and is unlikely to fade anytime soon. The San Diego City Council has unanimously voted to ban drinking on Mission Bay in an attempt to stop the "floatopia" booze parties that have been exploiting a loophole in the city's beach drinking ban. The parties, which involve hundreds of college-aged individuals drinking while floating on rafts, inner tubes, and other devices, have been deemed a safety hazard by police and lifeguard officials due to the potential for drownings and injuries from broken bottles.

Opponents of the ban argue that further restrictions on drinking could negatively impact tourism. However, Councilwoman Marti Emerald stated that the council's primary concern is ensuring the safety of beachgoers. The ban, which is set to take effect immediately, does not apply to drinking on boats.

The loophole that allowed the floatopia parties was discovered in 2008 by Bradford Boyle, an information technology engineer, who shared the information on a personal website. The parties have since grown in size, leading to concerns about public safety and potential negative impacts on tourism.

The alcohol-fueled riot on Pacific Beach during Labor Day weekend in 2008 prompted the initial one-year ban on alcohol consumption on city beaches, which was later made permanent by city voters. However, the ban did not cover drinking in the water. The recent vote to extend the ban to the water follows a series of incidents involving drunkenness and disorderly conduct at floatopia parties.

Sir Roger Bannister, the first person to run a mile in under four minutes, has passed away at the age of 88. His historic run of 3 minutes 59.4 seconds, achieved on May 6, 1954, at the Iffley Road sports ground in Oxford, stood as a record for just 46 days. However, his place in athletics history was secured. Apart from breaking the record, Bannister also won gold over the same distance at the 1954 Commonwealth Games. He was later diagnosed with Parkinson's disease in 2011.

IAAF president Lord Coe, who set a mile world record of 3:47.33 in 1981, expressed his sadness on the occasion. Bannister, who viewed running as a hobby during his medical studies at the University of Oxford, reached the biggest stages in the sport despite not being considered for the British team at the 1948 London Olympics. He set a new British record in the 1500 meters final at the 1952 Games in Helsinki.

Bannister aimed to become the first person to run inside four minutes for the mile after the Olympics and came close twice in 1953. American Wes Santee and Australia's John Landy were also targeting the record when Bannister finally achieved it in the spring of 1954. The men's mile record has since been broken multiple times, with Britons Sebastian Coe, Steve Ovett, and Steve Cram each holding the record at least once in the 1980s. The current record is held by Moroccan Hicham El Guerrouj, who ran a time of 3:43.13 seconds in Rome on July 7, 1999.

Bannister retired from athletics at the end of 1954 to focus on his medical studies full-time and later became a consultant neurologist. He continued to run until a car accident in 1975, the same year he was knighted. Bannister revealed his Parkinson's disease diagnosis in a BBC interview in 2014. He passed away peacefully in Oxford on March 3, surrounded by his family. His family's statement read, "He banked his treasure in the hearts of his friends."

A newly installed pedestrian bridge on Florida International University's campus collapsed on March 15th, resulting in at least four deaths. The bridge, which was touted as a feat of engineering, collapsed at around 1:30 p.m. and trapped at least eight vehicles under the rubble. Ten injured victims were transported to Kendall Regional Medical Center, with two in critical condition and eight in stable condition. The victims' ages ranged from 20 to 50 years old. The cause of the collapse is still under investigation by the National Transportation Safety Board, with no previous incidents of this type of bridge failure reported. The university expressed its condolences and promised to cooperate with investigators. The bridge was a $14.2 million project, funded by the U.S. Department of Transportation, and was expected to be completed in early 2019.

In a playful tradition of pranks during the transfer of power in Virginia, outgoing Governor Ralph Northam pulled a prank on his successor, Terry McAuliffe. Upon moving into the Governor's Mansion, Northam and his wife, Pam, found pillowcases emblazoned with McAuliffe's face and his favorite saying, "Sleep when you're dead." The newly inaugurated Northam was also greeted with several photos of McAuliffe around the residence and an early morning alarm clock that went off at 3 a.m. Northam found humor in the situation, thanking McAuliffe for the prank and joking that there was more to come.

This pranking tradition is unique to Virginia, as it is the only state where the governorship changes hands every four years. Previous governors have also participated in similar pranks. For instance, during Robert F. McDonnell's departure in 2014, he set an alarm clock to go off at 4 a.m., waking up McAuliffe on his first weekend in the Executive Mansion.

In 2010, Tim Kaine, who was then leaving the governorship to become a senator, hid cellphones in the mansion elevator shaft and periodically called them as a trick on McDonnell. It took a few days for McDonnell's team to locate them. Before that, Mark R. Warner, another senator, left a life-size cutout of himself in the governor's mansion shower for Kaine.

Despite the pranks, Northam took the oath to become Virginia's 73rd chief executive on Saturday, beating Republican Ed Gillespie in the November elections. The peaceful transfer of power in Virginia was marked by these light-hearted traditions, adding a touch of humor to the formal ceremony.

The New Vineyard Gazette, owned by Jerome and Nancy Kohlberg, has been sold for $2 million for the newspaper business and $1.5 million for the Gazette's real estate. Richard Reston, the paper's publisher since 1988, is retiring. The California Supreme Court refused to review lower-court rulings ordering SF Weekly to pay $21 million in damages for trying to drive a rival, the Bay Guardian, out of business.

In other news, Andrew McCarthy, a freelance travel writer, was named the 2010 Travel Journalist of the Year in the Lowell Thomas Travel Journalism Competition. The Washington Post asked McCarthy which award he would choose if he could win only one, to which he responded, "I'll take them all."

Afar Magazine, the Washington Post, and the San Francisco Chronicle won top honors as the best travel publications in North America in the 2010 Lowell Thomas Travel Journalism Competition. BudgetTravel.com won gold for the best online travel journalism site. Rick Steves earned top honors for the best travel book with "Travel as a Political Act."

The competition drew 1,161 entries, with judging done by faculty at the University of North Carolina-Chapel Hill School of Journalism and Mass Communication. The awards, recognized as the most prestigious in the field, were announced at the annual convention of the Society of American Travel Writers. The total prize money for individual winners was $20,600. The Grand Award earns the gold winner $1,500, the silver winner $750, and the bronze place $500. In individual categories, first-place gold winners each receive $500. Silver and bronze winners receive $250 and $150. The categories for Best Newspaper Travel Sections, Best Magazines, Best Online Travel Journalism Sites, and Best Travel Packages/Projects are not given monetary awards.

The article discusses a study by Forbes using IRS data to analyze moves between counties in the United States, focusing on the trend of wealthy individuals moving to counties with warm weather and low taxes. Other top counties include Greene County, Georgia; Nassau County, Florida; Llano County, Texas; and Walton County, Florida. The study suggests that the lack of an income tax in Florida and Texas, as well as lower personal tax burdens, are driving factors in the migration of wealthy individuals to these states. The study also reveals that six of the top 10 counties the rich are fleeing are located in states with high taxes, such as California, New Jersey, New York, and Maryland. The article uses data from the IRS, the Census Bureau, and real estate information services to support its findings.

In a controversial turn of events during a panel discussion on CNN, sports radio host Clay Travis made a crude statement, declaring that he believes in only two things completely: the First Amendment and "boobs." In a recent announcement, Salt Lake City Mayor Jackie Biskupski revealed that an internal affairs investigation has found that two Salt Lake City police officers, Detective Jeff Payne and Lt James Tracy, violated police codes of conduct in the forcible arrest of nurse Alex Wubbels, who refused to draw blood from an unconscious patient against hospital policy. The incident was recorded on a body camera, showing Detective Payne dragging and handcuffing Ms. Wubbels, who screamed "I've done nothing wrong!" as she was taken away. The hospital confirmed that Ms. Wubbels followed its policy correctly.

The investigation considered possible misconduct relating to lawful arrests and the police code of ethics. Mayor Biskupski described the footage of Ms. Wubbels' arrest as "unacceptable" and "not reflective of who we are as a city or as a police department." The officers have been placed on administrative leave and have up to 20 days to respond to the allegations.

The findings of the report will be sent to Salt Lake City police chief Mike Brown to decide on any further action. The police department has since amended its policy regarding blood sample requests to match that of the hospital. University of Utah Hospital policy states that blood can only be handed over without a patient's consent if they are under arrest or the police have a warrant, neither of which applied in the July incident.

Nurse Wubbels later released a statement, accepting the apologies from the city's mayor and police chief for the treatment she received. The investigation is not the final step in the process, with further action to be decided by the police chief.

The CNN debate on Monday night featured a controversial moment when Rep. Ron Paul was asked about a hypothetical uninsured individual in a coma. Some audience members cheered at the suggestion that society should let him die, a response that Gov. Rick Perry, who also participated in the debate, found surprising. Thomas Kinkade, the American painter known for his sentimental and religious-themed artwork, has been the subject of a legal dispute between his wife, Nanette, and his live-in girlfriend, Amy Pinto-Walsh. Nanette, who serves as the trustee and executor of the Kinkade Family Trust and the artist's estate, has filed a temporary restraining order against Pinto-Walsh.

The court documents, obtained by the Los Gatos Patch, allege that Pinto-Walsh breached a confidentiality agreement she signed in 2011 by disclosing private and confidential information about the Kinkade family and their businesses. The agreement was signed during her role as a personal assistant and companion to Thomas Kinkade.

Pinto-Walsh is accused of breaching the agreement by speaking to the media about Kinkade's non-public health condition and his death, which occurred on April 5, contrary to earlier reports. She is also said to have announced her intention to publicize confidential information about the Kinkade family and their businesses, including private photographs.

The restraining order seeks to prevent Pinto-Walsh from making statements or engaging in conduct that would defame, criticize, disparage, or discredit Kinkade, Nanette Kinkade, or any company owned by Kinkade. It also aims to prevent her from publishing any book, article, or report concerning the Kinkade family or their businesses.

The order also seeks to stop Pinto-Walsh from selling, trading, publishing, disclosing, producing, permitting access to, or otherwise revealing proprietary information to anyone. The hearing for the injunction request is scheduled for April 24.

Thomas Kinkade's death has left many unanswered questions, including the cause of his death, which remains pending after an autopsy was performed. Some former gallery owners have accused Kinkade of unfair business practices in the past. The recent legal dispute adds a new dimension to the circumstances surrounding his death.

Snoop Dogg, a 16-time Grammy nominee, received a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame on November 19, 2018, four days before the 25th anniversary of the release of his debut album "Doggystyle." The ceremony took place in front of the El Capitan Entertainment Center on Hollywood Boulevard where Jimmy Kimmel's show is taped. During his speech, Snoop Dogg thanked friends and family, including himself, for his success. He thanked himself for believing in himself, doing all the hard work, having no days off, never quitting, always being a giver, trying to do more right than wrong, and just being himself at all times. Snoop Dogg's rap career began by making mixtapes with his cousins Nate Dogg and Lil 1/2 Dead and friend Warren G. One tape was heard by Dr. Dre, who invited him to audition. "Doggystyle," released on Nov. 23, 1993, debuted at No. 1 on the Billboard 200 and sold more than 11 million copies worldwide through November 2015. Snoop Dogg has had a successful career in music, acting, television, and philanthropy, including establishing the Snoop Youth Football League in 2005. He has been nominated for nearly 20 Grammy awards and has released 18 studio albums, including "Snoop Dogg Presents Bible Of Love," which debuted at No. 1 on the Billboard charts in March 2018. Snoop Dogg's star is the 2,651st on the Hollywood Walk of Fame.

The oil and gas industry's expansion in the US, particularly in Oklahoma, has been linked to a significant increase in earthquakes. A study published in the journal Science suggests that massive injections of wastewater from the oil and gas industry could be responsible for the rise in earthquakes, with a forty-fold increase in the rate of quakes in Oklahoma between 2008-13. The researchers found that the disposal of water in four high-volume wells could be linked to a swarm of tremors up to 35km away.

The link between oil and gas extraction and earthquakes has been a topic of discussion in states like Arkansas, Texas, Ohio, and Oklahoma in recent years. If a fault is close to failure, the increased pressure at these locations could potentially push them over the edge, according to Dr Katie Keranen from Cornell University. In 2011, a 5.7 tremor in Prague, Oklahoma, injured several people and destroyed 14 houses, which was linked to the injection of wastewater from the oil industry.

The study found that more than 2,500 earthquakes greater than magnitude 3.0 have occurred around the small town of Jones since 2008, representing about 20% of the total in the central and western US in this period. Researchers have linked this increase to a near doubling in the volumes of wastewater disposed of in the central Oklahoma region between 2004 and 2008.

The high price of oil has driven the water-based approach in the oil and gas industry, but the law requires that drinking water must be protected from the salty flow. Four of the biggest wastewater wells in Oklahoma have been pumping around 4 million barrels of water a month to a depth of 3.5km beneath the surface. The study's authors are uncertain about the potential for the large-scale disposal of wastewater to trigger events of larger magnitude.

The authors of the study say that ongoing research will be needed to better understand the complexity of these processes as they continue into the future. The increase in earthquakes demands political and social discussion, with questions being raised about the importance of producing oil and gas in Oklahoma and whether the issues with disposal wells are worth dealing with to continue producing oil and gas.

The discovery of pottery fragments in two Neolithic villages in Georgia, dating back approximately 8,000 years, has revealed the earliest evidence of grape wine-making. The chemical analysis of the pottery revealed the presence of tartaric acid, a chemical "fingerprint" of wine residues, and other acids found in wine. The jars were similar to traditional winemaking vessels still used in Georgia today, and the grape decorations on the outside of the jars suggest that the people living at the time were grape lovers. The wine was likely produced in the nearby hills, close to where the grapes were grown, and may have been a seasonal drink, produced and consumed before it had a chance to turn vinegary. This discovery pushes back the world's earliest evidence of modern-style viticulture by up to 1,000 years, trumping earlier finds in the Zagros Mountains of Iran. The Eurasian grapevine, from which nearly all kinds of modern wine originate, has its roots in Caucasia. The findings are reported in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

Facebook, with over 1.39 billion active users worldwide, has updated its community standards to provide more clarity on what types of posts are not allowed on the platform. The social media giant walks a delicate line between banning violent or offensive content and encouraging free sharing of information. The company's decisions to block or allow content are often opaque and inconsistent, as seen in its handling of beheading videos, antigovernment protests, and the use of stage names by San Francisco's drag queens.

The updated rules ban terrorist organizations like the Islamic State, supporting or praising groups involved in "violent, criminal or hateful behavior," threatening people with physical or financial harm, bullying, content encouraging suicide or eating disorders, and sexual violence or exploitation, including revenge porn. Facebook has also clarified its stance on nudity, stating that it removes photographs of people displaying genitals or focusing on fully exposed buttocks, while allowing photos of women breastfeeding or showing breasts with post-mastectomy scarring.

Facebook will not automatically scan for and remove potentially offensive content. Instead, it will rely on users to report violations of the standards. The company has review teams working at all hours of the day around the globe, and every report is examined before a decision is made. The process can take time, with typical safety matters taking 48 hours.

Facebook's rulings can be appealed, and the company published its latest transparency report on Monday, disclosing country-by-country information on government requests for user data and the removal of content. In the second half of 2014, Facebook restricted 9,707 pieces of content for violating local laws, up 11 percent from the first half of the year. India requested the most takedowns, with 5,832, and Turkey was not far behind with 3,624. No content was restricted in the United States based on government requests.

Facebook's co-founder and CEO, Mark Zuckerberg, wrote that the company wants to give the most voice to the most people while also complying with government orders that require content to be restricted in certain countries. Zuckerberg believes that muting all voices in these countries would be detrimental to the millions of people who rely on Facebook to stay in touch with their friends and family every day.

The updated community standards aim to provide more clarity and examples, helping people understand what is and is not allowed on Facebook. The standards are broken into four sections: helping to keep users safe, encouraging respectful behavior, keeping accounts and personal information secure, and protecting intellectual property. Facebook continues to scrutinize each government request and push back when it finds deficiencies, while also pushing governments around the world to reform their surveillance practices to maintain safety and security while protecting rights and freedoms.

Florida's Orlando International Airport is set to become the first in the nation to require a face scan for all passengers on international flights, including U.S. citizens. This move, announced on Thursday, has raised concerns from privacy advocates who question the lack of formal rules for handling data obtained from the scans and the potential for wrongful denial of boarding.

Currently, airports in Atlanta, Boston, Chicago, Houston, Las Vegas, Miami, New York, and Washington already use face scans for some departing international flights, but not for all international travelers. The new program in Orlando would involve every international departure gate, marking a significant expansion of the number of people scanned.

U.S. citizens can opt out of the face scans at all airports, but concerns have been raised about the agency's effectiveness in informing travelers about this option. A notice about a possible rule change for the program states that U.S. citizens may be required to provide photographs upon entering or departing the United States.

Privacy advocates have expressed concerns about the accuracy of the face scans, particularly with regards to racial minorities, women, and children, as photos used to train the software may underrepresent these groups.

Two U.S. senators have sent a letter to the Department of Homeland Security, urging the implementation of formal rules before the program is expanded. They argue that this would ensure a thorough review of the potentially sweeping program that could impact every American leaving the country by airport.

The expansion of facial recognition technology in airports is part of a broader trend towards using biometrics to improve security and speed up the boarding process. Delta, for example, has announced plans to launch a self-service bag drop powered by facial recognition technology, and Clear, a private company, offers biometric verification for faster security lines at 24 airports nationwide.

The use of facial recognition technology in airports is expected to continue to evolve, potentially offering a more seamless travel experience for passengers. However, concerns about privacy and accuracy will likely remain a topic of discussion.

The article discusses the investigation into the disappearance of Malaysia Airlines Flight 370, which went missing more than a week ago. The possibility that one of the pilots may have deliberately crashed the plane by committing suicide is being considered by investigators. This is a sensitive topic, as such incidents are almost taboo and investigators are reluctant to conclude that a pilot purposely crashed a plane.

The article mentions several previous incidents where it was determined that a co-pilot's actions caused a crash, but the word "suicide" was not used in the official findings. For example, in the 1999 crash of EgyptAir Flight 990, the co-pilot was found to have switched off the autopilot, pointed the plane downward, and repeated the phrase "I rely on God" over and over. However, the National Transportation Safety Board did not use the word "suicide" in their report.

In addition to the investigation into the pilots, authorities are also examining engineers who may have had contact with the plane before it took off. One of the pilots' homes has been searched, and a flight simulator was taken from the home of the 59-year-old pilot, Zaharie Ahmad Shah.

The article also discusses the safety of flying in general, with a study by the Federal Aviation Administration indicating that pilot suicide is a rare occurrence in the U.S. During the 10 years ending in 2012, just eight of 2,758 fatal aviation accidents in the U.S. were caused by pilot suicide, a rate of 0.3%.

The article concludes by mentioning that Malaysia's government has announced that police are investigating the two pilots of the missing Malaysia Airlines jet, and that they are examining an elaborate flight simulator taken from the home of the 59-year-old pilot.

Actor Tom Sizemore, known for his roles in films such as Saving Private Ryan and Black Hawk Down, is accused of sexually molesting an 11-year-old actress on a movie set in 2003. The incident occurred during a photo shoot for the film Born Killers, and the actress' parents declined to press charges. The allegation has recently come to light in the wake of the Harvey Weinstein sexual harassment scandal.

The Hollywood Reporter spoke to a dozen people involved with the production, who confirmed that Sizemore was sent home over the alleged incident. The actress, now 26, has hired a lawyer to explore legal action against the actor as well as her parents. Sizemore has not commented on the situation.

The incident took place during a second-unit still portrait session, during which the young actress was required to be seated on Sizemore's lap for a holiday tableau. According to production manager Cassidy Lunnen, the girl was so young that it was unclear to her and her parents what had actually taken place.

Casting director Catrine McGregor, who hired the young actress, filed a complaint with the Screen Actors Guild legal department and advocated for Sizemore's immediate dismissal from the project. The producers of the film removed Sizemore from the set as soon as they heard about the assertion, but found the photographs from the portrait session to be inconclusive.

Sizemore has a history of drug use and convictions for battery against women, but has not previously been accused of molestation. He is currently represented by the boutique firm Pantheon.

The allegation comes at a time when the entertainment industry is moving towards greater transparency about sexual misconduct. The actress declined to address the matter except to note that she's exploring legal action. The producers of Born Killers have stated that they took the allegation extremely seriously, but lacked the evidence to pass judgment on Sizemore.

On September 26, 2011, Yosemite National Park Search and Rescue successfully conducted a high-angle helicopter rescue of an Austrian climber who had severed his thumb while climbing El Capitan. The incident occurred on the second day of the climbers' ascent, approximately 1,000 feet below the summit. The severed thumb miraculously landed on a small ledge and was retrieved by the climbing partner.

The park's contract helicopter, along with park rangers, flew to the scene and, despite the impending darkness, decided to attempt a short-haul extraction. The injured climber was transported to a hospital in San Francisco, where his thumb was successfully reattached. The rescue mission was complex and risky, but the team's skill, dedication, and commitment to service resulted in a successful outcome. Yosemite National Park Search and Rescue conducts hundreds of rescues each year, ranging from lost hikers to complex technical rescues like this one.

Ewan McGregor, the Trainspotting and Star Wars actor, was spotted sharing a passionate kiss with his Fargo co-star Mary Elizabeth Winstead in a busy London cafe. The pair spent over an hour at The Good Life Eatery in St John's Wood, where they were seen deep in conversation and appeared comfortable together. This encounter comes after Winstead announced her split from her husband Riley Stearns in May, while McGregor has been married since 1995.

In the US television show Fargo, McGregor and Winstead play lovers Ray Stussy and Nikki Swango. The third series of the show, filmed on location in Calgary, Canada, was aired between April and June. The pair played their roles convincingly, with Winstead portraying a recently-released prisoner who enjoys an affair with probation officer Ray Stussy, portrayed by McGregor.

McGregor and his wife Eve Mavrakis, a production designer, have been married for 22 years and have four daughters together. However, family sources have confirmed that they have been separated since May. A rep for McGregor did not immediately respond to requests for additional comment.

Mary Elizabeth Winstead is a versatile actress known for her roles in horror flicks, Die Hard, Scott Pilgrim vs. the World, and Smashed. She hit the headlines in 2014 when she became a victim of the iCloud hack, with intimate photos taken for her husband leaked online.

The kiss between McGregor and Winstead was captured by The Sun, and the pair were later seen leaving together on McGregor's motorbike. This incident has sparked speculation about the status of McGregor's marriage.

Carson Daly, a media personality, faced backlash after comments he made on his radio show regarding a recent JetBlue flight incident. Daly suggested that gay individuals may not be brave enough to handle dangerous situations, citing a hypothetical flight to a gay pride parade. This comment sparked criticism from the LGBT community, with many pointing out the bravery of Mark Bingham, an openly gay man who reportedly helped to stop a hijacked United Airlines flight during the 9/11 attacks.

Following the controversy, Daly issued an apology on Twitter, stating that his comments were unintentional and that he sincerely regretted offending anyone. GLAAD, the Gay & Lesbian Alliance Against Defamation, has been in dialogue with Daly and his team, with Daly expressing his commitment to fighting for the full equality of LGBT Americans. In a statement, Daly acknowledged his past support for LGBT rights and expressed regret for any offense caused.

Estella Havisham, a single mother from Australia, has received both praise and criticism for her tough-love approach to disciplining her 13-year-old son, Aaron, after he lied about doing his homework and was disrespectful to her. In response, Estella wrote a letter demanding that Aaron start paying rent, electricity, Internet, and food costs, as well as completing daily chores, in order to regain access to his room and belongings. The letter went viral on Facebook, with over 160,000 shares and nearly 14,000 comments. While some people agreed with Estella's parenting tactics, others thought they were unreasonable or attention-seeking. Despite the backlash, Estella maintains that she made the right decision and advises other parents to trust their instincts when it comes to disciplining their children. Aaron eventually apologized for his behavior and completed his chores, and Estella slowly began giving him his items back, including his precious Internet. In the end, both Aaron and Estella learned valuable lessons. The incident has sparked a wider discussion about parenting styles and the challenges of raising children in today's world.

Arturo Pierre Martinez, a 29-year-old American from El Paso, Texas, held a press conference in Pyongyang, North Korea on December 14, 2014, where he criticized the United States political and economic system. Martinez claimed to have illegally entered North Korea by crossing the river border with China, although the details of his entry are unclear. His mother stated that he is bipolar and had previously attempted to enter North Korea by swimming across a river, but was stopped and returned to the United States, where he was placed in a California psychiatric hospital. Martinez's mother also mentioned that the U.S. Embassy in Beijing is looking for him.

Martinez's statement at the press conference, which was held at the People's Palace of Culture, was approximately 4,000 words long. In it, he admitted to committing a crime by illegally entering North Korea but expressed gratitude for being pardoned and receiving a generous reception. He criticized American politicians, police, the electoral system, and the prison system, among other things. He also spoke about unidentified flying objects, CIA involvement in the cocaine trade, and the Western media's unfair portrayal of North Korea.

North Korea stated that Martinez entered the country in November, two days after American diplomat James Clapper arrived. Clapper negotiated the release of Kenneth Bae and Matthew Todd Miller, the last two American citizens known to be held by North Korea. The legal status of Martinez in North Korea is unclear, and it's unknown if he is free to leave the country.

Martinez's mother later released a statement expressing relief that her son was safe and appreciative to the North Korean authorities for pardoning and releasing him. She looks forward to spending Christmas with him after his release.

A Southwest Airlines flight from San Francisco to Phoenix was diverted to Los Angeles International Airport on Tuesday after a passenger went into labor mid-flight. The woman was assisted by the flight crew and two medical professionals on board, and the baby was delivered with the help of the medical team. The mother and newborn were taken to a hospital in good condition, and the aircraft was taken out of service for cleaning. The other passengers continued their journey to Phoenix on another plane, arriving over two hours behind schedule. The identity of the mother and baby has not been disclosed. This incident marks the second time a baby has been born on a Southwest Airlines flight, with a similar incident occurring in 2009. The airline did not release the baby's gender. Passengers on board praised the calm and efficient response of the crew and fellow passengers during the emergency.

In the small town of Manchester, Illinois, a tragic incident occurred on Wednesday when Rick Odell Smith, a 43-year-old man with a criminal history, burst into a home armed with a shotgun, a rifle, and a hunting knife. He proceeded to shoot and kill a grandmother, a young couple, and two small children, and seriously wounded a 6-year-old girl. Smith then carried the injured girl to a neighbor's house and sped off, leading to a chase and a shootout with police, in which he was killed. The motive for the attack remains unclear, as Smith was described as an "acquaintance" of the victims, and authorities declined to offer any reasons due to the ongoing investigation. The victims were identified as Joanne Sinclair, 67; Brittany Luark, 23; Luark's boyfriend, Roy Ralston, 29; 1-year-old Brantley Ralston, and a 5-year-old boy, whose name could not be confirmed. The 6-year-old girl survived the attack and was listed in serious condition at St. John’s Hospital in Springfield. The town of Manchester, which lacks even a stoplight and has not experienced a murder in decades, was left in shock and grief by the senseless violence.

Sen. Lisa Murkowski, a Republican from Alaska, has expressed that her views on same-sex marriage are evolving. In a conversation with the Chugiak-Eagle River Star, she acknowledged the changing perspective on marriage in the country and stated that her stance is under review. Murkowski has previously voted for constitutional amendments defining marriage as between one man and one woman, but she now seems to be reconsidering her position.

Murkowski's change of heart may be influenced by her children's generation, who appear to support same-sex marriage. She mentioned that when she asks her sons and their friends about the issue, they express a viewpoint that same-sex marriage should not even be a question.

Murkowski's stance on gay marriage may still align with the views of her constituents in Alaska, as they voted to ban same-sex marriages in 1998. However, she suggested that Alaska might reconsider its position on the issue in the future, and she is reviewing the matter closely.

Murkowski's comments come as the U.S. Supreme Court is currently considering two cases related to same-sex marriage. While her position remains undecided, she emphasized that there are more pressing issues facing the nation than debating who should be allowed to marry.

The incident report of Officer Lameen Barnes on the altercation involving inmate Dixon at a New York City jail, as stated in the report, portrays a peaceful medical examination without the use of excessive force. However, accounts from three anonymous sources, including a clinician's email, suggest a different narrative. According to these sources, Dixon was wheeled into an examination area without a security camera, where he was punched repeatedly by a group of correction officers.

Another inmate, Mr. Lane, who had also been involved in a similar incident, recalled being punched multiple times in the face. The newly appointed commissioner of the jail system, Joseph Ponte, is under scrutiny for violating city law by sending mentally ill inmates into 23-hour confinement without approval from mental health clinicians.

Ponte, who took over the jail system in March, claims he was trying to reduce rising levels of violence. However, the city oversight board rejected this argument, stating that the move jeopardized the health of some inmates, particularly those on psychotropic medications and those with seizure disorders.

Ponte has been criticized for moving inmates from air-conditioned mental observation units into uncooled solitary cells, which violates a federal judge's order. Nearly 40% of the inmates in city jails have a mental health diagnosis, with about a third suffering from serious mental illnesses such as schizophrenia and bipolar disorder.

The Associated Press has previously disclosed the deaths of two mentally ill inmates, prompting calls for reform. During a City Council oversight hearing on violence and mental illness at Rikers, Ponte was asked about a list of hundreds of inmates who owe time in solitary confinement but are in general population due to lack of space. Ponte stated that the number of such inmates is closer to 1,000, many of whom are high-risk for harming themselves and others and need to be separated to stem surging violence.

The incident involving Dixon and Lane highlights the ongoing concerns about the treatment of mentally ill inmates in New York City jails and the need for reform.

In Oregon, two pro-life county commissioners, Janet Carlson and Sam Brentano, have taken immediate action to halt the burning of aborted fetuses at a waste-to-energy incinerator near Portland. The controversy arose after a report in The B.C. Catholic newspaper claimed that "aborted and miscarried children" were being incinerated at the facility.

The waste-to-energy plant, owned and operated by Covanta Marion Inc., has been receiving biomedical waste from British Columbia, Canada, for five to seven years. This waste includes fetal tissue, cancerous tissue, amputated limbs, and other medical waste. The waste is collected by Stericycle Inc., a waste management firm, and sent to the Oregon facility for disposal.

The Marion County commissioners were shocked to learn about the practice and have expressed disgust. They held an emergency meeting and agreed to temporarily stop all biomedical waste shipments to the incinerator and amend local ordinances to bar any future shipments containing fetal tissue.

While the exact amount of fetal tissue from British Columbia that has been transported to the plant is unknown, the B.C. Ministry of Health confirmed that regional health authorities in the province have contracts with Stericycle and send biomedical waste, including fetal tissue, to the Covanta Marion plant.

The commissioners are planning to rewrite their ordinance to explicitly prohibit tissue from fetuses from entering the incinerator. They stressed that other medical waste would still be accepted, such as in the case of amputations.

The controversy comes after a similar issue was discovered in the United Kingdom, where health authorities were found to be using fetal remains to generate power at medical facilities. The practice was quickly banned.

Covanta, the company operating the Oregon facility, has cooperated with the suspension and stated that they do not seek out fetal tissue for disposal. However, they have also placed blame on Marion County for the controversy, stating that they have "no responsibility" for the medical waste program at their incinerator.

Stericycle, the waste management firm responsible for transporting the biomedical waste, has not responded to requests for comment. The issue has sparked outrage and calls for further investigation, particularly from pro-life groups and activists.

Yahoo is set to confirm a massive data breach that has potentially affected several hundred million user accounts. The hack, which is believed to be widespread and serious, has the potential to bring legal action and investigations from the government. Earlier this summer, there were claims that hackers had access to 200 million Yahoo user accounts, and one was selling them online. The announcement is expected this week and could have implications for the $4.8 billion sale of Yahoo's core business to Verizon, as the scale of the liability could cause headaches for the new owners. The deal is currently moving to completion, but regulatory agencies and Yahoo shareholders still need to approve it. The hack became known in August when an infamous cybercriminal named "Peace" claimed to be selling credentials of 200 million Yahoo users from 2012 on the dark web for just over $1,800. The data allegedly included usernames, easily decrypted passwords, and personal information like birth dates and other email addresses. Yahoo initially said it was investigating the information but did not issue a call for a password reset to users. Now, it is possible that Yahoo might have to. The confirmation of such an extensive hack is another blemish on the record of CEO Marissa Mayer, who has presided over numerous declines in the business since she arrived four years ago. The hack comes at an awkward time for Yahoo, as it is in the midst of a mega-acquisition by Verizon.

In Volusia County, Florida, a woman was carjacked while attempting to help crash victims on Interstate 4 early Saturday. The Volusia County Sheriff's Office is actively searching for the suspects, who allegedly stole a 2012 Ford Mustang convertible with Florida tag V83-4QC. The carjackers are described as three black males in their teens or early 20s, with one heavy-set and wearing a striped shirt and jeans, and the other two thin. The stolen vehicle was reportedly used to transport an unresponsive female, who was bleeding from her head, before driving away westbound. The victim, a 34-year-old woman, was not harmed during the incident. The Florida Highway Patrol is investigating the initial crash, and anyone who spots the vehicle or the suspects is asked to call 911.

The U.S. government shutdown has ended, but the political landscape for immigration legislation remains challenging. President Barack Obama has expressed his desire to see immigration reform passed by the end of the year, but some fellow Democrats are hesitant due to concerns about compromising with Republicans, who might dilute the issue's appeal to Hispanics, a crucial voting bloc for Democrats.

One of the hurdles facing legislation this year is the opposition of a majority of House Republicans to providing a pathway to citizenship for undocumented workers. The White House-backed push for immigration reform was derailed by the government shutdown and the subsequent fight over the debt limit.

The reluctance of some Democrats to push for immigration reform now is just one of the obstacles. Speaking on the issue, Texas Republican John Carter stated that there is currently no discussion about immigration by either party.

Obama has urged Congress to approve immigration legislation, casting it as a way to boost the U.S. economy. He has hinted at political repercussions for Republicans who prevent legislation from moving forward.

The fate of the legislation rests largely in the hands of House Speaker John Boehner, who must decide whether to bring a bill to the full House. The Senate passed an immigration bill in June that included a path to citizenship for the country's estimated 11 million undocumented workers.

Supporters of immigration legislation say if Obama pushes hard, it might make it tougher for Republicans to support a priority of the Democratic administration. Some Democrats have hinted that action could come further in the future, possibly in the early summer after primary election filing deadlines are past.

A coalition of business groups, religious leaders, and agricultural companies has spent much of the year lobbying for legislation. Next week, the Partnership for a New American Economy, an association of mayors and business leaders, is flying in 400 business, religious, and technology leaders to make the case for a bill on Capitol Hill. They're targeting House Republicans from more than 20 states.

The House has just 19 days in session before the end of 2013, and there are a number of reasons why immigration reform is stalled this year. The internal political dynamics within the House Republican Conference are tenuous, and a growing chorus of GOP lawmakers and aides are skeptical that any of the party's preferred piecemeal immigration bills can garner the support of 217 Republicans.

Obama is also ramping up his messaging on immigration reform, stating that it's good for the economy, national security, and the people, and should be done this year. However, getting immigration through this deeply divided Congress in 2014, an election year, would be incredibly difficult. Some prominent immigration supporters like Sen. Marco Rubio (R-Fla.) have also backed off any deal, saying the Obama administration has "undermined" negotiations by not defunding his signature health care law.

The article discusses the controversial practice of motorcycle lane splitting, where motorcyclists ride between lanes of moving or stopped traffic, particularly on busy highways. This practice, also known as white lining or filtering, is neither legal nor illegal in New Jersey, as there is no law explicitly forbidding it, but it is not encouraged. The New Jersey State Driver's manual warns against lane sharing with another vehicle and advises against riding in between rows of stopped vehicles.

Police can cite riders for failure to keep right if they lane split, and safety concerns are raised due to the potential for drivers changing lanes without seeing the motorcycle. Motorcycle advocacy groups cite safety reasons for lane splitting, including efficiency, fuel economy, and reducing traffic congestion.

The American Motorcyclist Association (AMA) states that stop and go traffic is the most dangerous situation for motorcyclists, and a study by the University of California at Berkeley concluded that motorcyclists who split lanes in heavy traffic are less likely to be struck from behind, suffer head or torso injuries, and sustain fatal injuries in a crash.

The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) seems to be divided on the topic, with no endorsement but acknowledging that lane splitting can offer an escape route for motorcyclists who might be hit from behind. The Motorcycle Industry Council supports state laws that allow lane splitting with reasonable restrictions, and an online petition to make it legal in New Jersey received over 700 signatures.

In contrast, California is on the verge of becoming the first state to create formal guidelines about lane splitting, with a bill authorizing the California Highway Patrol to set hard guidelines for the practice. The bill passed through the state assembly with a 69-0 vote and is expected to be signed by Governor Jerry Brown.

The article also mentions a separate bill in California that would impose a $1 fee on the purchase of lead-acid batteries, with the funds earmarked for cleaning up contaminated sites such as the former Exide battery plant in Los Angeles County.

The article discusses the consolidation of the pet care industry, focusing on the acquisition of veterinary clinics by large corporations such as Mars Inc. (which owns Banfield Pet Hospital and is set to acquire VCA Inc. and BluePearl Veterinary Partners). The consolidation is driven by the increasing trend of pet owners treating their pets like family members and spending more on their health care.

The article highlights the case of veterinarian John Robb, who lost his Banfield franchise in 2012 due to a dispute over vaccine protocols. Robb believes that Banfield's focus on profits led to over-vaccination and other questionable practices, and he has been vocal about his concerns through a Facebook page called "Boycott Banfield."

The article also discusses the concerns of pet owners who have been disappointed with Banfield's wellness plans, which include services that may not be necessary and could put pets at risk, such as annual teeth cleanings under general anesthesia and annual vaccines that may not be needed for immunity.

The article raises questions about the future of the veterinary care industry, suggesting that the consolidation trend could lead to a one-size-fits-all medical assembly line. The article also notes that the same sort of consolidation has occurred in certain niche care businesses, such as funeral homes.

Overall, the article highlights the concerns of pet owners and veterinarians about the consolidation of the pet care industry and the potential impact on the quality of care for pets.

In 2004, during the height of the Iraq War, a series of controversial photos emerged, allegedly depicting U.S. Marines in Fallujah mishandling and burning the bodies of Iraqi insurgents. The images, obtained by TMZ, show Marines pouring gasoline on the remains of two insurgents, setting their bodies on fire, and posing next to corpses, among other disturbing scenes. The Pentagon has confirmed that these photos have triggered a formal Marine Corps investigation, with the possibility of punishment for the soldiers involved.

The investigation aims to determine the authenticity of the photos and identify the soldiers depicted. The Uniform Code of Military Justice, which prohibits the mishandling of remains, is believed to have been violated. Notably, there is no statute of limitations on crimes against this code, meaning the soldiers could still face prosecution, potentially leading to imprisonment.

The full set of photos, which TMZ claims to have handed over to the military last week, also allegedly includes images of a dog eating one body and a Marine rummaging through a dead man's pockets. The photos were taken in Fallujah, a city that has recently seen a resurgence of Al Qaeda insurgents, sparking debate within the Iraqi military about whether to launch an attack to reclaim it.

Commander Bill Speaks, the Director of Press Operations for the Department of Defense, has stated that the photos, if authentic, are not representative of the honorable and professional service of the 2.5 million service members who served in Iraq and Afghanistan over the past decade.

The New York Stock Exchange (NYSE), a symbol of American capitalism for 220 years, is in discussions to be acquired by IntercontinentalExchange (ICE), an Atlanta-based commodities and derivatives trading platform, in a potential $8.2 billion deal. If successful, the merged company would operate 14 stock and futures exchanges and five clearing operations, making it the largest player in the market.

The NYSE's derivatives trading businesses, including the Liffe market in London, are the main attraction in the merger talks. ICE, founded in 2000, competes with the CME Group, a derivatives trading powerhouse. Last year, ICE and the NYSE's chief rival, the Nasdaq OMX Group, made a joint hostile bid for NYSE Euronext, aiming to break up its planned merger with Deutsche Börse. However, the deal was threatened by the Justice Department due to monopoly concerns.

The proposed merger with ICE might face fewer regulatory issues as it focuses on commodities, while NYSE Euronext primarily deals with stocks and derivatives. The deal would significantly expand ICE, which despite a larger market value, is a smaller company in terms of employees.

The trading of stocks has become less attractive, with the NYSE responsible for only about 11% of all stock trading. The average number of American stocks traded each day has been declining since 2009. A tie-up with ICE would link NYSE Euronext to one of the industry's fastest-growing exchanges, offering potential benefits from consolidation, greater scale, and cost savings.

Shares of NYSE Euronext rose more than 21% in after-hours trading following the news of the talks. The deal is expected to be announced as soon as Thursday morning, but talks may still break down. Other exchanges, such as the CME Group, Hong Kong, and Singaporean exchanges, could potentially express opposition or face nationalist concerns.

The Internet Archive is working on a project to archive web pages as they are created and preserve the pages they reference, aiming to fix broken links on the web. This project, known as "No More 404," involves crawling supported websites to archive pages and replace broken links with links to the archived versions.

The article also discusses the case of Walter Scott, a father who was killed by a police officer in North Charleston, South Carolina. Scott's death brought attention to the issue of child support debt and its impact on families.

In the past, Scott had struggled with child support payments, leading to jail time and the loss of his job. He admitted to making mistakes and sought help through a program called "Father to Father." However, he continued to fall behind on his payments and was eventually wanted by the authorities.

The article highlights the controversial practice of using jail time to pressure parents to pay child support, a policy employed by many states. Critics argue that this policy traps poor men in a cycle of debt, unemployment, and imprisonment.

The article also mentions a program called "Operation Work," which aims to help fathers who owe child support payments find ways to support their families. The program offers temporary reprieve, allowing participants to establish work skills and suspending their child support payments during the program.

The issue of child support debt and its impact on families has gained attention following Walter Scott's death, with some calling for a reevaluation of how we help families and a move away from punitive policies.

The MTV prank series "Punk'd" has returned, with Taylor Swift being pranked by her friend Justin Bieber in the first episode filmed in Los Angeles. The show, originally launched by Ashton Kutcher in 2003, went on hiatus in 2007 but is now back with Justin as the prankster. Meanwhile, Justin Bieber was involved in a minor car collision in Los Angeles, but there were no injuries or damage to his Ferrari or the other vehicle involved. The details of Friday's "Punk'd" prank on Taylor Swift are not yet available. Justin's Ferrari was slightly damaged in the collision, but no one was injured. The show is set to air soon, and fans are eager to see the prank on Taylor Swift.

The assassination of Ahmed Wali Karzai, the powerful half-brother of Afghanistan's president, has created a significant power vacuum in the volatile southern province of Kandahar. Karzai was a divisive figure, accused of corruption and alienating the American military, but his connections and ruthlessness made him a crucial force in the region. His death raises questions about the security gains made by the influx of American forces in the south and the potential for a leader with greater integrity to emerge.

Karzai's death underscores the complicated web of loyalties, interests, and contradictions that the U.S. has navigated for nearly a decade in Afghanistan. He was a politician working within the system and a criminal working against it; he ran militias on behalf of the CIA and funded drug networks that were the stated enemy of the U.S. military; he worked with trucking contractors that sold services to NATO and that funded anti-NATO warlords; he was a close ally of the U.S. and a tremendous drag on its mission to win over the Afghan people.

The U.S. mission both relied on and worked against men like Karzai, who were local "big men" with power inextricably linked with corruption. His death, like so much in the final ten years of his life, underscores the challenge that the U.S. has faced in the Afghan political system, which we rely upon in the short-term but which, in the long term, is a major hurdle in our effort toward peace and stability. Despite many efforts, we have not succeeded in unknotting this contradiction, and it's little wonder that President Obama appears bent on extricating the U.S. from a conflict that we have been unable to untangle, much less win.

The immediate implications of Karzai's death for the American-led war against the Taliban and the withdrawal of American troops beginning this month are uncertain. Many in the region warn that the Taliban, as well as competitors for Karzai's position, will try to take advantage of the power vacuum and that without him, the hard-earned security gains made by American and Afghan troops over the past year could erode. American military commanders have long argued that Karzai's reputation for blatant self-dealing undercut support for the government among many Afghans, and some wonder on Tuesday whether his death might make room for a leader with greater integrity. However, those commanders had clashed with Central Intelligence Agency officers who had long paid Karzai for information and other services and saw him as a crucial broker of intelligence and influence.

In conclusion, the assassination of Ahmed Wali Karzai has created a dangerous power vacuum in Kandahar, a focus of recent efforts by a surge of U.S. troops to turn the tide against the insurgency. His death underscores the challenge that the U.S. has faced in the Afghan political system, which we rely upon in the short-term but which, in the long term, is a major hurdle in our effort toward peace and stability. The immediate implications of his death for the American-led war against the Taliban and the withdrawal of American troops are uncertain, and many in the region warn that the Taliban will try to take advantage of the power vacuum.

A new advertisement campaign in Colorado, aimed at encouraging young people to enroll in the state's health insurance exchange, has sparked controversy and debate over its portrayal of women. The advertisement, produced by ProgressNow Colorado and the Colorado Consumer Health Initiative, features a young woman holding a packet of birth-control pills and standing next to a young man, with the text suggesting a promiscuous encounter. While the groups claim the aim is to encourage enrollment in the state's new health insurance exchange, a pillar of President Obama's Affordable Care Act, some have criticized the advertisement for belittling women and adding to the partisan back-and-forth over the new health care law. The enrollment of young adults is crucial to the new law as they tend to have low anticipated medical costs and can help keep insurance premiums lower. Other advertisements in the campaign feature young people doing keg stands and downing shots from a "shot ski." Amy Runyon-Harms, executive director of ProgressNow Colorado, defended the advertisements, stating that their intention is to raise awareness. However, critics have called the ads demeaning and an attempt to distract from those individual policy-holders who have been notified that their 2013 insurance will not exist in 2014. The advertisements have also been criticized for stereotyping millennials and for portraying women as independent. The state-run health care exchange, which is not associated with the ad campaign, declined to comment.

The fleece vest, often from Patagonia, has become the unofficial uniform for venture capitalists in Silicon Valley. The trend is so prevalent that San Francisco International Airport has a vending machine that dispenses vests, earning an average of $10,000 a month. The vest's popularity may be due to its practicality in the Bay Area's chilly weather, as well as its association with quality and groundedness. HBO's "Silicon Valley" also features a character wearing a Patagonia vest, adding to its popularity. Japanese retailer Uniqlo has added down vests to its vending machines at the airport, further catering to the tech industry's preference for the garment. Twitter has been poking fun at the trend, with one tweet going viral that reads, "SFO has a down vest vending machine for visiting VCs."

The document details a series of damaging messages sent by Rebecca Mansour, a top aide to former Alaska Governor and potential presidential candidate Sarah Palin, on Twitter. The messages, sent as direct messages to an online acquaintance, mock various political figures, including Red State Editor-in-Chief and CNN contributor Erick Erickson, Mitt Romney supporters, and then-California Senate candidate Chuck DeVore.

Mansour also expressed disdain for Palin's daughter, Bristol Palin, predicting that she would be held "at arm's length" by her mother. The messages were initially denied by Mansour, but later authenticated by The Daily Caller, causing a major headache for Palin's operation and leading to questions about Palin's staff.

Mansour served as Palin's domestic policy adviser, speechwriter, and gatekeeper, deciding who gets to see and talk to Palin. She also maintained Palin's online presence, including improving Palin's morale by urging activists to say nice things about the former governor online.

The messages show that, at least last summer, Palin was planning to run for president and calculating her political moves with a run in mind. Mansour also leaked damaging information about a liberal radio host in Alaska.

When contacted about the messages, Mansour initially lied and said none of them were from her. However, presented with evidence, she changed her story and admitted to sending some of the messages. Mansour refused to provide additional context or information about the messages.

The document raises questions about Palin's staff and the internal dynamics of the Palin family. It is unknown if Mansour has been let go by SarahPAC, but staff changes in Palin's camp are typically announced quietly only weeks or months after the fact.

A 15-year-old girl, Daejona M. Holmes, has been charged with the murder of her parents, Kinderly Holmes and Brian Starr, in Kansas City, Missouri. The charges include two counts of second-degree murder, two counts of armed criminal action, and tampering with physical evidence. The incident occurred on April 9 at their home in the 5000 block of Belmeade Road.

Upon arrival, police found both parents dead from apparent gunshot wounds. Daejona Holmes initially called 911 from a McDonald's, reporting a robbery and stating that her parents had been shot. However, her story later changed, claiming that her father had shot her mother, and she had then shot her father.
