During the investigation, police found evidence suggesting premeditation, including online searches for "scary movies where kids kill parents" and rap lyrics about wanting her father dead. A video was also found of Daejona Holmes holding a gun and dancing in her bedroom. A hand-drawn stick figure illustration was discovered in her backpack, depicting one labeled "me" pointing a gun at another labeled "dad."

A witness reported receiving calls from Daejona saying she needed help. He met her at McDonald's, where she told him her parents had been shot. Records show Daejona made nine phone calls with her mother's phone after the shooting, and she waited an hour to call 911. The gun in this case was ultimately located across the street from the home in a puddle of water.

Daejona Holmes has been certified to stand trial as an adult in this case, and prosecutors have requested a $150,000 bond. The case highlights the potential dangers of online content and its influence on young individuals.

The trial of Rudy Kurniawan, a renowned wine collector and dealer, concluded with his conviction on two counts of fraud in a Manhattan federal court. Kurniawan was found guilty of mail fraud for creating and selling counterfeit wine, potentially facing a sentence of up to 40 years.

Kurniawan, once known as one of the top-five wine collectors, had been living illegally in the United States since 2003. He rose to the top of his profession due to his exceptional palate, capable of identifying the finest wines, and spent millions of dollars each year. However, prosecutors claimed he sold ordinary wine that he blended in his kitchen "laboratory" and re-bottled to masquerade as vintage wines worth thousands of dollars.

In 2008, Laurent Ponsot, of the acclaimed Domaine Ponsot winery in France, was alerted by email about an auction in New York where 97 purported bottles of Domaine Ponsot were to be sold for $440,500-$602,000. Ponsot traveled to New York, arrived at the auction house 10 minutes into proceedings, and got the wines withdrawn from sale at the last minute. Kurniawan sat expressionless in court, chewing on mints as Ponsot spoke.

Several bottles were produced in court, and Ponsot pointed out the forgeries. He stated, "This one is very obvious... Clos Saint-Denis, and it says 1945. This cannot exist. And a label from Nicolas? We never sold to Nicolas," he said, holding the bottle.

Kurniawan was arrested at his home in Arcadia in 2012, after allegedly trying to sell more dubious wine at auction in London via an intermediary. Laurent Roumier of the Domaine Roumier winery also testified to forgeries, including a Bonne Mares, another vintage Burgundy dated 1923, again before bottling began.

The defense portrayed a young man who desperately wanted to fit into the richer, older world of rare wine collectors and painted a picture of a man being made a scapegoat. The jury deliberated for about an hour and 45 minutes before returning with the decision. Kurniawan gave no reaction and did not look at his lawyers.

The trial marked the first federal prosecution for selling fake wine in the U.S. Kurniawan faces a possible 40-year sentence and fines. The verdict brought relief to many in the wine community, with Laurent Ponsot stating, "I feel no pity for him. It's good justice."

Hurricane Irma, a Category 4 storm, is moving towards the Florida Keys, with its eye expected to make landfall soon. The storm's maximum sustained winds are 130 mph (215 kph), and it is currently centered about 20 miles east of Key West. The National Weather Service has reported wind gusts of 90 mph near its Key West office.

As Irma approaches, hundreds of thousands of people are without power in Florida, with Miami-Dade County having the most outages. The storm's eyewall has reached the Florida Keys, and authorities are urging people who chose to ride out the hurricane there to remain indoors until it passes.

In a humorous yet serious warning, the Pasco County Sheriff's Office in Florida has advised against shooting bullets at Hurricane Irma, stating that it will not make the storm turn around and could have dangerous side effects. The warning came in response to a Facebook event page created by two Florida men inviting people to shoot at Irma.

Meanwhile, France and the Netherlands have reported that their islands in the Caribbean were spared major damage from Hurricane Jose, which passed farther away from the islands than expected. The Dutch King Willem-Alexander is flying to the Caribbean to meet survivors of Hurricane Irma who were evacuated there from the hard-hit island of St. Maarten.

In Estero, Florida, evacuees filled Germain Arena, which is being used as a fallout shelter. The storm's impact on Florida is expected to be catastrophic, with tens of thousands of people huddled in shelters. Authorities are urging people who chose to ride out the hurricane in the Florida Keys to remain indoors until the storm has passed completely.

Lester Chambers, a 73-year-old musician and former member of The Chambers Brothers, was assaulted on stage during a blues festival in Hayward, California, after dedicating a song to Trayvon Martin. The attacker, identified as 43-year-old Dinalynn Andrews Potter, allegedly yelled "it's all your fault" before shoving Chambers. Witnesses and Hayward police stated that people on stage subdued Andrews Potter, and she was arrested on suspicion of battery. Chambers was taken to the hospital but has since been released. His family believes the attack was racially motivated due to Chambers' mention of Martin, and they are pressing police to file hate crime charges. Andrews Potter is white, while Chambers is black. Chambers has had a long-standing fight with record executives over royalty payments he claims he has never received. The Chambers Brothers will be part of the inaugural class inducted into the R&B Hall of Fame later this year.

Colin Kaepernick, the former San Francisco 49ers quarterback, has filed a collusion grievance against the NFL under the Collective Bargaining Agreement (CBA). The grievance alleges that Kaepernick remains unsigned due to collusion by NFL owners following his protests during the national anthem last season. Kaepernick started a national conversation about political activism by athletes when he decided to kneel during the anthem to bring attention to mistreatment of African-Americans by police. Other players have continued the protests this season, prompting an angry response from President Donald Trump.

Kaepernick opted out of his contract with the 49ers at the end of last season and remains a free agent despite a rash of injuries and poor play at the quarterback position. Mark Geragos, one of Kaepernick's attorneys, said in a statement that he filed the grievance "only after pursuing every possible avenue with all NFL teams and their executives." Geragos argued that athletes should not be denied employment based on partisan political provocation by the executive branch of the government.

The NFL players' union has stated that it will support the grievance, which was filed through the arbitration system that's part of the league's collective bargaining agreement. Kaepernick's goal, according to his attorney, is to be treated fairly by the league and return to the football playing field. San Francisco safety Eric Reid, Kaepernick's former teammate, has been kneeling during the anthem before games this season.

This grievance could potentially terminate the current CBA if proof of collusion is found. Kaepernick finished last season with 16 touchdowns and only four interceptions in 12 games, making him a quality option for NFL teams. However, some teams may be hesitant to sign him due to the media attention his protests have generated. Commissioner Roger Goodell has denied there has been any blackballing of the quarterback.

The Saudi government has announced ambitious economic reform plans to reduce its dependence on oil and diversify its economy, due to the significant drop in oil prices from over $110 per barrel in 2014 to less than $40 per barrel this year. The reforms aim to transform Saudi Arabia into a global investment power and end its "oil addiction."

As part of the reforms, the government will encourage tourism and establish new industries. Saudi Deputy Crown Prince Mohammad Bin Salman stated that the country can survive without oil by 2020. The government is addressing the issue of oil dependence as oil prices have slumped due to overproduction and weak demand.

In December, the Saudi government cut subsidies and raised fuel prices by 50 percent. Analysts believe that using oil wealth to diversify the economy is the only way forward for long-term survival. They also highlighted the challenges of being overly reliant on a single source of income and the need for changes to compete in the global market.

The Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) expects oil prices to recover, with the price of its basket of crudes expected to rise to $70 a barrel in 2020 and $95 a barrel in 2040. However, analysts predict an average price of $40 in 2016 and $45 in 2017.

The Saudi government registered a budget deficit of 16 percent of GDP in 2015 and is expected to register a deficit of 13 percent of GDP with the new reforms. The reforms include plans to increase non-oil revenue, alter the social structure of the ultra-conservative Muslim kingdom, and push for women to have a bigger economic role.

At the center of the plan is the restructuring of the Public Investment Fund (PIF), which is expected to become a hub for Saudi investment abroad, partly by raising money through selling shares in Saudi Aramco. The government aims to increase the PIF's capital to 7 trillion riyals ($2 trillion) from 600 billion riyals ($160 billion).

The plans also include the partial privatization of Aramco, with the government aiming to sell less than 5 percent of it through an initial public offering (IPO). The government expects Aramco to be valued at more than $2 trillion ahead of the IPO.

The reforms also include changes to the social structure of the kingdom, such as pushing for women to have a bigger economic role and offering improved status to resident expatriates. The government aims to raise non-oil revenue to 600 billion riyals ($160 billion) by 2020 and 1 trillion riyals ($267 billion) by 2030 from 163.5 billion riyals ($43.6 billion) last year.

The reforms aim to end Saudi Arabia's "oil addiction" and transform the country into a global investment power. The government plans to increase non-oil revenue, alter the social structure of the ultra-conservative Muslim kingdom, and push for women to have a bigger economic role. The reforms also include the partial privatization of Aramco and the restructuring of the Public Investment Fund.

In a bizarre incident, a woman from Bridgewater, New Jersey, has been charged with attempting to smuggle prescription drugs into the Somerset County Jail using children's drawings. The drugs, Suboxone, were hidden in the drawings, which were addressed to her incarcerated boyfriend, Michael Gill, from Oxford. The sheriff's office discovered the oddities in the mail on June 15, and a K-9 unit was called to confirm the presence of Suboxone. Further investigation revealed that Casey Giles, the woman in question, was trying to smuggle the drugs. Giles was charged with third-degree possession with intent to distribute a controlled dangerous substance and remanded to jail in lieu of $20,000 bail. Gill was charged with attempting to possess a controlled dangerous substance, and his bail was set at $10,000. The sheriff's office emphasized their commitment to maintaining a safe and secure environment in the jail. This incident underscores the ongoing efforts to prevent the smuggling of narcotics into correctional facilities.

Hillary Clinton announced her presidential campaign on April 12, 2015, aiming to be a champion for everyday Americans. Clinton, a seasoned politician with a diverse background, has served as Secretary of State, Senator from New York, First Lady of the United States, First Lady of Arkansas, a practicing lawyer, law professor, activist, and volunteer.

Born and raised in a suburban Illinois town, Clinton attended Wellesley College and Yale Law School. She began her career working for the Children's Defense Fund in Massachusetts, then moved to Arkansas where she taught law and founded Arkansas Advocates for Children and Families. As First Lady, she led the fight for healthcare reform and attended the UN Fourth World Conference on Women in Beijing, delivering a groundbreaking speech on women's rights.

Clinton was later elected to the U.S. Senate, working across the aisle to address issues such as the aftermath of the September 11 attacks. As Secretary of State under President Obama, she championed human rights, internet freedom, and opportunities for women, LGBT people, and young people worldwide.

The Hillary Clinton YouTube Channel provides updates on her 2016 presidential run, focusing on her platform, speeches, and campaign events. Clinton is expected to meet with voters in Iowa and host a formal kickoff event next month. Her campaign marks a new chapter in her public life, which has captivated and polarized the country since her husband, former President Bill Clinton, declared his presidential bid in 1991. Clinton enters the campaign with strong support, particularly among women, but faces the challenge of being associated with the 1990s and the Bill Clinton years.

Utah Senator Orrin G. Hatch, a member of the Senate Judiciary Committee, has stated that Christine Blasey Ford, who is testifying about her alleged assault by Supreme Court nominee Brett Kavanaugh, is "attractive" and "pleasing." Hatch stopped short of declaring Ford credible, stating it was "too early to say." When asked to clarify his use of the term "attractive," Hatch explained that he uses the term to describe compelling personalities, not appearances. Hatch's comments have sparked controversy given that all Republican members of the Senate Judiciary Committee are male and they have elected to have a female outside counsel, Maricopa, Arizona, Deputy County Attorney Rachel Mitchell, pursue their line of questioning during the hearing. Senator Lisa Murkowski, a key swing vote on Kavanaugh's confirmation, replied that she found Ford's testimony credible "thus far." The Judiciary panel will also hear from Kavanaugh later in the day, with a committee vote on his nomination scheduled for Friday.

The article discusses the ongoing quest to discover the smallest thing in the universe, with scientists exploring the possibility of miniature black holes, multiple dimensions, and parallel universes. The journey delves into the strange and complex, potentially requiring revisions to the fundamental laws of time and space.

One candidate for the smallest entity is the singularity at the center of a black hole. Historically, the understanding of the smallest components of the universe has evolved, from grains of sand to atoms, and then to quarks and electrons. However, the nature of quarks and electrons remains a mystery, as no evidence has been found of anything inside them.

Two theories aim to address this mystery: superstring theory, which posits that particles are loops of string, and the idea that space itself is made of discrete pixels or grains. Neither theory has been empirically verified yet.

Another contender for the smallest thing is the singularity at the center of a black hole, though it's believed that black holes are not infinitely dense. The true nature of black holes may be revealed when a theory of quantum gravity is formulated.

The Planck length, approximately 1.6 x 10^-35 meters, is thought to be the theoretical limit of the shortest measurable length and the demarcation line between general relativity and quantum mechanics. It's possible that all the universe's smallest things are roughly the size of the Planck length.

The article was provided by LiveScience and discusses the ongoing search for the smallest thing in the universe, the theories surrounding this search, and the potential implications for our understanding of physics.

The investigation into the slaying of a 17-year-old girl named Nabra Hassanen in Virginia is not being investigated as a hate crime at this time, according to the Fairfax County Police Department (FCPD). The girl attended a midnight Ramadan prayer at the All Dulles Area Muslim Society (ADAMS) mosque in Sterling and was walking back to the mosque from a nearby IHOP with a group of friends when they were confronted by a motorist. The motorist confronted the group, and all but one — Hassanen — ran back to the mosque. Remains believed to belong to Hassanen were later found in a nearby pond.

A 22-year-old man, Darwin Martinez Torres, has been charged with murder in connection with the case. The FCPD did not release any explanation as to why they weren’t investigating the murder as a hate crime.

The killing of Hassanen rattled the Muslim community, particularly during Ramadan, a month of religious observance in which adherents fast from dawn to sunset for about a month. The period culminates in the feast-like celebration Eid al-Fitr, which is expected to fall next weekend.

According to the Southern Poverty Law Center's 2016 hate census, the number of anti-Muslim hate groups in the U.S. increased dramatically last year, from 34 in 2015 to 101 in 2016. American Muslims faced the same level of bias-related violence in 2015 as they did in the post-9/11 era, according to the Pew Center's analysis of the FBI's anti-Muslim hate crime statistics.

Members of the Fairfax County Muslim community expressed their condolences and called for unity in the face of the traumatic event. Virginia officials also condemned the killing and expressed their condolences to Hassanen's family.

The ADAMS Center, which is Northern Virginia’s largest mosque and one of the nation’s most well-known congregations, has a paid armed security guard at the Sterling site. Many mosques have increased security since six Muslim worshipers were killed at a mosque in Quebec earlier this year.

The death of Hassanen sent a chill through the community when news spread Sunday. Many Muslims were concerned about the safety of their daughters, particularly those who wear traditional Muslim clothes. Virginia officials have urged all Virginians to show compassion and kindness in the wake of the tragedy.

A crowdfunding page to support Hassanen's family surged with donations Sunday night, jumping from $10,000 to nearly $18,000 in less than an hour. The fundraising page had met its $25,000 goal shortly before 10 p.m.

In a neighborhood full of Muslim immigrant families, Hassanen's apartment was the one overflowing with friends and laughter most days. On Sunday night, that apartment was crammed with more than 30 women in traditional Muslim garb, sobbing and comforting one another. At the center of the crowded, dimly lit living room was Hassanen's mother, Sawsan Gazzar.

Gazzar's phone rang constantly. To her brother and sister in her native Egypt, she said, “Pray for me that I can handle this . . . I lost my daughter, my first reason for happiness.” The night before, Gazzar had cooked a feast for Hassanen, the oldest of her four daughters, who wanted to host a big iftar break-the-fast dinner for all her friends from ADAMS and South Lakes High School, where she just finished 10th grade. The iftar was packed — Hassanen was always popular and sociable. And when it ended, a friend's mom drove some of the teens to ADAMS for the midnight prayers that mark the last 10 days of Ramadan. Family members said she frequented the mosque during Ramadan.

Gazzar said she thought Hassanen and her friends would eat at the mosque after the prayers, and she would have forbidden her from walking to IHOP in the middle of the night. But she also wasn’t surprised that the girl went out; she and other teens had done it safely last year. Other mothers in the apartment Sunday night echoed the same thought repeatedly — they and their children had always felt safe taking the sidewalk path to IHOP or McDonald’s for a fun meal on those final Ramadan nights.

Gazzar loaned her daughter an abaya to wear to the mosque Saturday night, since Hassanen didn’t typically wear traditional Muslim clothes. She heard from a detective that when the man in the car started shouting at the teens, Hassanen tripped over the long garment and fell to the ground, just before she was struck.

“I think it had to do with the way she was dressed and the fact that she’s Muslim,” Gazzar said. “Why would you kill a kid? What did my daughter do to deserve this?”

Hassanen was a diligent student, so much so that although she was extremely proud to get her first job ever at a McDonald’s, she quit when her manager didn’t understand that studying for a school exam took priority over a work shift. Family members were quick to note her interest in fashion and makeup, and her recently acquired nose ring.

All four Hassanen girls were born in the United States — the younger ones are 11, 10 and 3. Ali described Hassanen as a “daddy’s girl” who was close with her father, a bus-and-limo driver. Her father spent Sunday at the mosque, Ali said, beside himself with worry all day.

Gazzar's phone rang yet again, and this time she didn’t answer. She turned instead to the hundreds of photos stored on it, scrolling through them until she landed on one of Hassanen visiting her parents’ homeland in Egypt, laughing as she embraced two of the teen's little sisters.

“They’d all be laughing. They used to be really happy.” She gazed into the girls’ eyes, and cried harder.

Donald Trump has selected Rick Perry, the former Texas governor who infamously forgot the name of the Department of Energy during a 2011 presidential debate, to lead the agency. Perry's nomination comes after he criticized Trump during his 2016 presidential campaign, calling him a "cancer on conservatism."

Perry's selection is a surprise to some, as he had previously vowed to eliminate the agency during his 2012 presidential bid. During the debate, Perry blanked on the name of the department and said, "Oops."

If confirmed by the Senate, Perry will oversee an agency that plays a major role in President Barack Obama's climate agenda and nuclear deal with Iran. The department has a $29.6 billion budget and more than 100,000 federal employees and contractors.

Conservatives favor Perry for the job, viewing him as someone with management experience who will question the agency's status quo. They believe Perry might bring serious reform to the agency because he isn't wedded to energy programs that conservatives have criticized as unnecessary, market-distorting schemes.

The Heritage Foundation, a conservative think tank, has urged the next president to eliminate vast swaths of the department, including all the research, development, regulatory, and loan programs that the Obama administration has used to drive advances in green energy. Last week, Trump's transition team asked the department to supply the names of all agency employees who had worked on Obama's climate initiatives, a request that Democrats and former staffers denounced as a "witch hunt."

A Trump spokesman declined to rule out the possibility of dismantling the agency in its current form. Trump spokesman Jason Miller told reporters that the incoming president won't be shy about calling out taxpayer fraud or abuse and that he won't hesitate to take action against certain deals that aren't doing right by the taxpayers.

Perry, the longest-serving governor in Texas history, also had the Energy Department in his sights during the 2012 presidential campaign, when he called for eliminating it as part of his program to shrink the federal government.

In addition to his ties to energy companies, Perry is on the board of directors for Energy Transfer Partners, the developers of the controversial Dakota Access pipeline. If confirmed, Perry will likely have to step down from the board and sell any stock he might have in the company.

Environmental groups have criticized Perry's selection, calling it an insult to the functioning democracy. They fear that Perry will shift the department away from renewable energy and towards fossil fuels. During his 14 years as governor, Perry called for lighter regulation of the oil industry and referred to the science around climate change as "unsettled."

The oil business is a home state industry for Perry, and he has repeatedly called for "energy independence" and a rollback of regulations coming out of the Interior Department and the EPA. The Dakota Access pipeline, which would ship as much as 570,000 barrels a day of oil from the shale fields of North Dakota across four states, is a controversial project that has faced months of heated protests.

Perry's ties to energy companies may present potential conflicts of interest as he takes on his new role as energy secretary. If confirmed, Perry will oversee an agency that has ties in everything from funding energy research and providing loans for alternative energy efforts, to tracking and analyzing American energy production and consumption, to securing the safety of America's nuclear weapons.

A 17-year-old American teenager, Tristin Budzyn-Baker, was rewarded for his honesty after returning the lost wallet of Australian actor Chris Hemsworth, who plays Thor in the Marvel cinematic universe. Hemsworth lost his wallet while dining with his family in a "rough" area of Los Angeles. Budzyn-Baker found the wallet and returned it, even though it contained cash. As a reward, Hemsworth gave Budzyn-Baker a wad of cash and tickets for him and his mother to The Ellen Show, where Hemsworth was due to appear. Ellen DeGeneres, the host of the show, also gave Budzyn-Baker a further $10,000. In addition, Hemsworth wrote a special letter of recommendation for Budzyn-Baker's bid to earn the top scouting rank, Eagle Scout. This incident serves as a reminder that honesty is the best policy.

In Baton Rouge, a 13-year-old boy named Murrain Hawkins was accidentally shot and killed by Adonis Forbes, a 25-year-old man who was working on his handgun. The incident occurred on Saturday night, while Forbes was returning home to check on his kids. While trying to fix the malfunctioning gun, it discharged, striking Hawkins, who was babysitting Forbes' children at the time. The bullet hit Hawkins in the abdomen, and he was later pronounced dead at the hospital. Forbes was arrested and charged with negligent homicide, posting a $10,000 bond to be released from jail. It is unclear if Hawkins and Forbes are related.

In a lawsuit filed in Manhattan Supreme Court, Caitlin Sanchez, the voice actress for the popular animated character Dora from "Dora The Explorer," claims that Nickelodeon and its parent companies, Viacom and MTV Networks, exploited her with a contract that made millions for the network but left her underpaid. The 14-year-old actress contends that she was not adequately compensated for her work, including studio time, personal appearances, and profits from the show's merchandising empire.

Sanchez's lawyers allege that she and her parents were pressured into signing a "convoluted and inscrutable contract" in 2007, which they claim cheated her out of "millions, perhaps tens of millions." The suit names Nickelodeon, MTV Networks, and Viacom International as defendants.

Nickelodeon has responded that Sanchez's voice changed, and she was no longer able to portray the Dora character. The network also claims that Sanchez and her parents were well-compensated for their work and personal appearances. However, Sanchez's lawyer counters that the family often lost money on trips due to additional expenses not covered by the $40 per-diem provided by Nickelodeon.

Sanchez became Dora in 2007 and has also starred in four "Dora" TV movies and had a guest role on the short-lived show "Lipstick Jungle." The lawsuit seeks unspecified damages.

Littleton Police Officer Steven Beare, a Colorado National Guardsman, has been reported missing while climbing Mount Elbrus, the tallest mountain in Russia and Europe. Beare's wife, Olivia Beare, stated that he went missing on June 16 during his first solo climb without a guide. The last contact with Beare was on Monday night when he arrived in Russia. A severe storm and subsequent blizzard are believed to have caused his disappearance.

A Russian search and rescue team began looking for Beare on Sunday but had to call off their search due to weather conditions. Olivia Beare is currently organizing private search crews and two helicopters to resume the search once the weather permits.

Steven Beare is an experienced climber who has climbed more than 20 of Colorado's 14,000 foot mountains and has already climbed Mount Kilimanjaro. He was attempting to bag the seven highest peaks in the world.

The Colorado Police Officers Foundation is raising funds to help pay for expenses on the ground. Those interested in donating can make donations here or send a check to the Colorado Police Officers Foundation at 2701 W. 84th Ave. #211 in Westminster, CO 80031. In both instances, write Steven Beare's name in the notes section of the donation.

Beare has a 20-month-old son and Olivia is 11-weeks pregnant with their second child. The Littleton Police Department is keeping Beare and his family in their thoughts and prayers. The search for Beare continues, with hope that he will be found safe and returned to his family.

Gilbert P. Hyatt, a 76-year-old Las Vegas-based inventor, filed a lawsuit in January seeking action on two of the oldest pending U.S. patent applications, which have been waiting for over 43 years. Hyatt's patent applications include one for liquid crystal displays that has been in the Patent and Trademark Office for 35 years. Hyatt claims some of the delay is due to retribution for his past disputes with the agency.

Hyatt's 1990 patent on a "single chip integrated circuit computer architecture" effectively gave him a financial claim to most microprocessors, generating over $150 million through a licensing deal with Royal Philips NV. Intel Corp. co-founder Robert Noyce invested in Hyatt's first company in the 1960s.

Hyatt has taken the patent office to court more than 10 times to force reconsideration of rejected applications. He won a case at the Supreme Court in 2012 over what type of evidence can be presented in district court. Hyatt alleges in his latest lawsuit that the patent office's unofficial policy is to give him the runaround to avoid making a decision he can appeal, which may be why he hasn't received a patent since 1997.

Hyatt describes himself as a "frugal inventor" and doesn't expect to be placed in Silicon Valley's pantheon of founding fathers, but he wants a decision on his pending patent applications, either a patent or a final rejection that he can appeal to a U.S. court. The patent office won't comment on the lawsuit.

The ongoing delay in Hyatt's patent applications highlights the ongoing War on Inventors, where large high-tech corporations and their allies on Capitol Hill are trying to undercut small inventors under the guise of "patent reform." The latest attempt is the "Patent Transparency and Improvements Act of 2013," which would make it difficult for small inventors to file legitimate claims against large companies that infringe on their intellectual property.

A Crofton, Maryland man, Neil Edwin Prescott, was arrested and hospitalized for a psychiatric evaluation after repeatedly threatening to harm his former workplace, Pitney Bowes, and referring to himself as a "joker." Police found over 20 firearms, including assault rifles and handguns, and thousands of rounds of ammunition at his apartment. The threat was made in reference to the recent Colorado movie theater shooting, but investigators believe Prescott's actions were motivated by job-related animosity rather than a copycat attempt. Prescott has no criminal record and was either recently fired or in the process of being fired from Pitney Bowes. The company had previously contacted authorities about Prescott's concerning behavior.

In Harrisburg, a devastating fire on Lexington Street resulted in the death of a 3-4-year-old girl and left two other children in critical condition. The fire also claimed the life of a firefighter, Lt. Dennis DeVoe, who was responding to the scene when his car was struck by a stolen vehicle. The driver, Khanyae Kendall, 19, is now facing multiple charges, including aggravated assault by vehicle while DUI.

The fire, which gutted a row home, has left the neighborhood in shock, with neighbors recalling the harrowing sight of children trapped inside. Neighbor Crystal Benjamin, who was home during the fire, was advised to step outside by her neighbor. She witnessed the house engulfed in flames and heard her neighbors yelling that the children were still inside.

Firefighters, who were responding to the scene, were quiet and somber at the Mt. Pleasant Station 8, with a black curtain draped over the company's sign. Harrisburg Chief Brian Enterline expressed his grief over DeVoe's death, stating that the department's resolve remains strong.

GoFundMe campaigns have been set up for both the family of the fire victims and the family of DeVoe. The U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission has also been involved, investigating a possible link between the fire and a hoverboard explosion.

Federal law bars any person from selling products subject to a voluntary or mandatory recall by the Commission. To report a dangerous product or a product-related injury, consumers can go online to www.SaferProducts.gov or call CPSC's Hotline at 800-638-2772.

In 2007, an internal report at News of the World revealed 'smoking gun' evidence of criminal behavior, including reporters paying bribes to police. However, these emails were not handed over to Scotland Yard until last month, raising concerns of a cover-up by News International executives. The emails reportedly show a 'cabal' of six journalists acting as 'gatekeepers' to private investigator Glenn Mulcaire, who carried out hacking on a large scale. The total amount of alleged payments to police is said to be around £120,000.

The revelations have added pressure on News International's chairman, James Murdoch, who could face criminal charges in both Britain and America. Former home secretary Alan Johnson has suggested he could be prosecuted under anti-snooping legislation.

Assistant Commissioner John Yates of Scotland Yard has admitted he let down the victims of phone hacking and regretted not launching a second probe into the News of the World scandal two years ago. He is facing calls to resign after his apology in a newspaper.

In addition, at least nine journalists and three police officers face jail over the phone-hacking scandal. News International chief executive Rebekah Brooks is expected to be questioned by police in the coming days.

The scandal has threatened Murdoch's controversial bid to take full control of BSkyB. Labour leader Ed Miliband plans to attempt to postpone the deal until after the police investigation into phone hacking is complete.

The News of the World phone hacking scandal has led to calls for action against Rupert Murdoch and his newspapers due to their illegal activities, including phone hacking, corrupting the police, and compromising fair trials. The Regulation of Investigatory Powers Act of 2000, which was used to imprison News of the World reporter Clive Goodman and private investigator Glenn Mulcaire, contains a section that could potentially be used to charge News Corp. executives, including Murdoch himself, with criminal offenses.

The section in question, Section 79, states that if an offense under the Act is committed by a body corporate and is proved to have been committed with the consent or connivance of, or to be attributable to any neglect on the part of a director, manager, secretary, or other similar officer of the body corporate, they will also be guilty of the offense.

Rebekah Brooks, the CEO of News International, could potentially be charged under this section, as she was editor of the News of the World at the time it published stories that cited voice mail messages obtained through hacking. It is also possible to argue that Brooks had "Nelsonian ignorance" of the hacking, as she would have had to make it clear that she didn't want to know about it in order to avoid knowledge of the illegal activities.

The scandal has also threatened to derail News Corp.'s bid to gain control of British Sky Broadcasting, and could potentially affect who succeeds Murdoch at the top of his company. The public outcry over the phone hacking has led to rare condemnation of Murdoch in the British Parliament and even from Prime Minister David Cameron, who has enjoyed Murdoch's political support.

In response to the scandal, some observers have called for the dismissal of Rebekah Brooks, but both Rupert and James Murdoch have remained loyal to her. It remains to be seen whether charges will be brought under Section 79 of the Regulation of Investigatory Powers Act, and whether Murdoch and his executives will face criminal charges as a result of the phone hacking scandal.

Jennifer Houle, a 22-year-old business student and member of Pi Beta Phi sorority at the University of Minnesota, has been missing since Friday after a night of bar hopping in Minneapolis. Houle was last seen at Blarney Pub & Grill in the Dinkytown neighborhood, where she was separated from her friend. Her ex-boyfriend was reportedly encountered earlier in the night, which "set off some emotions." Police have spoken to the ex-boyfriend and people who were at the bar that night.

Houle was last seen between 1 a.m. and 2 a.m., and was wearing a green blouse, black leather jacket, black leggings, and boots. Her purse was found in the street about three blocks from the bar where she was last seen. Her sorority sisters have plastered missing posters across the neighborhood and spread her picture online, asking for help in finding her.

A prayer vigil was held for Houle on Sunday night at her old high school in Stillwater, where more than 200 friends and family members gathered to show their support. The university is working with police to help in the search, and a spokesman said they remain hopeful that Houle will be found safe and sound.

Anyone with any information concerning Houle's whereabouts is asked to contact the police immediately. The Minneapolis Police Department has urged the public to respect the privacy of Houle's friends, family, and sorority sisters as the situation continues to evolve. The University of Minnesota is offering support and counseling to any students who need it during this difficult time.

The Republican presidential debate on national security held on November 22, 2011, was a significant event that highlighted the candidates' positions on foreign policy and national security. The debate was sponsored by CNN, The Heritage Foundation, and AEI.

Newt Gingrich emerged as a winner in the debate, showcasing his debating skills and depth of knowledge on the issues. His rise in the polls afforded him more speaking time, and he took advantage of it to present his views on various topics, including immigration, where he took a more moderate stance than other candidates. However, his stance on immigration could potentially be a problem for him in a party that is vehemently opposed to anything that looks or sounds like amnesty.

Jon Huntsman also had a strong performance, particularly on issues related to foreign policy and national security. Given the focus of the debate, Huntsman's expertise in these areas helped him shine. He presented clear policy positions on Pakistan and Afghanistan and even managed to bring the conversation back to the American economy.

Mitt Romney had a relatively good performance, but it was not his most commanding. He avoided any significant miscues and focused on his positions on Iran and China. However, he did not have any standout moments, and his performance may have been overshadowed by other candidates.

Ron Paul had a strong debate, challenging many of his rivals on U.S. foreign policy. His views are not in line with mainstream Republican orthodoxy, but he is consistent in his beliefs and not afraid to express them. His fundraising numbers could increase due to his debate performance.

Michele Bachmann delivered a strong performance, demonstrating her confidence discussing policy issues and taking her competitors to task when they faltered. She sparred with Newt Gingrich over immigration and with Rick Perry over providing aid to Pakistan.

Herman Cain did not have the standout moment he needed to prove his command of foreign policy. He stumbled over a question regarding Libya and made a mistake by calling CNN anchor Wolf Blitzer "Blitz."

Rick Perry took some bold positions during the debate, but his policy stances were vigorously challenged by his colleagues. He almost seemed to immediately backtrack on his tough stance against foreign aid to Pakistan after being criticized by Michele Bachmann.

Overall, the debate was a meaty affair, with candidates making arguments to defend their differing positions. Newt Gingrich, Jon Huntsman, Ron Paul, and Michele Bachmann were the standout performers, while Herman Cain and Rick Perry struggled to make an impact. The debate was a double-edged sword for Newt Gingrich, as he had a strong performance but also found himself defending a position on immigration that could be problematic for him in the Republican primary.

In a closely contested Republican primary for an Alabama Senate seat, three candidates are vying for the nomination, with Sen. Luther Strange, Roy Moore, and Rep. Mo Brooks leading the race. Strange has the endorsement of President Donald Trump and significant financial backing from Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell, but questions about his appointment to the seat by a disgraced former governor have dogged him throughout the campaign.

Trump's endorsement and the support of the GOP establishment have been key factors in the race, but it remains unclear how much they will matter in the primary. Strange is struggling to secure a spot in the runoff, with Moore consistently leading in polls and Brooks battling for the runner-up position.

If no candidate reaches 50% of the vote, the top two candidates will advance to a runoff on September 26. The outcome of the primary will signal the strength of Trump's influence in Alabama and the viability of Strange's campaign.

On the Democratic side, seven candidates are running for the nomination, but former U.S. attorney Doug Jones and Robert Kennedy Jr. are the frontrunners. Jones is the favorite of the Democratic establishment and has been endorsed by former Vice President Joe Biden, while Kennedy is unrelated to the Kennedy political dynasty.

A Raycom News Network and Strategy Research poll released in late July found Kennedy leading the Democratic field with 49% support, while Jones trailed in second place with 28%. The primary results will determine whether a Democrat has a chance to win the seat, as no Democrat has held a U.S. Senate seat in Alabama since 1997.

In addition to the Senate primary, Florida is on high alert due to Hurricane Irma, with mandatory evacuations ordered for the Florida Keys and parts of Miami-Dade and Broward counties. The storm is expected to make landfall in Florida on Sunday, and the state is preparing for a potential mass evacuation.

The Carolinas and Georgia have also declared emergencies, and Delta Air Lines has added flights out of Miami, Fort Lauderdale, and Key West to Atlanta to accommodate evacuees. The White House has announced plans to evacuate people in the U.S. Virgin Islands and St. Martin in preparation for Hurricane Jose, which is expected to make landfall on some Caribbean islands on Saturday.

In other news, a major earthquake with a magnitude of 8.1 hit Mexico just off the Pacific coast on Thursday, killing at least 32 people. Mexican President Enrique Peña Nieto said it was the biggest earthquake to hit the country in a century. Hurricane Katia, now a Category 2 storm, is also threatening to close in on the coast of Mexico.

"Snow White and the Huntsman" is a darker and more menacing take on the classic fairy tale, directed by Rupert Sanders and starring Kristen Stewart as Snow White. The film, which opens nationwide on Friday, departs from the Disney version in many ways, with the dwarfs portrayed as industrious but haunting figures, and the evil queen, played by Charlize Theron, presenting a complex and terrifying character. Ravenna, the queen, is a woman with a legitimate grudge against a male-dominated world of sexual violence and patriarchal entitlement, and the film explores themes of innocence, terror, superstition, and sexual anxiety. Chris Hemsworth plays the Huntsman, a hard-drinking, belligerent widower who adds a gruff human presence to the fantastical world of the film. The film is rated PG-13 for blood, monsters, and whispers of sexual implication.

In addition, the British-born entertainer Richard Dawson, known for his work as an actor and comedian, died of esophageal cancer on Sunday. Dawson won a daytime Emmy Award as best game show host in 1978.

On August 16, approximately 350 U.S. newspapers published editorials as part of a coordinated effort to defend the freedom of the press and criticize President Donald Trump for consistently labeling news organizations as "enemies of the people." The initiative was organized by Marjorie Pritchard, the op-ed page editor of the Boston Globe, who aimed to unite editorial voices nationwide against the president's rhetoric, which some fear may incite violence against journalists.

The Boston Globe and The New York Times were among the biggest names to join the list, which also included the Houston Chronicle, the Minneapolis Star Tribune, the Miami Herald, and the Denver Post. However, the NOLA.com | The Times-Picayune editorial board chose not to participate, stating that a local news organization's voice should remain independent.

Not everyone in the media agrees with the Globe's strategy. Politico reporter Jack Shafer pointed out that an allegedly independent press engaging in "groupthink" may only reinforce the worst opinions held by many people. Trump's response to the editorials was critical, accusing the Boston Globe of being sold at a loss and colluding with other papers on free press issues.

Many of the newspapers participating in the coordinated effort are not just singing from the same hymnals but also preaching to the choir, as most either endorsed Hillary Clinton over Trump in 2016 or did not endorse at all. This endeavor is likely to have the same impact, with the legitimate defenses of the First Amendment and the importance of a free press getting lost in the partisan divide and strong feelings towards Trump's treatment by the mainstream media.

There is also the issue of the "Trump bump," the increase in circulation enjoyed by some outlets, most notably The New York Times, due to aggressive news coverage and editorial opposition to the president and his administration. The Boston Globe's inclusion of an ad in its online editorial asking readers to support a free press has raised questions about the objectivity of the effort.

The editorials conclude that lies are antithetical to an informed citizenry and that the greatness of America depends on the role of a free press to speak the truth to the powerful. The New York Times editorial calls for readers to subscribe to local papers, praise them when they do a good job, and criticize them when they could do better.

However, some critics argue that the coordinated effort only proves Trump's point about a biased media. They suggest that the media are bending the news to suit a leftist political agenda, and that the irony is that in participating in this "Antifa-inspired mob action," the media are proving what Trump says is true. The media's coverage of Omarosa Manigault-Newman's book and the extremist Islamist religious movement in New Mexico, as well as their economic bias, are examples of this alleged bias.

Speaking to reporters ahead of a cabinet meeting, Trump alluded to the editorials but did not comment further. The Senate passed a resolution in support of press freedoms, which included an affirmation that the press is not the enemy of the people. Trump took a swipe at The Globe by noting that The New York Times Company had sold the paper at a steep loss, though he incorrectly stated the price as $1. The Times Company sold The Globe and other properties for $70 million in 2013, after having paid $1.1 billion two decades before.

The president's tweets came a day after the White House announced that Trump had revoked the security clearance of one of his biggest critics, John O. Brennan, the former director of the CIA. Brennan said the president's action was an attempt to silence him and a warning to others who speak out against him and his administration's policies.

A 68-year-old grandfather, Roger Wilday, was walking his German Shepherd, Jade, in Stechford, Birmingham, when the dog discovered an abandoned newborn baby in a park. The baby, now named Jade after the dog, was found wrapped in a towel in a plastic carrier bag. The dramatic discovery took place in Marlborough House Community Park on Thursday afternoon. Roger raced to a friend's nearby house and dialed 999, then rushed back to pick up the infant. The little girl was taken to Heartlands Hospital where she is recovering. Jade, the faithful nine-year-old dog, is receiving extra special attention from Roger and his wife Catherine, who have five grandkids. West Midlands Police are continuing the search for the baby's mother and are urging anyone with information to call 101. The consequences of Jade not discovering the baby could have been serious, as even a few more hours exposed to the elements could have had fatal consequences. The police are keen to hear from witnesses, especially anyone who saw somebody with a carrier bag from The Entertainer toy shop.

The National Rifle Association (NRA) has announced that Vice President Mike Pence will speak at its annual convention in Dallas on Friday, with guns and weapons prohibited during his speech. This decision has sparked criticism from survivors of the February 14 mass shooting at Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School in Parkland, Florida, who argue that the NRA's hypocrisy is evident as they demand gun-free zones for their own events but advocate for armed guards in schools.

Students such as Matt Deitsch, Cameron Kasky, and David Hogg have expressed their skepticism and frustration on social media, questioning the NRA's commitment to school safety and suggesting that the organization prioritizes the protection of those who help them sell guns over children's lives. Fred Guttenberg, the father of a student killed in the Parkland shooting, has also highlighted the ban, stating that it is enlightening given the NRA's stance on the need for more guns in public places.

Some gun enthusiasts and apparent NRA members have also expressed their displeasure with the prohibition, viewing it as an attack on their Second Amendment rights. However, others argue that the Secret Service's involvement in security necessitates the ban to ensure the safety of the Vice President.

President Trump is also expected to speak at the NRA's annual meeting this week, marking his third consecutive appearance at the event. His speech comes nearly two months after the shooting in Parkland, which has prompted calls for gun law reforms from gun safety advocates and Democratic lawmakers. However, the Trump administration's proposal on school safety and gun restrictions did not address universal background checks or raising the age limit on certain gun purchases, leading to accusations of the President "chickening out" in the face of NRA pressure.

The new study reveals a link between certain drugs used to treat Parkinson's disease, such as dopamine receptor agonists, and abnormal behaviors like pathological gambling, hypersexuality, and compulsive shopping. The researchers analyzed 1,580 reports of such cases from 2003 to 2012, finding that 710 of them occurred in people taking dopamine receptor agonists, while the other 870 cases occurred in those taking other types of drugs. The study authors emphasize the importance of doctors and patients being aware of these potential side effects.

The researchers determined that the proportion of such reports was 277.6 times higher for people taking dopamine agonist receptor drugs than those taking other drugs. The drugs that were most closely linked to these behaviors were pramipexole and ropinirole, which have a significant effect on the D3 receptor.

The authors of the study suggest that these medications should be used less frequently and with caution, and doctors should pay close attention to possible untoward effects on behavior and impulse control. Thomas J. Moore, a senior scientist at the Institute for Safe Medication Practices, suggests that warnings about the potential side effects of these drugs should be introduced to make doctors aware of them.

The new findings may help researchers better understand how abnormal behaviors develop and how they may be related to the D3 receptor, which has also been investigated as a possible target for treatments for people with addictions. The researchers note that in some cases, the people taking these drugs had restless leg syndrome, not Parkinson's disease.

The study was published in the journal JAMA Internal Medicine on October 20, 2021. The researchers recommend that the Food and Drug Administration require these medicines to carry a black-box warning, one of the most prominent and serious cautions used for prescriptions drugs. The warning would help make the risk clearer to doctors and patients.

The North Carolina State Archives and State Library, partners with Archive-It since Sep 2005, are dedicated to preserving the state's historical resources. The North Carolina Office of Archives and History safeguards the documentary and material evidence of past generations, aiming to educate current and future residents about their history. This mission is to ensure the protection of democratic rights by providing a better understanding of the past. Users can access their web archives at http://webarchives.ncdcr.gov. By doing so, they contribute to the preservation of North Carolina's rich history for all citizens. #NorthCarolinaHistory #PreservationMatters

The video released by photographer Paul Nicklen and conservation group Sea Legacy on December 5, 2017, shows a starving polar bear on Somerset Island in the Canadian Arctic. The bear, featured in videos Nicklen published on social media, was in a critical condition, with its white hair limply covering its thin, bony frame. The bear was seen rummaging through a trashcan used seasonally by Inuit fishers, but found nothing and collapsed back down onto the ground.

Nicklen, a biologist and co-founder of Sea Legacy, said he filmed the bear's slow, beleaguered death because he didn't want it to die in vain. He hopes to convey a larger message about how a warming climate has deadly consequences for polar bears. Polar bears live only in Arctic regions and are often the first to feel the impacts of warming temperatures and rising seas. In 2002, a World Wildlife Fund report predicted that climate change could lead to polar bear endangerment or extinction. Fifteen years later, polar bears' icy hunting grounds are in even worse shape, with record lows in sea ice coverage expected to continue.

The video sparked controversy, with some questioning why Nicklen did not intervene to save the bear. However, Nicklen explained that he only would have been prolonging the bear's misery, as feeding wild polar bears is illegal in Canada. The footage served as a rallying cry for climate change awareness, with many expressing their sympathy for the bear and calling for action to address the issue. The video was viewed over 3.5 million times on Instagram and picked up news coverage from around the world.

Hilary Duff and Mike Comrie got married in an intimate ceremony in Santa Barbara, California on Saturday. The 22-year-old actress, dressed in a mermaid gown by Vera Wang, and the 29-year-old NHL hockey player exchanged vows in front of a sunset and 100 guests. Duff's sister Haylie served as her maid of honor. The couple, together for over two years, are excited to share their happy news. The wedding details and photos can be found in the new issue of OK! magazine.

In a Copenhagen court, Peter Madsen, a Danish inventor and engineer, faced charges for the murder of Swedish journalist Kim Wall, who went missing in August while researching a story on Madsen. The court heard that new evidence, including 15 stab wounds found on Wall's body and DNA traces on her body and Madsen's computer, have strengthened the case against Madsen.

The court also discovered violent footage of women being killed on Madsen's computer, though he claimed the computer was not his and was used by everyone in his laboratory. Madsen, who has denied the murder and mutilation charges, appeared calm during the pre-trial session.

Wall's headless, dismembered torso was found 10 days after she boarded Madsen's self-built submarine for an interview. Madsen has claimed that Wall died in an accident when a heavy hatch cover fell on her head, and he later attached a metal weight to her waist and planned to sink the submarine, taking his own life.

The court ordered Madsen to be detained for another four weeks as investigations continue. Wall, who had written for publications including the Guardian and New York Times, was last seen alive on Madsen's submarine on August 10. Madsen will appear in court again on October 31.

Rap Genius co-founder Mahbod Moghadam was fired from the annotation service following his posting of insensitive and misogynistic comments on the memoir of mass murderer Elliot Rodger, who carried out a shooting spree earlier this week. Moghadam's comments, which were removed from the site, included phrases such as "beautifully written" and "MY GUESS: his sister is smokin hot."

In a statement, Rap Genius co-founder and CEO Tom Lehman said that Moghadam had resigned as an employee and from the board of directors. Lehman stated that Moghadam's comments were contrary to everything the company is trying to accomplish and went beyond attempting to enhance anyone's understanding of the text.

Moghadam's departure from the company was a result of pressure from investors and others internally, as well as a conversation with Ben Horowitz of Andreessen Horowitz, a big backer of Rap Genius. Moghadam has a history of controversial behavior, including making offensive comments on social media and using spammy SEO tactics to boost the company's traffic.

Moghadam issued an apology on Twitter, stating that he needed to reflect and work on becoming a better person. This is not the first time Moghadam has apologized for his behavior, as he previously blamed a brain tumor for his impulsive outbursts.

Rap Genius is an annotation service that allows users to add explanations and comments to text, including poetry, music, legal documents, classic literature, and the news. The company raised $16 million from Andreessen Horowitz to expand its service. However, the company has faced criticism and negative press in the past due to Moghadam's behavior and other controversies.

The first significant winter snowfall of the season is expected to hit the Washington, D.C., area on Wednesday, with up to 10 inches predicted. The federal government has announced that non-essential employees will be granted excused absences. The storm, dubbed "Snowquester," has caused hundreds of flight cancellations, mainly at Dulles and Reagan National airports. However, the snowfall in Washington has been disappointing, with only fractions of an inch accumulating, while other areas have received significant amounts.

In nearby Virginia, Governor Bob McDonnell has declared a state of emergency, and over 215,000 residents are without power. The National Guard has been called up, and transportation officials report particularly nasty conditions on many roads. About 4,200 utility workers are trying to restore power.

The snowstorm has also affected tourism, with airlines canceling over 1,600 flights, leaving passengers stranded. The National Zoo is closed, but the Smithsonian museums remain open for visitors. The Washington Metrorail system is running, although some bus service is disrupted.

Along the coast, the problem isn't snow but high winds and the threat of flooding. Coastal flood warnings have been issued for parts of Massachusetts, New Jersey, New York, Delaware, Maryland, and Virginia. Officials in some areas have suggested residents evacuate from flood-prone areas.

The snowstorm is the same one that earlier dumped about a foot of snow in parts of Illinois, Minnesota, and North Dakota, causing delays and cancellations in air traffic in the Midwest. Chicago's O'Hare International Airport received 6 inches of snow, the first snowfall of 6 inches or more in the city since February 2011.

In summary, the Washington, D.C., area is bracing for its first significant snowfall of the season, but the snowfall has been disappointing, with only fractions of an inch accumulating. The storm has caused hundreds of flight cancellations and affected tourism. In nearby Virginia, a state of emergency has been declared, and over 215,000 residents are without power. The storm has also caused flooding threats along the coast.

A previously unknown fairy tale written by Hans Christian Andersen has been discovered in Odense, Denmark. The manuscript, titled "The Tallow Candle," was found by retired historian Esben Brage in a filing box at the National Archives of Funen in October. The story, which is believed to be one of Andersen's earliest works, tells the tale of a tallow candle seeking help from a tinder box to ignite itself.

The manuscript is dedicated to a vicar's widow named Bunkeflod, who lived across from Andersen's home. Andersen was known to have a close relationship with Bunkeflod, visiting her and borrowing books from her even after he moved to Copenhagen to attend university.

Experts believe the manuscript was written by Andersen in the 1820s, during his time at a grammar school. The simplistic style of the story suggests that it was written during this period.

The discovery of "The Tallow Candle" has been described as "sensational" by Andersen expert Ejnar Stig Askgaard. The manuscript is likely a copy of an original manuscript that has since been lost. The story's themes touch on perceptions of wealth and beauty, which are also present in many of Andersen's most famous works, such as "The Emperor's New Clothes" and "The Little Mermaid."

Andersen wrote hundreds of fairy tales, novels, poems, and travel journals throughout his life, many of which have been translated into more than 100 languages. The discovery of "The Tallow Candle" adds to the existing body of work by this celebrated Danish author.

The Senate Republicans have released their health care bill, titled the Better Care Reconciliation Act. The bill aims to repeal and replace the Affordable Care Act (Obamacare). The bill asks low- and middle-income Americans to spend significantly more for less coverage. The bill would roll back the Medicaid expansion and make changes to the individual market, including ending the individual mandate and providing smaller subsidies for less generous health insurance plans with higher deductibles. The bill also includes a six-month waiting period for those who want individual coverage but have had more than a two-month break in coverage in the last year. The bill would cut taxes for the wealthy and defund Planned Parenthood for one year. The bill has been met with criticism from Democrats and some Republicans, who argue that it would disadvantage sicker and lower-income Americans. Protesters, including members of the national disability rights group ADAPT, were dragged away by police from the hallway outside of Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell's office in protest of the bill.

The Norwegian ship captain, Håvard Melvaer, discovered the boat of missing teenagers Austin Stephanos and Perry Cohen while on a voyage from Louisiana to Norway. The discovery happened on March 18, 2016, when Melvaer stepped outside for fresh air and spotted the 19-foot SeaCraft bobbing in the water off the port side of his ship, the Edda Fjord. The boat was initially found by the US Coast Guard 67 miles off the coast of Daytona Beach two days after the Tequesta teens disappeared in July 2015, but it went missing during a subsequent search.

Melvaer was surprised that none of his 16-person crew noticed the boat, as it was in a shipping lane and could have posed a danger. He said it was a "stroke of luck" that he spotted the boat, and he notified the Coast Guard. The boat is now en route to Florida in a shipping container and is expected to arrive on May 16. Its contents, including Austin's iPhone, two fishing rods, and two small tackle boxes, have been returned to the families.

Melvaer said he felt a connection to the boys' families as a parent and a boater, and he and his crew made sure to handle the boat with care. He declined to discuss specific details about the boat or its contents, citing the ongoing investigation by the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission and concern for the boys' families. Melvaer hopes that the discovery of the boat might bring some peace to the families. The Coast Guard has called the discovery a "miracle."

A fugitive, identified as Jansen Simon, was arrested in Raceland, Louisiana, after he flagged down a Louisiana deputy for a ride on July 16. The Lafourche Parish Sheriff’s Office (LPSO) had been searching for Simon since 2013, when he allegedly struck another man with a hammer during a bar fight in Cut Off, Louisiana. The incident resulted in a fractured skull for the victim. Simon was also wanted for two additional contempt of court warrants from the same time period. Simon told the officer he was stranded by his friends, but the officer, upon verifying his identity, arrested him. Simon was booked into the Lafourche Parish Detention Center in Thibodaux for one count of Aggravated Second Degree Battery and two counts of Contempt of Court, and is being held without bond. The incident occurred when Simon flagged down a deputy in a marked police car along Highway 182, but it's unclear if he knew he was flagging down a deputy. Simon's current legal representation is unknown.

In a recent deposition, former Florida Republican Party chairman Jim Greer accused some party officials of being "liars and 'whack-a-do, right-wing crazies'" as he described turmoil within the party leading up to his resignation. Greer claimed that some GOP leaders were discussing ways to suppress black votes while others were constantly scheming against each other. He also accused legislative leaders and other party officials of orchestrating an investigation against him to avoid paying him money he was due. Greer has filed a lawsuit against the party and two officials in an attempt to collect $130,000 he was promised in a written agreement. The lawsuit is pending in Leon County and is unlikely to be resolved until after a criminal trial scheduled for mid-November.

Greer's testimony offers a glimpse into the level of animosity between him and the party he once led. He said the party was in turmoil due to disagreements with former Governor Charlie Crist, including the appointment of a liberal African-American judge to the Florida Supreme Court, Crist's endorsement of John McCain for president in 2008, and the hug Crist gave President Barack Obama in 2009. Greer also accused party officials of vetoing his attempts to open the party's books and credit card records, and of using party credit cards for personal expenses.

Senator John Thrasher, who succeeded Greer as party chairman, called Greer's accusations "absurd" and said he is making "baseless accusations on other people in an effort to divert attention from himself." Thrasher said party officials had no choice but to get rid of Greer once they discovered he had secretly created a company that was getting money from the party.

Many of Greer's accusations revolve around his creation of Victory Strategies LLC, a company that collected almost $200,000 from the party while he was running it. The criminal charges against Greer stem from that contract. Greer's animosity was evident throughout the deposition as he described the inner workings of the party.

Greer also claimed that during a December 2009 meeting with party officials, they discussed voter suppression and keeping blacks from voting. However, political consultant Jim Rimes said he recalls no such discussion. Greer's trial on corruption charges is scheduled for November.

In a statement made on the South Lawn of the White House, President Donald Trump expressed concern about the current political climate in America, stating that it is a "scary time for young men" as they can face sexual assault allegations even when they may be innocent. Trump's comments were in response to the ongoing controversy surrounding the nomination of Brett Kavanaugh to the Supreme Court, as multiple women have come forward with allegations of sexual misconduct against him.

Trump said that the current situation makes it difficult for individuals to refute allegations, and that some men are "guilty until proven innocent." However, when asked if he had a message for young women, Trump said it's a "great time for women."

The allegations against Kavanaugh stem from his time in high school and college in the 1980s. His first accuser, Christine Blasey Ford, testified to Congress last week that as a teenager Kavanaugh held her down, put his hand over her mouth, and tried to remove her clothes. A second woman, Deborah Ramirez, said that as a college student he exposed himself to her during a party. A third woman, Julie Swetnick, alleges that she was gang raped at a party that Kavanaugh attended.

Kavanaugh denies all of the allegations. During the 2016 campaign, Trump faced allegations of sexual misconduct from 18 women ranging from walking through women’s dressing rooms to unwanted kissing to touching their genitals without their consent. Trump denied all the allegations, calling the women "horrible, horrible liars." He's currently facing a defamation lawsuit from one of the women, former Apprentice contestant Summer Zervos.

The president's eldest son, Donald Trump Jr., also said in an interview this week that he's "scared most" for his sons, rather than his daughters. Trump warned Democrats that they risk turning Kavanaugh into a martyr on the right if they block his nomination, a move he said would energize conservatives ahead of the midterm elections. However, several GOP senators are withholding their support for Kavanaugh until the FBI investigation concludes. The White House agreed to allow the FBI to expand its investigation after senators accused the administration of limiting it too narrowly.

Trump's comments are likely to fuel the firestorm surrounding Kavanaugh's nomination and renew questions about his attitude toward the "Me Too" movement. The president has faced numerous allegations of sexual misconduct throughout his career, and has denied all of them.

An Indiana mail carrier, Kristopher Block, has been accused of not delivering thousands of pieces of mail and is now facing criminal charges. The incident occurred in La Porte County, where approximately 17,000 pieces of mail were reported missing. Block, who worked for the postal service from 2015 to 2017, is charged with felony Official Misconduct and misdemeanor Theft.

According to court records, for about six months in late 2016 to early 2017, a significant amount of mail never reached its intended destination, including the home of longtime LaPorte resident, Wally Bass. Bass reported that he often did not receive mail, including important documents like worker's comp checks.

Investigations by the U.S. Postal Service began when a deputy with the Berrien County Sheriff’s Office in Michigan found multiple tubs of undelivered mail in a ravine in February 2017. The recovered mail was traced back to the LaPorte Post Office and Block's assigned routes.

When first questioned, Block denied any involvement in the destruction of the mail. However, when shown some of the recovered mail, he reportedly said, "Looks like I’m going to jail." Block admitted to taking home mail he couldn't deliver before the end of his shift and paying a friend to burn it in Michigan.

Block resigned from his job at the post office on Feb. 7, 2017. An estimated 11,000 pieces were recovered from the ravine in Michigan, but police have not yet located Block's accomplice. The other man has not been formally charged with a crime at this time.

The U.S. Postal Service emphasized that most employees do their jobs diligently and that this type of behavior is not tolerated. Anyone can report alleged fraud, waste of funds, or resources, mail theft, and other postal crimes committed by postal employees or contractors by contacting the USPS OIG Hotline at 1-888-USPS-OIG (1-888-877-7644) or filing a complaint online at www.uspsoig.gov.

A Pinellas County man, identified as Christian Jose Gomez, aged 23, is accused of decapitating his mother, Maria Suarez-Cassagne, aged 48, on New Year's Eve using an ax. The incident occurred at their Oldsmar home, where they resided with two brothers. Gomez's older brother called 911 reporting the murder, and upon arrival, deputies found Suarez-Cassagne's headless body near garbage cans outside the house. The murder weapon was also recovered.

Gomez had fled the scene but was found a few blocks away following a 911 call about a suspicious person on a bicycle. After a brief foot chase, he was arrested and allegedly admitted to the crime during an interview with detectives. Sheriff Bob Gualtieri stated that Gomez had planned the murder for two days and was motivated by his mother's "nagging."

Gomez has a history of mental illness, with previous arrests for resisting an officer without violence, disorderly conduct, and loitering and prowling. The older brother was found unharmed. Gomez is charged with first-degree murder and is being held without bond in the Pinellas County Jail. The community expressed shock and sadness over the incident, with neighbors describing Suarez-Cassagne as a kind and wonderful person.

The article discusses a German passenger's successful lawsuit against Thomas Cook Airlines for a delayed flight that took off 22 hours late due to mechanical issues. The passenger was entitled to compensation under European Union regulations, but never received it. After four years of waiting, the passenger hired a claims company, FlightRight, to fight the airline for the payout. The court ruled in favor of the passenger, and an official at Salzburg Airport threatened to impound a Thomas Cook Airlines jet worth tens of millions of dollars until the outstanding debt was cleared. The airline's sister airline, Condor, promptly paid the money to avoid the impoundment. The incident highlights the tactic used by some airlines to stall on paying out claims, hoping people will give up. Only about 15% of EU residents who qualify for airline reimbursements actually file for them. The regulations also cover transatlantic flights from the US to Europe operated by EU-based airlines, and return flights from Europe to the US operated by any airline.

The Glassdoor Employees' Choice Awards for 2017 honored the Highest Rated CEOs across the U.S., Canada, UK, France, and Germany, with categories for large companies and small & medium-sized companies. In the U.S., the top ten Highest Rated CEOs were Benno Dorer of The Clorox Company, Jim Kavanaugh of World Wide Technology, Michael F. Mahoney of Boston Scientific, Craig B. Thompson of Memorial Sloan Kettering, Martin Rankin of Fast Enterprises, Jen-Hsun Huang of NVIDIA, Bob Bechek of Bain & Company, Elon Musk of SpaceX, Brian Halligan of HubSpot, and Mark Zuckerberg of Facebook. The top five Highest Rated CEOs at Small & Medium Companies were Justyn Howard of Sprout Social, Taylor Olson of Slingshot, Brady Harris of Eliot Management Group, Lane Rankin of Illuminate Education, and Ken McElrath of Skuid.

The awards are based on employee reviews and ratings of their CEOs and senior management, with an average CEO approval rating of 67%. The Clorox Company's Benno Dorer, SpaceX's Elon Musk, Cheesecake Factory's David Overton, and General Motors' Mary Barra were among the CEOs debuting as a Highest Rated CEO. The three highest-rated women CEOs were Enterprise Holdings' Pamela Nicholson, In-N-Out Burger's Lynsi Snyder, and Deloitte's Cathy Engelbert.

The Glassdoor Employees' Choice Awards are determined using the company's proprietary algorithm, considering the quantity, quality, and consistency of Glassdoor-approved company reviews shared by employees during a specific eligibility period. The winners can be found on Glassdoor's website in six categories: 100 Highest Rated CEOs – U.S., 25 Highest Rated CEOs at Small and Medium Companies – U.S., 25 Highest Rated CEOs – Canada, 50 Highest Rated CEOs – UK, 10 Highest Rated CEOs – France, and 10 Highest Rated CEOs – Germany.

The study from Glassdoor Economic Research reveals that highly rated CEOs are statistically linked to companies with great cultures, with employee satisfaction with senior leadership being the biggest driver of high CEO approval ratings. Glassdoor is showcasing interviews with winning CEOs, employee commentary, and best practices into how they lead.

The document from Medical News Today discusses two main topics: privacy policy and a research study on the relationship between vocal cues and power.

1. Privacy Policy: Healthline Media, Inc. seeks to process and share personal data, including mobile ad ID and site usage data, with third-party partners for various purposes such as personalizing content, communicating with users, and other reasons upon notice. The data will primarily be stored and processed in the United States, under the laws of the United States, which may offer lesser privacy protections than European Economic Area countries. By clicking "accept," users acknowledge and grant their consent for these activities, which can be withdrawn using the rights request form. More details can be found in the Privacy Policy.

2. The Sound of Status: A new research study published in Psychological Science reveals that people can identify high-power voices when they hear them. The study, led by Sei Jin Ko of San Diego State University, found that basic acoustic properties of the voice change when someone is in a position of power, and these changes influence how listeners perceive and behave towards the speakers. The researchers recorded college students reading a passage aloud twice, with the second recording capturing voices after participants were assigned high or low power roles. Comparing the recordings, the researchers found that high-power voices tended to go up in pitch, become more monotone, and vary more in loudness than low-power voices.
