Affleck and Garner have been in an ongoing custody battle since their separation in 2015, with Garner reportedly hesitant to finalize the divorce due to Affleck's sobriety. The couple has maintained an amicable relationship and co-parented their three children. Affleck has been spotted attending Alcoholics Anonymous meetings and meditation classes.

A 23-year-old Toronto resident named Chalipo, who lives at home with his mother, received an unexpected bill for $39,254 after an argument about personal information for a health insurance application. The bill, which was posted on Reddit and went viral, included charges for various expenses such as electricity, tuition, health care premiums, and a $1,000 fee for being unappreciative. The mother's intention was to teach Chalipo a lesson about being more appreciative, and the stunt worked as he apologized and acknowledged his poor behavior. The argument had started over an application for health insurance coverage for Chalipo's brother, and both parties agreed that Chalipo had acted like a jerk. Chalipo plans to repay his mother and hopes to be successful one day to support his family. The mother and son both agreed that the incident brought them closer together.

The MERS (Middle East Respiratory Syndrome) outbreak in South Korea has continued to spread, with at least 95 confirmed cases and seven deaths as of Tuesday morning. The outbreak began last month after a 68-year-old man returned from the Middle East and visited a doctor in Asan, a city south of Seoul. He was initially diagnosed with a minor ailment, but later tested positive for MERS.

The virus has spread to many hospitals, including mega-hospitals in Seoul, due to the crowded conditions and the practice of seeking referrals to bigger hospitals from smaller ones. The two hospitals with the most cases are among the biggest in their cities.

The hospital odyssey of the index case, the first infected patient, began after May 11, when he developed a fever and began coughing. He visited a clinic in his hometown Asan, and was later referred to Samsung Medical Center in Seoul, one of the largest hospitals in South Korea.

The outbreak has led to the closings of nearly 2,000 kindergartens and schools, the cancellation of concerts and religious and social gatherings, and a plummeting attendance at baseball stadiums. Sales of face masks and hand sanitizer have soared.

The WHO (World Health Organization) has not advised special actions at ports and airports in South Korea or travel or trade restrictions, "given the lack of evidence of sustained human-to-human transmission in the community." However, Hong Kong has raised its response level to "serious," which means ports of entry will exert tighter arrival controls and the Hong Kong Center for Health Protection has posted an advisory urging people to "avoid unnecessary travel" to South Korea.

The government has been criticized for its handling of the outbreak, with some experts faulting the way it initially handled information on the outbreak and the delay in revealing the names of the hospitals the patients had visited. The government has since released the names of all 29 hospitals affected by the disease.

The government has vowed an "all-out national response" and is using South Korea's advanced cellphone network to trace the signals of people who have defied quarantine in order to find them. The prospects for the virus weakening this week depend on whether there are many people who have evaded government quarantine measures and infected other people in various places.

The WHO has sent a team of experts to South Korea to investigate the outbreak. The government believes the disease can still be contained, as all infections have occurred at hospitals where at least one MERS patient had visited or stayed for treatment. The number of new infections and patients may begin to dwindle this week, according to government officials.

Agnes Nixon, a pioneering figure in daytime television and the creator of popular soap operas such as "All My Children" and "One Life to Live," passed away at the age of 93 on Wednesday. Nixon's contributions to the genre were significant, as she tackled various social issues, including child abuse, AIDS, racial segregation, and abortion, in her shows.

Nixon's impact was felt across the soap opera community, with numerous actors and writers expressing their condolences on social media. Susan Lucci, who played Erica Kane on "All My Children," wrote on Instagram, "I adored her and admired her — and I am forever grateful to her! May this liveliest and loveliest of women rest in peace."

Nixon's career began in the 1940s, where she wrote for radio soap operas before moving to television. In 1962, she created a storyline on "Guiding Light" that featured a character diagnosed with uterine cancer after waiting too long to undergo a Pap smear. Despite resistance from the show's owner and network, Nixon managed to push through the storyline, which was considered the first health storyline in a daytime drama. Thousands of women wrote in to thank her for the information, with one woman crediting Nixon for saving her life.

In 1968, Nixon created "One Life to Live," which ran for 43 years and featured many ethnic characters, including Jews, Polish-Americans, and African-Americans. Nixon also created "All My Children" in 1970, which ran for 41 years. Both shows were known for their progressive storylines and tackled various social issues, including drug addiction, depression, child abuse, and AIDS.

Nixon's work was widely copied by other soaps and networks, and she was often called the "queen of the modern soap opera." In 2010, she received a Daytime Emmy for lifetime achievement. Nixon is survived by her three daughters, Cathy Chicos, Mary Nixon, and Emily Nixon; their son, Robert; 10 grandchildren; and three great-grandchildren.

Nixon's passing has been met with an outpouring of condolences from the soap opera community, with many acknowledging her groundbreaking work and impact on the genre. Her legacy will undoubtedly live on in the many lives she touched and the progressive storylines she created.

Operation Blue Roof is a program initiated by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers to aid Florida residents affected by Hurricane Irma. The program provides fiber-reinforced tarps to homeowners with damaged roofs, allowing them to stay in their homes while arranging repairs. However, a mix-up occurred when a tweet from FEMA Region 4's account directed callers to a phone sex line instead of the correct number, 1-888-ROOF-BLU. The error has since been corrected, and the correct number is now being disseminated.

Owen Labrie, the former St. Paul's School student convicted of sexual assault and other charges last year, will be released from jail on bail while he awaits his appeal. The 20-year-old will be fitted with an electronic monitor that is tracked via GPS. Labrie was initially released on bail in October 2016, but his bail was revoked in March after he admitted violating his curfew. During the hearing on Monday, his lawyer argued that being in jail for two months had been a "life-changing" experience for him and he would comply with any additional conditions. A state prosecutor countered that Labrie did not like being in jail. The judge said he was not 100% sure that Labrie would comply, hence the need for monitoring. Labrie was arrested in 2014 after graduating from St. Paul's School in Concord and was convicted of sexual assault, endangering the welfare of a child, and prohibited use of a computer. During the trial, he testified that he and the girl had consensual sexual contact, but he denied having sexual intercourse with her. The encounter took place in a nearly deserted building on the school's campus. Labrie had been bound for Harvard University and had planned to take divinity classes before his arrest put everything on hold. He wept upon hearing the verdict last year. The New Hampshire Coalition Against Domestic and Sexual Violence has expressed concern that the decision sends the wrong message to victims of crime.

The legal dispute over the estate of the late Robin Williams, who passed away in August 2014, has escalated between his widow, Susan Schneider Williams, and his three children from previous marriages. The disagreement, which has been escalated to court, revolves around property and money.

Susan Williams, who was married to Robin for only three years, is accused by the children of attempting to seize some of their father's belongings, including personal effects, movie memorabilia, action figures, graphic novels, theater masks, and other items. The children claim that Robin had explicitly stated in his will and trust that these items should be left to his children.

However, Susan Williams argues that she has the right to items accumulated during their marriage, such as the tuxedo from their wedding and other "knickknacks." The children, on the other hand, claim that Susan is redefining the term "jewelry" to include items like Robin's watch collection, which they believe should be theirs.

The dispute has reportedly caused distress among those close to Robin, who believe the matter should have been resolved privately between family members. The court documents filed in December and January outline the details of the dispute, which centers around both wealth and cherished personal belongings.

A new law in France, effective from New Year's Day, will grant workers the "right to disconnect" from their work emails and smartphones outside of office hours. This law targets companies with over 50 employees and aims to combat the "always-on" work culture that often leads to overtime and intrusion into private lives. The law was first introduced in 2015 by French Labor Minister Myriam El Khomri, who warned about the health impacts of "info-obesity" in the workplace. A U.S. study has shown that checking emails outside of work hours can cause stress and emotional exhaustion due to the anticipation of responding. The law requires companies to negotiate measures with their staff about when they should work outside of contracted hours, or draw up a charter of good conduct outlining the hours when employees should not send or answer emails. France has had a 35-hour work week since 2000, but the new law addresses the hidden hours of work outside these hours. The measure has been welcomed by France's powerful trade unions, who argue that the overuse of smartphones results in many people working more than the 35-hour weekly limit. However, French workplace expert Xavier Zunigo has expressed concerns that workers may not appreciate losing the autonomy and flexibility offered by technology. In the UK, hardly any law prevents workers from digital burnout, according to Matt Gingell, an employment law partner at Gannons solicitors. Under the Working Time Regulations, British workers must not work more than 48 hours each week, averaged over 17 weeks. Workers can opt out provided they give a minimum of 7 days notice. There are also some general exceptions to the 48-hour week, including for those workers whose working time is not measured and are in control of their work.

In a significant development, a U.S. appeals court has ordered Justin Bieber and Usher to face a $10 million lawsuit alleging copyright infringement on their song "Somebody to Love." The lawsuit, initially dismissed in 2014, was revived by the 4th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in Richmond, who found that the choruses of the plaintiffs' song and the Bieber-Usher versions were similar enough to warrant a trial.

The plaintiffs, R&B singer Devin Copeland (De Rico) and his songwriting partner Mareio Overton, claimed that their 2008 song shared the beat pattern, time signature, and similar chords and lyrics with the three versions of "Somebody to Love" recorded by Bieber, Usher, or both. The court noted that the choruses were "similar enough and also significant enough" to suggest copyright infringement.

The case will now return to the lower court, involving other defendants such as Vivendi SA's Universal Music Publishing Group and Sony Corp's Sony/ATV Music Publishing. The defense lawyers have yet to comment on the matter.

The original version of "Somebody to Love," recorded by Bieber and credited as a co-writer, peaked at No. 15 on the Billboard Hot 100 in 2010. The plaintiffs allege that music scouts played their song for Usher, who then brought it to Bieber.

This ruling marks a significant step in the legal battle, potentially forcing Bieber and Usher to defend their song in court. The case is Copeland et al v. Bieber et al, 4th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals, No. 14-1427.

Gudrun Burwitz, the daughter of Heinrich Himmler, the top Nazi and architect of the Holocaust, died on May 24 at the age of 88. Burwitz was a member of West Germany's foreign intelligence agency (BND) in the 1960s, working as a secretary under an assumed name from 1961 to 1963. This was confirmed by the head of the spy agency's history department.

Burwitz remained unrepentant and loyal to her father, who commanded the SS, the Nazi paramilitary corps responsible for the murder of millions of Jews, Poles, Soviet prisoners-of-war, Roma, and others during the Holocaust. Himmler was captured by British forces in 1945 and killed himself to evade trial for war crimes.

Gudrun was a teenager when the war ended and was released in 1946 after testifying at the Nuremberg trials. She continued to attend neo-Nazi events throughout her life and was a prominent member of Stille Hilfe, a secretive group known to provide legal and financial support to former SS members.

The revelation about Burwitz's post-war involvement with the BND was first reported by German tabloid Bild following her death. The BND confirmed that Burwitz was a member of the agency for a few years until 1963. The timing of her departure coincided with the onset of a change in the understanding and handling of employees who were involved with the Nazis.

German organizations such as the BND have grappled with how to address their own Nazi links in the post-war era. Burwitz's death has sparked renewed discussions about the legacy of the Nazi era and the role of former Nazis in post-war Germany.

The National Security Agency (NSA) has been conducting extensive surveillance on Americans' email and text communications that cross international borders, according to intelligence officials. The NSA is not only intercepting communications of Americans in direct contact with foreigners targeted overseas, but also searching for people who mention information linked to those foreigners, such as little-used email addresses. This revelation adds to the ongoing debate about the NSA's activities and potential infringement on Americans' privacy.

The NSA's cross-border surveillance is authorized by a 2008 law, the FISA Amendments Act, which allows eavesdropping on domestic soil without warrants as long as the "target" is a noncitizen abroad. However, voice communications are not included in this surveillance, according to an NSA spokeswoman.

The NSA temporarily copies and sifts through the contents of most email and other text-based communications that cross the border. The agency makes a "clone" of selected communication links to gather the communications, but the volume of data that passes through these links is not specified. The NSA's system searches the data for identifying keywords or other "selectors" and stores those that match for human analysts to examine. The remaining communications are deleted, and the entire process takes a small number of seconds.

The NSA's activities are intended to gather intelligence on foreign powers, their agents, foreign organizations, foreign persons, or international terrorists, according to the NSA spokeswoman. However, critics argue that the NSA's surveillance practices are unconstitutional and infringe on Americans' privacy.

The FISA Amendments Act has been criticized for its broad authorization of surveillance without warrants and its weak protections for Americans' privacy. The Act permits the NSA to collect Americans' international communications, retain them, and possibly disseminate them to other U.S. government agencies and foreign governments. Americans' communications that contain foreign intelligence information or evidence of a crime can be retained forever, and even communications that don't can be retained for as long as five years.

The NSA's surveillance practices have been the subject of controversy and debate, with critics arguing that the agency is engaging in unconstitutional surveillance of Americans' communications, including their telephone calls and emails. The NSA's activities are under scrutiny, and the ongoing disclosures from Edward Snowden have shed light on the extent of the agency's surveillance practices.

A new study reports the discovery of an Earth-sized planet, Kepler-78b, that orbits a sun-like star 400 light-years away. The planet, which is 20% wider and about 80% more massive than Earth, has a density nearly identical to Earth's, suggesting a composition of rock and iron. The planet was found using the radial velocity technique, which measures the wobble in a host star's light induced by the gravitational pull of an orbiting planet. The study was conducted by a team of astronomers from various institutions, including the Observatoire Astronomique de l'Université de Genève and the Harvard-Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics. The extremely tight orbit of Kepler-78b puzzles astronomers, as it is thought to be an enigma in terms of its formation. The planet's days are numbered, as it will eventually be torn apart by the gravity of its host star. The discovery of Kepler-78b marks a milestone in the ongoing search for a true "Earth twin" and highlights the potential of upcoming missions like NASA's Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) to find such planets.

The document discusses a 3,700-year-old Babylonian clay tablet, known as Plimpton 322, which may contain the earliest evidence of trigonometry. The tablet, discovered in the early 1900s, has long been studied for its connection to Pythagoras' theorem, but its purpose and significance have been debated for decades.

Mathematician Daniel Mansfield from the University of New South Wales recently teamed up with Norman Wildberger to study Plimpton 322. They found that the tablet is a powerful, exact ratio-based trigonometric table, representing an entirely new way of looking at trigonometry. Unlike modern methods, which use angles, sines, and cosines, Plimpton 322 expresses trigonometry in terms of exact ratios of the lengths of the sides of right triangles, using the Babylonians' base 60 form of mathematics.

If the new interpretation is correct, Plimpton 322 would not only be the earliest evidence of trigonometry but also an exact form of the mathematical discipline. The tablet contains exact values of the sides for a range of right triangles, making it possible to find the ratios of the other sides using known ratio information.

However, some experts question the new interpretation, stating that it is speculative and that there is still a lack of proof that the Babylonians used this table for solving problems in the manner suggested in the new paper. The debate continues, with some arguing that the Babylonians could have used their tables for constructing palaces, temples, and canals.

The discovery has the potential to make maths education easier, as the Babylonian approach to calculating triangles is more straightforward than our current methods. If the hypothesis is confirmed, it could open new perspectives on right-angle triangles and angles, potentially making mathematics more engaging for students. The study has been published in Historia Mathematica, the official journal of the International Commission on the History of Mathematics.

In western Mexico, a violent gunbattle between rival drug gangs left 29 bodies in fake military uniforms scattered across a roadway and inside bullet-riddled vehicles in the Pacific coast state of Nayarit. The army reported the incident on Thursday, stating that the bodies were found Wednesday near the town of Ruiz, and that two suspects wounded in the battle were found at the scene. It is unclear if the two reported by the army were included in, or additional to, the state figure. The army also reported a separate shootout in a town about 35 miles north of Ruiz, where two suspects, a man and a woman, were killed.

Conflicting reports emerged from federal and state officials regarding the incident. Nayarit state police claimed that officers responding to reports of a kidnapping found four wounded men at the scene of the shootout, with one injured person dying later and three remaining at the hospital. The army, however, did not mention any kidnapping or wounded men in its statement.

The Sinaloa and Zetas drug cartels are believed to be involved in the fierce highway battle in Nayarit. The state has become a battleground for drug cartels fighting for control of the area, with the Sinaloa cartel, Mexico's most powerful, being active there for some time but recently being challenged by the Zetas and remnants of the Beltran Leyva cartel.

In nearby Michoacan state, officials said 500 marines and soldiers have been deployed to an area where at least 1,200 villagers fled their homes during three days of clashes between rival drug traffickers. The government provided shelter for the displaced families at five shelters in two nearby towns. Hundreds of villagers decided to return home by Thursday, with only 300 people remaining at the shelters.

The fighting in Michoacan is believed to involve rival factions of the Michoacan-based La Familia drug cartel, some of whose members now call themselves "The Knights Templar." Mexico still has fewer people displaced by violence than countries like Colombia, according to the Norway-based Internal Displacement Monitoring Centre, which tracks such figures. It estimates about 230,000 people in Mexico have been driven from their homes, often to stay with relatives or in the United States. An estimated 3.6 million to 5.2 million people have been displaced by decades of drug- and guerrilla-war violence in Colombia.

In Nayarit, the police chief admitted that he lacks the manpower and armament to patrol rural areas frequented by drug gangs, stating that sending ill-armed officers out there "would be certain death, and we're not thinking of putting our personnel at that risk." Drug violence has been on the rise in Nayarit, a Pacific Coast state known for its surfing and beach towns. In October, gunmen killed 15 people at a car wash in the capital of Tepic, an attack that police said bore the characteristics of organized crime. The bodies of 12 murder victims, eight of them partially burned, were found on a Nayarit dirt road a year ago. Officials have not identified the gangs fighting there.

In Durango state, which borders Nayarit to the north, authorities have been excavating dozens of corpses from mass burial grounds used by drug cartel killers. On Thursday, state police reported that two more bodies had been found in the latest excavation, bringing the total of bodies found at a seven lots in the state capital to 223.

The black box recording from the crashed Germanwings Flight 9525 suggests that co-pilot Andreas Lubitz deliberately locked the captain out of the cockpit and crashed the plane, killing all 150 people on board. The audio recording, leaked to German newspaper Bild, reveals a series of disturbing events in the final minutes of the flight.

Captain Patrick Sondenheimer can be heard pleading with Lubitz to open the cockpit door, but to no avail. The recording also includes the sounds of passengers screaming and Sondenheimer trying to break down the door with an emergency axe.

French authorities have said that Lubitz appeared to have crashed the plane deliberately, but they have not yet officially confirmed the transcript of the cockpit recording. The French accident investigation agency, BEA, has expressed dismay at the leak of the recording to the media.

Lubitz is believed to have locked Sondenheimer out of the cockpit before putting the plane on a rapid descent into the mountains. The flight took off 20 minutes late, and after reaching cruising altitude, Sondenheimer asked Lubitz to prepare the landing.

Once that was finished, Lubitz again told the captain he "can go anytime." There is the sound of a seat being pushed backward after which the captain says, "You can take over." At 10:29 a.m., air traffic radar detects that the plane is starting to descend.

Three minutes later, air traffic controllers try to contact the plane and receive no answer -- shortly after which an alarm goes off in the cockpit, warning of the "sink rate." Next comes the banging, followed by Sondenheimer begging Lubitz to let him in. Passengers then begin to scream, according to the transcript obtained by Bild.

Another three minutes pass. A loud metallic bang is heard at 7,000 meters (almost 23,000 feet). A minute and a half later and 2,000 meters (about 6,500 feet) lower to the ground, an alarm says "Terrain -- pull up!" "Open the damn door!" the pilot says.

It's 10:38, and the plane is at 4,000 meters (about 13,000 feet). Lubitz's breathing can still be heard on the voice recorder, according to Bild's report. Two minutes later, investigators think they hear the plane's right wing scrape a mountaintop. Screams can be heard one final time.

Cockpit recordings are some of the most sensitive and closely held parts of aviation crash investigations. They're never officially released, according to CNN aviation reporter Richard Quest. The leak of the black box audio is "unbelievable," Quest called it.

Communications between air traffic control and a plane's cockpit can be downloaded privately, but that's less common in Europe than it is in the United States. An edited and redacted version of the transcript is usually published in part of a final report on an incident.

Although search teams have recovered the cockpit voice recorder, the flight data recorder remains missing. That device could reveal crucial details about what happened during the final moments of the flight.

French authorities have said that Lubitz appeared to have crashed Germanwings Flight 9525 deliberately into the Alps on Tuesday as it flew from Barcelona, Spain, toward Dusseldorf, Germany. Much attention has focused on Lubitz's state of mind since then, with suggestions that he may have had mental health issues.

Lubitz, 27, passed his annual pilot recertification medical examination in summer 2014, a German aviation source told CNN. An official with Lufthansa, which owns Germanwings, said that the exam only tests physical health, not psychological health.

A Dusseldorf clinic said he'd gone there twice, most recently on March 10, "concerning a diagnosis." But the University Clinic said it had not treated Lubitz for depression. The speculation about Lubitz's mental state is based on a letter found in a waste bin in his Dusseldorf apartment.

The note, which was "slashed," said Lubitz was not able to do his job, city prosecutor Christoph Kumpa said Friday. The fact that investigators found "ripped, recent medical leave notes, including for the day of the offense, leads to the preliminary conclusion that the deceased kept his illness secret from his employer and his professional environment," prosecutors said.

Germanwings corroborated that assertion, saying it had never received a sick note from Lubitz. A handful of publications, citing unnamed sources, have reported that Lubitz suffered from various psychological maladies. CNN has not been able to confirm these reports.

Lubitz suffered from "generalized anxiety disorder," and from severe depression in the past, Le Parisien newspaper reported Sunday, citing sources close to the investigation. In 2010, Lubitz received injections of antipsychotic medication, the paper said. He was also prescribed a medication that influences neurotransmitters, but it's unclear when that happened, according to Le Parisien.

The newspaper said investigators found a handful of pills in his apartment in addition to two sick notes, which forbade him from working from March 16 to March 29. The New York Times and The Wall Street Journal, citing unnamed sources, reported Friday that Lubitz suffered from mental illness and kept his diagnosis concealed from his employer.

A subsequent report from the Times on Saturday, citing two officials with knowledge of the investigation, said Lubitz sought treatment before the crash for vision problems that might have put his career at risk. However, an official with Lufthansa, said that if Lubitz had vision problems, they would have been discovered during his pilot recertification medical examination.

Authorities have not ruled out the vision problems could have been psychosomatic, according to the Times. Citing an unidentified senior investigator, German newspaper Die Welt said that Lubitz suffered from a severe "psychosomatic illness" and that German police seized prescription drugs that treat the condition. Lubitz suffered from a "severe subjective burnout syndrome" and from severe depression, the source told the newspaper.

News reports also stated that antidepressants were found during the search of his apartment. Investigators are expected to question his relatives, friends and co-workers as they try to pin down what could have prompted the co-pilot to steer a jetliner full of people into a mountainside.

Lubitz had a girlfriend, a teacher at a school in Dusseldorf not far from his apartment, according to German media

Al-Qaeda, led by Ayman al-Zawahri, has announced the formation of a new branch called Qaedat al-Jihad in the Indian subcontinent. The group aims to spread Islamic rule and "raise the flag of jihad" across India, Myanmar, Bangladesh, and other regions. This expansion is part of a two-year effort to unite militants in the Indian subcontinent. Al-Qaeda has been overshadowed by the Islamic State, which has captured territories in Syria and Iraq and gained followers in India. The new group's leader, Essam Omar, has vowed to target Jews and Hindus, referring to them as "apostates of India." The announcement could pose a challenge to India's Prime Minister Narendra Modi, who has faced criticism for perceived anti-Muslim actions. Al-Qaeda is active in Afghanistan and Pakistan but is considered a minnow compared to local militant groups in terms of manpower and regional knowledge. The announcement did not mention Islamic State or its leader Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi, but it seems to take a subtle dig at the group's efforts at state-building. The Indian government has put several states on alert following the announcement, but there is no indication of an increased security presence.

Clint Bench, a Texas man born without arms due to a congenital deformity, is suing Six Flags for discrimination after being barred from riding the Aquaman Splashdown ride at Six Flags Over Texas in May 2012. Bench, who has led an active lifestyle, including mountain biking, college education, and frequent visits to amusement parks, claims that an employee refused to allow him to ride the Aquaman Splashdown, citing a new policy requiring riders to have at least one fully formed arm all the way down to the fingers. Bench's lawsuit states that this caused him considerable embarrassment, as his children had never witnessed discrimination against him due to his lack of natural hands.

Six Flags declined to comment on the ongoing lawsuit, but the move seems to be a departure from their historically accommodating policy towards those with disabilities. In 2008, Six Flags made a confidential settlement with Kaitlyn Lassiter, a 13-year-old guest whose feet were severed while riding the Superman Tower of Power. Bench is seeking damages for suffering and mental anguish, and he still wants to ride Aquaman. The lawsuit also aims to ensure that such discrimination doesn't happen again.

The investigation into the influence-peddling scandal surrounding Choi Soon-sil, a confidant of South Korean President Park Geun-hye, has shed light on the clandestine relationship between Choi and Ko Young-tae, a former national fencer and businessman. Ko, who is suspected of managing The Blue K and Wide Sports, underwent 40 hours of questioning by prosecutors after voluntarily appearing at the prosecutor's office. No details about the interrogation have been released yet.

Ko is known to have worked at host bars in Gangnam, southern Seoul, and is believed to have met Choi at one such bar around 2006. He later launched his accessory brand Villomillo with Choi's assistance, which became famous after President Park carried his bag in 2013. Ko is also reported to have been acquainted with Cha Eun-taek, another embattled man in charge of the Mir Foundation.

The political scandal engulfing South Korea has culminated in Park Geun-hye's impeachment. The scandal is said to have started with an argument over a puppy between Ko and Choi in 2014. Ko decided to exact revenge by going to the press about Choi and Park's relationship, which eventually led to the president's impeachment.

Ko testified at a parliamentary hearing this week that he got into an argument with Choi over walking her daughter’s puppy one day in 2014. He said Ms. Choi became upset when she found the dog alone at his home. From then on their relationship went downhill. "She treated me like a slave, swearing at me many times," he said in his candid account.

Angry and hurt, Ko decided to exact revenge by going to the press about Choi and Park's relationship. Over the months he collected evidence of Choi's power over Park's administration, including CCTV footage of Choi treating presidential aides as her personal servants. He eventually turned them over to a local broadcaster. Then, in October, he did a TV interview where he alleged Choi's "favourite thing" was to edit Park's presidential speeches. Reporters went digging for evidence to back it up, and obtained a tablet containing selfies of Choi and files of presidential speeches. The discovery, along with other revelations of Choi's allegedly suspicious business dealings, sparked public outrage and launched a wide-reaching corruption inquiry that has ensnared even corporate bigwigs and celebrities.

Park later admitted she gave Choi inappropriate government access - including to her speeches - and apologized. But she has denied the allegations of corruption that prosecutors have laid down. The president has now been impeached, while Ko is seen as a public hero, hailed by netizens for his "whistleblowing." One lawmaker during the public hearing even praised him for "opening Pandora's box."

At the Cannes Lions advertising festival in France, Michael Wolff, author of "Fire and Fury," predicted a bleak future for Donald Trump and the media. He stated that Vice President Mike Pence, whom he described as "the most boring man on earth," would become president, leading to a deep depression in the media business.

Wolff's comments were made in response to a question about the future of the media in light of the success of his book, which chronicles Trump's first nine months in office. The book has remained at the top of Amazon's bestseller list since its release in January.

The conversation between Wolff and Jeff Goodby, cofounder of Goodby, Silverstein & Partners, a San Francisco-based ad agency, also touched on the old-fashioned quality of Pence's relationship with his wife, Karen. It was reported that Pence refers to Karen as "Mother," a nickname that has become something of an obsession due to its unusual nature.

The Pences' distinctive relationship has been the subject of several news articles, including a 6,500-word profile in Rolling Stone. The article revealed that Pence has a practice of never dining alone with a woman other than his wife and avoiding events without her if alcohol is present. It is unclear if this practice remains in place.

The article also described a scene from a dinner at the governor's mansion where Pence was hosting Democratic state lawmakers. In the presence of his dinner guests, Pence was overheard shouting to Karen from one end of the table to the other, asking who prepared the meal and whose china they were eating on. The legislators found the nickname unusual, but it was unclear if it was a joke or not.

The old-fashioned quality of Pence's relationship with his wife has been a topic of interest since he became vice president. It was noted that President Trump has commented on Pence's "wingman" having a good marriage going.

The article also mentioned that Wolff had testified to Trump's ability to sell books, as his chronicle of Trump's first nine months as president remains at the top of Amazon's bestseller list.

Former President George H.W. Bush, 92, was hospitalized in Houston's Methodist Hospital due to an acute respiratory problem stemming from pneumonia. His wife, Barbara Bush, 91, was also admitted to the same hospital as a precaution after experiencing fatigue and coughing. Doctors performed a procedure on Bush to protect and clear his airway, which required sedation. The former president is stable and resting comfortably, but will remain in the ICU for observation.

A week before his hospitalization, Bush had sent a letter to President Trump stating that he couldn't attend the inauguration due to his age and health. President Barack Obama expressed his concern for the Bushes during his final news conference, stating that they have been a constant source of friendship and support for him and Michelle Obama.

Throughout his political career, Bush has had his share of health issues. He lost the 1964 U.S. Senate race in Texas, but was elected to the U.S. House of Representatives in 1966. He later served as the U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations, the Director of Central Intelligence, and was elected as the 41st President of the United States in 1988.

Bush has been married to Barbara for over 70 years and they have five children together. Despite his age and health issues, Bush has remained active, including leading a fishing trip for wounded warriors last summer. His office announced earlier this month that he and his wife would not attend Donald Trump's inauguration this week due to his age and health.

The Quinnipiac University National Poll released on July 2, 2014, found that 33% of American voters consider President Barack Obama the worst president since World War II. Another 28% pick President George W. Bush. Ronald Reagan is considered the best president since WWII by 35% of voters, with 18% for Bill Clinton, 15% for John F. Kennedy, and 8% for Obama.

 On the comparison between Obama and George W. Bush, 39% of voters say Obama has been a better president, while 40% say he is worse. Men say 43-36% that Obama is worse than Bush, while women say 42-38% he is better. Obama is worse, Republicans say 79-7%, and independent voters say 41-31% the same. Democrats say 78-4% that he is better.

 Voters say by a narrow 37-34% that Obama is better for the economy than Bush. America would be better off if Republican Mitt Romney had won the 2012 presidential election, 45% of voters say, while 38% say the country would be worse off.

 The Obama Administration is not competent running the government, 54-44% of voters say. The president is paying attention to what his administration is doing, 47% say, while 48% say he does not pay enough attention.

 President Obama's job approval rating is stalled at a negative 40-53%. Today, the president gets negative scores of 10-88% from Republicans, 31-59% from independent voters, 37-57% from men, and 42-49% from women. Democrats approve 79-13%.

 The economy and jobs are the most important problems facing the country today, 35% of voters say, with 12% listing politicians/campaigns/corruption, 6% each for healthcare and foreign affairs, 5% for the budget, and 4% each for education and immigration.

 Obama gets negative grades for his handling of most key issues: 40-55% for handling the economy, 37-57% for foreign policy, 40-58% for health care, 50-40% for the environment, 44-51% for terrorism, and 44-53% for leadership qualities.

 The poll was conducted from June 24-30, 2014, and surveyed 1,446 registered voters nationwide with a margin of error of +/- 2.6 percentage points.

Demi Lovato, 18, and Ryan Phillippe, 36, have reportedly been secretly dating for the past couple of months, according to E! News. The relationship was described as "really hot and heavy" before cooling down due to Phillippe's recent fatherhood and Lovato's busy promotion schedule for her new single "Skyscraper." However, a source close to Phillippe denies the relationship and claims he is currently single. The news comes after Phillippe's ex-girlfriend Alexis Knapp gave birth to their daughter Kai in July, and Phillippe has yet to take a DNA test to confirm paternity. Lovato has previously dated Wilmer Valderrama, Joe Jonas, and Trace Cyrus.

"The Book of Eli" is a post-apocalyptic film starring Denzel Washington as the titular character, a solitary survivor in a world devastated by war. Eli carries a leather-bound King James Bible, which he believes contains divine revelation and is on a mission to a place called "west." Gary Oldman plays Carnegie, a villainous dictator who seeks the book for nefarious purposes. The film, directed by the Hughes brothers, is set in a desolate landscape filled with marauding extras and features over-the-top violence. The story is didactic and humorless, with drab performances and a ponderous plot. The film is compared to other end-of-the-world movies such as "The Road" and "2012." Washington's performance is described as monosyllabic and lacking emotion, while Oldman is praised for his villainous portrayal. The film is visually moody, but ultimately hampered by its drab performances and heavy-handed message. The film is rated R for brutal violence and language. It opens nationwide on Friday.

A man, identified as Cary Joseph Heath, a teacher at Permenter Middle School in Cedar Hill, Texas, has been arrested and charged with capital murder after the fatal shooting of two of his neighbors in Fort Worth. The incident occurred early Sunday morning, and the victims, who have not been identified, were found outside their home on the 900 block of Buffalo Springs Drive. Police were initially called to the scene for a report of a robbery. Witnesses reported hearing gunshots and seeing Heath, who lived in the same neighborhood, unloading an assault rifle. Heath was arrested at the school the following day, and his bio on the school's website has since been removed. The school district placed Heath on administrative leave and notified parents via an automated phone message. Some parents expressed concern about Heath's arrest, as he was around children every day. The motive for the shooting is still under investigation, and police have not released the names of the victims.

In a radio interview, Senator Scott Brown (R-Mass.) made light of his Democratic opponent, Elizabeth Warren, not posing nude for a magazine to pay for college, as he had done in the 1980s. Warren, a consumer advocate and Harvard Law School professor, responded during a debate that she had borrowed money and worked part-time to fund her education. Brown's comment sparked criticism from the Massachusetts Democratic Party, who labeled it as "gutter campaigning" and a "dirty trick." The comment may not be well-received by women voters, potentially impacting Brown's popularity in the heavily Democratic state. Warren is currently leading a pack of Democratic candidates challenging Brown in the 2012 election.

The six-year-old boy, Jacob Hall, who was wounded in a shooting at Townville Elementary School in South Carolina on September 28, passed away on Saturday after three days on life support. His mother, Renae Hall, announced that his funeral service will be a superhero-themed event, reflecting Jacob's love for superheroes, particularly the Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles. The service will take place at Oakdale Baptist Church on Wednesday, and the pallbearers, Jacob's uncles and brothers, will dress as superheroes. The family encourages anyone who wants to attend and say goodbye to Jacob to wear their superhero costumes or t-shirts.

Jacob's family is holding strong to their faith as they struggle to let him go. Renae Hall has offered forgiveness to the teen accused in the shooting, something she said Jacob would have wanted. She believes that Jacob now has a new superpower: flying with the angels.

The Townville community came together for a balloon release in Jacob's memory on Sunday evening, following a special service at Oakdale Baptist Church. Batman and a special Batmobile will be attending the funeral service from West Virginia.

The funeral service was filled with superheroes, as boys and girls dressed as Batman, Superman, and Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles sat among adults and teenagers wearing capes and logo T-shirts. The reverend at the family's Oakdale Baptist Church celebrated Jacob as Townville's very own superhero.

Jacob's casket was decorated with Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtle stickers, and figurines of Ninja Turtles and Captain America were in a floral spray on top. Townville Elementary school teachers attended the funeral wearing handmade blue capes with a Ninja Turtle face and Jacob's name on the back.

The 14-year-old accused in the shooting now faces two murder charges in the deaths of his father and Jacob. He also is charged with three counts of attempted murder, as well as five counts of possession of a weapon during the commission of a violent crime.

The district announced a district-wide moment of silence at 1:42 p.m. Wednesday to mark one week since the shooting. Supporters also released hundreds of balloons Sunday in his honor, and people also crowded into the church Tuesday evening for Jacob's visitation. Students won't return to Townville Elementary until Thursday, but the district's other five schools will participate in Superhero Day, where everyone is invited to come to school in costume. Schools across the state also planned to participate in Superhero Day, but schools in central and coastal South Carolina were closed for the rest of the week because of the approach of Hurricane Matthew.

In the lead-up to the 2015-2016 US Presidential Election, Donald Trump repeatedly expressed concerns about the Obama administration's plan to accept 200,000 Syrian refugees. However, fact-checking organizations such as FactCheck.org and PolitiFact have debunked this claim, stating that the actual number of Syrian refugees the US was prepared to accept was significantly lower. The Trump campaign rarely responds to fact-check queries, and Trump's statements about the number of Syrian refugees were based on a misunderstanding. Trump's continuous use of the 200,000 figure for the number of Syrians the administration intended to accept has earned him a Four Pinocchio rating, indicating a pattern of false statements. Trump's statements about Syrian refugees were part of a larger pattern of spreading lies, appealing to fears, and stoking hatred during his campaign, which has been compared to the tactics of past demagogues.

Burger King has announced a change in its slogan from "Have It Your Way" to "Be Your Way," which is set to roll out across its marketing in the U.S. starting Monday. The new tagline is intended to remind people that they can and should live how they want and that self-expression is most important. Burger King aims to evolve from just being the functional side of things to having a much stronger emotional appeal. The company believes that "Be Your Way" is about making a connection with a person's greater lifestyle.

The switch comes as Burger King, along with McDonald's Corp., is fighting to boost sales at a time when people are moving toward foods they feel are fresher or higher quality. The new slogan was developed with ad agency DAVID, a unit of WPP. Burger King hasn't been actively using the "Have It Your Way" slogan for some time in the U.S., and the company will also stop using its more recent "Taste Is King" motto.

The switch is the latest in a series of marketing and menu changes under Burger King's new management, which was bought by investment firm 3G Capital in late 2010 and taken public again in 2012. The company has had a decent first half of 2014, with its stock up more than 9% over the first five months.

Meanwhile, McDonald's has introduced a new Happy Meal character named "Happy" as an ambassador for balanced and wholesome eating. The character has been met with criticism for its unsettling appearance. Brands are increasingly focusing on projecting a hip, non-corporate attitude to gain favor with customers.

Christopher Dorner, a former Los Angeles police officer and Navy reservist, is currently on the run after allegedly killing one police officer, injuring two others, and two civilians. Dorner sparked a region-wide manhunt after publishing an angry manifesto online, threatening at least 12 people by name, including police officers and their families. He is believed to be heavily armed, possibly with a .50 caliber rifle and a shoulder-fired missile launcher. Law enforcement officials are deeply concerned about Dorner's knowledge of police tactics, which he learned while working for the LAPD from 2005 to 2008. Dorner's killing spree began over the weekend, when a popular assistant women's college basketball coach, Monica Quan, 28, and her fiancé, Keith Lawrence, 27, were found dead in their car in Irvine, Calif. Dorner bears a grudge against Quan's father, retired LAPD Capt. Randy Quan, for his firing from the department. The search for Dorner has been ongoing, with dozens of law enforcement officers searching his home in La Palma, Calif., and Big Bear Mountain, where his burning car was found. However, his trail has gone cold, and police are currently searching over 200 empty cabins on the mountain to ensure that Dorner is not hiding out in them. The manhunt has caused a lockdown of businesses, homes, and ski resorts in Big Bear, and residents are preparing for a long, anxious evening.

In a groundbreaking rescue operation off Sydney, Australia, marine experts successfully saved a critically endangered grey nurse shark from a suffocating elastic cord wrapped around its gills. The shark, spotted off Magic Point, a critical shark habitat, was slowly dying due to the constricting cord. A team of divers and a veterinarian from SeaLife used a clear-plastic shark sock to capture the shark, coaxing it into the sock. However, other sharks also entered the sock, making the rescue more challenging. Once the injured shark was wrestled into a special stretcher, it was taken to the surface, where the cord was removed, and antibiotics were administered to prevent infection. Veterinarian Rob Jones stated that without intervention, the shark would have died. The shark swam away, and although the wound looks severe, officials expect it to heal in a month. With only an estimated 1,500 grey nurse sharks remaining off the Australian coast, this rescue is a significant conservation effort.

In related news, GrindTV reported on various marine life incidents, including a rare image of a great white shark losing a tooth during an airborne attack on a seal, a whale shark about to eat a diver, and scientists catching a shark within another shark off Delaware. These reports aim to preserve a record of web pages as they are created, fixing broken links on the web.

The Congressional Gold Medal will be awarded to Nisei veterans, Japanese Americans born to immigrants, who served in the 442nd Regimental Combat Team during World War II. These veterans, including Art Iwasaki and Kenji Yaguchi, faced discrimination and limitations, but their unit became one of the most decorated regiments of the war. The award recognizes over 6,000 Japanese-Americans who served and fought in Europe and Asia, and paves the way towards a more tolerant and just nation. The Congressional Gold Medal is one of the highest civilian honors in the U.S., previously awarded to figures like the Wright Brothers, Rosa Parks, and the Dalai Lama.

The University of Mississippi Medical Center (UMMC) has discovered approximately 1,000 bodies believed to be former patients of the Mississippi State Lunatic Asylum, which operated on the same campus from 1855 to 1935. The discovery was made during preparations to build a parking garage, but further testing indicates that up to 7,000 bodies may be buried on the 20-acre site.

The asylum, which was the first mental institution in Mississippi, housed thousands of patients over the years, many of whom died while in care. The UMMC is now considering various options for handling the remains, including creating a memorial with a visitors' center and a lab for research purposes.

Dr. Ralph Didlake, who oversees UMMC's Center for Bioethics and Medical Humanities, believes the lab would be a unique resource for studying life in the asylum during the 1800s and early 1900s. The lab would also provide insight into the remnants of clothing and coffins found with the bodies.

The discovery of the bodies has raised concerns about the cost of exhuming and reburying each body, which is estimated to be $3,000 per body, totaling up to $21 million. However, UMMC is exploring the possibility of handling the exhumations in-house at a lower cost of $400,000 per year for at least eight years.

The Asylum Hill Research Consortium, made up of anthropologists, archaeologists, historians, and an expert in dating the wood of the coffins, has developed plans for the memorial/visitors' center/lab. The consortium believes that the remains should be treated with care and respect, and that the lab would provide valuable research opportunities.

The discovery of the bodies has also sparked personal connections for some individuals, such as Karen Clark of Clinton, who is willing to donate her own DNA to see if it matches her great-great-great grandfather, who is believed to have died at the asylum.

The UMMC is currently working to determine the exact number of bodies buried on the campus and is seeking grants to fund further research and excavation efforts. The discovery has raised questions about the history of mental health care in Mississippi and the treatment of patients in the asylum during the 1800s and early 1900s.

A forklift driver named Arron Hughes from North Wales has made history by swimming across the Hoover Dam reservoir in the United States, becoming the first person to survive such a feat. The incident occurred during a stag do in Las Vegas, where Hughes was on a 37-hour bender. He swam from Arizona to Nevada, taking approximately 30 minutes, and narrowly escaped being dragged under due to nine of the ten hydroelectric turbines not being in operation. Hughes was fined $330 (£250) by the authorities after his arrest. The swim, which was drink-fuelled, has generated mixed opinions, with Hughes' friends calling him a legend, while his mother thinks he is an idiot. Despite the lack of official witnesses, Hughes' stunt has gained significant attention and he has been contacted by the Guinness Book of World Records, although it is unlikely that the effort will be marked in the record books due to the need for an official adjudicator. Hughes is not an avid swimmer but has a history of performing death-defying stunts.

Julian Edelman, a receiver for the New England Patriots, received a concerning direct message on his Instagram account while visiting his former teammate Danny Amendola in Texas last month. The message warned about a potential school shooting threat posted as a comment on one of Edelman's posts. The threat was reportedly directed toward Central Middle School in Port Huron, Michigan.

Upon receiving the message, Edelman, who is a father and had recently experienced the tragedy of the Parkland, Florida, school shooting, immediately alerted the authorities. The 14-year-old boy responsible for the threat was subsequently arrested.

During the investigation, police found two rifles at the boy's home, which belonged to his grandfather. The 14-year-old has been charged with making a false report of a terrorist threat, a four-year felony. He is currently being held at the Macomb County Juvenile Justice Center.

This incident underscores the importance of reporting potential threats and the swift action taken by authorities to ensure the safety of the community. The case is a reminder for everyone to remain vigilant and responsible in the digital age.

Starbucks is relocating its bottled-water production from California to Pennsylvania due to the ongoing historic drought in the state. The company aims to find a new water source for the West Coast and has committed to reducing water use in its California stores by more than 25%. The decision comes after criticism that Starbucks' Ethos water, sold in the Western United States, draws its supply from private springs in California, which is currently in "exceptional drought". Starbucks donates 5 cents for every bottle of Ethos water it sells to the Ethos Water Fund, which supports water and sanitation projects in developing countries. The company has distributed over $12 million since acquiring the water company in 2005. California's water board has approved a mandatory 25% urban water reduction in response to the drought crisis.

The American Cancer Society's estimates for melanoma skin cancer in the United States for 2015 are approximately 73,870 new cases and 9,940 deaths. Skin cancer is the most common type of cancer, with melanoma accounting for less than 2% of cases but causing most skin cancer deaths. The number of new melanoma cases has been increasing for at least 30 years, and the lifetime risk varies among different ethnicities.

Researchers at King's College London have developed a method that could help GPs quickly determine the number of moles on a patient's entire body by counting the number found on a smaller 'proxy' body area, such as an arm. This study, funded by the Wellcome Trust, used data from 3594 female Caucasian twins and found that the count of moles on the right arm was most predictive of the total number on the whole body. Females with more than seven moles on their right arm had nine times the risk of having more than 50 on the whole body, and those with more than 11 on their right arm were more likely to have over 100 on their body, indicating a higher risk of developing melanoma.

The findings could help GPs more easily identify those at the highest risk of developing melanoma and allow for more accurate estimates of the total number of moles in a patient. The area above the right elbow and the legs were also found to be predictive of the total body count of moles.

Skin cancer is the most common cancer, with about 5.4 million basal and squamous cell skin cancers diagnosed each year. Melanoma, the most deadly type of skin cancer, will account for about 76,380 cases of skin cancer in 2016. Skin cancer risk factors include too much exposure to ultraviolet (UV) radiation, pale skin, exposure to certain chemicals, family history of skin cancer, multiple or unusual moles, severe sunburns in the past, weakened immune system, and older age.

Signs and symptoms of skin cancer include any change on the skin, scaliness, roughness, oozing, bleeding, a sore that doesn't heal, the spread of pigment beyond its border, and a change in sensation. Skin cancer can be prevented by staying out of intense sunlight and practicing sun safety.

In conclusion, the study by researchers at King's College London has found that the number of moles on the right arm could be a useful indicator of the total number of moles on the whole body, which could help GPs identify those at the highest risk of developing melanoma. The findings could have a significant impact on primary care, allowing for more accurate estimates of the total number of moles in a patient and the identification of more patients at risk of melanoma.

Nelson Mandela's daughters, Makaziwe and Zenani, have launched a court case against three longtime associates of the former president - George Bizos, Tokyo Sexwale, and lawyer Bally Chuene - in a dispute over the control of two companies, Harmonieux Investment Holdings and Magnifique Investment Holdings. The companies were established to channel funds from the sale of Mandela's handprints, estimated to be worth over R15 million ($1.7 million), for the benefit of the Mandela family.

The court papers allege that the three defendants were not properly appointed as directors, and they have been accused of failing to perform their duties with due care, skill, and diligence. The sisters claim that the trio does not enjoy the support of most of Mandela's children and grandchildren and that their continued refusal to resign is not in the best interest of the beneficiaries.

The defendants have denied the allegations, with Bizos stating that the sisters are attempting to get their hands on the money in the companies. The case was filed in the Johannesburg High Court on Monday, and the defendants are preparing their response. The Nelson Mandela Foundation spokesman was not aware of the court application.

The mediation period in lawsuits related to Larry Nassar, a former Michigan State University (MSU) doctor accused of sexually assaulting at least 95 women and girls since 1992, is being extended by 30 days. The lawsuits, which also involve USA Gymnastics and other defendants, entered a 90-day mediation phase in September. Aly Raisman, a member of the Fierce Five squad that won gold at the London Olympics, has also come forward and said she was sexually abused by Larry Nassar.

Nassar worked for decades as a doctor at MSU and with USA Gymnastics. He was fired by MSU shortly after a story in the Indianapolis Star, and he left USA Gymnastics in fall 2015 with little notice. Nassar faces 22 sexual assault charges in state courts, all but three relate to his role as a doctor. In December, he will be sentenced on three federal child pornography charges.

MSU is paying five law firms for work related to the Nassar lawsuits, including one that the university has said is handling the "insurance aspects." Latham & Watkins, the law firm handling the insurance aspects, has billed MSU for $754,853 since June. Skadden, Arps, Slate, Meagher & Flom is the university's most expensive law firm, charging $990 an hour each for three different attorneys, plus hourly rates between $470 and $565 for four others. In September, the law firm sent MSU two invoices, each for more than $450,000, for work performed in May and June. In all, it has billed MSU for more than $2.7 million.

Aly Raisman, who has been openly critical of the way USA Gymnastics has handled complaints against Nassar, confirmed in an interview with 60 Minutes that she, too, was sexually abused by Nassar. Raisman's revelation comes a month after fellow Fierce Fiver McKayla Maroney came forward to say she was abused by Nassar for several years, beginning when she was 13. A third Olympian, Sydney bronze medalist Jamie Dantzscher, has also said she was abused by Nassar.

According to the Lansing State Journal, more than 140 women have alleged sexual abuse by Nassar, under the guise of medical treatment. Nassar was the USA Gymnastics’ team physician for nearly 20 years, beginning in 1996. He was fired by USA Gymnastics in the summer of 2015, but the federation waited five weeks before alerting the FBI. Raisman told 60 Minutes that she met with the FBI after the Rio Olympics, where she won a second team gold as well as silver medals in the all-around and floor exercise.

The mediation for the lawsuits, led by Jon Muth, has made substantial progress, but significant work remains to be done if a resolution is to be reached, according to court records. Attorneys representing the women and girls and all the defendants with the exception of USA Gymnastics filed a stipulation and proposed order to extend the mediation by 30 days, to Dec. 6. USA Gymnastics has not yet provided its position on the stipulation.

The rising legal fees for MSU are a concern, with the university's outside law firms having billed it for 6,812 hours worked and $4,174,361 as of Oct. 3. Nassar faces 22 sexual assault charges in state courts, all but three relate to his role as a doctor. In December, he will be sentenced on three federal child pornography charges.

In South Australia, a woman named Mary Anne Forster was attacked by a koala while walking her dogs, resulting in a four-day hospital stay and 12 stitches. The incident occurred two weeks ago in Williamstown, north of Adelaide. Forster was walking her dogs when they pulled her towards a koala at the base of a tree. The koala, feeling threatened, bit deeply into Forster's leg. In a struggle to free herself, Forster managed to pry the koala's jaws open and break free. She then hobbled over two kilometers to her home before being taken to the hospital.

The attack has raised concerns about the safety of humans and pets when encountering koalas in the wild. Dr Deb Kelly from the Environment Department advises keeping a safe distance from koalas and not allowing dogs near them, as they will defend themselves. Koalas and dogs have a history of conflicts, with 110 koalas killed each year by dog attacks. However, human involvement in such incidents is rare.

The Department of Environment and Heritage Protection warns that koalas are capable of defending themselves and any dog that attacks a koala may risk serious injury. Forster, despite her injuries, does not blame the koala for the attack. The incident serves as a reminder for people to exercise caution when encountering wildlife in their natural habitats.

The newly released court documents from the bail hearing for Huawei CFO Meng Wanzhou provide insights into her connection to Vancouver and potential legal defense. Meng, who was arrested in Vancouver on December 1 at the request of U.S. authorities, is wanted for fraud charges related to alleged violations of sanctions against Iran.

The documents reveal that Meng and her husband Xiaozong Liu own two homes in Vancouver, one purchased in 2009 and valued at $5.6 million in 2017, and another purchased in 2016 and valued at $16.3 million in 2017, currently under renovation for the family's use. Meng seeks to live at the 28th Avenue home if granted bail, and her family plans to move to Vancouver to live with her. The homes' equity is offered as collateral against bail.

The documents also speak to Meng and her family's 15-year connection to Vancouver. Two of her children attended school in the city between 2009 and 2012 while her husband completed a master's degree there. The family spent many weeks, sometimes months, in Vancouver during the summer, with Meng trying to spend at least 2-3 weeks in Vancouver every summer.

The court filings hint at Meng and Huawei's legal strategy ahead of a potential U.S. court case. The submission summarizes the U.S. government's case as alleging that Huawei "effectively 'controlled' an entity called Skycom" until about 2014, and that it had operated in violation of sanctions against Iran at some point between 2007 and 2013, while defrauding U.S. banks by misrepresenting its relationship with the smaller company. The submission highlights a specific date upon which fraud is alleged to have occurred, Sept. 3, 2013, in which Meng gave a PowerPoint presentation to an unnamed financial institution, misrepresenting Huawei's ownership and control of Skycom and its compliance with U.S. laws.

Meng's bail proceedings are set to resume on Monday in B.C. Supreme Court in Vancouver. Meng's defence argues that she does not pose a flight risk, owing in large part to her connection to the city, along with a moral obligation to see the case through. Crown prosecutors dispute that position, arguing that Meng has no meaningful connection to the jurisdiction, virtually inexhaustible resources, and is a citizen of a country with no extradition treaty with Canada and the U.S.

The 9-year-old Carlie Trent was abducted a week ago by her uncle Gary Simpson in Rogersville, TN. An East and Middle Tennessee Amber Alert remains in effect. Two Knoxville banking executives, Matt Daniels and Tim Williams, are offering a $10,000 reward for information leading to Carlie's return. Authorities suspect the pair might be in an isolated area, and the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation (TBI) has reached out to state park officials, as well as private campgrounds in Tennessee, North Carolina, Virginia, and Kentucky.

TBI spokesman Josh DeVine said they have specific, credible information that Carlie Trent is in imminent danger of serious bodily harm or death. They are pursuing tips on possible sightings of Carlie and Simpson in 11 states, including many in the Southeast. The TBI has yet to receive a credible sighting, and the Missouri Amber Alert has since been canceled.

Simpson was last seen traveling in a white 2002 Dodge conversion van, with Tennessee tag 173GPS. Authorities suspect the two might be in an isolated area, and DeVine suggested property owners in rural areas take a look around their land for anything suspicious.

Carlie is 4 feet 8 inches tall and weighs 75 pounds, with blond hair and blue eyes. Simpson is balding, about 5 feet 10 inches tall and weighs 157 pounds, with brown hair and brown eyes. Both are white. Anyone with information on Carlie or Simpson is asked to call the TBI at 1-800-824-3463. Anyone with immediate information on the pair’s location is asked to call E-911.

Authorities previously shared security video of Simpson taken at a Rogersville-area Walmart shortly before he picked up Carlie from her school, claiming her father had been in an accident. TBI officials initially described Simpson’s purchases as “camping supplies.” On Tuesday, DeVine said those items included a pink and purple “plush throw” blanket, a green men’s short-sleeve shirt, men’s black pants, girls’ khaki pants, two shades of lipstick, two shades of nail polish, a pink folding camp chair, a purple child-sized nightgown, a bikini, and a Fruit of the Loom brand girls’ multipack of underwear. Simpson also bought several “nonperishable items” at a Save-A-Lot grocery store Wednesday afternoon, shortly after picking up the girl.

The TBI is sifting through over 1,200 leads, and law enforcement in 19 states are working on possible sightings, but DeVine says so far they have had nothing credible. Anyone with information is urged to contact the Rogersville Police Department at (423) 272-7555 or 1-800-TBI-FIND.

In a 5-4 decision, the Supreme Court ruled in favor of Texas, allowing the state to maintain its current electoral maps in four counties, pending an appeal. The ruling was a victory for Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, who argued that a lower court's decision to invalidate the maps would have caused chaos in the electoral process. The decision means that the 2018 midterm elections will be conducted in the disputed congressional and legislative districts.

The ruling was met with disappointment by civil rights groups, who argued that the districts were drawn in a way that disadvantaged minority voters. The lower court had found that the districts diminished the influence of minority voters, and a three-judge panel had ordered new districts to be drawn.

The Supreme Court's decision was seen as a victory for Texas Republicans, who had drawn the disputed districts. The decision was also a significant win for President Trump's Supreme Court nominee, Justice Neil M. Gorsuch, as the court likely would have tied 4-4 without him, and Texas's request for a stay would have failed.

The decision is the latest in a series of losses for Texas in federal courts over the way it conducts elections. Over the summer, federal judges in four separate cases ruled that the Texas Legislature discriminated against minorities in drawing congressional and legislative districts, setting ID requirements for voters, and regulating who can assist voters whose first language is not English. Two courts are currently considering whether these actions were intended to discourage African American and Hispanic voters.

If the courts find that the actions were intentional, it could return Texas to the kind of federal oversight from which the Supreme Court freed it and other mostly Southern states in the landmark 2013 decision in Shelby County v. Holder. Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton called the rulings "outrageous" and "astonishing."

The article reports on the arrest of a 27-year-old man named Daniel Morley from Topsfield, Massachusetts, who is accused of threatening to hijack an airplane or ship and making bomb threats. The FBI Joint Terrorism Task Force is investigating the case, and the focus of their investigation is determining if Morley was influenced by others when he made the alleged airplane threat.

The police found a large stainless steel pressure cooker and a black duffel bag in Morley's bedroom closet, as well as materials to make a shrapnel bomb, such as black powder, igniters, and pieces of metal that included ball bearings. They also found a large assault rifle and a handgun, several hundred rounds of ammunition, and a drawing of what appeared to be the Boston skyline with an airplane in the left-hand corner and a figure of a man with a blue heart in his chest, holding a red heart in his hand.

Morley's mother told police that her son had the pressure cooker and other materials before the Boston Marathon attacks, and the FBI is looking into any potential links between the two cases. Morley is currently undergoing psychiatric evaluation at Bridgewater State Hospital, and his next court appearance is set for Thursday at Ipswich District Court in Newburyport.

The article also mentions that Morley was arrested on bomb scare charges on June 9 after a domestic disturbance call led the police to his home, where they found a pressure cooker in his possession. The Nunes memo, created by the staff of House Intelligence Committee Chairman Devin Nunes, alleges that the FBI abused its surveillance authority when seeking a secret court order to monitor a former Trump campaign adviser. The memo was approved for release by President Trump, despite concerns from the FBI and the Justice Department. The memo details the FBI's use of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA) during the 2016 presidential election cycle, specifically focusing on Carter Page, a US citizen who served as a volunteer advisor to the Trump campaign. The memo raises concerns about the legitimacy and legality of the FBI's interactions with the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court (FISC) and the breakdown of legal processes established to protect American citizens from abuses related to the FISA process. The memo also highlights the role of Christopher Steele, a longtime FBI source who was paid over $160,000 by the Democratic National Committee (DNC) and Hillary Clinton campaign, in the Carter Page FISA application. The memo suggests that material and relevant information was omitted from the FISA applications, including the political origins of the Steele dossier and Steele's numerous encounters with the media that violated the cardinal rule of source handling. The memo concludes by stating that no surveillance warrant would have been sought from the FISC without the Steele dossier information.

Arsenio Hall has filed a $5 million defamation lawsuit against Sinead O'Connor, alleging that she made false accusations against him regarding the supply of illegal drugs to the late musician Prince. The lawsuit, filed by Hall's lawyers, Marty Singer and Lynda Goldman, claims that O'Connor's Facebook post, in which she accused Hall of being Prince's drug supplier for decades and of spiking her with drugs in the past, is defamatory and seeks damages of at least $5 million. Martin Tripp, a former process technician at Tesla, has filed a countersuit against the company, alleging that Tesla is not living up to its environmental mission and is generating waste at its Gigafactory. Tripp claims that Tesla consistently reused battery parts that had been discarded as waste, and even intentionally damaged parts to prevent them from being used. He also alleges that Tesla discontinued systems to track vehicle parts, making traceability unknown. Tripp denies allegations that he hacked into Tesla's manufacturing operating system and claims that Tesla defamed him by accusing him of making false claims and threatening a mass shooting.
