Augustus "Gus" Lee, a 20-year-old University of Richmond football player and Paul VI Catholic High School graduate, died by suicide on December 11. His family has decided to donate his brain to the Veterans Administration-Boston University-Concussion Legacy Foundation Brain Bank to study traumatic brain injuries and chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE).

Lee was found dead in his car near the Richmond campus at 1:35 a.m. The cause of death was determined to be suicide by asphyxiation. Lee played football, lacrosse, and track at Paul VI Catholic High School and walked on to the University of Richmond football team after considering Delaware and Cornell.

Lee's mother, Phyllis Lee, expressed concern about the potential impact of concussions on her son's mental health, as he had suffered concussions in the past, including one that knocked him unconscious during a middle school lacrosse game. Doctors did not clear him to return to the field for several months after the injury.

Lee struggled to adjust to the larger, more competitive environment at the University of Richmond and the football team's rigorous training regimen took a toll on him. His mother noticed that he was homesick and "a little fried" during his freshman year.

Despite these challenges, Lee was making progress on the football field and was named the defensive MVP of the 2018 spring game. He played in all 11 of the Spiders' games this season, primarily on special teams.

In the weeks leading up to his death, Lee came home with bronchitis and was not himself when he returned to school. He spoke to his mother every day, which was unusual for them, and told her that he was not eating. On the night of December 10, he called home late and said he was driving from campus to Vienna, expressing feelings of loneliness and homesickness.

The next day, Lee saw a mental health professional and was scheduled for a neurological screening over winter break. However, he returned to campus for final exams and was last seen by his roommate several hours before his death.

Lee is survived by his parents, Phyllis and Chris, and older siblings, Gillian and Jackson. A funeral is planned for Saturday at 2 p.m. at Church of the Holy Comforter in Vienna.

Lee's death has been met with condolences from coaches, teammates, and others in the Richmond football community. Kyle Lauletta, a former Richmond quarterback who was drafted by the New York Giants, wrote on social media that Lee was "a terrific young man and a great member of our Richmond family."

The Concussion Legacy Foundation is a nonprofit that advocates for the study and treatment of brain trauma in athletes and other at-risk groups. Since 2008, the foundation has solicited donations of brains for researchers at Boston University to study, including the brain of former NFL player Aaron Hernandez, who was found to have CTE. The study of donated brains has contributed to a growing medical consensus that links football to CTE.

The family's decision to donate Lee's brain to the Concussion Legacy Foundation will allow researchers to study the potential impact of concussions and other brain injuries on his mental health and contribute to a better understanding of CTE in athletes.

On November 30, 2011, police in Philadelphia cleared out the Occupy Philadelphia encampment at Dilworth Plaza, ending the first phase of the Occupy movement in the city. The police operation was well-planned and executed, with 52 arrests made, mostly for failure to disperse and obstruction. The eviction began around 1 a.m., and the protesters responded by roaming around Center City, with police following them in a cat-and-mouse game that lasted until daylight. Three police officers and one female protester were injured during the operation. The protesters had initially agreed to move from the encampment when construction began on the $50 million renovation of Dilworth Plaza, but tensions had risen in recent weeks due to public urination, unsanitary conditions, and a reported sexual assault. The city had provided electricity for the protesters' computers and arranged for meetings with movement representatives, but the protesters' message of growing income inequality and other issues was not well-received by all. The eviction marked the end of the first phase of Occupy Philadelphia, but the protesters vowed to continue their activism elsewhere. The city had issued a permit for a splinter group, Reasonable Solutions, to protest on Thomas Paine Plaza, but as of Tuesday, the group had yet to set up there.

In a series of exclusive reports, Robin Thicke has been open about his desire to reconcile with his estranged wife, Paula Patton, following their separation. The article discusses the practice of microdosing, or taking small amounts of psychedelic drugs like LSD and magic mushrooms, and its potential benefits and risks. Martijn Schirp, a former poker player and graduate in interdisciplinary science, is one of the proponents of microdosing, which he claims improves his perception, mood, and focus without causing the hallucinations associated with higher doses. The practice has gained a following among a small group of hallucinogen enthusiasts, but it is uncharted territory in terms of scientific research. Matt Johnson, a psychologist at Johns Hopkins University, notes that while taking a smaller dose of a psychedelic is safer than taking a large dose, the regular use of small doses could have long-term side effects. The idea of taking small doses of psychedelics has been around for a while, with Albert Hofmann, the inventor of LSD, known to microdose in his old age. James Fadiman, a psychologist and researcher, has received anecdotal reports from microdosers around the world, most of whom report positive, barely perceptible shifts while microdosing. The effects are plausible from a physiological perspective, as all psychedelics work by activating a particular receptor in the brain known as the serotonin 5HT-2A receptor. However, there is no evidence to suggest that microdosing works as people claim it does, as the effects are so subtle that they are susceptible to the placebo effect. To prove that microdosing has an effect, psychedelics researchers would need to conduct a double-blind study, in which neither the people administering the drug nor the recipients know whether a particular participant is getting a microdose of a psychedelic or something inert. Some groups of people are allegedly doing these trials, but because LSD is illegal, they are off the grid and not publicizing their efforts. The article also mentions a separate issue of scientific censorship, as some researchers argue that outlawing drugs like marijuana and ecstasy hinders research into their medicinal properties. They argue that drug laws enacted in the 1960s and 1970s have impeded vital research into the drugs' functions and therapeutic uses, and that the restrictions are the most serious case of scientific censorship since the Catholic Church banned the works of Copernicus and Galileo.

John Heath, a 68-year-old retired painting contractor, pleaded not guilty to the 1984 murder of his wife, Elizabeth, in a Connecticut court on Tuesday. Heath's wife, Elizabeth, was reported missing in April 1984, just days after he filed for divorce. Her remains were found in a well under a barn in Newtown in 2010.

Heath was charged with murder on Monday and appeared in court wearing oxygen tubes. He was ordered to hand in his passport and is being held on a $1 million bond. The arrest warrant was issued after authorities were tipped about a moving truck outside Heath's rented home in Bridgewater over the weekend.

Elizabeth's body was found wrapped in bedding and placed head-first into a hole in the barn with a plastic bag covering her skull. When police questioned John Heath, he said he renovated the barn in 1990 and used a jackhammer to open a hole in the floor to put a cast iron pipe under concrete. He also reported his wife missing on April 6, 1984, telling police she took off with $600 cash, but telling several friends she left with no money.

The medical examiner previously ruled Elizabeth's death a homicide. She died from four blows to the head, and her left arm was broken, which authorities said was consistent with a defensive wound. Land records show that John Heath owned the property until 2005, when he lost it to foreclosure.

For years, John Heath's friends and family members have suspected him of committing the murder. Even his own mother believed "something wasn't right." The arrest warrant affidavit includes many interviews police conducted during the lengthy investigation, shedding light on the couple's faltering marriage and the suspicions of their friends, neighbors, and family members.

The case will continue on May 16, and a probable cause hearing is tentatively set for June 19. John Heath's friends described him as a Vietnam veteran with a volatile temper and still very disturbed by what he encountered in Vietnam.

Hope Hicks, the former White House communications director, has been appointed as the head of corporate communications for New Fox, the company that will emerge after 21st Century Fox completes the sale of assets to Disney early next year. Hicks will serve as exec VP and chief communications officer, reporting to Viet Dinh, Fox’s chief legal and policy officer. Danny O’Brien, who comes from GE Transportation, has also been appointed as exec VP and head of government relations.

Hicks' appointment follows her departure from the White House in February amid investigations into the 2016 presidential election and questions about the Trump campaign's ties to Russian entities. Her close association with President Donald Trump has made her appointment at Fox a topic of discussion on social media, with critics on the left viewing it as a sign that Fox News aims to promote the Trump administration's agenda.

Hicks' hiring further ties the company's cable news operation to Trump, as the Trump administration now includes national security adviser John Bolton, State Department spokesperson Heather Nauert, and White House communications adviser Mercedes Schlapp, all of whom have previously been Fox News contributors.

The appointment of Hicks and O’Brien is part of the executive transition at New Fox, which will be rooted in television and revolve around Fox Broadcasting Co., Fox News, and Fox Sports. Disney is buying the 21st Century Fox studio, FX Networks, National Geographic Partners, and other entertainment-focused assets for $71.3 billion.

Julie Henderson, the current PR chief at 21st Century Fox, and communications senior VP Nathaniel Brown, have opted not to make the transition to the New Fox entity. Hicks will be based in Los Angeles.

The hiring of Hicks and O’Brien is the latest in a long line of people who have moved between Fox and the White House. In June, former Fox News president Bill Shine took Hicks' former role with the Trump administration after her resignation in February.

On Monday, May 1, 2017, the bodies of Canadian national Francesca Matus and American national Drew Devoursney were found in Chan Chen Village, Corozal District, Belize. The couple had been reported missing on Wednesday after their friend, American national Joseph Milholen, found their home empty and their vehicle, a white Isuzu Rodeo, abandoned in a cane field. Since their disappearance, search parties had been organized, and the SUV was found on Sunday. The police have not yet released an official report, but it is suspected that the couple was murdered. Matus, 52, is originally from Sault Ste. Marie and spends winters in Belize. Devoursney, 36, is from Georgia. The couple had been dating for at least two months before they vanished. The Canadian government has not issued a travel advisory for Belize, but instructed Canadians to exercise a high degree of caution due to a high rate of violent crime throughout the country. The police are investigating the deaths as homicides, and it is reported that the bodies were found with duct tape wrapped around their wrists.

JPMorgan Chase, the largest U.S. bank by assets, has suffered significant trading losses estimated to surpass $3 billion from a hedging strategy that went wrong. The bank initially disclosed $2 billion of paper losses, with CEO Jamie Dimon indicating that additional losses could reach another $1 billion.

The losses are linked to an obscure group of indexes that track the performance of corporate bonds, with JPMorgan using one such index to bet on credit markets strengthening. The bank's position is believed to be large, with traders betting against JPMorgan in the hope of profiting as the bank's losses increase.

The index has been moving against JPMorgan in recent days, with Oppenheimer & Co estimating a potential additional loss for the bank of $5.9 billion on a straight line basis. However, this large loss is considered unlikely, according to Oppenheimer analysts, who believe the actual loss will be less.

The source of JPMorgan's problems is a credit default swap index tied to the credit quality of 121 North American investment-grade bond issuers, including Kraft Foods and Wal-Mart Stores. The bank is believed to have had offsetting bets to the same index maturing at the end of this year, aiming to protect against massive weakening in the credit market.

The Federal Reserve is examining the scope of the growing losses and the original bet, along with whether JPMorgan's chief investment office took risks that were inappropriate for a federally insured depository institution. The bank's overall health remains strong, but the huge trading losses have reignited the debate over how tightly giant financial institutions should be regulated.

The trading losses have caused concerns about the bank's dividend, with some analysts predicting that if the losses continue to mount, the outlook for the bank's dividend will grow uncertain. However, many analysts and investors remain optimistic about the bank's long-term prospects, with one widely followed analyst reiterating his buy rating on JPMorgan shares.

The underlying problem is that while these sharp swings are expected at a big hedge fund, they should not be occurring at a bank whose deposits are government-backed and which has access to ultralow cost capital from the Federal Reserve. Some experts argue that JPMorgan Chase has a big hedge fund inside a commercial bank, and should be taking in deposits and making loans, not taking large speculative bets.

The Internet Archive is working on a project to archive web pages as they are created and preserve the pages they refer to, aiming to fix broken links on the web. This project includes crawls of supported "No More 404" sites.

The summary also highlights the life and achievements of Aaron Swartz, an American computer programmer, writer, and Internet activist. Swartz was involved in the development of RSS, Creative Commons, Reddit, and web.py. He also focused on sociology, civic awareness, and activism, and in 2010, he became a research fellow at Harvard University.

Lastly, the summary mentions the release of a gospel album, Sunday Morning, by former Godfather's Pizza CEO Herman Cain. The album, which features Cain on vocals, was published 15 years ago but has recently resurfaced online. The album's standout track, "This is the Day," has been compared to "Footloose" and is available for listening on the Daily Caller's website. It is not yet confirmed whether the album is officially endorsed by the Cain campaign.

The endgame at hand, both Democratic and Republican congressional leaders expressed optimism on Thursday about reaching a swift compromise to extend Social Security tax cuts, keep long-term jobless benefits flowing, and avoid a threatened partial government shutdown at midnight Friday. President Barack Obama, House Speaker John Boehner, and Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid agreed on the need to extend the payroll tax cut, which is set to expire at the end of the year, and help create new jobs.

Negotiations are ongoing on legislation to extend the Social Security payroll tax cut and unemployment benefits. Democrats have abandoned their demand for a surtax on million-dollar incomes, removing a provision that Republicans strongly opposed. Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid said he hopes that they can come up with something that would get them out of there at a reasonable time in the next few days.

The long-moribund job market appears to be on the mend, with government figures showing a decrease in unemployment applications to the lowest number since the near-collapse of the financial system in 2008. The bristling rhetoric and partisan jabs from earlier in the week all but vanished in the Capitol, as both sides expressed a desire to reach a compromise.

The government would face a partial shutdown at midnight Friday unless Congress resolves its latest spending battle. The departments of Agriculture, Commerce, Housing and Urban Development, Justice, State, and Transportation, as well as NASA and some other smaller agencies, would be spared from the shutdown. However, many other agencies and departments would be shuttered, including National parks and processing of some passports.

The tension highlights the fact that neither side has come up with a way to pay for the tax cut that can get the 60 votes necessary for Senate approval. Senate Democrats say that the House bill is unacceptable and that they will vote against it, and the White House has said Obama would veto it. Their objections center on several GOP initiatives added to the bill to attract votes from conservatives, many of whom would not support the tax cut extension otherwise.

The bill would also extend a pay freeze for federal workers and raise Medicare premiums for upper-income seniors. The two sides are clashing over a provision that would force a decision on a construction permit for the Keystone XL within 60 days. The State Department, which is reviewing the pipeline issue, has said that if forced to make a decision so quickly, it would have to deny the permit.

Twice, the Senate has also blocked Democratic proposals for the millionaire surtax. If a government shutdown occurs, some agencies and departments would continue working, thanks to a partial spending bill passed in November. The showdown marks the fourth time this year that congressional disputes have dragged the government to the brink of a partial shutdown. Behind the white-hot rhetoric of their leaders, many rank-and-file lawmakers predict that there will be a last-minute compromise to extend the tax cut and prevent a shutdown. The only casualty of the fight, they say, will be Congress's already battered reputation.

Paul Manafort, former campaign manager for President Donald Trump, filed a lawsuit on Wednesday challenging the authority of Special Counsel Robert Mueller and alleging that the Justice Department violated the law in appointing Mueller. The lawsuit was filed in the US District Court in Washington, where Manafort and another former Trump campaign aide are charged.

The lawsuit challenges Mueller's decision to charge Manafort with alleged crimes that the suit claims have nothing to do with the 2016 campaign, but rather relate to lucrative lobbying work Manafort and his deputy did for a former Russia-friendly government in Ukraine. That work ended in 2014, the suit says. Manafort and his deputy Rick Gates deny the allegations in the charges.

The legal action represents a new tactic in a broader effort by supporters of the President to push back on the special counsel. Some Republicans have begun publicly calling for Mueller's probe to be shut down. Manafort's attorneys have echoed the President's criticism that Mueller's investigation into Russian meddling in the 2016 election is pursuing crimes that never happened.

The lawsuit alleges that Deputy Attorney General Rod Rosenstein and Mueller have unlawfully exceeded the authorities allowed under the law governing special counsel appointments. The lawsuit contends that the order Rosenstein signed to appoint Mueller "exceeds the scope of Mr. Rosenstein's authority to appoint special counsel as well as specific restrictions on the scope of such appointments."

A DOJ spokesperson responded with a statement, saying: "The lawsuit is frivolous but the defendant is entitled to file whatever he wants." The lawsuit escalates attacks by current and former Trump officials on the legitimacy of the government's investigation into campaign activities. Manafort, 68, and his longtime deputy, Rick Gates, 45, have pleaded not guilty and remain under home detention awaiting trial on charges including money laundering and fraud.

Their indictment, announced on October 30, marked the first criminal charges disclosed in probes into possible Russian influence in U.S. political affairs, which have also swept up former Trump national security adviser Michael Flynn and Trump campaign foreign policy aide George Papadopoulos. Both pleaded guilty to lying to investigators and are cooperating with investigators.

White-collar criminal defense attorney Jeffrey Jacobovitz said it is not unusual for a defendant to try to question the bounds of a special counsel. But he couldn't recall a single time that approach succeeded in tossing a charge. Trump, in social media postings after Christmas and New Year's Day, has attacked the special counsel investigation, the Justice Department and the FBI, including the FBI's former director, James B. Comey; former general counsel James Baker; and Deputy Director Andrew McCabe.

Trump, his spokeswoman and his attorney have cast the charges as having nothing to do with the president, who has called the probe a "witch hunt." Democrats and some Republicans have condemned the strategy of attempting to delegitimize law enforcement, warning that it will only feed the politicization and weakening of key institutions upholding law and order, outcomes Trump supporters say they oppose. Independent investigations set up by the Justice Department tend to have fairly wide jurisdiction, Jacobovitz said. He noted the charge that led to president Bill Clinton's Senate impeachment trial in 1998 was lying under oath about sexual liaisons with intern Monica S. Lewinsky, in a probe that began over his pre-presidency land deals.

"Look at what Ken Starr was looking at with respect to Bill Clinton and his dealings with Monica Lewinsky, and yet that was not shot down by any courts," Jacobovitz pointed out. "Ken Starr started looking at Whitewater and ended up looking at actions related to Monica Lewinsky."

In a trial held in Lueneburg, Germany, Oskar Groening, a 93-year-old former Nazi SS guard, is being charged as an accessory to the murder of at least 300,000 Jews at the Auschwitz-Birkenau death camp. Groening, who has admitted being "morally" guilty but denies having a direct role in the genocide, described the arrival of trainloads of Jews as "very orderly" and "not strenuous" for him.

Eva Kor, an 81-year-old Auschwitz survivor, confronted Groening in court, recalling her arrival at the camp where she was separated from her family and subjected to horrific medical experiments. Kor, who was prisoner A-7063 at Auschwitz, told the court how she and her twin sister were torn apart from their family within 30 minutes of arriving at the camp.

Kor, who was 10 at the time, said she had a "fierce determination to live one more day, to survive one more experiment." She also questioned Groening about his knowledge of Josef Mengele, the Nazis' so-called Angel of Death, and his experiments.

Groening is being tried for his role during a specific period between May and July 1944 when about 425,000 Jews from Hungary were taken to the Auschwitz-Birkenau complex. The charges against him relate to the murder of at least 300,000 Jews during this time. If found guilty, he could face between three and 15 years in prison.

The Auschwitz-Birkenau death camp, constructed in 1940, was a site of immense horror and tragedy. About one million Jews were killed at the camp, along with Roma (Gypsies), disabled people, homosexuals, dissidents, non-Jewish Poles, and Soviet prisoners. The camp grew to cover 40 square kilometers (15 square miles).

The Hawaii Senate Judiciary Committee, headed by State Sen. At a Senate hearing last week, lawmakers and the public expressed outrage at the exemption after it was reported that police officers had lobbied to keep it unchanged. Hee vowed to make the practice illegal, and the version of the bill moving through his committee on Friday will remove sexual penetration from the police exemption, leaving police with the ability to solicit sex in the course of an investigation.

Honolulu police spokeswoman Teresa Bell stated that officers have never been allowed to have sex with prostitutes under departmental rules, and making it illegal won't change how officers operate. Officers who have sex with prostitutes are subject to internal investigation and, on a case-by-case basis, the possibility of being fired or suspended. However, Bell said the department did not know of any cases in recent memory in which an officer was disciplined for having sexual contact with a prostitute.

Kathryn Xian, director of the Pacific Alliance to Stop Slavery, was surprised that the police agreed to changing the law, as the language never excluded their ability to solicit verbally. Xian drafted the language changing the exemption. The police department stated that they did not want the ability to have sex with prostitutes and only had a problem with the verbal part of the clause they pushed to be removed from the bill.

Rachel Dolezal, a former civic activist, appeared on NBC News on June 16, 2015, in an interview with Savannah Guthrie. Mikhail Popkov, a former police officer from Siberia, has been charged with an additional 47 murders, bringing his total to 81, making him Russia's most prolific serial killer. Known as the "Werewolf," Popkov was previously sentenced to life in prison for the murder of 22 women in the city of Angarsk between 1994 and 2000. He targeted women he considered immoral, offering them rides before taking them to remote locations where he killed them with axes, knives, or screwdrivers. Three of the murders were committed while he was on duty, using a police car.

Popkov has confessed to 59 new murders, and prosecutors are expected to bring charges for an additional 12 cases soon. The victims ranged in age from 17 to 38. If Popkov's confessions are confirmed by the court, he will rank among the most prolific serial killers in the world, behind Colombia's Luis Garavito and Pedro López.

Popkov's victims were found in Angarsk and Irkutsk regions of Siberia. He evaded capture for years because police could not contemplate that one of their own officers could be a mass killer. His daughter initially refused to believe he could be a mass killer, but his wife and daughter have since moved to another city to begin new lives.

The investigation began when women started disappearing from public places in Angarsk in the mid-1990s, at the time Popkov was a police officer. Later, authorities started finding mutilated bodies of the women around Irkutsk. Tire tracks from a Niva cross-country vehicle were found at some of the crime scenes, which ultimately led them to Popkov.

Popkov has been cooperating with investigators, and his testimony has been crucial to uncovering the 59 new cases. However, it is not ruled out that there are more cases than the 81 he admits. One theory is that he is deliberately rationing his confessions to delay the moment when he is sent from his current detention prison to a harsh penal colony to serve his life sentence.

The 2016 ISU World Figure Skating Championships took place in Boston, Massachusetts from March 28 to April 3, 2016. The competition featured figure skaters from around the world competing in men's singles, ladies' singles, pairs, and ice dancing. This was the first time Boston hosted the World Figure Skating Championships.

The event was organized by U.S. Figure Skating, with the Skating Club of Boston serving as the local organizing committee. The TD Garden was the primary venue, hosting all competitions and several practice sessions, while DCR Steriti Rink served as the secondary practice venue.

The competition determined the number of athlete slots for each federation at the 2017 World Championships. Argentina was represented by a skater at the World Championships for the first time in history.

Skaters were eligible for the event if they represented an ISU member nation and had reached the age of 15 before July 1, 2015, in their place of birth. National associations selected their entries according to their own criteria but were required to meet minimum technical elements scores (TES) at an international event prior to the World Championships.

Gracie Gold, a two-time U.S. figure skating champion and 2014 Olympic team bronze medalist, announced on Friday that she will be taking time off to "seek some professional help." Gold did not specify the nature of her struggles, but she has been dealing with weight issues and a decline in her performances in recent months. Her absence will likely impact her chances of qualifying for the 2018 Winter Olympics in PyeongChang, South Korea.

On March 13, an unprovoked attack on Prince George's County District III station resulted in the death of Officer Jacai Colson, a four-year veteran of the department. The attack occurred outside the station's front doors around 4:30 p.m., and Officer Colson was killed in the ensuing gunfight. The suspect was wounded and taken to a hospital, where he is in stable condition. Police have taken three brothers into custody in connection with the shooting, with two already in custody.

Officer Colson was described as a "cop's cop" and had an "infectious smile." He worked as an undercover narcotics officer and was known for his bravery and dedication to his fellow officers. The incident was described as "another horrific act of evil" by Prince George's County State's Attorney Angela Alsobrooks. Maryland Governor Larry Hogan ordered flags to fly at half-staff in honor of Officer Colson.

The shooting caused fear and panic in the Palmer Park and Landover areas, with police urging residents to shelter in place. One witness reported hearing what she thought were firecrackers and seeing a man dressed in black firing a handgun at the police station. The warning was lifted shortly after 7:30 p.m.

The shooting came 12 days after the funeral for Prince William County officer Ashley Guindon, who was shot and killed on her first day on duty. The incident prompted an aggressive investigation and prosecution of the alleged shooter, who is expected to survive, and another suspect arrested soon after the shooting. The names of the suspects were not immediately released.

The FBI and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives have begun assisting local police in the investigation, with the Prince George's County Police remaining the lead investigating agency. Maryland Governor Larry Hogan expressed his shock and sadness at Officer Colson's death and sent prayers to his family and loved ones.

George A. Romero, the influential horror filmmaker known as the "father of modern horror films," passed away on July 16, 2017 at the age of 77 following a brief battle with lung cancer. Romero was born in New York City in 1940 and gained fame with his 1968 cult classic "Night of the Living Dead," which he directed and wrote. The low-budget movie, made for $114,000, spawned an unrelenting parade of zombie movies and TV shows.

Romero's 1978 sequel, "Dawn of the Dead," was made for $1.5 million and grossed $55 million. He continued his work in the horror genre throughout the 1980s, directing several movies based on Stephen King's work, including the "Creepshow" films. Romero also penned a new version of "Night of the Living Dead" in 1990, which was directed by Tom Savini, his longtime collaborator and horror effects guru.

Romero's films were known for their social commentary, particularly against the military and materialism. His work was shot primarily in Pittsburgh, where he attended Carnegie Mellon University. "Night of the Living Dead" was rare for its time in featuring an African-American actor as a hero in a mainstream movie.

After directing several box-office failures in the early 1970s, Romero produced a series of TV documentaries focusing on Pittsburgh Steelers legends. He returned to the zombie milieu with "Dawn of the Dead," filmed at the Monroeville Mall outside Pittsburgh, which he said was a temple to consumerism.

Romero's manager, Chris Roe, announced his death on Facebook, saying he passed away peacefully in his sleep while listening to the score of "The Quiet Man," one of his all-time favorite films, with his wife and daughter at his side. He leaves behind a loving family, many friends, and a filmmaking legacy that has endured and will continue to endure the test of time.

Romero's work has been credited with reinventing zombies, which have become ubiquitous in movies, films, and books. Stephen King called Romero his "favorite collaborator." Without Romero, about 1/3 of nerd culture things wouldn't exist. RIP.

NASA has announced that astronaut Jeanette Epps will not be flying to the International Space Station (ISS) as expected in June, a historic mission that would have made her the first African-American crew member on the orbiting outpost. The space agency has not disclosed the reason for Epps' removal from the mission, citing it as a personnel matter.

Epps will now work in the Astronaut Office at Johnson Space Center and await another possible flight assignment. NASA has a history of changing flight assignments for various reasons, including health issues, as seen in the case of astronaut Ken Mattingly, who was pulled from the Apollo 13 crew due to exposure to German measles.

NASA has benched astronauts before flights for various reasons, including medical issues, family illnesses, and undisclosed personal reasons. The agency invests a significant amount of time, effort, and money in training its astronaut crews, and such decisions are not taken lightly.

Epps' removal from her planned flight is not without precedent, and her brother, Henry Epps, believes that "oppressive racism and misogyny in NASA" may be behind the decision. He started a petition on MoveOn.org calling for NASA to reinstate Epps to the mission. As of Sunday evening, the petition had gathered over 350 signatures.

Epps was born in Syracuse and attended Clary Middle School after Danforth. She graduated from Corcoran High School in 1988 and went on to 11 1/2 more years of schooling, beginning at Le Moyne College. She graduated with a degree in physics in 1992 and eventually earned her doctorate in aerospace engineering from the University of Maryland. Epps was part of NASA's 20th astronaut class, announced in 2009.

The crew for the ISS mission is set to go in June and spend at least six months in space. Serena Aunon-Chancellor, who previously was assigned to Expedition 58/59, has been reassigned to the ISS mission. She's a surgeon who spent nine months in Russia supporting medical operations for ISS crew members. Epps will now remain on the ground in Houston and work at the agency’s Johnson Space Center, awaiting future flight assignments.

A 10-year-old girl named Jasmine Martinez, who was visiting Six Flags Magic Mountain in Valencia, California, died on Saturday after collapsing at the park on Friday. The incident occurred at the park's Revolution ride, a roller coaster featuring a 90-foot tall vertical loop and reaching speeds up to 55 mph. Jasmine was airlifted from the park on Friday afternoon and was later pronounced dead at a hospital. The cause of her death is currently unknown, with an autopsy scheduled to determine the cause.

The ride was temporarily closed following the incident for a review, but was later reopened on Friday with no evidence suggesting it was related to the incident. It is not yet clear whether Jasmine had a pre-existing condition. Six Flags Magic Mountain expressed their condolences to Jasmine's family and friends. The park has stated that more than 45 million visitors have safely ridden the Revolution since it opened in 1976.

Lady Gaga attended a Silicon Valley fundraiser for President Barack Obama, held at the residence of Facebook COO Sheryl Sandberg. Gaga wore a black, sleeveless gown and high heels, and the event was attended by Silicon Valley elites who paid up to $35,800 per couple to attend. It was unclear if Gaga met with Obama to discuss her concerns about bullying.

In other news, Lady Gaga is planning to get diamond implants in her teeth to match her love for attention-seeking jewelry. Mick Hucknall of Simply Red once had a ruby implant in his tooth, but replaced it with a diamond.

There is also a dispute over the domain name LadyGaga.org. The artist formerly known as Stefani Germanotta submitted a complaint to the National Arbitration Forum alleging that the website was registered in bad faith and in violation of her trademark. However, the owner of the site argued that it was a non-commercial, unofficial fan site for Gaga that supports her fame and gives her free publicity. The National Arbitration Forum ruled in favor of the site owner, allowing it to continue.

Lady Gaga caused a stir at a Las Vegas hotel when she demanded a room with a private pool. After checking into the luxurious Cosmopolitan hotel and finding no private pool, she checked out and headed for The Palms Casino Resort. Gaga is in Las Vegas performing at the iHeartRadio music festival, along with several other artists. Arrangements around the concert seemed chaotic, with some artists reportedly not being paid and more concerned with their deals at the nightclubs.

A man, described as a carjacker, led police on a high-speed chase through the streets of Los Angeles, carjacking a vehicle at gunpoint and crashing at least six times. The chase, which started around 5pm local time, was captured live on television and continued through the city and its suburbs. The spree ended when the suspect failed to steal a third car and was shot by police. He is currently under arrest in the hospital.

The chase began when police tried to pull over the man for driving a car listed as stolen. The man refused to stop, leading to a high-speed chase that lasted for several hours. Footage captured by a helicopter showed the car speeding at around 60mph up a three-lane motorway, crashing several times at junctions before veering over pavements and into oncoming traffic on the wrong side of the road.

The car skidded and started spinning, hitting several other vehicles before coming to a stop in the middle of the road. The driver is seen jumping out of the crushed and smoking car before trying to carjack another vehicle, which sped away from him, and pulling what appeared to be a gun on the driver in the car behind it.

The woman whose car was stolen at gunpoint on live TV was not hurt but was deeply shaken. Elizabeth Yarahuan, 22, told KABC-TV Channel 7: “He just came up to me and pointed the gun at me and told me to get out of my car. I was just scared he was going to hurt me.”

At least eight LAPD cars and helicopters tracked the suspect as the chase continued on several motorways until heavy traffic in Montebello stopped the suspect’s escape. Stuck between stationary cars, cameras captured him jumping out of his vehicle and attempting to hijack two more.

Police attempt to stop the driver as he speeds off again

But as the second driver resisted and drove away, police running after the suspect on foot shot him as he fled down the road. He was handcuffed on the ground and taken to hospital in an ambulance. Last night, the suspect was alive in hospital being treated for “multiple” gunshot wounds.

“This individual acted with a complete disregard for other people's lives,” Los Angeles Police Department Commander Andy Smith told the LA Times. “He callously put innocent people's lives in danger, even after the police backed off the pursuit and tracked with the helicopter. Thank God no one was killed by this maniac.”

The University of Cambridge is seeking to appoint a new Professor, funded by the LEGO Foundation, in the field of educational or developmental psychology, with a focus on early years development and play. The role, titled the LEGO® Professorship of Play in Education, Development, and Learning, will lead the newly established Centre for Research on Play in Education, Development and Learning (PEDAL).

PEDAL, part of the Psychology, Education and Learning Studies Research Group at the Faculty of Education, was launched in October 2015 with funding from the LEGO Foundation. Its mission is to conduct academic research into the role of play in young children’s education, development, and learning to inform wider practice and policy.

The research will aim to understand the importance of play and playfulness in education globally, with an aim to produce research that supports excellence in education, equipping children with 21st-century skills like problem-solving, teamwork, and self-control. The successful candidate will have an outstanding research record of international stature and will be expected to teach, research, examine, supervise, and administer.

The LEGO Foundation has funded the establishment of PEDAL and has further funded the LEGO® Professorship. The Foundation believes play has a critical role in high-quality learning and hopes the professor will encourage more playful learning in schools, rather than testing. Applications close on 20 January 2017. The University values diversity and is committed to equality of opportunity.

State Representative Daniel B. Winslow, a former judge and aide to Governor Mitt Romney, has officially entered the special election for the US Senate, making him the first Republican candidate. Winslow, a second-term state representative from Norfolk, has donated $100,000 to kickstart his campaign, which he estimates will cost between $4 million and $6 million. He plans to meet with Republicans on Capitol Hill and the National Republican Senatorial Committee this week and will resign from his law firm next month to focus on his campaign. Winslow emphasized his commitment to the Second Amendment and fiscal conservatism.

Other potential Republican candidates include Senate Minority Leader Bruce E. Tarr, former congressional candidate Sean Bielat, private equity investor and former Navy SEAL Gabriel E. Gomez, and Jon Fetherston, a former chair of the Ashland Board of Selectmen. Two US House members, Stephen F. Lynch and Edward J. Markey, are running on the Democratic side. Candidates must gather 10,000 certified signatures by February 27 to qualify for the April 30 ballot, a hurdle that may weed out lesser-known candidates. Winslow expressed confidence in his ability to collect the necessary signatures.

In a chilling revelation, newly-released documents have disclosed that a nuclear bomb nearly detonated in North Carolina in 1961, during a military accident involving a B-52 bomber. The incident, which took place on January 24, 1961, saw two 4-megaton hydrogen bombs fall near Raleigh, NC. One of the bombs, named "Weapon I," came close to detonating as its arming mechanism switched to "armed" on impact, while the other bomb, "Weapon 2," would have exploded in mid-air if two cockpit wires had touched as the plane disintegrated.

Eric Schlosser, who obtained the documents a year before their release by the National Security Archive at George Washington University, stated that Weapon I, which was brought to Earth by a parachute, behaved as if it had been dropped over the Soviet Union. The bomb completed five of the six steps to detonation, and only a low-voltage switch prevented the explosion.

William Burr, an analyst from the National Security Archive, noted that the fact that the arming mechanism on Weapon 2 moved on impact showed its safety shortcomings. Had either bomb detonated, the consequences would have been catastrophic. According to Jack ReVelle, an Air Force weapons disposal specialist, the explosion would have created a crater eight football fields wide, destroyed every structure within a four-mile radius, and resulted in a 100-percent kill zone for eight and a half miles in every direction.

The B-52 was on a routine 12-hour mission when it suddenly lost 19 tons of fuel pressure within minutes. The pilot managed to straighten the plane at 10,000 feet and aimed it for nearby Seymour Johnson Air Force Base until its right wing broke off. One witness described the plane as streaking through the sky like a Roman candle. The pilots survived, and no one was killed on the ground.

The documents also reveal that three of the four safety switches on the other bomb failed to work properly, meaning only "one simple, dynamo-technology, low voltage switch stood between the United States and a major catastrophe." The parachute on this bomb deployed, but when it struck the ground, the final firing signal triggered, only to be halted by the fourth safety switch.

The Goldsboro incident is one of 32 pre-1980 accidents involving nuclear weapons that have been declassified. Weeks after Goldsboro, there was another close call in California. The US government had previously denied that its nuclear weapons stockpile had ever put the nation at risk. However, Schlosser stated that the documents shed light on how close the Air Force came to witnessing an atomic bomb explode on US soil.

Charles Hall, the inventor of the waterbed, is planning a comeback for the bed design 50 years after its initial debut. The new waterbed design aims to address the issues of the original design, such as the rigid frame and wave action, by using a foam collar around the water bladder, spandex covers, a fiber insert to quell waves, and an updated temperature system. The new waterbed will first be tested in a chain of Florida furniture stores later this spring or summer, before potentially being rolled out more broadly. The bed will be available in queen and king sizes, and will sell for about $2,000. Hall believes that the new waterbed will appeal to both those who remember the original design and a new generation of consumers. The waterbed first launched on the West Coast in the 1960s and became popular during the counterculture movement and sexual revolution of the 1970s. Hall laments the way the waterbed has been portrayed in movies and TV shows, as a joke or exploding. Waterbeds reached their peak in the 1980s before sales tapered off, and Hall moved on to other design projects, but returned to the concept in recent years with a few tweaks.

William Morgan, an American guerrilla fighter who fought alongside Castro during the Cuban Revolution, was executed by the Cuban government in 1961. His widow, Olga Goodwin, has been trying to bring his body back to his native Ohio for reburial for over a decade. The tussle over Morgan's remains could be ending as relations between the U.S. and Cuba thaw, with the release of Alan Gross, an American aid worker, and three Cuban members of the "Cuban Five" who were convicted of espionage-related charges. Morgan's body could be next in the deal.

Morgan was a charismatic American guerrilla who fell out of favor with Castro and Ernesto "Che" Guevara after the revolution and was executed. His body was placed in an unmarked grave in Havana. For more than a decade, Goodwin has tried to get Morgan's remains returned from Cuba to his native Ohio for reburial.

Morgan was a former paratrooper and high school dropout who worked as an enforcer for the mob before abandoning his life in 1957 to join Cuban fighters fighting Fulgencio Batista. In photos, Morgan cut a dashing figure with a thick beard and broad shoulders. While fighting in Cuba, Morgan met then Olga Rodriguez and married her. Their love story is at the center of the book "The Yankee Comandante: The Untold Story of Courage, Passion, and One American’s Fight to Liberate Cuba."

Morgan's life has attracted attention in recent years, with a new book written by Pulitzer Prize winners Mike Sallah and Mitch Weiss, and a possible movie adaptation in the works. Morgan was "like Holden Caulfield with a machine gun," according to a New Yorker article about him. He was the only American in the rebel army and the sole foreigner, other than Guevara, an Argentine, to rise to the army’s highest rank, comandante.

After the revolution, Morgan became disillusioned with Castro. Morgan's group supported a democratic form of government, while Castro began tilting toward the Soviet Union. When Castro canceled elections, seized properties, and imprisoned Morgan’s fellow freedom fighters, Morgan decided to take action. He began stockpiling guns to launch a counterrevolution in the Escambry. But he was betrayed by one of his men and executed by firing squad at the notorious La Cabana prison in March 1961.

Even his death was something out of the movies. Morgan gave his rosary to a priest, asking the man to return it to his mother in Ohio. When his executioners told him to kneel, Morgan reportedly said: “I kneel for no man.” The firing squad shot out his knees before killing him as he lay on the ground.

Goodwin has been trying to bring Morgan's body back to Ohio for reburial for over a decade. She has remarried, but she hasn't given up on her promise to Morgan. Getting his body back would finally repay him for sacrificing his life to liberate her country.

The return of Morgan’s remains will fulfill a widow’s promise and also close the book on the life of an American patriot, according to Sallah.

Simone Biles, the gold medal-winning gymnast from the 2016 Olympics, has come forward to say that she was molested by team doctor Larry Nassar. Biles' statement, posted on social media, comes just one day before Nassar's sentencing hearing, during which nearly 100 victims are expected to speak. Biles joins a growing list of gymnasts who have accused Nassar of sexual abuse, including members of the 2012 "Fierce Five" team – McKayla Maroney, Aly Raisman, and Gabby Douglas. Nassar pleaded guilty to sexually assaulting seven girls and is expected to receive up to 40 years in prison. The sentencing hearing will provide a platform for victims to tell their stories for the first time, in the midst of the #MeToo movement.

Biles' statement follows similar disclosures from other gymnasts, who have described feeling betrayed by Nassar and the institutions that enabled his abuse. Some victims are expected to blame not just Nassar but USA Gymnastics and Michigan State University, where Nassar had his sports-medicine practice. Both organizations are accused of giving Nassar unfettered access to vulnerable girls and women, ignoring signs or complaints of sexual misconduct, and trying to silence victims.

The sentencing hearing is expected to be emotional, with some victims planning to stand at a podium and speak directly to Nassar, while others will submit audio recordings or written statements. The hearing will provide a chance for victims to tell their stories and demand accountability from the institutions that failed to protect them.

The case illustrates the drive of the #MeToo movement to call out serial predatory behavior and the forces that enable it. Biles' statement is a powerful reminder that sexual abuse is not limited to any one individual or institution, and that it is important to speak out and demand change. Biles' courage in coming forward is a testament to the strength and resilience of survivors, and a call to action for those who have the power to prevent such abuse from happening again.

Kenny McKinley, a standout wide receiver for the Denver Broncos and the University of South Carolina, was found dead in his Colorado home on Monday. Authorities believe McKinley died from a self-inflicted gunshot wound. McKinley played for USC from 2005-08, setting records for receptions, receiving yards, and consecutive games with a reception. He was drafted by the Broncos in the fifth round of the 2009 NFL draft. McKinley's teammates and coaches described him as a positive and energetic individual. He is survived by a young son. The Broncos will hold a team meeting to discuss McKinley's death and grief counselors will be available for players. McKinley's death marks the third active Broncos player to die in the past four years.

Carrie Fisher, the actress best known for her role as Princess Leia in the Star Wars saga, passed away on Tuesday after suffering a heart attack on a flight from London to Los Angeles on December 23rd. Fisher was 60 years old.

Throughout her career, Fisher was known for her sharp wit and openness about her struggles with mental illness, drug abuse, and addiction. She was the daughter of two entertainers, actress Debbie Reynolds and singer Eddie Fisher.

Fisher's impact on Hollywood and the entertainment industry was significant, and her passing has been met with an outpouring of tributes and condolences from her colleagues and fans. Here are some memorable lines attributed to Fisher, who died Tuesday after suffering a heart attack during a flight:

* "If my life wasn't funny, it would just be true, and that is unacceptable." (2011)
* "There's no room for demons when you're self-possessed." (2014)
* "Instant gratification takes too long."
* “I act like someone in a bomb shelter trying to raise everyone’s spirits.”
* “Movies were meant to stay on the screen, flat and large and colorful, gathering you up into their sweep of story, carrying you rollicking along to the end, then releasing you back into your unchanged life. But this movie (Star Wars) misbehaved. It leaked out of the theater, poured off the screen, affected a lot of people so deeply that they required endless talismans and artifacts to stay connected to it.”

Fisher also left a legacy as an advocate for removing the stigma surrounding mental illness, changing minds by opening up about her own struggle with depression and bipolar disorder. Many have credited Fisher’s openness with breaking down stigma over mental health issues, and the topic was on the top of the minds of many of her admirers following her death.

Fisher is survived by her daughter, Billie Lourd, her brother, Todd Fisher, her mother, Debbie Reynolds, and her French bulldog, Gary.

The Morning Consult poll revealed that Star Wars fans favor Leia as their most loved character, with a 73% favorability rating. Luke Skywalker, Chewbacca, Yoda, and R2-D2 followed closely. Interestingly, Anakin Skywalker received a 55% rating, while Darth Vader, who is Anakin Skywalker, received a 49% rating. The poll also showed that Jar Jar Binks was not the most hated character, as he had a 37% approval rating, only one spot behind Rey. Supreme Leader Snoke finished at the bottom of the list with 26%.

The poll also examined the political leanings of Star Wars fans, with 53% of respondents not considering Star Wars to be political, and 41% of the 17% who do finding the series' political tone bothersome.

The poll results also shed light on the character of Jar Jar Binks' creator, Ahmed Best. Best, now 43, was a computer whiz and musician before landing the role of Jar Jar Binks. He has since launched The Afrofuturist Podcast, a series about the future that's closely linked to his past. Best was initially arrogant in his role in the theatrical production Stomp, which eventually led to him being cast as Jar Jar Binks.

The poll results were based on a survey of 2,200 people and provided a wealth of data that can be scavenged for weeks after the upcoming "Last Jedi" film drops.

A computer model has been developed that can predict first impressions based on facial features, according to a study published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. The model found that a smiling expression is key to an impression of approachability, large eyes signal youthfulness, and dominance is linked to a masculine face shape. The researchers believe this could lead to computer programs that help people choose the best photographs for creating a positive first impression.

The study found that first impressions are formed quickly and can have a significant impact on future behavior. The researchers used 1,000 photographs of people from the internet and asked six volunteers to rate their first impressions of the people in the photos on social traits such as trustworthiness and dominance. The faces were broken down into 65 physical features, such as the shape of a person's jaw, mouth, eyes, cheekbones or eyebrows. The researchers then analyzed these faces using an artificial neural network to learn which facial physical features might be linked to first impressions of social traits.

The model suggested that given enough data, it can accurately gauge people's likely impressions of a given image. If someone is thinking about attaching a picture to their CV, resume, or online dating profile, they may want to consider the findings of this study. The model found that mouth shape and area were linked to approachability, with a smiling expression being a key component of an impression of approachability. Eye shape and area were important for youthful-attractiveness, in line with views linking relatively large eyes to a youthful appearance. Dominance was linked with features indicating a masculine face shape, such as eyebrow height, cheekbones, as well as color and texture differences that may relate to either masculinity or a healthy or tanned overall appearance.

The researchers believe that this model could be used to select an image that conveys a desirable impression, perhaps even automatically. However, the researchers only looked at Caucasian faces in this study, and they are currently conducting cross-cultural studies to find out how culture impacts the results. The researchers also plan to use brain imaging to investigate how these social impressions are created in the brain and to look at ways in which first impressions can be influenced by directly manipulating specific features.

The study adds mathematical detail to a well-known phenomenon, according to Dr Tom Hartley, a neuroscientist at the University of York and the study's senior author. "If people are forming these first impressions, just based on looking at somebody's face, what is it about the image of the face that's giving that impression - can we measure it exactly?" Dr Hartley said. The findings could help film animators or anyone looking to create an instant impression on a social network.

The researchers believe that the commercial potential of this work is significant, particularly in today's world where people often only see one picture of a face on social media and have to form their impression based on that. The researchers plan to continue their research to better understand the role of facial features in first impressions and to develop ways to manipulate those features to create desired impressions.

Groupon, an e-commerce company, recently priced its IPO at $20 per share and started trading at around $30. However, the stock's current valuation of approximately $20 billion is deemed overvalued by some analysts due to the company's ongoing business transition and the deceleration in its growth rate.

The deceleration in Groupon's growth rate is primarily due to the law of large numbers and the company's decision to cut back on marketing costs. This deceleration could potentially be hazardous to the stock's value, as momentum investors typically dislike such deceleration.

Amazon's past experience serves as a cautionary tale. In 2000, Amazon underwent a similar transition from hyper-growth-and-losses to sustainable-growth-and-profitability, which led to a significant decline in its stock price.

Despite the short-term risks, long-term analysts are bullish on Groupon, citing its discovery of a new market and its scale as a barrier to entry. However, they warn that the transition may not be smooth and the stock's current valuation seems overvalued.

Institutional investors, who got the stock at $20, are already flipping it to other buyers. Analysts suggest that if the next few quarters are as rough as expected, the stock could trade down to around $8 billion or $12 per share, a significant drop from its current price.

In conclusion, while Groupon's IPO has been successful in the short term, its long-term prospects are uncertain due to its ongoing business transition and the deceleration in its growth rate. Investors should approach the stock with caution and consider the potential risks involved.

In a surprising turn of events, Dallas Cowboys wide receiver Lucky Whitehead was wrongfully implicated in a shoplifting arrest in Virginia last month, leading to his release from the team. The incident occurred on June 22 at a Wawa convenience store, where someone stole items, and the clerk pointed out the suspect at the scene. The suspect provided information that matched Whitehead's, leading to his arrest. However, police later confirmed that the information provided was falsely attributed to Whitehead, and they are currently seeking the identity of the actual suspect.

The police department expressed regret for the impact the incorrect information had on Whitehead, stating, "It cost my player his job. He deserved better from law enforcement." Whitehead's agent, David Rich, also expressed disappointment over the error, stating, "It cost my player his job. He deserved better from law enforcement. We all do."

Whitehead, who joined the Cowboys in 2015 with a three-year, $1.58 million contract, was given "a lot of different chances along the way going back to last year" by the team, according to Cowboys executive vice president Stephen Jones. However, the team decided it was time to go in a different direction, and Whitehead was released.

Whitehead has made headlines recently for other reasons as well, including a social media post about his dog being stolen and taken for ransom. The dog was later recovered. The Cowboys have not yet commented on the recent developments regarding Whitehead's innocence.

At a news conference, Dallas Cowboys coach Jason Garrett repeatedly stated that the team stands by the decision to cut Whitehead, refusing to elaborate further. When asked about the potential message being sent by rushing to judgment, Garrett replied, "Yesterday we made a decision that we felt that was in the best interest of the Dallas Cowboys. We're going to stand by that decision. We're going to move forward."

When asked about the possibility of Whitehead seeking his job back or why the team has kept other players who have courted controversy, his agent declined to comment. The Cowboys have not yet announced any plans to reinstate Whitehead.

Google's Security Rewards Year in Review for 2015 highlights the company's efforts to address security issues and reward those who discover vulnerabilities. In total, Google paid out over $2 million to more than 300 individuals. One of the more interesting recipients was Sanmay Ved, who briefly purchased Google.com for $12, a transaction that Google later reversed and offered him a $6,006.13 reward. The amount was significant because when viewed as letters, it spells out "Google." Sanmay donated his reward to charity, and Google doubled the amount.

Tomasz Bojarski was the most prolific researcher, discovering 70 bugs on Google. Android was added to the Security Reward program in 2015, resulting in payments of over $200,000 to researchers, including a $37,500 payment to the most significant single recipient.

Google also introduced Vulnerability Research Grants, providing researchers with funds before starting their investigations. One example of this program's success is Kamil Histamullin, a researcher from Kasan, Russia, who received a grant and found an issue in YouTube Creator Studio that would have allowed anyone to delete any video from YouTube. After the issue was fixed, he was rewarded $5,000 in addition to his initial research grant.

Google's established programs continued to grow in 2015, with highlights including Tomasz Bojarski's discovery of a bug in Google's vulnerability submission form and Sanmay Ved's purchase of Google.com. Google also announced a dedication of one million dollars specifically for security research related to Google Drive.

In conclusion, Google's Security Rewards programs have been successful in addressing security issues and rewarding those who discover vulnerabilities. The programs have grown significantly, with Android being added in 2015 and new initiatives like Vulnerability Research Grants being introduced. Google plans to continue the growth of these programs in 2016.

The document consists of two separate parts: a news article and a personal review of a restaurant in Lonsdale, Minnesota.

In this case, Spamhaus's Domain Name System (DNS) servers were targeted, the infrastructure that joins domain names, such as bbc.co.uk, with the website's numerical internet protocol address. The attack's power would be strong enough to take down government internet infrastructure, according to Mr. Linford.

The attack has caused a knock-on effect, hurting internet services globally. The attackers have targeted every part of the internet infrastructure that they feel can be brought down. Spamhaus has more than 80 servers around the world and has built the biggest DNS server.

The attacks typically happen in intermittent bursts of high activity. To cope, Spamhaus has received aid from companies like Google. The attacks are aimed at the victim from servers all over the world, making them difficult to stop because those servers cannot be shut off without halting the Internet. The only way to deal with this problem, according to security experts, is to find the people doing it and arrest them.

The heart of the problem is that many large Internet service providers have not set up their networks to make sure that traffic leaving their networks is actually coming from their own users. This potential security flaw has long been known by Internet security specialists but has only recently been exploited in a way that threatens the Internet infrastructure.

Archaeologists have successfully located a 16th-century Spanish fort, Fort San Marcos, on Parris Island, South Carolina, which was once the capital of Spanish Florida. The improved computer programs interpreting the data from radar and magnetometers played a crucial role in finding the fort.

The team is now working to map the entire town of Santa Elena, which is believed to have included around 60 homes, a church, shops, and taverns. They are also close to determining the location of Pedro Menendez de Aviles' home, which is distinguished by high-end Chinese wares no one else in the settlement could have afforded. DePratter and Thompson are working with a small team of doctoral students and undergraduates this summer.

The team's work is being done in open fields that were once fairways of the golf course, which has been moved to accommodate the archaeological work. The scientists have the cooperation of the Marine Corps and come and go as they please. The remote location behind the golf course means a protected site with few visitors, with Marines on their lunch break being the most recent visitors.

The new discovery will be published this week in the Journal of Archeological Science: Reports. The resulting information will be included in future exhibits at the Santa Elena History Center, which opened this year in downtown Beaufort to tell the story of the early settlement.

The finding of Fort San Marcos provides a unique view of the 16th-century landscape and sheds light on the "lost century" of South Carolina's history, 104 years before English settlers landed at Charles Towne. The work will allow researchers to tell the story of the land that would eventually become the United States and gain insight into how colonial powers in Europe vied for control over this corner of the New World.

The company owns a controlling interest in the Ekati Diamond Mine, which it operates, and owns 40% of the Diavik Diamond Mine. Both mines are located in the Northwest Territories of Canada.

The feud originated from a real estate dispute in 2007, where Rick Krlich attempted to buy a property adjacent to his own, which was owned by the Clemente family. The family, led by former fire chief John Clemente Jr., allegedly threatened Krlich and refused to sell the property.

Since then, Krlich claims that members of the Clemente family and their associates have honked their horns while driving past the Krlich's house as a form of harassment. Krlich has provided evidence of the honking, including recordings of city and county officials, police officers, and firefighters participating in the campaign. Despite this evidence, the police department has reportedly failed to take action or investigate the complaints.

In an attempt to bring peace to the town, ABC News' "20/20" invited the Clementes, the Krlich's, and the town of Hubbard to a Peace and Reconciliation Barbecue, which will be aired on May 2, 2023.

Recently, Garrick Krlich, a relative of Rick and Cindy Krlich, filed a lawsuit against the city of Hubbard, Police Chief James R. Taafe, and Trumball County, alleging a violation of the Equal Protection Clause. Krlich is seeking compensatory damages for his video recording equipment and legal fees, as well as punitive damages exceeding $75,000. The city of Hubbard did not respond to a request for comment.

North Korean leader Kim Jong-il has been re-elected as the leader of the ruling Workers' Party, with state media reporting that his youngest son, Kim Jong-un, has been appointed a four-star general. The appointment is seen as a significant step towards confirming Kim Jong-un as the successor to his father.

Kim Jong-un, who is believed to be around 27 years old, has little experience but has been groomed as the successor to his father, Kim Il-sung, since the mid-1970s. He has been given military and party roles, including a position in the Workers' Party secretariat in 1980.

The announcement about Kim Jong-un is his first mention by name in state media and is reminiscent of his father's rise to prominence. Kim Jong-un's elder brother and half-brother appear to have been ruled out of the running for the succession.

Kim Jong-il's sister, Kyong-hui, has also been named a four-star general, and analysts believe she may play a role in ensuring a smooth transfer of power to Kim Jong-un.

The appointment of Kim Jong-un as a four-star general without military experience has raised concerns about the lack of experience and the potential for instability in North Korea, which has a nuclear program and is hostile towards South Korea.

Kim Jong-il is reported to be suffering from several illnesses, including diabetes and a kidney ailment, and there have been fears about instability and a possible power struggle in the country if he were to die without anointing a successor.

The Workers' Party has not met for decades, and observers believe Kim Jong-il may be cementing the family dynasty by anointing Kim Jong-un as his chosen successor. The succession is being closely watched because of the North's nuclear program and hostility with the South.

The state television announcer was quoted as saying that Kim Jong-il had been reappointed as general secretary of the Workers' Party as an "expression of absolute support and trust." She said a "crucial" development was underway but gave no further details. The state news agency said the leader had been re-appointed with "the unanimous will and wishes" of North Koreans.

The appointment of Kim Jong-un as a four-star general and the re-election of Kim Jong-il as general secretary of the Workers' Party are seen as strong signs that the authoritarian state intends to continue its quasi-religious leadership cult for another generation. Final confirmation would come if Kim Jong-un's portrait appears alongside that of his father and grandfather in every home and workplace.

The analysis of a tablet device belonging to Germanwings Flight 9525 co-pilot Andreas Lubitz reveals that he researched suicide methods and cockpit door security in the days leading up to the crash on March 24, 2015. The tablet, retrieved from Lubitz's Dusseldorf apartment, showed searches concerning medical treatment, suicide methods, and cockpit doors and their security measures. The co-pilot is suspected of deliberately bringing down the plane, killing all 150 on board.

Investigators have also found the second 'black box', the flight data recorder, which will provide details about the plane's speed, altitude, and the pilot's actions during the crash. A female police officer discovered the recorder in a ravine, and despite fire damage, it is expected to yield useful information.

Authorities have found 470 personnel effects at the crash site in the French Alps, including 40 cell phones, though their condition makes it unlikely that any useful information can be retrieved. 150 different sets of DNA have been recovered, corresponding to the number of people on the flight.

The crash has led to calls for enhanced crash avoidance software that could take control of an aircraft away from a pilot and steer it to a safe altitude. This software was previously developed but ultimately scrapped over a decade ago.

It is becoming increasingly clear that Lubitz was "very afraid" he would lose his license to fly due to his medical issues. He had battled depression for years and concealed recent medical leave notes from his employer, Germanwings. Lubitz saw at least five doctors in the weeks leading up to the crash, seeking help for his severe depression and stress.

The investigation is ongoing, with a new task force looking into medical procedures for pilots and cockpit door locking mechanisms. The cockpit door on the plane was strengthened following the events of September 11, 2001, making it impossible for the captain to force his way in. German Transport Minister Alexander Dobrindt has emphasized the need for quick but careful decisions regarding these issues.

A large caravan of approximately 1,200 migrants, primarily from Honduras, is making its way towards the United States, bypassing Mexican authorities and gangs. The migrants are fleeing poverty, political unrest, and violence in their home country, which worsened after the election of President Juan Orlando Hernández. The group, organized by Pueblos Sin Fronteras, or People Without Borders, aims to help migrants safely reach the United States. The migrants are divided into groups and committees for security, food, and logistics, and they hope to find asylum or cross the border illegally once they reach the US. Some migrants, like Yonis, are hoping to settle in other parts of Mexico instead. The caravan has been moving along highways, hitchhiking and using trucks and freight trains, and has been welcomed by local townspeople and churches who provide food and shelter. President Trump has expressed opposition to the caravan, tweeting that Mexico should stop it at their northern border and that the US needs a wall and proper border legislation to secure its borders.

Mel B, a British singer and former Spice Girl, has filed for divorce from her husband Stephen Belafonte, but is still wearing the expensive wedding ring he gave her in 2014. The couple has been separated since December, but Mel B claims that Belafonte physically and emotionally abused her throughout their nearly decade-long marriage.

In her divorce documents, Mel B alleges that Belafonte would beat her, choke her, and throw her to the ground on multiple occasions. She says that he destroyed her self-confidence and self-esteem, especially because she was struggling to lose her pregnancy weight. Mel B also claims that Belafonte threatened to release sex tapes of them he recorded, threatening to ruin her career. She says he threatened to release the videos to Children's Services in an attempt to have the kids taken away.

Mel B says that the abuse was witnessed by many people around her, but most of them bought her stories that made no sense. She was forced to miss a filming of 'X Factor' (UK) in late 2014 because her injuries were so bad they could not be covered by theatrical makeup. When she finally returned, she still had visible facial and body wounds yet no one sounded the alarm.

Mel B also claims that Belafonte harassed and intimidated her agents, producers, and co-stars, and they complained to her that he was "abusive and demanding," and he was adversely affecting her business.

Belafonte has not commented on the allegations. Mel B has been granted a restraining order, forcing Belafonte to stay away from her and their three children and ordering him to leave the family home. The judge has also ordered Belafonte to surrender all firearms, as he is prohibited from carrying firearms as part of a domestic violence conviction involving another woman.

Krishna Maharaj, a British businessman who has spent the past 27 years in a Florida prison for a double murder, is seeking a retrial with new evidence that his lawyers claim will prove his innocence. The case is being considered by Judge William Thomas, who granted Maharaj a full evidentiary hearing on April 24, 2023.

Maharaj was sentenced to death in 1987 for the murders of his business partner Derrick Moo Young and Young’s son Duane in the Dupont Plaza hotel in Miami on 16 October 1986. He was taken off death row in 2002 and resentenced to life imprisonment.

The newly released documents underline the massive case for exoneration that has been built up by Maharaj’s lawyers. They plan to call 53 witnesses and present 498 documents to persuade the court to order a retrial. Among the witnesses to be called are six people who can testify that Maharaj was 30 miles away from the Dupont Plaza hotel when the murders happened. Further testimony will be provided alleging that another named individual carried out the killings, and illuminating the motive for him doing so.

Maharaj asserts that he was framed as the murderer to help cover up the involvement of Colombian drug cartels in the killings. The prisoner will present the court with evidence that the victims had been laundering huge sums for the Medellin drug cartel.

The case is being considered by Judge William Thomas. Ordering a full evidentiary hearing on 24 April, he stated that Maharaj would be granted a new trial if he could persuade the court that the new evidence that will be presented at the full hearing was of “such nature that it would probably produce an acquittal on retrial”.

Lawyers for the state have claimed much of the new material is hearsay and inadmissible in any new trial. The judge said he would take a view on admissibility at the evidentiary hearing.

The case has gained attention due to the allegations that Maharaj was framed for the murders by Colombian drug cartels, with evidence suggesting that the murders were committed by former members of Pablo Escobar’s infamous drug cartel. The defense team also alleges Florida prosecutors covered up evidence in the 1987 trial that could have proved Maharaj’s innocence.

Despite the challenges, Maharaj’s wife, Marita, has been fighting to keep his spirits up. "He and his wife talk every day on the phone," defense attorney Clive Stafford Smith told CNN.
