"And she goes to see him every Sunday." Smith and the defense team successfully pressed Florida courts to reduce Maharaj’s death sentence to life in prison in 2002. Smith says new witnesses have been found who will testify that the killings were hits ordered by Escobar and that Maharaj was framed. But Florida state attorneys say none of the witnesses has firsthand knowledge of the case or can provide admissible testimony or evidence.

In Los Angeles, anonymous street artists have posted posters depicting Meryl Streep as a Harvey Weinstein enabler, with the phrase "She knew" referring to Weinstein's alleged sexual abuse of women. The posters, inspired by the work of artist Barbara Kruger, were hung near Streep's house, the SAG-AFTRA building, and the 20th Century Fox studio lot. The artists are referencing accusations that Streep had knowledge of Weinstein's predatory behavior but did not speak up. This comes after Rose McGowan, who alleges she was raped by Weinstein, criticized Streep for her professional relationship with Weinstein. Streep has since issued a statement denying any knowledge of Weinstein's crimes. The posters also follow a Twitter feud between McGowan and Amber Tamblyn over McGowan's criticism of Hollywood actresses planning to wear black to the Golden Globes in protest of sexual harassment. The clash originated over speculation that actresses, including Streep, plan to wear black gowns to the upcoming Golden Globes on Jan. 7 to protest sexual harassment of women.

Two women, Lizandra Cosme, 32, and Susana Gonzalez, 27, have been arrested and charged in connection with an incident at the Children's Learning Place daycare in Chicago, where five toddlers were injured with a hot glue gun on December 1. The incident occurred while Cosme was watching 16 children. Surveillance footage allegedly shows Cosme applying hot glue to the hands and arms of the five 2-year-olds, causing them to grimace in pain. Gonzalez, an assistant at the daycare center, can be seen laughing nearby.

Cosme faces five felony counts of aggravated battery to a child, while Gonzalez faces five misdemeanor counts of causing the circumstances of endangering a child. The extent of the children's injuries is unclear, and it is not immediately known what prompted the burnings.

During a court hearing, Cosme's defense attorney said her actions were not malicious, but rather a mistake. Prosecutors allege that Cosme brought the hot glue gun from home to work on a Christmas project.

The Children's Learning Place is a licensed child-care facility with four locations in Chicago. The daycare center immediately terminated the two employees involved in the incident and is cooperating with investigators. The Department of Children and Family Services is also investigating the incident.

Lizandra Cosme was ordered held without bail and is scheduled to return to court on December 26. Susana Gonzalez's next court appearance is not immediately known. The incident has raised concerns about the safety and well-being of children in daycare centers.

Burberry, a British luxury fashion house, announced on Thursday that it will cease the practice of destroying unsaleable products, effective immediately. This decision aligns with the company's five-year responsibility agenda, which aims to drive positive change, become carbon neutral, and positively impact one million people.

The fashion house has already been implementing measures to reuse, repair, donate, or recycle unsaleable products, and plans to expand these efforts. Burberry's commitment to sustainability extends beyond product waste, as they have also partnered with the Ellen MacArthur Foundation's Make Fashion Circular Initiative and established a Material Futures Research Group with the Royal College of Art to invent new sustainable materials.

In addition to addressing waste, Burberry has pledged to phase out the use of real fur, starting with Riccardo Tisci's debut collection for Burberry later this month. The company has historically limited its use of fur to rabbit, fox, mink, Asiatic racoon, and Angora, but these materials, along with Angora, will now be banned.

Burberry's commitment to sustainability and ethical practices has been recognized with its inclusion in the Dow Jones Sustainability Index for the third consecutive year. The company's efforts have also included supporting young people in disadvantaged communities, developing a more inclusive and sustainable cashmere industry in Afghanistan, and establishing partnerships to support and accelerate innovation and sustainable business practices.

The decision to stop burning unsold goods and use of real fur follows criticism on social media and from environmental activists. Burberry had previously destroyed clothes and perfume worth over $36 million in 2017, a common practice among fashion firms to prevent the sale of unwanted goods cheaply. The animal rights group Human Society International welcomed Burberry's decision to go fur-free, describing it as a "compassionate stance" and brands who continue to use fur as "isolated and outdated."

The article discusses the iconic dunk by Benny Anders, a swingman for the Houston Cougars, during a Final Four game against Louisville 30 years ago. Anders stole the ball near the free throw line, slalomed through traffic, and performed a spectacular dunk that was described as a "midair shark attack." The dunk galvanized Houston, who eventually pulled away to win the game. However, Anders' career never reached the same heights again, and he disappeared from the public eye. Despite efforts to find him, his whereabouts remain unknown. The article also discusses the upcoming documentary "Phi Slama Jama" which features Anders and the Houston Cougars' dynasty of the 1980s.

President Trump has announced that he is open to a path to citizenship for approximately 690,000 undocumented immigrants known as "Dreamers" as part of a potential immigration deal being negotiated by Congress. This potential breakthrough comes with the condition that $25 billion is allocated for a wall on the southwest border with Mexico and $5 billion for additional border upgrades. The president also plans to continue his push to curb legal immigration as part of the deal.

Trump's remarks represent a significant shift from his hardline stance on immigration during his campaign and his rejection of a bipartisan Senate proposal last week that included citizenship. The White House is expected to release a complete "framework" on Monday, which will likely grant immediate provisional legal status to those immigrants covered by the Obama-era Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) program, making them eligible to pursue full citizenship over 10 to 12 years.

Lawmakers face a February 8 deadline for a must-pass spending bill to keep the government open, but Democrats and some Republicans have expressed their unwillingness to support a long-term deal that does not address the future of the DACA program. The impasse over immigration led to a brief, partial government shutdown this week before lawmakers agreed to a three-week funding extension.

Congress members have expressed exasperation over Trump's unclear demands and fluctuating stance on the issue. A senior White House official stated that the framework will give lawmakers a clearer set of guidelines to help break the impasse.

Trump's proposal for citizenship would be limited to the 690,000 who were enrolled in DACA when he terminated the program. However, Democrats and some Republicans have pushed to extend legal protections to a far larger group of Dreamers – up to 1.7 million under the latest version of the DREAM Act.

Many of those who were eligible for DACA never applied, with immigrant rights advocates attributing this to fears of registering with the government and costs associated with applying. White House officials stated that it would be left to Congress to negotiate over expanding protections beyond the DACA recipients.

Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.), who drafted the bipartisan immigration plan that Trump rejected last week, welcomed Trump's statement as a sign of "presidential leadership on immigration." Graham stated that the offer of a path to citizenship will help in modernizing a broken immigration system and securing strong border security measures.

The White House announcement on immigration comes as 35 senators gathered to figure out how the chamber will proceed on its immigration debate. Sens. John Cornyn (R-Tex.) and Richard J. Durbin (D-Ill.) have been asked to serve as a clearinghouse and sort out the parameters and timetable for the debate.

If lawmakers fail to agree on a spending plan by February 8, the government could shut down again. The White House encourages the Senate to bring the new immigration plan to the floor, stating that it represents a compromise that members of both parties can support.

The Hope Diamond, one of the world's most famous jewels, is currently on display at the Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History, where it has been since 1958. Despite its infamous reputation for bringing misfortune to its owners, the museum has not experienced any negative effects. The diamond's supposed curse is often attributed to the numerous tales of its owners meeting tragic ends, but many scholars believe these stories were embellished or fabricated by the diamond's various owners to increase its value.

The Hope Diamond's history can be traced back to 1653, when a French merchant named Jean Baptiste Tavernier obtained the original 115-carat blue diamond in India. The story goes that Tavernier plucked the gem from one of the eyes of a Hindu idol, but this is a myth as Tavernier returned to France and sold the gem to King Louis XIV for a significant sum before retiring to Russia and dying peacefully.

Louis XIV also escaped misfortune despite owning the diamond, which was then known as the "French Blue." However, one of Louis' descendants who inherited the stone was not so lucky. King Louis XVI and his queen, Marie Antoinette, lost their heads to the guillotine during the French Revolution, and their crown jewels, including the diamond, were stolen.

The diamond resurfaced in London two decades later and was purchased by Henry Philip Hope in 1839. The stone's "curse" skipped over Henry but came down with a vengeance on a descendant, Lord Francis Hope. After Lord Francis received his inheritance at the age of 21, he married an American showgirl named Mary Yohe and lived beyond his means, eventually declaring bankruptcy and being forced to sell the diamond. The showgirl ran off with one of his rivals and died in poverty.

The Hope diamond changed hands a few times before being purchased by American jeweler Pierre Cartier in the late 1800s. Cartier is suspected of embellishing some of the curse rumors to entice the diamond's next buyer, the glamorous Washington socialite Evalyn Walsh McLean, who became the modern poster child for the stone's curse. McLean and her husband obtained the diamond in 1912, and their lives were marked by tragedy, including the death of their young son, the suicide of their daughter, and the husband's eventual institutionalization.

The Hope diamond was eventually sold to the Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History in 1958, and the museum has thrived since its acquisition. However, the postman who delivered the diamond met with misfortune, being hit by a truck (not fatally), losing his wife and dog, and experiencing a house fire.

The Hope Diamond is worth a quarter of a billion dollars today, leading some to question whether the curse is real. The diamond's complex history and unique properties continue to fascinate scholars and the public alike. Recently, a team of researchers discovered that the Hope Diamond was likely placed on a gold background and specially cut to produce an effect reminiscent of a sun at its center during the late 17th century, when it was part of the personal collection of King Louis XIV of France. This new discovery sheds light on the diamond's history and the secrets it may still hold.

In addition to its scientific and historical significance, the Hope Diamond has also inspired a video game called "Hidden Expedition: Smithsonian Hope Diamond," which was released in December 2020. The game takes players on an adventure around the world as they try to find pieces of the Hope Diamond before a group of thieves gets to them. The game is littered with trivia and teaches players about the real Hope Diamond and its history.

In August 2010, a video surfaced that allegedly showed CBS Evening News anchor Katie Couric making a comment about the unique names of Sarah Palin's children, which some perceived as mockery. The video was from the day John McCain announced Palin as his running mate in 2008, and it appears to show Couric rehearsing news copy and recording promotional spots. The comment in question was, "Where the hell do they get these names?" in response to the names of Todd and Sarah Palin's children.

However, the context of the video suggests that Couric was likely unfamiliar with Palin at the time, and the comment might have been a genuine reaction to the unusual names. The video also shows Couric making a joke about female basketball players and making a negative comment about Palin's hometown.

Conservatives have criticized CBS for the way they framed Palin's life in their story, focusing on moose burgers, her children, and her being a former beauty queen, rather than her accomplishments as a governor. Some have suggested that this video is evidence of Couric's bias against Palin.

CBS has not disputed the authenticity of the video but has not commented on its content. The video has sparked debate about media bias and the role of news outlets in political campaigns. It remains to be seen whether Sarah Palin herself will comment on the video.

The article discusses the development and testing of a new top-secret unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV), known as the RQ-180, by Northrop Grumman. The RQ-180 is designed for intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR) missions and is believed to be currently in flight testing at the Air Force's Area 51. The aircraft is equipped with stealth technology and aerodynamic efficiency, making it suitable for operations in hostile airspace where current U.S. drones are not welcome.

The RQ-180 is the successor to the Lockheed Martin RQ-170 Sentinel, which has been in operation since 2007. The new UAV is expected to address the problem of flying in hostile airspace by incorporating improved stealth design and better aerodynamics. This will allow the Air Force to expand ISR capabilities beyond "permissive environments" such as Iraq and Afghanistan, where current drones such as the Global Hawk and Predator/Reaper operate.

Financial reports from Northrop Grumman suggest the possibility of the new airplane, and satellite images of the company's facility in Palmdale, California, and Area 51 show new hangars capable of holding aircraft with a wingspan of at least 130 feet, larger than a Boeing 737. The Air Force has declined to comment on the existence of the RQ-180.

The RQ-180 is expected to have a stealth design with greatly improved aerodynamics, translating to longer missions and greater efficiency for ISR work. Northrop Grumman has also been publicly flight testing its X-47B unmanned combat aircraft, which is aimed at combat as well as intelligence gathering, and is being developed for the Navy. The use of unmanned aircraft for spying continues to rise, but most of the work is done by slow flying aircraft such as the Global Hawk and Predators, which are far from invisible to radar and require protection from manned fighter aircraft.

On July 23, 2012, Earth narrowly avoided a catastrophic solar storm that was the strongest ever recorded, with a strength more than twice that of any solar storm in the last 150 years. The storm, which was actually two storms that combined their energy, missed Earth by a week. If it had hit, the storm would have caused widespread electrical blackouts, destroyed transformers, and damaged satellites, with an estimated economic impact of over $2 trillion. The storm was captured by NASA's STEREO-A spacecraft, and scientists are now studying the event to better understand the risks posed by extreme solar storms and to prepare for future events. The odds of a similar event occurring in the next 10 years are estimated to be 12%. The study of space weather, including solar storms, has been ongoing for at least 150 years, and solar storms pose a threat to our electrical grid, satellite systems, and modern electronics.

The Florida couple, Chris and Dana White, have expressed their intention to never set foot on a Carnival Cruise ship again after discovering a hidden recording device in their stateroom during a three-day Caribbean cruise last October. The device, which was found among TV wires and pointed at their bed, was initially dismissed by Carnival as a non-camera. However, Chris and Dana insist it was a functioning camera that was warm to the touch.

In an exclusive interview with Inside Edition, Chris recorded a Carnival employee dismantling the device. The couple is speaking out now because they feel Carnival did not handle the situation properly. Initially, a representative for the company said the device was not a camera, according to the pair.

Carnival later acknowledged a "video transmitter" was found during a full investigation by the shipboard team, but notes it "was not connected to an electrical source and not capable of recording." The company stated that the safety and security of their guests and crew is of paramount importance and measures have been taken to prevent such incidents in the future.

The device was turned over to the FBI for further inspection. Dana White felt their privacy had been invaded, stating, "I just immediately felt like we had been invaded; our privacy had been invaded."

In a separate incident, a cruise operated by Royal Caribbean International was overrun with around 1,300 men from a tobacco company who held wild parties featuring women dressed as Playboy bunnies. The cruise on the Voyager of the Seas, which left from Sydney, Australia, was inundated with men who took over the pool decks, bars, and buffets. They were also said to have brought burlesque dancers onboard, who starred in parties on deck. The men would also harass other passengers and film young girls on their mobile phones, passengers said.

Passengers were forced to take refuge as the scantily clad women danced on the decks. The workers brought “crates and crates” of their own food onto the ship, which underwent extensive refurbishments in 2014. Even bingo, a popular pastime on cruises, was canceled due to a lack of interest from the passengers, who were more interested in the cabaret.

Passengers were dismayed by their experience and felt Royal Caribbean should have notified them about the large group being onboard. Royal Caribbean issued full refunds to passengers and is currently investigating the incident to ensure it does not happen again.

A West Virginia Department of Transportation worker, Thomas Keith Henderson, was arrested on charges of driving a state snow plow while under the influence of alcohol. The incident occurred on Burke Mountain near Keystone on January 29, during a traffic stop where the deputy found Henderson's breath smelled of alcohol and his eyes were bloodshot and glassy. Henderson, a 56-year-old resident of Elkhorn, was given a field sobriety test and a breathalyzer test that registered a blood alcohol content of 0.09, exceeding the 0.04 legal limit for commercial driver's license holders. Henderson was released on a $500 bond after being arraigned on charges of DUI (CDL) and Defective Equipment.

In a significant event at the New Museum in New York, artist Nari Ward engaged in a conversation with Massimiliano Gioni, the museum's Edlis Neeson Artistic Director, on the occasion of Ward's exhibition, "We the People." Ward is renowned for his transformative sculptures that address personal memory and complex political and social issues.

Meanwhile, a controversial video titled "A Fire in My Belly, A Work in Progress," produced by the late David Wojnarowicz, has been exhibited at the New Museum after being banned from a Smithsonian museum. The video, which includes graphic content and depicts Jesus covered by insects, has sparked controversy and renewed opposition from religious groups.

Catholic League President Bill Donohue criticized the artistic community for alleged insensitivity towards Christians, comparing it to the prohibition of depictions of the Holocaust, black slavery, and Mohammed. The video was previously removed from a Smithsonian exhibit following Donohue's protests and petition for funding cuts.

However, the New Museum has defended freedom of expression and opposed censorship, with director Lisa Phillips stating that they cannot afford to take civil liberties for granted. The video is currently displayed in the museum's lobby and can be viewed free of charge. The controversy has led to requests from numerous art galleries to show the video, with some expressing concern over potential censorship.

The second most wanted man on the Simon Wiesenthal Centre's list of Nazi war criminals, Vladimir Katriuk, a Canadian resident of Ukrainian ancestry, has died at the age of 93 after a long illness. News of his death emerged just hours after the Centre for Israel and Jewish Affairs urged Ottawa to take necessary steps to ensure he be held accountable if found guilty of war crimes.

Katriuk was accused of participating in a village massacre in 1943 in what is now Belarus, and was a member of a Ukrainian battalion of the SS, the elite Nazi storm troops, between 1942 and 1944. He had denied the accusations against him.

The Russian embassy in Ottawa called on the Canadian government to support a criminal case against Katriuk, but Canada ignored the request and said it would never recognize Moscow's annexation of Crimea and its interference in Ukraine.

A study three years ago alleged Katriuk was a key participant in a village massacre during the second world war. Katriuk allegedly deserted his SS unit when it moved to France from eastern Europe in 1944. He lived in Paris before moving to Canada in 1951, and later became a Canadian citizen and lived with his French-born wife in Ontario, working as a beekeeper.

In 1999, Canada's federal court ruled Katriuk obtained Canadian citizenship under false pretenses, by not telling authorities about his collaboration with the Nazis, but could find no evidence he committed atrocities. In 2007, the Harper cabinet decided not to revoke his citizenship.

Katriuk repeatedly refused to discuss anything about himself, other than his passion for honey bees. He died peacefully after years of unwarranted harassment, according to his lawyer. The death of Katriuk may have ended the possibility of him facing justice for the alleged war crimes.

In a significant development, nearly half of the US states have backed Montana in its fight against the US Supreme Court's 2010 Citizens United decision, which lifted restrictions on corporate spending in politics. Led by New York, these states are asking the high court to preserve Montana's state-level regulations on corporate political expenditures. The states argue that local restrictions are necessary to prevent corruption, as corporate money can have a more corroding effect at a local level than on national politics.

The case stems from Montana's century-old Corrupt Practices Act, which was struck down by a Montana court following the Citizens United ruling. However, the Montana Supreme Court has since upheld the state law, putting it in conflict with the Citizens United ruling. If the Supreme Court agrees to take up the case, it is unlikely to overturn Citizens United, but it could hand down a decision that would give state legislatures greater leeway in limiting corporate money in politics.

The case has been challenged by a conservative interest group, American Tradition Partnership, which has asked the US Supreme Court to overturn the Montana ruling. The court blocked its implementation in February and is now considering whether to hear arguments in the case or simply issue a ruling reversing the Montana judgement.

Senator John McCain, who authored the campaign finance law struck down by the US Supreme Court in Citizens United, has backed the Montana action. In his brief, McCain argues that there is already evidence since the Citizens United ruling that large sums of money thrown into the political process are having a corrupting effect.

The states that have filed a brief in support of Montana are New York, Arkansas, California, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawaii, Idaho, Illinois, Iowa, Kentucky, Maryland, Massachusetts, Minnesota, Mississippi, Nevada, New Mexico, North Carolina, Rhode Island, Utah, Vermont, Washington, West Virginia, and the District of Columbia.

Minnesota Representative Michele Bachmann has requested the withdrawal of her Swiss citizenship, which she automatically received upon marrying her husband, a Swiss immigrant, in 1978. The news of her and her children's recent application for Swiss papers caused a stir, leading to Bachmann's statement clarifying her allegiance to the United States. She emphasized her American birth and her unwavering commitment to the U.S. Constitution and the United States.

The former Republican presidential candidate, known for her criticism of President Obama's "socialist" policies, had seemed an unlikely American politician to have dual citizenship with a European country ruled in part by the Social Democratic Party. The statement also mentioned that Bachmann's husband's Swiss citizenship made her eligible for dual citizenship since their marriage.

However, this contradicts earlier statements by Bachmann and her spokeswoman, Becky Rogness, who said the family had sought the citizenship. The family had recently applied for the citizenship, with some of their children wanting to exercise their eligibility for dual citizenship.

Bachmann initially tried to downplay the citizenship, calling it a "non-story" and saying the family had "just recently updated our documents." Her Democratic challenger, Jim Graves, had earlier called the news a "distraction." Graves also noted that he and his family were "proud to be Americans."

The issue of Bachmann's dual citizenship raises questions about her judgment and potential conflicts of interest, given her membership on the House Intelligence Committee. However, members of Congress are not subject to the same rules regarding "foreign preference" as federal employees and contractors seeking a formal security clearance. Nonetheless, Bachmann's statement used language that implied an attempt to talk her way out of the problem.

The NYPD has arrested Isaiah Thompson, 22, for subway surfing, a dangerous act of riding on the outside of a moving train, which was caught on video last week. This is at least the third time Thompson has been arrested for the same offense, with previous incidents occurring in March and November of 2017. The most recent incident occurred between the Clinton-Washington and Lafayette Street stations on the C line. The NYPD considers this act incredibly dangerous, disruptive, and foolish, as it can cause major delays and potentially result in death. Thompson has been charged with reckless endangerment and disorderly conduct. The NYPD could not confirm a fourth arrest in September, as reported by the NY Post. The subway surfing incident caused alarm among commuters, with one commuter, Matt Beary, capturing the video and expressing both awe and fear. New York City Transit chief Andy Byford has urged against such stunts, citing the potential for serious injury or death. Thompson could not be reached for comment. The incident serves as a reminder of the risks associated with subway surfing, and commuters are advised to wait for the next train or consider riding an MTA bus for an adrenaline rush.

Title: Wikipedia Outlink Crawl of 2016 and Physical Inactivity Among Americans

In March 2016, a comprehensive outlink crawl from Wikipedia.org was initiated, marking several years since the last such event. Notably, these files are currently not publicly accessible. The collection, unique in several aspects, was meticulously prepared to ensure completeness, as it was anticipated that the data might be shared.

One significant change implemented for this collection was the deactivation of duplicate detection. This decision was made to simplify the potential sharing of data, as linking to random collections poses a complex problem.

Another novelty was the inclusion of all different wikis, not just the English one (enwiki), as the seed list was built from all 865 collections.

In a separate development, a new survey revealed that the number of Americans leading a sedentary lifestyle reached its peak since 2007. Approximately 83 million Americans aged 6 and over, representing about 28% of the population, reported no participation in any of 104 specific physical activities throughout the previous year. This concerning trend underscores the need for increased awareness and initiatives promoting physical activity among Americans.

In a tragic incident during the Hajj pilgrimage, at least 717 people have been killed and 863 injured in a stampede near Mecca, Saudi Arabia. The incident occurred during the last major rite of the pilgrimage, known as "stoning the devil," at Mina, a valley about 5km from Mecca. The stampede is the deadliest incident to occur during the Hajj in 25 years. King Salman has ordered an urgent review of this year's Hajj plans to improve organization. The supreme leader of Iran, which lost at least 95 of its citizens in the crush, has criticized Saudi Arabia's preparedness. The incident is the second disaster to strike Mecca in two weeks, following a crane collapse at the Grand Mosque that killed 109 people.

The pilgrims travel to Mina to throw seven stones at pillars called Jamarat, which represent the devil. The stampede occurred at around 09:00 local time as pilgrims were walking towards the Jamarat Bridge. The Saudi civil defense directorate said the victims were of "different nationalities," without providing details. In addition to victims from Niger witnessed by the BBC's correspondent at the scene, Iran's state news agency, Irna, said at least 95 Iranians were among the dead, with another 150 injured. The BBC understands at least three Indonesians are among the dead.

The Saudi authorities have spent billions of dollars on improving transport and other infrastructure to try to prevent such incidents. The Hajj is the fifth and final pillar of Islam, and it is the journey that every able-bodied adult Muslim must undertake at least once in their lives if they can afford it. The number of people attending Hajj has risen from 57,000 in 1921 to a high of 3.2 million three years ago, according to the Saudi Central Department of Statistics and Information. The figure dropped to just over two million last year.

The stampede occurred when two large groups of pilgrims converged from different directions on to one street, according to Maj Gen Mansour al-Turki, a spokesman for the Saudi interior ministry. Photographs showed the bodies of dozens of pilgrims on the ground, some piled high. They were all dressed in the simple white garments worn during the Hajj.

Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Nayef, who headed an emergency meeting after the stampede, has ordered an investigation. The Saudi health minister, Khaled al-Falih, said the crush occurred because many pilgrims moved "without respecting the timetables" established by authorities. Saudi-owned al-Arabiya TV reported that the head of the central Hajj committee, Prince Khaled al-Faisal, blamed the stampede on "some pilgrims with African nationalities." However, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, Iran's supreme leader, said the Saudi government "must accept the huge responsibility for this catastrophe," adding that "mismanagement and improper actions" were to blame. The UK Foreign Office said it was urgently seeking more information about whether British nationals were involved.

Tiger Woods is accused of fathering a secret love child by adult film star and escort Devon James, according to RadarOnline.com. James, who gave birth to her son in early 2001, claims that Woods is the father, and a source familiar with the situation told RadarOnline.com that Tiger has not taken or been asked to take a paternity test. James recently disclosed her secret on the set of a forthcoming porn movie.

The allegations come just a day after reports of Tiger having a secret love child, but without naming the alleged mother. James claims to have had a two-and-a-half-year affair with Woods, during which they engaged in unprotected sex, and she became pregnant. However, it wasn't until a chance encounter with Woods, six years later, that she told him that she believed her son was his.

RadarOnline.com has found no evidence that Woods has paid James. Previously, it was reported that another alleged mistress, Theresa Rogers, had a baby while seeing Woods, but sources close to her told RadarOnline.com that Tiger is not the father.

The claims are set to be featured in a new TV documentary, Tiger Woods: The Rise and Fall, on Channel 4 this week. Journalist Neal Boulton, who helped Woods hide affairs, claims that there is more to come out, and Tiger will eventually admit to fathering a child. The allegations come as Tiger is set to play in the U.S. Open, and his wife Elin is in China with their two children, visiting her brother in Shanghai.

In the late 1980s and early 1990s, California experienced its worst measles epidemic in over a decade, with 16,400 reported cases, 3,390 hospital admissions, and 75 deaths. The majority of patients were young children, particularly infants under 12 months, and the outbreak centered in low-income Hispanic communities in southern and central California. The main cause of the epidemic was low immunization levels among preschool-aged children and young adults. The cost of medical care and outbreak control for the epidemic is estimated at $30.9 million. Unless the level of immunization in preschool-aged children is increased, similar epidemics are likely to recur.

Bill Gates, co-founder of Microsoft and the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, has become one of the most influential philanthropists in history. Through the foundation, Gates and his wife have funded various global health and development initiatives, including polio eradication and sewage-treatment plants. They have also convinced 127 other billionaires to sign their giving pledge, an oath to donate the majority of their wealth to philanthropic organizations.

In their annual letter, the Gates Foundation lays out a series of ambitious goals for the next 15 years, including cutting childhood deaths by half, eradicating polio and three other diseases, and making Africa capable of feeding itself. The letter predicts that the lives of people in poor countries will improve faster in the next 15 years than at any other time in history.

The Gates Foundation is also launching a new program called Global Citizens, aimed at educating and inspiring action among the general public. The foundation will ask its Global Citizens to push for a meaningful reboot of the UN's Millennium Development Goals and to hold their governments accountable for meeting those targets.

California health officials are urging those who have not been vaccinated against measles, including children too young to be immunized, to avoid Disney parks where the spread of the disease originated. The outbreak has spread to five U.S. states and Mexico, with 70 people infected, most of whom were not vaccinated. The California Department of Public Health reports that the vaccination exemption rate among kindergarten students in California is 3.1 percent, but there are pockets of the state where the rate jumps into the double digits.

In response to the outbreak, the Gates Foundation has announced that it will be increasing its efforts to deliver vaccines to remote areas of the world. Gates has also expressed frustration with the anti-vaccination movement, which he believes creates risk and has led to pertussis and measles deaths.

Gates also discussed his views on global inequality, climate change, and President Obama's tax proposals in a wide-ranging phone conversation with WIRED. He expressed optimism about the world's progress in the fields of health, agriculture, and poverty, but warned that climate change poses a significant challenge. Gates also expressed support for progressive tax policies and the role of philanthropy in moderating income inequality.

In conclusion, the California measles epidemic of the late 1980s and early 1990s was a significant public health crisis, particularly affecting low-income Hispanic communities in southern and central California. The main cause of the epidemic was low immunization levels among preschool-aged children and young adults. The cost of the epidemic was estimated at $30.9 million. Bill Gates and the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation have become influential philanthropists, funding various global health and development initiatives. The foundation's annual letter lays out ambitious goals for the next 15 years, including cutting childhood deaths by half and eradicating polio and three other diseases. The foundation is also launching a new program called Global Citizens, aimed at educating and inspiring action among the general public. The California measles outbreak has highlighted the importance of vaccination and the dangers of the anti-vaccination movement. Gates has expressed support for progressive tax policies and the role of philanthropy in moderating income inequality.

The Republican presidential race is narrowing down to three candidates, with Speaker Paul Ryan being a potential dark horse candidate for the nomination. Despite RNC Chairman Reince Priebus stating that it's highly unlikely for a non-candidate to become the nominee, some top Republican insiders are still pushing for Ryan to be the nominee. Ryan has repeatedly stated that he does not want to run for president, but his past actions suggest that he may be open to the idea if offered the position.

Meanwhile, the government is in a state of crisis, with a government shutdown entering its 27th day, TSA employees working without pay, and Speaker Nancy Pelosi rescinding her invitation for President Trump to deliver the State of the Union address from the Capitol. The shutdown shows no signs of ending, with both parties dug in and ratings agencies and economic forecasters warning of severe consequences.

In other news, former House Speaker John Boehner has been replaced by Steve King of Iowa, who was admonished by his leadership for voicing support for white supremacy. Pelosi and Trump are in open war with each other, with Pelosi privately referring to Trump as the 'whiner in chief' and questioning his manhood.

In the world of media, David Haskell has been named the new editor in chief of New York magazine. The magazine will cover topics such as fashion, food, shopping, and politics.

Finally, tariffs imposed by the government are having a negative impact on Main Street retailers across the country, according to the National Retail Federation. Scroll down to learn more.

On July 19, 2018, a tourist boat carrying passengers capsized and sank on Table Rock Lake in Branson, Missouri during a thunderstorm. The accident resulted in at least 17 fatalities, including children, and seven injuries. Four people remain missing. The National Transportation Safety Board is investigating the incident. The boat, operated by Ride the Ducks Branson, was on a regular tour around the lake when the storm hit. The company, owned by Ripley Entertainment, has been operating in Branson for over 40 years and is a popular tourist attraction. The boat was updated with modern safety equipment, but it is unclear whether the operator received a severe thunderstorm warning before the storm. The incident is the latest in a series of fatal accidents involving duck boats, which are amphibious vehicles used for sightseeing tours. Critics argue that the boats have varying safety requirements due to numerous agencies regulating them. Duck boats were originally used by the U.S. military in World War II to transport troops and supplies.

Two men, Kenneth Burke (46) and Timothy Foote (38), from Ocean Township and Asbury Park, respectively, are facing burglary charges after allegedly using a taxi to rob a house in Deal, New Jersey, on November 4. According to the Deal Police Department, the men called for a taxi to a house on Norwood Avenue and asked the driver to wait outside while they burglarized the house. Upon their return, they took a TV and liquor bottles and refused to pay the fare when the driver took them to an apartment in Asbury Park. The driver reported the unpaid fare and suspicious activity to the Asbury Park Police Department, leading to the men's arrest. The stolen items were returned to the homeowner, and the men are being held in the Monmouth County jail on $20,000 bail each. Their court dates are pending.

In Virginia Beach, a tractor-trailer driver named Joseph Chen, aged 47, from Greenville, North Carolina, died after his vehicle went over the Chesapeake Bay Bridge-Tunnel (CBBT) on Thursday afternoon. The accident occurred at mile marker 15 around 12:30 p.m. on the southbound side. The driver was hauling seafood for Evans Transports and was rescued by a Navy crew before being taken to the hospital, where he later succumbed to his injuries.

The Medical Examiner’s Office ruled Chen's death as accidental, caused by drowning and hypothermia. Chen was a father, husband, and the founder and president of Turn-N-Burn Motorcycle Club.

The CBBT was closed for a short period due to the incident, and a Level 2 wind restriction was in effect, requiring tractor-trailers to have a gross payload of 30,000 pounds or more. The accident occurred during a windy day, with the water temperature at 45 degrees and wave height between five and seven feet.

The Virginia Trucking Association expressed their condolences to the victim's family, friends, and colleagues. This was not the first incident of a tractor-trailer going overboard on the CBBT; previous accidents occurred in May 2014 and January 2016. Stay with WAVY.com for updates on this developing news.

On June 11, 2014, taxi drivers across Europe staged mass protests against Uber Technologies Inc., a San Francisco-based car-sharing service that has been causing controversy among cabbies in the U.S. and Europe. The demonstrations took place in cities including London, Madrid, Berlin, and Paris, with more than 30,000 taxi and limo drivers participating.

The protests were sparked by the smartphone application's threat to the livelihoods of traditional taxi drivers, as it allows customers to order rides from drivers who don't need licenses that can cost up to 200,000 euros ($270,000) each. In London, black-cab drivers were joined by private car services and trainees to protest what they saw as the government's failure to hold Uber to the same standards as other car services and taxis.

The biggest city-center protest was in London, where traffic was disrupted as thousands of black cabs and private hire cars descended on tourist hubs such as Trafalgar Square and Parliament Square. Drivers in Paris blocked the Charles de Gaulle and Orly airports, preventing private-car services from picking up passengers, and slowed down traffic on the A1 highway that circles Paris, leading to a 200-kilometer (120-mile) jam.

Uber took the demonstrations as an opportunity to promote its service, saying in a statement that its teams across Europe would keep the cities moving. The company also opened its service in London to black-cab drivers, describing its 5 percent commission as the lowest of all booking systems in the city.

The protests have a deeper significance beyond the taxi industry, as they underscore the growing backlash against technology companies such as Airbnb Inc. and Aereo Inc. that are clashing with traditional industries and arguing that they should be subject to the same regulations.

Uber raised $1.2 billion in new financing last week, valuing the company at about $17 billion. The company had earlier raised $307.5 million from investors including Google Ventures, TPG Capital, and Menlo Ventures. However, finance professor Aswath Damodaran wrote on his blog this week that the company's assets may be worth just $5.9 billion, based on optimistic assumptions about the taxi industry's growth and Uber's market share and profitability.

Uber's CEO, Travis Kalanick, has pushed the company into 37 countries and says the low prices and ease of use that their drivers can offer will lead to a base of support from consumers that regulators won't be able to ignore. A typical journey from Finsbury Square, near London's financial district, and Paddington Station takes between 20 and 30 minutes by car to travel approximately four miles. Uber estimates that that journey would cost between 14 pounds ($24) and 16 pounds, while London's transportation authority estimates that the trip could cost between 15 pounds and 22 pounds.

Uber says it is responsible for 20,000 new jobs per month, and the median income for drivers using the UberX platform, Uber's low-cost service, is $90,000 per year in New York and more than $74,000 in San Francisco. The company advertises itself to prospective drivers as a way to start your own business, drawing users who aren't professional chauffeurs. That's different from apps such as Hailo, which recruit from the industry. Uber customers can tap the app on their smartphone and see the locations of taxis in real time, pay via a stored credit card, and rate their driver.

The protests in Europe highlight the challenges for Uber's expansion, as well as the tensions between technological innovation and traditional industries. European cities have tended to regulate taxi drivers more than the U.S., and regulators and courts are struggling with the disconnect between the desire to protect a regulated industry and the need for more technological innovation.

The study published in the Journal of Applied Ecology has raised concerns about the potential extinction of at least one species of Darwin's finches in the Galápagos Islands. The medium ground finch (Geospitza fortis) is threatened by the parasitic nest fly Philornis downsi, which lays its eggs in bird nests, causing significant harm to the finch's reproductive success.

Researchers used five years of field data to predict the species' long-term viability and found that, in two out of three scenarios, medium ground finches could be gone within the next century. The study focused on the medium ground finches, which are the most abundant and have the most accessible nests, but the problem likely extends to other species of Darwin's finches.

The researchers manipulated the parasite load in actual nests, creating a control group of nests that were sprayed with plain water, while a second set of nests was sprayed with permethrin, an insecticide that is also used to kill mosquitoes, lice, and ticks. The use of treated and untreated nests allowed the team to determine the direct effects of the flies on the birds. They then used that data in models of good, bad, and neutral years for the birds' reproduction and ultimate survival.

The team predicts that if the finches were to run into a series of bad reproductive years in which extreme weather cuts off their food supply, they'd go extinct in about 50 years. A model weighted toward neutral years indicates they'd be extinct within about 80 years. Unsurprisingly, a run of good reproductive luck would spell longer survival for the species: about 100 years. Reducing the number of flies could help the birds hold on even longer, or even prevent them from going extinct at all.

The study highlights the importance of the Galápagos Islands to biologists, as it is home to an intact native population of birds, including Darwin's finches, which are prized as one of the best examples of speciation. If any species of Darwin's finches were to go extinct, it would be a disaster not just for biodiversity, but for researchers who see the finches as an example of real-time evolution due to their rapid adaptations.

Luckily, there are ways that the finches could beat both P. downsi and time. The team estimates that if nest fly infestations were reduced by just 40 percent, the birds won't go extinct. Scientists are batting around ideas such as flooding the island with sterile male flies or allowing birds to fumigate their own nests with permethrin.

In a separate study, researchers have discovered that eggs of various bird species often match the color and pattern of their environment, providing camouflage against predators. The study, published in Current Biology, supports a centuries-old theory that shell variation, at least for some birds, helps to camouflage eggs. The masters of egg disguise turn out to be Japanese quail, whose mother quails somehow learn the patterning of their own eggs and choose laying spots to hide them best. The ground-nesting birds often perfectly match the eggs to substrate, helping to prevent the precious contents from being some hungry predator's dinner.

A video of a newborn Scottish Highland calf named Diego, born during a snowstorm at Yankee Farmer's Market in Warner, New Hampshire, has gone viral on Facebook, attracting both positive and negative attention. The video, which has garnered over 12 million views and 138,000 shares since Thursday, shows Diego being warmed with a hair dryer after his birth. While some have expressed love for the adorable calf, others have criticized the farm for potentially slaughtering the animal. The farm owner, Brian Farmer, has defended his practices, stating that the calf was returned to his mother shortly after the video was taken and that the farm raises its animals ethically, with most roaming and eating freely in pastures and raised without antibiotics or hormones. The farm has faced negative reviews on Facebook, with some offering to adopt Diego to save him from his fate. Despite the controversy, Farmer plans to continue posting about his animals to educate the public on their living conditions. Diego is the heir to one of the first herds of Scottish Highlanders ever raised in the country, and his thick neck, strong body, and gentle disposition make him a good candidate for breeding stock.

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) issued a safety alert for Philips Lifeline's Personal Help Button, a neck-worn emergency response device, due to a potential choking hazard. The FDA is aware of at least six reports, including three deaths in the U.S. and one in Canada, from choking incidents caused by the device's cord becoming entangled with other objects. The device is primarily used by seniors living independently, and over 750,000 users in the U.S. and Canada are affected.

Philips Lifeline has sent letters to its customers and changed the product's labeling to include a warning against the potential choking hazard. The FDA recommends that users consult their healthcare providers to determine the most beneficial emergency button style, including wrist-worn devices, to minimize risks.

In a related incident, an 86-year-old woman from New Cumberland, Pennsylvania, died after her medical alert necklace caught on her walker and strangled her. The lanyard, which apparently lacked a breakaway feature, caused her upper torso to be suspended above the floor level, cutting off air and blood flow. The death was ruled accidental.

The FDA emphasizes that these widely used devices provide critical emergency care access for those at risk of falls or medical emergencies. While the number of adverse events is small compared to the number of users, the severity of these events is a concern. Users and their healthcare providers should assess the options provided by each style of button and choose the one that best fits their condition.

Healthcare professionals and users can report serious adverse events or product quality problems with the use of these devices to the FDA's MedWatch Adverse Event Reporting program.

The small secluded village of Kuşköy, located on the Black Sea coast of Turkey, is unique due to its distinctive language known as "bird language" or kuşköy dili. This whistled language, which adapts standard Turkish syllables into piercing tones, has been the subject of interest for linguists and researchers for decades.

Recently, Turkish-born German biopsychologist Onur Güntürkün conducted a study in Kuşköy to understand how the brain processes a language that is more akin to music than traditional speech. His study, published in Current Biology, suggests that both hemispheres of the brain play significant roles in the early stages of comprehension for whistled Turkish, challenging the assumption that the left hemisphere plays a dominant role in language understanding.

Whistled languages, although rare, have been documented in various parts of the world, including the Atlas Mountains, the highlands of northern Laos, and the Brazilian Amazon. They are often used in areas with steep terrain or dense forests where it might be hard to communicate at a distance.

However, the use of whistled Turkish in daily life is rapidly declining in Kuşköy. Once a common method of communication among children, women, and men, it is now mainly used by older generations and is increasingly being replaced by texting for privacy. Despite this, the villagers still use whistled Turkish when communicating with Güntürkün, who is based in Germany, demonstrating its continued utility in certain contexts.

Güntürkün's findings could have implications for people with stroke-damaged speech, as they suggest that some individuals might learn to communicate using a whistled dialect. However, the opportunity to study and preserve whistled Turkish is dwindling, making it a valuable and unique linguistic phenomenon that is worth preserving.

Dominique Strauss-Kahn, the former head of the International Monetary Fund, is currently on suicide watch at New York City's Rikers Island jail complex. He was transferred there after being charged with attempted rape, sex abuse, and other related offenses following an incident at a Manhattan hotel. Due to his stature and potential suicide risk, Strauss-Kahn is being housed in a wing that normally accommodates inmates with contagious diseases. He is being monitored 24 hours a day, has a medical device to prevent sleep apnea, and is being checked every 15 to 30 minutes as a precaution. Despite the special measures, Strauss-Kahn is allowed to leave his cell for recreation and court appearances. His lawyer maintains his innocence, and the maid involved in the incident is reportedly in hiding. Strauss-Kahn's arrest has raised questions about his political future in France, where he was considered a strong contender for the Socialist party's presidential nomination.

The study, titled "Estimating the Reproducibility of Psychological Science," conducted by a large collaborative research project, aimed to replicate 100 studies published in major psychology journals. The findings revealed that only 39 of the studies' results could be replicated, raising concerns about the reproducibility of psychological research. The study's authors suggest that this issue is more about the difficulty of designing a reproducible study rather than the accuracy of the studies themselves.

The study's results underscore the importance of reproducibility in science, as it allows scientists to confirm the effects of their research. The National Institutes of Health has already announced initiatives to address these concerns, but there are still no widely established reproducibility guidelines.

The study also found that of the 39 studies that were replicated, 83% had smaller effects than initially reported, with the drop in effect size usually around 50%. The researchers identified three possible reasons for the discrepancies: the original result may not have been real, the researchers may have failed to detect a real effect during the reproduction, or both studies may have been accurate but with differing methodologies.

The researchers emphasize that this is not a failure of science but a demonstration of its self-correcting nature. They suggest that the focus on novelty in research and the desire for publication may encourage the publication of results that are less reproducible. To move toward more repeatable studies, researchers and journals need to shift their interests away from novelty.

The study also highlights the issue of how exact a replication should be, especially when moving from one location to another. The researchers hope that the establishment of replication standards will help answer this question and lead to a clearer view of each finding's accuracy.

In conclusion, the study reveals that a significant portion of psychological research findings may not be reproducible. The researchers emphasize the importance of reproducibility in science and suggest that a shift in focus away from novelty is necessary to move toward more repeatable studies. The study also highlights the need for replication standards to help ensure the accuracy of scientific findings.

Santa Ono, the President of the University of Cincinnati (UC), revealed over the weekend that he had attempted suicide twice in his youth. In an interview with The Enquirer, Ono, 53, said he wanted to erase the stigma attached to mental illnesses and send the message that depression is treatable. Ono recovered from depression and being suicidal, and he credited medication, professional help, and support from others for his recovery.

In the immediate aftermath of UC student Brogan Dulle’s May 2014 death by suicide, Ono was instrumental in finding resources for UC to provide any student with five free sessions of mental health counseling. Ono attended an Indian Hill fundraiser for a group called 1N5, named for the statistic that one in five people will suffer from mental illness, and told about 200 people about his suicide attempts. The event raised more than $115,000.

After the event, Ono took to social media and told his more than 70,000 followers on Twitter about his suicide attempts. He said he wanted to get the message out to a broader audience. Dr. Phil Diller, who oversees the University Health Service in his role as chairman of UC’s department of family and community medicine, said Ono’s revelation did not surprise him. More than a year ago, Ono met with Diller and other mental health care providers at UC following Dulle’s death.

College students are particularly vulnerable to depression and suicide, with 174 Ohioans between 15 and 24 dying by suicide in 2012, and more than 100,000 college students nationwide attempting suicide in 2012. Ono said he has been passionate about suicide prevention since his research into mental illness during his time at Emory University. He said he is inspired by the empathy and awareness of his students and believes they are motivated to do something about mental health issues.

Ono is the son of a noted mathematician who emigrated from Japan after World War II and held research posts in Princeton, New Jersey, and at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore. Ono, an accomplished cellist as well as a college administrator, became UC president in 2012. Ono said he did research into mental illness during his time at Emory University under his mentor, Earl Lewis, now president of the Andrew W. Mellon Foundation. They focused on the high suicide rates among Korean students who felt extreme shame in failure.

Twitter responded warmly to Ono’s revelations, with many people thanking him for speaking out. Resources for mental health services are available at the University of Cincinnati Counseling & Psychological Services, the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline, Crisis Text Line, Hamilton County Mental Health and Recovery Services Board, Lindner Center of HOPE, Active Minds, and other organizations. Ono said he hopes his story will encourage legislators to support more programs for mental health.

The control of Virginia's House of Delegates is in limbo after a three-judge panel declined to certify the recount of a key House race, leaving it tied between Democrat Shelly Simonds and Republican Del. David Yancey. The judges ruled that a questionable ballot should be counted in favor of Yancey, tying the race at 11,608 votes each. The ballot in question contained a mark for Simonds as well as a mark to strike out her name, and the voter had also selected every other Republican on the ballot. The fate of the chamber will be determined by a lottery, scheduled for Dec. 27, where names will be placed in film canisters and drawn from a glass bowl. The turnaround shocked Democrats, who had celebrated their unlikely rise to power in the House of Delegates, and the House Democratic Caucus vowed to fight the judges' decision. Republicans, who had conceded the recount and pledged to share power with Democrats, issued a new statement after Wednesday's turn of events. The recount is just one of several taking place this week, with at least one other race likely to reshuffle politics in Richmond. The House Democrats were meeting to elect their own leadership for the coming General Assembly session, but held off on voting for speaker due to the uncertainty in the Simonds-Yancey race and in District 28.

In a concert by superstar DJ Avicii at the TD Garden in Boston on Wednesday night, dozens of concertgoers, mostly young adults, were hospitalized due to issues related to dehydration, drugs, and alcohol. The Massachusetts General Hospital received 13 patients between the ages of 16 and 19, and Boston EMS reported that most of the patients they saw were between the ages of 16 and 25, with no serious injuries.

The incident was a result of heavy alcohol consumption and drug use, which is common at such concerts, according to Boston EMS Deputy Superintendent Michael Bosse. Boston Police issued citations for intoxicated patrons and patrons consuming drugs on the premises, and three men were arrested near the TD Garden on drug charges.

Concert promoter Live Nation stated that most of the people taken to the hospital were stopped before entering the concert. Avicii, who became an international star as a DJ and producer in electronic dance, expressed concern for those affected and their families via a tweet.

Officials are taking the incident seriously, with Commissioner Evans and Mayor Walsh planning to meet with TD Garden officials next week to discuss the incidents. TD Garden has been cited several times in the past few years for various issues, but the number is not unusual for an entertainment venue of any size. The TD Garden has implemented increased precautions such as restricted alcohol sales, additional security, and provided two cooling off areas for guests.

Burger King is testing a new menu item called the Whopperito, a hybrid of their iconic Whopper and a burrito. The Whopperito consists of flame-grilled beef, American cheese, tomatoes, lettuce, mayo, ketchup, pickles, and white onions wrapped in a tortilla. The test is currently being conducted in several Burger King locations in Pennsylvania. The creation of the Whopperito has sparked mixed reactions on social media, with some expressing excitement and others voicing disapproval. It remains unclear if the Whopperito will be released in other cities or states. The combination of a Whopper and a burrito is not a new concept, as some have previously created their own version by combining ingredients from both Burger King and Taco Bell.

The Chinese Foreign Ministry has urged the United States to prevent a Taiwanese delegation from attending President-elect Donald Trump's inauguration, citing concerns about potential interference in China-US relations. The delegation, led by former Taiwan premier Yu Shyi-kun, includes a Taiwan national security adviser and some lawmakers. This is a new point of contention between China and the incoming Trump administration, as Trump has broken with decades of precedent by taking a congratulatory call from Taiwan President Tsai Ing-wen and has stated that the "One China" policy is up for negotiation, a position Beijing strongly rejects. China considers Taiwan a breakaway province and opposes any diplomatic relations with other countries. The delegation plans to hold talks with politicians, academics, and overseas Chinese community representatives in addition to attending the inauguration. Tensions between China and Taiwan have risen since Tsai's election last year, with Beijing cutting off contacts and working to deepen Taiwan's diplomatic isolation. The U.S. has no formal relations with Taiwan but maintains robust informal ties, selling Taiwan arms and regarding any threat to the island as a matter of grave concern. The Trump administration has not yet responded to China's request.

The President of Palau, Tommy Remengesau, has proposed a new law to attract high-end tourists and reduce the number of visitors by allowing only five-star hotels to operate on the islands. This move aims to shift the focus from quantity to quality tourism, encouraging wealthy travelers who spend more, thereby generating more tax revenue.

The proposal is part of a strategy to address concerns about the impact of mass tourism on the islands, including damage to coral reefs, overcrowding, and wildlife disturbance. Chinese tourists, who visit on package holidays and spend little locally, have been particularly problematic. In 2015, the Palau government halved the number of charter flights from China, which seemed to increase tourist spending.

Palau, known for its pristine beaches, world-class scuba diving, and forest-covered volcanic islands, relies heavily on tourism for 85% of its GDP. The new law encourages high-end hotels that would be responsible for their own water treatment systems, power backups, and infrastructure development, with tax breaks and exemptions as rewards.

The exact locations for the new five-star resorts are yet to be determined, but with 500 islands, there is no shortage of potential sites. However, the sustainability and harmony with Palau's natural assets of these future resorts remain uncertain.

In a 6-2 decision, the Supreme Court upheld the federal law that prohibits individuals convicted of domestic violence from owning guns. The ruling maintains that the law applies to both intentional and reckless acts of abuse, overturning arguments from two Maine men who pleaded guilty to hitting their partners. The men argued that their misdemeanor convictions should not disqualify them from gun ownership. The decision was supported by advocates for domestic abuse victims, who asserted that the law should cover all forms of abuse. Gun rights groups, on the other hand, contended that the men's constitutional right to bear arms should not be infringed upon due to misdemeanor abuse convictions. The case was previously ruled against by a federal appeals court.

Boko Haram, a militant group in Nigeria, has been linked to the abduction of over 200 schoolgirls in April and several other recent attacks, including an assault on villages near Chibok that killed at least 40 people and a bomb attack on a shopping district in Abuja. The group has demanded the release of imprisoned militants in exchange for the kidnapped girls. The military has raided a Boko Haram intelligence unit and arrested its leader, Babuji Ya'ari, who is accused of being involved in the abduction and coordinating deadly attacks in Maidugiri since 2011. The group, founded in 2002, is known for opposing Western education and has launched military operations since 2009 to create an Islamic state. Thousands have been killed, mostly in north-eastern Nigeria, and over three million people have been affected. The US declared Boko Haram a terrorist group in 2013. The military's claims could not be independently verified, and the group has not yet commented on the allegations. The government says it knows where the abductees are, but a rescue could lead to the girls being killed. The military's slow response to the abductions and failure to swiftly rescue the girls has been criticized, and negotiations appear stalled.

The International Association of Athletics Federations (IAAF) has barred Russia's track and field team from competing in the upcoming Rio Olympics due to a widespread doping conspiracy. This historic decision, made in a unanimous vote, is unprecedented in Olympics history and will prevent Russia from competing as a team. However, individual athletes may still have a chance to compete as neutrals if they can demonstrate that they have been subject to effective anti-doping systems and have not been tainted by the Russian system.

The IAAF's decision comes after a World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) independent commission report in November concluded that Russia was running a state-sponsored doping program in athletics. Despite significant progress in some areas, the IAAF task force monitoring the verification process found that Russia has not sufficiently addressed the deep-seated culture of tolerance or worse for doping in its athletics program.

Russia won 18 medals in track and field, including eight golds, at the last Summer Olympics. However, when the Rio Games begin on August 5, no track and field athletes will compete under the Russian flag. This punishment is more severe than the one faced by East Germany, which conducted a notorious doping scheme throughout the 1960s, '70s, and '80s.

The IAAF's decision is already facing challenges, with pole vaulter Yelena Isinbayeva, a two-time Olympic gold medalist, announcing that she will file a discrimination case in the court for human rights. The Russian Ministry of Sport has also appealed to the International Olympic Committee (IOC), which is holding a summit on Tuesday to discuss the issue.

In a news conference announcing the IAAF decision, Rune Andersen, chair of the IAAF task force, said that efforts to test athletes in Russia have encountered serious obstacles. Additionally, RusAF is unable to enforce all doping bans, and the Russian Anti-Doping Agency is 18-24 months away from compliance with the WADA code.

The IAAF council accepted the following recommendations from its task force monitoring the verification process:

* That Russia's track and field federation not be reinstated.
* That the council pass a rule amendment allowing individual athletes who can "clearly and convincingly" show they have been subject to effective anti-doping systems and have not been tainted by the Russian system be able to apply to compete in international competitions as a neutral athlete.
* That athletes who have made "an extraordinary contribution to the fight against doping" be able to apply for that exception, particularly that the case of whistleblower Yuliya Stepanova be viewed favorably.
* That no RusAF officials, athletes, or support personnel take part in international competition or IAAF affairs.

Andersen made clear that the exception for athletes would be narrow, saying the task force was advised by legal counsel to head off legal challenges that could come to the Court of Arbitration for Sport. "The crack in the door, or the opening to apply for this is quite narrow," Andersen said, "so there won't be many athletes that will manage to get through the crack of that door because it's clearly, they have to demonstrate that they have been subject to a credible anti-doping control system and that they are not tainted by the system in Russia."

The culture of doping in Russia is deeply entrenched, according to the IAAF task force's report. Despite improvements such as replacing the entire council, barring athletes with serious anti-doping rules violations from being considered for Olympic team selection, and teaching anti-doping classes in schools, the federation has fallen short of several other criteria. In interviews with the task force, Isinbayeva and Yuriy Burzakovskiy, the head coach of the Russian national team, acknowledged that they have not read the independent commission report, although both have made public statements dismissing its contents.

The IAAF's decision is a significant step towards protecting clean athletes and ensuring the integrity of international competition. However, it is likely to face challenges, particularly from Russian athletes and officials who feel they have been unfairly targeted.

The article discusses the potential military intervention in Syria by the United States and its allies, with a focus on President Obama's decision to bomb Syria and the calls for him to seek authorization from Congress. The article argues that going to Congress is necessary for several reasons, including the need for deliberation, accountability, and the establishment of clear objectives for the military action.

The article notes that Britain's Prime Minister David Cameron has called for a vote in Parliament, and a draft resolution has been submitted to the United Nations Security Council to authorize military action in Syria. However, it is expected that the resolution will fail due to the veto of Russia and China.

In the United States, a letter has been signed by 114 members of Congress, led by Scott Rigell, a Virginia Republican, urging Obama to reconvene Congress and seek authorization for any attack. The article suggests that Obama could do so if he wanted to, and it is argued that not doing so would be a mistake.

The article also discusses the potential risks and disadvantages of military intervention in Syria, including the possibility of escalation, civilian casualties, and the creation of a civil war in a broken country. It is noted that Obama's policy towards Syria has failed, and a tougher approach is needed.

The article concludes by stating that the Administration needs Congress, and it needs deliberation, as it needs to be interrogated sharply about the objectives and consequences of military action in Syria. It is suggested that the Administration should consider non-military options, such as providing humanitarian aid and diplomatic efforts to bring about a negotiated settlement.

Overall, the article argues that Obama should seek authorization from Congress before bombing Syria, as going to Congress is necessary for accountability, deliberation, and the establishment of clear objectives for the military action. It also discusses the potential risks and disadvantages of military intervention in Syria and suggests that the Administration should consider non-military options to bring about a negotiated settlement.

The article discusses two separate events related to the song "Hail Mary" by Tupac Shakur. The first part focuses on the song from the Makaveli album, which was recorded in 1996 and features verses by the Outlawz. The song is described as a spiritual and chilling piece, with Tupac expressing his thoughts on violence and seeking a conversation with his spiritual mother. The music video depicts Tupac rising from the dead to answer the prayers of a wrongfully convicted prisoner.

The second part of the article reports an incident that occurred in Sri Lanka in 2016, where churchgoers at a Christmas carol service received booklets containing the lyrics to Tupac's Hail Mary instead of the traditional Christian prayer. The lyrics, which include profanity and references to violence, shocked and amused many attendees. The incident was widely shared on social media, and no explanation was given by the organizers.

Both versions of Hail Mary ask Mary, the mother of Jesus, to intercede on behalf of sinners, though Tupac's version is more explicit in detailing the sins in question. The article concludes with a quote from Andrew Choksy, who attended the service in Sri Lanka, expressing his surprise and amusement at the incident.

On December 22, 2017, a barber named Khaled A. Shabani, aged 46, was arrested at Ruby's Salon in Madison, Wisconsin, for allegedly inflicting harm on a 22-year-old customer during a haircut. The customer had requested a specific haircut, but Shabani reportedly became angry due to the customer's movements during the service.

According to police spokesman Joel Despain, Shabani allegedly retaliated by shaving the customer's head down the middle and snipping his ear with scissors, causing bleeding. The victim left the salon and called the police upon returning home. Shabani was arrested on suspicion of mayhem and disorderly conduct while armed.

Despain clarified that while giving a bad haircut is not a crime, intentionally snipping a customer's ear with scissors is. On Wednesday, Shabani pleaded not guilty to disorderly conduct, a violation of a county ordinance, not a criminal charge. The Madison Police Department had no further information when reached by BuzzFeed News.

Trevor Story, the Colorado Rockies' shortstop, made history on April 8th, 2016, by homering in each of his first four games in the team's home opener against the San Diego Padres. This feat, according to Elias Sports Bureau, made him the first player in 100 years to achieve this milestone. He is also the fifth player since 1900 to homer in each of his team's first four games in a season, joining Chris Davis (Orioles, 2013), Nelson Cruz (Rangers, 2011), Mark McGwire (Cardinals, 1998), and Willie Mays (Giants, 1971).

After hitting home runs in the fourth and ninth innings, Story now has six home runs and 11 RBI in his first 19 major-league at-bats. His impressive performance has not been limited to Coors Field, as he belted his first four home runs in the Rockies' season-opening series at Arizona.

Rockies manager Walt Weiss described Story's performance as "legendary," while slugger Carlos Gonzalez praised him as fearless and playing like a Hall of Famer. Story's historic start has earned him a place in the National Baseball Hall of Fame, with his helmet and batting gloves already on display.

The Padres, who were the first team in big league history to be shut out in their first three games, broke loose in this game. Despite Story's impressive performance, the Padres won 13-6. Even the Padres acknowledged Story's talent, with outfielder Matt Kemp commenting on his great swing and impressive feat of hitting six homers in four games.

Rockies owner Dick Monfort commented on the ongoing suspension of shortstop Jose Reyes, stating that if Reyes "did something wrong, he should pay for it." Reyes was suspended with pay under the sport's new domestic abuse policy just before the start of spring training for an alleged incident with his wife at a Maui resort hotel on Oct. 31. Monfort expressed uncertainty about the potential impact of the suspension on the team's public relations and fan base.

The Internet Archive, on behalf of the National Library of New Zealand, has conducted crawls of data that is currently not publicly accessible. Meanwhile, the political landscape in the United States is shifting as Donald Trump's Republican primary win in South Carolina solidifies his status as a serious contender for the White House.
