In response to this, a humorous parody video titled "Winter is Trumping" has emerged, combining footage and speech audio of Trump with key scenes from Game of Thrones. The video depicts Trump negotiating with Littlefinger, facing off against Daenerys Targaryen, and preparing for battle with Tyrion Lannister, among other scenarios. The video's creators have imaginatively placed Trump in the ruthless world of Game of Thrones, albeit in a somewhat harsh comparison to the show's characters. David Mack, a deputy director of breaking news for BuzzFeed News, reported on this development.

A large military convoy believed to be led by Tuareg rebel leader Rissa ag Boula, who is allegedly a supporter of Libya's former dictator Moammar Gadhafi, has entered the city of Agadez, Niger. The convoy, consisting of more than a dozen pickup trucks with well-armed Libyan troops, reportedly came from the direction of Arlit. The convoy's arrival has sparked speculation about the presence of Gadhafi or his family members, but it is not yet confirmed. Meanwhile, negotiations are ongoing between tribal elders and Gadhafi loyalists holed up in the Libyan town of Bani Walid, as rebel forces try to persuade them to surrender. Gadhafi's regime is believed to have financed the Tuareg rebellion in Niger, making the country one of the last to recognize the rebels that ousted Gadhafi. The convoy's arrival in Agadez has raised concerns about the ongoing conflict and the potential for further instability in the region.

Jonathan Trappe, a balloonist, was rescued on Friday after attempting to cross the Atlantic Ocean in a boat suspended by over 300 helium-filled balloons. He left Caribou, Maine, on Thursday and was forced to land in a remote area on Newfoundland's west coast due to insufficient ballast. Trappe contacted his crew via satellite message to assure them of his safety and that there was no emergency. He had intended to become the first person to fly across the Atlantic using only cluster balloons. Trappe, known for his adventurous use of balloons, including flying a house, like in the Disney-Pixar animated film Up, landed in an inaccessible area south of Lark Harbour. Residents tried to reach him on ATVs, but with no success due to the impassable terrain. Trappe expressed his gratitude to the media and said the journey was about the adventure, not the destination. He wrote on Facebook, "Hmm, this doesn't look like France," indicating he hadn't reached his European destination. Trappe's rescue was facilitated by a helicopter chartered by CBC for an aerial survey of the area.

The hiring of Jason Van Dyke, a white Chicago police officer charged with murder for shooting a black teenager in 2014, by the Fraternal Order of Police (FOP) has sparked outrage and promises of protests. Van Dyke, who is currently stripped of his police powers and on unpaid status, has been hired as a janitor and "jack-of-all-trades" at the FOP hall in the West Loop, making $12 an hour. The FOP stated that they made the decision to "assist the Van Dyke family" due to the notoriety of the incident, threats of harm, and other issues that caused him to become unemployable. The union president, Dean Angelo, defended the decision, stating that it is not unprecedented and that the union would do the same for any CPD officer in a difficult financial situation. The move has drawn quick criticism, with activists planning demonstrations outside the FOP and Father Michael Pfleger blasting the move on Facebook. Protests are expected on Thursday.

The Internet Archive is working on a project to archive web pages as they are created and preserve links to archived versions of pages that are later changed or removed. This is part of an effort to fix broken links on the web. The project, called "No More 404," is currently being tested on supported websites.

In a separate news item, Oliver Stone's documentary "The Putin Interviews" features the filmmaker and Russian President Vladimir Putin watching Stanley Kubrick's 1964 film "Dr. Strangelove" together. Stone gifted Putin a DVD of the film, but the Russian leader joked that it was a typical American gift as the DVD case was empty.

"The Putin Interviews" is a four-part series that offers "unparalleled access to the most controversial man in the world" and presents Putin's perspective on various issues. However, the documentary has been criticized for spouting Kremlin propaganda and falling back on American clichés about Russia. Some have criticized Stone for not challenging Putin and for ceding him the floor to spin his own narrative.

In the documentary, Putin discusses topics such as his rise to power, his hesitancy to delegate, and his views on the United States. He also denies that Russia was the aggressor in various global conflicts and champions Russia's economy over that of the U.S. Stone asks Putin questions such as whether gays can serve in the military in Russia and whether the U.S. provided technical support to the Chechens during the Second Chechen War.

Overall, "The Putin Interviews" has been criticized for humanizing Putin and demonizing America, and for failing to challenge Putin on important issues. Some have also criticized Stone for his past associations with dictators such as Fidel Castro and Hugo Chavez.

The Clarion nightsnake, a species that was believed to be extinct for nearly 80 years, has been rediscovered on a remote Mexican island. The snake was first spotted by American naturalist William Beebe in 1936, but subsequent attempts to find more nightsnakes on Clarion Island were unsuccessful. The existing dead sample was assumed to be a labelling error and the snake was largely struck from taxonomic registries.

However, Daniel Mulcahy, a researcher for the National Museum of Natural History in Washington, suspected the snake might still exist. He and Juan Martinez Gomez of Mexico's Ecology Institute set out to find it, using Beebe's original field notes as a guide. One of Martinez Gomez's graduate students, Juan Alberto Cervantes, was the first to spot one of the snakes for the first time since 1936.

DNA analysis was performed to establish the long, dark spotted snake as its own species and see where it had come from. The tests showed it is most closely related to snakes from Mexico's Sonora-Sinaloa coast more than 500 miles away. Martinez Gomez said the snake's ancestors may have made the trip from the mainland on a tree trunk felled by a storm and washed out to sea.

The rediscovery of the Clarion nightsnake is significant because of the fragility of island ecosystems. One inhabitant of the Revillagigedo Islands, the Socorro dove, went extinct in its natural habitat sometime in the 1970s. But live specimens had been taken off the islands in the 1920s, and their descendants were recently re-introduced to the islands.

The National Museum of Natural History said Mulcahy "uncovered the controversy surrounding the inclusion of this snake in the scientific record, and found that it appears to be the only species ever to be discarded due to a presumed locality error." The museum stated that the rediscovery of the Clarion nightsnake is an incredible story of how scientists rely on historical data and museum collections to solve modern-day mysteries about biodiversity in the world we live in. The team plans to continue monitoring the species to learn more about its role in the delicate Clarion Island ecosystem.

In Parsippany, New Jersey, a driver identified as Domingo Moreno, 27, is facing multiple charges after allegedly crashing his 1999 Nissan Quest into a mailbox and a fire hydrant, causing the hydrant to be dislodged and driven away. Moreno fled the scene but was later found at a nearby diner. The incident occurred on Edwards Road at around 1 a.m. on Tuesday.

The police investigation revealed a fluid trail leading from the crash site to a residence on Norman Avenue, where Moreno's vehicle and the missing fire hydrant were found among the garbage cans. Moreno was arrested and charged with criminal mischief, tampering with evidence, hindering apprehension, failure to report an accident, unlicensed driving, careless driving, reckless driving, and failure to maintain lane. He was remanded to the Morris County Correctional Facility pending a court appearance. The police are still investigating the cause and other details of the crash.

Gene and Pat Warrington, an Ohio couple who were married for 69 years, passed away eight hours apart on December 27, 2022, in Findlay. Both were in hospice care and had been dealing with health issues. Their son, Phil, shared that they spent time together in Pat's room the day before their deaths, with Gene holding his wife's hand. Knowing Pat's condition was critical, Gene returned to his room and began to pull out his intravenous tubes, expressing that life wouldn't be fun without her. Gene died, and eight hours later, Pat passed away. The couple met in junior high school and secretly wed while Gene was home from boot camp before leaving for World War II. They raised three children, had seven grandchildren, and twelve great-grandchildren. Throughout their marriage, they were nearly inseparable, even in failing health.

Sen. Saxby Chambliss (R-GA) announced his retirement from the Senate in 2014, citing frustration with the lack of leadership from the White House and Congress, particularly on economic issues. Chambliss' retirement opens up a highly contested seat, with several Republican House members and former Georgia Secretary of State Karen Handel expressing interest in running.

Democrats are also showing interest, with Atlanta Mayor Kasim Reed and Rep. John Barrow being considered top prospects. Chambliss' retirement could provide a significant opportunity for Democrats, as the seat is considered one of their best pick-up opportunities of the cycle due to changing demographics and the potential for a divisive GOP primary.

Herman Cain, former presidential candidate, is the Republican who would pose the greatest threat to Chambliss in a primary, leading him by 14 points in a hypothetical match-up. Cain has a favorable 68/20 approval rating among GOP primary voters, compared to Chambliss' 45/36 approval spread. Other potential candidates, such as Allen West and Erick Erickson, trail Chambliss in hypothetical match-ups.

Chambliss is particularly weak with Republican voters describing themselves as very conservative, with 61% wanting to replace him compared to only 23% who would like to see him nominated again. In the general election, the Georgia Senate race resembles the Indiana contest this cycle, with a safe Republican seat if Chambliss is the nominee, but a potential opportunity for the Democrats if a far-right candidate wins the primary.

"Swamp People," a reality series airing on The History Channel, focuses on Cajun alligator hunters in Louisiana's Atchafalaya Swamp during the 30-day hunting season. The show, now in its third season, is a ratings success, with last week's episode pulling in 3.8 million viewers. The series is praised for its authenticity and departure from typical reality TV.

Recently, one of the show's stars, Mitchell Guist, passed away during a hunting trip. The incident occurred in St. Martin Parish along the Belle River, where Guist suffered a fall in the boat and later died despite resuscitation attempts. The cause of death is currently unknown.

The History Channel expressed their sorrow over Guist's passing, stating that he was a beloved member of the "Swamp People" family. They plan to air all scheduled episodes and find a way to honor his memory. The show's fans, who appreciate its authentic portrayal of Cajun life, have expressed their condolences and respect for Guist and his family.

Tunisian Prime Minister Mohammed Ghannouchi, who was seen as too closely linked to the old regime, announced his resignation on state TV, a key demand of demonstrators. Ghannouchi, 69, had served under former President Zine al-Abidine Ben Ali since 1989. His resignation followed a week of protests demanding a new government and a new constitution, with at least three people killed in clashes between demonstrators and security forces. The government had promised reforms and elections by July, but those promises did not satisfy the protesters. Beji Caid-Essebsi, 84, a former government minister, was named as his replacement. The resignation and appointment followed renewed street protests, and it remains unclear if they will quell the violence. The change in leadership comes at a time when Tunisia is attempting to rebuild its tourism industry and cope with an influx of refugees from neighboring Libya.

The Boston Marathon bombings and subsequent shootings have left four dead and over 170 injured, with the reasons behind the attacks still unknown. The suspects, Chechen-American Muslim brothers Dzhokhar Tsarnaev and Tamerlan Tsarnaev, are under investigation for potential ties to a terrorist organization and unclear motives, with some reports suggesting struggles with assimilation after immigrating to the United States.

Following the capture of Dzhokhar Tsarnaev and the death of Tamerlan Tsarnaev, the Muslim community faces questions about accepting the brothers as Muslims given the allegations against them. Many mosques and Islamic groups have distanced themselves from the brothers, with some expressing reluctance to provide an Islamic burial.

Tamerlan Tsarnaev, the older brother, has been described as more attuned to radical Islamic movements in recent years, with federal authorities investigating a six-month trip he took to Chechnya and Dagestan in 2012.

Islamic tradition dictates that the body of the deceased should be tended to as soon as possible, with a ritual washing, shrouding, funeral prayer gathering, and burial. However, it is unclear where Tamerlan Tsarnaev's body currently is, and it is not known if a mosque will step forward to conduct a funeral.

The next-of-kin to take custody of Tamerlan Tsarnaev's body would be his wife, Katherine Russell, who has expressed her dismay at the actions of her husband. It is not known if she will request a funeral, and mosques have been hesitant to comment on the matter.

Investigations are ongoing to uncover the motives and potential ties to terrorist organizations behind the attacks, with authorities stating that the brothers may have been inspired by Al Qaeda propaganda and learned bomb-making techniques from the group's online magazine. The surviving brother, Dzhokhar Tsarnaev, is being treated at a Boston hospital and is reportedly telling authorities about their actions.

Oklahoma State Senator Ralph Shortey, a conservative Republican, was accused of child prostitution on March 9, 2017. He was charged with three felony counts, including engaging in child prostitution, engaging in prostitution within 1,000 feet of a church, and transporting a minor for prostitution. The allegations stem from an incident where Shortey was found in a hotel room with a 17-year-old boy, whom he had met through a Craigslist personal encounter ad.

The evidence against Shortey includes a graphic online conversation where the two discussed having sex and smoking marijuana, which was found on the teenager's Kindle tablet. Shortey, using the online name "Jamie Tilley," at one point during the discussion about sex called the teenager "baby boy." Police also found an open box of condoms in Shortey's backpack and a bottle of lotion in the teenager's backpack.

Governor Mary Fallin, Lt. Governor Todd Lamb, Senate leaders, and many others called for Shortey to resign. He was stripped of most of his privileges at the Capitol, including his office and parking space, by the state Senate on Wednesday. Shortey has been a senator since 2010 and has championed law-and-order issues. He is married to his high school sweetheart and has three children.

Shortey turned himself in at the Cleveland County Detention Center and was released after posting bail. He had no comment. The maximum punishment, if convicted, is 25 years in prison. The teenager was not charged because prosecutors consider him to be a victim. He is listed on the charge, by his initials, as a witness against Shortey.

The teenager had a history of soliciting himself on Craigslist for sexual conduct and also had a history of drug abuse. The teenager told police he had known Shortey for about a year and the two were smoking marijuana in the hotel room when police knocked on the door. Police also reported seizing a green plastic container with the label, "Colorado Retail Marijuana."

Shortey had studied in college to do mission work in Uganda but decided to go into the oil and gas industry after having his first child. He later went into politics, both as an elected senator and as a paid political consultant. Last year, he helped former state Rep. Mike Christian, who lost a bid to become Oklahoma County sheriff. Christian is running again for sheriff this year in a special election but has a different consultant. Christian was among those calling for Shortey to immediately resign.

Authorities are searching for a 23-year-old man named Jesus Henry Kong, also known as Jessie Eloah Calix and Jesus Matute, in connection with threatening messages posted on Twitter that targeted several schools in Orange County, Florida. The threats included encouragement for people to shoot students and plans to place pipe bombs inside two schools. The schools affected are William R. Boone High School, Edgewater High School, Colonial High School, Colonial Ninth Grade Center, and Liberty Middle School. The FBI, Orlando Police Department, and Orange County Sheriff's Office are investigating the threats, but do not believe they are credible. Kong has a history of law enforcement encounters and is a transient who has lived in Florida, California, Virginia, and Maryland. Parents of students at the schools were alerted to the threats, but classes were not affected. On Thursday, more than 900 students were absent from three of the four schools named in the threats, with large numbers of students staying home from at least three schools. The attendance numbers for Orlando's Colonial High School, the fourth school named in the threats, are not yet available.

The study, published in the Journal of the American Medical Association, suggests that income plays a significant role in determining life expectancy in the United States. The researchers analyzed over one billion tax and Social Security records and found that the life expectancy gap between the richest one percent and the poorest one percent is widening. For men, the difference is 14.6 years, and for women, it's 10.1 years.

However, the study also found that geography plays a crucial role in life expectancy, especially for the poor. The poor have a higher life expectancy in prosperous urban areas like San Francisco and New York City compared to more rural areas and some rust belt states. The authors attribute this to local public health programs and policies, such as restrictions on tobacco and bans on trans fats.

In contrast, life expectancy for the poor is especially low in cities like Detroit, where the poorest men have a life expectancy comparable to those living in Sudan and Pakistan. The study shows that the richest men in America have a better life expectancy than any men in the world, while the poorest men have a life expectancy comparable to those in developing countries.

The study suggests that more discussion needs to happen at a local level to address the disparities in health and lifespan. The authors found that health behaviors, such as smoking, are a significant factor in life expectancy, even when there is access to healthcare. For example, life expectancy is on the rise for the poor in Birmingham, Alabama, but in Tampa, Florida, the poor are on the downslide when it comes to life expectancy.

In an accompanying editorial, Dr. J. Michael McGinnis of the National Academy of Medicine wrote that "community is powerfully associated with life expectancy." He suggests that individual leaders working together to strengthen community-wide attention and action on behalf of health could make a difference.

The study results also suggest a revamp of Social Security and Medicare might be in order, as men and women in the top one percent are on track to claim these benefits for 11.8 and 8.3 more years than men and women in the bottom one percent of the income distribution.

Overall, the study offers insights on how to help blunt some of the adverse health issues faced by Americans who are not affluent. The authors suggest that focusing on health behaviors, such as smoking, and supporting community-wide action on health could help address the disparities in life expectancy across income groups.

The United Kingdom general election held on May 7, 2015, resulted in a victory for the Conservative Party, led by Prime Minister David Cameron. The Conservatives are poised to retain their office at 10 Downing Street, with a projected 316 seats in the House of Commons, which is close to the number needed for an absolute majority. The Labour Party, led by Ed Miliband, suffered a significant defeat, with projections showing they will win 239 seats. The Liberal Democrats, the current coalition partner in the Tory-led government, are projected to lose significantly, with a drop from 57 seats to a projected 10. The Scottish National Party (SNP) is expected to make a significant gain, with projections showing they might take all of Labour's seats in Scotland and advancing from 6 to 58 seats in all. The election results have major implications for the UK's global role, the possibility of a referendum on whether to stay in the European Union, fears of a fractured country, and clamping down on immigration. The Conservatives have promised a referendum on EU membership by 2017, and the results of this referendum would be unpredictable. The SNP's rise could lead to yet another referendum on Scottish independence in 2016. The election results have also led to resignations from key political figures, including Ed Miliband, leader of the Labour Party, and Nick Clegg, leader of the Liberal Democrats. The UK Independence Party (UKIP) leader Nigel Farage lost his bid to win a seat in Parliament, but the party's surge to third in the popular vote nationwide could have a significant impact on the Conservative Party's policies. The election results have also raised concerns about the UK's influence globally, as the UK has been increasingly taking a back seat to Germany in world affairs.

The Australian radio hosts Mel Greig and Michael Christian, who made a prank call to the hospital where the Duchess of Cambridge was staying, have apologized for their actions following the death of nurse Jacintha Saldanha, who took the call. The hosts, who have been in hiding and undergoing counseling since the incident, broke their silence in interviews on Australian television, expressing their deep regret and sympathy for Saldanha's family. They stated that they had not expected the call to be put through to the Duchess's room and that it was supposed to be a simple, harmless prank. Southern Cross Austereo, the owners of the radio station, have canceled the hosts' show and suspended all prank calls by its broadcasters. The incident has sparked demands for tougher regulation of the electronic media, with Australia's press regulator considering whether to initiate an inquiry beyond its usual process. The case has also led to calls for the radio station to be held accountable for its actions, with some accusing the hosts of having blood on their hands.

The article discusses the potential economic consequences of a debt ceiling standoff between the U.S. government and House Republicans. The author, Jon Favreau, recalls drafting a speech for President Obama in 2011 that outlined the dire consequences of failing to raise the debt ceiling, including delayed Social Security checks, veterans' benefits, and government payments to businesses, which could lead to a global financial crisis.

The author argues that the confusion surrounding the debt ceiling and the term "raising the debt limit" contributes to the public's lack of understanding of the issue. He suggests that the phrase "government shutdown" is more relatable and understood by the public, as it has historical context and can be visualized.

The author warns that a failure to raise the debt ceiling could result in an "economic shutdown of epic proportions," causing financial hardship and ruin for millions of Americans. He emphasizes that a vote to raise the debt limit will not cost taxpayers any money or increase the deficit, but a failure to do so could lead to economic catastrophe.

The author criticizes House Republicans for their stance on the issue, stating that they are willing to risk default in order to pass policies that Mitt Romney ran and lost on in the 2012 election. He concludes by expressing concern over the potential consequences of a debt ceiling standoff and the need for political leaders to prioritize the well-being of the American people over ideological agendas.

Former International Monetary Fund chief Dominique Strauss-Kahn and the hotel maid who accused him of sexual assault have reached a settlement in a lawsuit stemming from the 2011 incident. The agreement, which comes after criminal charges were dropped last year, will likely be confidential due to a non-disclosure agreement. The two parties, represented by lawyers William W. Taylor III and Kenneth P. Thompson, are scheduled to appear in court next week to finalize the settlement. Strauss-Kahn was arrested in 2011 after the maid accused him of sexually assaulting her during a hotel cleaning, leading to his resignation from the IMF. The case fell apart due to concerns about the maid's credibility, and the charges were dropped in August 2011. Strauss-Kahn has also faced legal troubles in France, where he was charged with participating in an organized prostitution ring.

A U.K. Royal Marine named David Hart, who was killed by a Taliban bomb in Afghanistan, will posthumously fund a Las Vegas vacation for 32 of his friends and their girlfriends. Hart, described as "the perfect Marine" by fellow officers, had taken out a £250,000 insurance policy before his deployment, with instructions that £150,000 of the amount should be used for the Las Vegas trip. Hart's friends have been supportive of his family since his death, and the remaining insurance money will also go toward a charity group of injured Marines and Hart's family. Additionally, Hart's family and friends are planning a charitable U.K. bike ride to raise money in Hart's memory this fall. The funds raised will be donated to the Royal Marines Charitable Trust Fund. Hart, who was 23 years old, joined the Royal Marines in 2009 and served with 40 Commando. His Commanding Officer, Lt Col Paul James, described him as "a perfect commando" who was "fiercely courageous and always thinking of others before himself."

Thailand's Prime Minister Abhisit Vejjajiva declared a state of emergency on Wednesday following a storming of the country's parliament by anti-government demonstrators. The emergency measure, effective in Bangkok and nearby provinces, limits certain rights of people, bans gatherings of more than five persons, and prohibits the publishing, broadcasting, or spreading of information deemed a threat to national security.

The decree allows authorities to take actions without court orders, such as summoning, arresting, and detaining people, and embarking on searches. It also grants access to communications like fax or telephone and the power to end communications. People are prohibited from staying in certain areas, and authorities are permitted to stop Thai citizens from leaving the country.

The demonstrators, supporters of former Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra, have been demanding that Abhisit call elections, claiming he took office illegitimately in 2008 with the help of military pressure on parliament. The group, United Front for Democracy Against Dictatorship, disregarded calls to disperse from Bangkok's commercial hub, potentially affecting tourism by about 10%.

The unrest in Thailand disrupted a summit of Southeast Asian leaders, with Prime Minister Abhisit Vejjajiva forced to abandon his trip due to fears of violence. The tensions raised concerns among ASEAN leaders, who were focused on economic discussions among member countries with diverging political systems. The Red Shirts, the demonstrators, are calling for Abhisit to dissolve Parliament within 15 days and call new elections.

A girl named Wati, who was believed to have perished in the devastating 2004 tsunami in Indonesia's Aceh, has miraculously returned home after seven years. Wati was 8 years old when she was separated from her mother during the tsunami. For years, her family believed she had drowned. On Wednesday, Wati's grandfather received a visit from a girl claiming to be lost and seeking her home. The girl, who was initially thought to be a beggar, was later identified by Wati's parents as their daughter based on a mole and a scar. The 2004 tsunami, triggered by the world's most powerful earthquake in 40 years, resulted in nearly 170,000 deaths and almost 130,000 people going missing across more than 10 countries. The circumstances surrounding Wati's disappearance and reappearance remain unclear.

Title: Oklahoma's Unwired Electric Chair in Dispute as Lethal Injection Procedures Face Review

The Oklahoma Department of Corrections (DOC) is in a dispute with the city of McAlester over ownership of the state's unwired electric chair, which may be reinstated for use if challenges to Oklahoma's lethal injection procedure are upheld. The electric chair, nicknamed Old Sparky, is currently in storage, and corrections spokesman Jerry Massie has stated that it could be rewired and used again, but only if lethal injection is deemed unconstitutional.

The dispute over the electric chair predates the current execution crisis, which began after the botched lethal injection of Clayton Lockett on April 29, 2014. Lockett writhed, groaned, and attempted to speak during the execution, which took 43 minutes to complete. Since then, there have been no executions in the US. Attorneys for Charles Warner, who was scheduled to die the same night as Lockett in a rare double execution, are closely watching the review of Oklahoma's execution procedures. Warner was granted a stay of execution after Lockett's death and is now scheduled to die on November 13.

McAlester Mayor Steve Harrison believes the electric chair should be on display for the public to see, as it is a historical artifact. The chair was previously housed in a museum in McAlester, a town of about 18,000 that is home to the state's death chamber. However, the chair was taken back by the corrections department a number of years ago, and its current location is unknown. Harrison expects that if Oklahoma were to electrocute an inmate, the state would obtain a new electric chair, as the current one has not been used since 1966.

The electric chair, first used in 1915, was used to execute 82 inmates before it was retired. The last inmate to sit in it was James French, who was killed on August 10, 1966, for the murder of his cellmate. As states grapple with a European-led boycott over lethal injection drugs, some have proposed returning to old methods such as the electric chair and the firing squad. Tennessee's governor recently approved the use of the electric chair for executions where drugs cannot be acquired. Some states, such as Florida, Alabama, and Virginia, have long listed electrocution as an optional execution method. The last US inmate to die by electrocution was Robert Gleason, who chose it over lethal injection and was killed on January 16, 2013, in Virginia.

In Kearney, Nebraska, a man named Jason Behrens was arrested for drunk driving with his children in the car, marking the second time he was caught driving under the influence with minors in the vehicle. The incident occurred during a family vacation, and Behrens' children became increasingly nervous as they noticed the car swerving and making close calls, nearly causing a head-on collision. The children, aged 14 and 12, sent text messages to 911 detailing their father's intoxicated state, eventually leading to his arrest at a Burger King.

The children, Mackenzie and Ethan Behrens, expressed their gratitude to the Kearney Police, stating that they had saved their lives. Mackenzie and Ethan said this wasn't the first time their father was driving drunk while they were in the car. The children's mother, Amy Brooks, stated that the children were scared enough during this incident to take action and send the text messages to the police.

Behrens blew nearly three times the legal limit when arrested. He is charged with DUI and two counts of driving drunk with minors in the vehicle. The children are currently in the care of their mother.

Texting 911 was launched in Buffalo County, Nebraska, last year, and it has since been rolled out in select municipalities and counties across the country as an option for reaching help during emergencies. The incident highlights the importance of this service and the bravery of the children in taking action to protect themselves.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) is investigating a multistate outbreak of Shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli O157:H7 (E. coli O157:H7) infections, which has affected 62 people from 16 states and the District of Columbia as of January 9, 2019. The outbreak appears to be over.

Public health investigators used DNA fingerprinting techniques such as pulsed-field gel electrophoresis (PFGE) and whole genome sequencing (WGS) to identify the outbreak. WGS provided a more detailed DNA fingerprint and showed that the strains were closely related genetically, indicating a common source of infection.

Illnesses started from October 7, 2018, to December 4, 2018, with a median age of 25 and 66% of ill people being female. Forty-six percent of the 54 people with information available were hospitalized, including two cases of hemolytic uremic syndrome, a type of kidney failure. No deaths were reported.

Investigations revealed that romaine lettuce from the Central Coastal growing regions of northern and central California was the likely source of the outbreak. Traceback evidence from the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) indicated that ill people in this outbreak ate romaine lettuce harvested from specific counties in the region.

The FDA, along with CDC and state partners, investigated farms and cooling facilities in California that were identified in traceback. CDC analyzed water and sediment samples from an Adam Bros. Farming, Inc. farm in Santa Barbara County, which was one of the farms identified in the traceback investigation. The outbreak strain of E. coli O157:H7 was found in sediment within an agricultural water reservoir on the farm. WGS results showed that the E. coli O157:H7 found in the agricultural water reservoir was closely related genetically to the E. coli O157:H7 isolated from ill people.

This outbreak does not appear to be linked to a spring 2018 multistate outbreak of E. coli O157:H7 infections linked to romaine lettuce. People in the spring outbreak were infected with E. coli O157:H7 bacteria with a different DNA fingerprint.

The FDA is continuing to investigate to learn more about how the E. coli bacteria could have entered the agricultural water reservoir and ways romaine lettuce from the farm could have been contaminated. The FDA is able to confirm that Adam Bros. Farming, Inc. has not shipped romaine since November 20, 2018. Romaine lettuce from Adam Bros. Farming, Inc. linked to this outbreak is no longer available for sale.

Federal health officials are warning about a fresh outbreak of E. coli linked to romaine lettuce on November 20, 2018. At least 32 people are sick, and 13 hospitalized in the outbreak, with no deaths reported. The CDC advises consumers not to eat any romaine lettuce, including whole heads, hearts, bags, boxes, and salad mixes that contain romaine, even if some of it was eaten and no one has gotten sick. The FDA is working closely with the leafy greens industry and other state and federal partners to implement safety practices to reduce the risk of such outbreaks. There's not enough information to identify a specific supplier yet, so it's safest to just throw out all romaine lettuce for now.

To clean a refrigerator after a food recall, follow these steps: throw out recalled food, empty the refrigerator, wash removable parts, clean and sanitize inside the refrigerator, return shelves, drawers, and food, and wash hands and towels used during the cleaning process.

The article provides an exclusive update on the casting process for the upcoming Marvel Studios film, The First Avenger: Captain America. The studio, along with director Joe Johnston, is reportedly considering Chris Evans, who previously portrayed a Marvel Comics character in the Fantastic Four films, as a potential candidate. Mike Vogel (Cloverfield) and Garrett Hedlund (Tron: Legacy) remain the top contenders, with Hedlund initially not testing but now being reconsidered due to scheduling issues. Previous candidates such as Chace Crawford, John Krasinski, Scott Porter, Michael Cassidy, and Patrick Flueger are no longer in the running. The film is set for release by Paramount Pictures on July 22, 2011, and Garrett Hedlund can currently be seen in the new trailer for Tron Legacy.

The study published in the Journal of the American Medical Association reveals that China has the highest number of smokers globally, with approximately 281 million smokers in 2012. This number has increased despite a decrease in smoking prevalence from 30.4% to 24.2% between 1980 and 2012. The study, conducted by researchers at the Seattle-based Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation, highlights the need for China to address tobacco control due to the significant health, economic, and environmental costs associated with smoking.

The study found that the leveling off of smoking prevalence in China and globally can be attributed to varying degrees of addictiveness. The average number of cigarettes consumed daily per smoker in China has increased from 15 in 1980 to 22 in 2012. Despite government measures to restrict smoking, such as bans in restaurants and public places, these measures are rarely enforced.

Interestingly, the gender ratio of China's smoking population has become more pronounced, with only about 4% of smokers being female in 2012, down from about 8% in 1980. This is surprising, considering that greater independence and improved economic conditions have been associated with a rise in smoking among women in the West.

Recently, the Chinese government announced plans to ban indoor smoking in public areas by the end of the year. The country's health authorities estimate over a million deaths from tobacco-related diseases every year, and the World Health Organization warns that if tobacco use is not decreased in China, these deaths will increase to 3 million by 2050. The latest moves by the Chinese government are seen as hopeful by Dr. Judith Mackay, the senior adviser at the World Lung Foundation, who examines tobacco issues in China.

The article by David Leonhardt discusses a new study that suggests Republicans are slightly more likely to report being happily married than Democrats, even after accounting for demographic differences between the two parties. The study, conducted by Brad Wilcox of the Institute for Family Studies, found that among married people between the ages of 20 and 60, 67% of Republicans report being "very happy" with their marriages, compared to 60% of Democrats and independents.

The study also found that whites and the religiously observant are both more likely to be Republicans and more likely to report having happy marriages. However, the gap between Republicans and Democrats did not disappear completely, even after controlling for demographic factors.

The study's findings are consistent with previous work that found Republicans are generally happier with their lives and more likely to be married. However, the authors acknowledge that the gap could stem from people's attitudes toward life and survey questions, rather than from the quality of their marriages.

The study also notes that conservatism may have cultural attitudes that improve the environment in which children grow up, including a greater respect and reverence for the idea of marriage. The study's findings challenge the notion that blue states are more conducive to stable family life than red states.

The study's findings are significant because they remind us that conservatism also has values and cultural attitudes that seem to improve the environment in which children grow up. Given the widespread anxiety about upward mobility in the United States, it's worth looking for potential lessons from any political ideology.

The study conducted by Kaiser Permanente has found that the HIV-preventing drug Truvada, which was approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration in 2012, is 100% effective in preventing HIV infections. The study followed over 600 patients for nearly three years, and none of them tested positive for HIV. The drug, which contains the antiviral drugs emtricitabine and tenofovir, was originally created as an anti-retroviral drug used to treat HIV, but it has been shown to reduce the risk of HIV infection in people who are at high risk by up to 92% when taken consistently.

The study was published in the medical journal Clinical Infectious Diseases, and it found that the drug was effective in a real-world setting, even among participants who did not use condoms for prevention and who were diagnosed with other sexually transmitted diseases. The study did find a significant decrease in condom use among the participants, which has been a concern among critics of the drug.

The drug has been criticized by some health providers and advocates who worry that it may encourage unsafe sex because of a false sense of security. One of the loudest critics has been Michael Weinstein, president of the AIDS Healthcare Foundation in Los Angeles, who has publicly called Truvada a “party drug.” However, the CDC and public health advocates disagree, and they recommend the drug as a prophylactic for those at highest risk of becoming infected, such as sex workers, men with HIV-positive partners, or those who engage in high-risk behaviors, such as IV drug use.

The study did not have a control group for the sake of comparison, but the participants clearly weren’t abstinent. After six months, about 30% of the PrEP users had been diagnosed with at least one sexually transmitted infection, with that number rising to 50% after a year. But there were no HIV infections, the study found. When the participants were asked about any changes in behavior, 74% reported no change in their number of sexual partners, while 15% reported a decrease and 11% said the number increased. Condom use was unchanged in 51% of the participants, while 41% said they had decreased their condom use and 3% had increased the use of condoms.

For study participant Paul Marcelin, a San Francisco Kaiser patient who lives in Alameda, the drug allows him to protect himself while maintaining his relationship with his HIV-positive boyfriend. Marcelin, 40, a database expert, participated in a separate PrEP study conducted in 2013 by the San Francisco Department of Public Health and stayed on the drug for the Kaiser study. He said he thinks any hesitancy about Truvada is starting to dissipate, and people are accepting it as another prevention option.

The study suggests that HIV is very close to being managed like any other chronic disease, such as diabetes or asthma. The drug costs Kaiser patients about $50 a month, and it is not without controversy. However, the CDC and public health advocates agree that it is an important tool for those at high risk of HIV infection, and it can help prevent new HIV infections, deaths, and stigma.

A DreamWorks animator, Young Song, aged 40, has been accused of brutally beating a 1-year-old German Shepherd with a hammer and shooting it with a pellet gun. The incident occurred on April 20 in Pasadena, California, and was captured on surveillance video. The dog is now missing and presumed dead. Song, who worked on several children's movies such as "Kung Fu Panda" and "Madagascar 2," pleaded not guilty to felony animal cruelty and theft of the animal in court on Thursday. The Humane Society is investigating the case alongside local police, suspecting an ongoing dispute between the neighbors as the cause. If convicted, Song could face several years in state prison. The Humane Society described the incident as one of the worst cases of animal abuse they've ever seen, causing shock and sadness among its workers.

The escalating violence in Syria, as stated by Maj. Gen. Robert Mood of the United Nations, is hindering the ability of UN monitors to observe, verify, and report on the situation, and reviving the mission requires a cease-fire. Syrian President Bashar al-Assad, in an interview with Turkey's Cumhuriyet newspaper, showed no readiness to heed calls for a cease-fire or a transitional government plan proposed by Kofi Annan, the special envoy on Syria. The interview provided insights into Assad's thoughts on the Syrian crisis and regional relationships, strained by the downing of a Turkish warplane by Syrian gunners last month.

The bodies of the two Turkish pilots were recovered and sent to Malatya, Turkey, with a memorial service planned. Syria and Turkey dispute whether the plane was in international or Syrian airspace at the time. In the interview, Assad discussed his survival through 16 months of uprising, his determination to suppress the revolt, and his insistence on having the support of the majority of Syrians. He compared his situation to that of the Shah of Iran, who was overthrown by the Islamic revolution in 1979, but argued that his position was different due to popular support among Syrians.

Iraq's foreign minister stated that the government has "solid information and intelligence" about al-Qaida militants infiltrating Syria from Iraq to carry out attacks. Iraq has reinforced security along its border with Syria, making it the most heavily guarded Iraqi frontier, due to concerns about a spillover of violence from Syria to the rest of the Middle East. Al Qaeda operatives were reportedly communicating through underground networks of militants.

In summary, the violence in Syria is escalating, making it difficult for UN monitors to observe and report on the situation. Syria's President Assad has shown no readiness to heed calls for a cease-fire or a transitional government, and tensions between Syria and Turkey remain high following the downing of a Turkish warplane. Iraq is concerned about the spillover of violence from Syria and has reinforced security along its border with Syria due to the infiltration of al-Qaida militants.

Nine-year-old Elina Childs, a Girl Guide member, sold out of cookies in 45 minutes outside an Edmonton cannabis store on the first day of legal sales. Her father, Seann Childs, came up with the idea a day before, as selling cookies in their neighborhood had been slow. Elina, who has cystic fibrosis, managed the sale politely and used the opportunity to educate herself about cannabis. The Girl Guides praised Elina's strategy, and her father used the experience to teach her about the implications of legalization. Elina's national TV interview focused on her joke, "Why did the cookie go to the doctor? Because it was feeling crummy."

A 19-year-old individual, suspected of network intrusions and distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks against international businesses and intelligence agencies, has been arrested by the Metropolitan Police Central e-Crime Unit. The arrest took place in Wickford, Essex, and the suspect is currently in custody at a central London police station. The investigation involved the FBI, and it is speculated that the attacks may be linked to the LulzSec and Anonymous activist groups.

LulzSec has previously targeted various organizations including the US Senate, the CIA, the NHS, and several games and entertainment companies. On Sunday, LulzSec teamed up with Anonymous to launch an operation called AntiSec. The UK's Serious Organised Crime Agency (Soca) was the first reported victim of AntiSec, confirming a DDoS attack on Monday.

However, there is confusion within the AntiSec campaign as to who has been arrested. Initial reports suggested the arrested individual was involved with LulzSec, but later updates from self-proclaimed Anon members and LulzSec's official Twitter account indicate that the suspect may be Ryan Cleary, a previous target of Anonymous due to his alleged attempts to attack Anonymous's network servers. LulzSec has distanced itself from Cleary, stating that he only houses one of their legitimate chatrooms on his IRC server.

The U.S., having secretly flown unmanned surveillance aircraft over Iraq since last year, has been assessing the situation as Islamist militants, led by the Islamic State in Iraq and the Levant (ISIS), have seized two major Iraqi cities, Mosul and Tikrit, during a rapid advance. The insurgents are planning to push further south towards Baghdad and regions dominated by Iraq's Shia Muslim majority. U.S. President Barack Obama has stated that his government is considering all options, including military action, to help Iraq fight the Islamist militants, but has no intention of sending ground troops. The White House is moving defense contractors working with the Iraqi military to safer areas. The insurgency could lead to a break-up of Iraq on sectarian lines, deepening the sectarian conflict between Sunnis and Shias that is already the most dangerous fault line in the Middle East. The U.S. invasion and occupation of Iraq in 2003 helped create and strengthen jihadist groups, limiting the options available to the U.S. in the current situation. Iraq's ambassador to the U.S. has described the current situation as the most serious in recent years. The Iraqi parliament has failed to achieve a quorum to vote on emergency powers, reflecting the fragmented state of Iraqi politics. Kurdish forces have claimed control of the oil city of Kirkuk, historically claimed by the Kurds, and have slowed the insurgents' advance on Samarra, a city just 110km north of Baghdad. The insurgents have bypassed Samarra and seized the town of Dhuluiya, 90km north-west of the capital. Security in Baghdad has been stepped up after a video emerged of the militants threatening to march on the city. The U.N. Security Council has unanimously supported Iraq's government and people in their "fight against terrorism."

The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) has developed the world's most precise clock, known as the ytterbium optical lattice clock. This table-sized clock has a stability that does not change by more than one part in 10^18, making it 10 times more stable than any other atomic clock. The clock uses ytterbium atoms and optical light to measure time with an unprecedented level of precision, approaching one quadrillion oscillations per second.

The ytterbium clock has the potential to significantly impact timekeeping and various sensors measuring quantities such as gravity, magnetic fields, and temperature. The high stability of the ytterbium clocks allows for precise results to be achieved quickly, within a second of averaging time, compared to the five days required by the current U.S. civilian time standard.

NIST physicist Andrew Ludlow stated that the stability of the ytterbium lattice clocks opens the door to various practical applications of high-performance timekeeping. The clocks rely on about 10,000 rare-earth atoms cooled to 10 microkelvin and trapped in an optical lattice. The ticks of the ytterbium clocks can be measured and improved by constructing a second version of the clock.

Although the ytterbium clocks have set a new record for stability, more research is needed to determine their accuracy. The research is funded in part by the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency and the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA). The potential applications of this groundbreaking technology include testing Einstein's theory of general relativity, improving global positioning systems, and developing navigation and communication systems. However, the total cost of the clocks is on the order of a half-million dollars, making them impractical for everyday use.

A woman stole a wedding ring from a deceased woman at the Sunset Funeral Home in Odessa, Texas, on April 8th. The suspect is described as a heavy-set white female wearing a brown long sleeve sweater, black sweat pants, and black sandals. The theft occurred a day after the deceased woman, Lois Hicks, died. The family is still grieving and is asking anyone with information about the theft to come forward. The incident is being investigated as a State Jail Felony, and no arrests have been made yet. The funeral home has released a higher quality video of the suspect and a photo of her vehicle. Anyone with information can contact the Odessa Police Department or Odessa Crime Stoppers at 432-333-TIPS. The theft of jewelry from the dead at funeral homes is not uncommon, but the brazen nature of this incident is unusual. The funeral home had little information about the theft, but the family has a video recording of the theft which has alleviated some of their concerns. The family is still seeking the suspect and is offering a reward for information leading to her arrest.

The House Intelligence Committee has voted to release a classified memo alleging improper use of government surveillance during the investigation into Russian election interference and contacts with President Donald Trump's campaign. The memo, written by Republicans, addresses a dossier of allegations against Trump compiled by a former British spy and questions over whether it was used to obtain surveillance warrants. Democrats on the committee voted against its release. The White House has not yet decided whether to authorize the release of the memo, with President Trump favoring "full transparency." Two Republican senators, Lindsey Graham and Susan Collins, have urged President Trump to maintain silence on an independent investigation into his 2016 campaign's contacts with Russia. The memo has been a source of escalating partisan tension in Congress, with Republicans arguing it shows wrongdoing by FBI officials involved in the surveillance of a Trump campaign aide, while Democrats say it mischaracterizes intelligence and is an attempt to distract from Special Counsel Robert Mueller's probe into Russia's interference in the 2016 election. The FBI director, Christopher Wray, has been shown the memo by House intelligence committee Chairman Devin Nunes and has expressed concerns with its contents. The White House now has five days to either object to the committee's request or clear the way for the memo's release.

President Donald Trump has been blaming the Democrats for the separation of immigrant children from their parents at the border, claiming it's a law created by them. The increase in family separation is due to a zero-tolerance policy introduced by the Trump administration and Attorney General Jeff Sessions.
