The bill requires the government to keep families together when in the custody of the Department of Homeland Security, but it does nothing to stop the current policy.

Democrats want the administration to reverse the policy, but they see the mechanism for addressing it sitting purely with the executive branch. They are going to the border to highlight the issue and have marched to do so. They believe the answer to separating families is not to put them behind bars.

The bill touches on the issue but is hardly a fix, and Democrats aren't in negotiations with Republicans about a legislative fix. The Trump administration implemented the current separation policy, but it's also a negotiating play to try and force Democrats to the table on immigration legislation the President favors. However, Democrats aren't in the room on those legislative efforts, and the President just nuked the lone House GOP effort that had a shot at passage. The prospects of any effort in the near future to prevent families from being separated at the border aren't looking good.

The article discusses the declaration by Bishop David L. Ricken of Green Bay that Our Lady of Good Help in Champion, Wisconsin, is an official site of Marian apparitions, making it one of only a dozen worldwide and the first in the United States. The Virgin Mary is said to have appeared to Adele Brise, a Belgian immigrant, in 1859, instructing her to teach Catholic beliefs to children. After a two-year investigation, the church found no evidence of fraud or heresy and declared that Adele's encounters were of a supernatural character, worthy of belief.

Since the declaration, there has been an increase in visitors to the shrine, with some driving several hours to pray and feel the presence of Mary. The shrine's grounds were spared during the Great Peshtigo Fire of 1871, which caused over 1,200 deaths, adding to the belief in the divine intervention.

The church's scandals did not influence Bishop Ricken's decision, but he hopes that the shrine can become a source of hope and healing for people, including victims of errant priests. The Vatican gives primary responsibility for evaluating apparitions to local bishops, and over the 20th century, only a dozen were recognized as valid.

Visitors to the shrine on Wednesday afternoon seemed to have no doubts about the apparitions, with one woman stating that there is a lot of power there and you can feel the presence of Mary. The declaration has not changed anything for two women who have made a weekly pilgrimage to the shrine for years, as they already knew that the visits were real.

The article concludes by emphasizing the profound message of the Holy Mother's visitation to Adele Brise, that there is no one anywhere who is beyond the reach of God's generous love. The church encourages everyone to celebrate this visit and open the message to anyone and everyone who answers the call.

On May 15, 2015, D.C. police discovered the deaths of a family and their housekeeper in an upscale neighborhood in Northwest Washington. The victims were identified as Savvas Savopoulos, 46, his wife, Amy Savopoulos, 47, their son, Philip, 10, and housekeeper Veralicia Figueroa, 57. The events leading to their deaths may have begun on Wednesday.

D.C. police have released video images of a person of interest in the case, dressed in dark clothing, captured on surveillance video near the house. They are also seeking information about a 2008 blue Porsche 911, which was seen near the house on Thursday. The car was later found torched and unoccupied in the parking lot of St. Christopher's Episcopal Church in Lanham, Maryland.

The deaths are being investigated as a homicide arson, and police believe the fire was intentionally set. There is no sign of forced entry into the home. The family had an extensive art collection, which was on display during a Christmas house tour.

Police are examining surveillance video from the neighborhood and have found at least two cameras outside the Savopoulos' home. The days and hours leading up to the deaths had come into sharper focus, with new details from police records showing attempts by friends and relatives to reach the victims on Thursday morning before they were found dead in a burning home.

The deaths have shocked the community and District's society circles. The couple were active donors to both social and political causes, and attended St. Sophia Greek Orthodox Cathedral. Savvas Savopoulos was president and chief executive of American Iron Works, a leading custom steel and iron manufacturing company.

Relatives of the Savopouloses have spoken briefly about the family and the incident, but have been too overwrought for more in-depth interviews. The couple have two surviving daughters, Abigail Savopoulos and Katerina. Philip was a student at St. Albans School in the District.

Gutierrez, who was close with Figueroa, said her friend had planned to soon return to her native El Salvador. Figueroa was at her wedding, and was there for her baby shower and, later, her daughter's first communion.

D.C. Police Chief Cathy L. Lanier said Friday that police were still working on a timeline, and looking for a motive. It remains unclear whether anything was taken from the two-story red brick house. Lanier asked anyone who saw the Porsche on Wednesday or Thursday to contact police.

Stephen Bannon, the former White House chief strategist, will not be joining Fox News or CNN following his departure from Breitbart News. This decision comes after Bannon made controversial remarks about Trump's family to author Michael Wolff, which were published in the book "Fire and Fury: Inside the Trump White House." Bannon had been executive chairman of Breitbart News since 2012 and left the publication to join the Trump campaign, becoming the president's chief strategist. He was fired six months into that job and returned to Breitbart. However, after his comments to Wolff about the president's mental fitness, Breitbart began to distance itself from Bannon, leading to his resignation.

Bannon's career has been in flux since the publication of Wolff’s book. In the book, Bannon was quoted as calling Donald Trump Jr. "treasonous" and "unpatriotic" for meeting with a Russian lawyer during his father’s presidential campaign. Trump slammed Bannon in a statement, claiming that the former Goldman Sachs investment banker had "lost his mind" after the comments on Trump Jr. first came to light. Bannon has since apologized for the comments, but the White House has rejected the overture.

Bannon's association with controversial figures like former Breitbart editor Milo Yiannopoulos and Roy Moore has also contributed to his downfall. During his tenure at Breitbart, the publication became increasingly devoted to promoting Bannon, welcoming him back as a "populist hero" after he returned following his ouster from the White House. However, after the release of Wolff's book, Breitbart began to distance itself from Bannon, leading to his resignation.

In addition to losing his positions at Breitbart, SiriusXM, and potentially Fox News, CNN, and MSNBC, Bannon's wealthy conservative patron Rebekah Mercer has also cut ties with him. Mercer had been unhappy with Bannon for some time, and in a rare public statement, she announced that her family was no longer supporting his political projects. Breitbart's board reportedly debated firing Bannon, and the company may face consequences as a result of his actions.

Overall, Bannon's career has taken a significant hit as a result of his controversial comments about the Trump family and his association with controversial figures. His future in the conservative media landscape remains uncertain.

The study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences suggests that a microbe called Methanosarcina, which produces large amounts of methane, may have caused the worst mass extinction in Earth's history 252 million years ago, known as the end-Permian extinction. The extinction event, which wiped out up to 97% of all species, has previously been attributed to massive volcanic eruptions. However, new research indicates that volcanic activity may have only played a minor role in the catastrophe.

The researchers found that Methanosarcina, a single-celled organism distinct from bacteria, thrived in the oceans and released enormous quantities of methane into the atmosphere. This methane contributed to global warming and ocean acidification, creating unlivable conditions for many species. The microbe's growth was facilitated by an increase in nickel concentrations in the oceans, which were driven by volcanic eruptions in Siberia.

The end-Permian extinction was the most severe of five known mass extinction events and resulted in the disappearance of various marine and land species, including trilobites, sea scorpions, and many mammal-like reptiles. The first dinosaurs appeared 20 million years after the extinction event.

The researchers argue that the changes in the carbon cycle during the end-Permian extinction cannot be fully explained by volcanic activity alone. They suggest that microbial life may have played a significant role in causing the environmental shocks that led to the mass extinction. The study broadens the conversation about the potential causes of mass extinctions and emphasizes the importance of considering various natural fluctuations in Earth's carbon cycle when making future predictions.

The executive order issued by U.S. President Donald Trump restricting immigration from seven Muslim-majority countries has been blocked by judges in at least five states. The order, which halted travel by people with passports from Iran, Iraq, Libya, Somalia, Sudan, Syria, and Yemen for 90 days, and stopped the resettlement of refugees for 120 days, has been met with widespread criticism and protests.

The rulings by judges in California, Massachusetts, Virginia, Washington state, and New York have complicated the administration's effort to enforce the order. The growing number of rulings has raised questions about the constitutionality of the order. Lawyers representing people covered by the order have reported that some authorities were unwilling to follow the judges' rulings on Sunday.

Attorneys general from 15 states and Washington, D.C., have issued a joint statement condemning the order as unconstitutional. The states taking part in the joint statement are Washington, California, New York, Pennsylvania, Massachusetts, Hawaii, Virginia, Oregon, Connecticut, Vermont, Illinois, New Mexico, Iowa, Maine, and Maryland.

The U.S. Department of Homeland Security has said it will comply with judicial orders while enforcing the order in a manner that ensures those entering the United States do not pose a threat to the country or its people. However, there have been reports of confusion and chaos at airports as immigration lawyers work to help travelers and protesters gather to show their opposition to the order.

The order has sparked a global backlash, with U.S. allies viewing the actions as discriminatory and divisive. Supporters of the order have argued that it is necessary to protect the American people from terrorist attacks by foreign nationals admitted to the United States.

Lawsuits on behalf of more than 100 individual travelers have been filed nationwide, with some coming from large corporate firms including Mayer Brown, Kirkland & Ellis, and Cleary Gottlieb Steen & Hamilton. Some have come from large corporate firms including Mayer Brown, Kirkland & Ellis, and Cleary Gottlieb Steen & Hamilton.

In Boston, U.S. District Judge Allison Burroughs temporarily blocked the removal of two Iranians who have taught at the University of Massachusetts, and had been detained at the city's Logan International Airport. Burroughs' ruling appeared to go further than Donnelly's by barring the detention, as well as the removal, of approved refugees, visa holders, and permanent U.S. residents entering from the seven countries. Donnelly's order forbade only removal.

The U.S. Constitution's First Amendment guarantees the free exercise of religion. Trump's order sought to prioritize refugees fleeing religious persecution, which the president said was aimed at helping Christians in Syria. However, critics have argued that the order is discriminatory and unconstitutional.

The order has also caused confusion and outrage across the country, with travelers detained at airports, panicked families searching for relatives, and protesters gathering at airports and other locations to show their opposition to the order. Protests have been reported in cities including New York, Washington, D.C., Boston, and Miami.

The order has also been met with criticism from foreign leaders, including the Dutch Prime Minister Mark Rutte, who said the order goes "in the wrong direction" and that measures taken to prevent terrorism must "respect fundamental rights as well as international law." The Swiss foreign minister Didier Burkhalter also expressed concern that the order breaches the Geneva Conventions by imposing a general ban on people coming from Syria.

Overall, the executive order has been met with widespread criticism and protests, with many arguing that it is discriminatory, unconstitutional, and goes against American values of welcoming refugees and immigrants. The order has also caused confusion and chaos at airports and sparked a global backlash from U.S. allies.

A passenger plane approaching Heathrow Airport in London is believed to have been struck by a drone, according to a police investigation that is currently underway. The British Airways flight from Geneva, which had 132 passengers and five crew members on board, was hit as it approached the airport at 12:50 BST on Sunday. If confirmed, this would be the first such incident in the UK. The plane was hit by the drone at about 1,700ft (580m) while flying over the area of Richmond Park, in south west London. No debris has been found and police have asked for anyone who finds drone parts in the Richmond area to come forward. The Metropolitan Police's aviation security unit, based at Heathrow, is leading the investigation.

After safely landing the plane, the pilot reported an object had struck the front of the Airbus A320. British Airways said the plane was inspected and cleared for the next flight. The incident has highlighted the "very real dangers of reckless, negligent and some times malicious use of drones," according to Chief Superintendent Martin Hendy, head of the Met's aviation policing command.

The Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) has said it is "totally unacceptable" to fly drones close to airports. Steve Landells, from the British Airline Pilots Association (Balpa), said it had been "only a matter of time before we had a drone strike." He called for greater enforcement of existing rules.

Flying a drone near an airport can already be punished with up to five years in prison, and rules also forbid flying them "beyond the direct unaided line of sight" of the operator or near buildings and crowds of people. Drones may not fly above 400ft (122m). The latest incident will only add to the pressure for further steps to be taken.

The US recently introduced a compulsory registration scheme so any drone recovered from an accident can be traced back to its owner. In addition, officials could make it mandatory for drones to run geo-fencing software - that would prevent them flying in restricted areas. The Department for Transport has promised to publish a strategy for unmanned aircraft this year. Pilots have also called for it to fund tests into what would happen if a drone got sucked into an engine or crashed into a plane's windscreen.

Last month, the British Airline Pilots Association noted that while the threat of bird strikes had been well researched, there was little data about how much damage a drone could cause a plane. The incident follows a warning earlier this year by the head of the International Air Transport Association Tony Tyler that drones flown by the general public are "a real and growing threat" to civilian aircraft. The UK Air Proximity Board - which investigates near-miss incidents in UK airspace - said there had been a number of serious near-misses at UK airports involving drones.

David Black, from Blackwing Aerial Services - a company that specialises in licensed commercial drones - said education and enforcement of the current rules were important, particularly for hobbyists. "I think a register is a good idea," he said. "With firearms it has shown it's a good thing... but it has not stopped bad guys from getting guns. If you're going to use them as weapons, bad guys can build them themselves. You need enforcement, but the problem with enforcement is that it costs money and people to carry it out.... There needs to be better technology for detection and avoidance."

Geo-fencing is available in some drones - a database within the drone will not let it take off if it is near an airport so that operators cannot accidentally fly into trouble. Mr Landells from Balpa added: "The law as it stands says you're not supposed to go above 400ft (122m) or 500m away from the base unit, depending on the drone you're using, but we've been seeing incidents up at 8,000 feet, where drones just have no place to be, so we've got to do something. That's a registration process, some sort of tracking, some sort of electronic security - we've got to do something about this."

This incident marks the latest in a series of close encounters between drones and manned aircraft in the UK and US. Experts have warned that the growing popularity of drones poses a serious threat to civilian aircraft and have called for greater regulation and enforcement of existing rules.

Former CIA Director David Petraeus, who resigned last week after admitting to an extramarital affair, will testify before the House Intelligence Committee on Friday. Petraeus' biographer and mistress, Paula Broadwell, is at the center of the scandal, with her government security clearance suspended pending investigations into her contacts with General John Allen, the top U.S. commander in Afghanistan. Broadwell is accused of sending harassing emails to Tampa socialite Jill Kelley, who in turn had been in contact with Allen. The FBI is investigating whether Broadwell released classified information, but a senior law enforcement official close to the Broadwell investigation said it is unlikely she will be prosecuted. Petraeus has not been following the media firestorm surrounding his resignation and instead is focusing on his family. He has offered to testify on the Benghazi attack, which he was scheduled to discuss in private hearings on Capitol Hill this week. The affair ended four months ago, but the two remained in contact, mostly in a professional capacity. President Obama has praised Petraeus' service to the country and said he has no evidence of any potentially damaging breach in national security stemming from the affair. Lawmakers from both parties have complained about not being notified sooner about the investigation that led to Petraeus' resignation.

In the past 11 days, a serial-like killing spree has occurred in the Seminole Heights neighborhood of Tampa, Florida, with three people being shot and killed. The latest victim, Anthony Naiboa, was a 20-year-old who had taken the wrong bus and was shot near a bus stop. The shooter remains at large, and authorities are urging residents to stay vigilant, turn on their porch lights, and walk in groups. The FBI, Hillsborough County Sheriff's Office, St. Petersburg Police, Crime Stoppers, and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives are all assisting in the investigation, which is offering a $25,000 reward for information leading to a suspect's arrest. The victims, Naiboa, Benjamin Edward Mitchell, 22, and Monica Caridad Hoffa, 32, were all connected by proximity and timeframe, but there is no known motive or connection between the type of weapon or ammunition used in the killings. The community is in shock, and residents are encouraged to stay informed and report any suspicious activity.

In a shocking turn of events, a 75-year-old Detroit-area grandmother, Sandra Layne, was convicted of second-degree murder for fatally shooting her 17-year-old grandson, Jonathan Hoffman. The verdict was delivered on Tuesday, March 15, 2013, in Pontiac, Michigan. Layne's son-in-law, Michael Hoffman, and his ex-wife, Jennifer, described the verdict as a "vindication" for their son, whose actions and lifestyle were questioned during Layne's trial.

Jennifer Hoffman expressed her dismay, calling her mother a "monster" and stating that it was hard to comprehend such an act from her own mother. She added that her son is now in heaven, a place Layne will never reach. Sandra Layne testified that she bought a gun due to fear of Jonathan and his friends after he moved in with her during his senior year in high school.

The jury found Layne guilty of second-degree murder, using a gun during a felony, and likely faces at least 14 years in prison. Defense attorney Jerome Sabbota stated that Layne was "devastated" by the verdict and is sorrowful over her grandson's death.

During the trial, Layne portrayed herself as a caring grandmother who felt overwhelmed when Jonathan was hospitalized for drug use a year ago. However, the jury was swayed by an incriminating 911 call made by Jonathan, in which he pleaded for help as Layne shot him. The jury reportedly played the call repeatedly in the jury room, which they found crucial to their decision.

The Hoffmans, who are divorced and moved to Arizona, had initially agreed to let Layne take in Jonathan for his final year of school in 2011. The tragic incident has left the family devastated, with Jennifer Hoffman expressing her grief and anger towards her mother.

Tyler Hadley, a 17-year-old from Port St. Lucie, Florida, is accused of brutally murdering his parents with a hammer. The double murder occurred on Saturday, and Hadley allegedly confessed the crime to his best friend, Michael Mandell, stating that he had taken three ecstasy pills before the incident. Hadley reportedly told Mandell that he believed the devil possessed him and intended to commit suicide.

The partygoers, who arrived later that night, were unaware of the gruesome events that had taken place earlier. Hadley, who was on suicide watch, made his first court appearance on Tuesday and was charged with second-degree murder. The prosecution plans to argue for life in prison, as Hadley is not eligible for the death penalty due to his age.

Details of the crime emerged from a police affidavit, which revealed that Hadley confessed to killing his parents and then hosting a party for about 60 friends while their bodies were hidden in a locked bedroom. Mandell, who has known Hadley since they were 8, was initially skeptical of his friend's confession but was convinced when he saw Blake Hadley's body.

Hadley allegedly took his parents' cell phones and credit cards to prevent them from contacting the authorities and to access their money. The police arrived at the scene after receiving an anonymous tip and found the bodies of Mary Jo Hadley, 47, and Blake Hadley, 54, beneath furniture piled into the bedroom from other rooms in the house.

Dr. Julie Holland, an assistant professor of psychiatry at New York University, stated that ecstasy is not known to cause violent reactions. The tablets Hadley allegedly took may have been sold as ecstasy, but could have been anything else. Mandell's mother, Michele Mandell, described Hadley as a "great kid."

In a gruesome discovery, 18 dismembered and beheaded bodies were found inside two vans near Lake Chapala, a tourist spot near Guadalajara, Mexico. The Jalisco state Prosecutor, Tomas Coronado, confirmed that the bodies were dismembered and that three more severed heads were found along with the body parts. The area has been a site of violent turf battles between the Jalisco New Generation gang, allied with the Sinaloa cartel, and the Zetas drug cartel.

The killings may be linked to the abduction of 12 people who later escaped in the same area on Tuesday. A woman allegedly watching the captives was detained and told investigators that the kidnappings were a repercussion of events in Tamaulipas. This could be a reference to the slayings of 23 people found in Nuevo Laredo, a city on the border with Texas, where drug cartels are engaged in an escalating turf war.

Handwritten messages were found in the vans, which were signed by the Zetas, suggesting that the massacre was part of an ongoing conflict between the Zetas and the Sinaloa cartel. The Zetas have been battling the Jalisco New Generation gang, a minor cartel allied with the Sinaloa cartel, for dominance of the Mexican drug trade. The Zetas cartel, known for its brutality, controls most of eastern Mexico and much of the north.

The United States is home to an estimated 70 to 80 million pet dogs, making up 37 to 47 percent of all American households. In a new genomic study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, researchers offer strong evidence that domesticated dogs originated in Central Asia, around modern-day Nepal and Mongolia.

Previous genetic studies of dog lineages have concluded that domestication occurred in Southern China around 16,500 years ago, but the earliest archaeological evidence of domesticated canines is found in Europe and Siberia. The new study, led by Adam Boyko of Cornell University, analyzed DNA samples from 5,392 dogs, including 549 "village dogs" from 38 countries, making it the largest ever of worldwide canine genetic diversity.

The study found that genetic diversity is highest in Central Asia, specifically Nepal and Mongolia. Genetic diversity then fans out like ripples in a pool, with areas like Afghanistan, Egypt, India, and Vietnam—all ringing around the possible center of origin in Central Asia—having the next highest levels and so on. Dogs studied in geographic regions farther away, like the South Pacific and Americas were almost exclusively of European origin.

The researchers broke new ground by analyzing DNA samples from so-called “village dogs,” which have lived alongside humans throughout the world since dogs first evolved from wolves and were domesticated around 15,000 years ago. "Although they associate with humans, village dogs are more or less expected to make it on their own," says Boyko. "They are very different from pure-bred dogs genetically because they are free-breeding, so in a genetic sense, they are a natural population."

The study suggests that hunter-gatherers in central Asia domesticated dogs from grey wolves. A combination of increasing human population density, better hunting methods, and climate change may have reduced the availability of prey and pushed some wolves towards scavenging, which favored tameness and smaller size. This would in turn have reduced their hunting prowess further, setting them on the path to domestication.

Other researchers have welcomed the tracing of domestication to the neighborhood of central Asia, although some dispute the precise site. "They are actually putting the origin very close to where we put it, just 1000 kilometres away in parts of Asia south of the Yangtze river," says Peter Savolainen of the Royal Institute of Technology in Solna, Sweden. "So I would say the consensus pointing to south and east rather than central Asia is quite clear."

The study is significant because it reaches a clear conclusion that can be tested further. "We are excited to be working with Boyko’s group and others," says Greger Larson of the University of Oxford. "Having collected more than 1500 ancient dogs and wolves over the past few years, our lab has begun our next-generation sequencing effort." The genetic data will then be compared with morphological data from more than 4000 specimens going right back into the late Pleistocene.

In the aftermath of the earthquake in Haiti, a local eatery named Muncheez has transformed into a community kitchen, providing free meals to those in need. Co-owner Gilbert Bailly initiated the initiative when he realized his ingredients were about to spoil, and since then, the restaurant has been serving rice, beans, chicken, and spaghetti to over 1,000 people daily. Bailly's nephew gathered additional food supplies from local businesses and even the Dominican Republic when donations ran out. The restaurant's Facebook page is now being used to seek further assistance.

Leonce Bell, a 40-year-old resident who lost his home and job in the earthquake, is among those receiving meals. He and his family currently reside in a public park where food is scarce. Bell, who hasn't eaten in three days, is saving the meal he received at Muncheez for his child.

International aid group World Vision has learned about Muncheez's improvised soup kitchen and is now delivering trucks of dry food to the restaurant. Along with their meals, people are now receiving bags of bulgur and lentils to share with their families. Bailly hopes this additional aid will alleviate some of the suffering in the community. In small ways, people across Port-au-Prince are banding together to share food and support each other during this time of despair.

In an effort to support local businesses, cities are imposing restrictions on tech companies offering free meals to their employees. This comes as tech giants like Facebook, Google, and LinkedIn have long provided high-end dining options for their workers, including pizza ovens, sushi counters, and ice cream.

The city of Mountain View has barred Facebook from serving free food to its employees when they move into a new office later this year. This restriction was enforced after local restaurants complained that free meals at Google had damaged their business. The city of San Francisco hopes to follow suit with similar regulations.

Facebook's new office in Mountain View will not have a corporate cafeteria with free food for about 2,000 employees. Instead, the company can cover the cost of employees’ food if they dine in restaurants that are open to the public. This rule is designed to encourage tech workers to spend money in and integrate with the local community, rather than arriving in a bus each day and never leaving the building.

The absence of an in-house cafeteria will help boost local retailers, according to Steve Rasmussen, owner of the Milk Pail Market, a produce market blocks from Facebook’s future office. Rasmussen is in talks with local restaurants to stock ready-to-eat meals at Milk Pail Market, which currently lacks such fare.

Mountain View has been seeking other concessions from tech giants, such as subsidizing the rent for small businesses on their property or having agreements with retailers to patronize their businesses. Google didn't respond to a request for comment on its North Bayshore plans regarding small businesses.

In San Francisco, restaurants have opened in the Mid-Market neighborhood in hopes of gaining customers from the tech companies there, but a number have shuttered and struggled. Chris Foley, co-owner of the Market, a food hall underneath Twitter’s headquarters in San Francisco, hopes that one day the city will follow Mountain View’s lead and ban on-site workplace cafeterias.

This move is part of a larger trend of cities seeking to balance the needs of tech companies with the needs of local businesses and communities. As tech companies come under increasing pressure to deliver more value to the communities they inhabit, cities are clamping down on campus cafeterias in an attempt to support local restaurants.

In August 2015, a tragic incident occurred during a bungee jumping event in Spain. A 17-year-old Dutch girl named Vera Mol, who was part of a group of teenagers, died after jumping from a 130-foot-high bridge on the northern coast. The instructor, working for Aqua21 Aventura, had given the command "No jump," but due to his poor English pronunciation, Vera apparently heard "Now jump" and leaped to her death before her harness was secured.

An appeals court in Cantabria recently upheld a ruling that the instructor could face criminal charges, including accidental homicide, if prosecutors decide to proceed with the case. The court's judgment stated that the instructor's use of "no jump" could be misunderstood as an explicit order to jump by the victim.

The court also criticized the instructor for not checking Vera's ID to ensure she was over 18, as bungee jumping from the road bridge where the incident occurred is allegedly banned under Spanish regulation. The case highlights the importance of clear communication and safety measures in adventure sports activities.

A practitioner of Chinese herbal medicine, Dr. Weidong "Henry" Han, his wife Huijie "Jennie" Yu, and their 5-year-old daughter Emily Han were found dead in their California home on Wednesday. The crime scene was discovered during a welfare check, and authorities are investigating the case as a homicide. Dr. Han owned and operated the Santa Barbara Herb Clinic since 1991, providing traditional treatments such as acupuncture and herbal formulas. The family resided in a modern home in a gated 7-acre ranchette outside Santa Barbara. Authorities have not yet released the details of the incident or the names of the victims pending next-of-kin notification. The community is in shock, especially the Foothill Elementary School where Emily was enrolled in kindergarten. The Sheriff's Office will provide an update on the case on Friday at noon.

A Dallas pet-sitting company, Prestigious Pets, filed a $1 million lawsuit against a Plano couple, Michelle and Robert Duchouquette, for a one-star review they posted on Yelp. The lawsuit accused the couple of defamation, business disparagement, and breach of contract. However, the case was dismissed after the Duchouquettes argued that it should be dismissed based on the Texas Anti-SLAPP statute, which allows judges to dismiss frivolous suits filed against people who speak out about a matter of public concern.

The Duchouquettes had hired Prestigious Pets in October 2015 to watch their two dogs and betta fish while they were on vacation. In the Yelp review, they stated that their betta fish's tank looked murky in a video feed, the billing was messed up, and the company tried to charge to return the keys to the family. Prestigious Pets claimed that the Duchouquettes violated a non-disparagement clause in their contract by posting the review, and that their statements were false and defamatory.

The judge agreed to dismiss the case, and the Duchouquettes are now entitled to recover court costs and reasonable and necessary attorney fees from Prestigious Pets. The judge's decision was based on the Texas anti-SLAPP law, which allows defendants in cases involving issues of speech to seek a dismissal if the plaintiff cannot establish a prima facie case for each essential element of the claim in question.

The Duchouquettes expressed their relief and gratitude regarding the ruling, stating that "we should all have the opportunity to express our opinions without the fear of a lawsuit." The case has attracted attention from advocates for consumers and free expression, and Yelp has begun publicly flagging certain companies that are believed to be making questionable legal threats over online reviews.

The Internet Archive is implementing crawls to archive web pages as they are created and preserve links to the original versions of pages, even if they are changed or removed from the web. This initiative aims to fix broken links on the web. In a separate news, a tragic incident occurred in Seattle where a University of Washington student was severely beaten by her boyfriend, also a UW student, who is identified as Casey Henderson. The victim, a 22-year-old woman, was taken to Harborview Medical Center but later succumbed to her injuries. Henderson was arrested and his bail was set at $1 million. The case is now being investigated as a homicide, and formal charges are expected to be filed. The Seattle Times typically does not identify suspects until they are charged. The incident was reported to the police by a neighbor who heard a violent confrontation next door.

In an interview with CNBC, Target's CEO, Gregg Steinhafel, defended the four-day delay in informing customers about a security breach that occurred between November 27 and December 15, affecting as many as 110 million customers. The breach involved hackers infecting Target's point-of-sale terminals with malware to steal personal information, including payment card information, names, mailing addresses, phone numbers, and email addresses.

Steinhafel explained that the delay was necessary for investigators to identify and eliminate the malware, prepare stores and call centers for consumer reactions, and initiate the investigation work and forensic work.

Target's breach is not an isolated incident, as Upscale department store Neiman Marcus and at least three other unidentified retailers also suffered security breaches during the holiday shopping season. The practice of payment card skimming at point-of-sale terminals has become more frequent in recent years, with retailers like Barnes & Noble and Subway also being victims.

Target is now facing criticism for the delay in disclosing the breach, but Steinhafel argues that the four-day delay was a swift response from Target's perspective. The company is now trying to woo back customers with a public relations effort, including full-page newspaper advertisements and an interview with Steinhafel on CNBC.

Steinhafel also expressed his support for the adoption of payment card technology that stores customer information on computer chips and requires users to type in personal identification numbers. The National Retail Federation has called for tougher security standards following the breaches at Target and other retailers.

The breaches could mark a watershed moment for security standards, with calls growing for changes in the protection of consumer information. The new enthusiasm for "Chip-and-PIN" payment cards, which have computer chips built into them and require users to type in PINs, is a sign of the change. However, it is not clear whether "Chip-and-PIN" technology would have prevented the breaches at Target and elsewhere.

The Forbes Celebrity 100 list ranks celebrities based on a combination of their earnings and media visibility, including print, television, radio, online exposure, and social media power. The list includes actors, musicians, athletes, authors, and TV personalities. The earnings are calculated by talking to industry insiders and consist of pretax income between May 1, 2011, and May 1, 2012, without deducting management, agent, or attorney fees. The fame is measured using Google blogs, Factiva, LexisNexis, The Nielsen Co., Pollstar, Box Office Mojo, Euromonitor International, Publishers Weekly, and IMDBPro. Jennifer Lopez tops the list this year with $52 million in earnings and massive fame, unseating Lady Gaga who drops to fifth place with $52 million in earnings, down from $90 million last year. Oprah Winfrey ranks second with $165 million, followed by Justin Bieber in third place with $55 million. Newcomers to the list include Kim and Khloe Kardashian, Ashton Kutcher, and others. The full list can be found on Forbes' website.

In the Town of Paradise, a contract has been awarded to ARRB Group to assess the damage caused to roads by large trucks and equipment during the cleanup process following the devastating Camp Fire. ARRB uses innovative technology, including lasers, to collect data before and after the debris removal process. The Town of Paradise expressed gratitude to the North Valley Community Foundation for their donation that helped fund this survey.

However, the peace was disrupted when photos posted by Rob Freestone, a Camp Fire cleanup worker, on his Facebook page drew outrage from social media users. The images, which were later published on the Town of Paradise Facebook page, showed Freestone and other workers posing in destroyed properties, a dead cat with a beer bottle near its mouth, and him jumping on a burned-out trampoline.

Paradise police have announced they will pursue criminal charges against Freestone for his disrespectful actions. The possibility of charges includes being in an evacuated area, as Freestone was operating outside of his responsibility as a cleanup worker when taking the photos.

Freestone worked as a third-party contractor for Pacific Gas and Electric Co. (PG&E). Following the incident, PG&E confirmed that Freestone has been removed from the Camp Fire cleanup. Bigge Crane and Rigging Co., the company Freestone worked for, also terminated the employment of three employees involved in the incident.

The Town of Paradise condemned the insensitive behavior, calling it unacceptable and reprehensible. The Paradise Police Department is investigating the matter, and Bigge Crane and Rigging issued a statement expressing regret for the residents of Paradise and Butte County having to endure such an egregious insult during an already devastating time.

PG&E did not immediately respond to a request for comment regarding the incident. This incident underscores the need for sensitivity and respect during the cleanup and recovery process following the Camp Fire, a tragedy that has already caused immense suffering for the residents of Paradise and Butte County.

Stephanie Clifford, also known as Stormy Daniels, a pornographic film actress, has publicly accused President Donald Trump and his attorney Michael Cohen of using intimidation and legal tactics to silence her regarding their relationship. In an effort to void a non-disclosure agreement (NDA) that Trump never signed, Daniels filed a lawsuit in Los Angeles, California. Instead of acknowledging the NDA's invalidity, Trump and Cohen have threatened Daniels with millions of dollars in damages if she speaks out.

Daniels recently offered to return the $130,000 she was previously paid in exchange for the right to speak openly, but Trump and Cohen did not respond. Daniels is seeking funds for legal fees, out-of-pocket costs associated with the lawsuit, arbitration, and her right to speak openly, security expenses, and potential damages.

In a statement to The Daily Beast, Daniels accused her lawyer, Michael Avenatti, of filing a defamation suit against Trump against her wishes and speaking on her behalf without her consent. Daniels also claimed that Avenatti had ignored her requests for accounting information about a legal defense and safety fund and launched another crowdfunding campaign without her knowledge.

Avenatti responded, stating that the money raised through the crowdfunding effort has primarily been used for Daniels' security expenses and other costs. He also argued that he hasn't received any fees from the crowdfunding effort and that his firm has spent over a thousand hours on the case.

The situation between Daniels and Avenatti has raised ethical concerns, with a New York University Law School professor suggesting that Avenatti could face serious problems if he sued Trump against Daniels' wishes. The current CrowdJustice site is one of three fundraisers highlighted on CrowdJustice's homepage, with an earlier site raising over $580,000 for Daniels' legal defense.

Daniels and Avenatti have become prominent figures since the revelation of a hush-money payment made by Cohen during the presidential campaign. Daniels claims she had an affair with Trump years before his presidency, a claim Trump denies. Cohen admitted in court in August that he made illegal payments during the campaign at Trump's direction.

Avenatti has also faced personal and professional challenges, including allegations of domestic violence and criticism for his handling of cases involving migrant children and tax issues. Despite these challenges, he has become a prominent figure in the #Resistance and has openly considered a 2020 presidential bid.

SpaceX, the space transportation company owned by Elon Musk, has announced that Japanese billionaire Yusaku Maezawa, the founder and CEO of online fashion retailer Zozo, will be the first private passenger on a voyage around the moon. The mission is planned for 2023 aboard SpaceX's Big Falcon Rocket (BFR) spaceship, which is yet to be built. Maezawa, who made headlines last year for purchasing a painting by Jean-Michel Basquiat for $110.5 million, plans to invite six to eight artists to join him on the lunar flyby. The BFR, a super heavy-lift launch vehicle, is expected to conduct its first orbital flights in two to three years and could eventually fly humans and cargo to Mars. The mission is subject to successful test flights to ensure safety. Maezawa's identity was revealed at an event at SpaceX's headquarters in Hawthorne, California. In a country known for its staid corporate culture, Maezawa is one of a small group of mould-breaking billionaires widely recognized by the general public.

The announcement marks an important step towards enabling access for everyday people who dream of traveling to space. Only 24 humans have visited the moon, all of them Americans; 12 of them landed on the moon. Nasa's Apollo 17 in December 1972 marked the last time humans landed on the moon, or went beyond low Earth orbit. Maezawa will not land on the moon but will travel on a free return trajectory, which will bring his BFR ship back to Earth after it has gone around the far side of the satellite.

The BFR has never flown, but Musk has released some technical details about it. The rocket is expected to stand 118m high and have a diameter of 9m. Eventually, the BFR should be able to lift a whopping 150 tonnes into low-Earth orbit - that is more than the US Saturn V rockets that lofted the Apollo spacecraft.

Musk has previously said he wants the rocket to be ready for an unpiloted trip to Mars in 2022, with a crewed flight in 2024, though his ambitious production targets have been known to slip. The amount Maezawa is paying for the trip was not disclosed, but he told Reuters the total sum was "much higher" than the cost of a Basquiat painting. Musk said Maezawa had outlaid a significant deposit and would have a material impact on the cost of developing the BFR, which he estimated at about $5 billion.

Maezawa is one of Japan's most colorful executives and is a regular fixture in the country's gossipy weeklies with his collection of foreign and Japanese art, fast cars, and celebrity girlfriend. He made his fortune by founding the wildly popular shopping site Zozotown. His company, Zozo, officially called Start Today Co Ltd, also offers a made-to-measure service using a polka dot bodysuit, the Zozosuit. In a country known for its staid corporate culture, the businessman is one of a small group of mould-breaking billionaires widely recognized by the general public.

With SpaceX, Amazon.com founder Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin and entrepreneur Richard Branson’s Virgin Galactic battling it out to launch private-sector spacecraft, Maezawa will join a growing list of celebrities and the ultra-rich who have secured seats on flights offered on the under-development vessels. Those who have signed up to fly on Virgin Galactic sub-orbital missions include actor Leonardo DiCaprio and pop star Justin Bieber. A 90-minute flight costs $250,000. Short sightseeing trips to space aboard Blue Origin’s New Shepard rocket are likely to cost around $200,000 to $300,000, at least to start, Reuters reported in July. These trips were not attractive given the limited amount of time spent in zero-gravity, Maezawa told Reuters. "If I’m going to go to space, I’d rather go as far as I can," he said.

Zozo shares fell as much as 4.7 percent and closed down 2.4 percent after the announcement. Still, a jaunt around the moon would provide publicity for Zozo, which has ambitious overseas sales targets to be driven by its custom-made private clothing line. The diminutive Maezawa, who as a young man struggled to find clothes that fit, hopes to revolutionize the fashion industry through his Zozosuit, which, once donned, allows users to upload their body measurements and order a growing number of made-to-measure items.

SpaceX has already upended the space industry with its relatively low-cost reusable Falcon 9 rockets. The company has completed more than 50 successful Falcon launches and snagged billions of dollars’ worth of contracts, including deals with NASA and the U.S. Department of Defense. When asked about Boeing Co CEO Dennis Muilenburg’s prediction that the first humans will be carried to Mars on a Boeing rocket, Musk responded, "Game on," to the sound of cheers from employees assembled at the event.

The Colorado Tourism Office has released a survey indicating that legal recreational marijuana is becoming a significant factor in attracting visitors to Colorado. The survey, commissioned by the office and presented to the board of directors, shows that nearly 49% of potential summertime visitors were influenced by Colorado's marijuana laws when considering a trip. The state's "Come to Life" ad campaign, which does not mention marijuana, has been successful in attracting visitors, with the campaign reaching 11.1 million households and generating an economic impact of $2.6 billion this summer. However, only 8% of tourists who responded to the survey said they visited a marijuana dispensary during their trip to Colorado. The survey's director noted that the questions may not have captured the opinion of people who opted out of Colorado travel because of legal pot. The new tourism chief, Cathy Ritter, has stated that legal cannabis is a topic for discussion and further research. The survey results suggest that marijuana is having both positive and negative influences on travel decisions. The survey was conducted among 3,254 tourists from target markets in various cities, with about 10% of those surveyed having vacationed in Colorado between April and September. The retail sales of recreational marijuana became legal in Colorado in January 2014. The survey also found that while some people surveyed were purchasing marijuana legally for the first time, 200 of the 325 people used marijuana daily. Many people said they preferred to buy products legally because legal weed is more likely to have been tested, making it safer to use. The survey results indicate that marijuana is not the primary reason for tourists to visit Colorado, but it is becoming a significant factor in their decision-making process.

The article discusses a clash between Haredi worshippers and Israeli police in Jerusalem's Old City, which occurred during a court-authorized prayer session by the Women of the Wall group at the Western Wall. The Women of the Wall, a group challenging the Orthodox monopoly over rites at the Western Wall, were seeking a greater role in prayer ritual. The police presence at the site was seen as a sign of progress by some women worshippers, and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has asked former cabinet minister and Jewish leader Natan Sharansky to seek a compromise to permit the Women of the Wall to hold prayers without exacerbating tensions with the ultra-Orthodox Jews. Sharansky has proposed a formula to widen a separate zone at the Western Wall for egalitarian prayer, but neither side nor the government has yet embraced the proposal. The article also mentions that when tweeting, Twitter stores the location of the tweet, and users can switch location on/off before each tweet and always have the option to delete their location history.

A team of physicists at CERN, the world's largest physics lab, has reported a surprising discovery that could potentially challenge Einstein's theory of special relativity. The researchers found that subatomic particles called neutrinos appear to travel faster than light, which contradicts the theory that nothing can travel faster than light. The results come from the Oscillation Project with Emulsion-tRacking Apparatus (OPERA) experiment, which detects neutrinos fired through the Earth from CERN in Switzerland. The OPERA researchers measured the time it took for roughly 16,000 neutrinos to travel 730 kilometers from CERN to a detector in Italy and found that they arrived 60 nanoseconds faster than expected if they were traveling at light speed. The researchers acknowledge that the result is extraordinary and will likely be met with skepticism. They are inviting the broader physics community to scrutinize their measurements and are looking to the US and Japan to confirm the results. If confirmed, the discovery would force a fundamental rethink of the laws of nature and could have significant implications for modern physics. The researchers are currently looking for systematic errors that could explain the result.

Tova Gerson, a 32-year-old New Jersey housewife and mother of four, has filed a $5 million federal lawsuit against Century 21, alleging the department store defrauded her and other customers by ripping off 80 cents using a coupon-fraud scheme. Gerson claims she used a $5 off coupon during a January shopping spree at Century 21's Paramus, NJ store, but was refunded 80 cents less than expected when she returned a $17.97 item, as the coupon was pro-rated over all the goods she purchased. Gerson's lawsuit, filed by her lawyer father, Harry Katz, seeks damages for herself and other shoppers who may have been affected by the store's alleged fraudulent and misleading promotion. Century 21 has not yet commented on the matter. Gerson's lawyer, Harry Katz, has a history of suing retailers over alleged coupon schemes, with previous suits against Dick's Sporting Goods, Casual Male, and The Children's Place either dismissed or settled. Gerson refused to comment when approached at her home.

In a significant rescue mission, FOUR PAWS International, a global animal welfare organization, has successfully evacuated two surviving animals, Simba the lion and Lula the bear, from the war-torn Mosul Zoo in Iraq. The animals were found abandoned and in dire conditions, suffering from various diseases due to malnutrition and lack of care. The Montazah al-Morour Zoo, located in the eastern half of Mosul, was nearly destroyed during the battle, with most of its animals perishing due to the conflict. This rescue mission marks a rare moment of hope amidst the ongoing conflict in Mosul, where hundreds of thousands of civilians have been displaced.

In a heart-wrenching turn of events, Bill Hudson, the father of actresses Kate Hudson and Oliver Hudson, has vowed to cut ties with his eldest children following a series of public jabs on Father's Day. In this news article from CNN, it is reported that Andrew Shirvell, an assistant attorney general in Michigan, has been waging a six-month-long online campaign against Chris Armstrong, the openly gay student assembly president at the University of Michigan in Ann Arbor. The study published in the journal Socioaffective Neuroscience and Psychology challenges the notion of sex addiction, as it found no evidence to support the idea that hypersexual brains react differently to sexual stimuli than brains with high libidos. The research, led by UCLA's Nicole Prause, measured brain responses to sexual images using electroencephalography (EEG) and found that the P300 response, which is higher when a person notices something new or interesting, was only related to sexual desire, not hypersexuality or sexual compulsivity.

The study involved 52 volunteers, aged 18 to 39, who reported having difficulties controlling their viewing of sexual images. They filled out questionnaires covering various topics, including sexual behaviors, sexual desire, sexual compulsions, and the possible negative cognitive and behavioral outcomes of sexual behavior. Participants had scores comparable to individuals seeking help for hypersexual problems.

While the debate over sex addiction continues, this study provides a significant challenge to the existing theories of sex addiction. However, it is important to note that a 2012 study by Prause's colleague Rory Reid supported the reliability of the proposed DSM-5 diagnostic criteria for hypersexual disorder. Yet, this study did not focus on the validity of sex addiction or impulsivity and did not use biophysiological data in the analysis.

The study's findings could have significant implications for the understanding and treatment of sexual compulsive behavior, as they question the addiction model and force a reconsideration of how we think and talk about these problems. The debate about sex addiction underlines important questions about how psychiatrists should categorize the difference between a clinical mental illness that can be demonstrated in a lab, such as substance addiction, and other forms of mental distress, which deserve equal care and compassion but don't necessarily indicate a medical mental illness.

The study was funded by an Idaho State University Graduate Student Committee grant and involved collaborations with the University of New Mexico and Idaho State University. The research was conducted at the UCLA Department of Psychiatry and Biobehavioral Sciences, which is part of the Semel Institute for Neuroscience and Human Behavior at UCLA.

The Confederate submarine H.L. Hunley, which sank the Union ship USS Housatonic during the American Civil War in 1864, has been a mystery for over 150 years regarding the cause of death for its eight-man crew. A new study published in the journal Plos One suggests that the crew died instantly from the shockwave generated by the submarine's own torpedo explosion.

The study, led by biomechanist Rachel Lance, involved constructing a 6-1/2-foot scale model of the submarine and subjecting it to pressurized air blasts and black powder explosions while monitoring the effects with a series of onboard sensors. The findings suggest that the ensuing shockwave travelled through the soft tissues of the crewmen's bodies, causing catastrophic injuries, particularly to their lungs and brains.

The study's conclusions fill in an important gap in US Civil War history and offer fresh insights into human physiology and the physical forces we are able to endure. The crew's skeletal remains, found seated at their hand-crank stations, exhibited no broken bones, and the submarine was startlingly intact, with only a hole in one conning tower and an apparently broken window as noticeable blemishes.

The findings have been met with some skepticism, with the Friends of the Hunley, part of the Hunley Project, declining to comment on the research. However, the study's authors believe they have solved a significant part of the mystery surrounding the H.L. Hunley and its crew's fate.

Barbara Walters, a veteran journalist and co-host of ABC's "The View" and "20/20," announced her retirement, effective summer 2014. Walters, who has been with ABC News for over 37 years, will continue as co-executive producer of "The View" and will be involved in selecting new co-hosts to replace Joy Behar and Elisabeth Hasselbeck. Walters, who turns 84 in September, will remain on "The View" through the next season.

Rumors of Walters' retirement first surfaced in March following a health scare and hospital stay. Despite brushing off retirement rumors in recent weeks, Walters confirmed the news on Monday's edition of "The View."

Walters began her career in 1961 as a researcher for NBC's "Today" and went on to become the first woman to host an evening newscast when she was paired with Harry Reasoner on the ABC Evening News in 1976. Walters landed dozens of important interviews throughout her career, including Anwar Al Sadat and Menachem Begin, the Shah of Iran, Boris Yeltsin, Vladimir Putin, China's Jian Zemin, Margaret Thatcher, Fidel Castro, Indira Ghandi, Hugo Chavez, Michael Jackson, and Monica Lewinsky.

ABC News president Ben Sherwood praised Walters, saying "There's only one Barbara Walters. And we look forward to making her final year on television as remarkable, path-breaking and news-making as Barbara herself."

Walters' retirement will include retrospectives of her many Oscar and Ten Most Fascinating People specials as well as a multi-part career retrospective to air on ABC. Walters plans to sit back and admire the women and some men who will take her place on "The View."

On Monday, a woman died and dozens of people were hospitalized, with three remaining in critical condition, after a smoke-filled incident at the L'Enfant Plaza Metro station in Washington, D.C. The incident occurred when a Yellow Line train filled with smoke in a tunnel just south of the station around 3:20 p.m. Passengers reported difficulty breathing and being trapped inside the train's cars as the tunnel filled with thick, black smoke. Firefighters gained access to the tunnel and evacuated the passengers, with one injured firefighter being transported from the scene.

The exact cause of the smoke and fire is unknown, but NTSB investigators reported an electrical arcing involving the third rail and the power supply cables to that rail prior to the fire. There was water along the tracks near the accident scene, which may have facilitated smoke along the third rail. The FBI is assisting Metro Transit Police in determining the cause, which is standard procedure for incidents in the capital region.

The woman's cause of death and identity remain unknown. Metro General Manager and Chief Executive Officer Richard Sarles expressed his condolences and said that thoughts and prayers go out to the family of the passenger who passed away. D.C. Mayor Muriel Bowser also expressed her condolences and thanked the first responders who assisted passengers during the evacuation and at the scene.

Green Line trains are operating on a normal schedule, while Blue Line trains will replace the Yellow Line from Huntington to Largo Town Center. The L'Enfant Metro station reopened for Orange, Silver, and Blue line service on Monday evening, but Green and Yellow line service remained suspended through the end of the day between the Gallery Place and Navy Yard/Pentagon stations. It is unknown if service will be restored for the Tuesday morning commute.

The incident has caused some controversy, as a tweet from the Netflix series "House of Cards" was criticized for its poor timing, as it was posted on the same day as the incident and referenced a storyline on the show in which one character pushes another in front of a subway train. The tweet has since been deleted.

Crystal Matrau-Belt, a 24-year-old woman from Michigan, recently gave birth to her son, Jeremiah James Matrau-Skokan, at the Bronson Medical Hospital in Kalamazoo. Unfortunately, her fiance, Emil Skokan III, and her mother, Peggy Nichols, were killed in a car accident on their way to meet her at the hospital.

Matrau-Belt had called Skokan before her emergency cesarean section to tell him they were going to deliver the baby. However, it was the last time she spoke to him, as he lost control of the car and died in the crash. Nichols was also in the car and was killed as well.

Matrau-Belt's extended family, including her stepfather and stepmother, were there to help her during the delivery. Hours after delivering her son, Matrau-Belt's family broke the news that her fiance and mother had been killed in a car accident.

Matrau-Belt named her son Jeremiah, a name she and Skakon had agreed on just before her delivery. She sees a lot of her fiance's personality in her young son already. Matrau-Belt is expected to be discharged from the hospital tonight so that she can attend the funerals for her fiance and mother later this week.

Matrau-Belt said she wants others to "chereish every moment" and not take life for granted. She is struggling to balance the joy of welcoming her son into the world with the grief of losing her fiance and mother.

Skokan was a caring, hard-working, and intelligent man who loved tinkering with his fish tank and their 20-plus fish. He spent all night Friday cleaning the house for the baby and setting up his bassinet. Skokan was also handy around the house and had been helping Matrau-Belt's mother and stepfather work on their house, which had caught fire in February 2015.

Nichols was the most caring person Matrau-Belt had ever met. She treated Skokan like her own son and was excited to meet her first biological grandchild. Nichols had bought "his entire wardrobe," a car seat, and a stroller for the baby.

Authorities have said speed was a factor in the crash that killed Skokan and Nichols. Matrau-Belt said they were trying to get to the hospital as quickly as possible because a lot of medical stuff was happening and they wanted to be there for her.

Jeremiah has his mother's lips, but his facial features and mannerisms already mirror his father's, especially when he furrows his brow when he doesn't like something. Matrau-Belt thinks he'll have curly, dirty blond hair like Skokan's, who spent four years growing out his hair to shoulder-length curls.

Matrau-Belt is struggling to balance her grief for both her fiance and her mother, as they were both important figures in her life. She will soon have to face the difficulty of burying the man she was going to marry and her own mother. Skokan's funeral will be at 11 a.m. on Wednesday, December 16, at Langeland Family Funeral Homes, Memorial Chappel, and Nichols' funeral will be at 11 a.m. on Friday, December 18, with interment following at Mt. Ever-Rest Memorial Park South.

Matrau-Belt is receiving support from her family during this difficult time. She said she wants to celebrate Jeremiah's first Christmas, but it will be a difficult one without her loved ones.

The article discusses the unrest in Milwaukee's Sherman Park neighborhood for the second consecutive night, which occurred on Sunday, August 14th.
