A Southwest Airlines flight from Chicago to New Jersey was forced to land in Cleveland due to a cracked window on Wednesday, with no reported injuries. The plane, Flight 957, never lost cabin pressure and the pilots did not declare an emergency. The plane was taken out of service for a maintenance review. The incident comes two weeks after a Southwest Airlines plane made an emergency landing in Philadelphia due to an engine explosion and a blown-out window, resulting in a fatality.

Aviation experts suggest that even the slightest defect or micro-crack in a plane window can cause cracks. Windows are periodically polished to remove tiny cracks caused by exposure to chemicals and the sun's rays. Experts say problems with windows should be detected during regular inspections and maintenance.

The damaged window on the Cleveland flight affected only one layer of the multiple acrylic layers. Plane windows are built to withstand such damage, with each pane designed to withstand two to four times the amount of pressure it would normally experience while in flight. The outer pane takes the pressure of the aircraft, and the inner one takes over when the outer one breaks.

Jim Lee, the founder and CEO of Lee Aerospace, expects investigators to be able to determine the cause of the damage easily. He assures that while the damage may startle passengers, it is not dangerous.

The Loughner family, residing in Tucson, Arizona, is in deep mourning following the mass shooting perpetrated by their son, Jared, who is the main suspect in the attack that left six people dead and 13 others injured, including Congresswoman Gabrielle Giffords. The family's neighbor, Wayne Smith, reported that Randy and Amy Loughner have been devastated by the events and are preparing to release a public statement.

The Loughners are known for their preference for privacy, with Randy being described as a reclusive individual who seldom engaged in neighborhood activities. Federal investigators are working to build a case against Jared, who they believe had psychological problems and planned the attack.

The Loughners' home is secluded, with its front entirely covered by shrubbery. Neighbors, who barely knew the family, have shared mixed experiences with Randy, with some reporting hostile interactions. The family's last name was unknown to many neighbors until after the shooting incident.

The Loughners' statement, which is yet to be released, is expected to express their deep sorrow for the victims and their families. The family has been unreachable since the attack, and it is reported that they were unaware of the severity of their son's problems.

Bruno, a seven-year-old chocolate Labrador retriever, was rescued from an abandoned well in Estevan, Saskatchewan, after spending nearly a month without food. The dog's story gained international attention, and after 22 days of recovery at the University of Saskatchewan’s Western College of Veterinary Medicine, he was released and headed home.

Bruno's owners, John and Cindy Billesberger, had been searching for him since he went missing from their farm near Hitchcock on September 17. They found him on October 14, lying in a muddy well three meters below, injured and near death from starvation.

Initially, Bruno was treated at the Prairie Animal Health Centre in Estevan, but after a few days of good news and promising test results, he experienced "refeeding syndrome," a condition that can result in the body not functioning properly and lead to death. This led to his transfer to Saskatoon for further treatment.

At the veterinary college in Saskatoon, Bruno was monitored 24 hours a day by clinicians in the intensive care unit. His paws were treated with cold laser therapy, and his electrolyte levels, which were affected due to refeeding syndrome, were constantly monitored and supplemented intravenously.

Bruno's case will be documented as a case study for veterinary professionals to use for future cases. He will now continue recovering at home, with a special diet and physiotherapy. His owners are grateful for the staff at the veterinary college, as Bruno's survival was unlikely if his rescue had come any later.

Bruno's story has attracted international attention, with newspapers across North America, the U.K., and Russia reporting on his rescue. His owners are happy to have him back, and Bruno seems to be doing well, wagging his tail and playing with a squeaky toy on his release day. Despite his ordeal, Bruno still looks thin and wears a cast on one paw.

The San Fermin Festival, a renowned eight-day event in Pamplona, Spain, attracted thousands of participants from around the world on July 9, 2017. The third running of the bulls during the festival was deemed tranquil, resulting in only minor injuries, according to hospital spokesman Tomas Belzunegui. Four men, three Spaniards, and one Frenchman were treated for minor injuries caused by falls and knocks.

The bulls from the Puerto de San Lorenzo ranch made their debut at the festival, completing the 930-yard (850-meter) cobbled-street course in 2 minutes, 22 seconds, which is well under the average of three minutes. One bull, named Huracan, broke away early and sped ahead through the crowd, nearly catching a runner and causing a brief scare.

Notably, Bill Hillmann, an author who has been participating in the annual tradition for 12 years, was gored during the run. Despite this, he plans to run again on Monday. Hillmann was initially inspired to run with the bulls after reading Ernest Hemingway's novel "The Sun Also Rises."

On the previous day, two Americans were gored during the second running of the bulls. One of them, Bill Hillmann, was in stable condition after being gored in the buttocks. Despite his injury, he expressed his intention to run again before the festival's end. Another American, Jack Capra, was in serious condition after his left arm was impaled and he was dragged for several meters before the bull flung him off.

The festival, which attracts tens of thousands of partygoers from Spain and abroad, was popularized by Hemingway's novel. This year, Hillmann is being filmed by a crew working on an interactive documentary called ¡Fiesta Pamplona! with Hillman as the main character in the "foreign runner" section of the story.

The San Fermin festival has been marked by several gorings over the first two days, but none of the injuries have been life-threatening. Despite the risks, participants like Bill Hillmann continue to be drawn to the festival and the thrill of running with the bulls.

The Big Island of Hawaii is currently experiencing a volcanic eruption from the Kilauea volcano, which has been active for over a week. Residents in the southeast corner of the island have been alerted to rising levels of toxic gas from lava-oozing fissures, with sulfur dioxide gas being particularly dangerous if inhaled in large quantities. Hawaii County authorities have warned residents of a wind change that will bring higher levels of sulfur dioxide gas to the area.

Governor David Ige has warned that mass evacuations may be necessary as more fissures open and spew lava and gas into residential areas on the east flank of Kilauea. Geologists have warned that new areas east of the erupting volcano may be at risk of molten rock bursting from the ground. During an evening meeting with community members, an official with the United States Geological Survey’s Hawaii Volcano Observatory said that while no new fissures have opened during the last 24 hours, there has been "quite a bit" of ground cracking over the last day and that they were releasing steam.

Authorities have completed the removal of highly flammable chemicals from a nearby geothermal power plant that was in the path of creeping lava. The latest upheaval at Kilauea began last week after the crater floor of a long-active side vent collapsed suddenly, triggering a similar plunge in the molten lake inside the larger crater at the volcano’s summit.

Geologists have warned that Kilauea may be entering a new phase of explosive eruptions not seen in nearly a century that could hurl "ballistic blocks" weighing up to 12 tons for half a mile, and rain pebble-sized fragments for another mile or two. The immediate vicinity around the summit, an area controlled by the National Park Service, was to be closed to visitors indefinitely, starting on Thursday night.

The Leilani Estates community remains in greatest danger, with 15 volcanic fissures so far having destroyed 36 structures, most of them homes, and forcing the evacuation of about 2,000 residents. However, as the eruption progresses, "other areas of the lower East Rift Zone may also be at risk," the Hawaiian Volcano Observatory said in a bulletin.

In addition to the threat of explosive eruptions at Kilauea’s summit, new vents and the wrath of lava, Hawaii island residents also have acid rain to worry about. Rain forecast mostly for the windward side of Hawaii island today and Friday brings with it the possibility of sulfur dioxide from the volcanic vents mixing and reacting with water, creating acid rain. University of Hawaii meteorologist and professor Steven Businger said the rain is not dangerous.

Local meteorologists said the change in prevailing winds could send Kilauea’s volcanic smog, or vog, northwest to Maui and other islands in Hawaii. Surfers bobbing in the ocean off Kona on the west side of the Big Island complained of the smog that could be seen in a haze over the coast.

Hawaii police said they arrested Alexandru Stingu-Dragomir, 29, on suspicion he burgled four houses in Leilani Estates after the mayor declared an emergency the area on last week.

Governor David Ige has requested federal disaster assistance as he said a mass evacuation of the lower Puna District, where Leilani Estates is located, would be beyond current county and state capabilities.

Gloria Chapman, the wife of Mark Chapman who assassinated John Lennon, revealed that Mark told her two months before the murder that he planned to kill Lennon. However, she claimed he never carried out the threat due to his love for her and had discarded the gun. After Lennon's death, Gloria knew Chapman was the assassin. Now, Chapman is facing a parole hearing for the 10th time, and Gloria hopes he may soon be released. Despite being abused during their marriage, Gloria has remained devoted to Chapman, citing their religious beliefs and marriage vows. The couple has only been allowed to spend 44 hours each year together during conjugal visits. Chapman's parole hearing is scheduled for the week starting August 20.

In the early hours of Sunday, June 12, 2016, Omar Mateen, the gunman responsible for the deadliest mass shooting in American history, reportedly placed a phone call to the News 13 newsroom in Orlando, Florida, as the shooting was unfolding at the Pulse nightclub. Matthew Gentili, a producer at News 13, answered the call and spoke with the shooter, who claimed responsibility for the attack and stated that he was doing it for the Islamic State. The caller spoke fluently in a foreign language, but Gentili asked him to speak in English. The call ended with the shooter stating that he had no further words and hanging up. The FBI interviewed Gentili after his 12-hour shift, and although they did not confirm whether it was the gunman on the phone, News 13's managing editor was able to research the phone number and match it to Mateen. The timing and content of the phone call align with Mateen's 911 calls made during the shooting. The shooting at Pulse nightclub resulted in the deaths of 49 people and injuries to 53 more.

A Pennsylvania man, Ryan Collins, has agreed to plead guilty to hacking into the email and online accounts of over 100 individuals, including several female celebrities, and stealing private information such as nude photos and videos. The U.S. Attorney's Office in Los Angeles announced this on Tuesday. Collins is charged with violating the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act and faces a maximum of five years in prison, although prosecutors will recommend a sentence of 18 months.

Between November 2012 and September 2014, Collins sent fake emails that appeared to be from Apple or Google, tricking victims into revealing their usernames and passwords. He then used this information to gain access to their email accounts, sometimes downloading full backups from Apple’s iCloud and swiping nude photos in some instances.

The hacking investigation began in September 2014, following the leak of nude photos of celebrities such as Jennifer Lawrence and model Kate Upton. However, Collins is not suspected of being involved in the release of these images. The ongoing investigation is also looking into the posting of the photos.

Collins' case will be transferred to Harrisburg, Pennsylvania, and this is the first arrest in connection with the security breach. At least 50 iCloud accounts and 72 Gmail accounts were compromised, officials said.

David Bowdich, the Assistant Director in Charge of the FBI’s Los Angeles Field Office, stated, "By illegally accessing intimate details of his victims' personal lives, Mr. Collins violated their privacy and left many to contend with lasting emotional distress, embarrassment, and feelings of insecurity." He also encouraged users of internet-connected devices to strengthen passwords and be skeptical when replying to emails asking for personal information.

Bill Watterson, the creator of the iconic comic strip Calvin and Hobbes, has released a new cartoon after a nearly 20-year hiatus. The new work is a movie poster for the documentary Stripped, which explores the state of the newspaper industry and features interviews with over 60 cartoonists, including Watterson. In addition to providing a voice-over for the documentary, Watterson also agreed to create the film's poster, marking the first time he has shared new artwork with the public since Calvin and Hobbes ended. The new cartoon is bawdier than Watterson's previous work and features human nudity. Stripped was funded through Kickstarter and will be available on iTunes on April 1 and on DVD on April 2.

In a separate event, Watterson also created a piece of artwork for the Team Cul de Sac fundraising project for Parkinson's research. The artwork features the character Petey Otterloop from Richard Thompson's comic strip "Cul de Sac." This is the first new artwork from Watterson that his syndicate has seen in the 16 years since Calvin and Hobbes ended. The Team Cul de Sac project aims to raise $250,000 for Parkinson's research through the sale of a book of "Cul de Sac"-inspired art created by Thompson's professional colleagues, including Watterson.

Rob Porter, a senior White House official and staff secretary, has resigned after his two ex-wives accused him of physical and emotional abuse. Porter served as Chief of Staff John F. Kelly's top enforcer and was the gatekeeper to the Oval Office, determining which articles and policy proposals reached the president's hands. Aides were aware of the accusations against Porter since late last year, but learned of the specifics late Tuesday when approached by a reporter from DailyMail.com. Porter's ex-wives said they informed the FBI in January 2017 of their allegations against him while they were being interviewed as part of Porter's security clearance review. It is unclear when or whether the FBI informed the White House. Porter denied the accusations but said he was stepping down from his job, although it was unclear when he will officially leave the White House. Porter's first wife, Colbie Holderness, said in an interview with The Washington Post that he was continually abusive during their marriage, including punching her in the face during a trip to Florence in 2005. Porter's second wife, Jennie Willoughby, received a temporary emergency protective order in 2010 after saying he refused to leave her residence, in violation of their separation agreement. The White House initially gave Porter its full support, but just hours after the second set of revelations, Porter resigned while still protesting his innocence.

The article discusses the practice of swaddling babies, which involves wrapping them in blankets to calm them and promote sleep. While swaddling has been used in many cultures throughout history, recent concerns have been raised about its potential risks, particularly regarding the development of hip dysplasia.

Professor Nicholas Clarke of Southampton University Hospital argues that swaddling can be damaging to developing hips as it holds the legs out straight and restricts movement, which can alter the development of the hip joint. He advises against swaddling, stating that there is no health benefit but a risk for adverse consequences of the growing and often immature hips.

The Royal College of Midwives and other experts also advise against tightly swaddling a child, citing the risk of overheating and a raised risk of cot death. They emphasize the importance of individualized advice to ensure that mothers know how to keep their baby safe, able to move, and not get overheated.

Andreas Roposch, a consultant orthopaedic surgeon at Great Ormond Street Hospital, agrees that swaddling should not be employed due to the risk of adverse consequences for the growing and often immature hips. He suggests that similar effects may be seen in all devices or manoeuvres that place the legs in a purely straight position for prolonged periods in early infancy.

The article also provides guidance on how to swaddle a baby safely, emphasizing the importance of allowing the baby's legs to move into a 'frog position' rather than being held straight. It is recommended that parents avoid using heavy materials for swaddling, not cover the baby's head, and never place a swaddled baby on their stomach.

In conclusion, while swaddling has been used for centuries to calm and soothe babies, recent concerns have been raised about its potential risks, particularly regarding the development of hip dysplasia. Experts advise against tightly swaddling a child and emphasize the importance of individualized advice to ensure that babies are kept safe, able to move, and not get overheated.

Arizona Congresswoman Gabrielle Giffords is in critical condition after being shot in the head during a public event on Saturday. The bullet went through her brain, but a doctor at the University Medical Center in Tucson is optimistic about her recovery. Surviving a gunshot wound to the head is rare, with a survival rate of about 5%, and those who do survive often face significant neurological deficiencies. The severity of the injury depends on factors such as the size of the bullet, its trajectory, and where it hits in the brain. If the bullet enters one hemisphere, it's possible to make a reasonable recovery, but if it crosses from one side of the head to the other, it can be fatal. Giffords' friend, state Sen. Linda Lopez, confirmed that the bullet entered Giffords' head at her temple and exited through her forehead. The next three to four days are considered critical for Giffords' recovery, and she may face years of rehabilitation. The survival story of a British soldier who was shot near the ear and survived with some memory loss and deafness in one ear is cited as a hopeful example.

On April 29, 2013, Ramineh Behbehanian, a 50-year-old corporate chemist and pharmacist from South San Jose, was arrested on suspicion of attempted murder. Police allege that Behbehanian attempted to poison a Starbucks in San Jose by placing bottles of orange juice containing a lethal amount of rubbing alcohol into the store's refrigerated display case.

An alert customer and a sharp-eyed employee noticed Behbehanian's suspicious behavior and reported it to the store manager. After Behbehanian fled the scene, the employee managed to get her license plate number. The store employees then called 911 after noticing the bottles had a toxic smell.

Firefighters on the scene tested the contents and determined that the bottles contained a "lethal quantity" of isopropyl rubbing alcohol mixed with the juice. No one drank from the bottles, and the customer's quick actions were praised by the police.

Behbehanian was arrested at her San Jose home later that night and placed into custody on suspicion of attempted murder and felony poisoning. Police are still looking for a motive for the alleged poisoning attempt.

The Starbucks store in San Jose was closed after the incident but reopened the next morning. As a precaution, the store pulled all of its remaining juices from the open-air refrigerator and destroyed them. Other Starbucks nearby were also alerted and told to check all their juice bottles to make sure none of its seals were broken.

Behbehanian could make her first appearance in court as soon as Thursday. Her LinkedIn page states she has a master's degree in physical chemistry and chemical engineering from Lehigh University in Pennsylvania and worked as a scientist, engineer, or project manager for a string of high-profile corporations including Pfizer, Boston Scientific, and Johnson & Johnson. At the time of her arrest, she was working at Janssen, a pharmaceutical subsidiary of Johnson & Johnson.

In Richmond, California, a horrific incident occurred at Richmond High School where a 15-year-old girl was allegedly raped and beaten during a school picnic area after her homecoming dance on October 24, 2009. The attack, which lasted for over two hours, was reportedly witnessed by up to two dozen people, many of whom did not intervene or report the crime to authorities.

The victim, a sophomore, had left the dance and joined a group drinking in a school courtyard when she was attacked. Two suspects were in custody, with one being a 19-year-old former student, Manuel Ortega, who is charged with rape, robbery, and kidnapping. Another suspect, a 15-year-old student, was also arrested.

The attack has caused outrage in the city, which is known for its high crime rate. The incident has prompted calls for increased security measures, including the installation of surveillance cameras at the school. The attack has also led to some students transferring out of the school due to safety concerns.

The police are offering a $20,000 reward for information leading to the conviction of any of the assailants and are expecting to make more arrests. The incident has been described as one of the most heinous crimes in the memory of the police officers involved. The girl remains hospitalized with non-life-threatening injuries.

The article discusses an unusual wood ant colony living in an abandoned Soviet nuclear weapons bunker in Templewo, Poland. The ants, belonging to the species Formica polyctena, have created an ant society unlike any other, due to their isolation and the harsh conditions in the bunker.

The Soviets built the bunker during the Cold War to store nuclear weapons, sinking it below ground and planting trees on top as camouflage. A massive wood ant colony took up residence in the soil over the bunker, but due to a ventilation pipe, thousands of worker ants fall down the pipe every year and cannot climb back out. The survivors have continued to build a nest and maintain it in typical wood ant fashion, despite the unusual circumstances.

Researchers from the Polish Academy of Sciences discovered the nest after a group of other zoologists found that bats were living in the bunker. The ants live in a state of near-starvation, producing no queens, no males, and no offspring. The massive group tending the nest is entirely composed of non-reproductive female workers, supplemented every year by a new rain of unfortunate ants falling down the ventilation shaft.

The ants' lives are so strange that the researchers hesitate to call them a "colony." Conditions in the bunker are so harsh, constantly cold, and mostly barren, that the ants seem to live in a state of near-starvation. The ants have created an "ant cemetery" around the nest mound, with a tiny ecosystem where mites and a few other invertebrates feed on the bodies of the dead wood ants. The question is, what are the ants eating? It's possible they have figured out how to eat the creatures who feast in their cemeteries, essentially making them cannibals at one remove. But Czechowski and his team dismiss this as unlikely. It's also possible that there are nutrients growing in the bat guano from the ants' only living neighbors in the bunker. But in their years of observation, the scientists still haven't figured out for certain what the ants' source of food is.

The paper's conclusion reads like a dystopian science fiction scene from the 1970s, describing the wood ant colony as an example of survival in a hostile environment with constant darkness, low temperatures, and no ample food supply. The continued survival of the colony is dependent on new workers falling in through the ventilation pipe. The supplement of workers more than compensates for the mortality rate of workers, such that through the years the bunker workforce has grown to the level of big, mature natural colonies.

Life in an abandoned nuclear weapons bunker is nightmarish, even for the humble ant. It appears that the legacy of the Soviet occupation of Poland doesn't just haunt the country's human population. It has affected the social structures of insects too. The article was published in the Journal of Hymenoptera Research.

On April 10, 2017, a man was forcibly removed from an overbooked United Airlines flight from Chicago to Louisville, causing widespread outrage after a video of the incident was posted online. The airline initially asked for volunteers to give up their seats, offering $400 and a hotel stay, but no one accepted. When the airline used a computer to randomly select passengers who had already boarded the flight to be removed, a doctor who refused to leave was forcibly dragged off the plane, resulting in injuries and a two-hour delay. The incident sparked a series of reactions, including apologies from United Airlines, investigations, and calls for accountability. The man, identified as Dr. David Dao, was eventually allowed to re-board the plane with visible injuries. The incident has led to a significant backlash against United Airlines, with many calling for improved customer service and fair treatment of passengers.

Apple unveiled its latest touch-screen device, named iPad, on Tuesday, sparking a wave of criticism and humor, particularly from women, due to the perceived connection between the name and menstruation. Twitter users, particularly women, expressed their concerns about the lack of female representation in Apple's marketing and business development departments. The study "Marital Characteristics and the Sexual Relationships of U.S. Older Adults" published in the Archives of Sexual Behavior, analyzed the relationship between marital characteristics and sexual outcomes among 1,656 married adults aged 57-85. The results showed that individuals in their first marriage had more frequent sex than remarried individuals, and marital duration had a curvilinear relationship with frequency of sex, with a slight rebound occurring for those whose marriages endured longer than half a century. However, marriage order did not affect physical pleasure and emotional satisfaction.

Researchers speculate that the permanency of the relationship may drive the greater sexual activity in first marriages, and sicker men in younger marriages may drive frequency of sex for women in younger marriages. The study also notes that the findings may challenge societal stereotypes about older adults and sexual activity.

The study's authors include Samuel Stroope, Ph.D., now an assistant professor of sociology at Louisiana State University, Michael McFarland, Ph.D., assistant professor of sociology and public health at Florida State University, and Jeremy Uecker, Ph.D., an assistant professor of sociology at Baylor University. The researchers suggest that future studies could explore the reasons behind the findings, such as the role of relationship permanency and the impact of declining health and the death of a spouse on sexual activity in older adults.

On the second anniversary of the Egyptian uprising that ousted President Hosni Mubarak, five people were shot dead in Suez during nationwide protests against President Mohamed Mursi. A total of 280 civilians and 55 security personnel were injured in demonstrations across Cairo, Alexandria, Suez, and Port Said, fueled by anger towards Mursi and his Islamist allies in the Muslim Brotherhood. Thousands of Mursi's opponents gathered in Cairo's Tahrir Square, rekindling the demands of the revolution they believe has been hijacked by Islamists who have betrayed its goals. Street battles erupted, and state-owned buildings were targeted, including an office used by the Muslim Brotherhood's political party. The schism between Islamists and their secular rivals is hindering Mursi's efforts to revive an economy in crisis and reverse a plunge in Egypt's currency. The anniversary laid bare the deep divide between the two groups, with thousands of opposition protesters demanding a complete overhaul of the constitution and freedom of expression, among other things. The Muslim Brotherhood, however, stayed off the streets to avoid conflict after last month's violence. The opposition accuses the Brotherhood of seeking to dominate the post-Mubarak order, while the Brotherhood denies these accusations. The clashes resulted in injuries and property damage, and the anniversary marked a continuation of the internal strife that has plagued Egypt since the revolution.

On September 5, 2017, an Air Force pilot, Lt. Col. Eric Schultz, tragically lost his life during a training mission at the Nevada Test and Training Range, approximately 100 miles northwest of Nellis Air Force Base. The aircraft involved in the crash is classified and not available for release. Lt. Col. Schultz was a 1991 graduate of Annapolis High School and held multiple graduate degrees. He joined the Air Force in 2001 and became a flight training officer. He was the 28th pilot to fly the F-35 fighter jet in 2011. The crash is under investigation, and the cause is yet to be determined. This incident was one of two Air Force crashes near Nellis on Wednesday, September 6, 2017. Two A-10C Thunderbolt II jets also crashed on the test range at approximately 8 p.m., but the pilots ejected safely. Lt. Col. Schultz is survived by his wife, Julie, and five children, Noah, Elijah, Zion, OliviaMae, and Naomi; parents Larry and Linda Schultz of Annapolis; brother Lars (his children Ava and Tristan) of Alexandria, Virginia; and many more aunts, uncles, nieces, and nephews. The investigation into both crashes is ongoing.

On Tuesday, a shooting occurred at Brigham and Women's Hospital in Boston, resulting in the death of Dr. Michael J. Davidson, a well-respected cardiac surgeon and assistant professor at Harvard Medical School. The shooter, identified as 55-year-old Stephen Pasceri from Millbury, reportedly fired two shots at Davidson and then turned the gun on himself.

Davidson, a father of three, was the director of endovascular cardiac surgery at the hospital and had been working there since 2006. The incident occurred in the Shapiro Cardiovascular Center just after 11 a.m., causing a brief lockdown and evacuation of the second floor. Witnesses reported hearing loud voices and gunshots before the emergency announcement was made.

Investigations suggest that Pasceri may have had issues with prior medical treatment of his mother at the hospital, who passed away on November 15. The Boston Police Department described the incident as a "senseless act of violence" and praised the hospital staff's response.

The hospital lowered its flag on Wednesday in honor of Dr. Davidson, who was known for his passion for running and medicine. He was part of a team that performed a landmark heart-valve procedure and helped establish one of the most advanced operating rooms in the nation.

Pasceri's family issued a statement expressing their condolences to Davidson's family and friends. Neighbors described Pasceri as a calm, pleasant individual who was active in the community and church.

This tragic incident has brought attention to the rare but serious issue of hospital shootings. The Brigham and Women's Hospital has been one of the first hospitals in the country to train staff on how to respond to an "active shooter" situation, working closely with the Boston Police Department. The hospital has also produced a training video to guide staff in such situations.

In a groundbreaking development, Swiss scientists have broken a four-decade-long informal ban on LSD research by conducting a study on terminally ill cancer patients. The study, published in the Journal of Nervous and Mental Disease, aimed to assess the safety and efficacy of LSD when combined with talk therapy to help patients confront their fears of death.

The research involved 12 patients who underwent 30 supervised 10-hour-long "trips" over two months. One patient described the experience as a "mystical experience" that brought up distressing memories. These periods of distress were considered therapeutically valuable as they allowed patients to address their emotions.

A year after the sessions ended, patients who received a full dose of LSD (200 micrograms) experienced a 20% improvement in their anxiety levels. However, the group given a lower dose saw their anxiety symptoms increase.

Despite the small number of participants, the study's results were not statistically significant. However, the fact that the research took place at all is significant for psychedelic drug research, as LSD caused no serious side effects.

Rick Doblin, executive director of the Multidisciplinary Association for Psychedelic Studies, believes that revisiting LSD-based treatments is worthwhile. He stated, "We want to break these substances out of the mold of the counterculture and bring them back to the lab as part of a psychedelic renaissance."

This study marks a significant step forward in the exploration of LSD's potential therapeutic benefits, particularly in managing anxiety disorders. However, further research with a larger sample size is needed to confirm these findings.

The city of Akron, Ohio, is distributing palm cards titled "You and the Law" to middle and high school students, aimed at advising citizens on how to behave when stopped by police. The cards, created by the Akron PeaceMakers, a group of high school students, contain 15 bullet points, including advice to engage politely with officers, answer questions about identity, and keep hands visible. The initiative was sparked by the deaths of Tamir Rice in Cleveland and other high-profile police shootings in Missouri and New York. Akron Mayor Don Plusquellic and PeaceMakers President Myia Culbreath presented the cards to the media at Akron City Council chambers. The cards will first be distributed to Akron Public School students, but will also be distributed to churches, community houses, and other locations. The cards have personal significance for Billy Soule, the PeaceMakers' assistant to the mayor for community relations, whose son was stopped by police while carrying a toy gun years ago. The cards will also include advice on reporting police misconduct. The PeaceMakers conceived the cards two weeks ago and were advised by Akron Assistant Police Chief Charles Brown and retired police Sergeant Willa Keith. The cards are getting praise from adults, but are now heading out to a tougher audience of high school students, who are showing interest and engaging in debate over the responsibility of officers in encounters. The cards are part of an effort to bridge police-citizen divides and build trust, and mayors across the country are looking at this approach as a way to do so.

The shooting at a congressional baseball practice earlier this week in Alexandria, Virginia, involved a suspect, James Hodgkinson, who was carrying a list of names, including GOP Reps. Mo Brooks of Alabama, Jeff Duncan of South Carolina, and Trent Franks of Arizona. Although Duncan and Brooks were present at the field, the shooting occurred before Duncan left, and neither of them was injured. The list was not considered an "assassination list," but it is clear that Hodgkinson had a focus on certain individuals.

Doctors provided an update on the condition of House Majority Whip Rep. Steve Scalise, who was critically injured in the shooting. Although his condition has improved over the last 36 hours, he will require further surgeries, hospitalization, and rehabilitation. Hodgkinson died of his wounds on Wednesday.

Federal authorities are investigating Hodgkinson's motives, including examining social media posts that included anti-Trump and anti-Republican sentiments. Hodgkinson had moved from Illinois to Alexandria in recent months and was living in his vehicle.

The Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF) traced the two weapons recovered from the scene, a 9 mm handgun and a 7.62 caliber rifle, and found no evidence that the suspect obtained the weapons illegally.

The list found with Hodgkinson also included pictures of the ballpark, and it is not clear whether it was an attack list. None of the victims injured in the attack were on the list. Rep. Mo Brooks, who was on the list and present at the practice but unharmed by the shooting, has advised his office personnel and friends to be extra wary in his presence.

In a groundbreaking study, scientists have discovered evidence that air pollution particles can travel through the lungs of pregnant women and lodge in their placentas, potentially affecting the fetuses. The research, presented at the European Respiratory Society International Congress in Paris, involved five non-smoking women living in London who delivered healthy babies. Researchers found sooty particles in the placentas' macrophage cells, which are part of the body's immune system and engulf harmful particles such as bacteria and air pollution.

While further analysis is needed for confirmation, the researchers believe these particles could also move into the fetuses. The study adds to growing evidence that air pollution causes health problems beyond the lungs, including a reduction in intelligence and the discovery of toxic nanoparticles in human brains.

Air pollution has been linked to an increased risk of premature birth, low birth weight, and lifelong health damage. A large study of over 500,000 births in London confirmed the link, with doctors warning of the implications for millions of women in polluted cities worldwide.

The research suggests a possible mechanism of how babies are affected by pollution while being theoretically protected in the womb. Stricter policies for cleaner air are needed to reduce the impact of pollution on health worldwide, as harm to fetuses can occur even below current European Union pollution limits.

Separate research presented at the same congress found that children with early onset and persistent asthma fared less well in education than those without the condition. Asthma in children has long been linked to air pollution.

The study, conducted over 20 years in Sweden, showed that children with asthma were three and a half times more likely to leave school at the age of 16 with only basic education and were also twice as likely to drop out of university courses. The researchers suggest that children with asthma may have lower school attendance as a possible reason for their poorer educational outcomes.

In conclusion, the new study provides evidence that air pollution particles can travel from the mother's lungs to the placenta, potentially affecting the fetus. Stricter policies for cleaner air are needed to protect pregnant women and their unborn babies from the harmful effects of air pollution. Additionally, the study highlights the link between asthma in children and poor educational outcomes.

The federal government initially planned to withhold 11 words from the declassified copy of the Pentagon Papers, a 7,000-page report detailing the U.S. government's study of the Vietnam War, which was published by The New York Times in 1971. The decision to censor these words sparked a guessing game among historians, security analysts, and the report's authors. Daniel Ellsberg, who leaked the report, and Leslie H. Gelb, the director of the task force that wrote the report, expressed their inability to guess which words were being withheld. The New York Times invited readers to speculate on Twitter using the hashtag #pentagon11, and is currently compiling the guesses.

The article discusses two separate but related topics: a powerful coffee drink called the Ass Kicker and the issue of cookies not being properly set in certain browsers, particularly the Facebook in-app browser.

The Ass Kicker is a coffee drink served at Viscous Cafe in Adelaide, Australia. It contains an extremely high amount of caffeine, equivalent to 80 standard cups of coffee, and is designed to keep customers awake for extended periods. The drink was initially created for an emergency department nurse who needed to stay awake for long hours. Despite being toned down since then, it still comes with a warning that it is not for the faint of heart. The drink is popular and has become a talking point, but the cafe owner actively discourages customers who are only interested in a gimmick.

On the other hand, there is a problem with the Facebook in-app browser intermittently making requests to websites without cookies that had previously been set. This appears to be a defect in the browser which should be addressed soon. The simplest approach to avoid this problem is to continue to use the Facebook app but not use the in-app browser. This can be done by turning on the option "Links Open Externally" in the app settings.

The article also provides instructions on how to enable cookies in various browsers, including Internet Explorer, Firefox, Google Chrome, and Mobile Safari (iPhone, iPad).

Lastly, the article mentions that caffeine, the stimulant found in coffee, is the most commonly used drug in the world. While it has been linked to some health risks, such as increased blood pressure, gastrointestinal problems, and raised cholesterol, it is also believed to have health benefits, such as protection from Parkinson's disease and cognitive decline. However, the Ass Kicker, with its high caffeine content, is considered a dose too far by experts.

A YouTube clip from the 1928 film The Circus by Charlie Chaplin has sparked a debate about time travel, as a woman in the film appears to be using a mobile phone. The woman, dressed in a hat and coat, is seen walking and talking into a black object, which some viewers believe is a mobile phone. The clip, posted by George Clarke, a self-proclaimed Chaplin fan from Belfast, has garnered over 1.3 million views and has led to various theories, ranging from secret government operations to a crazy old person using a hand-held vibrator. The clip, which Clarke has been studying for over a year, has been shown at film festivals and has left many viewers baffled. The clip can be found on YouTube, with viewers encouraged to share their own theories.

On July 3rd, an 18-year-old college student named Connor Golden from Fairfax, Virginia, was severely injured in a blast that occurred in Central Park, New York. The incident happened around 11 a.m. near East 60th Street and Fifth Avenue, and it is believed that Golden stepped on a homemade firecracker that caused the explosion.

Golden was with two friends, Thomas Hinds and Matthew Stabile, who were also visiting from Virginia. The three were high school buddies and were in town for the Fourth of July holiday. According to Hinds, they had arrived in New York the previous evening and were planning to go slacklining in Central Park.

During their visit, they climbed on rocks to get a good look at the area for slacklining, and it was on their walk down that Golden stepped on the explosive device. The blast resulted in the amputation of part of his leg below the knee.

Investigators from the NYPD Bomb Squad were called to the scene to confirm whether the explosion was caused by a firecracker or something more sinister. They determined that the blast was indeed the result of "explosive experimentation" or the making of homemade fireworks.

Lt. Mark Torre, head of the NYPD Bomb Squad, explained that it is not unusual for people to make or try to create homemade fireworks around the Fourth of July. He added that the explosion was likely the result of someone trying to make a loud noise or create a flash.

Investigators believe that whoever left the device was not trying to cause any intentional harm to anyone. They found wet matches near the explosive, suggesting that it may have been left over from a previous attempt to ignite it on Friday night but did not go off due to the rain.

Golden was transported to Bellevue Hospital, where he underwent surgery. Witnesses in the area reported that the makeshift firecracker could be heard outside the funeral of Holocaust survivor and Nobel Peace Prize winner Elie Wiesel.

The friends of the victim, Hinds and Stabile, were questioned by the police to find out whether they were playing with fireworks at the time of the incident. However, they were able to prove that they were not involved in the construction of the explosive device.

Golden is a student at the University of Miami in Florida, Hinds attends Northwestern University, and Stabile is enrolled at Bard College. The incident has left his friends and family in shock, and they are hoping for a speedy recovery.

The NYPD has cordoned off a two- to three-block area of the park near the blast site and sent bomb-sniffing dogs into the area to search for other explosives. Lt. Torre of the NYPD bomb squad said the material didn't appear to have been "shock-sensitive" and that there was no evidence that it was meant to explode if stepped upon.

Mayor de Blasio took to Twitter to reassure the public that the explosion appeared to be an "isolated incident, unrelated to terrorism." He encouraged people to come out and enjoy the park for the Fourth of July celebrations. The incident serves as a reminder to leave fireworks to the professionals and to exercise caution when in public spaces.

Former President George W. Bush's official presidential portrait was unveiled at the White House, featuring Bush in the Oval Office with a look typical of political portraits. The painting, titled "A Charge to Keep," was a favorite of Bush, who often shared a story about its origins as depicting Methodist missionaries. However, this story has been disputed, with some claiming it is not the true story behind the painting.

Presidents choose their own painters for their official portraits, with the process involving many applicants and the selection often involving interviews. The cost of these portraits is paid for via private donations channeled through the nonprofit White House Historical Association. The official portraits are significant as they provide a visual representation of the presidents' history and are displayed at the National Portrait Gallery, individual presidential libraries, and the White House itself.

During the unveiling ceremony, President Obama and Bush interacted graciously, leading to speculation about the process of selecting the artists for official presidential portraits and the funding of these paintings.

The article discusses the upgrade of charges against Jesse L. Matthew Jr., the man accused of abducting and killing University of Virginia (U-Va.) sophomore Hannah Graham. The charges have been upgraded to capital murder, which means if convicted, Matthew could face the death penalty. The charges were upgraded at a court hearing in Charlottesville, Virginia, due to allegations of aggravating factors, including abduction or sexual assault.

Graham, an 18-year-old from Fairfax County, Virginia, went missing in September from an outdoor mall near the U-Va. campus. Matthew was the last person seen with her, and her body was found in a wooded area about 10 miles from campus weeks later. Matthew was charged with her killing.

Authorities have alleged that Matthew abducted Graham "with intent to defile," indicating that police believe he intended to sexually assault Graham. Albemarle County Commonwealth’s Attorney Denise Lunsford initially did not seek a capital murder charge, but after consulting with Graham's family and weighing the impact on the community, she decided to upgrade the charges.

Matthew is also facing charges related to a sexual assault from nearly a decade ago. He is awaiting trial on charges that he attacked and attempted to kill a woman in Fairfax City in 2005. Police found Matthew's DNA under one of the victim's fingernails.

Graham, a U-Va. sophomore who graduated from West Potomac High School, disappeared after a night out in Charlottesville on Sept. 12. She had been socializing with friends earlier in the night but left the group with plans to meet up with them later. She never showed up, and police believe she became disoriented while walking through Charlottesville.

Vice President Joe Biden has chosen Supreme Court Justice Sonia Sotomayor to administer his oath of office, making her the first Hispanic and fourth woman to do so. President Barack Obama will be sworn in by Chief Justice John G. Roberts Jr., who infamously stumbled through the ceremony four years ago. Both ceremonies will take place on January 20 and 21, with Sotomayor also swearing in Biden on the 20th. Three women have previously sworn in presidents and vice presidents, including Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg in 1997.

Formally embarking on his second term, President Obama will take the oath of office surrounded by family in an intimate inauguration at the White House on January 20, before re-enacting the ceremony before an excited crowd of hundreds of thousands outdoors at the Capitol on January 21. Roberts will administer the oath of office both days.

Vice President Biden will be sworn in on January 20 in a small, early morning ceremony at the Naval Observatory. Once the celebrations are over, Obama will plunge into a second-term agenda still dominated by the economy, with the president seeking to cement his legacy with sweeping domestic changes, pledging to achieve both an immigration overhaul and stricter gun laws despite opposition from a divided Congress.

The relationship between Obama and Roberts has been tumultuous since their first awkward public interaction during the botched oath of office four years ago. However, the pair seemed cordial during Sunday's ceremony, with Roberts reading the oath from a piece of paper and both men seeming relieved when it was over. The historical fates of Obama and Roberts are more intertwined than those of any chief justice and president in recent decades, and experts predict the Roberts-led court will continue to challenge the president's policies in areas that will shape the future of the nation, including affirmative action, immigration, and the environment.

A Cincinnati woman, Shawntelle Turley, has filed a lawsuit against the University of Cincinnati Medical Center (UCMC) and several individuals, including an employee named Ryan Rawls, after an employee allegedly posted her medical records, including her diagnosis of syphilis, on Facebook. The records were posted to a Facebook group called "Team No Hoes" in September 2013, and were followed by comments referring to Turley as a "hoe" and a "slut." Turley is seeking more than $25,000 in damages for invasion of privacy, emotional distress, malice, and negligence. The lawsuit also claims that Rawls, along with an unnamed nurse at UCMC, posted the records online at the request of Turley's ex-boyfriend, Raphael Bradley. UCMC has not commented on the pending litigation, but has sent a memo to employees reminding them of the seriousness of unauthorized access or sharing of medical records. Turley's lawyer, former Hamilton County prosecutor Mike Allen, did not return a call seeking comment.

In an incident that occurred last month in Niger, four US soldiers and five Nigerien troops died in an ambush during a joint patrol. The US special forces detachment fought alone for hours after the local Nigerien forces they were accompanying fled in the first minutes of the engagement. The trapped soldiers also made repeated efforts to convince French warplanes sent from neighboring Mali to engage the enemy, but the pilots refused due to poor weather, rough terrain, and an inability to differentiate friend from foe.

The incident has been the focus of an intense debate in Washington over the executive branch's extensive powers to use military force abroad without congressional approval and with little oversight. The Niger incident has been described as an "intelligence failure" by Republican senator John McCain, who blamed it on budget cuts. The US troops were part of a "train and equip" program, but the incident has prompted questions in Congress on where such missions blur into counter-terrorist combat.

Controversy flared after President Trump was accused of mishandling a phone call to the widow of La David Johnson, one of the dead soldiers. The timeline of the controversy shows that Trump initially discussed his calls to bereaved families, saying that most presidents did not make calls. Trump then dragged White House chief of staff John Kelly into the developing row, asking if Kelly had received a call from Obama, a reference to the death of Kelly's son in Afghanistan. Trump later phoned the widow of Sgt La David Johnson and reportedly said Johnson "knew what he was signing up for," according to Frederica Wilson, a Democratic congresswoman who heard the call. Wilson criticized Trump's reported remark as "so insensitive."

In response, Trump claimed Wilson's account was "totally fabricated" but Johnson's mother supported Wilson's version of events. White House press secretary Sarah Huckabee Sanders said Kelly was "disgusted and frustrated" by the politicization of his son's death – even though it was Trump who first mentioned him.

The Pentagon has launched a special investigation to be carried out by officers from US Africa Command, which is due to report within two months. A defence department spokesman said that there would be no further comment on the incident until then. But defence department leaks have fuelled anger within the US special forces community at what one retired senior officer called “a massive blame game.”

The email contains new details of the engagement, which took place on the immediate outskirts of the remote village of Tongo Tongo in south-western Niger, in the center of the volatile Sahel region. The Pentagon has said the unit that was attacked comprised 12 soldiers from the 3rd Special Forces Group which had recently arrived in Niger for a six-month tour, and about 30 Nigerien troops.

The ambush took place at 11:40pm on 4 October after the unit had spent two hours in Tongo Tongo, talking to local elders. The previous night, the Americans had destroyed a camp used by Djoundjoun Cheiffou, a lieutenant of Abu Waleed al-Sahraoui, an Islamic extremist based in neighboring Mali who last year pledged allegiance to Islamic State.

About 50 men attacked the US and Nigerien unit with small arms, rocket-propelled grenades, and mortars. The retired special forces officer said he had been told by servicemen with detailed knowledge of the incident that “approximately half of the US/Nigerien force was allowed to pass through the ambush killzone before the ambush was sprung, trapping the rear half.” On hearing firing, the lead group of soldiers turned around to engage the militants. “Except for those already dead or wounded, all of the Nigerien soldiers bugged out and left the Americans to fight … all by themselves. Two groups, roughly six Americans per group, fighting for their lives alone against a superior ALQ force,” the retired officer said.

A US drone was on the site of the engagement within minutes, but was unarmed. An hour passed before the trapped unit on the ground called for airstrikes against the militants who surrounded them. The delay has surprised and concerned experts and veterans. “Airstrikes were requested as the Americans fought on. Several French Mirage fighters responded, but refused to engage citing poor weather, rough terrain, and an inability to differentiate friend from foe. American SF [Special Forces] requested ‘danger close’ support and attempted to talk the CAS [close air support] in, but the French Mirages alleged continued to refuse to engage,” the officer wrote in the mail, based on his own discussions with serving and retired special forces soldiers with knowledge of the incident.

A spokesman for the French defence ministry did not respond to a request for comment on the allegations. According to a CNN account of the incident, the attackers set fire to the dry bush around the encircled special forces soldiers to cover the battleground with smoke. The account quoted a Nigerien soldier as saying that the surviving troops from the patrol were fighting off their attackers, standing back to back in a last stand, when reinforcements finally arrived.

After two hours, French special forces flown by helicopter from their base in Mali reached the site of the ambush, prompting the attackers to withdraw. The French soldiers searched the immediate vicinity and evacuated survivors, including several who were wounded. Four US special forces soldiers were left behind. Three are thought to have been dead at the site. It is unclear when Johnson was killed, but the 25-year-old mechanic had become separated from the rest of the unit almost immediately after the ambush started, sources within the special forces community said. The Pentagon has now said that a second team of US and Nigerien forces was close to the ambushed patrol. It was believed to have been on a mission to kill or capture al-Sahraoui. That operation was called off, and the troops eventually retrieved the bodies of three of the US soldiers several hours after the ambush had ended. Johnson’s remains were discovered by Nigerien troops near the site of the attack two days later. The five Nigeriens killed in the ambush died in its first moments, sources within the special forces community said. They described how one of the light, unarmored trucks used by the patrol became stuck in sand after the attack started. Almost all the Nigerien troops it was carrying were killed or wounded. One source said the vehicle was hit by a mortar round. Most of the ambushed US unit had no combat experience, and had not been warned to expect any encounter with hostile forces. This assessment has surprised some and has been a focus of congressional attention. A United Nations assessment indicated that there have been at least 46 attacks by armed groups in the districts around Tongo Tongo since February 2016.

Tiger Woods struggled in the first round of the PGA Championship, shooting a 77 and finishing tied for 129th place. This is one of Woods' worst performances, as he was tied for the lead early but made three double bogeys and five bogeys. Woods is in danger of missing the cut and ending his PGA Tour season early, as he is currently 129th in FedEx Cup points and needs to advance to the playoffs. This is Woods' highest opening round in a major championship and his highest ever at the PGA. Woods expressed frustration and anger, stating that he thought he could play by feel but his motor patterns got in the way and he started fighting his swing.

A former Oklahoma City police officer, Daniel Holtzclaw, has been sentenced to 263 years in prison for raping and sexually assaulting more than a dozen black women while on duty. The victims, who were mostly drug addicts and prostitutes, testified that Holtzclaw coerced them into having sex after threatening to arrest them for possessing drug paraphernalia or on outstanding warrants. The sentence was in line with what the jury recommended. Holtzclaw's attorney claimed that his client was denied a fair trial due to discovery violations and misrepresentations by the government. The defense team filed for a new trial and an appeal, but both were denied. The victims' stories were shared, including a 57-year-old grandmother who was forced to perform oral sex and a 24-year-old woman who was raped while handcuffed to a hospital bed. The case has been criticized for an all-white jury and has sparked discussions about race and police misconduct.

In 1890, Thomas Edison introduced the world to some of the first talking dolls, which are now infamous for their eerie sound. Standing at about 2 feet tall, these dolls have wooden limbs, a metal body, and a spring-activated miniature phonograph in their back that plays pre-recorded verses. The recordings, which were most likely read by a female factory worker imitating a child, are unsettling and have been described as super creepy.

Edison aimed to market the wax cylinder phonograph for home use through these dolls, but they flopped in the market due to their high cost and lack of realism. People wanted moving mouths and understandable voices from the dolls. Edison stopped producing the dolls after about a month, referring to them as "little monsters."

The fear and fascination surrounding talking dolls can be attributed to their uncanny nature, as they occupy a middle ground between human and inanimate objects. According to Georgetown University horror scholar Caetlin Benson-Allott, talking toys belong in an unsettling middle space, being both familiar and different, and we don't fully understand if they are entirely dead or entirely alive. This feeling of the uncanny is a subconscious holdover from childhood, when we pretended our dolls were real.

Recently, a government laboratory was able to scan the fragile recordings from Edison's talking dolls and make them available to the public, providing a chilling soundtrack to our nightmares. Despite their failure in the market, these dolls remain an intriguing piece of history, embodying the uncanny and sparking our fear of technology turning against us.

The Hamilton County coroner in Ohio released a report on Wednesday stating that Otto Warmbier, an American student who died in June after being released from North Korean imprisonment, died due to a lack of oxygen and blood flow to the brain. The coroner's report cited complications of chronic deficiency of oxygen and blood supply to the brain in Warmbier's death. The cause of the brain damage remains unknown, and the coroner stated that the manner of death was listed as "undetermined." The report was based on an external examination of the body, as Warmbier's family declined an autopsy. North Korea has denied mistreating Warmbier, who was sentenced to 15 years of hard labor in March 2016 for allegedly stealing a propaganda poster. The Warmbier family has accused North Korea of torturing him, and President Donald Trump tweeted that Otto was "tortured beyond belief by North Korea." The coroner's report did not find any evidence of trauma to Warmbier's teeth or broken bones, contradicting the Warmbier family's claims that his teeth had been disfigured. Warmbier died days after returning to the United States in a coma. The report also noted multiple scars and bruises on Warmbier's body, some of which appeared to stem from medical procedures. The Warmbier family has not yet responded to the coroner's report.

The stovepipe hat, believed to have belonged to Abraham Lincoln, is under scrutiny as two investigations suggest there is little evidence to support its connection to the former president. The hat, valued at $6.5 million, is a significant attraction at the Abraham Lincoln Presidential Library and Museum, but it is currently not on display due to its delicate condition.

The hat's authenticity was questioned by the Chicago Sun-Times in 2012, and since then, investigations have been conducted, including a previously undisclosed FBI analysis and a report by top curators from the Smithsonian National Museum of American History and Chicago History Museum. These investigations found inadequate documentation to prove that Lincoln ever owned the hat.

In 2015, an FBI analysis, conducted with secrecy, compared DNA samples from the hat with Lincoln's blood-spattered handkerchief and other items from the night of his assassination. However, the results were inconclusive. The DNA testing was apparently done with such secrecy that FBI agents were encouraged to disguise themselves as a news crew while at the museum.

The recent revelations come as the Abraham Lincoln Presidential Library Foundation is seeking millions of dollars in state taxpayer support and private donations to repay outstanding loans on the purchase of the hat and 1,600 Lincoln-related artifacts. The foundation said it summarized the findings by the FBI and historians for the museum’s current leadership and Governor Bruce Rauner’s administration while lobbying unsuccessfully for state subsidies earlier this year. However, the foundation did not give the full reports to current museum officials or Rauner’s office.

The Lincoln Museum’s executive director, Alan Lowe, expressed frustration that he only recently learned about the reports, but he sought to downplay their significance, stating that neither of these initiatives produced new evidence about the hat’s origins. Lowe also mentioned that James Cornelius, who had been curator of the museum’s Lincoln collection, has been discharged, but his departure did not involve the foundation or the hat.

In conclusion, the stovepipe hat, which is one of the most historically sacred objects displayed at the Abraham Lincoln Presidential Library and Museum, is under question due to insufficient evidence to prove its connection to Abraham Lincoln. The hat's authenticity has been investigated by the FBI and top curators from various museums, but the results have been inconclusive, and the foundation has been accused of withholding full reports from current museum officials and Governor Rauner’s office.

Richard Grenell, an openly gay foreign policy spokesman for Mitt Romney's presidential campaign, has resigned due to pressure from anti-gay conservatives. In a statement, Grenell expressed that the hyper-partisan discussion of personal issues during the campaign had diminished his ability to speak clearly and forcefully on foreign policy matters. He thanked Romney for his support and belief in his abilities, stating that being openly gay was a non-issue for the campaign.

Grenell's resignation came after being kept under wraps during a time when national security issues, including the president's ad concerning Osama bin Laden, had emerged as front-runners in the campaign. The controversy surrounding Grenell's appointment was reflected in pieces from the National Review and Daily Caller, with some social conservatives expressing outrage over his appointment.

Despite the controversy, the Romney campaign did not publicly support Grenell or enlist supportive social conservatives to calm the waters. The campaign manager, Matt Rhoades, responded to Grenell's resignation by stating that they were disappointed he decided to leave for personal reasons, emphasizing that he had superior qualifications for the position he was hired to fill.

Since joining the campaign, Grenell faced criticism over deleted tweets about the physical appearances of certain high-profile Democratic women, as well as heat from the anti-gay group American Family Association. In a statement, Grenell pointed to the public discussion over his sexual orientation as a reason for leaving the campaign.

Grenell's short tenure was marked by controversy, and his resignation leaves a gap in the Romney campaign's foreign policy team. The ongoing pressure from social conservatives and the reluctance of the Romney campaign to send Grenell out as a spokesman while controversy swirled left Grenell essentially with no job. The Romney camp has not responded to further requests for comment.

The billionaire businessman Barry Sherman and his wife, Honey, were found dead in their Toronto mansion on Friday, December 15. The couple, who were both 75 years old, died from "ligature neck compression," which is a form of strangulation. The homicide squad is now investigating their deaths, although they are still classifying the deaths as "suspicious" rather than a homicide.

The Shermans were known for their philanthropy and had four children and a new grandchild. Honey was a gregarious philanthropist who was involved in various causes, including higher education, health care, and the Jewish community. Barry was the founder of Apotex Inc., a generic pharmaceuticals giant, and had a net worth of $4.77 billion.

The couple's deaths have shocked their friends and colleagues, who have described them as kind, generous, and dedicated to their work and community. The family has dismissed the suggestion that a murder-suicide was behind the deaths, stating that it is inconsistent with their parents' enthusiasm for life.

The Shermans had recently listed their North York home for $6.9 million, and a real estate agent discovered their bodies on Friday morning. There was no sign of forced entry, and no note was left behind to explain what happened.

Tributes and condolences have poured in from various leaders, including Prime Minister Justin Trudeau and Toronto Mayor John Tory. Friends and colleagues in Toronto's tight-knit Jewish community are struggling to find an explanation for the couple's deaths.

The investigation into the deaths is ongoing, and the police have not released any further details about the case. The Sherman family has requested privacy during this difficult time.

In his first visit to Europe since taking office, US Vice President Mike Pence delivered a stern message to Nato allies at the Munich Security Conference, urging them to increase their defense spending contributions. Pence criticized some of the largest allies for not having a credible path towards meeting their financial obligations, without naming specific countries such as Germany, France, and Italy. The speech was met with lukewarm applause, and German Chancellor Angela Merkel responded by stating that Germany would fulfill its commitment to increase defense spending over the next decade, rather than being forced into faster rises.

Pence's speech followed Merkel's call for more multilateralism and her avoidance of direct references to President Trump. Merkel emphasized the importance of freedom of the press as a pillar of democracy, in response to attacks on the media by the Trump administration.

Pence also addressed the ongoing controversy surrounding ties between the Trump administration and Russia. He called for Russia to honor the 2015 Minsk peace agreement aimed at ending violence in Ukraine and stressed that the US would continue to hold Russia accountable, while also searching for new common ground. Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov rejected accusations that Russia was responsible for destabilizing peace and described Nato as stuck in "Cold War" thinking.

The conference marked the first major meeting between the Trump administration and leaders from across Europe since Trump took office. Pence was scheduled to hold bilateral talks with Merkel and the leaders of Ukraine and the Baltic states. The US will be "unwavering" in its support for Nato, according to Pence, but European countries are "failing to pay their fair share" on defense, which "erodes the foundation of our alliance." Only the US, UK, Greece, Poland, and Estonia currently meet the 2% GDP defense spending target set by Nato.

The giraffe, the world's tallest land mammal, has been classified as vulnerable to extinction by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) due to a dramatic decline in its population over the past 30 years. The giraffe population has decreased from around 155,000 in 1985 to 97,000 in 2015. The decline is attributed to habitat loss, poaching, and civil unrest in many parts of Africa.

The giraffe is undergoing a "silent extinction" as its numbers have been plummeting, with some populations declining by up to 95% in the last three decades. The rapid growth of human populations has resulted in the expansion of farming and other forms of development that have fragmented the giraffe's range in many parts of Africa. In war-torn areas, giraffes are considered "war fodder" and are hunted for food.

The IUCN has updated its Red List of threatened species, and the giraffe is now listed as vulnerable, meaning that over three generations, the population has declined by more than 30%. Researchers believe that some local populations may not survive, but there is optimism that the long-term future of these tall creatures can be secured.

The success in keeping giraffe numbers high in Southern Africa has much to do with the management of game parks for tourists. Experts believe that the extra attention that the IUCN listing will now attract will benefit the species. South Africa is a good example of how wildlife can be managed effectively for conservation purposes.

The latest edition of the IUCN Red List now contains over 85,000 species in total, with more than 24,000 threatened with extinction. The update also includes the first assessment of crops including wild oats, barley, mango, and other wild relative plants. The publication also includes the first assessment of the Java sparrow, which is now regarded as vulnerable in the Red List classification.

The IUCN Red List is a critical indicator of the health of the world's biodiversity. It provides information about range, population size, habitat and ecology, use and/or trade, threats, and conservation actions that will help inform necessary conservation decisions. The update shows that the scale of the global extinction crisis may be even greater than previously thought.

Rudy Giuliani, Trump's new attorney, is adopting a more aggressive strategy towards special counsel Robert Mueller's investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 election. Giuliani has been pushing dubious theories and making unfounded claims about the case, such as accusing Mueller's office of trying to frame Trump and asserting that the FBI implanted a spy in Trump's campaign.

Trump and his legal team have also been attempting to undermine key witnesses, such as James Comey, the former FBI director fired by Trump. The president's penchant for half-truths, exaggerations, and outright falsehoods has made it difficult for the public to decide whether to believe him or Comey.

Giuliani views his tactics as a success, stating that public opinion is shifting in their favor. He has also been setting new terms for a potential Trump-Mueller interview, requiring Mueller to show evidence that Trump committed a crime and that an interview is necessary.

The delays in scheduling the interview are part of Trump's strategy to sway public opinion and damage the investigation's credibility. Giuliani has been waging a PR campaign against Mueller and the investigation, which has been echoed in Trump's Twitter feed.

Trump's lawyers have suggested that Mueller will abide by Department of Justice guidance that says a sitting president cannot be indicted, which would mean Mueller's most likely option is a written report, which could be presented to Congress. If such a report is damning against Trump, and if Democrats retake the House of Representatives in the fall, the chance of impeachment increases. However, if the public can be convinced that the investigation is a "WITCH HUNT," lawmakers might be more reluctant to take on the president.

Giuliani, Trump, and their allies in Congress have been working to discredit Mueller. Giuliani has played up the debunked "Spygate" conspiracy, admitting that the drama was conjured up "for public opinion." The House of Representatives has also been waging war against Deputy Attorney General Rod Rosenstein, Mueller's boss, sanctioning him on the House floor for failing to turn over requested documents about the investigation.

Recent polls show that Mueller's favorability rating has dipped sharply, particularly among Republicans. A Politico/Morning Consult poll in June put Mueller's favorability at just 32 percent, while more people (36 percent) had an unfavorable opinion of him. The war against Mueller appears to be working, as public opinion becomes increasingly important in the lead-up to the midterm elections.

Michael Bay, the director of "Transformers 4," was involved in an incident in Hong Kong during the filming of the movie. Initially, reports suggested that Bay was injured in an attack, but a press representative later clarified that Bay had fended off an attacker who was wielding an air-conditioning unit as a weapon. The attacker, along with two other men, were arrested for assault and blackmail. The incident occurred when the men demanded money from Bay and his crew, and when Bay refused, they attacked him. The older brother also attacked three police officers who tried to intervene. Bay was injured on the right side of his face but the injuries were not serious, and filming resumed after the episode. It is speculated that the men may have been seeking "disturbance fees" from shops and businesses affected by the "Transformers 4" production. In a statement, Bay provided a different account, stating that the man was under the influence of a narcotic substance and attacked Bay with the air-conditioning unit. The man had earlier accosted several other crew members and rushed onto the set to attack Bay. Bay was able to prevent a serious accident by wrestling the air-conditioner from his attacker. The incident was described by Bay as similar to a scene from the movie "World War Z." In an interview, Bay had previously mentioned that he is a recognizable figure when he travels the world.

The study published in Clinical Psychological Science, a journal of the Association for Psychological Science, suggests that there is no significant change in personality when people become intoxicated, contrary to popular belief. The research was conducted by Rachel Winograd and her colleagues from the University of Missouri, St. Louis, and other institutions.

Participants in the study reported experiencing changes in all factors of the Five Factor Model of personality when they were intoxicated, but extraversion was the only factor that was perceived to be different by outside observers. The researchers believe that this discrepancy may be due to differences in point of view, with both the participants and observers being accurate and inaccurate in their assessments.

The study involved 156 participants who were recruited and brought to the lab in friend groups. They completed an initial survey about their typical alcohol consumption and their perceptions of their own "typical sober" and "typical drunk" personalities. Each participant consumed beverages designed to produce a blood alcohol content of about .09, and the friends worked through a series of group activities to elicit a variety of personality traits and behaviors.

The participants completed personality measures at two points during the lab session, and outside observers used video recordings to complete standardized assessments of each individual's personality traits.
