As expected, participants' ratings indicated changes in all five of the major personality factors, but observer ratings indicated reliable differences in only one personality factor: extraversion.

The researchers acknowledge that they cannot rule out other influences, such as participants' own expectations of their drunk personality, that may have contributed to the discrepancy in ratings. They plan to replicate the study in real-world settings and explore its relevance in the clinical realm to help reduce the negative impact of alcohol on people's lives. The co-authors on the research include Douglas Steinley, Sean P. Lane, and Kenneth J. Sher from the University of Missouri, Columbia.

On a JetBlue flight from Portland, Oregon to JFK, an 18-year-old passenger, Robert Vietze, was accused of urinating on a sleeping 11-year-old girl during the flight. The incident occurred when the girl was left alone for a few minutes while her father and sister used the lavatories. Vietze, who claimed to have consumed eight alcoholic beverages, was removed from the plane and issued a federal summons for indecent exposure. However, federal prosecutors later dropped the case.

The flight was not without further incident, as another passenger complained of chest pains and vomited. The flight crew attempted to manage both situations, using liquid soap from the bathrooms to clean up.

Robert Vietze is a member of the US Ski Team, but his actions may have jeopardized his chances of competing in the 2014 Winter Games in Russia. Vietze refused to apologize for his actions and was subsequently removed from the team's developmental roster. The family refused to comment on the incident when approached by media.

The young victim and her family were on their way to see her grandmother on eastern Long Island for the first time since her father's cancer diagnosis. The family attempted to recover from the incident by attending a Yankee game after the flight.

The neighbor of Vietze described him as a "very nice boy, one of the nicest, most respectable young people I've ever met." However, the incident has raised questions about the selection process for the US Ski Team and the behavior of its members.

Title: Ridley Scott's "Prometheus" - A Science Fiction Film with Philosophical and Horror Elements

Ridley Scott's "Prometheus," released in 2012, is a science fiction film that combines elements of philosophy, pulp fiction, and horror. The film, which shares some DNA with Scott's earlier work, particularly "Alien," stands on its own for those unfamiliar with the earlier film.

The story begins in 2089, on the Isle of Skye, where archaeologists Elizabeth Shaw and Charlie Holloway make a startling discovery - a 35,000-year-old pictogram suggesting that beings from outer space played a significant role in creating life on Earth. They convince the world's richest human, Peter Weyland, to fund a space expedition to find these aliens and answer fundamental questions about the origin and purpose of human life.

The film's cast includes Noomi Rapace as Elizabeth Shaw, Michael Fassbender as David, the spaceship's android, and Charlize Theron as Meredith Vickers, a representative of Weyland Industries. The film is notable for its expert use of 3-D, spooky production design influenced by H.R. Giger, fluid cinematography, and Ridley Scott's moment-to-moment storytelling skill.

The crew lands on a distant planet and enters a vast dome or pyramid, where they find alien humanoids in suspended animation. These aliens have DNA that matches humans, leading the crew to believe they could have brought life to Earth. The film then develops horror scenes comparable to "Alien," with the crew exploring the pyramid and experiencing the alien beings.

One of the key members of the crew is David, an android who knows or can figure out everything, even alien languages. Fassbender's performance as David is praised, particularly his ability to convey the can-he-be-trusted aspect that comes with android territory. Rapace's performance as Elizabeth Shaw is hit and miss, with her never quite connecting with the tree-hugger aspects of her character but coming into her own once things start to go south.

The film raises questions about the origin of human life and doesn't provide clear answers, which adds to its intrigue. It is compared to golden age sci-fi and echoes Scott's "Alien," but it creates a world of its own. Despite some plot twists being predictable, the film's visuals, special effects, and pitch-perfect casting make up for it.

In conclusion, "Prometheus" is a science fiction film that combines elements of philosophy, pulp fiction, and horror. It is a visually stunning film with expert horror scenes, mind-challenging ideas, and enough unanswered questions to prime the inevitable sequel. The film's cast, particularly Fassbender and Rapace, deliver strong performances, and the film's use of 3-D, production design, and cinematography are commendable.

In an exclusive report, actress Daniele Watts, known for her role in 'Django Unchained', has found herself in a controversial situation after pictures were obtained showing her in a seemingly intimate encounter with her white boyfriend, Brian James Lucas, outside the CBS lot in Studio City. The pictures, taken on Thursday, depict Watts straddling Lucas with her breasts exposed, and the couple engaging in explicit behavior.

An eyewitness reported that Watts and Lucas were asked to stop due to the inappropriate display, but they continued. The incident led to an indecent exposure complaint being made to the police.

However, the Los Angeles Police Department (LAPD) is refuting Watts' account of the incident, claiming that she is making "malicious and false statements." LAPD Sgt. Jim Parker contends that he was already near the location when he received a call about public nudity.

According to Parker, he recorded the incident from the moment he got out of his car. He states that Watts and Lucas were not just making out, but were engaged in sexual activity. Parker also mentions that Watts initially refused to identify herself when asked, leading to her being handcuffed.

In contrast, Watts claimed on her Facebook page that she was handcuffed and detained by the LAPD after refusing to agree that she had done something wrong by showing affection, fully clothed, in a public place. She alleged that the police accused her of prostitution due to her being publicly affectionate with her white boyfriend.

The LAPD is conducting an internal investigation into the incident due to the widespread publicity it has received. Watts' agent has not yet commented on the matter.

In Anaheim, California, a Ku Klux Klan (KKK) rally on February 27 resulted in a violent brawl, with three people being critically stabbed and two others assaulted. The KKK members had arrived at a park to denounce "illegal immigration and Muslims," while counter-protesters were several dozen in number. The encounter quickly turned violent, with one KKK member using the decorative end of a flag pole as a weapon and another stabbing a counter-protester.

The KKK's presence in Anaheim dates back to 1924, when it took control of the city's council, with four out of five seats occupied by Klansmen. This was during a time when the Klan's membership roster in Orange County was 1,280 names-strong. The council's actions reflected the KKK's objectives, as they organized a parade with 10,000 Klansmen and a fireworks display in the city park.

This recent rally was significantly smaller, with only six Klan members attending. Five of them were initially arrested, but were released on Sunday as evidence showed they acted in self-defense. Seven counter-protesters remain in custody for allegedly beating, stomping, and attacking the Klansmen with wooden posts.

The brawl was met with criticism for the police response, with some spectators applauding as they watched the Klansmen being arrested. Brian Levin, who directs Cal State San Bernardino’s Center for the Study of Hate and Extremism, was present at the protest and pushed a ringleader of the Klan rally away from the crowd as counter-protesters approached.

The KKK's membership has been on the decline for decades, falling from a peak of 4 million in 1925 to between 5,000 and 8,000 Klansmen today, according to the Southern Poverty Law Center. However, the rise of Republican presidential candidate Donald Trump may be turning the tide for latent white nationalists.

Rachel Pendergraft, a national organizer for a Ku Klux Klan subgroup known as the Knights Party, stated that Trump's ascendance has opened "a door to conversation." Trump has garnered support for proposals such as building a wall between the U.S. and Mexico and barring all Muslims from entry, which some believe aligns with the KKK's ideologies.

The critically injured counter-protester is now in stable condition. The incident serves as a reminder of the ongoing tension and violence that can arise from opposing ideologies, and the importance of peace and dignity in responding to such situations.

The article discusses the use of military equipment by campus police departments in the United States, specifically focusing on the University of Central Florida and Hinds Community College. Both institutions have acquired military equipment, including a grenade launcher, through a federal program known as the 1033 program, which transfers military surplus to law-enforcement agencies across the country. The equipment is obtained at little cost to the departments, with colleges paying only for shipping.

The acquisition of such equipment has been met with both support and criticism. Supporters argue that it provides necessary gear for departments, particularly those with limited budgets, and can be useful in situations such as active-shooter incidents. However, detractors argue that the procurement of tactical gear does not help with the types of crimes that occur more frequently on college campuses, such as alcohol-related incidents and sexual assault. Additionally, there are concerns that military equipment may have a chilling effect on free expression on college campuses.

The 1033 program has received renewed scrutiny in the wake of protests in Ferguson, Missouri, where police officers were criticized for using military-grade weapons and equipment. Some lawmakers have called for a review of the program, and there have been suggestions that local police departments that enjoy cost savings from free military equipment be required to receive additional training.

The University of Central Florida and Hinds Community College both received their grenade launchers from the Department of Defense, and Central Florida also acquired 23 M-16 assault rifles through the program. At least 117 colleges have acquired equipment through the 1033 program, with the most popular weapon procured being the M-16 assault rifle.

The article also discusses the value of transparency in the use of military equipment on college campuses, as well as the importance of administrative oversight and communication between campus police departments and administrators. It is noted that many campus police departments use the 1033 program to acquire basic supplies along with tactical equipment.

Overall, the article raises questions about the appropriateness of the use of military equipment by campus police departments and the potential impact it may have on college campuses.

One year ago, the Hollywood landscape was drastically altered as allegations of sexual assault and harassment against prominent figures in the industry surfaced. The initial accusations against Harvey Weinstein sparked a wave of similar allegations against other high-profile figures such as Kevin Spacey, Morgan Freeman, and Mario Testino. The #MeToo movement, which began as a hashtag on social media, gained momentum as hundreds of famous men were exposed as sexual predators and abusers, leading to their termination from various roles.

Rose McGowan, who was previously known for her role in the TV show Charmed, was one of the eight women who accused Weinstein of sexual assault. Her allegations set off a wildfire of accusations that swept through Hollywood, causing numerous reputations to crumble.

Recently, Bill Cosby, a once-respected comedian and actor, was found guilty of sexual assault. Rose McGowan took to Twitter to express her feelings about the anniversary of this tumultuous year, stating that it was one of the hardest years of her life and expressing pride in the survivors of sexual assault. She also clarified that her previous statements about the #MeToo movement were not meant to imply that the movement is a lie, but rather that she was referring to Hollywood and the Time's Up movement. McGowan ended her tweet by expressing her determination to move forward, using the hashtag #RoseArmy.

A new study suggests that exposure to bright light, similar to light boxes used to treat depression, can increase testosterone levels and sexual satisfaction in men with low sexual desire. The study, conducted by the University of Siena in Italy, involved 38 men diagnosed with disorders causing a lack of interest in sex. Half of the group was treated with a light box for half an hour each morning for two weeks, while the other half received an adapted light box with significantly less light. The group exposed to the bright light tripled their sexual satisfaction scores, while the control group's scores remained the same. The researchers also found that testosterone levels increased in men who had been given the active light treatment, from around 2.1 ng/ml to 3.6 ng/ml, but the control group showed no increase. The increased levels of testosterone were attributed to the greater reported sexual satisfaction. The light box treatment works by simulating exposure to sunlight and passing messages to the part of the brain that controls sex drive, among other functions. The researchers believe that the light therapy may inhibit the pineal gland in the brain, allowing for more testosterone production. They hope that light therapy may offer benefits similar to medication but with fewer side effects, although more research is needed before it can be recommended as a clinical treatment. The paper will be presented at the European College of Neuropsychopharmacology (ECNP) Congress in Vienna.

A stolen statue of the Virgin Mary from a Vermont nativity scene in Lyndonville, missing since January 2016, has been found and returned to its owner. The statue was discovered in an apartment house storage area by Lyndonville Police Chief Jack Harris, acting on a tip. The statue was identified by Municipal Administrator Justin Smith, who recognized it in photos of the building's interior taken during an inspection. The building is primarily occupied by college students, making it impossible to determine how the statue ended up there. Unfortunately, a statue of the baby Jesus stolen at the same time remains missing. This news was reported by The Caledonian Record.

In her will, legendary actress Lauren Bacall, who passed away at the age of 89, bequeathed $10,000 for the care of her beloved dog, Sophie. The majority of Bacall's estate, worth over $26 million, will be split among her three children: Leslie Bogart, Stephen Bogart, and actor Sam Robards, who was also tasked with caring for Sophie. Bacall, known for her iconic roles and marriages to Humphrey Bogart and Jason Robards, was a lifelong dog lover. She left additional monetary sums to two of her employees and $250,000 to each of her six grandchildren. Bacall's will also included provisions for the use of her likeness and movie and book royalties, and requested that her personal papers remain private. This is not an unusual practice among celebrities, with examples such as Leona Helmsley leaving $12 million to her Maltese, Trouble, and Dusty Springfield including provisions for her cat, Nicholas, in her will.

In a recent development, a neighborhood group in Washington, D.C., known as the Shaw Dupont Citizens Alliance, proposed a moratorium on new liquor licenses for the vibrant nightlife corridors on 14th Street and U Street. This move was aimed at controlling the growth of bars and restaurants in the area, citing local nuisance effects and fears of becoming "the next Adams-Morgan," an area that is already under a moratorium. However, a counter-group called In My Backyard—D.C. has emerged, advocating for growth-friendly policies.

The proposed moratorium is part of a larger trend across the United States, where similar fights over liquor licenses play out in cities. In New York, a group of residents on the Lower East Side attempted to halt the issuance of new liquor licenses last fall. Chicago has areas that have voted to become completely "dry," and moratorium zones where existing businesses can stay open but no new licenses can be issued. In California, many whole counties, including all of San Francisco, have gone into moratorium status.

Proponents of curtailing licenses typically cite local nuisance effects as the key reason. They fear a "Wild West atmosphere" and the nightmare of becoming like Adams-Morgan. However, these complaints should be understood in the larger context of urban economics. Moratorium boosters often think there's something unnatural about the heavy concentration of booze-serving establishments in a single area. They also think restricting bars and restaurants will cause the kind of thriving local retail they remember from old Jane Jacobs books to magically appear.

In reality, there's nothing particularly unusual about similar firms clustering together. Drinking and dining establishments want to be where people are likely to look for them. And people want to go to places where they'll find options. Complicated interdependencies and complementarities can arise. The late-night pizza joint's proximity to the dive bar increases the value of both. Forcing the cluster to disperse destroys its value. Preventing new firms from entering the cluster fosters high prices and mediocrity, as underperforming bars and restaurants can essentially free-ride on the rest of the cluster.

Providing these kinds of dense networks of related but independent small undertakings is exactly what cities are good at. Refusing to grant liquor licenses won't undo the decades of history that brought us big-box stores. It just leads to empty storefronts and car rides out to Ikea or Costco. The good news is that lately, Amazon has been crushing the big-box sector, and e-commerce levels the shopping playing field between traditional urban neighborhoods and suburban ones.

Under the circumstances, promoting the development and expansion of nightlife hubs should be a key economic development priority for cities. This means making decisions about liquor-licensing rules at a higher level, with consideration of the full citywide effects in terms of tax revenue and job creation. It also means attempting to directly address perceived problems with crime and trash. Instead of refusing to issue new liquor licenses, why not send more cops and offer more frequent street cleaning in the hubs?

Furthermore, it's important to note that excessive alcohol use can lead to numerous health risks, including premature death, increased disease and injury, property damage, alcohol-related crime, and lost productivity. The economic costs of excessive alcohol consumption in 2010 were estimated at $249 billion, or $2.05 a drink. Therefore, cities should not only focus on promoting nightlife hubs but also address the issue of responsible drinking.

In a separate context, a blogger-pundit, Matt Yglesias, has been advocating for more bars, arguing that the current licensing system leaves us with a paucity of public drinking spots where they're wanted. However, increasing the number of bars could contribute to the ongoing public health crisis of alcohol abuse, which already kills tens of thousands of Americans annually and costs hundreds of billions of dollars a year in lost productivity, health care, and property damage.

In contrast, there's growing evidence that marijuana could be a substitute for alcohol, with potentially lower social costs. As more states move towards legalizing recreational marijuana use, there's a demand for marijuana bars or weed cafes, a demand that's being suppressed far more strongly than the demand for more alcohol bars. However, the responsible common use of marijuana in public remains a topic that needs to be addressed.

In conclusion, while the proposed moratorium on new liquor licenses in Washington, D.C., is part of a larger trend across the United States, it's important to consider the economic and health implications of such decisions. Cities should focus on promoting the development and expansion of nightlife hubs while addressing the issue of responsible drinking and exploring the potential of marijuana as a substitute for alcohol.

On May 30, 2018, thousands of residents in McDowell County, North Carolina were allowed to return home following a mandatory evacuation due to a landslide near the Tahoma Dam. The evacuation was prompted by heavy rains that caused widespread flooding, with McDowell County reporting 4 to 6 inches of rainfall over the past 24 hours. The flooding was triggered by the remnants of Tropical Depression Alberto, the first named storm of the Atlantic hurricane season.

Residents living below Lake Tahoma were ordered to evacuate early Wednesday morning after an engineer determined that the landslide had compromised the dam's integrity. The National Weather Service issued a flash flood emergency for McDowell County, which includes the cities of Marion and Old Fort. The evacuation order was lifted later in the day after an engineer deemed the dam safe.

The flooding was particularly severe, with the Catawba River near Pleasant Gardens cresting at its highest level since its record crest set during Hurricane Frances in September 2004. Schools were closed in McDowell County, and flooding was also reported in the town of Old Fort. Multiple semi trucks were reported stuck in floodwaters in the Greenlee community just east of Old Fort.

In addition to the flooding, a landslide shut down all westbound lanes on Interstate 40 at the top of Old Fort Mountain Tuesday night, but the roadway has since been cleared and reopened. Elsewhere, parts of U.S. 176 were shut down from flooding in Polk County, North Carolina, between Saluda and Tryon. At least five mudslides were reported in Henderson County blocking roads near the towns of Bat Cave and Hendersonville.

The flooding and mudslides led to five minor injuries during water rescues, and a state of emergency was declared in McDowell County. Shelters were set up at two churches and a YMCA, and some 2,000 people from campgrounds and residential communities near the dam and lake had evacuated, with roughly 200 at shelters. Old Fort and Marion were the hardest-hit communities.

This is a developing story, and check back for updates on weather.com.

In a political standoff, House Speaker John Boehner has asked President Obama to address a joint-session of Congress on Thursday, September 8, instead of the originally requested September 7. The White House has accepted the new date. The initial request for September 7 conflicted with a Republican presidential debate scheduled for the same night. Boehner requested the change citing logistical difficulties, but did not mention the debate conflict in his letter. The response by Boehner sets up an early showdown between Obama and the Congress just returning from its August recess. The White House downplayed the scheduling conflict with the GOP debate as a coincidence, but the Republican National Committee accused the Obama administration of politicking by scheduling the speech simultaneously with the debate. This year's opener of the NFL season, traditionally a ratings winner, will also compete with the presidential address. The speech will focus on creating jobs and putting aside politics. The House Democratic leadership was not consulted about the change in date for the president's address.

A 54-year-old man has been arrested and is being questioned in connection with a series of fake bomb incidents that occurred across Staten Island, New York, over the past few weeks. The suspect is believed to have been motivated by jealousy, as he had a crush on a woman who recently married a man living on his block. Three inert devices were found, with threatening notes in Spanish attached to them, and the devices were made with propane cylinders, gasoline, nails, and screws. The devices were found in laptop bags or suitcases, and at least one had a nine-volt battery attached to it. The devices spurred evacuations of nearby homes and triggered an all-out manhunt by the NYPD. The suspect's name has not been released, and charges are pending. The NYPD formed a task force to investigate the incidents and believes that terrorism was not a motive.

The family of Bart Palosz, a 15-year-old student who committed suicide in August 2013 after the first day of his sophomore year at Greenwich High School, is suing the town and its board of education for $15,000 in damages. The lawsuit alleges that school officials were aware of Palosz's years-long history of bullying at Western Middle School and Greenwich High School, and failed to protect him despite their knowledge of the bullying he endured.

According to the complaint, Palosz faced name-calling, teasing, physical violence, and property theft from classmates. He was kicked and hit on the back of the neck, had his pencil stolen and thrown at him, and his brand new smartphone smashed. School administrators, teachers, and counselors are accused of leaving Palosz "unprotected and unsupported" despite their knowledge of the bullying he endured.

The lawsuit claims that Greenwich High School "failed to comply" with its anti-bullying policy, which requires staff members to provide victims with emotional support, intervene in and investigate known cases of bullying, file oral and written reports on bullying instances, contact the parents of bullying victims, and discipline bullies. The complaint cites Greenwich First Selectman Drew Marzullo as saying, "We as a community failed this child."

The family's attorney, Randy Savicky of Silver Golub & Teitell LLP, said the town is required to respond by Sept. 8. The lawsuit seeks changes to how the Greenwich school system responds to students in need of help and aims to prevent further needless deaths. The case sheds new light on the case and again raises the question of whether the school district should share the blame in Palosz's decision to take his life.

French economist Thomas Piketty, author of the influential book "Capital in the 21st Century," has declined France's highest award, the Legion d'honneur. Piketty, who is known for his critique of income inequality, stated that it is not the government's role to decide who is honorable. He expressed his concern that the government should focus on reviving economic growth in France and Europe instead.

Piketty was once associated with the Socialist Party but has distanced himself from their policies. His book, which examines income inequality, became a surprise hit, topping the bestseller list in the US. It is rare for anyone to turn down the Legion d'honneur, with notable refusals including philosopher Jean-Paul Sartre and radiology pioneers Pierre and Marie Curie.

Piketty's book, which is almost 600 pages long, sold half a million copies in English and was widely debated, particularly in the US. Nobel Prize-winning economist Paul Krugman called it "the most important economics book of the year - and maybe of the decade." Last year, cartoonist Jacques Tardi also turned down the Legion d'honneur.

A homeless man named Glen James, residing in Boston, returned a backpack containing over $42,000 in cash and traveler's checks to the police, earning him praise for his honesty. Ethan Whittington, a resident of Midlothian, Virginia, was so moved by James' act that he started a fundraising campaign on Go Fund Me with the goal of raising $250,000 to help James buy a house. The campaign has already garnered over $110,000 in donations. Whittington believes this initiative serves as a positive statement for America, demonstrating that collective efforts can bring about significant change. Despite facing skepticism, Whittington aims to meet James and distribute the funds to him soon.

Google has provided a closer look at its futuristic eyewear, Google Glass, by revealing more details about its user interface, features, and potential applications. The device, which is worn above and to the right of the right eye, features a small screen visible through a mirrored glass block. The UI allows users to take photos, record videos, search Google, receive reminders, and share content through messaging or Google+ Hangouts. Users can engage the device by saying "OK, Glass."

Google is also accepting applications for a limited number of public testers, who can apply by writing a 50-word post on Google Plus or Twitter with the hashtag #ifihadglass. Winners will receive a pair of Google Glass, but will have to pay $1,500 plus tax. Google has also launched a contest to encourage creative uses for the glasses, with winners getting the opportunity to purchase their own.

Google has also shared some potential use cases for Google Glass, such as a ballerina streaming live video, a tourist translating foreign languages, and a family video chatting with a long-distance relative. Google is looking for "bold, creative individuals" to join the testing process and help shape the future of Google Glass.

The article discusses the critical condition of former Russian double agent Sergei Skripal and his daughter Yulia, who were poisoned with the nerve agent novichok in Salisbury, UK. Ross Cassidy, a friend of the Skripals, believes they are so critically ill that they should be allowed to die due to the severe mental impairment they are expected to face if they survive. Cassidy met the Skripals in 2010 when they moved in next door to him in Salisbury. He describes them as friendly and generous, and he introduced Sergei to English beer while Sergei introduced him to vodka. Cassidy has spent many hours with counter-terror detectives investigating the poisoning but would not discuss the police operation. He drove Mr Skripal to Heathrow to collect Yulia on March 3, 2018, and the next day they were found collapsed in Salisbury city centre. Cassidy has been upset by the suggestion that there isn't anyone who cares enough to want to go and see the Skripals, as he has asked the police several times if they could go and see them, but was told categorically that they were not allowed. Viktoria Skripal, Mr Skripal's niece, told the BBC she is hoping for a miracle but believes the prognosis for both Sergei and Yulia is not good. The article also mentions that countries across the world have joined the UK in taking diplomatic action against Russia, which has been blamed for the attack.

A 14-year-old boy, identified as Brandon Clegg, died from a self-inflicted gunshot wound after a shootout with police at Dennis Intermediate School in Richmond, Indiana, on Thursday. The chaos unfolded after Clegg's mother called 911 to report potential violence at the school, prompting a police response and a lockdown. The teen was not a student at the school but lived in the area.

A candlelight vigil was held on Sunday to support Clegg's mother, who is being praised for her actions in preventing a potential mass shooting. Dozens of community members attended the vigil, meeting with the mother and praying with her.

Investigators say it was Clegg's mother who called 911, reporting that her son was armed and headed to the school. Clegg was met by police at the school and took his own life after a shootout with officers.

Clegg's family says he was bullied, and they believe this may have contributed to his actions. The middle school remains closed on Monday. The investigation into the incident is ongoing.

In the 2011 Values Voter Summit, Ron Paul won the presidential straw poll, with 36.9% of the votes, followed by Herman Cain, Rick Santorum, Rick Perry, Michele Bachmann, Mitt Romney, Newt Gingrich, and Jon Huntsman. Paul's victory was attributed to his well-organized campaign, as his Campaign for Liberty organization bought tickets for the event. Herman Cain, who delivered a well-received speech, was a popular choice, but his stance on immigration and Perry's likability may have dampened his potential supporters' enthusiasm. Perry, who had a poor showing, focused on Iowa instead of the event. Santorum, who rose from a 5% showing in 2010, benefited from the departure of fantasy candidates like Mike Huckabee and Sarah Palin. However, social conservatives did not receive much help from FRC President Tony Perkins in choosing a candidate to unite behind to prevent a potential Romney win. The event was not Romney-friendly, as he only won 13% of the vote in 2010, and his path to the nomination does not require a massive embrace from religious conservatives.

Oliver Stone, a renowned controversial director, has announced plans to write and direct a film about Edward Snowden, the former NSA contractor who leaked massive amounts of classified documents to the media. The film will be based on "The Snowden Files: The Inside Story of the World's Most Wanted Man," a book by Guardian journalist Luke Harding. Stone has advocated for Snowden, calling him a hero for revealing the alleged violations of the Fourth Amendment by the US government.

Sony Pictures has also acquired the big-screen rights to Glenn Greenwald's "No Place to Hide: Edward Snowden, the NSA and the U.S. Surveillance State." The film is being produced by James Bond producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael G. Wilson.

Stone and long-time producing partner Moritz Borman have secured the rights to the book and have started working on the screenplay. They aim to start filming before the end of the year. The New York Times described "The Snowden Files" as a fast-paced, cinematic thriller. Both Stone and Guardian editor-in-chief, Alan Rusbridger, expressed excitement about the project.

Charlie Sheen, known for his past endorsement of the 9/11 conspiracy theory, has faced backlash from a group of conspiracy theorists. They are planning to protest at his live shows, as they believe Sheen has abandoned the cause by shifting his focus away from questioning the events of 9/11 and towards personal controversies such as drug use and encounters with sex workers. Mark Dice, a prominent member of The 9/11 Truth Movement, has reached out to Sheen, expressing disappointment and urging him to address the issue. If Sheen does not respond, the protesters plan to demonstrate at his upcoming shows.

The study led by Dr. Marcos A. Espinal, the director of communicable diseases at the Pan American Health Organization, found a significant correlation between the Zika virus and Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) in seven Latin American countries. The increase in GBS cases was substantial, with a 877% increase in Venezuela, 211% in Colombia, 150% in the Dominican Republic, 100% in El Salvador, 144% in Honduras, 400% in Suriname, and 28% in men compared to women across all the countries.

The study included both confirmed and suspected Zika infections reported by national health officials. The continental United States lacks a formal monitoring system for GBS, which could pose challenges as the number of Zika cases increases.

Puerto Rico reported its first death from GBS related to a Zika infection. The victim was a man between 35 and 45 years old from the San Juan metro area. Puerto Rico has a total of 13,186 confirmed Zika cases, with 102 hospitalizations and 34 cases of GBS. The number of Zika cases is believed to be much higher due to the high number of asymptomatic infections.

A study published in JAMA Pediatrics estimates that up to 10,300 pregnant women in Puerto Rico could be infected with Zika, and between 100 to 270 babies could be born with microcephaly through mid-2017. The study also suggests that some babies infected with Zika may present with other complications such as eye abnormalities, hearing loss, and inflexible joints.

Doctors are fairly certain that Zika can cause GBS, a condition in which the immune system attacks the nerves, causing temporary but often severe paralysis. In extreme cases, patients may require ventilators. Zika's worst effect is the brain and nerve damage it causes in developing fetuses, which cannot be prevented or reversed.

Pregnant women in Zika-affected zones are advised to avoid mosquito bites if possible by using repellents, covering up with clothing, and staying inside behind screens and air conditioning. However, these facilities are often not available in some of the worst-hit places.

The researchers found more women than men reported Zika infections, but men were more likely to develop GBS. The study suggests that monitoring GBS cases could be a useful way to spot Zika outbreaks. Approximately 500 million people in Latin America and the Caribbean are at risk for Zika virus infection, and increases in the incidence of GBS impose a substantial burden on populations and health services in this region.

On New Year's Day, the minimum wage will increase in 10 states, ranging from a dime to 35 cents. The wage hikes are either part of automatic adjustments to keep up with cost of living or due to state laws. In Rhode Island, the minimum wage is increasing for the first time in five years. The increase is good news for workers like Sydonia Lary, but a concern for business owners like Julio Fonseca who worry about rising costs. Bill Vernon from the National Federation of Independent Business argues that higher wages will harm young workers looking for entry-level jobs. The wage increases will benefit nearly a million workers, with Washington state raising its wage to $9.19 an hour, almost double that of neighboring Idaho. The research shows that rising minimum wages have no impact on employment and can actually reduce turnover. The automatic adjustments are expected to continue in many states this year, with lawmakers considering a federal minimum wage increase of about $2.

The article discusses the establishment of Lumos, a charity founded by J.K. Rowling in response to a disturbing photograph of a caged child in a residential institution. The photograph, published in 1996, sparked outrage and led to the creation of Lumos, named after a spell from Rowling's Harry Potter series. Lumos aims to shed light on the lives of the 8 million children worldwide who are separated from their families and institutionalized due to poverty, disability, and discrimination.

The article highlights the deplorable conditions in these institutions, where children are often caged, malnourished, and abused. The majority of these children have parents who could care for them, but are placed in institutions due to a lack of resources or alternatives. Lumos works to keep families together, support vulnerable families, and promote family-based care alternatives for children who cannot be with their parents.

The article emphasizes that institutionalization causes children measurable and sometimes irreparable harm, including developmental delays, psychological trauma, and a lifetime of poverty and dependency. However, the problem is solvable, and Lumos estimates that institutionalization of children can be eradicated globally by 2050.

The article also discusses the economic benefits of ending institutionalization, as it is far more cost-effective to support a child in a family than in an institution. Lumos has achieved significant success in reducing the number of children in institutions in countries like Moldova, the Czech Republic, and Bulgaria.

Finally, the article introduces the social media campaign #Letstalklumos, launched by Rowling to raise awareness and keep the issue alive. Rowling has also committed to becoming president of Lumos for life, with the dream of ending the practice of institutionalization in her lifetime.

The article discusses the rise of background check services for online daters, aimed at protecting individuals from scammers, identity thieves, sexual predators, and felons on dating websites. The services, such as MyMatchChecker and various mobile apps, allow users to perform background checks on potential partners they meet online for a small fee.

The increase in online dating usage, with over 20 million Americans using dating sites, has led to concerns about safety and violence. While no definitive numbers exist on the amount of crime stemming from dating sites, there have been reported cases of sexual predators and serial rapists using online dating platforms to meet victims.

In response, some states, like New York and New Jersey, have begun regulating Internet dating sites, with New York's Internet Dating Safety Act requiring sites to post safety tips. However, the effectiveness of background checks is debated, as state and county databases are incomplete, and databases vary in quality and availability.

Online dating companies argue that background checks may give users a false sense of security, as the checks may not be comprehensive or accurate. Critics also point out potential issues with the handling of personal information by background check companies and the potential misuse of information by mobile apps.

Despite these concerns, the article emphasizes the importance of safety in online dating and encourages users to be cautious and vigilant when meeting people online.

In Suffolk, Virginia, a shooting incident occurred on Thursday morning at a local barbershop. The dispute started over an argument about Halle Berry playing Aretha Franklin in a movie, according to a witness. The argument escalated into a physical fight, and 44-year-old Michael Jermell Hatton pulled out a firearm, shooting the other man outside the shop. Both victims received emergency medical treatment before being transported to local hospitals. The gunshot victim, Tony Jonathan Lundy, is in critical condition. Hatton was treated, released, and arrested, and is currently held without bond at the Western Tidewater Regional Jail. The investigation is ongoing. The incident highlights a dispute over the casting of Halle Berry as Aretha Franklin in an upcoming biopic, a role that was eventually given to Jennifer Hudson.

Nancy Reed, a 77-year-old community volunteer from Kingwood, Texas, died on September 15 due to complications from necrotizing fasciitis, a flesh-eating bacterial infection. The infection was acquired after Reed fell and injured her arm in her flooded home during Hurricane Harvey. This makes Reed the 36th official Harvey-related death in Harris County. Another case of the bacteria was reported in a rescuer, J.R. Atkins, who survived after contracting the infection through an insect bite while assisting flood-ravaged victims in suburban Missouri City. Necrotizing fasciitis is a serious bacterial skin infection that can cause organ failure and is usually fatal if not treated promptly with antibiotics. The infection is not a reportable disease in Texas, but doctors are required to report certain organisms that cause the disease. Reed is remembered as a kind and generous member of the Kingwood community who was active in her church and various charities. Her family and friends are mourning her loss.

Tensions between Russia and Ukraine escalated on March 1, 2014, as Russian President Vladimir Putin requested authorization from the Russian Parliament to use military force in Ukraine. Putin's justification was the protection of ethnic Russians and personnel of a Russian military base in Crimea, a strategic region with a Russian majority. The move came after pro-Russian forces took control of key airports and a communications center in Crimea, prompting accusations of a "military invasion and occupation" from Ukraine. The crisis has deepened the schism between Russia and Ukraine, with the latter appealing to NATO for help. The Ukrainian government, led by a new government that took power after the ouster of President Viktor Yanukovich, warned of war and placed troops on high alert. The situation is particularly tense in Crimea, where the new authorities suspect Russia of fomenting tension and potentially bidding for separation. The crisis has raised alarm bells among world diplomats, with Ukraine's ambassador to the United Nations calling Russia's actions a "clear act of aggression." Russia, however, has rejected these calls and blamed the EU for causing the unrest in Ukraine. The situation remains fluid, with ongoing negotiations between Ukrainian and Russian naval chiefs aimed at easing tensions. The crisis marks the biggest confrontation between Russia and the West since the Cold War.

The Political TV Ad Archive, a project of the Internet Archive, is collecting political TV ads and social media content from key 2016 primary election states to provide reliable information on political influence. In a separate news, a 13-year-old student named Austin Lacey from Ethan A. Chase Middle School in Menifee was asked to remove his Elsa costume during a Disney-themed school spirit day. The school principal felt the costume was causing a disruption, but many students, including Kassandra Melara, 14, and Natalia Alvarez, an eighth-grader, stated that it was not a disruption and everyone was taking pictures with Austin. Austin, who is running for ASB president, wore the costume for fun and his classmates loved it. The school district's superintendent, Dr. Julie Vitale, stated that the action was taken in accordance with district policies and that there was no indication that Austin was expressing any particular message. Austin and his mother were surprised by the reaction of school officials, but Austin completed the school day without facing any discipline. The incident sparked controversy among students and parents, with some supporting Austin's right to express himself and others supporting the school's decision to maintain order.

On Wednesday, security cameras captured a sinkhole opening at the National Corvette Museum in Bowling Green, KY, swallowing eight iconic sports cars. The museum has released videos of the incident on their YouTube channel, showing the cars being sucked into a 40-foot deep hole. No timeline has been set for the cars' removal or museum repairs, as engineers ensure safety before working inside the pit. The museum offers a variety of exhibits and attractions, including a 50s-themed Corvette Cafe and a large Corvette store.

Margaux Sainte-Lagüe, a French entrepreneur, has launched an online store named Mon Pavé Parisien, selling hand-painted cobblestones directly from Paris's iconic streets. The city of Paris began selling thousands of tons of cobblestones from its most famous roads and secret-trodden alleyways in early 2016 as part of its circular economy initiative to reduce waste and save energy.

Sainte-Lagüe, inspired by the sight of jackhammers tearing up cobblestones on Paris's Champs-Élysées, bought five tons of the stones and now offers three styles: a classic version hand-painted in the colors of France's flag, one gilded in 22.5 carats of gold, and the May 68 series stone, whose bottom half is sheathed in sand and features the inscription “sous les pavés,” a popular phrase used during the protests of the May 1968 revolution.

Customers can also request custom designs, and Sainte-Lagüe has already personalized stones for Paris's mayor, Anne Hidalgo, and for a Chinese bride and groom. Each cobblestone is available at Mon Pavé Parisien’s online store, with prices ranging from $63 to $157.

The activity is rooted in a movement to create a circular economy, promoted by the French government, European Commission, and some builders, to reduce waste and save energy through recycling and reuse. Paris may sell as many as 3 million tons of cobblestones, first laid in the 11th century, with some going to small companies for paving terraces and driveways.

The sales could add about 400,000 euros ($371,000) annually to municipal coffers if 10,000 tons are extracted from under asphalt every year. At between 60 euros and 150 euros a cobblestone, Sainte-Lague is making a tidy profit from her central Parisian workshop where she cleans and custom decorates each stone. With the possibility that some of the cobblestones were trod on by famous artists like Vincent Van Gogh or Pablo Picasso, buyers can own a piece of Paris’s history.

The article discusses a tragic incident that occurred during the Oklahoma State University (OSU) homecoming parade, where a car plowed into a crowd of spectators, resulting in four deaths and numerous injuries. The driver, Adacia Chambers, is a 25-year-old woman who has been charged with four counts of second-degree murder and driving under the influence of drugs.

Chambers' attorney, Tony Coleman, stated that she was not intoxicated and suffers from mental illness. He believes that she may have experienced a blackout due to underlying physical or mental problems. Coleman also mentioned that Chambers has diabetes but is not being treated for it, and she reportedly suffers from insomnia.

The victims of the crash include Marvin Stone, a retired OSU professor, his wife Bonnie, who had worked for the university for over 30 years, Nicollete Strauch, an OSU employee, and 2-year-old Nash Lucas, the son of an OSU student. Several others were injured, including 11 victims younger than 13.

Family members of the injured and deceased are coping with the aftermath of the tragedy. Mark McNitt, a relative of one of the injured victims, described the chaotic scene and the ongoing support from hospital staff and the community.

OSU President Burns Hargis called the incident an "incomprehensible tragedy." The football game scheduled for that day was allowed to proceed, with the team kneeling in solemn prayer at the 25-yard line before the game.

Chambers is being held in jail without bail and is expected to appear in court on Monday. The investigation is ongoing, with toxicology results still pending. The community is mourning the loss and offering support to those affected by the tragedy.

This week, a joke made by actor Robert De Niro at a fundraiser with First Lady Michelle Obama sparked controversy. De Niro joked about the possibility of a white first lady, referencing the wives of Newt Gingrich, Karen Santorum, and Ann Romney. The first lady's press secretary deemed the joke inappropriate, and De Niro apologized, stating his remarks were not meant to offend.

Meanwhile, President Obama's chief political strategist, David Axelrod, used the term "Mittzkrieg" to describe Mitt Romney's constant advertising barrage in Illinois, which the Republican Jewish Coalition found offensive due to Holocaust and Nazi imagery. They demanded an apology from Axelrod and a public rebuke from Representative Debbie Wasserman Schultz.

In a New York Times op-ed, HBO's Bill Maher called for an end to insincere demands for apologies from those who have supposedly offended others. He argued for a permissive rule, suggesting that if one finds something offensive, they should simply change the channel. Maher's argument, however, is self-serving as he has faced criticism for using vile words to refer to former Alaska governor Sarah Palin and her family.

The debate over civility and incivility in politics continues, with some arguing for higher standards and civil discourse, while others, like Maher, advocate for freedom of speech. The issue remains complex, with both parties using it for political gain, but the call for a more united America persists.

The federal court has approved a $25 million settlement in a lawsuit against President Donald Trump and his defunct Trump University, which was accused of using false advertising and high-pressure sales techniques to lure students into expensive seminars. The settlement was first approved by a judge in March 2017, but was held in escrow until the court upheld it. The students had claimed that Trump University, which operated from 2005 to 2010, promised to teach them the secrets of success in the real estate industry but instead led to the loss of thousands of dollars in tuition. The most expensive program, a "one-year apprenticeship," cost $1,495; a "membership" cost over $10,000; and "Gold Elite" classes cost $35,000. Trump faced two lawsuits in California and one in New York, which were combined into one class action suit after he was elected. Trump paid the $25 million in January 2017, but the settlement was delayed until the court approved it. The court ruled that plaintiffs are expected to receive 80-90% of what they paid for Trump University programs. Trump, who has boasted about his real estate and investing acumen, rebuffed the claims of fraud during his 2016 presidential campaign but quickly settled after the election. The appeals court also rejected a challenge brought by Florida bankruptcy lawyer Sherri Simpson, who wanted to take Trump to trial over the $19,000 she paid for classes and a mentorship program. The court ruled that the notice sent to participants in the litigation only promised one opportunity to opt out of the class-action suits. The settlement clears the way for about 4,000 Trump University participants to receive their payments. Simpson could delay the settlement further through an appeal to a larger set of 9th Circuit judges or to the Supreme Court, but her attorney said she is giving up the fight. The decision was made to distribute the settlement money to the former students so that they can receive their payments. The three appeals court judges assigned to the case were appointed by President Barack Obama.

The document is a press release issued by U.S. Senator Bernie Sanders on January 16, 2016, calling for the resignation of Michigan Governor Rick Snyder over the lead-poisoning crisis in Flint, Michigan. The crisis began in April 2014 when Flint switched its water supply from Detroit's system to the Flint River, resulting in lead contamination of the city's water supply. The crisis has sickened thousands of children and exposed many more to potential brain damage from lead. Sanders argues that Snyder knew about the lead in Flint's water but did nothing, and that families will suffer from lead poisoning for the rest of their lives.

The press release provides a timeline of key events in the development of the Flint water crisis, starting in April 2014 when Flint began drawing its water from the Flint River, and continuing through January 2016 when Snyder declared a state of emergency in Flint and requested federal aid. The crisis has received widespread attention and criticism, with many calling for Snyder to resign or be held accountable for his role in the crisis.

In addition to the press release, the document includes a series of news articles and photographs related to the Flint water crisis, including a photo of a line of families at a school in Flint waiting for lead testing, and a map showing the number of Flint children under the age of 6 who have been exposed to lead. The articles provide more details on the crisis, including the fact that the state of Michigan has acknowledged that all children who drank the city's water since April 2014 have been exposed to lead, and that the crisis has been linked to an increase in cases of Legionnaires' disease in the county that includes Flint.

Overall, the document provides a comprehensive summary of the Flint water crisis, including the timeline of events, the call for Governor Snyder to resign, and the ongoing efforts to address the crisis and provide aid to the affected families.

A team has created an interactive visualization of military conflicts using data from Wikidata and DBpedia. The visualization, created in nodegoat, includes over 2600 battles with both location and date. The data was gathered by querying the Wikidata and DBpedia sparql-endpoints and cleaning the results in Open Refine, LibreOffice Calc, or Excel. The visualization allows users to scroll through time and click on dots to access information about each battle in Wikidata. The team also connected the events to people involved, such as those in the American Civil War, and included births, deaths, and movement between battles. The data used for the visualization was generated from slash pages from various domains on the web.

On May 8 (in the Americas or Pacific) and May 9 (for the rest of the world), Earth will pass between the sun and the largest planet in our solar system, Jupiter, marking its opposition. This event occurs when Jupiter rises in the east as the sun sets in the west. This is the best time to view Jupiter as it is up all night and generally closest for the year. Jupiter's opposition date this year is May 9 at 1 UTC, translating to May 8 at 8 p.m. Central Daylight Time in North America.

Jupiter will be brighter than any star in the evening sky, except for Venus, which will be blazing low in the west. Venus will set as Jupiter ascends in the eastern sky. At this opposition, Jupiter will be located in the constellation Libra, with Zubenelgenubi, Libra's alpha star, nearby. Jupiter outshines Zubenelgenubi by over 100 times.

Jupiter's opposition occurs approximately every 13 months due to the time it takes Earth to travel once around the sun relative to Jupiter. As a result, Jupiter's opposition comes about a month later each year. Last year, it was on April 7, and next year, it will be on June 10.

There is a NASA spacecraft, Juno, currently orbiting Jupiter, providing never-before-seen glimpses of the giant planet's polar regions. Jupiter is not a rocky planet like Earth but a failed star, not massive enough or hot enough inside to spark thermonuclear fusion reactions.

For stargazers, this is an excellent opportunity to observe Jupiter and its moons. The four largest moons, known as the "Galilean Moons," are visible with just a set of binoculars. On the night of March 14, stargazers will get a chance to see Europa and Io transit in between Jupiter and the Earth.

This opposition of Jupiter is a great opportunity for stargazers to appreciate the beauty and magnitude of our solar system.

The Robert Gordon University has revoked Donald Trump's honorary degree due to his statements during the US election campaign that are incompatible with the university's ethos and values. A petition has been launched to ban Trump from entering the UK, citing his hate speech and divisive comments. The petition has gained over 300,000 signatures and is being reviewed by Parliament's petitions committee. If it reaches 100,000 signatures, it could be debated in the Commons. Trump's comments about Muslims have caused controversy and have been condemned by British politicians, including David Cameron, Jeremy Corbyn, and Boris Johnson. A petition on the UK government website calling for a ban on all immigration until ISIS is defeated has also gained over 440,000 signatures but was rejected by the British government. A separate petition was launched to strip Trump of an honorary degree from Aberdeen's Robert Gordon University, which has gathered nearly 9000 signatures.

The execution of Lawrence Russell Brewer, a convicted hate crime killer, has led to a ban on final meal choices for death row inmates in Texas. Brewer, who was executed on Wednesday, had requested a lavish meal consisting of two chicken fried steaks, a triple-meat bacon cheeseburger, fried okra, a pound of barbecue, three fajitas, a meat lover's pizza, a pint of ice cream, and a slab of peanut butter fudge with crushed peanuts. However, prison officials reported that Brewer did not consume any of the meal. The ban on final meals for death row inmates was proposed by Senator John Whitmire, following the belief that it is inappropriate to grant such privileges to individuals sentenced to death.

The Church of Kopimism, a group of 3,000 Swedish file sharers, has been recognized as an official religion by the Swedish authorities. The church, which believes in the sanctity of communication and sharing, has been seeking official recognition since 2010. The church's name, "Kopimi," means "copy me," and its followers consider CTRL+C and CTRL+V as sacred symbols.

The church's founder, philosophy student Isak Gerson, is thrilled about the recognition, hoping it will encourage more people to openly embrace their beliefs. Although the official status does not make copyright infringement legal, Gerson hopes that their beliefs will be considered in future legislation. The church has tripled its members from 1,000 to 3,000 over the past six months and expects another surge in followers following the news. Gerson encourages everyone with an internet connection to continue sharing information.

Eric Swenson, a co-founder of Thrasher magazine and a significant figure in the skateboarding community, died by suicide on June 20, 2011, at the age of 64. Swenson was a private individual who struggled with a debilitating motorcycle injury for many years. His longtime partner in skateboarding ventures, Fausto Vitello, passed away five years prior to Swenson's death.

Swenson co-founded High Speed Productions Inc., which includes magazines Thrasher, Juxtapoz, and Slap, as well as Independent Trucks, a skateboard truck manufacturer that revolutionized the sport by enabling skateboarding on vertical surfaces. Swenson's contributions to skateboarding helped establish it as a subculture with its own music, dialect, and fashion style.

Swenson's partner, Fausto Vitello, was the more outgoing face of the company. Together, they manufactured the revolutionary skateboard trucks at a foundry in the Hunters Point Shipyard and started the distribution company Deluxe Distributions. The magazine side of the business was started as a way to advertise the skateboard products.

Swenson was known as a behind-the-scenes workhorse who preferred hard work to glory or being in the spotlight. He was a humble man who didn't flaunt his wealth and was extremely successful in his passions.

The skateboarding world paid tribute to Swenson on social networking websites, with skaters and industry figures expressing their condolences and appreciation for his contributions to the sport. Swenson leaves behind his wife Linda McKay, sisters Rebekah Engle and Sonja Taylor, and a tremendous number of admirers.

China and the United States are in discussions to resolve the incident involving the seizure of a U.S. Navy unmanned underwater glider by the Chinese navy, which occurred in the South China Sea. The glider, used for oceanic research, was seized on Thursday while collecting unclassified scientific data about 92 kilometers northwest of Subic Bay near the Philippines. The U.S. has issued a formal diplomatic complaint and demanded the return of the drone, which costs about $150,000 and is largely commercial, off-the-shelf technology. The incident is being viewed as one of the most significant disputes between the two countries' militaries in recent years, and has the potential to further strain already tense relations between the U.S. and China. The seizure occurred within the exclusive economic zone of the Philippines, not China, and has been criticized as a violation of international law. China's foreign ministry has stated that the two sides are working to appropriately handle the matter through military channels, but has not provided further details. The incident comes amid increased tensions between the two countries over Beijing's ongoing military buildup in the South China Sea and President-elect Donald Trump's comments regarding Taiwan. Trump has used Twitter to accuse China of an "unpresidented" act in seizing the drone, and has suggested that the U.S. should not want it returned. The Chinese foreign ministry has responded that the U.S.'s "hyping up" of the incident is not conducive to a smooth resolution.

Following a divisive election campaign, Donald Trump was elected as the 45th President of the United States on November 9, 2016. Throughout the campaign, Trump made several controversial remarks about America's relationship with other countries, raising concerns and speculation about the potential impact of his presidency on international relations.

In Indonesia, many on social media questioned why Americans had voted in large numbers for Trump, who is perceived as intolerant and reactionary. Indonesians feared that under a Trump administration, they may be prevented from visiting relatives and friends in the U.S. or traveling there as tourists. Approximately 100,000 Indonesians live in the United States.

In Cuba, the normalization of relations with the U.S. that had been underway for the past two years was put at risk by Trump's promise to reverse Obama's opening with Cuba unless President Raul Castro agreed to more political freedom on the island. This was a concession considered a virtual impossibility.

In Mexico, the peso declined sharply in international markets as news of Trump's lead hit hard. Many Mexicans were shocked and anxious about the prospect of a President Trump, who had made numerous controversial Mexico-related policy plans, including vowing to build a wall along the entire U.S.-Mexico border, large-scale deportations, and threatening to nix trade deals with Mexico.

In China, some participants at a U.S. Embassy event in Beijing welcomed a Trump presidency, while others expressed concern that he projects a flawed image of the United States. Some Chinese participants hoped that a Republican president would do more to encourage freedom of speech in China.

In Australia, Foreign Minister Julie Bishop expressed readiness to work with whoever the American people chose as their president, noting that the U.S. is Australia's major security ally and largest foreign direct investor.

In New Zealand, a student named Sarah Pereira expressed dread at the prospect of Donald Trump winning the presidency, as she was looking forward to working as an intern in the U.S. Congress.

In Japan, Prime Minister Shinzo Abe followed the vote count in his office, with analysts on both sides of the Pacific discussing the potential changes in U.S. policy toward Japan and the rest of Asia if Trump were to win.

In the Vatican, the first reaction to Trump's election focused on the hope for global peace. Pope Francis did not comment directly on the election, but his secretary of state, Cardinal Pietro Parolin, offered Trump congratulations and expressed hope that his government could be "fruitful."

In the Taliban, the group called on Trump to withdraw all U.S. forces from Afghanistan once he takes office. In China, President Xi Jinping conveyed his congratulations to Trump, expressing hope for constructive relations between the two countries. In Kenya, President Uhuru Kenyatta congratulated Trump, noting the close historical connection between Kenya and the U.S. In Slovenia, the home country of Melania Trump, the president expressed hope that relations with the U.S. would further improve during Trump's presidency.

In Iran, the government expressed hope that America would implement its part of multilateral international commitments under the historic nuclear deal. In Iraq, the government expressed confidence that relations with the U.S. would remain strong, especially in the fight against terrorism. In Germany, Chancellor Angela Merkel offered Trump "close cooperation" on the basis of shared trans-Atlantic values. In the European Union, leaders invited Trump to visit as soon as possible to assess trans-Atlantic ties.

In South Sudan, the government welcomed Trump's election, expressing hope for better relations with the U.S. In Cambodia, Prime Minister Hun Sen congratulated Trump, noting his support for the candidate during the campaign. In Egypt, President Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi congratulated Trump and invited him to visit Egypt.

In the Philippines, President Rodrigo Duterte congratulated Trump and expressed hope for further enhancement of the treaty allies' relations. In Hungary, Prime Minister Viktor Orban congratulated Trump, calling his victory "great news" and showing "democracy is still alive." In Turkey, Prime Minister Binali Yildirim called on Trump to extradite a U.S.-based Muslim cleric Fethullah Gulen as soon as he is sworn in.

In India, Prime Minister Narendra Modi congratulated Trump, expressing appreciation for the friendship he had articulated toward India during his campaign. In the United Kingdom, Prime Minister Theresa May congratulated Trump, noting that the two countries will remain "strong and close partners on trade, security, and defense."

In Israel, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu congratulated Trump, calling him a "true friend of the State of Israel." In the Palestinian territories, President Mahmoud Abbas expressed hope that peace will be achieved during Trump's term.

In Russia, President Vladimir Putin expressed readiness to try to restore good relations with the U.S. In the Netherlands, anti-Islam populist lawmaker Geert Wilders congratulated Trump, calling his victory "A revolution." In France, populist, anti-immigrant politician Marine Le Pen congratulated Trump even before the final results were known.

In Canada, the prospect of Americans moving there due to the U.S. election caused so much online interest that it knocked out the country's immigration website. In Mexico City, many gathered at an American-themed bar to watch the election results roll in, with some viewing thundershowers that lashed the capital as a sign of turbulent times to come.

Overall, Trump's election as president was met with a mix of shock, anxiety, and hope in various countries around the world, with many expressing concern about the potential impact of his presidency on international relations and global stability.

A Cook County judge set a $1.5 million bond for Chicago police officer Jason Van Dyke, who is facing first-degree murder charges for shooting 17-year-old Laquan McDonald 16 times in 2014. The shooting was captured on a squad car video, which was released last week. Van Dyke had been in custody since turning himself in on November 24. The judge watched a few minutes of the grainy dashcam video before setting the bail. Four hours later, Van Dyke posted $150,000 bond and was released from Cook County Jail. Protests and demonstrations have been held across the city in response to the shooting and the release of the video. The mayor's office announced plans to create a "Task Force on Police Accountability" to review the system of accountability, oversight, and training for Chicago's police officers. The task force is expected to present recommendations to the mayor and the City Council by March 31, 2016. The dashcam video of the shooting was made public last week, and since then, hundreds of demonstrators have rallied to mostly peaceful protests across the city. Ten people were arrested on Monday at a "small gathering" outside City Hall. Activists, pastors, and other city residents called for Chicago Police Supt. Garry McCarthy to resign during a demonstration outside Chicago Police headquarters on Monday evening. The shooting of Laquan McDonald has touched off demonstrations across the city, and the images were not enough for a Cook County judge to order Van Dyke held without bail pending trial.

An off-duty California Highway Patrol (CHP) sergeant, who wished to remain anonymous, is being praised for her integrity after finding $120,000 in cash on a Concord, California roadside and returning it to its rightful owner. The sergeant, a 20-year CHP veteran, had to swerve to avoid two large bank deposit bags, picked them up, and discovered the large sum of money. She immediately reported the find to authorities, who were able to track down the owner. The sergeant, raised by a single mother in Los Angeles, saw this as an opportunity to teach her children a lesson about honesty. CHP Golden Gate Division Chief Avery Browne praised the sergeant, noting that many officers do not receive recognition for simply doing their job.

Hurricane Harvey, a Category 4 storm, made landfall in Texas late Friday, August 25, 2017, causing widespread destruction and flooding. The storm hit northeast of Corpus Christi, Texas, with sustained winds of 130 mph. Emergency personnel in coastal communities reported widespread damage to buildings, loss of power, and communication outages. The storm has since been downgraded to a Category 1 hurricane, but is expected to hover over the region for days, dumping as much as 40 inches of rain and causing potentially catastrophic flooding. President Donald Trump has commended the head of the Federal Emergency Management Agency for his handling of the hurricane, which is posing the first major emergency management test of Trump's administration.

Archaeologists are set to conduct a geophysical scan on Tuesday at Waltham Abbey Church in Essex to determine the accuracy of the Bayeux Tapestry's depiction of King Harold II's death at the Battle of Hastings in 1066. The scan, funded by amateur historian Peter Burke, aims to investigate whether Harold may have survived the battle and lived as a hermit for another 40 years.

Burke, who has lived near Waltham Abbey for 29 years, initially dismissed the theory of Harold's escape from the battle, but after discovering an anomaly in the Abbey's stonework and studying a 12th-century document called Vita Haroldi, he became convinced of its validity. The document suggests that Harold was wounded in the eye by a Norman arrow but survived the battle, living until his eighties as a hermit.

The scan, conducted by the Stratascan team, will be filmed for a documentary exploring this alternative theory. If the scan provides evidence, excavation may still be a while off due to the consecrated nature of the site. English Heritage granted permission for the ground-penetrating radar to scan the area, but further consent would be required for excavation.

If the scan does find evidence supporting the alternative theory, it could potentially lead to a rewriting of history books, as the commonly accepted account of Harold's death by four Norman knights after being struck by an arrow to the eye would be called into question. Despite potential criticism, Burke remains hopeful that the scan will provide significant findings.

Kim Kardashian West was robbed at gunpoint in a private residence in Paris by five armed men disguised as police, who made off with millions of pounds worth of jewellery. The incident took place early Monday morning local time, while Kardashian West was in Paris attending fashion week shows. The robbers tied her up in the flat's bathroom before fleeing the scene, and she was "badly shaken but physically unharmed." The stolen items included a jewellery box containing valuables worth €6m (£5.2m) and a ring worth €4m. The robbers escaped on bicycles. The private apartment where Kardashian West was staying was built in 1838 and is now a listed building, popular with the wealthy and famous. The incident has sparked a manhunt in Paris and criticism from political opponents to the Socialist government. Kanye West, Kardashian West's husband, abruptly ended his performance at the Meadows music and arts festival in New York on Sunday night, citing a "family emergency." The family has been uncharacteristically silent on social media since the report involving Kardashian West. This was not the first time Kardashian West has been ambushed in Paris; she was also attacked outside of a Paris fashion week show in 2014. Paris has been a special place for Kardashian West and her husband, who spent the weekend there before marrying in Florence in May of 2014.

The Boston Marathon bombing suspect, Tamerlan Tsarnaev, was found to have a broad interest in far-right conspiracy theories, as revealed by extremist publications discovered in his apartment. These publications were passed on to him by a 67-year-old man he cared for, who had a history of anti-U.S. government beliefs. The man, Donald Larking, suffered brain damage from a 1974 shooting incident and shared theories such as the Sept. 11 attacks and the Newtown shooting being orchestrated by the U.S. government.

Tamerlan Tsarnaev and his brother, Dzhokhar, befriended Larking through their mother's health care aide job. Larking shared his views with the brothers, who found anti-U.S. government websites and became increasingly irrational. Larking also has literature questioning the Holocaust.

Authorities claim the Tsarnaev brothers orchestrated the April 15 marathon bombing, which killed three people and injured over 260 others. Dzhokhar Tsarnaev pleaded not guilty to charges including using a weapon of mass destruction. Tamerlan died after a shootout with police a few days after the bombing.

Larking converted to Islam and still attends the mosque the brothers took him to. He seems to have been close to Tamerlan, who was kind and helpful to Larking and his wife. However, it's unclear if the Tsarnaev brothers fully understood the extent of Larking's brain damage.

In a federal indictment in June, authorities found on Dzhokhar Tsarnaev's computer a publication advocating violence against Islam's perceived enemies and a magazine with instructions for building bombs using pressure cookers.

A man named Brian Howard, aged 36, from Naperville, has been charged with one felony count of Destruction of Aircraft or Aircraft Facilities after allegedly setting a fire in the basement of an Aurora FAA facility, causing significant damage to the host computer and radar lines. The incident led to a ground stop at Chicago's O'Hare and Midway international airports, resulting in thousands of flights being cancelled and delayed. The Air Route Control Center in Aurora, which monitors high altitude aircraft before landing in Chicago or flying through the area, was left in disarray, with much of its work being handled by facilities in surrounding states at a much more limited capacity. The economic impact of the disruption was substantial. Illinois Senator Mark Kirk called for an immediate review by the FAA of the screening process and changes to prevent similar incidents in the future. Authorities believe this was an isolated incident and that Howard acted alone.

Howard allegedly entered the FAA facility with a black hard-sided roller board suitcase and sent a Facebook message referencing the three-letter call number for the facility before starting the fire. He was found by paramedics lying on the floor, slicing his throat with a knife, and remains hospitalized with self-inflicted stab wounds. Howard had worked for the Control Center as a contract employee for approximately eight years and was authorized to be in the building. No firearms were found on the scene.

The incident could result in days of potential radar outages at the Aurora facility, causing significant flight delays in the Great Lakes region. Planes are currently moving in and out of Chicago at a "reduced rate" after airspace management was transferred to adjacent FAA facilities. There are only three routes out of Chicago right now: east toward South Bend, north to Milwaukee, and west to Rockford. Planes have to stay at a lower altitude for a longer time to maintain contact with those smaller facilities, which can only handle about 25 percent of normal operations.
