The FAA is beefing up staffing at those facilities and others in the area, and has not said when the repairs will be made to the Aurora building and when controllers can come back to work.

Hundreds of Chicago flights were canceled, delayed, and re-routed as a result of the incident. Airlines are urging travelers to check the status of their flights at www.fly.faa.gov. The incident is a reminder of the critical role air traffic control centers play in the safe and efficient operation of the aviation industry.

United Airlines has introduced a new boarding process to address congestion at its gates, which has been a source of frustration for customers. The new process, which was tested since last fall, involves reducing the number of boarding lanes from five to two, and urging passengers to wait until their boarding group is called. The lanes will be color-coded, with lane 1 being the "blue" lane for elite and priority passengers, and lane 2 being the "green" lane for other passengers. The new system, which will be rolled out to all United locations starting Tuesday, aims to reduce waiting times, improve communication, and better recognize Premier customers. The airline says the changes were made based on customer feedback. However, it remains to be seen how the new process will affect the distribution of elite customers on flights with a large number of them.

In addition to the new boarding process, United Airlines has also launched push notifications for passengers with the airline's mobile app. These notifications will alert passengers when boarding begins, which will be particularly useful in case of flight delays or early boarding.

Separately, United Airlines, Copa Airlines, and Avianca have reached an agreement for a joint business agreement (JBA) that is expected to provide substantial benefits for customers, communities, and the marketplace for air travel between the United States and 19 countries in Central and South America. The JBA is expected to offer customers many benefits, including integrated, seamless service in more than 12,000 city pairs, new nonstop routes, additional flights on existing routes, reduced travel times, and economic benefits for consumers and the communities served. The carriers expect the JBA to drive significant traffic growth at major gateway cities coast to coast, which is expected to help bring new investment and create more economic development opportunities. The JBA is expected to provide customers with expanded codeshare flight options, competitive fares, a more streamlined travel experience, and better customer service. The carriers plan to apply for regulatory approval of the JBA and an accompanying grant of antitrust immunity from the U.S. Department of Transportation and other regulatory agencies in the near term. The JBA currently includes cooperation between the U.S. and Central and South America, excluding Brazil, but the carriers are exploring the possibility of adding Brazil to the JBA.

In a historic referendum, Ireland legalized same-sex marriage, becoming the first country to do so via a popular vote. With a landslide 62% in favor, Ireland has made a significant social shift, marking a transformation in a traditionally Catholic country that only decriminalized homosexuality two decades ago. The Catholic Church, which teaches homosexual activity as a sin, saw its influence in Irish politics decline after child sex abuse scandals in the 1990s. The archbishop of Dublin acknowledged the result as a social revolution and called for a reality check within the Church. The Yes vote was particularly pronounced in Dublin, with Dublin Midwest recording a Yes vote of 70.9%. The No campaign, led by the Iona Institute, conceded the victory and expressed concerns about the implications for freedom of religion and freedom of conscience. The result has been widely celebrated, with US Vice President Joe Biden tweeting, "We welcome Ireland's support for equality #LoveWins." The referendum has attracted international attention, with a large international contingent in attendance at Dublin Castle.

In a heartwarming story, Giovanni DeGarimore, owner of Giovanni's Fish Market in Morro Bay, California, purchased a 70-pound octopus named Fred for $200 with the intention of releasing it back into the wild. The octopus had been accidentally caught by a crab fisherman in San Luis Obispo County. DeGarimore, an avid diver and lover of the ocean, felt conflicted about selling octopus due to their sentient nature. He released Fred back into the water the following day.

In a separate incident, a two-spotted octopus caused a 200-gallon seawater flood at the Santa Monica Pier Aquarium in California. The octopus disassembled a water recycling valve and directed a tube to spew out of the tank for about 10 hours.

Octopuses have been found to be intelligent creatures, capable of navigating mazes, solving problems quickly, and remembering solutions for short periods. They can change colors, squirt out poison, and exert a force greater than their own body weight. Scientists have been studying octopuses for 35 years to gain insight into the evolution of intelligence.

Jennifer Mather, a comparative psychologist at the University of Lethbridge in Alberta, Canada, has been studying octopuses for 35 years. She has found that octopuses can figure out how to open clams and mussels, using different techniques depending on the species. They have also been observed playing with floating objects in a tank.

Octopuses have personalities, with variations in activity, reactivity, and avoidance. They have a large nervous system, with about one third of the neurons located in the brain and the rest in the arms. This allows them to have a hundred pincer grasps, enabling them to manipulate their environment effectively.

Octopuses have evolved big brains to navigate the complex environment of tropical coral reefs, which is the most complex environment in the world. They have a unique nervous system with two areas of the brain dedicated to memory storage.

In the Facebook post about Fred, Giovanni DeGarimore said, "It might not change the world, but I'm going to do one thing and if it only makes me and Fred happy, that's okay too." Since sharing Fred's story, the post has been shared hundreds of times.

House Republicans have initiated an impeachment resolution against IRS Commissioner John Koskinen, alleging he violated public trust, failed to comply with a congressional subpoena, and misled Congress during the investigation of the IRS's targeting of conservative groups. The resolution was introduced by Oversight Committee Chairman Jason Chaffetz, who accused Koskinen of destroying backup tapes containing emails from Lois Lerner, the central figure in the scandal.

The Justice Department concluded its investigation into the IRS targeting scandal last week without filing any charges. Chaffetz argues that Koskinen was not truthful when he said all relevant emails were handed over, given the destruction of the backups. He also accused Koskinen of failing to notify Congress about the missing evidence.

The impeachment charge centers around the destruction of several backup tapes that could have contained emails sent by Lerner. Republicans claim that Koskinen, who took over the IRS after the controversy emerged, failed to preserve 422 backup tapes that could have contained Lerner emails.

Democrats have denounced the move as political grandstanding, with Rep. Elijah Cummings, the committee's top Democrat, calling it "ridiculous" and a waste of taxpayer money. Cummings argued that there is no evidence to support the accusations against Koskinen and pointed out that the IRS has spent $20 million and 160,000 employee hours cooperating with investigations.

Pursuing impeachment against an agency leader is highly unusual, and this would be the first time such a move has been made against an IRS commissioner. More than a century ago, Congress brought articles of impeachment against War Secretary William Belknap in 1876, after the House of Representatives uncovered evidence supporting a pattern of corruption. He resigned during the proceedings.

On August 9, 2014, a 12-foot, 120-pound Burmese python was captured by Port St. Lucie police in Florida. Neighbors suspected the snake was responsible for the disappearance of several cats in the area, with one confirmed death. The python was found hidden in waist-high brush by Sgt. John Holman, who also discovered a dead cat. The captured python was reportedly owned by an individual with a license to keep it, despite a ban on Burmese pythons in Florida since 2012.

On June 30, 2017, a shooting occurred at the Bronx Lebanon Hospital in New York, resulting in one death and six injuries. The gunman, Dr. Henry Bello, who previously worked at the hospital, was identified as the shooter. Dr. Kamran Ahmed, a colleague of Bello, expressed surprise at being targeted, stating that Bello had issues with many people and had threatened to return and kill him. Bello had been forced to resign from the hospital in 2015 due to a sexual harassment scandal and had made threats against his former colleagues.

Before the shooting, Bello sent an email to the Daily News, blaming colleagues he said had forced him to resign. Bello arrived at the hospital with an assault rifle, which he had purchased in upstate New York a week earlier, hidden under his lab coat. He asked for a specific doctor he blamed for his resignation, but the doctor was not present at the time. The victim of the shooting was Dr. Tracy Sin-Yee Tam, a family medicine doctor who was working a shift in the main hospital as a favor to someone else.

Bello died from a self-inflicted gunshot. The six injured people were hospitalized. Detectives searched Bello's home and found the box where the gun came from, which was purchased at a gun shop in Schenectady on June 20. Ahmed, who was not working on the day of the shooting, praised Tam as an excellent colleague who was loved by everyone. He attended a staff meeting with a hospital official the day after the shooting and plans to visit the other victims.

Al-Qaeda has claimed responsibility for the kidnapping of 70-year-old American development expert Warren Weinstein in August in Lahore, Pakistan. Weinstein, who was working on US Agency for International Development (USAID) projects, was abducted from his home by unidentified gunmen. During the long period of silence following the kidnapping, it is suspected that Weinstein may have been passed through various criminal and terrorist networks before being held by Al-Qaeda.

Weinstein was the country director for J.E. Austin Associates, a US-based firm that advises various Pakistani business and government sectors. His work included enhancing Pakistan's dairy and gem trades, importing dairy chillers to boost the productivity of Pakistan’s milk industry, and providing scholarships for Pakistanis to study the gem trade.

In a video message, Al-Qaeda leader Ayman al-Zawahri demanded the United States stop airstrikes in Afghanistan, Pakistan, Somalia, and Yemen, and release all al-Qaida and Taliban suspects around the world in exchange for Weinstein's release. Weinstein's health is reported to be poor, and his family and employers have appealed to his captors to provide him with necessary medications. The incident has left many in Pakistan who knew Weinstein shocked and saddened, describing him as a kind and helpful individual.

The Boy Scouts of America (BSA) has revoked the charter of a church-sponsored troop in Seattle due to the church's refusal to dismiss an openly gay scoutmaster, Geoff McGrath. The church, Rainier Beach United Methodist Church, has vowed to keep McGrath as troop leader, going against the BSA's policy that bans gay adults from membership.

The BSA contacted the leaders and parents of the children in Troop 98 and its affiliated Cub Scout pack to inform them that the church is no longer authorized to be a charter partner. The organization expressed sadness over the situation, stating that the church no longer agrees to the terms of the BSA chartered organization agreement, which includes following BSA policies.

The BSA's top leader in Seattle has offered a local community center as a potential new home for the pack and troop. The church's pastor, Rev. Monica Corsaro, has called the BSA's decision a "unilateral decision" and stated that the church's anti-discrimination beliefs are not being respected.

Corsaro also mentioned that the church would still offer a youth program but has not yet discussed what that would look like. About 15 boys participate in either the troop or the pack.

This incident marks the first known case of a gay adult being booted from the Boy Scouts of America since last May's vote that allowed gay youth but not adults to join Scouting. McGrath, who is married, said he was "shocked" by the BSA decision.

The BSA has been grappling with its controversial membership policy barring gays in recent years. In an historic ballot last May, its 1,400-member National Council voted to allow gay youth but not adults to join Scouting. Troop 98 was formed shortly after this contentious ballot.

McGrath, a member of the Methodist Church, was approached by local clergy to lead a Boy Scout unit due to a lack of youth programs in the area. He hesitated due to concerns about his sexual orientation, but the Seattle BSA official claimed she never knew he was gay.

The gay fathers of a child who joined Troop 98 after the news article have received a letter from the BSA's top leader in Seattle with the offer to transfer to a troop at a local community center. However, they have no plans to go elsewhere. Their son, Adrian Benitez, 14, expressed his displeasure with the situation, stating it was offensive to him and his fathers.

The Seattle-based investigative reporter Chris Halsne, from KIROTV- CBS- COX MEDIA GROUP, has returned from El Salvador where he interviewed a U.S. government subcontractor who worked with the Secret Service advance team in San Salvador before President Obama's trip in March 2011. The eyewitness claims that several Secret Service agents visited a strip club in San Salvador, drank heavily, and paid for sexual favors. These alleged incidents occurred a year before the recent revelations of Secret Service agents using prostitutes in Cartagena, Colombia.

Halsne interviewed the owner of the San Salvador strip club, who confirmed that a large number of U.S. Secret Service agents (and some military escorts) visited his club before President Obama's visit. The owner claims the agents were there at least three nights in a row. He says his club is popular among high-ranking U.S. embassy employees, FBI, and DEA agents due to its reputation for security and privacy. The owner denies allowing prostitution inside the club and ensures that all his "girls" are at least 18-years-old.

The Secret Service is investigating the report, and the Department of Defense did not respond to a request for comment. House Oversight Committee Chairman Darrell Issa believes there were instances of misconduct by Secret Service agents prior to the Colombian prostitution scandal. Sen. Chuck Grassley has called for independent investigations into the agency due to the latest allegations. However, Homeland Security Secretary Janet Napolitano insists there is no evidence of additional misconduct. The investigation is still developing, with Halsne having names of some of the agents allegedly involved and viewing records that add credibility to the subcontractor's eyewitness testimony. KIRO-TV is set to air a series of television stories beginning at 5 p.m. on Thursday, April 26.

The resignation of Michael Flynn as President Trump's national security adviser has caused a fresh crisis for the Trump administration. Flynn's resignation came after it was revealed that he had not been entirely truthful about a phone call he had with Russia's ambassador, and investigators believed that he was not forthcoming. The acting attorney general decided to notify the White House about the situation, setting in motion a chain of events that led to Flynn's resignation.

Flynn's short tenure as national security adviser was marked by controversy and questions about his relationship with Russia. The revelation that he had discussed sanctions with the Russian ambassador before Trump entered office raised concerns about the Trump administration's relationship with Russia, particularly given American intelligence reports of Moscow's intervention in last year's elections in the United States.

Conservative radio host Rush Limbaugh has accused the media of helping to force Flynn out of his position. Limbaugh claimed that the media has become the "full-fledged resistance" to Trump and is constantly impeding the Trump administration. He argued that the media is trying to get Trump out of office and that the extensive news coverage of Flynn's past phone conversations with Russian ambassador Sergey Kislyak is evidence of this.

Flynn resigned late Monday and blamed the "fast pace of events" for why he "inadvertently" gave "incomplete information" to Vice President Mike Pence and others about the talks. He said that he spoke with the ambassador specifically about the 35 Russian officials that were expelled from the U.S. as part of the Obama administration's sanctions, but that "no lines were crossed."

Reports emerged last week that Flynn and Kislyak discussed sanctions against Russia during a series of phone calls in December. Pence had previously denied that Flynn and Kislyak ever spoke about sanctions. White House press secretary Sean Spicer said Tuesday that Trump asked for Flynn's resignation once the president's faith in his adviser "eroded" following the reports.

Leading members of the US Republican Party have joined calls for a wide investigation into Flynn's links with Russia. However, some senior Republicans have expressed resistance to an investigation. The New York Times has reported that phone records and intercepted calls show that members of Trump's presidential campaign, as well as other Trump associates, had repeated contacts with senior Russian intelligence officials in the year before the election. However, officials spoken to by the newspaper said they had not yet seen evidence that the Trump campaign colluded with Russia on the hacking of the Democratic National Committee or to influence the election.

Both the Senate and House intelligence committees are already examining Russian involvement in the election. It is not yet clear whether the latest claims will be included in their scope. The development comes as senior US officials are mounting a major effort to reassure uncertain allies in Europe about the Trump administration's intentions. The resignation of Flynn is likely to raise further questions about the relationship between the Trump administration and Russia.

On June 27, 2017, a police helicopter attacked the Venezuelan Supreme Court and Interior Ministry in what President Nicolas Maduro described as a "terrorist attack" aimed at ousting him from power. The helicopter, which carried an anti-government banner, was piloted by a man identified as Oscar Pérez, who claimed to be part of a coalition of military, police, and civilian officials rising up against what he called "tyranny." The incident occurred during a time of political and economic crisis in Venezuela, with widespread protests against Maduro's government. The attack was met with suspicion by some, who accused the government of staging the incident to justify a crackdown on dissent. The whereabouts of Oscar Pérez are unknown.

The trial of Captain Francesco Schettino, who is charged with manslaughter and abandoning ship following the 2012 Costa Concordia disaster, was electrified by the testimony of a Moldovan dancer, Domnica Cemortan. Cemortan, who was on the bridge with Captain Schettino when the ship ran aground, admitted to being his lover. She testified that she had worked for the company that operated the Costa Concordia for about three weeks in December 2011 and had met Captain Schettino on a previous cruise.

On the night of the crash, Cemortan had dinner with the captain before joining him on the bridge. Local press have speculated that the captain may have been distracted by her presence or even showing off. After the ship hit the rocks, Cemortan said the captain urged her to "save herself." She helped other passengers to abandon ship before getting into a lifeboat herself.

The court is expected to hear evidence from about 1,000 surviving passengers and crew during Captain Schettino's trial. In testimony earlier in the day, ship maitre d' Antonello Tievoli told the court that he had asked the captain to sail close to the island of Giglio because he has family there. The captain obliged on 6 January, but was apparently disappointed with the result, and ordered the ship's helmsman to plot a closer route for next time. A week later, the ship ran aground on rocks after veering too close to the island, with 3,206 passengers and 1,023 crew aboard.

Captain Schettino has acknowledged fault in the tragedy, but his defence team is arguing the ship sank in part because watertight doors did not function on the ship. He also told the court in late September that his Indonesian helmsman was to blame for steering the ship onto rocks and ignoring orders to slow down. However, an Italian naval expert told the trial these were not crucial factors and the crash would have happened anyway.

The helmsman, Jacob Rusli Bin, is one of five employees who were granted plea bargains in return for mild sentences in a separate proceeding. He was given a sentence of one year and eight months. The 290m-long vessel was righted last month in one of the largest, most complex salvage operations ever that took 18 hours and followed months of stabilisation and preparation work by a team of 500 engineers and divers. That operation allowed divers to retrieve the remains of one of the two people still missing in the disaster, believed to be an Italian passenger, Maria Grazia Trecarichi. An Indian waiter, Russel Rebello, is still unaccounted for. Plans are now being made to attempt to remove the wreckage of the ship next year.

Nick Stoeberl, a 24-year-old artist and comedian from California, has set a new world record for the longest tongue, measuring 10.1cm (3.97in) from the tip to the middle of his closed top lip. This record is featured in the Guinness World Records 2015 book, which is the 60th anniversary edition and is currently on sale. The previous record holder, Brit Stephen Taylor, held the title since 2002 with a tongue length of 9.8cm.

Nick's father was a fan of the band KISS, and as a child, Nick would imitate Gene Simmons' famous tongue pose, realizing his tongue was longer than others. Nick enjoys the attention his tongue receives, boasting that he can lick his nose and elbow, although brushing his tongue takes longer in the morning due to its size.

Adrienne Lewis from Michigan might challenge Nick's record, as she believes her tongue to be 4 inches long. She has been promoting her massive tongue on Facebook and YouTube for years, and her videos have gained thousands of views. Adrienne can touch her tongue to her elbow, nose, and even her eye with a little help from her hand. She is currently in talks with Guinness World Records to see if she has officially broken the new world record.

The Guinness World Records 2015 book is packed with incredible feats, facts, and achievements and features new Augmented Reality technology. To learn more about the book, visit www.guinnessworldrecords.com/2015. For the latest on world records, follow Guinness World Records on Facebook, Twitter, Google+, and Instagram, and subscribe to their YouTube channel for the latest record-breaking videos.

ABC has announced a revival of the iconic sitcom "Roseanne," bringing back the Connor clan after a 20-year absence. The revival, set for midseason, will consist of eight episodes and feature returning stars Roseanne Barr, John Goodman, Sara Gilbert, Laurie Metcalf, Michael Fishman, and Lecy Goranson. The series will address the economic challenges of living paycheck to paycheck in 2018.

The revival was spearheaded by Sara Gilbert, who currently hosts and exec produces CBS daytime show The Talk. Original exec producers Barr, Tom Werner, and Bruce Helford will return, along with Whitney Cummings and Tony Hernandez. A police lieutenant in Georgia, Greg Abbott, is being terminated after a 2016 traffic stop video surfaced where he was heard saying "we only shoot black people." The comment was made during a traffic stop where a woman was scared to move her hands to get her cellphone. Abbott, who had been an officer for 28 years, was placed on administrative leave while the department investigated the video.

The police chief, Mike Register, announced the decision to fire Abbott, stating that such comments have no place in law enforcement. Register emphasized that the statements were inexcusable and not indicative of the values he is trying to instill within the Cobb County police department.

Register learned of the comments after the television station WSB-TV obtained the video through an open-records request. Abbott's attorney, Lance LoRusso, did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the firing. Previously, LoRusso stated that Abbott's comments were meant to "de-escalate a situation involving an uncooperative passenger."

Register has been working hard since becoming chief to strengthen the relationship between the department and the community. He expressed concern that the video could potentially harm this relationship. Register stated that the badge and uniform should mean justice and fairness for all.

Black community leaders applauded Register's quick action. Deane Bonner of the Cobb County chapter of the NAACP found the officer's introduction of race into the stop particularly troubling, suggesting it could be a systematic issue within the department. Ben Williams, chairman of the Cobb County chapter of the Southern Christian Leadership Conference, focused on the police chief's behavior, stating that the real story is the behavior of the police chief in Cobb County, Georgia.

On the night of Thursday, a mysterious event occurred over Cyprus, leaving residents baffled. Witnesses reported seeing a meteor streaking across the sky, with a blue glow and a loud explosion that some felt caused the ground to shake. The Cyprus Geological Department and police are investigating, with no reports of casualties or damage. Authorities are searching for debris from the potential meteorite fall. Although confirmation is still pending, it is likely that the object was a meteor, a piece of comet or asteroid from outer space that creates a fireball upon entering Earth's atmosphere. If confirmed, the meteorite could provide valuable information about the early solar system for scientists. The civil aviation authority confirmed that all flights operated normally during the incident.

In Venice, four Japanese tourists were shocked by a €1,100 bill they received after dining at a restaurant near St. Mark's Square. The bill included four steaks, a fried fish platter, water, and service. Three women with them, who chose another restaurant, also faced a high bill of €350 for seafood pasta. The mayor of Venice, Luigi Brugnaro, has expressed outrage and vowed to investigate the incident.

The Japanese students filed a complaint upon their return to Bologna, where they are studying. The case has been taken up by Marco Gasparinetti, a spokesperson for a Venice residents' forum called "Gruppo 25 Aprile." The forum has reported that only 1.1% of restaurants in that part of Venice are owned by locals, with 50% being owned by non-locals in the historic center as a whole.

The incident has sparked criticism from the residents' forum, who plan to post advice for tourists on Facebook to help them avoid overpriced restaurants. The forum stated that such incidents harm the reputation of Venice and its residents.

This is not the first incident of overcharging tourists in Venice. In a previous incident, a British tourist accused a restaurant of overcharging him for seafood dishes he hadn't ordered, racking up a bill of €526. The mayor, Luigi Brugnaro, defended the restaurant and criticized the tourist for not speaking Italian.

Despite the criticism, Brugnaro has been working to manage Venice's vast tourism industry, which residents have long complained makes the city unlivable. Earlier this year, he introduced measures to reduce the crowds at popular sites, including limiting tourist accommodation and installing automatic people-counters in high-traffic areas. Last week, Italy's national government approved plans to ban cruise ships from the center of Venice.

The wreck discovered off the coast of Haiti, which was initially believed to be that of Christopher Columbus's flagship Santa Maria, has been determined not to be the ship by a team of experts from Unesco. The experts found that the artifacts at the site were of copper alloy, while the Santa Maria should have had iron and/or wood fixations. The Santa Maria was the flagship of Columbus's first voyage to the Americas, which set sail in August 1492. The ship ran aground on a reef near Haiti on 24 or 25 December 1492. US underwater investigator Barry Clifford had previously claimed that the wreck was that of the Santa Maria, but Unesco's experts concluded that the fasteners found at the site indicated a technique of ship construction that dates the ship to the late 17th or 18th century rather than the 15th or 16th century. The report also ignored evidence from an expedition which may have visited the site in 1960 and failed to carry out tests on the ballast from the wreck or detailed analysis on the bronze objects found on the site. Unesco now plans to look for the Santa Maria in a number of different locations, both on land and on the seabed. The report has been criticized for ignoring photographic evidence for what could be Columbus-era cannon on the site and for suggesting that the Santa Maria could be buried under sediments on what used to be seabed and is now coastal marshland, a theory that many scholars find questionable. The report may also have implications for the US's relationship with Unesco, as a US-led investigation of the site has been replaced by a partly European team.

The report released by Conflict Armament Research (CAR) on Thursday reveals that some weapons bought by the U.S. military in 2015 ended up in the hands of Islamic State (IS) fighters within two months. The findings are based on three years of meticulous documentation of weapons recovered from ISIS on the battlefields of Iraq and Syria.

CAR used serial numbers or key markings on the weapons to trace them back to their origin and try to piece together how they were obtained by the militants. Some of the weapons found on the front lines after ISIS was driven out include Chinese-manufactured machine guns laced with amphetamines, drones modified in sophisticated terrorist factories, and even a rifle made in Nazi Germany.

One anti-tank missile sold to the U.S. Army made its way to ISIS in just 59 days. It was purchased from a Bulgarian manufacturer by the U.S. Army, but only weeks later it was property of ISIS. However, it is not entirely clear how the weapon got from the Bulgarian plant to ISIS fighters in Iraq.

Under at least two different programs, the U.S. government has supplied weapons to Syrian armed groups, first to fight the Assad regime and then to assist the Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) in the fight against the Islamic State. Some of ISIS’ weapons are also thought to have been pilfered from military stockpiles while others were purchased illicitly.

According to CAR's report, Iraqi police recovered a Bulgarian-made missile tube during the battle of Ramadi on Feb. 9, 2016. The company confirmed to researchers that the weapon had been exported to the U.S. Army through an arms broker on Dec. 12, 2015. It is not entirely clear how the weapon got from the Bulgarian plant to ISIS fighters in Iraq.

However, a Syrian opposition group called Jaysh al-Nasr posted a series of photographs on Dec. 21, 2016, showing fighters posing in a snowy landscape. A closer inspection shows that one of their anti-tank weapons bears an identical lot number and a similar serial number to the item seized in Iraq. That suggests, the report says, that they "were part of the same supply chain."

CAR says the United States has not yet replied to a trace request for the weapon. Kiesler Police Supply Co., which CAR says brokered the anti-tank missile's sale to the U.S. military, declined to comment.

Based on the anti-tank missile tube found in Ramadi and other examples of weapons purchased by U.S. suppliers from European manufacturers, CAR says there is evidence that many weapons obtained by various Syrian rebel groups supported by the U.S. were diverted to ISIS.

When asked to comment on U.S.-purchased arms potentially ending up in the hands of ISIS, Eric Pahon, a spokesman for the Department of Defense, said, “Any alleged misuse or diversion of U.S. support will be taken seriously and lead to the possible curtailment of support, if verified.” Pahon added that he had not seen the CAR report.

The report highlights the enormous risks that come with handing weapons "to unprepared, not very well-trained armed groups, or even so-called organized militaries." The weapons recovered from ISIS and documented in the report come from a wide range of manufacturers and sources. Many were looted from Iraqi and Syrian government stockpiles as ISIS rampaged across both countries. By early 2015, the group controlled around 35,000 square miles of territory — an area about the size of Indiana.

However, the introduction of new weapons into the Syrian conflict significantly improved the “quantity and quality of weapons available” to ISIS. In propaganda videos, ISIS frequently showcases the U.S.-made weapons in its arsenal, much of it presumed to have been seized from Iraqi military stockpiles. In 2015, CAR found one American-made M-16 in Kobani, Syria, with an Islamic State commander’s name inscribed on the magazine — a clear status symbol. But in reality, American weapons make up only a minor portion of the small arms documented by CAR. Chinese and Russian arms account for more than 50 percent, with the ubiquitous AK-47 in heavy use.

CAR found most of ISIS' weapons were made before 1990, the year Iraq came under an arms embargo. The report highlights the enormous breadth and depth of ISIS' arsenal. Its researchers found rockets made in the former Yugoslavia as well as guns and ammunition exported from Belgium more than 30 years ago. James Bevan, CAR's director, found a Mauser rifle manufactured in Nazi Germany in 1941 in an ISIS cache in Baghdad alongside 150 other weapons and improvised explosive devices.

Spleeters said the fact that ISIS used older weapons “shows the extent of how long such a weapon can live and go through different owners and keep shooting and keep killing." CAR says it has documented more than 40,000 individual items during visits to Iraq and Syria, recording everything from tanks and rocket launchers, to bullets and bits of detonation cord. But it uncovered some surprises as well. In September, the group's researchers made the unusual discovery of 122 Chinese-made light machine guns at a former ISIS site south of Mosul. The serial numbers were mostly in sequence, indicating they were diverted from a single intended recipient. At least one pouch of amphetamines was attached to each. CAR concluded that ISIS "had stockpiled the weapons together with individual rations of performance-enhancing drugs for issue to its fighters."

The document discusses the role of John McCone, the Director of Central Intelligence (DCI) during the Kennedy and Johnson administrations, in the aftermath of President Kennedy's assassination in 1963. McCone, an outsider to the intelligence community, replaced Allen Dulles after the failed Bay of Pigs invasion in Cuba.

After Kennedy's assassination, McCone became an important witness for the Warren Commission, the panel created to investigate Kennedy's murder. He testified that the CIA had no evidence suggesting Lee Harvey Oswald, the assassin, was part of a conspiracy. The commission's final report agreed with McCone's depiction of Oswald as a delusional lone wolf.

However, a once-secret report written by the CIA's top in-house historian in 2013, declassified last fall, suggests that McCone and other senior CIA officials were "complicit" in keeping "incendiary" information from the Warren Commission. The report accuses McCone of being at the heart of a "benign cover-up" intended to keep the commission focused on the belief that Oswald acted alone.

The most significant information withheld from the commission, according to the report, was the existence of CIA plots to assassinate Fidel Castro, some of which involved the Mafia. Without this information, the commission never considered the possibility that Oswald had accomplices in Cuba or elsewhere who wanted Kennedy dead in retaliation for the Castro plots.

The report does not question the essential findings of the Warren Commission, including that Oswald was the gunman in Dallas. However, it raises questions about McCone's motivations and whether the Johnson White House may have directed him to hide the information.

The report also mentions other information that McCone did not reveal to the commission, such as evidence that the CIA might have been in communication with Oswald before 1963 and that the agency had secretly monitored Oswald's mail after his attempt to defect to the Soviet Union in 1959.

The declassification of the report suggests a new openness by the CIA in trying to resolve the lingering mysteries about the Kennedy assassination. However, there are still sensitive information gaps in the public version of the report.

The document also discusses the contacts between McCone and Robert Kennedy in the days after the assassination, and the special gravity these communications had given Robert Kennedy's role in overseeing the administration's secret war against Castro. The report raises the question of whether Castro's actions against Kennedy were in retaliation for the administration's obsession with Cuba.

The next day, she visited a cardiologist who informed her that she had a "widow maker" heart attack, caused by a 99% blockage in her LAD artery. She emphasized the importance of recognizing heart attack symptoms, particularly for women, and urged others to listen to their bodies and call 911 if needed. The article from Pacific Coast News discusses two main topics: the departure of actor Neal McDonough from the ABC show Scoundrels due to his refusal to participate in a sex scene, and the book "Sex at Dawn: The Prehistoric Origins of Modern Sexuality" by Christopher Ryan and Cacilda Jethá, which argues that monogamy and the nuclear family are not natural for humans and are causing problems in modern relationships.

Neal McDonough, a 44-year-old actor known for his roles in Band of Brothers, Desperate Housewives, and Scoundrels, left the show after three days of filming due to a sex scene with Virginia Madsen. McDonough has a strict policy against sex scenes, which has cost him roles in the past. ABC has called the departure a "casting change."

The book "Sex at Dawn" argues that humans were not meant for lifelong monogamous unions and that the current state of marriage in the West, particularly in the United States, is in a grim state, with a high divorce rate and many couples trapped in sexless, passionless unions. The authors use evidence from human physiology, archaeology, primate biology, and anthropological studies to support their argument that monogamy and the nuclear family are more recent inventions than most people believe.

The authors also argue that the bonobos, our closest relatives, provide evidence of our natural inclinations, as they live in egalitarian and peaceful groups with high rates of sexual interaction. While the book is often hard to follow, its provocative argument is impossible to dismiss.

In an interview with Salon, author Christopher Ryan discusses the problems with American marriages, why gay men understand relationships better than straight men, and the hidden meaning of human testicle size. Ryan argues that marriage in the West is in direct confrontation with the evolved reality of our species and that the best way to increase marital stability is to develop a more tolerant and realistic understanding of human sexuality.

Ryan also discusses how the advent of agriculture around 8000 B.C. changed everything about human society, including sexuality, politics, economics, health, diet, exercise patterns, and work-versus-rest patterns. He argues that property was not a very important consideration when people were living in small, foraging groups where most things were shared, including food, childcare, shelter, and defense. It makes sense that sexuality would also be shared in such a society, as paternity was not an issue.

However, when agriculture was introduced, men started to worry about paternity and the accumulation of property, leading to a more possessive culture and the notion of lifelong coupling. Ryan and Jethá argue that this is not in line with our natural inclinations and is causing problems in modern relationships.

Overall, the article discusses the departure of Neal McDonough from Scoundrels due to his refusal to participate in a sex scene and the provocative arguments of the book "Sex at Dawn," which argues that monogamy and the nuclear family are not natural for humans and are causing problems in modern relationships.

In a significant ruling, U.S. District Judge Denise Cote found that Nomura Holdings Inc. and Royal Bank of Scotland Group Plc made false statements in selling mortgage-backed securities to Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac before the 2008 financial crisis. The ruling, which may lead to $450 million in damages for the banks, is part of a series of lawsuits filed by the Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA) over $200 billion in mortgage-backed securities sold to the government-owned mortgage companies.

The judge's 361-page opinion, following a three-week trial, stated that the banks misled Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac by providing inaccurate information about the mortgage loans. The FHFA is entitled to judgment against Nomura and RBS, with the exact damages to be determined.

Nomura has expressed confidence in its transparency and professionalism in dealings with Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac and plans to appeal the ruling. RBS did not comment on the decision.

This is the first trial out of 18 lawsuits the FHFA filed in 2011. The FHFA has previously secured nearly $17.9 billion in settlements with banks including Bank of America, JPMorgan Chase, and Deutsche Bank.

The seven deals at issue in Nomura's case were issued from 2005 to 2007. Nomura was the securities' sponsor, and RBS underwrote four of the deals. The judge found that the securities sold to Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac "were supported by loans for which the underwriting process had failed," with deals comprised of 45% to 59% "materially defective" mortgages.

The banks argued that any losses incurred by Fannie and Freddie were not their fault and were due to overall market conditions. However, the judge noted that the banks have not quantified the loss due to macroeconomic factors and that there is a link between the securitization frenzy associated with shoddy practices and the macroeconomic factors causing the losses.

The case is Federal Housing Finance Agency v Nomura Holding America Inc, U.S. District Court, Southern District of New York, No. 11-06201.

In a significant development, a judge has allowed Leslie Merritt Jr., the suspect charged with freeway shootings that caused panic in Phoenix last year, to be released from jail. The judge reduced Merritt's bond to zero, allowing him to return home under electronic monitoring, expected to be released later in the day. This decision comes amid questions about the evidence linking Merritt to the crimes, with his defense lawyers contending that ballistic tests cast doubt on the claims by authorities that he was behind four of the freeway shootings.

The shootings, which occurred in August and September of 2015, caused panic on Phoenix-area freeways, with 11 vehicles being hit. The head of the Arizona Department of Public Safety had earlier labeled the shootings as the work of a domestic terrorist, prompting increased patrols and surveillance.

Merritt was taken into custody on September 18, 2015, with Governor Doug Ducey declaring "We got him!" on Twitter five minutes after the arrest. However, Merritt adamantly denied shooting any cars in court the next day, and his lawyers have since been raising questions about the evidence, citing ballistics information and phone records they claim provide an alibi for their client.

The judge in the case, Warren Granville, has imposed a gag order on lawyers, preventing them from discussing the evidence that prompted the shift in bond. The Arizona Department of Public Safety and the Maricopa County Attorney's Office have declined to comment, citing the gag order.

Meanwhile, in a separate incident in Brooksville, Alabama, a driver suspected of firing a gun at motorists on an Alabama highway and exchanging gunfire with officers has been killed. The details of the incident, including the suspect's name and the officer's race, have not been released.

In Libya, thousands of individuals have gone missing during the six-month-long conflict against Moammar Gaddafi, with over 60,000 reported missing. The rebels, who are still searching for Gaddafi, have opened his prisons in Tripoli, freeing thousands, but only about 10,000 prisoners have been accounted for. This has left families and friends in fear that thousands may be in underground prisons or mass graves. One individual, Abdul Rauf, was held for 48 days at the notorious Abu Salim facility, known for its brutality and where many political opponents vanished. After his release, Abdul Rauf shared his harrowing experience of being beaten, deprived, and held in a small cell with 70 people. Another individual, Muneer Masoud Own, survived an ordeal in which nearly 150 prisoners were slaughtered by Gaddafi's forces as rebels closed in on Tripoli. Own was detained, handcuffed, blindfolded, and put in a warehouse with about 60 others. Over the next 18 days, Gaddafi's forces kept bringing detainees, and about 175 people were crammed inside the warehouse. Own endured horror and deprivation, and in the three days before he made his escape, the detainees had no food or water, and the warehouse filled with the stench of human waste. Just before sunset on the promised day of release, guards opened the warehouse doors but tossed a grenade inside and started shooting, killing dozens. Own managed to escape, but he lost track of his brother in the chaos and has not heard from him since. The rebels' efforts to locate missing individuals and bring justice to the victims continue.

In this summary, the Libyan leader Col Muammar Gaddafi has denied any protests in Tripoli and claimed that he is loved by all his people. He laughed off suggestions that he would leave Libya and accused Western countries of abandoning the nation. US Ambassador to the UN Susan Rice described Gaddafi as "delusional" and "unfit to lead." Gaddafi is facing a massive challenge to his 41-year rule, with protesters in control of towns in the east. He accused Western countries of wanting to colonize Libya and claimed that power was already in the hands of the people. The US, EU, and other foreign ministers have condemned attacks on Libyan civilians and imposed sanctions on Gaddafi and his entourage. Gaddafi showed no signs of giving up in Tripoli and challenged those who accused him of having money abroad, saying he would "put two fingers in their eye." He claimed that the protesters were under the influence of drugs supplied by al-Qaeda. The US has frozen $30bn in Libyan assets, the largest sum it has ever frozen. Protesters have secured towns in the east, but Gaddafi shows no signs of giving up in and around Tripoli. About 100,000 people have fled anti-government unrest in Libya over the past week. Gaddafi conducted an interview with several journalists, including Christiane Amanpour, in a beachfront restaurant in Tripoli, where he denied using force against his people and blamed al-Qaeda for the protests. He felt betrayed by the US and accused it of wanting to colonize Libya. US Ambassador to the UN Susan Rice called Gaddafi's assertion that the Libyan people are behind him "delusional."

The Syrian Deputy Prime Minister Qadri Jamil dismissed President Obama's warning about the potential use of chemical weapons by the Syrian regime as mere election politics. The Pentagon has made contingency plans to send small teams of special operations troops into Syria to secure chemical weapons depots controlled by President Bashar Assad's security forces. President Obama warned that any effort by Assad to move or use chemical munitions would cross a "red line," implying it could prompt swift U.S. intervention. The Pentagon plans to protect or destroy any Syrian stockpiles that are left unguarded and at risk of falling into the hands of rebel fighters or militant groups. The chemical agents are stored in bunkers and other sites around the country, with four production facilities near Aleppo, Hama, Homs, and Latakia. U.S. intelligence agencies believe Syria has over the years produced or acquired hundreds of tons of sarin nerve agent and mustard gas, and has sought to develop VX, another powerful nerve gas. The toxicity of some chemical agents degrades significantly over time, so it is unclear how lethal the stockpiles are. The actual killing may be less important than the panic the chemical agents would induce, according to Leonard Spector, who heads the James Martin Center for Nonproliferation Studies at the Monterey Institute of International Studies. Although he did not make an explicit threat, Obama's comments at the White House on Monday were widely seen as a direct warning to Assad that the U.S. would take military action if necessary to stop the use of chemical weapons. However, officials said no large-scale U.S. intervention is likely unless it is part of an international coalition. The Syrian army shelled southern Damascus on Wednesday, and helicopters fired rockets and machineguns during an assault meant to shore up President Bashar al-Assad's grip on the capital 17 months into an uprising, opposition activists said. The army has this week used tanks and helicopter gunships in an offensive around Damascus that coincided with the departure of U.N. military observers, their mission to stop the bloodshed and nudge Syria towards a peaceful transition a failure. The United Nations estimates that more than 18,000 people have been killed in what has become a civil war after the state's violent response to peaceful street protests triggered an armed rebellion in the pivotal Arab country.

Amazon, Berkshire Hathaway, and JPMorgan Chase have announced a partnership to address the high costs and complexities of the U.S. healthcare system for their combined workforce of over 1.1 million employees. The new company, which will be independent and free from profit-making incentives, aims to focus on technology solutions to simplify and improve healthcare services. The three companies hope their collective resources will enable them to tackle the issue effectively.

The announcement has caused shares of multiple healthcare companies to fall sharply, indicating the potential threat posed by the new entity to the current healthcare system. Some experts are skeptical about the partnership's ability to significantly lower costs and improve outcomes, but others believe it could be a disruptive force in the industry.

The three companies have appointed Todd Combs from Berkshire, Marvelle Sullivan Berchtold from JPMorgan, and Beth Galetti from Amazon to lead the project. The longer-term management team, headquarters location, and operational details will be communicated in due course.

The partnership is in its early planning stages, and further details are expected to be released in the future. The companies aim to create solutions that benefit their U.S. employees, their families, and potentially all Americans.

The article discusses Frank Taaffe, a neighbor and friend of George Zimmerman, who was acquitted in the shooting death of Trayvon Martin in 2012. The daughter of former Russian spy Sergei Skripal, Yulia Skripal, is improving rapidly and is no longer in a critical condition, according to doctors at Salisbury District Hospital. Yulia Skripal, who was poisoned along with her father nearly four weeks ago, has responded well to treatment but continues to receive expert clinical care 24 hours a day. Her father, Sergei Skripal, remains in a critical but stable condition.

The police have placed a cordon around a children's play area near Sergei Skripal's home as a precautionary measure. Officers are investigating the case as an attempted murder, and have been treating more than 5,000 hours of CCTV footage and examining over 1,350 exhibits.

The nerve agent used in the attack, Novichok, was found at other locations in Salisbury but in lower concentrations. A police officer who fell seriously ill after responding to the attack, Det Sgt Nick Bailey, was treated in hospital and was discharged on March 22.

The British government has accused the Russian state of involvement in the attack, a claim that has been denied by Moscow. In response, the Kremlin has expelled an equal number of British diplomats and closed down the British Council. More than 20 governments, including the US, have expelled diplomats in their countries in a coordinated action.

The incident has caused widespread concern and condemnation, with at least 26 countries expelling Russian diplomats suspected of being spies. In response to the closure of National Park areas in Utah due to the ongoing government shutdown, San Juan County, Utah, has declared a state of emergency and threatened to take control of some parks and reopen them to the public. The county commission has decided to storm National Park Service barricades and mobilize local resources, including law enforcement, search and rescue volunteers, and portable toilets, to manage the parks. The commissioners argue that the closure is causing financial hardship for local businesses that depend on visitors to the parks. The county, which is as large as Connecticut and Delaware combined, has a history of resisting federal land management policies. A Bronxville resident, William McCormack, is suing Lawrence Hospital Center and Dr. Michael Kerin, a Tuckahoe surgeon, for medical malpractice. The lawsuit alleges that McCormack underwent an appendectomy at Lawrence Hospital in January 2013, but a year later, he had to undergo another emergency appendectomy in the Adirondacks after his appendix was found to still be inside him.

According to the lawsuit, McCormack experienced severe stomach pains during a visit to Lake Placid in early March. The second operation revealed that the appendix was never removed during the first operation. The hospital is investigating the claim and has not commented on the pending litigation.

The lawsuit includes a copy of a January 27, 2013 Operative Report from Lawrence Hospital stating that McCormack's appendix had been removed, electronically signed by Dr. Kerin. However, a report from Lawrence Hospital's Pathology Department states that there was no evidence of an appendix in the specimen received.

The lawsuit alleges that the hospital and Dr. Kerin realized the mistake and carelessly ignored it, leading to McCormack having to undergo a second surgery. McCormack is seeking unspecified damages for the pain and suffering, as well as for having to undergo surgery twice. The hospital and Dr. Kerin have not returned calls seeking comment.

A Jacksonville, Florida pediatric dentist, Dr. Howard Schneider, is facing a class-action lawsuit and an investigation by the Florida Attorney General's Office for alleged abuse, assault, battery, false imprisonment, and intentional infliction of emotional distress. The lawsuit accuses Schneider's practice of being a "house of horrors" where children were strapped down, left with visible injuries, and threatened to avoid exposure. The plaintiffs are seeking damages exceeding $15,000 and a jury trial.

The lawsuit follows protests outside Schneider's office and complaints from parents alleging physical abuse, botched dental work, and stonewalling when his methods were questioned. The Florida Attorney General's Office confirmed that Schneider's practice is under investigation for alleged Medicaid fraud.

The complaint alleges that Schneider's practice specifically targeted low-income, uneducated, and non-English speaking clients to limit their ability to protect their children from his "deviant and violent" methods. The suit accuses Schneider of being a "pathological sadist" who derives sexual excitement from inflicting pain or humiliation on another person, consenting or otherwise.

Schneider, 78, has been practicing in Jacksonville for over 40 years and has never been charged with a crime in connection to the jarring allegations. The allegations include choking children to unconsciousness instead of using appropriate anesthetic, performing non-medically necessary dental procedures without anesthetic, and using fear and threats to scare and silence his victims.

Twice, the Jacksonville Sheriff's Office has been called to Schneider's practice to deal with complaints about his use of excessive force on young patients. Court records show that there were two malpractice suits brought against him in 1995 but they were later dismissed.

The lawsuit alleges one mother called the Department of Children and Families after a visit to the dentist's office on April 15 when she said he pulled four of her 2-year-old son's baby teeth instead of two. The complaint is one of four accounts detailed vividly in the lawsuit, which says attorneys for the plaintiffs have identified at least 60 victims of Schneider's, some of whom are now adults. The suit suggests there could be as many as 1,000 victims from over the years who have yet to come forward.

John Harrell, a spokesman for the Department of Children and Families, said it was possible the department received a call about that complaint, but noted that the agency does not have jurisdiction over doctors and dentists. It's not clear whether the Florida Board of Dentistry, which investigates allegations of malpractice and could revoke his license if the claims are founded, has intervened. The board's investigations remain confidential until they're complete.

An attorney representing Schneider did not return calls for comment about the lawsuit. However, in an earlier interview, Schneider dismissed the allegations. "I'm sure in my lifetime I've done something that is off color, but it ain't mistreat kids," he said.

The Brevard County Hall of Fame is aiming to relocate the remains of Jim Morrison, the lead singer of The Doors, from his grave in Paris to Melbourne, Florida, where he was born. Born in 1943 at the former Brevard Hospital, Morrison gained notoriety as the frontman of The Doors, known for his controversial and magnetic persona. Although his grave in Paris is a popular tourist destination, there is little evidence in Melbourne of his local ties.

John Tice, the president of the Brevard Hall of Fame, has expressed his desire to bring Morrison's remains to Melbourne for display at the Brevard Hall of Fame. Tice, who is also a West Melbourne city councilman, plans to contact authorities at the Père Lachaise Cemetery in Paris to discuss the potential move. If successful, a fundraising drive would be organized to cover the costs of the relocation.

Tice claims that French cemetery officials previously offered to move Morrison’s remains to his birth home in Melbourne, but the homeowner declined the offer. The Morrison display at the Brevard Hall of Fame currently includes posters, two record albums by The Doors, and a framed copy of his last will and testament.

Tice believes that Morrison, who is considered the most popular public figure from the area, deserves more recognition in his birthplace. The display serves as the centerpiece of the Brevard Hall of Fame, alongside memorabilia from other famous figures with Space Coast residential ties, such as Kate Upton and pro wrestler "Hacksaw" Jim Duggan.

Tice is still waiting to hear back from officials in Paris regarding the potential relocation of Morrison's remains. Some residents of Brevard County may support the move, while others may express opposition. If the move is successful, Morrison's remains would join the other notable figures honored at the Brevard Hall of Fame.

Kimberly Pappas, a 25-year-old woman from Wyandotte, Michigan, has been ordered to stand trial for murder charges after allegedly giving birth at her workplace, CEVA Logistics in Redford, and suffocating her newborn baby. The baby was found dead in a plastic bag hidden in a desk drawer on March 31, 2015.

Pappas' co-workers discovered blood in the bathroom and called 911. Pappas initially told officials she had a miscarriage, but an autopsy revealed the baby's death to be a homicide. The Wayne County Medical Examiner's Office determined the cause of death to be asphyxiation.

Pappas' attorney has stated that she suffers from serious mental health issues and has sought treatment. However, in July, Pappas was found mentally competent by the Redford Township District Judge Karen Khalil. The case was described as "very difficult" by Judge Khalil during a preliminary examination.

Pappas will be arraigned on August 31 in Wayne County Circuit Court on charges of first-degree premeditated murder, felony murder, and first-degree child abuse. If convicted, she faces up to life in prison.

The incident was reported by local news outlets, including the Detroit Free Press and Hometown Life. The details of the case, including Pappas' alleged actions leading up to the discovery of the baby's body, were presented during a preliminary examination.

Pappas' sister, Cassie Pappas, stated that Kimberly did not tell anyone about the pregnancy before the child was delivered. The sister also testified that she brought a change of clothes to the bathroom at work after receiving a text from Kimberly asking for them. Kimberly was found fading in and out later, prompting her sister to call 911.

The case has been described as difficult due to the sensitive nature of the allegations and the potential mental health issues involved. Pappas' legal team has argued for dropping the murder charges and moving forward with manslaughter charges, but Judge Khalil has bound her over on the three counts after taking a short recess in her chambers.

The Associated Press reports that White House senior adviser Jared Kushner, who is also President Donald Trump's son-in-law, has denied any collusion with Russia during the 2016 presidential campaign. Kushner spoke to reporters at the White House on Monday after meeting with Senate investigators probing Russian meddling in the election and possible ties to the Trump campaign. Kushner told reporters he "did not collude with Russia nor do I know of anyone else in the campaign who did so." Kushner also said he "had no improper contacts" with Russia and that his actions were entirely "proper." Kushner left his private meeting with Senate investigators, nearly three hours after it began, and delivered a brief statement upon his return to the White House but did not answer reporters' questions.

In a written statement released before the committee meeting, Kushner said he never colluded with Russians looking to help Trump beat Hillary Clinton and does not know of anyone who did. He disclosed four interactions with Russians during the campaign and transition, saying he had nothing to hide. Those were with the Russian ambassador to the U.S., a Russian banker, and a Russian lawyer said to have damaging information about Clinton.

Kushner is also set to meet with the House intelligence committee on Tuesday.

House Speaker Paul Ryan said special counsel Robert Mueller, who is investigating ties between the Trump campaign and Russia, is not a biased partisan. Ryan's comments come as President Trump repeatedly has dismissed Mueller's investigation as a political witch hunt.

President Trump has also called the top Democrat on the House intelligence panel "sleazy" for conducting what he says is a "biased" Russia investigation. Trump tweeted Monday that "Sleazy Adam Schiff, the totally biased Congressman looking into 'Russia,' spends all of his time on television pushing the Dem loss excuse!"

Trump has also questioned why those investigating Russian meddling in the 2016 election and possible collusion by members of his campaign aren't digging into Hillary Clinton's "crimes & Russia relations." Trump took his latest swipe at Attorney General Jeff Sessions, including him in the list of people who he says should be investigating Clinton's potential Russia links.

Kushner also revealed in a statement that he received a "random email" during the presidential campaign from someone claiming to have Trump's tax returns and demanding ransom to keep the information secret. Kushner says he interpreted the email as a hoax and showed it to a Secret Service agent, who told him to ignore it.

Kushner also blamed his assistant for filing a version of his security clearance questionnaire that left off any contacts with foreign governments. He says the assistant accidentally filed the questionnaire while it was still being prepared. He says the initial form left off all foreign contacts, not just ones with Russians. Kushner says he eventually disclosed more than 100 contacts with people from more than 20 countries.

Kushner is also denying that Russians finance any of his business in the private sector.

In a statement, Kushner said he "did not collude, nor know of anyone else in the campaign who colluded, with any foreign government." He also said he "had no improper contacts" with Russia and that none of his actions were improper. Kushner also said he has tried to be transparent and that he hopes this puts the matter to rest.

However, Kushner's account of a December meeting with Russian Ambassador Sergey Kislyak raises questions. Kushner confirmed that he asked Kislyak about communicating through a secure line at the embassy, but he denies that there was any effort to hide communications between the Trump camp and Russia from US snooping. The Washington Post reported that Kislyak recounted the meeting to his superiors at the Kremlin, suggesting that there was an effort to hide communications.

Kushner also met with a Russian banker, Sergey Gorkov, at the Russian government's urging. Gorkov is known to be close to Russian President Vladimir Putin and graduated from the Russian FSB's spy academy. Kushner says the meeting was not about business, but Gorkov has a different account. Kushner also denies that he asked for a secret backchannel with Russia, but the Washington Post reported that this was one of the topics discussed in the December meeting with Kislyak.

Kushner's statement also raises questions about a June 2016 meeting at Trump Tower with a Russian lawyer who was said to have damaging information about Hillary Clinton. Kushner says he was late to the meeting and only stayed for a short time, and he denies that the meeting was about colluding with Russia. However, emails released this month show that Donald Trump Jr. accepted the meeting with the idea that he would receive damaging information about Clinton.

Overall, Kushner's statement denies any collusion with Russia, but it raises new questions about his interactions with Russian officials during the campaign and transition, and it contradicts some reports about those interactions. The Senate and House intelligence committees are investigating Russian interference in the 2016 election and any possible collusion by Trump associates.

A great white shark named Mary Lee, tagged in 1996 by the organization Ocearch, has been cruising the East Coast of the United States. The tracking of Mary Lee can be followed on Ocearch's website. This shark's journey is significant as it is being monitored as part of ongoing research on great white sharks.

The data collected from Mary Lee and other tagged sharks is often donated by Alexa Internet to the Internet Archive. Alexa Internet has been donating their crawl data since 1996, with the data being added to the Wayback Machine after an embargo period. This data contributes to the understanding and conservation of marine life.

Mary Lee's journey has taken her from the Atlantic Ocean off the coast of Massachusetts to the Gulf of Mexico and back, covering thousands of miles. Her movements are being closely watched by researchers, providing valuable insights into the behavior and migration patterns of great white sharks.

The tracking of Mary Lee and other tagged sharks is part of a larger effort to understand and protect these apex predators. Great white sharks are a keystone species in marine ecosystems, playing a crucial role in maintaining the balance of marine life.

Email notifications can be set up to receive updates on Mary Lee's movements, as well as other marine life research and conservation efforts. This allows individuals to stay informed and engaged in efforts to protect and understand our oceans and the creatures that inhabit them.

In a significant development, Democratic presidential candidate Hillary Clinton announced on Saturday a compromise to expand mandatory healthcare funding over the next decade, a move that is seen as a concession to her rival Bernie Sanders. The announcement came during a meeting of the Democratic Party draft platform committee in Orlando, Florida, where efforts by Sanders to influence the committee to adopt strong language opposing the Trans-Pacific Partnership (TPP) trade pact failed.

Clinton's healthcare proposal includes doubling funding for primary care services at Federally Qualified Health Centers, which serve populations with limited access to health care. This is a key priority for Sanders, who successfully fought for the inclusion of $11 billion in funding for such centers in the Affordable Care Act of 2010.

Clinton also affirmed her commitment to giving Americans in every state the choice of a "public-option" insurance plan, a proposal she supported during her 2008 presidential campaign and one that Sanders pushed for during the ACA debate. She also proposed allowing people below Medicare age to opt into the program, starting at 55.

Sanders, who has made combating healthcare costs a central theme of his campaign, praised the updates to Clinton’s proposal as a step in the right direction. He indicated that the proposal brings the two camps closer together and is a significant step forward in expanding access to health care and addressing a crisis in primary health care.

The compromise on healthcare comes as Sanders has been pushing for more liberal policies and campaign language from Clinton to endorse her for the November 8 general election against Republican presumptive nominee Donald Trump. Sanders has yet to officially endorse Clinton, but this healthcare proposal is seen as a significant step towards that endorsement.

The announcement follows a higher education proposal Clinton released earlier in the week that Sanders called a “bold initiative” to “revolutionize the funding of higher education in America.” This proposal is designed to eliminate college tuition for working families and reduce debt.

The compromise on healthcare and education proposals are seen as efforts by Clinton to court Sanders' supporters ahead of his possible endorsement. The New York Times reported on Thursday that an endorsement is imminent, and Sanders is expected to officially throw his support behind Clinton at a campaign stop in New Hampshire early next week.

The failure of Sanders to influence the committee to adopt strong language opposing the TPP is a significant blow to his efforts to push the party further to the left. Sanders has headed the effort on the U.S. left to oppose the TPP and trade deals like it, arguing that they are unfair to American workers. Clinton has also come out as opposed to the agreement.

Despite Clinton having already secured the requisite delegates to clinch the party’s nomination at the July 25-28 convention, Sanders remains in the race to be the party’s nominee. He has indicated that he would hold off on endorsing Clinton until she adopted policies and campaign language that more closely resemble his own more liberal tone.

The compromise on healthcare and education proposals are seen as a step towards a possible endorsement from Sanders, which could open the door to many of his supporters who have been reluctant to support the more moderate Clinton. The endorsement could be a crucial factor in the November 8 general election against Republican presumptive nominee Donald Trump.

In Wiltshire, England, archaeologists have unearthed a 4,300-year-old house, believed to be one of the best-preserved Neolithic structures ever found in the UK, on the edge of Marden Henge. The house, which was adorned with white chalk plaster, is as regular and neat as modern postwar bungalows and was likely used for grand feasts, as indicated by pig bones and scorch marks from a charcoal firepit.

The house is part of a vast archaeological site that includes Marden Henge, an enormous enclosure with ramparts three meters high and a ditch that once surrounded a 15-hectare area, far larger than the Avebury or Stonehenge circles. The purpose of Marden Henge is believed to be a display of wealth and power, as it required a massive workforce to construct.

The site also includes Wilsford henge, where a 4,000-year-old Bronze Age skeleton, believed to be that of a child, was recently discovered. The child was found wearing an amber necklace, and scientific analysis will provide information on its gender, diet, pathologies, and date of burial.

The three-year Vale of Pewsey dig is a partnership between the University of Reading, Historic England, the Arts and Humanities Research Council, and Wiltshire Museum. The aim is to gain a better understanding of the people who lived in the areas surrounding Stonehenge, and findings to date include flint arrowheads and blades, decorated pottery, shale and copper bracelets, and a Roman brooch.

The site welcomes visitors every day, and an open day will feature finds on display, tours, and activities as part of the national festival of archaeology. The discoveries at Marden Henge and Wilsford henge are expected to shed new light on the ancient landscapes of the area.

The online retailer Accessory Outlet has been criticized for a clause in its Terms of Sale that fines customers $250 for complaining about purchases or threatening to do so. The clause, which is buried at the bottom of the Terms page, forbids customers from making public statements about their orders or the retailer for 90 days, or threatening to do so within that period, or it is considered a breach of the terms, creating liability for damages in the amount of $250, plus additional fees. The Terms also claim that the customer agrees to binding arbitration to take place in New York City, with all expenses paid by the respective parties.

One customer in Wisconsin was fined $250 for threatening to issue a chargeback on her credit card because an iPhone case she ordered did not arrive after 10 days. The customer has sued Accessory Outlet in a New York state court, arguing that the $250 "debt" she is now being hassled over is bogus. The customer claims that she was never required to acknowledge that she had read the Terms of Sale during the purchase process.

Accessory Outlet has a history of using threatening emails to bully customers into keeping quiet about their bad experiences with the company. The retailer has been accused of deceptive practices and has been sued by the advocacy group Public Citizen, which recently won summary judgment and damages of over $300,000 in a related case in Utah involving the French parent company of KlearGear, a similarly unscrupulous vendor.

The Better Business Bureau has given Accessory Outlet an "F" rating and has served the company a cease-and-desist demanding it remove the BBB badge from its site. The company is not certified by buySAFE, Angie's List, or Trusted Shops, which are organizations touted on the site.

The story began on July 6, 2014, when Cindy Cox, a disabled veteran and substitute teacher, placed an order for an iPhone case. When the item did not arrive, she contacted Accessory Outlet and was threatened with a $250 penalty and collections action. Cox eventually received the item, but it was warped and would not snap closed. She is seeking declaratory judgment that the company's self-imposed "debt" of $250 is invalid and that the company engaged in deceptive practices. Accessory Outlet did not immediately respond to Ars' request for comment.

However, new analysis reveals that the prevalence of malaria parasite infection has decreased significantly in Africa since 2000, with the number of people infected falling from 173 million in 2000 to 128 million in 2013.

However, drug and insecticide resistance pose a significant threat to current malaria control strategies.

Recent research has identified a "super mosquito" hybrid in Mali that is resistant to insecticide-treated bed nets. This hybrid is a result of interbreeding between Anopheles gambiae and A. coluzzii, two major malaria vectors. The insecticide resistance came as no surprise, as growing resistance has been observed for some time.
