The article discusses the trend of downsizing in consumer products, specifically in toilet paper, with rolls becoming narrower, cardboard tubes growing in diameter, and the number of sheets per roll and the size of the sheets decreasing. This practice, known as "desheeting," is aimed at reducing the number of sheets per box.

Kimberly-Clark Corp. recently introduced new Kleenex tissue that is 15% "bulkier," but each box contains 13% fewer sheets than before. This has sparked concern among consumers, who argue that they should decide how much toilet paper they need.

Consumer Reports conducted tests on various toilet papers for strength, softness, disintegration, and tearing ease. The top performers in their latest tests were White Cloud 3-Ply Ultra, sold at Walmart, and Charmin Ultra Strong. White Cloud 3-Ply Ultra, priced at 25 cents per 100 sheets, received excellent marks for strength and softness, and very good marks for disintegration and tearing ease. Charmin Ultra Strong, costing 41 cents for 100 sheets, received excellent marks for tearing ease but did not perform as well on the other three attributes.

Other products that did not fare well in the tests include Scott 1000, Marcal Small Steps, and Cottonelle CleanCare with Touch of Soft Cotton. Scott 1000 was found to be neither soft nor strong, Marcal Small Steps was almost as harsh as Scott 1000 and did not tear easily, and Cottonelle CleanCare with Touch of Soft Cotton was less soft than many and more expensive than all but one other tissue in the tests.

The article advises consumers not to buy toilet paper solely based on brand, as various products from the same brands can perform differently. It also suggests that consumers should be aware of downsizing trends in the toilet paper industry and choose products that meet their needs and provide good value for money.

Jamaica's parliament has passed a bill to decriminalize small amounts of marijuana, known locally as ganja, and establish a licensing agency to regulate the medical cannabis industry. The new law makes possession of up to 2oz (56.6g) of marijuana a petty offense that would not result in a criminal record. Cultivation of five or fewer plants on any premises is now permitted in Jamaica, where marijuana has long been culturally entrenched but illegal.

The legislation paves the way for a "cannabis licensing authority" to be established to deal with regulating the cultivation and distribution of marijuana for medical and scientific purposes. Rastafarians can now legally use marijuana for religious purposes for the first time on the island where the spiritual movement was founded in the 1930s. Tourists prescribed medical marijuana abroad will be able to apply for permits at a cost authorizing them to legally buy small amounts of ganja.

Peter Bunting, the island's national security minister, said the legislation does not mean Jamaica plans to soften its stance on transnational drug trafficking or cultivation of illegal plots. William Brownfield, the US assistant secretary for counter-narcotics affairs, noted that the trafficking of marijuana into the US remains illegal.

The move by Jamaican lawmakers adds to an international trend of easing restrictions on marijuana for medical or personal use. More than 20 US states allow some form of medical marijuana, and last year Colorado and Washington legalized personal use. In the Americas, Uruguay last year became the first nation to create a legal marijuana market. In Argentina, personal possession of marijuana was decriminalized under a 2009 Supreme Court ruling that jail time for small amounts of drugs violates the country's constitution.

Jamaican officials hope the island could become a player in the nascent medical marijuana industry, health tourism, and the development of innovative pot-derived items. Local scientists already have a history of creating marijuana-derived products, such as "Canasol," which helps relieve pressure in the eyes of glaucoma patients. Commerce Minister Anthony Hylton said the cannabis industry holds "great potential" for Jamaica, which is laboring under its latest loan program with the International Monetary Fund.

A San Francisco federal judge has ordered Wells Fargo to pay $203 million in restitution to customers for manipulating debit transactions to maximize overdraft fees. In a 90-page opinion, Judge William Alsup accused Wells Fargo of profiteering by processing transactions from the highest to the lowest, rather than in the order they occurred. This practice, known as "high-low," helped drain customer bank accounts faster and boost overdraft fees, which can cost up to $35 per transaction.

Wells Fargo garnered over $1.4 billion in overdraft fees in California alone from 2005 to 2007, and nationwide, banks and credit unions collected almost $24 billion in overdraft fees in 2008. The bank has said it will appeal the decision, stating that its transactions have been "consistent with the laws and rules of governing regulatory authorities."

The ruling could have implications for a separate class-action lawsuit in Florida, where Richard Heimann, the lead attorney for the Wells Fargo customers in California, is also representing plaintiffs. Heimann believes the decision could influence the outcome of the Florida case, even though the judge there is not legally bound to follow it.

The ruling also criticized Wells Fargo for allowing overdraft purchases after accounts had been drained by offering a "shadow line of credit" that customers were unaware existed. The case comes as new federal regulations are set to kick in, requiring banks to obtain customers' permission to provide overdraft protection. Historically, most banks have automatically provided the service, unless customers opt out.

The ruling is part of the case Gutierrez vs. Wells Fargo, heard in the U.S. District Court for Northern California. Wells Fargo shares closed down 5.3 percent on Wednesday, reflecting broader market concerns and the impact on banks.

The Phoebe ring, Saturn's largest and most mysterious ring, has been found to be significantly larger than previously thought. The ring, which can't be seen with the human eye, is now estimated to stretch from approximately 3.75 million to 10.1 million miles, making it over 270 times the radius of Saturn. The ring is made mostly of tiny particles, with 90% of them being smaller than the size of a soccer ball.

The findings, published in the journal Nature, could shed fresh light on the evolution of the Saturnian ring system. The research team, led by Douglas Hamilton from the University of Maryland, discovered the ring in 2009 using NASA's Spitzer Space Telescope. At the time, they estimated that the ring stretched from 4.8 million to 7.76 million miles. However, with the use of NASA's Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer telescope, they were able to determine its true extent.

The Phoebe ring's immense size and unusual particle distribution have puzzled scientists. The team theorized that the dark material on Iapetus, one of Saturn's moons, was caused by unseen particles from the Phoebe ring. Iapetus is tidally locked with Saturn and can't rotate fast enough to get an all-around coating.

Understanding why the particle size distribution is so skewed could offer researchers "a window into the history of the Saturn system," Hamilton said. The researchers suspect that the material in the ring is probably very old, perhaps in the billions of years. They also suspect that the tiny particles are material ejected from the distant moon Phoebe.

The discovery of Saturn's largest ring could have implications for our understanding of other planetary systems. The researchers suspect that Jupiter likely has a massive unseen ring around it as well. The Phoebe ring's quirks are a reminder that the universe still holds a lot of surprises, and that there are lots of mysteries out there that we don't yet understand.

In the tumultuous 2010 election year, the Tea Party, a grassroots political movement, has emerged as a significant force, challenging the established political order. However, a Washington Post investigation reveals that the Tea Party is not a unified, organized movement, but rather a loosely connected network of local groups with varying beliefs and goals.

The investigation, which contacted hundreds of local Tea Party groups across the nation, found that 70% of these groups have not participated in any political campaigning this year. Many have no official candidate slates, have not rallied behind any national leader, have little money on hand, and remain ambivalent about their goals and the political process in general.

The local groups stand in contrast to larger national groups that claim the Tea Party label, such as FreedomWorks and Tea Party Express, which have used their resources and know-how to help elect several candidates. The findings suggest that the breadth of the Tea Party may be inflated, with one organization, the Atlanta-based Tea Party Patriots, claiming a listing of over 2,300 local groups, but The Post only being able to identify a fraction of that number.

The Tea Party's lack of a clear leader, platform, and organizational structure has made it difficult for President Barack Obama to engage with the movement effectively. Obama has tried various strategies to counter the Tea Party, such as elevating John Boehner as a worthy opponent, attacking the U.S. Chamber of Commerce, and going after Big Business and Evil Finance, but these efforts have been met with mixed results.

The Tea Party's primary emotion is anger, driven by a desire for change and a general distrust of government. While the movement has been tainted by racism, its grievances can be co-opted and absorbed into the engine of change that Obama himself once represented. The Tea Party's existence is largely due to the Internet, which allows like-minded people to connect and organize without the need for a traditional political party.

McDonald's, a global fast-food giant with over 31,000 restaurants serving 58 million people daily, faced an unexpected challenge in Bolivia. Despite its success in other parts of the world, McDonald's struggled to gain traction in Bolivia for 14 years, eventually closing its doors in 2002, marking the first time the company had left a country in the Americas. The documentary 'Why did McDonald’s Bolivia go Bankrupt?' suggests that the failure was due to Bolivians' cultural preference for home-cooked meals prepared with love, dedication, hygiene standards, and proper cook time. This contrasts with McDonald's fast-food offerings, which are often criticized for their nutritional value and eco-friendly practices. The closure of McDonald's in Bolivia is celebrated as a victory for those who value wholesome, home-cooked meals over fast food.

The Tully monster, a prehistoric creature discovered in 1955 in Illinois, has been a puzzle in the field of paleontology for over half a century. Due to its unique features, scientists have struggled to classify it, with theories ranging from it being a mollusk, arthropod, or worm. However, a recent study published in the journal Nature has revealed that the Tully monster is, in fact, a vertebrate closely related to lampreys.

The research team, comprising scientists from Argonne National Laboratory, the Field Museum, Yale University, and the American Museum of Natural History, utilized advanced imaging techniques and a collection of over 2,000 Tully monster specimens to reach this conclusion. They found that the creature's chemical composition, eye structure, and gut trace were similar to those of vertebrates, particularly lampreys.

The Tully monster's discovery has been a significant mystery in the field of paleontology, even earning it the status of Illinois' official state fossil. The finding resolves a debate that has lasted for over 50 years and provides valuable insights into the evolution of early vertebrates.

The study's lead author, Victoria McCoy, expressed her excitement about the discovery, stating, "The coolest thing is finding out that as weird as it looks, it is part of a familiar group of animals." The finding changes the Tully monster from a mysterious creature to a fish-like organism that is likely on the lineage leading to lampreys.

The study's findings have significant implications for the understanding of early vertebrate evolution and the classification of unusual fossils. The Tully monster's classification as a vertebrate also highlights the importance of continued research and the use of advanced technology in solving long-standing mysteries in the field of paleontology.

The University of California's Board of Regents approved a 32% increase in undergraduate fees, equivalent to a 32% tuition hike, during a meeting at UCLA on Thursday. The increase will bring the basic UC education fees to approximately $10,300, with additional campus-based charges and other expenses pushing the total cost to around triple the UC cost a decade ago. The fee hike, which will be implemented in two steps by next fall, was met with protests from hundreds of students from various campuses across the state.

Students expressed concerns about the impact of the fee increase on illegal immigrant students, minority students, and low-income families. Protesters linked arms to block regents from leaving the building, and about 14 demonstrators, including 12 students, were arrested for disrupting the Regents meeting. Groups of UC students from several other campuses joined the demonstration against the fee hike, and a group of protesters occupied a UCLA classroom building.

UC President Mark G. Yudof urged students to explore all financial-aid possibilities to avoid being scared away or dropping out. Only student regent Jesse Bernal voted against the undergraduate fees. The protests continued, with students issuing e-mail statements and campus police surrounding the occupied classroom building, but no arrests were made. The increased fees have raised concerns about an exodus of faculty and the ability of low-income students to afford the cost of education.
