The Australian Football League (Aussie Rules) and the National Rugby League are under the most scrutiny. The commission's findings draw parallels with the USADA investigation into Lance Armstrong, with the key difference being that the Australian issue is current, crosses sporting codes, and is evolving. The Australian Rugby Union CEO, Bill Pulver, was not directly implicated in the report. The report comes amidst an ongoing Federal Drug Administration (FDA) investigation related to the Armstrong case.

Nicole "Snooki" Polizzi, a reality TV star known for her role on Jersey Shore, is reportedly pregnant with her first child, according to the New York Post and People.com. Despite denying the pregnancy on ABC's Good Morning America on February 2, sources claim that Polizzi is three months pregnant and the baby's father is her boyfriend, Jionni LaValle.

This news comes at a time when single American women, particularly young ones, are experiencing a rise in births outside of marriage. According to the New York Times, more than half of births to American women under 30 occur outside of marriage, a trend that has been labeled as the "new normal."

Snooki's pregnancy, if true, could have significant implications for her career. Known for her wild antics on Jersey Shore, which often involved excessive drinking, Polizzi has lined her pockets with endorsement deals for energy drinks and diet pills, which are definite no-no's for a mommy-to-be. It remains to be seen whether she will be able to continue her party-girl lifestyle while also fulfilling her responsibilities as a mother.

The pregnancy news could also impact the upcoming spin-off of Jersey Shore that Polizzi is filming with costar Jenni Farley in Jersey City, New Jersey. While the premise of the show is still unknown, it is expected to follow the pair's lives as they navigate adulthood and motherhood. It is unclear whether Polizzi's pregnancy will be a central focus of the show or if it will be kept under wraps until a later reveal.

Overall, Snooki's pregnancy, if confirmed, highlights the challenges that many young, single women face when unexpectedly becoming pregnant. While the circumstances of her pregnancy may be more public than most, the issues she is facing are similar to those faced by millions of women across the country. It will be interesting to see how she navigates this new chapter in her life and how it impacts her career and personal relationships.

The inspector general for the intelligence community has informed Congress that some material from Hillary Clinton's private email server contained classified information, but it was not identified as such at the time. The IG reviewed a "limited sampling" of her emails and found that four contained classified information. Clinton has previously denied sending classified information from her personal server. The Justice Department is considering launching a criminal investigation into Clinton's possible mishandling of classified email. The New York Times reported that inspectors general for the intelligence community and the State Department have asked the Justice Department to launch a criminal investigation. The Clinton campaign has denied the report. The request for the Justice Department investigation came after a June memo from the State Department's inspector general stating that a review of 55,000 pages of Clinton emails found "hundreds of potentially classified emails within the collection." A follow-up memo from both the State Department and intelligence community inspectors general to Undersecretary of State Patrick Kennedy on July 17 said they had received confirmation that "several of the emails contained classified (Intelligence Community) information, though they were not marked as classified." Officials were additionally concerned that possible classified material would be posted in future releases of Clinton's emails. Clinton has been criticized by Republicans for using a private email server for official business. The reported request for a criminal investigation is likely to renew fierce Republican criticism of Clinton's email practices. House Speaker John Boehner called on Clinton to relinquish her server and questioned her judgment. South Carolina Rep. Trey Gowdy, chairman of the Select Committee on Benghazi, echoed Boehner's criticism. The top Democrat on the Benghazi Committee, however, pushed back on the attacks, saying that the inspector general did not ask the Justice Department to launch a criminal investigation of Clinton's email usage. Clinton has said she has nothing to hide and would like the process of making her emails public to be expedited. The State Department has been publicly releasing some of the tens of thousands of emails from the private account that Clinton handed over to it in December. Clinton's successor as secretary of state, John Kerry, wrote to the State Department inspector general in March asking for recommendations on the department's practices on document retention and its freedom of information process. Clinton has been a front-runner for the Democratic presidential nomination.

Pete Kostelnick, a 29-year-old financial researcher from Nebraska, has set a new record for the fastest time to run across the United States, completing his 3,100-mile journey from San Francisco to New York City in 42 days, 8 hours, and 34 minutes. Kostelnick's run is still awaiting verification by the Guinness Book of World Records, but Frank Giannino, who previously held the record for the California-to-New York run in 1980, was present to congratulate him. Kostelnick faced challenges during his journey, including falling twice and going through eight pairs of sneakers, but was supported by fans along the way. He plans to spend time with his wife and have a beer upon completing his run. Kostelnick took up running to lose weight and has since become a successful ultrarunner, winning the Badwater Ultramarathon two years in a row and setting the course record in 2016. He set his sights on running across the country and breaking the Guinness record, and his route took him through various landscapes, including the Rockies, the plains, and the Poconos. Kostelnick maintained a consistent nine-minute-mile pace, and his crew tracked his mileage and caloric intake to ensure he stayed on course and met the requirements for the Guinness record. The former record holder, Frank Giannino, was happy to see his record broken by "an athlete at the top of his running game."

In a groundbreaking study, scientists have successfully restored bladder control in paralyzed rats with severe spinal cord injuries. The treatment involves transplanting nerve cells from the rats' ribs into the damaged section of the spinal cord, followed by the addition of an enzyme that breaks down scar tissue and a growth factor to encourage cell growth. This method has allowed the damaged nerves to regenerate and regain function, marking the first time bladder control has been restored in animals with such extensive spinal cord injuries. The study, published in the Journal of Neuroscience, could potentially lead to similar treatments for paralyzed patients in the future. However, further animal experiments and human trials are needed before such treatments can be considered. The findings offer hope for the restoration of bladder function in people with severe spinal cord injuries, which is a high priority for the spinal cord injury community. The treatment involves growing axons, nerve fibers, to bridge the gap in the spinal cord, allowing the brain to communicate with muscles below the line of paralysis. The researchers focused on the scar tissue barrier and used an enzyme to minimize scar tissue and a growth factor to encourage cell growth and axon recovery in the graft. The rats were able to urinate without assistance six months after the treatment. Larger animal trials are planned before moving on to human trials, which could potentially take several years.

A Shorewood man, Robert D. Monroe, has been charged with over a dozen counts of illegal voting in multiple elections between 2011 and 2012, including the 2012 gubernatorial recall. The 50-year-old allegedly used addresses in Shorewood, Milwaukee, and Indiana, and even cast votes in the names of his son and his girlfriend's son.

Monroe is accused of voting twice in the 2011 Supreme Court election, twice in the 2011 Alberta Darling recall election, five times in the Scott Walker-Tom Barrett recall, once illegally in an August 2012 primary, and twice in the November 2012 presidential election.

In the presidential election, Monroe is said to have cast an in-person absentee ballot in Shorewood on November 1 and then drove a rental car to Lebanon, Indiana, where he voted in person on election day, November 6. The complaint alleges that Monroe owns a house in Indiana.

The 26-page criminal complaint was filed in Milwaukee County Circuit Court and is being prosecuted by Assistant District Attorney Bruce Landgraf, who was involved in the John Doe investigations of Gov. Scott Walker's staff.

The investigation reportedly started in Waukesha County, where there were suspicions about Monroe's son voting in Waukesha and applying for an absentee ballot at the Shorewood Village Hall. The son denied any knowledge of requesting an absentee ballot from his father's Shorewood address, and the investigation shifted back to Milwaukee County.

The complaint includes text messages between Monroe and his family, urging them to vote. Monroe is an executive in the health care industry and earned a master's degree in business administration at the University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee in 2013. He faces various counts of election fraud and could face up to 18 months in prison, two years of extended supervision, and a $10,000 fine for each charge.

Monroe is not in custody, and his initial court appearance is scheduled for July 17. He is represented by Milwaukee attorneys Franklyn Gimbel and Steven McGaver, who have declined to comment on the matter.

The U.S. Transportation Security Administration (TSA) has announced a policy change that will allow passengers to carry small pocket knives, golf clubs, hockey sticks, and other sporting equipment onto planes for the first time since the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks. The change, which takes effect on April 25, aims to align the list of prohibited items on U.S. flights with those of international carriers and speed up security screening. However, the move has been criticized by flight attendants who argue that it creates an unnecessary risk and further crowds the already limited space in the overhead bins. The TSA will still prohibit some knives, including those with locking blades or molded handles, and will continue to ban box cutters and razor blades. The changes are based on recommendations from a TSA working group that's trying to weed out commonly confiscated items that don't present a security threat. The TSA Administrator, John Pistole, has stressed the use of intelligence and "risk-based" security during his tenure leading TSA, and the agency is moving away from uniform procedures that apply to every passenger and toward efforts to perform background checks on passengers before they arrive at an airport. The greatest threat to U.S. travelers is currently believed to be small, non-metallic bombs, not knives or sporting equipment. The TSA policy changes will let more passengers go through screening lines more quickly.

The Mayor of Florence, Dario Nardella, has initiated a unique measure to address the issue of tourists eating and making a mess on church steps, starting with the Basilica of Santa Croce and Santo Spirito church. The initiative involves city workers spraying water over the church steps during lunchtime, aiming to discourage tourists from sitting there. The mayor emphasized that Florence has numerous cafes with outdoor seating, and churches are religious and cultural sites, not restaurants.

The response to this measure has been mixed, with some locals criticizing it on social media, claiming it could deter tourists or be perceived as elitist. However, others believe that in the current 30C heat, picnickers might not mind being showered with water.

Mayor Nardella clarified that the city would not be using water cannons on tourists but would simply clean church steps and pavements during lunchtime. He also emphasized that the city is not against tourists but against those who do not respect Florence.

The mayor has taken several steps to protect Florence's ancient heritage from problems caused by mass tourism. For instance, he blocked an application from McDonald's to open a restaurant in the main square, and the city has passed regulations ordering new restaurants in the historic centre to sell food that is at least 70% locally sourced.

This is not the first radical measure taken by Florence to tackle overcrowding. Venice, another popular tourist destination, has introduced measures such as live people-counters, limits on tourist accommodation, and bans on new takeaway food shops in the historic centre.

In summary, the Mayor of Florence has started a unique initiative to discourage tourists from eating on church steps by spraying water over them during lunchtime. The measure is part of a broader effort to protect Florence's ancient heritage from problems caused by mass tourism.

The Syrian President Bashar al-Assad delivered a defiant speech on Sunday, refusing to negotiate and promising trouble for both his allies and enemies. This defiance may prompt Lakhdar Brahimi, the international envoy, to decline continuing his mission, leaving the "Friends of Syria" – a group of nations supporting the opposition – with a difficult choice between intervening more aggressively or allowing the conflict to continue indefinitely. The United Nations estimates that over 60,000 people have died in the civil war, which began as a peaceful protest movement but turned into an armed struggle. Neither side appears ready to give up the prospect of military victory, though analysts say neither side is close to achieving it. Mr. Assad's speech was met with criticism from Western nations, who accused him of clinging to power and continuing to kill his own people. The opposition called the speech a pre-emptive strike against diplomatic solutions. The speech came just a few miles from fighting that raged across Syria on Monday, with clashes reported near the road to the city's international airport. The government restricts access by international media, making it difficult to verify accounts of the fighting. Despite the ongoing conflict, some Syrians expressed frustration with the speech, saying it was eloquent but empty and that military operations would continue in full swing.

The Kansas House of Representatives has passed a controversial bill, House Bill No. 2453, which allows businesses and government employees to deny service to same-sex couples on religious grounds. The bill, criticized as a step back to the 1890s and reminiscent of Jim Crow laws, covers almost all public accommodations, including grocery stores, movie theaters, hotels, gyms, and restaurants. The bill also authorizes anti-gay discrimination by state employees, potentially affecting services like ambulances, park management, state hospitals, and public welfare agencies.

If the bill becomes law, businesses can refuse service to same-sex couples without facing civil suits, and the couples would have to pay their opponents' attorney's fees. The bill has been met with national criticism, with opponents arguing it promotes discrimination.

Senate President Susan Wagle has stated that the bill does not have the support of a majority of Republicans in her chamber, and with fewer than half the Senate Republicans supporting the bill, it would need Democratic support to pass the 40-member chamber, an unlikely prospect since Democrats are lined up against it.

Supporters of the bill argue it is intended to protect religious liberties, citing cases of photographers, bakers, and florists who have faced legal action for refusing to provide services to same-sex weddings. However, critics argue the bill's language is broad and vague, opening the door for discrimination.

The bill is currently under review and revision in the Senate, with legislative leaders planning to make substantial changes to address business and community concerns. The bill's future remains uncertain, but opponents hope the revisions will protect the religious liberties of all Kansans while ensuring the dignity of gay and lesbian couples across the state.

In September 2017, William Hannah, a 68-year-old grandfather from England, died after being accidentally given cleaning detergent instead of saline during a medical procedure at Salford Royal Hospital. The incident occurred while Hannah was being treated for a head injury and multiple fractures following a car accident.

According to the Hannah family's lawyers, a healthcare assistant mistakenly handed the doctor a bottle of cleaning detergent instead of saline, leading to the error. The doctor realized the mistake after the procedure, but Hannah's condition worsened, and he died the next day.

An internal investigation by the Salford Royal NHS Foundation Trust found that multiple factors contributed to the mistake, including an un-stocked trolley, distractions, lack of clear communication, no labeling of the bottle, inadequate staff training, and a lack of risk assessment. The report noted that the clinical impact of the errors on the patient is unknown at this point.

The Trust has apologized for the incident and introduced new measures to prevent such mistakes from happening again. However, Hannah's daughter, Lisa, has expressed dissatisfaction with the hospital's handling of the investigation, stating that it has added to the family's distress and upset.

The Hannah family has instructed lawyers and is suing the hospital to hold it accountable and ensure lessons are learned. Hearings are scheduled to begin in February 2019. The exact cause of Hannah's death will be determined during a future inquest at Bolton Coroner's Court.

In Irvington, New Jersey, a tragic incident occurred on Saturday where a 15-month-old girl, Sania Cunningham, was shot and killed by a stray bullet while playing inside her home. The shooting took place during a gun battle between two groups of men, with several bullet holes found in the area, including the house where Sania lived, a car on the street, and a neighbor's air conditioner.

The family had recently moved into the apartment, and the girl was rushed to the hospital but later pronounced dead. The Essex County Prosecutor's Office is investigating the case and has scheduled a press conference. A $10,000 reward is being offered for information leading to an arrest.

Neighbors have expressed concern over the ongoing violence in the area, with some describing it as a "O.K. Corral" and stating that it's especially disturbing that the shooting happened during daylight hours. The community is urging anyone with information to come forward.

Minister Thomas Ellis, of Newark, visited the neighborhood to offer comfort to residents and put up an orange sign outside the home that reads "Enough is Enough!" The family of the victim is not known to Minister Ellis.

The shooting has drawn an outpouring of concern and anger from the community, with some residents complaining that it took a toddler's death to bring attention to the area that is under siege. Essex County Sheriff's CrimeStoppers is offering $10,000 for information, and Mayor Tony Vauss has posted condolences on his Facebook page. The township recently received $1 million to hire more police officers.

Investigators are searching for three men who were wearing hooded sweatshirts as they fired multiple shots on the block. The acting Essex County prosecutor, Carolyn A. Murray, stated that bullets struck the home where the toddler was staying, the Houston family's house, and a car. The motive behind the shooting remains unclear.

The article discusses the infiltration of a small New York dam by Iranian hackers in 2013, which was previously undisclosed. The hackers did not take control of the system but were probing its defenses. The incident occurred during a wave of Iranian hacks on U.S. banks and three years after a computer worm believed to be built by the U.S. and Israel damaged nuclear infrastructure in Iran. The article highlights the increasing concerns about cyberattacks on critical infrastructure networks, including the power grid, and the potential for devastating consequences if hackers move from grid-mapping to a deliberate attack. The article also mentions the outdated technology governing industrial systems and the lack of preparedness of utilities to cope with the threat of such an attack. The U.S. has more than 57,000 industrial-control systems connected to the Internet, and the Department of Homeland Security has responded to an increasing number of hacking incidents related to industrial controls in recent years. The article also mentions the potential for ISIS to perpetrate cyberattacks and the need for clear standards governing the U.S. response to different incidents. The article ends by discussing the murky guidelines surrounding cyberwarfare and the need for clear standards to define what constitutes an act of war, the appropriate response, and the line between crime and warfare.

In the final installment of the Planet of the Apes trilogy, "War for the Planet of the Apes," Caesar, the intelligent chimpanzee leader, embarks on a revenge mission against a ruthless human colonel who has caused him significant loss. The film, directed by Matt Reeves, is a stirring and soulful conclusion to the trilogy, combining old and new elements while creating its own rich mythology.

The movie picks up shortly after the last film, with Caesar leading a community of intelligent apes hoping for peaceful coexistence with humans. However, a military attack on their forest home by the colonel and his renegade forces quickly destroys these plans, prompting Caesar to pursue vengeance.

The apes are eventually captured, leading to a series of events reminiscent of "The Great Escape." The film also features ample brutality inflicted by the humans on their simian prisoners, with a saving grace coming in the form of a young girl who the apes reluctantly take in.

The apes' war against the humans takes a darker turn, with references to internment camps, the Bible, and even the Holocaust. The film's imagery and non-stop horror can be heavy-handed at times, and it lacks sympathetic human characters within the base. However, the film's message about humanity's blindness to the humanity in other species is poignant.

Despite its dark themes, War for the Planet of the Apes is a well-crafted and intelligent movie that treats its audience like adults. The physical action is clear, the character motivation is fully thought out, and the special effects support the story rather than supplanting it. The film's climax has true emotional sweep, making it a fitting conclusion to the trilogy.

In the latest update of Apple's iOS 7, a significant change is the sleek, minimal aesthetic, however, the introduction of numerous motion effects has caused issues for some users, particularly those with motion sickness. The new animations, such as zooming, parallax, and sliding, have been reported to cause symptoms like dizziness and nausea.

The severity of these symptoms varies, but for some, it has become a significant problem. iOS user and power-user Jenni Leder, for example, has experienced headaches and feelings of motion sickness due to the new animations. These symptoms were not present under iOS 6, which had fewer triggering animations.

The issue is not new, as 3D effects can cause intense nausea, dizziness, and vertigo for people with vestibular disorders. The vestibular system, which gives us our sense of balance and spatial awareness, can conflict with visual systems, leading to distressing symptoms.

The number of people affected is hard to pin down, but it is estimated that 69 million US adults over 40 experience vestibular system dysfunction. The problem is compounded by the fact that many people do not believe the issue exists, and there is currently no fix.

Apple provides a "Reduce Motion" option within the iOS 7 Settings app, but it only disables the parallax effect, not zooming or sliding. Apple has not responded to requests for comment regarding the issue.

Independent iOS developer Matt Gemmell suggests that those with neurological conditions that cause central dizziness may find the new iOS 7 interface uncomfortable or disorienting. The Ménière's Society, a UK charity for people with disorders causing dizziness or balance disorders, explains that these disorders can be extremely debilitating, despite there being no visible symptoms.

Technology writer Kirk McElhearn questions whether Apple is ignoring people with vision and balance problems, and suggests that Apple should acknowledge the issue and initiate an open dialog with those affected, developers, and Apple's own accessibility team.

In the meantime, developers can do their part by considering all categories and ability levels of users, enabling users to disable anything that could be annoying or intrusive, and ensuring UI effects have a useful function.

Individual developers like James Thomson of the popular calculator app PCalc have recognized the accessibility concerns and provided the option to remove full-screen transitions throughout the app. However, Thomson hopes Apple will add this option at the system level, so individual developers don't have to.

Gemmell urges Apple and developers alike to react accordingly regarding animations and transitions, simply because it's the right thing to do: "Designing for accessibility levels the playing field, and increases the utility of devices for everybody."

Tennis legend Jennifer Capriati, a three-time Grand Slam winner and Olympic gold medalist, was hospitalized after a suspected drug overdose at a Riviera Beach hotel. According to TMZ, Capriati's father reported that she is recovering well. Known as a child prodigy, Capriati's career was marred by personal struggles, including legal issues and a stint in rehabilitation. Despite these challenges, she made a comeback in the early 2000s, winning the Australian and French Opens, and defending her Australian title in 2002. However, she has not returned to tennis due to further injuries and reports of depression.

The United States has reported at least 16 incidents targeting U.S. staff and government officials in Cuba, according to U.S. officials. These incidents, described as unprecedented, have caused a variety of physical symptoms, including headaches, vision issues, balance and walking issues, and memory loss. The incidents are believed to have started in late December 2016, and some U.S. officials were exposed to a sonic device in Havana that caused serious health problems.

The Cuban government denies any involvement and is cooperating with the ongoing U.S. investigation, but the two governments are not working together on the matter. The FBI is among those investigating on the ground in Havana, with the State Department's Bureau of Diplomatic Security taking the lead.

Some U.S. officials have been evacuated to Miami for medical treatment and testing, and medical professionals have been sent to Cuba to treat and test the affected individuals. The University of Miami has been consulted by the State Department regarding the health care issues of the U.S. diplomats.

The State Department has expelled two Cuban embassy officials in Washington as a response to the attacks, but there are signs that the U.S. may be privately moving forward with plans to make it easier for Americans to visit and do business with Cuba. The Treasury Department's Office of Foreign Assets Control has removed hundreds of internet domain names primarily focused on travel to Cuba from its Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons list.

The investigation into the incidents is ongoing, and the U.S. government is working to find the source of these incidents and the perpetrator. The U.S. takes the matter very seriously and is trying to provide the affected individuals with the best medical attention possible.

This is a heartwarming story about Linda Hooper, a teacher, and one of her students, Cruz Riojas, who eventually became her adopted son. In the fall of 1981, Cruz was a troubled student at Brown Elementary School in Lubbock, Texas, known for his frequent violent outbursts and academic struggles due to dyslexia. Linda, a veteran teacher, found it difficult to connect with Cruz, often describing him as a "holy terror."

However, over the course of six years, Cruz and Linda formed a unique bond. Cruz would often misbehave in class, using his dry humor to distract from the lesson, or even throw chairs and stab his peers. Despite these challenges, Linda became a refuge for Cruz, who was living in a one-room lean-to with his mother, stepfather, and siblings in "total squalor." Cruz wore the same clothes to school every day and was sent home with lice 12 times that year.

In December of that school year, Cruz changed, starting to help around the classroom and eventually working for the Hoopers on odd jobs for cash. As their relationship improved, Cruz's home life worsened, leading to a cold, snowy day in February 1983 when Cruz had the last fight he would have with his stepfather and was kicked out at the age of 12. Cruz's mother took him to hide at a nearby truck stop, and Linda agreed to keep him for the weekend - a decision that would ultimately lead to Cruz living with the Hoopers permanently.

Cruz's adoption by the Hoopers was not formalized until 1998, but he legally became part of the family in a ceremony that brought great joy to Linda and her husband, Gale. Cruz has since grown up to have a successful career and a loving family of his own, while Linda credits Cruz with changing her approach to teaching and her life in general. Linda now looks back on Cruz as the "one thing in my life I've done right."

Actress Melissa Gilbert, known for her role in "Little House on the Prairie," faced a tax debt of over $360,000 from the IRS in 2014. The debt was attributed to a stalled acting career, the economy, and divorce. Gilbert, along with her husband and fellow actor Timothy Busfield, moved from Howell, Michigan to a log house in Livingston County, citing the move as unrelated to the tax debt. Gilbert has a history of tax problems, with California filing tax liens against her since 2013. The IRS filed a $360,551 tax lien against Gilbert in February 2014, accusing her of owing federal income taxes from 2011, 2012, and 2013. Gilbert has since negotiated a payment plan with the IRS to pay off the debt. The couple has been living in Michigan since their marriage in April 2013 and have been active in the local community, participating in charity events and filming projects. Gilbert has also written a cookbook called "My Prairie Cookbook" and has done book signings in Livingston County.

Dylann Roof, the suspected gunman responsible for the killing of nine people in a Charleston, South Carolina church on Wednesday, was apprehended in Shelby, North Carolina early this morning. Debbie Dills, a bookkeeper in Kings Mountain, North Carolina, spotted Roof's car and white tag, which matched the police description of the shooting suspect, and called 911. Police in Shelby received a tip at 10:32 am about a possible sighting of the suspect and arrested Roof at a traffic stop 12 minutes later. Roof cooperated with the officer who stopped him. Charleston police Chief Greg Mullen said he was pleased the case was resolved quickly. Roof waived extradition in North Carolina and is cleared to return to South Carolina.

In recent weeks, Roof reconnected with a childhood friend who said Roof started railing about the Trayvon Martin case, black people "taking over the world," and the need for someone to do something for the sake of "the white race." Roof displayed a Confederate flag on his license plate and wore a jacket with the flags of the former white-racist regimes of South Africa and Rhodesia on his Facebook page. The Southern Poverty Law Center, a civil rights group that tracks hate organizations and extremists, said it was not aware of Roof before the rampage. Some other friends interviewed said they did not know him to be racist.

The shooting at the historic black church in Charleston was decried as a hate crime by community leaders and politicians. Roof had at least two recent run-ins with the law, with a felony drug case pending against him and a misdemeanor trespassing charge from April. Juvenile records are generally sealed in South Carolina. Court records list no attorney for him. Roof's mother and her boyfriend live in Lexington, and his father lives in Columbia.

A researcher named Dr. Gordon Hamilton, a climate scientist from the University of Maine, died in a snowmobile accident on October 22, 2016, in Antarctica. The accident occurred in a heavily crevassed area known as the Shear Zone, approximately 25 miles south of McMurdo Station, which is one of the three U.S. research stations in Antarctica. Dr. Hamilton was part of the U.S. Antarctic Program (USAP), managed by the National Science Foundation (NSF).

Dr. Hamilton's research focused on studying the stability of the Ross and McMurdo Ice Shelves using two robots with ground-penetrating radar instruments. At the time of the accident, he was driving a snowmobile and fell into a crevasse, which is still under investigation. His body has been recovered and will be returned to his family in Maine.

The NSF manages the USAP, coordinating all U.S. research and logistical support on the continent and aboard ships in the Southern Ocean. The two teams involved in the accident, science and Traverse operations, were experienced and had received crevasse and glacial safety training. They were working together to identify and remediate crevasses in the area.

Deaths in Antarctica are rare, and this incident serves as a reminder of the risks involved in field research, especially in extreme environments. Dr. Hamilton is survived by his wife, Fiona, and their two children, Martin and Calum. His loss is deeply mourned by the scientific community.

A Pembroke Pines Police Officer, Sgt. Jennifer Martin, was allegedly denied service at an Arby's restaurant on Tuesday, with the reason being that she was a police officer. The incident has sparked a controversy and a potential boycott of the fast-food chain. According to a police report, the shift manager stepped in for an employee and said he didn't want to serve Martin because she was a police officer. The manager has since claimed it was a misunderstanding and a bad attempt at humor.

The incident has received widespread criticism on social media, with comments such as "Goodbye Arby's" and "I don't think I will ever eat there again." The Broward County Police Benevolent Association is calling for a public apology to every law enforcement officer instead of the one given to the chief of the Pembroke Pines Police Department. The CEO of Arby's has apologized to the chief, but the company has yet to respond to further requests for comment.

The incident occurred on the same evening that a woman and her daughter visited the Pembroke Pines Police Department to drop off cookies and a "thank you" card. The police union is calling for the employee who refused to serve the officer to be fired, and a group of police officers' wives held a protest outside the restaurant on Wednesday. The police union has also asked for a national boycott of the fast-food chain.

The police chief of Pembroke Pines, Dan Giustino, has expressed his disappointment and called the incident unacceptable. He has contacted the Arby's corporate office and received an apology on behalf of the organization. The company has stated that the employee's behavior was unacceptable and not representative of the company's values. The incident is considered to be isolated.

Jeffrey Zaslow, a renowned author and journalist known for his best-sellers such as "The Last Lecture" and "Gabby: A Story of Courage and Hope", was tragically killed in a car accident in northern Michigan on Friday. Zaslow, aged 53, was a Philadelphia native, married to Fox 2 Detroit news anchor Sherry Margolis since 1987, and the father of three daughters. He lost control of his car on a snow-covered road near Elmira, M-32, and was hit by a semi-truck.

Zaslow began his career as a Wall Street Journal reporter, winning the contest to replace Ann Landers and becoming her replacement at the Chicago Sun-Times. He later became a columnist for the Wall Street Journal, focusing on relationships. His books inspired millions, including "The Last Lecture" about Randy Pausch, a Carnegie Mellon professor dying of pancreatic cancer, and "Gabby" about U.S. Rep. Gabrielle Giffords' recovery from a gunshot wound to the head.

Zaslow's latest book, "The Magic Room," chronicles the stories of eight brides from a bridal store in Fowler, Michigan. He drew inspiration for the book from his own three daughters. In an interview last week, Zaslow spoke about the importance of hugging his children and making the most of each moment, inspired by Prof. Randy Pausch's advice to him.

Zaslow's work touched and inspired millions around the world, and he was twice named best columnist by the National Society of Newspaper Columnists. In a statement, the editor of the Wall Street Journal said, "Jeff's writing, for the Journal and in his books, has been a source of inspiration for many people around the world and his journalistic life has been a source of inspiration for all journalists."

The mother of Peter Fedden, a 29-year-old Commack man and the owner of a popular local deli, has filed a federal wrongful death lawsuit against Suffolk County police, claiming that they failed to arrest him for driving under the influence (DUI) after a crash on July 30, 2013, which ultimately led to his death. The lawsuit, filed in Central Islip, alleges that police drove Fedden home after the initial crash, despite his severe intoxication and visible injuries.

According to the lawsuit, Fedden later drove off in one of the cars parked in his driveway and was killed in a subsequent crash in Hauppauge. The complaint states that Fedden was served excessive amounts of alcohol at a Ruby Tuesday restaurant before the crashes, and the lawsuit names the restaurant as being responsible for his intoxication.

The lawsuit alleges that Fedden started the night at Ruby Tuesday's bar, where he was served two 10-ounce glasses of Jack Daniel's whiskey. After leaving the bar with another customer, they drove directly to Fedden's deli, where they smoked marijuana. The lawsuit also claims that Fedden was driving at speeds over 100 mph when he crashed.

Suffolk County police have not commented on the pending litigation, and county officials could not be reached for comment. The owner of the marketing firm that suffered $100,000 in damage when Fedden crashed into it called the lawsuit frivolous. The Ruby Tuesday's spokesman could not be reached for comment.

The lawsuit seeks $130 million in damages and alleges that the police conspired to avoid charging Fedden with any crimes due to their relationship with him through his deli, where officers were known to receive big discounts. The lawsuit also claims that the defendants carelessly disregarded Fedden's safety and created the events leading to his wrongful death. Kathi Fedden's attorney, Harry M. Thomasson of Wantagh, could not be reached for comment.

Ken Mehlman, a former Republican National Committee (RNC) chairman, has come out as gay in an interview with The Atlantic's Marc Ambinder. Mehlman managed President Bush's re-election campaign in 2004 and chaired the RNC from 2005 to 2007. His announcement is significant as it may help normalize homosexuality within the Republican party and could potentially shift public opinion on gay rights.

Mehlman's announcement has been met with support from his colleagues, including the current RNC chairman, Michael Steele, who said, "I am happy for Ken. His announcement, often a very difficult decision which is only compounded when done on the public stage, reaffirms for me why we are friends and why I respect him personally and professionally."

Mehlman plans to advocate for gay rights within the GOP and believes that it is consistent with the party's philosophy of individual freedom, limited government, and encouraging adults who love each other to get married. He hopes to persuade Republicans that supporting gay marriage is compatible with their social conservative values.

Mehlman's announcement is seen as a step towards greater respect and civility in the same-sex marriage debate. It is also a reminder that an openly gay RNC chief might still face challenges within the party. Mehlman's personal journey and decision to come out publicly is a significant moment in the ongoing conversation about gay rights and the role of homosexuality within the Republican party.

The burning of Korans by U.S. military personnel in Afghanistan has led to a series of violent events that have escalated tensions and potentially exposed a vulnerability in the U.S.'s strategy to wind down the war. The U.S. strategy involves replacing large NATO combat units with smaller advisory teams working alongside Afghan partners. However, the killing of two high-ranking NATO officers by an Afghan security official has raised doubts about the reliability of Afghan security forces to protect Western partners. This erosion of trust could have severe consequences, as it may signal the endgame of the partnership.

The recent killings of U.S. officers were perpetrated by Afghan troops with alleged Taliban loyalties or due to tensions arising from perceived insults to their faith. Afghan President Hamid Karzai initially responded with outrage but later sought to calm the situation by recalling NATO advisers from his ministries. Protests continued, resulting in violence and casualties on both sides.

The U.S. remains committed to its partnership with Afghanistan, but much of the cooperation between U.S. advisers and their Afghan partners is on hold due to the increased threat level. The smaller U.S. advisory force may be more exposed to fratricidal attacks than conventional military units, as these attacks often stem from cultural differences. To mitigate this risk, advisers are encouraged to build closer relationships with their Afghan partners.

Current plans call for the U.S. force in Afghanistan to decrease from 100,000 troops to about 68,000 by the end of the summer, with further reductions expected later this year and in 2013. By the end of 2014, all NATO combat troops are expected to be withdrawn. To maintain security, NATO could rely on as few as 25,000 advisory troops, who would live without large bases, dining facilities, and quick-reaction forces. The more willing advisers are to accept risk, the more effective they will be. The current strains in the U.S.-Afghan relationship could impact the success of this strategy.

The third National Climate Assessment, a federal report released on Friday, warns that climate change is already affecting U.S. residents through heat waves, droughts, and other changes, and predicts that temperatures could increase by as much as 10 degrees Fahrenheit if global carbon emissions continue to soar. The report, developed by a federal advisory panel, concludes that there is "unambiguous evidence" that the Earth is warming, and that climate change over the past 50 years is primarily driven by human activity, especially from burning fossil fuels.

The report tallies the wide-ranging effects of climate change, such as water supplies stressed by declining runoff and increased risk of heat stress and waterborne disease, and notes that U.S. infrastructure is already being harmed by sea-level rise, storm surges, and heavy downpours. Environmentalists have seized on the report to call for more aggressive steps to drive down emissions, with one scientist stating that it could help restart a national conversation about climate change.

The report finds that U.S. temperatures will continue to rise by 2 degrees F to 4 degrees F in most areas in the coming decades, but it's unclear how high temperatures will climb in the long term. The report provides a range of 3 degrees F to 5 degrees F by the end of the century if global emissions are reduced sharply after 2050, and up to 10 degrees F if they're not. Average U.S. temperatures have risen roughly 1.5 degrees F since 1895, with more than 80 percent of that increase occurring since 1980.

While climate advocates are pushing for stronger executive actions, such as Environmental Protection Agency carbon emissions standards for existing power plants, it's unlikely that the report will fundamentally change the politics of climate change on Capitol Hill, where bills to cap emissions or impose carbon taxes are moribund. However, green activists are continuing to press for action, with one former climate czar calling for strict carbon pollution standards for power plants and significant investments in community resiliency to protect against extreme weather events such as floods, droughts, wildfires, and heat waves.

The report is just the latest broad study or statement by a scientific body to conclude that there is overwhelming evidence that global warming is underway and that human activities are a major cause. However, some Republicans dispute this conclusion, with one representative stating that climate change is due to a combination of factors, including natural cycles, sun spots, and human activity. The report is in draft form and will be open for public comment for three months before being finalized.

The document discusses the potential collaboration between the Roswell Park Cancer Institute in the United States and Cuba's Center for Molecular Immunology to develop a lung cancer vaccine, Cimavax. The vaccine, which has low toxicity and is relatively cheap to produce and store, was developed in Cuba over 25 years and made available to the public in 2011.

Cuba's focus on biotechnology and medical research, particularly preventative medicine, has led to several significant breakthroughs, including their own vaccines for meningitis B and hepatitis B, and monoclonal antibodies for kidney transplants. The Obama administration's efforts to normalize relations with Cuba have facilitated this collaboration, with the Roswell Park Cancer Institute aiming to bring Cimavax to the US for FDA approval and clinical trials.

The document also mentions another vaccine, Racotumomab, with a different mechanism, which is being developed in collaboration with a biologist at the Feinstein Institute for Medical Research. The lifting of some restrictions against medical and research equipment by President Obama is a step towards further collaboration, but the Cuban embargo must be lifted by Congress for more extensive collaboration to occur.

Governor Andrew Cuomo's visit to Cuba was significant in finalizing the agreement between the Roswell Park Cancer Institute and Cuba's Center for Molecular Immunology. The visit also saw a deal between software company Infor and a Cuban university for the provision of healthcare software. The normalization of relations between the US and Cuba is seen as beneficial for both parties, with the potential for Cuban researchers to share their innovative approaches to medical research with their US counterparts.

The document also highlights the economic challenges faced by Cuba, with the average worker earning $20 a month, yet the country's healthcare spending per individual being a fraction of that in the US, yet the average Cuban having a life expectancy on par with the average American. The document concludes by emphasizing the innovative nature of Cuban biotech and medical research, particularly given the country's economic constraints.

Russian President Vladimir Putin showcased his hockey skills at the All-Russia Festival of Night Hockey League in Sochi, scoring one goal and assisting five others during a friendly match. Putin, wearing the number 11 jersey, played alongside retired Soviet hockey legends and Olympic medal winners, while his opponents were reportedly amateurs. In at least two attempts, Putin just missed the goal, but his teammates helped him score. The match was part of a league that began as a casual event for over-40s but has grown to include 108 teams from 11 countries. Putin's participation in the league is the latest in a series of macho publicity stunts, including cuddling a tame snow leopard, tranquilizing a polar bear, and shooting a whale for scientific research. The Russian premier, 61, has a history of such stunts, which are often intended to boost his image as a strong leader.

Snap Inc., formerly known as Snapchat, has made its camera-enabled sunglasses, Spectacles, available for purchase online in the U.S. Previously, the glasses were only sold through vending machines and a pop-up store in New York City. Due to high demand and limited supply, some pairs were resold for up to $5,000. The online sale aims to prove to investors that Spectacles can generate revenue for the company ahead of its IPO.

Spectacles, priced at $129.99, are available in three colors: teal, coral, and black. The purchase limit is six pairs per household, and shipping is estimated to take two to four weeks. Snapbots, the roving vending machines, will continue to appear in unexpected locations across the U.S. after a brief hiatus.

The online sale comes as Snap reported a loss of $514.6 million in 2016, making the sale of 4 million pairs of Spectacles enough to break even this year. The company plans to use Spectacles to increase user engagement on its Snapchat app, but it also aims to demonstrate the potential for hardware revenue. The future holds anticipation for what new camera devices Snap Inc. will release.

Facebook is set to launch its long-rumored music service next month, according to Mashable and other sources. The service will be announced at Facebook's f8 developer conference on Sept. 22 and will allow users to listen to music from within Facebook.com. The music and media platform will not directly host or stream any music or media, but will instead rely on partners like Spotify, Rdio, and MOG to provide the content. Facebook's plan is to become a platform for media content in the same way it is a platform for applications and games. The music platform is expected to be deeply integrated into users' home pages and will enable users who are subscribers to a service to share songs and playlists seamlessly with each other and to see what friends are listening to. The digital music services hope Facebook users will sign up with them after seeing friends sharing playlists that require subscription. Facebook declined to comment on the new music platform, but it is expected to be a significant boost to its partners as they compete in the digital music sector dominated by Apple Inc's iTunes's download store. The launch of the music service is part of Facebook's strategy to increase the amount of time users spend in the Facebook environment and to partner with other media content owners like movie studios. However, Facebook has not yet confirmed whether it will go beyond music with the platform.

Russian hackers infiltrated the White House's unclassified computer system last year, gaining access to sensitive information about President Obama's schedule. The hack was connected to a Russian cyberattack that also breached the State Department's network. The intrusion began when hackers sent a phishing email from a State Department account, infecting a White House computer with malware.

The White House breach is significant because the White House maintains tight control over information about the president's activities. While a general outline of the day's events is available to the press, Obama takes many meetings and phone calls throughout the day that are not publicly disclosed. The president's precise whereabouts are also not always known, and the press pool that covers Obama on a daily basis is restricted from accessing many parts of the White House building and grounds.

Intimate knowledge of Obama's activities would be seen as valuable to foreign intelligence agencies like Russia's. Officials with knowledge of the investigation told CNN that Russian hackers were able to break into the White House system through their foothold within networks at the State Department.

The State Department has been battling its own highly sophisticated cyber intrusion for months, though exactly which portions of its network remain breached is unclear. Private security experts had suspected there was a link between the State Department and White House break-ins.

Russia is a key adversary of the United States in cyberspace, and is believed to have infiltrated most U.S. critical infrastructure, including installing malware in software that controls everything from oil and gas pipelines to wind turbines to nuclear power plants.

The White House breach made headlines last year as a sign of hackers’ increasing access to the highest levels of the U.S. government. White House officials confirmed in October that its unclassified system had been breached. Computers and systems were not damaged, officials said, though some services were disrupted as cybersecurity experts sought to limit hackers’ activity in the months that followed. The “vast majority” of systems were back online as of late February, White House press secretary Josh Earnest said at the time.

The investigation into the breach is being led by the FBI, Secret Service, and U.S. intelligence agencies. The intrusion was routed through computers around the world, as hackers often do to hide their tracks, but investigators found tell-tale codes and other markers that they believe point to hackers working for the Russian government.

The White House and State Department have not commented on the breach, but National Security Council spokesman Mark Stroh said that "any such activity is something we take very seriously." Ben Rhodes, President Barack Obama's deputy national security adviser, said the White House's use of a separate system for classified information protected sensitive national security-related items from being obtained by hackers.

The hack is the latest in a series of cyberattacks on U.S. government systems that have been attributed to Russia. The attacks have been seen as a sign of increasing tensions between the United States and Russia, particularly over issues such as the Russian aggression in Ukraine and U.S. military operations in Syria.

Senator Susan Collins has called for legislation to encourage the government and private companies to bolster their cyber defenses in response to the breach. The attacks on the State and White House systems is one reason why Director of National Intelligence James Clapper told a Senate hearing in February that the "Russian cyberthreat is more severe than we have previously assessed."

The hack is also raising concerns about the security of Hillary Clinton's private email server, which she used to conduct government business during her time as Secretary of State. Critics say her private server likely was even less safe than the State system, and the Russian breach is believed to have come after Clinton departed State.

Hackers have long made Clinton and her associates targets. In 2013, a hacker known as Guccifer broke into the AOL email of Sidney Blumenthal, a friend and advisor to the Clintons, and published emails Blumenthal sent to Hillary Clinton's private account. The emails included sensitive memos on foreign policy issues and were the first public revelation of the existence of Hillary Clinton's private email address, which is now at the center of controversy. The address is no longer in use.

The solar-powered MS Turanor PlanetSolar, a catamaran conceived by Swiss electrical engineer Raphael Domjan in 2004, completed its journey around the world on Friday, marking the end of an 19-month voyage. The boat, designed by New Zealander Craig Loomes, is made of a lightweight carbon material and covered with 38,000 solar cells that feed power to six blocks of lithium-ion batteries. The ship's journey took it through the Atlantic, Pacific, Panama, and Suez canals, and various ports including Miami, Cancún, Brisbane, Singapore, and Abu Dhabi.

Domjan's goal was to demonstrate the capabilities of solar power and promote its use as an alternative to fossil fuels in sea travel. The boat's arrival in Monaco was met with a light show powered by the energy stored in its batteries. Domjan plans to take some time off before working on a book and a film documentary about the journey, which will be ready by September 27, two years after the boat set off from Monaco.

In other news, Yahoo confirmed misleading information on its new CEO's resume, California is expected to reap a windfall from Mark Zuckerberg in Facebook's IPO, and 3-D holographic video conferencing is reportedly possible.

The upcoming foreign trip of President Donald Trump, starting on May 19, is a nine-day, five-country tour that includes visits to the homelands of all three Abrahamic faiths - Judaism, Christianity, and Islam. The trip aims to project American power abroad, build relationships with world leaders, and "broadcast a message of unity" to Jews, Christians, and Muslims.

The itinerary includes Saudi Arabia, the birthplace of Islam, where Trump aims to erase his Islamophobic image and urge Muslim leaders to address extremist ideologies. In Israel, Trump wants to jumpstart the stalled peace negotiations between Israelis and Palestinians, while visiting touchstones like the Western Wall. In Europe, the President seeks to repair frayed relations with two of the continent's most venerable institutions, the Vatican and NATO.

Trump's speech in Saudi Arabia is expected to be a contrast to the vision Obama laid out in his first trip to the region. In Israel, Trump will meet with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, looking to smooth over fresh tensions. In Rome, Trump will call upon Pope Francis, the popular, liberal-minded pontiff. In Brussels, Trump will attend a meeting of NATO, the World War II-era alliance which Trump has repeatedly mused about abandoning. And in Sicily, the President will meet with the other leaders of the G7, a gathering of Western economic powers.

The trip comes at a critical moment for Trump's young presidency, as he tries to calm allies worried about his "America First" message, and deliver specifics about his worldview to a global audience that has watched his initial, chaotic months in the White House with a mix of amusement, befuddlement, and alarm. However, the trip also carries considerable risks, especially for someone with a tendency to improvise in delicate diplomatic situations.

In Saudi Arabia, Trump risks alienating or even insulting many Muslims who are weary of Western politicians conflating their faith with terrorism. In Israel, Trump will have to address the embassy question, as he had promised to move the US embassy to disputed Jerusalem, a change that would irk Palestinians and other Arabs. In Rome, Trump will have to navigate his relationship with Pope Francis, who has criticized Trump in the past.

Overall, the trip offers Trump opportunities to make real news and change the subject from domestic scandals, but it also risks being dominated by domestic-style questions. The White House believes the unexpected move of going to Saudi Arabia first was meant to underscore the seriousness of the United States' commitment to fighting extremist groups like the Islamic State. Trump, whose denunciations of Iran have been welcomed by the Saudis, wants to frame the conflict not as one between the West and Islam, but simply between good and evil.

The trip also marks Melania Trump's first international trip as First Lady, where she will engage with foreign women and children and deliver remarks to U.S. military families and personnel. The Trumps will leave Washington on Friday for a trip to Saudi Arabia, Israel, Rome, Brussels, and Sicily.

The article discusses the struggles of Jeb Bush's presidential campaign, which many attribute to the early stages of his campaign being held in Dallas, Texas. The meetings at a Dallas airport hotel were seen as ungainly and disjointed, with rapid hiring by new advisers causing friction among older Bush hands. The campaign's initial optimism and strategic errors were exacerbated by unexpected stumbles by Bush and internal strife within his team, leading to a staff shake-up.

Bush's candidacy was based on the premise that a bold, fast start would scare off potential rivals and help him overcome the burden of his last name, but this has proven to be misguided. Bush's middle-of-the-road positions on immigration and education have come off as out of step with the base of his party, and his wonky question-and-answer exchanges with voters sometimes resemble college lectures rather than a disarming appeal for votes.

The troubles have eroded Bush's image as the one Republican uniquely ready for the presidential stage, and he has slipped in polls from presumed front-runner to one of several candidates jumbled toward the top of an increasingly crowded field. Bush and his team are now preparing plans to attack the records and experience of his GOP competition, especially Sens. Marco Rubio (Fla.) and Rand Paul (Ky.) and Wisconsin Gov. Scott Walker.

The original premise of Bush's candidacy has proven to be misguided, and his operation's ability to rake in large checks has fueled inflated expectations. Supporters acknowledged this week that an allied super PAC was likely to fall short — perhaps substantially — of predictions that it would bring in $100 million in the first half of the year.

On the stump, Bush has stuck to his pledge not to shift to the right to win the nomination, but his middle-of-the-road positions on immigration and education have come off more as out of step with the base of his party than shrewdly pragmatic. His wonky question-and-answer exchanges with voters sometimes resemble college lectures rather than a disarming appeal for votes.

The troubles have eroded the image Bush has sought to present as the one Republican uniquely ready for the presidential stage. He has slipped in polls from presumed front-runner to one of several candidates jumbled toward the top of an increasingly crowded field.

Speaking in Berlin during an overseas trip, Bush expressed confidence. "It's June, for crying out loud, so we've got a long way to go," he said, adding later: "I'm going to compete everywhere. If I'm a candidate, there's no fifth-place, you know, kind of mentality in my mind."

Forced to make up lost ground, Bush, his aides and his super-PAC allies are now preparing plans to attack the records and experience of his GOP competition, especially Sens. Marco Rubio (Fla.) and Rand Paul (Ky.) and Wisconsin Gov. Scott Walker. A summer envisioned as a season of slow and warm introductions to voters is poised to be a battle as Bush tries to recapture his place atop the pack.

"The Bushes have always underestimated the depth of the base's dissatisfaction with their policies, and they take the criticism personally," Laura Ingraham, a conservative radio host, said in an interview. "Jeb has to try to understand the reasons why conservatives have problems with him instead of crowing about how principled he is."

Aides bristle at what they consider the media's relentless focus on Bush's personal and professional past. They say that out on the campaign trail, in visits to more than a dozen states, he has been doing exactly what he should.

"Interacting with people on the road who deal with real issues . . . that's what brings true joy to Jeb," Sally Bradshaw, a longtime consultant, said in a recent e-mail.

Bush started with an aggressive series of steps late last year and early this year — a kind of "shock and awe" entry that caught fellow contenders by surprise. The moves were designed to send an unambiguous cue to fundraisers and party activists and to reinforce a natural advantage Bush had with establishment donors.

At the same time, Bush's inner circle operated on the theory that there was little that could be gained by trying to speed up the political clock and that most voters in early states would not begin paying attention until later in the year.

Bush revived a 650-member alumni network of aides who worked for him as governor, and he recruited 21 veterans of his father's and brother's administrations to advise him on foreign policy. He hired state directors in the first four early states, aides for outreach to evangelical Christians and Hispanics, and a spokeswoman dedicated to fielding questions from the Spanish-language press.

As Bush travels the country, he has fielded more than 900 questions from donors, reporters and voters, according to aides. He has maintained a busy schedule that stretches from the early-voting states of Iowa, New Hampshire, South Carolina and Nevada — where conservative Republicans remain skeptical — to places visited less frequently at this early stage by presidential candidates, including Denver, Seattle and Puerto Rico.

Despite those efforts, some recent surveys put Bush in a five-way tie for the lead. Recent polls touted by his advisers give him a wide lead in New Hampshire, while others taken nationally and in the early states put him behind Rubio and Walker.

Sensing Bush's vulnerabilities, Ohio Gov. John Kasich this week hired two experienced GOP operatives as he prepares to jump into the contest and make a play for the same donors Bush has already wooed.

"I didn't think I was going to be back up here again, because frankly I thought Jeb was just going to suck all the air out of the room, and it just hasn't happened," Kasich told New Hampshire business leaders last week.

In a series of counter-terror raids, 15 suspected jihadis were arrested and two were killed in shootouts with police in Belgium and France. The arrests and shootouts occurred as part of an effort to dismantle an active terror cell spanning both countries, with the intention of averting an imminent terrorist attack aimed at police officers and buildings in Belgium. The two gunmen killed in the shootout in Verviers, Belgium, were Belgian nationals and are believed to have belonged to a homegrown cell of jihadis that recently returned from Syria. The arrested suspects were found with ammunition, weapons, explosives, police uniforms, walkie-talkies, radios, mobile phones, and false documents, as well as a "significant amount of money." The operation was intended to dismantle a terrorist cell and its logistical network. There was no link between the events in Verviers and last week's terror attacks in Paris, but an atrocity on a similar scale was averted at the last minute. Several Jewish schools in Belgium have been closed amid warnings that they could be targets for Islamist militants, and cities across the country remain on a heightened state of alert. European authorities are on high alert for further potential terrorist attacks, with as many as 20 sleeper cells of between 120 and 180 people believed to be ready to strike in France, Germany, Belgium, and the Netherlands. Intelligence officials are trying to determine the nature of the wider threat and are monitoring groups of men who have returned from fighting in Syria. The threat is evolving, with cells controlled by a clear commander being replaced by "thousands of independent actors or semi-independent terrorist suspects" who are difficult to track. European security and law enforcement agencies need to cooperate more closely to foil every terror attack.

In southeastern Laos, a hydroelectric dam under construction by a joint venture led by South Korean companies, Thai, and Lao partners, has collapsed, leaving an unknown number of people dead and hundreds missing. The Xepian-Xe Nam Noy hydropower dam in Attapeu province collapsed on Monday evening, releasing large amounts of water that swept away houses, making more than 6,600 people homeless. The dam was still under construction, and the portion that collapsed was a "saddle dam," an auxiliary dam used to hold water beyond what is held by the main dam.

The accident has caused at least 19 deaths and left dozens missing. Boats have been brought in to help evacuate people as water levels rise, with reports that the flash flooding has left more than 6,000 people homeless in six villages in Laos. The Red Cross has staff and volunteers on the ground helping with the response to the disaster.

The $1.2 billion dam is part of a project by Xe-Pian-Xe Namnoy Power Company, a joint venture that also includes Thailand's Ratchaburi Electricity Generating Holding, South Korea's Korea Western Power, and the state-run Lao Holding State Enterprise. South Korea said 53 of its nationals were taking part in the construction and were evacuated in advance of the collapse.

Environmental groups have long voiced fears about hydropower ambitions in impoverished and landlocked Laos, with around 10 dams in operation, another 10 to 20 under construction, and dozens more in the planning stages. Concerns have been raised about the impact on the Mekong River, its flora and fauna, and the communities that depend on it for their livelihoods.

Rescue efforts are underway, and top government officials have rushed to the site. Public appeals have been launched for aid, and provincial authorities have issued a call for emergency aid, including clothing, food, drinking water, medicine, cash, and other items. The prime minister of Laos has suspended the planned monthly meeting of the government for August and led his Cabinet members and other senior officials to Sanamxay (district) to monitor rescue and relief efforts being made for flood victims.

Laos, one of the poorest countries in Asia, has transitioned from communism to a market economy but remains a single-party state where freedoms are limited. There is virtually no freedom of the press, and foreign reporters who visit operate under tight restrictions, limiting the flow of information. Electricity from several hydroelectric dams provides a large share of Laos' export earnings, with Thailand being a major buyer.

The 2019 Golden Globes nominations have been announced, with several surprises and snubs in both the TV and movie categories. On the TV side, NBC's The Good Place was finally honored for best comedy series, while Sacha Baron Cohen unexpectedly won best actor in a comedy for Showtime's Who Is America? The BBC/Netflix thriller Bodyguard received a nomination for best drama series, and Candice Bergen was nominated for CBS' Murphy Brown reboot. However, The Handmaid's Tale, Westworld, and Atlanta were all snubbed in the top categories, despite being on prediction lists. In the movie category, Sam Elliott was surprisingly omitted for his work in A Star is Born, while Mary Poppins Returns was snubbed in the best original song category. Ethan Hawke's performance in First Reformed was also overlooked, and Peter Farrelly and Adam McKay were criticized for their straightforward direction in Green Book and Vice. Other notable snubs include Ryan Gosling, Ryan Coogler, Ryan Reynolds, Chadwick Boseman, Michael B. Jordan, Clint Eastwood, The Grinch, Atlanta, A Quiet Place, Widows, Mamma Mia! Here We Go Again, Amandla Stenberg, Hugh Jackman, and Meryl Streep.

A Baltimore County police officer, Amy Caprio, was killed in a confrontation while responding to a call in Perry Hall, Maryland, on May 21, 2018. The incident occurred during an afternoon call regarding a suspicious vehicle. The officer, who was a four-year veteran of the force, was pronounced dead at MedStar Franklin Square Hospital Center. A 16-year-old suspect, Dawnta Anthony Harris, has been charged with her murder, and three other suspects are still being sought. The enormous manhunt for the remaining suspects took place in a suburban community, where schools were placed on alert status for hours. The officer's body was taken to the Medical Examiner's office for autopsy, and her identity will not be released until after the autopsy and body camera footage review. The officer's family, friends, and colleagues mourned her death, and Governor Larry Hogan offered condolences. The officer's body camera footage will be reviewed to determine what happened during the confrontation. The cause of death has not yet been determined. The officer's death is the 11th to occur in the line of duty in Baltimore County since 1932.

In a groundbreaking study led by academics from the Universities of Nottingham and Bristol, the link between the breeding season and the hormone melatonin has been discovered for the first time. The research, published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS), reveals how animals link changes in seasons to their fertility.

The study found that melatonin, produced in the pineal gland during long winter nights, controls the production of two different types of a protein called vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) within a specific region of the pituitary gland. This region is separate from where sex hormones are made.

In winter, sheep make forms of VEGF that stop blood vessels growing. In summer, they make a different VEGF that makes vessels grow between the two areas of the pituitary. This allows VEGF to act as a messenger to control sex hormone-producing cells and fertility, marking the first time that the molecule linking long winter nights to sex hormones has been found.

The discovery could help farmers control when sheep start lambing, enabling them to respond to climate change. The findings also have wider implications for how animals, and potentially humans, use this system in health and disease.

The research team included Professor David Bates of the University of Nottingham, PhD student Dr Jennifer Castle-Miller, and Dr Domingo Tortonese of the University of Bristol. The paper, titled "Mechanisms Regulating Angiogenesis Underlie Seasonal Control of Pituitary Function," is published by PNAS and will be available on the PNAS website after the embargo has lifted.

The study has significant implications for the farming industry and is anticipated to have an impact in human medicine. The search for the missing link between the different parts of the pituitary has been going on for nearly 30 years. Knowing how this works could help farmers control when sheep start lambing, enabling them to respond to climate change. The findings also have wider implications for how animals, and potentially humans, use this system in health and disease.

President Barack Obama will not attend the funeral of Justice Antonin Scalia, who passed away on Saturday at the age of 79. Instead, Obama will pay his respects on Friday when Scalia's body lies in repose at the Supreme Court building. Vice President Joe Biden will attend the funeral at the Basilica of the National Shrine of the Immaculate Conception.

Obama has faced criticism for not attending the funeral, with some viewing it as a partisan snub. However, the White House has clarified that the president will pay his respects at the Supreme Court on Friday, and he believes it is important to honor Scalia's life and service.

There is no substantial historic precedent for presidents attending the funerals of sitting justices, with the last justice to die in office being Robert H. Jackson in 1954. President George W. Bush not only attended but also eulogized Supreme Court Chief Justice William Rehnquist in 2005.

Scalia's death has opened a political seam, with Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell calling for Scalia's replacement to be delayed until the next president is in office. Obama has announced his intent to nominate a fair-minded legal heavyweight to replace Scalia, but has not yet tipped his hand as to top candidates or whether he will consider a moderate who could be palatable to the Republican-controlled Senate.

Some Republicans have signaled they are open to at least holding hearings, if not also allowing a confirmation vote. However, Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell is still making hay of the Senate's oppositional force, penning a letter to donors that said, "Senate Republicans have made a commitment to ensuring that the American people have a voice in the selection of the next Supreme Court Justice."

The optics of paying his respects to Scalia are tricky for Obama, who would have been the subject of constant cutaways to his reactions and interactions with members of Congress during the funeral, distracting from memorials for the giant of American legal thought. Obama has taken pains to show reverence for Scalia, even as he urged Republicans to keep an open mind about a replacement.
