The study published in the journal Science has found that Neanderthal DNA, inherited by people of Eurasian origin, has a subtle but significant impact on modern human biology. The research, led by John Capra from Vanderbilt University, compared Neanderthal DNA in the genomes of a significant population of adults of European ancestry with their clinical records.

The study confirmed that Neanderthal DNA influences a wide range of traits, including immunological, dermatological, neurological, psychiatric, and reproductive diseases. Some of the associations discovered confirm previous hypotheses, such as the influence of Neanderthal DNA on skin biology and the risk of developing sun-induced skin lesions.

There were also surprises, such as a specific bit of Neanderthal DNA significantly increasing the risk for nicotine addiction and a number of variants influencing the risk for depression, both positively and negatively. The researchers found a surprising number of snippets of Neanderthal DNA associated with psychiatric and neurological effects.

The pattern of associations discovered suggests that today's population retains Neanderthal DNA that may have provided modern humans with adaptive advantages 40,000 years ago as they migrated into new non-African environments. However, many of these traits may no longer be advantageous in modern environments.

The researchers used a database containing 28,000 patients' anonymized electronic health records to make these discoveries. They plan to analyze other information contained in the medical records, such as lab tests, doctors' notes, and medical images, in a similar fashion.

The study was funded by the National Institute of Health and the National Human Genome Research Institute. The research establishes a new way to investigate questions about the effects of events in recent human evolution.

The Philae lander, which landed on Comet 67P/Churyumov–Gerasimenko as part of the Rosetta mission, has run out of power after a last-ditch attempt to move it into a sunnier spot came too late to charge its batteries and keep systems running. The lander had been receiving only 1.5 hours of sunlight instead of the expected 6-7 hours, due to its awkward orientation and surrounding rocks.

On Friday, mission controllers prepared to "hop" the robotic probe in an attempt to move it to a sunnier spot. Later that day, a message was posted on the lander's official Twitter account announcing that its rotation was successful and it appeared to be viewing a whole new comet from its new angle. However, it was soon announced that the lander would have to use up its last battery power in sending a final burst of data back to Earth before going into hibernation.

The lander's legs have a built-in spring action, and commands were uploaded on Friday night to fire them in an attempt to move the lander. Another strategy under discussion was to spin up an internal flywheel that could make Philae cartwheel out of its predicament, but this risked using up the last of its battery power.

Early on Saturday, it was announced that Philae was on the move and attempting to optimize its solar power. Despite the awkward landing, by Friday Stephan Ulamec, Philae lander manager, estimated that 80% of the science Esa was hoping for had been achieved. If the drilling operation succeeded in delivering samples to onboard instruments, it would rise to 90%, he said.

The COSAC (Cometary Sampling and Composition experiment) instrument was chosen to study the first samples rather than the UK-built PTOLEMY instrument, as COSAC uses less power and provides data that can be more easily compared to that taken from the Rosetta orbiter. PTOLEMY still generated data by working in "sniffing" mode.

Despite the lander shutting down for now, all might not be lost forever. The comet is currently out beyond the orbit of Mars, heading for its closest approach to the sun in August 2015. This will bring it as close to the sun as Earth's orbit, where the sunlight will be brighter and may just allow Philae to reboot and power up.

Philae made history on Wednesday when it was dropped by Esa's Rosetta satellite to the surface of 67P - the first time this feat has been achieved. The probe has been returning pictures and other scientific data ever since. It is not known precisely where on the comet the robot is located, but the pictures it has returned indicate it is in the shadow of a cliff. The limited sunlight the probe receives means its solar panels cannot keep the battery systems properly topped up. Engineers doubt Philae in its current position can stay powered beyond Saturday.

Harper Lee, the author of the Pulitzer Prize-winning novel "To Kill a Mockingbird", spent a crucial year writing the book in New York City, thanks to a generous gift from a New York couple, Joy and Michael Brown. In 1956, Lee was working as an airline reservations clerk and couldn't afford to take time off for the holidays. She spent Christmas Eve at the Browns' apartment, where she found an envelope with a year's salary as a gift, allowing her to focus on writing. The Browns' role in bringing "Mockingbird" to publication has been little known until now, as revealed in Mary McDonagh Murphy's documentary, "Hey Boo: Harper Lee & To Kill a Mockingbird".

Lee wrote about the evening in McCall's magazine after the book's publication in 1960, recalling the Brown's generosity and their faith in her work. However, the Browns have become reticent again due to a controversy over an as-yet-unpublished biography of Lee. Excitement spread when Penguin Press announced that "The Mockingbird Next Door" had been written by a former Chicago Tribune reporter with input from Lee. Lee made a statement through her 99-year-old sister Alice's law firm that she had not "willingly participated" with author Marja Mills. The matter is unresolved.

Michael Brown, a Broadway lyricist who performed in supper clubs around town, explained in the documentary that in 1949 he received a letter from his friend Truman Capote, asking him to look after Capote's childhood soulmate, Nelle Harper Lee, who had quit the University of Alabama to become a writer. Those first years in Manhattan were rough going, but Lee had an exceptional social life, following Capote around and gaining entree into the literary world.

"To Kill a Mockingbird" was published in 1960, and for nearly a half-century afterward, the Browns and Lee kept their secret. The Browns were astonished upon hearing what the book's original publisher, J. B. Lippincott & Company, planned for it in 1960, as they thought only 5,000 copies would be printed. However, the book's demand far exceeded the initial printing, with over 30 million copies sold worldwide. Lee, who is now 85 and suffered a stroke in 2007, made a statement through her sister's law firm that she had not willingly participated in the biography, creating controversy.

A 14-year-old Chilean girl named Valentina Maureira, suffering from cystic fibrosis, has made a plea for euthanasia in a video uploaded to her Facebook page. In the video, she expressed her desire to speak with President Michelle Bachelet and requested authorization for a lethal injection. Valentina's brother had previously passed away due to the same condition. Her father, Freddy Maureira, confirmed that she had undergone five surgeries, which caused her significant pain and suffering.

The video surprised her father and sparked a debate in Chile about euthanasia. However, the government spokesman, Alvaro Elizalde, ruled out euthanasia as an option, stating that current Chilean law does not allow for such a request to be granted.

Valentina Maureira is a patient at the Universidad Catolica clinic in Santiago, where a spokeswoman confirmed her hospitalization but stated that she was stable with no immediately life-threatening conditions. The health ministry is reportedly in contact with the family to ensure Valentina receives necessary psychological and medical treatment.

Euthanasia is illegal in Chile, much like in many other countries, and the Catholic Church holds significant influence over the society. Chile is one of the few countries that ban abortion under any circumstances. President Bachelet, who is in her second term, has introduced reforms, including a bill being debated in Congress that would relax the abortion law, but euthanasia has not been a part of her agenda.

Following the video's virality, President Bachelet visited Valentina on Saturday, sparking further debate about euthanasia in Chile. Valentina was diagnosed with cystic fibrosis at the age of 6 and has endured constant vomiting and headaches. Her family has already experienced the terminal nature of the disease with the death of her older brother.

Pete and Alisha Arnold, a tech-savvy couple from Minneapolis, have created a controversial website, Birthornot.com, where they are allowing the public to vote on whether they should have their unborn child or opt for an abortion. The couple, both 30 and married for 10 years, have been blogging about their pregnancy since September, posting health updates, ultrasound pictures, and videos. A poll on the site, hosted by PollDaddy.com, asks the question "Should We Give Birth or Have an Abortion?" with "Give Birth" currently receiving 46% of the vote and "Have an Abortion" at 54%. The poll will close on December 7th, and the couple plans to use the results to make their decision, although they maintain that the poll is not binding.

The Arnolds have stated that they are unsure about whether they are ready to be parents and have decided to ask the public for advice. They have experienced two miscarriages in the past year and a half, and during the second pregnancy, they purchased the birthornot.com domain. When Alisha became pregnant again a few months ago, they decided to launch the website.

Pete, who identifies as a Libertarian, views the majority-rule abortion as a civics lesson that brings the abortion debate home. However, critics argue that the vast majority of people who are pro-choice are not pro-abortion, and the poll may be skewed by trolls who want to upset pro-lifers. Some believe the Arnolds are attempting to gain media attention through an outrageous stunt, while others see it as a pro-life publicity stunt. Regardless of the motivation, many find the idea of using an Internet poll to decide the fate of an unborn child to be despicable and inappropriate.

The article, titled "Bill Ayers: Yeah, I wrote ‘Dreams from My Father’" was posted on March 28, 2011, by Allahpundit via the American Thinker. The article discusses Bill Ayers, a controversial figure known for his radical political activities, and his claim that he wrote former President Barack Obama's book "Dreams from My Father."

Ayers has a history of making this claim, particularly when approached by conservatives. In October 2009, a conservative blogger encountered Ayers at Reagan Airport and he unprompted offered to admit that he wrote the book and suggested splitting the royalties. When the blogger pointed out that she thought he had at least edited the book, Ayers continued to insist that he was the author.

The article suggests that Ayers enjoys mocking people who believe he ghostwrote the book, and that he likely makes this claim to see if listeners can detect the mockery. The author of the article believes that Ayers's response is a stock response whenever the book is mentioned in his presence. However, the article acknowledges that interpretations may vary.

The New York Times is reportedly preparing another attack piece on Brett Kavanaugh, this time focusing on a letter he wrote in the 1980s to organize a beach trip with classmates. The letter, which was shared among Georgetown Prep alumni as an example of Kavanaugh's organizational skills, details the plans for the trip, including the location, costs, and items to bring. The letter also includes inside jokes and references to alcohol and obnoxious behavior, as well as a note about inviting girls to the party. Classmates confirm that Kavanaugh organized the event, which was a popular tradition among students in the D.C. metro area. This is not the first time the Times has faced criticism for its coverage of Kavanaugh and his high school friendships, as a previous article scrutinizing inside jokes in the 1983 yearbook was found to be sourced to a political opponent of Kavanaugh. The Senate is currently awaiting the completion of a supplemental background check investigation before voting on Kavanaugh's confirmation to the Supreme Court.

President Barack Obama unveiled a $3.8 trillion budget proposal for the fiscal year 2013, aiming to cut $4 trillion from the deficit over the next decade through spending restraints and higher taxes on the wealthy. The budget emphasizes investments in infrastructure, education, and domestic manufacturing, while also proposing cuts to various programs to meet spending caps.

The budget proposes a six-year plan to spend $476 billion on surface transportation, a significant increase from current levels. However, it also includes cuts to many programs, with 210 places where programs will be cut or eliminated, resulting in savings of $24 billion in 2013 and $520 billion over a decade.

The budget also includes tax hikes of $1.5 trillion, primarily by allowing the Bush tax cuts to expire for high-income earners. The proposal also includes the Buffett Rule, a guideline to ensure that the wealthiest do not pay a lower overall tax rate than those who earn substantially less money.

However, the budget does little to address the long-term threat posed by entitlement programs such as Medicare and Social Security. The budget would cut more than $360 billion from Medicare, Medicaid, and other health programs over a decade, but this is a small fraction of the expected rapid expansion of costs for these programs.

The budget is a political document as much as a spending plan, setting Obama apart from Republicans who are opposed to higher taxes and believe the only way to cut government red ink is to slash the heavy burden of social programs. The budget is expected to intensify the deep partisan divisions that have kept Washington in gridlock since Republicans regained majority control of the House of Representatives in the 2010 election.

The budget request is just a starting point, and it's one that Congress can accept, reject, or modify. Even if Obama's budget is adopted, the estimates for deficit reduction may or may not pan out depending on how close to reality the administration's forecasts for unemployment, interest rates, and economic growth prove to be. The budget process involves no less than 40 congressional committees, 24 subcommittees, countless hearings, and a number of floor votes in the House and Senate. If all goes well, a formal federal budget for government agencies will be in place by Oct. 1, the start of the 2013 fiscal year.

The Texas Rangers are investigating an incident involving catcher Yorvit Torrealba, who allegedly struck an umpire in the face during a winter league game in Venezuela. The incident, captured in a viral video, shows Torrealba, playing for Leones del Caracas, pushing the umpire's facemask after a heated argument over a disputed strike call. Rangers general manager Jon Daniels stated that they are aware of the incident and will look into it, but the circumstances may determine any potential disciplinary action. Torrealba, entering the second year of a two-year contract with the Rangers, had a .273 batting average with seven home runs and 37 RBIs in the regular season, but his playing time diminished in the postseason. The incident has been widely criticized as an inexcusable and disappointing display of poor sportsmanship.

The Internet Archive is working on a project to archive web pages as they are created and preserve the pages they reference. This aims to maintain a link to the version of a page that was live when it was written, even if the page is later changed or removed. The goal is to fix broken links on the web and provide a link to the archived version of a page when the original link is broken.

Meanwhile, Allison Williams, the star of HBO's Girls, made her debut at 92Y in conversation with Seth Meyers. Williams discussed her role in Girls, her performance in Peter Pan Live!, and addressed the controversy surrounding her father, Brian Williams, who was suspended from NBC News for six months.

Williams defended her father during the Q&A, expressing support and trust in him despite the controversy. She spoke about her father's integrity and his care for journalism, and shared a personal story about how he had promised to attend a father-daughter dance when she was in ninth grade but was deployed in Iraq at the time.

Williams is best-known for her role as Marnie in Girls, which is currently in its fourth season. She has been involved in theater since a young age and honed her skills in improv comedy at Yale. Williams is trained in acting and singing.

The summary of the article provides an overview of the Internet Archive's web archiving project and Allison Williams' 92Y debut, where she discussed her career and addressed the controversy surrounding her father.

On Tuesday, a packed Aeromexico-operated Embraer jet crashed shortly after takeoff in Mexico's Durango state, resulting in 103 people on board, including two infants and four crew members, escaping before the plane was engulfed in flames. The crash occurred at around 4 p.m. local time, and while there were no fatalities, around 85 people suffered mostly light injuries.

Passenger Jackeline Flores reported that the plane crashed shortly after taking off in heavy rain. She and her daughter escaped from a hole in the fuselage as the aircraft filled up with smoke and flames. Durango Governor José Rosas Aispuro attributed the crash to a gust of wind that rocked the plane before it plunged suddenly, causing the left wing to hit the ground and two engines to break off.

The plane's pilot was the most severely injured but is reportedly in a stable condition. Among the passengers was Chicago-born priest Esequiel Sanchez of the Shrine of Our Lady of Guadalupe. The United States will send two people to assist the Mexican investigative team.

Aeromexico has not had any fatal crashes in the past 10 years. However, the Embraer 190, the model involved in Tuesday's incident, was previously involved in one fatal crash when a Henan Airlines flight overshot a Chinese runway in 2010 and another in Africa in 2013 during a hostage-taking incident.

Embraer has delivered more than 1,400 E-Jets, and Aeromexico leased the 10-year-old aircraft involved in Tuesday's incident from Republic Airlines in the United States in 2014. The aircraft, the serial number of which was 190-173, was delivered in May 2008.

The Mexican pilots association reported 66 accidents and 173 incidents in Mexican aviation last year, calling for more supervision of flying schools, more funds for maintenance, and oversight of fleets, and shorter flying hours for pilots. The cause of the crash is still under investigation, and it could take months to determine.

The Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) has come under criticism for live-tweeting the raid that led to the death of Osama Bin Laden, the leader of al-Qaeda, five years after the event occurred. The tweets, which began at 1:25 pm EDT and ended at 7:01 pm, provided a minute-by-minute account of the mission, including details such as the approval of the operation, the departure of helicopters, and the eventual killing of Bin Laden. The decision to tweet the account was made to mark the fifth anniversary of the raid and to remind the public of the CIA's role in the historic operation. However, the tweets prompted an outpouring of criticism on Twitter, with many users calling the move "grotesque and embarrassing." Some users posted memes and gifs of people rolling their eyes and putting their heads in their hands. The tweets also prompted more supportive responses, with some users praising the CIA for their transparency. Bin Laden, who was thought to have ordered the 9/11 attacks on New York and Washington, was shot dead at a compound in Abbottabad, Pakistan in May 2011 after evading capture by the US and its allies for nearly a decade. Speaking on the fifth anniversary of his death, CIA director John Brennan said the United States had destroyed a large part of al-Qaeda but "it's not completely eliminated, so we have to stay focused on what it can do." He also discussed the importance of removing Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi, head of the so-called Islamic State (IS), as a key focus for the CIA. The tweets have sparked a social media backlash, with many users questioning the CIA's decision to relive the event in such a public manner.

Bryan Singer, the director of the upcoming Queen biopic 'Bohemian Rhapsody', has been fired by 20th Century Fox due to his prolonged absences from the set and clashes with lead actor Rami Malek. The studio initially cited Singer's "unexpected unavailability" as the reason for halting production on Dec. 1. However, Singer claims he was terminated because Fox would not let him tend to a gravely ill parent and his own health.

Trouble began when Singer went missing during production on several occasions, resulting in cinematographer Newton Thomas Sigel having to step in to helm some of the days while Singer was absent. Actor Tom Hollander, who plays Queen manager Jim Beach, is said to have briefly quit the film due to Singer's behavior but was persuaded to return.

Malek complained to the studio, charging Singer with not being present on set, unreliability, and unprofessionalism. Singer had been warned before production began by Fox Film chairman and CEO Stacey Snider and Fox Film vice chairman and president of production Emma Watts that they wouldn't tolerate any unprofessional behavior on his part. A representative from the Directors Guild of America also arrived on set to monitor the situation.

The growing tension led to a confrontation between Singer and Malek, which, while it did not become physical, did involve Singer throwing an object. Subsequently, however, the two are said to have settled their differences, and filming was expected to resume.

But then Singer did not return to the set after the Thanksgiving break and is believed to have been in the U.S. for about the last 10 days, according to one source. In his absence, Sigel stepped in to helm several days of shooting before the production was shut down. Singer's prolonged absence was the final straw, and so the studio decided to terminate him under his pay-or-play contract.

Singer has claimed he is suffering from post-traumatic stress disorder because of the tensions on the set. In his statement, Singer said, "Rumors that my unexpected departure from the film was sparked by a dispute I had with Rami Malek are not true. While, at times, we did have creative differences on set, Rami and I successfully put those differences behind us and continued to work on the film together until just prior to Thanksgiving."

The studio, which has about two more weeks of principal photography remaining on the film, is expected to name a new director within the next few days.

In a controversial statement, Donald Trump's lawyer, Michael Cohen, claimed that it is legally impossible for a spouse to rape another spouse. The statement was made in response to a decades-old allegation that Trump had forced himself upon his then-wife, Ivana. Cohen's remarks were met with outrage and criticism, with many pointing out that marital rape was illegal in New York in 1984, the year the alleged incident occurred. Cohen's aggressive behavior towards reporters who asked about the allegation, including threats of legal action and personal attacks, further fueled the controversy. The Trump campaign has since distanced itself from Cohen's comments, with a spokesperson claiming that the incident was "old news" and never happened. Ivana Trump herself has since released a statement denying the allegations and expressing her support for her ex-husband's presidential campaign. The incident has once again brought attention to the issue of sexual assault and the treatment of women in politics.

The Internet Archive is working on a project to preserve and archive web pages, aiming to fix broken links on the internet. This includes crawling supported websites under the "No More 404" initiative. In a related news, historians in Poland have published the most comprehensive list of Nazi SS commanders and guards at the Auschwitz concentration camp. The list, compiled by historian Aleksander Lasik, contains over 8,500 entries and is based on data from various international archives. The goal is to bring justice to as many of the Auschwitz guards as possible, with estimates suggesting that up to 200 former guards could still be living. The list, available in Polish, English, and German, includes details such as date and place of birth, nationality, education, military service, and party affiliation. The entry for Rudolf Hoess, the camp's commander from 1940-43, includes a photocopy of his death sentence. Nazi hunter Efraim Zuroff has praised the publication of the names, stating it has practical implications for Nazi crime investigators in Germany. The list is not complete, and Lasik continues his search. The project aims to preserve historical records and bring justice to victims of the Holocaust.

The shooting of Walter Scott, a 50-year-old black man, by North Charleston police officer Michael Thomas Slager has resulted in Slager's firing and murder charges. The incident was recorded by a bystander, showing Slager firing eight shots at Scott as he ran away. The video was released to the media on Tuesday, the same day Slager was charged. The shooting has sparked protests in North Charleston, led by the Black Lives Matter group, and has raised questions about police use of force and racial profiling. The shooting comes amid a plunge in trust between law enforcement and minorities after the officer-involved killings of Michael Brown in Ferguson, Missouri, and Eric Garner on Staten Island, New York. The FBI and the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division are investigating the shooting. Slager, a five-year veteran with the North Charleston police, appeared without a lawyer at his first appearance and was denied bond, facing 30 years to life in prison if convicted of murder. The shooting has also led to calls for body cameras to be worn by every officer on the North Charleston force. The city has purchased 150 body cameras to complement the 101 cameras it had already ordered through a state grant. The mayor has also vowed to start a community discussion about police policies this spring. The shooting has been widely condemned, with the mayor and police chief both expressing their condolences to the Scott family and promising a full investigation. The video of the shooting has been described as "the most horrible thing" by the slain man's mother, and as "heartbreaking" by a former police chief. The shooting has also led to calls for police reform and for the justice system to work more effectively in cases involving police use of force.

On January 8, 2014, a U.S. military helicopter carrying live ammunition crashed into a nature reserve on the east coast of England, killing four American airmen. The Air Force HH-60 Pave-Hawk helicopter was practicing flying at low altitudes when it went down, near the village of Cley in Norfolk. The airmen were identified as Capt. Christopher S. Stover, Capt. Sean M. Ruane, Tech. Sgt. Dale E. Mathews, and Staff Sgt. Afton M. Ponce. The crash site was cordoned off due to scattered live ammunition, and British police took jurisdiction over the investigation. The bodies were removed from the scene after a daylight assessment by the British coroner. The commander of the 48th Fighter Wing, Colonel Kyle Robinson, paid tribute to the fallen airmen and thanked the British people for their support. The helicopter was assigned to RAF Lakenheath, the British base that is also home to the U.S. Air Force's 48th Fighter Wing.

The article critiques the current state of corporate publishing, using Lena Dunham's $3.7 million book deal with Random House as an example. The author, a former employee of Random House, argues that the publishing industry has become corporate, bottom-line driven, and reactionary, prioritizing big deals over nurturing talent and literary value. The Dunham deal is seen as a search for the next big thing, similar to Tina Fey's successful book "Bossypants."

The author acknowledges that Dunham is a target due to her youth, family background, and success in the entertainment industry, but also points out an element of sexism in the backlash against her large advance. The author supports Dunham's agent for securing a good deal for her client in a competitive market.

The article then compares the current publishing landscape to the approach of Barney Rosset, the founder of Evergreen Review and Grove Press, who was known for publishing groundbreaking authors and paying them small advances. The author argues that a more selective and risk-taking approach, similar to Rosset's, could lead to the discovery of new literary talents and cultural touchstones.

The article also mentions the success of small publishers like Bellevue Literary, Graywolf, McSweeneys, and others, who are winning awards and cultural relevance. However, the author notes that there are pockets of risk-taking within the major publishers as well.

The article concludes by expressing concern that the corporate publishers' focus on big deals and short-term profits is leading to a loss of cultural relevance and potential solvency. The author suggests that a more selective and long-term approach could lead to the discovery of new literary talents and the publication of enduring works.

Pope Francis, during his weekly audience at St. Peter's Square, denounced a "culture of waste" in the increasingly consumerist world, stating that throwing away good food is equivalent to stealing from the poor and hungry. He emphasized that this is especially deplorable given the prevalence of hunger worldwide. The pontiff has been advocating for the Roman Catholic Church to defend the poor and practice greater austerity since taking office in March, and has also made several calls for global financial reform.

The United Nations World Environment Day was the focus of the audience, with Francis urging people to care for the environment and reduce waste. He added that cultivating and caring for creation is a responsibility given to each individual, and transforming the world into a habitable place for everyone is essential.

The Pope's speech was welcomed by Coldiretti, Italy's largest agricultural organization, who recognized the importance of farmers' contribution to agriculture and cultivation. It was also noted that around 1.3 billion tonnes of food are lost or wasted every year, according to the United Nations' food agency.

In his speech, Francis criticized the media for considering a 10-point drop in stock markets as a tragedy, while the death of homeless people on the streets is no longer considered news. He emphasized that human ecology and environmental ecology are interconnected.

In February 2016, Amanda Carpenter, a former communication director for Senator Ted Cruz, found herself trapped in an out-of-date elevator at Baltimore–Washington International Airport. In an attempt to seek help, she tweeted her predicament to her 90,000 followers. Seven months later, Amtrak, the company responsible for the elevator, responded to her original tweet, asking if she was still trapped, unaware that the initial tweet was from several months prior. Amtrak later clarified that someone had recently retweeted the call for help, bringing it back to their attention. After the incident gained attention, Amtrak offered Carpenter a free ride on its Acela service as a gesture of goodwill. The incident, while an honest mistake, sparked humor on the internet.

In the southern Brazilian city of Cascavel, a riot at a prison has resulted in the deaths of four inmates, with two decapitated and two pushed off a building. The riot, which began on Sunday morning, involved over 700 prisoners who were reportedly dissatisfied with the prison's management, food, and hygiene conditions. The rioters took over parts of the jail, ransacking and setting fire to much of it.

The riot broke out when warders delivering coffee to inmates were overpowered. Rival prison gangs are suspected of taking advantage of the chaos to settle scores, with the leaders of the rebellion holding at least two prison guards hostage. The authorities restarted negotiations with the rioters on Monday morning in an attempt to end the stand-off.

The prison, which has a capacity for 1,181 inmates, houses 1,140, with overcrowding being a significant issue. The prison guard union in Parana state has called for investment in the facility, stating that a lack of investment in the prison system is a major problem. The union also claimed that workers often have to use their own money to purchase necessary items for their jobs.

Brazil has the world's fourth-largest prison population, with half a million inmates in facilities meant to hold 300,000. Earlier this year, the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights called for an investigation into the high number of violent deaths in Brazil's prisons after previous riots at a jail in the north of the country left dozens of people dead. The authorities reached a deal with the rioting prisoners on Monday, with prisoners being transferred to another jail and the hostages being freed. However, the police still need to enter the jail to assess the damage and determine if there are more victims.

A Mount Sinai Hospital doctor, Dr. David Newman, was arrested and appeared in court on Tuesday on charges of sexually abusing two female patients while they were under his care. The 40-year-old doctor is accused of drugging and sexually abusing a 22-year-old woman in January, and another 22-year-old woman who claims she was groped during a chest exam in September. The initial sex assault allegations came from a woman who was being treated for a shoulder injury, and the second alleged victim came forward after the first story was reported.

Dr. Newman was ordered held on $150,000 bond, or $50,000 cash. He is a highly-regarded emergency room doctor and has no criminal record or claims of malpractice against him. Mount Sinai Hospital suspended him after the allegations surfaced.

The alleged victim from January kept her hospital gown and bedding as evidence, and police are awaiting lab results on the DNA found on her body. In court, an assistant district attorney said only nurses are given access to morphine, concluding that Newman must have had his own stash.

Mount Sinai employees were upset by the news, with one employee saying it's disappointing when people abuse their power or position. Police believe there may be more victims and are urging those patients to come forward.

In a separate report, it was revealed that Dr. Newman is also accused of ejaculating on a patient's face in another incident in September. The patient claimed she went to Mount Sinai suffering from a severe head cold and Newman's "treatment" included fondling her breast. Newman has yet to make any comment on the vile charges against him.

Dr. Newman is a prominent Manhattan doctor, an Iraq War veteran, and a published author. He is due back in court on February 23. Mount Sinai Hospital has confirmed that he remains on suspension as the investigation goes forward.

The Missouri Supreme Court has appointed Judge Roy L. Richter to take over Ferguson's municipal court to implement reforms following a highly critical report by the U.S. Department of Justice. The report, prompted by the fatal police shooting of Michael Brown, highlighted racial profiling, bigotry, and a profit-driven municipal court system in Ferguson, a predominantly black St. Louis suburb. The court system was found to function as a money-making enterprise, with fines and fees generating nearly one-quarter of the city's budget.

Judge Ronald J. Brockmeyer resigned, citing the need to promote public confidence and aid Ferguson's healing process. The city council held a closed-door meeting, and the city manager and mayor declined to comment. The new judge, Richter, will take charge on March 16, and the Supreme Court has assigned staff to aid him in reviewing Ferguson's municipal court practices.

The federal report also cited instances of favoritism in Ferguson's court system, with tickets being forgiven for officials and friends. The change in the court system has drawn mixed reactions, with some seeing it as a step towards rebuilding Ferguson, while others call for more radical changes, including the elimination of the police force, courts, and judges.

Missouri Governor Jay Nixon praised the Supreme Court's actions, and the first session under Richter saw some fines being lowered. The resignation of the court clerk and the firing of the former clerk are also part of the reforms. The reforms are not just limited to Ferguson, with the Supreme Court also examining statewide reforms.

In Emeryville's biotech corridor, food startup Ripple Foods is set to launch its pea-based milk products, funded by $15 million in venture capital. The company, co-founded by Adam Lowry and Neil Renninger, aims to disrupt the $2 billion plant-based dairy market, joining established brands like Almond Breeze and So Delicious.

Ripple's founders, who have backgrounds in climate science and sustainable product development, have developed a method to isolate proteins from split yellow peas, creating a high-protein, neutral-tasting substance. This substance is blended with water, sunflower oil, stabilizers, and flavoring to produce a variety of "milks" - plain, sweetened, vanilla, and chocolate. The result is a vegan drink containing 8 grams of protein, similar to cow's milk, and free of common allergens like soy and nuts.

Ripple also boasts lower sugar content and higher calcium content compared to cow's milk, with a serving providing 45% of daily calcium needs. The company emphasizes its environmental benefits, claiming its product uses 96% less water than almond milk and 98.5% less water than cow's milk. However, the current use of French-raised peas contributes to a carbon footprint similar to almond milk, which is expected to improve with the switch to U.S.-grown peas.

Ripple plans to launch its products in an unnamed national chain this month, with Bay Area stores to follow. The company is also working on an organic label and aims to source all ingredients from the U.S. by the end of 2016. With its unique technology and health and sustainability benefits, Ripple could potentially disrupt the plant-based dairy industry.

Thomas S. Monson, the 16th president of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, has died at the age of 90 after nine years in office. Monson, who spent over five decades in top church leadership councils, was a well-known figure to multiple generations of Mormons. He became a church apostle at the age of 36 and served as a counselor for three church presidents before assuming the role of the top leader in 2008.

Monson's presidency was marked by a low profile during a time of intense publicity for the church, including the 2008 and 2012 campaigns of Mormon Mitt Romney for President. Monson's most public acts were appearances at church conferences and devotionals, as well as dedications of church temples. He will be remembered for his emphasis on humanitarian work, leading the faith's involvement in the passage of a gay marriage ban in California in 2008, continuing the religion's push to be more transparent about its past, and lowering the minimum age for missionaries.

Monson was known for his warm, caring, and approachable leadership. He was known for dropping everything to make hospital visits to people in need, and his speeches at the faith's twice-yearly conferences often focused on parables of human struggles resolved through faith. He put an emphasis on the humanitarian ethic of Mormons, evidenced by his expansion of the church's disaster relief programs around the world.

The next president of the church is expected to be Russell M. Nelson, the next longest-tenured member of the church's governing Quorum of the Twelve Apostles. Monson's legacy will be tied to the religion's efforts to hold tight to its opposition of same-sex marriage while encouraging members to be more open and compassionate toward gays and lesbians as acceptance for LGBT people increased across the country.

Monson was a World War II veteran and served in the Navy. He earned a business degree at the University of Utah and a master's degree in business administration from the church-owned Brigham Young University. Before being tabbed to join the faith's church's governing Quorum of the Twelve Apostles, Monson worked for the church's secular businesses, primarily in advertising, printing, and publishing, including the Deseret Morning News.

Monson married Frances Beverly Johnson in 1948. The couple had three children, eight grandchildren, and 11 great-grandchildren. Frances died in 2013 at the age of 85. Throughout his life, Monson was an avid fisherman who also raised homing pigeons, specifically, roller pigeons who twirled as they flew. He was known for his love of show tunes, Boy Scouts, and the Utah Jazz.

Two sisters, Nazila Sharaf and Lida Sharaf, have pleaded not guilty to charges of child abuse and neglect in Alameda County Superior Court. The sisters, who are both pregnant, were arrested last week and are accused of endangering infants' lives by binding them too tightly in swaddling blankets at their Livermore preschool, Universal Preschool LLC. Authorities claim that the sisters used heavy-duty knots and sometimes threw blankets over the infants' faces, impairing their ability to move and breathe.

The sisters maintain that their swaddling methods were not abusive, but prosecutors argue that evidence shows otherwise. Doctors found no signs of injuries, but the sisters are being held at Santa Rita Jail on $340,000 bail each. The preschool has been closed following a surprise March 12 investigation that revealed improper swaddling techniques.

Lida Sharaf had previously lost a license to operate a preschool in 2010 due to a similar swaddling offense. The school is now closed, and parents of 19 infants have spoken with police during the investigation. The sisters' attorney stated that they are "greatly embarrassed" and "shaken" by the situation. Both women are in protective custody at Santa Rita Jail.

The investigation began after the Department of Social Services requested assistance in closing the center due to multiple licensing violations discovered during an unannounced visit on March 12. Swaddling is a common technique used on newborns, but it is prohibited by state licensing and is usually intended for newborns between 1 month and 2 months old. The case will likely trail the criminal proceedings, as the women have filed an appeal against the ban on working at any state-licensed child care facilities.

On June 27, 2012, assailants attacked the offices of Microsoft in Athens, Greece. The attackers drove a van through the front doors and set off an incendiary device, causing significant damage but no injuries. The van contained three inflammable gas canisters and five cans of gasoline. The attack occurred at about 1:45 AM, and at least two individuals wielding pistols and a machine gun kept security guards away.

Police are investigating the attack, but no group has claimed responsibility yet. The attack is part of a pattern of arson attacks against banks, foreign firms, and local politicians in Greece, which have become more frequent as the country battles high unemployment and a deepening recession exacerbated by austerity policies.

Microsoft has temporarily closed its office in Athens to assess the damage, which is estimated to be around €60,000. The attack follows a series of violent incidents in Greece, including a small bomb left on an empty subway train in Athens in February, which a far-left group claimed responsibility for. The growing public anger at the impact of austerity measures was reflected in two parliamentary elections in May and June, in which parties opposed to the terms of Greece's international bailout performed strongly.

In a significant turn of events, a judge in Los Angeles has overturned a $417 million jury award to a woman who claimed that her use of Johnson & Johnson's talc-based baby powder led to her developing ovarian cancer. The judge, Maren Nelson, ruled that there were errors and jury misconduct in the previous trial, and that the award for damages was excessive. The woman, Eva Echeverria, has since passed away, but her attorney has announced plans to appeal the decision.

Echeverria's lawsuit alleged that Johnson & Johnson failed to adequately warn consumers about the potential cancer risks associated with talcum powder. She used the product for feminine hygiene on a daily basis from the 1950s until 2016, and was diagnosed with ovarian cancer in 2007. Her attorney contended that documents showed that Johnson & Johnson knew about the risks of talc and ovarian cancer for three decades.

This ruling comes after a Missouri appeals court threw out a $72 million award to the family of an Alabama woman who died from ovarian cancer. The court ruled that Missouri was not the proper jurisdiction to hear the lawsuit, citing a U.S. Supreme Court ruling that placed limits on where injury lawsuits could be filed.

Johnson & Johnson has faced hundreds of lawsuits over the same allegations, with jury awards totaling hundreds of millions of dollars. However, a mistrial was declared in a Missouri state court in another lawsuit against the company that involved three plaintiffs, two from out of state.

Talc, a soft mineral widely used in personal care products, has been a subject of controversy due to conflicting research on its link to ovarian cancer. While most major health groups have said talc is harmless, some smaller studies have found a small link, and the International Agency for Research on Cancer classifies genital use of talc as "possibly carcinogenic."

Ovarian cancer accounts for about 22,000 of the 1.7 million new cases of cancer expected to be diagnosed in the U.S. this year. Risk factors for ovarian cancer include age, obesity, use of estrogen therapy after menopause, not having any children, certain genetic mutations, and a family history of breast or ovarian cancer.

The company has maintained that its products are safe, and has appealed all the awards against it. The fate of awards in similar cases remains uncertain, with the appeals court's decision potentially setting a precedent for future cases.

On Monday, August 14, 2017, a century-old statue of a Confederate soldier was toppled by protesters in Durham, North Carolina, during a rally against racism. The monument, which was dedicated in 1924, was pulled down using a rope and a ladder, with dozens of protesters cheering as it fell. After the statue was brought down, some protesters began kicking it, while others took pictures with it.

The protest was in response to a white nationalist rally held in Charlottesville, Virginia, over the weekend, where one woman was killed after a white nationalist drove his car into a group of peaceful counter-protesters. Although the violence in Virginia has prompted fresh talk by government officials about bringing down symbols of the Confederacy around the South, North Carolina has a law protecting them.

The Durham protest was attended by various groups, including members of the Triangle People’s Assembly, Workers World Party, Industrial Workers of the World, Democratic Socialists of America, and the antifa movement. Protesters chanted "No Trump! No KKK! No fascist USA!" and demanded that people fight racism in their communities and across the South.

After the statue was pulled down, protesters blocked traffic on East Main Street and continued to walk down the street, with police accompanying them. No arrests were made, and the line of protesters eventually returned to the old courthouse. Some protesters took photographs with the fallen statue, while others yelled at police officers standing on the steps of the old courthouse recording the event.

Democratic North Carolina Gov. Roy Cooper criticized the action, tweeting that "the racism and deadly violence in Charlottesville is unacceptable but there is a better way to remove these monuments." Durham County sent out a statement expressing their understanding of the unrest in the nation and community, particularly following the events in Charlottesville, and their commitment to ensuring Durham remains a community of excellence where all residents can live peacefully, grow, and thrive.

The protests, which began in December 2010, were fueled by anger over high unemployment, corruption, and repression. Al Jazeera's coverage of the unrest was credited with forging a sense of solidarity among the protesters, and social media platforms like Twitter were used to organize and spread information about the protests. The protesters targeted Ben Ali's second wife, Leila Trabelsi, and her family, who were accused of amassing conspicuous fortunes through corruption. The protests continued despite Ben Ali's attempts to placate the protesters, including firing his interior minister, pledging a corruption investigation, and promising new freedoms and a resignation at the end of his term in 2014. In the end, Ben Ali was forced to dismiss his entire cabinet and announce his resignation. The protests were significant not only for Tunisia but also for the region, as they were seen as a potential catalyst for change in other Arab countries.

Greece's banking stocks continued to plummet for a second day on Tuesday, causing the main Athens index to decline despite gains in non-financial sectors. The banking index lost over 29%, reaching its daily loss limit, as lenders struggle with recapitalization needs due to a flight of euros from deposits this year. However, the non-financial sector showed signs of recovery, with the blue chip retail sector up over 11% and other gainers including OPAP and Aegean Airlines. The gains suggest that investors are attracted by historically low valuations and that fears of further turmoil between Greece and its international lenders are primarily confined to banks. The main index lost around 16.2% on Monday, following a five-week shutdown as indebted Greece sought to maintain eurozone membership.

Greece is currently in bailout talks with its European Union partners, and a deal is expected to be concluded by August 18. However, the threat of political and economic instability remains high. The economy is projected to shrink by 2-4% this year, returning to the recession that plagued Greece for six years until 2014. A survey showed that Greek manufacturing activity plunged to a record low, and economic sentiment hit its lowest in almost three years in July.

Despite the ongoing crisis, U.S. investors have little to fear as their mutual funds typically have only a small percentage of their portfolios invested in Greek stocks. International stock funds and emerging-market stock funds are the most likely to have Greek investments, with an average of 0.5% and nearly 40% respectively. Even funds that don't specialize in foreign markets can have Greek holdings, such as those investing in master limited partnerships. Across all categories, the average amount is 0.3%, not including funds that are entirely clear of Greek stocks.

A gold-rush has commenced at a beach in Kent, England, following the burial of £10,000 worth of gold bars by German artist Michael Sailstorfer as part of the Folkestone Triennial arts festival. The 30 gold bars, hidden on Folkestone's Outer Harbour beach, are up for grabs once the tide recedes at 4pm on Thursday, with prospectors allowed to keep any bars they find. The Folkestone Digs project is one of several installations for the festival, which runs from August 30 to November 2 and features work by Yoko Ono and others.

Lewis Biggs, curator of the Folkestone Triennial, said the project is an artwork that has been kept secret due to the potential treasure hunt. He hopes the mass digging on the beach will create a work of art by forming sand castles. Biggs also raised questions about what people would do with any gold they found, suggesting it might be worth more as an artwork or kept as a collector's item.

The gold bars, of varying sizes and standard gold bullion marked "Made in London," could be worth several hundred pounds each. Biggs said the work aims to change the perception of public art, with temporary projects like Folkestone Digs having as much impact as more permanent installations.

The Folkestone Triennial is in its third edition and aims to revitalize the fading seaside town. This year, more than 20 artists have been commissioned, including Yoko Ono, Andy Goldsworthy, and Pablo Bronstein. The overall theme is Lookout, exploring ideas of looking at the town's past and envisioning its future.

The Berlin-based Sailstorfer, who chose not to be present for the gold rush, has previously created artworks that change people's perception of a place. For example, he collected fallen autumn leaves, painted them green, and reattached them to a tree to make it look like spring.

Safety measures are in place for the gold rush, and metal washers have also been buried to confuse those using metal detectors. The Folkestone Triennial has gained international attention, with artists and visitors engaging with the town's history to envision its future.

The incident serves as a reminder of the importance of safety and respecting restricted areas when visiting popular tourist destinations.

The state's shift towards conservative Republicans makes it easier to criticize Democrats like Sen. Mark Pryor, but the state's Republican legislature's implementation of a "private option" for Medicaid expansion has divided the Tea Party and the Chamber of Commerce, preventing a unified Obamacare rebellion.

Washington state has become the third state to approve same-sex marriage by popular vote, following Maine and Maryland. The victory was narrow, with 52% of the vote in favor of Referendum 74, which upholds the state's new same-sex marriage law. The law was signed by Governor Chris Gregoire in February but has been on hold pending the election's outcome.

The campaign for Referendum 74 was led by Washington United for Marriage, which outraised its opponents by a significant margin, with contributions from big names like Amazon.com CEO Jeff Bezos, Microsoft Corp. co-founder Bill Gates, and New York Mayor Michael Bloomberg. Opponents of gay marriage raised just $2.7 million.

The measure was losing in 31 of the state's 39 counties, but it had its strongest lead in King County, which holds about a third of the state's voters and is home to Seattle. Gay couples in Washington could start picking up their marriage certificates and licenses from county auditor offices on December 6, a day after the election is certified.

The path to gay marriage in Washington state began several years ago. In 2006, a state Supreme Court ruling upheld a 1998 law banning same-sex marriage. However, a gay civil rights measure passed in 2007, signaling a change of mindset in the Legislature. The state's first domestic partnership law passed in 2007, and the law allowing gay marriage was passed this year.

The victory in Washington state is significant because it marks the first time that gay marriage has won a statewide vote anywhere in America. It also means that six other states and the District of Columbia already allow gay marriage, and Maryland, Maine, and Washington are the first to approve it by public vote. The other states' laws were enacted either by lawmakers or court rulings.

The anti-gay rights National Organization for Marriage had a string of successes until Tuesday, including California's Prop. 8 and Maine's earlier rejection of marriage equality. However, opponents of gay marriage "significantly outperformed the Republican ticket in nearly every state," according to NOM president Brian Brown.

The victory in Washington state is being celebrated by gay rights activists, who see it as a step forward in the fight for marriage equality. Supporters of Referendum 74 were giddy even before Wednesday's vote totals confirmed its victory, with Democratic gubernatorial candidate Jay Inslee describing it as "a grand step forward in the arc of the moral universe."

The great-niece of the late singer Johnny Cash, Courtney Cash, was found stabbed to death and stuffed in a box at her home in Cookeville, Tennessee. The incident occurred on Wednesday morning, and her boyfriend, William Austin Johnson, was found with multiple stab wounds and is currently being treated at Vanderbilt University Medical Center in Nashville. Courtney Cash's body was discovered in a chest just inside the front door of the house. The suspect, Wayne Gary Masciarella, has been charged with first-degree murder. The altercation that led to the stabbings is believed to have taken place in the house where Johnson and Cash lived with their young child. Masciarella is being held without bond and is due in court on April 21. The motive for the murder is suspected to be drug-related. Tommy Cash, Johnny Cash's brother, issued a statement asking for prayers for the family following the loss of his granddaughter.

The city's Executive Director Michael Ryan cited security as a reason for keeping voting materials under lock and key before Election Day, but election expert Tammy Patrick suggested that setting up early would allow for the identification and resolution of issues such as misdelivered materials, missing signs, pen shortages, and absent poll workers.
