The biggest of these alliances is Electionland, a project involving over 400 newsrooms across the country. Participating reporters and editors are connected to an online platform that shares real-time data and tips on everything from long lines and voter intimidation to hoax tweets. The project aims to provide no-strings-attached data, technology, and information to help journalists cover one of the most challenging days of their year.

While some major media outlets declined invitations to join Electionland, it was a no-brainer for many local outlets struggling with layoffs and budget cuts. The project has already led to several stories, including one about poll workers in Harris County, Texas, giving voters incomplete instructions about photo identification, and the debunking of internet hoaxes about stuffed ballot boxes and immigration officers arresting voters.

The collaboration among journalists is historic given the competition among newsrooms, but it may expose them to heightened scrutiny from critics in Trump's camp who may interpret their work as collusion. Despite this, many news organizations will make election integrity issues a central part of their coverage plans, given accusations of Russian cyber espionage and Trump's allegations of vote tampering and rigging.

Additionally, a new startup called Votecastr aims to publish detailed projections on Election Day based on real-time turnout figures and pre-polling surveys on voting preferences. The project will be pulling information from about 700 precincts in eight key battleground states and publishing on Slate, with a live video stream available on Vice Media. Sasha Issenberg, one of the founding partners of the project, hopes that it will be a generator of leads and hypotheses for reporters to chase.

The article discusses two separate but related topics: the donation of crawl data by Alexa Internet to the Internet Archive and a study on the link between low intelligence and the appreciation of pseudo-profound, intellectual-sounding statements, often referred to as "bulls***."

Since 1996, Alexa Internet has been donating their daily crawl data to the Internet Archive, which is added to the Wayback Machine after an embargo period.

In a study titled 'On the reception and detection of pseudo-profound bulls***,' researchers from the University of Waterloo in Ontario, Canada, found a correlation between being impressed by such statements and low intelligence. The study, which uses the term "bulls***" over 200 times, tested hundreds of people to determine this link.

Pseudo-profound statements are grand-sounding but meaningless, often found on social media platforms like Instagram. An example given is: "Hidden meaning transforms unparalleled abstract beauty." The study explains that these statements may seem profound but are merely collections of buzzwords without adequate meaning or truth.

Researchers used a website that generates pseudo-profound sentences to test participants, who were asked to rate the profundity of these sentences. Most participants struggled to differentiate between these made-up quotes and actual philosophy quotes or tweets from Deepak Chopra, a writer.

The study also found that those who were more receptive to pseudo-profound statements were less reflective, had lower cognitive ability, were more prone to ontological confusions and conspiratorial ideation, and were more likely to hold religious and paranormal beliefs, as well as endorse complementary and alternative medicine.

In summary, the article discusses the donation of data by Alexa Internet to the Internet Archive and a study that links the appreciation of meaningless, intellectual-sounding statements to low intelligence, less reflection, and other personality traits.

The United States has apologized for a deadly airstrike on a hospital run by Doctors Without Borders (MSF) in Kunduz, Afghanistan, which killed 22 people, including 12 MSF staff. President Barack Obama called MSF's president, Joanne Liu, to express his condolences and apologize for the incident. However, MSF is pushing for an independent investigation by the International Humanitarian Fact-Finding Commission (IHFFC), a panel created under the Geneva Conventions, to establish what happened in Kunduz, how it happened, and why it happened. The IHFFC requires the consent of the parties involved, and neither the United States nor Afghanistan recognizes the commission. MSF has condemned the attack, which it calls a war crime, and has demanded an independent investigation to gather facts and evidence from the United States, NATO, and Afghanistan, as well as testimony from MSF staff and patients who survived. The White House has said that a U.S. investigation would provide a transparent, thorough, and objective accounting of the facts and circumstances of the incident, and that Obama would implement changes to prevent similar tragedies from occurring in the future. The United Nations has condemned the attack but has not yet decided whether to support an independent probe.

In the aftermath of the Boston Marathon bombings, the city is grappling with the identification of three victims, including an 8-year-old boy named Martin Richard from Dorchester. Martin was killed, and his mother and sister were injured in the explosions. Hundreds attended a vigil for Martin at Garvey Park in Dorchester. Martin's father, Bill Richard, released a statement expressing his grief and asking for privacy. Martin was at the race to watch his father, a community leader in Dorchester.

In another tragedy, Krystle Campbell, a 29-year-old restaurant manager from Medford, was also killed in the bombings. Her parents were initially told that she had survived, but later learned she was dead in a hospital mix-up. Krystle was waiting near the finish line to cheer on a friend who was running.

The third victim was a Boston University graduate student from China who was watching the race with two friends near the finish line. The student's name and gender have not been released pending family approval. One friend was injured and listed in stable condition at a Boston hospital, while the other friend was not hurt.

Across the city, the Salvation Army provided food, drinks, and emotional and spiritual care. The First Corps of Cadets Armory in downtown Boston became a staging area for runners looking for their gear bags, trying to find lost phones and passports, or trying to make travel arrangements.

The blasts occurred just before 3 p.m., just hours after Ethiopia's Lelisa Desisa won the 26.2-mile race. Bloodied spectators were carried to a medical tent intended for runners. Organizers stopped the race and locked down the marathon headquarters. The Federal Aviation Administration announced a temporary flight restriction over Boston.

President Obama praised first responders and others who helped the injured. "If you want to know who we are, what America is, how we respond to evil, that's it: selflessly, compassionately, unafraid," he said. The president will travel to the city on Thursday for an interfaith service.

Pope Francis also sent a message of condolence, expressing his grief and offering prayers for the victims and their families. He called for unity in the face of evil and a determination to build a more just, free, and secure society.

Boston District Attorney Daniel Conley said that moments like this define who the city is. He praised the city's response to the bombings, noting its strength, compassion, and determination to see justice done.

In the aftermath of the bombings, FBI officials have promised to "go to the ends of the Earth" to find whoever is responsible. They have also assured the public that there are no known additional threats. The city is working to heal and move forward, with significantly enhanced security at bus and train stations and airports. Boston's Mayor Thomas Menino has promised that the city will not be intimidated by terror.

In an update on December 15, 2016, it was revealed that five of the seven bullets fired by Officer Selman hit 73-year-old Francisco Serna, with at least one bullet passing through him. Three bullets also hit a neighbor's home. On December 14, the Kern County Sheriff's Office confirmed that Serna's cause of death was multiple gunshot wounds, and the manner of death was a homicide.

On the morning of December 12, Bakersfield Police shot and killed Serna, who was reportedly brandishing a gun. However, no gun was found at the scene, and it remains unclear if Serna was holding anything when he was shot. The family claims that Serna was suffering from early stages of dementia and had police called to his home several times without incident.

The family also stated that Serna was lying naked in the driveway, but he was covered in a yellow tarp until the crime lab photographer arrived. The coroner's officer later cut Serna's clothes off to search him, according to the family. An autopsy was performed on December 14.

The officers involved in the shooting have been placed on administrative leave, and the incident remains under investigation. Serna leaves behind five children, 16 grandchildren, and five great-grandchildren. He had worked at a cotton gin in California's Central Valley until retiring about a dozen years ago. His son stated that Serna did not own a gun and that he was a peaceful, unarmed elderly man.

A proposed bill in Washington state aims to allow licensed gun owners to bring firearms into stadiums, including the Seattle Mariners’ Safeco Field and CenturyLink Field, home of the Seattle Seahawks and MLS's Seattle Sounders. The bill, House Bill 1015, would prevent stadium operators from banning guns from stadiums on public land. The NFL has expressed opposition to the bill, citing its policy against carrying weapons into stadiums. The bill is likely to face strong opposition, particularly in Washington's Democratic-leaning state. If passed, the law would allow licensed gun owners to bring firearms into stadiums, raising concerns about fan safety and potential violence, especially considering the presence of alcohol and passionate sports fans. The logistics of bringing a pistol into a stadium legally would be complex, given current restrictions on items allowed into NFL games.

Florida Governor Jeb Bush, a potential 2016 Republican presidential candidate, has published over 250,000 emails he received during his time as governor of Florida. The emails, which are easily searchable by date, contain both the content of messages and the email addresses of the people who wrote to him. The publication of these emails has raised concerns about privacy, as many of the emails contain personal information such as full names, home addresses, phone numbers, and social security numbers.

Some of the emails contain sensitive information about government operations, and some include personal appeals from citizens with medical or employment issues. One email, for example, contains information about a child with a life-threatening medical condition and the mother's name, home state and phone number, her social security number, and her healthcare identification number.

Florida's freedom of information laws are very broad, and social security numbers are protected under state law. However, it is unclear whether Bush or those who facilitated the publication of the records took any steps to redact potentially sensitive personal information from the emails.

The publication of these emails has been criticized as a breach in trust, as many of the people who wrote to Bush did not expect their emails to be released in such a public way. Some of the people whose emails are included in the publication have expressed embarrassment or concern about how they come across in the emails.

Jeb Bush's camp has not responded to requests for comment on the matter. It is unclear whether the personal information in the emails will be removed, and it is also unclear whether Bush or his team will take any steps to prevent similar incidents in the future.

"Baby Driver" is a high-octane action-comedy film directed by Edgar Wright, known for his Cornetto Trilogy. The movie stars Ansel Elgort as Baby, a skilled getaway driver with a love for music and chronic tinnitus. To drown out the constant ringing in his ears, Baby always wears earbuds, and the film's soundtrack is carefully synchronized with his movements.

The story revolves around Baby's work for crime boss Doc (Kevin Spacey), who hires him for various heists. Baby's crew includes characters like Bats (Jamie Foxx), Buddy (Jon Hamm), and Darling (Eiza Gonzalez). Baby falls in love with a sweet-faced waitress named Debora (Lily James), but his life becomes complicated when Doc sets up one more job.

The film is praised for its unique blend of action, humor, and music, with the action sequences being particularly well-timed and expertly executed. The performances are also noted as spectacular, with Jon Hamm's role receiving special mention for his bracing, nutty portrayal.

"Baby Driver" is set in Atlanta and has elements of a semi-fantastical folk tale, with familiar archetypes and classic conflicts. It has been compared to films like "Pulp Fiction" and "La La Land," and it pays homage to the works of Walter Hill.

The film received positive reviews, with critics praising its originality, dark humor, and energetic action sequences. It is considered one of the most entertaining thrill rides of the year and has been a passion project for director Edgar Wright.

The article discusses a year-long billing dispute between a Northern California man named Conal O'Rourke and Comcast, which ultimately led to O'Rourke being fired from his job at PriceWaterhouseCoopers (PWC) in San Jose. The dispute began in February 2013 when O'Rourke moved to a new place in San Jose and signed up for Comcast TV and Internet service.

O'Rourke noticed several issues with his first bill, including a misspelled name, charges for additional HD outlets and cable boxes he never activated, and the disappearance of premium channels after three months instead of the promised nine. O'Rourke attempted to resolve these issues by calling Comcast multiple times, but to no avail.

In October 2013, O'Rourke's Internet speeds dropped off, becoming "unworkable." He again contacted Comcast, but the company allegedly never addressed the problem. In December 2013, O'Rourke returned home to find several boxes at his doorstep containing equipment he did not order, along with a monthly bill for over $2,000.

O'Rourke took the equipment back to the same San Jose Comcast store and was given a service ticket, but when he discovered that he was Ticket #395 and the store was only on Ticket #251, he decided to return later in the day to ensure that someone would address his problems.

When O'Rourke returned to the store, a Comcast employee named Matt Doblias helped him, took back the equipment, and cleared the charges. However, the root of the errors persisted for months. O'Rourke provided Doblias with a detailed spreadsheet outlining the billing errors, but Doblias allegedly never followed up.

In January 2014, O'Rourke became frustrated and wrote a sarcastic letter recommending Doblias for Comcast's Employee of the Month award. The letter included lines like: "Their blatant disregard for the customer has made resolving my issues next to impossible."

Despite the letter, O'Rourke heard nothing and the billing errors continued, resulting in Comcast allegedly sending a collections agency after him. O'Rourke has since hired a local attorney and is threatening to file a lawsuit against Comcast if the company does not agree to his demands, which include a full retraction and apology, his re-employment with his former employer, and $100,312.50 by October 14.

The article includes pages and pages of Comcast invoices, a spreadsheet, photos, notes, business cards, and complaint letters that O'Rourke provided to Ars, which is the publication that the article was published in. The article also includes a listing image by Alyson Hurt.

The report published in the Journal of Medical Toxicology warns about the danger of a widely used dietary supplement, yohimbe tree bark extract, which is often taken for sexual enhancement. Between 2002-2012, at least 275,000 calls were made to poison control centers due to exposure to various dietary supplements, with yohimbe having the largest proportion of serious outcomes. Yohimbe can cause heart beat rhythm changes and kidney failure in children.

Yohimbe is an evergreen tree found in Africa, and its bark contains the chemical yohimbine, which is used to make medicine. It has been used for centuries as an aphrodisiac and to treat fever and leprosy, but its most popular use is for treating erectile dysfunction and low libido. However, there is scant evidence that it works.

As a dietary supplement, yohimbe is available in capsule, tablet, and tea forms. Since the dose range is narrow, its use is not recommended due to the risk of seizures and kidney failure. Even "safe" dosages can cause dizziness, nausea, insomnia, anxiety, a rise in blood pressure, and rapid heartbeat. Overdose can be fatal.

The study found that 78% of yohimbe exposures occurred in children, ages six or older, although most supplement exposures occur in children under six. Among reported exposures, 3.2% were admitted to a critical care unit for treatment, with one reported death. At least 1.3% of cases were serious and more than a quarter caused moderate harm.

The vast majority of exposures were unintentional. Henry Spiller, co-author of the study and director of the Central Ohio Poison Center at Nationwide Children Hospital, says the findings show the need for child-resistant packaging, caregiver education, and FDA regulation of yohimbe and other energy supplements.

The study also found that between 2005 and 2012, the rate of supplement-related calls to poison centers increased 49.3%. In the final year of data, the centers were getting calls at a rate of nearly 10 adverse exposures per 100,000 people. The majority of exposures were in children under six, and most were unintentional.

The authors of the study conclude that the FDA needs to do more to regulate yohimbe and energy products in the US, as was done successfully with ma huang products in 2004. They also recommend that parents keep dietary supplements out of reach of children and consider whether the potential benefit outweighs the risk of accidental ingestion.

A Michigan man named Kristopher Oswald was fired from his job at Walmart after he intervened to help a woman who was being assaulted in the store's parking lot. Oswald, who was on his lunch break, heard a woman screaming and a man hanging onto the hood of her car. He walked over to investigate and the man attacked him, punching him in the head while yelling "I'm going to kill you." Oswald was able to get on top of the man, but two other men then jumped him from behind. Livingston County Sheriff deputies arrived and stopped the fight. However, Walmart fired Oswald, citing a violation of company policy during his lunch break. Oswald had only been working at Walmart for seven weeks and had not yet completed his 180-day probation. Oswald says Walmart's policies against workplace violence do not allow for employees to assist in situations of imminent danger and self-defense. Walmart has not responded to requests for comment.

On March 22, 2014, a mudslide in Oso, Washington, resulted in the deaths of at least 16 people. Rescuers expanded their search on March 25, finding additional bodies in the debris. An interactive map and collection of stories and visuals were made available to provide a detailed view of the affected neighborhood, the lives of the victims, and the possible reasons for the disaster. Navy Cmdr. L. John Regelbrugge III, a 32-year veteran, was among the victims found on his shattered property on Steelhead Drive. His wife, Kris, a mother of five, was also found later. Officials believe they have located eight more bodies that have not been recovered. The number of those unaccounted for remains at 176, a figure officials are still trying to reduce by verifying names. The search has been challenging due to worsening weather conditions and difficult terrain. Teams from the Washington Army National Guard and Federal Emergency Management Agency have been aiding the search, using specially trained dogs and technologies such as sonar. The slide is likely to keep creeping, and it's unclear whether another large slide could follow. The disaster has been compared to other deadly natural disasters in the United States, such as the Hanukkah Eve Windstorm, Mount St. Helens eruption, Columbus Day Windstorm, Blizzard of 1950, Great Fire of 1910, Stevens Pass Avalanche, and the La Conchita mudslide in California.

The article discusses the false claim of "death panels" in the political discourse surrounding the Democratic health care reform proposals in 2009. The claim, made by Sarah Palin on her Facebook page, asserted that the government would set up boards to determine whether seniors and the disabled were worthy of care. The claim spread rapidly through various media outlets, talk shows, blogs, and town hall meetings, and was widely criticized as inaccurate and sensationalist.

The editors of PolitiFact.com, a fact-checking website, chose the "death panels" claim as their "Lie of the Year." In a national poll, nearly 61% of voters chose it as the biggest lie of the year from a field of eight finalists. The claim was found to be false by PolitiFact, as there were no mandatory counseling sessions or euthanasia provisions in the health care reform proposals.

Despite the fact-checking and criticism, some prominent Republicans continued to support the claim, including Sen. Charles Grassley and former House Speaker Newt Gingrich. Democrats responded by saying the accusation was untrue and highlighting the actual Medicare provision and what it said. The controversy touched a nerve of anxiety among seniors and was exploited by Republicans to mobilize opposition to the health care reform.

The controversy also raised concerns about the state of political discourse, with some experts saying that the episode suggests that political distortions need to be confronted faster and more forcefully. The episode also led to increased conversations about making end-of-life decisions and giving people more control over their care.

Sarah Palin has stood by her claim, stating that she sees the "death panels" as a metaphor for the potential rationing of health care under the Democratic health care reform proposals. She has continued to criticize the proposals and the use of the term "death panels" to describe them.

In this summary, the Army band members of the United States Army Band, "Pershing's Own," were chosen to stand in for President-elect Donald Trump and Melania Trump, Vice President-elect Mike Pence, and Karen Pence during the 2017 Inauguration Day dress rehearsal on January 15, 2017, in Washington. The band members were selected based on their height to match their counterparts, and they went through an audition process to secure their roles.

Sgt. Maj. Greg Lowery, who played the part of President-elect Donald Trump, said he aimed to "look the part as much as possible" and bought a red tie for the assignment. Army Spc. Sara Corry, who played the part of Melania Trump, is from Capistrano Beach, California.

The rehearsal aimed to practice events to ensure everything goes off as flawlessly and on time as possible for the real thing on Friday. The stand-ins will have to re-enact everything from the swearing-in to moving around with security detail.

The stand-ins understand the importance of their roles, as their actions could impact the safety of the people they're impersonating and how it airs to the world. MSG Neil Ewachiw, who played the role of Vice President-elect Mike Pence, said, "It's crucially important because the escorts to the President and First Lady will need to know their route."

The peaceful transfer of power is a keystone of American democracy, and the stand-ins are thrilled to be part of this historic event. M SGT Leigh Ann Hinton, who played the role of Karen Pence, said, "To take part in it, I just think it's thrilling."

The stand-ins are also aware that they need to dress the part on rehearsal day, and SPC Sara Corry said, "It's really going to be really fun to wear a nice pair of heels and have some camera time."

The Joint Task Force National Region is directing rehearsals, and the stand-ins have one chance to fix any kinks at the one and only dress rehearsal to be held this Sunday, Jan. 15th.

A homeless man with a violent criminal history, Bodio Hutchinson, was arrested for the unprovoked stabbing of two Boston park rangers on Boston Common, the nation's oldest public park. The 46-year-old ranger sergeant is in critical condition at Massachusetts General Hospital, while the 23-year-old ranger is in stable condition at Tufts Medical Center. Witnesses provided cellphone video and followed Hutchinson, leading to his arrest in the Public Garden. Hutchinson faces attempted murder charges, assaulting a police officer, and drug charges. The incident has prompted discussions about the need for more equipment and manpower to ensure the safety of the parks.

The western Indian state of Gujarat has passed a new law that makes the slaughter of cows punishable with life imprisonment, and transporting beef will result in a 10-year jail term. This makes Gujarat's laws the toughest in the country regarding cow protection. Offenders will also face heavy fines. The cow is considered sacred by India's Hindu majority, and killing cows is already illegal in many states. The new law is set to come into effect once approved by the state's governor.

In a separate incident, a Muslim man named Pehlu Khan died from injuries sustained after being brutally beaten by a mob in Rajasthan state, three days earlier. The mob accused him of transporting cows for slaughter. The men had bought the dairy cows at a cattle fair and were taking them home when the mob stopped them, pulled out the men, and beat them. No arrests have been made.

Since Prime Minister Narendra Modi took office in 2014, there has been a rise in the activities of self-styled Hindu cow-protection groups that stop trucks on highways and attack anyone transporting bovine animals. Rumors of beef eating by Muslims have sparked violence in several places in northern India.

These incidents highlight the sensitive issue of cow protection in India, as cows are considered sacred by the Hindu majority, and eating beef is taboo for many. The new law in Gujarat underscores the government's commitment to enforcing these cultural norms.

Facebook, a leading technology company, has recently unveiled its new search feature, Graph Search, at its Menlo Park headquarters. This new feature is designed to help users find content within their network of social connections without having to leave the site. With over one billion users and vast amounts of content, Facebook aims to make it easier for users to find relevant information based on their network. The search parameters focus on games, videos, pictures, and people.

Google, with its Search Plus Your World feature, is attempting a similar approach, but Facebook's one-billion-strong network gives it an advantage. This development could potentially impact companies like Yelp, Foursquare, and Path, which offer recommendation services based on user history. Facebook has partnered with Microsoft's Bing search engine to provide any web content not shared within the social network.

The new search feature is part of Facebook's ongoing efforts to build products that create utility for users, developers, and advertisers. Users can stay connected with friends and family, discover what's happening around the world, and share their interests. Developers can use the Facebook Platform to build applications and websites that integrate with Facebook, reaching its global network of users. Advertisers can engage with over 900 million monthly active users, targeting them based on information they have chosen to share with the company.

Recently, Facebook acquired Mobile Technologies, a developer of online applications, and Onavo Inc. In September 2013, Mail.Ru Group Limited sold its remaining shares in Facebook Inc. These acquisitions and the development of Graph Search demonstrate Facebook's commitment to innovation and growth. The new search feature is expected to enhance user experience by keeping them inside Facebook, reducing the need to leave the network for information.

A Good Samaritan named Derrick Deanda, who rescued a family from a crashed van in Elk Grove, California, in September 2015, has received a bill for a 'first responders fee' of $143. Deanda, who was driving by the scene, stopped to help a man standing inside the overturned van holding a two-year-old child. He broke the window to check on the passengers and sustained a small cut in the process. Paramedics arrived and checked Deanda over after attending to those inside the car.

Months later, Cosumnes Community Services District sent Deanda a bill for the 'first responders fee.' Deanda expressed his disappointment, stating, "I mean why would I want to stop to help somebody if I'm going to get a bill for $150?" On Facebook, he posted a picture of the bill and a scary image of the crashed van.

Deputy Chief Mike McLaughlin confirmed that his district billed Deanda, stating, "We're obligated to provide the same level of service, the same billing, the same everything, for every patient we encounter." However, McLaughlin also noted that this was a unique situation and expressed a desire to have the fee waived. The district implemented the fee two years ago to prevent fire station brownouts.

Deanda plans to appeal the bill and hopes the matter is resolved before it goes to collections. The incident has raised questions about the appropriateness of charging a Good Samaritan for their unselfish act of helping others.

The study published in the journal Nature reveals that Antarctica is shedding ice at an accelerating rate, with approximately 200 billion tonnes of ice being lost annually. This has resulted in a 0.6mm annual increase in global sea levels, a three-fold increase since 2012. The losses are predominantly occurring in the West of Antarctica, where warm waters are melting the fronts of glaciers that terminate in the ocean. The researchers, including Andrew Shepherd from the University of Leeds, used data from satellites that have been monitoring Antarctica since the early 1990s to compile their findings. The study incorporates 24 independent satellite assessments, providing a comprehensive look at what's happening to the world's vulnerable ice sheets in Antarctica and Greenland. The melting of Antarctica is expected to contribute about half a foot to sea level rise by the end of the century, making it a significant player in global sea-level rise. The study also found that East Antarctica is losing relatively little ice a year, with about 31 billion tonnes being lost since 2012. However, it is unclear whether this trend will continue, as it is likely due to natural variability rather than climate change. The study emphasizes the need for governments to take account of the accelerating trend in Antarctic ice loss as they plan future defences to protect low-lying coastal communities.

On January 27, 2016, Brittany Daniel, a 26-year-old woman from Fort Worth, was fatally shot during a suspected road-rage incident on Interstate 30 in Arlington. The shooting occurred between 6:45 and 7 p.m. as Daniel was driving home from work with a friend. According to a passenger who called the police, a man riding in the back of a car opened fire on Daniel, and the incident was described as road rage.

The gunman is described as a light-skinned black or Hispanic man in his mid-20s, sitting in the back of a small four-door sedan with tinted windows. The car is believed to be dark-colored. Police are asking for anyone who was driving on I-30 near Cooper Street between 6:45 and 7 p.m. on Wednesday and saw or knows something about the incident to come forward.

Brittany's father, Malcolm Daniel, is grieving along with his daughter's mother, four brothers, friends, and extended family. He expressed his desire to find the person responsible for his daughter's death and bring them to justice. The Arlington police are currently investigating the case and are asking for the public's help in solving it. Anonymous tips can be submitted to Tarrant County Crime Stoppers at 817-469-TIPS.

A France Telecom worker, aged 57, has reportedly committed suicide by setting himself on fire in a work car park. The employee, who had four children and had worked for the company for over 30 years, was reportedly unhappy about several transfers within the firm in recent years. This incident follows a series of suicides at France Telecom, with more than 30 reported cases in 2008 and 2009. The company, which employs 100,000 people and runs the major mobile provider Orange, has faced criticism for its handling of the crisis, leading to the resignation of its deputy CEO in October 2009.

In a separate incident, the former head of France Telecom, Didier Lombard, along with six other executives and the company Orange, are set to stand trial over alleged workplace bullying. They are accused of engaging in or assisting psychological harassment, following an April 2010 report from labour inspectors that found 19 employees took their own lives, 12 attempted suicide, and eight suffered from deep depression or were forced to stop work as a result. The trial is scheduled for the coming months.

The suicides at France Telecom have raised concerns about workplace conditions and the use of harsh restructuring methods such as forcing people into new jobs and giving unattainable performance objectives. The crime of "moral harassment" can be punished with two years in prison and 30,000 euros ($35,000) in fines.

If you or someone you know is experiencing emotional distress or suicidal thoughts, please call Samaritans for help on 116 123, or email jo@samaritans.org in the UK.

A former Indiana University (IU) student, John Enochs, has been sentenced to one year of probation and one day in jail after pleading guilty to battery with moderate bodily injury. The charges stem from two rape cases, one in April 2015 and another in 2013, that occurred at the Delta Tau Delta fraternity house.

In the most recent case, the victim, who had been drinking, claimed she was in the courtyard with friends when she went inside for the bathroom. She later woke up in a private room, naked, with an unknown man having sex with her. She was able to escape after being held down and suffering a laceration to her genitals.

In the 2013 case, authorities found DNA evidence and witness statements that led to Enochs' arrest. Rape is a level 3 felony in Indiana, which can carry up to 16 years in prison upon conviction. However, it's unclear why prosecutors settled for a probationary sentence, dropping the rape charges.

The decision has sparked outrage on social media, with users comparing Enochs' light sentence to that of former Stanford student Brock Turner, who was given a lenient sentence for sexual assault. Critics argue that Enochs' race may have played a role in the leniency of his sentence.

Indiana University Bloomington has faced criticism for its handling of sexual assault cases on campus, with three open Title IX complaints against it. The university spokesman confirmed that Enochs is no longer a student at the school.

The document provides a comprehensive history of the Apollo 11 mission, which marked the first time humans landed on the moon. It includes a series of photographs and captions that depict various stages of the mission, from the pre-launch preparations to the historic moon landing, and the subsequent return to Earth. The document also provides information about other Apollo missions, including Apollo 17, which was the last mission to visit the moon. Additionally, it discusses the challenges faced by astronauts in terms of personal hygiene and waste management in space, and the solutions that were developed to address these issues. The document also provides some context about the historical significance of the Apollo missions and their impact on society.

Pope Francis, the first Pope to visit South Korea in 25 years, arrived in Seoul on August 14, 2014, for a five-day trip aimed at spreading the faith on a continent where only 3% of the population is Catholic. The visit, which is his third abroad and the first papal trip to Asia since St. John Paul II went to India in 1999, includes meetings with bishops, South Korean President Park Geun-hye, and other government officials.

In his first speech, Francis called for renewed efforts to forge peace on the war-divided Korean Peninsula and for both sides to avoid "fruitless" criticisms and shows of force. The Pope's message of reconciliation came hours after North Korea fired five projectiles into the sea. Organizers of the pope's trip had invited a delegation of North Korean Catholics to attend his Aug. 18 Mass for peace and reconciliation at Seoul's main cathedral, but North Korean authorities declined the invitation.

The Pope's visit to South Korea is significant as the Catholic Church in the country has been growing steadily over the last half century and is seen as a model for the future. Local church officials hope for a continuing increase in believers in a country that once welcomed missionaries to help spread the faith but now sends its own priests and nuns abroad to evangelize in other countries.

During his visit, Francis will beatify 124 Korean martyrs who founded the church on the peninsula in the 18th century, hoping to give South Korea's vibrant and growing church new models for holiness and evangelization. The Pope will also attend a Catholic youth festival for young believers from around Asia and meet with some families of the South Korean ferry sinking in April.

The Pope's visit to South Korea is also significant as it includes a rare opportunity for an exchange between the Holy See and China, as Francis sent a telegram of greetings and prayers to Chinese President Xi Jinping on his way to South Korea. The Holy See and Beijing have no diplomatic relations, and this exchange furthers a low-key push for better ties with China and efforts to heal a rift between the Chinese authorities and those Catholics who worship outside the state-recognized church.

Overall, Pope Francis' visit to South Korea is a significant event for the Catholic Church in Asia, as it aims to spread the faith on a continent where only a small percentage of the population is Catholic. The Pope's message of peace and reconciliation, particularly in the context of the ongoing tension between North and South Korea, is a powerful one that resonates with many people in the region.

General Mills has initiated a nationwide recall of approximately 10 million pounds of flour, including products from the Gold Medal, Wondra, and Signature Kitchens brands, due to a potential contamination with E. coli O121. The recall was announced after an investigation by state and federal health authorities found that about half of the 38 individuals who fell ill reported making homemade food with flour, and some reported using a General Mills brand of flour. No deaths have been reported, but E. coli O121 can cause bloody diarrhea and dehydration, particularly among the elderly, young children, and people with weakened immune systems. The recall involves six SKUs of Gold Medal branded flour, two SKUs of Signature Kitchens branded flour, and one SKU of Gold Medal Wondra branded flour. Retailers that received shipments of the recalled flour include Safeway, Albertsons, Jewel, Shaws, Vons, United, Randalls, and Acme. General Mills has advised consumers never to eat raw dough or batter, and has set up a hotline and a web page for consumers to check if their flour is affected by the recall. This is the second significant recall for General Mills in less than a year, following a recall of gluten-free Cheerios and Honey Nut Cheerios in October 2015. Kashi Co, owned by General Mills' rival Kellogg Co, also announced a recall of one variety each of its granola and granola bars due to potential contamination with Listeria monocytogenes bacteria.

Taco Bell is under fire for a class action lawsuit alleging that their beef contains only 36% meat, with the rest being "extenders" and other non-meat substances. However, Taco Bell's President and Chief Concept Officer, Greg Creed, has released a statement claiming that the lawsuit is baseless and filled with inaccuracies. Creed states that Taco Bell's beef is 100% USDA inspected, slow-cooked, and simmered with proprietary seasonings and spices to provide the signature taste and texture. The seasoned beef recipe contains 88% USDA-inspected beef, 3-5% water, 3-5% spices, 3-5% oats, starch, sugar, yeast, citric acid, and other ingredients. Taco Bell plans to take legal action against the lawyers for making false statements about their products. The controversy highlights growing concerns about the quality and authenticity of food products in the market.

The Tamiment Library Economic and Social Justice Web Collection, initiated in 2010, archives web pages of organizations advocating for economic and social justice from a left and progressive perspective. The collection encompasses a wide range of issues such as corporate accountability, immigrant rights, unemployment, homelessness, urban justice, healthcare reform, wealth redistribution, and more. A significant portion of the collection focuses on the Occupy Wall Street Movement, a social movement that aims to reform both the private and public sectors, established in New York City in September 2011.

The collection includes various media types like YouTube videos, PDFs, blog postings, petitions, news feeds, audio, and more. These websites document and update on the organizations' activities, schedule upcoming events, build awareness of their cause, and more. Websites are captured quarterly, but during periods of rapid updates, they are captured weekly or monthly.

The collection also houses Micah White's book, "The End of Protest," published in 2016. In this book, White, co-creator of Occupy Wall Street, argues that traditional protest methods are outdated and proposes eight principles of tactical innovation to catalyze future social movements. He discusses the limitations of contemporary activism, the need to re-conceive protest in a broader timescale, and the emergence of increasingly sophisticated movements.

White's book offers a vision of a comprehensive revolution of revolution, encompassing spiritual, political, and social changes. He is an influential social activist with a twenty-year record of innovative activism, including conceiving the debt-forgiveness tactic used by the Rolling Jubilee and popularizing the critique of clicktivism. White currently directs Boutique Activist Consultancy, an activist think tank specializing in impossible campaigns.

"The Road" is a film adaptation of Cormac McCarthy's Pulitzer Prize-winning novel, which presents a post-apocalyptic world where the protagonist, a man, and his son struggle to survive. The film, directed by John Hillcoat and written by Joe Penhall, is generally depressing and lacks the emotional depth of the novel, despite strong performances by Viggo Mortensen and Kodi Smit-McPhee as the father-son duo. The film is visually realistic, but fails to capture the transformative prose of McCarthy's work, resulting in an honorable attempt at filming an unfilmable book. The story explores themes of human survival and the horrors humans inflict on each other, with the characters' greatest fears revolving around cannibalism and losing their humanity. The film is powerful, but falls short of transcending the horrors it portrays, leaving viewers with an endurance test rather than a more elevated experience.

The Senate Judiciary Committee is set to vote on Brett Kavanaugh's nomination to the Supreme Court on Friday, with key Republican senators still undecided. The vote comes after a heated hearing featuring Kavanaugh and Christine Blasey Ford, who accused him of sexual assault. Senators Jeff Flake, Susan Collins, Lisa Murkowski, and Joe Manchin met to discuss the nomination, with Flake expressing doubt about moving forward. GOP senators are optimistic about Kavanaugh's nomination being favorably reported out of the committee, with at least one undecided senator, Bob Corker, announcing his support. President Trump praised Kavanaugh's testimony as "powerful, honest, and riveting." The vote will determine whether Kavanaugh's nomination advances to the full Senate for a vote.

The article discusses the possibility that Craig Steven Wright, an Australian computer scientist and entrepreneur, may be the creator of Bitcoin, also known as Satoshi Nakamoto. The evidence presented includes blog posts, emails, and leaked documents that link Wright to Nakamoto's pseudonymous identity and bitcoin's creation. However, the article also acknowledges that the evidence could be a hoax and that Wright has demonstrated a talent for obfuscation and a love of privacy. In a historic ruling, U.S. District Judge Bernard Friedman struck down Michigan's ban on same-sex marriage, making it the 18th state to allow gay and lesbian couples to marry. The decision came after a nine-day trial that focused on testimony from scholars and researchers on opposing sides of the gay marriage debate. Judge Friedman's ruling was criticized by Michigan Attorney General Bill Schuette, who vowed to continue fighting to uphold the Michigan Marriage Amendment Act, which was approved by 2.7 million voters in 2004. However, the judge's ruling was not stayed, prompting Schuette to file an emergency stay request to prevent gay couples from marrying immediately. The plaintiffs in the case, Hazel Park nurses April DeBoer and Jayne Rowse, were overjoyed with the ruling, as it allows them to marry and adopt each other's special needs children. The ruling has been met with mixed reactions, with some hailing it as a victory for the gay rights movement, while others argue that it violates the will of the voters. The case is expected to be appealed to the U.S. 6th Circuit Court of Appeals.

On July 13, 2014, heavy fighting erupted between rival militias in Libya's capital, Tripoli, resulting in at least seven deaths and 36 injuries. The clashes centered around the international airport, which was closed for three days due to security concerns. The Zintan militia, which had controlled the airport since the overthrow of Moammar Gadhafi in 2011, was reportedly under attack by militias from Misrata.

The fighting was the worst in Tripoli since November 2013, when over 40 people were killed in clashes between militias and armed residents. The United Nations temporarily relocated some of its international staff due to the violence.

The central government denounced the attackers as illegal, while comments on pro-Misrata websites suggested that the force was freeing the airport from Zintani control to hand it over to authorities. The violence occurred amidst security concerns and political tensions, as Libya awaited the results of the June 25 parliamentary elections.

Libya, an OPEC member, has been divided since July 2013 due to rival militias from urban communities and tribes, as well as Islamist and more moderate forces. The loss of oil revenues due to the unrest has caused a budget crisis in the country. The US expressed concern over the ongoing violence in Libya, fearing it could lead to widespread conflict. Tripoli has seen a surge in kidnappings but has been relatively spared the kind of violence that has rocked the eastern city of Benghazi.

The document expresses strong criticism towards LeBron James, who is set to announce his decision on which NBA team he will join tomorrow. The author believes that James has become the most unlikable person in American sports due to his self-aggrandizing behavior and perceived manipulation of the media.
