Oprah Winfrey has apologized for causing a media frenzy after stating that she experienced racism during a trip to Switzerland, specifically at an upscale Zurich boutique named Trois Pommes. Winfrey claimed that a clerk refused to show her a handbag, stating that she could not afford it. However, the sales assistant at the boutique has since denied these claims, stating that she felt 'powerless' after the accusations. The sales assistant insists that she only sells a handbag costing nearly £25,000 a few times a year and that she would never refuse to show a customer a bag based on their race. Winfrey's encounter with the sales assistant occurred in July while she was in Switzerland for Tina Turner's wedding. The sales assistant has expressed a desire to apologize to Winfrey and hopes the incident will soon be resolved.

The article introduces kGoal, a revolutionary smart Kegel trainer designed to help women exercise and manage their pelvic floor muscles. The device, which functions as both an exercise tool and a performance monitoring system, aims to provide a fun, interactive platform for guiding, measuring, and tracking pelvic floor exercises. The device is like having a personalized gym and tracking system in the palm of one's hand.

Pelvic floor muscles are crucial for various aspects of health, including pregnancy, bladder control, musculoskeletal stability, and sexual pleasure. However, tools to help exercise and manage these muscles have been lacking. kGoal aims to address this gap by providing real-time biofeedback, suggesting exercise plans tailored to the user's current capabilities, tracking performance, and making exercise more comfortable and enjoyable.

The device consists of a squeezable pillow that is inserted into the vagina and an arm that stays outside the body, holding the device in place and providing additional vibrational feedback. The system communicates with an app, where users can find their exercise history, suggested workouts, and track their performance over time. kGoal is made with Class VI medical-grade silicone and is splash-resistant for easy cleaning.

kGoal was developed by Minna Life, a startup in San Francisco that includes designers, engineers, and health experts. The team has a deep level of experience in product development and manufacturing and has successfully developed and launched two previous products. The company turned to Kickstarter to gather user feedback and help cover manufacturing costs.

The article also highlights the importance of pelvic floor muscles and the benefits of strengthening them, including improved sexual function, urinary control, and overall health. It mentions that Private Gym, another fitness program that strengthens the pelvic muscles, has been successful in boosting sexual performance and preventing the onset of erectile dysfunction in men.

Overall, the article presents kGoal as a groundbreaking advance in pelvic floor health, offering a fun, interactive, and effective way for women to exercise and manage their pelvic floor muscles. The device aims to fill a gap in the market for tools to help women maintain pelvic floor health and improve their overall well-being.

AirAsia Flight 8501, which crashed on December 28 with 162 people on board, has had four large parts found on the sea bed, according to the head of Indonesia's search and rescue agency. The multi-national search and rescue team has been searching the northern Java Sea and coastline of southern Borneo to recover the victims and locate the wreckage and black box flight recorders. The breakthrough came as authorities announced that Indonesia AirAsia had violated the terms of its licence for the Surabaya to Singapore route by flying on a Sunday, the day the plane went down. No survivors have been found, and much effort has focused on finding the mostly Indonesian victims. The cause of the crash remains unexplained, but a report from Indonesia's weather bureau suggests that the plane may have flown into bad weather, which would have been difficult to avoid. The plane was flying at 32,000 feet and the pilot had asked to climb to 38,000 feet just before contact was lost. Indonesia AirAsia has been ordered to stop its Surabaya to Singapore flights, and the transport ministry has announced a full review of all AirAsia flights. Divers, including a team of Russian specialists, may be able to investigate the suspected wreckage on Sunday if the weather improves.

The Coast Guard has issued a stern warning to Taylor Energy, the owner of an oil platform off southeast Louisiana, which has been leaking oil for over 14 years. The new federal estimates put the daily leak rate at 10,500 to 29,000 gallons, making it one of the largest and longest-running oil spills in North America. The Coast Guard has ordered Taylor Energy to devise a new containment plan and hire a contractor to execute it, with fines of up to $40,000 per day for non-compliance.

Taylor Energy disputes the new leak estimates and the cause of the chronic sheens, often stretching for miles from the well site. The company claims that the sheens are caused by oil and gas bubbling up from the oil-saturated seafloor, not leaky wells. The platform, known as MC-20 Saratoga, was destroyed by Hurricane Ivan in 2004, triggering an underwater mudslide that buried a cluster of wells.

Several environmental groups have long disputed Taylor's claim that its containment effort has limited pollution to a trickle. In 2013, an environmental group measured the sheen at over 20 miles long. The Gulf Monitoring Consortium estimated a daily release rate of between 100 and 400 gallons.

Federal regulators began investigating the leak in 2016, and Taylor Energy sued the federal government over the remaining $432 million from a trust created to pay for the leak response. The company argued that its response worked and that the remaining funds should be returned.

In a 2017 legal filing, the Bureau of Safety and Environmental Enforcement estimated the leak's range at 42 to 2,300 gallons per day. However, this year, the government cited the vastly larger daily estimate of up to 29,000 gallons. The Coast Guard noted the new rate in its recent order for additional containment work.

The Coast Guard's order is seen as long overdue by environmental groups, who accuse Taylor Energy of negligence. Taylor Energy, however, questions the government's new estimates, calling them "ridiculous" and based on "erroneous science."

The wells at the Taylor Energy site were relatively low in pressure, and it's unlikely the platform site could leak at the new estimated rates without pressurization, according to a marine scientist hired by Taylor Energy. A more likely source of the sheen is the sediment, which is heavily contaminated with oil.

Despite the ongoing controversy, the sheen has never been documented reaching the shore, nor has it caused large-scale damage to fisheries or wildlife. However, environmentalists argue that any release of oil into the Gulf of Mexico can have significant environmental impacts.

This summary also includes a brief mention of the Deepwater Horizon oil spill in 2010, which was the largest marine oil drilling disaster in history, resulting in the death of 11 workers and the release of 4 million barrels of oil over 87 days. The U.S. filed a complaint against BP Exploration & Production and several other defendants, leading to a record-setting settlement of $5.5 billion for a Clean Water Act penalty and up to $8.8 billion in natural resource damages.

Kathleen Dawn West, a 42-year-old mother from Calera, Alabama, was found dead outside her home on January 13, 2018. The police have classified her death as a homicide, but have not released the cause of death or made any arrests. The investigation is ongoing.

West was known to have a subscription-only website where she went by the name Kitty Kat West and posted revealing photos. Her neighbors described her as keeping to herself and living a quiet life with her husband, an unsworn Birmingham Southern College campus police officer, and their 12-year-old daughter.

West's mother has launched an online fundraising campaign to help with funeral expenses. In a statement, her mother wrote that she is seeking prayers and support during this difficult time. West's family has been tight-lipped about her death, and no further public statements have been made.

Two private Facebook groups have been created to discuss West's death and have over 3,000 members combined. The discussions offer a litany of conspiracy theories about what happened to West, with posts featuring local hearsay, screenshots of her and her family's social media accounts, and even a bloody photo of the street where she died.

The police have not confirmed the details of the Facebook groups' accounts, and have stated that much of the information and speculation shared by media outlets and on social media has hindered their investigation into West's death. The Associated Press has reported that West's online activities may have played a role in her death, but no publicly disclosed evidence or statements from authorities have connected her social media activities to her killing in any way.

The overriding tone of the Facebook discussions is a mixture of lurid interest and small-town hysteria, with users desperate for clues to inspire or reinforce their own unproven theories. The police have encouraged the public to avoid spreading rumors and to wait for official updates on the investigation.

The United States has handed over Ali Musa Daqduq, a Hezbollah prisoner suspected of the deaths of five U.S. soldiers, to the Iraqi government. The Obama administration had sought to keep Daqduq in U.S. custody but was legally obligated to transfer him due to a security agreement negotiated in 2008. The decision to transfer him to Iraqi custody was criticized by Republicans and some senators, who wanted him transferred to Guantánamo Bay for a military tribunal. The senators expressed concern that the Iraqi government may release Daqduq for political reasons. The U.S. has discussed transferring him to a U.S. military commission, but the administration has stated that it wants to close the detention facility at Guantanamo Bay. The U.S. marked the end of the Iraq war on Thursday and is in the process of withdrawing troops from the country by the end of the month.

The document discusses a bizarre trend of people dressing as clowns and scaring people in the streets, particularly in Greater Manchester and Cheshire, UK. The police have issued warnings against this behavior, stating that it is unacceptable and could potentially constitute an offense. There have been several reports of clown sightings, with some instances involving people wearing clown masks while driving cars and chasing children. The police have received a small number of reports in Cheshire and Gloucestershire, with no arrests made due to the suspects fleeing before the police arrive. The incidents in the UK appear to be inspired by similar clown-related threats in the United States. The trend has left many children terrified and parents concerned, with some expressing their disapproval on social media. The police have urged anyone who witnesses any suspicious activity or feels intimidated by this behavior to report it immediately.

In the final episode of her long-running talk show, Chelsea Handler, who is moving to Netflix for a new stand-up and talk show deal, marveled at her seven-year run on Chelsea Lately, calling it "seven years of ridiculous stupidity." The show, which mixed a panel of comedians, superfluous and silly skits, and free-wheeling, often ribald celebrity interviews, was a hit with audiences and celebrities alike. Handler's irreverent attitude and willingness to joke about tabloid culture made her a funnier version of our own inner monologue and a popular stop for celebrities on their press tours. The finale featured a star-studded musical number and a fake intervention with Sandra Bullock, Jennifer Aniston, and Mary McCormack. Handler will continue her career on Netflix, where she will host a talk show and release a stand-up special.

In the aftermath of Rush Limbaugh's controversial comments about a female law student, Sandra Fluke, seven advertisers have temporarily suspended their ties with his radio show. The latest company to do so is ProFlowers, citing Limbaugh's comments as going beyond political discourse and not reflecting their company values. The pressure to end relationships with Limbaugh's show came from women's groups, with UltraViolet reporting 91,000 signatures on a petition urging ProFlowers to take action. Other advertisers who have suspended their advertising with Limbaugh include Quicken Loans, Sleep Train, Sleep Number, Citrix Systems Inc., Carbonite, and LegalZoom.

Republican presidential hopefuls Newt Gingrich, Rick Santorum, and Ron Paul criticized Limbaugh's remarks, while Eric Fehrnstrom, an advisor to Mitt Romney, thought Limbaugh's apology was appropriate. Fehrnstrom also expressed a desire for a more civilized public discourse, acknowledging extreme rhetoric on both sides of the political spectrum.

David Friend, CEO of Carbonite, issued a statement saying that Limbaugh's comments were offensive and that they have decided to withdraw their advertising from his show. Friend emphasized that the outcry over Limbaugh was the worst they've ever seen and that they are taking this matter very seriously. He has scheduled a face-to-face meeting with Limbaugh to express the offense his comments caused to many of their customers and employees.

The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) has apologized for an intern mistakenly confirming offensive and inaccurate names of the pilots involved in the Asiana Airlines flight 214 crash on July 6. The intern, acting outside his authority, confirmed the names to a media outlet, which were later aired by local station KTVU. The NTSB does not release the names of crewmembers involved in transportation accidents to the media. KTVU has since issued multiple apologies for the error and is reviewing its procedures to prevent such incidents in the future. Asiana Airlines is considering legal action against both KTVU and the NTSB for the damage to the pilots' reputation. The incident has sparked criticism from the Asian American Journalists Association for the offensive nature of the names.

A 23-year-old woman, Laura Cunliffe, from Hoyland near Barnsley, has been sentenced to 14 weeks in jail for causing unnecessary suffering to her pet kitten, Mowgli. The incident occurred when Cunliffe put the kitten in a microwave and turned it on for five minutes, believing it had attacked her goldfish. The kitten initially survived but died 90 minutes later due to its internal organs being cooked. The court deemed this act as "an act of utterly horrendous cruelty." Cunliffe has been banned from keeping animals for life and cannot appeal the ban for at least five years. Her defense attorney stated that Cunliffe has longstanding problems with psychotic depression and has been sectioned under the Mental Health Act 20 times. The RSPCA expressed sympathy for the kitten's suffering and hoped that other animals would not have to endure such cruelty in the future.

Google and Microsoft are offering free Wi-Fi services to travelers during the holiday season. Google's free Wi-Fi will be available in 47 airports across the United States until January 15, 2010, and on Virgin America flights within the continental United States. Notable absences from Google's free Wi-Fi list include major hubs and popular destinations like Chicago O'Hare, LAX in Los Angeles, and all three New York-area airports. Microsoft, in partnership with JiWire, is offering free Wi-Fi in nationwide hotels and airports in exchange for one Bing search.

Google is also encouraging users to donate to charities via Google Checkout when using the free Wi-Fi. The airport that generates the most donations by January 1, 2010, will receive $15,000 to donate to the charity of their choice. A photo contest is also being held, where users can submit photos of themselves using free in-flight or airport Wi-Fi during the holidays to win prizes.

Google's free Wi-Fi offer does not require credit card or payment information, but users should be careful when selecting a network to avoid paid hotspots. Google will have access to some aggregate, non-personally identifiable information. For more information, check out Google's free Wi-Fi FAQ page.

A former employee of Brink's Company, Stephen Dennis, has been charged with stealing nearly $200,000 worth of quarters while working as a money processing manager at the company's Birmingham, Alabama, branch. The theft was discovered during an April 2014 audit, which found four ballistic bags containing beads and only $1,000 in quarters.

Investigations revealed that Dennis had replaced the quarters with beads in the ballistic bags belonging to the Federal Reserve Coin Inventory. In total, he swapped 784,000 quarters, or nearly 10,000 pounds of quarters, for beads at the Brink's facility.

The FBI announced the charges and stated that Dennis had entered a plea agreement with the U.S. Attorney's Office to plead guilty to the charge and repay $196,000 to Brink's. The armored service had already reimbursed the Federal Reserve Bank for the loss.

FBI Special Agent Roger C. Stanton stated that Dennis may have thought he was stealing a small amount, but the theft was equivalent to a major bank heist. U.S. Attorney Joyce White Vance added that Dennis must now repay the money and face a federal sentence.

The maximum penalty for bank theft is 10 years in prison and a $250,000 fine. The case was investigated by the FBI, and Assistant U.S. Attorney Henry Cornelius is prosecuting.

In a heated exchange at an AARP event on Friday, President Barack Obama and GOP vice presidential nominee Paul Ryan traded sharp criticism over health care reforms and Medicare. Both accused each other of being untruthful regarding the Affordable Care Act, also known as Obamacare.

Obama argued that the health care law strengthened Medicare, stating that the claim by Ryan and other Republicans that $716 billion is being cut from Medicare to fund the bill is "simply not true." Ryan, in response, said that Obama's contention that the health care law strengthened Medicare was "just not true," adding that the legislation "turned Medicare into a piggy bank for Obamacare."

The debate over Medicare is a major issue in the November election campaign, especially in the battleground state of Florida. Both candidates are campaigning aggressively in key states, with Romney heading to Las Vegas, Obama to Virginia, Biden to New Hampshire, and Ryan to Florida.

In a separate development, Romney released details of his 2011 income tax return, showing he made $13.7 million last year and paid $1.94 million in federal taxes, giving him an effective tax rate of 14.1%. Despite this release, Romney has been criticized for not releasing more than two years worth of taxes, with Democrats and some Republicans calling for more transparency.

Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid called the new tax information insufficient, stating that "When will the American people see the returns he filed before he was running for president?" Obama's deputy campaign manager Stephanie Cutter also criticized the disclosure, stating it "continues to mask Romney's true wealth" and income from the private equity firm he once led, leaving the American people in the dark about critical details of his finances.

The exchange at the AARP event is part of a larger campaign battle over Medicare, with both candidates emphasizing their positions and attacking each other's plans. The debate is expected to continue as the election approaches.

On Wednesday evening in Mendon, a Toyota Corolla driven by Nabila Altahan was suspended from a telephone guy wire after a quick reaction to GPS unit instructions to turn around. The car veered off Route 4 while westbound, leaving the lane of traffic, following sudden directions from the GPS due to passing the intended destination. Altahan and her passenger were unharmed, and emergency services including State Police and Rutland City Fire Department responded to the incident, which occurred across from Sugar & Spice Restaurant. A witness at a nearby miniature golf course reported seeing Altahan jump out of the car as it was suspended from the pole. The incident was captured by photographer Ray Ault.

The Solar Impulse 2 plane successfully took off from Nagoya, Japan on Monday, marking the end of a four-week hiatus during its historic attempt to circle the globe without fuel. The solar-powered plane, which is driven by four electric propellers and banks of solar panels, had been grounded since June 1 due to unfavorable weather conditions.

After a pre-dawn scramble, the plane took off from Nagoya Airport and is expected to land in Hawaii after a nonstop flight of roughly five days and nights. The plane aims to reach the United States mainland and cross the Atlantic while summer conditions persist. Its round-the-world voyage will end at its starting point, Abu Dhabi.

The team spent nearly two months waiting for clear weather to cross the Pacific, and a developing cold front forced the plane to make an unscheduled landing in Japan earlier this month. The Pacific crossing is the eighth leg of Solar Impulse's journey around the world, but this stage has proven to be the most difficult, with weeks of delays.

Swiss pilot and Solar Impulse co-founder Andre Borschberg, who is flying the experimental single-seater craft, spent weeks in Nanjing, China, waiting for the right flying conditions to present themselves. He finally took off on May 31, but a deterioration in the forecast a few hours into the mission meant that he had to divert to Japan.

The rainy season in Nagoya has meant another long wait there, but after the false start last week, meteorologists are now confident they have found a weather window to make the five-day, five-night crossing to Hawaii. The plane will be heading straight out across the Pacific.

The experimental craft, which has 17,000 solar cells, is powered only by the Sun. Once over the ocean, if it fails to soak up enough rays to fully charge its batteries and make it through the night, the pilot could be forced to bail out. Mr. Borschberg has been trained for that eventuality and has a dinghy and enough supplies for several days while he waits for the team to identify a vessel to go pick him up.

If this flight succeeds, the plane will continue its journey around the world, with Bertrand Piccard taking the controls for the next Pacific crossing from Hawaii to the US mainland. The plane will then continue across North America, before attempting to fly over the Atlantic. However, the build-up of delays could impact on the later stages. Ideally, the plane needs to cross the Atlantic before August, when the hurricane season reaches its peak.

In a move to prevent professional sports leagues from aiding the Obama administration in promoting Obamacare, Senate Republican leaders have sent letters to the heads of the National Football League, Major League Baseball, National Basketball Association, National Hockey League, Professional Golf Association, and NASCAR. The letters, dated June 27th, express concerns that partnering with the administration could damage the leagues' reputations and warn of potential policy retaliation. The letters come after Health and Human Services Secretary Kathleen Sebelius mentioned a potential partnership with the NFL to promote the Affordable Care Act. The Republican senators argue that the law is unpopular and point to polls that reflect this sentiment. The letters also suggest that the Obama administration may be threatening the pro sports leagues to extract support for Obamacare. An HHS spokesperson declined to comment, and the White House did not immediately respond. The NFL has since stated they have "no plans" to engage on Obamacare.

In response to the Ebola outbreak in West Africa, three states – New York, New Jersey, and Illinois – have implemented mandatory 21-day quarantines for healthcare workers returning from treating patients in the affected region. However, top federal health official, Dr. Anthony Fauci, director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, expressed concerns that such quarantines could discourage healthcare workers from volunteering, as they may find the measures uncomfortable and potentially stigmatizing.

Fauci emphasized that active and direct monitoring can accomplish the same level of protection as a quarantine, as people infected with Ebola do not become contagious until they start showing symptoms. He made these remarks on various news shows, including "Fox News Sunday," ABC's "This Week," and NBC's "Meet the Press."

New York Governor, Chris Christie, defended the quarantine, stating that it was necessary to protect the public health of New Jersey residents. He also mentioned that the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) would likely come around to their point of view on the matter.

Rep. Darrell Issa, who chairs the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee, expressed concerns about the public's lack of confidence in the Obama administration's ability to handle the Ebola crisis. He suggested that mandatory quarantines might not be the best approach for containing the disease.

Samantha Power, the U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations, highlighted the need to ensure that returning U.S. healthcare workers are treated as heroes rather than stigmatized for their efforts in combating Ebola.

The debate over quarantines and their potential impact on healthcare worker volunteering continues, with Fauci advocating for respectful treatment and active monitoring as more effective strategies for protecting public health.

Commissioner Rob Manfred has rejected Pete Rose's bid for reinstatement into Major League Baseball (MLB), maintaining his permanent ban for gambling on baseball. Rose, who holds the all-time hits record, was placed on the permanently ineligible list in 1989 for betting on baseball games while both a player and manager for the Cincinnati Reds.

Manfred's decision does not address Rose's eligibility for the National Baseball Hall of Fame, stating that the considerations for reinstatement and Hall of Fame eligibility are different. The National Baseball Hall of Fame has also reiterated that Rose remains ineligible for consideration due to his placement on the permanently ineligible list.

Rose formally appealed his case in 2015, and Manfred conducted a comprehensive review of the issues before delivering a three-page decision. In the decision, Manfred reiterated the importance of MLB's Rule 21, which prohibits betting on baseball, and stated that Rose has not demonstrated a fundamental change in his life or a grasp of the scope of his violations.

The decision references a notebook obtained by the Commissioner's Office after the publication of an ESPN report in 2015, which appears to show that Rose bet on the Reds as an active player in 1985 and 1986. Rose has admitted to wagering on the team after becoming the manager but has denied betting on baseball while he was a player.

Manfred's decision also disputes Rose's contention that he bet on the Reds to win every game. While noting that the specific games do not matter regarding the violation of Rule 21, it points out that his decision to pass on certain games may have been a tip-off to those aware of his activity.

Rose may not associate with any Major or Minor League club, but the rules do not cover relationships with third parties that do business with MLB. Therefore, he may pursue such opportunities unless it involves an association with a Major League club, in which case the proposal must be submitted to the Commissioner's Office for review.

Manfred did acknowledge that Rose had an exceptional career, and he will continue to allow him to participate in ceremonial activities that present no threat to the integrity of the game, provided that the activities are approved by him in advance.

Newly uncovered documents obtained by Outside the Lines provide the first written record that Pete Rose bet extensively on baseball, and on the Reds, while he was still a player. The documents go beyond the evidence presented in the 1989 Dowd report that led to Rose's banishment and provide the first written record that Rose bet while he was still on the field.

For 26 years, Rose has maintained that he never bet on baseball while he was a player. However, the newly uncovered documents show that Rose bet on baseball, and on the Reds, as he racked up the last hits of a record-smashing career in 1986. The documents reflect betting records from March through July 1986, showing that Rose bet on at least one MLB team on 30 different days and on the Reds on 21 of those days. Most bets were about $2,000, with the largest single bet being $5,500 on the Boston Celtics, a bet he lost.

John Dowd, the former federal prosecutor who led MLB's investigation, said that the newly uncovered documents are the final piece of the puzzle on a New York betting operation with organized crime. He believes that the evidence strengthens the case for Rose's banishment from the game.

Rose, through his lawyer, has issued a statement that he will not comment on specific matters relating to reinstatement. He has a meeting with Manfred scheduled after the All-Star break to discuss his entire history and his long personal journey since baseball.

The Reds president and CEO, Bob Castellini, issued a statement that they respect Manfred's decision on the matter of Pete Rose and are grateful for his diligence and the amount of time he spent on the matter. They appreciate that the Commissioner stated that Hall of Fame consideration is a separate issue and believe that Rose deserves that opportunity. They are pleased that they have had and will continue to have opportunities to commemorate Pete's remarkable on-field accomplishments. Any future plans to celebrate Pete's career with the Reds will be discussed with the Commissioner and then will be communicated publicly at the appropriate time.

The Silk Road, an online black market for illegal drugs and other illicit goods, was shut down in October 2013, and its operator, Ross Ulbricht, was convicted of multiple charges in February 2014. Ulbricht, who operated under the pseudonym Dread Pirate Roberts, is facing potential life sentences for distributing narcotics on the internet and engaging in a continuing criminal enterprise. The site generated over $213 million in revenue from January 2011 to its closing, with Ulbricht taking millions of dollars in commissions.

The trial also accused Ulbricht of commissioning the murders of five people he saw as threats to his enterprise, although no evidence of harm was found. Meanwhile, Charlie Shrem, a known name and early advocate in the bitcoin community, pleaded guilty to bitcoin-related crimes in December 2014. Shrem was arrested in January 2014 and charged with failing to report suspicious banking activity, laundering money from BitInstant accounts for Silk Road customers, and operating an unlicensed money-transmitting business.

The case of Ulbricht and Shrem has raised concerns about the safety and reputation of bitcoin, with some viewing it as a negative for the community. However, some in the bitcoin world see the prosecution as a positive sign that traditional law enforcement tactics are working, even in the bitcoin world.

Recently, it was revealed that two agents involved in the investigation to take down Silk Road allegedly stole proceeds from the underground site and hid their booty in offshore accounts. Former DEA agent Carl Force and former Secret Service agent Shaun Bridges are charged with money laundering, wire fraud, theft, and conflict of interest. Force and Bridges worked on the Maryland investigation where Ulbricht was also the target.

Force allegedly used several online aliases to extort hundreds of thousands of dollars worth of bitcoin from Ulbricht, while Bridges allegedly stole more than $800,000 worth of bitcoin that he controlled during the Silk Road investigation. Both agents have resigned from their respective agencies and are facing charges.

The cases of Ulbricht, Shrem, Force, and Bridges highlight the ongoing challenges of regulating and policing the use of digital currencies like bitcoin, as well as the potential for corruption and abuse by law enforcement officials.

The Syrian military is preparing for a possible invasion of Aleppo, Syria's largest city and a major commercial hub, where rebels have been embedded for over a week. The city's civilian population is reportedly gripped by foreboding as government forces mass on the southern outskirts. Fierce street clashes have sporadically erupted, but military commanders appear to be awaiting reinforcements before issuing invasion orders.

The United States has expressed alarm about the possibility of mass civilian casualties in Aleppo, a UNESCO World Heritage site, and has indicated that it is not reconsidering its stance against military intervention. The US favors defected Brigadier General Manaf Tlass as a potential successor to President Bashar al-Assad, but others question whether he would be acceptable to Syrians.

In a separate development, Turkey's prime minister has injected tension into the Syrian conflict by asserting that Syrian forces have abandoned territories close to the Turkish border that have since been occupied by Kurdish militants hostile to Turkey. This has led to fears of possible Turkish military incursions into Syria, similar to Turkey's incursions into northern Iraq.

In Aleppo, rebels have set up checkpoints and sniper positions and claim to be in control of half of the city. Thousands of people are leaving the city as fears grow that an intense battle is looming. Rebels are reinforcing their ranks with more fighters, medical supplies, and ammunition, but are reportedly lacking in weapons.

In Damascus, where government forces have largely repelled a sustained assault by rebels, state TV reported more clashes in the southern district of Qadam. The violence also spread to the Yarmouk Palestinian refugee camp, where street battles have taken place between rebels and soldiers.

Over 16,000 people have been killed in Syria since the start of anti-regime protests in March 2011. Repeated diplomatic attempts to stop the violence have foundered, with the UN Security Council bitterly divided. Thousands of refugees have already sought shelter in Turkey, Lebanon, Jordan, and Iraq. Conditions throughout the country have worsened as the fighting has spread and intensified in the two main cities in recent weeks.

The film "Selma," directed by Ava DuVernay and starring David Oyelowo as Martin Luther King Jr., has been released and is receiving critical acclaim. The film focuses on the 1965 march from Selma to Montgomery, Alabama, and King's fight with President Lyndon B. Johnson to secure the Voting Rights Act. The film is unique in that it does not use King's most famous speeches, as the rights to those speeches are controlled by the King family and have been sold to DreamWorks SKG with Steven Spielberg producing. The filmmakers instead paraphrased King's speeches to capture his cadence and meaning, while avoiding the need for permission from the King family. The film is a nuanced portrayal of King as a strategic and conflicted figure, rather than a forbidding icon or flawless secular saint. The filmmakers believe that an African American director was necessary to achieve this portrayal, as there has historically been an allergy to black powerful men driving the narrative in films about the civil rights movement. The film has sparked a debate about historical accuracy and artistic license in biopics, as well as the degree to which the King estate's control of copyright has affected the portrayal of King in films and other media. The King estate has a long history of enforcing its copyright to maximize revenue and control King's image, and has sued several media outlets and producers for using King's speeches without permission. The estate has also licensed King's speeches for use in commercials and other products, and has demanded licensing fees for the use of King's likeness and quotes in the King Memorial on the National Mall. Critics argue that the estate's actions are devaluing the message of "I have a dream" and that the speeches should be entering the public domain. The estate insists that it is protecting the King brand and ensuring that the King family is fairly compensated for the use of King's image and words.

Bernardo Bertolucci, the acclaimed Italian film director, has been the subject of controversy after a resurfaced video interview revealed that he and Marlon Brando conspired to film a graphic rape scene in their 1972 film 'Last Tango in Paris' without the knowledge of the 19-year-old actress, Maria Schneider. In the interview, Bertolucci admitted that he wanted Schneider's reaction as a girl, not as an actress, and that the graphic nature of the scene was improvised on set. Schneider had previously stated that she was not informed of the details of the scene beforehand and felt humiliated and "a little raped" during the filming. The revelations have sparked outrage on social media, with celebrities such as Jessica Chastain, Chris Evans, and Ava DuVernay expressing their disgust and calling for Bertolucci to be stripped of his awards or prosecuted. The controversy has also brought attention to the treatment of actresses in the film industry and the importance of informed consent in filmmaking.

The Florida Senate race between Democratic incumbent Sen. Bill Nelson and Republican Rick Scott is heading for a recount due to a margin of less than 0.5 percentage points, as per Florida law. Sen. Nelson announced his disappointment in the election night results but did not concede, stating that the race remains tight. The recount is mandatory due to Scott's lead of slightly more than 30,000 votes out of over 8.1 million votes cast.

Scott's campaign criticized Nelson for pushing for a recount, while Nelson's campaign is sending monitors to every county across the state and working with attorney Marc Elias. Elias has highlighted potential areas of concern, such as comments made by a GOP supervisor of election in Madison County.

The recount process involves the 67 county supervisors of election rechecking the total tally, and the Nelson campaign contacting voters whose ballots were not counted due to issues like a lack of ID or a matching address. The deadline for determining whether the recount proceeds is noon on Saturday, but it may be extended under certain circumstances.

During his speech, Rick Scott vowed to bring a business-like approach to Washington and change the direction of the federal government, as he did in Florida during his eight years as governor. He also paid tribute to his mother and a former aide who died in a boating accident this year.

A Chicago TV station, WGN-TV, has apologized for using a Nazi-era symbol during a news segment about Yom Kippur, the holiest day in the Jewish year. The graphic displayed behind anchor Tom Negovan was a yellow Star of David badge emblazoned with the German word "Jude," or Jew, on striped material similar to the uniforms used in Nazi prisoner camps. The mistake was noticed by Marc Karlinsky, an editor at Chicago Lawyer magazine, who shared a photo of the segment on Twitter, sparking a widespread backlash. In a statement, WGN General Manager Greg Easterly and News Director Jennifer Lyons admitted that the picture came from their image bank and they failed to recognize it as an offensive Nazi symbol. The station has promised to review its in-house policies and make changes to prevent such oversights in the future. They expressed deep regret for the error and apologized to the Jewish community and their viewers.

The article discusses the mythical Hydra, a multi-headed serpent-like creature from Greek mythology, and the possibility that its creation was inspired by real-life polycephalic animals, or those with more than one head. The Hydra was a fearsome creature that Heracles, the son of Zeus, had to defeat as part of his twelve labors. Heracles enlisted the help of his nephew Iolaus to prevent the Hydra's heads from regrowing after they were chopped off.

Scientists have documented cases of polycephalic animals in the wild and in laboratories, including two-headed fish, sharks, dolphins, and even humans. These cases are often the result of conjoined twins or mutations in embryonic development. The shape and composition of a face are determined by an organism's genes, specifically the Sonic Hedgehog (SHH) gene.

The article also discusses the low survival rate of polycephalic animals and the possibility that the authors of classical myths may have been inspired by real-life observations of these creatures. The Hydra is not the only mythical creature with multiple heads, as there are also stories of the multi-headed dog Cerberus, the eight-headed snake Yamata no Orochi, and the three-headed dragon Zmey Gorynych.

The article concludes by noting that there is still much to be discovered about polycephaly in animals, and that it is likely to remain extraordinarily rare in real life. The authors of classical myths may have been inspired by real-life observations of polycephalic animals, but the exact origins of these stories are still unknown.

A head-on train collision occurred in western Switzerland on Monday evening, injuring at least 44 people, four of them seriously. The crash happened on a route between Payerne and Lausanne, and one locomotive's driver is missing. Search crews are trying to access the train's crushed cab. The cause of the collision is under investigation. The incident will disrupt train service between Payerne and Moudon until at least midnight. This tragic event follows a high-speed derailment in Spain earlier this month that resulted in 79 fatalities.

On November 12, a massive explosion occurred at a military base in Iran, which the Iranian authorities initially described as an accident causing a minor setback in research work. However, a recent analysis of commercial satellite images reveals extensive damage across the base, with most buildings destroyed or extensively damaged. The Institute for Science and International Security, which made the images public, stated that the force of the explosion was so great that it shook windows in surrounding towns. The blast, which killed 17 military personnel, including a founder of Iran's missile program, General Hassan Tehrani Moghaddam, occurred while researchers were working on missile technology. The exact cause of the explosion remains unclear, with possibilities ranging from an accident to sabotage. The satellite images were taken on November 22, 2011, by DigitalGlobe, and the institute's sources suggest that the blast occurred during a volatile procedure involving a missile engine. The analysis also indicates that the damage seen in the images is likely due to the explosion and not subsequent demolition or debris removal.

The Tonight Show, hosted by Jay Leno, is undergoing significant budget restructuring, resulting in a pay cut for Leno and the layoff of approximately 20-25 staff members. The show remains the top-rated late-night program, but financially, it only breaks even due to a high production budget and low ad sales. Leno voluntarily agreed to a salary reduction to save jobs, with his new salary estimated to be around $20 million. NBC declined to comment on the situation, but other senior staffers also agreed to pay cuts.

The weekly budget for Leno's prime time show was approximately $2.3 million, which remained unchanged when he returned to late night. The budget is now expected to be closer to $1.7 million, similar to what it was during Leno's previous late-night stint. Leno is not the first late-night host to agree to a salary reduction, as CBS restructured David Letterman's deal in 2009.

The exact reasons for the budget cuts are unclear, but some speculate it is due to Comcast wanting to review NBC's finances. The layoffs come just five days after Michelle Obama appeared as a guest on The Tonight Show for the third time. Leno's new salary is reportedly $27 million to $30 million, with additional earnings from his personal appearance schedule.

Leno replaced Johnny Carson as host of The Tonight Show in 1992 and resumed hosting in 2010 after a brief hiatus, following a payoff to Conan O'Brien. Leno's ratings have been criticized in the past, but he continues to be a valuable asset to NBC. The downsizing is part of a wave of cost trims recently imposed by Comcast at NBC.

The preliminary report from an investigation reveals potential financial ties between President Donald Trump's personal lawyer, Michael Cohen, and a Russian billionaire, Viktor Vekselberg. Stormy Daniels' attorney, Michael Avenatti, claimed that Cohen received $500,000 from a company controlled by Vekselberg, deposited into an account used to pay off Daniels.

Avenatti also detailed other transactions he deemed suspicious, including deposits from pharmaceutical giant Novartis, the state-run Korea Aerospace Industries, and AT&T. Novartis and AT&T confirmed they paid Cohen's company, Essential Consultants, for "insights" into the Trump administration.

Avenatti's claims, supported by financial documents, could suggest a new dimension to the federal investigation into Cohen. Columbus Nova, a U.S.-based affiliate of Vekselberg's company, stated that it hired Cohen as a business consultant after Trump's inauguration. However, Columbus Nova denied that Vekselberg was involved or provided any funding for Cohen's engagement.

AT&T and Novartis have since confirmed their connections, while Korea Aerospace Industries did not respond to requests for comment. The White House has stated that Trump denies having an affair with Daniels, and Cohen has said he himself put up the $130,000 Daniels was given in a non-disclosure agreement.

This investigation adds to the legal troubles for Cohen, whose home and office were raided last month as part of a criminal investigation by federal prosecutors in Manhattan. The questions asked of Vekselberg suggest that Mueller investigators have been examining some of Cohen's business relationships as part of the investigation into Russian meddling in the 2016 presidential election. Vekselberg was one of two Russian oligarchs the FBI stopped earlier this year as part of Mueller's investigation.

Supreme Court Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg will officiate at a same-sex wedding this weekend, marking a historic first for a member of America's highest court. The wedding is between Kennedy Center President Michael Kaiser and John Roberts, a government economist. Ginsburg, who is an opera lover and frequent guest at the Kennedy Center, expressed admiration for Kaiser and agreed to officiate. The private ceremony will take place at the Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, a national memorial to President John F. Kennedy.

Same-sex marriage is legal in the District of Columbia and 13 U.S. states. Ginsburg has been a strong advocate for same-sex marriage rights, arguing for equal treatment in a case heard by the Supreme Court earlier this year. The wedding comes after the court's landmark ruling in June to expand federal recognition of same-sex marriages.

Justices generally avoid taking stands on political issues, but Ginsburg's involvement in the wedding is seen as a significant statement in support of same-sex marriage. Ginsburg has another same-sex wedding planned for September.

Ginsburg and Kaiser are close friends, and she is known for her support of the fine arts, especially opera. Kaiser has been at the helm of the Kennedy Center since 2001 and is an internationally recognized expert in arts management and one of Washington's most influential civic leaders.

The wedding brings together the nation's highest court and the capital's high society and marks a new milestone in the recognition of same-sex unions. Such marriages were virtually unheard of a little more than a decade ago but are now legal in several states and countries. After victories at the Supreme Court earlier this summer, a wave of litigation is challenging bans on same-sex marriages in states where they remain prohibited.

Ginsburg has been a trailblazer in her own right, becoming the second woman ever appointed to the Supreme Court in 1993. She has been a strong voice for women's rights and has been a champion for gender equality throughout her career. Her involvement in this wedding is another example of her commitment to social justice and equality.

A powerful and viral video advertisement, launched by the Kuwaiti telecom company Zain during Ramadan, challenges terrorism by featuring victims of terrorism confronting a suicide bomber. The three-minute music video, which has been viewed nearly 2.4 million times on YouTube, features a young girl questioning the bomber's actions, and Emirati star Hussain Al Jassmi singing about peace and love. The ad has been viewed as a beautiful attempt to tackle extremism, but has also been criticized for its use of an actor to play Omran Daqneesh, a Syrian boy who was wounded in an airstrike by the Syrian government rather than in an attack by Muslim extremists. Some have also criticized the ad for being exploitative and oversimplifying the complex issue of extremism.

The heroin epidemic is not limited to Iowa, as heroin use is spreading across all demographics, with women and 18-25 year-olds seeing the biggest increases in recent years. The heroin epidemic is not limited to urban centers, as heroin is making its way into the suburbs, with once-sleepy towns finding themselves hotbeds of drug activity. The heroin epidemic is a serious issue, not just because of the presence of heroin, but because of the effects that heroin is having on users. The number of overdoses and the number of overdose deaths is very concerning.

The Danish toy manufacturer, Lego Group, has surpassed Mattel and Hasbro to become the largest toymaker globally in terms of revenue and profit. This achievement is largely attributed to the success of the Lego Movie, which boosted sales by 11% in the first half of the year. The Lego Movie, released by Time Warner, made $69 million in its opening weekend and has grossed nearly $260 million so far. Sales across Europe, the Americas, and Asia increased by double digits compared to the same period in the previous year.

Lego's CFO, John Goodwin, expressed satisfaction with the reception of the Lego Movie products. He anticipates the business momentum to continue into the second half of the year, with the release of the Lego Movie on DVD. However, the majority of Lego sales occur in a short time-span leading up to the holiday season, and it remains to be seen how the line will develop.

Lego toys have gained immense popularity, with even big-time criminals reportedly involved in Lego theft schemes involving over $300,000 in toys this summer. Despite its success, Lego Group remains a privately owned family business founded in 1932 by the Kirk Kristiansen family.

The Lego Movie has attracted attention not only for its commercial success but also for its positive impact on sales of popular Lego sets, including a new set featuring female scientists, which sold out on Lego's website over the course of a weekend. The Lego Group, with approximately 12,000 employees, continues to dominate the global toy market.

The study published in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition suggests that fast food may not be the primary cause of childhood obesity, but rather a symptom of poor dietary habits learned at home. Researchers from the University of North Carolina, led by nutrition professor Barry Popkin, analyzed data from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) collected between 2007 and 2010. The study categorized nearly 4,500 children between 2 and 18 years old as non-consumers, low consumers, or high consumers of fast food.

The researchers found that fast food is only a small portion of a larger dietary pattern established by children's parents and caregivers. Obese children's diets often include too few fruits and vegetables and too much processed food and overly-sweet beverages. This unhealthy diet pattern is often reinforced in the meals students are offered as school lunches.

The study's authors suggest that public health efforts targeted at fast-food restaurants may be necessary but not sufficient to reduce child obesity if the remainder of the diet is not addressed. They emphasize that a better understanding of the patterns behind childhood obesity is important in the attempt to foster healthier habits, such as the reduction of sugary drink consumption and the greater inclusion of fresh vegetables and fruits.

Another study published this week from University of Illinois researchers found three main predictors for preschool obesity risk: a lack of adequate sleep, having parents with high body mass index (BMI), and having their eating habits restricted for weight control purposes. The study concluded that improving parents' health status, changing the food environment of the home, and encouraging an early bedtime could potentially reduce children's weight status.

In a groundbreaking study published in The Journal of Experimental Biology, researchers have discovered that the Southeast Asian flying snake, Chrysopelea paradisi, adopts a unique, UFO-like shape to aid in its gliding abilities. This shape, which is unlike any other animal or engineered flyer, provides the snake with the necessary aerodynamic properties for gliding.

The study, led by biomechanics researcher Jake Socha from Virginia Tech, found that the snake's body compresses and flattens into a saucer-like shape when it glides. This shape, when tested in a water tunnel, was found to be more aerodynamically efficient than a cylindrical shape.

The flying snake's performance in air is surprisingly comparable to that of other gliding animals, such as flying squirrels, lizards, and ants. However, the researchers are still investigating why the snake undulates while gliding.

The team created physical models of the snake's cross-section and tested them in a water tunnel to understand the aerodynamic forces at play. The results suggest that the snake's undulating shape generates enough lift to account for its gliding ability.

Despite the findings, don't expect to see flying-snake-shaped planes anytime soon. The shape would not be as aerodynamically effective at a plane's size and speed, according to Socha.

The study provides insights into the engineering solutions that nature has evolved over time, and the team is now focusing on understanding other aspects of the flying snake's aerial performances. The flying snake remains an Unexplained Flying Ophidian in many aspects.

The document discusses the elimination of the adoption tax credit in the House GOP's tax overhaul bill. The adoption tax credit, which was created in 1996 as part of the Small Business and Job Protection Act, helps reduce financial barriers to adoption by subsidizing costs for agency and attorney fees, travel, and post-adoption services. The credit offers up to $13,570 in 2017, but it is nonrefundable, meaning it only benefits taxpayers who owe federal taxes.

Adoption advocates have been bracing for the end of this credit, as House Ways and Means Chair Kevin Brady, one of the architects of the tax overhaul bill, mentioned the adoption tax credit as a provision that could be eliminated during a speech at the Heritage Foundation in December. The elimination of the adoption tax credit is concerning to adoption advocates, as it could have a chilling effect on adoption and increase costs for families who choose to adopt.

The number of taxpayers claiming the adoption tax credit is relatively small, but the credit has a significant impact on families who adopt, particularly those adopting from foster care. The credit can help families afford the high costs of adoption, which can range from $30,000 to $40,000 for private adoptions. The credit also helps families adopt multiple children at once, keeping siblings together and the family unit intact.

Two separate bills have been introduced in the Senate and the House this year to make the adoption tax credit refundable, which would make it more accessible to lower-income families. The elimination of the adoption tax credit is a significant loss for the adoption community, and advocates are staging a fight to make the credit refundable.

The consequences of cutting the adoption tax credit are still hard to predict, but it is likely that it will make it harder for lower- and middle-income families to adopt, especially privately and internationally. The credit is one of the government's most important pro-life policies, as it helps ensure that every child is a wanted child and extends the pro-life ethic beyond birth. The elimination of the adoption tax credit is intolerable, as it goes against the GOP's "pro-life" platform and could make it more difficult for children to find loving homes.

On May 11, a 40-person team at VCU Medical Center in Richmond, Virginia successfully delivered sextuplets to Ajibola Taiwo, a native of Western Nigeria. The team included experts from various fields such as maternal-fetal medicine, labor and delivery, nursing, anesthesia, respiratory, neonatal medicine, social work, nutrition, cardiology, and chaplain services. The babies, three boys, and three girls, ranged in weight from 1 pound, 10 ounces to 2 pounds, 15 ounces. All six are doing well and are currently in the Children’s Hospital of Richmond at VCU neonatal intensive care unit.

The Taiwos had been trying to conceive for 17 years and were overjoyed when they saw four heartbeats at their first ultrasound in November. It was not until January when they learned they were expecting sextuplets. The delivery required hours of planning and coordination, including pre-delivery drills and resuscitation exercises.

Kangaroo care, also known as skin-to-skin contact, was provided to the babies as soon as safely possible. This practice has been shown to maintain skin temperature regulation, increase successful breastfeeding, and ease the transition to life outside the womb. The Taiwos actively participate in the sextuplets’ care in the NICU.

Ajibola Taiwo was discharged from the hospital on May 18. She and her husband hope for their children to grow up and return to VCU to study and care for others. The hospital and family are not facilitating media requests at this time, but a media availability may be provided once the babies are discharged from the hospital.

Delivering sextuplets is a rare event, with only 24 such births reported by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention in the U.S. in 2015 out of nearly 4 million live births. The successful delivery and care of the sextuplets at VCU Medical Center is considered an amazing medical accomplishment.

Hillary Clinton made a surprise appearance at the UNICEF Snowflake Ball on Tuesday, where she presented Katy Perry with the Audrey Hepburn Humanitarian Award. The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force has recommended that women in their 40s should avoid routine mammograms for early detection of breast cancer, causing controversy and confusion. The recommendation is not government policy, and Health and Human Services Secretary Kathleen Sebelius advises women to continue discussing their individual histories with their doctors. The task force's recommendations are aimed at reducing false positives and unnecessary biopsies, but critics argue that it could lead to rationing of healthcare. The American Cancer Society disagrees with the findings and continues to recommend annual screening for all women over 40. Rep. Debbie Wasserman-Schultz, who was diagnosed with breast cancer at 41, finds the recommendations "disturbing" and "irresponsible." Hearings on the advisory board's recommendations are planned. Breast cancer is the most common cancer for U.S. women, with nearly 200,000 women expected to be diagnosed with the invasive form of the disease this year.

NBC News chairman Andrew Lack has reached a tentative agreement with Brian Williams to keep him at the network after his six-month suspension ends in August. The deal will see Williams taking on a new role at NBC, with Lester Holt expected to permanently take over as anchor of "NBC Nightly News." The scandal erupted in February when Williams admitted to misremembering an incident in which he claimed his helicopter was struck by enemy fire in Iraq. NBC launched an internal investigation to fact-check the anchorman and identified several other times when Williams exaggerated. The network said it would not publish the detailed results of the investigation, but offered a two-paragraph summary of the findings. Williams has since embarked on an "apology tour," meeting with NBC staffers and admitting to his mistakes. He will take a "substantial" pay cut and will serve as an anchor of breaking news and special reports on NBC's MSNBC cable news channel, as well as a breaking news anchor for NBC News live special reports when Holt is not available. The new arrangement is seen as a demotion for Williams, but it avoids an awkward scenario where he could show up on a rival network or website and potentially embarrass NBC. The move back to MSNBC will be a homecoming of sorts for Williams, who anchored a signature 9 p.m. newscast on the cable channel back in the late 1990s before ascending to "NBC Nightly News." In a recent interview at the Code Conference in California, former presidential candidate Hillary Clinton discussed her loss in the 2016 election and the factors she believes contributed to her defeat. Clinton pointed to suspected Russian cyberattacks, the Democratic National Committee's data operation, and a "very broad assumption" that she would win as key factors. She also criticized the media for their coverage of the email scandal, which she dubbed "the biggest nothingburger ever." Clinton also accused the news media of not providing substantive policy reporting during the campaign.

Clinton again brought up the FBI's investigation into her private email server, stating that it was a significant factor in her loss, particularly in the final days of the campaign. She also criticized the Democratic National Committee for providing her with an inferior data operation, while the Republicans had invested heavily in data infrastructure between 2012 and 2016.

On the topic of Russian interference in the election, Clinton described the hacks into the DNC and her campaign chairman's private email account, as well as various "fake news" websites, as the country "weaponizing" technology in an unprecedented misinformation campaign against her. While she did not explicitly accuse Trump's campaign of colluding with the Russians on the cyberattacks, she suggested that the Kremlin had help from Americans in some form.

Clinton also commented on the state of the Democratic Party, declining to name possible 2020 presidential candidates but calling on people to focus on coming gubernatorial elections in New Jersey and Virginia, as well as the 2018 midterms. She also stated that she is not running for office again but has no intention of vacating the public stage.

Throughout the interview, Clinton took hits at Donald Trump, calling him a "very impulsive, reactive personality" and describing his reported plan to withdraw from the Paris climate change agreement as "totally incomprehensible." She also made a joke about Trump's much-scrutinized relationship with Russia, stating that his tweet of the non-word "covfefe" was a "message to the Russians."

Overall, Clinton's interview provided insight into her thoughts on the 2016 election and the factors she believes contributed to her defeat. She also expressed her continued involvement in politics and her commitment to the Democratic Party.

In a candid conversation at the 2017 Ted Talks conference, tennis champion Serena Williams revealed that her accidental Snapchat pregnancy announcement was sent out to the world due to a mistake. Williams, who is engaged to Reddit co-founder Alexis Ohanian, admitted that she had been taking weekly pictures to track her pregnancy progress but had not intended to share the image. The slip-up did not cause her stress, and she plans to continue documenting her pregnancy journey.

Later, Williams announced on social media that she is 20 weeks pregnant and will welcome her first child in the fall. Her representative confirmed the news to PEOPLE. The mother-to-be also posted a moving love note to her unborn baby at the Ted Talks event.

Regarding her career plans post-baby, Williams expressed optimism about returning to championship form, citing Roger Federer as an example of a player who continues to excel at an older age. She also shared her excitement about her baby being in the stands to cheer her on. Williams' accidental pregnancy announcement serves as a reminder that even a tech giant's fiancée can still make social media blunders!

Tom Cruise and Katie Holmes' divorce, which shocked the world in June, has been officially finalized. The couple reached a settlement two weeks after Holmes filed for divorce, granting her primary physical custody of their 6-year-old daughter, Suri. The details of the agreement remain confidential. Cruise's representative stated that the actor is happy and relieved to be moving forward, with his priority being a good father. Scientists at the National University of La Plata in Buenos Aires have discovered that the larvae of the Argentine horned frog, a carnivorous species known for its aggressive behavior, emit a metallic-like sound when threatened. This is the first evidence of sound production by the larvae of anurans (frogs and toads). The discovery was made during a study of the mating calls and croakings of adult frogs. The distress calls, described as brief, clear, and metallic, are produced by pushing air out of the tadpoles' lungs, which develop very early. The tadpoles are naturally aggressive and carnivorous, but do not eat each other, possibly due to the distress calls. This discovery raises the possibility that other tadpoles may also produce sounds underwater. The researchers plan to study how and why the ability to produce sounds develops so rapidly, and how the sound is perceived by other tadpoles. The discovery could have far-reaching implications for our understanding of the behavior and ecology of amphibians, many of which are threatened by disease, habitat destruction, and illegal trade.

The article discusses the reunion of the cast from the popular romantic comedy film, Love Actually, for a special charity event called Red Nose Day Actually. The event was aired on BBC and featured cameos from many of the original cast members, including Hugh Grant, Liam Neeson, Keira Knightley, Bill Nighy, Rowan Atkinson, and Colin Firth. At the 90th Academy Awards, Ashley Judd, Annabella Sciorra, and Salma Hayek, three of Harvey Weinstein's most vocal accusers, presented a video montage emphasizing equality and representation. The video featured several other industry figures, including Mira Sorvino and Kumail Nanjiani, discussing the importance of representation in Hollywood.

Judd, who initially spoke out against Weinstein in an exposé by The New York Times, recounted his inappropriate behavior during a business meeting, where he asked her to watch him shower. Hayek detailed her experiences with Weinstein, including his threats to kill her when she refused his advances, in a New York Times op-ed. Sciorra shared her harrowing encounters with Weinstein, including an incident where he allegedly forced sexual intercourse on her, in an expose for The New Yorker.

The women called attention to the #MeToo and #TimesUp movements, praising the "powerful sound of new voices" that have emerged to combat sexual harassment and inequality in Hollywood. They expressed hope for a future of equality, diversity, and inclusion, and encouraged support for the Time's Up Legal Defense Fund, which provides subsidized legal support to those who have experienced sexual harassment, assault, or abuse in the workplace.

Harvey Weinstein, once a powerful figure in Hollywood, has been accused of sexual harassment and assault by dozens of women. He has denied all allegations of non-consensual sex and claims of retaliation against those who rebuffed him. The 2018 Oscars were held on March 4 at the Dolby Theatre at Hollywood & Highland Center and were broadcast live on ABC.

The Internet Archive is working on a project to archive web pages and preserve broken links by crawling pages and archiving the pages they refer to. This aims to fix all broken links on the web. In a separate development, Wolfram Alpha, a search engine, has launched a new project that identifies anything in a picture. The system was trained with millions of images to learn what objects are. Although it's not always accurate, it shows remarkable human-like mistakes. The technology can be used to identify and categorize large collections of photos and could potentially be integrated into other apps.

Wolfram Alpha's new image identification project joins similar tools like Google's Goggles and Amazon's Firefly. However, it differs in that it doesn't aim to sell products based on the images it identifies. The site, ImageIdentify.com, allows users to upload photos and receive a computer-generated guess about the picture's content.

In testing, the system showed promising results, correctly identifying a miniature pinscher, the type of flower from a hike in Los Angeles, and a pizza. However, it struggled with tech products and other images, often providing vague or incorrect guesses. The site sometimes threw up an error message.

CEO Stephan Wolfram acknowledges the tool's limitations and encourages users to help improve it by indicating when the system is right or wrong. With potential improvements, the tool could have various applications, such as itemizing discoveries on a vacation or translating images of food into dietary information. Developers can use Wolfram's programming and cloud computing tools to build these applications.

The video, posted by a pro-Syrian government television presenter, shows Omran and his father living in Aleppo, now under the control of President Bashar al-Assad's forces. Omran's father stated that he did not want to leave Syria and had changed his son's name and hairstyle to protect him from being kidnapped. In a surprising declaration following his third-place finish in the Iowa caucus, Republican presidential candidate Ron Paul proclaimed, "We are all Austrians now." This statement refers to the economic philosophy known as "Austrian economics," which is more radical and libertarian than standard free-market thinking. The term "Austrian economics" can be misleading, as it originally referred to a group of classical liberal thinkers from the Austro-Hungarian Empire, but in Paul's context, it specifically refers to the thought of Ludwig Von Mises and his student Murray Rothbard.

Austrian economics rejects the legitimacy of any government intervention to protect the poor or regulate the economy. It also disagrees with the idea that the government can stabilize macroeconomic fluctuations through policies like the 2009 stimulus bill, carbon taxes, wireless spectrum auctions, or even the tweaking of short-term interest rates by central banks. Instead, Austrians believe that stimulative policies cause recessions by producing unsustainable bubbles.

However, the Austrian story of investment booms and busts doesn't actually explain recessions and unemployment. Spending patterns shift all the time without sparking a recession. The interesting question is what to do about it, and many of the original Austrians found their business cycle ideas discredited by the Great Depression, in which the bust was clearly not self-correcting and country after country stimulated real output by abandoning the gold standard and engaging in deficit spending.

Economic forecasting is a mug's game, but the application of economic theory should help us avoid the commonplace error of assuming that the future will be like the past. The conventional wisdom is that the relatively strong growth in the fourth quarter was a false dawn, and the economy is destined to stall out. However, some tragic unforeseen disaster could hit us, but if it doesn't, we should be in for a string of increasingly strong quarters and accelerating growth that put us back on the path to full employment.

The important thing to note is that each month of recovery closes the gap between the natural rate and the rate the Federal Reserve is willing to set. The downward creep of unemployment from 10.1 percent in October 2009 to 8.6 indicates a rising natural rate of interest. Improvement will lead to further improvement, with the economy growing rapidly as idle resources—workers, machinery, storefronts—are put back into use.

The recovery will be seen in concrete terms such as an increase in total bank credit, a return to a more normal level of construction, and a boost in state and local tax revenue, among other things. While this recovery won't result in a tight labor market and rapidly rising wages like in the late '90s, it will look like a magnificent boom compared to the past four years.

The U.S. Department of Labor has filed lawsuits against the Fundamentalist Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-Day Saints (FLDS) and some of its leaders, accusing them of using child labor, violating child labor laws, and not paying members for their work during the 2012-13 pecan harvest. The lawsuits, filed in federal court, allege that top church leaders, including FLDS Bishop Lyle Jeffs and Dale Barlow, pulled children out of school for weeks to work without pay.

As many as 175 children under the age of 13 were found among the 1,400 children and adults who harvested pecans at the Southern Utah Pecan Ranch in Hurricane but were not paid, according to one of the lawsuits. The lawsuits seek back wages for the 1,400 workers, but due to a lack of record-keeping, it is unclear how much is owed.

Another federal court filing accuses Paragon Contractors Corporation, a Hildale construction company that manages the pecan groves, and the company's owner, FLDS member Dan Jessop, of violating a 2007 injunction handed down when child labor violations were discovered at the pecan ranch.

The Department of Labor is seeking $1.9 million in penalties for the alleged child labor violations and has taken administrative action to collect the money from FLDS Church members Dale Barlow and Brian Jessop, and Paragon Contractors Corp. The department has also filed a lawsuit against the FLDS Church Bishop Lyle Jeffs and Barlow to claim back wages and initiated a contempt of court action against Jessop and Paragon for violating the 2007 court order that restrained them from violating child labor laws.

FLDS leaders are accused of directing schools in Hildale, Utah, and nearby Colorado City, Arizona, to close so children and adult laborers could collect pecans. David Weil, administrator of DOL’s Wage and Hour Division, said in a prepared statement that such violations of labor laws, especially concerning children, cannot be tolerated.

The article discusses the economic and political fallout of Russia's annexation of Crimea from Ukraine. Demonstrators in Kiev, Ukraine, hold a large flag combining the Ukrainian, Crimean, and Tatar flags in protest. In Russia, President Vladimir Putin's popularity soared after the annexation, but the country is facing economic sanctions from the US and EU, which are pushing Russia toward a recession. The Russian Micex stock index has plunged 13.7% this year, making it the worst performer among emerging markets, and the ruble is the second-worst performing currency against the dollar. The sanctions have targeted individuals close to Putin, including billionaires Gennady Timchenko and Arkady Rotenberg, and have led to the suspension of services for Bank Rossiya, whose main shareholder is reputed to be close to Putin. The sanctions have also led to a bill in Russia's parliament to ban transaction services based outside of the country. The article also mentions the arrest of Ukrainian billionaire Dmitry Firtash on a US warrant for bribery and other charges, and the potential for him to provide information about deals involving Russian state gas exporter OAO Gazprom that could be considered corrupt. The article concludes with the announcement that the G8 summit will not take place in Russia this year due to the crisis in Ukraine.

A group of women named Nicole at the University of Calgary have united thanks to a mass email sent by a man named Carlos Zetina, who was trying to locate a missed connection he met at a bar. The network of Nicoles can trace its start to a woman named Nicole from the Netherlands, who accidentally gave Zetina the wrong phone number. In an attempt to find the "original Nicole," Zetina emailed 246 women named Nicole or one of its variants at the university. The women started exchanging messages about the email and formed a Facebook group called "Nicole From Last Night." They planned a get-together to find the woman Zetina was looking for, which was dubbed the "Congress of Nicoles." The unusual gathering drew attention on Twitter, with users tweeting their support with the hashtag #nicolefromlastnight. Alas, the intended Nicole was not in attendance, but she eventually posted on the Facebook group, revealing herself as "the real Nicole." The women helped the original Nicole connect with the student who sent the email, and they plan to meet monthly. The whole situation, from the formation of their "little girl gang," to the matchmaking, to the story going viral, has been described as "wild" and "fun."

A Reddit user demonstrated heroism by extinguishing a fire on a boat without a fire extinguisher at hand, earning praise for their quick actions. Despite initial skepticism, the individual successfully put out the fire, showcasing bravery and resourcefulness. The incident serves as a reminder of the importance of fire safety equipment, but also highlights the spirit of good Samaritans ready to help in emergencies.

In northern India, a 47-year-old man named Feroz Khan was arrested for allegedly selling his newborn grandson on Facebook. The baby was reportedly kidnapped shortly after birth by Khan, who sought help from two temporary hospital employees to arrange the sale. The deal was made for 45,000 rupees ($830). The baby was rescued and returned to his mother, Noori Khan, who had lodged a complaint against her father. Five people, including Khan, have been charged with kidnapping and will appear in court. This incident is believed to be the first reported case of child trafficking over a social networking site in India. The case highlights the ongoing issue of child trafficking in India, with tens of thousands of children thought to be trafficked annually for various purposes, including adoption, bonded labor, begging, and sexual exploitation.
