On August 14, 2014, President Obama addressed the ongoing crises in both Ferguson, Missouri, and Iraq from his vacation at Martha's Vineyard, Massachusetts. In Ferguson, Obama called for calm amid violent protests following the death of 18-year-old Michael Brown, urging police and protesters to work together for peace and healing. He also criticized the arrest of journalists during the protests and called for openness and transparency from local police. In Iraq, Obama stated that a rescue operation for religious minorities trapped on Mount Sinjar would not be necessary, as most had already escaped. He praised the military's humanitarian efforts and continued airstrikes against militants threatening U.S. personnel and others in northern Iraq. Additionally, Missouri Governor Jay Nixon appointed an African-American captain of the Highway Patrol to oversee security in Ferguson, and U.S. Attorney General Eric Holder offered technical assistance to help maintain public safety without excessive force. The Justice Department, the FBI, and the St. Louis County prosecutor's office are all investigating Brown's death.

In a surprising turn of events, Senator John McCain has tentatively agreed to publish a column attacking Russian President Vladimir Putin's leadership in the Russian news site Pravda. This follows Putin's criticism of the United States in a column published in The New York Times. Dmitry Sudakov, the English editor of Pravda, welcomed the offer, despite their differing political views. The agreement marks a significant development in U.S-Russian relations, and it's noteworthy that McCain did not need to hire a public relations firm for this arrangement. Pravda, once an official organ for the Communist Party, is now distinctly anti-Western but no longer operates as such. The column is expected to address issues such as democracy, human rights, and Russia's involvement in Syria. This new chapter in U.S-Russian relations is being welcomed by The Cable, who played a part in facilitating the agreement.

Twenty-five years after the infamous art heist at Boston's Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum, law enforcement officials have released new surveillance footage showing an unauthorized visitor entering the museum the night before the robbery. The video, captured by museum security cameras, shows a security guard granting access to an unidentified man at about 12:49 a.m. on March 17, 1990, nearly exactly 24 hours before the heist. The man is also seen getting out of a car matching the general description of one reported to be parked outside the museum minutes before the theft.

Law enforcement officials hope that releasing the footage will assist in identifying the man or the vehicle in the video, and are seeking the public's help in doing so. The stolen artwork, including Vermeer's "The Concert" and Rembrandt's "The Storm on the Sea of Galilee," is worth at least $500 million. No one has ever been charged in the heist, and a $5 million reward has been offered by the museum for information that leads to the recovery of the stolen artwork in good condition.

The video footage was recently examined by investigators and was not released earlier. US Attorney Carmen Ortiz said that a team of investigators began reviewing the original evidence, and that one of them, Assistant US Attorney Robert Fisher, requested the video, which was in the custody of the FBI. Officials then decided to release it to the public in hopes it could lead to new information.

The release of the video refocuses the spotlight on Richard Abath, a rock musician moonlighting as a security guard who fell under suspicion soon after the robbery. Authorities did not say Abath was the guard in the video, but three officials familiar with the investigation confirmed to the Globe that it is he. It is not immediately clear why the surveillance footage of the night before the robbery had not been made public before, and whether it was viewed by the FBI in the initial investigation.

The heist remains Boston's most enduring mystery, and authorities are hopeful that the release of the new video will bring new leads in the case. The museum remains committed to the return of all 13 works to their rightful place, and has offered a $5 million reward for their recovery.

The U.S. and China have imposed new sanctions against North Korea at the United Nations, aiming to hinder the development of Pyongyang's nuclear and missile programs following its recent atomic bomb test. Meanwhile, IBM's Sequoia supercomputer has taken the top spot on the list of the world's fastest supercomputers, installed at the US Department of Energy's Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory in California. Sequoia, which is capable of calculating in one hour what would take 6.7 billion people using hand calculators 320 years to complete, will be used for simulations to extend the life of aging nuclear weapons and avoid the need for real-world underground tests. The U.S. has reclaimed the lead in high-performance computing, but its tally of three computers in the top 10 was worse than six months ago. China and Germany both have two supercomputers, while Japan, France, and Italy have one. IBM proved to be the leading manufacturer, claiming five out of the top 10 spots. Sequoia is more energy-efficient than the Fujitsu model, consuming 7.9 megawatts compared to the K computer's 12.6 megawatts. Government laboratories in Europe have already expressed interest in the IBM supercomputer. The first computer to take the top position on the list was the CM-5/1024 in 1993, designed by Thinking Machines. According to Prof Dongarra, Sequoia is 273,930 times faster. The list is published every six months by German Professor Hans Meuer and US-based Professor Jack Dongarra, who stated it is unlikely that another manufacturer will overtake IBM in the next year.

West Virginia Democratic state Senate candidate Richard Ojeda was brutally beaten during a cookout on Sunday, just two days before his primary election. The attacker, Jonathan Porter, was arrested and charged with malicious assault. Ojeda suffered multiple fractures to his head and face and was transported to a hospital in Charleston. He initially planned to delay surgery until after the election but later had to undergo surgery to fix his face. Ojeda believes the attack was politically motivated, citing the intense poverty, corruption, and nepotism that plagues the region and his campaign for transparency and good government. Porter rammed vehicles and escaped after the attack, and others at the cookout tried to stop him. Ojeda's primary opponent, incumbent state Sen. Ark Kirkendoll, wished him a speedy recovery and condemned violence in politics. Ojeda has received threatening phone calls for weeks while campaigning for the District 7 State Senate seat. He will be released from the hospital on Monday to campaign and be with his family ahead of tomorrow's primary election. The attack is being investigated by the West Virginia State Police.

The document discusses the importance of habeas corpus, a legal procedure that prevents the government from holding individuals indefinitely without showing cause, and its historical significance since the signing of the Magna Carta in 1215. The Founders of the United States Constitution enshrined habeas corpus as a fundamental right in the first article of the Constitution. However, the Military Commissions Act (MCA) of 2006 revoked the right to habeas corpus for individuals detained at Guantánamo Bay and for foreigners labeled as "enemy combatants" anywhere in the world, including legal residents of the U.S.

The document also focuses on the application of habeas corpus to the detainees at Guantánamo. The government has little evidence against most of the men detained, and many were sold into captivity by warlords for bounties. Only 10 have ever been charged with any crime. CCR has been filing habeas corpus petitions on behalf of the detainees since 2004, but the Bush administration has prevented them from getting a fair hearing in the courts.

The document further discusses the recent court ruling in favor of two research chimpanzees, Hercules and Leo, at Stony Brook University in New York, granting them the right to have their day in court through a writ of habeas corpus. This is the first time in U.S. history that an animal has been covered by a writ of habeas corpus, and the ruling could force the university to release the primates and potentially sway additional judges to do the same with other research animals.

The MCA has eroded the foundation of the legal and constitutional framework by compromising the core legal value and necessary protection against the executive branch. The document argues that if we do not defend the right to habeas corpus, we all lose. The document ends with an update on the court case involving Hercules and Leo, which has been moved back from 6 May to 27 May. The judge will hear legal arguments regarding whether Hercules and Leo should remain at Stony Brook. The case is seen as a significant step forward in the fight for the rights of non-human animals.

The British government has given the go-ahead for a controversial four-lane highway to be constructed under Stonehenge, a prehistoric landmark and one of Britain's top tourist attractions. The new 1.8-mile tunnel is aimed at solving a decades-old traffic problem caused by the busy A303 trunk road that runs past Stonehenge. The tunnel is part of a $2.45 billion program of investment in the region and is expected to cut traffic congestion.

The plan has been met with opposition from some campaign groups, who argue that the tunnel would cause irreparable damage to the landscape and archaeology of the area. However, supporters of the plan, including heritage charity National Trust, argue that it will make Stonehenge a better place to visit by removing the sight and sound of traffic for visitors.

The Stonehenge Alliance, a campaign group, has called for a much longer tunnel to minimize the road's impact on the landscape and archaeology. The group argues that any tunnel shorter than 2.7 miles would do irreparable damage to the site. The public consultation on the scheme will run until March 5.

The A303 currently passes within a few hundred meters of Stonehenge and has been a source of frustration for visitors and locals alike due to the traffic congestion. The tunnel is expected to improve journey times and reduce congestion on the road.

The proposal for a tunnel past Stonehenge has a long and chequered history, with plans for a tunnel first being mooted in 1995. However, the plan has been shelved multiple times due to concerns about the environmental impact and rising costs of construction. The idea resurfaced in 2014 and was given support by the coalition government in December of that year.

The construction of the tunnel is expected to take several years and will be a significant investment in the region's infrastructure. The project has been met with mixed reactions, with some welcoming the improvement in travel times and others expressing concern about the impact on the landscape and archaeology of the area. YouTube, Google's video site, is set to renew funding for 30-40% of its original channels, following a $100 million investment in over a hundred new channels last year. Channels that failed lacked a commitment to the platform and a focus on audience building. The top 25 new channels now average more than a million views a week, and the top 33 have over 100,000 subscribers.

The investment in original channels marks a significant shift for YouTube as a funding source for programming, with premium producers now considering producing original content for YouTube.

In a weekly news conference on Capitol Hill, House Democratic Leader Nancy Pelosi of California rejected the idea of funding President Donald Trump's proposed border wall in exchange for helping hundreds of thousands of young immigrants avoid deportation. Pelosi stated that funding for the wall and legal protections for the Dreamers should not be linked, as they are two separate subjects.

The House and Senate approved a stopgap bill on Thursday to keep the government funded through Dec. 21. The measure now goes to the White House for Trump's signature, allowing for ceremonies honoring former President George H.W. Bush, who passed away on Nov. 30. However, Trump has expressed his desire for the next funding package to include at least $5 billion for his proposed wall, a demand that Democrats have rejected.

Trump and Pelosi are set to meet at the White House on Tuesday. In a tweet on Thursday, Trump warned of potential danger at the U.S.-Mexico border in Arizona and demanded that Pelosi and Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer approve border security and the wall.

Pelosi stated that the lame-duck Congress should pass a half-dozen government funding bills that key committees have already agreed on, along with a separate measure funding the Department of Homeland Security, which oversees the border. Funding for the homeland agency should address border security and does not necessarily include a wall, Pelosi said.

Most Democrats consider the wall "immoral, ineffective, and expensive," Pelosi said, noting that Trump promised during the 2016 campaign that Mexico would pay for it, an idea Mexican leaders have repeatedly rejected. Even if Mexico did pay for the wall, "it's immoral still," Pelosi said.

Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer said a bipartisan Senate plan for $1.6 billion in border security funding does not include money for the 30-foot-high concrete wall Trump has envisioned. The funding "can only be used for fencing" and technology that experts say is appropriate and makes sense as a security feature, Schumer said.

If Republicans object to the proposal because of pressure from Trump, Schumer suggested lawmakers should approve six appropriations bills and a separate measure extending current funding for Homeland Security. Either option would avert a partial government shutdown, which lawmakers from both parties oppose.

Schumer called the spat over the wall unnecessary, noting that the administration has not spent more than $1 billion approved for border security in the budget year that ended Sept. 30. "The idea that they haven't spent last year's money and they're demanding such a huge amount this year makes no sense at all," he said.

Senate Appropriations Committee Chairman Richard Shelby prefers to include Homeland Security in an omnibus package containing seven unresolved spending bills for the current budget year. "I believe the best route is to keep all seven together and pass them," the Alabama Republican told reporters on Thursday. Lawmakers have made significant progress in recent weeks on the seven spending bills. "I'd like to conclude it," he said.

Missouri Sen. Roy Blunt, a member of Republican leadership, stated that the key question is whether Trump will sign a bill without funding for the wall. "It doesn't matter how much appetite there is for a shutdown anywhere else, if he is willing to have a shutdown over this issue," Blunt said. "He has given every indication that he would."

In a dramatic turn of events, Senate Minority Leader Mitch McConnell has successfully averted a fiscal crisis by brokering a deal with Democrats to reopen the federal government and prevent a federal debt default. This marks the fourth time in less than three years that McConnell has played a key role in fiscal matters, negotiating two tax deals and two debt-limit measures that have averted potential financial meltdowns.

However, McConnell's involvement in these bipartisan deals may impact his re-election bid. In Kentucky, he faces a primary challenger from the right who accuses him of selling out conservative principles, and a fresh-faced Democratic challenger from the left who depicts him as part of the "disease of dysfunction" in Washington.

Initially, McConnell's muted involvement in the early rounds of the government shutdown fight led some to believe he was avoiding his role. However, McConnell has now announced his intention to make his bipartisan efforts a hallmark of both his primary and general election campaign next year.

The latest deal, which defied the skeptics, includes the extension of the Bush-era tax cuts for more than 98 percent of workers and a permanent estate tax exemption up to $5 million. McConnell argues that this exemption will benefit family farms and small businesses in his state.

The spending cuts in the 2011 Budget Control Act, also known as the sequester cuts, represent real reductions in government funding that McConnell mentions every chance he gets. During the negotiations for reopening the government and avoiding default, McConnell's main goal was to protect his winnings from the two previous deals.

The government shutdown and potential default were a result of a series of complicated relationships, internecine Republican warfare, and rare Democratic unity. House Speaker John Boehner was overrun by his own conference, and even Vice President Joe Biden was shut out of direct negotiations with lawmakers this time around.

McConnell's strategy was to protect his winnings from the two previous deals, such as the repeal of an unpopular tax on medical devices that helps fund the Affordable Care Act. However, Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid outfoxed McConnell, shutting down the bipartisan group and forcing the talks into just a negotiation between the two Senate leaders.

The final deal gave Reid everything he wanted but set up new fights, in January over government funding and later next year over the next debt-ceiling increase. McConnell admitted that his hand was weak, but he was trying to get a better position on the field.

In a separate development, House Speaker John Boehner was pulled aside by President Barack Obama for a grilling during the second day of the government shutdown. Boehner admitted that he had been overrun by his own conference. The fiscal drama turned on a series of complicated relationships, internecine Republican warfare, and rare Democratic unity.

The shutdown was a result of the GOP's Obamacare strategy, which McConnell now admits was a mistake. Obama and Reid stuck together, emerging as the political victors. Their hard-ball tactics were designed to "break the fever" brought on by the tea party, but it also helped drive the country to the edge of default.

Republicans cycled through every option possible during the three-week standoff to save face. Their Obamacare demands devolved from repeal and defund to a delay of the individual mandate. They revived the idea of a "grand bargain" on taxes and government spending but Reid openly laughed when Boehner raised it during a White House meeting. They offered a more narrow proposal to replace the sequester cuts for two years. Then, they went back to Obamacare.

Nothing worked. By Wednesday, Republicans just needed a way out, agreeing to a bill that looked almost identical to what they rejected three weeks earlier: a debt-limit increase until Feb. 7, an extension of federal funding through Jan. 15, and no binding strings attached.

This account of the behind-the-scenes drama was drawn from dozens of interviews with key players in Congress and at the White House. The look back reveals how Republicans waged a fight on Obamacare that their leaders knew they would probably lose but pushed anyway because many in their ranks truly believed that Democrats, like they've done so often before, would fold — especially under the threat of an historic default on U.S. debt.

McConnell told his colleagues this week that his party should "never" be put in the same political position again. Boehner told WLW radio on Wednesday, "We fought the good fight. We just didn't win." The buildup to shutdown began in late August when Boehner promised a "whale of a fight." Obama and Reid got on the same page early on, agreeing during strategy sessions over the summer that they wouldn't give up anything until Republicans renewed the debt limit and government funding. Democrats never believed that Boehner could deliver the 217 House votes he needed to cut a deal. They stood firm, and Boehner was forced to fold.

The document discusses President-elect Donald Trump's intervention in federal procurement, specifically targeting the F-35 fighter jet contract held by Lockheed Martin. Trump's actions could potentially be used as a weapon against individual companies to further his own political and policy agendas, which is unprecedented in federal contracting.

The most famous example of the federal government canceling a contract came in 1991, when Defense Secretary Dick Cheney terminated a contract with General Dynamics and McDonnell Douglas to design and build the Navy’s A-12 stealth attack plane. Trump could potentially terminate a contract for convenience, which would involve a disruption in the bureaucracy. Contracting officers are independent of their superiors, including the president, and must make an independent determination that terminating a contract is in the best interest of the country. Trump's actions could have significant implications across the government and economy, creating new uncertainty for both companies and contracting officers. His tweets can have an immediate impact on a company’s share price, and even when he doesn't make an explicit threat, his willingness to involve himself in individual contracts can influence a company’s decision-making. The ultimate result of Trump threatening to terminate federal contracts could be higher costs for the government, as companies faced with the increased risk of termination or negative publicity from an angry tweet from the president would likely raise their prices in response.

However, the AP found that the tweet "fell short of AP standards by omitting essential context."

The AP review found that among the individuals Clinton met with at the State Department who were outside of government, an extraordinary proportion had donated to her family's foundation personally or by way of some other entity. The AP wrote that this indicated "her possible ethics challenges if elected president." Specifically, the AP found that 85 of the 154 people who'd had in-person or phone meetings scheduled with Clinton and who weren't government officials were also foundation contributors, according to the State Department calendars that were available.

However, the AP tweet promoting the article "omitted the important distinction between discretionary meetings and official meetings." The now-deleted tweet gave the impression that a far higher percentage of Clinton's total meetings while secretary were with donors than was concluded by the story's analysis, given that the 154 people included in the review did not encompass the many government officials she was interacting with during her tenure, meetings that made up the bulk of her workday.

Clinton and her campaign blasted the story not long after it was published. Speaking with CNN's Anderson Cooper last month, the Democratic presidential nominee said of the growing controversy regarding the relationship between the State Department under her leadership and the Clinton Foundation: "I know there is a lot of smoke and there is no fire." Of the AP report, Clinton said: "It draws a conclusion and makes a suggestion that my meetings with people like the late, great Elie Wiesel or Melinda Gates or the Nobel Prize winner Muhammad Yunus were somehow due to connections with the foundation instead of their status as highly respected global leaders."

Clinton campaign spokesman Brian Fallon said the AP "cherry-picked a limited subset of Secretary's Clinton's schedule to give a distorted portrayal of how often she crossed paths with individuals connected to charitable donations to the Clinton Foundation." The AP review included only the portion of Clinton's daily schedules it had acquired following a Freedom of Information Act request. Last week, the State Department said it would produce the remainder of Clinton's schedules by Oct. 17 after having previously said they would not be released until December, weeks after the election.

The AP memo explaining the decision regarding the Clinton tweet also addressed the organization's new policy regarding the deletion of tweets, a practice it said was formally left to "AP news managers to decide on a case-by-case basis." "We have to be the AP, wherever our work is being distributed," says executive editor Kathleen Carroll in the memo, which announced that messages on Twitter would now be given "the same internal review and response process as other AP content."

The 1917 painting "Nu couche (sur le cote gauche)" by Amedeo Modigliani was auctioned at Sotheby's in New York for over $157 million on May 14, 2018. This sale was part of Sotheby's "Impressionist & Modern Art" evening sale, which also featured works by Pablo Picasso, Claude Monet, Edvard Munch, and Georgia O'Keeffe. The painting had the highest pre-auction estimate at $150 million, but failed to set a new record for the most expensive painting ever sold, with Leonardo da Vinci's "Salvator Mundi" selling last year at Christie's for $450 million. The painting caused a scandal when exhibited at Modigliani's first solo show in Paris in 1917, with the police demanding the immediate closure of the show. The painting was consigned by John Magnier, who had purchased it in 2003 at Christie's for $26.9 million. The painting was recently included in Tate Modern's exhibition of Modigliani's work in London.

Researchers at Johns Hopkins University and the National Institutes of Health have discovered a compound that significantly enhances learning and memory in mice with Down syndrome-like conditions. The compound, a sonic hedgehog pathway agonist, was injected into mice on the day of birth, and it was found to normalize the growth of the cerebellum, a part of the brain that is typically smaller in individuals with Down syndrome.

The researchers, led by Roger Reeves, treated Down syndrome-like mice with the compound and found that it enabled the animals to perform as well as normal mice in tests, such as navigating a water maze. The compound has not yet been proven safe for use in humans with Down syndrome, but the researchers are hopeful that it could lead to the development of drugs like it.

Reeves and his team used mice that were genetically engineered to have extra copies of about half of the genes found on human chromosome 21, which caused them to have many characteristics similar to people with Down syndrome. The compound was injected into the mice just once, on the day of birth, while their cerebellums were still developing.

The researchers caution that the compound's potential to become a human drug is complicated, as altering an important biological chain of events like sonic hedgehog could have many unintended effects throughout the body, such as raising the risk of cancer by triggering inappropriate growth. However, the team plans to continue researching the compound to find more targeted ways to safely harness its power in the cerebellum.

Down syndrome is a condition that occurs when people have three, rather than the usual two, copies of chromosome 21. As a result, people with Down syndrome have extra copies of the more than 300 genes that are housed on that chromosome, leading to intellectual disabilities, distinctive facial features, and sometimes heart problems and other health effects. Since the condition involves so many genes, developing treatments for it is a formidable challenge.

The study was funded by the Down Syndrome Research and Treatment Foundation, Research Down Syndrome, the National Institute of Child Health and Human Development, the intramural programs of the National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism, the National Institute of Mental Health, and the National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke. The findings were published in the Sept. 4 issue of Science Translational Medicine.

Rodney King, the former Los Angeles motorist whose 1991 beating by police was captured on video and sparked the 1992 Los Angeles riots, died early Monday morning at his home in Rialto, California. He was 47. Just hours before his death, King spoke with Damon Feldman, a friend and organizer of a celebrity boxing match in which King was scheduled to fight Jose Canseco in August. Feldman said King was excited about the upcoming event and looked forward to getting back in the ring. However, King's fiancée, Cynthia Kelley, told friends that King had been drinking all day Saturday and smoked marijuana in the hours leading up to his death. Kelley said she found King naked and screaming in the backyard around 5:00 AM, and discovered him in the bottom of the pool shortly after. Paramedics attempted to revive King, but were unsuccessful. The cause of death is not yet known.

In a shocking turn of events, a New Jersey psychotherapist, Diane Sylvia, has been charged with soliciting a violent attack on a man who she claimed had been blackmailing her for years. According to a criminal complaint unsealed on Monday, Sylvia, a licensed clinical social worker, conspired with an FBI agent posing as a hitman to carry out the assault.

The plot unfolded after one of Sylvia's patients, who had past connections to an unspecified organized criminal gang, revealed this information during therapy sessions. Sylvia, 58, allegedly expressed her desire for revenge and provided the undercover agent with details about her intended victim.

During their meetings, Sylvia reportedly requested that the victim's "pretty little face" be bashed in, and suggested breaking one arm and messing up his face. She also specified that the attack should render him unable to work out.

Investigators found that Sylvia went as far as to buy a prepaid cellphone to communicate with the undercover agent and provided the "hitman" with her victim's license plate. She ultimately paid the undercover agent $5,000 to carry out the assault.

Sylvia was charged with one count of solicitation to commit a crime of violence in federal court in Camden. If convicted, she faces up to five years in prison and a $250,000 fine. She was released on $50,000 bail and is scheduled to make her initial appearance before a federal magistrate in Camden.

Sylvia's professional profile on Psychology Today describes her therapy practice as treating individuals, couples, families, and children. Her profile also states, "Our words and thoughts are powerful and help create the life we desire. The most important component of therapy is the relationship between the client and therapist and the client's willingness to make the decision to change."

This incident raises serious questions about the ethical boundaries of therapy and the potential misuse of professional relationships for personal gain. The investigation is ongoing, and further details are expected to be released as the case progresses.

The Parnell's mustached bat (Pteronotus parnellii) is a species of bat native to North, South, and Central America. It prefers a habitat within moist areas but can also live in arid deciduous forests. The bat can have a wingspan of up to 1.9 feet and bears squat, pointed ears. It does not have a nose leaf, but its lips are pointed upwards creating a funnel-shaped mouth. The bat prefers to roost in caves and tunnels and will occasionally roost with other bat species. The Parnell's mustached bat appears on the IUCN Red List with a conservation status of "Least Concern."

A recent study published in Frontiers of Neuroscience has shown that like humans, mustached bats use the left and right sides of their brains to process different aspects of sounds. The study found that the left hemisphere is better at processing fast sounds, while the right hemisphere is better at processing slow sounds. This asymmetrical sound processing is thought to be important for communication and sonar use in bats. The study was supported by grants from the National Institute on Deafness and Communication Disorders and the Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute of Child Health and Human Development. The authors report having no personal financial interests related to the study. The findings of this study could potentially help in understanding certain human language disorders and improving computer speech recognition.

The Internet Archive is working on a project to archive web pages as they are created and preserve links to the versions of the pages that were live when a page was written. This is aimed at fixing broken links on the web by replacing them with links to the archived pages or providing companion links to the original intended content.

In a heartwarming incident, a woman named Debbie Bolton, the co-founder and global chief sales officer at Norwex, was praised for her kindness after she helped a father who was struggling to find a ticket for his two-year-old daughter on a plane. The father was denied a free seat for his daughter as she was over the age limit by two months. Kevin Leslie, a fellow flier, shared the story on Facebook, which quickly went viral with over 45,500 shares.

Without hesitation, Debbie Bolton paid for the $749 ticket for the little girl. The father was overwhelmed with joy and tried to thank her, but she refused and walked away. It was later identified that the woman was Debbie Bolton, and her company, Norwex, confirmed her identity. Employees of Norwex praised her for her act of kindness and described her as kind, caring, and generous.

The story was shared by Leslie because he believes "people like this need to be heard about." Debbie Bolton said she just "did what anyone else would do," but since the story reached many people, she hopes her action might inspire others to make a positive impact in someone's life. The Internet Archive's project and Debbie Bolton's act of kindness highlight the importance of kindness and generosity in our society.

"Popstar: Never Stop Never Stopping" is a comedy film written by Andy Samberg, Akiva Schaffer, and Jorma Taccone, and directed by Schaffer and Taccone. The film stars Samberg, Imogen Poots, and Bill Hader, and is classified as 14A.

The film is a satire of the modern pop music industry, with a focus on the life and career of a Bieber-like superstar named Conner4Real (played by Samberg). The film follows Conner's struggle for relevance and the effects of a business that prioritizes either youth or nostalgia. The film features numerous celebrity cameos, including Questlove, Nas, Mariah Carey, A$AP Rocky, and Usher, among others.

The film is a homage to documentaries such as Bieber's Never Say Never, Backstreet Boys' Show 'Em What You're Made Of, and One Direction's This Is Us, and combines straightforward filming with interviews from celebrities offering their takes on Conner4Real as a musician and what the Style Boyz meant to them. The film is less a spoof than it is a homage, and it holds a magnifying glass up to the culture that we've all had a hand in creating.

The film is well-received, with critics praising its humor, thought-provoking commentary, and the performances of the cast, particularly Samberg's portrayal of Conner4Real. The film is a pitch-perfect take on modern-day pop stardom, the music industry, and celebrity culture. It is a must-see for fans of the Lonely Island and anyone interested in a hilarious and insightful look at the world of pop music.

The Graham-Cassidy ObamaCare repeal bill, which aims to give states more control over health care, is facing significant opposition, according to a new poll by the left-leaning Public Policy Polling. The poll found that only 24% of voters support the bill, while 50% disapprove. The Senate is set to vote on the bill next week, but without a Congressional Budget Office analysis of its impact on premiums and the number of people covered. The poll was highlighted by several Democratic groups seeking to defend the Affordable Care Act.

The bill would convert ObamaCare's insurer subsidies and Medicaid expansion funds into block grants, allowing states to design their own health care programs. However, the poll found that 77% of voters agreed with late-night host Jimmy Kimmel that no one should be denied coverage because they cannot afford it.

Sen. John McCain announced on Friday that he cannot "in good conscience" vote for the bill, likely ending Republicans' latest effort to repeal and replace the Affordable Care Act. McCain's "no" vote means it is unlikely Republicans will be able to repeal and replace Obamacare before September 30, as Sen. Rand Paul of Kentucky and Sen. Susan Collins of Maine have also expressed opposition to the bill. It's unclear where Alaska Sen. Lisa Murkowski stands on the issue.

The bill appears to be polling at least somewhat higher than the earlier GOP ObamaCare repeal bill, which got just 12% approval in a USA Today/Suffolk University poll in June. A study from the Brookings Institution found that at least 21 million people would lose health-care coverage under the new plan by 2026.

The latest survey comes as Republicans are struggling to pass the bill, with key senators expressing concerns and the White House continuing to engage with senators to try to solidify support for the bill. Democrats are praising McCain for his decision to oppose the bill and are open to bipartisan talks to stabilize Obamacare marketplaces.

The 51st Country Music Association Awards, held on November 8, 2017, began with a tribute to the victims of the Las Vegas shooting and other recent tragedies. Hosts Carrie Underwood and Brad Paisley also took the opportunity to poke fun at the CMA's previous ban on journalists asking artists about politics and gun rights. The duo performed a parody song titled "Before He Tweets," which mocked President Trump's Twitter habits and nuclear tensions with North Korea. The CMA Awards, which aired on ABC, were filled with memorable moments, including Taylor Swift's surprise win for Musical Event of the Year. The event was a political-free zone, but Paisley and Underwood couldn't resist making light of the political climate. They joked about being unable to sing political songs like "Harper Valley DNC," "Hold Me Closer, Bernie Sanders," and "Stand By Your Manafort." The highlight of their parodies was "Before He Tweets," which took down the President's habitual, early-morning tweeting. The payoff line was a chorus as cutting as it was humorous, referencing the high-stakes game some believe Trump is playing with North Korea. This marks Paisley and Underwood's 10th consecutive time hosting the CMA Awards.

The article discusses two main topics: millennials' home-buying habits and the introduction of six-second ads in sports broadcasts.

Regarding home-buying trends, a report from real-estate website Zillow reveals that millennials are the largest group of homebuyers in the US, with the median age of a homebuyer being 36. Spencer Rascoff, Zillow's CEO, attributes the delay in first-time home purchases by millennials to limited starter-home inventory, causing them to rent longer and buy more expensive homes when they do decide to purchase.

On the other hand, Fox Sports is experimenting with six-second ads during sports broadcasts, starting with the Cowboys-Broncos game. T-Mobile will be the first to test these ads, with Visa following suit for its Hurricane Harvey relief efforts. The shorter ad format is part of Fox's strategy to improve the TV viewing experience and compete with platforms offering fewer or no commercials.

The shorter ads are expected to become commonplace in Fox's sports broadcasts, including Major League Baseball and NFL games, as well as college football and Major League Soccer on FS1. Advertisers are charged similar rates for six-second spots as for 15-second ads, with a 30-second ad in Fox's Sunday games costing about $775,000 this season.

In conclusion, millennials are indeed interested in purchasing homes but are waiting longer due to limited starter-home inventory, and Fox Sports is introducing six-second ads to improve the TV viewing experience and compete with digital platforms.

The U.S. housing market is experiencing a significant downturn, with home prices falling at an accelerating rate in major cities across the country. The Wall Street Journal's latest survey found that prices declined in all 28 major metropolitan areas tracked during the fourth quarter compared to a year earlier. The housing market may take five to six more years to recover, according to TrimTabs Investment Research. The size of the year-to-year price declines was greater than the previous quarter's in all but three of the markets. Inventory levels are rising in many markets as the number of unsold homes piles up. Home values dropped the most in cities that have already been hard-hit by the housing bust, including Miami, Orlando, Atlanta, and Chicago. However, price declines also intensified in several markets that so far have escaped the brunt of the downturn, including Seattle and Portland, Oregon. The biggest risk to the housing market is that job growth doesn't pick up, and the threat of future price declines has led to a standoff between buyers and sellers. Bargains abound, but few are interested or eligible to take advantage. The home ownership rate has taken a big plunge, despite the fact that home prices have fallen, affordability is much improved, and inventories of new and existing homes are still running quite high. Eleven percent of the houses in America are empty, and younger Americans have seen what home ownership has done to their friends and families and many want no part of it. Credit has become very nearly elitist, and banks, Fannie, and Freddie are holding on to hundreds of thousands of properties, and we don't know exactly when or how they'll sell them.

The New York Times has decided not to include Ted Cruz's new biography "A Time For Truth" on its forthcoming bestsellers list, despite selling more copies in its first week than all but two of the Times' bestselling titles. The book, published on June 30, sold 11,854 copies, surpassing 18 out of the 20 titles that will appear on the bestseller list for the week ending July 4. The Times stated that the book did not meet their criteria for inclusion, citing an analysis of book sales that goes beyond just the number of books sold. The Times spokesperson, Eileen Murphy, explained that their goal is to reflect authentic best sellers, considering not just numbers, but patterns of sales for every book. HarperCollins, the book's publisher, and the Cruz campaign declined to comment on the matter. The book has sold more copies in a single week than Rand Paul's "Taking a Stand" and Marco Rubio's "American Dreams," and is currently ranked high on various other lists. The Times later clarified that the overwhelming evidence suggested that sales were limited to strategic bulk purchases.

The upcoming NATO summit will see leaders approve a rapid-reaction military force to respond more quickly to threats, particularly in light of Russia's continued efforts to destabilize and break up Ukraine. This force, known as a "spearhead" unit, will consist of troops from various member countries and will be capable of deployment within two days. The unit will have a permanent command center and supply depots located in different regions, reducing the need for troops to fly in all their equipment.

NATO Secretary-General Anders Fogh Rasmussen stated that the spearhead could include several thousand troops, supported by air, sea, and special forces. The existing response force currently takes five days for the first units to arrive.

The summit, originally intended to mark the end of the NATO-led mission in Afghanistan, will instead signal a shift towards the defense of Europe as the alliance's primary concern. Canadian Prime Minister Stephen Harper is set to attend the summit, visiting London to promote trade and investment before joining NATO member country leaders in Wales.

The rapid-response force will not assist Kiev, which is currently battling pro-Moscow rebels and is taking steps to apply for membership in NATO. It remains unclear when or if Kiev might be admitted into the alliance, which has an agreement to defend member countries against attack.

NATO appears to have shelved a proposal to permanently station alliance troops in new bases along its eastern flank, a measure sought by members such as Poland as a means of providing a deterrent to further Russian aggression. Member countries such as Germany rejected the idea due to concerns it could provoke Moscow.

Canada will be asked to contribute soldiers and equipment to NATO's new high-alert force. However, the Canadian government has not yet committed to regular contributions, stating they will "consider all measures accordingly" and look forward to discussions at the summit.

The summit marks a significant moment for NATO, as it faces its greatest crisis since the Berlin and Cuban crises of the Cold War. NATO can demonstrate its commitment to standing up to Russian incursions or risk fading into irrelevance by issuing empty communiqués, according to Fen Hampson, director of the Global Security and Politics program at the Centre for International Governance Innovation in Waterloo, Ontario.

In related news, Ukrainian President Petro Poroshenko accused Russia of "direct and undisguised aggression" in a speech on Monday. Poroshenko stated that Russian forces are helping the rebels to turn the tide of the war, a claim dismissed by Russia, which continues to deny actively supporting the rebels. The latest setback for Ukraine occurred in the south, where troops had to retreat from a new rebel advance near the city of Mariupol.

Russian President Vladimir Putin called for immediate negotiations on the "statehood" of southeast regions of Ukraine, blaming Kiev's leadership for refusing to enter into direct political talks with the separatists. European Union leaders decided at a summit on Saturday to step up economic sanctions against Russia unless it pulls its soldiers back from the war.

The Harper government is wary of proposals to permanently station NATO troops in new bases due to insufficient detail on costs, troop contributions, and rules of engagement. The Canadian government has also balked at a push for NATO countries to boost military spending to at least 2% of GDP, a commitment being called for at the summit. Canada currently spends roughly 1% on defense.

Ottawa has a ship, six fighter jets, and rotating shifts of Canadian Armed Forces members on training exercises in Europe to reassure NATO member countries concerned about further Russian aggression in the region. Canada has also matched sanctions imposed on Russians and Ukrainians linked to Moscow's efforts to menace Ukraine.

In southeast Ohio, a manhunt is underway for 23-year-old Arron Lawson, who is wanted for multiple murders and aggravated murder charges. On October 12, 2017, authorities found multiple people fatally shot and another stabbed and critically wounded at a pair of residences in the area. The victims, who have not been identified, include a 7-year-old boy, Devin Holston, whose body was found hidden in a home.

Lawson was last seen in a blue truck in Ironton, Ohio, and a brief chase ensued when deputies tried to apprehend him, but he crashed into a ditch and fled into the woods. The investigation is being assisted by the Ohio Bureau of Criminal Investigation, and agents from the crime-scene and cyber-unit are involved.

The initial report of the slayings recalled details from a still-unsolved homicide case that occurred in rural southern Ohio last year. However, investigators have no indication of a connection between the cases. The deaths occurred roughly 40 miles southeast of the Piketon area, where eight people from the Rhoden family were found shot to death in four homes in April 2016.

The schools in the Rock Hill district were closed on October 12 due to the attacks. The bodies have been sent to the Montgomery County Coroner’s Office for autopsy, and the names of the victims have not been released yet as next of kin are still being notified. Law enforcement agencies from across Ohio and the Tri-State area are assisting in the search for Lawson.

The Hillary Clinton campaign and the Democratic National Committee (DNC) funded research that led to the creation of a dossier containing allegations about President Trump's connections to Russia. The research was conducted by Fusion GPS, a Washington-based firm, and the dossier was compiled by Christopher Steele, a former British intelligence officer. Marc E. Elias, a lawyer representing the Clinton campaign and the DNC, retained Fusion GPS in April 2016 to conduct the research. Before that, Fusion GPS's research into Trump was funded by an unknown Republican client during the GOP primary. The Clinton campaign and the DNC continued to fund Fusion GPS's research through the end of October 2016, days before the election. It is unclear how much of the information gathered by Fusion GPS was shared with the campaign and the DNC, and who in those organizations was aware of the roles of Fusion GPS and Steele. The dossier has become a central focus of investigations into the Trump campaign's possible connections to Russia, and the president and his allies have argued that the investigations are politically motivated. The FBI has been investigating whether Trump associates helped the Russians in their efforts to disrupt the 2016 election. The dossier was published by BuzzFeed News in January, and Steele previously worked in Russia for British intelligence. Some of the details in the dossier have been confirmed by U.S. intelligence agencies, while others have not been verified. The Clinton campaign and the DNC have not commented on the arrangement, and Fusion GPS has declined to comment.

JPMorgan Chase, the largest bank in the U.S., is set to invest $100 million over five years to aid Detroit's housing repairs, blight removal, job training, and economic development projects. This investment, a mix of loans and grants, comes as Detroit nears the end of the nation's largest municipal bankruptcy proceedings, with an estimated $18 billion in long-term debt. The city is currently lobbying for nearly $200 million in funding from Michigan lawmakers, who are cautious about using taxpayer dollars for a major metropolis bailout.

The funds, to be announced publicly by Jamie Dimon on Wednesday, will focus on city revitalization efforts. Half of the money will support community projects lacking capital, with $25 million allocated to organizations like the Detroit Land Bank Authority and the Detroit Blight Removal Task Force. The remaining funds will be divided among workforce training, small-business assistance, and economic growth projects such as a new streetcar system.

JPMorgan's investment follows a five-year initiative announced in December that infused $250 million into Detroit and other major cities for job-skills training. The bank has faced regulatory scrutiny, settling a $13 billion case in November over the sale of questionable mortgage securities before the financial crisis. Goldman Sachs, another bank dealing with regulatory issues, pledged $20 million to Detroit in November for job creation and economic development.

The investment was initiated by a phone call from Jamie Dimon to Dan Gilbert, the billionaire behind Quicken Loans, who owns or controls over 40 downtown buildings in Detroit. The investment is aimed at reshaping and rebuilding Detroit's economy and making it an attractive place to live, work, and invest.

The study decoding the genome of the coelacanth, a prehistoric-looking fish often referred to as a living fossil, provides insights into the genetic changes that occurred during the transition of aquatic vertebrates to land. The coelacanth, whose genome is similar in size to a human genome, is found to be genetically closer to tetrapods (the first land-dwelling vertebrates) than the lungfish, another air-breathing fish.

Researchers have identified genes in the coelacanth genome that may have helped its ancestor adapt to life on land, including a gene related to placenta development and a limb-forming gene enhancer. The coelacanth's genome shows evidence of slower evolution compared to mammals, possibly due to a stable habitat and lack of predators, despite significant environmental changes over the past 400 million years.

The study also reveals that the coelacanth's genome contains conserved non-coding elements (CNEs) that originated in the most recent common ancestor of tetrapods. These CNEs are enriched for gene regulatory elements and are associated with categories such as smell perception, morphogenesis, cell differentiation, and immunoglobulin VDJ recombination, reflecting the body-plan changes required for the transition from water to land.

The study also examines the Hox regulation of limb development in ray-finned fish, coelacanth, and tetrapods. An analysis of the HOX-D locus and its surrounding gene desert identifies a conserved limb enhancer (island 1) that was a lobe-fin developmental enhancer in the fish ancestor of tetrapods and was coopted into the autopod enhancer of modern tetrapods.

The adaptation to a terrestrial lifestyle necessitated major changes in the physiological environment of the developing embryo and fetus, resulting in the evolution and specialization of extra-embryonic membranes of the amniote mammals. The study identifies a region of the coelacanth HOX-A cluster that may have been involved in the evolution of extra-embryonic structures in tetrapods, including the eutherian placenta.

Changes in the urea cycle provide an illuminating example of the adaptations associated with the transition to land. The widespread and almost exclusive occurrence of urea excretion in amphibians, some turtles, and mammals suggests that the use of urea as the main nitrogenous waste product was a key innovation in the vertebrate transition from water to land. The study finds evidence of adaptive evolution in the hepatic urea cycle during the vertebrate land transition.

In conclusion, the study of the coelacanth genome provides valuable insights into the genetic changes that occurred during the transition of aquatic vertebrates to land, shedding light on the evolution of key features such as limbs, the placenta, and the urea cycle. The study also highlights the importance of the coelacanth as a model for understanding the evolution of vertebrates and their adaptation to different environments.

An arrest has been made in the 18-year-old cold case of Kirsten Hatfield's disappearance in Midwest City, Oklahoma. 56-year-old Anthony Palma, a neighbor of the Hatfield family, was arrested on complaints of first-degree murder and kidnapping and is currently in Oklahoma County Jail. DNA evidence collected in 1997, which was not tested until recently, linked Palma to the case. The evidence included cigarettes, a syringe, a beer bottle, and blood found on Kirsten's partially ripped underwear and window sill. Midwest City Police Chief Brandon Clabes stated that they have worked continuously on this case for 18 years and are emotionally invested in it. Kirsten's family, who have been living with the nightmare for 18 years, expressed hope that this could be the end of their ordeal. Police believe that Palma targeted Kirsten for sexual assault and that she was killed shortly after her abduction, but her body has not been found. The investigation is ongoing, and police believe there could be additional suspects. The break in the case came when the case was reassigned to Midwest City police Detective Darrell Miller, who discovered that crucial evidence was never tested 18 years ago.

Ben Affleck and Ted Kennedy Jr. have both announced they will not run for the vacant Massachusetts Senate seat, currently held by John Kerry who is expected to be confirmed as Secretary of State. Affleck, a well-known actor and activist, stated his focus is on his charity work, supporting veterans, and addressing hunger and Iran issues. Ted Kennedy Jr., son of the late Senator Edward Kennedy, lives in Connecticut and considers it his home, but did not rule out a future run for office. The potential Democratic candidates for the seat include Massachusetts Reps. Michael Capuano, Stephen Lynch, and Ed Markey, while former Sen. Scott Brown, who lost to Elizabeth Warren in November, is the strongest likely Republican candidate. If Kennedy had run, the Democratic field might have been smaller due to the attention he would have received.

The article discusses Walmart's experiment with increasing wages and training for its employees, a move that challenges the prevailing ethos of cost-cutting on Wall Street. The idea, known as "efficiency wages," suggests that employers who pay workers more will receive more loyal, harder-working, and productive employees in return.

Walmart, the largest private employer in the United States, faced pressure from investors to reverse a slide in business and combat threats from competitors. In early 2015, the company announced "the investments," a plan to spend more on wages, training, and predictable scheduling.

The results have been promising, with customer service ratings rebounding and sales increasing. However, the immediate impact on earnings and the company's stock price has been less rosy. The question for Walmart is whether this short-term hit will make the company a stronger competitor in the long run.

The future health of the U.S. economy and the well-being of its workers may depend on whether Walmart's changes mark a shift in how large companies think about their workers. The experiment tests the theory of efficiency wages, which suggests that higher wages can lead to increased productivity and improved economic results.

The article also explores the potential benefits of a good jobs strategy, where a retailer builds its operating philosophy around better-compensated staff members who are empowered to make decisions. Companies like Costco and Wegman's have a base pay closer to what labor activists seek and are successful by many measures.

In conclusion, Walmart's experiment with higher wages and training could have significant implications for the U.S. economy, testing the theory of efficiency wages and potentially setting a precedent for other large companies. The results so far show improved customer service and sales, but the long-term impact on profits and the company's stock price remains to be seen.

In a recent interview, former Senator Rick Santorum expressed dissatisfaction with his 38-31% loss to Mitt Romney in the Conservative Political Action Conference (CPAC) presidential straw poll. Santorum suggested that Romney may have had an advantage due to the buying of tickets for supporters, a practice he does not condone. Romney's campaign denied any such allegations, stating that Romney won the CPAC straw poll and a separate nationwide survey of conservatives.

Ron Paul, another Republican presidential contender, was also puzzled by Romney's description of himself as a "severe conservative." Paul expressed interest in understanding the definition, but Romney has yet to clarify.

In other news, Jack Lew, the newly appointed White House chief of staff, asserted that President Obama's position on birth control and Catholic institutions has been consistent. Lew stated that the recent "accommodation" is the furthest the administration will go to appease the bishops. Lew also claimed that health insurers would pay less for birth control-inclusive plans due to a reduction in pregnancies.

This summary covers the opinions and statements of Rick Santorum, Mitt Romney, Ron Paul, and Jack Lew on various topics, including CPAC, conservatism, and birth control.

The Irish parliament passed a groundbreaking law on Thursday, allowing for limited abortion rights in the republic. The Protection of Life in Pregnancy Bill, which was pushed through by Prime Minister Enda Kenny and his coalition government, will only permit abortions when a woman's life is at risk if her pregnancy continues or if she is suicidal. The law was passed after a marathon two-day debate in the Dáil, despite threats of excommunication from cardinals and bishops.

The legislation, which passed after 24 hours of tortuous debate, will not stop the annual abortion trail from Ireland to Britain. According to Irish department of health figures released on Thursday, about 4,000 Irish women traveled to British hospitals and clinics to terminate their pregnancies last year, including 124 who were under 18. The new law does not include women who were raped, meaning the annual abortion trail will continue.

Pro-choice and anti-abortion groups have already threatened court cases to challenge the new law. Mara Clarke, director of the London-based Abortion Support Network, a charity that raises money to help women afford the cost of traveling and paying for an abortion in England, condemned the restriction on an Irish woman's right to choose. She argued that even if the law is enacted, only a very small percentage of women who need abortions will be able to access them in Ireland.

The debate and vote inflicted damage on Kenny's 2-year-old coalition government, with Catholic conservatives vowing to drive his centrist Fine Gael party from power for violating its 2011 campaign pledge not to legislate on abortion. The government drafted the bill in response to last year's case of a miscarrying woman who died in an Irish hospital from blood poisoning nearly a week after being refused a termination. The death highlighted Ireland's failure for two decades to draft abortion legislation in support of a 1992 Supreme Court judgment ruling that life-saving abortions, including to prevent suicides, should be legal in Ireland.

During the debate, the Europe minister Lucinda Creighton was expelled from the Fine Gael parliamentary party for voting against the abortion law reform. She is now expected to lose her ministerial job as well. The marathon debate took its mental toll on lawmakers, with one accidentally pressing the wrong button during a 5 a.m. vote to reject opposition amendments, and another grabbing a female colleague by the hips during a 3 a.m. amendment vote. Both incidents caused controversy and prompted apologies.

The passage of the bill has sparked divisions, with many lawmakers expressing hopes or fears that it will put Ireland on a slippery slope to granting wider abortion rights, as has already happened in the rest of Europe. The island of Malta is the only other European Union member to outlaw the practice.

The Muslim Brotherhood, an outlawed Egyptian Islamist opposition group, is experiencing internal rifts between young and old, reformist and hard-liner, and between urban politicians and rural preachers. The group became poised for a growing role in Egypt's political life following the resignation of President Hosni Mubarak amid the region's most dramatic grassroots uprising since the Iranian Revolution in 1979.

Two faces of the Brotherhood emerged: Moaz Abdel Karim, a 29-year-old activist who advocates for democracy and human rights, and Mohamed Badi, a 66-year-old conservative leader who pledged to continue jihad against Jews and called for the establishment of an Islamic state. The Brotherhood's moderate wing, represented by Abdel Karim, played a key role in organizing the protests that led to Mubarak's downfall, but the more conservative old guard still dominates the group's leadership.

The Brotherhood's conservative leadership's autocratic style, lack of tolerance for dissenting opinions, and preference for conducting business behind closed doors have raised skepticism among outsiders about the group's commitment to democracy. Israel, which shares a long and porous border with Egypt, fears that if a moderate wing of the Brotherhood exists, it could be shoved aside by more extreme factions within the group. The U.S. appears to be taking a wait-and-see approach, with officials saying the group should be given a chance.

The Brotherhood's conservative wing has a history of anti-Israel comments and has funded Hamas, the Palestinian militant group. It has also spoken out in support of attacks against U.S. soldiers in Iraq and Afghanistan. Egypt's government has long highlighted the group's hard-line wing as a threat to the country, but its selective crackdowns have historically empowered the very hard-liners it has sought to undermine, analysts and Brotherhood members say.

In recent years, the group's pragmatic wing has forged a historic alliance with secular opposition activists. The Brotherhood's role in the unseating of Mubarak appears to have given them a boost in a struggle for influence with the Brotherhood's fiery old guard. The question for many is: Which Brotherhood? Whether the more moderate Brothers will have lasting clout is one of the key unknowns in Egypt's political evolution.

Casey Kasem, the legendary radio host known for "America's Top 40," is in a critical condition due to advanced Parkinson's disease and potential early onset dementia, according to new legal documents obtained by TMZ. The documents were filed by one of Casey's daughters, Julie, who is seeking to become a conservator to control Casey's health care decisions. Julie alleges that Casey's wife of 33 years, Jean, has isolated Casey from his children, denying them phone contact. Julie currently holds a power of attorney for health care decisions, but has been denied contact with Casey for the past three months. This situation has been ongoing for the last 3 to 4 years, with Casey's health deteriorating significantly. The documents outline Casey's severe impairments in short-term, long-term, and immediate recall memory, verbal communication, simple calculations, task planning, logical reasoning, disorganized thinking, and moderate hallucinations. The WARC files associated with this crawl are not currently available to the general public.

A jawbone discovered in Romania belonging to a man who lived approximately 40,000 years ago has been found to have the highest percentage of Neanderthal ancestry among modern humans. The study, published in the journal Nature, indicates that this individual, an early modern human, had a Neanderthal ancestor within four to six generations of his family tree. This finding suggests that interbreeding between Neanderthals and modern humans occurred more recently than previously thought, not just in the Middle East but also in Europe.

The study focuses on a jawbone from Oase 1, one of Europe's earliest modern humans, found in Peștera cu Oase ("Cave with Bones") in southwestern Romania in 2002. The researchers chose to study Oase 1 because the jaw showed some Neanderthal characteristics. DNA extracted from the Oase 1 jawbone showed one of its human ancestors interbred with a Neanderthal.

The Neanderthal contribution to the Oase 1 genome is between 2.3- and 3.6-fold larger than the Neanderthal DNA found in the genomes of populations living today outside sub-Saharan Africa and those of four other early modern humans from Russia and Luxembourg whose genomes have been sequenced. This indicates that more interbreeding happened with the ancestors of eastern non-Africans than with Europeans.

The study suggests that humans and Neanderthals continued interbreeding later than previously thought, even in Europe. However, Oase 1 didn't leave a significant genetic impact on later European populations. The findings revise our understanding of when and where humans and Neanderthals interbred, and they provide evidence that Neanderthals were not just our close cousins but also our sexual partners in Europe. Despite an outdated reputation as our dimwitted cousins, scientists say Neanderthals were highly intelligent, as shown by their complex hunting methods, likely use of spoken language, and sophisticated use of fire.
