In a different context, the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Department in Florida used an unorthodox approach to resurrect the story of 8-year-old Christy Luna, who disappeared in 1984. The department let Christy's imagined voice "take over" their Facebook and Twitter accounts to recount her kidnapping in real time on the 33rd anniversary of her disappearance. The campaign aimed to inspire someone to come forward with fresh tips that might lead to a break in the case.

Christy Luna disappeared on Memorial Day weekend in 1984 while searching for food for her cats. She was last seen wearing a turquoise body suit and no shoes, walking down the street to Belk’s General Store in Greenacres, Florida. For decades, detectives chased leads, investigated multiple suspects, and kept in contact with Christy's mother, Jennie Johnson, who was napping when her daughter disappeared. The case stalled, producing no arrests and no Christy.

Over the holiday weekend, the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Department used social media to resurrect Christy's story. Beginning on May 26, the date before Christy disappeared, authorities let her imagined voice "take over" their Facebook and Twitter to recount in real time what she could have been thinking and feeling during her kidnapping. The tweets and Facebook posts continued through May 27, the anniversary of her disappearance, and May 28, when Johnson went on the news to plead for the safe return of her child.

The tweets and Facebook posts in Christy’s voice seemed to speak directly to Christy’s mother, followers, and the public. The campaign aimed to inspire someone, somewhere to come forward with fresh tips that might lead to a break in the case. It's unclear what impact the social media campaign had on the case, although the goal was to inspire someone to come forward with fresh tips that might lead to a break.

The case of Christy Luna remains unsolved, and it's unclear if the social media campaign will lead to any new developments. The National Center for Missing and Exploited Children developed a composite sketch of how Christy might look today, with blue eyes and wavy, chestnut brown hair. The case has had a lasting impact on the community, with a lingering sense of fear and paranoia in the neighborhood where Christy disappeared.

In Memphis, a man named Kelton Griffin is accused of stealing a woman's car during a date and using it to take another woman on a date later that evening. The initial victim, Faith Pugh, reported her black Volvo stolen after Griffin, whom she knew from high school, asked her for a ride and then drove off with the car. Pugh's mother picked her up, but she received a surprising text from her God sister, stating that Griffin had asked her out.

The God sister, unaware of the car theft, agreed to a date with Griffin. Using the GPS on her phone, Pugh and her family trailed Griffin and found him at a drive-in movie theater on Summer Avenue with her God sister in the stolen Volvo. The God sister paid for their entry to the drive-in so Pugh could retrieve her car.

Griffin was arrested that night and charged with theft of property. This is not his first arrest, as in 2016, police reported that he and two other men robbed a restaurant after dining there. Faith Pugh expressed her desire for Griffin to spend a long time in jail and never want to speak to him again.

The new privacy policy for Samsung's Smart TVs has caused concern among internet users, with comparisons being drawn to George Orwell's dystopian novel 1984. The policy allows Samsung and its partners to listen in on everything users say, even when voice recognition software is activated. The policy states that data is encrypted and users can disconnect the TV from wifi to keep their data safe. However, Samsung will still collect data about how people use the TV if voice recognition is turned off. The policy has been criticized for its similarities to the telescreens used in 1984, as it allows Samsung to collect associated texts and other usage data. The policy has raised concerns about the internet of things and the potential for companies to collect more data on users than ever before. Samsung has stated that data is encrypted and users can disconnect the TV from wifi to keep their data safe.

In addition to the Smart TV service, Samsung's privacy policy also covers Voice Recognition, Gesture Controls, Facial Recognition, Fitness Services, and Kids Services. The Voice Recognition feature allows users to control their Smart TV with voice commands, but the data collected is used to provide the Voice Recognition features and evaluate and improve them. The Gesture Controls and Facial Recognition features use a camera to enable advanced services, but the camera can be covered and disabled at any time. The Fitness Services allow users to create a profile that contains basic information about themselves, and Kids Services make available educational videos and other content appropriate for children.

Microsoft's new Xbox One also has privacy concerns, as the new Kinect is always listening and has a constant connection to the internet. The new Kinect is so sensitive that it can read heartbeats and recognize individual voices. Microsoft claims that the new Kinect will run in an extremely low-power state for listening mode, and the company has stated that it has strong privacy protections in place and will continue to be a responsible steward of user data. Microsoft has not provided additional details on how the system operates in listening mode or if any safeguards have been considered against potential privacy threats.

In a series of tweets on July 28, 2017, President Donald Trump called for a change in Senate rules to require only a 51-vote majority for legislation, instead of the current 60-vote threshold. This proposal came after the failure of the Republican health care bill, which needed 50 votes plus Vice President Mike Pence's tie-breaking vote, but only received 49 votes. Three Senate Republicans, John McCain, Lisa Murkowski, and Susan Collins, voted against the bill, with McCain's decision being a surprise. Trump's call for a change in Senate rules would not have saved the Obamacare repeal effort, as the bill was being passed through the budget reconciliation process, which only required a 51-vote majority. The president has expressed frustration with the pace of policy and has threatened to let the Affordable Care Act collapse, a move that was criticized by Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer as a threat to "hurt innocent people." The failure of the health care bill marked a significant setback for the Republican agenda, as other key measures such as government spending bills will require Senate Republicans to win over at least eight Democrats to reach the 60-vote threshold.

Defense Secretary James Mattis delivered a pep talk to U.S. troops stationed abroad during his recent trip to Jordan, Turkey, and Ukraine. In a video that surfaced on social media, Mattis expressed concern about the current state of the U.S., stating, "Our country right now, it’s got problems we don't have in the military. You just hold the line until our country gets back to understanding and respecting each other and showing it."

Mattis spoke about the U.S. having "two powers" - "inspiration" and "intimidation." He acknowledged the troops' role in intimidation, saying, "The power of intimidation — [and] that’s you, if someone wants to screw with our families, our country, and our allies." He also expressed gratitude for the troops' service and mentioned that he came out of retirement to "serve alongside young people like you who are so selfless and, frankly, so rambunctious."

The video was likely taken in Jordan, and Mattis's comments were made during a week of national turmoil following violence at a white supremacist rally in Charlottesville, Virginia. Mattis's remarks were perceived as a veiled criticism of President Trump, as they came before Trump signed a presidential memo ordering the Defense Department to stop allowing transgender people to enlist in the military.

Mattis's comments were widely interpreted as possible veiled criticism of Trump, and many observers suggested they could be a response to White House economic adviser Gary Cohn's reported comments about the administration's handling of far-right and neo-Nazi activists.

In July, Trump announced his decision to ban transgender people from serving in the military "in any capacity." The decision reportedly took the Pentagon by surprise, and military chiefs made it known they considered a ban unnecessary and detrimental. Late on Friday, John McCain, chair of the Senate armed services committee, criticized the decision, stating it would be a step in the wrong direction. According to Military Times, as many as 250 service members are transitioning gender or have been approved to formally change gender within the Pentagon’s personnel system.

In Detroit, activists have resorted to civil disobedience to protest the Detroit Water and Sewerage Department's (DWSD) plan to cut off water for tens of thousands of non-paying residents. On Thursday, 50 demonstrators held a protest outside the offices of Homrich, a company contracted by DWSD, resulting in the arrest of nine activists for disorderly conduct. The activists argue that in a city with a high poverty rate and expensive water bills, DWSD should work with poor residents instead of cutting off their water.

Critics claim that DWSD has been unnecessarily aggressive in pursuing delinquent accounts, with some families, elderly, and disabled residents affected. DWSD argues that it needs to shut off water to recoup $175 million in outstanding bills, but has been accused of ignoring the debts of large entities while going after individuals who owe as little as $150.

DWSD says there are sufficient payment plans and assistance programs in place to help those who fall behind on their bills, but nearly 50% of DWSD's accounts are behind on payments, and Detroit's water prices are on the rise, now averaging $75 a household - almost double the national average. Activists say these high numbers give residents no choice but to protest.

Last month, Detroit activists successfully petitioned a U.N. panel to call the water shutoffs a violation of human rights. In response, DWSD announced a $1 million fund for residents struggling to pay. However, activists say many others are likely to lose access to water over the summer if the shutoffs continue.

The pressure seems to be working, as DWSD announced plans to intensify efforts to collect unpaid debts from its delinquent commercial customers, which make up about 12% of the approximately 90,000 accounts that are at least 60 days past due. Activists have criticized DWSD for ignoring commercial deadbeats while going after residential customers.

The protests have been ongoing, with a group from Windsor, Ontario, delivering 1,000 liters of water in support of Detroit residents, and protests held outside DWSD's offices every Friday since the shutoffs began. Detroit congressman John Conyers has sent off letters requesting federal action to address the issue.

On Monday, a French-Canadian university student named Alexandre Bissonnette was charged with six counts of first-degree murder and five counts of attempted murder in a shooting rampage at a Quebec City mosque. The attack, which occurred during evening prayers on Sunday, left six people dead and 19 injured, all men. Bissonnette, who has espoused support for the French far-right party of Marine Le Pen and had liked U.S. President Donald Trump on his Facebook page, was known to those who monitor extremist groups in Quebec. He was an anthropology and political science major at Laval University in Quebec City. The mosque where the attack happened has been a target of hate crimes in the past, including last summer when a pig's head was left on its doorstep during Ramadan. Prime Minister Justin Trudeau and Quebec Premier Philippe Couillard both characterized the attack as a terrorist act, which came amid heightened tensions worldwide over Trump's travel ban on seven Muslim countries. The suspect was arrested in his car on a bridge near d'Orleans, where he called 911 to say he wanted to cooperate with police. Police did not give a motive for the attack. The victims were businessmen, a university professor, and others who had gathered for evening prayers. The suspect was described as an introverted young man by his neighbors. The White House pointed to the attack as an example of why Trump's policies were needed, while Trudeau condemned the attack and reiterated Canada's welcoming stance towards immigrants and all religions. The prime minister later attended a vigil outside the mosque.

The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has approved the first genetically engineered animal for human consumption - the AquAdvantage salmon. The salmon, produced by Massachusetts-based AquaBounty, contains a growth hormone from a Chinook salmon and a gene from the ocean pout, allowing it to grow twice as fast as a natural Atlantic salmon in about 1.5 years.

The FDA's decision was based on a comprehensive review of extensive data submitted by AquaBounty Technologies and other peer-reviewed data. The agency found that the genetically engineered salmon is as safe to eat as a normal Atlantic salmon, with no discernible difference in its nutritional value. The approval is conditional on the salmon being raised only in land-based, contained tanks in two specific facilities in Canada and Panama, with regular inspections.

Critics, including food-safety activists, environmental groups, and the salmon fishing industry, have long opposed the approval of the fish, citing concerns about its potential impact on wild Atlantic salmon populations if it were to escape and mate with wild fish. AquaBounty has argued that its fish are all female and sterile, making it impossible for them to breed with other salmon.

The FDA will not require a special label for the genetically engineered salmon, despite outcry from consumer and health advocates who say Americans should know if the salmon they are buying has been genetically altered. FDA officials suggest that looking for 'wild-caught' salmon could ensure that consumers are not eating genetically engineered salmon.

The approval of AquAdvantage salmon has raised concerns about the potential for other genetically engineered animals with their own health and environmental concerns. Critics argue that the FDA's decision sets a dangerous precedent, while supporters say it is a step forward for science, aquaculture, and consumers.

During a speech at a university in Jerusalem on March 21, 2013, President Barack Obama was interrupted by a heckler demanding the release of former U.S. Navy Intelligence officer Jonathan Pollard, currently serving a life sentence for leaking military secrets to the Israeli government. Obama jokingly stated that the incident was planned to make him feel at home, as he had been heckled twice before in the U.S. The heckler received boos from the crowd, and Obama brushed off the interruption, stating that it was part of the lively debate he had mentioned earlier. Obama reiterated that there are currently no plans to release Pollard, as he had committed a serious crime. The heckler's shout was reported by the White House pool, and Obama added that he felt more comfortable with at least one heckler present.

Sean Penn, an Oscar-winning actor, has been charged with battery and vandalism following an altercation with a photographer outside a Brentwood store in October. The incident was captured on camera and shows Penn charging towards the photographer, taking a punch and kick while shouting "get out!" The actor could face up to 18 months in jail if convicted. This is not Penn's first run-in with the law; twenty-five years ago, he received a suspended sentence for attacking two British journalists.

Meanwhile, Penn has been spending time in Port-au-Prince, Haiti, where he has been highlighting the need for more aid in the earthquake-leveled nation. A year after the devastating earthquake, Penn, along with Paul Haggis, Maria Bello, and others, are still fighting for Haiti's survival amid unspeakable horror.

Penn has been a fixture in Haiti since moving there almost immediately after the earthquake. He has been leading a camp that houses 55,000 displaced persons and has been working tirelessly to provide aid and rebuild the country. Despite the challenges, Penn remains committed to Haiti and plans to continue his efforts there.

In a rare personal revelation, Penn discussed his divorce from Robin Wright during an interview about his work in Haiti. He mentioned that the divorce had cost him half of his assets and that he would have to start working again soon. Penn and Wright finalized their divorce in July 2010 after several failed reconciliations over the course of three years.

Oklahoma Governor Mary Fallin signed a bill into law that prohibits cities in the state from implementing mandatory minimum wage, vacation, or sick-day requirements. Critics argue that the bill specifically targets Oklahoma City, where a petition is underway to raise the city's minimum wage from $10.10, a rate advocated by President Barack Obama, to a level higher than the federal minimum wage of $7.25 an hour. David Slain, the lawyer who wrote the petition, expressed disappointment over the state legislature's decision, stating it infringes on the people's right to decide minimum wage. The grassroots effort will continue, with hopes of gathering 4,000 signatures by the end of April, and a total of 80,000 to bring the initiative to a statewide vote.

Supporters of the ban argue it will help local businesses, with Oklahoma state Rep. Randy Grau stating an artificial raise in the minimum wage could derail local economies. Sen. Dan Newberry contends the measure provides a safer business environment that will allow Oklahoma to remain economically competitive and see continued job growth.

Governor Fallin stated that raising the minimum wage is not an effective way to bring people out of poverty, citing a Congressional Budget Office report indicating a national minimum wage increase could lead to a loss of half a million jobs in the US. However, numerous studies have challenged this stereotype, stating that most minimum-wage workers are older than 20, with an average age of 35, and more than a quarter have children to support and over half work full-time.

State Rep. Eric Proctor argued against the bill, contending it was "immoral" to have a minimum wage so low that a person could work full-time and still be classified as living in poverty. The Oklahoma City group circulating the petition is contemplating a constitutional challenge to the law, citing infringement on the people's right to have an initiative petition.

In a statement released on Friday, President-elect Donald Trump announced that former New York City Mayor Rudy Giuliani will not be serving in his administration. Giuliani had been a top surrogate and adviser to Trump during his campaign and was being considered for the position of Secretary of State, one of the most important positions in a president's cabinet.

Giuliani removed himself from consideration for a position last month, according to the transition team's statement. However, CNN reported that Giuliani was told he would not get the Secretary of State position this week. Trump praised Giuliani in the statement, calling him "an extraordinarily talented and patriotic American" and expressing appreciation for his dedication to the campaign and wise counsel.

Trump also said that he will call upon Giuliani for advice and sees an important place for him in the administration at a later date. Giuliani explained his decision to withdraw, saying that the process was becoming confusing and difficult for Trump and that he had a lot of terrific candidates for the position. He added that he could play a better role being on the outside and continuing to be Trump's close friend and adviser.

Giuliani said that Secretary of State was the only position he had pursued and was not interested in others. He advised Trump not to pick Mitt Romney, who had disparaged Trump during the 2016 campaign, and expressed support for former UN ambassador John Bolton as a potential Secretary of State.

Giuliani's allies cast his withdrawal as a gracious move by one of Trump's most dedicated supporters. Tony Carbonetti, a close Giuliani associate, said that the former mayor did not want another job in the administration and removed himself from consideration when he realized it was becoming a distraction.

Several people close to the transition expressed concern that Giuliani lacked the energy necessary for the rigors of the Secretary of State position, which demands long hours of tedious discussions with foreign counterparts and thousands of miles of travel. Others questioned whether Giuliani was his old self and wondered why he would want to endure confirmation hearings that were likely to be highly contentious.

Trump's incoming chief of staff Reince Priebus dismissed talk that Giuliani's business ties were the reason for his withdrawal. Priebus said Giuliani was vetted by the team for any possible conflicts and passed with flying colors. However, others acknowledged that Giuliani's paid work for foreign governments had hurt his chances.

Giuliani will remain on as a "Vice Chairman of the Presidential Transition Team." He is expected to continue advising Trump in a different capacity at a later date. The search for a Secretary of State continues, with ExxonMobil CEO Rex Tillerson emerging as the leading contender, according to two transition aides. Others still in the mix include retired Adm. James Stavridis, Foreign Relations Committee chair Sen. Bob Corker (R-Tenn.), and former U.N. ambassador John Bolton. Former Ford CEO Alan Mulally also met with Trump recently to discuss the position.

The World Health Organization and the U.S. National Cancer Institute have published a study stating that smoking costs the global economy over $1 trillion annually and is projected to cause an additional 2 million deaths by 2030, with the majority occurring in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). Currently, 80% of smokers live in these countries, and although smoking prevalence is decreasing globally, the total number of smokers is rising.

The economic costs are expected to continue rising, and while governments have the tools to reduce tobacco use and associated deaths, most have not used them effectively. The study recommends increasing tobacco taxes and prices, implementing comprehensive smoke-free policies, banning tobacco company marketing, and using pictorial warning labels. Governments spent less than $1 billion on tobacco control in 2013-2014.

In related news, Australia has won an international legal battle to uphold its plain packaging laws, with tobacco giant Philip Morris failing in its attempt to challenge the laws using a clause in a 1993 Hong Kong bilateral trade deal. The decision could give other countries greater confidence to follow Australia's lead in outlawing tobacco company logos on cigarette packets and moving to drab, uniform designs dominated by graphic health warnings.

The economic costs of tobacco use are significant, with the WHO estimating that tobacco taxes generated about $269 billion in 2013-2014. However, the costs of tobacco-related health care and lost productivity are likely to outweigh these revenues. The study, which was peer-reviewed by over 70 scientific experts, highlights the need for effective tobacco control policies to reduce the global burden of tobacco-related deaths and economic costs.

In a separate news, British biologist John Bradshaw suggests that cats may perceive humans as larger cats due to their behavior. According to Bradshaw, the way cats greet humans (with their tails up and rubbing on legs) is similar to how they greet other cats. This behavior, he explains, is a way for smaller cats to show affection and submission to larger ones.

Bradshaw, who has studied cats for decades, argues that understanding cat behavior is key to living happily with them. He advises cat owners to take their time when approaching their cats, and to wait for the cat to put its tail up before making contact. He also suggests keeping an ear out for purring, as it can indicate contentment or a request for help.

According to Bradshaw, a cat's affection can be shown through three behaviors: the tail-up/rub ritual, resting in contact, and grooming. If a cat is doing any one of these behaviors, it indicates that it likes its owner.

Bradshaw's book, Cat Sense: How the New Feline Science Can Make You a Better Friend to Your Pet, has recently gained renewed interest on social media. For more information about the book, visit the publication's website.

In a study published in Scientific Reports, researchers from the University of Auckland and the University of Lincoln in the UK have confirmed that the local strains of yeast used to ferment grapes do indeed alter the outcome of Sauvignon Blanc fermentation, providing evidence for a microbial aspect to the concept of terroir.

The researchers isolated 3,900 strains of Saccharomyces cerevisiae from native forests, vineyards, and the spontaneous ferments of Vitis vinifera var Sauvignon Blanc fruit from six major regions in New Zealand. They found 295 different genotypes, with significantly distinct sub-populations residing in each of these regions.

The researchers used the genetic ancestry profiles produced from Bayesian analysis, in combination with regional allele frequencies, to select S. cerevisiae genotypes from each regional sub-population that span and represent the genetic diversity within each region. They included at least one genotype that harbored regionally unique alleles.

All ferments were conducted using the same commercially derived batch of homogenized and sterilized Sauvignon Blanc juice from Marlborough in NZ. The chemical profiles produced by single genotype ferments correlated with the region of microbe origin, with a significant correlation between the region of isolation of S. cerevisiae and aroma profiles in wine.

The researchers found that roughly half of the chemical compounds that determine a wine’s unique traits came from yeast during fermentation, with most of the ‘fruity’ notes in wine being derived from yeast, not the fruit. The compounds are a by-product of fermentation. Some winemakers add yeast to grape juice for fermentation, but many rely on microbes naturally found in the fruit.

The researchers found that the chemical signatures of the wines showed a large degree of overlap, but that the profiles of those produced by yeast strains from the same region tended to cluster, indicating the wines did indeed exhibit a regional character. The most distinct regional signature belonged to those wines produced by strains of yeast from Nelson, with particularly high concentrations of compounds that are known to impart apple and sweet fruit sensory effects.

The researchers concluded that this is the first quantitative demonstration of a microbial component of terroir, and that further study is needed to determine whether other fungi and bacteria may also be contributing to regional wine characteristics. The study provides evidence that the types of metabolites that different strains of yeast can generate in the ferment play a role in the unique characteristics of wine.

Steve Jobs' resignation as Apple Inc.'s CEO, while surprising in timing, may not significantly alter the company's trajectory. Jobs, who has been on medical leave, has handed over daily operations to Tim Cook, the company's former COO, who has been appointed as CEO. Despite stepping down as CEO, Jobs remains chairman of the board and has been involved in major decisions this year, such as the unveiling of the iPad 2.

The transition from Jobs to Cook is not unprecedented, as Apple has been preparing for this event for at least two years. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has reported an increase in cases of acute flaccid myelitis (AFM), a polio-like illness that affects the nervous system, particularly the spinal cord. The cause of AFM is unknown, but it has been linked to viral infections such as polio, enteroviruses, adenoviruses, and the mosquito-borne West Nile virus. Symptoms of AFM include pain in the arms and legs, difficulty passing urine, and respiratory failure. There is no specific treatment for AFM, and the degree of paralysis in the first month has generally improved only slightly over the course of a year. The 2014 outbreak of AFM occurred at the same time as a larger outbreak of enterovirus D68, but the CDC did not detect traces of the virus in AFM specimens collected that year. This year, no similarly widespread outbreak of EV-D68 respiratory infections has been reported, although cases of it and other enteroviruses have been seen in some areas. The CDC is advising people to wash their hands, avoid close contact with sick people, and clean surfaces with a disinfectant to prevent illness. The case of Carter Roberts, a 3-year-old boy from Chesterfield, Virginia, who was diagnosed with AFM in July, highlights the perplexing nature of the condition. Carter lost control of his right arm, then over his legs and other muscles within a few days, and can now only wiggle a toe and move the left side of his face. He is one of at least 50 people in the US who have been diagnosed with AFM this year.

The Capnocytophaga bacterium, commonly found in dogs and cats, can cause severe infections in humans, particularly in individuals with weakened immune systems. The most common infections occur in tissues connected to the mouth and throat, including periodontal (gum) disease, respiratory tract infections, eye infections, and can lead to complications such as septicemia, endocarditis, abscesses, inflammation of various body tissues, and inflammation of the eyes, face, lymph nodes, or brain membranes.

In a groundbreaking discovery, researchers believe that Saturn's moon, Enceladus, has a warm ocean with ongoing hydrothermal activity, making it the most life-friendly habitat found outside of Earth. The lawsuit also claims that written and unwritten policies and practices for evaluations and promotions discriminate against blacks.

Two named plaintiffs in the lawsuit are Celeslie Henley, a former executive administrative assistant at CNN, and Ernest Colbert Jr., a senior manager at TBS. Henley alleges that she was mistreated in the workforce based on race, sex, and pregnancy, while Colbert claims he was consistently paid below grade level compared to comparable white employees.

The lawsuit also mentions DeWayne Walker, a CNN producer who sued CNN individually in January for $50 million for racial discrimination and retaliation for filing a complaint with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission. Meachum said he has been collecting information about CNN and Turner for three years before filing the class-action suit. The Australian ship Ocean Shield, towing a US pinger locator, has detected four signals in the Indian Ocean that are consistent with the black boxes of missing Malaysia Airlines Flight MH370. The signals were first detected on Saturday and again on Tuesday, with the latest two signals lasting for five minutes and seven minutes respectively. The development revives hopes for the discovery of the plane's wreckage, as the signals are believed to be consistent with those of a flight data recorder. The search area has been refined to a single zone, about 75,423 square kilometres in size, 2261 kilometres northwest of Perth. Up to 11 military aircraft, four civil aircraft and up to 14 ships will assist in the search on Wednesday, while the Ocean Shield will also conduct a sonar voice search. The signals are getting weaker, which means that either the search area is moving away from the signals or the pinger batteries are dying. The batteries powering the flight recorders' locator beacons are certified to be working for 30 days. The first signal, at 4:45 p.m. Perth Time on Saturday, lasted 2 hours 20 minutes. The second, at 9:27 p.m. Saturday, lasted 13 minutes. The third signal was picked up Tuesday at 4:27 p.m. That lasted 5 minutes 32 seconds. The fourth, at 10:17 p.m. Tuesday, was 7 minutes long. The search for the missing plane, which went missing on March 8, has been ongoing for over a month and has involved extensive international search efforts.

The operation scared Wayne's family, and even the cowboy himself a little. His estranged wife, Pilar, wanted a reconciliation, but Wayne stated, "You can never go back." The screen's most famous cowboy discovered the problem in his artery in a strange way. He had been having respiratory trouble, and then he found he was losing his voice. A doctor explained that there is an artery that goes from the heart to the vocal cords, which worried Wayne as an actor relies on his voice to make a living.

After the operation, Wayne admitted that he was scared at losing his voice. He joked that he could still take a belt of Scotch but had been taking it easy since he came back from Boston. Wayne can out drink anyone in Hollywood and has a reputation for being colorful and outspoken.

Wayne's 150-odd movies, spanning a 50-year career, have grossed a half-billion dollars or more. The movie is a contemporary family story, and if the movie is as good as the novel, it could be a hit. Wayne's family and friends are sure there will be more westerns in the old cowboy's future.

Wayne may be tough, but he's not too tough to indulge in a little sentiment. He admits that the outpouring of good wishes from fans concerned about his illness "made me cry." Love bombing is a manipulative tactic used by predators to gain control over their victims, often through excessive flattery, praise, and promises of a deep alliance. This tactic is commonly used by abusers, cult leaders, and emotional predators to exploit their targets and fulfill their own agendas.

In relationships with pathological predators, love bombing is combined with intermittent reinforcement, creating an unstable and coercive environment. Intermittent reinforcement involves cruel treatment mixed with occasional affection, causing victims to seek their approval and settle for occasional positive behavior.

Children of narcissistic parents are particularly susceptible to love bombing, as they have been subconsciously programmed to seek approval, engage in people-pleasing habits, and look for external validation. When they meet emotional predators in adulthood, they are especially vulnerable to becoming ensnared in the web of a malignant narcissist.

Love bombing, intermittent reinforcement, and the effects of trauma work together to strengthen an intense trauma bond between target and abuser. Targets of emotional and psychological violence seek the love bombing that was so nourishing in the idealization phase, even as they are now being devalued and discarded by their abusers.

There are three ways children of narcissists are vulnerable to the tactics of love bombing:

1. Love-bombing disarms victims initially, making them feel a sense of belonging and kinship. Narcissists and sociopaths are skilled at "hooking" victims by pointing out their desirable physical attributes, personality traits, and accomplishments, but their affection is often short-lived and transient.

2. Victims of love bombing often fall for predators who make them feel special and unique, a type of attention they craved in childhood. However, they later become retraumatized by these manipulators when they are "triangulated" with former or new harem members and lovers.

3. Victims mistake superficial alliances for deep, meaningful connections, holding onto even the most superficial of connections for indications that they have finally found a "home" for their tattered hearts and weary souls.

To resist these manipulation tactics, victims should seek internal validation for their qualities, pinpoint what makes them irreplaceable, and differentiate between connection and flattery early on to avoid investing in people who may not have their best interests at heart. Building authentic relationships with what makes them stand out can help victims become more selective about who they let into their lives.

In this article, it is revealed that Tamerlan Tsarnaev, one of the Boston Marathon bombers who was killed in a confrontation with police, sought to change his name to Muaz, after a well-known rebel fighter, in January 2013, less than three months before the bombings. The name change petition is part of a growing body of evidence that portrays Tsarnaev as more radical and organized than previously believed.

Tsarnaev's name change request was part of a Homeland Security Department petition form, which was obtained by The Times. According to a federal law enforcement official close to the Boston bombing case, Tsarnaev described the decision in political terms, stating that he was frustrated with the Russian people for terrorizing his home country.

The emerging picture of Tamerlan Tsarnaev is likely to play a key role in the upcoming defense of his brother, Dzhokhar Tsarnaev, who is accused of using a weapon of mass destruction and other federal charges in connection with the bombings. Defense attorneys for Dzhokhar Tsarnaev are expected to argue that his older sibling took the lead role in what became the worst domestic terrorist attack since Sept. 11, 2001.

U.S. authorities believe Tamerlan was deeply radicalized during his 2012 visit to Dagestan, which, along with adjoining Chechnya, is home to an Islamist insurgent movement. They say he made an unsuccessful attempt to join the rebels and was either sent back to the U.S. to carry out a terrorist strike or took it upon himself.

Defense attorneys for Dzhokhar Tsarnaev claim that Tamerlan may have been set off by what he believed was FBI pressure and attempts to recruit him as an informant. They say that the FBI's involvement went further than previously reported, with multiple visits to talk with Tsarnaev and his parents, questioning him about his Internet searches, and asking him to be an informant.

The FBI has said that it met once with Tsarnaev to discuss his visit to the Caucasus region, but lawyers for his brother claimed in court filings that federal agents interviewed him multiple times, a process that they say increased his anger against the U.S.

In 2011, the Russian government asked the FBI to check on Tsarnaev, warning he might be preparing to travel to the Caucasus region. The FBI said it ran a series of checks, spoke with him and his parents, and reported back to Moscow that it had uncovered no links to terrorism.

The new revelations about Tsarnaev have prompted defense lawyers for his brother to characterize him as the key player who "supplied the motivation, planning and ideology behind the Boston Marathon attack." Dzhokhar Tsarnaev has pleaded not guilty to using a weapon of mass destruction and other federal charges. If convicted at his trial this fall, he faces a death sentence.

The defense wants to investigate those factors as it seeks to portray Tamerlan as a dominating family figure who may have pushed the younger Dzhokhar to take part in the attack. The lawyers’ allegation, based on conversations with family members and other sources, was made in a 23-page court filing Friday in which the lawyers sought a court order forcing prosecutors to turn over more evidence in the case.

Prosecutors did not immediately respond to the defense request, though defense lawyers conceded that they have a March 14, 2014, letter in which prosecutors said they had “no evidence that Tamerlan Tsarnaev was solicited by the government to be an informant.” Although the FBI does not comment on court matters, the bureau cited a statement Friday that it made Oct. 18, 2013, which said, “The Tsarnaev brothers were never sources for the FBI, nor did the FBI attempt to recruit them as sources.”

Dzokhar Tsarnaev, now 20, faces a 30-count indictment in his alleged role in the bombings, which killed three people and injured more than 260. He and Tamerlan also allegedly shot and killed an MIT police officer before the confrontation with police in Watertown. Tsarnaev is being held at the federal prison at Fort Devens in Ayer. He is slated to go to trial in November.

Prosecutors have described him as a young Muslim extremist who wanted to carry out jihad, or holy war, against the United States. They alleged the brothers learned to build the bombs through websites that supported Al Qaeda. In court requests filed late Friday, the defense lawyers sought a court order to force prosecutors to turn over a list of records, including reports related to the fatal shooting of MIT police Officer Sean Collier, the Watertown confrontation, and any evidence that an MBTA police officer was shot by fellow officers, rather than by Dzokhar Tsarnaev, who the lawyers say was unarmed. The request also targets records of the brothers’ Internet searches.

One of the court requests asked for any information prosecutors collected under the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act including any surveillance of Tamerlan’s return visits to Dagestan and the Chechnya region before the bombings. A recent US House of Representatives homeland security report indicated FBI officials in Moscow may have collected “electronic communication” between Tamerlan and a jihadist named William Plotnikov.

The lawyers are also seeking the immigration records of Tsarnaev’s family members, including his mother, father, and brother. His father, Anzor, sought the family’s asylum in fleeing torture in Kyrgyzstan close to two decades ago, and the defense lawyers argued that the records would illustrate Tsarnaev’s family history. They also said that Tamerlan’s immigration records could yield more evidence about his encounters with federal authorities, specifically after his visits to Dagestan that caught the attention of Russian officials.

The lawyers plan to argue that the unknowns about Tsarnaev’s “formative environment and relative moral culpability” and the possible “psychological domination” by his brother would support their case against the death penalty.

A Melbourne-made treatment that combines peanut flour and a high dose of the probiotic Lactobacillus rhamnosus has shown promising results in curing peanut allergies in children. In a clinical trial conducted at the Murdoch Children's Research Institute, 82% of the treated children were able to eat peanuts without any issues, and four years later, 80% of those cured children continue to show no signs of allergic reaction. The treatment, known as PPOIT, works by reprogramming the immune system's response to peanuts and developing a tolerance. If confirmed by larger clinical studies, this treatment could have a significant impact on the high rates of food allergies among children in Western societies. The researchers are now working with a venture capital firm to fund the commercialization of the treatment, which involves daily doses of powder for 18 months. The findings were published in the Lancet Child & Adolescent Health.

In a surprising turn of events, Chicago Mayor Rahm Emanuel failed to secure more than 50% of the vote in the city's mayoral election on Tuesday, forcing him into a runoff against second-place finisher Jesus "Chuy" Garcia in April. Despite a significant financial advantage, Emanuel was unable to fend off Garcia, a Cook County commissioner and progressive Democrat with a minimal campaign fund.

The setback for Emanuel, who served as President Barack Obama's chief of staff, came despite a visit from Obama last week. Emanuel outspent his four opponents by a large margin, receiving millions of dollars from campaign donors, including Hollywood directors and hedge fund executives, as well as Obama's support.

Garcia, who entered the race last October after the teacher's union president, Karen Lewis, dropped out due to a brain cancer diagnosis, held a low public profile before his campaign. However, he gained support from the powerful Chicago Teachers Union and its president, Lewis, who endorsed him.

The runoff election will take place on April 7. With 98% of precincts reporting, Emanuel had 45.4% of the vote, while Garcia had 33.9%. Polls before the election had shown Emanuel close to 50%, and Garcia at about 20%.

Emanuel sounded emotional as he addressed supporters, urging them to continue their fight. "Tomorrow morning I will be seeing you at the L stops," he said. "We will get back out there talking to our friends and families and neighbors as they make a critical choice about who has the strength, who has the leadership, who has the ideas to move this great city forward."

Emanuel won the mayoral seat outright when he first ran in 2011, but controversial decisions such as closing 50 public schools and continued high crime contributed to the city's first runoff mayoral election since 1995. Garcia has argued that Emanuel paid more attention to the city's upper class and downtown than to the poor and communities outside the commercial center.

In a television ad, Garcia turned one of Emanuel's apparent strengths - an ability to lure corporations to Chicago - into a negative by casting the incentive packages as tax breaks that favored big companies while taking money away from spending on police. "We have something to say," Garcia told his euphoric supporters Tuesday night. "We want change."

Suzy Broz, a former Emanuel supporter, said she thought Garcia could win. "A lot of people are upset with a one percent mayor and people feel that there's a great chance for change," Broz said.

Emanuel has argued that he had to make tough choices to rein in the city's budget deficit, which is expected to grow to $1.2 billion by next year due to an increase in payments to public pensions. As the election loomed, Emanuel turned more attention to lower income residents, passing a city ordinance to raise the minimum wage.

The runoff election will be closely watched as it marks a significant challenge to Emanuel's political career. Garcia will need to consolidate the votes of those who backed other candidates in the first round, including businessman Willie Wilson and Alderman Bob Fioretti. Despite his financial advantage, Emanuel will need to address the concerns of voters who have criticized his tenure for clashes with teachers, a wave of violent crime, and backlash over his plan to increase taxes.

Ursula K. Le Guin, a renowned fantasy fiction writer, passed away on Monday at the age of 88. Known for her influential work in the genre, Le Guin authored over 20 novels, numerous books of poetry, short stories, essays, children's books, and translations. Her work has been translated into over 40 languages and has sold millions of copies worldwide. Le Guin's writing is recognized for its feminist sensibilities and its contribution to "high literature" in the fantasy genre. She received multiple Hugo and Nebula awards, as well as the National Book Award's Medal for Distinguished Contribution to American Letters.

Upon her death, Le Guin left a significant void in the world of fantasy fiction. Notable authors, including Stephen King, N.K. Jemisin, Neil Gaiman, and many others, expressed their sadness and shared stories of how much Le Guin's work inspired them. Stephen King called her a "literary icon," while N.K. Jemisin stated that Le Guin was one of the reasons she became a writer. Neil Gaiman, who presented Le Guin with the National Book Foundation's lifetime achievement award, expressed deep affection for her both as a person and a writer.

In response to her passing, numerous authors and readers shared heartfelt messages on social media, praising Le Guin's influence on their work and expressing their admiration for her as a writer and a person. Le Guin's passing has left a profound impact on the literary world, and her legacy will continue to inspire generations of writers and readers.

In this article, the third round of parliamentary elections in Egypt took place on January 2, 2012, with the final round covering nine provinces. The Muslim Brotherhood's Freedom and Justice party was expected to consolidate its gains, having taken the lead in earlier rounds. The trial of former Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak resumed on the same day, with prosecutors accusing him of being a "tyrant" responsible for violence and oppression during his rule. Mubarak's trial is a reminder to future rulers that they will be held accountable for breaking the law, the prosecutor said.

The election and Mubarak's trial are taking place amid growing opposition to the ruling generals, who say they won't cede power before presidential elections are held by the end of June. It's unclear what powers the elected assembly will have and how a new government will be formed. Clashes in Cairo last month between security forces and demonstrators calling for an earlier end to military rule left at least 17 people dead. Protesters are preparing to take to the streets on January 25 to mark the anniversary of the mass rallies that drove Mubarak from power.

Economic growth has slowed as the unrest deters tourists and investors. Foreign-currency reserves declined by 44 percent to $20.2 billion in the first 11 months of 2011. The benchmark EGX 30 stock index lost 49 percent last year, making it the third-worst performer among world markets tracked by Bloomberg.

About 14 million voters are eligible to vote in this round, and 150 parliamentary seats are up for grabs. In Minya, one of the provinces where balloting is being held today, Mina Magdy, a Christian, said gains by Islamists in previous rounds encouraged him to vote for the secular Egyptian Bloc alliance. "We're trying to balance things out," he said. "We want more liberals in parliament."

The court trying Mubarak adjourned until tomorrow, state television reported. It showed Mubarak carried on a gurney to and from the makeshift courtroom in a police academy. Prosecutor Moustafa Soliman told the court Mubarak was a "tyrant" who sought to install his son, Gamal, in his place, the state-run Middle East News Agency reported. His trial is a reminder to future rulers that they will be held accountable for breaking the law, the prosecutor said. Mubarak allowed former Interior Minister Habib el-Adli to "practice oppression and violence against Egyptians so he could remain in office," Soliman said, according to MENA. Police seeking to block protesters from reaching Cairo's Tahrir Square targeted their heads and chests, and some were run over by police vehicles, he said. Prosecution arguments against the former president, who has pleaded not guilty to charges of corruption and conspiring to kill protesters, will continue over the next two days, state television said. At least 846 people were killed during the revolt. Gamal Mubarak and the former president’s other son, Alaa, are facing corruption charges, and el-Adli and six of his aides are also on trial.

A 51-year-old woman named Sara Beebe was rescued by helicopter after she got stuck on a 50-foot cliff in Silverado Canyon while trying to rescue her kitten that had run off on Monday morning. Beebe climbed up the slope behind her home in the 14900 block of Kitterman Drive, but slipped and slid down, injuring her ankle and scraping her arms and legs. She was unable to climb up or down and had to call for help. A firefighter rappelled down from a helicopter and pulled Beebe onto the aircraft to safety. The kitten made its way back down the hill on its own. Beebe learned a lesson and plans to let her cat be more independent in the future. The Orange County Fire Authority advises putting food out for the cat if it gets stuck in a tree or on a roof, as they usually come down on their own.

The Federal Reserve Bank of New York is under scrutiny for potentially knowing as early as August 2007 that the global benchmark interest rate system was flawed. In spring 2008, they shared proposals for reform with British authorities following an inquiry with Barclays Plc. The role of the Fed may raise questions about their response to concerns about Libor rate manipulation, as they struggled to maintain the banking system during the financial crisis.

In a statement, the Fed admitted receiving occasional reports from Barclays about Libor issues in late 2007 and early 2008, and further inquiry was made in spring 2008. They shared their analysis and suggestions for reform with British authorities before the first media report on the subject.

Legislators on Capitol Hill have requested transcripts of communications between the New York Fed and Barclays regarding Libor from August 2007 to November 2008. Both the House Financial Services Committee and the Senate Banking Committee plan to question Treasury Secretary Timothy Geithner and Federal Reserve Chairman Ben Bernanke about the allegations.

Barclays agreed to pay $453 million to settle allegations of Libor manipulation in July. The rates, set daily by a group of international banks in London, have an impact on borrowing costs for many people and companies, affecting $550 trillion in loans, securities, and derivatives.

The scandal has been more of a British affair so far, with Barclays' top three executives resigning, the British government expressing concern, and questions about the lack of oversight from British regulators. However, the investigation is expected to uncover problems beyond Barclays and British banks, with more than a dozen banks, including Citigroup, JPMorgan Chase, Deutsche Bank, HSBC, UBS, and Royal Bank of Scotland, being investigated.

Regulators, including the New York Fed, had a responsibility to ensure greater integrity and cooperation, but their focus was on preventing a global economic disaster during the autumn of 2008. Barclays first contacted Fed officials to discuss Libor on August 28, 2007, and communicated with them another 10 times between then and October 2008 about Libor submissions and related problems during the financial crisis.

Officials with the New York Fed talked to British authorities about problems with the calculation of Libor and heard from market participants about the need for an alternative. In April 2008, a "Fixing LIBOR" meeting was held at the New York Fed, but it is unclear what was discussed or who attended. The New York Fed was not part of the Barclays settlement, which was the first major resolution in the Libor probe.

In a chilling case reminiscent of the movie Seven, a former bank manager named Kenan Oner in Bursa province, western Turkey, is accused of murdering his parents and burying their dismembered bodies in his garden. The police found the remains six years after Oner's parents went missing. Oner is also suspected of killing his wife, who disappeared in 2005, and burying her remains inside the walls of his apartment.

Oner's alleged crimes have shocked the country, not only due to the gruesome details but also because of the precision and planning that went into the killings. The police believe Oner's main motivation was money, as he was embroiled in a bitter dispute with his parents and siblings over his inheritance.

Oner's criminal history dates back to 1980 when he was a philosophy major and a member of a radical communist group in Turkey. Fearing arrest, he fled to France, where he allegedly killed a Turkish friend for his money. Oner was sentenced to life in prison in 1998 but received parole in 2005.

After returning to Turkey, Oner discovered his wife was having an affair, and they divorced. In 2005, his wife disappeared, and Oner claimed she ran away to Europe with her lover. However, the police now believe he killed her and buried her remains in his apartment.

Oner's meticulousness ultimately led to his capture, as he saved thousands of documents, including hourly notes of his movements and a hand-drawn map of his parents' garden with an "x" marked on it. The notes around the dates of his parents' disappearance read, "What am I going to do with these now?" and "I dug my dad's garden, I am very tired."

The police say Oner is not a psychopath or a serial killer but was motivated by money. If found guilty, he may spend the rest of his life behind bars, and his murder trial is likely to be a media frenzy of epic proportions. The press is already sensationalizing the case with headlines such as "Man chopped his parents into 300 pieces."

The story revolves around Manti Te'o, a Notre Dame linebacker, who became the center of a controversial hoax in 2013. Te'o claimed to have a romantic relationship with a woman named Lennay Kekua, who supposedly died of leukemia in September. However, it was later revealed that Kekua never existed, and the entire relationship was a hoax.

Te'o's story gained attention due to its heartwarming nature, as he played through adversity while grieving the loss of his grandmother and his supposed girlfriend. The revelation of the hoax left many questioning whether Te'o was a victim or a participant in the scam.

The university and Te'o claimed that he was drawn into a virtual romance with Kekua, and was fooled into believing she died of leukemia. Their only contact was via the internet and telephone. Te'o's agent stated that he had no plans to make any public statements.

The story raised questions about whether Te'o was truthful about his relationship with Kekua, and whether he embellished the details to gain sympathy. It also raised concerns about the media's role in spreading the story without verifying its authenticity.

The hoax has left many wondering whether Te'o was a victim or a participant in the scam, and whether he will face consequences for his actions. The NFL is expected to investigate the matter before drafting Te'o. The story has also sparked discussions about the dangers of online relationships and the importance of verifying information before spreading it.

A domestic Egyptian flight, EgyptAir MS181, was hijacked by a passenger claiming to have a suicide explosive belt. The flight was diverted to Cyprus, where the hijacker surrendered after a morning of tension, releasing all hostages unharmed. The hijacker, identified as Seif Eldin Mustafa, reportedly wanted to speak with his estranged Cypriot wife or seek the release of female prisoners in Egypt. The incident was not terrorism-related, according to the Cypriot president.

The hijacking raised concerns about aviation security, particularly how the passenger was able to carry materials resembling a bomb through Alexandria airport. It is unclear how the man was able to pass through security with such materials.

The incident is a further blow to Egypt's tourism industry, which has yet to recover from a previous airline bombing in October 2015. The hijacker's surrender came shortly after several people were seen fleeing the aircraft, including a crew member who escaped by climbing out of the aircraft's cockpit window.

Local media reports suggest that the hijacker handed over a four-page letter in Arabic after the plane landed at Larnaca on Tuesday morning, and that later a woman thought to be his wife arrived at the airport.

Egypt has taken steps to improve airport security following the October 2015 bombing, including a review of security at Cairo, Sharm El-Sheikh, and Marsa Alam airports, increased and more thorough checks, and a $1bn investment in airport security. However, checks remain patchy and inconsistent, with many VIPs refusing to be searched and MPs claiming immunity.

EgyptAir said the Airbus A320 was carrying 56 passengers from Alexandria to Cairo, along with six crew and a security official. The plane had initially said 81 passengers were on board. Larnaca airport, on the south coast of Cyprus, has been closed and scheduled flights diverted elsewhere.

In the aftermath of the Squirrel Hill synagogue shooting on October 27, a Jewish nurse named Ari Mahler, who treated the shooter Robert Bowers at Allegheny General Hospital, shared a lengthy Facebook post over the weekend. Mahler, a registered nurse at Allegheny General since May, did not reveal his Jewish identity to Bowers. In his post, Mahler described his own experiences with anti-Semitism and his lack of surprise at the attack on Tree of Life Congregation, where 11 people were killed and six injured. Mahler wrote that he did not see evil when he looked into Bowers' eyes, but rather a lack of depth, intelligence, and confusion. He also mentioned that he felt it was important to treat Bowers with compassion and empathy, and to honor the victims by proving Bowers wrong. Mahler grew up the son of Rabbi Mark Joel Mahler, who retired as rabbi of Temple Emanuel of South Hills, a Reform synagogue, in June. He said he experienced anti-Semitism from other school children but more from ignorance than from hate. Mahler worked as a loan officer and a financial consultant before taking a job as a nurse at Magee-Womens Hospital in 2014, according to his LinkedIn.com profile. Dr. Jeff Cohen, the president of Allegheny General Hospital, praised the two Jewish medical professionals who treated Bowers for putting their emotions aside and doing their job. Cohen said that the registered nurse, whose own father is a rabbi, broke down in tears after treating Bowers. Cohen also said that he became more and more curious about meeting Bowers and wanted to have his own impression of the suspect. Cohen described the Tree of Life Congregation as a safe place where people gather daily to pray and socialize, and said that he knew several of the victims personally.

The article discusses the mystery surrounding Czech supermodel Karolina Kurkova's lack of a belly button, which was noticed during a catwalk show for lingerie giant Victoria's Secret. While most people have an "outie" or "innie," Kurkova has a smooth indentation. The absence of her belly button is referred to as the "riddle of the £2.5m beauty."

The reasons for Kurkova's lack of a belly button could be due to an abdominal operation in infancy, or the umbilical cord being left to detach naturally. Other possibilities include adults losing their navel after stomach surgery or cosmetic reshaping, or having an artificial navel created. However, Kurkova has not spoken publicly about the matter.

The article also explores other cases of people lacking a belly button, including a man named Rob Swainson who was born with a hole in his abdominal wall and had to undergo surgery as a newborn. Another man, David Elliott, has a small belly-popper due to being born premature.

The article also mentions British heptathlete Kelly Sotherton, who also has a smooth indentation. The article concludes by stating that Kurkova's lack of a belly button does not seem to be hindering her career, as she was ranked as the eighth highest-paid model in the world last year.

The article also includes comments from readers who share their own experiences of lacking a belly button, including one who suspects being born premature via caesarean section may have caused their indentation, and another who lost their belly button after abdominal surgery. Other readers share their stories of having an artificial belly button created after stomach surgery or having a large scar instead of a belly button.

The article ends with a statement that Kurkova does have a belly button, as evidenced by a photo on her own website. However, industry sources have revealed that the perfect belly button in magazines and catalogs is usually the result of photo retouching.

On Monday, Israel beefed up security for the funeral of former Prime Minister Ariel Sharon, who passed away at the age of 85 after eight years in a coma. The funeral will take place near the Gaza border, a location within range of rockets from the Palestinian territory. Two rockets were fired from Gaza hours before the funeral, but they did not appear to have landed in Israel. The military said the rockets were fired into the sea, causing no injuries or damage. The Iron Dome anti-missile system was reportedly deployed near Sharon's ranch in southern Israel to protect against rockets during the funeral.

Israeli police have deployed increased forces for Sharon's funeral, and the US Vice President Joe Biden will attend the state ceremony in Jerusalem and the burial at Sycamore Farm's Poppy Hill. The United States was among 18 countries to send delegations to the state ceremony for Sharon.

There was no immediate response from Hamas, the governing authority in Gaza, regarding Israel's warning not to allow rocket fire during the funeral. Egyptian officials, who have served as mediators between Israel and Gaza in the past, were unavailable for comment.

Israel has deployed an Iron Dome rocket interceptor near Sycamore Farm, which has been hit by Gaza-launched rockets in the past. The rockets are often inaccurate and cause relatively little damage, but when fired in salvoes, they spread panic and paralyze routine life in southern Israel.

During his visit to Israel, Biden will discuss the ongoing peace negotiations with Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas and address Israel's concerns about the interim nuclear deal with Iran, which takes effect on January 20. Biden is seen as one of Israel's best friends in Washington, with a career dating back to his decades on Capitol Hill.

Israeli authorities braced for any potential rocket attacks during the funeral, with the southern police commander stating that they are taking the full range of possible scenarios into account. The IDF is prepared, informed, and ready to respond if necessary.

In East Liverpool, Ohio, an officer named Chris Green accidentally overdosed on fentanyl during a drug-related traffic stop on Friday night. The incident occurred when Green, while following protocol for handling drugs, inadvertently came into contact with the powder while searching a blue Monte Carlo. The suspects, Justin Buckle and Cortez Collins, were arrested for tampering with evidence and each had a bond set at $100,000.

The traffic stop took place at the bottom of Lisbon Street at W. 8th Street, where officers had blocked in the Monte Carlo after observing a suspected drug transaction. According to East Liverpool Captain Patrick Wright, Buckle and Collins attempted to dispose of the evidence in the vehicle.

After the arrest, Green showed signs of overdose and was given Narcan, both at the station and later at the hospital, where he received three additional doses. As of Sunday, Green is reportedly recovering.

The incident serves as a stark reminder of the dangers associated with the drug epidemic, forcing police to alter aspects of their job, such as no longer field-testing drugs due to accidental exposures. The East Liverpool Police Department is urging caution when dealing with suspected fentanyl, a potent opioid that can be absorbed through the skin and is 50 times more potent than heroin.

Both Buckle and Collins are facing charges, and the police expect to file more charges. The incident has left the East Liverpool Police Department shaken, but they are relieved that Officer Green is recovering.

In a groundbreaking development, a Swedish medical team has initiated embryo transfers into four of nine women who have received transplanted wombs since 2012. The women, who either lacked a uterus at birth or lost it due to cancer, have ovaries and were able to produce eggs for in vitro fertilization. The team, led by Dr. Mats Brannstrom, predicts that three to four of the nine women might successfully give birth, marking a world first if successful.

Previous attempts at womb transplants in Saudi Arabia and Turkey have not resulted in live births. In Sweden, two women had to have their transplanted wombs removed due to complications, and four experienced mild rejection episodes. The Swedish team's method is unique as they use wombs donated by living relatives or friends of the recipients, while other countries use wombs from deceased donors.

The recipients will need to take drugs throughout their pregnancy to prevent rejection and will be closely monitored due to potential concerns about the transplanted uterus's ability to support a growing baby. Dr. Charles Kingsland, a spokesman for Britain's Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists, emphasized the need for careful observation of the physiological changes in the uterus and its suitability for a growing baby.

The transplants aim to benefit women who cannot conceive due to uterus loss or absence. However, the long-term effects and success of the procedure remain uncertain, and further research is necessary to ensure the safety and success of the transplants.

The St. Joseph Abbey, a monastery in Louisiana, has been involved in a legal dispute with the state over the sale of handcrafted caskets. The abbey, which is part of the Order of Saint Benedict, has been making caskets for years but recently decided to turn it into a business to help support the monastery. However, Louisiana law only allows licensed funeral directors to sell "funeral merchandise," which means that the abbey must either give up the casket-selling business or become a licensed funeral establishment. The abbey has argued that this law is unconstitutional, as it violates due process and equal protection. The case went to federal court, where the monks won round one in July, with U.S. District Judge Stanwood R. Duval Jr. ruling the restrictions unconstitutional. The Louisiana State Board of Embalmers and Funeral Directors has appealed, and the case will be heard in early June. The monks are represented by the Institute for Justice, a libertarian legal group that takes on cases involving government regulation of free enterprise. The group is hoping that the case will be taken up by the Supreme Court, as it presents an opportunity to challenge government economic regulations. The monks argue that the law is protectionist and does not serve the interests of consumers, as Louisianans are free to purchase caskets online from companies like Wal-Mart and Costco but not from in-state casket-makers. The funeral directors board argues that the law protects consumers from improper sales tactics and is necessary due to Louisiana's unique burial practices.

In a recent interview on The Howard Stern Show, Jason Alexander, best known for his role as George Costanza in Seinfeld, revealed the backstory behind the death of his character's fiancée, Susan Ross, played by Heidi Swedberg. Alexander explained that the lack of comedic chemistry between him and Swedberg was the primary reason for Susan's untimely demise in the show's seventh season.

Alexander admitted that he struggled to find the right comedic tone with Swedberg, and his castmates initially dismissed his concerns. However, after Jerry Seinfeld and Julia Louis-Dreyfus performed scenes with Swedberg, they too acknowledged the issue. According to Alexander, Julia Louis-Dreyfus even joked about wanting to kill off Susan. This comment, according to Alexander, provided showrunner Larry David with the inspiration for the season finale, in which Susan dies after licking poisonous envelope glue, symbolizing the toxic impact of the relationship on her life.

Alexander clarified that no one on the cast disliked Swedberg, and he issued an apology to her, stating that it was his intention to defend her from rumors when he told the story on the Howard Stern Show. He also emphasized that the comments about killing off Susan were directed strictly toward the character and not toward Swedberg herself, who he described as "generous and gracious."

Following her role as Susan Ross, Swedberg continued acting, appearing in shows such as ER, Gilmore Girls, and Bones. These days, she plays and teaches ukulele music and performs as the lead in the Sukey Jump Band.

On February 14, 2013, Oscar Pistorius, the South African double-amputee sprinter known as the "Blade Runner," was charged with the murder of his girlfriend, Reeva Steenkamp. The incident occurred at Pistorius's home in the gated community of Silver Woods Country Estate in Pretoria, one of South Africa's capitals. Pistorius claimed that he mistook Steenkamp for a burglar and shot her in self-defense. However, the evidence against him is strong, including the fact that he shot Steenkamp through the closed bathroom door, which is reckless behavior. The case has attracted international attention and has been described as the crime story of the year. The athlete is depicted as an aggressive narcissist addicted to caffeine pills and energy drinks, a thrill-seeking womanizer who let fame go to his head and used foul language around children while training at the gym. Some sources, including Hilton Botha, the police detective who initially investigated the case, argue that the evidence against Pistorius is strong and that he is guilty of murder. However, Botha's credibility has been called into question due to his own legal troubles and inconsistent testimony. The case is set to go to trial in June 2013.

The heirs of Alfred Flechtheim, a prominent German Jewish art collector, have filed a lawsuit against the German state of Bavaria, seeking the return of eight paintings by Max Beckmann, Juan Gris, and Paul Klee that they claim were looted by the Nazis. Flechtheim was forced to leave the paintings behind when he fled Berlin for Paris in 1933 to escape Nazi persecution. Some of the paintings may have passed through the hands of Hildebrand Gurlitt, a Nazi art dealer who was allowed to sell "degenerate" art. The lawsuit joins others seeking to reclaim artworks taken, sold, or left behind after the Nazis took power in Germany. The case is Hulton et al v, Bayerische Staatsgemaldesammlungen et al, U.S. District Court, Southern District of New York, No. 16-09360. Alfred Flechtheim was one of the most important German art collectors at the beginning of the 20th century, but his work came to an abrupt end with the Nazis. He died impoverished in London in 1937, and his widow Betti committed suicide as she faced deportation. Flechtheim's grand-nephew Michael Hulton and his stepmother Penny Hulton are the plaintiffs in the lawsuit. The paintings in question include Beckmann's "Duchess of Malvedi" (1926), "Still Life with Cigar Box" (1926), "Quappi in Blue" (1926), "Dream—Chinese Fireworks" (1927), "Champagne Still Life" (1929) and "Still Life with Studio Window" (1931); Gris' "Cruche et Verre Sur un Table" (1916) and Klee's "Grenzen des Verstandes" (1927). The defendants are the Bavarian State Paintings Collections and the State of Bavaria. The case is being filed in the U.S. District Court in Manhattan.

The Supreme Court has upheld a regulation by the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) aimed at reducing air pollution that travels across state lines, in a 6-2 decision. The regulation, known as the "good neighbor" rule, requires 28 eastern states to reduce power-plant emissions that contribute to smog and soot particles in downwind states. The EPA's formula for dealing with cross-state air pollution was deemed "permissible, workable, and equitable" by the court. The decision delivers a significant victory to the EPA and downwind states, such as Connecticut, where 93% of air pollution originates from out-of-state sources. The ruling was met with criticism from some states and power companies, who had argued that the EPA should allow them to create their own plans to cut emissions. Justice Antonin Scalia, in his dissent, argued that the EPA rule was an "undemocratic revision" of the Clean Air Act. The decision has implications for the ongoing debate over the role of the EPA and the extent of its regulatory powers.

The Officer Down Memorial Page (ODMP) has announced a new memorial program, ODMP K9, to honor police dogs that have been killed in the line of duty. The program aims to recognize the hundreds of canines that have sacrificed their lives while serving alongside law enforcement officers in America.

One such case involves Primo, a Belgian Malinois K-9 with the New Orleans Police Department, who died in 2009 after being left in a hot police SUV. The dog's body temperature spiked to nearly 110 degrees, and he suffered three seizures before dying due to heat stress. Primo's death is one of more than two dozen police K-9 deaths due to heat-related symptoms since 2007.

The animal rights group PETA identified 20 such deaths, with BuzzFeed News confirming those and finding an additional nine based on local and national news reports. The deaths of police dogs can be particularly heartrending because they put their lives on the line, much like uniformed officers. New technology can help prevent such tragedies by warning handlers who've left their K-9s in cars.

Police K-9s are more susceptible to heat stroke due to their thicker coats and darker hair. Ike, a Department of Corrections K-9 in Phoenix, died last year after being left in a police vehicle for seven hours, while two police K-9s in Bexar County, Texas, perished after being left in a vehicle for nearly 30 hours in 2012.

Many of these K-9 deaths occur in local police forces, but they also happen in airport police, corrections departments, and other types of law enforcement agencies. Forgetting the dog in the car is one problem, but some handlers intentionally put their dog in the vehicle, trusting the air-conditioning system to keep running for hours.

The vast majority of such K-9 deaths occur in local police forces, but dogs also sweltered to death while in vehicles belonging to airport police, corrections departments, and other types of law enforcement agencies. Forgetting the dog in the car is one problem, but some handlers intentionally put their dog in the vehicle, mistakenly trusting the air-conditioning system to keep running for hours.

In a particularly ghastly case, police K-9 Sasha was found in her handler's SUV after three hot August days in Warwick, Georgia. Lt. T.J. Frye, Sasha's K-9 handler, told investigators the dog must have made it into the vehicle on her own. Sasha's final moments in the car were eerily similar to Primo's. Both dogs apparently tried to chew through the car to escape. After Frye found Sasha's bloated and decomposing body in the vehicle, he buried the eight-year-old Dutch shepherd in his backyard. Local residents and city officials expressed shock and grief, demanding that the dog receive a proper burial. An online petition for an investigation into the dog’s death received more than 4,000 signatures.

Across America, there are at least 20,000 working police dogs. No one knows how many police dogs die annually in hot cars. No federal agency keeps track. The Connecticut Police Work Dog Association tallies K-9s that died in service from all causes. K-9s who died of excessive heat because they were left in vehicles are not listed explicitly, but some of those deaths can be found on the website under the category of “Heat Exhaustion.”

The 29 deaths confirmed by BuzzFeed News occurred in 14 states from North Carolina to California, and only between April and September. Even on mild summer days, closed vehicles act like a greenhouse. When it’s 85 degrees outside, one study found that in 20 minutes, the temperature inside a car can rise almost to 114°F — almost 30 degrees. After an hour, the inside temperature can hit a scorching 128 degrees.

The Officer Lewis case in New Orleans is one of the most controversial cases. Lewis returned to his police SUV to find his K-9, Primo, battling for his life.
