Lewis had left the dog inside the police vehicle while he got ready for his shift. Primo tore, clawed, and bit into the upholstery on the seats, apparently trying to escape to cooler air. When Lewis returned to the vehicle he saw Primo “lying in the back coughing.” The officer hosed down the dog then rushed him to a local veterinary clinic, where the dog subsequently collapsed, suffered three seizures, and died. Cause of death: “shock due to heat stress.”

Lewis was charged with aggravated cruelty to animals, a felony. Lewis later pleaded guilty to a misdemeanor animal cruelty charge. He was ordered to pay $11,500 to the police department. After almost three years, a court of appeals found that Lewis was not negligent, and reinstated the officer with full pay and benefits.

Many police K-9 units use heat alert systems sometimes known as “Hot Dog” or “Hot-N-Pop” systems. The technology varies, but if the vehicle’s interior gets too hot, the alert system automatically rolls down the windows, activates a cooling system or fan, and sets off the vehicle’s siren. According to an investigation by San Antonio’s ABC affiliate, KSAT 12, the Bextar County Sheriff’s Office bought two Hot Dog systems prior to the death of police K-9s Hades and Vegas, but “sat in boxes, untouched on a training room floor for over a year.” It is unclear why the systems, which were bought from a $27,000 grant, were not installed.

The ODMP K9 program aims to honor the sacrifices made by these brave animals and raise awareness about the dangers they face. The program will work to ensure that police dogs receive the recognition and protection they deserve.

CVS, the largest pharmacy chain in the United States, has announced that it will stop selling cigarettes and other tobacco products in all of its 7,600 stores by October 1. This decision marks the first time any drugstore has ever dropped tobacco sales, and it is part of a major shift in direction for the company. The move is intended to align CVS with its long-term goal of becoming a central player in the U.S. health care system, focusing on delivering healthcare services and interacting more closely with patients.

The decision to exit the tobacco category is expected to cost CVS approximately $2 billion in annual revenues, equating to approximately 17 cents per share. However, the company has identified incremental opportunities to offset the profitability impact. The decision has been praised by various health organizations, including the American Medical Association, the American Heart Association, and the American Cancer Society.

In addition to stopping the sale of tobacco products, CVS plans to launch a national smoking cessation program this Spring. The program will offer information and treatment on smoking cessation at CVS/pharmacy and MinuteClinic locations, as well as online resources. The program will be available broadly across all CVS/pharmacy and MinuteClinic locations and will offer additional comprehensive programs for CVS Caremark pharmacy benefit management plan members to help them quit smoking.

CVS Caremark is dedicated to helping people on their path to better health as the largest integrated pharmacy company in the United States. Through its more than 7,600 CVS/pharmacy stores, its leading pharmacy benefit manager serving more than 60 million plan members, and its retail health clinic system, the largest in the nation with more than 800 MinuteClinic locations, it is a market leader in mail order, retail and specialty pharmacy, retail clinics, and Medicare Part D Prescription Drug Plans.

The company continually strives to improve health and lower costs by developing new approaches such as its unique Pharmacy Advisor program that helps people with chronic diseases such as diabetes obtain and stay on their medications. The decision to stop selling tobacco products is consistent with the positions taken by various health organizations that have all publicly opposed tobacco sales in retail outlets with pharmacies.

The article discusses the launch of a new mobile application called Yo, which allows users to send the word "Yo" to their contacts. The app was created by Or Arbel, a former iOS designer at Mobli, at the request of Mobli's CEO Moshe Hogeg, who wanted a simple way to notify his assistant when he needed her. The app was initially met with skepticism, but has since gained attention and investment, with $1 million raised from a group of angel investors led by Hogeg.

Yo is a simple app that allows users to send a push notification to anyone else with the app, with all notifications saying the same thing: "Yo." The app's inventor, Or Arbel, believes that "you usually understand what the Yo means based on who you get it from and when you get it." The app has been popular among other start-ups and has attracted over 50,000 users who have sent about 4 million Yos.

Arbel has big plans for Yo, including using it for notifications from newspapers and blogs, and for embedding a Yo button on blogs to notify readers of new stories. The app is also being used to follow the World Cup, with anyone who sends a Yo to "WORLDCUP" receiving notifications whenever a goal is scored.

The simplicity of the app has been both its appeal and its criticism, with some seeing it as a joke and others seeing it as a new way to get lightweight, non-intrusive notifications. The app has been compared to Facebook's original Poke button, Foursquare's new Swarm app, an RSS reader, and WhatsApp without so many words.

Arbel has moved to San Francisco to work on Yo full-time and is seeking "strategic partners." The app is available on iOS and Android. The article also discusses the potential for Yo to represent a new tech bubble, with investors throwing money at any app that fits into the social/mobile category. However, Arbel is confident in the potential of Yo and is working on developing an API to partner with brands.

In the 30th District state house election in Washington State, the incumbent Democratic state Rep. Roger Freeman, who was one of two black representatives in the state legislature, passed away at the age of 48 due to colon cancer at the end of October. At the time of his death, about 15% of the district's voters had already mailed in their ballots, and Freeman had a six-point lead over his Republican opponent, Jack Dovey. Since Freeman's death was so recent, many voters were unaware and continued to vote for him or on a party line.

The two counties that make up the 30th district will select a temporary legislator from three possibilities offered by local Democrats. A special election will then be held next year to fill out the final year of the two-year House term.

Voters electing people who are no longer alive is not an uncommon occurrence. Last year, Oregon voters elected a man to the Aberdeen City Council five months after he died, and Missouri elected a dead man who was running unopposed to serve as county commissioner in 2010.

Roger Freeman, who died last week, is leading his race for a seat in the state House of Representatives. Early results show Freeman is taking 53% of the vote. Freeman's supporters still want folks to vote for him, because if he wins he'd be replaced by a democrat. The democratic precinct leaders would offer three potential replacements to the county councils of King and Pierce counties who would select one. If no agreement is reached, the governor gets to choose.

The election in Washington state is noteworthy for several reasons. Voters will decide the fate of two competing gun background check initiatives. Washington's 4th Congressional District features two Republicans on the fall ballot, the first time that's happened in a federal race under the state's 'Top 2' primary system. Democrats need to win two or more seats to regain control of the Senate, but Republicans had strong showings in the primary. Voters in Washington state will vote yet again on class sizes. Education advocates are pushing a measure limiting class sizes, but opponents say Initiative 1351 could make a bad budget situation worse as lawmakers scramble to pay for court-ordered reforms.

The Olsen twins' luxury fashion brand The Row is experiencing a surge in demand with their $39,000 backpack selling out at Barneys New York. Ashley Olsen, one of the twins, revealed that the backpack was the first item to sell off the shelf. Barneys New York began carrying the crocodile-skin bags in July as a strategy to compete with other high-priced handbags. The bag, designed to appeal to a younger crowd willing to spend a significant amount on a long-lasting, classic design, has been a successful gamble for Barneys New York, according to Amanda Brooks, the fashion director. The bag's exclusivity also adds to its allure. However, with the bag flying off the shelves, the chances of being the only one who owns it are diminishing.

The film "Old Fashioned," produced by Freestyle Releasing, is set to challenge the highly anticipated "Fifty Shades of Grey" on Valentine's Day 2015. The faith-based romantic drama, with the tagline "Chivalry makes a comeback," aims to offer a Christian alternative to the sexually explicit "Fifty Shades."

Written, directed, and starring Rik Swartzwelder, the film revolves around a former frat boy and a free-spirited woman, who attempt an old-fashioned courtship in contemporary America. Swartzwelder emphasizes that the film explores the possibility of a higher standard in relationships, without condemning those who have made mistakes.

"Old Fashioned" is the first faith-based theatrical release to specifically target the Christian singles audience. The film's producers include Skoche Films, Motion Picture Pro Studios, Dave DeBorde, Nini Hadjis, and Nathan Nazario.

The announcement comes four days after the debut of the "Fifty Shades" trailer, which features several sex and bondage scenes. Fox is also releasing its "Poltergeist" reboot on the same weekend.

"God's Not Dead," another successful faith-based film by Freestyle Releasing, topped $60 million earlier this year, making it the highest-grossing film for the studio.

"Old Fashioned" promises to offer a wholesome, God-centered love story as a counterpoint to the erotic themes of "Fifty Shades of Grey." The film's release on Valentine's Day will provide Christian audiences with an alternative option for the holiday.

The Discussion and Action group aims to promote discussions on Liberty, Freedom, and the Constitution, with a focus on the Second Amendment and Open Carry Events in Kentucky. The group's logo is the 2nd Amendment Dollar, and more information can be found at budsgunshop.com.

Recently, a controversial incident occurred involving a woman named Lauren Valle from MoveOn.org, who was assaulted during an encounter with Rand Paul, the Republican nominee for Senate in Kentucky. The incident, captured on video, shows Valle being pushed to the ground and stomped by a supporter of Paul. The perpetrator, Tim Profitt, admitted to the Associated Press that he stepped on Valle's head. Profitt was the Bourbon County coordinator for Paul.

Lexington police have identified Profitt as the suspect and have served him with a criminal summons. The Paul campaign has distanced itself from the incident and the volunteer involved. The violence occurred before Paul's debate with his Democrat rival, Jack Conway, on Monday night. This incident has raised concerns about the level of aggression and violence in political campaigns in 2010.

Damien Hirst's latest exhibition at the Tate Modern in London features his most famous works, including a shark suspended in formaldehyde and a platinum human skull covered in 8,601 diamonds, estimated to be worth £50 million. The exhibition includes a gift shop offering limited-edition items, such as a plastic skull titled Hallucinatory Head, priced at £36,800, and a £10,500 set of plates. Critic Julian Spalding has criticized Hirst's work as "con art," but Hirst defends his art, stating that its value is determined by demand. The exhibition, which runs from 4 April to 9 September, has been met with controversy, with some questioning the high prices of the limited-edition items.

The Pentagon's Excess Property Program, also known as the 1033 Program, has been under scrutiny since August, following civil unrest in Ferguson, MO. The program, which supplies excess military equipment to police departments across the country, has released a detailed breakdown of its supplies for the first time. The data, released on Nov. 21, shows a wide range of equipment, from mundane items like battery chargers to powerful equipment like armored mine-resistant vehicles and helicopters. Surprising items include trumpets and snowshoes, while hundreds of organizations have received armored vehicles. The most common items issued were rifles, supplied to departments large and small. Unusual items include 500 pairs of snowshoes, French horns, and over 372 televisions for personal use. The program has supplied more than $4.3 billion in gear since 1997, with over $160 million going to agencies in California. The data highlights the distribution of military equipment to small police forces, raising concerns about the militarization of police.

On Thursday night, investigators were reviewing surveillance video from a gas station near the Clinton Correctional Facility, where two convicted killers, David Sweat and Richard Matt, escaped over the weekend. The escapees were last seen at the gas station, where K-9 units picked up their scents and followed them east towards Cadyville. A Subway restaurant is located at the gas station, and it is believed that the pair may have been trying to find food in a trash bin.

The search effort intensified in Cadyville on Thursday night, with officials using infrared technology to help locate the escapees. Cringle Road was closed to traffic, while Trudeau Road and Route 374 remained open. Investigators have also found an imprint from a shoe or boot, as well as a food wrapper in the area, and are trying to determine if this is an area where the escapees bedded down and how long ago they were there.

Residents in Cadyville and surrounding communities were urged to stay in their homes and lock their doors, with Saranac Central School shutting down for the day. New York State Police closed State Route 374 east of the village of Dannemora to West Plattsburgh as they investigate what they called a "lead involving the escapees from the Clinton Correctional Facility."

Police sources classified a tip to the Press-Republican as their best lead by far, with "We are close. This could be it" being the sentiment expressed. While the focus appears to be in Dannemora and nearby Cadyville, authorities are also searching neighboring woods, farms, fields, and woods in Willsboro after a driver saw two "suspicious" men run off during a late-night driving rainstorm. There was also a turn toward Vermont due to "information that would suggest (that state) was discussed as a possible location."

Authorities have not ruled out the possibility that Matt and Sweat have left New York, with the possibility of them heading to Canada or most anywhere in the United States or beyond. To this point, 50 digital billboards with the fugitives' photos have gone up in New York, New Jersey, Massachusetts, and Pennsylvania.

The escape in 1903 by a former bank burglar serving a life sentence and three other inmates under the walls of Clinton prison in far northern New York State is similar to the recent escape. Over the years, other inmates have tried different methods, scaling gates, donning disguises, or simply walking away when guards were not looking.

Since Clinton opened in 1845, dozens of inmates have escaped over, under, or through the prison’s thick walls, their exploits detailed in breathless, often sensationalistic, newspaper reports of earlier eras. Among the earliest escapes from Clinton occurred in 1860, when James F. Whiting, known as “The Gay Deceiver,” donned a suit of civilian clothes and walked out, according to an article in The New York Times. He was arrested a year later for defrauding a Philadelphia jeweler of $670.

Inmates at Clinton can be locked away for years, for decades, sometimes their whole lives in a prison that is among the oldest and most remote in the state. They are battered by extremes of heat and cold and worn down by boredom. For many, the idea of escape can offer a semblance of hope.

"Escape. Making a beat. That was all I thought of,” John Resko, an inmate at Clinton in the 1920s and ’30s, wrote in “Reprieve,” his best-selling memoir. “That was all any of the cons thought of, spoke of, dreamed of."

The document summarizes two movie reviews, "Bitch Slap" and "Wonderful World."

"Bitch Slap," a tribute to hot-women-in-peril movies, features a plot about buried treasure and the CIA, but its focus is on the actresses' assets and girl-fighting. The movie has moments of enjoyment, such as an oh-so-gratuitous water fight and the lusty sadism of the most unhinged of the three actresses, but it also suffers from a surfeit of fistfights and a lack of Zoë Bell. The film is surprisingly puritanical, substituting plentiful violence and a howlingly predictable "shock" ending for the payoff it promises.

"Wonderful World" stars Matthew Broderick as Ben Singer, a once moderately successful children's music performer who has retreated from the world, becoming a self-styled, self-hating curmudgeon. His ex-wife now lives in a huge mansion with her new husband, and Singer's teenage daughter rarely wants to see him. He works as a proofreader in a law office, making a long-term career of a job most people use as a temporary landing pad. His only solace comes from smoking pot and playing chess with his Senegalese roommate Ibou (Michael Kenneth Williams). When Ibou goes into a diabetic coma, Ben finds himself with a new roommate in Ibou's sister (Sanaa Lathan). The film uses immigrants to open the eyes of closed-off main characters, but it never fully explores the hidden corners of Ben's character's psyche.

Both movies received R ratings and were released in general theaters. "Bitch Slap" was rated R for brutal violence, strong sexual content and language throughout, and brief drug use, while "Wonderful World" was rated R for language, some drug use, and sexual content.

The ninth-century Qarawiyyin library in Fez, Morocco, considered the oldest library in the world, is set to reopen after years of restoration. The library, which was founded by Fatima al-Fihri in 859 and houses priceless manuscripts dating back to the seventh century, was in dire need of restoration due to structural problems, lack of insulation, and a blocked drainage system.

Canadian-Moroccan architect Aziza Chaouni, who grew up in Fez, was tasked with the restoration project. The library boasts a new sewerage and underground canal system to drain away moisture that threatened to destroy many of its prized manuscripts. An elaborate lab was also set up to treat, preserve, and digitize the oldest texts.

The most ancient works are housed in a special room with strict security and temperature and humidity controls. The most precious is a ninth-century copy of the Qur’an, written in ornate Kufic script on camel skin. The library's restoration comes at a time when extremists are rampaging the region’s heritage, with the Islamic State carrying out cultural atrocities in Syria and Iraq.

The library's reopening is part of a plan to restore Fez to its status as a spiritual and cultural capital, which it was for centuries before Rabat became the center of political life. Renovations are also taking place in other quarters of the city, and Sufi and music festivals have injected fresh blood into the medina. Plans are being made for an exhibition that would showcase the most prized collections in the library.

Chaouni's sustainable architecture philosophy means the library cannot be a relic of ages past but a breathing part of the city. She also drafted a plan to restore the river in Fez, which was once known as the river of jewels but was gradually drenched in waste from the local tannery and sewage from surrounding residences. The river is slowly coming to life now.

The library is expected to be reopened for visitors later this year, and King Mohammad VI is expected to inaugurate the reopening. The restoration is a testament to the value of preserving heritage for future generations and the importance of cultural and spiritual capital in Morocco.

The Transparency International's 2013 Global Corruption Barometer surveyed over 114,000 people in 107 countries, revealing that 27% of respondents had paid a bribe in the past year. The survey, which measures the views of everyday people, found that police and the judiciary are the most prone to bribery, with nearly one-third reporting bribes paid to police and 24% for the judicial system. The situation is particularly dire in countries known for police and judicial corruption, with an average of 53% of people asked to pay a bribe by police and 30% by the judicial system in the worst-affected countries. Over half of those surveyed reported an increase in corruption over the past two years, with Liberia and Mongolia scoring the worst on a five-point corruption scale. Respondents also identified political parties as the most corrupt institution, and have less faith in their leaders to combat corruption than in 2008. The survey was conducted by Samuel Rubenfeld, who can be reached at Samuel.Rubenfeld@dowjones.com and followed on Twitter at @srubenfeld.

Toronto Mayor Rob Ford, who is battling a rare form of cancer, stated on Thursday that he has a 50-50 chance of survival. Despite his health challenges, Ford is considering participating in debates for his old council seat in Ward 2, Etobicoke North, where he is running as a candidate. Ford's decision to run for office while undergoing chemotherapy has been met with criticism from some residents, but he defended his decision, stating that many residents support his candidacy.

One of Ford's opponents, business professional Andray Domise, called Ford's decision "highly irresponsible." Domise expressed concern that Ford has not released a platform, has not been canvassing, and has not been knocking on doors. However, community developer Luke LaRocque expressed a different view, stating that the people in the community are focused on ensuring their community gets the things it needs, and if Ford is focused on those things, he should be allowed to run.

Ford represented Ward 2 for 10 years, from 2000 to 2010, and polls suggest he holds a big lead over the field. Ford has been seen canvassing at least once since he was discharged from the hospital. He skipped a Ward 2 all-candidates’ debate held by Rogers television on Wednesday night, instead attending a mayoral debate in which his brother Doug Ford was participating.

Ford spoke with City Hall reporters for the first time about his cancer diagnosis and his decision to pull out of the mayoral race. He stated that cancer has been the "worst event" that's ever happened to him, and that it has been especially difficult given the effect on his family. Ford's voice was hoarse, and he had to stop mid-sentence several times to gather his thoughts.

At the same time that Ford spoke with reporters at City Hall, Doug was in Etobicoke, unveiling his transit plan at a press conference. Doug's $9-billion, 32-kilometre subway plan is almost identical to the plan unveiled by Rob when he was still running for mayor, with one notable exception. Whereas Rob's plan placed Sheppard and Finch subways as his first priorities, Doug said that a downtown relief line would instead be his number one priority. As with his brother, Doug promised to build the subways at no cost to residents.

In the wake of the fatal shooting of University of Utah student-athlete Lauren McCluskey on campus, separate reviews will be conducted into campus safety and the university police department's response to a complaint from McCluskey about her killer. Melvin Rowland, a convicted sex offender who was free on parole, had dated McCluskey for about a month after they met at a bar where he worked as a bouncer. After the relationship ended on October 9, Rowland attempted to extort McCluskey and stalked her residence before assaulting her in a parking lot and shooting her several times in the back seat of a car on October 22. Rowland killed himself hours later in a church as police closed in.

McCluskey had reported receiving numerous emails and messages using different names trying to lure her to locations. Investigators now believe they all came from Rowland, who was described as a master manipulator. After shooting McCluskey, Rowland was picked up on campus by a woman he had recently met on a dating website, and they went to her apartment where Rowland took a shower. The woman later contacted police when she saw Rowland's name in news reports about the shooting and is not expected to face charges.

Rowland was convicted of forcible sexual abuse and enticing a minor, both felonies, in 2004 in Utah. He was granted parole in February and released in April, but was later returned to prison for parole violations. During one parole hearing, he described himself as a womanizer who manipulated women to get what he wanted and said he was attracted to teenage girls and vulnerable women.

University of Utah president Ruth Watkins said outside investigations are being launched to assess campus security and police protocols to determine if improvements can be made to prevent future shootings. Watkins said so far she has found no mistakes in how police handled the case. Brophy said he welcomes the reviews. Gov. Gary Herbert said corrections and parole officials had approved independent investigations into the handling of Rowland's parole.

In the early stages of the investigation, police did not have enough information to pass on to any other law enforcement agency, Brophy said, adding that there were no indications from McCluskey that Rowland was threatening physical violence. University of Utah athletics paid tribute to McCluskey by writing her name on the sneakers of star player Donovan Mitchell before a game against the Houston Rockets. "It was a scary feeling to be close to that. It's just so sad," Mitchell told NBA TV after the game. "I have a little sister. My mom raised me. Women have to be protected more. She was being harassed for two straight weeks. That's so tough. She was defenseless. She couldn't do anything about it. For a man to do that, that's terrible. For me, I just wanted to be able to dedicate this game to her and her family."

The article from The Guardian investigates the alarming issue of women in prisons across the United States being targeted by sex traffickers, who force them into prostitution upon their release. The investigation found that traffickers are using government websites to obtain personal information, such as mugshots, release dates, and charge sheets, to identify potential victims while they are still incarcerated.

Pimps also use inmates in prisons and jails nationwide to befriend incarcerated women, who are later trafficked into the $9.5bn US commercial sex industry. The investigation revealed cases of the bail bond system being exploited in sex trafficking operations in at least five different states. Pimps and sex buyers are locating incarcerated women awaiting a court date by using personal data such as mugshots and bail bonds posted online, or through corrupt bondsmen.

Once released, women are told they must work as prostitutes or have their bond rescinded, and be sent back to jail. The investigation found numerous cases of this exploitation in Florida, Texas, Ohio, North Carolina, and Mississippi. One trafficking survivor from Tampa, Florida, stated, "The pimps would use bail as a way to control us and keep us in debt bondage."

Diane Checchio, a former prosecutor for the district attorney’s office in Orlando, Florida, said the bail bond system was routinely exploited by traffickers. Up to 80% of the trafficking cases she worked on in 2016 involved bondsmen found to be illegally passing on information about women arrested on prostitution charges to suspected traffickers.

The investigation gathered testimony from more than 20 trafficking survivors in 11 states across the country, as well as correctional officers, convicted sex traffickers, law enforcement officials, lawyers, prosecutors, and frontline workers. All corroborated that prisons and jails were being used as recruiting grounds for human traffickers.

There are currently 1.2 million women under the supervision of the criminal justice system in the US. Women now comprise a larger proportion of the prison population than ever before, with the number incarcerated eight times higher than in 1980. Many women are jailed for non-violent offenses, with 25% incarcerated on drug-related charges.

The article emphasizes that prisons and jails are perfect hunting grounds for traffickers due to the isolation and trauma experienced by many inmates. Traffickers first identify potential victims, then establish a relationship by using letters, phone calls, promises of money and housing, and prison bank accounts to send money and establish a debt.

The article concludes by stating that correctional facilities must prioritize the safety and protection of inmates and ensure staff understand the vulnerability of their institutions to human trafficking. Anti-trafficking campaigners argue that prisons and jails are failing women by not offering alternative options upon release and by not adequately addressing the issue of human trafficking within their facilities. The US Department of Justice declined to comment.

The U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) has declared the deaths of 30 large whales in the western Gulf of Alaska since May an "unusual mortality event." This event is three times the historical average for the region and has triggered a more intense investigation to determine the cause. The leading hypothesis for the deaths is harmful algal bloom toxins, but no conclusive evidence has been found yet.

Officials have only been able to get samples from one whale due to challenges in accessing carcasses, which are often floating, rarely beached, and difficult to reach. Large-scale whale deaths are among the toughest to investigate, as they pose safety concerns for researchers who want to collect samples due to bears feeding on washed-up whale carcasses.

Scientists and researchers are looking at environmental factors, historical information, and mortality among seabirds or other sea creatures to gain a better understanding of the situation. However, they are limited in what they can do without better access to the carcasses.

In Canada, six large whales have been reported dead off the coast of British Columbia since May. Necropsies were conducted on two of the more recent carcasses, but the results are pending. This does not appear to be a "coast-wide" event at this point, as large whale deaths have not increased during the same timeframe near California, Washington, and Oregon.

NOAA is urging the public to report any sightings of dead whales or distressed animals they encounter. The agency plans to work with colleagues in Canada to investigate the cause of death for the stranded whales. The investigation will involve scientists from NOAA and partner organizations, as well as members of the Alaska Marine Mammal Stranding Network.

This kind of investigation generally requires months, or sometimes even years, of data collection and analysis. NOAA will publish information on its unusual mortality event website as it becomes available. The public can assist in the investigation by immediately contacting the Alaska Marine Mammal Stranding Network hotline at 877-9-AKR-PRD (877-925-7773) if they see a stranded or dead marine mammal. Only specially trained marine mammal experts are authorized to respond to marine mammals in distress. The public should not touch stranded or floating whales.

In a recent development, members of the Pi Kappa Alpha fraternity at California State University in Chico are facing federal charges for an alleged tree-cutting binge and vandalism in Lassen National Forest. The incident occurred during an initiation ceremony for new pledges in April. The group is accused of illegally chopping down over 32 trees and firing guns, leaving a mess at a campground.

The U.S. Forest Service released surveillance photos of the young men buying the tools believed to have been used in the vandalism. Each member now faces charges of vandalism, illegal firearms, and degrading U.S. territory. The fraternity and its president, Evan Jossey from Pleasant Hill, are scheduled to appear in court on June 26, 2017.

The incident has caused backlash from the community and fellow fraternities. The Pi Kappa Alpha fraternity, however, denies some of the allegations and claims to have faced threats. The incident is part of an ongoing effort to archive web pages and fix broken links on the internet. More charges may be headed the fraternity's way as the investigation continues.

A 14-year-old girl named Ayvani Perez, who was abducted from her home in Ellenwood, Clayton County, early Tuesday morning, has been safely returned to her family. The neighbor reported seeing Ayvani return to her home early Wednesday night, but she did not spend the night there. Clayton County Police Chief Greg Porter confirmed that Ayvani was in good health after being found at a home in Conyers.

Authorities have arrested Wildrego Jackson, 29, and Juan Alberto Rodriguez, 40, in connection to Ayvani's abduction. Police said two armed men broke into Ayvani's home early Tuesday and kidnapped her after asking her mother for money and jewelry. However, Rodriguez and Jackson are not the same men pictured in the sketches investigators released on Tuesday, and the men in the sketches remain at large.

Federal agents haven't disclosed how they found Ayvani at the Conyers home. Rodriguez has a criminal background, having been arrested in December 2012 in Henry County under the name Juan Aberto Contreras-Ramirez, and charged with trafficking marijuana. Ayvani's mother was also arrested in that incident.

Jackson faces conspiracy to commit kidnapping charges, and Rodriguez is currently being held on immigration-related charges. Jackson has an extensive criminal background dating back to at least 2001, with charges that include assault, child cruelty, sale and distribution of cocaine, marijuana possession, being a convicted felon in possession of a firearm, and obstruction charges.

Neighbors are relieved and grateful that Ayvani has been returned safely. However, questions remain about the circumstances surrounding her kidnapping. The community is now seeking more information about the incident.

Sienna Miller, a British actor, is set to join the legal battle against Scotland Yard and the News of the World over the phone-hacking scandal. Miller's lawyers plan to seek a judicial review of the police's handling of the case, alleging that her privacy was invaded by the newspaper. The actor discovered that the News of the World's private investigator, Glenn Mulcaire, had obtained her mobile phone numbers, account number, and secret PIN code.

Sean Hoare, a former News of the World journalist who exposed hacking at the paper, has been interviewed by police under caution, indicating he is being treated as a suspect. Another former staffer, Paul McMullan, has also been contacted by detectives for questioning.

The police had been in possession of information about Miller being targeted since 2006 but failed to inform her until her lawyer inquired. Miller plans to join the legal action led by Bindmans law firm, which includes former deputy assistant commissioner at Scotland Yard, Brian Paddick, and investigative journalist Brendan Montague, among others.

Meanwhile, MPs are investigating whether parliamentary privileges were breached by Mulcaire. The Commons Standards and Privileges Committee will consider whether phone hacking is a contempt of parliament.

Andy Coulson, the former editor of the News of the World and now Prime Minister David Cameron's communications chief, has denied Hoare's claims of phone hacking. Additionally, representatives of comedian Steve Coogan and presenter Chris Tarrant have announced legal action after confirming their clients' personal details were in Mulcaire's possession.

California is experiencing its driest year on record, with reservoirs throughout the state having low water levels, including Santa Clara County reservoirs that are at 3 percent of capacity or lower. Governor Jerry Brown has declared a drought emergency to speed up assistance to local governments, streamline water transfers, and potentially ease environmental protection requirements for dam releases. The order focuses on urban life, requiring cities to stop watering median strips, replace grass with drought-tolerant landscaping, and install drip or microspray systems in new developments. State agencies will create a temporary rebate program to encourage homeowners to replace water-guzzling appliances with high-efficiency ones. Golf courses, campuses, and cemeteries must cut their water use, and water agencies will discourage water waste with higher rates and fees. The order aims to reduce the amount of water used statewide in urban areas by 25%.

Some critics argue that the order does not do enough to address agricultural uses, which account for roughly three quarters of Californians' water usage. The water board will release draft regulations in mid-April to implement the order, and local agencies will receive targets for cutting water use based on how well they've done so far. Local agencies that have been slow to conserve since then will feel the order's effects most dramatically. Most of the burden of enforcement will fall on local agencies, with fines of up to $10,000 a day for non-compliance.

Many Southern California agencies are already taking steps called for in Brown's order, such as a turf rebate program administered by the Metropolitan Water District of Southern California. Although some cities may find it challenging to meet the 25% target, they welcome Brown's action.

The order also requires agricultural districts in depleted groundwater basins to share data on groundwater use with the state. For the second year in a row, Central Valley growers without senior water rights are likely to get no supplies from the valley's big federal irrigation project, idling about 500,000 acres last year and potentially leaving even more cropland unplanted this year.

California's drought crisis is causing significant changes in water use habits, with many institutions and individuals taking steps to conserve water. The order aims to reduce water consumption statewide and emphasizes the need for everyone to do their part in these tough times.

On Tuesday night, a rare Blue Moon graced the clear sky, prompting many to take photographs. The Blue Moon, which is not actually blue, is the second full moon in a month according to popular belief, although the U.S. Naval Observatory describes it as the third full moon in an astronomical season with four full moons. This phenomenon occurs once every three years, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. The Blue Moon is also known by other names such as the Full Sturgeon Moon, Green Corn Moon, Grain Moon, or Full Red Moon. The next Blue Moon will take place in 2015. The Blue Moon has inspired romantic songs, popular phrases, and social media buzz, with people sharing photos and jokes about the event. The Blue Moon can appear blue in history due to moonlight traveling through a cloud of particles from forest fires, as was the case in Edinburgh, Scotland in 1950. The Blue Moon tonight is the first full moon of August and will be visible until Wednesday morning.

In Cleveland, Ohio, three women who had been missing for years were found alive on Monday, having reportedly been held captive by 52-year-old Ariel Castro. Fernando Colon, a former security guard in the neighborhood and step-father to Castro's four children, was questioned by the FBI in 2004 about the disappearance of Gina DeJesus and Amanda Berry. Colon was convicted of molesting two of Castro's daughters in 2004 and maintains that Castro orchestrated the case to divert attention away from his own crimes. Colon claims he identified Castro as a more likely suspect in the abductions of the young girls in 2004, and veteran Cleveland private investigator Chris Giannini, who worked for Colon's defense team, agrees that authorities should have taken a closer look at Castro. Arlene Castro, Ariel Castro's daughter, told America's Most Wanted in 2004 that she was the last person to see Gina DeJesus alive. The FBI has not yet returned calls about the allegations made by Fernando Colon.

The article highlights Maria Rose Belding, a 20-year-old American University sophomore, who co-founded MEANS Database, a platform that connects organizations, businesses, and individuals with excess food to food banks and pantries in need. In its first year, MEANS rescued approximately 4,000 pounds of food, won several competitions, and took home a $10,000 prize from L'Oreal Paris. The platform aims to become self-sufficient by developing a system for companies to claim tax benefits for their food donations.

Belding's inspiration for MEANS came from volunteering at a local soup pantry in her Iowa hometown, where she witnessed the waste of food donations. The platform operates through a website and an app, allowing donors to list available food, nearby recipients to receive notifications, and someone to claim and arrange for pick-up.

MEANS addresses the paradox of food waste in America, where 48 million people live in food insecurity but 40% of the country's food is wasted. The platform aims to solve this problem by connecting the supply and demand of food. Hunger is a growing issue, even affecting college students, with several campus food pantries listed on MEANS.

Belding's idea for MEANS became a reality when she met her co-founder, Grant Nelson, who developed the technology while Belding found the donors, food banks, and pantries. The technology and wide reach of MEANS make it different from other food rescue organizations. The platform allows small organizations and individuals to participate on a scale that might be too small for larger organizations like City Harvest, but crucial to the people they help.

MEANS now has a staff of 11 people, 10 interns, and volunteers. The platform aims to become less grant-dependent by developing a system for companies to claim tax benefits for their food donations. The platform is free for users, with MEANS taking a small fee.

Belding hopes to launch the tax benefit program next year, grow and improve the existing program, and create a public, searchable directory of food pantries. She is focused on finals and maintaining her impressive academic record as a student.

Belding shares her journey from hating math in high school to realizing its importance in developing strategies and discovering big-picture solutions for hunger and food waste. Math matters for MEANS, which lives in the space where empathy and entrepreneurship meet. Charity can and should have a big brain to match its big heart. MEANS Database is an example of a simple idea with an extraordinarily complicated execution, using math and data science to connect food banks and pantries, reduce food waste, and feed those in need.

Nicky Hilton Rothschild, a fashion heiress, is expecting her first child with husband James Rothschild this summer. The couple, who married in a lavish ceremony at Kensington Palace in 2015, have been excited about their new life as husband and wife. Paris Hilton, Nicky's older sister, has also expressed her desire for children in the future. The pair were recently spotted baby-shopping in Los Angeles, and close friends and family have been informed of the pregnancy. Nicky is reportedly feeling great and is excited to become a mother.

On November 9, 2013, hundreds of protesters gathered in Santa Rosa, California, and in cities throughout the Bay Area and the state to protest the police killing of 13-year-old Andy Lopez. The protests were part of a "National Day of Action for Andy Lopez" organized by the Answer Coalition and the California Statewide Coalition Against Police Brutality. Andy Lopez was walking and holding a toy AK-47 rifle in rural Sonoma County on October 22, 2013, when he was shot and killed by Sonoma County Sheriff's Deputy Erick Gelhaus. The killing has sparked outrage within the community, state, and nationwide, with many decrying the incident as a tragic example of police brutality that protesters say often targets low-income black and Latino citizens.

During the protests in Santa Rosa, volunteers were collecting stories from attendees about their own experiences with police brutality. In Oakland, more than 100 protesters marched from the Fruitvale BART station to the Alameda County Sheriff's Office, and in San Francisco, more than 100 protesters gathered at the 24th and Mission BART station to speak out against Andy's death.

On July 7, 2014, Sonoma County District Attorney Jill Ravitch announced that no criminal charges will be filed against Deputy Gelhaus in the shooting of Andy Lopez. In announcing her decision, Ravitch released a 52-page summary of her findings that includes several new details about the shooting, including that Lopez was likely high on marijuana at the time he was killed. Blood samples taken from Lopez's body during the autopsy revealed significant levels of THC, the psychoactive compound in marijuana. The levels were consistent with Lopez smoking marijuana 60 to 75 minutes prior to his death. Lopez also had a joint and a bottle of Visine on his body at the time he was killed.

The decision was met with outrage outside the press conference, where protesters denounced Ravitch's decision and vowed to press for justice for Lopez. Activists gathered in Roseland for a march to the Moorland Avenue location where Lopez was killed and planned a rally for the following day in Old Courthouse Square. The decision comes eight months after the fatal encounter on the outskirts of southwest Santa Rosa. The Lopez family's attorney, Arnoldo Casillas, said he received a personal phone call from Ravitch informing him of her decision, and that the family and his office are greatly disappointed with the decision. The family's federal civil rights lawsuit against Gelhaus and the county will now proceed.

The United States has seen a decrease in violent crime rates since 1995, with the national violent crime rate falling from 685 to 366 per 100,000 people. However, the country remains far from the most peaceful, with states like Louisiana being the least peaceful and Maine being the most. Factors contributing to violence in a community include low incomes, the presence of 15-25 year old men, and environmental conditions such as vacant housing and burned-out streetlights. Arizona, South Carolina, Florida, Missouri, Arkansas, and Alabama are among the least peaceful states, with high violent crime rates, low median household incomes, and large law enforcement operations.

The federal government is in the third week of a shutdown as Congress works to fund its operations and avoid a possible default due to the debt limit. The shutdown has caused displeasure among furloughed federal workers. The negotiations to lift the debt limit have slowed down, with Republicans and Democrats at odds. Senate Minority Leader Mitch McConnell asked Majority Leader Harry Reid to elevate negotiations to the highest level. Democrats are now on the offensive, seeking to undo the sequester spending cuts, which Republicans had initially demanded. The Treasury Department is due to exhaust its borrowing power in four days, and a default could lead to massive disruption worldwide. Christine Lagarde, managing director of the International Monetary Fund, warned that a failure to make scheduled payments to investors would mean a recession. Republicans oppose any agreement that backs away from the sequester cuts, while Democrats have no interest in rolling back the sequester cuts now. The fight over the debt limit is a point where reforms and deficit reduction are typically sought, but any agreement would require approval in the Republican-controlled House. Democrats are pressing for a quicker deadline on a temporary measure to fund federal agencies and reopen the government, while Republicans support a longer deadline for raising the debt limit. A deal could involve reopening the government immediately before the sequester hits in January and then having serious discussions to undo the sequester. The White House and congressional leaders are meeting to work out a deal, with a deadline of Thursday when the Treasury Department may run out of borrowing capacity.

President Barack Obama will meet with congressional Democrats on Capitol Hill on Wednesday to discuss strategies for protecting the Affordable Care Act (Obamacare) from Republican efforts to dismantle it. The meeting, which will take place at 9 a.m. in the Congressional Visitors Center auditorium, will involve both House and Senate Democrats.

Republicans have pledged to begin repealing Obamacare as soon as the 115th Congress convenes next week. They plan to use a parliamentary move called "reconciliation" to bypass the filibuster and pass legislation with a simple majority. However, they may delay the repeal's effective date for up to three years to allow time for a replacement.

Democrats are divided on how to salvage Obamacare. Some are open to working with Republicans on a replacement, while most oppose repeal efforts. Incoming Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer has vowed to block Republican repeal efforts and any conservative replacement.

Obamacare has provided insurance for more than 20 million people, including young adults under the age of 26 and those with pre-existing conditions. The law has slowed the growth in healthcare costs, but its critics have pointed to rising premiums in certain states.

President-elect Donald Trump has promised to keep some popular aspects of Obamacare, such as prohibiting insurance from denying coverage to people with pre-existing conditions. However, health policy experts consider such selective preservation to be unworkable, as the popular elements of the law are funded by less popular ones, like the individual mandate.

Democrats are also planning a broader health care offensive against Republicans, focusing not only on their push to repeal Obamacare but any efforts to overhaul Medicare and Medicaid. They will host a "day of action" on January 15 to rally grassroots support for protecting social safety net programs.

Incoming House Democratic Caucus Chairman Joe Crowley said the meeting will likely discuss other policy matters, including the Dodd-Frank financial law and environmental issues. Obama is retiring from public office and wants to ensure that the advancements he's made are defended, not only by the party but by the people.

On September 18, 2014, Jack McAtee, a resident of Breckenridge, Colorado, crashed his car into Dillon Reservoir. The accident occurred at around 6:40 p.m., and his black sedan veered onto a paved bicycle path, cutting through a 10-foot opening between a steel guardrail and a concrete highway barrier. The car rolled for about 135 feet across dirt and gravel, went airborne for 110 feet, and crashed into the water, almost entirely submerging.

Miraculously, McAtee swam to the surface with only a laceration above his left eye. He claimed he had fallen asleep at the wheel. A state trooper interviewing McAtee did not suspect that he was under the influence of drugs or alcohol. However, McAtee had recently stopped taking his medication for bipolar disorder, according to family members.

The trooper did not know about McAtee's mental health condition as he took McAtee to St. Anthony Summit Medical Center for medical clearance and then to the Summit County jail for a mental evaluation. The trooper just knew that McAtee was acting erratically, his moods swinging from irritated to chatty.

At one point, McAtee asked the trooper if hitchhiking was legal in Colorado. Within certain guidelines, it can be, the trooper explained. McAtee then asked him where he would hitchhike if heading west on Interstate 70. Just making conversation, the trooper said, “Moab.” The trooper left McAtee in a holding cell at the jail. At first, McAtee was in high spirits. Then he cried in his cell. Then, before the trooper departed, McAtee seemed to be in a good mood again.

The next day, McAtee met with a psychologist. He was released at around 11 a.m. on September 19. He was wearing a red hoodie and a tan hat. He had $67 in his pocket. Since then, McAtee's friends and family haven't seen him or heard from him.

McAtee, a gregarious and adventuresome 27-year-old who had lived in Breckenridge for about 5 years, had gone missing three times after going off his medication, but never for this long. Picking up on the hitchhiking theme in the trooper's report, his family quickly assembled a team of volunteers, getting the word out to truck stops stretching from Salt Lake to St. Louis, where the McAtee family is from.

The Moab Times-Independent published a story on McAtee’s disappearance just in case he followed up on the trooper’s suggestion. The story generated more than 10,000 clicks, but no one there has yet to report a sighting. However, a trucker in the Wheat Ridge area near Denver was convinced he saw McAtee.

Because of that tip, and the fact McAtee has made no bank transactions since his disappearance, the family is now focusing efforts closer to home. They now believe it’s possible he is still in the Summit County area. Posters have been put up all over town and along trailheads.

McAtee’s father, Steve McAtee, is currently leading search efforts from Breckenridge. “In case you are reading this, Jack, your mother and I and your four sisters Megan, Maddy, Katherine, and Ali love you with all our hearts,” he wrote in an email. “And we want to be with you now, more than ever. We love you. Come home.”

Summit County sheriff’s spokeswoman Taneil Ilano told the Moab Times-Independent that McAtee’s disappearance is being investigated as a missing-person case. Anyone who has seen McAtee — who is 5 feet, 10 inches tall, weighs 170 pounds and has green eyes — or who has information concerning his whereabouts is asked to call the Summit County Sheriff’s Office at (970) 668-8600.

The article "When the Taliban Takes the Girl Next Door" by Dave Gilson, published in Philadelphia magazine in November 2016, tells the story of Caitlan Coleman, a young woman from a small town in Pennsylvania who was kidnapped in Afghanistan by the Taliban in 2012, along with her husband Joshua Boyle. The article details the couple's travels through Central Asia before their kidnapping, their change of plans to travel to Afghanistan, and the subsequent disappearance and captivity of Caitlan and Joshua.

The article also discusses the efforts of the U.S. government to secure the release of the couple, including the creation of the Hostage Recovery Fusion Cell in 2015. The article notes that Caitlan gave birth to two children while in captivity, and that the couple has appeared in several videos released by the Taliban, the latest of which was released in August 2016. The article also discusses the public's indifference to the couple's plight, as well as the vicious online comments directed at Caitlan and Joshua.

In addition to the main article, the document also includes a brief Associated Press report on a video released by the Afghan Taliban in September 2016, showing Caitlan and Joshua warning that their captors will kill them and their children unless the Kabul government ends its executions of Taliban prisoners. The video was not independently verified by the AP, but the State Department said it was evaluating the video for its validity and continuing to urge for the immediate release of Caitlan and her family on humanitarian grounds.

An 89-year-old Nazi war crimes suspect, Johann Breyer, died on Tuesday night at a Philadelphia hospital, a day before a judge approved his extradition to Germany to face trial for aiding and abetting the murder of hundreds of thousands of Jewish men, women, and children during his time as an Auschwitz death camp guard. Breyer was accused of 158 counts of aiding and abetting the deaths of 216,000 Jews, and a judge found probable cause that he was the same person sought for aiding and abetting murder in Germany. The judge's ruling stated that "no statute of limitations offers a safe haven for murder." Breyer, a retired tool-and-die maker, had been arrested in June outside his home in northeast Philadelphia based on a 2013 German warrant. He had previously acknowledged being an SS guard at Auschwitz during World War II but claimed he was stationed outside the death camp section and had nothing to do with the slaughter. Breyer had been held without bail due to his frail health, with mild dementia and heart issues. The US government had yet to approve the extradition motion.

The European Commission is investigating allegations that some television manufacturers, including Samsung, may be using software to skew energy efficiency ratings during testing. A study by ComplianTV, a consortium of non-governmental organizations, found that a Samsung LCD TV reduced its power requirement significantly during the standardized energy efficiency test. The discrepancy was attributed to Samsung's "motion lighting" feature, which controls the backlights of TV screens.

Samsung denies any wrongdoing, stating that the feature is a standard out-of-the-box setting that delivers energy savings and helps reduce the company's environmental impact. The European Commission plans to explore the findings and may tighten energy efficiency regulations to outlaw the use of so-called "defeat devices" in TVs or other consumer products.

Another study by the Swedish Energy Agency found that a manufacturer's TV sets "clearly recognized" the test film and adjusted their energy use to avoid detection during the test. The Commission has not disclosed which company's televisions were tested, but the BBC understands that sets belonging to a single manufacturer other than Samsung were affected.

The apparent discrepancies between real-world and test performance of the TVs are reminiscent of the Volkswagen diesel scandal, in which the car company admitted to programming its cars to deliberately cheat emissions tests.

Environmental campaigners claim that EU testing procedures are overly generous, and there is no suggestion that Samsung or any other manufacturer has behaved illegally. However, concerns have been raised about the potential for manufacturers to game energy efficiency tests, and the Commission has pledged to investigate any allegations of their use.

Perez Hilton, the popular celebrity blogger, announced the birth of his first child, a healthy baby boy, on his eponymous blog. The 34-year-old shared the news in a heartfelt post, expressing gratitude to his fans for their support. Although details about the child's mother, name, and the method of conception were not disclosed, a photo of Hilton cradling the baby was shared. Known for his snarky comments and celebrity gossip, Hilton has become a household name and has even interacted with the celebrities he often writes about. The website, which receives 300 million page hits a month, has now become a platform for Hilton to express his newfound role as a father.

An American man, William Jacob Raak, was injured during a shooting at a nightclub in Istanbul, Turkey on New Year's Eve. Raak, a small-business owner from Greenville, Delaware, survived the attack by playing dead and remaining motionless even after being shot. He was with a group of nine people, seven of whom were also shot. Raak was shot in the hip and the bullet traveled to his knee. The Islamic State group has claimed responsibility for the attack, which left 39 people dead, mostly foreigners. The gunman is still at large, and Turkish authorities are pursuing leads to identify and capture him. Raak's mother, Grace Raak, said he was in Istanbul to celebrate his birthday and is expected to return home on Tuesday. The attack occurred at the Reina nightclub, a popular spot for the Turkish jet set and foreign tourists. The incident bears similarities to the 2015 attack on the Bataclan music hall in Paris.

President Donald Trump pardoned former Maricopa County, Arizona sheriff Joe Arpaio on August 25, 2017. Arpaio was convicted of contempt of court for defying a federal judge's order to stop detaining people based on suspicion of being undocumented immigrants. Trump had been considering intervening in Arpaio's case since spring, but was advised by Attorney General Jeff Sessions that it would be inappropriate. Trump waited for Arpaio to be found guilty of contempt before issuing the pardon, which bypassed the traditional review process and spared Arpaio from any prison time.

The pardon raised protests from some Republicans and threatens to become a stain on Trump's legacy. Critics argue that Trump's efforts to intervene in Arpaio's case showed a troubling disregard for the traditional wall between the White House and the Justice Department, and could undermine respect for the rule of law. Arpaio was a controversial figure during his 23 years as sheriff, accused of racial profiling, failure to investigate sex crimes, poor treatment of prisoners, and other instances of police misconduct.

Trump and Arpaio became allies five years ago, during the "birther" movement to undermine President Barack Obama. Trump admired Arpaio as a law-and-order icon and saw him as a symbol of his own immigration policies. Arpaio's age weighed on Trump, who did not want to see the 85-year-old sheriff waste away in jail.

Trump's pardon of Arpaio is consistent with his alleged attempts to influence the federal investigation of Michael Flynn, the former national security adviser, and his separate appeals to Director of National Intelligence Daniel Coats and National Security Agency Director Michael S. Rogers to deny the existence of any evidence of collusion between the Russians and the Trump campaign during the 2016 election.

The pardon was announced on a Friday evening, as a hurricane was bearing down on the Texas coast, in a move that some see as a deliberate attempt to bury the news and avoid scrutiny. The move was widely criticized by Democrats and some Republicans, who argue that it undermines the rule of law and deepens divisions in the country.

Astronomers from the University of California, Santa Cruz have made a significant discovery by capturing the first direct images of a part of the cosmic web, a network of filaments believed to link galaxies. This network is mainly composed of dark matter, an invisible substance that exerts gravitational forces on visible light and ordinary matter. The team used the 10-meter Keck telescope in Hawaii to observe an extremely large, bright nebula of gas, approximately 2 million light-years across, which they believe is a part of this cosmic web.

The discovery was made possible by exploiting the fact that a luminous object called a quasar can act as a natural "cosmic flashlight". The quasar, located 10 billion light-years away, shines light in just the right direction to reveal the cold gas cloud, which appears to trace out filaments of underlying dark matter. This is a new way to detect filaments, and it seems that they have a very bright quasar in a rare geometry, according to Prof Alexandre Refregier of the ETH Zurich.

The cosmic web suggested by the standard model is a giant web-like structure made up of dark matter and ordinary matter like gas, stars, and everything else. For some years, cosmologists have been running computer simulations of the structure of the universe to build the "standard model of cosmology". They use the cosmic microwave background, corresponding to observations of the very earliest Universe that can be seen, and recorded by instruments such as the Planck space observatory, as a starting point. Their calculations suggest that as the Universe grows and forms, matter becomes clustered in filaments and nodes under the force of gravity, like a giant cosmic web.

The new results from the 10-meter Keck telescope in Hawaii are reported by scientists from the University of California, Santa Cruz and the Max Planck Institute for Astronomy in Heidelberg. They are the first direct observations of cold gas decorating such cosmic web filaments. The observations support the cosmological simulations' general picture of a cosmic web of filamentary structures but suggest around 10 times more gas in the nebula than predicted from typical computer simulations. This may be due to limitations in the spatial resolution of the current models or, more interestingly, may be because the current grid-based models are missing some aspect of the underlying physics of how galaxies form, evolve, and interact with quasars.

The discovery of the cosmic web filaments is a significant step forward in understanding the structure of the universe and the distribution of dark matter. It provides a new way to detect filaments and may lead to further insights into the formation and evolution of galaxies. The researchers' results are published in the journal Nature.

Archaeologists have discovered a significant ancient tomb in Greece's northeast Macedonian region, dating back to 300-325 B.C. The tomb, located in Amphipolis, is believed to be the largest ancient tomb found in Greece and is expected to be opened by the end of August. Although there is no evidence linking the tomb to Alexander the Great or his family, it is thought to belong to a prominent Macedonian of that era. The tomb is guarded by two sphinxes and features frescoed walls, a 4.5-meter-wide road, and a 497-meter-long marble outer wall. Experts believe a five-meter-tall lion sculpture previously discovered nearby once stood atop the tomb. Prime Minister Antonis Samaras visited the site and declared the discovery "extremely important." The tomb's occupant is yet to be identified, but it is believed to be a senior ancient official. The discovery has sparked great interest, with the Associated Press reporting on the find.

The ongoing conflict between Israel and Hamas in Gaza has resulted in a significant increase in violence and casualties. As of Monday, August 4, the death toll in Gaza has risen above 1,100, according to a Palestinian health official, with at least 8 children killed at a refugee camp. Eighteen people, including eight children, were also killed in Gaza City early Tuesday morning due to powerful air strikes. On the Israeli side, five soldiers were killed in a militant tunnel attack, and another ten soldiers were killed in combat and mortar fire.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has stated that the military will not end its incursion into Gaza until it has destroyed tunnels that Hamas is using to attack civilians outside Gaza. The tunnels are a central goal of Israel's military operation, and Hamas has been accused of using civilian facilities such as homes, schools, mosques, and hospitals to launch attacks and store weapons.

Despite calls for a humanitarian cease-fire, fighting has intensified, with reports of carnage at a hospital and a refugee camp. World leaders, including U.S. President Barack Obama, British Prime Minister David Cameron, German Chancellor Angela Merkel, French President Francois Hollande, and Italian Prime Minister Matteo Renzi, have pleaded for a lasting cease-fire. However, Netanyahu has said that Israel needs to be prepared for a protracted campaign in Gaza.

The conflict has also had a devastating impact on civilians, with UNICEF reporting that about two-thirds of the children killed were 12 or younger. Israel has been accused of sending bombs that killed people in Gaza, while Hamas has been accused of encouraging people to stay in their homes despite Israeli warnings that strikes are coming.

The Israeli military has denied responsibility for the deaths of 16 people last week when an "errant Israeli mortar" hit a U.N. school that was sheltering many Gaza residents. However, a CNN team that visited the shelter several hours after the mortar attack saw evidence that people were badly wounded at the courtyard. The IDF has released a high-altitude aerial video of the round hitting the school, but it does not have high resolution and it is impossible to tell if anybody was sitting on the courtyard edge.

UN Secretary General Ban Ki-moon has urged an immediate halt to violence in Gaza, saying the Palestinian territory is in a "critical condition." He has been critical of both sides for firing into civilian areas of the small coastal strip. He reiterated the UN's call for an immediate, unconditional humanitarian ceasefire in Gaza during the Muslim Eid al-Fitr holiday, which marks the end of Ramadan. Both sides have been accused of behaving in an irresponsible, "morally wrong" fashion, allowing the violence to continue despite the efforts of the UN and US Secretary of State John Kerry.

The study published in the journal PLOS ONE reveals that whale sharks, the largest living fish, are increasingly using volcanic islands off the western coast of Europe, specifically the Azores, as a new home due to rising sea surface temperatures. This shift could be a result of climate change and may provide insights into how fish behavior might change globally.

Whale sharks, known for their gentle nature and filter-feeding habits, prefer warm tropical waters. However, in recent years, they have been increasingly sighted around the Azores Islands, which lie along the colder northern edge of their historically preferred waters. The researchers analyzed data on whale shark sightings gathered over 16 years by observers on tuna fishing boats to better understand this phenomenon.

The study found a sharp rise in whale shark sightings in the exceptionally warm year of 2008, and the giant fish have become regular visitors to the region since then. Higher water temperatures around the southernmost Azores Island of Santa Maria were associated with more sightings of the fish. Observers also spotted the sharks more often in areas with underwater hills and mountains, which coincide with large amounts of photosynthetic organisms that feed the creatures the whale sharks eat.

The findings suggest that large marine animals like whale sharks can change their oceanic distributions depending on regional conditions as climate changes globally. Future research could investigate why whale sharks remain in this area during the summer, whether it's only for food or for mating purposes. The study underscores the potential for the Azores to become an important oceanic habitat for whale sharks in the North Atlantic and the need to consider such shifts in the context of long-term changes in the ocean.

President Donald Trump spent Thanksgiving at his Mar-a-Lago estate in Palm Beach, Florida, where he gave a thumbs-up to photographers. On the day after Thanksgiving, Trump took to Twitter to demand funding for a border wall as part of a "major Border Security package." Trump called on both Republicans and Democrats to come together for this initiative, stating that it's "finally time for action."

Trump also expressed his support for criminal justice reform legislation, stating that Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell and Democratic leader Chuck Schumer "have a real chance to do something so badly needed in our country." However, Trump mistakenly tagged a Schumer fan instead of the senator in his tweet.

Trump's call for border security funding comes as Congress has until December 7 to fund the rest of the government, with a potential government shutdown looming if an agreement does not include funding for a border wall. The GOP lost the House in the midterm elections, and liberal lawmakers are strongly opposed to funding Trump's long-promised border wall.

Trump's criminal justice reform bill has caused divisions within the GOP, with Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell expressing doubts about passing the measure during the lame-duck session. Trump's border security initiative and criminal justice reform remain key legislative priorities for his administration.

The article discusses the competition between two popular pastry creations, Maury Rubin's pretzel croissant and Dominique Ansel's Cronut, both of which are baked in New York City. The pretzel croissant, a combination of a croissant and a pretzel, has been a staple in lower Manhattan for years, while the Cronut, a deep-fried croissant-doughnut hybrid, has gained popularity and created lines that start early in the morning.

The article explores the history of innovation in pastry and cooking, with a focus on the role of pastry chefs in leading the way. It also delves into the competitive nature of the baking world, with different types of bakers living in an atmosphere of mutual recrimination and suspicion.

The article also discusses the impact of innovation on the costs of baking, with the price of ingredients such as flour and butter increasing significantly in recent years. It also mentions the case of Dunkin' Donuts, which plans to roll out a croissant-doughnut hybrid in the U.S. next week, but the company has asked not to be called a "Cronut."

The article also features interviews with Maury Rubin and Dominique Ansel, the creators of the pretzel croissant and the Cronut, respectively. Rubin discusses the creation of the pretzel croissant and his views on the Cronut, while Ansel talks about his classical French culinary education and the opening of his bakery in SoHo.

Overall, the article provides an interesting exploration of the world of pastry and baking, with a focus on innovation, competition, and the impact of rising costs on the industry.

The Syrian government has opened a dialogue with religious and community leaders who have influence on the ground with fighters, marking a subtle shift in tone from the government's portrayal of the armed rebellion as a foreign-led conspiracy. However, the question of who within the diffuse opposition could deliver results and be an acceptable negotiating partner to the government remains a challenge in attempts to reach a political solution to the war in Syria, which has killed over 100,000 people and forced millions from their homes.

Syrian Foreign Minister Walid al-Moualem exuded confidence that the government had taken the upper hand against the rebels, and said that even as it pledged to give up its chemical weapons to avoid a US airstrike, the government had achieved diplomatic and military victories. He suggested that the natural next step was an international push for Israel to relinquish its nuclear weapons, which the neighboring state has never formally acknowledged and which was never linked to Syria's agreement to give up its chemical weapons stockpile.

However, his statement that the government was "100 percent sure" that rebels, not government forces, fired the chemical weapons that killed hundreds of people in the Damascus suburbs in August was dismissed by American officials and at odds with some of the scientific findings of UN inspectors sent to investigate the chemical attack.

The article also includes a series of photos depicting the unrest in Syria, showing the destruction caused by the conflict, including damaged buildings, dead bodies, and people fleeing their homes. The photos were taken between March 2011 and January 2013.

In Tampa, Florida, a tragic accident occurred on Wednesday when a mother, Jessica Raubenolt, and her 21-month-old daughter, Lillia, were struck and killed by a speeding car while crossing the street in a stroller. The driver of the car, 18-year-old Cameron Herrin, was allegedly racing another vehicle, driven by a 17-year-old, according to witnesses. Both Herrin and the 17-year-old were charged with street racing, vehicular homicide, and reckless driving resulting in serious bodily injury. Tristin Herrin, the older brother of the driver, was also charged with a misdemeanor count of racing.

Jessica Raubenolt was visiting Tampa from Ohio with her family, as her husband was waiting to obtain his certification as a single-engine airplane pilot. The family had been in Tampa for a week due to bad weather, which delayed the husband's certification. Raubenolt was a devoted mother, wife, and niece who had recently married and was passionate about health, exercise, and gardening.

The accident occurred on Bayshore Boulevard, a main road for the two teen drivers who lived nearby. The Herrins, the family of the driver, live in a house they purchased for $1.4 million in 2005. Cheryl Herrin, the mother, is a former member of the Citizens Property Insurance board of governors, and Chris Herrin works as a videographer/editor.

Following the accident, the uncle of the victim, John Reisinger, expressed words of forgiveness for those involved. "We’re praying for those young boys and their families," he said. "We hope something good will come of this foolish accident. That’s what Jessie would want."

Late Thursday, Lillia passed away at the hospital. The family is mourning their loss and remembering Raubenolt as a woman who made a mark on the world that her death will not diminish. The Catholic Diocese of St. Petersburg confirmed that the three drivers are recent graduates of Tampa Catholic High School. In a statement, the diocese said it is praying for the victims.

The Associated Press has documented numerous cases of misuse and overuse of pesticides in Argentina, a nation that has become the world's third-largest soybean producer due to the adoption of genetically modified crops and chemicals. The misuse of these chemicals has led to health problems among the 12 million people living in Argentina's farm belt, with cancer rates and birth defects increasing significantly.

The misuse of pesticides includes spraying in windy conditions, application in populated areas, and the use of toxic chemicals without protective gear. Farmworkers, such as Fabian Tomasi, have been exposed to chemicals without proper training, leading to health issues like polyneuropathy.

The Argentine government relies on industry research approved by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, which states that glyphosate, the key ingredient in Monsanto's Roundup brand of pesticides, is safe if used properly. However, a molecular biologist at the University of Buenos Aires found that even low doses of glyphosate can cause changes in levels of retinoic acid, which can lead to spinal defects in frogs and chickens.

The misuse of pesticides has led to numerous complaints, but the federal government has never cited a single agrochemical user for failing to follow national spraying regulations. A presidential commission was formed to study the health impacts of these violations, but it hasn't met in three years.

The misuse of pesticides is not only harmful to human health but also to the environment.
