The AP documented cases where poisons are applied in ways unanticipated by regulatory science or specifically banned by existing law, with the chemicals drifting into schools, homes, and settling over water sources.

Doctors are warning that uncontrolled pesticide applications could be the cause of the growing health problems in Argentina's farm belt. In response, the government insists that the problem is not a lack of research, but misinformation that plays on people's emotions. However, the AP's investigation highlights the need for stricter regulations and enforcement to protect the health of the people and the environment in Argentina.

The article discusses a study by Action on Sugar that reveals high levels of sugar in many hot flavored drinks sold at popular coffee shops in the UK. The study found that 98% of the 131 hot flavored drinks analyzed would receive a 'red' (high) label for excessive levels of sugars per serving. Starbucks' Hot Mulled Fruit - Grape with Chai, Orange and Cinnamon Venti was the worst offender, containing 25 teaspoons of sugar, which is more than three times the maximum daily intake of free sugars for adults. The study also found that 35% of the hot flavored drinks contain the same amount or more sugar than a can of Coca Cola. Action on Sugar is calling for stricter product reformulation of sugar and fat, a ban on promotions and marketing of unhealthy products, and a 20% tax on sugar-sweetened drinks. The study highlights the need for more transparency on sugar content and compulsory labelling of sugar content. Starbucks has committed to reducing added sugar in its indulgent drinks by 25% by the end of 2020 and offers a variety of lighter options, sugar-free syrups, and sugar-free natural sweetener. The article also mentions Cameron's comprehensive plan to prevent childhood obesity and type 2 diabetes, which includes setting up an independent agency for nutrition, banning of all forms of advertising/marketing/promotion of unhealthy foods and drinks to children and adolescents, and a hypothecated 20% duty on all sugar-sweetened drinks.

The Supreme Court heard arguments over the constitutionality of President Obama's healthcare law, with many journalists reporting a challenging day for the Obama administration. Solicitor General Donald Verrilli was criticized for his performance in defending the law, and Justice Anthony Kennedy, a potential swing voter, expressed skepticism towards the individual mandate at the heart of the law. CNN's Jeffrey Toobin described the proceedings as a "train wreck" for the administration, while Mike Sacks of the Huffington Post noted opposition to the law seemed "almost unequivocal" from Kennedy. However, it's important to note that the court's conservatives, including Kennedy, exhibited aggressive skepticism towards the individual mandate, and its fate depends on at least one of them siding with the administration. The individual mandate may still be struck down, but the court's notorious opacity and the high stakes of the case have led to speculation and overreaction. The case requires the use of RealPlayer or Windows Media Player to stream audio files, and Mac users can use Windows Media Components for QuickTime.

In northern Afghanistan, at least 21 people were killed and eight others were wounded in a gunfight that erupted at a wedding party on Sunday. The incident occurred in Deh Salah district, Baghlan province, which has recently experienced a surge in insecurity due to the Taliban insurgency. According to provincial police spokesman Jawed Basharat, the clashes began when a local security official fired in the air during a verbal altercation, leading both sides to exchange fire. The victims were all male guests at the wedding, ranging in age from 14 to 60. Baghlan police spokesman Sultan Mohammad Ebadi dispatched an official delegation to investigate the matter.

Fatal gunfights and celebratory gunfire are unfortunately common at Afghan weddings, given the country's history of nearly 40 years of war. In December 2014, Afghan soldiers mistakenly fired mortars at a wedding party in the southern province of Helmand, killing 17 women and children. Previous incidents include a suicide bomber killing a prominent Afghan lawmaker and 16 other people at his daughter's wedding party in 2012, and gunmen storming a wedding party in eastern Afghanistan in 2011, resulting in the groom's death and eight other casualties.

Despite ongoing peace talks between the Afghan government and Taliban cadres, militant attacks continue to take a heavy toll on civilians. A suicide bomber killed 19 people, including women and children, in a crowded market in the northern province of Faryab in July 2015, as insurgents intensified their annual summer offensive.

The Afghan government is planning a second round of talks with insurgents this week, aiming to secure a ceasefire during negotiations likely to be held in China. However, the willingness to engage in talks has not led to a reduction in militant attacks.

The Backstreet Boys have announced new dates for their Las Vegas residency, adding 21 shows from July 25 to Nov. 17. During a recent Q&A session, the band revealed that a new single is imminent, with Kevin Richardson stating it's "coming out real soon." While the exact release date remains unclear, AJ McLean hinted it could be within the next few days or weeks. The band also shared a short, upbeat snippet of the new single, titled "Don't Go Breaking My Heart." The single marks their first new music since 2013 and will be part of their upcoming 10th studio album, expected later this year to coincide with their 25th anniversary. Presale tickets for the Vegas shows are available now, with general sale starting Friday. The new single, "Don't Go Breaking My Heart," was officially released on Feb. 15.

The article discusses the arrest of a Baton Rouge mother, Schaquana Evita Spears, who was charged with child cruelty after she physically disciplined her three sons, ages 10, 12, and 13, for breaking into a neighbor's house. The incident occurred on June 22, 2016. Spears admitted to using an RCA cord to whip her sons, resulting in injuries to two of them, including cuts and bruises. The neighbor, Lisa Nicholson, supported Spears, stating that she believed the mother was acting in self-defense and that the boys could have been killed during the break-in.

The incident sparked a debate about the line between well-meaning discipline and child abuse. East Baton Rouge Parish District Attorney Hillar C. Moore III stated that it was reasonable for a parent to discipline a child who is burglarizing other people's homes, but the seriousness of the boys' injuries would be reviewed. Moore also noted that Spears has no prior convictions.

The case attracted defenders from across the country, including state Treasurer John Kennedy, who wrote an open letter to the Department of Children and Family Services (DCFS) Secretary Marketa Garner Walters, calling for leniency on Spears. Kennedy argued that sparing the rod led to a spoiled child in biblical times, and in modern times, sparing the rod leads to an imprisoned child.

DCFS Secretary Walters released a statement on June 23, 2016, stating that the way to tell when disciplining a child has gone too far is when a child is left bleeding or with cuts, burns, or bruises. Walters did not specify any particular case she was addressing.

Spears was released from jail on June 21, 2016, after a judge reduced her bail. She is working to regain custody of her six children, who are currently being cared for by their grandmother. Spears' attorney, Brenden Craig, stated that he believes the arresting agency should have taken more time to investigate before arresting Spears. Craig also stated that just because Spears' children had cuts or were bleeding does not mean his client is guilty of a crime.

The article also includes information about RCA connectors, which are commonly used to carry audio and video signals. RCA connectors were originally designed for internal connection of a phonograph turntable to a radio receiver, but they have since been adopted for other uses, including as a DC power connector, an RF connector, and as a connector for loudspeaker cables. The connector consists of a central male connector surrounded by a ring, with the ring being slightly larger in diameter and longer than the ring on the plug, allowing the plug's ring to fit tightly over it. The jack has a small area between the outer and inner rings which is filled with an insulator, typically plastic. The connector was initially used for audio signals, but it has been adopted for other uses, including as a connector for composite video signals. RCA connectors and cable are also commonly used to carry S/PDIF-formatted digital audio, with plugs colored orange to differentiate them from other typical connections.

In December 2015, 8-year-old Safyre Terry, who lost her family in an arson fire three years prior, received an overwhelming response to her request for Christmas cards. Her story went viral, and she received hundreds of thousands of cards, letters, and packages from all over the world. The family's post office box was flooded with mail, and they needed two 2-ton mail trucks and a rented cargo truck to deliver it all.

Volunteers helped Sa'fyre and her family open the influx of cards and packages they received. The community's support was overwhelming, with one 5-year-old boy in Hong Kong sending Sa'fyre his favorite teddy bear with a note that said "Let's be friends."

Today, the charity Baking Memories 4 Kids surprised Safyre and her family with a trip to Walt Disney World in February 2016. The family will be traveling to Orlando, Florida, where they will stay at Give Kids the World, an Orlando resort designed to house the recipients of such trips during their week-long vacations.

Safyre has undergone more than 50 surgeries since the fire, including the amputation of her foot in March 2015. The news of the trip came at a difficult time for the family, but it was exactly what they needed to hear. Safyre's aunt, Liz Dolder, said she was emotional and happy when she learned about the trip.

Baking Memories 4 Kids provided a similar vacation to Safyre's classmate Zachary Cunniff's family last year. Zachary's brother, Caleb, has spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) and their father, Trooper David Cuniff, was tragically killed in 2013 after being struck by a vehicle while conducting a traffic stop.

Safyre's post office box has been flooded with cards, gifts, and letters since her story went viral last week. The family's YouCaring fundraiser site, which once had a modest goal of raising $15,000, has raised more than $300,000 to date, as support pours in from around the world. Cards for Safyre can be mailed to P.O. Box 6126, Schenectady, NY, 12306.

The U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) and IBM Watson Health have announced a public-private partnership to bring Watson's precision oncology technology to 10,000 American veterans with cancer over the next two years. The collaboration aims to help VA doctors identify precision treatment options for a larger number of patients than previously possible.

Scientists and pathologists will sequence DNA for cancer patients, then feed de-identified genetic alteration files into Watson. The supercomputer will generate a report for physicians that identifies likely cancer-causing mutations and possible treatment options to target those specific mutations through a comprehensive review of existing medical literature.

The partnership is expected to greatly speed up the ability of VA doctors to help identify precision treatment options for veterans. IBM's Watson for Genomics technology is designed to provide insights that match what a team of scientists and clinicians would uncover when analyzing genome sequencing data and suggesting potential treatment options to target cancer mutations.

The VA serves 3.5 percent of the nation's cancer patients, the largest group of cancer patients in the country. Watson is expected to facilitate rapid access for veterans to personalized care, particularly for patients with advanced cancer.

IBM's commitment to VA follows more than 2 years of collaboration with more than 20 leading cancer institutes to train and validate Watson for Genomics. Early results from academic medical centers that are using Watson for Genomics show that the technology provides insights that match what a team of scientists and clinicians would uncover when analyzing genome sequencing data and suggesting potential treatment options to target cancer mutations.

The collaboration between IBM and the VA is also expected to help advance genomic research. Findings related to the identified treatment options in the literature will be shared with the academic community.

The partnership is part of Vice President Joe Biden's Cancer Moonshot program, which aims to achieve a "decade worth of advances in 5 years." The program offers funding, targeted incentives, and increased private-sector coordination to accelerate cancer research and treatment. The Cancer Moonshot is focused on more than a 100 different types of cancers and is meant to galvanize efforts to find a cure for cancer.

Supreme Court Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg, aged 85, was hospitalized on Thursday after falling in her office the previous evening, resulting in three fractured ribs on her left side. The court's oldest member, Ginsburg has a history of health issues, including multiple bouts with cancer and a heart stent procedure in 2014. This is not the first time Ginsburg has fractured her ribs while on the court, as she experienced a similar injury in 2012.

Ginsburg, a key figure in shaping jurisprudence on gender discrimination, women's reproductive health, and international law, has served on the bench for 25 years. She is known for her work ethic and has expressed intentions to serve until she is 90.

The fall prevented Ginsburg from attending the formal investiture ceremony for new Associate Justice Brett Kavanaugh, which took place on the same day. The event was attended by President Donald Trump, first lady Melania Trump, and other Supreme Court justices.

Ginsburg's health has been a matter of concern due to her age and the potential for conservative control of the court if another opening were to occur. She is a beloved figure among liberals, who refer to her as the "Notorious RBG." A documentary titled "RBG" and an upcoming feature film, "On the Basis of Sex," are dedicated to her life and work.

Breitbart News' application for permanent press credentials to cover Congress has been tabled by the Capitol Hill Standing Committee of Correspondents, and their temporary credentials will not be renewed when they expire at the end of May. The committee has expressed concerns about Breitbart's editorial independence, particularly due to its ties to Steve Bannon, who is now chief strategist in President Trump's White House. The committee has also questioned Breitbart's office space and staffing, as well as potential conflicts of interest with the Government Accountability Institute, a non-profit Bannon used to run that is funded by the Mercer family. Breitbart can reapply for credentials if they address these concerns, but their current staff members will lose access after May 31. Breitbart has asserted that it is an editorially independent news organization and is entitled to permanent Senate Press Gallery credentials.

In a significant ruling, a Criminal Court judge in Manhattan has ordered Twitter to hand over private messages sent by a Brooklyn writer during the Occupy Wall Street protests last year. The judge, Matthew A. Sciarrino Jr., ruled that while private speech is protected, public comments on Twitter are not. The writer, Malcolm Harris, was one of about 700 protesters arrested in October while walking on the roadway of the Brooklyn Bridge and charged with disorderly conduct. Prosecutors are interested in Harris's messages because they may contradict his argument that the police led or escorted protesters off the pedestrian paths and into the bridge’s roadway.

The case raises significant issues in the still-new area of social media. Prosecutors requested Harris's postings and member information directly from Twitter, which then notified him. The American Civil Liberties Union filed a friend-of-the-court brief, arguing that prosecutors should be required to obtain a search warrant for each request and that the person whose posts were being sought should have an opportunity to oppose the demand in court.

Twitter itself sought to quash the subpoena but was ordered to turn over Harris's messages. The company is disappointed with the ruling and is considering its options. The judge held that public speech, regardless of the forum, does not enjoy the same protections as private speech.

According to new data released by Twitter, American police are leading the charge to get users’ info from the popular San Francisco-based microblogging service. Overall, from Jan. 1 through June, the company received 849 law enforcement requests for individual users’ information, granting 63% of those requests. American law enforcement accounted for 80% of those information requests compared to other nations.

The widespread data generated by social media use represents one of the next frontiers of privacy’s collision with police surveillance. The U.S. Department of Homeland Security monitors public posts on social media for potential threats. The numbers released by Twitter on Monday show requests for “user information.” According to the company’s privacy policy, that can include your location, IP addresses, search terms, pages visited, and data from when you visit third-party websites with Twitter buttons on them.

Some of this data is deleted after 18 months, according to the company’s privacy disclosure, if not sooner. The company accepts requests from law enforcement to preserve information for longer periods of time. Twitter is one of the more transparent social-media sites out there, with a standing policy to notify users of requests for their information, unless barred by a statute or a court order.

In May, according to the Associated Press, Facebook cooperated with Pakistani authorities trying to block users participating in an inflammatory competition to post pictures of the prophet Muhammad, which is forbidden under Islamic law; Twitter, however, refused to cooperate and saw its services briefly blocked in Pakistan as a result.

The ruling and the data released by Twitter highlight the growing tension between privacy and law enforcement in the digital age. As more and more personal information is shared online, the question of who has access to that information and under what circumstances becomes increasingly important.

Mike Huckabee, a former Arkansas governor and 2008 presidential candidate, is reportedly launching a new online news publication called the Huckabee Post. The website will cover news on politics, U.S., international, media, sports, and other general news. Huckabee served as governor from 1996 to 2007 and briefly led the race for the Republican nomination during the 2008 presidential election before John McCain secured the nomination. His campaign featured an endorsement from Chuck Norris. Huckabee has recently indicated that he is considering another run for the presidency in 2016. Conservative personalities have found success leveraging their personal popularity into media brands, most notably with subscription service TheBlaze and The Dish. Representatives for the Huckabee Post did not immediately respond to an email in response to its Craigslist ad.

The article discusses the failure of an early warning system for tsunamis in Indonesia, which could have potentially prevented some deaths in the recent tsunami that hit the island of Palu on September 30, 2018. The high-tech system, which includes seafloor sensors, data-laden sound waves, and fiber-optic cable, was intended to replace an existing system set up after a 2004 tsunami that killed nearly 250,000 people in the region. However, inter-agency wrangling and delays in securing funding have stalled the project, leaving the system in the testing phase for years.

The tsunami that hit Palu killed at least 832 people in the cities of Palu and Donggala, highlighting the weaknesses of the existing warning system and low public awareness about how to respond to warnings. Louise Comfort, a University of Pittsburgh expert in disaster management who has led the U.S. side of the project, expressed her disappointment at the failure of the new system and the tragic consequences for the Indonesian people.

The article also discusses the backbone of Indonesia's current tsunami warning system, which includes tidal gauge stations, land-based seismographs, sirens, and a system to disseminate warnings by text message. However, the system has limitations, particularly in providing advance warning, as none of the 22 buoys connected to seafloor sensors are functioning.

The article also discusses the response to the tsunami warning issued by the meteorology and geophysics agency, which warned of potential for waves of 0.5 to 3 meters (2 to 10 feet). The warning was lifted at 6:36 p.m., but it's unclear exactly what time the tsunami waves hit Palu. The agency's head said the warning was lifted after the tsunami hit.

The article also discusses the importance of training and trust in disaster preparedness, as the fact that people were still milling around Palu's shoreline when waves were visibly approaching shows that the lessons of earlier disasters have not been absorbed.

Overall, the article highlights the need for improved tsunami warning systems and disaster preparedness in Indonesia, one of the world's most earthquake and tsunami-prone countries.

The sixth edition of Merriam-Webster's "Official Scrabble Players Dictionary" was released on September 20, 2018, in New York, featuring over 300 new words. Among the additions are long-awaited words like "OK" and "ew." The dictionary update was done in consultation with Scrabble owner Hasbro Inc. and the North American Scrabble Players Association.

One of the significant additions is "qapik," a unit of currency in Azerbaijan, which adds to the 20 playable words beginning with "q" that don't require a "u." Scrabble players are excited about the inclusion of "OK" as it is a much-anticipated two-letter word.

The new edition also includes words with high Scrabble scores, such as "bizjet," worth 120 points on an opening play, and words with magical vowel dumps, like "arancini," Italian balls of cooked rice. However, "bizjet" can only score high if it's made into a plural with an "s."

Merriam-Webster sought advice from the North American Scrabble Players Association while updating the book to ensure the words are desirable. Lexicographer Peter Sokolowski, editor at large at Merriam-Webster, has a favorite among the new words, not primarily because of Scrabble scores but because of its meaning, "macaron," a delicate French sandwich cookie featuring different flavors and fillings.

Other new words include "aquafaba," "beatdown," "zomboid," "twerk," "sheeple," "wayback," "bokeh," "botnet," "emoji," "facepalm," "frowny," "hivemind," "puggle," and "nubber." The dictionary also includes foreign words like "schneid," a sports term for a losing streak, and words like "bibimbap," "cotija," and "sriracha" that are no longer considered foreign due to their widespread use in English.

The goal of this update is to keep the game fresh and exciting for Scrabble players. The first official Scrabble dictionary was published in 1976, and updates have been made every four to eight years since then. This update aims to archive pages as they are created and preserve the pages they refer to, fixing broken links on the web.

An elderly woman in Bedford, Pennsylvania, was shocked to discover that an unknown man had been living in her home for several weeks, hidden in an upstairs closet. The woman, who is in her 80s and has difficulty moving, had a caretaker and was introduced to the caretaker's boyfriend, Mark Potts. However, when the woman's daughter visited, they found Potts living in the house. Police found several suitcases, a duffel bag, and personal items belonging to Potts in the upstairs room. Potts was also found to be in possession of a small handgun. Potts is facing criminal trespassing charges, and the caretaker could face additional charges for aiding him. The caretaker's name has not been released yet, but police are investigating and expect charges to be filed against her as well. The incident has left the woman feeling fearful and insecure in her own home.

The article discusses the nuclear crisis at the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear power plant in Japan following a powerful earthquake and tsunami. The explosion at reactor No. 1, caused by a buildup of hydrogen, damaged the outer wall and roof of the building but did not collapse the steel containment of the reactor. The explosion was likely due to the failure of the cooling system, which allowed pressure to build up beyond the design capacity of the reactor.

Radiation levels at the plant were reported to be far above normal but still too small to pose a significant hazard to human health. However, as many as 160 people may have been exposed to radiation, and three workers were reported to be suffering from radiation sickness. The Japanese authorities are preparing to distribute iodine to protect the thyroid gland from radiation exposure to people living near the plant.

Experts believe that the explosion was caused by a hydrogen formation, which could have begun inside the reactor core. The plant's design differences from Chernobyl mean that the release of radiation is likely to be much smaller, even if there is a complete core meltdown. However, the presence of spent nuclear fuel in a pool inside the same reactor building poses a significant risk to workers trying to prevent a meltdown.

The emergency at the plant began shortly after the earthquake struck, and the loss of power and damage to the plants' generators crippled the cooling systems. The malfunctions allowed pressure to build up beyond the design capacity of the reactors. Early Saturday, officials had said that small amounts of radioactive vapor were expected to be released into the atmosphere to prevent damage to the containment systems and that they were evacuating people in the area as a precaution. However, safety officials urged people who were not evacuating but still lived relatively nearby to cover their mouths and stay indoors.

The situation is still serious, and it is too early to say that a catastrophe has been averted. The cause of the explosion has yet to be determined, and the integrity of the fuel inside the reactor is uncertain. The Japanese authorities are working to cool down the reactor and reduce pressure by flooding the core with seawater.

Researchers at the Georgia Institute of Technology have created a miniature replica of Leonardo da Vinci's Mona Lisa, named "Mini Lisa," which is approximately 30 microns in width, making it 25,000 times smaller than the original. The Mini Lisa was created using a technique called ThermoChemical NanoLithography (TCNL) and an atomic force microscope. The team, led by Associate Professor Jennifer Curtis, heated tiny spots on a plastic substrate to trigger chemical reactions that created new molecules, resulting in variations in surface concentration and grayscale shades. Each pixel was 125 nanometers wide, smaller than the smallest known bacteria. The creation of Mini Lisa demonstrates the potential for nano-manufacturing of devices due to the team's ability to vary the surface concentration of molecules on such short length scales. The researchers hope that TCNL will enable a wide range of experiments and applications in various fields, including nanoelectronics, optoelectronics, and bioengineering.

Astronaut Scott Kelly, who spent 340 days aboard the International Space Station (ISS), returned to Earth on Thursday, finding himself two inches taller due to the effects of microgravity on his spine. This temporary change occurred as the gel-filled discs between his vertebrae expanded without the full force of gravity.

Kelly's twin brother, Mark, a retired astronaut, was in Houston to welcome him. The twin study, which began last year, aims to measure the effects of long-term spaceflight on the human body. Scott Kelly's mission was the longest single spaceflight by an American astronaut and the longest on the ISS.

The scientific experiments involved in the twin study are ongoing, focusing on cellular behavior, physiological changes, psychological tests, and microbial changes. The data collected will help scientists understand the challenges of long-term space travel, with the ultimate goal of enabling human exploration of Mars by the 2030s.

Upon landing, Kelly was greeted by his family, second lady Jill Biden, and NASA officials. He expressed gratitude for the support and achievement, emphasizing that the mission was not his alone but a collective effort by NASA and the United States. He also mentioned his plans to take a swim in his pool as soon as possible.

The execution of 9-year-old Tyshawn Lee, a fourth-grader from Chicago, has been charged to Dwright Boone-Doty, a 22-year-old gang member. The murder took place on November 2, 2015, in an alley near his grandmother's South Side home. Boone-Doty lured Tyshawn from a park by offering to buy him treats and then shot him execution-style in the right temple.

Prosecutors allege that Boone-Doty initially planned to torture Tyshawn and cut off his fingers and ears, and kill his grandmother. Boone-Doty was charged on Monday with Tyshawn's murder and an earlier shooting that left a woman dead and a man wounded. He was held without bail during a bond hearing.

An informant secretly recorded Boone-Doty making incriminating statements about the fatal shootings. Boone-Doty was already in the Cook County Jail on a separate gun charge. An inmate agreed to wear a wire after telling authorities that Boone-Doty bragged about shooting Tyshawn.

Boone-Doty had laughed about the shooting, saying he "seen that bitch go in his head," prosecutors said, adding that he was writing a rap song in jail that mentioned the killing. Boone-Doty's mother, Michelle Doty, expressed her regret about her son's actions, saying, "You don't think I would try to do all I could to turn my baby around?"

Cook County State's Attorney Anita Alvarez called the child's killing "among the worst I've ever seen in my 30 years as a prosecutor." Interim Police Supt. John Escalante said, "I have never witnessed such an act of savagery and treachery."

Two other men have already been implicated in Tyshawn's murder. On November 27, Corey Morgan, 27, of Lansing, was charged with murder, and police have a warrant for the arrest of a third suspect, Kevin Edwards, 22. The murders were part of a gang feud over the murder of Tracey Morgan, 25, authorities said.

On October 13, Morgan, a parolee, was shot to death and his mother was wounded after they left a police-sponsored meeting intended to resolve gang conflicts. His brother Corey Morgan allegedly vowed to target "mothers, grandmothers, babies, and all" because his brother was killed and his mother was shot.

Corey Morgan and Boone-Doty are members of the Bang Bang Gang faction of the Black P Stones. They were gunning for rivals in the Killaward faction of the Gangster Disciples, who they believed were responsible for Tracey Morgan's death, prosecutors said.

On October 18, Jenkins, 19, and Bowens, 20, were sitting in a car about 4:30 p.m. in the 7800 block of South Honore when they were shot, police said. Jenkins was pronounced dead at the scene, authorities said. Friends drove Bowens to Advocate Christ Medical Center in Oak Lawn, where his condition stabilized. Boone-Doty said he went to the hospital to finish off Bowens, but was unable to do so, prosecutors said.

Boone-Doty allegedly said he didn't know who was in the car before he opened fire, but he thought Bowens was a rival because he shouldn't have been parked on that block. Tyshawn was shot about two weeks later, on November 2, because of his father's ties to the Killaward gang faction, police said.

Boone-Doty was on parole when he allegedly killed Tyshawn, authorities said. He was sentenced to five years in prison in July 2013 for unlawful possession of a firearm by a felon and drug possession in downstate Sangamon County, prison records show. Officers had found a stolen handgun under the seat of a car he was in. They also found cocaine on him. He was paroled in August 2015, three months before Tyshawn was lured into the alley in the 8000 block of South Damen and shot to death.

Boone-Doty is the father of three children, ages 4, 3, and 6 months, an assistant public defender said. Before he was jailed, he worked for his father's construction company and his grandfather's landscaping business, his attorney said. Boone-Doty completed 10th grade and has a certificate in technology.

The spiraling cycle of gang violence that claimed Tyshawn's life is all too common in the city, but the grade-schooler's murder marked a chilling break even from the bloody norms of Chicago's gang warfare. "The murder of Tyshawn Lee was something far more sinister. This was a targeted assassination by Dwright Doty, Kevin Edwards, and Corey Morgan," Escalante said. "Tyshawn was an innocent child betrayed by these three men. Sadly, he paid the ultimate price for gang violence, senseless gang violence, that plagued his neighborhood."

Joan Fontaine, a renowned actress from the 1940s, known for her delicate beauty and romantic vulnerability, died on December 15, 2013, at the age of 96. Fontaine was best recognized for her roles in Alfred Hitchcock's films "Suspicion" and "Rebecca," for which she won an Oscar in 1942, beating her older sister, Olivia de Havilland.

Fontaine and de Havilland endured a long-standing sibling feud that began in childhood and was fueled by their ambitious stage mother. Their rivalry continued over the years, with disputes over movie roles and the attention of powerful men such as Howard Hughes. The relationship became strained, and they rarely spoke after their mother's death in 1975.

Born in Tokyo to English parents, Fontaine began her Hollywood career in 1935. Initially, she struggled to break out of low-budget films despite occasional opportunities. However, she gained widespread recognition in 1939 with her role in the all-female comedy "The Women."

Fontaine's career peaked in the early 1940s with memorable performances in "Rebecca" and "Suspicion." She earned an Oscar nomination for "Rebecca" and won the award for "Suspicion," becoming the only actor to win an Oscar in a Hitchcock film.

The rest of Fontaine's career was a mix of good and mediocre roles, but she stepped out of type in several films, including "Ivy," "Serenade," and "Tender is the Night." She faced criticism for playing opposite black entertainer Harry Belafonte in "Island in the Sun."

Fontaine received the Eleanor Roosevelt Humanitarian Award for her work with children at a New York school for the deaf in the mid-1960s. She continued to act in soap operas and television series until the 1990s.

Fontaine was married and divorced four times, and she had two daughters. She was the niece of British airplane manufacturing pioneer Sir Geoffrey de Havilland and was a skilled pilot, balloonist, Cordon Bleu chef, and excellent tuna fisherman.

Fontaine's feud with her sister, Olivia de Havilland, who is still alive at 97 and living in Paris, is well-documented in Fontaine's autobiography, "No Bed of Roses." The two sisters never reconciled, and their rivalry remains one of the longest-running sibling feuds on record.

The United States is experiencing heightened fear and concern about national security, according to a new NBC News/Wall Street Journal poll. Following the brutal beheadings of journalists by Islamic extremists, 47% of Americans believe the country is less safe now than before the September 11, 2001 terrorist attacks, a significant increase from the immediate aftermath of 9/11. The poll also found that 94% of Americans have heard about the beheadings, making it the most widely-known news event in the past five years.

President Obama is set to deliver a primetime speech outlining his plan to combat the terrorist group ISIS, which has taken over parts of Iraq and Syria, beheaded two American journalists, and launched a social media campaign to extend its reach. The poll suggests that more than six in ten respondents believe taking military action against ISIS is in the nation's interest.

The poll results indicate a shift in public opinion, with a "very war-weary country" now recognizing the threat that ISIS poses. The beheadings are seen as particularly chilling, with one pollster comparing them to the self-immolations during the Vietnam War.

The poll comes as President Obama prepares to outline his plans for expanded operations against ISIS, which could include intensified airstrikes and a heavy reliance on allies. The role of Middle East nations could be crucial, as they may provide crucial support for the U.S. effort.

The conflict with ISIS is seen as part of a continuous conflict that has been ongoing for over a decade, dating back to the Iranian revolution of 1979. The U.S. has been at war against various factions of Islamic militants and terrorists, including the Taliban and al-Qaida, as well as offshoots in Yemen, Somalia, and elsewhere.

Some experts argue that the U.S. government's policies in the Middle East have contributed to the rise of extremist groups like ISIS. Ibrahim Hooper, spokesman for the Council on American-Islamic Relations, contends that the U.S. government's tolerance of authoritarian regimes and lack of criticism of Israel's policies toward the Palestinians have exacerbated the conflict.

Others argue that the U.S. government's policies have been inadequate in addressing the threat posed by ISIS. James Jay Carafano, a national security expert with the conservative Heritage Foundation, argues that the U.S. government's withdrawal of troops from Iraq in 2011 emboldened ISIS fighters.

Looking ahead, experts familiar with the Middle East say it's hard to foresee a total victory for the U.S. and its allies any time soon. Some argue that the U.S. government's intervention in the region has been selective and counterproductive, making things worse rather than better.

Overall, the poll suggests that the American public is willing to back aggressive, long-term engagements overseas, as long as they are seen as necessary and effective. The conflict with ISIS is likely to be a long-term struggle, with experts suggesting that it could last for decades.

The article discusses the role of alcohol in the lives of modern women, particularly those of a certain socioeconomic status, and the argument that excessive drinking is a coping mechanism for living in a sexist society. The author, who is newly sober, describes her own experiences with alcohol and the societal pressures that contribute to the normalization of drinking among women.

The author cites an essay by Kristi Coulter, who argues that women drink to escape the realities of living in a still-too-sexist world. Coulter describes blowing off steam after serving on a sexist panel at work by drinking Manhattans and eating tapas with her female friends. She criticizes women who insert alcohol into every social scenario, from a morning walk through the farmers market to a trip to the waxing salon.

The author agrees with Coulter's argument to some extent, but also acknowledges that it is difficult to prove that women drink to cope with the pressures of living in a sexist society. She notes that women are also shaped by the culture they consume, which muddies the waters even more. The author also discusses her own experiences with alcohol, including drinking with friends on her podcast and selling a portable wine tumbler branded with their podcast logo.

The author also discusses the role of alcohol in the workplace, describing the prevalence of alcohol at her office and the pressure to drink at company events. She describes a particularly difficult experience at a wine tasting event, where she was the only person not drinking and felt out of place.

Overall, the article provides a thoughtful and nuanced exploration of the role of alcohol in the lives of modern women, and the societal pressures that contribute to the normalization of drinking among women. The author raises important questions about the role of the patriarchy in shaping women's lives and choices, and the ways in which alcohol can both empower and disempower women. The article is well-written and thought-provoking, and will likely resonate with many readers.

The Trump administration has announced that it will end the temporary protected status (TPS) for approximately 200,000 Salvadoran immigrants living in the United States since 2001. The decision, made on September 9, 2019, means that these immigrants will have 18 months to either leave the country or seek lawful residency. The TPS was granted in 2001 in response to two devastating earthquakes in El Salvador that left hundreds of thousands homeless.

The move is part of the Trump administration's broader push to tighten immigration laws and expel those living in the United States illegally. Critics argue that the decision ignores the ongoing violence in El Salvador and gives the Salvadorans few options but to leave the United States or remain illegally.

Salvadorans are by far the largest group under TPS, a program that administration officials say is supposed to provide a temporary haven for victims, not a permanent right to remain in the United States. Critics have complained that TPS has allowed participants to repeatedly extend their stays in 6-month to 18-month increments.

Patricia Hernandez, a Salvadoran immigrant who has lived in North Carolina for 18 years, expressed her concern about the decision, stating that most TPS holders pay taxes and are not living off the government or committing crimes. The family plans to move to Honduras with their children and do not intend to return north, though they worry about violence and political instability in Central America.

Trump administration changes to the TPS program mean that over the next two years approximately 250,000 people who previously had permission to live and work in the United States will be subject to deportation if they remain. Haitians and Nicaraguans will lose their protected status in 2019, and Hondurans, the second largest group in the program, could lose their rights later this year.

Advocates of the program argue that long-term resident Salvadorans and their children should not be sent back to El Salvador, a country struggling with a weak economy and gang violence that has given it one of the world's highest murder rates. Critics argue that the U.S. government is complicit in breaking up families and further destabilizing neighboring countries.

The U.S. Chamber of Commerce had urged the government to extend TPS protections for Salvadorans, Haitians, and Hondurans, stating that the loss of employment authorization for these populations would adversely impact several key industries. Congressional Democrats have expressed support for finding a permanent solution to help Salvadorans in the United States, but it will be politically difficult at a time when there are rival immigration priorities, including providing permanent protection for "Dreamers" - undocumented immigrants brought to the United States as children.

The article discusses two significant developments in the realm of space exploration and international law. Firstly, Alexa Internet has been donating their crawl data to the Internet Archive since 1996, which is added to the Wayback Machine after an embargo period.

Secondly, a project to establish the first space nation, named Asgardia, has been proposed by a team of scientists and legal experts, led by Russian scientist Dr. Igor Ashurbeyli. The aim of Asgardia is to create a space area beyond the control of individual nations, offering an independent platform free from the constraints of a land-based country's laws. The new nation aims to foster peace, open up access to space technologies, and protect Earth from cosmic threats.

Asgardia, named after one of the mythical worlds inhabited by the Norse gods, will initially consist of a single satellite, scheduled to be launched next year. Citizenship is open to anyone living on Earth, with over 1000 individuals having already signed up. The project's ultimate aim is to create a legal platform to ensure protection of planet Earth and provide access to space technologies for those who do not have that access.

However, the project faces significant hurdles, including getting UN recognition for Asgardia and addressing issues around liability. Experts in space law have expressed doubts about Asgardia's ability to be recognized as a country due to the specific criteria required for an entity to be recognized as a nation.

The project is seen as a potential way to sidestep the Outer Space Treaty or do an end-run around government regulations that are key to making the treaty work. Previously, American James Mangan claimed all of space beyond Earth as the "Nation of Celestial Space" in 1949, but his claim was largely ignored.

In conclusion, the establishment of Asgardia represents an ambitious attempt to create a space nation, offering an independent platform for space activities and fostering peace and protection for Earth. However, the project faces significant challenges in terms of recognition and legal implications.

The Leona M. and Harry B. Helmsley Charitable Trust has awarded a $6.3 million grant to the Iowa Department of Health to enhance cardiac arrest response across Iowa. The grant aims to purchase LUCAS 2 Chest Compression System devices for ambulances and hospitals, which provide automated chest compression for more consistent CPR delivery. Each device costs $10,000, and studies suggest they can improve CPR outcomes by 5-50%.

Leona Helmsley, the late New York City businesswoman famously known as the "Queen of Mean," is the source of the grant. However, a recent development in her estate's distribution has caused a stir in a New York court. The state attorney general has contested a $100 million fee sought by the estate's executors, including two of Mrs. Helmsley's grandchildren, arguing it is "astronomical" and should be significantly reduced, potentially by 90%.

Mrs. Helmsley was a prominent figure in the real estate industry, owning a vast portfolio that included the Empire State Building. The ongoing court battle over her estate's distribution underscores the complexities that can arise in estate planning and distribution, even for individuals of significant wealth. The grant to Iowa for cardiac arrest response, however, demonstrates the positive impact that such wealth can have in saving lives.

The 111th Congress, dominated by Democrats, passed more landmark legislation in two years than any since the era of Lyndon B. Johnson's "Great Society." The Congress approved an $814 billion economic stimulus, a massive healthcare overhaul, new regulations on Wall Street trading, and consumer credit cards. The list grew longer during the lame-duck session with tax cuts, a nuclear arms treaty, and the repeal of the "don't ask, don't tell" policy on gays in the military.

However, the Congress was also marked by endless filibuster threats, volatile town hall meetings, and the rise of the tea party, symbols of a dissatisfaction that peaked on Nov. 2 with a Republican rout in the midterm elections.

The 111th Congress will be remembered for its productivity, passing more laws affecting more Americans since the "Great Society" legislation of the 1960s. The Congress took the biggest step toward achieving a national health-care system, giving 32 million Americans access to insurance. They rewrote the rules for Wall Street in the most comprehensive way since the Great Depression and spent over $1.67 trillion to revive an economy on the verge of a depression.

The Congress also ended an almost two-decade ban against openly gay men and women serving in the military, and today ratified a nuclear arms reduction treaty with Russia. Before adjournment, Congress approved legislation to help rescuers and clean-up crews suffering from illnesses linked to the wreckage caused by the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks in New York City.

Despite the ambitious achievements, the 111th Congress also witnessed a voter-backlash driven by a 9.6 percent unemployment rate that cost Democrats control of the House and diminished their Senate majority. The Congress was unable to approve a single one of the 12 annual appropriations bills that fund the government.

As lawmakers wrap up the session, Wall Street firms are positioned to complete their best two years in revenue, General Motors has emerged from bankruptcy with more than $23 billion repaid to the U.S. Treasury, and American International Group was able to sell $2 billion of bonds in its first offering since the company’s 2008 bailout. The S&P 500 Index has gained 38.9 percent since Congress convened in January 2009, the biggest increase for a two-year congressional session since 1997-1998.

Stimulus money created and saved jobs across the country, helping strapped state governments retain their workforces. The careers of many lawmakers didn’t fare so well. Fiscally conservative Tea Party activists channeled their frustration with government spending and debt into political campaigns, most often to the benefit of Republicans challenging Democratic incumbents. In the Nov. 2 elections, Democrats lost 63 House seats, costing their party control of the chamber in next year’s Congress. In the Senate, the Democratic majority was shaved by six seats; the party will have 53 votes in next year’s session, Republicans 47.

Party-line votes on most of the major measures engendered ill will among Republicans and helped stall in the Senate initiatives requiring significant bipartisan support. Blocked legislation included limits on greenhouse-gas emissions, a bill offering undocumented immigrants a path to citizenship, and the administration’s attempts to curb growing income inequality with tax increases for higher earners. These are unlikely to be tackled next year, when the House’s Republican majority will turn its attention to dismantling the health-care law and cutting domestic government spending by $100 billion.

Congress this year was also unable to approve a single one of the 12 annual appropriations bills that fund the government. "I think it was a disaster," said Senator Jeff Sessions, an Alabama Republican, of the congressional session. Senator Richard Durbin of Illinois, the chamber’s No. 2 Democratic leader, saw it differently: “This whole two-year session has been dramatic in terms of its achievement and the changes that it’s brought about.” Outgoing House Speaker Nancy Pelosi praised the accomplishments of Congress in remarks to reporters today. “We’re very, very proud of the work that was done by this Congress,” the California Democrat said. “We came here to do a job and we got much of it done.”

The XPRIZE Foundation, a non-profit organization dedicated to fostering innovation, has launched a new global competition focused on ocean mapping, offering a $7 million prize purse. The three-year competition aims to push the boundaries of ocean exploration technology, with participants required to complete a series of tasks using devices launched from shore or air, capable of operating at a depth of up to 4,000 meters.

The tasks include creating high-resolution sea-floor maps, taking high-definition images of specific objects, and identifying key features in a "treasure hunt" style challenge. There is also a bonus $1 million challenge for technology that can monitor specific chemical and biological compounds in the water column.

The competition is part of XPRIZE's Ocean Initiative, a series of five multi-million dollar prizes aimed at addressing critical ocean challenges and inspiring innovation. The past two ocean prizes focused on Oil Spill Clean-Up and Ocean pH Sensor technologies.

The announcement was made during the American Geophysical Union (AGU) Fall Meeting in San Francisco, and is a partnership between XPRIZE, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), and Shell Oil Company. The competition is open to anyone, with registration currently open.

According to XPRIZE head Peter Diamandis, only a small percentage of the deep sea has been mapped, making it one of the planet's greatest unexplored frontiers. The competition aims to address this critical ocean challenge by accelerating innovation in deep-sea exploration.

Teams' creations will be tested first at 2,000 meters, then at 4,000 meters, at which point the robots will be required to complete the aforementioned tasks. The top prize is $4 million, with a chance to win an extra million if the robot manages to follow a chemical or biological signal back to its source.

Registration for the competition ends in September 2016, with the first tests scheduled for a year after that. For more information and to register, visit oceandiscovery.xprize.org.

This year, NORAD, the North American Aerospace Defense Command, has partnered with Microsoft Bing to track Santa's Christmas Eve journey, marking a shift from their previous partner, Google, who will continue to track Santa independently. NORAD has been tracking Santa since 1955, a tradition that started as a result of a department store ad error.

NORAD's Santa tracking system uses four high-tech systems: radar, satellites, Santa Cams, and fighter jets. They will provide updates via their website, Windows Azure cloud-computing platform, and Bing Maps, as well as through apps for Windows 8, Windows Phone 8, and Android. People can also call the official Santa tracking phone number or send emails to noradtrackssanta@outlook.com for live updates.

Google, on the other hand, will track Santa using its Google Maps and Google Earth tools. They have developed a new route algorithm for this purpose. Google's Santa tracking will be available on its Santa Tracker website, a new Chrome extension, Android app, and its Google+, Facebook, and Twitter pages. Google-owned YouTube will continue to host dispatches from NORAD concerning Santa's whereabouts.

The switch from Google to Bing's mapping service by NORAD is a mutual decision, and Google continues to maintain a loose affiliation with NORAD through YouTube. This year, over 1,250 volunteers from Canada and the US will maintain the tradition. The shift in partnership may not significantly impact Santa's journey, and it remains to be seen whether it will help or hinder his progress.

Liana Barrientos, a 39-year-old woman from the Bronx, has been arrested and is facing felony charges for allegedly participating in a marriage scam. In addition to her current charges for theft of service and criminal trespass, Barrientos was previously arraigned for two counts of filing a false instrument. The false instruments in question were a marriage license application and the signed marriage license from 2010, which stated it was her first and only marriage.

However, authorities believe that Barrientos has been marrying men to help them enter the country. She is currently believed to be married to four people, and at one point, she was married to eight men simultaneously. The case was brought to the attention of the Bronx County District Attorney's Office by Immigration and Customs Enforcement and the Department of Homeland Security's Investigation Division. Seven of the men involved are from countries considered "red-flagged," including Egypt, Turkey, Georgia, Pakistan, and Mali.

In 2006, one of the grooms, Rashid Rajput, was deported to Pakistan following an investigation by the Joint Terrorism Task Force. Barrientos lived in a Bronx building with her boyfriend, who is not one of the 10 men she is alleged to have married.

National security expert Manny Gomez stated that this case is a significant breach in security, as someone could potentially enter the country illegally and plot or recruit for terrorist activities. Barrientos' history of serial marriages began in November 1999, and she has since married 10 men in various towns across New York State.

If convicted, Barrientos faces up to four years in prison. The men whom Barrientos is alleged to have married, most without benefit of divorce, are identified as Mohamed Gebril, Ahmed Allam, Habibur Rahman, Davit Koridze, Duran Goktepe, Aliaksandr Paharelau, Vakhtang Dzneladze, Rashid Rajput, Kakhaber Khorbaladze, and Salle Keita. Seven of the men filed for permanent status based on their marriages to Barrientos.

Peggy Sue Gerron Rackham, the Texas woman who inspired the 1958 Buddy Holly song "Peggy Sue," has passed away at a Lubbock hospital. She was 78 years old. The news of her death was confirmed by Eric Finley, a spokesperson for University Medical Center, where she died on Monday. Gerron's family granted permission for the hospital to confirm her death, but requested that no further information be disclosed.

In 2008, Gerron released her autobiography "Whatever Happened to Peggy Sue?: A Memoir by Buddy Holly's Peggy Sue" to commemorate the 50th anniversary of the song. The book was based on approximately 150 diary entries she made during her time knowing Holly. Gerron was born in Olton, Texas, but later moved to Lubbock where she attended high school and met Holly and his friends.

Gerron was married to drummer Jerry Allison, a member of Holly's rock 'n' roll band The Crickets. The couple later divorced. Tom Stathos, Gerron's son-in-law, reminisced on Monday and told KCBD-TV in Lubbock that the song "Peggy Sue" initially had a different name. Stathos said that Allison wanted to impress Gerron, so he convinced Holly to change the name of the song.

Holly wrote several other popular songs, including "That'll Be The Day" and "Maybe Baby." He also penned the song-sequel "Peggy Sue Got Married." Holly died in a plane crash in Iowa on February 3, 1959, along with Ritchie Valens and J.P. "The Big Bopper" Richardson.

A 1978 movie, "The Buddy Holly Story," featured Gary Busey in the title role. A 1986 movie called "Peggy Sue Got Married" featured actress Kathleen Turner as a character also named Peggy Sue who faints during her 25th high school reunion, then believes she's gone back in time and reconsiders how her life turned out. The Buddy Holly Center in Lubbock pays tribute to the singer, musician, and songwriter who is described as "Lubbock's most famous native son."

The ghost town of Cerro Gordo, nestled in the Inyo Mountains of California, has been purchased for $1.4 million by a group of investors led by Brent Underwood and Jon Bier. The town, which was listed for $925,000, was once the largest producer of silver and lead in California and has a rich history dating back to the 19th century. The sale closed on Friday the 13th, and the new owners plan to restore and preserve the town while introducing amenities to attract more visitors. The town has 22 structures remaining, including an abandoned hotel, church, and bunkhouse, and has a long history of averaging a murder a week in its heyday. The new owners hope to create a unique destination by hosting events such as writing retreats, concerts, photo shoots, and theater, while maintaining the historic nature of the property. The sale attracted numerous offers, with the winning offer being appreciated by the sellers for its plan to preserve and publicize the town's history. The town has been in the hands of the same family for decades and was previously open to the public for tours. The new owners plan to renovate select buildings and bring WiFi to the property, while also addressing necessary refurbishments to ensure the buildings are structurally sound. The long-term goals for Cerro Gordo include hosting high-level programming such as writing retreats, music events, dining experiences, photo shoots, theater, special events, and more. The sale of Cerro Gordo is one of many examples of entire towns being sold these days. The Hard Luck Castle, another example, is a self-sustainable, off-grid property located in Nevada and encompassing 40 acres of land and 8,000 square feet of living space. The castle has a long list of offerings, including two kitchens, three full baths, a wood shop, wine cellar, theater and game room, glass solarium / planetarium, fountain room, large main entrance with afternoon view deck, two 1920's pipe organs, and more. The castle has become a tourist attraction and a landmark in Esmeralda County.

"Get Out" is a horror film written and directed by Jordan Peele, marking his debut in feature films. The movie is a terrifying and topical satire that combines elements from various horror classics such as "Guess Who's Coming to Dinner," "Rosemary's Baby," and "Invasion of the Body Snatchers." However, it stands out as more than just a parody, with its social critique being a significant part of the narrative, unlike other horror films where it is usually subtext.

The film tells the story of Chris, a 26-year-old photographer, who visits the affluent family of his white girlfriend, Rose, after she fails to disclose his race to her parents. Chris is wary but trusts Rose, despite warnings from his TSA agent friend, Rod. The family's behavior towards Chris is initially overly accommodating, but as the weekend progresses, he encounters a series of disturbing discoveries that lead him to an unsettling truth.

Peele's direction is commended for maintaining a high level of tension throughout the film, with his handheld camera contributing to the anxiety in scenes where Chris expresses his concerns to Rose. The performances of the cast, particularly Daniel Kaluuya as Chris, are also praised for their authenticity and intensity.

The film's opening scene sets the tone, with a young black man walking down a suburban street at night, a car following him, and a 1939 novelty song playing. This scene, reminiscent of the Trayvon Martin case, is a powerful statement about the fears and dangers faced by black individuals in America.

"Get Out" is a memorable horror film that successfully combines entertainment with a sharp social critique, making it a significant addition to the horror genre. Its release date is February 24, 2017.

The It Gets Better Project is a campaign aimed at providing resources and support for LGBT youth. The project encourages donations to fund suicide prevention and anti-bullying programs, and encourages individuals to share their personal stories of hope. The project also offers the opportunity to take a pledge, purchase merchandise, and buy the project's book. For a $25 donation, a copy of the book can be sent to a local library or school. The project also invites individuals to send in their own It Gets Better videos or stories, and offers to share some stories in the coming months.

The Airbus A350 XWB jet, debuted in early 2015, aims to revolutionize air travel by addressing common issues such as energy efficiency, aerodynamics, and comfort, while ensuring technological relevance for its projected 30-year lifespan. The plane's structure is made from 50% carbon fiber-reinforced plastic, making it lighter and more durable than traditional aluminum planes. The larger, wider wings and improved flap system contribute to a 25% improvement in fuel economy compared to similarly sized planes from competitors.

To combat jet lag, the A350 is equipped with LED lights that mimic the sun's natural glow, adjusting color temperature according to natural circadian rhythms. The cabin's air is refreshed every 2-3 minutes, and it is pressurized to 6,000 feet, aiming to improve passenger comfort and minimize jet lag effects.

The fuselage is wider to accommodate larger economy class seats and easier aisle movement. The interior design is adaptable, allowing carriers to swap out seats and tweak configurations more easily than in the past. This philosophy extends to the way computer hardware integrates with the design, making avionics and software upgrades less cumbersome.

Airbus is hoping that its no-nonsense approach to design and engineering will help it best the competition, namely the Boeing 787 Dreamliner and 777 long-distance planes. However, the A350's first trip to the United States was aborted due to a short runway, and the plane has faced no reported problems aside from lengthy delivery times.

In summary, the Airbus A350 XWB jet is a significant advancement in air travel, integrating design and engineering tricks to address common issues such as energy efficiency, aerodynamics, and comfort, while minimizing jet lag effects through innovative LED lighting and cabin air systems. The plane's wider fuselage and adaptable interior design aim to improve passenger comfort and convenience. With $15 billion in funding and 2,600 hours of test flights, the A350 is expected to be in service for the next 30 years.

The United Kingdom has announced plans to ban the sale of new gasoline and diesel cars starting in 2040 as part of an effort to improve air quality and reduce emissions. The decision marks a significant shift towards low-emission technologies and has major implications for the auto industry, society, and the environment. The ban is expected to be a heavy lift, as electric and fuel cell cars, along with plug-in hybrids, currently account for less than 3% of the market.

Experts believe sales of clean cars will continue to increase, but the industry is concerned about the cost of new technologies and consumer willingness to adopt battery, plug-in hybrid, and hydrogen cars. Consumers have expressed concerns over affordability, range, and charging points. The deadline was announced as part of a plan to reduce air pollution, with approximately £1.4 billion ($1.8 billion) in government investment earmarked to help ensure that every vehicle on the road in Britain produces zero emissions by 2050.

The decision to phase out internal combustion engines mirrors one proposed by France, where President Emmanuel Macron has given the auto industry the same deadline to make the switch to cleaner technology. The move is aimed at addressing health problems caused by gasoline and diesel engines, which contribute to cancer, asthma, stroke, and heart disease, among other health issues. Roughly 40,000 deaths in Britain each year are attributable to outdoor air pollution, according to a study published last year by the Royal College of Physicians.

The ban is expected to have a significant impact on the auto industry, which supports over 800,000 jobs in the U.K. Andy Palmer, CEO of British luxury automaker Aston Martin, has stated that ditching conventional engines will require much more planning and investment. "To make a moonshot work, you need to have a NASA," he told CNNMoney. "If you don't want to export jobs out of the U.K., you need to create that capability and that infrastructure ... we're a long, long way from having that capability today."

Other countries have been even more ambitious than the U.K., with India planning to stop selling gas-powered vehicles by 2030. The German car industry and government officials will meet in early August to discuss the future of diesel engine technology, as manufacturers try to avoid diesel cars being banned from German towns and cities.

The final plan, which is due by the end of July, comes after a draft report that environmental lawyers described as "much weaker than hoped for." The environment secretary, Michael Gove, will be hoping for a better reception when he publishes the final document on Wednesday following months of legal wrangling. The plan includes measures to help councils improve air quality in specific areas where emissions have breached EU thresholds, such as retrofitting buses and other public transport, changing road layouts, altering features such as roundabouts and speed humps, reprogramming traffic lights, and providing funding for a targeted scrappage scheme. Some want the countrywide initiative to follow in the footsteps of London, which is introducing a £10 toxic "T-charge" that will be levied on up to 10,000 of the oldest, most polluting vehicles every weekday.

On November 29, 2018, the office of Elizabeth Midlarsky, a Jewish professor who teaches and researches the Holocaust at Columbia Teachers College, was vandalized with swastikas and anti-Semitic slurs. The incident occurred around 1 p.m. and was discovered by Midlarsky herself. The graffiti was drawn in the entryway to Midlarsky’s office, which is not shared with other staff.

Midlarsky found the graffiti when she came to her office and notified security. According to the NYPD, a different staff member entered the room at approximately 11:47 a.m. Wednesday and did not observe anything unusual at that time. The incident remains under active investigation by the NYPD Hate Crimes Task Force and is being treated as an aggravated harassment.

This is not the first time Midlarsky's office has been vandalized. In 2007, a swastika was spray-painted on her door and anti-Semitic flyers left in her mailbox. Midlarsky attributes this second incident to a broader national rise in anti-Semitic crimes and a changing culture.

Both the Office of University Life and Barnard College issued statements on Thursday morning strongly denouncing the anti-Semitic act and showing support for Jewish students. Teachers College president Thomas Bailey also released a statement condemning the act and expressing the college's commitment to providing a respectful and welcoming environment for all.

In addition to Midlarsky, three other professors and a former professor at Columbia University's Teachers College received hate mail this week, including a former professor who was sent a manila envelope containing an image of a noose. The NYPD Hate Crimes Unit is leading the investigation into the incident, and no arrests have been made.

The incident has been widely condemned, with the Teachers College community deploring the hateful acts and expressing support for the affected professors. Midlarsky, who has worked at the university for 28 years, has written about the Holocaust and has been a repeated target of anti-Semitic vitriol. The Police Department is investigating the vandalism as a hate crime.

In a significant development, Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell has publicly stated that Alabama Republican Senate nominee Roy Moore should step down from the race following allegations of sexual misconduct. The allegations, detailed in a report by The Washington Post, involve Moore pursuing relationships with teenage girls while he was in his 30s, with one woman claiming she was 14 years old at the time of the alleged encounter. Moore has denied the allegations and threatened to sue The Washington Post.

Moore responded to McConnell's statement by tweeting that it is McConnell who should step aside, accusing him of failing conservatives and needing to be replaced. The allegations against Moore have increased pressure on Republicans to disavow him, given his controversial history of racially-charged and homophobic commentary.

McConnell's comments on Monday represent a further step in the party's distancing from Moore. The National Republican Senatorial Committee, one of the party's main campaign arms, has already cut its fundraising ties with Moore. The Republican Party is now exploring the possibility of a write-in option as an alternative to Moore. This story is ongoing and will likely continue to develop in the coming days.

Donald Trump called for a ban on burning the American flag, suggesting that the offenders could face consequences such as loss of citizenship or a year in jail. This proposal contradicts two Supreme Court rulings that protect flag burning as a form of free speech. The article from Bloomberg Businessweek reveals that retail giant Target was aware of a security breach on their system nearly two weeks before they took any action to address it. The breach occurred on November 30, 2013, and was detected by FireEye, a security firm that Target had hired to monitor their servers for malware. The Bangalore-based response team at FireEye alerted Target's headquarters in Minneapolis, but the company's security team failed to respond.

The breach eventually compromised up to 40 million customers' credit card data, with personal information like email addresses and phone numbers being compromised for 70 million customers, affecting a total of 110 million people. This contradicts Target's previous statements about the incident, which claimed they only learned of the attack in mid-December.

The report suggests that Target's inaction was a series of "blunders," including the disabling of an automatic malware deletion feature by the company's security team. The article also speculates that the perpetrator of the hack may be Andrey Khodyrevskiy, a Ukrainian hacker known as Rescator. However, there is no definitive proof that Rescator and Khodyrevskiy are the same person.

Target's President and CEO Gregg Steinhafel has issued a statement, saying the company is conducting a company-wide probe to determine what happened. Target's CIO during the hack, Beth Jacob, resigned earlier this month. The full article can be found on Businessweek's website.

The article discusses the challenges faced by individuals with dysphagia, a condition that impairs the ability to swallow, often due to damage to the nerves or muscles involved in swallowing. One of the main issues is the difficulty in consuming and digesting food, particularly bread, which can be hard to swallow and absorb saliva, leading to discomfort and potential blockages.

To address this problem, companies like EN Otsuka Pharmaceutical Co. Ltd have developed engineered substitutes for bread, such as iEat Bread, which has been treated with enzymes to alter its physical properties, making it easier to swallow. Researchers are also experimenting with moulds that shape purées into more natural-looking dishes and using 3D printing to design nutritious and appealing foods with a gel-like consistency.

For those who lack the strength in their throat muscles to swallow, devices like the Swallow Expansion Device, which resembles a stud earring, are being developed to mechanically move the larynx forward and open the upper oesophageal sphincter. Other approaches include nerve-aiding medications, muscle stem cell therapy, and methods to limit collateral damage from radiation therapy and dilate the oesophagus.

The article also shares the personal story of Samantha Anderson, a woman who developed dysphagia after a case of shingles damaged four of her cranial nerves. After months of misery, she was diagnosed and underwent treatment, including high doses of donepezil, strengthening exercises, and training to practise a new swallowing technique. With these interventions, she has slowly regained her strength and is able to eat solid foods again, albeit with precautions.

The article underscores the importance of awareness and understanding of swallowing disorders, which can affect both young and old, and the need for continued research and development of treatments to help those suffering from dysphagia.

The article discusses the findings of a study on a controversial ancient Egyptian papyrus fragment known as the "Gospel of Jesus's Wife." The fragment, which refers to Jesus as being married, has been under scrutiny since it was introduced by Harvard professor Karen L. King in 2012. New scientific tests have revealed no evidence of modern forgery, supporting King's argument that the document is authentic.

The tests included carbon dating, which found that the papyrus probably dates to the 8th century, carbon-based ink analysis, and microscopic imaging to detect any suspicious ink pooling. The results suggest that the ink's composition is consistent with that used by ancient Egyptians, and there is no ink out of place at the microscopic level.

However, the tests do not definitively prove that the text was written in ancient times. Specialists have suggested that a highly skilled modern forger could have obtained the right kind of ink and applied it to a blank piece of ancient papyrus.

The controversy over the fragment's authenticity is likely to continue, with some scholars dismissing it as a modern-day cut-and-paste job with several grammatical blunders. Leo Depuydt, an Egyptologist at Brown University, believes the document is a forgery and argues that the similarities between the Gospel of Jesus's Wife and the Gospel of Thomas are too close to be coincidental.

King maintains that the document was probably part of a debate among early Christians about the role of women, family, and celibacy in spiritual life. She believes the document may have been copied from a much earlier Greek text and sees it as an important addition to the study of the development of Christianity.

The latest tests do not prove definitively that the text was written in ancient times, but groundbreaking work by Columbia University researchers may soon uncover a way to date the ink without harming the fragment, which would offer a more definitive verdict about its authenticity. Meanwhile, the controversy over the fragment seems likely to continue.

In his commencement address at Howard University, President Barack Obama praised the efforts of black activists, including those involved in Black Lives Matter and "black Twitter," for raising national awareness about inequality in the criminal justice system. He urged activists to focus on electoral politics and compromise to bring about structural change. Obama also highlighted the progress made by black Americans since his graduation from Columbia University in 1983, and encouraged the graduates to embrace their heritage and affect systemic change through the political process.

Both Packnett and Mckesson agreed that policy and street protests inform one another, and that engagement on all fronts is necessary for creating change.

Samuel Sinyangwe, who works with McKesson and Packnett on Campaign Zero, a policy thinktank on police violence, said that Obama's remarks highlighted a truth: awareness is important, but it is not enough. He added that awareness matters in terms of understanding cultural biases and the need for change.

Obama also cautioned protesters against silencing or interrupting political opponents, and instead encouraged them to rebut and teach them.
