The study titled 'The Biggest Lie on the Internet: An Empirical Investigation of Privacy Policy and Terms of Service Policy Reading Behavior' reveals that the majority of internet users do not read the Terms of Service (TOS) and Privacy Policies (PP) before agreeing to them. The researchers created a fictitious social networking site to test this behavior, with policies modeled on LinkedIn. The policies included clauses that should have raised concerns, such as data sharing with the NSA, third parties, and even requiring participants to sign over their firstborn child. Out of 543 participants, 74% skipped the PP and TOS entirely, and those who did read them spent an average of 73 seconds on the PP and 51 seconds on the TOS. The study found that 98% of participants missed the existence of the 'gotcha' clauses, indicating a lack of understanding and awareness of the terms they are agreeing to. The study highlights the need for more user-friendly policies and increased awareness about the importance of reading and understanding TOS and PP.

The Worldwide Cost of Living Index 2014 report, published by the Economist Intelligence Unit (EIU), ranks Singapore as the most expensive city in the world. This is primarily due to the strong Singapore dollar and high costs of cars, utilities, and clothing. Singapore's rise in the rankings has been gradual, having been the 18th most expensive city ten years ago. The EIU's survey, conducted bi-annually, compares the cost of living in over 160 cities across 400 individual prices, including food, housing, transportation, and utilities, among others. The survey is designed to help businesses calculate cost-of-living allowances and build compensation packages for expatriates and business travelers. The report can be downloaded for a fee, and the EIU is renowned for its comprehensive global coverage and uncompromising integrity. The report also reveals other expensive and affordable cities worldwide.

The Republican National Convention (RNC) officially nominated Mitt Romney as the party's presidential candidate on Tuesday, August 28, 2012. The convention, which was delayed due to Hurricane Isaac, was held in Tampa, Florida, and was scripted to propel Romney into a close race for the White House. Key figures at the convention included Ann Romney, wife of Mitt Romney, and Paul Ryan, the Republican vice presidential candidate. The convention also approved a conservative platform that calls for tax cuts to stimulate the economy, and featured speeches from various Republican leaders, including New Jersey Governor Chris Christie. The convention was marked by a heated campaign for the nomination, with Texas Rep. Ron Paul drawing several dozen delegate votes. The convention took place in an atmosphere of security, with thousands of police, National Guard troops, Secret Service, and others present. The convention was followed by the Democratic National Convention (DNC), which will be held in Charlotte, North Carolina, next week.

The Internet Archive is working on a project to preserve web pages as they are created and maintain archived versions of pages that are referenced, aiming to fix broken links on the web. This is done by replacing broken links with links to the archived versions of the pages. Meanwhile, a Burger King in Morro Bay, California, has been closed since Sunday due to an incident where employees received a prank call about a fake gas leak. The call led employees to smash all the windows, causing an estimated $35,000 worth of damages. The fast-food chain is expected to reopen on Tuesday. The manager on duty, who used a car to ram into the building, has been suspended. The police are encouraging anyone with information, pictures, or video of the incident to contact them.

The Democratic National Convention featured a speech by former President Bill Clinton, who endorsed President Barack Obama for re-election. Clinton's speech was a comprehensive case for Obama's re-election, tackling important topics such as the economy, healthcare, and fiscal policies. Clinton praised Obama's policies, including the 2009 stimulus, his expansion of college aid, and his efforts to boost renewable energy. He also explained how Obama's healthcare law would benefit ordinary Americans and warned that Republican healthcare cuts would hurt the poorest and most vulnerable members of society. Clinton unraveled Republican attacks on Medicare spending and welfare that have been deemed misleading by independent fact-checkers and warned that proposed Republican cuts to healthcare would hurt the poor and disabled, not just the middle class. Clinton also addressed the question of whether Americans are better off than they were four years ago, stating that while the details may not be known, Romney's policies would either balloon the national debt, shift more of the tax burden to the middle class, or hollow out programs such as child nutrition and transportation. Overall, Clinton's speech was well-received by Democrats and Republicans alike, with many praising his ability to communicate complicated subjects in a way that resonates with the American people. However, some criticized his speech for being too long and self-indulgent.

Martin Gill and his partner have been fostering two brothers for four years in North Miami, with the hope of adopting them since their parental rights were terminated in 2006. However, due to a Florida state law that bans adoptions by gay people, their adoption has been delayed. Martin is challenging this ban with the help of the ACLU, and a juvenile court judge granted the adoption last November. The case is currently under appeal by Florida's attorney general.

Separately, a large-scale web crawl was conducted from March 2011 to December 2011, using the new HQ software for distributed crawling. The crawl used Alexa's top 1 million web sites as the seed list and captured 2,713,676,341 URLs, 2,273,840,159 unique URLs, and 29,032,069 hosts. The crawl was somewhat experimental due to operational issues with the software, such as not crawling all embedded and linked objects in a page and repeated crawls of some Argentinian government sites. The data is available for those interested, but access may not be granted to all requests as the organization is still determining whether this is a good idea.

In a series of interviews, President Barack Obama and General David Petraeus, head of U.S. Central Command, have stated that the U.S. does not plan to send troops to Yemen or Somalia, despite the growing threat of Islamic militants in both countries. Al Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula (AQAP), based in Yemen, is believed to have trained and directed the Nigerian man accused of attempting to bomb a U.S. airliner in December 2009. AQAP and Al Shabaab, an al Qaeda-inspired insurgency in Somalia, have seized large areas of their respective countries.

The U.S. intends to increase its security assistance funding to Yemen from $70 million last year to at least $150 million this year, and has also provided additional economic aid. Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates have also pledged significant funds to help Yemen fight terrorism and promote development.

Yemen President Ali Abdullah Saleh has expressed a preference for handling al Qaeda on its own, and the U.S. plans to honor this request. The U.S. has provided intelligence on al Qaeda targets to Yemeni authorities, but has not disclosed whether U.S. aircraft or ordnance were used in any strikes.

General Petraeus has expressed concern about AQAP's growth in Yemen, which has been a haven for the group as it was pushed out of other countries such as Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Pakistan, and Afghanistan. The U.S. embassy in Yemen was briefly closed last Sunday due to intelligence suggesting a possible attack on the compound, but reopened on Tuesday.

Despite the increased focus on Yemen, General Petraeus has stated that the western Pakistan-Afghanistan border area remains the most important locale in the U.S. war on terror. The U.S. has made significant strides in the fight against terrorists, but must continue to maintain pressure on Al Qaeda wherever it is found.

In a significant development, the Kern High School District has agreed to pay $10.5 million to Mitch Carter, a former student who was injured in a violent dog pile that occurred during a 2010 pep rally at Bakersfield High School. The incident took place during a skit where Carter, wearing a chicken costume to mock an opposing team's mascot, was roughed up by members of the football team.

The jury had already found the district liable for Carter's injuries, which included brain damage. The district's insurance company, Everest National Insurance Company, will pay the majority of the settlement. Mitch Carter will use the money for healthcare-related costs.

Attorney Nicholas Rowley, representing Carter, stated that the jury was expected to award more than $45 million, but the school district would have appealed, potentially prolonging the process for years. However, Carter needs the money now, according to Rowley.

The settlement ends a seven-day civil trial that highlighted shoddy safety practices, questionable policies, and disorganization within the Kern High School District. The incident has led to accusations of conspiracy and cover-up.

Defense attorney Michael Kellar described the incident as "embarrassing and inexcusable," and it came as a surprise to school staff. He stated that the district's insurance company made the decision to settle to reduce the risk of a higher jury award.

Kern High School District officials have accepted responsibility for the incident and will reevaluate their safety policies to ensure a safe and secure environment for students. They expressed their best wishes for Carter and his family.

Mitch Carter, who suffered brain damage during the incident, expressed his hope to attend law school in the future so he can stand up for those who need their voices heard. He stated that he bears no bad blood towards Bakersfield High School but wants top administrators to be held accountable for their actions.

The trial was marked by accusations of conspiracy and cover-up, with witnesses testifying about a school culture that prioritized football and protected star players. Mitch Carter testified that he was shunned by school administrators after reporting a starting player for theft.

The settlement is expected to force the Kern High School District to change its policies to prevent such incidents from happening in the future. Carter's attorney, Ralph Wegis, has been vocal about the district's "despicable" actions and wants top administrators to be held accountable.

In Texas, a controversial proposal to require the cremation or burial of fetal remains instead of disposal in sanitary landfills has been finalized by health officials. The rules, which take effect on December 19, will apply to all medical facilities, hospitals, and clinics, regardless of the period of gestation.

Opponents of the rules, led by abortion rights advocacy group NARAL Pro-Choice Texas, have voiced concerns that the requirements could be costly and create more obstacles for people seeking abortions. Critics argue that the rules are an attempt to deny access to abortion and target abortion providers.

The new rules were introduced by the Department of State Health Services, which found that the proposed rules would not increase total costs for healthcare facilities. The department also clarified that the requirement does not apply to miscarriages or abortions that take place at home, and does not require birth or death certificates to be filed.

Abortion providers generally use third-party special waste services to dispose of fetal remains. Previous rules allowed fetal remains to be ground up and discharged into a sewer system, incinerated, or handled by some other approved process before being disposed of in a landfill.

The move has been met with fierce opposition from abortion rights advocates and the medical community, who argue that the rules are unnecessary and create an undue burden on women. Some groups, like the Center for Reproductive Rights, have said they would likely challenge the new rules in court.

Meanwhile, Republican lawmakers in the state have expressed support for the proposed rule, with one state senator saying, "Life begins at conception." The rules fall under the rulemaking authority of the state health department, and do not require legislative approval. However, Republican lawmakers have already filed legislation to write the rules into statutory law when the legislature reconvenes in January.

Other states have also passed restrictions on the use of fetal remains. For example, a law in Indiana would have prohibited abortions sought solely because a fetus had been potentially diagnosed with a disability such as Down syndrome. However, a federal judge suspended the law from going into effect, finding that it violated U.S. Supreme Court precedents protecting a woman's right to choose an abortion and the right to privacy in making that decision.

The legal status of fetal remains is a complex and murky area, with deep philosophical, religious, and legal questions that have yet to be fully addressed.

The Watergate parking garage, a historic site where Washington Post reporter Bob Woodward met his anonymous source "Deep Throat" during the Watergate scandal, is set to be demolished as part of a redevelopment plan by Monday Properties. The company plans to replace two aging office buildings, located at 1401 Wilson Blvd and 1400 Key Blvd in Arlington, Va., with a mixed-use development. The redevelopment will go through Arlington's site plan process, which can take 1-4 years.

The Watergate parking garage, built in the early 1960s, is nearing the end of its useful life. Monday Properties plans to preserve the historical marker outside the garage and may incorporate it into the new development. The marker will likely be removed and stored during the redevelopment process.

The new development will consist of a 32-story apartment or condo building and a 29-story office building. In total, the buildings will have 500,000 square feet of office space, 385,000 square feet of residential space, and 60,000 square feet of retail space, including a planned full-service grocery store. About half of the land will be used as a public open space.

Monday Properties has not yet set a timeline for the demolition and subsequent construction, pending county approval. The Arlington County Site Plan Review Committee is scheduled to hold a meeting about the development proposal on Monday, Oct. 21. The company is receptive to ideas for preserving some part of the garage's history and appreciates the historical significance of the site.

In a heated exchange during a House hearing on Tuesday, Republican Representative Louie Gohmert and Attorney General Eric Holder clashed over documents related to an Islamic charity based in Texas and the Fast and Furious scandal. Gohmert accused Holder of not doing his job and of making personal choices in prosecutions, while Holder snapped back, "You don't want to go there, buddy."

The following day, Gohmert appeared on "Fox & Friends" and stated that there was no personal bad blood between him and Holder. He reiterated his belief that Holder was not fulfilling his duties as the highest law enforcement officer in the country. Gohmert argued that Holder should produce the documents that would allow for proper oversight and transparency.

During a speech at Al Sharpton's National Action Network on Wednesday, Holder addressed the contentious exchange and took a jab at Gohmert, stating that no Attorney General had ever had to endure such treatment. Holder also highlighted the Obama administration's efforts to "advance the cause of justice" in the face of "unprecedented, unwarranted, ugly, and divisive adversity."

In addition to Gohmert, Republican Blake Farenthold also criticized Holder, stating that he should be in jail. The exchange between Holder and Gohmert was captured on video and can be viewed below.

In summary, the exchange between Holder and Gohmert during a House hearing on Tuesday was contentious, with both parties accusing the other of inappropriate behavior. The following day, Gohmert maintained that there was no personal animosity between him and Holder, but reiterated his belief that Holder was not doing his job. Holder, in turn, addressed the exchange during a speech on Wednesday and took a jab at Gohmert, while also highlighting the Obama administration's efforts to advance justice in the face of adversity.

In northern India, a young girl, believed to be between 10 and 12 years old, was found living in a forest with a group of monkeys. The girl, now known as the 'Mowgli girl' due to comparisons to the character from Rudyard Kipling's Jungle Book, was discovered in a malnourished state, unable to communicate, and displaying "monkey-like" traits. She was first spotted by villagers in the Katarniaghat wildlife sanctuary, on the Indian border with Nepal, and was later rescued by police.

The girl was initially taken to a hospital in Bahraich, where she was treated for her physical condition and began to improve. She has started walking normally and eating with her hands, but is still unable to speak. Indian police are reviewing reports of missing children to try to identify the girl and determine her parents.

The girl will be sent to a home for juveniles until she is identified, and is expected to be handed over to child welfare agencies and medical specialists to slowly reintroduce her to the world. The hospital's chief medical officer, DK Singh, has stated that although she is still in hospital, she will be transferred to the Lucknow Medical College once she has been given a clean bill of health.

Local District Magistrate Ajaydeep Singh has named the girl "Forest Durga," a reference to a Hindu warrior goddess. Many in India are comparing the girl's story to that of Mowgli, the character from The Jungle Book who was raised by wolves. It is not clear, however, how long the girl has been living in the forest.

In the primary elections held on Tuesday, U.S. Senator Orrin Hatch, R-Utah, won the GOP primary in Utah, defeating a challenge from tea party forces led by former state senator Dan Liljenquist. Hatch, 78, who has been in office since 1976, spent about $10 million on his campaign, blanketing the airwaves and building a campaign operation unlike anything Utah had seen before. Liljenquist, who survived a 2008 plane crash in Guatemala that killed 11 of 14 on board, faced an overwhelming financial and organizational disadvantage.

In New York, 82-year-old Rep. Charlie Rangel won the Democratic primary despite a House censure 18 months ago for failing to pay all his taxes and for filing misleading financial disclosure statements. Rangel's career was put in jeopardy after a 2010 ethics investigation that culminated in him being censured on the House floor.

In another closely-watched House race in the Empire State, state Assemblyman Hakeem Jeffries crushed New York councilman Charles Barron, a former Black Panther with a history of fiery rhetoric whose candidacy spooked the Democratic establishment.

In Oklahoma, GOP Rep. John Sullivan lost the seat he has held since 2002 to a little-known, tea party-backed opponent.

Senator Hatch's race was the premier event in Tuesday's primaries. Hatch, learning from the defeat two years ago of his Senate colleague Robert Bennett, spent about $10 million blanketing the airwaves and building a campaign operation unlike anything Utah had seen before. Hatch's race was considered vulnerable like Bennett and six-term Republican Sen. Richard Lugar, who lost in last month's Indiana GOP primary. But Hatch got a huge endorsement from Republican presidential candidate Mitt Romney, who said he would need Hatch in the Senate if he wins the presidency.

Hatch seemed to have an answer to every criticism in his quest for a seventh term. For those who said that 36 years in office was enough, he said that he wouldn't be running again if it weren't for the opportunity to serve as chairman of the Senate Finance Committee if the GOP wins control of the Senate. He also announced it would be his last term. For those who said he wasn't conservative enough, he gravitated to the right with his comments and his votes, scoring a 100 percent rating from the American Conservative Union in 2010 and 2011. His lifetime rating of 89 percent from the ACU would place Hatch among the Senate's most conservative lawmakers, but Hatch at times took stands that didn't sit well with the right. Liljenquist, 37, a relative newcomer to the Utah political scene, seized on voters' concerns about the growing national debt and tried to make the case that Hatch had been a major contributor to that debt.

With the primary victory, Hatch was a huge favorite to win the general election in November against Democratic candidate Scott Howell. Rangel's triumph marked his latest display of survival instincts. He was dogged by a bad back and ethics controversy and managed to overcome a redistricting process that forced him to fight for reelection on less friendly political terrain. Rangel's career was put in jeopardy after a 2010 ethics investigation that culminated in him being censured on the House floor. Adding to his problems, earlier this year his seat was refashioned to include more Latino voters than blacks. That gave an opening to Rangel's lead primary opponent, Espaillat, a 57-year-old state senator who is Dominican American. Making matters worse, Rangel had to compete with three lesser known black candidates who threatened to siphon African American votes from him. And the incumbent was incapacitated for three months this year by health problems, including a bad back and a viral infection. Rangel revealed last week that he had been receiving a daily IV infusion of antibiotics. But on Tuesday, Rangel said he had shown he's just fine.

Bob Dylan, in an exclusive interview with Bill Flanagan on his website, discussed his latest album of standards, Triplicate, and his musical influences and relationships with various artists. Dylan explained that the three discs of music were released together because they are thematically interconnected, with each disc resolving the previous one. He also discussed his approach to singing with a live horn section and working with tight arrangements and charts, stating that it required a new way of thinking but that he was able to focus on the melodies within the arrangements. Dylan also spoke about his relationship with Frank Sinatra, stating that Sinatra was a guide and that he had to make believe that he never heard of Sinatra when recording Shadows in the Night. He also discussed his feelings about the passing of various music legends, including Muhammad Ali and Merle Haggard, and his experiences with Elvis Presley.

The U.S. Department of Justice announced on Thursday that there is reasonable cause to believe that the Cleveland Division of Police engages in a pattern and practice of using excessive force. This conclusion follows a federal investigation that examined nearly 600 cases of use of force that occurred between 2010 and 2013. The investigation was launched in March 2013, following a number of high-profile use of force incidents and requests from the community and local government.

The investigation found several unreasonable practices, including unnecessary and excessive use of deadly force, unnecessary, excessive or retaliatory use of less lethal force, excessive force against persons who are mentally ill or in crisis, and employment of poor and dangerous tactics that place officers in situations where avoidable force becomes inevitable. The division was also found to not adequately review and investigate the use of force by its officers or fully investigate misconduct allegations or identify and respond to patterns of at-risk behavior.

Attorney General Eric Holder went on to say that Cleveland and the Justice Department had agreed on a statement of principles that will lead to a consent decree. The agreement will require an independent monitor who will oversee necessary reforms. The details of the agreement will be worked out in the coming months.

Holder invoked the names of Michael Brown, Eric Garner, and 12-year-old Tamir Rice, who was killed in Cleveland in November, noting that there are ongoing federal civil rights investigations for each of those incidents. The Justice Department's investigation predates the recent shooting of Rice, but it will be considered as an agreement on changes that must be made within the Cleveland Division of Police.

The Cleveland investigation is the same kind of investigation the Justice Department launched into the Ferguson Police Department after one of its officers, Darren Wilson, shot and killed Michael Brown, an unarmed 18-year-old. Holder made his announcement in Cleveland, where he is hosting a round table discussion as part of a tour of several U.S. cities where he will meet with local leaders and discuss relations between the community and law enforcement. He is also expected to visit Memphis, Chicago, Philadelphia, and Oakland in the coming weeks.

In this summary, we discuss the tragic shooting of Javon Wilson, the 15-year-old grandson of U.S. Rep. Danny Davis, D-Ill. The shooting occurred on November 18, 2016, in the Englewood neighborhood of Chicago. The incident was a targeted attack stemming from an argument over gym shoes, according to Chicago police.

Two juvenile suspects have been taken into custody, and first-degree murder charges are expected. The shooting took place at Wilson's home while his mother was out picking up dinner for the family. Javon Wilson was a sophomore at Perspectives Charter High School, and calls to the school were not immediately returned.

U.S. Rep. Danny Davis, who was re-elected this month to his 11th term in the 7th Congressional District, expressed his grief over the loss of his grandson. He wondered how the shooter obtained the gun and said he would continue to try to combat gun violence. Davis described his grandson as a "typical 15-year-old" who loved playing basketball, music, and was improving his grades after a rough patch.

The shooting is a reminder of the dramatic rise in shootings and homicides in Chicago this year. The city has seen 673 homicides so far this year, including the fatal shootings of the cousin of Chicago Bulls basketball star Dwyane Wade, a Chicago police officer's son, and the son of a famed percussionist.

Former U.S. House Speaker Newt Gingrich took to Twitter, saying, "The murder of Congressman Danny Davis’ 15-year-old grandson in a Chicago home invasion is a reminder we need a federal strategy to save lives." However, Chicago police corrected Gingrich, stating that it was not a home invasion but a dispute among teens over gym shoes that ended in a senseless shooting.

Family friend Charles Raymond believes that prayer, community involvement, and a more personal relationship with police are necessary to eliminate senseless killings. Javon Wilson's family and friends are grieving the loss of a young life taken too soon.

In the recent primary elections held in New York City, Bill de Blasio, a Democratic mayoral candidate, emerged as the surprising front-runner, with approximately 40.2% of the votes. However, he is still short of the 40% threshold needed to avoid a runoff, which would pit him against former city Comptroller Bill Thompson. The runoff, if necessary, will take place in October, with the general election scheduled for November 5.

De Blasio's campaign focused on fighting economic inequality in the city, a message that resonated with voters. His primary opponents, including Christine Quinn, the early front-runner, and former city Comptroller Bill Thompson, could not match his momentum. Anthony Weiner, another prominent candidate, was derailed by a sexting scandal.

On the Republican side, Joseph J. Lhota, a former chairman of the Metropolitan Transportation Authority, won the nomination, defeating John A. Catsimatidis. Both candidates have pledged to maintain the city's record low crime rates, similar to the policies of outgoing Mayor Michael R. Bloomberg.

In the Democratic primary for public advocate, Letitia James and Senator Daniel L. Squadron of Brooklyn will face each other in a runoff election. Scott M. Stringer, the Manhattan borough president, repelled a last-minute comeback attempt by Eliot Spitzer, who resigned as governor over his use of prostitutes.

The election comes at a critical juncture for the city, which has been led by Bloomberg for 12 years. The city is experiencing shrinking crime rates yet widening income inequality, and the nearly completed One World Trade Center building symbolizes a new era after the terrorist attacks of 2001.

The winner of the mayor's race in November will assume the helm of the nation's largest city. Democratic leaders may pressure Thompson to drop out of the race in the name of party unity, as exit polling shows that de Blasio would handily defeat Thompson in a runoff. However, Thompson has indicated he will compete in a potential runoff.

This document provides an overview of China's economic development and military spending from the late 1970s to the present. China has transitioned from a centrally planned economy to a more market-oriented one, experiencing significant growth and becoming the world's largest economy on a purchasing power parity basis. The reforms included the liberalization of prices, fiscal decentralization, increased autonomy for state enterprises, growth of the private sector, development of stock markets and a modern banking system, and opening to foreign trade and investment.

China's economy has faced numerous challenges, such as reducing its high domestic savings rate, managing corporate debt, controlling off-balance sheet local government debt, facilitating higher-wage job opportunities, dampening speculative investment, reducing industrial overcapacity, and raising productivity growth rates. Economic development has progressed further in coastal provinces than in the interior, and China's population control policy has resulted in it becoming one of the most rapidly aging countries in the world. Deterioration in the environment, notably air pollution, soil erosion, and the steady fall of the water table, especially in the North, is another long-term problem.

China's military spending has been increasing, with a 11.2 percent increase planned for this year. This spending is driven by China's expanding global commitments and lingering territorial disputes. China's defense spending is the second highest in the world after the U.S., and it has risen in tandem with the expansion of its economy. China's neighbors and the U.S. have expressed concerns about China's territorial claims in the South China Sea and the Senkaku/Diaoyu islands.

China's economic development and military spending are driven by a combination of domestic and international factors, and the government faces numerous challenges in balancing these competing interests. The government's 13th Five-Year Plan emphasizes the need to increase innovation and boost domestic consumption to make the economy less dependent on government investment, exports, and heavy industry. However, China has made more progress on subsidizing innovation than rebalancing the economy. The government continues to favor state-owned enterprises and emphasize stability, which threatens to discourage private initiative and make the economy less efficient over time. The slight acceleration in economic growth in 2017 gives the government more latitude to pursue its economic reforms, focusing on financial sector deleveraging and its Supply-Side Structural Reform agenda.

In a recent court hearing, Halle Berry's attorney accused her ex-boyfriend, Gabriel Aubry, of attempting to make their 6-year-old daughter, Nahla, appear less African American by straightening and highlighting her naturally curly hair. The judge ruled that neither parent can alter Nahla's hair color or texture, and her hair is to grow back naturally. This is the latest point of contention in the contentious shared custody arrangement between the two.

Berry and Aubry, who dated for two years before splitting in 2010, have been embroiled in a bitter custody dispute since then. In November 2012, Aubry was arrested after getting into a fistfight with Berry's then-fiance, Olivier Martinez. Recently, Berry reportedly moved to reduce her child-support payments to Aubry from $16,000 a month to less than $4,000 to motivate him to get a job.

In 2011, during the height of their custody dispute, Berry told Ebony magazine that she wanted her daughter to choose how she's identified but considered Nahla to be black. Aubry is white. The actress was referring to the controversial legal and sociological notion of the "one-drop rule," pre-dating the civil rights movement, by which any person with even "one drop" of black blood was deemed to be black.

Berry's attorney did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The case highlights the complexities of racial identity and the challenges of raising a child in a multiracial family.

U.S. President Barack Obama visited Jamaica on April 8, 2015, marking the first visit by a U.S. president since 1982. The visit aimed to address energy security concerns and counteract growing Chinese influence in the Caribbean. Obama's agenda includes meeting with Jamaican Prime Minister Portia Simpson Miller, other Caribbean leaders, and young regional leaders in a town-hall setting.

During his visit, Obama paid tribute to the late reggae star Bob Marley at his museum, touring Marley's former home while "One Love" played through the building's sound system. The president's trip follows increased attention to the region by the U.S. president over the past year, including immigration executive orders, efforts to slow the influx of Central American minors to the U.S. border, and diplomatic outreach to Cuba.

Energy security is a significant concern for the U.S. in the Caribbean, as Venezuela's oil diplomacy has scaled back, leaving a potential void. In response, the U.S. has been working to promote energy security through cooperative solutions with Caribbean countries. Meanwhile, China has been expanding its economic alliances in the region through 'checkbook diplomacy.'

Obama's visit to Jamaica is the prelude to his attendance at the Summit of the Americas in Panama, which will gather heads of government from across the Western Hemisphere. The visit is part of Obama's efforts to capitalize on mutual needs and address regional issues, particularly in light of weakening power by Venezuela and expanding Chinese influence.

The incident at the White House press briefing has sparked a debate about workplace sexism, following a comment made by US President Donald Trump towards Irish reporter Caitriona Perry. During a call with Irish Taoiseach Leo Varadkar, Trump interrupted to compliment Perry's smile, which has since been retweeted over 8,000 times. The exchange has led to a discussion on social media, with some describing Trump as a "creeper" while others argue his comments were a compliment.

In a video posted on Twitter, Perry described the encounter as "bizarre." The exchange begins with Trump mentioning the number of Irish reporters present and then pointing to Perry, beckoning her over. Perry replies that she is from RTE news, to which Trump tells Varadkar that she has a nice smile and treats him well.

The incident has raised questions about whether a male reporter would be spoken to in the same way, with some Twitter users questioning whether a male journalist would be called upon to explain his good looks. In contrast, many have defended Trump's remarks as complimentary, with one Twitter user asking, "Can't women take compliments anymore?"

In a separate news item, CNN is facing criticism after three journalists resigned over a retracted story about a Donald Trump Russian connection. The White House quickly took advantage of the situation, with blistering presidential tweets and a media scolding at the afternoon press briefing. Conservative provocateur James O'Keefe also released a video with a CNN producer caught on camera talking about the network's Russia coverage being ratings-driven.

CNN has accepted the resignations of journalists Thomas Frank, Eric Lichtblau, and Lex Haris over last week's web story about Trump aide Anthony Scaramucci's pre-inaugural meeting with the head of a Russian investment fund. The network retracted the story on Friday and apologized to Scaramucci. Trump has been unhappy with CNN since he was a candidate and has been particularly annoyed by its reporting on connections with Russia. The misstep on a relatively minor story has left some White House staff members jubilant, believing it handed them a new talking point to use as a cudgel against mainstream media organizations they feel are largely biased against them.

In Geneva, Swiss authorities have arrested two Syrian men on suspicion of manufacturing, concealing, and transporting explosives, as well as violating laws against organizations like Al-Qaeda and the Islamic State (IS). The arrests followed the discovery of traces of explosives in their car, and the city has been on high alert due to fears of an IS cell in the area. The tip-off about the potential terror cell originated from the United States, and the arrests come after increased vigilance by Geneva police. The two Syrians, who recently arrived in Switzerland and could not speak French, were stopped due to their behavior and nationality. No evidence of toxic gas was found, and authorities have confirmed that the arrests are not directly linked to the coordinated November 13 attacks in Paris that left 130 dead. The UN has stated that there is no specific threat to the UN in Geneva or its personnel.

In a significant legal setback for Johnson & Johnson, a Philadelphia jury awarded $2.5 million in damages to an Alabama man named Austin Pledger, who developed gynecomastia (abnormal breast development in males) after taking the company's antipsychotic drug Risperdal. The lawsuit was brought by Pledger's family, who claimed that J&J failed to warn about the risk of gynecomastia. This is the first such lawsuit to go to trial, following a handful of cases that were settled earlier.

The case gained attention due to several factors. First, J&J had previously paid a $2.2 billion settlement two years ago for illegally marketing Risperdal to children and the elderly. Second, former FDA commissioner David Kessler testified as a paid expert witness for the family, stating that J&J was aware of the risks.

Pledger, who has autism, was prescribed Risperdal in 2002 at the age of 8, a time when the drug was not approved for use in children. In 2006, the FDA approved Risperdal for use in children and updated the label to include high levels of prolactin, a hormone that promotes breast growth. By this time, Pledger had already begun to develop breasts.

Janssen Pharmaceuticals, a Johnson & Johnson subsidiary, disputes the claims, stating that the FDA-approved label "properly warned" of the drug's potential side effects. They also claim that Pledger's quality of life was significantly improved while on Risperdal.

Pledger's case is the first of over 1,200 similar cases pending in the Philadelphia court to reach a jury verdict. If the verdict stands, it could potentially lead to significant payouts for other victims.

The Mayo Clinic offers appointments in Arizona, Florida, Minnesota, and various Mayo Clinic Health System locations. The clinic's general interest e-newsletter keeps readers updated on various health topics, including symptoms of Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA). DKA symptoms often develop quickly and may include excessive thirst, frequent urination, nausea and vomiting, abdominal pain, weakness or fatigue, shortness of breath, fruity-scented breath, confusion, high blood sugar level, and high ketone levels in urine. If these symptoms are experienced, it is advised to contact a doctor immediately.

In a separate news item, two Sydney parents have been charged with the manslaughter of their six-year-old diabetic son who died after attending a "self-healing" course where he was allegedly deprived of insulin and food. The boy died at the Ritz Hotel in Hurstville on April 30, 2015, after the workshop held at a nearby clinic. The man who ran the course, Hongchi Xiao, continues to elude police in Australia and Britain, where he was recently detained on suspicion of manslaughter over another death.

Hongchi Xiao, a self-described "healer" who practices a therapy called "paidalajin", was treating a 71-year-old diabetic woman, Danielle Carr-Gomm, when she died suddenly during a retreat he ran in south-west England. Police then released him on bail. Paidalajin involves fasting, stretching, and slapping the skin to the point of bruising.

The parents, granted conditional bail, were due to appear before local courts this week, facing a maximum of 25 years' jail if convicted. It is important to seek medical attention when experiencing symptoms of DKA and to be cautious when attending alternative healing courses.

The article discusses the ongoing competition among coffee brands to produce the strongest coffee, with Black Insomnia, a South African company, recently claiming the title of the world's strongest coffee. The brand boasts that its blend has "dangerously high levels of caffeine," with 702 milligrams per 12-ounce cup, compared to Death Wish Coffee's 660 milligrams. Both brands offer significantly more caffeine than the recommended daily limit of 400 milligrams, and even a "normal" cup of coffee contains about 150 milligrams.

Black Insomnia also emphasizes that its coffee is "strictly pure coffee" and is made from highly caffeinated Robusta beans, which are said to offer a nice walnut and sweet taste profile without a burnt and high acidic flavor. The brand's coffee is now available in the US through Amazon.

The article also includes a Mayo Clinic article on the dangers of consuming too much caffeine. The article explains that up to 400 milligrams of caffeine per day is considered safe for most healthy adults, but heavy caffeine use can cause unpleasant side effects such as migraines, insomnia, nervousness, irritability, restlessness, frequent urination, stomach upset, fast heartbeat, muscle tremors, and jitters. The article also advises that women who are pregnant or breastfeeding should talk to their doctors about limiting caffeine use.

The article concludes by offering tips for those who want to reduce their caffeine intake, such as keeping track of caffeine consumption, cutting back gradually, switching to decaffeinated beverages, brewing tea for less time, and choosing herbal teas. The article also notes that some over-the-counter pain relievers contain caffeine, so it's important to look for caffeine-free options.

In the article "Obama's Midterm Loss Record Could Make History," Stuart Rothenberg discusses President Barack Obama's upcoming midterm elections, which are expected to result in significant losses for the Democratic Party. The losses could potentially surpass those of any two-term president in the past 50 years, including those of Harry S. Truman, Dwight Eisenhower, George W. Bush, and Ronald Reagan.

In Truman's two midterms, he lost a total of 83 House seats, while Eisenhower lost a combined 66 House seats in his midterms. Obama had one midterm where his party lost 63 House seats, and Democrats are expected to lose another 5 to possibly 12 House seats (or more), taking the sitting president’s total midterm House loses to the 68 seat to 75 seat range.

In the Senate, Democrats lost 6 seats in 2010 and seem likely to lose from 5 to as many as 10 seats next week. That would add up to Obama midterm Senate losses of from 11 seats to as many as 16 seats. Democrats will likely not exceed the number of Senate losses they incurred during the two Truman midterms, in 1946 and 1950, when the party lost a remarkable net of 17 seats.

The article also discusses the impact of the increasingly partisan nature of elections and the makeup of the past two Senate classes on the Democrats' losses. The answer, according to the article, is that both factors are responsible for the Democrats' losses.

Finally, the article mentions that the Senate Democrats have long awaited the 2010 tea party wave to splash back on Republicans during the 2016 election cycle. The upcoming midterm elections are expected to shift the focus from red-state Democrats to blue-state Republicans, with several first-term Republicans up for reelection in states that Obama won in both 2008 and 2012. The leftward-tilting map means a GOP-controlled Senate could be short-lived if the party prevails on Tuesday. Even in the best-case scenario for the party, a Republican majority is certain to be slim.

On the 13th of February, two 17-year-old students from Plano East Senior High School, Ritu Sachdeva and Hillary Kate Kuizon, were found dead within hours of each other. Police in Murphy are investigating the deaths, which they believe to be suicides.

Ritu's body was discovered in her home by relatives, while Hillary's remains were found in a wooded area near Kimbrough Stadium. No motives have been identified, and no evidence of foul play has been detected.

Rumors of a suicide pact have circulated, and investigators are speaking with relatives to determine if there is any connection between the two deaths. Friends of the girls have described them as bubbly, energetic, and well-liked.

Plano ISD officials are assisting with the case, and flags flew at half-staff at the school on Monday. Twenty counselors were on campus for grieving students and faculty.

The causes of death will be determined by the medical examiner. No evidence of foul play has been found, and Murphy police believe there is no threat to area residents.

Grief counselors have been provided at the school, and the Plano East Fellowship of Christian Athletes will hold a prayer meeting. Classmates have taken to Twitter to express their heartbreak and remember the teens.

The investigation is ongoing, and it is not yet clear if the deaths are related. Anyone contemplating suicide or dealing with the suicide death of someone they know is encouraged to call the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline.

A 12-year-old boy named Reginald Fields, also known as "Mr. Reggie," from Maple Heights, Ohio, has experienced a significant increase in his lawn care business following an incident where a neighbor called the police on him for accidentally cutting their grass while mowing a customer's lawn. The incident, which was captured in a viral video, sparked outrage on social media, with many people expressing support for the young entrepreneur and offering him more business.

Lucille Holt, the customer whose lawn Reginald was mowing, posted a video on Facebook detailing the incident. In the video, she explained that the neighbor had a history of calling the police for seemingly innocuous incidents, such as her children playing loudly in the snow. The video has garnered over 184,000 views and 700 shares on Facebook as of Friday afternoon.

Holt has received hundreds of messages and calls from people wanting to use Reginald's lawn care business, "Mr. Reggie's Lawn Cutting Service." She said that his business has picked up so much that someone even offered to create an online scheduling system to prevent overbooking.

Reginald started the business last year to help his mother, who cares for his grandfather, who uses a wheelchair. He plans to use the money he earns this summer to buy new equipment and expand his business. The incident has left Reginald feeling discouraged, but the support he has received since the video went viral has helped to lift his spirits.

The Maple Heights Police Department confirmed that they were called to the scene but took no action against Reginald. The neighbor who called the police has not come forward to speak about the incident. The community's support for Reginald and his business has been overwhelming, with people from all over the city reaching out to him for lawn care services.

The discovery of a rock shelter in the Flinders Ranges, Australia, has unveiled evidence of human settlement dating back 49,000 years. The site, known as Warratyi, is considered one of the most important prehistoric sites in Australia, pushing back the earliest known dates for the development of key technologies such as bone and stone axes, ochre use, and the interaction with megafauna. The site was found by archaeologist Giles Hamm and Aboriginal elder Clifford Coulthard during a survey of gorges in the northern Flinders Ranges. Excavations revealed around 4,300 artefacts and 200 bone fragments from 16 mammals and one reptile. The site also provides the first reliably dated evidence of human interaction with megafauna, including the extinct giant wombat-like Diprotodon optatum and an ancient giant bird. The discovery challenges the assumption that Indigenous Australians were not as innovative as similar populations elsewhere in the world and suggests that humans arrived in the arid interior of Australia some 10,000 years earlier than previously thought. The study has been published in Nature.

The excavation methods used at Warratyi rock shelter included hand excavation within two 2 × 1 m trenches, using a 1-m grid system, and dry-sieving through (8, 5 and 2 mm) sieves. Optical dating of quartz grains was also used to determine the age of the site, which was found to be 49,000 years old. The site was dated using single-grain optically stimulated luminescence (OSL) dating of quartz and single-grain TT-OSL dating of quartz for cross-checking the reliability of the OSL-dating approach. The site also underwent radiocarbon dating of hearth charcoal and eggshell samples, and Bayesian age modeling was used to integrate all stratigraphically reliable chronological information within a unified statistical framework. Use-wear and residue analyses were also conducted on some artefacts.

The discovery of Warratyi rock shelter provides valuable insights into the early history of human settlement in Australia and challenges previous assumptions about the ingenuity of Indigenous Australians. The site's age and geographic location are significant, as it pushes back the earliest known dates for the development of key technologies and provides the first reliably dated evidence of human interaction with megafauna. The study has been published in Nature.

In Moses Lake, Washington, an 89-year-old store owner named Miyo Koba successfully defended her store from a sword-wielding robber using a golf club. The incident occurred on Sunday morning at Frank's Superette, a store Koba has owned for 60 years.

The robber, described as tall and slender, entered the store wearing a ski mask and dark sunglasses. Koba found him standing behind the cash register and refused to open it for him. The robber became agitated, pulled out a 3-foot-long sword, and began pounding on the register to open it.

Koba, who weighs around 125 pounds, grabbed a golf club and attempted to hit the robber. Although she couldn't reach his head, she managed to hit his legs, causing him to drop the cash register and flee on a BMX bike. Koba's son reported that she was not injured during the incident, and she later recovered the cash register with the money still inside.

Police are still searching for the suspect and are asking anyone with information to contact Moses Lake Police. The robber apparently removed his clothing after leaving the store, and police later recovered his clothes. Koba expressed that the robber never made her feel threatened, and she even felt a bit more brave during the ordeal.

In a forum at St. Ambrose University in Davenport, Iowa, Republican presidential candidate Jeb Bush declined to rule out the resumption of torture by the U.S. government under certain circumstances. Bush stated that he believes torture is generally inappropriate, but suggested there may be instances where brutal interrogations are necessary to keep the country safe. He also defended his brother, former President George W. Bush, for largely ending the CIA's use of enhanced interrogation techniques, which included waterboarding, slapping, nudity, sleep deprivation, humiliation, and other methods. The CIA's use of these techniques has been criticized for being more brutal than previously disclosed, with the CIA lying about them, and failing to produce unique, life-saving intelligence. Jeb Bush believes that the techniques were effective in producing intelligence, but acknowledges that "now we're in a different environment."

In addition to discussing torture, Bush also addressed the Iraq War, which his brother initiated. Bush has been walking a careful path, seeking to disassociate himself from some of the unpopular aspects of his brother's legacy while praising him. Bush blames the rise of the Islamic State group on what he said was Obama's failure to negotiate an agreement to leave U.S. troops there in 2011. Asked if it was true that there would be no IS without a U.S. invasion of Iraq, Bush said there was no way to know. He repeated his call for a more aggressive posture toward the Islamic State group but, like the Obama administration, he opposes sending in regular U.S. ground forces. He does favor putting special operations troops on the battlefield.

Bush spoke at a foreign policy forum sponsored by Americans for Peace, Prosperity and Security, a group chaired by Mike Rogers, a former Republican congressman from Michigan who chaired the House Intelligence Committee. The Associated Press also contributed to this report.

Ryan Gosling, known for his kindness and heroism, saved a dog from a busy California highway during a weekend getaway with his girlfriend, Eva Mendes. The incident occurred while they were on their way to pick up take-out. Gosling jumped out of the car to save the dog, handing it back to its owner. The couple, along with their 1-year-old daughter, Esmeralda, enjoyed a four-day stay at Frank Sinatra's former ultra-luxurious estate in Palm Springs, which they rented for $10,400.

In a separate incident, Hilary Duff adopted a French bulldog named Peaches, the sister of her late dog Beau. Gosling's act of kindness echoes his previous deeds, such as breaking up a fight in New York City and saving a reporter from an oncoming taxi. His actions continue to inspire and earn him the title of a human angel.

Jamaica's lawmakers are set to debate a constitutional amendment that would replace Queen Elizabeth II as the head of state and make the island a republic. This move is a significant action item on the new government's 2016-2017 legislative agenda. The proposal would establish a Non-Executive President, replacing the current Governor-General, Sir Patrick Allen.

The Jamaican Labour Party, led by Andrew Holness, won a narrow victory in the February general elections, with promises of tax cuts and a higher minimum wage. The legislative agenda also includes proposals for fixed election dates and term limits for the Prime Minister, as well as the full legalization of marijuana for "specified purposes."

Other proposed measures include setting up a single anti-corruption body, reforming the tax and pension system, and implementing a new Special Economic Zones regime. The government also plans to pursue an active legislative agenda, with key bills including the Arbitration Bill, a Constitution (Amendment) Bill to replace the Queen, a bill to address the judicial review of the Director of Public Prosecutions, and the Criminal Justice (Plea Negotiations and Agreements) (Amendment) Bill.

The government aims to sever colonial ties with Britain by replacing the Queen with a non-executive president, who would perform a representative and civic role but have no policy-making powers. This move aligns with former Prime Minister Portia Simpson Miller's proposal in her 2011 inauguration speech.

Additional legislation includes the Impeachment Bill, which will allow for criminal proceedings against corrupt public officials and parliamentarians, and the Integrity Commission Bill, which will establish a Single Anti-Corruption Body. Other bills in progress include amendments to the INDECOM Act, the Constitution to address the judicial review of the Director of Public Prosecutions, and the Criminal Justice Amendment Bill to provide for reduced sentences on guilty pleas.

The 2016/2017 session of Parliament officially opened on April 14, with the traditional pomp and pageantry. The Governor-General, Sir Patrick Allen, announced the plan to move to republican status, while outlining other measures on the legislative agenda. Lawmakers are expected to carry through other pieces of legislation that are already in progress, such as the Integrity Commission Bill, the Arbitration Bill, and the Judicature (Resident Magistrate) (Amendment) Bill.

A middle school teacher, Julie Marburger, from Cedar Creek, Texas, has gained international attention after venting her frustration with the perceived bad behavior of students and parents on Facebook. Marburger's post, which has been shared over 400,000 times, details incidents of disrespect from parents and students, including drawings in books, theft of personal items, and a particularly embarrassing incident involving a disrespectful phone call from a parent in front of her class. Marburger, 45, expressed her intention to leave teaching at the end of the year due to these issues, stating that administration often prioritizes parent satisfaction over the teacher's ability to do their job effectively.

Marburger's post has sparked a broader conversation about the challenges faced by teachers, particularly those related to support and pay. Teachers in several states, such as Oklahoma and West Virginia, have recently taken action, with classes canceled in Oklahoma for the seventh day and teachers in West Virginia ending a nine-day strike after a 5% pay hike was agreed upon.

Ericka Souter, the editor of mom.me, a parenting website, emphasized the importance of parents viewing their relationship with their child's teacher as a partnership. Souter suggested three tips for parents to build stronger relationships with teachers: being involved, being proactive, and ensuring their child understands the consequences of bad behavior.

Marburger's post has surprised her with the positive reaction it has received, despite initial concerns about offending people. She is currently weighing her options regarding her future in teaching. The attention garnered by Marburger's post highlights the ongoing issues faced by teachers and the need for support and collaboration between parents and educators to provide the best educational experience for children.

J.J. Barea, the only active NBA player of Puerto Rican descent, has been actively involved in hurricane relief efforts for his native country following the devastation caused by Hurricane Maria. Barea's parents were finally contacted on Sunday, and they are safe, although the situation in Puerto Rico remains dire.

To aid in the recovery, Dallas Mavericks owner Mark Cuban loaned the team's plane to Barea, who left on Monday to transport food, water, and supplies. Barea plans to return on Tuesday, missing the first day of Mavs training camp. Cuban expressed pride in Barea's quick and dedicated response to the crisis.

Coach Rick Carlisle stated that the team supports Barea's efforts and that he will be taking his mother and grandmother back with him. Barea's father is expected to stay in Puerto Rico to assist with the recovery efforts.

Barea and his wife, Puerto Rican actress and model Viviana Ortiz, organized an online fundraiser after the hurricane, which has already generated over $140,000. The fundraiser aims to provide aid to those affected by the storm, which caused major flooding, knocked out electricity and phone service, and left much of the island without power for months.

In Baltimore, a mother gained widespread praise after a video emerged of her confronting and disciplining her son who was participating in riots and throwing rocks at police. The incident was captured by a WMAR news photographer and later went viral. The mother, identified as Toya Graham, expressed her concern for her son's safety and the potential consequences of his actions, stating, "That's my only son, and at the end of the day, I don't want him to be a Freddie Gray." Baltimore Police Commissioner Anthony Batts commended the mother's actions, stating that he wished more parents had taken similar steps to control their children during the unrest. The video sparked a wave of positive sentiment on social media, with users praising the mother as "Mom of the Year." The riots in Baltimore followed the death of resident Freddie Gray, who died of a severe spinal injury while in police custody. The city has been grappling with violence and unrest in the aftermath of Gray's death, with many residents taking to the streets to clean up the damage caused by the riots.

In a recent court hearing, Molly Wei, a former Rutgers University student, admitted her role in a high-profile invasion of privacy case linked to a student suicide. Wei was charged with secretly taping two male students engaging in sex and agreed to cooperate with authorities in the ongoing case. In exchange, she was permitted to enroll in a pretrial intervention program, which could result in the charges against her being dropped.

Wei, who was charged with two counts of invasion of privacy, declined to comment after the hearing but her lawyer stated that she was cooperating with authorities and should not be considered the "poster child" for this case. Her lawyers have consistently maintained that Wei played a minor role in the controversial case.

Wei and Dharun Ravi, another student, were charged in September with the secret taping of Ravi's roommate, Tyler Clementi, while Clementi engaged in a sexual encounter with another male in their dorm room. Clementi, 18, committed suicide a few days later by jumping off the George Washington Bridge.

Ravi was charged in a 15-count indictment handed up in April with invasion of privacy and bias intimidation. Authorities alleged that he targeted Clementi and the other male because they were homosexuals. Ravi, who could be sentenced to up to 10 years in prison if convicted, is to be arraigned on May 23. He has remained free on $25,000 bail.

Clementi's parents, who attended Friday's hearing, agreed with the more lenient sentence for Wei. In a statement released after the hearing, they said that "based on the information supplied to us, we understand that Ms. Wei's actions, although unlawful, were substantially different in their nature and their extent than the actions of Tyler's former roommate."

Wei will be enrolled in the PTI program for three years and must complete 300 hours of community service and undergo counseling on issues like cyber-bullying and alternate lifestyles. She has also agreed to cooperate in the investigation and to testify for the prosecution in the case against Ravi.

The incident has become a focal point for gay rights advocates who view it as an example of the type of bias members of the gay community face. The case has also been cited by groups concerned about the Internet becoming a vehicle for violating basic privacy rights. Supporters of Ravi have termed his actions a college prank run amok and have argued that authorities have turned the incident into a more serious criminal offense.

The SS United States, a historic ocean liner launched in 1952, is currently moored in Philadelphia. Known as the world's fastest ocean liner, it was built as a secret Cold War project to create the world's fastest ship. The ship is 990 feet long, longer than the Titanic, and was designed to pass through the Panama Canal with two feet of clearance on either side.

Recently, the SS United States Conservancy announced that it had raised over $100,000 from supporters worldwide, temporarily sparing the ship from being scrapped. The conservancy aims to repurpose the ship as a museum and mixed-use destination. However, the nonprofit had previously sent a virtual SOS last month due to unsustainable expenses, even retaining a broker to explore selling the ship to a metals recycler. The conservancy needs more than $60,000 per month to keep the rehabilitation project afloat.

The SS United States is a symbol of American pride and accomplishment, with notable figures such as Jim Nantz, Herb Douglas, William Jefferson Clinton, Peter Knego, and Walter Cronkite expressing their support for its preservation. The ship represents the golden era of ocean liners and is considered an important part of US history and technology.

Supporters of the SS United States Conservancy are urging donations to save the ship, emphasizing its significance as a symbol of American character and pride. The ship's future is uncertain, but efforts are being made to preserve this engineering marvel and piece of American history.

The situation in Libya remains volatile as fighting continues between rebels and forces loyal to Muammar Gadhafi. The United Nations, regional organizations, and world powers are urging a smooth transition to democracy, emphasizing inclusiveness, reconciliation, and national unity. The fighting has caused widespread shortages of fuel, food, and medical supplies, and there are reports of revenge killings by both rebels and loyalists. The International Criminal Court has issued an arrest warrant for Gadhafi, and the opposition National Transitional Council is moving its political base to Tripoli. The rebels are pushing to consolidate their power, with clashes occurring in Sirte and Tripoli. NATO forces are bombing Gadhafi's regime in Tripoli and Sirte, and the rebels are making gains. The rebels are also struggling to secure areas still held by Gadhafi loyalists, such as an airport in Tripoli. Amnesty International has gathered accounts of abuse in Zawiya by both pro-Gadhafi soldiers and rebel forces. The rebels have pleaded with the United States and other countries to unfreeze more money to establish peace and stability in Libya.

In the Vermont gubernatorial election, incumbent Governor Peter Shumlin, a Democrat, is leading Republican challenger Scott Milne, but neither candidate has secured the required 50% plus one vote to win the election outright. As a result, the election will be decided by the state Legislature in January, with Shumlin's fellow Democrats controlling both houses. Shumlin had been expected to easily win re-election for his third term, but Milne's campaign appears to have tapped into voter discontent with the governor. The race remained close throughout the night, with Shumlin receiving approximately 46.7% of the vote and Milne receiving just over 45%. This is the 24th time in Vermont's history that the gubernatorial race has gone to the Legislature, with the Legislature typically awarding the election to the candidate who received the most votes. Shumlin was chosen by the Legislature for his first term in 2010, when he won 49.5% of the vote. The most recent time the race involving an incumbent governor was decided by the Legislature was in 1986. The close election results could potentially impact Shumlin's signature agenda item, a universal health care system covering all Vermonters.

Shinichi Mochizuki, a mathematician from Kyoto University, Japan, claims to have proven the ABC conjecture, one of the longest-standing mysteries in mathematics. However, his 500-page paper, published in 2012, has been difficult for fellow mathematicians to understand due to the dense framework of new maths, Inter-universal Teichmüller Theory, that he developed. Mochizuki has been criticized for not making his work more accessible, but he argues that most mathematicians are not qualified to issue a definitive statement on the proof without a deep understanding of his theory. The ABC conjecture is a complex problem in number theory that questions the true nature of numbers, and solving it would be highly significant for mathematics. Mochizuki's work remains in limbo, with no definitive answer on its correctness, and the scientific community is awaiting further verification.

A Florida police officer, Officer Laurie Graber, demonstrated extraordinary kindness by replacing an elderly woman's stolen engagement ring, worth approximately $4,500 today, after it was taken from her finger at a hospital. The woman, Betty Wagner, who has Alzheimer's, had worn the ring for 67 years. Upon learning the story of the couple's long-lasting relationship, Officer Graber purchased a replacement ring from J.C. Penney and delivered it to the hospital. The original ring remains missing, but the new ring has brought some comfort to Mr. Wagner, who is still at his wife's bedside. The Plantation Police are investigating the theft and are reviewing hospital surveillance footage for any leads. The act of kindness by Officer Graber has received widespread attention in the media.

On July 21, 2010, authorities confirmed that a body found in a rural field in Moreno Valley, California was identified as that of 17-year-old Norma Lopez, who had been missing since July 15 after failing to return from a summer school class. The discovery of the body came just hours after her family held a press conference pleading for her return. The autopsy confirmed her identity, but the cause of death was not released.

Residents of Moreno Valley, where Lopez attended Valley View High School, gathered for a vigil at the school's athletic field, remembering Lopez as a talented dancer who loved merengue and salsa. Police and the FBI are investigating the case, but have not identified a suspect. Authorities are offering a $35,000 reward for information leading to the arrest and conviction of whoever abducted Lopez.

Lopez was last seen heading to meet a friend after leaving her summer school class. When she did not show up, her younger sister and a friend went to look for her and found some of her personal items in a field near the school. The field, a popular shortcut among students, is off a street that dead-ends at the base of boulder-studded hills cut with trails.

The body was found in a remote section of town surrounded by wheat fields, just off the 60 Freeway. Exposed to the elements during the recent heat wave, the remains were so decomposed that authorities could not immediately determine the sex of the deceased, let alone whether it was Norma's body.

The teen's disappearance drew wide attention across Southern California, where the high-profile abduction-murders of two other teenage girls in San Diego County led to a sex offender who ultimately admitted the killings and is now imprisoned. Lopez was described as a very good student and a quiet girl who never got into trouble.

Authorities are urging anyone with information about the case to call (877) 242-4345, or send an e-mail to findnorma@riversidesheriff.org.

Title: Internet Archive Aims to Fix Broken Links on the Web and David Harbour's Support for Mental Health Awareness

The Internet Archive is implementing a new initiative to archive web pages as they are created and preserve the pages they reference. This is aimed at preserving the original intent of a page's authors, especially when the referenced pages are altered or removed from the web. The archived pages are intended to replace broken links or serve as companion links, allowing people to view the original versions.

In a related development, actor David Harbour, known for his role in Stranger Things, has shown his support for mental health awareness. In an interview with TooFab, he acknowledged the commonality of mental health issues in today's society. He suggested that his podcast, "WTF," could provide comfort and understanding for those who may be struggling with mental health issues or supporting loved ones who are. He emphasized that the podcast could offer solace to those who still feel shame about a diagnosis or worry about the future of a bipolar child.

Harbour's comments come at a time when mental health awareness is increasingly being discussed in the media and society at large. His support for mental health initiatives underscores the importance of destigmatizing mental health issues and providing resources for those who need them.

In conclusion, the Internet Archive's initiative to fix broken links on the web and David Harbour's support for mental health awareness are significant steps towards preserving the web's history and addressing mental health issues, respectively. Both initiatives highlight the importance of understanding, empathy, and the preservation of information in today's digital age.

A federal judge in Manhattan has ordered the Metropolitan Transportation Authority (MTA) to display an advertisement from the pro-Israel group, American Freedom Defense Initiative (AFDI), on buses, after the agency declined to run it last year. The advertisement, which was initially intended to parody a "My Jihad" campaign by the Council on American-Islamic Relations (CAIR), features a man wearing a Palestinian keffiyeh and quotes "Hamas MTV" as saying "Killing Jews is worship that draws us close to Allah." The judge ruled that the ad qualified as protected speech and granted a preliminary injunction ordering the MTA to run the ad. The MTA had argued that the ad could be seen as a call to violence against Jews, but the judge found no evidence that seeing the ad on the back of a bus would prompt a violent reaction. The MTA has expressed disappointment with the ruling and is reviewing its options. The AFDI's leader, Pamela Geller, called the ruling a "triumph for liberty and truth." The MTA had previously declined to run the "My Jihad" ads, which were part of the reason they didn't want to run the AFDI's ads. The MTA had asked for an injunction against the AFDI, but the judge determined that the MTA could not prove the ads would lead to violence that would outweigh the AFDI's freedom of speech. The judge also noted that the ads had essentially already run without incident in Chicago and San Francisco. The MTA has not yet decided what to do in response to the ruling. The AFDI's ads have been controversial in the past, with the Southern Poverty Law Center labeling the group a hate group and the Anti-Defamation League denouncing the group's lawyer for his "record of anti-Muslim, anti-immigrant and anti-black bigotry." The MTA's political leaders have also expressed opposition to the ads, with Mayor Bill de Blasio's spokeswoman calling the ads "outrageous, inflammatory and wrong."

The police report regarding Lindsay Lohan's alleged theft of a $2,500 necklace from an L.A. jewelry store presents two inconsistencies in the jeweler's account, which could potentially aid Lohan in her defense. Initially, the jeweler claimed Lohan had visited the store three times before the theft, focusing on the necklace in question. However, the following day, the jeweler recanted and stated it was a ring that Lohan had been interested in on previous visits.

Another inconsistency concerns the surveillance footage. Initially, the owner claimed Lohan removed the necklace and placed it in her bag, but the next day, the owner changed her story, stating that Lohan left the store with the necklace around her neck. The owner attributed the discrepancy to reviewing the video on a different monitor the second time.

Lohan is eager to reach a plea bargain for her felony grand theft case due to fears of incarceration. A court hearing has been set for February 23 to discuss the plea bargain. Lohan is willing to plead guilty, provided she avoids jail or prison time. However, the prosecutor insists on jail time, creating an impasse.

In cases with a single charge, the defendant can propose a deal directly to the judge, potentially bypassing the District Attorney. If Lohan offers to plead guilty to felony grand theft, with the judge's assurance of no imprisonment, the case could be resolved. Additionally, it's common for the judge to reduce the offense to a misdemeanor if Lohan maintains good behavior for 12 months.
