In an open letter to Dylan Farrow, Mira Sorvino, an actress who won an Oscar for her role in Woody Allen's 1995 film Mighty Aphrodite, has publicly apologized for working with Allen and for overlooking Farrow's accusations of sexual abuse against him. Sorvino, who had previously defended Allen, admitted that she had been naive and had accepted the media's portrayal of Farrow's allegations as a result of a custody battle between Allen and Farrow's mother, Mia Farrow.

Sorvino wrote that she had spoken with Farrow's brother, Ronan Farrow, about her experience being sexually harassed by Harvey Weinstein, which prompted her to re-examine her decision to work with Allen. In her letter, Sorvino expressed regret for not investigating Farrow's allegations further and for turning a blind eye to her story.

Sorvino also revealed that she had no personal experience of inappropriate behavior by Allen towards young girls, but acknowledged that this did not excuse her previous lack of support for Farrow. She wrote that it was difficult to sever ties with her heroes and benefactors, but that she now believes Farrow's story and will never work with Allen again.

Sorvino's letter comes after Ellen Page and Greta Gerwig also publicly distanced themselves from Allen and expressed regret for working with him. The allegations against Allen date back to 1992, when Dylan was 7 years old and reportedly told her mother, Mia Farrow, that Allen had inappropriately touched her. Although Allen has denied the allegations and was not criminally charged, a judge granted Mia Farrow full custody after finding Dylan's testimony credible in 1993. Dylan has maintained her allegations in recent essays.

The study published in the New England Journal of Medicine reveals a temporary decline in gunshot-related deaths and injuries during the National Rifle Association (NRA) annual conventions. The researchers, Dr. Anupam Jena of Harvard Medical School and Andrew Olenski of Columbia University, found a 63% decrease in gun-related injuries in the states where the conventions were held, and a 20% decrease nationally. The drop in injuries was most prominent among men, particularly in states with high rates of gun ownership and in the South and West. The study suggests that the decrease in injuries is due to lower rates of firearm use during the convention period, as many gun owners and venues where firearms are used may be attending the event. The NRA did not respond to a request for comment. The study comes amidst ongoing debates about gun control in the United States, where an estimated 265-300 million guns are owned by Americans, with 30% owning at least one gun. In 2014, 461 people died from accidental firearm discharge, and nearly 2,000 children were injured. The study's findings have been met with mixed reactions, with some accepting the analysis and its conclusions, while others, including the NRA, have called it "absurd."

On May 2, 2013, a shooting incident occurred at Houston's George Bush Intercontinental Airport in Terminal B. A man identified as Carnell Marcus Moore entered the airport and fired a gun into the ceiling near a ticketing counter. A Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) agent confronted Moore, who refused to drop the gun. In the ensuing confrontation, Moore was shot by the agent and killed, while it is unclear who fired the fatal shot. The incident caused panic among passengers and employees, with some people running and hiding. No other individuals were injured in the shooting.

Moore had posted on social media earlier in the day that he intended to commit a mass shooting. A handwritten note found on his body indicated that he had changed his mind and wanted to kill himself. An autopsy was scheduled for the following day. Moore's neighbors described him as a reserved individual of few words.

The terminal was closed immediately after the shooting, but parts of it were later reopened to passengers. Some passengers who were scheduled to depart from Terminal B were rerouted to other terminals. The rest of the airport remained open. The incident disrupted flights, with Terminal B being shut down for hours, and incoming passengers being rerouted to enter through terminals C and E.

The shooting scene was chaotic, with passengers and employees reporting shouts to "run!" and hiding behind walls as gunfire rang out. Employees at a nearby McDonald's heard the shots and were told to get down. The incident also prompted interviews with several individuals by Houston police and the FBI. There was no visible damage to the facility.

Starbucks has announced a significant change to its dress code, allowing employees more freedom in their appearance. The new policy permits baristas to wear shirts in colors outside of solid black or white, including gray, navy, dark denim, and brown. Dark wash jeans are also allowed, and suitable hats such as beanies and fedoras are now permitted.

Perhaps the most notable change is that Starbucks workers are now allowed to dye their hair any color, as long as the coloring is permanent or semi-permanent. This change comes after years of complaints from employees about the coffee giant's hair policy.

The new dress code is not a free-for-all, with permitted clothing colors still being subdued, and the chain's "no list" remaining extensive. Banned items include brightly colored shirts, hoodies, socks with distracting graphics, and UGG boots.

The shift in the dress code is intended to be more reflective of what Starbucks baristas wear outside of work and to boost employee morale. The changes are being implemented gradually, with the Broadway coffeehouse and select Reserve stores being the forerunners for all company stores in the U.S. and Canada.

The new dress code is part of a series of changes made by Starbucks to benefit employees, including its college achievement plan and a wage increase announcement set to go into effect in October. The company had previously barred its employees from dyeing their hair unnatural colors, such as pink and purple.

The new dress code has been welcomed by customers and employees alike, with many taking to social media to celebrate the change. The policy states that hair should look natural, with no bright or unnatural colors, but allows for a wider range of options than before.

The change in dress code is part of a growing trend of individual expression in the workplace, and it invokes a more hipster, average Joe coffee shop feel. The new wardrobe is available here.

Two men, Michael Mancil and James Dryden Jr., were arrested in Coffee County, Georgia, last week for planning a domestic terrorism attack on the High Frequency Active Auroral Research Program (HAARP) owned by the University of Alaska Fairbanks. The men were found with an arsenal of weapons, including AR-15 rifles, Glock handguns, a Remington rifle, and thousands of rounds of ammunition, which investigators described as "something out of a movie." The men confessed that they were planning to blow up the facility, believing it to be used for mind control and trapping souls.

The HAARP facility, originally a U.S. Air Force facility, studies the properties and behavior of the Earth's ionosphere, a part of the atmosphere that can affect communication and navigation systems. The facility has been the subject of conspiracy theories for many years, and in August, it hosted an open house to dispel such theories.

The men were initially investigated for possible drug sales, and a local gun shop also alerted investigators to Mancil's attempts to buy a large amount of weapons. Officials at HAARP said they have had threats before but nothing of this magnitude. They expressed gratitude to the law enforcement agencies in Georgia for their work in making the arrests.

Mancil and Dryden are charged with selling Methamphetamine, possession of marijuana, possession of a weapon during the commission of a crime, and use of a telecommunication device in committing or facilitating a felony. More charges are pending.

In December 2018, Steve Aisthorpe, a Scottish mountaineer, experienced a sense of closure after the remains of his two friends who went missing in the Himalayas over 30 years ago were found. Aisthorpe, a mission development worker for the Church of Scotland, was part of an expedition to Pumori on the Nepal-Tibet border with Kristinn Rúnarsson and Þorsteinn Guðjónsson in 1988. The group had established a base camp, but during the expedition, Aisthorpe fell ill and returned to a village to consult a doctor. He sent a message to his friends suggesting they make a summit attempt without him, and they were never seen again.

Their remains were discovered last month by an American mountaineer at the snout of the glacier below the climb route, suggesting they fell into the crevasse at its base. The bodies were brought back to Kathmandu, the capital of Nepal, by a group of local climbers, and a cremation service was attended by relatives of the men who took their ashes home to Iceland. Aisthorpe said the positioning of the ropes implied that his friends had either reached or almost reached the ridge at the top of the face when disaster struck. He believes the remains were slowly carried down the mountain by a retreating glacier over the last 30 years.

Aisthorpe became friends with Guðjónsson in 1987 after they were introduced by a mutual friend who was also a mountaineering enthusiast. Pumori, which is nearly 23,500ft high, is one of Mount Everest’s more challenging neighbors. The four-man expedition, which included Jon Geirsson, established a base camp, 17,388ft below a glacial lake west of Kala Patthar. Over a 12-day period, the group moved on to set up a high camp on the upper Changri Shar glacier, and it was during this time that Geirsson fell ill and decided to return home.

Aisthorpe had also begun to suffer from a gastric flu and on October 16, 1988, he descended to the village of Pheriche to consult the doctor there. He was told that it would take a week for him to recover, so he sent a message back to the high camp suggesting that Guðjónsson and Rúnarsson “should feel free” to make a summit attempt without him. They set off and were never seen again.

Recalling the tragic episode, Aisthorpe said, “I’ve never felt as alone as the day I arrived back at our high camp. As I worked my way upwards, I desperately hoped that Kristinn and Torsteinn had descended safely and were now lying in their sleeping bags in the tiny red tent camp. As it came into view, I called out at the top of my voice – my calls echoed from the rocks and ice before fading. But the silence was palpable.”

Aisthorpe said he summoned help, and a helicopter search was finally launched five days after the men were last seen. He left a couple of weeks later after no signs of his friends were found. He hadn’t heard anything about what happened to his two friends until three weeks ago when an Icelandic filmmaker, who was already in touch with Aisthorpe about making a documentary about his experiences, called him. “It was him who contacted me while I was in holiday in Morocco, about three weeks go, and said have you heard the news,” Aisthorpe said. “What ran through my mind first of all was: ‘Is it really their bodies?’”

The remains were transported to Kathmandu, and the authorities contacted Aisthorpe asking if he had any photographs of Rúnarsson’s and Guðjónsson shortly before they died. Aisthorpe sent some through, and the authorities were able to identify some articles of clothing and equipment. “The two things that’s happened over the last three weeks is closure and the other thing is that it’s brought us all together again,” he said. Aisthorpe is planning to go to Reykjavík in Iceland soon to meet their families and pay his respects.

Aisthorpe said his faith was “vital” in helping him make sense of the tragedy. “This week, I dug out my diary from that period and it was interesting to see how vital my faith was at that time. I recorded in my diary the sense of loving presence and how prayer and what I was reading in the scriptures on particular days really seemed to speak to the situation,” he said.

Alec Baldwin, the renowned actor known for his impersonation of Donald Trump on Saturday Night Live (SNL), will continue his portrayal of the President this fall despite a busy schedule. The announcement was made during a promotional event for Baldwin's new movie, "Blind."

Baldwin's Trump impression has become one of his most memorable sketches on SNL, and he has hosted the show a record 17 times. However, due to his busy schedule, fans can expect fewer Trump impersonations, with Baldwin referring to them as "a couple celery sticks" rather than a "whole meal" of blonde wigs and orange bronzer.

In the past, Baldwin has been non-committal about continuing his Trump impersonation on SNL, expressing concerns about the audience's ability to handle more of it. However, he has now confirmed that it will return this fall.

The announcement was made at an event where Baldwin was honored for his three-decade career at Harlem's Apollo Theater. The event was attended by co-stars, family, and notable figures such as former President Bill Clinton and Robert De Niro, who both took jabs at Trump during the event. Clinton praised Baldwin's genuine interest in helping others and his early political aspirations, while De Niro praised Baldwin's Trump impression and encouraged him to continue mocking Trump.

During the event, Baldwin's daughter, Ireland, also paid tribute to her father, recalling a controversial voicemail he left her in 2007 and expressing her love and pride for him. The event concluded with Baldwin making harsh zingers to his colleagues and family rather than thanking them. One Night Only: Alec Baldwin airs on July 9 at 9 p.m. on Spike TV.

The family of Walter L. Scott, an African-American man who was fatally shot by a white police officer in North Charleston, South Carolina, has reached a $6.5 million settlement with the city. The settlement was approved by the North Charleston City Council and precludes the Scott family from bringing civil claims over his death. The shooting, which was captured on video, sparked a national conversation about policing methods and the treatment of African-Americans by some officers. Michael T. Slager, the police officer involved, was fired and indicted on a murder charge, and remains in jail. The settlement is the largest payout in recent high-profile killings of black men by police officers.

The settlement was reached after several months of negotiations between the city and Scott's family. City officials said they wanted to avoid a lawsuit and the potential for a large verdict due to the video evidence and the fact that Slager is charged with murder. The family of Walter Scott will receive the settlement, with a portion of the funds being donated to aid flood victims.

The shooting of Walter Scott was one of several high-profile cases of unarmed black men being killed by police officers in late 2014 and early 2015, and sparked protests in dozens of cities. The settlement in the Scott case follows similar settlements in the cases of Eric Garner and Freddie Gray.

The officer involved, Michael Slager, remains imprisoned while he awaits trial on murder charges. If convicted, he faces 30 years to life in prison with no possibility of parole. Slager's attorney has refused to comment on the settlement.

So far this year, police officers have shot and killed more than 750 people, according to a Washington Post database tracking police shootings. There are just five cases this year that have resulted in charges for the officers involved, and in all but one of those cases video evidence was crucial to prosecutors' decision to bring charges.

Anthony Scott, Walter Scott's brother, said the settlement was a "bittersweet victory" and that the family will focus on the criminal trial. "As long as we win the war, and get a conviction for murder, we will be pleased and feel like we got justice," he said.

A Pittsburgh man, Robert Trostle, and his wife, Krystsina, have filed a lawsuit against Kennywood Entertainment Inc. after Robert allegedly contracted a harmful parasite known as microsporidia from the water used in the Raging Rapids ride at Kennywood Park. The incident occurred on July 2, 2021, when Robert was splashed in the left eye with dirty water during the ride.

According to the lawsuit, the water surrounding the Raging Rapids was "dirty, stagnant, and sludge-like," and the waterfall was not operating. The parasite embedded in Robert's eye caused his left eye to become inflamed, itchy, red, photosensitive, and severely painful. He was initially diagnosed with acute conjunctivitis on July 5 and given antibiotics, but his condition worsened, and he was later diagnosed with microsporidia keratitis on July 14.

Robert underwent a painful surgery to remove the parasite from his eye, but the entirety of the parasite could not be removed. He still suffers from inflammation, blurry vision, redness, and pain in his left eye. The Trostles claim that Kennywood did not have adequate policies and procedures to inspect the water used on the Raging Rapids to eliminate and reduce the dangers posed by microsporidia.

The suit was filed in Allegheny County Common Pleas Court, alleging negligence against Kennywood Entertainment and claiming damages in excess of $35,000. The Raging Rapids simulates a whitewater rafting excursion and opened in 1985, according to Kennywood's website.

The Allegheny County Health Department took samples from the ride's water after the incident, but the results have not been disclosed. The health department is still investigating the matter, and no further information is available. Kennywood spokesman Nick Paradise said he could not comment on pending litigation, but safety is a top priority at Kennywood.

This is not the first time a water park has been sued for a similar incident. In June 2016, the family of a teen who contracted a brain-eating amoeba after rafting at a North Carolina water park sued the facility. The park was found to have inadequate filtration and disinfection systems, and the water quality caused raft guides to routinely contract staph infections, ringworm, and other skin illnesses. The park wound up changing its filtration and disinfection system.

Wind shear is a critical factor in the formation and destruction of hurricanes, particularly in the vertical direction within the troposphere, the atmospheric layer where active weather occurs. Hurricanes fill the entire vertical extent of the troposphere and are steered by the average wind through this layer. Wind shear is typically measured as the difference in wind speed between the top of the troposphere (40,000 feet altitude or 200 mb pressure) and a layer where a pressure of 850 mb is found, about 5,000 feet above the surface. This wind shear is computed over a large area, such as a circle of 700 miles in diameter centered on the hurricane.

Wind shear hurts hurricanes by removing heat and moisture they need for development, and by distorting their shape, making them less efficient heat engines. Dr. Bill Gray of Colorado State University was one of the first scientists to study the effect of wind shear on hurricane formation. He found that large vertical wind shears do not allow for the concentration of heat and moisture, making it difficult for tropical cyclones to develop. He also discovered that the east-west or "zonal" component of the wind shear is what matters most to hurricanes, while wind shear in the north-south or "meridional" direction does not significantly affect storms.

A general rule of thumb is that the shear must be 20 knots or less for intensification to occur. Most instances of rapid intensification of hurricanes occur when the wind shear is 10 knots or less. However, large and powerful hurricanes can be resistant to shear values as high as 40 knots, as demonstrated by Hurricane Wilma.

Current wind shear values can be diagnosed using the University of Wisconsin CIMSS site, which computes upper level winds by looking at cloud motion from satellites. A mean low level wind, averaged over a layer between 925 mb and 700 mb (1500 feet to 10,000 feet), is subtracted from a mean upper level wind, averaged over a layer between 300 mb and 150 mb (30,000 to 45,000 feet). If a tropical cyclone is present, the winds due to the circulation around the storm are removed, so that one can just look at the environmental wind field the storm is embedded in.

An example of the effect of wind shear on a tropical storm is Tropical Storm Gabrielle of 2007. Gabrielle had a well-defined circulation from the surface to 850 mb, but could not develop any heavy thunderstorm activity near the center because strong upper level winds from the southwest blew away the thunderstorms as quickly as they formed. The winds carried high, wispy cirrus clouds from lower left to upper right, creating 20 knots of wind shear over the center of Gabrielle (where the winds were calm). Just north of the Gabrielle's center, the surface to 850 mb flow was out of the northeast at about 10 knots, due to the counter-clockwise flow of air around the vortex. As a result, the shear was 20 knots at 200 mb minus negative 10 knots at 850 mb, for a total wind shear of 30 knots.

While much attention remains on Texas and the destruction left by Hurricane Harvey and its historic rainfall, powerful Hurricane Irma is rapidly intensifying in the open Atlantic and poses a major threat to the Caribbean and potentially to the United States next week. Irma was designated a tropical storm Wednesday morning, and by Thursday afternoon, it had strengthened into a large Category 3 hurricane, with winds of 115 mph. Such explosive strengthening is known as "rapid intensification," defined by the National Hurricane Center as having its wind speed increase at least 30 knots (35 mph) in 24 hours.

Irma is a classic "Cape Verde hurricane," a type of hurricane that forms in the far eastern Atlantic, near the Cape Verde Islands, then tracks all the way across the Atlantic. Cape Verde storms frequently become some of the largest and most intense hurricanes. Examples are Hurricane Hugo, Hurricane Floyd, and Hurricane Ivan. Irma is forecast to continue to strengthen as it moves westward over the next five days, and the official forecast from the National Hurricane Center puts a dangerous Category 4 Hurricane Irma on the doorstep of the Caribbean by the end of the five-day forecast on Wednesday.

A strong high-pressure ridge to the north of Irma, over the Atlantic, is steering the storm to the west and limiting the wind shear in the upper levels of the atmosphere, which has allowed the storm to grow so quickly. Unfortunately, Irma will remain in a low-shear environment for the next several days, so there isn't much hope that Irma will weaken any time soon. There is considerable confidence that Hurricane Irma will track to the west through the weekend and then take a slight jog to the southwest early next week in response "to a building ridge (of high pressure) over the central Atlantic." From there, the forecast becomes a lot less clear, with some major differences among some of the key models meteorologists use to forecast hurricanes. The differences are so drastic that one prediction has Irma sliding harmlessly back out to sea, while in another, it makes multiple disastrous landfalls in the Caribbean and likely hits the United States after that.

In this comprehensive summary, a European bison, a protected species, was shot by authorities in Germany, sparking outrage from conservation groups. The bison had wandered from the Ujście Warty National Park on the German-Polish border and was killed by local hunters under the instruction of the head of the local public order office. The European bison is the largest land mammal in Europe and had not been seen in the wild in Germany for over 250 years.

The shooting of the bison has led to charges being filed against the head of the public order office in Brandenburg, with conservation groups arguing that giving permission to shoot a protected animal without a clear potential threat is a criminal offence. The incident has highlighted a lack of professionalism in the treatment of wild animals in the area, with the state of Brandenburg previously criticized for its handling of wolves and elk.

The European bison has enjoyed a renaissance in Europe in recent decades after years of suffering at the hands of hunters. The last wild bison in Poland was shot in 1921, leaving only 50 in zoos scattered across the continent. Since the end of World War II, successful conservation programmes, especially in Poland, have led to bison numbers growing to over 4,600 worldwide. They have also been slowly re-introduced to the wild, with Poland now boasting 1,212 free-ranging animals.

The shooting of the bison has also brought attention to the issue of wolf numbers in Europe. Both bison and wolves have been reintroduced to the wild and have enjoyed a resurgence in numbers. Estimates of wolf numbers in Poland now range from 800-900.

The incident has also highlighted the importance of nature reserves and the need for proper management and protection of endangered species. The Bialowieza Forest, a refuge for bison, bears, wolves and lynx, among other species, is an example of a successful conservation effort. However, the forest faces challenges, including a shallow gene pool due to a low genetic diversity among the bison population.

The European bison is a symbol of the success of conservation efforts in Europe, but incidents like the shooting in Germany highlight the need for continued vigilance and proper management of endangered species. The shooting has also brought attention to the issue of wolf numbers in Europe and the need for proper management of these animals as well.

Facebook and Microsoft have entered into a deal where Facebook will acquire a significant number of patents from Microsoft, which Microsoft recently acquired from AOL. This deal is part of a larger strategy by both companies to strengthen their intellectual property portfolios, particularly in the face of patent lawsuits from companies like Yahoo.

The deal will see Facebook acquiring approximately 650 patents and patent applications from Microsoft, while Microsoft will retain ownership of around 275 AOL patents and a license to the remaining 650 patents that Facebook will own. This deal will significantly increase Facebook's patent portfolio, bringing the total number of patents it owns to over 1,000.

The patents being acquired by Facebook cover various technologies, including mobile, Web, and instant messaging. For Microsoft, this deal allows it to retain valuable patents related to search technology.

The deal is seen as a strategic move by both companies to counter the growing influence of Google in the tech industry. Google has been a significant competitor for both Microsoft and Facebook, with Google Plus being introduced as a rival social service, and Google's search engine posing a threat to Microsoft's Bing search engine.

The deal could potentially give Facebook additional ammunition in its ongoing patent dispute with Yahoo. Yahoo had previously sued Facebook, claiming violations of Yahoo patents related to online advertising. Facebook countersued Yahoo, and this patent deal could provide Facebook with more patents to use in its defense.

The deal also highlights the growing importance of stockpiling patents in the tech industry. As both Facebook and Microsoft approach their respective initial public offerings, they are looking to protect their interests over the long term by building strong intellectual property portfolios.

Microsoft and Facebook have a history of collaborating, with Microsoft using data from Facebook in its Bing search engine to create more relevant search results. Despite this collaboration, Microsoft had previously tried to acquire Facebook but was rejected by Facebook's CEO, Mark Zuckerberg.

The deal between Microsoft and Facebook is expected to close pending regulatory scrutiny. If it goes through, it will represent a significant boost for Facebook's patent portfolio and could potentially shift the balance of power in the tech industry.

The intellectual property story of the week revolves around the shutdown of a popular website, PonyArchive.org, offering downloads of the cartoon My Little Pony: Friendship is Magic. The website was a key resource for the "brony" community, a group of adult male fans of the show. Hasbro, the trademark holder, sent a take-down notice to PonyArchive, which resulted in a heated response from the website's administrators. The incident sparked a rift in the brony community, with some viewing the response as immature and others defending it as a justified response to Hasbro's actions. The shutdown has left international fans, who couldn't access the show on TV or iTunes in their country, disappointed. Despite the controversy, illegal torrents of episodes are still available for motivated fans, and the brony community shows no signs of disappearing anytime soon.

A former employee of the Royal Canadian Mint in Ottawa, Leston Lawrence, has been sentenced to 30 months in prison and fined $190,000 for stealing 22 gold "pucks" worth approximately $130,000. Lawrence, who worked in the mint's testing department, was found guilty in November of 2020 for breach of trust, possession of property obtained by crime, and conveying gold out of the mint.

The theft took place between 2014 and 2015, and Lawrence managed to sell 17 of the pucks through Ottawa Gold Buyers. He used the money to buy a house in Jamaica and a boat in Florida. The remaining 5 pucks were recovered from a safety deposit box.

The evidence presented in court was mostly circumstantial, as no one actually saw Lawrence taking the pucks, and there was no video evidence. However, the pucks exactly fit the unique ladle used at the mint, and Vaseline and latex gloves were found in Lawrence's locker at work.

Lawrence set off the metal detector more often than any other employee, but subsequent checks with a wand did not set off alarms. The Mint has since improved its internal security measures, including upgrades to their facility's security checkpoint and screening process, upgrades to their camera system, and working closely with CATSA to establish more robust scanning training of their employees.

During sentencing submissions, the Crown attorney argued for a three-year prison sentence, while the defense lawyer argued for an 18-month sentence. The judge ruled that Lawrence would have to serve an additional 30 months if he doesn't pay the $190,000 fine within three years of being released from prison.

Lawrence's defense lawyer called the judge's decision careful and meticulous, and said Lawrence accepts the outcome of the trial. The Mint responded by stating that they are confident they have the right security measures in place to effectively operate their business.

The ideal candidate should have a minimum of 18 years of dad experience and 10 years of grilling experience. The chosen 'dad' must bring his own grill, but food and beer will be provided. Dane Anderson of KHQ-TV reports that these men don't live with their fathers and are not prepared to take on the role of barbecue dad. Additional requirements include discussing dad-related topics like lawnmowers, building decks, and musician Jimmy Buffet. Several potential 'barbecue dads' have responded to the ad. Ford announced on Wednesday that it will phase out most cars it sells in North America, focusing instead on trucks, SUVs, and commercial vehicles. The automaker will transition to two vehicles, the Mustang and an unannounced vehicle, the Focus Active, being the only traditional cars it sells in the region. Ford sees 90% of its North America portfolio in trucks, utilities, and commercial vehicles due to a reduction in consumer demand and product profitability. The company is not investing in the next generation of sedans, and several models such as the Taurus, Fusion, Fiesta, and C-Max will no longer be sold in North America. Ford also plans to bring hybrid-electric powertrains to the F-150, Mustang, Explorer, Escape, and upcoming Bronco. This shift in focus reflects a broader trend in consumer preferences, with North American consumers increasingly turning to crossovers, trucks, and SUVs over sedans and small cars. Ford aims to become the leader in the U.S. hybrid vehicles market by sales by 2021, surpassing current leader Toyota. The Mustang, which has been in production since 1964, will remain a staple in Ford's lineup.

The document details the growing presence of armed civilian groups and border vigilantes in response to President Trump's warnings about the threat posed by caravans of Central American migrants moving through Mexico towards the U.S. border. These groups, such as the Texas Minutemen, are preparing to head for the Rio Grande and offer aid in stopping the migrants. The Texas Minutemen have around 100 volunteers en route to the Rio Grande, with more likely on the way. However, the prospect of armed vigilantes showing up beside U.S. troops and border patrol agents is causing concern, with military planners issuing warnings to Army commanders about the arrival of unregulated militia members. The military is concerned about the potential for incidents involving these militias, including the alleged theft of National Guard equipment during deployments. Some landowners in the area have expressed concerns about the militias, with one rancher, Michael Vickers, stating that he will not let militia members from outside the area onto his property and that he doubts most area landowners would trust outsiders. Other landowners, such as Lucy Kruse and Joe Metz, also worry about the potential for harm or property damage from the militias. Stephen J. "Tio" Kleberg, the heir to the state's largest and most influential ranch, has stated that he will not allow private militias onto his property. Manuel Uribe, formerly recognized as the world's heaviest man, passed away on Monday at the age of 48. Uribe, who was confined to his bed in Monterrey, Mexico for years, had a record peak weight of 1,230 pounds (560 kilograms) in 2006, certified by Guinness World Records. He was admitted to a hospital in his native Nuevo Leon state a few days ago due to cardiac arrhythmia and other health complications. Uribe had been bedridden since at least 12 years and required a crane to be transported to the hospital by emergency and civil defense workers. He lost 593 pounds after getting married in 2008, and in a 2008 interview with the Daily Record, he expressed hope for a happy life with his new wife. Uribe had a history of obesity, weighing more than 250 pounds (115 kilograms) as an adolescent. The cause of his death has not yet been certified by doctors, but he was also believed to have suffered from liver problems.

House Speaker Paul Ryan released a campaign-style video on Friday, fueling speculation about his potential involvement in the Republican presidential race at a contested convention. The video, titled "Politics These Days," is part of Ryan's agenda for House Republicans, called "#ConfidentAmerica." In the video, Ryan criticizes identity politics and expresses his desire to unify the party.

Despite his repeated denials, Ryan's name has been floated as a potential nominee due to concerns about a likely contested convention and the possibility of a Donald Trump or Ted Cruz nomination. Ryan's predecessor, John Boehner, has suggested that Ryan should be the party's pick if they are unable to select a candidate on the first ballot.

Ryan's political office has released similar videos in the past, and his communications-savvy team has moved quickly to shut down any "Draft Ryan" for president movements. However, Ryan's reluctance to immediately accept the speakership last year has led some to question his statements about 2016.

In 2015, Ryan initially insisted that he would not be a candidate for speaker of the House following John Boehner's retirement announcement. Three weeks later, he was sworn in as speaker of the House after another alternative failed to materialize.

Ryan has aggressively downplayed the possibility of a presidential run, but his latest video has added fuel to the fire. Many on Twitter have speculated that the Speaker may be planning a shadow run at the convention, despite his previous denials. Ryan's office has come out most forcefully against the possibility of a presidential run, with spokeswoman AshLee Strong stating that he is not interested and will not accept a nomination.

The term "Shermanesque statement" has been used to describe Ryan's denial, originating from Civil War Gen. William Tecumseh Sherman, who didn't want to be nominated in the 1884 election. President Lyndon B. Johnson also used a similar statement in 1968 when he announced he was not going to seek re-election.

All eyes will once again be on Ryan when he returns to Washington, D.C., next week. Despite the denials, the release of the campaign-style video has reignited speculation about Ryan's potential involvement in the presidential race.

The Humane Society of Missouri's Disaster Response Team successfully rescued a small white dog named Soshe who was trapped in a flooded house in Pender County, North Carolina, during Hurricane Florence. The owner, who had evacuated a week earlier and was now stranded in Wilmington, North Carolina, was distraught about her dog's situation. The Humane Society's team made three attempts to locate the house, as the floodwater had reached the roofs, making homes difficult to identify. After dealing with a broken-down boat and paddling half a mile, they finally reached Soshe's home and heard barking coming from inside. Upon entering, they found Soshe marooned on a floating living room couch. The team carefully removed the dog, dried her off, and reunited her with her grateful mother. The Humane Society of Missouri's Disaster Response Team spent 10 days in North Carolina, rescuing dogs, cats, chickens, goats, and horses from the flood waters, and assisting the Coast Guard with the unloading of animals. Anyone interested in helping pets affected by Hurricane Florence can donate online or by calling (314) 951-1542.

Army Staff Sgt. Robert Bales, charged with the murder of 16 Afghan villagers in one of the worst atrocities of the Afghanistan war, will plead guilty to avoid the death penalty. His attorney, John Henry Browne, revealed this to The Associated Press on Wednesday. Bales was "crazed" and "broken" during the attack, but his mental state did not meet the criteria for a legal insanity defense. The plea deal, which requires Bales to recount the horrific attack for the first time, must be approved by a judge and the commanding general at Joint Base Lewis-McChord, where Bales is being held. The outcome of the case carries high stakes, as the Army had been trying to have Bales executed, and Afghan villagers have demanded it. The plea hearing is set for June 5.

Bales, an Ohio native and father of two from Lake Tapps, Wash., had been drinking contraband alcohol, snorting Valium, and taking steroids before the attack. He slipped away from his remote southern Afghanistan outpost at Camp Belambay early on March 11, 2012, and attacked compounds. Most of the victims were women and children, and some of the bodies were piled and burned. The slayings drew such angry protests that the U.S. temporarily halted combat operations in Afghanistan.

Bales' attorneys have said that he suffers from post-traumatic stress disorder and sustained a traumatic brain injury during a prior deployment to Iraq. They believe the Army is attempting to escape responsibility for sending Bales to Afghanistan for his fourth deployment, knowing that he had PTSD and a concussive head injury. The defense team has determined that Bales would not be able to prove any claim of insanity or diminished capacity at the time of the attack.

The plea deal could inflame tensions in Afghanistan, and Browne expressed concern about a potential backlash. However, his primary goal is to save Bales from the death penalty. The sentencing-phase trial set for September will determine whether Bales is sentenced to life in prison with or without the possibility of parole.

A new footbridge, known as the Golden Bridge, has recently opened in Vietnam's Ba Na Hills mountain resort. The bridge, held up by two giant stone-colored hands, is suspended approximately 4,600 feet above sea level and is 150 meters long. The bridge, which took under a year to construct, is part of a $2 billion investment to attract more tourists to the area.

The Ba Na Hills was a popular holiday destination for French authorities in the early 20th century but fell into disrepair after the revolution against colonial rule in 1945. The area now features a replica French village, gardens, a cable car, and an amusement complex.

The Golden Bridge is the latest in a series of unusual footbridges around the world, including the Fan Bridge in London, the Rolling Bridge in London, the Lucky Knot bridge in Changsha, China, and the living root bridges in Meghalaya, India.

The bridge has attracted a significant number of visitors, who are drawn to its unique design and the uninterrupted views of the landscape below. The design of the bridge was inspired by the image of "giant hands of Gods, pulling a strip of gold out of the land."

The Ba Na Hills received over 2.7 million visitors last year, and the Golden Bridge is expected to contribute to this number. The bridge has received both local and international attention for its unusual design.

Visitors to the bridge have expressed their awe and admiration for the structure, with one tourist saying, "I feel like I'm walking on clouds. It's so unique." Another tourist commented, "The two, smooth, giant hands look real. It makes me feel like humans can do anything."

The Golden Bridge is the latest addition to the list of attractions at the Ba Na Hills, which already includes Fantasy Park, French Gardens, and the world's longest and highest cable car. The bridge is expected to attract even more visitors to the area, further boosting the local tourism industry.

The study published in the journal Psychological Science, led by Christopher Thorstenson from the University of Rochester, has found a direct connection between a person's emotions and their ability to perceive color. The research suggests that sadness affects color perception, specifically along the blue-yellow color axis, but not along the red-green color axis.

The study involved two experiments where participants were randomly assigned to watch either a sad film clip, a neutral screensaver, or a comedy skit. Afterward, they were asked to identify desaturated colors. The results showed that people who watched the sad film clip had difficulty differentiating between shades along the blue-yellow color axis, while those in the amused and neutral groups did not experience any problems.

Psychologists believe that perception along the blue-yellow axis is linked to the neurotransmitter dopamine, which is associated with mood disorders like depression and ADHD. The study's findings suggest that sadness affects dopamine's other tasks, including transmitting visual information about blue and yellow light.

The researchers speculate that this could be due to a dopamine deficiency, but they did not measure dopamine levels in the study. The study's findings highlight the possibility that our understanding of the world happens "top-down" as much as "bottom-up," meaning higher-level cognition can determine what and how we perceive.

The study's findings have implications for understanding the relationship between emotions, color perception, and neurotransmitters like dopamine. Further research is needed to confirm the role of dopamine in color perception and to explore other possible factors that may influence color perception based on emotions.

The Fukushima Daiichi nuclear power plant in Japan faced a potential meltdown after a magnitude-8.9 earthquake and tsunami on March 11, 2011, crippled its cooling system. The disaster led to a hydrogen explosion at Unit 1, which was vented to prevent a total nuclear meltdown. Officials were aware of the risks involved in venting the radioactive steam, as it contained hydrogen and could potentially cause an explosion.

The chain of events started when the earthquake and tsunami severed electricity to the Fukushima Dai-ichi nuclear complex, located 170 miles northeast of Tokyo. Backup power did not kick in properly at one of its units, leading to worsening conditions. Initially, officials said things were improving, but crisis after crisis continued to develop or be revealed.

Without power, and with plant pipes and pumps destroyed in the explosion of the most-troubled reactor's containment building, authorities resorted to drawing seawater in an attempt to cool off the overheated uranium fuel rods. This was a desperate measure, and the success of using seawater and boron to cool the reactor would depend on the volume and rate of their distribution. The restoration of electrical power was also crucial, as it would allow for the restoration of normal cooling systems.

Officials placed Dai-ichi Unit 1, and four other reactors, under states of emergency. An additional reactor was added to the list, for a total of six reactors in emergency status. Local evacuations have been ordered at each location. Japan has a total of 55 reactors spread across 17 complexes nationwide.

If the temperature inside the Fukushima reactor vessel continued to rise, the uranium fuel pellets would start to melt. This would cause the fuel to eat through the bottom of the reactor vessel, the floor of the already-damaged containment building, and potentially cause an explosion much bigger than the one caused by the hydrogen. Such an explosion would enhance the spread of radioactive contaminants.

If the reactor core became exposed to the external environment, officials would likely begin pouring cement and sand over the entire facility, as was done at the 1986 Chernobyl nuclear accident in the Ukraine. The estimated death toll from Japan's disasters climbed past 10,000, making it the nation's worst crisis since World War II.

The disaster also caused widespread destruction along the northeastern coast, with hundreds of thousands of people struggling to find food and water. Rescuers pulled bodies from mud-covered jumbles of wrecked houses, shattered tree trunks, twisted cars, and tangled power lines while survivors examined the ruined remains. One rare bit of good news was the rescue of a 60-year-old man swept away by the tsunami who clung to the roof of his house for two days until a military vessel spotted him waving a red cloth about 10 miles offshore.

Dozens of countries have offered assistance, and two U.S. aircraft carrier groups were off Japan's coast and ready to help. Helicopters were flying from one of the carriers, the USS Ronald Reagan, delivering food and water in Miyagi. Two other U.S. rescue teams of 72 personnel each and rescue dogs arrived Sunday, as did a five-dog team from Singapore. However, large areas of the countryside remained surrounded by water and unreachable. Fuel stations were closed, though at some, cars waited in lines hundreds of vehicles long.

The United States and several countries in Europe urged their citizens to avoid travel to Japan. France took the added step of suggesting people leave Tokyo in case radiation reached the city. Community after community traced the vast extent of the devastation, with one town reporting that nearly two-thirds of its population have not been heard from since the tsunami wiped it out.

Fitch Ratings has placed the United States' AAA credit rating on a negative watch due to the ongoing political impasse over raising the debt ceiling and the government shutdown. The agency's decision comes as the U.S. is set to hit its debt ceiling on October 17, leaving cash reserves of just $30 billion. The prolonged negotiations over the debt ceiling could undermine confidence in the role of the U.S. dollar as the preeminent global reserve currency, casting doubt over the full faith and credit of the U.S. The 'AAA' rating reflects the U.S.'s strong economic and credit fundamentals, including its highly productive, diversified, and wealthy economy, extraordinary monetary and exchange rate flexibility, and the exceptional financing flexibility afforded by the global reserve currency status of the U.S. dollar. Fitch expects to resolve the rating watch by the end of Q114, but the timing will depend on developments and events, including the duration of any agreement to raise the debt ceiling. The agency's medium-term fiscal projections imply federal and general government debt stabilizing next year and over the remainder of the decade at around 72% and 104% of GDP, respectively, which is below the 80% and 110% thresholds that Fitch previously identified as being inconsistent with the U.S. retaining its 'AAA' status. However, public debt stabilization at such elevated levels still leaves the U.S. economy and public finances vulnerable to adverse shocks. The rating watch could result in a downgrade of the ratings if the government fails to honor interest and/or principal payments on U.S. Treasury securities or if there is a similar episode occurring in the future.

Chelsea Handler, the popular late-night talk and comedy host, has moved her show to a new studio at Universal Studios, which was previously used by Jack Benny and Conan O'Brien. Handler is particularly excited about the new set's private shower, as it eliminates the need for her to walk past her guests semi-nude, an issue she faced in her previous studio.

The new studio offers more space, allowing for more audience members and the possibility of Chuy Bravo, Handler's sidekick, entering on elephants and other animals. Handler aims to maintain an intimate vibe with her audience, involving them in the show in creative ways.

On the first day in the new studio, Handler's close friend Jennifer Aniston was the first guest. Other guests for the week include Fergie, Miley Cyrus, and Christina Aguilera. Handler values having a space where guests can have fun and looks forward to welcoming more celebrities.

The new studio is equipped with improved sound and lighting systems. Handler, who has hosted "Chelsea Lately" since 2007, sees this move as a commitment to stay and continue her work. The show airs weeknights at 11 p.m. on E!.

The article discusses the discovery of a child's skeletal remains found in a suitcase in South Australia, which has led to speculation about a possible connection to the 2007 disappearance of Madeleine McCann, a three-year-old British girl who went missing from her family's holiday apartment in Portugal. The remains, believed to be of a fair-haired child aged between 2 ½ and 4 years old, were found on the side of a rural highway in South Australia.

UK police have made inquiries with Australian authorities, but Australian police have stated that there is currently no evidence to suggest that the remains are those of Madeleine McCann. South Australian police believe that the child was killed at a different location at some point since the start of 2007. The remains were found in a suitcase along with items of clothing and a degraded quilt.

Police have released images of the quilt and some of its patches in an attempt to identify its origins and potentially solve the mystery. The quilt was homemade using a sewing machine and a polyester material was used to line its inside, indicating it was made for a child. Police believe that some of the quilt fabric was manufactured in New York in about 2008.

Researchers have discovered a large reservoir of melt water under the Greenland ice sheet, which could provide important insights into sea level rise. The water is stored in the air space between ice particles, similar to the way juice is stored in a slush drink. The aquifer, which covers an area the size of Ireland, is estimated to hold roughly 140 billion tonnes of water, equivalent to half of the annual contribution of Greenland to sea level rise. The water is prevented from freezing by the large amounts of snow that fall on the surface of the ice sheet late in the summer. The ultimate destination of the water in the reservoir is unknown, and scientists are planning to return to Greenland to further study the aquifer and its implications for the future of the ice sheet. The discovery may help explain disparities between climate models and satellite observations of Greenland's ice loss. The researchers used a drill rig to extract cores from the snow aquifer and found that liquid water was flowing back to the surface even when air temperatures were below freezing. The discovery was a surprise to the researchers, as they had thought that the water was stored in the air space between subsurface rock particles, not ice particles. The research was published in the journal Nature Geoscience.

The study published in Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B reveals that understory fires in the Amazon rainforest, previously hidden due to their location beneath the forest canopy, are causing extensive damage to the forest, exceeding the impact of deforestation in recent years. These fires, which occur when climatic conditions are suitable, are responsible for burning over 33,000 square miles (85,500 square kilometers) of forest between 1999 and 2010.

Unlike fires in the Amazon's grassy areas, understory fires burn nearly undetected, killing between 10 and 50 percent of the trees in the affected areas. The fires are likely an important source of carbon emissions that have not been adequately accounted for in climate models.

The study also found no correlation between understory fires and deforestation; instead, climate conditions, particularly low nighttime humidity, appear to be the primary factor determining fire risk in the Amazon at a regional scale. Researchers are currently investigating the climate mechanisms that predispose the southern Amazon to burn, with soil moisture being a leading suspect. NASA is using satellite data to monitor the evolution of dry conditions during the fire season, providing valuable insights into the factors contributing to severe fire seasons in the Amazon.

The findings of this study could have significant implications for estimates of carbon emissions from disturbed forests and our understanding of the Amazon's vulnerability to fire.

Initially classified as a light sport aircraft by the FAA, the TF-2, despite being 120lb over the limit, received an exemption due to its unique design. The two-seater Transition can drive on roads at 30 miles per gallon and take off from suitable spots, folding its wings electrically.

The Transition cruises at 115mph, has a range of 460 miles, and can carry 450lb. It requires a 1,700-foot runway for take-off and fits in a standard garage. Terrafugia, the manufacturer, claims the Transition's safety advantage lies in its ability to drive home during inclement weather instead of being grounded or flying in unsafe conditions.

So far, 70 people have placed deposits for the Transition, priced at $194,000. Deposits are held in escrow to ensure refunds in case of company bankruptcy before delivery. This news was reported by The Register.

Iran has announced its intention to increase its naval presence in the Gulf, particularly around three disputed islands claimed by the United Arab Emirates (UAE). The islands, located near strategic oil shipping routes, have been a source of tension between the two countries for over 40 years. The Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has stated that the security of these islands is part of their naval force's strategies, and they are expanding their naval defense capabilities in five zones, with the fifth zone specifically responsible for the defense of the Iranian islands. The dispute between Shi'ite Iran and Sunni UAE has nationalist and ethnic overtones, and has strained relations between the two countries.

In a separate development, Iranian media is reporting that Iran has produced a domestically-made drone capable of hovering in midair and flying in silence. The drone is expected to be displayed in February. Iran has also claimed that it obtained images of sensitive Israeli bases using a drone launched by Lebanon's Hezbollah movement, although these claims have been disputed by Israel. Iran frequently makes claims about military technology breakthroughs and other achievements, many of which are difficult to independently confirm.

The incident, which was captured on surveillance video, led to the man, identified as Dallas Swonger, being cited for trespassing and public urination. The decision to drain the reservoir was made to ensure no health risks to Portland water customers, despite experts stating that the risk was minimal. Critics argue that the decision was a public relations move and a waste of resources. Swonger, in an interview with Vocativ, claimed he urinated on a wall next to the reservoir and not in it, and expressed his dismay at the national attention the incident has received. The incident has sparked debate about the city's water management and the proposed switch of control of the city's water away from the City Council to an independently elected water district board. The city has stated that politics did not play a role in the decision to drain the reservoir.

The Manchester Arena bomb attack, which occurred on May 22, 2017, has led to a rift in intelligence sharing between the UK and the US due to leaks to the media. The leaks have caused outrage among UK officials, with photos of debris from the attack appearing in the New York Times and the name of bomber Salman Abedi being leaked to US media just hours after the attack. The leaks have caused much distress for families of the victims and have potentially compromised the ongoing investigation.

The UK's acting ambassador to the US, Lewis Lukens, has unequivocally condemned the leaks, describing them as "reprehensible" and "deeply distressing." He has stated that communications at the highest level of the US government have taken place to identify and stop the leaks.

Meanwhile, the Queen has visited the Royal Manchester Children's Hospital, where some of the injured from the attack are being treated. During her visit, she paid tribute to Manchester and the "extraordinary" way the city has responded to the attack.

Eight men are currently in custody following the bombing, which was carried out by Manchester-born Abedi, a 22-year-old from a family of Libyan origin. The arrests have been described as "significant" and searches of premises have yielded items "important to the investigation."

It has also emerged that two people who had known Abedi at college made separate calls to a hotline to warn the police about his extremist views. A Whitehall source has stated that Abedi was one of a "pool" of former subjects of interest whose risk remained "subject to review" by the security service and its partners.

In other developments, Greater Manchester Police hope to resume normal intelligence relationships with the US soon but is currently "furious," the BBC understands. The force's chief constable, Ian Hopkins, has stated that the recent leak has caused "much distress for families that are already suffering terribly with their loss."

All other US-UK intelligence is still being shared, while five terrorist plots have been disrupted in the UK since the Westminster attack in March. Home Secretary Amber Rudd has stated that she is "confident" the leaks will now end, after having voiced her irritation following the leak of the attacker's name.

However, the pictures of debris - which appear to show bloodstained fragments from the bomb and the backpack used to conceal it - were subsequently leaked to the New York Times, prompting an angry response from within Whitehall and from UK police chiefs. UK officials believe that US law enforcement rather than the White House is the likely culprit for the leaks.

The police decision to stop sharing information specifically about the Manchester attack with their security counterparts in the US is a hugely significant move and shows how angry British authorities are. The information from the crime scene wasn't shared on a whim: the British and Americans have a lot of shared world-leading expertise in improvised explosive devices and scientists would be discussing whether the Manchester device tells them something new that could, ultimately, track down a bomb-maker. Other sharing will continue. The UK and US share a vast amount of information about terror and espionage threats - it is a tight-knit network that also encompasses Canada, Australia and New Zealand. That system is based on trust and the "control principle": if a piece of intelligence is shared, the receiving nation has no right to further disseminate it without permission. The UK's National Police Chiefs' Council described the "unauthorised disclosure" as a breach of trust which had potentially undermined a "major counter-terrorism investigation." Counter-terrorism detectives have spoken in the past about how a delay of about 36 hours before the public know who is being investigated can allow known associates of the suspect to be arrested without being tipped off. Lord Blair, who was the head of the Metropolitan Police at the time of the bombings in London on 7 July 2005, said a similar leak had happened then. "It's a different world in which the US operate in terms of how they publish things and this is a very grievous breach but I'm afraid it's the same as before," he said.

What's happening with the investigation?
Eight men have been arrested in the UK since Monday night, including Abedi's older brother Ismail, 23. Abedi's younger brother Hashem, 20, was held by special forces linked to the interior ministry in the Libyan capital Tripoli, as was their father. Speaking on Wednesday, Greater Manchester Chief Constable Ian Hopkins said: "It's very clear that this is a network that we are investigating." As part of their investigation, raids involving controlled explosions have been carried out at a block of flats near Manchester Piccadilly station in the city centre on Wednesday and at an address in the Moss Side area of Manchester in the early hours of Thursday. Anyone with information can call the anti-terror hotline on 0800 789321.

Who are the victims?
The youngest so far known to have died is eight-year-old Saffie Roussos. Off-duty Cheshire police officer Elaine McIver was also among the dead. The latest victims to be named are Wendy Fawell, 50, from Otley, west Yorkshire and Eilidh MacLeod, a 14-year-old from Barra in the Outer Hebrides, and 19-year-old Courtney Boyle. Of the 116 injured, 75 remain in hospital. Of those 23 are in critical care, five of them children.

Who was the attacker?
Salman Abedi was a 22-year-old born in Manchester to Libyan parents, and a former University of Salford student. He attended Burnage Academy for Boys in Manchester between 2009 and 2011, and The Manchester College until 2013. A former classmate told the BBC that Abedi was a "very jokey lad" but also "very short tempered" and would get angry at "the littlest thing." The man, who did not want to be identified, said Abedi had hung around "the wrong crowd and was very, very gullible." A Muslim community worker, who did not want to be identified, has told the BBC that two people who had known Abedi at college had made separate calls five years ago to a hotline to warn about his extremist views. In an exclusive interview following her release from a military prison, Chelsea Manning, formerly known as Bradley Manning, discussed her motivation for leaking over 700,000 classified documents to WikiLeaks. Manning, a transgender U.S. Army soldier, was convicted by a military tribunal under the Espionage and Computer Fraud and Abuse Acts and sentenced to 35 years in prison. However, her sentence was commuted by former President Barack Obama in his final days in office.

Manning said she felt a "responsibility to the public" to leak the documents due to the human toll of the "death, destruction, and mayhem" she witnessed as an Army intelligence analyst in Iraq. She emphasized that no one directed her to leak the documents and that she has accepted responsibility for her actions.

Manning spent seven years in prison at the U.S. Disciplinary Barracks at Fort Leavenworth, Kansas. During her imprisonment, she struggled with her gender transition and attempted suicide twice. She fought for and eventually received hormone treatments that she claimed were essential for her survival.

Manning remains in the Army but is off duty while she appeals her court-martial conviction. She has been documenting her life on her Instagram and Twitter account since her release. Manning has been praised by some as a hero, while others have labeled her a traitor. When asked how she sees herself, Manning simply replied, "I'm just me."

Manning's leaked documents included low-level battlefield reports from Iraq and Afghanistan, evidence of civilian deaths, Guantanamo prison camp detainee profiles, and U.S. diplomatic correspondence. Manning said she leaked the documents to spark public debate and did not believe they would threaten national security.

Manning pleaded guilty to some charges and was acquitted of the most serious charge brought against her: aiding the enemy. Her imprisonment was the longest of any leaker in U.S. history. President Obama commuted her sentence to time served three days before he left office.

Manning came out as transgender while in prison, and the military eventually provided her with treatment for her gender dysphoria. Fighting for hormone treatment was important for Manning because, she said, "it's literally what keeps me alive." Manning was released from prison on May 17, 2017, and has been documenting her life on her Instagram and Twitter account since.

In Switzerland, voters will decide on June 5th whether to implement a nationwide guaranteed income for all citizens and legal residents. The proposal, if passed, would provide $2,600 per month tax-free to every adult and $650 to each child. This income would be given regardless of work status, income level, or wealth. The idea of an unconditional basic income is gaining traction globally, with Switzerland being the first country to vote on it at a national level.

The proposal has been put forward by a group of artists, writers, and intellectuals, utilizing Switzerland's direct democracy system. Supporters argue that the stipend would offer people the option to reduce their working hours while maintaining a decent standard of living. They claim it would lead to a more motivated workforce and a more stable, productive economy.

However, the proposal has many critics. Opponents argue that it could put at risk the current system that motivates people to work and get training. They also note that financing the scheme, estimated to cost about $200 billion a year, would strain the government’s coffers.

The initiative's backers propose funding the plan through increases in value-added tax and other sources of revenue. The government counters that other taxes would have to rise and spending slashed to afford such a generous giveaway.

The proposal has sparked discussions about the potential adoption of a similar policy in the U.S., with some experts suggesting it could become a serious topic of discussion a decade from now, given the inevitable job and wage losses due to technological disruption.

Despite the proposal's likelihood of failure in the upcoming vote, it marks a significant step for the basic income movement, being the first time an entire nation will put the idea to a vote. However, critics argue that the current proposal is not perfectly conceived, and if children were excluded, it would be more affordable.

The article discusses the concerns of Admiral Mike Mullen, the Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, regarding an anticipated increase in service member suicides and family crises as troops return from multiple deployments in Iraq. With the drawdown of US forces in Iraq, a significant number of troops are returning to bases, particularly at Fort Lewis and Fort Hood. This influx of soldiers and aviators poses a challenge for commanders as they deal with troops returning with personal challenges for the first extended period with their families.

Mullen is particularly concerned about the rising suicide rates in the military, which have hit record highs in the Army, the branch most affected by repeated deployments. He mentioned five suicides in the Army last weekend alone. The article also highlights the issue of suicides at Fort Hood, where there have been 14 confirmed suicides and six suspected suicides of soldiers since the beginning of the year. This puts Fort Hood on pace to shatter its annual record for suicides since the beginning of the Iraq and Afghanistan wars.

Military officials are taking steps to address these issues, such as increasing the length of time between deployments and conducting reviews to identify soldiers at risk for suicide. Fort Hood officials are also reviewing the post's privately owned weapons registration and visiting soldiers living off-post to stem the rise in suicides.

The article emphasizes the need for leadership and encourages soldiers to watch out for warning signs among their comrades and seek help if needed. It also quotes a soldier, Sgt. Cassandra St. Amand, who acknowledges the emotional impact of the recent increase in suicides at Fort Hood.

The article is a reminder of the ongoing mental health challenges faced by service members and their families, particularly those who have been deployed multiple times in recent years. The military is taking steps to address these issues, but the challenges remain significant.

Trump also discussed the White House, denying reports of chaos within the White House but also saying he’s watching his back. He stated that he doesn't trust everybody in the White House and that Washington D.C. is a "vicious, vicious place."

The San Jacinto fault, a 130-mile long strike-slip fault that traverses East County, has the potential to produce larger earthquakes than previously believed, according to a study led by Tom Rockwell, an SDSU seismologist. The study, published in the journal Pure and Applied Geophysics, reveals that the central and northern sections of the San Jacinto fault can fail together, resulting in earthquakes of magnitude 7.6 to 7.7. If the San Jacinto fault were to rupture onto the San Andreas fault, it could potentially reach a magnitude 8.0, although there's no evidence of such an event in the past couple of thousand years.

Tom Rockwell, one of the world's foremost authorities on the San Jacinto fault, oversaw field studies that examined 21 seismic events that have occurred on the fault over the past 4,000 years. The San Jacinto fault is part of the larger San Andreas fault, the dividing line between the Pacific and North American plates, and is responsible for roughly 80% of the slippage along the plates. The fault has produced notable earthquakes in the past, such as a magnitude 6.5 quake in April 1968 and a 6.7 quake in November 1987 from a different strand known as Superstition Hills.

The study's findings suggest that earthquakes on the San Jacinto fault could potentially rival those on the San Andreas fault. This revelation underscores the importance of understanding and preparing for the potential seismic risks in the region. Michel Fourniret, a notorious French serial killer known as the 'Ogre of the Ardennes', has confessed to the murder of British student Joanna Parrish, who was 20 years old at the time of her death in 1990. Fourniret was already serving a life sentence for the rape and murder of seven other young women, but until now, police had been unable to prove his involvement in Parrish's murder.

Parrish, a student at Leeds University, was working as a language assistant at a secondary school in Auxerre, France, when she was abducted and murdered. Her body was found in the River Yonne near Auxerre, and an autopsy revealed that she had been raped, beaten, and strangled.

Fourniret's confession came after he was interviewed by two instructing magistrates in Paris last week. According to Parrish's family lawyer, Didier Seban, Fourniret made detailed and repeated confessions admitting to Parrish's murder. Seban also mentioned that Fourniret admitted to the murder of French teenager Marie-Angele Domece, who disappeared in 1988 and whose body has never been found.

Seban hopes that a trial will soon go ahead now that Fourniret has confessed to the murders. Paris prosecutors have not yet commented on the revelations, as investigations are still ongoing. Fourniret's lawyer has also remained silent on the matter.

Parrish's father, Roger Parrish, spoke of his relief at the confession, stating that his family would finally have "closure at last." However, he also expressed concern that this could be another false lead, as Fourniret had always denied his involvement in Parrish's murder in the past.

Fourniret's wife, Monique Olivier, had previously accused him of the two unsolved murders but later retracted her statements. Olivier was found guilty of complicity in five murders and is serving a life sentence with an order to serve at least 28 years behind bars. In May 2008, Fourniret was sentenced to life in prison for the joint rape and murder of seven girls.

The blast took place outside the arena, catching people as they exited, and also triggering chaos inside the venue. Initial reports indicated that some of the injuries might have been caused by a stampede of concertgoers.

The biography "Private Wealth and Public Life" by Peter Ascoli highlights the life and work of Julius Rosenwald, a German Jewish immigrant who transformed Sears, Roebuck and Company into the country's most significant retailer and became a notable philanthropist. Known as "JR," Rosenwald apprenticed for his uncles, major clothing manufacturers in New York City, before joining Sears, Roebuck and Company, where he eventually became the CEO.

Rosenwald was not just a philanthropist but also a subtle critic of racial democracy, as W.E.B. DuBois noted. He made significant contributions to African-American education, culture, and community development. He founded Chicago's Museum of Science and Industry and helped build over 5,300 schools in the American South, many of which still bear his name.

Rosenwald's charitable fund during World War I ceased to exist in 1948 at his expressed wish. Ascoli's biography provides a fascinating account of Rosenwald's meteoric rise in American business and his lifelong dedication to philanthropy.

The story of Rosenwald's philanthropy towards African-American causes is little-known, but a new documentary by Aviva Kempner, titled "Rosenwald," aims to change that. The documentary reveals how Rosenwald's philanthropy changed the course of education for thousands of children in the rural South and helped foster the careers of prominent artists like Langston Hughes, Marion Anderson, and Jacob Lawrence.

Alex Bethea, the son of cotton and tobacco farm workers, recently learned that his school in North Carolina was named after Julius Rosenwald, thanks to a screening of the documentary at the NAACP convention in Philadelphia. Bethea expressed that this revelation helped him understand the impact Rosenwald had on his life.

Rosenwald's philanthropy extended to providing seed money to build YMCAs for blacks in cities around the country and developing a huge apartment complex in Chicago to improve living conditions for migrants from the Jim Crow South.

The documentary "Rosenwald" celebrates the affinity between African-Americans and Jews that started long before the civil rights movement and speaks to the powerful Jewish tradition of tikkun olam, or repairing the world. The film features interviews with prominent African-Americans like Maya Angelou and U.S. Rep. John Lewis (D-Ga.), both of whom attended Rosenwald schools.

Kempner hopes that her film will motivate others to continue the tradition of American Jewish philanthropy started by Julius Rosenwald. She notes that while not everyone can be Rosenwald, everyone can do something. The official opening of the documentary in theaters is scheduled for mid-August.

In a significant breakthrough, astronomers have discovered that the comet Hartley 2 contains water with a composition similar to Earth's oceans, providing a substantial boost to the theory that comets played a significant role in supplying water to a thirsty early Earth. The finding, published in Nature, suggests that comets could have contributed more to the Earth's water supply than previously thought.

The research, led by Paul Hartogh of Germany's Max Planck Institute for Solar System Research, used infrared instruments on the Herschel Space Observatory to measure the deuterium fraction in the comet's water. Deuterium, a rare type of hydrogen, has a different molecular weight than regular hydrogen and can serve as a unique identifier for water sources.

Previous studies of other comets suggested they could have delivered no more than 10% of today's oceans due to differences in their deuterium composition. However, Hartley 2's deuterium fraction was found to be much closer to that of Earth's oceans, hinting at the possibility that comets could have been a more significant source of water.

Comet Hartley 2 is unique because it originates from the Kuiper Belt, a region of the solar system located about 30 to 50 times further from the sun than the Earth, while other comets studied come from the Oort Cloud, which is much further away. This difference in origin could explain the discrepancy in deuterium composition between Hartley 2 and other comets.

The discovery challenges the long-held assumption that asteroids were the primary source of water for the early Earth. It also opens up new questions about the early solar system and the mechanisms that brought water to Earth. The Atacama Large Millimeter Array of telescopes in Chile, which recently released its first results, is expected to provide further insights into these questions in the future.

Storm Barney, the second named storm of the season, is sweeping across the UK, bringing disruptive winds, power cuts, fallen trees, and diverted flights. The storm has led to a warning by the Environment Agency and the Royal Society for the Prevention of Accidents (RoSPA) that people taking "storm selfies" are putting themselves at risk to capture dramatic moments. David Walker, leisure safety manager at RoSPA, said, "We understand the temptation to view powerful tides and weather conditions, however, if you get caught up or swept out to sea in these events your life will be at risk very quickly and our rescue services will also be at great risk."

The storm follows a year of dangerous selfie incidents, with dozens of injuries and fatalities reported. In January, three Indian college students were killed by a train when they stopped on the road to Agra and tried to take a photograph of themselves in front of it. In the same month, two men in the Ural mountains died while taking a selfie with a hand grenade – after they had removed the pin.
