In a shocking turn of events, court records unsealed on Tuesday revealed the details of a December slaying in Griswold, Connecticut, where a couple and their son were murdered. The suspects, Ruth Correa and her brother Sergio Correa, conspired with the son, Matthew Lindquist, to exchange drugs for guns kept in his parents' home.

According to a 17-page arrest warrant affidavit, Matthew Lindquist had planned to make the exchange look like a robbery. In a text exchange, he wrote to one of the suspects, "If u pull up street from my house and give me a stack, I’ll show u right where the safe is." The texts came hours before authorities discovered the burned-out Kenwood Estates home and the bodies of Kenneth and Janet Lindquist on December 20.

Matthew Lindquist had told Ruth Correa that his father usually went to bed after dinner, around 6 or 7 p.m., and they should wait until then before carrying out the plan. Ruth Correa told investigators that the plan included tying up Matthew and blaming the theft of the guns on two black men.

Ruth Correa admitted to investigators that she had gone to the Griswold neighborhood with her brother, Sergio Correa, and that he was responsible for much of the violence that night. On the day of the slayings, Ruth Correa told investigators that a man who she did not know got into her brother's car asking about the drugs, which she thought was heroin.

Sergio Correa told the man that he was not going to get the drugs until Sergio got what he wanted, and the two men discussed a fake robbery and that the basement door to the home was unlocked. When they drove down the street and parked the car, the man got out and panicked, and the affidavit reveals the brutal details of what happened next.

When the man ran off, Sergio Correa ran after him with a machete, hitting him in the back of the head. He then threatened to tie Matthew Lindquist up with tape and zip ties, but Matthew began to yell and "freak out." Sergio Correa then began to stab the man, and at one point, he handed Ruth the knife and guided it into the man. The stabbing happened about 50 feet from the road in some trees.

Ruth and Sergio Correa then went into the house through the open basement and found the safe bolted to the floor. They went upstairs and were confronted by the man's father, who went after Sergio Correa. The two men fought over the keys to the safe, which he refused to hand over. Sergio Correa struck the man multiple times with a bat.

Ruth Correa said the man's wife came out from another room, but Ruth guided her into a bedroom, according to the affidavit. When the woman asked Ruth why they were doing this, she responded it was because the woman's son had set them up. While with the woman, Ruth said her brother had gotten the keys to the safe and brought a gun to the bedroom, which he pointed at the woman.

With her brother having the gun trained on the woman, Ruth walked around the house collecting items, including a purple laptop from an office in the home. She then returned to the bedroom and told her brother it was time to go, but left again to grab more items. When she returned to the bedroom a second time, she said she saw her brother with a rope or string around the woman's neck and his foot in her back. She told police that the woman appeared to be choking.

After the woman stopped making noise, Ruth and Sergio Correa started taking bags of items out to the car. During their last trip back into the house, Ruth said she saw her brother again using the rope or string to choke the woman because she was going for her phone. He grabbed a bat and hit the woman four or five times, Ruth told investigators.

On their way out, Ruth said her brother told her to look for something flammable. She said Sergio handed her cans of strong-smelling liquid, and she dumped a whole can in one spot and went outside. She returned briefly to see her brother on the first floor ignite an exercise ball. They loaded all the stolen property into a silver car outside the home and drove to her brother's car. She got into her brother's car and they drove off, following her brother out of the neighborhood.

They drove for about 30 minutes until they found an abandoned building and parked, and they put all the stolen property into Sergio's car before he drove off in the stolen car. Matthew Lindquist's car was found ablaze in a parking lot of a Glastonbury apartment complex not long after.

Ruth Correa, 23, of Hartford, was charged with murder, murder with special circumstances, robbery, arson, and home invasion in connection with the deaths of 56-year-old Kenneth Lindquist, his 61-year-old wife, Janet Lindquist, and their 21-year-old son, Matthew Lindquist on Dec. 20, 2017. Sergio Correa, 26, has not been charged in the case, but his attorney said he has been made aware an arrest warrant has been issued for his client for murder in the case in New London County. The attorney said his client maintains his innocence.

The affluent Connecticut couple, Jeffrey and Jeanette Navin, have been reported missing since August 7, three days after they were last seen near their home in Easton. Their car was found in a park-n-ride off Exit 42 of the Merritt Parkway in Westport on Aug. 9. The couple's disappearance comes a week after they lost an appeal over a debt of more than $2.2 million they owe in a foreclosure case with HSBC Bank USA.

The Navins, who run a sanitation company and work as a paraprofessional at Weston Intermediate School's library, are known for taking spur-of-the-moment vacations, but they usually inform their relatives about their travel plans. However, authorities are not suspecting foul play in their disappearance.

The debt on their 8,265-square-foot house, which has six bedrooms and a 10-acre wooded property, nearly doubled by December 2014. The case is still pending, but it is not the only debt-related case against the Navins. In November, a power company claimed Jeffrey owed $139,000 in unpaid electric fees for the same house.

The couple sold a house in 2012 to resolve another foreclosure filed by OCWEN Financial Corp. in 1999. The sale was linked to a 2002 civil case involving Jeffrey and Essex Savings Bank, although the details of that case were not immediately available.

Relatives have denied that the couple's money problems caused them to go missing, noting their bank accounts are "untouched" during this "overwhelming and troubling time." The family stated, "Financial issues recently reported by the media have not been proven to be a factor for our family members' disappearance."

The investigation into the Navins' disappearance has been turned over to the state police, and detectives are searching a Bridgeport home belonging to their son. The state police are poring through a ton of paperwork trying to backtrack where the Navins may have been before they disappeared. The couple earned up to $216,000 a year, and they moved into a custom-built 4,000-square-foot house in Westport in 1994 and sold it for $900,000 in June. They soon began renting a home in Easton, where the median household income is $142,000.

Jeffrey's company, J&J Refuse, began with "one man in a truck in 1985 and has been growing ever since," according to its website. Jeanette is a "beloved employee" for the Weston Public Schools district, where she has worked for 18 years. The Navins' longtime attorney, Kenneth Davis, said he hasn't seen them in about a month and that he doubts their debt would lead to physical harm against them.

The FBI agents Peter Strzok and Lisa Page, who were part of the investigation into alleged collusion between President Donald Trump's campaign and Russia, exchanged text messages that were critical of Trump, as well as other prominent figures. These texts were uncovered during a Justice Department inspector general investigation into potential political influence on investigative decisions during the campaign. Strzok was removed from the Russia probe "immediately" after the texts were discovered in late July, while Page had already ended her assignment to Mueller's office.

The texts show the pair expressing negative views of Trump as early as mid-2015, with Strzok calling Trump an "idiot" in response to a Washington Post story about Trump's comments on Russian President Vladimir Putin. In March 2016, Page exclaimed, "God trump is a loathsome human," to which Strzok replied, "He’s awful."

The agents sometimes expressed respect or outright support for Democratic presidential candidate Hillary Clinton. Strzok wrote, "God Hillary should win 100,000,000 - 0," calling himself a "conservative Dem." In another exchange, Page said, "Also did you hear [Trump] make a comment about the size of his d*ck earlier? This man can not be president," to which Strzok replied, "He’s awful."

The texts also reveal the agents' concerns about Russian influence on the campaign, with Page expressing concern that "sandernistas" might undercut Clinton’s campaign in July 2016. They also seem to have been assessing Trump’s chances while at work, with Strzok writing in August 2016, "I want to believe the path you threw out for consideration in Andy’s office — that there’s no way he gets elected — but I’m afraid we can’t take that risk." It’s unclear how helpful these texts will be to Trump allies seeking to prove that Mueller’s probe was tainted by bias, as the last of the messages are from last December.

The texts also show the pair mocking other politicians, with Strzok calling former Maryland Gov. Martin O’Malley a “douche.” Page speculated on Ohio Gov. John Kasich’s sexuality, saying he was “long suspected of being gay.” The agents also don’t seem to have been fans of Attorney General Eric Holder.

The Justice Department provided Congress with more than 350 text messages exchanged between Strzok and Page. It’s unclear why the texts were released before the public IG report is finished, but Democrats have called for a full review of the Department of Justice's decision making that led to their release. The texts have sparked partisan debate, with Republicans seizing on them as evidence of "extreme bias" in both Mueller's Russia probe and last year’s FBI investigation into Clinton's use of a private email server, while Democrats counter that the texts were private exchanges protected under the First Amendment.

Susan Olsen, best known for her role as Cindy Brady on "The Brady Bunch," has been fired from her job as a Los Angeles-based radio DJ after posting a homophobic rant on Facebook. The incident occurred during a radio interview with openly gay actor Leon Acord-Whiting on LA Talk Radio's "Two Chicks Talkin' Politics" segment on December 7.

Following the interview, Acord-Whiting accused Olsen of being "dangerous" and "unprofessional" on Facebook, citing her spread of "outrageous misinformation." He also expressed his intention to boycott the radio station until Olsen was removed.

The next day, Olsen responded with a derogatory and expletive-laden private message to Acord-Whiting, which he later shared on social media. The message contained offensive language and homophobic slurs.

LA Talk Radio announced Olsen's termination on December 9, stating that they will not tolerate hateful speech from anyone associated with their radio station. The station takes pride in its close relationship with the LGBT community and aims to provide a platform for hopeful and positive messages.

This incident highlights the importance of respectful discourse, especially in public forums, and the consequences that can arise from spreading hate speech. It also underscores the growing awareness and intolerance towards homophobic remarks in today's society.

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has announced heightened security measures at federal buildings in the District and nationwide, following the shooting at the Canadian Parliament and threats from terrorist groups to attack the U.S. The increased security, which started over the weekend, is a precautionary step to safeguard U.S. government personnel and facilities. The new security measures will be law-enforcement sensitive, varying and shifting from location to location, and will be continually re-evaluated. The DHS action follows last week's shooting in Ottawa, Canada, where a gunman killed an honor guard soldier and opened fire inside the Parliament building. President Obama condemned the violence, expressing shock. The DHS emphasized that the heightened security is not based on any specific, credible information about an active plot against U.S. officials, but rather due to ongoing terrorist threats and recent acts of violence.

The United States military is set to withdraw from Iraq by the end of 2011, with the Obama administration planning a significant civilian effort to fill the void. The State Department will assume responsibility for training the Iraqi police, a task largely carried out by contractors. To protect civilians in a country still plagued by insurgents and militias, the State Department is planning to double its private security guards to as many as 7,000. These security contractors will operate radars, search for roadside bombs, fly reconnaissance drones, and staff quick reaction forces to aid civilians in distress. The transfer of civilians, numbering around 2,400, is expected to be carried out on schedule, with the aim of helping bring stability to Iraq. However, some veteran Iraq hands suggest that thousands of additional troops may be needed after 2011. The administration is also planning to negotiate with Iraqi officials for a potential future military presence. The mission after 2011 will focus on providing support and economic development assistance. As the last of the military troops leave at the end of 2011, the Obama administration is planning to more than double the number of private security guards it has in Iraq. This move is aimed at protecting civilians from Al Qaeda-linked insurgents and Iranian-backed militias. At the same time, Afghanistan is asking the United States to remove a bulk of its private contractors from the country. The U.S. still has a significant amount of influence in Iraq, and the mission will be to preserve that investment and integrate Iraq into a more peaceful situation. The withdrawal of troops is seen as a historic moment, but the U.S. is not ending its involvement in Iraq, with a long-term commitment to the country remaining.

A scene of Cruise's character firing off a semi-automatic weapon is being removed from promotional spots.

Another Christmas release, Quentin Tarantino's "Django Unchained," is also known for its violent content. The film, which opens on Christmas Day, stars Jamie Foxx as a slave-turned-bounty hunter. In response to the shooting, the premiere of "Django Unchained" in Los Angeles was canceled, and a screening for cast and crew will still take place.

The Weinstein Company, the studio behind "Django Unchained," has not yet announced any changes to its marketing materials for the film. Meanwhile, Warner Bros. used NFL football to advertise its upcoming period pic "Gangster Squad," which is heavy on gunfire. The film was originally scheduled to open in September but was pushed back after the Colorado shootings to remove a scene depicting a gunfight in a movie theater.

Other events and premieres have also been affected by the shooting, with moments of silence observed at NFL games and celebrities expressing their condolences online. Pop star Justin Bieber tweeted, "My prayers go out to all those suffering in this tragedy. it's just wrong. Everyone please pray for them." Singer Rihanna added, "God have mercy!!!! No one deserves this! Praying for the families of the victims of the Connecticut shooting!! What a Christmas it will be."

The Crimson published a story detailing a "scouting report" written by members of the 2012 men's soccer team regarding incoming female recruits on the women's soccer team. Six members of the Harvard Women’s Soccer recruiting class of 2012, Brooke Dickens '16, Kelsey Clayman ’16, Alika Keene '16, Emily Mosbacher '16, Lauren Varela '16, and Haley Washburn '16, have spoken out against the report, expressing their frustration, disgust, and concern for the future. The report attempted to pit the women against each other, reducing them to their physical appearance. The women have called for men to join them in combatting this type of behavior and to help prevent it in the future.

The Harvard men’s cross country team has also been found to have produced yearly spreadsheets about members of the women’s team, sometimes writing "sexually explicit" comments about them. The team created the spreadsheets each year ahead of an annual dance with the women’s team. The men guessed which women would invite certain men to the event and added comments about the women’s physical appearance in certain spreadsheets.

The men’s cross country team has expressed regret for their past behavior and have taken steps to change their culture. The team's captain, Brandon E. Price ’17, has asked the team to "come clean with anything that we have typed down in the past." The team has also been working with University officials to educate themselves and to help others come to the same realizations that they reached.

The women of the Harvard Women’s Soccer team have called for men to join them in combatting this type of behavior and to help prevent it in the future. They have expressed their hope that the release of these reports will lead to productive conversation and action on Harvard’s campus, within collegiate athletic teams across the country, and into the locker room that is our world. The women have also expressed their hope that this will catalyze the cultivation of an environment and a culture that strives to lift up all of its members.

The six members of the Harvard Women’s Soccer recruiting class of 2012 have expressed their hope that this experience will serve as an opportunity to encourage their fellow women to band together in combatting this type of behavior, because they are a team and they are stronger when they are united. They have also invited men to join them, because ultimately they are all members of the same team. They have expressed their hope that this will lead to a culture that strives to lift up all of its members.

In a recent development, Casey Anthony's former lawyer, Jose Baez, is threatening to sue over claims made by a private investigator, Dominic Casey, who alleges that Baez had a sexual relationship with Anthony before her trial. The accusations were made in an affidavit filed in Anthony's bankruptcy case last month. In the affidavit, Dominic Casey also claims that he witnessed a naked Casey Anthony in Baez's office and that Baez confessed to him that Anthony had murdered her daughter Caylee.

However, Baez has strongly denied all the allegations, stating that he never had a sexual relationship with Anthony and that he has always conducted his practice consistent with the high ethical standards required of members of the Florida Bar. He further stated that legal action is forthcoming.

This isn't the first time Dominic Casey's claims have raised eyebrows. In a 2011 deposition, he floated several theories about Caylee's disappearance and death, and even expressed doubts about whether the remains found near Anthony's house were indeed Caylee.

The allegations come as part of a civil lawsuit connected to the Casey Anthony scandal, with Roy Kronk, the man who found Caylee's body in 2008, filing a suit against Anthony in 2011, alleging that she, through her attorneys, falsely accused Kronk of killing the girl. The case is still grinding through Central Florida bankruptcy court.

Dominic Casey has written two books with unsubstantiated claims about the case. Lawyers for Casey Anthony don't want him to provide testimony in the Kronk case, according to documents filed in the case. Dominic Casey has been deposed by Kronk's attorneys, and a transcript of that was filed on the court docket. Casey Anthony's lawyers have filed motions to strike Dominic Casey's deposition and are demanding to see records he claims to have.

The Kronk case was delayed when Anthony filed for bankruptcy in 2013 but was eventually moved over to the bankruptcy court, where Kronk is now arguing that her bankruptcy should not prevent him from recovering damages related to his claim of defamation.

The hormone kisspeptin, discovered in 1996, plays a crucial role in initiating and maintaining puberty and reproductive function. It is a protein that triggers the cascade of biochemical changes leading to the maturing of testes in boys and ovaries in girls. The KiSS-1 gene, which produces kisspeptin, was named after the Hershey's Kiss chocolate confectionary due to its discovery in Hershey, Pennsylvania.

Kisspeptin stimulates the secretion of gonadotropins, hormones that stimulate the production of testosterone in men and estradiol in women. Injections of kisspeptin have been found to advance the age of puberty in immature rats. Recent research suggests that kisspeptin may also boost behavioral circuits associated with sex and love, potentially aiding in the treatment of psychosexual disorders.

A study conducted by researchers from Imperial College London found that after an injection of kisspeptin, volunteers showed enhanced activity in brain regions associated with sexual arousal and romantic love. The researchers are now exploring the possibility that kisspeptin could be used to treat psychosexual disorders and potentially help couples who struggle to conceive.

However, the new age verification law in the UK, announced last week, may potentially censor any UK site that carries adult content, including educational and historical sites like www.thewhoresofyore.com. The site, which archives historical images of sexuality, may be liable to fall foul of the new laws, despite not being for profit and signposting the content as intended for adults.

The proposed censorship has raised ethical concerns and questions about its effectiveness, as it will have no power over social media sites and messenger apps that allow users to share pornographic images and videos. The researchers suggest that open and honest conversations about sex and pornography are necessary to keep children safe and educate them effectively.

The Juneau Police Department confirmed the death of Juneau Mayor Greg Fisk, who was found deceased inside his residence on Kennedy Street on Monday. The cause of death is currently unknown and is being investigated by the State Medical Examiner. An autopsy is expected to be completed within several days.

Rumors of an assault in connection with Fisk's death have surfaced, but the police have stated that these are merely speculations and the investigation is ongoing. The City and Borough of Juneau cancelled Assembly meetings scheduled for Monday night following the news of Fisk's death.

Fisk was elected mayor in October, securing nearly twice as many votes as incumbent Merrill Sanford. Juneau Deputy Mayor Mary Becker, a long-time family friend of Fisk, expressed her shock and sadness at his death. Becker will assume the responsibilities as acting mayor in accordance with state law.

The investigation into Fisk's death is ongoing, and further details are expected to be released as the investigation progresses. For more coverage on this developing story, visit KTOO's website.

Lady Gaga has confirmed a residency in Las Vegas at MGM's Park Theater, set to begin in late 2018. The deal, worth nearly $100 million, will see Gaga performing approximately 74 dates, with the potential for more. Each show is expected to earn her over a million dollars, totaling $75 million over two years. This residency marks Gaga's long-held dream of becoming a Las Vegas performer. The announcement was made through her social media channels, accompanied by photos of the deal signing and a toast with MGM Resorts International's president, Bill Hornbuckle, among others. Other headliners at the Park Theater include Bruno Mars and Cher. Gaga's last touring run saw an average box office gross of $2.5 million, according to Pollstar.

On Thursday, the National Archives released the final batch of documents related to the assassination of President John F. Kennedy, marking the largest release to date under a directive from President Trump. The documents, totaling 19,045, were released to comply with the President John F. Kennedy Assassination Records Collection Act of 1992.

President Trump had encouraged the release of the long-anticipated files last year to put any conspiracy theories to rest. However, he provided agencies with a temporary certification until this Thursday to allow for re-review of all documents withheld for release. Ultimately, at the request of the FBI and CIA, Trump blocked the release of some of the original records, which were not part of the final batch released Thursday and may never be released.

The administration released all related JFK documents other than the names and addresses of any living person mentioned in the documents. Trump said in October that he had no choice but to accept the redactions rather than allow potentially irreversible harm to the nation's security.

The National Archives released 19,045 documents on Thursday, which can be downloaded along with previously released records. The documents include secret 1978 testimony from a former CIA station chief in Mexico City, David Atlee Phillips, who called assassin Lee Harvey Oswald "loony" and insisted that Oswald had acted alone.

The transcript of the four-decade-old testimony was in the batch of documents released on December 15. Historians, assassination buffs, and conspiracy theorists are still digging through the documents for insights into the investigation and countless unrelated topics.

President Trump issued an order on Thursday, keeping some of the most sensitive records from the Kennedy assassination files sealed for another 3 1/2 years. Trump ordered agencies to review the remaining documents in the next three years to determine which should be released.

The releases include FBI, CIA, and other agency documents identified by the Assassination Records Review Board as assassination records. The National Archives released documents previously withheld in accordance with the JFK Assassination Records Collection Act. The vast majority of the Collection (88%) has been open in full and released to the public since the late 1990s. The records at issue are documents previously identified as assassination records, but withheld in full or withheld in part.

The Rock am Ring music festival in Germany was temporarily closed down on June 2, 2017, due to a suspected terror threat. The three-day event, which attracts approximately 90,000 people, was evacuated on Friday evening after police received "concrete elements" that suggested a possible terrorist threat could not be ruled out. The incident occurred less than two weeks after a terrorist attack at a concert in Manchester.

Police increased their security forces to 1,200 officers in response to the Manchester attack. After an intensive search of the festival site, the fears of an imminent danger were not confirmed, and the festival was given the go-ahead to resume at 1:30 pm on Saturday. The evacuation came after three individuals, suspected of being members of a Salafist group, were detained but later released. One of the individuals had access to backstage areas.

Last year's Rock am Ring programme was curtailed by violent storms, and the country remains on high alert following a jihadist attack on a Christmas market in Berlin on December 19, 2016. The attack claimed 11 lives and wounded dozens. The region's interior minister defended the decision to evacuate the festival, stating that "we cannot take risks." The festival resumed on Saturday, with German band Rammstein as Friday night's headliners.

The Groupon Super Bowl commercial featuring a mock public service announcement about Tibet has caused controversy and potential consequences for the company's expansion plans in China. The ad, which features actor Timmothy Hutton, humorously turns into an advertisement for group-buying deals, but has offended viewers in both the U.S. and China.

Rumors have been circulating for weeks that Groupon, a fast-growing Internet company based in Chicago, is planning to expand into China, which has more Internet users than any other nation. Reports suggest that Groupon is in talks with Chinese Internet giant Tencent to partner and offer its services in China, with plans to employ 1,000 people within three months.

However, the Tibet ad may not please Chinese officials, who will need to approve any operations in the country. The ad was one of three the company aired during the Super Bowl, each of which makes fun of a different charitable cause. The charity associated with the Tibet ad is the Tibet Fund, an organization backed partially by the U.S. State Department.

The ad was reportedly posted on a Chinese video site after it aired in the U.S., but has since been taken down. Chinese Internet users have been disapproving of the ad, slamming it as a bad business move and criticizing the company for mixing business with politics.

Groupon has a history of philanthropy, as it started as a collective action and philanthropy site called ThePoint.com. In response to the criticism, Groupon has offered to match donations to charities associated with the causes it parodies.

The Super Bowl commercials were a mix of the best and worst, with Volkswagen being the biggest winner and Pepsi and Doritos peppering the Super Bowl with hit or miss adds. The worst commercials included a Careerbuilder.com ad featuring more monkeys, a Pepsi MAX commercial featuring a man addicted to Doritos cheese dust, and a GoDaddy.com ad featuring a woman in a bikini.

Overall, the Groupon Tibet ad has caused controversy and potential consequences for the company's expansion plans in China, as it may not please Chinese officials and has been criticized by Chinese Internet users. The ad was one of three the company aired during the Super Bowl, each of which made fun of a different charitable cause. The charity associated with the Tibet ad is the Tibet Fund, an organization backed partially by the U.S. State Department. Groupon has offered to match donations to charities associated with the causes it parodies in response to the criticism.

Cesar Millan, the star of the Nat Geo WILD Channel's "Cesar 911" and former host of "Dog Whisperer With Cesar Millan," is currently under investigation for animal cruelty following a complaint made against his Santa Clarita, California, dog psychology center. The complaint involved a dog attacking and injuring a pig during a training session, as reported by TMZ.

Millan, a self-taught dog behaviorist, quickly rose to fame with his series "Dog Whisperer With Cesar Millan," which was broadcast in more than 80 countries worldwide from 2004 to 2012. "Cesar 911" premiered on the Nat Geo WILD Channel in 2014.

In response to the investigation, a Nat Geo WILD spokesperson issued a statement clarifying that Cesar took precautions, such as putting the dog on a long lead to assess its behavior, before making initial corrections and removing the leash. The pig that was nipped by the dog was tended to immediately afterward, healed quickly, and showed no lasting signs of distress.

However, critics argue that Millan's methods are inhumane and that he uses animals as bait, which is against the law. A complaint has been filed to Animal Control for animal cruelty, and people are being encouraged to come forward with concrete evidence of any abuse witnessed while working, volunteering, or as a trainee at Millan's dog psychology center.

The American Humane Association, responsible for the protection of animals during the filming of any movie or TV, has received complaints regarding an episode of a Nat Geo reality television series featuring Cesar Millan. They call on the entertainment industry to have American Humane Association on all of their productions with animals to ensure that all animals in entertainment are safe and humanely treated.

California State Law prohibits malicious and intentional maiming, mutilating, torturing, or wounding of animals, as well as causing unnecessary suffering or inflicting unnecessary cruelty upon animals. The law is also stated in the petition being circulated to demand that Cesar Millan shows be taken off the air. Critics argue that Millan's shows cause the public to imitate his behavior with their own dogs, leading to abuse in homes.

The document discusses the ongoing controversy surrounding NFL players protesting during the national anthem, with a focus on recent events during preseason games. President Donald Trump criticized the players for their protests, accusing them of being unable to define what they are protesting and suggesting they should be happy and cool. The NFL players, however, have been vocal about their protests, which began two seasons ago in opposition to racial injustice and police brutality.

On Thursday night, several players, including Philadelphia Eagles safety Malcolm Jenkins and Miami Dolphins wide receivers Kenny Stills and Albert Wilson, showed signs of protest during the national anthem. Jenkins and Eagles cornerback De'Vante Bausby raised their fists, while Stills and Wilson kneeled.

The NFL Players Association did not immediately return a request for comment. The protests have sparked controversy and led to the NFL approving a new policy in May that allows teams to fine players and other personnel who fail to stand during the national anthem. Enforcement of that policy has been put on hold as the league negotiates with its players over the controversy.

Critics argue that players are disrespecting the American flag and national anthem when they protest during the song, but many protesting NFL players argue that it is important to use their national platform to speak out against injustice, and that they have a right to free speech.

The protests began years ago, sparked by then-San Francisco 49ers quarterback Colin Kaepernick's refusal to stand for the anthem in 2016. Kaepernick, a free agent who went unsigned and did not play in the league last season, tweeted his support for the players who protested on Thursday night.

The issue gained significant attention last year when Trump labeled kneeling players as a "son of a bitch" and suggested they be thrown out of the league at a rally in Alabama. Trump's attention to the issue prompted more players to protest, turning the sports debate into a nationwide controversy.

Notable players such as New England Patriots quarterback Tom Brady have broken with the president on the issue, praising the protests in an interview with Oprah Winfrey during the offseason.

North Korean leader Kim Jong-Un has climbed Mount Paektu, the country's highest mountain, according to state-run media. Photos show a smiling and windswept Kim standing on the snow-covered peak, surrounded by troops. The mountain is considered sacred in Korean folklore and is a key part of propaganda glorifying the Kim family. Kim Jong-Un's father, Kim Jong-Il, is said to have been born on the mountain, although many historians believe he was born in Russia. The climb is seen as a significant event in the Kim dynasty's rule, which has been marked by an iron fist and a pervasive personality cult. Kim Jong-Un has made frequent public appearances across the country as part of an effort to portray himself as an energetic man of the people. North Korea has a troubled economy, with two-thirds of the population struggling to find food, according to the UN. The country has also been developing its nuclear weapons, with its last test taking place in February 2013. The regime has been criticized for spending large amounts of government money on the "supreme leader" and the advancement of his personality cult, while neglecting the needs of its people.

Josh Greenberg, the co-founder of Grooveshark and a prominent figure in Gainesville's student startup movement, was found dead in his home on Sunday at the age of 28. His death was reported by his girlfriend, Abby Mayer, who returned home to find his body. Police investigations found no evidence of injuries or drugs, and his mother, Lori Greenberg, stated that he had never been sick and was not prescribed any medication.

Greenberg and Sam Tarantino, both from the Tampa area, founded Grooveshark as 19-year-old freshmen at the University of Florida in March 2006. At its peak, the company had up to 40 million users a month and 145 employees. The company shut down in April 2015 after losing a copyright-infringement lawsuit filed by major record labels and reaching a settlement with the industry.

Greenberg was widely regarded as a mentor to budding entrepreneurs and computer programmers, helping people get started in the tech industry through Grooveshark University classes, the Summer with the Sharks internship program, and as a partner in the Founders Pad business incubator. He was a founding member of the Gainesville Area Chamber of Commerce's Gainesville Technology Council.

Greenberg was working on another music-related mobile application and was involved in the Gainesville Dev Academy, which launched this summer to offer training in computer programming. He started MaidSuite with Student Maid founder Kristen Hadeed to provide an online scheduling application for cleaning companies and other service providers.

The cause of Greenberg's death remains unknown, with the medical examiner's autopsy finding no explanation. Toxicology results will take two or three months. Greenberg is survived by his younger brother, Jacob, and grandparents, Jerry and Sandy Greenberg. A memorial service is being arranged in Gainesville.

Greenberg was known for his keen intellect, wonderful sense of humor, and love for animals. He was a vegetarian for ethical reasons and adored his three cats. Duncan Kabinu, a friend of Greenberg, described him as "a legend" and said the community wants to continue his legacy by continuing to mentor and contribute back.

A 20-year-old man in Thailand, identified as Wuttisan Wongtalay, filmed himself killing his 11-month-old daughter on Facebook Live before taking his own life at an abandoned hotel in Phuket province. The incident occurred after an argument with his wife, and the video was made inaccessible by Facebook late Tuesday. The company expressed condolences to the family and pledged a review of its processes following the incident. The footage was also available on YouTube but was removed after being alerted by the BBC. The incident comes less than two weeks after a man in Cleveland, Ohio, broadcast himself on Facebook Live shooting a man to death. Facebook founder Mark Zuckerberg acknowledged the need to improve the platform's safety measures in response to the US killing. In Thailand, social media users reacted with anger to the footage, while offering condolences to the family of the girl. Relatives picked up the bodies of the girl and her father from the hospital. The incident also highlights the global scope of the problem as Facebook pushes to further integrate itself into users' lives. Accidents and crimes have occasionally shown up on the platform, making it difficult for the company to patrol the content.

Scientists have made a significant breakthrough in heart disease treatment with a stem cell therapy that can partially repair damaged heart tissue. The treatment involves creating heart cells from the skin of a donor, who is carefully selected to be a genetic match for the recipient. Tests on monkeys showed that the freshly-made heart cells were quickly incorporated into damaged areas of the heart and helped the organ to pump more vigorously. However, the monkeys also developed unusual heart rhythms, indicating that more work is needed before the treatment can be considered safe enough for human trials.

Heart attacks are a leading cause of death in the developed world, with nearly 200,000 cases occurring annually in the UK alone. While most patients survive, many are left with tissue damage that affects the heart's functionality. One idea for treating heart attack survivors is to take skin cells from the patient and convert them into pumping heart cells. The advantage of this approach is that the heart cells will not be rejected by the immune system, but the procedure is time-consuming and expensive.

In the latest work, researchers in Japan took a different approach. They induced heart attacks in five macaques and then treated the damage with heart cells created from the skin of a donor monkey. The donor was selected to be a close genetic match, but the recipients still needed drugs to prevent their bodies from rejecting the cells. The scientists injected the monkeys with 400m lab-made heart cells and found that they replaced about 16% of the damaged tissue. The new cells were wired up with healthy ones in the heart and over 12 weeks started to help the organ to pump more strongly. However, all of the monkeys developed unusual heart rhythms after the therapy.

The scientists are now trying to understand the precise cause of the abnormal heart rhythms, but they are hopeful that they can be managed. The work is exciting because it is a step towards the possibility of repairing a damaged heart following a heart attack. Currently, the only long-term option for these patients is heart transplantation, but there are not enough donors to meet the current demand. Ideally, immune rejection would be eliminated if the cells could be derived from the same patient, but this is costly and time-consuming at a time when the patient requires immediate treatment. Another concern is that the incomplete integration of the transplanted cells could result in irregular heartbeats, which can be deadly.

The Japanese team's work is a significant step forward, and they hope to continue refining the treatment to make it safer and more effective for human trials. The arrhythmias seen in the study were not fatal and are expected to decrease with time. Clinical strategies for preventing sudden cardiac death from arrhythmia may be necessary as adjunct therapy for some months after implantation.

The White House recently corrected a transcript from President Donald Trump's Monday press conference, where he insulted ABC News reporter Cecilia Vega during a Rose Garden event marking the trade deal agreement between the U.S., Canada, and Mexico. Trump initially said, "I know you’re not thinking, you never do," to Vega, who was waiting for a microphone. Vega responded, "I’m not, thank you, Mr. President," and later asked a question about Supreme Court nominee Brett Kavanaugh that Trump initially refused to answer. The exchange went viral online, with Vega tweeting, "#FirstAmendment." The initial transcript, released several hours after the press conference, incorrectly quoted Trump as saying, "I know you're not thanking. You never do." The White House later corrected the transcript to reflect the accurate quote.

On Friday, a bug on Facebook caused a memorial banner to appear on the profile pages of many users, including CEO Mark Zuckerberg, incorrectly labeling them as deceased. The error was quickly rectified, and Facebook apologized for the incident. The memorial feature, introduced in 2015, allows users to opt for their account to be turned into a memorial page upon their death, where friends can leave messages and share memories. An alternative option is to have the account deleted after death. The confusion led to numerous posts from users reassuring their friends and family that they were indeed alive. The incident sparked humor among technology reporters and users, with some jokingly referring to it as a fitting end to a tumultuous week, which included the presidential election. Facebook has stated that memorialized accounts can only be requested after a person has passed away.

In a recent development, North Korea has threatened to conduct a new form of nuclear test, escalating tensions following the UN Security Council's condemnation of its recent ballistic missile launch. The North Korean foreign ministry, in a statement released on the official Korean Central News Agency (KCNA), accused the UN of ignoring US nuclear war exercises and condemning North Korea's self-defensive rocket launching drills. The statement also warned of a new form of nuclear test for bolstering up North Korea's nuclear deterrence, without providing specific details.

The threat comes after North Korea fired two medium-range Rodong ballistic missiles into the sea off the east coast of the Korean peninsula on Wednesday, which was followed by the UN's condemnation. This was North Korea's first firing of mid-range missiles since 2017 and marks a significant escalation in its missile program.

Analysts have suggested that North Korea may be preparing for multiple nuclear tests at its Punggye-ri nuclear test site, based on patterns of excavation at the site. If this is the case, it could indicate that North Korea is planning to conduct nuclear tests on a much more regular basis, posing a significant threat to regional and global security.

The UN and international community have condemned North Korea's nuclear and missile tests, calling for the country to abandon its nuclear weapons program and comply with UN resolutions. However, North Korea has continued to defy international pressure and has shown no signs of abandoning its nuclear ambitions.

The situation remains tense, and it is unclear how the international community will respond to North Korea's latest threat. The UN has warned that further nuclear tests by North Korea would be met with "stronger measures" to pressure the country to abandon its nuclear weapons program. The US and its allies have also reaffirmed their commitment to defend against any threats from North Korea.

In conclusion, the latest threat by North Korea to conduct a new form of nuclear test has raised tensions in the region and poses a significant threat to global security. The international community must continue to pressure North Korea to abandon its nuclear weapons program and comply with UN resolutions, while also preparing for the possibility of further nuclear tests by the country.

Mitt Romney, the presumptive Republican nominee for President, discussed gun control legislation during an interview on Monday, stating that the shooting in Aurora, Colorado was not a time to discuss politics associated with the event. Romney signed a law as Massachusetts governor that banned weapons like the AR-15, used in the shooting, but emphasized that it was a result of a combination of efforts from both sides of the gun control debate. Romney believes that the Second Amendment is the right course to preserve and defend and does not believe that new laws would make a difference in such tragedies. He stated that the challenge is not the laws, but individuals who are disturbed and commit unthinkable acts. Both Romney and President Obama have avoided discussing new gun control laws in the aftermath of the Colorado shooting. The interview took place after both campaigns paused their political activities following the tragedy, but Romney admitted that the pause was over. Romney criticized Obama's campaign for being negative, stating that he has not seen the healthy, important debate coming from the president's team. A recent study found that both campaigns were similar in their use of negative ads.

On November 29, 2016, a chartered airplane carrying the Brazilian first division soccer team Chapecoense crashed in a mountainous area outside Medellin, Colombia, resulting in the deaths of 71 people, with six survivors. The British Aerospace 146 jet, operated by charter company LaMia, was en route to Medellin for the first game of the Copa Sudamericana final against Atletico Nacional.

The crash occurred after the plane suffered an electrical failure and was in a holding pattern due to heavy rain and poor visibility. Authorities are investigating the possibility of the aircraft running out of fuel minutes before landing. The cockpit voice recorder and flight data recorder have been found and are being studied by experts.

The Chapecoense team had a fairy tale season, having worked its way into Brazil's top league for the first time in decades and advancing to the championship of one of South America's most prestigious tournaments. The loss of the team has been felt across the region, with South America's soccer federation canceling all scheduled matches in a show of solidarity, and Real Madrid and Barcelona clubs interrupting their training sessions for a minute of silence.

Three players were among the survivors, with Alan Ruschel reported in the most serious condition, facing surgery for a spinal fracture. Teammates Helio Zampier and Jakson Follmann also suffered multiple trauma injuries, and Follmann's right leg was amputated. A journalist and two Bolivian crew members were also among the survivors, with the journalist undergoing surgery.

LaMia, the charter company that operated the plane, is based in Bolivia and has a close relationship with several premier South American soccer squads. The plane involved in the crash had transported Barcelona forward Lionel Messi and Argentina's national team earlier in the month, as well as the national squads of Brazil, Bolivia, and Venezuela in the last three months.

The crash has sparked an outpouring of grief and support, with fans of the Chapecoense team gathering in Chapeco, Brazil, to mourn the loss of their beloved team. Brazilian President Michel Temer declared three days of official mourning, while FIFA President Gianni Infantino called it a "tragic loss."

The Chapecoense club is a modest team from a small city in southern Brazil, and the team's dream of soccer greatness was cut short by the tragic accident. The team's coaching staff had praised the airline, saying it brought them good fortune when it flew them to Colombia for the championship's quarterfinals, which they won.

The investigation into the crash is ongoing, with investigators looking closely at the reported electrical outage and the aircraft's fuel levels. The crash has raised concerns about air safety in South America, with retired Bolivian air force general Gustavo Vargas, president of the airline, saying, "I would be concerned that the pilots may have been cutting it too close."

The Sudbury Police Department has shared a humorous reminder about responsible Christmas tree transportation, following an incident where a vehicle was largely obscured by a large conifer. The incident occurred on Route 20, with the police department posting a photo of the incident on their Facebook page. The car's occupants received a warning in the spirit of the holidays, and the officer at the scene assisted in securing the tree more safely, marking it with caution tape. The police department shared the photo to emphasize the importance of moving all items, including Christmas trees, responsibly on vehicles during the holiday season.

The launch of myONE Perfect Fit by ONE® Condoms marks a significant shift in the U.S. market, offering 60 different condom sizes to address the long-standing issue of poor fit and discomfort. With combinations of 10 lengths and 9 widths, myONE aims to cater to a wider range of penis sizes, including those smaller and larger than what was previously available. The company pledges to give away 1 million free condoms to emphasize the importance of proper fit.

The need for better-fitting condoms stems from common complaints about existing condoms being too long, too short, too wide, or too tight. These issues can lead to loss of sensation, loss of erection, difficulty achieving orgasm, and an increased risk of unintended pregnancies and sexually transmitted infections (STIs). Surprisingly, previously available condoms properly fit only 12 percent of men.

myONE Perfect Fit addresses these issues by offering a range of 60 condom sizes, including 28 sizes larger than the leading XL condom and 27 sizes smaller than the average condom. The lengths range from 4.9 to 9.4 inches, while prior condoms available ranged from 6.7 to 8.3 inches in length. The circumferences available from myONE range from 3.5 to 5.0 inches, while prior condoms available ranged from 3.9 to 4.5 inches.

The development and introduction of myONE Perfect Fit have been a seven-year process, requiring extensive work among researchers, standards organizations, and ONE’s R&D and manufacturing experts. This effort resulted in updated testing standards and the eventual FDA clearance for myONE Perfect Fit in the United States.

To purchase myONE Perfect Fit condoms, customers use a FitKit or a measuring tape to measure their length and circumference, and receive a unique product code that corresponds to their myONE size. The FitKit comes as a printable measuring tool complete with instructions, downloadable at www.myonecondoms.com.

The public health impact of myONE Perfect Fit is significant, as it has the potential to increase condom use, reduce the number of unintended pregnancies, and decrease STI occurrences. The company is committed to bringing a smart solution to market by offering comfortable condoms at affordable pricing.

In a related study, researchers assessed men's erect penile dimensions in a sample of 1,661 men. The mean erect penile length was 14.15 cm, and the mean erect penile circumference was 12.23 cm. The self-reported erect penile dimensions in this study are consistent with other penile dimension research. The findings suggest that mode of getting an erection may influence erect penile dimensions and that how a man becomes erect for self-measurement may be associated with his erect penile length and/or circumference.

The launch of myONE Perfect Fit represents a historic shift in the condom industry, offering a more personalized and comfortable condom experience to a wider range of men. The public health implications are significant, as improved condom fit and comfort may lead to increased condom use, reduced unintended pregnancies, and decreased STI occurrences.

David Neevel, a physicist from Portland, has built a machine to remove the creme from Oreos due to his dislike for it. The machine, called the OSM, is made from scrap aluminum, wood, a hatchet, and floss, and was constructed in a Portland garage. The OSM splits the Oreo, collects the cookie halves, and removes the creme using a router table. The machine took about two weeks to build and was commissioned by Oreo as part of their "Cookies vs. Creme" campaign. Three other inventors were also commissioned by Oreo to create concepts, with the next one set to be unveiled later this week.

In a separate study, researchers examined 45-year trends in time-use, household management (HM) and energy expenditure in women. The study found a significant decrease in the time allocated to HM by women, with non-employed women decreasing by 16.6 hours per week and employed women by 6.7 hours per week. This decrease in HM resulted in a considerable decrement in household management energy expenditure (HMEE), with non-employed women experiencing the largest decrease of 10.5 MJ per week (1.5 MJ per day; 2518 kcal per week; 360 kcal per day). In parallel with the decrement in HMEE was a substantial increase in the amount of time spent in screen-based media use, with women spending more time in screen-based media use than in cooking, cleaning, laundry, and leisure time physical activity (LTPA) combined by the 1990s. The study suggests that the reallocation of time from active behaviors such as HM to sedentary activities has significant health consequences, particularly for future generations.

A 15-year-old girl from Mississauga, Ontario, was cautioned by the Ontario Provincial Police (OPP) after she called 911 to report that her parents had "forced" her to go on vacation with them. The incident occurred at a rental cottage in Trent Hills, approximately 180 kilometers northeast of Toronto. Police responded to the scene, but determined that there was no real emergency, stating that it was a case of a teenager being a teenager. The girl's call tied up police resources, potentially impacting the safety of others in the community who were in real need of assistance. The girl was cautioned for misuse of the emergency number. The incident has sparked collective sighs and eye rolls from teenagers across Canada.

In an unexpected turn of events, Miranda Levy, a soon-to-be bride, unintentionally revealed her pregnancy along with her engagement news on Facebook. In her excitement, she posted a picture of herself with her fiancé and her new engagement ring. However, a pregnancy test tucked away in the lower left corner of the picture caught the attention of her friends, who began asking if she was pregnant. Unaware of the oversight, Miranda was initially confused but soon realized the error and confirmed the double joyous news. The incident serves as a reminder for social media users to carefully check and crop photos before posting to avoid such embarrassing situations. Congratulations, Miranda, on your upcoming marriage and new addition to the family!

A man named David Weaver, aged 37, from Nelson, B.C, is wanted by Toronto police for two separate incidents that occurred on October 12. The first incident took place at Medieval Times where Weaver allegedly assaulted a 34-year-old man outside the venue after being asked to leave for being disruptive. The victim suffered serious injuries, including black eyes and a broken tooth.

Later that same evening, Weaver is suspected of skinny-dipping in the shark tank at Ripley's Aquarium of Canada. Security footage shows him entering the aquarium, taking off his clothes, climbing over the security barrier, and jumping into the water. He swam with the sharks for a while before being escorted out. No injuries were reported to the man, animals, or patrons.

Ripley’s Aquarium of Canada is cooperating with authorities and is willing to press all appropriate charges once Weaver is apprehended. Videos captured by onlookers show the naked man swimming in the tank as sharks darted by. Weaver is described as 35-40 years old, five-foot-ten, and 220 pounds. He has a shaved head, a dark goatee, a tattoo on his lower leg, and is missing a front tooth. He was last seen wearing a dark hoodie, dark jeans, a green teal T-shirt, and grey and white shoes. Police say he may be driving a green Dodge Caravan with the British Columbia license plate number PL120G.

Anyone with information is asked to contact police at 416-808-5200 or call Crime Stoppers anonymously at 416-222-TIPS (8477). The aquarium incident has received significant attention, with videos of the event receiving over 5,000 views on YouTube. The aquarium was hosting a monthly Friday Night Jazz event at the time of the incident. The Toronto Police Service and the Toronto Star are investigating the incidents.

Amy Winehouse, the troubled singer, died accidentally due to alcohol toxicity at her north London home in 2011, a second inquest has confirmed. The coroner, Dr Shirley Radcliffe, recorded a verdict of misadventure, matching the original inquest in October 2011. The inquest was reopened due to irregularities in the first inquest, where the deputy coroner, Suzanne Greenaway, was found to lack the required qualifications.

On the day of her death, Winehouse was described as her usual bubbly self, and there was no evidence of illicit drugs in her system. However, the level of alcohol in her blood was over five times the drink-drive limit, and two empty vodka bottles were found in her bedroom.

The court heard that Winehouse had a history of struggling with an eating disorder, where she made herself sick. Her GP, Dr Christina Romete, stated that Winehouse had specifically said she did not want to die the night before her death.

The move to hold another inquest came after an investigation found that Suzanne Greenaway, who oversaw the first inquest, did not have the correct qualifications for the role. Dr Andrew Reid, the senior coroner for the inner north London area and Greenaway's husband, resigned from his position after disciplinary proceedings were launched against him.

None of Winehouse's family were present at the second inquest, as they were happy with the first inquest, which they said had brought them some relief to have finally found out what had happened to Amy.

On Tuesday afternoon, a woman in her 80s committed suicide using a toxic chemical, sodium azide, at the historic Berkeley City Club. The incident resulted in the evacuation of hotel guests and residents, and the closure of Durant Avenue for several hours. The woman, who lived on the third floor, left a suicide note warning authorities of the hazardous situation. It remains unclear if the substance contaminated the entire building or just her unit. The Berkeley Police are investigating the incident, and the coroner is yet to arrive on the scene. The Berkeley City Club has confirmed that no members or staff were harmed. The club is a hotel and private social club with an indoor swimming pool, restaurant, hair salon, and meeting spaces. This story is ongoing, and updates will be provided as more information becomes available.

Hayden Kennedy, a renowned 27-year-old alpinist, tragically took his life on October 7, 2017, following a fatal avalanche that claimed the life of his girlfriend, Inge Perkins. The incident occurred while they were skiing near Bozeman, Montana.

Kennedy was a highly accomplished climber, known for his numerous first ascents and bold climbs. He grew up climbing with his father, Michael Kennedy, a renowned alpinist, and began taking the sport seriously at age 13 or 14. His passion for climbing led him to skip college and focus on his climbing career.

Some of Kennedy's notable achievements include the first ascent of Carbondale Short Bus (5.14), an all-free ascent of the Hallucinogen Wall (VI 5.13+ R) in Colorado’s Black Canyon, and climbing new routes up K7 and the South Face of the Ogre (Baintha Brakk). His career highlights also include the controversial removal of over 100 bolts from Cerro Torre's Compressor Route in Patagonia.

Kennedy's death was preceded by a letter his father published in the Alpinist, praising his son's decision to remove the bolts and reminding climbers to abide by their ideals. In a final essay published on the climbing blog Evening Sends, Kennedy contemplated climbing, loss, and mortality, acknowledging the fleeting nature of friends, summits, and crux moves in the sport.

Kennedy's passing has left a profound impact on the climbing community, with many expressing their grief and admiration for the humble and talented alpinist. His legacy will continue to inspire future climbers, and his story serves as a poignant reminder of the risks and rewards of pursuing one's passion.

In Atlanta, a father named Lester Chaney experienced a harrowing incident when his car was carjacked at a gas station, with his one-year-old twin daughters, Nadia and McKenzie, inside. The incident occurred on a Saturday night at a Texaco gas station on Martin Luther King Jr. Drive. Chaney had trouble with his card at the gas pump, prompting him to go inside to pay. Unfortunately, he left his car running, which allowed a suspect to quickly jump in and drive away with the children in the backseat.

The suspect was later found to have abandoned the car in an apartment complex parking lot, with McKenzie still in her car seat in the back. Nadia, however, was removed from the car and left in a wooded area. Remarkably, both girls slept through the entire ordeal. The police were able to locate the girls a quarter of a mile away from the initial carjacking site. The incident has understandably left Chaney shaken, and he expressed his relief that his daughters were safe.

In a campaign rally in Buffalo, New York, Republican presidential front-runner Donald Trump made a mistake by referring to the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks as "7-11." Trump, who is leading the Republican nomination race by a significant margin in New York, spoke passionately about revamping trade agreements, repealing Obamacare, and restoring jobs to Buffalo and other parts of New York. He criticized his opponents, including "Lyin' Ted Cruz" and "Crooked Hillary Clinton," and blamed politicians for the economic struggles in New York, particularly the loss of manufacturing jobs. Trump's speech was well-received by the crowd, with boisterous cheers for his proposals and his promise to build a wall at the Mexican border. The event took place on the eve of the New York primary, the biggest prize yet in the 2016 presidential nominating process. The mistake in Trump's speech about the 9/11 attacks has since been widely criticized.

In Indianapolis, a pet pig named Dumplin is being credited for potentially scaring away home intruders. The back door of the home was broken into, but the thieves did not steal anything, leading police to speculate that they may have been deterred by the presence of Dumplin. The homeowner, a single mother, was fortunate that her family was not home during the break-in. Dumplin was rescued by its owner earlier this year, and the family recently moved into the east side neighborhood where break-ins are common. The homeowner is relieved that Dumplin was not harmed during the crime and encourages others to consider adopting pet pigs. The police are still searching for the suspects.

In a landmark case, serial killer Stephen Port has been sentenced to spend the rest of his life in prison for the murder of four young gay men he drugged and raped before dumping their bodies near his east London flat. The 41-year-old chef, who had a fetish for sex with unconscious boyish-looking men, was convicted of the murders of Anthony Walgate, a 23-year-old fashion student from Hull, Gabriel Kovari, 22, originally from Slovakia, Daniel Whitworth, 21, a chef from Kent, and Jack Taylor, 25, a forklift driver from Dagenham.

Sentencing Port to a whole-life order, Mr. Justice Openshaw said: “I accept his intention was only to cause really serious harm rather than cause death but he must have known and foreseen there was a high risk of death, the more so after the death of Anthony Walgate, the first victim.”

The judge said: “The murders were committed as part of a persistent course of conduct of the defendant surreptitiously drugging these young men so that he could penetrate them while they were unconscious. A significant degree of planning went into obtaining the drugs in advance and in luring the victims to his flat. Having killed them by administering an overdose, he dragged them out into the street in one case, or took them to the churchyard in the other cases, and abandoned their bodies in a manner which robbed them of their dignity, and thereby greatly increased the distress of their loving families.”

The judge highlighted Port’s attempt to cover up two of his murders with a fake suicide note as “wicked and monstrous”. All four men died after being given fatal overdoses of the date-rape drug GHB, also known as G or liquid ecstasy. Port was convicted of 22 offences against 11 men, including drugging and sex offences against seven men who survived their encounters with him.

Despite striking similarities between the four murders, which were carried out over 15 months, the Metropolitan police failed to link them until the family of Taylor, his final victim, forced them to re-examine all the deaths. The Taylor family are planning to sue the force, and believe Port would not have been stopped if they had not fought for a full investigation.

The Independent Police Complaints Commission is investigating the Met’s initial response to the murders, including whether “discrimination played any part in actions and decisions”.

The public gallery at the Old Bailey court was packed, and all the members of the jury had returned to court to hear the sentencing. Ahead of sentencing, Jonathan Rees QC, prosecuting, read aloud to the court from victim impact statements. Relatives of Walgate described their “devastation”. His mother said her son was clever, funny and talented and wanted to be a famous fashion designer. Port had not only destroyed their family, but had destroyed his own, she said.

Kovari’s brother, Adam, said the impact on his family of the loss of his only brother could “hardly be described in words”, said Rees. His murder had “changed their lives for ever”. Adam Whitworth, father of Daniel Whitworth, described living two parallel lives, where grief tainted everyday life. Friends had told him that “the light had gone out of his eyes”, said Rees, and he had a “life sentence of grief”. His partner and Daniel’s stepmother, Amanda Pearson, said she had become “bitter and cynical”, that the “rich and fulfilling life ahead of us with Dan has been stolen from us”. It had been painful for the family when they had first wrongly been told he had taken his own life, Rees said.

Taylor’s family said their lives had been destroyed, and they had had to suffer the “devastating effect” of his body being exhumed. They endured endless sleepless nights, and family members had taken time off work sick. The loss of the son, brother, uncle, brother-in-law had left “a black hole that will never be filled”.

Port’s family later said they continued to believe he was innocent, ITV news reported. Speaking anonymously to the broadcaster, Port’s mother said: “I know he’s my son – he’s a kind boy.

“He said all along, ‘I didn’t murder anyone mum,’ he said. Honest truth. ‘I didn’t murder anyone’ - that’s what he told me last Sunday on the telephone.”

David Etheridge QC, for Port, said in mitigation that at that period in Port’s life, he had descended into a “vortex” of drug-taking, where “gratification of his sexual life was central”. Port’s fetish for sex with drugged young men had “graduated to fixation, and fixation to compulsion”. He added the prosecution had not alleged “any intent to kill these young men”. The premeditated planning “was to drug to unconsciousness and not to end someone’s life”, said Etheridge.

As Port was convicted, Stuart Cundy, a police commander who leads the Met’s specialist crime and operations unit, offered personal letters of apology to the victims’ families for the missed opportunities to catch Port sooner. During the trial it emerged that Port, a bus depot canteen chef, had been arrested and charged for lying about how the body of his first victim, Walgate, came to be found dumped outside the communal entrance to his flat in Barking, east London, in June 2014. Port was bailed. He went on to murder his second and third victims, Kovari and Whitworth, in August and September 2014. Their bodies were found within three weeks, by the same dog walker, propped up in a sitting position in a graveyard near his flat.

As part of an elaborate cover-up, Port faked and planted a suicide note purporting to have been written by Whitworth claiming he had taken his own life by overdosing on GHB in guilt over accidentally giving Kovari a fatal dose of the drug during sex. The note, which was taken at “face value” by investigating officers, included the line: “BTW, please do not blame the guy I was with last night, we only had sex, then I left. He knows nothing of what I have done.” Had police attempted to trace that “guy’, which they did not, it could have led them to Port.

In a significant turn of events, the Miami Dolphins have terminated the contracts of offensive line coach Jim Turner and head trainer Kevin O'Neill following the release of an independent investigation report on misconduct in the team's locker room. The report, conducted by Ted Wells, detailed instances of language and behavior that were against the Dolphins' core values. The team's owner, Stephen Ross, conducted an internal review and concluded that both Turner and O'Neill exhibited poor judgment.

Turner, who was not scheduled to attend the annual pre-draft event in Indianapolis, has been under scrutiny due to his involvement in the harassment of Miami players, as detailed in the report. He was accused of tolerating and even participating in the harassment, lying to investigators, and attempting to convince Jonathan Martin to publicly defend teammate Richie Incognito.

A new study by Pecan Street Research Institute challenges the conventional wisdom that solar panels in the Northern Hemisphere should face south for optimal energy production. The study, conducted in Austin, Texas, found that west-facing solar panels produced 2% more electricity during a normal day and 49% more during peak demand hours (3-7pm). West-facing panels reduced peak energy usage by 65%, compared to 54% for south-facing panels.

The study suggests that west-facing panels are more effective due to lifestyle factors, as they capture solar energy late in the afternoon, a time when most people turn on their air conditioning. The findings could significantly impact the residential solar market, particularly for homeowners with east-west roof pitches who were previously thought to be poor candidates for solar.

However, the study was conducted during summer months, and its results may vary during winter when the sun sets earlier. The study has not been publicly released, but it's hoped that it will prompt utility companies to reconsider their opposition to west-facing panels. The study is not the first to suggest that west-facing panels may be more effective, but the precise quantification could motivate both consumers and utilities to fine-tune their use of solar installations.

The benefits of adjusting solar panel orientation vary depending on the region, and the structure of incentives provided by utility companies also plays a role in consumer decisions. The study raises the point that testing solar panel performance in practice is important, rather than assuming that angling south is always the best approach.

On May 17, 2018, it marks one year since Robert Mueller was appointed as the special counsel to investigate any links between the Russian government and individuals associated with President Donald Trump's campaign. Mueller's appointment followed Trump's decision to fire FBI Director James Comey, who was leading the initial investigation. Allegations arose that Trump had asked Comey to scale back the probe into former National Security Adviser Michael Flynn.

Mueller, a Marine veteran who received a Purple Heart during the Vietnam War, served as FBI director from 2001 to 2013 and has a career spanning both the public and private sectors. He left his position at the law firm WilmerHale to take on the special counsel role.

In its first year, the Mueller investigation has been tight-lipped about its activities, primarily focusing on indictments and plea deals. The investigation has obtained five guilty pleas and multiple indictments. The team has faced criticism from Trump and his allies, who claim partisan bias and label the investigation a "disgusting, illegal, and unwarranted witch hunt."

The investigation's endgame could involve complex legal decisions about whether presidents can be subpoenaed or indicted, and whether Trump can fire Mueller or use pardons to hinder the probe.

Mueller's team consists of 17 attorney staff members, with at least 12 registered Democrats, two unaffiliated, and the status of two others remains unconfirmed. Mueller himself is a registered Republican in the District of Columbia.

The investigation has produced several key developments, including indictments against former Trump campaign officials Paul Manafort and Rick Gates, and guilty pleas from George Papadopoulos, Michael Flynn, and Dutch lawyer Alex van der Zwaan.

Legal experts suggest that being president does not offer blanket protection against a subpoena, but there are enough gaps in legal precedent that Trump's team could raise serious legal challenges. The question of whether Mueller can indict Trump remains unresolved, with widespread assumptions among legal experts that courts would rule against the idea of prosecuting a sitting president.

Trump's potential removal of Mueller falls into a legal gray area, with various scenarios possible, such as Rosenstein refusing to fire Mueller if he believes there has been no misconduct. Trump could also seek to rescind the Justice Department regulations or narrow Sessions' recusal to curb the scope of Mueller's probe.

Trump's use of pardons to get around the investigation is a complex issue, with questions surrounding whether a president can pardon themselves. A self-pardon could potentially supercharge impeachment efforts, and a blanket amnesty to protect a presidency has never been enacted before.

A 6-year-old autistic boy was found driving a miniature battery-powered ATV on the Bronx River Parkway in Mount Vernon, New York, on Sunday evening. The boy had initially gone missing from a city park, and his family reported him missing to the Mount Vernon police. Good Samaritans, including Ana Rubio and her husband Joel Reyes, helped to block the child from other traffic and safely bring him to the side of the parkway. The boy was then taken to Montefiore Mount Vernon Hospital for observation and was found to be okay. The incident is currently under investigation. The good Samaritans are being hailed as heroes for their quick actions in protecting the child.

The article announces the release of a new, Ford-licensed body shell for a 1967 Ford Mustang Convertible. This body shell, priced at $15,995, is the fourth reproduction classic Mustang body available to restorers, joining the '65 convertible, '67 fastback, and '69 fastback.
