Justice Sonia Sotomayor granted a temporary stay on Tuesday, preventing the Obama administration from enforcing a part of the Affordable Care Act that requires some religious-affiliated groups to provide health insurance coverage for birth control. The stay was granted at the request of the Little Sisters of the Poor, a Catholic order of nuns based in Colorado, and applies to them and other Roman Catholic nonprofit groups using the same health plan. The order was issued just hours before the requirement was to go into effect on New Year's Day, and the Obama administration has until Friday to respond to the Supreme Court.

The contraception requirement has been a contentious aspect of the health law since its announcement in mid-2011, with religious opponents of abortion objecting especially to the requirement for emergency contraception pills. The Obama administration has offered compromises, such as separate coverage not paid for by employers, but has refused to offer accommodations to secular businesses whose owners have religious objections to contraception.

The Little Sisters of the Poor operate nursing homes for low-income people in the United States and around the world. Without the stay, they would have faced large fines for non-compliance. The contraception requirement has led to a series of lawsuits, and last month, the Supreme Court agreed to hear a pair of cases on whether corporations may refuse to provide insurance coverage for contraception.

The Obama administration argues that the Little Sisters can opt out of the contraceptive coverage requirement by completing a self-certification form and providing it to the entity that administers their health benefits. However, the Becket Fund, which represents the nuns in the lawsuit, argues that the "accommodation" still violates their religious beliefs by forcing them to find an insurer who covers sterilization, contraceptive, and abortion-inducing drugs and devices.

The Obama administration has repeatedly defended the birth control requirement, with White House press secretary Jay Carney stating that "the president believes that no one, including the government or for-profit corporations, should be able to dictate those decisions to women." The pending Supreme Court cases, filed by Hobby Lobby and Conestoga Wood Specialties Corporation, challenge the constitutionality of the birth control mandate.

The Arctic Ocean is experiencing a significant transformation due to climate change, with warm waters from the Atlantic Ocean creeping up from below, contributing to the rapid melting of sea ice. This phenomenon, known as "Atlantification," is a new and powerful driver of melting, alongside losses due to rising air temperatures.

The study, published in Science, shows a "massive shift" in the behavior of the Arctic Ocean over a short time, with both the Amerasian and Eurasian basins losing ice at an alarming rate. Across the entire Arctic Ocean, ice is disappearing at a rate of 13% per decade since satellite data was available, and it has thinned by 1.7 meters since the 1970s.

Warm Atlantic waters, delivered by an offshoot of the Gulf Stream, have long been known to prevent ice formation north of Scandinavia. However, over the last decade, ice has also begun to disappear in the eastern side of the Eurasian basin, north of Siberia. This region used to have ice that persisted through the sunny summers, allowing several years of ice growth to accumulate. Now, the ice melts in summer, causing the total time without floating ice in the region to jump from less than 1 month per year to more than three.

To understand this new trend, scientists installed sensors on lines tethered to the floor of the Eurasian basin, called moorings, in 2002. When they retrieved data from the moorings in 2015, they found that the ocean had experienced a dramatic change over the previous decade, especially during the winter.

Between Norway and Greenland in the western Eurasian basin, Atlantic currents flow into the Arctic at a depth of 200 to 250 meters, about 4°C warmer than the surface water. In winter, cold air cools surface waters until they fall and mix with the warm waters below. That creates an overall warmer, well-mixed ocean over the top 250 meters, and one with little sea ice.

On the eastern side of the basin, however, the warm Atlantic waters were kept at bay until recently. The currents lurked at a depth of about 150 meters, but they didn't mix much with surface layers, because of a barrier called the cold halocline layer (CHL)—a boundary between salty deep waters and fresher water on top. Summer ice, as it forms, rejects salt, leading to the creation of dense, salty waters just below the ice. Those waters are heavier, and as they fall they create a highly stratified ocean.

The result is an increased "Atlantification" of the Arctic, where the eastern side of the Eurasian basin is becoming more like the western side. The top of the Atlantic water, according to one mooring, had risen from a depth of 140 meters in the winter of 2003–04 to a depth of 85 meters just a decade later. Without summer sea ice forming to establish the CHL, less ice forms.

Air temperatures were the main culprit for ice melting in the 2000s on the eastern side of the Eurasian basin. Now, however, researchers believe air temperatures and warm waters share the blame about equally. They also caution that the addition of massive flows of freshwater from Siberian rivers, bolstered by thawing permafrost, could affect the system. That new freshwater could encourage more sea ice to form on the basin, unless winds wash the new water away.

The changes in the Arctic Ocean could affect everything from how freshwater is stored and delivered to how the ocean itself responds to increasing acidity. The Arctic's eastern Eurasian Basin has been basically ice-free for nearly six years. The changes will have impacts on the people, plants, and animals that call the Arctic home, and could also create more geopolitical tension as resources previously locked under ice become available and shipping lanes open up.

Jian Ghomeshi, a popular host of the Q radio show on CBC, has been fired due to information received by the public broadcaster that precludes them from continuing their relationship with him. Ghomeshi has since announced that he is launching a $50-million lawsuit against the CBC, claiming breach of confidence and bad faith.

Three women have come forward with allegations of physical violence and sexual assault by Ghomeshi. The women allege that he struck them, bit them, choked them, covered their nose and mouth, and verbally abused them during and after sex. Ghomeshi has stated that he has been open with the CBC about the allegations and that he voluntarily showed evidence last week that everything he has done was consensual.

Ghomeshi has blamed a woman he describes as an ex-girlfriend for spreading lies about him and orchestrating a campaign with other women to "smear" him. In a Facebook posting, Ghomeshi wrote that he has "done nothing wrong" and that he engages in "adventurous forms of sex that included role-play, dominance and submission."

Over the past few months, the Star has approached Ghomeshi with allegations from three young women who say he was physically violent to them without their consent during sexual encounters or in the lead-up to sexual encounters. Ghomeshi, through his lawyer, has said he "does not engage in non-consensual role play or sex and any suggestion of the contrary is defamatory."

A fourth woman, who worked at CBC, has said that Ghomeshi told her at work: "I want to hate f--- you." Ghomeshi has paid homage to his "fantastic team" of journalists at Q in his Facebook posting, but it is unclear whether he will continue to work in the industry following the allegations against him.

The CBC has not responded to the allegations against Ghomeshi, citing both privacy rules related to the employer-employee relationship and Ghomeshi's intention to file a lawsuit. It is unclear whether any police reports have been filed in connection with the allegations.

Terry Ward's funeral service was a unique and memorable event that reflected his humorous and unconventional personality. His daughter, Jean Lahm, wrote an atypical obituary that went viral and was shared by numerous news outlets across the country. The obituary, filled with personal anecdotes and humor, perfectly encapsulated Ward's life and spirit.

Ward, who died on January 23 at the age of 71, worked for AT&T for 39 years, accumulating thousands of rolls of black electrical tape during his career. His obituary described him as a man who couldn't care less about material things and had a youthful spirit that could be compared to a 17-year-old, 37-year-old, or even a 7-year-old, depending on his mood.

The funeral service was held at Geisen Funeral Home in Crown Point, where Lahm works and where she said her final goodbye to her one-of-a-kind father. The service was filled with laughter and stories about Ward's life, including a story about a time when Lahm saw him working on a large box of wires while driving by his AT&T truck.

Lahm's obituary for her father was well-received by her family and has since been shared by many people across the country. It has brought attention to Ward's life and has made many people wish they had met him while he was alive. The obituary has also served as a reminder of the importance of laughter and celebrating life, even in difficult times.

Many people who did not know Ward attended his funeral as a result of his obituary, and some even sent flowers and donations in his memory. Lahm has expressed that this experience has made her think about the importance of living a life that is worth celebrating, and she hopes that Ward's obituary will inspire others to write obituaries that reflect their loved ones' personalities and lives in a memorable way.

Julian Assange, the founder of WikiLeaks, claims that his organization's revelations are just the tip of the iceberg, and more damaging information will be revealed in the future. In an exclusive interview with RT, Assange expressed concern about the hidden world that people are not aware of, and called on people not to believe that the information they receive from the media is all that is happening.

Assange also criticized Facebook, stating that it is the most appalling spying machine ever invented, and that users are doing free work for US intelligence agencies by adding their friends to the site. He claimed that Facebook, Google, and Yahoo have built-in interfaces for US intelligence to access user data.

In the interview, Assange also discussed the recent developments in the Middle East and North Africa, stating that there is genuine change in some parts of the Middle East, but that the situation in Libya is not normal and is driven by state actors. He also discussed the role of social networking sites like Facebook and Twitter in the revolutions in the Middle East, stating that Facebook in particular is a spying machine for US intelligence.

Assange also discussed the UK as a haven for extremism, with at least 35 Guantanamo detainees having passed through the UK. He stated that the UK is a haven for oligarchs and former regime dictators, and that there is a disconnect between the UK's support for free-speech activists and its support for people like the sons of Gaddafi.

Assange is currently awaiting extradition to Sweden to face sexual assault charges, and has been fighting extradition to the US. He stated that his No. 1 enemy is ignorance, and that media in general are so bad that the world would be better off without them. He also stated that nearly every war that has started in the past 50 years has been a result of media lies.

In a separate report, Assange called Facebook a spy tool for the US government, stating that it has the world's most comprehensive database about people, their relationships, their names, their addresses, their locations, their communications with each other and their relatives, all sitting within the United States, all accessible to US Intelligence. He stated that everyone should understand that when they add their friends to Facebook, they are doing free work for US intelligence agencies. Facebook has denied these claims, stating that they only respond to compulsory legal process.

On June 26, a family's outing off the coast of Noank, Connecticut, turned into a distressing event when their 8-month-old Shiba Inu puppy, Ryder, slipped out of his harness and fell into the ocean. The family, including owner Clare Shaw, spent hours searching for Ryder with the Coast Guard's assistance, but to no avail. They assumed Ryder had drowned. In an attempt to find Ryder, Shaw posted on Facebook, and her post was shared over 100 times.

Meanwhile, three friends, Phil Q. Bigelow, Patrick Jullarine, and Tommy Nahornick, were out fishing when they decided to rescue Ryder instead. They found the scared and shivering pup about a half mile out and brought him on board. They named him Nemo and took care of him until they could reunite him with his family.

Bigelow and his friends are not considered heroes, as they believe they were simply in the right place at the right time. Shaw and her family were overjoyed at Ryder's safe return and expressed their gratitude to everyone who helped find him. The incident underscores the power of social media and the caring community in Noank.

The Italian Supreme Court is set to announce its decision on the appeal of Amanda Knox, an American, and her Italian ex-boyfriend, Raffaele Sollecito, regarding their guilty verdicts for the brutal 2007 murder of Knox's British roommate, Meredith Kercher. The possible outcomes include confirmation of the verdicts, a new appeals round, or an acquittal.

In 2007, Meredith Kercher, a 21-year-old British student, was found dead in the apartment she shared with Knox in Perugia, Italy. Knox and Sollecito were convicted of the murder by a trial court in 2009 and spent four years in jail. However, they were acquitted in 2011 by a Perugia appellate court. The acquittals were overturned in 2013, and last year, an appeals court in Florence convicted the pair, sentencing Knox to 28 ½ years and Sollecito to 25 years.

If the high court upholds the Florence convictions, the prosecutor's office in Florence would issue an order to execute the sentences. For Knox, the situation is more complicated due to the extradition process. If the high court orders a new trial or acquits, it would be a significant development in the long-running case that has captivated audiences on both sides of the Atlantic.

Recently, one of the civilian jurors on the panel that convicted the pair in the Florence appellate case gave an interview suggesting there was not enough evidence for such a severe conviction, potentially indicating that the guilty finding was not unanimous. However, this is unlikely to have a bearing on the decision of the high court.

The decision of the Italian Supreme Court is expected on Wednesday, with potential implications for Knox and Sollecito's future and the course of the case.

"Everybody's Fine," starring Robert De Niro, is a remake of the 1990 Italian film "Stanno Tutti Bene." De Niro plays Frank, a widowed retiree who travels across America to visit his four adult children, only to find that each is hiding secrets and unhappiness. The film's plot revolves around Frank's journey and his discovery of his children's lies.

However, the film has been criticized for its lack of authenticity, with characters and emotions feeling forced and inauthentic. De Niro's performance is strenuous, and the film's syrupy score adds to the overall feeling of artificiality.

One of the film's most notable flaws is its portrayal of Frank, who is supposed to be a simple man but is shown to be unworldly to the point of absurdity. For example, Frank is shown carrying his rolling bag instead of pulling it, despite the fact that he worked in the telephone industry.

The film has also been criticized for its Americanization of the original Italian film, with a British director at the helm and a cast of American actors delivering trite and shallow performances. The film's message about the need for truthfulness rings hollow, as the characters and situations feel predictable and unoriginal.

Overall, "Everybody's Fine" is a disappointing film that fails to live up to its potential. The film's lack of authenticity, predictable plot, and shallow characters make it a missed opportunity for both De Niro and the filmmakers.

The Trump administration is facing a lawsuit from Twitter over an attempt to unmask the user behind the anti-Trump account @ALT_uscis. Twitter argues that the request for personal information, including login details, phone number, mailing address, and IP address, is a threat to free speech and infringes on political speech protected by the First Amendment. The account, which has over 40,000 followers, claims to represent dissenting members of US Citizenship and Immigration Services and has been critical of the Trump administration's immigration policies.

The lawsuit names several individuals from the Department of Homeland Security and Customs and Border Protection as defendants. Twitter contends that the request for user information lacks sufficient legal authority and that unmasking the account would have a chilling effect on free speech, particularly on other "alternative agency" accounts that have emerged to voice dissent against government policies. The American Civil Liberties Union has pledged to support Twitter in the case.

The @ALT_uscis account, which has seen a surge in followers since the news of the lawsuit, has been posting criticism of the administration for weeks. The account has been active since Trump's inauguration, and it is unclear whether it is operated by a government employee or not. The Department of Homeland Security and the White House have declined to comment on the matter.

Twitter has a history of litigating in favor of user privacy and has previously challenged government demands for information on its users. The lawsuit is currently pending in the Northern California District Court.

The High Court of England and Wales has ruled against the extradition of Lauri Love, a British-Finnish hacker accused of breaking into US government websites, to the United States. The court's decision was based on concerns about Love's mental health and the conditions he would face in US prisons, which were deemed to pose a risk of suicide.

Lauri Love, who lives in Suffolk and has Asperger syndrome and severe depression, had been accused of hacking into US government websites between October 2012 and October 2013 and stealing data. His lawyers argued that he should be tried in the UK instead of being extradited, citing the risk of suicide and the potential for inhumane treatment in US prisons.

The court heard evidence from psychiatrists who work in the US prison system and questioned the adequacy of safeguarding procedures in US prisons. The judges also raised concerns about the possibility of Love being held in solitary confinement and facing a jail sentence of up to 99 years in the US.

The Crown Prosecution Service (CPS), which acts on behalf of the US authorities in the case, has 14 days to decide whether or not to appeal the decision to the Supreme Court. If the CPS does not appeal, it will be up to the CPS to prosecute Love in the UK for the alleged offenses.

Lauri Love expressed relief and hope that his case would set a precedent for the future, stating that he hoped it would help spur discussion about how people with mental health issues are handled by the justice system. His supporters had gathered outside the Royal Courts of Justice before the hearing, carrying placards declaring "Free Love" and "Trial at home."

The ruling was welcomed by human rights groups and lawyers as a precedent for trying hacking suspects in the UK in the future. Emma Norton, the head of legal casework at Liberty, which intervened in the case, said: "We are delighted that the court has today recognised Lauri’s vulnerability, close family connections to the UK and the potentially catastrophic consequences of extraditing him." She added that the case could have been prosecuted in the UK and it was shameful that Lauri and his family had been put through this terrible ordeal.

Nick Vamos, a solicitor at the law firm Peters and Peters and a former CPS extradition specialist, said the judgment would mean that US and UK prosecutors would need to be very careful in future about how they decide who should prosecute cases of concurrent jurisdiction, and would have to focus far more than previously on a suspect’s connections to the UK.

The article discusses the concerns of a professor at the University of Texas, Lisa Moore, regarding the new law that allows the concealed carry of guns in dorms, classrooms, and buildings at state universities and community colleges in Texas. Moore is a founder of Gun-Free UT, a group that formed in response to the controversial campus-carry bill that was passed in May. The law makes Texas the eighth state to allow firearms on campus.

Moore and others in Gun Free UT hope to influence how the university system applies the new statute and keep weapons out of classrooms, dorms, and offices. They argue that guns in classrooms could lead to a grave shift in how students learn and teachers educate, as the classroom is a safe space where students should be able to become uncomfortable with certain ideas without fear of violence.

Moore shares personal experiences where she has faced acts of vandalism and a disruptive student with mental illness, and how the presence of guns in the classroom would have made these situations more dangerous. She also expresses concern that the law will lead to self-censorship and a dulling of provocative lessons.

The article also mentions Daniel S. Hamermesh, the Sue Killam Professor Emeritus of economics at the University of Texas at Austin, who has decided to stop teaching in Texas after guns become legal in his classroom due to the heightened risk of a disgruntled student bringing a gun into the classroom and starting shooting.

The article concludes by discussing the opposition to the law from faculty members, students, and parents, and the efforts of Gun Free UT to gather signatures on an anti-campus carry petition and hold anti-campus carry forums on campus. The article also mentions other faculty members who have spoken out against the campus carry law, such as Javier Auyero, the Joe R. and Teresa Lozano Long Professor of Latin American Sociology at Austin, and David Smith-Soto, a senior lecturer of multimedia journalism at the University of Texas at El Paso.

In this summary, the focus is on the escalating tension between Israel and Iran over Iran's nuclear program. Other news items in the document include reports of political developments in Syria, Egypt, Jordan, and the United States, as well as local incidents in Israel, such as the shooting down of a fighter jet by rebels and the arrest of extremist group members by Hamas. The media company Media Rights Capital (MRC) has set up an anonymous complaint hotline, crisis counselors, and sexual harassment legal advisors for the crew of Netflix's "House of Cards" following allegations of sexual harassment against Kevin Spacey. The allegations include inappropriate behavior, nonconsensual touching, and crude comments, with one former employee claiming that Spacey sexually assaulted him. The new accusations follow an explosive article published by BuzzFeed News, in which actor Anthony Rapp said Spacey made sexual advances towards him in 1985, when Rapp was 14 years old. Spacey has since apologized for his behavior, but did not respond to CNN's request for comment on the new allegations. Production of Season 6 of the series has been halted, and MRC has stated that they have consistently reinforced the importance of employees reporting any incident without fear of retaliation and have investigated and taken appropriate actions following any complaints. MRC also added that they will continue to investigate all claims brought to their attention. Other people with whom CNN spoke describe behavior similar to that recounted by the crew member, with colleagues never complaining out of fear of losing their jobs. The entertainment world is currently reckoning with the fallout from the Harvey Weinstein sexual harassment scandal.

TransCanada Corp, a Calgary-based pipeline company, has announced plans to launch a North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA) claim seeking over $15 billion in damages and file a lawsuit in the U.S. Federal Court in Houston, asserting that the U.S. government's denial of the Keystone XL pipeline permit exceeded its power under the U.S. Constitution. The Keystone XL pipeline, designed to transport Canadian oil sands and some Bakken crude to Gulf Coast refineries, was rejected by the Obama administration in November 2015, marking the first time a cross-border oil pipeline from Canada has been denied.

TransCanada expects to take a writedown of $2.5-2.9 billion after tax in the fourth quarter related to the Keystone XL permit denial. The company argues that the decision was politically motivated and unfair, violating the NAFTA requirement of fair and equitable treatment. In its notice to claim to arbitration under Chapter 11 of NAFTA, TransCanada's lawyers argue that environmental activists turned opposition to Keystone XL into a litmus test for politicians to prove their environmental credentials.

The U.S. government has yet to comment on the lawsuit, but the Liberal government in Canada expressed its disappointment when President Obama announced the decision. The rejection of Keystone XL was justified by activists who opposed the pipeline due to concerns about rising greenhouse gas emissions in the oil sands and local pollution from pipeline spills. However, TransCanada argues that the denial was not based on the merits of the project but was a symbolic gesture based on speculation about the perceptions of the international community regarding the administration’s leadership on climate change.

The lawsuit and NAFTA action come as Prime Minister Justin Trudeau is due to visit the U.S. for a state dinner in March, and as Washington, Ottawa, and Mexico work towards forging a North American energy and climate agreement. The Keystone XL pipeline has become a contentious issue in U.S. politics, with Democratic candidates opposing the project while most Republican candidates are in favor. The legal action is unlikely to get the pipeline built, but TransCanada appears to have a solid case in arguing that it was unfairly treated and that the decision was politically motivated.

A legislative committee in Wyoming is drafting a bill to allow firing-squad executions as the state faces difficulties in obtaining execution drugs. The state currently has no execution drugs, and the only inmate on Wyoming's death row is Dale Wayne Eaton, convicted for the 2004 murder of an 18-year-old woman. Meanwhile, in Utah, State Rep. Paul Ray plans to introduce a bill to bring back firing squads, citing it as the most humane way to execute prisoners.

In a separate development, Tennessee has become the first state to enact a law to reintroduce the electric chair without giving prisoners an option. The law was signed by Governor Bill Haslam, who faced no opposition from legal experts. However, it is expected to face legal challenges on the grounds of constitutional protections against cruel and unusual punishment.

The move towards alternative execution methods comes after a European-led boycott on drug sales to prisons, which has left several states struggling to obtain execution drugs. The Supreme Court has upheld the use of firing squads, the electric chair, and lethal injection in the past, but has never declared a method of execution unconstitutional on the grounds of cruelty.

The bills in Wyoming and Utah are a response to the botched lethal-injection execution in Oklahoma earlier this year. Thirty-two states currently have the death penalty, with Tennessee, Oklahoma, and Texas leading the way in executions.

On April 2, 2015, a tentative framework for a nuclear deal between Western powers and Iran was reached in Lausanne, Switzerland. The agreement aims to limit Iran's nuclear program in exchange for sanctions relief. However, several key issues remain unresolved, including Iran's research into next-generation centrifuges and the fate of its low-enriched uranium stockpile.

The agreement allows Iran to conduct "limited research and development" into advanced centrifuges, but the specifics of this research and the timeline for it remain unknown. Critics argue that this could potentially lead to a faster path to a nuclear weapon for Iran.

Another contentious issue is the disposition of Iran's low-enriched uranium, which is material that has been enriched much of the way toward the purity needed for a nuclear weapon. The agreement requires Iran to reduce its supply of nuclear material, but it does not specify how this will happen. Initially, Iran had agreed to export most of its low-enriched uranium, but it later toughened its position, insisting that it would merely dilute the uranium on its own soil to a form unsuitable for weapons use.

The framework deal requires Iran to uninstall more of its centrifuges than earlier reports had suggested would be required, subjects Iran to extensive international inspections, and mandates the redesign of a nuclear reactor so that its spent fuel can't be used to make a bomb.

However, the agreement is vague on several points, including the research into bomb-making that Iran is suspected of having conducted in the past. The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) has accused Iran of stonewalling on questions about its past research into nuclear weapons production, including bomb designs and detonators.

Key players in Congress, including Republicans and Democrats, are skeptical of the deal and want to review the details. There is a possibility of a push for new Iran sanctions or a measure requiring President Obama to get congressional approval, both of which the White House strongly opposes.

Leading lawmakers from both parties in Congress responded cautiously to the deal, demanding to review any final agreement but refraining from a vow to kill the accord. The committee's leadership is looking for ways to shape a bill that would gain broad approval in both parties.

The jousting between the White House and Congress is likely to continue for months, and pressure could mount on Republican leaders to toughen their stand. Negotiators must turn a framework into a detailed agreement by this summer, and legal sanctions imposed by the United States will not have to be lifted anytime soon, possibly not for years. The agreement is not likely to require action from Congress until the next presidential administration.

Some Democrats hailed the deal as a potential paradigm shift, while others tried to find a middle ground between embracing the accord and undermining it. The bill demands that the administration submit the full text of any agreement to Congress, including classified annexes. It would prohibit the removal of any congressional sanctions for 60 days after a final accord, and would require the president to certify Iranian compliance every 90 days. Without that certification, it mandates a quick return of sanctions.

The original version of the congressional review bill was written by Senator Bob Corker and Senator Robert Menendez, but Menendez's indictment on corruption charges and his decision to step down from the top Democratic spot on the Foreign Relations Committee elevated the more diplomatic voice of Senator Benjamin L. Cardin.

In general, the most senior Republicans, while cool to the deal, spoke in measured tones. However, some Republicans, such as Representative Michael McCaul, have expressed concerns about the deal's potential consequences for the U.S. and its allies in the region.

Overall, the framework deal is a significant step towards resolving the nuclear standoff between Iran and the West, but several key issues remain unresolved and are likely to be the subject of intense debate and negotiation in the coming months.

The U.S. 2014/15 total rice supplies are projected to increase by 2.8 million cwt due to higher production, with the first survey-based forecast of the U.S. 2014/15 rice crop at 228.8 million cwt, up nearly 21 percent from the previous year. The average all rice yield is forecast at 7,560 pounds per acre, up 91 pounds per acre from last month’s projection, but down nearly 2 percent from last year’s record. The U.S. 2014/15 total rice use is projected at 243.0 million cwt, 12 percent above the previous year.

In California, the historic drought is expected to cause a 25 percent drop in the production of specialty rice used in sushi, as farmers planted just 420,000 acres, about a quarter fewer than usual, due to water restrictions. The real pain will be felt at sushi restaurants, which will have to make a decision about whether to pass on the expected added cost of their product or see a reduction in profit margins.

On a global scale, the projected decrease in global 2014/15 total supply is greater than the drop in total use, resulting in a decrease in world ending stocks. Global production is lowered 2.1 million tons to 477.3 million, due primarily to forecast reductions for Bangladesh, Brazil, Indonesia, and India, offset partially by an increase in the United States. India’s 2014/15 rice crop is lowered 1.0 million tons to 103.0 million, attributed mostly to a slower rate of planting of the kharif rice crop due to the late start of the monsoon and below normal precipitation in some rice growing areas.

Overall, the sharp reduction in California rice planting is expected to result in higher prices for rice in the U.S. and potentially worldwide. However, rice growers in other parts of the country are expecting a bumper crop, with overall rice production in the U.S. expected to increase by as much as 21 percent this year.

In the aftermath of Mariah Carey's troubled performance on Dick Clark's New Year's Rockin' Eve, several conflicting reports have emerged. The performance, which took place on New Year's Eve, was marred by technical difficulties, with Carey reportedly unable to hear through her in-ear monitors.

Following the performance, Carey's manager, Stella Bulochnikov, issued a statement to Billboard, claiming that the in-ears were not working 10 minutes before the performance. Despite repeated attempts to alert the stage managers, they were reportedly reassured that the issue would be resolved once the show went live, which did not happen. Bulochnikov further claimed that Dick Clark Productions (DCP) did not cut the West Coast feed, and that the company's foremost concern is not artist-friendly, especially when the artist cut her vacation short for the event.

However, a production source denies these claims, stating that Carey had ample time to rehearse and chose not to. The source also claims that Carey used a body double to rehearse in her place earlier on New Year's Eve day, and that all technical issues were resolved on the production end. Audio producer Robert Goldstein of Maryland Sound International, who worked on the event, confirmed that all monitors and in-ear devices worked perfectly.

Following the performance, Carey took to Twitter to respond to the buzz surrounding her show, writing, "Shit happens. Have a happy and healthy new year everybody! Here’s to making more headlines in 2017." Josh Groban also weighed in on the situation, joking in a since-deleted tweet that "Any time one of the greatest voices of my generation lip syncs, an angel loses its wings." Groban later deleted the tweet and apologized, stating that it was made in humor but taken way more meanly than intended.

In conclusion, the incident has left many people questioning what happened and who is to blame. While Carey's camp claims that DCP set her up to fail, the production company denies these allegations and emphasizes their concern for the artist. The exact cause of the technical difficulties remains unclear, with conflicting reports from both sides.

The draft United Nations report warns that nations are not doing enough to combat climate change, with another 15 years of carbon emission inaction potentially making the problem impossible to solve with current technologies. The report suggests that future generations may need to develop technologies to suck greenhouse gases out of the atmosphere and store them underground to preserve the planet's livability. However, it is uncertain whether such technologies will ever exist at the necessary scale, and even if they do, they would likely be expensive.

The report criticizes governments for spending more money on subsidizing fossil fuels than on accelerating the shift to cleaner energy, thus encouraging continued investment in projects like coal-burning power plants that pose a long-term climate risk. The spread of technologies like solar power and wind farms is overtaken by rising emissions from fossil fuels, especially in fast-growing countries like China. Nuclear power, a significant source of low-carbon energy, is declining over time as a percentage of the global energy mix.

The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, a United Nations panel of climate experts, found that efforts to reduce emissions and adapt to climatic changes are lagging. The political willingness to tackle climate change is growing in many countries, but the rapid growth of fossil fuels is outpacing these efforts. Emissions appear to have fallen in some wealthy countries, but this is somewhat of an illusion due to the outsourcing of greenhouse gas emissions to countries like China.

The Kyoto Protocol, an international treaty meant to limit emissions, has not been as successful as intended. The treaty exempted developing countries from taking strong action, a decision that many experts now say was a mistake. Efforts are underway to negotiate a new international treaty to replace Kyoto, but it is unclear whether countries will agree on ambitious goals to limit emissions.

Business leaders will tackle many of the problems raised in the draft report next week at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland. The Obama administration is pushing for a new international treaty, but any treaty would have to be ratified by the Senate, and many Republicans and some coal-state Democrats are wary, fearing economic damage to the country.

The new report suggests that the real question is whether to take some economic pain now or more later. Nations have agreed to try to limit the warming of the planet to 3.6 degrees Fahrenheit above preindustrial levels. Even though it will be exceedingly difficult to meet, this target would still mean vast ecological and economic damage. However, having no target would risk catastrophic disruption. The report warns that if countries permit continued high emissions growth until 2030, the target will likely be impossible to meet.

A coalition of environmental groups is calling on President Barack Obama to put greater emphasis on combating climate change in his energy policy, pressing the administration as it weighs approving the Keystone XL pipeline. The administration's pursuit of increased domestic oil and gas production jeopardizes progress made toward lowering carbon pollution linked to climate change, according to the groups. The letter emerged as the U.S. State Department completes work on a final environmental assessment of TransCanada Corp.'s proposed $5.4 billion pipeline that would carry oil sands crude from Canada to refineries along the Gulf of Mexico coast. The summary of the news articles provided focuses on two main topics: the donation of $25 million by Facebook CEO Mark Zuckerberg and his wife, Priscilla Chan, to the CDC Foundation to aid in the fight against the Ebola epidemic, and the infection of a nurse at Texas Health Presbyterian Hospital who had cared for Thomas Eric Duncan, the first Ebola patient to die on U.S. soil.

The Zuckerberg-Chan donation will be used by the CDC's Ebola response effort in Guinea, Liberia, Sierra Leone, and other affected areas. The grant follows a previous donation of $9 million by Microsoft co-founder Paul Allen. The donation is being made from the couple's fund at the nonprofit Silicon Valley Community Foundation.

On Tuesday, the World Health Organization (WHO) reported that West Africa could see up to 10,000 new Ebola cases a week within two months, and confirmed that the death rate in the current outbreak is now 70 percent. The disease has killed more than 4,000 people, nearly all of them in West Africa. The WHO has called the outbreak "the most severe, acute health emergency seen in modern times."

In Dallas, Texas, a nurse who provided care to Thomas Eric Duncan, the Liberian man who died of Ebola in the U.S., has tested positive for the virus. The infection of the nurse means the CDC must broaden the pool of people getting close monitoring. The nurse's infection occurred despite the hospital's intense effort to save Duncan's life, and suggests that many other people could have been exposed to the virus during Duncan's time in an isolation unit.

The medical records of the caregivers who treated Duncan offer clues to what happened and who was involved, but the hospital has refused to answer questions about their specific duties. The CDC has been actively monitoring 48 people who might have had contact with Duncan after he fell ill with the infection but before he was put in isolation. The number includes 10 people known to have contact and 38 who may have had contact, including people he was staying with and health care professionals who attended to him during an emergency room visit from which he was sent home. None is sick.

The CDC has not yet established a firm number of health care workers who had contact with Duncan. Dr. Tom Frieden, director of the CDC, said that if this one individual was infected — and they don't know how — within the isolation unit, then it is possible that other individuals could have been infected as well. The expanding monitoring "is an abundance of caution that's probably beyond what needs to be done" because medical caregivers will notice if they're getting a fever, and they're not contagious until that point.

In a separate story, a 33-year-old freelance cameraman who contracted Ebola in Liberia is fighting for his life at the University of Nebraska Medical Center. The cost of his medical bills could run in excess of $500,000, as his travelers' insurance policy excludes "catastrophic events or outbreaks." NBC has agreed to cover his medical bills.

Finally, the WHO reported that the death rate in the current Ebola outbreak has increased to 70 percent, up from previous estimates of around 50 percent. The WHO is still focused on trying to get sick people isolated and provide treatment as early as possible.

A video circulating online shows a staged human sacrifice at the European Organisation for Nuclear Research (CERN), home of the Large Hadron Collider. The video depicts hooded figures engaging in a ritual under a statue of a Hindu deity, culminating in a woman being stabbed. However, the footage appears to be part of a prank by CERN scientists, and the identities and motives behind the video remain unknown.

The video shows multiple people wearing long, flowing black robes, with one wearing hiking boots underneath. The woman moves onto the floor and is apparently stabbed. The person recording the video reacts and runs away, causing the camera to move away before it is cut off.

The ceremony took place under the statue of Shiva, a gift from India to celebrate its association with CERN. The Shiva statue was chosen because of a metaphor drawn between the cosmic dance of the Nataraj and the modern study of subatomic particles. CERN confirmed that the video was filmed there, but said it was made without permission or knowledge, and does not condone such spoofs as they can give rise to misunderstandings about the scientific nature of their work.

CERN has been associated with the occult and the mystical due to the highly specialized and often terrifying work that goes on there. Conspiracy theories suggest that the Large Hadron Collider could bring about a black hole in the Earth, allow access to new forms of power, or open a portal to another dimension. CERN has had to rebut claims that its work is meant to prove that God doesn't exist.

The campus has security measures to ensure that everyone on the grounds is either an official scientist or a visitor. The identities of those involved in the prank remain unknown, but the woman in the video appears to be identifiable. CERN has added an article to its FAQ page stating that the video is a work of fiction and that the prank was the result of some visitors letting their sense of humor go too far.

On an Aeroflot flight from Moscow to Bangkok, severe turbulence injured 27 passengers, with some suffering broken bones. The incident occurred in clear skies, known as clear air turbulence, which is difficult to predict and cannot be identified by the naked eye or conventional radar. The turbulence happened about 40 minutes before the Boeing 777 carrying 313 passengers was due to land in Bangkok.

The Russian embassy in Thailand reported that 24 Russian nationals and three Thai citizens were injured. Fifteen people, including one child, were admitted to hospitals in Bangkok, with three needing surgery. By early evening on Monday, 14 passengers remained in hospital, and Aeroflot has stated it will pay the medical costs of the injured.

The turbulence was "impossible to foresee," and the crew was unable to warn passengers to return to their seats and fasten their seatbelts. The pilot, with over 23,000 flight hours, operated the flight. Clear air turbulence is a common occurrence in civil aviation, with about 750 cases reported annually.

Passenger Yevgenia described being "hurled" up to the ceiling during the turbulence, which felt like it wouldn't stop. Images taken by a passenger show the aircraft's cabin in disarray, with passengers lying in the aisles and items scattered on the floor.

Aeroflot's safety record has improved since the collapse of the Soviet Union, but it still experienced an accident in 2008 that killed 88 passengers and crew. The airline is ranked 37 out of 60 in the 2017 airline safety rankings.

United Airlines has awarded one million air miles to a security researcher named Jordan Wiens as the first reward in their bug-bounty program. Wiens discovered a remote-code execution flaw in United's website and submitted the information to the airline. This is the first time Wiens, the owner of the Florida-based security firm Vector 35, has participated in a bug-bounty program.

United's bug-bounty program, announced in May, is the first of its kind in the airline industry. The company offers bounty submitters only air miles as a payout, with the amounts varying depending on the type of bug reported. For example, cross-site scripting bugs earn 50,000 miles, while authentication bypass bugs can earn up to 250,000 miles. Remote-code execution flaws, which allow an attacker to remotely run malicious code on a vulnerable web site or system, earn the top payout of 1,000,000 miles.

Wiens was surprised to receive the massive payout, as he thought his submission would only earn him 50,000 miles or less. He had submitted two bugs that he believed were remote code execution, but he wasn't sure if they were on parts of the infrastructure that qualified. After confirming his U.S. citizenship and that his research was done in the U.S., United told him to check his mileage account, where he discovered the deposit.

One million miles will travel quite far, and Wiens plans to use them for coach class trips for his family, though he is considering one splurge in the 'premium' cabin. The miles are worth around $25,000 in cash, which is a better payout than most commercial bug bounties. Wiens said he was boasting that he earned 1,000,000 airline miles without ever leaving the ground.

United's bounty was announced shortly after the incident with Chris Roberts, a security researcher who tweeted during a flight that he had access to the aircraft's in-flight entertainment system. Roberts was questioned by the FBI, who allegedly said Roberts told investigators he took control of the airplane and caused it to climb and turn. Wiens, who is bound by the rules of the bounty not to share details on the vulnerability he found, said he wasn't particularly worried about the ramifications of the Roberts incident on his work.

Remote code execution bugs are one of 10 bug classes eligible for bounties under United's program. Others include authentication bypass vulnerabilities, vulnerabilities on customer-facing websites and the United mobile app, cross-site request forgery, cross-site scripting, information disclosure, timing and brute-force attacks. Bugs on internal sites, partner sites and apps, on-board Wi-Fi, entertainment and avionics systems are out of scope.

Wiens said he salutes United for hosting the ongoing contest and plans to continue participating in bug bounties in the future. He encourages other companies to follow United's lead and offer bug bounties to help improve their security.

Brandon Jenkins, a prospective student at the Community College of Baltimore County (CCBC), is suing the institution for allegedly denying him admission into the radiation therapy program due to his religious beliefs. Jenkins was asked during an interview about what is most important to him, to which he responded "My God." However, according to the American Center for Law and Justice (ACLJ), which is representing Jenkins, this was the only time Jenkins mentioned God during the application process.

Adrienne Dougherty, director and coordinator of the radiation therapy program, reportedly told Jenkins that religion is not appropriate in the field and that he should leave his thoughts and beliefs out of future interviews. The ACLJ claims that Dougherty also mentioned Jenkins' 3.2 GPA being lower than other applicants and a 10-year-old criminal charge on his record as reasons for his denial.

The lawsuit, filed in U.S. District Court of Maryland, seeks unspecified damages and an injunction requiring that Jenkins be admitted into the program. The ACLJ argues that denying admission based on religious beliefs is unlawful and violates the Constitution.

CCBC spokeswoman Hope Davis declined to comment on the pending litigation but stated that the college is committed to diversity. A response from CCBC's attorney also stated that the school seeks applicants "motivated by an individual passion in the field," and that Jenkins' statement about being pursuing the program at the behest of God or others "was not a good answer."

This case highlights the ongoing debate about the intersection of religion and education, and whether institutions should be allowed to deny admission based on an applicant's religious beliefs. The ACLJ is arguing that such discrimination is unlawful and violates the Constitution, while CCBC maintains that it seeks applicants who are passionate about the field and able to separate their personal beliefs from their professional duties.
