The Secret Service leaked sensitive personal information about Representative Jason Chaffetz, a prominent critic of the agency, to the press in an attempt to intimidate and embarrass him. The Department of Homeland Security Office of the Inspector General issued a report on Wednesday that accused Secret Service Assistant Director Edward Lowery and other agency officials of plotting to leak information about Chaffetz, including his unsuccessful attempt to join the organization. The report found that between March 24 and April 2, 2015, 45 Secret Service employees accessed Chaffetz's personal information nearly 60 times, with only 4 of the 45 employees having a legitimate need to access the information. The report also found widespread dissemination of the personal information, with Lowery emailing employees saying, "Some information that he might find embarrassing needs to get out. Just to be fair." Chaffetz blasted the agency for the alleged leaks, calling it a tactic designed to intimidate and embarrass him. The Oversight Committee launched an investigation into the Secret Service earlier this year after a series of embarrassing security incidents at the White House. The panel is also investigating reports that Secret Service agents paid for sex during a presidential visit to Colombia. Rep. Elijah Cummings, the top Democrat on the panel, said the Secret Service should issue an "immediate apology."

A team of international scientists, led by the British Antarctic Survey, is heading to Antarctica to investigate a newly exposed marine ecosystem that was hidden for 120,000 years under an Antarctic ice shelf. The ecosystem was revealed when a massive iceberg, known as A-68, calved off from the Larsen Ice Shelf last July. The team will spend three weeks on board the research ship RRS James Clark Ross to collect samples from the newly exposed seabed, which covers an area of around 2,200 square miles. The scientists aim to study marine life as it responds to a dramatic environmental change and gather as much information as possible in a short time. The calving of A-68 offers a new and unprecedented opportunity to establish an interdisciplinary scientific research program in this climate-sensitive region. The team will investigate the area previously under the ice shelf by collecting seafloor animals, microbes, plankton, sediments, and water samples. Their findings will provide a snapshot of what life under the ice shelf was like, so that changes to the ecosystem can be tracked. The team will also investigate the impact of climate change on the polar regions and the sustainability of polar continental shelves under climate change. The hope is that the team will gain deeper insight into the life that lives in frigid Antarctic waters and how to protect it if it becomes threatened by further ice breaks and melting sea ice. The mission is part of a wider campaign to turn a huge section of the Antarctic region into the world's largest ocean sanctuary.

A Central California woman, Myrna Arias, has filed a lawsuit against her former employer, Intermex Wire Transfer LLC, alleging that she was fired for refusing to install an app that tracked her location 24/7, even during non-work hours. The app, Xora's StreetSmart, was used to monitor employees' movements, including their driving speed, roads taken, and time spent at customer locations.

Arias, a sales executive and account manager, claims that her boss, John Stubits, admitted to monitoring employees while off duty and bragged about knowing her exact location. She found this invasion of her privacy offensive and compared the app to a prisoner's ankle bracelet. Despite meeting all her quotas and earning around $7,250 a month, Arias was fired a few weeks after uninstalling the app to protect her privacy.

According to Arias' attorney, Gail Glick, an employer can legally monitor employees at work if there is a legitimate business interest, but if an employee cannot stop it, it violates California and federal laws against invasion of privacy. Arias objected to the app because there was no way to turn it off when she was at home, and it would still run in the background.

Intermex is accused of going "above and beyond a normal wrongful termination" by interfering with Arias' ability to earn a livelihood by informing her former employer, NetSpend, that she had been disloyal to them. Arias seeks an injunction and damages for invasion of privacy, retaliation, labor code violations, intentional interference with contract, wrongful termination, and unfair business practices.

The Xora app, which enables employees to create electronic timecards on their phones, is not a party to the complaint. Intermex did not respond to comment requests by press time. Arias' attorney, Gail A. Glick, is with Alexander, Krakow & Glick of Santa Monica, and they intend to pursue the case aggressively to get Arias the justice she deserves.

In a significant shift, Senators Heidi Heitkamp (D-N.D.) and Joe Donnelly (D-Ind.) have expressed their support for gay marriage, joining a growing number of Democratic senators who have recently endorsed the cause. Both senators hail from deeply conservative states, making their support particularly notable.

In statements, both senators emphasized the importance of equality and non-discrimination in personal relationships. Heitkamp stated that she believes the federal government should not interfere in personal, private, and intimate relationships, while Donnelly highlighted his past votes in favor of repealing 'don't ask, don't tell' and opposing workplace discrimination based on sexual orientation.

Their announcements come as support for same-sex marriage continues to increase among the general public. According to a logistic regression analysis, the two most significant factors influencing a senator's stance on same-sex marriage are their ideology rating and the estimated support for same-sex marriage among voters in their state.

The shift in senators' positions mirrors the shift in public opinion, but the increase in endorsements has been exponential over the past few years, with a notable jump in the last two weeks. This rapid change may be due to a "momentum" effect, with senators learning from each other's experiences and encouraging others to follow suit.

Only four remaining Democratic senators have not publicly backed gay marriage: Mark Pryor (D-Ark.), Joe Manchin (D-W.Va.), Mary Landrieu (D-La.) and Tim Johnson (D-S.D.). Landrieu and Pryor face re-election in 2014 in Southern red states, while Johnson is retiring in 2014, but there is a movement to draft his son to run for his seat. Manchin, like Donnelly and Heitkamp, is not up for reelection until 2018.

The analysis suggests that the model does not do a particularly good job of replicating the exponential increase in same-sex marriage support in the Senate over time, but a "majority model" that takes into account the likelihood of same-sex marriage having reached majority status in both the state and nationally does a modestly better job of predicting endorsements among senators and matching the change in support over time. The model suggests that the recent surge in endorsements may be due to the perception of same-sex marriage having reached a national majority or plurality in some polls.

Wesley Snipes, the actor known for his roles in films such as 'White Men Can't Jump', 'Demolition Man', and the 'Blade' trilogy, began serving a three-year prison sentence on December 9, 2010, at the Federal Correctional Institution McKean in Pennsylvania. The minimum-security prison camp, located in the small town of Lewis Run, is a stark contrast to the harsh prison fortresses depicted in Snipes' films. The prison doesn't have fences around its perimeter and houses 300 nonviolent inmates in two-man rooms with daily showers and double-feature movie showings on weekends. However, the prison's rules prohibit NC-17, R, or X-rated movies, which eliminates much of Snipes' action-heavy repertoire.

Snipes was convicted in 2008 in Florida for willful failure to file income tax returns and owed $2.7 million in taxes on $13.8 million in income from 1999 to 2001. He was a member of a tax-protest group that challenges the government's right to collect taxes and described himself at his sentencing as a naive truth-seeker. Snipes attempted to delay his arrival while he took his appeal to the U.S. Supreme Court, but the trial judge said he had received a fair trial.

At McKean, Snipes can pursue his spirituality at weekly meetings of various religious groups, exercise through sand volleyball, indoor basketball, or workout machines, and engage in activities like badminton, bocci, or bridge. The prison's infirmary copay is $2, and contact in the visitors room is limited to a kiss. Snipes made a last-minute request for a new trial, citing misconduct allegations against the jurors, but the judge denied the request. Snipes' prison term marks the end of his options in his tax-related conviction.

Robin Roberts, the popular host of ABC's "Good Morning America," returned to her anchor desk on Wednesday, five months after undergoing a bone marrow transplant to treat a rare blood disorder known as myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS). The return was celebrated by fans and industry professionals alike, with many praising Roberts for her resilience and determination.

Roberts' illness was first diagnosed in August 2012, after she felt exhausted while covering the Academy Awards. She underwent the transplant in September and took a leave of absence from the show. During her absence, her co-hosts and the show's producers kept her in the loop and shared her updates with viewers.

Roberts' return to the show was a significant moment for both her and ABC, as she defied expectations and returned to the anchor desk despite predictions that she might be unwilling or unable to do so. The broadcast gave ABC fresh optimism that "Good Morning America" can continue to beat NBC's "Today" in the morning ratings.

Roberts' return also marked the end of a difficult chapter in her life, as she had been warned by her doctors that she would feel like dying at one point during her recovery. However, she persevered and is now back on the air, albeit with a gradual return schedule. She will appear on the show for a few days a week at first, depending on how she and her doctors feel about her progress.

Roberts' story has been widely covered in the media, with some critics accusing ABC of exploiting her illness for ratings gains. However, the show's producers and viewers have generally been supportive of Roberts and her television family, who remained firmly No. 1 among total viewers while she was away.

Ben Sherwood, the president of ABC News, said that the experience had reminded them to take nothing for granted and that they felt like they were just getting started. He also said that he hoped Roberts would eventually return to a five-day-a-week schedule.

Roberts' return was even cause for a temporary ceasefire in the long-standing rivalry between "Good Morning America" and "Today." "Today" sent a gift basket to the ABC studio and welcomed Roberts back during its 8 a.m. hour.

Overall, Roberts' return to "Good Morning America" was a triumphant moment for both her and the show, and a testament to her strength and determination in the face of adversity. She is expected to continue appearing on the show on a gradual basis, with a special edition of "20/20" airing on February 22 to offer a candid look at her experience.

On August 7, 2016, a family of five, including three children, was found dead in their home in Sinking Spring, Pennsylvania. The victims were identified as Mark Short, 40, his wife Megan, 33, and their children Liana, 8, Mark Jr., 5, and Willow, 2. The family dog was also found dead. Police discovered a handwritten "murder-suicide" note in the home, along with a gun near one of the deceased adults. The family had been dealing with "domestic issues" and Megan Short had reportedly planned to leave her husband.

Megan Short had been active in raising awareness for congenital heart disease, as their youngest daughter Willow had undergone a heart transplant at just one week old. Megan wrote about her experience dealing with post-traumatic stress disorder throughout her ordeal with Willow on a blog.

Neighbors described Megan as unhappy in her relationship, and she had made no secret of her plans to leave her husband. About a week before the murder-suicide, Megan posted on Facebook that she needed help moving from their home on August 6.

Counseling was made available for parents and children at the school where Liana would have attended third grade, and will also be available at Green Valley Elementary School. The Wilson School District Superintendent Curtis Baker asked district parents to include the Short family in their prayers, saying the tragic event had shaken the Wilson family.

The Shorts were parishioners at St. Ignatius Loyola Parish, and their story was featured in local and national news due to Willow's heart condition. Megan wrote for Phillyheart.com, a website associated with the nonprofit Mended Hearts Inc., that shares the stories of families battling congenital heart defects. She once described having to deal with the post-traumatic stress of having her daughter undergo a heart transplant after only six days of life. The family was featured in an October 2014 story in the Reading Eagle.

Mark and Megan shared dozens of photos of their children with friends and family on Facebook, and Mark wrote that Megan was "the most beautiful girl that I've ever met." Many of the posts on Willow's Heart Journey appear to be written by Megan, and while the page was meant to inspire hope, it also captured Willow's hardship. Posts tracked days in the hospital, the fear of a parent whose child is sick, and the daily burden on the family's shoulders. The New York Times published a feature story on the family in July 2015, detailing their struggles with specialty pharmacies and obtaining anti-rejection medication for Willow.

Neighbors expressed sadness over the tragedy, with one neighbor, Angie Burke, describing how she had a sense that Megan was unhappy in her relationship. Burke and Megan had kept in contact mostly through Facebook, and Burke provided screen grabs of a July 23 conversation in which Megan commented on a link to an online article about emotional abuse in a marriage and said she was leaving her marriage after 16 years. Burke offered to help Megan with the move, but Megan declined as she was planning to move to Yardley.

The investigation into the murder-suicide is ongoing, and no further details have been released. The community is in mourning, and counseling is being made available for those affected by the tragedy.

The U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) announced the completion of Operation Sunflower, an international operation targeting child pornography and sexual abuse. The operation resulted in the arrest of 245 suspects, with 23 arrests made outside the U.S. ICE identified 123 child victims, some as young as 3, with 44 children being rescued from their abusers. The operation spanned 46 states and six countries, including the Bay Area, and involved the arrest of 37 individuals in California.

One of the suspects, Michael Lindsay, 53, of San Jose, was arrested for engaging in child sex tourism. ICE continues to search for additional victims, as evidence suggests Lindsay had sexual contact with additional children.

Operation Sunflower was named to commemorate a successful operation in 2011 that rescued an 11-year-old Kansas girl from rape. The operation is part of ICE's new Victim Identification Program.

ICE is asking for the public's help in identifying three men and a woman in three unsolved Operation Sunflower cases. Tips can be reported anonymously by calling 1-866-DHS-2-ICE or visiting www.ICE.gov/tips.

The operation underscores ICE's commitment to protecting children from sexual exploitation and abuse, with ICE Director John Morton stating, "We are defending the defenseless."

Ken Bone, the undecided voter who gained internet fame during the second presidential debate, discussed his experience and the event's contentious nature in an interview on CNN. Bone, wearing his now-iconic red sweater, lamented the bickering and name-calling that dominated the debate, but praised the moderators for their efforts. He acknowledged that the debate became uncomfortable at times but found some substantive answers amidst the rhetoric.

Bone's sudden internet popularity led to a surge in his Twitter followers, and he joked about his sweater being more famous than him. He also revealed that he wore the sweater as a backup plan due to a wardrobe malfunction.

Bone was unaware during the debate that Donald Trump had invited women who claimed to have been wronged by the Clintons to sit in the audience. While he stated that this move would not affect his voting decision, he felt it was uncalled for. Bone admitted that Clinton's composure and answers during the debate had impressed him, although he initially leaned towards voting for Trump.

The debate, however, did not provide Bone with any clarity on whom to vote for in November. He remains an undecided voter. The internet has since been abuzz with people trying to find and purchase the same red sweater that Bone wore during the debate. Several retailers have capitalized on this trend by offering similar sweaters at various price points.

The study published in the journal Science Advances reveals that Earth is currently experiencing a sixth mass extinction, with animal species dying out at a rate that is 100 times higher than the normal rate without human impact. The study, led by Gerardo Ceballos of the National Autonomous University of Mexico, used conservative estimates to arrive at this conclusion. Even when using the most conservative rates, the rate at which vertebrates are being lost forever is far higher than in the last five mass extinctions. The study found that modern rates of extinction were eight to 100 times higher than the background rate, with 477 vertebrates having gone extinct since 1900, rather than the nine that would be expected at natural rates. The authors of the study argue that rapid, intensified efforts are needed to stop or slow the extinctions currently underway. The study's findings echo those of previous studies, such as WWF's Living Planet Report, which highlighted a 52% decline in vertebrate populations over the last 40 years. The study was published on June 19, 2015.

On Sunday morning, two churches in Las Cruces, New Mexico, were rocked by nearly simultaneous explosions. No one was injured in either incident, but the damage to each church was described as relatively minor. The first explosion occurred at Calvary Baptist Church around 8 a.m., with the device placed in a mailbox. Parishioners were inside the church at the time, but services had not yet begun. Less than half an hour later, an explosive device went off in a trash can near the entrance of Holy Cross Catholic Church, causing the service to be evacuated.

Both churches remained closed on Sunday afternoon while multiple law enforcement agencies investigated the nearly simultaneous blasts. Holy Cross Catholic Church announced that activities at their adjoining school would be canceled on Monday. The churches' pastors and parishioners expressed their concern and called for increased security measures.

Governor Susana Martinez of New Mexico called the bombings cowardly and vowed that the person responsible would be caught. State Police Chief Pete Kassetas said the acts were intended to terrorize churchgoers but could not confirm whether the two explosions were related. The Dona Ana County Sheriff's Office Bomb Squad, New Mexico State Police, an NMSU canine unit, the FBI, ATF, and Department of Homeland Security are all assisting in the investigation.

During a rally on Sunday night, faith leaders from throughout the community called for forgiveness and a stronger sense of community. Bishop Oscar Cantú expressed thanks that no one was hurt and vowed that church services would continue, but with more prudence. The Las Cruces Police Department advised other churches in the area to be on the lookout for anything suspicious.

The study conducted by Andrew Reece from Harvard University and Christopher Danforth from the University of Vermont reveals that Instagram photos can potentially serve as indicators of mental health, specifically depression. The researchers analyzed 43,950 photos from 166 volunteers, recruited from Amazon Mechanical Turk, and found that depressed individuals tend to post photos with increased hue, decreased brightness, and decreased color saturation, resulting in "bluer, grayer, and darker" images. Depressed participants also tended to post more frequently and use more Instagram filters, with the most popular one for depressed participants being Inkwell.

The study's findings suggest that computers can correctly identify instances of depression at a better rate than the typical physician, with a success rate of 70%. Valencia was the most popular filter among users who were not depressed, while depressed users favored Inkwell. The researchers believe this method could lead to an unobtrusive, inexpensive way to use social media for health screening.

Michael Thase, the director of the Mood and Anxiety Program at the University of Pennsylvania, supports the idea, suggesting that users might opt-in to receive screening feedback from social media. However, he emphasizes the importance of protecting users' privacy and ensuring that the information is not misused.

The study is the latest example of how valuable insights can be derived from digital footprints left online, and it highlights the potential for tech companies to assist patients and their healthcare providers. The researchers plan to continue investigating how artificial intelligence can impact mental health, with a focus on developing tools for early detection and intervention.

A far-right activist and writer, Dominique Venner, committed suicide at Paris's Notre Dame Cathedral on Tuesday, in an act that has been described as political by France's far-right National Front party leader, Marine Le Pen. The 78-year-old Venner, known for his essays against immigration and the decline of European civilizations, shot himself in front of the cathedral's altar, causing the evacuation of approximately 1,500 visitors.

In a statement posted on his website the day before, Venner expressed his opposition to France's recent legalization of gay marriage and immigration from Africa. He also left a message on a conservative radio station, expressing his belief that his suicide was necessary to awaken slumbering consciences and break the lethargy overwhelming France.

Marine Le Pen hailed Venner's act as "eminently political," while adding that France will renew and save itself through life and hope. Bruno Gollnisch, a senior National Front figure, referred to Venner as an "extremely brilliant intellectual" and believed his suicide was a protest against the decadence of society.

Venner had a long career publishing right-wing essays, military histories, and books on weaponry and hunting. He fought for France in the Algerian War of Independence and was a member of the OAS, a paramilitary group that opposed Algeria's independence from France.

This suicide follows another dramatic incident in Paris less than a week ago, where a 50-year-old man shot himself dead in a primary school near the Eiffel Tower, in front of a dozen stunned children.

The gay marriage bill, which has sparked numerous protests in France, was finally signed into law by President François Hollande on Sunday. Venner denounced this law, along with immigration from North Africa, in his final statements.

The Notre Dame Cathedral, one of France's top tourist attractions, was visited by 13.6 million people in 2011. The cathedral's rector, Monsignor Patrick Jacquin, expressed shock and sadness over the incident, stating that masses had been cancelled and a vigil would be held later on Tuesday.

James Wesley Howell, a 20-year-old from Indiana, appeared in Superior Court in Los Angeles on June 14, 2016, facing felony weapons charges. Authorities found assault rifles and explosive chemicals in his car in Santa Monica, California, on June 12, before a major Los Angeles gay pride parade. The discovery was made hours after an attack at a gay nightclub in Orlando, Florida left 49 people dead, which may have contributed to heightened security measures at the LA Pride event.

Prior to his arrest in California, Howell was charged in Indiana with child molestation. Clark County Prosecutor Jeremy Mull stated that Howell allegedly had sex with a 12-year-old girl on May 31, and the molestation charges apparently spurred his cross-country journey to Los Angeles. If convicted, Howell could face up to 16 years in prison.

Howell has pleaded not guilty to the weapons charges in California, and a Los Angeles County judge set his bail at $2 million. Federal agents searched Howell's Jeffersonville home on Monday, but declined to release any details.

Friends in Indiana described Howell as a gun enthusiast with a short temper. In October, he was accused of pulling a gun and making threats, once against a boyfriend and once against a neighbor. Howell was convicted in April of misdemeanor intimidation for the incident with his neighbor, and under the terms of his probation, he was not allowed to have weapons or leave Indiana.

The child molestation case in Indiana is ongoing, and it is unclear whether Howell will be extradited to face the charges. The discovery of weapons and explosives in his car in California has raised concerns about potential threats to public safety.

Jeffrey Sandusky, the son of convicted sex abuser and former Penn State football coach Jerry Sandusky, pleaded guilty to 14 counts of child sexual abuse on Friday. The charges include soliciting sex from a child younger than 16 and soliciting child pornography. The plea deal comes a week before his scheduled trial, which was nearly six years after his father was arrested in a child molestation case that shook Penn State. Jeffrey Sandusky will spend up to six years in state prison, but the judge could impose a sentence of as much as eight years. He will also become a Tier III sex offender, the highest level in Pennsylvania. The charges involve incidents with two girls, one in 2013 and one in 2016. The district attorney's office did not immediately return a call seeking comment from Jeffrey Sandusky's lawyer. This development comes six years after Jerry Sandusky's arrest in a child molestation case that is still working its way through criminal and civil courts.

Bill Cosby was sentenced to three to 10 years in prison for drugging and sexually assaulting Andrea Constand at his home outside Philadelphia in 2004. Judge Steven T. O'Neill also classified Cosby as a "sexually violent predator" under state law. After the sentencing, Cosby's publicist, Andrew Wyatt, made fiery accusations of racism and sexism, framing Cosby's downfall as an unjust product of the #MeToo era. Wyatt compared Cosby's trial to the accusations of sexual misconduct against Judge Brett M. Kavanaugh, stating that both Cosby and Kavanaugh were victims of a "sex war" that is "going on in Washington today." Wyatt also claimed that Cosby's trial was the most racist and sexist in U.S. history, and criticized the psychologists who testified against Cosby, as well as the authenticity of audio footage played in the courtroom. In a bizarre moment, Wyatt referenced the persecution of Jesus while discussing Cosby. Cosby spent his first night behind bars at SCI Phoenix, a new 3,830-bed state prison in suburban Philadelphia. Wyatt has repeatedly argued that racism played a role in Cosby’s conviction, invoking Emmett Till, a black boy murdered after a white woman falsely accused him of whistling at her. Kavanaugh's nomination has been embroiled in controversy after two women accused him of sexual assault and misconduct in incidents dating back to the 1980s. Christine Blasey Ford came forward earlier this month to accuse him of attempted rape during a high school party in the '80s, and a second accuser, Deborah Ramirez, stepped forward with her own story of sexual misconduct on Sunday. Both accusers have called for the FBI to investigate their claims before a vote on Kavanaugh takes place. However, there's a strong chance Kavanaugh could be confirmed anyway.

The article discusses the economics behind rotisserie chickens in supermarkets, revealing that they are often made from unsold chicken nearing its expiration date. This practice is a strategic way for grocery stores to minimize losses and offer fresh, prepared food at lower prices. The prepared-foods section of supermarkets uses up unsold produce and meat, similar to hunter-gatherers using every part of an animal.

This innovation in grocery store management has significantly improved the economy over the past few decades by reducing spoilage and lowering prices for consumers. The article encourages readers to consider the unsung heroes in the innovation economy, such as the individuals who spit-roast chickens and streamline factory production, in addition to well-known tech companies like Facebook and Google.

The article also addresses the misconception that prepared meals are always more expensive than homemade meals. In contrast, rotisserie chickens are an exception due to the cost-effective practices of grocery stores, which recycle unsold food items into prepared meals.

The article concludes by emphasizing that sell-by, use-by, and best-by dates are estimates of food quality rather than safety indicators. Consumers can extend the shelf life of their groceries by using resources like StillTasty.com and avoiding food waste, which contributes to 60 billion pounds of wasted food annually in the US. By purchasing rotisserie chickens, consumers can help reduce food waste, lower prices for others, and contribute to environmental conservation.

The U.S. government has issued a warning about the Islamic State (ISIS) potentially creating fake Syrian passports, using seized Syrian government assets such as passport printing machines and blank passport books. This intelligence report, obtained by ABC News, suggests that ISIS has been able to print legitimate-looking Syrian passports since taking over cities like Deir ez-Zour and Raqqa, which have passport offices. The report indicates that ISIS's access to biographical data and fingerprint information on Syrian citizens raises the possibility of identity theft. The State Department and FBI have acknowledged the concern, with State Department spokesman John Kirby stating that they are "mindful" of the threat. The report notes that the primary source for the information was rated at "moderate confidence," and fake Syrian passports have already been discovered in Europe. The U.S. is on high alert for ISIS attacks, and this potential threat could pose a significant security risk.

The French Laundry, a renowned restaurant in Yountville, California, was the victim of a Christmas Day robbery, with thieves making off with a collection of highly valuable wines worth at least $300,000. The majority of the 76 bottles stolen were from the Domaine de la Romanée Conti, including bottles from the Romanée Conti vineyard, which are worth around $15,000 each. The restaurant's chef, Thomas Keller, has taken to Twitter, appealing for help from the wine community to find the thieves. The French Laundry, which is one of only 13 restaurants in the United States to earn three stars from the Michelin guide, is currently undergoing a kitchen remodel and had just served its last meal on Christmas Eve before the incident. The stolen wines, mostly collectible and traded on private and auction markets, include bottles of DRC Romanée Conti from vintages spanning 2004-2010, which range in price from $11,000 to $15,000 per bottle, and several bottles of California cult Cabernet Sauvignon Screaming Eagle, with prices ranging from $2,100 to $7,500. The restaurant is cooperating with local law enforcement in the ongoing investigation and is seeking any information from the community that could help identify the offenders.

Sinn Féin leader Gerry Adams was arrested and questioned for four days at Antrim police station over the 1972 IRA murder of Jean McConville. Adams, who denies any involvement in the murder, criticized the timing of his arrest during an election campaign. The McConville family, who have been fighting for justice for 42 years, expressed their determination to continue their fight. Adams was released, and a file will be sent to the Public Prosecution Service to decide if charges will be brought. The arrest and release have sparked debates about the timing and political implications of the arrest. The case against Adams is based on interviews he allegedly gave to researchers at Boston College in the US.

The fourth Republican presidential debate on Tuesday night was held in Milwaukee and featured eight candidates, including front-runners Donald Trump, Marco Rubio, and Ted Cruz. Jeb Bush, who entered the debate with the most to gain, turned in his strongest performance to date but it is unlikely to significantly change his position in the broader field. Rubio and Cruz continued to outshine their rivals, exploiting a more subdued debate format and showcasing their mastery of the facts and ease under the bright lights.

The debate was marked by a series of sharp exchanges, particularly on the issue of immigration, with Trump and Cruz on one side and John Kasich and Bush on the other. Kasich criticized Trump's proposal to build a wall along the U.S.-Mexico border and to deport 11 million undocumented immigrants, while Trump took a dig at Kasich's state's economic recovery. Bush followed by mockingly thanking Trump for "allowing me to speak at the debate" and chided Trump for the mass deportation proposal, calling it "impossible."

Rubio, who is viewed as one of the strongest candidates, stayed out of the fray and landed his own memorable moment when he tangled with Rand Paul over military spending. The debate is unlikely to dramatically alter the race as it now stands, with the next GOP debate 35 days away and the month of December effectively a dead zone for campaign fundraising.

In addition to the immigration debate, the candidates also clashed over government spending and how to handle Russia's Vladimir Putin. The audience got involved at times, with boos and applause for various candidates. Overall, the debate was seen as more substantive than previous debates, with a focus on policy questions.

In terms of winners and losers, Marco Rubio and Ted Cruz were seen as the standouts, with Rubio delivering a particularly strong performance on military spending and the role of the United States in the world. Donald Trump had a rough night, with a lackluster performance and several missteps, particularly on the issue of immigration. John Kasich struggled to find his footing and was criticized for his interruptions and aggressive tone. Jeb Bush had a somewhat improved performance but it was not enough to significantly change his position in the race. Ben Carson had a shaky debate, struggling with policy questions and taking up the least amount of speaking time despite his position in the center of the stage. Carly Fiorina was also seen as underwhelming, with a low-key performance that did not stand out.

Overall, the debate was seen as a more subdued affair than previous debates, with a focus on policy rather than personal attacks. However, it is unlikely to significantly alter the race as it now stands, with the next debate 35 days away. The status quo may hold through the end of the year, with the GOP field still dominated by Trump, Cruz, and Rubio.

Shia LaBeouf has withdrawn from his Broadway debut in the play "Orphans," citing creative differences, a month before the production's scheduled opening. The production, directed by Daniel Sullivan, still features Alec Baldwin and is set to open at the Schoenfeld Theater on April 7, with previews commencing on March 19. LaBeouf, who rose to fame in the "Transformers" series and the latest "Indiana Jones" installment, had little theater experience prior to "Orphans." His departure leaves the role of one of the brothers uncast.

Meanwhile, Tom Hanks is making his Broadway debut in the play "Lucky Guy," based on the life of New York City tabloid columnist Mike McAlary. Hanks, who won Academy Awards for "Philadelphia" and "Forrest Gump," was initially hesitant about the role due to McAlary's unlikable character. However, he later felt drawn to McAlary's swagger and drive. The play, directed by George C. Wolfe, is a tribute to McAlary, who died of colon cancer at the age of 41, and to his collaborator Nora Ephron, who died of leukemia last June. Ephron spent years rewriting the script, which was originally titled "Stories About McAlary."

The Afghan government has stated that it will accept a Taliban liaison office in Qatar to initiate peace talks, but has emphasized that no foreign power can be involved in the process without its consent. The government's peace council has set out ground rules for engaging the Taliban, including the cessation of violence against civilians, cutting ties to al Qaeda, and acceptance of the Afghan constitution which guarantees civil rights and liberties. The council also stated that any peace process with the Taliban would require the support of Pakistan, as members of the insurgent group are based there. The government prefers an office in Saudi Arabia or Turkey, but is open to Doha as long as the authority of the Afghan state is not compromised. The Afghan government has recalled its ambassador from Doha due to concerns about the latest round of contacts with the insurgent group, and is also concerned about reports of the transfer of Afghan prisoners from Guantanamo Bay to Doha. The tension between the Karzai administration and the United States over engaging the Taliban underscores the challenges of seeking a political settlement as the West prepares to withdraw most combat troops from Afghanistan by 2014. The peace council has laid down tough conditions for talks, including the cessation of violence, cutting ties to terrorist groups, acceptance of the constitution, and honoring the gains made in the last 10 years. The Taliban have not publicly responded to these demands and have vowed to continue fighting until all foreign troops have left the country. The insurgents have also expressed confidence in their ultimate victory and compared the NATO forces to the Soviet invaders who withdrew from Afghanistan in 1989. A gunman wearing an Afghan army uniform opened fire on coalition troops in western Afghanistan, wounding several soldiers and killing the gunman. This shooting is the latest in a series of attacks by Afghans against coalition partners, raising fears of Taliban infiltration as NATO speeds up the training of Afghan security forces. The expansion of the army and police is a critical element in NATO's exit strategy from Afghanistan.

The Supreme Court has ruled unanimously that farmers cannot use Monsanto's patented genetically altered soybeans to create new seeds without paying a fee. The ruling has implications for various industries, including agriculture, vaccines, cell lines, and software. The decision is narrow and emphasizes that it only applies to the specific case before the court.

The case, Bowman v. Monsanto Company, involved an Indiana farmer, Vernon Hugh Bowman, who had signed contracts for his main crop but discovered a loophole for a second, riskier crop. He bought seeds from a grain elevator, hoping some would contain Monsanto's patented Roundup Ready gene. After planting and spraying them with Roundup, many plants survived, and he replanted their seeds.

Monsanto sued Bowman, and a federal judge in Indiana ordered him to pay over $84,000. The United States Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit, which specializes in patent cases, upheld that decision, stating that by planting the seeds, Bowman had infringed Monsanto's patents.

Justice Elena Kagan agreed with the lower courts, suggesting that Bowman had been too clever for his own good. Bowman's main argument was that a doctrine called patent exhaustion allowed him to do what he liked with products he had obtained legally. However, Justice Kagan said this doctrine did not apply to the way Bowman used the seeds.

The ruling protects biotechnology entrepreneurs from potential predators and bolsters the argument that self-replicating products can be protected from patent infringement even if their challengers go through third parties. However, it may lead to higher prices for consumers, as three corporations control much of the global commercial seed market, and the cost to plant 1 acre of soybeans has risen significantly since 1995.

The ruling does not settle all future cases involving self-replicating products, and it remains to be seen how such inventions will be handled in other cases. The Supreme Court is still pending a decision on whether human genes can be patented.

In a recent study, Facebook analyzed over a million status updates from English speakers in the United States, using the Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count (LIWC) Dictionary to categorize words and identify patterns in usage.

The findings reveal that older users tend to write longer updates, use more prepositions and articles, and discuss family and social processes more frequently. Younger users, on the other hand, use more curse words, express anger, and swear more. The use of the word "you" indicates a large number of friends.

The study also found that people are most positive in the morning and negative emotions peak after 10 p.m. References to time peak in the morning, possibly due to posts about late nights or being late for work. Updates with negative emotions receive more comments than those with positive emotions, suggesting friends offering consolation.

Interestingly, people tend to use similar words as their friends, particularly when referring to family, religion, or swearing. The study could be useful for advertisers and marketers, as it provides insights into user behavior and preferences. For example, a rock band targeting younger users might use more curse words and sexual references, while an event planner might aim for a promotional push around 4 p.m., when references to leisure activities begin to spike.

Google, ahead of the 2014 Winter Olympics in Sochi, Russia, made a pro-LGBT statement with a rainbow-colored doodle on its homepage worldwide, including Russia. The doodle, featuring silhouettes of athletes, links to the Olympic Charter's principle against discrimination. The charter states that sport is a human right, and everyone should have the opportunity to practice it without discrimination.

The move comes amidst Russia's controversial anti-gay propaganda law, which restricts the rights of gay citizens and has been a contentious issue leading up to the Olympics. AT&T and American Apparel have spoken out against the law, but other official sponsors, including Coca-Cola, Visa, and Procter & Gamble, have yet to make statements in favor of LGBT rights in Russia.

Google declined to comment on the matter. The change isn't limited to the U.S. homepage, as Google.ru also displays the pro-LGBT doodle. The move by Google is seen as a stand against Russia's anti-gay laws and a show of support for LGBT rights at the Sochi Olympics.

In a tragic turn of events, a mother in Georgia, Nicole Bahret, discovered that her son, Mackean Robertson, had died in a car crash when she arrived at the scene of the accident unaware of the unfolded events. The accident occurred on July 17th, involving a three-car collision on a road near the Sawnee Mountain Preserve in Forsyth County.

According to the Forsyth County Sheriff’s office, a white 2010 Mercedes SUV, driven by a 17-year-old Natalie D’Allen from Suwanee, collided with a white 2005 Honda Accord driven by Robertson. The Honda slid sideways into the path of a westbound green Nissan Pathfinder, resulting in Robertson's death at the scene. The other drivers and passengers were transported to the hospital to be treated for injuries.

Robertson was a student at Forsyth Central High School and had graduated from Georgia Cyber Academy in May. His aunt described him as an amazing person who was loved by everyone he came into contact with. Hundreds of people attended his funeral, and a fundraising page has been set up to help cover funeral costs, which has raised over $15,000 as of Wednesday.

Nicole Bahret shared several photos of her son with Channel 2’s Chris Jose, expressing that she will miss his smile the most. She said that the past two weeks have been difficult since losing Mackean, but she finds comfort surrounded by close friends and family. Forsyth Central High School has scheduled a memorial for Robertson on August 12th.

Natalie D’Allen turned herself in to law enforcement on July 23rd and posted bond, according to the sheriff's office. The investigation into the crash remains ongoing, and no charges have been filed yet.

In Beijing, ten individuals were arrested for the illegal killing and dismemberment of a wild giant panda, as reported by Chinese state television. The incident occurred in December in Yanjin, Yunnan province, where police discovered the panda's skin, bones, and 22 pounds of meat during a raid on a house. Two of the suspects, brothers, admitted to hunting the animal after it allegedly killed their goat. DNA tests confirmed the panda was an adult female.

The case has sparked strong reactions on social media, with some expressing shock and dismay at the heartlessness towards the endangered species. However, others argue that the demand for panda parts fuels such killings.

The giant panda is a protected species in China, and poaching them is rare due to their high value on the black market. The arrested suspects could face years in jail if convicted. The wild panda population in China has grown slightly since the last census in 2003, with 1,864 pandas currently estimated.

However, economic development remains a significant threat to pandas, with hydropower plants, roads, and mining projects disrupting their natural habitats. The World Wide Fund for Nature has noted a decline in poaching but emphasizes that it remains a problem, and Chinese authorities are increasing efforts to combat acts endangering rare animals.

A new study published in the European Journal of Personality suggests that an individual's personality traits can be discerned through their scent alone. Researchers from the University of Wroclaw in Poland asked participants to wear white cotton t-shirts for three consecutive nights without using fragrances, deodorants, or soaps. The shirts were then collected and rated by 200 participants who evaluated five personality traits of the donors, on a scale of one to 10.

The judges' ratings matched up with the self-assessments of the donors for three personality traits: extroversion (the tendency to be outgoing and sociable), neuroticism (the tendency to feel anxious and moody), and dominance (the urge to be a leader). While the matches were far from perfect, the raters predicted the donor's level of extroversion and neuroticism through smell about as accurately as participants in a different study predicted personality traits based on a video depicting a person's behavior.

Judgments of dominance were most accurate in the case where an individual rater was assessing the odor of someone who was the opposite sex, suggesting such judgments are especially important when it comes to choosing a mate. The findings are preliminary and more studies need to be done to confirm the results, but the researchers believe that personality traits may be expressed physiologically, including through our emotions and hormones, which could alter a person's scent.

Taylor Swift has posted a cryptic video on her social media accounts, hinting at a possible return with new music. The video, which features a snake-like figure, was shared on both Instagram and Twitter. Joseph Kahn, a music video director who has worked with Swift on videos such as "Bad Blood" and "Wildest Dreams," seemed to confirm the news by replying to the post with a smiley face and a tweet suggesting that Swift would "blot out the sun" in 30 minutes, a reference to the upcoming 2017 Solar Eclipse.

In May, Us Weekly reported that Swift has been quietly recording a new album during her time off, with a source stating that she is aiming to release the album this fall. The singer has been keeping a low profile in recent months, but her social media accounts were wiped clean on August 18, and her official website was changed to a black screen.

Fans noticed that the blackout occurred exactly three years after the announcement of Swift's most recent album, 1989. Swift shared a video on Monday, August 21, which features a snake-like figure slithering as the lights flicker. The return is just as mysterious as the disappearance of posts.

Fans have been speculating about the meaning of the video and whether it signals the release of new music. Some have pointed out that Swift has been associated with snake imagery since her drama with Kim Kardashian last year, and that she has embraced the nickname "Snake" on social media. Others have joked that Swift is trying to outshine the solar eclipse, which is happening on the same day as the video was shared.

One date that Swift fans should keep in mind is September 30, the end of the eligibility period for next year's Grammy awards, which would give the singer a hard deadline if she wants any new music to qualify.

This weekend, a 10-mile stretch of Interstate 405 in Los Angeles will be closed for 53 hours due to a bridge demolition project. The closure, dubbed "Carmageddon" or "Carpocalypse," is expected to cause significant traffic congestion, potentially bringing Los Angeles to a standstill. To help Angelenos cope with the closure, various businesses are offering discounts and deals. Bark Pet Photography is offering a 20% discount on pet portraits, while merchants such as hotels, bars, florists, jewelers, and tattoo parlors are offering deals to attract customers. Some businesses are even going as far as hiring a man dressed in a chicken suit to attract weary drivers. JetBlue Airways is offering a $4 one-way flight from Burbank to Long Beach to allow people to fly over the traffic. Briles Wing & Helicopter is offering luxury helicopter rides for $150, allowing passengers to view the traffic from above. The closure has also spawned a website, Car-mageddon.com, which sells T-shirts and serves as a regional clearinghouse for shutdown events, deals, and commentary. Amid the pre-emptive panic, a cluster of Carmageddon capitalists is emerging to combat the shutdown's impact on the local economy. Some businesses are worried that the deals won't be enough to pry spenders from home. A new study published in the journal Occupational & Environmental Medicine has linked a common chemical, pyrethroids, found in head lice treatments to behavioral difficulties in children. The study found that children with higher levels of certain pyrethroid metabolites in their system were more likely to display abnormal behaviors at age 6 than those who didn't. The study found a correlation between pyrethroids and behavioral issues in children, but did not establish causation.

Pyrethroids are synthetic chemicals used in insecticides like head lice treatments and some mosquito repellents. For the study, researchers measured levels of five pyrethroid metabolites in the urine of women in the early stages of pregnancy and, later, in their 6-year-olds. Mothers with higher levels of cis-DCCA in their urine during pregnancy were more likely to have children with a higher risk of internalizing behaviors. Higher levels of another metabolite, 3-PBA, in the children’s urine was linked with a higher risk of externalizing behaviors.

The study found that there was a correlation between pyrethroids and behavioral issues in children, not a causation. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention estimates that up to 12 million head lice infestations happen each year among children aged 3 to 11. While pyrethroids are the main recommended treatments for lice, other compounds can be used, like alcohol-based treatments and an anti-parasitic drug called ivermectin. More rigorous studies are needed to confirm the findings and determine if pyrethroids cause behavioral problems in children.

The study demonstrates that cigarette smoke alters the cell walls of MRSA, making it more resistant to reactive oxygen species and antimicrobial peptides, which are chemicals used by immune cells to kill pathogens. Furthermore, the increased resistance persisted for 24 hours after exposure, suggesting it could be inherited.

In lab studies, MRSA exposed to cigarette smoke extract were four times more resistant to macrophage killing than non-exposed MRSA. Additionally, the smoke-exposed MRSA became more resistant to antimicrobial peptides, which pierce bacterial cell walls.

The study's findings suggest that cigarette smoke not only harms smokers but also aids pathogens by making them more resistant to the immune system's defenses. The research adds another reason for individuals to refrain from smoking.

The discovery was made on Sunday after a Massachusetts State Police helicopter spotted what appeared to be a body in the river. The body was later recovered by Tyngsboro police and firefighters.

Goulet, a student at Nashua High School North, had gone missing on Friday night during a storm, and a missing person's report was filed by his parents on Saturday. His family had been frantically searching for him, and his uncle and cousin had yelled for him into storm drains throughout the city.

Goulet was described as being 5 feet 8 inches tall and weighing around 200 pounds. He had short, black hair on the sides with longer hair along the top of his head, blue eyes, and was last seen wearing a denim vest with metal studs, a gray T-shirt, black shorts, and black Converse All-Star sneakers.

Based on the description, Nashua police believe the body found is that of Goulet, but a positive identification will not be made until the Massachusetts Medical Examiner's Office confirms it. The storm drain that Goulet may have fallen into is an "interceptor" that connects to the waste water treatment plant over several miles of pipeline.

The interceptor is said to have a steep drop and could be 20 feet deep. It is unclear how the cover came off of the storm drain, but it was resecured with bolts on Sunday afternoon. Grief counselors will be available at Nashua North on Monday to talk to Goulet's classmates.

The high school is putting together a list of his friends and reaching out to them. The principal said they will also send a note to parents on Sunday evening to update them on the situation. Many people in Nashua, some who didn't even know Goulet, were emotional over the situation.

A tribute to Goulet grew by the hour Sunday night, with friends sitting together and consoling each other while many people -- some total strangers to Goulet -- left flowers at the site. "I wouldn’t want it to be one of my boys. That shouldn’t have happened," Diana Bela said.

Nicholas Brown, one of Goulet’s best friends, left a Converse shoe -- Goulet’s favorite brand -- with a note inside at the memorial. Brown said he saw Goulet on Friday, just hours before he disappeared while walking home from a friend’s house.

"Anything sad, he would just like, try to be happy about it," Brown said. "Or he’d try to make a joke of something, just to get him by, you know."

"It doesn’t seem real to me that something like this could happen, where I could be making jokes with him in second block of school, and then a day later, he turns up missing," Brown said.

The search for Goulet began on Friday after officers responded to a drain behind 75 Main St. and the north side of Water Street for a report that a person may have fallen down a storm drain. Despite there being no witnesses, Nashua police believe Goulet fell down the storm drain, and a massive search began on Saturday.

Police found items, including a baseball cap and an umbrella, near the drain, but no identifying information. Based on information given by Goulet’s parents and surveillance footage, police had reason to believe that the items could belong to Goulet. Officers searched areas including the Nashua River, the Merrimack River, and the entire underwater storm drain system north of Water Street and south to Sawmill Drive.

The Nashua Fire Department and its dive team, the city of Nashua Waste Water Department, Division of Public Works, New Hampshire State Police, Massachusetts State Police, and New Hampshire Fish and Game assisted with the effort. Public works assisted in the search, and a private contractor was called in to search the sewers with cameras, according to Nashua Mayor Jim Donchess.

Donchess said that approximately 1,000 feet of the sewer system had been searched as of Sunday afternoon. Donchess described the storm drain that Goulet may have fallen into as an "interceptor," which connects to the waste water treatment plant over "several miles" of pipeline. The interceptor is said to have a steep drop and could be 20 feet deep.

Officials are unsure how the cover came off of the storm drain. The storm drain cover was resecured with bolts on Sunday afternoon. "No one has ever potentially fallen into the sewer system as far as we know, and these covers don’t typically come off," Donchess said.

Donchess said that grief counselors will be available at Nashua North on Monday to talk to Goulet’s classmates. "We feel so badly for the family -- for Jacob’s family, his parents, for the kids who know him at the high school. We’ve asked that the school department have grief counselors available for the kids at Nashua High School North," Donchess said.

Meanwhile, his friends and family are reeling after the latest developments. The high school is putting together a list of his friends and reaching out to them. The principal said they will also send a note to parents on Sunday evening to update them on the situation.
