In a fascinating study, researchers have discovered that Cuban boas, the largest native terrestrial predators in Cuba, coordinate their attacks on fruit bats that emerge from sinkhole caves. The boas, which are typically solitary, position themselves in strategic locations within the cave passageway, waiting to strike as the bats fly past.

Vladimir Dinets, a research assistant professor at the University of Tennessee, Knoxville, observed this behavior during a bird- and mammal-watching tour in Desembarco del Granma National Park, Cuba. Dinets found that the snakes would take turns occupying the same positions, suggesting a level of coordination rather than mere preference for specific locations.

The coordination proved beneficial for the snakes, as they were significantly more likely to capture a meal when hunting together. Dinets published his findings in the journal Animal Behavior and Cognition, challenging the long-held belief that reptiles are mostly solitary and not particularly intelligent.

This is not the first instance of snakes hunting bats mid-flight. Similar behavior has been observed in Puerto Rico and at the Cavern of Serpents in Mexico. However, further research is needed to confirm the coordination of these hunts.

The Cuban boa population is dwindling due to hunting for food and the pet trade, making it increasingly difficult to observe this unique behavior. Dinets expressed concern that if their numbers in a cave fall, they may die out, as coordinated hunting might be crucial for their survival.

The study provides valuable insights into the hunting tactics of snakes, which are often thought to be solitary creatures. It also underscores the importance of preserving these unique ecosystems and the species that inhabit them.

In a remarkable medical feat, doctors at Stony Brook University Hospital on Long Island performed the first-ever operation on triplets born with a rare skull condition called craniosynostosis. The Howard triplets - Hunter, Jackson, and Kaden - underwent surgery in January to correct the condition where their skulls did not form properly. The chance of this occurring in triplets is one in 500 trillion, and it's particularly unusual because they are not all identical.

The condition is not only a cosmetic issue but could restrict brain growth. The triplets' skulls fused too early in utero, causing their heads to have abnormal shapes. The babies will have to wear helmets for the next few months as they recover, but then they will lead normal lives.

The Howards, who conceived their triplets without the help of fertility drugs, are grateful for the life-changing surgery their boys received. The triplets - Kaden, the laid-back one, Hunter the talker, and Jackson the tough one - are already full of life and have made medical history as the first-known case of triplets all born with craniosynostosis. The surgeries took place over two days in January, and the boys were back home two days after their surgeries. For the next six to nine months, they must wear orthotic custom-made helmets 23 hours a day to help mold their skulls.

The couple is still adjusting to life with three boys and three cats, finding it a little chaotic but awesome. They'd like to have a girl join the family, but aren't planning to have more kids, fearing another set of triplets. The Howard triplets are a testament to the power of modern medicine and the resilience of the human spirit.

The Cleveland police officer Timothy Loehmann, who shot and killed 12-year-old Tamir Rice in Ohio last year, has given his first public account of the shooting, arguing that he was engaged in an "active shooter situation" and believed Tamir was 18 years old. Loehmann shot Tamir, who was black, within two seconds of arriving at a local park on 22 November 2014, after a 911 caller reported that there was a juvenile in the area with a weapon that was "probably fake."

In his statement, Loehmann said he shot because Tamir pulled a gun - which turned out to be a pellet gun - from his waistband. He told grand jurors that he had been trained that "the cruiser is a coffin" and that he had repeatedly told Tamir to raise his hands as the boy was "reaching into his waistband."

Loehmann and his partner, Frank Garmback, are currently being investigated by a grand jury for potential criminal charges. The officers, who had previously declined to be interviewed by county investigators, provided written testimony that was released by prosecutors after being read to grand jurors on Tuesday.

Garmback, who was the driver of the patrol car on the day of the shooting, concedes that the patrol car had slid along the ground and "did not stop where and when I intended."

Lawyers for the Rice family have repeatedly dismissed claims that Loehmann and Garmback could have given the 12-year-old sufficient warnings or commands, given the fraction of time that passed between the officers arriving on the scene and opening fire. On Tuesday, Rice family lawyers described the prosecutor's decision to allow the officer's unsworn statements before the grand jury as "a stunning irregularity."

The steady release of evidence presented to the grand jury, including three expert testimonies that concluded the shooting was justified, has been staunchly criticized by Tamir's parents and protesters in Cleveland, who argue that the drip feed of information is designed to prepare the public for a non-indictment. Rice family lawyers have requested the grand jury also hear testimony from two experts who concluded the shooting was not justified.

Asked for a statement on the officers' behalf, their attorney, Henry Hiler, said in an email on Tuesday: "We respect the grand jury process and have faith in our judicial system."

The officers' statements were read to the jurors a day after Tamir's mother, Samaria, testified to the panel about the loss of her son. In a statement, her attorney said she had asked the jurors whether the officers' actions "could possibly be 'reasonable' or 'justifiable'."

"She believes that the answer is plainly no," the statement said, "and hopes and prays that the grand jury agrees that there is probable cause to indict the officers and hold them accountable for her son's death."

The shooting of Tamir Rice has sparked widespread protests and calls for justice, with many arguing that the police officers' actions were unjustified and that the boy was unfairly targeted due to his race. The case is currently being investigated by a grand jury, with a decision expected in the coming months.

The search for remains from AirAsia Flight QZ8501, which went missing on Sunday with 162 people aboard, continued on Wednesday despite challenging weather conditions. Debris and seven bodies, including a flight attendant, were found 100-200 kilometers from the aircraft's last known location over the Java Sea.

Search teams are looking for other bodies and parts of the plane, including its black boxes, which could provide crucial information about the cause of the crash. Sonar equipment has been used to search the bottom of the sea, but strong currents have made it difficult to locate the wreckage.

The discovery of the debris and bodies has been a heartbreaking blow for families whose loved ones were on board the flight. Dozens of ambulances have been lined up in Surabaya, Indonesia, ready to carry any bodies recovered.

The search and rescue effort has been hampered by heavy wind, rain, and big waves. The United States is among several nations contributing resources to the effort, with the USS Sampson and USS Fort Worth being prepared to deploy.

AirAsia CEO Tony Fernandes expressed his condolences to the families affected by the crash and said the focus for now must remain on the recovery effort. He also indicated that changes may be made to the airline's operations once the investigation is complete.

The cause of the crash is still unknown, but some experts have suggested that the aircraft may have experienced an aerodynamic stall due to a lack of speed or flying at too sharp an angle. The key to understanding what happened will likely be contained in the aircraft's flight recorders.

The mood at the airport in Surabaya has been somber, with many relatives increasingly frustrated by the lack of concrete news over the past 24 hours. Some have given DNA samples to help with the identification process, while others have prayed for a miracle.

The crash of AirAsia Flight QZ8501 is the latest in a series of aviation disasters in Asia, following the disappearance of Malaysia Airlines Flight 370 in March and the downing of Malaysia Airlines Flight 17 in July. The victims of the AirAsia crash were primarily Indonesian, with nearly all of them frequent visitors to Singapore. The Indonesian government has urged cities to tone down or cancel New Year's Eve celebrations out of respect for the victims and their families.

The album "Before I Self Destruct" by 50 Cent, released after a backlash over his pop-rap crossover hits, aims to revive his career by returning to the tropes and narratives of '90s gangsta rap. The study published in The Cryosphere reveals that Greenland's ice sheet has been darkening over the past two decades, absorbing more heat from the sun and increasing snow melt. This trend is likely to continue, with the surface's reflectivity, or albedo, decreasing by as much as 10 percent by the end of the century. The darkening is caused by two feedback loops created by the melting itself. One of the processes isn't visible to the human eye, but it is having a profound effect.

The first process involves tiny impurities, such as dust and soot grains, buried just beneath the surface of the ice sheet. As fresh snow melts in the summertime, deeper and dirtier layers of ice are exposed, rendering the surface a bit darker. The researchers suggest that especially warm summers can cause several years worth of impurities to become concentrated at the ice sheet's surface.

The second reason for the darkening has to do with a change in the reflective properties of the ice itself. As snowpack melts and refreezes, individual ice grains tend to get larger. Larger grains have less surface area and scatter less sunlight, therefore absorbing more solar energy. This effect, the authors say, is strongest in the infrared range, which is invisible to human eyes but can be seen with satellites.

While soot blowing in from wildfires contributes to the problem, it hasn't been driving the change, the study finds. The real culprits are the feedback loops created by the melting itself. The researchers used satellite data to compare summertime changes in Greenland's albedo from 1981 to 2012. The first decade showed little change, but starting around 1996, the data show that due to darkening, the ice began absorbing about 2 percent more solar radiation per decade.

The study also raises questions about whether Greenland's high plateau is darkening as previous reports have suggested. The scientists found no long-term trend of darkening at the top, and they suspect that the Terra MODIS satellite sensor that has detected darkening in the past may actually be degrading, as previous studies have suggested. At lower elevations, the signal is much stronger.

The scientists also ran a computer model to simulate the future of Greenland's surface temperature, grain size, exposed ice area, and albedo. Over the current century, the model projects that the average albedo for the entire ice sheet will fall by as much as 8 percent, and by as much 10 percent on the western edge, where the ice is darkest today. Those are conservative estimates – the change could be twice that, the researchers said.

The study has global implications, as fresh meltwater pouring into the ocean from Greenland raises sea level and could affect ocean ecology and circulation. "It's a complex system of interaction between the atmosphere and the ice sheet surface," said lead author Marco Tedesco, a research professor at Columbia University's Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory and adjunct scientist at NASA Goddard Institute of Space Studies. "Rising temperatures are promoting more melting, and that melting is reducing albedo, which in turn is increasing melting."

The study was co-authored by Sarah Doherty of the University of Washington; Xavier Fettweis of University of Liege; Patrick Alexander of NASA Goddard Institute of Space Studies and City University of New York; Jeyavinoth Jeyaratnam of the City College of New York; and Julienne Stroeve of University of Boulder.

A new study published in the medical journal JAMA Pediatrics suggests that the use of acetaminophen during pregnancy may be associated with ADHD-like behavioral problems in children. The study, which analyzed data from over 64,000 children enrolled in the Danish National Birth Cohort study between 1996 and 2002, found that prenatal exposure to acetaminophen may increase the risk of a child being diagnosed with ADHD or being prescribed ADHD medications and exhibiting ADHD-like behaviors.

The study authors concluded that taking acetaminophen for longer periods and later in pregnancy is associated with higher risks, with mothers reporting use for 20 weeks or more having a 50% increased risk for receiving ADHD medication. However, it's important to note that the study did not find a cause-and-effect relationship between acetaminophen and ADHD.

The study's authors suggest that acetaminophen may increase the risk of ADHD by interfering with maternal hormones that are critical for fetal brain development. However, some experts have criticized the study, pointing out that the literature cited by the authors is not relevant to the human condition and that ADHD runs in families.

The makers of Tylenol, which contains acetaminophen, have stated that when used as directed, Tylenol has one of the most favorable safety profiles among over-the-counter pain relievers. They also note that there are no prospective, randomized controlled studies demonstrating a causal link between acetaminophen use during pregnancy and adverse effects on child development.

The study's authors suggest that pregnant women should try to avoid taking painkillers as much as possible until more is known about the potential risks. Alternatives for relieving pain during pregnancy, such as massages, baths, and acupuncture, were suggested as alternatives to medication.

The study conducted a meta-analysis to examine the risk of sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS) for infants swaddled for sleep. The study included four observational studies that measured swaddling for the last or reference sleep. The overall age-adjusted pooled odds ratio (OR) for swaddling in all four studies was 1.58, indicating a significant association between swaddling and SIDS. However, the heterogeneity among the studies was substantial, with a random effects model being used for analysis.

When the most recent study conducted in the United Kingdom was removed, the heterogeneity was reduced, and the pooled OR was 1.38, using a fixed effects model. The risk of SIDS varied according to the position placed for sleep, with the highest risk for prone sleeping, followed by side sleeping and supine sleeping. Limited evidence suggested that the risk of SIDS increased with infant age, and swaddling should be discouraged after a certain age.

The study also found that swaddling was more common among younger infants, and the risk of SIDS linked to swaddling seemed to increase in older infants. The advice given in the Netherlands, a country with low rates of SIDS, is to encourage swaddling to reduce excessive crying but to stop swaddling as soon as the child signals he or she is trying to turn over and never to initiate swaddling after the fourth month.

The study concluded that the current advice to avoid placing infants on their front or side to sleep may especially apply to infants who are swaddled. Given the marked increase in infants swaddled and found prone, coupled with an increased risk of swaddling with increased age regardless of sleeping position, health professionals and current guidelines should consider an appropriate age limit at which swaddling should be discouraged.

The Monroe County Heritage Museum in Alabama is facing a trademark infringement lawsuit from author Harper Lee, who is best known for her Pulitzer Prize-winning novel "To Kill a Mockingbird." The lawsuit, filed in Mobile's federal court, seeks to prohibit the museum from using the book's name or characters to promote activities or sell merchandise.

Lee's attorney, Clay Rankin, declined to comment on the matter. The lawsuit alleges that the museum has been using the book's name and characters without permission, and that it has become more "brazen" in its violations as Lee's health has declined. The museum's attorney, Matt Goforth, denies the allegations and claims that the museum has been honoring Lee's legacy for over two decades.

The museum is a substantial business that generated over $500,000 in revenue in 2011, according to the lawsuit. Goforth describes it as a nonprofit that would be put out of business if Lee's suit succeeds. The lawsuit also cites an example of a cookbook that traded on a fictional character created by Lee.

Conflict between the museum and author erupted earlier this year when the museum moved to block Lee from registering her trademark. Lawyers in that case will begin taking sworn testimony and exchanging documents on Oct. 28. That dispute will be decided by the Trademark Trial and Appeal Board.

In May, Lee sued the son-in-law of her former literary agent in an attempt to re-secure her copyright on the book. She settled that in September. The latest lawsuit is the latest salvo in the conflict with the museum.

The town of Monroeville, where Lee was born and raised, has been divided by the legal dispute. Some believe that Lee's lawsuit is an attempt to protect her legacy, while others see it as an attack on the museum that honors her. The museum's logo features an image of a mockingbird and the cupola of the Old County Courthouse, which was the setting for the dramatic trial in "To Kill a Mockingbird." The lawsuit alleges that the museum falsely proclaims its mission to be history, but the museum denies this.

The lawsuit cites various examples indicating how closely the museum is tied to the book, right down to the website, tokillamockingbird.com. Researchers at MIT, the University of Sheffield, and the Tokyo Institute of Technology have developed a tiny origami robot that can be ingested in a capsule and unfold itself in the stomach to perform tasks such as removing swallowed objects or patching wounds. The robot is made of dried pig intestine and a magnet, and its movements are controlled using external magnetic fields. The team tested the robot in a synthetic stomach model and successfully removed a button battery. The robot is still a work-in-progress, but its creators believe it could have promising applications in healthcare. The research will be presented at the International Conference on Robotics and Automation this week. The team is planning to add sensors to the robot and redesign it to control itself without the need for external magnetic fields. The robot could potentially be used to retrieve swallowed batteries, which can cause tissue burns and other complications, especially in young children.

Ford Motor Company announced on Thursday, March 19, 2013, that it will be closing its two auto plants in Australia and cease production in the country by October 2016. The decision comes due to sliding sales, high costs, and a strong Australian dollar. The company's engine plant in Geelong and assembly plant in Broadmeadows, both in Victoria, will be closed. The move will result in 1,200 job losses and marks the end of over 90 years of car production in Australia. The government has invested heavily in the country's automobile industry, and this decision is a significant setback. Ford cited unsustainably high business costs, with wages being a particular concern.

The article discusses ways to protect personal information from the National Security Agency (NSA) due to its broad powers to capture private data. The methods include:

1. Browse anonymously with Tor: Tor is a distributed network that bounces traffic among several proxy computers, making it difficult for the NSA to trace the user's IP address.

2. Keep chats private with OTR: OTR is an instant messaging extension that offers end-to-end encryption, making conversations unreadable to the server and thwarting eavesdropping.

3. Make secure calls with Silent Circle: Silent Circle is an Internet telephony application that offers end-to-end encryption, making it difficult for the NSA to intercept calls.

4. Make secure calls with Redphone: Redphone is another application that makes phone calls with end-to-end encryption, similar to Silent Circle.

5. Remove cellphone battery to thwart tracking: The NSA can track a user's location through cellphone tower data. To prevent this, the user can turn off their cell phone or remove the battery.

The article also notes that while it's possible to protect the contents of communications from government spying, there's no easy technological fix to prevent the government from finding out who a user is communicating with.

Additionally, the article provides instructions on how to download and use Tor Browser for anonymous web browsing.

Joe Miller, who won Alaska's Republican U.S. Senate primary and lost the general election to incumbent Republican Senator Lisa Murkowski in a write-in campaign, has finally conceded the race after two months of legal battles. Miller addressed supporters at a news conference on Friday, stating that he would not appeal Murkowski's 10,000-vote victory, effectively ending the legal disputes.

Murkowski was officially certified as the winner on Thursday, allowing her to be sworn in on January 5 alongside the other newly elected senators. Her victory marks the first time a senator has won as a write-in candidate since Strom Thurmond in 1954.

Miller had sued the state over what he considered its improper attempts to determine voters' intent, arguing that voters should have had to spell Murkowski's name correctly. However, a federal judge ruled against Miller, stating that voter intent was paramount, and Miller's interpretation "would erode the integrity of the election system."

Despite not pursuing an appeal to the U.S. Supreme Court, Miller defended his legal actions, stating that they would lead to "more transparent, clearer standards" in Alaska. Miller also indicated that he had not yet contemplated any plans for another campaign, though there has been speculation that he might run for the state's House seat in 2012.

After the brutal campaign, Miller addressed any unresolved issues with the Murkowski camp, stating that they had no ill will towards Murkowski and had significant differences of opinion about the direction of the nation. Miller also clarified that his highest-profile backer, former Alaska Governor Sarah Palin, took a lower profile in the campaign while the courts sorted out a resolution, but SARAHPAC still donated to Miller's recount fund.

The article discusses the efforts of scientists and conservationists to resurrect an ancient species of super-cow, known as the auroch, which went extinct nearly 400 years ago. The auroch was a powerful and fearsome creature that roamed the grassy plains of Europe for 250,000 years until its extinction in Poland in 1627. Adolf Hitler's followers tried to breed a similar beast as part of their Aryan mythology.

Now, conservationists believe the auroch was key to preserving the continent's ecosystem and have launched the Tauros Project to 'rewild' the fourth generation of their experimental auroch replacement. The Tauros are bred from a number of current species with auroch ancestry and have been released into areas of Spain, Portugal, Croatia, the Czech Republic, and Romania, where they have had to contend with wolves and other predators.

Ecologist Ronald Goderie, founder of the Tauros Project, believes that by 2025, the seventh generation of neo-aurochs will be as close as possible to the originals. The aggressive breed was produced by German zoologists and brothers Heinz and Lutz Heck, whom the Nazi party commissioned to produce a breed of cattle based on the aurochs.

In 2015, a British farmer was forced to kill off half his herd of auroch-derived Heck cattle because they kept trying to kill him. The aurochs were the largest land mammals in Europe until the rise of human civilization decimated their numbers, and the last of the species died in Poland in 1627 -- one of the first recorded cases of extinction.

Conservationists now believe the loss of the keystone herbivore was tragic for biodiversity in Europe, arguing that the aurochs' huge appetite for grazing provided a natural "gardening service" that maintained landscapes and created the conditions for other species to thrive. The theory is now being put to the test, as a "near 100% substitute" of the beast is returned to the forests.

The Tauros Project is a part of a larger rewilding initiative led by Rewilding Europe, which supports the restoration of natural processes through projects that range from rebuilding rivers to introducing apex predators. The Tauros are being tested in the wild and are showing signs of de-domestication, adapting to the presence of large packs of wolves.

Critics have raised concerns about the unintended consequences of introducing new species, but proponents argue that the aurochs were formidable grazers and are expected to restore dysfunctional ecosystems. The successful introduction of bison in the US shows that such initiatives can have a positive impact, but one intervention can lead to another. The International Union for the Conservation of Nature (IUCN) has issued new guidelines to manage such impacts.

A teacher at Union County Career & Technology Center in South Carolina, Leigh Anne Arthur, has resigned after a nude photo of her was spread through the school by a student. The incident occurred on February 19, when the student took Arthur's phone from her desk while she was out of the room and took pictures of the nude photo on her phone. The student then shared the photo throughout the school.

Arthur claims that the week before Valentine's Day, she had some personal pictures on her phone intended for her husband. She left her phone on her desk to go out and be a hall monitor between classes, and in that time, a student went and took pictures of her phone from his phone and shared them with anyone in class who wanted them.

Arthur said the student then said at the end of class, "your day of reckoning is coming." Later, she was told what had happened, and she checked with the student's parents who she said were 100% on her side. The student went to the principal and admitted it, and two witnesses also went to the principal.

Arthur says the principal asked for her resignation the next Tuesday. She says the district told her there was no policy about "inappropriate material on her cell phone," but they were firing her for that reason. She was also in trouble for "making her phone easily accessible," according to Arthur.

Arthur made a police report, and the student's phone is now in possession of the Union County Sheriff's Office. However, the interim superintendent, David Eubanks, has dismissed the petition as "insignificant." Eubanks has also said that he has seen evidence that suggests Mrs. Arthur routinely allowed students to use her phone, which Arthur denies.

The student is under investigation by authorities and will face consequences for his actions. The petition to reinstate Arthur has garnered over 8,000 signatures. Arthur has filed a lawsuit against the Union County School District and David Eubanks, alleging false accusations and policies and due process not appropriately followed by the school district.

Hurricane Sandy, yet to make landfall in the United States, is already impacting the upcoming election. The storm has forced President Obama and Mitt Romney to rework their campaign schedules, and temporarily suspended early voting in Maryland and the District of Columbia. The storm could potentially affect early voting between the East Coast and the Great Lakes, with the possibility of impact ranging from "some" to "a whole lot."

A study by Boston University's Andrew Reeves and Carnegie Mellon's John Gasper suggests that electorates punish presidents and governors for severe weather damage, but the response of attentive electorates to the actions of their officials is more significant. The storm's effects on voters' psyches could be significant, as the study shows that electorates are able to separate random events from governmental responses and attribute actions based on the defined roles of politicians.

The storm may also affect the number of polls issued, with some polls suspending until the storm passes. The Northeast, a Democratic-leaning region, could potentially impact Mr. Obama's standing in the polls if 15 million Americans, who are 20 points Democratic-leaning, are unable to reply to surveys due to the hurricane.

The storm could also depress turnout along the Eastern Seaboard on Election Day, potentially reducing Mr. Obama's national popular vote without hurting his standing in the Electoral College much, increasing the risk of a split outcome. However, the Northeast is a wealthy region with better infrastructure, allowing them to recover more quickly after a disaster, and the after-effects could be felt in red-leaning areas as well.

The storm will also affect the plans of the campaigns and the tenor of news coverage about them. Academic studies on the effects of natural disasters on elections have produced ambiguous results, but suggest that a well-managed disaster response could help an incumbent, while a botched response could harm him. The immediate political consequences of the storm may be limited, as most studies evaluate the political effects of disasters on elections held months or even years later.

The report commissioned by Nestle, conducted by Verite, reveals abusive labor practices in Thailand's seafood industry, supplying global companies like Nestle. Migrant workers are subjected to hazardous, inhumane living and working conditions, with some being trapped in debt and forced labor. The report found indicators of forced labor, trafficking, and child labor among sea-based and land-based workers in the Thai seafood sector, posing a challenge to any company sourcing seafood.

Nestle, one of the world's largest food companies, has pledged to address these issues by finding ways to track the source of seafood ingredients, training boat captains on proper practices, and conducting audits. The company has also promised public updates periodically.

The issue of forced labor in Thailand's seafood industry has also been highlighted in lawsuits against Costco and Nestle. In August, a federal lawsuit was filed against Costco in California, demanding that it label much of the shrimp it sells as the product of human slavery. A week later, a class action suit was filed against Nestle alleging its Fancy Feast cat food was the product of slave labor, imported from its partner, Thai Union Frozen Products.

Thailand's military government has acknowledged the issue and is working to address concerns, but the European Union has threatened to ban Thai seafood imports if the country fails to improve regulation.

Nestle has adopted a strategy similar to one it used for its chocolate business to address labor issues. In 2001, Nestle and other leading chocolate makers agreed to a plan to prevent child labor on farms in West Africa. Nestle agreed to monitoring by the Fair Labor Association in 2012, and the non-profit organization makes random visits to farms that supply Nestle with cocoa.

In response to the report, Nestle's Magdi Batato, executive vice president of operations, said, "Nestle is committed to eliminating forced labor in our seafood supply chain in Thailand, working alongside other stakeholders to tackle this serious and complex issue." The company aims to make significant progress in the months ahead.

The University of New Hampshire has announced that it will become the first flagship state university in the United States to accept scores from the Chinese university entrance exam, known as the Gaokao. This move is aimed at attracting more Chinese students, who currently make up over one-third of all international students in the US. The Gaokao is a highly competitive, nine-hour exam that plays a crucial role in determining a student's future prospects in China, with nearly 10 million students taking it each year. The University of New Hampshire has launched a recruiting website in Chinese and English and will accept Chinese students who submit their Gaokao results, high school transcripts, participate in a video interview, and take an English test. Students who are accepted will be able to start classes in Durham, New Hampshire in January, allowing them to start a semester early. The University of San Francisco, a Jesuit college, already has a similar program that allows Chinese students to bypass US standardized tests and instead submit just their Gaokao score, grades, and English language interview. The decision by the University of New Hampshire comes amid a federal crackdown on Chinese student visas, with the Trump administration considering limiting visas as part of a broader package of measures against China. Details have not been officially announced, but students studying high tech manufacturing fields, such as aviation and robotics, are expected to now receive visas with shorter lengths of stay.

The Apolipoprotein E (APOE) gene, with its three variants e2, e3, and e4, has been extensively studied as a risk factor for various conditions, including cardiovascular diseases, rare disorders, and age-related macular degeneration.

Carrying at least one copy of the APOE e4 allele increases the risk of developing atherosclerosis, a condition characterized by the accumulation of fatty deposits and scar-like tissue in the arteries, which can lead to heart attacks and strokes. On the other hand, the APOE e2 allele significantly increases the risk of Hyperlipoproteinemia type III, a rare condition characterized by increased blood levels of cholesterol, triglycerides, and beta-very low-density lipoproteins (beta-VLDLs). This condition can result in the formation of small, yellow skin growths called xanthomas and the development of atherosclerosis.

APOE gene variants have also been studied as a potential risk factor for age-related macular degeneration, a leading cause of vision loss among older people worldwide. Some studies suggest that having at least one copy of the APOE e4 allele may protect against this disease or delay the onset of vision loss, while having at least one copy of the APOE e2 allele may increase the risk or cause symptoms to appear earlier. However, other studies have not found these associations, indicating a need for further research to clarify the role of APOE gene variants in the development of age-related macular degeneration.

Individuals with one or two e4 variants are significantly more likely to develop Alzheimer's, while adults with e2 variants have more plaques in their brains but are less likely to have symptoms of dementia. The complex relationship between APOE gene variants and these conditions highlights the importance of continued research in this area.

Jared Kushner, President Trump's son-in-law and senior adviser, has had his permanent security clearance restored after a year of uncertainty. The study conducted by the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) and the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service has revealed that 85% of male smallmouth bass and 27% of male largemouth bass in 19 national wildlife preserves in the Northeast U.S. are intersex. Intersex is a condition where one sex develops characteristics of the opposite sex, and it is tied to the exposure of fish to endocrine-disrupting chemicals that can affect the reproductive system and cause the development of characteristics of the opposite sex, such as immature eggs in the testes of male fish.

The researchers found that the fish were exposed to estrogens such as compounds that enforce the female physiology. These chemicals are found mostly in the organs of the fish, rather than the flesh that people eat. The study suggests that endocrine disrupting chemicals (EDCs) are the most likely culprit for the intersex fish, as they are being dumped into rivers, streams, swamps, and lakes from various sources, including hormones in livestock manure, herbicides and pesticides, and trace amounts of pharmaceuticals like birth control pills discharged from wastewater treatment plants.

The problem of intersex fish has been documented over the past two decades in nearly 40 fish species worldwide. Scientists believe their prevalence is more widespread than previously thought and could be starting to take a toll on some populations, either by reducing a fish's ability to reproduce or weakening its immune system and making them more vulnerable to disease.

The study does not conduct a chemical analysis on the water, so they could not say for sure what was to blame for the intersex fish. However, the findings suggest that EDCs were the most likely the culprit. The researchers are concerned about the potential effects of these chemicals on other wildlife and the human dimension.

The study's lead author, Luke Iwanowicz, emphasized that the findings show the increasing threat of EDCs on refuge lands using bass as an indicator for exposures that may affect fish and other aquatic species. The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service encourages management actions that reduce runoff into streams, ponds, and lakes, both on and off of refuge lands, to help address this issue. The journal article, Evidence of estrogenic endocrine disruption in smallmouth and largemouth bass inhabiting Northeast U.S. National Wildlife Refuge waters: a reconnaissance study, is available online in Ecotoxicology and Environmental Safety.

Title: Unusual Awakening: Midazolam, a Sedative, Helps Regain Consciousness in Minimally Conscious State Patient

Midazolam, a sedative used for sleepiness and anxiety relief before surgeries and procedures, has shown an unexpected "awakening" effect in a minimally conscious state patient in Italy. The 43-year-old man, who was in a coma for 40 days following a car accident, regained consciousness after being administered midazolam during a CT scan.

Initially, the man was in a minimally conscious state, able to open and close his eyes, have a sleep-wake cycle, but unable to communicate or respond to commands. After the accident, his cognitive ability declined, and he exhibited aimless, repetitive behaviors.

Two years post-accident, the man's doctors administered midazolam for a CT scan. Within minutes, he began to talk and interact with others. The man was able to perform simple math problems, read, and understand simple sentences. The researchers identified brain regions affected by the drug, which were previously linked to catatonia symptoms.

However, the effect was temporary, lasting only about two hours, and the man returned to his previous state. The researchers tried using lorazepam, another drug from the same class as midazolam, but the patient became agitated and aggressive. They then switched him to carbamazepine, a drug used to treat epilepsy, which allowed him to maintain the improvement in his ability to interact and communicate with people.

The study, published in the November issue of Restorative Neurology and Neuroscience, is the first report of midazolam having an "awakening" effect. However, it is unclear whether the patient suffered from catatonia or merely exhibited catatonic symptoms. Midazolam is typically given to patients in intensive care units, where they can be monitored continuously.

John Sidney McCain Sr., born in Mississippi in 1884, was a prominent figure in the United States Navy, serving as a commander during World War II. He attended the United States Naval Academy and the University of Mississippi, and his son, John S. McCain Jr., and grandson, John McCain III, also served in the navy and held the rank of admiral. McCain's great-grandson, John S. (Jack) McCain IV, is currently attending the United States Naval Academy.

McCain's naval career began with assignments on ships of the Asiatic Squadron, and he served during the American occupation of Veracruz in the Mexican Revolution. In the years between the world wars, he served on various ships, including the Maryland (BB-46) and New Mexico (BB-40). His first command was the Sirius (AK-18). In 1936, at the age of 51, he was designated a Naval Aviator, and from 1937 to 1939, he commanded the aircraft carrier Ranger (CV-4), contributing to the development of carrier tactics for the war to come.

During World War II, McCain served as Commander of Air Forces for Western Sea Frontier and the South Pacific Force. However, a lapse in his leadership led to heavy losses and the Allied defeat in the Battle of Savo Island in 1942. Despite this, McCain later became Chief of the Bureau of Aeronautics and rose to the rank of Vice Admiral as Deputy Chief of Naval Operations (Air). He returned to the Pacific Theater in 1944, succeeding Marc Mitscher as commander of the Fast Carrier Task Force, and his exceedingly skillful tactics earned him the Navy Cross.

McCain died in September 1945, just after returning to the United States, and was posthumously appointed Admiral. He was buried in Arlington National Cemetery, among other family members, including his brother, William Alexander McCain, Brigadier General, U.S. Army, and John Sidney McCain Jr., Admiral, United States Navy. The USS John S. McCain (DDG-56) was named in his honor, along with his son.

The study led by researchers at the University of Southern California reveals that the significant difference in life expectancies between men and women first emerged at the turn of the 20th century. This was due to the adoption of positive health behaviors, such as improved diets and infectious disease prevention, which led to a decrease in mortality rates. The team found that female death rates decreased 70 percent faster than those of males, with heart disease being the primary cause of excess deaths in adult men over 40. The study, titled "Twentieth century surge of excess adult male mortality," was published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

Researchers also suggest that sex may play a role in defining not only lifespan but also the specific portion of a lifespan that's healthy, or "healthspan." They argue that future research should emphasize the importance of controlling for sex in studies in which age is a variable.

In a separate study, it was found that out of the 53 living supercentenarians – people over 110 years old – 51 are women. Researchers are now looking into how hormones like estrogen and testosterone might modify lifespan by affecting stem cell populations. The goal is to understand how genetics might have an impact on stem cell aging in males and females and to potentially find ways to ameliorate the aging process and maintain the regenerative capacity of stem cells.

Daniel Perlman, a biophysicist at Brandeis University, has invented a wine bottle that doesn't drip when pouring, aiming to solve the long-standing issue of wine dripping down the side of traditional wine bottles. Perlman's solution involves adding a small groove around the lip of the bottle opening, which changes the behavior of the liquid during pouring. Instead of hugging the bottle, the wine falls directly into the intended vessel until it stops coming out. The grooved tip is only two millimeters wide and has shown significant improvement in preventing drips compared to the original wine bottle design. However, the innovation would require bottle manufacturers to build the groove into their products, potentially increasing production costs. The process of adopting Perlman's design by manufacturers is still in its early stages, so the use of napkin bandanas to absorb drips may not be phased out immediately.

Selena Gomez underwent a kidney transplant this summer, with her best friend Francia Raisa serving as the donor. Gomez revealed the news on Instagram, stating that she had been recovering from the procedure due to complications from her Lupus. North Korea claimed to have successfully tested a hydrogen bomb on Wednesday, a move that would significantly advance its nuclear capabilities if confirmed. The test, which registered as a 5.1 magnitude earthquake, was met with skepticism from the international community, including the United States, which disputed North Korea's claim of a successful hydrogen bomb test. The test drew immediate condemnation from China, the North's main economic and diplomatic backer, and the United Nations Security Council announced plans to impose new sanctions on North Korea. The test also added to a list of foreign policy failures that Republican presidential candidates in the United States accused President Barack Obama of enabling. The test took place two days before what is believed to be North Korean leader Kim Jong Un's birthday, and North Korea called the device the "H-bomb of justice." It will likely take several days to determine more precisely what kind of nuclear device North Korea set off. Hydrogen bombs are much more powerful than atomic bombs and use a two-step process of fission and fusion to release substantially more energy. The United States believes North Korea had set off the latest in a series of tests of old-fashioned atomic bombs, rather than a hydrogen bomb. The test caused a drop in global stocks and added to geopolitical worries, including fears about China's economy. The test also prompted calls for stronger missile defenses and further sanctions against North Korea.

The Museum of Fine Arts, Boston opened an exhibition in 2009, showcasing artifacts from Tomb 10A in Deir el-Bersha, Egypt, dating back to 2000 BC. The tomb belonged to an early Middle Kingdom governor named Djehutynakht, and his wife, also named Djehutynakht. The tomb had been plundered in antiquity, but many artifacts were still found, including a large burial assemblage, pottery, canopic jars, models, model boats, and a famous processional group. The governor and his wife were buried in finely decorated coffins made of cedar of Lebanon boards.

When the tomb was looted, the mummies were damaged, and a mummified head was found on top of the governor's coffin. For over a century, researchers have debated whether the head belonged to the governor or his wife. In 2005, the head was analyzed with computerized tomography, but the absence of facial bones and lack of comparative data made it impossible to determine the sex definitively.

In 2018, a team of forensic scientists managed to extract DNA from a molar extracted from the head in 2009, producing 105 milligrams of tooth dust. After amplifying the DNA, they found it belonged to a biological male, suggesting that the head likely belonged to Djehutynakht and not his wife. The results were confirmed by a team at the Department of Homeland Security. However, it remains unclear which Djehutynakht the head and tomb belonged to, as there were two governors with that name during that period.

The successful extraction of DNA from the 4,000-year-old mummy marks a significant breakthrough in forensic science and opens up new possibilities for understanding Egypt's ancient past. The research was published in the journal Genes.

A genetic study has revealed that some Burmese pythons, an invasive species in Florida's Everglades, are hybridized with the Indian rock python, creating a potential super-predator. The study, published in the journal Ecology and Evolution, analyzed the tail tissue of 400 snakes captured in South Florida and found that 13 had genetic markers from the Indian pythons, a species that prefers high, dry ground compared to the Burmese python's preference for swampy areas.

The discovery of this hybridization could have significant implications for the Everglades ecosystem, as the Indian pythons are smaller, faster, and arguably more aggressive than Burmese pythons. This could lead to a better ability to adapt to environmental stressors and changes, potentially allowing the hybrid pythons to expand their range more rapidly than any species before them.

The researchers believe that the cross-breeding occurred before the pythons secured their foothold in Florida. However, the impact of so-called "hybrid vigor" on an individual snake is still unclear. Steve Johnson, associate professor of wildlife ecology at the University of Florida, noted that the hybrid snakes would likely share traits of both species, but how that translates to behavior is still unknown.

The discovery of the hybrid pythons is an unwelcome development for wildlife officials, who have been struggling to reduce or eliminate the invasive species, which has decimated native species including bobcats, foxes, rabbits, and raccoons from the Florida Keys to north of Lake Okeechobee. Wildlife officials admit they are fighting a losing battle, with failed initiatives including training dogs to sniff out the snakes and releasing pythons with radio transmitters to lead hunters to females carrying up to 100 eggs at a time.

The Florida Fish and Wildlife Commission has recorded more than 500 invasive or non-native species in the state, including tegu lizards from South America that eat rodents, Cuban tree frogs that prey on smaller species of amphibians, and green iguanas that feast on native plants. The study's lead author, Margaret Hunter, stressed that the genetic markers found in the snakes do not mean a new species of super-snake has suddenly been unleashed on the Everglades. Instead, she sees it as a potential development that could hamper already unsuccessful efforts to control the invasive python population.

The Duke of York, Prince Andrew, has joined Twitter, becoming the first member of the Royal Family to do so. His handle is @TheDukeOfYork. His first tweet, "Welcome to my Twitter account - AY," indicates that the tweets will be written by him personally. China has announced plans to send the first-ever lunar probe to the dark side of the moon by 2020, marking a significant milestone in its space exploration program. Known as the Chang'e mission, this endeavor aims to examine the geological conditions on the moon's far side, with the ultimate goal of installing a radio telescope. This mission would be the first successful landing on the dark side of the moon, a region currently inaccessible via radio transmissions from Earth.

The Chang'e program, named after a mythical Chinese goddess, has already made strides in lunar exploration, having launched a pair of orbiting lunar probes and landing a craft on the moon with a rover in 2013. China's next lunar mission is scheduled for 2017, where it will attempt to land an unmanned spaceship on the moon and return with samples, a feat that would make China only the third country to achieve this after the United States and Russia.

The dark side of the moon, also known as the far side, is of particular interest due to its unique geological conditions and the fact that radio transmissions from Earth cannot reach it. To address this communication issue, China plans to deploy a spacecraft orbiting the moon to relay radio signals from the far side back to Earth. This would enable the placement of radio transmitters on the far side, providing astronomers with a new and valuable tool for studying the universe.

China's space program has been progressing steadily, having sent its first astronaut into space in 2003 and deploying an experimental space station. The country has also hinted at a possible crewed mission to the moon in the future. This latest lunar probe mission is expected to fill a void in humanity's understanding of outer space and contribute to the ongoing advancements in space exploration.

The case of the drowning deaths of William and Michelle Becker, a police officer and his beautician wife, is being re-examined after 35 years, with a $15,000 reward offered for new information. The couple, who were married for 17 years and parents to three children, spent the evening of March 10, 1981, at a friend's house in Mattituck, Long Island, and left shortly before midnight. Their bodies were found the next day, with William's body discovered in a marina and Michelle's body found the following day. The Suffolk County Police Department deemed the deaths an accident, but relatives and colleagues have expressed doubts and nagging questions.

Michael Malkush, Michelle Becker's brother, said investigators told him that the theory was that the couple went to the marina to find the boat that belonged to the dinner party host and "get romantic." However, Malkush and other family members feel that the couple did not go to the marina on their own and accidentally drowned.

DEC Police Maj. Scott Florence, who began looking into the mystery in the 1990s, noted that a kitchen table on the boat had come apart, and Becker's clip-on uniform tie was found on the floor, potential signs of a struggle. He said the 35th anniversary of the drownings was seen as an opportunity to bring attention to the case and perhaps dislodge some long-held secrets.

The police union and a fraternal organization came up with the reward for information leading to the arrest and conviction of anyone who might have been involved in the Beckers' deaths. In a statement, the Suffolk County Police Department said Homicide Squad detectives are "open to receiving any new information anyone had to provide."
