The study, published in The New England Journal of Medicine, estimates that approximately 5,000 people may have died in Puerto Rico due to reasons related to Hurricane Maria in 2017. The research team, led by scientists from the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, conducted a randomized survey of 3,299 households from January 17 through February 24, 2018. The survey aimed to detect a 50% increase in the annual mortality rate from a historic baseline rate, using a hybrid census method to collect information about each household member.

To ensure a representative sample, the population was stratified according to remoteness, with barrios grouped into eight categories based on travel time to cities with a population of at least 50,000 persons. The survey included questions on age, sex, cause of death if after the hurricane, hurricane-related migration, neighborhood deaths, and access to electricity, water, and cellular network coverage.

The researchers calculated a statistical term called a 95% confidence interval, which encompasses a broad range – from 800 to 8,500 deaths. Their figure of 4,645 lies near the middle of that range, and they round up to something over 5,000 to account for some assumptions they made. The findings suggest that the mortality rate in Puerto Rico had jumped 62% in the three months following the storm, with 83% of the households without electrical power for the time period looked at.

The study notes that this death rate is a contentious subject, as federal and island governments haven't responded as rapidly to the disaster as they have in other hurricane emergencies. The government of Puerto Rico commissioned researchers from George Washington University's Milken Institute School of Public Health to estimate excess deaths, with results due out this summer.

The Harvard study covers a greater time period than previous estimates, which could partly account for the much higher figure. The household survey is a widely accepted technique for estimating casualties following a disaster, but it can be misleading if the sample isn't truly random or if some households have been wiped out altogether and are therefore missing from the survey. The researchers suggest that the government in Puerto Rico could use their methods in an even larger survey to reduce the large uncertainties in their findings.

In Chesterton, Cambridge, a mysterious protest took place, with a series of three-foot-high Latin phrases painted on four upmarket houses flanking the River Cam. The phrases, "Locus in domos loci populum," which translates to "the place into homes, the people of the place," are considered nonsensical and have sparked a flurry of speculation and debate. The graffiti is thought to be a protest against the development and the high cost of housing in the city, where the average house price is £500,000, 16 times higher than the average local salary. The developer, HC Moss (Builders) Ltd, is taking steps to remove the graffiti and has reviewed security measures at the site. The incident has been reported to the police, who are investigating the criminal damage. The graffiti has been compared to previous protests in Cambridge, such as a 2015 incident where a threat was written in Greek and Latin to remove or destroy bicycles chained to railings in the city center. The incident has been described as a "different class of graffiti in Cambridge" and has sparked debate about the cost of housing and the use of Latin as a form of protest.

On July 21, 2018, a gunman identified as Gene Evin Atkins, 28, took dozens of people hostage at a Trader Joe's supermarket in Los Angeles' Silver Lake section. The incident began when Atkins shot and killed a woman, later identified as 27-year-old Melyda Corado, who worked at the store. Atkins' grandmother was hospitalized in critical condition after the shooting.

Authorities believe that Atkins shot his grandmother seven times and wounded another woman, whom he forced into a car, at a South Los Angeles home around 1:30 p.m. Officers tracked the car, gave chase, and exchanged gunfire with the man, who crashed into a pole outside the supermarket and then ran inside. The unidentified woman, who suffered a graze wound earlier, was taken out of the car by police.

Customers and workers dove for cover as police bullets fired at the man shattered the store's glass doors. Some people inside the supermarket climbed out windows, and others barricaded themselves in rooms as scores of police officers and firefighters and 18 ambulances converged on the scene and prepared for mass casualties.

Heavily armed officers in riot gear stood along the side of the store and used mirrors to look inside as hostage negotiators tried to coax the man into freeing his 40 to 50 hostages and surrendering. At around 6:30 p.m., Atkins agreed to handcuff himself and walked out the front door, surrounded by four of the hostages. He was immediately taken into custody.

Mayor Eric Garcetti congratulated police and firefighters for their work and mourned the loss of life at the Trader Joe's, where he and his wife regularly shopped when they lived in the neighborhood. Among those who survived the harrowing afternoon was 91-year-old Don Kohles, who lives in the neighborhood and was walking into the supermarket when he saw the man crash into the pole.

Christian Dunlop, a real estate agent and actor who lives nearby and frequents Trader Joe's, was on a corner near the store when he saw four people run out. One person, an employee, was dragging an injured woman by the hands. He then saw five employees hang out a second-floor window and drop to the ground and around 15 others run to safety from the back of the store. Among them was a police officer carrying a small child, he said.

Atkins is being held on $2 million bail and is suspected of murder. It is unclear if he has an attorney. The incident caused panic and fear among the customers and employees of the supermarket.

In a speech at Georgetown University, Senator Bernie Sanders, a Democratic presidential candidate, positioned himself as the successor to President Franklin D. Roosevelt's democratic socialist ideals. Sanders emphasized that his democratic socialism is centered around economic rights as essential to American values, while clarifying that he does not advocate for government ownership of businesses. He drew comparisons between his political views and the fight for economic rights led by Roosevelt and Martin Luther King Jr.

Sanders also discussed the need for a new international security organization to address current threats, such as terrorism. However, the majority of his speech focused on explaining his democratic socialist policy goals, including health care as a right, free college tuition, investment in jobs and a living wage, and public funding of elections.

Sanders acknowledged that some people are uncomfortable with the term "socialist," but he argued that Roosevelt faced similar criticism when he "reinvigorated democracy" and "transformed our country." Sanders emphasized the importance of achieving the vision for a "second Bill of Rights" that Roosevelt outlined in his 1944 State of the Union address, which links economic security to the concept of freedom.

Some critics, such as Bhaskar Sunkara, founder of the socialist magazine Jacobin, argue that Sanders's vision lacks the socialist emphasis on ownership and control. However, political scientist Daniel Schlozman points out that Sanders's project aims to bridge the gap between socialism and liberalism, reviving a political framework that was operative during the Great Depression and World War II but collapsed soon after.

Sanders's speech drew support from college students, with some expressing concerns about the attainability of his policy goals in a deadlocked Congress. Sanders acknowledged these concerns but emphasized the need for a political movement to challenge the "greed" of the billionaire class.

The Metropolitan Opera in New York faced protests on Monday over the performance of the opera "The Death of Klinghoffer," which is based on the 1985 hijacking of the Achille Lauro and the subsequent murder of a 69-year-old Jewish man, Leon Klinghoffer. The opera has been a source of controversy since it was first premiered in 1991 and has been criticized by some as anti-Semitic and glorifying terrorism. Former Mayor Rudolph Giuliani joined the demonstrators outside the opera house, stating that the opera romanticizes terrorists. However, opera expert Fred Plotkin argued that the opera presents the Klinghoffers as its moral spine and that the terrorists are not portrayed in a favorable light. The performance went on with some disruptions, including boos and a voice shouting from a balcony, but ended with a standing ovation. The Met canceled the international movie theater and radio broadcasts of the opera in November amid pressure from Jewish groups, including the Anti-Defamation League. The opera runs through November 15. The controversy surrounding the opera has sparked discussions about artistic freedom, the portrayal of historical events in art, and the role of cultural institutions in society.

The search for Malaysia Airlines Flight 370, which disappeared on March 8, 2014, is entering a new phase due to the fruitlessness of the previous efforts. Australian, Malaysian, and Chinese officials will meet in Canberra, Australia, on Wednesday to discuss the next stage of the hunt. The new phase will involve a detailed mapping of the ocean floor, which has never been mapped, and the use of more advanced technology, including towed side-scan sonar and autonomous underwater vehicles. The cost of the new phase is estimated to be $60 million, and it is expected that most of the new equipment will come from the private sector. The search has been challenging, with the plane's disappearance occurring in deep water that has never been mapped, and the search area expanding to areas that have not been previously searched. Despite the challenges, officials remain optimistic that the new technology and equipment will help in the search for the missing plane.

In a response to Dan Brown's portrayal of Manila as "the gates of hell" in his latest novel "Inferno," Philippine authorities have expressed anger and displeasure. The book depicts Manila as a city with horrible traffic jams, suffocating pollution, massive poverty, and a thriving child sex trade. The chairman of the government agency managing Manila, Francis Tolentino, sent a letter to Brown and his publishers criticizing the "inaccurate portrayal of our beloved metropolis."

Tolentino, who is also the traffic czar, disputed the six-hour traffic jams mentioned in the book, stating that Manila's traffic is only around two hours long at most. He also took issue with the book's religious insinuations against Manila, calling them a "diabolic description."

Tolentino has previously criticized Brown's work, writing an article in 2006 slamming "The Da Vinci Code." He even asked local theaters not to show the movie version of the book. This time, Tolentino wants Brown to visit the Philippines and rectify his portrayal of Manila in his newest book.

On the other hand, some Filipinos on cyberspace agreed with Brown's portrayal, with one person tweeting, "It looks like (Tolentino) is the one who hasn't been to Manila." Last month, the government announced that despite years of economic growth, 27.9 percent of the Philippine population lived in poverty, a figure practically unchanged since 2006.

Senator-elect JV Ejercito has also called for a "massive rehabilitation" of Manila, stating that the city has been neglected and needs to be cleaned up. Ejercito's father, former President Joseph Estrada, has recently been elected as mayor of Manila and has promised to bring the city back to its former glory.

Dilated Cardiomyopathy (DCM) is the most common type of heart disease, primarily affecting adults between the ages of 20 and 60. The condition affects the heart's ventricles and atria, with the left ventricle often being the initial site of the disease. As the heart chambers dilate, the heart muscle weakens, leading to heart failure, which is characterized by symptoms such as shortness of breath, fatigue, and swelling in various parts of the body.

DCM can also lead to heart valve problems, arrhythmias, and blood clots in the heart. The disease can have various causes, including alcohol abuse, diabetes, high blood pressure, thyroid disease, viral infections, and certain medications. In some cases, the cause of DCM is unknown, and up to one-third of those affected may inherit it from their parents.

Alcohol-related fatty liver disease (ALD) is a condition caused by excessive alcohol consumption, which can lead to a buildup of fat in the liver. ALD can cause symptoms such as pain or discomfort in the upper right abdomen, and if left untreated, it can progress to alcoholic hepatitis, alcoholic cirrhosis, and liver failure.

George Michael, the British singer, died of natural causes due to heart disease and a fatty liver, according to a British coroner. The singer died at his home in Oxfordshire county, southern England, on December 25, 2017, at the age of 53. An initial autopsy failed to determine the cause of death, but a post-mortem found that Michael died of "dilated cardiomyopathy with myocarditis and fatty liver." The coroner stated that no inquest would be held because Michael died of natural causes.

In an exclusive interview, Kenny Goss, George Michael's partner for 13 years, spoke about his support for the singer's family during the grieving process. Goss revealed that he flew to England to help the family during the painful and drawn-out process while investigations continue. The family is still awaiting the results of toxicology tests before the coroner can release the body for a funeral. Goss plans to be present for the funeral and expressed a desire for closure.

Mantecore, the white tiger that was involved in a near-fatal incident with Roy Horn of Siegfried & Roy in 2003, passed away on March 19 at the age of 17 after a short illness. The tiger, who was often referred to as Montecore in press reports, was seven years old at the time of the incident during a show at The Mirage. Although Horn suffered significant blood loss from the bite, it was a stroke and brain-swelling that followed the injury that left Horn partially paralyzed, ending his stage career.

Following the incident, Mantecore was quarantined for 10 days but was later returned to exhibit at The Mirage's Secret Garden of Siegfried & Roy attraction. In the years that followed, Mantecore spent most of his time alternating between the Secret Garden attraction and Horn's estate.

Horn, who was adamant that the tiger was not attacking him but rather reacting protectively, always maintained that the tiger was not to blame for the incident. As recently as his 69th birthday party last October, Horn chided a columnist for using the word "attack" to describe the incident.

In a statement released today, Horn said, "The world has lost one of its most majestic creatures and I have lost a brother. I will forever believe it was his concern for my safety and well-being that caused him to act as he did on that night long ago." Horn added that Mantecore's contribution to conservation and preservation efforts made him unforgettable.

Siegfried & Roy are mourning the loss of their prized pet and former costar. Mantecore lived at the Siegfried & Roy Secret Garden and Dolphin Habitat at the Mirage hotel in Las Vegas until his death.

Christopher Kennedy Lawford, the nephew of President John F. Kennedy and son of Peter Lawford, died on Tuesday, September 4, 2018, in Vancouver, Canada. He was 63 years old. Lawford was a well-known advocate for sobriety and recovery, having struggled with substance abuse and addiction throughout his life. He was living in Vancouver with his girlfriend and working to open a recovery center. Lawford died of a heart attack, according to his cousin, former U.S. Representative Patrick J. Kennedy.

Lawford was born into political and Hollywood royalty. His parents were Patricia Kennedy, sister of John, Robert, and Ted Kennedy, and Peter Lawford, an English actor and socialite who was a member of Frank Sinatra's "Rat Pack." Lawford wrote about his struggles with drugs in his 2005 book, "Symptoms of Withdrawal: A Memoir of Snapshots and Redemption." He began using LSD while at boarding school at the age of 14, and his drug use escalated in the 1970s Hollywood scene, where his father also struggled with addiction. Lawford was estranged from his sisters for a time but eventually reconciled with them.

In addition to his work as an advocate for recovery, Lawford was an actor and author. He appeared on TV shows such as "Frazier" and "The O.C." and had recurring roles on the soaps "All My Children" and "General Hospital." He also authored several books on addiction and recovery, including "What Addicts Know." Lawford is survived by his sisters, Sydney, Victoria, and Robin, and his children, David, Savannah, and Matt.

The article discusses the arraignment of Ariel Castro, a former school bus driver in Cleveland, Ohio, who is accused of kidnapping and raping three women and holding them captive in his home for a decade. Castro is being held on $8 million bail and is facing charges of kidnapping and rape. Prosecutors have announced that they will seek additional charges, including "aggravated murder" for the termination of the captives' pregnancies, as Ohio law allows for murder charges for the killing of unborn children. The women were found on May 6, 2013, after one of them, Amanda Berry, managed to escape and call for help. The article also mentions the writings found in Castro's home, which authorities believe were written by him and contain details of his actions and reasons behind them, including justification for his behavior based on his own history of abuse. The article also includes interviews with Castro's mother, who expresses remorse, and his daughter, who says she had no idea about the alleged depravity. The women are currently recovering with their families.

The Casey Anthony verdict, which found her not guilty of first-degree murder or manslaughter of her two-year-old daughter Caylee, has sparked a campaign for "Caylee's Law." This proposed law, initiated by an Oklahoma mother, Michelle Crowder, aims to make it a federal offense and a felony for a parent or guardian to fail to report a child's disappearance to law enforcement. The outcry stems from Casey Anthony's failure to report Caylee's disappearance, which occurred on June 16, 2008, a month before her grandmother notified the police. The "Caylee's Law" petition on Change.org has garnered nearly 2,000 signatures each hour since its creation, making it the fastest-growing campaign on the site. Additionally, a Facebook campaign has amassed nearly two million people pledging to leave their porch lights on for Caylee. The Casey Anthony trial has been a subject of widespread media attention, with articles discussing the verdict, the media's reaction, and the court of public opinion. The L. Tom Perry Special Collections Web Archive at Brigham Young University documents the case and other aspects of Mormonism online.

The study, published in Pediatrics, finds that serious complications related to vaccines are extremely rare and there is no evidence that immunizations cause autism. The report comes amid a resurgence of vaccine-preventable diseases, such as measles, in communities with low vaccination rates. The analysis found strong evidence that the measles vaccine is not associated with an increased risk of autism, debunking a myth that gained popularity in 1998.

The report notes that some vaccines, including flu shots and the combined vaccine against measles, mumps, and rubella, are associated with an increased risk of fever-related seizures in small children. Although these seizures can be frightening for parents, they're typically benign and cause no long-term problems.

The study also found that vaccines against rotavirus, a common cause of severe diarrhea and dehydration in children, increase the risk of a serious type of intestinal blockage called intussusception. However, the vaccines against it, RotaTeq and Rotarix, cause an additional one to five cases of intussusception for every 100,000 doses given.

The new analysis may not convince parents who are strongly anti-vaccine. The report highlights the importance of doctors promoting vaccines to their patients, especially since recent medical school graduates are more skeptical about the effectiveness of vaccines than older doctors.

The study emphasizes that the benefits of vaccines, such as the prevention of millions of illnesses and thousands of deaths annually, outweigh the rare risks of serious side effects. The report also notes that the most dangerous aspect of giving your child vaccines is driving to the office to get them.

The US Geological Survey (USGS) has revised its forecast for a magnitude 8.0 or greater earthquake in California, raising the probability from 4.7% to 7% in the next three decades. This increase is due to a better understanding of the interconnected nature of earthquake faults in California, which can lead to simultaneous ruptures of multiple faults.

Scientists have observed instances of earthquakes jumping faults, such as the 2010 Easter Sunday earthquake near the California-Mexico border, which directed tectonic stress northward and increased the risk for future quakes. The southern San Andreas fault, which hasn't ruptured in over three centuries, is considered the greatest threat.

While the risk of a mega-quake is higher than past estimates, it's more likely, greater than 99%, that California will experience a magnitude-6.7 quake similar to the 1994 Northridge disaster. The chance of a Northridge-size quake was slightly higher in Northern California than Southern California – 95% versus 93%.

The report emphasizes that California is earthquake country, and residents should live every day as if it could be the day of a big one. The report does not predict the exact location or time of the next big earthquake, but efforts are being made to develop an early warning system to provide a few seconds of notice before a quake strikes. However, the public alert system is still in the pilot phase and needs more funding before it can be rolled out statewide.

The U.S. Navy is investigating whether a cyberattack may have caused the collision of the USS John S. McCain with a merchant vessel on August 21, 2017. The Navy is sending investigators to the McCain to determine if hackers infiltrated the ship's computer systems before the crash. However, the Navy is not considering the possibility that the USS Fitzgerald collision, which occurred on June 17, was the result of hacking. The two collisions resulted in a total of 17 sailors dead and raised concerns about the readiness of the American Pacific fleet. The Navy has already set aside $1.5 billion between fiscal years 2014 and 2023 to improve cybersecurity defenses. If hackers breached the McCain's digital defenses, it would represent a significant development in naval warfare, as hackers could potentially manipulate a ship's computer systems and blind its commander, leading to a collision. The Navy is preparing for potential digital warfare and plans to make cybersecurity a standard part of accident investigations in the future. The Navy is currently investigating the McCain collision as part of Operation Orion's Hammer, which is focused on the reported failure of the aft steering mechanism that may have contributed to the collision. The Navy is also investigating the possibility of a cyberattack in the USS Fitzgerald collision, although no evidence of a cyberattack has been found in either incident. The Navy is taking steps to institutionalize cybersecurity investigations as part of any mishap investigation in the future.

The Dark Web, a notorious part of the internet known for its anonymity, has been under scrutiny due to a recent study conducted by Gareth Owen, a computer science researcher from the University of Portsmouth. The study, presented at the Chaos Computer Congress in Hamburg, Germany, reveals that a majority of traffic on the Dark Web is driven by the sexual abuse of children.

The researchers ran 40 "relay" computers in the Tor network, a collection of thousands of volunteer machines that anonymize traffic, to gather data about the Dark Web. They found that over four out of five visits to Tor hidden services were to online destinations with pedophilia materials, which is over five times as many as any other category of content, such as gambling, bitcoin-related sites, or anonymous whistle-blowing.

However, the creators of Tor, known as the Tor Project, have raised concerns about the study's findings, suggesting that factors like visits from law enforcement and anti-abuse groups, denial of service attacks, unstable sites, and sites visited through Tor2Web could have artificially inflated the number of visits to child abuse sites.

Despite these concerns, the study's results are still alarming, as they suggest that Tor users who seek child abuse materials use Tor much more often and visit sites much more frequently than those seeking to buy drugs or leak sensitive documents to a journalist. The study also found that child abuse sites represent only about 2% of Tor hidden service websites, with drug-related sites and markets accounting for about 24% and whistleblower sites accounting for 5%.

The study raises questions about the darkest subcultures of the Dark Web and law enforcement's response to them. In November, the FBI and Europol staged a massive bust of Tor hidden services, but none of the site takedowns mentioned pedophilia sites. The study could lead to difficult questions for the Tor support community and could shift the larger public conversation around the Dark Web.

The study also suggests the possibility of blocking access to certain Tor hidden services, although the researcher behind the study cautioned that this is merely an introduction of the concept and not a suggestion. The study's findings could have significant implications for the ongoing debate about the balance between privacy and the fight against child abuse on the internet.

A 10-year-old girl named Britton Joniec from Houston underwent emergency surgery after accidentally swallowing a metal bushing from a fidget spinner. The incident occurred on the way home from a swim meet, when Britton made a retching sound and appeared to be choking. Her mother, Kelly Rose Joniec, shared the terrifying ordeal on Facebook, explaining that Britton had put the metal bushing in her mouth to clean the fidget spinner, but somehow swallowed it.

The family was initially taken to an urgent care center, but medical workers were unable to determine whether the bushing was lodged in Britton's airway or esophagus. They were then rushed to Texas Children's Hospital in The Woodlands, where X-rays showed the bushing was stuck in her esophagus. A doctor used an endoscope to remove the object, and Britton made a full recovery.

Joniec warned fellow parents about the potential choking hazard posed by fidget spinners, particularly for young children under 8 years old. The toys have become popular in recent weeks and have been banned in some schools. The incident has received widespread attention, with over 500,000 shares and comments on Facebook. It serves as a reminder for parents to be cautious when allowing their children to play with fidget spinners.

On July 4, 2017, Joey Chestnut won his 10th Nathan's Famous International Hot Dog Eating Contest in New York, eating a world-record 72 hot dogs in 10 minutes. The contest was disrupted by the arrest of five animal rights activists who tried to unfold a black banner amidst the crowd. In the women's division, Miki Sudo won her fourth title, eating 41 hot dogs and buns in 10 minutes. Joey Chestnut's victory surpassed his own record of 70 hot dogs from the previous year, consuming a total of 20,160 calories, 1,296 grams of fat, 2,160 milligrams of cholesterol, and 56,160 milligrams of sodium. The average American eats 70 hot dogs a year, according to the Hot Dog & Sausage Council. The men's competition included a rematch between Chestnut and Matt "Megatoad" Stonie, who finished second and third, respectively.

The study published in the journal Climatic Change reveals that rising global temperatures due to climate change will make it harder for aircraft to take off, particularly during the hottest parts of the day. The research, led by Ethan Coffel, a PhD student at Columbia University, suggests that 10-30% of fully loaded planes may have to remove fuel, cargo, or passengers, or wait for cooler hours to fly. This is because warmer air has lower density, reducing the lift generated by plane wings during takeoff.

The study, which is the first global analysis of its kind, projects that heat waves will become more common, with annual maximum daily temperatures at airports worldwide projected to rise 4-8 degrees Celsius (7.2-14.4 Fahrenheit) by 2080. This could lead to substantial economic and logistical impacts on the aviation industry, as airports in hotter regions, such as Dubai, and those with shorter runways, like New York's LaGuardia, may be particularly affected.

The study also highlights the potential for cascading effects on the global economy due to flight delays and cancellations. Some aircraft with lower temperature tolerances will be more affected than others, and certain airports, such as those at higher elevations or in hotter parts of the world, will suffer more.

The authors suggest that modifications, such as new engine or body designs, or expanded runways, could mitigate some of these effects, but these would come at a cost. The study emphasizes the need for climate to be incorporated into mid- and long-term plans for the aviation industry to adapt effectively.

The paper, titled "The impacts of rising temperatures on aircraft takeoff performance," is available from the journal Climatic Change. The authors are Ethan Coffel, Radley Horton, and Terence R. Thompson. For more information, contact Elizabeth.hawkins@springer.com, Ethan Coffel (ec2959@columbia.edu), Radley Horton (rh142@columbia.edu), or Kevin Krajick (kkrajick@ei.columbia.edu).

Trojan has released a new state-of-the-art vibrator called Triphoria, which is advertised as a "personal massager" to bypass cable networks' restrictions on advertising sex toys. The commercial, produced by Sullivan Productions, uses humor and innuendo to describe the product's benefits, such as "screams of ecstasy" and "intense waves of pleasure."

The use of camouflage language in advertising sex toys is not new; in the early 1900s, vibrators were advertised in women's magazines and the Sears catalog as relaxation aids. However, their appearance in stag films in the 1920s led to their "social camouflage" being undone, and such ads disappeared.

Trojan's Triphoria campaign is the largest advertising campaign for a vibrator and is expected to be carried at major retailers like CVS, Walgreen's, and Wal-Mart beginning in the first half of 2011. The company spent $22.4 million on advertising in 2009, most of it focused on condoms. According to Trojan-financed studies published in the Journal of Sexual Medicine, 52.5 percent of women and 44.8 percent of men have used vibrators, with 40.9 percent of women and 40.5 percent of men reporting having used them with sexual partners.

Not everyone views television networks' greater acceptance of ads of a sexual nature as a victory. On Monday, the American Academy of Pediatrics issued a policy statement urging that ads for erectile dysfunction drugs like Viagra be shown only after 10 p.m. and "not be overly suggestive."

Trojan's approach of advertising the Triphoria subtly on cable networks increases the likelihood of eventually gaining approval for the commercials on the major broadcast networks. The company aims to approach networks for approval, possibly in the early part of next year.

Sophia Chua-Rubenfeld, the eldest daughter of Amy Chua, the author of the controversial book "Battle Hymn of the Tiger Mother", gave the commencement address at her high school graduation. As valedictorian, she made light-hearted jokes about her mother, who has been a subject of intense criticism and praise this year for her parenting methods. During her speech, Chua-Rubenfeld joked about reading from her mother's bestselling memoir. She was chosen as the sole valedictorian for the class of 2010-2011, with the other student speaker being the class president.

Earlier this year, Chua-Rubenfeld started a personal blog to address rumors about her family. She hinted in an April blog entry that she had chosen Harvard University, using a popular Massachusetts phrase to describe it. Amy Chua made Time magazine's 2011 list of the world's most influential people, but faced backlash after the January release of her book, which was seen as promoting strict child-rearing techniques. Chua later clarified that she intended the book to be a satirical take on rigid Asian parenting, not a parenting guide.

In a historic turn of events, a 76-year-old man, Jack McCullough, convicted for the 1957 murder of 7-year-old Maria Ridulph in Sycamore, Illinois, was ordered released from prison and granted a new trial by Judge William Brady. McCullough had been serving a life sentence for the cold case, which was the oldest ever brought to court.

The judge's ruling was based on "clear and convincing evidence" that McCullough was wrongly found guilty. After the hearing, McCullough was released and was driven away by a family member. His stepdaughter, Janey O'Connor, who was present at the hearing, shared a tearful moment with him.

Maria Ridulph's murder remained unsolved for half a century until detectives pursued a tip and brought McCullough to trial in 2012. However, questions about the fairness of the trial were raised in Ann O'Neill's 2013 series, "Taken."

Charles Ridulph, the older brother of the victim, expressed disappointment at the ruling. He had helped search for Maria when she vanished from a street corner near their home while playing in the snow with a friend.

McCullough's lawyers and DeKalb County state's attorney Richard Schmack argued that McCullough's conviction was based on false testimony, improper legal rulings, and a tweaked timeline that ruled out McCullough's alibi. McCullough had long insisted that he couldn't have abducted and killed the child because he was 40 miles away in Rockford, Illinois, trying to enlist in the U.S. Air Force when she was taken.

McCullough repeated this alibi when he spoke with CNN in prison in March 2013. He claimed that when Maria was kidnapped, the telephone in his home in Sycamore was ringing, and he was on the other end of the phone in Rockford.

An Illinois appeals court upheld McCullough's conviction last year. However, McCullough made a last-ditch appeal in a jailhouse motion last December, stating that police and prosecutors had buried evidence supporting his alibi. He asked a judge to find him innocent.

Schmack, who inherited the case from predecessor Clay Campbell, was placed in the position of having to defend the conviction. He launched a six-month investigation that included a review of over 4,500 pages of documents, including old police and FBI reports, grand jury transcripts, trial transcripts, affidavits for search and arrest warrants, and even CNN's five-part series on the case, "Taken," which raised questions about the courtroom reconstruction of history being unfairly one-sided.

Schmack concluded that he had found "clear and convincing evidence" that McCullough had been convicted of a crime he didn't commit. The precise time of Maria's abduction has been in dispute almost from the beginning. The dark-haired second-grader with big brown eyes was with her playmate, Kathy Sigman, on December 3, 1957, when they were approached by a stranger who said his name was Johnny. He gave Maria two piggyback rides, Sigman told police at the time. Sigman, now a grandmother known as Kathy Chapman, said she went home to fetch her mittens. When she returned, Maria and Johnny were gone.

Over 600 volunteers combed the fields and woods around Sycamore in search of Maria, and within 24 hours, dozens of FBI agents descended on the small farming community about 65 miles west of Chicago. Despite the work of nearly three-dozen FBI agents, the investigation turned up no solid leads to Maria's whereabouts. Her body was discovered 144 days later by a couple looking for mushrooms near the Iowa border. She was under a fallen tree, some 100 miles from home.

The Illinois State Police began to look into the Ridulph case again in 2008, after McCullough's half-sister, Janet Tessier, emailed a tip. She said her dying mother had pulled her close some 14 years earlier and whispered, "Those two little girls, and the one that disappeared, John did it. John did it, and you have to tell someone." McCullough was questioned in Seattle and arrested in late June 2011. A judge hearing the case without a jury found McCullough guilty after a week-long trial.

Schmack, the state's attorney, said he sat through the trial and always doubted whether there was enough evidence to support the conviction. In his review of the case, he said he found new evidence that verified McCullough's long-standing alibi. He subpoenaed records from AT&T and found that a collect call had indeed been placed at 6:57 p.m. to McCullough's home in Sycamore from a pay phone at the post office in downtown Rockford on December 3, 1957, just as McCullough said he had done.

At his sentencing, McCullough vehemently professed his innocence. "Look in the box. The truth is in the box," he said, pointing to a cardboard box in the courtroom. It was filled with old FBI reports and other documents that the judge, James Hallock, kept from the trial, saying it was inadmissible hearsay. Prosecutor Richard Schmack reviewed the case and asked for McCullough to go free.

Schmack did look at those documents. He built a timeline based on the statements of 21 people - Maria Ridulph's family members, friends, neighbors, and passersby - that confirmed the FBI's original timeline, ruling out McCullough as a suspect. Maria was taken that day some time between 6:45 and 7 p.m., and not as early as 6 p.m., as alleged during McCullough's trial. It would have been impossible for him to have been in two places at once.

Campbell, the state's attorney who brought the case, was defeated by Schmack in an election just weeks after McCullough was convicted. Campbell has declined to comment since Schmack released his findings. Cold cases are particularly difficult to prosecute because evidence is often lost or destroyed, memories fade, and witnesses die. This case raises questions about the evidence used to convict McCullough and whether it was strong enough. No physical evidence ties him to the crime.

A report published by the right-wing news website WND claims that a significant explosion occurred at Iran's Fordow nuclear facility, located deep within a mountain, on Monday, March 18th. The blast is said to have partially destroyed the site and trapped approximately 240 people underground. Iran has accused Israel of being responsible for the explosion. However, the report has yet to be verified by any independent sources, and Iran's deputy head of the Atomic Energy Organisation has denied that any explosion occurred.

Israeli officials have been unable to confirm the reports, but Avi Dichter, Israel's home defence minister, welcomed the news, stating that any explosion in Iran that doesn't harm people but damages its assets is a blessing. Officials in Israel's foreign ministry, who are known to have an extensive surveillance network monitoring Iran's key nuclear sites, claim they have no reliable intelligence of an explosion at Fordow.

One theory suggests that Tehran may have deliberately leaked false reports about a blast to prevent international inspectors from entering the site. The Fordow facility is immune to air strikes or bunker bombs and contains more than 2,700 centrifuges enriching uranium to more than 20%. Iran has repeatedly blamed Israel for a string of explosive disasters that have hit Iranian nuclear targets in the past.

The U.N. International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), which regularly inspects Iranian nuclear sites, had no immediate comment on the matter. The alleged explosion at Fordow follows speculation that global powers and Iran could resume talks on Iran's disputed nuclear program on Monday and Tuesday. However, the European Union, the lead negotiator on the nuclear talks, has stated that there is no such agreement.

Diplomats in Vienna, where the U.N.'s nuclear agency is based, have stated that they have no knowledge of any incident at Fordow but are looking into the reports. One Western diplomat has said they do not believe the reports to be correct. The U.N. IAEA is expected to release a report on Iran's nuclear program later this week.

North Korea is suspected of moving an intercontinental ballistic missile (ICBM) following a briefing by South Korea's National Intelligence Service (NIS). The exact timing, direction, and mode of transportation of the projectile are unclear. The suspicion arises after North Korea conducted its sixth nuclear test on September 3, which was the most powerful ever detonated by the country, according to nuclear experts. North Korea claimed it was a hydrogen bomb, which could be fitted onto a long-range missile capable of reaching the United States.

The South Korean Navy conducted live-fire drills off the east coast of the Korean Peninsula in response to North Korea's nuclear test. The United Nations condemned the test, with the US ambassador, Nikki Haley, urging for the strongest sanctions against North Korea. South Korean President Moon Jae-in and US President Donald Trump agreed to lift current restrictions on the payload weight of South Korea's ballistic missiles in a phone conversation.

However, there are signs of a rift between the two leaders despite the decades-long alliance between Seoul and Washington. Moon has advocated for more dialogue and diplomacy with North Korea, while Trump has stated that "talking is not the answer." North Korea could potentially launch another ICBM test on September 9, the country's founding day.

South Korean President Moon Jae-in and Japanese Prime Minister Shinzo Abe will attend an economic summit in Vladivostok, Russia, on September 6-7. They will be joined by Russian President Vladimir Putin, who has called for North Korea to stop nuclear tests but also emphasized the need for dialogue. Putin has criticized sanctions as ineffective and potentially harmful to North Korea's citizens.

In response to the nuclear test, the US is planning to circulate a resolution at the United Nations to impose the strongest possible sanctions against North Korea. The international community has expressed concern over North Korea's continued nuclear and missile tests, which pose a threat to regional and global peace.

North Korean leader Kim Jong-un delivered his first New Year's speech on state TV, emphasizing the need for economic improvement and reunification of the Koreas. The speech, which came less than a month after the election of South Korea's conservative President Park Geun-hye, seemed to refocus North Korea's sights on the economy. Kim called for a "radical turnabout" that would transform the impoverished, isolated state into an "economic giant" and raise living standards.

While Kim stressed the importance of military power, he also called for an end to confrontation between North and South Korea, and for both sides to respect and implement previously-agreed declarations. The focus on the economy and detente, however, was met with skepticism, as analysts await concrete evidence of Pyongyang's willingness to implement these agreements.

Kim's speech came amidst UN Security Council discussions on how to punish North Korea for a recent long-range rocket launch, which the US, Japan, and South Korea are seeking a response to in the UN Security Council. Under Kim's leadership, North Korea has conducted two long-range rocket launches, with the latest attempt appearing to be a success, placing a satellite into orbit.

Kim Jong-un saw in the new year by watching a musical performance with his wife, according to North Korean state media. The speech marked a departure from the previous New Year's messages delivered by North Korea's founder, Kim Il-sung, in 1994, and from the lengthy editorial carried by state-run newspapers during Kim Jong-il's tenure. The speech was scrutinized by outside analysts for hints about policymaking in the family-run police state, but did not mention the North's destitution and food shortages, nor did it mention the United States or the North's nuclear weapons program.

The seasonal decline in gas prices, typically occurring earlier, has been delayed this year. Despite a recent drop to $3.72, gas prices remain at a record high for this time of year. The summer was marked by refinery and pipeline complications, leading to a 27% increase in prices compared to last year. However, with rising inventories and decreasing demand, gas prices are expected to plunge up to 50 cents from the October peak of $3.86 over the next few weeks. This decline could provide a boost to consumer spending and potentially influence the upcoming presidential election, especially in battleground states. California, the nation's priciest state, still has higher prices, averaging $4.51, but is expected to follow the national trend.

The New York Times inadvertently published an article titled "For Women in Weiner Scandal, Indignity Lingers" on June 10, 2023, before quickly deleting it. The article, written by reporter Michael Barbaro, provided a sympathetic look at the women involved in Anthony Weiner's sexting scandal, many of whom went public in exchange for cash. The article was reconstructed from Google's cache and portrayed the women as victims of a harsh media environment who have banded together to reclaim their lives.

The article discussed Lisa Weiss, a blackjack dealer who leaked her emails with Weiner to RadarOnline, and Traci Nobles, a fitness instructor in Georgia whose salacious messages with Weiner were leaked without her permission. Both women support Weiner's mayoral campaign, with Nobles stating, "A perfect comeback story, ya know?"

The article also mentioned Ginger Lee, a porn star who capitalized on the situation by staging a press conference with Gloria Allred, calling on Weiner to stay out of the race to spare women like her further anguish. Weiss and Nobles both said they have been overwhelmed by the reaction to the scandal, with Weiss stating, "I cannot tell you the devastation."

Weiner issued a statement to the Times, saying, "I am deeply sorry that my behavior caused so much upheaval in the lives of those who were unwittingly involved." The article also discussed the complex feelings of the women towards Weiner, with some still supporting him despite their travails.

Several hours after the story was posted, the New York Times republished their story, stating that their editors decide when a story is ready for publication and outside coverage does not play a role in that decision. Weiner responded to the New York Times in an interview with City and State, stating, "I want to reiterate that sense of apology, and I’ve never talked about the private exchanges that we’ve had and I never will, because I think that they’ve already been put through enough."

North Korea issued an air raid warning on Thursday, which appeared to be part of a defense drill, according to South Korea's Unification Ministry. The warning was issued at 0032 GMT and carried a message to military units to stand ready. This incident comes amidst heightened tensions between the two Koreas, as North Korea has been conducting large-scale military drills and has expressed anger over the U.S. flying B-52 bombers over South Korea as part of annual military exercises. The North Korean military has threatened U.S. military bases in Guam and Japan, stating that they are within its "striking range." This threat follows the announcement by the United States that its B-52 bombers were making flights over South Korea. Tensions have been escalating since North Korea's latest nuclear test, which prompted the United Nations Security Council to respond by toughening sanctions on the secretive regime. The sanctions have further enraged North Korea, which has ratcheted up its threats, suggesting it could carry out a pre-emptive nuclear strike on the United States and South Korea. Analysts suggest that the North's threats are largely driven by domestic concerns and are intended to prop up the regime. The U.S. is currently formulating a new strategy to address the changed situation in North Korea, as the regime's unabashed declarations about its nuclear weapons show that "it's not the same North Korea as 10 years ago."

A Pakistani court has sentenced four individuals, including Farzana Parveen's father, brother, cousin, and former fiancé, to death for brutally murdering Farzana Parveen, a pregnant woman who married against her family's wishes. The killing, which occurred in broad daylight outside Lahore's high court, sparked global outrage. Farzana had testified against her family in a lawsuit accusing her husband of abducting her, but it later emerged that her husband had killed his first wife to be with her. The case is unusual as death sentences for family members in such cases are rare, but the defendants have the right to appeal. The incident highlights the prevalence of so-called honor killings in Pakistan, with hundreds of such cases reported each year. Despite Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif's condemnation, arranged marriages remain the norm in many conservative communities, making it unthinkable to marry against the family's wishes.

Pakistan's army has ordered a reduction in U.S. military personnel operating within the country, following the unilateral American commando raid that led to the death of Osama bin Laden. The army's decision comes in response to criticism over allowing the country's sovereignty to be violated during the operation in Abbottabad, a garrison town near Islamabad. The army statement also acknowledged "shortcomings in developing intelligence on the presence" of bin Laden in Pakistan, but claimed that initial information was provided to the CIA.

Pakistan's army chief, General Ashfaq Kayani, warned that any repeat of such U.S. commando operations would be viewed as a violation of Pakistani sovereignty and could imperil military and intelligence cooperation between the two countries. The U.S. has around 275 declared military personnel in Pakistan at any given time, some of whom help train the Pakistani army.

The Pakistani army also threatened to review its military and intelligence cooperation with Washington if the U.S. carries out any more similar raids. Ties between the two countries were already strained due to American allegations that Pakistan was failing to crack down on Afghan Taliban factions sheltering on its soil, and Pakistani anger over U.S. drone strikes on its territory.

The discovery of bin Laden's refuge in Pakistan has deepened belief in Washington that elements of Pakistan's army had provided him sanctuary. However, Pakistan's military and intelligence establishment has chafed at U.S. expressions of victory and shown acute resentment about what it deems a lack of gratitude for Pakistan's partnership.

The Obama administration has asked Pakistan for details about the compound where bin Laden lived in Abbottabad and who had access to it. However, they have largely refrained from criticizing Pakistan in recent days while trying to keep the counterterrorism partnership from completely unraveling.

In a week in which Pakistan's army and intelligence services have faced a rare onslaught of criticism, the Pakistani statements also appeared to reflect a concerted effort to redirect the public discourse towards anger at the United States, with violations of sovereignty being a sensitive issue in Pakistan. The army has promised an investigation into how bin Laden could have lived undetected in Pakistan, but past inquiries have rarely been revealing.

A historian, Dr. Paul Booth, from Keele University in the UK, has made a significant discovery in the Chester county court plea rolls dating back to 1310. He found the name 'Roger Fuckebythenavele,' which is believed to be the earliest known reference to the swear word 'fuck.' The man was named three times as part of a process to be outlawed, with the final mention being on September 28, 1311.

Dr. Booth suggests that the surname could mean an actual attempt at copulation by an inexperienced youth, later reported by a rejected girlfriend, or an equivalent of the word 'dimwit.' Prior to this discovery, the previous earliest use of the word was in a poem written around 1475.

Dr. Booth plans to publish an article about his discovery in the journal Notes and Queries. He also mentioned that he has come across other interesting curse words while studying the legal records of Cheshire during the reign of Edward II, such as 'Humphrey of the golden testicle' and 'Roger God-save-women.'

The word 'fuck' is of Germanic origin and is related to words in several other Germanic languages that have sexual meanings as well as meaning 'to strike' or 'to move back and forth.' This discovery is significant as it is the first instance of the word being used with a sexual connotation. The OED has been informed about this discovery, but it is up to them to decide whether to include it.

In a shocking incident in Kansas City, a couple was shot and robbed while attempting to purchase a car listed on Craigslist for their teenage son. The 53-year-old father suffered four gunshot wounds, while his 55-year-old wife was shot in the upper right arm. Their 16-year-old son, who witnessed the attack, was unharmed.

The robbery and shooting occurred around 7:30 p.m. on Wednesday at an apartment complex in the 5500 block of East 84th Street. The family had gone to inspect a 2007 Hyundai Sonata advertised for sale on Craigslist. They spoke to a man who identified himself as "AJ," but when they discussed the purchase, he walked away to call his wife. Two armed men then approached them, demanding money.

When the gunmen pointed their weapons at the woman, the father stepped in front of her, resulting in a barrage of gunfire. One robber grabbed the woman's purse, which contained $3,000, before they fled in the Hyundai. The abandoned vehicle was later found, but the cash was missing.

Detectives are questioning four people in connection with the incident, although details about their arrest are scarce. The four are considered persons of interest in the case. The shooting may be linked to an armed robbery hours earlier, where a man was robbed of an Xbox he was trying to sell on Craigslist.

Liberty-based Ferrellgas has contributed $5,000 to a reward for information leading to the arrest of the robbers, bringing the total reward to $7,000. Anyone with information is asked to call the TIPS Hotline at 816-474-TIPS. The injured man works for Ferrellgas, and his colleagues have praised his bravery in shielding his wife and son from the gunfire.

In a groundbreaking decision, a North Carolina judge ruled that a condemned killer, Marcus Robinson, should be removed from death row and serve a life sentence due to racially biased decisions by prosecutors during his trial. This is the first case to test North Carolina's Racial Justice Act, a law that allows death row prisoners to challenge their sentences based on racial discrimination. The judge found that race played a significant role in jury selection, with prosecutors eliminating black jurors more than twice as often as white jurors. The ruling could impact over 150 pending cases, and prosecutors have announced plans to challenge the decision. The case centers around the 1991 murder of a white teenager, Erik Tornblom, by Robinson and his co-defendant, Roderick Williams Jr. Robinson's mother, Shirley Burns, advocated for the law, which is under threat from a new Republican majority in the state's General Assembly. The Michigan State University study, central to Robinson's case, reported that nearly all-white juries were common among North Carolina's death row inmates. The Racial Justice Act represents a landmark reform in capital sentencing in North Carolina, according to the judge.

In Fort Worth, Texas, eight bodies were found at Johnson Family Mortuary on Tuesday after police were called to investigate an abandoned building. The owner, Dondre Johnson, claims a misunderstanding led to the police being called, as the building's landlord arrived to evict him but found the bodies instead. The mortuary's state license expires this month, and the business is the focus of five separate commission investigations. Johnson insists the business will be vindicated and that they are operating legally. No one has been arrested, and the medical examiner's office is now responsible for identifying the bodies and notifying next of kin. The Johnson Family Mortuary has had an active funeral director's license with the state since July 2011 and has no previous disciplinary history. The investigation is ongoing, and any concerned family members are asked to call the Tarrant County medical examiner’s office. The Johnson twins, who began working in the funeral business in the 1990s, have faced previous complaints but have not been found guilty of wrongdoing.

A strong winter storm caused significant disruptions across the eastern United States, resulting in at least eight deaths, tens of thousands of power outages, and numerous flight cancellations. The storm initially hit the Midwest, causing a mix of snow, rain, and ice that led to school closures, traffic accidents, and hours-long delays for commuters. The storm moved eastward, dumping up to a foot of snow in some parts of the Northeast and causing widespread freezing rain and ice accumulations.

In the Northeast, the snow was expected to end Saturday morning, but gusty winds and coastal flooding were expected to continue. Another cold front was expected to drop additional snowfall from the Great Lakes to the New England interior through Sunday.

The storm contributed to traffic crashes that killed people in several states, including a tour bus crash in Mississippi that resulted in two deaths and several injuries. In Indiana, a woman died after losing control of her vehicle in slick road conditions, and another person was killed in Canton, Ohio, and in Maryland. Arkansas reported two separate incidents in which three people were killed after drivers lost control of cars on icy roads.

The storm snarled traffic in the New York City area, with about 6 inches of snow accumulating around Central Park and in Newark, New Jersey. More than 8,200 flight delays and 1,900-plus cancellations were reported Thursday in the United States, with Newark Liberty International appearing the most affected.

The storm forced long waits at Manhattan's Port Authority Bus Terminal, where the terminal was packed with commuters waiting for buses that struggled to access the site. Some students in West Orange, New Jersey, were forced to sleep at their schools after their buses turned back, while others were taken to a diner to eat because snow-covered roads were clogged with traffic.

New York Mayor Bill de Blasio said the city was caught off guard by the storm, and he promised a full review of what happened. New Jersey Gov. Phil Murphy said the storm was a "regional nightmare," and he offered apologies to commuters who experienced a difficult commute home.

Schools in northern New England were delayed or closed after the region saw anywhere from four to eight inches of snow. Interstate speeds in New Hampshire and Maine were lowered to 45 mph. Schools were closed or were opening with delays in upstate New York, including in the Albany and Syracuse areas.

UPS recently conducted a test in Lithia, Florida, using an octocopter drone for residential package delivery. The drone, developed by Workhorse Group, was launched from a custom-built electric UPS delivery truck and docked on the truck's roof when not in use. A driver loads a package into the drone, which then flies autonomously to its destination. The drone's battery recharges during docking, and it has a 30-minute flight time limit.

For the test, the drone was launched from a truck a quarter mile away to a blueberry farm, where it delivered a package to a home. The truck then moved down the road to allow the driver to make another delivery. UPS sees potential in this system for reducing costs and emissions, particularly in rural areas where delivery vehicles often travel long distances to make single deliveries.

However, there are still obstacles to commercial drone deliveries, such as Federal Aviation Administration regulations that prohibit drones from flying over humans not involved in operation and require them to remain within the pilot's line of sight.

Amazon has also been exploring drone deliveries, having completed its first residential drone delivery in England in December and filing a patent for a drone that could use parachutes, electromagnets, or spring coils for package delivery.

UPS aims to make drones compatible with any type of delivery vehicle for last-mile deliveries. The HorseFly drone used in the test weighs 9.5 pounds, is powered by a lithium 18650 battery pack, and can fly for 30 minutes at a top speed of 45 miles per hour, carrying packages up to 10 pounds. UPS has previously collaborated with Mercedes Benz and drone startup Matternet on similar delivery van and drone projects.

The Hollywood Reporter published an investigative article titled "Animals Were Harmed," which alleges that the American Humane Association (AHA), a nonprofit organization responsible for monitoring film and TV productions for animal abuse, has concealed animal deaths to maintain positive relationships with Hollywood producers. The article cites several instances of animal mistreatment and neglect, including the death of three horses during the filming of HBO's Luck, a dog being punched by its trainer on the set of Eight Below, and the death of dozens of sheep and goats during the filming of The Hobbit: An Unexpected Journey. The AHA defends its actions by stating that the incidents were unintentional or occurred off-camera.

The AHA, which receives most of its funding from industry groups, is criticized for its response to the deaths of animals during filming. In an interview with The Hollywood Reporter, Candy Spelling, a national AHA board member, defends the organization's "No Animals Were Harmed" end credit by stating that people believe it means that animals don't die during filming, and that the AHA's monitoring only occurs when the cameras are rolling.

In response to the article, the AHA released a statement denying the allegations and stating that it has a high safety record of 99.98 percent on set. The AHA also clarified that it does not have jurisdiction over post-production and transit, and that it only monitors animals when they are on the set. The AHA also stated that it has made changes to its No Animals Were Harmed program, including the creation of a Scientific Advisory Committee, the hiring of licensed veterinarians to serve as Certified Safety Representatives, and the implementation of a policy for an independent, third-party investigation in the event of animal injury or death.

The AHA emphasized that it is a mission-driven small nonprofit that has worked to protect millions of animals on movie and television production sets for over 70 years. The AHA's overall record is one of caring and success, with a remarkable safety rate of 99.98 percent. The AHA stated that abuse in film and entertainment is not pervasive, and that most people in production settings want to do right by the animals, as does the AHA.

Prince Philip, the Duke of Edinburgh and husband of Queen Elizabeth II, announced his decision to stop carrying out public engagements this fall, according to Buckingham Palace. The 95-year-old prince will continue to head numerous charitable organizations but will not attend events. Speculation about the royal couple's health arose earlier due to a report in the Daily Mail about a meeting of royal household staff. Meanwhile, a new book titled "Where's the Birth Certificate?" by Jerome Corsi rekindles the "birther" issue, claiming President Obama is not a natural-born U.S. citizen. The "birther" controversy resurfaced earlier this year with Donald Trump's repeated discussions about Obama's birthplace while considering a presidential bid. The article discusses two main topics: the planned but ultimately abandoned Eddie Murphy Bill Cosby impersonation sketch for Saturday Night Live (SNL) 40th anniversary special, and Eddie Murphy's underwhelming performance during the actual event.

In the Paris area, a 62-year-old man named Regis Levasseur died during a hunt in the Compiègne national park after being gored by a deer with its antlers. The incident occurred around 10am local time, and the man was acting as a beater, helping to corner the animal. The hunter, who was not carrying a rifle, died of internal bleeding before emergency services arrived. This type of death is reportedly uncommon.

The incident has sparked discussions about hunting safety, with Guy Harlé, the president of the local hunters federation, stating that the accident serves as a reminder of the inherent risks involved in hunting wild animals. However, the fatal goring of Levasseur comes just a week after an outcry in France over hunters and their hounds tracking a stag to a private house and shooting it at close range.

Animal rights groups have called for hunting to be banned, and protests have been held in nearby towns. The hunting group involved in the incident was banned for a month, and the hunter who shot the stag was subject to death threats.

The death of Levasseur also comes after several tragic hunting accidents since the start of the season in September, including a grandfather who accidentally killed his own grandson during a hunt in western France and a woman who was shot dead in her garden after a bullet from a hunter's gun passed through her garden hedge.

France's national hunting office insists that the majority of accidents are caused by people not respecting the rules of the hunt, with 27 percent of accidents due to mishandling of the firearm and 17 percent due to hunters firing off bullets without having identified a definite target. Last year, 18 people were killed in hunting accidents in France, and 351 have been killed since 2001, most of whom were involved in the hunt.

The murder of Drummer Lee Rigby, a 25-year-old soldier, in London has sparked a controversy over whether the UK security services missed signs that could have prevented the attack. The two suspects, Michael Adebolajo and Michael Adebowale, were known to MI5 for eight years, and a Commons inquiry has been initiated to investigate their monitoring. Eric Pickles, the Communities Secretary, defended the security services, stating that it is impossible to control everyone all the time. Drummer Rigby was murdered on a street in Woolwich, south-east London, and footage emerged showing one of the suspects, Adebolajo, stating that he carried out the attack because British soldiers kill Muslims every day. The attack was filmed by a passer-by, and armed police arrived on the scene 13 minutes after the first 999 call. Both suspects remain under armed guard in separate London hospitals in stable conditions with non-life-threatening injuries.

The former head of counter-terrorism at MI6, Richard Barrett, stated that it is hard to detect attacks of the type seen in Woolwich, even with the suspects having been known to MI5 for eight years. He noted that it is difficult to determine when a person who expresses radical views will become a violent extremist. The radical Islamist preacher Anjem Choudary, who was once the leader of the banned al-Muhajiroun organization, said that Adebolajo had made comments that "I think not many Muslims can disagree with." He also said that one man killed in the street does not equate to the hundreds and thousands, in fact, who've been slaughtered by the British and American foreign policy.

Thousands of members of the Ahmadiyya Muslim community are expected to gather in London to offer prayers for the dead soldier and his family and to "express solidarity against extremism." The National President of the Ahmadiyya Muslim community, Rafiq Hayat, said, "We hope that the perpetrators of this crime, that is based on a twisted and warped ideology, are brought to justice." On Thursday, Drummer Rigby's family paid tribute to "a loving son, husband, father, brother, and uncle, and a friend to many." They said in a statement that Drummer Rigby, who had a two-year-old son, "would do anything for anybody - he always looked after his sisters and always protected them."

The footage obtained by the Daily Mirror reveals how, after beheading the soldier, they hatched a plot to ambush and murder the first police officers to come to his aid. The brave WPC first on the scene at the Woolwich beheading comes within inches of death, a dramatic Daily Mirror video shows. The driver, unable to draw her firearm, is saved by a male colleague in the back who fires his machine-gun through his window at a suspect who is charging at her. The callous Islamic extremists had lured police to the scene by dragging the body of the murdered fusilier – named yesterday as Lee Rigby, 25 – into the middle of the road. When they see the first police car arrive, the pair split up. Blade-wielding Michael Adebolajo, 28, runs at officers head-long towards the driver's side of the marked silver patrol car, in an apparent attempt to attack officers. Turkey has shared audio recordings related to the murder of Saudi journalist Jamal Khashoggi with Saudi Arabia, the United States, Germany, France, and Britain, according to President Recep Tayyip Erdogan. The recordings reportedly document the killing of Khashoggi, a critic of the Saudi government, who was killed at the Saudi consulate in Istanbul on October 2.

Erdogan stated that Saudi Arabia is aware of the identity of Khashoggi's killer, as the individual is among a group of 15 people who arrived in Turkey the day before the murder. The Turkish president called on Saudi Arabia to cooperate with Turkey in the investigation and to rid itself of the "stain" of Khashoggi's murder.

The existence of the audio recordings has not been officially confirmed, and it is unclear whether they have been verified or what they contain. Turkish police have ended the search for Khashoggi's body, but the criminal investigation into his murder will continue.

Saudi Arabia has changed its narrative about Khashoggi's murder several times amid international outcry and intensifying skepticism over its account. After initially insisting that Khashoggi had left the consulate, Saudi Arabia later admitted that he had died in a fistfight inside the building. Riyadh later conceded that Khashoggi was killed in a premeditated murder, but that the murder was an unplanned "rogue operation."

Erdogan has accused the "highest levels" of the Saudi government of ordering the hit, while some officials have pointed the finger at the crown prince, a charge Riyadh denies. Erdogan may meet with US President Donald Trump in Paris during the commemorations for the 100th anniversary of the end of World War I.

The Turkish and Saudi governments have carried out joint inspections of the consulate and the consul-general's residence, but Erdogan said some Saudi officials are still trying to cover up the crime. Saudi officials have reportedly refused to cooperate with their Turkish counterparts and may have tampered with the ongoing investigation by sending in chemical experts to destroy evidence.

The article discusses the misconception that the winter solstice of 2021 would feature the longest night ever due to the Earth's rotation slowing down. However, the Earth's rotation is actually speeding up slightly over the past forty years, and the longest night in Earth's history likely occurred in 1912.

The Earth's rotation is slowing down due to the moon's gravity, which causes tidal acceleration. This phenomenon allows the moon to drift slightly farther away from Earth over time and also causes the Earth to spin more slowly.

On a year-to-year basis, geologic factors such as melting ice at the poles and the resulting redistribution of the Earth's mass can alter the speed of the Earth's rotation.

Tonight, December 21, 2021, is the winter solstice, and it is the longest night of the year for locations in the Northern Hemisphere. This is because the Earth orbits around the sun on a tilted axis, and the Northern Hemisphere gets the shortest duration of sunlight all year on this day.

The days will gradually lengthen as the Earth begins to tilt back toward the sun, and the shortest days will not be the coldest. The coldest days of the year on average across the U.S. occur in mid-January, as the Northern Hemisphere continues to lose more heat than it gains for several more weeks.

The winter solstice offers a ray of light for everyone, as snow lovers can rejoice that the coldest days are still upon us, while warm weather fans can look forward to the lengthening days as a sign that spring is just a few more months away.

The article discusses the ongoing bourbon shortage that has been affecting the United States in recent years. The shortage is due to a combination of factors, including increased demand for bourbon, a shortage of new American oak barrels, and poor decisions made by distillers in the 1990s regarding production levels.

Making bourbon is a process that involves aging the whiskey in oak barrels for a period of time, with the length of aging affecting the flavor and quality of the bourbon. Traditional methods of aging can take anywhere from two to more than 20 years, but new distilleries are experimenting with unconventional aging methods to speed up the process.

Some of these methods include using smaller barrels, adding oak chips to the barrels, and using increased oxidation to mimic aging. These methods have been met with skepticism from whiskey connoisseurs, who argue that the secret to a refined bourbon is time.

The popularity of bourbon in the past decade has led to a significant increase in sales, with the U.S. selling 19 million cases in 2014, generating $2.7 billion in revenue. However, the shortage of bourbon has led to a panic-buying mentality among drinkers, with many buying up limited release bourbons from well-established companies.

The shortage is expected to continue for some time, as traditional brewing methods require a decade or more for the bourbon to mature. However, new distilleries are continuing to experiment with new aging methods in an attempt to find a solution to the shortage.

The article also mentions the announcement of synthetic diamonds in 1955, which was met with similar skepticism and alarm as the claims of accelerated bourbon aging. The article concludes by stating that the future of bourbon is uncertain, but that the shortage is temporary and that new bourbon is already being brewed. It is just not ready to arrive quite yet.

The study published in PLoS Medicine reveals that a mother's height directly influences the risk of preterm birth. Researchers from the March of Dimes Prematurity Research Center Ohio Collaborative found that a mother's height, determined by genetic factors, shapes the fetal environment, influencing the length of pregnancy and frequency of prematurity. The study analyzed 3,485 Nordic women and their babies and observed consistent associations between maternal height and birth length, birth weight, and gestational age.

The researchers used a height genetic score as a powerful genetic instrument for maternal height and observed significant associations of maternal height genetic score with birth length, birth weight, and gestational age. The study suggests that the observed correlations between maternal height and birth length or birth weight were mainly due to fetal genetic effects rather than confounding effects.

The findings indicate that birth weight and birth length are mainly defined by fetal genetics, making it difficult to define abnormal fetal growth without taking genetic variance into account. In contrast, gestational age at birth might be causally influenced by maternal height, in which case maternal height might operate as an important factor that shapes the intrauterine environment and influences the gestational age.

The study also found that shorter maternal height is a risk factor for preterm birth, with an estimated 3% increase in risk if the mothers are 1 cm shorter. The researchers acknowledge that further replication studies in independent cohorts are needed to confirm the findings.

The March of Dimes is raising $75 million to support its five prematurity research centers, which bring together the brightest minds from various disciplines to find answers to prevent premature birth. The centers are located at Stanford University School of Medicine, the University of Pennsylvania, Washington University in St. Louis, the University of Chicago, Northwestern University, and Duke University. Preterm birth is a major health issue, as it is the number one killer of newborns in the United States, and more than 450,000 babies are born too soon in the U.S. annually. Worldwide, 15 million babies are born preterm, and more than one million die due to complications of an early birth. Babies who survive an early birth face serious and lifelong health problems.

The 2013 Nathan's Hot Dog Eating Contest took place on July 4th, with Joey Chestnut defending his title for the seventh consecutive year. He broke his own record by consuming 69 hot dogs in 10 minutes, surpassing his previous record of 68 set in 2009 and 2012. Matt Stonie finished second with 51 hot dogs, while Tim Janus, better known as Eater X, came in third with 50 hot dogs.

In the women's competition, Sonya Thomas, also known as the Black Widow, won for the third time, narrowly defeating Juliet Lee by a quarter of a hot dog. Thomas had set a record with 45 hot dogs last year, but fell short this time with just under 37.

The contest, which has been a city tradition for 97 years, was held at Coney Island and attracted thousands of spectators. New York City Mayor Michael Bloomberg attended the event and made an effort to use as many hot dog-related puns as possible during his speech. The contest took place despite concerns about a swaying observation tower near the amusement park.

In this news roundup, Kanye West is reported to have been affectionate towards Kim Kardashian at a party following their LA concert with Jay-Z. Kendall Jenner discusses handling criticism from haters in an interview for Teen Prom. Rooney Mara criticizes her early work on Law and Order: SVU, and later talks about merkin artistry.
