Hurricane Sandy, which made landfall on the East Coast on October 29, 2012, has caused significant disruptions to the upcoming Halloween celebrations. The storm, which has caused multiple fatalities, halted mass transit, and left millions without power, was originally expected to generate $8 billion in spending coast-to-coast. However, its impact on Halloween purchases is unclear as many stores and pumpkin patches along the East Coast are closing due to the storm.

The storm has also affected the Halloween parade in New York City's Greenwich Village, which was scheduled for Wednesday night. The number of viewers and participants is expected to be cut in half, and the city's Halloween-related revenue is projected to be sliced from $90 million to $45 million. Many East Coast merchants that rely on Halloween day for a big chunk of business appear to be in trouble.

The storm has also washed out takeout business, as Halloween is not a huge holiday for eating out, but roughly one in five Americans opted for takeout food last Halloween. This number could take a hit this year if the storm or its aftermath forces a number of East Coast restaurants to close.

Pumpkin patches have also been affected, with Cox Farms pumpkin patch in Centreville, Va., closing on Monday and Tuesday. Reservations for both days were being switched to Wednesday, when the weather is supposed to improve.

The Goodwill Gridiron Halloween Party with the Baltimore Ravens, hosted by Goodwill of the Chesapeake, has been postponed. It's the group's biggest, annual fundraiser, with proceeds helping job-train people with disabilities.

New Jersey Gov. Chris Christie addressed the issue directly by tweeting that if conditions are not safe on Wednesday for trick-or-treating, he will sign an Executive Order rescheduling #Halloween. Many communities in New Jersey and elsewhere are already pushing festivities back until this weekend or next week.

Many parents are worried about taking their children out on Halloween night due to conventional Halloween safety advice such as being mindful of traffic, wearing bright colors, and staying away from downed tree limbs and power lines. The Boston Police Department’s Virtual Community urges trick-or-treaters to “stay away from downed tree limbs and power lines,” avoid neighborhoods with no power and stick with short costumes that won’t get "caught in debris from trees or slippery wet leaves.”

Some children may be feeling fearful of trick-or-treating, even if their parents aren't. Heading into the spookiest of holidays on the heels of a threatening natural disaster may take a toll on a young person's psyche.

Parents are being advised to show their kids on the radar maps that the storm is gone, and to act as if everything is okay and try to return to a normal routine as soon as possible. If you can’t get outside for a conventional evening of trick-or-treating, the Internet is brimming with ideas such as setting up an in-home candy hunt or having a "Trunk or Treat" (dispensing candy from the backs of cars) in a local cul-de-sac.

Governor Chris Christie has signed an executive order postponing Halloween festivities in New Jersey until Nov. 5. Gov. Christie said in a statement: "As Governor, it is my responsibility to use all available resources of the state government to protect against the emergency created by Hurricane Sandy -- postponing Halloween celebrations by five days is a commonsense and necessary step to accomplish that." On Wednesday afternoon, he tweeted, "Its just not safe yet to be out trick-or-treating tonight, so Halloween has officially been postponed until Monday," following up with "I better see you all out there on Monday with your costumes on and candy in tow."

On October 30, 2015, a 20-year-old man named Richard Pananian from Burbank died in a high-speed rollover crash on the southbound Golden State (5) Freeway. The accident occurred near Colorado Boulevard and the Ventura (134) Freeway interchange.

According to the California Highway Patrol (CHP), Pananian was driving his 2004 Ford Fiesta at a high speed and passing vehicles on the right shoulder. He veered out of control and collided with a 2004 Ford F-150, which was in the No. 4 lane going 50 mph. The Fiesta then overturned multiple times, ejecting Pananian who landed on a freeway sign.

Pananian was not wearing a seatbelt, and it is unclear what exactly caused his death, as the collision report stated that the injuries sustained and force of impact were unclear. The F-150 driver and his passengers were not injured.

The incident caused all southbound and northbound lanes of the 5 Freeway to be temporarily blocked, and the two southbound right lanes were closed for an extended period. The lanes reopened about 11 a.m., according to CHP's Southern Division.

Pananian worked at an automobile sales company called L.A. Autostore in Van Nuys, and the company expressed their condolences on Facebook. The CHP is investigating the crash, and it is not yet known if drugs or alcohol were a factor.

The original map of The Hundred Acre Wood, featured in A.A. Milne's Winnie-the-Pooh, is set to be auctioned by Sotheby's in July. The map, illustrated by E.H. Shepard, is expected to sell for between £100,000 and £150,000. The map, which also appears in the Disney film released in 1966, is considered one of the most famous maps in English literature due to its iconic status and the unique illustrations by Shepard. Four other illustrations by Shepard, including one of Christopher Robin and Pooh saying goodbye, will also be auctioned. The auction comes amid increased interest in illustrations from collectors, according to Sotheby's senior specialist Dr Errington. The map and illustrations are valued highly due to their association with the beloved Winnie-the-Pooh characters and their iconic status in literature and popular culture. The map was first sold by Sotheby's in 1968 and has since changed hands twice. The auction comes as a new film based on Milne's characters, "Christopher Robin," is due to be released by Disney in August.

A Vancouver Police officer, identified as Peter Colenutt, was praised for his heroic actions after he rescued a dog that had fallen through the thin ice at Lost Lagoon in Stanley Park. On Friday afternoon, the dog chased a ball onto the frozen lake and broke through the ice. When officers arrived, they saw the dog struggling to stay afloat. Const. Peter Colenutt removed parts of his uniform, took hold of a rescue rope, and with his colleagues holding the other end, he made his way to the dog. Both the dog and the officer were uninjured but cold when they reached the shore. This is not the first time Colenutt has been recognized for his bravery; he received the Chief Constable's Commendation this past week for his part in a Stanley Park water rescue in June 2016, where he and another officer swam 100 meters to aid a person in distress. Social media users have praised Colenutt for his act of kindness, with many expressing gratitude for his actions.

Cardinal Donald Wuerl, the Archbishop of Washington, announced on Tuesday that he will travel to Rome to discuss his resignation with Pope Francis. This decision comes amidst a growing sexual abuse scandal within the U.S. Catholic Church. The move marks a significant phase in the ongoing crisis, as accountability shifts towards those who covered up abuse rather than the perpetrators.

The Pittsburgh Diocese, where Wuerl served as bishop from 1988 to 2006, removed his name from a high school following a grand jury report that found he had reassigned priests accused of abusing children, rather than taking stronger action. The report did not accuse Wuerl of personally sexually abusing children.

The grand jury investigation in Pennsylvania found evidence of sexual abuse by at least 1,000 people, mostly children, over the past 70 years by approximately 300 clergymen. The actual numbers could be much higher. The report revealed that Wuerl notified the Vatican in 1989 of several priests accused of sexually abusing children, but he later granted requests for reassignment or early retirement, and in one case, approved a loan to assist a priest with personal debts.

Wuerl canceled a planned speech at the World Meeting of Families in Dublin, making him the second high-ranking U.S. Church official to do so. Last week's report was the most wide-ranging U.S. investigation into sexual abuse by priests since the scandal became public in Boston in 2002.

In a letter to priests, Wuerl stated that he will meet with Pope Francis about the resignation he presented three years ago at age 75, the mandatory retirement age for Catholic bishops. Wuerl expressed the need for this decision to enable the archdiocese to move forward and bring healing. The meeting's date is yet to be determined.

Wuerl's announcement follows calls for his resignation from some of his priests and parishioners since the release of the Pennsylvania grand jury report, which included accounts of his allowing several priests accused of sexually abusing children to remain in ministry. Despite his association with his predecessor, the former Cardinal Theodore E. McCarrick, who recently stepped down due to accusations of molestation and coercion, Wuerl had gained the confidence of both Pope Francis and his predecessor, Benedict XVI.

In a significant move, President Obama announced on Thursday that he would halt deportations for millions of immigrants living in the country illegally. This action, however, was framed by Democrats as just the first step towards a comprehensive overhaul of the immigration system, which they assert can only be achieved through Congress.

Democrats, including House Minority Leader Nancy Pelosi, welcomed the executive actions but emphasized the need for a legislative solution. They argued that the president's actions provide an opportunity for Republicans to pass an immigration bill when Congress reconvenes in December.

Republicans, on the other hand, were furious with what they perceive as an unconstitutional power grab by Obama. They believe his actions make it harder for lawmakers to reach a deal on broader reforms. Speaker John Boehner accused Obama of lawlessness and damaging his remaining credibility.

The Democrats' strategy is clear: they welcome the president's actions but do not want them to impede Congress's efforts to enact a more permanent comprehensive reform law over the next two years. The Senate had passed such a reform bill in June 2013 with broad bipartisan support, but House Republican leaders refused to consider it.

The debate is also a test of whether the Republican Party can contain the controversial and sometimes offensive comments that have often hindered attempts to bolster support for Republicans among Hispanics. The party leaders are urging their colleagues to avoid playing into the president's hands and to respond strongly but measuredly.

Republican leaders are considering several moves, including filing a lawsuit over Obama’s executive authority, pursuing stand-alone legislation on immigration policy, and removing funding for immigration agencies. However, they are also trying to avoid a fiscal clash during the lame-duck session, shortly before the GOP takes control of the Senate in January.

The Democrats and Republicans are set for a confrontation over immigration reform, with both sides urging strong but measured responses. The outcome of this confrontation could have significant implications for the future of immigration policy in the United States.

In the 1995 episode "Lisa's Wedding" of the animated series "The Simpsons," the writers presented a vision of what 2010 would look like. The episode, which aired six seasons into the show's run, served as a precursor to the more famous "Back to the Future Part II" predictions. This summary will focus on the 11 accurate predictions made by "The Simpsons" about the year 2010.

1. Cryogenic freezing: While we are not yet at the point where people can be frozen and thawed like bottles of Jagermeister, advancements in cryonics are being made.

2. Fox News: Instead of transitioning to a hardcore sex channel, Fox spawned Fox News, which has become a dominant force in the media landscape.

3. Jim Carrey's career: The episode did not anticipate Jim Carrey's future efforts to be taken seriously as an actor, and his return to rubber-faced comedy when things didn't work out.

4. News channel consolidation: Each network decided to tackle the 24-hour news cycle head-on, providing a similar amount of actual news as in 1995, supplemented with additional hours of people screaming at us.

5. Redesigned planes: Airlines have not redesigned their planes to turn passengers upside-down and shake loose change, but the experience remains less than comfortable.

6. Robot librarians, British servants, and inanimate carbon rod handlers: While we are not yet at the point where we have robot butlers or inanimate carbon rod handlers, advancements in technology are moving in that direction.

7. Fully sponsored education: While corporations have not yet taken over the education system, there is a growing trend of corporate involvement in education.

8. Ubiquitous video phones: Video conferencing has become more common, but it still falls short of the seamless, face-to-face communication depicted in the episode.

9. World War III: The episode humorously mentions a World War III, but it is not clear if this was meant to be taken seriously.

10. Big Ben going digital: The episode shows Big Ben being replaced by a VCR clock, but it is unlikely that this will happen in the near future.

11. Soy snacks: Soy-based snacks, such as SoyJoy, have become more common, and "The Simpsons" accurately captured their poor taste.

Overall, "The Simpsons" did a good job of predicting some aspects of 2010, particularly in the areas of technology and media. However, it is important to remember that the episode was meant to be humorous and should not be taken as a completely accurate prediction of the future.

In a clear indication of an impending showdown, House Speaker John Boehner has reiterated that Republicans will not raise the U.S. borrowing authority without substantial spending cuts. Boehner's stance comes as President Obama prepares a series of speeches on the economy, which the GOP leaders view as a precursor to a push for higher taxes. The Speaker criticized Obama for ignoring House-passed legislation aimed at boosting job growth and accused him of using speeches as a setup for tax increases.

Republican leaders, including Majority Leader Eric Cantor, have expressed frustration over Obama's focus on speeches rather than action. They cited House legislation such as the Keystone oil sands pipeline, regulatory reform, and delaying the implementation of the 2010 healthcare law as proposals that could help the economy but are opposed by the White House.

The debate over raising the debt ceiling could collide with negotiations to fund the government for the 2014 fiscal year, which begins on October 1. Both Democrats and Republicans are concerned about repeating the events of 2011, when a fight over the debt limit led to a potential government shutdown.

Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid has stated that Democrats are "not negotiating on the debt ceiling," while Senate Democrats want to replace the automatic, across-the-board cuts with a mix of spending cuts and tax revenue. The White House Office of Management and Budget has projected the caps in 2014 would be $967.4 billion for security and non-security spending unless the sequester is repealed.

The economy is showing signs of growth, with government tax receipts climbing 14 percent above the level a year ago. However, the recovery is still sluggish, and funding at the lower levels could lead to a disaster for the country, according to Senator Reid. The need to increase the nation's borrowing authority will likely lead to a fall showdown between the White House and Congress.

The Pentagon has concluded that a senior Defense Department official, Michael Vickers, leaked restricted information to the makers of the film 'Zero Dark Thirty' about the hunt for Osama bin Laden. The case was referred to the Justice Department in September, but no criminal prosecution has been launched yet. The leaked information involved the name of a U.S. Special Operations Command officer who helped plan the raid on bin Laden's hideout in Pakistan, which is against the law in certain circumstances.

Vickers is the top intelligence adviser to Defense Secretary Leon Panetta and oversees the Pentagon's vast intelligence operations. He has been frequently mentioned as a candidate to replace retired Army Gen. David Petraeus as CIA director. The Justice Department review could potentially hurt Vickers' chances of being nominated to the CIA post, but it's unclear whether it will.

The Pentagon inspector general's office is continuing to examine whether there were any other leaks of restricted information to the makers of the film. The inquiry was launched at the request of Rep. Peter King, who has expressed concerns that classified information may have been given to the filmmakers that could compromise tactics used by U.S. special forces and the methods used by the CIA to gather intelligence.

The film, directed by Kathryn Bigelow and written by Mark Boal, was delayed amid Republican complaints that it could bring Obama votes by glorifying the bin Laden operation. The premier was held last week and the film is due for a limited public release on Wednesday.

The investigation is emblematic of an ongoing debate over what information the government deems to be secret, who can disclose classified material, and to what degree leaks of such information jeopardize national security. Obama's Justice Department has prosecuted a record number of U.S. officials for leaking secret information to the news media that critics contend shouldn't have been classified or did no harm to national security.

The case raises questions about the boundaries of what is and what is not classified, and whether the government's classification system is fraught with problems, as a presidential advisory panel found in a recent report. The Public Interest Declassification Board recommended an extensive overhaul of the system.

The investigation will create more controversy for the movie, which has been criticized by human rights groups and others for scenes of the CIA's brutal interrogation of al Qaida detainees that erroneously imply that torture provided crucial intelligence that led to bin Laden's hiding place in Abbottabad, Pakistan. King requested the investigation in letters to the Pentagon and CIA inspectors general in August 2011 over concerns that classified information may have been given to the makers of the bin Laden movie. Bigelow and Boal have said that they didn't receive classified information and didn't request it.

The article tells the story of Johnny "Thumper" Duckworth, a busboy at Randy's Southside Diner in Grand Junction, Colorado, who found $3,000 in cash on the floor and turned it in to his employer. Duckworth, who has worked at the diner for nine years, is known for his honesty and hard work. He lives house to house with friends and family and is currently struggling due to car breakdowns and medical bills that garnish his paycheck.

To help Duckworth during his hard times, a GoFundMe page was set up to collect donations. The page has now exceeded its listed goal of $3,000 in donations. The money was originally lost by Darrell Cox, who came to the diner for breakfast and left the envelope with the cash behind. Duckworth found the envelope and handed it over to his boss, Randy Emmons, who returned the money to Cox through the bank.

Cox returned to the diner on Thursday and gave Duckworth a $300 tip as a reward for his honesty. The article concludes by stating that Duckworth continues to work hard at the diner, despite his struggles.

The article details the capture of David Sweat, one of two convicted murderers who escaped from the Clinton Correctional Facility in Dannemora, New York, on June 6, 2015. Sweat was found and apprehended by a New York State Police sergeant on June 28, 2015, in the town of Constable, near the Canadian border, after a more than three-week manhunt. Sweat was shot twice in the torso during the encounter and was transported to the Albany Medical Center in critical condition.

The search for Sweat's accomplice, Richard Matt, ended on June 26, 2015, when he was shot and killed by law enforcement officers. Matt was sick and drunk at the time of his death, and investigators believe he had been outdoors for a long time and possibly consumed spoiled food or bad water.

The escape of Sweat and Matt from the maximum-security prison was facilitated by their cozy relationship with a prison tailor and a guard who allegedly provided them with tools. They cut their way through multiple barriers and underground passageways to escape through a manhole in the middle of a street.

Authorities are hoping to interview Sweat to gather more information about the escape and to prosecute anyone found to have assisted them. Investigators believe that Sweat and Matt had been gathering information about hunting cabins and the surrounding terrain for almost a year to help them navigate during their escape.

The manhunt for Sweat and Matt captivated the nation and led to wild speculation about their whereabouts. The search for Sweat continued even with heavy downpours of rain, and authorities were hopeful that they could be close to finding him after encountering Matt. It is believed that Sweat may have used pepper to throw off the scent of tracking dogs during the manhunt.

The capture of Sweat brings an end to the statewide search for him and his prison-break partner, Richard Matt. New York Governor Andrew Cuomo described the arrest as the end of a "nightmare" and expressed relief that Sweat was captured without injury to any law enforcement officers.

The U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) announced on September 19, 2018, that Cargill Meat Solutions is recalling approximately 132,606 pounds of ground beef products due to potential contamination with Escherichia coli O26. The products were produced and packaged on June 21, 2018, and were shipped to retail locations nationwide. The ground beef items were identified following an investigation related to Recall 072-2018, where ground beef products were recalled in connection with the E. coli O26 outbreak.

The products subject to recall bear establishment number “EST. 86R” inside the USDA mark of inspection. The affected products include 3-, 10- and 20-pound packages of ground beef under the Our Certified, Excel, Sterling Silver, Certified and Fire River Farms brands with July 11 use or freeze by dates. Consumers are advised to check their freezers for these products and either throw them away or return them to the place of purchase.

E. coli O26 is a serovar of Shiga toxin-producing E. coli (STEC) that can cause illnesses with onset dates ranging from 2 to 8 days after exposure. Symptoms include diarrhea (often bloody) and vomiting, and most people recover within a week. However, some infections can be more severe and may lead to kidney failure, hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS), and even death.

The USDA is concerned that some product may still be frozen in consumers' freezers and is urging consumers not to consume these products. The USDA routinely conducts recall effectiveness checks to verify that the recalled products are no longer available to consumers.

Cargill Meat Solutions has stated that all affected products have been removed from supermarkets, and food safety teams are reviewing the Fort Morgan facility and others to ensure safe food delivery. The USDA did not release information about the people who died or became ill, including locations.

The Cargill plant had a smaller recall of Excel ground beef in August, but no illnesses had been reported at that time. Consumers with questions regarding the recall can call 1-844-419-1574. Media with questions regarding the recall can contact April Nelson with Cargill corporate affairs at (952) 742-9150 or at april_nelson@cargill.com.

In November 2015, an email about Halloween costumes by Yale University lecturer Erika Christakis sparked a student uprising over racial bias and insensitivity at the Ivy League institution, with similar issues being echoed at colleges across the country. The email, combined with allegations of racial insensitivity at a Yale fraternity, provoked outrage among students of color who demanded action to improve the university's racial climate.

Christakis, who was known for her courses on child development and psychology, became the focus of intense scrutiny after her email critiquing a college-wide request that students think twice before wearing culturally insensitive Halloween costumes. In the email, she expressed concern about the increasing censorship and prohibition on college campuses.

The email and the allegations against the fraternity led to protests, with hundreds of students demanding answers from the college's first black dean. The controversy also sparked a national debate about free speech and racial sensitivity.

Through a set of initiatives unveiled last month, including faculty growth in fields dealing with race and ethnicity, Yale President Peter Salovey took a major step in quelling the tensions. However, Christakis and her husband, Silliman Master Nicholas Christakis, remained at the helm of the college.

An open letter expressing support for the right of the Christakises to free speech and freedom of intellectual expression was signed by nearly 70 faculty members. However, another open letter expressing solidarity with students' concerns about "racism and devaluation" was signed by a larger number of faculty members.

While many student protesters called for the Christakises' dismissal from Silliman, few mentioned their presence in the classroom. Christakis has now decided to resign her teaching role to return to her work with young children and families. Nicholas Christakis, a physician and sociologist, will take a sabbatical in spring 2016 and not teach his popular lecture, Health of the Public.

The resignation of Christakis has been met with mixed reactions. While some students understand her rationale for leaving the classroom, others are disappointed by her decision, as her courses on child development and education were highly valued. The university has not yet commented on the matter.

Elizabeth Rathburn, 56, of Grosse Pointe Park, Michigan, pleaded guilty on Monday to her role in a scheme where she and her husband, Arthur Rathburn, ran a shady cadaver business, International Biological, Inc., that sold or rented human remains to medical and dental students. The couple was indicted in January, and Elizabeth Rathburn was charged with wire fraud, mail fraud, and lying to a police officer. She reached a deal with prosecutors that had her plead guilty to wire fraud and is set to be sentenced on July 18.

Arthur Rathburn was also charged with transporting hazardous materials and making false statements. He has pleaded not guilty and is scheduled to begin trial on April 5. The couple is accused of purchasing diseased specimens from suppliers at a discount and misrepresenting the remains to maximize profit, defrauding customers and exposing them to infection.

Elizabeth Rathburn admitted selling human remains she claimed were disease-free, but which had tested positive for HIV and Hepatitis B. In one instance, she shipped the head of a person who died from sepsis and pneumonia among seven other severed heads on a Delta Cargo flight. The heads were stuffed in trash bags inside coolers that also contained pools of human blood.

Under the terms of her plea deal, Elizabeth Rathburn faces four to 10 months in prison and has to pay $55,225 in restitution to the American Anesthesiology Association, which had rented the diseased body parts from the Rathburns' company. Arthur Rathburn's case is headed toward trial, which will be full of grisly exhibits and allegations that he committed many crimes, like cutting up bodies with chainsaws, shipping blood-filled coolers of fresh heads on commercial airliners, and storing more than 1,000 body parts on ice at his warehouse. If convicted, he could face up to 20 years in prison.

Before getting into the body parts trade as a private dealer, Arthur Rathburn was the coordinator of the University of Michigan's anatomical donation program from 1984-90, but he got fired after he was caught selling bodies. In 1989, he started his own business supplying body parts.

The state of Louisiana's refusal to install air conditioning on death row at the Louisiana State Penitentiary in Angola has resulted in over $1 million in legal fees, according to records obtained by The Associated Press. The case, which has been ongoing for three years, involves three death-row inmates with medical problems who filed a lawsuit against the state. Most of the money spent has gone to private attorneys on both sides of the case, with the state accruing at least $1,067,000 in expenses.

Expert witnesses and state contractors have also received tens of thousands of dollars, and the prison itself has incurred over $100,000 in expenses, including a payment of nearly $29,000 to a firm monitoring the heat and humidity every 15 minutes.

The judge has questioned whether the state's refusal to install air conditioning is based on prison management concerns, politics, or ideology. He suggested that the litigation is already more costly than the fix, estimating that it would cost about $1 million to install air conditioning on death row's six tiers.

The state has argued that the consequences of installing air conditioning would be far-reaching, potentially spawning more lawsuits from prisoners across the country demanding air-conditioned cells. However, the judge has cited a state remediation plan, suggesting that the litigation is already more costly than the fix.

The case is "another example of elected officials taking a stand as long as the taxpayers pay for it," said Bill Quigley, a Loyola University law professor. He described the situation as a waste of money.

The hearing on Wednesday will determine whether the state's current heat remediation measures are adequately protecting the plaintiffs as Louisiana's sweltering summer approaches. The inmates' attorneys are urging the judge to reconsider air conditioning as a requirement.

Neale stressed that public pressure was helping to move the needle on the issue, and said that management at the facility had already implemented some of his group's recommendations, including providing piles of snow for its two polar bear hybrids.

Animals Asia and the China Cetacean Alliance have contacted Haichang Holdings, the largest Chinese operator of ocean parks, to outline the numerous animal welfare issues at the Grandview Aquarium. There has been no response to date.

Neale said, "As long as businesses are allowed to use animals in this manner, wealth will always be put ahead of welfare. We all need to continue to publicly object to such facilities."

Animals Asia and the China Cetacean Alliance will continue to monitor the situation and push for an end to this cruelty. The aquarium did not respond to requests for comment.

Mariner Energy, an oil and gas company, has been involved in numerous offshore accidents and pollution incidents in the Gulf of Mexico, resulting in investigations by federal regulators. Senior Democrats on the House Energy and Commerce Committee have requested a briefing on the incident from Mariner Energy by September 10. The cause of the fire remains under investigation.

Pewee has since spoken out about the incident, saying that retailers should be aware that "times have changed" and that consumers should be made aware of any dress code before shopping.

In an incident that occurred on November 15th, a three-year-old girl named Aubri Degeffered was abducted during a carjacking in Milwaukee. The incident took place around 6:50 p.m. in the 4900 block of W. Chambers St. A red 2014 Volvo SUV was stolen, with Aubri inside.

An Amber Alert was issued, and later in the evening, Aubri was found safe in Jefferson County. The suspect, a 32-year-old individual, was also apprehended. The vehicle was located and recovered in Jefferson County.

The red Volvo SUV was later involved in an attempted strong-arm robbery in Brookfield. The suspect, believed to be the same individual who stole the SUV, attempted a robbery at a gas station in Brookfield around 7:35 p.m.

The investigation is ongoing, and charges are expected to be presented to the Milwaukee County District Attorney's Office. The family of Aubri Degeffered was en route to Jefferson County to reunite with her. This developing story will continue to be monitored on FOX6 News and FOX6Now.com.

A Mormon missionary, Gavin Paul Zimmerman, aged 19, from the US state of Utah, died after falling from a cliff at Cape Solander in Kurnell, Sydney, while taking photos for a friend. The incident occurred on Monday afternoon during a whale-watching outing with other missionaries. Zimmerman had been in Australia for almost a year serving his mission. His parents, Raymond and Jeanette Zimmerman, released a statement through The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, describing their son as a "bright light" who loved his mission and was a great example to them.

This is the second fatal incident at Cape Solander in six weeks, following a similar incident involving a man in his 30s last month. Police have urged visitors to stick to the whale-watching platform and not to climb onto the rocks below for safety reasons. The local council is considering whether further safety measures are needed, and there are plans to educate people more about the dangers.

The incident has brought attention to the popular whale-watching spot, which is managed by NSW National Parks and Wildlife Service. June and July are the best times to see humpback whales off the NSW east coast as they migrate north to warmer waters. NSW Police Chief Inspector Chris Hill has urged anyone visiting the area to take heed of warning signs and stay on the whale-watching platform for safety reasons.

Lacey Spears, a 26-year-old mother, has been charged with the second-degree depraved murder and first-degree manslaughter of her 5-year-old son, Garnett, who died in January due to sodium poisoning at Westchester Medical Center. Authorities believe that Spears tortured her son medically for years, possibly suffering from Munchausen syndrome by proxy, a psychiatric illness in which a parent sickens a child to gain attention and sympathy.

Spears often blogged about Garnett's deteriorating medical condition, and prosecutors claim that she fed her son lethal amounts of salt, conducting Internet research about the effects salt would have on him. Garnett was brought to Nyack Hospital on January 17 with seizure-like symptoms before being transferred to Westchester Medical Center on January 19 after his sodium levels rose with no medical explanation.

The state Office of Children and Family Services had already launched an investigation into whether Spears was harming her son before Garnett died on January 23. Spears turned herself in to Westchester County police after an indictment against her was handed up, and police obtained an arrest warrant. She was ordered held without bail and is due back in court on July 2.

Authorities suspect that Spears poisoned Garnett at least twice, once before he experienced seizures that sent him to Nyack Hospital and again on January 19 at Nyack when his sodium level spiked. As Garnett lay dying in the hospital, a Chestnut Ridge neighbor reported that Spears called and told her to dispose of a bag Spears used to feed the boy through a tube.

The case may be one of the first involving Munchausen by proxy in the era of social media, as Spears was constantly documenting her son's medical crises on social media. Spears lived with Garnett in the Fellowship Community, an idyllic communal community in Chestnut Ridge, Rockland County, where she cared for the elderly and farmed, and the boy attended school.

Residents of the community have expressed shock and disbelief, asking how so many people could live around the story and not know what was happening. The investigation involved numerous detectives traveling up and down the East Coast, conducting multiple interviews, examining multiple documents, and following a tremendous amount of leads. Spears faces a maximum sentence of 25 years to life in prison if convicted.

The New York Times reporter James Risen is facing criticism for his Page One story about Afghanistan's mineral deposits, with some accusing it of being part of an orchestrated campaign to boost the American effort in Afghanistan. Risen dismissed these criticisms, stating that the story was based on the work of a Pentagon team led by Paul Brinkley, who is charged with rebuilding the Afghan economy. The story reported that the US has discovered nearly $1 trillion in untapped mineral deposits in Afghanistan, including lithium, copper, iron, and other minerals. The story has been criticized for its timing, coming as it did on the heels of a series of troubling reports about the stability of the Karzai government and one day before Gen. David Petraeus was scheduled to testify before Congress about the war. Risen defended the article against claims that Afghanistan's mineral wealth was largely a matter of public knowledge prior to his story, and explained that he based his report on the work of Brinkley's team, which used geological data from the Soviet era and USGS surveys conducted in 2006 to search for minerals on the ground. Risen also defended himself against criticisms from bloggers, stating that they should do their own reporting instead of sitting around in their pajamas. The story has been met with mixed reactions, with some praising Risen for his reporting and others questioning the timing and motivations behind the story.

President Donald Trump is spending his weekend at his Bedminster, New Jersey golf club, reviewing potential candidates for the Supreme Court vacancy left by Justice Anthony Kennedy's retirement. Trump has narrowed his list of candidates to about five, including two women, and plans to announce his pick on July 9. The candidates under consideration are Brett Kavanaugh, Amy Coney Barrett, Thomas Hardiman, Raymond Kethledge, and Amul Thapar. Trump has been consulting with White House Counsel Don McGahn regarding the candidates' rulings, judicial philosophies, and temperaments. No interviews with candidates have taken place yet, but Trump may interview one or two candidates over the weekend. The confirmation process is expected to be partisan, with Republicans having a majority in the Senate. Trump has stated that he will not ask candidates about the 1973 Roe v. Wade abortion-rights ruling, a decision that could potentially be overturned by the new court. The confirmation process could be challenging due to the political divide, with senators such as Susan Collins and Lisa Murkowski, who support abortion rights, holding critical votes.

In 1990, a schoolgirl named Zoe Lemon, now Zoe Averianov, tossed a message in a bottle into the North Sea during a family holiday. The bottle was discovered 23 years later in the Netherlands by Piet Lateur, who found it while walking his dog near Rotterdam. The letter contained Zoe's contact details and information about her hobbies and pets.

Over Christmas, Zoe received a reply from Piet and his wife, Jacqueline. The letter contained Zoe's original message and a response detailing how Piet found the bottle. Zoe, who now lives in Salford and works in a jewellery shop, was surprised and emotional upon receiving the letter. She has since been in contact with Piet via email and requested photographs of the location where the bottle was found.

Zoe's original letter, written when she was 10, detailed her love for ballet, playing the flute and piano, and her pets, a hamster named Sparkle and fish named Speckle. The discovery of the reply has been a surprising and emotional experience for Zoe, who had long since forgotten about the letter she tossed into the sea.

Jeb Bush, the former Governor of Florida, has announced that he will not be running for President in the 2012 race, putting an end to speculations about his potential candidacy. Bush is currently in Louisville to discuss education reform at the National Conference of State Legislatures, where he highlighted Florida's success in improving educational performance, particularly among Latino students.

During his appearance, Bush praised President Barack Obama's contribution to education policy while also supporting the local control of education, as advocated by Republican U.S. Senate candidate Rand Paul, whom he hosted a fundraiser for on Monday. Bush emphasized the importance of education in addressing social issues and stated that all children have the potential to learn.

The goal is to fix broken links on the internet and ensure that references to archived pages replace broken links, providing a historical record of the original content.

Three French workers are facing charges of theft after discovering a hidden treasure worth over €900,000 ($1.2 million) while working on a house in Normandy. The workers, aged 20, 33, and 40, found the loot, which included six gold bars and 600 gold coins, in jars and decided to steal it instead of informing the house owner. They sold the treasure to a local coin collector, but their crime was uncovered when one of the workers deposited high-value cheques. The workers confessed to their crime, and police seized several vehicles, motorcycles, and hundreds of thousands of euros as part of the investigation. The three workers and the coin collector will appear in court in Evreux, northwest of Paris, at an unspecified date. The house owner, who wishes to remain anonymous, jokingly told the workers to inform her if they found any treasure. The treasure, estimated to have been hidden during World War II, may have been buried on the property. The house owners have found it difficult to sleep since the police informed them about the discovery.

The paper published in Science on Thursday suggests that up to half of the water on Earth is older than the sun. This discovery was made by measuring the ratio of deuterium, or heavy hydrogen, to hydrogen in Earth's water. The findings indicate that some of Earth's water predates the sun, as heavy hydrogen levels on Earth are higher than they would have been in the protoplanetary disk that formed around the sun during its birth.

This research has significant implications for the search for life outside our solar system. If water can survive a star's birthing process, as it seems to have done in our case, it suggests that water might be a common ingredient in the formation of other planets.

Professor Tim Harries from the University of Exeter's Physics and Astronomy Department, one of the authors of the paper, stated that this finding indicates that the way our solar system was formed will not be unique, and that exoplanets will form in environments with abundant water. This raises the possibility that some exoplanets could have the right conditions for life to evolve.

Last spring, scientists announced that there could be up to 11 billion exoplanets, planets outside our solar system, that are at the right distance from their stars to have liquid water, and potentially life as well. This discovery further supports the idea that water may be a common ingredient in the formation of planets, increasing the likelihood of finding life beyond Earth.

In a remarkable tale that seems fit for a Hollywood movie, Jack Yufe and his identical twin brother Oskar Stohr, separated at birth in 1933, lived vastly different lives under contrasting circumstances. Jack was raised as a Jew in Trinidad, while Oskar grew up in Nazi Germany and joined the Hitler Youth.

Their first meeting at a German train station in 1954 was awkward, as they found themselves disliking each other due to their striking similarities rather than their differences. They shared numerous idiosyncrasies, such as wearing the same outfits, reading books from back to front, and even having the same nervous habits.

Despite their initial animosity, they eventually grew to care for each other deeply. Their complex relationship was a subject of fascination for researchers involved in the landmark Minnesota twin study, which aimed to identify the impact of environmental and genetic factors on psychological traits.

The study brought the brothers back together, and they discovered even more shared traits, such as a hot temper and competitive drive. However, they also had disagreements, particularly over political and religious issues.

Yufe passed away on Monday at a San Diego hospital, while Stohr died in 1997. Their unique relationship and the study's findings have contributed to a better understanding of the interplay between nature and nurture in shaping human behavior.

This summary highlights the extraordinary story of Jack Yufe and Oskar Stohr, two identical twins who lived vastly different lives but shared striking similarities, ultimately providing valuable insights into the complex interplay between nature and nurture.

Bobbi Kristina Brown, the 22-year-old daughter of Whitney Houston and Bobby Brown, passed away on July 26, 2015, after being in a coma for six months. She was found unresponsive in a bathtub at her Roswell, Georgia, home on January 31 and was placed in a medically induced coma to deal with swelling of the brain. In March, she was moved to a rehab facility near Atlanta, but her condition worsened on June 24, leading to her transfer to Peachtree Christian Hospice to live out the rest of her days peacefully.

Brown's family confirmed her death with a statement to the media, expressing their gratitude for the tremendous amount of love and support they received during these last few months. Numerous celebrities and friends of Brown took to Twitter to offer their condolences, including Monica, Taraji P. Henson, Reggie Bush, Jermaine Dupri, ErykahBadoula, and Sherri Shepherd.

Before the news of Bobbi Kristina's death, her father Bobby Brown spent his Sunday connecting with family members to share the news. Bobby traveled back to Atlanta from his home in California shortly after the birth of his new daughter Bodhi Jameson Rein, to continue his vigil by Bobbi Kristina's side.

An autopsy will be needed to evaluate what led to Bobbi Kristina's death, as the time that elapsed from when she was found unresponsive until her death will complicate the medical examiner's effort to reconstruct what happened. The medical examiner also mentioned that interpreting autopsy findings will be challenging, but it could be helpful to address questions about what caused her to become unresponsive.

Bobbi Kristina was the only child of Houston and singer Bobby Brown.

Sureshbhai Patel, a 57-year-old Indian man, was severely injured after an encounter with the Madison Police Department in Alabama. The incident occurred less than a week after Patel arrived in the United States to help his son and daughter-in-law care for their 17-month-old child.

Patel, who does not speak English, struggled to communicate with the police during the incident. In an attempt to search him, Patel was forced to the ground by an officer, resulting in injuries that left him partially paralyzed. He underwent surgery at Huntsville Hospital and faces a long recovery, with limited mobility in his limbs.

The family has hired a local attorney to sue the Madison Police Department. A GoFundMe campaign has been set up to help the family with their mounting medical bills, as Patel has no insurance. The family expects a long road to recovery.

Madison Police Chief Larry Muncey has recommended that Officer Eric Parker, who was involved in the incident, be fired for his use of force. Parker turned himself in to face assault charges and was released on a $1,000 bond. The FBI is conducting a civil rights inquiry to determine if further actions will be taken.

Attorney Hank Sherrod filed a lawsuit against the City of Madison and the Madison Police Department, arguing that excessive force was used and that there was no cause to stop Patel on a public sidewalk and search him. Sherrod has criticized the initial statement from the police suggesting that Patel had been looking into garages or was in any way responsible for the incident.

Members of the local Hindu community, who are known for their principle of non-violence, have shown their support for Patel. The family of Sureshbhai Patel and the GoFundMe campaign have received offers of help from as far away as California. As of Thursday afternoon, the GoFundMe campaign had raised over $13,000 towards its goal of $25,000.

The article, "The Problem With Saints: On the lifeless Jackie Robinson biopic 42. Plus, Danny Boyle's twisty Trance," by Wesley Morris, discusses two films released in 2013: 42, a biopic about Jackie Robinson, and Trance, a film by Danny Boyle.

Morris argues that when icons become saints, it is difficult to create a good movie that captures their naturalism, idiosyncrasy, and personality. In the case of 42, the film focuses on Robinson's debut with the Brooklyn Dodgers in 1947 and his encounters with racism, but the movie lacks depth and character development, with Robinson serving as a lesson in tolerance rather than triumph. The film also fails to imagine how it must have felt for Robinson to be subjected to relentless slurs.

Trance, on the other hand, is a high-order, film noir nonsense movie by Danny Boyle that takes him back to the thrillers he made at the start of his career. The film concerns an auction-house art heist that goes south when the job's inside man, an auctioneer named Simon, takes a shot to the head that erases his memory of where he put the Goya painting he helped steal. The movie features group hypnosis, sex, and multiple plot twists that reroute and rewire the movie.

The article also includes a personal anecdote about the author's encounter with Jackie Robinson when he was 9 years old. The author notes that Robinson made his country a better place by simply being better than the people who hated him.

In summary, the article discusses the challenges of making a good movie about icons and the lack of depth and character development in the biopic 42. It also praises Danny Boyle's film Trance as a high-order, film noir movie with multiple plot twists. The article also includes a personal anecdote about the author's encounter with Jackie Robinson.

The Nokia 8, HMD Global's first flagship smartphone under the Nokia brand, has been launched with a unique feature called 'bothie', a hybrid of selfie and normal photo. The phone is designed to compete with high-end devices like the iPhone 7 and Samsung's Galaxy S8, featuring a polished aluminum body, Carl Zeiss cameras, spatial audio, and a high-resolution 5.3-inch screen. The Nokia 8's 'bothie' function uses Dual Sight technology to shoot video or photos from both the rear and front-facing cameras simultaneously, which can be shared live on Facebook or YouTube.

The Nokia 8 has similar specifications to other top-end smartphones but lacks the super-slim bezel designs of the best devices from 2017. The phone has dual 13-megapixel cameras for the back, and spatial audio technology that was previously used in Nokia's high-end 360-degree camera.

Ben Wood, chief of research at CCS Insight, said that the Nokia 8 has innovative features like the dual-sight function on the camera and 360-degree audio recording but it's not yet clear whether these are game-changing features that will lure consumers away from established rivals such as Apple and Samsung.

The Nokia 8 will cost €599 (£546) and will go on sale in early September, placing it in the middle of the launch season for new smartphones from both Samsung and Apple. Wood said that aggressive pricing and marketing would be needed for the Nokia 8 to successfully compete with established market leaders.

Nokia dominated the mobile phone market for more than a decade from the late 1990s but was left trailing behind Apple and Samsung in the smartphone era following the launch of the iPhone in 2007. The Finnish company sold its loss-making mobile devices division to Microsoft in 2013 to focus on its telecoms network equipment business. Now, a group of former Nokia executives, backed by private equity, have formed a new company called HMD Global and bought back their former employer’s feature phone business from Microsoft, aiming to bring the Nokia handset brand back to its former glory with a range of new smartphones.

A feminist group at the University of Mary Washington has filed a complaint with the U.S. Department of Education, accusing the school of failing to act on online threats against its members, one of whom was killed last month. The victim, Grace Rebecca Mann, was a vocal member of the group and was murdered in April. Mann was harassed on the anonymous messaging app Yik Yak before her death, with more than 700 sexist, threatening messages being posted about Feminists United or its individual members. The group alleges that the university's administration did not take sufficient action to protect them from the harassment, despite repeated requests throughout the year. The university has denied the group's request to shut down access to Yik Yak on campus, citing First Amendment concerns. The complaint also alleges that Yik Yak has a responsibility in the matter, as the app has been used for cyberbullying and has not responded to the group's requests for help. The university has not yet responded directly to the complaint, but has said that it acted on all threats of violence or sexual assault on the social-media site and that student safety is its top priority. The case highlights the ongoing issue of online harassment and the challenges of regulating anonymous speech on social media platforms.

Weight Watchers International Inc., a leading dieting company, reported a loss in the holiday quarter and a decline in membership, citing increased competition from digital methods and fitness trackers. The company's shares dropped significantly, marking the largest decline since their market debut over 13 years ago.

Weight Watchers has faced challenges in keeping pace with the digital age, as consumers increasingly use apps and fitness trackers to manage their calorie intake and exercise. The company's subscriptions and revenue have been declining for eight consecutive periods.

In response, Weight Watchers plans to cut $100 million in costs this year and has announced a partnership with health-care company Humana Inc. to offer diet programs at discounted rates on certain health insurance plans. The company's CEO, Jim Chambers, acknowledged that the turnaround will take longer than anticipated.

Meanwhile, the market for fitness trackers is expected to triple by 2018, with about 57 million devices in use worldwide. Fitbit will remain the leading player for fitness tracking, but smartwatches, particularly Apple's Watch, are expected to gain popularity and become the most-worn wearable device by 2018.

Juniper Research predicts that there will be two types of fitness trackers: less expensive ones like the Xiaomi MiBand, which will compete mainly on price, and more complex devices like the Fitbit Surge, Microsoft Band, and Samsung Gear Fit, which will offer additional features beyond fitness.

Weight Watchers has embraced activity trackers, allowing subscribers to use FitBit, Jawbone, and the company's own ActiveLink gadget to track diets and exercise. However, the company is struggling to keep pace with the digital age and has not yet been able to effectively remake its image and offerings to appeal to a more digital consumer base.

Analysts believe that Weight Watchers' best bet is to focus on providing weight-loss programs for corporations and health plans, which have been seeking ways to keep employees healthy and insurance costs low. The company's decision not to integrate with Apple Health may harm its market share in the short term.

Mexico is deploying additional troops and federal police in the northeastern states of Tamaulipas and Nuevo Leon, aiming to reinforce government authority and curb drug cartel violence. The region has been a battleground for the Gulf and Zetas gangs since their split, resulting in intense violence, including regular roadblocks, assassinations, and attacks on civilians. The operation, called "Coordinated Operation Northeast," aims to prevent the cartels from regrouping after the loss of key leaders. The government has been criticized for its handling of the drug war, with 49% of Mexicans viewing the government's drug war as a failure, according to a recent opinion poll. The Mexican government has similar operations in other parts of the country, including Chihuahua state, where the border city of Ciudad Juarez is considered one of the most violent cities in the world. The deployment comes after the arrest of the new leader of the Beltran Leyva gang, Carlos Montemayor, marking a fresh blow against the remnants of the once-formidable gang. The in-fighting has stoked months of killings and beheadings across the states of Morelos and Guerrero, home to the resort city of Acapulco. The Mexican and Texas governments have expressed support for the buildup, with Texas Governor Rick Perry praising the increase in patrol presence along the border.

The 2017 Golden Globes were filled with laughter, drama, and political commentary. Goldie Hawn and Amy Schumer brought some good laughs to the event as they presented an award while joking about their new film, Snatched. Viola Davis delivered a heartfelt speech about Meryl Streep, this year's Cecil B. DeMille Award recipient. Jimmy Fallon poked fun at Mariah Carey's New Year's Eve performance drama, and Hugh Laurie made jokes alluding to President-elect Donald Trump. The musical La La Land was the big winner of the night, taking home seven awards, including Best Actor and Best Actress honors for its stars, Emma Stone and Ryan Gosling. Jimmy Fallon stayed true to his word that Donald Trump jokes would be aplenty at the Golden Globes, making several jabs at the soon-to-be President-elect throughout the night.

The Internet Archive is working on a project to archive web pages as they are created and preserve links to archived versions of pages that are changed or removed. The goal is to fix broken links on the web. Meanwhile, Dr. Prabhjot Singh, a Sikh American professor at Columbia University, was brutally attacked in a hate crime on a public street in New York City. The assailants taunted him with racist slurs and called him "Osama" and "terrorist." Dr. Singh, who wears a beard and a turban as part of his faith, was hospitalized with a fractured jaw and other injuries. The NYPD Hate Crime Task Force is investigating the incident.

Dr. Singh is a well-respected figure in the community, serving as the Director of Systems Management at the Earth Institute and an Assistant Professor at Columbia University's School of International and Public Affairs. He is also a resident physician at Mt. Sinai Hospital and has dedicated his life to improving the health of underserved communities.

This attack is part of a larger trend of hate crimes against Sikh Americans, who are often targeted due to their religious and cultural differences. A national study released by Stanford University researchers shows that more than 50 percent of Americans associate the Sikh turban with Osama bin Laden than with any other figure.

The incident has sparked calls for increased efforts to build bridges between different communities and combat hate and ignorance. Dr. Singh's friend Simran Jeet Singh, who is also a Sikh, emphasized the importance of tracking and counting anti-Sikh hate crimes. The attack on Dr. Singh is a reminder of the ongoing challenges faced by minority communities in America.

The article discusses the growing discontent among travelers due to the intrusive airport security measures implemented in the United States following the 9/11 attacks. The author argues that the Transportation Security Administration (TSA) has created a security theater that has not made air travel safer but has instead invaded travelers' privacy and caused unnecessary inconvenience.

The author uses the example of John Tyner, who refused a full-body pat-down by a TSA agent and warned him not to "touch my junk," as a symbol of the growing frustration among travelers. The author argues that the TSA's equal-risk assumption, which treats every passenger as a potential threat, is flawed and has led to unnecessary and invasive security measures.

The author proposes a risk-based screening system that would divide passengers into three categories: low, medium, and high-risk. Low-risk passengers, such as cockpit crews and frequent travelers who have undergone a rigorous background check, would be subject to minimal security checks. High-risk passengers, such as those on watch lists, would be subject to more extensive screening. Medium-risk passengers would undergo standard security checks.

The author concludes that the current security measures are not only ineffective but also a violation of travelers' privacy and dignity. The author calls for a shift to a risk-based screening system to make air travel safer and more convenient for everyone.

R&B legend Etta James, best known for her hit "At Last," is gravely ill, suffering from dementia and leukemia, according to court documents. Her husband Artis Mills seeks control of over $1 million of her funds for her health care, while her son Donto James wants a third party to oversee the funds to prevent family conflicts. James has not performed since 2010 and caused a stir in 2009 when she was not chosen to sing at President Obama's inauguration. The next hearing on the matter is scheduled for Friday. James, who has battled obesity and drug addiction, has a long list of hits from the 1960s, including "Tell Mama" and "All I Could Do Was Cry."

In the latest episode of "The Simpsons" titled "Fraudcast News," Lisa Simpson publishes a newspaper accusing power plant tycoon Montgomery Burns of being a hateful man. In response, Burns purchases every media outlet in Springfield, leading the townspeople to create their own newspaper. Burns is forced to acknowledge that controlling all media is difficult, except for those with immense power like Rupert Murdoch. The episode caused a Twitter sensation, with viewers commenting on the show's apparent dig at Murdoch, who is currently embroiled in a phone hacking scandal in the UK.

Rupert and James Murdoch have been summoned to appear before the British Parliament next week to answer questions about the actions of their newspapers in the phone hacking scandal. News International, News Corp.’s British newspaper arm, has stated they will cooperate. The summons is not binding on the Murdochs as they are not British citizens, but it will increase public pressure on the company.

In a related development, it has been revealed that five senior police investigators discovered that their own cellphone messages had been targeted by The News of the World during their initial criminal inquiry of phone hacking in 2006. This raises questions about whether senior investigators feared retaliation from the tabloid if they aggressively investigated.

The lead police investigator on the phone-hacking case, Andy Hayman, left the Metropolitan Police in 2007 after questions were raised in the media about his business expenses and relationship with a woman who worked for the Independent Police Complaints Commission. John Yates, the assistant commissioner who has become a lightning rod for the police’s handling of the phone-hacking case, had reportedly used frequent flier miles earned in the line of duty for personal vacations.

Members of Parliament will question Mr. Hayman, Mr. Yates, and several other senior police officials at a hearing to determine why the Metropolitan Police decided to limit the initial phone-hacking inquiry in 2006. They are also concerned about whether the investigators had a conflict of interest because they themselves were victims of the people they were investigating.

The episode of "The Simpsons" and the ongoing phone hacking scandal in the UK highlight the power and influence that media moguls can wield, and the potential for abuse when that power is not checked.

Fiat Chrysler Automobiles (FCA) has announced a recall of 1.4 million vehicles due to software security concerns, following a demonstration by hackers who took control of a Jeep driving at 70 mph. The vulnerability affects cars equipped with 8.4-inch touch displays, including models like the Dodge Viper, Ram pickups, Jeep Grand Cherokee, Dodge Durango, Chrysler 200, Chrysler 300, Dodge Charger, and Dodge Challenger.

The hackers, Charlie Miller and Chris Valasek, developed code that could control the vehicle's dashboard functions, steering, brakes, and transmission from a distant laptop. They plan to present their research at the Black Hat conference in Las Vegas next month. FCA has already applied network-level security measures and delivered patches over the air, with affected customers receiving USB devices for additional security upgrades. Despite the media demonstration, FCA is unaware of any related injuries, complaints, accidents, or warranty claims.

In response to the White House's announcement that the minimum wage for federal contract workers would increase to $10.10 an hour in 2015, apparel retailer Gap Inc. announced plans to raise the hourly pay for its U.S. employees to $9 in June 2014 and $10 in June 2015, affecting approximately 65,000 store employees. Gap's Chairman and CEO, Glenn Murphy, stated that the wage increase is not a political issue but a business decision expected to benefit the company.

Meanwhile, Wal-Mart Stores Inc., the largest private employer in the United States, initially expressed support for an increase in the federal minimum wage, as reported by Bloomberg. However, Wal-Mart spokeswoman Brooke Buchanan later clarified that Wal-Mart remains neutral on the issue and that the majority of its hourly associates already earn above the state and federal minimum wage.

President Barack Obama signed an executive order last week to raise the minimum wage for federal contract workers to $10.10 an hour starting January 1, 2015, and encouraged employers nationwide to increase wages for their workers. Wal-Mart is expected to report its fourth-quarter results on Thursday.

On August 31, 2017, a Salt Lake City nurse named Alex Wubbels was arrested after refusing to draw a blood sample from an unconscious patient without a warrant, consent, or the patient being under arrest. The incident occurred at University Hospital, where Wubbels works, and was requested by a Salt Lake City police detective. The detective had arrived seeking a blood sample from 43-year-old William Gray, who was involved in a fiery collision on July 26, 2017, in northern Utah.

Hours after the incident, Salt Lake City's mayor and police chief apologized for the officer's conduct and announced that a criminal investigation into the episode would be conducted by the Unified Police Department. The internal affairs investigation by Salt Lake City police into the officer, Detective Jeff Payne, is also ongoing, and both Payne and a second unnamed officer were placed on administrative leave.

The video footage of the arrest became public on Thursday during a news conference held by Wubbels' attorney, Karra Porter, who stated that no claim or lawsuit has been filed. In the footage, Wubbels explains that blood cannot be taken from an unconscious patient unless the patient is under arrest, unless there is a warrant allowing the draw, or unless the patient consents. Payne acknowledges in the footage that none of those requirements is in place, but he insists that he has the authority to obtain the draw.

Governor Gary Herbert tweeted that the arrest was "disturbing" and that the city's police should "rectify the situation." City offices, including the police department, were bombarded with social media backlash and phone calls as the video skipped around the country. Several city and state officials weighed in on Payne's conduct, including Sen. Todd Weiler, R-Woods Cross, who heads the Senate’s judiciary committee, who said he would "stand against any form of unnecessary police brutality or inappropriate behavior."

The updated policy, provided by the department, states that a blood draw requires consent by the subject, or a search warrant — noting that "implied consent" by the subject of the draw is no longer allowed. The updated policy also notes that "blood draws are subject to established search and seizure laws."

National nursing associations weighed in, too. "It is outrageous and unacceptable that a nurse should be treated in this way for following her professional duty to advocate on behalf of the patient as well as following the policies of her employer and the law," American Nurses Association President Pam Cipriano said in a statement. The babbler birds use two sounds, A and B, in different arrangements to convey specific meanings. For instance, a flight call (AB) has a different meaning than a feeding call (BAB). This demonstrates that the two calls are rearrangements of the same sounds.

The researchers believe that the birds rearrange sounds to code new meaning because it is quicker than evolving a new sound altogether. Their findings, published in the journal PLOS Biology, reveal a potential early step in the emergence of the elaborate language systems used by humans today.

This discovery could help in understanding how language evolved in humans. Co-researcher Dr Andy Russell, who has been studying babblers since 2004, expressed surprise at the findings, stating that he would be amazed if other animals couldn't do the same. Co-researcher Dr Simon Townsend from the University of Zurich added that this is the first time the capacity to generate new meaning from rearranging meaningless elements has been shown to exist outside of humans.

The authors report that in the chestnut-crowned babbler, the first sound element "B" is what seems to differentiate the meaning between flight and prompt vocalisations, akin to cat and at in English, where the c represents the meaning differentiating element, or phoneme. This simple form of phoneme structuring could help us understand how the ability to generate new meaning initially evolved in humans.
