A 12-year-old boy embarked on a solo drive across Australia, traveling approximately 1,300 kilometers from Kendall, New South Wales, to Broken Hill, an isolated mining city in the outback. The boy intended to complete the 4,000km journey to Perth, but was stopped by police on Saturday morning for driving with a hazardous vehicle. The grueling journey, which takes around 40 hours by car and involves driving through the arid Nullarbor Plain, raises questions about how the boy managed to travel such a distance without being noticed. The boy was arrested and taken to Broken Hill police station, and inquiries are continuing. The distance between Broken Hill and Perth is about 4,300 kilometers, or 2,700 miles, which is similar to the drive from New York to Los Angeles. The boy's journey is unusual and has sparked awe and questions among Australians, including how he paid for gas, who taught him to drive, and what compelled him to take on such an expedition. The police have not yet released further details about the incident.

A 2-year-old girl named Leasia Carter has tragically passed away in Baltimore after being left in a hot car for more than 16 hours. The incident occurred in the Belair-Edison neighborhood, and her father, Wilbert Carter, has been arrested and charged with second-degree murder and child abuse.

According to the police, Carter discovered his daughter unresponsive in the car around 5:30 p.m. on Monday on the 3400 block of Juneway. The girl was rushed to Johns Hopkins Children's Center, but she later succumbed to her injuries.

Investigators found that Carter had been drinking on Sunday night into early Monday morning and had little memory of the incident. He reportedly left his daughter in the car for 16 hours, most of which was during the day when the temperature neared 90 degrees. The girl suffered second-degree burns, and by the time she was taken from the car, she was already deceased.

Witnesses reported seeing Carter crying and saying that someone was dead when he discovered his daughter in the car. Neighbors also stated that Carter had sole legal custody of his daughter and had another child with him when he went looking for Leasia.

Authorities are urging people never to leave elderly people, pets, or children unattended or in vehicles, especially during the summer heat. This incident serves as a grim reminder of the dangers of heatstroke, which is among the leading causes of vehicle-related deaths among children under 14.

Research shows that more than half of the children who died from heatstroke in a car over a 17-year period had been forgotten by a caregiver. Seventeen percent died because a caregiver had intentionally left the child in the vehicle, and about 30 percent of the deaths were the result of a child playing in an unattended vehicle.

This tragic incident has sparked concern and awareness about the dangers of leaving children in hot cars, and authorities are urging everyone to take extra precautions to ensure the safety of children during the summer months.

Archaeologists in Burgas, Bulgaria, have discovered a lead vessel containing ashes from the alleged grave of John the Apostle, one of the Twelve Apostles of Jesus Christ. The reliquary, dated to the 6th century C.E., was found in an early Christian basilica that was part of an ancient and medieval fortress site. The vessel, less than an inch long and decorated with crosses, is considered one of the most important discoveries in the museum's history.

In addition to the relic, archaeologists also uncovered a 10th-century Bulgarian royal seal at the fortress site. The structures at the site include an Early Christian basilica from the 6th century A.D., a building complex from the 5th-6th century A.D., and a Roman villa from the 3rd century A.D.

Milen Nikolov, director of the Burgas Regional Museum of History, explained that early Christians would have believed the relic had healing properties. John the Apostle's grave in Turkey was also a pilgrimage site for early Christians seeking healing.

The Bulgarian archaeologists believe that the reliquary was likely donated to the basilica on Foros by a pilgrim who had visited John the Apostle's grave in Ephesus, Turkey. The reliquary is one of only 43 known lead tubes from this time period, and the images on it are identical to those on clay tube reliquaries produced in ancient Ephesus.

The discovery of the reliquary resembles another relic discovery from the same region, Bulgaria's Southern Black Sea coast, where archaeologists discovered a reliquary containing relics of St. John the Baptist in 2010. The relics of St. John the Baptist have received international interest, with Oxford University scholars confirming their authenticity in 2015.

The ancient and medieval fortress and port of Burgos (Poros) on Cape Foros was first excavated in 2008 and dates back to the Late Antiquity/Late Roman period. The site has been in use throughout this entire period by different states, including the Roman Empire, the Byzantine Empire, the Bulgarian Empire, and the Ottoman Empire. Some of the more interesting finds include a stone block with an Ancient Roman inscription in Greek mentioning the name of Roman Emperor Gordian III, a 2nd-century A.D. inscription carved into stone stating that "burgi" (fortifications) were built on the border of the Roman colony of Deultum, and a basilica.

The Foros peninsula was marked on Italian and Catalan maps from the 13th-17th century as an old fortress and port under the name Poro (strait) or Poros, which means that the fortress defended the waterway entry point of the nearby Lake Mandra which flows out into the Black Sea. The area of the Burgos (Poros) fortress and the Cape of Foros is also famous for being the site of a major battle during the Second Bulgarian Empire in 1304 A.D.

In 2006, during the construction of a shopping center in Tulln, Austria, archaeological excavations uncovered a unique find - a complete skeleton of a camel, which is rare and significant for Central Europe. The skeleton, found in a large refuse pit, belonged to a male individual of slender stature, exhibiting a few characteristic pathological changes, indicating it was not a beast of burden but a valuable riding animal.

The camel's remains were subjected to anatomical, morphometrical, and molecular genetic analyses, which revealed it was a hybrid of a dromedary and a Bactrian camel. The hybrid camel, known as a Tulu, was most likely around seven years old and castrated.

The find was dated to the late 17th century, based on artifacts such as ceramic plates and a coin from the time of Louis XIV. The camel's presence in Tulln during the Ottoman-Habsburg war suggests it may have been an exotic acquisition, possibly acquired through an exchange with the Ottoman army.

The discovery of the Tulu hybrid camel in Tulln provides valuable insights into the history of Austria during the 17th century and the use of camels by the Ottoman army. The study was published in the scientific journal PLOS ONE.

Gabino Zavala, a prominent Catholic bishop in the Archdiocese of Los Angeles, has resigned after it was revealed that he fathered two children. Zavala, who oversaw the church's San Gabriel region and was known for his advocacy for social and economic justice, submitted his resignation in December after informing the Vatican of the children. The Vatican accepted his resignation, but did not name a successor.

Zavala's fatherhood violates the canon law of celibacy for priests, and his resignation is likely to spark renewed debate over the ecclesiastical laws of celibacy. The earliest popes were married men, but in the fourth century, church officials concluded that men who were not celibate should be deprived of the honor of the clerical life.

Zavala, who is no longer in ministry but remains a priest and bishop, could not be reached for comment. The archdiocese has offered financial support to help pay for the children's college expenses.

Zavala was raised in Los Angeles and ordained in 1977. He had overseen the San Gabriel region since 1994, and was known for his work with California's Hispanic community. He served as the president of Pax Christi USA, an influential group that lobbies against war and violence, and was a member of the United States Conference of Catholic Bishops. He also advocated for an end to capital punishment, immigration reform, and a path to citizenship for illegal immigrants.

Archbishop Jose Gomez wrote a letter to worshippers announcing Zavala's resignation, describing the news as "sad and difficult." He said that Bishop Zavala had been living privately and not participating in ministry since resigning. The Pope has shown no sign of relaxing the Roman Catholic Church's rule on priestly celibacy, which has been in place since the 11th Century.

The 51st State Initiative, aimed at creating a new state called North Colorado, has been rejected in Weld County, the most populous of the counties considering secession. The movement, fueled by frustration with the state government's focus on urban areas, asked county commissioners to pursue secession. However, voters in six of the 11 rural counties have voted against the proposal. The initiative received strong support in five counties, with Kit Carson County, Phillips County, Sedgwick County, Cheyenne County, and Yuma County voting in favor. The proposal was intended as a straw poll, and if successful, would require a vote of the state electorate or legislature, and then the U.S. Congress. Despite the rejection, organizers of the 51st state movement plan to continue their efforts, backing a new initiative to model the State Senate after the United States Senate, where counties would be given equal representation, and supporting statewide candidates who understand and support rural issues. The movement's spokesman, Jeff Hare, stated that the initiative will have a lasting legacy, and that in the 2014 election cycle, candidates running for office must have good information about the urban vs. rural divide. The results of the vote in Moffat County, on the Western Slope, are still pending.

Tracy Rosner, a non-Spanish-speaking teacher at Coral Reef Elementary in Miami-Dade County, has filed a federal lawsuit against her employer, alleging employment discrimination. The lawsuit claims that Rosner was denied a job teaching an hour of Spanish per day due to her race (white) and the school's policy of requiring foreign language teachers to speak the language they teach.

Rosner's attorneys argue that the school's policy is discriminatory as it could have assigned someone else to teach the foreign language component while Rosner taught the rest of the curriculum. After being denied the job, Rosner claims that the school's principal retaliated by increasing her workload and asking her to teach all subjects instead of just reading and language arts.

The lawsuit further states that non-Spanish speakers are a minority population in Miami-Dade County, and seeking employment solely from Spanish speakers "disproportionately affects" Rosner and others like her. The school board has not yet responded to the lawsuit, and the case is currently pending in the Southern District of Florida.

Rosner did not respond to a message from New Times seeking comment. The lawsuit seeks damages for emotional pain, suffering, inconvenience, mental anguish, and loss of enjoyment of life.

The 40-piece Chicken McNugget is the most calorie-dense meal at McDonald's, with 1,880 calories, followed by the Big Breakfast with Hotcakes and a large biscuit at 1,310 calories. A 16-ounce McFlurry with M&M's and a Large Oreo Frappe each contain around half the recommended daily intake of calories. A plausible lunch order of a chicken sandwich, medium fries, and a McFlurry totals over 2,000 calories.

24/7 Wall St. analyzed the calorie content of approximately 500 McDonald's menu items, finding that most high-calorie options are larger sandwiches or large portion items. However, calories alone do not fully represent a food's nutritional value, as an item with fewer calories may have higher sodium content.

The Premium Grilled Chicken Bacon Clubhouse Sandwich, with 630 calories, is a typical meal in calorie count but has nearly the most sodium on the menu. McDonald's meals have more calories than home-cooked meals and food served at most non-fast food chains. While there is no direct link between McDonald's and adverse health outcomes, high concentrations of fast food restaurants are associated with obesity and other negative health outcomes.

In an unusual solution, Savell and her boyfriend allegedly armed themselves with a .22 caliber handgun and shot at the guests' feet from the doorway of the home. The 12-year-old jaguar named Salman, who was on a breeding loan from the Thiruvananthapuram Zoological Garden in Kerala, is being sent back to his original zoo due to his obesity. Salman has shown no interest in mating with the female jaguar, Kalpana, at the Delhi zoo, where he has been since October 2014. Despite efforts to reduce his weight through a strict diet and increased exercise, Salman continues to eat excessively and shows little interest in mating. The Delhi zoo officials have given up hope that Salman will ever be interested in mating, as jaguars have no breeding season and can mate at any time. Salman's weight is estimated to be over 100kg, which is considered too much for breeding. The zoo officials believe that Salman's excessive eating and laziness may be causing his lack of interest in mating. This is not the first time an Indian zoo animal's lack of mating interest has drawn criticism, as earlier this year experts at Alipore zoo in Kolkata said a white tiger named Vishal had spurned the advances of a tigress, despite being de-wormed and given libido-enhancing vitamins. Jaguars are native to the Americas and are listed as "near threatened" on the International Union for Conservation of Nature's red list.

Graham, a GOP presidential contender, expressed concern that the party could lose its moral authority and the Latino vote if they continue to embrace Trump's divisive comments. The article discusses the sale of a unique and viral online business, ShipYourEnemiesGlitter, which allowed customers to anonymously send glitter to their enemies for $9.99. The founder, Mathew Carpenter, a 22-year-old Australian, launched the site as a joke but was overwhelmed by the sudden influx of orders, totaling over $20,000 in sales in just four days.

Carpenter, who described the glitter as "the herpes of the craft world," decided to sell the site due to its popularity and the negative impact it had on his life. The site was sold on Flippa for $85,000, with the buyer being a legitimate individual who had previously spent $83,000 on the site.

The site gained fame due to its snarky tone and clever advertising, but Carpenter faced criticism for not capitalizing on the opportunity and selling the business prematurely. However, he argued that he launched the site as a joke and was not prepared for the attention it received.

Since Carpenter closed orders, several copycat sites have emerged, including Glitterbombs from the UK and Mat Won't But We Will from the US. The site's new owner will find themselves with more competition but will also have the opportunity to explore future opportunities, such as introducing other annoying products and allowing users to send customized notes for an additional charge.

O.J. Simpson, the former football star and actor, is set to appear before a Nevada judge on October 3rd for a parole hearing. If granted parole, Simpson could be released from prison as early as October 1st. Simpson's net worth is estimated to be $250,000, a significant decline from his days as a high-earning football player. He was earning $55,000 per month in 1992, with much of his income coming from Hertz, where he served as spokesperson for nearly 20 years. However, Simpson has faced financial difficulties since his infamous murder trial, including a default on his mortgage and a failure to pay the Brown and Goldman families the $33.5 million awarded to them in a civil suit.

Simpson's football career was nothing short of legendary. He won the Heisman Trophy while playing for the University of Southern California and was chosen by the Buffalo Bills as the first pick in the 1969 NFL draft. In 1973, he made history as the first NFL player to rush more than 2,000 yards in a season. Simpson retired from the NFL in 1979 and went on to act in nearly three dozen films and television shows from 1968 to 2008.

The murder trial of Simpson's ex-wife Nicole Brown Simpson and Ronald Goldman in 1995 was dubbed the "trial of the century." Regarded as a national obsession, the trial ran from January to October and was watched by 150 million viewers. Simpson was acquitted of the murders, but was found guilty in a subsequent civil suit and ordered to pay $33.5 million to the Brown and Goldman families.

Simpson is currently serving a prison sentence for crimes unrelated to the murder trial. He was convicted in 2008 for a September 2007 robbery, where he and five other men forced their way into a Las Vegas hotel room and robbed sports memorabilia collector Bruce Fromong at gunpoint. If paroled, Simpson will be able to live on his NFL pension, which is an estimated $25,000 per month.

In anticipation of Simpson's parole hearing, there has been much speculation about what he will do upon his release. The article from CNN discusses the aftermath of Hurricane Harvey, which hit Houston, Texas in August 2017, and the potential impact of climate change on the storm. The article highlights that while the storm itself was not directly caused by climate change, certain factors related to climate change, such as sea level rise and warmer ocean temperatures, made the storm more severe and increased the risk of flooding.

The article notes that sea level rise, caused in part by climate change, contributed to a higher storm surge, leading to more flooding and destruction. Additionally, the water in the Gulf of Mexico was warmer than normal, providing more fuel for the hurricane. The warmer air and water associated with climate change also mean that hurricanes can hold more water, leading to heavier rainfall and potentially more intense storms.

The article also discusses the role of climate change in the stalling of the storm, which led to prolonged and devastating flooding in Houston. Some scientists suggest that changes in the jet stream and weather patterns caused by melting sea ice in the Arctic may have contributed to the blocking fronts that caused Harvey to stall.

The article notes that while it is not yet possible to definitively determine the exact role of climate change in Hurricane Harvey, the storm serves as a warning of the type of extreme weather events that may become more common in the future due to climate change. The article emphasizes the need for action to address climate change and reduce greenhouse gas emissions in order to prevent future disasters.

The article also touches on the politicization of the storm by some media outlets, with Fox News criticizing CNN for discussing the potential impact of climate change on the storm. The article notes that while it is premature to definitively blame climate change for the storm, it is important to consider the role of climate change in extreme weather events and to take action to address the underlying causes.

Overall, the article from CNN discusses the potential impact of climate change on Hurricane Harvey and emphasizes the need for action to address climate change and prevent future disasters. The article also touches on the politicization of the storm by some media outlets and the importance of considering the role of climate change in extreme weather events.

The article discusses the discovery of a 2.7-million-year-old soil buried under the Greenland ice sheet, which was once a verdant tundra. The soil, found in 2013 and published in the journal Science, provides insights into the history of the ice sheet and its endurance through periods of global warming.

The soil was discovered by scientists from the University of Vermont, who were surprised to find that the landscape beneath the ice was preserved for over two miles. Paul Bierman, the lead study author, stated that the ice sheet has been frozen to its bed, acting as a refrigerator that preserved the antique landscape.

The researchers tested 17 ice samples from the lowest 40 feet of an ice core extracted from the glacier in 1993. From the sediment, they extracted a rare form of the element beryllium, which acts as a geological clock. The high concentrations of beryllium-10 found in the soil suggest that it had been stable and exposed at the surface for between 200,000 and one million years before being covered by ice.

The findings indicate that the Greenland ice sheet has endured previous periods of global warming, even during the warmest periods of history. This information is crucial as the stability of the Greenland ice sheet will significantly impact sea level rises resulting from man-made climate change.

The scientists are now searching for ancient landscapes in Antarctica, as the continent froze earlier than Greenland. The discovery of the ancient soil under the Greenland ice sheet helps unravel an important mystery surrounding climate change, as it provides insights into how big ice sheets melted and grew in response to changes in temperature.

On Friday, April 13, 2018, President Donald Trump announced that the United States, France, and Britain launched military strikes on Syria in response to a suspected chemical attack on civilians by Syrian President Bashar Assad's government on April 7. The strikes were aimed at punishing Assad and deterring him from using chemical weapons again. The U.S. military response included missile strikes launched from outside Syrian airspace.

Syrian air defenses responded to the attack, and Syrian television reported explosions over Damascus. President Trump did not provide details on the joint U.S.-British-French attack, but it was expected to include cruise missiles. Trump described the main aim as establishing a strong deterrent against chemical weapons use.

The decision to strike came after days of deliberations, and it was Trump's second order to attack Syria. In April 2017, he authorized a barrage of Tomahawk cruise missiles to hit a single Syrian airfield in retaliation for Assad's use of sarin gas against civilians.

He did not give details about what equipment is involved in the operation or what sites it is targeting.

President Trump reiterated his call to have other nations take on more of the burden in Syria and asked for increased engagement from countries including Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, and Egypt to ensure that Iran does not profit from the defeat of the Islamic State group. Trump also warned Russia and Iran about their association with Assad's government and called on Moscow to change course and join the West in seeking a more responsible regime in Damascus. Trump added that America does not seek an indefinite presence in Syria and looks forward to the day when they can bring their warriors home.

The UNICEF report, titled "Harnessing the Power of Data for Girls: Taking stock and looking ahead to 2030," reveals that girls between the ages of 5 and 14 worldwide spend 40% more time, or approximately 160 million additional hours daily, on unpaid household chores compared to boys their age. This disparity includes tasks such as cooking, cleaning, caring for family members, and collecting water and firewood.

The report highlights that the burden of domestic work begins early, with girls aged 5 to 9 spending 30% more time on chores than boys, and the disparity growing as girls reach adolescence, with 10 to 14-year-olds spending 50% more time.

Anju Malhotra, UNICEF's Principal Gender Advisor, stated that the overburden of unpaid household work starts in early childhood and intensifies as girls reach adolescence, causing them to miss out on important opportunities for learning, growth, and enjoying their childhood. This unequal distribution of labor among children also perpetuates gender stereotypes and the double burden on women and girls across generations.

The report also notes that girls' work is often less visible and undervalued, with adult responsibilities such as caring for family members being imposed on them. Time spent on chores limits a girl's time to play, socialize with friends, study, and be a child. In some countries, collecting firewood and water puts girls at risk of sexual violence.

The report found that girls between 10 and 14 years old in South Asia and the Middle East and North Africa spend nearly double the amount of time on household chores compared to boys. The countries where girls between 10 and 14 years old bear the most disproportionate burden of household chores compared to boys are Burkina Faso, Yemen, and Somalia.

Girls in Somalia spend the most amount of time on household chores, totaling 26 hours every week. The report also includes data on girl-related issues addressed by the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) such as violence, child marriage, female genital mutilation, and education.

UNICEF Chief of Data and Analytics Attila Hancioglu stated that quantifying the challenges girls face is the first critical step towards meeting the SDG on gender equality and breaking down barriers that confront the world's 1.1 billion girls. The report aims to drive economic growth, promote peace, and reduce poverty by achieving the SDGs that address these issues and empowering girls with the knowledge, skills, and resources they need to reach their full potential.

The study of the Last Universal Common Ancestor (LUCA), the ancestor of all life on Earth, has provided new insights into its lifestyle and environment. Researchers, led by William Martin, analyzed over 6 million genes from various prokaryotic genomes to identify genes likely inherited from LUCA. They found 355 gene families that are broadly distributed across modern organisms, suggesting that LUCA was an anaerobic, CO2-fixing, H2-dependent organism with a thermophilic nature. The genes also indicate that LUCA's biochemistry was rich in FeS clusters and radical reaction mechanisms, and it required specific cofactors such as flavins, S-adenosyl methionine, and molybdopterin.

The findings support the theory that LUCA inhabited a geochemically active environment rich in H2, CO2, and iron, which aligns with the hypothesis that life originated in extreme environments like deep-sea vents or volcanic areas. The study provides a more specific understanding of LUCA's genetic makeup, offering valuable insights into the origins of life on Earth. However, the debate about the exact environment where life first emerged continues, with some favoring more normal settings like Darwin's "warm little pond."

In a recent investigation, cyber intelligence firm iSight Partners discovered a five-year cyber espionage campaign by Russian hackers, dubbed "Sandworm Team," exploiting a bug in Microsoft Windows and other software. The hackers targeted NATO, the European Union, Ukraine, and companies in the energy and telecommunications sectors. The operation, still ongoing, used various methods to attack targets, with a focus on diplomatic, energy, and telecom issues, particularly related to the Ukraine crisis.

The hackers began exploiting a vulnerability in most versions of Windows only in August. Microsoft was informed about the bug, and an automatic update to affected versions of Windows was planned for release on Tuesday.

Researchers believe the hackers are Russian due to language clues in the software code and their choice of targets. The hackers are suspected to be engaged in espionage rather than cybercrime, as they targeted NATO, regional Ukrainian governments, and an academic working on Russian issues in the United States.

The malicious software used was highly sophisticated, using a previously unknown attack method to bypass most security protections. iSight alerted some victims of Sandworm Team but declined to elaborate. The firm plans to release a 16-page report on Sandworm Team to its clients on Tuesday.

This is the latest in a series of private sector security reports linking Moscow to sophisticated cyber espionage. In August, Russia's Kaspersky Lab revealed a campaign that attacked two spy agencies and hundreds of government and military targets across Europe and the Middle East.

With the release of the patch, Microsoft users are advised to update their systems promptly to avoid potential exploitation by other hackers. However, it is expected that some hackers may attempt to exploit the vulnerability before systems are updated.

Fox News host Laura Ingraham mocked Taylor Swift after the candidate Swift endorsed, Phil Bredesen, lost the Tennessee Senate race to Rep. Marsha Blackburn. Ingraham tweeted a reference to one of Swift's songs, "#hatersgonnahate #shakeitoff." Swift had publicly supported Bredesen, stating that she could not support Blackburn due to her political views. Blackburn's victory likely thwarts Democrats' chances of taking the Senate. This is a rare political stance for Swift, who had previously advocated for voting for women in office.

The Massachusetts court has approved the release of Mitt Romney's 1991 testimony related to the divorce of Staples Inc founder Thomas Stemberg. The testimony shows that Staples issued a new class of shares to help fund Stemberg's divorce, with Romney, a former Massachusetts Governor and current Republican presidential candidate, testifying that it was done as a favor. The "D" class of shares at issue could be converted to common stock, unlike earlier shares sold in previous fundraising rounds, which held greater voting rights. Thomas Stemberg, who spoke on Romney's behalf at the Republican National Convention, and his ex-wife Maureen Sullivan Stemberg have been subject to a gag order preventing them from discussing terms of their divorce. Gloria Allred, Sullivan Stemberg's attorney, sought the release of the transcripts and the lifting of the gag order. The court approved the release of the documents but declined to lift the gag order. The office-supplies retailer, in which Bain Capital, a private equity fund that Romney worked for before entering politics, was an early investor. The release of the documents and the ongoing court proceedings have sparked discussions about the accuracy of Romney's description of the value of Staples, with an independent filmmaker claiming that Romney inaccurately described the value of the company during his testimony. Romney's attorney has denied the allegations, stating that there is no new information in the released documents.

The Internet Archive is working on a project to archive web pages as they are created and archive the pages that they reference. This project aims to preserve links to the original versions of pages even if they are changed or removed from the web. The goal is to fix all broken links on the web. The Internet Archive is also supporting "No More 404" sites, which are websites that have implemented measures to ensure that broken links are redirected to the archived versions of the pages they reference.

Bob Dylan, a musician and songwriter, has recently been awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature. Some people have questioned whether Dylan's work can be considered literature, while others believe he deserves a special Nobel Prize for his contributions to music and culture. Dylan's songs are often seen as reflecting the concerns and issues of his time, and many of his lyrics have been interpreted as poetic and thought-provoking.

The admiration for Dylan's work is not limited to his music. In a commentary for CNN, poet and novelist Jay Parini writes that Dylan's songs have "filled our heads with language that both interprets and transforms the realities we confront." Parini goes on to say that Dylan's work is "deeply personal and yet universal, speaking to our deepest concerns as human beings."

The Internet Archive's project to archive web pages and fix broken links is an effort to preserve the web and ensure that information remains accessible. The goal is to create a permanent record of the web, ensuring that future generations can access and learn from the information and resources that are currently available online.

In addition to the Internet Archive's project, there are other organizations and initiatives working to preserve and archive digital content. For example, the Library of Congress has a program called the National Digital Information Infrastructure and Preservation Program (NDIIPP), which aims to ensure the long-term preservation of digital content. The NDIIPP works with a variety of partners, including libraries, archives, and museums, to identify and preserve at-risk digital content.

Overall, the Internet Archive's project to archive web pages and fix broken links is an important step towards preserving the web and ensuring that information remains accessible. The project is part of a larger movement to archive and preserve digital content, and it is an example of the efforts being made to ensure that the wealth of information and resources available online is preserved for future generations.

Ana-Alecia Ayala, a 32-year-old mother of a 3-year-old, passed away on Wednesday after a year-long battle with uterine sarcoma. Diagnosed in December 2015, the rare cancer spread to her ovaries and the lining of her stomach. Despite undergoing surgery to remove the majority of the tumor, a new one appeared on her spleen in July, requiring a more aggressive chemotherapy approach.

Ayala found solace and distraction in her dance partner, Danielle Andrus, whom she met through a fitness group in 2015. Andrus would visit Ayala during her chemotherapy sessions, bringing magazines, arts and crafts to keep her entertained. The duo shared a dance video on social media in November 2016, dancing to the song "Juju On That Beat," which quickly gained popularity, garnering about 25,000 views in the first 19 hours.

Ayala's spirit remained positive throughout her battle, encouraging others not to view cancer as a death sentence and to make the most of difficult situations. She also encouraged loved ones of cancer patients to step out of their comfort zones, be silly, and have a good time, believing that laughter is the best medicine.

Ayala's GoFundMe page is still active for those who wish to donate. Her story serves as an inspiration to many, demonstrating the power of resilience, positivity, and the healing power of dance during challenging times.

In a tragic turn of events, a Georgia couple, Elrey "Bud" Runion and his wife, June E. Runion, were found dead after going missing during a road trip to buy a car. The bodies were discovered on Monday, and both victims were shot in the head. The man initially charged with false statements in the case, Ronnie Adrian "Jay" Towns, is now facing charges of murder and armed robbery.

The couple had posted an ad on Craigslist on January 19, seeking a 1966 Mustang convertible. They set out for a small farming community in southern Georgia to meet a potential seller, but never returned. Police believe Towns, who was the person who answered the ad, lured the couple for cash, as the car he claimed to have didn't exist.

Towns was arrested on Monday and is currently being held in the Dodge County jail in Eastman. He is charged with malice murder, armed robbery, making a false statement, and criminal attempt to commit theft by deception. The sheriff stated that a cellphone used to make the last known contact with the Runions had been traced to Towns.

The Runions' daughters reported them missing last week after they didn't show up to babysit their grandchildren. They told WSB-TV their parents left home with their cellphones and chargers, but no one had heard from them since 3:30 p.m. Thursday.

Investigators found the couple's SUV in a lake a few miles outside McRae, a city of 5,700 about 80 miles southeast of Macon. Searches discovered two bodies - a man and a woman - nearby, now identified as the couple.

Towns comes from a well-established family in the small community, and his family reacted with shock and anger at Tuesday's developments. Towns' father, also named Ronnie, expressed his belief that someone else might be involved and that evidence could have been planted.

The Runions were known for their charitable works throughout the South, from storm-damaged Alabama towns and impoverished pockets of West Virginia to housing projects in the Atlanta suburbs. They had a charity called "Bud's Bicycles," where they donated food, household items, school supplies, coats, blankets, and even Thanksgiving turkeys.

The community is a peaceful one despite difficult economic times, with Telfair County being among the poorest counties in the country. The sheriff stated that when they see violent crimes, they pull out all the stops to investigate.

The investigation is ongoing, and authorities have a "mountain of evidence" to go through. The family of the accused has expressed their sympathy for the victims' family and their belief in Towns' innocence.

U.S. Representative Elizabeth Esty, a Democrat from Connecticut, is facing criticism for her handling of sexual harassment and violence allegations against her former chief of staff, Tony Baker. The allegations include physical harm, death threats, and sexual harassment, which were reported to Esty in 2016. Despite learning about the allegations, Esty did not suspend or fire Baker until three months later.

Esty has apologized for her actions and regrets not moving forward with an internal investigation into the allegations more quickly. She also regrets providing any assistance to Baker as he sought a new job. Baker has since left his position as the Ohio state director of Sandy Hook Promise, an anti-gun violence advocacy group.

In response to the controversy, Esty has asked the House Ethics Committee to investigate whether she did anything wrong in her handling of the firing of her former chief of staff. She has also announced that she will not seek re-election at the end of her current term.

The controversy has sparked calls for Esty to resign from some state politicians, including fellow Democrats. However, Esty has dismissed these calls and has said that she will work to improve workplace protections during her final months in office.

Karen Jarmoc, executive director of the coalition against domestic violence, has said that Esty reached out to her last weekend and asked to meet at Jarmoc's office. Jarmoc said that Esty's priority was looking out for the survivor of the harassment, and that she seemed to have a genuine desire to make things better for employees in the workplace.

The Hartford Courant has called on Esty to resign, saying that her answers so far have been disappointing and that "time is up for Elizabeth Esty." The state Republican Party chairman has also called on Esty to step down, accusing her of being "complicit in covering up assault."

Esty has received mild criticism from fellow Democratic members of Connecticut's congressional delegation, with nearly all noting that Esty acknowledged she had made mistakes. U.S. Senator Richard Blumenthal has said that Esty needs to talk to her constituents about whether she should resign.

In a groundbreaking study, scientists suggest that black rats may not have been the primary cause of the repeated outbreaks of the bubonic plague, also known as the Black Death, across Europe during the 14th century. Instead, they believe that the plague may have originated from gerbils in Asia, which thrive under specific weather conditions.

The study, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, challenges the long-held belief that black rats, which carry the plague-causing bacteria, were responsible for allowing the plague to establish in Europe. The researchers compared tree-ring records from Europe with 7,711 historical plague outbreaks to determine if the weather conditions would have been optimal for a rat-driven outbreak. However, they found no relationship between the appearance of plague and the weather.

Instead, the team believes that specific weather conditions in Asia may have caused an increase in the population of giant gerbils, which are also carriers of the plague-causing bacteria. When the weather is favorable, these gerbils thrive, increasing the chance of plague transmission. The fleas that also do well in these conditions would then jump to domestic animals or to humans, potentially causing epidemics in Europe.

The researchers believe that the plague was most likely brought to Europe along the Silk Road, as trade between the East and West was at a peak during this time. They plan to analyze plague bacteria DNA taken from ancient skeletons across Europe to support their theory. If the genetic material shows a large amount of variation, it would suggest that the different waves of the plague coming from Asia would show more differences than a strain that emerged from a rat reservoir.

The plague died out in Europe after the 19th century, but outbreaks continue to this day in other parts of the world. In another study, published in the American Journal of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene, researchers in the US found that the expansion of agriculture in East Africa is placing the region at an increased risk of the plague. As cropland increases, rodent populations are also rising, creating "the perfect storm for plague transmission."

The plague is caused by the bacteria Yersinia pestis, which is usually found in small mammals and their fleas. People infected with Y. pestis often develop symptoms after an incubation period of one to seven days, with two main clinical forms of plague infection: bubonic and pneumonic. Bubonic plague is the most common form and is characterized by painful swollen lymph nodes or 'buboes.' Plague can be a very severe disease in people, with a case-fatality ratio of 30% to 60% for the bubonic type, and is always fatal for the pneumonic kind when left untreated. Antibiotic treatment is effective against plague bacteria, so early diagnosis and early treatment can save lives.

From 2010 to 2015, there were 3248 cases reported worldwide, including 584 deaths. Currently, the three most endemic countries are the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Madagascar, and Peru. Plague is easily treated with antibiotics and the use of standard precautions to prevent acquiring infection.

The study published in the Journal of Gerontology: Social Sciences suggests that being emotionally closer to one's mother among siblings may increase the risk of depression in adulthood. Researchers from Purdue University, led by Jill Suitor, analyzed data from 725 adult children from 309 families as part of the Within-Family Differences Study. The study found that adult children who felt they were emotionally closer to their mother than their siblings and those who believed they were the sibling their mother was most disappointed in reported the highest levels of depressive symptoms.

The researchers looked at four measures of favoritism and disfavoritism: emotional closeness, conflict, pride, and disappointment. They found that sibling rivalry due to favoritism may induce depressive symptoms. The study also found that black adult children were particularly distressed when they were the children in whom mothers were most disappointed.

The authors suggest that the association between psychological well-being and both favoritism and disfavoritism can be accounted for by processes involving social comparison rather than equity for both black and white adult children in midlife. The team plans to investigate whether similar results arise from studying adult children's perceptions of favoritism and disfavoritism from fathers and predicting favoritism between mothers and adult children.

Previous studies conducted by the research team have shown that mothers really do have a favorite child. The Within-Family Differences Study, which began in 2001, aimed to achieve a greater understanding of relations in aging families. The researchers collected data from 725 adult children (average age of 49) within 309 families in which mothers were between the ages of 65 and 75 when the project began. The study occurred in two phases seven years apart.

The study results indicate no differences based on gender, with both sons and daughters feeling the weight of their mother's opinion, whether good or bad, equally. The constant appraisal and judgments among siblings were found to be the root cause of unhappiness. Those adults who were perceived to be closer to the mother experienced more tension from their siblings, while also feeling greater responsibility for taking care of their aging mothers. Meanwhile, those who argued with their mothers or felt they'd disappointed her also suffered.

Google's UK Marketing Director, Dan Cobley, discussed Apple's decision to remove Google Maps from iOS 6 with Bloomberg TV. Cobley suggested that users could still access Google Maps by downloading them or visiting the Google Maps website, but it's unclear what he meant by "downloading." Google Earth, available in the App Store, is not a suitable replacement for Google Maps. Google has expressed a desire to make Google Maps accessible to all users, regardless of device or operating system. In response to a question about a new Google Maps app for iOS and its potential features, Google stated that they aim to provide the most comprehensive, accurate, and user-friendly maps worldwide. Users missing Google Maps can explore alternative third-party apps.

Additionally, the article mentions a Tumblr called "theamazingios6maps.tumblr.com" that has been created to mock the issues with iOS 6 Maps. Other topics include a multi-tool ax, a giveaway for a free iPhone 6S, a discounted 6-month subscription for Pandora One, and various tech-related items like USB cables and a dwarf-themed tool.

Florida prisoners are planning a statewide strike on Martin Luther King Jr. Day to protest against what they consider modern-day slavery, including being used as unpaid labor and being paid nothing for their work. The strike is in response to inmates being forced to work in sweltering conditions after Hurricane Irma, as well as longstanding grievances such as price gouging on food and other necessities, and the lack of parole for those with long-term sentences. The prisoners have dubbed their protest Operation Push, after civil rights leader Jesse Jackson's campaign to improve economic conditions for African Americans. Florida has the third-largest prison system in the country, with allegations of abuse of inmates and violence rife. In 2017, officers were cleared of blame for the death of a mentally ill patient left in a scalding shower for two hours as punishment, and investigations uncovered large numbers of rapes, beatings, and cover-ups in the state's non-air-conditioned jails. The prisoners are demanding a reasonable wage for their labor, an end to price gouging, and the return of parole as an incentive for those with long-term sentences. Solidarity rallies are being held outside several prisons and department of corrections offices on Monday. Tensions are running high in the Florida prison system, with all facilities placed on lockdown last August in response to unspecific threats of rioting. The Florida Department of Corrections has not addressed detailed questions about the planned response to Monday's protests.

In this extensive article, details emerge about Robin Williams' last known photos before his suicide, which occurred on Monday morning, three days after he was seen at an art gallery reception near his Bay Area home. The actor, who seemed in good spirits at the event, was there with his wife and spoke to the artist's students. The pictures were taken at 5:45 PM on Saturday.

Robin Williams' spokeswoman, Mara Buxbaum, addressed the speculation about financial problems potentially contributing to his suicide, stating that Williams had no such issues. She added that the actor's comments about financial stability in previous interviews were made in jest.

Williams' net worth was estimated to be $50 million, with two properties, a Napa Valley mansion and a waterfront home in Tiburon, California, valued at approximately $29.9 million and $6 million, respectively. The properties have mortgages totaling $7.25 million as of 2011, leaving real estate with an estimated equity of around $25 million, subject to the sale of the Napa Valley mansion.

Buxbaum also clarified that Williams took the role in "The Crazy Ones" for creative reasons, not due to financial necessity. The show, which was canceled after one season, earned Williams an estimated $165,000 per episode.

Williams' personal life was marked by battles with depression, which he often joked about. In the days leading up to his death, he was reportedly sleeping up to 18 hours a day and had no appetite, indicating a dark depression.

The individual who discovered Williams' body was his longtime confidante and friend, Rebecca Erwin Spencer. Williams was found in his bedroom with a belt secured around his neck, with no note. Toxicology reports are expected back in five to six weeks.

The article concludes with a reminder for anyone struggling with thoughts of suicide to immediately seek help. The National Suicide Prevention Lifeline can be reached at 1-800-273-TALK (8255).

The mass shootings of eight members of the Rhoden family in Pike County, Ohio, have prompted an ongoing investigation. Ohio Attorney General Mike DeWine and Pike County Sheriff Charles Reader confirmed that the victims were targeted and that the investigation is lengthy. The killings occurred at four rural locations, and all eight autopsies have been completed. A marijuana grow operation was found at three of the crime scene locations, and while it is unclear if the drugs were connected to the shooting, they will be a significant part of the investigation.

Facebook threats against one of the Rhoden family members are also being examined by investigators. Sheriff Reader warned the surviving members of the Rhoden family to be armed and take precautions. The investigation has involved more than 100 personnel, and authorities have refused to discuss many details, including any evidence or the search for the assailant or assailants.

A memorial fund has been established to benefit the family at Fifth Third Bank, and anyone with information on this case is asked to call 1-855-BCI-OHIO (224-6446) or the Pike County Sheriff's Office at 740-947-2111. The community has been on edge since the killings, with many people scared to come out due to fear of the assailant or assailants still being at large. The victims were identified as 40-year-old Christopher Rhoden Sr., his 16-year-old son, Christopher Rhoden Jr., 44-year-old Kenneth Rhoden, 38-year-old Gary Rhoden, 37-year-old Dana Rhoden, 20-year-old Clarence "Frankie" Rhoden, 20-year-old Hannah Gilley, and 19-year-old Hanna Rhoden. The investigation is ongoing.

In this news summary, actor Ron Livingston, known for his roles in Sex and the City and Office Space, has issued a statement in defense of his sister Jennifer Livingston, a news anchor in La Crosse, Wisconsin. Jennifer Livingston went viral for her emotional response to an insulting letter from Kenneth Krause, who criticized her weight and suggested she was not a suitable role model for the community's young people.

In response to the viral video of Livingston's response, Krause issued a statement, showing no remorse for the emotional impact his words had on Jennifer. He instead expressed hope that Jennifer would take advantage of her position to influence the health and psychological well-being of the community by transforming herself over the next year.

On Thursday, Soledad O'Brien discussed Jennifer Livingston's story on Starting Point, asking if she had to ask her bosses if she could address the email writer on air. Livingston explained that there had been some discussion prior to her response, and her news director supported her decision, particularly after the positive response she received.

While Livingston chose not to name the man who wrote the email, O'Brien did, revealing him to be Kenneth Krause. In his statement, Krause offered to give Jennifer advice and support should she want it. This news summary highlights the ongoing controversy surrounding Jennifer Livingston's response to a critical email and the subsequent reactions from both the sender and supporters.

In this summary, two news articles are presented, both involving undocumented immigrants facing threats of deportation or detention in Texas.

The first story revolves around a Guatemalan migrant mother and her son who have been residing at an Austin, Texas church for over a year due to their fear of being deported. They have no intentions of leaving the church.

The second story focuses on a 10-year-old girl named Rosamaria Hernandez, who has cerebral palsy, and her mother, Felipa Delacruz. Rosamaria underwent gall bladder surgery at Driscoll Children’s Hospital in Corpus Christi, Texas, but is now under threat of deportation or detention after crossing a U.S. Customs and Border Protection checkpoint to get to the hospital.

Delacruz's niece, Aurora Cantu, accompanied Rosamaria past the checkpoint, but federal agents escorted them to Corpus Christi from there. Federal immigration agents are reportedly waiting outside Rosamaria's hospital room, and Delacruz is in Laredo.

Rosamaria was a recipient of the Texas Health and Human Services program that helps children with special health-care needs. She was first treated at Driscoll Children's Specialty Center in Laredo, where it was revealed to a nurse that the child is undocumented.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) policy discourages enforcement actions at sensitive locations, including hospitals, schools, places of worship, public ceremonies or demonstrations. However, federal immigration agents detained Rosamaria just out of emergency surgery on Wednesday, taking her to a detention center in San Antonio.

This incident highlights the newfound relentlessness in immigration arrests and detentions under the current administration, as schools, churches, courthouses, and hospitals—once “safe zones” from immigrant detention—are now open to arrests.

The story is still developing, and updates can be found on Caller.com.

The article recounts a meeting between the author, a former White House intern, and Ken Starr, the independent prosecutor who investigated her in 1998 during the Bill Clinton impeachment scandal. The meeting took place on Christmas Eve 2017, and the author was initially hesitant to approach Starr due to the traumatic experiences she had endured during the investigation. However, years of personal-counseling work had helped her to embrace opportunities to break out of old patterns of retreat or denial, and she decided to introduce herself to Starr.

The meeting was awkward and uncomfortable, with Starr asking several times if the author was "doing OK." The author felt the need to remind Starr of the ways in which his investigation had affected not only her but also her family. Starr did not apologize, instead saying that the situation was "unfortunate."

The author reflects on the impact of the scandal on her life and on the nation as a whole, describing it as a low-grade collective trauma that has had an epigenetic quality, lingering in the collective consciousness for the past 20 years. She discusses the ways in which the Internet and social media have changed since the scandal, allowing for the democratization of support networks and the amplification of women's voices through the #MeToo movement.

The author acknowledges that her experiences may not fit neatly into the #MeToo movement, as they did not involve sexual assault, but she is still moved by the courage of the women who have spoken up and confronted entrenched beliefs and institutions. She is still working on processing and healing from the trauma of the investigation, but she is hopeful that the movement will lead to a systemic transformation.

The article ends with a quote from Haruki Murakami, "When you come out of the storm you won't be the same person who walked in. That's what this storm's all about." The author reflects on who she was then and who she is now, and the ways in which the scandal has shaped her and the nation's collective consciousness.

In August 2012, archaeologists discovered the remains of a 14-year-old girl at Jamestown, Virginia, who they believe was a victim of cannibalism during the "starving time" winter of 1609-10. The girl, named "Jane" by researchers, had marks of butchery on her skull, including shallow chops and a split cranium, indicating her flesh, tongue, and brains were removed. The Jamestown colony, founded in 1607, was besieged by Powhatan Indians, and the settlers had been joined by new colonists late that summer, among them women and children, whose main supply ship had disappeared in a storm, leaving them without food. Only 60 of 300 people survived the winter. The butchery marks on Jane provide stronger evidence for cannibalism at Jamestown, though not all colonial-era historians agreed that it took place. An exhibition devoted to the discovery will open this Friday at the Historic Jamestowne site, and her reconstructed face will be displayed at the Smithsonian museum.

Robin Williams, the acclaimed actor and comedian, was found dead at his home in Tiburon, California, on August 11, 2014, at the age of 63. The Marin County coroner's office confirmed that his death was ruled a suicide by asphyxia and hanging. Toxicology reports revealed that antidepressants, caffeine, and levodopa, a drug used to treat Parkinson's disease, were found in his system.

Williams had been struggling with severe depression for years and had recently been diagnosed with Parkinson's disease. He also had a "recent increase in paranoia," according to a medical history recorded at the scene. The night before his death, he had given away several wristwatches to someone because he was worried about their safekeeping.

When Williams returned home, he seemed "OK" to his wife, Susan, who told investigators that he handed her magazines and seemed in a good mood. However, he was later found dead in an empty bedroom belonging to his stepson, who was away visiting his father. The actor was dressed in a long black T-shirt and belted black jeans, hanging by a nylon belt in a closet door frame.

Personal items, including an iPad and two different kinds of antidepressants, were found on a chair near his body. An engraved pocketknife with a dried red substance, later confirmed as Williams' blood, was also found. No efforts were made to revive him, and his death was declared at 12:02 p.m.

Despite a long and well-documented history of depression, Williams' wife and assistant said he never expressed suicidal thoughts or behavior. His pill dispenser had been refilled the day before, but the medications remained undisturbed in their appointed daily slots. The investigator asked Susan if Robin had ever mentioned suicide "as a solution to a significant health issue." After searching through Williams' iPad, which was near his body, Investigator D. Harris found only web browsers open to information about medications. A sweep of his iPhone revealed no texts or messages that indicated he was suicidal.

The Marin Sheriff's Office drew criticism for releasing candid details about Williams' death but said the disclosure was necessary under the California Public Records Act. The final autopsy report was originally scheduled to be released on September 30 but had been delayed twice.

The article discusses the impact of World War II's German battleship Tirpitz on a forest in Norway, as revealed by tree rings. Winston Churchill, the British wartime leader, nicknamed the Tirpitz "the beast" due to its significant size and the Allies' repeated attempts to sink it.

In 2016, researchers from Johannes Gutenberg University in Mainz, Germany, discovered that the trees in a forest near Kafjord, Norway, had unusually narrow or nearly absent rings in 1945. Initially, they suspected insect infestation, but no known insects in northern Scandinavia could have caused such damage in the mid-20th century.

After speaking with a local scientist, they connected the tree damage to the Tirpitz. The ship had retreated to northern Norway's watery labyrinth to evade detection, and Allied aerial scouts eventually found it. The Germans countered with a plan to produce artificial fog to hide the ship and surrounding area from aerial view.

The artificial fog, likely made from chlorosulphuric acid, caused significant damage to the trees. The smoke drifted into the forests surrounding the fjord and left a distinctive "fingerprint" on the trees. The study of tree rings, or dendrochronology, was used to trace the damage, revealing that more than 60% of the trees near where the ship once lay showed virtually no growth in 1945.

The artificial fog likely caused arboreal fatalities as well, as gaps in the forest suggest. As far as four kilometers away, more than half the trees were severely affected, taking eight years on average to fully recover. Pine trees, which keep their needles for up to seven years, were hit hardest.

The Tirpitz never saw much action and was eventually sunk by a squadron of British Lancaster bombers in late 1944. The relentless campaign to find and sink the Tirpitz left its mark on the landscape, with the effects still evident in the forests of northern Norway more than 70 years later. Researcher Claudia Hartl believes similar cases may be found elsewhere, suggesting potential for further exploration in the field of "warfare dendrochronology."

The EgyptAir flight 804, carrying 66 passengers, crashed into the Mediterranean Sea on May 19, 2016, while flying from Paris to Cairo. French air accident investigation agency reported smoke was detected in the plane moments before it disappeared from radar. The cause of the crash remains unclear, with no hard evidence of terrorism or equipment failure emerging so far. The aircraft's black boxes, which hold crucial data, are being searched for in the deep waters of the eastern Mediterranean.

Investigators are looking into the possibility of a bomb blast or a struggle in the cockpit due to the plane's erratic flight. No militant group has claimed responsibility for the crash, unlike the downing of a Russian jet in Egypt's Sinai Peninsula in October 2015. The passenger manifest for Flight 804 contained no names on terrorism watch lists, according to three European security officials.

French aviation investigators are questioning all ground crew members at Charles de Gaulle Airport who had a direct or indirect link to the plane before it took off. In June 2016, a tragic incident occurred at Walt Disney World in Florida, where a 2-year-old boy was killed by an alligator while wading in the Seven Seas Lagoon. This event followed warnings issued two months prior to firefighters at Reedy Creek, the tax district for Walt Disney World Resort, to stop feeding alligators at one of the resort's fire stations.

Emails obtained through a public-records request revealed that firefighters were feeding at least one of two alligators near Fire Station 3, located less than half a mile from Seven Seas Lagoon. One gator was a baby, and the other was estimated to be between 4 and 5 feet long.

The emails indicated that the feedings were causing concern among employees, with communications captain Claude Rogers warning that staff needed to stop giving food to the animals. However, it is unclear if any action was taken to remove the alligators following these warnings.

Feeding alligators is illegal in Florida as it causes the animals to lose their natural fear of humans, making them more aggressive. The alligator that attacked the boy was estimated to be between 4 and 7 feet, larger than the alligators being fed by the firefighters.

After the tragedy, Disney installed warning signs about the presence of alligators and snakes and removed crocodilian characters from its attractions. The family of the victim sought privacy, and it is not clear if the feeding of alligators at the fire station is connected to the June attack.

This incident highlights the dangers of feeding wild animals, particularly alligators, which can become aggressive when they lose their fear of humans. It also underscores the importance of following laws and regulations regarding wildlife interactions to ensure the safety of both humans and animals.

On Friday night, a 19-year-old man named Allen Ivanov allegedly shot and killed three people at a party in Mukilteo, a Seattle suburb, using an AR-15 rifle. However, instead of using the rifle for its intended purpose, Ivanov brought it to the party that his ex-girlfriend, A.B., was attending.

From the master bedroom balcony, he fired at two more people in the driveway, and climbed to the roof, discovering that he had emptied his rifle.

Ivanov, who is being held without bail at the Snohomish County Jail, was charged with two counts of first-degree murder and one count of first-degree aggravated murder. It is not yet clear if he has a lawyer.

According to the affidavit, Ivanov told detectives that he viewed the AR-15 as a "symbol of power." He had broken up with A.B. two months prior but decided he wanted her back. After seeing photos of A.B. on Snapchat with other young men, he became angry and decided to commit the shooting.

The victims of the shooting were all recent graduates of Kamiak High School. A vigil was held for A.B. at the University of Washington's Bothell campus, where she and Ivanov were students. She was remembered as a "bright light" who was considering a career in medicine.

The mass shooting has shocked the tight-knit group of friends who attended Mukilteo's Kamiak High School. Sultan Akbar, who had classes with Ivanov and the victims, attended court to express support for the victims' families. He described Ivanov as having an explosive temper and once threatening to get Akbar kicked out of school after Akbar reported to a teacher that Ivanov had copied his work.

Ivanov's parents retained Seattle defense attorneys Tim Leary and Zach Wagnild over the weekend. Leary expressed concern that Ivanov was able to buy an assault-style rifle but was too young to buy a six-pack of beer. He also highlighted the police contention that Ivanov read the weapon's instruction manual just before the shooting, which he said "speaks volumes to his youth and inexperience and highlights the lethality of the weapon involved."

The police report also states that someone from Kentucky told officers that Ivanov had sent them text messages about committing a mass shooting. Ivanov's attorneys told KOMO News that Ivanov's family is grief-stricken and that he is "very quiet and having some trouble right now." Prosecutors have until Wednesday to file formal charges, and Ivanov's formal arraignment has not yet been scheduled.

On February 4, 2004, Mark Zuckerberg launched thefacebook.com, a social networking site exclusively for college students, from his Harvard dorm room. Initially, Facebook faced competition from established platforms like Friendster and MySpace. However, its focus on college students, clean layout, and lack of immediate monetization strategies made it an instant hit.

By December 2004, the site had 1 million users, and it didn't even have a photo-upload feature yet. Over the years, Facebook added numerous features, some of which, like News Feed and the Like button, significantly impacted the internet. Others, like Facebook Gifts, were less successful.

On the occasion of Facebook's 10th anniversary, the company released a timeline of significant events in its history. This timeline omits less successful ventures such as Facebook Gifts, Beacon, and its experiment with democracy.

On the eve of the anniversary, Facebook unveiled a product called "A Look Back," which allows users to create a personal movie or slideshow of their favorite moments on Facebook. The company also launched a new iPhone app, Paper, on the App Store.

Mark Zuckerberg, in a statement, expressed gratitude for the journey so far and expressed optimism about Facebook's future. He stated that Facebook has the opportunity and responsibility to connect everyone and continue serving the community.

In 2006, Zuckerberg launched Facebook from his Harvard dorm room. The site combined elements of a standard House facebook with extensive profile features. Over 650 students had registered to use the site within a week of its launch, and Zuckerberg anticipated 900 students would join by the next morning.

Director of Residential Computing Kevin S. Davis stated that an official Harvard facebook was in the works, but the creation of Zuckerberg's site raised concerns about privacy and the compilation of directory information without authorization.

Zuckerberg's site allowed people with Harvard email addresses to upload their pictures and personal and academic information. It also allowed users to search for people according to their interests and create an online network of friends.

The extensive search capabilities were restricted by a myriad of privacy options for members who did not want everyone to be able to look up their information. Zuckerberg hoped the privacy options would help restore his reputation following student outrage over facemash.com, a website he created in the fall semester.

Today, as Facebook celebrates its first 10 years, users will receive a notification for a video summary of their life on Facebook, known as "Look Back." Each user's video contains 15 or so of their most-liked photos, statuses, and life events set to a catchy tune. The videos are a reminder that for many, Facebook has become a normal way to document daily lives.

The film "Detroit," directed by Kathryn Bigelow, is a harrowing portrayal of the 1967 Algiers Motel incident in Detroit, where three unarmed black men were killed by police during the city's riots. The film is set against the backdrop of the larger story of the Detroit riots, which left 43 people dead, nearly 1,200 injured, and 7,200 arrested. The film explores the systemic oppression and mistreatment of black people in the United States, and the resulting anger and frustration that led to the riots.

The film is written by Mark Boal, who previously collaborated with Bigelow on "Zero Dark Thirty" and "The Hurt Locker." The film is less of a character study and more of a situational one, focusing on the events leading up to and during the Algiers Motel incident. The film features a large cast of characters, including rising R&B singer Larry Reed, private security guard Melvin Dismukes, a Vietnam vet named Greene, and two white visitors from Ohio.

The film is visceral and brutal, with little to no reprieve for the audience. It opens with a history lesson about the movement of poor southern black people to white-dominated northern cities, and the resulting powder keg of inequities that exploded in Detroit and across America. The film depicts the Algiers Motel incident as a cascading series of bad choices, evil intentions, and escalating violence.

The film has been criticized for its lack of character development and nuance, as well as its historical inaccuracies. Some have accused the film of demonizing all authority figures, while others have praised it for its powerful depiction of the events and its message about the ongoing struggle for racial justice in America.

Overall, "Detroit" is a powerful and disturbing film that offers a stark portrayal of the systemic oppression and mistreatment of black people in the United States. It is not an easy watch, but it is an important one.

The study titled "Axillary Dissection vs No Axillary Dissection in Women With Invasive Breast Cancer and Sentinel Node Metastasis" is a randomized clinical trial that aimed to determine the effects of complete axillary lymph node dissection (ALND) on survival of patients with sentinel lymph node (SLN) metastasis of breast cancer. The trial was conducted by the American College of Surgeons Oncology Group Z0011 trial, involving 115 sites and enrolling patients from May 1999 to December 2004.

The trial included women with clinical T1-T2 invasive breast cancer, no palpable adenopathy, and 1 to 2 SLNs containing metastases identified by frozen section, touch preparation, or hematoxylin-eosin staining on permanent section. All patients underwent lumpectomy and tangential whole-breast irradiation. Those with SLN metastases identified by SLND were randomized to undergo ALND or no further axillary treatment. Those randomized to ALND underwent dissection of 10 or more nodes. Systemic therapy was at the discretion of the treating physician.

At a median follow-up of 6.3 years, 5-year overall survival was 91.8% with ALND and 92.5% with SLND alone; 5-year disease-free survival was 82.2% with ALND and 83.9% with SLND alone. The hazard ratio for treatment-related overall survival was 0.79, indicating that SLND alone compared with ALND did not result in inferior survival.

The study concluded that among patients with limited SLN metastatic breast cancer treated with breast conservation and systemic therapy, the use of SLND alone compared with ALND did not result in inferior survival. This finding challenges the long-standing practice of removing cancerous lymph nodes from the armpit in breast cancer patients, as it has been shown to cause complications like infection and lymphedema without improving survival or changing the treatment plan. The study suggests that taking out just one or a few nodes should be enough for these patients.

In a recent court ruling, a Pennsylvania judge has determined that two men who were texting a driver at the time of a fatal motor vehicle accident could potentially be held liable as defendants in the case. This decision follows a 2013 appellate ruling in New Jersey that recognized the same cause of action against third parties in motor vehicle accident litigation, but the New Jersey ruling did not apply in the case at hand because the remote texter did not know the recipient of the messages was driving at the time.

The Pennsylvania ruling sets a high bar for plaintiffs to prevail in suits against third parties, as it requires proof that the third party knew the recipient was driving and that the texts were likely to be read behind the wheel. This decision could open up a new avenue for litigation against remote texters in motor vehicle accident cases, potentially requiring them to appear, retain counsel, and participate in discovery to establish a lack of knowledge.

The New York Personal Injury Attorney Law Blog provides a copy of the Gallatin ruling, in which Pennsylvania Common Pleas Judge John Hodge points to both the New Jersey appellate decision and Section 876 of the Restatement (Second) of Torts, which provides for liability when one person acts in concert with another. Under Pennsylvania law, texting while driving is illegal.

Attorney Skippy Weinstein, who represented the plaintiffs in the distracted driving case that won the appellate ruling in New Jersey, has reported receiving calls from lawyers around the country after the decision was publicized and knows of new filings in his home state since then that assert text-related claims against remote third parties.

This development could have significant implications for remote texters in motor vehicle accident cases, potentially expanding the liability of distracted driving accidents beyond the driver. Legal experts have suggested that putting people on notice that engaging in texting activities with a driver who they know is actually driving a vehicle could potentially lead to some form of liability if there is an injury, which could help reduce texting-related accidents. However, proving that a third-party texter was aware the driver was texting and would view the text while on the road could be difficult to prove.

The Ebola crisis in West Africa is escalating, with over 670 deaths reported so far, making it the deadliest outbreak in history. The outbreak has crippled parts of Liberia, Sierra Leone, and Guinea, prompting heads of state to cancel travel plans to address the situation. The World Health Organization has recorded the highest death toll from an Ebola outbreak, and the numbers are increasing.

Residents in affected villages have accused international medical workers of bringing the disease into the country, and some have barricaded their towns or blocked access to Ebola victims. A nurse with Doctors Without Borders stated that the most challenging aspect of helping people is that they are often not welcome in the communities due to fear and denial about Ebola.

Several humanitarian organizations have pulled out of the affected countries, including Samaritan's Purse and the Peace Corps, which have recalled all non-essential personnel. The United States is considering raising the travel alert to discourage non-essential travel to the affected countries. Liberia's president has urged residents to avoid public amusement and entertainment areas and to take extra measures announced by the Ministry of Health to keep themselves safe.

The virus spreads through the transmission of bodily fluids, and those most at risk are loved ones of those infected and health care workers tending to the ill. The outbreak has taxed the capacity of local health clinics and doctors, prompting concern for those who remain in the country. The Peace Corps has evacuated its volunteers from Liberia, Sierra Leone, and Guinea, and two U.S.-based missionary groups have ordered the evacuation of their non-essential personnel from Liberia after a doctor and a missionary both contracted Ebola.

Officials from Charlotte, Desoto, Sarasota, Palm Beach, Broward, and Miami Dade counties have children attending the camp.
