Greece is facing a deep financial crisis, as the country will not pay a 1.6 billion euro loan installment to the International Monetary Fund (IMF) due on Tuesday, June 30. This decision comes after talks between Greece and its creditors broke down over the weekend, leading to the imposition of capital controls on Greek banks. The IMF has warned that Greece will be in default as of July 1 if it fails to pay the money, though it may classify Greece as "in arrears".

The missed payment could potentially lead to Greece exiting the eurozone if the European Central Bank (ECB) cuts off emergency funding that Greek banks rely on. However, the ECB is expected to maintain the lifeline at least for this week. The Greek government's decision to call a referendum on bailout terms presented by creditors on July 5 has further complicated the situation.

European leaders have urged Greeks to vote "yes" in the referendum, warning that a "no" vote could lead to Greece's exit from the euro. If Greece defaults, it would be the first time the country is cut loose from international rescue loans since it joined the bailout program in 2010. The outcome of the referendum and its impact on Greece's future in the eurozone remains uncertain.

In a new video released by ISIS, suspected fighters threaten to carry out attacks in France, Italy, the United States, and other countries. The video features two fighters threatening to blow up the White House, launch attacks on Paris, and conquer Rome. The Vatican's St. Peter's Square was recently featured on the cover of ISIS's online magazine.

In response to the video and magazine, Italy has deployed 1,000 members of the army to beef up security around the country. The U.S. Embassy in Rome has urged Americans visiting Italy to remain vigilant and aware of their surroundings, warning that St. Peter's Basilica in Rome, as well as Milan's Duomo and La Scala, could be terrorist targets. The Embassy also warns that "general" venues such as houses of worship, restaurants, theaters, and hotels in Rome and Milan could be targeted.

Wednesday, ISIS released a video warning of an impending attack on New York City, featuring Times Square and purporting to show an explosive device being put together and a bomber zipping his jacket over a suicide belt. The New York City Police Department said it was aware of the video and was deploying additional members of its new anti-terrorism squad out of an abundance of caution.

Mayor Bill de Blasio and Police Commissioner Bill Bratton vowed that New York City would not live in fear of threats from ISIS. "The people of New York City will not be intimidated," de Blasio said, standing in the middle of Times Square, one of the locations featured in the ISIS propaganda video. "We understand it is the goal of terrorists to intimidate and disrupt our democratic society. We will not submit to their wishes."

Officials insisted that there had been no specific threat against New York City, but cops remained on high alert. ISIS has claimed responsibility for the Paris attacks that killed 129 people and injured hundreds more. The terror group has also released a video threatening Washington, D.C. in the past.

ISIS first drew international attention for taking over swaths of Iraq and Syria, leaving a trail of violence and destruction in its wake. Its efforts to bring terror to the global stage seem to be growing.

Title: Kurt Cobain: Montage of Heck

Kurt Cobain: Montage of Heck is a riveting and intimate documentary directed by Brett Morgen, offering a comprehensive and fresh perspective on the life of the late Nirvana frontman. The film, which premiered on May 4, 2015, and received an A rating, delves into Cobain's life from his early years to his tragic death at the age of 27.

The documentary begins with home movies of a young Cobain, showcasing his innocent and bright personality. It then explores his struggles with depression, his rise to fame with Nirvana, and his tumultuous relationship with Courtney Love. Interviews with Love, bandmate Krist Novoselic, and Cobain's first girlfriend provide additional insights into his life.

One of the most challenging scenes to watch is a home movie where Cobain seems to nod off on drugs while Love cuts their daughter's hair. This scene, along with others, demonstrates Morgen's commitment to presenting the real Kurt Cobain, warts and all, rather than perpetuating the myth.

Frances Bean Cobain, who was just 20 months old when her father died, found the film allowed her to understand her father in an unfiltered way, discovering that he truly loved her.

Montage of Heck is a two-hour-plus film that is both an artful mosaic and a hammering barrage, featuring various montages of visuals and sounds. It offers a highly constructed narrative, stopping short of Cobain's suicide, which is recounted in a one-sentence title card. The film presents Cobain as relentlessly self-aware and self-critical, while also advancing a theory involving insecurity and shame.

The documentary's reliance on Cobain's personal material and its sparse use of interview subjects create a sense of mystery and intrigue. Despite the limited number of interview subjects, the film provides a captivating exploration of Cobain's life, music, and art.

In a recent study published in the Archives of Gynecology and Obstetrics, it was found that women who consume apples regularly may experience improved sexual function. The research was conducted on 731 sexually active Italian women aged 18 to 43, with no history or complaints of sexual disorders. The women were divided into two groups: those who ate one to two apples daily (Group A) and those who ate none (Group B). The participants filled out the Female Sexual Function Index (FSFI), which includes questions about desire, arousal, lubrication, orgasm, satisfaction, and pain.

Group A scored higher on the FSFI, indicating increased lubrication and overall sexual function. The researchers suggest that apples may improve sexual function due to their polyphenols and antioxidants, which can stimulate blood flow to the genitalia and vagina, aiding arousal. Apples also contain phloridzin, a phytoestrogen structurally similar to estradiol, a female sex hormone, and play a significant role in vaginal lubrication and female sexuality.

However, the study has limitations, such as a small sample size and difficulty separating correlation from causation. Despite these limitations, the researchers find the results "intriguing." They speculate that the sexual health benefits might come more from apple peels, which have high concentrations of phenolic compounds, than from the apples themselves. Future studies may focus on the role of apple peels in female sexuality.

The study adds to the growing body of evidence suggesting a positive correlation between phytoestrogens, polyphenols, antioxidants, and women's sexual health. While more research is needed, the findings suggest that eating apples could potentially improve sexual function for some women.

In this article, it is reported that freelance journalist Natasha Exelby was temporarily removed from her on-air role at ABC24 after a blooper during a live news shift went viral. Exelby was caught off guard and looked startled when she realized the cameras had returned to her after a prerecorded package had finished. The incident sparked waves of support for the "mortified" news professional, with many viewers and fellow journalists sharing their own embarrassing mistakes on social media. The ABC has denied that Exelby has been banned or sacked, stating that live television is a demanding art and slip-ups will happen. The broadcaster also confirmed that Exelby will continue working various shifts she has been rostered for, subject to normal performance management. The ABC director of news, Gaven Morris, has assured Exelby that the broadcaster wants her to continue working for them. The incident comes after the ABC was widely criticized for failing to vet the audience of its panel program "Q&A" and allowing one-time terror suspect Zaky Mallah to join the live TV debate.

Former New York Governor George Pataki has suspended his bid for the Republican presidential nomination, citing insufficient resources and a mismatch between his moderate politics and the party's rightward shift. Pataki announced his decision in a two-minute video message on NBC affiliates in Iowa, New Hampshire, and South Carolina, securing free airtime after Donald Trump hosted the network's "Saturday Night Live."

Pataki, who served as governor from 1995 to 2006, highlighted the need for a president who can confront and defeat radical Islam, shrink the size and power of Washington, and unite the nation. He expressed confidence that the right candidate could be elected, but acknowledged that his moment had passed.

Throughout his campaign, Pataki struggled to gain traction, rarely polling above 1% nationally and 2% in New Hampshire, the key moderate-leaning state he visited frequently. He never made it to the main debate stage and failed to secure significant funding, raising just $153,513.89 in the third quarter, leaving him with $13,570.55 in cash on hand at the end of September.

Pataki's departure leaves 12 candidates in the Republican field, making him the fourth current or former governor to exit the race, following Rick Perry, Scott Walker, and Bobby Jindal. His campaign, which focused heavily on New Hampshire, was overshadowed by better-known politicians like Sen. Marco Rubio (Fla.) and New Jersey Gov. Chris Christie, who are also targeting moderate voters.

The Senate Intelligence Committee has recommended Gina Haspel as the next CIA director, with a 10-5 vote. Haspel, Trump's pick, is expected to become the first woman to lead the agency. She currently has the support of the majority of Republicans and at least six Democrats, ensuring her confirmation. The committee's chairman, Richard Burr, praised Haspel's qualifications and ethical conduct. However, some Democrats, including Ron Wyden and John McCain, have expressed concerns about Haspel's nomination due to her past involvement in controversial CIA programs, particularly waterboarding and other "stress" techniques. The vote could take place this week or slip into next week.

In a significant turn of events, the Seattle City Council voted to repeal a tax on large businesses, including Amazon and Starbucks, that was intended to combat a growing homelessness crisis. The tax, which was passed unanimously last month, aimed to raise approximately $48 million annually for affordable housing and homeless services. However, the repeal came after a campaign led by businesses, including Amazon, raised over $285,000 to put the tax to a referendum vote this fall.

The vote exposed deep divisions within the city, with supporters of the tax facing off against those advocating for its repeal at a raucous city council meeting. The meeting was marked by chanting, jeering, and booing, with both sides expressing strong opinions. Supporters of the tax held signs reading "Tax Amazon" while opponents displayed signs stating "No tax on jobs."

The repeal was seen as a victory for Amazon, the city's largest employer with over 45,000 workers. Amazon's CEO, Jeff Bezos, was named the world's richest man in March. The company paid $25,000 toward the referendum effort, and Amazon, Starbucks, and investment company Vulcan each contributed to the campaign.

The tax was proposed as a progressive revenue source aimed at addressing one of the nation's highest homelessness numbers. However, businesses and residents demanded more accountability in how Seattle funds homelessness and housing, and many worried that companies like Amazon would leave the city if the tax was implemented.

The repeal of the tax has raised questions about its potential impact on other cities considering similar taxes on big tech companies to help mitigate the effects of growth. The City Council in Mountain View, California, where Google is based, is set to vote on a similar measure on June 26.

Mountain View Mayor Lenny Siegel said that Seattle's retreat hasn't changed his support for the tax, and he believes that Google and other companies have a better relationship with the city than Seattle does. However, he also acknowledged that Google hasn't taken a position on the proposal and that no significant opposition has materialized from the company.

In Seattle, the tax would have charged companies about $275 per full-time worker each year. It targeted nearly 600 businesses making at least $20 million in gross revenue and was set to take effect next year. The city government said it would only affect about 3% of the city's employers.

Critics of the tax argued that the city's homeless problem was growing despite large amounts of spending by the city already. Seattle spent $68 million on fighting homelessness in 2017, and the tax would have raised roughly $48 million annually. However, a one-night count in January found more than 12,000 homeless people in the Seattle and surrounding region, a 4% increase from the previous year.

Many supporters called the repeal a betrayal and said the tax was a step toward building badly needed affordable housing. They booed council members, imploring them to keep it and fight a coalition of businesses trying to get a referendum overturning the tax on the November ballot.

The repeal of the tax has sparked debate about the role of big businesses in local politics and the balance between supporting economic growth and addressing social issues like homelessness. It remains to be seen how this development will impact future efforts to combat homelessness in Seattle and other cities.

David Knowles, a 77-year-old retired nurse and St John Ambulance volunteer, had a heart attack during a CPR training class he was teaching at his local church in Exeter. As he started feeling unwell, he instructed his trainees on what to do before passing out. The trainees, thinking he was role-playing, quickly called 999 and performed CPR until paramedics arrived. Knowles went into cardiac arrest but survived due to their quick actions. He was later hospitalized for five weeks and suffered another heart attack and a pulmonary embolism. Despite the severe condition, he is now making excellent progress and is mentally alert, able to walk unaided, and continuing to recover at home. His trainees' quick response saved his life, and he is now helping St. John Ambulance celebrate its 140th anniversary.

Antony Britton, a British escapologist, narrowly escaped death during a failed attempt to escape from a six-foot grave, a stunt inspired by Harry Houdini. The incident occurred at the Escape for Life event in Slaithwaite Spa, West Yorkshire. Britton was handcuffed and buried under six feet of soil, but after nearly nine minutes, he failed to break free and had to be rescued unconscious. He was later found to have a cracked rib and minor injuries.

Britton revealed that he almost died during the escape, with the soil crushing him as he struggled to breathe. He was saved by his well-drilled crew who managed to locate him and dig him out. Britton expressed his disappointment at being just two feet from the surface when he had to be rescued.

This Buried Alive escape bid was the highlight of an event that also featured magicians, bands, and circus acts. The event was organized to raise funds for Leukaemia & Lymphoma Research, which will be changing its name to Bloodwise this month.

Britton is only the third person in 100 years to attempt the Buried Alive escape. Previous attempts by Harry Houdini in 1915 and British escapologist Alan Alan in 1949 also ended with them having to be dug out by their crews. Britton said he would think carefully before attempting the challenge again, despite nearly reaching the surface.

The dramatic scenes unfolded at Britton's fourth Escape for Life event, which was initially scheduled for March but was postponed due to unexpected snowfall. The event was also in doubt due to rain earlier in the week, but Britton was given the all-clear after consulting experts. However, Britton has decided not to attempt the Buried Alive escape bid again and will take some time to recuperate.

A Chinese tourist, identified as Mr. L, was mistakenly processed as a refugee in Germany after attempting to report a stolen wallet. The incident occurred when Mr. L, who spoke only Mandarin, visited the city of Heidelberg, believing it was a police station. Instead, he signed an asylum application, leading to his two-week detention in a refugee shelter in Duelmen.

German authorities discovered their mistake after turning to a local Chinese restaurant for interpretation assistance. Christoph Schluetermann, head of a Red Cross refugee center in Duelmen, stated that the man was trapped in the country's bureaucratic system due to the language barrier.

The man, from Beijing, had been robbed upon arriving in Stuttgart and then traveled to Karlsruhe, where he signed an asylum application at the Patrick Henry Village processing camp. He was then taken to the refugee shelter in Duelmen.

Over the past year, more than one million refugees have arrived in Germany, primarily fleeing war and poverty in Syria, Iraq, Afghanistan, and other countries. However, the number of Chinese asylum seekers has been minimal, according to Schluetermann.

The man was fingerprinted and given a medical exam, but his well-dressed appearance and unusual behavior drew attention. He repeatedly tried to communicate his situation to staff but was unable to do so due to the language barrier.

With the help of a translation app and a translator from a Chinese restaurant, it was determined that the man wished to travel to France and Italy, not seek asylum. After 12 days, German officials were able to rectify the situation and send him on his way.

Schluetermann described the man as being happy to leave but not upset, stating, "What would you expect if you had come to Europe as a tourist and spent 12 days sleeping on a camping bed in a refugee center?" The incident highlights the challenges faced by both refugees and non-German speakers navigating the country's complex bureaucracy.

Nazi Hunter Eli Rosenbaum, Director of the Justice Department's special investigation unit, has dedicated his career to tracking down and deporting Nazi war criminals who moved to the U.S. after World War II. Rosenbaum, who grew up in a Jewish family that did not discuss the Holocaust, was inspired to pursue this work after watching a reenactment of the Auschwitz trial as a child. He finds the most memorable part of his work to be questioning the suspects, which he describes as "surreal."

Rosenbaum and his team face time pressures as the number of remaining Nazi war criminals decreases each year. In the early part of his career, he felt guilty taking a day off, as he knew the time was running out for many of the victims. However, he eventually returned to the Justice Department to continue his work.

One of the most notable cases Rosenbaum has worked on is that of Jakiw Palij, a 92-year-old man living in a modest apartment in Queens, New York. Palij, who worked at the Trawniki concentration camp in Poland, is the only remaining active case from the Nazi era being pursued by the Justice Department. Despite multiple deportation attempts, Palij is unlikely to be deported due to the refusal of three European countries to take him.

Palij has denied any wrongdoing and claims he was coerced into working for the Nazis. However, Rabbi Marvin Hier, dean and founder of the Simon Wiesenthal Center, dismisses Palij's denials, stating that only those who were eager and brutal were chosen to work at the camps. Justice Department officials say that since 1979, their investigations have resulted in 73 former Nazis being stripped of U.S. citizenship and 59 of them being deported.

Rosenbaum is resolute that pursuing every last Nazi is the least owed to the victims of the Holocaust. He believes that what Palij did prevented other people from reaching old age, as he served at the Trawniki SS training and base camp, where he trained on live Jews and everyone who was held there was eventually massacred. The U.S. Holocaust Memorial Museum has helped support Rosenbaum's work by providing access to documents it has collected on war crimes.

David Welch, a 54-year-old retired Pepsi Co. representative, spent his last days trapped in a ravine in the Utah desert after driving away from his home in Manhattan, Kansas, without any explanation in September 2013. For nearly seven weeks, his family searched for him, unaware that he was injured and writing love letters to them from his mangled car. His car veered off the road and plummeted into the ravine, and he was found dead by a hitchhiker on October 18. The exact cause of his death and the contents of his love letters remain private. Welch was an avid outdoorsman who loved landscaping, scuba diving, and snowskiing. The circumstances surrounding his disappearance and death remain a mystery.

On April 8, 2017, a suspected terror attack occurred in central Stockholm, Sweden, when a hijacked beer truck plowed into a crowd of shoppers outside the popular Ahlens department store. Four people were killed, and 15 were injured. The suspect, a 39-year-old native of Uzbekistan, was previously known to Swedish authorities as a marginal figure with no clear links to extremist groups.

Swedish Prime Minister Stefan Lofven declared Monday a national day of mourning, with a minute of silence at noon. The prime minister urged citizens to "get through this" and strolled through the streets of Stockholm to chat with residents. The police chief said they were confident they had detained the man who carried out the attack, but they could not exclude the possibility that others were involved.

Police found something in the truck that "could be a bomb or an incendiary object," but they are still investigating it. The suspect has not yet spoken to authorities, and it is not clear whether he was a legal resident of Sweden. Anders Thornberg, head of the Swedish Security Service, said security services were working with other nations' security agencies to investigate the attack.

Many in Sweden were shocked by the attack, questioning whether Swedish society had failed in some way. Sweden's health service said 10 people were still hospitalized for wounds from the attack, and four of them were seriously injured. Visiting the attack site, Sweden's Crown Princess Victoria laid roses on the ground and wiped away a tear.

The crash was near the site of a December 2010 attack in which Taimour Abdulwahab, a Swedish citizen who lived in Britain, detonated a suicide bomb, killing himself and injuring two others. He had rigged a car with explosives but the car bomb never went off. In February, U.S. President Donald Trump suggested that Sweden could be the next European country to suffer the kind of extremist attacks that have devastated France, Belgium, and Germany.

Sweden has taken in nearly 200,000 refugees and migrants in recent years, more per capita than any other European country. However, there was a drop in numbers last year after the country introduced new border checks. Sweden is believed to have the highest number of Islamic State group fighters per capita in Europe. About 140 of the 300 who went to Syria and Iraq have since returned, leaving the authorities to grapple with how best to reintegrate them into society.

Papa John's has released a new advertisement addressing customer outrage over comments made by its former chairman, John Schnatter, regarding the NFL and the use of a racial slur. The video features actual customer tweets expressing disappointment and demanding changes from the company. Papa John's has acknowledged the concerns and stated that it is reviewing its culture from top to bottom and intends to earn back customers' trust through action.

The company has also announced plans to implement mandatory bias training for its workers, starting in October. The training will cover topics such as unconscious bias, racial and cultural sensitivity, and managing bias. Papa John's is also conducting an internal audit on diversity and inclusion practices, launching a program to support minority-owned franchises, and starting a foundation focused on local communities.

CEO Steve Ritchie has stated that he is personally committed to adding more diversity to the leadership team of Papa John's. The company has hired Bank of America and Lazard to help stabilize the business, and it seems to be following a similar playbook to that of Starbucks, which mandated anti-bias training after a PR crisis.

In an open letter, Ritchie emphasized the company's core values of equity, fairness, respect, and opportunity, and expressed a commitment to continuously striving for better. The letter outlined the steps the company has taken so far to address diversity, equity, and inclusion, and highlighted upcoming initiatives such as the Papa John's minority-owned franchise expansion and development program and the formation of a new foundation focused on making a positive impact in communities.

Scott Brown, the former Massachusetts Senator, has been working as a bike mechanic at Gus' Bike Shop in North Hampton, New Hampshire, after losing his seat in 2012 and a comeback bid in 2014. Brown developed a passion for cycling after an eye injury from basketball and has raced in Europe, including the Spanish Pyrenees. He has also experienced grueling races, such as one in Maryland where he needed intravenous fluids after the race. Brown's training regimen involves a triathlon-like workout daily, and his favorite place to ride is Route 1A starting in Portsmouth. He also enjoys riding a tandem bike with his wife. Brown has been nominated by President Trump to serve as ambassador to New Zealand, and he endorsed Trump in 2016. Recently, Brown was accused of making sexually inappropriate comments and putting his hands on a former Fox News host, Andrea Tantaros, while on set. Brown denied the allegations.

Jennifer Love Hewitt and her husband Brian Hallisay have welcomed their first child, a daughter named Autumn James Hallisay, on November 26. The couple, who met on the Lifetime show The Client List, secretly got married as well. Hewitt lost her mother to cancer less than a year and a half ago, and has expressed her eagerness to pass on her mother's love to her child. The couple decided to keep the sex of their baby a surprise and celebrated with a gender-neutral baby shower in October.

The Internet Archive is working on a project to preserve and fix broken links on the web by archiving pages as they are created and archiving the pages they refer to. This aims to maintain a record of the original intended content of a page when a link is broken or changed. The project, called "No More 404," is being implemented on supported websites.

In India, which is home to 430 million children, child sexual abuse is a significant issue. In 2007, the government published its first survey on the topic, revealing that more than half of the children interviewed had been subjected to some form of sexual abuse. The survey found that very few cases are ever reported, with most perpetrators known to the child. The problem is not limited to poor families, as even wealthy families have been affected.

Other studies have shown similar results, with one survey conducted in 2005 finding that at least 48% of boys and 39% of girls interviewed had faced sexual abuse. Official crime records also indicate the severity of the problem, with one in three rape victims being a child.

The Indian government has taken steps to address the issue, including enacting a law outlawing child sexual abuse in 2012. The National Commission for the Protection of Child Rights (NCPCR) was also established in 2007 to monitor the implementation of laws and policies related to child rights. However, the government has yet to create an effective social services network to protect children and prevent crimes against them.

The media and nongovernmental organizations have played a leading role in increasing awareness of child sexual abuse in India and putting pressure on the government to act. However, there is still much work to be done to protect children from abuse and provide them with the support they need.

Congressman Dennis Kucinich has filed a lawsuit against the Longworth House Office Building cafeteria and related companies for serving him a sandwich with an unpitted olive in 2008, causing dental injuries. The lawsuit, seeking $150,000, alleges negligence and breach of implied warranty. Kucinich claims the incident resulted in multiple oral and dental surgeries. A spokesperson for Kucinich described the matter as private, and Restaurant Associates could not be reached for comment. The lawsuit details are available online. Kucinich appeared normal on video footage from the day after the incident.

In a shocking turn of events, Muhammad Iqbal, the husband of Farzana Parveen who was brutally murdered outside Lahore's high court, admitted to strangling his first wife six years ago. This confession comes after Iqbal's pregnant second wife was beaten to death by her family on Tuesday.

Iqbal, who is now facing public scrutiny, avoided a prison sentence for the first murder due to Islamic provisions in Pakistan's legal system that allow family members to forgive the perpetrator. This is a situation he has previously criticized in relation to his wife's killers.

Parveen's family is believed to have killed another daughter of Iqbal in the past, a claim that has not been confirmed by the Aurat Foundation, a women's rights organization.

The killing of Parveen, who was killed after marrying without her family's consent, has sparked outrage both domestically and internationally. Pakistani Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif has ordered an urgent investigation into the matter, stating that the crime is "totally unacceptable and must be dealt with in accordance with the law promptly."

The UN High Commissioner for Human Rights, Navi Pillay, has condemned the incident, stating that Pakistan must take "urgent and strong measures to put an end to the continuous stream of so-called 'honour killings' and other forms of violence against women."

The Human Rights Commission of Pakistan reported that nearly 900 women were killed in 'honour' crimes in 2013 alone, with the actual figure likely to be much higher.

The media's response to the incident has been criticized for its lack of coverage, with one journalist stating that the country's media reflects its audience, which is primarily composed of semi-tribal societies in rural areas.

The case has highlighted the prevalence of 'honour' killings in Pakistan, a practice that is deeply rooted in cultural and religious traditions. The government and human rights organizations are under pressure to take action and ensure justice for victims like Farzana Parveen.

The mystery surrounding the identity of a mummified head, believed to be that of King Henry IV of France, has caused a stir in the scientific community. The head, discovered in 1919 and found to belong to Henry IV in a 2010 study, has been challenged by a new study published in the European Journal of Human Genetics.

The new study, conducted by researchers from the University of Leuven in Belgium, found a genetic mismatch between the head and three living male relatives of the 17th-century French king. The researchers concluded that the head did not come from anyone in the royal lineage.

King Henry IV, known as the "Green Gallant" and "Good King Henry," was one of France's best-loved kings, credited with bringing religious peace to the country and building Parisian landmarks like the Pont Neuf bridge during his reign from 1589 to 1610. He was the first of the Bourbon monarchs and grandfather of the Sun King Louis XIV.

The same study also found a blood sample previously attributed to King Louis XVI, one of Henri's descendants, lacked any royal ties. The researchers could not determine who the head or the blood sample belonged to, as the DNA from both failed to match samples from other royal families on record.

The original conclusion was based largely on facial reconstruction techniques and signs the skull had injuries similar to those suffered by the monarch. The new study looked at DNA instead. Philippe Charlier, author of the 2010 study that identified the head as Henri IV, dismissed the new research, stating that a three-dimensional comparison of the ancient head and Henri IV's death mask showed an exact match.

The researchers from the University of Leuven have called for the retraction of the 2010 study, stating that "robust scientific arguments... negate the conclusions." The mummified head is currently in a Parisian bank vault awaiting reburial, but there are no exact plans yet. The identity of the head remains a mystery, causing a divide among forensic scientists.

In this interview, Will Smith and his son Jaden discuss their upcoming film After Earth, a post-apocalyptic drama where a father and son are stranded on Earth a thousand years in the future. Will, who came up with the story, sees parallels between their adventures in Hollywood and the characters' journey in the film.

Will, who considers himself a "student of patterns," believes there is a single equation or theory of everything that governs life. Jaden agrees, stating that a new mathematics would be needed to find this equation.

The Smiths are not religious but study world religions. They discuss the patterns they see in the Best Actor Oscars, with Will noting that almost 90% of winners portray historical figures or characters with mental illness.

Jaden describes working with Will on After Earth as a collaboration, starting from teaching him about filmmaking during The Karate Kid, to a more equal partnership on this film. The family dynamic on set includes Willow, who demands the most attention, and Jada, who is very opinionated and ensures Jaden follows instructions.

The interview also touches on the dangers they faced while filming in Costa Rica, including venomous snakes. Jaden discusses the challenges of fame, stating that he enjoys it except when people create false stories about him.

Regarding their family business, Will and Jaden emphasize their focus on creating valuable lives and pursuing their passions. They reject the idea of exploiting their fame and prioritize transparency. Will shares that he would never push his children into acting against their will, and that Willow chose to stop her music career to focus on school.

The interview ends with Jaden discussing his father's influence, stating that Will lets them have their freedom as long as they can control it. He also mentions that Will watches TED talks and often shares life lessons with him.

On April 19, 2013, a manhunt for Dzhokhar Tsarnaev, a suspect in the Boston Marathon bombings, took place in Watertown, Massachusetts. The search followed a violent night that left another suspect, Tsarnaev's brother Tamerlan, dead and a police officer critically wounded. Residents of Boston were ordered to stay in their homes as authorities searched for the surviving suspect.

The manhunt began after a shootout between the suspects and police that left Tamerlan dead. Dzhokhar Tsarnaev was later apprehended after a standoff that lasted several hours. He was found hiding in a boat in a Watertown backyard.

Tamerlan Tsarnaev had previously been interviewed by the FBI in 2011, on behalf of an unspecified foreign government that suspected he had ties to a terrorist organization. However, the FBI found nothing warranting further investigation.

The Tsarnaev brothers were of Chechen heritage and had emigrated legally to the United States. Both had embraced American passions, with Tamerlan being an accomplished boxer and Dzhokhar a wrestler at Cambridge's public high school.

The bombings occurred on April 15, 2013, killing three people and injuring over 260. The brothers were identified as the suspects after authorities released photos of two men carrying backpacks near the Marathon's finish line.

The bombings sparked a massive manhunt and lockdown of the greater Boston area, with authorities issuing a stay-at-home order for the entire city and several surrounding towns. The investigation into the bombings is ongoing, with authorities still seeking to understand the brothers' motives and any potential help they may have received.

In North Korea, voting is compulsory for citizens over the age of 17, and the recent elections held on March 9th were for local representatives on provincial, city, and county People's Assemblies. However, the elections were not democratic in nature, as the results had already been decided by Kim Jong Un's central government. Voters were handed ballot papers but did not mark them; instead, they deposited them in a ballot box, signifying their support for the pre-approved candidates. The elections served as an unofficial census, checking citizens were where they should be, and also provided an opportunity for the government to see if any established names were absent and to oust any dissident behavior.

North Korea's Supreme Leader Kim Jong-Un, who exercises complete control over the country's 24.9 million citizens, was also seen casting his ballot in the capital, Pyongyang. The elections were Mr Kim's first at a local level since he inherited the position in 2011, with voters reportedly "singing and dancing" as they cast their vote at polling stations "clad in a festive atmosphere."

Local elections are held every four years, and voters choose mayors, local assemblies, and governors, who meet twice a year to approve budgets and endorse leaders that have been approved by the ruling party. In the 2011 elections, which also saw a 99.97% voter participation rate, 28,116 representatives were elected as deputies without a single vote of opposition. Ballot papers only present one candidate to choose from, which has been overseen by Mr Kim's Workers' Party, and any dissenting votes are considered acts of treason.

The elections have been denounced as an effort by North Korea to appear democratic, but they also serve as a means for the government to keep track of its population's whereabouts and to check up on the populace. Defectors have reported that elections are an opportunity for the government to find out about defectors and people who have been missed.

The results of the election are expected to be officially announced early next week. The elections highlight an odd thing about sham or rigged elections held in autocratic countries, as even the most despotic leaders feel the need to pay democracy the back-handed compliment of imitating its outward appearance, if not its underlying political model. North Korea's leaders seem to take their pantomime polls seriously.

In Bentonville, Arkansas, James Andrew Bates was arrested on suspicion of first-degree murder in the death of Victor Parris Collins, a Centerton resident, in November 2015. The investigation began after Bates called 911 to report Collins' death in his hot tub. Bates had invited Collins and two other friends to his home for a Razorback football game, during which they drank beer and vodka. After one friend left, Bates and Collins continued drinking in the hot tub until Bates went to bed, leaving Collins alone.

The next morning, Bates found Collins floating face down in the hot tub. An initial examination of the crime scene showed the water was tinted red and contained bodily fluids and blood, and Collins had a black eye, a cut on his eyelid, swollen and bruised lips, and was bleeding from his mouth and nose. The crime lab later determined the blood belonged to Collins.

Over the course of the investigation, detectives interviewed Bates and several witnesses, collected evidence, and obtained water and electrical usage data from the Bentonville Utilities Department. The data showed the residence used 50 gallons of water between 1 to 2 a.m. on the night of the incident and an additional 90 gallons of water between 2 and 3 a.m. This was consistent with the patio being sprayed down, and was unusual given the freezing temperatures.

The investigation also revealed that Bates had several smart home devices, including an Amazon Echo. Police sought stored Echo information, but it's unclear what information they were able to access. Amazon declined to release customer information without a valid and binding legal demand, but did hand over Bates' account details and purchases. Police say they were able to pull data off of the speaker, but it's not clear what info they were able to access.

The case raises questions about privacy and the use of smart home devices in criminal investigations. Bates' attorney argues that there should be an expectation of privacy in one's home, and that law enforcement should not be able to use technology against citizens. However, the reliability of information from smart home devices is also a concern, as accuracy can be an issue for any number of IoT gadgets.

As in the San Bernardino case, it will be interesting to see how authorities and the companies who make smart home devices work out the tension between serving customers, maintaining privacy, and pursuing justice. The case is currently ongoing, and Bates is being held at the Benton County Jail without bond.

A serviceman, Jeffrey Michels, who disappeared from an Air Force Base in North Dakota in 1977 has been arrested and charged with desertion after living under an alias in Florida for over four decades. Michels, now 64, was found using the name Jeffrey Lantz and was discovered last week by the US Air Force. He had used this alias to obtain a business license in Florida in 1998. There is no statute of limitations for desertion, and Michels will stand trial in a military court.

The military rarely enforces the highest sentences for desertion, ranging from a dishonorable discharge to a prison term of up to three years. However, soldiers are only executed for desertion during wartime, and even then, it has to be demonstrated that their action left serving personnel in danger.

This week, Army Sergeant Bowe Bergdahl, who was held captive by the Taliban in Afghanistan for five years, pleaded guilty to desertion and misbehavior before the enemy. Bergdahl's lawyers have argued he cannot get a fair trial following criticism from Donald Trump during the 2016 presidential campaign.

The Air Force does not keep strict records for servicemen and women who have deserted, but the outstanding number is estimated to be around 50,000 based on internal military data. This case highlights the ongoing issue of military desertion and the challenges in enforcing desertion laws.

In recent weeks, there have been multiple sightings of bald eagles, the national symbol of the United States, in various locations across Massachusetts. The most recent sighting was by Tom Palmer, a resident of Milton and an employee of the Neponset River Watershed Association, who spotted two bald eagles perched in a tree along the Neponset River shoreline. This marks the second time in less than 10 days that someone in the area has witnessed the giant birds of prey, with their impressive seven-foot wingspans, in their natural habitat.

Previously, two bald eagles were seen on the frozen Charles River, not far from the Longfellow Bridge, on January 21. Photographs of the birds were shared to the community message board, Reddit. Residents in Arlington have also reported seeing the birds at Spy Pond.

The species was reintroduced in Massachusetts at the Quabbin Reservoir in 1982. The first nest in the wild with eaglets was reported in 1989. As numbers grew, the winged predators’ status was changed from “endangered” to “threatened” in 2012. State officials say there were around 46 eagle territories in 2014, but they are confident that that number has grown.

Eagle sightings increase in the winter, as birds come down to Massachusetts from northern New England and Canada, where rivers and lakes may be frozen, for better access to food. The birds primarily stick to shoreline habitats.

In a separate incident, a driver on I-95 recently spotted a bald eagle soaring above the traffic. The eagle was seen swooping down to check out a dead deer by the side of the road, but the driver was afraid the eagle would get hit by a car. Unfortunately, getting hit by a vehicle is a common occurrence for bald eagles, with about 15% of the eagles admitted to the Wildlife Center of Virginia for rehabilitation in the past five years having been hit by a vehicle.

The increased sightings of bald eagles in Massachusetts are a positive sign of the species' recovery since it was threatened with extinction in the 1970s due to DDT contamination, illegal shooting, and habitat loss. However, 80% of the eagles treated at the Wildlife Center of Virginia have measurable levels of lead in their systems, which is bad for the birds' nervous system and can make them more susceptible to being hit by cars.

Overall, the increased sightings of bald eagles in Massachusetts are a testament to the success of conservation efforts and the improving health of the state's waterways.

The local women's clinic, Isis Women's Health Care, is changing its name due to confusion with the terrorist group ISIS. The clinic, which has been in operation for ten years, has received numerous death threats from individuals who believed the clinic was associated with the terrorist group. The name "Isis" was originally chosen for its tie to the Egyptian goddess of motherhood, but due to the association with the terrorist group, the clinic is changing its name for the safety of its employees and patients. The clinic employs dozens of people in three offices and is affiliated with North Fulton Hospital and Emory Johns Creek Hospital. The unveiling of the new company name will be held on March 31 at its 1015 Mansell Road office. The clinic is encouraging its clients to submit ideas for a new name as they move into the next decade.

The research published in The American Journal of Gastroenterology reveals that the combination of smoking and drinking significantly increases the risk of developing esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC), a type of esophageal cancer. The study, led by Dr. Anoop Prabhu, is the first meta-analysis to examine the interaction between alcohol and tobacco in the risk of ESCC. The research confirms that both alcohol and tobacco are independent risk factors for ESCC, and the combination of their use markedly increases their potency as carcinogens.

In a separate study, researchers investigated the factors contributing to hangovers. The study found that the severity of a hangover is primarily influenced by the alcohol content and the presence of congeners, substances produced during fermentation that give drinks their color and flavor. Clear drinks such as white rum, vodka, and gin tend to cause fewer and less severe hangovers due to their relatively low levels of congeners.

However, the study did not find evidence to support the claim that mixing drinks increases the severity of hangovers. The researchers suggest that the strength of the drinks may play a more significant role in determining hangover severity, with beer being weaker than wine or spirits, which could lead to less intoxication if consumed first.

In conclusion, the research highlights the dangers of smoking and drinking, particularly in combination, in the development of esophageal cancer. Meanwhile, the evidence on hangovers suggests that the high congener count and alcohol content of drinks are the primary factors contributing to their severity, rather than the order in which they are consumed.

The court-martial of U.S. Army Major Nidal Hasan, accused of the 2009 Fort Hood shooting rampage, is ongoing. Hasan is acting as his own attorney and declined to address jurors during the closing argument. Prosecutors urged the jury to convict Hasan of premeditated murder, which would allow them to seek the death penalty. They presented evidence suggesting that Hasan had planned and carried out the attack, which was the deadliest mass shooting ever on a U.S. military base. Hasan is facing numerous counts of premeditated murder for the attack that killed 13 people and wounded more than 30 others at the Army post in central Texas. The jury will continue deliberating on Friday. Hasan has been unapologetic about saying the rampage was necessary to protect Muslim insurgents abroad from American soldiers preparing for combat in Iraq and Afghanistan, but most of his arguments have played out through leaks to the media or directly to the judge, so they couldn't be considered by the jury.

A San Jose man, Robert Farmer, was sentenced to 16 years in jail for the torture and dismemberment of up to 16 cats in San Jose. The cats' disappearances had caused fear and distress among pet owners in the Cambrian Park neighborhood, where most of the cats were abducted. Farmer, who had previously lived with mental health issues and a methamphetamine addiction, was arrested in October 2015 after police found a dead cat in his car. He pleaded guilty to 21 felony counts of animal cruelty, but the court did not require him to register as a sex offender, despite allegations that he had sexually abused one of the slain felines. The victims and their supporters were relieved by the sentence, but disappointed that Farmer would not have to register as a sex offender. He will serve his time in county jail, not state prison, and will have to stay away from Cambrian Park, not own or care for any animal for 10 years, and undergo mandatory psychological treatment upon his release.

The article discusses the release of Hillary Clinton's emails, which were sent through her private email account while she served as Secretary of State. Under pressure from the House Select Committee on Benghazi, the State Department has announced that it will speed up the release of about 900 pages of Benghazi-related emails. The review of the broader set of approximately 55,000 pages of Clinton emails is expected to take several months.

Steven Aftergood, who directs the Project on Government Secrecy at the Federation of American Scientists, expressed his suspicion that if a researcher or journalist had sought all of Clinton's emails under the Freedom of Information Act, some of the emails might have been withheld on the grounds of classification. He pointed out that as Secretary of State, Clinton was the top classification authority for the entire State Department, with broad discretion to determine which department documents were classified and which were not.

Clinton aides argued that there was no need to use the personal email account for sensitive matters, as Clinton was almost always accompanied by one or more aides with secure government devices that could be used to send classified material. They also stated that Clinton communicated with foreign officials in person, through correspondence, and by telephone, and that her staff's review of her emails revealed only one email with a foreign official, one from the United Kingdom.

John M. Deutch, a former C.I.A. director, was previously punished for storing classified information on a personal device, but Clinton has stated that she never discussed classified information in emails sent through her private account. Clinton has welcomed the State Department's decision to release the records and is eager to see them made public soon. The State Department has acknowledged that its review of the documents will include checking them for classified national security information that is exempt from release under the Freedom of Information Act.

The article discusses the impact of Paul Ryan as Vice Presidential pick for Mitt Romney in the 2012 U.S. presidential election. The author argues that Ryan's selection could significantly influence the election, making it more ideological and nationalizing the campaign.

Ryan's selection could counter the Democrats' "Mediscare" strategy, which portrays the Republicans as wanting to privatize Medicare and harm seniors. The Republicans plan to emphasize that their Medicare plan does not affect those over 55, and to go on the offensive by pointing out that President Obama's healthcare reform cuts Medicare by $700 billion.

The author also suggests that Ryan's selection could have long-term implications for the Republican Party, potentially making him a dominant figure for a generation. The history of vice-presidential picks shows that they can ascend to party leadership and even become future presidential nominees.

The author compares Ryan to Ronald Reagan, who was a movement conservative and the first modern leader of his kind to achieve the presidency. Ryan represents a new kind of conservatism that rejects the moderate accommodationism of previous Republican leaders and offers a serious approach to structural problems.

The author concludes by suggesting that if Ryan performs well in the campaign, he could become a dominant national force, shaping the conservative future for years to come. The selection of Paul Ryan as Vice Presidential candidate is seen as a strategic move that could have significant implications for the 2012 election and beyond.

The Most Holy Redeemer church in San Francisco's Castro district is facing challenges due to controversial decisions regarding the church's leadership, policies, and potential closure. The controversy began with the archdiocese's refusal to allow drag queens to serve as emcees for charity events, which was perceived as antigay sentiment. The incoming Archbishop Salvatore Cordileone, an opponent of same-sex marriage, is seen as the cause of this decision by some, but the issue is larger than just drag queens at a fundraiser.

The decision calls into question the church's responsibility to the community, its acceptance of all walks of life, and the tenets of religion. The new pastor, the Rev. Brian Costello, has been learning about the unique culture of the Castro and has been open to reconsidering the drag-queen decision. However, his attempts to reconsider were rejected by the archdiocese.

Most Holy Redeemer has a robust congregation of over 450 to 550 members, with more than 80% being gay or lesbian. The church is known for its renowned music and welcoming atmosphere, with services attended by visitors from all over the country. Despite these positive aspects, many gay and lesbian Catholics worry about their future with the arrival of Archbishop Cordileone, who has been a key player in the passage of Proposition 8.

Cordileone has stated that gays and lesbians in sexual relationships should not receive the sacrament of Holy Communion, and he is expected to be firm in his beliefs when he arrives in San Francisco. The church must reach out, support people, and move them along to understand, according to Cordileone. The future of Most Holy Redeemer and its relationship with the incoming archbishop remains uncertain, but many are hoping for an open-minded approach from both sides.

In a series of tweets on Saturday, Donald J. Trump, the U.S. Presidential candidate, commented on the shooting death of Nykea Aldridge, a cousin of NBA star Dwyane Wade, in Chicago. Trump initially linked the incident to his campaign to win African-American votes, stating, "Just what I have been saying. African-Americans will VOTE TRUMP!" However, he later posted a separate tweet offering his condolences to the family. Trump's approach to courting African-American voters has involved portraying minority communities as plagued by poverty, violence, and dysfunction, particularly in urban areas. Trump's tweets were criticized for their insensitivity and lack of empathy towards the victim's family, and for exploiting a tragic event for political gain. This incident highlights the ongoing debate about Trump's approach to race relations and his ability to connect with diverse communities.

In a series of interviews and speeches, political figures have discussed the implications of Mitt Romney's appearance at the NAACP convention, where he faced boos from the audience. House Minority Leader Nancy Pelosi suggested that Romney's boos were a calculated move to appeal to racist voters within the GOP. Guest Goldie Taylor agreed with Pelosi's assessment, arguing that Romney's speech was more about appealing to small factions of the GOP base rather than engaging with the black community.

Taylor criticized Romney for not repudiating voter ID laws, which she compared to a "poll tax." She also argued that Romney needs to take action to address the concerns of African-Americans, rather than just appealing to their dissatisfactions.

Mitt Romney's speech at the NAACP convention was met with boos, particularly when he discussed his plans to repeal the Affordable Care Act. Rep. Emanuel Cleaver (D-Mo.) was not pleased with Romney's comments on healthcare, stating that if Romney had staff members who vetted his speech, they should be fired. However, Cleaver did give Romney an "A" for effort for speaking to the NAACP.

In response to the criticism, Rush Limbaugh argued that Romney was unfairly criticized for being successful and out of touch with the struggles of the black community. Limbaugh also questioned why being successful is seen as a negative and suggested that Romney's wealth and success disqualified him from understanding the struggles of the black community.

Overall, the discussions surrounding Romney's appearance at the NAACP convention highlight the ongoing tensions and divisions between the Republican Party and the African-American community, as well as the challenges faced by Romney in appealing to diverse voter groups.

The Internet Archive is working on a project to archive web pages as they are created and preserve the pages they refer to, aiming to fix broken links on the web. This is done by archiving pages that are referenced and preserving a link to the version that was live when the page was written.

In a recent development, the upcoming film "Blind," starring Alec Baldwin as a blind novelist, has drawn criticism for casting an able-bodied actor in the lead role. The Ruderman Family Foundation, an organization advocating for disability rights, has accused the film of "crip-face," a comparison to blackface, for having Baldwin portray the main role. The foundation argues that it is unacceptable for able-bodied actors to portray disabled characters, citing that those with disabilities represent almost 20% of the country’s population, yet 95% of disabled characters on television are played by able-bodied performers.

Last summer, the foundation criticized the 2016 romantic drama "Me Before You" for casting Sam Claflin as a young banker who was left paralyzed from an accident. The trailer for "Blind" was released recently, with Demi Moore co-starring as a married socialite who cares for Baldwin's character as part of a plea bargain. The film, directed by Michael Mailer, premiered at the Woodstock Film Festival on Oct 13 and is scheduled to release worldwide on July 14 by Vertical Entertainment.

The shooting of Michael Brown, an 18-year-old African-American, by a police officer in Ferguson, Missouri, has led to widespread protests and violence. Witnesses say Brown was surrendering with his hands up when the officer opened fire, but authorities claim Brown assaulted the officer and tried to take his gun. The shooting has sparked a federal civil rights investigation and national debate. Tensions are high in Ferguson, where there is a history of distrust between the predominantly black community and the largely white police force.

Michael Brown was spending the summer with his grandmother in Ferguson and was set to start classes at Vatterott College. According to witnesses, Brown and a friend were walking to his grandmother's house when they were confronted by a white police officer who told them to get onto the sidewalk. Dorian Johnson, a friend of Brown's, said the officer drove forward and almost hit them, causing them to hit the officer's car. Johnson said the officer then grabbed Brown by the neck and tried to pull him into the car, leading to a physical altercation. Johnson said the officer drew his weapon and fired, hitting Brown.

Witness Tiffany Mitchell said she saw Brown and the officer "tussling through the window" of the police car. Mitchell and another witness, Piaget Crenshaw, said Brown appeared to be trying to pry himself away from the officer's grasp. Brown then broke free and started running, but was shot multiple times by the officer and died on the spot.

St. Louis County Police Chief Jon Belmar said the preliminary investigation showed that the Ferguson officer tried to exit his vehicle, but Brown pushed him back into the car and physically assaulted the officer. Belmar said a shot was fired inside the police car, and Brown was eventually shot about 35 feet away from the vehicle. It is unclear how many times Brown was shot.

The officer who shot Brown is on paid administrative leave and will be required to undergo two psychological evaluations before returning to duty. His name has not been released by authorities. Brown's family has retained attorney Benjamin Crump, who also represented the family of Trayvon Martin, an unarmed black teen who was shot and killed by a white neighborhood watch volunteer in Florida.

The shooting has sparked protests and violence in Ferguson, with some demonstrations turning violent and resulting in looting, vandalism, and attacks on police officers. The NAACP and other community leaders have called for nonviolent protests and for witnesses to come forward with information. The shooting has also fueled a national debate about race and police violence. Brown's parents have urged people to remain calm and to seek justice for their son.

Mitch Daniels, a conservative figure considered for the presidency in 2012, delivered a speech on education policy to a conservative think tank in Washington. In an unexpected turn, Daniels praised the Obama administration's education policies, including support for national standards and federal involvement. This move was seen as a departure from traditional conservative views and a strategic move to differentiate himself from other Republican candidates.

Daniels' speech echoed George W. Bush's campaign as a "compassionate conservative" in 2000, focusing on education and the needs of disadvantaged children. However, unlike Bush, Daniels is not perceived as a natural politician and his intellectual approach may wear off as opponents portray him as an old drug-industry executive.

In the speech, Daniels proposed teacher ratings based on student growth, advocated for social justice, and softened his support for private-school vouchers by requiring two semesters in public school. He also boasted about increasing education spending in Indiana and claimed that the state had the highest share of its budget committed to education.

Daniels employed a folksy, humorous style during the speech to deflect questions about entering the presidential race. Despite his moderate stance on social issues, he announced plans to sign a bill stripping Planned Parenthood of Medicaid financing, drawing criticism from pro-choice groups.

The speech was seen as a strategic move to position Daniels as a moderate alternative to the current Republican field, which is focusing on social issues like abortion and homosexuality. However, Daniels' moderate stance on social issues may be at odds with his fiscal conservatism, as he has been vocal about eliminating government intervention in personal decisions, except in the case of abortion.

The speech received mixed reactions, with some praising Daniels for his moderate stance and others criticizing him for his inconsistency on social issues. Overall, the speech was seen as a strategic move to position Daniels as a potential presidential candidate and to differentiate himself from the current Republican field.

The comedy series "Who Is America?" by Sacha Baron Cohen, which is now available on SHOWTIME, features a prank on former U.S. Senate candidate Roy Moore. Moore appeared on the show on July 29, 2018, and was subjected to a fake pedophile detector test by Cohen's character, Col. Erran Morad. Moore walked off the set after the device beeped in front of him, claiming that the technology was faulty.

Before the episode aired, Moore threatened legal action against Cohen, criticizing the show's satire of American values. Moore stated that he was invited to Washington D.C. in February 2018 to receive an award for his support of Israel and that he accepted the invitation without knowing that it was part of Cohen's series.

In a statement, Moore said that he does not apologize for his belief in God or his support of Israel, and that he stands for truth and honesty. He also said that he is involved in several court cases to defend his honor and character against false political attacks by liberals like Cohen. Moore added that Alabama does not respect cowards who exhibit traits like trickery, deception, and dishonesty.

Moore's appearance on "Who Is America?" is just one example of the show's pranks on various public figures. Other guests include former Alaska Governor Sarah Palin, former Vice President Dick Cheney, and U.S. Senator Bernie Sanders. In the first episode, Cheney agreed to autograph a waterboard kit, which was described as a "waterboard kit" by Cohen's character in a "Borat" voice.

In a ranking of the guests in episode three of "Who Is America?," Moore is ranked third, with Chip Limehouse, a former Republican State representative from South Carolina, being ranked second, and the Quinceañera Commandos, who were recruited to bait and trap undocumented immigrants, being ranked first. The Quinceañera Commandos were criticized for their willingness to conflate the innocent idea of a quinceañera with the rape of 15-year-olds, and for their eagerness to participate in a fake quinceañera featuring a rubber vagina and Rohypnol-laced guacamole.

The article discusses a controversial Tumblr page that showcases selfies taken at funerals and uploaded to social media platforms, often with insensitive captions and hashtags. The creator of the page, who remains anonymous, expresses dismay at the behavior and the lack of respect shown towards the deceased and their families. The page has caused an uproar, with many finding the selfies disrespectful and inappropriate. The creator of the page provides context in interviews on "Q" and "The List." The creator also mentions that they are unlikely to continue updating the Tumblr page, but may consider it if offered a significant amount of money. The creator encourages followers to follow them on Twitter or take a selfie at a funeral and risk being mocked globally as their only two options.

Alexander Shulgin, a renowned psychedelic chemist and advocate for cognitive liberty, died on June 3, 2014 at the age of 88. Known for his work on MDMA (Ecstasy), Shulgin synthesized over 100 previously unknown psychoactive compounds during his 30-year career in his California backyard lab. He was a dear friend, mentor, and role model to many, including the author. Shulgin's books, TIHKAL and PIHKAL, detail his research and the effects of various psychedelic drugs. The DEA initially had a good relationship with Shulgin, but became cold towards him after he published his books. Despite this, Shulgin remained an icon in the psychedelic community, particularly during the rise of the rave scene in the 1990s. Ecstasy was outlawed by the federal government in 1985, but Shulgin continued to work on other psychedelic compounds. He was diagnosed with terminal liver cancer and passed away peacefully.

The Iranian government has executed a currency trader known as the "Sultan of Coins," Vahid Mazloumin, and another associate for amassing approximately two tonnes of gold coins, deemed a violation of international law by Amnesty International. The executions were carried out following a series of fast-tracked trials by special courts set up to deal with financial crimes, established after Ayatollah Ali Khamenei's approval in August.

The demand for gold coins and US dollars in Iran has surged due to the country's currency, the rial, plummeting in value by about 70% against the US dollar, following renewed US sanctions targeting Iran's oil and finance sectors. The sanctions have caused instability in Iran's financial markets since April, when the government attempted to stabilize currency prices by introducing a single official dollar exchange rate.

In response to the economic crisis, demonstrators have taken to the streets, protesting perceived corruption. On the day before the executions, about 130 small-time currency and gold dealers were arrested in downtown Tehran and the Grand Bazaar. The rial was trading at 12,900 to the dollar on Wednesday, slightly better than the day before but down from about 40,000 a year ago.

A Georgia mother, Rachel Lehnardt, has lost custody of her five children after being arrested for hosting a wild party at her home, which included alcohol, drugs, a hot tub, and a game of naked Twister with her 16-year-old daughter and her friends. The party took place at Lehnardt's home in Evans, an Augusta suburb. Lehnardt was charged with two counts of contributing to the delinquency of a minor.

The party began after Lehnardt's 16-year-old daughter texted her asking if she could bring friends over "to party." Lehnardt replied, "Come on, let's party." Lehnardt provided marijuana and alcohol to the partying teens and joined them in a game of naked Twister. She then had sex with an 18-year-old boy in the bathroom, according to the police report.

Lehnardt later woke up to find her daughter's 16-year-old boyfriend having sex with her. The boy is not facing charges because "there is no evidence of rape" since Lehnardt "refuses to discuss the case."

Lehnardt, who works in an Augusta bridal shop, had been attending a sexual-addiction workshop at her local Mormon church. She was released after posting a $3,200 bond. The party forced Lehnardt to lose custody of her children, ages 4, 6, 8, 10, and 16, on April 6.

Growing up in the Mormon Church, Lehnardt never touched a drop of alcohol before her husband of 15 years came back from a deployment to Iraq with Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder and anger issues in 2010. The party made Lehnardt decide to go sober, and she met with a woman in Alcoholics Anonymous who she knew from her Mormon church four days later. She spilled the salacious details and reportedly admitted to showing photos of her having sex with her boyfriend to her 16-year-old daughter. The sponsor, who "struggled" to look like she wasn't judging Lehnardt during the tale, reported the rager to police.

Lehnardt was arrested on two counts of contributing to the delinquency of a minor and was released on $3,200 bond. Her attorney, Shawn P. Hammond, told the Daily News that some of the accusations "were exaggerated." Lehnardt plans to attend counseling and will continue to attend AA meetings.

The $1.1 trillion spending bill, unveiled by House-Senate negotiators on Monday, aims to restore order to government funding for the next year. The bill, which is a compromise between Republicans and Democrats, fills in the blanks of the December budget agreement and avoids another government shutdown.

The bill keeps a tight rein on new funding for Wall Street regulators and effectively freezes appropriations for President Obama’s health care program at the reduced, post-sequester level. However, the White House retains the flexibility to find the financing it needs to implement the health exchanges and appears satisfied to have avoided the most contentious restrictions proposed by conservatives.

President Obama secured significant new funding for pre-kindergarten education initiatives, although more through existing programs like Head Start than the new format he envisioned. The new $8.6 billion funding level for Head Start reflects one of the biggest investments in the bill, with an estimated $1 billion, or 13 percent, increase over current funding and $612 million over its initial 2013 enacted appropriation.

House Appropriations Committee Chairman Hal Rogers (R-Ky.) came away with two coal-related riders, one affecting mountaintop mining regulations and the other challenging new Export-Import Bank guidelines on the financing of coal-fired power plants overseas.

One legislative provision that all sides embraced would exempt disability pensions for veterans from a cost-of-living cut included in the December budget deal. The very evident give-and-take caps more than six weeks of often intense bargaining within the Appropriations Committees and sets the stage for what the leadership hopes will be a rapid series of floor votes sending the bill on to Obama by this weekend.

The bill would fund federal agencies through the rest of the fiscal year, with significant new funding for pre-kindergarten education initiatives, albeit more through existing programs like Head Start than the new format President Obama envisioned. It would also give all federal workers a 1 percent raise. However, in a blow to the District, it provides only partial funding to continue constructing buildings for the Department of Homeland Security’s campus in Anacostia.

The Fukushima Daiichi nuclear power plant in Japan has been upgraded to a level 7 on the International Nuclear Event Scale (INES), making it the only other event besides the 1986 Chernobyl disaster to receive this rating. This decision was made after Japan's nuclear safety body determined that the plant released 10,000 terabecquerels of iodine-131 for several hours, which meets the criteria for a level 7 accident.

The INES scale, designed by the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) and the Nuclear Energy Agency of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, ranges from 1 (anomaly) to 7 (major accident). Level 7 accidents are defined as having a major radioactive release with widespread impact on the environment and public health.

Despite the upgrade, the amount of radioactive material being released at Fukushima today is less than 1 terabecquerel, and to date, Fukushima has released only about 10% of the total radiation released 25 years ago at Chernobyl. The long-term death toll due to exposure from Chernobyl could eventually be as high as 4,000, compared to the immediate aftermath of Chernobyl, where about 30 people, mostly workers, died.

The decision to upgrade the Fukushima crisis level comes after a minor fire was spotted outside Fukushima's Reactor 4 and following a series of aftershocks, including a 7.1-magnitude aftershock that triggered landslides, resulting in three deaths. The government also expanded the exclusion zone around Fukushima to include several towns within a 19-mile (30 km) radius.

Greenpeace conducted a survey last week, finding radiation levels 75 times higher than the government recommendation in 11 samples of vegetables from gardens and small farms in Fukushima. The environmental group also found radiation levels equivalent to an annual exposure of 5 millisieverts — the evacuation threshold for Chernobyl — at a playground in Fukushima City, pop. 300,000. Greenpeace is urging the government to delay the start of the school year.

The upgrade of Fukushima's level to 7 may not herald any immediate worsening of events but is sure to add to many residents' growing concern over what could happen at dozens of other nuclear reactors spread across Japan. Anti-nuclear protests have been held in Tokyo, with more than 17,000 people protesting against nuclear power on Sunday.

The change in Fukushima's level to 7 signifies a "major accident" that includes widespread effects on the environment and health. However, Japanese officials stressed that the harm caused by Chernobyl still far outweighs that caused by the Fukushima plant. The revision was not a cause for worry, according to a nuclear physicist at Kyoto University Research Reactor Institute, as most of the radiation was released early in the crisis, and the reactors still have mostly intact containment vessels surrounding their nuclear cores.

Prime Minister Naoto Kan urged the public not to panic and to focus on recovering from the disaster. Continued aftershocks following the 9.0-magnitude megaquake on March 11 are impeding work on stabilizing the Fukushima plant, with the latest a 6.3-magnitude one on Tuesday that prompted plant operator Tokyo Electric Power Co., or TEPCO, to temporarily pull back workers.

The document discusses the discovery and exploration of subglacial aquatic environments, specifically in Antarctica, and the life forms found within these environments. Scientists have used ground penetrating radar and other remote sensing tools to discover that under the Antarctic ice sheets lies a vast hydrological system of liquid water, maintained by geothermal heat flow, pressure, movement, and the insulating nature of the ice sheet.

The Whillans Ice Stream Subglacial Access Research Drilling (WISSARD) project was organized to explore Subglacial Lake Whillans and the nearby grounding zone on the southeastern edge of the Ross Sea. The project uses radar, seismic equipment, and GPS stations to profile the overlying ice sheet and the underlying water, sediments, and rock.

During the 2014-2015 season, the team's focus was on the grounding zone, where the West Antarctic Ice Sheet meets the Ross Sea. The work aimed to assess the stability of the West Antarctic Ice Sheet, which is the last ice sheet on Earth resting in a deep marine basin and is the most likely player in any future, rapid sea-level rise.

Tomorrow's edition of the journal Nature will include a paper documenting the existence of microorganisms living far beneath Antarctic ice. The microbes, called Archaea, convert ammonium and methane into energy to survive and grow. This discovery raises questions about the potential for life in extreme environments on Earth and beyond, such as Saturn's moon Titan and Jupiter's moon Europa.

The conditions below the Antarctic ice sheet have certain characteristics in common with known places on other worlds in our solar system, leading many to wonder if life might be more inevitable in those distant locales than previously thought. The discovery of life beneath the Antarctic ice sheet could have significant implications for our understanding of the potential for life on other planets.

Weinstein is currently under investigation by multiple law enforcement authorities and has been accused by dozens of women of sexual harassment and assault. In a throwback to the 90s, Mayim Bialik, known for her role as Blossom, is now dishing out sex advice on Kveller.com, a Jewish parenting website. In the third Republican presidential debate of the week, former Governor Mitt Romney and Governor Rick Perry of Texas engaged in a heated exchange over immigration, health care, and entitlements. The debate, held in Orlando, Florida, was sponsored by Fox News, Google, and the Republican Party of Florida.

The debate focused on the candidates' records and consistency, with Romney criticizing Perry's policy on illegal immigration, particularly the Texas law that allows illegal immigrants to qualify for in-state tuition rates at public colleges and universities.
