The article discusses the mysterious origins of a painting by Pierre-Auguste Renoir, known as "On the Shore of the Seine," which was recently discovered to have been stolen from the Baltimore Museum of Art in 1951. The painting was brought to an auction house in Alexandria, Virginia, by Martha Fuqua, who claimed to have found it at a flea market in West Virginia. However, it was later revealed that Fuqua had previously taken the painting to a different auction house, Quinn's Auction Galleries, in June 2011, where she claimed to have obtained it from an estate and believed it would fetch $1 million at auction.

The article also includes accounts from several people who knew Fuqua's mother, Marcia Fouquet, who was a fine arts major at Goucher College and ran an art studio out of her home in Fairfax County, Virginia. Robert Musser, who dated Fouquet in the 1980s, recalls seeing the Renoir in her studio and being told it came from a museum in Baltimore. Another acquaintance of Fouquet's, Bobby J. Fontaine, also recalls seeing the painting in the studio in the early 1990s.

The FBI is currently investigating the theft of the Renoir and has seized the painting from the Potomack Company auction house. A federal judge in Alexandria is set to decide who should keep the painting, either Fuqua or the Baltimore Museum of Art. Fuqua's attorney has declined to comment, and neither Fuqua nor her mother have returned messages seeking comment.

The article also mentions that Fuqua filed for bankruptcy in 2009 after being laid off from her job as a physical education teacher. She was interviewed by The Washington Post in 2010 as she trained to work as a blackjack dealer in West Virginia.

In summary, the article discusses the mysterious origins of a stolen Renoir painting, known as "On the Shore of the Seine," which was recently discovered to have been in the possession of Martha Fuqua. The painting was brought to an auction house in Alexandria, Virginia, where it is currently being investigated by the FBI. The article includes accounts from several people who knew Fuqua's mother, Marcia Fouquet, who was a fine arts major at Goucher College and ran an art studio out of her home in Fairfax County, Virginia. Fuqua has not returned messages seeking comment, and the FBI is currently investigating the theft of the Renoir.

In France, a 23-year-old suspect has been charged with plotting to assassinate President Emmanuel Macron during the Bastille Day parade on July 14. The man, who was arrested in a Paris suburb, was found with three kitchen knives in his vehicle and had conducted internet searches on potential targets. He had previously been convicted of condoning terrorism for praising Norwegian mass murderer Anders Breivik.

Meanwhile, Macron is delivering a state-of-the-nation-style address in Versailles, outlining his priorities. However, the French president is facing criticism from far-left leader Jean-Luc Mélénchon, who accused Macron of behaving like a "pharaoh."

The Bastille Day parade, which commemorates the start of the French Revolution, takes place on the Champs-Elysées avenue in Paris. In 2002, then-President Jacques Chirac was the subject of a Bastille Day assassination attempt. This year, the Champs-Elysées has seen two attacks on police, including one in April where a gunman shot dead police officer Xavier Jugelé.

The suspect's plans were vague and not yet finalized, and he appeared to be acting alone. Macron will oversee the military parade in Paris on Bastille Day alongside President Donald Trump. After the parade, Macron will head to Nice to mark the anniversary of the Islamic extremist truck attack that killed 86 people in the southeastern city.

In a tragic incident on September 24, 2015, six people died and seven were injured in a high-speed police chase involving a Ford Explorer on U.S. Highway 59 near Edna, Texas. The chase began when the driver refused to stop during a routine traffic stop. The vehicle, registered in Corpus Christi, lost control and flipped multiple times, ejecting four passengers who died at the scene. Nine other passengers were injured, three of whom later died. Two people from the vehicle fled on foot and were later apprehended by police.

The rear seats of the Ford Explorer were folded down, and the middle seat removed, suggesting the vehicle was overcrowded to accommodate more passengers. Preliminary investigations suggest that the vehicle was being used for human smuggling, with some of the victims identified as being from Honduras, Guatemala, and Mexico. The Department of Public Safety is investigating the crash, and federal immigration officials are conducting a criminal investigation into the incident.

This incident is not the first of its kind in southeast Texas, where traffic stops of vehicles carrying immigrants are common, and many of the immigrants try to evade capture. The area is a major corridor for human and drug trafficking, according to authorities.

In the ongoing federal budget discussions, a bipartisan collaboration between Democratic Senator Harry Reid, backed by Nevada casino interests, and Republican Senator Jon Kyl is aiming to introduce an online-gambling bill. This bill, if passed during the lame-duck session, could potentially expand certain forms of online wagering while limiting others. Notably, it proposes the establishment of an Office of Online Poker Oversight under the Department of Commerce.

This initiative, which has been discussed privately but not publicly introduced, seeks to regulate online gambling. The bill, if passed, could bring significant changes to the online gambling landscape in the United States. The collaboration between Reid and Kyl, despite their contrasting views on gambling, underscores the potential for compromise and progress in this contentious issue.

In the Irkutsk region of Russia, a mass poisoning has occurred due to the consumption of a bath lotion disguised as a safe alcoholic drink called Hawthorn. This incident is now the worst such case in modern Russian history, with at least 58 deaths reported and over 37 individuals still being treated, many in critical condition. The bath lotion contained poisonous methanol, a chemical found in antifreeze, which can cause blindness, nausea, vomiting, and in severe cases, death.

The victims, aged between 25 and 62, include a doctor and a kindergarten teacher. Many were discovered dead in their homes due to a lack of time to call an ambulance. The labels on the contaminated lotion claimed the product contained ethyl alcohol, leading people to consume it as a cheap alternative to alcohol, a common practice in Russia.

Authorities have arrested the owners of an illicit workshop where the bath oil was being produced, along with bootleg vodka. The situation has been exacerbated by two years of Western economic sanctions. Up to 12 million Russians are reported to drink cheap surrogate alcohol, including household products like perfume, aftershave, anti-freeze, and window cleaner.

Survivors of the poisoning have expressed their hope that the perpetrators will be found and brought to justice. The authorities have declared a state of emergency in Irkutsk and have confiscated about 500 liters of bath oil and other liquids from stores in the area. This tragic incident serves as a stark reminder of the dangers of consuming illicit alcohol and the importance of proper distillation processes to ensure safety.

Rush Limbaugh, a conservative radio host, criticized the Republican establishment for being "shocked" by Rick Santorum's three-state win, stating they were insulated and unaware of the growing support for Santorum. Limbaugh also rejected the media's notion that he was influencing conservative voters, emphasizing that voters were genuinely dissatisfied with Mitt Romney and found Santorum to be the least corrupted and most conservative candidate. Santorum, on the other hand, addressed a group of pastors in Texas, denying he was running to be "pastor in chief" and urging clergy to work harder. He also spoke about his personal testimonial, religious awakening, and the loss of his son Gabriel and daughter Bella. Santorum also addressed the California Proposition 8 ruling, criticizing the decision for labeling those who oppose same-sex marriage as "bigots." The event concluded with the pastors praying for Santorum's health, safety, and candidacy.

In a groundbreaking lawsuit, a Montclair couple, Marianne and Erin Krupa, along with two other women, are suing the commissioner of the New Jersey Department of Banking and Insurance, claiming the state's insurance mandate discriminates against their sexual orientation. The mandate forces infertile homosexual women to pay for costly procedures to try to become pregnant, while heterosexual couples are covered.

The state mandate requires most major insurance companies to cover medically necessary treatments for infertile clients. However, the language used in the mandate, which defines infertility based on the inability to impregnate another person, carry a pregnancy to live birth, or conceive after one or two years of unprotected sex, is said to violate the constitutional rights of nonheterosexual women.

The plaintiffs, all lesbians trying to conceive, are seeking damages for the cost of their treatments, including artificial insemination and in vitro fertilization. The lawsuit, brought by lawyer Grace Cretcher, targets Richard J. Badolato, commissioner of the Department of Banking and Insurance. The agency declined to comment on the litigation.

Fifteen states, including New Jersey, require insurance companies to cover fertility treatment. However, the specific wording of the New Jersey mandate is particularly egregious and one of the most specific and exclusionary, according to Cretcher. California and Maryland have updated the language in their mandates to require fertility coverage regardless of sexual orientation.

The New Jersey Legislature has two bills that propose changing the definition of infertility to include a "determination of infertility by a physician." Neither bill has emerged from committee.

Dr. William Ziegler, the medical director of the Reproductive Science Center of New Jersey, said the issue of insurance coverage had long weighed on the field of fertility treatment. He stated that insurance played a big role in the type of treatment his patients were able to undergo.

Another plaintiff in the case, Sarah Mills, expressed concerns about raising a child with debt from unsuccessful fertility treatments. Mills, an elementary school teacher from Union City, N.J., has used credit cards to pay for her failed cycles of artificial insemination and anticipates taking out a loan.

Horizon, Mills' insurance company, stated that it covered "infertility services equally, regardless of sexual orientation," and that it interpreted the law "in a gender- and orientation-neutral manner and our coverage standard complies with federal nondiscrimination requirements."

After being denied coverage by Horizon, Erin Krupa appealed the claim and began paying out of pocket for artificial insemination - $6,000 for three cycles. Each was unsuccessful. Her appeal was then denied.

The Krupas worry they are running out of time to conceive. Both women are now undergoing in vitro fertilization, even though the procedures are no longer covered. They have paid about $50,000 out of pocket for treatments since they first tried to start a family.

Erin Krupa hopes that the lawsuit means other women will not need to endure the financial burden they have. "If this is what good can come out of it," she said, "I guess I would do it all again to improve treatment for other women."

The Justice Department and FBI have launched a review of thousands of criminal cases to determine if any defendants were wrongly convicted due to flawed forensic evidence. This is the largest post-conviction review ever done by the FBI, involving cases conducted by all FBI Laboratory hair and fiber examiners since at least 1985. The review comes after reports that the Justice Department had known for years about flawed forensic work that may have led to the convictions of innocent people, but had not performed a thorough review of the cases.

The review will include cases from federal and local cases across the country, often in violent crimes such as rape, murder, and robbery. The FBI is starting with more than 10,000 cases referred to all hair and fiber examiners, and the focus will be on a smaller number of hair examinations that resulted in positive findings and a conviction.

The review will include help from the Innocence Project, a New York-based advocacy group for people seeking exoneration through DNA testing, and the National Association of Criminal Defense Lawyers. The Justice Department has vowed to conduct a more expansive review and dedicate considerable time and resources to addressing the issues.

The review comes as the National Academy of Sciences is urging the White House and Congress to remove crime labs from police and prosecutors' control, or at least to strengthen the science and standards underpinning the nation's forensic science system.

In April, The Washington Post identified two District men convicted largely on the testimony of FBI hair analysts who wrongly placed them at crime scenes. Since the Post report, one of the convictions was vacated, and prosecutors moved to overturn the other's conviction and declare him innocent. The Justice Department had not previously reviewed their cases.

The last time the FBI abandoned a forensic practice was in 2005, when it ended efforts to trace bullets to a specific manufacturer's batch through analyzing their chemical composition after its methodology was scientifically debunked. The bureau released files in an estimated 2,500 bullet-lead cases only after "60 Minutes" and The Post reported the problem in 2007.

Michael R. Bromwich, a former Justice Department official who investigated the FBI Laboratory in the mid-1990s, said the review is important as the nation's crime labs come under scrutiny. He said the review is a departure from one-sided government reviews that left defendants in the dark.

The review will focus on exaggerated testimony by FBI examiners, but it is unclear whether it will also focus on scientifically unfounded statements made by others trained by the FBI, or made by prosecutors. It is also unclear at what point government officials will notify defense attorneys or the Innocence Project. In past reviews, the department kept results secret and gave findings only to prosecutors, who then determined whether to turn them over to the defense.

The FBI and Justice Department have acknowledged that nearly every examiner in an elite FBI forensic unit gave flawed testimony in almost all trials in which they offered evidence against criminal defendants over more than a two-decade period before 2000. Of 28 examiners with the FBI Laboratory's microscopic hair comparison unit, 26 overstated forensic matches in ways that favored prosecutors in more than 95 percent of the 268 trials reviewed so far, according to the National Association of Criminal Defense Lawyers (NACDL) and the Innocence Project, which are assisting the government with the country's largest post-conviction review of questioned forensic evidence.

The cases include those of 32 defendants sentenced to death. Of those, 14 have been executed or died in prison, the groups said under an agreement with the government to release results after the review of the first 200 convictions. The FBI errors alone do not mean there was not other evidence of a convict's guilt. Defendants and federal and state prosecutors in 46 states and the District are being notified to determine whether there are grounds for appeals. Four defendants were previously exonerated.

The admissions mark a watershed in one of the country's largest forensic scandals, highlighting the failure of the nation's courts for decades to keep bogus scientific information from juries, legal analysts said. The question now, they said, is how state authorities and the courts will respond to findings that confirm long-suspected problems with subjective, pattern-based forensic techniques — like hair and bite-mark comparisons — that have contributed to wrongful convictions in more than one-quarter of 329 DNA-exoneration cases since 1989.

The FBI and Justice Department have vowed to continue to devote resources to address all cases and said they "are committed to ensuring that affected defendants are notified of past errors and that justice is done in every instance. The Department and the FBI are also committed to ensuring the accuracy of future hair analysis testimony, as well as the application of all disciplines of forensic science."

Peter Neufeld, co-founder of the Innocence Project, commended the FBI and department for the collaboration but said, "The FBI's three-decade use of microscopic hair analysis to incriminate defendants was a complete disaster." He said an exhaustive investigation is needed to determine how the FBI, state governments that relied on examiners trained by the FBI, and the courts allowed this to happen and why it wasn't stopped much sooner.

Norman L. Reimer, the NACDL's executive director, said, "Hopefully, this project establishes a precedent so that in future situations it will not take years to remediate the injustice." He added that his organization will "fully assist in finding and notifying all those who may have been affected."

Senator Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.), a former prosecutor, called on the FBI and Justice Department to notify defendants in all 2,500 targeted cases involving an FBI hair match about the problem even if their case has not been completed, and to redouble efforts in the three-year-old review to retrieve information on each case.

The FBI is waiting to complete all reviews to assess causes but has acknowledged that hair examiners until 2012 lacked written standards defining scientifically appropriate and erroneous ways to explain results in court. The bureau expects this year to complete similar standards for testimony and lab reports for 19 forensic disciplines.

The Congressional Budget Office (CBO) has released a report outlining over 100 options for reducing budget deficits, with several proposals targeting veterans' programs. These proposals include capping military pay raises, raising TRICARE fees for military retirees, reinstating the ban on "concurrent receipt" for military retirees with disability ratings below 50%, narrowing eligibility for VA compensation, and tightening Individual Unemployability (IU) benefits for older veterans.

The report suggests that capping military pay raises could save $25 billion from 2015 to 2023, as military pay now exceeds wages of 90% of civilian counterparts. Raising TRICARE fees for retirees aged 65 and older could slow TRICARE costs by $31 billion, but could also discourage preventive care. Restoring the ban on concurrent receipt could save $108 billion, but could financially impact retirees. Narrowing eligibility for VA compensation could save $20 billion, but could be difficult to administer. Tightening IU benefits for older veterans could save $15 billion.

These proposals are not recommendations, but are intended to inform lawmakers as they negotiate a new debt-cutting deal. The impact of these proposals on military recruitment and retention, as well as the financial impact on veterans, is a subject of debate. The CBO report is timely, as House and Senate conferees strive to negotiate a new deal to replace automatic budget cuts of sequestration by mid-December.

Mark Williams, a prominent Tea Party Express leader and conservative radio host, referred to President Barack Obama as "our half white, racist president" in an email to colleagues in September. The email was obtained by TPMmuckraker. Williams defended his record on race and claimed to have marched for civil rights in the past. However, in a 2009 interview with CNN's Anderson Cooper, Williams admitted to using the term "Nazi" to refer to President Obama on his website. The Tea Party Express, a series of anti-Obama bus tours, has been criticized as "astroturf" or fake grassroots by other aspects of the Tea Party movement. Robin Stublen, a leader of the Tea Party Patriots, described Williams as an "arrogant, self-promoting, egotistical jerk." Despite the controversy, Williams declined to comment to TPMmuckraker.

Joy Milne, a woman from Perth, Scotland, has an extraordinary ability to detect Parkinson's disease through a unique odor. Her husband, Les, who was a consultant anesthetist, was diagnosed with Parkinson's at the age of 45 and passed away from the disease earlier this year at the age of 65. Joy noticed a change in Les's odor years before his symptoms appeared, describing it as a heavy, slightly musky aroma.

Researchers at Edinburgh University were intrigued by Joy's ability to identify Parkinson's sufferers from T-shirts they had slept in, dubbing her as a "super-smeller." They believe that changes in the skin of people with early Parkinson's produce a particular odor linked to the condition. The researchers aim to find the molecular signature responsible for the odor and develop a simple test such as wiping a person's forehead with a swab.

Parkinson's UK, a research charity, is funding researchers at Manchester, Edinburgh, and London to study about 200 people with and without Parkinson's. A diagnostic test for Parkinson's could be life-changing, according to Katherine Crawford, the Scotland director of Parkinson's UK. Such a test could enable people to go in and see a consultant, have a simple swab test, and come out with a clear diagnosis of Parkinson's. This could potentially offer more opportunities for people living with Parkinson's to get involved in research.

The research is still in its early stages, but if proven, it could have a significant impact on early diagnosis and identifying people to test drugs that may slow or stop Parkinson's. Joy hopes that her discovery will make a real difference to people starting out on their own journey with Parkinson's.

The Calexit movement, advocating for California's secession from the United States, has gained momentum following President Donald Trump's election. The Yes California campaign, also known as Calexit, is aiming to collect 585,407 signatures to place a constitutional amendment on the 2018 ballot, which, if approved, would delete California's adherence to the United States and authorize a 2019 referendum on independence.

The arguments for Calexit include California's cultural and policy differences with the rest of the country, particularly on immigration and environmental issues. California's size and wealth, similar to France's GDP, make it a potential contender for independence. However, the process to make Calexit a reality is daunting, requiring a high voter turnout and approval from both California and the rest of the country.

The main driver for the sudden interest in Calexit is Donald Trump, with his policies perceived as threatening California's preferences on various issues. The latest Trump provocation, threatening to cancel federal funds for sanctuary cities, is seen as primarily aimed at California. The state's sanctuary status, which prohibits local jails from holding immigrants beyond their sentence, is further expanding through legislation.

Despite the challenges, a successful Calexit referendum would only take effect if the rest of the country agreed, requiring a constitutional amendment with two-thirds votes in Congress and ratification by three-fourths of the states, or the first constitutional convention since 1787. Unilateral secession, as attempted in 1861, did not work out well.

The Calexit movement primarily represents a defiance against Trump and his policies, which are perceived as harmful to the environment, promoting racial profiling, and criminalizing abortion. The movement is expected to gain more interest from conservatives who view California as a haven for hippies, sodomites, and border-crashers. However, the likelihood of Calexit becoming a reality is low, but it serves as a symbol of the deep divisions among Americans.

New Jersey Governor Chris Christie has expressed outrage and sadness over newly released documents linking a senior member of his staff to the closure of lanes on a major bridge in September 2013, which caused significant traffic jams and sparked allegations of political retribution. The documents, obtained by The New York Times and other news outlets, indicate that Christie's staff, appointees at the Port Authority, and his campaign office were all involved in discussing the growing scandal and how to react to it.

Bridget Kelly, a deputy chief of staff to Christie, and David Wildstein, a Port Authority official and Christie ally, are at the center of the controversy. In an email on August 13, 2013, Kelly wrote to Wildstein, "Time for some traffic problems in Fort Lee," to which Wildstein replied, "Got it." In September, two of Fort Lee's lanes to the George Washington Bridge were closed, causing traffic backups for a week and delaying emergency responses to several medical calls, including one involving a 91-year-old woman who died after reaching the hospital.

Christie initially denied his staff played a role in the lane closures, even mocking reporters for asking about the issue. However, the emails tell a different story and potentially undercut Christie's reputation as a truth-teller who doesn't play political games. In a statement, Christie said he was "outraged and deeply saddened to learn that not only was I misled by a member of my staff, but this completely inappropriate and unsanctioned conduct was made without my knowledge." He vowed that "people will be held responsible for their actions."

It is unclear if Kelly or anyone else has been fired, as Christie's office did not respond to follow-up inquiries. Wildstein and Bill Baroni, Christie's top appointed staff member at the Port Authority, resigned in December after port officials testified in a legislative hearing that the men had violated protocols and had sought to hide their plans for the lane closings from Fort Lee officials, the police, and even other Port Authority officials.

The longer the scandal goes on, the bigger a problem it could be for Christie's national ambitions. Some New Jersey Democrats have accused Christie supporters of retaliating with the lane closures, and Fort Lee's Democratic mayor, Mark Sokolich, has called the incident "the lowest level of political venom you could possibly even make up." Sokolich has called for Christie to publicly address the people impacted by the lane closures, apologize, and implement reforms to prevent such an incident from happening again.

At least one Christie confidant tied to the controversy appears shielded from immediate fallout: Bill Stepien, the governor's former campaign manager and newly appointed state party chairman, is expected to continue advising the Republican Governors Association in a senior role. Stepien was included on several emails last fall referring to traffic turmoil in Fort Lee, but has not been linked to the actual decision to snarl traffic near the bridge.

The article discusses the arrest of controversial Indian guru Sant Rampal, who was wanted for a 2006 murder case and contempt of court. The standoff at his ashram in Hisar, Haryana, resulted in the deaths of at least six people, including an 18-month-old child, and injuries to many more. The situation was reminiscent of other religious standoffs, such as Operation Blue Star in 1984 and the Waco siege in 1993.

The article highlights the challenges faced by law enforcement in dealing with cult leaders in India, where religion plays a significant role in society. The guru's followers saw him as divine, and their reaction to the authorities was serious enough to prompt police to step back after an attempted invasion of the ashram on Tuesday.

The government sent 14 Central Reserve Police Force companies to handle the situation, but their task was not to invade with shock and awe. Instead, they were instructed to apprehend the cult leader with as little bloodshed as possible.

The article also discusses the memory of a similar incident three years ago when a large yoga meet in the middle of the capital was broken up by the Delhi Police, leading to criticism for the use of excess force. The current government would not want to risk a similar backlash.

Rampal was arrested late Wednesday night and remanded in custody until November 28. The bodies of four women and a child were found at the site on Wednesday, and a fifth woman died at a local hospital after leaving the ashram. The causes of their deaths are being investigated. Rampal denied police allegations that he had used his followers as human shields during clashes and denied all the charges against him.

The article concludes by noting that Rampal is a worshiper of Kabir, a 15th-century Indian mystic, and that authorities were carrying out arrest orders for him after he had repeatedly failed to appear in court in connection with a 2006 murder case. Officials at the ashram could not be reached for comment.

A 52-year-old woman identified as Rosa Ayala-Goana or Rosy Esparza, according to conflicting reports, died from multiple traumatic injuries after falling from the Texas Giant roller coaster at Six Flags Over Texas on Friday night. The Tarrant County Medical Examiner's Office confirmed the death, stating the manner of death as accident. The ride will remain closed until Six Flags and the German firm Gerstlauer Amusement Rides, which manufactured the coaster's cars, complete their investigations, which could take months.

The Texas Giant has reported 14 injuries since 2008, according to Texas Department of Insurance records, though the most serious were a concussion and muscle strains. Amusement park safety analyst Ken Martin noted that such injuries are self-reported and may not be entirely accurate.

Witnesses reported that Ayala-Goana expressed concern before the ride that the safety bar had not fully engaged. An amusement park ride safety inspector, Walter Reiss, speculated that either Ayala-Goana managed to slip out from behind a locked mechanism or that the harness mechanism failed and opened.

Six Flags Entertainment Corp. President and CEO Jim Reid-Anderson offered no details during a conference call to discuss the company's earnings, stating that the company was using "both internal and external experts" to investigate the accident. The Texas Giant first opened in 1990 as an all-wooden coaster but underwent a $10 million renovation in 2010 to install steel-hybrid rails before reopening in 2011.

As a precautionary measure, Six Flags has temporarily closed the Iron Rattler roller coaster at its Six Flags Fiesta Texas. Officials with Gerstlauer Amusement Rides are expected to inspect the Texas Giant. The Dallas Morning News has reported that officials with the roller coaster's German-based car manufacturer could not be reached for comment.

In a trial that began on Tuesday in Stillwater, Stephen Allwine, a Cottage Grove man, is accused of plotting and executing the murder of his wife, Amy Allwine, in November 2016, rather than divorcing her due to his esteemed role in a local church. The prosecution alleges that Allwine, who was initially charged with second-degree murder, later indicted for first-degree premeditated murder, accessed the dark web to hire a hitman, but the defense argues that the state's evidence is filled with "distractions" and "red herrings."

Amy Allwine, a loving mother, dog lover, business owner, and woman of faith, was found dead in her Cottage Grove home with a gunshot wound to the head. A medical examination revealed excessive doses of scopolamine, a drug used to treat nausea, in her body, which she did not have a prescription for.

The prosecution claims that after several plans to hire a hitman fell through, Allwine poisoned his wife and shot her with the family's 9mm gun. However, the defense attorney, Kevin Devore, disputes this timeline, stating that the state has built a case on "theories with gaps" and used speculation to "bridge those gaps."

Stephen Allwine was a marriage counselor and served as a deacon and later a church elder at a Newport Church. Through these roles, it is alleged that he learned about Ashley Madison, a dating website catering to married people seeking affairs. Investigators identified at least two women Allwine met through the website, but Devore acknowledges the affairs but states that having affairs does not mean Allwine killed his wife "or even didn't love his wife."

The prosecution argues that Allwine's role as an elder and longtime congregant at the church could have kept him from divorcing his wife, despite wishes to end the marriage. Officials with the FBI had been in contact with the family since July 2016 about anonymous emails Amy Allwine received graphically threatening to harm her family if she did not commit suicide.

Investigators who searched Stephen Allwine's computer found searches for the names of his wife's family members and emails sent through a Tor, an anonymous router used to access the dark web, soliciting Amy Allwine's murder under the username "dogdaygod" on "Besa Mafia," a website associated with hired murders and assaults. The user provided Besa Mafia with Amy Allwine's description and whereabouts and discussed two possible attempts to kill Amy Allwine, neither of which transpired.

Several months later, the same user inquired on a different dark web site about buying scopolamine, the drug found in Amy Allwine's body, using a virtual currency called bitcoin. In the search of the Allwine home following Amy Allwine's death, detectives found a document backup on Stephen Allwine's computer from his phone containing a bitcoin code, a sequence that Kreuser said would have been "virtually impossible to replicate." Investigators found the same code posted to the Besa Mafia website by user "dogdaygod."

The trial continues this week in District Judge B. William Ekstrum's court in Washington County.

The Lakota Hope faith ministry in Whiteclay, Nebraska, has initiated a fundraising campaign to purchase the four beer stores in the town, which sell millions of cans of beer annually, located just 200 yards from the Pine Ridge Indian Reservation in South Dakota. The reservation, home to the Oglala Sioux Tribe, is plagued by high rates of alcoholism, fetal alcohol syndrome, and poverty.

The ministry aims to raise at least $6.3 million to close the stores, which have faced decades of investigations, lawsuits, and protests, some of which turned violent. Ministry founder Bruce BonFleur believes the beer store owners are ready to sell out.

However, some activists have expressed doubts about the buyout's success. Olowan Martinez, an Oglala Lakota activist, suggests replacing the stores with recreational facilities like a roller skating rink, movie theater, or park to entertain young people. On the other hand, Native American activist Frank LaMere wants the state to revoke the liquor licenses and not reward the owners with a payout.

The Nebraska Liquor Control Commission is set to meet on March 7 to discuss the stores' liquor licenses, amid concerns about the lack of adequate law enforcement in Whiteclay. The local county board has recommended renewing the licenses, partly due to concerns about increased intoxicated drivers in Nebraska if the stores were closed.

The ministry's new effort is called "B.O.B.S. Whiteclay P.L.A.N.," which stands for "Buy out the beer stores" and "Promote the Lakotas as a nation." The ministry plans to replace the old liquor store buildings with a Makerspace, providing a safe place to work, access to art supplies, and state-of-the-art equipment. The space will also offer an online store for local artists to establish a more reliable income and teaching/mentoring opportunities.

The situation in Whiteclay is complex, with concerns about alcoholism, poverty, and the potential impact of closing the beer stores on the community. The fundraising campaign and proposed Makerspace represent an effort to address these issues and promote the Lakota nation.

Amy Schumer, the Snatched star, showed her kindness and generosity while jogging in Chicago when she stopped at a local Six Corners Mattress Firm in need of an emergency bathroom. The store employee, Sagine Lazarre, graciously allowed Schumer to use the restroom, unaware that the desperate jogger was the famous comedian. Grateful for the help, Schumer bought a $2,000 mattress as a gesture of appreciation. Lazarre and her daughter had just recently moved into a new apartment, making the new mattress a perfect addition. It wasn't until later that Lazarre realized her generous benefactor was Amy Schumer. Lazarre expressed her shock and gratitude, stating that she had watched Schumer's stand-up comedy and was surprised by the encounter. Schumer's new film with Goldie Hawn, Snatched, is set to hit theaters on May 12th.

A hacker, using the handle "thedarkoverlord," has leaked the first 10 episodes of "Orange Is the New Black" season 5 online, after allegedly failing to receive a response from Netflix to their extortion demands. The episodes were shared on the Pirate Bay, with a total file size of 11.46 gigabytes. The hacker claimed to have obtained unreleased shows from ABC, Fox, National Geographic, and IFC, which were stolen in an attack on post-production studio Larson Studios in late 2016. Netflix has set June 9 for the release of season five of "Orange Is the New Black," and it is possible that the streamer will move up the premiere date due to the leak. Netflix has not responded to a request for comment. The hacker has threatened to release the remaining episodes and other stolen shows unless "modest" ransoms are paid. This is not the first time "thedarkoverlord" has made such demands, as they previously threatened to release unreleased movies and TV show episodes but later claimed they would not make them publicly available. Netflix is counting on "Orange" to help it add 3.2 million subscribers from April through June, and any impact on subscriber growth and the company's stock price due to the leak remains to be seen. The FBI and other authorities are investigating the breach.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average reached an all-time high of 19,000 for the first time on Tuesday, following a multisession rally in equities. This surge comes after President-elect Donald Trump's victory, with his proposals for deregulation and infrastructure investment boosting the broader equity market. Other major stock-market benchmarks, including the S&P 500, Nasdaq Composite, and small-cap index Russell 2000, also hit record highs. Global stocks also rose, buoyed by the U.S. market's close at a record high and hopes for OPEC's support in oil price stabilization. The yuan, however, weakened as Chinese authorities set the yuan's official "parity rate" at 6.8779, breaking a 12-day losing streak. The dollar rose to 110.84 yen and the euro edged down to $1.0629. The optimism continues over the potential economic boost from Trump's policies, but investors remain cautious due to policy uncertainty.

Sinead O'Connor, the Irish singer known for her shaved head, outspoken opinions, and haunting voice, caused a stir at the Bray Music Festival in Ireland with her recent appearance. Sporting a short dark bob, eyeglasses, a belly-revealing mesh top, and a more ample figure than fans remember, O'Connor's changed appearance sparked a wave of criticism and astonishment online, with many commenting on her weight gain and calling her a "shameless blimpo" and a "pig." Despite the backlash, O'Connor seems to have embraced her new look and enjoyed her performance at the festival.

The public's reaction to O'Connor's changed appearance highlights the pressure that celebrities, particularly women, face to maintain a certain image and the harsh judgment that is often meted out when they do not conform to these expectations. O'Connor, who has been open about her struggles with bipolar disorder and her history of child abuse, has always rejected conventional beauty standards and has continued to perform and release music throughout her career.

The outpouring of criticism and shock over O'Connor's appearance is a reminder that the entertainment industry can be unforgiving and that celebrities are often judged harshly based on their appearance. Despite this, O'Connor's talent and ability to move and astound audiences with her voice remains undiminished. The lyrics of her songs, such as "Feel So Different," "I Do Not Want What I Have Not Got," and "Three Babies," have become even more poignant with the passage of time. O'Connor's continued success and resilience in the face of adversity is a testament to her strength and talent as an artist.

Autumn Veatch, a 16-year-old teenager, survived for two days in rugged terrain after a plane she was traveling in with her step-grandparents, Leland and Sharon Bowman, crashed in the North Cascades. Autumn was found on Monday and taken to an Okanogan County hospital with minor injuries. The Bowmans' condition remains unknown.

Autumn's voice on the phone to her father, David Veatch, was a miracle for many who had feared the worst. During a brief hospital call, Autumn explained that the small plane had crashed and she had tried to pull her step-grandparents from the wreckage. She stayed by the scene for some time, hoping for help, but eventually decided to leave the mountains on her own.

Autumn followed drainage down to a river, then the river via a trail, downstream to the nearest road, where she caught a ride with hikers to the nearest community and contacted authorities. The trail she followed was the Easy Pass trail, a popular but difficult hike in the rugged mountain terrain.

Autumn was taken to Three Rivers Hospital in Brewster with non-life-threatening injuries, but she was suffering from dehydration and exposure to the elements. She was admitted overnight and diagnosed with treatable rhabdomyolysis, a breakdown of muscle tissue that leads to damaging protein in the blood.

Autumn's father, David Veatch, was overwhelmed with joy when he arrived at the hospital late Monday. Autumn had one request: McDonald's. The couple's downed plane has not been found as of Tuesday morning, but information provided by Autumn helped narrow down the search area where the plane is believed to have crashed.

The search for the plane is difficult due to the rugged terrain and the many nooks and crannies in the area. The Beech A-35 left Montana about 1 p.m. PDT Saturday and crossed the Idaho-Washington border about 2:20 p.m. PDT, but it dropped off the radar near Omak, Okanogan County, about an hour later. The last cellphone signal from one of the plane's occupants was detected around 3:50 p.m.

The jubilation over Autumn's survival was tinged with regret at the possible deaths of the Bowmans. Autumn Veatch, a former Sehome High School student, continued to live with her father after her parents divorced and her mother, Misty Bowman, relocated to Montana a couple of years ago. The mother declined to comment Monday night.

Autumn is described as an amazing, witty, creative, loving human being who loves art, music, and is a quirky, sarcastic girl. Even as Autumn was making her way out of the mountains, a data trail from previous activity on her cellphone was helping searchers locate the plane's last known position.

The deficit reduction talks between the White House and Congressional Republicans were disrupted on Thursday, as House Majority Leader Eric Cantor (R-Va.) and Senate Minority Whip Jon Kyl (R-Ariz.) withdrew from the negotiations. Cantor announced his decision due to the insistence of Democrats for including tax increases in a deal to cut deficits while raising the debt ceiling. The withdrawal of Cantor and Kyl leaves only Democratic negotiators in the group, with Vice President Biden, Treasury Secretary Timothy Geithner, and other top White House officials cancelling their scheduled meeting at the Capitol. The Republicans' move is a high-stakes gamble to change the dynamic of the talks and push back hard on the revenue question, a central tenet for the party. However, it also betrays a growing defensiveness inside the GOP, as the debt ceiling gets closer with no deal in sight and pressure for negotiators to consider defense cuts and eliminating some tax subsidies. The withdrawal of Cantor and Kyl has added to the intrigue, with some Democrats suggesting they were quitting so that Speaker John Boehner (R-Ohio) would take the fall if Republicans end up agreeing to some tax increases.

The American Customer Satisfaction Index (ACSI) has published a report on car buyer satisfaction, revealing that Fiat, a brand owned by Fiat Chrysler (FCAU), is the least favored among American consumers. The survey also found that Jeep and Dodge, other brands under FCAU, are also poorly regarded. The auto industry recalled nearly 64 million vehicles last year due to safety issues, with General Motors, Honda, and FCAU among the largest offenders. Consumers rated their satisfaction with their cars at 79 points out of 100, a decline of 3 percentage points from a year earlier. The economy's improvement is causing a return to normal pricing, which may be contributing to the decline in consumer satisfaction. Interestingly, luxury brands such as Toyota's Lexus and Honda's Acura are the most liked by consumers, with scores of 84 and 83 points respectively. Fiat vehicles have received negative reviews, with the Fiat 500 being criticized for its lack of appeal and cramped rear row. The ACSI survey asks consumers about their experiences with cars they bought six months to three years prior to the survey, making it a valuable resource for those considering a new car purchase. The full report, including ratings for all 27 auto brands, can be found on the ACSI website.

In a recent interview with televangelist Pat Robertson, President Donald Trump expressed his frustration and anger over the potential failure of the Republican effort to repeal Obamacare. Trump stated that he would be "very angry" if the bill fails, and added that he is waiting for the bill to reach his desk. Trump reiterated his belief that Obamacare is a failed experiment and needs to be replaced.

Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell is currently trying to win support from several moderate Republicans and key conservatives to move the healthcare reform legislation forward. McConnell announced that the Senate will stay in session through the first two weeks of August, shortening the summer recess considerably.

One obstacle to the bill's passage is Sen. Ted Cruz, who has been insisting on an amendment that would allow insurance companies to sell any kind of health plan they want as long as they offer at least one that complies with federal regulations. Critics argue that this amendment could lead to higher costs for those with pre-existing conditions.

McConnell can only afford two defections if he is to pass the bill, as Republicans control 52 seats. Vice President Pence would break a 50-50 tie. Sen. Rand Paul is expected to oppose the bill, and many observers believe it will be impossible to win support from Sen. Susan Collins.

Despite the tough odds, there is generally a "more positive feeling" that the motion to proceed to the bill will pass next week, but no one has expressed support for the bill yet. Several Republican senators left a recent lunch voicing frustration with McConnell's strategy of keeping the details of the bill secret until the last minute.

The bill is expected to be posted publicly sometime Thursday morning, and McConnell has scheduled a special meeting of the conference at 11:30 a.m. Thursday to discuss the detailed contents of the legislation. Sens. Mike Rounds and Bill Cassidy are negotiating with Cruz and Lee to modify their amendment so that it could gather at least 50 votes on the floor.

Country music legend Merle Haggard, a native of Bakersfield, California, passed away on his 79th birthday on April 6, 2016. Haggard's manager confirmed his death, stating that he died at home in Palo Cedro, California, due to pneumonia. Haggard had been hospitalized for double pneumonia recently and had to cancel his tour with Willie Nelson.

Haggard was a pioneer of the Bakersfield sound and was involved in the Outlaw Country movement. He had numerous hits, including "Mama Tried," which was recently selected for preservation in the National Recording Registry. Haggard was inducted into the Country Music Hall of Fame in 1994 and the Oklahoma Music Hall of Fame.

Haggard's son, Ben, posted a statement on social media following his death, saying that his father had predicted he would pass away on his birthday. Willie Nelson also expressed his condolences, stating that Haggard was his brother and friend. Haggard's last interview was in July 2015, where he discussed the moving of a historic boxcar on his family's property in Oildale to the Kern County Museum to be restored.

The San Francisco City Attorney's Office has issued a cease and desist letter to three electric scooter rental companies operating in the city, citing public safety concerns and violations of state law. The companies, including Bird, LimeBike, and Spin, have flooded the city's streets with scooters, which have become a popular mode of short-distance transportation. However, the city has received numerous complaints about riders disregarding helmet laws, operating on sidewalks, and parking scooters inappropriately, creating a public nuisance.

The city's complaints come as the scooters represent a wave of venture capital money pouring into short-distance transportation tools. The presence of scooters in San Francisco has been particularly noticeable, with some residents claiming to have broken their toes tripping over them. Supervisor Aaron Peskin is working on a municipal law to regulate scooter usage, while the San Francisco Board of Supervisors has approved legislation requiring the scooter companies to have transit agency permits and to allow public workers to remove scooters from streets or sidewalks.

The companies have responded to the city's concerns, with Bird stating that it wants to work with city officials to solve traffic problems in San Francisco. The company has started a pilot program requiring San Francisco riders to take a photo showing how they parked the scooter at the end of their trip. Lime has also stated that it is taking the city's concerns seriously and plans to update its community outreach plan to address pedestrian safety, parking compliance, and rider education. Lime will also provide helmets to users, which will be available for pickup starting April 22.

The city's crackdown on electric scooters comes after a series of incidents involving the devices, including a collision between a scooter and a pedestrian that left the pedestrian with a broken leg. The city's move to regulate electric scooters is part of a broader effort to address the growing number of shared mobility programs in the city and ensure that they are operated safely and responsibly.

In a recent interview on Good Morning America, Democratic strategist James Carville offered his assessment of the current Republican presidential candidates. Carville was particularly critical of Herman Cain, calling him a "national distraction" and stating that he "is not going to be the Republican nomination for president." Regarding Mitt Romney, Carville described him as a "serial windsock," implying that he frequently changes his political positions. Carville was even more scathing in his criticism of Texas Governor Rick Perry, stating that he "is evidently not up to this" and is "in over his head." Carville added that Perry's wealth, amounting to $150 million, is irrelevant as he is "incapable of running for president." Carville also commented on a recent video of a Cain adviser smoking a cigarette, calling the adviser either "drunk or stoned." Overall, Carville's comments suggest that he does not see any significant obstacles standing between Mitt Romney and the Republican nomination.

The Internet Archive is working on a project to archive web pages as they are created and preserve links to the archived versions of pages that are changed or removed. This initiative aims to fix broken links on the web. The archive also hopes to replace broken links with links to the archived versions or provide companion links for users to view the original intended content.

Heinz Ketchup has released its first Super Bowl ad in 16 years, featuring a humorous and heartfelt spot showcasing Americana imagery and comic moments. The ad encourages consumers to share photos of themselves with Heinz products as part of a larger "Show Us Your Heinz" campaign.

In related news, mayonnaise has surpassed ketchup in popularity in the United States, with Americans buying $2 billion worth of mayonnaise last year compared to $725 million in ketchup. Chefs are divided on their opinions about mayo, with some, like restaurateur Fabio Viviani, praising its combination of eggs and olive oil, while others, like chef Stephen Jones, dislike its taste and consistency.

Mayo-hating chef Stephen Jones avoids mayo by making flavorful aïoli with whole grain mustard, bacon fat, roasted garlic, shallots, and herbs. Philadelphia-based marketing professional Craig Horwitz hates mayo so much that he started a website, holdthatmayo.com, and co-directed a mockumentary film called "The Mayo Conspiracy." He advocates for using tomato, avocado, and Greek yogurt as alternatives to mayo.

In the world of restaurants, mayo is often used in dishes that may not be immediately apparent, according to Texas-based chef Tim Love, a spokesperson for Hellman's. He believes that mayo haters are missing out on its versatility and encourages them to try it in various dishes to be won over.

In a thrilling NFL divisional playoff game on January 14, 2012, the San Francisco 49ers defeated the New Orleans Saints 36-32, advancing to the NFC championship for the first time since 1997. The 49ers' defense played a crucial role in the victory, setting the tone with hard-hitting plays and forcing five turnovers.

Defensive tackle Justin Smith and rookie Aldon Smith harassed Saints quarterback Drew Brees all day, while Patrick Willis and NaVorro Bowman shut down the running game. Dashon Goldson made punishing hits and key plays from the secondary. The defense's performance was a significant factor in the 49ers' resurgence, with a record of 14-3.

The 49ers will play the Giants next Sunday at Candlestick Park, after New York defeated the defending Super Bowl champion Green Bay Packers 37-20. The 49ers beat Eli Manning and the Giants 27-20 at home on November 13.

Cornerback Carlos Rogers expressed his relief at playing at home, stating it was better than traveling to Wisconsin and that it was not as hard to prepare for a team they had already faced. San Francisco's defensive coordinator, Vic Fangio, has developed the unit into one of the NFL's best under his guidance.

The 49ers' defense was stingy all season, not allowing a 100-yard runner or a rushing touchdown until the second-to-last game of the year. Hall of Famer Ronnie Lott praised the current team for not "giving up inches."

The Niners' offense featured four lead changes in the final five minutes of the game, capped by Alex Smith's 14-yard touchdown pass to Vernon Davis with 9 seconds remaining. However, it was the defense that got things going, with safety Donte Whitner delivering a crushing blow that knocked out running back Pierre Thomas and forced the first of five Saints turnovers.

Whitner's jarring, legal helmet-to-helmet hit on Thomas was a blow to the Saints' psyche as well as to their depth chart. Whitner was unfazed by his pass interference penalty moments earlier that briefly sent shaken-up tight end Jimmy Graham to the sideline.

In the AFC, the Baltimore Ravens defeated the Houston Texans 20-13, advancing to the AFC championship. The Ravens' defense and ball protection were key to their victory, with almost as many punts as first downs and only three points scored over the final 46 minutes. Baltimore didn't commit a turnover, intercepted rookie quarterback T.J. Yates three times, and totaled four takeaways.

Veteran defensive stars Ed Reed and Ray Lewis led the unit, with Reed sealing the victory with the Ravens' fourth takeaway, an interception near the goal line in the closing minutes. The Ravens will visit the New England Patriots next Sunday, with the winner advancing to the Super Bowl in Indianapolis on February 5. The Patriots lead the series 6-1, but Baltimore's lone win came in the postseason.

Vanilla Ice, whose real name is Robert Van Winkle, revealed in an interview that he dated Madonna in 1991. At the time, Ice was 24 years old, and Madonna was 33. The rapper admitted that it was "exciting" to have a relationship with an older woman but ended it when Madonna published her 1992 coffee-table book 'Sex,' which featured intimate photographs of the pair and images of her with other men. Ice expressed that he felt "hurt" and "embarrassed" as he was portrayed as being part of a "slutty package." He stated that Madonna claimed she didn't have sex with the other men in the book, but it appeared otherwise. Currently, Vanilla Ice is participating in the U.K. reality competition 'Dancing on Ice.'

In a significant ruling, a US federal judge has determined that the music publishing company Warner/Chappell does not hold a valid copyright to the lyrics of the popular song "Happy Birthday To You." The song, originally composed by two Kentucky sisters in 1893 as "Good Morning To All," has been under copyright since 1935, with Warner/Chappell acquiring the rights in 1988. The company is estimated to have made $2 million annually by charging fees for the use of the song in films, television, advertisements, and other public performances.

The case was launched in 2013 by Rupa Marya and Robert Siegel, who are making a film about the song. When Warner/Chappell asked for a $1,500 fee for the right to use the song in their film, the plaintiffs argued that the song was in the public domain and should not be subject to copyright fees. Judge George King ruled that Summy, the original copyright holder, never acquired the copyright to the song's words.

Mark Rifkin, one of the lawyers who acted for the plaintiffs, expressed his delight at the judge's decision. He stated that exhaustive historical research revealed no evidence that the publisher owned anything other than copyrights to four specific piano arrangements. The plaintiffs are now planning to ask the court to order Warner/Chappell to return all the money collected from licensing fees for the use of the song since 1988.

Despite the ruling, the song still remains under copyright in the UK and other countries. Intellectual property lawyer Mark Owen cautioned film-makers to exercise caution over its use, as some rights to the song may still be owned. Warner/Chappell has stated that it is considering its options following the ruling.

The song "Happy Birthday To You" has been a source of controversy for years, with many believing it to be in the public domain. The ruling could potentially undo Warner/Chappell's lucrative licensing business around the song.

A recent study published in the journal PLoS ONE has found that feeling cold is contagious. The research, conducted by neuroscientists from the University of Sussex, found that watching videos of someone's hand in cold water caused a significant drop in the temperature of the participants' own hands. The study involved 36 participants who watched videos of actors placing their hands in either warm or cold water, while their hand temperatures were closely monitored. The results showed that the temperature of the participants' right hands fell by an average of 0.1 degrees Fahrenheit, and the temperature of their left hands fell 0.4 degrees. The study adds to the growing body of evidence on emotional contagion, which is the tendency for two individuals to mimic each other's expressions and emotional states. The study also suggests that this phenomenon may help humans empathize with each other and live in communities. The research was led by Dr. Neil Harrison, a neuropsychiatrist at the Brighton and Sussex Medical School.

The article from Reactions, published on November 3, 2015, offers a scientific explanation for the perfect grilled cheese sandwich. The article delves into the chemical process of cheese making and the factors that determine how different cheeses melt when grilled.

The article explains that cheese is made up of casein proteins that form micelles, which are held together by calcium and fat. The surface of a micelle is negatively charged, causing the little balls to repel each other. However, when lactic acid gets involved, the micelles smack into each other and create chains that trap water and turn into a mess of cheesy goo.

Cheeses that age longer contain more lactic acid, lowering its pH. This means sharper cheeses have a lower pH than their counterparts, which don’t age as long. The ideal pH level for a cheese used to make grilled cheese is between 5.3 to 5.5. Any lower and cheese will release all its oil when heated, leaving curdled, clumpy clusters.

The article suggests that gouda, gruyére, and manchego are ideal choices for a grilled cheese sandwich. If choosing between mild and sharp cheddar, go with mild, as it has the texture you want, and won’t break down like its sharp counterpart.

The article also mentions a video from the series Reactions, hosted by the American Chemical Society, which delves further into the science of cheese and its melting properties. For more information on how to cook the grilled cheese once you’ve selected your cheese, the article suggests checking out the We Tried It investigation.

Former South African President Nelson Mandela is currently hospitalized for a recurring lung infection and is responding positively to treatment, according to a statement from the presidency. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) has released the first high-resolution images from its newly-launched GOES-16 satellite, a $1.2 billion satellite that is expected to revolutionize weather forecasting. The images, captured by the satellite's Advanced Baseline Imager (ABI), have an image resolution four times greater than the existing GOES satellites, allowing for more accurate forecasts and advanced warnings for severe weather or tropical systems.

The first images were taken on January 15 and released to the public on January 23. One of the images shows the moon and Earth, while another shows an ice storm that caused damage and fatalities across the U.S. on January 15. Dust moving off the coast of Africa is also visible in one of the images, as well as Florida and some of the clear blue waters of the Caribbean. GOES-16 is able to photograph the entire Western Hemisphere.

In addition to offering more channels, the ABI can provide a full disk image of the Earth every 15 minutes, one of the continental U.S. every five minutes, and has the ability to target regional areas where severe weather, hurricanes, wildfires, volcanic eruptions or other high-impact environmental phenomena are occurring as often as every 30 seconds.

NOAA plans to announce the planned location for GOES-16 in May, with the satellite expected to be operational as either GOES-East or GOES-West by November 2017. The second satellite in the GOES series, GOES-S, is already in development and is undergoing environmental testing at Lockheed Martin’s Corporation facility in Littleton, Colorado.

The release of the first images from GOES-16 marks the latest step in a new age of weather satellites, with the higher resolution images allowing forecasters to pinpoint the location of severe weather with greater accuracy. The satellite's advanced capabilities are expected to lead to more accurate and timely forecasts, watches and warnings.

The article, produced in collaboration with the Houston Chronicle, discusses the decline of the heart transplant program at Baylor St. Luke's Medical Center in Houston, Texas. The program, which was once renowned for its excellence in heart surgery, has faced a series of challenges in recent years, including an outsized number of transplants resulting in deaths or unusual complications, the loss of several top physicians, and a scaling back of its ambition for treating high-risk patients.

The heart transplant survival rate at St. Luke's now ranks near the bottom nationally, with only 85% of patients surviving at least one year after transplant, compared to 91.4% nationally. This means that twice as many St. Luke's patients died within a year as would have been expected, taking into account patient characteristics and illnesses.

The hospital has made changes in response to these problems, including hiring a new surgical director and becoming more conservative in its approach to transplants. However, the program has continued to struggle in other ways. For example, in one case, the surgeon sewed shut one of the major veins that carry blood back to the heart, leading to the patient's death a few weeks later. In another case, the surgeon stitched through the other major vein, causing blood to pool in the patient's head and leading to an emergency repair, weeks of follow-up operations, a three-month hospital stay, and ongoing health struggles.

The hospital has also faced criticism for its marketing practices, as it has continued to promote itself as a standout program despite its poor outcomes. In response to these issues, the hospital has agreed to put reporters in touch with heart transplant patients who were pleased with their care, as well as to provide data showing that patient survival rates have improved since the arrival of the new surgical director.

The article also discusses the experiences of several patients and their families, including David Kveton, who died after a failed heart transplant at St. Luke's, and Lazerick Eskridge, who suffered severe complications after his transplant. In both cases, the patients and their families raised concerns about the quality of care they received at the hospital.

Overall, the article provides a detailed and critical examination of the heart transplant program at Baylor St. Luke's Medical Center, highlighting its struggles and raising questions about the quality of care provided to patients.

The article discusses the medical term "zebra" as a metaphor for diagnosing rare or exotic medical conditions when a more common explanation is more likely. The term was coined by Dr. Theodore Woodward in the late 1940s, who advised his medical interns to consider common diseases first, likening rare diseases to zebras, which are less common than horses in Maryland.

The tendency for medical novices to make rare diagnoses is due to the availability heuristic and the phenomenon that striking and novel events are more easily remembered. The aphorism serves as a caution against these biases when teaching medical students to weigh medical evidence.

However, it is important to hold rare diagnoses in mind until the evidence conclusively rules them out. The term for an obscure and rare diagnosis in medicine is fascinoma.

Examples of misdiagnoses include necrotic skin lesions in the United States being diagnosed as loxoscelism, even in areas where recluse spiders are rare or not present, and Ehlers–Danlos syndrome and hypermobility syndrome being underdiagnosed and misdiagnosed.

In popular culture, the theme of considering common diagnoses first is featured in television series such as Scrubs, House, and Law & Order: Special Victims Unit. The Harvard Medical School and Harvard School of Dental Medicine's 2017 music video "IT'S NOT A ZEBRA!" also depicts this theme.

Other medical aphorisms include Sutton's law, Occam's razor, Leonard's Law of Physical Findings, Hickam's dictum, and the Unfalsifiable Hypothesis.

In an unrelated incident, two zebras escaped from a circus in West Philadelphia and were safely recaptured later that day. The incident caused a stir on social media as startled Philadelphians shared photos and videos of the zebras running through the streets.

The article discusses two main topics: Budweiser's heartwarming Super Bowl commercial and the NFL's dilemma regarding the Roman numerals used in the Super Bowl logo.

California Governor Jerry Brown signed a bill on October 3, 2013, allowing immigrants who are in the U.S. illegally to obtain driver's licenses. The bill, AB 60, adds California to the growing list of states that offer driver's licenses to undocumented immigrants. The licenses will have a special designation on the front and a notice stating that they are not official federal identification and cannot be used for employment or public benefits.

The bill was supported by Latino activists, police chiefs, and insurance authorities. Governor Brown predicted that other states would follow California's example. The licenses are expected to become available no later than January 2015.

State officials estimate that 1.4 million drivers will apply for licenses under the law during the first three years. The measure, written by Democratic Assemblyman Luis Alejo, will grant licenses to anyone who passes the written and road tests, regardless of immigration status.

Proponents of the bill argue that with more licensed drivers, hit-and-run accidents will decrease, and the percentage of drivers who are insured will increase. However, opponents of the bill have raised concerns about identity fraud and the potential for employers and landlords to be in conflict between complying with state and federal laws.

The bill is one of several immigrant-friendly measures passed by the California Legislature this year, including overtime pay for domestic workers and an effort to scale back collaboration between local law enforcement and federal immigration officials.

California is home to nearly one in four immigrants who live in the U.S. without legal status. The state can learn a lot about potential problems from New Mexico, which has issued more than 90,000 driver's licenses to foreign nationals since 2003. However, New Mexico has experienced issues with identity fraud related to the licenses.

Some immigrant advocates initially raised concerns that a different license in California would contribute to racial profiling. The new law bans discrimination based on the license and states that the license cannot be used as a basis for arresting someone for being in the U.S. illegally.

The bill is likely to face legal challenges, with one of the leading opponents, businessman Don Rosenberg, considering a possible legal challenge to the new law. Rosenberg lost his 25-year-old son in an accident with an unlicensed immigrant driver and testified against the legislation, criticizing it for not requiring any training or other measures to make sure the new drivers are safer.

Overall, the bill is seen as a significant expansion of immigrant rights in California and is likely to have a major impact on the lives of undocumented immigrants in the state.

In the Northern Hemisphere, an unusual phenomenon is occurring where birds appear to be intoxicated due to their consumption of fermented winter berries. The alcohol forms in the berries as they ferment with the first frosts, and birds that gorge on these fruits may get drunk more often than expected. This year, large numbers of birds in various locations, including Whitehorse, Yukon, and Duluth, Minnesota, have been affected.

In Whitehorse, several Bohemian waxwings were admitted to the Animal Health Unit after bingeing on fermented rowan tree berries. Although there's no Breathalyzer for birds, their intoxicated state was evident by their inability to coordinate flight movements or walk in a coordinated manner. The birds generally recover after a few hours, but some unfortunately die in collisions with buildings.

In Duluth, Minnesota, a large number of birds have been flying into buildings and cars due to what is believed to be avian inebriation caused by fermented mountain ash berries. Local authorities have advised that there is no need to call law enforcement about these birds, as they should sober up within a short period of time.

Scientists believe that the relatively large livers of waxwings and other berry-reliant species help them handle alcohol. However, young birds may be more vulnerable. The increased risk of collisions during this season, with or without fermenting berries, is a common occurrence. To reduce the risk of bird strikes, experts recommend adorning windows with stickers, suncatchers, or strings.

Climate change may play a role in making these incidents more frequent, as freezing causes the berries to convert starches into sugars, and subsequent thawing allows yeast to speed up the fermentation process. As global temperatures continue to rise, longer-term trends will need to be monitored to assess the impact of climate change on this phenomenon.

The display of military prowess came at the end of Putin's state-of-the-nation speech, which lasted almost two hours and covered everything from health care to the annual grain harvest. Earlier, the leader pledged to improve the lives of Russians by cutting poverty by half, boosting pensions, and creating more daycare places. On November 23, 2015, a California man named Luis Vargas was exonerated after spending 16 years in prison for sexual assault convictions. The Los Angeles Superior Court Judge William Ryan overturned Vargas' conviction after DNA evidence linked the crimes to another man, known as the "teardrop rapist." The teardrop rapist, who has been linked to over 30 rapes in the Los Angeles area since 1996, has never been identified. Vargas was misidentified as the rapist due to a similar teardrop tattoo.

Vargas maintained his innocence and reached out to lawyers and students at the California Innocence Project at California Western School of Law. After his name was cleared, Vargas was taken into custody because his green card was revoked when he was convicted of the crimes. His lawyers believe he will be released soon.

Vargas' daughter, Cristal Nora Vargas, expressed her relief and gratitude, stating that she had believed in her father's innocence since the day he told her he was innocent. She described the impact of her father's imprisonment on her life and her dreams of him walking her down the aisle and reading bedtime stories to her 7-year-old daughter.

The teardrop rapist gained his nickname for a teardrop tattoo under his eye. The rapist was known for grabbing his victims and threatening them with a weapon before pulling them into a secluded area and raping them. The attacks by the teardrop rapist continued while Vargas was in prison, fighting for his release.

Vargas' case caught the attention of the California Innocence Project in 2011. The case was riddled with textbook post-conviction red flags, including eyewitness misidentification. The prosecution's entire case relied on the wavering identifications of three traumatized young ladies. Vargas was convicted solely on the victims' accounts of the savage attacks.

In 2013, the California Innocence Project decided to test the only remaining physical evidence available in Vargas' case: the rape kit and clothing from one of the victims. The DNA test results revealed Vargas did not commit the rape, but the teardrop rapist did. The teardrop rapist is attributed to having committed 35 attacks, not including the three attacks for which Vargas was convicted.

This exoneration marks the California Innocence Project's 3rd DNA exoneration and 20th freed client overall. The project continues to work on other cases of wrongfully convicted individuals.

In the Dallas suburb of Irving, Texas, an anti-Islam group called the Bureau of American Islamic Relations (BAIR) publicized the names and addresses of over 60 Muslims and Muslim "sympathizers" on its Facebook page. The publication of this list comes after a controversial Irving City Council vote on Islamic tribunals, where the council backed a state bill that would limit Muslim influence. The publication of the list has caused alarm among Muslim leaders, with Alia Salem, executive director of the Dallas/Fort Worth branch of CAIR, stating that this is the first time she has felt alarmed over anti-Islamic sentiment. The publication of the list is far from the first Islam-related controversy in Irving, Texas. The teenager subsequently received support from President Obama, Hillary Clinton, Facebook CEO Mark Zuckerberg, and Google, among others, and his family is now seeking $15 million from the city. Irving Mayor Beth Van Duyne also attracted national attention this year, when she railed against what she described as a "Sharia Law Court" in her city. Critics say Van Duyne blew out of proportion a voluntary and non-binding dispute mediation service.
