In a significant ruling, a federal court in Virginia has supported a transgender student, Gavin Grimm, who sought to use the boys' bathroom at his high school. The court denied the Gloucester County School District's motion to dismiss Grimm's lawsuit, which has been ongoing for four years since Grimm's graduation.

Grimm's lawyers, from the American Civil Liberties Union, argued that Title IX, a federal law prohibiting sex discrimination in education programs, also protects against discrimination based on gender identity. Judge Arenda L. Wright Allen of the US District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia agreed, stating that Grimm had sufficiently pleaded a Title IX claim of sex discrimination under a gender stereotyping theory.

This ruling follows a similar decision by a federal appeals court in Chicago in May 2017. Grimm, who identifies as male, was barred from using the boys' restrooms in high school and sued the school board in 2015, claiming the policy violated his constitutional rights and federal protections against sex discrimination. The case was sent back to a lower court last year, and in September, the school board argued for its dismissal.

The judge has now ordered a settlement conference for both parties. This decision marks a significant step forward in the recognition and protection of transgender rights in education.

A woman named Jane Wilson, an academic engagement librarian at the University of Manchester, fell to her death while descending Snowdonia's Tryfan peak with her husband Gary, an experienced climber. On March 25, the couple decided not to summit as dusk approached and used only Gary's smartphone to find a route down. They traversed the mountain's west face, known for its loose rocks and steep inclines. Jane went ahead to find a suitable route and asked if it was safe. After a series of exclamations and a rock fall, Gary realized she had fallen and raised the alarm. The Ogwen Valley Mountain Rescue Team led Gary to safety, finding Jane's body over 150 meters lower down. She had fractured her skull and sustained several other severe injuries.

The inquest heard that Jane was a fit and active woman who had been mountain walking and scrambling for six years. Detective Constable Tim Bird, the leader of the rescue team, stated that Jane had fallen 20-30 feet down a vertical cliff, then tumbled about 150 meters down into an area known as Notch arrete. He suggested that the light boots worn by Jane were not suitable for such rough terrain, and she may have slipped. After abseiling two days later to the spot where her body was found, DC Bird was hit by falling rocks.

DC Bird told the hearing that the change in route was an attempt to traverse the west face to avoid the summit. He advised that it would have been better to have retreated the way they had come or gone to the North Ridge. He also noted that the smartphone app used for navigation would have had less detail than a normal map.

The coroner recorded a conclusion of accidental death. Chris Lloyd, a member of the Ogwen Rescue team, described the route the pair had taken as "not a straightforward path." He added that Tryfan is responsible for "about 30 percent" of the incidents the Ogwen Rescue team had to attend. He advised that anyone climbing the North Ridge for the first time might well be advised to go with someone who has experienced the North Ridge before.

After the incident, Mountain Rescue England and Wales urged walkers to use a map and compass in addition to electronic navigation aids. Speaking at the inquest, DC Bird said Mr. Wilson had been using an Ordnance Survey app on his smartphone. He emphasized that there is no easy way up Tryfan but there are easier routes. The inquest was told that Mrs. Wilson was a fit and active woman and that she and her husband had been mountain walking and scrambling for six years.

Eisenhower and served in Kabul, Afghanistan, as chief of staff of Joint Task Force 435 and later Combined Joint Interagency Task Force 435. An American World War II veteran, Norwood Thomas, and his wartime girlfriend, Joyce Morris, have reunited after over 70 years apart. Title: The State of Education in the United States: Many Students Not Being Challenged

The report, "Do Schools Challenge Our Students? What Student Surveys Tell Us About the State of Education in the United States," reveals that a significant number of students in the U.S. are not being challenged in school. The findings are based on a federal survey of students in elementary and high schools across the country.

Key findings include:

1. Many students find their schoolwork too easy: 37% of fourth-graders, 29% of eighth-grade math students, 51% of eighth-grade civics students, 57% of eighth-grade history students, 21% of 12th-graders, 56% of 12th-grade civics students, and 55% of 12th-grade history students report that their work is often or always too easy.

2. Students are not engaged in rigorous learning activities: Almost a third of eighth-grade students read fewer than five pages a day, and approximately one-third of students write long answers on reading tests twice per year or less. High school students also report similar issues, with 39% of 12th-grade students saying they hardly ever or only once or twice a month write about what they read in class.

3. Students don't have access to key science and technology learning opportunities: 72% of eighth-grade science students say they are not taught about engineering and technology.

4. There are racial and socio-economic gaps in understanding and access to rigorous learning opportunities. Students from disadvantaged backgrounds and minority students are less likely to have the same access to robust learning opportunities.

The report recommends that policymakers push for higher, more challenging standards, and that researchers and educators continue to develop student surveys to gain more insights into the student experience. The report suggests that the U.S. needs to do more to improve the learning experience for all students.

The report is available for download in various formats, and an interactive state-by-state map is also provided on the Center for American Progress website. The report was authored by Ulrich Boser and Lindsay Rosenthal.

A rare case of a Canadian boy developing allergies to fish and nuts after a blood transfusion has been reported. The 8-year-old, who had no previous history of food allergies, was undergoing treatment for medulloblastoma and received a blood transfusion. A few weeks later, he experienced anaphylaxis within 10 minutes of eating salmon, and four days later, he had a reaction to a chocolate peanut butter cup. The doctors suspected that the blood transfusion had triggered the allergic reactions, as the boy's body had received the protein that triggers an allergic reaction to fish and nuts. The protein, called immunoglobulin E, is an antibody associated with food allergies. The boy's allergies were temporary, and he was able to gradually reintroduce nuts and fish back into his diet after five months.

Acquiring allergies from a blood donor is rare but not unprecedented. The researchers found two other case reports, both in adults, where patients acquired temporary allergies from blood plasma. In the new case, the boy also received plasma, and the researchers traced the problematic blood product back to a donor with several allergies. Canadian Blood Services barred the donor from making future donations as a precaution.

Doctors typically ask blood donors if they are currently experiencing any allergy symptoms at the time of donation, but they are not usually screened for allergies or asked to defer donation if they have a history of allergy. The field will likely get a better sense of how common this effect is if doctors are on the lookout for the development of allergies after a blood transfusion. The safety of the blood supply is of everyone's utmost concern, but more research is needed to determine how best to avoid the transfer of allergies and how frequently this happens.

The New York Court of Appeals is set to hear arguments on Wednesday regarding a case involving the strip club Nite Moves, challenging a tax bill of over $124,000. The club argues that their nude dancing should be considered an art form and exempt from sales tax under state law, similar to theater or ballet performances.

Nite Moves, located in suburban Albany, contests the tax bill following a 2005 audit, claiming that sales taxes were paid on non-alcoholic drinks, but not on admission fees and "couch sales" for private or lap dances. The club relies on testimony from a cultural anthropologist who has studied exotic dance and visited Nite Moves.

The state Tax Appeals Tribunal and a mid-level court have previously ruled against Nite Moves, stating that the club did not present sufficient proof that it qualifies for the exemption. The Appellate Division court also found "no merit" to the club's constitutional claims.

The court's decision could have implications for other strip clubs, as some states are considering imposing taxes on such establishments. This case represents a trend of cash-strapped statehouses targeting strip clubs, which have few allies in government.

The attorney general's office is representing the state tax department, while Nite Moves is represented by Andrew McCullough, a prominent attorney for adult-themed businesses. The case has drawn support from the proprietors of "Larry Flynt's Hustler Club."

The outcome of the case could influence the debate on the taxation of strip clubs moving forward. If Nite Moves wins, it could set a precedent for other strip clubs to claim tax exemptions for their performances. However, if the court rules against the club, it could encourage more states to impose taxes on these establishments.

The American Cancer Society has released guidelines for the prevention and early detection of cervical cancer. The guidelines recommend that women begin cervical cancer testing at age 21, with Pap tests every 3 years for those aged 21 to 29. From age 30, the preferred method is co-testing, which involves a Pap test combined with an HPV test every 5 years. Another reasonable option is to get tested every 3 years with just the Pap test. Women at high risk of cervical cancer may need to be screened more often, and women over 65 who have had regular screening in the previous 10 years can stop cervical cancer screening if they haven't had any serious pre-cancers found in the last 20 years. Women who have had a total hysterectomy should stop screening, but those who have had a hysterectomy without removal of the cervix should continue screening. Women who have been vaccinated against HPV should still follow these guidelines.

A study published in the journal Cancer on Monday found that the death rate from cervical cancer in the United States is considerably higher than previously estimated, with black women dying at a rate 77% higher than previously thought, and white women dying at a rate 47% higher. The study found that previous estimates did not account for women who had their cervixes removed in hysterectomy procedures, which eliminates the risk of developing cervical cancer. The study used data from the Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System to adjust the cervical cancer death rates.

The study found that the racial disparity in cervical cancer death rates for black and white women was underestimated by 44% when hysterectomies were not taken into account. The researchers noted that the data were limited to only 12 states in the country, but the data still provided a nationally representative sample of women. The researchers emphasized the need for a better understanding of the reasons underlying the racial disparity in cervical cancer mortality.

The study adds to the current understanding of cervical cancer's impact on different communities, and experts have called for initiatives focusing on better access to prevention or screening programs, better access to HPV vaccination programs, and improved access and adherence to standard of care treatment for cervical cancer. The new findings highlight the need for more women to have access to screenings and other preventive measures, and the expected repeal of the Affordable Care Act and the closing of family planning clinics are of particular concern.

The House of Representatives passed a health care bill on Saturday, which includes a provision that restricts the use of federal subsidies for insurance policies that cover elective abortions. Abortion rights advocates argue that the provision could deprive women of abortion coverage, as insurers may drop the procedure from their plans to sell them in the newly expanded market of people receiving subsidies. The subsidized market would be large, as anyone earning less than $88,000 for a family of four would be eligible for a subsidy under the House bill. The president and Democratic leaders have long promised that their proposed health care overhaul would not direct taxpayer money to pay for elective abortions, but have yet to spell out how this will be achieved in the novel program of offering insurance subsidies or a government-run plan to millions of poor and middle-class Americans. The abortion issue has caused deep divisions within the Democratic caucus, with some House Democrats vowing to oppose any final bill that includes the restrictive provision. The focus now turns to the Senate, where some Democrats are pushing to incorporate the same restrictions in their own bill. The outcome is uncertain.

On April 3, 2017, a bomb blast occurred on a subway train in St. Petersburg, Russia, killing 11 people and injuring over 40. The explosion took place deep under the city, and authorities immediately launched an investigation to find the perpetrators. The National Anti-Terrorism Committee stated that they were looking for the "perpetrators and organizers of the terror attack."

The bombing occurred while President Vladimir Putin was visiting the city, his hometown. In the past two decades, Russian trains and planes have been frequent targets of terrorism, usually blamed on Islamic militants. Initially, police were searching for two suspects, but later reports suggested that the blast may have been the work of a suicide bomber linked to radical Islamists.

The explosion occurred in the afternoon as the train traveled between stations on one of the city's north-south lines. The driver chose to continue on to the next stop, Technological Institute, a decision praised by the Investigative Committee as aiding evacuation efforts and reducing the danger to passengers who would have had to walk along the electrified tracks.

Within two hours of the blast, authorities had found and deactivated another bomb at another busy station, Vosstaniya Square. That station is a major transfer point for passengers on two lines and serves the railway station to Moscow.

The main suspect in the attack was identified as Akbarzhon Jalilov, a 23-year-old who came from ex-Soviet Central Asia and was linked to radical Islamist groups. Jalilov had rented an apartment in St. Petersburg a month before the blast, and authorities found explosives and bomb-making equipment during a raid on the apartment.

The bombing drew widespread condemnation, with President Donald Trump stating that it was "absolutely a terrible thing." The incident tested Russian President Vladimir Putin's policy of military intervention in Syria, as some Russians may decide that their country's intervention is making them a target for reprisal attacks by Islamists instead of making them safer.

The entire St. Petersburg subway system was shut down and evacuated, but partial service resumed after about six hours. Security was immediately tightened at all of the country's key transportation sites, including the subway in Moscow. Russian law enforcement agencies confirmed that the suspected suicide bomber left the bomb at the Vosstaniya Square station before blowing himself up on the train.

The bombing in St. Petersburg marked the first major terrorist attack in the city in over six years. The city, a major tourist destination famed for its imperial palaces and lavish art museums, had been spared previous attacks. The explosion occurred in a busy part of the city, and many people were left injured and traumatized by the event.

The bombing also raised questions about the security measures in place to protect the city's residents and visitors. The city's mayor, Georgy Poltavchenko, stated that the city would increase security measures in response to the attack. The Russian government also promised to provide financial assistance to the victims and their families.

The bombing in St. Petersburg was a tragic event that left many people injured and traumatized. The investigation into the attack is ongoing, and authorities are working to find the perpetrators and bring them to justice. The bombing also raised questions about the security measures in place to protect the city's residents and visitors, and the Russian government has promised to increase security measures in response to the attack.

The article discusses the testing of children's headphones to determine their safety and effectiveness in limiting volume to prevent hearing loss. Brian Fligor, a member of the World Health Organization's working group on safe listening devices, advised on comparing the results to the 85-decibel workplace limit, which was originally devised for open areas, not headphones.

Lauren Dragan, an editor at The Wirecutter, organized a group of children aged 3 to 11 to test and rate various models of headphones. The overall pick for the children was a Bluetooth model called the Puro BT2200, which was well-liked by both toddlers and tweens, had excellent sound quality, offered some noise cancellation features, and adequately restricted volume as long as the cord wasn't used.

The battery life of the Puro BT2200 lasts an impressive 18 to 22 hours, and the wired connection is used only as a backup. However, the cord must be plugged in correctly, with one end to the headphones and the other to the music device, or it will play very loud.

Most of the other models tested relied on resistors inside the cord to reduce volume, but they sometimes failed to work. The Onanoff Buddyphones Explore and JLab JBuddies Studio were also top picks, with toddlers liking the fit of the Onanoff Buddyphones but likely outgrowing them, and the JLab JBuddies Studio being the pick for older children.

The headphones' ability to reduce ambient noise was also assessed, as children often wear headphones in noisy places like car back seats and planes. Without noise cancellation, the natural tendency is to pump up the volume to hear over the background noise.

The article also mentions that there is no governing board that oversees the safety of children's headphones, and that it is up to adults to monitor their child's overall noise exposure. The Wirecutter team tested the headphones using audio-testing equipment and found that almost all of them could produce dangerously high volume if used with certain gear, such as a headphone amplifier. The Puro BT2200 was the only model that employed a digital limiter to stop the sound from playing any higher than a certain volume level.

The fetus, which showed signs of microcephaly and severe brain injury, had high levels of the Zika virus in its brain tissues, exceeding levels typically found in blood samples. This finding strengthens the association between Zika virus infection and microcephaly.

The Zika virus is transmitted by mosquitoes, and there is no treatment or vaccine. The discovery of viral particles and a high load of Zika virus RNA in the brain samples, coupled with the absence of other possible pathogens, and a complete viral genome present "strong evidence" of the Zika virus' potential for causing birth defects.

Twenty-three of 29 mothers reported suspected Zika virus infection signs and symptoms during pregnancy, 18 in the first trimester, four in the second trimester, and one in the third trimester. Of the 29 infants, 17 eyes (29.3 percent) of 10 children (34.5 percent) had ocular abnormalities.

The funeral of Michael Brown, an 18-year-old African-American who was unarmed and fatally shot by a white police officer in Ferguson, Missouri, took place on Monday, August 25, 2014, at Friendly Temple Missionary Baptist Church in St. Louis. Thousands of mourners, including celebrities, civil rights leaders, and White House officials, attended the service. The funeral was a celebration of Brown's life, a search for meaning in his death, and a call to action for change in policing in America.

Brown's family and friends remembered him as a "gentle soul" with a deep faith in Christianity, ambitions to be known by the world, and a love for computer games, Lil Wayne, Drake, "Grown Ups 2," and "Family Guy." They urged the crowd to go to the polls and push for change, saying the community has had "enough of the senseless killings."

The Rev. Al Sharpton delivered one of two eulogies during the service and had sharp words for those who looted stores and clashed with police after Brown's death. He criticized police who pointed rifles at peaceful protesters in Ferguson and urged mourners to respect the Brown family's wish for silence on Monday and to make protests peaceful in the future.

The Rev. Charles Ewing, Brown's great-uncle, drew parallels between Brown's life, death, and Scripture during his eulogy on behalf of the family. He said, "Michael Brown's blood is crying from the ground, crying for vengeance, crying for justice." He also called for justice for other victims of violence, including Trayvon Martin, the children at Sandy Hook Elementary School, and those affected by black-on-black crime.

A new study suggests that a pesticide present in milk in the early 1980s, specifically heptachlor epoxide, may be linked to signs of Parkinson's disease in people today. The researchers looked at Japanese-American men in Hawaii, where the pesticide was frequently used, and found that those who drank more than two cups of milk daily at the start of the study had 40% fewer brain cells in an area of the brain called the substantia nigra 30 years later, on average, compared with similar men who drank less than two cups of milk per day. The loss of brain cells in this area of the brain may be an early sign of Parkinson's disease, and can start decades before any visible symptoms of the disease occur.

The link between the higher consumption of milk and the loss of cells in this brain area was not found among the men in the study who had ever smoked cigarettes, the researchers noted. Previous research has shown that people who smoke cigarettes may have a lower risk of developing Parkinson's disease, the researchers said.

The researchers also found that residues of the pesticide were present in the brains of 90% of the men who drank the most milk, compared with 63% of those who did not drink any milk. High levels of the pesticide were found in the milk supply in the early 1980s in Hawaii, where the chemical was used for insect control in the pineapple industry. The commercial sale of the pesticide in agriculture was banned in the United States by 1988, according to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency. However, a related compound can still be used today for controlling fire ants in electrical grid machinery, according to the Agency for Toxic Substances & Disease Registry.

The researchers noted that they do not have direct evidence that the milk the men drank contained the pesticide. However, they "just have no other explanation for how heptachlor epoxide found its way into the brains of men who consumed milk," said study author Robert D. Abbott, of the Shiga University of Medical Science in Otsu, Japan.

The findings suggest that diet may play a role in the development of Parkinson's disease, the researchers said. However, the new results do not show a cause-and-effect relationship between the pesticide or milk and Parkinson's disease. Rather, they show there is an association between these factors, they said.

The study was published in the journal Neurology. The researchers followed about 450 Japanese-American men for more than 30 years until they died, and then performed autopsies on them. They looked at the cells in the substantia nigra, and also measured the amount of the pesticide residue in 116 of the men's brains, according to the study.

The researchers also found that the men who smoked and who also drank milk showed none of the brain cell loss. The study adds to the literature that diet may indeed play a role in Parkinson's, and suggests that further investigation is needed to understand the potential link between dairy products, pesticides, and the development of Parkinson's disease.

The study published in the Annals of Internal Medicine suggests that drinking hot tea, particularly for people who also smoke and drink alcohol, could increase the risk of esophageal cancer by five times. The research, which involved over 456,000 Chinese adults, found that drinking "hot" or "burning hot" tea was associated with a higher risk of esophageal cancer, but only for those who also smoked or drank alcohol. The study, which followed participants for an average of 9.5 years, found that very hot drinks could make the esophagus more vulnerable to known cancer-causing agents such as alcohol and smoke. However, drinking hot tea alone was not a predictor of esophageal cancer for people who did not smoke or drink alcohol excessively. The study's main limitation was that participants did not objectively measure the temperature of their tea. The findings add to the ongoing debate about the potential risks and benefits of tea consumption, as tea has been associated with both cancer-fighting and cancer-causing properties in previous studies. The researchers emphasized that abstaining from high-temperature tea, smoking, and excessive alcohol use is the most important means for esophageal cancer prevention.

The Supreme Court has declined to hear a case brought by Republican-led states seeking to defund Medicaid funding for Planned Parenthood and other organizations that provide women's reproductive health services. The case does not involve federal money for abortion-related services, which is barred by federal law. Instead, it involves an effort by two states to block Medicaid funding for some abortion providers that also receive Medicaid funding for providing other services to low-income women, such as cancer screenings, prenatal services, birth control, and ultrasounds.

Three conservative justices - Clarence Thomas, Neil Gorsuch, and Samuel Alito - dissented and would have heard the challenges brought by Kansas and Louisiana. However, two other conservatives, Chief Justice John Roberts and Justice Brett Kavanaugh, did not. They were joined by the court's four liberals. The court's decision not to decide strongly suggests that a majority of justices, led by Roberts, would like to keep a low profile this term.

The justices' decision to stay out of the Medicaid issue goes back to discredited videos purporting to show Planned Parenthood officials inappropriately looking to sell fetal parts. Planned Parenthood, which says that only 3% of the services it provides are abortions, contended in this case that the states were singling them out for disfavored treatment because they separately provide constitutionally protected abortion services. The court's decision Monday to stay out of the issue for now leaves in place a conflict in lower court decisions. It lets stand decisions in five federal appeals courts that have ruled in favor of Planned Parenthood and other women's health service providers, and one appeals court that has ruled the other way.

Six remaining circuits, most of them in geographical areas dominated by Democrats, have not ruled on the issue; presumably, most, if not all, of the states in those circuits have not enacted a ban on Medicaid funding for women's health service providers if those organizations also provide separate and privately funded abortion services. Some 70 million Americans are on Medicaid, and Justice Thomas observed in his dissent that the court should have heard the case and resolved the legal conflict.

Leana Wen, president of Planned Parenthood Federation of America, praised the decision in a statement, saying, "Every person has a fundamental right to health care, no matter who they are, where they live, or how much they earn." Students for Life of America, an anti-abortion-rights group, focused on Planned Parenthood's role in abortions, though Medicaid funds cannot be used to fund abortions. The group's president, Marjorie Dannenfelser, said in a statement, "Abortion is not healthcare, and women's needs are better met by real, full-service medical locations, not abortion vendors."

The United States and China, the world's two largest economies, consumers, and emitters of greenhouse gases, have announced ambitious targets to reduce carbon emissions in the post-2020 period. This joint action is aimed at addressing the global climate change issue, which neither country can solve alone.

The United States intends to reduce net greenhouse gas emissions by 26 to 28 percent below 2005 levels by 2025, a target that is both ambitious and feasible. This target doubles the pace of carbon reductions in the period from 2020 to 2025 as compared to the period from 2005 to 2020.

China, on the other hand, is announcing a peak year for its carbon emissions, around 2030, and a commitment to try to reach the peak earlier. China also plans to expand the share of total energy consumption coming from zero-emission sources (renewable and nuclear energy) to around 20 percent by 2030.

Both countries hope that this joint action will spur other nations to be equally aggressive as they work to finalize a worldwide climate treaty next year. The U.S. will submit the new 2025 emissions reduction target by the end of the first quarter of 2015 as the intended U.S. contribution to the U.N. Framework Convention on Climate Change.

This collaboration marks a significant step forward in the fight against climate change and in the U.S.-China relationship. The targets themselves are important as they provide a foundation for building the low-carbon global economy needed to combat climate change. The U.S. has made significant strides in reducing emissions, with wind energy production tripling and solar energy increasing by a factor of ten since President Obama took office.

The Chinese targets also represent a major advance. China's goal to peak emissions before 2030 and expand the share of energy consumption from zero-emission sources to 20 percent by 2030 sends a powerful signal to investors and energy markets around the world. To meet its goal, China will need to deploy an additional 800 to 1,000 gigawatts of nuclear, wind, solar, and other renewable generation capacity by 2030.

This joint action is a fresh beginning in climate diplomacy, with the two countries, traditionally viewed as leaders of opposing camps in climate negotiations, coming together to find common ground and make lasting progress on the unprecedented global challenge of climate change. The aim is to create a more prosperous and secure world.

Scientists are on the hunt for a potential ninth planet in our solar system, which they call "Planet Nine." This planet, if it exists, is believed to be 10 times the mass of Earth and located approximately 20 times farther from the sun than Neptune. The search for Planet Nine is being led by Konstantin Batygin and Mike Brown of Caltech, who have found five different lines of observational evidence pointing to its existence.

One of the pieces of evidence is the elliptical orbits of six known objects in the Kuiper Belt, a distant region of icy bodies. These orbits point in the same direction and are tilted about 30 degrees "downward" compared to the plane in which the eight official planets orbit the sun. Using computer simulations of the solar system with Planet Nine, Batygin and Brown showed that there should be even more objects tilted a whopping 90 degrees with respect to the solar plane. Further investigation revealed that five such objects were already known to fit these parameters.

Since then, the astronomers have found new evidence that further supports the existence of Planet Nine. With help from Elizabeth Bailey, an astrophysicist and planetary scientist at Caltech, the team showed that Planet Nine's influence might have tilted the planets of our solar system, which would explain why the zone in which the eight major planets orbit the sun is tilted by about 6 degrees compared to the sun's equator.

Finally, the researchers demonstrate how Planet Nine's presence could explain why some Kuiper Belt objects orbit in the opposite direction from everything else in the solar system. "No other model can explain the weirdness of these high-inclination orbits," Batygin said.

The search for Planet Nine is ongoing, and the team plans to use the Subaru Telescope at Mauna Kea Observatory in Hawaii to find it. If discovered, Planet Nine could turn out to be our missing "super Earth." The most common type of planets discovered around other stars in our galaxy has been what astronomers call "super Earths" — rocky worlds that are larger than Earth but smaller than Neptune. However, no such planet has yet been discovered in our solar system, meaning that Planet Nine could be our missing "super Earth."

Scientists have discovered the partial tail and feathers of a 99-million-year-old baby dinosaur preserved in amber, offering a rare and valuable glimpse into the structure and organization of dinosaur feathers. The find, published in the journal Current Biology, was led by Lida Xing of the China University of Geosciences and Ryan McKellar of the Royal Saskatchewan Museum.

The dinosaur's tail, which belonged to a coelurosaur about the size of a sparrow, consists of eight vertebra surrounded by highly preserved feathers. The feathers had an underdeveloped main stem, or rachis, and were dark on top and light on the underside, suggesting they may have been used for camouflage or signaling.

This discovery is significant because it is the first time that scientists are able to clearly associate well-preserved feathers with a dinosaur, and in turn gain a better understanding of the evolution and structure of dinosaur feathers. Previous findings of individual dinosaur-era feathers in amber and evidence for feathered dinosaurs in fossil impressions have been limited in their ability to provide insight into the origins of feathers and their evolution for flight.

The amber sample, formally called DIP-V-15103 and nicknamed "Eva," was collected by Xing and his research team in 2015 at a well-known amber market in Myitkyina, the capital of Kachin state, northern Myanmar. The majority of Burmese amber is used in jewelry and carvings, but the modification of the sample had a silver lining: it offered a nice cross section through the tail that enabled the scientists to study the chemistry of the exposed surface.

The discovery of this dinosaur tail in amber is just one of many exciting findings that may come from increased scientific access to the amber mines in Myanmar, as the conflict between the Myanmar government and the Kachin Independence Army nears its end. The researchers are continuing to search amber markets, hoping to get lucky once again.

Audrey Parker, a 57-year-old Halifax woman diagnosed with Stage 4 breast cancer in 2016, passed away on November 1st after choosing to end her life with medical assistance. Parker's death was a result of Canada's medically assisted dying law, which requires patients to be lucid at the time of death and to give last-minute consent. Parker felt this law forced her to die earlier than she wanted, as she feared losing her mental capacity due to the progression of her cancer.

Parker's final Facebook post, shared thousands of times, expressed her frustration with the current law and called for its amendment to eliminate late-stage consent in situations like hers. MP Darren Fisher, representing the riding where Parker lived, expressed his support for Parker's request, stating that if Canadians are in favor of changes, it is the job of politicians to advocate for those changes.

The medically assisted dying law, passed two years ago, allows adults to request medical assistance to die. However, the law stipulates that people who want to die must be able to give late-stage consent, meaning they must reassure the doctor of their choice immediately before going through with it. Parker argued that this stipulation cut her life short, as she couldn't predict when her condition would worsen.

Parker's death has reignited a debate over Canada's legislation on medically assisted death, with some critics stating that the law forces terminally ill people to choose between a premature death or a painful one. A government panel is studying the existing legislation and is expected to release a report in December, but it will not make any recommendations, and the government will not be required to act.

Parker's friends and family will host a public celebration of life at Pier 21 in Halifax on November 9th at 2 p.m. Parker's final request was for the public to maintain pressure on legislators to amend the medical assistance in dying (MAID) law.

In the aftermath of the deadly school shooting at Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School in Parkland, Florida, which claimed at least 17 lives and injured over a dozen others, the nation is once again grappling with a tragic event. The suspected gunman, 19-year-old Nikolas Cruz, opened fire with a semi-automatic AR-15 assault rifle, setting off fire alarms to lure students out of their classrooms.

Three Junior Reserve Officers' Training Corps (JROTC) cadets who were killed in the shooting have been posthumously awarded the U.S. Army's Medal of Heroism. Alaina Petty, Peter Wang, and Martin Duque were recognized for their bravery and acceptance of danger during the incident. Wang, a 15-year-old who held open a door to allow his classmates to escape, was remembered as "funny, caring, and selfless." Petty, 14, was an excited member of the female color guard team, while Duque, also 14, was a football fan and regular churchgoer.

In response to the tragedy, an outpouring of support has been received by the Broward community. Comfort dogs from the Lutheran Church Charities (LCC) have been deployed to the high school to offer comfort to students and faculty. The dogs, which are trained to the level of a service dog, are available to parents, first responders, and anyone in the Broward community struggling with the aftermath of the shooting.

A GoFundMe campaign has been set up by the Broward Education Foundation to raise funds for the victims of the Stoneman Douglas shooting. As of Monday morning, the fund had received over $1.5 million of its $2 million goal. Memorial bracelets are also being created to honor the victims, and a text-to-donate option has been set up by the foundation.

Additionally, a scholarship fund has been established in the name of one of the shooting victims. Florida residents are encouraged to donate blood, as at least four shooting victims are still being treated at local hospitals. Florida Attorney General Pamela Bondi has announced that her office will cover the funeral expenses of the 17 victims. JetBlue Airways is providing free transportation for family members of victims traveling to Florida, and ride-sharing service Lyft is offering free ground transportation in partnership with JetBlue.

Alex Schachter, a 14-year-old victim of the shooting, was a member of the Eagle Regiment Marching band and is being remembered by his family and friends. A fund has been created in his memory to support a nationwide school safety commission and increased safety measures in schools across the nation.

The Broward Education Foundation's official Stoneman Douglas Victims’ Fund has stopped accepting donations as of June 30, 2018, with distributions taking place in July. The fund will be used to provide relief and financial support to the victims and families of the shooting. The National Center for Victims of Crime is advising the committee, assisting with ongoing fundraising efforts, administering victim application and vetting processes, and coordinating the distribution of proceeds from the Foundation’s official GoFundMe campaign, other fundraisers, and third-party donation sources. GoFundMe has donated $50,000 to the Fund to cover operating costs associated with developing and implementing the distribution plan.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has released a draft of federal guidelines on circumcision, recommending the procedure for male newborns in the United States due to its potential health benefits. The guidelines suggest that circumcision can lower the risk of sexually transmitted diseases (STDs), urinary tract infections, and penile cancer. The CDC's Dr. Jonathan Mermin stated that the benefits of circumcision outweigh the risks, particularly in reducing the risk of HIV transmission from an infected female partner by 50-60%.

The guidelines are based on a systematic review of all available evidence on the health risks and benefits of circumcision and consultation with experts in HIV prevention and related fields. The CDC emphasizes that the decision to circumcise should take personal, cultural, religious, and ethical beliefs into account. The guidelines also state that all uncircumcised, sexually active straight males and adolescents should be counseled by their doctors on the key risks and benefits of circumcision.

The CDC notes that the risk of adverse events from circumcision is low, with minor bleeding and inflammation being the most common complications. The agency states that complications arise in less than one-half of 1% of newborns, 9% of children, and about 5% of adults. The guidelines also state that sex with circumcised men is safer for women, as they are less likely to become infected with HPV, bacterial vaginosis, and trichomoniasis.

The CDC's draft guidelines are subject to a 45-day public comment period and a formal external peer review. The release of the draft recommendation has sparked controversy, with opponents of circumcision arguing that it is wrong to perform permanent elective surgery on a newborn. Some have expressed concerns about the potential for complications and the decision-making capacity of newborns.

The CDC's guidelines largely mirror the position of the American Academy of Pediatrics, which states that the benefits of circumcision are sufficient to justify access to the procedure for families choosing it and to warrant third-party payment for circumcision of male newborns. About 58% of newborn boys in the U.S. are currently circumcised before they leave the hospital. The CDC notes that circumcision is simpler, safer, and less expensive for infants than it is for adults.

A nine-year-old boy caused a disruption at Oakdale Elementary School in Rock Hill, South Carolina, last week. The incident began when the boy was upset after a teacher confiscated his iPad for inappropriate behavior. The boy responded by flipping over chairs, crawling under a desk, and stomping on the teacher's feet repeatedly. The teacher, along with two other teachers and an administrator, managed to restrain the boy. The boy was later released to his mother, and no arrest was made. Two other students were also reported to have been disorderly during the incident.

The document presents two separate but related topics: a scientific study on the experiences of people who hear voices and a discussion on the role of dreams in the historical evolution of religions.

The study, published in The Lancet Psychology, surveyed 153 people who reported hearing voices. Contrary to popular belief, the researchers found that the experiences of these individuals are diverse and complex, often involving internal conversations rather than the stereotypical angry voices associated with schizophrenia. Some people even experience physical sensations like tingling in their hands and feet. The study suggests that psychology researchers need to talk to more people who hear voices to understand the full range of these experiences and develop effective clinical interventions.

The second part of the document discusses the role of dreams in the historical evolution of religions. Researchers argue that in traditional societies, people treated dreams as the source of their religious ideas, including their concepts of gods and the supernatural. Dreams were considered proof of the gods and a spirit realm because they were involuntary and emotionally vivid experiences that involved the dreamer’s soul encountering other beings.

The document also presents a theory from evolutionary psychology that suggests humans are inclined to presume intelligence or agency in unlikely places, which might have helped them recognize patterns for better survival. Dreams offer a perfect setting to "converse" with a deity, as they bring forth mental stimulations of alternate realities, involve theory of mind attributions, and allow us to give value or significance to our experiences.

The conclusion of the document is that all humans are endowed with brains innately primed to daily generate god concepts in dreaming. The document does not provide specific references for the information presented.

On Wednesday, a disruption occurred at the Supreme Court during an oral argument in a patent case. A man identified as Noah Newkirk from Los Angeles interrupted the proceedings, shouting slogans against the 2010 Citizens United v. Federal Election Commission ruling, which allowed increased independent corporate and union spending during federal elections. Newkirk was charged with violating a law that prohibits loud, threatening, or abusive language in the Supreme Court building. The justices ignored the incident, and none of them commented on the scuffle from the bench. This was the first such outburst in the Supreme Court since 1983, when Hustler magazine publisher Larry Flynt was ejected for shouting obscenities during a libel case. The court continued its October term, hearing arguments in several cases, including Weyerhaeuser Company v. U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, Gundy v. U.S., and Knick v. Township of Scott, Pennsylvania.

Ivanka Trump and Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau attended a Broadway show titled "Come From Away" together on Wednesday night. The musical, which tells the true story of a group of 6,579 people on 38 planes forced to land unexpectedly in Gander, Newfoundland after the September 11 attacks, was well-received by the political power crowd in attendance, including several foreign ambassadors to the United Nations. Trudeau spoke to the audience before the show, thanking the cast and praising the story of friendship between individuals and countries. Ivanka Trump was also spotted chatting with Foreign Affairs Minister Chrystia Freeland and Nikki Haley, the U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations. The unlikely friendship between Trudeau and Trump was noted, as they had previously met during a roundtable discussion about women in the workforce in February. The play, which had successful runs in Ontario, San Diego, Seattle, and Washington, D.C., before opening on Broadway, offers a hopeful message and features a recurring subplot involving prejudice against Muslims. The attendance of Ivanka Trump and Trudeau at the show comes at a time when the United States is facing criticism for its executive action freezing refugee processing and limiting travel from a handful of majority-Muslim countries.

Spc. Hilda I. Clayton, a visual information specialist and member of the U.S. Army's 55th Signal Company, also known as Combat Camera, was killed during a training exercise with Afghan forces in the eastern Laghman Province on July 2, 2013. She was 22 years old and from Augusta, Georgia. Clayton was photographing an Afghan National Army (ANA) mortar validation exercise when a mortar tube accidentally exploded, killing her alongside an Afghan photographer she was training and several ANA soldiers.

The image of Clayton's final moments was recently released by the military and published in the May-June issue of Military Review, a journal of the army. The article accompanying the image noted that Clayton's death symbolizes the increasing exposure of female soldiers to hazardous situations in training and combat, on par with their male counterparts.

The story emphasized the importance of the partnership between U.S. and Afghan forces in stabilizing Afghanistan, with Clayton playing a crucial role in documenting activities aimed at shaping and strengthening that partnership. The article also highlighted Clayton's dedication to her work and her unit's respect for her.

The release of Clayton's final image has sparked a renewed interest in her story, with many expressing admiration for her courage and sacrifice. This incident is reminiscent of the story of LIFE photographer Paul Schutzer, who continued to shoot in his final moments during the Six-Day War in 1967.

Clayton's service and sacrifice were recognized with memorial ceremonies at Forward Operating Base Gamberi and at the Defense Information School (DINFOS) in Fort Meade, Maryland. Additionally, Combat Camera named an annual best combat camera competition after her, the Spc. Hilda I. Clayton Best Combat Camera (COMCAM) Competition.

Country singer Jason Aldean, who was performing at the Route 91 Harvest festival when a shooting occurred, visited patients at University Medical Center in Las Vegas one week after the incident. The shooting claimed 58 lives and injured hundreds. Aldean's wife, Brittany, posted a photo of them on Instagram, stating that the visit helped in the healing process. The hospital expressed gratitude for Aldean's visit, stating that it helped to cheer the wounded victims. Aldean declined to participate in a UFC ceremony to honor the victims and first responders the day before, instead choosing to focus on visiting patients. Brittany Aldean posted on Instagram, expressing her feelings about being back in Vegas and meeting the strong victims. The post ended with the hashtag #vegasstrong.

The discovery of three effigies of African-Americans hanging from nooses on the University of California, Berkeley (UC Berkeley) campus has sparked debate over whether the images are a powerful form of protest art or a racially insensitive act. The effigies, which included the names of historical lynching victims and the dates of their deaths, were found on Saturday morning ahead of a noon-time "#blacklivesmatter" protest in Sproul Plaza.

Two of the effigies were found hanging from the arches at Sather Gate, and another was discovered in a tree near Bancroft Lane. It is unclear whether the effigies were placed by supporters or opponents of the protests. UC Berkeley spokeswoman Claire Holmes said it is unclear if the effigies were a racially motivated act or not, and police are investigating the matter.

Many on social media have reacted with confusion and disgust, with some viewing the effigies as a form of "guerrilla art" and others finding them offensive and triggering. UC Berkeley professor Rodolfo Mendoza-Denton said he sees no redeeming quality in the images, while Leigh Raiford, an associate professor of African American studies at UC Berkeley, suggested that the effigies may have been created to provoke thoughtful discussion about historical black repression.

The black student union at UC Berkeley is also mystified about who hanged the effigies and why. Spencer Pritchard, a Berkeley student who helped organize the protest, said the group hopes that the effigies were placed by someone who wanted to bring attention to the issue.

The protest, which was mostly peaceful, attracted about 300 people. Many of them later joined a larger demonstration in Oakland, where 45 people were arrested. The incident has sparked a larger conversation about race and police brutality on college campuses and beyond.

The sun is preparing for a magnetic field flip, a routine event that occurs every 11 years and marks the peak of the star's solar cycle. NASA-supported observatories have confirmed the imminent reversal, which is expected to take place within the next three to four months. This change will have effects throughout the solar system, including some stormy space weather around Earth and potential changes in cosmic rays for astronauts in orbit. Despite the event's significance, it is considered routine and historically poses no threat to Earth. The current solar cycle is the weakest in 100 years, with minimal sunspot activity. NASA has released a video explaining the magnetic field reversal process in detail.

The latest Quinnipiac University poll shows a significant shift in the Iowa Democratic caucus race, with Bernie Sanders leading Hillary Clinton for the first time among likely participants, with 41% support compared to Clinton's 40%. Joe Biden, who has yet to declare his 2016 intentions, received 12% support. The results suggest a candidate struggling to put down a rebellion on her left flank and reeling from the controversy over her emails. Clinton remains the front-runner for the nomination, but the results reflect serious movement for Sanders, who trailed Clinton by a 52-33 percent margin in Quinnipiac's last poll of Iowa's likely Democratic caucus-goers in July.

The poll also shows that Sanders and Biden have a higher net favorability rating than Clinton and higher ratings for honesty and empathy. Clinton has the best scores for leadership and temperament to handle an international crisis. Biden drew a net favorability rating of +70 points, while 91% said he is honest and trustworthy, compared to 5% who did not think so. By a count of 84% to 11%, likely caucus-goers said Biden cares about the needs and problems of people like them. On the leadership front, 81% to 14% gave him high marks, while in terms of his ability to handle crises, 81% to 13% said they approved of his capabilities.

The poll was conducted in the weeks around Labor Day, from Aug. 27-Sept. 8, surveying 832 likely Democratic caucus participants in the Hawkeye State via landlines and cellphones, with a margin of error of plus or minus 3.4 percentage points. The results suggest a tightening race in the Hawkeye State, with Sanders edging Clinton in New Hampshire as well. The results come as Clinton's campaign has been working to address concerns about her email use and her seeming difficulty connecting with voters.

British Airways (BA) is facing a major IT meltdown that has disrupted over 75,000 passengers' flights, with the airline's chief executive, Alex Cruz, apologizing "profusely" for the chaos. The outage, which occurred on Saturday, has caused significant travel disruptions, with many passengers stranded in airports and some even sleeping on terminal floors.

Cruz revealed that the airline is making progress towards getting their services back to normal on Monday, but admitted that the IT issues were a "tragedy." He denied claims from the GMB union that the problems were due to BA cutting "hundreds of dedicated and loyal" IT staff and outsourcing work to India to save money. Cruz insisted that the parties involved in the weekend's problems had not been outsourced to foreign countries, but were instead local issues managed by local resources.

Cruz said there was "no evidence whatsoever" a cyberattack was behind the computer problems, and instead cited a "power surge" around 9.30am on Saturday morning as the cause of the "catastrophic effect" on all of BA's systems. He added that the backup system failed to work properly.

BA is operating more than 95% of its flights on Monday, with all of its Gatwick services and long-haul flights from Heathrow going ahead. More than 90% of BA short-haul flights from Heathrow would also be operating, while more than two-thirds of passengers affected on Saturday and Sunday would make it to their final destination by the end of Monday. Other passengers whose flights were disrupted over the weekend will have the option to re-book their flights for any time over the next six months.

Experts predict BA is facing a huge compensation bill, estimated at more than £100m, over the disruption. Passengers have been left queuing for hours in packed terminals over the last few days and some had to bed down on terminal floors on Saturday. Many complained of scant information from staff.

Cruz promised an "exhaustive investigation" into the meltdown, adding that the airline is committed to finding the root causes of the event and ensuring it never happens again. He also vowed to provide compensation to passengers and make up for any personal events that were interrupted during the chaos.

In addition to the IT outage, video has emerged of a BA employee at Venice Airport threatening to call the police on a woman who asked about the policy on customers who do not have money to pay for hotel rooms. Some experts expect the disruption to linger for several days, as planes and aircrew are returned to their positions and the backlog of passengers is cleared.

The End of Term Web Archive conducted a pre-inauguration web crawl in the Fall and Winter of 2016, preserving publicly-accessible government websites and social media materials. Meanwhile, in Punta Gorda, Florida, 73-year-old Mary Knowlton was accidentally shot and killed during a lethal force simulation as part of a citizens police academy. The officer involved has been placed on administrative leave, and an independent investigation by the Florida Department of Law Enforcement has been initiated to determine how live ammunition was used during the class. The tragedy has deeply affected the community, with city officials providing grief counseling. Mary Knowlton was a beloved member of the Punta Gorda community, having worked as a librarian and serving on the Friends of the Punta Gorda Library board of directors. The citizens police academy, organized by the chamber of commerce, aims to improve relations between officers and the community, and is part of a broader trend of such programs across the U.S. The first known citizens academy was established in 1985, and they have been recognized as an integral way to improve community relations by the International Association for Chiefs of Police.

In a controversial plea deal, Benjamin Lawrence Petty, a legally blind Oklahoma man, was sentenced to 15 years of probation for raping a 13-year-old girl at a church camp in 2016. Petty, who was a cook at the Falls Creek church camp, tied the girl's wrists, raped her, and threatened her with physical harm if she told anyone.

The plea deal was negotiated by Murray County Assistant District Attorney David Pyle, who cited Petty's legal blindness as a major factor in not insisting on prison time. Under the terms of his probation, Petty will be required to wear an ankle monitor for 24 months, register as a sex offender, and obtain treatment.

However, the Oklahoma Coalition Against Domestic Violence and Sexual Assault criticized the sentence, stating that it sends the wrong message to victims of crime. They argued that monitoring systems do not prevent sexual assaults and that state agencies that monitor sex offenders suffer from a lack of resources.

The victim's family filed a civil lawsuit against the church that brought her to the camp, County Estates Baptist Church in Midwest City, and the Baptist General Convention of Oklahoma, alleging that they failed to perform background checks, which may have protected the teen.

The Baptist General Convention of Oklahoma released a statement saying they are saddened to see the church stooping to victim-blaming. The church's attorneys have asked the judge to reconsider their decision to question the rape victim about her "prior history of voluntary sexual activity."

The Falls Creek church camp is owned and operated by the Baptist General Convention of Oklahoma and is the largest youth camp in the nation. Sen. James Lankford, an Oklahoma Republican, was director at the camp for 13 years before stepping down in 2009 to run for Congress.

The case has sparked controversy and criticism, with some arguing that Petty's legal blindness should not have been a factor in the plea deal, while others argue that the sentence sends the wrong message to victims of crime. The case is currently pending in the civil court.

In March 2014, three college students - Reese Werkhoven, Cally Guasti, and Lara Russo - found $40,000 in cash inside a second-hand couch they had bought from a Salvation Army store. After discovering the money, they faced an ethical dilemma about whether to keep it or return it to its owner. The group began a thorough search of the couch to find more money, and after a while, they found a woman's name on one of the envelopes.

They had a series of moral discussions about the money and sought advice from their parents. The parents advised them not to spend the money, not to tell anyone about it, and to find the woman from the envelope to determine if it was her money. They considered various scenarios, such as the money belonging to a criminal or being counterfeit, but ultimately decided to return the money to its rightful owner.

After some investigation, they were able to track down the woman, who was a 91-year-old widow. The woman explained that her husband had given her money each week to put away for when he passed, and she had stored her savings inside an old couch for 30 years. When her husband passed away, she continued to store her money in the couch until she had an operation on her back and went to a rehabilitation center for several months.

Upon the doctor's advice, the woman's daughter and son-in-law replaced the couch she slept on with a full-size bed. The couch ended up at the Salvation Army store in New Paltz and was bought for $20 by the three students. The woman gave $1,000 to the students as a reward for returning the $40,000. The students returned the money to the woman, who was grateful and cried in gratitude. They felt that it was not their money and that returning it was the right thing to do.

The PlayStation 4 (PS4) was unveiled by Sony at an event, marking the next generation in gaming. The PS4 is designed to provide a seamless gaming experience across various platforms, focusing on ease of development and accessibility. The system's architecture is based on an x86 PC CPU, with an 8-core combined CPU/GPU and 8 GB of unified GDDR5 memory.

The PS4's DualShock 4 controller includes a touchpad, share button, headphone jack, and a light bar for motion tracking. The system also features instant boot-up from sleep mode, background downloading, and a dedicated video-processing chip for sharing gameplay videos.

The PS4 will offer remote play capabilities, allowing gamers to continue playing on other devices, with the PlayStation Vita being the primary small-screen device. The system will also support streaming video apps like Netflix, Hulu, and Vudu.

Social integration is a key feature of the PS4, with the ability to easily upload and share gameplay videos, spectate "celebrities" gaming, and network using real names and profile pictures. The system will also integrate with Facebook, allowing users to connect with their existing online network.

The PS4 is expected to offer improved graphics, but not a revolutionary leap compared to its predecessor, the PS3. Demos showcased realistic facial detail, spectacular lighting, and massive cityscape scenes. However, no native PS3 backwards compatibility was announced, with Sony instead offering PlayStation Cloud for streaming access to old titles.

The PS4 is set to release during the 2013 holiday season, but the cost and final design have yet to be revealed. The system aims to build upon the success of the PS3, offering a more powerful and accessible gaming platform.

In the early hours of March 27, a domestic dispute between Latina Verneta Herring and Allen Dion Cashe escalated into a shooting rampage that resulted in Herring's death, the fatal shooting of her 8-year-old son, and injuries to her 7-year-old son, her father, and two bystanders. The incident occurred in Sanford, Florida.

The dispute between Herring and Cashe was first reported to the police at 3:20 am, when they were called to a gas station where the couple was arguing over the keys to Herring's house and car. The police body camera video shows Cashe and Herring yelling at each other, with Cashe accusing Herring of having an attitude and being drunk after returning from a club.

Twenty minutes later, the police were called again to Herring's home. In the police video, Cashe is handcuffed and placed in a patrol car, but he is then released after officers conclude that it is a civil matter, not a criminal one. The officers are heard saying that Herring was making false accusations and that it was the second time she had done so.

Three hours later, Herring was dead, both of her sons and her father were critically wounded, and two bystanders suffered non-life-threatening gunshot wounds. Cashe admitted to firing an entire magazine from his AK-47-style rifle, shooting Herring, and possibly accidentally shooting both children while they were sleeping.

Allen Dion Cashe is currently in jail without bond, pending arraignments on April 17 on a charge of violating parole and on May 2 on two counts of first-degree premeditated murder, five counts of attempted homicide, and a count of possession of a weapon by a convicted felon. The Sanford police have not yet responded to requests for comment on how officers handled the scene.

The shooting has sparked criticism from Herring's friend, Ladasha Beasley, who said that the Sanford police should have done more to protect Herring. Beasley stated, "Sanford PD's a big disappointment to me and to others. To protect and serve who man? Justice needs to be served."

The summary of the news article from The New York Times and CNN reports that President Trump's attorneys are advising him against agreeing to an interview with Special Counsel Robert Mueller, citing concerns that Trump might incriminate himself through false statements and potentially be charged with lying to investigators. The attorneys are reportedly urging Trump to refuse an extensive interview, and they believe that Mueller may not subpoena Trump to compel a presidential interview if refused.

Last month, Trump expressed eagerness to speak with Mueller under oath, stating that he had no collusion or obstruction of justice. However, his lawyers' stance puts them at odds with the President's public and private sentiments.

The decision about whether Trump will speak to prosecutors is expected in the coming weeks, and it will significantly impact the investigation into possible ties between Trump's associates and Russia's election interference, as well as whether he obstructed justice.

Refusing to sit for an interview with Mueller could lead to a court battle over whether the President must answer questions under oath, potentially reaching the Supreme Court. Additionally, rejecting an interview could have political consequences, as it would likely prompt accusations that the President is hiding something, and a court fight could prolong the special counsel inquiry, casting a shadow over Republicans as the midterm elections approach or beyond into the President's re-election campaign.

The University of Canterbury is working on a project to make a 600-year-old medieval manuscript, known as the Canterbury Roll, more accessible to the world. The Roll, which dates back to the Wars of the Roses, is the only genealogical scroll in the southern hemisphere and is considered a significant and substantial medieval artefact in New Zealand. The Roll features contributions from both the key players in the Wars of the Roses and tells the history of England from its mythical origins to the late Middle Ages.

A team of British scientists is set to visit Christchurch in January to carry out in-depth testing of the Roll to look for hidden information about its origins. The team will use specialized equipment to test the Roll for any hidden writing and features. The digitized Canterbury Roll will be available to the public in 2018, and the digital version will be more advanced than any other document of its kind, with a fully scrolling, online, and zoomable text.

The Canterbury Roll Project is also providing a fantastic way for students to develop transferable skills such as teamwork and coding. The Latin transcription and English translation of the Roll have been spearheaded by students at the University of Canterbury. The Roll is both an important part of European history and an important part of the New Zealand story, embodying the way attitudes to colonialism have changed over time.

The Roll was owned by the famous Cantabrian known as Nurse Maude, Sybilla Maude, and was acquired by the University of Canterbury in 1918. The Roll is visually striking and is considered a unique item in the University of Canterbury's Special Collections. It is particularly significant because it tells the history of England during the Wars of the Roses, which served as the inspiration for George R.R. Martin's popular fantasy series, Game of Thrones. The Roll is both an important part of European history and an important part of the New Zealand story, embodying the way attitudes to colonialism have changed over time.

The article discusses the unique approach taken by Gravy, an event finding app, to measure the "greenness" of American cities. Instead of focusing on energy efficiency or carbon footprint, they looked at the number of "green-friendly" events happening in a year. While this method doesn't guarantee a city's commitment to environmentalism, it does indicate a public commitment. Gravy's list of the most Earth-friendly cities, compiled since 1996, includes unique Earth Day activities for each city. These cities, when ranked based on other environmental metrics, tend to be among the greenest in America. The article does not specify the top five cities on the list.

The families of victims from the 2012 Sandy Hook school shooting are taking their lawsuit against Remington, the manufacturer of the military-style weapon used in the attack, to the Connecticut Supreme Court on Tuesday. The lawsuit was initially dismissed due to federal law protecting gunmakers from liability in shooting deaths. However, the families' lawyers claim that Remington knowingly marketed its AR-15 assault rifle to a high-risk group of young men, including shooter Adam Lanza.

In a brief submitted to the court, attorneys representing 10 Sandy Hook families argue that Remington targeted a "younger demographic" by "linking the AR-15 to macho vigilantism and military-style insurrection" to boost sales. The families are seeking to hold Remington accountable for the weapon's role in the mass shooting, with Nicole Hockley, whose six-year-old son Dylan was killed by Lanza, leading the charge.

Remington's marketing campaigns have been criticized for portraying the firearm alongside phrases like "perform under pressure," "bow down," and "consider your man card reissued." The families argue that this marketing increased the risk of the weapon falling into the wrong hands, leading to the mass shooting.

The case rests on the families' ability to prove that Remington's negligence allowed the weapon to fall into the hands of a dangerous user. Legal analysts say the appeal's success depends on demonstrating that the manufacturer's marketing campaigns contributed to the weapon's misuse.

If the appeal is successful, the case will advance to the discovery phase, during which Remington's marketing campaigns could be scrutinized. Remington did not respond to CBS News' request for comment.

The Sandy Hook shooting is one of over 1,500 mass shootings that have occurred since then, according to the Gun Violence Archive project. The families' legal argument is a novel approach to overcome the federal law enacted in 2005 that shields gun manufacturers from liability for how their products are used.

The Connecticut Supreme Court will now decide whether the families can proceed with a trial seeking to hold Remington, along with a gun wholesaler and local retailer, responsible for the carnage based on its marketing. A decision is yet to be made.

Archaeologists in Poland have discovered a group of vampire graves during the construction of a roadway near Gliwice. The graves contain skeletons with their heads severed and placed on their legs, indicating a ritualized execution to prevent the dead from rising. This practice was common in Slavic lands during the early Christian era, stemming from superstition and lack of knowledge about decomposition.

The belief in vampires was widespread in medieval Europe, with people attributing unexplained calamities such as plagues and crop failures to vampires. In some cases, suspected vampires were decapitated or hung from a gibbet, with their heads placed on their legs to prevent them from rising.

The practice of decapitating suspected vampires before burial was common in Slavic countries, and in 2012, archaeologists in Bulgaria found two skeletons with iron rods piercing their chests, indicating they may have been considered vampires.

The exact burial date of the skeletons found in Poland is unknown, as they were found with no jewelry, belt buckles, buttons, or other artifacts that could assist in determining their age. Unlike the classic image of a caped, blood-sucking aristocrat, the definition of a vampire in the Middle Ages was broader, and even people who followed old pagan customs could be accused of vampirism and executed.

In a controversial move, an anonymous group of anti-NSA pranksters have launched a project in New York City, claiming to be contractors of the National Security Agency (NSA). The project, named "We Are Always Listening," involves planting micro-cassette recorders under tables and benches around the city, secretly recording people's conversations. The group has posted some of these recordings on their website, including conversations about personal matters, work, and intimate details.

The group's intention is to highlight the issue of mass surveillance and the NSA's tactics. They argue that if people are not bothered by their conversations being listened to, they should express their dissatisfaction to their government representatives. The group has taken measures to protect people's identities, not releasing anyone's first and last names on the recordings, and deleting sensitive information such as bank account numbers and passwords.

However, the project is against the law in New York State, as consent is required from at least one person being recorded. The group claims they are not worried about legal repercussions and believe they are helping the NSA in their mission to keep the country safe. They have an email address for people who want their recordings removed, but no such requests have been received so far.

The project has sparked a debate about privacy and the NSA, with the group aiming to add awareness to the conversation. They argue that even the most mundane conversations reveal a lot about a person's life and patterns of behavior. The group has not revealed their identities to avoid legal controversy. The NSA and the ACLU have not responded to requests for comment.

Citizens are advised to be cautious about what they say in public, especially in New York City, as untold numbers of recorders could still be planted around the city. The group plans to roll out the initiative across the United States, under the slogan "We Are Always Listening."

President Obama has authorized two major military actions in Iraq: targeted airstrikes against the Islamic State (ISIL) militants if U.S. interests or personnel are threatened, and humanitarian assistance for thousands of civilians trapped on a mountain in Iraq. The humanitarian mission on Mount Sinjar began with airdrops of food and water, but may require targeted airstrikes to break the siege at the base of the mountain. The advance of the Islamic State near Irbil, where U.S. diplomats, civilians, and military personnel are located, has been a line in the sand for the Obama administration, and the U.S. has authorized airstrikes if necessary to protect the city. The U.S. military launched one C-17 and two C-130 cargo planes near Mount Sinjar on Thursday, dropping supplies, and the possibility of more airdrops in coming days has been left open. The U.S. has also increased its support to Iraqi forces and is working with Iraqi leaders to form a new government that can fight back against the threats posed by ISIL. The U.S. will continue to consult with Congress and other countries on these actions.

Title: Iceland's Tourism Boom: From Volcano Eruptions to Game of Thrones

 Iceland, a Nordic island nation with a population of 350,000, is experiencing a significant surge in tourism, with an estimated 2.4 million tourists expected this year. This increase is attributed to the country's stunning natural landscapes, increased global attention due to media coverage and tourism campaigns, and the popularity of Iceland as a filming location for TV shows and movies.

 The country's unique attractions, such as glaciers, waterfalls, volcanoes, lava fields, geothermal pools, and geysers, have always been present. However, it was the 2010 eruption of the Eyjafjallajökull volcano, followed by cameo roles in TV and film, and quirky tourism campaigns that grabbed the world's attention.

 Inga Hlin Palsdottir, Director of Visit Iceland and Creative Industries at Promote Iceland, stated that the initial response was crisis communications due to the 2008 recession and the volcano's eruption during the peak summer tourism season. However, the tourism industry and the government collaborated to save the summer season and promote Iceland as a year-round destination.

 Unique initiatives like inviting tourists to local homes, renaming Iceland, and creating the Iceland Academy, a series of offbeat videos, have further boosted tourism. Tourists are now drawn to Iceland for its connection to musicians like Björk, Of Monsters and Men, and Sigur Rós, as well as its role in TV series like Game of Thrones and movies such as The Secret Life of Walter Mitty.

 The Northern Lights, a spectacle on most travelers' wish lists, also contribute to Iceland's allure. Foreign and local tour operators have expanded schedules and itineraries, and the inventory of hotel rooms and vacation rentals has grown significantly.

 HomeAway's listings in Iceland have grown by 68 percent in the past year, while demand for stays grew 81 percent. This influx of visitors from North America is facilitated by increased air service, particularly by Wow Air and Icelandair, which offer passengers the option of an Iceland stopover for no additional airfare charge.

 Icelandair's stopover option, promoted since the 1950s or 60s, encourages passengers to experience Iceland for a few days before continuing their journey to Europe. The airline has also introduced Northern Lights-themed and glacier-themed planes to offer passengers a taste of Iceland's unique experiences.
