 Tourists flock to attractions such as the Jökulsárlón Glacial Lagoon, the Blue Lagoon, Skogafoss waterfall, and the Solheimasandur plane wreck site. However, some attractions, like the Breiðamerkurjökull Glacier, may not match the images in advertisements due to melting and changes from one year to the next.

 In Reykjavik, visitors can see the Sun Voyager sculpture by Jón Gunnar Árnason and witness geysers at a geothermal field in Geysir. Construction facades and the Svínafellsjökull Glacier in Skaftafell National Park are also popular sights. Despite the challenges, Iceland's unique landscapes and growing tourism industry continue to attract visitors from around the world.

The Senate unveiled a broad tax bill on Thursday, aiming to prevent a spike in income taxes for most Americans from January 1. The bill, which has a 10-year price tag of $858 billion, includes extensions of tax cuts for all income brackets and subsidies for ethanol and other alternative energy sources. The bill is expected to pass with the support of most Senate Republicans and a substantial number of Democrats. However, House Democrats have voiced opposition to the tax deal, urging leaders not to bring it up for a formal vote. The rebellion among House Democrats reflects their opposition to the tax treatment of wealthier Americans and their frustration with being frozen out of negotiations that produced the agreement. The White House and key lawmakers are working to clear the way for swift Senate action, with a test vote scheduled for Monday. The tax provisions in the package will cost $801 billion over 10 years, with a 13-month extension of enhanced benefits for the long-term unemployed adding $57 billion. The bill identifies no offsetting cuts in federal spending, adding to the deficit. The bill also includes a more generous estate tax provision, which has infuriated Democrats already unhappy with the agreement. The two-year cost of the plan is estimated at about $850 billion, further swelling record federal deficits. Despite significant criticism from fellow Democrats, President Obama has said the sweeping measure is necessary to help the struggling economy recover from the worst recession in decades. With unemployment at 9.8 percent, a top White House official warned Democratic critics that blocking the measure could send the economy back into recession. The emergence of bipartisan legislation indicates progress for the White House and Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid towards possible year-end passage of other major items on their agenda, including ratification of a new arms control treaty with Russia and ending the Pentagon's 17-year ban on openly gay members of the military.

In a video posted online, Chechen warlord Doku Umarov, the self-proclaimed leader of the "Caucasus Emirate" and head of the Islamist militant insurgency in the North Caucasus, claimed responsibility for the deadly suicide bomb attack on Moscow's Domodedovo International Airport on January 24, 2011. The attack left 36 people dead and 180 injured. Umarov stated that the attack was a response to "Russian crimes in the Caucasus" and threatened that similar suicide attacks would continue. Umarov has been linked to previous acts of terror, including the March 2010 suicide bombings on the Moscow Metro and the November 2009 bombing of a train from Moscow to St Petersburg.

Following the attack, the Russian authorities have taken measures to prevent similar attacks, including new security regulations at Russian airports, tighter controls outside airport buildings, and more document checks. Several law enforcement officials have been sacked and a new head of transport security has been appointed in the Interior Ministry. However, many Russians do not believe that these measures will prevent future terror attacks.

Umarov's claim of responsibility for the Domodedovo bombing will not come as a surprise to Russians, as he has previously claimed responsibility for other acts of terror. His declaration that there are hundreds more suicide bombers ready to strike at any moment will spread fear across the country. The attack at the airport, which was the busiest serving the Russian capital, resulted in the deaths of at least seven foreigners and 16 Russians. Russian President Dmitry Medvedev has sacked several officials in response to the bombing, blaming them for poor security.

On October 1, 2015, a mass shooting occurred at Umpqua Community College in Roseburg, Oregon. Armed with multiple guns, Chris Harper Mercer opened fire in a classroom, killing nine people and wounding nine others. The gunman spared one student and gave the "lucky one" something to deliver to authorities, according to the mother of a student who witnessed the rampage.

Authorities have not disclosed whether they have an envelope or package from Harper-Mercer, who Douglas County Sheriff John Hanlin said killed himself as officers arrived. A law enforcement official said a manifesto of several pages had been recovered.

Relatives of other survivors of the shooting described Harper-Mercer giving something to a student in the class. Pastor Randy Scroggins, whose 18-year-old daughter Lacey escaped without physical injuries, said she told him that the gunman called to a student, saying: "'Don't worry, you're the one who is going to survive.'" Harper-Mercer then told the student that inside the shooter's backpack was "all the information that you'll need, give it to the police."

Scroggins also said his daughter heard the gunman tell one victim he would spare that person's life if the student begged, then shot the begging victim anyway. Lacey Scroggins also spoke about students being ordered to crawl to the middle of the room before being shot. Scroggins said his daughter survived because she was lying on the floor and partially covered by the body and blood of a fellow student. The gunman thought Lacey Scroggins was dead as well, stepped over her and shot someone else.

The law enforcement official who disclosed the existence of the manifesto did not reveal its contents but described it as an effort to leave a message for law enforcement. The official is familiar with the investigation but was not authorized to disclose information and spoke on the condition of anonymity.

The official said the document was left at the scene of the shooting but wouldn't specify how authorities obtained it. Boylan, a freshman at Umpqua Community College, also told her grandmother the gunman asked students about their faith. "If they said they were Christian, he shot them in the head," Willis said, citing the account given by her granddaughter. However, conflicting reports emerged about Harper-Mercer's words as he shot his victims.

The dead ranged in age from 18 to 67 in the attack in Roseburg, a rural timber town about 180 miles south of Portland. Harper-Mercer wore a flak jacket and brought at least six guns and five ammunition magazines when he went to the campus that morning. Oregon's top federal prosecutor said the shooter used a handgun when he opened fire.

Several years ago, Harper-Mercer moved to Oregon from Torrance, California, with his mother Laurel Harper. Harper-Mercer's social media profiles suggested he was fascinated by the Irish Republican Army and frustrated by traditional organized religion. Scroggins said he was grateful his daughter survived Harper-Mercer's attack. "There's been a lot of emotion," he said. "But others don't get their children back."

The family of Christopher Sean Harper-Mercer released a statement Saturday, saying they are "shocked and deeply saddened by the horrific events," which resulted in 10 deaths, including that of their son. The statement did not provide a possible motive for the killings.

Paul Ryan, a 45-year-old Wisconsin congressman, has been nominated as the new Speaker of the House of Representatives by House Republicans. He defeated Florida Republican Daniel Webster in a secret-ballot vote with 200 votes versus 43. The full House of Representatives will officially approve the nomination on Thursday, marking the end of John Boehner's tenure as Speaker. Ryan, who has been seen as a top contender for the presidency, has pledged to unify the House Republicans and get the House back on track. He faces challenges from the right wing, but is expected to receive the necessary 218 votes to win on the House floor. The change in leadership comes after weeks of turmoil among House Republicans, following Boehner's abrupt announcement that he was stepping down.

In a series of interviews, Melania Trump, the wife of Republican presidential nominee Donald Trump, spoke out for the first time since a 2005 tape was released in which her husband made lewd comments about women. In an interview with Fox News, Melania Trump said that the comments were offensive and inappropriate, but that she accepted her husband's apology and they are moving on. She also accused the mainstream media of trying to damage her and her family by spreading lies.

In a separate interview with CNN, Melania Trump defended her husband against allegations of sexual misconduct, calling them "lies" and saying Trump was "egged on" into "boy talk" during the 2005 tape. She specifically attacked a first-person account in People Magazine, in which journalist Natasha Stoynoff said Trump made an unwanted advance while she worked on a story about his one-year wedding anniversary. Melania Trump said the story was "lies and not true stuff."

Melania Trump also defended her husband's criticism on the campaign trail of his accusers' looks, saying he is "real" and "raw" and that because of his years as an entertainer, he faced an especially tough challenge transitioning into politics. She said she jokes that her husband at times behaves like an overgrown boy, and that she saw his "Access Hollywood" remarks as emblematic of that.

In other news, Billy Bush, who was fired from NBC following the release of the lewd tape, has reportedly reached a financial agreement with the network that ends his employment. The settlement amount will remain confidential. Bush reportedly felt like a "scapegoat" following the tape and felt his dismissal was simply for PR reasons.

In a series of tweets on Tuesday, President Trump publicly denigrated Omarosa Manigault Newman, his former White House aide, calling her "that dog" and a "crazed, crying lowlife" after her allegations against him of mental deterioration and racism. Manigault Newman, in response, claimed that Trump treats women differently from men and talks in derogatory ways about minorities.

In recent weeks, Trump has also publicly criticized Don Lemon, a CNN anchor, LeBron James, a star basketball player for the Los Angeles Lakers, and Representative Maxine Waters, Democrat of California, questioning their intelligence and calling Waters "low I.Q."

The White House was unable to guarantee that no recordings exist of Trump using the racial epithet "N-word." At a White House briefing, press secretary Sarah Sanders said she had never heard Trump use the racial epithet in question. Manigault Newman, however, claims to have heard a tape of Trump using the N-word during his time on The Apprentice.

Manigault Newman has been promoting a memoir, Unhinged, and has released several secret recordings related to her firing from the White House and claims that Trump used the "N-word" during his career in reality TV. The Trump campaign has accused her of breaching a 2016 non-disclosure agreement and has filed an arbitration against her.

In an interview on MSNBC, Manigault Newman also confirmed that she has been interviewed by special counsel Robert Mueller, who is investigating Russian interference in the 2016 election and links between Trump aides and Moscow.

Manigault Newman's claims and the release of her book have infuriated the president, who has denied using the racial slur. However, a new recording obtained by CBS News seems to back up Manigault Newman's story that several Trump advisers discussed an alleged tape during the 2016 campaign. The authenticity of the recording has not been verified, but it appears to confirm Manigault Newman's claims that Trump campaign officials were aware of the existence of the tape in which then-candidate Trump uses a racial slur.

A video of a middle school student named Keaton Jones from Knoxville, Tennessee, discussing his experiences with bullying at school has gone viral. In the video, Keaton describes being bullied both verbally and physically, with his bullies making fun of his appearance and pouring milk on him. The video has received widespread support on social media, with celebrities such as Chris Evans, Mark Ruffalo, and Snoop Dogg offering words of encouragement and inviting Keaton to events. Tennessee Volunteers wide receiver Tyler Byrd has also announced that the team will visit Keaton's school to show their support. The video has been viewed over 21 million times on Facebook and has sparked the #StandWithKeaton hashtag on Twitter.

On August 28, 2005, meteorologist Robert Ricks, working at the National Weather Service office in Slidell, Louisiana, issued an urgent and dire weather forecast for the approaching Hurricane Katrina. The forecast, titled "URGENT... SPECIAL MESSAGE," predicted catastrophic damage, including roof and wall failures of most homes, widespread tree damage, and water shortages leading to immense human suffering. Ricks' forecast, considered the most dire in the history of the National Weather Service, was issued a day before the storm made landfall in New Orleans. The forecast, now in the Smithsonian Museum of American History, was a result of Ricks' personal experience surviving Hurricanes Betsy and Camille. Despite the devastating forecast, Ricks felt a sense of responsibility to warn people of the impending disaster. The forecast was accurate, and Ricks, a lifelong resident of New Orleans, returned to work alongside colleagues who had lost their homes and were wearing the same clothes they wore during the storm. Ricks' forecast is now recognized as a heroic act that helped save lives.

"Water for Elephants," a film adaptation of Sara Gruen's novel, fails to capture the quirky charm and period atmosphere of the source material. Directed by Francis Lawrence, the film is criticized for its squeamish attitude towards gritty circus life and overuse of James Newton Howard's musical score. The novel's central character, Rosie, a gentle elephant who understands Polish, is a heroine for all seasons in the book, but in the film, her connection with the audience is barely felt. The romantic chemistry between leads Reese Witherspoon and Robert Pattinson is nil, and the film's monotonous tone lacks the necessary cathartic release. The film is rated PG-13 and opens nationwide on April 21, 2011.

Richard Dunn, a creative individual, spent his overnight wait at Las Vegas' McCarran Airport filming a unique music video for Celine Dion's 1996 hit "All By Myself." Using only his iPhone, a wheelchair, and a water bottle, Dunn ingeniously repurposed the airport's escalators and moving walkways to create various shots. He taped his iPhone to the wheelchair and computer bag handles, and used different items to adjust angles. For the escalator shot, he had to sprint up the steps to avoid his bag falling back down.

Dunn also paid homage to the 1983 film Flashdance by recreating the iconic waterfall silhouette shot using a water bottle. The video, uploaded on Vimeo, has already garnered nearly 500,000 views. Remarkably, Celine Dion has expressed interest in meeting the man behind the viral video. This creative endeavor showcases Dunn's resourcefulness and passion for music and pop culture.

The events in Charlottesville, Virginia, on August 12, 2017, were marked by violence and tragedy. A white nationalist rally was held in the city, which led to clashes between the nationalists and counter-protesters. Three people died during the day, including a 32-year-old woman who was killed when a car plowed into a crowd of protesters. The driver, James Alex Fields Jr., a 20-year-old from Ohio, was charged with second-degree murder. Two Virginia state troopers also died when their helicopter crashed in the woods on the outskirts of town.

Three more men were arrested in connection to the violent clashes, including Troy Dunigan, Jacob L. Smith, and James M. O'Brien. U.S. officials opened a civil rights investigation into the circumstances of the car attack. President Donald Trump tweeted about the violence, calling for peace and condemning hate.

The organizer of the rally, Jason Kessler, disavowed the violence and encouraged attendees to leave town after authorities declared an unlawful assembly and police ordered people to disperse. First Lady Melania Trump also called for peace. The NHL's Detroit Red Wings denounced the use of their logo at the rally and are considering legal action to stop it.

Following the car incident, a suspect, James Alex Fields of Maumee, Ohio, was arrested and held without bond at Albemarle-Charlottesville Regional Jail. He is facing charges of second-degree murder and three counts of malicious wounding. Vigils were held for the victims in McGuffey Park and on the Downtown Mall. The Richmond FBI Office also opened a civil rights investigation into the deadly car attack.

In a heated encounter at a Senate Intelligence Committee hearing, InfoWars host Alex Jones clashed with Senator Marco Rubio (R-Fla.). Jones, who was banned from Twitter, YouTube, and Facebook, made a surprise appearance at the hearing and approached Rubio during a recess, accusing the U.S. of censorship akin to China's. The exchange escalated when Jones touched Rubio's shoulder, prompting the senator to warn him not to do so again. Jones continued to taunt Rubio, calling him a "little gangster thug" and a "frat boy." Rubio responded by saying he would "take care of" Jones, and Jones later insinuated that Rubio had threatened to physically harm him. The incident occurred as Facebook COO Sheryl Sandberg and Twitter CEO Jack Dorsey testified before the committee about foreign interference on social media. Jones livestreamed his entrance into the building and took a seat in the first row of the hearing room, sitting close to the tech executives. The incident highlights the ongoing tension between technology companies and conservative critics who accuse them of bias.

The document discusses the midterm elections in the United States, focusing on the potential outcomes for the Democratic Party and President Donald Trump. The article suggests that Trump is distancing himself from the possibility of a Republican defeat in the elections, stating that he sees the midterms as not a referendum on himself but rather as a prelude to his 2020 reelection bid. Trump is reportedly telling confidants that he holds House Speaker Paul Ryan and Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell responsible for protecting their majorities in Congress.

The article also mentions that Trump is poised to shift the blame for any Democratic takeover of the House on Nov. 6 down Pennsylvania Avenue, with aides anticipating lots of unfiltered, early-morning tweets casting blame on everyone but the president. The themes for Trump's potential response to a Democratic victory are predicted to include claims that he wasn't on the ballot, that people didn't fully appreciate his policies, and that the media opposed him.

The document also discusses the Democratic Party's efforts to tamp down expectations for a "blue wave" two weeks before the midterm elections, as key races in the House tighten and winning back the Senate majority looks increasingly out of reach. Democratic National Committee chairman Tom Perez and Senator Bernie Sanders have both stated that they don't believe in a blue wave.

The article also mentions that President Trump has escalated his immigration rhetoric at a midterm rally in Texas, falsely accusing Democrats of "encouraging millions of illegal aliens to break our laws, violate our borders, and overwhelm our nation." Trump is seeking to drive Republican turnout with his hard-line immigration policies, targeting a migrant caravan heading to the U.S. southern border.

The document also discusses the early voting turnout in Houston, Texas, where thousands of people were camped out at a key early voting location hours before voting began. The article also mentions that Republican-affiliated voters have outpaced Democratic-affiliated voters in early voting in seven closely watched states, according to data provided by TargetSmart and independently analyzed by the NBC News Data Analytics Lab. The states in question are Arizona, Florida, Georgia, Indiana, Montana, Tennessee, and Texas, with only Nevada showing Democratic-affiliated voters exceeding Republican-affiliated voters so far in early voting. The data suggests robust enthusiasm among early Republican voters that could put a dent in Democratic hopes for a "blue wave" in next month's midterm elections.

The shooting at Santa Fe High School in Texas left 10 people dead, most of them students, and 10 others wounded. The suspect, a 17-year-old student named Dimitrios Pagourtzis, has been charged with capital murder. He is believed to have used a shotgun and a .38-revolver, both of which were legally owned by his father. The shooting occurred on May 18, 2018, and was the deadliest school shooting in the United States since the massacre at Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School in Parkland, Florida in February. The victims included a 15-year-old freshman named Kyle McLeod, a 15-year-old student named Sabika Sheikh who was an exchange student from Pakistan, and a substitute teacher named Cynthia Tisdale. The shooting sparked calls for gun control and increased school security measures. President Donald Trump offered his condolences and pledged to work with Texas Governor Greg Abbott to provide all appropriate federal assistance. Vice President Mike Pence also expressed his sympathies. The shooting also led to the cancellation of the premiere of the second season of the Netflix show "13 Reasons Why."

The Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) has suspended trading of Cynk Technology Corp., a social network operator with no revenue, assets, or full-time employees, due to concerns about the accuracy and adequacy of information in the marketplace and potentially manipulative transactions. The SEC's suspension follows a halt by the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority and a "buyer beware" warning by OTC Markets Group Inc., which runs venues for trading penny stocks.

Cynk's stock price has skyrocketed since mid-June, rising as much as 36,000% from May 15 to its intraday high on July 17. The surge may have occurred due to difficulty in shorting the stock and brokerage compliance systems preventing owners from selling after the suspicious jump in price.

Cynk's headquarters are listed as being in Belize City, Belize, but the Matalon office building, where the company claims to be located, does not have a Suite 400, and there is no main company with the name Cynk Technology. The company's website, Introbiz.com, is registered through a Scottsdale, Arizona-based proxy company and offers services to buy the contact information of various types of people, including celebrities such as Nicole Kidman and Johnny Depp.

The SEC is investigating how Cynk Technology Corp. was able to achieve a $6 billion valuation despite reporting zero assets, no revenue, and one employee. The investigation is ongoing, and further details have not been disclosed.

In a series of interviews on Sunday, several political figures weighed in on various issues. Treasury Secretary Timothy Geithner criticized Mitt Romney's claim that the majority of jobs lost under the Obama administration were among women, calling it a "ridiculous way" of looking at the country's economic challenges. Republican National Committee Chairman Reince Priebus dismissed President Barack Obama's proposed Buffett Rule as insignificant in addressing the budget deficit.

Rep. Darrell Issa predicted that the Secret Service scandal that occurred during Obama's trip to Colombia was not an isolated incident. He suggested that the investigation would focus on how such incidents have happened in the past and questioned whether the entire organization needed changes to ensure the safety of government officials. Eleven Secret Service personnel and five military members were reported to be involved in the scandal involving local prostitutes.

Rep. Michele Bachmann attacked Hilary Rosen for her remarks that Ann Romney has "never worked a day in her life." Bachmann defended Mitt Romney and engaged in a sharp exchange with Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand (D-N.Y.) over their respective parties' records affecting women, particularly on the issue of contraception. Bachmann indicated that she is seriously considering endorsing Romney.

In other news, the Secret Service is facing criticism following the Colombia scandal, with concerns about the agency's culture and the safety of government officials. The Buffett Rule, a proposed minimum tax rate on millionaires, is also a topic of debate, with some arguing it won't significantly reduce the budget deficit. The economy, jobs, women's issues, and the Secret Service scandal are all hot topics in the ongoing presidential campaign.

Marco Lavoie, a 44-year-old experienced outdoorsman, was rescued after spending over three months in the wilderness of northwestern Quebec, where he survived a bear attack and faced extreme conditions. The bear reportedly ate Lavoie's food and destroyed his equipment, leaving him without essential resources. Lavoie's German shepherd protected him during the attack but did not survive.

Lavoie began his adventure on July 16, and his family reported him missing on October 21 after too much time had passed without his return. Police conducted searches for eight days, but they could not locate him due to harsh weather conditions. On Wednesday, rescuers in a helicopter finally spotted Lavoie, but they could not land safely, so officers had to hike in to pick him up and carry him more than a mile to the chopper.

Upon finding Lavoie, authorities reported that he was barely able to speak and drink water due to his critical condition. He suffered from hypothermia, dehydration, and starvation, and had lost about half of his body weight. Lavoie made the heartbreaking decision to kill and eat his beloved German shepherd to stay alive.

Survival experts have praised Lavoie for his determination and good decisions that helped him survive the ordeal. They noted that after 30 days in the wilderness with no food, Lavoie's body would have gone into shock from starvation, and he would have craved non-traditional food sources such as slugs and bugs.

Lavoie is currently hospitalized in critical condition, and police are waiting for him to recover before continuing their interview to learn more about his experience and the measures he took to survive. The incident serves as a reminder of the dangers of venturing into remote wilderness areas without proper preparation and equipment.

The article, titled "The Terrorist Inside My Husband's Brain," is a personal account by Susan Schneider Williams, the wife of the late Robin Williams, who passed away in 2014 due to Lewy body disease (LBD). The author shares her husband's struggle with the little-known neurological disorder, which caused symptoms such as constipation, urinary difficulty, heartburn, insomnia, and a poor sense of smell, among others.

Robin Williams' case was particularly severe, with about 40% loss of dopamine neurons and Lewy bodies throughout his entire brain and brainstem. His diagnosis came too late, and he took his own life three months after his death. Susan Schneider Williams emphasizes that almost 1.5 million people in the US are suffering from similar neurological diseases.

The author describes the loving relationship she and Robin shared, which helped them navigate the challenges of life together. However, when LBD began sending a "firestorm of symptoms" their way, their foundation of friendship and love became their armor.

The story details Robin's decline, including his struggle with fear and anxiety, memory loss, and paranoia. He was diagnosed with Parkinson's disease (PD) in May 2014, but it was later determined that he had diffuse LBD. Despite his best efforts, including therapy, physical therapy, and self-hypnosis techniques, Robin's symptoms continued to worsen.

Susan Schneider Williams' hope is that sharing her husband's story will help those working in the field of neurology understand the impact of these diseases on patients and their families. She serves on the Board of Directors for the American Brain Foundation and encourages continued research and discovery towards cures for brain diseases.

The concept of digital natives, individuals born after 1980 who are allegedly more adept at technology compared to older generations, has been widely debated. The term was coined by Marc Prensky in 2001, and since then, it has gained widespread attention, with notable figures like Bill Gates and Rupert Murdoch using it. However, a recent editorial in Nature and a paper published in Teaching and Teacher Education argue that the idea of digital natives is a myth.

The paper published in Teaching and Teacher Education claims that there is no evidence to suggest that digital natives are more tech-savvy or good at multitasking than older generations. Research has shown that millennials do not necessarily possess special skills at basic computer programs compared to older generations, and multitasking is neither a special domain of the young nor an effective way to get good results for virtually anyone.

The idea of digital natives has influenced various aspects of society, including education and corporate work environments. However, if the idea of digital natives is a myth, it raises questions about the validity of the assumptions that underpin these changes.

Jean Twenge, a professor of psychology at San Diego State University, argues that categorizing people into distinct generations can be useful for certain things. She points out that millennials show significant differences from older peers in terms of their workplace preferences, life goals, religious participation, alcohol and drug use, and trust in institutions. However, she emphasizes that the way people learn won't change so quickly.

A better approach might be to rethink how we define generations. Instead of focusing on the idea of digital natives, it may be more productive to recognize and understand the unique characteristics and differences that define each generation, while acknowledging that basic human cognition remains consistent across generations.

Marc Prensky, the originator of the digital natives concept, has largely moved on from using this metaphor and now focuses on finding "Digital Wisdom" together, emphasizing the importance of mutual respect and collaboration between digital immigrants and natives.

The Tomah VA Medical Center in Wisconsin has announced that nearly 600 veterans may have been infected with Hepatitis B, Hepatitis C, or HIV due to a dentist's violation of infection control procedures. The dentist, who used his own equipment and reused it without proper sterilization, has been removed from patient care and is now working in an administrative role. The VA is offering free screenings to those veterans and will provide free medical treatment to those who test positive for an infection. This incident is not the first time the Tomah VA has come under fire for its medical practices, as it has previously been investigated for allegations of over-prescribing prescription painkillers to patients. The VA is currently reviewing patient records and contacting those who may be affected. The dentist's actions were found to be purposeful and against VA regulations, and the case has been referred to the inspector general for assessment of any criminal charges. The news has alarmed many veterans in Western Wisconsin, with some expressing concerns about the level of care provided at the Tomah VA.

The phone-hacking trial in London revealed that Rupert Murdoch's 'News of the World' intercepted private voicemails of Kate Middleton and Prince Harry, allegedly gaining embarrassing personal details about them. This is the first time the Murdoch media empire has been accused of illegally accessing a member of the royal family's phone. The court heard that a series of messages between Middleton and Prince William, including one where William calls her "babykins," were unearthed as part of the police investigation. The jury was told about eight voicemail messages recorded by Glenn Mulcaire, a private investigator who pleaded guilty to phone hacking earlier this year. The trial involves former News of the World editors Rebekah Brooks, Andy Coulson, and five others, who are accused of conspiring to intercept communications without lawful authority between October 2000 and August 2006. The allegations are part of a series of damning claims of corrupt and illegal practices that the prosecution says were endemic at the News of the World. The trial is ongoing.

The study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences suggests that oxytocin, often referred to as the "love hormone," may help individuals with autism spectrum disorders (ASD) improve their social interactions. The study, led by Angela Sirigu from France's Center of Cognitive Neuroscience, involved 13 adults with high-functioning autism or Asperger's syndrome. The participants were given a nasal spray containing oxytocin, and their social behavior was observed. The results showed significant improvement in social tasks, such as making eye contact and responding to others in a ball tossing game.

The study's findings are promising, as they suggest a potential therapeutic use of oxytocin for individuals with ASD. If confirmed, early administration of oxytocin could potentially help children with autism develop more normally. However, more research is needed to confirm the findings and explore the long-term effects and safety of using oxytocin as a treatment.

Oxytocin is a hormone that plays a key role in social interaction, promoting maternal behavior and monogamy in animals. Previous studies have found that people with autism who received oxytocin intravenously were less likely to engage in repetitive behavior and were more able to identify emotions in voices. The latest study adds to the growing body of evidence indicating that oxytocin could lead to ways to help people with autism function better.

Advocates for families with children with autism welcomed the findings, as many families have already been using oxytocin as an "alternative" therapy with reported improvement. However, it is important to note that more research is needed on children and additional patients to ensure the safety and effectiveness of oxytocin as a treatment for autism.

Target has announced the launch of a new line of affordable wines called California Roots, priced at $5 per bottle. The collection includes five blends made from California grapes: chardonnay, pinot grigio, moscato, cabernet sauvignon, and a red blend. The wines are described as having various fruit flavors and being suitable for pairing with different foods. The new line is part of Target's strategy to expand its alcohol selections, particularly craft beer, as a way to boost sales. The company plans to add alcohol to 300 stores nationwide, including seven in Southern California. The California Roots wines will be available at all Target stores that sell alcohol starting September 3. Target's Chief Merchandising Officer Mark Tritton said the move to beef up its beer, wine, and spirits offerings was prompted by mid-single digit sales increases in the adult beverage business for the first quarter. The company has recently remodeled many stores and plans to remodel more than 600 of its 1,800 stores, including the location in Orange, California. The expansion includes adding alcohol in "300 stores through increased footprints, remodels and new liquor licenses." The seven stores in Southern California adding alcohol include six small-format stores opening this year in Irvine, Orange, Los Angeles (Eagle Rock and USC Village), Mission Hills and Burbank; along with a traditional store slated to open in Oceanside. Beyond adding liquor to new or existing stores, Target also plans to shore up current wine and beer shelves with a wider selection of options, particularly from local craft breweries. California craft breweries contributed $7.28 billion to the state's economy in 2015, up 12% from 2014. The first small-format Target store in Orange County is set to open soon, and the company is focusing on expanding the brand in urban areas and college campus markets.

The Secret Service supervisor, David Chaney, who was ousted from the agency in the ongoing Colombia prostitution scandal, made light of his protective work for former Republican vice presidential candidate Sarah Palin in a Facebook post. Chaney joked about a picture of himself standing watch behind Palin during the 2008 campaign, commenting that he was "really checking her out." This incident has raised questions about accountability and personal conduct within the Secret Service, with two high-level managers being involved in the misconduct. Chaney and another supervisor, Greg Stokes, have been accused of participating in heavy drinking, visits to a strip club, and payments to prostitutes during a night of carousing in Colombia ahead of President Obama's visit to the Summit of the Americas. Both men have worked at the Secret Service for nearly two decades and have served significant time with the presidential protection detail. The disclosure that two high-level managers were involved in the misconduct has raised concerns about a deeper cultural problem within the institution. The scandal has resulted in three Secret Service employees being dismissed, with more expected to follow. The incident became public after one man got into a dispute over payment with a woman on the morning of April 12, drawing the attention of hotel staff and Colombian authorities. The Secret Service recalled its 11 employees and replaced them with another team before Obama arrived on April 13. All of the recalled members were placed on administrative leave, and their top-secret security clearances were revoked.

A Philadelphia man was caught using an illegal cell phone jammer on a SEPTA bus, disrupting fellow passengers' calls. The man, identified as Eric, admitted to using the device, stating he was taking the law into his own hands to prevent public cell phone use that he found irritating and rude. The device, which Eric bought online, is illegal under federal law, with potential penalties including jail time and a $16,000 fine.

The use of cell phone jammers is concerning due to their potential to block not only personal cell phone use but also GPS, two-way radios, and even police radio if they're close enough. This could lead to public safety issues, such as cutting off communication between public officials, dispatch centers, and the public's access to 911.

The SEPTA bus route where the incident occurred has received complaints about lost calls, but SEPTA insists that riders are safe, and their system would not be affected by a handheld jammer. However, a passenger named Marie, who first reported the incident, expressed fear and anger whenever she encounters the man on the bus.

The practice of jamming cell phones is not unique to Philadelphia, as it is also common on the rails in New York and Washington DC. Some commuters use jammers to silence loud talkers on their daily commute, justifying their actions as a means of controlling an increasingly inconsiderate society. However, the use of such devices poses significant public safety risks.

After being informed that the cell phone jamming device was illegal, Eric called to say he would dispose of the device. The incident highlights the need for awareness and enforcement of laws against the use of cell phone jammers to maintain public safety and communication.

The article discusses allegations that Supreme Court nominee Brett Kavanaugh, while serving as a federal judge on the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit, had a preference for hiring female clerks who had a "certain look." The allegations come from a former Yale Law School student who was warned by professors Jed Rubenfeld and his wife, Amy Chua, about Kavanaugh's preferences. The student was told that Kavanaugh liked his female clerks to have a "certain look," but neither Rubenfeld nor Chua said that the judge did anything untoward regarding the women he worked with. The student found the counsel off-putting and decided to interview with Kavanaugh, but ultimately clerked for another judge. Chua has since defended Kavanaugh, stating that he only hires the most qualified clerks and has been an exceptional mentor to his female clerks. The allegations have raised questions about whether Rubenfeld and Chua were feeding into Kavanaugh's preferences and whether they did the same for other judges. The article also mentions an internal investigation at Yale into Rubenfeld's conduct with female law students.

The article discusses the rise of IV hangover cures, specifically focusing on a service called the I.V. Doctor, started by New York urologist Dr. Elliot Nadelson and his surgical resident son Adam. The service provides intravenous hydration and medication to alleviate hangovers for clients in New York City and the Hamptons. The service is popular among finance professionals who work long hours, entertain clients late into the night, and need to perform at a high level early the next morning.

The I.V. Doctor charges a few hundred dollars for the service, which includes a nurse setting up clients with about 200 ml of fluid and any combination of anti-nausea, anti-heartburn, and anti-inflammatory or headache medicine. The full cocktail of all the drugs is the most popular request and costs $249.

The article also mentions other similar services, such as Hangover Heaven, which opened two years ago in Las Vegas and offers services from $129 to $239 in the clinic, with an additional fee for a nurse to come to a client's hotel room.

The I.V. Doctor is expanding to Chicago this summer and is making a big social media play for potential clients in the Hamptons. The service has been successful in treating tens of thousands of tourists for hangovers in Las Vegas, and they encourage clients to pre-book their appointments, as treatment slots for IV therapy can be limited on weekends.

The article also mentions that as doctors face financial pressures, they are turning to side businesses to supplement their income, with one example being a classmate of the author who offers cosmetic G-spot injections. The author's friend justifies this by saying that it probably doesn't hurt anyone and is probably not necessary.

Overall, the article highlights the growing trend of IV hangover cures and the financial pressures facing doctors, leading them to explore new revenue streams.

A team of divers has connected two underwater caverns in eastern Mexico, revealing what is believed to be the world's largest flooded cave, known as the Gran Acuifero Maya (GAM). The cave system, located near Tulum, connects the Sac Actun and Dos Ojos systems, measuring a combined length of 347 kilometers (216 miles). The discovery could provide new insights into the ancient Maya civilization, as the region was dominated by the Maya before the Spanish conquest. The Yucatan peninsula is studded with monumental relics of the Maya people, whose cities drew upon an extensive network of sinkholes linked to subterranean waters known as cenotes. Some cenotes acquired particular religious significance to the Maya, whose descendants continue to inhabit the region. The discovery of the world's largest underwater cave system is the result of years of work by the GAM, led by underwater archaeologist Guillermo de Anda. The cave holds an important freshwater reserve and supports great biodiversity, with evidence of America's first settlers, Mayan culture, and extinct animals. The team plans to connect the Sac Actun system with other nearby underwater cave systems. The discovery was made after ten months of work by the Underwater Exploration Group of the Great Maya Aquifer Project (GAM), led by German explorer Robert Schmittner. The team dedicated their achievement to Bil Phillips, an underwater cartographer who dedicated his life to understanding the depths of the site through the investigation of these ancestral waters. The discovery has been hailed as "amazing" and is expected to provide new insights into the Maya civilization and the relationship between humans and these ancestral waters.

In this summary, we will discuss two main topics: Bradley Wiggins' award and Saudi Arabia's shift in weekend.

Bradley Wiggins, the British cyclist, concluded his successful year by winning the prestigious award in a ceremony held in London.

Moving on to the second topic, Saudi Arabia is set to change its weekend from Thursday and Friday to Friday and Saturday, starting next week. This decision aligns Saudi Arabia with other Gulf Cooperation Council countries and is aimed at opening its $400 billion stock market to foreign investors. The shift is expected to facilitate global business transactions, as the current system only allowed three days for business, with limited hours due to time zone differences.

The decision to change the weekend was taken based on economic considerations and international obligations. The move is seen as a step towards opening up the Saudi Arabian market for foreign investors. Global banks such as Deutsche Bank AG, HSBC Holdings Plc, and Morgan Stanley have already set up offices in Riyadh in anticipation of the market opening up.

The Tadawul All-Share Index (SASEIDX) declined 0.8 percent to 7,500.69 on the day of the announcement, trimming its year-to-date advance to 10 percent. However, the shift is expected to attract as much as $30 billion of inflows, according to John Burbank, founder of Passport Capital LLC.

The changes to the working week are expected to lead to greater convergence with global markets and put an end to negative effects and lost economic opportunities from having different working days than regional and international institutions. Schools and educational institutions will also change their weekend in the next academic year.

In conclusion, Bradley Wiggins' award and Saudi Arabia's shift in weekend are significant events that will impact their respective fields. The changes in Saudi Arabia are expected to boost its economy and attract foreign investments, while Bradley Wiggins' award marks the end of a successful year for the cyclist.

An 11-year-old girl named Evha Jannath died after falling from a water ride at Drayton Manor theme park in Staffordshire, UK. The incident occurred on a school trip, and Evha was later pronounced dead at Birmingham Children's Hospital. The Splash Canyon ride, where the incident took place, was temporarily closed, and a Health and Safety Executive (HSE) investigation was initiated. Evha's family described her as a "beautiful little girl who was full of love and always smiling." The theme park and Evha's school were closed for the day as a mark of respect. This tragic incident is the first reported death at a UK theme park since 2004. The death at Drayton Manor has raised concerns about the safety of similar rides, leading to the closure of rides at other theme parks as a precautionary measure.

Barnes & Noble (BKS) is reconsidering its strategy for the Nook, its e-reader and tablet line, following a 34% sales decline in the company's fiscal fourth quarter. The bookseller plans to partner with another manufacturer to produce Nook HD tablets, with future devices potentially bearing both the new manufacturer's name and the Barnes & Noble logo. CEO William Lynch confirmed that Barnes & Noble will not exit the device business. The company did not disclose the identity of the potential partner, but more details are expected in the coming months.

The decision comes amid industry speculation that Microsoft (MSFT) might acquire the Nook brand, as Microsoft already holds a 17.6% stake, acquired in April 2012. Microsoft declined to comment on its future plans for the Nook.

Barnes & Noble's stock dropped by about 18% following the release of the earnings report on Tuesday. The company reported a net loss of $118.6 million for the fourth quarter, nearly double the loss from the previous year, and a 7.4% revenue decline to $1.3 billion.

Despite the decline in device sales, Barnes & Noble will continue to expand its digital catalog, adding thousands of e-books weekly. The company attributes the decline in digital sales to the drop in device sales and the fact that popular novels, such as The Hunger Games and Fifty Shades of Grey trilogies, were best-sellers a year ago.

Consistent with prior years, Barnes & Noble expects to open five new stores while closing between 15 and 20 stores in the coming year.

Twitvid is rebranding as Telly, inviting users to preview the new platform at telly.com using their existing Twitvid accounts. A passenger named Stefanie Gordon, on a flight from New York City to Palm Beach, unexpectedly captured the last launch of the space shuttle Endeavour on her iPhone and shared it on Twitter, gaining media attention and thousands of new followers. Despite other passengers taking photos, Gordon seems to be the only one who posted them on Twitter, making her the unintentional documenter of the historic event. Gordon, who is currently job-seeking, has also used Twitter to share her LinkedIn resume, leveraging her newfound popularity.

A man named Alex Van Der Zwaan, an associate at law firm Skadden, Arps, Slate, Meagher & Flom, has pleaded guilty to making false statements to the FBI in Special Counsel Robert Mueller's probe into Russian election interference. The charges against Van Der Zwaan involve his work on a report prepared for the Ukrainian Ministry of Justice in 2012, which was related to the trial of Yulia Tymoshenko, a former Ukrainian prime minister.

Van Der Zwaan allegedly lied about his last communications with former Trump campaign adviser Richard Gates and deleted emails requested by the special counsel's office. The false statements were made as part of his work on the report.

The new charges come as Gates is reportedly nearing a plea deal with Mueller, which could lead to his testimony against Paul Manafort, President Trump's former campaign chairman. Gates and Manafort were indicted together last year for allegedly laundering money and acting as unregistered foreign agents.

The law firm Skadden, Arps, Slate, Meagher & Flom terminated Van Der Zwaan's employment in 2017 and has been cooperating with authorities in connection with this matter. The New York Times reported last year that the law firm's report was arranged by Manafort as part of his work for Yanukovych, a former president of Ukraine allied with Russia.

The charges against Van Der Zwaan are the latest development in Mueller's ongoing investigation into Russian election interference and any links between the Trump campaign and Russia.

The White House Counsel Kathryn Ruemmler, who served as a federal prosecutor in the trial of Enron executives in 2006, was faced with a challenge when she learned about an upcoming inspector general's report on the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) in April 2013. The report revealed that the IRS had improperly targeted tea party and other conservative groups.

Ruemmler, along with White House Chief of Staff Denis McDonough and other senior White House aides, decided to withhold the information from President Obama until the independent audit was completed and made public. This was done to protect the president from any appearance of trying to influence an investigation.

However, the IRS's attempt to get ahead of its own story on May 10, 2013, created a communications disaster for the administration. Senior White House officials were stunned by the IRS's actions, which left them scrambling to contain the public damage.

Ruemmler's focus on the law sometimes conflicts with political imperatives, and the absence of dominant first-term personalities like former adviser David Axelrod and former chief of staff Rahm Emanuel has left the White House struggling to cope with recent scandals.

In the IRS case, many prominent Washington lawyers believe Ruemmler made the sensible legal call by distancing President Obama from a politically sensitive problem and ensuring that he could not be accused of meddling in an inquiry. However, inconsistencies in the White House's public statements undermined their credibility and invited scrutiny.

Ruemmler is known for her lawyerly focus and for advising Obama on the law and protecting executive branch prerogatives. She is considered one of the most cool-headed people in the White House and is a regular presence in the Situation Room and the Oval Office. However, her lack of political and media savvy has been criticized, with some arguing that she should have given the president a heads-up about the IRS situation to allow for crisis management planning.

The controversy over Ruemmler's handling of the IRS situation was further fueled by a Washington Post story that focused on her shoe habit, which some critics argue was undermining and trivializing. The story described Ruemmler's fabulous shoes, including a pair with a jeweled paisley pattern and another that was black and strappy.

The incident highlights the challenges faced by women in public life and the media's tendency to focus on their appearance rather than their professional accomplishments. A recent study found that hearing descriptions of a female candidate's appearance had detrimental impacts on her candidacy, while it had no effect on a male candidate.

The IRS scandal is just one of several challenges facing the Obama administration in recent weeks, including the continued fallout from the Benghazi attack and the Justice Department's tracking of journalists as part of leak investigations. The administration is struggling to contain the damage and maintain the president's agenda.

In a recent development, Peter Madsen, a Danish inventor, has admitted to the death of Swedish journalist Kim Wall on his homemade submarine, the UC3 Nautilus. Madsen claimed that Wall died in an accident on board and he "buried" her at sea in Koge Bay, south of Copenhagen. The police have been conducting a search for Wall's body since her disappearance on August 10th.

Madsen was initially charged with negligent manslaughter, but the charges have been upgraded to aggressive manslaughter, which can lead to a sentence of up to eight years in prison in Denmark. The submarine was deliberately sunk by Madsen, according to the police, and he was rescued before being arrested.

Kim Wall, a 30-year-old journalist who wrote for several international publications, was reported missing by her boyfriend after she failed to return from a short trip on the UC3 Nautilus submarine. She was researching a feature about Madsen and his submarine, which was the largest privately-made vessel of its kind at one stage.

The search for Wall's body by both Danish and Swedish authorities is continuing, with divers, helicopters, and ships involved in the effort. The route taken by the submarine in Koge Bay and the Oresund strait before sinking has been mapped out by maritime authorities.

Madsen's lawyer, Betina Hald Engmark, said her client had not admitted any wrongdoing and still pleads not guilty to the charges against him. The court case is being heard behind closed doors.

Wall's family had feared the worst, and until Madsen confessed, police from Denmark and Sweden and members of the voluntary Swedish Lifesaving Society had conducted a search of the waters of the Oresund straits and parts of their coastlines with dwindling hopes of finding her alive. At one point, chief investigator Jens Moeller Jensen acknowledged that "it is our clear presumption that we are looking for a dead person."

The investigation is ongoing, and no further information has been released by the police. The case has garnered international attention, with media outlets reporting on the developments in the case.

On August 23, 2018, Raymond Reinke, a 55-year-old man from Pendleton, Oregon, pleaded guilty to four charges related to misconduct in Yellowstone and Grand Teton national parks. The charges included being under the influence of alcohol, disorderly conduct, and disturbing wildlife. Reinke was sentenced to 130 days in jail, 5 years of unsupervised probation, and a ban from entering Yellowstone, Grand Teton, and Glacier National Parks.

The charges stemmed from multiple incidents in the weeks leading up to his arrest, including open container and public intoxication. The most infamous incident was a video that surfaced online in late July, showing Reinke aggressively provoking a bison by waving his arms and running towards it. This incident led to Reinke being cited for harassing wildlife.

Reinke initially pleaded not guilty to the charges, but changed his plea during Thursday's hearing to guilty. He apologized to the bison, stating, "I'm sorry to the buffalo. He didn't deserve what I did to him. I'm sorry, I really didn't mean to hurt that buffalo."

Judge Mark Carman described Reinke's behavior as the most "egregious" case of animal harassment they'd seen in Yellowstone. Reinke has a criminal history dating to 1991, although no felony offenses. He will also be required to serve five years of unsupervised probation, in which he cannot use drugs or alcohol. He is also barred from Yellowstone, Glacier, and Grand Teton parks during his probationary period.

Separately, a bear attacked a 10-year-old boy in Yellowstone National Park on Thursday, causing puncture wounds to his back, wounds around his buttocks, and an injured wrist. The boy was transferred to a Montana hospital for treatment. It is unclear what caused the bear to charge or what species it was.

Visitors to Yellowstone National Park are advised not to run if they encounter a bear and to stand their ground if the animal charges. The last reported bear attack in Yellowstone was in 2015, and the park averages one bear attack per year. Several park visitors had been injured in animal encounters earlier this year, including a woman who was gored by a bison in June following two separate elk attacks that injured two women in May.

The El Cerrito Police Department is seeking public assistance to identify a violent suspect who attacked a teenage girl and stole her iPhone. The suspect, who is seen in selfies taken with the stolen phone, may have unintentionally uploaded the selfies to iCloud. The victim, a student at El Cerrito High School, was walking to class when the suspect demanded her phone and backpack, and then assaulted her, causing minor injuries and loss of consciousness. The victim later recognized the suspect in the selfies and reported the incident to the police. Authorities believe the suspect may not have been aware that the selfies would be uploaded to iCloud. The incident serves as a reminder for students to protect their smartphones and avoid displaying valuable items publicly.

In Sedro-Woolley, Washington, the owner of Lucky Teriyaki restaurant has requested local law enforcement, including the Skagit County Sheriff's Office, not to dine at the establishment. This decision was made after a misunderstanding that occurred when deputies were eating at the restaurant and were asked to leave by the owner.

According to the restaurant owners, an employee noticed some customers at another table had spilled soup and water, and mistakenly thought they were upset due to the presence of the deputies. The employee asked the deputies if they were about to leave, but the misunderstanding persisted when the deputies tried to clarify what had happened.

The request from the restaurant owner took Sheriff Will Reichardt by surprise, as the Skagit County community generally shows appreciation for law enforcement. The incident sparked a wave of reactions on social media, with some expressing support for the restaurant's right to refuse service, while others criticized the decision.

In response to the incident, the owners of Lucky Teriyaki have invited law enforcement to eat for free at the restaurant on Monday, July 18. The owners also clarified that they welcome police officers to the restaurant.

Dave North, owner of The Bullpen Sports Bar & Grill in Sedro-Woolley, is planning a police appreciation day in Skagit County for early August. This event will be a fundraiser for the Behind the Badge Foundation, and the date and participating restaurants will be announced once the details are worked out. Anyone interested can contact North on his Facebook page.

Paula Deen, a popular TV chef, restaurateur, and cookbook author, has faced a series of business separations following her admission of using a racial slur in the past. QVC, Target, Home Depot, Wal-Mart, and Sears & KMart are among the companies that have ended their relationships with Deen. In a statement, QVC announced it would phase out Deen's product assortment over the next few months and pause her appearances on the network. Deen's book publisher, Ballantine Books, also canceled a deal for multiple books, including an upcoming cookbook that was the No.1 seller on Amazon.com and Barnes & Noble. Diabetes drug maker Novo Nordisk also suspended its patient education activities with Deen. However, Deen's annual "Paula Deen Cruise" has seen an increase in bookings, and she is still scheduled to make appearances at cooking shows in Houston, Dallas, and Washington, DC. The fate of her magazine "Cooking with Paula Deen" remains uncertain.

In a significant escalation of the ongoing Syrian conflict, twin blasts targeted Syria's army command headquarters in Damascus on Wednesday, resulting in sporadic gunbattles and a fire inside the heavily guarded compound. The explosions, one of which was a car bomb, were followed by hours of heavy gunfire and caused significant damage, including the death of Iranian Press TV correspondent Maya Nasser.

The blasts, which occurred near the landmark Omayyad Square, were heard several miles away and caused extensive damage to nearby buildings, including the Dama Rose hotel. The army command building was in flames, sending thick black smoke over Damascus for several hours.

Witnesses reported that rebels may have been holed up inside the army command building, with gunfire heard from the area. The British-based Syrian Observatory for Human Rights reported heavy clashes inside the compound, with casualties on both sides.

The Syrian conflict, which began in March 2011, has escalated into a civil war that activists estimate has killed nearly 30,000 people. Over the past few months, rebels have increasingly targeted security sites and symbols of regime power in an attempt to turn the tide in the fighting.

The unrest in Syria was the focus of attention at the U.N. General Assembly's annual meeting in New York this week, with U.N. Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon calling for international action to stop the war. However, the U.N. Security Council remains paralyzed due to vetoes by Russia and China, leaving the conflict in a stalemate.

The Syrian government regularly refers to rebels fighting to topple President Bashar Assad's regime as terrorists. The army statement said a number of guards were wounded in the blasts, but Information Minister Omran Zoubi said that all military commanders and personnel were fine.

The conflict in Syria has had regional and global ramifications, with the U.S. pledging support for Syrians trying to oust Assad. The death of Maya Nasser, an Iranian journalist covering the conflict, has added to the growing list of casualties in the region.

In a significant development in the Jessica Ridgeway murder case, authorities have released the description of a man suspected in an unsuccessful abduction attempt on a 22-year-old woman near Ketner Lake on May 28. The police are linking this case to Jessica's abduction and subsequent murder on Oct. 5, 2012, to uncover any potential leads. The suspect is described as white or light-skinned, between 18 and 30 years old, with brown hair, medium build, and standing about 5 feet, 8 inches tall. The woman claimed the man used a chemical-soaked rag during the attempted abduction.

Police are investigating whether there is a connection between the two cases, as Ketner Lake Open Space is only half a mile from Jessica's home and south of the Witt Elementary School where she was headed on the day she disappeared. Law enforcement has no description of a vehicle related to the May 28 case.

Westminster police are also examining other attempted abductions in the Denver metro area to determine if the suspects could be linked to Jessica's kidnapping. Authorities are asking the public for any information about unusual behavior or changes in appearances or habits around Memorial Day or Oct. 5. Anyone with information can contact Westminster police at 303-658-4336 or send an email to PDamberalert@cityofwestminster.us. The police are particularly interested in anyone with a cross similar to the one the suspect may carry or wear.

Air Force Staff Sgt. Luis Walker, an instructor at Lackland Air Force Base in San Antonio, Texas, was found guilty on all charges of sexual misconduct on Friday, July 20, 2012. Walker was accused of sexually assaulting or having improper sexual contact with at least 10 female recruits from October 2010 through January 2011. The allegations are part of a sweeping sex scandal involving several Lackland instructors. Walker could face up to life in prison and dishonorable discharge.

The trial was dominated by the graphic and emotional testimony of female recruits, with some testifying that Walker gained their trust to get them alone in his office or an empty dormitory, where he then forced them into kissing, touching, or intercourse. The alleged sexual misconduct among instructors at the base apparently began in 2009, but the first woman didn't come forward until last year.

Walker is among 12 Lackland instructors investigated for sexual misconduct toward at least 31 female trainees, and among the six charged on counts ranging from rape to adultery. Other instructors charged in the case include Staff Sgt. Craig LeBlanc, who is accused of sexual misconduct, obstruction of justice, and making a false official statement. No trial date has been set for LeBlanc.

The sexual abuse scandal is among the worst to hit the military in over a decade. In 1996, dozens of women at the Aberdeen Proving Ground in Maryland accused male supervisors of rape, sexual assault, and other offenses. A few years earlier, more than 80 women were assaulted during several days of drunken revelry at the Tailhook Association convention in Las Vegas, a case that led to the resignation of the Navy secretary and two admirals.

Air Force officials said more instructors could be charged as a result of the current investigations, with recruits being encouraged to report episodes anonymously through a 24-hour tip line. The two-star general’s review has also been expanded to include three other Air Force training bases.

The scandal has been deeply painful for the Air Force. Nine years ago, a survey by the Pentagon’s inspector general found that 12 percent of the women who graduated from the Air Force Academy that year said they had been victims of rape or attempted rape while at the school. The vast majority said they did not report the episodes to the authorities out of fear of being punished.

The rigorously hierarchical nature of the military makes it especially conducive to sexual abuse, critics say, and basic training is even more so, with instructors looming as intimidating, all-powerful figures to young recruits. The Pentagon rejects such assertions, but amid growing criticism from advocacy groups and Congress, Secretary of Defense Leon E. Panetta announced in April new steps to combat sexual assault, including having higher ranking officers handle sexual assault complaints, a change expected to lead to more prosecutions.

Artist Ryan Mendoza, who moved Rosa Parks' old Detroit home to Germany last year, aims to return the house to the United States. Mendoza believes that the house, which was once home to civil rights icon Rosa Parks, should be a monument to the civil rights movement rather than the Confederacy. However, Detroit's cultural institutions have shown little interest in bringing the house back. The house may end up in a museum or venue elsewhere in the U.S., such as Washington, D.C., or New York.

Mendoza, who lives in Germany, believes that the house should return to the U.S. as communities debate what to do with Confederate monuments and memorials, and some fear that white nationalism is on the rise. The house was dismantled, moved, and rebuilt at a cost of over $130,000, with Mendoza spending much of the money from the sale of his other artwork.

One foundation, the Nash Family Foundation, based in New York, has committed up to $40,000 to ship the house back to the U.S., and dozens of museums have been receptive to Mendoza's appeals to display it. The vice chancellor of Germany, Sigmar Gabriel, is also helping to champion Mendoza's efforts to return the house to the U.S.

Rosa Parks, a soft-spoken seamstress, became an international civil rights icon after being arrested for refusing to give up her bus seat to a white passenger in 1955 in Montgomery, Alabama. The bus, No. 2857, which was assigned to the Cleveland Avenue route, has been restored and is now at the Henry Ford Museum in Dearborn, Michigan.

Parks left the South in 1957 and came to Detroit to stay with family. She first settled at the home on South Deacon Street, and later moved to a home on Wildemere on the city's west side. In 1994, she was assaulted and robbed by an intruder. She then moved to an apartment in Riverfront Towers in downtown where she lived until her death in 2005.

The Rosa Parks Family Foundation, founded by McCauley, bought the house on South Deacon Street in November 2014 for $500 from the Detroit Land Bank Authority with the hopes of restoring it. Mendoza learned about the Parks house through McCauley after he worked on the "The White House" project, in which he dismantled an abandoned house in Detroit and re-created it in Europe as artwork. That project, however, also angered some of the people who lived near the home's crumbling remains.

In a groundbreaking development, researchers from the University of Tokyo and Kyoto University have successfully created human ear cartilage from induced pluripotent stem cells. The scientists implanted the grown ear on the back of a rat, and after two months, it developed into a 5-centimeter human ear. This new technology could potentially help individuals born without ears or with small ears.

In the United States, around 10% of adults have chronic kidney disease, with 600,000 patients currently suffering from chronic kidney failure. To address this issue, scientists from the University of California, San Francisco are working on a sophisticated artificial kidney device made with human kidney cells, silicon nanofilters, and powered by blood pressure. The project aims to begin testing the kidney device in 2017.

Advances in bioengineering are also being made in the field of regenerative medicine. For instance, scientists have been growing bioengineered intestines in the lab to diagnose digestive disorders and help patients born without a piece of intestine. In 2011, a team led by John March from Cornell University began collaborating on a small artificial intestine using collagen and stem cells.

In the realm of spinal discs, treatment for chronic back pain is limited. Over the past several years, artificial discs have emerged as an alternative, but they can wear out. In 2011, a research team from Cornell University bioengineered implants using gel and collagen seeded with rat cells, which were then successfully placed into rat spines. This summer, Duke bioengineers took things further, coming up with a gel mixture they think can help regenerate tissue when injected into the space between discs.

In April, Hannah Warren, a 32-month-old patient, became the youngest person to ever receive a bioengineered organ. Scientists had made a windpipe for her using her own bone marrow cells. Despite the high risks, bioengineers say they will continue to move ahead.

The liver is one of the largest and most challenging organs to recreate. In 2010, bioengineers at Wake Forest University Baptist Medical Center grew miniature livers in the lab using decellularized animal livers for the structure and human cells. This month, a team from the Yokohama City University Graduate School of Medicine published results of a study where they reprogrammed human adult skin cells, added other cell types, and got them to grow into early-stage liver “buds.”

Artificial heart devices have been surgically implanted since the 1980s, but no device has been able to replace the human heart as effectively as a healthy biological one. Recently, scientists have made advances in adding more biological material to artificial heart devices. In May, the French company Carmat prepared to test an artificial device containing cow heart tissue, and at Massachusetts General Hospital, surgeon Harald C. Ott and his team are working on a bioartificial heart scaffold.

In the field of vascular biology, being able to make blood vessels in the lab from a patient’s own cells could mean better treatments for cardiovascular disease, kidney disease, and diabetes. In 2011, the head of California-based Cytograft Tissue Engineering reported progress in a study where three end-stage kidney disease patients were implanted with blood vessels bioengineered in the lab.

Finally, surgeon Anthony Atala directs the Wake Forest Institute for Regenerative Medicine and is known for growing new human cells, tissues, and organs, particularly ones that advance urology. Atala and his team’s bioengineered bladders succeeded in clinical trials. The bladders were constructed from patients’ cells that were grown over two months on a biodegradable scaffold and then implanted. Patients included children with spina bifida who risked kidney failure. It’s been several years since then, and the results are positive.

Florida Governor Rick Scott, along with top state lawmakers, proposed a significant move towards gun control on Friday, defying the National Rifle Association (NRA). The plan aims to raise the minimum age to buy any firearm, including semiautomatic rifles, from 18 to 21, and strengthen rules to keep weapons away from people with mental health issues or injunctions against them for stalking or domestic violence.

The proposal comes in response to the school shooting in Parkland, Florida, which left 17 people dead. Student protesters who rallied at the State Capitol on Wednesday demanded a complete ban on military-style assault rifles, but the plan stops short of this demand.

Governor Scott stated, "I want to make it virtually impossible for anyone who has mental issues to use a gun. I want to make it virtually impossible for anyone who is a danger to themselves or others to use a gun."

The plan also calls for tougher background checks and waiting periods to buy firearms, requiring mentally ill people who have been involuntarily committed to temporarily surrender weapons, and the allocation of hundreds of millions of dollars toward improving security in schools and mental health services.

The Broward County Sheriff, Scott Israel, was pleased with the news, stating, "Thank you Gov. Scott and state legislative leaders for proposing a gun and school safety package that incorporates nearly all the ideas (Broward Sheriff's Office) and other sheriffs suggested."

However, other Democrats believe the proposals would not go far enough, with Florida Senate Democratic Leader Oscar Braynon stating, "We can beef up mental health screenings, raise the age for gun purchases and dream up other stop-gap measures, but the threat to our children and our citizens will continue until we finally take bold action to ban assault weapons designed for the battlefield from easy access in our communities."

Scott, who is a member of the NRA, said he is not calling for a ban on all firearms, stating, "I know there are some who are advocating a mass takeaway of Second Amendment rights for all Americans. That is not the answer."

The plan is divided into three parts:

1. Keep guns away from dangerous people: The plan will address strengthening gun laws to keep "guns away from dangerous and violent people." This includes creating a "Violent Threat Restraining Order," strengthening gun purchase and possession restrictions for mentally ill individuals, and prohibiting people subject to certain injunctions from possessing or buying a firearm.

2. Keeping students safe: The plan proposes a $450 million initiative for student safety, including the presence of a resource officer in every public school, mandatory active shooter training, increased funding for safe school infrastructure, and crisis intervention training for all school personnel.

3. Expand mental health initiatives: The plan outlines a $50 million allocation for mental health initiatives, including the expansion of mental health service teams, a Department of Children and Families case manager embedded in every sheriff's department, and matching grants for sheriff's offices to set up special law enforcement teams to work with DCF case managers.

The proposal has received mixed reactions, with some students calling it a step in the right direction, while others are disappointed that it does not go far enough in banning certain types of firearms. The governor's focus is on bringing in law enforcement to keep schools safe, rather than arming teachers.

The University at Albany has charged seven men for the 2014 hazing death of student Trevor Duffy, where they allegedly forced him to drink a 60-ounce bottle of vodka. The men claim to be part of Zeta Beta Tau (ZBT) fraternity, but the national fraternity based in Indianapolis has denied any affiliation with the rogue group. The fraternity has retained legal counsel and plans to sue the men for falsely representing themselves, deceiving the public, and damaging the fraternity's reputation.

The rogue group was not recognized by the university or the fraternity, and the men were never members of ZBT. The fraternity has stated that its name, symbols, slogans, and materials are protected by United States copyright and trademark law, and anyone found to be using them unauthorized may be subject to legal action.

ZBT was founded in 1898 as the world's first Jewish fraternity and has chapters on over 90 campuses across North America. Attorney Paul DerOhannesian is representing one of the accused students, and while he acknowledged the new lawsuit, he was not yet ready to state his client's case in regard to the new allegations.

The Bramble Cay melomys, a small rodent endemic to the Great Barrier Reef, has been declared extinct following extensive searches on its only known habitat, a sandy island in far northern Australia.
