The study, led by the Queensland Department of Environment and Heritage Protection and the University of Queensland, found no evidence of the species during a six-night survey, confirming its extinction. The key factor behind the extinction was attributed to climate change, with rising sea levels and increased incidence of extreme weather events over the past decade causing habitat loss. The Bramble Cay melomys, also known as the mosaic-tailed rat, was first discovered in 1845 and was considered Australia's only endemic mammal species on the Great Barrier Reef. The last known sighting was in 2009, and a 2014 study found no sign of the species, prompting the most extensive survey possible in the hope of conserving the species. The study's findings suggest that the Bramble Cay melomys may be the first mammal to be driven to extinction solely by anthropogenic climate change. The main hope for the species lies in the possibility of another population existing in neighboring Papua New Guinea. The extinction of the Bramble Cay melomys highlights Australia's ongoing extinction crisis, with the nation having the worst rate of mammal extinction in the world. The study's authors emphasize the need for significant funding towards protecting Australia's threatened species to prevent further extinctions.

Sebastian Gorka, a deputy assistant to President Donald Trump and a close ally of former chief strategist Steve Bannon, was ousted from the White House on Friday. In a resignation letter, Gorka cited "forces" that do not support President Trump’s "MAGA promise" as those that drove him out of the White House. The letter stated that the individuals who embodied and represented the policies that would "Make America Great Again" have been internally countered, systematically removed, or undermined in recent months, specifically mentioning the removal of any mention of Radical Islam or radical Islamic terrorism from the president's speech on Afghanistan as a significant factor. Gorka's departure came one week after Bannon was fired from his White House position. The news of Gorka’s departure was greeted with resignation by Trump loyalists, who believe the president has handed over too much power to military officers and former generals and is losing any connection to the base that elected him.

In addition, a pair of House Democrats, Jared Huffman and Barbara Lee, unveiled proposals to cut off the salaries of controversial White House aides Stephen Miller and Sebastian Gorka, citing their encouragement of white supremacists and their involvement in policies that have been criticized as racist. The lawmakers accused Miller and Gorka of promoting white supremacist views, specifically mentioning Miller's involvement in the travel ban on several Muslim-majority countries and Gorka's work at Breitbart. It is unlikely that the amendments submitted by Huffman and Lee will be granted time on the House floor, given GOP leaders’ desire to stay out of Trump’s personnel controversies.

Gorka's tenure at the White House was marked by personal attacks against him and his family by left-leaning media organizations and the Democratic Party. He has been accused of having ties to Nazi groups in his family's home country of Hungary, but has strenuously objected to these allegations. In his resignation letter, Gorka made clear that he believes in the promise of the Trump presidency despite being concerned about its present direction. He expressed hope that the president's base will help rebalance the current reality and that the MAGA platform will ultimately be successful.

On Monday, an Amtrak train derailed on its inaugural trip through a faster railway route between Portland and Seattle, killing three people and injuring over 70. The train was supposed to slow to 30 mph before entering a curve where the crash occurred, but it was reportedly traveling at 80 mph in a 30 mph zone when it derailed. The derailment occurred on a new route that was part of a $180.7 million project designed to cut 10 minutes off the stretch between Tacoma and Olympia by running alongside Interstate 5 instead of hugging the Puget Sound. The tracks were equipped for positive train control equipment, but the train controls weren't operating yet in that area. The National Transportation Safety Board is investigating the cause of the derailment, but it appears to have been caused by speed. The incident highlights the need for positive train control systems, which can prevent dangerous situations such as excessive speed, to be fully implemented. The train controls were mandated by Congress in 2008, but the implementation has been delayed until the end of 2018, and there is a possibility of another delay until 2020.

A 5-year-old girl, Allison Anderwald, is being hailed as a hero after she saved her unconscious mother, Tracy Anderwald, from a swimming pool in Portland, Texas. The incident occurred during a family outing at Tracy's sister's house. Tracy, 34, had a seizure and sank to the bottom of the pool, where Allison, who had been swimming with her, noticed her mother had not resurfaced after five minutes. The brave little girl jumped in, pulled her mother to the shallow end, and flipped her body over so her head wasn't submerged.

Tracy's sister, Tedra Hunt, 32, who was nearby, was alerted by the children's screams and immediately called 911. Emergency services took Tracy to CHRISTUS Spohn Hospital Corpus Christi-Memorial. The doctors informed the family that had Tracy been underwater any longer, she might not have survived.

Initially, doctors had low expectations for Tracy's recovery and anticipated she might have neurological damage. However, Tracy woke up the next day and was deemed fit for release after a few tests and assessments on Tuesday afternoon. She will soon follow up with a neurologist to determine the cause of the seizure, as she had never experienced one before.

Tracy's sister, Tedra, believes their late father, who passed away almost exactly two years ago, was a "guardian angel" watching over them that day, guiding Allison to help save Tracy. The family hopes their story will raise awareness for the importance of teaching children how to swim and what to do in an emergency at an early age. Allison, affectionately known as a "water bug," has been swimming since she was 2.5 years old.

The incident has been widely reported by local media, with photos of the family at the hospital being published in the Caller-Times. Tracy and Allison are grateful for the support they have received and are looking forward to a full recovery.

The US Ambassador to New Zealand, Scott Brown, has admitted to being under investigation for inappropriate comments made during his inaugural trip to Samoa, where he also served as the US representative. The allegations stem from comments Brown made at a party in Apia, where he told attendees they looked "beautiful" and could make hundreds of dollars working in the hospitality industry in the US. Brown and his wife, Gail Huff, claimed they were unaware the comments would be considered offensive.

The investigation was conducted by the US State Department, which sent investigators to Wellington to look into the matter. Brown stated that the complaints related to his cultural insensitivity, as he transitioned from being a politician to an ambassador. He acknowledged the need to be aware of different cultures and sensitivities in his new role.

Brown also mentioned that politics is a "blood sport" and there were many attendees at the event who did not support US President Donald Trump. Brown was Trump's first ambassadorial appointment after he took office.

Huff stated that the incident served as a lesson for them to be more careful with their words and how they are perceived. The Guardian reported that complaints against Brown came from two serving female members of the peace corps.

The US State Department, US embassy in Wellington, and the US high commission in Samoa did not respond to requests for comment regarding the incident in August. On Wednesday, a spokesperson for the US embassy in Wellington stated that Ambassador Brown had nothing further to add to his comments made in the afternoon interview.

The first court hearing for six Baltimore police officers charged in the death of Freddie Gray, a 25-year-old black man who died a week after suffering a critical spinal injury in police custody, took place on September 2, 2015. During the hearing, Judge Barry Williams refused to dismiss the charges against the officers, denying a defense motion for prosecutorial misconduct on the part of State's Attorney Marilyn Mosby. Williams also rejected a defense motion seeking to have Mosby recused from the case, stating that her husband's position as a councilman in a district that experienced a disproportionate amount of violence during the riots that Gray's death sparked was not a reason for recusal. The officers face charges ranging from second-degree assault to second-degree "depraved-heart" murder. The case has sparked widespread protests in Baltimore and has become part of a national dialogue about police treatment of black citizens. Outside the courtroom, dozens of protesters gathered in peaceful demonstrations and marches through downtown, resulting in one arrest and snarled traffic. Inside the courtroom, Williams sought to maintain order and frequently interrupted the attorneys during their arguments. The officers had waived their rights to attend the hearing, and Gray's family did not attend. The case will proceed with six separate trials.

The article from Gizmodo UK discusses the decline in popularity of the internet slang term "LOL" (laugh out loud) on Facebook, with "haha" and "hehe" remaining the most commonly used expressions of laughter. The decline in the use of "LOL" is believed to be due to a shift in demographics on the social network, with older users being more likely to use the term. The article suggests that this could be due to older users being more comfortable with the term, struggling to find the emoji keyboard, or misunderstanding the acronym. The article concludes that "LOL" is becoming less popular as emoji becomes the preferred method of expressing laughter among younger users. The report does not address the ironic use of "LOL" or variations of it.

The study published in Global Environmental Change reveals that approximately 47% of the edible U.S. seafood supply, amounting to about 2.3 billion pounds, is wasted annually. The waste occurs at various stages of the food supply chain, with the majority (51-63%) occurring at the consumer level. The study, led by David Love from the Johns Hopkins Center for a Livable Future, also found that 16-32% of waste is due to bycatch, while 13-16% is lost in distribution and retail operations.

The wasted seafood contains enough protein to meet the requirements of more than 10 million people each year, according to the study. This finding is significant as U.S. dietary guidelines recommend that most Americans increase their seafood intake. However, the global seafood supply is threatened by overfishing, climate change, pollution, habitat destruction, and the use of fish for purposes other than human consumption.

The study suggests that reducing seafood waste could support increased seafood consumption without further stressing aquatic resources. Suggested approaches to reduce seafood waste include limiting bycatch at the production level, packaging seafood into smaller portion sizes at the processing level, and encouraging consumer purchases of frozen seafood. The researchers hope these estimates and suggestions will stimulate dialogue about the significance and magnitude of seafood loss and contribute to a more efficient and sustainable seafood system.

The 18th Annual Critics' Choice Movie Awards were held in Santa Monica, California, where Ben Affleck won the Best Director Award for his film 'Argo'. The film also won the Best Picture Award. Jennifer Lawrence won in two actress categories, Best Actress in an Action Movie for 'The Hunger Games' and Best Comedic Actress for 'Silver Linings Playbook'. Daniel Day-Lewis was named the Best Actor winner for his role in 'Lincoln'. The Critics' Choice Awards are often a reliable predictor for the Academy Awards, and many stars who were nominated for Oscars were in high spirits at the event. Matthew McConaughey, who was nominated for Best Supporting Actor for 'Magic Mike', was also there to support his indie comedy, 'Bernie'. The awards were hosted by Sam Rubin and found a new home at the Barker Hangar in Santa Monica, as well as a new television home on the CW. The winners of the full list from the Critics' Choice Awards were also announced.

A powerful storm swept across northern Europe on Friday, causing significant damage and disruptions. The storm, known as Xaver, brought hurricane-force winds and the highest tidal surge in 60 years, flooding numerous homes and prompting evacuations along the eastern English coast. In Britain, over 1,400 properties were flooded, and several communities were at risk of high tides and large waves. The Thames Barrier in London was closed for a second time in two days to protect the city from the surge.

The storm also caused numerous accidents, resulting in at least eight deaths across Europe, from Britain to Sweden, Denmark, and Poland. In Denmark, a collection of Viking ships was threatened by the high winds, and museum workers boarded up the expansive windows of the Viking Ship Museum in Roskilde amid fears that water from the fjord would rise and shatter the glass.

In the United States, a frigid winter storm system hit Dallas, causing temperatures to plummet and resulting in at least seven storm-related deaths. The high temperature at the Dallas/Fort Worth airport on Saturday was 26 degrees, the coldest high temperature ever recorded there on December 7 and the coldest December day in Dallas/Fort Worth in 23 years. The storm caused hundreds of car crashes and forced the cancellation of hundreds of departures at Dallas/Fort Worth International Airport.

Across the country, temperatures were much colder than usual, with winter coming much earlier than expected in many sections. In Indiana, up to 10 inches of snow fell on Thursday, and temperatures dropped into the single digits at night. In Michigan, temperatures were currently at zero degrees, with average temperatures in the 20s.

The storm is expected to continue affecting Europe and the United States in the coming days, with high winds and heavy snow expected in some areas. In Europe, further tidal surges are expected to hit Hamburg on Friday evening, and Hamburg airport has warned of cancellations due to wind and snow. In the United States, snow, ice, or freezing rain is expected to fall on Washington, Philadelphia, New York City, and Boston on Sunday, with temperatures expected to rise into the 40s and any accumulation starting to melt on Monday.

Beyonce and Jay-Z's daughter, Blue Ivy, while unique, is not the most unconventional baby name in Hollywood. Celebrities like Gwyneth Paltrow and Chris Martin's daughter Apple, and others with names like Audio Science, Pilot Inspektor, Moon Unit, and Stranger, hold that title. Despite potential teasing in kindergarten, Blue Ivy's name is relatively tame compared to some Hollywood offspring names. U.S. Representative Gabrielle Giffords, who is recovering from a gunshot wound to the head, has shown remarkable progress in her recovery. During a visit to Houston, her rabbi, Stephanie Aaron, reported that Giffords sang the folk-rock song "American Pie" and knew all the words. Giffords was shot on January 8 at a supermarket in Tucson, Arizona, where she was holding a meet-and-greet event. Six people died, and Giffords is currently undergoing treatment at TIRR Memorial Hermann in Houston, where her husband, astronaut Mark Kelly, lives.

Giffords' medical team has been encouraging her to mouth the words to songs as part of an exercise known to rebuild the brain. During her visit to Houston, Giffords overheard the rabbi talking about getting matzo-ball soup and responded by saying "Soup?" The rabbi also brought a large poster-board card from students at Emily Gray Junior High School, where Giffords was once a student. When she saw the picture, Giffords touched the part of the picture that showed her with Kelly.

Meanwhile, a veteran city firefighter, Mark Ekstrum, may have slowed his Tucson Fire Department unit's response to the shooting spree on January 8. Ekstrum retired from his 28-year career two days later, while his supervisors were still considering how to discipline him. In a memo obtained by the Arizona Daily Star, fire Capt. Ben Williams wrote that when Ekstrum first told him he would not go out on the call, he mentioned something about "political bantering" and did not want to be part of it. Ekstrum has since stated that he was distraught over the shootings and had no problem with Giffords, who is recovering from a bullet wound to the brain.

Experts have said it's a good sign that Giffords is talking, but that she still has a long, difficult road to recovery. The first reports of Giffords speaking came last week, when a staff member confirmed the congresswoman asked for toast with her breakfast. There have also been reports of her mouthing the words to "Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star," as friends sang along. Giffords was shot in the left forehead and the bullet went clear through the left side of the brain, which typically controls right-side strength, sensation, and speech. Traumatic brain injuries can affect a person's ability to concentrate and remember, as well as cause problems with balance and coordination. Many survivors are severely disabled.

The Federal Reserve, led by Chairman Ben Bernanke, held a meeting on Wednesday where they decided to maintain the key interest rate at a historic low of 0% to 0.25% and end their $600 billion bond-buying program on June 30th. The Fed stated that the economic recovery is progressing at a moderate pace, but inflation has picked up and the jobs market remains a concern. The decisions were expected, with the FOMC making only minor changes to the language of the policy statement. Attention now turns to Bernanke's first-ever news conference, scheduled to begin at 2:15 p.m. Eastern, where he will be asked tough questions about the Fed's decision to accept high unemployment for an extended period, despite the power to reduce it. Critics argue that Bernanke's hesitance to use that power could lead to years of widespread unemployment, with severe consequences for the economy and society. The news conference offers a chance to hold Bernanke accountable for his decisions.

In a dramatic turn of events at the Oscar Pistorius murder trial, the double-amputee Olympian became emotional in court as graphic images of the night he shot and killed his girlfriend, Reeva Steenkamp, were displayed. Pistorius' defense called pathologist Jan Botha to the stand, who testified that Steenkamp died quickly after sustaining a head injury. Pistorius was seen sobbing, retching, and covering his head as images of his blood-covered toilet and Steenkamp's wounds were shown. Despite his emotional state, Pistorius is expected to testify next.

Pistorius, 27, is accused of the premeditated killing of Steenkamp, a model and law graduate, at his home in Pretoria, South Africa, on Feb 14, 2013. He maintains that he thought she was an intruder when he opened fire through a bathroom door.

During his testimony, Pistorius expressed remorse for Steenkamp's family, saying there is "not a moment" when he does not think about them and prays for them daily. He also spoke about his fear of crime, his religious faith, and the impact of a speedboat accident in 2009 on his mental state.

Earlier in the day, the first defense witness, pathologist Prof Jan Botha, questioned prosecution evidence that Steenkamp must have eaten about two hours before her death at 3am, which contradicts Pistorius's statement that they went to bed at 10pm. Botha was aggressively questioned by prosecution counsel Gerrie Nel, foreshadowing the intense cross-examination Pistorius will likely face.

The trial continues.

The article discusses concerns about the accuracy and reliability of China's reported gross domestic product (GDP) figures, with some analysts suggesting they may be manipulated to meet political targets. Li Keqiang, a vice premier of China, reportedly stated in 2007 that the figures were "man-made" and "for reference only."

China's GDP growth rate for the second quarter of 2012 was 7.6 percent, the slowest pace in three years. This has raised concerns among investors, bankers, and economists, who face difficulties in interpreting the numbers from China's statistics bureau. Combining all officially reported provincial GDP numbers for last year produced a total exceeding national GDP by about 10 percent, due partly to double counting of items including factory production.

The government is good at measuring some pieces of the economy, such as industrial production and profits, but the statistical system may be less capable of measuring the service economy or getting an accurate reading of consumption by the middle class. Retail sales include purchases by government offices and big state enterprises, which may explain why retail sales haven't fallen during downturns.

Investment banks have searched for an indicator that will predict an economic turning point, but many have found that traditional indicators such as GDP, electricity consumption, and rail cargo volume are not reliable. Bank loans, however, are still considered a good proxy for the economy.

One new effort to gauge the economy is the China Beige Book, a quarterly survey of about 2,000 bankers and company executives. This report measures growth in eight key industries across China's major regions and is seen as a more accurate reflection of the economy than the official GDP figures.

China's growth has slowed to its lowest rate since the depths of the global financial crisis in 2009, though analysts voiced optimism on Friday that the economy may have bottomed out already. The government has already cut interest rates twice in a month and lowered the amount of cash that banks must hold as reserves three times since November, and analysts expect further easing of monetary policy. However, officials have insisted they will not launch a stimulus package comparable to the 4 trillion yuan (£405 billion) package of 2008.

The article discusses the origins of traditional Thanksgiving dishes, focusing on turkey, cranberry sauce, pumpkin pie, and apple cider. Contrary to popular belief, turkey may not have been present at the first Thanksgiving feast in 1621, as there is no explicit mention of it in the accounts of the event. However, turkey became a popular choice for Thanksgiving meals in the 19th century, when Bradford's journals were reprinted and highlighted the colonists' hunting of wild turkeys.

Cranberry sauce was also not a part of the first Thanksgiving, as sugar was a rare luxury at the time. Cranberries were used by Native Americans for various purposes, including making pemmican, a mixture of equal parts ground dried meat and cranberries. Cranberries were also used as a medicinal remedy and as a source of energy.

Pumpkin pie did not appear at the first Thanksgiving either, as the colonists lacked the necessary ingredients to make a pie crust. Pumpkin pie became a popular dish on 17th-century American tables, but it may not have been served at Thanksgiving until the 1623 celebration.

Apple cider was likely the drink of choice at the first Thanksgiving, as it was a popular beverage in England during the 16th and 17th centuries. Cider's history dates back to ancient times, with the cultivated apple originating in the Tien Shah Mountains.

The article also discusses the history of cranberries, which were a key ingredient in the original energy bar, pemmican. Cranberries were used by Native Americans for a wide range of purposes, including cooking, dyeing textiles, and medicinal treatments.

In conclusion, while many believe that the traditional Thanksgiving dishes of turkey, cranberry sauce, pumpkin pie, and apple cider have been a part of the holiday since its inception, this is not entirely accurate. These dishes became popular choices for Thanksgiving meals in the 19th and 20th centuries, with turkey gaining traction after Bradford's journals were reprinted and highlighted the colonists' hunting of wild turkeys. Cranberries, pumpkins, and apples were all used by Native Americans for various purposes, but it was not until later that they became associated with the Thanksgiving holiday.

The discovery of a vast Roman villa, believed to be one of the largest ever found in Britain, was made by Luke Irwin, a rug designer, in his backyard in Wiltshire. The villa, which dates back to AD 175-220, was found during renovations for a table tennis room, when Irwin insisted on an underground cable instead of an overhead one, leading to the discovery of a mosaic layer. The villa, which was three-storey high and similar to those found at Chedworth, is thought to have belonged to a wealthy and influential Roman family.

Archaeologists from Historic England confirmed the discovery and found evidence of the villa's luxurious lifestyle, including discarded oyster and whelk shells, which were transported in barrels of salt water from the sea, indicating the villa's owners were extremely wealthy. Other discoveries included a perfectly preserved Roman well, a stone coffin of a Roman child, and "extremely high status" pottery, brooches, coins, and bones of wild animals.

The villa's walls are still more than a meter high, although buried under alluvial sediment from a nearby river, and the mosaic has been revealed to be of particularly high quality. The discovery is of "national significance" and gives researchers a unique opportunity to understand Roman and post-Roman Britain. The site has now been protected to preserve it, and further research will be continued when more funding becomes available. Luke Irwin, who stumbled upon the find, described it as "mind blowing" and said it was "unbelievable" to have found it so close to his home.

The document discusses the nerve agent attack on a former Russian spy, Sergei Skripal, and his daughter, Yulia, in Salisbury, England. The UK government has accused Russia of being behind the attack, expelling 23 Russian diplomats and freezing the assets of Russians under suspicion. The US has yet to publicly condemn Russia, with President Trump only stating that he will condemn Russia if the facts support it. The silence of the US has been criticized by former US diplomats, who argue that the US should have backed its closest international ally from the beginning. The US Ambassador to the UN, Nikki Haley, has since stated that the US stands in absolute solidarity with Great Britain and believes Russia is responsible for the attack. The UK's expulsion of the Russian diplomats marks the largest such expulsion since the Cold War. The document also mentions the history of Russian involvement in the UK, including the murder of former Russian spy Alexander Litvinenko in 2006. The Russian government has dismissed the UK's accusations, calling them a "circus show." The document concludes with comments from former US diplomats, who express concern about the US's silence on the matter and its potential impact on the US-UK relationship and international relations.

This report, authored by Maria Owings, Sayeedha Uddin, and Sonja Williams, presents estimates of male newborn circumcisions performed during the birth hospitalization from 1979 to 2010, using data from the National Hospital Discharge Survey (NHDS). The national rate of newborn circumcision declined by 10% over the 32-year period, from 64.5% to 58.3%. The report also highlights regional trends, with the West showing the most significant decrease, while the Midwest and South exhibited fluctuating rates. The Northeast region had a relatively stable rate throughout the period.

In a series of tweets on Sunday, President Donald Trump accused the media of treating his son unfairly and distorting democracy, following reports of a meeting between Donald Trump Jr., Paul Manafort, and a Russian lawyer. A group of 18 House Republicans have formally nominated President Donald Trump for the Nobel Peace Prize in recognition of his efforts towards denuclearizing the Korean Peninsula and potentially ending the 68-year-old war between North and South Korea. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer has expressed concerns over the sudden termination of FBI Director James Comey, suggesting it may be part of a cover-up to halt investigations into Russian interference in the 2016 election on behalf of President Donald Trump. Schumer questioned the timing and reason for Comey's dismissal, stating that if the mishandling of Hillary Clinton's email investigation was the true reason, the administration could have acted earlier.

President Trump fired Comey on Tuesday, ending the career of the man who was investigating whether members of his campaign team colluded with Russia in its interference in the 2016 election. Senior White House officials appeared to have misjudged the impact of Trump's sudden move, as critics immediately concluded it was because of the Russia probe. Schumer, along with many of his Democratic colleagues, is now demanding the appointment of a special prosecutor to take over the Russia investigation that Comey was leading at the time of his termination. The United States Special Operations Command is collaborating with various industries, universities, and laboratories to develop a high-tech suit of armor, named TALOS (Tactical Assault Light Operator Suit), inspired by the Iron Man suit from the Marvel movies. The suit aims to provide enhanced ballistic protection, superhuman strength, and advanced technology for soldiers.

A new grave has been discovered on Beacon Island, off the coast of Western Australia, shedding light on the Batavia shipwreck massacre that occurred in 1629. The Batavia was a Dutch East India vessel on its maiden voyage that was wrecked on Morning Reef within the Abrolhos Islands, resulting in the deaths of over 300 people. The survivors swam to Beacon Island, but about 40 people drowned. The events that followed on the island were a 17th-century tale of mutiny and systematic murders of the survivors, inspiring movies, books, and plays, and remaining one of the darkest chapters in Australia's maritime history.

Recently, a skeleton was discovered almost four centuries later, making it the 11th found on Beacon Island since the 1960s. Two musket balls were found near the body, which was about 1.5 meters underground. A forensic team is examining the remains and believes it to be that of an adolescent. The WA Museum's head of maritime archaeology, Jeremy Green, stated that the find is a major step forward in better understanding this internationally significant chapter in history.

The human tooth found on the final day of an expedition at the island in 2013 led archaeologists to examine the same area where they eventually discovered the skeleton. Surprisingly, it appears the skeleton was not the owner of the tooth, indicating that there is another grave very close. A mass grave was discovered on Beacon Island in 1999, but archaeologists had to wait 15 years before old fishermen shacks were removed so they could comb the entire island for clues left behind in 1629.

The team of researchers is studying the island as part of the Australian Research Council-funded project, led by UWA archaeologist Professor Alistair Paterson. Professor Paterson stated that experts traveled from as far away as Holland to help piece together the Batavia story. He said that the chapter in history needed more recognition, and that West Australians know the story well, but there is still more to be learned elsewhere in the country.

The Batavia was carrying gold and silver when it sailed from Texel for the Dutch East Indies in 1628 to obtain spices. However, the vessel went off course and was wrecked in the Abrolhos on June 4, 1629. A total of 180 people – among them 30 women and children – were ferried off the ship, while about 70 men remained. The survivors landed on Beacon Island, and some, including the ship's captain, navigated a longboat to Java to find help after it became clear they could not survive long on what was left of the ship's provisions. Undermerchant Jeronimus Cornelisz assumed charge of the group, and began picking off survivors, by sending them in search of water on nearby islands, where he thought they would not survive. His men drowned many others. He also murdered women and children, the ill and infirm. He kept a number of women alive to subject to repeated rapes. He was eventually overcome by a force he had sent to one of the islands, as he tried to lure them into a trap. When the captain returned to the site of the shipwreck, he sentenced the mutineers to having their right hands chopped off, then put them to death on the gallows. Some of the lesser offenders were returned to Holland, while another two men were left stranded on the mainland as punishment.

Professor Paterson stated that the chapter in history needed more recognition and that West Australians know the story well, particularly in Geraldton and other places, but there is a lot more of that story to be picked up elsewhere in the country. The team of researchers is hoping to create a virtual reality website that will allow visitors to see Beacon Island as it has stood over time, which is expected to be online later this year.

On August 6, 2015, an estimated 1 million gallons of acidic wastewater containing heavy metals were released from the Gold King Mine in San Juan County, Colorado. The wastewater flowed into Cement Creek, which then merged into the Animas River, causing it to turn orange-brown. The disaster forced the city of Durango to halt the pumping of raw water from the river and led to the closure of the Animas River to public use by La Plata County Sheriff Sean Smith.

The accident occurred on Wednesday, August 5, during a cleanup project by a mining and safety team working on behalf of the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA). The team was attempting to secure and consolidate a safe entry to the mine and access contaminated water, according to Richard Mylott, an EPA spokesman in Denver. The project aimed to pump and treat the water and reduce metal pollution flowing out of the mine into Cement Creek.

The contaminated water made its way through Durango by Thursday evening, prompting La Plata County health officials to advise against recreational use of the Animas River. The closure, which applies to all flotation devices, will remain in effect until the river is deemed safe. The closure was made in consultation with the EPA, the Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment, San Juan Basin Health Department, representatives of the Southern Ute Indian Tribe, and Colorado Parks and Wildlife.

The city of Durango stopped pumping water from the Animas River on Wednesday to prevent contamination of the city reservoir. The city also suspended the transfers of raw water to a local golf course and Fort Lewis College. Pet owners were advised to keep dogs and livestock out of the Animas.

The disaster had an impact on wildlife as well. There are no fish in the Cement Creek watershed due to longstanding water-quality issues, according to the Colorado Department of Public Health and the Environment. Colorado Parks and Wildlife placed cages containing fish in the Animas River to monitor their survival and to ensure no infiltration into the hatchery.

The contaminated water made its way to Bakers Bridge in La Plata County by Thursday morning and crossed the New Mexico state line between 4 and 5 a.m. on Friday. Farmington city officials shut down all water-supply intake pumps to avoid contamination, and advised citizens to stay out of the river until the discoloration has passed. Local officials also asked all agricultural water users to shut off water intakes.

The wastewater contained high concentrations of iron, aluminum, cadmium, zinc, and copper. The pH level dropped from 7.8 to 5.8 when the toxic plume arrived, indicating a significant increase in acidity. The EPA will be sampling and investigating downstream locations over the next several days to confirm the release has passed and poses no additional concerns for aquatic life or water users.

The disaster has raised concerns about the EPA's handling of the situation, as New Mexico Governor Susana Martinez criticized the agency for waiting too long to inform New Mexico's environmental agencies about the spill. The incident has also raised questions about the EPA's relationship with the town of Silverton, where some residents and local officials have been opposed to a Superfund listing for the area.

The disaster is not the first time there has been a water-related accident at one of the mines, but it came as a surprise to the town. It remains to be seen whether the toxic metal concentrations flowing downriver will impact the few fish species living below Bakers Bridge. The EPA teams will continue to sample and investigate downstream locations to monitor the situation.

A British chef named Ryan Lock, aged 20 from Chichester, West Sussex, died on December 21 in northern Syria while fighting against the Islamic State of Iraq and the Levant (Isil) in the city of Raqqa. Lock's body was transported to Iraq in preparation for return to the UK, and his father expressed gratitude to the YPG for bringing him home. Lock is the third British man to die fighting alongside the Kurds against IS. The Foreign Office continues to advise against all travel to Syria.

Title: With Charity for All: A Critique of the American Nonprofit Sector

The book provides insights into the charity selection process and current recommendations for donors.

A campaign to recall Judge Aaron Persky of Santa Clara County, California, who handed a lenient sentence to former Stanford athlete Brock Turner for sexually assaulting an unconscious, intoxicated woman, was officially launched on Monday. The campaign filed a notice of intent to recall Persky with the county registrar of voters, with about 35 people gathering to show support, holding signs such as "Soon to be unemployed. Aaron Persky" and "Recall Aaron Persky. Enough is enough."

The campaign submitted a scathing statement branding Persky as an apologist for rapists and batterers, and if approved by the county registrar of voters, it will appear on petitions that proponents plan to begin circulating in August. Recall proponents must collect 58,634 valid voter signatures within a 160-day period ending in January to qualify the measure for the June 2018 countywide ballot.

The campaign, spearheaded by Stanford law professor Michele Dauber, has already hired a firm to help collect signatures. Dauber is a friend of the victim's family and a longtime activist against campus sexual assault.

Judge Persky, who has not commented on the uproar over the Turner sentence, could not be reached for comment on Monday. But a key supporter, District Attorney Jeff Rosen, noted that the case has already had a significant impact, including his successful effort to get a state law passed requiring a prison term for sexual assault of an unconscious or intoxicated person.

Rosen said he has also tried to raise national awareness by organizing a campus sexual assault symposium and crafting a ground-breaking protocol on how colleges and law enforcement handle such assaults.

"Judge Persky’s sentence in that case was wrong, in my opinion, but he had the right to give it," Rosen said in a written statement. "My focus as we move forward is less about an individual judge than it is to the victims of campus sexual assault."

The judge now has seven days to submit his up to 198-word response. If the recall qualifies, voters will also have a chance on the same ballot to immediately pick his replacement, just as they did when they ousted Gov. Gray Davis in 2003 and chose Arnold Schwarzenegger to replace him out of 134 other candidates.

Any lawyer in California may run for judge; there is no requirement in judicial races that candidates must live in the county. If the recall qualifies and Persky loses, whoever gets the most votes would serve out the rest of Persky’s six-year term, ending in 2022. The winner needs only a plurality of the votes, not a majority.

So far, only one candidate has surfaced as a potential replacement: assistant district attorney Cindy Hendrickson, an executive in Rosen’s administration. Hendrickson supports the recall.

Dauber predicted the campaign's biggest challenge would be managing what she said has already been a huge outpouring of support and offers by volunteers to collect signatures. Persky's backers include dozens of law school professors in California, including UC Irvine’s Erwin Chemerinsky and Santa Clara University’s Gerald Uelmen. The professors, including 11 who teach at Stanford, are opposed to the proposed recall on the grounds that the sentence was lawful and dovetailed with a probation officer’s recommendation.

Persky's ouster, they wrote, would cause great harm, because judges may well feel pressured into making decisions based on public opinion. Other groups, including the California Judges Association, have issued similar statements expressing concern about judicial independence.

County officials are still conducting research but have said it would cost slightly more than $1.1 million to put the recall on the June 5, 2018, ballot, far less than the $6.8 million cost of holding a special countywide election in November. However, recall proponents believe it would cost half that, and are still negotiating with the county on the issue.

The incident and the judge’s sentence spawned national outrage. The woman Turner sexually assaulted read a letter to him in court about how the incident affected her mental health. Persky faced widespread criticism for the sentence, and more than 1.3 million people signed a Change.org petition calling for his removal from the bench. California legislators passed a bill mandating prison sentences for people who sexually assault unconscious or intoxicated victims.

Malaysia Airlines Flight 370, which disappeared on March 8, 2014, remains a mystery with no definitive answers about its location or cause of disappearance. However, statistical tools, particularly Bayesian statistics, can help refine and focus the search for the plane and provide insights into its possible location and cause of disappearance.

Bayesian statistics, named after Thomas Bayes, a British Presbyterian minister, allows hunters to update their estimates of the probability of finding their target in any latitude-longitude combination or even in three dimensions, accounting for depth in the water. Bayesian methods have been used in previous search operations, such as the hunt for U-boats in World War II, a U.S. submarine in the 1960s, and Air France Flight 447 in 2011.

In the case of Malaysia Airlines Flight 370, new developments, such as information about how the plane's communication systems were shut off, have lowered the probability that the plane disappeared because of an accident and increased the likelihood of a deliberate diversion. This, in turn, affects the probability of finding the plane at any given location, as a deliberate act has made spots farther from the takeoff point of Kuala Lumpur more likely.

Bayesian inference formalizes what seems like common sense. Its founding principle is that most new situations can be assessed and assigned probabilities. Initially, we might guess that the probability is uniform, but new information is layered on to update the probability distribution.

The Metron team, which worked on the Air France Flight 447 search, outlined its success in a paper that makes plain the subjectivity inherent to the approach. For instance, the team had to account for the possibility that an earlier search covered an area including the wreckage site but missed it. So they examined each prior search, one by one.

In the second search for Air France Flight 447, in June and July 2009, two U.S. Navy ships listened for acoustic signals from beacons on the flight data recorder (also called the black box) and the cockpit voice recorder. Searchers designed the ships' path to ensure that they got within 1,730 meters (a little over a mile) of every point in the area of the Atlantic they were scanning. Metron searchers had to calculate the probability that this search failed not because it was in the wrong area but because the beacons malfunctioned. This step alone, critical in determining how likely it was that a repeat search in that area would yield the wreckage, required several intuitive estimates, or educated guesses.

The extra layers of complexity in the Malaysia Airlines search, including the new estimates of the plane's location and mounting evidence of a deliberate act, complicate the Bayesian calculations and estimates. Some statisticians, such as Bradley Efron of Stanford University, argue that Bayes is a bad fit for the Malaysia Airlines hunt because new evidence changes the situation drastically. However, other advocates of Bayesian statistics argue that it is the perfect situation for Bayesian techniques, which should make searchers most effective in adapting to changing information, so long as they properly assume from the get-go that the plane might not be in the initial search area.

Despite the widespread use of Bayesian methods in searches, not every airline or government uses them. There's no evidence the Malaysian government nor Malaysia Airlines has used Bayesian methods in the current search, though they are getting help from a team of French government investigators who worked on the Air France hunt. The search for Malaysia Airlines Flight 370 continues, and it remains to be seen whether Bayesian statistics will play a role in finding the missing plane.

In a groundbreaking discovery, researchers have confirmed that a fossil found in Sussex, England, in 2004, is the first example of fossilized dinosaur brain tissue. The fossil, most likely from a species similar to Iguanodon, displays similarities to the brains of modern-day crocodiles and birds. The fossilized brain was preserved due to the dinosaur's brain being pickled in a highly acidic and low-oxygen body of water shortly after its death.

The fossil was discovered by Jamie Hiscocks, a fossil hunter, and was studied by Professor Martin Brasier of the University of Oxford and Dr. David Norman from the University of Cambridge. The research was published in a Special Publication of the Geological Society of London, in tribute to Professor Brasier who died in 2014.

The fossilized brain tissue is rare, making understanding the evolutionary history of such tissue difficult. The researchers used scanning electron microscope (SEM) techniques to identify the tough membranes, or meninges, that surrounded the brain, as well as strands of collagen and blood vessels. Structures that could represent tissues from the brain cortex (its outer layer of neural tissue), interwoven with delicate capillaries, also appear to be present.

The structure of the fossilized brain shows similarities with the brains of modern-day descendants of dinosaurs, namely birds and crocodiles. However, the researchers caution against drawing any conclusions about the intelligence of dinosaurs from this particular fossil. They believe that during death and burial, the head of this dinosaur became overturned, causing the brain to collapse and become pressed against the bony roof of the cavity.

Jamie Hiscocks, the man who discovered the specimen, said, "I have always believed I had something special. I noticed there was something odd about the preservation, and soft tissue preservation did go through my mind. Martin realized its potential significance right at the beginning, but it wasn't until years later that its true significance came to be realized."

The discovery of this fossilized dinosaur brain could potentially shed new light on the intelligence of dinosaurs and their evolutionary history. However, further research and scrutiny are needed to confirm the findings and draw definitive conclusions.

The parent company of Joe's Crab Shack, Ignite Restaurant Group, is pioneering a new approach to federal minimum wage policies by implementing a no-tipping policy in 18 of its 131 locations. This policy, currently being tested, aims to replace tips with higher wages for restaurant workers. The CEO, Ray Blanchette, believes that this model will help the company navigate the ongoing national debates about minimum wage increases.

The test locations include restaurants in Utah, Ohio, Indiana, Kentucky, Missouri, Pennsylvania, Illinois, Michigan, Nebraska, and Kansas. The wages of employees at these locations have been raised based on factors such as historical compensation and their importance to the business. However, specific salary details have not been disclosed.

Notably, the restaurants testing the policy are not adding service charges to checks, although there have been small increases in menu item prices. Blanchette anticipates that this change will reduce employee turnover due to the fixed rate of pay, which he compares to a $14 hourly wage, compared to the current $2.25 an hour for tipped workers in some states.

This move by Joe's Crab Shack follows a similar announcement by famed New York restaurateur Danny Meyer, who plans to eliminate tipping at all of his New York City restaurants. Meyer operates Union Square Hospitality Group, which includes Union Square Cafe, Gramercy Tavern, and Blue Smoke, among others.

This shift towards a no-tipping policy is part of an effort to archive pages as they are created and preserve the original intended content of web pages, even if they are later changed or removed from the web. This initiative aims to fix all broken links on the web.

On January 14, 2014, a school shooting occurred at Berrendo Middle School in Roswell, New Mexico. A 12-year-old seventh-grader, Mason Campbell, is the suspected shooter, who brought a 20-gauge shotgun with a sawed-off wood stock into the school. Campbell warned several students not to attend school that day and injured two students, an 11-year-old boy and a 13-year-old girl, who were airlifted to a Lubbock hospital. The boy remained in critical condition, while the girl's condition was updated to satisfactory.

Campbell was taken into custody by New Mexico State Police Lt. Gary Smith, who was dropping off his child just as the school principal was locking the front doors. After a hearing, Campbell was transferred to a psychiatric hospital in Albuquerque. Police are serving search warrants for Campbell's school locker, his home, and the bag he used to conceal the gun.

John Masterson, an eighth-grade social studies teacher at Berrendo Middle School, is being credited for stopping the shooter. Masterson, who also coaches track and soccer, talked Campbell into putting the gun down, and Smith took the boy into custody. The school's faculty members had participated in "active shooter" training, and they responded appropriately, according to Superintendent Tom Burris.

Governor Susana Martinez said a staff member received very minor injuries but declined medical care because he wanted to stay and help. Students were reunited with their families at a mall parking lot nearby, and a prayer vigil was scheduled at the Roswell Convention Center. School will resume on Thursday. The community is described as strong and resilient, and the shooting is expected to bring the community together in prayer and support.

UPMC Presbyterian Hospital is currently investigating the potential link between the deaths of two heart transplant patients and fungal infections they may have contracted in the cardiothoracic intensive care unit (CTICU). Two patients, one who died in October 2014 with lichtheimia and another who died in June with rhizomucor, had stayed in the same room where mold was recently discovered.

The discovery of mold in the CTICU earlier this month prompted its closure for cleaning and analysis by UPMC infection prevention experts and a private remediation company. It's unclear when the unit may reopen. Dr. Cyril Wecht, a former Allegheny County medical examiner, stated that mold is rarely fatal and it's uncommon for it to contribute to or cause death.

The mold contamination in the unit was first detected after a patient tested positive for mold in his lung tissue on Sept. 3. Fifteen patients remained in the ICU until they were removed last week upon the discovery of more mold in the 20-bed unit. UPMC has yet to determine the cause of the mold contamination.

News of the mold outbreak and the two deaths came as a shock to the relatives of some patients. UPMC's chief quality officer, Tami Minnier, stated that the hospital regrets the loss of the loved ones and is committed to transparency. She also mentioned that the complicated nature of the patients' illnesses and the sporadic and limited scope of the infections made it difficult to find the mold problem sooner.

Wecht expressed concern about the lack of autopsies on the deceased patients and called for them to be conducted. The mold cases under review at UPMC Presbyterian Hospital are under jurisdiction of Pennsylvania's health department. Allegheny County's health department declined comment on the case.

David Namey, program chief of housing and community environment for the county health department, stated that mold is typically not a serious health risk, with common health risks being allergic reactions such as runny nose, watery eyes, or nasal congestion. People who are severely immuno-compromised could be at a higher risk.

Namey also emphasized the importance of taking precautions for those with severely compromised immune systems, especially in situations where mold is present. Transplant patients are on drugs that suppress their immune systems to prevent organ rejection.

The investigation into the mold outbreak and the two deaths is ongoing, with UPMC launching an online blog to report new information as it occurs.

A new species of ancient predatory cockroach, named Manipulator modificaputis, has been discovered preserved in amber, dating back 100 million years. This tiny, unusual creature, measuring just under 1 cm, possesses a unique combination of features, resembling a chimera of a crane fly, a praying mantis, and a cockroach. The discovery adds to the known ferocious cockroaches that lived during prehistoric times.

Manipulator modificaputis belongs to the ancient family of cockroaches called the Manipulatoridae. It has a triangular, maneuverable head with large eyes, set upon a long neck, likely used for hunting. The cockroach also had a narrow body and wings, elongated legs, and mouthparts, and an extra set of modified eyes located on the top of its head, which likely helped it spot predators.

The cockroach was a solitary hunter, able to run fast and seize its prey with strong spines on its feet. However, some scientists argue that it was more likely to surprise its prey, using its long limbs to traverse gaps between forest leaves.

In a separate discovery, paleontologists found a fossil of a bizarre sea creature, Aegirocassis benmoulae, an early member of the arthropod family tree. This extinct animal lived about 480 million years ago in a shallow sea that once covered part of the Sahara Desert. Aegirocassis benmoulae is an early ancestor of cockroaches, butterflies, and shrimp and is one of the biggest arthropods that ever existed, far bigger than any arthropod today.

The discovery of these ancient creatures provides valuable insights into the evolution of arthropods, the most morphologically diverse group of animals on the planet. The fossils were well-preserved, allowing researchers to see previously hidden features on the body of these early arthropods, helping them to solve a longstanding evolutionary mystery. The success of arthropods is associated with their ability to adapt to a wide range of environments due to their bodies and legs being made of multiple segments that can be modified for various purposes.

The 2014 International Consumer Electronics Show in Las Vegas is set to be a significant milestone for the automotive industry as auto manufacturers aim to make cars connect to the internet in a major way. Companies like General Motors Co. and Audi AG are planning to use the event to announce strategies for equipping cars with built-in 4G high-speed broadband.

The rise of smartphones and tablets has put pressure on traditional automotive technology, with free mapping services and entertainment apps becoming compelling alternatives to built-in systems. To address this, several automakers and technology companies, including Google, have formed the Open Automotive Alliance. This group aims to customize Google's Android software for vehicles, providing an opportunity for technology companies to place their products into hundreds of millions of cars while allowing automakers to modernize their software.

The automotive industry has traditionally preferred stable, proven technology, but the rapid evolution of smartphones and tablets has necessitated change. Car companies have responded with custom in-car software systems, but this approach requires software companies to write different applications for each carmaker, a costly and time-consuming process.

Partnerships have been attempted to solve this problem, such as the Genivi Alliance, a collaboration around the Linux operating system and supporting software. Android, a variant of Linux, has an advantage due to its dominance in the mobile device industry, offering access to newer, better technology and lower costs for testing equipment.

Tesla Motors, known for its all-electric Model S sedan with a 17-inch touch screen, is among the cutting-edge automakers popularizing the concept of a computer on wheels. Silicon Valley startups like CloudCar are also working to bridge the technology and automotive realms, developing computing devices that can be plugged into cars to provide modern infotainment systems. Ford has opened a research center in Palo Alto and open-sourced some of its car's control software to encourage customization.

In summary, the 2014 International Consumer Electronics Show marks a significant shift in the automotive industry as car manufacturers and technology companies collaborate to bring the internet to cars, aiming to modernize software and keep pace with mobile devices.

A former police officer, Roy Oliver, has been charged with murder for the shooting of 15-year-old Jordan Edwards in Balch Springs, Texas, on April 29, 2017. The shooting occurred after Oliver opened fire on a car full of teenagers, including Edwards, who were leaving an unruly house party. The initial police account stated that the car was backing up aggressively towards the officers, but this was later revised after reviewing body-camera footage, revealing that the car was actually driving away when Jordan was shot.

Oliver turned himself in on Friday and was released after posting a $300,000 bond at the Parker County Jail in Weatherford, about 95 miles west of Dallas. The sheriff's office issued a warrant for his arrest based on evidence suggesting that Oliver "intended to cause serious bodily injury and commit an act clearly dangerous to human life that caused the death."

The shooting has led to protests calling for Oliver to be fired and charged. The news comes amidst other high-profile cases involving the shooting of black men by white police officers, such as the decision not to charge two white police officers in Baton Rouge, Louisiana, in 2016, and a white officer in North Charleston, South Carolina, pleading guilty to federal civil rights charges in 2015.

Jordan Edwards' family has filed a wrongful death lawsuit against Oliver, the Balch Springs Police Department, and the city of Balch Springs. The family's attorney, Lee Merritt, stated that the family is grateful that investigators sought a murder charge and that it gives the appearance that the state is not going to sweep the incident under the rug. However, Merritt also emphasized that they still have some ways to go before securing a conviction.

Balch Springs Police Chief Jonathan Haber expressed his condolences to the Edwards family and acknowledged that the incident did not meet the department's core values. He also emphasized the need for the community to learn from the incident and push for change together. The investigation into Edwards' death will continue, according to the Dallas County Sheriff's Office.

Celia Barquín Arozamena, a 22-year-old Spanish golfer and Iowa State University student, was found dead on an Iowa golf course on Monday, with several stab wounds to her head, neck, and upper body. Collin Daniel Richards, also 22, has been charged with first-degree murder in her death.

On January 31, 2018, a unique astronomical event will take place, a total lunar eclipse of a Super Blue Moon, visible from Australia and the western United States. The Virtual Telescope Project, in partnership with several astrophotographers from both countries, will provide a live broadcast of this event. The team includes astrophotographers Dean Hooper, John Stevenson, Chris Stockdale, John W. Johnson, Andrew Wall, Ron Delvaux, James McCue, Gerard Lazarus, and coordinator Gianluca Masi. The online, free lunar total eclipse session is scheduled for 31 Jan. 2018, starting at 11:30 UT.

In addition, the Virtual Telescope Project will show the Super Blue Moon rising above Rome's legendary monuments on the same day, starting at 16:00 UT. Donations to the project will provide supporters with unique images of the stars above Rome.

The eclipse will be a total eclipse and will be a Blue Moon, a term used for the second full moon in a month. Such a skywatching event hasn't happened for more than 150 years. The Pacific Ocean will be turned toward the moon at the time, and central and eastern Asia, Indonesia, New Zealand, and most of Australia will get a fine view of this moon show in the evening sky.

To the east, Alaska, Hawaii, and northwestern Canada will see the eclipse from start to finish. Moonset will intervene for the rest of North and Central America. A timetable for the main stages of the moon's passage through the Earth's shadow for six time zones has been provided.

The upcoming eclipse on Jan. 31 will be the first total eclipse of a Blue Moon in nearly 152 years! The next time that a Blue Moon passes through Earth's umbra will be on Dec. 31, 2028, and, after that, on Jan. 31, 2037. Both of these eclipses will be total. Before 2017, there was an 8 percent partial eclipse on Dec. 31, 2009, but, for a total eclipse of a Blue Moon, we have to go all the way back to March 31, 1866.

Visible supermoons—full moons that appear when the moon is at its closest orbital point to Earth—aren’t very rare. Having three in a row certainly is. The first supermoon appeared when the moon swung by Earth 26,500 km (approximately 16,500 miles) closer than usual on Dec. 3. It will reappear as a visible supermoon on New Year’s Day 2018 and again on Jan. 31. Visible supermoons appear 14% bigger and 30% brighter than full moons that occur at the farthest point in the moon’s orbit. If you only have time to catch one episode of the trilogy, NASA recommends catching the last one, which will be extra special.

A high school teacher in Visalia, Margaret Gieszinger, has been arrested and is currently in jail after an incident where she forcibly cut a student's hair in class. The incident occurred at University Preparatory High School, which is located on the College of the Sequoias campus. On Wednesday, a video surfaced showing Gieszinger, 52, chasing students with scissors between desks while singing the "Star Spangled Banner."

Students reported that Gieszinger came into class with a pair of scissors and declared it was "hair cut day." One student, who wished to remain anonymous, said Gieszinger started cutting a student's hair and continued to sing the national anthem loudly as she tossed a chunk of hair behind her. The student ran to the main office for help, but Gieszinger followed him out with scissors. Other students tried to intervene, and eventually, other staff managed to stop her.

Gieszinger was arrested on suspicion of felony child endangerment by the College of the Sequoias Police. Her bail was set at $100,000. The Tulare County Office of Education released a statement regarding the incident, expressing concern for the students who were subjected to Gieszinger's disturbing behavior.

The incident is out of character for Gieszinger, according to one of her students, Lilli Gates. However, trouble reportedly started on Monday when a test went missing, and Gieszinger blamed students. During Monday's incident, Gieszinger made a student's friend cry, and students reached out to administrators for help but were told they had to go back to class.

The Tulare County Office of Education is investigating the incident, and Gieszinger will not return to her UPHS classroom. A highly-qualified substitute teacher will take over for the rest of the semester. About 225 students are enrolled in the Tulare County Office of Education high school, which opened on the COS campus in 2009. The Commission on Teacher Credentialing is also investigating Gieszinger's credentials, which were suspended in 2007 and 2016 for immoral or unprofessional conduct.

Florida's coral reefs have been experiencing a multi-year outbreak of coral disease since 2014, which is unprecedented due to the number of affected coral species and the ongoing nature of the event. The disease outbreak has resulted in the mortality of millions of corals, with widespread disease confirmed across approximately 55 linear miles of reef, including locations as far north as St. Lucie Inlet in Martin County and as far south as Biscayne National Park.

Response efforts have been ongoing since 2015, with DEP and numerous partners working together to document the distribution, prevalence, severity, and impacts associated with the disease outbreak; identify likely pathogens; understand potentially contributory environmental factors; experiment with treatments and other interventions; seek additional capacity and funding; and facilitate stakeholder assistance through a region-wide Reef Ambassador program and maintaining SEAFAN and C-OCEAN citizen science programs.

The exact cause and contributing factors for this event are still unknown, but addressing other known coral stressors such as water quality, turbidity, and sedimentation will increase the ability of the corals to recover. The Florida Coastal Office has partnered with coral disease experts to deliver workshops on coral disease identification, ecology, and investigation techniques, as well as discuss the next phase of coral disease response efforts.

The disease outbreak is believed to be a bacterial disease, and for about half of the state's species of coral it's deadly. The disease has moved from one patch of coral to another, and has moved north, affecting reefs all the way up to the St. Lucie inlet, and is now moving south, through the Florida Keys. A large number of researchers are working to tackle the disease on many fronts, including DNA analysis to try to identify the pathogens involved and looking for ways to stop the disease from spreading.

Mote Marine Lab is raising healthy corals in the lab and transplanting them onto reefs, with the hope of planting 35,000 of its lab-raised corals onto reefs in the Keys this year. So far, corals raised in the lab have shown resistance to the mystery disease, giving scientists hope they may yet be able to save Florida's reefs.

Verizon Communications Inc. has agreed to buy Yahoo Inc.'s main web businesses for $4.8 billion, ending a two-decade run as an independent company for the pioneering internet company. The deal includes Yahoo's real estate but excludes some intellectual property, which will be sold separately. Yahoo will be left with its stakes in Alibaba Group Holding Ltd. and Yahoo Japan Corp., with a combined market value of about $40 billion.

Verizon will add Yahoo's web services, which still draw 1 billion monthly users, including mail, news and sports content, and financial tools. The largest U.S. wireless carrier also gets smaller but faster-growing assets such as mobile applications and advertising technology for video and handheld devices.

The deal comes after a drawn-out auction process for Yahoo, which has been struggling to compete with nimbler online rivals such as Google and Facebook Inc. Yahoo shares closed 1.4 percent higher on Friday at $39.38, giving the company a market valuation of $37 billion. Verizon on Friday ended 1.3 percent higher at $56.10, with a market capitalization of $229 billion.

The driving force behind the deal on the Verizon side is Marni Walden, a longtime Verizon executive who has been leading the company's moves beyond telecommunications, particularly its expansion into video and advertising. Walden has been instrumental in the acquisition of AOL and is expected to play a key role in the integration of Yahoo.

The sale of Yahoo comes with access to Yahoo's news operation and Yahoo Finance, a website for investors keeping tabs on Wall Street. It includes Yahoo's popular destination for fantasy sports, and its question-and-answer platform, Yahoo Answers. Plus, Yahoo owns the microblogging site Tumblr and the photo-hosting site Flickr.

The deal may face potential land mines, such as new privacy rules on Internet providers and the Federal Communications Commission's requirement for Internet providers to get their customers' explicit permission before using their data for third-party advertising. However, Verizon's ambitions in the media and content realm are evident, and the company may continue to look for more acquisitions to reach its goals.

The sale of Yahoo marks the end of an era for the company that once defined the Internet. Yahoo's seventh and final CEO, Marissa Mayer, will reportedly depart upon the deal's conclusion with severance pay worth more than $50 million. The sale leaves Yahoo as a company focused on its Asian asset equity stakes, with a much smaller operating business.
