Gaga lost the Oscar to Sam Smith's James Bond track "Writing's on the Wall," but her performance was still widely praised.

Following the ceremony, Gaga thanked the survivors who joined her on stage and expressed gratitude for their strength and bravery. She also credited her fiance, "Chicago Fire's" Taylor Kinney, for standing by her and supporting her throughout the process.

Gaga's performance and subsequent Instagram post have been hailed as a milestone for sexual abuse survivors, as she used her platform to speak out about her experiences and offer support to others who have gone through similar situations. The performance was particularly poignant given that Gaga first opened up about her abuse in a 2014 Howard Stern interview, where she revealed that she had been assaulted by a man who was 20 years older than she was.

Overall, Lady Gaga's performance at the 2016 Academy Awards was a powerful and moving moment that brought attention to the issue of sexual abuse and offered support to survivors. Her bravery in speaking out about her own experiences and using her platform to support others is commendable and serves as an inspiration to many.

The start of 2013 brought a mix of celebrations, fiscal cliff drama, and new state laws. Among the thousands of new state laws that took effect quietly, some are quite peculiar. In Illinois, motorcycle wheelies are now illegal, and strip clubs must charge a $3 door fee with proceeds going to charity. Kentucky has made it illegal to release wild pigs into the wild, and stealing unused cooking oil worth over $1000 is now a felony in North Carolina. California has legalized "driverless" cars, but a human must always be in the passenger seat. In Wellington, Kansas, households are limited to no more than four cats, and Concord, Massachusetts has outlawed plastic bottles. Illinois has also banned the sale and trade of shark fins.

California coaches and administrators who have regular contact with children are now mandated to report suspected child abuse. "Caylee’s Laws" take effect in both California and Illinois, imposing strong penalties for a parent or guardian who fails to report the disappearance or death of a child within 24 hours. Gay marriage becomes legal in Maryland and Maine, and same-sex couples from other states are now recognized in Maine. New Hampshire enacts a ban on so-called “partial-birth abortions,” and Montana now requires parental notification for any minor who wants to have an abortion.

California becomes the first state to write into law expanded official authority to investigate mortgage fraud, and large lenders are now prohibited from foreclosing while evaluating a homeowner request for loan modifications. Pennsylvania now requires that contractors on public-works projects use the E-Verify system to confirm employees’ citizenship. Montana moves to withhold state services from illegal immigrants. After civil liberties groups and others criticized the practice of employers asking job applicants for passwords to their Facebook and Twitter accounts, that is now illegal in Illinois.

These new laws reflect a range of concerns, from child protection to environmental issues, and address a variety of public concerns. Despite low opinions of legislatures, some argue that these new state laws demonstrate that state governments are indeed addressing public concerns. However, the question remains whether legislation is the proper avenue through which to fix or solve these problems.

The Ontario Provincial election held on June 7, 2018, resulted in a majority victory for the Progressive Conservative Party, led by Doug Ford. The Progressive Conservatives defeated the Liberal Party, which had been in power for 15 years, and the New Democratic Party (NDP). Doug Ford's election promises included income tax cuts and opposition to a carbon tax.

Doug Ford is the brother of the late Toronto Mayor Rob Ford, who became famous for his drug use and controversial tenure as mayor. Despite his controversial past, Ford was able to capitalize on voter dissatisfaction with the Liberals and the unpopularity of their leader, Kathleen Wynne. Ford's campaign was characterized by simplicity, control, and a focus on tangible deliverables such as tax cuts and reduced prices for gas, beer, and hydro rates.

Ford's victory was a vindication for his team against naysayers, including some within his own party. His campaign was relatively last-minute and disorganized, but his simple and effective message resonated with voters. Ford's control during the debates and his ability to stay on point helped counter the image his opponents tried to create, that he was a radical, hard-right conservative and Donald Trump clone.

Ford's victory was also a rebuke of the party elites by an outsider, as he narrowly edged out Christine Elliott in the party's leadership race. Elliott was expected to win, but Ford's victory was a stunning rebuke of the party establishment. Ford has promised to cut spending by $6 billion without slashing public-sector jobs, but his platform was never fully costed.

The Ontario election results marked the end of the Liberals' 15-year reign and the beginning of a new era for the province. The election was characterized by a desire for change, and Ford's victory was a vindication for his team against the naysayers. Despite his controversial past, Ford's simple and effective message resonated with voters, and he was able to capitalize on voter dissatisfaction with the Liberals to win the election.

Rachel Uchitel, known for her high-profile affairs with Tiger Woods and David Boreanaz, has married her boyfriend Matt Hahn in Nevada. The couple, who have been together for several months, got married in October. Uchitel, 36, is currently pregnant and shared a photo of her baby bump on Twitter. Aside from her scandals, Uchitel has appeared on reality shows like "Celebrity Rehab With Dr. Drew" and "Famous Food."

The U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) has announced a recall of approximately 6,937,195 pounds of raw, non-intact beef products produced by JBS Tolleson, Inc., due to potential contamination with Salmonella Newport. The products, which include ground beef, were packaged between July 26 and Sept. 7, 2018, and were shipped to retail locations and institutions nationwide.

The recall was initiated after an investigation linked the products to 57 reported cases of salmonella illness in 16 states, with 14 hospitalizations. The first store receipt linking the purchase of the contaminated products to a case-patient was received on September 19, 2018, and traceback investigations identified JBS as the common supplier of the ground beef products.

Consumers are urged not to consume the recalled products and should throw them away or return them to the place of purchase. Consumers with questions regarding the recall can contact the JBS USA Consumer Hotline at (800) 727-2333. The USDA advises all consumers to safely prepare raw meat products and only consume ground beef that has been cooked to a temperature of 160°F.

The USDA will continue to work with public health partners and will provide updated information as it becomes available. Consumers with food safety questions can contact the USDA Meat and Poultry Hotline at 1-888-MPHotline (1-888-674-6854).

In a controversial move, Danish radio station Radio24syv killed a baby rabbit named Allan on air as part of a stunt aimed at exposing the hypocrisy of those who claim to be animal lovers but consume meat. The rabbit was killed with a bicycle pump and later skinned and eaten by one of the radio station's hosts, Asger Juhl, and his family. The station defended the stunt, stating that it aimed to highlight the conditions faced by animals in Denmark's agriculture sector, including the crowded living conditions and lengthy transport to slaughterhouses. The stunt received widespread criticism, with many calling for a boycott of the radio station. Reality star Linse Kessler, who was brought on the program as an outspoken advocate for animal rights, tried to prevent the rabbit from being killed but was asked to leave. The stunt drew comparisons to the Copenhagen Zoo's controversial killing of a giraffe named Marius last year. Asger Juhl, the host who killed the rabbit, has since defended his actions, stating that he wanted to spark debate about our meat-eating habits and that the rabbit was killed in a humane manner. However, many have criticized the stunt as being insensitive and inappropriate.

Edvard Munch's iconic artwork, "The Scream," sold for a record-breaking $119.9 million at Sotheby's auction in New York City. The 1895 piece, the only one still in private hands, was sold by Norwegian businessman Petter Olsen. Proceeds from the sale will fund a new museum, art center, and hotel in Hvitsten, Norway. The auctioned artwork is the most colorful and vibrant of the four versions, with a hand-painted frame by the artist and a poem detailing its inspiration. "The Scream" is renowned for its popularity in pop culture, being as famous as the Mona Lisa. The previous auction record was held by Picasso's "Nude, Green Leaves, and Bust."

The mystery novel "O: A Presidential Novel," set during the 2012 presidential election, is causing a stir due to its anonymous author, who is rumored to have had close ties with President Obama. Speculations about the author's identity include Joe Klein, Robert Gibbs, Rahm Emanuel, Ben Smith, and even President Obama himself. The novel, published by Simon & Schuster, mixes fact with fiction, similar to the 1996 novel "Primary Colors" about Bill Clinton.

Joe Klein, the author of "Primary Colors," has denied any involvement, but his past denials have proven to be untrue. Robert Gibbs' profile as White House press secretary fits the publisher's description, but he is considered less likely due to his busy schedule and lack of literary flair. Rahm Emanuel is also a possibility, but the smart money is on Joe Klein. Ben Smith, a Politico correspondent, has been leading a hunt for the anonymous author, but has denied any involvement.

President Obama himself is also a speculated author, given his established status as a bestselling author. However, White House spokesperson Bill Burton declined to comment on the speculation. The author's anonymity adds an element of intrigue, with the author's grasp of campaigns and Obamaland suggesting a political reporter or press staffer as the author's identity. The novel, while bogged down by campaign details, is described as a fast-paced, well-plotted bit of campaign fiction.

US senators, Carl Levin and John McCain, have expressed concern over the sentencing of a Pakistani doctor, Shakeel Afridi, to 33 years in prison for aiding US intelligence in the search for Osama bin Laden. Afridi was accused of treason by a tribal court in Khyber, a lawless district and extremist hotbed, for collecting DNA to verify bin Laden's presence. The senators called the sentence "shocking and outrageous," stating that Afridi's actions were heroic and patriotic. They urged Pakistan to pardon and free Afridi, warning that his continued imprisonment could harm US-Pakistani relations and potentially affect US financial assistance to Pakistan.

The US has provided Pakistan with over $18 billion since joining the war in Afghanistan following the September 11 attacks, but relations between the two countries have been strained due to concerns about Pakistani support for extremists. The US has been pushing Pakistan to reopen supply routes to NATO forces in Afghanistan, which were closed in November after a border air raid killed 26 Pakistani troops.

Tensions between the US and Pakistan have also been raised by US drone strikes in Pakistan's North Waziristan region, which are seen as violations of sovereignty and inflict civilian casualties. Pakistan's parliament has demanded an end to these drone strikes. The CIA's ability to target high-value al Qaeda or Taliban militants is believed to rely on cooperation from Pakistani authorities, unless intelligence from informants on the ground has significantly improved.

In summary, the situation in the Donetsk region of Ukraine has escalated significantly, leading to the cancellation of President Petro Poroshenko's visit to Turkey. The town of Novoazovsk, strategically positioned in southeastern Ukraine, is now under the control of Russia-backed separatists, raising concerns about a new front in the Ukraine conflict. The Obama administration has accused Russia of orchestrating a new military incursion, while the Russian government denies these allegations. The Ukrainian government has reported that an increasing number of Russian troops are involved in the fighting, and international leaders such as Angela Merkel, Francois Hollande, and the OSCE are demanding explanations and action from Russia. The Ukrainian forces are reportedly withdrawing from Novoazovsk and reinforcing Mariupol's defenses. The conflict has resulted in a significant loss of life, with at least 2,119 people killed and 5,043 wounded since mid-April, according to a UN report. The human cost of the war in eastern Ukraine continues to rise, with many civilians and soldiers killed and displaced.

During a Salvation Army fundraiser at a Tega Cay Wal-Mart, an anonymous individual donated a rare coin worth $1,200. The coin was appraised at Brownlee Jewelers, a local store. The coin is expected to be sold, with all proceeds going to the Salvation Army. For more information, contact David Thackham at dthackham@heraldonline.com. The generous donation highlights the spirit of giving during the holiday season.

The article emphasizes the importance of Operations Security (OPSEC) in the military, particularly in the age of social media. The use of social media platforms can potentially reveal sensitive operational information to adversaries, putting military members at risk. Islamic State sympathizers and 'lone wolves' are identified as potential threats who can use social media to track down and harm military personnel.

Capt. Jonathan McDonald, AFCENT Force Protection chief, emphasized the need for military personnel to avoid posting vital mission-related information and personal details on social media to ensure safety. He also advised checking security settings and being cautious about what is posted and shared.

Master Sgt. Aaron Miller, AFCENT Information security program manager, highlighted the consequences of OPSEC violations, stating that it could impact missions, resources, and members, potentially affecting national strategic and foreign policies.

The article also provides tips for maintaining OPSEC, such as protecting information on the Critical Information List, using secure phone lines, encrypting emails, and shredding paper documents. The public affairs office coordinates all media interviews, and any suspected OPSEC incidents should be reported to the unit's OPSEC manager.

The Air Force has adopted the phrase "Loose Tweets Destroy Fleets" as a modern-day twist of the World War II slogan, "Loose Lips Sink Ships," to remind servicemembers to guard what they share on social media. The phrase has been well-received by some, with one commenter stating its relevance in today's digital age, while others have humorously suggested that the Navy should reclaim the slogan.

The iron gate with the infamous Nazi slogan "Arbeit Macht Frei" ("Work sets you free") from the Dachau concentration camp in Germany, which was stolen in 2014, has been found in western Norway. The gate was discovered following an anonymous tip-off, and police believe it is highly likely to be the stolen gate due to its similarity in appearance. The gate was initially installed at Dachau in 1933 and was used as a symbol of the concentration camp's brutal history. More than 41,000 people, including many Jews, were murdered at Dachau during World War II. The camp was liberated by US troops in 1945, and it is now a memorial that attracts hundreds of thousands of visitors from around the world. The gate was replaced with a replica in 2015, and its recovery is being hailed as a significant find. The police did not release further details about the location of the gate or the identity of the informant. This is not the first time a gate with the same inscription has been stolen; a similar gate was stolen from Auschwitz in Poland in 2009.

A hammer-wielding man was arrested at Salisbury Cathedral on suspicion of attempted theft, possession of an offensive weapon, and criminal damage, after an attempted smash and grab of the Magna Carta. The incident occurred on Thursday, and the suspect was held by staff and volunteers before being apprehended by police. The Magna Carta, one of Britain's most influential legal documents, was not damaged, and nobody was injured. The document has been removed for safe-keeping, and a facsimile copy will be displayed instead. The incident caused the cathedral to be evacuated, and fire crews were called but were not needed. The Magna Carta, dating back to 1215, is considered the foundation of constitutional liberty in the English-speaking world and is on permanent display at Salisbury Cathedral.

Minnie Driver, a British actress known for her roles in films like Good Will Hunting and Hunky Dory, discusses her career and personal life in a new interview. Driver's latest film, Hunky Dory, is a small British indie set in Wales during the 1976 heatwave. She plays a high school teacher who sings in the film, but the humour is specialized and the film lacks funding. Driver reveals that she has been trying to get on the TV show Glee since its inception, but was beaten out by Gwyneth Paltrow.

Driver's career took a turn for the worse in the late 1990s, with negative press surrounding her behavior on the set of the film Hard Rain and the end of her relationship with Matt Damon. She was also criticized for comments she made about Dame Judi Dench that were taken out of context. Driver vowed never to speak to the press again, but has since opened up about the difficult period in her life.

Physically, Driver is similar to the woman she was in her 20s, but she says she is much changed. She had a "crisis" in her 30s and started making music in a beach trailer in Santa Monica as a way to cope. Driver has lived in LA for the past 14 years and also has a house in the hills, but the trailer fits an image of her as boho and hippy.

Driver's personal life has been the focus of intense press scrutiny, particularly regarding her son, Henry, who was born in 2008. She revealed his father's identity in a recent interview, stating that he was a writer on the TV show The Riches. Driver says she chose to protect her son from the public eye because he was not directly in the business.

Driver describes herself as a "robust person" and is proud of her ability to handle herself in Hollywood. She is in two minds about whether to stay in America in the long-term, but enjoys the outdoor life and the fact that she can pick up her son from school. She has set her sights on a return to the small screen, with ambitions to work with directors like Danny Boyle and Martin Scorsese. Motherhood has changed Driver's perspective on her career, and she says she now takes it less seriously.

In a separate article, Driver has revealed the identity of her son's father, stating that he was a writer on the TV show The Riches. She says he has increased his involvement in their son's life since the revelation.

The Drudge Report has been criticized for its coverage of Ted Cruz's recent wins in the Republican primaries, with the site being accused of becoming a propaganda tool for Donald Trump's campaign. The Report has been linking to several stories with sensational headlines about the Colorado Republican convention, including accusations of corruption and voter disenfranchisement. Cruz himself has spoken out against the Report, claiming that it has become an attack site for the Trump campaign and no longer covers news. The Report responded by posting a link to a previous interview where Cruz praised the site. The increasing scrutiny from the Drudge Report comes as the delegate wrestling and wrangling intensifies in the Republican race, and Cruz will need the support of grassroots activists to win the nomination at a contested convention in Cleveland. Meanwhile, the Democratic National Committee has begun to train more of its fire at Cruz, after focusing almost single-mindedly on Trump for months.

In other news, Donald Trump has identified with Howard Roark from Ayn Rand's "The Fountainhead." Trump praised the novel and its protagonist in a broader interview with USA Today, and columnist Kirsten Powers wrote that he pointed out that "The Fountainhead" is "in a way about the tyranny of groupthink." Roark is an architect who dynamites a housing project he designed because he is angry about changes that others made to his blueprints. He is then put on trial for arson, but a jury acquits him after he delivers an eloquent speech about the need to always stay true to one's self.

In other political news, Phyllis Schlafly is facing backlash after endorsing Trump, including an attempt to oust her as the head of the Eagle Forum, the conservative group she founded 44 years ago to stop the Equal Rights Amendment. John Kasich will call his candidacy the GOP's only way out of a "path to darkness" in a speech today in Manhattan. Ben Carson continues to be a poor surrogate for Trump, admitting that his support for Trump is "purely pragmatic" and saying he would probably oppose him "if the stakes weren’t so high."

In other news, Forty percent of former NFL players show signs of traumatic brain injuries, according to a groundbreaking study that will be presented at next week’s American Academy of Neurology. This is one of the largest studies performed on living NFL players, and it offers "the most conclusive evidence yet" of a definitive link between brain injury and playing football.

In other news, Trump spoke last night during a campaign event in Albany, NY. Phyllis Schlafly is facing backlash after endorsing Trump, including an attempt to oust her as the head of the Eagle Forum, the conservative group she founded 44 years ago to stop the Equal Rights Amendment. John Kasich, speaking today in Manhattan, will call his candidacy the GOP's only way out of a “path to darkness.” “Without naming Cruz or Trump, Kasich plans to indict them both,” writes Weigel, who reviewed the planned remarks. Ben Carson continues to be the worst surrogate of the cycle. He admitted yesterday that his support for Trump is “purely pragmatic" and said he'd probably oppose him “if the stakes weren’t so high.” (BuzzFeed) Trump told USA Today he could envision putting Marco Rubio in his cabinet. “Yes. I like Marco Rubio. Yeah. I could,” he said. “There are people I have in mind in terms of vice president. I just haven’t told anybody names. ... I do like Marco. I do like Kasich. … I like [Scott] Walker actually in a lot of ways. I hit him very hard. ... But I’ve always liked him. There are people I like, but I don’t think they like me because I have hit them hard.”

In other news, Trump also got outgunned last weekend in Virginia and Indiana, losing delegates in both states. The delegate scoreboard since Rubio got out: Cruz 120, Trump 65, Uncommitted 29, Kasich 0. In the Democratic race, Clinton devoted a Long Island campaign event entirely to gun control, all but blaming Sanders for crime in New York City. Sanders called for a national ban on fracking and released a new ad to highlight his opposition, narrated by actress Susan Sarandon. Biden said Sanders calling Clinton "unqualified" was not sexist but something said in the heat of a campaign. During an interview with Mic.com, the vice president was asked about Sanders’ comment and if he thought Hillary is held to a higher standard because she is a woman. “No, I don’t think she’s held to a higher standard,” he replied. “This country’s ready for a woman,” Biden elaborated. “There’s no problem. We’re going to be able to elect a woman in this country.” When the female interviewer asked Biden if he’d like to see a woman elected, a male aide to the VP interrupted from off camera and tried to end the interview. “That’s it,” he said. “I would like to see a woman elected,” Biden said. “I don’t mind,” he told the staffers standing off camera. “The president and I are not going to endorse because we both when we ran said, ‘let the party decide.’ But gosh almighty, they’re both qualified,” he added. “Hillary is overwhelmingly qualified to be president.”

In a Washington County court, Jessica Dutro, a 25-year-old mother, is on trial for the murder of her 4-year-old son, Zachary Dutro-Boggess, who died from injuries related to a beating in August 2012. Dutro's 8-year-old daughter testified that her mother used to give them "lickins" when they were bad. Brian Canady, Dutro's 24-year-old boyfriend, pleaded guilty earlier this month to first-degree manslaughter for his part in the abuse. Prosecutors claim that both defendants abused Dutro's three children and neglected to seek medical attention for Zachary until it was too late.

In a Facebook message to Canady, Dutro expressed her belief that Zachary was gay, which she considered to be the motive for the deadly beatings. The trial revealed that Zachary was put in timeout for long periods, forced to "face the wall" with his hands in the air, and punished with "lickins" that hurt and left marks. The girl also recalled a time when Zachary was hit in the stomach but couldn't remember the specifics.

After jurors were released for the day, Judge Don Letourneau ruled that a Facebook message from Dutro and web searches thought to be done by her would be admissible evidence. The message established Dutro's motive for inflicting a pattern of torture and abuse on Zachary, while the searches suggested a lack of remorse or concern for her actions.

The girl and her two surviving brothers now live with Dutro's relatives, and she described it as fun. The trial continues as Dutro faces charges of murder, murder by abuse, and second-degree assault.

The article discusses the movie "The Other Guys" directed by Adam McKay, starring Will Ferrell and Mark Wahlberg. The film is a comedy that satirizes the financial industry, with shocking data about bloated CEO bonuses and bank bailouts displayed during the closing credit sequence. However, the film's plot is not its main focus, with Ferrell's character, Allen Gamble, being aggressively passive and his foil, Terry Hoitz, being an unlucky detective. The movie provides good laughs through nonsensical verbal riffing and broad slapstick, with Dwayne Johnson, Samuel L. Jackson, and other actors making fun of their action-hero personas.

In addition, the article mentions that Alexa Internet has been donating their crawl data to the Internet Archive since 1996, with the data being added to the Wayback Machine after an embargo period. The data is used to create a ranking of URLs with more than one incoming inter-domain link, with the top ranked pages being selected from every linked-to domain using the Wide00012 inter-domain navigational link graph. Up to a maximum of 100 most highly ranked URLs per domain are selected for this purpose.

An Egyptian court has sentenced singer Shyma, also known as Shaimaa Ahmed, to two years in prison for "inciting debauchery" and publishing an indecent film. The sentence was handed down after a music video featuring Shyma suggestively eating a banana sparked controversy in the conservative country. The video's director was also sentenced to two years in prison, but in absentia.

The video for Shyma's song "I Have Issues" attracted over a million views in a few days but also sparked outrage among conservatives due to its strong sexual gesturing. In the video, Shyma is seen dancing in underwear, pouring milk over a banana, and licking an apple and a slice of chocolate cake.

Shyma, who is an Arab Idol competitor originally from Tanta, in northern Egypt, appeared at court on Tuesday wearing a niqab covering her face and was seen reading the Quran while waiting for the sentence to be issued. She can appeal the verdict to a higher court.

This is not the first time that Egyptian courts have imprisoned women for "inciting debauchery." Last year, three women were jailed for six months each for dancing in music videos. Another singer, Sherine Abdel Wahab, is currently facing trial for "spreading provocative publicity" after suggesting that drinking from the Nile River could make someone sick.

In a now-deleted Facebook post, Shyma apologized to people who took the video for the song in an inappropriate way. She wrote, "I didn't imagine all this would happen and that I would be subjected to such a strong attack from everyone."

The sentencing of Shyma comes after dozens of young Egyptians were arrested in September for attending a concert in Cairo where a rainbow flag was raised. They were also accused of debauchery, harming public morality, and other accusations.

In Epping, New Hampshire, a woman named Leslie Kahn found herself stuck in her swimming pool after the ladder broke while she was swimming on August 11. With no one else at home and her cellphone inside, she turned to social media for help. She posted a message on a community Facebook page, labeling it "911" to attract attention. A nearby resident responded, followed by the police and a neighbor. Leslie, a breast cancer survivor, expressed gratitude for the help she received, stating that sometimes one helps others and other times, one asks for help.

In a separate incident, also in Epping, Leslie had a mishap in her backyard pool when the ladder broke, leaving her stranded in four feet of water. She tried to climb out but couldn't due to a lack of agility and upper body strength. With her phone inside and her iPad on a chair out of reach, she used a pool pole to drag the chair and posted a plea for help on a community Facebook group. Offers of help poured in, but none of the suggested solutions worked until they tried a step ladder, which allowed Leslie to climb out. Leslie expressed her gratitude for the help she received, stating that she was laughing about the situation even then.

In the latest round of stress tests by U.S. regulators, most of the largest banks passed, allowing for increased dividends and share buybacks. However, Citigroup Inc., the third-largest U.S. bank by assets, failed to meet minimum capital standards and was denied a request to raise its dividend and expand its buyback. The Federal Reserve objected to Citigroup's capital plan, which may have included a higher dividend request. Citigroup's CEO, Vikram Pandit, expressed optimism about returning capital to shareholders, but the Fed's decision is a setback. Ally Financial Inc., SunTrust Banks Inc., and MetLife Inc. also fell short in the Fed's test, with Ally and SunTrust planning to submit revised capital plans. The stress tests aim to assess how banks would fare in a deep recession and a second housing crisis. The results are a blow to Pandit, who has been selling riskier assets to rebuild the bank's strength. Shares in Citigroup declined 3.2 percent, while JPMorgan Chase & Co. and Wells Fargo & Co. saw minimal changes. Citigroup still has over $200 billion of unwanted assets in the Citi Holdings unit, including over $100 billion of mortgages. The Fed's decision "is disappointing, but we remain very optimistic about the long term," Pandit wrote in a memo. The tests may also set back Ally, which had planned an initial public offering to repay its bailout.

Cory Booker, the 44-year-old Newark mayor, won the Democratic primary for the special election to replace the late Sen. Frank Lautenberg (D-N.J.) with a landslide victory, taking 59% of the vote against two U.S. congressmen and the speaker of the New Jersey State Assembly. His opponent in the October election will be Republican Steven Lonegan, a former mayor of Bogota, N.J., who has promised a vigorous campaign against Booker's liberal policies.

However, Booker's victory has been met with criticism from some progressives who argue that he is too cozy with Wall Street and Silicon Valley, and that he uses his connections to enrich himself. Critics also claim that he tries to hide his elitist and corporatist tendencies by promoting himself as a champion of the little guy.

Despite these criticisms, Booker's poll numbers have remained high, and he is expected to easily win the general election in October. Some argue that the liberal opposition to Booker is misplaced, as he has a track record of getting things done and could be a valuable advocate for liberal causes in the Senate.

Booker's parents were some of the first black executives at IBM, and he was a star football player at a well-regarded public high school before going on to attend Stanford University, where he became class president, and Oxford and Yale, where he received honors. He has also been involved in charitable work throughout his life.

Some liberal pundits have criticized Booker for being an avatar of the wealthy elite and a political cipher who has never proposed any solutions to the structural causes of the problems he claims to care about. They argue that he represents the interests of Wall Street and Silicon Valley, and that Democrats should be working to take control of the party away from people like him.

Despite these criticisms, Booker is expected to be a reliable Democratic vote in the Senate, and some argue that he could be a valuable advocate for liberal causes. The general election in October is not expected to be close, and Booker will likely serve in the Senate for many years to come.

The protest initiated by San Francisco 49ers quarterback Colin Kaepernick, who kneels during the national anthem to protest racial injustice, is gaining traction within the sports world, particularly among the Seattle Seahawks. Seahawks players Jeremy Lane, Doug Baldwin, and Bobby Wagner have expressed interest in joining the protest, with the possibility of the entire team taking a stand in solidarity. Wagner stated that any action taken by the team would be a collective decision, emphasizing unity and teamwork. The Seahawks' organization and coaches have expressed support for the players' freedom of expression, with coach Pete Carroll stating that Lane's actions were "simple" and that he understands the responsibility of his decision. The team's wide receiver Doug Baldwin has been in contact with Kaepernick and has received support from veterans who believe the protest aligns with the values for which they fought. The Seahawks host the Dolphins on September 11, and the public will be watching to see if the team decides to take a stand during the national anthem.

The Brussels Appeals Court has ordered the retired King of Belgium, King Albert II, to take a DNA paternity test regarding a claim by 50-year-old artist Delphine Boel. The court's decision overturns an earlier ruling and gives Albert three months to comply. If he fails to do so, he will be legally presumed to be Boel's father. Albert, who abdicated in 2013, has contested Boel's claim for over a decade. Previous DNA tests have proven that she is not the daughter of Jacques Boel, a member of one of Belgium's richest industrial dynasties.

Boel's lawyers expressed satisfaction with the court's decision, stating it affirms the principle of acting in the interests of the child. The court's decision comes after the publication of a biography of Queen Paola, Albert's Italian wife, in 1999, which alleged a long-term extramarital relationship between Albert and another woman, resulting in a daughter born in the 1960s. Albert has acknowledged marital difficulties with Paola, but their children are all older than Boel. The next in line to the throne is 17-year-old Princess Elisabeth, daughter of Albert's successor, King Philippe, and Queen Mathilde.

In the 2012 U.S. Senate elections, Democratic candidates Jon Tester in Montana and Heidi Heitkamp in North Dakota secured victories over their Republican opponents. Tester, a farmer from Big Sandy, won by a margin of 16,000 votes over U.S. Rep. Denny Rehberg, while Heitkamp won by fewer than 3,000 votes in North Dakota.

Tester, speaking in Great Falls, emphasized the need for Congress to address pressing issues such as the federal deficit, taxes, and the economy. He also criticized the influx of "relentless, secretive political spending" in elections, calling for transparency in political funding. Tester's wilderness/jobs bill, which has been stalled in Congress since 2009, aims to create new wilderness in western Montana forests while identifying new acreage for logging.

Heitkamp's victory in North Dakota was unexpected, as Rick Berg, the Republican congressman, was favored to win. Berg could have requested a recount, but he conceded the race with a qualifier, stating he would step aside barring any unforeseen circumstances during the state canvasing board's certification process, which is set to begin on Friday.

In other Senate races, Democrat Elizabeth Warren defeated incumbent GOP senator Scott Brown in Massachusetts, and Democrat Claire McCaskill won re-election in Missouri, following the withdrawal of her Republican opponent, Todd Akin, after controversial remarks about rape. In Wisconsin, Democrat Tammy Baldwin became the first openly gay senator in U.S. history, defeating former governor Tommy Thompson.

In the presidential election held in Taiwan on January 16, 2016, pro-independence candidate Tsai Ing-wen of the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) took a commanding lead, while the China-friendly Nationalist Party's candidate, Eric Chu, conceded a massive loss. Tsai is poised to become Taiwan's first female president, as she garnered about 60% of votes while Chu had about 30% with half of votes counted.

Chu, the Nationalist Party's chairperson, admitted defeat and apologized to the voters, stating that the party had not worked hard enough. He also announced his resignation as party chief. Outgoing Nationalist President Ma Ying-jeou, who has served eight years and is constitutionally barred from another term, presided over a complicated relationship between Taiwan and mainland China.

The outcome of the contest for a majority in the 113-seat legislature remained uncertain, with independents and smaller parties posing a threat to both the Nationalists and the DPP. The election took place amid concerns that Taiwan's economy is under threat from China and broad opposition to Beijing's demands for political unification.

Voters expressed concerns about the slowdown in Taiwan's once-mighty economy, with providing opportunities to the next generation being the most important issue. A win for Tsai would introduce new uncertainty in the relationship between Taiwan and mainland China, which claims the island as its own territory and threatens to use force if it declares formal independence.

Beijing has made maintaining negotiations that have produced a series of pacts on trade, transport, and exchanges its baseline for continuing negotiations with Taiwan. Observers say China is likely to adopt a wait-and-see approach to Tsai's presidency, but might use diplomatic and economic pressure if she is seen as straying too far from its unification agenda.

Tsai has pledged to maintain the status quo of de-facto independence for the island of 23 million, although she has refused to endorse the principle that Taiwan and China are parts of a single nation to be unified eventually. She has also vowed to co-operate with other political parties on major issues and to ensure that no provocations or accidents take place in cross-strait relations.

In her victory speech, Tsai emphasized that both sides of the Taiwan Strait have a responsibility to find mutually acceptable means of interaction that are based on dignity and reciprocity. She also thanked the US and Japan for their support and vowed that Taiwan would contribute to peace and stability in the region.

On July 24, 2013, a Spanish train derailed near Santiago de Compostela in northwestern Spain, killing at least 80 people and injuring over 200. The train was traveling from Madrid to Ferrol and was carrying 247 passengers and five crew members. The accident occurred on a high-speed stretch of track, and video footage showed the train hurtling into a concrete wall and overturning. The driver of the train, Francisco Jose Garzon, was under police guard in hospital and was being formally investigated for the accident. He was reported to have boasted about speeding on Facebook and may have been traveling at twice the speed limit on the section of track where the accident occurred. The accident was one of Europe's worst rail disasters and brought misery to Santiago de Compostela, which was set to celebrate one of Europe's biggest Christian festivals on the day of the accident. The Galicia regional supreme court said that the judge investigating the accident had ordered police to take a statement from the driver, who was being formally investigated but not under arrest. It was not clear what kind of injuries he had suffered. The disaster stirred memories of a train bombing in Madrid in 2004, which killed 191 people. Spain's rail safety record is better than the European average, but the accident was the country's deadliest since 1972. The disaster happened at 8.41 p.m. (2.41 p.m. ET) on the eve of a festival dedicated to St. James, one of Jesus' 12 disciples, whose remains are said to rest in Santiago de Compostela's centuries-old cathedral. The apostle's shrine is the destination of the famous El Camino de Santiago pilgrimage across the Pyrenees, which has been followed by Christians since the Middle Ages. The disaster prompted an outpouring of sympathy from around the world, including the White House and the European Commission. The Spanish government declared three days of national mourning for the victims of the disaster.

A Disneyland employee, Christian Barnes, was arrested on suspicion of placing a dry ice bomb in a theme park trash can, causing an explosion that led to a brief evacuation of the Mickey's Toontown section. The 22-year-old Long Beach resident, who worked as an outdoor vendor, is being held on $1 million bail and is cooperating with investigators. No one was injured, and the explosion did not cause significant damage. The incident is being investigated as an isolated incident with unanticipated impacts. Disneyland is working closely with local authorities to ensure the safety of visitors. The dry ice bomb appears to have been placed in a plastic bottle left in a trash can in Toontown. This incident does not seem to be connected to similar dry-ice explosions in Anaheim in recent months. The mixture exploded around 5:30 p.m. on Tuesday, forcing officials to evacuate people from the area for two hours. Visitors expressed shock and concern about the incident, reminding everyone to prioritize safety. Other news includes a probe into a Palmdale boy's torture death and disputes over Justin Bieber's Ferrari story.

The United States has begun aid drops and conducted airstrikes in the Iraqi town of Amerli, which is surrounded by ISIS fighters. The town is home to many Shiite Turkmen, who face the threat of an "imminent massacre" according to the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights. The U.S. military has dropped humanitarian aid to help the trapped residents, and conducted coordinated airstrikes against ISIS targets to support the operation. The town has been besieged by ISIS since mid-June, and its residents are without power, facing severe food and water shortages, and a complete absence of medical services.

In Syria, ISIS has reportedly sold Yazidi girls and women, with the Syrian Observatory for Human Rights claiming that about 300 women have been abducted and distributed to ISIS fighters. The group considers the Yazidis as "captives of the spoils of war with the infidels."

In a separate development, ISIS has beheaded a Lebanese soldier who was one of 19 captured when militants seized a Lebanese border town earlier this month. The soldier's beheading was shown in a video posted on social media sites.

In Iraq, at least three Iraqi soldiers were killed in a suicide car bombing south of Iraq's capital, dealing a blow to the military in that area for a second straight day as government forces fight ISIS militants across the country.

In the U.S., former NSA director Keith Alexander is charging companies up to $1 million a month to help them protect their computer networks from hackers. Alexander claims to have invented a new technology to detect malicious hackers and cyber-intruders, and says his insider knowledge gives him a competitive advantage in the cybersecurity market. However, his decision to start a security business and apply for patents has raised eyebrows on Capitol Hill, with some questioning whether he is effectively selling classified information in exchange for his huge consulting fee.

In Saudi Arabia, King Abdullah has warned that extremists could attack Europe and the U.S. if there is not a strong international response to terrorism after Islamist extremists seized a wide territory across Iraq and Syria. The king's statement appears aimed at drawing Washington and NATO forces into a wider fight against ISIS and its supporters in the region.

The article discusses the growing tension between traditional theater etiquette and the increasing use of mobile devices by audience members during Broadway shows. The issue has recently gained attention due to several high-profile incidents, including Patti LuPone snatching a phone from a texting audience member during a performance of her Off Broadway show, "Shows for Days," and Nick Silvestri, a 19-year-old college student, charging his phone on stage during a performance of "Hand to God."

Silvestri held a press conference on July 10 to apologize for his actions and to educate himself about theater etiquette. He admitted that he was not aware that the stage was considered off-limits and that he had been drinking before the incident. Silvestri's actions were met with criticism from the theater community, with LuPone famously being tough on folks who use cell phones during her shows.

The press conference was used by producers of "Hand to God" to gain publicity for the Broadway comedy, which has struggled to gain momentum at the box office despite earning strong reviews and five Tony nominations. Silvestri took the opportunity to apologize to the Broadway community and to express his regret for his actions.

The article also mentions other incidents of cell phone use during Broadway shows, including Madonna reportedly texting during a performance of "Hamilton." The article highlights the generational divide between the traditionally older-skewing theatergoing demographic and the younger audiences who have grown up in the digital, mobile era.

The article concludes by stating that Silvestri has learned a lot about the theater in the past few days and that he will not be setting foot on a stage again unless he decides to become an actor. The article also mentions that LuPone is known for being tough on folks who use cell phones during her shows and that she has even stopped shows in the past to upbraid audience members for using their phones.

In Texas City, a 13-year-old girl named Brittany Baker lost her beloved 10-year-old beagle, Bailey, after four pit bulls from a neighboring house escaped and attacked her pet. The incident occurred on October 27, when Brittany returned home from school and heard yelping, screaming, and barking from her backyard. Upon opening the back door, she saw the four dogs ganging up on Bailey. The neighbor, Emerald White, who owned the dogs, was also injured during the incident.

The Texas City Police Department declared the four dogs dangerous under the city's ordinance. As a result, the owners must abide by several regulations, including keeping the dogs in an enclosed space, micro-chipping and tagging the dogs, posting a sign on their premises warning of a vicious animal, and showing the city animal control department a certificate of public liability insurance in the amount of $100,000.

Brittany's family, who had owned Bailey since she was three, was devastated by the loss. However, they are pleased with how the city and police have responded to their family's tragedy. Brittany does not hold a grudge against her neighbors, who have since repaired the hole in the fence.

Recently, Emerald White filed a lawsuit against the deceased dog's owner, Steve Baker, seeking up to $1 million in damages. Steve Baker was shocked by the lawsuit and felt that justice had already been served since the dogs were declared dangerous and awareness was raised. The lawsuit alleges that White suffered multiple serious injuries and ongoing medical treatment as a result of the attack. Multiple calls made to White's attorney were not returned.

The incident has raised awareness about the importance of responsible pet ownership and the need for secure fences to prevent such tragedies from happening in the future. The city of League City recently toughened its dangerous dog ordinance, requiring a microchip tag, a fluorescent orange collar, and up-to-date photos of the animal to be on file with the city's animal control. Any dog declared dangerous would also be held at the animal shelter until a court hearing is held to determine the dog's future. The League City ordinance was adopted soon after a two-year-old girl was attacked by a pit bull that belonged to her mother's boyfriend.

In Bellefonte, Pennsylvania, a preliminary hearing was held for 18 Penn State fraternity brothers, including Craig Heimer, who are accused of involvement in the hazing death of Timothy Piazza, a 19-year-old pledge. State College Police Detective David Scicchitano testified that surveillance footage from the Beta Theta Pi fraternity house showed Piazza, who died two days after a hazing ritual on February 2, 2017, looking like a corpse after being carried upstairs the morning after the event. The video showed Piazza was injured after his first serious fall at 11:22 p.m., and he was left alone on a couch by about 3 a.m. He later fell several times in the house's great hall and other areas, hitting his head and stomach, and staggering severely. Piazza was not seen on tape again until two hours later, when brothers found him in the basement. The defendants face charges including involuntary manslaughter and felony aggravated assault. Piazza's father, Jim, was in the courtroom as his son's final hours were described, but left when the video was shown. The fraternity chapter is also a defendant, and Penn State has permanently banned the fraternity for a persistent pattern of excess drinking, drug use, and hazing. The goal of the hearing was to determine if there is enough evidence to send the case to court for trial.

On Friday, May 4, 2018, residents of the Big Island of Hawaii faced a day of heightened anxiety as a powerful 6.9 earthquake struck their homes, adding to the existing threats posed by an ongoing volcanic eruption. The earthquake, which was one of over 110 in a 24-hour period, knocked out power for some residents who were already dealing with mandatory evacuation orders, lava flows, and high levels of sulfur dioxide in the air.

The situation continued to deteriorate, with five volcanic vents reported open, and at least one home and another structure destroyed by lava. The vents were unusually far from the Kilauea volcano, causing concern among authorities. Hundreds of people evacuated from Leilani Estates, a community of about 1,700 people, and Lanipuna Gardens. The government pledged support for residents, including those who wished to return to their homes to gather belongings.

Residents were advised to be prepared for potential inconveniences, with people allowed to check on their homes in designated neighborhoods. One resident, Stephen Clapper, was among those who evacuated, forced to do so due to his mother's need for portable oxygen and the imminent threat posed by lava setting trees ablaze and threatening homes.

The Kilauea volcano, one of the world's most active, is located in Hawaii Volcanoes National Park, which closed on Friday. The tremors had been jarring residents, who reported nearly constant ground vibrations and cracks in roads. Concerns about sulfur dioxide levels were also raised, with potentially dangerous amounts detected in the evacuation area.

The Hawaii National Guard was activated to assist with evacuations and security, and the Red Cross opened shelters for displaced residents. The situation remained volatile, with authorities urging residents to stay informed and vigilant.

In a twist of reality TV drama, Jon Gosselin, the father of eight from the hit show "Jon & Kate Plus 8," is embroiled in a controversy involving his girlfriend Hailey Glassman and Octo-mom Nadya Suleman. Hailey accused Gosselin of emotional abuse, but a source close to Gosselin claims this was a staged confession for TV. The insider alleges that Gosselin orchestrated Hailey's appearance on "The Insider" to generate attention for a potential reality show and to secure financial stability.

Contrary to Gosselin's denial, emails obtained by Fox411 and RadarOnline.com show he was indeed considering a reality show with Suleman, despite his initial denial. The source claims Gosselin was hoping to earn close to a million dollars for a series of fake dates with Suleman.

Despite the controversy, Gosselin and Glassman have reportedly not split, with Gosselin expressing regret for any pain he caused Glassman and claiming they are slowing things down. Glassman, however, has clarified on Twitter that she is not yet ready to start dating again. The story continues to unfold as Gosselin seeks to reconnect with his spiritual self and mend his relationships.

The Mega Millions jackpot has grown to an estimated $502 million after no winning tickets were drawn on Tuesday. This is the fourth time the jackpot has surpassed half a billion dollars in the game's 16-year history. The next drawing will take place on Friday, March 30, with a cash payout option of $301 million. Since the last winning jackpot on January 5, there have been 33 winners of $1 million or more. The three largest Mega Millions jackpots have been $656 million, $648 million, and $536 million, won in 2012, 2013, and 2016 respectively. The game can be played in 44 U.S. states, Washington D.C., and the U.S. Virgin Islands.

In the Super Bowl, U.S. Senate candidate Pete Hoekstra faced criticism for a controversial ad featuring a young Asian woman speaking broken English, which was perceived as racially insensitive. The ad, which was meant to be satirical, portrayed the woman thanking Michigan Senator Debbie Stabenow for spending too much money, thereby weakening the U.S. economy and benefiting China.

The Asian & Pacific Islander American Vote group's Michigan chapter expressed disappointment over the ad, stating that it uses harmful negative stereotypes that encourage anti-Asian sentiment. GOP consultant Nick De Leeuw also criticized Hoekstra for the ad, calling it "appalling" and "racism and xenophobia."

Hoekstra defended the ad, stating that it has yielded an "overwhelmingly positive response" and should only offend Stabenow. He argued that the ad does not criticize the Chinese but instead points out the strength of an international competitor that is benefiting from America's declining economic status.

Despite the backlash, Hoekstra's campaign is spending $75,000 to air the ad statewide. The ad is set to run over the next two weeks on cable TV shows targeted at GOP voters. The controversy has not deterred Hoekstra's chief rival for the GOP nomination, school charter advocate Clark Durant, who questioned Hoekstra's congressional record but did not comment on the uproar over the approach.

"Daybreakers" is a vampire film starring Ethan Hawke, Claudia Karvan, Willem Dafoe, and Sam Neill. The movie is set in a world where vampires have taken over, with humans becoming a rare resource. Vampires drive anti-sunlight cars, and there is a ghoul military force, with baristas serving blood-spiked coffee. The plot revolves around a vampire hematologist, Edward Dalton (Hawke), who hates his supernatural diet and is working on an ineffective blood substitute for his boss. Edward finds a group of renegade humans led by Audrey (Karvan) and Elvis (Dafoe), and he defangs himself for the greater good. The film has a satiric tone and adds vamp-mobiles to the usual mythology, but it eventually devolves, with the Spierig brothers losing interest in what they've created. The film is a B movie, with lowbrow pleasures, and while it has holes, it brims with fierce retro fun. The film is a dark mirror of the human world, with a looming problem of the blood farms running dry, causing mass panic and the evolution of vampires into scary bat-like creatures. The film has clever ideas and resonant concepts, but the action eventually settles into lulling rhythms, and the plot digs into a rut. Overall, Daybreakers is a visually flair-filled film with a unique take on the vampire genre.

Deborah Skouson, a mother from St. George, turned to social media on August 7 to find a specific pink flowered shirt for her autistic daughter Cami, who has been fixated on the shirt for five years. The shirt, a particular brand and style, had become unwearable and was unavailable even on eBay. Skouson posted a plea on Facebook, offering to pay for the shirt and shipping if someone would sell it to her. The post quickly went viral, with over 22,000 shares, including one from a local TV news anchor and the Love What Really Matters page, which has over 4 million fans. Skouson has since received over 150 shirts, some coming from as far away as Germany and England. Cami, who started the fifth grade on August 11, was initially confused but happy to see more than one of her favorite shirts. Target also contacted Skouson, offering to make larger versions of the shirt to fit Cami into adulthood. The support Skouson has received has changed her perspective on the internet, making her feel more connected to people. However, she has also faced criticism for "feeding into her daughter's obsession." Skouson believes that as the mother, she knows what is best for her daughter, and if the shirt makes her happy, she will do everything in her power to find it for her. The Internet Archive is archiving pages to fix all broken links on the web.

The Danish inventor Peter Madsen has been sentenced to life in prison for the premeditated murder and sexual assault of Swedish journalist Kim Wall on his submarine in August 2017. The court found Madsen guilty of all three main charges of premeditated murder, aggravated sexual assault, and desecrating a corpse. The judge, Anette Burkø, stated that the murder was a cynical and pre-planned sexual assault of a particularly brutal nature. Madsen confessed to dismembering Wall's body but denied the murder charge, claiming that she died accidentally inside the submarine. However, the court found Madsen's version of events to be not credible and inconsistent with the evidence presented. The trial, which gripped Denmark, heard from a woman to whom Madsen had confessed that he was a psychopath, but a loving one. The cause of Wall's death has never been established.

On June 2, 2015, a fatal crash involving a Chicago Transit Authority (CTA) bus occurred during rush hour, resulting in one death and eight injuries. The victim, Aimee Coath, a 51-year-old woman from Flossmoor, died at Northwestern Memorial Hospital. The crash occurred at North Michigan Avenue and East Lake Street, where the bus collided with several vehicles. Witnesses described the scene as chaotic, with people screaming and running towards the bus. The bus driver was among the injured and was hospitalized with non-life-threatening injuries. The driver was later cited for not stopping at a red light and for "failure to exercise due care." The CTA is reviewing footage from the bus at the time of the crash and is investigating the accident's cause. Parts of Michigan Avenue and Lake Street were closed to traffic for several hours, and several buses were rerouted around the crash scene.

Two couples, Kelly Tousley and Curtiss O'Rorke Stedman, and Kristin Connolly Schillaci and Tony Schillaci, have embraced the tiny house movement by downsizing their living spaces and embarking on cross-country travels.

Kelly and Curtiss, a high school English teacher and musician, sold most of their possessions and moved into a 98-square-foot trailer, leaving their Juneau, Alaska, home in June. They aim to tour the Alaska road system and the Lower 48 for a year, with Curtiss pursuing his music career. The trailer, which cost $8,600, features a queen-sized bed, solar panels for electricity, and a small bathroom and kitchenette.

Meanwhile, Kristin and Tony, both UAF graduates, spent a year on the road in an 18-foot-long trailer, traveling 25,000 miles to 30 juried art shows in 35 states to sell Kristin's fine art photographs. They returned to Santa Fe, New Mexico, after their journey.

Both couples faced challenges in downsizing and adapting to their new living arrangements. For Kelly, it was parting with sentimental items like her high school track sweatshirt. For Curtiss, it was giving away his plants, which were grown from his great-great-grandmother's clippings.

The couples' journeys reflect the growing trend of the tiny house movement, which encourages downsizing, simplicity, and self-sufficiency. While some may view their lifestyle as unconventional, both couples are excited about the adventure and freedom it offers.

To follow Kelly and Curtiss' journey, visit paygasnotrent.com. Their song "Here and Now" reflects their new nomadic lifestyle.

A strong earthquake of magnitude 7.2 hit the eastern Van region of Turkey on Sunday, resulting in at least 85 confirmed deaths and over 1,140 injuries. The town of Ercis was the worst-hit area, with many buildings destroyed. Rescue teams are working tirelessly to find survivors trapped under the rubble, with several survivors already being pulled out. The death toll is expected to rise as outlying areas are reached. The prime minister, Recep Tayyip Erdogan, has expressed concern for residents of outlying villages yet to be reached by rescue workers. The earthquake occurred in a region known for its vulnerability to earthquakes, and Turkey's seismology institute estimates the casualty count to be between 500 and 1,000. The government, Turkish Red Crescent, and several foreign countries have offered aid. The aftermath of the earthquake has left many homeless, with over 1,000 tents and 500 food packages sent to Van. The earthquake was the largest to strike Turkey since 1999 when two earthquakes with a magnitude of over 7 killed almost 20,000 people in densely populated areas.

In the lead-up to the 2012 presidential election, Funny or Die, a popular comedy website, has announced plans for dedicated coverage. On November 8th, they launched "Live Funny or Die" with a video featuring comedians impersonating several presidential candidates. Notable performances include Mike Tyson as Herman Cain, Darrell Hammond as Rick Perry, and Reggie Brown as President Obama. The video humorously showcases each candidate's unique personality and highlights the importance of cats and breasts in capturing an online audience. Mitt Romney, Ron Paul, Michele Bachmann, and Rick Perry are among the candidates parodied, with Tyson's Herman Cain character singing a song about pizza. The video ends with Obama explaining the formula for internet success: cats and breasts. The video aims to provide a humorous take on the upcoming election.

The former Stanford University swimmer, Brock Turner, was sentenced to six months in jail and three years' probation for sexually assaulting an unconscious woman in January 2015. The sentence has sparked outrage due to the perceived leniency, with critics arguing that Turner, a star athlete from a privileged background, received special treatment. Despite the sentence, Turner is expected to be released from jail three months early on September 2, due to good behavior. Turner's statement following the sentencing blamed the assault on the "party culture" at Stanford and portrayed himself as the victim, while his father's statement described the conviction as a "steep price to pay for 20 minutes of action." The incident occurred at a fraternity party, where Turner was found assaulting an intoxicated, unconscious woman. Two Swedish students intervened and prevented Turner from fleeing the scene. The incident has caused widespread outrage and sparked discussions about sexual assault and privilege on college campuses.

In August 2014, Firas Jumaah, a Ph.D. student in Analytical Chemistry at Lund University in Sweden, sent a distress message to his supervisor, Charlotta Turner, stating that he might not complete his thesis if he did not return within a week. Jumaah, a member of the Yazidi ethno-religious group, was hiding with his family in a disused bleach factory in Iraq, as ISIS fighters were roaming the town. Jumaah had returned to Iraq after his wife called to inform him that ISIS had taken over their neighboring village, killing all the men and enslaving the women.

Turner was determined to help her student and contacted the university's then security chief, Per Gustafson. Over a few days, Gustafson organized a rescue operation, hiring a security company that arranged for four heavily-armed mercenaries to pick up Jumaah, his wife, and their two small children from their hiding place and transport them to Erbil Airport.

Jumaah and his family were fortunate to survive the ISIS occupation, and Jumaah returned to Sweden to complete his Ph.D. He now works for a pharmaceuticals company in Malmö. The family is almost finished paying the university back for the rescue operation.

Gustafson stated that this was a unique event, as far as he knows, no other university has ever been involved in anything like it. Jumaah expressed his gratitude, stating that he had never felt so privileged and VIP, but at the same time, he felt like a coward for leaving his mother and sisters behind.

The article discusses the increasing trend of superhero movies in the early 2000s, with a focus on Warner Bros.' ambitious plan to produce 10 DC Comics movies between 2016 and 2020. However, the article warns that this saturation of superhero movies might lead to their decline in popularity. The article highlights Warner Bros.' past struggles with DC Comics adaptations, such as the "Catwoman" catastrophe of 2004 and the bombs "Jonah Hex" and "The Green Lantern."

Warner Bros. is betting on its golden boys, including Ben Affleck as Batman and Henry Cavill as Superman, and plans to release two other Justice League movies. The upcoming release "Suicide Squad" is another attempt to replicate the success of Marvel's "Avengers" franchise. However, the article suggests that the dark tone of the movie, directed by David Ayer, may not appeal to audiences who enjoy the humor in Marvel's superhero movies.

The article also discusses Marvel's exceptional casting and Warner Bros.' reliance on newcomers for their superhero roles, such as Gal Gadot as Wonder Woman and Ezra Miller as The Flash. The article also mentions the upcoming reboot of "Green Lantern" in 2020, not even a decade after the Ryan Reynolds incarnation bombed.

The article concludes by suggesting that Warner Bros. may be running hard to catch up with Marvel, but it might be smarter to focus on the next big thing instead. The article also mentions other superhero movie news, such as Captain America 3 potentially featuring Iron Man as the villain, Michael Keaton expressing interest in reprising his role as Batman, and Jeremy Renner hinting at a possible Hawkeye solo movie. The article also mentions the fast-tracking of a movie featuring Will Arnett's Lego Batman.

The documentary film "Virunga," produced by Leonardo DiCaprio's Appian Way and distributed by Netflix, centers on the protection of endangered mountain gorillas in Virunga National Park, Democratic Republic of Congo. The film, directed by Orlando von Einsiedel, follows a team of park rangers, including an ex-child soldier, a gorilla caretaker, and a Belgian conservationist, as they battle armed militia, poachers, and other threats to the park. The film has won numerous awards and will be released in select theaters in New York and Los Angeles on November 7, as well as on Netflix the same day. DiCaprio, who serves as executive producer, called the partnership with Netflix an "exciting opportunity to inform and inspire individuals to engage on this topic." The film highlights the ongoing battle between theater owners and Netflix, with the latter planning to release the sequel to Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon on its streaming service and in select Imax theaters, causing displeasure among exhibitors.

In a series of leaked emails, former Secretary of State Colin Powell criticized both Donald Trump and Hillary Clinton. Powell, a Republican, called Trump a "national disgrace" and "international pariah" for his racist "birther" movement and his attempts to question President Obama's citizenship and religion. He also accused Trump of trying to destabilize Obama's presidency.

In another email, Powell dismissed Trump's overtures to African-American voters, saying that Trump takes voters for idiots and cannot overcome his past actions against Obama. Powell also criticized the repeated investigations into the 2012 attack in Benghazi, calling it a "witch hunt."

Powell's emails were obtained by the website DCLeaks.com, which is believed to have ties to Russian intelligence services. The emails were first reported by Buzzfeed News.

Powell's emails have been a topic of controversy due to his connection to Hillary Clinton's use of a private email server. In one email, Powell expressed frustration about being linked to Clinton's email issues and wrote that he had to disclose his past use of emails and had a gig cancelled because of it.

Powell has not endorsed any candidate in the 2016 election, and some of his friends and advisors have asked when he will endorse Hillary Clinton. However, Powell has not made any public endorsements as of yet.

The leaked emails mark the latest in a string of headlines around Powell's email correspondence, and Congressional Democrats are bracing for more leaked data. The FBI is currently dealing with a data breach that revealed the personal data of nearly 200 current and former House Democrats.

The Internet Archive is working on a project to preserve web pages as they are created and archive pages that they refer to, aiming to fix all broken links on the web. The archive hopes that references to these archived pages will replace broken links or serve as a companion link to show the original intended content.

In other news, Michael Lohan, father of Lindsay Lohan, has proposed to Jon Gosselin's ex-partner, Kate Major. Lohan, 49, expressed his appreciation for Major's long-term support, stating that their relationship is the strongest in his life. He revealed that he waited for the situation with Lindsay to resolve before announcing the engagement.

Major, 27, isn't currently pregnant but plans to have children with Lohan in the future. The couple is planning to get married later this year at Oheka Castle in New York. Major described the engagement ring as "gorgeous," but has yet to receive well wishes from Jon Gosselin.

The Netflix political drama "House of Cards" has been announced to end with its sixth season, a decision made months ago and not in response to recent sexual misconduct allegations against lead actor Kevin Spacey. The allegations, made by actor Anthony Rapp, involve an incident from over 30 years ago. Spacey apologized for any inappropriate behavior but also revealed he is gay, which sparked backlash from the gay community. The final season will premiere in 2018, with production already underway. The show's creator, Beau Willimon, has also released a statement regarding the matter.

In a series of interviews on Sunday, Secretary of State John Kerry accused Russian-backed separatists in Ukraine of shooting down Malaysia Airlines Flight 17, which crashed on Thursday, killing 298 people. Kerry stated that the separatists received military aid from Russia, including a convoy of armored personnel carriers, rocket launchers, tanks, and artillery, which crossed the Russian border into Eastern Ukraine within the last month. He also pointed to evidence that the missile system used to shoot down the plane passed through two towns in the vicinity of the launch site, and that separatists tampered with evidence and stole pieces of the plane. Kerry expressed optimism that the ongoing conflict between Israel and Hamas in Gaza would soon end in a ceasefire, and he defended Israel's right to defend itself against rocket attacks. However, Kerry also criticized the Israeli government's assurances about the limited scope of its attack and ground invasion of Gaza, and he called for a ceasefire to be implemented as soon as possible. Kerry also expressed concern about the investigation into the crash of Malaysia Airlines Flight 17, stating that it has been "seriously compromised" by the actions of separatist soldiers and the removal of evidence from the crash site. Kerry called for full access to the site and accused Russia of having a "moment of truth" in the matter. In an off-camera conversation before an interview with Fox News Sunday, Kerry was caught on an open mic criticizing the Israeli government's operations in Gaza as a "hell of a pinpoint operation." Kerry later defended his comments, stating that he was reacting to the loss of civilian lives in the conflict.

The United Nations food agency, the World Food Programme (WFP), has faced criticism for withdrawing a report that revealed desperate hunger among the persecuted Rohingya population in Myanmar's northern Rakhine state. The report, which warned of more than 80,000 children under the age of five living in majority-Muslim areas being "wasting" - a potentially fatal condition - was removed at the request of the Myanmar government. The WFP has since announced plans to republish the report, stating that it stands firmly behind its findings.

The report was replaced with a statement saying that Myanmar and the WFP are collaborating on a revised version, but the original report's removal has added to a series of recent criticisms that the UN did not push the Myanmar government hard enough for the rights of 1.1 million Rohingya in Myanmar or sound the alarm on their spiraling oppression. The issue exploded on August 25 when Rohingya insurgents attacked security forces, leading to a severe counteroffensive by the military that has resulted in more than half a million Rohingya fleeing to neighboring Bangladesh.

The UN's most senior official in Myanmar will leave at the end of the month amid allegations she suppressed another report and attempted to shut down public advocacy on Rohingya suffering. The WFP, along with other humanitarian aid agencies, has been denied access to the conflict zone and is urging the Burmese authorities to lift the restriction.

Meanwhile, half a million Rohingya have fled to Bangladesh, with the UN calling it the world's "fastest developing refugee emergency" and a "textbook example of ethnic cleansing." Bangladesh is trying to register the Rohingya and restrict their movement, but the Rohingya are not recognized as refugees and face limited access to education and employment. There are concerns that Bangladesh's own Islamist extremists may try to exploit the new arrivals, and some religious hardliners in Muslim-majority Bangladesh are stirring the pot, calling for the Rohingya to be armed and even talking about war with the Buddhist majority neighbor.

The WFP has not responded directly to questions about whether food aid cuts had left vulnerable people in need or whether it prioritized good relations with the government over the immediate humanitarian needs of the Rohingya. The agency's purpose in Myanmar is to address the food and nutrition needs of vulnerable people.

On January 27, 2016, authorities released new images of Bac Duong, a suspected gang member, in connection with the escape of three inmates from the Orange County Central Men's Jail. Five arrests were made in connection with the escape, and more arrests are expected. The three fugitives, Hossein Nayeri, Jonathan Tieu, and Bac Duong, were awaiting trial for various violent crimes before they escaped on Friday, January 22. The trio escaped by cutting through 1/2-inch-thick steel bars and plumbing tunnels to gain access to the unsecured roof, which they used to rappel to the ground and flee on foot.

Sheriff Sandra Hutchens described the escape as "every sheriff's nightmare" and said that the department is looking into the policies and procedures conducted at the jail to prevent any future attempts. She added that she believes Nayeri, who faces charges such as kidnapping and torture, is the mastermind behind the elaborate escape plan based on his military background.

The escape has prompted changes at the jail, including the way deputies count prisoners, and a $200,000 reward has been offered for information leading to the inmates' arrests. Anyone with information on the inmates' whereabouts was urged to call the Orange County Sheriff's Department hotline at (714)628-7085. Those wishing to remain anonymous may call Crime Stoppers at (855) 847-6227.
