Freedom Industries Inc., embroiled in lawsuits and investigations following a chemical spill on January 9, has filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in the Southern District of West Virginia. The company's assets and liabilities are listed as being between $1 million and $10 million, with over 200 creditors and $3.66 million owed to its top 20 creditors. The spill occurred when a chemical used for coal cleaning leaked from a storage tank at the company's facility, contaminating the Elk River and the state's largest water system.

The bankruptcy filing suggests that the storage tank may have been pierced by an unknown object, and a possible theory for the hole is a broken local water line near the Charleston plant, which could have caused the ground beneath the tank to freeze before the spill. Following the spill, residents in a nine-county area around Charleston were advised not to use the water for anything other than flushing toilets, leading to temporary closures of businesses and schools. Water restrictions have since been lifted for most residents.

It is worth noting that the terminal that leaked had not been inspected by state officials since 2001, when it was owned by a different company operating under more stringent rules. State officials stated that Freedom Industries purchased the terminal last month. This filing marks a significant development in the aftermath of the chemical spill, which has had far-reaching effects on the community and environment.

Title: Lunar Tides in Loch Ness: A Natural Level Indicator

Researchers from the National Oceanography Centre in Liverpool, UK, and the University of Porto, Portugal, have discovered that Loch Ness in Scotland behaves like a giant carpenter's level due to lunar tides in the nearby North Sea. The subtle movement of the loch is caused by ocean tidal loading, where the increased pressure on the seafloor from the incoming North Sea tide deforms the Earth.

The researchers used pressure sensors distributed throughout Loch Ness to measure depth changes with an incredible accuracy of 0.1 mm (0.004 in) over its 35 km (22 mi) length. They found that the depth of the loch changed by 1.5 millimeters (0.06 inches) at its different ends depending on whether the North Sea tide was in or out.

This discovery makes Loch Ness one of the world's longest and most accurate tiltmeters, according to the researchers. This could potentially be the first measurement of land shifting tides due to ocean tidal loading in a European lake. The findings were published in the Journal of Geophysical Research.

The study provides new insights into the geophysical processes of Scottish lochs and could have implications for understanding similar phenomena in other bodies of water. The researchers hope that their findings will contribute to a better understanding of the Earth's dynamic system.

The news articles from Fox News and Bloomberg reveal that Susan Rice, former National Security Adviser under President Barack Obama, requested the unmasking of the identities of Trump transition officials who were incidentally caught up in surveillance. The unmasked names were then shared with various officials at the National Security Council, the Defense Department, the Director of National Intelligence, and the CIA. The news comes in the wake of Evelyn Farkas' television interview last month, in which she urged her former colleagues to gather as much intelligence as they could before President Obama left office. Rice herself has been involved in controversy in the past, including her appearance on Sunday news shows to defend the administration's later debunked claim that the Benghazi attack was prompted by a video.

The unmasking of Trump transition officials adds an important element to the ongoing investigations into ties between Trump associates and a Russian influence operation against Hillary Clinton during the election. Both the House and Senate intelligence committees are probing these ties, and the chairman of the House intelligence committee, Representative Devin Nunes, is also investigating how the Obama White House kept tabs on the Trump transition after the election. Rice has not spoken directly on the issue of unmasking.

In his final address to the United Nations General Assembly as President, Barack Obama urged world leaders to address the global refugee crisis and work together to promote democracy, human rights, and international law. He criticized isolationist and nationalistic movements, stating that a nation ringed by walls would only imprison itself. Obama also spoke out against strongman leadership models, emphasizing the importance of independent news institutions and democratic governments. He highlighted his administration's accomplishments, including normalizing relations with Cuba, reaching a nuclear agreement with Iran, and pushing for Myanmar's transition to democracy. The retirement of Justice Anthony Kennedy from the Supreme Court has sparked a heated debate over the nomination process, with Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell vowing to confirm Trump's nominee before the midterm elections, while Democrats demand a delay until the new Congress is seated in 2019. The fight over Kennedy's replacement follows a pattern of escalating partisanship in Supreme Court nominations, with both parties breaking norms and rules to gain an advantage.

In 2016, Senate Republicans blocked President Obama's nominee Merrick Garland, citing an unwritten rule that open seats on the Supreme Court should not be filled in an election year. Democrats, in response, filibustered Neil Gorsuch's nomination in 2017, leading to the elimination of the filibuster for Supreme Court nominations.

The current state of the process leaves the minority party with no power over Supreme Court picks, as the majority party can and will jam whomever they want onto the Court, where they will serve for life. This dynamic creates a situation where seats on the Court may remain open for years, and when they are filled, they will be filled with more extreme candidates.

The high stakes of Supreme Court nominations, combined with the fact that justices serve for life and no one knows when the next seat will open, have turned the process into a bloodsport. To deescalate Supreme Court fights, some have proposed limiting terms for justices, such as a 10-year, nonrenewable term, which would lower the stakes of individual nominations and make the timing of fights more predictable.

The fight over Kennedy's replacement is already underway, with McConnell vowing to act quickly, and Democrats demanding a delay. The nomination process is expected to be contentious, with abortion likely to be a flashpoint, as Kennedy was the fifth vote for upholding Roe v. Wade, the landmark case that established a right to abortion in 1973. Sens. Susan Collins and Lisa Murkowski, two Republicans who support abortion rights, are likely to exert significant influence on the debate.

In Doral, Florida, Pedro Viloria, a cashier at a McDonald's, displayed heroism by jumping through the drive-thru window to help a woman who suddenly lost consciousness while operating her vehicle. The woman, an off-duty Miami-Dade police officer, was ordering breakfast for herself and her two children. After preparing the order, Viloria noticed the driver struggling to breathe and, without hesitation, jumped through the window to assist.

Surveillance footage shows Viloria pulling the off-duty officer from the SUV as it rolled forward. A second McDonald's employee, along with paramedics who were in the restaurant, helped to revive the woman at the scene. She was then taken to the hospital for further treatment.

McDonald's commended Viloria's bravery, praising him as an excellent employee who acted quickly and selflessly. Another employee also assisted with CPR. As of Wednesday, Miami-Dade Police Detective Daniel Ferrin has yet to release any information on the woman's condition. The incident highlights Pedro Viloria's heroic actions and the quick thinking of the McDonald's team in Doral, Florida.

Central Europe is experiencing severe flooding due to record high water levels in the Danube and Elbe rivers. The Danube, Europe's second-longest river, is expected to reach unprecedented levels in Budapest, Hungary, where a state of emergency has been declared. Thousands of volunteers are reinforcing the riverbanks, and emergency workers have set up camps. The river is expected to peak near the border with Slovakia on Saturday and in Budapest on Monday, potentially causing the country's worst floods ever.

Meanwhile, the Elbe River is threatening Saxony-Anhalt in eastern Germany, where thousands of people are being evacuated. The cost of damage to homes, businesses, and agriculture is expected to run into hundreds of millions of euros. The water is still rising in the Elbe and is expected to peak in Saxony-Anhalt on Tuesday.

In the Czech Republic, the focus has shifted to the clean-up operation, and offers of help with equipment and manpower from Poland and Slovakia are being accepted. The flooding has caused at least 15 deaths across the region since last weekend, with eight deaths reported in the Czech Republic.

Hungary has expressed concern over a toxic waste reservoir in Almasfuzito, near Komarom, which could be breached by the surging Danube, potentially leading to water pollution. Environmental campaign group Greenpeace has raised concerns that some toxic sludge could be washed into the water system through the groundwater. The reservoir is being closely monitored, but the government remains anxious about its safety.

The flooding follows heavy rain in the region last weekend, after a wet spring left the ground saturated. Scattered showers are likely over the coming days, but there is hope that Europe's worst river floods for more than a decade could soon be over due to recent dry weather in Austria and Germany and a hot forecast for Hungary over the weekend.

Kirstin Blaise Lobato, who spent over a decade in prison for the murder and mutilation of a homeless man in Las Vegas in 2001, has had her case dismissed by a judge after prosecutors declined to proceed with a third trial. Lobato, who has consistently maintained her innocence, was convicted twice for the crime, with the only evidence against her being a third-hand rumor.

In October 2017, a hearing was held during which several renowned entomologists and a medical examiner testified that the state's theory of the crime, which claimed that Lobato had killed the victim in the early morning hours of July 8, 2001, and left his body outside all day, was scientifically implausible. The testimony demonstrated that if Bailey had been killed and left outside as the state claimed, blowflies would have quickly colonized his remains, leaving visible clusters of eggs in his various wounds. However, Bailey's body had no blowfly eggs on it.

The state's prosecutor, Sandra DiGiacomo, attempted to argue that flies in Las Vegas behave differently than flies elsewhere in the world, but this argument was not successful. In a detailed opinion filed on December 19, Judge Stefany Miley concluded that the testimony of Lobato's experts was credible, and had a jury heard such evidence, they might have acquitted her. Miley granted Lobato a new trial.

On Friday, District Attorney Steven Wolfson chose to dismiss the charges against Lobato "with prejudice," meaning the state can never seek to prosecute her again for the crime. It is unclear when Lobato will be released from prison, as prison officials have stated that she "could be transported to another location" before being released.

Lobato's case was taken on by the Innocence Project, which fought to overturn her conviction. Lead defense attorney Vanessa Potkin said that prison had a "devastating impact" on Lobato's life and expressed elation at the dismissal of the charges. Clark County District Attorney Steve Wolfson declined to comment on the ruling.

In 2007, Lobato was found guilty of voluntary sexual conduct between a prisoner and another person, which added another year to her sentence and was expected to be served after she finished serving her time for the killing. Potkin has stated that she will push for Lobato's immediate release and revisit the prison crime conviction, as Lobato "served over 15 years for a crime she did not commit."

Lobato filed a petition in May 2010 to challenge the legality of her detention, alleging 79 grounds for relief. The Supreme Court last year ordered an evidentiary hearing on 25 of the claims.

The study published in The Journal of Nutrition found that a diet high in meat, fast food, and instant noodles is associated with increased abdominal obesity and high LDL cholesterol in South Koreans. However, the study did not find a link between this diet and metabolic syndrome as a whole. The study also found that women who eat instant noodles at least twice a week have a 68% higher likelihood of having metabolic syndrome, while this effect was not apparent in men. The study was based on surveys of over 10,000 adults in South Korea and was conducted by researchers from South Korea and the United States. The findings have caused a heated reaction in South Korea, where instant noodles are a popular and essential part of the diet. Many South Koreans have vowed not to quit eating instant noodles, while others have offered up techniques they believe keep them healthy, such as adding vegetables and using less seasoning. The study raises questions about the nutritional value of instant noodles, as they provide a high amount of sodium and are not considered a healthy food. The study also highlights the cultural significance of instant noodles in South Korea, where they are often seen as a symbol of convenience and affordability.

In a tragic incident that occurred in Chantilly, Virginia, a wedding caterer, Tyonne Johns, was stabbed to death during a dispute over folding chairs at a wedding reception in Ellanor C. Lawrence Park. The 35-year-old owner of the Chef Tyonne catering company was pronounced dead at a local hospital after the altercation with Kempton A. Bonds, a 19-year-old seasonal employee of the Fairfax County Park Authority.

The dispute began when Johns was packing up the folding chairs, with Bonds insisting that they belonged to the park authority. The argument escalated, and Bonds allegedly pulled out a pocketknife and stabbed Johns in the upper body. Bonds has been charged with second-degree murder and is being held without bond at the Fairfax County Adult Detention Center.

Earlier in the day, Bonds had called the police after becoming aggravated by the behavior of the wedding guests. Bonds' bizarre conduct was noticeable to guests throughout the night, according to a bartender working at the reception.

Tyonne Johns was remembered as a rising chef, a kindhearted, loving spirit, and a professional by her colleagues and friends. The investigation is ongoing, and calls to relatives of Bonds seeking an interview were not returned. The Fairfax County Park Authority has expressed shock and condolences to Johns' family. Bonds has worked for the park authority since 2015 and has been fired pending the outcome of the investigation.

Facebook is set to implement face recognition technology to aid users in tagging photos of friends, starting next week. The new service will not change existing privacy settings, as users will still receive notifications when tagged and have control over who tags them. The technology will not be automatic; when uploading an album, Facebook will attempt to recognize the people in it and ask for confirmation before tagging. Users can opt-out of having their name suggested during the photo tagging process. Facebook will initially roll out the service to a small number of U.S. users, following previous updates such as group tagging and higher-resolution images. Facebook's revenue is projected to reach $2 billion in 2010, more than double the 2009 figure. The company's popularity among consumers and advertisers has made it an attractive target, surpassing Yahoo in global users in October. Facebook's growth has also sparked concerns about privacy, but the company has introduced simpler privacy controls and reduced the amount of user information that's publicly available.

"Sausage Party" debuted at the box office this weekend, earning $33.6 million and providing a much-needed win for Sony Pictures. The animated comedy, which features a foul-mouthed cast including Seth Rogen, Kristen Wiig, and Edward Norton, holds the record for the largest August opening ever for an animated film. "Suicide Squad" topped domestic charts for a second week, but its second-week business dropped by 67%, indicating that the film's negative reviews are starting to impact its performance. Disney's remake of "Pete's Dragon" faltered, earning $21.6 million despite positive reviews. "Jason Bourne" and "Bad Moms" rounded out the top five. In limited release, the Western heist film "Hell or High Water" performed well, earning $592,000 from 32 locations. Total box office receipts were up nearly 15% from the year-ago period.

The Curiosity rover is set to land on Mars at 1:31 a.m. Eastern time, with confirmation expected within minutes. However, silence from the rover could be due to interplanetary communications glitches or the landing site rotating out of view. The Odyssey orbiter will attempt to pick up signals, but if it fails, a second orbiter, Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, will also listen. If no signal is received after 18 hours, concerns about Curiosity's safety will arise.

The landing is historic as Curiosity is larger, more complicated, and more ambitious than previous rovers. It will use a hovering rocket stage and a sky crane for descent, a method never tested in full on Earth. NASA's chief scientist John Grunsfeld has called it "the most important NASA mission of the decade."

The landing is generating worldwide interest, with parties scheduled in various cities globally, including New York's Times Square. Mars exploration is notoriously challenging, with only about one-third of missions since the late 1960s successfully reaching, orbiting, and landing on Mars. The United States has been the only nation to land a vehicle on Mars and complete its mission, having done so six out of seven times.

The University of Alberta has cancelled a scheduled spoon bending workshop, which was to be presented by Anastasia Kutt, an energy healing therapist and registered reiki master. The workshop was part of the Pediatric Integrative Medicine rounds, intended to address existing information about reiki and other energy therapies. The cancellation followed criticism from law professor Timothy Caulfield, who called out the university's faculty of medicine for scheduling the workshop. The event was widely criticized on social media by doctors, scientists, and others skeptical of spoon bending and energy healing. The original poster for the workshop described it as a guided meditation/energy transfer technique that would teach participants to bend cutlery using the power of their minds. The cancellation was met with a protest against what was deemed as "unethical institutional support for medical quackery" from the University of Alberta. This incident highlights the ongoing controversy surrounding the integration of pseudoscientific practices like reiki and energy healing in mainstream medicine.

The manhunt for Christopher Dorner, a former Los Angeles police officer accused of a deadly rampage, continued in the snow-covered San Bernardino Mountains. Over 100 officers searched the area, including SWAT teams and search dogs, after Dorner's burned-out pickup truck was found near Big Bear Lake. The search was hampered by heavy snowfall, but authorities pledged to continue until they find Dorner or definitive evidence that he is no longer in the area. Dorner is described as African American, 6 feet tall, and 270 pounds.

Authorities believe Dorner is on a vengeful rampage, killing three people and injuring others in a campaign to take revenge on those he blamed for his dismissal from the LAPD four years ago. Investigators are scrutinizing a conspiracy-laden manifesto that they believe was published on Dorner's Facebook page, in which he threatened "unconventional and asymmetrical warfare" against police officers and their families.

The search for Dorner has been extensive, with false leads and erroneous sightings reported throughout California, Nevada, Arizona, and northern Mexico. Authorities have searched Dorner's home in Las Vegas and his mother's home in La Palma, carrying out bags of potential evidence.

Dorner's familiarity with the terrain and preparedness to brave a winter storm are unknown, but cold weather poses a tremendous threat to human survival, and Dorner would need layered, insulated clothing and avoid getting wet to survive for very long. The search is expected to resume at daybreak on Saturday, with authorities hoping clearer skies will allow airplanes to help in the search.

The Central African Republic (CAR) was suspended by the African Union on Monday after rebels, led by Michel Djotodia, seized power in a rapid assault on the capital, Bangui. The international community expressed concern over the deteriorating security situation in the impoverished, landlocked country, which has largely untapped mineral wealth including uranium, gold, and diamonds. The Seleka rebellion began in December 2012, accusing Bozize of reneging on a peace deal and demanding his resignation. The accord brought several prominent figures from Seleka into the government but collapsed after the rebels said their demands had not been met. Seleka launched its first offensive on December 10, accusing Bozize of failing to honor an earlier peace agreement.

Oscar Pistorius, the South African double amputee and former Paralympian, is set to be released from prison in August after serving 10 months of his five-year sentence for culpable homicide in the death of his girlfriend Reeva Steenkamp. Pistorius was convicted of the lesser charge in a 10-month trial last year, a decision the state is appealing. He shot Steenkamp, a 29-year-old law school graduate and model, through a locked door in his bathroom on Valentine's Day 2013, claiming that he mistakenly believed an intruder was in the house when he fired his gun. Pistorius has been incarcerated at the Pretoria Central Prison since his conviction last fall and is expected to be released on August 21.

The family of Reeva Steenkamp reacted with dismay, stating that Pistorius' ten months in prison is "simply not enough" of a punishment for his crime. They expressed their forgiveness towards Pistorius but emphasized the importance of accountability for his actions. In a separate development, South Africa's Supreme Court of Appeal set a date for prosecutors to appeal the runner's conviction for manslaughter. If successful, Pistorius could face a longer prison sentence, potentially even life in prison.

During his time in prison, Pistorius has been held in a single cell due to fears of attacks from violent inmates. Despite the isolation, he is reportedly managing and is eager to work with disadvantaged youngsters upon his release. His legal team is working to arrange opportunities for him to do so.

Throughout his legal fight, Pistorius' solicitor, Barry Roux, has maintained that Pistorius will be released in August and will serve the remainder of his sentence under house arrest. Roux also revealed that Pistorius has rejected numerous Hollywood film offers and book deals, despite being broke due to the high costs of his legal defense.

In Laurel County, Kentucky, a man named Ernest Chumbley has been charged with murder after admitting to shooting and killing his wife, Virginia, who was battling cancer. According to Chumbley, he carried out the act as a mercy killing, stating that Virginia had asked him to end her suffering. The discovery of ancient tools and pigments in Kenya's Olorgesailie Basin suggests that dramatic shifts in the East African climate may have driven toolmaking advances and the development of trading networks among early humans or their close relatives by the Middle Stone Age, around 320,000 years ago. The newly excavated tools, including hand axes and smaller, more specialized implements, are the oldest of their kind and were made from obsidian that came from far away, indicating long-distance contacts and trading among hominid populations. The researchers propose that these behavior changes were a response to unpredictable food sources on changing landscapes. The findings, published in three papers in Science, challenge the previous belief that modern behaviors such as symbolism, innovation, and art suddenly arose 40,000-50,000 years ago and suggest that these behaviors occurred much earlier in Africa. The discovery of red pigment chunks also indicates the earliest known use of pigments to color rocks in the archaeological record.

The study published in JAMA Pediatrics analyzed 20 years of nationwide mortality data to examine trends in suicide among US children aged 5 to 11 years. The overall suicide rate remained stable during the 29-year period, going from 1.18 to 1.09 per one million. However, the stability resulted from divergent trends in suicide for black and white children during those 20 years.

The suicide rate increased in black children from 1.36 to 2.54 per one million, while the suicide rate decreased in white children from 1.14 to 0.77 per one million. The statistically significant racial differences were confined to both black and white boys, with an increase in the suicide rate among black boys (1.78 to 3.47 per one million) and a decrease in the suicide rate among white boys (from 1.96 to 1.31 per one million).

Hanging/suffocation was the predominant method of suicide, accounting for 78.2% of the total suicides, followed by firearms (17.7%) and other methods (4.1%). The analysis showed a significant decrease in the firearm suicide rate during the study, both overall (IRR = 0.69; 95% CI, 0.57-0.85) and among white boys (IRR = 0.72; 95% CI, 0.59-0.88).

The study's findings highlight a potential racial disparity in suicide rates among school-aged children that warrants attention. The researchers suggest that factors such as disproportionate exposure to violence and traumatic stress, aggressive school discipline, and an early onset of puberty may influence increasing suicide rates among young black children. However, it remains unclear if any of these factors are related to increasing suicide rates.

The authors recommend ongoing surveillance to monitor these emerging trends and research to identify risk, protective, and precipitating factors associated with suicide in elementary school-aged children to frame targets for early detection and culturally informed interventions.

The study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences reveals a paradoxical trade-off in the evolution of Antarctic notothenioid fishes, which have developed antifreeze proteins (AFPs) to prevent their blood from freezing. While AFPs are essential for survival in frigid waters, they also inhibit the melting of ice crystals in the fish's body, a potentially harmful side effect.

Researchers found that AFP-stabilized ice resists melting at temperatures above the expected equilibrium freezing/melting point (eqFMP), both in vitro and in vivo. Superheated ice was observed inside notothenioid fishes and solutions of purified AFPs, and ice persisted inside live fishes at temperatures more than 1°C above their eqFMP for at least 24 hours, and at a lower temperature for several days.

Field experiments confirmed that superheated ice occurs naturally inside wild fishes. Over the long-term record (1999–2012), seawater temperature surpassed the fish eqFMP in most summers, but never exceeded the highest temperature at which ice persisted inside experimental fishes. This suggests that summer warming may not reliably eliminate internal ice due to AFP-induced melting inhibition.

The study exposes a potentially antagonistic pleiotropic effect of AFPs: beneficial freezing avoidance is accompanied by melting inhibition that may contribute to lifelong accumulation of detrimental internal ice crystals. The researchers suggest that further investigation is needed to understand the long-term cost of having the protein and whether the fishes have evolved mechanisms to deal with these ice crystals inside their bodies.

The U.S. job market and economy experienced a setback in September due to Hurricanes Harvey and Irma, resulting in a loss of 33,000 jobs, the first decline in nearly seven years. The job losses were primarily in the restaurant and bar industry, reflecting the damage to Florida's tourism industry. Approximately 1.5 million people were unable to work due to the weather, the most in 20 years. The average hourly wage rose 2.9 percent from a year earlier, but this figure was artificially inflated by the loss of lower-paid workers in hurricane-hit areas.

Despite the hurricane-related losses, other recent indicators point to a solid economy and job market. A survey of services firms found that they expanded at their fastest monthly pace since 2005, while a survey of manufacturers showed an equally strong gain. Factory activity expanded at the fastest pace in more than 13 years.

Auto sales, which had been lackluster this year, jumped 6.1 percent in September due to replacement of cars destroyed by the storms. This increase in purchases should soon lead automakers to step up production.

The economic losses from Harvey are estimated to be between $76 billion and $87 billion, making it the second-worst U.S. natural disaster after Hurricane Katrina in 2005. Irma is expected to cause between $58 billion and $83 billion in economic losses, while Maria, which hit Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands, could cost between $45 billion and $95 billion.

In many ways, the September jobs report is a mixed bag, with the market focusing on the average hourly earnings number, which showed an accelerated pace but may be artificially inflated by the effects of hurricanes. The unemployment rate falling to 4.2 percent, despite labor force participation rising, is a positive sign of underlying strength in the U.S. economy.

Title: Pennsylvania Inheritance Tax Rates, Exemptions, and Payment Details

The document discusses the Pennsylvania Inheritance Tax, a levy imposed on the value of a decedent's estate that is transferred to beneficiaries. The tax rate varies based on the relationship between the decedent and the heir.

- Transfers to a surviving spouse or a parent from a child aged 21 or younger are exempt from tax.
- Direct descendants and lineal heirs are subject to a 4.5% tax rate.
- Siblings face a 12% tax rate.
- Other heirs, excluding charitable organizations, exempt institutions, and government entities, are taxed at a rate of 15%.

Property owned jointly between spouses is exempt from inheritance tax. Effective for estates of decedents dying after June 30, 2012, certain farmland and other agricultural property are exempt from Pennsylvania inheritance tax, provided the property is transferred to eligible recipients. For more details, refer to Inheritance Tax Informational Notice 2012-01.

Inheritance tax payments are due upon the death of the decedent and become delinquent nine months after the individual's death. A 5% discount is allowed if the tax is paid within three months of the decedent's death.

For further information and answers to commonly asked questions, the document suggests reviewing the brochure, Pennsylvania Inheritance Tax and Safe Deposit Boxes. For detailed and historic Pennsylvania inheritance tax information, consult the Tax Compendium.

The HMS Illustrious aircraft carrier is being sent by the UK government to aid the relief effort in the Philippines following the devastating Typhoon Haiyan. The typhoon, which hit on Friday, has killed at least 2,300 people and displaced more than half a million. HMS Illustrious is expected to arrive in the Philippines on 24 November and will relieve the destroyer HMS Daring, which is already on its way to the country. The carrier will provide helicopters to transport food and water to people stranded in remote areas of the Philippines, which is made up of more than 7,000 islands. The UK is also sending aid by air, with the first flight arriving on Tuesday. The Royal Navy has almost all of its ships equipped with supplies and equipment for use in emergencies, and its crews are trained for dealing with humanitarian disasters. HMS Daring has more than 200 personnel on board, including a doctor, a dentist, engineers, and a chaplain. It is also carrying members of the Royal Marines band, who are trained first aiders. The ship holds 700 ration packs, can provide more than 20,000 liters of water, and has other equipment including generators and thermal-imaging cameras. The UK has given more than £20 million in aid and the Disasters Emergency Committee (DEC) has raised £23 million in its first 48 hours. A huge international aid effort is underway, but widespread infrastructure damage is hampering efforts to distribute aid to some areas. The DEC, which brings together 14 major UK charities, launched its appeal on Monday and said the response from the public has been "remarkable." The British Red Cross is also sending aid and equipment to the Philippines. The typhoon has affected more than 11 million people, according to the UN. The UK government is also sending a team of 12 medical experts to the country, and a Royal Air Force C-17 military transport aircraft is being deployed in the early hours of Friday morning. Justin Forsyth, chief executive of Save the Children, said the aid effort is allowing aid to get "right into the heart of this catastrophe." British couple Andrea Agarwal and Trevor Holmes, who own a dive center in the island of Malapascua, have been helping with the aid effort. They were not on the island at the time the typhoon hit but said their bar and restaurant were destroyed. They have been coordinating aid efforts from the island of Cebu, 360 miles south of Manila. Major relief packages have continued to pour into the typhoon-devastated city of Tacloban, including food aid, medicine, and search-and-rescue teams. Despite the arrival of aid and a concerted effort by the military to restore order to the town, thousands of stricken residents are still crammed at the airport desperate for a way out of the city. On Wednesday night, the Tacloban mayor led a mass burial in a graveyard just outside the city. Officials said every effort had been made to ensure those buried could be identified in the weeks to come. The official death toll of 2,357 is a considerably lower figure than that estimated by aid workers, who say the lack of information coming from various areas could mean that the devastation is far greater than yet realized. Most casualties seem to have been around the islands of Samar and Leyte, where the storm first made landfall at 195 mph on Friday morning, with accompanying sea surges of up to 20 feet. The resulting damage in the region, a coastal flatland that has seen whole villages blown apart by the storm's heavy winds and rain, has created a state of pandemonium in Tacloban, where survivors have had to loot shops and malls for water, while others have resorted to scavenging for food among the bloated bodies of the dead. On Wednesday stories of heightened violence and tension circulated around the city as eight were killed after stampeding a rice warehouse looking for food. A Philippine Red Cross convoy was allegedly hijacked by armed men who were later shot dead by police, and a 13-year-old boy was knifed in the neck and stomach by unknown men, AFP reported. There were unverified reports that prisoners from the local jail, who had successfully broken out of their cells after the storm, were ambushing people carrying supplies across San Juanico bridge, which connects Tacloban with Samar island. A Facebook status warning of traffickers posing as relief workers and targeting women and children circulated on Thursday but the Guardian was not able to verify the report. Officials urged people to stay calm and not believe everything they heard. "There have been so many reports of looting and rape which have turned out not to be correct," Ricky Caradang, a spokesman for President Benigno Aquino III, told the local ABS-CBN TV channel. A nighttime curfew has been in place since Monday and in a televised report on Wednesday the BBC correspondent Rupert Wingfield-Hayes said Tacloban had turned into a "war zone." Footage showed tanks rolling through the center of the devastated town and soldiers crouching behind walls with automatic rifles. Just what the threat was to the city had not been made clear, he said. Some aid agencies, fearing for the safety of their employees, have ordered teams to evacuate. Plan International has withdrawn all 15 of its employees – normally permanently based in Tacloban – until security is restored in the city, according to spokesman Ian Wishart. The fact that many aid workers had arrived in Tacloban but little aid had yet been distributed was creating a security concern, one aid worker told the Guardian. A memo was circulating among relief workers advising them not to move around in Tacloban as some UN staff had already been pulled out for security reasons. But officials have pointed to an increased presence of police and military, and the arrival of aid, as a turning point for the ravaged city. Caradang said 26 of 138 barangays (neighborhoods) in Tacloban had received aid, with many of the roads previously blocked by fallen trees and debris now cleared. Oxfam has sent enough emergency water supplies for 20,000 families in Tacloban on a first-run delivery of effort, although the charity added that delivery was dependent on a stable security situation in the town itself. Plans are to provide half a million people affected by the super storm with emergency shelter, water, and construction materials to rebuild their homes and boats. The World Food Programme successfully delivered nearly 25 tonnes of high-energy biscuits on Wednesday and another 10 tonnes were on their way, the UN body said.

NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft, launched in 1977 to explore the outer solar system, has entered a new region near the edge of the solar system, referred to as a "magnetic highway." This region connects the sun's magnetic field lines to interstellar magnetic field lines, allowing lower-energy charged particles from inside the heliosphere to zoom out and higher-energy particles from outside to stream in.

Scientists believe this is the final region Voyager 1 has to cross before reaching interstellar space. Voyager 1's environment has been stable since August 25, 2012, when it entered the magnetic highway region for the second time. The spacecraft's magnetic-field reading instrument indicates it is still within the heliosphere, as the direction of the magnetic field lines has not changed.

Voyager 1 may remain within the heliopause, the outer boundary of the solar system, for another two to three years, but it's hard to anticipate how long it will be until the probe leaves the solar system. The spacecraft's data will continue to be analyzed to determine when Voyager 1 first reaches interstellar space.

Voyager 1 and its twin, Voyager 2, are the longest-serving spacecraft, with Voyager 1 currently 122 AU from Earth and Voyager 2 about 100 AU away. One AU, or astronomical unit, is equivalent to the distance from Earth to the sun. The Voyager missions are a part of NASA's Heliophysics System Observatory, sponsored by the Heliophysics Division of the Science Mission Directorate at NASA Headquarters in Washington. For more information about the Voyager spacecraft, visit: http://www.nasa.gov/voyager and http://voyager.jpl.nasa.gov.

On April 9, 2014, a 16-year-old boy named Alex Hribal went on a stabbing rampage at Franklin Regional High School in Murrysville, Pennsylvania. The attack occurred in the crowded halls of the school, just minutes before the start of classes. Hribal, who was armed with two kitchen knives, flailed away at students and a security guard, injuring 22 people, including at least five who were critically wounded.

The rampage set off a "screaming stampede," left blood on the floor and walls, and brought teachers rushing to help the victims. Police shed little light on the motive for the attack, but investigators were looking into reports of a threatening phone call between Hribal and another student the night before.

Hribal was taken into custody and charged with four counts of attempted homicide and 21 counts of aggravated assault. He was jailed without bail and would be prosecuted as an adult. His attorney did not immediately respond to a message for comment.

The attack unfolded in the morning and was over in about five minutes. Hribal ran wildly down about 200 feet of hallway, slashing away with knives about 8 to 10 inches long. One student, Nate Moore, 15, said he saw the boy tackle and stab a freshman. Moore tried to break it up, but the boy got up and slashed his face, opening a wound that required 11 stitches.

Assistant Principal Sam King finally tackled the boy and disarmed him, and a Murrysville police officer who is regularly assigned to the school handcuffed him, police said. King's son told reporters that his father was treated at a hospital, though authorities have said he did not suffer any knife wounds.

In addition to the 22 who were stabbed or slashed, two people suffered other injuries during the melee. The security guard, who was wounded after intervening early in the melee, was treated and released.

Governor Tom Corbett visited the stricken town and said, "There are a number of heroes in this day. Many of them are students."

While several bloody stabbing rampages at schools in China have made headlines in the past few years, schools in the U.S. have concentrated their emergency preparations on shooting rampages. Nevertheless, there have been at least two major stabbing attacks at U.S. schools over the past year.

The attack at Franklin Regional High School was the latest in a string of school violence that has occurred across the nation. Mass stabbings, such as the one at the high school, are rare. The attack has rattled the town, a residential enclave with a population of about 20,000. Information on what led to the stabbings and the conditions of the injured are still unfolding.

Arnold Schwarzenegger, the former California Governor and action movie icon, is set to return to films after a hiatus of nearly 16 years. His agent, CAA, has received the green light to consider offers for Schwarzenegger, who is best known for his roles in "Terminator" films. He has been considering three scripts, one of which portrays him as a kind-hearted Nazi soldier. Schwarzenegger acknowledges the need to adapt his roles due to his age and aims to focus more on acting. He served as California's Governor from 2003 to 2011, during which he took on bit parts in films like "Around the World in 80 Days" and "The Expendables." Despite speculations about a presidential run due to his high popularity in 2003, Schwarzenegger's approval rating fell significantly in recent years. Now, he expresses a desire to return to Hollywood.

Senator John Thune announced on February 22nd, 2011, that he will not be running for president in 2012. Despite encouragement from supporters across the country, Thune decided to stay in the Senate, citing his role in the ongoing fiscal crisis and economic uncertainty as a reason to fight for America's future from within the Senate. Thune's decision was influenced by his family, the timing of his political career, and the potential for further opportunities in the Senate.

The Metropolitan Police is under pressure to expand their phone-hacking inquiry to include private investigator Jonathan Rees, who is accused of targeting politicians, royal family members, and high-level terrorist informers on behalf of Rupert Murdoch's News International. The former prime minister Tony Blair is among the suspected victims, along with Jack Straw, Peter Mandelson, Alastair Campbell, Prince Edward, the Countess of Wessex, the Duke and Duchess of Kent, Kate Middleton, and several high-level officials. Rees is also accused of using a specialist computer hacker to steal information about MI6 agents who had infiltrated the Provisional IRA. The Metropolitan Police have not confirmed or investigated these cases, and it is not yet clear precisely what form of surveillance Rees and his agency, Southern Investigations, were using. The Labour MP Tom Watson has urged the prime minister to ensure that a cover-up does not occur. The News of the World, which employed Rees, has denied the allegations and stated that they have not been asked for any information regarding Rees by the Metropolitan Police.

Alexa Internet, a web traffic analysis company, has been donating their crawl data to the Internet Archive since 1996, with the data added to the Wayback Machine after an embargo period. In a separate incident, a Spokane man named Carlo M. Cerutti, 50, was arrested on Saturday following an assault charge. The incident occurred at his duplex near the NorthTown Mall, after his neighbor called the police. The dispute between Cerutti and his neighbor reportedly started over garbage cans, with Cerutti's wife accusing the neighbor of throwing his garbage into her can. The neighbor then claimed that Cerutti came out of his house wielding a large sword-type weapon with multiple blades, attempting to swing it like a hatchet. The victim put his hands up to block the blade and was able to pull the sword away from Cerutti. Another neighbor witnessed the fight. Cerutti now faces assault charges as a result of this incident.

On March 24, 2015, a Germanwings passenger jet carrying 150 people crashed in the French Alps, killing all on board. The victims included two babies, two opera singers, and 16 German high school students and their teachers returning from an exchange trip to Spain. The Airbus A320 operated by Germanwings, a budget subsidiary of Lufthansa, was less than an hour from landing in Duesseldorf when it unexpectedly went into a rapid descent. The pilots sent out no distress call and had lost radio contact with their control center, deepening the mystery.

The crash site was located in a remote, snow-covered area in the French Alps, not far from the Italian border and the French Riviera. Debris from the plane was scattered across the mountainside, with larger airplane body sections and white flecks of debris. A black box was recovered from the scene, which will be immediately investigated to provide investigators with a second-by-second timeline of the plane's flight.

The town of Haltern, Germany, was rent with sorrow after losing 16 tenth graders and their two teachers. Students and teachers at the Joseph-Koenig-Gymnasium high school in Haltern am See gathered outside the school, embracing and crying in front of lit candles that read 'In silent sympathy.' The students had been on a week-long Spanish exchange program at the Institut Giola in Llinars del Vallès near Barcelona, and were on their way home when the plane crashed.

German Chancellor Angela Merkel, French President Francois Hollande, and Spanish Prime Minister Mariano Rajoy were to visit the site on Wednesday. The White House and the airline chief said there was no sign that terrorism was involved, and Merkel urged reporters not to speculate on the cause. Lufthansa CEO Carsten Spohr called it the "blackest day of our company's 60-year history." He insisted, however, that flying "remains after this terrible day the safest mode of transport."

Germanwings said 144 passengers and six crew members were on board. Authorities said 67 Germans were believed among the victims, as well as many Spaniards, two Australians, and one person each from the Netherlands, Turkey, and Denmark. The crash was Germanwings' first involving passenger deaths since it began operating in 2002. The Germanwings logo, normally maroon and yellow, was blacked out on its Twitter feed.

In 2014, Robin Williams' suicide was the most popular search on Google, surpassing other significant events such as the World Cup, the Ebola outbreak, and the Ice Bucket Challenge. Other trending topics included the addictive smartphone game "Flappy Bird," bearded drag queen Conchita Wurst, the Middle East extremist group ISIS, the hit Disney movie "Frozen," and the Winter Olympics in Russia.

The list of top searches was similar worldwide, with a few exceptions. In the US, the Ferguson confrontation and Ukraine's conflict with Russia held more interest compared to the rest of the world. Apple products did not make the list for the first time in a few years.

Google's list of top searches provides insights into people's collective mindset, as Google processes about two out of every three search requests made on the internet. Yahoo's search lists indicated a focus on entertainment, with celebrities and entertainers occupying several slots. Microsoft's Bing separated its lists into different categories, such as athletes, celebrities, vacation destinations, and musicians.

PayPal has banned Infowars, a controversial media outlet, citing violations of its "acceptable use policy" for promoting hate and discriminatory intolerance. The decision comes weeks before the mid-terms and follows a string of bans from other major platforms. Infowars had been using PayPal for transactions on its online store. The company claims it conducted a comprehensive review of Infowars' site, but no specific examples were provided. Off the record, Infowars was told that criticism of Islam and opposition to transgenderism being taught to children were two of the examples of "hate." The ban was instituted despite InfowarsStore.com containing no political content, leading to concerns that it is a broader attack on the Infowars platform. PayPal representatives said they were giving Infowars 10 days to switch payment processors, after which all services would be terminated. The ban was handed down just weeks after a George Soros-funded group called for PayPal to terminate its agreement with Infowars. Right Wing Watch, which routinely violates copyright by uploading entire sections of other people's videos to YouTube without any pretense of fair use, has not had its channel deleted. The Jeff Bezos-owned Washington Post published an article less than two weeks ago that served as a dog whistle for PayPal to ban Infowars. The article bemoaned the fact that despite Alex Jones being banned by every other Big Tech platform, the censorship had left intact key elements of his moneymaking machinery. The article then specifically mentions how Infowars uses PayPal to generate a "high rate of sales." This is yet another example of a competing media outlet abusing its dominant position to lobby to shut down a smaller media outlet. Critics argue that PayPal's decision represents politically motivated financial discrimination by a giant corporation abusing its monopolistic status to attack the basic right to engage in commerce.

A French court has ordered Air France to pay a fine of 10,000 euros and damages of 3,000 euros to a pro-Palestine activist, Horia Ankour, who was forced off a flight to Tel Aviv in 2012 due to her non-Jewish status. The court ruled that Air France had discriminated against Ankour, who was attempting to participate in a "Welcome to Palestine" campaign. The incident occurred amidst heavy Israeli pressure that led to the cancellation of about 300 flights in Europe. Air France claimed Ankour's name was on a list of undesirables provided by Israeli authorities, but French prosecutors argued it was a clear case of discrimination.

Swiss mountaineer Erhard Loretan, renowned for summiting all 14 peaks above 8,000 meters, died in a climbing accident on his 52nd birthday. Loretan, from Fribourg, began climbing at 11 and ascended his first 8,000-meter peak in 1982. He completed the rest over 13 years, becoming one of three climbers to achieve this feat. In 1986, he climbed Mount Everest in 40 hours without oxygen, and climbed 38 Swiss peaks in 19 days. However, his career was marred by a family tragedy in 2001 when he was convicted of manslaughter for shaking his 7-month-old son to death. Loretan and a client fell during a climb in the Bernese Alps, with Loretan dying at the scene and his client being flown to hospital in serious condition.

Jerry Seinfeld, a renowned comedian, has launched a new web series titled "Comedians in Cars Getting Coffee" on Crackle and the series' own website. The show features Seinfeld picking up his comedian friends in vintage cars and driving to have coffee and casual conversations. The first guest is Larry David, co-creator of the Seinfeld sitcom. The series is highly produced, crisp, and rich-looking, with quick edits to different perspectives. The conversations are entertaining and occasionally touch upon the intricacies of comedy and life. The show feels like a casual, spur-of-the-moment event, but it is meticulously produced. Seinfeld does not need the web, but it seems better suited to his current interests of casual comedy and schmoozing with friends.

Tom Hanks also recently launched his web series, "Electric City," a dystopian animation series, on Yahoo. Hollywood stars are increasingly turning to the web for opportunities and freedom of expression that they cannot get in traditional media. This trend is driven by the growing portion of ad spending on the web and changing viewer habits due to the ubiquity of smartphones and tablet computers. The web allows established stars to experiment creatively without network executives, clunky TV timeslots, spiraling budgets, and other Hollywood blights.

In a series of tweets, President Donald Trump responded to reports that an FBI informant had contacted multiple campaign advisers during the 2016 presidential campaign, suggesting that such an action was politically motivated and could potentially be a major scandal. The informant, described as an American academic who teaches in Britain, is said to have made contact with Trump advisers George Papadopoulos and Carter Page.

The alleged informant's name has been published by conservative media outlets and circulated widely on Twitter. Trump maintained that the truth about the informant could only be revealed with the release or review of documents that the House Intelligence Committee and Senate Judiciary are seeking from the Justice Department.

Congressional Republicans have been engaged in an intense fight with the Justice Department over access to highly sensitive and classified information related to the investigation into the Trump campaign, and the identity of the FBI's informant. The investigation, which started after Trump advisor Papadopoulos' April 2016 conversation with an Australian diplomat indicating the Russians had dirt on Democratic nominee Hillary Clinton, has led to special counsel Robert Mueller's probe into whether Trump campaign officials colluded with the Russian government during a Kremlin campaign to meddle in the 2016 election.

Republican lawmakers have expressed frustration with the Justice Department's refusals to grant access to the documents, with House Freedom Caucus co-founder Rep. Jim Jordan (R-Ohio) stating that if the reports about an informant are true, "that is as wrong as it gets."

Supreme Court Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg has made a series of politically charged remarks against Republican presidential nominee Donald Trump, raising concerns about judicial ethics. In interviews with CNN and The Associated Press, Ginsburg called Trump a "faker" and criticized his refusal to release his tax returns. Trump responded by calling on Ginsburg to resign, tweeting that she should "apologize to the court."

Ginsburg's comments are highly unusual for a justice to make, and some critics say she crossed the line by making politically charged remarks. House Speaker Paul Ryan said the comments were "out of place" and suggested that they could be seen as inherently biased.

Despite the criticism, Ginsburg expressed no regret for her comments and said she was not surprised that Trump has gotten so far in the election cycle. She also drew a contrast between what she believes is tougher media treatment of Democratic candidate Hillary Clinton and Trump's refusal to release his tax returns.

Ginsburg has been a vocal critic of Trump in the past, and her comments are likely to further fuel the controversy surrounding the presidential election. Some have praised Ginsburg for speaking out against Trump, while others have criticized her for violating judicial ethics by making political remarks.

Ginsburg was appointed to the Supreme Court by President Bill Clinton in 1993 and is now the senior member of the liberal wing of the court. She has been a strong voice in countering conservative Chief Justice John Roberts and has drawn a cult-like following among young people who have nicknamed her The Notorious R.B.G., a play on American rapper The Notorious B.I.G.

Throughout her career, Ginsburg has been known for her frankness and her willingness to speak out on issues she cares about. In 2009, she was being treated for pancreatic cancer yet made sure to attend President Barack Obama's televised speech to a joint session of Congress, explaining that she wanted people to know the Supreme Court was not all men. "I also wanted them to see I was alive and well, contrary to that senator who said I'd be dead within nine months." She was referring to Sen. Jim Bunning, a Kentucky Republican, who had said she would likely die within nine months from the pancreatic cancer. Bunning later apologized.

It is unclear how Ginsburg's comments will affect the Supreme Court or the presidential election, but they are sure to continue to be a topic of discussion in the coming weeks. Some have speculated that Ginsburg may be trying to influence the election, while others have praised her for standing up to Trump. Regardless of one's political views, it is clear that Ginsburg's comments have sparked a lively debate about the role of the judiciary in politics and the appropriate behavior for Supreme Court justices.

In a tragic incident that occurred on April 9, 2015, an Egyptian man named Ali Elmezayen intentionally drove his car off a pier at the Port of Los Angeles with his severely autistic children and domestic partner. The car sank, and two of his children, aged 8 and 13, drowned. Elmezayen had purchased accidental death insurance policies on their lives, totaling over $6 million, and collected over $260,000 in insurance payouts.

Elmezayen was arrested on November 7, 2020, and charged with defrauding insurance companies. He is accused of posing as his domestic partner in communications with the insurance companies, making false statements, and orchestrating a scheme to profit off his children's deaths. The charges against him include mail fraud, wire fraud, and aggravated identity theft.

Elmezayen's domestic partner survived the incident, but his other son was at camp at the time of the tragedy. Elmezayen and his partner came to the U.S. in 2000 and overstayed their tourist visas. Both later entered into sham marriages in an attempt to become permanent residents.

The investigation into this case involved the Federal Bureau of Investigation, IRS Criminal Investigation, Los Angeles Police Department, Los Angeles Port Police, and the Los Angeles City Attorney's Office. Elmezayen is due in court on November 29 for an arraignment, and if convicted, he could face a statutory maximum sentence of 20 years in prison for each fraud count, along with a mandatory consecutive sentence of two years for aggravated identity theft.

A new genus and species of shrew rat, named Hyorhinomys stuempkei, has been discovered in the remote, mountainous island of Sulawesi, Indonesia. The species is unique with a large, flat, pink nose, large ears, long hind legs, long white incisors, and very long urogenital hairs. The discovery was made by a research team from Australia, Indonesia, and America in 2013, and the species is so genetically different that it represents a new genus. The loss of the coronoid process in the dentary bone indicates a weak jaw musculature and a diet that does not require vigorous chewing, and the new species eats earthworms and beetle larvae. The island of Sulawesi is geographically complex and challenging to scientifically sample, and little research has been conducted on the island since the early 20th century. The scientists described the Few-toothed shrew rat, or Paucidentomys vermidax, in 2012, and the Sulawesi water rat, Waiomys mamasae, in 2014. The Hog-nosed rat is the third new genus described by this group of scientists since 2012. The discovery is the cover story of the Journal of Mammalogy this month.

A 6-year-old girl named Lexi, who has lived with a California foster family for four years, was removed from their home due to her Native American heritage, as determined by the Indian Child Welfare Act of 1978. The girl is 1.56% Choctaw Native American, and the law seeks to keep American Indian children with American Indian families.

Lexi was placed with the Pages, who have three other children, in December 2011 after two unsuccessful foster homes. In 2011, extended family in Utah became aware that Lexi was with a foster family and expressed interest in adopting her. The Utah couple is not Native American but is related to Lexi through her step-grandfather.

The California Court of Appeals originally ruled in August of 2014 that Lexi could stay with the Pages and they could continue to fight the Utah family for custody of the child. However, a decision earlier this month ordered the Los Angeles County Department of Children and Family Services (LA DCFS) to place Lexi with the Utah family "in accordance with the federal Indian Child Welfare Act."

The Pages addressed an online petition called "Keep Lexi Home" to several California and LA DCFS officials, stating that Lexi considers the Pages her family and that she would be devastated by being taken away. The petition had over 40,000 signatures by Monday afternoon.

Dozens of supporters gathered outside the Page's home on Monday in an attempt to block LA DCFS officers from taking Lexi. The emotional scene was livestreamed on Facebook, with the teary child, wearing a pink shirt and grasping a teddy bear, being carried out of the home by Rusty Page and placed in a social worker's car.

The Pages' lawyer said they had been willing to offer the Utah family visitation rights, but they "never responded to offers of compromise." The LA DCFS said in a statement that the department always seeks to act in the best interest of the children it serves.

The National Indian Child Welfare Association argues that the decision to re-place Lexi was the right one because "the purpose of foster care is to provide temporary care for children ... not to fast-track the creation of new families when there is extended family available who want to care for the child." The Choctaw Nation echoed this sentiment, stating that following the Choctaw Nation's values is in Lexi's best interest.

The Pages have appealed the decision to the California Supreme Court, and custody of Lexi has been returned to them pending the appeal. The case highlights the ongoing debate over the application of the Indian Child Welfare Act and whether it serves the best interest of the child.

In a breaking news report, Bill Cosby's wife, Camille Cosby, underwent a contentious six-hour deposition in February as part of a defamation case filed against her husband by seven women who accuse him of sexual assault. The deposition was released on Friday, revealing that Camille Cosby invoked spousal privilege and refused to answer many questions. The case involves allegations that Bill Cosby portrayed the accusers as liars after they came forward with their accusations in late 2014. Camille Cosby was asked about her husband's honesty and whether he deceived her, but she refused to answer. She also refused to answer whether it is dishonest or deceitful to give Quaaludes to someone for the purpose of sex. The deposition was conducted as part of a defamation suit filed against Bill Cosby, who has counter-sued the seven women who filed suit, also alleging defamation. Camille Cosby is not named in the suit. Bill Cosby faces a criminal case in Pennsylvania for allegedly drugging and molesting a former Temple University employee in 2004. He has not yet entered a plea in that case, but his attorneys have said he is innocent of the charges. About 50 women have publicly accused Bill Cosby of sexual misconduct going back decades. Camille Cosby invoked spousal privilege when asked whether her husband has been truthful with her. She also said she never obtained Quaaludes for her own use or someone else's use. In a separate lawsuit, Playboy magazine founder Hugh Hefner provided sworn testimony on Wednesday in a sexual battery lawsuit filed in Los Angeles. The lawsuit was filed by Judy Huth, who alleges that Cosby forced her to perform a sex act on him at the Playboy Mansion around 1974, when she was 15. Bill Cosby's former lawyers have accused Huth of attempting to extort him before filing the case and have tried unsuccessfully to have it dismissed. The contents of Hefner's testimony were sealed. Hefner was also named as a defendant in a case filed on Monday by former model Chloe Goins, who accuses Bill Cosby of drugging and sexually abusing her at the Playboy Mansion in 2008.

In a historic ruling on October 8, 2018, a Spanish court found an 85-year-old doctor, Eduardo Vela, guilty of stealing a newborn child nearly five decades ago during Spain's 20th-century dictatorship. However, the court acquitted Vela due to the statute of limitations having expired. The case, which is the first in relation to the wide-scale child trafficking that took place from the onset of the country's Civil War in 1936 to the death of dictator Gen. Francisco Franco in 1975, was a test case for thousands of families who are thought to have been affected by the illegal practice.

Vela, the director of a Madrid clinic considered to be at the epicenter of the scandal, was accused of taking Inés Madrigal from her biological mother in the spring of 1969 and giving her to a couple who were not her parents. Prosecutors sought an 11-year prison sentence for Vela on charges of unlawful detention, falsifying official documents, and certifying a nonexistent birth.

Judges at Madrid’s provincial court found that Vela had committed the three offenses and it was "crystal clear" that he had faked official documents and handed the baby over to a couple who were not her parents. However, they ruled that too much time had passed for a conviction since Madrigal could not have been unlawfully detained once she became an adult and had only brought her complaint against Vela six years ago.

Madrigal, who learned at 18 that she wasn't living with her biological parents, argued that she couldn't have lodged her complaint earlier because she only learned about the scheme in 2010, when her adopting mother, who died three years later, disclosed the details of what had happened at Vela's clinic. Madrigal, now 49, said she considered the provincial court's verdict to be "bittersweet" and announced she would be appealing it to the country's Supreme Court.

Spain only started investigating the "stolen babies" cases a decade ago, when National Court magistrate Baltasar Garzon opened a probe on the more than 30,000 children that were under the care of the regime. According to some estimates, as many as 300,000 babies may have been taken from their birth mothers and placed with families who supported the Franco regime. Some of the stolen children are thought to have been placed with families in the US and Latin America.

Among those women targeted were single mothers, those with "degenerate" political views or those from poor backgrounds. Madrigal, a railway worker and president of the Murcia branch of the SOS Stolen Babies association, had also acknowledged that the proceedings were unlikely to bring her real closure or help her find her birth mother. She said she hoped her legal action would be the first of many brought by stolen babies and their families, arguing that people like her had been torn from their parents, trafficked, and ignored for too long.

McDonald's is giving away 10,000 bottles of its iconic special sauce to promote the launch of two new sizes of the Big Mac: the Mac Jr. and the Grand Mac. This is the first time the sauce is being bottled and given away in the U.S. The giveaway is scheduled for Thursday at participating restaurants nationwide. The Mac Jr., a smaller version of the Big Mac, and the Grand Mac, a larger one, will be launched on the same day. The Mac Jr. is a smaller version of the Big Mac, while the Grand Mac features larger beef patties. McDonald's is hoping to boost sales, particularly among Millennial consumers, with this move. The company has faced a dip in sales over the last quarter, with the All-Day Breakfast program being a notable exception. In response to McDonald's announcement, a Twitter user jokingly posted a photo of Kraft's Thousand Island dressing.

In South Dakota, Dakota Layers, a large-scale egg-laying farm, has become the first in the state to be infected with the highly pathogenic H5 avian influenza virus. The virus has led to the deaths of millions of chickens and turkeys in the Midwest, primarily in Minnesota and Iowa. The farm, which accounts for nearly half of South Dakota's egg-laying chickens, had taken extensive biosecurity measures to prevent an outbreak. The state veterinarian, Dustin Oedekoven, confirmed the presence of the virus and crews began euthanizing the chickens. The farm produces over 90,000 dozens of eggs daily and ships about 70 percent of its eggs to California. Officials have stressed there is no danger to the supply and very low risk to humans.

The bird flu outbreak has also affected the supply of liquid eggs used by industrial food producers. Wholesale breaker-eggs, which are cracked and sold in liquid form for use by wholesale bakers and restaurants, have more than doubled in price in the past three weeks. This surge in prices is due to the worst-ever American outbreak of the bird flu virus, which has affected more than 33.5 million chickens, turkeys, and other birds. Iowa, the top U.S. egg producer, was hardest hit, losing 40 percent of its laying hens. The disease has prompted the government to forecast the first annual drop in egg production since 2008.

The liquid eggs are a staple in industrial food production for everything from imitation crab meat to ice cream. Higher costs will "find their way more widely downstream into large industrial users," according to David Swenson, a regional economist at Iowa State University. Governors in several states have made resources available to stem the spread of the disease, and the USDA has authorized $330 million for bird-flu assistance to farmers. Warmer weather is also expected to slow the outbreak.

The bird flu outbreak has caused shortages of liquid eggs, with some food makers turning to shell eggs sold in cartons as a substitute. The shelled substitutes are fetching higher prices than the five-year average for the month of May. The cost of breaker eggs could go up another 25 percent by the summer for some bakers, such as Joe Greco, who owns a bakery near Chicago.

In response to the outbreak, Dakota Layers has increased biosecurity measures, including washing the tires and undercarriages of all vehicles that come onto their farms. Center Fresh Group, which houses about 5.5 million hens, also increased measures to prevent more infections. The industry is working together to find ways to get through the outbreak.

The death of Freddie Gray, a 25-year-old man who died from a severe spinal injury while in police custody in Baltimore, has sparked violent protests and unrest in the city. Six Baltimore Police officers have been charged in connection to Gray's death, with charges ranging from second degree murder to assault. Award-winning musician Prince is set to play a concert in Baltimore on Sunday, May 10th at the Royal Farms Arena to promote peace following the violent protests. The concert will feature special guests and tickets will go on sale Wednesday at 5 p.m. Attendees are being asked to wear something gray.

Prince has recorded a new song in response to Gray's death and the protests, titled "Baltimore." The song addresses the unrest in Baltimore and the socio/political issues around the country in the wake of a slew of killings of young black men. An official statement from Prince's publicist describes the song as "a tribute to all of the people of the city of Baltimore."

Prince sat at his electric keyboard on the soundstage at Paisley Park to record the song, with 3rdEyeGirl joining him. The song is described as a soul/rock number, with a pre-chorus slightly reminiscent of Prince's "The Holy River." The lyrics of the song address the violence and unrest in Baltimore and call for peace and an end to the gun violence.

This is not the first time Prince has injected political or social commentary into his music. In the past, he has addressed issues such as the Cold War, police brutality, and economic inequality in his songs. The "Baltimore" concert and song are part of Prince's ongoing efforts to promote peace and address social issues through his music.

The film adaptation of Alice Sebold's bestselling novel "The Lovely Bones" directed by Peter Jackson, co-written with Fran Walsh and Philippa Boyens, was one of the most anticipated films of the year. The story follows a 14-year-old girl named Susie Salmon (Saoirse Ronan) who is savagely murdered in 1973 and watches for years from a state she calls "the blue horizon between heaven and earth" as her friends, family, and killer go on with their lives.

Jackson's best move was casting Ronan as the murdered Susie Salmon, who brings naturalness, honesty, and radiance to the part of a young woman just on the cusp of life. The film's imaginative notion of what Susie's afterlife looks like is strong, but the focus on the murderer George Harvey (Stanley Tucci) undermines the story's balance. Tucci's performance as Harvey is unsettling and toxic, and the film's decision to give him a more prominent role and show the bizarre decorations of the underground murder site in grotesque detail disturbs the story's emotional tone.

The film also features strong performances from Mark Wahlberg and Rachel Weisz as Susie's father and mother, both devastated in their own ways by their daughter's death. Susan Sarandon as Grandma Lynn is encouraged to be too over the top for anyone's good. The dreamscape look of the in-between world where Susie spends her time watching her murderer scheme, her sister Lindsey (Rose McIver) grow up, and her parents fall apart is consistently involving.

Despite its flaws, "The Lovely Bones" has moments that resonate with the book's comforting notion of a sentient afterlife. Ronan's performance as Susie is the only element of the film that is exactly as it should be. The film's erratic mixture of emotional tones, its decision to go back and forth from missing-Susie sadness to serial-killer sadism, undercuts the ability of the actors to give resonant performances. The film's tendency to push things too hard undermines its effectiveness, and it never overcomes its focus on the off-putting aspects of the story that would have prevented the book from finding the huge audience it did.

Poland's Senate has approved a controversial bill that makes it illegal to accuse the Polish nation or state of complicity in Nazi Germany's crimes, including the Holocaust. The bill sets fines or a maximum three-year jail term as punishment. President Andrzej Duda supports the bill, stating Poland's right to defend historical truth. However, the bill has outraged Israeli MPs, who view it as an attempt to rewrite history and deny the Holocaust.

The bill states that anyone who accuses the Polish nation or state of being responsible or complicit in Nazi crimes will be subject to a fine or a three-year jail term. The law includes a caveat that it does not apply to artistic or scientific activities. The bill passed with 57 votes to 23, with two abstaining.

Poland has long objected to the use of phrases like "Polish death camps," which suggest the Polish state shared responsibility for camps such as Auschwitz. The camps were built and operated by Nazi Germany after it invaded Poland in 1939. However, the more contentious point raised by the bill is whether it will outlaw references to acts of individual complicity by Poles with the Nazis. Historians say there is clear evidence for such acts.

Israeli MPs are furious about the bill, with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu describing it as an attempt to rewrite history and deny the Holocaust. Following the bill's passage, Israel's Foreign Ministry asked to postpone the visit of a senior Polish official. Pavel Solosh, the head of the Polish National Security Council, will not arrive in Israel on Sunday as planned.

In response, Israeli MPs are backing a bill that would expand Israel's existing Holocaust denial laws to include a five-year jail sentence for anyone denying or minimizing the role of Nazi collaborators, including Poles, in crimes committed during the Holocaust. The amended law would also give legal aid to any Holocaust survivor telling their story who is prosecuted in a foreign country.

The US State Department has also urged the Polish government to rethink the bill. Polish politicians have expressed bafflement at the Israeli response. The bill is supported by Poland's nationalist party, Law and Justice, which is keen to show the world how Poland was ruthlessly victimized by its German and Soviet neighbors during the war.

Historians say individual Poles denounced their Jewish neighbors to the Germans and participated in Nazi-instigated massacres, including in Jedwabne where hundreds of Jews were murdered by their neighbors. Critics say this bill may act as a muzzle on people trying to uncover the full complexity of the Holocaust.

This article discusses a unique collaboration between Bathrooms.com and U.K.-based chocolatiers Choccywoccydoodah, resulting in a chocolate-made bathroom suite called the Maderno Sweet. The set includes a bidet, sink, bathtub, and toilet, all made from Belgian chocolate, and is listed for sale on Bathroomsweets.com. The entire set contains approximately 9.4 million calories and is priced at $133,040. The chocolate bathroom is not intended for use as a functional bathroom due to the risk of melting in direct sunlight, heat, or contact with hot liquids. The suite is designed to be a novelty item, with a six-month shelf life or the ability to be preserved with a layer of varnish. The idea for the chocolate bathroom stemmed from Bathrooms.com CEO Ian Monk noticing a high number of Google searches for "bathroom sweets" instead of "bathroom suites."

Manti Te'o, a Notre Dame football star, has been embroiled in a hoax involving his non-existent girlfriend, Lennay Kekua. Te'o claimed he spent hours talking to Kekua on the phone, even falling asleep with her on the line.
