Katie Couric's show has released three voicemails from Kekua, which were allegedly left on Te'o's phone. The hoaxer, Ronaiah Tuiasosopo, admitted to disguising his voice over the phone and posing as a woman. The voicemails include one from Kekua before her first chemotherapy session, one accusing Te'o of having someone else in his room, and one left on September 11, 2012, the day Kekua claimed she was released from the hospital. Couric reviewed Te'o's phone records and found dozens of calls, some hours long, to one phone number, which Te'o claimed belonged to Kekua. The authenticity of these voicemails and the identity of the person on the other end of the phone remains unclear.

On Monday, the New England Holocaust Memorial in Boston was vandalized for the second time in two months. A 17-year-old male from Malden allegedly threw a rock through one of the glass panels, causing damage. The suspect was quickly apprehended by two bystanders and is charged with willful destruction of property. Police are investigating whether the incident was a hate crime.

The memorial, which was installed in 1995, had never been vandalized before the June incident. The glass towers, etched with numbers representing Holocaust victims, were damaged in the latest attack.

The vandalism occurred just two days after a white nationalist rally in Charlottesville, Virginia turned violent, and less than two months after a similar incident at the Boston memorial. The suspect's motive is currently under investigation.

Robert Trestan, regional director of the Anti-Defamation League, expressed concern over the vandalism, stating that it was a reminder of the need for unity against hate. He also noted that the destruction was jarring, regardless of the suspect's motive.

Mayor Martin J. Walsh of Boston expressed his disappointment, stating that Boston stands against hate. Boston Police Commissioner William Evans also condemned the senseless and shameful behavior.

The memorial reopened around 9 p.m. on the night of the incident, with at least one officer posted there throughout the night for security. The community has expressed shock and sadness over the vandalism, with many viewing it as a representation of hate and evil, rather than the city of Boston.

The International Court of Justice (ICJ) has dismissed claims of genocide by both Serbia and Croatia during the Croatian war of secession from Yugoslavia. The Croatian government had alleged that Serbia committed genocide in the town of Vukovar and elsewhere in 1991, while Serbia filed a counter-claim over the expulsion of more than 200,000 Serbs from Croatia. The war resulted in the death of approximately 20,000 people, mostly Croatians. The town of Vukovar was devastated when it was occupied by Serbs for three months in 1991, resulting in the displacement of tens of thousands of ethnic Croats and the death of about 260 Croat men. Four years later, the Croatian military's Operation Storm bombarded the majority ethnic-Serb Krajina area, forcing about 200,000 people from their homes. The ICJ's ruling was posted online, with Judge Peter Tomka dismissing both the Croatian claim and the Serbian counter-claim. The court stated that neither side had provided sufficient evidence to demonstrate the "specific intent required for acts of genocide." The ruling has been met with mixed reactions in both Croatia and Serbia, with some expressing disappointment and others hoping it will lead to a period of lasting peace and prosperity in the region. The cases were filed 16 years ago and are part of the long legal fall-out from the break-up of Yugoslavia into seven states in wars that lasted eight years and left more than 100,000 dead.

Dan Adler, a Democratic candidate in California's 36th district, is generating controversy with his unconventional campaign ads. In one ad, Adler, a Jewish entertainment executive married to a Korean woman, attempts to appeal to Asian voters, but the ad features a heavily-accented Korean immigrant woman asking "What's a mensch?" The ad has gone viral. Adler's campaign strategy appears to mimic the "Demon Sheep" ad, aiming for shock value or weirdness. Another ad features Patty Duke declaring "Dan Adler: He Gets Shit Done," and a third features Adler's son delivering a catchphrase and performing a basketball dunk that rivals NBA star Blake Griffin. The campaign's unusual approach has drawn attention, but its effectiveness in the primary race remains uncertain.

A mummified monk was discovered in Mongolia, sitting in the lotus position and wrapped in cattle skins. Senior Buddhists claim the monk is in a deep meditative trance and not dead, but is instead in a rare state of meditation called "tukdam." Forensic examinations are underway to determine the cause of the monk's preservation, with some speculating that Mongolia's cold weather may be a factor. Dr Barry Kerzin, a physician to Tibetan spiritual leader the Dalai Lama, believes the monk is in a state of tukdam, where if the meditator can remain in this state for more than three weeks, their body will gradually shrink and they can become a Buddha. The monk was stolen and was about to be sold on the black market before being arrested by Mongolian police. The monk is now being guarded at the National Centre of Forensic Expertise. The monk's identity is unclear, but there is speculation that he may be the teacher of Lama Dashi-Dorzho Itigilov, a Buryat Buddhist Lama who was also found mummified in 1927 and is now worshipped for eternity in a Buddhist temple.

President Obama was interrupted from his vacation in Hawaii on Monday due to a minor beach injury suffered by the son of one of his friends, Dr. Eric Whitaker. The incident occurred during a golf outing at the Luana Hills Country Club, causing a sudden and dramatic departure from the golf course. The White House initially kept the incident private out of respect for the Whitaker family's privacy, but later confirmed that the first family was unharmed. Obama returned to the golf course after ensuring the boy was safe and was treated and released from the hospital. The president continued his vacation, playing golf until sundown. The incident did not affect Obama's public statement regarding the attempted Christmas Day bombing of a Northwest Airlines flight and the government crackdown of protestors in Iran. The president also condemned the violent suppression of innocent Iranian citizens. Obama's vacation in Hawaii has provided opportunities for interactions with military personnel and local residents.

A scuba diver named Christopher Le Cun is filing a lawsuit against Florida Power and Light (FPL) after he was sucked into an intake pipe at the St. Lucie Nuclear Power Plant in July 2015. Le Cun was scuba diving off the coast of Hutchinson Island with a friend when they tied their boat to a buoy and dove into the water to investigate large submerged structures. They claimed there were no warnings posted, and FPL disputes this, stating that the buoy has always read "stay back 100 feet."

Le Cun was pulled into the pipe, which is 16 feet across, about a quarter-mile long, and sucks in around 500,000 gallons of water per minute. He spent four to five minutes tumbling through the darkness of the pipe, fearing for his life and thinking about his family. He eventually emerged from the pipe into a pond at the nuclear plant and was able to call his wife.

This is not the first time an incident like this has occurred. In 1989, another diver named William Lamm was also sucked into the same pipe and survived. Le Cun says he does not know if he will ever embrace scuba diving again.

FPL released a statement saying that safety is their top priority and that there is a protective cap over the intake piping. They also stated that the diver intentionally swam into one of the intake pipes after bypassing a piece of equipment to minimize the entry of objects. However, Le Cun claims that the cap is not designed to keep anyone or anything out.

Le Cun is hoping that the lawsuit will lead to safety improvements and prevent a third incident from happening.

On March 18, 2014, a significant sewer main break occurred in the Valley Creek Trunk Sewer Force Main near the intersection of Routes 252 and 23 in Tredyffrin Township, Pennsylvania. The break caused extensive flooding in the Valley Forge National Historical Park, leading to the closure of several roads. The initial estimate suggested that approximately 5 million gallons of raw sewage were spilled into the Valley Creek.

Crews worked through the night to repair the 30-inch main, shared by Tredyffrin Township, Easttown Township, East Whiteland Township, Malvern Borough, and Willistown Township. Overnight, the damaged pipe was removed, and a new one was expected to arrive on site by 7 a.m. on Wednesday.

The sewage leak did not pose a threat to humans but could be a safety concern for wildlife in the area. Officials from the Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection have not yet responded to inquiries regarding the potential impact on the surrounding area and towns downriver. Road closures are expected to last several days as construction crews repair the damaged water main and resurface affected sections of the street.

At the 2020 Golden Globes, Ricky Gervais and Mel Gibson had an awkward encounter, with Gervais making jokes about Gibson's past alcohol problems and legal issues. Gibson responded with a joke about colonoscopies, leading to one of the most unusual moments in Globes history. Gervais' monologue also included jabs at Sean Penn, Caitlyn Jenner, and the inclusion of "The Martian" as a comedy film.

This was not the first time Gervais had caused a stir at the Golden Globes. In 2010, his acerbic remarks stunned Hollywood stars, and he continued to provoke the A-list audience in 2011. In 2012, he made a homophobic joke about Jodie Foster, and in 2016, he was involved in a dispute with Madonna.

Gervais' 2010 monologue included jokes about cosmetic surgery, actors, writers, and the third world. He joked about his own penis reduction and made fun of Angelina Jolie, saying that she could be a child's "mummy" in the third world. He also made fun of writers, saying that actors were more important because of their good looks.

In summary, Ricky Gervais has a history of making controversial and offensive jokes at the Golden Globes, and his 2020 appearance was no exception. He made jokes about Mel Gibson's past issues, and the two had an awkward encounter on stage. Gervais' monologue also included jabs at other celebrities, and he continued his tradition of making acerbic remarks that stunned Hollywood stars.

The document outlines a process for selecting top-ranked pages from various domains on the web, using a specific inter-domain link graph (Wide00012). The selected pages are limited to a maximum of 100 per domain. Simultaneously, a new ISIS propaganda video has emerged, featuring two deaf-mute militants delivering a sign language message. The video calls on Muslims in Europe to join ISIS, threatens enemies, and showcases the fighters' traffic policing duties in Mosul. The video, titled "From Who Excused [sic] To Those Not Excused," implies that disability is no excuse for not participating in jihad, and ends with the militants launching rockets claimed to be aimed at Peshmerga fighters.

The document describes a web-wide crawl conducted from March 2011 to December 2011, using the new HQ software for distributed crawling by Kenji Nagahashi. The crawl captured a total of 2,713,676,341 web pages, with 2,273,840,159 unique URLs and 29,032,069 hosts. The seed list for this crawl was the Alexa top 1 million websites, and the scope was not limited except for a few manually excluded sites. However, operational issues with the software led to some embedded and linked objects not being crawled, and repeated crawls of some Argentinian government sites, which may skew results by country.

The researchers have made this data set available for public use, but access may not be granted to all requests due to potential issues. The document also mentions a separate research study on the DNA of a tammar wallaby, a kangaroo species, which identified a gene responsible for the kangaroo's hop. The researchers sequenced the tammar wallaby genome, making it the third marsupial genome to be sequenced, and hope their work may help produce future treatments for human disease.

Tim Tebow, the New York Jets backup, has canceled his scheduled appearance at the Dallas megachurch of controversial pastor Robert Jeffress. The cancellation follows mounting criticism over Jeffress's controversial views on other religions and homosexuality. Tebow's planned visit had drawn intense criticism, with critics viewing his appearance as a tacit endorsement of Jeffress's beliefs. In a statement, First Baptist Church responded to Tebow's cancellation, stating that he was pressured by the media to back out due to misrepresentations of Jeffress's past comments on homosexuality and AIDS. Jeffress has been quoted as saying that 70% of the gay population has AIDS and has described Judaism, Islam, and Mormonism as religions from the "pit of hell." Tebow, however, expressed his desire to speak at First Baptist Dallas at a future date. The church emphasized that Jeffress shares a message of hope, not hate.

Sir Elton John, in an interview with TODAY's Matt Lauer, revealed that listening to his album "Goodbye Yellow Brick Road" brought him to tears, reminding him of a time when he was innocent and the album was a huge breakthrough for him. However, the success of the album also led John into a downward spiral of drug and alcohol abuse. John has been sober for over two decades and expressed no anger but regrets his past decisions.

John also discussed his upcoming nuptials with partner David Furnish, who he has been in a civil partnership with since 2005. The pair plan to wed as early as May, now that gay marriage is legal in England. They have two children together, Zachary and Elijah.

John shared his love for music, stating that it has been with him through "sadness, through laughter, through love." He also expressed his admiration for young musicians like Lorde, who inspire him to write the best song in the world.

Furnish, in a separate interview, announced that John and he will get married in an English registry office in May, with their two kids and a few friends in attendance. Furnish also revealed that they have tattoos of their children's names on their bodies.

Furnish spoke about their civil partnership, stating that it had a huge impact on their commitment and brought a sense of happiness they didn't anticipate. Furnish also shared his struggles with coming out and the pain of being forbidden from marrying when he was younger.

Furnish believes that exposure to gay, lesbian, bisexual, and transgender people through media has helped break down barriers and increase acceptance. He also mentioned his friendship with Eric McCormack, who starred in the TV series "Will & Grace," as an example of how life can take unexpected turns.

The Associated Press reports that Republican presidential candidate Ben Carson has maintained a business relationship with a close friend, Alfonso A. Costa, who was convicted of health care fraud. Costa pleaded guilty to a felony count of health care fraud in 2008 after an FBI probe into his oral surgery practice found he had charged for procedures he never performed. Despite Carson's calls for harsh punishment for such crimes, he helped petition for leniency for Costa, who was sentenced to one year of house arrest and 100 hours of community service, and ordered to pay over $294,000 in fines and restitution. Costa has served on the board of Carson's charity, the Carson Scholars Fund, and continues to lead the charity's fundraising efforts in the Pittsburgh area. Carson and his wife have made investments through Costa that earn them between $200,000 and $2 million a year, according to financial records. Costa also continues to promote his involvement with Carson's charity as part of his real estate business. The breadth of the two men's business ties has not been previously reported, partly because details can be obscured in property and incorporation records. Costa's company and its affiliates own properties in at least five states and overseas. In 2007, a pair of corporations was established in Pennsylvania called BenCan LLC, and INBS LLC. Carson and his wife are listed as the sole members of the companies. The AP contacted Carson's campaign spokesman Doug Watts, who confirmed that the two men are best friends and that they do hold business investments together. Costa did not respond to messages seeking comment. The report contradicts the draconian criminal penalties Carson called for in his 2013 political treatise, "America the Beautiful." In his book, Carson wrote that anyone found guilty of health care fraud should face what he called the "Saudi Arabian Solution," which includes the loss of one's medical license for life, no less than 10 years in prison, and loss of all of one's personal possessions. Despite this, Carson and his wife have kept their investment with Costa in the years since his conviction. The report raises questions about Carson's stance on health care fraud and his business dealings with Costa.

A 19-year-old suspect, Erich Nowsch, has been arrested in connection with the fatal shooting of Tammy Meyers, a mother of four, following a road rage incident in Las Vegas last week. The shooting occurred outside Meyers' home on February 12th, and she passed away two days later. Nowsch faces charges of murder, attempted murder, and discharging a gun in a vehicle.

The road rage incident began earlier that night when Meyers was confronted by an angry driver during a drive home with her daughter. After getting home, Meyers and her 22-year-old armed son went out looking for the driver and followed a car they believed was involved in the earlier incident. They stopped following the car and returned home, but a silver or gray car pulled up and someone inside began shooting.

Nowsch is believed to be the only shooter, but police are searching for at least one more suspect. Robert Meyers, Tammy's husband, stated that they knew Nowsch and that he had been familiar with the suspect, having interacted with him at a local park where Tammy used to console him.

Meyers' son, Brandon, defended his actions in a vigil, stating that he acted to protect his family. Nowsch also had registered firearms, but the number and type of weapons are not specified.

The standoff at Nowsch's home occurred on Thursday afternoon, and he was taken into custody. A court hearing has been scheduled for Monday morning. The Meyers family has been criticized for their actions during the incident, but Robert Meyers expressed his frustration towards the media, stating that they had portrayed his wife and son in a negative light.

The death of Cecil the lion, a 13-year-old iconic lion living in Zimbabwe's Hwange National Park, has caused international outrage after it was allegedly killed by an American tourist, Minnesota dentist Walter James Palmer, in July. Palmer is accused of shooting Cecil with a bow and arrow, injuring him, and then tracking him down and killing him with a gun. Cecil was then beheaded and skinned.

Zimbabwean authorities have charged two Zimbabwean men, professional hunter Theo Bronchorst and land owner Honest Trymore Ndlovu, with poaching offenses and not having the required hunting permit. They appeared in court on Wednesday and were granted bail of $1,000 each. Palmer could also face charges, as authorities are investigating whether he killed Cecil without a permit.

Palmer has said that he deeply regrets the killing of Cecil and that he believed he was on a legal hunt, as he had relied on professional guides to find a lion and obtain the necessary permits. He added that he hasn't been contacted by American or Zimbabwean officials but will assist them in any inquiries they may have.

The death of Cecil has sparked a wave of international outrage, with angry commenters inundating Palmer's dental practice's Yelp and Google Review pages and vilifying him across social media. Local police are now monitoring Palmer's office, and protesters have placed a small pile of stuffed animal toys at the dental practice's front door.

According to conservationists in Zimbabwe, Palmer and the two Zimbabwean men allegedly lured Cecil out of the national park using a dead animal tied to a vehicle. The lion's death on private land outside the park's boundary was condemned by the Zimbabwe Professional Hunters and Guides Association.

Cecil was one of Africa's most famous lions and was part of a study by Oxford University. The lion's death has set off a debate about the big business of big game trophy hunting and the role of professional hunters and land owners in such cases.

A 37-year-old caretaker was mauled to death by a Bengal tiger at Terra Natura zoo in Benidorm, Spain. The incident occurred at around 5pm while the victim was cleaning the tiger's enclosure. The tiger was anaesthetized to allow recovery of the victim's body. The park was open at the time, but the attack was not witnessed by visitors as the cage was away from the main area. An investigation is underway, and it is believed the woman came into direct contact with the tiger during her cleaning tasks. The zoo staff are deeply affected by the tragedy, and this is the latest in a series of incidents involving the death of zoo employees by big cats. The Terra Natura zoo promotes itself as a "new generation immersion park" with more than 1,500 animals of 200 different species.

In a tragic accident on the Bronx River Parkway, seven family members, including three generations, were killed when their SUV plunged off the highway and into a wooded area near the Bronx Zoo. The driver, Maria Gonzalez, was believed to have been speeding and lost control, causing the vehicle to skid across three lanes of traffic, hit a concrete curb, and go airborne over a 4-foot-tall fence before landing six stories below in an unoccupied part of the zoo. The medical examiner's office ruled the deaths accidental, and autopsies showed that all seven died from blunt force trauma. The crash site has been called the "Bermuda Triangle" of the Bronx River Parkway by a lawyer who previously sued the city and state over a similar accident near the same location in 2006. The lawyer, Eric Buckvar, claimed that traffic tends to slow suddenly there, and that officials have considered adding a new lane, but did not due to plans to replace the viaduct. Buckvar also stated that after settlements in the 2006 case, the city replaced the troublesome median barrier, but it hasn't stopped the accidents. The accident came as the victims drove to a family party with grandparents visiting from the Dominican Republic. The family has opened a bank account and is asking for donations to cover the cost of the funerals. The crash was the second in the past year in which a vehicle fell off the same stretch of road. The investigation is ongoing.

Thousands of tins of Heinz baked beans with sausages were stolen from a parked lorry on the A441 in Cookhill, near Redditch, Worcestershire. The theft occurred between 8.45pm on Monday and 5.30am on Tuesday, with the driver asleep in the cab. The thieves cut a large hole in the white Scania vehicle and made off with 6,400 tins. Police are appealing for information, particularly about anyone trying to sell large quantities of Heinz baked beans in suspicious circumstances.

Nine-year-old Kieran Sorkin, born with a rare condition called microtia that left him without fully formed ears, underwent a groundbreaking procedure at Great Ormond Street Hospital in London. In a six-hour operation, surgeons led by Neil Bulstrode harvested cartilage from both sides of Kieran's chest and crafted it into frameworks for his ears. The ears were then grafted onto Kieran's head under pockets of skin and shaped using a vacuum.

Kieran, who has been using a hearing aid since birth, can hear but is still about 90% deaf without it. His parents, David and Louise, expressed their joy over the procedure, stating that it would significantly boost his confidence and improve his quality of life. Kieran, who has struggled with bullying due to his appearance, expressed his excitement about looking like his friends and being able to wear sunglasses and earphones.

The surgery was primarily cosmetic, but it brings psychological benefits, as it can significantly improve a patient's confidence and alter their trajectory in life. Advances in tissue engineering may make this kind of reconstructive surgery less invasive in the future, as scientists are creating stem cells from patients' fat tissue and inducing them to make cartilage or bone.

Three days after the surgery, Kieran was delighted with his new ears, expressing his excitement with a "wow" and a giggle. He will need a follow-up operation in six months to make his ears stand out more from his scalp. The surgery was a success, and Kieran's new ears should last because they are cartilage and not prosthetics.

The Nina, a historic racing sailboat built in 1928, has gone missing with seven people on board, including six Americans and one British national. The vessel, equipped with modern tracking and communication devices, dropped out of contact a week after leaving port in the Bay of Islands, New Zealand, on May 29, bound for Newcastle, Australia.

The last known communication was on June 4, when a meteorologist received a satellite phone call from the boat, with a woman inquiring about the weather conditions. The boat's emergency locator beacon has not been activated, and attempts to contact the crew by radio and an aerial search have been unsuccessful.

The skipper of the 70-foot (21-meter) vessel is American David Dyche, accompanied by two other American men, three American women aged between 17 and 73, and a British man aged 35. Messages posted online by friends suggest the boat originally left from Panama City, Florida.

Authorities are considering several scenarios, including the boat losing communications, drifting off course, or the crew taking to lifeboats. They are also investigating the possibility of a catastrophic failure that led to the sinking of the boat before anyone could react.

Rescue efforts have been ongoing, with an Air Force plane searching the area where the boat went missing, but no signs of life have been found. The crew had hoped to arrive in Australia mid-June, but given the conditions, a realistic arrival date was estimated to be around June 25. The Nina is a well-maintained vessel with a new engine installed recently, which reportedly caused some initial leaking problems.

The disappearance of the Nina and its crew has raised concerns, and authorities are urgently searching for any signs of their whereabouts.

On June 26, actor Terry Crews testified before the Senate Judiciary Committee about his experience with sexual assault, advocating for the Sexual Assault Survivors' Bill of Rights. However, his testimony was met with mockery from rapper 50 Cent, who posted memes on Instagram making light of Crews' assault. The memes, which were since deleted, included a split meme with Crews flexing and holding a rose, with the top saying "I got raped ... My wife just watched," and the bottom saying "Gym time." The post received over 125,000 likes and a crying-laugh emoji from Russell Simmons, who has been accused of raping several women.

The backlash against 50 Cent was swift, with many on social media calling his behavior "disgusting" and "alarming." One user wrote, "The reaction to Terry Crews and people laughing along with 50 Cent is alarming, this includes people like @UncleRush. There are countless Black Men and Boys who have been violated sexually who don't tell you their stories because of reactions like these. Likely people you know."

Crews himself took the high road when asked about 50 Cent's comments by TMZ, saying, "I prove that size doesn’t matter when it comes to sexual assault." He also revealed that he declined a role in "Expendables 4" after being pressured by the film's producer to drop a sexual assault lawsuit against his former agency.

This incident highlights the ongoing problem of toxic masculinity and the need for greater empathy and understanding when it comes to sexual assault. It also underscores the importance of the Sexual Assault Survivors' Bill of Rights, which aims to remove the burden of sexual assault from victims and provide them with access to proper counseling services, among other things. The bill was originally signed into law in 2016 under President Obama and is currently being implemented in all 50 states.

The Tubbs Fire, which started in California's North Coast region on October 8, 2017, was one of the most destructive wildfires in the state's history. The fire, named after its origin near Tubbs Lane, quickly spread at a pace of about 3 mph, burning up an acre a minute and spewing burning embers a half-mile or more ahead. The firestorm forced entire neighborhoods to flee in the middle of the night, causing widespread destruction and killing at least 40 people in four counties.

The fire's speed and intensity were attributed to powerful winds, which fueled an unprecedented number of wildfires across the region. The Tubbs Fire made a horrific 12-mile run from Calistoga, in the northern edge of the Napa Valley, into a dense city neighborhood in west Santa Rosa. It raced through ranches and rural communities, sweeping through million-dollar homes in Santa Rosa’s hillside Fountaingrove development and tract neighborhoods in Larkfield-Wikiup. At 2 a.m., the ferocity of the firestorm propelled it across Highway 101, an unprecedented leap that spread flames into a commercial district on Cleveland Avenue and hundreds of tightly packed homes in Coffey Park.

Fire scientists said the Tubbs Fire unleashed a series of fiery tornadoes powerful enough to flip cars, yank trees out of the ground, and rip homes apart. Gusts of up to 73 mph were recorded, but the extraordinary damage documented during postmortem evaluations indicated that much more powerful forces were at play. The homes destroyed in the city’s Fountaingrove and Coffey Park neighborhoods burned in rapid succession. As flames driven by powerful winds slammed into the neighborhoods, the heat rose up, pulling the wind with it and creating a kind of vortex of air that circled around at hurricane-force speeds.

The whirling winds blew fire sideways into homes in Santa Rosa, peeled off roofs, and even lifted and turned vehicles. Survivors recounted running out of their homes into the equivalent of a blast furnace, with embers flying everywhere amid a terrible gale. The Tubbs Fire was the worst fire that Scott Upton, the northern region chief for the California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection, had ever seen in his 30-year career.

The battle to contain the fires covering more than 178,000 acres across the region continues still. Authorities have not yet determined the cause of the fire. The Tubbs Fire is just one example of the destructive power of wildfires, which can be made even more dangerous by the formation of fire tornadoes or fire devils. These fiery vortices can whirl up during a wildfire due to the heat and wind conditions during those events and can carry fire and ash high into the air, causing widespread destruction and posing a significant hazard to human life.

In a significant development, North Korean leader Kim Jong Un has agreed to allow international experts to monitor the dismantling of a key missile test site and launch pad, and to permanently close the site if reciprocal measures are taken by the United States. This agreement was made during a summit with South Korean President Moon Jae-in in Pyongyang. The two leaders also agreed to connect two rail lines across the heavily militarized border, and Kim pledged to visit Seoul in the near future, a move that would make him the first North Korean leader to visit the South's capital.

The leaders of the two Koreas also agreed that the Korean Peninsula should turn into a "land of peace without nuclear weapons and nuclear threats." The agreement signed in Pyongyang is expected to open a higher level for the improvement in relations between the two Koreas.

In addition, North Korea will shut down the Dongchang-ri missile engine testing facility and missile launch pad, and may close its main Yongbyon nuclear complex if the United States takes unspecified reciprocal measures. However, it is unlikely that Washington would agree to give up any part of its own nuclear arsenal.

The United States has expressed readiness to resume talks with North Korea following these developments. U.S. Secretary of State Mike Pompeo has invited North Korea's foreign minister to meet in New York next week, with the aim of completing North Korea's denuclearization by January 2021.

China, North Korea's most important economic backer and diplomatic ally, has warmly welcomed the agreement reached in Pyongyang and strongly supported it.

However, some U.S. officials have expressed skepticism about the agreement, fearing that Kim is trying to drive a wedge between Washington and Seoul. They believe that Kim is trying to ease the economic pressure on him to curb his nuclear programs and to undercut the rationale for U.S. troops being based in South Korea by improving relations with Seoul.

The agreement signed in Pyongyang is a significant step towards peace on the Korean Peninsula, but it remains to be seen whether North Korea will take concrete steps towards denuclearization and whether the United States will be able to negotiate a deal that is acceptable to both sides.

Bon Jovi, an American rock band, was set to perform in Beijing, Shanghai, and Macau for the first time in mainland China. However, the concerts in Beijing and Shanghai were abruptly cancelled due to unforeseen reasons, with the promoter AEG Live Asia citing permit issues. It is believed that the cancellation stemmed from a 2009 music video featuring imagery from the Tiananmen Square protests in 1989 and a 2011 video showing Bon Jovi performing in front of images of the Dalai Lama. The band's management was unable to provide comment, and there were no official statements regarding refunds for ticket holders.

This incident follows a series of political controversies involving Western acts in China. In July, Maroon 5 cancelled shows planned in Beijing and Shanghai due to permit issues, and many speculated that it was due to Jesse Carmichael, the band's keyboard player, attending the Dalai Lama's birthday party in California and tweeting about it. China regards the Tibetan spiritual leader as a separatist due to his calls for autonomy for the Himalayan region.

American singer-songwriter Taylor Swift also faced scrutiny after planning to sell merchandise featuring her initials and the name of her album, "1989," direct to fans in China. The events might be seen as a reference to the Tiananmen Square pro-democracy protests of 1989, where hundreds, if not thousands, of civilians were killed when the Chinese army moved in to clear the square.

Western performers in China have sparked political controversies before, with Icelandic singer Bjork being criticized by the Ministry of Culture after she chanted pro-Tibet slogans at a concert in Shanghai in 2008. A number of musical acts, including American singer Bob Dylan and British band Oasis, subsequently had to cancel tours due to their perceived political leanings.

This year has seen an unusually high number of events cancelled at the last minute, causing concern among those involved in organizing the events. Chinese music fans have expressed disappointment and frustration at the cancellations, with one fan commenting, "Better go abroad if you want to go to concerts. It's too risky in China."

The 2017 Oscar nominations were announced on Tuesday, with La La Land and diversity being major winners. However, there were several notable snubs and surprises in the nominations.

Silence, directed by Martin Scorsese, was a surprising omission despite its prodigious 12 Oscar nods and one win to date. The religious epic only managed to secure a nomination for best cinematography.

Amy Adams, a five-time Oscar nominee, was also overlooked for her understated performance in Arrival, despite the sci-fi drama receiving eight nominations including best picture.

Finding Dory, which earned more than $1 billion at the global box office, couldn't swim to a nomination for best animated feature.

Denzel Washington, who earned his seventh acting Oscar nod for his acclaimed performance in Fences, was edged out of best director by Mel Gibson (Hacksaw Ridge) and Denis Villeneuve (Arrival).

Annette Bening, a four-time Oscar nominee and member of the Academy's Board of Governors, missed out on Nomination No. 5, with a crowded field of other well-respected actresses including Meryl Streep (Florence Foster Jenkins) and French icon Isabelle Huppert (Elle) being favored.

Deadpool, for a second there, looked like it might score a nomination for best picture, but even with the boost of Ryan Reynolds' delightfully unconventional awards campaign, the R-rated superhero couldn't go the distance.

Aaron Taylor-Johnson, who won best supporting actor at the Golden Globes, was passed over for his creepy Nocturnal Animals turn in favor of his wry co-star, Michael Shannon. Tom Ford's stylish second feature was otherwise missing from the nominations.

Taraji P. Henson, who starred in Hidden Figures, failed to score a nomination for her portrayal of Katherine Johnson, the African-American mathematician who helped send the first American astronauts into space. Despite Hidden Figures receiving four nominations including best picture and best supporting actress (Octavia Spencer), the Empire star couldn't manage a best-actress nod for her powerful turn as Johnson.

Sully, Clint Eastwood's workmanlike take on the Miracle on the Hudson, was also overlooked in major categories, despite its stellar box office and likable star in Tom Hanks.

Overall, the Oscars certainly kept viewers on their toes with several notable snubs and surprises in this year's nominations.

In response to the bullying of Robin Williams' daughter on Twitter, the social media platform has vowed to improve and expand its policies. The incident involved several users sending abusive messages, including blaming Zelda Williams for her father's suicide and sending altered images of him. Twitter has since suspended several accounts and announced plans to update its policies, focusing on self-harm, private information, and improving support for deceased users' families.

However, the issue of abuse on Twitter is not isolated to this incident. Imani Gandy, a senior legal analyst, has detailed her daily experience of racial, gender, and medical condition-based abuse on the platform. Despite blocking and reporting abusive accounts, she continues to face harassment, with Twitter's current tools proving ineffective against persistent attackers who create new accounts.

Soraya Chemaly, a media critic and feminist activist, has expressed concern that Twitter's commitment to free expression may be hindering its ability to address this issue effectively. She suggests that Twitter could learn from third-party software like "Block Together," which automates the blocking of new accounts sending direct messages.

The incident involving Robin Williams' daughter has brought renewed attention to the problem of abuse on Twitter. Many believe that more needs to be done to protect users, particularly those who are most vulnerable to harassment. Twitter's response to this issue will be closely watched in the coming days.

On September 2, 2010, an oil platform exploded and caught fire approximately 200 miles west of the site of the BP spill in the Gulf of Mexico. The incident occurred about 100 miles south of Louisiana's Vermilion Bay, in waters 340 feet deep. All 13 crew members were rescued and were reported to be uninjured, with some huddling together in insulated survival suits known as "Gumby suits." The Coast Guard initially reported an oil sheen a mile long and 100 feet wide, but later stated that crews were unable to find any spill. The company that owns the platform, Mariner Energy, is investigating the cause of the explosion. The platform was producing 58,800 gallons of oil and 900,000 cubic feet of gas per day, and can store 4,200 gallons of oil. The platform is considered less stable than the Deepwater Horizon rig, which exploded in April 2010 and caused a three-month leak that totaled 206 million gallons of oil. The Coast Guard is continuing to monitor the situation.

Seth Meyers, the host of Late Night with Seth Meyers, welcomed his second child, a son named Axel Strahl, on April 8th in an unexpected and dramatic fashion. The baby was born in the lobby of Meyers' apartment building, with the New York Police Department assisting in the delivery and cutting the cord. Meyers' neighbors helped keep the newborn warm until more help arrived. The proud father shared the heartwarming story on his show the following day, expressing gratitude to the NYPD and his neighbors. Axel's middle name honors Meyers' wife's grandparents, who met in a hospital in Austria after being liberated from a concentration camp. Meyers' first child, Ashe Olson, was born in March 2016. The couple announced their second pregnancy on the show in November 2017. Social media users congratulated the couple on their new addition and praised Meyers for his emotional storytelling.

The Trump administration has announced that there are no future plans to halt joint U.S.-South Korea military exercises, contrary to the suspension of exercises announced in June. The decision comes amid a stalemate in diplomatic efforts with North Korea over its nuclear weapons. Defense Secretary Jim Mattis said that the U.S. has no plans to suspend any more exercises, but left open the possibility that future exercises could be halted if it would enable negotiations. The U.S. has about 28,500 troops in South Korea. The resumption of regular U.S.-South Korea military exercises may be a sign that the Trump administration is growing impatient about having made concessions to North Korea without tangible steps on denuclearization. The decision to resume military exercises comes after President Trump's decision to halt the "very expensive" annual military exercises with South Korea following his June 12 meeting with Kim Jong Un. The next military exercise, Foal Eagle, had been set for next spring, but its status is uncertain. The U.S. and North Korea have made little progress since the June summit, with North Korea giving no indication it is willing to give up its nuclear weapons unilaterally as the Trump administration has demanded. The U.S. has implemented three rounds of sanctions against North Korea in August, and additional sanctions are likely. The U.S. has yet to cite any progress from North Korea on efforts to denuclearize.

The article discusses numerous allegations of sexual misconduct against Harvey Weinstein, a prominent Hollywood producer, by over 50 women, including well-known actresses such as Asia Argento, Lysette Anthony, and Gwyneth Paltrow. The allegations range from rape to sexual harassment and date back to the 1980s. Some of the women have reported the allegations to the police, and Weinstein has been charged with rape and sexual misconduct. The article also discusses the #MeToo movement, which was started by Alyssa Milano, and encourages women to share their stories of sexual harassment and assault using the hashtag. The article highlights the prevalence of sexual harassment and assault in the entertainment industry and calls for change.

In a Senate hearing, Senator Elizabeth Warren called for the resignation and criminal investigation of Wells Fargo CEO John Stumpf over a cross-selling scandal that has engulfed the bank. Warren accused Stumpf of "gutless leadership" and "cheating customers" to drive up the bank's stock price and enrich himself. She also criticized the bank's culture, stating that if a teller took money from the cash drawer, they would face criminal charges, but Stumpf squeezed employees to cheat customers.

Wells Fargo, the second-largest bank in the US, has been accused of illegal cross-selling to millions of customers without their knowledge. The bank has paid $185 million in penalties for acts dating back to at least 2011, and fired over 5,300 employees found to have created false accounts.

Warren's comments came amidst testy questioning of Stumpf, who has been accused of failing to hold himself or any other senior executives accountable for the company's actions. Other senators also pressed Stumpf on whether the bank regards the case as one of fraud, whether it will "claw back" any of the millions paid to former executive Carrie Tolstedt, and how it will help customers whose credit ratings have been hurt by the fake accounts.

Donald Trump is expected to announce that he plans to recognize Jerusalem as Israel’s capital on Wednesday. The decision is a compromise, as Trump had previously pledged to move the US embassy to Jerusalem, which would have set off an international firestorm. The administration has insisted that it still plans to move the embassy to Jerusalem, but Trump will sign another six-month waiver, meaning that no change is imminent. The decision has been met with predictable criticism, with Pope Francis calling on the US to respect the status quo in Jerusalem. Violent protests are expected in response.

The decision comes amidst a broader shift in Middle East politics, with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman presenting a peace plan to the Palestinian Authority that would be more tilted toward the Israelis than any ever embraced by the American government. The Palestinians would get a state of their own but only noncontiguous parts of the West Bank and only limited sovereignty over their own territory. The vast majority of Israeli settlements in the West Bank, which most of the world considers illegal, would remain. The Palestinians would not be given East Jerusalem as their capital and there would be no right of return for Palestinian refugees and their descendants. The Saudis have denied the contents of the report. With both Saudi Arabia and the US growing closer to Israel, it’s becoming increasingly doubtful that Trump will uphold his previous pledge to be a fair broker in negotiations between the Israelis and Palestinians.

Meghan Markle and Prince Harry have revealed details about their upcoming wedding, set for May 19. Meghan's parents, Doria Ragland and Thomas Markle, will attend and spend time with the British royal family, including Queen Elizabeth II and the Duke of Edinburgh, before the wedding. Meghan's mother will accompany her to Windsor Castle, while her father will walk her down the aisle. The couple plans to honor the memory of Princess Diana, Harry's mother, during the ceremony. Meghan will not have a maid of honor, but Prince William will serve as best man. All bridesmaids and page boys will be children, and the style and designer of Meghan's wedding gown will remain a secret until the moment she arrives at the chapel. The couple will spend their first night as a married couple in Windsor Castle, and Prince Philip's health will be closely monitored for the wedding. The Order of Service will be published on the palace's website, and the couple will not leave for their honeymoon immediately after the wedding. Alexi Lubomirski, who took their engagement photos, will photograph the wedding.

The Washington Navy Yard shooting, which resulted in the death of 12 Navy personnel, has led to recommendations for improved security reviews within the Navy. The Secretary of the Navy, Ray Mabus, has suggested that future reviews should include any available police reports, even if they did not result in charges or convictions. This recommendation was made following a detailed review of the military career of Aaron Alexis, the gunman, who had an honorable discharge, a Secret-level clearance, and a history of firearm incidents in his law enforcement files.

In 2004, Alexis was involved in an incident where he brandished a .45-caliber pistol and fired at the tires of a construction worker's car. In another incident in September 2010, commanders halted efforts to force Alexis out of the Navy due to a lack of cooperation from the police. This incident was not entered into his military file.

The Navy's review also revealed that Alexis obtained a secret-level security clearance despite a 2004 arrest involving a firearm, which was not mentioned in the federal personnel report. The Office of Personnel Management knew about the arrest due to a fingerprint check when Alexis joined the Navy Reserve in 2007, but Alexis did not disclose the offense on his security questionnaire.

Alexis' violent tendencies and apparent mental illness were missed opportunities for intervention by both the Navy and his civilian employer, a military contractor. Alexis had complained about hearing voices and being bombarded by microwaves, and because of his job, which required a security clearance, he had a valid ID card that allowed him entry to the Navy Yard.

The Navy cleared Alexis based on the information available at the time, but the events suggest different activity when viewed in retrospect. The Navy is now recommending that all personnel office investigative reports include "any available police documents related to the subject being investigated for clearance eligibility." This recommendation has been sent to Defense Secretary Chuck Hagel.

Alexis' security clearance form did not mention any felony charges, arrests by law enforcement, or incidents from his 2004 arrest. Alexis said he did not disclose this information because the charge was dismissed and he was told by his attorney that it would be removed from his record.

The Navy's review also revealed several other incidents involving Alexis, including an arrest in DeKalb County, Ga., in September 2008, and another in Fort Worth in September 2010, where he was arrested for discharging a firearm in his home after an altercation with a neighbor. No charges were filed in either case. Alexis left the Navy three months later with an honorable discharge.

A group of predominantly white militiamen, led by Ammon and Ryan Bundy, occupied the Malheur National Wildlife Refuge headquarters in Oregon over the holiday weekend, leading to a tense standoff with law enforcement. The militia is demanding that the federal government give up publicly managed land to local ranchers, loggers, and miners. The media's response to the armed takeover has been criticized for being timid, with many on social media arguing that the coverage would have been more alarmed if the protesters were black or Muslim.

The media's reaction to Black Lives Matter demonstrators over the past few years has been significantly different, with protests being characterized as wholly violent and leading to a wave of crime and violence. In contrast, the Oregon militia members have been characterized as armed protesters, and the media has generally shied away from using language about the threat of violence.

The discrepancies in coverage have sparked accusations of skewed reporting, with some arguing that the media seems to be quick to treat minority groups as violent, while giving a predominantly white group a pass. The underlying issue is implicit bias, or subconscious prejudices that can change how we approach and treat people of a different race, ethnicity, and religious affiliation.

Research has shown that these biases are real and can contribute to greater use of force by police. Media outlets and pundits should be aware of these biases and strive to report objectively, recognizing that their own biases could be coloring how they approach stories.

The Oregon standoff is ongoing, with the militia showing no signs of leaving the refuge anytime soon. The federal government has not yet made any moves to remove the militia, and tensions remain high in the area. The standoff has brought attention to the issue of public land ownership and the ongoing conflict between the federal government and rural communities over the management of those lands.

The Florida gun shop, Florida Gun Supply, has been sued by the Council on American-Islamic Relations (CAIR) for declaring the store a "Muslim-free zone." The lawsuit, filed in the U.S. District Court in Fort Lauderdale, alleges that the store's policy violates federal law and seeks an injunction to stop the discrimination.

CAIR Florida's Chief Executive Director, Hassan Shibly, stated that American Muslims have the right to browse and purchase guns, take classes on gun safety, and shoot guns at a range without being profiled or discriminated against. He added that such discrimination is not only illegal but also harmful to the country.

The store's owner, Andy Hallinan, made the announcement on a controversial Facebook video earlier this month, citing the shooting of four Marines and a Navy sailor in Chattanooga, Tennessee, as the reason for the policy. He argued that he had a moral and legal responsibility to ensure the safety of his community and would not arm or train those who wish to harm his fellow patriots.

Hallinan's attorney, Robert Muise, called the lawsuit "completely frivolous" and said it contained no factual allegations. He also threatened to seek sanctions against CAIR for filing a frivolous lawsuit. Muise argued that Hallinan has an obligation to not train or equip terrorists and refused to do so.

CAIR says the store's policy violates federal law and has gone above and beyond to amicably reach a resolution outside of court with Florida Gun Supply regarding its discriminatory policies. The group wants to make it clear that religious discrimination is still illegal in the United States and that American Muslims are entitled to their rights just like every other American.

Hallinan later rescinded an invitation to meet and train Hassan Shibly, CAIR-FL's executive director, after receiving a flood of emails and calls warning him about CAIR's inclusion on the United Arab Emirates' list of designated terrorist groups. Shibly is not named as a plaintiff in the lawsuit, and he stressed that the lawsuit is about countering what he said was an "illegal" policy by the store to discriminate against Muslims.

The lawsuit comes after federal agents advised Hallinan to shut down his shop due to concerns about the intentions of a Muslim convert who had traveled from California to attend a class at Florida Gun Supply scheduled for that day. It is unclear how agents learned about the convert's plan.

The study published in JAMA Internal Medicine suggests that proton pump inhibitors (PPIs), commonly used drugs to reduce stomach acid, may be associated with an increased risk of chronic kidney disease. The study, which was conducted using data from the Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities (ARIC) study and the Geisinger Health System in Pennsylvania, found that PPI users had a higher risk of incident chronic kidney disease (CKD) in both groups. The results were replicated at Geisinger.

The study authors note that PPIs are one of the most commonly prescribed medications in the United States, and an estimated 25 percent to 70 percent of these prescriptions may have no appropriate indication for use. Other observational studies have linked PPIs to serious adverse health outcomes, but no population-based studies, to their knowledge, have looked at the association between PPI use and the risk of chronic kidney disease (CKD).

The study findings suggest that up to 70 percent of PPI prescriptions may be unnecessary, and that 25 percent of long-term PPI users could discontinue therapy without developing symptoms. The authors note several study limitations, including that participants who are prescribed PPIs may be at higher risk of CKD for reasons unrelated to their PPI use.

The study concludes that more research is needed to determine whether PPI use causes kidney damage, and that the widespread use of PPIs could have a considerable public health effect given the widespread extent of use. More than 15 million Americans used prescription PPIs in 2013, costing more than $10 billion.

A related editorial summarizing recent data on the adverse effects of PPI use was also published in JAMA Internal Medicine. The editorial notes that a large number of patients are taking PPIs for no clear reason, often for remote symptoms of dyspepsia or "heartburn" that have since resolved. The editorial concludes that PPIs should be stopped to determine if symptomatic treatment is needed.

In a separate study, researchers found that PPIs might increase the risk for dementia. The study, published in JAMA Neurology, found that people 75 or older who regularly take PPIs had a 44 percent increased risk of dementia, compared with seniors not using the drugs. The study only found an association, however, and not a cause-and-effect link. The study authors note that more research is needed to confirm the findings and to determine the mechanism by which PPIs might increase the risk for dementia.

The study findings are surprising, as earlier studies have linked another type of antacid, H2 blockers, with an increased risk of dementia. Up to now, experts have recommended that patients use PPIs to treat acid reflux and steer clear of H2 blockers like Tagamet, Pepcid, and Zantac. The new findings suggest that patients may want to discuss the potential risks and benefits of PPI use with their doctors.

The Washington Post reported that the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) has concluded that Russia intervened in the 2016 U.S. election to help Donald Trump win. This bombshell report comes after Trump's victory in one of the slimmest margins in U.S. history. The report also includes the revelation that Republican Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell played a key role in keeping the explosive information under wraps during the election.

According to the Post, McConnell voiced doubts about U.S. intelligence and threatened to publicly accuse the Obama administration of partisan politics if the White House challenged the Russians publicly. After the election, Trump chose McConnell's wife Elaine Chao to be secretary of transportation, a position that requires approval by Congress, and McConnell has rejected calls to recuse himself from the confirmation process.

The New York Times reported that intelligence agencies have "high confidence" that Russians hacked the Republican National Committee but "conspicuously released no documents" related to Republicans. This raises the question of whether Russia is holding onto these materials to use as leverage, perhaps over the Trump administration.

Julian Assange of Wikileaks, which published the hacked Clinton emails, has denied that it received the materials from the Russian government. Russia also has denied the allegations. The latest news has set off a firestorm, with Evan McMullin, a former CIA agent and Republican presidential candidate, tweeting that Republican leaders knew Russia was undermining the democracy during the election and chose to ignore it.

Trump's team issued a statement attacking the CIA's credibility, comparing it to the false claims about weapons of mass destruction in Iraq. Trump has been using Twitter to issue statements and go after critics, often going off on unrelated tweet storms after major news stories break about him. For example, after Trump agreed to pay $25 million to settle a Trump University fraud lawsuit, Trump tweeted attacks on the cast of the Broadway show, Hamilton.

Trump has said he'll have a press conference on December 15th, his first since July 27th. At the last conference, he told reporters that he hoped Russian intelligence agencies had hacked Hillary Clinton's emails and would publish whatever they found. "Russia, if you’re listening, I hope you’re able to find the 30,000 emails that are missing," Mr. Trump said. "I think you will probably be rewarded mightily by our press."

This report is a nuclear bombshell, with the potential for a foreign government to have determined the outcome of a presidential election. The Obama administration and the CIA should put this information out publicly, and if the evidence is persuasive, it will be a genuine crisis. The guy who got 2.8 million fewer votes to begin with may have made it over the finish line with a push from Vladimir Putin. Democrats should demand the release of the information, demand a real investigation, pin McConnell's ears to the wall, discredit him as much as possible, and agitate from the outside. The media needs to get the message that conservatives aren't the only people who get pissed off. In a word: Fight. Like hell.

President Obama addressed a growing scandal involving 11 U.S. Secret Service agents who were sent home from Cartagena, Colombia, for alleged involvement in a prostitution scandal. The agents were providing protection for Obama during the Summit of the Americas. Obama emphasized the importance of thorough and rigorous investigation, stating that if the allegations are true, he will be angry as the agents are representing the U.S.

The controversy has shifted attention away from Obama's trip to the economic summit, with the media focusing on the accusations of heavy drinking and womanizing. The Secret Service placed the agents on administrative leave pending an internal investigation. The agents were returned to Washington and interviewed by the Office of Professional Responsibility, the agency's internal affairs unit.

Meanwhile, the Defense Department has ordered its own inquiry after determining that five of its personnel, who were staying at the same hotel as the Secret Service agents, violated curfew on Wednesday night. All of the U.S. personnel were part of Obama's advance team that was preparing logistics and security for his arrival.

The alleged misconduct came to light after one of the agents became involved in a dispute with a woman over a payment, and Colombian police reported the matter to the U.S. Embassy. The controversy has raised concerns about the systems in place to prevent such incidents in the future, with lawmakers in Washington pressing for more details about the investigation.

The incident has also caused embarrassment for Colombia, a country that had hoped to showcase its modern face during the Summit of the Americas. Colombians expressed disappointment that the global media coverage focused on the scandal rather than the country's achievements. The incident unfolded just as the heads of state began discussing weighty issues such as trade protectionism, Cuba, and the war on drugs.

Donald Trump, the Republican Party's presidential nominee, is scheduled to receive his first classified briefing tomorrow at the FBI's New York Field Office. He will be accompanied by New Jersey Gov. Chris Christie and retired Lt. Gen. Michael Flynn, a former Defense Intelligence Agency director. The career staffers from the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (DNI) will lead the briefing, which is expected to cover major threats and emerging concerns around the world. Trump's session comes two days after he laid out a series of foreign policy proposals, including plans for subjecting immigrants to "extreme vetting" and temporarily blocking immigration from "the most dangerous and volatile regions of the world."

The decision to take Christie and Flynn with him could stoke speculation that Trump is considering them for positions in his Cabinet. Both spoke in support of Trump at the Republican National Convention in Cleveland last month. As for Trump, many of his critics, including top Democratic senators, have questioned whether he is fit to receive classified information, citing controversial statements he has made on the campaign trail.

The FBI will have no role in the briefing beyond playing host. The decision to brief the presidential candidates is a long-standing tradition in the U.S., dating back more than 60 years. Each of the campaigns decides the location for the classified briefings. Both Trump and Democratic nominee Hillary Clinton are expected to receive two or three classified briefings before Election Day. These briefings resemble the annual Worldwide Threat Assessment issued by the intelligence community, which releases an unclassified version each year. While some top-secret information could be discussed, the briefings will not include the nation's most sensitive secrets, particularly information on sources, methods, and operations.

Senior officials in both parties have sought to turn this year's closed-door briefings into a campaign issue. After the FBI director said this month that Clinton had been extremely careless but had broken no laws by using a private email server while secretary of State, House Speaker Paul Ryan (R-Wisc.) urged Clapper to deny classified material to her. Giving the Democratic nominee access, he wrote in a letter, would “send the wrong signal to all those charged with safeguarding our nations’ secrets." Clinton is scheduled to accept her party's nomination tonight at the Democratic National Convention in Philadelphia.

On Friday, October 24, 2014, Josephine Crook, a 49-year-old woman, was arrested in Alhambra for allegedly stealing ladies' undergarments from a Kohl's department store. According to the Alhambra Police Department, Crook was accused of concealing the items in an empty purse and failing to pay for them. She was taken into custody around 7:15 p.m. and booked at the Alhambra Police Department. Crook's bail was set at $20,000, and she is scheduled to make her first court appearance on Wednesday at the Alhambra Municipal Court. Additionally, it was reported that Crook was suspected of possessing burglary tools, including wire cutters and scissors. No further details were immediately available.

In Lincolnshire, over 1,000 meters of overhead cabling were stolen, causing a village-wide power outage in Newton-on-Trent. The incident occurred overnight on Friday, leaving the village without power for several hours. This is the second such theft of overhead cabling in the county, with a similar incident happening in August at Normanby-Le-Wold. Authorities are emphasizing the severe risks associated with such crimes and are urging anyone with information to contact them at 0300 111 0300. The theft has disrupted power supply and poses potential dangers due to the extreme nature of the stolen equipment.

In a significant cybersecurity breach, a group of Russian hackers infiltrated the servers of Dow Jones & Co., the owner of the Wall Street Journal and several other news publications, reportedly stealing information for potential stock trading. The Federal Bureau of Investigation, Secret Service, Securities and Exchange Commission, and the Manhattan U.S. Attorney’s Office are investigating the matter. Dow Jones, however, has denied any knowledge of such an investigation, stating they have found no evidence to support the allegations.

The infiltration, which began at least a year ago, is described as more serious than a previous breach disclosed by Dow Jones last week. The hackers are suspected of seeking information including stories being prepared for publication. It's unclear whether the company's news-gathering operations were affected.

This hacking incident marks a shift in insider trading tactics, with hackers now stealing sensitive information and selling it to traders. Law enforcement officials are struggling to keep pace with the rapidly evolving schemes of cybercriminals.

Dow Jones publishes the Wall Street Journal and Barron’s, and provides information through services like Dow Jones Newswires. The company says its Factiva service provides global business content to about 1.1 million active users.

In a related development, U.S. authorities have been ramping up their pursuit of hackers following a series of high-profile attacks on corporations. In August, federal authorities made several arrests in a years-long scheme that combined insider trading and hacking. Russian-speaking hackers working from Ukraine were indicted, along with traders, for siphoning more than 150,000 press releases containing data that could be used to anticipate stock market moves.

The hacking investigation underscores the growing vulnerability of information companies to cyber attacks, particularly in the financial sector. Potentially market-moving scoops often develop in-house for days or weeks, providing intruders a long pre-publication window to mine information and execute trades. Data being held for public release at a specified time can also be a valuable target.

The Karlbox, a limited-edition art supply storage box, was launched earlier this month in collaboration between Karl Lagerfeld and Faber-Castell. Designed by Lagerfeld, the black box holds 350 Faber-Castell art tools for drawing and painting, with a wood exterior resembling a Chinese wedding cabinet and removable drawers for storage. The box includes a variety of premium artists' tools, such as Albrecht Dürer and Polychromos color pencils, Pitt Artist ink pens, Castell 9000 graphite pencils, and Pitt crayons and pastels.

Lagerfeld, known for his extensive career in luxury goods, has used Faber-Castell products throughout his career. He stated that drawing is like breathing and writing for him, and he turns to pen and paper to concretize his ideas. The Karlbox is priced at $2,850 and includes a serial number and certificate of authenticity, with only 2,400 produced.

Faber-Castell is a family-owned company founded in 1761 in Germany and is known for its high-end pens and exclusive artist products. The company has a long history of working with renowned artists, including Vincent van Gogh, Paul Klee, Oskar Kokoschka, and Neo Rauch.

The Karlbox is available at select department and specialty stores, Faber-Castell stores, Karl Lagerfeld boutiques worldwide, Harrods, London, and Gump's of San Francisco. The box is a symbol of the long-term relationship between both brands and represents the symbiosis of the fashion, art, and design worlds.

The Archbishop of Philadelphia, Charles Chaput, has issued new guidelines for Catholics in the archdiocese, which include rules for divorced and remarried individuals, as well as those who are attracted to people of the same sex. The guidelines, which took effect on July 1, call on priests to help Catholics who are struggling with same-sex attraction to find chastity and frequent penance. The guidelines also state that two people in an active, public same-sex relationship offer a serious counter-witness to Catholic belief and can produce moral confusion in the community.

Divorced and remarried Catholics are welcome in the community but are required to abstain from sex and live out their relationships like "brother and sister" to receive Holy Communion. Cohabitating unmarried couples are also required to refrain from sexual intimacy to receive Holy Communion. The guidelines also state that allowing persons in "irregular" relationships to hold positions of responsibility would offer a serious counter-witness to Catholic belief and produce moral confusion in the community.

The guidelines come three months after Pope Francis urged bishops to be more accepting of Catholics who lived outside of the church's social teaching and doctrine, including people who have divorced and remarried, and people in same-sex relationships. The pope's views were published in April in a document titled Amoris Laetitia (Joy of Love), which was hailed as potentially groundbreaking.

The Philadelphia archdiocese is known for its conservative leadership, with Archbishop Chaput being one of the staunchest conservative leaders in the US Catholic church. The guidelines issued by the archdiocese reflect this conservative view. It is believed that Philadelphia may be among the first archdiocese to publish such rules based on its interpretation of Amoris Laetitia.

John Allen, a veteran Vatican journalist, said he believed that more progressive bishops would not put out documents to say so, but would quietly make it clear to priests that it is OK under certain circumstances to allow some people to quietly come back to communion. Allen said that he did not think Pope Francis would be surprised by Chaput's reading of the papal document, since he is likely aware of traditional interpretations of his document.

The guidelines state that some people with same-sex attraction can still live out a vocation of heterosexual marriage with children, notwithstanding "some degree of same-sex attraction." The guidelines also state that those with predominant same-sex attractions are called to struggle to live chastely for the kingdom of God. In this endeavor, they have need of support, friendship, and understanding if they fail.

The guidelines also address cohabitating unmarried couples, stating that if a priest senses that one person in the couple is reluctant to take the plunge, the archdiocese recommended trying to break up the pair. If the cohabitating couple seems ready to tie the knot but is just a bit slow, the priest should encourage them to practice chastity.

Overall, the guidelines issued by the Archdiocese of Philadelphia require divorced and remarried Catholics, as well as cohabitating unmarried couples, to refrain from sexual intimacy to receive Holy Communion. The guidelines also state that allowing persons in "irregular" relationships to hold positions of responsibility would offer a serious counter-witness to Catholic belief and produce moral confusion in the community. The guidelines reflect the conservative view of Archbishop Charles Chaput and may be the first of its kind issued by the bishop of any American diocese in response to Amoris Laetitia.

Charlie Sheen, the actor known for his role in "Two and a Half Men," was hospitalized last week due to severe abdominal pains. Before his hospitalization, an adult film star named Kacey Jordan attended a party at Sheen's home, where she claimed to have witnessed excessive drug and alcohol use. Jordan described Sheen as being covered in wine stains, having "tennis ball size" chunks of cocaine delivered, and consuming so much alcohol and cocaine that she feared he was on a "suicide binge."

During the party, Jordan claimed that Sheen asked her to move into a mansion he was setting up for a 24-hour party and to babysit his children. Sheen is currently in rehab, and production on "Two and a Half Men" has been put on hold indefinitely.

Sheen's publicist stated that he was rushed to the hospital with severe abdominal pains on Thursday. ABC News reported exclusive details about the raucous party that took place at Sheen's home the night before he was hospitalized. She also claimed that there were four other women at the party, at least two of whom were porn stars.
