The study conducted by Nationwide Children's Hospital has revealed high levels of bacteria, including disease-causing bacteria, in breast milk purchased online. The research analyzed 100 samples of breast milk bought from a public milk-sharing website and found that 75% of the samples were contaminated with either high levels of bacterial growth or disease-causing bacteria, including fecal contamination. The contamination was likely due to poor hygiene during milk collection, the use of unclean containers, unsanitary breast milk pump parts, or compromised shipping practices. The study, published in Pediatrics, emphasizes the risks associated with buying breast milk online from unknown sellers, as it may not be the safest way to obtain breast milk for infants whose immune systems are vulnerable. The Food and Drug Administration warns against feeding babies breast milk acquired directly from individuals or through the Internet, citing safety concerns. However, the study does not apply to situations where milk is shared among friends or relatives or donated rather than sold. The study's findings highlight the importance of following strict guidelines set by the Human Milk Banking Association of North America to ensure the safety and quality of breast milk for infants in need.

A new blood test has been developed that could potentially screen for Alzheimer's disease during routine health check-ups, making it more accessible and less expensive than current methods such as PET-scans and spinal taps. The test works by measuring the relative amounts of different forms of beta-amyloid, a protein that forms plaques in the brains of people with Alzheimer's. The test was developed by comparing ratios of beta-amyloid types in 41 people's blood with PET scans showing how much beta-amyloid had aggregated in their brains.

Early detection of Alzheimer's disease is important as amyloid plaques start developing 15 to 20 years before the symptoms of the disease start to show. The test could help identify people at risk of developing the condition and allow for early intervention, potentially slowing the progression of the disease. However, testing positive for the presence of amyloid plaques does not necessarily mean that a person will develop Alzheimer's.

The hunt for a drug that can effectively treat Alzheimer's disease continues, but in the meantime, evidence is growing that healthy lifestyle interventions such as exercise and a healthy diet can reduce the risk of developing the disease by as much as 30%. In theory, the blood test could reassure some people that they are not at risk of developing the condition, while identifying others who might benefit from further tests and lifestyle changes.

In addition to the blood test, a major study is underway to see how PET scans could change the nature of Alzheimer's diagnosis and treatment. So far, the results have been dramatic, with just 54.3% of MCI patients and 70.5% of dementia patients having the plaques. A positive test for amyloid does not mean someone has Alzheimer's, though its presence precedes the disease and increases the risk of progression. But a negative test definitively means a person does not have it. The findings could change the way doctors treat people in these hard-to-diagnose groups and save money being spent on inappropriate medication.

A $20 million two-year clinical trial has also been launched to see if lifestyle changes can prevent cognitive decline. The trial will work with 2,500 older adults at risk for cognitive decline and test whether two years of intervention that includes physical exercise, nutritional counseling, social and cognitive stimulation, and improved self-management will help cognitive function in participants 60 to 79 years old. Similar studies are also underway in Singapore and Australia. Research has shown that each of these factors contributes to cognitive health, but researchers believe that, as with heart disease, combating Alzheimer's is likely to require a multipronged, or "cocktail" approach combining drugs and lifestyle changes.

In Windsor, Vermont, a survey conducted by WISE, a domestic violence prevention and advocacy group, has sparked controversy among parents. The survey, administered to fifth-grade students, inquired about students' sexual history, preference, and gender identity. Parent Vanessa Beach expressed concern, stating that the questions were inappropriate for her 10-year-old daughter's age group, likening the concept of a 10-year-old having a sexual partner to sexual abuse.

Beach also mentioned that she never received a notice about the survey, which allowed parents to opt-out of their children's participation. WISE officials stated that students are informed before the survey is distributed that they are not required to participate and can choose not to do so without consequence.

The survey, developed with researchers from the University of New Hampshire, aimed to collect data that WISE would share with the researchers. Beach reported voicing her concerns to the school and WISE, and both parties are working to address the parental complaints. Beach acknowledged the group's efforts in raising awareness about domestic violence. School administrators are currently addressing the concerns raised by parents.

George Brinkman, a suspect in five homicides, contacted a local television reporter before his arrest during a standoff in Brunswick, Ohio. Brinkman exchanged messages with a WOIO-Channel 19 reporter, who initially reached out to him due to his friendship with three women found dead in North Royalton. Officers, including those on break, conducted sweeps but found no suspicious items. The stations were reopened hours later. Authorities urge the public to avoid crowds, public transportation, and train stations as the situation is still developing.

In a significant development, federal prosecutors in Boston have seized approximately $20 million found under a mattress in a Westborough, Massachusetts apartment, following the arrest of a Brazilian man, Cleber Rene Rizerio Rocha, on charges of money laundering. The cash seizure is connected to an investigation into TelexFree Inc, an internet telecom company that authorities allege was a massive global pyramid scheme.

TelexFree, based in Marlborough, Massachusetts, was founded by James Merrill, a U.S. citizen, and Carlos Wanzeler, a Brazilian. The company promised to sell voice-over-internet telephone service but, according to prosecutors, made little to no money from this service. Instead, it made millions by recruiting thousands of people to become promoters who would post ads online for the company.

TelexFree filed for bankruptcy in April 2014, owing $5 billion to its participants. In total, 965,225 victims in the United States, Brazil, and various other countries lost $1.76 billion when it collapsed. Merrill was arrested in May 2014 and pleaded guilty to conspiracy and wire fraud charges in October. Wanzeler fled to Brazil and could not be extradited.

The current case involves an attempt to transfer millions of dollars of hidden TelexFree assets to Brazil by laundering the cash through Hong Kong, according to court documents. Rocha, acting as a courier for Wanzeler's nephew, flew from Brazil to the United States, met with a cooperating witness, and gave him a suitcase containing $2.2 million. After the meeting, federal agents followed Rocha to the Westborough apartment and later arrested him. Upon returning to the apartment, they found a substantial amount of cash hidden under a mattress, which Rocha claimed totaled $20 million.

The case is U.S. v. Rocha, U.S. District Court, District of Massachusetts, No. 17-mj-05007.

Wilson's Hollywood career spanned over five decades, with notable roles in films such as 'In Cold Blood', 'The Great Gatsby', and 'Dead Man Walking'. He earned a Golden Globe nomination for Best Supporting Actor for his role in 'The Ninth Configuration'. In recent years, he starred in 'Pearl Harbor' and had a recurring role on 'CSI'. Wilson's return to 'The Walking Dead' for season 9 was announced at New York Comic-Con, but he passed away peacefully at his home in Los Angeles just an hour after the announcement. A tribute was aired at the end of the season premiere, and tributes poured in from current and former cast members and producers on social media.

In a disturbing development, a video posted online by the Islamic State (IS) militant group shows a child shooting and killing an Israeli Arab, Mohamed Said Ismail Musallam, who was accused by IS of being an Israeli spy. The 19-year-old Musallam, a citizen of Palestinian descent, had left his home in East Jerusalem for Turkey last year, reportedly to fight in Syria. However, his family and Israeli officials have denied that he was an Israeli spy.

The video, published by IS's Furqan media outlet, shows Musallam sitting in a room wearing an orange jumpsuit, confessing to being recruited and trained by Mossad, Israel's intelligence service. He is then escorted to a field and shot in the head by a boy, described by an older, French-speaking fighter as one of the "cubs of the caliphate." The video, which is about 13 minutes long, has not been independently verified, and Israeli officials could not confirm its authenticity.

Musallam's family said he had left for Turkey four months ago without telling them. Soon after his departure, he told his brother that he planned to join IS in Syria. According to his father, Musallam had become disillusioned and wanted to return home but was captured by IS militants. The family believes that IS forced Musallam to say he was a spy before killing him for show.

The video comes after an interview published by IS's English language magazine Dabiq in February, in which Musallam claimed he had joined IS to report to the Israelis on weapons caches, bases, and Palestinian recruits. However, Israel and his family denied that he was an Israeli spy. In the latest video, Musallam repeated his confession, saying, "I tell my father and my son: Repent to God. I say to the spies who spy on Islamic State: You will not be successful, they will expose you."

The killing of Musallam is the latest in a series of brutal executions carried out by IS, which has attracted international condemnation. The group has been accused of committing war crimes and human rights abuses, including the use of child soldiers and the execution of prisoners. The United Nations has called for an investigation into IS's actions, and several countries have pledged to take action against the group.

The killing of Musallam has sparked outrage among his family and friends, who have condemned IS for its actions. His family wept at their home in East Jerusalem when they learned of his death, with his mother saying, "A spy of 19? How is that possible? Why would he have gone there if he were a spy?" The family has called for an investigation into his death and for justice to be served.

The killing of Musallam is a reminder of the brutal and violent nature of IS, which continues to pose a threat to security and stability in the Middle East and beyond. The international community must take action to combat the group and bring an end to its reign of terror.

Bernie Sanders has declared that the Democratic Party's convention will be "contested," unless Hillary Clinton garners enough pledged delegates to secure the nomination without the aid of superdelegates. Sanders's campaign has been advocating for superdelegates to switch their allegiance, particularly in states where he has won by double-digit margins. While Clinton currently has the backing of 520 superdelegates, Sanders has only 39. Sanders argued that he is entitled to superdelegate support if he wins a state by a large margin.

Sanders called on superdelegates from states like Washington and Minnesota to change their allegiances, citing his strong performance in those states. However, during the press conference, Sanders contradicted himself by stating that superdelegates should follow the popular vote from their states but also consider backing him even if he does not win the majority of pledged delegates.

Sanders's campaign distributed factsheets showing general election polling in battleground states and nationwide where he outperforms Clinton against Republican candidates. Sanders acknowledged that Clinton is currently winning the race by a significant margin and would need to win 65% of the remaining pledged delegates to pull ahead of Clinton.

Philip Bump from The Fix explains that a contested convention is still unlikely for Bernie Sanders, as he trails Clinton by a significant margin in actual votes. Sanders's campaign has been asking superdelegates to set aside Clinton's lead in actual votes because of his strong performance in certain states and national polling. However, it is unlikely that Sanders will be able to convince superdelegates to switch their allegiance, as Clinton currently has a lead of over 3 million votes.

In summary, Bernie Sanders has declared that the Democratic Party's convention will be "contested" unless Hillary Clinton garners enough pledged delegates to secure the nomination without the aid of superdelegates. Sanders has been advocating for superdelegates to switch their allegiance, particularly in states where he has won by double-digit margins. However, it is unlikely that Sanders will be able to convince superdelegates to switch their allegiance, as Clinton currently has a lead of over 3 million votes.

The article "Brain Wars: How the Military is Failing its Wounded" by ProPublica and NPR investigates the U.S. military's traumatic brain injury (TBI) testing program, which was established in 2007 to screen soldiers for TBIs caused by roadside bombs in Iraq. The article claims that the program has failed to deliver on its promise, offering soldiers the appearance of help, but not the reality.

The military chose a test called the Automated Neuropsychological Assessment Metric (ANAM) that was not proven to detect TBIs. More than a million troops have taken the test at a cost of over $42 million to taxpayers, yet the military still has no reliable way to catch TBIs. When such injuries are left undetected, it can delay healing and put soldiers at risk for further mental damage.

The investigation found that the people who invented ANAM and stood to make money from it were involved in the military's decision to use it, prompting questions about the impartiality of the selection process. No other tests received serious consideration. A report by the Army's top neuropsychologist circulated last year labeled the selection process "nepotistic."

The Pentagon's civilian leadership has ignored years of warnings that there was insufficient scientific evidence that the ANAM could screen or diagnose TBIs. The military's highest-ranking medical official said the test was "fraught with problems." Compounding flaws in the ANAM's design, the military has not administered the test as recommended and has rarely used its results. The Army has so little confidence in the test that its top medical officer issued an explicit order that soldiers whose scores indicated cognitive problems should not be sent for further medical evaluation.

Top Pentagon officials have misrepresented the cost of the test, indicating that because the Army invented ANAM, the military could use it for free. In fact, because the military licensed its invention to outside contractors, it has paid millions of dollars to use its own technology.

The military has not conducted a long-promised head-to-head study to make sure the ANAM is the best available test, delaying it for years. Instead, a series of committees have given lukewarm approval to continue using the ANAM, largely to avoid losing the data gathered so far.

Several current and former military medical officials criticized the Defense Department's embrace of a scientifically unproven tool to use on hundreds of thousands of soldiers with TBIs. Retired Brigadier General Dr. Stephen Xenakis, a former adviser on mental health issues to the chairman of the joint chiefs of staff, said, "The test was not developed for the purposes of identifying the kinds of problems that we see in concussions."

Army Surgeon General Eric Schoomaker acknowledged there have been problems with the testing program and called it a "first step." He added that the Army has tried to improve the ANAM test and is comparing it to alternatives.

Many experts in the field say Congress' mandate for testing went beyond what science can provide. There is no computerized test that, on its own, allows doctors to diagnose TBIs. Yet studies have indicated the ANAM shows promise when used immediately after a blast, helping doctors determine if soldiers are sharp enough to return to duty. Other studies, as yet unpublished, show the test may also be able to detect certain cognitive problems months after a brain injury.

Those most familiar with the ANAM program insist that testing can be of significant value if used properly -- and that this is where the military has gone wrong. Retired Colonel Mary Lopez, who used to manage the Army's testing program, said, "We have failed soldiers. It is incredibly frustrating because I can see first-hand the soldiers that we've missed, the soldiers that have not been treated, not been identified, [or] misdiagnosed. And then they struggle."

A 73-year-old man's impeccable driving record was overshadowed during a traffic stop on Tuesday night when he attempted to snort cocaine in front of an officer. Upon approaching the vehicle, Officer Abts-Olsen noticed the driver portioning out cocaine from a small glass vial.

Anthony J. Lescowitch Jr., a 35-year-old man from Drifton, was arrested after he shared a wanted poster of himself on his own Facebook profile, mocking the Freeland police department. The police had posted the wanted poster on their Facebook account on Monday, seeking assistance from the community to locate Lescowitch, who was wanted for aggravated assault and other charges since November 27, 2013.

In an attempt to track down Lescowitch, an undercover officer posed as a female on Facebook and began conversing with him about his wanted picture. The two talked back and forth for about 30 minutes, with police gathering key information that eventually led to Lescowitch's arrest. The officer then asked Lescowitch to meet at an undisclosed location, and he agreed. However, when Lescowitch arrived, police were waiting and took him into custody without incident.

According to court papers, Lescowitch was also wanted by Luzerne County Adult Probation. He was arraigned on Tuesday by Magisterial District Judge Martin Kane, Wilkes-Barre, and set bail at $25,000. Lescowitch was unable to post bail and was taken to jail.

Four other people were charged in the incident, including Heather Mumie, Clayton R. Spohr, and Janine K. Brotzman. The incident occurred during an argument on July 14, 2013, during which Lescowitch was alleged to have hit the victim in the head, causing him to fall to the street, become unconscious, and be robbed while incapacitated. The victim's wallet, which contained $53 and an ATM card, were among the items taken, police wrote. The victim's ATM card was later used to withdraw $100, according to an affidavit filed by Officer Denna Krammes, who investigated the case.

The Freeland police department encouraged the community to like and follow them on Facebook to stay informed about local news and events.

In a recent interview, Donald Trump, the presumptive Republican presidential nominee, suggested that racial profiling could be a preventative tactic in the United States, citing Israel and other countries as examples of successful profiling. Trump's comments come in the wake of the Orlando nightclub shooting, the deadliest mass shooting in U.S. history. Trump renewed his calls for a temporary ban on Muslims entering the U.S., stating it would have prevented the attack, despite the shooter being a U.S. citizen.

Trump also discussed gun reform, stating that attacks like Orlando would stop if those in the Muslim community would "report" suspicious activities. He mentioned the San Bernardino case as an example, where people saw bombs in the suspects' apartment but did not report them.

Trump added that Mateen, the Orlando shooter, had "red flags" before the attack, citing his past and school record. He is working with the National Rifle Association on a policy that would ban people on the no-fly list from purchasing guns.

Trump's proposal of racial profiling has been met with criticism from civil libertarians who decry the practice as discriminatory. Trump defends his stance, stating it is a matter of choosing "common sense" over "political correctness."

In a recent development, Derek Benson, a Connecticut resident, has been arrested on additional burglary charges due to a unique circumstance. Benson, already facing charges from a series of burglaries, was identified by a victim who recognized a stolen sweatshirt he was wearing in a mugshot. The sweatshirt, bearing the logo of Coco Libre, a brand the victim works for, was taken during a burglary in 2014. The investigation was reopened after the victim contacted the police in February 2023. The stolen sweatshirt, along with jewelry, was reportedly taken during the burglary. Apple is set to launch the iPhone 4S in China on January 13, making it available in 22 countries, including mainland China. The iPhone 4S, one of Apple's best-selling devices, accounts for nearly half of Apple's annual revenue and more than 60% of its profits. China, with its vast mobile device market of nearly a billion cellphone users, is a significant market for Apple. Apple currently partners with China Unicom, one of the larger carriers with close to 200 million cellular subscribers.

However, Apple has not yet announced a partnership with China Mobile, the country's largest carrier with over 630 million subscribers. Rumors of such a deal have been circulating for months, and millions of China Mobile customers are already using the iPhone by modifying the device to work on their network.

Siri, the voice-activated assistant, will not be able to understand Mandarin when the phone launches in China next week. Apple plans to add official language support for Chinese, including Mandarin, later in 2012. The iPhone 4S is expected to be in high demand in China, following its quick sell-out in Hong Kong.

The iPhone 4S prices in China are expected to be similar to those in 2010: 4,999 yuan ($793) for the 16GB model and 5,999 yuan ($952) for the 32GB model, without a long-term carrier contract. The 8GB iPhone 4, which sells for $99 in the U.S. with a two-year contract, goes for 3,880 yuan ($633) in China without a contract.

In addition to China, over 20 other countries will also see the iPhone 4S launch on January 13, including Bolivia, Dominican Republic, Jamaica, and Senegal.

A California pioneer named Granville P. Swift, whose great-uncle was the legendary explorer Daniel Boone, is known for his role in the Bear Flag Revolt and his extensive fortune in gold. In 1846, Swift, along with 33 other Americans, captured Sonoma during the Bear Flag Revolt and stayed on in Sonoma for another year, commanding a company and earning the rank of captain. Upon the announcement of gold being discovered at Sutter's Fort, Swift set off for Bidwell's Bar and struck it rich. He made an immense amount of gold, estimated to be over $100,000 each for him and his companions. Swift had his gold minted into octagonal slugs, $50 each, with a special mark designating them as Swift's.

Loaded down with gold and without a banking system to receive it, Swift decided to start burying his haul around the Bay Area, primarily in the Sonoma area. However, Swift was very bad at remembering where he'd hidden it all, and although he died in 1875, the secret died long before then, forgotten by the scatter-brained settler. Over time, some of the gold was found. In 1903, a worker on a ranch in Sonoma County dug up $7,000 in Swift's $50 slugs. A year later, $30,000 in gold was pulled from a chimney hiding place on Swift's old ranch near present-day Sears Point. The biggest discovery came in 1914, when a Sonoma Valley rancher, A.W. Lehrke, found $42,600 in gold coins under his home, believed to have contained one of Swift's hidden hoards.

Since 1914, the remainder of Swift's enormous haul has gone undiscovered. Today, we have one meager hint, courtesy of a misspelling-laden note written by Swift himself: "1 tin box & 1 Little Bottle Boath in the saim hoal." Swift's life was marked by both glorious and sad moments. He lost most of his non-buried treasure after investing in a non-existent Comstock Lode mine and lost $80,000 of gold panned by his sister Polly when he buried it near a creek. Winter floods washed the whole lot away. Hoping to turn his luck around, Swift moved his family to Solano County in 1864 and set out into the Berryessa area to prospect once more. He was visiting his quicksilver mine one day in 1875 when his mule returned home without a rider. His worried family retraced his steps and found his mangled body in the hills. It seemed Swift had been thrown by his mule and then dragged, foot caught in the stirrup, until his head was fatally struck.
