In Southgate, Michigan, a group of students at Anderson High School are facing disciplinary action and are required to retake a final exam, after they were caught cheating. Two juniors reportedly took photos of the exam's answer key while the teacher was out of the classroom and shared the answers with other students. The teacher noticed unusual perfect scores and alerted the administration, leading to the discovery of the cheating incident. The entire class, which consisted of approximately 30 students, had to retake the final exam during summer break. The school administration is still determining the appropriate punishment for the students involved. This is the first time the school administration has dealt with cheating of this magnitude among 11th-grade students.

The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) has unveiled a comprehensive plan to regulate high-frequency trading (HFT) and increase oversight of dark pools and other secretive trading practices in the U.S. equity market. The plan aims to bring more transparency to the markets and address concerns about unfair advantages held by HFT traders, who account for about half of U.S. stock executions.

Proprietary traders who use computers to buy and sell stocks in milliseconds will have to register with the SEC, while operators of dark pools will have to provide the regulator with their rules for matching buyers and sellers. The SEC is also considering new rules to require more oversight of traders' algorithms and to minimize speed advantages held by some HFT firms.

The plan could affect stock exchanges, brokerages, and a class of proprietary traders who have so far escaped oversight. The SEC's new scrutiny comes as HFT has drawn scrutiny from law enforcement and regulators, including the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC), which has previously said it was considering registration for high-speed traders of futures.

Senator Carl Levin, chairman of the Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, has also asked regulators to provide information on risks posed by HFT in advance of a hearing this month. High-frequency trading accounts for about 48 percent of all U.S. share volume, and firms such as Chopper Trading LLC, Jump Trading LLC, and Tower Research Capital LLC have been subpoenaed as part of an investigation by New York Attorney General Eric Schneiderman.

The SEC's plan also includes proposals to address claims of unfairness in how order and price data reach the public, and to require brokers to tell investors where their stock trades are executed. The measures outlined by SEC Chair Mary Jo White are intended to prevent failures and excessive fragmentation and complexity in the market, and the agency will create a new advisory committee of investors and others to help inform its initiatives and rule changes.

In Fairfield, California, a couple, Ina Rogers and Jonathan Allen, have been charged with various offenses including child cruelty, child torture, and neglect, following the discovery of their 10 children living in squalid conditions. The children, aged 4 months to 14 years, were found living in unsanitary and unsafe conditions, with filth, garbage, and animal and human feces present in the home. The children described incidents of intentional abuse resulting in puncture wounds, burns, bruising, and injuries consistent with being shot by a pellet or airsoft gun.

Rogers, who is out on bail, defended herself and her husband, stating that they are good parents and that the allegations are unfounded. She claimed that the home's condition was left messy by police during their search. Allen was arrested on Friday after a six-week investigation and is being held on $5.2 million bail.

The children have been placed in the custody of Rogers' sister and mother in the Bay Area. The investigation was initiated by the Fairfield Police Department's Family Violence Unit with the assistance of Child Welfare Services and the Solano County District Attorney's Office. The investigation revealed a long and continuous history of severe physical and emotional abuse of the children.

In a separate case, David Turpin, a father accused of shackling and starving some of his 13 children, has had eight new charges filed against him in Riverside County, California. The case has received international attention since his 17-year-old daughter escaped the family's home in January and called 911. Turpin and his wife previously pleaded not guilty to torture, child abuse, and other charges.

Netflix announced a significant new program for its employees on Tuesday, introducing an unlimited maternity and paternity leave policy for the first year following a child's birth or adoption. The policy aims to provide employees with the flexibility and confidence to balance their personal and professional lives without financial or work-related concerns. Under this policy, employees can take off as much time as they need, returning part-time, full-time, or taking subsequent time off as necessary. Netflix will continue to pay employees normally, eliminating the need to switch to state or disability pay.

Netflix's Chief Talent Officer, Tawni Cranz, emphasized that the company's culture fosters a "freedom and responsibility" approach, giving employees context about the business and the freedom to make decisions with the accompanying responsibility. This new policy is part of Netflix's strategy to attract and retain top talent, recognizing that employees perform better when they are not preoccupied with home-related issues.

This policy update follows the trend set by other tech giants like Yahoo, Facebook, and Google, who have previously expanded their maternity and paternity leave policies to remain competitive. The focus on work-life balance is a shift from the earlier-2000s, when perks like ping-pong tables, Xboxes, snacks, and free lunches were common to keep employees in the office. However, the unlimited leave policy has its potential drawbacks, such as the need for employees to coordinate with their managers and teams to avoid jeopardizing projects or deadlines, and the potential strain on workplace relations due to extended absences.

In summary, Netflix's unlimited maternity and paternity leave policy is a notable step towards prioritizing work-life balance for its employees, aiming to support them during significant life changes and ultimately improve their productivity and dedication.

Steven Seagal, the American action movie star known for films like Under Siege, has been barred from entering Ukraine for five years due to national security concerns. The Ukrainian security service cited Seagal's socially dangerous actions and support for Russia's seizure of Crimea as the reasons for the ban. Seagal, who has a history of showing affection towards the former Soviet Union, has been vocal in his support for Russian President Vladimir Putin and his policies. This support has earned him the enmity of the Ukrainian authorities, who included him in a proposed blacklist of foreign cultural figures in 2015. Seagal's ban comes after he was granted Russian citizenship last year and follows Ukraine's decision to ban Russia's entry to the Eurovision song contest, which Kiev is hosting next week. This cultural war with Moscow continued this year when Kiev banned Russia's Eurovision entrant, Yulia Samoilova, for performing in Crimea in 2015. The ban on Seagal and Samoilova highlights the ongoing tension between Ukraine and Russia, particularly over the Crimean region.

The Gulf of Mexico oil spill, caused by a ruptured underwater well, has tripled in size, causing growing concerns among experts. The spill, which is currently over 3,850 square miles, threatens to become more devastating than initially estimated. The approaching oil slick is a concern for environmentalists, as it could destroy habitats and affect wildlife, including birds, dolphins, and various marine species. The spill could potentially reach the Florida Keys, home to the only living coral barrier reef in North America, which would be devastating.

BP is using chemicals to break up the oil, but these dispersants contain harmful toxins that could create new environmental problems. If the leak continues for weeks or months, the stockpile of dispersants could run out. The exact makeup of the dispersants is kept secret, but they are associated with health issues at high doses.

The spill threatens hundreds of species of wildlife and could affect the seafood industry in the Gulf Coast region. The cause of the explosion is still under investigation, with lawsuits claiming it was caused by improper cementing during the well-capping process. The Coast Guard has shut down two offshore platforms near the spill as a safety precaution.

BP has already used over a third of the world's supply of dispersants, and if the leak continues, there may not be enough to contain the spill. The use of dispersants is a trade-off, as they help prevent oil from reaching the shore but can also harm the ecosystem offshore. The decision to use dispersants should be made carefully to minimize environmental damage.

On July 15, a hiker died while climbing the iconic Half Dome trail in Yosemite National Park, California. The incident occurred during thunderstorm activity around 4:30 p.m., and the hiker's body was recovered the following day. The National Park Service reported that the hiker was scaling the steepest part of the trail where cables are installed to aid hikers during the 4,800-foot ascent. The companion hiker was assisted by park rangers and was unharmed.

The cables are installed each summer to help the thousands of hikers who make the popular 14-mile round trip. While hikers can clip safety harnesses to the cables, the vast majority do not. The National Park Service is still investigating the cause of the fall, but it's unclear if the hikers were climbing in the rain, and the trail was wet.

Half Dome is one of Yosemite's symbols, and the trail to the top is one of the most popular routes in the park, requiring reservations to prevent overcrowding. The National Park Service declined to release the hiker's name pending notification of his family, stating that it's the first fatal fall from Half Dome since 2010. The park requires hikers to obtain permits to hike the popular trail during the peak summer season.

In a recent development, Rudy Giuliani, President Donald Trump's attorney, has revealed that Trump's legal team has not received a response from special counsel Robert Mueller's office in nearly three weeks regarding their latest letter. Giuliani suggested that Mueller's team could be planning to issue a report without speaking to the President, issue a subpoena, negotiate with what Trump's team offered, or wait until after the midterm elections to make their next move.

Meanwhile, Roger Stone, a longtime associate of President Trump, has predicted that he will soon be indicted as part of the investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 presidential election. Stone made this prediction in an email to his supporters, stating that he is being targeted by the special prosecutor to silence him and pressure him to testify against President Trump. Stone's prediction comes a week after Trump's former campaign chairman, Paul Manafort, was convicted of federal crimes, and his former personal lawyer, Michael Cohen, pled guilty to similar charges.

Mueller's investigation has also made reference to Stone in the indictment of Russian military officers in the 2016 hacking of the Democratic National Committee. Stone has acknowledged that messages included in the indictment matched ones that he exchanged with hacker Guccifer 2.0, whom Mueller has alleged was a front for Russian operatives. Mueller has also investigated multiple people linked to Stone as part of its probe.

In June, Stone had previously predicted that Mueller could indict him as part of the investigation. The latest developments suggest that the Mueller investigation is continuing to probe individuals close to President Trump and could result in further indictments.

The Bloom Energy Server, a low-emissions energy server, was announced in Silicon Valley, drawing attention to its potential benefits. The server, developed by NASA, is said to have a 2-to-1 efficiency over electric utilities, making it attractive for various uses. The energy server requires a fuel source, such as natural gas, to operate, but it's important to note that energy is converted from one form to another to make electricity.

The Bloom Energy Server is currently priced at $700,000-$800,000, making it affordable for corporations but not for regular households. Bloom Energy aims to reduce the price to a few thousand dollars for home use, but this could take a decade or more as the technology improves.

The Bloom Energy Server has been met with skepticism due to the lack of details about its long-term reliability, cost, and energy efficiency. Some experts have expressed concerns about the technology's potential downtime, heat production, and the need for subsidies to make it economically viable.

Despite these concerns, Bloom Energy claims that its server can produce more energy with less environmental damage than other fuel cells on the market. The company has been secretive about its technology, but it's known that the server can use various energy sources, including wind, solar power, and natural gas.

Competitors in the fuel cell market exist, but Bloom Energy claims to have an integrated system and package ready for commercial sale, putting them ahead of the pack. The potential exists for a competitor to introduce an even more attractive system, and Bloom Energy's announcement has put pressure on competitors to make their announcements as well.

There are several important unknowns about the Bloom Energy Server, including its life span, downtime, and what will be done with the heat produced. The Bloom Energy Server is an exciting development, but its challenges and potential competition should be considered.

Netflix has officially renewed the critically acclaimed series "13 Reasons Why" for a second season, set to premiere in 2018. The show, which is an adaptation of Jay Asher's bestselling 2007 YA book, revolves around the suicide of a high school girl and the subsequent complicated journeys of the characters towards healing and recovery. The series, produced by Selena Gomez, has been a breakout success, receiving positive reviews and generating significant attention on social media.

Tony Award- and Pulitzer Prize-winner Brian Yorkey, who wrote the adaptation and served as an executive producer on the series, will take over as the sole showrunner for Season 2. Diana Son, who was executive producer/co-showrunner on the drama's first season with Yorkey, is leaving.

The first season follows teenager Clay Jensen (Dylan Minnette) as he discovers cassette tapes recorded by Hannah Baker (newcomer Katherine Langford), his classmate and crush, who tragically committed suicide two weeks earlier. On the tapes, Hannah explains the 13 reasons why she decided to end her life. The series, which deals with sensitive topics such as teen suicide, bullying, drunk driving, and rape in graphic detail, has been the subject of active discussion and criticism by some mental health experts who express concerns about potential health risks for certain young people, especially those with suicidal thoughts. In response, Netflix has amped up its content warnings.

"13 Reasons Why" is directed by Oscar winner Tom McCarthy, written by Yorkey, and executive produced by Gomez, Yorkey, McCarthy, Joy Gorman, Michael Sugar, and Steve Golin from Anonymous Content, Kristel Laiblin, and Mandy Teefey. The series is produced for Netflix by Paramount Television. The second season will also consist of 13 episodes.

The study published in The New England Journal of Medicine analyzed data from Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services carrier files for a 20% random sample of beneficiaries from 2008 to 2011. The research aimed to identify emergency room doctors who are more likely to prescribe opioids to older patients, and the potential risks associated with such prescriptions.

The study defined an index visit as the earliest visit at an emergency department where a beneficiary had an evaluation and management claim by an emergency medicine physician. They included only one index visit per beneficiary, excluded visits resulting in hospital admission, and limited the analysis to beneficiaries who had been continuously enrolled in Medicare Part D for at least 18 months.

The researchers assigned each index emergency department visit to a physician according to the billing National Provider Identifier (NPI) and linked each visit to a hospital by matching to facility claims. They excluded physicians with fewer than five emergency department visits and hospitals with fewer than five physicians billing for emergency department visits in their sample.

The main exposure was treatment by a "high-intensity" or "low-intensity" opioid prescribing physician within the same hospital. The researchers calculated the proportion of all emergency department visits after which an opioid prescription was filled for each physician and grouped them into quartiles of rates of opioid prescribing within each hospital.

The primary outcome was long-term opioid use, defined as 180 days or more of opioids supplied in the 12 months after an index emergency department visit. Secondary outcomes were rates of hospital encounters (emergency department visits, hospitalizations, or both) in the 12 months after an index emergency department visit.

The study found that patients treated by high-intensity opioid prescribing physicians were at greater risk of using opioids chronically than those who saw doctors who prescribe them less frequently. The researchers performed additional sensitivity analyses to address potential selection bias and found similar results.

Dr. Lewis S. Nelson, the chairman of emergency medicine at Rutgers New Jersey Medical School, commented that the study provides important insights into the risk of a single exposure of a patient in an emergency room to an opioid. The research is significant as the opioid epidemic continues to affect communities across the country.

Amazon, the leading online retailer, is planning to open its first brick-and-mortar store in New York City, marking an attempt to connect with customers in the physical world. The store, set to open in time for the holiday-shopping season, will be located on the same busy street as Macy's Inc.’s flagship store.

The Manhattan location is expected to function as a "mini-warehouse" for same-day delivery in New York, product returns, and pickups of online orders. This move could potentially attract foreign tourists who shop on Amazon but find many products only available in the US.

Amazon has been a disruptor in the retail industry, offering competitive pricing and tools that encouraged "showroom buying." With a line of its own tech products, Amazon could put its homegrown goods in front of more customers and tout its growing offering of same-day delivery, which is available in 12 cities, including New York.

Analysts view this move as an experiment for Amazon to get its products in front of consumers, particularly those who prefer a more tactile shopping experience. The store is expected to devote much of the floor space to Amazon's successful products like Kindle e-readers and tablets, as well as underperforming products like the Fire set-top box and Fire smartphone.

The store's location, 7 West 34th Street, is across from the Empire State Building and a block east from busy Herald Square, home to the flagship Macy's and the site of the classic 1947 Christmas movie "Miracle on 34th Street." Amazon has yet to confirm the plans, but if it does, it could significantly impact the retail landscape in New York City.

Former South Carolina Governor Mark Sanford, running for his old House seat, has faced a series of setbacks in recent weeks. His ex-wife filed a lawsuit against him for trespassing, national Republicans withdrew their support for his campaign, and a poll showed him trailing his Democratic challenger by a significant 9-point margin in a traditionally Republican district.

In response to these challenges, Sanford's campaign took an unconventional approach by staging a debate with a cardboard cutout of House Minority Leader Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.). This move appears to be inspired by Clint Eastwood's controversial speech at the 2012 Republican National Convention, where he delivered a rambling address to an empty chair symbolizing President Obama.

At a press event on Wednesday, Sanford accused his opponent, Elizabeth Colbert Busch, of running a "stealth campaign" by refusing to debate him publicly. He justified debating a cardboard cutout of Pelosi as a last resort. During the mock debate, Sanford posed a question to the cutout about a National Labor Relations Board lawsuit that aimed to prevent Boeing from building a new plant in South Carolina. Republicans claimed the lawsuit was politically motivated and would have denied the state much-needed jobs.

The Congressional Candidate Website project, led by political scientists at Northwestern University, The University of Minnesota, and Oberlin College, is archiving all major-party House and Senate candidate websites during the 2008 and 2010 campaigns. This initiative aims to preserve digital records of political campaigns for future research and analysis.

On March 20, 2015, triple suicide bombers attacked two mosques in Sanaa, Yemen, during midday prayers, resulting in the deaths of 46 people and injuring over 100 others. The mosques targeted were controlled by Shiite rebels, known as Houthis, who seized Sanaa in September 2014. The attacks occurred at the Badr and al-Hashoosh mosques, with at least two suicide bombers attacking the Badr mosque. One witness described the scene as chaotic, with bodies and body parts scattered on the floor, and many injured by shattered glass. The al-Hashoosh mosque was also targeted, with one witness being thrown two meters away by the blast.

The Islamic State group (ISIS) claimed responsibility for the bombings, marking their first large-scale attack in Yemen. The attacks come a day after intense gun battles in the southern city of Aden between rival troops loyal to Yemen's former and current president, leaving 13 dead and forcing the closure of the city's international airport.

The Houthis, who are Shiites in a predominantly Sunni country, already face resistance from Al Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula (AQAP) and supporters of ousted President Abdu Rabu Mansour Hadi. If ISIS committed the attack, it would be a new challenge to the Houthis and a challenge to ISIS's rival, AQAP. The attacks also mark one of the worst days of recent violence during a complicated struggle for control of Yemen.

Among those killed in Sanaa was prominent Houthi religious leader Murtatha Al Mahathwari, and a separate explosion rocked a government compound in the Houthi stronghold city of Saada, killing two people and wounding a third. The Houthis have Sanaa, launched airstrikes in Aden, and clashes between Houthi-controlled forces and military units still loyal to Hadi have stepped up this week in Aden.

The United States strongly condemned the attacks and expressed its condolences to the victims' families and loved ones. The attacks underscore that terrorism affects all Yemenis and that Yemen and its people must remain unified to confront these challenges. Officials in Saudi Arabia urged all Yemeni political groups to take part in talks in Riyadh.

India has elected Ram Nath Kovind, a Dalit and member of the ruling BJP party, as its 14th president. Kovind secured a majority in a nationwide ballot involving nearly 5,000 lawmakers from the central parliament and state legislatures. His victory is seen as part of a strategy by Prime Minister Narendra Modi to widen support among India's 200 million-strong Dalit community. Kovind's election is also expected to strengthen Modi's grip on power, as the president's role in India is largely ceremonial but can delay key legislation and symbolically signal disapproval of controversial bills. The election of a Dalit president is significant as it represents progress in addressing India's ancient system of discrimination, but caste and religious divisions continue to be major issues in Indian politics. The election of Kovind is also seen as a move to address disillusionment among the Dalit community and to win support from important voting blocs, such as the Koli ethnic group in Modi's home state of Gujarat. The election of a Dalit president is a step forward in addressing India's caste system, but the country continues to grapple with persecution and exclusion of Dalits, and caste and religious divisions remain major issues in Indian politics.

In a groundbreaking event, a humanoid robot named Athena boarded a commercial flight at Los Angeles International Airport (LAX) on December 15, 2014, marking the first time a robot has flown as a paid passenger on a commercial jet. The robot, developed by Sarcos, was purchased by Germany's Max Planck Society, and the scientists accompanying it aimed to use Athena for tasks too dangerous for humans, such as cleanup after the Fukushima nuclear disaster.

Athena, wearing stylish red sneakers and accompanied by Alexander Herzog and Jeannette Bohg, was treated as a regular passenger, receiving special treatment such as a cut to the front of the ticket line in the first-class lane. Despite being in an off position during the flight, Athena was strapped into a seat and received a special electronic pat-down from the Transportation Security Administration (TSA).

The robot created a scene at the Tom Bradley International Terminal, with television crews, camera flashes, and cell-phone cameras capturing the moment. Athena's software to make her legs move and stand is still in development, but her arms can operate, and her mouth glows blue on a white head fitted with cameras and sensors.

LAX spokeswoman Nancy Suey Castles stated that the scientists wanted to see how humans responded to a robot sitting in a plane, and it was cheaper to get a seat for Athena than to ship her in a box. Lufthansa representatives could not be reached for comment.

This event could pave the way for more robots to fly as passengers on commercial jets in the future. Robots offer several advantages as passengers, such as not complaining about legroom, not kicking the seat in front of them, and not finding it unconscionable that even a soda can cost $2 aboard some flights.

A significant medieval cemetery, believed to be one of the largest in Britain, was discovered beneath the Old Divinity School at St John's College, Cambridge University during recent refurbishments. The graveyard, which contains approximately 1,300 burials, including around 400 complete skeletons, dates back to the 13th to 15th centuries. The cemetery served the medieval Hospital of St John the Evangelist, the origin of St John's College.

The excavation revealed that many graves were pre-dug, possibly in anticipation of winter deaths when ground conditions would make digging graves more difficult. The bodies found showed few signs of serious illnesses, suggesting the hospital's primary focus was spiritual and physical care for the poor and infirm rather than medical treatment.

The cemetery had gravel paths and a water well, and the presence of seeds from various flowering plants suggests it was a place for people to visit their deceased loved ones, much like modern-day cemeteries. The vast majority of burials were without coffins or shrouds, indicating the cemetery primarily served the poor.

Grave-goods such as jewellery and personal items were rare, with only a few exceptions, including a jet crucifix and the head of a woman. Despite local rumors linking the hospital cemetery to the Black Death, no evidence of this disease was found on any of the remains.

The excavation, led by Craig Cessford from the Cambridge University Department of Archaeology and Anthropology, was one of the largest medieval hospital osteoarchaeological assemblages from the British Isles. The findings shed significant new light on life and death in medieval Cambridge.

In a new study, it is suggested that Vincent van Gogh's infamous act of self-mutilation, where he cut off his ear, was inspired by the news that his brother Theo was about to marry after a whirlwind romance. Previously, it was believed that Van Gogh learned of the marriage only after the incident, but new evidence indicates that he learned of it in a letter from Theo delivered on December 23, 1888. The letter contained 100 francs and also news that Theo had met and quickly married an old friend, Jo Bonger, within a week of the letter. The news of Theo's marriage likely caused Van Gogh distress, as it could have threatened their close relationship and left Theo unable to financially support his brother. Later that night, there was a quarrel between Van Gogh and fellow artist Paul Gauguin, but it was not the trigger for Van Gogh's despair, according to the new study. The razor slash left Van Gogh bleeding copiously, and he gave the piece of ear to a young woman at a brothel. The bed depicted in Van Gogh's famous painting "The Bedroom" survived until after the Second World War and was donated to a community in the Netherlands. The bed was later donated by Van Gogh's nephew to an appeal for furniture to help villagers whose homes had been destroyed, but its current whereabouts are unknown. Van Gogh's paintings from this period in his life are among his best-loved works. The study, "Studio of the South: Van Gogh in Provence," is published by Frances Lincoln on November 3.

The Republican members of the House Ethics Committee have called for the public trials of Reps. Charlie Rangel (D-N.Y.) and Maxine Waters (D-Calif.) to be held before the November elections. The Republicans, led by Jo Bonner (R-Ala.), accused the committee chairwoman, Zoe Lofgren (D-Calif.), of stalling the proceedings and refusing to set trial dates. Bonner and his colleagues criticized Lofgren for not scheduling the trials even as the House prepares to adjourn until after November 2. The Republicans argued that it is in the best interest of transparency and fairness to complete the trials before the elections. The clash over the schedule for the Rangel-Waters trials is the worst public fight for the ethics committee since early 2005. Democrats were privately furious over the decision by Bonner and the other four Republicans to go public with their complaints about Lofgren. The Democratic aide also said that Lofgren "has lost control of the process." The Republicans stand to gain seats in the November election and possibly retake the majority, and have every interest in showcasing the ethics charges against two prominent Democrats. Rangel and Waters have both expressed a desire to have a chance to clear their names before the midterm vote.

The $43,000 phone booth installed by former EPA administrator Scott Pruitt in his office, initially estimated to cost $25,000, has come under scrutiny as newly released records show only one call was made to the White House, lasting five minutes. The phone booth was installed last year and was likened to a Sensitive Compartmented Information Facility (SCIF) for secure conversations, but the EPA has a SCIF at its headquarters on a different floor. Pruitt resigned last month amid ethics and management scandals, and the Government Accountability Office concluded that he violated federal spending laws by building the phone booth without providing advance notice to Congress. The new documents do not show how many incoming calls Pruitt received in the soundproof booth, and the EPA has not released complete phone logs. The Sierra Club, an environmental advocacy group, played a significant role in exposing Pruitt's spending decisions and has filed a lawsuit against his successor, acting administrator Andrew Wheeler, seeking more communications from EPA staff.

On Monday, a Denver man named Christopher Myers was attacked by a great white shark off Ballston Beach on Cape Cod. Myers and his 16-year-old son, J.J., were swimming several hundred meters offshore, close to known seal colonies, when Myers was bitten on his lower legs. Myers believes the shark grabbed his left foot and he kicked at what he thinks was the creature's snout, causing it to release him. Myers suffered serious injuries, including deep puncture wounds and severed tendons, and required over 40 stitches to close the gashes.

The attack was the first in 76 years on Cape Cod and set off a media furor. Lifeguards were on high alert, hundreds of spurious dorsal fin sightings were reported, and airborne spotters scanned the offshore swells for great white sharks. Massachusetts marine biologist Greg Skomal confirmed that the growing grey seal population is the reason for the increased presence of great white sharks in the Cape Cod area.

After the attack, Massachusetts tourism officials were battling to prevent a single attack from turning into a marketing nightmare. Betsy Wall, executive director of the Massachusetts Office of Travel and Tourism, advised people to stay away from seals. Myers, who is expected to make a full recovery, said he wishes shark warnings had been posted.

George Burgess, director of the Florida Program for Shark Research, said that humans disregarding the rules, such as swimming with seals in the area, can lead to attacks. Great whites, while not as ferocious as depicted in the movie Jaws, are dangerous and have been sighted with greater frequency in recent years off Cape Cod as seal populations have re-established themselves.

Myers vowed to return to the waters off Ballston Beach but said he will take to the waters with a bit more care. "I think I'll stick a little closer to the shore," he said. Myers is thankful for all who came to his aid and said he's not holding a grudge against the shark. "I'll be biting into a nice steak tonight and probably not thinking too hard about it," he said. "So I can't get too mad at the shark either."

Melvin Johnson, a community activist who advocated for an end to violence in Oakland after his son and grandson were killed in a shooting three years ago, was shot and killed on December 27, 2016, near a street memorial for his family. The shooting occurred on the east side of Oakland, not far from the memorial for his 16-month-old grandson and 20-year-old son, who were fatally shot in August 2013. Police have made no arrests and have not released a motive for Johnson's killing.

Johnson had moved his son, Andrew "Drew" Thomas, and grandson, Drew Leon Deon Jackson, to the central California city of Fresno to get them away from Oakland's street violence, but they were slain while in town for a birthday party. A shooter fired into a relative's home in the middle of the night, killing the sleeping pair. The slayings are still unsolved.

Johnson's mother, Carolyn Smith, spoke of her late son as a good person who was committed to his family following a series of tragedies. Another of his sons, 8-year-old Jahmel Johnson, died last month after a battle with lymphoma.

Johnson's business, Drewski Designs, which made T-shirts and clothing for picnics, anniversaries, funerals, and special events, helped people in the community. Authorities are offering up to $10,000 for tips on who killed Johnson, and a reward of up to $30,000 for information leading to an arrest in his son and grandson's killings is still being offered.

Oakland has seen triple-digit annual homicide rates and has been on the FBI's list of the 10 most dangerous cities in the country. Poverty is rampant in some areas, with gangs and drugs linked to as much as 90 percent of the killings. This year, the mayor said Oakland has seen a double-digit drop in overall shootings and violent crime. However, the blue-collar city of about 410,000 has yet to see the economic boom underway in neighboring San Francisco.

Joaquin "El Chapo" Guzman, the notorious Mexican drug lord and leader of the Sinaloa cartel, was transferred from a maximum-security prison in central Mexico to a prison in Ciudad Juarez, a city on the border with the United States. The move was made to improve security at the Altiplano prison where Guzman was previously held, but it has sparked speculation about his possible extradition to the US. Guzman has been indicted on drug trafficking charges in several US states, including New York, California, and Texas, and the US government has been preparing for his transfer for months. Guzman's lawyers have said that their client may be willing to plead guilty to drug trafficking charges in the US if certain conditions are met, but it is not clear when he will be extradited. Guzman has a history of escaping from prison, including a dramatic escape through a tunnel in 2015, and his transfer to a prison near the US border has raised concerns about his security. Guzman is accused of smuggling tons of drugs into the US and is wanted in several US jurisdictions.

The Internet Archive is working on a project to archive web pages as they are created and preserve links to archived pages when the original pages are changed or removed. This initiative aims to fix broken links on the web. In a separate news, Lonnie David Franklin Jr., a former garbage truck driver and LAPD garage attendant, was found guilty of murdering nine women and one girl over a span of three decades in Los Angeles. Known as "The Grim Sleeper," Franklin was convicted of all charges, including attempted murder, and is facing the penalty phase of his trial starting May 11. The trial featured the testimony of 61 witnesses, with prosecutors portraying Franklin as a sexual predator who killed his victims and dumped their bodies. The defense argued that the government's case was circumstantial and lacked evidence. The verdict follows a three-month trial, and Franklin's defense attorney has apologized for his behavior during the trial. The case was solved using DNA technology that did not exist when the initial killings occurred in the 1980s. Franklin had been charged with killing 10 victims, ranging in age from 15 to 35, from 1988 to 2007. The DNA evidence, including Franklin's saliva on many of his victims' breasts, along with ballistic evidence and the testimony of a surviving victim, were crucial in building the case against him. The prosecutor reminded jurors of a videotaped police interrogation of Franklin, in which he did not appear surprised about the allegations against him. The verdict brings some closure for the families of the victims.

In Houston, a 19-month-old girl named J'zyra Thompson died after being accidentally burned in an oven while her three siblings, aged 5, 3, and 3, were left home alone. The mother, Racquel Thompson, and her boyfriend were questioned by police, but it's unclear if they'll face charges.

An emergency hearing was held, and a judge ruled that the three surviving siblings will remain in foster care. The 5-year-old girl claims to have been sleeping when the incident occurred, while one of the 3-year-olds admitted to putting the baby in the oven.

CPS is providing counseling for the children to help them cope with the traumatic event. The next hearing regarding the custody of the children is scheduled for December 2.

Fredrick Price, the ex-boyfriend of Racquel Thompson, was looking for his two 3-year-old children who were also in the apartment during the incident. He had been trying to contact Racquel but had not received a response.

Court records show that CPS has concerns about Racquel Thompson and her boyfriend, including leaving the children home alone, driving without a license or car seats, and Thompson's pregnancy. The surviving children are currently in foster care as no suitable relatives could care for them.

Thompson has an older child living with his father and is seven months pregnant with her current boyfriend's child. No charges have been filed against Thompson or her boyfriend yet, but CPS workers expect criminal charges to be filed.

The U.S. Department of the Interior has announced that it will cancel two potential Arctic offshore lease sales in the Beaufort and Chukchi seas off Alaska's northern coast, citing current market conditions and low industry interest. This decision follows Royal Dutch Shell's announcement last month that it will stop Arctic activity due to "disappointing" test results. The government's decision has been welcomed by environmentalists, who argue that offshore drilling will pollute and damage a natural wilderness and must be avoided to prevent runaway climate change. The existing leases in the Beaufort and Chukchi seas will expire in 2017 and 2020, respectively. Shell has spent about $7bn on Arctic offshore development in the Chukchi and Beaufort seas, but has not found sufficient amounts of oil and gas to warrant further exploration. The US Geological Survey estimates that the Arctic holds about 30% of the world's undiscovered natural gas, as well as 13% of its oil. The U.S. government's decision to cancel the lease sales and deny lease extension requests from Shell and Statoil comes as the current low price of oil makes Arctic exploration even less attractive.

In a high-profile case that has reignited the debate over immigration policy, a jury on Thursday found an undocumented immigrant, Jose Ines Garcia Zarate, not guilty of murder and involuntary manslaughter charges in the 2015 death of Kate Steinle, a 32-year-old woman who was shot on a popular pier in San Francisco. The jury convicted Garcia Zarate of being a felon in possession of a firearm, which could bring a three-year sentence.

The shooting touched off a national immigration debate, as Garcia Zarate had been deported from the United States five times prior to Steinle's death. Before the shooting, officials in San Francisco released Garcia Zarate from custody instead of turning him over to immigration authorities, citing a sanctuary city law that limits cooperation with U.S. immigration authorities.

Prosecutors argued that Garcia Zarate intentionally shot Steinle with a Sig Sauer .40-caliber handgun as she and her father walked on the pier. However, Garcia Zarate's defense attorney said the shooting was accidental and the bullet ricocheted off the ground and traveled about 80 feet before hitting Steinle.

Reaction to the jury's decision was swift, with President Donald Trump calling the verdict "disgraceful" and Attorney General Jeff Sessions saying that San Francisco's sanctuary city policy was largely to blame for what happened that summer day. Conservative pundit Ann Coulter said Steinle "would still be alive if we had a wall," referring to the President's call for the construction of a border wall between the US and Mexico.

However, one of Garcia Zarate's lawyers said the debate over immigration didn't belong in the case. "From day one, this case was used as a means to foment hate, to foment division and to foment a program of mass deportation," public defender Francisco Ugarte said. "Nothing about Mr. Garcia Zarate's ethnicity, nothing about his immigration status, nothing about the fact that he is born in Mexico had any relevance as to what happened on July 1, 2015," the defense attorney said.

Steinle's family expressed disappointment in the verdict, with her father saying "justice was not served." The family did not attend court to hear the verdict and told the San Francisco Chronicle that they were looking forward to no longer being in the spotlight.

Immigration officials said they will try to deport Garcia Zarate, and the Department of Justice is considering bringing charges against him. U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement deputy director Tom Homan criticized San Francisco's sanctuary city policy and said that "following the conclusion of this case, ICE will work to take custody of Mr. Garcia Zarate and ultimately remove him from the country."

On August 5, 2013, two Sumatran tiger cubs were born at the Smithsonian's National Zoo in Washington, D.C. The mother, Damai, had been closely monitored by keepers who knew she was pregnant after observing her weight gain and unusual behavior. The cubs were delivered at 6:08 p.m. and 8:24 p.m., and both appeared healthy. The birth was a significant event as Sumatran tigers are critically endangered, with only 400 to 500 existing in the wild and only 65 in accredited zoos in North America. The cubs were described as weighing about two pounds, and their eyes were not yet open. The births followed a calculated, months-long keepers' vigil, which involved color-coded calendars. The cubs will not go outside for about 16 weeks and will undergo a series of health exams and vaccinations before being put on public exhibit. The cubs' sexes will not be known for four to six weeks, when they'll get their first physical exam. The births were a huge relief for keepers, who were anxious about the cubs' health and well-being. The cubs' father is the zoo's male Sumatran tiger, 12-year-old Kavi. The cubs' birth was celebrated as a conservation success, as every Sumatran tiger cub born in captivity helps to increase the population of this critically endangered species.

The article discusses the perceived privacy violations by tech companies like Facebook and Google, suggesting that critics focus excessively on these corporations while ignoring other privacy concerns, such as gossip among friends and acquaintances. The author proposes that the issue might be more about control than privacy, as people feel uncomfortable with the loss of control over their personal data. The author also questions the effectiveness of proposed solutions, such as legislation or self-reforms from media and tech companies, in addressing the control problem.

In a separate incident, George Mason economist and blogger Tyler Cowen was pepper-sprayed and placed under citizen's arrest while teaching a class on vigilante justice. The motive behind the attack is unclear, but it is speculated that it could be due to Cowen's libertarian beliefs. The author does not directly connect these two events, but suggests a broader reflection on the nature of privacy concerns and public discourse.

High Street retailers Barratts and Blockbuster have entered administration, putting over 3,000 jobs at risk. Duff & Phelps has been appointed as administrator for Barratts, citing difficult trading conditions as the cause. Blockbuster, with 2,000 employees, will continue trading while administrators Moorfields seek a sale of the business. Blockbuster's last in-store rental was made on Saturday, marking the end of in-store rentals. Customers who rented before the last day can return movies at any Blockbuster drop box location. Seth Rogen, star of the rented movie "This Is the End", has expressed his thoughts on the news on Twitter.

J.K. Rowling, the author of the Harry Potter series, was revealed to be the author of the crime novel "The Cuckoo's Calling" under the pseudonym Robert Galbraith. The book, published in April, features a private investigator named Cormoran Strike, who lost a leg in Afghanistan. The book quickly rose up the charts after Rowling's identity was disclosed. The book was published by Mulholland Books, an imprint of Hachette Book Group, and by a sister imprint in the U.K.

The book was initially described as being written by an author with military experience, which helped shape the novel. After the revelation, the book became a bestseller, with sales soaring on Amazon.com. A reprint of the book is underway, and the revised author biography will state that Robert Galbraith is a pseudonym for J.K. Rowling.

Rowling said in a statement that she hoped to keep her identity a secret, as writing under a pseudonym allowed her to write freely without expectations from her audience. The book received praise before Rowling's identity was revealed, but sales skyrocketed after the disclosure.

In other news, President Obama signed a new law that makes it a Federal crime for an individual to fraudulently claim military decorations or medals with the intent to obtain money, property, or other tangible benefits. The law is aimed at protecting real military heroes from phonies. The original Stolen Valor Act of 2005 was ruled unconstitutional by the Supreme Court, but a new version of the bill was introduced in 2012 and signed into law today. The law narrows the act to say the liar must be attempting to materially profit from the lies.

Mayor Rahm Emanuel of Chicago filed a lawsuit on Monday to block the Department of Justice from withholding police grant funding from sanctuary cities, as per the new conditions outlined by Attorney General Jeff Sessions' Justice Department. The lawsuit was filed in federal court and seeks to block the enforcement of three new conditions that Sessions included in applications for Edward Byrne Memorial Justice Assistance Grant money. The city uses this grant to fund an anti-violence program, purchase police cars, and other equipment.

The new conditions require sharing immigration status information with federal officials enforcing deportation laws, providing unlimited police station access to those officials, and giving them 48-hours notice of an arrested person's release in cases of potential immigration violations. City officials contend that they do share immigration status information when they have it, but that's rare because the city doesn't keep it in the normal course of business. Providing unfettered station access would interfere with police department practices, delay the release of people being held, and violate the 10th Amendment by "commandeering" local government functions, the lawsuit states. Holding people for 48 hours without a warrant or probable cause that they have committed a crime would violate 4th Amendment search and seizure limitations, it adds.

The suit also contends that the Justice Department has no authority to set conditions on the Byrne grant funding and is attempting to usurp the Congressional power of the purse. In short, the suit deems the conditions "unlawful and unconstitutional." This year, the city was counting on receiving $3.2 million from the grants in question, a relatively miniscule portion of the city's overall $9.8 billion budget.

The fate of Chicago's grant application would also affect other local Illinois governments that include their funding requests in Chicago's application, according to the lawsuit. They are Cook County, Bellwood, Calumet City, Chicago Heights, Cicero, Dolton, Evanston, Harvey, Maywood, Riverdale, and Skokie. The outcome of the suit could have ramifications for far-flung local and state governments with sanctuary laws on the books, including New York, Philadelphia, Miami, and the state of California.

The lawsuit has received mixed reactions. Some representatives of Chicago's immigrant community praised Emanuel for going to court to block the Trump administration's efforts, while others contend that Emanuel should do more to prevent police from helping federal officials deport Chicago immigrants who entered the country without the required legal documentation. U.S. Attorney General Jeff Sessions criticized Emanuel, saying "no amount of federal taxpayer dollars will help a city that refuses to help its own residents."

Groups like the Illinois Coalition for Immigration and Refugee Rights backed the mayor's move, with senior policy counsel Fred Tsao stating, "We are all for defending Chicago's policy with respect to immigration, and the law is on the side of the city." However, Tsao's group is part of a broader coalition that has been pushing Emanuel to remove four exemptions from the city's Welcoming City Ordinance, which sets its status as a sanctuary city.

Ald. Carlos Ramirez-Rosa, who has been pushing to get Chicago to join other cities that have eliminated similar exemptions, criticized Emanuel, stating, "It's quite funny and hypocritical that at the same time as (Emanuel is) putting forward this lawsuit saying that we want to defend the Constitution, here the ACLU has said that our own sanctuary city policy is in violation of the supreme law of the land." Ramirez-Rosa's view runs counter to the image Emanuel has tried to portray on the issue in mostly Democratic Chicago, which has a significant Latino population that's become increasingly politically active.

The article discusses the event "Phelps vs. Shark: Great Gold vs. Great White," which aired on Discovery Channel as part of Shark Week. The event was a simulated 100-meter race between 28-time Olympic medalist Michael Phelps and a great white shark. However, many viewers were disappointed as Phelps did not swim side-by-side with a real shark, but instead raced against a computer-generated image of a shark based on its swim rate. The event was filmed in Cape Town, South Africa, and Phelps was equipped with a monofin and a specially designed wetsuit to help him compete. In the end, the shark won the race by two seconds. The event received mixed reactions, with some viewers expressing disappointment and others understanding the safety concerns involved in swimming with a real shark. The article also mentions that Phelps has no hard feelings towards the sharks and hopes to raise awareness about the species.

Rutgers University has dismissed five football players following their arrests earlier this week, including four charged with aggravated assault, riot, and conspiracy to commit a riot for a fight that left a man with a broken jaw. The players, Nadir Barnwell, Dre Boggs, Ruhann Peele, Delon Stephenson, and Razohnn Gross, were also at the center of an investigation into whether coach Kyle Flood broke school and NCAA rules by contacting a teacher about a grade received by Barnwell. Boggs was also charged in two home-invasion robberies in April and May. The dismissals will leave Rutgers' secondary very thin, as three of the five were defensive backs expected to be key contributors this season. The investigation is part of an ongoing legal matter, and Rutgers officials have declined to comment. The revelation of a video capturing the assault is the latest wrinkle in a scandal that rocked the Rutgers University football program.

In a controversial move, New York Magazine published a profile on Soon-Yi Previn, wife of filmmaker Woody Allen, written by Daphne Merkin, a longtime friend of Allen. The article, published on Vulture, sees Previn breaking her silence on the longstanding controversy surrounding her husband, adoptive daughter Dylan Farrow, and ex-partner Mia Farrow. Previn alleges years of abuse by Mia Farrow.

Merkin's friendship with Allen, spanning over 40 years, has raised concerns about bias. The writer has publicly acknowledged her friendship with Allen, and her website mentions that Allen was her first fan letter recipient. Merkin has also gushed over Allen in her book The Fame Lunches, stating that he was her alter ego and that she wrote him a letter in her early 20s.

Critics, including several journalists and New York colleagues, have condemned the publication for allowing a sympathetic figure to write the profile. Dylan Farrow's brother Ronan, a strong supporter of Dylan, issued a statement criticizing the story, stating that it was a hit job written by a longtime admirer and friend of Woody Allen's. Dylan also tweeted a lengthy statement, expressing disappointment in allowing a friend of an alleged predator to write a one-sided piece attacking the credibility of his victim.

New York Magazine spokesperson Lauren Starke defended the story, stating that Soon-Yi Previn is telling her story for the first time and that the piece is transparent about being told from Previn's point of view. Starke also mentioned that Merkin approached Previn about doing the piece, not vice versa.

Merkin's history with Allen beyond their friendship is not extensively detailed in the article. However, her previous encounters with Allen, such as his support during her depression and encouragement as a writer, have raised questions about a potential conflict of interest. Critics argue that having someone with an apparent conflict of interest defend an accused child molester, without a response from the accuser, is questionable journalistically.

The controversy has sparked a debate on social media, with many expressing disappointment in the decision to have Merkin write the profile, given her history with Allen. Critics argue that the piece lacks journalistic integrity and brings no understanding of Previn, instead focusing on attacks on Mia Farrow.

Greece is under pressure to find an additional 1.5 billion euros in savings to satisfy its creditors, who are currently evaluating the country's progress in complying with the terms of its latest bailout. The Greek government has agreed on most of the austerity measures but is struggling to reach a consensus on pension and wage cuts among the three parties in the conservative-led administration. The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has expressed its willingness to stay in Athens until the savings plan is finalized.

Greece is facing a fifth year of recession, record unemployment, and repeated waves of austerity cuts. The country's leaders are discussing possible layoffs of contractors in the public sector, a cap on pensions, cuts in welfare benefits, reductions in tax exemptions, lower salaries for public employees, and raising the retirement age to make up the shortfall in savings.

German Finance Minister Wolfgang Schaeuble has stated that he cannot see room for further concessions to Greece and is insisting that the country must implement far-reaching reforms and cut its budget deficit. The inspectors' report, expected in September, will determine whether Greece continues to receive rescue loans or faces a disorderly bankruptcy and exit from the euro. The public mood in Greece is increasingly angry towards the troika and the austerity measures they have imposed.

The Utah legislature has passed a bill that could potentially criminalize miscarriages and certain instances of induced abortion, causing concern among women's rights advocates. The bill, which is awaiting the governor's signature, amends Utah's criminal statute to allow the state to charge a woman with criminal homicide for inducing a miscarriage or obtaining an illegal abortion. The bill's uniqueness lies in its punitive nature towards pregnant women, rather than those who might assist or cause an illegal abortion or unintended miscarriage.

The bill criminalizes an intentional attempt to induce a miscarriage or abortion, and creates a standard of "reckless behavior" that could make women legally responsible for miscarriages caused by actions thought to increase the risk of miscarriage, even if the woman did not intend to lose the pregnancy. This could potentially lead to prosecution for actions such as drinking too much alcohol, failing to wear a seatbelt, or falling down stairs.

Critics argue that the bill is dangerous and could lead to the criminalization of many common actions, leaving a large number of pregnant women vulnerable to arrest. They also express concern that the law could drive pregnant women with substance abuse problems "underground," afraid to seek treatment lest they have a miscarriage and be charged for murder.

The bill does exempt fetal deaths due to failure to follow medical advice, accept treatment, or refuse a cesarean section. However, critics argue that the standard is too broad and could potentially lead to the prosecution of pregnant women for actions that are not intended to cause a miscarriage.

The bill has been met with opposition from organizations such as Planned Parenthood and the ACLU of Utah, who have worked to amend the bill and mitigate its worst aspects. However, the bill's passage has sparked debate and concern about the potential impact on women's rights and reproductive health in Utah.

The court hearing for actress Lindsay Lohan has concluded, with the focus now on her reactions and potential responses to questions. Currently, she is still inside the courtroom, discussing matters related to her SCRAM bracelet fitting. In an exclusive interview with Sheeraz Hasan of HOLLYWOOD.TV, Lohan addressed various rumors, including the controversy surrounding a "cocaine" photograph, her DUI court situation, her relationship with her father, Michael Lohan, allegations of drug use, and her emotional admission about missing her brother's graduation. The interview took place on May 23rd, 2010, in Beverly Hills.

The article discusses the ongoing electricity crisis in Pakistan, which has been exacerbated by a $5 billion "circular debt" of unpaid bills across society. This debt has crippled the power sector, leading to frequent power outages and slowdowns in power plants. The crisis has hit hardest in Punjab, with businesses like Malik Mazhar Iqbal Awan's small marble factory suffering as a result.

The crisis has become a significant political issue, with the public galvanized more so than by Islamist militancy. Nawaz Sharif, a former steel baron, won the May 11 election in part due to his promises to deliver a "shining Pakistan" and end the darkness. However, analysts question whether Sharif has the political will to make the tough decisions needed to change the system, particularly as some of his own supporters are among the bill defaulters.

Experts say that while easing the $5 billion "circular debt" is the principal problem, money is only part of the solution. Deep-rooted structural issues, exacerbated by political interference and systemic graft, lie at the heart of Pakistan's power crisis. Electricity theft, both by rich and poor, is common, with slum dwellers stealing power through illegal connections and powerful politicians and government departments simply refusing to pay their bills.

Corruption is also rampant in the private power sector, with political supporters winning lucrative contracts at inflated costs or without even producing a megawatt of power. In 2011, the auditor general noted that the government had committed to $1.7 billion in such contracts, yet added just 62 megawatts to the national power grid.

The crisis is estimated to be equivalent to at least 4% of the country's gross domestic product, greater than the estimated economic cost of the Taliban insurgency. In the short term, Sharif will seek foreign cash or fuel to get dormant power stations back online, with Saudi Arabia offering up to $15 billion worth of emergency oil supplies on favorable terms. However, oil and money can only provide temporary relief, and Sharif may also seek foreign assistance to tackle the structural problems.

The United States has spent $225 million since 2009 in refurbishing Pakistan's hydroelectric power plants, adding 900 megawatts to the national grid. However, large-scale infrastructure projects take years to come to fruition, and international donors are reluctant to commit further funds without signs of strong reform from Pakistan's political leadership. Pakistan's leaders know they are running out of time, as the country's rapidly growing population adds 1,000 megawatts per year to the country's electricity needs.

Two Northwestern University freshmen, Anthony Morales and Matthew Kafker, were arrested and charged with vandalizing a campus chapel. The vandalism included racist, homophobic, and anti-Semitic slurs, a swastika, and the word "Trump" spray-painted on walls and furniture. The incident occurred around 12:45 a.m. on Friday, and the freshmen were captured on surveillance video entering the chapel without permission. The vandalism was discovered later that morning, and the university estimated the damage to be over $300. The judge ordered both men held in lieu of $50,000 bail for charges of institutional vandalism, hate crime to a place of worship, and criminal damage to property. The freshmen appeared in court wearing T-shirts and jeans, and neither spoke during the hearing. The judge expressed her disapproval of their actions, and the mother of one of the defendants cried during the hearing. The chapel continued with its usual Sunday service after most of the graffiti was removed over the weekend. The motive for the vandalism is unknown.

A Belgian woman, Florence Heene, has found her biological father after a lifelong search, thanks to a Canadian family who recognized their late grandfather in photos published in a news article. Herbert Louis Hellyer, a Canadian soldier, was stationed in Ghent, Belgium during World War II and had a relationship with Heene's mother, Augusta Ryckoort. Hellyer died in 1948, and his family, who live in British Columbia, have been in contact with Heene through Facebook.

Heene's mother, Augusta, had a difficult childhood after her father left for the war and was infected with tuberculosis. The children were sent to foster homes, and it wasn't until her father returned that the family was reunited. However, the reunion was not happy, as her father was temperamental and despondent, likely due to his brain injuries.

Hellyer's family has filled in some details about his life. He was born in England and emigrated to Canada as a boy. He became a printer by trade and had five children before enlisting as a soldier in 1939 and heading off to Europe. During the war, he was injured and later died by suicide in a Vancouver hospital in 1948.

Heene is sad that her father died tragically, but is happy to have found a "new family" in Canada. She first saw the man she believes is her biological father while rummaging through a box of photos as a child. Her mother originally told her the soldiers in the photos were uncles, but eventually admitted that one of them was her biological father, with whom she had a relationship when he was stationed in Ghent.

The family hopes to meet Heene and welcome her into their family. Despite her own family dynamics, Janes, one of Hellyer's daughters, wants to get acquainted with her newly discovered half-sister. She hasn't yet been in contact with Heene, but hopes to soon.

The search for Herbert has gained some traction in Canada, but it's far from over. Florence still needs help finding out more about him, including if he is still alive or how and when he died, and if she has any other (half) brothers or sisters. If anyone recognizes the photo of Herbert, they are asked to contact Florence.

Astronauts on spacewalks consistently encounter an unusual odor in space, which they describe as a mix of seared steak, hot metal, and welding fumes. This peculiar smell is attributed to atomic oxygen and high-energy vibrations of ions. Upon returning to the space station, the interior smells more mundane, a mix of machine shop, engine room, laboratory, and roast beef from food packages. Rookie astronauts, including Kevin Ford and Nicole Stott, have described their first spaceflight experiences as having a distinct smell and a different environment than expected. The space station, a $100 billion collaboration of 16 countries, is currently home to 13 astronauts, with Discovery's seven-astronaut crew delivering fresh supplies, new science gear, and a $5 million treadmill named after comedian Stephen Colbert. The astronauts are also enjoying an international smorgasbord of food from various partners.

On Thursday, a shooting occurred at a Rite Aid distribution center in Harford County, Maryland, near Aberdeen. A temporary employee, identified as Snochia Moseley, 26, from Baltimore County, fatally shot three co-workers and injured three others before taking her own life. The motive for the shooting is unknown.

The shooting began outside the facility and continued inside, according to Harford County Sheriff Jeffrey Gahler. Deputies arrived at the scene within five minutes of receiving a call about the shooting. The gun used in the shooting was a 9 mm Glock handgun, which was legally owned by Moseley.

The victims were taken to Johns Hopkins Bayview Medical Center and Christiana Hospital in Newark, Delaware. Two victims died at the scene, and two more died at the hospital. The other three victims are reported to be in stable condition.

The shooting is one of three to occur in U.S. workplaces in the past 24 hours. On Wednesday, shootings occurred at a software company in Middleton, Wisconsin, and at a municipal building in Masontown, Pennsylvania. The shooters in both of those incidents were killed by police.

The shooting in Harford County marks the third high-profile shooting in the county in the past year. In June, a gunman stormed the Capital Gazette newsroom in Annapolis, killing five staff members. In October 2017, three co-workers were killed at a kitchen countertop company in Edgewood, less than 10 miles away.

The shooting has sparked outrage and calls for action against gun violence. Former U.S. Representative Gabrielle Giffords, who was shot in the head at a "Congress on Your Corner" event in 2011, said, "Three workplace active shooting attacks in just the last 24 hours should spark outrage in every American." Giffords has become an anti-gun violence activist.

The Rite Aid distribution center has been closed, and grief counselors are being made available to employees. The facility will remain closed until it is reopened and assessed for safety. The Harford County Emergency Operations Center has been partially activated, and a family reunification center has been set up at the Level Fire Company in Havre de Grace. The Harford County Information Hotline at 410-838-5800 has been activated for people trying to get in touch with family and loved ones.

The New York Police Department is investigating the theft and subsequent return of two high-value photograph prints, worth $105,000, from the MoMA PS1 Annex in Long Island City, Queens. The stolen works, part of the exhibit "Carolee Schneemann: Kinetic Painting," were discovered missing on October 30, but were anonymously mailed back to the museum on November 3.

Surveillance video from a shipping store in Williamsburg, Brooklyn, shows a woman mailing the photos in a large box. The woman is described as white, in her twenties, wearing a dark cap, glasses, a black overcoat, tan pants, and tan shoes. The NYPD is asking for the public's help in identifying the woman, and anyone with information is encouraged to contact the Crime Stoppers Hotline.

The theft and return of the photographs remain a mystery, with speculation that the thief may have had a change of heart or that the works were returned by a third party. The museum does not have surveillance cameras, and there was no sign of forced entry or damage to the photographs. The security alarm was activated but did not go off.

The two works are titled CS in the broken mirrors on the back of Four Fur Cutting Boards (1965) and CS With Gloves (Radiator), 1965, and are on loan from the artist and New York galleries P.P.O.W. Gallery and Galerie Lelong. The museum declined to comment on the ongoing investigation.

The article discusses the group known as Antifa, a left-wing activist movement that emerged as a response to the growing presence of right-wing extremism. Antifa is not a monolithic organization but rather a collection of local groups concentrated in Texas and the Northwest, with no national structure. The group's members have varying political ideologies, with some identifying as anarchists, Marxists, or simply anti-fascists.

Antifa's primary goal is to confront, expose, shame, and sometimes convert white supremacists. Their methods are often aggressive, and they are not afraid to use force when necessary. This has led to clashes with right-wing extremist groups, most notably during the violent events in Charlottesville, Virginia, this month.

The article notes that while Antifa has not been responsible for any politically motivated killings, right-wing extremists have been responsible for a disproportionate number of such incidents over the past decade. Antifa's aggressive tactics have been criticized by some on the left, including Noam Chomsky, who considers them a distraction from practical tasks and a gift to the right.

The article also discusses the hypermasculine bravado that is prevalent within Antifa circles, with a majority of members being men who prioritize muscularity. Some Antifa activists draw inspiration from left-wing paramilitaries of Weimar Germany and the Black Panther Party, despite the historical precedent of these groups being crushed by authoritarian regimes.

The article concludes by noting that Antifa is likely to grow as a result of the anti-Trump wave, increasing the potential for armed clashes, especially in open-carry states. Right-wing extremist groups, emboldened by the Trump administration, are also training and preparing for confrontations with Antifa. The article warns that more Charlottesville-like incidents may occur in the future.

Racked, a consumer culture publication, is ceasing operations and its staff is moving to Vox.com's The Goods. Over 200 women in 40 states have filed a class action lawsuit against Wen by Chaz Dean and its infomercial owner Guthy-Renker, alleging that Wen's cleansers cause hair loss and scalp injuries. The lawsuit claims that Guthy-Renker removed negative online reviews about the products and blocked comments about hair loss from Wen's Facebook page.

The complaint alleges that Wen's products contain a caustic ingredient that damages hair and follicles. Guthy-Renker denies that Wen is defective or responsible for hair loss. The first four ingredients in many Wen cleansers are water, glycerin, cetyl alcohol, and cetearyl alcohol, which are commonly used in hair products. Wen does contain a chemical banned in the EU, hydroxycitronella.

Amy Davis, the Dallas-based attorney and lead counsel for the plaintiffs, said that her firm hired chemists to test Wen. "What we understand about the product and how it causes hair loss is it contains virtually no cleanser," she told a local CBS station. "It’s like using lotion to wash your hair, so instead of removing the product, when you rinse it off, it just becomes impacted in your hair follicle."

The lawsuit could have a tough road ahead, as determining the cause of hair loss in women can be extremely complicated. The plaintiffs are heading to mediation, and both sides have agreed to refrain from making extrajudicial statements about the case.

The Internet Archive is working on a project to preserve web pages as they are created and archive pages that they refer to. This aims to maintain a record of the original content even if the linked pages are altered or removed. The goal is to fix broken links on the web by replacing them with links to the archived versions or providing a companion link to view the original content.

In a separate development, the identity of a victim from the 1992 Los Angeles riots, Armando Ortiz Hernandez, has been revealed after 25 years. Hernandez, who was 18 at the time, died from smoke inhalation, thermal burns, and carbon monoxide poisoning during the looting and violence that ensued after the acquittal of four white police officers in the beating of black motorist Rodney King. His body was found inside an auto parts shop that was set ablaze during the riots in South Los Angeles.

Investigators were able to lift a single fingerprint from Hernandez's left middle finger, but it's unclear if his fingerprints had been run through databases previously. Attempts to reach Hernandez's family members were unsuccessful. The riots, which were one of the deadliest race riots in American history, resulted in 53 deaths and over 2,000 injuries.

This summary covers the efforts to preserve web pages and the identification of a victim from the 1992 Los Angeles riots after 25 years.

Nine former professional hockey players have filed a lawsuit against the NHL, alleging that the league intentionally created, fostered, and promoted a culture of extreme violence, leading to long-term negative health consequences for the players. The lawsuit, filed in federal court in Manhattan, claims that the NHL failed to take adequate steps to warn players of the dangers of the sport and deliberately promoted violence for profit.

The complaint is more graphic than other suits brought by former hockey players, highlighting the role of enforcers in the NHL over many years and mentioning movies that celebrated fighting in hockey. The plaintiffs include former players Dan LaCouture, Dan Keczmer, Jack Carlson, Richard Brennan, Brad Maxwell, Michael Peluso, Tom Younghans, Allan Rourke, and Scott Bailey. Some of the players were brawlers, like Carlson, who racked up 1,111 penalty minutes in the NHL and the World Hockey Association. Peluso, who played in the NHL from 1990 to 1998, led the league with 408 penalty minutes in 1991-92 and fought 179 times in his nine-year career.

The case will be heard by Judge Shira A. Scheindlin of Federal District Court in Manhattan. This is the latest lawsuit involving violence in the NHL. In May, the family of Derek Boogaard filed a wrongful-death lawsuit against the NHL, saying the league was responsible for the physical trauma and brain damage Boogaard sustained in six seasons as one of the league's top enforcers. Boogaard died of an accidental overdose of prescription painkillers and alcohol in 2011.

In November, a group of players who were in the league in the 1970s, '80s, and '90s filed a lawsuit in federal court in Washington, saying NHL officials should have done more to address head injuries but instead celebrated a culture of speed and violence. The NHL set up a concussion study program in 1997, the first in North American major league sports, and has in recent years modified rules to address head trauma. However, the lawsuit calls those moves "untimely and ineffective."

The plaintiffs are seeking unspecified compensatory and punitive damages, and the NHL has stated that it intends to defend the case vigorously. The lawsuit comes as the NHL faces increased scrutiny about its policies regarding head injuries and concussions, with players like Sidney Crosby missing large chunks of games due to concussion symptoms and former players like Derek Boogaard dying tragically due to brain injuries.

The October issue of Elle magazine features Gabourey Sidibe on one of its four covers, marking her first fashion magazine cover. Lifetime's new reality show, Born in the Wild, is causing controversy as it documents pregnant women giving birth outdoors, unassisted by doctors. A remote Brazilian island, Fernando de Noronha, has welcomed its first baby in 12 years, breaking a long-standing ban on births. The unidentified 22-year-old mother, who was unaware of her pregnancy, gave birth at home on Saturday. A tragic nightclub fire in Santa Maria, Brazil, claimed at least 245 lives and injured over 200 people on January 27, 2013. The fire, caused by pyrotechnics used by a band for visual effects, set the building ablaze, causing a stampede towards blocked and overcrowded exits. Most victims died from smoke inhalation, while others were crushed in the ensuing panic. The tragedy occurred in a region known for its strict and organized culture, and authorities are investigating safety violations at the club.
