The cause of the fire is still under investigation, and authorities are offering support and condolences.

The orca whale named J35, also known as Tahlequah, has finally dropped her dead calf after carrying it for 17 days and over 1,000 miles off the Pacific Northwest coast. This prolonged mourning behavior, which drew international attention, is a confirmation of the complex emotional lives of orcas and similar animals like dolphins. J35 is a 20-year-old member of the J Pod of Southern Resident Killer Whales, a group of orcas that inhabit a large territory including waters off Seattle, Vancouver, and Victoria, British Columbia.

Researchers were concerned about J35's health during her "tour of grief," but she appears to have made it through physically unharmed. Experts believe that J35's grief may be deeper because she had the chance to form an emotional connection with her baby before it died, after a 17-month gestation period. The death of the calf is a significant blow to J Pod, which hasn't seen a successful birth in three years. The three pods have a total of 75 members, and experts give the population five more years before it becomes extinct.

The lack of food is cited as the main culprit for the orcas' struggles, as they are dependent on Chinook salmon for their primary food source, which is also endangered. Experts expressed relief that J35 survived, as she is a crucial member of the pod in her prime. However, they emphasize that the population is in crisis and needs stewardship and support to survive.

J35's actions are unprecedented, and the traumatic scene has weighed on scientists who closely monitor the whales. J35 is in good health and is being fed by her close family, including her son J47. An audio recording of what appeared to be J35 making "mournful and prominent" calls was also released.

Government officials, scientists, and volunteers are warning off vessels approaching J35 and her pod, and are urging mariners to respect the rules and regulations put in place to ensure the whales are protected and not disturbed. The population of Southern Resident killer whales is endangered, with only 75 whales in J-pod, and a four-year-old whale known as J-50 is cause for concern as she looks underfed. Researchers plan to use photogrammetry from a distance in the coming days to see how she's faring.

Members of the pod are now taking turns floating the body of the newborn calf that died more than a week ago, sparking concerns that they may tire themselves out. The Whale Museum released an audio recording of the mother communicating with her pod, using a series of calls and whistles to communicate and echo-location to pick up food sources and map their underwater environment. Researchers believe the whales are holding their own version of a wake or funeral for the calf.

Mike Megna, a former Marine and police officer, is suffering from a rare kidney disease that he believes was caused by his work at Ground Zero following the September 11 attacks. Megna spent three weeks at the site, helping in the rescue efforts, and has since developed a condition where his bone marrow produces defective antibodies that attack his kidneys. His illness is not currently covered by the fund set up to help 9/11 workers who developed health problems as a result of their work at the site.

Megna's kidney ailment was only recently named by researchers at the Mayo Clinic, and his case is so rare that it has only been found in 20 people so far. In his frustration, Megna has taken out two billboards, one on Route 3 across from MetLife Stadium and another on an approach to the Holland Tunnel, pleading his case and urging motorists to call the top administrator of the World Trade Center Health Program. The billboards also mention his website, www.DoRightByMike.com, where his story is told.

John Howard, the director of the Fund, had no comment, and the National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health, the federal agency that determines which diseases qualify for compensation, also declined to comment. Megna has been told he needs to wait until medical researchers can prove a link between 9/11 exposure and his illness. However, Megna argues that he should not have to wait, as he did not wait to go to Ground Zero to help with the rescue efforts.

Megna was working as a police officer in Pompton Lakes on the day of the attacks and went to the city with his two brothers, who were sheriff's deputies in two counties. They had not heard from their father, a Port Authority police officer, and went to the site to help with the rescue efforts. After locating their father safe and sound, Megna and his brothers stayed to help with the rescue efforts, often working as part of the "bucket brigade" clearing debris.

Megna returned to the site nearly every day after work for as long as hope remained there might be survivors. In 2007, he started urinating blood, and after countless rounds of testing, his doctors could determine only that his bone marrow was producing some substance that was slowly attacking his kidneys. As his condition worsened, he became chronically anemic from the blood loss and was eventually forced to go on disability.

Megna's financial situation has also been affected, as he has stopped paying his mortgage and assuring his bank he would catch up on payments once he got money from the September 11th fund. When his application for a compensation award was rejected, the bank began foreclosure proceedings.

Megna had a follow-up biopsy earlier this year, and this time, to the surprise of his Veterans Administration doctor, the lab report came back with a diagnosis: "Monotype atypical anti-GBM nephritis." The disease had been documented by the Mayo Clinic, which had found it in just 20 people so far. Megna headed to Minnesota recently to meet with doctors, a trip funded by New York State's Workman's Compensation, which has a special fund set up for Ground Zero volunteers.

Stephen Erickson, Megna's Mayo Clinic nephrologist, explained his ailment is a rare variation of an already rare kidney disease. The antibodies of the human immune system are produced in the bone marrow. Any defective antibodies are usually filtered out by the kidneys. In Megna's case, however, his defective antibodies actually attack the kidney filters, Erickson said. Since chemotherapy might do more harm than good, Erickson recommended more waiting – in this case, waiting until a better treatment comes along.

Megna's mood changes moment to moment these days: He can be agitated, perched excitedly on the edge of his couch, raging against all the closed doors he has encountered. The very next minute, he'll slump back and say with a resigned wave of his hand, "I hate them all." Megna's brother Christopher, a retired sheriff's officer who has his own crop of 9/11-related medical problems, describes Megna as depressed and says he has gained weight and grown a beard as a sign he has given up. Megna insists he is not asking for a pity party and wonders how much sicker he has to get before he is compensated.

The problem is that the Fund awards compensation only if a person's illness has been scientifically associated with exposure to the terrorist attack sites. The Zadroga Act, which sets aside taxpayer funds to deal with the long-term health damage of 9/11, lays out the steps that must be taken to qualify for money: Researchers must first gather information about how many 9/11 responders have developed a condition, then compare it with the percentage of the general population that would come down with the same disease. Only if the 9/11 group's rate is higher than that of the general population can an illness be placed on the list of ailments that entitles the victim to a payout.

The World Trade Center Health Program funds some of the research projects aimed at establishing a connection between 9/11 exposure and illnesses. One of those grants is to researchers at Mt. Sinai Hospital to look into kidney ailments. An earlier study had pointed to a link, but not a strong enough one to get kidney problems on the list. That could change with new information, Spring said. "Some health conditions will take decades to show up," she said.

Megna's case is a reminder of the long-term health effects that many 9/11 responders are still facing, and the struggle to get the compensation they deserve.

The updated guidelines for Alzheimer's disease, released by the National Institute on Aging and the Alzheimer's Association, expand the definition of the disease to include patients with early-stage symptoms. The new guidelines divide Alzheimer's into three stages: dementia, mild cognitive impairment, and a recently discovered phase with no symptoms but brain changes.

The guidelines emphasize the importance of studying biomarkers, physiological indicators that someone is likely to develop dementia, for earlier diagnosis. However, the tests for these biomarkers are not yet standardized, and their results are not ready for clinical usage.

The guidelines also clarify diagnosis criteria for people with dementia symptoms, distinguishing Alzheimer's from other dementias, such as vascular, fronto-temporal, and Lewy body. The guidelines note that the earliest symptom of Alzheimer's dementia is not always memory loss but could be mood changes or problems with language, spatial perception, or reasoning.

The new guidelines aim to encourage more research to develop drugs to attack early brain changes and identify people who might benefit from such drugs when they become available. The goal is to extend the range of our ability to investigate Alzheimer's disease and find the treatment necessary to avoid the epidemic of Alzheimer's disease over the next 40 years.

The biggest impact of the guidelines is expected to be seen with people who fall into the middle phase, those with mild cognitive impairment linked to Alzheimer's. Experts suggest that at least as many people experience this phase as the 5.4 million people estimated to have Alzheimer's dementia.

The guidelines also acknowledge that earlier diagnosis would enable patients to make plans about their lives when they are better equipped to make such decisions. Once medications become available that are proven to slow the progress of the disease, doctors hope that Alzheimer's patients can begin taking them earlier.

However, there is no conclusive evidence that currently available drugs are effective in slowing down the disease, and several clinical trials of experimental treatments have been disappointing in recent years. The guidelines urge caution because there is currently no drug known to halt or significantly delay the onset of symptoms.

Paul Ceglia, the man who sued Facebook and CEO Mark Zuckerberg for 84% of the company in 2010, has been indicted on federal charges of wire and mail fraud. On July 11, 2014, a Florida court sentenced Ivins Rosier, then 17, to a 23-year prison term for the shooting of a retired Florida Highway Patrol (FHP) trooper's police dog, Drake. The incident occurred on November 21, 2012, when Rosier was questioned by Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office Detective Philip DiMola regarding a burglary. During the interrogation, DiMola emphasized that shooting the dog and causing its death would be considered the murder of a law enforcement officer.

Rosier confessed to the shooting and Drake was euthanized two days later. He was charged as an adult and stood trial, although not for the murder of a police officer due to Drake's retirement status. The jury found him guilty of cruelty to animals with a firearm, burglary of a dwelling with a firearm, and shooting into a building.

Circuit Judge Robin Rosenberg ordered Rosier to be held without bail at the Palm Beach County Jail. Defense attorneys Jack Fleischman and Rachel Preefer announced plans for a new trial and legal challenges, including revisiting the argument that Rosier's indictment violates his right to be sentenced as a juvenile, which would result in less prison time for the offenses.

Fleischman also intends to reiterate his closing arguments from Thursday, stating that there is insufficient evidence to prove Rosier's guilt beyond a reasonable doubt, despite the defendant's confession and GPS ankle monitor records showing Rosier was inside the trooper's home on the night of the crimes.

In a significant political shift, top House and Senate Democrats announced an agreement with President Donald Trump on Wednesday to protect hundreds of thousands of young undocumented immigrants, known as Dreamers, from deportation. The deal, reached after a White House dinner, would enshrine protections for the nearly 800,000 immigrants who had benefited from the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) program, which provided temporary work permits and protection from deportation.

The agreement specifies bipartisan legislation called the DREAM Act, which provides eventual citizenship for the young immigrants. The deal, however, does not include funding for Trump's long-sought border wall. Trump ended the DACA program earlier this month, giving Congress six months to come up with a legislative fix before the statuses of the Dreamers begin to expire.

The apparent deal is the latest example of Trump's sudden pivot to bipartisanship after months of railing against Democrats as "obstructionist." The president has urged them to join him in overhauling the nation's tax code, among other priorities. The agreement on DACA is a positive step towards the president's commitment to bipartisan solutions, according to the White House.

During a White House meeting with moderate House members from both parties earlier Wednesday, Trump had urged lawmakers to come up with a bipartisan solution. "We don't want to forget DACA," Trump told the members at the meeting. "We want to see if we can do something in a bipartisan fashion so that we can solve the DACA problem and other immigration problems."

The agreement on DACA is a significant political development, as it represents a major shift for a president who made promises of tougher border control policies the centerpiece of his campaign and pledged to build a "big, beautiful wall" along the U.S.-Mexico border. A majority of Republicans, especially in the House, have long opposed offering legal status, and a path to citizenship, to the nation’s more than 11 million undocumented immigrants.

The deal, however, is not without controversy. Some conservative supporters of Trump have criticized the agreement, with Rep. Steve King (R-Iowa), an immigration hard-liner and early Trump supporter, writing that if reports of a potential immigration deal are accurate, the president’s “base is blown up, destroyed, irreparable, and disillusioned beyond repair. No promise is credible.”

The agreement on DACA is a positive step towards addressing the plight of the Dreamers, but the details of the deal, particularly regarding border security, are still being negotiated. The deal is a significant political development, as it represents a major shift for a president who made promises of tougher border control policies the centerpiece of his campaign. The agreement is also a positive step towards bipartisanship, as Trump has urged Democrats to join him in overhauling the nation's tax code, among other priorities. However, the agreement is not without controversy, as some conservative supporters of Trump have criticized the deal.

The hacked online cheating service Ashley Madison, owned by Avid Life Media, is facing allegations of hypocrisy after leaked emails suggest that a former executive hacked into a competing dating service in 2012. Emails released from the recent hacking leak indicate that Raja Bhatia, Ashley Madison's former CTO, informed CEO Noel Biderman of a security hole in Nerve.com's website and used it to exfiltrate the competitor's entire user database. Bhatia also claimed the ability to alter records and turn non-paying users into paying users.

Bhatia was the founding CTO of Avid Life Media but left the company by 2010. In the email exchange, he posted a sample of the stolen database on GitHub, although the post is no longer available online. Six months later, Biderman discussed whether he should disclose the vulnerability to Nerve.com, but there is no apparent response among the leaked emails.

If Bhatia did hack Nerve.com and exfiltrate its database, he could be criminally charged under the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act. The irony lies in Bhatia discussing a vulnerability in Nerve.com's website, as other emails show that he was aware of AshleyMadison.com's own security issues, which the Impact Team exploited in the recent hack.

In 2012, Nerve.com was a dating platform that Avid Life Media considered purchasing. Emails show that Avid Life Media began considering the purchase after a suggestion from Rufus Grissom, a VP with Babble.com. However, it's unclear if Avid Life Media disclosed the vulnerability to Nerve.com.

The emails also reveal that Ashley Madison was approached with offers to partner with or invest in Nerve.com and Flirts.com, but Ashley Madison ultimately declined to pursue a deal. Neither Bhatia nor Biderman responded to requests for comment from WIRED.

The hack on Ashley Madison has caused significant damage, with the Impact Team releasing personal data on more than 30 million users. The leaked emails also show that Ashley Madison's parent firm was aware of its own vulnerabilities, including XSS/CRSF vulnerabilities and SQL injection/data leaks. The Toronto Police have announced a $500,000 reward for information leading to the arrest and prosecution of the hackers, but some critics argue that the reward should have been offered earlier. The Impact Team has not yet released data from the other Avid Life Media property they claim to have hacked, Establishedmen.com.

This news article discusses the highest-paid public university presidents in the United States for the 2011-12 fiscal year, as reported by The Chronicle of Higher Education. Graham B. Spanier, the president of Pennsylvania State University, topped the list with a compensation of $2.9 million, including severance and deferred pay, despite being forced out due to a child sex abuse scandal involving a football coach.

Other presidents with compensation exceeding $1 million were Jay Gogue of Auburn University, E. Gordon Gee of Ohio State University, and Alan G. Merten of George Mason University. Notably, Mr. Gee's base salary was the highest among the 212 chief executives, at $830,439.

Cigarroa of the University of Texas system.

The town of Amesbury, located in Wiltshire, has been confirmed as the longest continuously inhabited settlement in the United Kingdom, dating back to 8820BC. This discovery was made during an archaeological dig at the Blick Mead site, which also unearthed evidence of frogs' legs being eaten in Britain 8,000 years before France. The findings suggest that the first monuments at Stonehenge, another famous historic site in Wiltshire, were built by the same people who lived in Amesbury.

David Jacques, from the University of Buckingham, led the dig and stated that the site provides evidence for people staying put, clearing land, building, and presumably worshipping monuments. He believes that Amesbury was a hub point for people to come from many miles away and was a forerunner for what later went on at Stonehenge. The first monuments at Stonehenge were built by these people, according to Jacques.

The River Avon, which runs through Amesbury, would have been like an A road with people traveling along it, and there would have been feasting, according to Jacques. Remains of big game animals, such as aurochs and red deer, and an enormous amount of burnt flint from their feasting fires were found during the dig.

Previously, Thatcham in Berkshire held the record for the longest continuous settlement in the country. The dig in Amesbury also uncovered 31,000 worked flints in 40 days, as well as animal bones such as frogs' legs. Jacques stated that our ancestors were eating a "Heston Blumenthal-style menu."

The findings provide evidence which suggests that Stonehenge, rather than a Neolithic new-build sitting in an empty landscape, should be viewed as a response to long-term use of the area by indigenous hunters and home-makers. The discoveries put a date to the activities of those who built the first monuments at the Stonehenge site, using enormous pine posts. It shows their communities lived in the area for a further 3,000 years, close to the dawn of the Neolithic era when Stonehenge itself was built.

The dig was filmed and made into a documentary by the BBC, Smithsonian, CBC, and others to be screened later in the summer. The project was led by the University of Buckingham. The findings have been recognized by the Guinness Book of Records.

The Old Rag hike in Shenandoah National Park is both popular and dangerous, with numerous blogs and websites attesting to its appeal and the need for caution. A scientist, Michael Dillon from the Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory in California, has published a guide to help minimize deaths from fallout after a city is hit by a nuclear bomb. The guide provides mathematical models for the "optimal shelter exit time" to minimize radiation risk. According to the study, if adequate shelter is 15 minutes away, individuals should remain in their initial, poor-quality shelter no longer than 30 minutes after detonation. If the better shelter is only five minutes away, individuals should move there immediately. The study, published in Proceedings of the Royal Society A, suggests that reaching adequate shelter rapidly could save between 10,000 and 100,000 individuals from fatal exposure in the event of a single, low-yield detonation. The guide is intended to assist emergency planning officials in the development of an optimal low-yield nuclear detonation response strategy. The threat of smaller-scale nuclear attacks has increased in recent years, and the best way to protect against radioactive dust and ash of nuclear fallout is to seek shelter underground. More than 20% of U.S. households do not have basements, and those people must decide when and how far to travel in search of higher-quality shelter in the event of an attack. The guide simplifies the decision process by providing rules people can abide by to protect themselves from fallout. The first order of business is to determine the quality of shelter that one has immediate access to at the time of an attack. Underground concrete shelters are best, while thin-walled homes made of wood or other flimsy materials are considered poor-quality shelters. The study is detailed in the journal Proceedings of the Royal Society A.

The Syrian Observatory for Human Rights (SOHR) has reported that the Islamic State (ISIS) has executed 1,878 people in Syria since declaring their "caliphate" on June 28, 2014. The majority of the victims were civilians, with 1,175 civilians killed, including four children and eight women. Of these civilians, 930 were members of the Shaitat tribe in the eastern countryside of Deir Ezzor.

ISIS also executed 502 soldiers and pro-regime militiamen, and around 120 of its own members, mostly for trying to flee to their home countries. Additionally, 80 members of the rival Al-Nusra Front, the Al-Qaeda affiliate in Syria, were executed.

The SOHR believes that the real number of people killed by ISIS is higher due to the large number of missing and detained individuals, as well as the loss of communication with about a thousand men of the Shaitat tribe and dozens of Kurds who have been missing since the beginning of the ISIS attack on the countryside of Ayn al- Arab "Kobani" in September 2014.

ISIS often records such killings on video and posts footage on the internet, which experts say is meant to sow fear among civilians and rival groups, as well as to attract new recruits. To quash ISIS, U.S.-led forces have conducted air strikes against the militant group in Syria and Iraq.

George Herbert Walker Bush, the 41st President of the United States, passed away at the age of 94. Born in Milton, Massachusetts in 1924, Bush served in World War II as a Navy pilot, earning the Distinguished Flying Cross. After the war, he married Barbara Pierce and moved to Texas to pursue a career in business.

Bush's political career began in the 1960s, and he served as the U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations, Chairman of the Republican National Committee, and Director of the CIA before becoming Vice President under Ronald Reagan in 1980. He succeeded Reagan as President in 1988, winning the election with a campaign slogan of "Read my lips: No new taxes."

During his presidency, Bush led the U.S. to a swift and decisive victory in the first Persian Gulf War, and presided over the peaceful dissolution of the Soviet Union and unification of Germany. However, a recession and a primary challenge from the right cost him a second term, and he lost the election to Bill Clinton in 1992.

In subsequent years, historians have been kinder to the Bush presidency than voters were at the time. Bush also won some degree of vindication when his eldest son, George W. Bush, won the White House in 2000, making Bush the only American since John Adams to be both a president and father of a president.

Bush was a prominent figure in the Republican Party and served as Vice President for eight years before becoming President. He was known for his loyalty to President Reagan and his diplomatic skills, particularly in handling the aftermath of the 1981 assassination attempt on Reagan and the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989.

Upon retiring from politics, Bush undertook a few diplomatic missions and celebrated his birthday into his mid-80s with a parachute jump. He developed postpresidential friendships with former foes, including Bob Dole, and built a strong bond with Bill Clinton. Bush stayed largely in the background during his son George W. Bush's presidency, but made headlines for staying away from the 2016 Republican convention.

Bush's wife, Barbara, died earlier this year at the age of 92. Bush is survived by his five children, including former President George W. Bush and former Florida Governor Jeb Bush. He will be remembered as a statesman who served his country with distinction and grace.

The Israeli Prime Minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has vowed retribution against Hamas, the militant Palestinian group, after the bodies of three Israeli teenagers were found in the West Bank. The teenagers, Naftali Frenkel, Gilad Shaar, and Eyal Yifrach, had been missing for over two weeks. Israel launched over 30 air strikes on the Gaza Strip in response to 18 rocket attacks from Gaza since Sunday night. The Israeli military also flooded into the Palestinian town of Halhul, where the bodies were found under a pile of rocks near the town. Israel named two suspects, Ayoub al-Kawasma and Abu Aisheh, and set off explosives while raiding their homes. Pictures showed extensive damage at the home of Abu Aisheh. One Palestinian was also shot dead after throwing an explosive device at Israeli forces carrying out an operation in the West Bank town of Jenin early on Tuesday. Hamas denies any involvement in the abduction and murder of the teenagers. The funerals of the teenagers will take place on Tuesday, and Israel's response will be calibrated to match the huge sense of anger and outrage felt in the country. Israel has the military capacity to target Hamas's stockpiles of missiles and rockets in a sustained campaign. Hamas said Israel was using the abductions "story" to justify a war on Palestinians. The deaths of the students, who were last seen at a junction between Hebron and Jerusalem as they hitchhiked home, has sparked international condemnation. Over 400 Palestinians were arrested, while five were killed by Israeli troops during the search operation. The Israeli government spokesman, Mark Regev, said that Hamas "must pay a price" for the killings. Hamas spokesman Sami Abu Zuhri accused Israel of "trying to take advantage" of the situation "to open war against our people." Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas called an emergency meeting of the Palestinian leadership. His spokesman Abdallah Abdallah expressed "regret" for the deaths. "We wanted peace to be created in this part of the world so no mother or no family will be bereaved for the loss of their beloved ones, Palestinian or Israeli." The Israeli Deputy Defence Minister, Dan Danon, told the BBC that Hamas "must pay a price" for the killings. The teenagers' funerals, which will be held on Tuesday afternoon, will be the focus of intense grief and national anger. Late on Monday, rockets were launched from Gaza into south Israel. Israel then began air strikes against militant sites in the Gaza Strip. The ministry of health in Gaza said at least four people were wounded when an air strike hit a police station in central Gaza. Hamas and Islamic Jihad training facilities were also targeted, local sources said. Air strikes on electricity stations also caused widespread blackouts. A BBC reporter in Gaza says that Hamas denies carrying out the rocket attacks.

In a large study involving 4,676 healthy women, greater adherence to the Mediterranean diet was associated with longer telomeres, which are protective structures at the end of chromosomes. Shorter telomeres are linked to age-related chronic diseases and reduced life expectancy. The study, published in the British Medical Journal, controlled for various factors and found that the higher the score for adherence to the Mediterranean diet, the longer the telomeres. The difference in telomere length for each point on the adherence scale was equivalent to an average of 1.5 years of life. The Mediterranean diet, characterized by a high intake of vegetables, fruits, nuts, legumes, and grains, a high intake of olive oil but a low intake of saturated lipids, a moderately high intake of fish, a low intake of dairy products, meat, and poultry, and a regular but moderate intake of alcohol, has been linked to numerous health benefits, including reduced overall mortality and reduced incidence of major cardiovascular diseases. The study suggests that the Mediterranean diet may have anti-aging effects, potentially due to its protective effects on oxidative stress and chronic inflammation. However, the study's cross-sectional design precludes establishing a temporal association between dietary habits and telomere length, and the findings may not be generalizable to other ethnicities.

The Alaska Senate primary election between incumbent Lisa Murkowski and challenger Joe Miller is still undecided as over 20,000 absentee and questioned ballots remain to be processed. Miller currently leads Murkowski by 1,668 votes. The state has received back 11,266 out of over 16,000 requested absentee ballots, with 658 early votes and 8,972 questioned ballots still to be counted. A ballot can be "questioned" for several reasons, often due to voters casting ballots in precincts other than where they live.

Miller expects to maintain his lead with the help of military absentee voters and has expressed concern about a potential legal battle from Murkowski to save her seat. He is concerned about a lawyer from the National Republican Senatorial Committee assisting Murkowski's campaign during the ballot count, stating it could lead to "improper meddling" in the primary.

Murkowski's campaign manager has stated that they are focusing on the ballots that are left to be counted and are not considering any speculation about third-party candidacies or write-in efforts. However, there is a possibility that Murkowski could run on the Libertarian ticket in the November general election if she loses the Republican primary. The Alaska Libertarian Party is discussing this possibility, and its Senate candidate, David Haase, has expressed openness to discussing Murkowski stepping aside.

Both sides are keeping close watch as the absentee ballots are counted, with officials planning to start counting them next Tuesday. The process is expected to be protracted, and the final count is scheduled for September 8. The number of remaining ballots changes daily as more absentees come in, and it is unclear how many will be disqualified. If all the current number of 20,896 remaining ballots were counted and three-fourths of them voted in the Republican Senate primary, Murkowski would need the vote on roughly 55% to win.

The study published in PLOS ONE reveals that domestic cats do not perceive their owners as a focus of safety and security in the same way that dogs do. The research, led by Professor Daniel Mills at the University of Lincoln, shows that adult cats are more autonomous and not necessarily dependent on others to provide a sense of protection. The study adapted the Ainsworth Strange Situation Test (SST), which has been used to demonstrate secure attachment in dogs and children, to cats.

The study observed the relationships between a number of cats and their owners, placing the pets in an unfamiliar environment together with their owner, with a stranger and also on their own. The results showed that cats vocalized more when the owner rather than the stranger left them with the other individual, but there was no other evidence consistent with the interpretation of the bond between a cat and its owner meeting the requirements of a secure attachment. The researchers believe this is because of the nature of the species as a largely independent and solitary hunter.

The study suggests that what we interpret as separation anxiety might actually be signs of frustration in cats. The researchers believe that alternative methods need to be developed to characterize the normal psychological features of the cat-owner bond. The results of the study reveal that while cats might prefer to interact with their owner, they do not rely on them for reassurance when in an unfamiliar environment.

The article discusses two separate but related topics: a news update about a tragic accident during the South by Southwest (SXSW) music festival in Austin, Texas, and a promotional piece about a remake of a Depeche Mode classic.

The SXSW accident occurred when a driver, Rashad Owens, allegedly attempted to evade police and drove his car through barricades, striking and killing two people and injuring 23 others. The victims included a cyclist from the Netherlands and a woman from Austin on a moped. Owens was apprehended and will face capital murder charges. The festival organizers have confirmed that the event will continue.

The promotional piece discusses a remake of a Depeche Mode classic in various modern genres. The campaign is gaining popularity with thousands of people requesting the release of full-length tracks. The article suggests that the remake might be released, and it praises Depeche Mode as the truth, comparing them to Volkswagen, which means People's Car.

The article concludes with an image gallery showing the aftermath of the SXSW accident, including photos of the crime scene, injured victims, and a vigil held for the victims.

In June 2016, British Prime Minister David Cameron resigned after the Brexit vote, and as he walked back to Number 10, he was heard humming a tune. The hum was compared to the West Wing theme, Winnie the Pooh, and the Dam Busters theme by various media personalities. Classic FM, a British radio station, analyzed the notes and declared them to be "Beethoven-esque." Some saw Cameron's relaxed demeanor as a sign he was pleased to be leaving Downing Street amid the chaos of the Brexit vote aftermath.

The hum has been analyzed, and it was found to have a brisk 3/4 time signature, with a crotchet roughly equating to 108 beats per minute, suggesting activity and positivity. However, the 3/4 time signature is not the most stable, and the hum has an ambivalent, confusing harmony. It starts with a confident leap of a fourth from G to C but quickly loses confidence when it mirrors the ascent later in the bar, plummeting down to D sharp. The hum also includes a percussive spoken 'Right,' which lands almost perfectly on the first beat of the next bar, demonstrating a reasonable knowledge of contemporary composition techniques.

There is a theory that Cameron was humming the opening of Shostakovich's Fifth Symphony. The hum has been described as Wagnerian fanfare, Beethoven-esque harmonic doubt, and a strange contemporary flourish at the end. Some interpret the hum as a reflection of Cameron's swift departure from office or a comment on what might be next for 10 Downing Street. Other interpretations of this new and invigorating work are welcome.

Leonardo DiCaprio will star in "The Devil in the White City," a film based on Erik Larson's book, with Martin Scorsese directing for Paramount. The project, which has been in development for over a decade, reunites DiCaprio with Scorsese, two years after "The Wolf of Wall Street." DiCaprio will play H.H. Holmes, a notorious serial killer who murdered between 27 and 200 people during the 1893 Chicago World's Fair. Billy Ray, known for "Captain Phillips" and "The Hunger Games," will write the script. The film tells the intertwining stories of fair architect Daniel H. Burnham and Holmes, who used a hotel near the fairgrounds to lure his victims. The project was previously owned by Tom Cruise and Paula Wagner, but the option lapsed in 2004. Paramount reacquired the film rights in 2007 and set it up with producers Michael Shamberg and Stacey Sher. DiCaprio first joined the project in 2010. This will be the next collaboration for DiCaprio and Scorsese, who have previously worked together on films such as "Gangs of New York," "The Aviator," "The Departed," and "Shutter Island." The film is expected to be a significant project for Paramount Film Group President Marc Evans. DiCaprio is represented by LBI, while Scorsese is represented by LBI and WME. Ray is represented by CAA, Management 360, and attorney Peter Nichols. The author is represented by APA.

A Colorado woman, Michelle Marie Thompson, was arrested for trespassing at the Mets' facility in Port St. Lucie, Florida, after she refused to stay away despite claiming to be in a relationship with Tim Tebow. The incident occurred on February 28 during the Mets' spring training season. Thompson had been hanging around the complex since early morning, asking questions about Tebow who had arrived for Minor League Baseball camp. She was found with a sticker on her driver's license stating "I (heart symbol) Jesus/Tim Tebow." When asked about her relationship with Tebow, Thompson claimed it was all-encompassing, but declined to provide more details. Despite being warned to leave, Thompson returned two days later, leading to her arrest. Tebow, a former University of Florida and NFL quarterback, expressed that he feels safe at the facility and enjoys interacting with fans, but finds it challenging to meet every fan due to the demands of his sport. The Mets have security measures in place to handle such incidents, and advise team members to seek help if needed.

Title: Collaborative Smartphone Launch and Apple's Operating System Updates

In the technology sphere, Samsung and Google have joined forces to introduce the Galaxy Nexus smartphone, running on a new version of Android. This launch comes shortly after Apple's unveiling of the iPhone 4S in various markets. The Galaxy Nexus was initially scheduled for an October 11 launch in San Diego, but the event was postponed.

Meanwhile, Apple has announced a public beta for its latest operating system, Yosemite, inviting users to test the Mac's newest OS before its official release. This move echoes Apple's strategy in 2000, when it introduced the first version of OS X.

Regarding digital cameras, a call to perspective is made, reminding users that complaints about their performance should be balanced with an understanding of the evolution of photography technology.

Lastly, a piece highlights the complexities of Apple's iCloud service, emphasizing its potential benefits when functioning properly, but also its history of outages and error messages, particularly for developers. The article suggests that a more open approach to iCloud could help alleviate these issues.

The US film censor, the MPAA, has been accused of homophobia after a film about two older gay men, "Love is Strange," was given a restrictive R rating, preventing anyone under the age of 17 from viewing it without a parent or guardian. The film, which stars John Lithgow and Alfred Molina, features no sex, nudity, or violence, but the MPAA has noted a number of uses of bad language in its decision to hand down an R rating. Critics have pointed out that two other new movies that feature far more obviously adult themes - but which do not focus on a gay relationship - have received the same grading. "Sin City: A Dame to Kill For" features scenes of prostitution, extreme violence, nudity, and drug use, while "Jersey Shore Massacre" includes scenes of graphic gore and violence towards women. The MPAA has a history of being criticized for its ratings system, with some claiming it is overly harsh on LGBT-themed films. The MPAA has not yet made any public comment on the accusations of homophobia.

The article discusses the increasing demand for cobalt, a key component in lithium-ion batteries used in electronic devices and electric cars. Cobalt mining has not occurred at scale in the United States for decades, but a handful of mining companies are now staking claims at sites in Idaho, Montana, and Alaska in search of this silvery blue mineral. The interest in cobalt is due to its rising prices and projected consumption growth of 8-10% annually.

About 300 companies worldwide are now searching for cobalt deposits, with mining giants such as Glencore boosting production in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), where most of the world's cobalt is found. In the US, limited cobalt production started in 2014 for the first time in about four decades. Canada-based First Cobalt bought a mine in Idaho this spring and hopes to get it developed in about three years, with cobalt being its main focus for the mine.

The global cobalt consumption is expected to exceed 122,000 tonnes this year, up from about 75,000 tonnes in 2011, according to CRU. The price per pound has risen above $40 this year, compared with about $20 in early 2011, and is now at about $32. Although increased production is likely to help meet demand in the next few years, analysts say shortages could occur as soon as 2022.

The market dynamics have helped to build confidence, and companies active in the US say they hope their "made in America" status will help speed up government approval for their plans and set their product apart from imports. They also cite concerns about corruption and child labor at mines in the DRC as pressure to find new sources of supply.

However, the realities of where large, high-quality cobalt deposits are found globally mean the US will never be able to completely stop importing cobalt. In fact, analysts expect the DRC's share of global production to increase as mining firms boost their activity there. China is also expected to remain the world's dominant player for refining cobalt, even as new facilities start operating in Europe, North America, and elsewhere in Asia.

The article also highlights the issue of child labor and poor working conditions in cobalt mines, particularly in the DRC. Thousands of children are being lured or forced into grueling and dangerous mine work due to the recent increase in global demand. The conditions described amount to modern-day slavery, according to law experts in Australia who think companies could do more to isolate their supply chains from exploitative practices. The Modern Slavery Bill currently awaiting a vote in the Australian Parliament would compel an estimated 3,000 Australian companies to conduct annual audits of their supply chain for signs of exploitative practices.

The City of Toronto is currently attempting to capture two elusive capybaras that have been missing for over two weeks. The capybaras, nicknamed Bonnie and Clyde, escaped from their pen at the High Park Zoo on May 24. One of them was spotted on June 5, but was not captured. City staff set traps the next morning, which were visible at High Park on Thursday.

Capybaras are the largest rodents in the world, reaching over four feet in height and weighing as much as 140 pounds. They are semi-aquatic animals that enjoy swimming and are native to South America. They have been known to eat other plants in the absence of their native grasses and can inhabit both wetlands and forest fragments. They are also capable of a range of vocalizations and can purr and bark.

The escape of the capybaras has led to a search party, a parody Twitter account, an online video game, and joking comments from Mayor John Tory. However, the zoo could face charges under the Ontario Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, especially given the zoo's history of animal escapes.

This isn't the first time an animal has run free from the High Park Zoo. Almost exactly a year ago, a peacock escaped from the zoo and was on the loose in Toronto for days before returning home on its own. In 2009, six animals – four llamas, one yak, and one wallaby – escaped from the zoo after someone opened their enclosures.

Capybaras have been known to bite humans from time to time, but they are more likely to retreat than stand and bite. The animals are far more likely to be a danger to themselves if they are not captured soon, as they do not possess the necessary fat reserves or thick coats to survive the harsh Canadian winter. The animals will also have to navigate roads and avoid vehicles while on the loose.

National Louis University, a private Chicago-based institution, is offering a deeply discounted deal on tuition for a graduate-level introduction to teaching course via Groupon. The deal, set to go live on Tuesday, will offer a 58% discount on the regular tuition of $2,232, reducing it to $950. The offer is open to up to 25 buyers who must possess an undergraduate degree. Prospective students will need to complete another 33 credits at full price to earn a graduate degree. The deal is part of an effort to boost interest in the graduate teaching program and encourage potential teachers to understand the realities of the profession. This is the first time an academic university has used Groupon in this manner, and it marks an experimental step for Groupon as well. The deal will run until it sells out or until Wednesday.

Former President Barack Obama criticized President Donald Trump's travel ban on immigration, stating that he fundamentally disagrees with faith-based discrimination. This is the first time Obama has publicly criticized the current president, breaking an unwritten rule that former presidents refrain from criticizing the current White House occupant.

Obama supports the protests against Trump's executive order, which was signed on January 27, 2017. The order bars Syrian refugees from entering the U.S. indefinitely and all other refugees for 120 days, and keeps out visitors for 90 days from seven predominantly Muslim countries: Iraq, Syria, Iran, Sudan, Libya, Somalia, and Yemen.

Trump has defended his policy by comparing it to Obama's actions in 2011 when he banned visas for refugees from Iraq for six months. However, the comparison is faulty as the Obama administration's actions were limited to one country and in response to a specific threat, while Trump's order is wider and does not identify a specific threat.

The Obama administration's actions in 2011 were prompted by the discovery of two Iraqi refugees living in Kentucky who had been involved in roadside bombing attacks on U.S. troops in Iraq. One of the refugee's fingerprints were found on a detonation device in Iraq, leading to the rescreening of about 58,000 Iraqi refugees in the U.S. and more than 25,000 Iraqis who had been approved to enter the U.S., but had not yet been admitted. The Kentucky case not only caused a backlog in processing Iraqi refugees in 2011, but it also resulted in an overhaul of the refugee screening process.

Trump's executive order has caused confusion at the nation's airports, with refugees, legal visa holders, and visitors affected by the new policy being detained and some even sent back to their home countries. Democrats and some Republicans have criticized Trump for overreaching his authority and jeopardizing Muslim relations in the fight against terrorism. A temporary stay has been granted in federal court to allow those already in the U.S., or en route to the U.S., to remain in the country.

The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) released its annual crime report on Monday, revealing a 3.9% increase in violent crimes and a 2.6% decrease in property crimes in the United States in 2015 compared to 2014. The report showed that while murder, rape, and assault remained below peak levels of the 1990s, the increase in violent crime could be a topic of debate for presidential candidates Hillary Clinton and Donald Trump.

Trump, a Republican, has portrayed himself as a "law and order" candidate and has supported aggressive policing tactics, including "stop-and-frisk." Clinton, a Democrat, has advocated for stricter gun control and national guidelines on the use of force by police officers.

The FBI report found that the crime rate was highest in the southern United States, with the murder and manslaughter rate in the region being more than twice as high as in the West, Midwest, and Northeast. The report also showed that crime was concentrated in big cities' segregated and impoverished neighborhoods.

FBI Director James Comey warned last year that violent crime in the United States might rise due to increased scrutiny of policing tactics. Experts suggest that crime in these areas can be best fought through better community policing and alternatives to incarceration for nonviolent crime.

In Chicago, there was a 13% jump in the city's murder rate in 2015, with 54 more people being murdered compared to the previous year. The report also revealed that crime was highest in big cities, with the violent crime rate increasing by 6.2% in cities with populations of 500,000 or more.

The FBI report provides valuable data on crime trends in the United States, which is likely to be a topic of discussion in the upcoming presidential debate on public safety.

Title: Uber Brings Flu Shots to Customers' Doorsteps in 35 Cities

On Thursday, Uber is partnering with UberHEALTH to deliver flu shots and wellness packs to customers in more than 35 cities across the US. The service, available between 11 am and 3 pm, aims to make flu prevention more accessible and convenient.

Customers can request a nurse via the Uber app, and upon arrival, they will receive a wellness pack for $10, which includes a water bottle, tissues, hand sanitizer, lollipop, and a recyclable UberHEALTH tote. The nurse will also offer up to ten free flu shots, administered by a registered nurse from Passport Health.

The initiative is part of Uber's efforts to boost vaccination rates, as only 30% of adults ages 18-49 get inoculated, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Last year, the company provided flu shots for a day in Boston, New York, Washington, and Chicago, with more than 2,000 vaccinations administered.

Interest in the service is expected to be high, and users may experience delays in receiving a nurse. The cost of the service is partially covered by Uber, Passport Health, and Epidemico, a public health data mining company owned by Booz Allen Hamilton.

John Brownstein, an epidemiologist at Boston Children's Hospital and Harvard Medical School, came up with the idea last year as a strategy for boosting vaccination rates. A study published in the Annals of Internal Medicine found that nearly 80% of consumers who used the service last year were unlikely to have gotten the vaccine if not for the on-demand delivery.

The cities where the on-demand flu shots will be available to Uber users are: Northeast - Baltimore, Boston, Hartford, Conn., Hoboken, N.J., Jersey City, N.J., New York, Philadelphia, Providence, R.I., Washington, Worcester, Mass.; South - Atlanta, Charleston, S.C., Charlotte, N.C., Dallas, Houston, Nashville, Tenn., New Orleans, Orlando, Raleigh/Durham, N.C., Richmond, Tampa Bay, Fla.; Midwest - Columbus, Ohio, Des Moines, Iowa, Detroit, Grand Rapids, Mich., Indianapolis, Kansas City, Mo., Milwaukee, Pittsburgh; West - Boise, Idaho, Los Angeles, Orange County, Calif., Phoenix, Portland, Ore., San Francisco, Seattle.

The service is intended to help address the convenience factor that often serves as a barrier to vaccination. Whether such efforts are practical depends on cost-effectiveness and scalability, which the researchers did not address in their paper. However, if such programs are shown to be practical, they could be extremely useful in scenarios where near-complete immunization of the population is necessary to prevent the circulation of infectious agents, especially those with severe consequences.

In an extraordinary turn of events, an 18-week-old baby named Megan from County Kildare, Ireland, has defied all odds and survived despite a series of complications that included a miscarriage, an abortion, and medical oversight. The mother, Michelle Hui, initially thought she had lost her baby due to a miscarriage, but doctors at Rotunda Hospital in Dublin confirmed the loss after five scans. However, Michelle was instructed to take abortion pills to clear her uterus, unaware that she was actually pregnant with twins.

A positive pregnancy test later revealed that Megan was alive, and doctors found her during a surgical procedure to remove dangerous blood clots. Megan, born on February 25, weighed just under 6 pounds and became a little sister to Mya, 4, and Noah, 2.

The mother of three, Michelle, expressed her disbelief and anger at the doctors' oversight, as the medical abortion could have potentially harmed her newborn. The doctors attributed the oversight to the presence of blood and clots creating shadows that made it difficult to see Megan on the scans.

This miraculous survival has been documented in medical journals, with medical professionals acknowledging the rarity of such a case. Katherine Hales, a spokesperson from the Association of Radical Midwives, admitted that while she had heard of rare cases of a miscarriage of one baby and the subsequent detection of another on a scan, she had never heard of such a case after the use of mifepristone, an abortion pill.

Megan is now thriving at 18 weeks, and her family is overjoyed. The doctors have called it a blessing, stating that they have never heard of anything like it. Michelle and her family believe that someone was looking over them during this challenging time.

President Obama announced on Tuesday that the United States formally recognizes the Syrian Opposition Coalition as the legitimate representative of the Syrian people in opposition to President Bashar Assad. This diplomatic shift grants new legitimacy to the rebel group and marks a new phase in U.S. efforts to isolate the Assad regime. The recognition allows for closer U.S. support of rebel efforts, including the organization of a future post-Assad government. However, the move does not include the provision of weapons, but it opens the door for that possibility in the future.

The president expressed caution about some Syrian factions involved with the coalition, warning that the United States will not support extremist elements. He specifically singled out the group Jabhat al-Nusrah for its alleged affiliation with Al Qaeda in Iraq. The State Department has already blacklisted al-Nusrah, imposing economic sanctions and branding it a terrorist organization.

The recognition of the Syrian rebel group has been expected, and the move does not change the military equation inside Syria, where Assad has clung to power despite gains by rebel fighters. Obama notably did not commit to providing arms to the rebels he is recognizing or to supporting them militarily with airstrikes or the establishment of a no-fly zone. The United States has played an active role behind the scenes in shaping the opposition, insisting that it be broadened and made more inclusive.

The American hope is that the opposition, in conjunction with local councils that are being formed in Syria, could help govern areas that have been wrested from Assad's control, provide public services like law enforcement and utilities, and perhaps even channel humanitarian assistance. However, the recognition does not confer on the opposition the legal authority of a state, and it is unclear to what extent the move might influence the situation inside Syria, where the pace of the fighting appears to have intensified.

A viral video on social media shows a man, later identified as Kino Jimenez, taking a teenager's "Make America Great Again" hat and throwing a drink at him at a Whataburger in San Antonio, Texas, on July 4th. The incident sparked outrage online, with the teenager, Hunter Richard, responding on Instagram. In the video, the man is shown shouting a racial slur. Jimenez has been arrested and charged with theft, and Whataburger has released a statement condemning the man's behavior. Donald Trump's 2020 presidential campaign manager has offered to send Richard a signed MAGA hat in support. The San Antonio Police Department is investigating the incident, and Jimenez has reportedly been fired from his job.

James Robert Jones, a former Army private convicted of murder in 1974, was arrested in Florida after 40 years on the run. Jones, who had been living under the false name Bruce Keith, was apprehended by US Marshals outside his work location in Pompano Beach. The arrest followed an investigation initiated by the Army in January, after they believed Jones to be living in Florida. Jones had escaped from the US Disciplinary Barracks at Fort Leavenworth, Kansas in 1977, the US Military's only maximum security prison. The Marshals matched a prison photo of Jones to a Florida driver's license first issued in 1981. Jones will be extradited back to Kansas to resume his sentence and may face additional charges related to his escape. The arrest came after Jones had been living a seemingly normal life in Florida for several years, with "significant others" and was only a year away from retirement.

The United States launched a missile strike on a Syrian airbase on April 7, 2017, in response to a chemical attack that occurred earlier in the week. The attack, which marked the first time the US has directly targeted Syrian President Bashar Assad's forces, was condemned by Assad's allies in Russia and Iran but welcomed by the Syrian opposition and its supporters. The bombing represents President Donald Trump's most dramatic military order since taking office and thrusts the US administration deeper into the complex Syrian conflict.

The US launched 60 Tomahawk missiles at the Shayrat airbase, southeast of Homs, which is used as a base for Syrian jets that bomb targets in northern and central Syria. The US missiles hit at 3:45 a.m. (0045 GMT) Friday morning and targeted the base's airstrips, hangars, control tower, and ammunition areas. The Syrian military reported at least seven people killed and nine wounded in the missile strike.

The attack was in retaliation for Tuesday's deadly chemical attack, which officials said used chlorine mixed with a nerve agent, possibly sarin. The Syrian government had been under mounting international pressure after the chemical attack, which killed 87 people, including 31 children. Even Russia has said its support is not unconditional.

Russia condemned the US strike as "aggression" and suspended crucial coordination with Washington in Syria's congested skies. The Kremlin said President Vladimir Putin believes the US strike is an "aggression against a sovereign state in violation of international law." Spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Putin believes the US launched the strikes under a "far-fetched pretext."

Russia's Foreign Ministry said it is suspending a memorandum with Washington — signed after Russia began an air campaign in support of Assad in September 2015 — under which the two countries exchange information about sorties over Syria. The Kremlin later moved to diminish the attack, saying that just 23 of 59 cruise missiles reached the air base, destroying six Syrian jets but leaving the runway intact. Moscow also confirmed it had been informed of the attack in advance.

A US-led coalition has been bombing Islamic State targets in Syria since 2014, while Russia's air force has been striking both extremist groups and Syrian rebels in order to aid Assad's forces. Saudi Arabia and Turkey, which support the Syrian opposition, welcomed the missile strike, with Riyadh calling it a "courageous decision" by Trump. Iran called it a "dangerous" unilateral action that would "strengthen terrorists" and further complicate the conflict.

The US had initially focused on diplomatic efforts after the chemical attack, and had pressed the UN Security Council to adopt a resolution drafted with Britain and France that would have condemned Syria's suspected use of chemical weapons. But the vote was canceled because of differences among the 15 members.

The attack on the Syrian airbase is the first direct military action by the US against Assad's forces since the start of the Syrian civil war in 2011. The US has provided support to various Syrian opposition groups, but has not previously targeted the Syrian government. The attack is likely to escalate tensions between the US and Russia, which have been supporting opposing sides in the Syrian conflict.

The US action is also likely to have significant implications for the Syrian conflict, as it represents a major shift in US policy towards the Assad regime. The US has long called for Assad to step down, but has not previously taken direct military action against his forces. The attack is likely to be seen as a warning to Assad and other leaders who use chemical weapons against their own people. It remains to be seen whether the attack will lead to a broader military intervention by the US in Syria, or whether it will be a one-time response to the chemical attack.

The attack on the Syrian airbase is also likely to have significant implications for US relations with Russia, which has been a key ally of the Assad regime. The US and Russia have been working together in Syria to combat the Islamic State, but the attack on the airbase is likely to strain that relationship. It remains to be seen whether the US and Russia will be able to continue to work together in Syria, or whether the attack will lead to a further deterioration of relations between the two countries.

Overall, the US missile strike on a Syrian airbase is a significant development in the complex Syrian conflict. It represents a major shift in US policy towards the Assad regime, and is likely to have significant implications for the Syrian conflict, US relations with Russia, and the broader Middle East region.
