In conclusion, the article highlights the financial success of large not-for-profit hospital systems and the resignation of Mike Dubke, President Trump's communications director, amidst ongoing staff changes in the White House.

In the primary elections held on August 5th, three-term Republican Senator Pat Roberts secured a narrow victory over Milton Wolf in Kansas, marking a win for the GOP establishment over the tea party movement. The National Republican Senatorial Committee (NRSC), chaired by Roberts' Kansas colleague Sen. Jerry Moran, played a significant role in Roberts' win. The NRSC sent workers to Kansas City for the final 10 days, knocking on over 10,000 doors in Johnson County alone, and made over 40,000 phone calls in the final three weeks. Roberts and the NRSC focused on turning out supporters in Wolf's home base to counteract Roberts' strength in the western side of the state.

In Michigan, businessman and lawyer Dave Trott defeated incumbent Kerry Bentivolio in the 11th Congressional District, marking a reversal of the recent political order of tea partyers targeting establishment favorites. Bentivolio, who was often described as the "accidental" congressman, was elected in 2012 when former Rep. Thaddeus McCotter turned in fraudulent voter signatures for a ballot spot.

The primary day launched a crowded stretch with Tennessee on Thursday, Hawaii on Saturday, and Connecticut, Minnesota, and Wisconsin next week. The primary results reflect a shift in the political landscape, with establishment candidates gaining momentum over tea party challengers.

Authorities ruled it a terrorist incident, although the shooter was not tied to a known group. The shooting at LAX is currently under investigation, with authorities still investigating the suspect's background.

In an unusual civil case out of Oakland County, Michigan, a woman named Lori Cichewicz is suing her doctor for emotional distress caused by an unplanned pregnancy. In 2008, Cichewicz went to get a permanent birth control procedure, but her doctor told her that her fallopian tubes were blocked, and she had no chance of getting pregnant. Three years later, Cichewicz gave birth to a child with Down syndrome.

Cichewicz is suing her doctor for "wrongful conception," alleging his negligence caused her emotional distress. The courts have already decided that damages are limited to the stress of the conception itself, not the costs of raising a child with special needs. The case is expected to go to a jury trial within the next few months, unless the doctor settles it before then.

Cichewicz described her daughter, Reagan, as "full of life, loving, kind, sweet, everything you could ever imagine." She said Reagan is adored by her big brother and her father, Cichewicz's boyfriend. However, Cichewicz said the thought of raising a child with special needs at her age, the added financial burden, and her doctor's broken promise all took an emotional toll.

The article discusses the claim that William Shakespeare may have written five additional passages in Thomas Kyd's "The Spanish Tragedy." English professor Douglas Bruster has recently published a textual analysis that suggests the proof lies in Shakespeare's trademark misspellings and bad handwriting. The findings reveal that Shakespeare's spelling was both old-fashioned and idiosyncratic. For example, with words like "spotless" and "darkness," Shakespeare would use a single "s." Past-tense words like "wrapped" and "blessed" he ended with a "t" (i.e., "wrapt," "blest"). Also telling is his habit of spelling the same word in two different ways (i.e., "alley" spelled "allie" and "allye" in the same line).

Bruster also argues that a particularly clumsy and nongrammatical stretch in the Additional Passages may be due to a printer's misreading of Shakespeare's handwriting. This discovery, if accepted by the broader world of Shakespeareans, would make the Additional Passages the first largely undisputed new addition to the canon since Shakespeare's contributions to "Edward III" began appearing in scholarly editions in the mid-1990s.

However, not everyone is convinced. Tiffany Stern, a professor of early modern drama at Oxford University, praised the empirical rigor of Bruster's paper but expressed skepticism about some new attributions driven by publishers' desire to offer "more Shakespeare" than their rivals.

The idea that Shakespeare may have written the Additional Passages was first broached in 1833 by Samuel Taylor Coleridge, but it remained a distinctly minority position well into the 20th century. The acceptance of these passages as Shakespeare's work is by no means assured.

The article also mentions that scholars have long cited the idiosyncrasies of Shakespeare’s handwriting to understand oddities in the earliest printed versions of his plays. For example, in the 1604 quarto version of "Hamlet," Gertrude is called "Gertrad" — probably a reflection of Shakespeare’s tendency to close up his u’s and drop his final e’s.

The discovery of these additional passages, if confirmed, would further support the theory that Shakespeare was a collaborative playwright who frequently worked with others, as argued by scholar Brian Vickers.

Cam Newton, football quarterback for the Carolina Panthers, introduced the dab to American sports in 2015, after being instructed by his younger brother. The move quickly spread to other athletes and even politicians, including Hillary Clinton, Loretta Sanchez, and Tom Watson.

The dab's association with cannabis culture, as claimed by Bow Wow, was met with opposition from other rappers and eventually debunked. However, in Saudi Arabia, the move was deemed illegal due to its perceived allusion to illegal substances.

Today, the dab is a common addition to dance routines, particularly in Korean pop music (K-pop) and among Manchester United footballers Paul Pogba and Jesse Lingard. The dance move has also been adopted by wrestler T.J. Perkins as a taunt or sign of disrespect.

In conclusion, the dab, a simple yet versatile dance move, has become a cultural phenomenon, propagated by celebrities and memes, and has made its mark in various fields, from sports and entertainment to politics and even royalty. However, its illegality in Saudi Arabia serves as a reminder of the cultural and societal differences that exist around the world.

Joy Covey, a groundbreaking tech executive and Harvard Law School graduate, passed away at the age of 50 in a bicycle accident. Covey was best known for her role as the chief financial officer of Amazon.com at the time of its initial public offering (IPO) in 1997.

Born in Boston, Covey grew up in San Mateo and dropped out of high school at the age of 15. She worked as a grocery clerk before returning to college at Fresno State, where she graduated in two and a half years. Covey then went on to earn dual law and MBA degrees from Harvard in 1989.

After leaving Amazon in 2000, Covey focused on environmental causes, establishing the Beagle Foundation and working with the National Resources Defense Council (NRDC). She also continued to work as an independent investor and consultant, serving on the boards of JetBlue Airways and other companies.

Covey was instrumental in Amazon's massive expansion and was known for her unconventional approach to business. She helped the company ignore Wall Street's short-term pressures and invest for the long-term, which was a radical idea at the time but ultimately contributed to Amazon's growth into a $61 billion retailing and entertainment behemoth.

In an interview with the Harvard Law Bulletin in 2002, Covey discussed her unique background and how it contributed to her success. She noted that her lack of a traditional liberal arts education and her independent spirit helped her think outside the box and make unconventional decisions that ultimately paid off.

Covey's death has been widely mourned by those who knew her, with many praising her intelligence, determination, and commitment to environmental causes. She is survived by her young son, Tyler.

Facebook's highly anticipated initial public offering (IPO) on Friday faced technical problems and a market-wide selloff, causing the stock to close at just $38.23, barely above its IPO price. The offering, which was the largest technology IPO ever, was marred by delays, confusion, and a lack of the expected first-day pop. Many factors contributed to the weak debut, including a broad-based selloff, complications due to the massive size of the offering, and concerns about Facebook's valuation and potential. Some believe the offering was priced too high, while others point to lingering questions about the company's business model and advertising effectiveness. Despite the rocky start, Facebook commands a market cap of about $104 billion, making it one of the largest tech companies in the US. The offering seemed to negatively impact other social networking companies, with Zynga, Yelp, and LinkedIn all seeing their shares fall on the day of Facebook's IPO.

The trial of two American hikers, Shane Bauer and Josh Fattal, arrested near the Iraqi border in July 2009, has been delayed by Iranian authorities due to the absence of a third suspect, Sarah Shourd, who was released on bail and returned to the United States. The trial was scheduled to begin on the 29th of May, but the court has delayed it to allow Shourd to return to Iran or for her case to be handled differently. Their lawyer was not aware of the trial postponement. The delay comes amidst ongoing negotiations between Iran and other powers regarding Iran's nuclear activities, which the international community fears are aimed at making an atomic bomb. Iran has expressed a willingness to resume talks, but no date has been agreed upon yet. The hikers, who claim they were hiking in northern Iraq and were not aware they had crossed into Iran, are at the center of a larger dispute between the United States and Iran. Ahmadinejad suggested in February that the Americans might be released as part of a prisoner swap for Iranians he claims have been abducted or tricked into going to the United States and jailed without due legal process. The trial delay and the prisoner swap possibility are being closely watched, as it could potentially ease tensions between the two countries.

The Panama Papers, a massive leak of documents from the Panamanian law firm Mossack Fonseca, reveal how the financial elite exploit secretive offshore systems to maneuver wealth anonymously and avoid taxes. The documents contain information about more than 214,000 shell companies, trusts, and foundations, which are often used to hold or transfer financial assets while hiding the identity of their real owners. The leak shows how some of the world's most powerful politicians, including eight members of China's Communist party elite, have taken advantage of offshore companies.

The documents show that Jasmine Li, the granddaughter of a powerful Chinese leader, became the sole shareholder in two British Virgin Islands companies while still a teenager. Her grandfather, Jia Qinglin, was the fourth-ranked politician in China at the time. Other prominent figures who have taken advantage of offshore companies include the brother-in-law of the president, Xi Jinping, and the son-in-law of Zhang Gaoli, another member of China's top political body.

The relatives of these politicians had companies that were clients of Mossack Fonseca, but there is nothing in the documents to suggest that the politicians in question had any beneficial interest in the companies connected to their family members. China's censors have been blocking access to the unfolding revelations about its most senior political families, and there have been reports of censors deleting hundreds of posts on social networks.

The leak comes amid Xi Jinping's crackdown on behavior that could embarrass the Communist party. Two more well-connected figures – the brother of former vice-president Zeng Qinghong and the son of former politburo member Tian Jiyun – are directors of a single offshore company. They have previously been linked in a court case that highlighted how some Chinese "princelings" have used political connections for financial gain.

The documents were obtained by the German newspaper Süddeutsche Zeitung and shared by the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists (ICIJ) with the Guardian, the BBC, and other media. China and Hong Kong were Mossack Fonseca's biggest sources of business, with clients from these jurisdictions linked to a total of 40,000 companies past and present. About a quarter of these are thought to be live, and in 2015, records show the firm was collecting fees for nearly 10,000 companies linked to Hong Kong and China.

There are many legitimate reasons to use offshore companies, but the leaks draw unwelcome attention to the wealth of leaders' families. In some cases, they show how secrecy havens are being used to create and hide potentially lucrative connections between big business and politics in the world's second-largest economy. Even as officials advertise their zeal in targeting corruption, they remain highly sensitive to the disclosure of the business interests of top leaders' families.

In 2014, the websites of the Guardian and several other media outlets were blocked for several months after revealing offshore holdings. Xi's brother-in-law Deng Jiagui and Li's daughter Li Xiaolin were named in those leaks, too. The new documents therefore indicate multiple offshore holdings.

Xi's harsh anti-corruption drive has brought down a host of high-ranking figures. In December, he urged politburo members "to strictly educate and supervise their children and other family members as well as subordinates, and to rectify their problems in a timely manner." He urged members of the 25-strong body to not only have integrity but "stay away from vulgar taste and set good examples for other cadres and the general public." In other words, avoiding wrongdoing is not enough, impressions count, too.

The following is a list of some of the other prominent figures named in the Panama Papers:

* Hu Dehua, the businessman son of Hu Yaobang, the Communist party's general secretary ousted in 1987 because he was seen as too liberal – and, some sympathisers say, for his attempts to root out corruption among leaders' families. Hu has interests in technology and energy, and is registered as sole shareholder of a BVI entity called Fortalent International Holdings.
* Lee Shing Put, the Hong Kong businessman married to the adoptive daughter of Zhang Gaoli, who is China's senior vice-premier. As a member of the politburo standing committee, he is one of the seven most powerful politicians in China.
* Zeng Qinghuai, the younger brother of Zeng Qinghong, who was China's vice-president until 2008. He is well known in Hong Kong, having worked there as an envoy for the ministry of culture.
* Tian Chenggang, son of the former vice-premier and politburo member Tian Jiyun. He is listed as a director of a company called Chinese Cultural Exchange Association Ltd, registered first in the tiny South Pacific island of Niue, then in Samoa.

The Panama Papers reveal that Zeng Qinghuai is a director of a company called Chinese Cultural Exchange Association Ltd, registered first in the tiny South Pacific island of Niue, then in Samoa. He sits on the board alongside another princeling, Tian Chenggang, son of the former vice-premier and politburo member Tian Jiyun. A 2012 court case, in which Tian Chenggang unsuccessfully sued a developer called Beijing Henderson Properties, shed new light on the business dealings of the red nobility. The court in Hong Kong heard that Tian and a company linked to Zeng had been separately engaged to lobby regulators on behalf of Henderson when it was under investigation for breaching foreign exchange regulations in 2006. An exchange of letters disclosed in court suggested Tian's father had written to the regulators to plead leniency. In the event, the fine imposed was smaller than expected. Companies linked to Zeng received fees of $2.1m and $650,000. Henderson rejected Tian's demand for $5.5m, so Tian sued for the money but lost. The judge's summing up said of him: "He tried to project an air of superiority … His attitude was contemptuous and disrespectful." Zeng and Tian did not respond to requests for comment.

In a shocking discovery in Mexico's Chiapas state, police found 513 migrants crammed inside two trailer trucks, bound for the United States. The migrants, mostly from Central and South America, Asia, and suffering from dehydration, were transported in dangerously crowded conditions, with some clinging to cargo ropes inside the containers. The trucks were arrested at a checkpoint in Tuxtla Gutierrez, where they were found to lack air and water.

The migrants, who were charged about $7,000 each for the journey, said they were told they would be loaded onto another set of vehicles for the trip to the U.S. border. Four alleged smugglers were arrested, but no drug gang involvement was confirmed. This is believed to be the largest shipment of migrants detained in Mexico in recent years.

The discovery highlights the increasing use of X-ray scanners by border security and police to inspect vehicles, including backscatter scanners, which are capable of seeing through clothes and walls. These scanners have been employed for years to check cargo for weapons and drugs, and also to catch human smuggling. However, their use has raised privacy concerns, particularly in the context of airport passenger screenings.

The image of the harrowing X-ray scan, showing the ghostly shadows of the migrants packed together, has drawn attention to the harsh realities faced by those attempting to illegally migrate to the United States.

In a heartwarming display of kindness, a new employee at Enterprise Rent-A-Car named John Goodlett has gained national attention for his exemplary behavior. Last week, Goodlett, who is only a few days into his job, assisted a customer named Coty Vincent, a mother of twin infants, by holding one of her sons while processing her rental car.

Vincent, who posted the viral photo on her Facebook page, expressed her gratitude for Goodlett's help. She had brought car seats for her boys but lacked a stroller that could accommodate both. Goodlett, without hesitation, helped her carry one of the babies while he worked, demonstrating an extraordinary level of compassion and multitasking ability.

The touching moment moved Vincent, who shared the photo with her Twin Mom groups. The post quickly went viral on various Facebook pages, receiving over 224,800 reactions and 24,600 shares on Vincent's own page. Goodlett, surprised by the attention, expressed his hope that the incident would serve as a reminder for people to treat each other with kindness and help one another more often.

Goodlett, who is a twin himself, lives with his sister and shares a "love-hate relationship" with her. Marlyn Jones, the Enterprise branch manager where Goodlett works, praised his performance and noted that his colleagues have also recognized his exceptional service.

Enterprise's corporate office offered Goodlett a gift card for his service, but he chose to donate the funds to his favorite charity, a local Boys & Girls Club run by the Salvation Army. The organization will receive scholarship money and new sports equipment. Vincent, too, received a double stroller from Enterprise's corporate office, which will allow her to leave the house without needing an extra set of hands to help.

Vincent expressed her hope that the simple act of kindness she witnessed would remind people of the importance of treating each other with respect and kindness, especially in these challenging times. She emphasized that there are many good people in the country, and it's up to everyone to turn things around by showing kindness and respect to one another.

On November 14, 2015, Arizona highway trooper Miguel Rincon was conducting a traffic stop when he was approached by a panicked driver who informed him that her granddaughter was about to give birth and needed an ambulance. However, the baby couldn't wait, and Courtney Benavidez gave birth in the car before Rincon could even reach her. Rincon, a seven-year veteran with the Arizona Department of Public Safety, stayed calm and handed Benavidez a blanket for the newborn. An ambulance arrived and took mom and infant to the hospital, where they were released the next day in good health. Rincon, who has three children of his own, said his instincts kicked in during the incident. The baby was named Carter Jett, a reference to his speedy arrival. Benavidez, a third-grade teacher, was shocked by how quickly things moved and expressed gratitude for Rincon's help. Rincon described the incident as the best experience since joining the force, stating that it was a welcome change from typical criminal activity.

A new trading exchange for investing in professional athletes has been announced by a start-up company, Fantex Holdings. The company plans to create stocks tied to an athlete's financial performance, with Arian Foster, a Pro Bowl running back of the Houston Texans, being the first athlete to have an initial public offering (IPO) for his stock. Investors in the deal will receive stock linked to Mr. Foster's future earnings, which includes the value of his playing contracts, corporate endorsements, and appearance fees. Fantex aims to sign up more football players and other athletes, as well as celebrities like pop singers and Hollywood actors.

The offering is intended to capitalize on the popularity of the National Football League and fantasy football. If thousands of fans are willing to pay for an Arian Foster jersey, the thinking goes, why wouldn't they pay up for a few shares of Arian Foster stock? The IPO is intended to track the economic performance of Mr. Foster's future brand income, but shareholders will not have a direct investment in Mr. Foster or any control over his brand. The company expects to pay a dividend to holders of the Foster stock.

Fantex has grand ambitions beyond the Foster IPO, and it hopes to sign up more football players and other athletes, as well as celebrities like pop singers and Hollywood actors. However, the offering is speculative, and in a filing for the Foster deal with securities regulators, Fantex laid out 37 pages of risk factors, including a possible career-ending injury or a performance slump.

The company is effectively financing the $10 million payment to Mr. Foster by raising money from retail investors in an IPO. In its filings, Fantex says it believes that the stock is intended to track the economic performance of Mr. Foster's future brand income. The company will market the IPO in the coming weeks, offering 1.06 million shares at $10 a share, or $10.6 million worth of stock. If demand is insufficient, the company may cancel the deal.

The company is backed by executives from Silicon Valley, Wall Street, and the sports world. The president of Fantex is John Rodin, co-president of the hedge fund Glenview Capital Management and a Goldman Sachs alumnus. Its chief technology officer is Joshua S. Levine, a former senior executive at E*Trade and Deutsche Bank.

The parents of First Lady Melania Trump, Viktor and Amalija Knavs, were sworn in as U.S. citizens in a private ceremony in New York. They have lived in the U.S. for over a decade and gained permanent legal residency before becoming citizens. The Knavses' immigration lawyer, Michael Wildes, stated that their process was no different from anyone else's, despite Donald Trump's anti-immigration stance and his criticism of the family visa system. The White House declined to comment on the Knavses' citizenship status, citing privacy concerns. It is believed that Melania Trump sponsored her parents for their green cards, which allowed them to live and work in the U.S. indefinitely and paved the way for citizenship. This type of family visa is one of the categories that the Trump administration has sought to end. The Knavses, who are in their 70s, are retired and maintain regular contact with the Trump family. Their citizenship has sparked controversy due to the administration's efforts to limit family-based immigration.

The article discusses the ongoing controversy between Dr. Jen Gunter, an obstetrician and gynecologist, and Goop, a lifestyle and wellness e-commerce company founded by Gwyneth Paltrow. The dispute began when Gunter criticized Goop for promoting pseudoscience and making unsubstantiated health claims, such as the suggestion that women should insert jade eggs into their vaginas to improve their sex lives.

Goop responded to Gunter's criticism with a post titled "Uncensored: A Word from Our Doctors," which defended the company's approach to health and wellness and accused Gunter of using her platform to critique Goop to gain attention. The post also included responses from two of Goop's featured doctors, including Dr. Steven Gundry, who criticized Gunter for using swear words and challenged her to have a friendly discussion about the pros and cons of lectins.

Gunter responded with a post titled "Goop's Misogynistic, Mansplaining Hit Job," in which she defended her credentials and expertise in the field of gynecology and reproductive health. She also accused Goop of promoting pseudoscience and putting women's health at risk with its unsubstantiated health claims.

The article also mentions that Goop held an In Goop Health conference last month in Culver City, California, for acolytes who paid $500 to $1,500 a ticket. The conference included panel discussions about topics such as leech facials and crystal therapy, as well as a mineral-infused oxygen bar and vegan ice cream.

The article also mentions that Goop has been under investigation by TINA.org, a non-profit organization that works to stop false advertising, for making unsubstantiated health claims in its marketing. TINA.org has provided Goop with a list of webpages containing illegal health claims, but the company has only made limited changes to its marketing to date. As a result, TINA.org has filed a complaint with two California district attorneys, urging them to investigate Goop's marketing and take appropriate enforcement action.

Overall, the article highlights the ongoing controversy between Dr. Jen Gunter and Goop over the company's promotion of pseudoscience and unsubstantiated health claims, and the efforts of TINA.org to hold the company accountable for its marketing practices.

In a rare press conference at the CIA's headquarters, Director John Brennan defended the agency's use of aggressive interrogation techniques in the aftermath of the 9/11 attacks, while acknowledging that some officers' actions were unauthorized and abhorrent. Brennan insisted that detainees subjected to these techniques provided useful information, but admitted that it's unknown whether the harsh treatment yielded that information.

Brennan's comments come two days after the release of a Senate Intelligence Committee report, which criticized the CIA for abusing detainees and mismanaging its interrogation program. The report details techniques such as mock executions, rectal rehydration, sleep deprivation, and beatings.

Brennan defended the agency, stating that the overwhelming majority of its workforce carried out their responsibilities faithfully during this difficult time. He also expressed sympathy for the agency's personnel, who have been under withering criticism in recent days.

However, Brennan conceded that the agency didn't do enough to supervise its officers and that some went too far in their interrogations. He admitted that the agency was unprepared to conduct a detention and interrogation program and that its officers inadequately developed and monitored its initial activities.

Brennan never used the word "torture" to describe the CIA's tactics and deflected a question about whether he supported the Senate Intelligence Committee's decision to release its report. He stated that there has been more than enough transparency in the past couple of days and that the report's release is over the top.

Senate Intelligence Committee Chairman Dianne Feinstein's staff ran a real-time fact-check of Brennan's remarks through her Twitter account, #ReadTheReport. Feinstein's office began tweeting even before Brennan began speaking, defending the accuracy of the study.

Brennan's appearance was intended to convey a message of support to a wider audience and quell concerns about the Senate report's impact on the agency's personnel, their reputations, and morale. Projecting an image of solidarity, about 30 senior agency officials sat directly in front of the director during the press conference.

Regardless of one's views on enhanced interrogation techniques, Brennan argued that the nation and, in particular, this agency did a lot of things right during this difficult time to keep the country safe and secure. He stated that the CIA's people have been touched by the outpouring of support from outsiders as the CIA came under criticism in recent days.

Brennan's comments come as former Vice President Dick Cheney is set to defend the use of techniques like waterboarding and confining suspects in small spaces on a Sunday television talk show. The CIA, Obama, and his close aides have made abundantly clear that they're eager to put this particular flurry of news coverage behind them.

CNN has announced changes to its primetime show "Parker Spitzer," with Kathleen Parker leaving her co-host role and the show being renamed "In the Arena." Eliot Spitzer will remain as the host, and starting Monday, E.D. Hill and Will Cain will join him, along with other contributors from within and outside CNN. The new format aims to provide balanced and thoughtful discussions with a wide range of guests representing various points of view. Parker will continue to appear on CNN occasionally, focusing more on her syndicated column. The changes come as the show has struggled with low ratings since its October debut, and as CNN looks to increase its audience share, particularly in the 8 p.m. hour. The new direction for the show is intended to elevate Spitzer, who resigned as New York governor in 2008 after a prostitution scandal. The move had been rumored for some time, and Parker's exit was reportedly imminent. The show was conceived last fall by former CNN president Jon Klein, who was dismissed two weeks before its premiere. The new program will aim to build on the show's policy-oriented conversation and analysis of important stories of the day.

The article discusses the ongoing winter cold snap in various parts of the world, including Britain, and the misuse of this weather event to question global warming. The author criticizes climate skeptics, such as Martyn Brown in the Express, Christopher Booker, and Richard North in the Telegraph and the Mail, for using the cold weather to support their claims that the Met Office is manipulating climate data to fit a political agenda. The author argues that these claims are baseless and that the Met Office's forecast for a warmer-than-average winter was not a prediction but an indication based on early indications. The author also highlights the difference between weather and climate, emphasizing that single events do not disprove long-term trends. The article concludes by noting that experts attribute the current cold snap to a natural variability in the atmosphere, and that it does not negate the ongoing global warming trend. The article also mentions the cold weather in other parts of the world, such as Beijing, Poland, Florida, and Bangladesh, and the impact it has had on people and wildlife in those areas.

The former US Army analyst and whistleblower, Chelsea Manning, was featured in the September issue of Vogue magazine. Manning was photographed by Annie Leibovitz in a red swimsuit on a beach for the magazine's 125th anniversary issue. Manning was sentenced to 35 years in prison in 2013 after leaking classified documents to WikiLeaks, including the video known as Collateral Murder. In 2007, while on leave from service in Iraq, Manning sent hundreds of thousands of classified and sensitive documents to WikiLeaks. Manning came out as transgender the day after she was sentenced and underwent hormone therapy while in prison. After six years behind bars, she was released from Fort Leavenworth prison on May 17, 2017, when President Obama commuted her sentence. Manning has been living in New York since her release. In an interview with Vogue, Manning spoke about her childhood in Oklahoma, her parents' separation, her growing awareness and confusion around her sexuality and gender identity, and her decision to enter the military in 2007 in the hope that it would help her "figure [herself] out." Manning accepted responsibility for her actions and spoke about the psychological toll of her time in prison, which included multiple suicide attempts and solitary confinement. Since her release, Manning's online persona has been a source of joy and positivity, despite relentless targeting by trolls and detractors. Manning is not the first trans woman to appear in Vogue, with models and trans women such as Hari Nef and Andreja Pejic having previously featured in the fashion magazine. Earlier this year, French Vogue made headlines when Brazilian model Valentina Sampaio was revealed on the cover of their March issue, marking the first time the magazine had featured a transwoman on the cover. In an unrelated incident, Manning was also featured in a controversial tweet, encouraging users to add a location to their tweets. Twitter stores the location of tweets, and users can switch the location on or off before each tweet and always have the option to delete their location history.

The romantic musical "Once," based on the 2006 film of the same name, won eight awards, including best new musical, at the Tony Awards held on Sunday. The musical, which uses songs by Marketa Irglova and Glen Hansard, tells the story of an unlikely love affair between a Czech flower seller and an Irish street musician in Dublin. Steve Kazee, who stars in the musical, won the award for best actor in a leading role in a musical. "Once" also won awards for director John Tiffany and playwright Enda Walsh, who wrote the book for the musical. The musical beat out "Newsies," `'Nice Work If You Can Get It" and "Leap of Faith." The Tony Awards ceremony was hosted by Neil Patrick Harris and took place at the Beacon Theatre in New York.

In addition to the awards for "Once," other notable winners at the Tony Awards included "Clybourne Park" for best play, "The Gershwins’ Porgy and Bess" for best revival of a musical, and Audra McDonald for best actress in a leading role in a musical. On September 21, 2012, a visitor at the Bronx Zoo in New York was mauled by a Siberian tiger named Bashuta after he jumped from a moving monorail train and breached a 16-foot-high perimeter fence. The man suffered bites and punctures on his arms, legs, shoulders, and back, and broke an arm and a leg. The incident occurred in the Wild Asia exhibit, where the train takes visitors through a forest past various animals, including tigers.

Bashuta was returned to a holding area and will not be euthanized, as the zoo director, Jim Breheny, stated that the tiger "did nothing wrong." The man was alone with Bashuta for about 10 minutes before zoo officials rescued him using a fire extinguisher to chase the animal away. The man was instructed to roll under an electrified wire to get to safety, and zookeepers then called the tiger into a holding area.

Bashuta is 11 years old and has been at the zoo for three years. The Bronx Zoo, one of the nation's largest zoos, contains hundreds of animals in habitats meant to resemble natural settings. Zoo officials will review safety procedures but stressed that the situation was unusual. The man is in stable condition, but his family has requested that no further information be released.

Bashuta's cubs were first featured in the Daily News in 2010. Breheny praised zoo workers for their quick response and preventing a potentially tragic situation. Bashuta will be back on exhibit tomorrow, according to zoo officials. The incident has raised questions about safety protocols at the zoo and the role of humans in causing harm to themselves and animals.

Meanwhile, Nora Ephron, an influential essayist, humorist, and filmmaker, passed away on June 26, 2016, at the age of 71. Ephron was a prolific writer, having worked as a journalist, blogger, essayist, novelist, playwright, Oscar-nominated screenwriter, and movie director. She was best known for her romantic comedy hits like "Sleepless in Seattle" and "When Harry Met Sally..."

Ephron was born on May 19, 1941, in Manhattan and raised in Beverly Hills, California. Her parents were Broadway playwrights, and all four of her sisters became writers. Ephron began her career as a journalist at the New York Post and later wrote for Esquire and New York magazines.

In 1976, Ephron married Washington Post journalist Carl Bernstein, with whom she collaborated on the screenplay for "All the President's Men." Their marriage ended in divorce four years later. Tom Colicchio, a renowned chef, has renamed his restaurant at the Beekman Hotel from Fowler & Wells to Temple Court, due to the discovery of the original name's racially charged past. Fowler & Wells were publishers and phrenologists in the mid-1800s, a time when phrenology, the study of skull size and structure to determine mental abilities, was widely used, often as a justification for discrimination and slavery.

Phrenology was not only used to justify slavery but also abolition. In Quentin Tarantino's Django Unchained, the character Calvin Candie, a southern slave owner, uses phrenology to assert the superiority of whites over African slaves. He claimed that an enlarged area in the brain associated with "submissiveness" was found in African slaves, justifying their enslavement.

However, phrenology has been thoroughly debunked, as the idea that the shape of the skull can be used to infer mental characteristics is incorrect. Despite this, it was popular during the 19th century, finding converts among reform-minded individuals worldwide.

Research reveals that even some abolitionists were advocates of phrenology, using it to justify their stance. Lucretia Mott, an American abolitionist, sent her children to phrenological lectures and spoke highly of phrenology. Horace Mann, another major figure in abolitionist politics, was an avid phrenologist.

Interestingly, the majority of phrenologists were against slavery. George Combe, a prominent phrenologist, explained that the apparent weakness and timidity of Africans served two purposes: it countered fears that they would take revenge on their masters if set free, and it provided a moral argument for helping them, not enslaving them.

In conclusion, the name change of Fowler & Wells to Temple Court reflects the growing awareness and rejection of historical practices that were used to justify discrimination and slavery. The intertwined history of scientific racism and abolition during the 19th century serves as a reminder of the complexities and contradictions of the past.

However, there is no record of her as a volunteer for the Nevada Democratic Party.

Another woman, Meagan Broussard from Texas, has also come forward, claiming she exchanged sexually charged messages with Weiner for a month. The controversy has prompted top Republicans to call for Weiner's resignation, with Democrats largely remaining silent on the issue.

In a separate incident, Jon Stewart of The Daily Show injured his hand during a mock press conference where he "resigned" for not being harsh enough on Rep. Weiner. The incident occurred while Stewart was making drinks during the bit, and John Oliver took over the show afterward, promising to be egregiously cruel to Weiner.

Wells Fargo CEO John Stumpf has agreed to forfeit $41 million in performance pay as the bank faces a scandal over the creation of millions of unauthorized accounts. The bank's former head of retail operations, Carrie Tolstedt, has also forfeited $19 million in bonuses and left the company. California has dropped Wells Fargo as its bond underwriter and broker-dealer due to the scandal. The US Consumer Financial Protection Bureau fined the bank $185 million earlier this month for "widespread illegal practice." Stumpf is expected to face tough questioning at a hearing before the House Financial Services Committee on Thursday. The bank's board has launched an independent investigation into the company's sales practices. The controversy has led to calls for Stumpf to resign, and he has faced criticism for his handling of the situation. The bank has fired more than 5,000 employees in response to the scandal.

The article discusses the controversy surrounding Terry Jones, a pastor who gained notoriety for threatening to burn the Qur'an on the anniversary of September 11. Jones claimed to have struck a deal to move a Muslim cultural center and mosque away from its current location in New York City. However, it is unclear if such a deal was actually made. Jones's threats have been met with criticism and concern, as they have the potential to incite violence and tension between different religious groups.

The media's coverage of Jones and his threats has been a topic of discussion. Fox News, CNN, and the Associated Press have all announced that they will not show images of the Qur'an being burned, citing a desire to avoid gratuitous offense. NBC has also announced that it will film the event but not show live coverage.

The article also mentions the Westboro Baptist Church of Kansas, which has also threatened to burn Qur'ans. However, their antics have been met with little interest from the media, as they are considered a fringe group.

Overall, the article suggests that Jones's threats have been subject to the law of diminishing returns, as the media has become more cautious in their coverage of him. The episode has also sparked some soul-searching within news organizations about the role they play in giving attention to controversial figures.

The document discusses two main topics: the donation of crawl data by Alexa Internet to the Internet Archive and the rise of fascism, particularly in the context of the 2016 U.S. presidential election.

Alexa Internet has been donating their crawl data to the Internet Archive since 1996. This data is added to the Wayback Machine after an embargo period. The goal is to archive pages as they are created and preserve the pages that they refer to, fixing broken links on the web.

The second topic revolves around the term "fascism" and its significance in 2016. Merriam-Webster reported that "fascism" was the most-looked-up word of the year, likely due to its association with the presidential election and related political movements. In response, Merriam-Webster's Twitter account attempted to encourage users to look up other words in an attempt to dethrone "fascism" as the word of the year. However, a word like "flummadiddle," defined as "something foolish or worthless," did not manage to surpass the popularity of "fascism."

In summary, the document discusses the efforts to preserve web data and fix broken links on the web, as well as the increased interest in the term "fascism" in 2016, particularly in the context of the U.S. presidential election.

In Mexico, the mayor of Doctor Gonzalez, located 30 miles east of Monterrey in Nuevo Leon state, was shot and killed by gunmen on Thursday. The attack is one of four public official killings in less than a month, with drug gangs being the suspected culprits. The mayor, Prisciliano Rodriguez, won the mayorship last year for the opposition Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI). The motive for the attack is unclear, but Nuevo Leon and neighboring Tamaulipas have become major drug war flashpoints. Another person traveling with the mayor was also killed in the attack.

In a separate incident, residents of a small town in the northern state of Chihuahua, Ascension, took justice into their own hands this week. An angry mob pursued and allegedly killed two suspected kidnappers, storming a military base to get at the alleged culprits who had kidnapped a teenage girl. The public fury happened due to the inability of the police to stop the violent crime epidemic in Mexico amid the brutal drug war. Ascension is a farming community of some 15,000 people, about 100 miles south of the border with New Mexico. In the past two years, kidnapping and extortion have been rampant.

President Felipe Calderon has condemned the killings and vowed to continue his fight against drug cartels, which have led to more than 29,000 people being killed in drug violence since Calderon sent more than 45,000 troops and federal police across Mexico in 2006 to battle warring drug gangs. The U.S. government has advised its consulate staff in Monterrey to send their children out of the city due to the high levels of drug-related violence. There have been more than 450 drug killings in Monterrey and Nuevo Leon state this year.

A sea slug named Chromodoris reticulata, found in the Pacific Ocean, has surprised scientists with its ability to detach, re-grow, and re-use its penis during mating. This is believed to be the first creature known to copulate using a "disposable penis." The sea slugs, also known as nudibranchs, are simultaneous hermaphrodites, possessing both male and female sexual organs. The Japanese team of researchers observed the animals as they mated, noting that the act took between a few seconds and a few minutes, after which the creatures would push away and shed their penises. Remarkably, the sea slugs were able to regenerate their male organs and mate again within 24 hours. The scientists discovered that the sea slugs had a large part of their penis coiled up in a spiral inside their bodies, which they would then use to replenish their missing part. The penis was also equipped with spines, possibly used to remove sperm left by competitors. This unique reproductive strategy allows the sea slug to ensure its genes are passed on by removing the sperm of previous partners before injecting its own. The team observed that the animals could copulate three times in succession, with each bout separated by about 24 hours. It is not yet clear whether the animal's sex life is effectively over once the internal penis is used up after these attempts or if the organ can regrow after a few weeks or months. Sea slugs are not the only animals that abandon their penis; orb weaving spiders, periwinkles, and certain land slugs also exhibit this behavior. However, Chromodoris reticulata is the first creature known to re-grow its appendage, giving it a sexual advantage.

The article discusses the experiences of Amanda Knox during her four-year imprisonment in Italy for the murder of her roommate Meredith Kercher. Knox's account of prison life, as presented in her upcoming memoir, has been compared to her earlier writings, including a personal prison diary.

Initially, Knox's diary portrayed the prison staff as kind and gentle, with no instances of physical abuse. However, in her memoir, she claims that prison guard Raffaele Argiro sexually harassed her, summoning her for late-night "chitchats" and asking inappropriate questions about her sexual partners. Argiro has since retired and denies the allegations.

Knox also recounts in her memoir that a female inmate attempted to start a lesbian affair with her, and that she was falsely told by officials that she was HIV positive.

The article also mentions that Knox's memoir, titled "Waiting to Be Heard," will be published by HarperCollins on April 30, 2013.

Since her release from prison in 2011, Knox has resumed her life in Seattle, taking classes and spending time with her family and boyfriend, James Terrano. Knox's first interview since her release will air during a primetime special on ABC on April 30, 2013.

The article concludes by mentioning that a new trial for Knox and her ex-boyfriend Raffaele Sollecito is expected to start sometime next year, as the Italian Supreme Court ordered a re-trial in January 2013. Knox has expressed disappointment and frustration about the decision, stating that it is "painful" and "completely unfounded and unfair."

In the sentencing hearing for Dzhokhar Tsarnaev, the Boston Marathon bomber, it is expected that he will be formally sentenced to death for his role in the 2013 attack that resulted in three deaths and over 260 injuries. However, it is unclear whether Tsarnaev will choose to address the court before the sentence is imposed. During the trial, Tsarnaev's remorse was only indirectly expressed, and legal experts suggest that there is little upside for him to make a statement.

Tsarnaev's lawyers have stated that he feels remorse for the attack, but his demeanor throughout the trial was impassive, making it difficult to know what he truly means. Sister Helen Prejean, a death penalty opponent, met with Tsarnaev five times and believes he is genuinely sorry for the carnage. However, prosecutors presented video evidence that showed Tsarnaev giving the middle finger to a security camera in a holding cell, suggesting a lack of remorse.

Legal experts suggest that Tsarnaev has little to gain by speaking, as the judge is required to impose the death sentence recommended by the jury. Some wonder if he could decide to apologize or make a political statement, but it is uncertain what he might say.

Convicted terrorists in the past have used their sentencing as an opportunity for diatribes, such as Zacarias Moussaoui, who proclaimed his support for Osama bin Laden, and Abu Hamza, who complained about the conditions he would face in prison. However, it is unlikely that Tsarnaev would follow this precedent.

Over 20 bombing victims are expected to speak during Tsarnaev's sentencing hearing, including family members of those who died and people who were injured in the explosions. Bombing survivor Celeste Corcoran has stated that she and her daughter will not attend the sentencing, as they believe it would add unnecessary stress and have no impact on Tsarnaev.

In the end, it is uncertain whether Tsarnaev will choose to speak during his sentencing hearing. Legal experts suggest that there is little to be gained, and it is unlikely that he would make a political statement or express remorse. The focus of the hearing will be on the victims and their families, who will have the opportunity to share their experiences and feelings.

In a significant development, actress Rose McGowan, who accused Harvey Weinstein of rape, expressed her joy over his arrest on "Megyn Kelly Today". The Hollywood community largely welcomed Weinstein's downfall following the allegations of sexual misconduct against him.

Separately, Morgan Freeman, an 80-year-old actor, issued an apology after multiple women accused him of harassment, including unwanted touching and inappropriate comments. Eight women, who have worked with Freeman on movie sets, for his production company, or interviewed him professionally, made these allegations. Several of the accusers stated they didn't report Freeman's behavior due to job fears.

Freeman responded to the accusations, stating he never intended to offend or make anyone uncomfortable. However, past interview footage shows more examples of questionable behavior, as described in a CNN report.

In 2015, Morgan Freeman made inappropriate comments about Janet Mock's appearance during an ET sit-down interview. Mock, who is currently writing and producing for Ryan Murphy’s new FX series, Pose, addressed the encounter, stating it was an example of men in power feeling entitled to women's bodies.

Entertainment reporter Chloe Melas, who co-authored the CNN piece on the accusations against Freeman, claimed she experienced her own inappropriate encounter with the actor at a press junket for his 2017 film, Going in Style. Melas, who was six months pregnant at the time, alleged that Freeman looked her up and down while shaking her hand and made suggestive comments, despite being surrounded by his co-stars and other junket personnel. However, Warner Bros. HR could not corroborate the account due to lack of video evidence and unnoticed behavior by employees present.

These incidents add to the growing list of sexual harassment allegations in the entertainment industry, following similar accusations against actors like Jeffrey Tambor and Harvey Weinstein.

A 19-year-old college student named Levy Thamba from the Democratic Republic of the Congo died in March 2014 after consuming an entire marijuana cookie containing 65 milligrams of THC, six times the recommended amount, while visiting Denver. The cookie was purchased at a marijuana store named Native Root Apothecary, and the group of four friends were instructed to divide the cookie into six pieces and consume one piece at a time. However, Thamba ate the entire cookie after not feeling any effects from the initial serving.

Over the next few hours, Thamba exhibited erratic behavior, including speaking in French, talking to a room lamp, and smashing room furniture. He eventually jumped off a fourth-floor balcony of a hotel and died from trauma from the fall. The autopsy found marijuana intoxication as a significant contributing factor, with Thamba's marijuana concentration in his blood being 7.2 nanograms of active THC per milliliter of blood, exceeding the legal limit for driving in Colorado.

This case illustrates the potential dangers associated with recreational edible marijuana use. The delayed effects of THC-infused edibles can lead to multiple servings being consumed in close succession before experiencing the "high" from the initial serving. High doses of THC can produce serious anxiety attacks and psychotic-like symptoms.

In response to this case and similar incidents, Colorado instituted new rules for the packaging and labeling of edible marijuana products in February 2015, requiring these products to contain no more than 10 mg of THC or to have clear marking of each 10-mg serving. However, the report suggests a need for improved public health messaging to reduce the risk of overconsumption of THC.

This story was first reported by CBS4, and the Denver police presented the case to the Denver District Attorney's Office. Prosecutors decided not to pursue criminal charges against Bessie Gondwe, the only person of legal age among the foursome who would be able to purchase recreational marijuana in Colorado. The Denver coroner listed "marijuana intoxication" as a significant condition contributing to Thamba's death.

This case highlights the need for clear instructions and warnings regarding the consumption of edible marijuana products, particularly for inexperienced users. It also underscores the importance of ongoing monitoring and regulation of recreational marijuana use to prevent adverse health effects.

Sally Hootnick, a resident of Manlius, NY, lost her iPad on an American Airlines flight that landed in New York City. Despite using a tracking software to locate her device, she was unable to retrieve it as authorities failed to act on her reports. Hootnick left messages with the airline's lost and found department and contacted the Port Authority of New York & New Jersey, but no action was taken. Frustrated, she sent messages to the iPad and used another application to make it beep every two minutes. The iPad was tracked moving from JFK Airport to Los Angeles, San Francisco, and back to JFK, leading Hootnick to suspect it was being used by an airline employee. American Airlines is not commenting on the ongoing investigation, and officials with the Port Authority have not returned calls. Hootnick has since replaced her iPad and turned off its wireless service, rendering it impossible to track.

Two Japanese citizens, Kenji Goto, a veteran war journalist, and Haruna Yukawa, a private military contractor, are being held hostage by the Islamic State extremist group in Syria. The hostages were warned by friends and colleagues to avoid the danger zones in Syria, but both disregarded the advice and entered the war-torn country for different reasons. Goto was seeking first-hand coverage of the conflict to shed light on the plight of innocent victims, while Yukawa was pursuing business opportunities.

In a video posted online, a masked man with a knife threatened to kill the hostages unless the Japanese government pays a ransom of $200 million (23.58 billion yen) within 72 hours. The Japanese government has verified the identities of the hostages and is using every possible diplomatic channel to secure their release.

Goto, the operator of the video news agency Independent Press, had a long career covering children in conflict-torn regions and had contributed to campaigns by the Japan Committee for UNICEF to raise awareness of children's rights around the world. Yukawa, who established a private military company called PMC in January 2014, had no military background but expressed excitement over having the chance to fire a gun in Syria.

The Japanese government has emphasized that its aid to Middle Eastern nations battling ISIS is humanitarian in nature and not intended to harm Muslims. The ransom demand is more than four-times the amount of money extorted by ISIS in exchange for hostages over the past year. The Japanese National Police Agency has dispatched a counter-terrorism team to Amman, Jordan, and is analyzing the hostage video for signs of manipulation.

Both hostages' families have been affected by the crisis. Yukawa's father has been unable to comment on the situation, while Goto's wife received an email demanding a ransom in December. The captors have used social media to disseminate their video as far and fast as possible in Japan, copying and pasting key phrases into trending hashtags to ensure quick spread.

Friends and colleagues are praying for the safe release of Goto and Yukawa, and many have expressed concern for their wellbeing. Goto's life work was to cover children in conflict-torn regions and convey the harsh realities they face to the world. Yukawa's venture into Syria was too dangerous, according to acquaintances, and his lack of experience and willingness to take risks may have played a role in his abduction.

In Grand Rapids, Michigan, the prosecutor's office has dropped the case against an 87-year-old man, Howard Klein, who was charged with soliciting a prostitute. The arrest took place on July 21, 2015, near Broadway Street NW and Leonard Avenue. Klein was not taken into custody due to his age and had no prior criminal record. He claimed he thought the woman he approached was someone he knew from church. The Kent County Prosecutor's Office reviewed the case and decided to dismiss the charges, stating that Klein, given his age and health issues, did not pose a danger to society. This case is notable as it may be the oldest person ever charged with this crime. Two other individuals, Tia Booth and Tammy Glautney, were also arrested for prostitution during the same sting operation.

On Saturday, a Trader Joe's employee, Melyda Corado, was killed by a police bullet during a shootout with a suspect, Gene Evin Atkins, in Silver Lake, Los Angeles. According to LAPD Chief Michel Moore, one of the officers accidentally shot Corado while engaging in a shootout with Atkins, who had crashed his car into a light pole outside the Trader Joe's store.

Corado, who was one of several people who ran to the front door of the store, was hit by a bullet that entered her body after it first hit her arm. Atkins, who had shot his grandmother and 17-year-old girlfriend before the incident, was charged with over 30 counts, including one count of murder, six counts of attempted murder, and 13 counts of false imprisonment of hostages.

Atkins' arraignment was postponed to Aug. 14, and his bail was set at $18.7 million. The slaying of Corado is attributed to Atkins even though he did not fire the fatal bullet because he is held to have caused the entire situation.

The Trader Joe's store remained closed on Monday, and a memorial of signs and flowers in memory of Corado continued to grow outside the building. The two officers involved in the shooting have been with the department for two years and six years, respectively.

The LAPD released dash-cam video leading up to the chase, and Atkins appeared in court on Tuesday for an initial appearance. The officers involved in the shooting are reportedly "devastated" by Corado's death. The incident has prompted mixed reactions, with some blaming the police for shooting directly towards the store, while others appreciate the precarious situation in which the officers found themselves. A GoFundMe page set up to help cover Corado's funeral expenses had raised nearly $25,000 as of midday Monday.

The Canadian UFO Survey for 2015, released recently, showed an increase in UFO sightings compared to 2014, with a total of 1,267 reports, second only to 1,981 in 2012. The survey, compiled by Chris Rutkowski, a science writer, includes reports from all provinces, with an unusual number of cases from Quebec. The survey defines a UFO as any object in the sky that cannot be explained. Most of the sightings were attributed to stars, planets, fireballs, aircraft, and police helicopters, but about 12% remained unexplained.

One "high-quality" unexplained case was from Manitoba in October 2015, where a couple saw a bright light that wasn't on a cellphone tower. They later saw a dark triangle moving with a red light in front and green and another color on the side. The object was silent and didn't look like an aircraft. The group investigating the sighting hasn't found an explanation yet.

The survey includes numerous strange stories, including accounts of lights, aircraft-shaped objects, silently hovering UFOs, and close encounters of the third kind. Only about 12% of the reports were classified as "unexplained." The data was collected from 17 sources across the country, including Transport Canada, Canada National Defense, and the National UFO Reporting Center.

Quebec led the country with 35% of all UFO reports in 2015. Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Nova Scotia, and Newfoundland also saw an increase in UFO sightings. Montreal had the most reports, followed by Toronto and Vancouver. The average sighting lasted about 16 minutes.

The survey has been conducted annually since 1989, and since then, they've compiled 16,905 sightings. By and large, Canadians mostly reported seeing strange lights in the night sky. The data becomes particularly strange in several isolated reports of one-on-one contact with alien beings.

The increase in UFO sightings could be linked to the popularization of drones, camera phones, laser pointers, and at-home strobe lights. However, Chris Rutkowski suggests that the increase likely relates to the country's collective curiosity. He added that, as writers like Stephen Hawking continue to pen popular books on outer space, humankind will continue to question the existence of extra-terrestrial life.

The Wolfman, a remake of the 1941 Universal horror film, was released in 2010. Directed by Joe Johnston, the film stars Benicio Del Toro, Anthony Hopkins, Emily Blunt, Hugo Weaving, Geraldine Chaplin, and Art Malik. The film attempts to blend the gothic storytelling of the original with modern horror elements, but the result is a hybrid that fails to work effectively.

The film takes place in rural England in the 1890s, where Lawrence Talbot (Del Toro) returns to his family's estate after receiving a plea from his brother's fiancée, Gwen Conliffe (Blunt). Upon arriving, Lawrence finds that his brother has disappeared, and a mangled body has been found. Lawrence becomes determined to find the beast responsible for his brother's death and begins a hunt that leads him to a gypsy camp, where he is attacked by a half-man/half-wolf.

Del Toro's portrayal of Talbot is criticized as muted and lacking emotional connection, while the film's attempts to recreate the original's haunting atmosphere are described as middling. The makeup provided by veteran Rick Baker is also criticized as campy, with the fangs looking like they were purchased at a Halloween costume store. The film's action takes a period piece flavor, and the supporting cast, including Anthony Hopkins and Emily Blunt, is described as wasted talent.

Overall, The Wolfman is criticized for its uneasy fusion of traditional makeup with CGI, its attempts to bridge the gap between classic and modern horror, and its campy appearance. The film is compared unfavorably to other classic horror remakes, including Dracula and Frankenstein, and is described as unnecessary and unintentional campy.

The Iranian supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, has responded to the US withdrawal from the 2015 nuclear deal by challenging President Donald Trump, saying "You cannot do a damn thing!" Khamenei made the comments during a meeting with school teachers in Tehran, a day after Trump announced the renewal of sanctions on Iran. Khamenei described Trump's speech as containing "more than 10 lies" and said it threatened Iran's people and government.

The nuclear deal, known as the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA), was a landmark agreement reached in July 2015 between Iran and a six-nation negotiating group, including the US, UK, France, Russia, China, and Germany. The deal limited Iran's nuclear program in exchange for sanctions relief. Under the deal, Iran unplugged two-thirds of its centrifuges, shipped out 98% of its enriched uranium, and filled its plutonium production reactor with concrete.

Khamenei has said it is not feasible for Iran to continue implementing the agreement without receiving enough guarantees from the UK, France, and Germany to withstand US pressure. The EU wants to keep the agreement but a US exit might trigger a collapse of the deal because US sanctions will hamper European business with Tehran.

The US exit from the agreement has been met with protests in Iran, with hardliners seizing on the opportunity to consolidate their power over reformists who championed the pact. On Wednesday, the commander of Iran's powerful Revolutionary Guards congratulated the nation on the US exit, while at the opening session of the Iranian parliament, a group of hardline MPs set fire to a US flag and the text of the JCPOA.

The US exit from the agreement has also been met with criticism from European allies, with France's Foreign Minister Jean-Yves Le Drian saying the deal is "not dead" despite Trump's decision to withdraw. Le Drian said there would be a meeting between France, Britain, Germany, and Iran on Monday to discuss the future of the deal. Russia and China have also expressed disappointment over the US decision, while Israel and Saudi Arabia have welcomed it.

The US Treasury has said the sanctions being reimposed will target industries mentioned in the deal, including Iran's oil sector, aircraft manufacturers exporting to Iran, and Iranian government attempts to buy US dollar banknotes. Major European and US companies are likely to be hit, with some exemptions due to be negotiated. The US National Security Adviser John Bolton is reported as saying that European companies doing business in Iran will have to stop doing so within six months or face US sanctions.

The US withdrawal from the nuclear deal has raised concerns about the future of the agreement and the potential for increased tensions in the Middle East. Experts say that it could still take Iran years to acquire a working nuclear arsenal, but the US exit has been criticized for undermining diplomacy and potentially bringing a new and catastrophic regional war closer.

The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) is set to vote on net neutrality rules on Thursday, aiming to preserve an open Internet and prevent Internet service providers (ISPs) from discriminating against content makers. The rules, proposed by FCC Chairman Tom Wheeler, aim to regulate ISPs as a utility under Title II of The Communications Act, a move that has been met with criticism from Republicans who argue it is overkill.

Net neutrality has become a polarizing issue, with more than 4 million comments on the subject filed with the FCC from various parties, including ISPs such as AT&T and Verizon, organizations such as the American Civil Liberties Union, and tech companies like Google and Netflix. The rules are expected to pass, but their impact will not be the last word as the agency's action will be challenged in court, by Congress, and by other entities.

The proposed rules have been met with opposition from some in the wireless industry, who argue that the rules would make it harder to manage congestion on their networks. However, some wireless companies, such as Sprint and T-Mobile, have publicly stated that they are not opposed to the new rules.

The battle over net neutrality has been ongoing for over a decade, with the FCC taking a different approach this time around compared to its last attempt in 2010. The new rules would allow for wireless carriers to discriminate against websites or applications in order to prevent congestion on their networks, a recognition that wireless is different from the wires that carry data into homes and businesses.

However, there are concerns about zero-rating, a practice where wireless providers promise not to count one app or group of apps against a consumer's monthly data cap. Critics argue that this creates an un-level playing field and interferes with user choice, while proponents argue that it is a good deal for consumers.

The FCC's proposed rules are expected to pass on Thursday, but their impact will not be immediately clear for the average consumer. The rules will give the FCC the authority to regulate ISPs and prohibit "fast lanes" that would grant faster access to companies that pay for the privilege. The debate over net neutrality is expected to continue, with potential legislative action and legal challenges in the future.

The First Step Act, a bipartisan bill aimed at reforming federal criminal justice sentencing laws, is gaining momentum with President Donald Trump's support. The proposed legislation focuses on improving prison conditions, preparing prisoners for re-entry into their communities, and reducing mandatory minimum sentences for drug-related crimes.

Key aspects of the bill include the creation of a risk and need assessment system to guide prisoners towards better outcomes, the expansion of time credits for good behavior, and the introduction of new credits for participating in job-training programs. The bill also addresses the specific needs of incarcerated women, prohibiting the shackling of pregnant inmates and requiring the Bureau of Prisons to locate prisoners in facilities close to their homes, if possible.

The Fraternal Order of Police and the National Sheriffs' Association have expressed support for the bill, despite initial objections from some law enforcement officials and conservative lawmakers. The bill's progress was bolstered by a letter from public figures, including Van Jones, Mark Cuban, Patricia Arquette, Kim Kardashian West, and Kanye West, urging Congress to recognize the humanity of inmates and act on the legislation.

The bill faces a crucial decision from Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell, who must decide whether to bring it up for a vote. The bill enjoys broad bipartisan support for prison reform, but sentencing reform, which would remove harsh sentencing minimums, is favored by Democrats but has divided Republicans.

The proposed sentencing reform would eliminate mandatory life sentences for defendants facing a third drug conviction, except for those with a prior "serious violent felony," and reduce federal mandatory minimum sentences for non-violent offenders. The bill could potentially release 4,000 people currently serving long sentences, invest tens of millions in re-entry programming, and retroactively extend the 2010 Fair Sentencing Act.

President Trump, who has been leery of appearing weak on crime, announced his support for the bill on Wednesday, stating that it would reduce crime while giving former inmates a chance at redemption. The bill's progress demonstrates the potential for bipartisan cooperation and compromise on criminal justice reform.

On October 22, 19-year-old Lucas Ransom, a fearless athlete and junior at the University of California, Santa Barbara, died after being attacked by a shark off the Santa Barbara coast. The attack occurred around 9 a.m. PDT, and three beaches in Santa Barbara County were immediately closed. Witnesses reported that the shark bit off Ransom's leg, and he bled to death.

Steve Blair, assistant curator of the Aquarium of the Pacific and a shark expert, believes that the great white shark is the likely culprit. Only a dozen out of the world's 400 shark species could inflict such a bite, and great whites are known to troll the coast of California and swim close to shore in search of seals and sea lions.

The attack occurred when Ransom and his friend were boogie boarding 100 yards off the beach. The shark, which was between 14 and 20 feet in length, pulled Ransom under the water. Ransom's friend apparently tried to get him out of the water, but it is believed that Ransom was dead before he made it to shore.

The shark was likely swimming around as the pair fled from the water, but it is unlikely that the shark is still in the area hunting humans. Federal and state wildlife officials are working to identify the type of shark that attacked Ransom.

Ransom was a chemical engineering major and was from Riverside County, just outside Los Angeles. The area where the attack occurred is a popular surfing spot and is adjacent to the Vandenberg Air Force Base, which responded to the incident. The last great white shark fatality in California was two years ago, when a triathlete swimmer was bitten in the leg off the coast of San Diego. He died a short time later from blood loss.

HBO Now, a standalone version of HBO without the need for a cable subscription, has officially launched on Apple TV and iOS devices. The service can be purchased through iTunes, with a free first month trial, and Cablevision is expected to start selling it soon. The HBO Now app on Apple TV is similar to HBO Go, offering the full library of original shows and movies.

Setting up an account was initially problematic due to high demand, but things seem to be improving. The user agreement reserves HBO's right to change the number of simultaneous streams and shut down password sharing if necessary. The service is intended for family use, but enforcement of this rule is unclear.

The Apple TV experience is functional but bland, with simple navigation and no significant issues during playback. The service is a no-brainer for those within Apple's ecosystem, offering a 30-day free trial. However, cord-cutting Android users will need to continue borrowing HBO Go logins for now. The service is expected to expand to other devices in the future.

The Washington Post's Philip Rucker reports that Republican presidential nominee Donald Trump has refused to endorse House Speaker Paul D. Ryan and Sen. John McCain (R-Ariz.) in their primary races, escalating his war with the GOP leadership. Trump's comments, an extraordinary breach of political decorum, came as President Obama delivered his sternest rebuke yet of Trump, calling him "unfit to serve as president" and "woefully unprepared."

In an interview with The Washington Post, Trump said he was not backing Ryan in his primary election next Tuesday in Wisconsin, or McCain in his Arizona primary later this month. Both have endorsed Trump but have criticized some of his policies and statements, most recently his belittling of the parents of dead U.S. Army Capt. Humayun Khan.

Trump praised Ryan's underdog opponent, Paul Nehlen, for running "a very good campaign" and said of Ryan: "I like Paul, but these are horrible times for our country. We need very strong leadership. We need very, very strong leadership. And I’m just not quite there yet. I’m not quite there yet."

Trump's comments underscore the continuing divisions in the GOP two weeks after the party's national convention in Cleveland, which was carefully choreographed to showcase unity. Also Tuesday, Rep. Richard L. Hanna (N.Y.) became the first sitting Republican member of Congress to declare publicly his plans to vote for Democratic nominee Hillary Clinton.

Trump said that Ryan has sought his endorsement but that he is only "giving it very serious consideration." Responding to Trump, Ryan spokesman Zack Roday said in a statement: "Neither Speaker Ryan nor anyone on his team has ever asked for Donald Trump’s endorsement. And we are confident in a victory next week regardless."

Trump made his comments during a wide-ranging 50-minute interview Tuesday afternoon over lunch at the Trump National Golf Club in Northern Virginia. He said he will work to negotiate the terms of general-election debates in his favor, saying that three is "the right number" but that they should not be scheduled on the same nights as National Football League games or the baseball World Series. He said that he should have influence in selecting "a fair moderator" for each debate and that third-party candidates Gary Johnson and Jill Stein should not be allowed on stage. "I’d rather have head to head" with Clinton, Trump said.

He took issue with the characterization of Clinton at last week's Democratic National Convention as a fighter and a change-maker. "Hillary’s not a change person. She’s going to be a person to keep it just the way it is," Trump said, biting into his cheeseburger. "It’s going to be four more years of Obama."

Trump lashed out at the media, including The Post, which he accused of turning sharply against him since he secured the nomination. "It’s myself really against the media," he said, citing what he views as "a tremendous bias against me."

Trump's statements about Ryan are the latest hiccup in what has been a fraught relationship for the two party leaders. Ryan endorsed Trump this spring and spoke on his behalf at the convention, but only after a period of public soul-searching. Ryan has disagreed with Trump on several key issues — including his proposed temporary ban on Muslims entering the United States — and he issued a statement over the weekend that indirectly criticized Trump's comments about the Khans.

In the Tuesday interview, Trump defended his commentary about the Khans by saying, "I was viciously attacked on the stage, and I have a right to answer back." However, his campaign acknowledged the crisis in an email sent to congressional supporters this week with the subject line "Urgent Pivot: Khan and TPs." The email asked allies on Capitol Hill to defend Trump's heavily criticized remarks about the Khans by underscoring his commitment to ending "radical Islamic terror" and deemphasizing his most confrontational comments.

In making his comments Tuesday, Trump may have been seeking retribution for Ryan's dragging his feet about endorsing Trump in May. Trump's phrasing of his uncertainty about Ryan — "I’m just not quite there yet" — echoes what Ryan told CNN's Jake Tapper in a May interview about endorsing Trump: "I’m just not ready to do that at this point. I’m not there right now."
