Trump's non-endorsement of Ryan and McCain is a significant departure from the usual practice of presidential nominees endorsing their party's incumbent members of Congress. The move is likely to further strain relations between Trump and the GOP establishment, and could have implications for the party's efforts to maintain control of Congress in the November elections.

The Supreme Court confirmation hearing for Judge Brett Kavanaugh is underway, with senators questioning him about his views on abortion, presidential power, and the independence of the judiciary. Kavanaugh, nominated by President Trump to replace retired Justice Anthony Kennedy, is treading carefully and not revealing his hand on key issues.

Democrats and liberal interest groups have expressed concern about Kavanaugh's nomination and its potential impact on abortion rights, as Kavanaugh could be a vote to uphold additional restrictions on the procedure and possibly overturn the 1973 Roe v. Wade Supreme Court decision that established a constitutional right to an abortion. However, Kavanaugh did not reveal his stance on Roe v. Wade during the hearing, calling it an "important precedent" that has been reaffirmed many times over the past 45 years.

Kavanaugh also declined to answer a series of questions about the powers of the president, particularly relevant given ongoing investigations surrounding President Trump. Kavanaugh said that he would not answer questions that could potentially come before the court, citing the need to decide issues only after hearing both sides of a case. Among the questions he declined to answer were whether the president has an absolute right to pardon himself, whether he can pardon someone in exchange for a promise not to testify against him, and whether he can be required to respond to a subpoena.

Repercussions of the "Me Too" era made an appearance at the hearing, as Kavanaugh was asked about his relationship with former federal appeals court judge Alex Kozinski, who resigned last year after several female former law clerks and colleagues accused him of sexual misconduct. Kavanaugh said that he was shocked and disappointed by the allegations and had no knowledge of them before they became public.

The hearing is expected to continue into the late evening, with Democratic senators expected to press Kavanaugh on issues such as gun rights, executive power, and his views on precedent. Kavanaugh's confirmation is likely, with Republicans holding a majority in the Senate and nearly all of them expected to support his nomination. However, several Democratic senators facing tough re-election races may vote to confirm him.

On Sunday, Santa Monica College confirmed the death of 26-year-old student Marcela Franco, making her the fifth victim of a shooting rampage that occurred on Friday. Marcela was with her father, Carlos Franco, 68, when the shooting took place. They were driving to the college to buy books for Marcela's summer classes when they were shot. Carlos died at the scene, while Marcela was taken to Ronald Reagan UCLA Medical Center but later passed away.

The shooting suspect, identified as John Zawahri, 23, was later killed by police during a confrontation in the college's library. The gunman had allegedly killed his father, Samir Zawahri, 55, and brother, Chris, 25, in a Santa Monica house before the rampage. He also killed a woman outside the library and wounded several others along the way.

The Santa Monica College Foundation has started the Carlos Franco Family Memorial Fund to honor the Franco family. Carlos Franco was a dedicated employee of the college, having worked there for 22 years. He was described as a hard worker who always tried to make people happy.

Police believe that the house was set on fire before the shootings, and the rampage spanned several parts of Santa Monica. The gunman was heavily armed and had about 1,300 rounds of ammunition during the rampage. The motive for the shootings is still under investigation, and there is no link to domestic or international terrorism.

Neighbors' stories suggest that the gunman forced a woman to stop her car at gunpoint and later hijacked another car during the rampage. The gunman was carrying an "AR-15 style rifle," pistols, and more clips for the rifle. The gunman was killed in a shootout with police in the college library.

Investigators are still trying to determine the motive for the shootings, which also left four people wounded. The gunman and a family member had been enrolled in Santa Monica College as recently as 2010. The gunman had reportedly suffered from mental health issues and had been hospitalized for treatment after allegedly talking about harming someone in the past.

Keith Urban and Nicole Kidman, both 45, maintain a strong relationship despite their busy schedules, with Urban touring and taping American Idol in the US, and Kidman filming in London. In an interview on The Ellen DeGeneres Show, Urban revealed that they communicate through phone calls only, and share intimate moments through sexting.

In a separate interview with Vanity Fair, Kidman reflected on her past marriage to Tom Cruise at the age of 23. She expressed gratitude for her current relationship with Urban, stating that she didn't know if she would find her "great love" again. Kidman also shared her experiences during the filming of The Hours, where she played Virginia Woolf, and the emotional impact it had on her.

Kidman discussed the level of fame she experienced during her marriage to Cruise, comparing it to the closeness and intoxicating nature of being in a celebrity couple. She also spoke about the challenges of balancing her career, family, and fame, particularly when explaining these concepts to her children.

Kidman revealed her preference for living in Nashville with Urban and their two daughters, stating that she finds it offers her a more idiosyncratic path and a peaceful life away from the dominating influence of Hollywood. She also discussed the healing effect her marriage has had on her, particularly in terms of personal growth and healing.

Though Kidman described her marriage as "very, very peaceful," she admitted to struggling between dedicating herself to her lover and her children, and her artistic desires. She acknowledged that this is an ongoing struggle, as she strives to balance her family life with her artistic ambitions.

The full interview with Kidman can be found in the December issue of Vanity Fair, available for download on tablet devices or iPhones.

American Airlines is facing a significant staffing issue during the busy holiday travel period next month due to a scheduling glitch that allowed pilots to take vacation at the same time. As a result, approximately 15,000 flights are without pilots assigned to them, according to the airline's pilots union, the Allied Pilots Association (APA). The problem occurred when pilots loaded up their schedules with flights in early December but many opted to take days off around the holidays after the system allowed it.

American Airlines is offering pilots 150 percent of hourly pay to work those dates and has reserve pilots to help cover flying in December. However, the APA has filed a grievance, saying the airline's solution violates the pilots' contract because of how the airline restricted overtime pay. The union estimates some 19,000 cockpit seats were left empty when the problem was discovered late last week, with about 15,000 flights scheduled without a captain, co-pilot, or both.

American Airlines declined to confirm the number of flights initially affected but said it is working diligently to address the issue and expects to avoid cancellations this holiday season. The airline's spokesman, Matt Miller, said they will work with the APA to take care of their pilots and ensure customers get to their destinations over the holidays. The scheduling issue predominantly affects the second half of December around the holidays when a computer system inadvertently gave pilots the opportunity to withdraw from flying.

This staffing shortage comes after budget airline Ryanair canceled some 2,000 flights in September due to pilot scheduling problems, stranding thousands of travelers. It is unclear how much the scheduling problem will cost American Airlines, but higher labor costs have concerned investors in the past. American Airlines shares tumbled after the airline announced pay raises for pilots and flight attendants earlier this year.

The airline representatives declined to say how many of the carrier's 15,000 pilots were allowed to take time off for the holiday. American Airlines operates on average 6,700 daily flights and has about 200,000 flights scheduled for December. The airline is working to resolve the staffing shortage and ensure flights are on schedule for the busy holiday travel period.

Jacob Brundage, a professional poker player from Lakeland, Florida, experienced an emotional jackpot after an Uber driver returned his lost bag containing $7,000 in cash and playing chips during the World Series of Poker in Las Vegas. Brundage realized his bag was left in an Uber minivan he had taken from The Venetian to the Rio around 9 p.m. on June 1. He frantically tried to contact the driver through the app but was unsuccessful.

Brundage then approached a group of Uber employees at the Rio, who assisted in tracking down the driver and the lost bag. After more than an hour, Brundage's phone rang, and the driver explained that his cellphone battery died. Brundage offered him $200 as a reward, which the driver accepted.

Uber spokeswoman Maui Cheska Orozco confirmed that this was likely the most expensive item ever left in an Uber car in Las Vegas. Brundage expressed his gratitude for the driver's honesty and integrity, feeling blessed by the experience.

On October 24, 2015, Academy Award-winning filmmaker Quentin Tarantino joined hundreds of demonstrators in New York City to protest police brutality. The protest was organized by RiseUpOctober and was the last of three demonstrations held in New York this week. The protesters marched from Washington Square Park to Sixth Avenue, waving signs and shouting through megaphones.

Speakers at the rally, including Tarantino, called for justice for those killed by police. Tarantino, who flew in from California for the event, said, "I'm a human being with a conscience, and if you believe there's murder going on then you need to rise up and stand up against it. I'm here to say I'm on the side of the murdered."

One of the organizers, academic and activist Cornel West, walked arm in arm with Temako Williams, whose son was killed by police in 2011 in Charlotte, North Carolina. Williams said, "It wasn't worth the price of my son's life. It's a wound that won't heal."

The protest came at a time of heightened awareness nationwide of the relationship between police officers and the people they serve. The event was peaceful, and no arrests were reported.

However, the protest was met with criticism from the city's police union, which called for a boycott of Tarantino's films after he referred to police as "murderers." The union president, Patrick Lynch, said, "The police officers that Quentin Tarantino calls ‘murderers’ aren’t living in one of his depraved big-screen fantasies — they’re risking and sometimes sacrificing their lives to protect communities from real crime and mayhem."

The protest also took place days after the shooting death of New York police officer Randolph Holder. The Rev. Al Sharpton dedicated his weekly radio broadcast and rally at his National Action Network headquarters to Holder. Sharpton and others went to the Brooklyn neighborhood where Holder served to lay a wreath and pray for him and his family.

Activist Carl Dix, who helped found RiseUpOctober with West, said that while he sympathized with Holder's family, the officer's death did not affect the need to hold the rally as scheduled. Dix said, "That's not what this is about. This is about all the people who are murdered by the police."

The protest was part of a larger movement to address police brutality and bring justice for those affected by it. The event was peaceful, and no arrests were reported. However, the controversy surrounding Tarantino's comments and the police union's response is likely to continue.

A New Jersey man, Joe Hornick, is facing a potential legal battle after being ticketed for flying a Donald Trump "Make America Great Again" flag on his property. The West Long Branch ordinance, which prohibits signs being posted more than 30 days before an election, is being challenged by a civil liberties group as unconstitutional due to its discrimination against political speech and the inability to differentiate between flags. The group argues that political signs cannot be time-limited and that a community cannot discriminate between flags. Hornick, who has been flying the flag since February, could face a fine of up to $2,000, a 90-day jail sentence, or both. The borough's attorney could not be reached for comment. Hornick is prepared to face a judge and potentially serve the sentence if necessary, stating that he will not take down the flag. The case highlights the ongoing debate over free speech and political expression in the United States.

Two men, Dereck James "D.J." Harrison (22) and his father Flint Wayne Harrison (51), were taken into custody following a day-long manhunt in Wyoming, in connection with the alleged kidnapping and assault of a Utah woman and her four daughters. The incident occurred on Tuesday, when the suspects lured the family to a Utah home under the pretext of a barbecue. Upon arrival, the family was allegedly tied up with wire and duct tape, and some of the young girls were assaulted with a baseball bat as they tried to break free.

The woman and some of the girls managed to escape and call for help, but by the time police arrived, the suspects had fled. The manhunt centered on Half Moon Lake Lodge in Pinedale, Wyoming, where authorities found a makeshift campsite.

Dereck Harrison was found and arrested without incident Saturday night, while Flint Harrison had turned himself in to authorities earlier in the day. Flint Harrison is registered as a sex offender in Wyoming for attempted forcible sexual abuse in 2001.

Both father and son are believed to have been armed and had made threats against law enforcement officials. They will be extradited to Utah to face charges, but it is unclear whether they will face additional charges in Wyoming. The motive for the attack appears to be retaliation against the mother.

Wheaton College, a conservative Christian college in Illinois, has removed the name of former Speaker of the House J. Dennis Hastert from one of its programs following federal charges against Hastert for lying to authorities about illicit payments he made to a man from his past. Hastert, who donated his Congressional papers to the school, resigned from the college's board of advisers and the J. Dennis Hastert Center for Economics, Government, and Public Policy was re-designated as the Wheaton College Center for Economics, Government, and Public Policy. The college said it would "pray for all involved, including Speaker Hastert, his family, and those who may have been harmed by any inappropriate behavior."

The indictment accuses Hastert of agreeing to pay $3.5 million to a longtime acquaintance to cover up wrongdoing in his past, then lying to the FBI when asked about the suspicious cash withdrawals from several banks. Federal law enforcement officials said Hastert was paying an individual from his past to conceal sexual misconduct that dates to Hastert's time as a high school wrestling coach and teacher in Yorkville.

Hastert attended Wheaton College as an undergraduate student and graduated with a bachelor's degree in economics in 1964. He remained an active alumnus over the years, and more than seven years ago, the college named the Hastert Center after him. According to its website, the center promotes ideas such as free enterprise, limited government, and individual responsibility through classroom teaching, research, and public discussion.

The college issued an initial statement Thursday saying it "was saddened to learn of the allegations against" Hastert. On Friday, the college said the center would continue to operate "in conformity with the highest ethical and academic standards of excellence and integrity."

The arraignment for Hastert is scheduled for June 4, 2015, in a Chicago federal court. The Illinois state legislature scrapped plans to construct a statue of Hastert earlier this month after the former U.S. House speaker asked that the project not move forward.

The college has not been implicated in or associated with any of the allegations in this matter. The college has committed to pray for all involved and to continue the work and mission of the Wheaton College Center for Economics, Government, and Public Policy.

In a tragic turn of events, a 19-year-old named Jonathan Brussow from Michigan was killed while vacationing in the Bahamas. The incident occurred while he was hiking with his girlfriend's brother, and a massive wave swept them away. The tragedy occurred shortly after Brussow had asked Athena Williams' family for permission to marry her.

Brussow and Williams, who met at a summer party in eighth grade, had been in a relationship since then. They bonded on the school bus the following year after Brussow moved down the street from Williams. Brussow, an adventurous "country boy" who loved dirt biking and hunting, had planned to propose to Williams during their vacation in the Bahamas. He had even sought permission from Williams' family before the trip.

On the day of the incident, Brussow and Williams' brother went for a hike to discuss the upcoming proposal. However, a freak wave hit them, sweeping both into the water. Although Williams' brother managed to survive, Brussow could not return to shore.

After days of searching, Brussow's body was recovered hundreds of yards from where the wave hit. The family has since shifted the focus of a GoFundMe page they had initially set up to raise reward money for anyone who found Brussow alive. Now, they aim to cover the expenses for Brussow's family to transport him back to Michigan and reimburse those who spent money to help in the search.

The family also plans to use the donations to purchase warning signs and safety gear near the Glass Window Bridge, where the incident occurred, and to help the local hospital acquire a mammogram machine. Williams expressed her gratitude towards the Bahamians who rallied together to help in the search and said that helping the locals in a meaningful and lasting way would be a great way to honor Brussow's memory.

Brussow's family released a statement comparing the storm that swept him into the sea to a straight-line wind storm that occurred on the day of his birth. They referred to him as "Jonathan 'Stormy' Brussow," a name that reflected his passionate and vibrant personality. The community is encouraged to celebrate Brussow's life, and Williams shared his last words with FOX 17.

Assemblyman Bill Nojay, a conservative Republican from New York, reportedly committed suicide on Friday morning at the Riverside Cemetery in Rochester. The news of his death came as a shock to state lawmakers, and it was later revealed that Nojay was facing criminal investigations and fraud charges.

According to reports, Nojay was to appear in court on Friday to turn himself in for fraud charges related to a trust fund he handled as an attorney. The FBI was also reportedly investigating a business deal related to a $1.3 billion school modernization program in Rochester, where Nojay played a central role.

In addition, Nojay was involved in unrelated business dealings that had fallen under legal scrutiny in Southeast Asia. Cambodian prosecutors sought to question him as part of a fraud investigation in 2014 after a dentist in that nation had accused him of defrauding her of $1 million. The trial in that case was delayed earlier this year.

Nojay was a member of Akra Group, a company promoting agriculture products in Southeast Asia, according to his 2015 financial disclosure form. He was also a vocal critic of the SAFE Act gun control law and an early supporter of Donald Trump's political ambitions.

Nojay was first elected in 2012 and represented the 133rd Assembly District, which includes Livingston County and parts of Monroe and Steuben counties. He faced a primary challenge on Tuesday from Rick Milne, mayor of Honeoye Falls. Milne and Democratic candidate Barbara Baer both suspended their campaigns on Friday.

Nojay was recalled by his colleagues as a staunch and outspoken conservative who was unafraid of attacking opponents regardless of party affiliation. He worked as one of two election attorneys for Assembly GOP Leader Brian Kolb in a hotly contested February 2000 special election that first sent Kolb to Albany.

When it came to legislative business, Nojay often went against the grain. He voted aye 59 percent of the time in 2016, one of the lowest percentages for any Assembly member, according to an analysis by New York StateWatch. He voted nay 32 percent of the time, the second highest percentage in the chamber. Nojay voted with a majority of his fellow Assembly Republicans 68 percent of the time, again one of the lowest percentages in the Assembly, even with Democrats factored in.

As further evidence of his outspoken nature, he also was a vocal critic of the election of Long Island Republican John Flanagan as Senate majority leader in 2015, so much so that earlier this year he said he was seeking GOPers to run against Sen. Michael Nozzolio, R-Seneca County, who backed Flanagan during the 2015 leadership battle. Nozzolio decided not to seek re-election.

Flanagan in a statement on Friday called Nojay "an outspoken advocate for conservative values, for his district, and for Upstate New York." An early supporter of Donald Trump's political ambitions, Nojay was among the Legislature's most relentless critics of the SAFE Act gun control law. As such, he was an organizer of the pro-Second Amendment concert called Freedompalooza, held in Altamont in August 2013.

Nojay was a conservative talk radio host, vice president and counsel for Commodity Resource Corp., a California commodity futures advisory and brokerage firm, and director and president of the Empire Page, a news aggregation website.

The news article discusses a controversy surrounding Bloomberg L.P., a financial information company, regarding the use of its terminals by reporters for journalistic purposes. The article reveals that several hundred Bloomberg reporters had used a technique to view a list of subscribers at a firm, access background information, contact details, chat information, and weekly statistics on their usage. This technique, using the "Z function" and the "UUID function," has been disabled in the newsroom.

The controversy started when Goldman Sachs raised concerns about Bloomberg reporters accessing confidential information, leading to the termination of the reporters' ability to monitor subscribers. The incident was followed by complaints from banking regulators at the Federal Reserve, who are examining whether their own employees were subject to tracking by Bloomberg reporters.

Bloomberg L.P.'s CEO, Daniel L. Doctoroff, stated that "client trust is our highest priority and the cornerstone of our business." He also emphasized that the limited customer relationship data previously available to reporters never included access to trading, portfolio, or other related systems or clients' messages.

The article also mentions that Thomson Reuters, a competitor of Bloomberg, seized on its rival's headache, stating that its Financial and Risk business and Reuters division operate independently, with reporters having no access to nonpublic data on its customers.

The controversy has raised concerns about the privacy of Bloomberg terminal subscribers and the potential for misuse of the information gathered through the terminals. The former Bloomberg employee who worked in the editorial section recalled using the functions to access information on high-profile officials like Ben Bernanke and Tim Geithner, though the specific functions and information accessed were not detailed.

The article concludes by stating that the incident has prompted Bloomberg to change its policy so that all reporters only have access to the same customer-relationship data available to clients.

President Donald Trump has expressed confidence in Veterans Affairs Secretary David Shulkin, despite reports suggesting his imminent dismissal. White House deputy press secretary Hogan Gidley stated that Trump has the power to make changes and that Shulkin's position could change at any time. Shulkin has faced criticism for excessive spending on travel and allegations of subversion within the VA. Reports indicate that Trump is considering replacing Shulkin, but no decision has been finalized. The White House has not commented on Shulkin's future, and Shulkin himself has not responded to requests for comment. If Shulkin is ousted, deputy VA secretary Tom Bowman would serve as acting head of the VA until a nominee is confirmed by the Senate. The VA provides medical care and benefits to over 9 million military veterans.

A human heart intended for donation was accidentally left on a Southwest Airlines flight bound for Dallas, causing the plane to return to Seattle-Tacoma International Airport. The heart was meant to be unloaded in Seattle but was forgotten, leading to a three-hour flight turnaround. The heart was eventually delivered to its destination and reached on time. The incident caused concern among passengers and on social media due to misinformation about the heart's viability. The heart was not a whole organ for transplant but donated heart valves, which have a longer transportation window. This incident is reportedly the first of its kind in the careers of the involved professionals. The heart donation was facilitated by Sierra Donor Services and LifeNet Health Inc., with the courier contracted by LifeNet inadvertently leaving the heart on the plane. The flight eventually took off for Dallas after a five-hour delay.

In a surprising turn of events, former Alaska Governor and political figure Sarah Palin offered an unconventional account of Paul Revere's famous midnight ride during a visit to his house in Boston. Instead of warning American patriots John Hancock and Samuel Adams about the approaching British army, as history records, Palin claimed that Revere was actually warning the British about the colonists' weapons. According to Palin, Revere used bells to send warnings and shooting signals to ensure the colonists' security and freedom. However, it is historically inaccurate as Revere was on a covert mission and did not rely on bells for communication. This new account, while not grounded in historical fact, has sparked a fresh wave of discussions about America's founding and the depth of knowledge some individuals may possess about the country's history.

The cybersecurity firm Trend Micro has released a report suggesting that the same hacking groups responsible for breaching the Democratic National Committee (DNC) emails, including Fancy Bear, APT 28, and Pawn Storm, have targeted French presidential candidate Emmanuel Macron and German political parties. These attacks were carried out using similar phishing schemes, with the Macron campaign allegedly contacted via the domain "onedrive-en-marche.fr." The DNC hackers had previously used the domain "actblues.com" to mimic the Democratic fundraising site ActBlue.

The report also mentions attacks on German political groups Konrad Adenauer Stiftung, associated with Angela Merkel's Christian Democratic Union, and Friedrich Ebert Stiftung, associated with the Social Democratic Party. All three countries have elections in 2017.

Fancy Bear is known for using phishing attacks as an entry point for their exclusive malware, X-Agent. The group is believed to have a unique characteristic of not minding being caught, as their servers have stayed active for an average of six months each, with some lasting for over a year.

The Macron campaign's digital campaign manager, Mounir Mahjoubi, confirmed attempted hacks but assured no party supporters' information had been compromised. Russian President Vladimir Putin has denied any interest in interfering with the French elections.

The report heightens concerns that Russia may attempt to influence the French presidential election, potentially benefiting Marine Le Pen, a pro-Trump, anti-NATO candidate who has backed Russia's annexation of Crimea. Le Pen met with Putin last month in Moscow. The increased use of command-and-control servers by Fancy Bear suggests the group has ramped up its operations.

The Heartland Institute, a conservative think tank known for promoting climate skepticism, has faced criticism for a controversial billboard campaign launched in May 2012. The campaign featured infamous criminals such as Ted Kaczynski (the Unabomber), Charles Manson, and Fidel Castro, who had expressed beliefs in man-made global warming. The billboards aimed to portray those who still believe in global warming as radical, extreme, and even insane.

The campaign drew criticism for its poor judgment and association of global warming advocates with criminals and tyrants. The Heartland Institute attempted to justify the campaign by citing the "Climategate" scandal and the release of internal documents detailing their funding and policy strategies.

The campaign led to questions about the future funding and support for the Heartland Institute, with some sponsors, such as General Motors, pulling their funding. The campaign also raised concerns about the speakers and attendees of the upcoming conference, with some questioning whether they would continue to associate with the think tank.

The billboard campaign was seen as an example of the increasingly extreme and divisive rhetoric used by some on the right to discredit global warming science and advocates. It also highlighted the growing divide between those who accept the scientific consensus on climate change and those who reject it.

The Gulf of Mexico is facing an imminent oil crisis as a slick, caused by a leaking well located 50 miles off the Louisiana coast, approaches sensitive ecological areas in the Mississippi River Delta. The slick, moving towards land, is estimated to be one of the worst spills in US history, with oil still leaking at a rate of about 42,000 gallons a day. Efforts to shut off the well using remote-controlled submarines have been unsuccessful so far. Coast Guard officials are considering a controlled burn of the oil slick, using fire-proof booms, to prevent further damage to marsh areas. The burn, if implemented, would be done during the day and could begin as early as Wednesday. The spill, stretching up to 42 miles by 80 miles, has already impacted marine life, with five small whales spotted nearby. The incident has political implications, as it may affect public support for offshore drilling. The well is expected to continue leaking until it is sealed, and several approaches are being tried to achieve this. The search for the 11 missing workers from the exploded rig has been suspended.

Vulfpeck, a small-time funk band, released an album called Sleepify, consisting of ten tracks of silence, as a business experiment to generate royalties from streaming services. The idea is for fans to stream the album continuously, with the band planning to use the proceeds for touring. The album has garnered over 1,115,000 plays on Spotify, earning the band between $6,700 and $9,400. Jack Stratton, a member of Vulfpeck, believes that Spotify is beneficial for the band, with about 10% of new fans coming through the service, although they make less on YouTube. The band's stunt has been met with approval by Spotify, although they prefer the band's earlier albums. However, if Vulfpeck wants to maximize digital earnings, they could focus on preventing bots from streaming their music, as bot-driven traffic is a problem in digital advertising. Spotify did not want to discuss the issue of bot-driven traffic, citing technical barriers and potential capture of attention. The band's strategy also raises concerns about gaming the system and potentially affecting other honest bands trying to make a living.

The body of former White House chef Walter Scheib, who served under Presidents Bill Clinton and George W. Bush, was found in New Mexico's Sangre de Cristo Mountains on Sunday night. Scheib, 61, went missing on June 13 after going for a hike near Taos Ski Valley and was reported missing the next day. His vehicle was found parked at a canyon trailhead on Tuesday. The cause of death and other details about the discovery of the body have not been released.

Scheib recently moved to New Mexico and served as the executive chef in the executive mansion for 11 years. He was hired in 1994 by former First Lady Hillary Clinton to infuse a distinctly modern American flair into 1600 Penn. menus. In 2005, after more than a decade and two administrations, Scheib was asked to resign.

According to the book “The Residence: Inside the Private World of the White House,” Scheib taught a teenage Chelsea Clinton to cook. After leaving the White House, Scheib started his own private chef business and co-authored a book, “White House Chef: Eleven Years, Two Presidents, One Kitchen.”

The search for Scheib's body has been ongoing due to the difficult terrain, according to New Mexico state police spokeswoman Sgt. Elizabeth Armijo.

Scheib's death comes as a shock to many, as he was known for his love of hiking and outdoor activities. He is survived by two sons.

The article discusses the impact of the Supreme Court's 2010 Citizens United v. Federal Election Commission decision, which granted corporations First Amendment free speech rights and allowed them to make unlimited donations for electioneering, on the 2012 presidential election. The article focuses on the Iowa caucuses, where super PACs, political organizations that can receive unlimited corporate contributions and make unlimited expenditures for federal candidates, played a significant role.

The article highlights the negative impact of super PACs on the campaign of Newt Gingrich, who finished fourth in the Iowa caucuses. The pro-Romney super PAC, Restore Our Future, spent over $2.8 million on attack ads against Gingrich, which were credited for his drop in polls and Mitt Romney's corresponding rise. Gingrich, who initially supported the Citizens United decision, has since expressed regret and accused Romney of colluding with the super PAC.

The article also mentions the Montana Supreme Court's recent decision to uphold the state's law limiting corporate election spending, which contradicts the Citizens United decision. The Montana court argued that the state has a compelling interest in maintaining its ban due to its history of corporate corruption.

The article concludes by discussing the ongoing debate over the impact of super PACs on American politics and the difficulty politicians face in balancing their support for free speech with their concerns about the influence of big money in elections.

In a surprising turn of events, two-time Oscar winner Tom Hanks played a pivotal role in a domestic assault case in Los Angeles. Hanks served as a juror in the trial, which started last week. The defendant, facing up to a year in jail, was prepared for closing arguments on Wednesday. However, the proceedings took an unexpected turn when the prosecuting attorney revealed that another lawyer had interacted with Hanks outside the courtroom, thanking him for his service.

Defense attorney Andrew Flier then requested a mistrial, citing prosecutorial misconduct. In a hearing on Wednesday, both sides settled on a reduced charge for the defendant: disturbing the peace and a $150 fine. The City Attorney's Office confirmed the interaction with Hanks, stating they would review the situation.

Initially, Flier was concerned that Hanks' celebrity status might unfairly influence the case's outcome. However, after interviewing Hanks during jury selection, Flier decided he was a fair juror. The resolution of the case did not disclose the alleged victim's reaction, and neither party has made a public statement.

Hanks' presence not only affected proceedings inside the courtroom but also drew a crowd of photographers and fans outside the courthouse. If the case hadn't ended in a plea, it's unclear how Hanks would have voted. He had been attentive and professional throughout the trial.

Jane Fonda, the Oscar-winning actress and activist, has had a life marked by controversy, as detailed in the HBO documentary 'Jane Fonda in Five Acts'. During her career, Fonda has been known for her roles in films such as 'Barbarella' and 'Coming Home', as well as her activism, which has often been a subject of controversy. In 1972, Fonda visited Hanoi during the Vietnam War, and was photographed sitting on an anti-aircraft gun, which earned her the nickname "Hanoi Jane" and caused decades of outrage from her critics. In a recent interview on The Late Show, Fonda admitted that she regretted the photo op, stating that she was not thinking about the implications of her actions at the time. Despite this, Fonda does not regret going to Vietnam, as she learned a lot during her visit. In 2011, Fonda wrote on her website that the photo was a mistake, and in 2005 she said it was a betrayal. Fonda continues to be a vocal activist, and has taken to the streets for the Women's March to protest Donald Trump's policies. The documentary 'Jane Fonda in Five Acts' provides an intimate look at Fonda's life and career.

Title: Two Families Battle Cancer and Legal Challenges, Seeking Support and Change in Medical Cannabis Laws

Two families in Australia are currently facing challenging circumstances as they navigate their children's cancer diagnoses and the legal hurdles surrounding the use of medicinal cannabis.

Sacha Maujean, a sole parent to two daughters, Romany and Rumer, recently discovered that Rumer, aged 2, has a large neuroblastoma tumor and stage 3 cancer. The family is currently residing at the Lady Cilento Children's Hospital in Brisbane, away from their home, family, and friends. Sacha has set up a GoFundMe page to help cover the costs associated with their extended stay and Rumer's treatment.

On a different note, Adam Koessler, a father in Cairns, was arrested in January 2015 for administering medicinal cannabis oil to his daughter, Rumer Rose, who was diagnosed with stage 4 Neuroblastoma. Adam's bail conditions prohibit him from having direct or indirect contact with his child, who is currently in the same hospital. Adam's case will be heard in the Brisbane Magistrates court on the 20th of January, and he is advocating for the reinstatement of his parental rights, the dismissal of charges against him, and the decriminalization of medicinal cannabis in Australia.

Both families are calling for support and change in the legal landscape surrounding medicinal cannabis. They argue that medical-grade cannabis oil has numerous beneficial effects for cancer patients with minimal side effects and risks compared to current drug treatments. In fact, when used in conjunction with recommended treatment regimes, medical cannabis has been proven to alleviate adverse side effects.

The case of Cooper Wallace in Victoria and his parents, Cassie Batten and Rhett Wallace, serves as a precedent. Although they were initially pursued for administering medical cannabis oil, they are no longer being charged, and the oil has had a significant positive effect on Cooper's seizures.

Close to 200,000 Australians support the decriminalization of medicinal cannabis, as evidenced by the Change.org petition in support of Dan Haslam.

You can support Sacha Maujean and her daughters by donating via the GoFundMe page: https://www.gofundme.com/rumer. Adam Koessler and Rumer Rose's GoFundMe page is also available for donations: https://www.gofundme.com/rumer_rose. For updates on Rumer's progress, visit facebook.com/rumersrecovery.

The second quarter of 2012 has been a challenging period for CNN, with ratings for the network's prime-time shows plummeting by 40% compared to the same period last year. This decline marks CNN's worst-ever performance for a second quarter, as the network struggled to attract viewers amidst a relatively quiet news cycle compared to the previous year.

All three cable news networks experienced declines among viewers aged 25 to 54, the demographic most valued by news advertisers. MSNBC saw a 18% drop, Fox News a 14% drop, while CNN's decline was more than double those figures.

CNN's 9 p.m. show, hosted by Piers Morgan, experienced a particularly steep decline, with a 32% drop in viewers in the 25-54 age group compared to last year. This is the first time a CNN 9 p.m. show has performed so poorly for a quarter.

In terms of total viewers, Fox News led easily with 2.14 million, followed by MSNBC with 817,000, and CNN with 470,000. The decline in CNN's viewership was the most significant, with a 35% drop compared to the same quarter last year.

CNN's struggles are attributed to the network's reluctance to embrace opinion-oriented programming, unlike Fox News and MSNBC, which have found success with personality-driven analysis. The network is facing an "identity crisis" as it struggles to make 24-hour news compelling while its competitors redefine the industry.

Despite the poor ratings, CNN has highlighted some increases in June, with Anderson Cooper's show up 5% and Piers Morgan's show up 9%. The network has also announced plans to expand Wolf Blitzer's The Situation Room to three hours and cancel poorly-rated politics show "John King USA."

Industry experts warn that without a coherent strategy, CNN could become largely irrelevant to the national conversation. The network's founder of the cable news genre is now registering its lowest ratings since the first Gulf War.

In a daring heist, a group of 15 armed and battle-hardened thieves ambushed two secure vans carrying millions in jewels on a French highway, making off with a haul worth €9m (£6.3m). The attack occurred on the A6 highway connecting Paris and Lyon, with no injuries reported. The drivers were forced out of the vehicles, and the vans were later found burnt and abandoned. The jewels remain missing, and authorities are currently searching the Burgundy region southeast of Paris for the perpetrators. This is the latest in a series of big jewel heists in France, with the case reminiscent of heists by the Pink Panther gang. France has seen repeated jewelry thefts, with the most spectacular heist being a double robbery at a Harry Winston shop in Paris in 2007 and 2008, worth over €100m.

On Monday morning, a shooting occurred at Butler High School in Matthews, North Carolina, resulting in the death of one student. The incident occurred during a fight in a crowded hallway, prompting a lockdown and causing chaos and fear among parents. The suspect, another male student, was quickly arrested by a school resource officer. The victim and suspect's identities were not immediately released.

Investigators reviewed surveillance footage showing the shooting, which was described as an "isolated incident." The weapon used in the shooting has been secured, but its type remains undisclosed. Charlotte-Mecklenburg Schools Superintendent Clayton Wilcox expressed sadness over the loss of life and concern about a student being the shooter. He also questioned how a young person could obtain a handgun in North Carolina, suggesting a review of security procedures.

Many students witnessed the shooting, and counselors and psychologists were made available to provide support. By late morning, the lockdown was lifted, and families could pick up students at the main entrance. Classes resumed for students who remained on campus. The school's diverse student body consists of about one-third white, one-third African-American, and one-quarter Hispanic.

Dozens of parents gathered outside the school during the lockdown, feeling confused and uncertain about meeting their children. Television footage showed students exiting the school, many in tears, hugging their parents. The investigation into the shooting is ongoing.

Andy Roddick, the top-ranked American tennis player for the past decade, announced his retirement from the sport after the US Open, which coincides with his 30th birthday. Roddick, who has a career record of 610-212 and career prize money of over $20 million, won the 2003 US Open and has 32 singles titles to his name. He will face 19-year-old Bernard Tomic of Australia in the second round of the US Open. Roddick revealed his decision to retire mid-tournament, stating that he felt it was time to leave the sport and that he was not sure he could physically and emotionally commit to another year of play. Roddick's career has been marked by injuries and ups and downs, but he is proud of the opportunities he had to play in major tournaments and be a part of the Davis Cup team. He has been a mentor to up-and-coming players such as Sam Querrey and Ryan Harrison and has been a vocal and witty presence in the tennis world. Roddick plans to remain active in the sport, working with his philanthropic foundation, doing radio work, and spending time with his family.

The U.S. government shut down for the first time in 17 years on October 1, 2013, due to a disagreement between Congress and the President over funding for federal agencies. The shutdown was caused by a failure to reach an agreement on a funding bill, with Republicans demanding concessions on President Obama's health care reform law, while Democrats refused to negotiate on the issue.

The shutdown affected more than 800,000 federal workers, with many being furloughed and not receiving paychecks. Essential services such as national security, the safety of people and property, and the management of benefits such as Social Security payments were maintained, but other services were interrupted. The U.S. Postal Service and air traffic control were among the services that remained operational.

The shutdown was the result of a standoff between Republicans and Democrats over the Affordable Care Act, with Republicans seeking to delay the implementation of the law's individual mandate and strip lawmakers and their aides of government health benefits. The Democratic-led Senate quickly rejected the House's proposal, and negotiations to resolve the impasse were ongoing.

The shutdown also raised concerns about the impact on the broader economy, with President Obama warning that it would take a substantial hit if the government's largest employer was shuttered. The shutdown was expected to last at least a week, with some Republicans predicting that it could last longer.

Privately, senior Republicans expressed concerns that the shutdown could harm the Republican Party, with some questioning the conventional wisdom that previous shutdowns had weakened the GOP. Democrats, on the other hand, predicted that the government-funding dispute could be merged into an even more serious battle over the federal debt limit, with the Treasury Department set to run out of cash to pay the nation's bills as soon as October 17 unless Congress approved additional borrowing authority.

The shutdown had a mixed impact on the public, with some services being delayed or interrupted, while others remained operational. Visitors to popular parks expressed frustration with elected officials, while tourists from other countries were confused by the impasse over the nation's health care system. The shutdown also raised concerns about the long-term impact on programs such as Head Start, which provides preschool learning programs for poor children, if the budget standoff dragged on.

On New Year's Day 2011, several tornadoes swept through the South and Midwest, resulting in seven fatalities and numerous injuries. The victims included three people in Missouri and three in Arkansas, with one additional death in Missouri occurring on Saturday. The tornadoes were fueled by unusually warm air, causing widespread destruction in several states.

In Arkansas, Chris Sisemore was thrown from his home by a tornado in Cincinnati. Despite sustaining bumps and bruises, he had no serious injuries. His mother, Margie Sisemore, described the incident, saying her son was carried across the street by the tornado.

In Missouri, a 69-year-old woman died in a trailer near Rolla when it was destroyed by a tornado. Another woman, Megan Ross, and her 64-year-old grandmother Loretta Anderson died at a farm in Dent County when their homes were hit by a tornado.

Governor Jay Nixon spent New Year's Day touring the damage in Missouri and Arkansas. Parts of Alabama and Florida were on tornado watch for much of Saturday, and flash flooding was reported in parts of Alabama.

In Cincinnati, Arkansas, the tornado caused significant damage, with residents spending New Year's Day sifting through the wreckage. At Fort Leonard Wood, a tornado with winds of 136 to 165 mph demolished about a dozen homes and caused lesser damage to many more in a neighborhood that houses military officers.

In Illinois, a tornado may have touched down in Petersburg, northwest of Springfield, causing damage to about two dozen homes. In southern Missouri, storms damaged buildings and boat docks around Table Rock Lake, leaving several boats adrift. Several homes and businesses were damaged in the St. Louis County town of Sunset Hills, and a church was damaged in nearby Fenton.

The region had been bracing for severe weather for much of the week, with Gulf moisture riding southerly winds pushing temperatures into the upper 60s and 70s on Thursday, ahead of a cold front expected to drop temperatures into the teens by Saturday morning.

The article discusses the appointment of three Democratic senators, Patty Murray, Max Baucus, and John Kerry, to a powerful new deficit panel known as the Joint Select Committee. The committee, which will consist of 12 members, is tasked with finding over $1 trillion in spending cuts by the end of the year as part of a bipartisan agreement to end the debt-limit fight. Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid made the appointments, with House Speaker John Boehner and Minority Leaders Nancy Pelosi and Mitch McConnell also selecting members.

Murray will serve as co-chairwoman of the committee. Her appointment has sparked controversy, with Republicans criticizing her for prioritizing fundraising and politics over the committee's mission. Reid's choices are intended to demonstrate his commitment to forging a bipartisan deal, particularly in the face of potential deep entitlement cuts.

The Democratic leaders aim to appoint loyalists who will resist a cuts-only approach that could target popular programs like Medicare and Social Security. They are also considering candidates who will advocate for revenues, as the panel's success may hinge on Republican agreement to new taxes.

The data set mentioned at the end of the article is unrelated to the appointment of the deficit panel but provides information about a web crawl conducted from March 2011 to December 2011, which captured over 2.7 billion URLs from Alexa's top 1 million websites.

The Chronicle of Higher Education's recent study shows a decline in graduation rates at American universities by 33% since 2002, with the recession being a likely cause. Harvard University has the highest undergrad completion rate of all research universities, with 98% of those enrolled in 2002 graduating by 2008. Yale University and the University of Notre Dame follow closely with rates of 97 and 96 percent, respectively. Among public research universities, the University of Virginia had the highest graduation rate in 2008 at 93%, followed by the College of William and Mary and the University of California-Berkeley.

On the other hand, some institutions have shown a decrease in graduation rates, with longer time to earn a degree being a possible factor. The study also includes a list of universities with the lowest graduation rates, with Clark Atlanta University having the lowest at 45%. The Chronicle's analysis includes data from over 1,000 four-year public and private nonprofit colleges and universities, focusing on research, master's, and Baccalaureate Colleges—Arts & Sciences by the Carnegie Foundation for the Advancement of Teaching in 2005. The rates are calculated as the percentage of all first-time, full-time students entering in the fall seeking bachelor's degrees who completed bachelor's degrees within six years. The study also accounts for changes in admissions selectivity and fluctuations in graduation rates over time.

The news article discusses a controversial Chinese talk show called "Interviews Before Execution," which aired on Henan Legal Channel for over five years. The show featured interviews with murderers on death row, conducted by reporter Ding Yu and her team. The interviews aimed to serve as a warning to others, with the slogan "human nature to awaken and 'perceive the value of life'."

The show was taken off air recently, following reports in foreign media, including a BBC documentary. Ding Yu, the host of the show, defends its format, stating that criminals want to be heard and find it therapeutic to discuss their crimes. The show was rated one of Henan's top 10 shows, with nearly 40 million viewers out of the 100 million who live in the province.

One notable case featured in the show was the murder of a grandmother and grandfather by a young, educated college graduate couple. Another case that gained attention was the murder of a mother by her daughter, Wu Yanyan, who was initially sentenced to death but later had her sentence suspended due to mitigating circumstances.

The show's cancellation is attributed to "internal problems," and requests for an interview with Ding Yu were denied. The show was not broadcast nationwide and was primarily known in Henan province. China is the world leader in executions, with an estimated 1,000 people put to death each year, although the exact number is a state secret.

The show's host, Ding Yu, is a subject in a documentary titled "Dead Men Talking," which offers an inside look at the making of the show. The documentary will be aired on BBC2 next week. The show's cancellation has sparked discussions about the toll the work takes on Ding Yu and the haunting images she lives with due to her close encounters with death row inmates.

Vint Cerf, one of the inventors of the Internet and a current Vice President of Google, warned at the American Association for the Advancement of Science annual meeting in San Jose, California, that future archaeologists may struggle to interpret the 21st century civilization due to the potential erasure of our digital trace. Cerf expressed concern that relying solely on digital data storage for books, texts, photographs, and other important documents could lead to a "digital Dark Ages," where crucial information is lost or becomes uninterpretable.

Comparing the future knowledge about the 21st century to the post-Roman period in Western Europe, Cerf stated that future generations may have great difficulty understanding our civilization due to the uninterpretable bits of information we leave behind. He emphasized that even though digitizing photographs may seem like a solution to make them last longer, it could potentially be wrong, and physical instances of important photos should be created.

Cerf also highlighted the potential issue of storing legal documents and the need to build preservation into our thinking. One possible solution he mentioned was "digital vellum," a concept being explored by computer scientists at Carnegie Mellon University, which involves taking a digital snapshot of all the processes needed to reproduce an item at a later date, including the software and operating system. This snapshot could then be used to reproduce the game, picture file, or spreadsheet on a "modern" computer, even centuries from now.

Cerf's concerns were echoed by the example of Doris Kearns Goodwin, an American Pulitzer Prize-winning writer who reconstructed conversations between Abraham Lincoln and his friends through the analysis of his correspondence. Future historians may struggle to do the same for current luminaries due to the either missing or unreadable digital record. Cerf concluded by stating that historians will tell us that sometimes documents and transactions images may turn out to have an importance which is not understood for hundreds of years, and failure to preserve them will cause us to lose our perspective.

Google's new social networking service, Google+, has seen a decrease in U.S. visitors and a reduction in the average time spent on the site, according to Experian Hitwise. Total visits fell 3% to 1.79 million in the week ended July 23, and the average time spent on the site declined 10% to 5 minutes and 15 seconds. Google+, which aims to help users better organize and manage contacts and sharing, was launched last month and has over 10 million users. Google co-founder Larry Page announced the user count earlier this month. Google+ is the company's latest effort to challenge services such as Facebook and LinkedIn. Google's shares fell $15.30, or 2.5%, to $607.22 today on the Nasdaq Stock Market. The shares have risen 2.2% this year. The research methods used by Experian Hitwise do not include mobile users and third-party application traffic. Google+ began a test version on June 28 by invitation only. The decline in traffic and time spent on the site may indicate that Google+ is experiencing a "sophomore slump" and that user retention may be a challenge. Google needs to provide a compelling reason for users to continue using the service and to engage with the content on the site. Hangouts are currently the major strong point of Google+ retention, while Sparks are a weak point. Circles, which allow users to organize their contacts into specific groups, are facing backlash due to their complexity and maintenance requirements. Traffic referred from Google+ is also dropping. Google needs to address these issues to ensure the long-term success of Google+.

Two former servers at Hard Rock Cafe's Universal Studios restaurant in Orlando have filed a lawsuit against the company, alleging that they were paid less than minimum wage and that their tips were shared with kitchen staff, which is illegal under Florida and federal law. Christopher Grant and Benjamin Aguda, the plaintiffs, claim that they were paid less than minimum wage for nearly three years, and that the company violated tip-sharing regulations by distributing their tips to kitchen employees. The suit alleges that the servers and bartenders were required to share their tips with "expediters," kitchen employees responsible for garnishing food. The lawsuit, filed by attorneys Sam J. Smith and Hillary Schwab, argues that this practice is unjust as it takes tips away from servers and bartenders who deserve them. The attorneys also criticize the current minimum wage, stating that it should be higher, especially in light of the economic situation.

In a groundbreaking discovery, U.S. researchers have found water in the Moon's soil, originating from solar winds. This new finding suggests that water on the Moon may have multiple sources, not just from comets and micrometeorites. The water is believed to be formed when hydrogen ejected from the Sun's atmosphere is carried in solar winds and implanted in the lunar soil, where it reacts with oxygen already present on the Moon's surface.

This discovery could potentially be a valuable resource for future human settlement on the Moon, as the water can be consumed, electrolyzed into hydrogen and oxygen, and used to make rocket fuel. However, geochemist Ross Taylor from the Australian Academy of Science has expressed skepticism about the feasibility of harvesting water from lunar soil for human settlement.

The researchers analyzed a collection of cemented regolith grains, a glass-like material, to find reacting hydrogen and oxygen molecules. The origin of water on the Moon's surface was previously unknown, but the researchers attribute it to solar winds. This finding "reshapes the perspective" of where water in the inner Solar System comes from, as it was initially believed that all water was delivered via icy bodies that came from further out in space.

It is still uncertain what percentage of the lunar soil contains water, and more research is needed to determine the extent of this resource. The study's lead author, Yang Liu, believes that this discovery emphasizes the potential for finding water on the surfaces of other airless bodies in the solar system. The researchers detailed their findings in the journal Nature Geoscience.

The White House has distributed a set of talking points to its allies, urging them to support President Donald Trump's stance on the violence in Charlottesville, Virginia. The memo emphasizes that Trump was "entirely correct" in his assessment that both sides were responsible for the violence, and that he has been a voice for unity and calm. However, the memo has been criticized for not including further rebukes of white nationalists, white supremacists, and neo-Nazis who organized and led the rally that left a woman and two policemen dead.

Trump's remarks on the Charlottesville violence have sparked outrage from both Republicans and Democrats. House Speaker Paul Ryan and other GOP leaders have criticized Trump for his equivocations about who is responsible for the violence. Senators Marco Rubio, Todd Young, and Tim Scott have also condemned Trump's remarks, with Rubio stating that Trump cannot allow white supremacists to share only part of the blame.

Senator Brian Schatz has stated that Trump is "not my president," and Sen. John McCain has tweeted that there is no moral equivalency between racists and Americans standing up to defy hate and bigotry.

The White House's talking points memo has been criticized for not including further rebukes of white nationalists, white supremacists, and neo-Nazis. Paris Saint-Germain (PSG), a prominent French Ligue 1 soccer team, will honor the victims of the recent Paris attacks by wearing a special "JE SUIS PARIS" jersey for their upcoming matches against Malmö on Wednesday and Troyes on Saturday. The jersey will replace the usual sponsor, Emirates Airlines, and will bear only the message "I AM PARIS" in the space typically occupied by the sponsor's logo. This gesture of unity comes as a tribute to the victims of the attacks that occurred on November 13, 2015. The team's home match against Troyes will be the first in the Parc des Princes stadium since the attacks. Emirates Airlines has approved this change and has been cooperative throughout the process. This is the second memorial design by PSG to honor the victims of the attacks. The team previously wore the words in smaller print just below the team's crest and over their hearts. The goal is to create a sense of unity and remember the victims of the tragic events.

Eminem's performance at the Bonnaroo music festival in Tennessee caused controversy when he used realistic gunshot sound effects during his song "Kill You," which triggered panic among some concertgoers. The rapper's decision to use the sound effects sparked a backlash on social media, with many people criticizing the noises as inappropriate given the prevalence of mass shootings in the U.S.

Fans defended Eminem, pointing out that he has incorporated gunshot sound effects into his music for many years, including just one week ago at the Governor's Ball Music Festival in New York City. Some also argued that the song was written in 2002, before recent mass shootings.

However, others argued that the sound effects were irresponsible and distasteful, especially given the current climate of heightened sensitivity to gun violence. Popular YouTube star Andrea Russett, who was in attendance at the festival, tweeted that the sound effects were extremely triggering and not funny or amusing.

Eminem's spokesperson issued a statement to TIME, saying that the effect used during the performance was a pyrotechnic concussion, which creates a loud boom, and that the rapper has used this effect in his live show for over 10 years without complaint.

The controversy continued on social media, with some fans defending Eminem and others criticizing him. Some argued that the sound effects were a regular part of his performances and that those who were triggered should not have attended his concerts. Others argued that the sound effects were inappropriate and that Eminem should have warned the audience if potentially traumatizing or triggering sound effects were going to be used.

UPDATE: Eminem's spokesperson gave E! News the following statement, "Contrary to inaccurate reports, Eminem does not use gunshot sound effects during his live show. The effect used by Eminem in his set at Bonnaroo was a pyrotechnic concussion creates a loud boom. He has used this effect—as have hundreds other artists—in his live show for over 10 years, including previous US festival dates in 2018 without complaint."

The article discusses the brutal murder of Peter Kassig, a 26-year-old American aid worker, by ISIS. Overall, the article discusses the brutal murder of Peter Kassig by ISIS, the group's demands for a ransom for the remaining American hostage, and the ongoing efforts by the United States to free American hostages held by ISIS. It also mentions the ongoing airstrikes against ISIS and the group's losses in Iraq and Syria.

The ceasefire agreement brokered by Turkey and Russia for the evacuation of civilians and rebels from the besieged districts of east Aleppo has stalled, with heavy shelling reported in the city. The agreement, which was expected to allow tens of thousands of trapped civilians to leave, has been delayed due to Iran-backed militias preventing opposition fighters and civilians from leaving the area. Shelling of the besieged districts resumed on Wednesday morning despite the agreement, which was brokered on Tuesday. It is unclear when residents will be allowed to leave and whether the deal will hold. Turkey's foreign minister, Mevlüt Çavuşoğlu, said discussions are ongoing with Russia and Iran to continue the planned evacuations. The Syrian military initially said it had no knowledge of the deal before backtracking and saying the evacuations would begin on Wednesday at 5am local time. However, none have yet to begin. The confusion over the deal highlights the splits and competing interests of Assad's supporters, which include Russia, Iran, and Iran-backed militias on the ground, who were implicated by the United Nations in execution-style shootings of civilians in opposition areas. Rebels inside east Aleppo have said they would support the agreement, but Iranian-backed militias on the ground are blocking it because the deal was reached without Assad or Iran's involvement. The United Nations has said it stands ready to facilitate the voluntary and safe evacuation of injured, sick, and vulnerable civilians from the besieged part of the city. The evacuation of rebel-held eastern Aleppo means the opposition will cede the entire city to the Assad regime, surrendering the last major urban stronghold where it maintained an active presence. The fighting in Aleppo has left residents in total despair and increasingly angry at the international community for abandoning them to their fate. The US ambassador to the United Nations, Samantha Power, has accused the Syrian government, along with Russia and Iran, of bearing responsibility for the deaths of civilians in Aleppo. She accused the three states of putting a "noose" around civilians in the city, asking "Are you incapable of shame? ... Is there no execution of a child that gets under your skin? Is there literally nothing that shames you?" The United Nations has received reliable reports from multiple sources that pro-Assad forces, including the Iraqi Shia militia Harakat al-Nujaba, have carried out summary killings of at least 82 civilians, including 11 women and 13 children, in four different neighborhoods of east Aleppo that have fallen under government control. Iranian leaders have self-congratulated on their role in the assault, with the chief military adviser to the supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, saying the city was "liberated thanks to a coalition between Iran, Syria, Russia, and Lebanon’s Hezbollah." Reports of killings by the advancing forces have raised grave concerns over the fate of tens of thousands of civilians, doctors, and activists who have remained in the shrinking rebel enclaves and face death if they stay there or being tortured and killed in regime-held areas if they flee over government lines.

The cannabis plant's genome has been sequenced by Medicinal Genomics, a young company that aims to explore the genomes of therapeutic plants. The raw sequence, containing approximately 131 billion bases, was released on Amazon's EC2 public cloud computing service. Although the sequence is currently fragmented into hundreds of thousands of snippets, the estimated size of the Cannabis sativa genome is about 400 million bases, roughly three times the genome of Arabidopsis thaliana. The sequencing project, which cost around $200,000, may lead to the development of treatments for cancer, pain, and inflammatory diseases. The data is being made public using Amazon's cloud-computing system, and McKernan's company aims to allow researchers to optimize the cannabis plant's therapeutic benefits and minimize its psychoactive effects. Alaska's Governor, Bill Walker, announced on Thursday that he will utilize his executive powers to expand the state's Medicaid health program for the underprivileged, bypassing political opponents and aiming to provide coverage to over 20,000 uninsured residents in the first year. The expansion would accept $146 million in federal funds made available under President Barack Obama's healthcare reform law.

Walker cited the decisions of nearly 30 other states that have expanded Medicaid coverage, stating that it benefits their residents, economies, and budgets. However, previous expansion efforts in Alaska, led by Walker since his election in 2014, have been blocked by the Republican-led state legislature.

The expansion of Medicaid under Obamacare has been stalled in states concentrated in the South and central West due to political divides. In Alaska, the Legislative Budget and Audit Committee has the authority to review requests for federal funds when the legislature is not in session. The committee has until September 1 to vote on whether to support the state's request for funds or recommend a special session to review expansion options.

Opponents of the expansion argue that Alaska should not risk the possibility of the federal government pulling the program and leaving the state with an unaffordable commitment. Republican state Senator John Coghill stated, "Today's spending will be paid for by tomorrow's taxpayers."

In a letter to the committee's chairman, Walker's budget director, Pat Pitney, cited benefits such as an estimated $1 billion in new federal healthcare dollars for the next six years, $100 million in savings to the state treasury, and 4,000 new jobs.

The expansion, if approved, would bring the number of states opting into the Obamacare expansion close to 30, making it more likely that other states would follow.

On Thursday night, CNN's New York offices and studios were evacuated due to a bomb threat received by phone. The New York Police Department (NYPD) responded swiftly, and an all-clear message was issued later in the night. CNN Worldwide president Jeff Zucker confirmed in an internal memo to staff that the building is secure and safe for employees to return in the morning. The NYPD stated that the threat was not substantiated. Initially, a caller claimed there were five devices in the building, but no explosives were found. The incident caused a temporary disruption, but CNN appreciated the quick action by the local authorities and the patience and professionalism shown by the employees.

The report by the Special Inspector General for Afghanistan Reconstruction raises concerns about a U.S. initiative to spend hundreds of millions of dollars on construction projects in Afghanistan, originally pitched as a vital tool in the military campaign against the Taliban. The report suggests that some projects may ultimately prove detrimental and questions the strategic rationale of U.S. development programs in the war-torn nation.

The report focuses on the Afghan Infrastructure Fund, which was authorized by Congress in 2010 to prevent the Defense Department from dipping into a discretionary account for military commanders to bankroll large projects. Among the projects criticized by the inspector general is a plan to provide electricity to residents of Kandahar, the country’s second-largest city, until a new hydropower turbine at a dam in Helmand province is installed. The report questions whether the Afghan government will have the financial ability to maintain many of the projects, creating an "expectations gap" among the population that could harm overall stabilization efforts.

The report also questions a new $23 million road in Helmand province and reveals that four electricity projects, costing a total of more than $300 million from the infrastructure fund, have not yet been awarded to contractors. Sen. Claire McCaskill, a frequent critic of Afghan reconstruction efforts, said the report raises fundamental questions about the strategic rationale of U.S. development programs in Afghanistan.

In response to the report, the U.S. Embassy defended the importance of large-scale development initiatives, stating that they have signaled to Afghan populations the U.S. government’s long-term commitment to Afghanistan. The report marks a shift in focus for the Special Inspector General’s office, which traditionally focused on contracting waste and fraud, but has now vowed to scrutinize how projects are conceptualized and designed, not just how they are implemented.

On August 15, a 2-year-old boy named Yoshiki Fujimoto was found safe and well after going missing for three days in Suo-Oshima, Yamaguchi Prefecture. The boy was discovered by a 78-year-old volunteer from Oita Prefecture who was participating in the search operation. Yoshiki was found sitting on a moss-covered rock in a mountain stream, just a few hundred meters from his great-grandfather’s home.

The boy's 37-year-old mother burst into tears when she saw him. Yoshiki had no problem conversing with his mother and grandmother, according to police. The boy was taken to a hospital in Yanai in the prefecture for a checkup. A doctor said he was suffering from dehydration and had scratches and tick bites on his skin, but no obvious injuries.

Yoshiki's 66-year-old grandfather took Yoshiki and his 3-year-old brother to swim in the sea about 400 meters from the home around 10:30 a.m. on Aug. 12. After walking 100 meters or so toward the beach, Yoshiki suddenly announced, “I want to go home,” and started walking back. The grandfather watched, apparently unconcerned that the boy could get lost. Yoshiki's mother and two other children who left the house soon afterward did not come across him, and the family then realized that he had gone missing.

About 150 prefectural police officers and firefighters had been searching for Yoshiki since Aug. 12, focusing on the area around his great-grandfather’s home. On Aug. 14, Yoshiki’s mother called out to him through a community wireless system, saying, “Yo-chan, say anything. Come out soon.” But there was no reply.

Experts were surprised that the boy was found alive as temperatures on the island topped 30 degrees Celsius (86 Fahrenheit) between Sunday and Tuesday. Paediatricians and experts said that the boy may have found shade near the stream and drunk water, which may have helped him survive.

The discovery of Yoshiki was touted as a "miracle", with experts pointing to some favourable conditions and unique characteristics of the toddler involved. According to Mieko Miyata, the head of a non-profit organisation promoting safety education for children, it is difficult for two-year-olds to objectively look at situations they are in.

The boy's grandfather took full responsibility for the incident and expressed his gratitude to the police, rescuers, and local people for their efforts in finding Yoshiki.

In a significant development, U.S. Representative Pete Sessions (R-TX) has withdrawn from the race for House majority leader, leaving only Kevin McCarthy (R-CA) as the remaining candidate to replace Eric Cantor (R-VA) who suffered a historic primary loss on Tuesday. Sessions, the House Rules Committee chairman and former head of the House GOP campaign committee, announced his decision due to concerns about creating unnecessary division within the Republican party.

McCarthy, the party's chief vote counter and top fund-raiser, is expected to become the second-ranking House Republican after the leadership election scheduled for June 19. Sessions' withdrawal was influenced by the advantage McCarthy had built up, as well as the quick turnaround for the election, which left little time for Sessions or other challengers to build enough support.

Three other top conservatives, Reps. Paul Ryan (Wis.), Tom Price (Ga.) and Jim Jordan (Ohio), have also passed on the race. Rep. Raúl Labrador (R-Idaho) is considering challenging McCarthy, but it's uncertain whether he could seriously threaten him.

With McCarthy likely to become majority leader, the more competitive leadership election becomes the race to replace him as whip. The race pits McCarthy's chief deputy, Rep. Peter Roskam (Ill.), against the chairman of the conservative Republican Study Committee, Rep. Steve Scalise (La.), and another conservative, Rep. Marlin Stutzman (Ind.), who entered the race on Thursday morning.

A British lawyer, Matthew Dick, proposed to his girlfriend Delyth Hughes using a creative and unique method - by hiding the proposal in the cryptic crossword of The Times newspaper. The proposal was accepted after Delyth was left "dumbfounded" by the gesture. The crossword included clues such as "Pretty Welsh girl widely thought not to be all there" with the answer "Delyth", and "'Will you marry me', say, that's forward also rude!" with the answer "proposal". Dick, a crossword enthusiast, underlined the words "will you marry me" and presented the proposal to Hughes during their birthday celebration in Cornwall. Hughes, who described Dick as "a smart-arse at the best of times", found the proposal "typical" but special.
