The late-night show host Stephen Colbert on CBS faced over 5,700 complaints to the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) following a sexually explicit joke about President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin on May 1. The joke, made during a monologue on Trump's first 100 days in office, was deemed "beneath the dignity of American broadcasting" by disgruntled viewers from various political backgrounds.

The complaints, released by the FCC in response to a POLITICO Freedom of Information Act request, included concerns about indecency, hate speech, and homophobia. Some viewers argued that the joke targeted Trump unfairly, while others raised qualms about its homophobic nature.

Despite the numerous complaints, legal experts believe that fines against Colbert and CBS are unlikely due to the time the joke aired (11:30 p.m., in what's known as the safe harbor) and the FCC's strict indecency and obscenity rules.

The number of complaints about Colbert's joke pales in comparison to the over half a million the agency received over Janet Jackson's "wardrobe malfunction" during the 2004 Super Bowl halftime show on CBS.

Andrew Schwartzman, an attorney with Georgetown University’s Institute for Public Representation, stated that the joke would likely pass the FCC's indecency test, and there is "zero chance" the FCC would bring an obscenity case against Colbert.

The FCC is currently reviewing the complaints, but no update has been provided. The review does not imply the complaints have merit, as it is standard protocol for the FCC.

China's currency, the yuan, depreciated further on Wednesday following a surprise change in its exchange rate mechanism on Tuesday, which rattled global markets and may escalate trade tensions with the United States and Europe. The People's Bank of China (PBOC) devalued the yuan by 1.9% against the US dollar on Tuesday, marking its biggest one-day fall in a decade, and it dropped another 1.6% on Wednesday.

The PBOC stated that the devaluation was due to changes aimed at making the tightly controlled currency more market-oriented. This move could potentially lead to further declines, benefiting Chinese exporters at the expense of foreign competitors and potentially boosting flagging economic growth.

Until now, the PBOC had set the yuan's value each day based on a basket of currencies, with the US dollar playing a significant role. However, the depreciation of the yuan over the past year, due to the strengthening US dollar, had hurt Chinese exporters and raised the threat of politically dangerous job losses. Exports in July plummeted by an unexpectedly steep 8.3% from a year earlier.

The PBOC announced that, starting Tuesday, the daily target for the yuan would be based on the closing price of the previous day and information from traders about supply and demand for the currency. This change presents a dilemma for China's trading partners, who have called for Beijing to let market forces set its exchange rate but don't want to see the yuan weaken.

The depreciation of the yuan is likely to see "continued strong influence" from the PBOC, with Tuesday's change "probably marking the start of an engineered depreciation," according to Mizuho Bank. Many economists cautioned against viewing Beijing's move as an effort solely to benefit its exporters, noting that the yuan, left to market forces alone, would have declined in value in recent months.

The depreciation "will not change the gloomy picture of global demand," said Vincent Chan of Credit Suisse. "The 2% devaluation cannot provide any meaningful help, but it caught the market by surprise." U.S. stocks tumbled on Tuesday, with the Dow Jones Industrial Average closing down 212 points.

China becomes the third major trader to take actions that lower the value of its currency, following initiatives by Japan and the European Union over the past two years. The yuan, also known as the renminbi, is allowed to fluctuate in a band 2% above or below a rate set by the PBOC based on its currency basket.

The change in the exchange rate mechanism has sparked complaints in Washington, where members of Congress have long complained that Beijing manipulates its currency to gain a trade advantage. "For years, China has rigged the rules and played games with its currency," said U.S. Sen. Chuck Schumer. "Rather than changing their ways, the Chinese government seems to be doubling down."

The U.S. Treasury Department's response was more measured, stating that China's move was another step in its move to a more market-determined exchange rate. The International Monetary Fund (IMF) also supported the change, stating that it appears to be a welcome step to give market forces a bigger role. However, the exact impact will depend on how the new mechanism is implemented in practice.

The IMF stated that China can, and should, aim to achieve an effectively floating exchange rate system within two to three years. The latest change will have no effect on the decision about whether to add the yuan to the dollar, the euro, the yen, and the British pound in the basket of currencies used to set the value of the Fund's in-house currency, called Special Drawing Rights. The IMF staff recommended last week that China wait until at least October 2016 to join. The Fund's board is due to consider that recommendation in October.

The depreciation of the yuan could further complicate the Federal Reserve's decision on when to raise interest rates. A rate hike would likely raise the value of the dollar, which has already jumped about 14% in value in the past 12 months against a basket of foreign currencies. The rising dollar has hurt U.S. exporters by making their goods costlier abroad, and China's devaluation could exacerbate this issue.

The Fed wants to be "reasonably confident" that inflation is returning to its 2% target before raising rates. Inflation has risen just 1.3% in the past 12 months. Michael Feroli, an economist at JPMorgan Chase, suggested that the dollar's rise poses a concern for some Fed officials, known as doves, who have been reluctant to raise rates. Should the U.S. economy stumble in the coming weeks, "dollar strength would only further embolden the doves at the next meeting" in September, Feroli said.

USB economist Tao Wang stated that Beijing would likely move cautiously, but investor expectations of further weakening "could quickly become entrenched" and cause the yuan to "depreciate quite quickly and significantly." She added that this would represent a "sea change in China's exchange rate policy" but would help to support flagging economic growth.

The surprising relationship between Madonna and Tupac Shakur, spanning back to the mid-90s, is the subject of a recently surfaced prison letter. In 1995, Tupac wrote a letter to Madonna expressing concerns about their relationship affecting his public image due to societal perceptions. The letter, which will be auctioned starting July 19, reveals Tupac's insecurities about being seen with a white woman, stating, "For you to be seen with a black man wouldn't in any way jeopardize your career, if anything it would make you seem that much more open and exciting."

However, Tupac felt that being in a relationship with Madonna would negatively impact his own image, saying, "But for me at least in my previous perception I felt due to my 'image' I would be letting down half of the people who made me what I thought I was." The letter also mentions a falling out, with Tupac quoting Madonna as saying, "I'm off to rehabilitate all the rappers and basketball players."

Tupac apologizes for any hurtful words and expresses growth since then, acknowledging himself as a "young man with limited experience with an extremely famous sex symbol." The letter is expected to fetch a high price, with a starting bid of $100,000. This poignant message underscores the shared human experience of insecurities and doubts, even among legendary figures like Tupac and Madonna. The letter also showcases Tupac's excellent handwriting.

In a separate report, it's mentioned that Alexa Internet has been donating their crawl data to the Internet Archive since 1996, with the data being added to the Wayback Machine after an embargo period. This data contributes significantly to the preservation of the internet's history.

Italy's national statistical agency, Istat, announced on Thursday that it will include the economic value of prostitution, illegal drug sales, and trafficking in contraband cigarettes and alcohol in the country's 2014 Gross Domestic Product (GDP) calculations. This update to the methodology is in line with European Union guidelines and will reflect a shift from the previous system implemented in 1995.

The inclusion of these illegal activities in the GDP calculations is expected to add between 1% and 2% to Italy's GDP. This expansion could potentially benefit the national government, particularly when calculating the deficit-to-GDP ratio.

Prime Minister Matteo Renzi, who is committed to reducing Italy's deficit to 2.6% of GDP this year, may find this boost to the economy beneficial. Italy's GDP, which stood at 1.56 trillion euros ($2.13 trillion) in 2013, has been stagnant due to four recessions in the last 13 years.

In addition to the inclusion of illegal activities, the change in methodology will also bring research and development and arms into the GDP calculation. Previously, research and development was excluded due to being classified as an intermediate cost.

The Finance Ministry declined to comment on the new system. The revised calculations will also adjust prior-year figures to reflect the change in methodology. The reporters for this story can be contacted at afrye@bloomberg.net and cvasarri@bloomberg.net.

In an interview with The Huffington Post, Senator Rand Paul defended his aide Jack Hunter, who has been criticized for his past comments praising John Wilkes Booth, criticizing Abraham Lincoln, and wearing a Confederate flag ski mask. Paul stated that he opposes such views and that Hunter has recanted many of them. He also emphasized that Hunter has never acted in a discriminatory way and that his earlier work in South Carolina was a form of youthful political showmanship. Paul stressed that he has a zero tolerance policy for any form of discrimination and that he would fire Hunter immediately if he showed any evidence of it.

Hunter, who co-wrote Paul's first book in 2010 and is now his social media adviser in Washington, is 39 years old and was a well-known figure in South Carolina for years before catching Paul's eye with some well-circulated YouTube videos. Paul said that he only knew vaguely about Hunter's work, but even if he had known all the details, he would not have shied away from hiring him because he is a talented conservative writer.

The controversy over Hunter's past writings and radio broadcasts has been widely seen as a drag on libertarian-leaning Republicans' mainstream political ambitions and a reminder of the elder Paul's newsletters. Hunter has now left Paul's office to resume his career as a political pundit and to clear his own name, which he argues is now unfairly associated with racism.

Senator Paul has been criticized for some of his statements on race and civil rights, which foes see as a throwback to the days when resistance to federal power was tantamount to defending the Old South. However, Paul insists that he is not an enemy of Lincoln and that he grapples with the tension between the grassroots tea party enthusiasm and libertarian online donors he inherits from his father and his own strategic plan to be seen as a mainstream-able GOP figure.

Paul is a freshman senator and a tea party libertarian who is hungering to climb his way through the GOP to the White House. He wins passionate fans for questioning the rise of the Security State at home and the drone wars abroad, but he also wins equally passionate critics for his statements on race and civil rights. Paul is known for his irritation at other people telling him what he should do, say, or think and is not about to distance himself from a writer who long called himself the "Southern Avenger."

Scientists have discovered the most distant galaxy ever confirmed, named z8_GND_5296, which is approximately 13.1 billion light-years away from Earth. The galaxy was found using the Hubble Space Telescope and the Keck Observatory in Hawaii. Light from this galaxy began its journey when the universe was about 700 million years old.

The discovery of this galaxy provides a snapshot of the early universe and helps researchers better understand the era of reionization, a period when newborn hot, massive stars and their galaxies transformed the opaque hydrogen fog that filled the cosmos in the first billion years after the Big Bang into the transparent intergalactic space we see today.

One unique trait about the record-breaker is its high rate of star formation, about 330 per year, which is more than a hundred times faster than the Milky Way galaxy. This could be a characteristic of the universe's early days, when hydrogen gas for star formation was more abundant.

The team of astronomers used images from the Hubble Space Telescope to identify 43 possible faraway galaxies and then used state-of-the-art spectrographic equipment at the W. M. Keck Observatory in Hawaii to confirm their distances. In the end, they could only retrieve data from this lone galaxy.

The find, described in a study published this week in the journal Nature, is expected to help researchers understand the early universe and its evolution. However, there is still much to learn, and astronomers continue to push the boundaries of detection capabilities to look even further back in time.

Richard Ellis, an astronomer not connected to the study, says it is possible to push the record back even further, closer to the Big Bang, but we do not yet have telescopes powerful enough to do the job. The conundrum for researchers is that looking at larger distances means looking further back in time, making galaxies ever fainter as we push closer to the birth of the universe and the Big Bang.

Advances in instrumentation technology will allow astronomers to continue stretching their detection capabilities further outward from the Milky Way, providing valuable insights into the early universe and its evolution.

In this summary, several political figures have expressed their opinions on the potential nomination of former Senator Chuck Hagel as the new Defense Secretary under President Barack Obama.

Senate Minority Leader Mitch McConnell has stated that Hagel should receive a fair confirmation hearing, but he will review Hagel's past statements to determine if his views align with the job requirements. McConnell had previously praised Hagel for his national security and foreign policy stance, but he has since expressed concerns about Hagel's views on Israel, particularly regarding the Iranian nuclear threat.

Texas Senator Ted Cruz and freshman Representative Tom Cotton have criticized Hagel's past policy positions and expressed their intention to vote against his confirmation. Cotton, a veteran of the Iraq and Afghanistan wars, believes there are more qualified Democratic defense professionals that Obama could nominate instead.

Senator Lindsey Graham has called Hagel's potential nomination "in-your-face" and "out of the mainstream" on foreign policy issues. Graham believes that if confirmed, Hagel would be the most antagonistic Defense Secretary towards Israel in U.S. history.

Senate Majority Whip Dick Durbin has defended Hagel, stating that he is a "serious candidate" due to his experience as a decorated Vietnam war veteran, his service on the Foreign Relations and Intelligence Committees, and his past service as a Republican senator.

The potential nomination of Hagel is likely to spark a contentious confirmation battle, with concerns being raised about his views on Israel, Iran, and his past comments regarding gays.

The United Nations Security Council has authorized a No-Fly Zone over Libya to prevent a humanitarian disaster, bringing the US and its allies into another Middle Eastern conflict. The intervention is a high-stakes gamble, with the potential for success quickly leading to Qaddafi's regime's collapse and aligning the US and the international community with the Arab protest movement. However, if the intervention degenerates into a long quagmire, it could lead to an Iraq-like rage against Western imperialism, potentially crushing the Arab uprisings' hopes.

The intervention is complicated by the ongoing bloody crackdowns in US-backed Bahrain and Yemen, raising questions about whether the Responsibility to Protect will extend beyond Libya. Gideon Rose, Foreign Affairs editor, warns that leaders should never go into a military intervention without thinking through the political endgame, a concern that remains relevant in the Libyan conflict.

Recent developments suggest that Libya has promised a cease-fire hours after the UN vote, but military experts and Libyan rebels view this as a tactical move by Col. Moammar Gadhafi to buy time and potentially neutralize US Secretary of Defense Robert Gates' stated desire to take out Gadhafi's defense as part of the no-fly zone. Reports from Misrata indicate that the city is still under bombardment, with civilians suffering deaths and destruction.

The clock is ticking, with Britain taking the lead by sending Tornado and Typhoon fighters to air bases in Italy and Cyprus, and a large naval flotilla stationed off the Libyan coast. The international community, including the US, France, and NATO, are holding emergency meetings to discuss the scope of military action under the no-fly zone. The hope is that the UN's resolution will quickly lead Qaddafi's regime to crumble and create the conditions for a rapid political process to change that regime without the actual use of military force.

In Bahrain, anti-government protests continued for a second day, with security forces opening fire on demonstrators, wounding at least 50 people. President Barack Obama condemned the violence and urged Bahrain's king to show restraint, hold those responsible accountable, and respect the rights of its people. The crown prince ordered the military to withdraw from the capital, and appealed for all political factions to join in dialogue for political reforms. The outcome of the uprising remains uncertain due to disunity within the opposition and the protesters' determination to continue demonstrating. The violence in Bahrain, along with Yemen and Libya, prompted Britain and France to halt arms sales to the affected countries.

The 2015 Academy Awards nominations were announced, with notable omissions and controversies. The critically acclaimed film Selma, directed by Ava DuVernay, was snubbed in the Best Director category, despite receiving rave reviews and being nominated for Best Picture. This marks the continued lack of recognition for black directors in the Academy Awards, with only three black men having ever been nominated in the best director category. The absence of DuVernay is particularly disappointing as she directed one of the best films of the year and would have been the fifth woman in history to receive a Best Director nomination. The Academy's voting members are predominantly white and male, and the lack of diversity in this year's nominations reflects this. The absence of DuVernay from the Best Director category is a missed opportunity to recognize a talented filmmaker and to promote diversity in the film industry. Selma's omission from the Best Director category has sparked controversy and criticism, with many arguing that the film's historical inaccuracies should not overshadow its artistic merit. The film's snub is a reminder of the challenges faced by black directors in the film industry and the need for greater diversity in the Academy Awards. The Academy's president, Cheryl Boone Isaacs, has been pushing for more diversity, but this year's nominations have failed to reflect that push. The absence of DuVernay from the Best Director category is a significant blow to the representation of black directors in the Academy Awards and in the film industry as a whole.

The mayor of Kharkiv, Hennadiy Kernes, was shot and critically wounded in a suspected assassination attempt on Monday in eastern Ukraine. Kernes was recovering after a two-hour operation to repair damage to his chest and abdomen, but his life remained in danger, according to his office. The shooting occurred while Kernes was out jogging in Kharkiv. The head of the hospital where Kernes is being treated said he had suffered a "very serious wound", and that a number of organs had been damaged.

On Monday, pro-Russian separatists also seized a local government building in Kostyantynivka, a town to the south of Kharkiv. The US has expanded sanctions to include targets linked to President Vladimir Putin's "inner circle". The list includes seven new individuals and 17 companies. The European Union is also expected to announce new sanctions.

Western nations accuse Moscow of supporting separatist gunmen who are occupying official buildings in cities across eastern Ukraine. The separatists continue to hold seven Western military observers who were seized last week in the region. Pro-Russian supporters and football fans clashed in Kharkiv on Sunday, resulting in several injuries.

Kernes was a supporter of the former pro-Moscow President Viktor Yanukovych, but dropped his support for the ousted president in favor of a united Ukraine. He has been described as a "mini-oligarch" - a successful businessman wealthy enough to launch a career in politics. He has been accused of starting his business career as an organized crime boss, a claim he denied while acknowledging that he was once jailed for fraud - a minor offence "partly fabricated" by his enemies, he insisted.

Kharkiv was also the scene of clashes on Sunday when football fans marching for a united Ukraine scuffled with pro-Russia supporters. On Monday morning, gunmen wearing uniforms with no insignias moved into the local administrative building in Kostyantynivka and raised the flag of the self-proclaimed "Donetsk Republic". They were also reported to be in control of the police station in Kostyantynivka.

'Not personal'

US President Barack Obama confirmed the stepping up of sanctions against Russia, which he said was part of a "calibrated effort" to change Moscow's behaviour in Ukraine, during a visit to the Philippines. He said the measures were in response to Moscow's failure to uphold an international accord aimed at peacefully resolving the Ukraine crisis. A White House statement said the new targets were "seven Russian government officials, including two members of President Putin's inner circle, who will be subject to an asset freeze and a US visa ban, and 17 companies linked to Putin's inner circle, which will be subject to an asset freeze".

Obama said the sanctions were not aimed at Russian President Vladimir Putin personally. "The goal is to change his calculus with respect to how the current actions that he's engaging in could have an adverse impact on the Russian economy over the long haul," he said. Meanwhile, ambassadors from the 28 EU member states are meeting in Brussels to agree new sanctions against Russia.

Eight foreign observers - who were operating under the auspices of the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE) - were led into Sloviansk town hall by masked gunmen and shown to the media on Sunday. German monitor Col Axel Schneider, who spoke for the group, stressed they were not NATO officers - contrary to claims made by the separatists - nor armed fighters, but diplomats in uniform. Later, one of the group - a Swede - was freed for medical reasons. The fate of five Ukrainian military officers accompanying the mission is unknown.

The US and EU already have assets freezes and travel bans in place targeting a number of Russian individuals and firms accused of playing a part in the annexation of Crimea last month. BBC Europe correspondent Chris Morris says it is expected that the ambassadors will add another 15 people in positions of power to the list of those to whom sanctions apply. Our correspondent says the White House wants a show of unity from the US and Europe, but there is little consensus within the EU at the moment for implementing broader economic sanctions against Russia.

The Lord's Resistance Army (LRA), a notorious rebel group known for extreme violence, has reportedly weakened as Joseph Kony, its leader, has appointed his son, Salim Saleh, as deputy leader. Salim Saleh, who is believed to be 22 years old and has spent his entire life with the LRA, is now responsible for field command, according to Ugandan General Sam Kavuma. This change suggests that Kony's control over the group has been weakened, with fighters now split into several autonomous gangs.

The LRA, which has been wanted by the International Criminal Court for war crimes and crimes against humanity, including murder, sexual slavery, and using child soldiers, has long been a target of international efforts to hunt them down. Despite being hunted by Ugandan troops with the support of US special forces, the LRA has shown resilience in avoiding capture and launching attacks.

Ugandan troops, led by General Kavuma, have reportedly weakened the LRA through defections and military campaigns. However, the group remains active, particularly in the Central African Republic. A UN official, Abou Moussa, reported a significant decrease in the number of killings, abductions, and displaced people due to LRA activities, but emphasized that there is "no room for complacency" while Kony is still operating.

Recent reports suggest that Kony and other senior LRA commanders may have sought refuge in an area known as Kafia Kingi, which is controlled by Sudan. However, Kony is known to move around the forested region that straddles the borders of Sudan, South Sudan, and the Central African Republic, making his capture challenging.

The Security Council has praised the progress made against the LRA and called for continued momentum until the rebels are no longer a threat. The number of people displaced by the LRA has significantly decreased, dropping from 420,000 people in March 2013 to 160,000 in March of this year, according to estimates from the UN humanitarian agency.

The LRA was initially a guerrilla war against the Ugandan government, led by Kony, but has since fled to the jungles of central Africa. Kony is believed to have no more than a few hundred fighters remaining.

The American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) of Michigan has filed a complaint with the U.S. Justice Department against the Detroit Police Department (DPD), alleging that they are forcibly removing homeless individuals from the Greektown entertainment district and abandoning them miles away, sometimes outside the city. The ACLU claims that this practice is inhumane, callous, and illegal, and that it discriminates against the homeless and endangers their lives.

The ACLU began receiving complaints last year, stating that the homeless are told they are not welcome in Greektown and are then forced into vans and driven away. They are often left late at night in unfamiliar neighborhoods, and their money is taken from them. The ACLU has listed the stories of five individuals who have experienced this treatment, including Andrew Sheehan, who has been "taken for a ride" at least four times since December 2011.

Detroit Police Chief Chester Logan has stated that he will look into the matter, as the DPD has not yet received a copy of the complaint. The ACLU is demanding an end to this practice and is calling for an investigation into the DPD's treatment of homeless individuals.

The ACLU's complaint comes as the number of homeless individuals in the Detroit area continues to rise, with nearly 19,000 people homeless in 2010, according to the Neighborhood Service Organization. The ACLU is urging the DPD to treat homeless individuals with dignity and to ensure their safety and rights are protected.

The Supreme Court has declined Virginia's Attorney General, Ken Cuccinelli's request to expedite the review of the Obama healthcare law, choosing instead to let the legal challenge proceed through the federal appeals courts. Cuccinelli had sought a speedy review to end the "crippling and costly uncertainty" surrounding the law. The court's decision means that the cases challenging the law's constitutionality will continue in the 4th Circuit Court of Appeals, 6th Circuit, and 11th Circuit.

The healthcare law, a signature legislation of President Barack Obama, is facing challenges from various states, including Virginia, Florida, and 25 others, claiming that the individual mandate, requiring most Americans to buy health insurance, is unconstitutional. So far, two federal judges have agreed with the states, while three others have found the law constitutional.

The cases are moving quickly through the appeals courts, with the Virginia cases set to be heard by the 4th Circuit Court of Appeals on May 10th, the Michigan case by the 6th Circuit on June 1st, and the Florida case, with challenges from over half the states, by the 11th Circuit appeals court on June 8th. The Supreme Court is expected to hear the case during the term that starts in the fall, with all nine justices participating.

Virginia Governor Bob McDonnell expressed disappointment at the court's decision, stating that the refusal to expedite the case would force states and businesses to incur increased costs and expend significant effort to comply with the law, which may ultimately be ruled unconstitutional.

Mischa Barton, the actress known for her roles in 'The Sixth Sense' and 'The O.C.', has filed a lawsuit against her mother and manager, Nuala Barton, alleging financial exploitation and fraud. According to the lawsuit, Nuala has withheld Mischa's career earnings, used her name for personal gain, and even kicked her out of her own home.

The complaint, filed in the Los Angeles Superior Court, accuses Nuala of being a "greedy stage mother posing as a talent manager" who defrauded Mischa. Mischa claims her mother lied about her compensation for acting in the horror film 'The Hoarder' and pocketed the difference, on top of her management fee. She also alleges that Nuala entered her into endorsement contracts without her knowledge and launched enterprises like a handbag line and a fashion boutique in London without compensating her.

The lawsuit further states that Nuala structured the purchase of Mischa's Beverly Hills home in 2006 to give herself co-ownership of the property, took out loans against it, and then kicked her out. Mischa is seeking unspecified damages, triple the amount the court finds her mother to have withheld, and legal fees.

Interestingly, Mischa did not sue her father, who is not her manager. The suit gets particularly nasty, with Mischa stating that her parents "sit back expecting their daughter's hard work and dedication to her craft to support their lifestyle." She adds that neither of them has had a job outside of Mischa Inc. in over a decade.

Mischa Barton is now represented by Jonathan Perry of APA and Adam Griffin of LINK Entertainment. Lawyers Alex Weingarten and Leslie Eggers of Venable LLP are representing her in the suit against her mother. As of the filing of this article, Nuala's attorney has not yet responded to the complaint.

The Global Slavery Index 2013, released by the Walk Free Foundation, reveals that approximately 29.6 million people are enslaved worldwide, with Mauritania and Haiti having the highest proportions of slaves. India, China, and Pakistan have some of the highest absolute numbers of enslaved individuals. Slavery takes various forms, including sexual exploitation, debt bondage, forced marriage, and hereditary servitude, particularly in West Africa and South Asia. Victims are often tricked, kidnapped, or sold into exploitative situations, such as unpaid labor, forced marriages, or domestic work. The 10 countries with the highest number of enslaved or exploited workers are India, China, Pakistan, Nigeria, Ethiopia, Russian Federation, Thailand, Democratic Republic of the Congo, Myanmar, and Bangladesh. Mauritania, with about 150,000 slaves, has the highest proportion of enslaved people, with aspects of "chattel slavery" that resemble the American institution, where human beings are considered full property of their masters. The index aims to serve as a baseline for governments and activists in the anti-slavery fight, with the hope of improving policies and resources to address the issue.

On April 1, 2016, Alaska broke a 101-year-old temperature record with a high of 71 degrees Fahrenheit in Klawock, located on Prince of Wales Island. The previous record, set in 1915, was 69 degrees in Ketchikan. This new record marks the warmest official temperature ever recorded in Alaska during the month of March.

Additionally, several other locations in southeast Alaska also set new record high temperatures for March 31. Juneau, Yakutat, Sitka, and Ketchikan all experienced record-breaking temperatures, ranging from 65 degrees in Ketchikan to 57 degrees in Yakutat.

Furthermore, March 2016 marked the warmest monthly average temperature on record for several locations, including Juneau, Sitka, Klawock, Haines, Petersburg, and Skagway. The high temperature recorded in Klawock today is currently preliminary and, if confirmed, will stand as the warmest official temperature ever recorded in Alaska during the month of March.

In the sixth Democratic presidential debate, Hillary Clinton and Bernie Sanders faced off in Milwaukee, with Clinton delivering her best debate performance of the election. She effectively criticized Sanders's health-care proposal and portrayed him as insufficiently loyal to President Obama, a point that resonates with black voters. Sanders, on the other hand, struggled to differentiate himself and came across as more combative than Clinton, particularly on foreign policy and relations with Obama.

Clinton's performance was aided by the lack of questions about uncomfortable topics for her, such as paid speeches and State Department investigations. However, she was uncomfortable when pressed on her super PAC being financed heavily by a few individuals.

Barack Obama was also a winner, as Clinton embraced him on every issue and even Sanders tried to tie himself to the outgoing president. The debate focused on domestic policy, which should have been Sanders's strong suit, but he struggled to score clean hits on Clinton and sounded repetitive, citing millionaires and billionaires to explain most of his answers.

Sanders also made a slip when he insisted that he would be better on race relations than Obama, a point that the Clinton campaign will undoubtedly use in the coming days and weeks. He was also criticized for his insistence that he would be a better president than Obama on race issues, which was seen as tone-deaf.

The debate also saw a strong focus on police reform, with both candidates promising to address systemic racism and reform the criminal justice system. Clinton spoke of the "dark side" of law enforcement and referred to "systemic racism," while Sanders promised to "end overpolicing in African-American neighborhoods."

Overall, Clinton's cool and collected demeanor played well, particularly on the topic of race, where she resisted the temptation to be critical. Sanders, on the other hand, was often on the defensive and allowed his feelings to affect his answers, particularly when Clinton attacked him for his criticisms of President Obama.

In terms of policy, Clinton defended her Wall Street fundraising by further punching the banking industry, while Sanders's proposals were criticized for not targeting a wide enough range of institutions. The debate also saw a surprising attack on Henry Kissinger by Sanders, who called him one of the most destructive secretaries of state in modern history.

In conclusion, Hillary Clinton delivered a strong debate performance, particularly on the topic of race, while Bernie Sanders struggled to differentiate himself and was often on the defensive. The debate also saw a strong focus on police reform and a surprising attack on Henry Kissinger by Sanders.

Rupert Murdoch's News Corp has sold a majority stake in three of its Chinese television channels to China Media Capital (CMC), a private equity fund backed by the Chinese government. This move marks a shift in News Corp's strategy in China, where it has struggled to break through despite a long-standing commitment. The deal includes Xing Kong, Xing Kong International, Channel [V] Mainland China, and the Fortune Start Chinese film library. News Corp will retain a significant stake but the financial details were not disclosed. The sale is part of a gradual retreat by News Corp from China's media market, where the government maintains tight controls. The deal is seen as beneficial for both parties, with CMC gaining access to overseas distribution channels and News Corp hoping to expand in the region. The combined assets of the three channels and the film library are valued at $300m, making the deal worth about $160m. This decision comes after a series of concessions made by Murdoch to the Chinese government, including barring the BBC from his satellite platform broadcasting in the region.

A white tiger named Riku attacked and killed a zookeeper, Akira Furusho, at the Hirakawa Zoological Park in Kagoshima, Japan. The incident occurred on Monday as Furusho was cleaning the tiger's enclosure. The tiger, which is about 1.8 meters in length and weighs approximately 170 kilograms, was sedated and will be kept alive following a request from the victim's family. Police are investigating the zoo's care of the four white tigers it keeps, and labor authorities are interviewing zoo workers to determine if safety regulations were violated. The zoo, which opened in 1972, is run by a public corporation under contract with the municipal government and remained open Tuesday, with restricted access to the tiger's display area.

In the recent elections, the Republican party has made significant gains in both the House and Senate. One of the potential Republican presidential candidates for 2016, Governor Scott Walker of Wisconsin, has successfully fended off a challenge from Democrats, despite previous conflicts with labor groups over a measure that diminished the power of public sector unions. Walker had previously survived a recall attempt two years ago.

The Republican advancement towards a Senate majority is evident, with the party making strides in various states. In the House, the GOP has secured victories over several veteran Democratic lawmakers. Notable among these is the defeat of 19-term lawmaker Nick Rahall in West Virginia by Republican Evan Jenkins, who was previously a Democrat. Rahall was one of the last white Democrats to survive in the South despite the Republican dominance in the region. Similarly, Rick Allen defeated five-term Rep. John Barrow of Georgia, another Southern Democrat.

These election results indicate a shift in political power towards the Republican party, with several key Democratic seats being lost in both the House and Senate.

Hillary Clinton, the presumed Democratic front-runner for the 2016 presidential nomination, was targeted with a shoe and papers during a speech at the Institute of Scrap Recycling Industries convention in Las Vegas. A woman threw multiple objects at Clinton, causing her to dodge a projectile near her head. Clinton handled the situation with poise, quickly getting back on track and joking about the incident. The woman was escorted out of the convention by security and Secret Service officers, and police were called. The rest of Clinton's address went smoothly, and she did not announce her plans for the 2016 presidential race. The woman who threw the objects was not affiliated with the organization and was not credentialed for the event. Clinton's speech focused on the recycling industry, international trade, the civil war in Syria, and U.S. relations with Russia. Clinton touched on the recycling industry, international trade, the civil war in Syria, and U.S. relations with Russia. Clinton's visit to Las Vegas was part of a cross-country tour in which she is giving paid speeches to industry organizations and appearing before key Democratic Party constituents.

On May 6, 2016, a suspected gunman, Eulalio Tordil, was arrested in connection with three deadly shootings that occurred in Montgomery County, Maryland. The shootings took place at Westfield Montgomery Mall and a Giant grocery store, leaving three people dead and three others injured. The first shooting occurred at the mall, where two men and a woman were wounded, one of whom later died. The second shooting took place at a Giant grocery store, where a woman was killed.

Tordil, who was an employee of the Federal Protective Service, was believed to be connected to a fatal shooting that occurred at a high school in Prince George's County on Thursday, where he shot and killed his estranged wife and injured a bystander. Tordil was wanted for this shooting, and police issued an alert for him, stating that he may have been wearing body armor and may be heavily armed.

Tordil was apprehended after being seen eating at a Boston Market, and police surrounded a silver Hyundai Elantra in the parking lot of an Aspen Hill Kohl's store, where he was found inside. Tordil was arrested in the same shopping center where the D.C. Beltway sniper attacks began in 2002.

The first shooting at the mall occurred at around 11:13 am, and the second shooting at the grocery store took place at around 11:50 pm. Police believe that Tordil shot two of the people who were wounded at the mall as they came to the aid of the first victim. The female victim at the mall is in stable condition with non-life-threatening injuries, while the second man is in critical condition at Suburban Hospital.

Westfield Montgomery released a statement regarding the shootings, expressing condolences to the victims and their families and encouraging people to follow official updates from the Montgomery County Police Department.

Prince George's County police officially charged Tordil with first-degree murder and related charges for the fatal shooting of his wife, and charges are pending against him in connection to the shootings in Montgomery County. Tordil was in custody Friday night at Montgomery County police headquarters being interviewed, and he will be arraigned in District Court on Monday afternoon.

A shelter-in-place order was issued for all Montgomery County schools out of an abundance of caution, but just before 2:30 pm, the order was lifted at all but five schools following Tordil's arrest. All shelter-in-place orders were eventually lifted.

The shootings have sparked a sense of foreboding in the area, as the same neighborhood suffered through the Beltway sniper rampage in 2002, which took 10 lives. Tordil was known to have eaten lunch at the same Boston Market where the snipers ate, and authorities are investigating whether there is a connection between the two incidents.

China's National Space Administration has released hundreds of high-resolution images taken by its lunar rover, Yutu or "Jade Rabbit," which landed on the moon in 2013. Despite initial problems and a three-month mission that ended in January 2014, the rover continued to transmit data until last October. The images show the moon's surface in vivid detail, marking a show of openness for China's usually secretive space program. The Chang'e-3 mission, which included a lunar lander, was the third nation to land on the moon after the US and Russia.

On Sunday, July 16, 2017, skywatchers in the northern United States and Canada may witness a spectacular display of the Northern Lights, also known as the Aurora Borealis. The event is a result of a geomagnetic storm caused by a solar flare that erupted from a sunspot on Thursday, July 13. The flare released a coronal mass ejection (CME) that took a couple of days to reach Earth.

NOAA's Space Weather Prediction Center expects a "moderate" geomagnetic storm, with a 2 out of 5 severity level. The aurora should be visible in states such as Montana, the Dakotas, Minnesota, Wisconsin, northern Illinois, Michigan, northern New York State, and much of New England. Cities like Minneapolis, Chicago, Detroit, Buffalo, Syracuse, Albany, and Boston have a fair chance of seeing the aurora.

The solar flare caused a minor radio blackout over parts of Asia, and the CME is mostly aimed ahead of Earth's orbital path. However, a significant portion of the CME will become snagged within the Earth's magnetic field and funneled down into the upper atmosphere near the planet's poles to produce bright auroras.

It is essential to have clear and dark skies to see the auroras, far from the light pollution cast by urban environments. Auroras are also known for being random and flighty, appearing and disappearing quite suddenly. If you plan on getting out to watch, choose your location carefully and be safe. Provincial parks are an excellent resource for skywatching. Give your eyes some time to adjust to the dark, and avoid all bright sources of light during that time. Look up and to the north to potentially see the auroras.

Brian Williams, during a GOP debate, asked Governor Rick Perry about the possibility of executing an innocent person through capital punishment, without explicitly mentioning the case of Cameron Todd Willingham. Perry responded that the state of Texas has a fair and thorough process for capital cases, and if someone commits a heinous crime against its citizens, they will face the ultimate justice. Meanwhile, Anthony Graves, who was wrongfully convicted and spent 18 years on death row, was finally exonerated and released. The district attorney for Washington and Burleson counties, Bill Parham, dismissed the charges against Graves, stating that there is no evidence connecting him to the crime. Williams also asked Perry about the audience's applause for his execution of 234 individuals, to which Perry replied that Americans understand justice and support capital punishment for heinous crimes. The article also details the tragic death of Cameron Todd Willingham and the investigation that followed, which ultimately led to his execution despite doubts about the cause of the fire that killed his children.

In a remarkable turn of events, a UPS driver played a crucial role in rescuing a woman who had been held captive and sexually assaulted at her home in Robertsville, Missouri. The driver, making a scheduled stop to pick up a package, noticed the words "contact 911" scrawled on it. He immediately contacted the police, leading to the swift response of a SWAT team. The team apprehended James Tyler Jordan, 33, who was allegedly holding the woman captive and threatening to harm her and himself.

Jordan's wife reported that he had refused to let her leave, physically assaulted her, and sexually assaulted her. During the standoff, Jordan allegedly made the woman write her plea for help on the package. The incident involved a 3-year-old child who lived in the home, prompting the activation of the SWAT team. Jordan surrendered to the police before the SWAT team arrived, and the child was found unharmed.

Jordan has been charged with domestic assault, sodomy, felonious restraint, unlawful use of a weapon, and endangering the welfare of a child. His bond has been set at $100,000 cash only. The UPS driver's quick thinking and the prompt response of the authorities are being hailed as significant in the woman's rescue.

Brad Pitt, in an interview with Matt Lauer on TODAY, clarified his previous remarks about his ex-wife Jennifer Aniston, stating that his comments were taken out of context and were not intended to be critical of Aniston. Pitt emphasized that his point was to acknowledge the importance of his children having a good mother, which he stated was not a reference to the past. Pitt also mentioned that he chooses to distance himself from the constant rumors surrounding his relationships with Angelina Jolie and Aniston, but felt the need to clarify his previous remarks due to their misinterpretation. The interview was conducted to promote Pitt's upcoming movie, "Moneyball," which is generating Oscar buzz. Pitt also shared that his son Maddox is a big baseball fan, and that they had a memorable experience watching a Yankees game together. The interview will air in its entirety on TODAY.

In related content, it was reported that Jennifer Aniston's team "went ballistic" after hearing Pitt's comments, and that Pitt's remarks came from a place of jealousy towards Aniston's current boyfriend, Justin Theroux. However, the validity of these claims is uncertain, as everything in Hollywood is taken with a grain of salt.

Pitt's previous remarks about Aniston caused controversy when he stated that he was "trying to pretend my marriage was something that it wasn't" and that he "wasn't living an interesting life" before meeting Angelina Jolie. Aniston's team reportedly reached out to Pitt's camp and "read him the riot act," leading Pitt to release a statement apologizing for any misunderstanding. Despite this, Pitt and Jolie continue to be in a happy relationship and are raising six children together. Aniston, on the other hand, is reportedly in a romantic relationship with Justin Theroux.

A woman in Jerusalem was arrested by Israeli police for allegedly setting a gas station petrol pump on fire after a driver refused to give her a cigarette. The incident occurred at a Paz Gas station on Derech Bethlehem, as depicted by security camera footage. The woman approached the man filling his car, asked for a cigarette, and when refused, lit the fuel pump handle, causing a fire. The suspect was arrested shortly after the incident but denied the accusations. The driver's brother, who was inside the car at the time, was not harmed. The woman is currently under investigation, with her arrest extended by five days for psychological evaluations.

The Rainbow Loom, a toy that involves a crochet hook and multicolored rubber bands, has caused a stir in two New York City schools due to its distraction during recess and classroom time. P.S. 87 on the Upper West side has banned anything related to Rainbow Looms, while P.S. 107 in Brooklyn allows students to wear the bracelets but not bring the looms and related paraphernalia to school. Some parents view the ban as a creative outlet for kids, while others applaud the schools for taking action due to disruptions in the classroom environment. The Rainbow Loom defies stereotypical gender norms as boys and girls are equally obsessed with making, trading, and giving the bracelets to their friends. The toy has been compared to previous fads such as Pokemon cards and Silly Bandz. The trend has not yet abated, despite some schools banning the wearing and trading of Rainbow Loom bracelets during school hours. The toy requires quiet concentration and fine motor skills, and its popularity among boys could be a sign of hope for gender equality.

French chef Sébastien Bras, who has been running the three-star restaurant Le Suquet in Laguiole for the past ten years, has requested to be removed from the Michelin Guide due to the immense pressure of maintaining the prestigious rating. Bras, who took over from his father, Michel Bras, who is credited with pioneering vegetable-focused haute cuisine, announced his decision on Facebook, citing the constant fear of being judged by Michelin's anonymous food critics as a major source of stress.

Bras's decision has been described as a first by Michelin executive committee member Claire Dorland-Clauzel, who noted that the process of removing a restaurant from the guide is not straightforward. Dorland-Clauzel also emphasized that the pressure associated with Michelin stars is a crucial aspect of culinary excellence in the guide's eyes.

Bras's decision to give up his restaurant's stars is not unprecedented, but it is rare for a French chef to do so without closing down or changing the concept of their restaurant. In the past, other chefs have given up their stars, such as Spain's Casa Julio, but this is believed to be the first time a French chef has requested to be removed from the Michelin Guide in this way.

The decision has significant implications in France, where Michelin stars hold major cultural clout, and where renowned chefs like Joël Robuchon are revered. Bras's request to be removed from the guide has sparked a debate about the role of pressure and stress in the competitive world of Michelin-star cooking.

In response to Bras's request, Dorland-Clauzel noted that the guide is not made for restaurateurs, but for customers, and that while the request would be considered, it is not guaranteed. Bras, who is one of only 27 French chefs to hold top rankings in the Michelin restaurant guide, has not yet announced his plans for the future of his restaurant.

A hacker is attempting to sell the account information, including emails and passwords, of 117 million LinkedIn users, which was stolen during a breach in 2012. The hacker, known as "Peace," is offering the data on the dark web marketplace The Real Deal for 5 bitcoins, approximately $2,200. The data includes 167 million accounts, with 117 million having both emails and encrypted passwords.

The breach was initially believed to have affected around 6.5 million users, but it appears that the number was much higher. The data was stored using the SHA1 algorithm, with no salt, making it easier to crack. According to Troy Hunt, a security researcher, 90% of the passwords were cracked within 72 hours.

LinkedIn has confirmed that the data is legitimate and is working to invalidate the passwords of affected accounts and contact users to reset their passwords. The company encourages users to use two-factor authentication and strong passwords to keep their accounts secure.

Users who had accounts during the time of the 2012 breach, have not changed their password since, and have reused their password on other websites should take precautions to protect their accounts. It is recommended to change passwords, especially on critical sites such as banking websites, email, and Facebook.

LinkedIn has implemented stronger security measures since the breach, including stronger encryption, email challenges, and two-factor authentication. However, these protections would not necessarily protect users from hackers who have obtained email and password combinations. The company advises users to visit its safety center to ensure they have two-step verification authentication and to use strong passwords to keep their accounts as safe as possible.

The Obama administration is planning to introduce a fee on banks as part of the upcoming budget to help recoup costs from the bailout. The fee aims to ease public anger towards financial firms, which are seen as having benefited from taxpayer support. The details of the fee, including who will pay, when it will be implemented, and how much banks will pay, are still under discussion. The fee is expected to cost large banks billions of dollars and could potentially affect bank customers if the costs are passed along. The proposal is aimed at large banks that have already repaid their bailout funds, and is not expected to target auto companies or American International Group (AIG) at this time. The administration believes that banks should bear the brunt of helping the government recoup costs, as they benefited the most from the overall financial rescue. The fee would need congressional approval and could face opposition from the banking industry, which is still recovering from the financial meltdown.

Supreme Court Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg, a prominent figure among liberals, expressed her intention to serve on the court until the age of 90, indicating that she plans to stay for at least five more years. Ginsburg made these comments during a visit to New York following a production of "The Originalist," a play about her late colleague and friend, Antonin Scalia. Ginsburg admired Scalia's intellectual rigor and considered him a formidable debating partner, often describing their relationship as a "ping-pong game."

Ginsburg's comments come at a time when the Supreme Court is facing significant changes, with the retirement of conservative Justice Anthony Kennedy and the nomination of Brett Kavanaugh to replace him, a move that could potentially shift the court's ideological balance. Ginsburg, who is 85, has already hired law clerks for at least two more terms, suggesting her commitment to her role.

The Supreme Court has gained celebrity status in recent years, with Ginsburg being particularly notable for her vehement dissenting opinions. She is the subject of a new documentary, RBG, and her fitness routine has been scrutinized. Ginsburg is a seasoned theatergoer and opera lover, sharing these interests with Scalia.

During her visit, Ginsburg spoke about the resilience of American institutions and the pendulum swing of political ideologies. She also discussed her experiences with discrimination as a Jewish woman and her role in landmark cases such as Brown v Board of Education, which ended school segregation.

The audience's favorite question during a discussion following the play was about Dean Dixon, a conductor who introduced Ginsburg to opera in 1944. Dixon's experiences with racial discrimination are chronicled in the book "Negro at Home, Maestro Abroad."

Ginsburg's comments and the play's themes are particularly relevant given the current political climate and the potential impact of Kavanaugh's nomination on the Supreme Court. Ginsburg's commitment to her role and her continued advocacy for equality and justice make her a significant figure in American politics.

The article discusses the controversy surrounding country sports tourism, particularly hunting, in Scotland, with a focus on a recent goat hunting trip by American media personality Larysa Switlyk. The Scottish Country Sports Tourism Group reports that country sports tourism brings in approximately $200 million to the Scottish economy annually. However, the display of animal trophies by well-heeled individuals, including members of the Trump family and Switlyk, on social media has sparked global condemnation.

The killing of Cecil the lion in Zimbabwe in 2015 and subsequent trophy hunts of his son Xanda and other animals have drawn international attention to the practice of paying to kill big game. Photographs of hunters posing triumphantly with the bodies of animals such as giraffes and baboons have stirred global outrage, leading to resignations in some cases.

While some defend hunting as an honorable, skilled, and bonding experience, others view it as unnecessary waste and detrimental to the environment and animals. The issue is complex, with some countries like Zimbabwe encouraging big-game hunting as a source of income, and others allowing it to manage herd populations and fund game reserves.

Switlyk's goat hunting trip in Islay, Scotland, caused an uproar after she shared photos of the dead goats on social media. Many found the images disgraceful and offensive, with some tagging Scottish legislators. First Minister Nicola Sturgeon and Secretary for Environment Roseanna Cunningham responded, expressing understanding for the concerns but stating that hunting wild animals such as deer and goats is not illegal. However, they plan to review the laws and consider if changes should be made.

Switlyk defended her hunting practices, stating that they serve as population control for wild goats, which have no other natural predators on the island of Islay. Some critics took issue with her response, questioning how killing animals connects with nature.

In response to the backlash, Switlyk posted on Instagram that she was on her way to her next hunting adventure and would be out of service for two weeks. Some critics took umbrage with this post as well, with one stating, "Hope you're 'out of service' for a lot longer than that!! You clearly haven't got the hint from Twitter today have you???"

The goat hunt on Islay has sparked a debate about the ethics of hunting and the role of country sports tourism in Scotland. The Scottish government plans to review the laws regarding hunting and consider potential changes in response to the public outcry.

Robin DiMaggio, a renowned drummer who has worked with artists such as Paul Simon, David Bowie, and Diana Ross, has been charged with embezzling $750,000 from a charity concert aimed at helping homeless and displaced children from conflict zones worldwide. According to federal prosecutors, DiMaggio, who is 47 and resides in Woodland Hills, promised to help the Peace for You Peace for Me Foundation, a Bulgaria-based non-profit organization, with organizing a charity concert in Sofia, Bulgaria.

In August 2016, the foundation's financial sponsor wired $750,000 to a DiMaggio-controlled account as a guarantee for future payments related to artists performing at the charity concert. However, instead of placing the money in an escrow account, as promised, DiMaggio allegedly deposited the funds into his personal bank account and used them for personal expenses, including the purchase of a home for his ex-wife in Calabasas.

DiMaggio has worked as a musical director for the United Nations and "The Arsenio Hall Show." He is expected to make his first court appearance following his arrest on Friday. If convicted, he faces up to 20 years in federal prison. The case has been investigated by the FBI.

DiMaggio has performed or recorded with numerous A-list artists throughout his career, which spans over 30 years. He has also composed the theme song for the Los Angeles County Sheriff's Department. The case is currently being investigated by the FBI, and if convicted, DiMaggio could face up to 20 years in federal prison.

In the primary elections held on August 28, 2018, Tallahassee Mayor Andrew Gillum won the Democratic nomination for governor in Florida, becoming the state's first African-American gubernatorial nominee. Gillum, an unabashed progressive, will face off against Trump-backed Republican Rep. Ron DeSantis in the general election. DeSantis gave credit to President Trump for his victory, stating that the president's endorsement "kind of put me on the map." Gillum's primary victory could help Democrats boost enthusiasm among minorities who often don't vote in large numbers in non-presidential years. Meanwhile, DeSantis will test Trump's grip on a crucial state he won in 2016 and wants to keep in his column in 2020. The results of the Florida governor's race will give an advantage to the winning party in a key political battleground heading into the 2020 presidential campaign. Florida Gov. Rick Scott is vacating the governor's mansion to run for Senate, setting up a showdown with Democratic Sen. Bill Nelson that is expected to be one of the nation's most competitive races. Democrats also eyed pickup opportunities in Florida as they try to flip control of the U.S. House, with one of their best chances being in South Florida, where Republican Rep. Ileana Ros-Lehtinen is retiring in a district that should favor Democrats. The contests in both Florida and Arizona were being closely watched for signs of how the political battlegrounds might tilt in the 2020 presidential election. The death of Sen. John McCain has highlighted anew the shift in the Republican Party since he captured the GOP nomination for president in 2008.

Relatives of a California Highway Patrol Officer, Mark Saylor, and three other family members who died in a high-speed crash caused by a Toyota Lexus in 2009, have filed a lawsuit against Toyota Motor Corp., Toyota Motor Sales U.S.A., and other U.S. Toyota entities, as well as the dealership that provided the loaner car. The lawsuit, filed in San Diego County Superior Court, alleges product liability against Toyota and negligence against the dealership, and seeks unspecified damages. The crash was caused by a wrong-sized floor mat that trapped the accelerator, leading to Toyota's recall of millions of cars for floor mat and gas pedal issues. The family testified before the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee last week, and the lawsuit does not specify an amount of money, but seeks responsibility and change. The automaker has not commented on the matter. The family is also facing a barrage of federal class-action lawsuits.

Egypt is experiencing escalating violence and unrest as protests against the military-led government continue for a third day. The clashes, which have resulted in at least 33 deaths and over 1,250 injuries, are the most significant challenge to the military leaders since the ousting of President Hosni Mubarak in February. The anger stems from the unfulfilled promise of a revolution that aimed to establish a new democracy, and the refusal of the military to relinquish power to a civilian government.

The violence began in Tahrir Square, the epicenter of the anti-Mubarak revolt, where protesters are demanding an end to military rule. The military council, headed by Field Marshal Mohamed Hussein Tantawi, has faced increasing hostility, particularly over attempts to establish new constitutional principles that would maintain the military's permanent control beyond civilian oversight.

The clashes have cast a shadow over Egypt's first free parliamentary elections in decades, which are due to start on November 28. The military has stated that the polls will proceed as planned, despite the violence. The United States, European Union, and United Nations have called for restraint on all sides and urged Egypt to proceed with elections.

The economic instability caused by the political uncertainty could lead to a currency crisis, prompting a sharp depreciation of the Egyptian pound and potential capital controls. The military plans to keep its presidential powers until a new constitution is drawn up and a president is elected in late 2012 or early 2013. Protesters are demanding a swifter transition.

The latest street clashes demonstrate the deep frustration in Cairo and other cities with the slow pace of change. Liberal groups are dismayed by the military trials of thousands of civilians and the failure to scrap a hated emergency law. Islamists, who are expected to perform well in the upcoming elections, suspect the army wants to limit their influence.

Analysts predict that Islamists could win 40% of assembly seats, with a significant portion going to the Muslim Brotherhood. The Revolution Youth Coalition has called for a "million-man march" in Tahrir Square on Tuesday to support demands for a new national salvation government to manage the transition phase, instead of the military council. The unrest in Egypt shows no signs of abating, and the future of the country remains uncertain.

The article discusses the popular websites Hipster Puppies and Hipster Kitty, which feature pets portrayed as hipsters, combining two popular internet trends: cute animals and humor towards hipster culture. The pets are depicted with hipster-like behaviors such as listening to Radiohead, wearing vintage clothes, and referencing highbrow culture. The sites have gained popularity due to their unique blend of humor and relatability. The article also mentions the launch of a new site, LOLcats-meets-Hipster Bingo, which has quickly spread across the internet.

On August 22, 2017, a customer in Hialeah, Florida, showed her Powerball tickets for the upcoming drawing. The jackpot was estimated at $700 million, with the option for the winner to take the annuity over 29 years or a cash prize of $443.3 million, minus taxes.

In Massachusetts, the winning ticket for the $758.7 million Powerball jackpot was initially reported to have been sold in Watertown, but it was later corrected that the winning ticket was actually sold at the Pride Station & Store in Chicopee. The owner of the store, Kamaljeet Kaur, expressed happiness and emotion upon learning her store sold the winning ticket.

The jackpot is the largest grand prize won by a single lottery ticket in U.S. history. The winning numbers were 6, 7, 16, 23, 26, and the Powerball number was 4. The store that sold the winning ticket will receive $50,000.

On August 24, it was reported that the winner of the $758.7 million Powerball jackpot has been identified as Mavis Wanczyk of Chicopee. Wanczyk, a mother of two adult children, came to lottery headquarters in Braintree to claim her prize. She said she found out she had won as she was leaving work Wednesday night with a colleague. Wanczyk has been working at Mercy Medical Center in Springfield for 32 years and has decided not to return to work.

The store where the winning ticket was purchased will receive $50,000 for selling the winning ticket, and the store owner has announced that they will donate the money to charity. There was also a winning ticket sold at a store in Watertown, but it was only worth $1 million. The Massachusetts Lottery initially reported that the winning ticket was sold at the Handy Variety store in Watertown, but later corrected the error.

In Portage, MI, Democratic state House candidate John Fisher has accused the Michigan GOP of sending out campaign mailers directing voters to call him at a number for his 91-year-old mother's room at a local nursing home. The mailers, paid for by the Michigan Republican Party, urged voters to call Fisher and express concerns about Obamacare and the health care policies supported by Democrats. Fisher's campaign manager, David Topping, stated that the number is registered under Fisher's name but is a direct line to his mother's room at Tendercare Portage, where Isabel Kramb is currently receiving hospice care for congestive heart failure.

Fisher, a 64-year-old Oshtemo Township pastor, is running against Republican Kalamazoo County Commissioner Brandt Iden and Libertarian Michael Stampfler in the state's 61st House District, which covers Portage and several surrounding townships. Fisher expressed his displeasure in a prepared statement, stating that directing people to call his suffering mother was "beyond the pale." He also called on Iden to distance himself from the Michigan GOP.

Iden, 31, said he does not condone the tactics used by his party in this instance and hopes Fisher would do the same. However, Iden's campaign was not immediately available for comment. The Michigan Republican Party spokesperson was also not available for comment.

This incident has been described as a case of politics at its worst, with fact and fiction being difficult to separate during political campaigns, especially in an election year. Both sides of the aisle have been working together to address the issue in the spirit of bipartisanship. The Republican Party has apologized for any distress caused and admitted responsibility for the mailer, stating that it wasn't their intention to have people call Fisher's mother. The incident has raised questions about the ethics and contempt for personal privacy displayed by the Republican Party, and the Michigan seniors' dignity and security are at the center of the debate.

The origin of the AIDS pandemic has been traced back to the 1920s in Kinshasa, now the Democratic Republic of Congo, according to a new study published in the journal Science. The study, led by researchers from the University of Oxford and the University of Leuven in Belgium, used a combination of viral archaeology and genetic sequencing to determine the pandemic's origin. The researchers found that a "perfect storm" of population growth, sex trade, and unsterilized needles used in health clinics likely contributed to the spread of the virus. Meanwhile, Belgium-backed railways facilitated the movement of the virus to neighboring regions. The study provides a fascinating insight into the early phases of the HIV-1 pandemic, with experts noting that the usual suspects, such as travel, population growth, and unsafe healthcare interventions, likely played a role in the virus's spread. The HIV virus, which attacks the immune system, has infected nearly 75 million people since it came to global attention in the 1980s. The pandemic has a much longer history in Africa, but the exact origin of the pandemic has remained a source of debate. The study's findings suggest that the answer lies in the era of black and white film and the tail-end of the European empires. In the 1920s, Kinshasa was part of the Belgian Congo, and the city's large and rapidly growing population, coupled with a high incidence of sexually transmitted diseases, likely contributed to the virus's spread. The virus spread to neighboring cities, eventually leading to a global pandemic. The study's findings are sure to spark debate within the field, with experts noting that more research is needed to fully understand the factors that contributed to the HIV-1 pandemic's spread.

The number of reported forcible rapes at four-year colleges increased by 49% between 2008 and 2012, according to an analysis by NPR's Investigative Unit of data from the Department of Education. This increase, while concerning, is seen as positive because it indicates more students are willing to come forward and report this underreported crime. The rise in reports can be attributed to increased education on college campuses about what constitutes sexual assault, as well as new rules and laws from Washington, D.C. that have pushed schools to take sexual assault investigations more seriously.

One school that has taken significant steps to prevent sexual assault is the University of Michigan. The school offers training sessions to first-year students on preventing sexual assault, teaches "bystander education," and encourages students to report incidents. However, the school has faced controversy over its handling of sexual misconduct allegations against a football player.

The data analyzed shows that reports of forcible sexual assaults at the University of Michigan have gone up 113% between 2010 and 2012. University officials have argued that the increase in reports is a sign that the school is taking sexual assault seriously and that students feel safe reporting incidents.

The White House has responded to the issue of sexual assault on college campuses by urging universities to take more action to prevent sexual assaults and to change reporting structures so that victims feel safe to come forward. The Campus SaVE Act, which demands more assault prevention education and better investigations, will be implemented by all schools around the country by next fall.

A quadriplegic man named Jamie Merrett, 37, from Devizes, Wiltshire, has been left brain-damaged after a nurse accidentally switched off his ventilator, an incident caught on camera. The incident occurred in January 2009, and the footage was released by the BBC on October 25, 2021. Merrett, who was able to talk, use a wheelchair, and operate a computer before the incident, has since seen his level of understanding drop to that of a young child.

The nurse involved, Violetta Aylward, worked for an agency contracted by the NHS Wiltshire Primary Care Trust. An internal investigation is ongoing, and the agency, Ambition 24hours, could not comment. A confidential report by Wiltshire social services found that the agency was aware it was required to supply a nurse with training in the use of a ventilator, but the company did not have adequate systems in place to check what training their staff had received.

Ms. Aylward has been suspended while the incident is investigated by the Nursing and Midwifery Council. The council's guidelines state that a nurse should work within their level of competence and have the skills to undertake whatever care they are delivering. The health authority responsible for Merrett's care has apologized and put measures in place to prevent such incidents from happening again. Ms. Aylward has not responded to requests for an interview. The program will be shown on Inside Out West and Inside Out South on BBC One at 1930 BST on Monday, October 25. Legal action is being considered by Merrett's family.

North Korea has announced that Kim Jong Un has assumed the supreme commandership of the army, following the death of his father, Kim Jong Il. The announcement was made by the state-run Korean Central News Agency on October 8. The change in leadership was met with a statement from North Korea's National Defense Commission, which declared that there would be no change in policy from the new regime. The statement criticized South Korea's decision to allow only a select group of private citizens to visit Pyongyang to pay their respects to Kim Jong Il, and expressed anger over South Korea's decision to put its military on alert after Kim Jong Il's death. The statement also warned of revenge over these perceived misdeeds.

Amid concerns over the change in North Korean leadership, a top U.S. diplomat, Kurt Campbell, plans to travel to the region early next year for talks on the situation in North Korea. The State Department announced that the "latest developments related to North Korea" will be on the agenda during Campbell's four-day visit to China, South Korea, and Japan. The statement from North Korea's National Defense Commission also expressed anger towards South Korean President Lee Myung-bak and warned that North Korea would "never deal" with him.

The new leadership in North Korea is an unknown quantity, and neighbors are watching to see whether the leadership change will affect Pyongyang's ties with the international community. North Korea remains technically at war with South Korea and is isolated on the international stage because of its dire human rights record and pursuit of nuclear weapons. Six-nation talks aimed at ending Pyongyang's nuclear ambitions have been stalled for months. The statement from the National Defense Commission also criticized South Korea's "unforgivable" decision to allow only two non-official delegations to cross the border to pay their respects to Kim Jong Il.

On Thursday, North Korea held a national memorial service for Kim Jong Il, ending the period of mourning. Hundreds of thousands of North Korean troops and citizens lined up for the ceremony in Pyongyang's main square. Top party and military officials hailed Kim Jong Un, the young and politically inexperienced new leader, in front of the huge crowd.

Walmart's Sam's Club has announced the closure of 63 stores across the United States, affecting thousands of employees. The decision follows a review of the company's real estate portfolio, with the aim of aligning locations with their strategy. The affected stores span various states, with some states like Alaska losing three stores, while others like Tennessee only lose one.

The closures are expected to result in job losses, and Walmart has stated it will provide severance pay and support to eligible employees. The company will also raise its starting hourly wage from $9 to $11.

The closure list includes locations in Alabama, Alaska, Arizona, California, Connecticut, Florida, Georgia, Illinois, Indiana, Louisiana, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, New Hampshire, New Jersey, New York, North Carolina, Ohio, Tennessee, Texas, Virginia, Washington, and Wisconsin. Three additional stores in Puerto Rico are also affected.
