However, the movie's performance is a letdown considering its high production budget of $230 million. The film, which features Johnny Depp as Jack Sparrow, is battling ghost sailors led by Javier Bardem's Captain Salazar. The movie's international appeal has helped it to make a whopping $208.4 million overseas, making a global total of $270.6 million this weekend.

On the other hand, Paramount's "Baywatch" has failed to make an oceanic summer splash, with a three-day total of $18.1 million and a four-day holiday weekend sum of $22 million. The movie, a reboot of the 1990s NBC drama, has a production budget above $60 million. The movie's poor performance is attributed to its low reviews, with a current 19% on Rotten Tomatoes.

"Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 2" has proven to be the only major hit to emerge from the summer box office so far, with a four-day total of about $340 million. Fox's "Alien: Covenant" is looking at $13.1 million over the four-day stretch, while "Everything, Everything" is a solid low-budget investment for Warner Bros., with a four-day total of about $7.6 million.

Universal's "Fate of the Furious" has become the sixth film to earn over $1 billion overseas, and Disney's "Beauty and the Beast" has passed $500 million domestically. Disney in general is keeping the box office afloat, as of Friday, the studio became the first to have earned over $1 billion in 2017, reaching the milestone in near record time. The only time a studio has earned so much so quickly was Disney last year.

The standoff between Occupy Wall Street protesters and the NYPD is escalating as the city plans to clean Zuccotti Park, where the protesters have been camping since September 17. The city has ordered protesters to remove their tents, sleeping bags, and tarps, claiming that conditions in the park have become unsanitary and unsafe. Protesters, however, view this as an attempt to evict them from the park. They have vowed to resist any attempt at evacuation and plan to link arms and fortify the park perimeter with a human chain, potentially leading to mass arrests.

Brookfield Properties, the park's owner, has complained about the deteriorating conditions in the park and plans to power wash it today. The NYPD has stated that if Brookfield complains about protesters interfering with the cleaning process, they will start making arrests. City Hall has assured protesters that they can return to the park after the cleanup, as long as they don't break the law. However, Police Commissioner Raymond Kelly has stated that sleeping bags and other camping gear will not be allowed back into the park.

A group of city politicians has rallied in support of the protesters, calling on Mayor Bloomberg to reconsider his "eviction notice" and warning him that the world is watching Zuccotti Park. Protesters have been cleaning the park themselves to prevent the city from doing so, and they have spent $3,000 from their donation fund on power washers, gardening supplies, and professional sanitation workers. However, the rented power washers proved to be useless since the park has no water supply.

The protesters' resistance to the city's orders has been fueled by sympathy and publicity generated by what they describe as heavy-handed police tactics. Hip-hop mogul Russell Simmons has offered to pay for the cleanup of Zuccotti Park to avoid confrontation. The controversy has led to a letter from a group of New York civil liberties lawyers offering to meet with Brookfield Properties to resolve the issue.

Donald Trump's former personal driver, Noel Cintron, has filed a lawsuit against the Trump Corporation, claiming he was underpaid and denied overtime for over 10 years. Cintron, who worked for Trump for more than 20 years, alleges that he received only two raises during his tenure, the last one in 2010 when he was forced to surrender his health benefits, saving the Trump Corporation nearly $18,000 annually.

The lawsuit also states that Cintron worked approximately 3,300 hours of uncompensated overtime during his last six years on the job, which he estimates would amount to about $178,000 in overtime pay. He is suing the Trump Corporation for lost wages and damages, seeking about $200,000.

Cintron's allegations echo those of other Trump employees and contractors who have sued the president or his businesses in the past, claiming underpayment and failure to honor promises for compensation. The Trump Organization has stated that Cintron was paid generously and in accordance with the law, and they expect to be vindicated in court.

Cintron, who lives in Queens, New York, started working for the Trump Organization about 30 years ago and worked his way up to chauffeuring Trump. He declined to comment to reporters outside his home. The case is Cintron v. Trump Organization LLC, Supreme Court, State of New York (Manhattan).

A suspect has been arrested and a body found in connection with the disappearance of an American woman, Denise Thiem, who went missing on a pilgrimage route in northwest Spain. Thiem, a 41-year-old woman from Arizona, was last seen on April 5 in the town of Astorga, along the Camino de Santiago, also known as the St. James Way. The suspect, Miguel Angel Munoz, was arrested in the town of Grandas de Salime in the province of Asturias, where he had fled. The body found on a rural property near Munoz's farm is believed to be Thiem's, according to Spanish Interior Minister Jorge Fernandez Diaz, who also stated that there are "well-founded suspicions" that Munoz is responsible for her death. The FBI cooperated in the search, which involved over 300 police and military personnel. The Camino de Santiago is a famous Christian pilgrimage route that leads to the city of Santiago de Compostela at Spain's northwestern tip, where the cathedral is believed to house the bones of St. James, one of the 12 apostles of Jesus. The U.S. Embassy in Madrid declined to comment on the case due to privacy laws. The arrest and discovery of the body have raised safety concerns about the pilgrimage routes, which are walked annually by tens of thousands of people.

In the wake of the Orlando shooting at an LGBT nightclub, a vigil was held in London's Soho district on Monday night. Thousands of people, including Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn and London Mayor Sadiq Khan, gathered to honor the 49 victims. The crowd observed a moment of silence, held Pride slogans, and released 49 rainbow balloons. The London Gay Men's Chorus performed Simon & Garfunkel's "Bridge Over Troubled Water" to a moving audience, as part of global tributes for the Orlando shooting victims.

Rush Limbaugh, a prominent conservative talk show host, has urged his listeners to call Congress over health care legislation, a move that is unusual for him as he typically avoids mobilizing listeners for coordinated political action. This is the second time Limbaugh has given out the Capitol's switchboard number on air, the first being in the 1990s for a U.S. News & World Report profile. Limbaugh stated that he did so to prove his point that he doesn't use his show for activism, as giving out phone numbers would overwhelm the system.

Limbaugh's call to action comes as he believes the current health care legislation would transform the country into something unfamiliar and undesirable. He stated that the American people have the power to prevent this transformation, and his urging listeners to call Congress is a means to express their disapproval of the legislation. Limbaugh acknowledged that by responding to questions on air, he would lose his "exclusivity," but he is concerned with ensuring the answers reach the public.

A tragic accident on Interstate 78 in Berks County, Pennsylvania, claimed the lives of Kathryn Schurtz, 35, and her fiancé, Joseph Kearney, both from Jersey City, New Jersey. The couple was on their way to their wedding in Pittsburgh when their vehicle was involved in a chain-reaction crash with five tractor-trailers. Three other people were injured in the accident.

Kathryn Schurtz was born in Elizabeth, New Jersey, and grew up in Fanwood. She graduated from Union Catholic High School in Scotch Plains, New Jersey, and earned her liberal arts degree from George Washington University before obtaining her MBA from Notre Dame University. She worked as the Head of Platform Partnerships for Oracle Data Cloud in New York City.

Visitation for Schurtz will be held at Immaculate Heart of Mary R.C. Church in Scotch Plains, New Jersey, on Monday from 4 p.m. to 8 p.m. and on Tuesday from 10 a.m. to 11 a.m., followed by a mass at 11 a.m. In lieu of flowers, donations should be made to the Kathryn M. Schurtz Scholarship Fund at Union Catholic High School in Scotch Plains, New Jersey.

The accident caused traffic to be tied up for hours, with vehicles being diverted off the interstate. The crash created traffic headaches for motorists, with some being diverted for over two hours. The highway was shut down for several hours between Hamburg and Lenhartsville in Windsor Township.

This is a tragic loss for the Schurtz and Kearney families, as well as their friends and colleagues. Our thoughts are with them during this difficult time.

The New York Giants, led by Eli Manning, returned to New York City on February 6th to celebrate their Super Bowl XLVI victory. A parade was held, starting at Battery Place and Washington Street, continuing through the Canyon of Heroes, and ending at City Hall Plaza. The parade was attended by all Giants players and thousands of fans. Meanwhile, some returned soldiers have questioned the timing of the parade, suggesting it might send the wrong message about the ongoing wars. Leslie Gelb of the Council on Foreign Relations stated that if such honors were delayed until wars ended, it could take a long time. The event is being extensively covered, with updates, pictures, quotes, and videos being shared.

The Obama administration is planning to announce regulations that will make it easier for banks to do business with legal marijuana sellers, according to Attorney General Eric Holder. Holder stated that the move aims to address public safety concerns related to large amounts of cash in marijuana businesses, which could be a target for robberies. However, the regulations will not amount to a federal endorsement of marijuana but rather an attempt to deal with the reality of legalization in certain states. The new rules, which are being worked out jointly by the Justice and Treasury departments, are expected to emerge "very soon." The regulations are intended to help legal marijuana businesses gain access to the American banking system, but they are not expected to give banks a green light to accept deposits and provide other services. The regulations will provide guidance to prosecutors not to prioritize cases involving legal marijuana businesses that use banks. The details of the guidelines will be crucial for deciding whether banks feel comfortable taking deposits, giving loans, or issuing credit cards to legal marijuana businesses. The regulations are expected to apply to states that have broadly legalized marijuana, but it is unclear if they will also apply to states that have legalized it for medicinal use. The new regulations come in the wake of decisions by voters in Colorado and Washington state to legalize the sale and possession of pot, creating legal tensions since marijuana remains illegal under federal law. The move is seen as a response to the vexing challenges faced by marijuana growers and retailers in the 20 states that have legalized the drug for recreational or medical use, particularly with regards to money and banking. Banks remain leery of accepting deposits from marijuana dispensaries, fearing they could lose their charter, attract unwanted attention from regulators, or even risk prosecution for money laundering. The new regulations are expected to provide clarity on the government's stance on banking and marijuana businesses, which could help alleviate some of the concerns held by banks.

North Korea fired a short-range missile into the Sea of Japan on Sunday, following a similar launch of three short-range missiles on Saturday, according to South Korea's news agency Yonhap. The missiles were fired in a northeastern direction, away from South Korean waters. Tensions in the region had eased since last month, but North Korea's actions have raised concerns about regional security. The U.N. Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon, a former South Korean diplomat, urged North Korea to refrain from further launches and return to stalled nuclear talks with world powers. South Korea criticized the missile tests as deplorable and urged the North to lower tensions and hold talks over a suspended inter-Korean industrial park in the North's border city of Kaesong. The recent tensions flared after North Korea's long-range rocket launch in December and underground nuclear test in February, both of which were widely condemned. Pyongyang's fiery rhetoric intensified in March as the U.N. Security Council voted to tighten sanctions on the regime following the nuclear test. Annual U.S.-South Korean military drills in South Korea also fueled the North's anger. North Korea is demanding recognition as a nuclear power, something the United States refuses to accept. Last month's crisis resulted in the closure of the Kaesong Industrial Complex, the last major symbol of inter-Korean cooperation.

The Israeli government has authorized the mobilization of up to 75,000 reservists in preparation for a possible invasion of the Gaza Strip, following rocket attacks from Palestinian militants towards Jerusalem and Tel Aviv. The Israeli air offensive, which began on Wednesday, has resulted in the deaths of at least 30 Palestinians in Gaza, according to Palestinian government sources, and three Israeli civilians. Rockets have been fired from Gaza into Israel, with some landing in populated areas, causing fear and anger on both sides.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu held a strategy session with senior ministers to discuss widening the military campaign, and it was reported that the current reserve troop quota for the Gaza offensive was more than doubled to 75,000. Egypt's Prime Minister, denouncing what he described as Israeli aggression, visited Gaza and said that Egypt was prepared to mediate a truce.

The siren that sounded in Jerusalem stunned many Israelis, as the city was last struck by a Palestinian rocket in 1970. The Israeli military has reported that 97 rockets fired from Gaza have hit Israel since Friday, and 99 more were intercepted by its Iron Dome anti-missile system. Dozens of Israeli bombing raids have rocked the Gaza Strip, and one flattened the Gaza Interior Ministry building.

Tanks and self-propelled guns have been seen near the border area, and the Israeli military has already called 16,000 reservists to active duty. The Israeli government has said that it will continue to hit Hamas hard and is prepared to broaden the action inside Gaza. Hamas spokesman Sami Abu Zuhri warned that the Israelis should be aware of the grave results of a possible ground invasion.

Egypt's Prime Minister Hisham Kandil visited Gaza on a solidarity visit, and Egypt is prepared to mediate a truce. However, a three-hour truce that Israel declared for the duration of Kandil's visit never took hold. The Gaza conflagration has stoked the flames of a Middle East already ablaze with two years of Arab revolution and a civil war in Syria that threatens to leap across borders.

The Israeli military's actions in Gaza have been condemned by the Nonaligned Movement, which called it an act of aggression against the Palestinian people. The onus has been placed on Hamas to stop the rocket attacks, according to the U.S. State Department. The violence has the potential to further erode Israel's fragile relationship with Egypt, which recalled its ambassador to Israel in protest over the ongoing strikes.

The Israeli military has accused Hamas of turning Gaza into "a frontal base for Iran," and has reported that more than 600 targets have been hit for terror activity and stifled rocket launches out of Gaza. However, scores of civilian casualties have been reported, including the death of a 4-year-old boy in Gaza City. The Israeli military has denied intentionally targeting civilians, but has been accused of using disproportionate force.

The Israeli military's actions in Gaza have been met with international condemnation, with the United Nations calling for an immediate end to the violence and a return to peace talks. The Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas has also denounced the Israeli military action, saying it is an aggression against all Palestinian people. The conflict has the potential to escalate further, with both sides showing no signs of backing down.

In New Port Richey, Florida, a woman named Felicia Nevins, who was trying to conceive a child through artificial insemination, called the Pasco County Sheriff's Office for help after she feared a thermos containing sperm and dry ice might explode due to an overlooked rubber O-ring. The Sheriff's Office posted details about the incident on their Facebook page, which led to Nevins' personal information being exposed.

Nevins was upset that the post was not removed, as it contained enough details for her to be identified. The Sheriff's Office defended their action, stating that it was important to provide safety information. Nevins, however, felt that the post should have been removed due to the disclosure of her personal and medical information.

The incident gained attention on social media, with some comments being unkind and accusing Nevins of seeking attention or money. However, many also sided with her, calling for the post to be removed. Nevins has since unfollowed the Pasco County Sheriff's Office on Facebook, stating that she no longer supports an agency that she feels belittles its community.

This incident highlights the potential risks of law enforcement using social media to announce news and seek information, as it can inadvertently expose personal information. The Pasco County Sheriff's Office has gained a large following on social media but has faced controversy in the past, including accusations of crossing the line with a previous post.

In late September 2017, a cloud of radioactive pollution over Europe, specifically ruthenium-106, indicated an accident in a nuclear facility in Russia or Kazakhstan. The French nuclear safety institute, IRSN, ruled out an accident in a nuclear reactor, suggesting it was likely to be in a nuclear fuel treatment site or center for radioactive medicine. No impact on human health or the environment in Europe was reported.

Based on weather patterns, the most plausible zone for the release of radioactive material was south of the Ural mountains, between the Urals and the Volga river, potentially indicating Russia or Kazakhstan. However, Russian authorities claimed they were unaware of any accident on their territory, and IRSN had not yet been in contact with Kazakh authorities.

The IRSN estimated that the quantity of ruthenium-106 released was major, between 100 and 300 teraBecquerels. If an accident of this magnitude had happened in France, it would have required the evacuation or sheltering of people in a radius of a few kilometers around the accident site.

The ruthenium-106 was probably released in a nuclear fuel treatment site or center for radioactive medicine due to its short half-life of about a year, which is used in nuclear medicine. The IRSN also ruled out the crash of a ruthenium-powered satellite and contamination with other radionuclides in a nuclear reactor accident.

Measurements from European stations showed high levels of ruthenium-106 in the atmosphere of the majority of European countries, with a steady decrease from October 6 onwards. The concentrations of ruthenium-106 in the air that have been recorded in Europe were of no consequence for human health and the environment.

The IRSN also stated that the probability of importing foodstuffs, notably mushrooms, contaminated by ruthenium-106 near the site of the accident is extremely low.

In an update from February 6, 2018, the IRSN confirmed the presence of ruthenium-106 in the atmosphere of Europe, with the most plausible zone of release lying between the Volga and the Urals. The quantity of Ruthenium-106 released was estimated to be very important, between 100 and 300 teraBecquerels, and the release would have occurred during the last week of September 2017.

Because of the quantities released, the consequences of an accident of this magnitude in France would have required to implement locally measures of protection of the populations on a radius of the order of a few kilometers around the location of the release. For foodstuffs, the exceeding of maximum permitted levels would be observed over distances of the order of a few tens of kilometers around the location of the release. However, the probability of a scenario that would see the importation into France of foodstuffs contaminated by Ruthenium-106 near the source of the release is extremely low and the potential health risk associated with this scenario is also very low. It does not therefore appear necessary to introduce systematic controls on the contamination of imported foods.

Soylent, a popular meal replacement product, is expanding its distribution by partnering with 7-Eleven to sell its drinks at 18 stores in the greater Los Angeles area starting July 10. This marks the first time Soylent will be available for purchase in a traditional brick-and-mortar store. The company, which has raised $74.5 million from investors, is known for its nutritious, complete meal replacement drinks that are popular among millennials and the "hacker" lifestyle. The drinks, available in flavors like Cacao, Cafe Coffiest, and Cafe Chai, are designed to provide essential vitamins, minerals, fats, carbohydrates, and protein. Soylent's drinks have faced some digestive issues in the past, with recent complaints on Reddit. The companies did not comment on whether the partnership will expand beyond greater Los Angeles, but called it the "first step in Soylent’s retail distribution plan." No details were provided on pricing.

The campaign of Democratic presidential nominee Hillary Clinton released a letter from her doctor detailing her recent diagnosis of mild bacterial pneumonia and providing an overview of her overall health. The letter, written by Clinton's doctor, Lisa Bardack, notes that Clinton is currently undergoing treatment with the antibiotic Levaquin and is expected to make a full recovery. The release of the letter comes after Clinton's sudden departure from a memorial service over the weekend due to illness, and follows concerns about her medical condition. The letter also includes information about Clinton's other medications, vital statistics, and past health conditions.

In addition to releasing Clinton's health information, the campaign also released a letter from the attending physician for Congress, Brian P. Monahan, stating that Clinton's running mate, Tim Kaine, is in "overall excellent health." The letter recommends that Kaine, who is 58 years old, add a daily vitamin D supplement to his diet.

The release of Clinton's health information comes as issues surrounding health and transparency have swirled around both Clinton and her Republican rival, Donald Trump, in the past several weeks. Clinton, who will turn 69 in October, would become the second-oldest president to enter the White House (after Ronald Reagan, who also was 69), while Trump, who turned 70 in June, would be the oldest. Neither has any known major medical problems.

Clinton has previously released more extensive health information than Trump, and has also been the subject of persistent rumors and conspiracy-minded claims about her health. Although her campaign has dismissed such theories as bunk and even sexist, Clinton's sudden departure from the memorial service and the campaign's delayed release of information on her health and whereabouts have fueled these rumors.

Trump discussed his own health during a taping of "The Dr. Oz Show" on Wednesday morning. He shared some of the results of his most recent physical examination, according to the show, even though earlier top campaign aides told reporters that he would not release any records on set and planned to talk about general wellness, not his personal health history.

Overall, the release of Clinton's health information is intended to put to rest concerns about her medical condition and provide transparency about her health. However, the campaign's handling of the situation, including the delayed release of information and Clinton's decision to continue with campaign events despite her illness, has fueled rumors and criticism.

The Facebook IPO, valued at $104 billion, faced unexpected challenges when Morgan Stanley, the lead underwriter, reduced its revenue forecasts for the company just before the IPO. This sudden caution during the investor roadshow reportedly contributed to the weak performance of Facebook shares, which dropped by 18% below the IPO price.

The change in Morgan Stanley's estimates came in response to a May 9 Facebook filing expressing caution about revenue growth due to a shift to mobile devices, where mobile advertising has been less lucrative than desktop advertising. It is unclear whether Morgan Stanley informed all clients or only top clients about the revised view.

JPMorgan Chase and Goldman Sachs, also major underwriters, also revised their estimates in response to Facebook's SEC filing. Analysts at lead underwriters typically operate independently of bankers and salesmen, as stipulated in a settlement with regulators following a scandal over tainted stock research during the dot-com boom.

However, a new development suggests that a Facebook executive informed the underwriter analysts to cut their estimates, which were then verbally conveyed to sophisticated institutional investors. This selective disclosure of the estimate cut may have influenced investment decisions and affected the price at which these investors were willing to buy Facebook stock.

This latest chapter in the Facebook IPO story raises concerns about fairness to investors and potential violations of securities laws. The SEC and FINRA may now investigate the situation.

The article discusses the controversy surrounding donations made to Florida Governor Charlie Crist's campaign in 2006, which are now being returned due to questions about their legitimacy. Jihan Nassar, a California homemaker, is one of the donors listed, but she insists she never made a donation. The donations were bundled by Harry Sargeant III, a defense contractor and finance chairman of the Florida Republican Party, who is a college friend of Crist's. Sargeant has said the donations were solicited by a business partner, Mustafa Abu Naba'a.

The McCain campaign announced that it would return $50,000 in donations tied to Sargeant, after news articles in the Washington Post and the New York Times raised questions about their legitimacy. In a letter to the donors, the campaign warned that foreign nationals cannot donate money to U.S. campaigns and contributors cannot be reimbursed by another donor as a way to get around contribution limits. Some donors whose contributions are being returned by McCain's campaign were also listed as contributors to Crist on June 19, 2006.

Zouhair El Srouji, another California donor, initially told a reporter that he had no memory of a $500 donation to the Florida governor. After reviewing campaign records, however, he said he recalled that a campaign contribution was requested by his employer, though he couldn't recall who asked him to give.

The controversy over the donations comes at an awkward time for Crist, who is one of several politicians auditioning to be McCain's vice-presidential candidate. Crist called Sargeant "a great patriot" earlier in the week, but later referred questions to his former campaign manager, George LeMieux. LeMieux said he would review the donations highlighted by The Miami Herald. He said every effort was made during the campaign to verify all donations and make sure they did not exceed campaign finance limits.

The article also mentions that Sargeant is among 63 McCain fundraisers nationwide who have bundled more than $500,000 in checks each. Donations to presidential candidates are capped at $2,300, but bundlers get around the limit by collecting checks from friends, business associates, and relatives. Sargeant also donated $30,000 of his own money to a joint McCain-GOP fund in May, records show. Before turning his attention to McCain, Sargeant also raised money for presidential candidates Rudy Giuliani and Hillary Clinton.

The article also mentions that Sargeant is under scrutiny for his Defense Department contracts to ship oil to the military in Iraq, and that he has been accused of fraud by the brother-in-law of the king of Jordan, who filed a lawsuit in West Palm Beach in April. The ex-partner, Mohammad Al-Saleh, said Sargeant and Abu Naba'a failed to pay him at least $13 million. In court papers, lawyers for Sargeant and Abu Naba'a denied any wrongdoing and said the suit should be moved to Jordan.

The New York Times Book Review published an interview with Alice Walker, the author of The Color Purple, in which she recommended a book by David Icke, a British figure known for his conspiracy theories that many consider antisemitic. The book, "And the Truth Shall Set You Free," contains ideas that revolve around concepts expressed in the fraudulent antisemitic propaganda text The Protocols of the Elders of Zion. Critics have accused Walker of promoting antisemitism, as this is not the first time she has expressed her affinity for Icke's work. The Times has defended the interview, stating that the subject's answers are a reflection of their personal tastes and opinions, and that the publication does not offer background or weigh in on the books named in the By the Book column.

David Icke is a controversial figure who has long claimed that a shadowy cabal controls the world, a familiar antisemitic trope. His book, "And the Truth Shall Set You Free," contains numerous references to Jews and the Rothschild family, and draws heavily from The Protocols of the Elders of Zion. Icke has been accused of anti-Semitism and has been criticized for his claims that Jews are behind various conspiracies, including the Holocaust and the slave trade.

This is not the first time that Walker has been accused of anti-Semitism. In 2013, she praised another Icke book in an interview and has been criticized for a poem she wrote last year that was also derided as antisemitic.

The New York Times has faced criticism for publishing Walker's recommendation without qualification, with critics arguing that the publication should have reacted to or qualified the contents of the book for its readers. The Times has defended the interview, stating that it is not a list of recommendations from their editors, and that the subject's answers do not imply an endorsement by Times editors.

Reactions to the interview have been mixed, with some arguing that the Times should have been more cautious in publishing Walker's recommendation, while others have defended the publication's decision to give Walker a platform to express her views. The controversy highlights the ongoing debate about free speech and the responsibility of media outlets to vet the views of the people they interview and publish.

The owner of Novus Health Care Services, Brad Harris, is under investigation by the FBI for allegedly directing nurses to overdose hospice patients with drugs such as morphine to speed up their deaths and maximize profits. The investigation, which started in October 2014, initially focused on allegations that the company recruited patients who did not qualify for services and charged the government for services that were not medically necessary.

Harris, an accountant who founded the company in July 2012, is accused of making comments like "You need to make this patient go bye-bye" and asking health-care executives to "find patients who would die within 24 hours." He is also alleged to have sent text messages asking a nurse to administer overdoses to patients and increasing a patient's medication to four-times the maximum allowed.

No charges have been filed against Novus or Harris, who did not return messages left with a receptionist and at his Frisco home. An FBI spokeswoman declined to comment on the investigation.

Novus' website states that the company offers hospice and home health-care services, and that it encourages employees to go the extra mile to make patients feel comfortable and secure.

The investigation revealed that Harris himself decided which home health care patients would be moved to hospice, and that if a patient was on hospice care for too long, Harris would direct the patient be moved back to home health, irrespective of whether the patient needed continued hospice care.

In a lunch meeting, Harris is alleged to have asked two health care executives to "find patients who would die within 24 hours" because that would "save my ass toward the cap." He is also said to have spoken of one of his patients, saying "words to the effect of, 'If this fu**** would just die.'"

Another Novus employee told agents that in late 2013, Harris sent a text message asking the worker to "administer an overdose of medication to a hospice patient … by increasing the patient's medication dosage to approximately four times the maximum allowed." The employee did not comply with the request because it would have killed the patient, the FBI said.

One worker said Harris regularly directed nurses to "overdose hospice patients when they have been on hospice service for too long" by sending text messages like, "You need to make this patient go bye-bye," the FBI said.

The search warrant required that a data storage company that Novus had hired, Smarsh, of Portland, Ore., turn over all of Novus' emails and medical records. The company turned over the information the same day, according to court records. The warrant refers to an FBI raid of Novus' offices in September 2015 but court records related to that search could not be found and appear to be under seal.

The FBI said investigators had interviewed several Novus employees. One worker said Harris regularly directed nurses to "overdose hospice patients when they have been on hospice service for too long" by sending text messages like, "You need to make this patient go bye-bye," the FBI said.

The owner of the Frisco hospice agency, Novus Health Services, filed lawsuits against several employees and two executives who quit in the days after an FBI raid. The company is accused of telling nurses to overdose patients on morphine to speed their deaths and maximize profits. No charges have been filed against Novus or Harris, who did not return messages left with a receptionist and at his Frisco home. An FBI spokeswoman declined to comment on the investigation.

Herman Cain, a Republican presidential candidate, is facing challenges in New Hampshire, a state crucial for the primary elections. Despite being behind in the polls, Cain remains optimistic about his chances, stating that even a second place finish would be considered momentum. However, Cain's campaign has been marred by controversies, including sexual harassment allegations, a stumbling answer on Libya, and a new controversy this week when he declined a meeting with the Union Leader, New Hampshire's largest and most influential newspaper. The Union Leader's endorsement is highly sought after and is often a significant factor in the New Hampshire primary.

During a rally in Nashua, Cain addressed the controversy surrounding his lack of knowledge on foreign affairs, stating that a leader should focus on assigning the right priorities and using experts, rather than having a deep knowledge of every country and situation. The event was marked by a last-minute decision by the Cain campaign to bar C-SPAN cameras and limit the interview with the Union Leader, which was refused. The Union Leader's no-show headline has added to Cain's woes in New Hampshire.

In other news, the Manchester aldermen are considering a pilot program to make trash collection safer, cleaner, and cheaper. Additionally, there has been a polarized reaction to a story about Manchester Police Chief Nick Willard's car accident in March. Lastly, responding to calls from people asking them to put out fires is costing the Portsmouth Fire Department millions of dollars per year, leading to discussions about whether homeowners should be billed for the service.

Lorde, a 16-year-old New Zealand singer, has been named VH1's You Oughta Know artist for September. Her single "Royals" has gained international recognition, topping the Billboard Alternative charts and becoming the fastest charting alternative song since Gotye's "Somebody That I Used To Know." The inspiration for the song came from a National Geographic photo of a baseball player signing baseballs with the word "Royals" on his shirt. Lorde's fascination with aristocracy and historical royals also played a role in creating the song.

In a surprising turn of events, a San Francisco radio station, 96.5 KOIT, has banned "Royals" from its airwaves until the conclusion of the World Series. This decision was made due to numerous requests from listeners who are fans of the San Francisco Giants and believe the song supports the Kansas City Royals. The first pitch for Game One of the World Series between the Kansas City Royals and the San Francisco Giants is scheduled for October 21.

President Obama has ordered flags at the White House and other federal buildings to be flown at half-staff as a mark of respect for the five U.S. service members killed in Chattanooga last week by a gunman. The White House and U.S. Capitol lowered their flags to half-staff by Tuesday afternoon, following criticism over the delay in honoring the fallen service members. The proclamation calls for the flags to remain at half-staff through Saturday. Obama expressed his condolences and gratitude to the police officers and first responders who stopped the shooting, and emphasized that the U.S. will not be divided by such acts of violence. The decision came hours after Speaker John Boehner ordered flags at the U.S. Capitol to be flown at half-staff. Conservatives had criticized the president for not lowering the flag earlier, noting that various governors around the country had done so and that the White House had lowered its flags after other mass shootings.

In a remarkable sentencing hearing, former U.S. Representative Jesse Jackson Jr. and his wife, former Alderman Sandi Jackson, were both sentenced to prison for their involvement in a scheme to misuse campaign funds. Jesse Jackson Jr. was sentenced to 2 ½ years in prison for stealing $750,000 from his campaign fund, while Sandi Jackson was sentenced to one year for filing false tax returns.

Sandi Jackson appeared stunned by the imposition of a prison term, while Jesse Jackson Jr. appeared emotional during his remarks to the judge. The judge took the unusual step of allowing the Jacksons to stagger their sentences, with Jesse Jackson Jr. set to report around November 1.

The judge rejected the Jacksons' arguments for leniency, stating that their crimes were "knowing, organized, joint misconduct repeated and then covered up." She also criticized Sandi Jackson for spending thousands of dollars illegally on personal expenses and noted that she had served as campaign treasurer, campaign manager, and consultant for her husband.

The Jacksons' sentences were lighter than prosecutors had recommended, but they were still significant. The judge's remarks came after emotional pleas from both Jacksons, with Jesse Jackson Jr. expressing remorse for his actions and Sandi Jackson asking for mercy for the sake of their children.

The sentencing marks a dramatic fall from grace for the son of the famed civil rights leader, the Rev. Jesse Jackson. Despite the sentencing, both Jackson Jr. and his father expressed hope for redemption. The Jacksons had hired a public relations consultant and crisis counselor to help them navigate the public fallout from the sentencing.

The sentencing of the Jacksons is particularly notable because it involves a powerful couple who together saw their political demise in the same courtroom. It is a reminder that even those in positions of power and influence are not immune from the consequences of their actions.

A rat infestation in a government office in Kissimmee, Florida, contaminated supplies that were intended for hurricane victims in Puerto Rico. The Puerto Rico Federal Affairs Administration (PRFAA) had collected the donated items, including water, food, and other supplies, from local organizations and private individuals following Hurricane Maria in 2017. However, the office was infested with rodents since August, a month before the hurricane, and the supplies were stored there despite this knowledge.

PRFAA's executive director, Carlos Mercader, stated that the agency could not afford to ship the supplies due to insufficient funding. Previous attempts to send the supplies through other organizations had been unsuccessful. Mercader also mentioned that the office in Kissimmee was in such a deteriorated state that the agency had decided to move to a new building.

The spoiled food comes amidst a series of administrative failings regarding aid sent to Puerto Rico. U.S. Representative Elijah Cummings and Stacey Plaskett, the congressional delegate from the U.S. Virgin Islands, have called for the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) to be subpoenaed over its failure to provide tens of millions to Puerto Rico.

In a separate incident, FEMA awarded a $156 million contract to a small Atlanta-based company, Tribute Contracting LLC, to deliver 30 million emergency meals to Puerto Rico. However, the company only delivered 50,000 meals, and the owner, Tiffany Brown, plans to sue the government for $70 million, citing being overwhelmed by the order.

The reports of the spoiled food and administrative failures have been met with criticism, with Juan Hernandez Mayoral, who ran the Kissimmee headquarters from 2013 to 2014, calling it "government negligence." Thousands of Puerto Ricans have relocated to Florida after Hurricane Maria, many of whom are expected to stay in Central Florida.

The newly-released deposition footage reveals that Ethan Couch, the Texas teen who was involved in a fatal DUI crash in 2013 and was sentenced to probation and rehab, lived a privileged life with no consequences before the accident. The document discusses the controversy surrounding Memories Pizza, a small-town pizzeria in Walkerton, Indiana. Amazon is expanding its delivery services with the launch of a new business called "Shipping with Amazon," which will compete directly with established delivery companies like FedEx and UPS. The service, set to debut in Los Angeles in the coming weeks, will involve Amazon picking up packages from businesses and delivering them to customers. This move is expected to be rolled out to other cities and businesses, with Amazon aiming to undercut UPS and FedEx on pricing. The announcement has caused a significant drop in the shares of both companies in pre-market trade on Friday morning. However, UPS has stated that it continues to support Amazon and remains a partner of the e-commerce giant. The full details of this development can be found in an article by Karan Deep Singh for the Wall Street Journal.

The studies published in the journal Pediatrics have linked the chemicals bisphenol A (BPA) and phthalates, found in processed foods and cosmetics, to obesity and insulin resistance in adolescents. The research found that teens with higher levels of DEHP, a phthalate, in their urine had increased rates of insulin resistance, which can lead to Type 2 diabetes. However, the studies do not prove a cause-and-effect relationship, and it is possible that insulin-resistant teens tended to eat food with higher phthalate content or excreted more DEHP in their urine compared to healthy children.

Another study found that children with the highest amounts of BPA in their urine had double the risk of being obese, compared with children with the lowest urinary BPA levels. The researchers cautioned against interpreting the results too strongly, as BPA is found in higher concentrations in fat tissue and it is possible that people with more body fat store more BPA and excrete more in urine.

Both BPA and phthalates have been the focus of intense research in recent years due to concerns over their potential to act like hormones in people who are exposed to them through food packaging. However, studies have been inconclusive, and scientists have not reached a consensus on the chemicals' effects on human health. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has maintained that current levels of adults' exposure to BPA is low and safe, but the chemical is more highly regulated in several countries as precautionary measures.

To avoid phthalate exposure, the researchers suggest avoiding unnecessary personal care products and opting for fresh foods instead of canned or plastic-wrapped foods. Certain kinds of packaging, like wax paper and aluminum wrap, don't contain DEHP. The studies add to the ongoing debate about the potential health effects of BPA and phthalates, and more research is needed to fully understand their impact on human health.

The Commerce Department has released a revised GDP report, indicating that the U.S. economy grew at a slower pace than previously estimated in both the first and second quarters of 2011. The second-quarter growth was revised down to 1.3% from an expected 1.8%, marking the weakest pace since the end of the 2007-2009 recession. The first-quarter growth was revised down sharply to 0.4% from the earlier estimate of 1.9%. Higher gas prices and reduced consumer spending were cited as culprits for the slower pace of growth. The revised GDP figures show that the 2007-2009 recession was even worse than previously thought, with the U.S. economy shrinking 5.1% during that period, 1 percentage point worse than the previous estimate. The government attributed the bigger declines in output in part to weaker consumer spending and business investment than previously estimated. The revisions showed that growth in 2010 was a bit stronger than previously estimated, with growth for all of 2010 at 3%, up from a previous estimate that the economy grew 2.9% last year. The unemployment rate remains elevated at 9.2%.

A prank April Fool's joke involving a false report of a shooting at Virginia College in Spartanburg, South Carolina, led to a full-scale response from law enforcement on Tuesday morning. Angela Timmons, an employee at the college, sent a text message to her daughter about hearing gunshots, which prompted her daughter to call 911. The ensuing 911 call brought out multiple patrol cars and deputies from the Spartanburg County Sheriff's Office, who responded at "breakneck speed" due to fears of another mass shooting like Columbine. However, it was soon determined that the report was a joke, and Timmons' daughter received a follow-up text from her mother confirming it was an April Fool's prank.

Diane Worthington, vice president of marketing for Virginia College, expressed disappointment over the poor judgment displayed by Timmons and apologized to the Spartanburg County Sheriff's Office, first responders, students, and staff. Worthington would not comment on Timmons' current employment status.

Timmons has stated that the prank was a simple joke between her and her daughters, something they do every April Fool's Day. However, she acknowledged that given today's times, it was a poor choice and expressed her apologies to her coworkers at Virginia College who were impacted by the incident. Timmons also mentioned that attorneys have been showing up at her home and she does have plans to hire one.

The incident has caused controversy and concern, with Wright stating that the joke was not funny and was not fair to the college, as the employee's actions do not reflect the institution.

In a series of tweets on July 16, 2018, President Donald Trump criticized Attorney General Jeff Sessions for bringing charges against two Republican Congressmen, Duncan Hunter of California and Chris Collins of New York, just before the midterm elections. Allies have advised Trump that firing Sessions before the November midterm elections would be damaging to the party, but some have indicated that Trump may make a change after the elections.

On Tuesday, a civilian working for Israel's Defense Ministry, Salah Shukri Abu Latyef, was shot and killed by a Palestinian sniper while working on the Gaza border fence. The incident occurred near the border, and the Palestinian militant group Popular Resistance Committees claimed responsibility. This marks the first Israeli civilian death near the Gaza Strip since last year's "Pillar of Defense" operation.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu characterized the attack as "very grave" and vowed a strong response. The attack, along with other recent incidents like a foiled bus bomb in Bat Yam, rocket fire from Gaza, and the knifing of a Border Patrolman outside of Jerusalem, have been viewed as serious breaches of the understandings that ended Operation Pillar of Defense.

Defense Minister Moshe Ya'alon advised Hamas not to test Israel's patience and urged Gaza's ruling regime to prevent further attacks. He also ordered the closing of the Kerem Shalom border crossing following the escalation on the Gaza border.

In a separate incident, a Palestinian youth approached the fence on the border with northern Gaza and was shot in the leg by Israeli soldiers after ignoring calls to vacate the area.

The events have raised concerns about the security situation along the Gaza border and the possibility of further escalation.

The Costa Concordia cruise liner captain, Francesco Schettino, has apologized for the accident that resulted in the death of at least 32 people, stating that he was distracted at the time of the incident. In his first full television interview since the accident on January 13, Schettino acknowledged his responsibility as captain and expressed remorse for the disaster. He was speaking after being freed from house arrest last week.

Schettino admitted to failing to act decisively once it became clear the 144,500-tonne vessel had come too close to the island of Giglio off the Tuscan coast where it ran aground. He insisted that the actual sailing of the ship was under the command of another officer at the time.

Investigators have severely criticized Schettino's handling of the disaster, accusing him of bringing the 290-meter-long vessel too close to shore, delaying evacuation, and losing control of the operation during which he abandoned ship before all the 4,200 passengers and crew had left the ship.

Schettino, who has been held up to abuse and ridicule following the accident, has always acknowledged making mistakes but has said he is not the only one who should be blamed for the tragedy. A pre-trial hearing was held in March, and investigations also target several other officers and officials of the ships owner, Costa Cruises, a unit of the world's largest cruise operator, Carnival Corp.

During the interview, Schettino broke down when asked about the youngest victim of the disaster. In a letter published recently in Italy's La Corriere della Sera newspaper, Mr. Schettino argued that he had saved many lives by steering the stricken vessel into shallow water. A phone call recorded during the rescue operation showed a local port authority chief chastising the captain and telling him to get back on board the ship to help stranded passengers. Mr. Schettino was arrested shortly afterwards.

The Internet Archive is working on a project to preserve web pages and their references, aiming to fix broken links on the internet. The project involves crawling supported websites and archiving pages as they are created. German authorities have recovered over 100 items belonging to the late Beatles star John Lennon that were stolen from his widow, Yoko Ono, in 2006. The items, which include three diaries, two pairs of Lennon's signature round glasses, a cigarette case, and a handwritten music score, were displayed at Berlin police headquarters on Tuesday.

The arrest of a 58-year-old German businessman of Turkish origin and another suspect who lives in Turkey was made after police searched the suspect's home and cars in Berlin. The second suspect, who is believed to be Lennon's former driver, is currently unattainable for the German authorities.

The items were confiscated from an auction house in Berlin in July, leading to an investigation to find the rest of the stolen items. Ono identified the objects from photos she was shown at the German consulate in New York.

Memorabilia connected to the Beatles can fetch huge prices at auction. In February, a leather jacket believed to have been worn by Lennon sold for £10,400 at an auction in England. In September, an original score for The Beatles' song Eleanor Rigby was removed from another auction in England amid claims it had been stolen.

The handwritten score, signed by Paul McCartney, was due to be sold with a guide price of £20,000. The recovered items are still being checked for further details on how they ended up at the auction house in Berlin and if the auctioneers were aware that they bought stolen goods from the two suspects.

The last entry in one of the diaries was made by Lennon on the morning of Dec. 8, 1980, a few hours before he was killed. It included a note on the famous photo shoot by Annie Leibovitz that same day showing a naked Lennon embracing his wife. It is not yet clear when Ono will get all the items back.

North Korea conducted an unidentified projectile launch from Pyongyang on Tuesday, August 29, 2017, which flew over Japan's northern island of Hokkaido and landed in the Pacific Ocean. The South Korean and U.S. militaries are analyzing the launch, but no damage was reported. This test-flight is considered especially aggressive, escalating tensions in the region.

The launch follows North Korea's firing of three short-range ballistic missiles into the sea earlier in August and a month after its second intercontinental ballistic missile (ICBM) test, which analysts believe could reach deep into the U.S. mainland when perfected.

North Korea's actions are often a response to U.S.-South Korean military drills, which are currently ongoing. Tensions are higher than usual due to threats by U.S. President Donald Trump to use "fire and fury" on North Korea, and Pyongyang's stated plan to consider firing missiles towards Guam.

North Korea views the U.S.-South Korean military exercises as an invasion rehearsal, while the allies claim they are defensive and intended to counter North Korean aggression. North Korea's U.N. ambassador, Ja Song Nam, recently described the exercises as "provocative and aggressive" in a letter, likening the Korean peninsula to a "time bomb."

This latest launch further intensifies the ongoing standoff between North Korea and its neighbors, particularly the U.S. and South Korea. The international community continues to monitor the situation closely.

The agreement on a DNA database expansion in New York is progressing as part of a series of legislative deals, including the state budget, new political districts, and a new pension plan. Skelos has expressed support for access provisions, provided they are implemented carefully.

The situation in Virginia highlights the need for transparency and accountability in the criminal justice system, particularly when it comes to DNA testing and the notification of exonerated individuals. The case of Bennett Barbour serves as a reminder of the potential for wrongful convictions and the importance of ensuring fairness and justice for all parties involved.

Scarlett Johansson and Ryan Reynolds were spotted having a friendly dinner at Blue Ribbon restaurant in New York City, sparking rumors of a possible reconciliation. The Gravity Blanket, a high-tech weighted blanket designed to reduce stress and anxiety, has raised over $3 million on Kickstarter. The blanket uses deep pressure touch stimulation therapy, simulating the sensation of being hugged, to target pressure points on the body linked to improved sleep, mood, and relaxation. It is made with high density plastic poly pellets and comes in three weight sizes: 15 lbs, 20 lbs, and 25 lbs, which should be between seven and 12 percent of the user’s weight. The duvet has a soft fleece cover and a cotton inner shell, making it durable, washable, and breathable.

The creators of Gravity claim that the blanket can be used to treat a variety of ailments, including insomnia, post-traumatic stress disorder, obsessive-compulsive disorder, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, as well as circumstantial stress and prolonged anxiety. However, the science behind these claims is scarce, and the blanket's creators have recently deleted the bold medical claims on their Kickstarter page after being questioned about their promotional statements.

Previous research has suggested that weighted blankets could have positive effects on sleep, with studies showing that they can provide a beneficial calming effect and aid in reducing insomnia. A study in 2015 published in the Journal of Sleep Medicine and Disorders reported that weighted blankets and vests can provide a beneficial calming effect, especially in clinical disorders.

Gravity is expected to be available for delivery this autumn in September and October, priced from $169. Other quirky blankets available for travellers include duvet suits, extra-padded pyjamas with a detachable hood and double up as a pillow, and the Slanket, a 60" x 95" fleece blanket with sleeves that lets you disappear under a warm cover without sacrificing the mobility of your arms.

However, the evidence behind the blanket’s claims is scarce, and it's not clear who, exactly, the blanket would benefit. Many cases of sleeplessness result from poor sleep hygiene, and underlying psychiatric disorders require treatment. Dr. Khalid Ismail, a sleep medicine researcher at Tufts Medical Center in Boston, said, "It's not a miracle therapy. I don't think it's ready for prime time yet."

Regardless of how it's promoted, the blanket's creators have recently deleted the bold medical claims on their Kickstarter page after being questioned about their promotional statements, which violated Kickstarter policy and went against FDA recommendations. The blanket's creators haven't posted an update about the changes for their buyers.

The article discusses the disappearance of a Texas couple, Forrest Sanco and Donna Grant, who went missing while on a honeymoon trip to the Bahamas. The study published in Circulation Research, an American Heart Association journal, reveals that long-term use of proton pump inhibitors (PPIs), a commonly used heartburn medication, may cause blood vessel cells to age faster in laboratory testing. This finding could potentially explain the link between long-term use of these drugs and several serious illnesses, including heart disease, kidney disease, and dementia.

The research indicates that PPIs, which are used to reduce acid production by the stomach, accelerate biological aging in human endothelial cells, the cells that line the inside of blood vessels. This aging process causes the endothelium to become more like Velcro, with blood elements sticking to the vessel to form blockages. The study also found that long-term PPI exposure impairs acid production by the lysosomes in the cells lining the blood vessel walls, leading to the buildup of waste and rapid cell aging.

Although PPIs can be effective for short-term use, they are not meant for extended treatment. The study suggests that the pharmaceutical industry and regulatory agencies may need to re-visit the specificity and safety of these agents due to their widespread use. The researchers emphasize that there are other approaches to long-term treatment for GERD, including H2 antagonists, lifestyle modifications, and in severe cases, surgical approaches.

The study has several limitations, including the fact that only one commercially available PPI, esomeprazole (brand name Nexium), was tested. Additionally, it did not show how PPIs actually impair the lysosome’s ability to produce enough acid to clear waste, and since the study was in a laboratory setting, long-term clinical trials are necessary to confirm the findings within the human body.

Harvard University has made history by appointing Evelynn Hammonds as the first black female dean of Harvard College. Hammonds, currently the senior vice provost for faculty development and diversity at Harvard, will take over from Acting Dean David Pilbeam on June 1. Her appointment comes after a year in which Harvard also appointed its first female president, Drew Gilpin Faust.

Hammonds' appointment is significant as she will be the first black and first female to hold the position of dean of the college. Yale, on the other hand, has never had a black or female dean of Yale College. Yale has recently reaffirmed its commitment to encouraging diversity in its top administrative ranks, particularly racial diversity.

Hammonds' role will involve overseeing matters ranging from academic affairs to student life to the general administration of Harvard College, the oldest undergraduate school in the United States. She came to Harvard in 2002 from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, where she served as founding director of the Center for the Study of Diversity in Science, Technology and Medicine.

The appointment marks the second milestone for the university in breaking down gender barriers; Harvard, America’s oldest university, went 371 years before appointing Faust, its first female president, last year. Faust was the permanent successor to former Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers, who was all but driven out of Cambridge in 2006 following a controversial comment he made about the relative aptitude of women in the sciences compared to their male counterparts.

However, Hammonds' tenure as dean has been marred by controversy. In March, it was reported that Harvard administrators searched the email accounts of 16 resident deans because of concerns about leaks that might have threatened the privacy and due process of students facing discipline in a cheating case. Hammonds announced her decision to step down on July 1, five years and one month after she became both the first African-American and first female to occupy the highest office in Harvard's undergraduate school. She will take a sabbatical before returning as head of a new program for the study of race and gender in science and medicine.

A group of fifteen former staff members from the Church Committee, a bipartisan intelligence watchdog committee active during the Watergate era, have urged President Barack Obama to negotiate a plea agreement with Edward Snowden, the NSA whistleblower who leaked classified documents. The former staff members argue that Snowden's disclosures led to public awareness and stimulated reform, and that leniency should be shown given past examples of leniency towards officials who have violated secrecy laws. The group includes Frederick Schwarz Jr., the Church Committee's chief counsel, and William Green Miller, the committee's staff director. The former staff members argue that Snowden's actions were more selfless than those of other officials who have been shown leniency, and that this should be taken into account. The group also notes that the government has been lenient towards senior national security officials who have divulged secrets, such as former CIA Director David Petraeus, who provided classified information to his biographer and pled guilty to a simple misdemeanor. The group does not advocate for a pardon, but instead urges the government to negotiate a settlement with Snowden that both sides can accept. The group argues that the public benefits of Snowden's leaks and his aim to help America should be taken into account in any settlement discussions. The group also challenges several assertions made by the House Intelligence Committee in its investigation into Snowden's motivations and actions. The former staff members note that the current political climate may stifle further reform, given the incoming administration and President-elect Donald Trump's known volatility. However, they remain hopeful that reform can still be achieved through watchful vigilance.

The Atlanta Journal-Constitution has published a new investigation revealing that 450 cases of doctors accused of sexual misconduct or sex crimes in 2016 and 2017 are still licensed to practice medicine. In nearly half of these cases, the doctors remain in practice, regardless of whether the victims were patients, employees, adults, or children. The investigation found that even some doctors who have been criminally convicted are back in practice, demonstrating that a system that forgives doctors has not changed.

The Associated Press also conducted an investigation, finding that even as Hollywood moguls, elite journalists, and politicians have been pushed out of their jobs or resigned amid allegations of sexual misconduct, the medical field is often more forgiving. When doctors are disciplined, the punishment often consists of a short suspension paired with mandatory therapy that treats sexually abusive behavior as a symptom of an illness or addiction.

The investigation by the Atlanta Journal-Constitution exposed the leniency of the physician disciplinary system in 2016, but little change has been made in the practices of state medical boards. The #MeToo campaign and the push for increased accountability for sexual misconduct in American workplaces have not sparked a movement toward changing how medical boards deal with physicians who act out sexually against patients or staffers.

The sentencing of Larry Nassar, a former doctor for the U.S. Olympic gymnastics program convicted of abusing more than 150 women and girls, has put a high-profile case of physician misconduct in the spotlight. However, most doctors accused of sexual misconduct avoid a medical license review entirely. A study last year found that two-thirds of doctors who were sanctioned by their employers or paid a settlement as the result of sex misconduct claims never faced medical board discipline.

Azza Abbudagga, a health services researcher with nonprofit advocacy organization Public Citizen, published a report detailing sexual misconduct among physicians. The report showed that of the 253 doctors reported to the National Practitioner Data Bank for having been sanctioned by their respective hospitals or health care organizations for sexual misconduct, or paid a settlement that stemmed from such an allegation, 170 of them were not disciplined by state medical boards, even though all boards have access to the reports filed with the data bank.

The current guidelines from the Federation of State Physician Health Programs, which represents doctor rehab programs in 47 states, are largely silent on handling sexual misconduct treatment and describe sexual harassment as a "cause of impairment" in a doctor. Programs to treat doctor impairment are inherently supposed to be "nondisciplinary," per the federation's guidelines.

Linda Bresnahan, who heads the federation, said its guidelines are being rewritten and, despite their language, should not be applied to sexual misbehavior. A statement provided by the federation says only about half of doctor rehab programs nationwide accept doctors accused of sexual misconduct, a choice the group considers to be "a local issue beyond the purview of national guidance."

The harm committed by sexually abusive doctors is aggravated by the personal nature of the doctor-patient relationship. When Marissa White came to Dr. Gunwant Dhaliwal in 2007 for neck pain after a car accident, he reached under her shirt and into her bra, grabbing her breasts. A jury convicted him of misdemeanor battery in the case, and Florida's medical board concluded that his crime demonstrated his "lack of good moral character" and "lack of worthiness" to practice medicine. However, despite that finding and at least six other similar allegations made by women patients and employees, Dhaliwal can still be found practicing at his Tampa-area urgent care clinics.

"I had to sit there in front of him, look him in the eye, they made their guilty verdict and that's it, nothing came of it," White told the AP of her experience at trial. She still lives in Florida, but won't even go to the neighborhood where Dhaliwal practices medicine. "He should have lost his license a long time ago. He should have lost it the first time it happened."

But his office manager told the AP that, while the Florida board referred him to the state's impaired physician network for evaluation, nothing came of it. "They did an evaluation and did not find anything wrong," the woman told the AP. "They don't do any treatment."

Examples of problematic behavior are easy to find in states across the country. In Arkansas, Dr. Robert Rook was allowed to keep his family practice open, so long as he's chaperoned, despite facing multiple criminal charges for rape. Prosecutors subsequently downgraded the charges to more than 20 counts of sexual assault in the second- and third-degree, charges for which Rook says he is innocent.

Rook did not return phone messages left with a secretary at his Conway office. He is set to face trial later this year. The Idaho State Board of Medicine in May reinstated the license of Richard Pines, a child and adolescent psychiatrist who lost his license in 2013 after the board accused him of having sexual relationships with four former patients, including taking nude photos of a 14-year-old and convincing the boys that he needed to practice giving naked massages to keep his medical license.

The state's highest court in 2015 ruled that Pines had engaged in sexual misconduct, but determined that two of the four alleged victims were not former patients. The court remanded Pines' case to a lower court and vacated his punishment, instead ordering the board to re-evaluate the scope of disciplinary action based on the charges the court upheld. The court's order also blasted the board for being impartial, accusing its members of "passionately railing" against Pines in its decision.

The AP reached out to Pines' former employers and contacted his most recent attorneys, but was unable to reach him. The AP also left a message for a biller at Sage Health Care, where Pines still processes invoices. The receptionist said Pines bills through the office but was unable to provide more details about his current practice.

State-authorized programs that attempt to oversee the rehabilitation of doctors who have committed sexual misconduct aren't always forthcoming about their methods. In Florida, the Professional's Resource Network, which the state medical board assigned to evaluate Gunwant Dhaliwal after his battery conviction, asked the AP to provide detailed questions and a list of sources before it would answer questions.
