The article discusses the selection of Pope Francis as TIME's Person of the Year for 2013. Pope Francis, born Jorge Mario Bergoglio, is the first Latin American and the first Jesuit Pope. In his short time in office, he has made a significant impact on the world stage, addressing issues of wealth and poverty, fairness and justice, transparency, modernity, globalization, the role of women, the nature of marriage, and the temptations of power.

Francis has challenged the world with his humility and compassion, embracing complexity and acknowledging the risks of a church obsessed with its own rights and righteousness. He has been praised for his focus on compassion, merriment, and his commitment to tending to the wounded rather than waging a culture war. However, he has faced criticism for not addressing issues such as the priest sex-abuse scandal and the sanctity of life.

The article also discusses Edward Snowden, who was awarded the Sam Adams Associates for Integrity in Intelligence award in Moscow. Snowden is a former CIA employee and NSA contractor who leaked classified information about the U.S. government's surveillance programs to the media. He is currently living in Russia, where he has been granted asylum.

The article also touches on the situation in Syria, where President Bashar al-Assad has been accused of brutal tactics in his efforts to maintain power. The article discusses Assad's rise to power and his recent use of chemical weapons, which led to international condemnation and a diplomatic crisis.

Finally, the article discusses the case of Edith Windsor, an 84-year-old woman who sued the U.S. government for a refund of estate taxes she had to pay when her spouse died. Windsor's case led to a landmark Supreme Court decision that declared the Defense of Marriage Act (DOMA) unconstitutional, making same-sex marriage legal in the United States.

Overall, the article discusses significant events and figures of 2013, including the selection of Pope Francis as TIME's Person of the Year, the situation in Syria, the case of Edward Snowden, and the legalization of same-sex marriage in the United States.

Lena Dunham, the actress and creator of the HBO series Girls, expressed her gratitude to Glamour magazine for not Photoshopping her cellulite on their February 2017 cover. In her Instagram post, Dunham shared her struggles with body image and self-confidence throughout her teenage years, and how she felt that the culture was telling her to hate her body. She also noted that throughout her career, people have celebrated her look but always through the lens of 'isn't she brave? Isn't it such a bold move to show THAT body on TV?'

Dunham went on to thank Glamour for letting her be real and for normalizing the female form in all forms. She concluded by stating that no one's body is fair game, regardless of size, color, gender identity, and that there's a place for everyone in popular culture to be recognized as beautiful.

On the cover, Dunham is seen with her Girls costars Jemima Kirke, Zosia Mamet, and Allison Williams in purple metallic booty shorts and platform heels. In their tell-all interview, which hits newsstands on January 10, Dunham revealed that as Girls’ creator and showrunner, she sometimes felt left out of the group on set.

The final season of Girls premieres on HBO on Sunday, February 12, at 10 p.m. ET. The show has been committed to portraying life as it is, with characters that look like people, dim and cramped apartments, relatable panic about work, money, and love, awkward sex, and bathroom scenes. The show has been controversial due to its nudity, homosexuality, and a character who is "super chill" about getting an abortion.

Girls has permeated our culture and has been a force, with conservative critics raging against it almost immediately. The show has inspired other shows like Broad City, Love, and Better Things, and Lena Dunham and Girls executive producer Jenni Konner have made it their mission to deepen the bench of women storytellers by founding a newsletter, Lenny Letter, and a production company, A Casual Romance Productions. The four women of Girls have further immersed themselves in politics, advocating for causes such as Planned Parenthood, reproductive rights, and sexual-assault survivors.

A group of truck drivers, known as "Truckers for the Constitution," are planning to protest the federal government by backing up the Capital Beltway around Washington, D.C. The protest is aimed at calling attention to their frustration with regulations from the Obama administration, high fuel costs, and overall political climate in the U.S. The truck drivers are also unhappy with reports of government spying on American citizens and the country's debt. The group is framing their protest as a necessity to get the attention of lawmakers and is appealing to the patriotism of American truckers. The truck drivers are planning to circle the beltway "three lanes deep" and are asking for the arrest of congressmen for allegedly disregarding the Constitution. However, it's almost certain that anyone attempting to "arrest" a member of Congress would be arrested themselves for attempted kidnapping. The truckers are also complaining about environmental regulations, high cost of diesel fuel, and perceived deterioration of Fourth Amendment rights. The protest is scheduled to take place on October 11, 2013.

The Syrian Centre for Policy Research (SCPR) has released a new report stating that the conflict in Syria has caused 470,000 deaths, nearly double the UN's previous estimate of 250,000. The report also highlights the devastating impact of the conflict on Syria's infrastructure, economy, and population.

The SCPR estimates that 11.5% of the country's population have been killed or injured since the crisis began in 2011. Life expectancy has dropped from 70 in 2010 to 55.4 in 2015, and overall economic losses are estimated at $255bn. The report also notes that the rest of the world has been slow to respond to the crisis, with global attention only intensifying when it had a direct impact on developed countries.

The report comes as warnings multiply about the situation in Aleppo, Syria's largest city, which is in danger of being cut off by a government advance aided by Russian airstrikes and Iranian militiamen. The Syrian opposition is demanding urgent action to relieve the suffering of tens of thousands of civilians. The International Red Cross has reported that 50,000 people have fled the upsurge in fighting in the north, requiring urgent deliveries of food and water.

Talks between US Secretary of State John Kerry and Russian counterpart Sergei Lavrov in Munich are closely watched for any sign of an end to the deadly impasse. UN-brokered peace talks in Geneva are scheduled to resume in two weeks, but are unlikely to do so without a significant shift of policy.

The SCPR was based in Damascus until recently and carried out research across Syria. It is careful not to criticize the Syrian government or its allies, but the findings are shocking. The report notes that the rest of the world has been slow to wake up to the dimensions of the crisis. "Despite the fact that Syrians have been suffering for five years, global attention to human rights and dignity for them only intensified when the crisis had a direct impact on the societies of developed countries."

The report also notes that the conflict "continues to destroy the social and economic fabric of the country with the intensification of international interventions that deepen polarization among Syrians. Human development, rights, and dignity have been comprehensively ruined." The report is entitled Confronting Fragmentation and is the latest in a series tracking the unfolding of the world's biggest humanitarian disaster.

The study published in the journal Pediatrics suggests that the use of e-cigarettes among teenagers in California has increased significantly since 2004, and the combined rate of e-cigarette or cigarette use in 2014 exceeded the rate of cigarette use in 2004. The study followed 5,490 high school seniors who graduated between 1995 and 2014, and the data suggest that rather than prompting teenagers to replace cigarette smoking with vaping, e-cigarettes have enticed an entirely new group of teenagers to use nicotine. The researchers say the numbers are consistent with national trends.

The study found that the combined adjusted prevalence of current cigarette or e-cigarette use in 2014 was 13.7%, which was substantially greater than the 9.0% adjusted prevalence of current cigarette use in 2004. The researchers say this suggests that e-cigarettes are not merely substituting for cigarettes and indicates that e-cigarette use is occurring in adolescents who would not otherwise have used tobacco products.

The study also found that the amount of nicotine in the liquids used with e-cigarettes varies, and users can purchase liquid with no nicotine or nicotine content ranging from 3 milligrams per milliliter to 18 milligrams per milliliter or even higher. While earlier studies have suggested that some teens are using nicotine-free vaping liquids, researchers say the majority of teens appear to be using nicotine-infused liquid in their e-cigarettes.

The researchers say that while e-cigarettes do appear to be safer than smoking tobacco, they are not risk-free. Nicotine disrupts neurotransmitter activity and is highly addictive, particularly in a developing brain. And the liquids contain solvents, formaldehyde, and other ingredients that pose health risks when inhaled.

The study also notes that the e-cigarette industry is not regulated, which makes it hard to know what ingredients are actually in any given product. Though the Food and Drug Administration recently took jurisdiction over e-cigarettes, it will be years before any regulations are put into effect. Currently, many products continue to be made in China with little, if any, oversight by the United States.

The study's lead author, Jessica Barrington-Trimis, said, "Kids are not just using e-cigarettes instead of cigarettes. That is what we were frankly hoping to find. All of the teenagers that were expected to be using cigarettes in 2014 are using them, and then there is a whole group of kids using e-cigarettes on top of that."

The study's findings have implications for tobacco control efforts, as they suggest that e-cigarettes may be recruiting a new group of kids to tobacco use who would not likely have initiated combustible tobacco product use in the absence of e-cigarettes. The researchers say that strong tobacco control interventions are needed to prevent the rise in e-cigarette use among youth and the potential for increased nicotine addiction.

A Blue Angels F/A-18 fighter jet crashed near Nashville, Tennessee on Thursday, killing the pilot, Marine Capt. Jeff Kuss. The crash occurred during an afternoon practice session, and no civilians on the ground were injured. The pilot was a native of Durango, Colorado, and had previously served in Afghanistan before joining the Blue Angels in 2014. This is the second fighter jet crash of the day for the military's elite fighter jet performance teams, as a member of the U.S. Air Force Thunderbirds crashed in Colorado following a flyover for the Air Force Academy graduation.

In Smyrna, Tennessee, a retired teacher named Brenda Lewis and her 21-year-old grandson spent much of the day watching the Blue Angels fly overhead. They heard a loud boom and saw smoke rising and police cars arriving, and Lewis was left heartbroken by the tragic incident. A manager at Auto Masters of Smyrna, Phil Dennis, was also watching the planes practice when he saw one plane coming out of a loop and flying too fast toward the ground. He watched as the plane disappeared behind a tree line and heard silence, and a massive fireball erupted from behind the trees.

Meanwhile, in Texas, three soldiers were killed and six were missing after an Army truck was washed from a low-water crossing and overturned in a rain-swollen creek at Fort Hood. The accident happened on Thursday, and Army aircraft, canine search teams, swift-water rescue watercraft, and heavy trucks were being used in the search for the six missing soldiers. Parts of Texas have been inundated with rain in the last week, and more storms are on the way that could dump up to 10 inches of rain from Thursday through Saturday and worsen flooding caused by rivers and other waterways that already have risen to record levels.

About half of Texas is under flood watches or warnings, including Fort Bend County, southwest of Houston, where about 1,400 homes have been affected by the Brazos River, swollen by heavy rainfall from last week. A storm system that moved through the Houston-area Wednesday night and Thursday morning dumped nearly 8 inches of rain in some of the city's northern suburbs, causing flooding in some neighborhoods. The river reached 54.8 feet in Fort Bend County — 4 feet higher than the record set in 1994 — with water spilling into neighborhoods that hadn't previously flooded. Officials say levels in the Brazos have not dropped much and additional rainfall could make the flooding worse.

In a series of events, CNN White House correspondent Jim Acosta found himself in a controversy after a direct message he sent to a GOP consultant and former aide to First Lady Melania Trump, Justin Caporale, was made public. The incident began when Acosta criticized the loud music at a Trump campaign rally, which he found difficult to work around during live TV. Caporale responded with a mocking tweet, which Acosta apparently found offensive, leading him to send a blunt two-word message before blocking Caporale. The message was later confirmed by Daily Caller reporter Peter Hasson, who had access to Caporale's Twitter account.

Acosta later apologized, stating that he had mistaken Caporale for an old friend from the campaign days. The incident has been widely mocked by conservatives, with some comparing it to a scene from a sitcom. This is not the first time Acosta has been a subject of controversy, as he is often a target for Trump-die hards and has had frequent jousts with the president and his press secretary, Sarah Sanders, during press events.

At the Trump campaign rally in Missoula, Montana, Acosta had earlier criticized the loud music, stating that it made it nearly impossible to do live TV and raised concerns about security for the Secret Service and local law enforcement, as they were unable to hear. This incident adds to the ongoing tension between the media and the Trump administration.

Dennis Rodman, the former NBA player, was arrested for driving under the influence (DUI) in Newport Beach, California on Saturday. According to TMZ, Rodman was pulled over for a traffic violation, and during a field sobriety test, he failed. He was subsequently handcuffed, put in a patrol car, and taken to the police station. Rodman reportedly blew over the legal limit in a breathalyzer test and remained in jail for seven hours. After being determined to be sober enough to care for himself, he was released. This is not Rodman's first DUI offense, as he was previously busted for DUI in 1999.

In a separate news, Dennis Rodman recently criticized President Donald Trump for his frequent Twitter tirades against North Korean leader Kim Jong-un. Rodman stated that he has not spoken with Trump in a while and expressed his desire for Trump to ask him about Kim. Rodman questioned Trump's lack of personal interaction with Kim, stating that he has never met him and has not talked with his people. He also questioned Trump's characterization of Kim as "crazy," asking what Kim has done to Trump personally.

Rodman's representative told TMZ that alcoholism has been a struggle for Rodman for the past 15 years, and they plan to discuss with him the possibility of returning to rehab.

The Obama administration has announced a new initiative to reduce food waste by 50% by 2030. The goal is part of the administration's efforts to combat climate change and address food insecurity. The USDA and EPA will lead a partnership with charitable organizations, private sector companies, and local, state, and tribal governments to reduce food loss and waste.

The announcement comes just a week before world leaders gather at the United Nations General Assembly to discuss sustainable development practices. The US enjoys the most productive food supply in the world, but an average family of four wastes an estimated $1,500 worth of food each year, and overall, retailers and consumers waste nearly a third of the country's food supply. This waste has far-reaching impacts on food security, resource conservation, and climate change.

Food waste is the single largest component of disposed U.S. municipal solid waste and accounts for a significant portion of U.S. methane emissions. Landfills are the third largest source of methane in the United States. Reducing food waste by just 15% would provide enough food for more than 25 million Americans every year, helping to sharply reduce incidences of food insecurity for millions.

The USDA will launch a consumer education campaign, including tips on how to reduce waste, and is partnering with food-service companies and state and local governments to carry out the plan. Food companies, including grocery chain Albertson's, grocery-delivery service FreshDirect, and food services company Sodexo, have expressed their support. Albertson's is working to divert food to hunger-relief organizations and repurpose scraps and leftovers for things like animal feed.

The USDA will also continue to encourage the private sector to set their own aggressive goals for reducing food loss and waste. The Consumer Goods Forum, which recently approved a new resolution to halve food waste within the operations of its 400 retailer and manufacturer members by 2025, is helping to lead the way. The Obama administration's initiative is part of its broader commitment to protecting the environment for future generations and addressing climate change.

The Bureau of Land Management (BLM) abruptly ended a week-long cattle roundup from rancher Cliven Bundy in southern Nevada due to safety concerns for employees and the public. The roundup, which aimed to remove hundreds of Bundy's cattle that were allegedly trespassing on public land, was halted after 400 cows were gathered, short of the BLM's goal of 900. The decision came as militia members and others gathered near the roundup site to protest the removal.

The BLM's director, Neil Kornze, made the announcement on Saturday, praising the agency for its willingness to listen to the state's concerns. Nevada Governor Brian Sandoval issued a statement praising the BLM for ending the roundup. The highway was reopened after protesters moved to the side of the road and stopped blocking it.

The controversy drew armed militia groups from across the country to Bundy's side, especially after a YouTube video captured a tussle teetering on violence between rangers and protesters. The BLM said Bundy owed about $1 million in back fees because his cattle grazed on federal land. It's unclear whether Bundy and the BLM have come to an agreement on how to end the long-running conflict.

The growing protest came amid the BLM's decision to put an early end to a roundup of Bundy's cattle, which the feds claim have been illegally grazing on federal land for 20 years. The dispute between Bundy and the government began in 1993 when the Bureau of Land Management changed grazing rules for the 600,000-acre Gold Butte area to protect an endangered desert tortoise. Bundy refused to abide by the changes and stopped paying his grazing fees to the federal bureau, which he contends is infringing on state rights.

The incident is under federal investigation, and Gov. Sandoval appealed for calm and urged out-of-state supporters to return home. U.S. Sen. Dean Heller, R-Nevada, also appealed for calm and asked all involved to return to their homes and allow the BLM officers to collect their equipment and depart without interference. The dispute is over, but emotions and tensions are still near the boiling point, and there is a need for a peaceful conclusion to this conflict.

A high-ranking North Korean diplomat, Thae Yong-ho, has defected to South Korea, marking the most significant defection in nearly two decades. Thae, the deputy ambassador, was responsible for promoting positive perceptions of North Korea's leadership in London. He was due to return to Pyongyang with his family but instead, he defected, citing disillusionment with the regime of Kim Jong-un. Thae had previously argued that Western countries were brainwashed into believing negative things about North Korea. The South Korean government confirmed that Thae and his family are under their protection. Thae's defection is significant as he is believed to be the highest-ranking North Korean official ever to defect. The reasons for his defection, according to a South Korean spokesman, include disgust with Kim Jong-un's regime, admiration for South Korea's democratic system, and concerns for his family's future.

In this article, a group of actors and producers, including Jeffrey Tambor, discuss their experiences and feelings regarding Tambor's behavior on the set of the TV show "Arrested Development." The conversation takes place after Tambor was accused of inappropriate behavior on the set of another show, "Transparent." Tambor admits to being difficult and mean at times, but denies the more serious allegations. The cast and crew express their support for Tambor, but also acknowledge the importance of addressing and learning from the allegations. The article also discusses the impact of the #MeToo movement on the entertainment industry and the complexities of the situation. The article was published in The Hollywood Reporter.

Tyra Banks has been announced as the new host for the 12th season of "America's Got Talent" on NBC. Banks, a supermodel, Emmy-winner, and creator of "America's Next Top Model," will join returning judges Simon Cowell, Mel B, Heidi Klum, and Howie Mandel. Banks takes over hosting duties from Nick Cannon, who left the show earlier this year after eight years. Contestants will showcase a variety of talents to compete for a $1 million prize. The live episodes will be aired this summer from the Dolby Theatre in Los Angeles, as part of an effort to preserve and fix broken links on the web.

The World Anti-Doping Agency (Wada) has announced that its database was hacked by a Russian cyber espionage group known as Fancy Bear, resulting in the leak of confidential medical data of several US athletes. The hacked athletes include tennis stars Serena and Venus Williams, gymnastics multi-gold medallist Simone Biles, and basketball player Elena Delle Donne. The hackers published records of Therapeutic Use Exemptions (TUEs), which permit athletes to use certain banned substances if they have a verified medical reason to do so.

Fancy Bear claimed the TUEs constituted evidence of doping by US Olympians, stating that dozens of American athletes had tested positive for illicit drugs. However, the US Anti-Doping Agency (Usada) chief Travis Tygart stated that the athletes had done everything right in adhering to the global rules for obtaining permission to use a needed medication.

The hack is believed to have been carried out using spear-phishing emails to gather passwords for the Wada Anti-Doping Administration and Management System (Adams) database. This comes after a similar hack of Yuliya Stepanova's account, a Russian 800-metre runner who blew the whistle on widespread doping among her country's Olympic team, less than a month ago.

Russia's track and field team was banned from the Rio Olympics over an alleged state-backed doping programme. All of its athletes are barred from the ongoing Paralympics. Wada has condemned the hack as an attempt to undermine the global anti-doping system, with director-general Olivier Niggli stating that these criminal acts are greatly compromising the effort by the global anti-doping community to re-establish trust in Russia.

The leaked documents allege that Serena Williams was granted permission to use drugs commonly used to treat muscle injuries, such as anti-inflammatories, while Biles is said to use Ritalin - a treatment for her ADHD. Former Australian Sports Anti-Doping Authority head Richard Ings stated that nothing he saw here gave him cause for alarm, adding it looked "totally normal".

The hackers have pledged to release confidential records from other national Olympic teams. This comes at a time when sport's leaders are desperately trying to restore trust following the biggest doping scandal in the history of sport. Many athletes will now be nervously wondering if their private medical details records are the next to be made public. The future of Wada is currently in question, and the fact its security was so badly compromised will raise more questions over the entire anti-doping system.

The Israeli military has launched a ground offensive against Palestinian militants in Gaza, marking an escalation in the 11-day-old military operation. Troops and tanks were sent into Gaza to target Hamas, with Israel stating its goal is to establish a reality where Israeli residents can live in safety and security. The ground offensive began on Thursday night, resulting in the death of a five-month-old child, 24 Palestinians, and one Israeli soldier. Over 200 Palestinians have been injured. Israel has killed 14 "terrorists" overnight, according to its claims.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ordered the invasion after days of intensive rocket fire and air strikes between the two sides. Since the start of the wider Israeli operation on 8 July, 258 Palestinians - three-quarters of them civilians - have died, according to officials in Gaza. An Israeli civilian was killed from mortar fire, and several Israelis have been seriously injured, Israeli medics say.

The Israeli military is testing the water, gauging the level of opposition before deciding whether or not to move deeper inside the Gaza Strip. The death of one of its own soldiers, at this early stage, will have come as a warning of the dangers ahead. However, Prime Minister Netanyahu seems determined to inflict greater damage on Hamas and that could mean sending his troops into densely populated areas, which could be devastating for Palestinian civilians.

The ground offensive follows attempts in Cairo to negotiate a new ceasefire. A temporary ceasefire was in place on Thursday to allow Palestinians to stock up on supplies and aid workers to distribute water, food, and hygiene kits. The truce lasted for five hours, although both sides reported violations.

Hamas chief Khaled Meshaal said that the Israeli ground operation was "destined to failure." Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas said the ground operation would lead to "more bloodshed" and called on Israel to stop. Mr. Abbas, whose Fatah party recently agreed to a unity government with Hamas, was meeting Egyptian officials in Cairo amid efforts to negotiate a truce.

The document discusses the unexpected speakers at the Republican National Convention (RNC), which includes soap opera stars Kimberlin Brown and Antonio Sabato Jr., as well as Dana White, the president of the Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC).

Dana White will also speak at the RNC, adding a colorful voice to the lineup. White is a political independent who has expressed gratitude to Donald Trump for helping the UFC succeed. He will speak on Tuesday night after RNC co-chair Sharon Day delivers a nominating speech for Trump's vice-president pick, Indiana Governor Mike Pence.

Tiffany Trump, one of Trump's children, will also take the stage. Tiffany graduated from the University of Pennsylvania this spring and has dabbled in music, with a single titled Like a Bird available on Amazon.

The RNC will officially nominate Donald Trump as the party's nominee on Tuesday, with unity being a major theme as the party seeks to put forth Trump as its standard bearer. Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell, House Speaker Paul Ryan, and House Majority Leader Kevin McCarthy are all scheduled to speak in a broad show of support for Trump. Tuesday's theme is "Make America Work Again," with speakers focusing on Trump's successful business career and his ability to lead the country's economy. Other speakers include Arkansas Governor Asa Hutchinson, Chris Christie, and Ben Carson, both of whom criticized Trump during the primary. Wisconsin Senator Ron Johnson is the only vulnerable Republican senator scheduled to deliver a speech on the convention stage. Tiffany Trump will make her national-stage debut on Tuesday night. The convention will also feature celebrities like Dana White and professional golfer Natalie Gulbis.

The controversy surrounding the cause of death of Sandra Bland, a 28-year-old woman found dead in a Waller County, Texas jail cell, has intensified, with some claiming she was already dead in her mugshot. However, leading forensic experts have dismissed this theory as "ridiculous," stating that there is no evidence to indicate Bland is dead in her mugshot. Dr. Michael Baden, who conducted a private autopsy for the family of Michael Brown, said it would be impossible to determine if someone is dead based on a low-resolution photo alone. The legality of Bland's arrest itself has also been called into question, with contradictions in her booking documents, allegations of excessive force by the arresting officer, and claims that she consumed a large amount of THC while in custody. Despite the controversies, Baden says the mugshot needs to be treated as nothing more than a low-resolution booking photo.

The article discusses a controversial tweet posted by Donald Trump on his Twitter account over the weekend, which featured an image of Hillary Clinton against a backdrop of $100 bills and a six-point star, which was later replaced with a circle. The tweet was accused of being anti-Semitic by Hillary Clinton's campaign and critics, who argued that the star was a reference to the Star of David and was meant to exploit stereotypes against Jewish people.

The House speaker, Paul Ryan, rebuked the tweet, stating that anti-Semitic images have no place in a presidential campaign. The Clinton campaign's director of Jewish outreach, Sarah Bard, called the tweet "blatantly anti-Semitic" and said that Trump should be condemning hate, not engaging extremists.

Trump defended the tweet, claiming that the star was a sheriff's star or a plain star, and not the Star of David. However, the image was traced by the news site Mic to a white supremacist message board, and some social media users disputed Trump's suggestion that the star was a sheriff's star.

The Anti-Defamation League condemned the tweet as further evidence of extremist sympathies within the Trump campaign, and called on Trump to speak out against white supremacists and make it clear that bigotry and anti-Semitism have no place in his campaign.

Trump's social media director, Dan Scavino, later stated that the star was not sourced from an anti-Semitic website, but was "lifted from an anti-Hillary Twitter user where countless images appear." Scavino also stated that he would never offend anyone and chose to remove the image.

This is not the first time Trump has been linked to anti-Semitic or white supremacist views, and his inconsistency on the issue is underlined by his family ties, as his daughter Ivanka converted to Judaism and is a key adviser to his campaign. Trump has also expressed support for Israel and condemned terrorist attacks against Israeli citizens. The latest incident has been criticized as an example of the Trump campaign's capacity to bring attention on itself even when it would be advantageous to remain silent.

In the wake of the shooting at Sandy Hook Elementary School in Newtown, Connecticut, which claimed the lives of 26 people, including 20 children, President Barack Obama urged Americans to come together and take meaningful action to prevent further gun violence. In his weekly radio address, Obama expressed his condolences to the families of the victims and called for a national conversation on how to address the issue of gun violence. However, he did not specify any proposed actions. New York City Mayor Michael Bloomberg, who runs a coalition of mayors on gun policy, called for immediate action and criticized the lack of leadership on the issue from the White House and Congress. The shooting has reignited a debate over gun control in a country with a flourishing gun culture and a strong gun lobby. President Obama mostly steered clear of the issue during his re-election campaign, and it remains unclear whether he will take a more assertive approach now that he has secured a second term. The shooting has put partisan bickering in Washington on hold, with House Speaker John Boehner canceling the Republican weekly address to allow President Obama to speak for the nation in mourning.

Prince Alireza Pahlavi, the youngest son of the late Shah of Iran, was found dead in his Boston residence on January 4, 2011, following an apparent self-inflicted gunshot wound. He was 44 years old. His brother, Reza Pahlavi, announced the news on his website, stating that Alireza had struggled for years to overcome his sorrow, particularly after the loss of his father and sister. Alireza's sister, Leila, died in 2001 from an accidental overdose of prescription drugs. Alireza had lived in the South End for many years but kept a low public profile. He was born in 1966 and attended schools in Tehran, New York, Cairo, and Massachusetts. He studied music as an undergraduate at Princeton University and ancient Iranian studies as a graduate student at Columbia University. He also did postgraduate work at Harvard University in ancient Iranian studies and philology. Alireza was not studying at the university at the time of his death. Neighbors described him as reserved and quiet, and he had placed satellite dishes with Arabic letters on the roof of his house so he could access Al Jazeera. The Pahlavi family has not played a major role in Iranian politics since the family left Iran, partly due to the ruthlessness of the shah's regime and the family's extravagant lifestyle while in power. Alireza's death has been met with sympathy from the Iranian-American community, but it is unclear how much weight exiled opposition forces have inside Iran or how many Iranians support the idea of a return to monarchy. Alireza's family has asked for privacy during their mourning period, and no funeral arrangements have been made.

Vice President Joe Biden officiated his first wedding, a same-sex ceremony for two longtime White House staffers, Brian Mosteller and Joe Mahshie, at the Naval Observatory on August 1, 2016. The ceremony was attended only by the grooms' families. Biden obtained a temporary certification from the District of Columbia to preside over the wedding. His wife, Jill, later tweeted her support, stating "Love is love!" Biden had publicly endorsed same-sex marriage in 2012. This marks a significant moment in the ongoing fight for marriage equality in the United States. ABC News' Arlette Saenz contributed to this report.

The FBI Director James Comey has sparked controversy in Poland by suggesting in a Washington Post article that some Poles were accomplices during the Holocaust. This statement was met with outrage and demands for an apology from the Polish government, as Poland lost six million citizens, half of whom were Jewish, during the Nazi occupation. The Polish President and Prime Minister both criticized Comey's comments, stating that Poland was a victim of World War Two and not a perpetrator. The US Ambassador to Poland, Stephen Mull, apologized and clarified that the US believes only Nazi Germany is responsible for the Holocaust. The controversy arose from two poorly worded sentences in Comey's article, which suggested that "murderers and accomplices" in Germany, Poland, and Hungary, among others, were responsible for the Holocaust. This statement is inaccurate, as Germany had a state policy of exterminating the Jews, while Poland was occupied and had no state during the war. The Holocaust was a result of specific German state terror, and not the actions of individuals in other countries. The controversy highlights the importance of accurate historical understanding and the need for Holocaust education.

The article discusses the contrast between childhood staring contests and the impressive eye contact skills of model Gigi Hadid. Hadid, known for her modeling career and "smizing," has been named one of Glamour's Women of the Year for 2017, joining a prestigious group that includes Nicole Kidman, Solange Knowles, Patty Jenkins, and Maxine Waters. The Women of the Year Summit will take place on November 13, and a live stream is available for those interested in learning more.

The article also highlights Gigi Hadid's success in the fashion industry, her strong work ethic, and her advocacy for various issues such as gun control, human rights, and women's personal safety. Hadid has amassed a large following on Instagram, and her followers appreciate her use of her platform to share her passions.

In a separate section, the article criticizes Glamour magazine for posting a video of Hadid staring into the camera for four minutes as an example of the magazine's struggle to adapt to the digital-first marketplace. The author finds the video uninteresting and argues that there are many celebrities they would rather watch do something other than stare at the camera.

Overall, the article provides an overview of Gigi Hadid's career and accomplishments, as well as a critique of Glamour magazine's video content strategy.

The study published in PLOS Neglected Tropical Diseases reveals that up to 25% of people infected with Ebola may show no symptoms, suggesting that the recent West African Ebola epidemic was more widespread than previously thought. The research, led by Gene Richardson of Stanford University, was conducted in the rural village of Sukudu in Sierra Leone, a major hotspot for the outbreak. Out of 187 villagers tested who had likely been exposed to Ebola, 14 were found to carry an antibody to the virus, with 12 denying any symptoms during the outbreak. This finding highlights the need for new methods to diagnose and contain the virus during an outbreak, as it may spread more rapidly and broadly through a population than previously believed. The study also raises questions about the potential for asymptomatic people to transmit the virus, though more research is needed to determine this. The researchers are now working in other villages in Sierra Leone to get a better handle on the true number of people affected during the crisis. If the 25% figure is correct, it presents a significant challenge for health officials in containing future outbreaks. Additionally, the Ebola virus mutated into a deadlier form during the last outbreak, adding to the urgency of finding new ways to combat the disease.

In Dorchester County, Maryland, a waterfowl hunter, Robert Meilhammer, was knocked unconscious after a goose fell from the sky and struck him during a hunting session on Thursday. The incident occurred near the Miles River, where Meilhammer was part of a larger hunting party. The goose was killed by one of the hunters, but it's unclear who was responsible. Meilhammer sustained head and facial injuries and was airlifted to Maryland Shock Trauma.

In a separate event, Orthodox Christians in Baltimore held a Saturday morning service to commemorate the first resurrection of Jesus Christ before observing Easter Sunday, known as Pascha.

Additionally, business and civic leaders attended a breakfast during the release of the annual State of Downtown Baltimore report. This event was not related to the goose incident.

On April 22nd, a shooting spree occurred in the Russian city of Belgorod, resulting in six fatalities and one injury. The gunman, identified as Sergey Pomazun, opened fire near an arms shop and is believed to be armed with a gas pistol and a semi-automatic rifle. Authorities have asked residents not to leave their homes due to the ongoing special operation. The suspect, who has a criminal record, is still at large, with over 1200 police personnel involved in the search. The city has declared April 23rd and 24th as days of mourning, and all churches in the region will hold memorial services for the victims. The shooting has caused panic among residents, with increased police presence and social media warnings for safety. The incident is reminiscent of previous mass shootings in Russia, such as the 2012 shooting in Moscow by a lawyer over a broken relationship.

Pope Francis, during a press conference aboard the papal plane, expressed his belief that the Roman Catholic Church should apologize to the gay community for historical mistreatment and discrimination. He stated that the Church should not discriminate against or marginalize gays, but instead, respect and accompany them pastorally. The Pope also expressed the need for the Church to seek forgiveness from various groups, including the poor, exploited women, and children forced into labor, as well as for having blessed weapons.

Francis' comments were hailed as a breakthrough by some Catholics, with the Rev. James Martin, a Jesuit priest, calling it a "groundbreaking moment." The Pope's apology to the LGBT community is significant as no pope has ever come close to apologizing to this group before.

In response to a question about a German Cardinal's statement that the Church should apologize for being "very negative" about gays, the Pope reiterated the Church's teaching that gays should not be discriminated against but also emphasized that certain behaviors can be condemned for political reasons, not theological ones.

The Pope's remarks were met with praise from the gay community, with Francis DeBernardo, executive director of New Ways Ministry, a Catholic gay rights group, calling them "an immense blessing of healing."

In other news, Pope Francis also addressed Brexit, stating that unity is superior to conflict and that the European Union should strive for creativity and fecundity to overcome its current challenges. He also reaffirmed his use of the term "genocide" to describe the murder of over a million Armenians in the early 20th century, despite Turkish protests. Lastly, when asked about the existence of two Popes, Francis clarified that there is only one Pope, with Pope Benedict serving as the Pope Emeritus and offering prayers for his successor.

The study published in Psychology of Addictive Behaviors analyzed data from the Pittsburgh Youth Study (PYS), a 20-year longitudinal study that tracked the development of antisocial and delinquent behavior among seventh-grade boys in Pittsburgh. The study focused on 506 boys, divided into four groups based on their marijuana use: those who rarely or never used marijuana (46%), those who mostly used it in their teens (11%), those who started using it in adulthood (21%), and those who started early and became chronic pot users (22%).

Researchers found that chronic marijuana users were not more likely than late-starting users, adolescence-limited users, or low/non-users to experience several physical or mental health problems in their mid-30s. The study controlled for factors like tobacco use and socioeconomic status.

The study's findings are surprising as they contradict previous studies that found a small but real link between chronic marijuana use and the development of psychological issues like depression or schizophrenia. However, the study has limitations, such as only focusing on men, only following participants for 20 years, and only considering certain diagnosable and self-reported health conditions.

The researchers suggest that individual differences may moderate the association between marijuana use and psychotic disorders, and that marijuana may not cause but rather accelerate the development of disorders like schizophrenia. The study's authors emphasize that their findings should be considered in the context of the larger body of work on the potential adverse consequences of early onset chronic marijuana use.

On Thursday afternoon, a Mountain View Police Department officer pulled over one of Google's self-driving cars on El Camino Real near Rengstorff Avenue. The vehicle was traveling at 24 mph in a 35 mph zone, causing traffic congestion. The officer stopped the car to educate the operators about impeding traffic and to inquire about the car's speed selection. The Google self-driving cars are considered "neighborhood electric vehicles" under the California Vehicle Code and can only be operated on roadways with speed limits at or under 35 mph. In this case, it was lawful for the car to be traveling on the street as El Camino Real is rated at 35 mph. No ticket was issued, and the Google Self-Driving Car Project appreciated the humor of the situation. The cars are designed to feel friendly and approachable, with a maximum speed of 25 mph for safety reasons. This was not the first time the self-driving cars have attracted attention, as they have driven over 1.2 million miles without receiving a ticket. The incident was captured by photographer Zandr Milewski, who was working nearby and rushed to the scene with his colleagues.

In a study published in the journal Nature, researchers have found that a decrease in a baby's attention to other people's eyes between 2 and 6 months of age is an early sign of autism. The study, led by Emory University School of Medicine in Atlanta, used eye-tracking technology to measure the way babies looked at and responded to social clues. The researchers found that children later diagnosed with autism showed a decline in eye contact from 2 months onwards, which could not be perceived by parents without the technology and expertise of an autism clinic. The study followed 59 infants at high risk of autism and 51 infants at low risk, and 13 of the children were diagnosed with autism spectrum disorders. The researchers hope that this early detection could lead to earlier interventions and therapies for autism. The study is significant because it provides an insight into the timing of atypical social attention in children who might go on to develop autism. However, the study is based on a small sample and needs to be replicated on a larger scale before any concrete conclusions can be drawn. Autism is a complex condition, and a holistic approach to diagnosis is required that takes into account all aspects of an individual's behavior.

Title: Twitter Introduces Location Feature for Tweets, Offers Control Over Location History

In a recent development, Twitter has introduced a feature that allows users to add their city or precise location to their Tweets, either from the web or via third-party applications. This feature provides a more personal and contextual touch to the Tweets. Users have the option to delete their Tweet location history at any time.

The introduction of this feature was preceded by a comprehensive crawl, where the starting point was a list of every host in the Wayback Machine. The crawl was conducted at a level 1, which includes URLs, their embeds, and the URLs of all outbound links, including their embeds.

However, it's important to note that the WARC files associated with this crawl are not currently accessible to the general public. This move may be aimed at maintaining privacy and security for users and the data collected during the crawl.

A new Confederate monument, commemorating "unknown Confederate soldiers" who died during the Civil War, was unveiled in Crenshaw County, Alabama, during a ceremony attended by over 200 people. The memorial, located in a Confederate memorial park, stands among existing monuments, replica cannons, and tall flagpoles. The event was organized by the Sons of Confederate Veterans, who stated that the memorial and ceremony were not responses to the racial discord in the nation, but rather a tribute to their ancestors.

The memorial resembles a standard stone gravestone and bears the words "Unkown AL Soldier CSA" and the quote "Mother, I have been found, I am home." The ceremony included speeches, a flag-raising ceremony, and the firing of blanks from multiple replica Civil War cannons. Members of the right-wing Three Percenters militia were present, wearing camouflage fatigues and body armor, carrying large guns, and standing in the back "in case anything were to happen."

The Sons of Confederate Veterans and other attendees wore Confederate T-shirts, black-leather motorcycle jackets, or similar attire, while some men dressed up in Confederate soldier uniforms, and several women wore period costume dresses. Many in attendance waved Confederate flags and other banners associated with the Confederacy and the South.

The event was met with criticism and widespread derision, but members of the Sons of Confederate Veterans expressed pride in their ancestors and their history. Wendy Osborne, a Tallassee resident and member of the Talisi Cotton Belles, a local chapter of the Order of Confederate Rose, said, "We are proud of our ancestors and we want to remember our history and where we came from, and that keeps us stronger as a people and brings us closer together. We stick together as a people."

The monument was surrounded by a black metal fence and flanked by two other monuments. As a red cloth was pulled to reveal it, five cannons were fired. The ceremony concluded with members of the Sons of Confederate Veterans kneeling down in front of the monument. The event was scheduled months ago and the monument was ordered last year.

In a heartwarming encounter during Black History Month, 106-year-old Virginia McLaurin danced with joy while meeting President Barack Obama and First Lady Michelle Obama at the White House. The video captures McLaurin's lively entrance, followed by her delight and laughter upon meeting the couple. President Obama declared, "She's 106!" while Michelle Obama hugged and held her hand. The Obamas then danced with McLaurin in the Blue Room, resulting in roars of laughter. McLaurin expressed her happiness, stating, "I thought I would never live to get in the White House. And I tell you. I am so happy: A black president." The sweet video can be viewed above. Subscribe to the Us Weekly newsletter for more inspiring stories like this.

In northern Iraq, the Islamic State, a Sunni militant group known for its extreme violence, has launched an offensive, causing thousands of civilians to flee. The Yazidis, a minority ethnic group considered "devil worshippers" by the Islamic State, are particularly at risk in the town of Sinjar. Tens of thousands of Yazidis have fled the town, which was attacked over the weekend, and are now surrounded by the Islamic State. The militants inflicted a humiliating defeat on Kurdish forces who had held towns in the area for years. The Islamic State has captured three towns and a fifth oil field, and reached Iraq's biggest dam, consolidating gains made after a lightning sweep through the north in June. The offensive poses the biggest threat to Iraq since the fall of Saddam Hussein.

Residents of Sinjar reported that about 50 people were killed after the Islamic State arrived in the town. While 20 were killed trying to defend the town, it's not clear how the others died. Many panicked Yazidis fled to the surrounding mountains, but some did not manage to escape. The United Nations children's agency (UNICEF) said that families who fled the area are in immediate need of urgent assistance, including up to 25,000 children stranded in the mountains. UNICEF reported that 40 children have died in the past 48 hours as a direct consequence of violence, displacement, and dehydration.

The Yazidis, followers of an ancient religion derived from Zoroastrianism, are spread over northern Iraq and are part of the country's Kurdish minority. Many of their villages were destroyed when Saddam Hussein's troops tried to crush the Kurds. Now they are on the defensive again, years after the fall of Saddam raised hopes of a brighter future for all. The U.S.-trained army crumbled when the Islamic State swept into northern Iraq, and thousands of soldiers fled. Kurdish fighters known as peshmerga, who often boast of their bravery in battles with Saddam Hussein's troops, stepped in, as did Shi'ite militias. But the Islamic State routed the Kurds in the weekend surge, using artillery, mortars, and machine guns seized from Iraqi soldiers compared to the Kurds' mostly AK-47 assault rifles.

Some of the most vulnerable Yazidis could not withstand the weekend offensive. Almost 70 children between the ages of one month and four died of thirst or hunger, according to a member of parliament from the Yazidi community. The Iraqi government has ordered its air force to help the Kurds, who have vowed to launch a counter-offensive against the Islamic State. But there is little sign of relief on the ground. The Islamic State's advance sets its sights on new territory, and there is no sign that Iraq's bickering politicians will be able to form a power-sharing government soon to counter the insurgency. Prime Minister Nuri al-Maliki is defying calls to step aside and make room for a less polarizing figure who could ease sectarian tensions causing the worst bloodshed since the height of a civil war in 2006-2007.

In a humorous and Swift-themed ruling, a California judge has dismissed a $42 million lawsuit against Taylor Swift, who was accused of stealing lyrics for her hit song "Shake It Off." The lawsuit, filed by R&B artist Jessie Braham, claimed that 92% of Swift's song came from his song "Haters Gone Hate."

Braham's song features the phrase "Haters gonna hate/ Players gonna play/ Watch out for them fakers/ They'll fake you every day," which bears a striking resemblance to Swift's chorus in "Shake It Off." However, Judge Gail Standish, in her ruling, pointed out the lack of factual evidence and the speculative nature of the allegations, leading to the dismissal of the lawsuit.

In a playful nod to Swift's music, Judge Standish quoted lyrics from several of Swift's other hits, including "We Are Never Ever Getting Back Together," "Blank Space," and "Bad Blood," as she dismissed the case. She wrote, "At present, the Court is not saying that Braham can never, ever, ever get his case back in court. But, for now, we have got problems, and the Court is not sure Braham can solve them."

If Braham can address the deficiencies in the lawsuit, he may file a new complaint, the court said. In conclusion, Judge Standish wrote, "At least for the moment, Defendants have shaken off this lawsuit." The dismissal of the lawsuit marks a victory for Swift, who has been embroiled in several copyright infringement lawsuits in the past.

The Neiman Marcus computer network was hacked as early as July, with the breach not being fully contained until Sunday, according to sources briefed on the investigation. The company disclosed the data theft of customer information late last week, stating that they first became aware of suspicious activity involving credit cards used at their stores in mid-December. Neiman Marcus has not publicly given an estimate of how many credit card numbers were stolen or how many customers were affected.

The hack appears to have gone on for significantly longer than the widespread attack on Target, where data from 40 million customers was stolen, along with encrypted PINs for debit cards, and other personal information belonging to 70 million people. Neiman Marcus has stated that it has no knowledge of any connection between its data breach and Target's.

Neiman Marcus only publicly acknowledged the data breach last Friday after facing inquiries from a journalist specializing in computer security, Brian Krebs. The company has faced criticism for not informing customers about the breach sooner, with some questioning Neiman's decision not to disclose anything to the public until the shopping season was over.

A growing group of state attorneys general, including those from Connecticut, New York, and Illinois, are jointly investigating both the Target and Neiman Marcus breaches. The authorities are examining whether the two attacks are related, with both appearing to have been committed by criminal groups in Eastern Europe.

A 17-page report from a computer firm hired to look into the massive data breach at Target stores provides new insight into the holiday hacking that endangered data for more than 100 million customers. The report details the type of software used in the hack, how it was effective, and mentions regions known to have the software coding prowess to pull off this kind of digital heist. The report, however, does not draw conclusions on who is ultimately responsible for the attack.

The data breach was caused by a type of malware, similar to a computer virus, placed in a store's point-of-sale systems. The malware works by getting the data on credit cards, which is encrypted, in the authorization stage while it is in the memory of the POS system, unencrypted. The tactic used during the Target holiday hackers is "new to eCrime," the report says, and "covertly subverts network controls and common forensic tactics to conceal all data transfers."

Since this style of POS hacking can net big rewards for the cyber crooks with little risk, cardholders can expect more of this type of breach, according to the report. The report concludes that the holiday data breach at Target Corp. appeared to be part of a broad and highly sophisticated international hacking campaign against multiple retailers.

The article discusses the findings of a research project conducted by the Van Gogh Museum in Amsterdam, which reveals that some of Vincent van Gogh's favorite paints have faded badly over time, changing the appearance of his works and making them less vibrant than they were originally. The exhibition, titled "Van Gogh at Work," examines van Gogh's practice as a painter, including his use of various types of canvas, his exchanges of ideas with other artists such as Gauguin and Toulouse-Lautrec, and his habit of reusing canvases.

The article also highlights a separate study by scientists in Belgium, who may have found the missing chemical link to explain why the reds in van Gogh's paintings are turning white. The study found that red lead or minium, a pigment used extensively by van Gogh, is being converted into plumbonacrite, a rare mineral, when exposed to light. This reaction forms a white degradation product that forms around the red paint.

The exhibition at the Van Gogh Museum includes a loan of van Gogh's Sunflowers from London's National Gallery, as well as van Gogh's palette and three tubes of paint that belonged to him. The article concludes that despite the changes in van Gogh's colors over time, his visionary art remains true to itself and brings viewers closer to him as they stand at his shoulder, watching him work. The article also emphasizes the importance of the research on the degradation of van Gogh's paintings for the conservation of works of art.

Kanye West recently performed in Kazakhstan, earning millions for a private concert at the Royal Tulip Hotel in Almaty. The event was a wedding for the grandson of President Nursultan Nazarbayev, who is known for his alleged dictatorial practices and wealth accumulated from oil resources. The exact amount Kanye was paid is unknown, but it's reported to be in the millions. This performance comes after Sting declined a paid gig in Kazakhstan due to concerns over oil workers' mistreatment. The wedding was attended by Kazakhstan's third richest person, Timur Kulibayev, who is married to Nazarbayev's second daughter. The performance marked Kanye's first public appearance since the release of his album Yeezus.

Death Valley National Park in California experienced its hottest month on record in July, with an average temperature of 107.4 degrees. This surpassed the previous record of 107.2 set in 1917. The average daily high temperature was an unbearable 119.6 degrees, making it the hottest average monthly temperature ever measured in the U.S. or the Western Hemisphere. The park, which is the hottest, driest, and lowest of all U.S. national parks, has no permanent residents except for a few park service staff and rangers.

Notably, the temperature did not drop below 89 degrees the entire month of July, and three days, the overnight low temperature was over 100 degrees. The hottest day was the 7th, when Death Valley hit 127 degrees, a temperature also reached on two June days.

Several other cities in the West also set record warm months, as did Miami, according to the weather service. Death Valley National Park announced the record-breaking heat on Twitter, stating, "We broke a record this July--the hottest month ever for Death Valley!"

The Apollo 11 lunar sample bag, used by astronauts Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin to collect the first samples of lunar rock, has become the center of a legal dispute. The bag was mistakenly sold at a government auction in 2015 for $995 to Nancy Carlson, an Illinois resident. The bag was discovered during a search of Max Ary's garage in 2003, who was the founder and former director of the Kansas Cosmosphere and Space Center. Ary was convicted in 2005 of stealing and selling hundreds of space artifacts, including the lunar bag.

Federal prosecutors are seeking to recover the bag, stating that it was not properly notified to NASA during the forfeiture process because of a clerical error. The government has called the bag "a rare artifact, if not a national treasure." The confusion arose due to two separate lunar bags being given the same inventory identification number. The other bag was from the Apollo 17 lunar mission in 1972, which Ary auctioned for over $20,000 in 2001.

In 2006, Ary was sentenced to three years in prison and ordered to pay over $130,000 in restitution. He was released on good behavior in 2010, having served about 70 percent of his sentence. Ary has consistently maintained his innocence, claiming that he accidentally mixed museum artifacts with items from his private collection.

Carlson has sued NASA in an Illinois federal court, seeking the return of the bag. Federal prosecutors have asked the federal judge who handled Ary's case to rescind the sale and refund Carlson. The legal dispute highlights the importance of proper inventory management and notification procedures in the handling of valuable historical artifacts.

Two friends, Phillip Boyle and Jamie Blyth, from Middlesbrough, England, embarked on an impromptu trip to Pattaya, Thailand, after a night of heavy drinking. The duo initially went out for a quiet pint at The Southern Cross in Marton, but ended up buying more alcohol from a gas station and staying up all night. The next morning, they hailed a taxi to Manchester Airport, where they purchased last-minute flights to Thailand. Despite a brief moment of hesitation on the flight, they had a memorable time, visiting restaurants and bars, and exploring the holiday resort. However, Phillip's new backpack and trainers were stolen during their stay.

The story gained international attention, with comparisons drawn to the movie "The Hangover Part II." Another similar incident occurred when a 19-year-old British teenager, Luke Harding, decided to visit Paris after a night of drinking, buying a flight from Manchester Airport and waking up in a bathroom at Charles De Gaulle airport.

Both Phillip and Jamie returned to work after their trip, with Phillip admitting he had fallen behind. Despite the chaos, they both expressed enjoyment and recommended the experience to others. However, they advised packing a proper suitcase before embarking on such adventures.

In Maine, a ballot measure to expand Medicaid, a health program that covers one in five Americans, is set for a vote on November 7. The measure, if approved, would provide health coverage to approximately 70,000 low-income Mainers. Governor Paul LePage, a staunch opponent of Medicaid expansion, has criticized hospitals for supporting the referendum, accusing them of wanting to take resources away from vulnerable Mainers. Hospitals, however, argue that Medicaid expansion would improve the population's health, create jobs, and lower the uninsured rate.

Governor LePage has vetoed five attempts by the Legislature to approve Medicaid expansion, citing concerns about the financial burden on Maine taxpayers. He claims that Medicaid expansion would cost Maine taxpayers $500 million over five years, but the Legislature's nonpartisan Office of Fiscal and Program Review states that state taxpayers would be responsible for $54 million per year, while Maine would receive $525 million per year from the federal government.

LePage's relationship with Maine hospitals has deteriorated since 2013, when he fought to pay off $105 million in unpaid MaineCare reimbursements to hospitals. Ann Woloson, public policy director for Maine Equal Justice Partners, the group behind Medicaid expansion, argues that rural hospitals are struggling financially due to providing free health care to the uninsured. She believes that Medicaid expansion would help these hospitals financially and attract more medical professionals.

Jeff Austin, vice president of government affairs and communication for the Maine Hospital Association, supports Medicaid expansion, stating that hospitals see tens of thousands of uninsured patients each year and believe that Medicaid expansion is the smartest way to care for this population. Despite LePage's criticism, expansion advocates argue that Medicaid expansion would not take away care from the elderly and disabled, as states have some leeway on how to spend Medicaid money.

Senator Susan Collins, who opposed the Obamacare repeal bills, is not taking a position on the ballot measure. Turnout may be a challenge for the advocacy groups leading the effort, as there are no national or statewide races this year to drive people to the polls. Governor LePage's stance on government safety net programs appeals to many voters in Maine's more rural regions. If approved, Medicaid expansion would make over 2.5 million poor uninsured adults across the country eligible for the program.

Tesla has filed a patent for a technology that aims to automate turn signals for drivers who often forget or neglect to use them. The system, if implemented, would utilize Tesla's Autopilot hardware to detect a driver's intent to change lanes or make a turn based on steering angle, and activate the turn signal accordingly. The technology is not exclusive to self-driving cars but is intended to assist manual driving.

The patent application describes a method where the vehicle's processor determines the intent to change lanes or turn based on a measured steering angle value within a stored value range, and then activates the turn signal source. A flowchart in the application illustrates the system's activation process.

Tesla's application for an international patent indicates that the technology is still in development, and it remains unclear when or if it will be integrated into Tesla vehicles. The patent could potentially be used to hinder competition, but if successful, it could significantly reduce accidents caused by drivers failing to use their turn signals.

The technology could serve as a precursor to Tesla's planned Autopilot 'On Ramp/Off Ramp' feature, which is expected to enable autonomous driving on the highway, including lane changes, in the upcoming version 9.0 update.

The study published in the Journal of Cancer Policy suggests that skin cancers caused by indoor tanning in the U.S. result in approximately $343 million in direct medical costs annually. This figure does not include indirect costs such as lost productivity and early deaths among patients with melanoma and other related cancers, which are estimated to exceed $127 billion over the lifetime of the affected individuals.

The study, co-authored by Hugh Waters of the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, found that an estimated 30 million people in the U.S. use tanning beds at least once a year, with approximately 25,000 tanning salons nationwide. To estimate the health costs associated with indoor tanning, the researchers tallied the average costs to treat skin malignancies, including melanoma, squamous cell carcinoma, and basal cell carcinoma.

In 2015, tanning beds were linked to 8,947 cases of melanoma, more than 168,000 cases of squamous cell carcinoma, and at least 86,000 cases of basal cell carcinoma. The average cost of treating melanoma was $5,054 per case, while the typical cost for other skin cancers was $1,168.

In addition to these medical costs, the researchers calculated the economic loss over the lifetime of individuals currently diagnosed with these cancers based on the value of a lost year of life. This estimate was calculated based on the size of the U.S. population and on a measure of the size of the economy known as gross domestic product (GDP) in 2015. Under this formula, a year of life lost resulted in a $55,266 reduction in GDP.

The study also noted that it's possible the number of skin cancers associated with indoor tanning was underestimated, and that the cost estimates did not include long-term medical and productivity costs associated with follow-up physician visits or additional care. However, it's also possible that the economic costs associated with indoor tanning were overestimated, according to Dr. David Leffell, a researcher at Yale School of Medicine in New Haven, Connecticut, who was not involved in the study.

The study's authors hope that putting an estimate on the social costs of indoor tanning will help reduce the use of tanning devices. The Food and Drug Administration has taken steps to regulate tanning beds, including requiring a black-box warning on tanning beds and classifying them as moderate-risk products. The Affordable Care Act also implemented a 10 percent excise tax on indoor tanning services.

Julian Assange, the founder of WikiLeaks, has expressed his displeasure with the upcoming DreamWorks film "The Fifth Estate," which is partly based on the book "Inside WikiLeaks" and stars Benedict Cumberbatch as Assange. In a letter to Cumberbatch, Assange criticized the film for its inaccuracies and its portrayal of him and WikiLeaks, stating that it is based on "deceitful books" and that it will distort events and bury the truth. Assange also expressed concern that the film will be used to harm him and WikiLeaks, and urged Cumberbatch to reconsider his involvement in the project. The film has already been criticized by WikiLeaks for its inaccuracies, and Assange has previously refused to meet with Cumberbatch to discuss the film. The film is set to be released in the United States next week.

Twitter, under the leadership of CEO Dick Costolo, is challenging traditional definitions of a media company. The platform, neither purely a technology nor media company, is considered an "entirely new thing" by Flipboard's Mr. McCue. Twitter has been vocal about protecting user privacy, taking legal actions against New York City courts and the U.S. Justice Department to safeguard user identities.

Dick Costolo joined Twitter in 2010 as CEO, after a move from Chicago to California. He brought back Jack Dorsey, one of the co-founders, in 2011 to address engineering issues. However, Dorsey's role was later reduced due to employee complaints about his work style.

Twitter is contemplating developing its own video-hosting technology, aiming to improve user experience and monetization opportunities. This move could potentially impact third-party video hosting services. The decision is still under discussion within the company.

Costolo's leadership style, characterized by quick decisions and high work ethic, has both positively influenced Twitter's growth and created friction among employees. His emphasis on creating a media-rich Twitter experience could lead to a more engaging platform for users and advertisers, but could also negatively impact third-party service providers.

The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has approved Plan B One-Step, an emergency contraceptive pill, to be available over the counter for women aged 15 and older. The decision partially complies with a federal court ruling in April that instructed the FDA to lift all age restrictions on the pill. The FDA's decision is based on research showing that women aged 15 and older can understand how the pill works, how to use it properly, and that it does not prevent the transmission of sexually transmitted diseases. The pill will still require ID verification at the pharmacy counter. The FDA's decision is a step in the right direction for increased access to emergency contraception, but the Center for Reproductive Rights is not satisfied as it still requires ID verification and may create barriers for some women. The FDA's approval of Plan B One-Step is independent of the ongoing litigation regarding the court ruling. The approval of Plan B One-Step does not affect the prescription status of other emergency contraceptive drugs. The FDA's decision is aimed at further decreasing the rate of unintended pregnancies in the United States.

Michael Cohen, President Donald Trump's personal attorney, is under criminal investigation for months due to his business dealings, according to the Justice Department. The revelation comes after Cohen's attorneys and Trump's attorneys fought with the US Attorney's Office in Manhattan over a massive raid of Cohen's records. Cohen did not appear in court and has not been charged with a crime.

The court filing did not detail what Cohen is under investigation for, but it mentioned that Cohen had done "little to no legal work" and that no emails were exchanged with President Trump. The prosecutors asserted that they have confidence that any seized material would not fall under the significant amount of attorney-client privilege that Cohen has claimed.

The raids covered Cohen's residence, hotel room, office, safety deposit boxes, and two cell phones. Previous search warrants allowed New York federal prosecutors to search multiple email accounts. The prosecutors noted that Cohen had personally not turned over any documents to Robert Mueller's Special Counsel investigation.

The prosecutors are setting up a "taint team" or "filter team" to review Cohen's documents to ensure nothing is used improperly or breaches client confidentiality. Cohen's lawyers have asked to review the material for themselves, a proposal which the Manhattan prosecutors are fighting.

The investigation potentially involves records related to the infamous "Access Hollywood" tape, Stormy Daniels, and Cohen's taxi medallion business. Cohen's lawyers have called the searches "completely inappropriate and unnecessary."

The hearing was put on hold until Monday after an attorney for Trump intervened and requested additional time. The judge ordered the parties to return to court on Monday for another hearing, where Cohen will have to be present. The Southern District of New York prosecutors are asking for a taint team to vet the material seized in the raids.

North Korea's senior diplomat, Choe Son-hui, has criticized US Vice President Mike Pence, calling his remarks "stupid" and threatening a "nuclear showdown" if diplomacy fails. Choe's statement, which was likely sanctioned by North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, came in response to Pence's warning that North Korea "may end like Libya" if it does not give up its nuclear weapons. The planned summit between Trump and Kim, scheduled for June 12, has been met with uncertainty, with both sides suggesting it could be delayed or cancelled. North Korea has insisted it will not give up its nuclear weapons unilaterally.

Choe Son-hui is a top aide to Kim Jong-un and has been involved in several diplomatic interactions with the US over the past decade. Her statement is significant as it indicates North Korea's hardline stance and may cast further doubt on the planned summit. The US had been warned about the sensitivity of comparing North Korea to Libya, as the Gaddafi regime collapsed and he was killed after renouncing nuclear weapons eight years earlier.

Meanwhile, North Korea is pressing ahead with plans to dismantle its only nuclear testing facility later this week. The Punggye-ri site is located in a remote part of the country and a group of international journalists have been invited to observe the event.

The timeline of events leading up to this point includes Trump announcing the summit on May 10, North Korea announcing the dismantling of the test site on May 12, North threatening to scrap the summit over comments by US National Security Advisor John Bolton about the "Libyan model" on May 16, Trump distancing himself from Bolton on May 18, and Trump insisting that unless certain conditions are met, the meeting will not take place on May 22.

Analysis from Laura Bicker, BBC News, Seoul, suggests that careful diplomacy requires careful messaging and careful language, and North Korea feels that the Trump administration has shown a lack of discipline in this regard.
