Marine archaeologists have recovered a bronze arm from an ancient shipwreck off the Greek island of Antikythera, where at least seven more priceless statues from the classical world are believed to lie buried. The ship, believed to have been sailing from Asia Minor to Rome in 1BC, foundered near the island between Crete and the Peloponnese.

The project team, from the Greek Ephorate of Underwater Antiquities and Lund University in Sweden, discovered the buried arm with a bespoke underwater metal detector which has revealed the presence of other large metal objects nearby under the seabed. The bronze arm, probably from a statue of a male, is the highlight of the team's 2017 excavation season.

Among other objects the divers recovered are a patterned slab of red marble the size of a tea tray, a silver tankard, sections of joined wood from the ship's frame, and a human bone. Last year, the team found the skull, teeth, ribs, and other bones of an individual who perished on the wreck. They have since extracted DNA from the skull and from it learned the individual's sex and where they came from.

The latest excavations uncovered a lump of material bearing a bronze disc that matches the size of geared wheels found in the Antikythera mechanism, a remarkable geared device that modelled the motion of the heavens. The team will return to the wreck in the spring, optimistic that they may pull up fresh treasures from the wreck, including the missing planetary gearing from the Antikythera mechanism, or a new piece of mechanism, or another mechanism that was being transported.

The Antikythera wreck first came to light in 1900 when Greek sponge divers happened on the scene in 50 metres of water. Archaeologists have since pulled up spectacular bronze and marble statues, ornate glass and pottery, stunning pieces of jewellery, and the Antikythera mechanism. The chance to recover another group of lifesize statues associated with the wreck is extraordinary, because bronzes are usually encountered randomly under the sea, picked up by fishing nets or chanced upon by divers.

The bronze recycling industry was huge in classical times and later in the medieval period, leading to the destruction of countless statues and other artefacts that would be priceless today. For this reason, many of the finest specimens of bronze statues that survive were once lost at sea. Any chance to recover more Greek sculptures in any medium, but particularly in bronze, should not be missed.

To recover the statues will take a massive effort. The divers must first remove boulders that are in their way, either by hauling them up, or by drilling holes in the rocks and filling them with grout that expands to fracture the stone. Another option is to crack the boulders open with small shaped charges that technical divers use to rescue people trapped when undersea caves collapse. But even if the statues can be lifted from the sea, they will be broken and need costly and time-consuming conservation and reconstruction.

The latest excavations uncovered a lump of material bearing a bronze disc that matches the size of geared wheels found in the Antikythera mechanism. Wound by a handle, the device showed the movement of the sun, moon, and planets in the sky, but not all of the machine was recovered. The disc may be something entirely different. Preliminary x-ray images reveal no teeth, but an image of a bull, suggesting the disc is not a cog but a decorative item.

The team will return to the wreck in the spring, optimistic that they may pull up fresh treasures from the wreck, including the missing planetary gearing from the Antikythera mechanism, or a new piece of mechanism, or another mechanism that was being transported. The chance to recover more Greek sculptures in any medium, but particularly in bronze, should not be missed.

The Harvard Crimson reported that a survey of over 1,300 incoming Harvard students revealed that 10% of the campus' new freshman class have cheated on tests and 42% have cheated on homework. Google has disclosed for the first time the number of requests it has received from government agencies for data about its users and to remove content from its services. The data, presented in a map, shows that Brazil made the most requests for user data during the last six months of 2009, with 3,663, followed by the US with 3,580. Brazil also led with 291 requests for removal of content, with Germany in second place and the US fourth, behind India.

Google's move comes as it faces criticism for not doing enough to explain how it uses the information it collects. A group of privacy commissioners from countries including Canada, France, and the UK have accused Google of privacy abuses, such as inadequate protections in its social-networking service Buzz and its procedures for retaining images it gathers for its Street View mapping services.

Google says it tries to notify users when information about their accounts has been requested and sometimes asks for account and log-in information. The company's new disclosure tool shows that government requests for user data go through Google's legal team, which examines each request to see if it is valid based on the law, narrows the request if possible, and complies only when it must legally do so. Some requests are backed by court order; others aren't.

Privacy advocates have praised Google's move, with Cindy Cohn, legal director of the Electronic Frontier Foundation, stating that it puts numbers behind all the stories we have. However, others have cautioned that the raw numbers are hard to interpret, in part because there is little to compare them with.

Google's disclosure tool also shows that the US made 2,576 requests for the removal of content, followed by Germany with 2,029, India with 1,834, and France with 1,181. The tool excludes data for China, where Google says numerating the requests would be illegal.

Google's chief legal officer, David Drummond, said the company decided to release the tool because it "thought it would be useful in conversations about this trend." He added that the company hopes the tool will shine some light on the scale and scope of government requests for censorship and data around the globe.

North Korea conducted a ballistic missile test on Sunday, marking the second launch in a week and the 10th this year. The missile, described as medium-range, was fired from Pukchang in South Pyongan province and traveled about 310 miles, according to South Korea's armed forces. The launch has sparked international condemnation and threats of tougher UN sanctions.

US Secretary of State Rex Tillerson described the launch as "disappointing" and "disturbing," but rejected the suggestion that the US strategy to tackle North Korea is not working. The latest missile test follows a test of an intermediate-range missile, the Hwasong-12, a week earlier, which according to Pyongyang flew almost 500 miles and was capable of carrying a "heavy" nuclear warhead. Analysts said the Hwasong traveled further than any previous ballistic missile launched by North Korea.

The launches have fueled tension with the administration of US President Donald Trump, who has vowed that such an ICBM launch "won't happen." He warned that no option is off the table in dealing with North Korea's weapons program, although Washington has so far opted for sanctions and diplomatic pressure, while looking to China, North Korea's closest ally, to step up economic pressure on Pyongyang.

Tillerson said the effects of these measures had yet to fully take effect. "I think we are early in the game of putting pressure on them, and one could also interpret that perhaps they are just acting out now in response to some of this pressure," he said in an interview with Fox News Sunday.

US allies South Korea and Japan issued sharp criticism of the latest missile test. Seoul's foreign ministry slammed the "reckless and irresponsible" firing as "throwing cold water on the hope and longing of the new government and the international community" for denuclearization and peace on the Korean peninsula. South Korea's incoming left-leaning government has taken a more conciliatory line with Pyongyang than its conservative predecessors, but has reacted strongly to the latest two missile tests.

Japanese Prime Minister Shinzo Abe said the missile launches "trample on efforts by the international community towards a peaceful solution and are a challenge to the world," Kyodo News reported. The US Pacific Command said it tracked the missile until it landed in the Sea of Japan (East Sea). "US Pacific Command stands behind our ironclad commitment to the security of our allies in the Republic of Korea (South Korea) and Japan," it added in a statement.

Pyongyang has long had missiles that can reach targets across South Korea and Japan. With an imputed range of 2,800 miles, the Hwasong-12 also puts US bases on the Pacific island of Guam within reach. The UN Security Council met behind closed doors last Tuesday to discuss tightening sanctions on North Korea after its May 14 launch. US ambassador Nikki Haley said the United States was working with Beijing on a new sanctions resolution and warned that all countries must step up action against North Korea or face measures themselves.

North Korea says it needs missiles and nuclear weapons to deter any attack by the United States, and state newspaper Minju Joson Sunday threatened more launches. "If the US persists in confrontation with the DPRK (North Korea), the latter will show how the crime-woven history of the US is put to an end," it said. "Many more 'Juche weapons' capable of striking the US will be launched from this land. This is the DPRK's answer to the Trump administration," it said, referring to the national philosophy of "Juche" or self-reliance.

In the aftermath of the deadly attacks in Paris that left 17 people and three gunmen dead, French Prime Minister Manuel Valls has stated that the hunt for accomplices to the attacks is ongoing, as there is "without a doubt" at least one accomplice. It is unclear if Valls was referring to Hayat Boumeddiene, the common-law wife of one of the attackers, or another suspect.

Turkish foreign minister Mevlut Cavusoglu revealed that Boumeddiene arrived in Turkey from Madrid on January 2, ahead of the attacks, and stayed at a hotel in Istanbul with another person before crossing into Syria on Thursday. Turkish intelligence tracked Boumeddiene via her cellphone and discovered that she had arrived in Istanbul's Sabiha Gokcen International Airport and stayed on the Asian side of the city. CCTV video from the airport emerged on Monday that officials say shows Boumeddiene and her traveling companion at the airport's passport control office.

Boumeddiene and her traveling companion, a 23-year-old man, toured Istanbul before leaving for a town near the Turkish border on January 4. Their last phone signal was on January 8 from the border town of Akcakale, where they crossed over into territory controlled by the Islamic State group. Their unused return tickets to Madrid went unused.

Meanwhile, France has ordered 10,000 troops into the streets to protect sensitive sites, with the deployment expected to be fully in place by Tuesday. The focus will be on the most sensitive locations, including Jewish schools, with 4,700 security forces assigned to protect France's 717 Jewish schools.

The common-law husband of Boumeddiene, Amedy Coulibaly, is believed to have killed a French policewoman on Thursday, the day before he killed four hostages at a kosher supermarket. In a video that emerged on Sunday, Coulibaly pledged allegiance to ISIS and defended the attacks on satirical magazine Charlie Hebdo. The SITE Intelligence Group said it had verified the video.

The latest issue of French satirical newspaper Charlie Hebdo, published by survivors of the deadly terror attack, features a cover cartoon of the Prophet Mohammed holding a sign that says "Je suis Charlie," an echo of the slogan of support for freedom of speech that spread across the globe after the tragedy. The press run is a huge jump from the normal circulation of 60,000 copies and reflects the strong outpouring of support from the public.

Some six terror-cell members may still be at large after the Paris terrorism attacks, French police say. Two French police officials have said that one of the at-large cell members has been spotted driving a car registered to the widow of one of the slain attackers, Hayat Boumeddiene, who Turkish officials say is now in Syria. Paris police are searching for a Mini Cooper car registered to Boumeddiene.

The unity rally on Sunday featured a procession led by French President Francois Hollande, who was joined by other world leaders, including German Chancellor Angela Merkel, British Prime Minister David Cameron, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, and Palestinian Authority leader Mahmoud Abbas. Hayat Boumeddiene is wanted in connection with the attacks in France.

The retailer has required manufacturers to provide documents proving that their vehicles comply with safety standards, with a particular focus on the battery and chargers. The move comes after a number of hoverboard fires, including one in a shopping mall in Washington state, and investigations by trading standards authorities in the UK and the US Consumer Product Safety Commission. The CPSC is investigating at least 10 reports of hoverboard fires in nine states. eBay continues to sell hoverboards, but Amazon has suspended sales of most devices on its websites in the US and the UK. Luca Guadagnino's films are known for their exploration of the transformative power of nature and the way it influences the characters' lives. In "Call Me By Your Name," set in the picturesque landscapes of northern Italy, Guadagnino masterfully portrays the summer of 1983 as a leisurely, sensual period where a life-changing romance unfolds between two young men, Elio and Oliver.

Elio, a 17-year-old prodigy with an intellect and wit beyond his years, and Oliver, an American doctoral student, initially seem worlds apart. However, their chemistry is undeniable, and they engage in intellectual banter while navigating their growing feelings for each other. James Ivory's adaptation of Andre Aciman's novel beautifully captures the characters' evolving dynamic, culminating in a powerful, authentic moment when they finally confess their love for each other.

Chalamet and Hammer deliver impressive performances, with Chalamet effortlessly transitioning between English, Italian, and French. Hammer balances Oliver's swagger with vulnerability, making their love scenes both heartbreaking and intensely erotic. The film's visual beauty, enhanced by Sayombhu Mukdeeprom's 35mm images, heightens the sensations and creates an inescapable tension.

Guadagnino's use of music, such as John Adams' "Hallelujah Junction – 1st Movement" and Sufjan Stevens' "Visions of Gideon," adds to the film's emotional depth. The Psychedelic Furs' "Love My Way" is used to great effect, capturing the joy and freedom of their relationship in its early stages and serving as a poignant reminder of their impending separation.

"Call Me By Your Name" is a lush, vibrant masterpiece that explores first love, self-discovery, and the bittersweet nature of fleeting relationships. Its stunning performances, beautiful cinematography, and evocative soundtrack make it a standout film of the year.

The article discusses the death of Toughie, the last Rabbs' fringe-limbed tree frog, at the Atlanta Botanical Garden. Toughie, whose age is unknown but is at least 12 years old, was collected in 2005 during a rescue mission to save frogs from the deadly chytrid fungus. The species was not described until 2008, and it occurred in a small range where the fungus proved especially deadly, leading to the extinction of up to 85% of the amphibians in Toughie's home turf. Toughie was named by Mandica's son and gained popularity as the last of his kind. He was silent for all the years he lived at the botanical garden until 2014 when his call was recorded for the first time.

Photographer Joel Sartore photographed Toughie for the Photo Ark project, which aims to showcase the planet's biodiversity and inspire people to fight the extinction crisis. Sartore has photographed over 6,000 species, many of which represent the end of the line for their kind. Sartore expresses sadness and anger that the plight of endangered species has not yet woken the world up to the extinction crisis.

Toughie had many admirers, and his image was even projected onto St. Peter's Basilica. Now that Toughie has died, an entire species has been lost. The loss of large numbers of animals and plants compromises the healthy ecosystems necessary for everyone's survival, including our own. The surgeries, which include shortening or lengthening toes, collagen injections, and other procedures, are often performed by doctors who specialize in aesthetic foot surgery.

The American Orthopaedic Foot & Ankle Society and the American Podiatric Medical Association are likely to issue statements condemning these medically unnecessary foot operations. Critics argue that it is reprehensible for a physician to correct someone's feet solely to enable them to wear high-end shoes. However, advocates for the procedures argue that they are fulfilling a need for women who invest significantly in their shoes and desire to look their best.

The article highlights the case of Dr. Suzanne M. Levine, a podiatrist who performs cosmetic foot surgeries and has a practice called Institute Beauté. She has been widely quoted in women's magazines and has appeared on network television promoting the procedures. The article also discusses the risks associated with these surgeries, including nerve damage and the inability to wear anything but specially designed shoes.

The article also mentions that foot fashion and function have long been in conflict. Chinese girls' feet were bound to shorten them by bending the toes backward, and high heels have been fashionable in the United States for decades, despite causing not only serious foot problems but also knee, pelvic, back, shoulder, and even jaw pain.

The article concludes by discussing the controversy surrounding these cosmetic foot surgeries and the disagreement among foot doctors over how to respond to such problems. Most advise patients to stop wearing the offending shoes, while an increasing number of doctors are performing delicate and expensive operations to allow women to continue to wear their favorite shoes.

Zig Ziglar, a renowned motivational speaker and author of over 30 books, died on November 28, 2012, at the age of 86, due to pneumonia. Known for his focus on positivity and balanced living, Ziglar was a prolific speaker who appeared alongside world leaders such as several U.S. presidents and former British Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher.

Born in rural Alabama in 1926, Ziglar was raised by his widowed mother and later served in the Navy during World War II. After leaving the University of South Carolina without graduating, he worked as a door-to-door cookware salesman, where he became fascinated with the power of self-help speakers.

Ziglar's first book, "See You at the Top," was published in 1974 and urged readers to re-evaluate their lives with a "checkup from the neck up" and to quit their "stinkin' thinkin'." He often spoke of his religious awakening in 1972 and invoked his faith in his books, such as "Confessions of a Happy Christian" (1978) and "Confessions of a Grieving Christian" (1998), which he wrote after the death of his eldest daughter.

Throughout his career, Ziglar was a regular presence at corporate retreats and conferences for firms such as IBM and J.C. Penney. He attracted millions of devoted followers with his faith-filled proverbs and earnest metaphors about setting goals and facing down adversity.

Ziglar's speeches were filled with corny one-liners, obvious advice, and real-life anecdotes about people who were once considered failures but turned themselves into successes. He was known for his positive attitude and ability to make everyone he met feel like a friend.

Ziglar's company, Ziglar Inc., offers motivation and performance training and features more than a dozen speakers advocating the "Ziglar Way." After a 2007 fall down a flight of stairs left him with a brain injury, Ziglar, along with another daughter, Julie Ziglar Norman, wrote "Embrace the Struggle," a book that described how his life changed after the injury.

Ziglar is survived by his wife, Jean, with whom he celebrated 66 years of marriage on Monday; his son, Tom Ziglar; and daughter Cindy Ziglar Oates. A memorial service is set for Saturday at Prestonwood Baptist Church.

In August 2021, several hundred Pacific walruses have gathered on a barrier island near Point Lay, Alaska, marking the earliest such haul out since the animals first appeared in 2007. The early arrival may be linked to this year's rapidly retreating Arctic sea ice, which has forced the walruses to seek land for rest after feeding.

Typically, adult female and young walruses in the region haul out on sea ice to rest while feeding. However, due to the early retreat of sea ice in the Chukchi Sea this year, the walruses have been forced to travel to the shore and haul out there to rest in between feeding periods.

The gathering of the walruses near Alaska's Chukchi Sea coastline is a result of retreating sea ice in recent years. Walruses typically use floating ice as platforms to rest between dives to forage for food, but summer and fall melt has forced them ashore.

The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service is currently deciding whether to list the Pacific walrus under the Endangered Species Act, with environmental groups arguing that the loss of sea ice threatens to drive the animals toward extinction.

As many as 40,000 animals have hauled out on the narrow islands in recent years, putting them at risk for overcrowding. The villagers of Point Lay are expressing concern about the potential disturbance to the animals, and the Fish and Wildlife Service is actively discouraging people from flying to the village to photograph the walruses.

The gathering of the walruses near Point Lay has happened almost every fall since 2007, a year notable for sea ice retreat. Observers from Point Lay have already reported several dead animals, and the tribal president has expressed concern about the potential disturbance to the animals by aircraft, boats, and ships.

Chelsea Manning, a transgender Army private serving a 35-year sentence for leaking national security secrets, was found guilty of four prison infractions on August 18, 2015. The infractions include disrespect, disorderly conduct, medicine misuse, and possession of prohibited property. As a result, Manning will face 21 days of restrictions on her recreational activities, including no access to a gym, a library, or the outdoors.

The charges against Manning include having books and magazines, such as Vanity Fair and Cosmopolitan, and possessing an expired tube of toothpaste. Prison documents also noted that the Cosmopolitan issue included an interview with Manning, and the Vanity Fair had Caitlyn Jenner on the cover.

Manning's lawyer, Chase Strangio of the American Civil Liberties Union, confirmed the restrictions to USA TODAY via an email. Strangio expressed concern that Manning had to face the disciplinary board for four hours without counsel, stating that it sets a "concerning precedent" for the remainder of her incarceration.

Manning's supporters reacted to the development on Twitter, with some comparing her situation to that of Edward Snowden, former government contractor now living in Russia after leaking information about the National Security Agency.

Manning was initially arrested in May 2010 as intelligence analyst Bradley Manning. He was accused of violating the Espionage Act after releasing about 700,000 classified or sensitive military and diplomatic documents to the Wikileaks website. Charges against Manning ultimately included aiding the enemy, which could have brought the death sentence.

Manning pleaded guilty in February 2013 to 10 of the charges and was later convicted of more charges, but acquitted of aiding the enemy. The day after Manning was sentenced, defense lawyers issued a press release announcing that Manning was a female and asked that she be referred to as Chelsea. Manning later sought hormone therapy and to be able to live as a woman. Transgender individuals were not allowed to serve in the U.S. military, and the Defense Department did not provide such treatment. The Army approved Manning's treatment early this year.

In June 2015, Defense Secretary Ash Carter issued a memo to top military brass and civilians outlining his plan to protect transgender troops from being discharged and directing officials to develop a plan within six months to incorporate those troops into the ranks.

The Motiva Enterprises' Port Arthur, Texas refinery, the nation's largest, may remain shut for up to two weeks due to damage from Tropical Storm Harvey. Historic flooding caused by Harvey has knocked one-fifth of the nation's refining capacity offline, according to S&P Global Platts. Experts said prices could increase as much as 35 cents a gallon as refineries remain offline during storm cleanup.

The U.S. dipped into the strategic oil reserve during other disruptions, such as the 2011 turmoil in Libya and during Hurricane Katrina in 2005. Earlier this year, President Trump proposed selling off half of the oil sitting in the reserve to raise revenue. Some analysts at the time criticized the proposal as risky.

The widespread disruption in the U.S. Gulf Coast has roiled global fuel markets and rerouted millions of barrels of fuel to the Americas to avert shortages. The storm, which lashed Louisiana with rain on Thursday, has pummeled the U.S. Gulf Coast, immersing Houston, Texas, and the surrounding area in several feet of water and forcing the closure of about a quarter of U.S. refining capacity.

The jump came after the Colonial Pipeline, the biggest U.S. fuel system, said it would shut its main lines to the Northeast by Thursday amid outages at pumping points and lack of supply from refiners. That artery can carry 3 million barrels of gasoline and other products daily.

At least two East Coast refineries have run out of gasoline for immediate delivery as they scrambled to fill barges for markets normally supplied by the Gulf Coast, two refinery sources said. Others were seen running at higher rates to boost profitability by filling shortages.

"This is going to be the worst thing the U.S. has seen in decades from an energy standpoint," said an East Coast market source, who declined to be named as he was not authorized to speak to the press.

Chris Kluwe, a former punter for the Minnesota Vikings, was released from the team in May 2013. Kluwe believes that his activism for same-sex marriage rights may have been a factor in his dismissal. In September 2012, Kluwe wrote a letter to a Maryland delegate criticizing him for trampling the free-speech rights of Baltimore Ravens linebacker Brendon Ayanbadejo. The letter went viral and Kluwe was called into the office of Vikings head coach Leslie Frazier, who told him to "be quiet, and stop speaking out on this stuff." Kluwe refused to promise to cease speaking out and was told by Frazier that "if that's what you feel you have to do."

Despite this, Vikings owner Zygi Wilf later told Kluwe that he was proud of his activism and encouraged him to continue speaking out. However, Kluwe claims that special teams coordinator Mike Priefer used homophobic language towards him throughout the 2012 season and that Priefer's behavior towards him worsened after Kluwe's activism became public. Kluwe also claims that Priefer said on multiple occasions that he would wind up burning in hell with the gays, and that the only truth was Jesus Christ and the Bible.

Kluwe believes that his activism for same-sex marriage rights played a role in his release from the Vikings, and he is calling for Mike Priefer to never hold a coaching position in the NFL again. Kluwe is also encouraging Leslie Frazier and Rick Spielman, the general manager of the Vikings, to reflect on their actions and to ensure that similar incidents do not happen in the future.

The Tennessee legislature has approved a resolution that allows the state to sue the federal government over the refugee resettlement program. Republican Governor Bill Haslam, however, has decided not to veto the measure, instead allowing it to go forward without his signature. Haslam has expressed concerns about the measure, stating that it goes against the principle of one branch of government not telling another what to do. He has also asked the state Attorney General to clarify whether lawmakers have the authority to hire outside attorneys to represent the state.

The resolution comes amid fears about refugees in Tennessee following terrorist attacks in Paris and San Bernardino. Supporters of the lawsuit believe that refugees are not being properly vetted by the Obama administration. However, opponents argue that the measure makes the state look unwelcoming and is intended to limit Muslim refugee resettlement.

Immigrant and refugee rights organizations have expressed disappointment that Haslam did not veto the measure. They argue that the resolution is constitutionally suspect and that attempting to dismantle the refugee resettlement program will not make communities safer. The Tennessee Immigrant and Refugee Rights Coalition has called on Haslam to act with greater moral authority and leadership in addressing the global refugee crisis.

The federal Office of Refugee Resettlement has stated that since the passage of the Refugee Act of 1980, over 3 million refugees from more than 70 countries have been given safe haven in the U.S. Tennessee pulled out of the federal refugee resettlement program in 2008, but Catholic Charities of Tennessee has been administering the program since that time.

The Attorney General of Tennessee has previously stated that the state cannot refuse to accept people the federal government has admitted to the country as refugees, as such a refusal would violate the Supremacy Clause of the U.S. Constitution. It remains to be seen how the lawsuit will proceed and whether the state will be able to hire outside counsel to represent it.

In a shocking revelation, secretly recorded phone conversations between Jared Fogle, the former Subway spokesman, and an unidentified individual were aired on Thursday's episode of "Dr. Phil." The conversations, which were allegedly made by Rochelle Herman-Walrond, a former journalist and former radio host from Florida, reportedly contain admissions of Fogle's sexual interest in children.

Fogle pleaded guilty in September to charges of having sex with minors and possessing child pornography, and is scheduled to be sentenced next month to between five and 12-and-a-half years in prison. The FBI has acknowledged receiving the tapes before raiding Fogle's Indiana home on July 7, but has not confirmed that Herman-Walrond ever worked with investigators as an undercover informant.

In one conversation, the speaker, allegedly Fogle, tells Herman-Walrond that he likes boys and girls of "all ages." In another, the speaker asks Herman-Walrond to describe her daughter's 7- and 8-year-old male and female friends, and wants specifics on those "you think are pretty hot" or "cute." The speaker also wants to know who "the most promising" of those children are.

Herman-Walrond told Dr. Phil that she notified Subway about the alleged Fogle recordings in 2011, but the chain issued a statement saying that the complaint came via Subway's website, and that "there was nothing that implied anything about sexual behavior or criminal activity involving Mr. Fogle." However, the chain added that it regretted that the comment was not properly escalated and acted upon.

The FBI declined to comment on the tapes until their investigation was complete. "Dr. Phil" will air more of the recordings on Friday's episode. Fogle's sentencing is scheduled for November.

The Mali coup, which ousted President Amadou Toumani Touré on March 22, has led to a Tuareg rebellion taking control of the northern part of the country. The rebels, primarily members of the nomadic Tuareg people, refuse to be called Malian and aim to establish an independent Tuareg state called Azawad. The Malian army is disintegrating, and potential reinforcements from neighboring countries in the Sahel region pose a threat. The coup has been met with swift response from West African leaders, who have formed a diplomatic emergency committee threatening the junta with heavy sanctions if it does not relinquish power. However, the self-preservation of the presidents of the region influences their desire to restore constitutional order in Bamako. The fighting in northern Mali could damage the World Heritage Site of Timbuktu, with Islamist fighters imposing Islamic law and ransacking bars serving alcohol and Western music. The UN Security Council is due to hold an emergency meeting on the crisis in Mali, and aid agencies warn that 13 million people need food aid following a drought in the region. The coup and Tuareg rebellion have exacerbated a humanitarian crisis in Mali and neighboring countries.

The study, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, suggests that the rise of the Mongol Empire in the 13th century may have been influenced by favorable climate conditions. Researchers analyzed the tree-ring records of Siberian pine trees in central Mongolia and found that the period of Genghis Khan's conquests was characterized by 15 consecutive years of above-average moisture, which is unprecedented over the last 1,112 years. This period of persistent moisture likely contributed to high grassland productivity, providing ample resources for the Mongol war horses. The study also indicates that the early 21st-century drought in central Mongolia was the hottest drought in the last 1,112 years, potentially indicating the impact of anthropogenic warming. The researchers propose that unusual climatic events at the decadal time scale can significantly affect ecosystems and societies in semiarid regions. The study suggests that the good weather conditions during the rise of the Mongol Empire may have provided the ideal conditions for a charismatic leader like Genghis Khan to emerge and unite disparate tribes into an efficient military unit that rapidly conquered its neighbors.

JK Rowling, the author of the Harry Potter series, has filed a £24,000 lawsuit against her former personal assistant, Amanda Donaldson, for alleged misuse of funds. The lawsuit, filed at Airdrie Sheriff Court in Scotland, claims that Donaldson, who worked for Rowling from February 2014 to April 2017, breached trust by using a business credit card for personal expenses and taking Harry Potter merchandise without authorization.

The alleged unauthorized expenses include £823 at Bibi Bakery, £1,482 at luxury candle company Jo Malone, £3,629 in cosmetic firm Molton Brown, £2,139 in card shop Paper Tiger, £1,636 in Starbucks, and various other purchases. Rowling also claims that Donaldson took three Harry Potter-related items worth over £6,000 without her knowledge or consent.

In addition, the lawsuit alleges that Donaldson took £7,742-worth of foreign money from a safe, bought two cats worth £1,200, and withdrew £400 in cash for a restaurant lunch but did not pay the deposit.

Donaldson has denied the claims and stated that Rowling has not suffered any loss and is not entitled to damages from her. The case is due back in court later this year.

Rowling's spokeswoman confirmed the legal action against Donaldson, stating that it was taken following her dismissal for gross misconduct involving a substantial breach of trust. The spokeswoman added that, as the case is not yet concluded, they are unable to comment further and there will be no comment from Rowling. Donaldson was unavailable for comment.

Following President Obama's call for acceptance of Donald Trump's victory, tens of thousands of protesters, including many too young to vote, took to the streets in cities across the United States to express their discontent with Trump's presidency. The demonstrations, which started on Wednesday, continued into the second night, with Portland, Oregon, experiencing a "riot" according to police. A small group of "anarchists" in a crowd of 4,000 reportedly smashed cars with baseball bats, threw rocks and Molotov cocktails, and spray-painted graffiti, leading to 26 arrests.

Protests also took place in Columbus, Ohio; Minneapolis; Madison, Wis.; and Milwaukee, among other cities. Trump addressed the protests on Twitter, calling them "professional protesters, incited by the media," but later issued a conciliatory message, stating that he appreciated the passion of the protesters and looked forward to unity.

The anti-Trump movement, barely 48 hours old, appears to lack strategy and coordination, but some activists are focusing on the electoral college, which is due to meet on December 19 to formally vote Trump into office. Political scientists say that while electors have in the past switched their votes, such occurrences are rare and have not altered the election outcome.

Clinton appears to be on track to win the popular vote, with a lead of 388,000 votes as of the last count. In the past, about 99% of electors have voted for the candidate to whom they are pledged, but defections do happen, and Democratic activists are working on persuading Republican electors who have expressed anti-Trump sentiments.

A petition on Change.org received over 2 million signatures in less than 24 hours, but it does not appear to have the support of Clinton, who has urged the American public to accept Trump. The protests, which have been less about supporting Clinton than opposing Trump, threaten to prolong an already painful and prolonged election process.

Many young voters were unenthusiastic about Clinton, failing to lend her campaign the energy they put behind Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders or for those old enough, behind Barack Obama in 2008. The protests have been marked by slogans such as "#notourpresident" and "#notmypresident," and have targeted Trump-branded buildings, with a Trump effigy being burned in Los Angeles and protesters blocking the 101 Freeway and spray-painting anti-Trump graffiti on vehicles and buildings.

In New York City, two separate marches converged in front of Trump Tower, where Trump lives in a penthouse condominium, forming a crowd that some reporters estimated at 10,000. The night was illuminated by hundreds of iPhones taking selfies of protesters gesturing with their middle fingers toward the Trump building. There were 65 arrests in New York City, mostly for disorderly conduct, obstructing governmental administration, and resisting arrest.

On November 4, 2016, a former student allegedly stabbed a faculty member and a student at Rutgers Business School in Piscataway, New Jersey. The incident occurred around 2:30 p.m. on the Livingston Campus. The suspect fled the scene but was later apprehended with self-inflicted injuries. Rutgers University issued a lockdown alert and advised students to shelter in place. The lockdown was lifted shortly after, but students were shaken up. The investigation is ongoing, and no charges have been filed. The university called the incident an "isolated incident."

A Jefferson Parish judge ruled on August 7 that there was probable cause to hold Shantel Wagner, the wife of Jefferson Parish Sheriff's Office Sgt. Troy Smith, on a charge of second-degree murder for Smith's shooting death. The judge reduced Wagner's bond from $500,000 to $300,000 and ordered that she be fitted with a GPS-enabled ankle monitor and confined to home at all times except for medical appointments.

The ruling came after a two-day hearing in which Sheriff's Office investigators presented evidence that physical evidence does not support Wagner's various stories to investigators that her husband committed suicide by a gunshot to the head. Prosecutors also accused Wagner of admitting guilt to a witness.

Defense attorneys for Wagner argued that Smith was suffering from PTSD, was depressed, had financial and relationship troubles, and had threatened to kill himself just the day before in a text message. They also pointed out that Wagner's DNA was not found on the gun used in the shooting.

The ruling marked the end of an unusually long, two-day hearing in commissioner's court. Smith, 44, died on June 24, one week after Wagner called 911 to report that he had tried to commit suicide inside their Waggaman home on Father's Day.

Sheriff's Office detectives arrested Wagner on July 11, noting that forensic evidence and interviews led authorities to determine that Smith's injury wasn't self-inflicted. Dr. Dana Trosclair, the forensic pathologist who conducted Smith's autopsy, took the stand Tuesday. But Trosclair and coroner's office attorney Chuck Credo told the court she could not yet provide an official opinion on whether Smith's death was a homicide or a suicide because the final autopsy report was not complete, according to court records. Toxicology samples are still being tested.

Palazzo, who employed Wagner as a paralegal at his Gretna law firm, did have Trosclair identify the location of Smith's entry wound, the "parietal scalp, right above the right ear," she said. The exit wound was on the "vertex" or top of the scalp. Trosclair described the trajectory as right to left, slightly front to back and upward.

Chief Deputy Tim Scanlan, commander of the Sheriff's Office Crime Lab, also took the stand Tuesday. He testified that his technicians are in the preliminary stages of reconstructing the shooting. Beevers pressed Scanlan with questions about bullet trajectory and whether he could he sure a hole found in the ceiling of the couple's home was made by a projectile fired at the time of Smith's shooting. Scanlan conceded that Wagner's DNA was not found on the gun recovered at the shooting scene. But he also testified that the totality of evidence is inconsistent with Smith shooting himself.

Palazzo passionately argued that the state did not prove probable cause to hold Wagner on a murder charge. None of the evidence presented during the hearing prove Wagner shot her husband, he said. In the end, Schneider agreed with Rish that Wagner's multiple inconsistent statements and the alleged confession to a witness rises to the level of probable cause.

Although Schneider lowered Wagner's bond, Palazzo said the family will not be able to meet the $300,000 amount and called her prosecution political. "It is an absolute tragedy," he said.

The wife of a Jefferson Parish Sheriff's Office deputy has been arrested and booked with second-degree murder in his death. Shantel Wagner, 35, of Waggaman, is accused of killing Sgt. Troy Smith, an instructor and hostage negotiator with the department, according to the Sheriff's Office.

Wagner called 911 on Father's Day, June 17, around 11:25 p.m. and reported Smith had tried to commit suicide in the bedroom of their Camellia Lane home, according to Lt. Jason Rivarde, spokesman for the department. Smith remained hospitalized for about a week before succumbing to his injuries. He was 44 years old.

But detectives determined through forensic evidence and interviews that Smith's injury wasn't self-inflicted, Rivarde said. Jefferson Parish Coroner Dr. Gerry Cvitanovich declined to comment about the case on Wednesday. Detectives obtained a warrant for Wagner's arrest and took her into custody around 1 a.m. Wednesday at a home in the 4900 block of Jean Lafitte Boulevard in Lafitte, Rivarde said.

Smith and Wagner married on Nov. 16, 2016, according to court records. Smith joined the New Orleans Police Department in 1995 and worked as a bomb technician and a member of the SWAT team. Smith joined JPSO in November 2013 as an instructor at the department's training academy, according to Rivarde.

NOPD Capt. Michael Glasser said those within NOPD who worked with Smith were "devastated" to hear of the shooting and subsequent death a few weeks ago, when they were unaware of the circumstances. "Now that (murder allegations have) become evident, we're even more devastated," added Glasser, the president of the Police Association of New Orleans. Smith's NOPD colleagues were sorry to see him leave the department, Glasser said, but happy he returned to law enforcement in the neighboring agency.

"Troy was extremely competent and extremely well thought of," Glasser said. Smith had also worked as a civilian contractor with the Department of Defense and was a 1st Lieutenant in the Mississippi State Guard. He was a member of the guard's 3rd Brigade and served as the group's Operations Training Officer, according to Lt. Russ Jones, spokesman for the Mississippi State Guard. Smith was named Non-Commissioned Officer of the Year in 2017 for both the Guard and the State Guard Association of the United States.

"We saw in Lt. Smith the same level of dedication and loyalty he displayed with his police work. He was a good soldier," Jones said in a statement released Wednesday.

A 99-year-old Dutch woman, known as Annie, fulfilled an unconventional wish on her bucket list by being arrested and spending time in a jail cell. Annie had expressed her desire to experience being in a police cell, and the local police in Nijmegen-Zuid granted her request. The police shared pictures of the smiling centenarian on their Facebook page, documenting the unique experience. The event was described as a "day to remember" for all involved.

In the realm of celebrity news, Heidi Montag, known for her reality TV stardom on The Hills, has released a new album titled Superficial. The album, which features the R-rated single "I'll Do It," where Montag invites a lover to "come eat my panties off of me," is a three-year labor of love. Montag, who is currently focusing on her pop star career, has put her plans for a family with husband Spencer Pratt on hold. The album's title, Superficial, Montag explains, is a double entendre, representing both the superficial nature of Hollywood and its deeper, more authentic side. Montag and Pratt have also taken up yoga to find inner peace and calmness. The album is now available for listening, despite its explicit lyrics that may raise eyebrows.

On Friday, a man attempted to jump the White House fence, causing a temporary lockdown and a brief closure of Pennsylvania Avenue. The incident occurred along the north perimeter of the Whitehouse, and Secret Service agents apprehended the individual before he could get over the fence. The man was not identified, and charges have not yet been placed. President Obama was not at the White House at the time, as he was in Michigan for a speech and the signing of the farm bill. The incident disrupted pedestrian traffic for over an hour.

The 25th anniversary edition of the amfAR Gala Cannes was held on May 17, 2018, at Hôtel du Cap-Eden-Roc in Cap d'Antibes, France. The event, presented by Bold Films and Chopard, was produced by AAB Productions/Andy Boose. Honorary chairs included celebrities such as Alessandra Ambrosio, Poppy Delevingne, Linda Evangelista, and Scarlett Johansson, among others.

The event featured spectacular performances by Sting and Shaggy, Grace Jones, Ellie Goulding, and Jason Derulo, as well as a fashion show curated by Carine Roitfeld. The looks were auctioned off as a collection, fetching $1.7 million. Other auction highlights included a Pierce Brosnan original painting, which sold for $1.4 million; a restored 1964 S3 Bentley Convertible, introduced by Heidi Klum and Benicio Del Toro, which sold for over $800,000; and a Joe Bradley painting, which brought in nearly $1 million.

Pierce Brosnan, who has been painting for more than 20 years, donated one of his original paintings, a portrait of Bob Dylan, for the auction. The painting sold for $1.4 million, and the new owner also won a lunch date with the actor. Brosnan described his art as "self-taught" and said he hopes to put on an exhibit and make a book shortly.

Other highlights of the event included the sale of an $800,000 restored 1964 S3 Bentley Convertible and a nearly $1 million painting by Joe Bradley. The evening also featured a fashion show presented by former Vogue Paris editor Carine Roitfeld.
