A new pill called Nalmefene, also known as Selincro, is now available to individuals in the UK who consume at least half a bottle of wine or three pints of alcohol per night. The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (Nice) has issued formal guidance recommending the drug, which reduces the urge to drink and can be prescribed alongside counselling support. The pill, which costs £3 per day, helps patients gradually cut back on their alcohol intake and is suitable for those who regularly drink high amounts of alcohol, as defined by the World Health Organisation.

Nalmefene is expected to be prescribed to more than 35,000 people in the first year, although the actual number may be lower. The drug is not suitable for those with severe alcohol problems who need to stop immediately. Lyndsey Dudley, a spokeswoman for Nice, stated that the drug is designed to support individuals who "probably don’t even recognize themselves as alcoholics."

Professor Carole Longson, Nice's health technology evaluation centre director, emphasized that regularly drinking over the recommended daily amount of alcohol can seriously damage one's health. She also noted that those who could be prescribed nalmefene have already taken the first steps towards addressing their alcohol dependency by visiting their doctor, engaging with support services, and participating in therapy programs.

Professor Jonathan Chick, a medical adviser for Drinkaware, clarified that the drug is intended for people who are concerned about their drinking, have tried to cut down, have been given brief advice/counselling by their doctor, and are still regularly drinking more than low-risk levels. He also pointed out that the risks associated with alcohol start at 14 units per week for women and 21 for men, but patients who will be prescribed nalmefene will be drinking higher amounts than that, and will have provoked changes in their brain patterns which have led to difficulty controlling their drinking.

In the primary election held on March 22, 2016, in Phoenix, Arizona, voters faced long wait times of up to four hours to cast their ballots. Gustavo Mendez, a 25-year-old voter, waited for four hours to vote for Sen. Bernie Sanders, with some voters waiting until 1 a.m. due to a significant reduction in polling places. Maricopa County, which has 2 million registered voters, had 200 polling places in the 2012 presidential primary and 400 in 2008, but only 60 polling places were available in 2016. The last polling place closed at 12:58 a.m., meaning the final voters had to wait nearly six hours. The U.S. Justice Department is investigating the election to determine if it disproportionately affected minority voters. The investigation comes after the Arizona Legislature slashed funding for counties to carry out the presidential election, leading to scaled-back polling. Despite the investigation, Arizona Secretary of State Michele Reagan certified the results of the presidential primary on March 28, 2016, with Donald Trump and Hillary Clinton winning. Lawyers for Bernie Sanders are considering challenging the results due to problems with voter rolls and the potential for additional delegates to the Democratic convention. The long wait times and other issues faced during the Arizona primary have been compared to the 2000 presidential fiasco in Florida.

The bankruptcy trustee of Sunland Inc., a peanut-processing plant that was at the center of a 2012 salmonella outbreak and subsequent nationwide recall, is dumping nearly a million jars of peanut butter at a New Mexico landfill due to refusal by Costco Wholesale to take the product. The peanut butter, estimated to be worth $2.6 million, was made with Valencia peanuts owned by Costco and had been sitting in the warehouse since the company shut down and filed for bankruptcy last fall.

After extensive testing, Costco agreed to a court order authorizing the trustee to sell it the peanut butter. However, after receiving eight loads, Costco rejected it as "not merchantable" because of leaky peanut oil. The trustee considered all options, including donation to food banks or repackaging or selling to brokers, but Costco declined all requests.

As a result, the estate is paying about $60,000 to haul the 950,000 jars of peanut butter to a Curry County landfill in Clovis, where it will be disposed of with regular waste and covered with dirt. The last of 58 truckloads was expected on Friday.

Sunland made peanut butter under a number of different labels for retailers like Costco, Kroger, and Trader Joe's, along with products under its own name. The plant was shut down in September 2012 after its products were linked to 41 salmonella cases in 20 states. It later reopened for about five months, but shut down last October after the company's Chapter 7 bankruptcy filing.

In a separate development, a Canadian company, Golden Boy Foods, has made a last-minute offer to buy the shuttered Portales peanut butter factory for $25 million, which has been deemed too good to ignore. The bankruptcy court judge has ordered that bidding for Sunland's assets be reopened, with Golden Boy's $25 million offer serving as the opening bid in an auction scheduled for 10 a.m. today in U.S. Bankruptcy Court in Albuquerque. The judge will consider final approval of the winning bid in a separate hearing set for 1 p.m.

Golden Boy's bid is $5 million more than the high bidder at the previous auction last week. Both Hampton Farms and Golden Boy say they would resume manufacturing operations at the Portales plant. The additional $5 million offered by Golden Boy would help settle more of Sunland's debt. The judge's decision to reopen bidding is expected to benefit the creditors.

The Maine Department of Transportation is announcing the results of its "My Maine Sign" contest, where participants submitted safety-themed messages to be displayed on humorous highway signs. Over 2,000 entries were received, and finalists will be chosen by the end of March. The public will then vote on the finalists' submissions using the department's website.

The winners will receive their message in neon lights on the highway signs, as well as various transportation-related prizes such as a ride to the Penobscot Narrows Bridge & Observatory, Maine State Ferry tickets, and a state park vehicle pass. The grand prize winners will also receive a personalized street sign from the state's sign shop.

The winning submissions for the smaller-sized road signs are: "Put Down UR Cell — Or You May End Up In One," by Katie Landry; "Spend Money On Lobstahs — Not Speeding Tickets," by Dan Zarin; and "Little Known Fact — Snow Is Really Slippery," by Tim Fahey. The winning submissions for the larger road signs are: "A Cold Suppah Is Bettah Thana Hot Ticket," by Craig Carver; "Be Protected — Not Projected – Buckle Up," by Laura Giuliano; "Keep In Mind — Moose Eyes Don't Shine," by Terry White.

The contest aimed to discourage unsafe behavior such as distracted or impaired driving, speeding, or texting behind the wheel. The department intends to archive the best ideas for future use. Drivers can expect to see the winning submissions posted along the highway in the coming year.

A barroom brawl occurred at Mackinac Island, Michigan, during a Republican political gathering, involving top aides for Senators Marco Rubio and Rand Paul. John Yob, a consultant for the Rand Paul campaign, alleged that Rubio's deputy campaign manager, Rich Beeson, assaulted him at Horn's Bar. Yob posted a grainy video of the incident on Facebook, but details are unclear. The Mackinac Island Police Department is investigating the alleged assault, and a formal report has not yet been completed. Police Chief Brett Riccinto stated that they have taken witness statements and security camera video from inside the bar. The county prosecutor will decide whether criminal charges will be filed. The incident has already become part of Michigan political lore, as a similar incident involving alcohol and a punch occurred at Horn's Bar in 2003. Sen. Rand Paul is expected to speak at the conference, while Sen. Marco Rubio is not in attendance.

In a lawsuit filed in New York County Court, Tricia Fraser, the mother of a 6-year-old girl named Anissa, is suing Heroic Media and anti-abortion group Life Always, claiming they violated her contract and used her daughter's image in a controversial and racist advertising campaign. The controversial ad, which initially caused a stir in February, featured Anissa in a sun dress and the warning, “The most dangerous place for an African American is in the womb.” The ad triggered outrage, culminating in the Reverend Al Sharpton threatening to picket its location near the Holland Tunnel in Manhattan.

The mother claims that she never agreed to have her daughter's image associated with the offensive and defamatory statement. She signed a release allowing her daughter to be photographed for stock "family photos," but the photo was purchased by Heroic Media from Getty Images with the agreement that it would not be used "in connection with a subject that would be unflattering or unduly controversial to a reasonable person."

Tricia Fraser alleges that the defendants used her daughter's picture in massive billboards on a busy street in Manhattan and in Jacksonville, Florida. She claims that the defendants bought a license to use the photo of Anissa as part of a campaign designed to shame African-American women from exercising their constitutional rights to reproductive freedom. The defendants erected the New York billboard in February, directing viewers to Thatsabortion.com, which is registered to Majella Cares.

The mother claims that the billboard was defamatory of Anissa and herself, giving the false suggestion that they approved of the racist and offensive message contained therein. She also alleges that the billboard caused substantial controversy, reported throughout international media and on the internet, and that her daughter's image was widely disseminated throughout the world in connection with an offensive, defamatory, and racist statement.

Tricia Fraser demands punitive damages for violation of New York civil rights law and breach of contract, disgorgement of any money the defendants raised from Anissa's image, and an injunction prohibiting them from using her image "in any way." The defendants, Heroic Media, Life Always, and Pastor Stephen Broden, did not immediately respond to calls for comment.

The Federal Reserve, in a statement following a meeting of its policy-making committee, acknowledged a slowdown in economic growth and a likely "moderate" pace over the coming quarters. The unemployment rate is expected to decline only slowly, prompting the central bank to promise additional accommodation if necessary to promote a stronger economic recovery and sustained improvement in labor market conditions.

The Fed did not take any new steps to support the economy, disappointing some equity investors. The Standard & Poor's 500-stock index and the Dow Jones industrial average both fell in response to the announcement.

Fed Chairman Ben Bernanke is expected to clarify his views at an annual monetary policy conference in Jackson Hole, Wyoming, at the end of August. Some economists anticipate a major new asset-purchase plan, including the buying of mortgage-backed securities, at the Fed's next policy meeting in September. However, others are not so sure that more purchases, or quantitative easing, are inevitable.

The Fed has already engaged in a wide-ranging effort to spur growth, including cutting interest rates, punishing savers, and rewarding borrowers. The central bank has held its benchmark rate near zero since late 2008 and plans to maintain that policy at least until late 2014. It has also put pressure on long-term rates by amassing a portfolio of almost $3 trillion in long-term Treasury securities and mortgage-backed securities.

The economy has been struggling for over three years, with unemployment remaining pervasive and more than 23 million Americans unable to find full-time jobs. Some Fed officials remain uncertain that the economy needs help, as economic indicators are imprecise in times of turbulence, and cheap loans are at best an indirect means of addressing problems like the decline in government spending, tight credit standards, and high levels of household debt.

The British government sent a Royal Air Force plane to Cyprus on Tuesday carrying one million euros ($1.3 million) in emergency loans for British military personnel and their families. The move was a contingency plan in response to the ongoing financial crisis in Cyprus, where banks have been closed due to a controversial eurozone bailout deal. The British government has also assured that it will fully refund any military or government personnel whose Cyprus bank accounts are affected by the levy imposed as part of the bailout deal. The RAF flight left the UK earlier this afternoon, with the money onboard designated for emergency loans in the event that cash machines and debit cards stop working on the crisis-hit Mediterranean island. The British government is proactively approaching personnel to ask if they want their March, and future months' salaries paid into UK bank accounts, rather than Cypriot accounts. The announcement comes amid concerns about the impact of Cyprus' banking problems on British troops posted to the island, with more than 3,000 British service personnel based at two military bases in Cyprus. The proposed Cypriot bailout is the first one that dips into people's bank accounts to finance the measures, and has sparked controversy and concerns about the security of bank deposits in Cyprus. The bailout package involves the International Monetary Fund (IMF), European Central Bank, and European Union.

In a new study published in the Journal of the American Heart Association, researchers from the University of California San Francisco have found that regular caffeine consumption, contrary to current medical beliefs, does not contribute to heart palpitations or extra heartbeats. The study, which is the largest to date to evaluate dietary patterns in relation to extra heartbeats, challenges the widely held clinical belief that caffeine products can lead to extra heartbeats.

The study involved nearly 1,400 randomly selected patients who were part of the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI) Cardiovascular Health Study database. The subjects were given a baseline food frequency assessment and 24-hour ambulatory electrocardiography monitoring with the frequency of regular consumption of coffee, tea, or chocolate determined by a survey.

Of the 1,388 subjects participating in the study, 840 or 61% consumed more than one caffeinated product daily. The researchers found no differences in the number of PACs (premature atrial contractions) or PVCs (premature ventricular contractions) per hour across levels of coffee, tea, and chocolate consumption. More frequent consumption of these products was not associated with extra heartbeats.

The study's senior author, UCSF Health cardiologist Gregory Marcus, MD, MAS, said, "Clinical recommendations advising against the regular consumption of caffeinated products to prevent disturbances of the heart’s cardiac rhythm should be reconsidered, as we may unnecessarily be discouraging consumption of items like chocolate, coffee, and tea that might actually have cardiovascular benefits."

The study's findings indicate that moderate coffee drinking may have potential health benefits, as it has been associated with a lower risk of type 2 diabetes mellitus and other cardiovascular risk factors such as obesity and depression. Furthermore, large observational studies have found that habitual coffee drinkers have lower rates of coronary artery disease and of cardiovascular and all-cause mortality.

However, the study did not examine the impact of acute consumption of caffeinated products on extra heartbeats, and further research is needed to determine whether excessive caffeine consumption can be harmful. The Food and Drug Administration has warned about sales of powdered caffeine, as one teaspoon delivers as much caffeine as 28 cups of regular coffee.

The study's findings may help to reduce uncertainty among doctors when it comes to counseling patients on the consumption of caffeinated products like coffee, chocolate, and tea. The study challenges the widely held belief that caffeine can cause dangerous heart rhythm disorders and provides another vindication for coffee as a safe drink.

Two former Nazi SS guards, aged 93 and 92, have been indicted by German prosecutors for being accessories to murder while they worked at the Stutthof concentration camp during World War II. The men, from Borken and Wuppertal, served at the camp from June 1942 to September 1944 and June 1944 to May 1945, respectively. The charges were filed last week at the state court in Muenster but only announced this week. Both defendants deny any knowledge of the killings at the camp.

Stutthof, located near Gdansk, Poland, was a concentration camp where approximately 65,000 people died, some from gas chambers, shootings, malnutrition, or freezing to death. The men served as guards and watched over prisoners who were taken outside the camp to work. During their tenure, hundreds of killings occurred at the camp.

Members of the SS killed more than 100 Polish prisoners and some 77 Soviet prisoners of war in the camp's gas chamber in 1944. An unknown number of Jews were also gassed there in late 1944. Between June 1944 and April 1945, SS members killed several hundred Jews by shooting them in the back of the neck. SS-physicians and nurses at Stutthof killed more than 140 prisoners, many of them Jewish women and children, by injecting their hearts with gasoline and the chemical compound phenol from late 1942 until late 1944.

German prosecutors have pursued Nazi suspects under new legal reasoning that allows them to be prosecuted if they helped camps operate, even without evidence of a specific crime. Holocaust survivor Judy Meisel, 88, from St. Louis Park, Minnesota, has provided essential testimony for prosecutors, including identifying one of the ex-guards, Johann Rehbogen, as a teenage SS officer who taunted her and other female prisoners.

Meisel could join prosecutors as a "co-plaintiff" in the case. The charges against Rehbogen and Harry Paul Fritz Schulz, 92, represent a new and vital chapter for survivors like Meisel. The trial could commence next summer if the defendants are deemed healthy enough. Meisel, her son, and other witnesses from Ohio, New Jersey, New York, and Florida have been named in the case.

Meisel has described her mother's death in the gas chamber at Stutthof and the wave of emotions the indictments have brought back. She welcomes any chance to tell her story "for the important lessons it teaches about tolerance and racism." The indictments are a determination not to "simply move aside and forget about" those responsible for the atrocities committed at Stutthof.

The deciphered coded text, believed to be part of an oath-taking process for the 'Ndrangheta, a powerful mafia network based in southern Italy, offers insights into their secretive initiation rituals. The document, discovered during a high-profile murder investigation in Rome, was found alongside weapons and ammunition. The script, written in a unique alphabet, was cracked by two Italian policemen with a passion for crosswords. The document is said to be the formula new members must recite to join the "San Luca" clan, and is rich in symbolism, describing the signs to recognize a mafioso, or "Man of Honour". The 'Ndrangheta, known as Europe's biggest cocaine smugglers, has surpassed Sicily's Cosa Nostra as Italy's most powerful mafia, and operates across Europe with connections to Colombian drug cartels. The discovery of this document sheds light on the mafia's quasi-mystical aura surrounding their recruitment process.

A fire aboard an empty Boeing 787 airplane operated by Ethiopian Airlines occurred at Heathrow Airport, leading to the temporary closure of both runways. The incident, treated as unexplained by British police, comes after the planes were grounded in January due to battery issues. The planes resumed flying in May after Boeing made redesigns to the battery system, with Ethiopian Airlines being the first to resume using the 787. Boeing shares fell 6.7 percent to $99.68 following the incident. Boeing personnel are currently investigating the event at Heathrow. The Ethiopian Airlines Dreamliner involved in the Heathrow incident, named the Queen of Sheba, had resumed flights after the grounding and was the first commercial flight since the grounding. The Air Accidents Investigation Branch has dispatched a team to the scene. Meanwhile, Thomson Airways experienced a technical issue with one of its Dreamliners, causing it to return to Manchester Airport. This is the second incident involving a Boeing 787 Dreamliner on Friday.

On June 17, 2015, a white man opened fire during a prayer meeting inside Emanuel African Methodist Episcopal Church (AME Church) in downtown Charleston, South Carolina, killing nine people and leaving the city and the nation in shock. The shooter, identified as 21-year-old Dylann Storm Roof, was later arrested in Shelby, North Carolina, following a massive manhunt.

The victims of the shooting ranged in age from 26 to 87 and included Clementa Pinckney, the primary pastor and a state senator, Cynthia Hurd, a county librarian, Sharonda Coleman-Singleton, a church pastor and coach of the girls' track and field team at Goose Creek High School, Tywanza Sanders, a college graduate, Ethel Lance, a retired church janitor, Susie Jackson, Lance's cousin and longtime church member, DePayne Middleton-Doctor, a pastor, Myra Thompson, a pastor, and Daniel Simmons Sr., a pastor who died in a hospital operating room.

The shooting was described as a hate crime by the U.S. Justice Department, and Roof has shown interest in racial segregation and the Confederacy. The tragedy renewed discussions about gun control and racial tensions in the United States.

The shooting took place during a Bible study and prayer service in the basement of the church, which has a long and complicated history involving race. The gunman sat quietly for 40 to 50 minutes before rising and opening fire.

The aftermath of the shooting brought local activists, Charleston's police chief, and South Carolina's governor to tears as they struggled to find words to ease the community's fear of further violence. President Barack Obama called the shooting a "dark part" of American history and said the nation needed to have a national introspection about the availability of guns.

The shooting also drew attention to the Charleston area, as it came just three months after the fatal shooting of Walter Scott, a black man shot in the back by a white North Charleston police officer, which prompted federal investigations. The FBI is examining potential civil rights violations in both cases.

The community mourned and searched for answers, with hundreds packing prayer vigils in a show of solidarity and support for the fallen and their families. Roof was charged with nine counts of murder and waived extradition, allowing him to be flown back to Charleston County to face charges in what has been called one of the worst hate crimes in the United States in decades.

The shooting at Emanuel AME Church is a tragic reminder of the long and complicated history of race in America, and the ongoing need for dialogue and action to address racial inequality and violence.

The United States is poised to finish atop the medals table at the London Olympics, potentially with the most golds ever collected by the Americans on foreign soil. The surge in medals has been driven by the track and field team, which has won 26 medals, including eight golds, through Friday. Bryshon Nellum, an Olympic silver medalist who was shot in the legs in 2008, will carry the U.S. flag at Sunday's closing ceremony. Nellum was part of the men's 4x400-meter relay team that finished second to the Bahamas on Friday night, and he also competed in the 400-meter dash in London, making the semifinal round. China, which beat the U.S. in gold medals at the 2008 Beijing Games, is currently in second place in both the gold and overall medals races. The Chinese started strong but are facing a challenge in swimming and track and field, where the U.S. has excelled. Britain, heavily promoting its athletes as Team GB, has excelled particularly in rowing and track cycling, thanks in large part to generous funding from the national lottery and the government-backed U.K. Sport body. U.K. Sport allocated $470 million for sports federations and athletes ahead of the London Games. South Korea has also performed well, asserting itself as an Asian power with 13 golds. The Russians, who have won plenty of silver and bronze, are third in the overall count but have failed to compete with the U.S. in track and field. Japan has performed strongly, with 35 medals, but has failed to turn them into gold, picking up only five. Australia and Germany have been among the biggest disappointments, with both countries lagging behind their projected medal counts.

President Donald Trump's nominee for Secretary of the Navy, Philip Bilden, a former military intelligence officer and private equity firm executive, has withdrawn from consideration due to concerns over privacy and separating himself from his business interests. This withdrawal follows a similar issue faced by Vincent Viola, Trump's nominee for Secretary of the Army, who withdrew earlier this month due to the same reasons.

Bilden, who served in the Army Reserve from 1986-1996 and relocated to Hong Kong to set up an Asian presence for HarbourVest Partners LLC, a global private equity management firm, recently retired from the firm after 25 years. In a statement, Bilden cited the need to avoid "undue disruption and materially adverse divestment of my family's private financial interests" to satisfy the Office of Government Ethics requirements.

Defense Secretary Jim Mattis will recommend a new nominee for the position in the coming days. The Pentagon had previously stated that Bilden remained committed to serving as Navy Secretary if confirmed by the Senate, but press reports suggested he might withdraw. Viola, a military veteran and businessman, also withdrew due to difficulties navigating the confirmation process and Defense Department rules concerning family businesses.

In a heartwarming turn of events, a 16-year-old named Chauncy Jones Black from Memphis, Tennessee, has gained widespread support after a chance encounter with a stranger named Matt White at a grocery store. The encounter, which took place at the "rich people's Kroger," led to Matt helping Chauncy with groceries and learning about his struggles.

Chauncy, who lives with his disabled mother, is a straight A student striving to make a better life for himself and his mother. He dreams of becoming a successful business owner and providing jobs and opportunities for others in his community. However, his circumstances have made it difficult for him to achieve these goals. He is in need of basic necessities such as food, a bed, and clothing, and he currently sleeps on the floor in a room with no air conditioning.

Matt, moved by Chauncy's story, created a GoFundMe page to help him get a lawnmower so he could start mowing lawns for money. The response to the campaign has been overwhelming, with over $92,000 raised to date. Matt is now working to provide Chauncy and his mother with new clothes, furniture, and a better living situation.

The story of Chauncy and Matt's encounter has touched many people, and the power of social media and kindness has been instrumental in helping this young man and his mother. Chauncy and Matt now attend church together every Sunday, and anyone interested in meeting them can join them at Hope Pres at the 11:15 service.

This story serves as a reminder of the power of kindness and the impact that one person can have on another's life. Despite the challenges that Chauncy and his mother face, their story offers hope and inspiration to many.

The article discusses the paradoxical state of the music industry, where album sales continue to decline, yet they remain crucial as marketing tools. The success of Lady Gaga's album "Born This Way" serves as a prime example. In its first week, the album sold 1.1 million copies in the US, with 662,000 being digital downloads, the highest ever. This achievement is attributed to Lady Gaga's popularity and a comprehensive marketing campaign.

Despite the decline in album sales, they no longer serve as the primary source of income for artists. Touring, endorsements, merchandise sales, and other revenue streams have become more significant. Lady Gaga has leveraged numerous branding and promotional deals in the past six months, further emphasizing this shift.

However, the extraordinary success of "Born This Way" was partly due to a 99-cent deal offered by Amazon, which led to sales exceeding a million. This move was met with criticism from brick-and-mortar retailers who saw their sales drop significantly.

The album's success is attributed to a well-planned promotional campaign that began nearly a year in advance and included various appearances, retail tie-ins, and media deals. The selling of "Born This Way" continued until the release date, making Lady Gaga inescapable in the weeks leading up to the release.

Despite the controversy surrounding the Amazon deal, the album's sales were still impressive, with no other releases coming close. The promotional campaign for "Born This Way" is expected to continue, underscoring the importance of albums as organizers of an artist's business, even with their declining sales.

The implementation of President Trump's executive orders on immigration has sparked fear and panic within Hispanic communities, particularly after the high-profile deportation of Guadalupe Garcia de Rayos, an undocumented mother of two U.S. citizens. The Trump administration's aggressive stance on immigration has led many to believe that all undocumented immigrants, not just dangerous criminals, are targets for deportation.

The Garcia de Rayos case has highlighted the uncertainty and confusion faced by undocumented, mixed-status communities, as well as legal residents and citizens. Community organizations are struggling to provide assurances and calm the trepidation, but under current law, undocumented immigrants have few options when they come into contact with federal enforcement officers.

Organizations such as the National Council of La Raza (NCLR) have set up legal defense structures and programs to inform immigrants of their rights. However, without significant changes to the law, undocumented immigrants remain vulnerable to deportation.

The Trump administration has expanded the definition of criminality to include misdemeanors like illegally crossing the border and has targeted a broader range of undocumented immigrants for deportation, potentially affecting millions. The lack of immigration judges and the use of expedited removal procedures could further exacerbate the situation.

Activists warn that going after easy targets, such as low-risk offenders, could damage communities by forcing economically active individuals into hiding, diminishing trust in law enforcement agencies, and allowing dangerous criminals to slip through the cracks.

In response to the growing concerns, community organizations and media are focusing on keeping people informed of their options and the government's ability to persecute undocumented immigrants. Telemundo anchorman José Diaz-Balart is hosting a town hall event to address the administration's immigration actions and answer questions from viewers.

Immigration raids have been reported in several states, including California, Texas, Virginia, North Carolina, Georgia, New York, and Kansas, targeting known criminals but also netting some immigrants without criminal records. The raids have sent shockwaves through immigrant communities, raising concerns that the U.S. government could start going after law-abiding people.

Activists suggest that the raids might be retaliation for cities' "sanctuary city" policies, which restrict the degree to which local law enforcement agencies collaborate with federal immigration enforcement. The Trump administration has also threatened to withhold federal funding from these cities.

Overall, the implementation of President Trump's immigration policies has created a climate of fear and uncertainty within Hispanic communities, with many feeling that they are under attack. Community organizations are working to provide support and information, but the situation remains volatile and uncertain.

A groundbreaking British study has discovered a potential pill for curing brain diseases such as Alzheimer's and Parkinson's. The study, published in the journal Science Translational Medicine, was conducted by the Medical Research Council's (MRC) Toxicology Unit at the University of Leicester. The compound used in the study works by inhibiting an enzyme, known as PERK, which plays a key role in activating a defense mechanism that stops essential proteins from being produced in the brain, leading to the death of brain cells.

The compound was tested on mice with prion disease, a model for human neurodegenerative disorders, and was found to prevent brain disease, restore proteins to protect brain cells, and stop the disease in its tracks, restoring some normal behaviors and preventing memory loss. Although the compound produced significant side effects in mice, including weight loss and mild diabetes, the researchers believe it is possible to develop a drug that protects the brain without the side effects.

Scientists are excited about the findings, as it is the first convincing report that a small drug can stop the progressive death of neurons in the brain, similar to that found in Alzheimer's disease. However, they caution that human trials are a long way off, and more research is needed to determine if the same approach will be viable for more common neurodegenerative conditions like Alzheimer's and Parkinson's.

The study comes at a time when the number of people living with dementia and Alzheimer's disease is set to break one million by 2021, representing an enormous health burden for the NHS and the social care system. The research is at a very early stage, and it could be a decade or more before the medicine is actually developed, but experts believe it could be a turning point in the search for medicines to control and prevent Alzheimer's disease.

In response to Donald Trump's presumptive nomination as the Republican candidate for the 2016 U.S. Presidential election, a new dating website called Maple Match has been launched to help Americans find Canadian partners. The website aims to provide a solution for those considering moving to Canada to escape a potential Trump presidency, as searches for "move to Canada" have spiked following Trump's Super Tuesday win. Maple Match promises to make it easy for Americans to find their "ideal Canadian partner" and offers a slogan of "making dating great again." The website has received a high level of interest, but has not yet officially launched, with users able to sign up for the waiting list. Maple Match founder Joe Goldman believes the service will fulfill a clear need in the dating space, as many Americans and Canadians have expressed frustration with current dating platforms. Goldman plans to launch the site as soon as possible, and believes that true love will overcome any obstacle, including borders. Canada offers a number of advantages, including universal health care, low business taxes, and a left-leaning political climate, as well as being a popular destination for sports fans due to its emphasis on hockey.

The Hollywood Reporter's comprehensive examination of Hollywood salaries reveals surprising earnings of celebrities. Robert Downey Jr. made $75 million for Iron Man, including 7% of the film's gross. Leo DiCaprio made over $25 million for The Wolf of Wall Street, while Jonah Hill made only $60,000. Jennifer Lawrence earns $20 million more than Jennifer Aniston, and product endorsements can make stars buy-an-island rich, such as Robert Downey Jr.'s $12 million from an HTC endorsement. Liam Neeson made $20 million for Taken 3, and Ashton Kutcher makes $750,000 an episode for Two and a Half Men, equating to $34,000 per minute. Alex Trebek makes $10 million per year, and Jon Stewart is the king of late-night paychecks with a $25 to $30 million annual salary. Reality TV can pay nothing, unless you're a Kardashian or a member of Duck Dynasty. The average SAG member earns $52,000 a year, while the vast majority take home less than $1,000 a year from acting jobs. Extras make $148 a day, and a monkey on Animal Practice made $108,000 for nine episodes. Celebrities like Christina Aguilera, Ryan Gosling, Jessica Simpson, Jennifer Aniston, Sandra Bullock, George Clooney, Mariah Carey, Tom Cruise, Tori Spelling, Britney Spears, Demi Moore, Kristen Stewart, Kim Zolciak, Lindsay Lohan, Cindy Crawford, Taylor Swift, Jim Carrey, Miley Cyrus, Kirstie Alley, Bruce Springsteen, Jennifer Lopez, Martha Stewart, Kate Gosselin, Johnny Depp, and Madonna are reported to have various quirks and habits at home.

The 115th US Congress is undergoing a spending review, during which Republican lawmaker Ron DeSantis has proposed an amendment to halt funding for the special counsel's Russia investigation after 180 days. The amendment also seeks to prevent special counsel Robert Mueller from investigating matters occurring before June 2015, which is when Donald Trump announced his presidential bid. Mueller is currently investigating Russia's interference in the presidential election and any potential ties between President Trump's campaign staff and Moscow.

In a related development, federal investigators working for Mueller are focusing on President Trump's role in crafting a response to a published article about a meeting between Russians and his son Donald Jr. Prosecutors want to know what Trump knew about the meeting and whether he sought to conceal its purpose. The meeting, which took place at Trump Tower in June 2016, was attended by Donald Trump Jr., Trump campaign chairman Paul Manafort, Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, Russian attorney Natalia Veselnitskaya, and former Soviet intelligence officer Rinat Akhmetshin.

Emails show that the meeting was scheduled to convey damaging information about Hillary Clinton and her campaign. In a June 3, 2016, email, publicist Rob Goldstone told Trump Jr. that a Russian prosecutor had offered to provide the Trump campaign with damaging information about Hillary Clinton. Trump Jr. responded, "If it's what you say, I love it."

The initial response by Donald Trump Jr. described the meeting as "a short introductory meeting. I asked Jared and Paul to stop by. We primarily discussed a program about the adoption of Russian children that was active and popular with American families years ago and was since ended by the Russian government, but it was not a campaign issue at the time and there was no follow up." However, by the next day, the meeting was reported to have been scheduled to convey damaging information about Hillary Clinton.

The DeSantis amendment faces uncertain prospects, as it must pass through committees and the Senate, and relations between President Trump and Senate Republicans are strained. DeSantis is expected to enter the 2018 Florida Governor’s race.

The Great Bear Rainforest, a wilderness area the size of Switzerland, is home to the spirit bear, a rare white bear that is more elusive than the giant panda. The spirit bear is one of many unique species found in the region, including whales, wolves, and eagles. However, the Great Bear Rainforest faces a threat from a proposed oil pipeline that could turn the area into a superhighway for supertankers, potentially harming the ecosystem and the native Gitga'at Nation who consider the spirit bear sacred.

Conservationists, including the International League of Conservation Photographers, are working to raise awareness about the plight of the spirit bear and the Great Bear Rainforest. The photographers spent time capturing images of the spirit bear, as well as the diverse wildlife and landscapes of the region. The Gitga'at Nation, who have traditionally spoken about the bears only in whispers, are also fighting to protect their home.

The pipeline proponents argue that the pipeline would skirt the Great Bear Rainforest and bring jobs to the region. However, the pipeline has already caused oil spills in other areas, raising concerns among the fishermen and native tribes who rely on the region for their livelihood. The search for the spirit bear continues, and conservationists hope that their efforts will help protect this rare and beautiful creature and its home.

The study published in Nature Climate Change reveals that global warming is projected to significantly decrease the population of Antarctica's emperor penguins by at least 19% by 2100. The study, led by biologist Stephanie Jenouvrier of the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution (WHOI), suggests that two-thirds of the penguin colonies will decline by more than 50%.

Emperor penguins, known for their distinctive golden head patches and ability to grow up to 1.2 meters tall, are heavily dependent on sea ice for their livelihoods. The researchers' analysis incorporates current and projected future sea ice declines, revealing that all colonies will be in decline by the end of the century due to climate change.

The study expands on previous research conducted in Terre Adélie, Antarctica, where researchers have been studying the penguin population for over 50 years. The data from Terre Adélie was crucial in predicting the future decline of all 45 known colonies across Antarctica.

The study urges governments to list the emperor penguin as endangered, which could impose restrictions on tourism and fishing companies. The listing could also provide tools to improve fishing practices and reduce CO2 emissions in the US.

The researchers recommend focusing conservation management strategies in the Ross Sea, as it will be the last place impacted by climate change. They also suggest identifying potential refuges for preserving penguin populations.

The study highlights the importance of long-term studies like the one in Terre Adélie, which provide valuable insights into the role of sea ice in the emperor penguin's life cycle. The study emphasizes the need for new international conservation paradigms to protect species threatened by future climate change.

The conflict in South Sudan, the world's youngest nation, entered its second month as the military battled rebels in the key northern oil town of Malakal on Wednesday. The battle for Malakal, the main town in Upper Nile state, has turned into one of the most bitter in the conflict, with tank battles reported in the streets by the United Nations. The army spokesman, Philip Aguer, dismissed rebel claims they had taken control of the town, stating that the fighting is ongoing. Rebel forces staged a fresh attack on Tuesday to seize Malakal, which has already changed hands twice since the conflict began.

The violence in South Sudan erupted on December 15 between forces loyal to President Salva Kiir and soldiers backing Riek Machar, his former vice-president. The conflict has seen reports of mass killings along ethnic lines, with over 1,000 people estimated to have died since the conflict began.

About 400,000 civilians have fled their homes over the past month, many of them to escape a wave of ethnic violence between members of Kiir's Dinka people, the country's largest group, and Machar's Nuer community. Up to 10,000 people are believed to have been killed in the fighting, including over 200 civilians who drowned in a boat fleeing the latest round of fighting in Malakal.

The East African regional bloc IGAD has been brokering peace talks in neighboring Ethiopia, although with still little sign of a hoped-for ceasefire agreement. The army is also trying to recapture the town of Bor from the rebels, the capital of restive Jonglei state.

In a tragic incident, more than 200 civilians drowned in a Nile ferry accident while fleeing fighting in Malakal. Thousands of civilians have been trying to escape the clashes by crossing the river, but many say they simply cannot afford to pay for a boat.

The negotiations in Addis Ababa are aimed at securing a ceasefire in South Sudan, with the key sticking point being the release of political leaders arrested in Juba. The army spokesman, Philip Aguer, said that the army was "still marching on Bor". Frontlines there have so far been quiet this morning, but clashes can break out at any time.

The television series based on the love story of Tejano music icon Selena and her husband Chris Perez is facing a legal challenge. Abraham Quintanilla, Selena's father, has filed a lawsuit against Endemol Shine North America and Perez, aiming to halt the production of the series. The suit alleges that only Selena's estate has the right to commercially exploit any material related to her life, including books, films, and TV series.

The controversy stems from a 1995 Estate Properties Agreement signed by Perez, which grants Quintanilla Jr. exclusive rights to Selena's entertainment properties, including contract, trademark, copyright rights, and rights of publicity. The agreement also states that Perez would receive 25% of the net profits derived from the exploitation of these properties.

The suit claims that Perez's book, "To Selena With Love," published in 2012, and the upcoming TV series are in violation of this agreement, as they are considered unauthorized. Quintanilla's estate attorney, Simran A. Singh, stated that Perez does not have the rights to publish a book or produce a television series based on any part of Selena's life. The lawsuit seeks a judicial declaration that Endemol and Perez have no right to exploit the series and to stop its production. As a result, the production of the Selena and Chris Perez love story series is currently on hold.

The article discusses the controversy surrounding Ian Buruma, the former editor-in-chief of The New York Review of Books (NYRB), who stepped down amidst a backlash over his decision to publish an essay by disgraced former radio host Jian Ghomeshi. Ghomeshi was acquitted of sexual assault charges in 2016 but faced multiple allegations of violent behavior from over 20 women. The essay, titled "Reflections from a Hashtag," was published in the NYRB last week and sparked an online backlash for giving Ghomeshi a prestigious platform to write an unchallenged first-person piece.

Buruma defends his decision to publish, stating that he expected intense reactions but hoped it would open a discussion about what to do with people who behaved badly but were acquitted in a court of law. However, he admits he did not gauge the forces of the #MeToo movement. Buruma claims he was not fired but felt forced to resign due to pressure from university publishers who advertise in the NYRB, fearing backlash on campuses.

The article also includes comments from Romayne Smith Fullerton, an associate professor at Western University, who criticizes the magazine's lack of transparency and expresses disappointment in the lack of progress towards gender equality in journalism.

The controversy has led to substantial discussion and letters responding to the article in the next issue of The New York Review, dated October 25, 2018. The article also mentions that Buruma was "publicly pilloried" and "convicted on Twitter." The NYRB has yet to give an explanation for Buruma's departure, and the magazine added an editorial note clarifying several details about the allegations against Ghomeshi, how they emerged, and the legal proceedings that followed.

The document discusses two main topics: the crawl of outlinks from Wikipedia.org, which started in March 2016 and is currently not publicly accessible, and a review of Jodi Kantor's book "The Obamas" in the New York Times Book Review.

Regarding the Wikipedia outlinks, the collection is complete, as duplicate detection was turned off, and all different wikis were included. The outlinks are not publicly accessible, and sharing data with pointers to random other collections is a complex problem.

In the review of "The Obamas," Douglas Brinkley, a historian, used the term "chick nonfiction" to describe Kantor's book, which raised concerns about the Times Book Review's alleged lack of respect for woman authors. The book documents the First Marriage, with an emphasis on Michelle Obama's influence on White House policy. Rebecca Traister, a writer for Salon, said the book is about people who had equal power in a marriage and one giving up the power.

Jennifer Weiner, a novelist who has accused the Times of bias against woman writers, criticized Brinkley's use of the term "chick nonfiction." Washington Post blogger Ezra Klein defended the book as a serious work of journalism. Brinkley has not responded to a request for comment.

The book broke news concerning Michelle Obama's frustration with a perceived failure to enact her husband's agenda, particularly with regard to health care and immigration reform. Some have criticized the book for various flaws, including errors of fact and speculative conceits. However, no review has questioned the book's basic seriousness as extensively as Brinkley's review.

Traister noted that much of the review was positive but found the allegedly condescending tone of certain parts puzzling. The Kolhapur sisters, Renuka Shinde and Seema Gavit, who were sentenced to death for kidnapping and murdering nine children between 1990 and 1996, may receive a temporary reprieve as their advocate, Sudeep Jaiswal, will move the Bombay High Court on Tuesday. On Monday morning, an "annular eclipse" was observed across a vast region spanning from Asia to the western United States. This celestial event occurs when the Moon is at its furthest from the Earth, resulting in a "ring of fire" phenomenon as the Moon does not completely block out the Sun. Millions of people witnessed this spectacle, with Tokyo being one of the prime viewing locations. In Japan, schools, parks, and even private airplanes hosted "eclipse tours." Similar events were held in China and Taiwan.

In Tokyo, the eclipse was broadcast live on TV, and despite initial light rain and cloudy conditions, the weather cleared up to provide near-perfect viewing. Kaori Sasaki, a resident in Tokyo, described the event as "a very mysterious sight - I've never seen anything like it." Japanese electronics giant Panasonic sent an expedition to Mount Fuji to capture the eclipse using solar-powered equipment.

Unfortunately, skywatchers in Hong Kong were not as fortunate. Heavy clouds obstructed the view despite hundreds gathering at the Kowloon waterfront for telescope viewings. In contrast, thousands attended viewing parties in Reno, Nevada, Oakland, California, and other locations in the US. The Petroglyph National Monument in Albuquerque, New Mexico, was hailed as one of the best vantage points, with Brent Veltri of Salida, Colorado, remarking, "That's got to be the prettiest thing I've ever seen."

The eclipse was fully visible across a 240 to 300km-wide swathe but partial views could be seen across much of east Asia and North America. The Slooh series of space telescopes covered the event on their website. The next solar eclipse is expected on November 13, and will be visible over northern Australia, according to NASA.

In this summary, Dennis McGuire, a man convicted of the 1989 murder of Joy Stewart, is set to be executed on Thursday, January 16th, 2014, in Ohio. The execution will be the first use of a never-before-tried lethal injection method, consisting of the sedative midazolam and the painkiller hydromorphone. McGuire's attorneys argue that he may suffer "agony and terror" as he struggles to breathe during the execution, while state attorneys dispute this scenario.

McGuire's execution was initially scheduled for last year, but was delayed due to a request for organ donation. However, his request for clemency was denied by Ohio Governor John Kasich. Stewart's slaying went unsolved for 10 months until McGuire, jailed on an unrelated assault charge, provided information about the woman's death. DNA evidence later confirmed McGuire's guilt, and he acknowledged his responsibility in a letter to Governor Kasich last month.

McGuire's attorneys argue that he was mentally, physically, and sexually abused as a child, which has affected his brain development and made him prone to impulsive behavior. They also argue that he should be allowed to donate his organs to family members, but Governor Kasich denied this request due to a lack of identified recipients.

The use of the new lethal injection method has raised concerns among McGuire's attorneys, who argue that it could cause "air hunger," a medical phenomenon that could result in McGuire experiencing terror as he struggles to catch his breath. However, the state disputes this scenario and argues that similar challenges have failed in the past. A federal judge sided with the state and allowed the execution to proceed, but ordered the state to photograph and preserve the drugs' packaging boxes and vials and the syringes used in the execution.

McGuire spent part of Wednesday visiting with his family, and requested a last meal that included roast beef and fried chicken. He was moved from death row in Chillicothe to the Southern Ohio Correctional Facility in Lucasville, where executions are carried out. The execution is scheduled to begin at 10 a.m. on Thursday.

The National Transitional Council (NTC) of Libya is expected to formally end the NATO mission over Libya on Wednesday, marking another milestone in the country's road towards democracy and free and fair elections in 2013. The decision comes after the death of Muammar Gaddafi and his son Mo'tassim, who were killed after being captured wounded but alive on Thursday. The bodies of both leaders were displayed in a Misrata meat locker, causing unease among the NTC's Western backers about Libya's prospects for stable government and respect for the rule of law. The NTC has promised to investigate the circumstances surrounding the deaths of Gaddafi and his son. The treatment of others who supported Gaddafi and fought alongside him is now a concern, according to US Assistant Secretary of State for Near Eastern Affairs Jeffrey Feltman. The NTC has emerged from 42 years of often brutal one-man rule, and many Libyans are savoring the end of eight months of bitter civil war won with NATO's backing. However, there are concerns about how Gaddafi met his end and how his body was treated afterwards. Some Libyans are unconcerned, with engineer Ali Azzarog saying, "Throw him in a hole, in the sea, in garbage. No matter. He is lower than a donkey or a dog and only foreigners say they care about how we killed him. And they are lying." The NTC is now likely to tussle for power during a planned transition to democracy in a nation riven with regional and tribal rivalries. With economic problems at home, NATO countries are expected to endorse an end to their U.N.-mandated mission in Libya on Wednesday after a preliminary decision last week to end it on October 31. Libyan interim Oil and Finance Minister Ali Tarhouni has requested that NATO maintain its mission for another month, but hopes for a swift end to United Nations sanctions to free up funds for the interim government to pay salaries and help reconstruction. The one remaining element from the old order is Gaddafi's sons, with the enigmatic Saif al-Islam remaining on the run. An NTC official said Saif al-Islam was in the southern desert near Niger and Algeria and was set to flee Libya using a false passport.

The study conducted by Anirban Mukhopadhyay, an associate professor of marketing at Hong Kong University Science and Technology, suggests that forcing a smile when feeling miserable may not help and could potentially make individuals feel worse. The research found that when people are forced to grin while feeling down, their brain starts to associate smiling with sadness rather than joy. The study results showed that faking a smile doesn't increase happiness but instead, the belief that one must already be happy to smile increases happiness. The study suggests that the idea of grinning and bearing it might not be the best solution after all. The researchers advise waiting for unhappiness to subside before attempting a grin to avoid linking happy acts to sadness. The study was published in the July issue of the Journal of Experimental Social Psychology.

Pope Francis delivered a historic speech to a joint session of Congress on Thursday, September 24, 2015, becoming the first pontiff to do so. During his speech, he called for an end to the death penalty, urging lawmakers to rehabilitate those convicted of crimes instead of executing them. He also expressed sympathy for American Indians and their turbulent history with European settlers, and lamented that the very basis of marriage and family life today is being put into question.

Francis also addressed the issue of climate change, urging a "courageous and responsible effort" to avert the most serious effects of environmental deterioration caused by human activity. He said he was convinced that working together, nations can make a difference to slow global warming, and that the U.S. and "this Congress" have an important role to play.

In addition, Francis denounced the arms trade, asking why weapons are being sold to people who intend only to inflict suffering on innocents. He has in the past denounced weapons makers and dealers as "the root of evil" and questioned how weapons manufacturers can call themselves Christian.

Francis also addressed the refugee crisis, calling on lawmakers not to be afraid of immigrants but to welcome them as fellow human beings. He said people are not things that can be discarded just because they are troublesome, and that the United States was founded by immigrants.

Overall, Pope Francis' speech to Congress was a call for compassion, cooperation, and a rejection of violence and extremism. He urged lawmakers to protect and defend human life at every stage of its development, and to work together to address the challenges facing the world today.

The Torti family from Franklin, Tennessee is raising awareness about a rare genetic disorder called LCHAD that affects one in 100,000 children. Their two-year-old son, Owen, has the disorder and requires constant feeding every hour to stay healthy. Due to LCHAD, Owen's body cannot break down certain fatty acids into energy, and if he goes without eating, his body would start to break down key muscles in search of energy.

Owen was diagnosed with LCHAD when he was just a week old. His parents, Kayla and Tyler Torti, found limited information online about the disorder, and they felt lonely initially. However, they are not alone, as people from their community have rallied around them. Two teams ran the Ragnar Relay through Tennessee to raise awareness for Owen and his metabolic disorder, raising $15,000 to help pay his medical bills.

The Torti family is both carriers of LCHAD, and if they have more children, there is a 25 percent chance they'll have the disorder as well. The family is unsure about the future but wants to get the word out to help other families who may be diagnosed with LCHAD in the future.

A Georgia family is also hoping to raise awareness for their 23-month-old boy who was diagnosed with LCHAD. Since the boy needs to constantly be fed, he doesn't quite understand the purpose of a meal, and he has a lot of oral aversion to eating. Despite the genetic illness, the boy still looks and acts much like any other toddler.

LCHAD was added to the newborn screening just six years ago, and the oldest living person with the disorder that the Torti's have contacted is now 25. The first LCHAD diagnosis wasn't until the 1990s. LCHAD is known as an orphan disease, which means no research or funding will be directed to finding a cure or long-term solution unless light is shone on the disorder or a celebrity/organization steps in.

Two teams, "All in for Owen," ran the Ragnar Relay through Tennessee to raise awareness for Owen and his metabolic disorder. The teams raised $15,000 to help pay Owen's medical bills and plan to run again in Chattanooga, TN, in October. The teams hope to bring light to the disorder and connect families around the world who are isolated by the disorder to see that they are not alone. The teams also aim to raise awareness for a family who refuses to give up and give hope to a family who is giving hope to others.

This was not Henningsgaard's first plane crash. In 2009, he crash-landed on Washington's Columbia River while flying with his 84-year-old mother to watch his daughter in a high school play.

The article discusses the decline of Pacific sardines, a crucial forage fish that supports a diverse marine ecosystem on the West Coast of North America. The sardine population has experienced a severe decline, affecting numerous species of seabirds, whales, sharks, dolphins, and commercially important fish such as salmon and tuna. The Pacific Fishery Management Council (PFMC) is urged to take action to help maintain a healthy Pacific Ocean by setting conservative catch limits on sardines and prohibiting unregulated fishing on other forage fish species.

The PFMC manages fishing in federal waters off California, Oregon, and Washington. In September 2013, the council committed to prohibiting unregulated fishing on forage fish species such as sand lance, saury, and lanternfish. However, it is suggested that the council should fulfill this commitment to help maintain a healthy Pacific Ocean.

The sardine fishery collapsed in the 1950s, and the November 2013 population estimate of 378,000 tons is the lowest in more than a decade, far below the peak of 1.5 million tons estimated in 2000. Forage fish account for more than one-third of the global catch of marine fish and are mostly used for industrial purposes such as feed for livestock, poultry, and farmed fish rather than being directly eaten by people. Most forage fish landed on the West Coast are exported for purposes such as bait in tuna longlining in Asia or as feed for farmed fish.

If sardines don't recover soon, experts warn, the West Coast's marine mammals, seabirds, and fishermen could suffer for years. The reason for the drop is unclear, but it is suggested that a naturally occurring climate cycle known as the Pacific Decadal Oscillation may be a factor. The decline is raising alarm, and some environmental groups have argued that the catch should be halted outright.

The Pacific sardine is the ocean's quintessential boom-bust fish, with numbers wildly unpredictable, surging up and down in decades-long cycles in response to natural shifts in the ocean environment. The article provides a historical context of the sardine fishery on the West Coast, including its collapse in the mid-20th century and the subsequent moratorium on sardine fishing that lasted 18 years.

In conclusion, the decline of Pacific sardines is a cause for concern, affecting numerous species in the West Coast marine ecosystem. The PFMC is urged to take action to help maintain a healthy Pacific Ocean by setting conservative catch limits on sardines and prohibiting unregulated fishing on other forage fish species. For further information, please visit pewenvironment.org/pacificfish, and write to the Pacific Fishery Management Council at pfmc.comments@noaa.gov.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit has struck down the Federal Communications Commission's (FCC) "open Internet" rules, effectively ending net neutrality in the United States. The ruling means that Internet Service Providers (ISPs) like Verizon, AT&T, Comcast, and Time Warner Cable can now discriminate against content they dislike, favoring their business partners while delaying or blocking websites they don't like. ISPs can also charge fees to websites that want quick content delivery, potentially slowing down poorer sites that can't pay up. This decision is bad for small businesses, as indie retailers and personal websites may suffer from slower content delivery, while ISPs may favor partner sites. In extreme cases, ISPs may hinder or block content that isn't produced by partners. Additionally, entire types of online traffic, such as Netflix and BitTorrent, may be in jeopardy, as ISPs can now discriminate against certain traffic types. Without net neutrality, ISPs can make even more money without actually improving the Internet, as they won't need to improve service or bring broadband to rural areas because they'll be able to keep growing (financially, at least) by charging content providers more for faster delivery and charging customers more for faster access. The FCC may appeal the ruling or reclassify the broadband providers to give itself back the authority to regulate them, but it is uncertain whether they will do so. Overall, the decision to end net neutrality will likely result in a more controlled and potentially slower Internet for consumers.

Scientists from the Cleveland Museum of Natural History have named a new species of praying mantis, Ilomantis ginsburgae, in honor of Supreme Court Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg for her work on gender equality. This is the first time a female-based genitalia system has been used to classify a praying mantis species, as male genitalia characters have historically been the standard. The new species, found in Madagascar, resembles Ginsburg's famous lace collar. The research, published in the journal Insect Systematics & Evolution, was led by Case Western Reserve University Ph.D. candidate Sydney Brannoch and co-author Dr. Gavin Svenson. The study establishes the validity of using female specimens in the classification of praying mantises and aims to set a precedent in taxonomy, encouraging scientists to equally consider both sexes in their research. The researchers examined 30 praying mantis specimens from three museums, analyzing their geographic distribution, external features, and both male and female genital characters. The female genital characters alone were found to define the species, and traditionally used character systems corroborated their findings. The study also resurrected Ilomantis as a valid genus from the related genus Nilomantis due to character differences observed on the female genitalia. This research reduces the impediment of identifying praying mantis species by characterizing both sexes for easier identification.

The satellite images released by the Committee for Human Rights in North Korea show that Camp 25, one of North Korea's gulags, has been expanding since 2003. The camp, which houses approximately 5,000 prisoners, has seen a 72% increase in size between 2009 and 2010 alone, and has grown to include several new buildings, agricultural fields, and almost two dozen guards. The expansion could be due to an intensified crackdown on attempted defectors, the purge of political dissidents after Kim Jong-un assumed power, or the consolidation of North Korea's political prison camp system. The gulags remain one of the most shadowy corners of North Korea, with few people managing to share stories from inside the camps. In a joint warning, ATM manufacturers Diebold Nixdorf and NCR Corp have alerted U.S. financial institutions about a rising threat of cyber attacks known as "jackpotting," in which hackers force ATMs to dispense cash. The attacks, which have been increasing globally, are believed to have started in Mexico last year.

NCR confirmed the first reported "jackpotting" losses in the United States, stating that their equipment was not targeted in the recent attacks, but the threat remains a concern for the entire ATM industry. Diebold Nixdorf warned that U.S. authorities have alerted the company about hackers targeting one of its out-of-production ATM models, the Opteva.

The attacks are carried out by gaining physical access to the ATM, replacing the hard drive, and using an industrial endoscope to depress an internal button. The U.S. Secret Service and the Federal Bureau of Investigation could not be reached for comment.

The Secret Service has reportedly warned about organized criminal gangs using the advanced Ploutus.D malware to target stand-alone ATMs in the United States, particularly those manufactured by Diebold Nixdorf. The gangs are said to deploy "money mules" to conduct the attacks and siphon cash from ATMs.

The Secret Service alert suggests that the attackers typically use an endoscope to locate the internal portion of the cash machine where they can attach a cord that allows them to sync their laptop with the ATM’s computer. Once this is complete, the ATM is controlled by the fraudsters, and the ATM will appear out of service to potential customers.

The attackers then install malware to force the machines to dispense cash at a rate of 40 bills every 23 seconds. The only way to stop the dispense cycle is to press cancel on the keypad, or the machine is completely emptied of cash.

Diebold Nixdorf and NCR have advised ATM operators to take appropriate steps to protect their ATMs against these forms of attack and to update to a version of Windows 7 to defeat this specific type of attack. This is a rapidly developing story and may be updated as more information becomes available.

Over the weekend, Chicago experienced a surge in shootings, with a total of 34 people being shot and five killed during a 24-hour period from Saturday morning to Sunday morning. The heaviest violence occurred between midnight and 3 a.m., with 30 people being shot, and five mass shootings accounting for 25 of the victims during a three-hour span. The majority of the shootings took place in the West and South sides of Chicago, with the most violent incidents occurring in the Lawndale neighborhood.

One of the most tragic incidents was the shooting of 17-year-old Jahnae Patterson, who was killed in a shooting on Sunday morning. The shooting took place during a block party in the 1600-block of South Avers Avenue, where two gunmen got out of a white Impala and shot four people. Later that morning, Patterson was killed and five other people, including an 11-year-old boy, were wounded in a shooting in the 1300-block of South Millard Avenue.

Chicago Police Chief of Patrol Fred Waller said that much of the violence is being traced back to gangs, and that the shootings were targeted and related to gang conflicts in those areas. He also noted that gunmen were shooting into large crowds. The police plan to focus their resources for the evening on neighborhoods where retaliation seems likely.

The aftermath of many of the shootings played out inside and outside the emergency room at Stroger Hospital, where extended family members and friends were prevented from entering as the staff dealt with the influx of trauma patients. The level of violence on Sunday made it difficult for police and hospitals to keep track, with resources at local hospitals being taxed as the wounded and their families poured in.

Activist Eric Russell, an organizer of the anti-violence protest Thursday that shut down Lake Shore Drive, spoke outside of the hospital, saying "This is the reason why we march." Russell harshly criticized Mayor Rahm Emanuel for not doing enough to address gun violence.

In a separate incident, police said a group of people, including three teens and five adults, were standing in a courtyard in the 1300-block of West 76th Street at about 12:40 a.m. when several people approached on foot and opened fire at the group. The victims range in age from 14-years-old to 35 years-old. Several had multiple gunshot wounds, and all were transported to area hospitals and are expected to survive. No one is in custody in connection with the shooting.

This comes just days after Superintendent Eddie Johnson visited ABC7 and talked about decreasing crime numbers and overall violence in Chicago. Johnson said, "I think some of our more challenging, communities, it’s just imperative that police and the community work together to reduce this gun violence. We just have too many guns on the streets of Chicago." Mayor Rahm Emanuel, who was downtown Sunday to announce plans for improvements to the Riverwalk, expressed the need to create more jobs, not just in the central business district, but on the South and West Sides as well.

The shooting incidents in Chicago have raised concerns about the city's safety and the need for increased efforts to address gun violence. The police are focusing their resources on neighborhoods where retaliation seems likely, and activists are continuing to call for more action from the city's leaders to address the root causes of violence in the community.

In a series of events, the Trump administration continued to apply pressure on North Korea regarding its nuclear ambitions. This escalated on Wednesday when President Donald Trump issued a warning to North Korea via Twitter, boasting about America's powerful nuclear arsenal.

During an appearance on Fox & Friends, former White House advisor Sebastian Gorka stated that Trump's message was clear: "don't test America and don't test Donald J. Trump." Gorka emphasized the U.S.'s military capabilities, describing it as a "hyper-power" that no other nation, including North Korea, could challenge.

Gorka also reiterated the hardline on North Korea, stating that Pyongyang should "stand down the rhetoric" and that North Korea posed a "very insignificant threat in terms of scale." Despite the escalating warnings from the White House, Gorka argued that the ball was in North Korea's court to de-escalate the situation.

Secretary of State Rex Tillerson had urged calm on North Korea hours before the president's tweets, stating that Americans should sleep well at night and that there was no imminent threat from Pyongyang.

During the interview, Gorka addressed criticism from Democratic lawmakers and some Republicans about Trump's "reckless" and "bombastic comments." Gorka invoked White House grievances about leaks and argued that Americans should come together to support Trump during this time of crisis.

In a separate development, US Defense Secretary James Mattis issued a dramatic ultimatum to North Korea, stating that the DPRK must choose to stop isolating itself and stand down its pursuit of nuclear weapons. Mattis warned that any actions leading to the end of North Korea's regime and the destruction of its people would be met with overwhelming force.
