The Democratic National Convention concluded with President Barack Obama delivering the shortest acceptance speech by an incumbent president in 36 years, lasting 38 minutes and 23 seconds. The speech was not as inspiring as some of his previous speeches, such as his 2007 Iowa Jefferson-Jackson dinner address, but it was well-received and is expected to energize supporters for the final 60 days of the campaign.

Some of the highlights of the convention included Gabby Giffords' emotional recitation of the Pledge of Allegiance, John Kerry's scathing assessment of Mitt Romney's foreign policy credentials, and John Lewis' stirring speech connecting the civil rights fight to the fight over voter ID laws. U2 and Foo Fighters also performed at the event.

On the other hand, Brian Schweitzer's folksy speech was not well-received, and Charlie Crist's attempt to win over the Democratic party was met with only polite applause. Caroline Kennedy's speech was also criticized for being flat and lacking energy.

Overall, the president's speech was not a standout moment of the convention, but it was not a colossal flop either. If there was a category between winning and losing, that's where Obama's speech would fall.

The president's speech focused on defending his and his party's belief in individual initiative, self-reliance, and earned success, while attacking Mitt Romney and his supposed plans to eradicate government for the sake of the wealthy. However, the president did not offer a discernible second-term agenda of his own, and his defense of his first term bore no resemblance to what that first term had involved.

The Democratic convention was overall strident and culturally liberal, while the Republican convention was mostly dull. However, neither convention offered much that is new, and it is expected that the election will be a referendum on the incumbent president.

The movie "Focus," starring Will Smith and Margot Robbie, is a caper film about a veteran con man and his young accomplice. The film, directed by John Requa and Glenn Ficarra, has a slick appearance but falls short in delivering a convincing portrayal of the underworld. The movie is criticized for being absurd and ludicrous, with no truth or substance to recommend it.

The relationship between Smith's character Nicky and Robbie's character Jess lacks emotional impact, and Smith's performance is described as withdrawn and serious, which eclipses the charm that made him a movie star in the first place. The movie's casting history is also mentioned, with various actors being considered for the roles initially.

The movie's plot revolves around Nicky teaching Jess the art of pickpocketing, with the focus being on the con artist's ability to convince anyone of anything. The movie approaches the modest goals and allure of a 60-year-old Hitchcock, and the performances of Smith and Robbie are praised, with Robbie being compared to a modern Grace Kelly.

The movie's con is that it presents a secret underworld, but it fails to deliver on that promise. The movie is criticized for being ridiculous and ludicrous, and the resolution of some scenes only makes it worse. Despite its flaws, the movie has some scattered good moments, such as the disconcerting sound of race cars and the performance of Adrian Martinez.

Overall, "Focus" is a movie about Will Smith's jaded charm and Margot Robbie's appearance, with the scenes disconnected from each other and lacking a coherent plot. The movie is criticized for being an elaborate con, but it can be enjoyed for its audacity and the performances of its stars.

Chris Christie, the embattled governor of New Jersey, sought to reconnect with the Republican base at the Conservative Political Action Conference (CPAC) on Thursday, delivering a low-key speech that emphasized traditional conservative themes. The speech was a far cry from his more brash and stirring performances in the past, but it earned a polite reception from the crowd.

Christie's attendance at CPAC is a sign that the frost between him and the party's base has thawed. He was snubbed by CPAC last year, just months after his public embrace of President Barack Obama in the aftermath of Hurricane Sandy. Many Republicans believed Christie's praise of the President during Obama's re-election campaign helped lift him over GOP nominee Mitt Romney.

During his speech, Christie defended the political activity of the billionaire Koch brothers, whose spending on 2014 races has become a rallying cry for vulnerable Senate Democrats. He urged conservatives to stress an economic platform that can lift Americans out of poverty and lambasted Obama for standing on the sidelines when Washington required leadership.

Christie framed himself as a conservative who has secured a governing majority in a reliably blue state. If the GOP can win in New Jersey, he said, it can borrow the blueprint to expand the political map in coming elections. He also took a rare foray into foreign policy, arguing in favor of "America being a leader in the world" and "a strong national defense... Not [a country] that allows us to get pushed around all over the world."

Christie's speech was delivered amid a media onslaught buffeting him, as he has been under fire in recent months amid revelations that aides initiated a traffic jam in an apparent act of political retribution. The harsh spotlight from a media conservatives see as biased has earned him new affection from the right.

In the speech, Christie also emphasized the need for the GOP to focus on what it is for, not just what it is against. He argued that conservatives must be confident that "our ideas are better than their [Democrats'] ideas." He proceeded to reel off accomplishments of several GOP governors in contrast to the "dysfunction" in Congress.

Overall, Christie's speech was an attempt to mend fences with the Republican base and remind them that he is a conservative who can get things done. He also emphasized the need for the GOP to focus on economic issues and strong national defense, and to not let the media define the party.

Arizona Sheriff Joe Arpaio, who is known as the "toughest sheriff in America," accused President Barack Obama of trying to make him the "poster boy" of Arizona's controversial immigration law. The UK government is planning to introduce compulsory lie detector tests for high-risk sex offenders, following a successful pilot scheme in the Midlands. MPs are expected to approve the use of polygraph screening for the most serious offenders across England and Wales from next year. The tests, which measure heart rate, blood pressure, breathing, and levels of perspiration, aim to monitor the behavior of 750 offenders who have served at least 12 months in jail. If offenders are found to have lied or breached the terms of their release, they could be sent back to prison. The move comes as part of a broader effort to create a tougher approach to managing sex offenders, including the creation of a National Probation Service tasked with protecting the public from high-risk offenders. The tests, however, are not admissible in any court in England and Wales due to continuing concerns about their reliability and misinterpretation of results. The government aims to roll out the tests next spring, subject to the parliamentary timetable.

Mohammed Tawfeeq, a CNN producer, editor, and Iraqi national, has filed a federal lawsuit challenging President Trump's executive order on immigration. Tawfeeq, a permanent legal resident of the U.S. since 2013, claims he was unlawfully detained at Hartsfield-Jackson International Airport in Atlanta on January 29, 2017, due to the executive order that bars people from Iraq, Iran, Syria, Yemen, Sudan, Libya, and Somalia from entering the U.S. for 90 days. The lawsuit alleges that Tawfeeq's detention violates the Immigration and Nationality Act and the Administrative Procedure Act.

Tawfeeq, who frequently travels to the Middle East for his CNN duties, says that when he presented himself for inspection at the airport, a U.S. Customs and Border Patrol officer notified him that he could be refused entry under the President's executive order. The officer scanned Tawfeeq's passport and green card and asked him pointed questions about the nature of his trip. Tawfeeq was eventually allowed to leave the airport without an explanation, documentation, or a passport stamp.

The lawsuit maintains that the implementation of Trump's executive order and Tawfeeq's detention at Atlanta's Hartsfield-Jackson International Airport has increased the uncertainty involved in current and future international travel for returning lawful permanent residents like Tawfeeq. The lawsuit seeks a declaration that the ban does not apply to legal permanent residents and an order of mandamus preventing it from being applied to those individuals.

The defendants named in Tawfeeq's lawsuit are the Department of Homeland Security, U.S. Customs and Border Protection, the State Department, Department of Homeland Security Secretary John Kelly, and acting Secretary of State Thomas Shannon. Tawfeeq is represented by Theresia Moser of Atlanta.

The events in Tunisia, a country traditionally outside the region's centers of power, have sparked widespread enthusiasm and hope for change in the Middle East. The protests, driven by economic woes, corruption, and repression, have echoed in many other countries in the region, including Egypt. The success of the Tunisian protests has gripped a region where residents have long complained about governments that seem incapable of meeting their demands and are bereft of any ideology except perpetuating power.

The protests were inspired by Mohamed Bouazizi, a university graduate who set himself on fire in December after the police seized his cart and mistreated him. Bouazizi was hailed as the symbol of the Tunisian revolution, and his name has been invoked in Egypt and other countries.

The momentum of the Tunisian protests has overshadowed other instances of dissent in the Arab world. In Egypt, protesters, often lacking in numbers, are occasionally beset by divisions between secular and religious activists. The mass protests in Lebanon that followed the assassination of Rafik Hariri in 2005 ended up deepening divisions in a country almost evenly split over questions of ideology, sectarian loyalty, and foreign patrons.

The Tunisian protests have also raised questions about American policy in the Middle East. During the Bush administration, democratization was at least a rhetorical priority, but the United States maintained its support for Egypt, Saudi Arabia, and other authoritarian governments in the region. On Thursday, as the protests in Tunisia were escalating, Secretary of State Hillary Clinton issued a scathing critique of Arab leadership and the region’s political and economic stagnation.

In the end, the most dramatic change in the old Arab order in years was inspired by Bouazizi. The protests have led to the ousting of President Zine El Abidine Ben Ali and the formation of a new interim government. However, the scene in Cairo might serve as a caution, as protesters in Egypt have been outnumbered and outmaneuvered by police officers.

The events in Tunisia have captivated Arabs who hope it will inspire the toppling of other entrenched authoritarian regimes. However, the continuing violence and chaos have raised the stakes for a people's power rebellion. Many Tunisians suspect that former members of Ben Ali's presidential guard, his most brutal adjutants in the Interior Ministry, and loyalists in his ruling Constitutional Democratic Rally have played a role in the unrest.

Overall, the events in Tunisia have sparked hope for change in the Middle East and raised questions about American policy in the region. The momentum of the Tunisian protests has overshadowed other instances of dissent in the Arab world, and the success of the protests has inspired hope for change in other countries. However, the continuing violence and chaos have raised concerns about the future of the region.

In this case, the Associated Press and other news outlets have reported on a controversial surrogacy case involving an Australian couple and a Thai surrogate mother. The concept of "meternity" leave, a sabbatical-like break for personal reflection and self-care, was inspired by Meghann Foye's jealousy towards co-workers who received maternity leave and early dismissals to pick up their children. Foye, author of the novel "Meternity," believes that every woman deserves mandated "me time."

Foye argues that a "meternity" leave would particularly benefit women who follow a non-traditional path and may not have the opportunity for self-reflection. She notes that the recession and the cultural expectation of being tethered to desks and smartphones have made it difficult for individuals to achieve a work-life balance.

Foye observes that her friends who took maternity leave returned with a clearer sense of what they wanted in life, and she believes that a "meternity" leave could provide the same benefits for women and men who have been in the workforce for a decade or more.

However, some critics argue that the concept of "meternity" is misguided, as it fails to acknowledge the challenges and exhaustion that come with maternity leave. Mothers point out that maternity leave is not about self-care, but rather about putting someone else's needs before one's own.

Foye acknowledges that her "meternity" leave allowed her to grieve the loss of her father and grapple with self-doubt, but she emphasizes that a "meternity" done right should be challenging and lead to personal growth.

Foye's novel "Meternity" explores the challenges of achieving work-life balance and the societal pressure to "have it all." She hopes that the take-away from her book is that parents and non-parents should support and not judge each other in their pursuit of balance.

Overall, the debate surrounding "meternity" leave highlights the ongoing struggle for work-life balance, particularly for women, and the need for societal support and understanding in this area.

In a hearing on Capitol Hill, the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee discussed the issue of Russian interference in the upcoming 2018 midterm elections. President Donald Trump, under pressure to address the threat, claimed without evidence that Russia will be working to help Democrats win. This contradicts Russian President Vladimir Putin's statement that he wanted Trump to win in 2016, and the findings of U.S. intelligence agencies that Russia interfered in the 2016 election to help Trump.

At the hearing, Christopher Krebs of the Homeland Security Department stated that while there have been continued malign influence operations in 2018, they are not at the same scope or scale as in 2016. An indictment this month accused 12 Russian intelligence officers of breaking into Democratic email accounts and attempting to penetrate state election systems, but there is no evidence that the vote count was affected.

Republicans, including some of Trump's closest allies, strongly criticized Russian interference and pointed to the indictment. However, they were careful not to directly disagree with the president. Democrats argued that Republicans haven't done enough to secure the vote this fall and called for more funding for states to secure their election infrastructure.

Congress has already allocated $380 million for election security upgrades, with most of the money disbursed. Democrats want to continue the funding through 2019, but Republicans have said new spending isn't needed. State and local election officials have been working with the Department of Homeland Security to shore up their efforts after at least 21 state systems were scanned for vulnerabilities by Russian hackers and at least one state saw its voter registration system breached.

In addition to helping state election officials obtain security clearances and offering remote scanning of their networks, Homeland Security officials also offer intensive cybersecurity reviews that involve onsite exams. Other threats remain, such as phishing attacks directed at candidates standing for election in the midterms, as revealed by Microsoft officials last week.

In a separate development, two senators introduced bipartisan legislation to impose new Russian sanctions, stating that the U.S. "must make it abundantly clear that we will defend our nation." The hearing and legislation come amid ongoing concerns about Russian interference in U.S. elections.

Former President George W. He emphasized that the library and museum aim to serve as resources for historians to judge him based on the facts he had access to as president.

The library and museum house the papers and records of the Bush presidency, including over 200 million emails, 70 million paper documents, and 43,000 artifacts. The center also includes the Bush Institute, which focuses on economic growth, education reform, global health, human freedom, wounded veterans, and helping women in the Middle East.

Bush appears at ease with his lower profile post-presidency and his handling of major episodes that defined his presidency. He is actively involved in post-presidential efforts aligned with initiatives of his presidency, such as fighting AIDS in Africa and empowering women in the Middle East. The museum focuses on critical periods of his presidency, including 9/11, the run-up to the Iraq War, Hurricane Katrina, and the 2008 financial crisis.

Bush, now a brand-new grandfather, said he is sleeping well and has no sleepless nights about the decisions he made as president. The presidential center, set on a 23-acre site on the campus of Southern Methodist University, officially opens on Thursday with attendance from President Obama and all four living former presidents, including George W. Bush's father.

A key message of the museum is to encourage people to serve and to show the pressure that the president feels in making high-impact decisions. The centerpiece is the "Decision Points Theater," which presents a series of critical decisions the president was faced with and asks the visitor to make a snap judgment based on that information.

The dedication of the George W. Bush Presidential Center comes at a time of broad reevaluation of the Bush legacy. A new ABC News/Washington Post poll found that 47% of people approve of the job Bush did as president, with negative sentiment softening considerably over the past few years.

Bush expressed comfort with staying away from day-to-day politics and declined to weigh in on raging debates over immigration reform, gun control, and gay marriage. He made an exception to advocate for the presidential candidacy of his younger brother, Jeb Bush.

The former president also spoke about his new passion for painting, saying it has changed his life in an unbelievably positive way. He became a grandfather for the first time this month when his daughter, Jenna Bush Hager, delivered a daughter, Mila. Asked what he wants to be called by his grandchildren, the former president joked, "El Jefe" - Spanish for "the chief" or "the boss."

The presidential center opens amidst national events such as the Boston Marathon bombings, which stirred memories of a defining episode of the Bush presidency - Sept. 11, 2001. A few days after the Boston attack, an explosion at a fertilizer plant not far from Bush's own Texas ranch stoked fears of further terrorism.

Bush told ABC News' Diane Sawyer that he remains comfortable with the decision to invade Iraq, stating that the removal of Saddam Hussein was the right decision for both U.S. security and giving people a chance to live in a free society. He added that history will ultimately decide those decisions.

Twitter has permanently banned right-wing conspiracy theorist Alex Jones and his "Infowars" show from the platform for abusive behavior. The decision comes after Jones posted a video on Wednesday that violated Twitter's policy against abusive behavior. The video showed Jones shouting at and berating CNN journalist Oliver Darcy for over ten minutes in a public hallway. Jones criticized Darcy's reporting and appearance, and at one point called him a "possum that got caught doing some really nasty stuff."

Twitter CEO Jack Dorsey testified at two congressional hearings focused on social media, but did not witness the confrontation. Jones had about 900,000 followers on Twitter, and "Infowars" had about 430,000.

Twitter had previously suspended Jones for a week, but until now had resisted muzzling him further. Other tech companies, such as Facebook, have taken more drastic measures, suspending Jones for longer periods and taking down his pages and radio stations.

Jones is currently active on Facebook, but his suspension there recently expired. Darcy has aggressively questioned social media companies about their treatment of Jones, asking why they have allowed him to remain on their platforms for as long as they have.

The ban comes weeks after Jones' accounts were removed or suspended by other major tech companies, including Apple, Facebook, and YouTube. Twitter said it wanted to be open about the action given the broad interest in the case.

In Queen Elizabeth National Park, Uganda, a leopard attacked and killed a 2.5-year-old child named Elisha Nabugyere at the Mweya Safari Lodge. The incident occurred on Friday evening at around 7:30 pm, near the Uganda Wildlife Authority (UWA) staff quarters. The child was seated with a maid when the leopard attacked and ran off with him. Despite efforts to rescue the child, his remains, including the skull and some bones, were recovered the following day.

The child's father, SSP Francis Manana Nabugyere, who is an officer at the police senior Command and staff college Bwebajja, expressed his grief and called for improved security measures from UWA to protect their staff and children. He also expressed his expectation for reasonable compensation from UWA, as they provided the coffin for the burial of his son's remains.

UWA communications manager Bashir Hangi described the incident as unfortunate but did not specify whether the parents would be compensated. He confirmed that efforts are underway to track down the killer leopard, with the intention of capturing it and removing it from the wild due to the increased risk of it attacking humans again.

The headquarters of the park, where the incident occurred, are reportedly in a protected area popular with tourists. The killing of the toddler marks the fourth unfortunate incident for UWA in recent weeks, following the deaths of 11 lions, a French tourist, and another lion in the park. The authorities are now focusing on capturing the leopard to ensure the safety of both tourists and park staff.

A Colombian-style band named Kombo Kolombia, consisting of 20 musicians and roadies, has gone missing in Mexico after a private gig in Hidalgo. Authorities have been searching for them since Friday, but have found no leads so far. The band members' vehicles were found abandoned at the venue, and gunshots and spent bullets were discovered nearby. The band, known for playing vallenato music, is not typically associated with drug gangs, but the venue of their last gig has links to drug violence. This incident comes amidst a surge in drug-related violence in Mexico, with over 70,000 people dying in such violence last year. The authorities are still investigating the disappearance of Kombo Kolombia.

The flu season, which has been the worst in a decade, is showing signs of abating, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). The number of visits to doctors for flu-like symptoms has decreased, with 6.4% of trips to the doctor being for flu-like symptoms, down from 7.5% the previous week. However, the CDC is cautious about declaring that the peak of the flu season has been reached, as more than half of the country is still reporting high levels of flu activity.

The decrease in child deaths from 22 the week before is encouraging, but it is not necessarily a sign that the severe flu season is abating, as each week's total from the CDC includes deaths from earlier in the season. The flu remained widespread in 48 states, according to the CDC's latest report.

The CDC recommends people get a flu shot, even though the effectiveness of this year's flu vaccine is estimated to be only 25% against the dominant H3N2 virus. However, the vaccine has been more effective for children, reducing illness by 59% among kids ages 6 months to 8 years old.

Work has already started on next season's flu vaccine, but experts are admitting that most vaccines will give at best mediocre protection, because they are based on outdated technology. The process of making flu vaccines starts months before the actual flu season gets underway because it takes a long time to make them using the current technology.

The CDC reports 13 more children died of the flu last week, bringing the number of pediatric flu deaths to 97 this season. Even at this point in the season, health officials recommend people get a flu shot.

The flu season has been driven by a formidable type of flu that tends to cause more hospitalizations and deaths. This year's flu vaccine is estimated to be only 25% effective against the H3N2 virus. The flu also killed an estimated 56,000 people, mostly older adults, during the 2014-2015 season. Most of the children who have died this year, as in past years, have not been vaccinated.

The CDC does not keep exact counts of adult flu deaths. All 10 regions reported flu-like illness reports that were at or above baseline levels in the areas. New York City, Washington, D.C., Puerto Rico, and 39 states experienced high flu-like visits. It's definitely not too late to get a flu shot, which remains highly recommended.

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has approved Yescarta (axicabtagene ciloleucel), a cell-based gene therapy, to treat adult patients with certain types of large B-cell lymphoma who have not responded to or who have relapsed after at least two other kinds of treatment. This is the second gene therapy approved by the FDA and the first for certain types of non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL).

Yescarta, a chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell therapy, is a customized treatment created using a patient's own immune system to help fight the lymphoma. The safety and efficacy of Yescarta were established in a multicenter clinical trial of more than 100 adults with refractory or relapsed large B-cell lymphoma. The complete remission rate after treatment with Yescarta was 51 percent.

The approval of Yescarta brings this innovative class of CAR-T cell therapies to an additional group of cancer patients with few other options. However, the treatment has the potential to cause severe side effects, including cytokine release syndrome (CRS) and neurologic toxicities, which can be fatal or life-threatening.

Yescarta is being approved with a risk evaluation and mitigation strategy (REMS), which includes elements to assure safe use (ETASU). The FDA is requiring that hospitals and their associated clinics that dispense Yescarta be specially certified. The treatment carries a bracing price tag of $373,000 per patient, not including the costs of dealing with Yescarta's side effects.

The FDA granted Yescarta Priority Review and Breakthrough Therapy designations, and it received Orphan Drug designation. The Yescarta application was reviewed using a coordinated, cross-agency approach. The clinical review was conducted by the FDA's Oncology Center of Excellence, while the Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research (CBER) conducted all other aspects of review and made the final product approval determination.

Yescarta is the second treatment of its kind, called a Chimeric Antigen Receptor T-Cell, or CAR-T, for the particular genetic modifications made to white cells. The first, Kymriah, for Novartis, was addressed at children with acute lymphoblastic leukemia, a small group of patients. Yescarta is being approved for a much larger population.

The approval of Yescarta marks another milestone in the development of gene therapy for deadly and largely untreatable forms of cancer. The FDA is committed to supporting and helping expedite the development of these products, and a comprehensive policy to address how it plans to support the development of cell-based regenerative medicine will soon be released.

A new record for the fastest illegal and dangerous lap of Manhattan has been claimed by an anonymous driver, who goes by the name AfroDuckProductions. The run was reportedly made on August 26th, 2013, using a stock 2006 BMW Z4. The driver started on FDR/East Side Drive at 116th Street, and the route included passing under the Williamsburg, Manhattan, and Brooklyn Bridges, shooting through the Battery Park Tunnel, and navigating red lights on West Street/West Side Drive. The course cut off the northern tip of Manhattan, turning right by the George Washington Bridge in Washington Heights, and the driver got across Manhattan at one of its narrowest points. The total distance was approximately 26.5 miles, with an average speed of around 66 miles an hour. The driver had to stop at six red lights during the run. The NYPD is investigating the incident, and technology such as license plate readers may be used to identify the lawbreaker. The stunt has received mixed reactions, with some praising the driver for his feat, while others criticize him for reckless driving and endangering other road users.

The article discusses two separate but related topics: a Tesla car fire incident and the career background of actress Mary McCormack.

The Tesla fire incident occurred on June 16, 2018, in West Hollywood, California. Actress Mary McCormack, who is married to British film director Michael Morris, tweeted a video of the incident, which showed a Tesla Model S suddenly catching fire while in traffic on Santa Monica Blvd. No one was injured, but the incident has raised concerns about the safety of electric vehicles, particularly Tesla's. Tesla is investigating the cause of the fire, and the company maintains that it takes extraordinary measures to protect passengers from fires, which it says are at least 10 times less likely in a Tesla than in a gas-powered car.

Mary McCormack is an American actress who has had leading roles in various TV shows and movies, including Murder One, The West Wing, In Plain Sight, and Private Parts. She was born in Plainfield, New Jersey, and began her acting career at age 12, performing in Gian Carlo Menotti's Christmas opera Amahl and the Night Visitors. She continued her stage work in musicals and finished an acting program at the William Esper Studio. She has worked in New York theater productions, including The Atlantic Theater Company, Alice's 4th Floor, and Naked Angels, where she appeared in Jon Robin Baitz's A Fair Country.

McCormack portrayed Justine Appleton on Murder One (1995–1997) and also starred in the HBO series K Street, which aired for only ten episodes. She starred in Howard Stern's movie Private Parts in 1997. In 2004, McCormack joined the cast of The West Wing as Deputy National Security Advisor and ex-CIA officer Kate Harper. Her character soon became a recurring role and remained throughout the last three seasons until the series finale. McCormack starred in the USA Network series In Plain Sight. She portrayed Mary Shannon, a deputy United States marshal attached to the Albuquerque, New Mexico, office of the Federal Witness Security Program (WITSEC), more commonly known as the Federal Witness Protection Program. On July 28, 2010, the show was renewed for its fourth and fifth seasons, to run in 2011 and 2012. The show was ended in 2011, making the fifth season its last. After its end, McCormack was cast as the lead in Kari Lizer's untitled comedy pilot on ABC.

McCormack was nominated for the 2008 Tony Award for Best Performance by a Featured Actress in a Play for the role of Gretchen in the 2008 Broadway revival of Boeing Boeing. In 2012, McCormack reunited with the cast of The West Wing to film a video that served both as a reminder that U.S. voters should vote for non-partisan candidates when they cast their ballots and as a video promoting McCormack's sister's ultimately successful judicial candidacy for the Michigan State Supreme Court. In 2016, McCormack played a supporting role in the Amazon.com exclusive special An American Girl Story - Maryellen 1955: Extraordinary Christmas.

In July 2003, McCormack married director and producer Michael Morris. Together they have three daughters, Margaret (born 2004), Rose (born 2007), and Lillian (born 2011). McCormack is the godmother of In Plain Sight co-star Fred Weller's daughter.

The TED conference in Vancouver featured a variety of speakers and topics, including technology designer Bran Ferren, who discussed the potential benefits of autonomous vehicles, and architect Marc Kushner, who spoke about the evolution of architectural history. Edward Snowden made a surprise appearance via a video chatbot, discussing his motivations for leaking NSA documents and calling for internet companies to encrypt web browsing as a default setting. The conference also featured discussions on urban planning, environmental efforts in China, typeface design, and documentary filmmaking. The former intelligence contractor left the audience divided, with some viewing him as a hero and others as a villain.

The Nasa spacecraft, New Horizons, is set to fly past Pluto on Tuesday, July 14, at a speed of over 45,000 kilometers per hour. The spacecraft, which is the first to reach Pluto on the outer edge of the solar system, has revealed that Pluto is larger than previously thought, with a diameter of approximately 2,370 kilometers, making it roughly two-thirds the size of Earth's moon.

Alan Stern, the lead scientist on the $700 million mission, stated that the increased dimensions mean that Pluto must hold more ice and less rock beneath its surface than researchers had expected. Pluto has been difficult to measure accurately from Earth due to its distance and the atmospheric mirages that can occur.

New Horizons has confirmed that Pluto's north pole bears an icy cap, with chemical signatures of methane and nitrogen ice detected in the polar cap. One early image received from New Horizons last week showed Pluto as an orangey globe bearing a large bright spot shaped like a heart. More recent images have revealed cliffs, craters, and chasms larger than the Grand Canyon.

The spacecraft will perform its historic flyby at 12.49 pm BST on Tuesday. However, scientists must wait until 2 am BST on Wednesday for the probe to make contact with Earth and confirm that it has survived the encounter.

The most dangerous hazards for New Horizons are dust particles trapped in orbit around Pluto after being dislodged from its moons by meteorite impacts. A strike from a dust particle the size of a grain of rice could destroy the spacecraft, but the risk of such a disaster is low, at around one in 10,000.

New Horizons has spent over nine years on its 4.8 billion-kilometer journey to Pluto, which was the last world in the solar system to be visited by a spacecraft. On board are seven sophisticated instruments and the ashes of Clyde Tombaugh, the astronomer who discovered Pluto in 1930.

When the probe blasted off in January 2006, Pluto was the ninth planet in the solar system. However, seven months later, astronomers at the International Astronomical Union voted to downgrade the icy body to a dwarf planet, as it does not dominate its region of space in the way the other major planets do.

The spacecraft will take scores of photographs as it speeds past Pluto and its five known moons, Charon, Hydra, Nix, Styx, and Kerberos. The images will provide the first close-up view of the mountains and valleys of the unknown world, and its tenuous atmosphere seen as the sun rises and sets behind it. Instruments on New Horizons might even find evidence that it snows on the tiny world.

Nasa officials expect the first images from the flyby to be released on Wednesday night. The snapshots from onboard cameras will capture details up to 100 meters across, a vast improvement on those taken on approach, which pick out features about 15 kilometers across.

However, scientists are in for a long wait to learn everything New Horizons sees. The probe will collect so much information as it passes Pluto that it will take 16 months to send it all back to Earth.

The mission marks the end of the US space agency's bid to explore every planet in the solar system, starting with Venus in 1962. Tuesday's flyby coincides with the 50th anniversary of the first ever fly-by of Mars by the Mariner 4 probe.

By studying other objects in the solar system, scientists can learn more about Earth's history. For example, studying Pluto can provide insights into how Earth formed, where Earth's water came from, how life began on Earth, Earth's atmospheric structure, and how the sun affects Earth.

Scientists are particularly interested in studying Pluto's atmosphere, as it is tenuous and extends much higher than Earth's atmosphere does. Observing Pluto's atmosphere can help scientists better understand global warming on Earth.

The New Horizons spacecraft is expected to provide a wealth of new information about Pluto and its moons, shedding light on the dwarf planet's geology, composition, and atmosphere. The mission is a significant milestone in the history of space exploration and will help scientists better understand the outer reaches of our solar system.

In the Florida Republican primary on Tuesday, Mitt Romney secured a commanding victory, rebounding from a defeat in South Carolina and taking a significant step towards the Republican presidential nomination. The former Massachusetts governor won 47% of the vote, while Newt Gingrich received 33%. Rick Santorum had 13%, and Texas Rep. Ron Paul garnered 7%.

Romney's victory was due to a majority of Florida GOP voters viewing him as the candidate best able to defeat President Barack Obama in a general election. Romney carried 60% of votes among those seeking a candidate who could defeat the president, while only about 30% said the same of Gingrich. Gingrich performed well among those seeking a true conservative and those seeking an experienced candidate, but Romney won over a majority of voters in both categories.

Conservatives were divided in their support for Romney, with about 40% saying his issue positions are not conservative enough. Strong supporters of the tea party movement also favored Gingrich over Romney, but Romney won 50% or more among those who support the movement somewhat, are neutral, or oppose it.

The gender gap played a significant role in the election, with Romney winning by a wide margin among women after a negative campaign in Florida that raised questions about Gingrich's character. Women were more likely to be influenced by campaign advertising and were more likely to prioritize a candidate's strong moral character in their vote. Only about half of women in the poll reported holding a positive opinion of Gingrich as a person, compared to nearly 80% who had a positive opinion of Romney.

Economic concerns were the top priority for about 60% of voters in choosing a candidate, with half saying foreclosures were having a major impact on their community, and 30% reporting they were falling behind financially.

Four in ten voters expressed a desire to see someone else run for the nomination, more than in New Hampshire a few weeks ago, though the window for another candidate to join the field is nearly closed. About half of voters said they would be satisfied if Gingrich or Rick Santorum became the nominee. More, about two-thirds, said they'd be satisfied with a Romney candidacy, including about 40% who voted for Gingrich and half who backed Santorum.

The survey of 2,739 Republican voters was conducted for The Associated Press and the television networks by Edison Research. The survey has a margin of sampling error of plus or minus 3 percentage points.

Romney's victory gave him all 50 of Florida's convention delegates, the biggest primary haul so far. The bigger prize was political momentum in the race to pick an opponent for Democratic President Barack Obama this fall. Romney headed west to campaign in Minnesota and Nevada after the victory, while Gingrich vowed to press on.

The president-elect, Donald Trump, has continued to express skepticism about the intelligence community's findings regarding Russian hacking of American political groups during the 2016 election. In a series of tweets, Trump claimed that intelligence officials delayed a scheduled briefing on the matter because they needed more time to build a case. He also cited WikiLeaks founder Julian Assange's claim that a "14-year-old kid could have hacked" the emails of Hillary Clinton's campaign chairman, John Podesta, and that Russia was not the source of the hack.

Intelligence experts both inside and outside of the government have stated that evidence suggests Russia attempted to influence the election, with the Obama administration stating that the hacking campaign went to the highest level of the Russian government. Trump has previously stated that it's nearly impossible to know who hacked what and when, and has antagonized the intelligence community over the weekend by stating that hacking is "a very hard thing to prove."

Trump has promised to reveal what he proclaims to know this week, but there has been some confusion over when he will receive new intelligence briefings. He initially stated that he would be meeting with high-level intel briefers mid-week, but that has been delayed. A senior U.S. intelligence official with direct knowledge of the situation told NBC News that the heads of the NSA, CIA, FBI, and the director of national intelligence were always scheduled to meet with Trump on Friday.

Trump's tweets have been criticized as adversarial by a senior intelligence official, who stated that "He's calling out the men and women of the intelligence community the way he called out Lockheed and Boeing, but these are public servants." Sen. Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., has also criticized Trump for taking on the U.S. intelligence community, stating that "You take on the intelligence community, they have six ways from Sunday to get back at you."

Meanwhile, CIA Director John Brennan stated that his report on Russian hacking was in the "final throes" and would be delivered to President Obama in days. Trump has also announced that he will hold his first news conference in over five months on January 11. The last time Trump held a pre-scheduled open media availability was on July 27, 2016.

The article discusses the controversy surrounding BP's decision to award its top executives, including CEO Bob Dudley, significant bonuses in 2015 despite the company's $5.2 billion loss and the challenging oil market conditions. The bonuses were criticized by a leading shareholder advisory group, Glass Lewis, which recommended that shareholders vote against the payment plans.

BP's compensation committee awards executive bonuses based on the company's performance in strategic areas, including safety record, operational cash flow, and underlying profits. The company defended the payouts, stating that Dudley and other executives had met or exceeded their targets in these areas. However, Glass Lewis expressed concerns that the payouts were not fully earned given the company's performance in 2015.

BP's shareholders will vote on the matter at the company's annual general meeting in London on April 16. This is not the first time Glass Lewis has raised objections to BP's executive pay. Last year, it also recommended that shareholders reject Dudley's pay package, noting that his compensation outpaced that received by chief executives at similar-sized firms "despite the company’s relative underperformance."

The article also mentions that BP's shareholders mounted an unprecedented protest against Dudley's pay, with 59% of proxy votes going against the company's decision to pay him nearly $20 million. This is the first time a top British company has been defeated over executive pay since the "shareholder spring" four years ago. The rebellion highlights a growing trend of institutional investors and advisers taking a more aggressive stance over pay.

The article concludes by stating that BP's chairman, Carl-Henric Svanberg, promised to review the terms on which pay is awarded in consultation with shareholders before next year. BP blamed the falling oil price and a $9.8 billion charge to settle claims related to the Deepwater Horizon disaster for its loss, among other factors. Svanberg told the meeting that the company would sit down with its largest shareholders to understand their concerns and return to seek their support for a renewed policy.

The Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) has announced the arrest of three Palestinians from East Jerusalem and the West Bank, recruited online by an al-Qaida operative in Gaza. The suspects, who were in the process of planning large-scale bombing and shooting attacks on multiple targets in Israel, were recruited separately and were meant to activate three independent terrorist cells. The intended targets included the Jerusalem Convention Center, a bus traveling between Jerusalem and Ma'ale Adumim, the US embassy in Tel Aviv, and emergency responders. The operative, named Ariv Al-Sham, received orders directly from al-Qaida's central structure leader, Ayman Al-Zawahri. The suspects were arrested between December 25 and January 3, and during questioning, they admitted to planning various attacks, including a double suicide bombing and a truck bomb attack. The investigation underlines the fact that the internet remains the main means of expansion for global jihadi elements, with terrorist operatives using it to create operational cells, local commanders, and transfer bomb-making know-how. The relationship between recruits and their handlers online is likened to that of a cow and a calf. The Gaza Strip is identified as a terrorism base for al-Qaida-affiliated elements, in addition to Hamas and Islamic Jihad. Hamas has reached an understanding with these elements, allowing them to act as they please, as long as they do not directly harm Hamas. The episode underscores the risk posed by al-Qaida's attempt to recruit east Jerusalem Palestinians, Israeli Arabs, and Palestinians in the West Bank.

French daredevil Tancrède Melet, a renowned slackliner, base jumper, and wingsuit flyer, died tragically on Tuesday while preparing for a hot air balloon stunt in the Drôme region of southern France. Melet was part of the "Flying Frenchies" and "Skyliners," a group of pioneering stuntmen known for their death-defying High-Line walks performed all over the world.

According to reports, Melet was anchored to a grounded balloon when it suddenly lifted off, leaving him suspended approximately 30 meters in the air. Despite the efforts of his crew, Melet was unable to release his anchor, and he fell to the ground, resulting in his death from trauma. The exact circumstances surrounding the accident are still under investigation.

Melet, who was 32 years old, had a passion for extreme sports and had previously basejumped off the Italian side of Mount Blanc and walked between hot air balloons thousands of feet off the ground as a "tightrope walker" or slackliner. He was also an accomplished climber, kayaker, kiter, and general lover of the outdoors.

Melet leaves behind his partner, Tiphaine Breillot, and a young child. His fellow "Skyliners" posted a tribute on his Facebook page, saying, "Tancrede Melet, a surprising lover of life, surprised us yesterday morning by leaving us too soon. He leaves behind wonderful memories, a taste of freedom, and a head full of dreams."

The Flying Frenchies gained international attention in 2014 when they attempted to walk between two free-flying hot air balloons thousands of feet in the air above the Spanish plains for an ABC News special. The group's YouTube videos, including one featuring a member catapulting off a cliff "Angry Birds-style," have received millions of views.

In Barcelona, Spain, on October 1st, Spanish riot police attempted to halt a disputed independence referendum in Catalonia by forcefully entering polling stations and firing rubber bullets at protesters. The Catalan government, which called for the vote, condemned the police actions and accused them of using excessive force. Tension has been escalating since the vote was announced in early September, with Catalonia, an affluent region contributing significantly to Spain's economy, expressing long-standing complaints about contributing too much to the state without receiving enough in return. Spanish officials, including Enric Millo, the Spanish government's representative in the region, defended the police actions, stating that they acted professionally to enforce court orders and that any attempt to claim the referendum as valid is doomed. Several people were injured during the clashes, and voting was prevented at many polling stations. Catalan President Carles Puigdemont was forced to vote elsewhere due to the police presence at his designated polling station. The Spanish government and its security forces are trying to prevent voting in the independence referendum, which is backed by Catalan regional authorities. The Spanish Constitution Court has suspended the vote, but regional separatist leaders have pledged to hold it anyway, promising to declare independence if the "yes" side wins.

The Great Barrier Reef is currently experiencing an outbreak of crown of thorns starfish, a coral-eating species, which could potentially become the worst on record, according to conservationists. The number of these starfish is estimated to be between four to 12 million, but a report commissioned by WWF-Australia predicts it could increase to 60 million by 2020. The starfish are believed to have caused the loss of around 60,000 hectares of live coral over the past 30 years.

Experts suggest that harmful chemical fertilizers from agricultural farming lands, which trigger algal blooms that feed the starfish, are contributing to the outbreak. They advocate for tougher measures to prevent future plagues, particularly by reducing pollution. Dr. Glen Holmes, co-author of "The Starfish That Eat The Reef," states that cutting catchment pollution can prevent the next outbreak and give the reef a chance to rebuild its coral cover.

Current government investment has not achieved the desired results, and more money is needed to reduce pollution, according to Dr. Holmes. If the outbreak follows the patterns of previous plagues, coral cover could be reduced to below 10%.

In a separate development, the Great Barrier Reef has been added to Google Maps, allowing anyone to explore and experience six of the ocean's most incredible living coral reefs, virtually. This initiative, in partnership with The Catlin Seaview Survey, aims to make these images available to millions of people through Google Maps' Street View feature. Whether you're a marine biologist, an avid scuba diver, or a landlocked landlubber, you can now dive in and explore the ocean with Google Maps.

The Sesame Street YouTube channel was hacked on Sunday, with all content being removed or made private. A 7-minute pornographic video was uploaded to the channel, and the banner was changed to "Sesame Street - It's where porn lives." The hack was claimed by YouTube users MrEdxwx and MrSuicider91. However, MrEdxwx later denied hacking the channel, stating he is an honest YouTuber. The channel remains unavailable at this time, but most of the videos appear to be back online. The incident has not been commented on by PBS, YouTube, or Google.

On September 29, 2016, an unidentified man caused chaos in an Apple Store in Dijon, France, using a steel ball typically used in the game pétanque. The incident was triggered by a refund dispute, with the man expressing his anger by destroying various Apple products, including iPhones, MacBooks, and iPads. During the rampage, he declared that Apple had violated European consumers' rights and demanded a refund, which was refused. The man was eventually apprehended by a security guard and arrested, causing significant damage to the store. A local news report and a video of his attempted escape from the scene were shared online. The incident gained attention due to the irony that the French word for Apple is "pomme," which is the root word for "pummel."

The Nobel Prize in Physics for 2018 has been awarded to three scientists: Arthur Ashkin from the United States, Gerard Mourou from France, and Donna Strickland from Canada. The prize recognizes their discoveries in the field of laser physics. Ashkin developed a laser technique known as optical tweezers, which is used to study biological systems. Strickland and Mourou paved the way for the shortest and most intense laser pulses ever created, a technique called Chirped Pulse Amplification (CPA). This technique has found applications in laser therapy for cancer and in the millions of corrective laser eye surgeries performed each year.

This marks the first time a woman has won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 55 years, since Maria Goeppert-Mayer in 1963. Donna Strickland expressed surprise and delight at winning the prize, and emphasized that her male colleagues also deserved recognition for their contributions. The award comes amid controversy at the CERN particle physics laboratory, where a physicist recently gave a controversial lecture suggesting that male scientists were being discriminated against.

The Nobel Prize in Physics is worth a total of nine million Swedish kronor (approximately £770,686 or $998,618). The Nobel Prizes are a series of annual international awards given in several categories, including Physics, Chemistry, Medicine, Literature, Peace, and Economic Sciences, to recognize outstanding achievements in various fields. The Nobel Prizes were established by the will of Alfred Nobel, the inventor of dynamite, and were first awarded in 1901.

In a tragic turn of events, 17-year-old Johran McCormick was fatally shot in a teenage girl's bedroom. "Deadpool 2" is a sequel to the 2016 hit film, continuing the trend of self-aware, gory, and obscenely funny superhero movies. The protagonist, Deadpool, played by Ryan Reynolds, is a smart-mouthed, unkillable mutant assassin who delivers fast, cheeky, and humorous commentary throughout the film. The movie lampoons earnest comic-book action movies with a creative chutzpah, embracing its bad ideas and shattering the fourth wall with meta precision.

The story revolves around Deadpool's quest to construct a substitute family and protect a defiant teen mutant, Firefist, from a Terminator-like soldier from the future, Cable. Along the way, they are joined by Domino, whose superpower is luck, and the film delves into topics such as gun violence, DC superhero movies, and pop culture addiction.

While the film benefits from Reynolds' superhuman charisma, it feels like more of the same, with an abundance of gross-out gags, irreverent jokes, and Deadpool's running commentary on the movie he's in. However, the film also launches an indictment of pop culture and its addicted fans, showing terrifying things that make viewers uncomfortable while asking if they are enjoying it.

Overall, "Deadpool 2" is a must-see for those who love films that keep them guessing, laughing, and surprised on the edge of their seat. The film delivers over-the-top mayhem and a refresher course on old Marvel comics isn't needed to appreciate what's happening on-screen.

The parent company of Applebee's and IHOP, DineEquity, plans to close up to 160 restaurants, with 105 to 135 Applebee's and 20 to 25 IHOP locations potentially shutting down. This move is aimed at improving overall franchisee financial health and enhancing the supply chain. The decision comes as the casual-dining segment faces increased competition from quick-service restaurants like Panera Bread and Chipotle Mexican Grill. Analysts have noted that Applebee's, in particular, has struggled to maintain favor with casual-dining consumers.

Despite the closures, DineEquity plans to open 125 restaurants globally between the two chains. The company also announced the appointment of Stephen Joyce as its new CEO, replacing Julia Stewart who resigned in February. DineEquity's stock was trading at $38.7, up $1.42 or 3.81%, in mid-afternoon trading. The company, based in Glendale, California, operates over 3,700 restaurants in 19 countries. The closures are part of a normal course of business in the industry, according to Amy Mason, senior vice president for global communications and consumer insights, as they involve underperforming restaurants in lapsed trade areas or locations with unsustainable economics.

A new study conducted by researchers at Dartmouth College has confirmed the authenticity of the famous backyard photo of Lee Harvey Oswald holding the same type of rifle used to assassinate President John F. Kennedy. The study, published in the Journal of Digital Forensics, Security and Law, used a new digital image forensics technique and a 3-D model of Oswald to analyze the photo in detail.

The researchers found that Oswald's pose in the photo is physically plausible, refuting claims that the photo was faked due to Oswald's seemingly implausible pose. The study also found that the lighting and shadows, rifle length, and facial features in the photo are consistent with other evidence.

The backyard photo of Oswald was particularly damning because it showed him holding the same type of rifle that was used to assassinate Kennedy. Oswald was arrested and charged for the assassination, but he died before his trial, fueling theories that he was part of a conspiracy.

The Warren Commission and the House Select Committee on Assassinations concluded that claims of photo tampering were unwarranted. However, previous studies only refuted claims about the lighting and shadows in the photo, and did not address claims about Oswald's pose.

In the new study, the researchers built a 3-D model of Oswald and manipulated it to stand in the same pose as the real Oswald in the photo. They added mass to different parts of the model in a "balance analysis" to see if the model remained stable. The analysis revealed that Oswald's pose in the photo is indeed stable.

The researchers believe that the type of detailed 3-D modeling performed in the study can be a powerful forensic tool in reasoning about the physical plausibility of an image. They plan to use the 3-D human model they created to analyze the pose, stability, and shadows in any image of people.

The study refutes purported evidence of manipulation in the Oswald photo, but it also provides a powerful forensic tool for analyzing the authenticity of other historical photos. Professor Hany Farid, the senior author of the study, is available to comment on the findings.

In Baltimore, a week-long curfew was imposed on Tuesday as thousands of police and National Guard troops patrolled the city to prevent further violence following a night of rioting, looting, and arson. The unrest erupted after the death of Freddie Gray, a 25-year-old black man who died from a spinal injury a week after being arrested by police. On May 14, 2016, a charter bus en route to a casino in Eagle Pass, Texas, crashed on U.S. Highway 83, resulting in eight fatalities and injuring 44 passengers. The accident occurred approximately 46 miles north of Laredo, Texas. The driver of the bus, operated by OGA Charters, survived the crash.

The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) has launched an investigation into the incident, with investigators arriving on the scene the following day. Preliminary reports suggest that the driver lost control and rolled over, but the cause of the accident remains under investigation.

Records from the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration (FMCSA) reveal that OGA Charters had been ordered to sideline one of its buses in 2015 due to brake and emergency exit problems. It is unclear whether this was the same bus involved in the crash or if the company addressed the issues between inspections.

The crash is one of the deadliest bus accidents in Texas in recent years, with the NTSB citing a retreaded tire and illegal bus operation as factors in previous fatal accidents. The owner of the Houston bus company involved in a 2008 crash was charged with making false statements but avoided prison in 2014.

The identities of the victims have been released, with seven dying at the scene and another passing away at a Laredo hospital. A Webb County official initially reported a ninth fatality, but later retracted the statement.

The small bus company, based in San Juan, Texas, had a "satisfactory" rating from the FMCSA in May 2014, but had reported six driver and vehicle inspections since 2014 that found a total of 15 violations, including brake connections with leaks and discolored windshields.

Officials at OGA Charters did not immediately return phone messages seeking comment. The highway at the accident scene was reopened by early evening, with Laredo approximately 150 miles southwest of San Antonio.

The Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM-5) was officially released this week, marking the fifth major revision of the manual used by clinicians in the U.S. to diagnose mental disorders. The DSM-5 was introduced in a conference call by the American Psychiatric Association (APA) and is expected to be a critical guidebook for clinicians. The APA received over 13,000 comments during the three separate drafts of the manual, making it the most open and transparent revision process ever.

The DSM-5 consists of three major sections: Introduction, providing clear information on how to use the DSM; Section II, which provides categorical diagnoses; and Section III, which includes self-assessment tools and categories that require more research. The DSM-5 has approximately the same number of conditions as the previous version, DSM-IV, but there are significant changes in specific disorders.

One of the major changes is the incorporation of four previous separate disorders into one condition called autism spectrum disorder (ASD). ASD is characterized by deficits in social communication and social interaction, as well as restricted repetitive behaviors, interests, and activities. Disruptive Mood Dysregulation Disorder, intended to address issues of over-diagnosis and over-treatment of bipolar disorder in children, is also a new diagnosis. Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) has been modified, with adults now being diagnosed if they meet one less symptom than children.

The DSM-5 also includes changes in the diagnostic criteria for PTSD, major and mild neurocognitive disorder, and new diagnoses such as binge eating disorder, premenstrual dysphoric disorder, and hoarding disorder. The DSM-5 has been met with controversy, with critics accusing it of lowering diagnostic thresholds across the board, making it easier for a person to be diagnosed with a mental disorder.

The release of the DSM-5 coincided with the APA's annual meeting, where 21 sessions will be dedicated to the new manual. The DSM-5 is not a pop-psychology book intended for consumers, but a guide for clinicians to help facilitate treatment. The APA hopes that the science of psychiatry will follow the direction of cancer research, moving from classifying disorders by where they occur in the body to characterizing them by their genetic and molecular signatures.

Some experts, such as Dr. Steven E. Hyman, a psychiatrist and neuroscientist at the Broad Institute, believe the DSM-5 is a scientific nightmare, with many people receiving multiple diagnoses for the same underlying condition. The National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH) has started a federal project called Research Domain Criteria (RDoC) to encourage researchers to investigate the biological underpinnings of disorders instead of relying on the DSM categories.

In conclusion, the DSM-5 is a critical guidebook for clinicians, with significant changes in specific disorders such as autism spectrum disorder, disruptive mood dysregulation disorder, and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder. The DSM-5 has been met with controversy, with critics accusing it of lowering diagnostic thresholds and some experts believing it is a scientific nightmare. The science of psychiatry is moving towards characterizing disorders by their genetic and molecular signatures, with the NIMH starting a project called RDoC to encourage this shift.

Gil Scott-Heron, a renowned poet and musician often referred to as the "godfather of rap," passed away on Friday at the age of 62 in New York. Scott-Heron was a significant figure in the development of hip-hop, best known for his spoken-word piece "The Revolution Will Not Be Televised."

Born in Chicago in 1949, Scott-Heron spent his formative years in Tennessee and New York, and began his recording career in 1970 with the album Small Talk at 125th and Lenox. His work has been influential to many in the hip-hop community, including Kanye West, who sampled Scott-Heron's voice on his platinum-selling album My Beautiful Dark Twisted Fantasy.

Throughout the 1970s and early '80s, Scott-Heron continued to record, but took a lengthy hiatus before briefly returning to the studio in 1994. In 2010, he released a new album, I'm New Here, to critical acclaim.

Scott-Heron struggled with substance abuse in the 2000s, spending time in and out of jail on drug possession charges. However, he returned to performing after his release in 2007.

In his personal life, Scott-Heron lived a reclusive lifestyle, often spending time in his Harlem apartment watching fight films and listening to his own music. He is remembered as a unique and influential figure in the world of music and poetry.

The article discusses a study that investigates the relationship between human brain size and intelligence, as measured by IQ tests. The study, which is a meta-analysis of 88 studies involving over 8,000 participants, found a weak but significant positive association between brain volume and IQ. However, the researchers conclude that brain size plays only a minor role in explaining IQ test performance and that brain structure and integrity are more important as a biological foundation of IQ. The study also found that publication bias may have overestimated the strength of the association between brain volume and IQ in the literature. Despite these findings, the researchers note that there are still indications that brain structure plays a role in cognitive performance within humans. The study was published in the journal Neuroscience and Biobehavioral Reviews.

The Utah Legislature passed a bill on Wednesday, eliminating the statute of limitations for lawsuits against perpetrators of child sexual abuse. The bill, HB277, was sponsored by Rep. Ken Ivory and Sen. Aaron Osmond, and is now awaiting Gov. Gary Herbert's signature. Deondra Brown, co-founder of the Foundation for Survivors of Abuse, watched the final debate and expressed excitement for the bill's potential to help victims of child sexual abuse in Utah.

Brown has personal experience with the issue, as three of her sisters, members of the 5 Browns piano quintet, were molested by their father, Keith Brown, as children. Keith Brown was sentenced to 10 years to life for sodomy on a child, and one to 15 years each on two counts of sex abuse of a child in 2011. The crimes occurred when the girls were 13 years old or younger.

Current Utah law limits civil actions to four years after a victim's 18th birthday. HB277 would remove those limitations and allow victims time to heal and muster the courage and maturity to take civil action and hold their abusers accountable.

Sen. Aaron Osmond stated that 1 in 6 boys and 1 in 4 girls in Utah will suffer or have suffered from sexual abuse. He added that most children who are sexually abused don't come to a realization or the ability to deal with the experience until after age 40. The bill gives victims a four-year window from the time of discovery or remembrance of the child abuse experience to file civil action, allowing them to overcome emotional obstacles that often bar them from taking action.

Sen. Scott Jenkins argued against HB277, stating that the statute of limitations was put in place for a reason and citing cases where individuals who realized repressed memories of child sexual abuse, but later discovered them to be wrong.

Deondra Brown stated that victims of child sexual abuse shouldn't have a "door closed in their face" because of time limits, and they should be granted the option if or when they decide they want to file civil actions against perpetrators. She stated that victims deal with medical bills and health issues for "the rest of their lives" and shouldn't have to shoulder the burden of paying for it, which she said costs the average victim up to $1 million over the course of their lives.

In a separate incident, a retired Rich High School teacher, Michael Layne Williamson, was sentenced to prison for sexually assaulting a former student 22 years ago. The 13 bald eagles found dead in Maryland's Eastern Shore in February did not die of natural causes, according to wildlife officials. The deaths, the largest single die-off of bald eagles in Maryland in 30 years, are now being investigated as a potential crime, with a $25,000 reward offered for information leading to a conviction. The birds showed no signs of trauma, and initial speculations of poisoned animal carcasses were dismissed, as the farm owner denied using poison. Necropsies also ruled out diseases such as avian influenza, a significant threat in the region due to its many poultry farms and migratory birds. The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and Maryland Natural Resources Police are working together to uncover the cause of the eagles' deaths, withholding further information to protect the investigation. Bald eagles, while no longer endangered, are still protected, and killing one is punishable by up to a year in prison and a $100,000 fine.

A 36-year-old woman from Florida developed an itchy skin lesion on her groin two months after her honeymoon in Belize. Initially, she thought it was an insect bite and sought treatment from several doctors, but the lesion persisted even after antibiotics. Doctors were puzzled and suspected it could be a cyst or an ingrown hair. However, upon further examination at Tampa's Memorial Hospital, they discovered that the lesion was a living creature – a human botfly larva, also known as a maggot.

The human botfly is rare in the US but common in the tropics. The insect lays its eggs on animals like flies or mosquitoes, which then become hosts and carry the eggs to human skin. The larvae burrow into the skin, causing itching, and live for 27 to 128 days. After its stay beneath the skin, the adult larva drops to the ground where it pupates for between 27 and 78 days before maturing into an adult botfly.

The woman underwent surgery to remove the larva, and her lesion was completely resolved a week later. The case was reported in the Journal of Investigative Medicine High Impact Case Reports. It's a reminder that skin problems are one of the medical issues travelers are most likely to bring home after visiting developing countries, and a skin infestation of developing larvae is the fourth most common skin disease travelers report.

The woman's experience underscores the importance of seeking medical attention for any unusual skin conditions, especially after traveling to tropical regions. In some communities in the tropics, home remedies like petroleum jelly, bacon strips, nail polish, or plant extracts are used to suffocate and extract the larvae. However, in this case, surgical removal was necessary.

Officials from the Bank of England, the Treasury, and the Financial Services Authority are drawing up contingency plans, anticipating that a Greek departure from the monetary union could be as damaging to the global economy as the collapse of Lehman Brothers in 2008. The governor of the Bank of England, Sir Mervyn King, warned that Europe is "tearing itself apart" without any obvious solution.

With a second election in Greece called for June 17, King hinted that the Bank could take further steps to stimulate growth if policymakers in Europe fail to address the sovereign debt crisis. The head of the International Institute of Finance banking lobby, Charles Dallara, stated that money is leaving Greece at an increasing pace due to political uncertainty, and a planned breakup of the single currency would cost 2% of EU GDP ($300bn) but a disorderly collapse would result in a 5% drop in output, a $1tn loss.

Capital flight from Greece has increased since it became clear that a coalition government could not be formed after the election earlier this month. The Greek president, Karolos Papoulias, said citizens are withdrawing their money amid "great fear that could develop into panic" at the risk of a debt default and exit from the Eurozone. In little more than a week following the election on May 6, €3bn was withdrawn from bank accounts, with €800m taken out in a single day earlier this week.

The Spanish prime minister, Mariano Rajoy, and the Irish finance minister, Michael Noonan, have expressed concerns about financing their respective countries due to the uncertainty surrounding Greece. The first meeting between French president François Hollande and German chancellor Angela Merkel helped to calm markets, with suggestions that Berlin might be more open to growth initiatives for Europe. However, foreign affairs analysts note that Obama's leverage with European leaders is minimal, and he is expected to use the G8 summit for quiet diplomacy, aiming to sway Merkel to endorse immediate actions to boost growth.

Sony Kapoor, of the Brussels-based Re-Define thinktank, stated that the high-stakes game of chicken between Greek and other EU politicians must end now. He warned that the social, political, and economic damage to the EU from a Greek exit is potentially incalculable. At the G8 summit, Obama is expected to press Merkel to lean more towards a growth package for Europe, instead of pushing for austerity measures that were rejected by Greek voters.

In a speech delivered at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland on January 26, 2018, President Donald Trump emphasized the resurgence of a strong and prosperous America, stating that it is now the best time to hire, build, invest, and grow in the United States. He highlighted the country's economic growth, low unemployment rates, and tax cuts as evidence of this resurgence. Trump also reiterated his "America First" policy, emphasizing that it does not mean America alone, but rather a commitment to international cooperation. He stressed the importance of fair and reciprocal trade, and criticized unfair trade practices that undermine all nations. The speech was met with mixed reactions, with some viewing it as a positive step towards international cooperation, while others criticized Trump's self-centered approach and lack of focus on global issues. The speech also included a call for the international community to work together on security concerns, such as fighting terrorism and addressing the threat posed by North Korea's nuclear program.

In this article, several notable figures from various fields have passed away. Gatling in the television series "Benson," died from a stroke on March 28. He was 94.

Actress Patty Duke, star of "The Patty Duke Show," died on March 29, at the age of 69. Duke won an Academy Award at age 16 for playing Helen Keller in 1962's "The Miracle Worker." Architect Zaha Hadid, whose designs include the London Olympic Aquatic Centre, died on March 31, a spokesperson from Zaha Hadid Design told CNN. She was 65. CBS News legend Morley Safer, whose work on "60 Minutes" embodied the show's 50 years on air, died at the age of 84 on May 19. Actor Alan Young, known for his role as Wilbur Post in the television show "Mr. Ed," died on May 19. He was 96.

Drummer Nick Menza, who played on many of Megadeth's most successful albums, died after collapsing on stage during a show with his current band, Ohm, on May 21. He was 51. Slice, whose real name was Kevin Ferguson, initially gained fame from online videos that showed him engaging in backyard bare-knuckle fights. A Florida man, Joseph Schreiber, was arrested on Wednesday for allegedly setting fire to a mosque in Fort Pierce, Florida, on Monday. The mosque was attended by Omar Mateen, the gunman who committed the deadliest mass shooting in U.S. history at a gay nightclub in June. The fire occurred on the Muslim holiday Eid al-Adha. Schreiber is being charged with arson and faces at least 30 years in prison if convicted. He was identified as the suspect after a tip and was found to have anti-Islamic posts on social media. The FBI is also investigating the fire for potential federal charges. The mosque has faced numerous threats of violence and intimidation since it was identified as Mateen's place of worship.

This document consists of two separate articles, one about privacy on a website and the other about human rights lawyer Amal Clooney's efforts to bring ISIS perpetrators to justice for their crimes against the Yazidi community.

Regarding privacy, the article explains that Meredith partners with third-party advertisers to serve digital ads, including personalized ads based on users' activity across the Internet and their devices. The second article focuses on Amal Clooney's visit to a refugee camp in northern Greece, where she met with members of the Yazidi community who have been affected by ISIS's genocidal campaign. Security Council. The diplomatic challenge does not daunt Clooney, who has taken on similar cases in the past, including the government of the Maldives.
