The city of Brussels, the capital of Belgium and home to EU and NATO headquarters, is facing a significant issue with chronic traffic jams due to the poor state of its underground tunnels. The tunnels' deterioration has led to repeated closures of key road tunnels, causing gridlock in the city. The Belgian capital's regional parliament has been informed that repairs are being delayed because the original construction plans for the tunnels have allegedly been eaten by mice.

The claim was made during an investigation into the dilapidated state of the tunnels, which span 7.1 miles. A special parliamentary commission has been set up to investigate the issue and determine if it's too late to save the tunnels.

During a hearing, Christian De Buysshcer, the former head of roads for the body in charge of the tunnels, was asked about the missing plans. He explained that the plans were archived in 1989 inside a pier under a viaduct linking the Liège motorway to the boulevard Reyers. The plans remained there for 20 years, and when workers finally moved them to a proper storage room in 2010, they were allegedly eaten by mice.

The state of the roads in Brussels, with an estimated repair bill of €1 billion, has become a hot political issue in Belgium. The city's political structure is complex, with 19 independent municipalities and a division of populations between French and Dutch speakers. The city's infrastructure is also shoddy, with roads often clogged by traffic.

Despite the humorous response to the news, the situation is causing frustration among residents and officials. The city's reputation is at risk, with some calling for the traffic jams to be given UNESCO World Heritage status. The city's political structure and infrastructure issues have been the subject of criticism in the past, and the latest mice-eaten-plans incident has added to the city's woes.

Julian Assange, the founder of WikiLeaks, has announced that he will accept arrest by British police if a United Nations working group on arbitrary detention rules in his favor, ending his three-and-a-half-year stay in the Ecuadorian embassy in London. Assange sought asylum in the embassy in 2012 to avoid extradition to Sweden over rape and sexual assault allegations, which he denies. The UN panel's decision, due to be published on Friday, is not legally binding but can be used to apply pressure on states in human rights cases. If Assange prevails, he expects the return of his passport and the termination of further attempts to arrest him. If he loses, he will exit the embassy and accept arrest. The UN panel's findings differ from those of the Swedish authorities, and the Swedish foreign ministry has stated that the legal process for Assange's case will be handled in court by Swedish prosecutors. The British government has stated that Assange has never been arbitrarily detained by the UK but is voluntarily avoiding lawful arrest by choosing to remain in the Ecuadorian embassy. The UK continues to have a legal obligation to extradite Assange to Sweden. The UN panel's decision could make it difficult for the UK and Sweden to bring pressure on other countries over human rights violations if they choose to ignore the decision. Assange's lawyers have demanded assurances from the UK that he will not be arrested and subjected to extradition proceedings to face potential prosecution over WikiLeaks' publishing activities. The British Foreign Office has stated that it will not pre-empt the panel's findings.

The lawsuit filed in Dallas County District Court on September 6, 2017, accuses the Boy Scouts of America (BSA) of negligence in the death of Reid Comita, a 15-year-old boy from Fort Worth. Reid died from heat stroke while hiking at Buffalo Trail Scout Ranch in June. The Comita family claims that Reid was sent on an aggressive hike in high temperatures, despite signing him up for an introductory backpacking class under adult supervision. The lawsuit also alleges that Reid did not receive proper training and was accompanied by only two teenagers, instead of the required two adults.

The circumstances surrounding Reid's death have left his mother, Copper, baffled, angry, and devastated. The lawsuit also outlines communication issues, claiming the Comita family was not notified of his death for more than four hours. The backpacking course would have been Reid's final task to accomplish Eagle Scout, an honor his troop awarded him posthumously.

The BSA issued a statement expressing their condolences and emphasizing the importance they place on the health and safety of their youth members. However, the Comita family has not received any communication from the BSA since Reid's death.

Reid was a bright student and active in choir, in addition to earning merit badges in the Boy Scouts. His father, John, grew up participating in the Boy Scouts and felt it was a bonding experience for them. However, he feels that the BSA's emphasis on their 12 points is more for the executives' convenience than for the safety and well-being of the scouts.

The lawsuit is seeking damages for the loss of life, mental anguish, and loss of companionship, among other things. The case is ongoing.

Warren Buffett, the renowned investor and chairman of Berkshire Hathaway, has expressed optimism about the Japanese economy despite the recent market plunge following the devastating earthquake and tsunami. Buffett, who is currently in South Korea, believes that the crisis presents a buying opportunity for Japanese stocks, stating that the economic future of Japan will not be altered. He also expressed confidence in the Japanese government and Tokyo Electric Power's efforts to contain the crisis at the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear power plant.

Buffett's optimism is shared by Yoji Takeda, director of Asian equities at RBC Investment (Asia) in Hong Kong, who believes that the market panic last week may have oversold shares due to overblown fears about the nuclear plant. The World Bank has estimated that it might take Japan up to five years and $235 billion to rebuild from the disaster.

Already, reconstruction-related businesses are seeing a boom, with shares of Daiwa House Industry, Japan's biggest home construction company, and other builders and contractors soaring since the disaster struck on March 11. Buffett is not new to acquisitions, with Berkshire Hathaway recently buying U.S. specialty chemicals maker Lubrizol for $9 billion. He has also expressed interest in buying entire businesses and large-cap shares in South Korea, where Berkshire is already a leading shareholder in steelmaker POSCO.

Buffett is scheduled to meet with South Korean President Lee Myung-bak and later head to India to launch his firm's insurance selling portal. His visit to South Korea has been met with admiration by ordinary South Koreans, many of whom have bad memories of the 1998 Asian financial crisis. Buffett's optimistic stance on Japan's economic future contrasts with the market's current pessimism, offering a glimmer of hope for investors.

In a media stir on Monday, Newsmax CEO Christopher Ruddy suggested that President Trump is considering terminating Special Counsel Robert Mueller, who is overseeing the Russia investigation. However, a source close to Ruddy stated that he did not actually speak to Trump about firing Mueller, but was reading between the lines of what others had said.

Sean Spicer, White House Press Secretary, confirmed that Trump had not discussed the matter with Ruddy. Jay Sekulow, one of Trump's lawyers, had previously not ruled out the possibility of Trump firing Mueller in an appearance on ABC's "This Week."

Deputy Attorney General Rod Rosenstein, who has the authority to hire and fire Mueller, stated at a Senate hearing that he has not seen good cause to fire Mueller. Rosenstein added that he is confident Mueller will have sufficient independence in the investigation into the Trump campaign’s potential ties to Russia.

Senator Susan Collins further pressed Rosenstein on reports that the administration is considering firing Mueller, asking whether he would if President Trump ordered him to do so. Rosenstein replied that he would not follow any orders unless he believes those are lawful and appropriate.

Democrats slammed Attorney General Jeff Sessions for canceling plans to testify at the hearing and sending Rosenstein in his place. The special counsel, Robert Mueller, was appointed by the Justice Department last month to investigate Russia's interference in the 2016 presidential election.

Christopher Ruddy, a confidant of Trump, has a history of floating trial balloons related to moves Trump is considering making. In February, after having a drink the night before with Trump at Mar-a-Lago, Ruddy criticized White House Chief of Staff Reince Priebus on CNN.

This situation highlights the ongoing tension between the Trump administration and the Russia investigation, with the President considering dismissing the special counsel assigned to the Russia investigation, and the Deputy Attorney General stating that he has not seen good cause to fire Mueller.

In an unexpected discovery, photographs from Nirvana's first concert in March 1987 have surfaced, shared by Maggie Poukkula, the daughter of Tony Poukkula, a member of Seattle band Laytem. The concert took place in Tony's basement, where Nirvana, consisting of Kurt Cobain, Krist Novoselic, and Aaron Burckhard, performed. During the show, Maggie joined the band on guitar for at least two Led Zeppelin covers. The photos, found within her father's biographies of Cobain and Nirvana, were recently shared on Twitter.

The concert's setlist included covers of Led Zeppelin's "Heartbreaker" and "How Many More Times," as well as early versions of "Aero Zeppelin," "Mexican Seafood," "Pen Cap Chew," "Hairspray Queen," "Spank Thru," and "If You Must." A recording of "Heartbreaker" and a bootleg version of "If You Must" are available.

The emergence of these photos follows a wave of rare Cobain and Nirvana artifacts, some of which were used in Brett Morgen's documentary, Montage of Heck. The film, which showcases Cobain's archives, including notebooks and audio cassette tapes, has been successful on the festival circuit, in limited theatrical runs, and on HBO. Montage of Heck will return to movie theaters starting August 7th.

This discovery and the subsequent documentary are part of an ongoing effort to archive web pages and preserve links to their original versions, aiming to fix broken links on the web.

Gwyneth Paltrow, the 43-year-old actress, is renowned for her wellness website, Goop.com, and her foray into the beauty industry, collaborating with Juice Beauty and launching her own Goop skin-care line. Living in Los Angeles, she shares beauty, hair, and life advice on the platform. Paltrow, who is a mother to Apple, 11, and Moses, 9, advocates for the use of oils in skin care, citing her Instant Facial product as a favorite due to its fruit acids and tingling effect.

However, a recent incident in Spain has raised concerns about an alternative therapy promoted by Paltrow, live bee acupuncture. A 55-year-old woman undergoing the treatment for two years suffered a severe allergic reaction and died weeks later due to multiple organ failure. This is believed to be the first reported death from live bee acupuncture, also known as bee venom apitherapy, of a patient who had previously not been allergic. The case highlights the increased risk of severe reactions with repeated exposure to the allergen. The report's authors, Ricardo Madrigal and Paula Vázquez Revuelta, emphasize the need for caution when considering alternative therapies.

On Thursday, a New Jersey Transit train crashed into the Hoboken station, resulting in one fatality and injuring 108 people. The train reportedly hit the station at high speed, according to Governor Chris Christie. The National Transportation Safety Board is leading the investigation into the cause of the crash. The engineer of the train, who was injured, is cooperating with law enforcement officials. The Hoboken station was thrown into chaos after the 8:45 a.m. crash, with passengers kicking through windows to escape the mangled wreckage. The majority of the injured were on board the train. The structural integrity of the station must be evaluated before service can resume, and there is no estimated timeframe for reopening. PATH service is expected to resume later in the day. A Family Reunification Center has been set up, and a hotline has been established for information. Alex Wulwick, a regular commuter on the train, was on board during the crash and described the scene as chaotic with "absolute panic" and "screaming." The speed of the train seemed normal before the crash, according to Wulwick. The Internet Archive is archiving pages to preserve links and fix broken links on the web.

The Yahoo annual shareholders meeting, led by CEO Marissa Mayer, was largely uneventful, with directors being re-elected and the executive compensation plan endorsed. Mayer highlighted the progress made since her appointment, citing a 70% increase in mobile email usage and a 50% rise in Flickr mobile app photo uploads. Despite a crass comment from an elderly shareholder, Mayer handled the situation professionally. Other shareholders asked trivial questions, including one about football team allegiances and another about Walmart, which Mayer deftly deflected. Yahoo's shares are up over 3% in afternoon trading.

The article discusses the ongoing conflict in Libya and the international response to it. President Obama is adopting a more passive role, allowing other nations to lead the search for solutions, a move that has been met with criticism from conservatives and some liberal interventionists. The administration is actively engaged in private diplomacy, including financial sanctions against Gaddafi's inner circle and military planning at NATO. France has taken a more aggressive stance, recognizing the Libyan National Council as the legitimate representative of the Libyan people and pledging to exchange ambassadors with them. The French move has been met with mixed reactions from other European powers and the United States. The Libyan National Council is facing challenges in establishing a transitional government and managing the tasks and challenges arising from the conflict. The article also reports on the ongoing fighting in Libya, with government forces making gains in key cities like Zawiya and Ras Lanuf. The conflict has resulted in a significant displacement of people, with nearly 250,000 forced to flee their homes. The United States is planning to send disaster relief teams to eastern Libya, but these teams should not be viewed as military operations. The article concludes with a condemnation of the detention and possible torture of a BBC news team by Libyan authorities.

Reynolds American Inc. (RAI) has agreed to acquire Lorillard Inc. (LO) in a $25 billion deal, excluding debt, reshaping the U.S. tobacco industry and making Newport menthols a stronger competitor against Altria Group Inc.'s Marlboro. The transaction will add Lorillard's Newport, the No. 2 U.S. cigarette brand, to Reynolds's portfolio, which includes Camel and Pall Mall cigarettes. British American Tobacco Plc (BATS) will fund $4.7 billion of the transaction, maintaining a 42% stake in Reynolds. Imperial Tobacco Group Plc (IMT) will acquire brands such as Kool and Blu e-cigarettes for $7.1 billion to address antitrust concerns.

The deal, valued at $27.4 billion including debt, will create a company with annual revenue of over $11 billion and operating income of about $5 billion, almost two-thirds the yearly sales and income of U.S. market leader Altria (MO) Group Inc. The combined company will account for almost 33% of the U.S. industry, leaving the U.S. with two competitors – Reynolds and Altria – selling nine out of every 10 cigarettes.

The deal faces challenges, and investors are uncertain it will close in its current form. Lorillard shares slid to $60.17 in New York, 13% below the purchase price. Reynolds shares also fell, dropping 6.9% to $58.84. Imperial Tobacco declined 3.7% to 2,638 pence in London, while BAT fell 1.8% to 3,532 pence. Altria dropped 3.7% to $41.76.

The companies will fight for customers in an industry where health concerns and smoking restrictions have eroded sales. Total U.S. cigarette shipments fell by a median of 2.9% in the first quarter among the nation’s top tobacco companies. Yet even amid the slump, the companies have remained profitable, with Altria, Reynolds, and Lorillard all boosting net income last year.

The deal will have to pass antitrust hurdles. As part of the effort to overcome those challenges, Imperial will acquire well-known brands such as Salem, Winston, and Maverick. Getting the Blu lineup also gives Imperial a foothold in the emerging market for e-cigarettes. The deal is expected to close in the fourth quarter of 2014.

The Federal Trade Commission is likely to take a hard look at the latest proposed transaction due to the consolidated market. Selling off minor brands to Imperial, and even unloading a bigger name like Camel, may not be enough to gain approval. The deal's likelihood of being approved is uncertain, and it would need to be more substantial than just Camel to pass regulatory scrutiny.

Whitney Houston's death was caused by a lethal combination of Valium, Xanax, and alcohol, according to an exclusive report by RadarOnline.com. The coroner is awaiting final toxicology results to determine the primary factor in her death, but it is believed that her heart stopped due to a suppressed respiratory system caused by the anti-anxiety meds and alcohol. Houston's final days were marked by scandal, as she became involved in an altercation at a Hollywood nightclub and was seen heavily intoxicated and injured. The final toxicology results for Houston should be released in the next several weeks. Additionally, there are reports that Bobby Brown, Houston's ex-husband, is planning to write a tell-all book about their relationship. However, a confidentiality agreement and the potential impact on his daughter, Bobbi Kristina, may stand in his way.

Uber's licence to operate in London has been revoked by Transport for London (TfL) due to concerns over safety, regulatory breaches, and corporate responsibility. The decision was supported by London Mayor Sadiq Khan and employment rights campaigners, but faced criticism from Uber users, drivers, and government ministers. Uber plans to appeal the ruling, stating that it disagrees with the decision but acknowledges the importance of a good reputation. The company's CEO, Dara Khosrowshahi, has called on Londoners to work with Uber to resolve the issue. The decision could have significant implications for Uber, as London is one of its biggest markets, and could also impact other gig economy companies. The decision was also criticized by some Uber users who rely on the service for affordable and accessible transportation options.

The nuclear talks between Iran and the United States, part of the P5+1 Group, are facing challenges as the deadline for a comprehensive deal approaches on July 20. U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry is in Vienna for face-to-face meetings with Iranian Foreign Minister Mohammad Javad Zarif, but no breakthrough has been achieved yet. The negotiations aim to curb Iran's uranium and plutonium programs in exchange for the end of nuclear-related sanctions.

The interim deal, which went into effect in January, offers the option of an additional six-month period for negotiations, an extension that appears increasingly likely. However, both sides may agree on a shorter window. The U.S. is leading the insistence on deep enrichment cuts, while Iran insists it needs to expand enrichment for reactor fuel and denies wanting atomic arms.

The state of U.S.-Iranian relations is adding a new wrinkle to the negotiations. While the two sides are arguably fighting proxy wars in Israel, Gaza, and Syria, they're talking cooperation in Iraq and Afghanistan. The nuclear matter is battling for full attention.

The negotiations won't succeed unless Iran wants a deal more than its international interlocutors do. The U.S.-led sanctions imposed by the international community have had a devastating bite, but their effectiveness is questionable if Iran doesn't consider failure to achieve economic relief an existential threat to the regime.

The talks are also complicated by crises across the Middle East and beyond, where the U.S. and Iran are often opposed. For example, Iran is Hamas' primary benefactor and the presumed source of its newfound drone capacity, while the U.S. provides billions in aid to Israel.

Despite these challenges, the U.S. and Iran have recently found increasing areas for cooperation, such as stemming a flow of Sunni extremists into Iraq. The nuclear matter is now one of many issues being discussed, and their discussions are broader than in years past.

An extension of the deadline makes sense for both sides, as terminating the nuclear talks could put Tehran back on a path toward isolation and potentially set the stage for U.S. military action if Iran proceeded again toward nuclear weapons capacity. However, both sides face internal pressures against a deal or an extension. In the U.S., some lawmakers have threatened to scuttle any emerging agreement if it would allow Iran to maintain some enrichment capacity. In Iran, hardliners oppose almost any concession by President Hassan Rouhani's government.

The acting director of the Transportation Security Administration (TSA), Melvin Carraway, has been reassigned following an internal investigation that revealed significant security failures at numerous busy airports. In a report by the Homeland Security Inspector General, TSA agents failed 67 out of 70 tests, allowing undercover investigators to smuggle mock explosives or banned weapons through checkpoints in 95% of trials.

The Homeland Security Secretary, Jeh Johnson, announced Carraway's reassignment to the Office of State and Local Law Enforcement at DHS headquarters, effective immediately. Acting Deputy Director Mark Hatfield will lead the TSA in the interim. Johnson expressed gratitude for Carraway's 11 years of service and 36 years of public service.

The security failures were highlighted in a six-point memo released by Johnson, which outlined actions taken to address the issues, including revising TSA's standard operating procedures for screening and directing training for all TSA officers and supervisors. Johnson also ordered more random covert testing at checkpoints and testing of airports' screening equipment.

Johnson emphasized that the findings were part of the continuous effort to improve aviation security as threats evolve. He also noted that President Barack Obama had nominated Coast Guard Vice Admiral Pete Neffenger to be the next TSA administrator, urging the U.S. Senate to confirm his nomination swiftly. The reassignment and subsequent actions aim to improve security at U.S. airports following the disconcerting findings.

Golden Corral, a popular restaurant chain, found itself in the spotlight on Reddit after images and a video surfaced, alleging poor kitchen conditions and improper food handling at one of its Florida locations. A user named GCWhistleblower posted pictures of a kitchen filled with garbage near food, and a video by an employee, Brandon Huber, showed food being stored near the dumpster. The chain responded by stating that the food in question was destroyed within an hour and the employee involved participated in the disposal. Huber's father attempted to sell the video for $5,000, but the offer was not accepted. The manager involved was terminated for failing to follow food handling procedures. The incident follows similar cases of poor hygiene practices in other restaurant chains, such as Taco Bell and Domino's Pizza. The chain's reputation may be affected by this incident, with comparisons being drawn to Edward Snowden. Huber has since filmed a follow-up video discussing his reasons for bringing the practice to light, but his current employment status remains unknown.

Comedienne Joan Rivers, 81, remains on life support at Mount Sinai Hospital in New York City after suffering cardiac arrest during a routine throat procedure on August 28. Her daughter, Melissa Rivers, has been by her side since the incident, and the family has received an outpouring of support from fans and fellow celebrities. Doctors are running tests to assess any damage caused by the incident and are hopeful that Rivers will make a recovery. Melissa Rivers has expressed gratitude for the support and asked for continued prayers. The taping of Rivers' show, Fashion Police, has been cancelled due to her hospitalization.

The first presidential debate between Donald Trump and Hillary Clinton took place at Hofstra University on Monday, and it was widely perceived that Clinton emerged victorious. The debate was marked by Clinton's focused and well-prepared performance, while Trump appeared defensive and wilted under her attacks. Trump's supporters in the debate hall groaned audibly as he struggled to answer questions, and his team seemed disheartened after the debate, while Clinton's team appeared relieved and energized.

Trump's strategy of turning himself into a reasonable facsimile of a presidential candidate unraveled during the debate, as Clinton launched a series of attacks on his business career, his net worth, and his job creation record. Trump's attempts to defend himself were often meandering and weak, and he failed to effectively counter Clinton's attacks.

One of Clinton's most effective attacks was on Trump's habit of stiffing contractors who have worked on his construction projects. She contrasted this with her own father's business ethics, and Trump's response was flippant and unconvincing. Clinton also effectively attacked Trump on his refusal to release his tax returns, suggesting that he may not be as rich as he claims and may have paid no federal income tax. Trump's response was that not releasing his tax returns made him smart.

Trump's performance in the debate was a departure from his usual aggressive and bombastic style, and he appeared to be on the defensive for much of the night. Clinton, by contrast, was focused and well-prepared, and effectively countered Trump's attacks on her email scandal and the Clinton Foundation.

Whether the debate will reverse Trump's momentum or reestablish Clinton's control of the race is an open question. However, it is clear that Clinton was the more effective debater on the night, and Trump's performance was widely criticized by both Democrats and Republicans.

Overall, the debate was a significant moment in the 2016 presidential election, and it will likely have a lasting impact on the race. Clinton's performance was seen as a strong showing, while Trump's performance was widely criticized as weak and defensive. The debate also highlighted some of the key issues and differences between the two candidates, and it will be interesting to see how they continue to campaign and debate in the coming weeks.

A US Secret Service agent, identified as Special Agent Noel E. Remagen, passed away after suffering a stroke during President Trump's visit to Scotland. Remagen, 42, was part of the presidential protection team and was working on protection for National Security Advisor John Bolton when he fell ill at Trump's Turnberry golf resort in Ayrshire on Sunday. He was quickly attended to by a White House doctor and Secret Service colleagues before being rushed to a hospital in Glasgow, where he passed away on Sunday. Remagen is survived by his wife and two small children. The President and First Lady Melania Trump departed for Joint Base Andrews to visit Remagen's family. The funds raised for Remagen's family through GoFundMe have been verified to go directly to the intended recipient.

In this article, Donald Trump, the President-elect of the United States, has threatened to upend longstanding U.S. nuclear weapons policy by suggesting an expansion and strengthening of the country's nuclear capabilities. Trump's statements, made in a series of impromptu comments and tweets, have caused confusion and concern among experts and officials, as they contradict ongoing efforts to modernize the U.S. nuclear arsenal and longstanding bipartisan support for preventing nuclear escalation.

Trump's comments come in response to Russian President Vladimir Putin's call for Russia to strengthen its nuclear forces. However, Putin seemed to normalize Trump's statements, calling them unsurprising. Trump's comments, if followed through, would represent an extraordinary shift in how the U.S. approaches the role of weapons of mass destruction in its own defenses and throughout the world.

Trump's advisers have attempted to clarify his intentions, with incoming press secretary Sean Spicer stating that there will not be an arms race, but also noting that Trump is not going to "take anything off the table." It remains unclear where Trump stands on the issue, but his comments have been criticized by experts and officials as perilous and potentially violating an arms control treaty with Russia.

The controversy started after Trump tweeted that the U.S. "must greatly strengthen and expand its nuclear capability" and called for the country to take part in an "arms race." Trump further escalated his call on Friday, telling MSNBC's "Morning Joe" that he is fine with the country taking part in an "arms race" if it puts the U.S. in a stronger position against foreign adversaries.

The potential consequences of changing U.S. nuclear weapons policy are unimaginable, according to John Tierney, a former Democratic congressman and current executive director of the Center for Arms Control and Non-Proliferation. Tierney warned that an expansion threatens a nuclear arms race and could have catastrophic consequences.

Joseph Cirincione, the president of the global security foundation Ploughshares Fund and a nuclear weapons expert, called Trump's actions "bizarre, unprecedented and completely out of bounds behavior for a president-elect." Cirincione noted that incoming presidents usually wait until they take office to make pronouncements on a topic like nuclear policy, and expressed alarm at Trump's cavalier attitude toward such a sensitive issue.

It is unclear how Trump's comments will be received by other countries and whether they will lead to an actual arms race. However, experts have warned that Trump's statements are dangerous and could have serious consequences for global security.

The survey published in the journal Pediatrics reveals that a majority of pediatricians and family physicians often or always acquiesce to parents who wish to delay vaccinating their children, despite the potential risks to the children's health. The survey, conducted in 2012, asked a nationally representative sample of 534 primary care physicians about parents postponing one or more vaccinations for children under 2 years old.

Ninety-three percent of doctors reported that at least once in a typical month, parents had asked them to delay vaccines, with 21% reporting that more than 10% of parents in their practices had made such requests. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention advises that children be vaccinated for 14 diseases before age 6, which entails roughly 29 shots, sometimes given all at once.

Physicians often agree to these requests to build trust with families and avoid losing them as patients. However, they feel that these decisions put children at risk for measles, whooping cough, and other ailments. The survey also found that dealing with changes to vaccine schedules had decreased job satisfaction for 40% of the doctors.

The American Academy of Pediatrics advises doctors to keep skeptics in the fold, lest they lose the opportunity to educate, cajole, or persuade them. Physicians reported trying various strategies to convince parents to vaccinate their children, such as telling them that they had immunized their own children or warning them about outbreaks if too few people are fully vaccinated.

However, the survey found that a disproportionate amount of time is spent discussing vaccines during doctor visits, with hesitant parents requiring up to 14 minutes or more of counseling. This is causing guidance on safe sleep or toilet training to be crowded out.

In response to the survey's findings, some doctors have started taking more drastic measures, such as ending their relationship with parents who refuse all vaccinations. Others, like Dr. Nivedita More, a pediatrician in Rancho Santa Margarita, Calif., allow delays most of the time but draw the line at refusal to vaccinate altogether.

The study's lead author, Dr. Allison Kempe, thinks that the idea that vaccine education can be handled in a brief wellness visit is untenable, and suggests that vaccine counseling should begin during pregnancy and be compensated separately when a substantial proportion of time is being spent on vaccines. Additionally, pro-vaccine parents and celebrities could be used in marketing campaigns to reinforce vaccination as a social norm.

Ohio Governor John Kasich postponed the execution of convicted child-killer Ronald Phillips, scheduled for January 16, due to Phillips' request to donate his organs to his mother and sister who suffer from kidney disease and a heart condition, respectively. The execution has been rescheduled for July 2, 2014, at Southern Ohio Correctional Facility in Lucasville.

Phillips, who was sentenced to death in 1993 for raping and killing a 3-year-old girl, is willing to donate organs to other people if he cannot help his relatives. His attorney, Lisa Lagos, stated that this was not a delaying tactic but an attempt by Phillips to make a final gesture for good.

The Department of Rehabilitation and Correction (DRC) initially denied Phillips' request due to logistics and security concerns, but Kasich allowed for the initial compatibility tests to be conducted by state prison officials. If a transplant of any non-vital organs is feasible, Phillips would undergo an operation at Ohio State University Medical Center before returning to death row.

This is an unprecedented situation in Ohio and the nation, as Phillips' execution is the first to be postponed to permit an inmate's organs to be harvested. Richard Dieter of the Death Penalty Information Center in Washington, D.C. noted that a Delaware inmate, Steven Shelton, was allowed to donate his kidney in 2005, but he was not facing immediate execution.

Phillips had ordered his last meal but did not have time to eat it due to the postponement of his execution. The cost of the transplant surgery will be paid by Phillips or the organ recipients, not by Ohio taxpayers, according to DRC policy. The surgery will be performed at the Wexner Medical Center at Ohio State University.

There was no immediate comment from Akron Prosecutor Sherry Bevan Walsh, who handled the case. Phillips' execution has drawn increased attention because he was scheduled to be the first person put to death in Ohio using a new and untried lethal-injection cocktail consisting of midazolam, a sedative, and hydromorphone, a morphine derivative.

Demi Lovato, the X Factor coach, has opened up about her past struggles with drug addiction, specifically cocaine, in a candid interview with Access Hollywood. At 19, Lovato admitted to smuggling drugs onto airplanes and using them in bathrooms, even with a sober companion watching her 24/7. She also confessed to abusing alcohol and hiding it in a Sprite bottle. Lovato's mother, Dianna, who also had an eating disorder, admitted to being in denial about her daughter's drug use but grew closer to her after seeking help together. Both Lovato and her mother have spoken about their mental health issues and how they have strengthened their bond as a family.

Exploding Kittens is a strategic card game created by Elan Lee, Matthew Inman, and Shane Small, inspired by Russian Roulette. The game involves players drawing cards from a deck until someone draws an exploding kitten and loses. The deck includes cards that allow players to avoid exploding, force opponents to draw multiple cards, or shuffle the deck. The game's intensity increases as the deck shrinks, making it more likely to draw an exploding kitten. The game's unique selling point is its Oatmeal-style artwork and humor. Within minutes of its Kickstarter launch, it surpassed its $10,000 goal and rapidly approached $1 million, indicating strong interest in the game.

The medical director of the NHS in England, Prof Sir Bruce Keogh, has called for an end to the incineration of aborted fetuses in hospitals, following a Channel 4 Dispatches investigation that revealed some NHS trusts have been burning fetal remains alongside clinical waste. The investigation found that ten NHS trusts have been burning fetal remains, with two more disposing of bodies in incinerators used to heat hospitals. Health Minister Dr Dan Poulter described this practice as "totally unacceptable" and has asked Prof Keogh to write to all NHS hospital trusts to stop the practice immediately.

The Human Tissue Authority has a code of practice for the disposal of human tissue, which includes fetal remains, that hospitals should follow. Women who have had an abortion or miscarriage should be informed that there are different options available - burial, cremation, and incineration. Incineration should be handled as "sensitive" and therefore should not be done alongside the burning of waste.

Professor Sir Mike Richards, chief inspector of hospitals, from the Care Quality Commission, expressed disappointment that some trusts may not be informing or consulting women and their families about the disposal of fetal remains. He also stated that the practice of incinerating pre-24 week fetuses is unacceptable and that cremation should be used instead.

Amanda Holden, who suffered a miscarriage herself in 2010 and delivered a stillborn son in 2011, is leading a campaign against the practice of incinerating fetal remains without the knowledge of the parents. In 2011, 189,931 abortions were carried out in England and Wales, mostly on the NHS. The Care Quality Commission has also said it will investigate the findings of the Channel 4 Dispatches programme.

The FBI Director, James Comey, sent a letter to Congressional leaders on Sunday, stating that the FBI found nothing in their investigation that changed their conclusions about Hillary Clinton's use of a private email server, meaning no recommendation of criminal charges. This letter came after Comey's previous letter in October, which raised concerns about new emails that could implicate Clinton. The news set Twitter on fire, with Comey being criticized from all sides for either "bowing" to Clinton pressure or for getting involved in the first place and disrupting the election.

Twitter users expressed their opinions on Comey's latest letter, with some praising him for clearing Clinton and others accusing him of caving to political pressure. Some tweets suggested that Comey's actions were intended to distract from the Wikileaks' ongoing release of emails hacked from Clinton campaign manager John Podesta. Others speculated that Comey was trying to protect Clinton and deflect attention away from the Wikileaks dump.

The anticipation of how Donald Trump and his campaign would react to the news was also a topic of discussion on Twitter. Some tweets suggested that Trump would continue to attack Comey and the FBI, while others speculated that Trump would now focus his attacks on Clinton.

Overall, the reaction on Twitter was divided, with some praising Comey for clearing Clinton and others accusing him of political bias and manipulation. The news came just two days before the presidential election and could have a significant impact on the outcome.

"Wonder Woman" dominated the weekend box office, earning an estimated $57.2 million, surpassing Tom Cruise's "The Mummy" which debuted with $32.2 million. The Gal Gadot-led film, produced by Warner Bros., has now earned over $205 million domestically in just two weeks. The poor opening for "The Mummy," which cost an estimated $125 million to produce, signals a weak start for Universal's "Dark Universe," a planned connected franchise of monster movies. Meanwhile, the A24 thriller "It Comes at Night," aimed at discerning horror fans, sold a modest $6 million in tickets in its debut weekend. "Captain Underpants: The First Epic Movie," "Pirates of the Caribbean: Dead Men Tell No Tales," and several other films rounded out the top 10.

The research paper by Jon Kleinberg of Cornell University and Lars Backstrom of Facebook suggests that the structure of a person's social network can predict their romantic partner more accurately than the number of mutual friends, a concept known as embeddedness. The researchers used data from 1.3 million Facebook users and found that a measure they call dispersion, which considers mutual friends and friends from various social circles, is a more reliable predictor. The algorithm correctly identified a user's spouse 60% of the time, significantly higher than random guessing. Interestingly, the algorithm's failures often indicated relationships that were likely to break up. The research has implications for Facebook, as it could help tailor content and ads to users based on their relationships. The study confirms the intuitive idea that a significant other occupies a unique place in a person's social network, characterized by dispersion rather than embeddedness. The researchers also found that relationships with higher dispersion were more likely to last. However, the study only considered Facebook users who identified their partners on the site, and future research could explore undeclared relationships.

In a visit to Washington, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov made a sarcastic remark about the firing of FBI Director James Comey, who was leading an investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 U.S. election. During a press conference at the State Department, Lavrov asked reporters if Comey was fired, to which they responded affirmatively. He then responded, "You're kidding, you're kidding." Lavrov's meeting with President Donald Trump at the White House later in the day was also closed to reporters.

The Russian diplomat's visit to the U.S. comes at a time of heightened scrutiny around investigations into the Trump campaign's possible ties to Russia. Comey was fired by Trump on Tuesday, which has sparked criticism from Democrats and some Republicans, and renewed calls for an independent investigator into Russian meddling in the 2016 election, including alleged collusion between the Kremlin and the Trump campaign.

During his meeting with Trump, Lavrov discussed efforts by Russia, Turkey, and Iran to set up "de-escalation zones" in opposition-held areas of Syria. The two governments still disagree on Assad's role in last month's chemical gas attack, which left dozens of civilians dead and spurred Trump to retaliate by launching 59 cruise missiles at a Syrian airbase.

The meeting between Lavrov and Trump also featured Russian Ambassador Sergey Kislyak, whose attendance is considered protocol. Kislyak's role is critical in the investigation into former National Security Advisor Michael Flynn, who met with the ambassador during the Trump transition and misled Vice President Mike Pence about the two men's discussions on Russian sanctions levied by the Obama administration.

The meeting between Lavrov and Trump is the highest-level Russian official to meet with Trump since he took office in January. The White House meeting also follows tensions over a U.S. airstrike against a Syria airbase blamed for a chemical attack by the regime of Syrian President Bashar Assad, a Russian ally. Trump said following that meeting that relations between the U.S. and Russia "may be at an all-time low."

Lavrov's meeting with Trump and Secretary of State Rex Tillerson in Washington comes less than 24 hours after news of the firing of FBI Director James Comey, which has ushered in a wave of criticism from Democrats and some Republicans with renewed calls for an independent investigator into Russian meddling in the 2016 election, including alleged collusion between the Kremlin and the Trump campaign. The meeting also comes at a time when U.S.-Russian relations are seen by the administration as "at a low point."

A teenager posing as a doctor was busted by West Palm Beach police after a month-long stint at St. Mary's Medical Center. The juvenile, whose age was redacted from the incident report, was spotted wearing a white doctor's lab coat with the St. Mary's logo and "anesthesiology" stitched on the front, carrying a stethoscope, and telling people he was a doctor. Hospital staff and police agreed not to charge him with a crime. The impostor was found in an OB/GYN examination room, where he had been with a patient when the real doctor, Dr. Sebastian Kent, conducted an exam. The hospital stated that the teenager never had contact with any patients and did not gain access to any patient care areas. The hospital is cooperating with the ongoing police investigation. The teen's mother arrived at the scene, stating that her son has an undisclosed illness and had not been taking his medication. The incident has left the medical community and patients shocked, with Dr. Kent expressing his surprise at the young doctors looking younger every year.

In a controversial ruling, a judge has barred a 20-year-old mother from breastfeeding her 11-month-old son due to her recent tattoo, which allegedly posed an unacceptable risk of HIV transmission. The mother, known as Ms Jackson, got a tattoo on May 6 without informing the tattooist that she was breastfeeding. The boy's father, Mr Macek, raised concerns about the mother's tattoo during a parenting dispute, leading to the case being brought before the Federal Circuit Court.

Judge Matthew Myers granted an injunction to prevent the mother from breastfeeding her son despite her testing negative for hepatitis and HIV. The judge argued that the tests were not conclusive, and the risk to the baby was still unacceptable. The decision has sparked outrage among breastfeeding advocates, with concerns that it could set a dangerous precedent.

Dr Karleen Gribble from the University of Western Sydney expressed shock, stating that many mothers who breastfeed get tattoos, including tattoos of their children's names. Rebecca Naylor, the Chief Executive Officer of the Australian Breastfeeding Association, also raised concerns about the potential implications of the ruling, questioning whether women who expose themselves to any blood-borne virus risks should be prevented from breastfeeding.

Despite the concerns, Judge Myers relied on material published by the Australian Breastfeeding Association, which states that HIV can be transmitted from mother to baby via breast milk. The case will be heard by a full bench of the Family Court in Sydney on Friday, as the mother appeals the ruling.

The decision has raised broader questions about a judge's right to control the risk-taking behaviors of women and the implications for breastfeeding mothers in Australia. The Australian Breastfeeding Association emphasizes the importance of considering the risk to babies while also acknowledging that mothers are individuals who engage in various activities. They stress that while caution is necessary, it should not restrict the natural bond between mother and child.

Al-Jazeera America, a Qatar-based news organization, is set to establish a firm foothold on American television on Tuesday, after a decade of trying. The network will replace Al Gore's former Current TV in more than 45 million TV homes. Al-Jazeera America has hired many veterans of U.S. television, including John Seigenthaler, Joie Chen, Antonio Mora, and Sheila MacVicar, and is promising a meaty diet of news that it believes will contrast with the opinionated talk that dominates American news networks.

The network has invested significantly in its launch, with dozens of flat-screen TVs and occupied desks scattered around marble pillars in AJA's New York office, and plans to establish bureaus in 11 other American cities. Until Al-Jazeera America revealed a prime-time schedule last week, there were few indications of what the network would look like. Scheduled shows include a nightly newscast anchored by Seigenthaler, a newsmagazine hosted by Chen, a news talk show with Mora, and a business program starring Ali Velshi.

It's still not clear what will be shown in the mornings and whether much of the broadcast day will be devoted to documentary-style programming or live news. Al-Jazeera is well-established overseas, and the American network will take advantage of its 70 bureaus. However, executives have been careful to stress that AJA will be geared toward American tastes.

The American launch has caused some internal dissension, with concerns that the network will water down its journalism for an American audience. Al-Jazeera America will be available in less than half of American homes at its launch, and the channel's location on cable systems may make it less accessible to viewers. Despite these challenges, Al-Jazeera America is confident that it can provide quality, in-depth content that will distinguish it from its competition.

In a recent interview with Fox News, US President Donald Trump defended Russian leader Vladimir Putin against accusations of being a killer, stating that "We've got a lot of killers. What, do you think our country's so innocent?" Trump's comments were met with stern criticism from Florida Senator Marco Rubio, who tweeted, "When has a Democratic political activist been poisoned by the GOP or vice versa? We are not the same as Putin."

Trump's respect for Putin and willingness to work with Russia has been a recurring theme, particularly in light of allegations that Russia interfered in the 2016 presidential election on Trump's behalf. The two leaders spoke by phone last weekend, and a summit meeting has been mooted by both governments.

Trump's comments about Putin being a killer were not the first time he has defended the Russian leader. In December 2015, MSNBC host Joe Scarborough told Trump that Putin kills journalists who don't agree with him, to which Trump replied, "Well, I think that our country does plenty of killing too, Joe."

Trump also reiterated his belief that millions of illegal immigrants voted in the 2016 presidential election, despite calls for him to provide proof and questions about whether he'll have an official probe into the issue. The full interview with Trump is set to air on Fox News before the Super Bowl.

The conversation between Trump and Putin, as well as the ongoing investigations into links between Trump aides and Russian actors, have raised concerns about the potential for improved relations between the two countries to come at the expense of democratic values and national security.

The article discusses the upcoming presidential race in the United States, with a focus on Hillary Clinton's announcement of her candidacy. The author expresses concerns about Clinton's approach to her campaign, including her reliance on pre-taped videos and a listening tour, which the author argues may not be effective in connecting with the broader public.

The article also touches on the political climate in the United States, noting that Clinton personifies the meritocracy that is seen as increasingly elitist by the middle class. The author suggests that Republicans will use this perception to paint Democrats as elitists, as they have done in previous elections.

The article also discusses the fundraising strategies of the Democratic Party, arguing that the need to serve donors keeps them from solving real problems and that they rely on paid propaganda to make up for it. The article concludes by discussing the three main problems with the current political system: the way they raise money, the way they craft their message, and policy.
