The Portsmouth High School Class of 2015 in New Hampshire broke the monotony of graduation ceremonies with a surprise flash mob performance to Taylor Swift's "Shake It Off." The idea was spearheaded by valedictorian Colin Yost, who wanted to send a positive message and go viral. The dance routine was choreographed by Yost, Brooke Matthews, Georgina Head, and Lauren Gagne, with the help of a stage manager and two friends with dance experience.

The students kept the dance a secret from the administration, but eventually gained their approval by presenting detailed outlines and a sneak peek of the performance. During the graduation ceremony, Yost ended his speech with the line "all you have to do is shake it off," and then began dancing awkwardly to the song, which was played over the gym's loudspeakers. The audience, initially surprised, soon joined in, and the performance went viral, receiving over 270,000 views on YouTube by Tuesday afternoon.

Yost, who plans to major in chemical and biological engineering at Princeton University in the fall, said the dance routine aligned with his valedictory address, which emphasized embracing one's inner nerd and being proud of who one is. The students were thrilled with the national attention the performance received, and it became the top-trending story on MTV.com later that evening. Yost, who works as an assistant in a cardiovascular operating room at a Portsmouth hospital, said the memory of the flash mob will stay with him forever.

A North Korean soldier who defected to South Korea was found to have antibodies against anthrax, a deadly disease caused by bacteria, sparking concerns about North Korea's biological weapons capabilities. The soldier, whose identity remains undisclosed, had either been exposed to or vaccinated for anthrax and developed immunity to the disease before defecting. The discovery of anthrax antibodies in the soldier's bloodstream has caused concern in Seoul, as anthrax can kill at least 80% of those exposed within 24 hours without antibiotics or vaccination.

South Korea's military is expected to have an anthrax vaccine developed by the end of 2019, but currently, it does not have one. The revelation adds to growing concerns about North Korea's biological weapons development, as the regime has been suspected of producing such weapons since the Pyongyang Biological Technology Research Institute was publicized in 2015. The institute, run by the Korean People's Army Unit 810, claims to specialize in pesticide research, but analysts suggest that the dual-use equipment on the site indicates biological weapons are being manufactured in North Korea.

The news of possible North Korea anthrax development comes at a time when South Korean newsmagazine Sisa Journal is reporting that the U.S. military in South Korea has continued to test live bacteria at local bases. The Joint United States Forces Korea Portal and Integrated Threat Recognition (JUPITR) program, aimed at shaping biological detection capabilities, is ongoing and budgeted to receive about $9 million. Concerns about biological weapons have spiked in South Korea after Seoul's defense ministry confirmed that the U.S. military in South Korea imported samples of anthrax 15 times since 2009, with a shipment in 2015 exposing as many as 22 people.

Jennifer Lawrence, the Hunger Games star, expressed her views on Hollywood's standards and her personal life in an interview with Elle magazine. Lawrence stated that she is often considered "obese" by Hollywood standards and vowed never to starve herself for a role, instead choosing to eat like a caveman. She also shared her experiences of getting in shape for the role of Katniss Everdeen, focusing on looking fit and strong rather than thin and underfed.

Lawrence also discussed her relationship with boyfriend Nicholas Hoult, whom she met on the set of X-Men: First Class. The couple, who have a laid-back lifestyle, enjoy watching TV together and have a sense of humor about it, often comparing women's bodies to those of The Simpsons characters.

The candid star also admitted her struggles with Hollywood's PR machine, often blurting out the first thing that comes to mind on the red carpet. Despite her success, Lawrence revealed that she is not planning to splurge on a mansion and will continue to live modestly, as she has done in the past.

In summary, Jennifer Lawrence discussed her views on Hollywood's standards, her relationship with Nicholas Hoult, her struggles with Hollywood's PR machine, and her decision to continue living modestly, despite her success.

Bloomingdale's, a luxury department store owned by Macy's Inc., has faced a wave of criticism on social media over an ad in their holiday catalog that some perceived as promoting date rape. The controversial ad features a woman laughing with her head turned as a young man looks her way, with the text "Spike Your Best Friend's Eggnog When They’re Not Looking." The ad has sparked over 3,868 negative comments on social media channels within the last 48 hours, with many calling it "creepy."

Bloomingdale's has since apologized for the ad, stating that the copy used was inappropriate and in poor taste. The company acknowledged that the ad was an error in judgment. It is unclear what the intention of the ad was, but branding experts suggest that marketers are under pressure to stand out amid the increasing amount of advertising messages consumers are exposed to daily.

This controversy comes at a crucial time, as the holiday shopping season approaches. Bloomingdale's is the latest company to experience a rapid spread of controversy, thanks in part to the influence of social media. Earlier this week, consumers took to social media to express their disapproval of Starbucks' new red holiday cups and to vent about the controversy itself.

The incident highlights the risks that marketers face when trying to grab attention in today's competitive advertising landscape. As Jonah Disend, CEO of Redscout, a branding firm owned by MDC Partners, notes, marketers have to work harder to get attention, but the harder they try, the riskier it becomes.

Hallie Twomey, a mother from Maine, USA, turned to social media in November 2013 to ask people across the world to scatter the ashes of her son, CJ Twomey, who took his own life in 2010 at the age of 20. One year later, CJ's ashes have been taken to over 100 countries and even sent into space.

The Scattering CJ Facebook page features numerous photographs of people holding CJ's ashes, often in unique locations such as Machu Picchu, Peru, a tea plantation in Tamil Nadu, India, and the Zugspitze, the highest mountain in Germany. Some of the ashes have been scattered from hot air balloons, skydiving, and even underwater near the Dominican Republic.

Hallie chooses people going to unique or previously unvisited locations to scatter CJ's ashes, and those who participate are asked to take a picture and share a few words about their chosen location. The Facebook page is filled with photographs from around the world, including famous landmarks, snowy mountains, and tropical islands.

CJ's ashes have been scattered across seven continents, including Antarctica, but there are still a few locations his family would like him to visit, such as the Christ the Redeemer statue in Rio de Janeiro, the Galapagos Islands, the Great Pyramid of Giza in Egypt, and under the ancient Angel Oak Tree in South Carolina.

CJ's ashes were also part of a rocket's payload launched from the New Mexican desert in October 2014, allowing his ashes to reach farther than his family ever imagined.

Hallie and her family have never measured the exact amount of ash in CJ's urn, but about two-thirds of what they planned to share has now been sent. They aim to post the remaining third by early 2015 but have no definite timeline. Hallie is unsure how she will feel when the Scattering CJ project draws to a close and she sends off the last packet of CJ's ashes, but she is glad she did it.

Postal systems around the world have different rules about sending cremated human remains by post. The US Postal Service allows the shipment of cremated remains both domestically and internationally, while the Royal Mail in the UK considers human remains, including ashes, a "prohibited item" and will not transport them. If posting ashes internationally, it is advised to check whether the destination country permits it or if certain procedures apply.

Hallie Twomey spoke to the BBC World Service about the Scattering CJ project, stating that she feels less alone due to the kindness of strangers who have helped scatter her son's ashes. She hopes that sending CJ on this journey will keep his memory alive.

In a study conducted by behavioral researchers Jason Rogers and Abbe Macbeth from Noldus Information Technology, it was found that the phenomenon known as Resting Bitch Face (RBF) is not just a popular internet meme, but a genuine expression detected by a sophisticated software program called FaceReader. The software, which maps over 500 points on a face to determine emotional expressions, found that while most faces register 97% neutrality, those with RBF have a higher level of emotion, specifically contempt, detected.

The study found that the big change in percentage came from 'contempt', which is detected by subtle signals such as one side of the lip pulled back slightly, the eyes squinting a little, or a tightening around the eyes and a slight raising of the corners of the lips. The software, being immune to gender bias, detected RBF in male and female faces in equal measure.

However, the researchers found that while RBF is not necessarily more common in women, it is more often noticed in women because women have more pressure to be happy, smiley, and to get along with others. Actress Anna Kendrick, who has publicly bemoaned the effect of RBF on her life, is an example of this.

The study also found that Kanye West, Queen Elizabeth, and Kristen Stewart are among the celebrities who are commonly associated with RBF. The researchers invited members of the public to submit their own faces for analysis, and those interested can email photos of their most "neutral" facial expressions to jason@noldus.com for analysis by FaceReader. The study has sparked interest and has been widely shared on the internet.

In this article, it is reported that hackers have threatened to release the upcoming Pirates of the Caribbean film, specifically Pirates of the Caribbean: Dead Men Tell No Tales, unless Disney pays a ransom in Bitcoin. The hackers allegedly gained access to the film and are threatening to release it in segments online. Bob Iger, Disney's CEO, confirmed the extortion attempt during a town hall meeting with ABC employees, stating that Disney has refused to pay the ransom and is working with federal investigators. The hackers are reported to have demanded a large sum of Bitcoin and threatened to release five minutes of the film initially, followed by 20-minute chunks until their demands are met. This incident marks a new twist in movie piracy, as ransoms appear to be a recent development. The article also mentions that several Hollywood agencies have been targeted by hackers with extortion plots in recent months. Disney did not immediately respond to a request for confirmation.

U.S. Representative Trey Radel, a freshman Republican from Florida, was arrested on October 29 for cocaine possession in Washington D.C. The arrest was made by the Drug Enforcement Agency, and Radel was charged with misdemeanor cocaine possession in D.C. Superior Court. He is scheduled to appear in court on Wednesday and faces a maximum of 180 days in jail and a fine of up to $1,000.

Radel, who was elected in 2012, has struggled with alcoholism and admitted in a statement that his "extremely irresponsible choice" led to his arrest. He apologized to his family, constituents, and the people of Southwest Florida, and said he will seek treatment and counseling to overcome his addiction.

Speaker John Boehner's spokesman said that members of Congress should be held to the highest standards, and the alleged crime will be handled by the courts. The U.S. Attorney’s office for the District of Columbia declined to comment on Radel’s arrest and case.

Radel's arrest has been met with disappointment and concern from fellow politicians, including Florida Sen. Garrett Richter and Miami-based Republican U.S. Rep. Mario Diaz-Balart. Radel's re-election bid may be affected by the arrest, as some believe it will put him under pressure.

The Associated Press reported that Radel was identified as a cocaine buyer by his suspected dealer, who had been previously arrested as part of a separate drug investigation led by a federal task force. Radel has missed all four votes in the House this week.

A 19-year-old Jewish resident of Israel with dual American-Israeli citizenship was arrested on Thursday in connection with a series of bomb threats against Jewish institutions and other targets worldwide. The arrest followed an intensive investigation spanning multiple countries, with the FBI and Israeli police working together to track down the suspect. The teenager, who has a history of behavioral issues and was diagnosed with an inoperable brain tumor when he was 14, is suspected of being behind hundreds of incidents involving threats to institutions around the world, including Israel, over a period of two or three years. The suspect's father was also arrested, and both were ordered to remain in custody for eight additional days. The arrest comes after more than 100 bomb threats were made this year against Jewish community centers, schools, and museums in the United States, prompting evacuations, heightened security, and fears of rising anti-Semitism. The suspect is not cooperating with police and has refused to grant permission to have his computers searched. The Israeli police are accusing him of extortion through threats and of false reporting spreading panic. The arrest was welcomed by Jewish leaders, who expressed relief but also concern about the suspect's background. The FBI and Israeli National Police have commended each other's work on the case, with US Attorney General Jeff Sessions stating that the Department of Justice is committed to protecting the civil rights of all Americans and will not tolerate the targeting of any community on the basis of their religious beliefs.

In an update from Charlottesville, Virginia, a pretrial hearing for Jesse LeRoy Matthew Jr. is underway, who is charged with capital murder in the 2014 disappearance and death of 18-year-old University of Virginia student Hannah Graham. Prosecutors are seeking the death penalty, and Matthew also faces first-degree murder charges in the 2009 death of 20-year-old Virginia Tech student Morgan Harrington.

During the hearing, a former detective testified that a police bloodhound detected traces of Hannah Graham inside Matthew's apartment and on his car door. The bloodhound also found Graham's scent at an industrial site about a mile from downtown Charlottesville, suggesting she may have been attacked near a mulch pile at the site.

The defense argued that the search warrant for Matthew's apartment and car should not have been issued, but the judge ruled that there were no instances of deliberate misstatements and reckless disregard in the affidavit supporting the search warrant. The judge also pointed out that witness statements put Graham and Matthew together on the night of her disappearance, and Matthew bought them drinks using his debit card.

The hearing also revealed that the defense is blaming police omission in the investigation, and the judge is doubting whether the search warrant should have been issued. The trial is expected to continue with more witnesses testifying.

The European air travel crisis caused by a volcanic ash cloud in Europe's skies has entered its fifth day, affecting over 6.8 million passengers. European airlines, including Air France-KLM and Deutsche Lufthansa AG, have questioned the basis of the ban after some successful test flights without passengers. KLM reported no problems or damage to aircraft after flying 10 test flights at normal altitudes. EU transport ministers are holding emergency talks to ease the crisis, with a proposal to allow passengers from countries like Britain to fly into Spain and continue their journey by train, boat, or coach. The ash cloud, a mixture of glass, sand, and rock particles, can seriously damage aircraft engines. The international airports council reported that 313 airports have been paralyzed by the restrictions. The crisis has also affected Kenyan agriculture, with refrigerated stores at Nairobi airport and on farms now completely full, and a huge amount of fresh flowers and vegetables destined for the European market in danger of perishing. The UK Transport Secretary, Lord Adonis, said information from various test flights on Sunday would be considered during the conference. European authorities are working to find a solution that does not compromise safety. The UK has extended its ban on most flights in its airspace until at least 1900 local time on Monday, while Ireland, Germany, and the Netherlands are keeping their airspace closed until 1200 GMT on Monday. Spain has re-opened its airspace after a brief closure, with officials suggesting its airports could be used as an entry platform into Europe. British Airways fears it may not be allowed to fly normal services until Thursday at the earliest, and the British government is discussing the possibility of deploying the Royal Navy to collect stranded Britons abroad.

The article reveals a chilling discovery at the home of Jared Lee Loughner, the accused gunman in the Tucson shooting that left six dead and 14 injured, including Congresswoman Gabrielle Giffords. Inside a camouflage tent in Loughner's backyard, investigators found an altar with a human skull replica, shriveled oranges, and ceremonial candles, suggesting an occult dimension to his mind. Loughner's online anti-government ramblings have been the focus of investigators, but the discovery of the shrine raises the possibility that he may have been driven by other forces.

Students and faculty at Pima Community College, where Loughner attended until his suspension last summer, describe him as clearly at odds with the world. Classmates recall his strange behavior, including laughing to himself in a creepy manner, asking bizarre questions in class, and expressing fears about his potential for violence. College officials sent campus police officers to Loughner's home with a letter informing him he could not return without a mental health professional's written assurance that his presence at college would "not present a danger to himself or others."

Loughner had once tried to join the military but was deemed unsuitable. He worked as a volunteer at the Pima Animal Care Center, where he was well-liked. However, a close friend of Loughner's, Bryce Tierney, reveals that Loughner held a grudge against Giffords and had repeatedly derided her as a "fake." Tierney says Loughner's animus toward Giffords intensified after he attended one of her campaign events and she did not, in his view, sufficiently answer a question he had posed.

The article also mentions that on the day of the shooting, Loughner called an old friend and said, "Peace out. Later." The friend, who did not answer the call, later felt a sickening feeling when he heard about the Tucson massacre and realized it was likely Loughner who had committed the crime. The article concludes by noting that federal prosecutors have charged Loughner with attempting to assassinate a member of Congress and unlawfully killing a federal employee.

In a tragic incident, a mother and son, Huong Pham (62) and Cody Ha (23), were found dead in their home in Wichita, Kansas, on Saturday night. The victims were identified by Wichita police, and their deaths marked the 29th and 30th homicides of the year in the city.

The incident came to light when a Houston man, Ashley Martinez, who was playing video games with Cody Ha as part of an online group, heard gunshots during their game. The loud popping noises were so intense that they hurt Martinez's ears under his headphones. Martinez and the other players started asking each other if they were gunshots, but they thought they might be overreacting.

When they called Ha's number, they could hear it ringing and ringing, but there was no answer. Martinez later learned that Ha's sister had found the bodies. The sister was panicking and said she didn't feel safe.

The next morning, Martinez and a friend had an online chat with a Wichita police detective to share what they heard. The detective said he would let them know if investigators needed anything else.

Ha's friend, Tommy Ong, said that Ha's playing was often interrupted by someone at the front door. Ha would stop playing long enough to go to the front door, saying it was someone wanting to buy prescription meds or tablets. It happened as recently as last week, and Ha said his mother gave him a share of the proceeds, Ong said.

Ha and his mother had lived in the house on the 7500 block of East Huntington for at least 10 years, according to court records. The house is appraised at $233,500.

Ha worked days at his mother's dry cleaning business and played video games through the night, said Ong. Ha and Ong had been friends since they were children, and Ha went to Southeast High School and worked in the family business, which has multiple dry-cleaning stores.

Ha was described as easy-going, and his mother, Pham, had conflicts with other people, according to Sedgwick County District Court records. It's not clear whether those conflicts had anything to do with her and her son's deaths.

Police are seeking tips to help solve the crimes and have not disclosed a possible motive. Neighbors who live near the house where Pham and her son were slain said they noticed different cars frequently arriving and leaving from the house.

Anyone with information is asked to call Wichita police or Crime Stoppers at (316) 267-2111. The city's 31st and 32nd homicides occurred the following day.

A middle school math teacher, Benjamin Nagurski, is facing felony charges for allegedly threatening a student with a knife during a pop quiz at Bernalillo Middle School. The incident occurred when Nagurski, who was only four feet away from the students, pointed a knife with a wooden handle and pointed tip towards them, according to the police report. The student reported the incident, and the teacher was arrested and booked into jail. Nagurski faces charges of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon and carrying a weapon onto school grounds. The school principal called the police, and it is unclear if Nagurski has an attorney. The Bernalillo Police Chief, Tom Romero, stated that the charges are serious, as both are felonies, and there could be significant consequences if found guilty. The Bernalillo Public Schools Superintendent, Allan Tapia, did not immediately return a message seeking comment.

On Friday, a car accident on Highway 55 in Craven County, North Carolina, resulted in a two-day ordeal for 9-year-old Jordan Landon. Jordan was trapped in the wreckage of a 1995 Chevrolet Monte Carlo, her father, Douglas Landon, having died in the crash. Jordan managed to survive by consuming Pop-Tarts, water, and Gatorade.

The accident occurred near Turkey Quarter Creek Road, and Jordan was found just before 6 p.m. on Sunday, 48 hours after the crash. She was transported to Pitt County Memorial Hospital. The investigation into the speed at which the car was traveling is ongoing, with troopers suggesting that Douglas Landon was driving over 100 mph. However, Jordan's mother, Cissy Leohmann, believes a tire blowout may have been the cause.

Douglas Landon and Jordan were believed to be returning home from a store in Jasper at the time of the accident. They were last seen at a Mini-Mart in Jasper just before the wreck, buying snacks and scratch-off lottery tickets. Leohmann filed a missing person report and searched for her daughter and husband on Saturday, but unfortunately, she was involved in a separate accident on Highway 55, less than 100 feet from the accident site.

Jordan's resilience during this traumatic event is commendable. She remained calm and managed to keep herself warm with a coat, despite the cold temperatures that dropped below 30 degrees overnight. Jordan suffered non-life-threatening injuries and is expected to make a full recovery. The speedometer recovered from the car was stuck at 110 mph, suggesting speed was a factor in the crash, although alcohol is not believed to have been involved.

On November 1, 2017, a truck attack occurred in Lower Manhattan, New York City, resulting in eight fatalities and 12 injuries. The suspect, Sayfullo Saipov, was shot by a police officer and is currently in custody. ISIS claimed responsibility for the attack in its weekly newsletter, al-Naba, without providing any evidence. The newsletter referred to Saipov as "one of the soldiers of the Caliphate" and stated that the attack instilled fear in America. However, the FBI has not found any connections between Saipov and any foreign terrorist groups.

Saipov has reportedly told authorities that watching ISIS videos inspired him to carry out the attack and that he closely followed the terror group's playbook. He has been charged with providing material support to ISIS, violence, and destruction of motor vehicles.

The attack has led to increased security measures and discussions about how to prevent similar attacks in the future. New York City has started installing concrete barriers along the bike path where the attack occurred to prevent larger vehicles from getting onto it. However, some local cyclists have expressed concerns about the barriers, stating that they will cause accidents.

The attack has also raised questions about the use of deadly force by police officers. Officer Ryan Nash, who shot Saipov, used a pellet gun and a paintball gun, which are not lethal weapons. Some have questioned whether Nash could have used de-escalation techniques instead of deadly force, but the head of a national police organization has defended Nash, stating that he followed his training to neutralize the threat.

The attack has had a significant impact on the victims, their families, and the community. Those who knew Saipov have expressed shock and disbelief, as he was described as a happy and peaceful person who had no signs of radicalization. The attack has also led to increased fear and tension in the city, with many questioning how to prevent similar attacks in the future.

The article discusses the ongoing search for debris from Malaysia Airlines Flight MH370, which disappeared in 2014 with 239 people on board. A group of relatives of the passengers, led by Blaine Alan Gibson, an American sleuth, are searching remote beaches in Madagascar for possible debris. They have found several pieces, including one found by Jiang Hui, a Chinese man who lost his mother on the flight. The piece has been handed to Malaysian investigators. The families are frustrated with the Malaysian-led official inquiry and have criticized it for failing to collect debris found on Madagascar six months ago. The sea search is being wound up soon, and the families will be the only ones looking for clues. The pieces found are being analyzed by experts to see if they are from the missing airliner. The debris is washing up thousands of miles from where investigators believe the aircraft came down, but it makes sense when you know how the oceans work. Thousands of clues are likely to be lying around undiscovered, because no one is looking for them. Some might be personal effects from passengers, others might hold small clues to what happened. If it's fire-damaged, that could point to an accident, not a deliberate act. The search is one of the world's biggest mysteries, and it's coming down to the loved ones, the bereaved, and an American who craves the truth, to keep this search alive.

President Donald Trump made an unannounced trip to Dover Air Force Base in Delaware on February 1, 2017, to honor the returning remains of a U.S. Navy SEAL, Chief Special Warfare Operator William "Ryan" Owens, who was killed in a weekend raid in Yemen. Owens was the first known U.S. combat casualty since Trump took office less than two weeks ago. The raid on an al-Qaida compound also resulted in the death of more than a dozen civilians, including the 8-year-old daughter of Anwar al-Awlaki, a radical cleric and U.S. citizen who was targeted and killed by a drone strike in 2011.

Trump's trip to Dover was shrouded in secrecy, with the president and his daughter, Ivanka, departing the White House in the presidential helicopter with their destination unannounced. The president met with Owens' family during a two-hour visit to the base, and the sailor's family had requested that Trump's visit and the return of Owens' remains be private.

Owens joined the Navy in 1998 and was the recipient of two Bronze stars, a Joint Service Commendation, and an Afghanistan Campaign Medal, among other honors. His death underscores the human costs of the military campaigns Trump now oversees, as thousands of U.S. troops remain in hotspots around the world, including Afghanistan, Iraq, and Syria.

Trump's trip to Dover comes as he begins weighing whether to reshape U.S. military activities around the world. As a candidate, he vowed to be tougher on the Islamic State and at one point said he would be willing to send up to 30,000 U.S. troops to fight the extremist group in Iraq and Syria. Last week, Trump gave the Pentagon and other agencies 30 days to submit a plan for defeating the Islamic State.

Trump has said little about his approach to Afghanistan, where America's longest war continues, with about 8,400 U.S. troops training and advising local forces. The president's relationship with the military community during the presidential campaign was uneven, with about 60 percent of voters who served in the military supporting Trump, compared with 34 percent who voted for Democrat Hillary Clinton.

Meanwhile, questions are mounting about what kind of first lady Melania Trump will be, as she has not been seen at official events since her husband's inauguration and is not living in the White House. The first lady has appointed a chief of staff, Lindsay Reynolds, and is expected to move to Washington, D.C. at the end of the school year, splitting her time between New York and D.C. in the meantime. The confirmation comes after a rumor sparked by tabloids early Wednesday morning that the First Lady and her 10-year-old son Barron Trump were not considering a move to Washington, D.C. from New York City.

"Mirror, Mirror" is a fantasy film directed by Tarsem Singh, opening in theaters on March 30. The film stars Julia Roberts, Lily Collins, Armie Hammer, and Nathan Lane. The story is a modern update of the Snow White fairytale, with a focus on female empowerment. The film takes a lighter approach, with slapstick humor and swashbuckling heroics, and references the classic Disney cartoon.

The film's visuals are stunning, with a high-concept snow-covered forest and a human form of a game of Battleship. The elaborate costumes were designed by Eiko Ishioka, who died in January. Julia Roberts delivers a strong performance as the evil stepmother, while Lily Collins does well in her first major leading role as Snow White.

The film has been compared to the upcoming "Snow White and the Huntsman," with both films taking a modern approach to the classic fairytale. However, critics have noted that "Mirror, Mirror" lacks substance and is more of a pretty, spun-sugar confection. The film is dedicated to Eiko Ishioka, who contributed significantly to its visual appeal.

In Syracuse, NY, a 30-year-old man named Michael Rotondo was ordered by the State Supreme Court to vacate his parents' home in Camillus. The court hearing followed multiple notices from his parents, Mark and Christina, who had asked him to leave since February 2018. Michael, however, refused to leave without a legal battle.

The case gained national and international attention, with media outlets such as the New York Post, Fox News, BBC, and The Late Late Show with James Corden covering the story. During the half-an-hour court appearance, Michael argued that he was entitled to six more months to find a new place to live. However, the judge, Donald Greenwood, ruled against him, citing an appellate court decision that family members don't receive special treatment unless in rare circumstances.

Michael Rotondo's legal research led him to believe that family members are given six months before an eviction. However, the judge provided a copy of a court decision that overruled the case Rotondo cited. Rotondo maintained that the judge's eviction order was wrong.

Rotondo's behavior during the court proceedings was unconventional, as he demanded an adjournment due to a notice error, tried to take the podium up with him, and called out to television camera crews for interviews after the hearing.

The judge expressed concern about the situation at home and ordered adult protective services to investigate. Rotondo's parents, who were present in the court gallery, said they had offered their son $1,100 to help him find a place of his own, but he claimed the money wasn't enough.

Rotondo, who runs a website business, moved back home eight years ago after losing a job. He said he plans to get some things from home and isn't sure where he will stay after the eviction. The judge asked the parents' lawyer to come up with an eviction order that Greenwood would sign, but no specific deadline was stated in court. Rotondo believes he is entitled to another 30 days, which would allow him to file an appeal and delay the eviction.

In a significant ruling, a Florida appeals court overturned the second-degree murder conviction of former FBI agent John J. Connolly Jr., who was found guilty of tipping off notorious mobster James "Whitey" Bulger about a murder in 1982. The decision raises the possibility that Connolly, a central figure in one of Boston's most notorious criminal chapters, could be freed.

By a 2-to-1 decision, the Miami appeals court ruled that Connolly's conviction should be overturned because he did not carry or discharge the gun used in the murder. The court faulted prosecutors for overreaching by using a firearms charge that skirted the state's statute of limitations, as Connolly was 1,500 miles away in Boston when the murder occurred.

The ruling sends Connolly's conviction to a lower court, where it will remain until post-appeal motions are finalized. Florida Attorney General Pam Bondi is considering an appeal to the state Supreme Court. Connolly's public defender, Manuel Alvarez, filed an emergency request to release Connolly immediately, but the court denied the motion.

The ruling has sparked mixed reactions. Mary Callahan, the widow of the Florida victim, expressed her disappointment, while others believe Connolly was a scapegoat for the FBI's top-echelon informant program in the 1970s and early 1980s.

Connolly's conviction was the second time he had been found guilty of charges linked to the Bulger gang. In 2002, he was sentenced to 10 years on federal racketeering charges for protecting Bulger and Stephen "The Rifleman" Flemmi, his longtime informants, while they continued a criminal rampage that included dozens of murders.

The appellate ruling turned on the prosecution's decision to charge Connolly with second-degree murder with a firearm, a crime that does not have a statute of limitations in Florida. Without the firearm component, the four-year statute of limitations that existed in 1982 for second-degree murders would have expired by the time Connolly was charged in 2005.

The ruling has sparked controversy and debate, with some arguing that Connolly's conviction should stand, while others believe he was unfairly targeted. The case remains ongoing, with the possibility of further appeals and legal battles.

A Pakistan government minister, Ghulam Ahmad Bilour, has offered a $100,000 reward for the killing of the creator of an anti-Islam film, sparking outrage and condemnation. Bilour, a member of the Awami National Party (ANP), made the announcement at a news conference, but clarified that he was speaking as an individual and not a government representative. A curling team led by Ryan Fry, an Olympic gold medalist, was disqualified from the Red Deer Curling Classic tournament in Alberta due to unacceptable behavior, including drunkenness and damaging property. Fry, who won gold for Canada at the 2014 Winter Olympics, and his teammates, Jamie Koe, Chris Schille, and DJ Kidby, were ejected from the World Curling Tour event and forced to forfeit their final match. The team reportedly broke brooms, damaged locker rooms, and engaged in offensive language. In a statement, Fry apologized for his actions and expressed regret for the negative impact on the curling community. The Red Deer Curling Classic is an annual event that counts towards rankings of the best curling teams in Canada. The team's behavior was widely criticized, and a sign was placed on the main board of the arena to make it clear that they were removed from the competition and future events at the club. Fry, who lives in Calgary, offered to pay for any damages caused. The team had won a Grand Slam title earlier this month. The team's skip, Brad Jacobs, expressed disappointment in the behavior and stated that they were handling the situation internally. The event committee was asked by the World Curling Tour to file a formal complaint.

Beijing is taking aggressive measures to combat air pollution, with authorities destroying over 500 outdoor barbecues as part of an emergency program. These barbecues, many operated by ethnic Uighur Muslims, are said to contribute significantly to air pollution in the city. The destruction of these barbecues aims to reduce PM2.5 levels, harmful particulate matter that can penetrate deep into the lungs. The campaign has been met with skepticism online, with some questioning the focus on small sources of pollution when larger sources remain. Beijing's pollution often reaches hazardous levels, causing long-term health issues such as lung cancer. The city government has implemented emergency measures, including odd-even car restrictions and school closures, in an attempt to reduce pollution.

The New York Times has excluded Ted Cruz's memoir, "A Time for Truth," from its bestseller list, sparking a controversy and accusations of partisan bias. The Times claims the book's sales were mostly "strategic bulk purchases," a claim disputed by Cruz's campaign and publisher, HarperCollins. The publisher has found no evidence of bulk orders or sales, and the book has ranked high on other bestseller lists. Cruz's camp sees the controversy as beneficial, as it has generated significant publicity and boosted book sales. The feud between Cruz and the Times is seen as a bonus for his 2016 campaign, as it has helped him gain attention and funds, putting him in a stronger position than many of his fellow candidates who have struggled since Donald Trump entered the race. On Monday, August 13, 2013, an American Airlines pilot died during a flight from Phoenix to Boston. The incident occurred approximately four hours into the flight, when the captain, identified as Capt. Michael Johnston, 57, fell ill. The co-pilot took over and diverted the plane to Syracuse, New York, where it landed around 7:10 a.m.

The nature of the pilot's sudden illness has not been disclosed. An airline spokesperson confirmed that one of the flight attendants is also a nurse and had tried to assist the ill pilot. The FAA requires two crew members in the cockpit at all times, and this was the case in this incident.

American Airlines confirmed the incident and expressed condolences to the pilot's wife, Betty Jean, and family. The airline stated that they are focused on caring for the family members and crew involved. The flight had 147 passengers and five crew members, including the pilot.

Passengers on the flight reported that they were not informed of the pilot's death until the second flight with a new crew. One passenger, Louise Anderson, said that American Airlines handled the situation professionally.

The pilot's death raised concerns among some passengers, but it is standard procedure for commercial airliners to have two crew members in the cockpit, each capable of flying the plane alone. The FAA also requires pilots to get two physicals per year after 40 years old and has a mandatory retirement age of 65.

This incident is a tragic reminder of the risks involved in air travel, but the airline industry takes safety very seriously. American Airlines has expressed their condolences and is focusing on supporting the family and crew involved in this unfortunate event.

Researchers have discovered the earliest known ancestor of humans, a microscopic sea animal named Saccorhytus coronarius, which lived approximately 540 million years ago in central China. The creature is the most primitive example of a category of animals called deuterostomes, common ancestors of a broad range of species, including vertebrates (backboned animals). Saccorhytus was about a millimeter in size and is thought to have lived between grains of sand on the sea bed. The study was carried out by an international team of researchers, from the UK, China, and Germany, and published in Nature journal.

Saccorhytus is significant because it provides insights into the evolutionary path that led to fish and eventually humans. The creature was covered with a thin, relatively flexible skin and muscles, and it probably moved around by wriggling. The researchers were unable to find any evidence that the animal had an anus, which suggests it consumed food and excreted from the same orifice.

The discovery of Saccorhytus also helps scientists understand the evolutionary history of deuterostomes, as until now, the earliest known deuterostome groups were from between 510 to 520 million years ago. These had already begun to diversify into not just the vertebrates but also sea squirts, echinoderms (animals such as starfish and sea urchins), and hemichordates (a group including things like acorn worms).

The study suggests that Saccorhytus had a bilaterally symmetrical body, a characteristic inherited by many of its evolutionary descendants, including humans. The creature had a large mouth, relative to the rest of its body, and probably ate by engulfing food particles or even other creatures. Small conical structures on its body may have allowed the water that it swallowed to escape, which could have been an early version of gills.

The findings also provide evidence in support of a theory explaining the long-standing mismatch between fossil evidence of prehistoric life and the record provided by biomolecular data, known as the "molecular clock." The microscopic scale of Saccorhytus, combined with the fact that it is probably the most primitive deuterostome yet discovered, appears to back up the theory that before a certain point, many of the creatures they are searching for were simply too small to leave much of a fossil record.

A Russian passenger plane carrying 71 people, including 65 passengers and six crew members, crashed near Moscow shortly after taking off from Domodedovo Airport on February 11, 2018. The plane, an Antonov An-148, disappeared from radar screens a few minutes after departure, and fragments of it were found in the Ramenskoye area, about 40 kilometers from the airport. No on-ground casualties were reported. According to preliminary information, no one survived the crash. The Russian Transport Minister, Maxim Sokolov, confirmed there were no survivors, and DNA tests were needed to identify the dead. The crash site showed wreckage of the plane, including at least one engine, lying in fields covered with thick snow. Helicopters and rescuers on snowmobiles were at the scene, and two bodies and a flight recorder were found. Debris and human remains were spread over a radius of a kilometer from the crash site. The Russian Investigative Committee opened a criminal case into the incident, and several possible causes were being considered, including weather conditions, human error, and the plane's technical condition. No distress signals were received from the crew. The plane was manufactured in 2010 and had been in service with Saratov Airlines since 2016. The crash is the latest in a series of plane crashes in Russia, where airlines often operate ageing aircraft in testing conditions. The last large-scale crash in Russia occurred on December 25, 2016, when a Tu-154 operated by the Russian Defense Ministry on its way to Syria crashed into the Black Sea minutes after takeoff from the southern Russian city of Sochi, killing all 92 people on board.

A service dog named Presley, who assists a 14-year-old boy named Joseph "Seph" Ware with Duchenne muscular dystrophy at Good Hope Middle School in Louisiana, has gained attention online after being included in the school's yearbook. Seph, who was diagnosed with the condition at the age of 3, has been using Presley as his service dog for the past four years. The school officials' decision to include Presley in the yearbook was well-received by Seph, who said, "Why not?"

Seph's mother, Lori Ware, shared that the school administrators' gesture was particularly meaningful as they had faced issues with Presley's acceptance at Seph's previous elementary school. Ware expressed her appreciation for the school's welcoming attitude towards Presley, stating that the students adore her, and she enjoys the attention.

The yearbook photo of Seph and Presley has garnered attention on social media, and a local newspaper, The News-Star, highlighted Presley's work for Seph. Presley and her canine sibling, Elvis, who works as a service dog in Wisconsin, were reunited last month after years apart. Both dogs help their young owners by performing tasks that their weakened muscles can no longer manage, such as picking up dropped items, turning on light switches, and opening drawers.

Duchenne muscular dystrophy, one of nine types of the disease, is caused by a missing protein that helps keep muscle cells intact. It primarily affects boys and leads to muscle deterioration, physical impairment, heart, and respiratory issues. However, advances in cardiac and respiratory care have expanded patients' life spans, making survival into their 30s more common. There are also cases of those affected living into their 40s and 50s.

The attention surrounding Presley and Seph has been overwhelming, with Seph drawing a paw print when classmates ask him to sign their yearbooks on behalf of Presley. Seph enjoys the attention and has been loving the experience.

On March 18, 2016, Salah Abdeslam, the main fugitive from the Islamic extremist attacks in Paris in November 2015, was arrested in Brussels, Belgium, following a four-month manhunt. The arrest took place during a major police operation in the Brussels neighborhood of Molenbeek, where Abdeslam was wounded and later hospitalized. Two other individuals were also wounded during the raid. Abdeslam, a Belgian-born French citizen, is believed to have driven a group of gunmen who took part in the Paris attacks that killed 130 people. The arrest comes after Belgian authorities found his fingerprints in an apartment raided earlier in the week in another Brussels neighborhood, where a man believed to have been an accomplice of Abdeslam was shot dead. The capture of Abdeslam is significant as he could provide valuable intelligence about the Paris attacks and potential future threats. The arrest was met with widespread praise and relief, with many expressing hope that it would bring some closure to the victims of the Paris attacks.

In a groundbreaking medical achievement, surgeons at the Glenfield Hospital in Leicester, England, successfully saved the life of a baby girl named Vanellope Wilkins, who was born with her heart outside her body due to a rare condition known as ectopia cordis. The condition, which occurs in five to eight cases per million live births, usually leads to termination of pregnancy or death. Vanellope, who had a less than 10% chance of survival, underwent three operations to relocate her heart, making it the first successful procedure of its kind performed on a newborn child in Britain.

Vanellope's parents, Naomi Findlay and Dean Wilkins, discovered during a nine-week scan that their first child had ectopia cordis, with the heart and part of the stomach growing externally. Despite being advised to terminate the pregnancy, the couple chose to continue with it, drawing inspiration from the baby's strong heartbeat.

The surgery to place Vanellope's heart inside her chest was a complex procedure involving a team of 50 medical staff, including obstetricians, heart surgeons, anaesthetists, neonatologists, and midwives. Within 50 minutes of birth, Vanellope underwent the first operation, and in the most recent surgery, her own skin was used to cover the hole in her chest.

Vanellope still faces a long road ahead, with the major risk being infection. The next step is to take her off a ventilator, which is being used to aid her recovery from surgery. Her parents, overjoyed at her survival, named her after a character in the Disney film "Wreck-It Ralph" who is a real fighter and turns into a princess at the end.

This remarkable story serves as a beacon of hope for parents facing similar challenges, demonstrating the power of determination and the incredible capabilities of modern medicine.

Raffaele Sollecito, the Italian boyfriend of Amanda Knox who was acquitted in the murder of Meredith Kercher, has revealed in an exclusive interview that he is planning to visit Knox in Seattle before Christmas. Sollecito and Knox, who were initially sentenced to 26 and 25 years respectively for the murder and sexual assault of Kercher, were released on appeal earlier this month. The couple was photographed kissing shortly after the death of Meredith Kercher.

Roger Ebert, a renowned film critic and television host, passed away at the age of 70. Known for his unique and insightful reviews, Ebert wrote for The Atlantic magazine and the Chicago Sun-Times for over four decades. His reviews were a combination of scholarly, witty, and sarcastic, and he was known for his ability to craft both exhilarating raves and stinging zingers.

In this article, we take a look back at some of Ebert's best reviews, including his review of E.T. - The Extra-Terrestrial, Casablanca, Toy Story, Raging Bull, Platoon, Beauty and the Beast, Titanic, Hoop Dreams, Star Wars, Fargo, and more. We also include some of Ebert's most biting takedowns, such as his review of Last Rites, Baby Geniuses, The Brown Bunny, Mad Dog Time, Valentine's Day, Deuce Bigalow: European Gigolo, Little Indian, Big City, Battlefield Earth, and North.

Ebert's love for the movies was evident in his writing, and his reviews will continue to be remembered and cherished by film enthusiasts for years to come. His autobiography, "Life Itself," was released in 2011.

The summary of the document discusses the pay disparity between Gal Gadot, who plays Wonder Woman, and Henry Cavill, who plays Superman, in the DC Universe movies. Initially, there were reports that Gadot earned $300,000 for Wonder Woman, while Cavill earned $14 million for Man of Steel. However, these reports have been debunked as unconfirmed, and it has been revealed that Gadot and Cavill were paid the same for their debut standalone outings.

The initial reports were based on a post from Elle magazine that did not differentiate between upfront salary and bonuses. The alleged $14 million figure for Cavill was deemed "ridiculous." Warner Bros., the studio behind both movies, declined to comment on the salary figures.

Standard fare for Hollywood tentpole movies is a salary in the low to mid-six figures for actors with short track records. For example, Chris Hemsworth made $150,000 for his starring debut in 2011's Thor, while Adam Driver was paid in the $500,000 range for his part in Star Wars: The Force Awakens. Felicity Jones, who had an Oscar nomination under her belt before landing the lead in Rogue One, was paid more than $1 million for the Star Wars stand-alone.

These salary figures do not take into account box-office bonuses, which hit when certain benchmarks are met, and actors receive substantial increases when it comes to sequels, especially if a movie is as successful as Wonder Woman. Gadot's deal will likely be renegotiated due to the film's success.

The document also mentions that one person cashed in on the Superman phenomenon, producer Jon Peters, who took home $80 million to $85 million combined for 2006's Superman Returns and Zack Snyder's Man of Steel, thanks to backend granted for his role in jumpstarting the franchise in the 1990s. Man of Steel earned $668 million worldwide.

In the Beach to Beacon 10K race in Maine, Jesse Orach, a 23-year-old runner from Gorham, collapsed due to heat stroke with about a quarter-mile to go. His top competitor, Robert Gomez from Windham, helped Orach to his feet and ran with him to the finish line, nudging him over the line. Both men completed the 6.2-mile course in 31 minutes, 31 seconds. Orach, who won the Maine division in 2016, is the first Maine man to repeat as champion since 2009. Gomez, who previously finished third in the race in 2010, didn't deserve to win, according to him, as Orach ran a better race. Orach's core temperature peaked at 107.3 degrees after the incident. After about an hour in the medical tent, Orach emerged, appearing weary-eyed and dazed. For the Maine women's division, Emily Durgin placed first in 34:43, followed by Michelle Lilienthal of Portland in second place. Lilienthal led for the first five miles before Durgin surged ahead. The touching moment of Orach's collapse and Gomez's assistance was captured by news photographers, and Gomez was praised for his selflessness in the running community.

In a significant advancement towards human bone reconstruction, researchers have developed a method to grow pig's own cells into bone in the lab, which was then used to restore a piece of missing jaw in pigs. This new technique, which is inching towards testing in humans, aims to replace large pieces of bone, addressing the challenges of precision, strength, and finding suitable donor sites in traditional autograft procedures.

The study, published in Science Translational Medicine, involved 14 pigs with facial bone damage. Researchers removed living cells from cow bone to create a porous scaffold that matched each pig's jaw. They then extracted mesenchymal stem cells from the pigs' fat and grew these cells in a bioreactor for three weeks, forcing them into the tiny spaces of the scaffold.

The seeded scaffolds were implanted in six pigs, while six others received unseeded scaffolds and the remaining two healed on their own. Over six months, pigs in the seeded graft group regrew a more complete portion of the missing jaw, with the grafts maintaining the height and mechanical strength of the original bone. The unseeded scaffolds shrank slightly, suggesting faster degradation of bone matrix.

While the use of a bioreactor to grow bone before grafting holds advantages, there is ongoing debate about the optimal recipe for a bone-stimulating scaffold. The researchers plan to gather more evidence to ensure the procedure is safe for human trials, which they hope to initiate in about three years.

The pigs recovered well after the procedure, with no signs of pain or rejection. The researchers, led by Gordana Vunjak-Novakovic, have founded a company, EpiBone, to commercialize the technology. This advancement could potentially revolutionize the field of bone reconstruction, offering a promising solution for large bone defects in humans.

In a recent study by Wealth-X, Hong Kong surpassed New York as the city with the largest population of ultra-high-net-worth individuals (UHNWIs), defined as people worth $30 million or more. The rise in Hong Kong's ultra-rich population was attributed to its booming stock market and growing financial links with China. China, with its rapid economic growth, has seen a significant increase in the number of ultra-rich individuals.

Despite Asia's growth, the United States remains the preferred country for the world's richest, hosting nearly a third of the world's UHNWIs. However, Asia, particularly China, is rapidly catching up, with a 20% increase in the number of ultra-rich individuals last year. The region's wealth is not concentrated in any one area but is distributed across the country, with tech tycoons like Jack Ma and Pony Ma contributing to this growth.

The study also noted that Asia-Pacific is forecast to close the wealth gap with other regions over the next five years. Despite challenges such as trade wars and high levels of debt, China's wealth is expected to continue growing, with China already having more billionaires than the United States by some estimates.

Global ultra-rich individuals increased by 13% last year, reaching over 250,000 with a combined total wealth of $31.5 trillion. Other cities in the top 10 for global wealth included Tokyo, Los Angeles, Paris, and London.

The bodies of a 36-year-old woman, Felicia Barahona, and her 4-year-old son, Miguel, were found dead in her Manhattan apartment on Monday, December 26, 2016. Barahona was found strangled, and Miguel was found unresponsive in a bathtub. Isaac Duran Infante, a former student of Barahona's and the father of her son, was arrested on murder charges on Tuesday, December 27, 2016, and confessed to the double killing. Duran Infante was reportedly dissatisfied with the way his son was being raised by Barahona. The medical examiner determined that Barahona died from strangulation by an electrical cord, and Miguel died of asphyxia from neck compression. The couple shared custody of the child. Duran Infante's grandmother, who lives in the Bronx, expressed her desire for justice and claimed her grandson's innocence. The investigation is ongoing. The relationship between Barahona and Duran Infante began in 2011 when he was still a student at DeWitt Clinton High School, where Barahona was a science teacher. The affair made headlines in 2013, and Barahona was fired from her job shortly after becoming pregnant.

On Father's Day, Eugene Blackwell Sr., a 46-year-old man from New Smyrna Beach, was arrested and charged with attempted first-degree murder after shooting his 18-year-old son, Eugene Blackwell Jr. The incident occurred at their Edward Street home, where the younger Blackwell had just graduated and was a star weightlifter at New Smyrna Beach High School.

According to Sgt. Eugene Griffith, the shooting took place after the son intervened in a physical altercation between his parents. The argument escalated when Blackwell Sr. asked his wife if she had been talking to a man named "Frank," and she denied the allegation, but also revealed her intention to seek a divorce. This led to Blackwell Sr. grabbing his wife by the neck, prompting the son's intervention.

After the son left the house, Blackwell Sr. shot him four times, wounding him in the abdomen, leg, hip, and arm. The son managed to flee to a neighbor's driveway, where he collapsed and called for help. Neighbor Richard Tredeaux, who is a shooting instructor at the Boy Scouts camp in Paisley, helped keep the victim calm until emergency services arrived.

Blackwell Sr. fled the scene but was later apprehended and arrested. He was denied bail at his first appearance hearing at the Volusia County Branch Jail. The younger Blackwell, who helped the New Smyrna Beach High School weightlifting team win a state title in April, was airlifted to Halifax Health Medical Center in Daytona Beach and was listed in satisfactory condition.

The incident is not the first instance of domestic violence in the Blackwell family, as court records show that Blackwell Sr. has been arrested several times on charges of battery and domestic violence. The mother, Windy Blackwell, told police that her husband has been abusive throughout their 23-year relationship and that he has been abusive with their son as well. The family has two other children, but they were not home during the incident.

In a series of tweets, President Donald Trump threatened to impose a retaliatory tax on European car exports in response to potential punitive taxes on U.S. goods from the European Union (EU). This escalation follows Trump's announcement of a 25% tariff on imported steel and aluminum, which has sparked concerns of a global trade war. In a bizarre turn of events, reality star Kim Kardashian was flour-bombed during a charity event in West Hollywood for her new fragrance, True Reflection. In China, a woman named Yang Xiaoyun paid over $1,000 to rescue 100 dogs from being eaten during a dog meat festival in Yulin, a city known for its annual festival devoted to dog meat consumption. The festival, which takes place during the summer solstice, has faced increasing backlash from animal protection activists who consider it cruel. Yang plans to rehouse the dogs at her home in Tianjin.

The festival has attracted criticism from celebrities such as Leona Lewis and Ricky Gervais, who have denounced it on social media. The consumption of dog meat is not illegal in China, but the government has called on meat vendors to respect food safety laws. However, the government has distanced itself from the event, stating that it is a commercial term and the city has never officially organized a "dog meat festival."

Despite the controversy, dog and cat meat traders report that business is booming, and it is expected that thousands of cats and dogs will be slaughtered this weekend to mark the summer solstice in Yulin. The slaughter of cats and dogs for meat is not outlawed in China, and the local government in Yulin says it cannot stop legitimate businesses preparing meat in the run-up to this year's solstice on June 21.

The dog meat industry is facing strong criticism inside China, with a growing army of animal lovers and pet owners believed to be 30 million strong. With their newfound bond with animals, this new generation of Chinese sees cats and dogs as thinking, feeling individuals deserving of compassion. Most importantly, they are friends, not food.

The dog meat trade is a serious threat to human health, and Chinese authorities have every reason to stand by the animal advocates. China has the world's second-highest incidence of rabies in humans, and Yulin is one of China's "top ten cities" for cases of human rabies. The handling and slaughter of vast numbers of unvaccinated dogs exposes the traders to a high risk of rabies infection.

Transporting the dogs to the festival is an intrinsically brutal operation, with the dogs often arriving malnourished, underweight, dehydrated, injured, or even dead. The festival is also a food safety disaster, with China's food safety regulations banning the processing, selling, and serving of products from diseased or dead animals of unknown causes.

In conclusion, the dog meat festival in Yulin, China, has faced increasing criticism from animal protection activists, celebrities, and the general public. The consumption of dog meat is a controversial issue in China, with a growing number of animal lovers and pet owners advocating for the protection of cats and dogs. The festival is a serious threat to human health, with the handling and slaughter of vast numbers of unvaccinated dogs exposing traders to a high risk of rabies infection. The government has distanced itself from the event, stating that it is a commercial term and the city has never officially organized a "dog meat festival."

The Will Ferrell and Kevin Hart comedy "Get Hard," which premiered at the South By Southwest Film Festival last week, has been met with criticism for its handling of race and homosexuality. During a Q&A session, an audience member accused the film of being racist, while early reviews have also questioned its portrayal of homosexuality.

The film's comedy revolves around Ferrell's character's fears of being raped in prison, with a scene involving an attempt to have oral sex with a gay man in a bathroom stall. Critics have criticized the film for its negative portrayal of homosexuality, with The Guardian writing that it "persisted in the mainstream in 2015." Variety described the film as having "some of the ugliest gay-panic humor to befoul a studio release in recent memory."

Director Ethan Cohen, along with Ferrell and Hart, have defended the film as a satire of stereotypes, not a representation of them. Ferrell stated that the film provokes and prods, and shows a mirror to what already exists in society. Hart added that the characters judge each other based on their initial impressions, but eventually realize that they are not who they thought they were.

"Get Hard" was conceived as a way to pair Hart and Ferrell, two of the most popular and bankable stars in comedy. The film is an attempt to comment on contemporary issues of inequality and race within the context of a broad, often crude comedy.

Adam McKay, Ferrell's longtime collaborator and a producer of "Get Hard," has criticized the backlash as being overinflated by "lazy journalism." McKay believes that the film is a satire of income inequality, and that seeing it as racist is "kind of ridiculous and disheartening." To claims of homophobia, he protested that the film's intention is to parody those who live in bubbles of wealth and prejudice.

Eric D. Snider, in his review for Vanity Fair, wrote that the film wasn't offensive to him as a homosexual, but it's just not funny enough. He concluded that it's disappointing, but not mean-spirited.

Despite the bad buzz, the goodwill both Ferrell and Hart have in storage, as well as Ferrell's dependably entertaining late-night appearances, may have helped alleviate any negative impact on the film's box office performance. The NAACP and GLAAD have not commented on the film.

Hart stated that he and Ferrell are no strangers to criticism, and that the critic's job is to critique. He added that he has never had a great review on a film that he's done, and that everyone always has something to say. Whether the talking around "Get Hard" will affect it at the box office remains to be seen.

In a new memo, Romney pollster Neil Newhouse argues that the poor state of the economy under President Obama, with high unemployment rates and increasing numbers of Americans on food stamps, will be the downfall of his presidency. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has retracted his statement that a Palestinian cleric gave Adolf Hitler the idea of annihilating Europe's Jews during World War II. In a Facebook post, Netanyahu clarified that he did not intend to absolve Hitler of his responsibility for the Holocaust. He stated that the decision to move from a policy of deporting Jews to the Final Solution was made by the Nazis and was not dependent on outside influence. Netanyahu's original comments, made during a speech at the World Zionist Congress, caused widespread outcry and were heavily criticized throughout Israel and the international community. Netanyahu's new statement aligns with the prevailing view of Holocaust historians, but contradicts his earlier speech where he claimed that the Mufti of Jerusalem, Haj Amin al-Husseini, convinced Hitler to adopt the Final Solution. On June 22, 2015, the University of Texas at Austin (UT-Austin) announced that the statue of Confederate President Jefferson Davis will be relocated to an exhibit in the Dolph Briscoe Center for American History. The decision comes after an advisory panel recommended the university relocate some or all of its statues of Confederate leaders. Four other statues, including ones of Confederate generals Robert E. Lee and Albert Sidney Johnston, will remain on the university’s South Mall, but may receive explanatory plaques to place them in historical context.

UT-Austin President Gregory Fenves stated that Davis had few ties to Texas and that it is not in the university’s best interest to continue commemorating him. The statue of former U.S. President Woodrow Wilson will also be relocated to another outdoor location due to symmetry reasons. The Davis statue will likely be removed in the next two days and refurbished before being relocated to the Briscoe Center in the next 18 months.

The advisory panel, which consisted of students, professors, and alumni, solicited over 3,100 opinions from the public and released its recommendations on Monday. The panel's report presented five options, four of which involved moving some or all of the statues to a history center on campus. Another option would have left the statues in place but called for explanatory plaques.

The Davis statue has been the most controversial of the ones commemorating Confederate leaders. In March, the student assembly passed a resolution asking UT to remove the statue of Davis. In April, it was vandalized with the phrase “Davis Must Fall.” A week after a deadly shooting at a black church in South Carolina, the statues of Davis, Lee, and Johnston were tagged with the phrase “Black Lives Matter.”

The other Confederate statues of Lee, Johnston, Confederate Postmaster General John Reagan, and one of former Texas Governor James Hogg have strong ties to Texas, Fenves said in his letter, noting Lee’s legacy "should not be reduced to his role in the Civil War." Moving the Davis statue, while leaving the other four in place, is a respectful decision that still honors the heritage of the United States and the university, Fenves said.

While applauding UT’s decision, state Senators Rodney Ellis and Judith Zaffirini reiterated their call for examination of Confederate monuments on the Capitol grounds. They hope the conversation at UT will encourage state leaders to have a similar debate about the numerous Confederate statues that dot the Capitol grounds.

The article discusses a new method called targeted error correction sequencing (TEC-Seq) developed by researchers at Johns Hopkins Kimmel Cancer Center. This method allows for the ultrasensitive direct evaluation of sequence changes in circulating cell-free DNA (cfDNA) using massively parallel sequencing. The method was used to examine 58 cancer-related genes encompassing 81 kb in plasma from 44 healthy individuals and 200 patients with colorectal, breast, lung, or ovarian cancer. The study found that the method was able to detect somatic mutations in the plasma of 71, 59, 59, and 68% of patients with stage I or II disease for colorectal, breast, lung, and ovarian cancer, respectively. The study also found that the amounts of ctDNA can serve as a predictive marker of patient outcome. The study suggests that TEC-Seq may be useful for noninvasive detection of early-stage tumors, which could potentially be used for cancer screening. The development of this method could lead to a new generation of diagnostic approaches for early detection of cancer. The study was published in the August 16 issue of the journal Science Translational Medicine.

Firefighters in Grande Prairie, Alberta, successfully rescued ten horses that had broken through an ice-covered slough on Sunday. The rescue was a challenging operation due to the horses being wild and the thin ice. Three horses later died from exhaustion and injuries sustained during the ordeal. The rescue team, consisting of 35 regional firefighters and a search and rescue team, used chainsaws to cut pathways to the shore and slings and boards to get the horses over the mud and melting ice at the edge of the slough. The seven remaining horses are reported to be in good shape. The rescue was particularly significant for the firefighters from La Glace, as several members are trained in large animal rescue. Regional Fire Chief Trevor Grant is urging landowners to be aware of their animals around sloughs at this time of year, as the ice can change rapidly. The rescue operation involved crews from Hythe, Beaverlodge, La Glace, and Grande Prairie.

Ruth Ann Steinhagen, a 19-year-old woman from Chicago, died at the age of 83 in December 2022. Steinhagen gained notoriety in 1949 when she shot and nearly killed former Cubs player Eddie Waitkus, an incident that inspired the book and movie "The Natural." The shooting, which put a spotlight on stalking crimes, temporarily sidetracked Waitkus' career and helped to draw attention to "baseball Annies" — young, hero-worshipping groupies who pursued major league ballplayers.

After her release from Kankakee State Hospital in 1952, Steinhagen lived in near obscurity for over 50 years. She spent much of her final years living in a modest house on the Northwest Side with her parents and sister. Steinhagen never spoke publicly about the Waitkus incident after her release from the hospital.

Steinhagen's death went unreported until it was discovered by the Chicago Tribune while searching death records for another story. Her neighbors were surprised to learn of her past, with one neighbor stating that he lived there for over 15 years before learning her history.

Steinhagen was born in Cicero, Illinois in 1929 and spent two years at Waller High School before earning a diploma from Jones Commercial High School. At some point in her teens, Steinhagen became obsessed with Waitkus, who was then a first baseman for the Cubs. After the Cubs traded Waitkus to the Phillies before the 1949 season, Steinhagen's obsession with him intensified.

It all came to a head on June 14, 1949, when Steinhagen lured Waitkus into a hotel room with a cryptic note and shot him, nearly killing him. The shooting made headlines and Steinhagen was committed to a mental hospital. She was released three years later, after doctors determined she had regained her sanity.

Details about the rest of Steinhagen's life are sketchy, but it is known that she lived with her sister in a house just a few miles from the hotel where she shot Waitkus. She made an effort to conceal her privacy and often refused to answer the phone or come to the door when visitors knocked.

The story of Steinhagen and Waitkus' near-fatal encounter has become part of both Chicago's colorful crime history and rich baseball lore. The incident inspired the novel "The Natural" by Bernard Malamud, which was later adapted into a movie starring Robert Redford. Steinhagen's life and the events that unfolded have been the subject of several books and articles.

The Menil Collection in Houston has confirmed an act of vandalism against a 1929 Pablo Picasso painting, "Woman in Red Armchair." A man was caught on video spray-painting the canvas with a stenciled message and a bull image, which defaced the original. The vandal and the photographer who captured the incident escaped. The damaged painting was immediately taken to the museum's chief conservator for repairs, and the painting's prognosis is reportedly good. The incident is being investigated as criminal mischief, and Houston Police are asking for witnesses or anyone with information to come forward. The Menil Collection, which has owned the painting since 1956, also owns 14 drawings, a terra-cotta sculpture, and over 100 prints by Picasso. The incident brought to mind a similar act in 1974 when artist Tony Shafrazi defaced Picasso's "Guernica" at the Museum of Modern Art. The Menil Collection's website can be found at http://www.menil.org/.

The massive distributed denial of service (DDoS) attack that occurred on Friday, October 21, targeted Dyn, a New Hampshire-based internet service company, causing widespread internet outages and extreme slowness on popular sites such as Twitter and Spotify. The attack was carried out in three waves and was traced back to hackers who weaponized video cameras and other internet-connected devices to send unmanageable amounts of traffic to Dyn's servers.

The investigation into the attack points to a group of hackers who may be associated with the English-language hacking forum community, specifically users and readers of the forum hackforums.net. The hackers used a type of malware called Mirai, which hacks poorly protected devices and uses them to hurl junk data at the target server. The attack was similar to recent DDoS attacks against other companies, such as the security blog Krebs on Security and OVH, a French internet service hosting provider.

The attack on Dyn was particularly significant because it involved millions of "Internet of Things" (IoT) devices such as digital video recorders and cameras, many of which cannot be patched, making them repeat offenders for future attacks. The sheer number of hackable devices makes it difficult for companies to prevent such massive assaults.

Researchers at Flashpoint believe that the primary target of the attack may have been a "well-known video game company" that happened to use Dyn for DNS services. The hackers are believed to be motivated by a desire to show off their power and cause disruption for sport, rather than for financial gain or political reasons.

In response to the attack, Senator Mark Warner, a co-chair of the Senate Cybersecurity Caucus, has called for manufacturers of insecure IoT devices to be held accountable and for ISPs to block insecure devices from their networks. Dyn has revised its estimate of the number of infected IoT devices used in the attack, stating that it was not tens of millions, but rather in the millions. The investigation into the attack is ongoing, and it remains to be seen what measures will be taken to prevent similar attacks in the future.
