On October 29th, a group of friends visited Nashville Nightmare, a popular Halloween attraction in Madison, Tennessee. During their visit, one of the friends was stabbed by another member of the group, who believed she was using a fake knife provided by an employee of the attraction. The incident occurred when the friend, Tawnya Greenfield, was approached by an employee dressed as a character, who asked if another friend was messing with Greenfield. Greenfield, thinking it was part of the attraction, said yes, and the employee handed her a knife, telling her to stab her friend. Greenfield, believing the knife was fake, complied, only to realize that it was real when she saw blood on the knife and her friend's arm. The friend, James Yochim, was taken to a nearby hospital for treatment. The employee who provided the knife has been placed on leave, and the group involved in the incident is seeking legal action. Nashville Nightmare issued a statement expressing concern for the safety and security of their patrons and stating that they have robust safety and security protocols in place, including metal detectors and onsite medical and security staff. They are cooperating with any official investigation and reviewing their safety protocols with their staff.

An Israeli woman, aged 25, reported being gang-raped by two men in the Himalayan town of Manali, India, on Sunday morning. The incident occurred after she hitchhiked a ride in a vehicle without a number plate, which was carrying six men. The woman alleged that two of the men raped her at an unidentified location and then dropped her off in Manali. The police have registered a complaint and are investigating the case, using CCTV footage from the area to identify the suspects. The Israeli Foreign Ministry has been informed about the incident. This is not the first rape incident reported by a foreigner in the Kullu district in the past four years. In 2013, an American woman was gang-raped in Manali by three Nepalese men, and in 2012, an Australian woman was allegedly raped in Kasol village of the same district. The Israeli woman is currently being treated in a hospital. India increased punishments for rapists as part of an overhaul of sexual assault laws in 2012, following a fatal gang-rape that shone a global spotlight on the levels of violence against women in India. However, rape and sexual assault remain commonplace in India, with incidents hitting the headlines almost every day.

Coach, a luxury handbag maker, has announced a $2.4 billion deal to acquire its smaller rival, Kate Spade & Co. This move is aimed at appealing to younger consumers, particularly millennials, as Coach CEO Victor Luis stated that Kate Spade has a unique and differentiated brand positioning with strong millennial consumer awareness. The deal is expected to close in the third quarter of 2017 and add to adjusted earnings in fiscal 2018.

The acquisition is seen as a sensible move by analysts, as it aligns with Coach's goal to become a global, multi-brand luxury company. The purchase is expected to generate $50 million in annual savings through combined inventory management and supply chain efficiencies. This cost savings will help bolster Kate Spade's image as a luxury brand by reducing online flash sales.

Coach has been working to turn its fortunes around after a decline in revenue in 2014 and 2015. In May 2016, it acquired popular shoe maker Stuart Weitzman. Kate Spade, too, has seen better days, with its shares hitting a three-year low in December before takeover rumors began to swirl.

The acquisition is expected to help both companies expand their international presence, as they primarily make most of their money in the U.S. However, the deal may not be favorable for bargain hunters, as the cost savings will likely lead to fewer online flash sales.

The acquisition is the latest step in Coach's strategy to broaden its customer base and create a portfolio of distinct and compelling luxury brands. The deal is expected to close by the end of the third quarter, and Coach plans to preserve Kate Spade's brand independence and retain key staff.

The parents of Megan Rondini, a University of Alabama student who died by suicide last year, have filed a federal wrongful death lawsuit against various parties, including the university, law enforcement officers, and a university Title IX official. The lawsuit alleges that Rondini was raped by a wealthy man in Tuscaloosa, Alabama in July 2015, and that law enforcement and university officials mishandled her allegations, leading to her mental and emotional decline and eventual suicide.

The lawsuit claims that Tuscaloosa Sheriff's Department deputies were dismissive when Rondini reported the rape, and that investigators conducted sloppy investigations. It also alleges that the university's Title IX coordinator and a therapist at the school's Women and Gender Resource Center failed to provide adequate support and counseling to Rondini.

The lawsuit names several defendants, including T.J. Bunn, Jr., the man accused of raping Rondini, Tuscaloosa Sheriff Ronald Abernathy, Beth Howard, the University of Alabama's Title IX coordinator, Cara Blake of the school's Women and Gender Resource Center, and two county officers, investigator Adam Jones and deputy Joshua Hastings.

The lawsuit seeks unspecified damages and asks for a court order requiring the sheriff's office to provide better training to officers and "to provide safe conditions to citizens around criminal investigations."

The University of Alabama has declined to comment on specifics of the lawsuit, but has said that school officials are trying to raise community awareness and support victims of sexual assault. A lawyer for T.J. Bunn, Jr. has denied the accusations against his client.

The lawsuit comes after a BuzzFeed News story detailed Rondini's growing frustration after she told Tuscaloosa law enforcement that she had been raped. Rondini accused Bunn in the assault, but Bunn said they had consensual sex. Tuscaloosa officers questioned why Rondini did not kick or hit Bunn and concluded the incident did not meet Alabama's legal requirements for rape. They also questioned Rondini about crimes she had allegedly committed, including taking money and a gun from Bunn's car as she fled his home after the alleged assault. Rondini ultimately dropped the case, left the University of Alabama, and moved back to her native Texas, where she hanged herself in February 2016. Bunn was never charged with a crime.

The article led to outrage in Congress, with Rep. Ted Poe, a Republican from Texas, describing Rondini's case and saying "she got the death penalty" after reporting she had been sexually assaulted. Poe criticized Tuscaloosa investigators, saying they treated Rondini "with disdain and disbelief." The lawsuit alleges that Tuscaloosa officers failed to test Rondini's rape kit, failed to interview witnesses, and failed to record all of the interviews they did conduct. Their behavior, the lawsuit alleges, "was intentional and due to Megan Rondini’s female gender."

The Bunn family, who are well-known in the Tuscaloosa area, have called the BuzzFeed News story "an intentional distortion of facts in a tragic case," and said Rondini's family had previously sought to sue "various parties who are the targets of these unfounded accusations." The University of Alabama has said the BuzzFeed News story "ignored some significant facts," including that it gave Rondini information about services available to her on campus. It also noted that it referred Rondini to another counselor because the first one she met with after the alleged assault knew the Bunn family and recused herself from the case. However, the Rondini family claims in the lawsuit that the second counselor Rondini was referred to, Cara Blakes, "inexplicably denied Megan counseling services" until she began taking anti-anxiety medication. The lawsuit alleges this was a violation of Rondini's rights under the Americans with Disabilities Act. The suit also says that Beth Howard, the University of Alabama's Title IX coordinator, ignored calls and messages from Rondini's family requesting help for their daughter. The suit was filed in US District Court in Alabama.

The investigation into a grisly crime spree in South Carolina, spanning over a decade, is expanding after a woman was found chained in a metal container on a property owned by Todd Kohlhepp. Kohlhepp, who is accused of the woman's kidnapping and confessed to a quadruple murder from 2003 at a motorcycle shop, was denied bond on Sunday.

Investigators found human remains on Kohlhepp's property on Sunday, which could be linked to at least seven deaths. The search for more remains will continue on Monday, and the investigation has expanded to other properties Kohlhepp currently or previously owned, not limited to South Carolina. The FBI and Department of Homeland Security are also involved in the investigation.

Kohlhepp was charged with four counts of murder in the 2003 killings, and more charges are expected. He was convicted of a kidnapping in Arizona in 1987 and was required to register as a sex offender in South Carolina.

The woman found chained in the container is not being named due to Kohlhepp being a sex offender, although authorities have not confirmed whether she was sexually assaulted. Kohlhepp appeared in court on Sunday wearing an orange jumpsuit and declined to make a statement.

Family members of the victims expressed a range of emotions, including relief that a suspect had finally been detained. Terry Guy, who lost a loved one in the 2003 murders, said he suffered depression in the wake of the crimes and lost 70 pounds. He expressed sympathy for Kohlhepp's family but also emphasized the need for justice to be served.

Tom and Lorraine Lucas, who lost their son in the quadruple murder, also spoke to the press outside of the courthouse. They expressed a desire to see Kohlhepp and to use the experience in healing. Kohlhepp's case was moved from juvenile to adult court in 1987 after he was arrested for allegedly kidnapping and sexually assaulting a 14-year-old girl. He pleaded guilty and was sentenced to 15 years in prison and required to register as a sex offender.

The investigation is ongoing, and investigators will continue to search for human remains and other clues on Kohlhepp's property on Monday.

In the Nevada caucuses held on February 4, 2012, Republican presidential front-runner Mitt Romney secured a victory, marking his second consecutive triumph in the nominating campaign. Romney, the former Massachusetts governor, held a double-digit lead over his nearest competitor, with former House Speaker Newt Gingrich and Texas Representative Ron Paul vying for a distant second. Former Pennsylvania Senator Rick Santorum trailed the field.

The caucuses drew little attention but are expected to be a fierce battleground in November between the Republican nominee and President Barack Obama. Nevada's unemployment rate was the highest in the U.S., at 12.6 percent in December.

Romney unleashed a sharp attack on Obama, criticizing his economic policies for prolonging the tough times. He emphasized America's role as a global leader in the 21st century.

Preliminary results of a poll of Nevada Republicans entering the caucuses showed that nearly half considered a candidate's ability to defeat Obama in the fall as the most important factor in their decision. About one-quarter of those surveyed were Mormon, similar to 2008 when Romney won with over half the vote in a multi-candidate field.

The entrance poll was conducted at 25 randomly selected caucus sites and included 1,553 interviews, with a margin of sampling error of plus or minus 4 percentage points. A total of 28 delegates were at stake in the state-by-state race to secure the Republican nomination.

Nevada awarded its delegates in proportion to the caucus vote totals, meaning that any candidate who captured at least 3.57 percent of the total number of ballots cast would be rewarded. By contrast, Romney's victory in the Florida primary on Tuesday netted him all 50 of the delegates at stake there.

From Nevada, the calendar turns to caucuses in Minnesota and Colorado and a non-binding primary in Missouri on Tuesday. Maine caucuses end next Saturday, and the next seriously contested states are expected to be primaries in Michigan and Arizona on February 28.

The Nevada caucuses were sedate, with little television advertising, no candidate debates, and only a modest investment of time by the contenders. The most memorable event was an endorsement by flamboyant billionaire Donald Trump, who bestowed his support on Romney in Las Vegas.

Romney, Gingrich, Paul, and Santorum are expected to continue campaigning, with Romney focusing on Obama more than his Republican rivals. Santorum is hoping to change the narrative of his sagging fortunes with sharper criticism and a strong showing in Missouri's non-binding primary. Paul is building off a decent base of support in Minnesota, where he drew nearly 16 percent of the 2008 vote.

On Tuesday night, a lunar occultation will occur, with the moon passing in front of the bright star Aldebaran, one of the most colorful stars in the sky. This event is not as well-known as eclipses or meteor showers. The occultation will be visible as a star vanishing behind the moon and reappearing an hour or so later for most of the eastern and southern U.S. However, in a few select locations, such as Los Angeles, Denver, and Minneapolis, the star will appear to slide right along the edge of the moon, creating a unique and visually striking spectacle. This event is part of a series of Aldebaran occultations that began in January 2015 and will end in September 2018, with the next occultation not occurring until 2033. To fully enjoy the spectacle, binoculars or a telescope are needed. Skies will be mostly clear across the southern tier of the U.S. late Tuesday and early Wednesday, making it an ideal night for stargazing.

The Trump administration has unveiled a tax reform framework aimed at simplifying and cutting taxes for individuals and businesses. The individual plan involves collapsing the current seven tax brackets into three, with rates of 12%, 25%, and 35%, and the option for Congress to create a fourth, higher rate above 35% to ensure the wealthy pay their fair share.

The plan seeks to benefit the middle class by doubling the standard deduction to $12,000 for individuals and $24,000 for married couples filing jointly. It also aims to increase the child tax credit and introduce a new tax credit for non-child dependents. Provisions such as the alternative minimum tax and the estate tax, a levy on inherited wealth, would be eliminated under the Republican proposal.

On the corporate side, the tax rate would be reduced to 20% from 35%, and a new 25% rate would be created for pass-through businesses, which are currently taxed at the rate of their owners. The plan also proposes reducing the corporate tax rate for small and midsize businesses to the lowest rate in over 80 years.

The tax reform plan faces challenges in Congress, where Republican leaders must sell it to lawmakers who have been divided this year. The push began at a House Republican retreat, where the Republican chairman of the Ways and Means Committee walked members through the blueprint and emphasized the importance of coming together to fix the tax code.

While conservative groups support the plan as a step towards economic growth, Democratic leaders have criticized it as an irresponsible boon to the rich. Some budget watchdogs have expressed concern about the long-term impact of a plan that could cost more than $2 trillion over a decade.

Trump, who has refused to release his tax returns, insists that wealthy people like him would not benefit from the plan. He framed the proposal in terms of his own self-interest, stating that the plan would protect low-income and middle-income households, not the wealthy and well-connected.

Democrats have criticized the plan, with Senator Ron Wyden of Oregon stating that it violates Trump's tax pledge that the rich would not gain at all under his plan. The plan still requires Congress to fill in many important details before bringing the legislation to a vote, and the missing information will show if the plan lives up to Trump's claims and how much the tax cuts would add to the deficit.

Each August since 1998, Beloit College has released the Beloit College Mindset List, which provides a look at the cultural touchstones that shape the lives of students entering college that fall. The class of 2014, for example, has never found Korean-made cars unusual on the Interstate, and "digital" has always been in their cultural DNA. They've never written in cursive and have no need for a wristwatch, as they can check the time on their cell phones.

The class of 2014 plans to enjoy college, but they will need to acquire the patience of scholarship, as they are accustomed to instant access. They will discover how to research information in books and journals, not just online. Their professors, who might be tempted to think they are hip enough and therefore ready and relevant to teach the new generation, might remember that Kurt Cobain is now on the classic oldies station.

The Mindset List website, Mediasite webcast, and Facebook page receive over 400,000 hits annually. The class of 2022, born in 2000, can't remember when a "phone" wasn't a video game and research library. They've always been searching for Pokemon and have never read a Peanuts strip that wasn't a repeat.

The Mindset List of Generation X, born between 1965 and 1980, has only a sixteen-year run, making their numbers small. Deidre McCloskey, an economic historian, suggests that the virtues of different social groups are strongly determined by their economic status. For instance, the peasant class, having no prospects for financial gain, glommed onto the virtue of humility, linked to the idea that God would reward them for their humility someday in Heaven. For the aristocratic class, whose financial prosperity was assured, courage became a dominant virtue.

It's a concise little manual for teachers, counselors, administrators, and anyone involved in the education and training of America's most talked-about generation.

Tom McBride and Ron Nief, co-authors of The Beloit College Mindset List and other books, speak frequently about the generation gap around the country and to a wide variety of organizations. They work with their readers to explore the underlying message of The Mindset Lists of American History and WeRHistory, a guide to discussion of the past and do-it-yourself history.

On Friday, the conservative website RedState, owned by Salem Media Group, fired several prominent writers, including top editors and critics of President Trump. Among those dismissed were Caleb Howe, Jay Caruso, Ben Howe, Patrick Frey (writing under the pseudonym Patterico), Neil Stevens, and Susan Wright. The layoffs were announced via email or a memo from Townhall general manager and vice president Jonathan Garthwaite, who stated that changes were necessary due to financial and political concerns.

RedState, founded in 2004, was once a prominent blog among Republican lawmakers and conservative activists. The dismissals mark a significant shift in the site's history, with some former contributors viewing it as a reflection of the conservative movement's drift during the Trump era.

Ben Howe, one of the fired contributors, lamented the lack of accountability in the modern conservative movement, stating that "Liberal tears" is the new operating principle. Erick Erickson, who no longer operates the website, suggested that the motivations for the layoffs were two-fold, relating to both financial and political concerns.

Sources noted that writers who brought in substantial traffic, such as Susan Wright, were often critical of President Trump and his supporters, while those who generated less traffic and were more pro-Trump remained with the site. The dismissals have been interpreted as a purge of anti-Trump writers by both staff and those let go.

Former staffers have suggested that the firings reflect the Trump-era incentive for conservative outlets to protect the Republican president at all costs. Erickson stated that he had spoken with roughly a dozen RedState writers on Friday, as the layoff notices went out, and noted that those fired had older contracts making more money-per-click.

Salem Media Group, which also owns radio networks and book publishers, has previously been criticized for its treatment of radio hosts who criticized Trump during the election. The internal memo obtained by CNNMoney confirmed the housecleaning, stating that changes were necessary once they reached the conclusion that they could no longer support the entire roster of writers and editors.

This move by RedState has sparked concerns about the suppression of dissenting voices within the conservative movement and the growing emphasis on supporting President Trump at all costs.

In a surprising turn of events, Johnny Bobbitt Jr., the homeless veteran who gained national attention for giving his last $20 to a stranded motorist, is suing the couple who led a $400,000 fundraising campaign on his behalf. The lawsuit, filed in the Superior Court of New Jersey, accuses Kate McClure, 28, and Mark D'Amico, 39, of committing fraud by taking more than half of the donated funds for personal use.

According to the lawsuit, Bobbitt, a Marine Corps veteran living on the streets of Philadelphia, gave McClure his last $20 in November 2017 after she ran out of gas on Interstate 95. McClure created a GoFundMe campaign to repay Bobbitt and thank him for his kindness. The campaign raised over $402,000 from more than 14,000 donors.

However, Bobbitt is now back on the streets and concerned that he may never see the bulk of the money. The lawsuit alleges that the couple has spent more than half of the funds raised, treating it like a personal piggy bank. Bobbitt's drug addiction has relapsed, and he is once again panhandling for money after completing two stints in rehab.

D'Amico told The Philadelphia Inquirer that he controls the money but would rather "burn it in front of him" than give Bobbitt the remainder of the funds. Bobbitt's attorneys have filed an application for an injunctive relief to prevent McClure and D'Amico from dissipating any of the donated funds and to ensure they are used only to benefit Bobbitt.

An update on the GoFundMe account indicated that the couple tried to ensure Bobbitt's financial future by setting up two trusts and a bank account for his everyday needs. However, a formal trust for Bobbitt's benefit has not been created, according to the lawsuit. Bobbitt is seeking compensatory damages, funds for counsel fees and costs, and the appointment of a receiver for the funds.

McClure and D'Amico did not respond to ABC News' request for comment. A hearing on the lawsuit is scheduled for Thursday. The relationship between Bobbitt and the couple has since soured, with Bobbitt accusing them of mismanaging the donations and ignoring his requests for a full accounting. The couple has repeatedly denied any wrongdoing or misuse of the funds.

The United Nations Migration Conference held in Marrakech, Morocco, on December 10, 2018, saw the adoption of the Global Compact on Migration by 164 out of 193 U.N. member states. The agreement, which is non-binding and voluntary, aims to ensure safe, orderly, and regular migration. The pact encourages countries to cooperate and fight discrimination against migrants.

German Chancellor Angela Merkel was a key backer of the agreement, while the United States, under President Donald Trump, did not participate in its drafting and did not support the final deal. The U.S. administration criticized the agreement for failing to distinguish adequately between legal and illegal immigrants and for potentially imposing policy.

The Global Compact for Migration is a response to the massive economic, social, political, and health issues caused by migration, which affects nearly every country. According to the U.N.'s International Organization for Migration, there are approximately 1 billion migrants worldwide, or nearly one in every seven humans.

The agreement aims to address the often dangerous and illegal movements across borders that have turned people smuggling into a booming worldwide industry. U.N. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres stated that unregulated migration bears a terrible human cost, with more than 60,000 migrants having died on the move since the year 2000.

Migration affects hundreds of millions of people across the globe, including farmers moving to cities, families fleeing war or persecution, impoverished workers seeking jobs in rich countries, and high-skilled workers looking for opportunities beyond their homelands.

Defenders of migration argue that it greases the wheels of the world economy by diversifying and rejuvenating workforces in aging rich countries and providing a needed source of cash to poorer countries through remittances sent home by migrants. Opponents often fear that an influx of migrants can dilute their countries' character, import poverty or crime, reduce wages, and take jobs from tax-paying citizens.

The conference in Marrakech was the capstone of efforts set in motion two years ago when all 193 U.N. member states, including the U.S. under President Barack Obama, adopted a declaration agreeing to work on a global compact. The Trump administration pulled out of the accord a year ago, citing clashes with U.S. immigration and refugee policies.

Some European Union countries, including Italy, Poland, and Hungary, now have anti-migrant populist governments that have reacted strongly after over 1 million migrants poured into Europe in 2015. Since then, right-wing and anti-immigration movements have enjoyed a surge in political support in pockets of Europe.

The suspected "Golden State Killer," a former police officer named Joseph DeAngelo, will be prosecuted in a combined trial in Sacramento, California, following his arrest in April. The case involves 13 counts of murder, spanning six jurisdictions across the state, and multiple kidnapping and weapons charges. The trial will bring an end to what is believed to be the most notorious unsolved serial-rape killing in California history, dating back to the 1970s and 1980s.

The "Golden State Killer" is accused of a string of murders, rapes, and home burglaries throughout California. The case remained unsolved for decades until investigators obtained the unknown killer's DNA in the early 2000s from the murders of Lyman and Charlene Smith in Ventura County. They then started reviewing rape kits from other jurisdictions, eventually using a genealogy database to build a family tree of the unknown killer's relatives. Investigators narrowed the search based on age, location, and other characteristics, leading them to DeAngelo.

DeAngelo is currently in custody in Sacramento County and has not entered a plea. The trial is set to begin on Thursday, with prosecutors committed to delivering justice for the victims and their families. The case has been described as ending a 40-year-long journey for justice.

Harper Lee, the author of the Pulitzer Prize-winning novel "To Kill a Mockingbird," has filed a lawsuit against her former literary agent's son-in-law, Samuel Pinkus, and others, alleging self-dealing and copyright infringement. The lawsuit, filed in federal court in Manhattan, claims that Pinkus took advantage of Lee's declining hearing and eyesight in 2010 to get her to assign the copyright of the book to him and a company he controlled.

Lee, who lives in Monroeville, Alabama, alleges that Pinkus continued to receive commissions from the book despite the copyright being reassigned to her last year. The lawsuit seeks unspecified damages and the forfeiture of the agent's commissions.

The complaint states that Lee, who was residing in an assisted-living facility in 2007 after suffering a stroke, signed a document assigning her copyright to Pinkus’s company without realizing it. The former agent's son-in-law and other defendants, including Leigh Ann Winick, the wife of Pinkus, and Gerald Posner, a New York lawyer and investigative journalist, did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

"To Kill a Mockingbird" won the Pulitzer for fiction and has sold more than 30 million copies worldwide. The case is Lee v. Pinkus, 13-3000, U.S. District Court, U.S. Bankruptcy Court, Southern District of New York (Manhattan).

During the interview, Spitzer choked up and expressed remorse for his past actions, stating that he had undergone a significant change due to the pain he endured. The hosts discussed whether Spitzer's tears were genuine, with one panelist stating that they felt real. Spitzer is now running for the position of New York City comptroller, a role that would give him the power to influence corporate America and the finance industry. As comptroller, he could use his position to pressure money managers and audit city agencies' dealings with financial companies, potentially causing headaches for Wall Street. Spitzer has made it clear that he intends to use the city's shareholder position to be a watchdog of corporate America, advocating for issues such as separating the roles of CEO and board chairman at large corporations. The interview came after Spitzer's surprise announcement that he would be running for comptroller, and he expressed confidence in his ability to convince voters to support him in the short amount of time before the election. The interview also touched on the common thread between Spitzer, Anthony Weiner, and Mark Sanford: an absence of shame and a neediness that is often seen in Washington politics. Bill Clinton set the modern standard for resilience after being impeached during the Monica Lewinsky uproar, and contemporary politicians like Weiner and Spitzer may be making a similar calculation that perceived character defects can be turned into assets through perseverance.

The Texas sheriff's deputy, Darren Goforth, was shot and killed at a gas station in Houston on Friday night. The suspect, Shannon Miles, was charged with capital murder and appeared in court on Monday. The prosecutor stated that Miles shot Goforth 15 times with a .40-caliber Smith & Wesson gun, which was matched to shell casings found at the crime scene. Goforth, a 10-year veteran of the force, left behind a wife and two children.

Investigators are still trying to determine the motive for the killing, but Miles has a history of run-ins with the law, including several incidents involving police. Miles spent four months in a mental hospital in 2012 after being declared incompetent to stand trial in an aggravated assault case.

The community has come together to honor Goforth's memory, with more than 1,000 people attending a walk in support of law enforcement and donations of cash for the family totaling over $150,000. President Barack Obama released a statement offering his condolences to Goforth's widow and praising the bravery of police officers.

Goforth's funeral will be held at Second Baptist Church in Houston on Friday, with a viewing an hour before the service. The officer will be buried at Woodlawn Cemetery.

In a highly publicized trial, former St. Paul's School student Owen Labrie was acquitted of raping a 15-year-old girl but found guilty on lesser sexual-assault charges. The jury deliberated for eight hours before determining that Labrie had sex with the girl, but prosecutors failed to prove he acted without her consent. The verdict left both teenagers in tears, with Labrie being devastated and the girl's family feeling a measure of justice was served.

Labrie could face several years in jail, with a maximum sentence of seven years on a computer enticement conviction, which is a felony, and as much as a year each on the four misdemeanors. Sentencing is set for October 29, and Labrie will have to register as a sex offender for life.

The trial revealed a toxic sexual culture at the prestigious boarding school, whose notable alumni include Secretary of State John F. Kerry and "Doonesbury" creator Garry Trudeau. The school did not directly respond to complaints that it had failed to curb such behavior.

The sexual-assault charges would commonly be referred to as statutory rape, but in this case, they were misdemeanors because the difference in age between Labrie and the girl was four years or less. Labrie's lawyer, J.W. Carney Jr., described the computer-enticement charge as "overreaching" and indicated he may appeal.

The girl's family felt betrayed by the school, stating that it allowed and fostered a toxic culture that left their daughter and other students at risk of sexual violence. The school praised the girl for her resolve and commended her "remarkable moral courage and strength."

The jury found Labrie guilty of three counts of misdemeanor sexual assault, endangering a child, and using computer services to lure a minor. Labrie's comments to several friends that he had sex with the girl were the "most damning" evidence against him. Labrie, whose acceptance to Harvard was rescinded, will remain free on bail, although prosecutors urged higher bail, saying Labrie could flee now that he has been convicted.

The Associated Press reported that Belgian officials are investigating the case of a woman with autism who was euthanized in 2010, marking the first criminal investigation in a euthanasia case since the practice was legalized in 2002. Three doctors from East Flanders are being investigated on suspicion of having "poisoned" Tine Nys, who was diagnosed with Asperger's syndrome two months before her death.

Belgium is one of two countries, along with the Netherlands, where euthanasia of people for psychiatric reasons is allowed if they can prove they have "unbearable and untreatable" suffering. Among Belgians euthanized for mental health reasons, the most common conditions are depression, personality disorder, and Asperger's. Many experts dispute whether autism should be considered a valid reason to be killed.

Last year, Nys' family filed a criminal complaint, alleging numerous "irregularities" in her death. Her doctors attempted to block the investigation, with one doctor writing that they must "try to stop these people." Sophie Nys, one of Tine's sisters, told the AP that the doctor who performed the euthanasia asked her parents to hold the needle in place while he administered the fatal injection, among other fumbling efforts.

The decision to refer the case to trial was made by the Court of Assize in Ghent, and the doctors involved will now face trial "due to poisoning," said Francis Clarysse, a Ghent prosecutor. Concerns have previously been raised about whether Nys' psychiatrist, Dr. Lieve Thienpont, too easily approved euthanasia requests from patients with mental illness.

The AP previously published documents revealing a rift between Thienpont and Dr. Wim Distelmans, who heads Belgium's euthanasia review commission. Distelmans voiced fears that Thienpont and colleagues may have failed to meet certain legal requirements in some euthanasia cases, and wrote that he would no longer accept referred patients from Thienpont.

In the 15 years since doctors were granted the right to legally kill patients, more than 10,000 people have been euthanized in Belgium. Only one case has previously been referred to prosecutors; that case was later dropped. The investigation into Nys' death is ongoing.

In a heartwarming turn of events, seven-year-old Josh Hardy, who has been battling a rare form of cancer and a life-threatening adenovirus, will receive a potentially lifesaving drug after days of pleas from his parents and a national campaign. The drug, brincidofovir, is manufactured by Chimerix and has not yet been widely available or FDA-approved.

Initially, Chimerix had denied the Hardy family's requests for the drug, citing concerns that it would slow down efforts to get the drug on the market. However, after a public outcry and media attention, the company agreed to release the drug for a new clinical trial starting Wednesday, with Josh as the first patient.

Josh's journey began when he was diagnosed with a rare form of kidney cancer at nine months old. Over the years, the cancer spread to his thymus, lung, and bone marrow, but each time, Josh managed to beat it. However, a bone marrow transplant left him with a weakened immune system, and in February, he was diagnosed with an adenovirus that has since ravaged his body, leaving him in critical condition in an intensive care unit.

St. Jude Children's Research Hospital in Memphis, where Josh is being treated, had also been pushing for the company to provide the drug. In a statement, the hospital expressed gratitude for the efforts of Chimerix, the FDA, and others who worked to achieve this outcome. They noted that the safety and effectiveness of the drug have not yet been established for use in children.

The FDA's "compassionate use" policy allows someone with a serious or life-threatening disease to ask a drug company for an experimental drug. While it's called compassionate use, pharmaceutical companies often say no, as Chimerix did at first to Josh Hardy. However, in this case, the company worked with the FDA to expedite additional trials and will release the drug to 20 patients, including Josh, in an open-label study.

The Hardy family and supporters have been vocal in their appeals to Chimerix, appearing on national television shows and launching online campaigns. The family hailed Chimerix president Kenneth Moch as a hero, praising his professionalism and integrity. Moch, in turn, expressed hope that the new FDA-approved study would help not just Josh, but other patients in need.

The story of Josh Hardy's battle for life and the drug that could save him has drawn national attention and sparked a discussion about the impact of an adenovirus infection and the need for additional clinical development to assess the drug's potential. The Hardy family played a key role in bringing this issue to light.

The article from CNN reports that US investigators wiretapped former Trump campaign chairman Paul Manafort under secret court orders before and after the 2016 election. The surveillance continued into early 2017, including a period when Manafort was known to be in contact with President Donald Trump. Some of the intelligence collected raised concerns among investigators that Manafort may have encouraged the Russians to help with the campaign, but the evidence is not conclusive.

The FBI's interest in Manafort dates back to 2014, partly due to an investigation of Viktor Yanukovych, the former Ukrainian president. Manafort's firm and other US consultants were probed for their possible role in a corruption case. However, last year, the Justice Department concluded that there wasn't enough evidence to bring charges against Manafort or anyone else in the probe.

The FBI surveillance was discontinued at some point last year due to lack of evidence, but it was restarted after obtaining a new FISA warrant that extended at least into early 2017. The second warrant was part of the FBI's efforts to investigate ties between Trump campaign associates and suspected Russian operatives.

The FBI conducted a search of a storage facility belonging to Manafort earlier this year, but it's unclear what they found. The conversations between Manafort and Trump continued after the President took office, but it's unclear whether Trump himself was picked up on the surveillance.

Special counsel Robert Mueller's team, which is leading the investigation into Russia's involvement in the election, has been provided details of these communications. The White House and Manafort's spokesperson declined to comment for this story.

The FBI wasn't listening in June 2016 when Donald Trump Jr. led a meeting that included Manafort, then campaign chairman, and Jared Kushner, the President's son-in-law, with a Russian lawyer who had promised negative information on Hillary Clinton. This gap could prove crucial as prosecutors and investigators under Mueller work to determine whether there's evidence of a crime in the myriad connections between suspected Russian government operatives and associates of Trump.

The article also mentions that Manafort has previously denied knowingly communicating with Russian intelligence operatives during the election and participating in any Russian efforts to undermine the interests of the United States. The FBI interest in Manafort and the investigation into Russia's involvement in the election is ongoing.

The article discusses the rise and popularity of Sophie the Giraffe, a French-made rubber teething toy, in the United States. The toy, which stands at 7.5 inches tall and costs $24.99, has become a go-to baby gift for the upper-middle class, with approximately 500,000 units sold annually.

Sophie's success story began in 2001 when French expatriate Hélène Dumoulin-Montgomery, who worked as a realtor's assistant, imported the toy to the US after being unable to find it in the country. Initially, the toy was met with resistance due to its high price and lack of recognition. However, in 2004, a meeting with Teri Weiss, owner of the Beverly Hills gift boutique Elegant Child, led to the toy's breakthrough. Weiss included Sophie in a gift basket for the actress Kate Hudson, who had just given birth, and demand for the toy grew as it was photographed with famous babies.

The toy's success continued to escalate after the 2007 recall of lead-tainted Chinese-made toys by Mattel. Sophie is made of natural rubber and food-grade paint, making it a popular alternative. The toy is now available in 75 different countries and has become a staple in many households with young children.

However, recent reports have surfaced of mold growing inside Sophie the Giraffe toys. Parents have shared their experiences of finding mold in their children's toys, leading to concerns about the toy's safety. The manufacturers of Sophie the Giraffe have acknowledged the issue and advise following the cleaning instructions provided with the toy to prevent mold growth.

In conclusion, Sophie the Giraffe has become a beloved teething toy for many families, but recent reports of mold growth inside the toy have raised concerns about its safety. Parents are advised to follow the cleaning instructions provided with the toy to prevent mold growth.

Ricki Lake, a former talk show host, announced the passing of her ex-husband, Christian Evans, on February 14, 2023. Evans, a jewelry designer, battled bipolar disorder, and Lake revealed this in an emotional Instagram post. The couple married in 2012 and split in 2014 due to Evans' manic episodes related to his disorder. Lake and Evans continued their relationship until last fall. Evans' death at the age of 45 compelled Lake to speak about bipolar disorder and the importance of seeking treatment.

Lake first met Evans in September 2010 and was drawn to his humor and charisma. When they married in 2012, they lived happily together, with Evans showing affection towards Lake's children. However, in September 2014, Lake witnessed one of Evans' manic episodes, during which he believed he could fly and cure cancer with his hands. This led to their divorce in 2015, although they continued their relationship until Evans' death.

Evans' mania returned in September 2022, and he moved out again. On February 11, 2023, Evans' sister informed Lake that he had emailed a suicide note. Evans was found two days later with a self-inflicted gunshot wound. Lake is now planning to scatter some of Evans' ashes on their favorite beach in Ibiza this summer.

Lake emphasizes the importance of recognizing and treating bipolar disorder, as Evans admitted to having the condition in his suicide note. She encourages anyone struggling with the disorder to seek help and offers resources for those in need. Lake plans to honor Evans by living a full and happy life.

In a 300+ page report, the US-China Economic and Security Review Commission revealed that for 18 minutes in April, China Telecom hijacked 15% of the world's internet traffic, including data from US military, civilian organizations, and allies. This incident, which received minimal attention due to its complexity, allowed China to potentially eavesdrop on unprotected communications, manipulate data passing through their country, or decrypt messages. The exact nature of what happened to the hijacked data is unknown, but the incident may be addressed in the Commission's annual report on the bilateral relationship, scheduled for release on November 17.

The hijacking took advantage of the trust-based system used by telephone giants, where machine-to-machine interfaces send out messages to the Internet informing other service providers about the fastest and most efficient routes for data packets. For 18 minutes on April 8, China Telecom Corp. told many ISPs of the world that its routes were the best paths to send traffic, potentially rerouting data from Arlington, VA, to the White House in Washington, D.C., even though the data would not have been noticeably delayed due to the speed of internet traffic.

McAfee, the world's largest dedicated internet security company, has briefed US government officials on the incident, but they were not alarmed, stating that their internet communications are encrypted. However, encryption also works on a basis of trust, and this trust can be exploited. Internet encryption depends on two keys: one private and not shared, and the other public, embedded in most computer operating systems. Unknown to most computer users, Microsoft, Apple, and other software makers embed the public certificates in their operating systems, trusting that this system won't be abused. Among the certificates is one from the China Internet Information Center, an arm of the Chinese Ministry of Information and Industry. If China Telecom intercepts an encrypted message and sends its public key with its public certificate, the recipient will not know any better, giving China the capability to decrypt encrypted communication links, whether it's web traffic, emails, or instant messaging.

The hijacking took advantage of the way the Internet operates and could happen again, anywhere and anytime. It is a flaw in the way the Internet operates, said Yoris Evers, director of worldwide public relations at McAfee. The Commission's report addresses the increasingly sophisticated nature of malicious computer activity associated with China.

Steven Avery, the convicted killer at the center of the Netflix series "Making a Murderer," has filed an appeal claiming that authorities used an improper warrant and that a juror was biased against him, among other issues. Avery was convicted of first-degree intentional homicide in the death of photographer Teresa Halbach a decade ago. He had previously been wrongfully convicted of a rape case and served 18 years in prison. The appeal, which bears Avery's signature and contains numerous spelling and grammar errors, takes issue with a search conducted during the murder investigation, stating that it improperly included multiple properties and that any evidence uncovered is "FRUIT OF THE POISONOUS TREE." Avery's new attorney, Kathleen Zellner, has uncovered new evidence that she claims will exonerate Avery, but has not yet revealed what it is. Wisconsin Governor Scott Walker has stated that he will not consider a pardon for Avery.
