The comedy series "Brooklyn Nine-Nine," starring Terry Crews as Sgt. Terry Jeffords, was saved from cancellation by NBC after Fox announced its termination on Thursday. Star Wars icon Mark Hamill played a significant role in the show's revival, expressing his disappointment over Fox's decision and using his social media influence to rally support for the sitcom. NBC quickly picked up the series, which was created by Dan Goor and Michael Schur and premiered on Fox in September 2013. The show centers around the goofballs of the New York Police Department's Brooklyn 99th precinct.

NBC Entertainment Chairman Robert Greenblatt revealed that the pickup was already in the works due to business considerations, as the show is produced by an NBC Universal-owned studio. Greenblatt stated that if he had known Andy Samberg would star in "Brooklyn Nine-Nine," NBC's studio never would have sold it to Fox in the first place.

NBC's revival of "Brooklyn Nine-Nine" is part of a trend of broadcast networks reviving canceled comedies. The network succeeded last season with a reboot of "Will & Grace," while ABC's revival of "Roseanne" has been even more successful.

In addition to "Brooklyn Nine-Nine," NBC plans to introduce five new dramas and two new comedies next season. The network is also taking steps to rectify its winter ratings slump, with a winter edition of "America's Got Talent," a competition series featuring judge Simon Cowell, and a new competition series from the producers of "American Ninja Warrior" featuring Dwayne Johnson.

On Wednesdays, NBC will air the dramas "Chicago Med," "Chicago Fire," and "Chicago P.D," all products of television veteran Dick Wolf's production studio. Wolf's long-running "Law & Order: SVU" will launch its 20th season on Thursday nights.

The midseason comedy "Abby," centered around a bar in San Diego, will be the first sitcom shot outdoors in front of a live audience. NBC's schedule includes three series that will premiere in the fall: "Manifest," a time-traveler series about passengers who find it's five years later when they get off a bumpy plane flight; "New Amsterdam," a medical series based in New York's Bellevue Hospital; and "I Feel Bad," a comedy about a working mom who is "perfectly OK with being imperfect."

Some series, such as "The Brave," "Law & Order True Crime," "Rise," and "Great News," were canceled, and decisions are pending on the fate of "Timeless" and "Champions."

The man accused of fatally shooting a stranger on San Francisco's Pier 14 pleaded not guilty to murder on Tuesday, with his attorney arguing that the evidence points to a tragic accident. Juan Francisco Lopez-Sanchez, who is 45 according to police and 52 in jail records, made his first court appearance, where he listened as Judge Daniel Flores read the charges against him in connection with the death of 32-year-old Kathryn Steinle. The circumstances of Steinle's killing remained unclear, but police have learned that the gun used in the shooting had been stolen just days earlier from a federal agent in a car burglary in San Francisco.

Lopez-Sanchez, who was asked for his plea through a Spanish interpreter, answered "no culpable" and repeated the statement throughout the hearing, even when he was not asked. He did not appear to understand what was happening, saying again that he was not guilty in Spanish in response to a question by the judge regarding his next court appearance.

Steinle had been walking along Pier 14 with her father when she was shot through the heart at about 6:30 p.m. on July 1. In a jailhouse interview with KGO, Lopez-Sanchez appeared to admit to firing the shot, saying the gun went off after he found it wrapped in a T-shirt under a bench and after he took sleeping pills he found in a trash can. However, Lopez-Sanchez's lawyer, Matt Gonzalez, suggested that the defendant did not understand what was being asked during the television interview.

Lopez-Sanchez was also charged with using a gun, which could add up to 10 years to his sentence if he is convicted of murder. The .40-caliber pistol that investigators believe Lopez-Sanchez fired had been stolen from a federal agent in a car burglary in San Francisco in late June.

The case has sparked outrage due to Lopez-Sanchez's history of drug crimes and his being deported five times to Mexico, but being released from San Francisco County Jail rather than being turned over to federal immigration agents for a potential sixth deportation. Lopez-Sanchez was brought to San Francisco in March after serving 46 months at a federal prison in Victorville for felony re-entry into the country. He had an old, outstanding warrant in the city, alleging that he fled marijuana charges in 1995. According to court records, the case was old enough that the evidence had been purged by the time Lopez-Sanchez appeared in court on March 27. Prosecutors discharged the case, and Lopez-Sanchez remained in County Jail until April 15, when the Sheriff's Department released him without alerting immigration.

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officials said they had asked to be notified before Lopez-Sanchez's release, so they could seek to deport him again. The Sheriff's Department said it had followed its own policy in not holding Lopez-Sanchez for immigration agents, as well as a 2013 city ordinance and a state law signed the same year by Gov. Jerry Brown. Steinle's parents did not attend Tuesday's arraignment, but an uncle who was present shook and rocked during the proceedings and scoffed as Lopez-Sanchez declared he was not guilty.

Gonzalez implored the media to look past the immigration debate raised by the case at the "ubiquitous nature of guns in our society." He said, "Every day in the United States, innocent people die from gun accidents. In contrast to that, I can say there are numerous studies that immigrants are far less likely to commit acts of violence than native-born persons." When asked about the immigration issue, Alex Bastian, a spokesman for the district attorney's office, demurred and said, "Today's about Kate." He added, "It's about this incredible family that has shown such strength during this incredibly difficult time. It's about bringing justice to that family and it's about doing everything we ethically can to prosecute this case and bring the justice this family rightfully deserves."

Assistant District Attorney Diana Garcia asked that Lopez-Sanchez be held without bail, while Gonzalez argued that he had the right to bail, even if he would not be able to afford it. Judge Flores then set bail at $5 million after the prosecutor requested $10 million. Lopez-Sanchez is scheduled to return to court July 27.

The study reports the use of functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) and an implicit attentional processing procedure to establish communication with patients suffering from advanced amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) in a completely locked-in state (CLIS). Four patients, two in permanent CLIS and two entering CLIS without reliable means of communication, learned to answer personal and open questions requiring a "yes" or "no" response using frontocentral oxygenation changes measured with fNIRS. The patients completed more than 46 sessions over several weeks, with online fNIRS classification of personal questions and open questions resulting in an above-chance-level correct response rate over 70%. The study suggests that this method could potentially be the first step towards abolishing complete locked-in states for ALS patients. The work was funded by various grants, including the German Ministry of Education and Research, the National Natural Science Foundation of China, and the EU grant LUMINOUS. The data is available on Zenodo. The study is open access and was published in Plos Biology.

Emma Kelty, a 43-year-old British woman, went missing on September 10 while kayaking the Amazon river. She had been joking about a warning she received about the stretch of the river near Coari, Brazil, two days before her disappearance. On September 12, Kelty posted about an encounter with armed men, describing them as having arrows and rifles. On September 11, she triggered a distress signal and has been missing ever since. On Tuesday, police arrested three males on suspicion of her murder.

Kelty, a former head of Knollmead primary school in Surbiton, had a history of solo adventures. She was only the sixth woman to ski solo to the south pole and hiked 2,600 miles alone across the US. She began kayaking in February with the intention of paddling the Amazon from its source in the Peruvian Andes to the Atlantic Ocean.

There were unsettling moments in her trip, particularly since crossing the border into Brazil's Amazonas state. On August 22, she told followers how she had paddled hard upstream to reach a beach to rest, only to find a man waving a machete and ravens eating whatever he had killed. In the following days, she complained of broken sleep, interrupted by strangers.

On August 28, Kelty said she was "officially beyond tiredness." She wrote about tent-bending storms and 85% humidity, but also moments of tranquility. On September 5, she recounted a peaceful stretch of the river.

Kelty is believed to have pitched her tent on Boieiro island, facing the town of Lauro Sodré, before she set off her locator flare last Wednesday. A 17-year-old suspect arrested on Monday in Codajás said that was where she was approached by two people. Five others arrived and the group stole her belongings, including her mobile phones, tablet computer, and GoPro camera. She was shot twice with a sawn-off shotgun and dumped in the river.

According to the teenager, whom police did not name for legal reasons, the group tried to sell her stolen items in local communities. Another 17-year-old from Lauro Sodré was also arrested, as well as a third man, named as Erinei Ferreira da Silva, whose age was not given. Police are looking for four further suspects.

Authorities launched a search operation involving 60 people, including divers scouring the riverbed. Residents of Lauro Sodré reported having seen Kelty alive, sailing past in her canoe. Fire officers and the Brazilian navy are continuing to look for her body and have searched the area where it was allegedly thrown.

River pirates are known to operate in the area where Kelty went missing. Local media reported two men were arrested in July after carrying out pirate attacks around Lauro Sodré and nearby communities. The remote stretch of the Solimões where Kelty is thought to have gone missing is the same section where the state’s previous civil police chief, Thyago Garcez, disappeared in December last year, after he and other police officers got into a firefight with drugs traffickers. His body has never been found.

The Foreign Office confirmed it was supporting the family of a woman who had died in Brazil and said it was in contact with the Brazilian authorities. Kelty's siblings, Piers, Giles, and Natasha, released a statement saying, "In a world that is today a much smaller place, the explorer in our sister found herself seeking ways to prove that challenges were achievable. We are extremely proud of our sister who was dearly loved by us all and her strength will be sorely missed."

In a significant legal victory, President Donald Trump celebrated the rejection of lawsuits by environmentalists and the state of California against his administration's efforts to construct a wall along the U.S.-Mexico border. The ruling was delivered by U.S. District Court Judge Gonzalo Curiel, whom Trump had previously criticized for his ethnicity during the 2016 presidential campaign. Trump's tweet on the matter made no mention of his past feud with Curiel.

The lawsuit, filed in a San Diego federal court, alleged that Trump's proposed wall violates federal environmental standards and constitutional provisions regarding the separation of powers and states' rights. The plaintiffs asked Judge Curiel to stop the administration from pursuing the barrier until it demonstrates compliance with environmental laws. However, Curiel ruled that such decisions should be left to other branches of government, not the judiciary.

The case grew out of a 1996 law that gave the executive branch power to construct a wall in and near San Diego and to waive environmental review when "necessary to ensure expeditious construction." The law also limited any federal court reviewing challenges to the construction to only consider Constitutional violations, not challenges based on the environmental laws.

California Attorney General Xavier Becerra renewed his complaint that the Trump White House was "ignoring laws it doesn't like in order to resuscitate a campaign talking point of building a wall on our southern border." Another plaintiff, the Center for Biological Diversity, announced that it would appeal the decision.

Trump is scheduled to visit California in mid-March to see prototypes for the proposed border wall. The federal government has already begun work to replace a section of barrier built in the 1990s in the border town of Calexico with a 30-foot (9.1-meter) high stretch of bollard-style wall. In his latest budget proposal to Congress, Trump requested $23 billion for border security, most of it for the wall.

Trump's criticism of Judge Curiel during the 2016 campaign prompted significant backlash, with House Speaker Paul Ryan (R-Wis.) labeling Trump's remark as the "textbook definition of a racist comment." It remains unclear what Trump meant about parts of the wall California wants built, given the state's opposition to the whole idea.

The death of Freddie Gray, a 25-year-old black man who died after suffering a spinal cord injury in police custody, has sparked protests in Baltimore and around the nation. The Baltimore Police Department has completed their investigation into Gray's death and delivered it to the city prosecutor, Marilyn Mosby, who is tasked with determining whether charges are warranted. The investigation revealed that Gray suffered a serious head injury inside a prisoner transport wagon, with one wound indicating that he struck a protruding bolt in the back of the vehicle.

New details of the investigation emerged, including a previously unknown stop by the transport van driver, which was captured on private security footage. Witnesses have said that police officers roughly handled Gray, who died a week after his arrest from injuries including a severed spine. The police have acknowledged that officers violated protocol by not buckling in Gray and providing medical help when he asked for it.

The van made several stops before arriving at the Western District police station, where Gray was found unresponsive and taken to the hospital. At one stop, the van picked up another prisoner, who was taken to the station on the other side of a metal partition. The prisoner initially told police that Gray was thrashing about, but later recanted part of his account.

The family of Freddie Gray and their lawyers have been seen leaving the state's attorney's office, and Mosby has stressed that her investigation is independent. The officers involved in Gray's arrest have been suspended with pay, and it is not yet known when Mosby will make a decision on whether to bring charges.

Protests over Gray's death have spread to other cities, including Boston, New York, and Washington, and have put pressure on city and police officials to explain what happened. Police Commissioner Anthony W. Batts noted that the investigation's first phase wrapped up a day before his self-imposed deadline of May 1, demonstrating the agency's sense of urgency around the case.

The American Civil Liberties Union of Maryland has criticized the police department for a double standard in investigations involving officers. The Justice Department is also working on an independent investigation into Gray's death. The family of Freddie Gray and their lawyers have expressed a desire for a thorough and accurate investigation, and have expressed willingness to wait for the results.

A Rosenberg man, Jason Griffin, has been charged with manslaughter, felon in possession of a weapon, and unlawful possession of body armor following a shooting incident at a party in the Heights, Houston. The victim, identified as Daniel Barber, was wearing a bulletproof vest when he was shot in the chest at a garage apartment on 23rd Street early Sunday morning. It is unclear if the bullet went through the vest or if the shooter missed. Griffin and another witness fled the scene, and Griffin was arrested Sunday while receiving medical treatment at a local hospital. In 2001, Griffin was charged with aggravated robbery in a Fort Bound County court, according to Harris County District Clerk court records. The incident is under investigation to determine if it was a result of a dare. Griffin's girlfriend told ABC13 that he didn't mean to kill his friend, and he didn't know his gun was loaded. Griffin is still in custody at the hospital.

The FBI has issued a warning to state election officials, advising them to enhance the security of their computer systems following evidence of foreign hacker penetration in two state election databases. The warning, contained in a "flash" alert from the FBI's Cyber Division, comes amid heightened concerns about potential cyber intrusions, possibly by Russian state-sponsored hackers, aimed at disrupting the November elections.

The FBI's warning refers to cyber intrusions against voter registration databases in Arizona and Illinois. In the Illinois case, hackers managed to download personal data on up to 200,000 state voters, forcing a 10-day shutdown of the state's voter registration system. The Arizona attack was more limited, involving malicious software introduced into its voter registration system but no successful data exfiltration.

The FBI bulletin lists eight IP addresses that were the sources of the two attacks and suggests that the attacks may have been linked. The FBI is investigating and has advised states to determine if any similar activity has been detected in their logs.

The FBI did not confirm the identity of the foreign hackers, but they are believed to be involved in the recent highly publicized attack on the Democratic National Committee and other political organizations, which U.S. officials suspect was perpetrated by Russian government hackers. However, other experts suggest that the hackers could also be common cybercriminals hoping to steal personal data for fraudulent purposes.

The FBI's warning comes just days after Homeland Security Secretary Jeh Johnson hosted a call with state election officials to discuss cybersecurity and election infrastructure. Johnson emphasized that Homeland Security was not aware of specific or credible cybersecurity threats to the election, but stressed the importance of securing election systems amid a rapidly changing threat landscape.

The FBI's warning underscores the growing concern about the potential for foreign hackers to interfere with the November elections, particularly given the recent hack of the Democratic National Committee. The FBI is urging states to take new steps to enhance the security of their computer systems to protect against such threats.

Bernie Sanders, a US senator from Vermont, has criticized the global economic system as becoming an "international oligarchy" controlled by a small number of billionaires, citing the Paradise Papers as evidence. The Paradise Papers are a massive leak of documents exposing the secrets of offshore investors, including details of tax avoidance schemes by wealthy individuals and corporations.

Sanders accused Congress and the Trump administration of providing tax breaks to profitable corporations like Apple and Nike, which have used offshore holdings to avoid paying taxes. He also pointed out that members of Trump's cabinet, who are billionaires, have avoided billions in US taxes by shifting American jobs and profits to offshore tax havens.

Sanders called for the closure of loopholes and a fair and progressive tax system. His intervention in the debate sparked by the Paradise Papers marks the most prominent political response to the leak in its opening 24 hours.

One of the most pointed disclosures in the Paradise Papers was that Wilbur Ross, Trump's commerce secretary, has continued to do business with the son-in-law of Russian president Vladimir Putin, as well as a member of Putin's inner circle who is under US sanctions. Ross has retained his investment in a shipping company, Navigator, that has a partnership with the Russian gas giant Sibur. In turn, Sibur is part-owned by Kirill Shamalov, the husband of Putin's daughter.

The emergence of Ross's ongoing ties to business interests so close to the Russian president at a time of intense scrutiny of the relationship between the Trump administration and the Kremlin has incensed prominent Democrats involved in Ross's confirmation to office. Richard Blumenthal, a Democrat who sits on the US Senate commerce committee, accused Ross of deceiving the public as well as lawmakers who had allowed the confirmation to go through having heard Ross promise to divest himself of any interests that carried potential conflict.

On Monday, Ross denied that he had done anything wrong in his handling of his investment in Navigator. In the course of a visit to London, he told UK media that "there is nothing wrong with it. The fact that it happens to be called a Russian company doesn’t mean there is any evil in it."

The Paradise Papers have also revealed that Nike, one of the world's best-known brands, has used complex tax schemes and offshore holdings to avoid paying taxes. Nike shoes are made in countries such as Vietnam and Indonesia, and from there, they are shipped to the company's futuristic warehouse in Belgium. Buy a pair of shoes in, say, London, and one would expect the cash to go to the company's main British subsidiary, Nike UK Ltd. However, the money from sales of shoes flows out of the UK to the Netherlands, where two companies at the heart of Nike's Dutch operations pay some tax on the near $8bn of revenue they receive from Nike sales across Europe, the Middle East, and Africa. From 2005 until 2014, Nike was able to shift vast sums of money out of the Netherlands to Bermuda, which is an offshore tax haven with zero tax. Nike did this through a Bermudan subsidiary, Nike International Ltd, which held the company's intellectual property rights for its sneaker brands – the crown jewels of the Nike empire. Even though this subsidiary did not appear to have any staff or offices in Bermuda, it charged large trademark royalty fees each year to Nike's European HQ for selling its trainers. The fees allowed Nike to legally shift profits away from Europe to Nike International Ltd.

In 2014, Nike had to think again. With the deal from the Netherlands due to expire, the company came up with a new plan, again with the agreement of Dutch authorities. This involved moving the company's intellectual property from Nike International Ltd in Bermuda to yet another subsidiary, Nike Innovate CV. This entity is not based in Bermuda. It is not actually based anywhere. The "CV" model allows Nike Innovate to avoid paying local taxes in the Netherlands. Nike Innovate is not being taxed anywhere else, either. Nike is not the only multinational to use the CV model. Many of the US's largest multinationals use similar subsidiaries.

The Paradise Papers have also revealed that Lewis Hamilton, the Formula One world champion, avoided paying European taxes on his private jet using an Isle of Man scheme that is to be investigated by HM Revenue and Customs. The big four accountancy firm EY and Appleby, the law firm at the center of the Paradise Papers leak, helped Hamilton and dozens of other clients set up seemingly artificial leasing businesses through which they rented their own jets from themselves.

The documents obtained from Appleby suggest that as much as £1.1m of the VAT that Hamilton appears to have reclaimed on his jet should have been paid, along with hundreds of thousands due on the continuing costs of flying the jet. Hamilton was asked about these arrangements and said he had instructed a senior lawyer to check his arrangements and was told they were lawful. He said his practice was to rely on professional advice, and he was not concerned with day-to-day management of his business.

The Paradise Papers have also revealed details of how Apple channels its earnings through tax haven companies in Guernsey, Malta, and the British Virgin Islands. In March 2015, data from the Malta companies registry shows that Hamilton incorporated 44IP, named after his racing number, in that country. Official documents describe the company's purpose as holding "image rights … trademarks, royalties, copyrights." Its shares are held by Inday Rose Ltd, the BVI company that also ultimately owns his jet, and BRV. As well as renting the jet, BRV holds Hamilton's contract with Mercedes, the data suggests. The purpose of 44IP appears to be to channel income from sponsorship deals via Malta, which charges foreign shareholders a 5% corporation tax rate.

The Paradise Papers have sparked calls for tax reform and transparency from politicians and activists around the world. Bernie Sanders has called for the closure of loopholes and a fair and progressive tax system, while Richard Blumenthal has accused Wilbur Ross of deceiving the public and lawmakers. The documents have also led to investigations into the financial dealings of prominent individuals and corporations, and have shed light on the complex web of offshore holdings and tax avoidance schemes used by the world's wealthiest individuals and companies.

In an exclusive interview with Fox News' Sean Hannity, President Donald Trump defended his forthcoming executive orders, which include suspending the U.S. refugee program and halting the issuing of visas to citizens of certain countries. Trump stated that the measures are necessary due to ongoing FBI terrorism investigations and the lack of proper vetting of refugees.

Trump also discussed the construction of a wall along the U.S.-Mexico border, a key promise of his presidential campaign. He asserted that the wall is necessary for protection and cited Israel as an example.

The president revisited the issue of torture, stating that he believes methods such as waterboarding are effective but would follow the advice of Defense Secretary James Mattis, who has argued against the use of such tactics.

Trump criticized the media, labeling it as "very hostile" and "very dishonest." He accused the media of making things up and spreading fake news. Trump also mentioned the controversy over a report that the bust of Martin Luther King, Jr. had been removed from the Oval Office, stating that it was a serious change and a reminder of the media's tendency to tweet first and check facts later.

Trump discussed other topics in the interview, including his goal of repealing and replacing ObamaCare, which he called a "horror show" and a "disaster." He also disclosed that he had decided on his nominee to the U.S. Supreme Court "pretty much in my mind."

Trump also mentioned the possibility of a pardon for Navy sailor Kristian Saucier, who was sentenced to a year in prison for taking photos of parts of a submarine's nuclear propulsion system. Trump contrasted Saucier's treatment with the FBI's decision not to charge Hillary Clinton for using personal email while secretary of state.

Overall, the interview showcased Trump's continued defense of his policies and his criticism of the media, as well as his focus on issues such as immigration, terrorism, healthcare, and the Supreme Court.

On December 18, 2017, an Amtrak train derailed in Washington, resulting in the death of three passengers and injuring over 70. The deceased were identified as Jim Hamre, Zack Willhoite, and Benjamin Gran. Hamre and Willhoite were rail enthusiasts and members of a local rail enthusiasts group. The third victim, Gran, was an avid Amtrak fan.

The train was on its inaugural run of a new route aimed at improving safety and reducing travel times. The preliminary investigation by the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) revealed that the engineer warned of an "over speed condition" six seconds before the derailment. The train was traveling at 78 mph, within the speed limit for the approach but exceeding the 30 mph limit at the crash site.

The train was not equipped with Positive Train Control, a system that could have prevented the derailment due to excessive speed. The NTSB also found no evidence of the crew using personal electronic devices during the incident. The full investigation is expected to take up to two years.

Scott Walker, the Wisconsin governor who entered the Republican presidential race as a front-runner in Iowa and a favorite of both conservative base and powerful donors, announced on Monday that he is dropping out of the race. Walker's campaign had been struggling due to poor debate performances and a lack of support from donors. He encouraged other trailing Republican candidates to follow his path and focus on a limited number of candidates who can offer a positive, conservative alternative to Donald Trump, the current front-runner. Walker's exit comes 10 days after former Texas Governor Rick Perry became the first Republican to drop out of the 2016 race. The field now stands at 15 candidates.

Walker made the decision to drop out after a plummet in the polls, which was a major factor in his decision-making. He sounded "upbeat" and his message to supporters was, "I did the best I could." Walker's decision was referred to as "The Pawlenty decision," named after former Minnesota Governor Tim Pawlenty's 2011 decision to drop out before piling up considerable debt.

Walker's exit is likely to set off a fierce scramble for his big-money backers, led by the Ricketts family, one of the GOP's most powerful financial contributors. Walker's campaign was bedeviled by a lack of hard dollars, which it needed to pay staff, travel the country, and pay filing fees to state parties. It will not be known how much money the Walker campaign raised or how quickly it burned through it until October 15, when the federal campaign finance reports are made public.

Walker's campaign had been struggling since the first two Republican debates, during which he gave lackluster performances. In a CNN/ORC poll released Sunday, Walker failed to garner even one-half of 1% nationally among likely GOP primary voters. A GOP strategist close to the campaign told CNN that Walker "is a pragmatist above all else and just didn't see the path to a comeback."

Walker's campaign was also hurt by reversals on a host of controversial issues, including birthright citizenship, on which he gave three different answers in the span of seven days. Those reversals were particularly damaging to his outsider image as non-politicians like Trump, Carson, and Fiorina climbed the polls.

Walker delayed entering the campaign in part to raise money for his super PAC, which posted a $20 million haul in the first half of 2015. However, once it launched, the campaign appeared to be bedeviled by a lack of hard dollars. The super PAC will "wind down our existing efforts and return remaining resources to supporters," according to a spokesman for the group.

Aimee Locke, a top Texas fundraiser for Walker, said she got no advance notice from the campaign, but said people in her network began to worry as CNN's new poll results showed Walker with less than 1% support nationally. "We were told that they were going to be some changes made, but we had no idea that this was the change that was going to be made," she said.

Walker's exit is now almost certain to set off a fierce scramble for his big-money backers, led by the Ricketts family, one of the GOP's most powerful financial contributors. Todd Ricketts, the campaign's finance chair, was scheduled to host a fundraiser for Walker in New York on Thursday.

Trump complimented Walker on Twitter after the news of his decision broke. "I got to know @ScottWalker well -- he's a very nice person and has a great future," he said.

South Carolina Senator Lindsey Graham, also a GOP presidential contender, said Walker made the decision that was "best for him and his family." "You are down to 15. You got three basketball teams. The bottomline is Scott made a decision best for him and his family," Graham said. "He's a very accomplished governor and it shows you just how hard it is running with this many people. That's what it shows."

AFL-CIO President Richard Trumka had some choice words for Walker -- best known for his anti-union efforts. "Scott Walker is still a disgrace, just no longer national," Trumka said.

A Brenham veterinarian, Dr. Kristen Lindsey, who was accused of killing a cat with a bow and arrow, will not face charges after an Austin County grand jury returned a "no-bill." The grand jury's finding indicates that there was insufficient evidence to charge Lindsey. The incident came to light when a Facebook photo surfaced, showing Lindsey holding up a dead cat with an arrow through its head, bragging about her kill. However, investigators were unable to determine where or when the incident took place, making it difficult to obtain a search warrant for any Austin County properties related to the case. Additionally, subpoenas to Facebook failed to produce usable evidence since Lindsey's account had been deleted. The cat, named Tiger, belonged to a pet sitter who was devastated by the incident and demanded justice. Many people protested outside the Austin County Courthouse, demanding an indictment. Since Lindsey has not been charged, her name and image were not released by KHOU 11 News. The veterinarian has since been fired from her job. The case has garnered attention from people all over the world, with posters voicing their support for Tiger and asking for an indictment. The investigation revealed that cat hunting is legal year-round in Wyoming, and the manner in which the cat was killed may have been considered humane according to guidelines from the American Veterinary Medical Association. The Washington Animal Clinic in Brenham, where Lindsey worked, issued a statement condemning her conduct and distancing itself from the incident.

Shannon Egeland, a convicted white-collar criminal, was sentenced to an extended prison term on Wednesday for persuading his son to shoot him in the leg as part of a staged insurance scam. The additional three years and ten months were added to his initial ten-year sentence for mortgage fraud. Egeland's insurance scheme involved a bogus disability insurance policy that he applied for seven days before the staged shooting, which led to the amputation of his left leg.

Egeland, who appeared in court on a prosthetic leg, expressed remorse for his actions, particularly the impact on his son. He acknowledged that he needed mental health counseling and treatment and was currently taking three medications. Egeland's son, Rylan, was 17 at the time of the incident and obtained a 20-gauge shotgun for the staged shooting, while Egeland provided the ammunition.

Egeland's criminal history includes fraud charges related to the Desert Sun housing scandal in 2009, where he was a co-owner of a company that raised millions from local banks through fraudulent business plans and falsified loan applications. During the sentencing, prosecutors sought a five-year sentence for the insurance scam, while Egeland's lawyer urged a two-year sentence to be served consecutively to the 10-year sentence he was already serving.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Scott Bradford described Egeland as a "menace to society" and a "self-absorbed, opportunistic narcissist" motivated by greed who recklessly manipulated his son. The psychological and emotional damage caused to his son was deemed unimaginable by Bradford. Egeland was also ordered to pay $90,011 he owes in child support and to undergo mental health treatment and counseling while in prison, as well as a new mental health evaluation upon his release.

The staged shooting backfired on Egeland, as it led to his extended prison sentence and the loss of his leg. The incident occurred a day before he was due to self-surrender to prison for a 10-year term for his role in an extensive mortgage-fraud scheme.

The Cleveland Browns, notorious for a dismal season, managed to win a game on Christmas Eve, thus canceling the planned 'Perfect Season Parade' organized by fans. The parade, initially intended to commemorate a 0-16 season, was to be held at the Factory of Sadness, a nickname for the stadium. Instead, the $10,000 raised for the parade will be donated to the Greater Cleveland Food Bank. The Browns have pledged to match this donation with an additional $10,000. The food bank announced the Browns' contribution on Twitter, expressing gratitude for the generous donations from Browns fans. The initial GoFundMe campaign aimed to cover costs for security, restrooms, and other necessities for the parade, surpassing its goal of $1,999 quickly.

The National Association of Theatre Owners (NATO) has announced plans for an off-night ticket-discount experiment in one U.S. state later this year. This move, while not a full-scale ticket price surrender, represents a significant concession in the industry's long-standing resistance to ticket discounting. The experiment is being carefully implemented to avoid violating antitrust laws and to ensure studio endorsement. NATO Chief John Fithian made the announcement at CinemaCon in Las Vegas, where tension between exhibitors and studios has been growing over issues such as shrinking theatrical windows, secret premium VOD, and now discounting. The experiment follows failed attempts by startups like Groupon and MoviePass to break into the ticket pricing market, which have faced intense exhibitor and studio pressure. Despite box-office grosses reaching new heights, actual ticket sales have been flat or in decline, with ticket prices and premium formats inflating revenues. This experiment could signal a shift in the industry's approach to ticket pricing, as exhibitors explore new strategies to boost ticket sales.

Martha Stewart has partnered with Triscuit to release a new flavor of crackers, Toasted Coconut & Sea Salt, which hit grocery store shelves in early May. Stewart said the flavor combination was her idea, as she is a fan of both salt and coconut. The crackers are part of a limited-time offering and are intended to be a gourmet snack, with suggested pairings such as crab meat and lime, avocado and hot pepper, melted cheese, crab and truffle, and even a Martha Stewart-approved s'more made with milk chocolate and a marshmallow. Stewart said she herself is not much of a snacker, but keeps crackers in the house for the salt factor. The new flavor is part of a broader trend of food items that are on trend and popular, including avocado, s'mores, and artisanal food products.

Netflix, a popular streaming service, has announced a price hike, causing a significant backlash from customers. The new pricing structure, effective from September, will see a split of the streaming video and DVD-by-mail services, with each costing $7.99 per month, and a combined subscription costing $15.98. This change has led to an influx of angry calls to Netflix's customer service, with some customers experiencing extended delays.

Netflix had anticipated the backlash and prepared its customer service representatives for an increase in calls. However, the volume of calls has been so high that even with extra employees, delays persist. Wall Street analyst Rich Greenfield, in a report, accused Netflix of being unprepared for the level of customer anger.

In response, Netflix spokesman Steve Swasey confirmed that they were aware of the reaction and were not surprised. He stated that the company had conducted tests, research, and analysis before making the decision.

The price increase has led to a flood of negative responses on Netflix's blog, with many customers threatening to cancel their subscriptions. However, Netflix employees have reportedly been advising those who threaten to cancel to wait until the new plan takes effect in September. This has led to criticism that Netflix is not concerned about losing customers.

Despite the controversy, Netflix has managed to renew its multi-year licensing agreement with NBC Universal, adding new content to its library. However, whether this new content will be enough to appease customers who are unhappy about the price hike remains to be seen.

The Broadway musical "Spider-Man: Turn Off the Dark" experienced another accident during a performance on Monday night, injuring a stunt double who fell from a platform into a pit below the stage. The actor, whose identity and condition are not yet disclosed, was taken to Bellevue Hospital. The incident occurred during a scene when Spider-Man was rescuing his love interest, Mary Jane, as she dangled from a rope attached to a bridge. The show's opening, initially scheduled for February 7, has been delayed due to safety concerns and artistic overhaul. This is the fourth accident since previews began last month, following injuries to an actor, a dancer, and actress Natalie Mendoza. OSHA, Actors Equity, and the New York State Department of Labor are meeting with the production to discuss additional safety protocols. The cause of the accident is reported to be human error.

The article discusses the strained relationships between Republican presidential candidate Ted Cruz and several high-profile Republicans, including Bob Dole, John McCain, George W. Bush, and John Boehner. The tension between Cruz and these politicians stems from various policy disagreements, personal animosity, and Cruz's perceived arrogance and lack of teamwork.

The article recounts anecdotes from Cruz's time as a policy adviser for George W. Bush's 2000 campaign, where he was described as hyper-arrogant, widely despised, and difficult to work with. Cruz's colleagues also noted his tendency to offer unsolicited opinions on matters outside his portfolio and his inability to be part of the team.

Cruz's relationship with Bob Dole soured in 2014 when Cruz led a last-minute push to defeat the UN Treaty on the Rights of Persons With Disabilities, which Dole had come to the Senate floor to support. Cruz's feud with John McCain began in 2013 when Cruz called McCain's failed candidacies evidence of the electoral impotence of mainline Republicans.

Cruz has also clashed with Sen. Lindsey Graham over national security measures and has been criticized by Rep. Peter King for his role in the government shutdown in 2013. Cruz's former classmates at Princeton and Harvard Law School have also described him as arrogant, abrasive, and difficult to work with.

The article also includes an 18-year-old video of a young Cruz joking about his life's goals, including world domination and a role in a teen tit film. Cruz's campaign spokesman replied that it was good to see he had always had a great sense of humor.

Overall, the article presents a portrait of Cruz as a divisive and polarizing figure who has strained relationships with many prominent Republicans due to his perceived arrogance, lack of teamwork, and policy disagreements.

A white man identified as Don Crandall, the general manager of Baymont Inn & Suites by Wyndham Hotels, was fired after a viral video showed him pulling a gun on four black students from Florida A&M University while they were waiting to enter their friend's apartment building late Saturday night. The incident occurred at Stadium Centre, an apartment complex marketed as off-campus housing for college students in Tallahassee.

Isaiah Butterfield, one of the students involved, captured the 10-minute confrontation on video and posted it on Twitter, where it received nearly 6,000 retweets. The video shows Crandall claiming to be a resident of the building and getting into a verbal altercation with the students before pulling out a gun.

According to Butterfield, the students were waiting at the garage entrance to the apartment building when Crandall walked past them and through the door. He then returned a few moments later and began harassing the students. Another man, whom Butterfield identified as "Chad," intervened on the students' behalf, and Crandall eventually backed down and allowed the students to enter the building.

The apartment complex's management issued a statement condemning Crandall's actions and stating that firearms are prohibited on the property. They also expressed their commitment to creating a diverse and inclusive residential community. The Pax Hotel Group, which owns the inn where Crandall worked, also issued a statement confirming that he had been fired and apologizing for his actions.

The incident has sparked outrage on social media, with many expressing their support for the students and condemning Crandall's actions as racist. The students have not yet commented further on the incident.

Jennifer Herold, a candidate for The Ohio House of Representatives-7th District, issued a statement on January 18th, condemning Tom Patton's discriminatory and insulting comments made on "America's Workforce Radio." In the radio interview, Patton, a 62-year-old Republican, questioned Herold's ability to serve as a state representative due to her status as a mother of two young children. He suggested that her responsibilities as a mother would conflict with the demands of the position, implying that she was unaware of the requirements of the role.

Herold, who has two sons aged 1 and 3, found Patton's comments to be insulting and discriminatory. She pointed out that numerous women, including former Vice Presidential nominee Sarah Palin, Cathy McMorris Rodgers, the fourth-highest ranking member of the Republican Leadership in the US House of Representatives, Lieutenant Governor Mary Taylor, and Ohio House Representative Christina Hagan, have served in office while raising a family.

Herold also highlighted the example of men who serve in public office while raising children, such as Governor John Kasich and Speaker of the House Paul Ryan. She questioned whether Patton's comments implied that these individuals were also unfit to serve.

In response to Patton's comments, Herold called on the Cuyahoga County Republican Party, The Ohio Republican Party, and any other organizations endorsing a candidate in this race to reconsider their support for Patton, as his comments reflect values that are not in line with the district's majority female population and parents who successfully balance demanding jobs and family life.

Patton later issued a statement claiming that his comments were misunderstood. He apologized for any misplaced words and stated that his intention was not to suggest that a young mother couldn't serve ably in the legislature. He acknowledged that millions of women balance raising young children and working every day, including his own daughters.

The winner of the House District 7 GOP primary on March 15 will face Democrat David Thurau, a former Berea School Board member, in November. The controversy surrounding Patton's comments has sparked a petition and social media campaign in support of Herold, using the hashtag #ISupportJen.

The article discusses a shocking murder case in Canada where a man, Luka Rocco Magnotta, is suspected of killing, dismembering, and mailing body parts to different locations, including the headquarters of the Conservative Party of Canada. The victim is a white male whose identity has not been disclosed. Magnotta, also known as Eric Clinton Newman, is a Montreal resident with no criminal background. The investigation began when a human torso was found in Montreal, and a human hand and foot were separately mailed from Montreal to Ottawa. Magnotta is believed to have known the victim, and his image and information were recovered from a pornographic website. The police are asking for the public's help in locating Magnotta, who is wanted for murder. The investigation is ongoing, and forensic testing is being conducted to confirm if all body parts belong to the same victim. The Conservative Party of Canada and the Canadian government have denounced the incident.

The study published in PLOS Biology has shown that bumblebees can learn to pull a string to retrieve a reward, and this skill can be passed on to other bees through social learning. This is the first time that such a behavior has been observed in insects, and it suggests that bumblebees have the cognitive abilities necessary for cultural transmission. The study involved training bumblebees to pull a string to obtain a sugar water reward, and then observing how the behavior was passed on to other bees. The researchers found that bees could learn the behavior from other bees, even if they had no prior experience with the task. The study also found that the behavior could spread through multiple generations of bees, suggesting that it could potentially be a form of culture. The findings challenge the notion that "big brains" are necessary for new skills to spread, and suggest that simpler mechanisms may be involved in cultural transmission. The study has implications for our understanding of animal cognition and the evolution of complex behaviors.

On December 18, 2013, William Morris Endeavor Entertainment (WME), a leading global talent, entertainment, and media company, announced an agreement to acquire IMG Worldwide (IMG). IMG is a market leader in college and professional sports, event management, client representation, fashion, and multi-media rights management. The acquisition aims to create a unique global sports and entertainment platform, operating across various continents.

WME Co-CEOs Patrick Whitesell and Ariel Emanuel expressed excitement about the deal, stating that IMG's global reach, exceptional management team, and leadership across sports, fashion, and media are a strong complement to their business. The combined company will have an unparalleled client roster, a broad relationship base with sponsors, brands, and broadcasters, and marquee assets in sports, events, film, television, and fashion.

Silver Lake, a global leader in technology investing, will continue its partnership with WME, supporting the combined company's growth. The transaction is subject to customary closing conditions, and financial details were not disclosed. Mubadala Development Company will be a minority investor in the transaction.

The deal represents the latest consequence of a rapid shift in the economics of Hollywood, as traditional talent agencies expand their reach beyond entertainment into sports and fashion. WME and IMG together will deliver a broad range of opportunities and resources to the companies and talent they collectively represent.

In a court case in Austin, Texas, James Miller, a retired police officer, was found not guilty of murder but guilty of criminally negligent homicide in the 2015 stabbing death of Daniel Spencer, 32. The jury sentenced Miller to 10 years of probation, 6 months in the Travis County Jail, a fine of $10,000 for restitution, an alcohol monitor for a year, 100 hours of community service, and payment of court costs.

The prosecution argued that Spencer was an upstanding member of the community who was killed by Miller for no good reason. The state called several witnesses, including Spencer's mother, who expressed her grief and pain over the loss of her son.

The defense argued that Miller acted in self-defense and should be eligible for the minimum punishment associated with the charge. They claimed that Spencer had made sexual advances towards Miller, which led to the altercation.

The "gay panic" defense, which allows a defendant to claim that they reacted violently due to fear of their own homosexuality being discovered, was used in Miller's case. This defense is legal in Texas, despite efforts by LGBT advocates and the American Bar Association to have it banned.

The case has sparked outrage among LGBT advocates, who argue that the law gives non-straight people second-class citizen treatment. D'Arcy Kemnitz, the executive director of the LGBT Bar Association, said the defense plays on the idea that LGBT people are considered "others" or outside what is normative in society.

Miller testified that he felt threatened in Spencer's home due to his height, arm length, and youth advantage. However, prosecutors argued that Spencer never threatened Miller or had any intention of hurting him.

The American Bar Association has urged lawmakers to curtail the availability and effectiveness of the "gay panic" and "trans panic" defense. Kemnitz said there is active legislation in several states to stop defense attorneys from using this defense. She also expressed concern that the defense re-victimizes the attacked person and sends a message of vulnerability to other marginalized members of society.

The document is a heartfelt plea for help in locating a lost dog named Jade in Yellowstone National Park. Jade's family, David Sowers, Laura Gillice, and David's daughter Angie Sowers, lost Jade during a car accident on July 23, 2015, while they were vacationing. The family has been making frequent trips from Denver, Colorado, to Yellowstone, a 550-mile journey, to search for Jade. Despite numerous sightings of Jade in the park, particularly in the Canyon Village area, efforts to catch her have been unsuccessful. The family is facing mounting medical bills and expenses from their frequent trips. The authors of the document are asking for small donations to help the family and for anyone visiting the park to join the search efforts. They emphasize that every little bit helps in bringing Jade home safely. The document ends with a quote, "Every once in a while a dog enters your life and changes EVERYTHING." The authors are asking for help in spreading the word to aid in finding Jade.

Rupert Murdoch, the media mogul, has filed for divorce from his wife Wendi Deng after 14 years of marriage. The couple, who have two daughters together, have reportedly grown apart in recent months. Rumors suggest that Wendi's socializing and friendships with men, including MySpace co-founder Chris DeWolfe, former British Prime Minister Tony Blair, and Google executive chairman Eric Schmidt, may have strained the marriage. A spokesman for the Murdochs declined to comment, and calls to Wendi's attorney were not returned.

In June 2012, The New York Times reported that Rupert rarely accompanies Wendi to charitable functions and that her social circle has grown to include Blair, David Geffen, Bono, and Nicole Kidman. Rumors of a romantic affair with DeWolfe surfaced in 2008, and both declined to comment at the time. Wendi was "chief of strategy" for MySpace.

More recently, there have been hints of a special relationship with Blair, who is said to be a godfather to at least one of Wendi and Rupert's daughters. In an article titled "Tony Blair and the Murdochs: A Family Affair" in The Guardian last year, author Michael Wolff described Blair as one of Wendi’s “first official social conquests” and suggested that she and Blair had joined forces to “handle” Rupert. Wolfe tweeted in May 2012, “Wendi Murdoch and Tony Blair: you heard it here first,” prompting journalist Jacob Weisberg to tweet, “Are you suggesting what I think?” A source close to Blair categorically denies any romantic relationship.

Schmidt, said to be friends with Wendi Murdoch, was mentioned in 2010 press reports as having invested with her in the New York-based startup Art.sy, meant to match art with prospective buyers. He has been estranged from his wife, Wendy, and according to media accounts has been linked to other women. The New York Times questioned Schmidt about such relationships in August 2012. His response: "I don’t think that is an appropriate question. We don’t comment on that -- rumors.” A Schmidt friend says it's "doubtful" the Google exec would be romantically linked to Wendi Murdoch.

Rupert Murdoch met Wendi Deng in 1998 when she was an employee of News Corp’s Star TV in Hong Kong. They married in 1999 and have two daughters, Grace, 11, and Chloe, 9. In recent years, China-born Wendi has played an increasing role in News Corp’s business in China, as well as producing the Fox Searchlight release Snow Flower and the Secret Fan. Sources say she has acted as an intermediary to Chinese officials for several Hollywood executives. Wendi gained national attention in 2011 when she came to her husband's defense after an assailant attempted to hit him with a pie during a hearing in connection with the News of the World phone-hacking scandal.

The divorce filing said that the “relationship between husband and wife has broken down irretrievably.” Rupert is represented by divorce lawyer Ira E. Garr. Pamela Sloan will represent Wendi. Murdoch’s divorce in 1998 from his second wife, Anna Maria Torv, cost him $1.7 billion, though he and Wendi are said to have a prenuptial agreement.

BBC reporter Robert Peston tweeted that the undisclosed reasons for Murdoch divorcing Deng are "jaw-dropping," and speculation about the reasons for the split is swirling. Some possible reasons include financial issues, infidelity, and Wendi's socializing and friendships with men. It remains to be seen what the true reasons for the divorce are, but it is certain to be a high-profile and closely watched case.

Charlie Hunnam, born on April 10, 1980, in Newcastle, England, began his acting career at 16 with a guest appearance on the popular TV series Byker Grove. He gained fame in Britain for his role as Nathan Maloney in Queer as Folk. Hunnam has since appeared in independent movies, television series, and auditioned for blockbusters like Star Wars: Episode II - Attack of the Clones.

Hunnam once turned down a million-dollar role due to scheduling conflicts and a desire to prioritize long-term career opportunities over immediate financial gain. He also had a role cut from the script of the independent film Anderson's Cross due to scheduling conflicts, with the director stating "No one replaces Charlie Hunnam."

The Cuban government has arrested an unidentified American contractor working for the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID) on charges that are yet to be disclosed. The contractor, employed by Development Alternatives Inc., was distributing cellphones and laptop computers to Cuban activists. The detention has raised concerns about the future of U.S.-Cuba relations, as it comes at a time when both governments have been working towards improved engagement. The contractor is being held in a secure facility in Havana, and consular officers are seeking access to him. The detention may be related to the contractor's efforts to connect Cuban activists with each other and with their affinity groups in the U.S., as well as to expand their access to the internet. The incident has sparked debate about the Obama administration's policy towards Cuba, with some questioning whether it breaks with the confrontational tactics of the past. The Cuban government has not commented on the matter. The detention of the American contractor threatens to strain relations between the two countries, as the Obama administration has been taking a "go-slow" approach to improving relations with Cuba. The new U.S. policy stresses that if Cuba takes concrete steps such as freeing political prisoners and creating more space for opposition, the United States will reciprocate.

In Lansdowne, Baltimore County, a 16-month-old girl named Sabriya Towels was found in cardiac arrest and later died at the hospital. She was discovered in a black Ford F-150, which is now under investigation by police. A relative, who was supposed to drop her off at the Highland Village Head Start Center, accidentally left her in the truck for four hours. The relative went home to sleep instead, and when he returned, he found the child unresponsive. The incident occurred in 88-degree heat, and the Office of the Chief Medical Examiner will determine the cause of death.

In a separate incident in Alexandria, an 8-month-old baby died after being left in a hot parked car. Zoraida Magali Conde Hernandez, the mother, has been charged with felony child neglect. The suspect car was towed from Inova Alexandria Hospital. The mother, who lives in Alexandria, intended to drop the child off at daycare on her way to work but forgot and went on to work. She only noticed the child was in the vehicle while driving and immediately drove to the hospital, but the child was declared dead upon arrival. The high temperature that day was 90 degrees. Both incidents have left neighbors and communities shocked and saddened.

On March 4, 2010, nationwide protests against deep education cuts took place on college campuses across the United States. The demonstrations were peaceful for the most part, but incidents of violence occurred in Wisconsin and California. In Wisconsin, 15 protesters were arrested after a confrontation with police at the University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee. In California, protesters blocked university gates and smashed car windows at the University of California, Santa Cruz. The protests were part of the March 4th National Day of Action for Public Education, with organizers estimating hundreds of thousands of students, teachers, parents, and others participating nationwide. The steep economic downturn has forced states to slash funding to K-12 schools, community colleges, and universities to cope with plummeting tax revenue. Experts warned that schools and colleges could face more severe financial trouble over the next few years as they drain federal stimulus money. Some university officials supported the protests as long as they remained peaceful.

The article from Time magazine, dated December 27, 2016, discusses the rising costs of producing the one-cent US coin, also known as the penny. In 2016, the cost to produce a penny increased to 1.5 cents, making it more expensive to manufacture than its face value. This trend has been ongoing since 2015, with the production cost of a penny reaching 1.43 cents in 2015 and 1.66 cents in 2014.

The high production costs of pennies and nickels are causing significant losses for the US Mint. Last year, the Mint produced over 8.4 billion pennies, resulting in a loss of $69 million due to production and shipping costs. This is the highest loss in nine years. The rising cost of zinc, a primary component in pennies, is attributed to its increased demand in heavy industry, construction, and electric car production.

Nickels, which are 75% copper and 25% nickel, also cost more to produce than their face value. The rising prices of copper and nickel, essential components in various industries, are contributing to the high production costs of both pennies and nickels. However, dimes and quarters are still cheaper to produce than their face value, helping the Mint offset the losses from pennies and nickels, as they reported making $391.5 million in seigniorage last year.

The article suggests that abolishing the penny could help reduce the budget and eliminate a coin that is often seen as unnecessary, as overseas bases do not use pennies and the only pennies seen overseas are those brought by new recruits.

Interior Secretary Ryan Zinke has recommended significant changes to nearly half of the geographic national monuments he reviewed at the request of President Donald Trump. The changes include reducing the boundaries of the Bears Ears and Grand Staircase-Escalante preserves in Utah, reopening protected oceans to commercial fishing, and altering several other monuments. The recommendations, which have not been officially released, also suggest reducing the size of two marine monuments in the Pacific Ocean and changing the boundaries of several other monuments, including Nevada's Gold Butte and Oregon's Cascade-Siskiyou.

The review of the national monuments was ordered by Trump earlier this year, following complaints about "land grabs" by former presidents, including Barack Obama. The monuments under review were designated by four presidents over the last two decades, with some being about the size of the state of Delaware.

Zinke's recommendations, if adopted by Trump, would mark the latest in a string of actions where Trump has sought to erode his Democratic predecessor's legacy. The changes could lead to increased public access, but conservationists have expressed concerns about potential losses of protections for areas that are home to ancient cliff dwellings, towering sequoia trees, deep canyons, and ocean habitats. They've vowed to file lawsuits if Trump attempts any changes that would reduce the size of monuments or rescind their designations.

The recommendations cap an unprecedented four-month review based on Trump's claim that the century-old Antiquities Act had been misused by past presidents to create oversized monuments that hinder energy development, grazing, and other uses. The changes have sparked controversy, with some arguing that they would protect tribal interests and historical land grants, while others fear they could lead to increased oil, gas, mining, logging, and other industrial activities.

In an auction, a rare album of photographs of Adolf Hitler, taken by a British Fleet Street photographer named Edward Dean, was sold. The photographs, which were carefully controlled by the Nazis to maintain a positive image of Hitler, show the dictator in a more casual and relaxed manner, including a shot of him giving a Charlie Chaplin-like salute outside his Berghof headquarters. The album was found in Eva Braun's bunker room after her and Hitler's suicide in 1945.

The auction, which was highly competitive, attracted bidders from various countries, including Britain, the United States, Germany, China, and South Africa. The buyer was not disclosed. The photographs are significant as very few artifacts from the Fuhrer Bunker in 1945 exist in the open market.

The ownership of Nazi memorabilia raises ethical questions, and there have been efforts to recover looted art from the Holocaust. Last year, a replica of a gate believed to have been stolen from the Dachau concentration camp was recovered.

Memorials dedicated to preserving the historical context of the Holocaust have called for the donation of personal items from survivors or collectors. In January, the memorial director of Auschwitz-Birkenau issued a statement appealing for such donations.

The sale of Hitler-related items, including this album, has been criticized as exploitative, given the horrific events of the Holocaust. However, the buyer is reportedly a historian, and such items are often collected for historical purposes. The photographs provide a unique insight into the personal life of one of history's most infamous figures.

Peaches Geldof, a British media personality and musician, was found dead at her home in Wrotham, Kent, on Monday. Her 11-month-old son Phaedra was with her at the time. Geldof's husband, Thomas Cohen, had spent the night away with their eldest child, Astala. The cause of death is currently unexplained, and plans for her funeral are being made.

Geldof was an advocate of attachment parenting and was often seen with her young son. The hope is that Phaedra was too young to understand what happened. Geldof's own mother, Paula Yates, was found dead in 2000, with her baby daughter Tiger Lily nearby.

In the weeks before her death, concerns were raised about Geldof's weight loss. She had been open about her extreme dieting, including juicing and subsisting on miso soup for extended periods. The Merck KGaA, Darmstadt, Germany, and the American Cancer Society have released a report highlighting that the top causes of cancer deaths in women worldwide are preventable or treatable early, with breast, colorectal, lung, and cervical cancers being the leading causes of death. The report, titled "The Global Burden of Cancer in Women," is the first output from a partnership aimed at raising awareness and strengthening advocacy around women's cancers.

The report examines the impact of cancer among women in low- and middle-income countries and outlines potential solutions to minimize the economic and societal impact of the disease. Cancer is the second leading cause of death in women, with the number of deaths expected to increase, particularly in low- and middle-income countries.

The study found that in 2009, the global economic burden of cancer was estimated at about $286 billion, with much of the cost due to premature death of members of the workforce. In the United States alone in 2008, years of productive life lost due to cancer in women corresponded to $82 billion.

The report was released at the World Cancer Congress during a panel moderated by Ambassador Sally Cowal, senior vice president, global cancer control at the American Cancer Society. The partnership will also catalyze the evolution of the American Cancer Society's All of Me Young Scholars program, which aims to educate and cultivate health and civil society professionals in Brazil, Mexico, Colombia, and India to affect meaningful change in prevention and early detection of cancers among women in low- and middle-income countries.

The report is part of the Healthy Women, Healthy Economies initiative, which aims to identify and implement policies that advance women's health and well-being to increase their economic participation in the societies in which they live. The full "Global Burden of Cancer in Women" report is available at cancer.org.

The report emphasizes the need for increased education and prevention efforts to address the growing global health crisis of cancer among women. The American Cancer Society and Merck KGaA, Darmstadt, Germany, encourage both the public and private sectors to find ways to reduce the impacts of cancer on women by increasing prevention and treatment.

The University of Warwick has conducted research that has established the first universal charts for the normal amount of crying in babies during the first three months. In a study involving nearly 8700 infants from various countries, it was found that on average, babies cry for around two hours per day in the first two weeks, peaking at around two hours fifteen minutes per day at six weeks, and reducing gradually to an average of 1 hour 10 minutes by the twelve week mark. Babies in the UK, Italy, Canada, and the Netherlands cry the most, while the lowest levels of crying were found in Denmark, Germany, and Japan. The highest levels of colic were reported in the UK, Canada, and Italy, and the lowest were reported in Denmark and Germany. The research, published in The Journal of Pediatrics, aims to provide modern parents and health professionals with new universal guidelines to assess normal and excessive levels of crying in babies. Professor Dieter Wolke, who led the research, stated that the new chart will help health professionals reassure parents about their baby's crying patterns and provide extra support if necessary. The research also highlights the need for parents to prioritize their own well-being to better care for their babies.

The research titled "Rethinking natural altruism: Simple reciprocal interactions trigger children’s benevolence" suggests that altruism in children, particularly 1- and 2-year-olds, is not solely innate but is also influenced by simple reciprocal interactions. The study, conducted by psychologists at Stanford University, found that a brief reciprocal activity, such as rolling a ball back and forth, significantly increased the likelihood of children helping others, compared to parallel play where each child played with their own ball.

The findings challenge the dominant claim that young humans are naturally and spontaneously altruistic, and that socialization cannot account for their altruistic actions. The researchers believe that these reciprocal experiences may communicate benevolent values or practices, thereby serving as a trigger for children's altruism.

The study was conducted in four parts, with the first part showing that children in the reciprocal play condition helped significantly more than those in the parallel play condition. The second part showed that the effects of a single reciprocal interaction carried over to affect how much children helped a second person in the situation. The third part demonstrated that reciprocity remained a potent cue for older (preschool) children, and the fourth part suggested that reciprocal interactions trigger an important belief in the mind of a child: the perception of benevolence in that situation.

The study has implications for adult-child interactions, suggesting that caregivers may engage in simple reciprocal activities to foster both the enactment of altruism in children and their expectation of altruism from others. The researchers plan to conduct further studies to verify the findings, particularly in children younger than 18 months. The study was published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

Trump and his wife, Melania, danced to the same song, "My Way," at the new president's inauguration in 2017. The McCain family chose a Russian dissident as a pallbearer, though Trump has professed his affinity and admiration for Russian President Vladimir Putin. Former prosecutor Marcia Clark, who was the lead prosecutor during O.J. Simpson's trial in 1995, is expressing skepticism about a recent development in the case. In a press conference on Friday, LAPD Capt. Andrew Neiman confirmed that the department is investigating the alleged discovery of a knife on the Rockingham property formerly owned by Simpson. In addition to the knife, several other knives have been proposed as the murder weapon over the years, though none have been conclusively linked to the slayings. Even if evidence is found linking the knife to the murders, Simpson cannot be tried again, as he was previously acquitted. The knife is currently being tested for fingerprints and hair, and samples may be contaminated through the years or degraded by the environment. It is unclear whether any useful evidence will be found on the knife.

The current bull market in stocks, which began on March 9, 2009, is turning eight years old this week. By the most commonly accepted definition, this bull market started when the Standard & Poor's 500 Index gained 20% two weeks after reaching a low of 676 on March 9, 2009. This bull market is the second-longest ever, with gains of over 250%.

However, some professional investors and market experts argue that the bull market truly got rolling well after the financial crisis climax. They cite alternative start dates such as September 2011, March 2013, and February 2016, when the market experienced significant setbacks.

The bull market's longevity has led to concerns about its potential demise. Some strategists warn of a correction of up to 10%, as the market is currently overvalued. However, analysts remain optimistic about further gains, citing stronger company earnings, lower taxes, and a corporate-friendly administration in Washington.

Despite the debate over the bull market's start date, it is clear that the market has delivered strong returns, with the S&P 500 gaining 250% since the 2009 low. Even if the bull market is considered mature, it is not over yet, and it is unlikely to be caused by old age. Instead, it is expected to end due to recession, financial panic, or action by the Federal Reserve.

In a significant development, all charges against Crystal Mason, a black woman who was sentenced to five years in prison for attempting to vote in the 2016 presidential election while on probation in Texas, have been dropped. This decision comes after a campaign to have the charges dropped, citing the disparity in sentencing between Mason and a white woman who was sentenced to probation for a similar offense in Iowa.

Mason's case has sparked controversy and discussions about voter suppression and white privilege. The issue of felons' voting rights has become a contentious issue in the United States, with more than six million Americans disenfranchised by felony disenfranchisement laws. The rules vary state by state, with some states revoking the right to vote for felons while they are incarcerated, on parole, or on probation. Some states, like Vermont and Maine, allow felons to vote even while they are in prison.

In Mason's case, the judge initially denied her motion for a new trial. However, a petition with over 38,000 signatures was started to have all charges against her dropped. The case has received widespread media attention and sparked debates about voter suppression and racial disparities in the criminal justice system.

The judge's decision to drop the charges against Crystal Mason is a step towards addressing these issues and ensuring that all citizens have the right to vote, regardless of their criminal history. It is crucial that all incarcerated people and formerly incarcerated people on probation or parole are aware of their inability to vote while they are on supervision. This decision sets a precedent and could potentially lead to further reforms in the criminal justice system and voting rights.

The new study published in Geophysical Research Letters provides the most accurate count yet of lakes on Earth, with 117 million lakes identified using high-resolution satellite data and supercomputers. The study found that these lakes cover 2 million square miles (5 million square kilometers), which is 3.7% of the land uncapped by glaciers. Most lakes are in the Northern Hemisphere, particularly in Canada, Russia, Alaska, Northern Europe, and the Great Lakes. The majority of Earth's lakes are at low altitudes, found at elevations less than 1,600 feet (500 meters) above sea level.

The Aral Sea, the world's largest lake, has been shrinking over the last half-century due to a massive Soviet irrigation project that diverted water from the rivers that fed it into farmland. Images taken from the Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer on NASA's Terra satellite show how the lake has increasingly shrunk until this year, when the eastern lobe dried up completely. The loss of the Aral Sea has brought dire consequences to the surrounding communities, with the water becoming polluted and the lakebed contaminating dust being blown up.

The new study plans to release the lake database and update the count with higher-resolution data from the Landsat 8 satellite. The researchers also noted that lakes are not static on the landscape and in some parts of the world, they are disappearing quickly due to climate change, higher temperatures, and overuse. In certain regions of Russia and Alaska, higher temperatures are causing permafrost to thaw, causing small lakes to dry up. Drought and overuse are also shrinking lakes in northern China.
