The visit was not without controversy, as Melania Trump's wide-brimmed hat drew comparisons to those worn by Beyoncé, Jude Law, and Kerry Washington. Some also noticed that while Brigitte Macron managed to kiss both of her fellow first lady’s cheeks, President Trump had trouble making contact and settled on air kisses instead. Overall, the visit was marked by a mix of diplomatic discussions and humorous moments, with the hand-holding and dandruff incidents becoming the main topics of conversation on social media.

This collection of images and captions showcases various moments in the life and career of Senator Orrin Hatch from Utah, who served as a senator from 1977 until his retirement in 2019. The images span over four decades, featuring Hatch with notable figures such as Muhammad Ali, Ronald Reagan, and Donald Trump, as well as his wife Elaine.

Hatch held several notable positions during his tenure, including Chairman of the Senate Judiciary Committee, where he played a role in the confirmation hearings for Supreme Court justices such as Elena Kagan, Samuel Alito, and John Roberts. He was also involved in various political events, including fundraisers and debates.

Throughout his career, Hatch was known for his work on healthcare, intellectual property, and other issues. He co-sponsored bills with senators like Edward Kennedy and was involved in the State Children's Health Insurance Program (SCHIP).

Hatch's career spanned multiple presidencies, from Reagan to Trump, and he was a prominent figure in the Republican Party. His retirement marked the end of an era in Utah politics, leaving a significant legacy behind.

In a recent interview, President Donald Trump criticized Nike for choosing former NFL quarterback Colin Kaepernick as the face of their 30th anniversary "Just Do It" campaign. Kaepernick, who began kneeling during the national anthem in 2016 to protest racial inequality and police brutality, has a new deal with Nike despite not being on an NFL roster. Trump stated that he believes Nike's decision sends a "terrible message" but acknowledges it's a matter of freedom of business in the United States.

Kaepernick's protest movement sparked controversy among NFL players and fans, with Trump frequently expressing opposition to players demonstrating during the anthem. In September 2017, Trump tweeted, "The issue of kneeling has nothing to do with race. It is about respect for our Country, Flag and National Anthem."

Nike's stock dropped 2% in early trading following the announcement of Kaepernick's new deal. Country singer John Rich of Big & Rich criticized Nike for endorsing Kaepernick, posting pictures of cut-up Nike socks on social media.

In response to the backlash, an NFL executive stated that social justice issues raised by players "deserve our attention and action." The league has been working with players and executives to learn about and address social issues, including community meetings, lobbying, and financially supporting local programs.

This controversy highlights the ongoing debate about protest during the national anthem and the role of athletes in addressing social issues.

In this article, several news stories are summarized, including a controversy surrounding Denis Finley, the editor of the Burlington Free Press, over a series of controversial tweets he posted regarding a gender-neutral driver's license policy in Vermont. Finley's tweets were met with widespread criticism and claims of canceled subscriptions. Another story discusses a heated exchange between CNN's Jake Tapper and White House aide Stephen Miller, during which Tapper cut off Miller after becoming frustrated with his evasive answers. The article also touches on the New York Times' new advertising campaign, declining TV news viewership, and a photo history of what actresses have worn to the Golden Globes over the years. Additionally, the article discusses the deportation of individuals to harm or death in Central America, the work of female soccer hosts, and the controversy surrounding ESPN's coverage of the New England Patriots. The article concludes with a discussion of the possibility that Deputy Attorney General Rod Rosenstein may not be investigating President Trump for obstruction, and the importance of informed readers in a democracy.

A 13-foot great white shark carcass was found ashore near the Rhode Island state line in Westport, Massachusetts on September 1, 2012. A Massachusetts marine biologist performed a necropsy on the 1,500-pound male shark, but found no signs of trauma, suggesting an unknown cause of death. The carcass was left where it was due to its large size, and officials hoped the tide would drag it back out to sea.

In a separate incident, shark sightings in Cape Cod, Massachusetts led to the closure of several popular beaches during the Labor Day weekend. The increased number of shark sightings is believed to be due to an increased population of grey seals, a staple of a shark's diet, along the North-Atlantic coast. The resident seal population shows no signs of slowing down, and beach goers will have to share the shore with the sharks until they migrate to warmer waters this winter.

A female Suncor Energy employee, identified as Lorna Weafer, was killed by a bear on the company's oil sands base camp site near Fort McMurray, Alberta. The incident occurred in a busy area of the industrial complex on Wednesday afternoon. The bear, a large male black bear, attacked Weafer shortly after she exited a washroom. Co-workers attempted to intervene but were unable to stop the attack. Suncor is conducting a full investigation into the incident. This is the third employee death on Suncor's oil sands site this year, although the two other incidents were work-related. The Royal Canadian Mounted Police and Alberta Environmental and Sustainable Resource Development responded to the incident, and the bear was put down. Suncor has expressed shock and condolences to Weafer's family, friends, and co-workers. The company is emphasizing personal safety and vigilance in dealing with wildlife. The bear was of above-average size, and no open food was found in the area at the time. Traps have been set up, and another bear has been caught. Suncor and Alberta Occupational Health and Safety are investigating to determine if anything could have been done to prevent the attack.

Anthony Bourdain, the renowned chef, author, and television host, was found dead of suicide in his hotel room in Kaysersberg, France on June 8, while in the country filming an upcoming episode of Parts Unknown. He was 61. A completed toxicology report revealed that he had no narcotics in his system at the time of his death, but there was a "trace of a nonnarcotic medicine in a therapeutic dose." Bourdain had a history of substance abuse, but he entered rehab and eventually got clean in the early 90s.

Bourdain's girlfriend, actress Asia Argento, is struggling to cope with his death. The two met in 2016 while filming an episode of Parts Unknown about Rome. Bourdain was an outspoken champion of Argento's work in the #MeToo movement, and supported her when she came forward to say she was raped by disgraced movie producer Harvey Weinstein.

Bourdain was a brash and opinionated figure who spoke openly about his use of drugs and addiction to heroin earlier in his life. He was the host of CNN’s food-and-travel-focused “Parts Unknown” television series, which catapulted him from washing dishes at New York restaurants to dining in Vietnam with President Barack Obama.

The grief-stricken Argento took to Instagram to share a photo of her and Bourdain smiling in front of a teal-blue body of water, captioning the shot, "Two weeks without you." Argento shared a heartbreaking statement on Twitter and Instagram after Bourdain's passing, expressing her love and admiration for him.

If you or someone you know is in crisis, call the U.S. National Suicide Prevention Lifeline at 800-273-8255, text TALK to 741741, or visit SpeakingOfSuicide.com/resources for additional resources.

The Trump administration's 90% cut in funding for Obamacare advertising has caused U.S. health insurers to increase their own advertising efforts to promote 2018 enrollment, which opened on November 1. Independence Blue Cross, Centene Corp, and tech-savvy newcomer Oscar Health are among the insurers ramping up their advertising efforts. Trump's actions have caused confusion among many people over the subsidies that help make coverage affordable and the existence of Obamacare itself. The government's advertising budget is now just $10 million for the 39 states that rely on the federal Healthcare.gov website to enroll consumers. The 11 states that run their own exchanges, like California and New York, set their own advertising budgets.

Insurers like Anthem Inc have sharply raised monthly premiums on the most popular Obamacare plans to account for reduced government funding, or pulled out of dozens of U.S. counties. As a result, many Obamacare customers may need to change health plans for 2018, either to work with a different insurer or in response to price increases.

Despite fears from Democrats that enrollment would fall off due to the Trump administration's cutbacks in outreach and advertising, a record number of people signed up for Obamacare in the first few days of open enrollment this year compared to the same period in previous years. It is still early in the process and it is unclear how the final sign-up numbers will come out.

The administration cut the outreach budget by 90% and cut back on grants to outside groups, called navigators, that help people enroll. This has added to the confusion and concerns about the future of Obamacare under Republican control of Washington. However, the spike in sign-ups in the first few days of open enrollment is some positive news for supporters of the health-care law.

Three House Republicans have introduced a measure calling for the resignation of Special Counsel Robert Mueller, who is leading the investigation into Russia's interference in the 2016 US election and potential collusion with the Trump campaign. The lawmakers, Matt Gaetz (R-Fla.), Andy Biggs (R-Ariz.), and Louie Gohmert (R-Texas), argue that Mueller should step down due to his professional relationship with James Comey, his successor at the FBI, and his role in the FBI's handling of a 2010 uranium deal with Russia. The resolution, while nonbinding, puts the House on record describing Mueller as unfit to lead the probe.

The move comes as Mueller issued his first indictments in the probe, charging former Trump campaign chairman Paul Manafort and his deputy Rick Gates with money laundering, and securing a guilty plea from George Papadopoulos, a low-level campaign foreign policy adviser, for lying to the FBI about his attempts to arrange a meeting between Russian officials and the Trump campaign. The anger from Republicans appears to mirror the feelings of President Donald Trump, who has been urging his own Justice Department to investigate Democrats for transgressions he says occurred during the 2016 election.

The resolution also includes a broader broadside against the FBI, accusing it of "willful blindness" over the uranium deal and calling for an investigation into the agency. Some on the left are urging Democratic lawmakers to step up their defense of Mueller, while other conservatives, like Reps. Trent Franks (R-Ariz.) and Ron DeSantis (R-Fla.), have already called for Mueller's departure. DeSantis has also pushed an amendment to curtail Mueller's probe and blamed Deputy Attorney General Rod Rosenstein for a "clumsy" decision to appoint Mueller without putting strict limits on his scope.

The new resolution is the latest sign of GOP resistance to the special counsel's Russia probe. While many of Gaetz's Republican colleagues have previously expressed support for Mueller and his investigation, some conservatives have latched on to the Uranium One deal, pointing to a report tangentially tying the deal to the 2016 Democratic presidential nominee, Hillary Clinton, who was the secretary of state at the time, and her husband, former President Bill Clinton. The House Intelligence Committee is also expected to end its separate investigation into Russian meddling in the 2016 presidential election soon.

A new case report links marijuana use to the deaths of two young men in Germany, with both deaths related to cardiovascular complications. Toxicological examinations found traces of THC, the main active ingredient in marijuana, in the men's blood and brain tissue. The men had a history of marijuana use, with one man having it in his pockets when he was found. The second man had also abused alcohol and drugs such as amphetamines and cocaine.

The researchers concluded that the men died from cardiovascular complications evoked by smoking cannabis, but noted that this assumption does not rule out that the men were predisposed to cardiovascular risks. The report has sparked controversy, with some experts arguing that marijuana does not cause heart problems, while others point to growing evidence of marijuana's potential cardiotoxic effects.

A recent French study also found a link between marijuana use and cardiovascular complications in young and middle-aged adults, with nearly 2% of reported complications being cardiovascular related. The study found that 25.6% of these complications resulted in death.

The case report in Germany was published in the April issue of the journal Forensic Science International, while the French study was published in the Journal of the American Heart Association. The reports highlight the need for further research into the potential health risks of marijuana use, particularly in young people and those with pre-existing cardiovascular weaknesses.

The documentary "Death of a Nation" is now available on DVD, Blu-ray, and Digital HD. The film explores the history of fascism and white supremacy, and examines the role of the Democratic Party in American politics. The film was directed by Dinesh D'Souza, a conservative writer and filmmaker who has been pardoned by President Trump after being convicted for violating campaign finance law. D'Souza is known for his provocative and controversial views, and has been a frequent critic of the Democratic Party. He can be found on social media platforms such as Facebook, Twitter, and Instagram, and his email is available on his website. In May 2016, D'Souza was pardoned by President Trump, who cited D'Souza's conviction as politically motivated. The pardon came after D'Souza's film "Hillary's America" was released, which portrays the Democratic Party as having ties to the Ku Klux Klan and slaveowners. The film also features cameos from Jonah Goldberg, a conservative writer who has been criticized for equating New Deal liberalism with European fascism. D'Souza's work has been controversial and divisive, but he has remained a prominent figure in conservative circles.

A British woman, identified as Kay Longstaff, was rescued after spending 10 hours in the Adriatic Sea following an accident where she fell from a cruise ship, the Norwegian Star, around 60 miles off Croatia's coast. The incident occurred late on Saturday night as the ship was en route to Venice, Italy.

Longstaff was found by a Croatian rescue ship and was immediately taken to a hospital in Pula, Croatia, for a 24-hour examination. She reported feeling "very lucky" to have survived and shared that she practiced yoga and sang to stay awake during her ordeal.

The cruise ship launched a search mission in the area of her fall but could not locate her. It was the Croatian coast guard that eventually found her 10 hours later. The circumstances of the incident are being investigated, and the British embassy in Croatia has been informed.

This incident comes weeks after another similar incident involving a cruise ship worker who fell overboard while traveling on the Norwegian Getaway, also operated by Norwegian Cruise Line, in the Gulf of Mexico.

The Norwegian Cruise Line has confirmed that they are pleased the individual is now safe and will soon be reunited with friends and family. The Adriatic Sea's warm temperature during the summer may have contributed to Longstaff's survival.

The article from AdAge.com discusses the ongoing "War on Christmas" in retail marketing messages, with the American Family Association (AFA) targeting Dick's Sporting Goods for promoting a "Holiday Shop" instead of using the term "Christmas." The AFA claims that the percentage of retailers recognizing Christmas in their advertising has risen from 20% to 80% over the past five years, with only eight retailers remaining on their list of "Companies Against Christmas."

Retailers such as Lowe's, Walmart, and Target have previously faced boycotts and media scrutiny for not using the term "Christmas" in their marketing, but have since changed their messaging to include it. This year, Dick's Sporting Goods will be the target of the AFA's annual boycott, with an expected Action Alert to be sent to the retailer's 2.3 million supporters.

The National Retail Federation (NRF) does not formally advise retailers on whether to use the word "Christmas," but provides statistics showing that 91% of consumers plan to celebrate Christmas, compared to 5% for Hanukkah and 2% for Kwanzaa. The pendulum seems to have swung back towards the use of the term "Christmas" in retail marketing, with retailers being careful not to alienate customers in the current economic environment.

The AFA's stance is that retailers should not profit from Christmas if they refuse to clearly acknowledge it. The AFA maintains that it is not bullying, but consumer advocacy. The AFA's list of "Companies for Christmas," "Companies Marginalizing Christmas," and "Companies Against Christmas" is provided in the article.

On February 12, a series of multi-vehicle crashes involving approximately 100 cars and dozens of tractor-trailers occurred on the Pennsylvania Turnpike between Willow Grove and Bensalem, Pennsylvania. The accidents, which stretched over several miles, resulted in the closure of the highway for most of the day.

A total of 30 people were injured and transported to local hospitals, with five of the injuries classified as serious but none considered life-threatening. Doylestown Hospital confirmed it was treating one victim who was in stable condition, while Abington was reportedly treating 16 people. St. Mary’s Medical Center, in Langhorne, was treating seven and Temple University Hospital was treating one.

Dr. John Kelly, chief of staff at Abington, stated that none of the injuries were serious. He explained that the injuries they were seeing were primarily soft tissue and bone injuries, with one patient having a closed-head injury but recovering well.

The incident began around 8:30am in the eastbound lanes between Willow Grove and the Route 1 exits in Bensalem, with another crash happening closer to the Route 1 exit. That accident area involved approximately 30 cars and included a jackknifed tractor-trailer.

Investigators are blaming icy conditions and sun glare as likely culprits in causing the pileup. Drivers reported that road spray on windshields plus the sun low in the sky may have hindered visibility as they found themselves suddenly upon a stopped vehicle ahead with insufficient room to stop on the slick pavement.

The Pennsylvania Turnpike Commission reported that the tractor-trailer blocking all eastbound lanes was moved to allow trapped backlog to get past the scene in the left lane to continue eastbound on I-276. Disabled commercial vehicles remained, but all passenger vehicles in the backlog had been removed.

The turnpike was reopened to traffic just before 4pm — about 7½ hours after the first crash occurred. The incident was described as "the worst accident I have seen in the 20 years I have been doing this" by CBS 3 traffic reporter Bob Kelly.

In Vietnam, a rare case of heteropaternal twins, born from different fathers, has been confirmed by genetic analysis. The twins, a boy and a girl, were brought to the Center for Genetic Analysis and Technologies (CGAT) in Hanoi for DNA testing due to concerns raised by their father and relatives about their dissimilar appearances. The father, from Hoa Binh Province, was pressured to take the test due to the baby girl's appearance being different from any family member. The results showed that the father is the biological father of only one of the twins, while the mother is the mother of both.

The news of this case has sparked concerns among other fathers in Vietnam who are in a similar situation. Le Dinh Luong, president of the Genetic Association of Vietnam, advised families not to take DNA tests unnecessarily, as twins looking different from each other is not uncommon and does not necessarily mean they are heteropaternal twins.

Heteropaternal twins are extremely rare, with only about 10 sets reported worldwide. They occur when two ova (egg cells) from the same menstrual cycle are fertilized by sperm from separate acts of sexual intercourse with two different males, a phenomenon known as heteropaternal superfecundation.

Vu Ba Quyet, director at the National Hospital of Obstetrics and Gynecology, confirmed that the probability of such occurrences is extremely low but not completely impossible. He explained that a female can bear twins from different males if she has engaged in sexual intercourse with the males within the same menstrual cycle, and her body has released two ova to be fertilized separately by their sperm.

Luu Thi Hong, a gynecologist, added that it is normal for fraternal twins to look different from each other, as the female body generally releases one ovum per month, though some women can release two at different times during a menstrual cycle.

The family involved in the case has not been identified to protect their privacy. The father is reportedly seeking the best way to deal with the situation. This case marks the first recorded case of heteropaternal twins in northern Vietnam.

Hillary Clinton delivered closing remarks at the Professional Business Women of California conference in San Francisco, addressing the "indignities" faced by women in their professional roles. She specifically mentioned the treatment of April Ryan, a White House journalist, who was patronized and cut off by White House press secretary Sean Spicer during a question-and-answer session. Clinton also referenced Bill O'Reilly's racist comment about Rep. Maxine Waters's (D-Calif.) hair.

Clinton also discussed the need for improved diversity and inclusion in Silicon Valley, citing the Uber sexual harassment scandal as an example of a company struggling with these issues. She praised Salesforce and the Gap for their commitments to equal pay and paid family leave. Clinton emphasized the importance of concrete solutions to address implicit bias and urged Silicon Valley to lead by example.

The article discusses the concern among conservationists that feral cat colonies in Hawaii are posing a threat to the endangered Hawaiian monk seals due to the bacteria Toxoplasma gondii found in cat feces. This bacterium can be deadly for the seals, as it has been linked to the deaths of several seals since 2001.

The debate over the issue is heated, with animal lovers on one side advocating for the protection of the feral cats, and conservationists on the other side arguing for euthanization of some of the cats to protect the seals. State Senator Mike Gabbard, who chairs a committee that proposed a ban on feeding stray cats on state land, states that the issue is emotional and difficult.

The problem of stray cats in Hawaii is significant, with an estimated 300,000 feral cats on the island of Oahu alone. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) is pushing for a way to shrink the population, either through adoption or humane euthanization.

NOAA's acting Hawaiian monk seal recovery coordinator, Angela Amlin, states that cats are not part of Hawaii's native ecosystem and that they are a threat to the seals. However, animal welfare advocates argue against euthanasia for healthy felines, and instead advocate for trapping, neutering, and spaying to help control the cat population.

The article also discusses the case of Hoku, a Hawaiian monk seal that died from Toxoplasma gondii in 2016. Hoku was one of two seals that died from the bacterium that year, and it is suspected that the bacterium may have been transmitted through cat feces and polluted runoff.

The article concludes by stating that the overall population of monk seals is declining at a rate of about 4.5 percent a year, and that interactions with humans are likely to increase as the seals come into contact with more contaminants and diseases. The article notes that no studies have been done in Hawaii on how and where toxoplasmosis reaches the ocean, and that there are few efforts to control it. The article states that the deaths of the seals from toxoplasmosis are "very concerning" and that the disease is one of the primary concerns for the species.

In 2017, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) reported a 46% increase in cases of syphilis in infants, marking a 20-year high with 918 cases. This surge has been attributed to a combination of factors, including a lack of access to prenatal care, the opioid epidemic, and insufficient testing and treatment of women during pregnancy.

Syphilis is a bacterial infection that can be easily cured with penicillin, but if left untreated, it can lead to severe health problems for infants, including miscarriage, stillbirth, newborn death, and lifelong physical and mental health issues. In 2017, 64 babies were stillborn, and 13 died as infants due to syphilis.

The increase in infant cases mirrors a broader rise in syphilis diagnoses overall, with 30,644 diagnoses in 2017, a 76% increase from the previous year. Gay and bisexual men make up a large majority of people diagnosed with syphilis, but the rate among reproductive-age women has been rising for the last five years, contributing to the increase in babies born with the disease.

Infants born with syphilis were reported in 37 states, with western and southern states being the hardest hit. Louisiana had the highest rate of congenital syphilis of any state. The spike in cases has been described as a "systemic public health failure" and a "crisis" by medical professionals.

David Harvey, the executive director of the National Coalition of STD Directors, is pushing for the Trump administration and Congress to declare the issue a public health emergency. He argues that the field is "starved for resources" and that more needs to be done to ensure pregnant women are tested for syphilis at the correct times and have access to prenatal care.

The surge in syphilis cases comes as diagnoses of other sexually transmitted diseases (STDs) have also reached record highs, with nearly 2.3 million cases of chlamydia, gonorrhea, and syphilis in 2017, according to the CDC's report. This marks the fourth straight year of a sharp increase in STD diagnoses.

The increase in STD diagnoses has been attributed to a decline in condom use and a decrease in STD prevention funding. Medical professionals are urging increased testing, treatment, and resources to address the growing crisis.

The Flint water crisis, which began in April 2014 when the city switched its water supply to the Flint River, continues to pose a threat as lead pipes have not been removed. Michigan Governor Rick Snyder admitted that he has no immediate plans to replace the corroded lead pipes, despite the fact that experts have stated that removing the pipes is the only permanent solution to the lead problem. Instead, the state is focusing on using phosphates in the water to coat the corroded pipes and keep the lead from leaching out. Flint Mayor Karen Weaver, however, has outlined a plan to replace all of the city's lead-contaminated pipes at an estimated cost of $55 million, with priority given to high-risk households. The funding for the project will be a collaboration between the Michigan legislature and US Congress. The project is expected to begin within a month and will be done in two phases, with the first targeting high-risk households. The second phase will ramp up to a "full-scale operation" that will bring in 32 crews to meet the one-year goal. The FBI is currently investigating the contamination of Flint's drinking water, and several lawsuits have been filed in connection with the crisis.

The U.S. News & World Report has released its Best Diets 2019 rankings, evaluating 41 popular diets based on factors such as short-term and long-term weight loss, nutritional completeness, ease of following, and ability to manage or prevent diabetes and heart disease.

Weight Watchers was ranked as the best diet for weight loss, followed closely by Jenny Craig and the Raw Food Diet. However, the DASH (Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension) diet was deemed the best overall diet, with the Mediterranean Diet coming in second.

The DASH diet also topped the list for the best diabetes diet, followed by the Mayo Clinic diet. The Ornish Diet captured the top spot for heart-healthy diets, with TLC (Therapeutic Lifestyle Changes) diet coming in second.

The rankings were determined by a panel of 22 experts in diet and nutrition, diabetes, and heart disease. The report emphasized that no single diet is ideal for everyone, and exercise plays a crucial role in overall health and weight management.

According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, approximately 34% of U.S. adults aged 20 and over are overweight, and an equal number are obese. The report aims to help individuals make informed decisions about their diet choices to achieve their health and fitness goals.

In a study conducted by researchers at Leiden University Medical Center in the Netherlands, it was found that watching horror movies increases levels of clotting agents in viewers' blood. This increase in clotting factors, particularly Factor VIII, is thought to be the body's response to fear, preparing it for potential blood loss during life-threatening situations. The researchers recruited 24 healthy volunteers aged 30 and under, showing them the horror movie "Insidious" and a documentary called "A Year in Champagne" in two groups, with one group watching the movies in reverse order. Blood samples were taken before and after each movie, and the horror movie was found to be scarier than the documentary, resulting in an increase in Factor VIII levels in 57% of participants during the horror movie, compared to only 14% during the documentary. The researchers concluded that frightening (in this case, horror) movies are associated with an increase in blood coagulant factor VIII without actual thrombin formation in young and healthy adults. They advised a "truly relaxing and merry Christmas, without exposure to frightening situations," to prevent venous thrombosis. The study was published in the British Medical Journal.

John Lasseter, co-founder of Pixar and a key figure in Disney's animation studios, has parted ways with the company after months of speculation and allegations of unwanted physical contact with female subordinates. Lasseter's departure follows a "day of listening" held by Disney in February, during which multiple staff members at Pixar and Walt Disney Animation expressed concerns about his increasingly domineering behavior.

The decision to part ways with Lasseter was a complex one, with some arguing that he had been unfairly swept up in the Time's Up movement and that his behavior did not warrant his ouster. However, retaining Lasseter would have divided employees, particularly women, who felt uncomfortable with his return. A #LoseLasseter campaign had appeared on Twitter, and a petition on Change.org demanding his ouster had attracted 68 signatures.

Pixar has been criticized as a boy's club, with only one of its 20 feature films having a credited female director. Lasseter's supporters have pointed out that he hired Jennifer Lee as a director of Frozen, which was praised for its departure from Disney's romantic "princess" formula.

Lasseter will serve in a consulting role at Disney throughout the end of the year, after which time he'll look for something new. Insiders expect Frozen director Jennifer Lee to be promoted at Walt Disney Animation, and Pete Docter, director of films Up and Monsters, Inc., to take on greater responsibilities at Pixar.

The departure of Lasseter comes amidst a broader movement in the entertainment industry to address and address sexual misconduct. Women in Animation President Marge Dean said the world changed last fall because courageous women spoke up, and that the safety of all employees has become a priority for the industry. The departure of Lasseter is expected to have a significant impact on the future of Pixar and Disney's animation studios.

U.S. stocks experienced a volatile session on January 20, 2016, with the S&P 500 closing lower but above session lows. The market saw a recovery in biotech stocks and small-caps, but the late-day rally lost momentum. The Dow Jones Industrial Average closed about 250 points lower, with IBM contributing the most to declines, while UnitedHealth contributed the most to gains. The S&P 500 ended at its lowest level since April 2014, and the major U.S. averages are down more than 9% for the year so far. The Nasdaq composite closed at its lowest since October 2014, and the iShares Nasdaq Biotechnology ETF (IBB) reversed a decline of more than 3% to end up 2.75%. Notable stocks like Netflix and Apple also showed a reversal in their intraday trade. The heavy trading volume indicated investor uncertainty, with about 11 stocks declining for every four advancers on the New York Stock Exchange. The number of new 52-week lows on the New York Stock Exchange and Nasdaq were the most on a single day since November 2008.

Veteran investor Mark D. Cook, who had pointed out red flags a year ago, feels vindicated as stock prices confirmed what he saw in 2014: We’re in a bear market and about to go over the cliff. Cook believes the oil and gas situation and China's economic problems are the main issues causing the bear market. He also pointed out that every rally in a bear market has no traction and that the NYSE Tick is registering no institutional activity on the buy side.

Investors are currently in the denial stage of a bear market, according to Cook, with many still buying the dips, which does not work in a bear market. As the market continues to struggle, investors will likely progress through stages of high anxiety, fear, and eventually panic, leading to a significant sell-off.

Michael James Rogan, a 42-year-old veteran of the United States Marine Corps, passed away on April 17, 2015, following an auto accident in Marshfield, Wisconsin. The accident occurred while he was driving his pregnant wife and seven children to the hospital for the birth of their eighth child. Despite the tragic loss of Michael, his wife and children survived with minor injuries.

Michael was born in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, and owned and operated Arnie's Farm Care for the past eight years, assisting organic farmers across the state. He was a member of St. Mary's Oratory, the church choir, and The Holy Name Society. He was a loving husband, father, and friend, and his faith was deeply important to him.

Michael is survived by his wife, Niki, and their children, Anne, Jon, Claire, Ben, Luke, Jacob, Gemma, and Blaise. He is also survived by his parents, Ron and Sue Bornbach, a sister, Beth Bornbach and her daughter, Johanna, and brothers, Joseph and Gabriel Bornbach. He was predeceased by his grandparents, John and Sylvia Rogan, an aunt, Sharon Nikolai, uncles, Charles Rogan and John Rogan, Jr., a cousin, Michele LaPorte, and his father-in-law, Arnold Richardson.

A Mass of Christian Burial will be held at 10:00 am on Saturday, April 25, 2015, at St. Mary's Roman Catholic Oratory, Wausau, with Canon Aaron Huberfeld, Rector, officiating. Burial will take place in St. Mary's Catholic Cemetery in Marathon, Wisconsin, where military rites will be conducted by the Veterans of Foreign Wars Post 6352 of Stratford. The visitation will be held on Friday from 4:00 pm until 8:00 pm at Sauter / Rembs Funeral Home, Stratford, and on Saturday from 9:00 am until service time at St. Mary's Oratory, Wausau.

A memorial will be established for the support of Michael's widow and children. Condolences may be sent online to www.rembsfh.com. Previous events include visitations and services at Sauter/Rembs Funeral Home in Stratford and St. Mary's Oratory in Wausau.

Michael's family and friends have set up a fundraiser on gofundme.com to help with funeral and medical expenses, as well as to create a safety net for the family's future welfare. Donations will be transferred directly to Niki Rogan. If you have any questions about the family, this campaign, or to make donations by mail, please reach out to roganfund@gmail.com.

The accident has received national coverage, with similar stories emerging about another father named Michael Draper from Texas who died in a traffic accident just two days before Michael Rogan. There has been some confusion between the two fundraisers, but Michael Draper's case was posted before ours, and it is legitimate, and you are encouraged to support it.

Jared Fogle, currently serving a 15-year sentence for child pornography and sex crimes, is attempting to overturn his plea deal by using the case of Larry Nassar, the disgraced Team USA doctor, as a comparison. In San Francisco, a treasure trove of 1,427 rare gold coins from the Gold Rush era, dating from 1847 to 1894, went on sale, with one coin selling for $15,000. The coins, valued at $11 million, were discovered by a California couple last year on their rural property. The couple, who wish to remain anonymous, found the coins in eight cans buried under a tree. Most of the coins were auctioned at the Old San Francisco Mint, with the remaining coins going on sale on Amazon.com and Kagins.com. The coins are extremely rare due to their pre-1870s origin and their mint condition. The collection includes four $5 gold pieces, fifty $10 gold pieces, and 1,373 $20 double eagles. Meanwhile, the United Nations Security Council has imposed new sanctions on North Korea for its continued intercontinental ballistic missile testing and violations of UN resolutions. The sanctions target North Korea's primary exports, including coal, iron, iron ore, lead, lead ore, and seafood, as well as banks and joint ventures with foreign companies. The sanctions are expected to reduce North Korea's annual export revenue by over a third, amounting to $3 billion.

North Korea's state-run newspaper Rodong Sinmun warned of self-destruction if the United States continues its "hostile policy" against Pyongyang. President Trump, vacationing in New Jersey, approved of the Security Council's resolution, praising China and Russia for joining the United States to condemn and crack down on North Korea's moneymaking ventures.

The resolution also bans countries from hiring additional North Korean workers, a move designed to shut off another source of hard currency for the Pyongyang regime. Nine people and four business entities, including a major North Korean bank, were placed on a UN blacklist, slapping all with asset freezes or travel bans. However, China opposed more severe restrictions that might have been urged by Washington, and North Korea is still allowed to receive oil.

Differences remain between the US and China, with the US taking prudent defensive measures to protect itself and its allies from the threat posed by North Korea, while China urges parties to halt the process of deploying the Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) anti-missile system in South Korea.

Experts on North Korea debate the impact of the sanctions, with some believing that the Kim regime will not respond to punitive measures and will continue to improve its nuclear and missile capability. Others believe that the sanctions could cause significant damage to the foreign currency income for North Korean elites and could potentially force Kim Jong Un to send a special envoy to China to make a deal.

The study published in Molecular Psychiatry suggests that there may be a genetic link between the risk of developing schizophrenia and the likelihood of using cannabis. Researchers studied over 1,000 cannabis users and found that those with a higher genetic risk for schizophrenia were more likely to use cannabis and use it in greater quantities. This finding challenges the notion that cannabis use increases the risk of schizophrenia and suggests that the association may be due to shared genes. The study highlights the complex relationship between cannabis use and schizophrenia and emphasizes the need for further research to understand the causal relationship between the two. The study's findings have important implications for the ongoing debate about the legalization of cannabis and its potential impact on mental health.

The Senate passed a legislation on Thursday that allows states to withhold federal funds from Planned Parenthood and other healthcare providers that perform abortions. The bill was passed with a tie-breaking vote from Vice President Mike Pence, who cast his first tie-breaking vote since assuming office. The legislation was opposed by Democrats who condemned it as an attack on women's health. The bill was a priority for anti-abortion groups and was a small but significant victory for them. The House had already approved the bill in February. The federal family planning program, created in 1970, serves 4 million clients at nearly 4,000 clinics and has a $286 million federal budget this year. Most of the money is for providing services like contraceptives, family planning counseling, breast and cervical cancer screening, and sexually transmitted disease prevention. The bill dismisses an Obama-era rule banning states from denying federal funds to such organizations. The Congressional Review Act was used to undo the regulation enacted by former President Barack Obama. The bill now goes to President Trump for his signature.

A new study published in the journal Heart suggests that regular consumption of chocolate may help prevent the development of atrial fibrillation, a type of irregular heartbeat. The study, conducted in Denmark, found that adults who ate chocolate at least once a month had rates of atrial fibrillation that were 10 to 20 percent lower than those who ate chocolate less than once a month. The strongest effects were seen in men and women who ate 1 ounce of chocolate, two to six times per week. The study found that the compounds in chocolate, particularly flavonoids, may play a role in preventing atrial fibrillation due to their anti-inflammatory and antioxidant properties. However, the study does not prove a cause-and-effect relationship between eating chocolate and a lowered risk of atrial fibrillation. The findings suggest that compared to other snack choices, a moderate intake of chocolate may be a heart-healthy snack, but people should choose chocolate with a higher cocoa content for the most health benefits. The study has limitations, including the fact that the participants were generally healthier and had lower rates of high blood pressure and diabetes than non-chocolate eaters, and the fact that people in Denmark are more similar to each other in race and ethnicity than people in other countries. The study's findings are interesting and warrant further consideration, according to an accompanying editorial.

In the late 20th and early 21st century, Brazil made significant strides in reducing deforestation and safeguarding the Amazon, making it a world leader in environmental conservation. However, the gains made over the years are now at risk due to the proposed environmental policies of far-right candidate Jair Bolsonaro, who is likely to become Brazil’s president in the upcoming runoff election on 28 October.

Bolsonaro has pledged to shut down Brazil’s environmental ministry, relax environmental law enforcement and licensing, open indigenous reserves to mining, ban international environmental NGOs such as Greenpeace and WWF from the country, and back out of the Paris climate accord. A study by the authors estimates that Brazilian deforestation and carbon emissions under Bolsonaro’s policies would cause unprecedented Amazon forest loss, and contribute to destabilizing the global climate.

Between 2005 and 2012, Brazil's annual deforestation rates decreased at a breathtaking speed, dropping to a historical low of 4,575 square kilometers (1,766 square miles) in 2012, a fall of more than 83 percent in just eight years. Building on these successes, the Brazilian government pledged an ambitious reduction of its greenhouse gas emissions – 37 percent by 2025, and 43 percent by 2030, below 2005 levels – a promise made at the 21st Conference of the Parties (COP21) in Paris in December, 2015.

The causes behind the sudden decrease in deforestation rates in the Brazilian Amazon include the expansion of protected areas and indigenous lands, better enforcement of existing environmental legislation, interventions in supply chains and credit restrictions, and fines and embargoes of illegal deforesters.

However, today, in the midst of an unprecedented economic crisis and political unrest, environmental protections are in danger of being rolled back. The annual deforestation rate in the world’s largest rainforest has been steadily growing since 2012. If environmental protections are removed by Brazil’s next president, the average annual loss of primary forest in the Amazon will quickly rise to 25,600 square kilometers (9,884 square miles) per year, a figure similar to the deforestation rates measured at the beginning of the 2000s and an increase of 268 percent from 2017. Within a decade, the scale of deforestation would be equivalent to the area of the UK or the US state of Oregon.

Carbon emissions would rise as deforestation increases. Under Bolsonaro’s proposed policies, from 2021 to 2030, accumulated emissions from clear cutting Amazon forest would attain 13.12 gigatons of carbon dioxide equivalent (GtCO2e), or an average of 1.31 GtCO2e per year, making it all but impossible for Brazil to fulfill its international commitments made in Paris. This annual carbon release corresponds to 3 percent of the current global emissions. Moreover, according to the latest literature 13.12 GtCO2e could represent up to 20 percent of the “free” carbon budget remaining to achieve the 1.5 Celsius IPCC goal.

In this election, and in the coming years, political will is needed to ensure that the Amazon forest and the ecosystem services it provides are conserved. The loss of biodiversity and climate regulation that could result from a dramatic change in policies would be a tipping point for both biodiversity and climate change, with global consequences.

George W. Bush, the 43rd President of the United States, recently appeared on The Ellen DeGeneres Show to discuss his new art book, "Portraits of Courage: A Commander in Chief’s Tribute to America’s Warriors." During the interview, Bush humorously addressed a viral moment from Donald Trump's inauguration when he struggled with a poncho. Bush expressed his willingness to collaborate with the Obamas on causes related to military personnel, military families, and veterans.

In a private moment after the inauguration, Bush was overheard saying, "That was some weird shit." Regarding the inauguration, Bush gave the same reason for attending as the Clintons – to honor the peaceful transfer of power. The book "The Secret Rescue" by Cate Lineberry tells the thrilling and moving story of Harold Hayes, an American hero who was part of a group of medics and nurses who crash-landed in Nazi-occupied Albania in 1943. Hayes was only 21 years old at the time. The group traversed more than 600 miles of brutal terrain, dodged German troops, faced desperate hunger and debilitating illnesses, survived blizzards, and were caught in crossfire. They were forbidden by the military from discussing the details of their experiences even after the war was over due to concerns for the safety of those who helped them. Now, almost 70 years later, Hayes, the only living member of the group, talks about his experiences with Lineberry. Hayes was a medic in the Army Air Forces serving in Catania, Sicily, when the plane he was on crash-landed in Nazi-occupied Albania in November 1943. The plane was carrying 30 people, including 13 nurses and 13 medics, and was bound for Bari, Italy, to evacuate wounded troops. The plane became lost in a storm and was attacked by German fighters and antiaircraft guns. The group was helped by Albanian partisans and villagers, who shared food and shelter with them. They eventually made it to the coast and were rescued by the British. Hayes's greatest concern while trapped behind enemy lines was that the American military and his family did not know where he was. The group got along well for the most part, but there were a few people who rubbed each other the wrong way. After the war, Hayes returned to civilian life and became an aeronautical engineer for North American Aviation. He married and had two daughters. Hayes is the last conduit for the story of the group's adventure, which has been related in several books, including Lineberry's "The Secret Rescue."

The situation in Eastern Ghouta, a rebel-held enclave near Damascus, has escalated into a humanitarian crisis, with hundreds of civilians killed in two days of "hysterical violence" by forces loyal to Syria's Bashar al-Assad. The area, which is home to 400,000 civilians, has been under siege for years and has been subjected to devastating chemical attacks. Amnesty International has accused the regime of committing flagrant war crimes on an epic scale, and hospitals in the region have been repeatedly bombed. The UN has expressed outrage at the casualties among Syrian children and has demanded an end to the targeting of civilians. The Syrian civil defense, a search and rescue organization, reported 61 deaths on Tuesday alone, while the Syrian Observatory for Human Rights reported 194 deaths in the last 48 hours. The escalating violence in Eastern Ghouta has included the use of notorious barrel bombs, which are seen as a war crime by human rights watchdogs. The regime has also used fighter jets and artillery bombardment, on top of the punishing siege. The first aid convoy to the region in months arrived a week ago but did not do much to alleviate the suffering. The latest violence in Eastern Ghouta, where 1,300 people died in 2013 after the Assad regime deployed sarin gas, has been described as a massacre. The situation is expected to worsen as forces loyal to Assad's regime and their Russian and Iranian backers seek an outright military victory instead of a negotiated political settlement.

On August 29, 2015, four shooting incidents occurred along Interstate 10 in Phoenix, Arizona, over a three-day span. The first two incidents happened on Saturday morning between 11:00 a.m. and 11:10 a.m. at 19th Avenue and 59th Avenue. The third shooting occurred around 10:15 p.m. on I-10 at 16th Street. A fourth shooting was reported at 4:25 a.m. on Monday on I-10, also near 19th Avenue.

Only one person was reported to have been injured, a 13-year-old girl who sustained a non-life-threatening cut to her right ear when a bullet pierced the windshield of the SUV she was in. The other bullets hit the sides of the vehicles and a headlight.

Authorities are investigating whether the same person is responsible for all four shootings. They are urging anyone with information to contact the Arizona Department of Public Safety and are asking for the public's help to report any suspicious behavior. The incidents occurred within an 8-mile stretch of the freeway, which runs through central Phoenix.

The Arizona Department of Public Safety is a state-level law enforcement agency whose mission is to protect human life and property by enforcing state laws, deterring criminal activity, and providing vital support to the State of Arizona and its citizens. The department is working non-stop to identify the shooter and is asking for the public's help in solving the case.

In a new study led by University College London PhD student Matthew Dodd, evidence of microscopic artwork etched into ancient rocks from Quebec's Nuvvuagittuq belt is suggested to be the oldest direct evidence of life on Earth. The rocks, which date back to at least 3.77 billion years, contain tiny tubes and filaments filled with hematite, an iron oxide mineral, that resemble iron-oxidizing bacteria found at hydrothermal vents today. The researchers also found carbon-rich material and minerals within blobs, which they believe support a biological origin.

The study is particularly interesting because it involves hydrothermal vent environments, which have been proposed as a logical place where life on Earth could have had its origins. If the findings are confirmed, it would suggest that there were at least two types of microorganisms living in different parts of the ocean by 3.7 billion years ago. The discovery also makes hydrothermal vents on other worlds more promising targets in the search for life beyond Earth.

However, the study is not without controversy, as some experts have called the patterns in the rocks "dubiofossils" and have expressed skepticism about the new findings. The researchers acknowledge that more research is needed to confirm their findings and to better understand the geology of the area. The study was published in Nature.

The arrest of Joseph James DeAngelo, a suspect in the Golden State Killer case, was made possible through the use of a genealogy website called GEDmatch. The site, which allows users to voluntarily share their genetic profiles for free, was instrumental in identifying a "distant relative" early this year, leading authorities to DeAngelo. The case sheds light on the potential use of genetic information in criminal investigations, as even distant relatives' data may be shared when one of them submits their DNA to a public site.

The investigation, which began six years ago, used genetic profiles based on DNA from crime scenes linked to the serial killer and compared it to information from genealogical websites. The hits on DeAngelo came from third and fourth cousins, and the tree that eventually linked to the Golden State Killer was so large, it contained about 1,000 people.

The use of genealogy websites in criminal investigations raises concerns about genetic privacy, as companies may be required to surrender genetic data if confronted with a search warrant. UC Berkeley's Andrea Roth expressed concern that the government may be looking at a lot of genetic information that most people want to keep private.

The East Area Rapist/Golden State Killer case demonstrates the promise and potential peril of DNA as a law enforcement tool. While it is a wonderful thing that police were able to find the suspect, there is a concern that the government may use genetic information for purposes beyond tracking down serial killers without accountability or further safeguards.

The Sacramento County District Attorney's Office confirmed that investigators tracked down DeAngelo using genealogical websites that contained genetic information from a relative. The investigation was conducted over a long period of time as officials in Sacramento County explored online family trees that appeared to match DNA samples from the East Area Rapist's crimes. The process finally came to fruition last Thursday, when the investigation focused on the possibility that DeAngelo might be a suspect. Sacramento County Sheriff Scott Jones' investigators set up surveillance on DeAngelo in his quiet Citrus Heights neighborhood and obtained his DNA from something he discarded. The crime lab began testing the material and Schubert received a call last Friday night confirming that the DeAngelo DNA matched that found at decades-old murder scenes in Ventura and Orange counties. DeAngelo was arrested outside his home Tuesday afternoon and booked into the county jail on two charges of murder in the February 1978 slayings of Katie and Brian Maggiore in Rancho Cordova. DeAngelo is expected to face charges in 12 homicide cases in Sacramento, Orange, Santa Barbara, and Ventura counties stemming from a rape and slaying spree that authorities say stretched from 1974 through May 1986.

The Defense Secretary Ash Carter revealed that only 60 Syrian rebels have been trained and vetted as part of a $500 million program aimed at equipping moderate Syrian rebels to fight against the Islamic State (ISIL). This number falls significantly short of the initial goal of training 5,400 fighters in the first year. The news has sparked criticism from Republicans who argue that President Obama's strategy for defeating ISIL is not effective. Democrats, on the other hand, are attempting to downplay the issue, citing reasons for the low number of recruits.

During a Senate hearing, Senator Bill Nelson (D-Fla.) pointed out that Carter's statement had caused a stir on cable news. Carter acknowledged causing a "firestorm" but emphasized that Congress deserved to know the current status of the program.

The low number of recruits can be attributed to stringent vetting standards, the U.S. requirement that rebels fight only ISIL and not Syrian President Bashar Assad, and the lack of a U.S. commitment to defend these troops from Assad's advanced weapons.

Despite the challenges, Pentagon officials remain optimistic about increasing the throughput at the four sites created for the train-and-equip program. Carter stated that about 7,000 volunteers are being screened, and as training progresses, they are learning more about the opposition groups and building important relationships.

However, many senators from both parties have raised questions about the viability of the train-and-equip program, expressing concerns about finding moderate rebels willing to take on ISIL. The "ISIL-first" strategy, which requires Syrian volunteers to agree only to fight ISIL and not the Assad regime, has been a significant factor in winnowing out potential recruits.

Senator John McCain (R-Ariz.) criticized the program, stating that he is doubtful they can achieve their goal of training a few thousand Syrian fighters this year. He also expressed concerns about the lack of solid commitments from the U.S. to the recruits, stating that people won't sign up to risk their lives unless they're certain the U.S. will provide support.

In response, Senator Jack Reed (D-R.I.), the panel's ranking member, stated that the pipeline is about 7,000 and that increased numbers will be seen as they reach a critical mass. However, he acknowledged that it will take time.

The low number of trained Syrian rebels has raised doubts about the effectiveness of President Obama's strategy for defeating ISIL and has sparked heated debates in Congress.

The document discusses the current political standoff in the United States over the automatic budget cuts, known as sequestration. The House of Representatives, led by the Republican party, is embracing the sequester, which will result in a 2.5% cut in all federal spending without any tax increases. President Obama, on the other hand, is advocating for tax increases and alternative spending cuts to replace the automatic ones.

In the midst of this, the House passed H.R. 667, a bill to rename NASA's Dryden Flight Research Center as the Neil A. Armstrong Flight Research Center. The bill, sponsored by Majority Whip Kevin McCarthy, was a deliberate move by House Republicans to honor Armstrong, the first man to walk on the moon. The bill passed without opposition in the last Congress but was not taken up by the Senate.

The document also highlights the lack of productivity in the House of Representatives, with lawmakers taking frequent recesses and spending a significant amount of time on ceremonial bills and time-wasting techniques. The House is scheduled to be out of session on the day the sequester is set to take effect and is planning another recess at the end of March, when the federal government is due to shut down for lack of funding.

The document concludes with a commentary by Dana Milbank, who expresses his skepticism towards the political panic over sequestration, comparing it to past disasters such as Vietnam, Watergate, and Disco. Milbank argues that the sequester was designed to be so horrible that both parties would recoil from it, but Congressional salaries are not affected by the cuts, leading to skepticism about the sincerity of the political standoff.

Jakiw Palij, a 95-year-old former guard at a Nazi labor camp in Poland, has been deported from the United States to Germany after being arrested by U.S. immigration authorities. Palij served at the Trawniki Labor Camp, where approximately 6,000 Jewish men, women, and children were killed in one of the single largest massacres of the Holocaust on November 3, 1943.

The United States had been trying to deport Palij since a 2004 deportation order, but no European country agreed to take him until Germany agreed to do so following talks with top members of Chancellor Angela Merkel’s government. Palij was taken to a home for the elderly in Ahlen, Germany.

Born in what is now Ukraine, Palij emigrated to the United States in 1949 and became a U.S. citizen eight years later. However, he concealed his Nazi service and involvement in human rights abuses, claiming he spent World War Two working on a farm and in a factory. In 2001, Palij admitted to the Department of Justice that he had trained at the Nazi SS Training Camp in Trawniki in 1943.

A federal judge revoked Palij's U.S. citizenship in 2003 and ordered him to be deported in 2004. However, no European country would accept him due to his age and questions over his health and possible lack of proof. It is unclear whether German authorities will attempt to prosecute Palij, as being a member of a criminal organization like the SS is not enough to be prosecuted in Germany.

The U.S. Ambassador to Germany, Richard Grenell, said the deportation was a result of a concerted effort by U.S. President Donald Trump. Germany has a mixed record on convicting Nazi war criminals, with critics saying it let many high-ranking Nazis and SS members escape justice while putting small cogs in the Nazi death machine on trial decades later.

Germany's Central Office for the Investigation of Nazi Crimes is still investigating individuals, including Palij, after the 2011 conviction of Sobibor death camp guard John Demjanjuk gave it a new impetus. It was the first time involvement in a camp was sufficient to be found culpable even without proof of a specific crime.

Before arriving in the United States, Palij and two other men worked as guards in their unit, which was part of the Streibel Battalion. All three guarded forced laborers who made uniforms and brushes. Their unit also conducted bloody reprisal campaigns against Polish partisans in the region around the town of Lublin, but it is unclear whether the men took part in such operations.

Palij's citizenship was revoked in 2003 after the Justice Department realized he had lied on his application. It was not until the early 1990s, after the fall of the Berlin Wall, that U.S. law-enforcement authorities figured out who Palij and the two other men were after finding a cache of Nazi records in Czechoslovakia. The Department of Justice accused all three of serving in the SS in Trawniki, and filed charges to take away their American passports and order them deported. All told, the Justice Department successfully charged and denaturalized 16 former SS members who served at Trawniki.

The article discusses the potential easing of water conservation rules in California, which have been in place due to the ongoing drought. The state water officials are considering a proposal that would allow local communities to decide their water usage regulations based on their anticipated water supply and demand for the next three years.

This proposal, if approved, would empower local districts to set their conservation targets, with some potentially imposing strict water-saving measures while others may lift existing mandates. The Irvine Ranch Water District in Orange County has spearheaded this regional approach, with confidence that districts across the state will carefully assess their supply and demand ratio.

California has been in a five-year-long drought, but this new approach is being considered as El Nino storms have delivered near-average rain and snowfall in Northern California, filling key reservoirs. However, Southern California remains deeply affected by the drought, and its future remains uncertain.

The proposed regulation would also make permanent bans on wasting water, such as hosing down sidewalks or washing cars without a shut-off nozzle. Despite these changes, Max Gomberg, a senior climate scientist for the state water board, believes that Californians will continue their water-saving habits, having demonstrated their commitment during the drought.

The article also includes brief mentions of unrelated topics, such as the opening of the Golden 1 Center, turkeys going wild in Davis, efforts to save the McClatchy High School newspaper, tips for navigating traffic to the Golden 1 Center, finding drinks in downtown Sacramento, the food options at the Golden 1 Center, using light rail for trips to the center, and development around the Golden 1 Center.

In this article, Ben Friberg, a Tennessee musician, successfully completed a historic 110-mile paddleboard journey across the Florida Straits from Cuba to Key West, Florida, on August 2, 2013. The journey took 28 hours, and Friberg's father watched from a support boat. Upon arrival, Friberg was dehydrated and exhausted but otherwise in good health. Fribergs's goal was to promote peace and understanding between Cuba and the United States and to encourage a healthy lifestyle.

During the trip, Friberg stood on his 14-foot-long board for most of the journey, only sitting for quick snacks. The support boat crew included a medic and a navigator. Friberg was dressed appropriately for the trip, with a long-billed cap, long-sleeved shirt, open-fingered gloves, and shorts cut off below the knee. Special socks shielded his feet.

Last year, Friberg broke the record for the longest distance stand-up paddleboard journey in 24 hours, traveling 238 miles on Canada's Yukon River. Friberg is believed to be the first person to cross the entire Straits on a paddleboard.

In 1992, Cuban-born doctor Ernesto Barral completed the journey on a windsurfing board in 19 hours, using the stars at night for navigation. In 2011, Miami lifeguard Cynthia Aguilar made the crossing by paddleboard from 14 miles off Cuba's coast. She was unable to set off from dry land because she did not have a Cuban government visa. Unlike Friberg, Aguilar completed the crossing on her knees, using her hands to paddle.

Several swimmers have attempted the journey, but only Australian Susan Maroney has succeeded, making the crossing in 1997 with the help of a shark cage.

In a separate story, Jerry Hall, a Tennessee scuba diver, set a new world record for the longest freshwater dive of six days, one hour, and 42 minutes. Hall spent six days submerged in South Holston Lake in Tennessee's northeast corner. The previous record of five days was also set by Hall. The dive was used as a fundraiser for the children's charity of Bristol Motor Speedway. Hall lost about 30 pounds during the dive due to lack of food and was on only liquids during the dive. Asked to describe Hall as he emerged, his trainer replied, "He's very, very cold, very wrinkled, and gray."

In the aftermath of former Senator John Kerry's resignation, Massachusetts Republican Party faces a challenge in finding a suitable candidate for the special Senate election. Tagg Romney, a wealthy private equity firm founder, was a visible surrogate for his father's presidential campaign.
