In April 2012, Anthony Hensley, a 37-year-old father of two from Villa Park, drowned in a retention pond at the Bay Colony condominium complex in Maine Township, Illinois. The cause of his death was an attack by a swan that had been nesting at the complex. The swan, which was aggressive, continued to lunge at Hensley as he attempted to swim to shore.

Hensley was a frequent visitor at the complex, where he was responsible for tending to the mute swans that had been brought in to control the geese population. He often brought his kayak and sometimes his dog to feed and care for the birds.

On Tuesday, Hensley's widow filed a wrongful death lawsuit in Cook County Circuit Court against the property management companies that owned and operated the complex. The lawsuit contends that the companies' negligence caused Hensley's death, as they should have known that the swans are territorial and have a dangerous propensity to attack. The companies are being sued for at least $50,000 in damages.

The Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) opened an investigation into Hensley's death and found no violations on the part of the company he worked for, Knox Swan and Dog. The property management companies were not part of the probe.

The lawsuit also states that the companies kept a pair of mute swans at the complex and should be held liable for "knowingly keeping dangerous animals on the premises." Hensley did nothing to provoke the swans prior to the attack.

Dive crews had to search the 50-foot-deep pond to locate Hensley, who was pronounced dead at Advocate Lutheran General Hospital in Park Ridge.

The case has brought attention to the issue of geese control and the use of swans as a deterrent. If you have a geese problem, there are several options for keeping them away, including setting up a swan decoy, making the water unattractive, using noise to scare them away, and using a goose and bird repellent spray. It is important to take action if geese are causing problems on your property.

In a dramatic rescue, DeKalb County firefighter Robert Sutton caught a baby tossed from a burning apartment building in Georgia. The father, trapped by the fire, threw his child from the second floor to save him from the smoke-filled apartment. Sutton, a 10-year veteran, was among the first firefighters to arrive at the scene. The family escaped without injuries. Sutton, who has two children of his own, was humble about the incident, deflecting credit to being in the right place at the right time. The video of the rescue was captured by a contracted plumber. Meanwhile, the Internet Archive is working on a project to fix broken links on the web by archiving pages as they are created and preserving pages that they refer to. This project aims to maintain the original intentions of page authors by replacing broken links with archived versions or providing companion links.

Researchers at the Scripps Research Institute in Florida have developed a potential blood test for Alzheimer's disease using antibodies, immune system proteins that can help detect foreign invaders. The study, published in the journal Cell, found that the test accurately identified Alzheimer's in six patients, and the researchers believe it could be extended to other diseases, including cancer. The test uses synthetic molecules called peptoids as antigen surrogates to screen for antibodies specific to Alzheimer's disease. The team has licensed the technology to Miami-based OPKO Health Inc, which plans to develop diagnostic kits within six to seven months. While the test still needs to be confirmed in larger numbers of patients, it could provide a simpler and less invasive method of diagnosing Alzheimer's and potentially other diseases. The true benefits of such a test for Alzheimer's patients would arise when effective treatments against the disease are developed.

On August 31, 2014, tensions escalated in Hong Kong as pro-democracy activists vowed to bring the city's financial hub to a standstill following China's parliament's rejection of their demands for a free election in 2017. The Standing Committee of the National People's Congress (NPC) endorsed a framework that allows only two or three candidates to run in the 2017 leadership vote, with all candidates needing majority backing from a nominating committee likely to be stacked with Beijing loyalists. This decision makes it almost impossible for opposition democrats to get on the ballot.

In response, hundreds of "Occupy Central" activists, who demand Beijing allow a real, free election, prepared to stage a small protest to formally launch a campaign of civil disobedience that will climax with a blockade at some time of the city's important Central business district. Benny Tai, a law professor and one of Occupy Central's main leaders, described it as the "darkest day in the history of Hong Kong's democratic development."

Meanwhile, in Macau, another special administrative region, leader and sole candidate Fernando Chui was re-elected uncontested by a select panel of 400 largely pro-China loyalists. This election followed a seven-day "civil referendum" in which 95% of 8,688 residents voted in favor of universal suffrage for the 2019 election. However, there were complaints of rights violations after police arrested several organizers of the referendum for allegedly breaching personal data laws.

The NPC's decision in Hong Kong has been met with cautious responses from the United States, which supports Hong Kong’s "traditions and Basic Law protections of internationally recognized freedoms, including the freedom of peaceful assembly and freedom of expression." The official also said "the legitimacy of the chief executive will be greatly enhanced if "the election provides the people of Hong Kong a genuine choice of candidates representative of the voters’ will."

Senior Chinese officials have repeatedly warned activists against their "illegal" protests, and say they won't back down. Some key members of the pro-democracy movement, including media magnate Jimmy Lai, have also come under pressure in the run-up to the Chinese parliamentary decision. China has also repeatedly warned against foreign interference, saying it will not tolerate the use of Hong Kong "as a bridgehead to subvert and infiltrate the mainland."

In Macau, Chui acknowledged shortfalls in his first term and promised to focus on economic diversification away from the gambling sector. Activists, however, continue to call for political reform. The Occupy Central movement in Hong Kong has not yet won broad support among Hong Kong's middle class, who are concerned about antagonizing China and disruptions to business. Any strong measures by China or the Hong Kong police could change that.

In the besieged Damascus suburb of Dariya, Syria, hundreds of people have been killed in what appears to be the largest mass killing since the 17-month conflict began. According to opposition and pro-government accounts, at least 320 people have been killed in Dariya since the military launched an assault five days ago. The Syrian Observatory for Human Rights, a British-based group opposed to President Bashar Assad, reported that the death toll could be as high as 334.

Opposition activists claim that many victims were executed after pro-government forces entered the town, while others were killed in shelling or shot by snipers. In one grisly discovery, more than 120 bodies were found in one basement, activists said. The government has accused the opposition of exaggerating death tolls and inventing massacres.

The numbers could not be independently confirmed as the United Nations monitoring mission in Syria has ended. The government places severe restrictions on media coverage. Opposition advocates blame government troops and plainclothes militiamen for the killings, while the government blames "terrorists," its usual term for armed rebels.

The violence in Dariya contributed to a death toll of over 400 throughout Syria on Saturday, according to the Local Coordination Committees, an opposition umbrella coalition. It appears to be the largest single-day death toll reported to date in the conflict. The government onslaught against Dariya began last week when regime forces began shelling from tanks, helicopters, and fighter jets.

The opposition says many victims in Dariya were executed after pro-government forces entered the town on Friday. The government has not commented on the allegations. The conflict in Syria has resulted in at least 17,000 deaths, mostly civilians, according to United Nations figures. The opposition puts the death toll at over 20,000. Verifying casualty counts in Syria has become more difficult with the departure of United Nations monitors.

The Belgian royal family will start paying taxes for the first time, following a government decision to reform the system of royal allowances. This change is in response to criticism over Queen Fabiola's plan to avoid paying tax on an estate in Spain. Under the new system, only the monarch, the heir, their spouse, and the widow or widower of a deceased monarch will continue to receive money from the state. The royal family will also lose their exemptions from paying income and value-added tax. The reform will significantly reduce Queen Fabiola's annual allowance, while the crown prince's siblings will continue to receive allowances. The king, who turns 79 on Thursday, will remain exempt due to constitutional restrictions. This change brings Belgium's royal system closer to those in countries like the Netherlands and Britain, where royal households also pay taxes.

A four-foot American alligator was discovered in Lake Michigan on October 8, 2018, by a kayaker fishing for salmon off Waukegan Harbor. The kayaker, David Castaneda, initially thought it was a dead salmon but upon closer inspection, he saw an alligator head. The animal was found with its mouth taped shut and appeared to be in poor health due to the cold water temperatures in Lake Michigan.

Waukegan's Animal Control responded to the call and retrieved the alligator, which was then transferred to the Lake Forest Wildlife Discovery Center. Rob Carmichael, curator for the Wildlife Discovery Center, stated that the alligator was on borrowed time and would be lucky to live another couple of weeks due to the dropping temperatures in the lake.

An investigation into the abandonment of the alligator, which is a crime, will be conducted by the city. The abandoning of exotic animals has decreased in recent years due to stricter state regulations around the ownership of endangered or threatened animals.

This is not the first time an exotic animal has been discovered in the area. In September 2012, a nearly 14-foot Burmese python was found near Waukegan Harbor, and in August 2010, an alligator was discovered in the Chicago River under the Belmont Avenue bridge.

Carmichael stated that the system for regulating the ownership of exotic animals seems to be working, as there have been fewer cases like this in the last five years. Dangerous animals like lions, bears, or coyotes are illegal to own under the state's Dangerous Animals Act.

The Nigerian military has announced the release of a second schoolgirl, Serah Luka, who was kidnapped by Boko Haram from the town of Chibok in 2014. The announcement comes two days after Amina Ali Darsha Nkeki, another Chibok girl, was found by a vigilante group. Luka was found along with 96 other women and children and 35 Boko Haram fighters were killed during the operation. If confirmed, Luka would be the second Chibok girl to escape from a Boko Haram camp in the Sambisa forest in the past two days. Amina Ali Darsha Nkeki met with President Muhammadu Buhari on Thursday, after being found by the vigilante group on Tuesday. She had been found on the edge of a Boko Haram stronghold after fleeing during an attack on the militants' camp. The president pledged to continue the search for the remaining Chibok girls, who number more than 200, and to fund Nkeki's education. Nkeki's brother confirmed that the president had pledged to look after Nkeki and her family. In what commentators called a "desperate bid to claim credit" for the escape of the first of the Chibok girls since the messy aftermath of the 2014 abductions, the Nigerian army initially claimed to have rescued a girl identified as Falmata Mbalala, but later admitted that her name was actually Amina Ali and that its troops had rescued her in conjunction with Civilian JTF, the local vigilante force. The army has made several mistakes in its statements about the Chibok girls, including using the wrong name and claiming to have freed more than 100 of them before later backtracking. In all, 218 girls remain missing since they were seized from Chibok secondary school in Borno state, north-eastern Nigeria, in April 2014.

The story revolves around the heartbreaking ordeal of Rosita Cage-Toaster, a nurse from Atlanta, whose daughter Crissita Elaine Cage-Toaster went missing in Detroit in October 2009. The young woman's abandoned car was found on Belle Isle, with her ID, purse, and cellphone inside. Despite the family's repeated attempts to find their daughter, they received no leads until September 2018 when they were informed that their daughter's body was found in the Detroit River five months after she went missing.

However, due to a mix-up in the records, the body was never linked to the missing-person report. The medical examiner performed a cursory death investigation, not a full autopsy, and tagged her as Jane Doe 10-3047. The cause of death remains undetermined. One major reason for the mix-up was that both Detroit police and the coroner recorded their daughter as either Caucasian or Hispanic, when she was actually black.

After spending nearly a year in the coroner's cooler, the body was buried in an unmarked grave at Knollwood Cemetery in Canton Township. Crissita Cage-Toaster has remained there since March 2011. The county has now notified the parents of their plans to exhume their daughter's body, and they will determine a final resting place this week.

The parents are left wondering how such a quiet, anonymous burial could have happened and are not getting clear answers. They suspect negligence and incompetence on the part of the Detroit Police Department and the Wayne County Medical Examiner's Office, which is one of the busiest in the nation. Both departments are reportedly pointing fingers at each other.

The National Institute of Justice maintains a public database of unidentified remains and missing persons, which usually includes details like tattoos that should have signalled a match, based on the description the parents initially reported. However, there are reportedly many inconsistencies in the case, leading the parents to question the competence of the professionals involved.

The family is planning a memorial service at a Southfield church on Nov 4. The Detroit Police Department and the Wayne County Medical Examiner's Office have not provided clear answers or explanations regarding the mix-up, citing privacy concerns. The family is still seeking answers and justice for their daughter.

In a historic settlement, survivors of one of Australia's deadliest wildfires, which occurred in Victoria in 2009, are set to receive approximately AUD 494.7 million ($470 million) in a class action lawsuit. This is the largest compensation settlement in Australian history. The fire, known as the Black Saturday bushfire, resulted in 119 deaths, making it one of the country's most devastating bushfires.

More than 5,000 people joined the class action against electricity provider SP AusNet, Utility Services Corporation Ltd., and the Victorian government, alleging negligence in power line maintenance and inadequate prevention measures. The settlement, yet to receive final court approval, will take 12 to 18 months to distribute.

Andrew Watson, the attorney representing the plaintiffs, stated, "No amount of money can compensate for the losses suffered, but this settlement of nearly $500 million represents a measure of justice and some real compensation to ease the financial burden of their suffering."

SP AusNet, in a statement, agreed to the settlement without admitting liability, claiming the conductor that sparked the fire was damaged by lightning. The settlement includes AUD 378.6 million from SP AusNet.

Carol Matthews, a lead plaintiff, expressed relief, saying, "There is so much pain that is still very real, but today there is also a sense of justice." The Black Saturday bushfire resulted in a total of 173 deaths across Victoria.

Bristol Palin, daughter of former Alaska Governor Sarah Palin, is expecting her third child with husband Dakota Meyer. The couple welcomed their daughter Sailor Grace last December and got married in June after a custody battle. Palin also has a 7-year-old son, Tripp, with ex-fiancé Levi Johnston. The couple expressed their excitement for the new addition and thanked God for their blessings. Palin and Meyer have been open about their ups and downs, but are happy to share their news with loved ones.

In Fresno, California, a burglary defendant named Bobby Pearson was mistakenly released from jail after a jury signed a not-guilty verdict, despite eight jurors believing him guilty. The judge, W. Kent Hamlin, had no choice but to release Pearson due to the verdict already being put on record. After being released, Pearson went home and got into a fatal fight with his sister's boyfriend, whose name remains undisclosed. The boyfriend is suspected of stabbing and killing Pearson.

The incident occurred hours after Pearson's release from jail. The jury in Pearson's trial had returned a guilty verdict against his co-defendant, Terrel Minnieweather, but the mistake with Pearson's verdict was discovered during lunch. Jurors were confused by the verdict forms, with one juror stating there was no form to indicate a deadlock.

The judge had polled the jury as a group to verify Minnieweather's guilty verdict, and no one questioned the not-guilty verdict in Pearson's case. However, it was later discovered that the jury was unable to reach a unanimous decision, with eight jurors voting for guilt and four for acquittal.

Prosecutor William Terrence expressed his disappointment over Pearson's death, stating, "There's not a death penalty on a burglary. I'm not sitting here thinking he got what he deserved." The case has raised questions about jury procedures and the importance of clear communication between jurors, judges, and lawyers during trials.

The polar vortex, a high-speed, high-altitude wind system that spins around the North Pole during winter, is currently stronger than average. According to Andrea Lang, an assistant professor of atmospheric and environmental science at the University of Albany, this could lead to a mild start to winter, but potentially a cold end. The vortex has been weakening due to retreating sea ice around the North Pole, which allowed extreme cold to plunge farther south in the Northeast during the last two winters.

The stronger-than-average polar vortex at the start of winter increases the likelihood of it becoming increasingly unstable as the season progresses, making it more likely that the vortex could become more misshapen, sending late blasts of cold air and snow to some southerly regions. The vortex is usually at its weakest from late December through February, increasing its volatility.

In terms of weather forecasts, a stronger El Nino warming effect in the Pacific Ocean is expected to result in a warmer winter. However, the stronger polar vortex at the start of winter could lead to a colder end. Consumers should remain snug in their homes without facing costly heating bills, as prices for propane, heating oil, and natural gas are near record lows and inventories are overflowing.

In New York, about a quarter-million homeowners, primarily in rural areas, heat with propane. Two years ago, a vortex-driven cold snap coincided with a nationwide propane shortage and rising prices, which added about $100 million to the heating bills in the state. This year, the average home propane bill should be about $3,300, down from more than $4,300 in 2013-14. For heating oil, the decline would be from $3,500 to about $2,300. For natural gas, the average bill for the period should drop from about $1,030 to about $930.

Propane users should breathe easy for the next few years, as supplies of propane, a byproduct of natural gas, are increasing, largely due to natural gas hydrofracking in Pennsylvania, Ohio, and other states. Since 2008, propane production in Eastern states has gone up more than 600 percent, about 10 times the rate of propane production overall.

In a tragic incident in Florida's Everglades, three people were killed and eight others were hospitalized following a chain reaction crash involving a black bear on Sunday evening. The initial accident occurred when a SUV hit and killed a 300-pound black bear on a dark, remote road at Big Cypress Seminole Reservation.

Three good Samaritans in a separate car stopped to help the passengers in the SUV. However, a third car, a Mercedes, plowed into the second car, resulting in the deaths of the three good Samaritans. The identities of the victims were not immediately released.

The SUV driver, who was injured, walked away unscathed, despite the vehicle being almost totaled. The Mercedes passengers sustained various degrees of injuries. Six patients were transported to Broward Health Medical Center in Fort Lauderdale, while two others were taken to Memorial Regional Hospital in Hollywood.

Gary Bitner, a spokesman for the Seminole Police Department, stated that he had never heard of a case of a bear being involved in a traffic accident. The bear died upon being struck by the SUV.

The Florida Fish and Wildlife Commission confirmed that the Everglades is the natural habitat of black bears. The incident is under investigation.

In Cahokia, Illinois, Ebony Conner, a single mother of five, was arrested and briefly jailed for failing to mow her lawn and clean up her yard, without being issued a ticket prior to the arrest. This incident is part of a broader issue where individuals, including a 70-year-old woman in Prichard, Alabama and a 75-year-old woman in Riesel, Texas, have been arrested for similar offenses. In Pagedale, Missouri, the Institute for Justice (IJ) has filed a class action lawsuit against the city due to its excessive use of municipal code enforcement, fining residents for trivial matters such as chipped paint, mismatched curtains, and walking on the wrong side of a crosswalk. From 2010 to 2014, the number of non-traffic tickets issued to residents increased by 495 percent, resulting in a significant financial burden for many residents.

The harm to Pagedale residents is significant, perpetual, and often completely overwhelming. Residents find themselves in a never-ending cycle of being fined because they cannot afford to maintain their homes to the city's standards, leading to more fines and ultimately threats of home demolition. Some residents have spent time in jail due to their fines and failure to appear in court.

The IJ has teamed up with some Pagedale residents to challenge the city's ticketing practices. Plaintiff Vincent Blount has accumulated $2,800 in fines, a significant portion of which comes from tickets regarding the home he lives in. Paying off his long-term payment plan prevented him from making the improvements the city sought, leading to more fines and ultimately a threat from the city to demolish his home. Plaintiff Valarie Whitner has received generic tickets for "house not up to code" without further explanation and has been arrested in front of her home. Mildred Bryant, an 84-year-old resident, faces a real threat of tickets, fines, and imprisonment due to the city's demands for modifications beyond her physical and financial abilities.

In a separate matter, Rudy Giuliani, President Trump's personal Russia investigation lawyer, has been described as being on a media tour to undermine Special Counsel Robert Mueller's investigation, which Giuliani himself admitted is "all just a big PR campaign." Giuliani's efforts are seen as a propaganda campaign to spread the "spygate" conspiracy, despite there being no evidence to support this claim.

The Air Force Academy announced on November 7, 2017, that racial slurs posted outside the dorm rooms of five black students were written by one of the students involved. The student is no longer at the school, but the academy did not disclose whether the student withdrew or was expelled due to privacy laws. The slurs were found in September at a dormitory that houses students attending the academy's prep school, which is on the academy grounds but not part of the four-year academy program.

The announcement came as a surprise, as the academy's superintendent, Lt. Gen. Jay Silveria, had given a stern speech to cadets shortly after the slurs were reported, warning that racists were not welcome at the school. The speech attracted nationwide attention, and a video of it was posted online and viewed thousands of times.

Silveria, a veteran fighter pilot who directed the air war in the Middle East, took command at the school in August. He graduated from the academy in 1985 and has repeatedly told cadets and staff that his highest priority is ensuring a climate of dignity and respect.

The academy has struggled with sexual misconduct problems in recent years, but few racial incidents have been made public. The academy, located outside Colorado Springs, has about 4,000 students, and the prep school usually accepts about 240 students.

The slurs appeared in the aftermath of racial violence in Charlottesville, Virginia, and amid a debate about NFL players kneeling for the national anthem. Silveria told cadets that they needed to be aware of the backdrop of what is going on in the country, including events like Charlottesville, Ferguson, and the protests in the NFL.

A 3-year-old girl named Mariah Woods has been missing since she was put to bed on Sunday night at her Jacksonville, North Carolina home. Her mother, Kristy Woods, reported her missing at 6:45 a.m. the following morning. Authorities, including the Onslow County Sheriff's Department and the FBI, are conducting a search for Mariah, who is described as having brown hair, blue eyes, and standing at 2 feet 9 inches tall and weighing 30 pounds.

The investigation is ongoing, and officials are still following tips and leads from the AMBER Alert and other sources. Kristy Woods has pleaded for the public's help in finding her daughter, stating that she loves her and wants to hold her tight.

Onslow County Sheriff Hans Miller has assured the public that authorities are using every available resource to search for Mariah, including drones and helicopters provided by the Marine Corps, the North Carolina State Highway Patrol, and a neighboring sheriff's department. An amber alert was issued for Mariah soon after she was reported missing.

Mariah's biological father, Alex Woods, has expressed skepticism about her disappearance. Officials have interviewed both Kristy Woods' mother and her live-in boyfriend and conducted a search of their home and vehicle. Neighbors in the area have been asked to check their yards, sheds, and other areas for any evidence of Mariah.

The FBI and Onslow County Sheriff's Office have released surveillance pictures taken Monday morning of a woman and child at a North Carolina Walmart, and are asking for the public's help in identifying both the woman and child to determine if they are Mariah Woods. Anyone with information about Mariah is asked to call the Onslow County Sheriff's Office at 910-989-4070.

The family of Dennis Lee Thian Poh, a 47-year-old businessman from Kuala Lumpur, is anxiously awaiting his return as he went missing during a trek in Ampurna, Nepal, on April 5. Lee was hiking with eight friends and was scheduled to return last Friday. His family has urged experienced volunteers to help with on-ground search efforts, as weather conditions in the Himalayas worsen. Search efforts have intensified with rescue teams combing the areas between Khopra and Bayeli as well as Dobasto and Tadatani. SAR Dogs Nepal, an independent Nepali search-and-rescue team, is leading the search efforts.

Lee's wife, Jennifer Peters-Lee, flew to Nepal to help coordinate the rescue team comprising professional rescuers, local police, and villagers. Those who are able to help in Nepal may contact rescuers at +977 9856025679 or email any information to finddennis@yahoo.com. Lee's friends have also set up a Facebook page called Find Dennis for the public to share information or express their support.

The night before he disappeared, Lee called his wife in Kuala Lumpur. They chatted about the bitter cold in Nepal's Annapurna range, and he said that dinner in his small lodge had consisted, yet again, of vegetable fried rice. Lee had been hiking for six days in Nepal's most visited trekking zone, the Annapurna Conservation Area. The area where Dennis disappeared is mostly above 11,800 feet elevation, between the tiny hamlets of Khopra Danda and Bayali in the center of the Annapurna Circuit, with an achingly beautiful panorama of mountains, rising nearly 26,000 feet above sea level.

The region is also one of Nepal's most dangerous for trekkers. The mountains collect moisture from the area, resulting in frequent rain, hail, and snow. Once a trekker heads higher into the mountains, like Dennis' group did, wide walking paths and stone steps are replaced by narrow, slippery, and unstable paths, often on the edge of vertical precipices. Last season, a sign was posted on the track to Bayali warning trekkers not to walk it solo. It's unclear whether the group guide warned Dennis, and no one knows whether he saw the sign.

The U.S. State Department warns visitors not to trek alone and urges everyone to register with the embassy in Kathmandu, where the consular section has pictures of missing American trekkers posted on the walls of its visitor area. Some trekkers' remains are not found for years. SAR Dogs Nepal, the country's main dog search and rescue organization, functions entirely on donations. In 2014, the agency rescued five foreigners and about 200 Nepalis. And it's not just the rugged terrain and weather that hinder rescue operations. Linguistic and cultural barriers, weak government infrastructure, and disorganized communication channels slow down searches.

The head of the SAR Dogs Nepal team searching for Dennis is a 29-year-old fine arts major from the village of Lamjung in the nearby hills. Karna Dura grew up around dogs and the search and rescue world. He knows intimately the odds and complexities of survival. In 2013, Dura and SAR Dogs Nepal found the body of a German trekker missing for 22 days after they believe he fell down a gorge as he left the trail to get a better angle to take pictures. He had managed to survive until a few days before SAR Dogs Nepal found him. The trekker had filmed his last few days and a message to his family on his camera.

In 1991, an Australian man disappeared in northern Nepal, surviving 43 days before being rescued. Unlike Dennis, both these men were trekking solo without a group and not on a set route. If a trekker is fully fit and does not have a head injury, trackers with SAR Dogs believe it's possible to survive three to four weeks in the mountains. Dennis, an avid and fit hiker, has a black belt in taekwondo. In his day-pack, he had a warm winter jacket, about 2 pints of water, a knife, a compass, and some muesli. Now the weather is Dura's biggest enemy.

Working with a 10-man team, three air-scenting dogs, and one dog that tracks a person, Dura and his team have identified four spots where Dennis was. One spot is a boulder, marking Dennis' last location on the main trail halfway to Bayali. The team is using Dennis' boots, sleeping bag, and clothes that the porters were carrying to give the dogs his scent. But large boulders below this site, combined with heavy fog and rain, make it impossible for the team to see down the ravine. Though they have been joined by 60 local villagers and six policemen, poor visibility has blocked helicopter assistance. Rappelling is the only way down the gorge, and the army is coming Thursday with professional rappellers.

Snow and hail for the past few days have kept nighttime temperatures below freezing. The trail is a slippery mud morass. "This is very stressful," Dura says in a phone call from Bayali, which at over 13,000 feet elevation is cloaked in snow. "I pray he is all right." Jennifer struggles to hold onto hope. But she also feels her world is crumbling. She has made fliers with Dennis' picture, with the offer of a reward, to be distributed to local Nepali villagers. "I am so desperate," she says. "I have written a letter to the prime minister of Malaysia asking him for help."

In a significant development, a prominent Iranian lawmaker has stated that Iran no longer needs more 20 percent-enriched uranium, a key concession sought by Western powers in ongoing nuclear negotiations. Hossein Naqvi Hosseini, a spokesman for the Iranian parliament's national security and foreign policy committee, indicated that Iran's current nuclear fuel supply eliminates the need for further production of 20 percent-enriched uranium, which could be used to build nuclear weapons.

However, Hosseini did not confirm whether Iran will halt enrichment altogether. He also mentioned that Iran is prepared to alleviate concerns over its stockpile of enriched uranium, suggesting a potential conversion of the stockpile to fuel rods.

The West fears Iran's nuclear program could lead to the development of an atomic bomb, while Iran maintains its program is for peaceful purposes such as medical research and power generation. Last week, Iranian diplomats met with negotiators from the United States, Russia, China, Britain, France, and Germany in Geneva, aiming to ease economic and oil sanctions imposed on Iran over its contested nuclear program.

Iran currently operates over 10,000 centrifuges, producing tons of fuel-grade material that can be further enriched for nuclear warheads. Iran also has nearly 440 pounds (200 kilograms) of higher-enriched uranium, enough to quickly produce a single warhead. Experts suggest that 550 pounds (250 kilograms) of 20 percent-enriched uranium are needed to produce a single warhead.

Among the key concessions sought by the West, according to two unnamed diplomats, is a halt to enrichment at the 20 percent level. The diplomats claim Iran offered to halt 20 percent enrichment during last week's Geneva talks, although this has not been publicly confirmed by the Iranian government.

Negotiators from Iran and the six powers are due to meet in Geneva for further talks on Nov. 7-8. The potential halt to 20 percent enrichment, if confirmed, could signal progress in the long-standing dispute over Iran's nuclear intentions. However, obstacles remain, including opposition from hardliners in Iran and skepticism from countries like Israel.

Blake Lively and Ryan Reynolds, former co-stars in "Green Lantern," are reportedly in a serious relationship. Despite neither confirming their relationship status, sources claim that Lively has visited Reynolds on the set of his current film "R.I.P.D." in Boston, and Reynolds previously visited Lively on the set of "Gossip Girl" in New York City. The couple, who have been spending more time together, were spotted having a romantic dinner in Boston, with Lively even picking up the check. Lively reportedly wanted to spend "a few days" with Reynolds but could only stay one night. The romance between the two has been a topic of interest, with Lively's ex-boyfriend Leonardo DiCaprio recently being linked to Australia's "Next Top Model" Alyce Crawford. Scarlett Johansson, Reynolds' ex-wife, has mentioned being "overcritical" and "incredibly impatient" in a recent interview. Neither Lively nor Reynolds' representatives have confirmed the relationship.

Goldman Sachs is facing a fraud lawsuit by the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) for allegedly misleading investors about a deal they helped structure and sell. The SEC claims Goldman failed to disclose that a hedge fund was helping create the investment while betting big that the deal would fail. Goldman denies the accusations, stating they did not structure a portfolio designed to lose money.

Similar practices were found in other major investment banks, including JPMorgan Chase, Merrill Lynch, Citigroup, Deutsche Bank, and UBS. These banks created CDOs with a hedge fund named Magnetar, which was both helping create and betting against the CDOs. The banks marketed and sold the CDOs to investors without disclosing Magnetar’s role or its interests.

Goldman's 25 Abacus CDOs, one of which is the basis of the SEC’s lawsuit, amounted to $10.9 billion. The SEC's suit states that CDOs like the ones Goldman built contributed to the financial crisis by magnifying losses associated with the downturn in the U.S. housing market.

The SEC did not sue the hedge fund involved in Goldman’s Abacus deals, Paulson & Co., or its manager, John Paulson. Notably, there's no evidence that what Magnetar did was illegal.

Other banks involved in Magnetar CDO deals, such as Bank of America, Citigroup, Deutsche Bank, Wells Fargo, and UBS, have declined to comment on potential lawsuits. Magnetar has responded to ProPublica's original reporting. Read ProPublica’s full Magnetar story for more details.

In a speech at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, Jack Ma, the CEO and founder of Alibaba Holdings, criticized the United States for squandering the benefits of globalization by not distributing the wealth more evenly throughout society. Ma argued that the U.S. has spent over $14 trillion on wars over the past 30 years instead of investing in infrastructure at home, which has contributed to economic anxiety among American citizens. Ma also expressed optimism about the potential for a more inclusive form of globalization, in which the benefits are more widely shared, and offered to help American small businesses sell their products in China and Asia through Alibaba's network. In a separate development, Alibaba announced a 12-year deal with the International Olympic Committee to supply technology for the organization of the Games, support a new shopping platform for merchandise, and run a Chinese version of the Olympic internet TV channel. The deal was hailed as a historic day for Alibaba by Jack Ma. However, the deal may face potential friction due to concerns about counterfeits on Alibaba's platforms, as the U.S. recently returned Alibaba to its "notorious markets list" for pirated goods.

The WikiLeaks release of a trove of documents allegedly from the CIA reveals the agency's extensive hacking capabilities, potentially taking surveillance into the homes and pockets of billions of users worldwide. The documents detail the CIA's ability to hack into a variety of everyday devices, including smartphones, televisions, and even anti-virus software.

The documents suggest that the CIA has developed ways to bypass encryption used by popular messaging apps, such as WhatsApp and Signal, without having to crack the encryption itself. Instead, the agency can intercept messages and calls before they are encrypted or after they are decrypted.

WikiLeaks claims that it has redacted names and other identifying information from the collection and will not release the computer code for actual, usable weapons until a consensus emerges on the technical and political nature of the CIA's program and how such 'weapons' should be analyzed, disarmed, and published.

The names used for projects revealed in the WikiLeaks documents appear to reflect the likely demographic of the cyber-experts employed by the CIA, with references to "Harry Potter," Pokémon, and Adderall, a drug used to treat hyperactivity. The documents also suggest that the CIA has studied whether it could infect vehicle control systems for cars and trucks, which could potentially be used for nearly undetectable assassinations.

At a time of increasing concern about the privacy of calls and messages, the revelations do not suggest that the CIA can actually break the encryption used by popular messaging apps. Instead, by penetrating the user's phone, the agency can make the encryption irrelevant by intercepting messages and calls before their content is encrypted, or, on the other end, after messages are decrypted.

WikiLeaks, which has sometimes been accused of recklessly leaking information that could do harm, said it has redacted lists of CIA surveillance targets, though it said they included targets and machines in Latin America, Europe, and the United States. The documents released Tuesday are the first batch of a series of releases that WikiLeaks plans, according to the group. This first group shows important differences from the 2013 revelations by the National Security Agency's former contractor Edward Snowden. His trove of documents largely described mass surveillance of Internet-based communications systems, while the WikiLeaks release more often describes attacks on individual devices.

The WikiLeaks revelations also will serve as a reminder that, for whatever the political backlash to revelations about digital spying, it is not going away and probably will continue to grow. Aside from the United States, many other advanced nations such as China, Russia, Britain, and Israel have extremely sophisticated tools for digital spying. Less advanced nations have gained access to powerful online spying technology through a robust and lightly regulated industry of surveillance contractors based throughout the world.

The WikiLeaks release has caused alarm in Silicon Valley, with technologists grappling with revelations of yet another U.S. government attempt to exploit their systems. Cybersecurity experts have reacted with alarm to the CIA's reported ability to hack into devices, even well-encrypted communications, without having to crack the encryption itself.

"I think a foreign power is much more likely the source of these documents than a conscience-stricken CIA whistle-blower," Mr. Lewis said.

The second sign-up season for Obamacare is underway, and Health and Human Services Secretary Sylvia Burwell reported that HealthCare.gov is functioning well, a significant improvement from last year's technical issues. Burwell expects a growth of around 2 million new enrollments, aiming for a total of 9 million people. During the first weekend, 100,000 new applications were submitted via the federal website serving 37 states, and 1 million people have been window shopping for insurance plans. The call centers have taken 100,000 calls, indicating consumer interest. President Obama praised the improvements made to HealthCare.gov. The website offers subsidized private coverage to people without insurance through their jobs, with the federal government running the health insurance exchange in most states. Some states, including Washington, are experiencing issues with their own exchanges. Premiums appear to be stable this year, but experts warn of potential significant cost increases for customers who already have coverage. The administration is under pressure to avoid another website meltdown, given the change in Congressional control.

Mark Herzlich, a rookie linebacker for the New York Giants, recently arrived in Indianapolis for Super Bowl XLVI against the Patriots. However, his journey to the Super Bowl is not just about football; it's a testament to his resilience against Ewing's sarcoma, a type of bone cancer. Diagnosed in 2009, Herzlich was given a grim prognosis, with the possibility of amputation or the cancer spreading. But he responded well to aggressive treatment, choosing to continue his football career despite the increased risk of the cancer returning. After missing the 2009 college football season, he played for Boston College in 2010 but went undrafted. He later signed with the Giants and is now preparing to play in the Super Bowl, a feat that seemed improbable just three years ago. Herzlich's story of survival has been a source of inspiration, with many fans supporting him despite rooting for the Patriots. His Twitter post upon arrival in Indianapolis expressed his gratitude for being alive and playing in the Super Bowl.

Long Vang, a 34-year-old man from Stewartville, Minnesota, is facing charges of third-degree murder, second-degree manslaughter, and stalking in connection with the suicide of Jessica Haban, the mother of his two children. Prosecutors allege that Vang inflicted ten years of relentless physical and emotional abuse on Haban, which led to her losing her will to live and ultimately taking her own life. This case is rare in Minnesota, as it involves charging an abuser with murder for another person's suicide.

The abuse inflicted on Haban was wide-ranging and persistent, and some of the interactions occurred despite a court order for Vang to have no contact with her. She was physically assaulted, threatened, and emotionally manipulated. The final emotional blow, according to charges, was Vang pressuring Haban to leave inpatient mental health treatment and return home, threatening to institutionalize her and take away custody of their children.

Haban's family has found comfort in the charges, with her mother stating, "While we know that it won’t bring her back, he will be held accountable." The case against Vang is being seen as courageous by some, as it could set a precedent for other county attorneys to bring criminal cases involving suspected abuse triggering suicide.

This case highlights the significant correlation between domestic violence and suicide, particularly among women. Research has shown that women who experience domestic violence have higher rates of suicide attempts and ideation than women who have not been victimized by an intimate partner. The stigma associated with these issues can make it difficult for victims to receive help and for perpetrators to be held accountable.

The case against Vang raises complex legal questions, with some worrying about prosecutorial overreach. However, for Haban's family, the charges offer some reassurance that authorities are taking her death seriously. It is hoped that this case will lead to further investigation into the connection between domestic violence and suicide.

The Obama Administration has taken several steps to address the issue of criminal justice reform, with a focus on rehabilitating and reintegrating formerly incarcerated individuals into society. The President is set to visit Newark, New Jersey, to highlight these efforts and announce new actions aimed at helping individuals who have served their time to rehabilitate and reintegrate back into their communities.

Each year, over 600,000 individuals are released from state and federal prisons. The Administration has taken a series of concrete actions to reduce the challenges and barriers faced by these individuals, including through the work of the Federal Interagency Reentry Council, a cabinet-level working group that supports cross-agency coordination and collaboration to promote public safety and economic opportunity.

The President has called on Congress to pass meaningful criminal justice reform, including the Sentencing Reform and Corrections Act of 2015, which aims to reduce recidivism and provide incentives for those incarcerated to participate in evidence-based treatment and training programs. The bill would also free up resources for investments in other public safety initiatives, such as reentry services, programs for mental illness and addiction, and state and local law enforcement.

Today, the President announced several measures to promote rehabilitation and reintegration, including:

1. Adult Reentry Education Grants: The Department of Education will award up to $8 million over 3 years to 9 communities to support educational attainment and reentry success for individuals who have been incarcerated.
2. Arrests Guidance for Public and other HUD-Assisted Housing: The Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) will release guidance to Public Housing Authorities and owners of HUD-assisted housing regarding the use of arrests in determining who can live in HUD-assisted properties. This guidance will clarify the Department’s position on “one strike” policies and include best practices from Public Housing Authorities.
3. Banning the Box in Federal Employment: The President is directing the Office of Personnel Management (OPM) to modify its rules to delay inquiries into criminal history until later in the hiring process. This action will better ensure that applicants from all segments of society, including those with prior criminal histories, receive a fair opportunity to compete for Federal employment.
4. TechHire: As part of President Obama’s TechHire initiative, over 30 communities are taking action to expand access to tech jobs for more Americans, including those with criminal records. Today, the Administration is announcing new commitments to expand tech training and jobs for individuals with criminal records in Memphis, TN, New Orleans, LA, Newark, NJ, New Haven, CT, and Washington, DC.
5. Establishing a National Clean Slate Clearinghouse: In the coming weeks, the Department of Labor and Department of Justice will partner to establish a National Clean Slate Clearinghouse to provide technical assistance to local legal aid programs, public defender offices, and reentry service providers to build capacity for legal services needed to help with record-cleaning, expungement, and related civil legal services.
6. Permanent Supportive Housing for the Reentry Population through Pay for Success: The Department of Housing and Urban Development and the Bureau of Justice Assistance at the Department of Justice have launched an $8.7 million demonstration grant to address homelessness and reduce recidivism among the justice-involved population.
7. Juvenile Reentry Assistance Program Awards to Support Public Housing Residents: With funding provided by the Office of Juvenile Justice and Delinquency Prevention at the Department of Justice, the Department of Housing and Urban Development will provide $1.75 million to aid eligible public housing residents who are under the age of 25 to expunge or seal their records in accordance with their applicable state laws.

These announcements stem from the President’s My Brother’s Keeper Task Force, which is charged with addressing persistent opportunity gaps facing boys and young men of color and ensuring all young people can reach their full potential. The Task Force has made considerable progress towards implementing its recommendations, many times creating partnerships across agencies and sectors.

The Administration has advanced numerous effective reintegration strategies through the work of the Federal Interagency Reentry Council, whose mission is to reduce recidivism and victimization; assist those returning from prison, jail or juvenile facilities to become productive citizens; and save taxpayer dollars by lowering the direct and collateral costs of incarceration.

In addition to the measures announced today, the Administration has taken several other steps to reduce barriers to employment, increase access to education and enrichment, expand opportunities for justice-involved youth to serve their communities, increase access to health care and public services, increase reentry service access to incarcerated veterans, and improve opportunities for children of incarcerated parents and their families. Private sector commitments to support reentry include the Center for Employment Opportunities (CEO), which has committed to more than double the number of people served from 4,500 to 11,000 across existing geographies and 3-5 new states, and Cengage Learning, which will roll out Smart Horizons Career Online Education in correctional facilities in up to four new states over the next 12 months, providing over 1,000 new students with the opportunity to earn a high-school diploma and/or career certificate online.

The article, "Make Sure Your College Tuition Pays You Back: Look Beyond College Costs, Check Your Return on Investment," discusses a study by compensation data site PayScale that calculates the return on investment (ROI) of over 850 colleges and universities. The study compares the cost of a school's degree with the average earnings of its graduates to determine the value of each institution. The California Institute of Technology (Caltech) has the highest ROI at $1,713,000, while Shaw University has the lowest ROI at $15,480. The article provides a list of the top 13 schools with the highest ROI scores and links to BusinessWeek's state-by-state breakdown of the data. The article encourages readers to consider the ROI of their college degree and share their experiences in the comments section.

The Justice Department has filed a lawsuit against California and two top state officials, accusing them of interfering with federal immigration enforcement efforts. The lawsuit, filed in federal court in Sacramento, alleges that California is blocking enforcement efforts by the Department of Homeland Security and imposing impermissible obligations on the federal government. The lawsuit points out that the Constitution gives the U.S. government sweeping authority over immigration, and that California's actions are a violation of this authority.

The lawsuit focuses on three immigration-related laws passed by California last year, which are under federal challenge. One bars private employers from voluntarily cooperating with federal immigration officials and requires businesses to notify workers in advance of a federal raid. A second law restricts state and local law enforcement from voluntarily sharing information with the feds about the release dates of undocumented people in their custody. The third law covers state inspections of detention facilities that hold noncitizens in federal custody.

The Justice Department is asking for a preliminary injunction to block these three laws. The federal government cites a 2012 Supreme Court dispute, in which the Obama administration sued Arizona over its punitive law meant to crack down on immigrants, as precedent. In that case, the court's five-justice majority ruled that federal law trumps state law in the immigration area, lest each state develop its own policy toward immigrants.

The case represents an escalation of the long-running battle between the Trump administration and California, whose Democratic governor, Jerry Brown, and attorney general, Xavier Becerra, have positioned themselves as ideological opponents to the White House on matters from immigration and climate change to criminal justice. The lawsuit comes as Attorney General Jeff Sessions is set to speak at an annual Law Enforcement Legislative Day hosted by the California Peace Officers' Association in Sacramento.

In response to the lawsuit, Governor Brown called it a "political stunt" and said that Sessions was "dividing and polarizing America." The case will test the power of the Trump administration to force California police departments and local governments to cooperate with deportations and other aggressive enforcement actions targeting people who entered the country illegally or overstayed their visas. It reflects the administration’s limited tolerance for state’s rights when states want to go in a sharply different direction than the administration.

Despite the charges, Richards was not sentenced to prison, but instead received probation and was ordered to participate in a sex offenders treatment program. The judge who sentenced Richards, Superior Court Judge Jan Jurden, noted that he "will not fare well" in prison and that treatment would be more beneficial for him. The article also mentions that Richards' ex-wife is suing him for compensation and emotional distress caused to their children. The case has raised questions about how the wealthy and powerful are treated by the legal system. The article also includes details about Richards' background, including his wealth, family connections, and properties.

Following a deadly attack at the French satirical magazine Charlie Hebdo, tens of thousands of people held silent vigils in Paris and other cities around the world. An estimated 35,000 people gathered in Paris's Place de la Republique to pay tribute to the victims, leaving candles and piles of pens in small memorials. Similar vigils were held in London, Buenos Aires, Washington DC, Vienna, Madrid, Berlin, Brussels, and other cities. People held placards and used mobile phones to convey the message "Je suis Charlie" (I am Charlie). Many took part in the vigils, such as in Lyon, held pens aloft as a symbol of press freedom. The attack on Charlie Hebdo, which left 12 people dead, has sparked messages of condolence, outrage, and defiance around the world. The inscription "I am Charlie" has become a popular slogan on social media, with many changing their profile pictures on Facebook and Twitter to show support for the victims. The attack on Charlie Hebdo, which had caricatured the Prophet Muhammad, has drawn condemnation and threats before, with the magazine being firebombed in 2011. Masked gunmen methodically killed the victims, shouting "Allahu akbar!" (Allah is the greatest) while firing, then fleeing in a car. The Newseum in Washington displayed "#JeSuisCharlie" on its atrium screen as a show of support for free expression. In every major city across France, hundreds of thousands gathered in a show of defiant solidarity against the gunmen who had invoked Allah as they shot dead 12 people in the offices of the weekly satirical magazine in a few horrifying minutes.

Same Ole Line Dudes is a professional line-sitting service based in New York City, founded by Robert Samuel in 2012 after he was laid off from his job at an AT&T store. The service aims to help individuals save time by waiting in line for them for various events, products, and experiences, such as Broadway shows, tech releases, designer sample sales, and even brunch waitlists.

Samuel's clients range from average everyday people to the wealthy, and he notes that they are more time-strapped than cash-poor. For example, mothers hire him because they cannot wait in lines in the mornings, and people with tight schedules hire him to purchase items they want but cannot get due to time constraints.

Samuel's business has grown since its inception, and he now makes up to $1,000 a week to stand in line. He recently spent 48 hours outside the Apple store in the Meatpacking District waiting for the iPhone 6s and even snagged $1,000 for the gig.

Same Ole Line Dudes joins a growing list of "Ubers" like Lugg, Doughbies On-Demand, Minibar, and Breather, which allow customers to buy their way to the front of various lines. However, Samuel's business faces competition from share economy start-ups like TaskRabbit and Agent Anything, where individuals can be purchased to do various small tasks.

Despite the publicity and success of his business, Samuel's mother remains skeptical and encourages him to go back to school. However, Samuel is unfazed by the challenges and continues to work full-time as a security guard for a financial services company while running his line-sitting service on the side.

In conclusion, Same Ole Line Dudes is a professional line-sitting service that helps individuals save time by waiting in line for them for various events, products, and experiences. The service has grown since its inception and faces competition from other start-ups, but Samuel remains committed to his business and continues to work full-time while running his line-sitting service on the side.

In the lead-up to the second US presidential debate on October 9, Melania Trump, the wife of Republican nominee Donald Trump, caused a stir by wearing a Gucci "pussy-bow" blouse. The style, which has a mixed history among feminists, became popular in the mid-20th century and was a signature look for former UK Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher. However, given the recent controversy surrounding Trump's lewd comments about women, many on social media saw the choice as ironic and in poor taste. Melania Trump condemned her husband's remarks, but refused to do a joint TV appearance with him to address the issue. The debate focused on various topics, including Trump's tax returns and his comments about women, which he labeled as "locker room banter." The controversy surrounding Trump's comments has led to the suspension of Billy Bush, the "Access Hollywood" host who was heard making inappropriate comments in the leaked video.

On December 20, 2017, a tragic incident occurred in Schertz, Texas, resulting in the death of a 6-year-old boy, Kameron Prescott, and a suspected car thief, Amanda Lene Jones, during a deputy-involved shooting. The incident took place at a mobile home park following a nearly two-hour manhunt for Jones, who was wanted for several felony warrants.

The Bexar County Sheriff's office, consisting of deputies John Aguillon, George Herrera, Jesse Arias, Johnny Longoria, and a reserve deputy, were involved in the shooting. According to Sheriff Javier Salazar, the incident began when a deputy spotted Jones with what he believed was a weapon. Jones allegedly threatened to shoot the deputy, and after evading capture for several hours, she was later found at the mobile home park where Kameron lived.

Jones forced her way into Kameron's home, threatened to shoot his family, and said she was taking their vehicle. When she left the home, the deputies were outside, waiting. Witnesses heard Jones threaten to shoot the law enforcement officers, and the deputies believed she was holding a weapon. They fired shots, killing Jones and striking Kameron, who died at a hospital.

The deputies involved in the shooting have been placed on administrative leave, and the local district attorney is investigating. The incident was captured on body camera, but the view was obstructed when the deputy raised his rifle to fire. The community is mourning the loss of Kameron, who was described as a kind, happy, and caring boy by his teacher and school counselor. A fund has been established to assist Kameron's family with expenses.

The U.K. has become the first country to allow the over-the-counter sale of Pfizer's erectile dysfunction treatment, Viagra. Men seeking the medication will be able to buy Viagra Connect, which contains the same active ingredient as regular Viagra, for approximately £19.99 for a pack of four pills and £34.99 for an eight-pack at pharmacies. Pfizer has been advocating for this change for nearly a decade, and the OTC version of Viagra will be available in the U.K. starting in spring 2018. The drug will only be available in pharmacies, and its supply will depend on pharmacists' assessment of its suitability for each individual.

Viagra has been one of the pharmaceutical industry's most successful prescription products since its launch in 1998. It achieved peak worldwide sales of over $2 billion in 2012 but has since declined as patents have expired. Pfizer is exploring extending the brand's value as a non-prescription drug. The U.K. is the first country to reclassify Viagra from a prescription-only medicine to a pharmacy status. The change follows a lengthy review by the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA).

The MHRA hopes the rule change will reduce the number of people buying counterfeit versions of the drug, which can be dangerous. The agency has seized over £50m ($67m) of unlicensed and counterfeit erectile dysfunction medications in the past five years. Pfizer will continue to make Viagra available as a prescription drug, but the over-the-counter option is likely to reduce demand for potentially ineffective and dangerous fakes.

In a 2012 interview, Kassig said he wanted to make a difference and believed that the exchange of ideas and experiences between people from diverse backgrounds was important. He also expressed frustration with delays in delivering aid to Syrian refugees and the loss of innocent lives as a result. Kassig was taken hostage in October 2013 and his family has been working to secure his release. On Wednesday, June 7, Iran was struck by a series of coordinated attacks on its parliament building and the mausoleum of Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, the founder of the Islamic Republic. The attacks, which left 12 people dead and 46 injured, were claimed by ISIS, marking the first time the terrorist group has carried out an attack in Iran.

The attacks targeted two symbolically significant sites in Iran. The parliament building is the heart of Iran's government, while the mausoleum of Ayatollah Khomeini is the spiritual heart of the Iranian revolution. The six known attackers, who were disguised as women, were killed during the assault, and five suspects were detained.

The attacks have been blamed by Iran's hardline Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) on Saudi Arabia, and it is likely that they will have a significant impact on regional tensions. ISIS has long viewed Iran as a religious and strategic competitor, and the attacks were intended to punish Iran for its meddling in Iraq, force Iran to commit even more forces to Iraq, and create alienation among Sunni Muslims in Iran.

The attacks also come at a time when ISIS is losing territory in Iraq and Syria, and the group is seeking to retain momentum and attract recruits by carrying out high-profile attacks. The attacks in Tehran are part of a series of attacks that have happened over the past few days, either inspired or directed by ISIS, and they are meant to show that the organization is still in the fight and can still recruit.

The attacks have been widely condemned, with Iran's foreign minister, Javad Zarif, tweeting that "terror-sponsoring despots threaten to bring the fight to our homeland. Proxies attack what their masters despise most: the seat of democracy." The United States has also condemned the attacks and called on states that sponsor terrorism to be held accountable.

The attacks are likely to increase public support for the Revolutionary Guards and for Iran's efforts to combat IS, but they will also increase the cost of Iran's involvement in Iraq and Syria, and they may create further tensions with Saudi Arabia and other Gulf states. The attacks are a reminder that the fight against terrorism is far from over, and that the region remains a volatile and dangerous place.

The Indian authorities have put on hold efforts to retrieve the body of an American missionary, John Allen Chau, who was reportedly killed by the Sentinelese tribe on North Sentinel Island in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands. The decision was made to avoid disturbing the endangered tribe and to prevent any potential confrontation. Chau was trying to convert the Sentinelese to Christianity when he was killed with arrows. His body is still on the island, and attempts to retrieve it have been unsuccessful. The authorities are in a quandary about how to proceed further due to the protected status of the Sentinelese and the risk of escalating tensions. The Sentinelese have aggressively resisted outsiders for years, and contact with the outside world could put them at risk of common illnesses such as flu and measles. The authorities are consulting experts to decide whether it is feasible to retrieve Chau's body without provoking a confrontation with the Sentinelese. The fishermen who ferried Chau to the island have been arrested, and Chau's family have forgiven those who killed him. The Sentinelese have lived in complete isolation on North Sentinel Island for tens of thousands of years, and India has protected the island for decades to prevent the Sentinelese from contracting modern illnesses and to keep outsiders safe. The island is roughly the size of Manhattan, and it is only about 50 kilometers west of Port Blair, the territory's capital. Chau traveled to the remote island knowing that his mission was illegal and risky, and he hoped to eventually share the gospel and translate the Bible.

The paper published in the American Journal of Physics by Alexander Klotz, a graduate student at McGill University, challenges the long-held belief that it takes 42 minutes for a person to fall through the Earth if they were to drill a tunnel through its center. Klotz's calculations, based on seismic data, suggest that it would take 38 minutes and 11 seconds instead.

Interestingly, Klotz also found that if gravity were assumed to be constant throughout the journey, the time taken would still be 38 minutes. This simpler assumption, while not entirely accurate, provides a good approximation to the actual results.

The difference in time is due to the varying density of Earth's layers. The classic problem assumes a uniform density, but in reality, Earth has a less dense crust and mantle and a denser core. This difference in density affects the force of gravity, making it stronger or weaker depending on the location within the Earth.

The new calculation not only provides a more accurate estimate but also explains why a crude assumption can still yield a relatively accurate answer. David Jackson, editor of the American Journal of Physics, finds this explanation gratifying and believes that the classic problem should be supplemented with the new findings.

This research highlights the importance of considering the internal structure of Earth when solving physics problems related to gravity. It also underscores the value of simple assumptions in physics, as they can sometimes provide useful approximations to complex real-world situations.

The Shin Bet, Israel's security agency, announced on Thursday the dismantling of a large Hamas terrorism network that was planning to carry out a series of attacks against Israeli targets. The network, which was directed by Hamas leaders in Turkey, had been recruiting operatives in Jordan and training them in various countries, including Syria and the Gaza Strip.

The intended targets of the network included the Teddy soccer stadium and the light rail system in Jerusalem, as well as Israeli communities in Judea and Samaria. The network also planned to carry out car bombings, kidnappings, and shooting and bombing attacks against Israeli military targets in the West Bank.

The network was discovered in September, following the detonation of explosive devices in the West Bank on August 31. The second explosive was timed to kill emergency responders, according to the Shin Bet's investigation. Following the attack, the agency arrested dozens of suspects, and learned during subsequent interrogations that some had joined Hamas as far back as 2012, in Jordan.

The network sought to recruit students who were friends of Hamas operatives, and identified students who supported the Muslim Brotherhood and Hamas, and had highly developed skills in various areas. Eventually, recruiters turned to selected prospective operatives with formal requests to join Hamas. Those who accepted came under the command of Hamas’s Turkey-based headquarters, which oversaw their military training.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu praised the Shin Bet and Israel Defense Forces for thwarting the attacks, saying that if carried out they could have exacted a heavy toll of casualties. While this operation has been made public, many other counter-terror actions against Hamas remain secret, he said. The Israeli government has been dealing with a surge in violence in recent months, with eleven Israelis killed in Palestinian attacks over the past month. Hamas did not immediately comment on the arrests.

A mysterious piece of space junk, WT1190F, is expected to collide with Earth on November 13th. Originally orbiting beyond the moon, it was first glimpsed by a telescope in early October. The object, three to six feet long and man-made, is believed to be a lost piece of space history, possibly a spent rocket or moon mission debris. Scientists are tracking its trajectory, which shows it will hit the Indian Ocean off the southern tip of Sri Lanka, with much of it burning up before reaching Earth. WT1190F is one of the few space objects whose impact can be accurately predicted, offering a scientific opportunity to study its descent. This event also tests the plans astronomers have in place to coordinate their efforts when a potentially dangerous space object appears. The object is only 1-2 meters in size, with a low density, suggesting it is artificial. Researchers are currently tracking only 20 such objects in distant orbits, with many more likely in existence but unidentified. This event highlights the need for increased funding and attention to tracking deep-Earth orbits, as there is currently no official, funded effort to do so.

Phil Mickelson, a professional golfer, was not criminally charged for allegedly profiting off an insider stock tip to repay a debt owed to sports gambler Billy Walters. The Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) charged Mickelson as a relief defendant for profiting without evidence of knowledge concerning the origin of the illegal tip. Mickelson has agreed to pay back $1.03 million, including interest, to settle the case.

Billy Walters, a noted sports gambler, was charged with insider trading and arrested by the FBI. He is scheduled to appear in court in June. The SEC also alleges that Walters' interaction with former chairman of Dean Foods Thomas Davis allowed him to make a profit of $32 million in stock trading while avoiding losses of $11 million. Davis is cooperating with the investigation and has already pleaded guilty to charges that include perjury and obstruction of justice.

The SEC is also looking to recoup gains from Davis and Walters. Mickelson is also tied to a federal money laundering case, but has not been charged with a crime.
