NBC Universal announced it was cutting ties with Trump as a result of his comments about Mexican immigrants.

On August 17, 2017, a van veered onto a promenade in Barcelona's Las Ramblas district and barreled down the busy walkway, swerving back and forth as it mowed down pedestrians, resulting in 13 deaths and over 100 injuries. The Islamic State group claimed responsibility for the attack, stating it was carried out by "soldiers of the Islamic State" in response to the extremist group's calls for followers to target countries participating in the coalition trying to drive it from Syria and Iraq.

The van attack was Spain's deadliest since 2004, when al-Qaida-inspired bombers killed 192 people in coordinated assaults on Madrid's commuter trains. In the years since, Spanish authorities have arrested nearly 200 jihadists. The only deadly attacks since then were bombings claimed by the Basque separatist group ETA that killed five people over the past decade but it declared a cease-fire in 2011.

Early Friday, Catalan police shot and killed five suspects in a seaside resort town south of Barcelona in response to a terrorist attack. Six civilians were injured in Cambrils but the exact connection to the Barcelona attack is still under investigation.

Spanish Prime Minister Mariano Rajoy called the killings a "savage terrorist attack" and said Spaniards "are not just united in mourning, but especially in the firm determination to beat those who want to rob us of our values and our way of life."

After the afternoon attack, Las Ramblas went into lockdown. Swarms of officers brandishing hand guns and automatic weapons launched a manhunt in the downtown district, ordering stores and cafes and public transport to shut down.

Several hours later, authorities reported two arrests, one a Spanish national from Melilla, a Spanish-run Mediterranean seafront enclave in North Africa, and the other a Moroccan. The arrests took place in the northern Catalan town of Ripoll and in Alcanar, where a gas explosion in a house is being investigated for a possible connection.

Media outlets ran photographs of one of the detained as Driss Oukabir, a French citizen of Moroccan origin. RTVE reported that Oukabir went to police in Ripoll to report that his identity documents had been stolen. Various Spanish media said the IDs with his name were found in the attack van and that he claimed his brother might have stolen them.

Barcelona is the latest European city where attackers used a vehicle as a weapon of terror against a popular tourist destination, after other deadly attacks in France, Germany, Sweden, and Britain.

The attack has been condemned by leaders around the world, including President Donald Trump and British Prime Minister Theresa May. Spain has been on a security alert one step below the maximum since June 2015 following attacks elsewhere in Europe and Africa.

The Benghazi Select Committee, a bipartisan panel established to investigate the 2012 attack on the U.S. diplomatic compound in Benghazi, Libya, has released its final report. The report includes new details about a two-hour video teleconference call held the night of the attack, which was led by White House Chief of Staff Denis McDonough and included Secretary of State Hillary Clinton and top Defense officials. The discussion, according to GOP investigators, centered on the attack's causes rather than rescue plans, with many action items written down during the meeting focusing on an anti-Islam video, which the administration would later incorrectly blame for the violence.

The report also reveals that a State Department official brought up concerns about whether Marines should wear civilian clothing instead of their uniforms during the attack, citing concerns that flags on the uniforms could hurt diplomacy in the region. However, a commander testified that Marines had to change in and out of their uniforms multiple times as they prepared to deploy, and the military never actually deployed to Benghazi.

The report also includes a timeline of public and private statements made by top Obama administration officials in the days following the attack, which contrasts the story they told the public with their private conversations. The timeline reinforces the committee's finding that the Obama administration knowingly provided the American people with a false story about the Benghazi attack, its causes, and its consequences.

Rep. Elijah Cummings (D-Md.), the panel's ranking Democrat, has criticized the panel's process, accusing Chairman Trey Gowdy (R-S.C.) of trying to prevent accountability for the panel's GOP lawmakers and of hiding transcripts from Democrats. Cummings has also stated that the panel's report does not alter the public's understanding of the 2012 attack in Benghazi.

The report also includes criticism of Secretary Clinton, accusing her of not adequately heeding concerns about growing extremism in Libya and of falsely blaming the violence on an anti-Muslim video. Clinton has since blamed her statements on changing information received from U.S. intelligence reports.

In this exclusive behind-the-scenes interview, BBC's State Department Correspondent Kim Ghattas gains access to Hillary Clinton during a recent diplomatic trip. The interview takes place on "special air mission 883" as it travels from the US to the Middle East and Africa. Clinton discusses various topics, including the mechanical issues with her plane, her work environment, jet lag, and her personal experiences.

Clinton shares insights about her plane, stating that it feels more like an office than a home due to its secure communications and capable team. She also mentions that jet lag is a challenge but manages it by sleeping on the plane, drinking water, and practicing deep breathing.

During the interview, Clinton also talks about her interactions with airport staff in Shannon, Ireland, and the concept of the "bubble" that surrounds her when traveling. She acknowledges that while the bubble can be isolating, it allows her to focus on her work and the goals of the United States.

Clinton discusses her encounters with leaders around the world, some of whom she has personal relationships with due to her prior roles. She also shares her thoughts on America's role in the world and the importance of restoring its leadership.

The interview concludes with Clinton discussing her personal life and her sense of humor, which is not often showcased in the public eye. Clinton expresses her intention to return to private life at the end of her current term as Secretary of State.

Japan, known for its longstanding issue of "karoshi" or death by overwork, is introducing a new initiative called "Premium Friday" to encourage workers to leave work early on the last Friday of every month. The goal is to spur consumption and improve work-life balance. The scheme suggests companies make employees go home at 3 PM on the designated day, starting in February. However, it is unclear how many companies will participate, and the government ministry behind the idea has not yet decided if its officials will join in.

The initiative comes after the suicide of a woman working over 100 hours of overtime a month at Japan's biggest ad agency, Dentsu. Her death was ruled a case of "karoshi," leading to an investigation, the resignation of the firm's CEO, and widespread concern about Japan's work culture.

Despite previous attempts to address excessive work hours, few have been successful. The government has tried to make employees take more of their entitled leave, increase public holidays, and encourage flexible hours, but with limited success.

The economy has stagnated for over two decades due to low consumption spending, a very low birth rate, and workers spending most of their waking hours at a desk. Productivity and efficiency also suffer from firms having staff perpetually on hand, as companies don't invest in labor-saving technologies.

If most workers participate, private consumption could rise by about ¥124 billion on each Premium Friday, according to calculations by Toshihiro Nagahama, chief economist at Dai-ichi Life Research Institute in Tokyo. However, Nagahama is concerned that workers at smaller companies may have difficulty leaving early or may simply make up the time on other days, limiting the campaign's impact.

Changing deeply-rooted attitudes to work will be difficult, but the effort might be helped by Japanese workers' declining corporate loyalty. Younger Japanese people, cut adrift by years of restructuring from the lifetime employment bargain that bound their fathers to a single firm, may find that the chance to head to the izakaya (pub) a bit earlier some Fridays is just the nudge they need to adopt a better work-life balance.

In an effort to become fossil fuel-free by 2020, a Swedish power plant in Vasteras is burning recycled wood and trash, including discarded clothing from H&M's central warehouse. The power plant, which supplies power to about 150,000 households, aims to eliminate the use of coal and oil by converting old plants to burn biofuels and garbage. The clothes burned by the plant are those that H&M deems unsafe for wearing due to mold or chemical contamination.

While Sweden is a leader in eliminating the use of fossil fuels, the fast fashion cycle encouraged by brands such as H&M is far from sustainable. The fast fashion industry is resource-intensive and encourages an environmentally catastrophic cycle of ever-increasing production to meet rising demands in markets such as Brazil, China, India, Mexico, and Russia.

Textiles can be recycled in various ways, with nearly half of donated clothing getting worn again, a large portion being recycled into things like insulation and carpet padding, and a slightly smaller portion being turned into industrial rags. The textile-recycling industry is now trying to clear up the confusion surrounding the proper disposal of old clothes, with the goal of changing the dialogue to "you're not just donating, you're reusing and recycling."

Charities have been the de facto national textile recyclers in the US for decades, but the system was set up in a pre-consumerist America, when we had neither a landfill crunch nor a waste crisis. With Americans now buying five times as much clothing as they did in 1980, charities have seen themselves transformed into dumps that accept clothes of varying condition in ever-increasing volumes.

The power plant in Vasteras burned about 15 tons of discarded clothing from H&M so far in 2017, making it a minuscule percentage of the 400,000 tons of trash it has burned. On December 28, 2016, President Barack Obama designated two national monuments in Utah and Nevada, marking the administration's latest move to protect environmentally sensitive areas before the end of his term. The Bears Ears National Monument in Utah covers 1.35 million acres in the Four Corners region and protects land considered sacred by Native American tribes and conservationists, as well as an estimated 100,000 archaeological sites, including ancient cliff dwellings. The designation was met with opposition from state Republican leaders and rural residents who argue it adds another layer of federal control and restricts energy development.

In Nevada, a 300,000-acre Gold Butte National Monument outside Las Vegas was established to protect a scenic and ecologically fragile area near where rancher Cliven Bundy led an armed standoff with government agents in 2014. The site includes rock art, artifacts, rare fossils, and recently discovered dinosaur tracks.

The White House and conservationists said both sites were at risk of looting and vandalism. Obama said in a statement, "Today's actions will help protect this cultural legacy and will ensure that future generations are able to enjoy and appreciate these scenic and historic landscapes."

The designations were criticized by Utah's Republican senators, who vowed to work towards reversing them. Sen. Mike Lee tweeted, "This arrogant act by a lame duck president will not stand." Sen. Orrin Hatch said Obama showed "an astonishing and egregious abuse of executive power."

The Antiquities Act, which allows a president to create monuments, does not give a president the authority to undo a designation, according to the White House Council on Environmental Quality. However, Congress could take action.

Opponents agreed that the areas are natural treasures worth preserving but worried the designations would restrict oil and gas development as well as residents' ability to camp, bike, hike, and gather wood. New mining or energy development will be banned, but existing operations won't be affected, federal officials said. Wood and plant gathering is still allowed as well as hunting, fishing, and other recreation, they said.

The Colorado River winds around the northern reaches of the proposed Bear Ears National Monument, with Canyonlands National Park in the background. The Navajo Nation, one of five tribes that will get an elected official on a first-of-its-kind tribal commission for the Bears Ears monument, called it an exciting day for their tribe and people of all cultures.

The Gold Butte site features Native American rock art and artifacts scattered amid rugged mountains, sandstone formations, and Joshua tree forests. Pioneers used the area for cattle ranching and mining, while campers and ATV riders enjoy it today. It's named for an early 1900s mining town.

Retiring Democratic Sen. Harry Reid pushed for protection of the remote area northeast of Lake Mead, but GOP members of Nevada's congressional delegation have been vocal opponents. The "designation is a wonderful capstone to a career of fighting to protect Nevada's pristine landscapes," Reid said in a statement. Nevada Sen. Dean Heller and Gov. Brian Sandoval, both Republicans, said Congress should make land designations. However, the governor said he "recognized the inevitability" of the move and met with landowners and White House officials to ensure it aligned with state water law and the land would be open to recreation.

Celebrity chef Anthony Bourdain, known for his CNN series "Parts Unknown," was found dead in a French hotel room on Friday, June 8th, in the ancient village of Kaysersberg. The French prosecutor, Christian de Rocquigny, stated that there is no evidence of foul play or violence, and preliminary findings suggest that Bourdain took his own life. There were no signs of violence on his body, but toxicology tests are being conducted to determine if he took any medications or other drugs. The luxury hotel owner, Olivier Nasti, paid tribute to Bourdain, expressing condolences to his family and the global community that he inspired. The French gastronomy community also mourned the loss of their esteemed colleague.

The Cleveland police released a 30-minute surveillance video showing the aftermath of the fatal shooting of 12-year-old Tamir Rice by a Cleveland police officer. The video, obtained by Northeast Ohio Media Group after protracted negotiations with city officials, shows Tamir's 14-year-old sister being forced to the ground, handcuffed, and placed in the back of a police car, just feet away from her wounded brother. The video also reveals that officers waited several minutes before administering first aid to Tamir, and that the first medical care he received was from an FBI agent, not from the police. The video has raised questions about the actions of the officers involved and has been criticized by Tamir's family and their attorney, who called the treatment of Tamir's sister "the cruelest thing I've ever seen." The investigation into the shooting has been handed over to the Cuyahoga County Sheriff's Department, and the case will be presented to a grand jury to determine if criminal charges should be filed against the officers involved. The city has not yet commented on the video.

In a significant development, soldiers in Mali, one of Africa's few established democracies, stormed the presidential palace on March 21, 2012, and announced they had seized control of the country. The mutinous soldiers ousted President Amadou Toumani Toure, just one month before he was due to step down at the end of his legal term. The coup was sparked by the government's perceived mishandling of an ethnic Tuareg insurgency in the country's north, which began in mid-January. The rebellion grew when fighters who had supported the late Libyan leader Moammar Gadhafi returned home heavily armed. The unrest has forced tens of thousands to flee and has prompted fierce criticism of Mali's government.

The soldiers formed the National Committee for the Reestablishment of Democracy and the Restoration of the State, or CNRDR, and suspended the constitution and dissolved institutions. They claimed they were overthrowing the government to combat the rebellion by the ethnic Tuareg separatists, who want to carve out a homeland in the country's northern desert. The CNRDR promised to return power to a democratically elected president as soon as national unity and territorial integrity are established.

The West African regional bloc ECOWAS strongly condemned the coup, describing it as "reprehensible" and a setback for the region's democracies. The ousted president, Amadou Toumani Toure, was hailed for handing power to civilians after coming to power in a 1991 coup, and later won the 2002 democratic election. His whereabouts were unknown on the day of the coup.

The coup was preceded by a mutiny at a military camp in the capital, where Defense Minister Gen. Sadio Gassama came for an official visit. In his speech to the troops, the minister failed to address the grievances of the rank-and-file soldiers, who were dissatisfied with the government's handling of the rebellion and the lack of supplies, including arms and food. The rebellion has claimed the lives of numerous soldiers.

The events culminated in gunfire throughout the capital, with the mutinous soldiers imposing a nationwide curfew and forcing a flight to the capital to make a U-turn in the air after the airport closed. Civilians in Bamako cheered as mutinous soldiers drove past, with gunshots still being heard late into the night. The coup is a major setback for Mali's democracy and regional stability.

NASA has launched a competition, the "Space Poop Challenge," to find solutions for managing human waste in space suits for up to six days. The goal is to award up to three $30,000 prizes for the most promising in-suit waste management systems. The challenge is crucial for future long-distance missions, as current diapers are only suitable for short-term use. The systems must be hands-free, operate in microgravity, and be compatible with NASA's Modified Advanced Crew Escape Suit. The deadline for submissions is December 20, 2016, and winners will be announced on January 31, 2017. The challenge aims to test the winning ideas within a year and implement them within three years, with the first human missions to Mars expected by the 2030s.

Currently, astronauts use a toilet on the International Space Station (ISS) with a vacuum and tube for fecal matter and a funnel and hose for urine. However, in emergency situations, astronauts may need to wear a spacesuit for extended periods, making waste management a significant challenge. In space, fluids can blob up and stick to surfaces, while solids float in the air. If waste is not properly managed, it could harm or even kill the astronaut.

NASA has been working on this challenge themselves, but they are seeking help from the crowd to come up with innovative solutions. The challenge is part of an effort to archive pages as they are created and archive the pages they refer to, to fix all broken links on the web. The goal is to ensure that the Space Poop Challenge guidelines and rules are preserved for future reference.

The Space Poop Challenge is an opportunity for innovators to take their place in the annals of space travel history and potentially make a significant contribution to human space exploration. The challenge is open to individuals, private teams, public teams, and collegiate teams, and no specific qualifications or expertise in the field of microgravity or waste management are required. Submissions must be made online and in English, and the deadline for submissions is December 20, 2016. The determination of the winners will be made by NASA specialists, and winners will be announced on January 31, 2017.

At a joint press conference in Warsaw, Secretary of State John Kerry was caught napping during his boss, President Obama's speech. The conference marked the start of Obama's European tour, during which he announced a $1 billion plan to boost U.S. military presence in Europe. Obama also addressed the Ukraine crisis, expressing a willingness to rebuild trust with Russia, but acknowledging it would take time. Kerry was also engaged in diplomatic discussions regarding defense and modernizing relations with Russia. The incident of Kerry dozing off was captured on video by ABC News.

The top Homeland Security official, Suzanne Barr, chief of staff for Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), has taken a leave of absence amidst allegations of a "frat-house"-style work environment. Two new affidavits have been submitted this week detailing lewd conduct inside ICE, including graphic comments made by Barr. These affidavits were given as part of a discrimination and retaliation suit filed earlier this year by James T. Hayes Jr., the head of the New York office for ICE. The new affidavits describe separate incidents in 2009, with one detailing Barr making inappropriate comments about a senior ICE employee's appearance and another describing a trip to Colombia where Barr and another official were accused of sending lewd messages and making inappropriate advances. ICE has referred these allegations to the DHS Office of Inspector General and the ICE Office of Professional Responsibility for review. The lawsuit also names Dora Schriro, who was brought on as a special adviser to Homeland Security Secretary Janet Napolitano, as a defendant. Hayes claims Schriro was not qualified for the job and was favored because of a long-standing relationship with Napolitano. The charges have added to a sense of unrest in ICE, which has been suffering major labor conflicts between senior officials and employees.

Daivon Reeder, a local college graduate from Eastern Michigan University, has gained significant attention on social media due to a viral tweet about his stepfather's skepticism towards his ability to graduate. Reeder, who majored in Criminal Justice and minored in Military Science, faced numerous obstacles throughout his college journey, including losing a scholarship, basic training for the Army, family problems, and being a black male student in a predominantly white university. Despite these challenges, Reeder persevered and formed an organization to mentor young boys, teaching them what he had to learn the hard way. His tweet, which has since gone viral, has received thousands of congratulations for proving his stepfather wrong. Reeder, who works two jobs to support his family, will walk with his entire EMU class on Saturday and officially accept his diploma. A former National Security Agency (NSA) contractor, Reality Winner, has agreed to a plea deal after being charged under the Espionage Act for leaking a top-secret government report about Russian meddling in the 2016 presidential election. Winner's mother believes this was the only way she could receive a fair sentence, despite her disagreement with the use of the Espionage charge. The plea agreement was reached after an 18-minute conference call on Wednesday with U.S. Magistrate Judge Brian Epps.

The leaked document, which was provided anonymously to The Intercept, is the most detailed U.S. government account of Russian interference in the election that has yet come to light. It reveals that Russian military intelligence executed a cyberattack on at least one U.S. voting software supplier and sent spear-phishing emails to more than 100 local election officials just days before the 2016 presidential election.

The NSA report indicates that Russian government hackers focused on parts of the voting system directly connected to the voter registration process, including a private sector manufacturer of devices that maintain and verify the voter rolls. The report raises the possibility that Russian hacking may have breached at least some elements of the voting system, with disconcertingly uncertain results.

The Obama administration's leak investigations usually ended in pleas to minor offenses, as shown by cases like John Kiriakou and David Petraeus. However, under the Trump administration, this will mark the second guilty plea in an anti-leak drive, following an FBI agent who pleaded guilty in April.

Reality Winner's plea hearing is scheduled for Tuesday, and the details of her plea arrangement will be revealed at the hearing. Her mother has stated that she will continue to support her daughter, who she believes is a patriot and a hero. The case has attracted international attention and garnered impassioned support from the left and rebuke from the right.

Russell Brand caused a stir at the GQ Men of the Year Awards after-party when he made offensive comments about the event's sponsor, Hugo Boss, and its historical links to the Nazis. Brand, who won an Oracle award at the event, took to the stage after Boris Johnson and made jibes about the use of chemical weapons in Syria and the sponsor's past. He also mimicked Hitler's moustache and goose-stepped on stage, which reportedly led to his ejection from the after-party. GQ editor Dylan Jones told Brand that his comments were offensive to Hugo Boss. Brand later took to Twitter to share an exchange he said he had with Jones, writing, "GQ editor: What you did was very offensive to Hugo Boss. Me: What Hugo Boss did was very offensive to the Jews." The fashion firm backed the event to the tune of £250,000 and would no doubt have been left reeling by Brand's tirade. The event, which was hosted by comic Rob Brydon, was attended by celebrities including Rita Ora, Rosie Huntington-Whiteley, and Justin Timberlake. Brand has run into trouble at the annual bash in the past, including a row with Rod Stewart in 2006. In 1999, GQ editor James Brown resigned after the magazine published a list of the 200 most stylish men of the 20th century, which included the Nazis and Field Marshal Rommel alongside Humphrey Bogart and John F Kennedy.

The New Jersey Supreme Court has ruled that more than 20,000 drunken-driving convictions could be in jeopardy due to issues with breathalyzer tests. The ruling stems from criminal charges brought against a State Police sergeant, Sgt. Marc Dennis, who was accused of falsifying calibration records on breath test devices used in five of New Jersey’s 21 counties. The court found that the test results from these counties are inadmissible as evidence.

The court's decision means that as many as 20,667 DWI convictions could now be challenged. The accusations against Dennis called into question any test result involving a machine he handled, including devices used by local police in Middlesex, Monmouth, Ocean, Somerset, and Union counties between 2008 and 2016.

The court ordered state authorities to notify anyone whose case involved results from machines Dennis calibrated that those results were not scientifically sound. It's unclear how state courts and law enforcement officials will now proceed, but the Supreme Court ruling does not automatically expunge all the drunken-driving convictions.

Attorney General Gurbir Grewal said his office was reviewing the decision and would issue guidance for county and municipal prosecutors on how to handle these cases. However, many of the defendants may have already served their sentences, and it remains to be seen how many will come forward to challenge their convictions.

The case was brought to the court by Eileen Cassidy, a New Jersey woman who died of a terminal illness in March. Her lawyer, Michael Hobbie, represented her in the case, which the justices ruled on because of the "significant public importance" of the issue.

Bristol Palin was eliminated from "Dancing with the Stars: All-Stars" this week, despite not receiving the lowest score from the judges. Kirstie Alley and Apolo Ohno were also in the bottom three. Palin's mother, former Republican vice presidential candidate Sarah Palin, was in attendance to see her daughter's elimination. Mark Ballas, Palin's partner, expressed disappointment but was proud of Palin's progress, as she had limited dance experience. The remaining all-stars will perform a team freestyle dance and an individual dance to their guilty pleasure song next week. The show airs on ABC on Mondays and Tuesdays at 8 p.m. ET. Some viewers on Twitter supported Palin's elimination, while Ballas and Palin's elimination did not come as a surprise to some. Ballas plans to root for Shawn Johnson and Derek Hough to win the mirror-ball trophy.

In a recent development, it has been clarified that Mitt Romney, a potential presidential candidate, is not planning to quadruple the size of his beachfront property as previously reported, but instead double it. The confusion arose due to a technicality in the measurement of non-living space, such as basements and garages, which were included in the initial estimate. The Union Leader, a New Hampshire newspaper, published this correction following a conversation with Romney. The publisher, Joe McQuaid, expressed his concern about the media's accuracy in reporting on Romney's wealth and emphasized the importance of fact-checking to avoid perpetuating preconceived notions. The incident serves as a reminder of the need for accurate reporting in the media, particularly when it comes to public figures' financial affairs.

Endo Pharmaceuticals has established a website for employees to donate to the American Red Cross Disaster Relief in support of the communities affected by the recent spring storms in Huntsville, Alabama. The company will match all donations made by March 21, 2012.

Meanwhile, in a historic event, U.S. cell phone users donated over $8 million by 8:25 a.m. EDT on Friday to the Red Cross for Haiti earthquake relief. The donations, made in $10 increments, represent the largest outpouring of support via mobile devices in history. To donate, mobile users texted "Haiti" to the number 90999. As of Thursday afternoon, over $5.1 million had been donated.

The Red Cross has released $10 million for earthquake relief in Haiti. Other charities, such as singer Wyclef Jean's Yele and the William J. Clinton Foundation, were also collecting mobile donations. Verizon Wireless reported that its users had pledged over $1 million to the Red Cross through text donations, surpassing earlier records for mobile giving.

Wireless carriers, including AT&T, Verizon Wireless, and Sprint, said they were not charging regular text-messaging fees on top of the donations. T-Mobile USA Inc. waived texting fees and enabled international calls to Haiti free of charge through January 31.

However, controversy arose when it was revealed that AT&T and Sprint were charging for the popular "text HAITI to 90999 to donate $10" meme, despite claims that they were not. Critics argue that this undermines the goodwill of the donations and takes advantage of the public tragedy for profit.

In conclusion, the response to the Haiti earthquake has seen an unprecedented outpouring of support via mobile devices, with over $3 million donated as of Friday. Endo Pharmaceuticals and other companies are also making donations to support disaster relief efforts.

The Ukrainian government has announced that it will only restart cease-fire negotiations with pro-Russian insurgents in the country's east once the rebels lay down their weapons, according to Ukrainian Defense Minister Valery Heletey. This statement comes after Ukrainian forces drove the insurgent militia from their stronghold of Slovyansk last week, a significant victory for Ukraine. The insurgents are unlikely to agree to negotiations in Svyatogorsk, a town controlled by Kiev, as they have suggested locations such as Donetsk, Russia, or Belarus.

The insurgency in eastern Ukraine has resulted in over 400 deaths and the displacement of thousands since February, when the ex-president was ousted. The rebels have called for Russian protection, but Russian President Vladimir Putin has yet to comment on the rebels' defeat in Slovyansk. The West has imposed sanctions on Russia for its role in the annexation of Crimea in March.

Ukrainian forces established a siege around Slavyansk in early May, but the blockade was fractured and the checkpoints were vulnerable to attacks by rebel forces based in the city. On Saturday, Ukrainian troops routed the rebels in Slovyansk, forcing hundreds of militants to regroup in Donetsk. Fears are growing of a similar siege in Donetsk, which has a population of one million, ten times that of Slavyansk.

The exact extent of the damage in Slavyansk is still difficult to assess due to strict control by the Ukrainians. Despite the victory, the city is still far from returning to pre-war normality, with no running water or electricity, few businesses open, and most of the civilian population having fled or remaining indoors. The war is far from over, and the rebels' dogged defense of Slavyansk and the breakout shows a level of motivation that will make any battle for Donetsk a bloody affair.

On the first anniversary of the Boston Marathon bombing, survivors, first responders, and family members of the victims gathered to commemorate the tragic event with solemn ceremonies. The ceremonies included a wreath-laying ceremony at the Forum restaurant, where one of the bombs exploded, and a moment of silence at the marathon finish line. Vice President Joe Biden was among the dignitaries in attendance.

The ceremony held at the Hynes Convention Center was attended by survivors such as Patrick Downes and Adrianne Haslet-Davis, both of whom lost their lower left legs in the bombings. Downes spoke of the sense of community that has developed among the survivors, while Haslet-Davis called on people to support those in their community who need help.

Former Mayor Thomas Menino told the audience that the heartbeat of Boston is a mighty force and that the city has inspired the world with its resilience. President Obama also released a statement recognizing the courage and leadership of Bostonians in the wake of the tragedy, and expressing gratitude to the first responders, medical professionals, and runners who displayed the spirit of Boston - perseverance, freedom, and love.

The Tsarnaev brothers, ethnic Chechens who lived in the former Soviet republic of Kyrgyzstan and the Dagestan region of Russia, settled in Cambridge, outside Boston, more than a decade ago after moving to the U.S. as children with their family. Prosecutors have said Dzhokhar Tsarnaev left a hand-scrawled confession condemning U.S. actions in Muslim countries on the inside wall of a boat he was found hiding in following the police shootout.

The anniversary was an emotional day for many, with Boston police Commissioner Williams Evans saying it brings back "some terrible memories." However, the city came together to honor the victims and show their strength and resilience. A moment of silence, flag-raising ceremony, and the tolling of church bells marked the occasion, with the American flag raised and the national anthem sung shortly before 3 p.m. on the spot where explosions, carnage, screams, and smoke interrupted one of the city's most joyous and popular events one year ago.

The impending retirement of Pope Benedict XVI, who will be the first living ex-pontiff in six centuries, has sparked a debate within the Vatican over his future status. On Ash Wednesday, Pope Benedict issued a warning to the cardinals who will elect his successor, criticizing internal rivalries that have plagued his eight-year papacy. He also made plans to appoint a new chief of the Vatican bank, which has been accused of money-laundering.

Pope Benedict will live inside the Vatican after his retirement on February 28, continuing to write and pray. He will retain his intellectual status as one of Roman Catholicism's leading theologians, but will give up all formal powers of his office. The pope will move to a renovated convent within Vatican walls, and some analysts have raised concerns about his potential influence over his successor.

The pope has made clear that he has no intention of interfering with his successor's work. The details of his retirement, including his title, writings, and the color of his vestments, will have significant ramifications for the church. The pope intends to keep a low profile and avoid any "dueling popes."

In the 13th century, Pope Celestine V resigned under pressure and was imprisoned by his successor out of fear of a rivalry. However, Pope Benedict has dispelled such fears by publicly stating that his resignation is his own choice.

Pope Benedict's final Ash Wednesday mass was attended by thousands of people, including dozens of cardinals who removed their miters in a sign of respect. The pope's voice was hoarse at times, and he expressed his intention to live a life of prayer, hidden from the world.

The Vatican has yet to decide on the pope's title or the color of his vestments. Some analysts suggest that he should be referred to as Cardinal Joseph Ratzinger and wear the robes of a cardinal rather than the white cassock of a pope. The pope's retirement marks uncharted waters for the Vatican, and experts are still navigating the complexities of his future role.

A mother of triplets, Rachel Park, has tragically passed away at her home in Whitehaven, Cumbria, just days after celebrating her first Christmas with her children. The triplets, Poppie, Mollie, and Evelyn, were born prematurely in March and spent several months in hospitals in Newcastle and Whitehaven. An online fundraising campaign has been launched to support Rachel's husband, Steven, in caring for the youngsters.

Rachel was a source of support for other mothers in similar situations, and her friend Lucy Dawson described her as a good friend and a good support to other ladies who had triplets in the area and across the UK. Julie Hodgson, who also helped set up the appeals, said the aim was to give Mrs Park's family the support they need now and in the coming months.

The triplets were born 14 weeks early and spent over three months in Newcastle's Royal Victoria Infirmary. The family was supported by The Sick Children's Trust, which provided free accommodation at its Crawford House site. After leaving Newcastle, the girls were admitted to West Cumberland Hospital as they still had feeding issues.

The combined birthweight of the triplets was just 5lb 2oz – three tiny sisters weighing together as much as one small newborn alone. The triplets fought for their lives in hospital for the first two months, and their parents were told to prepare for the worst. However, they have made great strides and are now home and weighing "roughly 14 pounds each."

Steven said, "When we look back on how poorly the girls were and where they are now – they’ve come so far and we’re just full of pride." He added that they have blips but nothing life-threatening and they're heading in the right direction. The family is planning to make their first Christmas extra special, as they were scared that the triplets may not make it this far.

GoFundMe has verified that the funds raised will go directly to the intended recipient. The family and friends of Rachel and Steven are asking for donations to help support the family during this difficult time. Tributes have been pouring in for Rachel, with many describing her death as "totally tragic and heartbreaking."

The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) is set to implement a new rule requiring cleaner gasoline and lower-pollution vehicles nationwide, one of President Obama's most significant air pollution initiatives. The proposed standards, which have faced resistance from the oil industry, would reduce the amount of sulfur in U.S. gasoline by two-thirds and impose fleet-wide pollution limits on new vehicles by 2017.

The automakers support the rule, as it aligns with stricter emissions standards they already adhere to in California. The EPA estimates that the annual health benefits of the new standards could reach up to $23 billion by 2030. However, oil industry officials argue that the cost of upgrading refineries to comply with the standards could be as high as $10 billion, with additional annual operating costs of $2.4 billion.

The automakers, represented by the Alliance of Automobile Manufacturers and Global Automakers, along with several major car manufacturers, met with White House Office of Management and Budget aides on March 22 to express their support for the EPA's planned "Tier 3" fuel and vehicle emissions rule. They argue that the costs for refiners to further reduce sulfur content have been overstated, as refiners are already producing ultra-low sulfur fuels in California and much of the developed world.

Oil industry officials, on the other hand, contend that the new standards will create billions of dollars in compliance costs while providing little benefit, as existing standards have already required steep cuts in sulfur content. They argue that the EPA is pushing ahead with tougher sulfur rules "without regard to the impacts on fuel prices."

The new standards have the potential to cut major contributors to smog-forming ozone and pollution by 80% and 70%, respectively, according to the administration official. However, critics remain skeptical, with some lawmakers appealing to the White House for a one-year delay in implementing the proposal. The final decision on the rule is expected to be announced on Friday.

The driver managed to stop the train soon after the accident, but the teenager was taken to John Hunter Hospital in critical condition. A 16-year-old girl has been charged as an adult for the murder of her 7-year-old nephew, Jordan Vong, in Denver. In a surprising turn of events, the defence of Dennis Oland, the accused in the 2011 second-degree murder of his father, prominent New Brunswick businessman Richard Oland, abruptly closed its case on Thursday. The trial, which began on September 16, has been one of the longest in New Brunswick's history.

Dennis Oland, the only son of a Canadian beer magnate, testified in his own defence on Tuesday and Wednesday, expressing his love for his father and asserting his innocence in the brutal killing. Richard Oland, 69, was found dead in his Saint John office on July 7, 2011, suffering from 45 sharp and blunt force injuries to his head, neck, and hands. No weapon was ever found.

The defence called only two additional witnesses, a bloodstain analyst and a forensic computer expert, apart from Dennis Oland. Witnesses expected to testify on his behalf included his mother, Connie, sister, Jacqueline Walsh, wife, Lisa Andrik-Oland, uncle, Jack Connell, and friend Mary Beth Watt.

The jurors are expected to receive the case as early as Dec. 16. The trial has been a long and detailed one, with testimony from nearly 50 witnesses over 47 days. Judge John Walsh has warned that his charge to the jury could be lengthy, possibly up to two days.

During his testimony, Dennis Oland acknowledged inconsistencies between his statement to Saint John police and his current testimony. He was "nervous, in shock, and sad" at the time of the statement, having just learned of his father's death, and remembers his comings and goings more clearly now. Among these inconsistencies, Oland told police he was wearing a navy blazer when he visited his father on the night in question, but video surveillance and witness testimony showed he was actually wearing a brown sports jacket. A brown sports jacket seized from Dennis Oland's bedroom closet had three bloodstains on it, and the DNA extracted from those areas matched his father's.

The Crown has suggested financial problems and Richard Oland's extramarital affair as possible motives in the slaying. Under questioning by his lawyer, Oland said he didn't discuss either of those issues with his father during their meeting. The trial is likely to wrap up earlier than expected, possibly as soon as Friday. If found guilty, Oland's legal team is expected to appeal all the way to the Supreme Court. The outcome of the trial has stirred up a lot of gossip and speculation in the community.

The report published by the Economic Policy Institute on Thursday reveals that the CEOs of America's top 350 companies earned an average of 312 times more than their workers in 2017, marking a significant increase from the previous year. The rise in CEO pay came after a 17.6% increase in average compensation, with CEOs taking home an average of $18.9 million. In contrast, worker wages stalled, rising just 0.3% over the year.

The pay gap between CEOs and workers has been on the rise since the 1990s, with some fluctuations. In 1965, the ratio of CEO to worker pay was 20 to one; by 1989 it had risen to 58 to one, and peaked in 2000 at 344 to one. Since then, CEO pay has dipped during economic downturns but has been rising rapidly since 2009.

The report highlights the CEOs of large firms now earning 5.5 times as much as the average earner in the top 0.1%. McDonald's CEO Steve Easterbrook earned $21.7 million in 2017 while the median wage for McDonald's workers was just $7,017, resulting in a CEO to worker pay ratio of 3,101 to one. The average Walmart worker earned $19,177 in 2017 while CEO Doug McMillon took home $22.8 million, resulting in a ratio of 1,188 to one.

The report attributes the astronomical pay gap to stock-related components of CEO compensation such as stock awards or the opportunity to cash in stock options. According to Lawrence Mishel, a distinguished fellow at the Economic Policy Institute, the rise in CEO compensation cannot be entirely explained by rising stock markets. Between 1978 and 2017, CEO compensation has increased by 979%, while the S&P 500 Index of the US’s largest companies grew 637%. The typical worker's pay package rose just 11.2% over the same time frame.

The report also notes that accidents at Amazon have been a concern, with workers left to suffer after warehouse injuries.

The report concludes that the outsize pay packets have had a direct impact on people down the corporate ladder, with Mishel claiming that the redistribution of wages to the top 5%, but particularly the top 1%, affected the wage growth of the bottom 90%. According to Mishel, had there not been the redistribution upward, the wages of the bottom 90% could have grown twice as fast as it actually did.

The report also includes a box on abnormalities in the fair value measure of stock awarded under plan-based awards in 2017. This affected the measure of CEO compensation based on stock-related awards for the year's report, causing the average CEO compensation to artificially fall by nearly $2 million on average per CEO.

The report also includes historical data on CEO compensation since the 1960s, showing a steady increase in CEO compensation, even during periods of stock market decline. The report also discusses the theory that CEOs are enjoying high and rising pay because their individual productivity is increasing, but notes that CEO compensation often grows strongly when the overall stock market rises and individual firms’ stock values rise along with it.

The report also discusses the new financial disclosure rule that forces companies to publish the ratio of CEO to worker pay, and the impact this has had on bringing the pay gap into sharper focus.

The report concludes by discussing policy options that could reverse the trend of excessive executive pay and broaden wage growth, including higher marginal income tax rates at the very top, setting corporate tax rates higher for firms with high ratios of CEO-to-worker compensation, and changes in corporate governance such as greater use of "say on pay."

A massive and mysterious bloom of pyrosomes, often referred to as the "unicorn of the sea" or "sea pickles", has swarmed the west coast of America, causing issues for fishermen and intriguing scientists. The tiny, translucent marine creatures, which are typically found in warm, tropical seas, have appeared in unprecedented numbers along the west coast, from Oregon to Alaska.

The pyrosomes, which are actually colonies of tiny organisms, have been ruining fishermen's nets and washing up on beaches, baffling locals. Researchers are scrambling to learn more about the bloom, with concerns about its potential impact on the ecosystem and the economy.

Ocean Networks Canada tweeted that they are seeing huge numbers of pyrosomes in the eastern Pacific. Pyrosomes are tubular, gelatinous creatures that can grow up to 30 meters long. They reproduce asexually by cloning themselves and have long fascinated seafarers.

Olivia Blondheim, a graduate student at the University of Oregon, is part of a new research team studying the bloom. She said no one knows how much surface area the bloom covers, but it has gathered in mammoth clusters right along the west coast.

Dr Lisa-ann Gershwin, a marine biology expert, said that while gargantuan blooms of pyrosomes have occurred in unlikely places before, the current bloom is unusual. She suggested that it could be a natural phenomenon, but also speculated that it could be due to warming sea temperatures caused by climate change, a change in the animals' diet, or unusual sea currents.

Researchers are collecting live pyrosomes to study in their labs, hoping to learn more about their feeding habits, swimming speed, and orientation in the water. The long-term effects of the bloom are unknown, but scientists worry that if all the creatures die off at once, they could create a dead zone for marine life by depleting oxygen as they decompose.

Facebook has revealed that a likely Russia-based group spent approximately $100,000 on political ads promoting divisive social and political messages during a two-year period leading up to the 2016 US election. The ads, which were spread through 3,000 ads and 470 "inauthentic" accounts and pages, touched on topics such as immigration, race, and gay rights, without explicitly backing a particular candidate.

Facebook's chief security officer, Alex Stamos, announced the findings in a blog post, stating that the company is cooperating with federal investigations into influence operations during the 2016 presidential election. The ads were mostly national in scope and did not appear to target political swing states.

The company did not release the names of the suspended pages, but some of them included words like "refugee" and "patriot." Although the spending is relatively small compared to overall campaign costs, the report from Facebook suggests that a Russian firm was able to target political messages, which could fuel questions about potential coordination between the Russians and the Trump campaign.

Facebook has been under criticism for serving as a platform for the spread of false information before the election. In a statement posted after the election, Facebook founder Mark Zuckerberg promised to explore the issue but later announced that it would begin flagging articles deemed false or fake with the assistance of fact-checking organizations.

The House Intelligence Committee will follow up with Facebook and other social media companies to investigate the extent to which they were able to confirm similar metrics. Representative Adam Schiff, the senior Democrat on the House Intelligence Committee, stated that the disclosure by Facebook serves as a "profound warning" about future elections.

The Internet Research Agency, a Russian "troll farm" with a history of pushing pro-Kremlin propaganda, is believed to be connected to the divisive ads. Although Facebook does not have the ability to determine whether the ads represented any sort of coordination, the company has taken steps to improve its ability to track fraudulent accounts and block fake accounts tied to election meddling in France and Germany.

Facebook's disclosure may be the first time a private entity has pointed to receiving Russian money related to US elections. The company declined to release the ads themselves, prompting criticism from some, including Pierre Omidyar, the billionaire founder of First Look Media. Omidyar stated that Facebook keeps the targeted political ads it publishes secret, emboldening criminals.

Two former Hooters employees, Paul "PJ" Cagnina and Scott Peterson, have filed a lawsuit against Hooters and their former supervisor, Rick Leukert, alleging sexual harassment and retaliation. The men claim that Leukert, who was their supervisor and CEO at various locations including Hollywood, subjected them to repeated instances of sexual harassment, including simulated sodomy, inappropriate touching, and sexually demeaning comments. The lawsuit also alleges that Leukert retaliated against the men when they complained about his behavior, eventually leading to Peterson's firing. Hooters of America has released a statement saying they have no independent knowledge of the facts and are unable to comment. The lawsuit seeks unspecified damages and a court order directing Hooters to stop allowing sexual harassment and retaliation in the workplace. Both men are no longer employed by Hooters, and their attorney wants to ensure that such behavior does not happen again.

A Trinidadian national, Bernard Charles, was arrested at John F. Kennedy International Airport on April 1st, 2014, for allegedly attempting to smuggle nearly two pounds of heroin, valued at over $70,000, hidden in his underwear. Customs and Border Protection officers became suspicious of Charles due to his nervous behavior and awkward gait. During a search, they discovered two plastic packages containing a brown paste-like substance that tested positive for heroin. Charles was ordered held without bail and faces up to 10 years in prison if convicted of drug smuggling charges. The arrest was hailed as an example of Customs and Border Protection's vigilance in protecting the United States from illegal drug distribution. This incident occurred back in 2014, as reported by CBS New York and the New York Daily News.

Schiller testified that during a 2013 trip to Moscow for the Miss Universe pageant, he rejected an offer from a Russian to send five women to Trump's hotel room. Schiller reportedly took the offer as a joke and informed Trump about it, who laughed it off. Schiller also denied knowing about the salacious allegations contained in the dossier compiled by former British agent Christopher Steele, which details alleged ties between Trump and his associates with Russians.

The dossier's claims about Trump's activities in Moscow are some of the most incendiary claims in the memos, and the FBI has corroborated some information in the dossier. However, federal investigators have not verified the most salacious allegations regarding Trump's activities on his 2013 trip for the Miss Universe Pageant in Moscow.

Schiller was also asked about a wide range of issues, including meetings between Trump associates and Russians, and he denied having knowledge of many of those interactions. He also denied knowing about the deliberations around the firing of FBI Director James Comey, saying he was only called into deliver a letter with the news to the FBI.

The document also mentions that Trump has long denied the allegations in the dossier and has ramped up his attacks after it became public that the Hillary Clinton campaign and Democratic National Committee paid for the opposition research that led to the dossier.

The document also mentions that Schiller, who is one of Trump's closest confidants, left the White House in September after serving as director of Oval Office operations. Schiller has been present for some of the most controversial moments of Trump's political career, including delivering Comey's termination letter to the FBI headquarters in May.

Overall, the document discusses the testimony of Keith Schiller regarding an offer of women to Trump's hotel room during a 2013 trip to Moscow, as well as his denial of knowledge about the salacious allegations contained in the dossier and other interactions with Russians. The document also mentions Trump's denial of the allegations in the dossier and his concerns about being recorded in Russia.

On August 29, 2018, a memorial service was held for Senator John McCain at the Arizona Capitol in Phoenix. Cindy McCain, accompanied by her sons Jimmy and Jack, attended the service. The public was also invited to pay their respects, with many Democrats, Republicans, and constituents waiting in line, some for hours, to honor the late senator.

Senator McCain, who died on August 25, 2018, at the age of 81 due to an aggressive form of brain cancer, served as a senator for Arizona since the 1980s. He was a decorated Navy pilot and prisoner of war during the Vietnam War.

The memorial service included a private ceremony in the morning, where family and politicians gathered to pay their respects. Gov. Doug Ducey and former U.S. Sen. Jon Kyl delivered remarks, with Kyl praising McCain's instincts on when to assert U.S. power and his contributions to national security. Sen. Jeff Flake offered a benediction.

Later in the afternoon, the Capitol was open to the public for a viewing, with the viewing going on as long as people were waiting in line. Many attendees spoke highly of McCain, praising his dedication to veterans and his down-to-earth demeanor.

The following day, there was a procession through Phoenix on the way to a memorial service at North Phoenix Baptist Church, with the public invited to line the route. The memorial service included tributes, readings, and musical performances, including a tribute from former Vice President Joe Biden and a recessional to "My Way" by Frank Sinatra.

From there, McCain's body was to be flown to Washington, D.C., for a ceremony at the U.S. Capitol and a memorial service at Washington National Cathedral, followed by a private memorial service and burial at the U.S. Naval Academy in Annapolis, Maryland.

Many attendees at the memorial service in Arizona spoke of McCain as a hero and a beloved figure in the state. One woman, Kassandra Morales, brought her children to the service to show them what a real hero was. Judith Hatch, a veteran from Phoenix, handed out flags to those assembled, saying Arizona had lost a champion for the military.

NASA's Curiosity rover, on Mars for over a year and a half, has delivered significant findings that suggest early Mars was habitable and may have shared many similarities with Earth. The rover's discoveries, detailed in six papers published in the journal Science, reveal that a lake existed in Gale Crater, which could have supported microbial life for extended periods, potentially millions of years.

The lake, which existed around 3.7 billion years ago, was fed by streams originating in mountains and covered a small portion of the 96-mile-wide Gale Crater. The rover analyzed fine-grained sedimentary rocks called mudstones, which formed in calm, still water, and found clay minerals that suggest an ancient freshwater lake. The mudstones also contained key chemical ingredients for life, such as sulfur, nitrogen, hydrogen, oxygen, phosphorus, and carbon.

The lake could have supported a class of microbes called chemolithoautotrophs, which obtain energy by breaking down rocks and minerals. These microbes are commonly found in habitats beyond the reach of sunlight on Earth, such as caves and hydrothermal vents on the ocean floor.

The lake's existence challenges the previous understanding that habitable environments on Mars were limited to the planet's early epochs. The discovery also raises the possibility that life may have existed on Mars in the past, although Curiosity was not designed to search for signs of life.

The new findings also provide insights into the geological history of Mars, suggesting that the lake may have been part of a larger system that included streams, lakes, and ancient groundwater systems. The lake's existence and potential longevity suggest that Mars may have been a more hospitable environment for life than previously thought.

The discoveries made by Curiosity have made the possibility of Martian life significantly more plausible, although further research is needed to confirm the presence of life on Mars. The rover's mission is ongoing, and it is currently en route to Mount Sharp, the primary destination of the mission.

Nelson Mandela, the legendary anti-apartheid leader and former President of South Africa, passed away at the age of 95 on December 5th. His death was mourned by many, including several notable musicians who have paid tribute to him through their music. U2, Hugh Masekela, The Special A.K.A., Youssou N'Dour, Public Enemy, Santana, Simple Minds, 2pac, Tracy Chapman, and Johnny Clegg are among the artists who have created songs and poems in honor of Mandela.

U2's "Ordinary Love" was made for the biopic "Mandela: Long Walk To Freedom," and the song's lyrics reflect Mandela's ideals. Hugh Masekela's "Mandela (Bring Him Back Home)" was recorded in 1987, and it expresses a desire for Mandela's release from prison. The Special A.K.A.'s "Free Nelson Mandela" is a protest song that calls for Mandela's freedom, and it was performed on the "Top of the Pops" in 1984. Youssou N'Dour's album "Nelson Mandela" was released in 1986 as a tribute to the future President of South Africa. Public Enemy's "Prophets of Rage" name-checks Mandela, and it is a powerful political statement. Santana's "Mandela" is an instrumental song that was performed at Mandela's 70th Birthday Celebration. Simple Minds' "Mandela Day" was performed at the same event, and it serves as a banner of hope. 2pac's poem "Just a Breath of Freedom (4 Nelson Mandela)" is a letter of praise to Mandela for his decades of struggle in the name of equal rights. Tracy Chapman's "Freedom Now" was written and performed as a Mandela protest song at his 70th Birthday Celebration. Johnny Clegg's "Asimbonanga" was written as a mix of Zulu and English, and it is a powerful statement of hope for Mandela's release from prison.

President Barack Obama eulogized Nelson Mandela as “a man who took history in his hands and bent the arc of the moral universe toward justice.” Obama spoke of Mandela’s impact on the world and on him personally, and he expressed his condolences to the people of South Africa. Obama is expected to travel to South Africa for the state funeral, which has not yet been scheduled. Mandela is considered the father of modern South Africa, and Obama praised the people of the nation for being an example to the world of “renewal and reconciliation and resilience.” Obama counted himself among the millions influenced by Mandela, and he expressed his gratitude for the example that Mandela set. The two met just once, but they did produce a well-known photo of Obama leaning over a seated Mandela, holding his hand. Mandela's death has been mourned by millions around the world, and his legacy will continue to inspire future generations.

Two Ohio men, Ricky Jackson and Wiley Bridgeman, were released from prison on Friday after being wrongly convicted of murder in 1975. They had spent nearly four decades behind bars for a crime they did not commit. Jackson was 19 at the time of his conviction, and Bridgeman's brother, Ronnie, was also convicted in the case.

The witness who testified against them, Edward Vernon, recanted his testimony last year, stating that he was coerced by detectives. Vernon wrote in a 2013 affidavit that he never saw the murder take place but was told by detectives that if he didn't testify against Jackson, his parents would be arrested.

Vernon confided in a pastor several years after meeting with Bridgeman and was encouraged to reach out to the Innocence Project. Vernon wrote that he had "been waiting to tell the truth about this for a long time."

Jackson and Bridgeman were released after a Cleveland judge dropped all charges against them on Wednesday. Jackson was originally sentenced to death, but that sentence was vacated due to a paperwork error. The Bridgeman brothers remained on death row until Ohio declared the death penalty unconstitutional in 1978.

"The bitterness is over with," said Wylie Bridgeman during his first moments of freedom on Friday. Jackson agreed, saying, "I had plans for my life, but time is just something that you can't get back, so I'm not going to really cry about it."

While Ohio provides compensation for those who are wrongfully imprisoned, not everyone is guaranteed money. The Ohio Innocence Project has set up a fund for Jackson. A story published in Scene Magazine in 2011 first raised new questions about the murder and whether Jackson and the Bridgeman brothers actually committed the crime.

Cuyahoga County Prosecutor Timothy McGinty said in court that without an eyewitness, there was not much of a case. "The state is conceding the obvious," he said, according to Reuters.

Jackson, who has served more time behind bars than anyone who has ever been released from prison on a wrongful conviction, according to the National Registry of Exonerations, thanked the Ohio Innocence Project and county prosecutors for showing integrity in dropping the case. He also had kind words for Eddie Vernon, the boy whose testimony helped convict him in 1975.

Vernon recanted his testimony, saying he lied to help police and was then manipulated by detectives. "I don't hate him," Jackson said. "He's a grown man today, he was just a boy back then." Jackson wished Vernon the best and said, "It took a lot of courage to do what he did."

The investigation into the death of music icon Prince, who passed away on April 21 at his home in suburban Minneapolis, has taken a criminal turn. Law enforcement officials are looking into whether an overdose of opioids led to Prince's death, and whether a doctor was prescribing him drugs in the weeks leading up to his demise.

Investigators are examining a plane incident less than a week before Prince's death, where he was found unconscious. First responders administered Narcan, a drug used in opioid overdoses, to Prince on the tarmac in Moline, Illinois, as he returned to Minneapolis following a performance in Atlanta.

Prescription pills were found at Prince's home, but it's unclear whether they were prescribed to him. Authorities are also trying to determine how Prince obtained the pills and who may have provided them. Prince's death came two weeks after he canceled concerts in Atlanta due to health concerns.

An autopsy has been performed, but results are not expected for three to four weeks. The search warrant for Prince's Paisley Park home and studio, carried out the day of his death, was filed under seal at the request of investigators to prevent hampering the investigation if contents were made public.

The federal Drug Enforcement Administration is not involved in the investigation at this time, according to Carver County Chief Deputy Jason Kamerud. The cause of death is still unknown, and it's expected that a cause of death won't be made public for weeks. Prince's body was cremated last week, and a private service was held at Paisley Park.

In recent weeks, more than 75 women have come forward to accuse movie producer Harvey Weinstein of sexual harassment or sexual assault. The stories that Weinstein’s accusers tell—of uncomfortable encounters in hotel rooms; of ostensible business meetings interrupted by requests to give him a massage, to watch him shower, to disrobe; and sometimes of sexual violence, including rape—echo each other in striking ways. In many cases, these women also describe having spent decades feeling isolated, alone, and ashamed of their brushes with Weinstein.

But they were far from alone. And so we invited three of these women to speak with each other about their experiences. In an honest and emotional conversation, they discussed what happened to them and how they’re feeling now about the cascade of Weinstein stories—and allegations against other powerful men—that has followed. (Through a spokesperson, Weinstein has denied all allegations of non-consensual sex, and of retaliation against women who rebuffed him or complained about his behavior.)

You can listen to their conversation here, or read a transcript that’s been condensed and edited for clarity below.

Alice Evans is an actress who has appeared on The Vampire Diaries and Lost. Katherine Kendall is a photographer and actress perhaps best known for her role in the film Swingers. Tomi-Ann Roberts is a professor of psychology at Colorado College who studies emotion, gender, and sexual objectification.

Slate: The Weinstein encounters you three have described took place in three different decades, which strikes me as a testament to the immense scope of what we’ve learned about Weinstein’s behavior, in the ’80s, the ’90s, and the early 2000s. Tomi-Ann, can you describe how and when you met Harvey Weinstein, and what happened?

Tomi-Ann Roberts: I was in between my junior and senior year in college, and a number of my college friends and I lived in New York that summer doing things like internships. I had been considering both a theater major and a psychology major at Smith College. That summer was an opportunity for me to do some auditions for commercials, get some head shots, things like that. I was working at a restaurant. It was at this restaurant that I met the Weinstein brothers, who introduced themselves to me as a production company. I remember learning about how they named their company Miramax after their parents.

Before I knew it, Harvey had indicated, when I said that I was an aspiring actress, that they were now going to be doing their first movie that they would be directing. They had been, I think, prior to that, importing foreign movies. That was very exciting, as you might imagine.

For the rest of the summer, I would receive scripts and updates about the movie. I remember going to the offices at one time. Then I was invited to an apartment. I presumed that other people involved with the movie would be at this evening event, because why would I be invited to something in the evening?

I arrived at this apartment to find Harvey. He called me down the hall. He was in the bathtub. I stood there frozen, of course. I’ve since wondered, why would something like that be so frightening? Here’s a man in a bathtub.

Exactly, and I don’t know, the temerity of him to think, “I’m just gonna present myself to you in this way.” Knowing that that would be very off-putting to me, he tried to calm me down and say that nakedness was something that I needed to be comfortable with, would I please take my top off because surely the movie would have some nudity scenes and I needed to show him that I was comfortable with that, which of course I wasn’t.

I wish I could remember my exact words. It was such a flooding experience. I do know, and I’m ashamed to say, that I was not aggressive in any way. I was terribly frightened of poking this bear. I very politely excused myself. I said I wasn’t sure that I was actually really cut out for this kind of thing and, “Please accept my apologies, but no thank you,” and exited.

I can’t probably say that there’s a direct line between that experience with Harvey Weinstein and my research on the sexual objectification and sexualization of girls and women, but there certainly is a dotted line.

These were the kinds of experiences that accumulated for me. That wasn’t the only time a man presented himself to me in an aggressive way, seeking something from me. It wasn’t the only time my physical appearance was commented upon in a context when I would’ve rather been recognized for my competence. That began to interest me.

I returned to Smith. I majored in psychology. I went on to earn my Ph.D. from Stanford. I began to study what the consequences are to girls and women of living in a culture that routinely treats us as though our sexualized bodies are the most valuable thing we have to offer.

Slate: Do you think that the experience affected your interest in acting, in the world of Hollywood?

Roberts: Absolutely. I really threw that aspiration in the wastebasket, I have to say. At the time I thought, as I said earlier, that this was just something I wasn’t cool enough to be able to participate in. Ugh! Looking back, I can’t believe that. I do think that there was a whisper inside of me, some sort of feminist whisper that said, “Get out now.” At the time, I think what I thought was, “OK, well that was a learning experience, and I am going to not pursue acting.”
