Ohio voters will decide on November 3 whether to legalize marijuana through a constitutional amendment, making it the sixth and most populous jurisdiction in the U.S. to do so if approved. The proposal, backed by a private investor group called ResponsibleOhio, limits cultivation of the commercial crop to 10 farms, with wealthy investors such as reality-TV star Nick Lachey and retired athlete Oscar Robertson among the owners. The group has pledged to spend $20 million on the election effort, including advertising and voter registration drives. However, a competing measure on the ballot, Issue 2, could potentially prohibit a monopoly or oligopoly in Ohio, which could potentially challenge the ResponsibleOhio proposal if both measures pass. The legalization proposal offers economic and social benefits, including generating over $2 billion a year by 2020, and saving millions of dollars currently spent on policing the black market and imprisoning people for low-level offenses. Opponents argue that the structure is a monopoly, while supporters say it will create a billion-dollar industry in the next four years.

In an incident that occurred in April 2014 in Billings, Montana, police officer Grant Morrison shot and killed an unarmed man named Richard Ramirez during a traffic stop. The shooting was ruled justified by a jury at a coroner's inquest, which took place this week. The jury's decision came after Morrison testified that he feared for his life because Ramirez was high on methamphetamines and he believed Ramirez was reaching for a gun.

Video footage of the incident showed Morrison shouting at Ramirez multiple times to put his hands up before firing three times into the car. The video also showed Morrison breaking down moments after the shooting, breathing heavily and crying, saying "I thought he was gonna pull a gun on me."

The ruling came after a two-day inquest, during which only three of the 15 witnesses called to testify were not from law enforcement. The Ramirez family, who allege excessive use of force and racial profiling, have said they intend to file a lawsuit against Morrison and the Billings Police Department.

Morrison had previously been cleared of wrongdoing in another shooting in 2013. He has since been assigned to a task force investigating prescription drug crimes. The police chief of Billings stated that this was the fifth officer-involved shooting in his eight years as head of the department, and each shooting was ruled to be justified.

The shooting of Richard Ramirez has come under increased scrutiny in light of recent police killings of unarmed suspects in Ferguson, Missouri and New York City. The Ramirez family and some community members have criticized the inquest as one-sided and have called for more transparency and accountability in police actions.

The United States has accused seven Russian spies of involvement in a series of cyber-plots across the globe, including targeting the global chemical weapons watchdog, anti-doping agencies, and a US nuclear company. The allegations are part of an organized push-back against alleged Russian cyber-attacks. Russia has dismissed the allegations as "Western spy mania."

The Netherlands has accused four Russians of plotting to hack the Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons (OPCW), which was investigating the chemical attack on a Russian ex-spy in the UK. The UK government accused the GRU of being behind four high-profile cyber-attacks, including firms in Russia and Ukraine, the US Democratic Party, and a small TV network in the UK. The US said its anti-doping agency, football's governing body Fifa, and the US nuclear energy company Westinghouse were targeted by Russian intelligence. Canada said with high confidence that breaches at its centre for ethics in sports and at the Montreal-based World Anti-Doping Agency were carried out by Russian intelligence.

The Dutch authorities have said a laptop seized from the four suspects in April was found to have been used in Brazil, Switzerland, and Malaysia. In Malaysia, it was used to target the investigation into the downing of Malaysia Airlines flight MH17 in 2014 over territory held by Russian-backed rebels in eastern Ukraine. All 298 people on board were killed.

The revelations about how the British and Dutch security agencies disrupted the operations of the GRU are astonishing in their detail and openness. This is not what secretive intelligence agencies normally do. The willingness of both countries to be so candid illustrates how determined both they and some other Western governments are to try to push back against what they see as a concerted pattern of Russian aggression.

The Russian foreign ministry released an official statement late on Thursday, saying it was the victim of "yet another stage-managed propaganda campaign." The US has indicted seven people, four of whom were the men expelled from the Netherlands, while the other three were among those charged in July with hacking Democratic officials during the 2016 US elections. They were also charged with wire fraud, identity theft, and money laundering. All seven men are thought to be in Russia, which does not have an extradition treaty with the US.

A joint statement from British Prime Minister Theresa May and her Dutch counterpart Mark Rutte said the alleged plot against the OPCW demonstrated "the GRU's disregard for global values and rules that keep us all safe." Meanwhile, British Foreign Secretary Jeremy Hunt said the UK was discussing further sanctions against Russia with its allies. The EU has also denounced the alleged cyber-plots.

The four suspects identified by Dutch officials had diplomatic passports, which meant the Netherlands could not arrest them as diplomats are in theory immune from prosecution in their host country. They included two IT experts and two support agents, officials said. The four hired a car and parked it in the car park of the Marriot hotel in The Hague, which is next to the OPCW office, to hack into the OPCW's wifi network, Major General Onno Eichelsheim from the Dutch MIVD intelligence service said. Equipment in the car boot was pointed at the OPCW and was being used to intercept login details, he said, adding that the antenna for the operation lay under a jacket on the car's rear shelf.

When the men were intercepted, they tried to destroy one of the mobile phones they were carrying, Maj Gen Eichelsheim said. He said one of their mobile phones was found to have been activated near the GRU building in Moscow, while another carried a receipt for a taxi journey from a street near the GRU to the airport. Maj Gen Eichelsheim said the group were planning to travel to Switzerland, to a laboratory in Spiez where the OPCW analyzed samples. They never made it. Instead, the four were immediately escorted out of the country, he added.

The suspects were named by the MIVD as hackers Alexei Morenets and Yevgeny Serebriakov, and support agents Oleg Sotnikov and Alexei Minin. Officials said they were from the GRU's Unit 26165, which has also been known as APT 28. The UK's ambassador to the Netherlands, Peter Wilson, said the unit had "sent officers around the world to conduct brazen close access cyber-operations" - which involve hacking into wifi networks. He said the hackers were planning to travel on to the OPCW-certified laboratory in Spiez near Berne in Switzerland, where the Novichok nerve agent used in March's attack on Sergei Skripal and his daughter in the British city of Salisbury was identified.

At the time the Russian operation was disrupted, the OPCW was investigating the Skripal case as well as an alleged chemical attack in April on the Syrian town of Douma near Damascus by Russian-backed government forces, the MIVD said. "With its aggressive cyber-campaigns, we see the GRU trying to clean up Russia's own mess - be it the doping uncovered by Wada [the World Anti-Doping Agency] or the nerve agent identified by the OPCW," Mr Wilson said.

A laptop seized from the suspects was found to have been used in Brazil, Switzerland, and Malaysia, the Dutch officials said. The cyber-operation in Malaysia targeted the attorney general's office and Malaysian police as well as the investigation into MH17's shooting down, Ambassador Wilson said. Earlier this year Dutch-led international investigators concluded that a missile that brought down MH17 belonged to a Russian brigade. Russia has denied any involvement in the plane's destruction, which led to the deaths of many Dutch citizens.

Data from the laptop showed it was also present in the Swiss city of Lausanne where it was linked to the hacking of a laptop belonging to Wada, which has exposed doping by Russian athletes.

Fan Bingbing, China's highest-paid movie star and a household name in China, has been ranked last in an academic report on social responsibility. The report, published by Beijing Normal University, evaluated celebrities based on professional work, charitable work, and personal integrity. Fan scored zero out of 100 points, while only nine celebrities made the cut, with Chinese actor Xu Zheng topping the list at 78%.

Fan's low score has sparked controversy online, with many fans defending her and questioning the report's methodology. Fan has been unusually quiet in recent months, following allegations of tax evasion in May. The report's authors studied the celebrities' behavior to assess their social responsibility but did not elaborate on their findings, stating that they were based on "research and web-scraping."

Fan's troubles began when Cui Yongyuan, a former presenter for state-run China Central Television (CCTV), posted purported contracts online that suggested Fan had received under-the-table payments. A statement released by Fan's studio said she was the victim of "slander" but did not dispute the authenticity of the documents Cui released. So-called "yin and yang" dual contract arrangements, with one contract for income declared to tax authorities and another kept secret, are reportedly used to evade taxes.

After the documents posted by Cui went viral, the state tax administration was reportedly investigating alleged use of such dual contracts in the entertainment industry in eastern Jiangsu province. Although Fan was not mentioned by name, she has businesses registered in Jiangsu. State news agency Xinhua reported in late June that government agencies, including the tax authority and the film and broadcast regulator, would crack down on excessive pay and tax evasion in entertainment.

Last month, nearly a dozen major Chinese film producers and video sites announced they would boycott "unreasonable" pay for actors. Fan is one of five leading international actresses cast in the upcoming Hollywood spy thriller "355," alongside Jessica Chastain and Penelope Cruz. China's state media reported last week that Fan was "under control." However, the Securities Daily report that Fan was "under control" and would "accept the legal decision" appeared to have been taken down hours after it was published.

Fan has been China's highest-paid actress since 2013, Forbes reported last year. She pulls in tens of millions of dollars for her acting roles, as well as several high-end endorsements. In June, Fan's studio denied allegations that Fan had signed multiple contracts to evade taxes, saying, "The studio and Fan Bingbing will fully cooperate with the relevant authority. We hope the investigation result can be released soon to answer the public doubt." The report by academics at Beijing Normal University ranked Fan the lowest in a "social responsibility assessment" of Chinese film and television stars.

The House Republican leadership has expressed support for Rep. Steve Scalise, the No. 3-ranking House Republican, following a controversy surrounding his 2002 speech to a white supremacist group. Scalise's position as House majority whip has been thrown into doubt by the revelation, and he had been calling members to gauge the level of support he had from his party. House Speaker John Boehner and House Majority Leader Kevin McCarthy issued statements supporting Scalise, stating that he has their "full confidence" as whip. Scalise himself issued a statement acknowledging that he spoke to the group while barnstorming the district to build support for a piece of legislation, and that speaking to them was a "mistake I regret." However, there is still uncertainty about how much Scalise knew about the group at the time of the speech, and it is unclear how much blowback he will receive from rank-and-file Republicans. The controversy has been a major distraction for Boehner and his leadership team, and has drawn national attention since the story was first reported on Monday.

The article details an account of a carjacking incident in Boston, which occurred three days after the Boston Marathon bombings. The carjacking victim, identified as "Danny," is a Chinese entrepreneur who was driving a Mercedes SUV. Tamerlan Tsarnaev, one of the suspects in the bombings, approached Danny's car, pointed a gun at him, and demanded that he cooperate. During the 90-minute ride, Tamerlan kept talking, detailing his hatred of Americans and asking about Danny's heritage and family. His younger brother, Dzhokhar, followed in another vehicle.

Tamerlan was the ringleader during the carjacking, giving orders and asking questions, while Dzhokhar responded to multiple orders, such as getting money from an ATM. The only question Dzhokhar asked was how much Danny paid for his Mercedes SUV. After the Chinese entrepreneur eventually escaped, police caught up with the brothers and engaged in a gun battle that left Tamerlan Tsarnaev dead. Dzhokhar, wounded, was found later and is in police custody.

Before forcing their way into Danny's vehicle, the brothers fatally shot a campus police officer at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, police said. Tamerlan Tsarnaev said right after he got in the vehicle that he was responsible for the bombings and the officer's death, according to Danny. Danny thought about a girl in New York whom he really liked during the carjacking, fearing he'd never see her again. The car sustained 32 bullet holes and is a total loss, but Danny is okay with that.

In a press conference, President Obama advocated for an end to high-end tax cuts, framing it as a test of societal priorities and a necessary step towards addressing the deficit. He specifically mentioned the corporate jet tax break, a proposal that would raise $3 billion, as an example of a perk that the wealthy are currently enjoying. Obama's goal was to provoke a reaction from Republicans, positioning them as defenders of the wealthy and escalating the debate over tax reform.

Obama emphasized that a balanced approach to deficit reduction, including both spending cuts and revenue increases, is necessary. He argued that the current low taxes for wealthy CEOs and hedge fund managers, which are at their lowest since the 1950s, can be increased without affecting their lifestyles.

The president also addressed the issue of entitlements, stating that while cuts will be necessary, they should not be at the expense of seniors. He stopped short of threatening to veto any deficit deal without a high-end tax hike but made it clear that he will continue to advocate for it.

The press conference was criticized for its class-warfare tone, with some commentators accusing Obama of being tiresome and out of touch. However, Obama's team is presenting the administration's stance as a commitment to debt reduction and broad sacrifice, while portraying the Republican position as one that prioritizes the wealthy over students and seniors. The debate over tax reform and deficit reduction is expected to continue as both parties prepare for negotiations.

The International Olympic Committee (IOC) has expressed dismay after the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) overturned the lifetime bans of 28 Russian athletes who were accused of doping at the 2014 Winter Olympics in Sochi. The CAS ruling also means that the athletes' results will be reinstated, returning Russia to the top of the medal table. The IOC had previously suspended Russia from participating in the 2018 Winter Olympics in Pyeongchang due to state-sponsored doping in Sochi. However, around 160 Russians have been granted permission to compete as neutrals under the banner of Olympic Athlete from Russia after being cleared of doping by an IOC anti-doping panel. The IOC has stated that the result of the CAS decision does not mean that athletes from the group of 28 will be invited to the Games, and it may consider an appeal to the Swiss Federal Tribunal. The IOC has also expressed concern that the ruling could have serious consequences for the fight against doping. The ruling comes after the IOC had already received criticism for allowing as many as 169 athletes to compete as neutrals in Pyeongchang, with the word 'Russia' emblazoned on their kit. The CAS decision may lead to further legal challenges from some of the athletes who now want to compete in Pyeongchang, causing last-minute havoc. The IOC has also been criticized for issuing lifetime bans in the first place when legal precedent shows that such sanctions are always doomed to fail once appealed. The ruling has been met with celebration in Russia, with sports minister Pavel Kolobkov stating that "our guys and all of us are happy that justice has finally triumphed." However, many have expressed concern that the ruling undermines the entire case built against Russia for state-sponsored doping, and fuels those who portray the scandal as a Western conspiracy.

The Badlands National Park's official Twitter account posted tweets about climate change contradicting the Trump administration's stance, stating that the current level of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere is higher than in the last 650,000 years. The tweets were deleted after a few hours, with the National Park Service (NPS) attributing them to a former unauthorized employee. The NPS clarified that the park was not instructed to remove the tweets but chose to do so when they realized the account had been compromised. The NPS also stated that their social media managers are encouraged to continue using Twitter to post information related to public safety and park information, except for content related to national policy issues. This incident marks the latest instance of a national park account sharing information that may contradict the administration's views on climate change.

The discovery of a baby dinosaur named "Joe" by high-school student Kevin Terris in 2009 has been highlighted in a virtual museum exhibit. The fossil skeleton, found in Utah's Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument, is the smallest, youngest, and most complete Parasaurolophus ever found. Parasaurolophus is a type of dinosaur known for its tube-shaped head crest, which may have been used for display or amplifying calls.

The discovery of "Joe" was a fortunate find, as two professional paleontologists had walked past the bones before Terris spotted them. The skeleton is named in honor of Joe Augustyn, a long-time supporter of the museum whose family sponsored the preparation of the fossil skeleton.

The research team, including Terris and other high-school students, discovered that "Joe" was less than a year old when it died, as it didn't have any growth rings in its bone tissue. The baby dinosaur was already 6 feet long, which is impressive considering that duck-billed dinosaurs hatched at about the same size as a human infant.

The discovery of "Joe" has provided valuable insights into the growth and evolution of Parasaurolophus. The team found that the baby dinosaur already had a crest bump, suggesting that Parasaurolophus started growing its crest earlier than other duck-billed dinosaurs. The skeleton of "Joe" will be on display at the Alf Museum beginning October 22, and a digital exploration of the skeleton will be available at dinosaurjoe.com.

Terris is now studying geology in college, and the discovery of "Joe" has sparked his interest in paleontology. The research paper on the discovery was published in the journal PeerJ on October 22. The research team included Andrew Farke, curator of the Raymond M. Alf Museum of Paleontology at The Webb Schools, and Sarah Werning of Stony Brook University, among others.

On Sunday, October 27, 2014, Perla Avina, a mother of four, was tragically shot and killed in an apparent road rage incident in East Oakland, California. The shooting occurred while Avina and her husband, Luis Lopez Gallegos, were returning home from grocery shopping. According to police, an angry motorist sprayed gunfire into their car, hitting Avina in the head. The couple was driving on 98th Avenue, somewhere between the 400 to 600 blocks, when the shooting took place. Gallegos drove the short distance to their home, where Avina died in the driveway. The shooter is still at large, and police are offering a reward of up to $30,000 for information leading to an arrest. Avina was a medical clerk at a pain rehabilitation center in Emeryville and is survived by her husband and their four children, ages 1 to 14. The family is mourning her loss, and a Go Fund Me page has been created to help with funeral expenses. The Oakland Police Department is urging residents and businesses in the area to check their surveillance cameras for potential evidence.

In May 2015, Harvard student Aran Khanna created a browser extension called Marauder's Map, which used data from Facebook Messenger to map the locations of users who sent messages. The app was downloaded over 85,000 times before Facebook asked Khanna to disable it and deactivated location sharing from desktops. The extension capitalized on a privacy flaw that Facebook had been aware of for about three years, as the Messenger app automatically shared users' locations with anyone they messaged.

Khanna's extension revealed that Facebook Messenger had been sharing users' geolocations since it launched in 2011, and that the data was visible to anyone in a group chat, regardless of their relationship to the sender on Facebook. The data was accurate to within three feet, and users could see the locations of people they barely knew.

Facebook responded by asking Khanna to disable the app and releasing a Messenger app update that required users to opt-in to sharing their location. However, the update did not mention the previous default settings, and users who did not activate the update continued to share their locations by default unless they manually altered their privacy settings.

Khanna created the extension to show the consequences of unintentionally sharing data and to give users the opportunity to decide for themselves whether or not it was a violation of their privacy. Facebook's response to the extension and the subsequent update raised questions about the company's commitment to privacy and its handling of user data.

Khanna's experience with Facebook and the creation of Marauder's Map is detailed in a case study published in Technology Science, a journal published by Harvard University. The study explores the issue of geolocation sharing on Facebook Messenger and the response from Facebook, a company with a reputation for encouraging outside-the-box thinking and hacking. The study raises questions about the privacy implications of automatic geolocation sharing and the need for transparency and user control over their data.

Facebook's response to the study and the creation of Marauder's Map highlights the ongoing tension between privacy and convenience in the digital age, and the need for companies to balance these concerns in their products and services. The study also underscores the importance of user awareness and control over their data, and the need for companies to be transparent about their data practices and give users the ability to make informed decisions about their privacy.

In a recent study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, researchers found that adopting expansive postures, such as spreading limbs and a stretched-out torso, can increase romantic interest in speed-dating situations. The study, led by Tanya Vacharkulksemsuk, a post-doctoral research fellow at the University of California, Berkeley, involved two studies.

In the first study, researchers watched videos of 144 speed-dates and found that people who sat in expanded postures were deemed more attractive. Postural expansiveness nearly doubled the chances of getting a "yes" response to a second date, even surpassing the effect of smiling and laughing.

In the second study, pictures of people in open and closed postures were posted on a dating site. Those in expansive postures were about 25 percent more likely to generate interest from another user. However, this strategy worked much better for men than women.

In a separate test, both the male and female "expansive" photos were considered more dominant than the "closed" photos. This dominance might suggest an abundance of resources and a willingness to share those resources.

The study suggests that in modern dating, where decisions are often made in a matter of seconds, displays of expansive posture can increase one's chances of initial romantic success. However, the findings should be viewed with skepticism, as previous studies on the power of posture have been met with controversy.

The report by Human Rights Watch reveals serious human rights abuses by militias and some units of the Afghan Local Police (ALP), a US-backed force, in Afghanistan. The abuses include killings, rape, arbitrary detention, abductions, forcible land grabs, and illegal raids in various provinces. The Afghan government has failed to hold these forces accountable, fostering support for the Taliban and other opposition forces. The report calls for the Afghan government and the US to sever ties with irregular armed groups and take immediate steps to create properly trained and vetted security forces that are held accountable for their actions. The US military is training and mentoring the year-old ALP force as part of its exit strategy. The report is based on over 120 interviews and documents serious abuses by the ALP in various provinces. The US and Afghan governments are urged to avoid rushing to set up new units of the ALP without proper vetting, oversight, and accountability mechanisms, and to investigate all allegations of abuse by the ALP and other police forces. The report also highlights the challenges of building up foreign armies and the need for proper training and oversight to prevent human rights abuses.

The article discusses Barack Obama's foreign policy approach, which has been labeled as "leading from behind." This style, according to an anonymous Obama adviser, is a result of two unspoken beliefs: the decline of the United States' relative power compared to rivals like China, and the U.S. being reviled in many parts of the world.

Obama's foreign policy has been criticized for being ad hoc, erratic, and confused, with examples given such as his passive approach during Iran's 2009 Green Revolution and his dithering on Libya. The adviser claims that this style is a deliberate attempt to accommodate American decline and appease those who revile the U.S.

The article also delves into Obama's intellectual and political development, highlighting his leanings towards conventionally left-leaning positions during his college years and his focus on civil-rights law and race during his career as a professor. Obama sought advice from various foreign policy experts, including Anthony Lake, Susan Rice, and Samantha Power, to educate himself on foreign affairs.

Power's book, "A Problem from Hell," which argued for liberal interventionism, particularly influenced Obama. He invited Power to dinner and later had her spend a year in his office as a foreign-policy fellow.

The article concludes by suggesting that the Republican Party needs to nominate a real leader to counter Obama's approach to foreign policy, which has been criticized as weak and indecisive. The article also questions the effectiveness of Obama's foreign policy, citing examples such as the ongoing conflict in Libya.

The article discusses the failure of Jeb Bush's presidential campaign, which ended on February 20, 2016 after a disappointing performance in the South Carolina primary. The article highlights several factors that contributed to Bush's downfall, including his underestimation of the anger and desire for change among Republican voters, his failure to connect with voters, and his perceived lack of energy compared to other candidates. The article also mentions Bush's struggles with his stance on the Iraq war, his attempts to distance himself from his family's political legacy, and his campaign's reliance on a super PAC for fundraising. The article concludes by noting that Bush's campaign was a disappointment for those who believed he had a strong chance of winning the nomination.

In a surprising revelation for the holiday cookie season, it has been discovered that the vanilla flavoring in various baked goods and candies could originate from the anal excretions of beavers. Known as castoreum, this substance is secreted by beavers to mark their territory and is considered safe by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA).

Castoreum, a chemical compound, primarily comes from a beaver's castor sacs, located between the pelvis and the base of the tail. Due to its proximity to the anal glands, it often contains a mix of castor gland secretions, anal gland secretions, and urine.

The fragrant, brown slime, which resembles molasses in consistency, has a musky, vanilla scent, making it an attractive addition to food recipes and perfumes. However, collecting castoreum involves anesthetizing the animal and "milking" its nether regions, a process that is both unpleasant and relatively uncommon, with annual consumption estimated at around 292 pounds (132 kilograms).

Manufacturers are not always required to list castoreum on the ingredient list, instead referring to it as "natural flavoring." This may raise concerns among consumers who are unaware that they might be consuming beaver-bum goop.

A 14-year-old boy named Stephen J. Brumby was accidentally shot and killed at High Noon Gun Range in Sarasota, Florida, on July 3rd, 2016. The incident occurred at around 3:15 PM, during a family outing with his father, William C. Brumby, and his siblings. According to the Sarasota County Sheriff's Office report, William Brumby was shooting in the last lane, and a spent shell casing deflected off the wall and fell into his shirt. While attempting to remove it, he accidentally pointed the gun behind him and fired, striking his son.

The investigation is ongoing, and at this time, no charges have been filed against William Brumby. A memorial fund has been set up on GoFundMe to help the family with expenses. The fundraising page describes Stephen Brumby as a passionate and wise young man who loved fishing, tennis, music, archery, and knife throwing, among other things.

This incident marks the second death at a local gun range in the past year. In August 2015, a man in his 70s shot himself at Take Aim Gun Range.

High Noon Gun Range, where the accident occurred, was described in a 2013 Herald-Tribune article as one of the safest indoor shooting ranges ever designed, featuring sound-dampening panels, strategically placed armored steel plates, and a large mound of granulated rubber material to absorb bullets. The walls are also lined with sound-dampening panels built to reduce noise and absorb stray rounds, preventing ricochets.

Taylor Swift's new album, "1989," is projected to sell over one million copies in its first week, making it the third consecutive album for Swift to achieve this milestone. This would make her the first artist in pop history to sell over a million copies in three separate weeks. The album, released on October 27, is expected to debut at the top of the Billboard 200 albums chart. The sales period started on October 26 and ends on November 2, with final sales figures to be released on November 5. The album is performing exceptionally well on iTunes and at Target, which carries an exclusive version with bonus tracks. Swift has been promoting the album extensively, appearing on various talk shows and participating in iHeartRadio's "Taylor Swift's 1989 Secret Session with iHeartRadio." If the sales figures hold, "1989" will be the second-biggest selling album of 2014, behind only the Frozen soundtrack and Beyonce's self-titled album.

Dr. George Doodnaught, an anesthesiologist, was sentenced to 10 years in prison for sexually assaulting 21 sedated women during surgeries. The assaults took place at the North York General Hospital in Toronto between 2006 and 2010. Doodnaught, 65, was found guilty of the crimes in November. The victims suffered emotional damage, including feelings of betrayal, anger, bitterness, and distrust of doctors. Many of the victims were in the courtroom during the sentencing and clapped as Doodnaught was handcuffed and led away. The judge described Doodnaught's conduct as "reprehensible in the extreme." Doodnaught intends to appeal his convictions, and a bail hearing for his release pending the appeal is scheduled for Wednesday. The hospital has apologized to the victims and made changes to how it addresses and tracks patient complaints. Doodnaught's medical license has been suspended, and he is set to face a disciplinary hearing with the Ontario College of Physicians and Surgeons. The notice of hearing contains allegations that Doodnaught sexually abused 30 patients, with one alleged assault dating back to 1992.

In an evening press conference, the NYPD, Mayor Bill de Blasio, and Brooklyn Borough President Eric Adams announced a suspect, Daniel St. Hubert, in the stabbing of two young children in an NYCHA building elevator in East New York. St. Hubert is a 27-year-old black male who stands 5'9" and weighs 210 pounds, resides in East New York, and has nine prior arrests. He is considered "armed and dangerous" and has been on parole since May 23 for a domestic violence incident. St. Hubert is accused of fatally stabbing 6-year-old Prince Joshua "P.J." Avitto and critically injuring 7-year-old Mikayla Capers in a building elevator at the Boulevard Houses on Schenk Avenue on Sunday. P.J. died at the hospital, while Mikayla survived but is unable to speak. Forensic evidence at the crime scene provided the link to St. Hubert. St. Hubert has been charged with assaulting a police officer and assaulting a Correction officer, which is the reason for his current parole status. It's been reported that St. Hubert may be behind the Friday night fatal stabbing of Tanaya Grant Copeland, though he is only named as a suspect in the stabbings of the children. The officials implored the public to contact 1-800-577-TIPS if they have any information about St. Hubert or call 911 if they see him. The NYPD arrested St. Hubert in Queens late Wednesday after a cell phone trace and a DNA hit led cops to him.

BP has agreed to the Obama administration's request to broadcast the "top kill" procedure, a complex method aimed at stopping the oil spill in the Gulf of Mexico, starting as early as Wednesday dawn. The procedure involves forcing drilling mud and cement onto the leak. This is the latest attempt to plug the oil leak, following pressure from the administration for live footage of the leak itself. The company will display the video after discussions with Coast Guard Adm. Thad Allen. The "top kill" operation may take up to two days to complete, and significant changes in the leak's appearance may occur without indicating the overall progress or success of the procedure. BP will provide updates as appropriate. Additionally, various live streams of underwater robots are available for viewing, though they may freeze or become unavailable at times.

The article discusses a surrogacy scandal involving an Australian couple, David and Wendy Farnell, and a Thai surrogate mother, Pattaramon Janbua. The couple hired Janbua to carry their twins, but when one of the twins, Gammy, was born with Down's syndrome, they decided to take only the healthy twin, Pipah, back to Australia. The surrogate mother refused to let Gammy go, and the couple has been criticized for abandoning the disabled child.

In an interview, David Farnell said that they wanted to take Gammy with them but were afraid that the surrogate mother would keep both children if they tried to take Gammy. He also said that they were angry that the surrogacy agency did not tell them about Gammy's condition until it was too late in the pregnancy to safely abort.

The case has brought attention to the lack of regulation of international surrogacy and has sparked calls for an overhaul of laws in Australia to reduce the number of couples traveling abroad for surrogates. The Australian government has asked the Thai authorities to allow for the completion of any current commercial surrogacy arrangements before introducing changes.

The Farnells have been criticized for their treatment of Gammy, and public outrage has been intensified by the fact that David Farnell was jailed in 1997 for sex offenses involving three girls under the age of 13. He has said that he has reformed and is no longer a risk to children.

Thailand has no clear legal framework for surrogacy, and commercial surrogacy is barred by the Medical Council of Thailand, but non-profit surrogacy is permitted for blood relatives, and exceptions are permitted on a case-by-case basis. A draft law banning commercial surrogacy in Thailand has been submitted to the military government.

The online appeal for Gammy's medical treatment and care has raised over A$241,000 ($224,000) so far, and Hands Across the Water, an Australian-run children's charity based in Thailand, will administer the funds.

Jeff Bezos, the founder of Amazon.com, achieved a significant milestone in space travel with his private spaceflight company, Blue Origin, as they successfully landed their New Shepard rocket back on Earth after a flight to the edge of space. This was the first time a Blue Origin rocket has been reused, marking a significant step towards the goal of making rockets reusable.

The New Shepard rocket reached a height of 100.5 kilometers, reaching a maximum speed of Mach 3.72. The rocket's engine reignited at 5,000 feet above the landing pad, and it landed back on Earth at a speed of just 4.4 mph. The rocket's landing was precise, landing only 4.5 feet off the center of the landing pad.

The capsule, designed to carry six people to suborbital space, returned to Earth via parachute. Blue Origin plans to offer suborbital flights to space aboard the New Shepard in the future, but the company's ambitions do not stop there. They also plan to build and launch an orbital rocket that would fly people and cargo to space from Florida.

Reusable rockets could significantly lower the cost of space travel, as currently, rocket components are effectively thrown away after one use. Bezos hopes to use these rocket parts again and again over the course of at least a few missions.

Elon Musk, the CEO of Tesla Motors and the owner of SpaceX, sent congratulations to Bezos and Blue Origin via Twitter. However, Musk also clarified the difference between "space" and "orbit," noting that getting to space requires a speed of Mach 3, but reaching orbit requires Mach 30 and 100 times the energy. SpaceX has attempted to land their Falcon 9 rockets on a drone ship in the ocean after orbit, although those tests have not yet been successful.

Blue Origin and SpaceX are two of the main players in the new business of private space launches, along with Richard Branson's Virgin Galactic. Bezos does not consider these companies as Blue Origin's competitors, stating that "Space is a big place. There's room for all of us."

Bezos plans to carry astronauts, including tourists, into space in the future. Blue Origin is taking names of people interested in hopping aboard a future flight, but they have yet to announce how much it will cost or how many people have signed up. SpaceX and Boeing have won contracts from NASA to carry astronauts to the International Space Station.

All three companies have had setbacks in their efforts to carry people into space. A Virgin Galactic spaceship crashed during a test flight in October 2014, killing one of the two pilots. An unmanned SpaceX supply flight to ISS exploded soon after launch in June. New Shepard had its first successful launch into space in April, but the rocket was not recovered due to a problem with the hydraulic system. However, this time, the rocket performed exactly as planned, traveling into the edge of outer space before returning.

Miranda July, the renowned filmmaker and author behind "You And Me And Everyone We Know," has confessed to a history of shoplifting, starting with stealing Neosporin during her freshman year of college. July continued to shoplift at grocery stores and even at Goodwill, including from charity. July's shoplifting spree extended to resetting Kinko's copy counters, cutting alarm tags out of clothes, and even stealing luggage from visitors to Portland. July's shoplifting was not limited to supermarkets, as she also stole from Goodwill and even put red "Sold" tags on large appliances and entire living-room sets for her friends to take. July's shoplifting ended when she started dating someone and decided to stop. July's shoplifting is not unique, as 10 other female celebrities have also (allegedly) shoplifted. July's confession was published in The New Yorker.

In the recent elections, Colorado voters approved a 15% excise tax on marijuana to fund school construction and a 10% sales tax for marijuana-related law enforcement. The measure, which generated strong support, is expected to bring in nearly $70 million in additional state tax revenue. Meanwhile, in 11 counties in northern Colorado, voters considered a secession plan to form a 51st state known as North Colorado, but the plan has no chance of becoming reality.

In Washington, voters considered a controversial initiative that would require labeling all foods containing genetically modified ingredients. The measure, which pits local consumer advocates against large agribusinesses, received 47% support but is still too early for CNN to call.

In New Jersey, voters were asked to amend their constitution to raise the state minimum wage from $7.25 to $8.25 per hour. In New York, voters considered a proposal to authorize seven casinos to generate new revenue for public schools and potentially cut property taxes.

Outside spending is on the rise in various states, with national interests influencing local elections. For instance, in the SeaTac minimum wage proposition, large contributions from out-of-state groups have dominated, with very little from city residents. This trend raises concerns about the core promise of the initiative process and representative democracy.

The GMO and minimum-wage ballot measures could have significant economic implications for companies and are seen as part of national movements. The biggest "no" donor for the GMO labeling measure in Washington is the Grocery Manufacturers Association, which has put in $11 million, while Monsanto has given more than $5 million. The total raised to combat Initiative 522 is the most ever raised for one side of an initiative election.

Nicole "Snooki" Polizzi, a former star of Jersey Shore, got married to her fiancé Jionni LaValle in a Great Gatsby-themed wedding at The Venetian in Garfield, New Jersey, on November 29. The couple, parents to Lorenzo, 2, and Giovanna Marie, 3 months, exchanged vows in a black and gold-colored event. Snooki donned two dresses for the occasion - an off-white, traditional lace gown for the ceremony and a more "fun and Gatsby-themed" dress for the reception. Her bridesmaids, including BFF Jenni “JWoww” Farley, wore black gowns with bows. The wedding was celebrated with a cigar and scotch bar, and an 18-piece band Time Machine provided the music for the reception. Snooki and LaValle have been together for over a year and got engaged in March 2012. They have two children together.

In a recent development, President Donald Trump has expressed support for a boycott of Harley-Davidson, a U.S. motorcycle manufacturer, following the company's decision to move some production overseas due to EU tariffs. The EU tariffs were a response to tariffs imposed by the U.S. on a variety of EU products. Harley-Davidson, based in Milwaukee, has stated that the new tariffs could cost the company up to $100 million annually. Trump's call for a boycott was made in a series of tweets, where he praised the potential move and suggested that it would level the playing field for American businesses. The President met with a group of "Bikers for Trump" supporters at his golf course in Bedminster, New Jersey, over the weekend. Harley-Davidson has not yet responded to requests for comment regarding the boycott.

Steve Vogelsang, a former Winnipeg broadcast personality and Red River College journalism instructor, has been charged with two counts of robbery involving two separate banks in Medicine Hat, Alberta. Vogelsang, who worked at CKY-TV (now CTV Winnipeg) from 1992 to 2002 and taught journalism at Red River College from 2002 to 2011, is accused of robbing a Royal Bank of Canada on October 19 and a Bank of Montreal on October 20 without the use of a disguise. He was arrested at a hotel in Medicine Hat on Saturday and is expected in court tomorrow.

Vogelsang's financial and legal difficulties are also highlighted in the report. Court documents show he faced charges of sexual assault in September 2016, which were stayed in October 2017. He was also granted a protection order in March 2017 and faces three charges of disobeying a court order, laid in August 2017.

In addition, Vogelsang is accused of harassing a former student he had dated off and on since 2004. The woman obtained a protection order against him in March and alleges that he continued to contact her despite police requests to leave her alone.

Vogelsang is fighting those allegations next month and has stated that the woman "has repeatedly misled police in an attempt to discredit me." He also claims that the woman "has actively interfered in my life."

Red River College confirmed that Vogelsang is no longer an employee there.

A video has gone viral showing a New York lawyer, Anna Lushchinskaya, engaging in a racially charged and violent attack on a fellow subway passenger. The incident, which occurred on a D train in Brooklyn, left a 24-year-old woman with cuts to her face. Lushchinskaya has been charged with two counts of felony assault and was apprehended at the 36th Street Station. The dispute began after Lushchinskaya bumped into the victim, and the attack escalated with Lushchinskaya using racial slurs and striking the victim with an umbrella and keys. A good Samaritan intervened, but Lushchinskaya also attacked him. Lushchinskaya has a prior arrest this year for a subway altercation at the same station in Brooklyn. The victim, who wishes to remain anonymous, expressed gratitude for the intervention of fellow passengers. The incident has sparked outrage and attracted millions of views on social media. Lushchinskaya could not be reached for comment, and it is unclear whether she is actively practicing law. The incident recalls another incident earlier in 2018 when another New York lawyer, Aaron Schlossberg, was caught on video making a racially charged, anti-immigrant rant. That incident also prompted intense blowback and a referral to attorney disciplinary authorities.

South Korean film legend Choi Eun-hee, who was once abducted and forced to make movies for the North Korean regime, has passed away at the age of 91. Choi, a leading actress in the South, began her film career in 1947 and rose to stardom in the late 1940s with movies like "The Sun Of Night" and "A Hometown in Heart." She later married Shin Sang-ok, a leading film director, and together they established Shin Film, leading the Korean film industry in the 1960s and 1970s.

In 1978, Choi was kidnapped by North Korean agents from Hong Kong and taken to Pyongyang. Her husband was also abducted six months later. In North Korea, the pair were forced by Kim Jong Il, the father of Kim Jong Un, to help revamp the country's film industry. Choi won the "Best Actress" award at the Moscow Film Festival in 1985 for her role in "Salt," produced in North Korea, becoming the first Korean to claim an award at an overseas film festival.

After eight years, the pair escaped captivity while in Vienna for a film festival, fleeing to the US embassy and, after ten years in the US, back to South Korea. Choi published her autobiography, "Confessions," in 2007. She died on Monday afternoon in a hospital in South Korea after a long battle with a chronic disease.

Choi is survived by two sons and two daughters. Her ex-husband Shin passed away in 2006. Choi's passing has been widely mourned across South Korea, with many remembering her as a beautiful and passionate actress. Her funeral will be held on Thursday in Seoul.

North Korea has always denied abducting the couple, saying they had sought sanctuary there. However, North Korean agents are suspected of abducting at least 17, and possibly more than 100, Japanese citizens, snatching them off streets and beaches and smuggling them to North Korea. Former U.S. President Jimmy Carter was taken to a hospital in Winnipeg on Thursday after experiencing dehydration while working on a Habitat for Humanity house. Carter, 92, was working outside in the sun for about 90 minutes when he appeared to feel faint and was taken to St. Boniface General Hospital for rehydration. His wife, Rosalynn, was with him.

The incident occurred during a Habitat for Humanity build that Carter and his wife are participating in as part of a week-long project. The couple has been longtime supporters of the organization and have helped build homes in various countries since 1984.

Carter had been working with volunteers to build a house for Todd Gauthier and his daughters Chloie and Carmin, aged nine and seven. The house is part of a larger project to build 25 homes in Manitoba as part of Canada's 150th anniversary celebrations.

Carter informed build leaders that he is feeling "OK," and encouraged volunteers to continue on with their regular workday. Any further information on Carter's condition will have to come from the Carter Center, a not-for-profit organization founded by the ex-president.

The last time Carter was in Manitoba was 1993, when he lent a hand at the construction sites for 18 other Winnipeg homes through the Habitat organization. The couple made a stop this month in Alberta to help with builds in Edmonton. The projects are part of a Habitat for Humanity "blitz" aiming to build 150 new homes across Canada between July 9-14.

An Ohio man named Matthew B. Matheny, 40, was found alive on Mount St. Helens in Washington state on Wednesday, nearly a week after he went missing during a day hike. Matheny, who was visiting friends in the area, survived by eating berries and bees he killed during his time lost in the wilderness. He was found in good condition, talking, and was flown to a hospital as a precaution due to dehydration.

Matheny set out for a hike on the mountain last Thursday, and his friends reported him missing when he failed to return. A search and rescue operation was launched, with about 30 search-and-rescue personnel, assisted by helicopters, tracking dogs, and a drone operated by the sheriff's office, searching for him daily.

Searchers focused on a 1-square-mile area based on cellphone signals and a computer model that sought to predict Matheny's movements. Matheny was found below a different trail, authorities said. He was scraped up and his feet were unprotected after the sandals he was wearing broke during the ordeal.

Matheny's parents, Linda and Carney Matheny, said during a press conference outside PeaceHeath Southwest Medical Center that he was being treated for dehydration and would likely stay overnight. They described their son as a former Boy Scout who is interested in fitness and nutrition with a sense of humor and a knack for getting himself into humorous situations.

The search for Matheny attracted a lot of attention, with at least 40 people participating in the search effort. Matheny's friends and family also were at the search scene. Charlie Rosenzweig, chief criminal deputy for Cowlitz County Sheriff's Office, called it "extremely unusual" that someone would survive such an ordeal. The parents of Matheny expressed their gratitude to all the emergency responders, volunteers, and his friends who aided in helping find their son.

Title: The Evolution of a New Species of Darwin's Finch Observed in Real-Time

 In a groundbreaking discovery, scientists have observed the evolution of a new species of Darwin's finch on the Galapagos Islands, a process that took just two generations. The study, published in the journal Science, was conducted over four decades by researchers from Princeton University and Uppsala University in Sweden.

 The new species, nicknamed "Big Bird," originated from the hybridization of two distinct species: the large cactus finch (Geospiza conirostris) and the medium ground finch (Geospiza fortis). The large cactus finch, a non-native species, arrived on the small island of Daphne Major 36 years ago and mated with a resident medium ground finch.

 The researchers followed the new lineage for six generations, taking blood samples for genetic analysis. They discovered that the original male parent was from Española island, more than 100 kilometers away. The offspring were reproductively isolated due to their unique song and differences in beak size and shape, which helped them compete for resources and mate within their own lineage.

 The study provides evidence that hybridization can lead to rapid speciation and that species can evolve quickly. It also challenges the traditional definition of a species as two populations that cannot produce fully fertile progeny when interbreeding.

 The research was supported by the Galapagos National Parks Service, the Charles Darwin Foundation, the National Science Foundation, the Knut and Alice Wallenberg Foundation, and the Swedish Research Council. The authors of the study include Sangeet Lamichhaney, Fan Han, Matthew T. Webster, Leif Andersson, B. Rosemary Grant, and Peter R. Grant.

 This discovery is significant as it demonstrates the value of long-term field studies and could help scientists better understand the process of speciation. Charles Darwin would have been excited to read this paper.

Oprah Winfrey, the media mogul, has announced plans to close Harpo Studios in Chicago by the end of the year, as her company's productions transition to OWN headquarters in Los Angeles. The move comes two months after OWN moved into a new space in West Hollywood, and it will impact approximately 200 employees. Winfrey delivered the news to her Harpo staff in person on Tuesday, expressing a mix of excitement and nostalgia about the 26-year history of the Chicago-based company.

OWN, co-owned by Winfrey and Discovery Communications, has posted three consecutive years of growth and ranked as the No. 20 ad-supported cable network among women. The closure of Harpo, which had produced over 800 hours of original programming exclusively for OWN, will allow the company to consolidate its team under one roof, particularly as the 4-year-old network is still in an early growth stage.

Winfrey, 61, will continue to pursue interests outside of the executive suite, including a cadre of film projects and a recurring role in Queen Sugar, a drama series from Selma’s Ava DuVernay. The high-end DuVernay drama is key to Winfrey's ongoing scripted push at OWN, with DuVernay set to deliver a pilot draft script to Winfrey in the coming days.

In addition to Queen Sugar, Winfrey has revealed plans for international speaking engagements and is set to reunite with Lee Daniels for his upcoming biopic, Pryor, in which she'll portray Richard Pryor’s grandmother Marie Carter. Winfrey's own Los Angeles-based Harpo Films will remain active, with a development slate that includes Henrietta Lacks at HBO and Oprah's Book Club 2.0 picks Ruby and The Invention of Wings.

The Harpo move comes nearly a year after real estate developer Sterling Bay Cos. closed a deal for the production company's four-building facility, reportedly paying a combined $30.5 million. A small group of the Chicago-based Harpo staffers will join the approximately 140 OWN employees who have moved into the network's newly constructed three-floor space at West Hollywood's The Lot. The remainder of Winfrey's lineup, including Master Class and Iyanla Fix My Life, will now be produced within Los Angeles-based OWN.

The exodus of Harpo Studios may be a tipping point for TV production in Chicago, with staffers doubting there will be enough jobs in the city to handle the influx of Harpo veterans. Winfrey leaves behind a monument to the "Oprah Effect" in the form of the massive facility she built, and the West Loop neighborhood she helped revive.

The document is a transcript of a speech given by President Donald Trump at a lunch with leaders from various African countries, including Côte d'Ivoire, Ethiopia, Ghana, Guinea, Namibia, Nigeria, Senegal, Uganda, and South Africa. The Miss World pageant, established in 1951, has announced the elimination of the swimsuit round after 63 years, marking a significant shift in the competition's focus. The decision aims to move away from physical appeal and emphasize the contestants' intellect, charity work, and service projects. The pageant's chairwoman, Julia Morley, stated that the swimsuit round did not align with the organization's "beauty with a purpose" philosophy.

In recent years, Miss World has placed more emphasis on the "beauty with a purpose" round, where contestants carry out charity work and raise awareness for worthy causes. The pageant's national director for Miss World America/Miss United States, Chris Wilmer, expressed that the contestants should be seen as ambassadors and spokespersons, rather than beauty queens.

To replace the swimsuit round, Miss World plans to introduce a beachwear round in competitions, focusing more on fashion than bikinis. Wilmer explained that the change sends a strong message and is a step towards modernizing the pageantry industry.

The Miss World competition, which was initially a publicity stunt featuring 26 women in bikinis on the River Thames in 1951, has evolved significantly over the years. In addition to the swimsuit round, contestants have competed in challenge events like sports, dance, talent, top model gown, Beauty with a Purpose video, and several interviews.

The 64th Miss World winner, Rolene Strauss of South Africa, was crowned on Dec. 14, 2014, marking the final event featuring contestants wearing bikinis. Strauss was judged on an in-depth interview, a service project dedicated to keeping girls in school, and her academic record.

Morley expressed her disapproval of the focus on physical appeal, stating that she does not want to see women just walking up and down in bikinis. She emphasized that the pageant is not about comparing women's bodies but about listening to their voices.

In contrast, The Miss Universe pageant, owned by Donald Trump, places a strong emphasis on the swimsuit element of the pageant and does not include an interview or a service element. Morley stated that following her husband's death, Trump phoned to ask if she was ready to throw in the towel, but she took out a $5 million loan to keep the company afloat.

The Miss World pageant has faced criticism from the feminist left, with protests occurring in the 1960s and 1970s. However, in recent years, the pageant has resurfaced as a cultural juggernaut, attended by a well-dressed and worldly crowd.

The elimination of the swimsuit round is a pioneering move for the pageantry industry, challenging the traditional focus on physical appearance and encouraging a shift towards judging contestants on their intellect, charity work, and service projects.

In a tragic turn of events, a Brooklyn man named Joseph Andrade, 44, and his adult son, Carlos, 22, died from a double opioid overdose while celebrating a family birthday party on Sunday. The incident occurred after the two excused themselves from the festivities, claiming they needed to go for a smoke. It is believed that Carlos, who was not known to use drugs, joined his father, a known addict, in taking a powerful opiate mix of heroin and fentanyl.

Carlos was discovered by his girlfriend, Jasmin Santos, just inside the foyer of his father’s building, showing signs of asphyxiation. Joseph was found outside the building on 27th Street near Fourth Avenue in Greenwood. Both men were administered Narcan, a drug that reverses the effects of an overdose, but it was too late, and they died at Lutheran Medical, authorities said.

Carlos had driven up from Maryland for the birthday bash with Jasmin and their children, ages 1 and 4. The distraught women called 911, and the incident is now under investigation, with the cause to be determined by the medical examiner.

The father and son's deaths are part of the ongoing opioid epidemic in the United States, which was declared a public health emergency in October 2017. The National Library of Medicine has been archiving a collection of websites and social media documenting various responses, perspectives, and impacts of the epidemic. The collection includes voices from the medical and public health communities, addiction researchers, policymakers, law enforcement, the addicted, and their families and communities.

Chinese tech billionaire Jack Ma, the executive chairman of Alibaba Group Holding Ltd., has retracted his promise to create one million jobs in the U.S., citing the ongoing trade dispute between the two economic powerhouses. Ma made the pledge during a meeting with then-President-elect Trump in January 2017, stating that the jobs would be generated by boosting sales by U.S. small businesses on Alibaba's e-commerce platforms.

However, in a recent interview with China's official news agency, Xinhua, Ma stated that the escalating tariffs imposed by both Washington and Beijing have made it impossible to fulfill the promise. He explained that the promise was contingent on friendly China-U.S. cooperation and reasonable trade relations, which no longer exist due to the current situation.

Analysts had already expressed doubts about the pledge, as it did not involve Alibaba investing in the U.S. to build factories or fulfillment centers. Instead, the plan was to stimulate trade by helping American small businesses and farmers sell their products to consumers in China and other Asian markets through Alibaba's platforms.

Alibaba held a conference in Detroit last year to encourage such sales, but the company has yet to disclose how many U.S. jobs have been created as a result. In the same interview, Ma expressed concerns about the prolonged trade war, predicting it could last for up to 20 years.

Ma, who founded Alibaba in his apartment nearly two decades ago, announced this month that he will step down as executive chairman next year, with current CEO Daniel Zhang set to succeed him. The 54-year-old tycoon, who was once an English teacher, plans to return to education.

Campbell Soup Company has announced changes to its iconic chicken noodle soup recipe, reducing the number of ingredients and making the product more transparent and health-conscious. The new recipe, which features in a limited-edition line of Star Wars-themed cans, contains 20 ingredients compared to 30 in the previous version. The changes are part of a broader strategy by Campbell to adapt to changing consumer preferences and address a decline in unit sales.

Under the leadership of Denise M. Morrison, who became CEO in 2011, Campbell has been working to modernize its approach to food production and marketing. This includes banishing ingredients that consumers dislike, engaging in conversations with consumers through advertising and social media, and making acquisitions to gain a foothold in new markets and bring new ideas to the organization.

The new chicken noodle soup recipe is part of Campbell's efforts to close the gap between kitchen and factory, using more common, kitchen-friendly ingredients. However, the changes carry risks, as these products are beloved and their profiles have become well-defined in consumers' minds over the years.

Soup sales have been stagnant globally since 2012, with sales expected to fall further this year. Smaller, organic brands like Annie's and Amy's Kitchen are doing relatively better, which may be due in part to consumer distrust of larger, established food companies. Early sales of Campbell's new line of organic soup in cartons have been strong.

Campbell, which relies heavily on the US market for its soup sales, has more to lose than most other big soup companies. In the US, Campbell accounted for almost three-quarters of the $1.6 billion in condensed soup sales last year, but its unit sales fell more than 5 percent.

Campbell has made several strategic acquisitions in recent years, including Bolthouse, Plum Organics, Kelsen Group, and Garden Fresh Gourmet. These acquisitions have given Campbell entree to new markets and brought new ideas to the organization. Campbell has also added new products like Skillet Sauces and Slow Kettle soups to its portfolio, offering kitchen cooks shortcuts and busy consumers a quick meal.

The new chicken noodle soup recipe was developed by a team of food scientists and chefs, who worked to create a broth and noodles that tasted the same or better than the previous version. The recipe eliminates several flavoring chemicals, including monosodium glutamate (MSG), and adds water, dehydrated onions, and dehydrated chicken broth. The process does not end when the food scientists and chefs finish their work, as the new formulation may add cost to the product, and Campbell may tinker with shipping cases and labels to bring the cost in line.

Campbell has also launched a new advertising campaign, "Made for Real, Real Life," which aims to reintroduce consumers to the idea that soup can be a staple in the kitchen. The campaign features a variety of families, reflecting the diversity of families in America today. The first spot in the series, which features a gay couple feeding their young son Campbell's Star Wars chicken noodle soup, caused a controversy, but Campbell shrugged it off. The second ad in the series features a mother and father preparing an organic tomato soup for their son.

Overall, Campbell's efforts to modernize its chicken noodle soup recipe and engage with consumers through advertising and social media are part of a broader strategy to adapt to changing consumer preferences and address a decline in unit sales. The new recipe reduces the number of ingredients, makes the product more transparent and health-conscious, and aims to close the gap between kitchen and factory. However, the changes carry risks, and Campbell will need to carefully balance the need for innovation with the need to preserve the beloved profile of its classic products.

NASA senior space scientist David Morrison debunked an apocalyptic claim that a planet called Nibiru is on a collision course with Earth, stating that there is no such planet, it's not a brown dwarf surrounded by planets, and it's not on a collision course toward Earth. A 4-year-old boy named Eli Waller from Hamilton Township, New Jersey, died last month due to Enterovirus D68 (EV-D68), a respiratory virus that has been spreading across the U.S. since August, affecting at least 43 states. Eli showed symptoms of pinkeye before his death, but no other symptoms. He was kept home from school on September 23 due to the pinkeye. The Mercer County medical examiner's office confirmed Eli's cause of death as EV-D68.

The U.S. is currently experiencing the enterovirus season, with the CDC expecting it to ease later in the fall. The relatively rare D68 strain appears to be the dominant type of enterovirus this year and may be contributing to an increase in severe respiratory illness. There are no special methods to treat or prevent EV-D68, and people are advised to follow typical hand hygiene practices.

Eli's father described him as a "beautiful mix of eagerness and hesitancy, need and striving, caution and surprise, all of which were grounded in a pure, unconditional love." The family is establishing The First Day of School Foundation to provide support for students involved in Special Education.

At least four other patients who tested positive for EV-D68 have died, and investigations are ongoing to determine if the virus played a role in their deaths. Another child in Rhode Island died last week from a combination of bacterial and viral infections, with the Rhode Island Department of Health stating the 10-year-old girl died of Staphylococcus aureus sepsis "associated with" enterovirus 68.

The respiratory disease is suspected of sickening children in at least 43 states, with symptoms often starting out like a common cold with coughing or a runny nose. In rare cases, the respiratory problems can become severe, particularly for asthmatic patients. In Colorado, CDC and local health officials are investigating whether limb weakness and paralysis reported in nine children was associated with the enterovirus 68. The Associated Press contributed to this story.

Title: Little Fockers (2010) - A Disappointing Sequel with a Depressing Tone

Little Fockers, released in 2010, is the third installment in the Focker series, following Meet the Parents (2000) and Meet the Fockers (2004). The film stars Robert De Niro, Ben Stiller, Owen Wilson, Dustin Hoffman, Barbra Streisand, and Jessica Alba. Directed by Paul Weitz, the film's running length is 1 hour and 35 minutes, and it has a PG-13 rating for profanity and sexual content.

The film continues the story of Greg Focker (Ben Stiller) and his family, including his wife, Pam (Teri Polo), and his father-in-law, Jack Byrnes (De Niro). The plot revolves around Jack's decision to make Greg the "Godfocker" - the patriarch of the next generation of Byrnes and Fockers. To do so, Jack conducts background checks and spying, which uncovers Greg's apparent dalliance with a drug company representative, Andi Garcia (Jessica Alba). This stokes Jack's anger, leading to an all-out war between him and Greg.

Critics found Little Fockers to be a disappointing sequel, with many feeling that it brought an overpowering sense of sadness. The film was particularly criticized for its reliance on recycled humor and a lack of character development. Researchers from Canada have discovered a protein called cardiotrophin 1 (CT1) that can trick the heart into growing in a healthy way, potentially treating heart failure. This growth is reversible, similar to that which occurs in response to endurance exercise or pregnancy. The team, including members from the Ottawa Hospital and the University of Ottawa in Ontario, Canada, reports the finding in the journal Cell Research.

Heart failure is a serious condition in which the heart cannot pump enough oxygen-rich blood to meet the needs of the body and its organs. The condition commonly results from heart muscle damage following a heart attack, the main cause of which is coronary artery disease. There are around 26 million people living with heart failure worldwide, and numbers are rising.

The outlook for patients diagnosed with heart failure are poor; their survival rates are worse than those of patients with breast, prostate, and bowel cancer. In the United States, where around 5.7 million adults are living with heart failure, around half of patients die within 5 years of being diagnosed. If heart failure is diagnosed and treated early, it is possible to improve survival and quality of life. Treatment usually consists of drug therapy, reducing dietary sodium, and exercising regularly.

The new study represents a step forward in a regenerative medicine approach to the treatment of heart failure, where the aim is to treat or even cure the disease by regrowing damaged tissue or restoring function. Co-senior study author Lynn Megeney, a professor at the University of Ottawa, explains that when part of the heart dies - as it does in heart failure - "the remaining muscles try to adapt by getting bigger, but this happens in a dysfunctional way and it doesn't actually help the heart pump more blood."

However, in animals with heart failure, they found that CT1 caused the heart muscles to "grow in a more healthy way," and it also stimulated the heart to grow new blood vessels. "This actually increases the heart's ability to pump blood, just like what you would see with exercise and pregnancy," he adds.

The researchers investigated the effects of CT1 in laboratory-grown heart muscle cells, rats, and mice. They also compared the effects of CT1 with those of phenylephrine (PE), which is a drug that stimulates the "bad kind of heart growth," such as the harmful, irreversible enlargement that occurs in heart failure. The researchers found that, when treated with CT1, heart muscle cells grow into longer, healthier fibers, whereas treatment with PE just results in wider growth. Also, with CT1, the new heart muscle tissue formed with new blood vessels alongside, which helps the heart to pump better. PE did not have this effect.

Furthermore, the heart growth that occurs with CT1 is reversible; when treatment stops, the organ returns to its original size, as it does when exercise stops or after pregnancy. The unhealthy heart growth that results from PE, on the other hand, is irreversible; when treatment stops, the heart remains dysfunctionally enlarged.

In two animal models of heart failure - one caused by heart attack, which damages the left side of the heart, and the other caused by pulmonary hypertension, or high blood pressure in the lungs, which damages the right side - CT1 treatment led to "dramatic improvements" in heart function.

The team is excited by these findings because, if they translate to humans, they could vastly improve the prognosis for patients with heart failure. Co-senior author Prof. Duncan Stewart - cardiologist, senior scientist, and executive vice president of research at the Ottawa Hospital - explains that, at present, the "only treatment for right heart failure is a transplant." "And although we have drugs that can reduce the symptoms of left heart failure," he adds, "we can't fix the problem, and left heart failure often leads to right heart failure over time."

The researchers are hopeful that CT1 will work in humans with heart failure because it did so in several animal models of the condition. They also point out that, while in theory, exercise is an obvious way to reap the benefits that CT1 appears to offer, this route is not open to people with heart failure, who can only exercise in a limited way.

Profs. Megeney and Stewart already have patents pending for using CT1 to treat heart problems, and they hope to partner with others to test the protein in human patients. Nevertheless, they say that it will be several years, even if the tests are successful, before the treatment is ready for widespread clinical use.

The document discusses an investigation into the FBI's handling of a tip regarding Nikolas Cruz, the perpetrator of the school shooting at Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School in Parkland, Florida on February 14, 2018. Greece is facing an economic crisis as a deal to form a national unity government has collapsed, reviving the chances of former European Central Bank vice president Lucas Papademos heading the coalition. Prime Minister George Papandreou failed to install an old-politician ally as premier, and the country is running out of money next month unless emergency funding is agreed with the European Union and International Monetary Fund. In a separate development, the Italian government presented economic overhaul measures to the Senate Budget Committee, confirming its plans to raise the pension age and giving more details on how it intends to privatize state-owned real estate. The Italian government is attaching economic overhaul measures to the annual fiscal policy legislation in a bid to hasten its approval at a time when investors are frustrated with Italy's perceived reform inertia.

The article discusses the ongoing controversy surrounding the detention of an American diplomat, Raymond Davis, in Pakistan. The article discusses a new research finding about male black widow spiders adopting an unusual strategy to increase their reproductive success. Traditionally, mature female black widow spiders consume their male partners after mating, a practice known as sexual cannibalism. However, a significant number of male spiders are now copulating with immature females, who are too young to consume their mates. These young females have internal genitals protected by a tough shell, which the males penetrate to deposit sperm. This tactic, discovered by researchers from the University of Toronto Scarborough, allows male spiders to have multiple partners, a departure from their usual monogamous behavior.

The researchers found that one-third of the immature females they collected had been violated in this way. The male spiders use their fangs to cut through the exoskeleton and deposit sperm in the female's sperm receptacle, causing no apparent injury. This tactic, while currently uncommon, has the potential to change the sexual preferences and evolutionary trajectory of the black widow spider species. The researchers suggest that this sexual experimentation may be a response to the evolutionary advantage of sexual cannibalism, but its long-term impact remains to be seen.
