The unemployment insurance system in the United States is facing a crisis due to record-high unemployment and, in some cases, poor planning. Thirty-six states have increased the annual tax businesses pay to finance unemployment benefits, with the average tax per worker ranging from $267 in Alabama to $1,070 in Hawaii. These tax increases are hitting employers nationwide, with business owners in Virginia facing an average tax increase from $95 per employee in 2009 to $171 this year. The recession has depleted many state unemployment insurance trust funds, forcing states to borrow from the federal government, raise taxes, or cut benefits. In some states, unemployment compensation funds are still in the black, but reserves are rapidly dwindling. The situation is particularly dire for seniors, with many facing benefit cuts or reductions in benefits. For example, James Hay, a 70-year-old in Roanoke, Virginia, had his monthly unemployment benefits cut from about $800 to $100 because state law limits payments to Social Security recipients when the state's fund runs low. The cuts to unemployment benefits are controversial, with some arguing that they undermine the fundamental goals of the program, which is to boost the economy and keep people out of poverty during an economic downturn. The unemployment insurance system's crisis is expected to continue as long as high unemployment persists, and some states may need to impose further tax increases or benefit cuts if the situation does not improve.

The Universal Paid Leave Act of 2015 was introduced in Washington D.C. by council members Elissa Silverman and David Grosso. The bill aims to provide 16 weeks of paid leave for medical or family reasons to all D.C. residents and workers, including those who work for federal government and opt in by paying their own contributions to a city-managed leave fund. The bill would offer the most generous paid leave in the country and would work much like unemployment insurance.

The bill would be funded by contributions from employers, with 1% for every employee making over $150,000 per year, 0.8% for those in the $50,000-150,000 range, and so on down. Self-employed residents would be allowed to opt out. An employee taking leave would file a claim with the fund, which would pay out the benefits. Under the bill, the fund would cover 100% of the first $1,000 an employee makes per week and 50% thereafter, for a maximum of $3,000 per week over the course of the leave taken.

The bill is being co-sponsored by several council members, giving it enough votes to pass the Council. The business community has expressed concerns about the costs of providing paid leave and the potential impact on the business climate in Washington, D.C. Supporters of the bill argue that it will benefit all D.C.-based employees, particularly low-income workers, and will make the District more competitive regionally. The bill has been assigned to a Council committee for a hearing and markup, after which it would go to the full Council for voting.

The bill draws from research done for a $96,000 grant from the U.S. Department of Labor, and it is being supported by the Obama administration. The bill is part of a larger strategy by the Obama administration to address rising income inequality and to use local law to forge a policy bulkhead for bigger changes nationally. The bill is also part of a larger trend of states and local governments designing paid-leave policies that work for their citizens, as the United States is one of the few countries on Earth without national paid leave.

In a blog post, Chris Urmson, the director of Google's self-driving car project, discussed a recent collision involving one of their autonomous vehicles. The incident occurred on July 1 in Mountain View, California, where Google's self-driving cars have been testing for several years. The Lexus SUV, equipped with sensors and cameras, was stationary at a green light, having stopped along with two other vehicles due to traffic congestion on the opposite side of the intersection. A fourth vehicle, driven by a presumably distracted individual, rear-ended the Google car at approximately 17 mph, causing minor whiplash to the three Google employees on board and resulting in damage to both vehicles.

Urmson emphasized that this incident, the 14th accident involving Google's self-driving cars since the project's inception in 2009, was not the fault of the autonomous vehicle. In fact, human error and inattention were identified as the primary causes of the collisions. Google's self-driving cars are designed to pay attention to hundreds of objects in all directions and never tire, get irritable, or become distracted. Urmson compared human driving behavior to watching a television show on TiVo, suggesting that people often treat the road as if they can pause it and return without missing a beat.

Google has logged nearly 2 million miles with their autonomous vehicles and adds around 10,000 new miles each week. The company believes that self-driving cars will be safer and more efficient than human drivers. Urmson also mentioned that they are exploring ways to alert distracted drivers before a potential collision, although concerns about annoying residents of Mountain View have been raised regarding the use of honking as a warning signal.

Urmson concluded the blog post by urging drivers to remain attentive on the road, especially during the summer months when road accidents tend to increase. He emphasized that the fight against distracted driving is everyone's responsibility, until the day when self-driving cars become widely available and people can simply relax and enjoy the ride.

The 89th Academy Awards nominations were announced on January 24, 2017, with the candy-colored musical "La La Land" leading with a record-tying 14 nominations, matching "Titanic" and "All About Eve." The film earned nods for best picture, its stars Emma Stone and Ryan Gosling, its songs, and its 32-year-old writer-director, Damien Chazelle.

The other nominees for best picture are "Moonlight," "Arrival," "Manchester by the Sea," "Hell or High Water," "Lion," "Fences," "Hidden Figures," and "Hacksaw Ridge." Following two years of "OscarsSoWhite" furor, the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences fielded a notably more diverse field of nominees, led by Barry Jenkins' luminous coming-of-age portrait "Moonlight," Denzel Washington's "Fences," and Theodore Melfi's "Hidden Figures."

The nominees for best actor are Casey Affleck ("Manchester by the Sea"), Andrew Garfield ("Hacksaw Ridge"), Ryan Gosling ("La La Land"), Viggo Mortensen ("Captain Fantastic"), and Denzel Washington ("Fences"). The nominees for best supporting actor are Mahershala Ali ("Moonlight"), Jeff Bridges ("Hell or High Water"), Michael Shannon ("Nocturnal Animals"), Lucas Hedges ("Manchester by the Sea"), and Dev Patel ("Lion").

The Oscars will take place on February 26, with Mel Gibson receiving a best director nomination for his World War II drama "Hacksaw Ridge." The dearth of blockbusters among the best picture nominees poses a test for host Jimmy Kimmel, who will be presiding over the Oscarcast for the first time. The regular business of today's corporate-driven Hollywood is increasingly set apart from the industry's awards season, where smaller, critically adored films like "12 Years a Slave," "Birdman," "Boyhood," and "Spotlight" have recently dominated.

Amazon landed its first best picture nomination for Kenneth Lonergan's "Manchester by the Sea," which the streaming retailer partnered with Roadside Attractions to distribute. The Oscars also rejiggered its nominations format, with pre-produced videos of previous winners introducing each category on Tuesday morning. The Academy Awards will be the first Oscars voted on since academy president Cheryl Boone Isaacs ushered in new membership rules and added 683 new members as a way to diversify a predominantly white, male, and elderly group, which now numbers 6,687.

The article discusses the decline of the chick lit genre and the rise of a new genre called "farm lit." In farm lit, the heroines leave urban cities for rural areas, engaging in activities such as raising goats, opening cupcake bakeries, and tending to farms. David Goodall, a 104-year-old Australian scientist and respected botanist, ended his life in a medically assisted suicide at a Swiss clinic on Thursday. Goodall, who was not terminally ill, had campaigned for the legalization of assisted dying in Australia but was forced to travel to Switzerland due to its ban. He died while listening to Beethoven's "Ode to Joy." Goodall had lost his independence when he lost his driver's license at 84, which prompted his decision to seek assisted suicide. He hoped his story would lead to the legalization of assisted dying in other countries. Goodall was a pro-euthanasia advocate and a member of Exit International, which represented him in his final journey. He was born in London in 1914 and held academic positions across the world before retiring in 1979. In 2016, he was awarded the Order of Australia Medal. Goodall's family and friends were with him at the Life Circle clinic in Basel, Switzerland, when he died.

In this article, Debra Harrell, a mother from South Carolina, was arrested for leaving her 9-year-old daughter alone at a park while she went to work at McDonald's. The girl had a cellphone to call her mother in case of emergency. Most commentators believe that authorities went too far in arresting Harrell, as they think the child is now in more danger in the custody of the department of social services.

Dorothy Roberts, a professor of law, sociology, and civil rights at the University of Pennsylvania, explains that state laws are vague about how parents should behave, and there are no specifics about how long a child can be left alone without supervision. Roberts also points out that states determine whether to treat neglect as a crime or as a child welfare matter, and the vagueness of the statutes leaves room for discretion by social workers, police, judges, and prosecutors, which can allow race, class, and gender biases to influence decisions.

Jonathan Chait argues that the arrest of Harrell is concerning because it comes at a time when the state is suffering from a shortage of foster families and a child protective services workforce that is overwhelmed. He also points out that the state's decision to arrest Harrell and take custody of her child has caused the child more trauma than she was ever likely to suffer in the park.

The article also discusses a cultural shift in society where most people believe a child can not be out of sight for one second and needs constant, total adult supervision. This shift is not rooted in fact and is rooted in irrational fear, according to Lenore Skenazy, the founder of Free Range Kids.

In conclusion, the arrest of Debra Harrell for leaving her 9-year-old daughter alone at a park while she went to work has sparked a debate about the role of the state in parenting decisions, the vagueness of child welfare laws, and the cultural shift towards constant adult supervision of children. Many believe that the state went too far in arresting Harrell and causing her child more trauma than she was ever likely to suffer in the park.

In a groundbreaking six-year study, scientists have identified and reconstructed the likely common ancestor of placental mammals, a group that includes humans, whales, bats, and elephants. The ancestor, named Protungulatum donnae, is believed to have lived around 200,000 to 400,000 years after the Cretaceous-Paleogene (K-Pg) extinction event, which occurred approximately 66 million years ago. The research, published in the journal Science, combined genetic and anatomical data to establish the ancestor's standing as an early placental mammal.

The study suggests that the common ancestor emerged later than previously estimated based on genetic data alone. The researchers found that Protungulatum had several anatomical characteristics associated with full-term live births, such as a two-horned uterus and a placenta in which the maternal blood came in close contact with the fetus's membranes, as in humans.

The findings challenge the theory that the breakup of the supercontinent of Gondwana around 120 million years ago was a direct factor in the diversification of mammals. The evidence of the common ancestor was found in North America, but the animal may have existed on other continents as well.

The research team used a vast online database called MorphoBank to build a composite of the hypothetical ancestor based on the morphology of existing and extinct animals, along with DNA data. The ancestor was a small, furry creature that weighed no more than a half-pound, had a long furry tail, and lived on insects.

The study also contradicts the molecular clock-based theory that placental mammals developed into different species because of the fragmentation of the supercontinent Gondwana, millions of years before the dinosaurs vanished. In addition, the study concluded that a subset of placental mammals known as Afrotheria, which includes elephants and aardvarks, did not originate in Africa as commonly believed; instead, authors say they arose in the Americas.

The research team drew on combined fossil evidence and genetic data encoded in DNA in evaluating the ancestor's standing as an early placental mammal. The findings were not a total surprise, but they are an important discovery because they rely on lots of information from fossils and also molecular data. The study is expected to be widely applied in years ahead to similar investigations of plants, insects, fish, and fowl.

Felicia Pearson, also known as "Snoop" from the HBO series "The Wire," pleaded guilty to conspiring to distribute heroin in a joint federal-state drug investigation known as "Operation Usual Suspects." The plea, accepted a day before her trial, suspended a seven-year sentence with credit for time served and ordered three years of supervised probation. Pearson was accused of allowing drugs and cash to be stored in her apartment. She was one of 64 people indicted in March in connection with the operation. The actress, who originally pleaded not guilty, has since stated that she would have been found not guilty. Pearson, who is moving to Los Angeles to avoid legal trouble in the future, has been involved in the drug trade since her teenage years, but has now learned a valuable lesson about loyalty. Pearson played a Baltimore drug gang assassin in "The Wire" and has since been working on two movies. Roger Ebert, a renowned film critic and television co-host, passed away on Thursday at the age of 70 in Chicago. He had been working for The Chicago Sun-Times for over 40 years and was best known for his thumbs-up or thumbs-down approach to movie reviews that significantly influenced the film industry.

Ebert was diagnosed with cancer in 2002 and suffered from related health problems throughout his life. Despite losing his ability to eat, drink, and speak, he continued to write reviews and commentary, becoming a prolific presence on Facebook and Twitter.

Ebert's work was highly influential, and he was respected for his dry wit, occasional sarcasm, and quirky opinions. His reviews ran the gamut from classics to independent cinema to cartoons, and he was known for his put-downs, which could be withering.

President Obama reacted to Ebert's death with a statement that praised him as someone who advised moviegoers about what to see and how to think about what they saw. Ebert's struggle with cancer gave him a public image as someone who refused to surrender to illness.

In recent years, Ebert became a popular figure on social media, with over 800,000 followers on Twitter. He commented on various topics, including pro football, James Joyce short stories, and untold numbers of movies and television shows.

Ebert was the first film critic to win a Pulitzer Prize, in 1975, and his columns were syndicated to more than 200 newspapers in the United States and abroad. He wrote more than 15 books, many of which were based on his columns. In 2005, he became the first film critic to be honored with a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame.

Ebert's collaboration with Gene Siskel popularized television film criticism, and their partnership began in 1975. Despite initially having no desire to team up with Ebert, Siskel came to appreciate his work and the two became close friends.

Ebert's death was met with an outpouring of tributes from the film industry and beyond. He will be remembered for his impact on film criticism, his love of movies, and his indomitable spirit in the face of illness.

In a groundbreaking study, researchers have found that brain scans of infants at high risk for autism can predict with 80% accuracy which babies will develop autism by the age of 2. The study, published in Nature, was conducted on 106 infants with older siblings diagnosed with autism, using magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) at 6 months, 12 months, and 24 months of age.

The findings reveal that early brain development biomarkers could help identify high-risk babies who will go on to develop autism. The study showed an increased rate of growth in the outer surface of the brain, known as the folds, in the first year of life, which was followed by an overgrowth of the brain in the second year. This overgrowth coincided with the behaviors typical of autism that start to emerge when the child reaches their second year.

The potential for earlier diagnosis and intervention is significant, as the sooner autism is recognized, the sooner families and doctors can employ intervention strategies like behavioral and communication therapies. Early diagnosis and intervention can significantly improve a child's condition and possibly even eliminate symptoms.

The study raises hopes for earlier care and interventions for those affected, as affected children could be helped with specialized care and interventions to help their social abilities before any behavioral symptoms start to appear. However, the technology is not yet ready for use in clinics, and more research is needed to confirm the findings and develop a tool that can predict autism in high-risk babies before their first birthday.

The study offers a potential breakthrough in the care of children with autism, as early intervention before the age of 2 could change the clinical course of those children whose brain development has gone awry and help them acquire skills that they would otherwise struggle to achieve. The technology could help families who already have an autistic child to access earlier diagnosis for subsequent children, allowing them to receive the right support as early as possible. However, it is important to note that autism is a complex condition that manifests in many different ways, and no single test is likely to be able to identify potential autism in all children.

Billionaire David Tepper, the founder of Appaloosa Management, has relocated his tax residency and corporate headquarters from New Jersey to Florida, a move that could save him hundreds of millions of dollars in taxes and potentially impact New Jersey's state budget significantly. Tepper, who has earned over $6 billion over the past three years, could have paid over $500 million in taxes to New Jersey if he had been taxed at the state's top rate of 8.97%.

Tepper's decision to move to Florida highlights the stark income difference between America's rich and poor and the subtle side effects of trying to solve it through taxation. New Jersey has one of the highest tax burdens in the country, with a marginal income tax rate of almost 9% for top earners and an array of estate and inheritance taxes. Florida, on the other hand, has one of the country's lowest tax burdens, with no personal income or estate taxes.

New Jersey's struggling state budget relies on income taxes for 40% of its revenue. The state's legislature is concerned about the potential impact of Tepper's departure on the state's tax revenue forecasts. Frank Haines, a budget officer with New Jersey's Office of Legislative Services, testified before a Senate committee that the state may be facing an unusual degree of income-tax forecast risk due to Tepper's move.

Tepper's move also sheds light on the economic puzzle and the perils of resolving it through increasing taxes. Economists argue that the relief for middle-class families should come from increasing their wages rather than tax cuts. The decision by Tepper to move to Florida for tax-friendly reasons highlights the inadequacy of pre-tax income for middle-class families, who are struggling to pay for housing and childcare.

In conclusion, the departure of one of New Jersey's richest citizens, David Tepper, could complicate estimates of how much tax money the struggling state will collect. Tepper's move to Florida for tax-friendly reasons underscores the stark income difference between America's rich and poor and the subtle side effects of trying to solve it through taxation. The state's legislature is concerned about the potential impact of Tepper's departure on the state's tax revenue forecasts, and economists argue that the relief for middle-class families should come from increasing their wages rather than tax cuts.

In the aftermath of the 2016 presidential election, President-elect Donald Trump reiterated his hard-line stance on immigration, vowing to deport approximately 2 to 3 million undocumented immigrants with criminal records. However, experts question the feasibility of such a plan, as the actual number of individuals who fit this criteria may be significantly lower than Trump's estimates.

In a "60 Minutes" interview, Trump emphasized his focus on deporting or incarcerating undocumented immigrants who are gang members, drug dealers, or have other criminal convictions. He suggested that there are "a lot of these people, probably 2 million, it could be even 3 million."

However, the Department of Homeland Security reports that there are roughly 1.9 million non-citizen immigrants who have been convicted of crimes and are subject to deportation. This total includes both undocumented immigrants and noncitizens in the country legally. The Migration Policy Institute estimates that there are roughly 11 million immigrants in the U.S. illegally, and approximately 820,000 of them have criminal records.

Trump's plan mirrors the approach taken by President Obama in his first term, when he prioritized deporting undocumented immigrants with criminal convictions. Deportations soared under Obama, topping 400,000 in 2012. However, in recent years, the Obama administration has shifted focus to deporting immigrants convicted of more serious crimes or for repeat offenses.

Chicago, a sanctuary city, has pledged to maintain its status, defying Trump's past promise to cut off funding to such cities. Chicago's elected officials, including Mayor Rahm Emanuel, are expected to hold a news conference to discuss the city's commitment to sanctuary status. Aldermen are expected to call on Republican Governor Bruce Rauner to pressure Trump to back off his vow to interfere with funding.

The move is largely motivated by elected officials who say they’ve heard from terrified residents, including so-called Dreamers (children whose parents entered the country illegally), who fear imminent deportation. On Sunday, Emanuel’s office released a statement directing those with questions or in need of legal resources to call 311.

Since Trump’s election, other cities that have affirmed their commitment to remaining sanctuaries include New York, Los Angeles, Seattle, Philadelphia, and San Francisco. There are dozens of sanctuary cities in the United States and more than 100 jurisdictions have policies on the books that limit compliance with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

Trump's immigration policy was a central part of his campaign message, framed by his pledge to build a wall along the U.S.-Mexico border. However, the realities of actually building the wall have begun to set in. The Mexican government has publicly reminded Trump that Mexico will not pay for the wall, and Trump transition co-chair Newt Gingrich has suggested that the wall could be part wall and "some fencing," in accordance with what congressional Republicans have proposed.

Barack Obama, in his final press conference as president, urged Trump to "think long and hard" before endangering young undocumented immigrants who received protections from deportation under his executive actions. Obama did not address the issue of protecting their information, which has some beneficiaries of the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) program concerned.

In the agricultural sector, rural Americans voted to remove the low-wage workers that are, arguably, the linchpin of the rural economy. Farming is a high-risk, low-margin business, largely propped up by government subsidies and a marginalized workforce willing to toil at appallingly low rates of pay. Millions of undocumented farmworkers are in a state of panic, fearing Trump's immigration policies.

Immigration experts have said Trump’s mass deportation plan is implausible and would likely be ineffective at reversing the tide of immigrants from south of the border. The Trump campaign has even acknowledged that his initial statements on deportation may have been more bluster than substance. More likely than rounding up all 11 million illegal immigrants, is that Trump would reverse DACA, President Obama’s executive order, which granted legal status – and a work permit – to immigrants who entered the country illegally prior to their 16th birthday. The paper trail associated with DACA workers would make them easy targets for deportation, compared to the millions of undocumented workers hiding in the shadows.

There will undoubtedly be intense political pressure from a coalition of immigrant rights groups to soften Trump’s anti-immigrant stance. The United Farm Workers, a Latino agricultural union based in California, which also advocates nationally on behalf of immigrant farm workers, will no doubt be one of those, leveraging its deep ties in Washington to block the president-elect’s deportation efforts.

Apple has filed a patent for a protective mechanism aimed at reducing damage to electronic devices, particularly the iPhone, during accidents such as drops. The system involves a sensor that detects when a device is falling and how it is positioned relative to the ground. The sensor data is processed by a system that determines the best way for the device to land, and a mechanism is deployed to reorientate the device mid-air or protect sensitive components.

The patent suggests various methods for this, including the movement of a weighted mass within the device, aeroplane-like foils that extend out from the device's surface, and a thrust mechanism like a small gas-propulsion device. The system also explores the possibility of ejecting cables to prevent the device from being pulled to the ground.

While the system is not close to production, it could potentially save the most fragile components of an iPhone, such as the glass screen, by controlling the device's landing. The patent was filed in September 2011 and credits Nicholas V. King and Fletcher Rothkopf as its inventors. However, given the iPhone's trend towards a thin-and-light design, it is unlikely that this complex system will be integrated into an iPhone anytime soon.

The disgraced cyclist Lance Armstrong is set to give his first television interview since being stripped of his Tour de France titles, in a 90-minute "no-holds-barred" interview with Oprah Winfrey, scheduled to air on January 17. The interview will address doping allegations against Armstrong, following the release of a 202-page report by the United States Anti-Doping Agency (USADA) in October, which detailed Armstrong's alleged use of performance-enhancing drugs and blood transfusions.

In the past, Armstrong has argued that he took more than 500 drug tests and never failed. However, the USADA report states that it had tested Armstrong less than 60 times and the International Cycling Union conducted about 215 tests.

The interview will take place at Armstrong's home in Austin, Texas, and is expected to be simulcast on Oprah.com. Armstrong has been training for triathlons in Hawaii since the ban, and has won two of the five events he has entered.

In October 2012, Armstrong was stripped of his titles and banned from cycling.

It is unclear whether Armstrong would face criminal prosecution for perjury should he confess. Armstrong was involved in several cases where he gave sworn testimony that he never used banned drugs. The interview with Oprah Winfrey may provide insight into Armstrong's thoughts and actions regarding the doping allegations against him.

The fast-track trade bill, introduced by Senators Orrin G. Hatch (R-Utah) and Ron Wyden (D-Ore.), moves forward President Obama's bid to complete the Trans-Pacific Partnership (TPP), a 12-nation trade agreement in the Asia Pacific. The bill allows the president to present a final agreement to Congress for an up-or-down vote without amendments, a move that would grant him vast new powers to close the deal. The bill faces fierce opposition from many Democrats, labor unions, and environmental groups who argue that the TPP will harm U.S. jobs and benefit large corporations.

The White House considers the fast-track authority crucial to wrapping up negotiations on the TPP, which Obama has touted as a cornerstone of his second-term agenda. The bill includes provisions mandating protections for workers and the environment, and a stipulation that human rights be a priority, although the details are lacking.

The legislation places Obama against a majority of House Democrats and a significant number of Senate Democrats, many of whom believe previous trade deals have hurt U.S. workers. Sen. Charles E. Schumer (D-N.Y.), expected to take over as Senate Democratic leader in 2017, has expressed skepticism towards the TPP due to its lack of protections against currency manipulation.

The bill's passage in the Senate is expected in May, setting up a more significant fight in the House, where the margins are narrow. The legislation faces opposition from several dozen House Republicans who either come from manufacturing districts or are opposed to giving Obama any new authority. To win passage in the House, Obama would need to deliver more than 30 Democrats, a feat that insiders on both sides of the aisle say is not guaranteed.

Rep. Rosa L. DeLauro (D-Conn.), a leading liberal opponent of trade deals, has stated that the legislation is wrong and that members of Congress will not stand for it. The fight over the fast-track trade bill is expected to escalate, potentially leading to a significant political battle.

On Independence Day, the majority of fireworks used across the United States are imported from China, with nearly 98-99% of consumer fireworks and 75% of professional-grade pyrotechnics coming from there. This is a notable exception to the growing "Buy American" sentiment in Washington and corporate America, particularly during patriotic events.

The shift towards Chinese production began shortly after the U.S. and China reestablished trade ties in 1979. By the early 1990s, China was generating over $60 million in annual pyrotechnic exports to the U.S., and by 2013, the U.S. was importing $213 million worth of fireworks, almost all from China.

The high labor-intensity of making fireworks and stricter environmental and safety regulations in the U.S. make domestically produced fireworks significantly more expensive than Chinese imports. The industry's quality control has also improved over the years, with organizations like the American Fireworks Standards Laboratory conducting safety inspections before fireworks are shipped from China to U.S. buyers.

However, specialty fireworks manufacturers in the U.S. continue to innovate, with a big assist from the U.S. Army. The Army is working on more environmentally friendly ingredients for pyrotechnics used on the battlefield, which could potentially improve the quality of neighborhood Fourth of July fireworks shows.

Innovations in the fireworks industry also include creating complex patterns, letters, and numbers in the sky, and incorporating video projections in theme park fireworks displays. Despite the reliance on Chinese imports, the future of fireworks continues to hold promise for new colors, shapes, and technologies.

The Phunky Elephant restaurant in Staten Island has removed a dessert called 'Roofie Colada' from its menu following public backlash on social media. The Connecticut Supreme Court has ruled that authorities can forcibly medicate a mentally ill doctor, Lishan Wang, to make him competent to stand trial for the murder of Yale doctor Vajinder Toor. The court's 7-0 decision overturned Wang's appeal, which argued that medicating him against his will would violate his constitutional rights.

Wang, a Chinese citizen, has pleaded not guilty to the 2010 shooting and has insisted he is competent and doesn't need medication. He was charged with attempted murder for shooting at Toor's pregnant wife, who was not injured. The shooting was believed to stem from a workplace dispute Wang had with Toor and other doctors.

The court found that it was substantially likely that Wang would be made competent by the medication and that it was unlikely he would suffer from side effects. They also determined that no less-intrusive option existed, and that the drugs were in Wang’s medical best interest.

The case has been a subject of debate, with Wang's public defender, Mark Rademacher, arguing that a projected success rate of mid-50s to 70 percent did not make it "substantially likely" that Wang would be restored to competency. However, the Supreme Court defined "substantially likely" as "more likely than not, or a greater than 50 percent probability."

Rademacher is considering appealing the state Supreme Court ruling to a federal court, possibly the U.S. Supreme Court. The ruling allows for the use of forced medication in rare instances where it is deemed necessary for a defendant to stand trial.

The Nobel Peace Prize for 2012 was awarded to the European Union (EU), marking the first time an organization has been honored with the prestigious award. The EU was recognized for its significant contributions to peace and reconciliation, democracy, and human rights, which have prevented the continent from experiencing another major conflict since World War II.

The EU, a supranational group of 27 states, is unique in its ability to communalize some of the powers of its sovereign national governments. The European Parliament, representing all member states, plays a crucial role in influencing legislation, and citizens of the EU can live and work in any member state. However, national governments take the lead in the Council of the European Union, where conflicts between national and European interests often arise.

The EU's achievements include integrating former military dictatorships and communist states, as well as uniting Germany and its former enemies. The current enlargement project aims to include the fragile western Balkans. Despite its bureaucratic and undemocratic criticisms, the EU has a structured legal system for addressing grievances, and the European Court of Justice is a globally unique institution.

However, the EU is currently facing economic turmoil, with Germany taking on a leadership role due to its economic strength. The financial and sovereign debt crisis poses one of the most serious predicaments in the EU's history. Critics argue that awarding the prize to the EU in 2012 seems odd, given the ongoing economic problems. Some view the decision as a pep talk for a continent that needs encouragement, while others see it as a mockery due to the current money problems.

The decision to award the prize to the EU was leaked early by Norway's NRK public radio, despite Norway not being a member of the EU. The prize money of $1.2 million will be shared among the EU's four presidents of the Council, Parliament, Commission, and the Euro Group. However, many argue that the real winners are the 500 million citizens of the EU, who have supported integration, reforms, enlargement, and have borne the costs incurred.

The Nobel Peace Prize for the EU highlights the continent's long-term work towards peace, democracy, and human rights. Despite the ongoing economic challenges, the EU continues to strive for unity and normality, embracing diversity in unity. The award serves as a reminder of the EU's historic achievements and the potential for continued progress.

U.S. Secretary of State Mike Pompeo traveled to Pyongyang, North Korea, on July 6, 2018, for talks aimed at filling in details on the dismantlement of North Korea's nuclear program and the recovery of the remains of U.S. troops missing from the Korean War. Pompeo met with North Korean officials, including Kim Yong Chol, who played a key role in arranging the summit between U.S. President Donald Trump and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un in Singapore last month.

The talks lasted nearly three hours, and it was uncertain whether Pompeo would meet Kim Jong Un. Pompeo said he was seeking to "fill in" some details on North Korea's commitments and maintain the momentum towards implementing the agreement from the summit. He also aimed to agree on at least an initial list of nuclear sites and an inventory that could be checked against available intelligence.

The issue of the remains of U.S. soldiers missing from the Korean War was also high on the agenda, with Trump saying after the Singapore summit that Kim had agreed to send the remains back to the United States. Both issues are considered essential tests of whether Kim is serious about negotiations. North Korean officials have yet to demonstrate that in working-level talks, according to U.S. intelligence officials.

Pompeo's talks will be closely watched in the region, and he is due to meet officials from allies South Korea and Japan in Tokyo also on July 7. Some officials in the State and Defense Departments and in U.S. intelligence agencies are worried that Trump has put himself at a disadvantage by overstating the results of the Singapore summit.

In a bid to build trust, Pompeo brought a CD of Elton John's Rocket Man as a gift for Kim Jong Un, along with a letter from Trump. The gifts reflected Trump's belief that Kim would follow through on commitments the leaders agreed at their summit in Singapore last month. Trump raised the rocket man reference during their meeting, and Kim said he had never heard the song, prompting the president to ask Pompeo to take the CD with him to Pyongyang on what is his third trip to North Korea since April.

Pompeo's visit to Pyongyang is the latest in a series of diplomatic efforts aimed at resolving the long-standing issue of North Korea's nuclear program. The talks come after a historic summit between Trump and Kim Jong Un in Singapore on June 12, 2018, where Kim made a broad commitment to "work toward denuclearization." However, the details of how or when North Korea would dismantle its nuclear program were not discussed during the summit.

The CD is not the first bizarre White House offering to Pyongyang. During their summit, the US and North Korean delegations watched a four-minute video, made in the style of a Hollywood trailer, setting out the North's stark choice: conflict with a powerful enemy or a peaceful and prosperous future as America's (denuclearised) partner. The film, a copy of which was given to Kim, casts him and Trump as the architects of a new chapter in world history – "two men, two leaders, one destiny."

As concerns grow that North Korea is upgrading its nuclear capability, despite agreeing to work towards the denuclearisation of the Korean peninsula, Pompeo said he expected the North to "fill in some details" outlined in the leaders' Singapore declaration. Pompeo said: "Since the summit the consultations have continued. On this trip I'm seeking to fill in some details on these commitments and continue the momentum towards implementation of what the two leaders promised each other and the world. I expect that [North Korea] is ready to do the same."

This document details a web crawl conducted from March 2011 to December 2011 using the new HQ software by Kenji Nagahashi. The crawl utilized the top 1 million Alexa websites as the seed list and Heritrix (3.1.1-SNAPSHOT) crawler software. The crawl resulted in 2,713,676,341 captures, 2,273,840,159 unique URLs, and 29,032,069 hosts. However, due to operational issues with the software, not all embedded and linked objects in pages were crawled, and some Argentinian government sites were repeatedly crawled, potentially skewing results by country. Despite these issues, the data set is available for public use upon request to info@archive.org. The document also includes a sign-in section for accessing rewards.

The University of Granada scientists have discovered a phenomenon they've named 'The Pinocchio Effect,' where the tip of the nose heats up due to anxiety, particularly when lying. This rise in temperature is countered by making a 'great mental effort.' The researchers used thermal imaging cameras on volunteers and found that this technique can also detect sexual desire and arousal in both men and women, indicated by an increase in temperature in the chest and genital areas. The study also demonstrated that men and women become aroused at the same physiological level, although women may not subjectively acknowledge it. The scientists' findings suggest that the brain's insular cortex, which is involved in body temperature regulation, is altered when people lie about their feelings. The researchers have published some of their results in scientific journals, while others remain unpublished, as reported by El Mundo newspaper. Additionally, the scientists found thermal footprints for aerobic exercise and distinct types of dance, such as ballet, where the temperature in a Flamenco dancer's buttocks lowers, and it rises in their forearms.

The city of Chicago has been named America's funniest city in a new study conducted by the University of Colorado at Boulder. The study, which was released on Sunday, evaluated several data sets, including the number of comedy clubs, famous comedians, humorists, and traveling comedians' ratings of local audiences. Chicagoans were hailed for their witty banter and observational humor, particularly their ability to poke fun at the city's brutal weather and public transportation system.

However, the study found that despite their funny ranking, Chicagoans are not great joke tellers. They prefer to mine humor from the situations they find themselves in rather than telling zingers. The study also ranked Boston, Atlanta, Washington, Portland, Ore., New York, Los Angeles, Denver, San Francisco, and Seattle in the top 10. Indianapolis, Detroit, and Milwaukee ranked 25th, 34th, and 39th, respectively.

The study was led by Peter McGraw, an associate professor of marketing and psychology at CU-Boulder’s Leeds School of Business. The project grew out of McGraw's new book, “The Humor Code: A Global Search for What Makes Things Funny,” which he co-authored with journalist Joel Warner. The study aimed to provide a window into the humor profiles of each of the top 10 cities. Boston residents were found to balance high-brow intellectualism with drunken rowdiness, while Washington, D.C., found humor in the absurdities of political systems. Portlanders were described as being just plain weird.

On September 18, 2016, an explosion occurred in Manhattan's Chelsea neighborhood, injuring 29 people. The incident took place on West 23rd Street, and Governor Andrew Cuomo stated that there was no evidence linking the explosion to international terrorism. The injured individuals were mostly released from hospitals, and additional law enforcement officers were deployed as a precaution.

Authorities found a second device a few blocks away from the explosion site and safely removed it. Surveillance videos showed a man near the blast site and another location where a pressure cooker device was found. The man was seen with a duffel bag near the West 23rd street explosion about 40 minutes before the blast, and later on West 27th street. Investigators are still searching for evidence and transporting it to the FBI lab in Quantico, Virginia, for review.

The increased police presence around the city is common during the United Nations General Assembly meeting, but it will be even more intense due to the explosion. New York Governor Andrew Cuomo added that 1,000 additional New York State Police officers and National Guard troops will be deployed to patrol bus terminals, airports, and subway stations for safety measures. The increased policing is intended to ensure New Yorkers' confidence as they return to work on Monday.

The NFL is currently experiencing a nationwide backlash following the controversial ending of the Monday Night Football game between Green Bay and Seattle, particularly among sports bettors. The game's final play, which resulted in a Seahawks victory, was marred by a questionable call by replacement referees. The NFL spokesman, Brian McCarthy, stated that negotiations with the referees union are ongoing, and they hope to reach an agreement soon. President Obama expressed his disapproval, calling the ending "terrible" and stating that the referees need to be reinstated.

In response to the botched finish, New Jersey State Senate President Stephen Sweeney announced plans to introduce legislation prohibiting the use of replacement officials in professional sports due to concerns over increased injury risks and lower quality of play. Sweeney believes that the replacement officials lack the ability to control a game, especially in a highly physical sport like football, and that they devalue the investments fans have made in tickets. Sweeney's proposed legislation aims to ensure the safety of players and maintain the integrity of the game.

The controversial call had a significant impact on gamblers, with an estimated $150 million in total bets worldwide shifting from those who bet on the Packers to those who took the underdog Seahawks. The shift in money was particularly noticeable in Las Vegas, where the sportsbook at the Wynn and the Las Vegas Hotel reported a significant increase in bets on the Seahawks following the call. Oddsmakers estimate that the worldwide impact of the call could be as high as $1 billion.

Sweeney's proposed legislation aims to address concerns over the use of replacement officials and ensure the safety of players and the integrity of the game. The legislation is a response to the NFL's ongoing dispute with the referees union and the controversy surrounding the use of replacement referees in professional sports.

The article in Vanity Fair portrays Erik Prince, the CEO of Blackwater, as a controversial figure who has led a double life as a secret agent for the CIA. Prince has been accused of being a war profiteer and a rogue military contractor, with his company Blackwater being involved in numerous controversies, including excessive force and bribery allegations. However, Prince claims he has been working as a CIA asset, helping to craft, fund, and execute operations, including targeted assassinations. The article suggests that Prince's activities may have contradicted statements made by CIA Director Leon Panetta and others to Congress about the operational status of the targeted assassination program. The article also describes Prince as a complex and intense individual who sees himself as destined for a special mission.

On June 1, a violent brawl erupted between two factions of inmates at the Clinton Correction Facility, five days before two inmates, Richard Matt and David Sweat, escaped from the maximum-security prison. The fight involved some Muslim inmates and suspected members of the Bloods gang, and ended with an inmate suffering a broken leg. The prison was partially locked down the next day, but only the yard and two cellblocks were searched, despite concerns from correction officers that the entire facility should have been searched.

Matt and Sweat used a small electrical saw and a sledgehammer to cut their way out of their cells on an "honor block" tier, and then made their way through a utility tunnel and a 24-inch steam pipe that led to a sewer outside the prison. The inmates may have received the saw and other tools from a female civilian employee who had developed a relationship with Matt. The investigation is also examining whether the employee or someone else may have given Matt access to a cellphone.

The FBI is assisting in the search for Matt and Sweat, who are believed to still be within a five- or 10-mile radius of the prison. The inmates' assignment on the honor block allowed them to wear and keep regular clothing, and the green prison uniforms were found left behind. The manhunt for the escaped inmates is ongoing, and a reward of $100,000 is being offered for information leading to their capture.

The escape has raised questions about security at the prison, as well as about the relationship between Matt and a female employee. The family of Matt's son, Nicholas Harris, is concerned about the escape and the possibility that Matt may come to their area. Harris recounted stories of his father's criminal past and his own memories of meeting his father in jail. Despite these concerns, Harris said he hopes for the best outcome for everyone involved.

The race between Hillary Clinton and Donald Trump has tightened, with Clinton's lead over Trump decreasing from a peak of 8 percentage points to a current 4-5 percentage points, according to recent polls. The tightening of the race has been gradual over the past few weeks, with evidence of the shift being particularly clear in polls taken just after the conventions and retaken now.

The tightening of the race does not guarantee that Trump will continue to gain ground, as polls have fluctuated throughout the year between showing a dead heat and a lead of 8-10 percentage points for Clinton. Despite the recent shift, Clinton is still ahead, with a 74% chance of winning according to the polls-only model and a 70% chance according to polls-plus.

However, if the race continues to tighten, there are concerns that Clinton's position in the swing states may not protect her in the Electoral College. While Clinton's superior field operation is expected to eventually pay dividends, her swing state results have ebbed and flowed with her national numbers.

For example, in Wisconsin, Clinton's lead has declined from a double-digit lead at her peak to an estimated 7 points as a result of the trend line adjustment and data from the Ipsos 50-state tracking poll. Two highly rated, traditional telephone polls of Wisconsin showed Clinton up by just 3 points and 5 points, compared to a 13-point lead just after the Democratic National Convention.

The trend line adjustment helps the model predict what forthcoming polls will look like in a state even if there haven't been many recent polls. When Clinton established an 8-point lead nationally in August, the model predicted she would have leads of 10-12 percentage points in some of her better swing states, such as Michigan and Colorado, and leads of 5-6 percentage points in swing states that are just slightly redder than the country as a whole, such as Ohio and Florida. This is what the model saw, on average. Now that the race has tightened to 4 or 5 points nationally, the model expects to see narrower leads, along with some polls showing a tie or Trump slightly ahead in the more red-leaning swing states.

Overall, Clinton's leads in the tipping-point states average about 4 percentage points, close to her numbers in national polls. With a tighter race, the model's expectations for Clinton are lower, and a new poll showing her up by 5 or 6 points in Florida or Ohio could be a terrific one for her today, depending on the pollster.

In terms of Trump's campaign, it is facing challenges and is teetering on the brink of collapse. The campaign is running short on time, with just 22 days until the start of early voting. There have been issues with deploying field staffers, opening up swing-state headquarters, and establishing field offices in battlegrounds that will decide the election. These issues have been wracked by confusion, false starts, and a lack of quick decision-making.

The deployment plan has been delayed due to the departure of Paul Manafort, Trump's former campaign chairman, who abruptly quit following withering scrutiny surrounding his work overseas. His departure created a chain reaction, delaying the talks for days on end. By late August, finger-pointing had begun, with a Trump aide accusing the RNC of slow-walking the process, while RNC officials blamed the lag on dysfunction within the campaign.

Trump's son Eric made a pilgrimage to RNC headquarters in hopes of expediting the delayed field programs, but the RNC shrugged off any talk of tension with the Trump campaign. The absence of a clear plan has spread to something even more fundamental — the campaign's path to 270 electoral votes.

The campaign's big donors are also slowing to a trickle, and aides are confused about who's calling the shots. Donald Trump's campaign is facing significant challenges as the election approaches, with a lack of clear leadership, a delayed deployment plan, and a lack of funding threatening to derail the campaign's efforts to win the Electoral College.

In an exclusive interview with CNN's Piers Morgan, U.S. Supreme Court Justice Antonin Scalia downplayed reports of personal and ideological rifts within the court following the recent landmark health care reform ruling. Scalia, who was on the losing side of the ruling upholding the Affordable Care Act, argued that the court should not be perceived as a political institution and that judges should not be questioned personally for their legal conclusions.

Scalia, along with Bryan Garner, is co-author of a new book, "Reading Law: The Interpretation of Legal Texts." The men describe their legal philosophy, and how to make sense of the law and the U.S. Constitution. They call their approach "textualism."

Scalia would not specifically address the health care decision or other recent or current case issues, such as immigration enforcement, affirmative action or gay marriage. He also declined to discuss how the court reached its health care ruling in internal deliberations.

In the interview, Scalia expressed his dismay at the criticism of Chief Justice John Roberts, suggesting those who may have leaked information were not entirely privy to the internal discussions over the health care decision. On abortion, Scalia said the 1973 Roe v. Wade decision legalizing the medical procedure should be overturned, believing it remains an issue best left for states to decide.

Scalia reiterated his firm views over the 2000 ruling effectively handing the presidency to George W. Bush after the Florida ballot recounts, stating that supporters of Al Gore should "get over it." In his new book, Scalia argues interpreting laws and the Constitution properly requires a strict approach to look at the actual text of the law itself. He warns that squishy, unprincipled decision-making is bad for the country and for the reputation of judges themselves.

Scalia is known for his often brash demeanor and wicked sense of humor, and he displayed that in the hourlong conversation with Morgan. Despite his reputation as an intellectual fighter, Scalia described himself as "a peaceful man." When asked if he had ever broken the law, the justice said, "I've had a few speeding tickets, though none recently." His outgoing personality and sharply written opinions have made him among the most recognizable of justices, and a particular favorite of conservative activists, scholars, and lawmakers.

Groupon is facing another lawsuit from employees over unpaid overtime, making it the second such lawsuit in two months. The latest lawsuit, filed in Chicago, involves 50 "deal vetters" who claim they were not compensated for working more than 40 hours per week. This is similar to a class action filed in August by over 1,000 salespeople seeking overtime pay. The deal vetters' lawsuit comes after a string of staff departures, SEC disputes, and the postponement of Groupon's IPO in September. The company has not yet responded to requests for comment. The lawsuits highlight concerns about compensation for employees at Groupon, particularly following the distribution of $810 million in bonuses to top executives before the IPO.

Fiat Chrysler Automobiles (FCA) CEO Sergio Marchionne has stated that the company's chances of meeting its 2018 financial targets are "significantly greater than 50 percent." The targets, set in 2014 and updated in 2016, include revenue of 136 billion euros ($144 billion) and adjusted net profit of between 4.7 billion euros and 5.5 billion euros. FCA had no comment on Marchionne's remarks.

Last January, FCA raised its 2018 targets and forecast adjusted operating profit of 8.7 billion to 9.8 billion euros, and adjusted operating margins of 6.4 percent to 7.2 percent. However, many analysts have expressed doubts about the company achieving these targets.

FCA shares have been performing well, with shares in Milan closing at 10.47 euros on Wednesday, up 21 percent since the end of December, and shares in New York closing at $11.09, up 21.6 percent this year.

Marchionne confirmed on Monday that he will retire at the end of 2018. However, FCA has been accused of violating pollution laws with 104,000 diesel vehicles, sending the shares plunging on the prospect that the automaker may face billions of dollars in fines.

The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) alleged that FCA put software in Jeep Grand Cherokee and Ram 1500 models that allows them to exceed pollution limits. The EPA stopped short of calling the software a "defeat device" but said the carmaker failed to disclose its use. FCA said it meets all applicable regulatory requirements and will work with President-elect Donald Trump's administration to contest the allegations.

FCA becomes the second automaker in less than three years the EPA has accused of violating the law by using software to pass laboratory emissions tests. Volkswagen, which admitted to using defeat devices in September 2015, agreed to pay a $4.3 billion fine on Wednesday, boosting the cost of the scandal to about 20.5 billion euros ($21.9 billion).

Marchionne said on Thursday that FCA's case is "completely different" from Volkswagen's, and called the timing of the EPA's notice of a violation "very strange." He also said that the company had been discussing emissions with the EPA for more than a year.

The alleged violations could result in fines of as much as $44,539 per vehicle, with a total potential penalty of as much as $4.6 billion, based on the cost per vehicle and the number of 2014 through 2016 model year SUVs and trucks. When the EPA first revealed Volkswagen's wrongdoing in September 2015, the company faced punishment of up to $18 billion.

"Our meetings with Fiat Chrysler to date have not produced a viable explanation" for the software, said Cynthia Giles, the EPA's enforcement chief. "This is a clear violation of the Clean Air Act."

New York Attorney General Eric Schneiderman said his office will investigate the EPA's claims against FCA, saying in a statement he was "deeply troubled" and would work with state and federal partners.

FCA plans to work with the Trump administration to "present its case and resolve this matter fairly and equitably," the automaker said in a statement.

The company's bonds also fell, with its $1.47 billion of 5.25 percent coupon notes due in 2023 sinking 4 cents to 99.7 cents at 11:19 a.m. in New York, according to Trace, the bond-price reporting system of the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority. That's the biggest decline since the notes were sold in July 2015.
