Alexa Internet, since 1996, has been donating their crawl data to the Internet Archive, which is added to the Wayback Machine after an embargo period. A woman in Tempe, Arizona, identified as Alaina Marie Limpert, was arrested on charges of child abuse. The incident occurred when Limpert's almost-two-year-old daughter consumed macaroni and cheese made with THC butter, a chemical in cannabis that causes intoxication.

Limpert's home was reported to the Department of Child Safety, who found THC in the infant's system. The police report states that Limpert and her husband laughed about the child's side effects and placed her in their backyard pool. The Department of Child Safety took custody of all three children living in the home two days later.

Upon searching the home, police found two marijuana grow tents in the garage, mushrooms, bongs and pipes, containers of hash oil, and other drug paraphernalia. In the refrigerator, they discovered three large tubs of THC butter. Limpert later admitted to making the mac and cheese with THC for her husband, but was unaware that her daughter had consumed it.

Limpert is scheduled to appear in court on April 19. The full police report can be accessed by clicking the provided link. The copyright for this news article belongs to KPHO/KTVK (KPHO Broadcasting Corporation).

A Tulane Medical School student, Peter Gold, is fighting for his life after being shot in an attempted abduction in New Orleans. The incident occurred on Friday morning in the 1000 block of St. Mary Street, where Gold stopped his car to help a woman who was being dragged by a hooded man. The gunman demanded money from Gold, who did not have any, and shot him once. The gun jammed, and the suspect attempted to shoot Gold three more times, but the gun malfunctioned. The suspect took the woman's purse and fled the scene.

The suspect is described as a black man wearing a dark hooded jacket, and police have offered a $10,000 reward for any information leading to his arrest and indictment. The woman seen in the surveillance video was treated for minor injuries and released. Gold remains in "guarded" condition at the hospital.

On Sunday, police identified the suspect as 21-year-old Euric Cain, who is wanted on charges of attempted first-degree murder, second-degree kidnapping, and armed robbery. Tulane University and Crimestoppers are offering up to $12,500 for information leading to his arrest and indictment. The woman who was abducted continues to cooperate with the police.

Gold is a fourth-year Tulane Medical School student and is expected to make a full recovery. Tulane University President Michael Fitts expressed his shock and sadness at the news of the shooting and asked the community to keep Gold and his family in their thoughts and prayers.

The incident has sent shockwaves through the Uptown neighborhoods, which have been shaken by several brazen armed robberies in recent months. Anyone with information about the shooter is asked to call Crimestoppers at (504) 822-1111 or post a tip at crime stoppersgno.org.

A Boston police officer, Michael Doherty, a 16-year veteran, was arrested and charged with assault and battery, using a motor vehicle without authority, and using racial slurs during an incident involving an Uber driver in South Boston early Sunday. The incident occurred at around 2:45 a.m., and the Uber driver reported that Doherty became agitated because he thought he was in the wrong location. Doherty allegedly used racial slurs against the Uber driver, and when the driver stopped, he began hitting him, prompting the driver to seek help from a good Samaritan. Doherty then stole the Uber driver's car and chased the driver and the good Samaritan. The Uber driver and the good Samaritan gave chase, and Doherty eventually pulled over and approached both parties, using racial slurs and attacking them. Doherty was released on bail and ordered to stay away from the victims and to refrain from drugs and alcohol. The Boston Police Department placed Doherty on administrative leave, and the department's Anti-Corruption Unit is investigating the incident. Uber has barred Doherty from using their service, and the company has offered to assist law enforcement in the investigation. Doherty's lawyer maintains that his client was the victim in the incident and disputes the prosecutor's account. Additionally, Doherty's ex-girlfriend, Mary Niland, had a separate hearing in the same courtroom prior to Doherty's arraignment, where a charge against her was amended from unarmed burglary to breaking and entering during the night time with intent to commit a felony.

Jackson Odell, a 20-year-old actor and singer-songwriter, best known for his role as Ari Caldwell in ABC's "The Goldbergs," has tragically passed away. The Los Angeles County Coroner's Office confirmed his death on June 8, at his Tarzana residence in San Fernando Valley, with no foul play suspected. The cause of death is yet to be determined, pending an autopsy.

Odell began his acting career at the age of 12, and apart from "The Goldbergs," he had roles in shows like "The Fosters," "Modern Family," and "iCarly." He also starred in the 2011 film "Judy Moody and the Not Bummer Summer."

As a musician, Odell wrote original songs for the soundtrack of the 2018 romantic drama film "Forever My Girl," including "Wings of an Angel," sung by "American Idol" contestant Lauren Alaina. He also posted several covers and original songs on his YouTube channel, with one of John Mayer's "Dreaming with a Broken Heart" garnering over 16,000 views.

A new Canadian study published in the Canadian Medical Association Journal suggests that artificial sweeteners, commonly found in diet drinks, do not aid in weight loss and may be linked to weight gain, high blood pressure, diabetes, and other health issues. The study, led by Dr. Meghan Azad of the University of Manitoba, reviewed 37 previously published studies that looked at the diet habits of over 400,000 people. The research found no evidence that regularly consuming artificial sweeteners led to weight loss, and longer observational studies showed a link between the sweeteners and higher risks of weight gain, obesity, high blood pressure, diabetes, and other health issues. The study noted a lack of good, rigorous studies on artificial sweeteners and called for more research, particularly studies that could compare the different sweeteners to determine if one is better than another. The study also suggested that artificial sweeteners may disrupt healthy gut bacteria, confuse metabolisms, or cause people to overcompensate for missed calories from sugar. Dr. Azad advises consumers to think twice about consuming artificial sweeteners regularly, as there is no evidence to suggest they are truly harmless alternatives to sugar.

The article discusses a unique application of dance music, specifically Balearic techno, originating from Ibiza. Polish cybersecurity researcher Krzysztof Szczypiorski has utilized this genre to transmit secret messages, hidden in nearly imperceptible changes in tempo, resembling Morse code. This innovative method allows for the communication of entire sentences during open-air beach raves, without most people realizing they are listening to coded messages.

The system works by assigning a dot-and-line series to letters, where a "dot" is a slight increase in tempo, and a "line" is a slight decrease. By subtly modulating the tempo, messages can be transmitted over time. To decode the messages, one can use an algorithm that analyzes the beats per minute or listen very closely if the ear is finely tuned enough.

Szczypiorski's paper, published on the arXiv preprint server, describes two experiments with the system, called StegIbiza. In the first experiment, twenty people (half with musical backgrounds) listened to dance music manipulated to contain messages. Results showed that none of them could identify a difference in the audio when the tempo was changed by less than one percent.

In the second experiment, Szczypiorski DJ'd an open-air summer party with about 70 people in attendance. Results were similar to the first experiment, but the experiment had to be stopped when Szczypiorski manipulated the tempo too much, causing the rest of the party to lose interest in the music.

It is worth noting that music steganography is an old practice, and Szczypiorski acknowledges that hiding messages in musical compositions and scores dates back at least 500 years. However, this application with club music is a novel approach, offering a more entertaining twist compared to the past.

In conclusion, Szczypiorski's StegIbiza system demonstrates a creative use of dance music to transmit secret messages during raves. However, it is essential to find a balance between the coded messages and maintaining the enjoyment of the music for the partygoers.

Pret a Manger, a British restaurant chain, is facing controversy after a second customer died from an allergic reaction to a sandwich containing an undisclosed allergen. The incident occurred in December 2017, and the customer collapsed and died after purchasing a "super-veg rainbow flatbread" that was supposed to be dairy-free.

Pret a Manger has blamed the death on a dairy-free yoghurt supplied by CoYo, a vegan brand. However, CoYo has denied any responsibility, accusing Pret of hampering its investigation by failing to provide vital information. CoYo recalled its yoghurts in February 2018 after dairy traces were found, but denies that the recall is related to the death.

The second death follows criticism and an inquest into the death of 15-year-old Natasha Ednan-Laperouse in 2016, who died after eating a Pret baguette containing sesame. Pret a Manger has promised to improve its labeling following the criticism. The parents of Ednan-Laperouse, who are campaigning for stronger allergen warnings, expressed their condolences for the second death.

Pret a Manger has ended its contract with CoYo and is taking legal action. The company agreed to full labelling of ingredients on all its freshly made products last week following the case of Natasha Ednan-Laperouse. Both Pret and CoYo are urging all parties to work together to find the true cause of the death, which is still being investigated by the coroner's court.

The Senate passed a sweeping tax overhaul early Saturday morning, marking a significant victory for Republicans and putting them one step closer to revamping the U.S. tax system for the first time in more than three decades. The bill, which includes approximately $1.4 trillion in tax cuts, lowers the corporate rate to 20% from 35%, reshapes international business tax rules, and temporarily lowers individual taxes. The Senate narrowly passed the bill with a 51 to 49 vote, with only Senator Bob Corker of Tennessee opposing the measure.

The legislation also touched on other Republican goals, including opening the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge to oil drilling and repealing certain provisions. The House passed its own plan in November, and House and Senate Republicans will now have to settle the differences between their tax bills before President Donald Trump can sign a final bill.

The Senate Majority Leader, Mitch McConnell, praised the bill's passage, stating that "every single member of our conference wanted to get to yes, and all but one did." President Trump praised McConnell and Senate Finance Chairman Orrin Hatch in a tweet after the bill passed, adding that "we are one step closer to delivering MASSIVE tax cuts for working families across America."

Democrats harshly condemned the legislation and the way it came together. Senator Ron Wyden of Oregon, the top Democrat on the tax-writing Finance Committee, stated on the Senate floor that "millions of Americans must be watching in stunned disbelief tonight as the Republican Senate betrays the middle class for the benefit of faceless multinational corporations."

The bill faces further debate and amendments in the House and Senate, and it remains to be seen whether the final bill will be signed into law by President Trump before the end of the year.

A 6.5 magnitude earthquake struck Eureka, California at around 4:30 p.m. on Saturday, causing widespread damage and power outages. The quake, which lasted for around 30 seconds, resulted in several injuries, with over 30 people visiting hospitals. Many buildings, including the Bayshore Mall and Eureka Natural Foods, sustained damage, with reports of light fixtures falling out of the ceiling, floor tiles popping up, and chunks of the ceiling falling onto customers. The epicenter of the quake was 20 miles west-northwest of Ferndale, and aftershocks have been reported since. As of 7 p.m., about 27,000 PG&E customers were without power, and broken gas lines and downed power lines were the most common calls coming across the scanner. The office of Humboldt County administrative officer and public information officer for this incident through the Office of Emergency Services confirmed the quake's magnitude and classified the damage as minor to moderate. Crews will work around the clock to restore power, with estimates of power being restored in some areas as late as Sunday night. Residents in the affected areas are advised to stay away from downed power lines and report them to 911 or 1-800-PGE-5000. The temblor was felt at least as far east as Willow Creek, and according to the U.S. Geological Survey Web site, six aftershocks have struck since the major shaking began, none of which approached the original magnitude of the quake.

In Boulder, Colorado, a mountain lion broke into a home, killing a family's cat named Klondike. The homeowner returned to find the big cat inside, having pushed through a screen and unable to exit. Neighbors watched from their windows as the mountain lion wandered around the house for over an hour. Animal control officers used non-lethal rounds to scare the mountain lion out of the house and away from the neighborhood. The incident has prompted local authorities to advise residents to keep ground-level doors and windows locked at night to prevent similar occurrences. The mountain lion was later found in the wilderness near Boulder Canyon, uninjured. The homeowner, Kayla Slaughter, expressed her grief over the loss of Klondike but was reassured by officers that the mountain lion is unlikely to return after being hit with the bean bags.

Rutgers University, New Jersey's premier public university, has approved a 2.3% increase in undergraduate tuition and fees for the 2015-2016 academic year, amounting to about $300 more for the typical in-state undergraduate. The increase in tuition and fees will bring the total annual cost to $14,131. Room and board costs are also going up by about 2.6%. The average student living on the New Brunswick campus will pay a total bill of $26,185, a $624 increase from last year.

The Rutgers Board of Governors approved the tuition hike during a meeting on the New Brunswick campus. The increase is necessary to cover several rising costs, including new contracts with various unions calling for a 2% raise for Rutgers employees and a 3.7% cut in state funding for Rutgers operations.

Under Rutgers' system, tuition and fees vary by campus and school. On the Rutgers-Newark campus, the typical undergraduate will pay $13,597 in annual tuition and fees, a $300 increase from last year. On the Rutgers-Camden campus, the typical undergraduate will pay $14,000 in annual tuition and fees, a $317 increase from last year. Similar increases of about 2.3% have been approved for most graduate students. Out-of-state students will see their tuition and fees go up slightly more, by about 3.4%.

Rutgers continues to have one of the highest tuition rates in the nation among state universities. However, New Jersey is considered a high aid state in which low-income students receive relatively generous financial aid packages to help cover tuition. Less than half of Rutgers students pay the full tuition and fee rate, university officials said. The rest get grants and scholarships to help cover some of their tuition.

The Rutgers board also approved a 3.2% increase in the university's financial aid program. The Rutgers Assistance Grant program will include $32.5 million to help low-income students cover the tuition increase, Winterbauer said.

In a separate report, the Center for American Progress found that 20 universities received one-fifth, or $6.5 billion, of the total amount of loans the government gave graduate students in the 2013-2014 academic year. Those schools, however, only educate 12% of all graduate students. What's striking about the Center's findings is that a majority of the debt taken to attend the 20 schools on its list is not for law or medical degrees that promise hefty paydays. Most graduate students at those schools are seeking master's degrees in journalism, fine arts or government, according to CAP.

The April jobs report, released by the Labor Department, showed a significant discrepancy from market expectations, with only 160,000 new jobs produced, compared to the anticipated 205,000. The unemployment rate remained steady at 5%. Over the past three months, an average of 200,000 new positions have been added.

Hourly earnings demonstrated growth, increasing by 2.5% over the past year. However, the labor force participation rate decreased to 62.8%.

The economy's performance in the first quarter of the year was sluggish, with a 0.5% annual growth rate, raising concerns about the longevity of the seven-year-old economic expansion.

The economy is currently at a crossroads, with contradictory indicators. Crude oil prices have seen a recovery from $35 a barrel in early 2016 to $45 due to decreasing fears of a global recession. The stock market has also rebounded, with the Standard & Poor’s 500 index increasing by nearly 8% over the past three months.

Private sector jobs are consistently growing, and consumer confidence is improving. Long-term unemployment is decreasing, and initial jobless claims have reached a 43-year low. Wage growth is stronger than post-recession norms.

However, the bond market is less optimistic, with the yield on 10-year Treasury bonds dropping from 2% at the start of the year to 1.8% currently. This indicates that investors are buying more government debt, which is more desirable in times of stagnation.

Other economic indicators are less encouraging, such as persistently low inflation and slow growth in the first quarter of 2016. These contradictory data points have led the Federal Reserve to hold off on raising interest rates, as they did for the first time in nearly a decade in December 2015.

The next Fed meeting is in June, and if the jobs report remains as ambiguous as the past few, the Fed's decision-making process will be more complex.

On June 25, 2017, an overturned oil tanker burst into flames in Pakistan, resulting in the death of at least 153 people and injuring over 100, many with severe burns. The accident occurred on a national highway outside Bahawalpur, in Punjab province, while the tanker was en route from Karachi to Lahore. The tragedy occurred when hundreds of people gathered to collect leaking fuel, and a fire erupted when someone attempted to light a cigarette near the spilled fuel.

The death toll could rise further as dozens of people remain in critical condition. DNA testing may be required to identify some of the victims, and many were burned beyond recognition. Pakistan's Prime Minister, Nawaz Sharif, has expressed deep grief over the incident and has immediately returned to Pakistan to respond. The disaster occurred on the eve of the Muslim holiday of Eid al-Fitr, which marks the end of the fasting month of Ramadan.

The tanker was carrying about 6,600 gallons of oil, and at least three cars and over 70 motorcycles were destroyed in the flames. Firefighters took more than two hours to put out the fire, and dozens of people are being treated in hospitals, with several airlifted by helicopter. The incident has sparked outrage and calls for improved safety measures on Pakistan's highways.

The incident that occurred on a United Airlines flight on Sunday, April 9, 2017, in Chicago, where a passenger was forcibly removed from the plane, has caused widespread outrage and criticism. The flight was overbooked, and when passengers were asked to voluntarily give up their seats, four were chosen at random when no volunteers came forward. One passenger, who identified himself as a doctor, refused to leave and was violently removed from the plane by airport security.

The airline's initial response to the incident was met with criticism, as it was seen as insensitive and lacking empathy. United CEO Oscar Munoz initially apologized for the overbooking situation but not for the violent removal of the passenger. However, in a later statement, Munoz defended the airline's ground staff and described the passenger as "disruptive and belligerent."

The incident has raised questions about the terms and conditions of air travel in the United States, as it is legal for airlines to overbook flights, and passengers can be involuntarily bumped if necessary. Passengers who are bumped involuntarily are entitled to compensation, but the airlines have great latitude to set their own priority rules for bumping travelers.

This incident is just the latest in a series of bad behavior by United Airlines, which has been criticized for refusing to allow three young girls to board a flight because they were wearing leggings, refusing to accommodate an autistic child, and refusing to give an unopened can of Diet Coke to a Muslim chaplain.

In response to the incident, there has been a call for a boycott of United Airlines, with many people urging others to stop flying with the airline and to choose other airlines instead. The incident has also led to calls for reforms in the airline industry, including changes to the way airlines handle overbooking and the way they treat passengers.

The incident has also highlighted the need for better training for airline staff in dealing with difficult situations, as well as the need for airlines to prioritize the safety and well-being of passengers over their own interests. The incident has been widely condemned, with many people calling for the airline to take responsibility for its actions and to make changes to ensure that such incidents do not happen again in the future.

The National Park Service (NPS) has proposed a significant increase in visitor fees for 17 of the most popular national parks, including Yosemite, Grand Canyon, and Yellowstone, during their peak seasons. The increase aims to generate revenue for the renovation and restoration of aging infrastructure within these parks.

The proposed new fee structure would establish peak-season entrance fees at the following national parks: Arches, Bryce Canyon, Canyonlands, Denali, Glacier, Grand Canyon, Grand Teton, Olympic, Sequoia & Kings Canyon, Yellowstone, Yosemite, Zion, Acadia, Mount Rainier, Rocky Mountain, Shenandoah, and Joshua Tree. The peak season for each park would be defined as its busiest contiguous five-month period of visitation.

During the peak season at each park, the entrance fee would be $70 per private, non-commercial vehicle, $50 per motorcycle, and $30 per person on bike or foot. A park-specific annual pass for any of the 17 parks would be available for $75. The cost of the annual America the Beautiful- The National Parks and Federal Recreational Lands Pass, which provides entrance to all federal lands, including parks for a one-year period, would remain $80.

The proposal is open for public comment from October 24, 2017, to November 23, 2017, on the NPS Planning, Environment and Public Comment (PEPC) website. The National Parks Conservation Association has criticized the proposal, stating that it could make these parks unaffordable for some families to visit.

The increased fees could generate an estimated $70 million in new national park revenue, a 34% increase over the $200 million collected in Fiscal Year 2016. Under the Federal Lands Recreational Enhancement Act, 80% of an entrance fee remains in the park where it is collected, while the other 20% is spent on projects in other national parks.

In addition to the entrance fee adjustments, the NPS is also proposing entry and permit fee adjustments for commercial tour operators. The proposal would increase entry fees for commercial operators and standardize commercial use authorization (CUA) requirements for road-based commercial tours, including application and management fees. These fees will fund rehabilitation projects for buildings, facilities, parking lots, roads, and wayside exhibits that would enhance the visitor experience. The fees will also cover the administrative costs of receiving, reviewing, and processing CUA applications and required reports.

The NPS manages more than 417 national parks and works with communities across the nation to help preserve local history and create close-to-home recreational opportunities. The public is invited to provide comments on the proposed peak season fee increases during the open comment period.

On May 12, 2015, an Amtrak train derailed in Philadelphia, resulting in eight fatalities and over 200 injuries. Investigations revealed that the assistant conductor on the train overheard radio transmissions indicating that the engineer of a Southeastern Pennsylvania Transportation Authority (SEPTA) train reported being hit by a rock or shot at, with a broken windshield, and placing his train into emergency stop. The Amtrak engineer also reportedly mentioned being struck by something. The FBI is now investigating damage to the windshield of the Amtrak train, particularly a circular pattern of damage on the lower left windshield.

The engineer, Brandon Bostian, was interviewed for the first time since the accident and reported no memory of the crash, having only recalled ringing the train bell as required at the North Philadelphia station. Bostian was cooperative and demonstrated good knowledge of the territory, speed limits, and other relevant details.

Investigations are ongoing, considering various factors such as speed, track conditions, and human error. Passengers aboard other trains reported being struck by objects before the crash, adding to the mystery of the incident. The Philadelphia District Attorney's office is monitoring the investigation but has not found any conclusive evidence of criminal recklessness on Bostian's part.

Bostian, a 32-year-old transportation enthusiast, had a reputation for being professional and knowledgeable. His attorney has stated that he was not under the influence of alcohol, drugs, or distracted by his cell phone during the accident. The conductors aboard the train described Bostian as "very professional" and "great to work with."

The crash has sparked discussions about the need for positive train control (PTC) technology, which could have prevented the accident if it had been in place. PTC systems are designed to override human error and have been advocated by Bostian himself in online posts. The Amtrak CEO has pledged to implement PTC on the Northeast Corridor by December 31, 2015. However, questions remain about the slow implementation of such safety upgrades due to underfunding of transportation infrastructure nationally.

Ricky Gilmore, a 49-year-old paraplegic, endured a harrowing ordeal when he was left stranded in the New Mexico desert without his wheelchair for three days. The incident occurred after Gilmore hitchhiked with a woman and a man near Shiprock, who later dropped him off in the desert. With no food, water, or coat, Gilmore had to drag himself for about four miles down a dirt road. He spent two nights in the cold desert, enduring freezing temperatures and wild animals. Gilmore's body shows the toll of the ordeal, with shredded skin, a sprained wrist, and kidney problems due to dehydration. He was found by a motorist and is currently receiving treatment at the Northern Navajo Medical Center. The incident is being investigated by the Shiprock Police Department, and Gilmore has described the suspects as Native American, with the male suspect having a cursive tattoo on his neck. Gilmore feels fortunate to have survived and plans to stop hitchhiking for a while once he recovers.

In Thailand, wildlife authorities are currently in the process of removing over 130 tigers from a controversial Buddhist temple in Kanchanaburi Province, west of Bangkok. The temple, known as the "Tiger Temple," has been a popular tourist attraction, allowing visitors to walk among the tigers and take photos. However, Thailand's Wildlife Conservation Office (WCO) has accused the temple of mistreating the animals and posing a danger to visitors.

When WCO staff arrived to remove the tigers on Monday, temple officials initially refused to let them in. After a half-day standoff, wildlife officers were able to sedate eight tigers and enter the temple. The operation, involving approximately 1,000 state personnel, is expected to continue for a week.

The tranquilized tigers will be taken to three government animal refuges elsewhere in Thailand. The temple has been criticized by animal rights activists for allegedly not having the proper facilities to care for the animals and for flouting regulations restricting their trade. The monks have resisted previous efforts to take away the tigers, but relented this time after police obtained a court order.

The temple had recently made arrangements to operate as a zoo, but the plan fell through when the government determined that the operators failed to secure sufficient resources. The WCO director, Teunjai Noochdumrong, stated that the temple intentionally released some tigers to obstruct the removal process, causing "mayhem" when the wildlife officers arrived.

In this news summary, several celebrity relationships have come to an end.

Firstly, Mariah Carey and Nick Cannon's divorce is reportedly a 'done deal' as they have been living apart since May. The separation was allegedly triggered by an incident in March when Nick named five celebrities he had slept with on a radio show, including Mariah, which caused a rift between them. Mariah felt humiliated, and their relationship never fully recovered. Nick has been taking on various projects, which Mariah believes keeps him away from their children, causing further tension. On the other hand, Nick feels Mariah is difficult to handle due to her surrounding herself with 'yes men.'

Secondly, Ronnie Ortiz-Magro and Sammi "Sweetheart" Giancola from Jersey Shore have ended their five-year relationship for good. The couple, who had a tumultuous on-off relationship on the reality show, officially parted ways two months ago. Ronnie is now focusing on being an uncle to Jenni "JWoww" Farley's 5-week-old daughter.

Lastly, Meg Ryan and John Mellencamp have ended their three-year relationship due to the long distance between them. The pair, who kept a low profile during their relationship, are now focusing on their individual projects. Meg Ryan is set to make a major return to Hollywood with her directorial debut, Ithaca, while John Mellencamp is preparing to release his 22nd album, Plain Spoken, in November.

All three couples have ended their relationships, with distance and personal differences being the main causes.

A 25-year-old woman named Lauren Mann, originally from Colorado, United States, was found dead in her Vienna, Austria apartment on Tuesday, January 26, 2016. The autopsy did not reveal the cause of death, and toxicological tests are pending. Mann had been working as an au pair in Vienna and was reported missing by her employer after she failed to show up for work.

Mann graduated from the University of Colorado-Boulder's College of Music in 2012. The family for whom she worked described her as "very reliable, trusted, caring, and socially active." Her neighbor, Peter Kratochwill, found it "extraordinary" for such an incident to occur in their quiet and safe neighborhood.

Austrian police are treating Mann's death as a homicide, as a third party's involvement cannot be excluded. However, the initial autopsy did not reveal any signs of strangulation, stabbing, or shooting. The final autopsy results showed that Mann died of suffocation. Toxicology testing is ongoing, and final results may take up to a couple of weeks.

The U.S. Embassy in Vienna is providing consular assistance. Mann's friends and neighbors have been contacted by the police. Mann had been living in Vienna for several years, studying while working as an au pair. She grew up in the small Colorado town of Paonia.

Norway is set to become the world's first country to transition entirely to digital radio, with the switch-off of FM radio channels scheduled for January 11, 2017. The move is driven by cost savings, as digital audio broadcasting (DAB) is eight times cheaper than FM, resulting in an estimated annual savings of 200 million Norwegian Krone (approximately $23.5 million). The transition will provide more radio channels and improved quality. However, critics argue that the move could lead to missed emergency alerts, as many cars and homes lack DAB receivers. The Norwegian government has been planning this transition for years and has made efforts to inform citizens about DAB and guide them through installing adaptors or accessing digital radio via the internet.

The switch to digital-only radio is opposed by the majority of the Norwegian population, with 66% expressing their opposition in a recent opinion poll. The transition will start in the northern city of Bodø and will be completed by the end of the year. The shutdown of the FM network, introduced in the 1950s, will render almost eight million radio sets obsolete.

The move is being closely watched by other countries, including Denmark, Sweden, Switzerland, and South Korea, considering a similar transition. The transition to DAB radio in Norway will offer over 20 crystal-clear channels, with more expected to follow. Britain plans to review the need for a switchover once digital listening reaches 50%.

The switch to digital radio in Norway is a significant step towards modernizing the country's radio infrastructure, but it has been met with resistance from the majority of the population. The transition will be closely watched by other countries considering a similar move.

A taxi driver named Wang Mingqing, from southwest China, has been reunited with his daughter Qifeng, who went missing in 1994, after a 24-year search. Wang's daughter wandered off while he and his wife were running their fruit stall in Chengdu, Sichuan province. Over the years, Wang and his wife searched for Qifeng, even taking out advertisements in newspapers and setting up online appeals. In 2015, Wang became a taxi driver and used his job to broaden the search by asking passengers to help him find his daughter. He also distributed 10,000 fliers with details about the case.

In March 2021, a 27-year-old woman named Kang Ying contacted Wang via social media after reading about his search and realizing she might be the girl in question. Kang had been told she was adopted as a child and grew up under the name Kang Ying in a town only 20 kilometers away from her birth parents. With the help of a non-governmental organization, Kang took a DNA test that confirmed she was Wang's daughter. She is flying to Chengdu on Tuesday to meet her birth parents.

The story of Wang's reunion with his daughter has swept China, with many celebrating the happy ending. Wang and his wife were fruit sellers, selling their wares at a roadside stall in Chengdu. On one particularly busy day, Wang ran out of change and briefly went to a neighboring stall to change money for a customer. When he returned minutes later, his daughter was nowhere to be found. Wang and his wife spent years searching for her in the city and surrounding areas, but DNA tests ruled out several women who could have been Qifeng.

A breakthrough finally came late last year, when a police sketch artist read about Wang and decided to help by producing a drawing of what Qifeng might look like as an adult. The picture was circulated online, and Kang saw it and was shocked by how much it resembled her. Kang contacted Wang earlier this year, and they quickly arranged for a DNA test. This time, the result was positive - Wang had finally found his long-lost child. On Monday, Wang and Kang spoke for the first time via a voice messenger app, and Wang shared the news with his friends on social media. On Tuesday, the pair were reunited in person when Kang flew to Chengdu with her husband, son, and daughter. They hugged each other tightly and cried as they were reunited, and were quickly joined by the rest of the family. Kang told reporters tearfully, "The whole world told me I didn't have a mother - but I do!"

In a 90-minute conference call on Thursday, White House officials presented their case for possible military action against Syria to congressional leaders. The evidence presented included an intercepted phone call involving a high-level Syrian official, which was offered as proof of a government chemical-weapons attack. The focus of the administration's action is to prevent President Bashar al-Assad from using chemical weapons again.

The administration is seeking international support for its actions but is not letting it dictate its policy. Several lawmakers came away from the briefing with a conviction that the Assad regime was behind the attack, but President Barack Obama must do more to persuade the country of the need for military action and to rally international support.

Senator Carl Levin called for a continuing effort to win international support for strikes against the Assad regime, while Senator Bob Corker opposed deploying American troops in Syria but supported "surgical, proportional military strikes." Senator Bob Menendez said the briefing reaffirmed for him that a decisive and consequential U.S. response is justified and warranted.

Unease among members of Congress about the prospect of U.S. involvement in a new military conflict in the Middle East continued to escalate, with the numbers of lawmakers signing a letter to Obama calling for an authorization vote for any potential military action increasing to 137 signatories from 116 on Wednesday. The call did little to change anyone's mind, with members reiterating their long-held views on Syria.

Senate Armed Services Committee Chairman Carl Levin urged the administration to increase military pressure on the Assad regime by providing lethal aid to vetted elements of the Syrian opposition. Meanwhile, Senator Jim Inhofe was undeterred in his opposition to military operations in Syria until there's a clear plan to pay for them. The White House said 15 members of Congress asked questions during the call and that it would continue reaching out to lawmakers.

The new research by an international team of scientists has significantly increased the estimated population of Adelie penguins in East Antarctica. Previous estimates put the number at around 2.3 million, but the new study suggests there are actually 5.9 million Adelie penguins living in a 5,000 km stretch of coastline. This new figure represents an increase of 3.6 million birds.

The study, which used aerial and ground surveys, tagging and resighting data, and automated camera images, took into account non-breeding Adelie penguins, which were previously difficult to count due to their tendency to forage at sea rather than nesting in colonies on land. The new estimate suggests that non-breeding Adelie penguins may be as, or more, abundant than the breeders.

The research has implications for conservation, as more Adelie penguins may be interacting with humans in Antarctica and the Southern Ocean than previously thought. The study also estimated the amount of krill and fish needed to support the Adelie penguin population, which is also sought after by seals and whales. The dietary information will be used by the Commission for the Conservation of Antarctic Marine Living Resources to set sustainable krill fishery catch limits.

Adelie penguins are slick and efficient swimmers that live on the Antarctic continent and on many small, surrounding coastal islands. They spend the winter offshore in the seas surrounding the pack ice. The study's findings will help better understand the entire population's foraging needs and ensure enhanced protection for significant penguin breeding populations near research stations in the future.

The United States has announced that it will not recognize the result of Venezuela's presidential election held on Sunday, May 20, 2018, as U.S. Deputy Secretary of State John Sullivan stated during a meeting ahead of the G20 Meeting of Foreign Ministers in Buenos Aires, Argentina. The election, which was boycotted by the opposition, was won by Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro with 67.7% of the vote. Maduro's main rivals, Henri Falcon and Javier Bertucci, have declared the election illegitimate due to alleged widespread irregularities. The U.S. is considering oil sanctions on Venezuela, and a response to the election will be discussed at the G20 meeting in Buenos Aires on Monday. Maduro dismissed international condemnation and allegations of vote buying and electoral fraud, vowing to work swiftly to stabilize his country's economy. The 14-nation Lima group of Latin American countries plus Canada has issued a statement saying it does not recognize the legitimacy of Venezuela’s presidential election and will call their ambassadors back from Caracas for consultations. The election board put turnout at just 46.1%, way down from the 80% registered at the last presidential vote in 2013, due to a boycott by Venezuela's mainstream opposition.

Fresh clashes have erupted in South Sudan's capital, Juba, resulting in the death of at least 66 soldiers, according to local doctor Ajak Bullen. The US Embassy has advised all citizens to depart immediately due to the ongoing violence. The fighting between army factions is believed to be a power grab attempt by former Vice President Riek Machar, who was sacked by President Salva Kiir in July. The two men, from different ethnic groups, have a history of political rivalry.

The UN reports that about 16,000 civilians have sought refuge in two UN compounds due to the violence. Sporadic gunfire is still being heard in Juba, and the city's international airport remains closed. The US Department of State has warned against all travel to South Sudan and recommended that US citizens currently in the country leave immediately.

The government has arrested at least 10 very senior former government officials, including six cabinet ministers, according to South Sudan's Information Minister Michael Makuei Lueth. There are conflicting reports about the whereabouts of Riek Machar, with the government claiming he is on his way to Unity State, while Machar's spokesperson says he is still in Juba.

The violence has put a strain on resources in the UN compounds, with many people requiring healthcare, food, water, and security. The UN deputy special representative for South Sudan, Toby Lanzer, said that many people who are coming require health care of all types. The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) is providing support to Juba's two major hospitals to cope with the heavy influx of patients.

The African Union has expressed concern about the events in South Sudan and has urged the government, leadership, and other stakeholders to exercise maximum restraint and avert any further escalation. The US Embassy in South Sudan has suspended normal operations until further notice and cannot provide routine consular services to US citizens in South Sudan. US citizens who choose to remain in South Sudan are advised to enroll in the Smart Traveler Enrollment Program (STEP) to stay updated on safety and security announcements.

A Canadian sniper from the elite Joint Task Force 2 (JTF2) has set a new world record for the longest confirmed kill shot in military history, hitting an Islamic State (ISIS) insurgent at a staggering distance of 3,540 meters (approximately 2.17 miles) during an operation in Iraq within the last month. The Canadian Armed Forces confirmed the record-breaking shot, stating that the sniper used a McMillan TAC-50 sniper rifle while firing from a high-rise. The shot took under 10 seconds to hit the target and disrupted an ISIS attack on Iraqi security forces.

The JTF2 operation falls within the strictures of the government's advise and assist mission, and the sniper's identity remains undisclosed for operational security reasons. The shot was independently verified by video camera and other data, and military sources have described it as an "incredible feat" that might never be equaled.

The previous world record was held by British sniper Craig Harrison, who shot a Taliban gunner with a 338 Lapua Magnum rifle from 2,475 meters away in 2009. Canadian Corporal Rob Furlong had set the world record in 2002 at 2,430 meters, and Canadian Master Cpl. Arron Perry briefly held the record after he fatally shot an insurgent at 2,310 meters during the same operation.

JTF2 special forces are primarily tasked with counterterrorism, sniper operations, and hostage rescue. The unit's snipers and members of Canadian Special Operations Regiment, who are training Kurdish forces, have been operating in tough conditions in Iraq. The Trudeau government pulled CF-18 fighter jets out of Iraq in 2016 but expanded the military mission, which will see the number of Canadian special forces trainers climb to 207 from 69 in an assist, train, and advise mission. Canadian commandos are not supposed to be involved in direct combat, but are authorized to go up to the front lines on training missions with Kurdish Peshmerga fighters and to paint targets for coalition air strikes.

The skill of the JTF2 sniper in taking down an insurgent at 3,540 meters required math skills, great eyesight, precision of ammunition and firearms, and superb training. The shooter would have had to take into consideration wind conditions, the curvature of the Earth, and other factors to make such a long-distance shot. Canadian snipers are considered some of the best in the world, with a reputation for their high-quality training and cross-training of soldiers above their existing rank.

The Canadian military has a history of producing skilled snipers, with former corporal Rob Furlong shooting a Taliban fighter in Afghanistan in 2002 from a distance of 2,430 meters, breaking the record set just a few days earlier by another Canadian, former master corporal Aaron Perry, who shot an insurgent from a distance of 2,286 meters. Cpl. Francis Pegahmagabow, an Ojibwa member of the 1st Canadian Infantry Battalion, was the deadliest sniper of the First World War, with a record of 378 kills. He still stands as one of Canada's most decorated First Nations soldiers.

The Canadian mission in Iraq has been the subject of much debate over whether Canada's troops are involved in a combat mission. The debate was reignited recently when the Chief of the Defence Staff Gen. Jonathan Vance revealed Canadian troops were operating inside Mosul. In a statement confirming the sniper's successful shot, the Canadian Forces insisted its mission in Iraq is still to merely "advise and assist" Iraqi forces.

In Eagle, Colorado, Juan Jose Vidrio Bibriesca, a 43-year-old defendant, found himself in deeper legal trouble after a court appearance. Bibriesca was already facing a felony drug charge and was in court for a bond violation. The document discusses a three-step plan for a species to become a universal superpower, as proposed by Russian astronomer Nikolai Kardashev in 1962. Kardashev's plan, known as the Kardashev scale, categorizes technologically advanced civilizations based on their energy consumption.

1. Harvest all resources on the home planet (Level I).
2. Harvest energy from the nearest star (Level II).
3. Harvest energy from all stars in the local galaxy and move on to another galaxy (Level III).

A recent paper by Dan Hooper, a senior scientist at the Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory, revives Kardashev's model and adds an apocalyptic twist. Hooper argues that harvesting energy from distant stars is not only a means to increase a civilization's resources but also a necessity due to the expanding universe caused by dark energy. Over time, stars beyond our Local Group will become inaccessible, limiting the energy that can be extracted from them.

To prevent this, advanced civilizations would capture stars from other galaxies, reel them in, and harvest their energy before they become inaccessible forever. This process would involve the creation of a colossal cloud of satellites, known as Dyson spheres, which would hover around a star, beam energy back to a nearby planet, or even use the star's energy to accelerate it back toward the planet.

Hooper's paper suggests that humans are currently at Level I (0.7) on the Kardashev scale, but advanced civilizations thousands or even millions of years older than ours might already be in their Level III, star-harvesting phase. If another civilization has indeed begun rearranging the stars, it may not be long before Earthlings notice them, as they would likely produce significant fluxes of electromagnetic radiation.

Astronomers could watch for stars being dragged unceremoniously across distant galaxies or look for unusual galaxies that have had their prime stars ripped away by advanced civilizations. These civilizations would likely be picky, choosing stars with a mass about 20 to 100 times the mass of our sun. The light signatures from these galaxies would be dominated by massive stars and would peak at longer wavelengths than usual.

Physicist Freeman Dyson proposed similar structures in a scientific paper in 1960, and science fiction author Olaf Stapledon described spherical, energy-trapping alien structures in his 1937 novel "Star Maker." Dyson spheres and other mega-structures appear frequently in science fiction.

In conclusion, the document discusses the Kardashev scale, a three-step plan for a species to become a universal superpower, and the potential for advanced civilizations to harvest energy from distant stars to prevent the ever-expanding universe from leaving them alone in space. The document also mentions Dyson spheres, a concept of a colossal cloud of satellites used to harvest energy from a star.

The study of Europe's best-known mummy, Ötzi, reveals that he had severe dental issues, including gum disease, cavities, and heavily worn teeth. Ötzi's genetic profile places him in the rare G2A4 haplogroup, linking his paternal genes to a population that migrated from the Near East to Europe at the beginning of the Neolithic era. His genetic makeup suggests a close relationship with small populations living in Sardinia, Corsica, Georgia, and remote areas of Russia.

The genome analysis also reveals that Ötzi had brown eyes, brown hair, type-O blood, and shared the lactose intolerance common among Neolithic Europeans. He was also the first known carrier of Lyme disease, as the sequencing yielded genes from the Borrelia burgdorferi bacterium. Although it's unclear if Lyme disease affected Ötzi during his lifetime, the discovery of 60% of a B. burgdorferi genome from a Neolithic carrier shows that this pathogen has been present for thousands of years.

The new findings contribute to our understanding of Neolithic life, with mummy expert Frank Ruehli stating that Ötzi's well-preserved state and extensive information make him an important source of insights. Separately, Twilight actor Kellan Lutz is participating in a charity auction of celebrity baggage to raise funds for youth groups across the country. The first round of items auctioned off raised over $15,000, and Lutz's bags, along with items from Taylor Swift, Jessica Simpson, and others, will be a part of the second round, which started on May 31.

Finally, a film reel owned by collector Morace Park is set to command a six-figure sum at auction. The film, Charlie Chaplin in Zepped, is the only known surviving copy and shows the famous British actor bringing down a German Zeppelin during a London raid. The seven-minute long reel is thought to contain some of the earliest known animation.

A US court has awarded $500 million to Zenimax Media Inc, a video game publisher, for violations of a non-disclosure agreement by Facebook, Oculus, and other defendants. The jury found that Oculus, a virtual reality company owned by Facebook, breached a contract with Zenimax when launching its own VR headset, the Rift. Oculus stated it was disappointed and plans to appeal. The ruling came at a time when Facebook reported strong financial results for the fourth quarter, with net profit more than doubling to $3.6 billion and advertising revenues increasing by 53%. Facebook is on track to reach two billion users in the first half of 2017. The court case threatened to overshadow Facebook's results, as it involved allegations of intellectual property theft and breach of contract. The case also involved Palmer Luckey, co-founder of Oculus, who was found to have broken a non-disclosure agreement with Zenimax. The ruling could have significant implications for Facebook, as it faces criticism over the spread of fake news and partisan propaganda on its platform, particularly in the context of the US presidential election. Facebook is also investing in video content to compete with next-generation television companies like Netflix. Despite the setback, Facebook's mobile ad revenue is expected to grow significantly in 2017, with about 90% of its users accessing the network through mobile devices.

In a surprising turn of events, Greg Gianforte, the Montana congressman-elect, pleaded guilty to misdemeanor assault for his infamous "body-slamming" incident involving a reporter last year. The incident occurred the night before Montana's congressional election. Judge Rick West sentenced Gianforte to a 180-day deferred sentence, 40 hours of community service, 20 hours of anger management, and a $300 fine, along with a $85 court fee.

Initially, West had sentenced Gianforte to four days of jail time, but due to the ineligibility of those guilty of assault charges for the work program, the sentence was amended. A misdemeanor assault conviction in Montana carries a maximum penalty of up to six months in jail and a fine of up to $500, according to the state government website.

Gianforte has apologized to the journalist, Ben Jacobs, and pledged to donate $50,000 to the Committee to Protect Journalists, an organization that promotes press freedom. President Trump, however, showed no regret for making light of the incident at a Montana rally, stating, "Any guy that can do a body slam, he is my type!"

The White House Correspondents' Association has since come out to condemn the president's comments, stating, "All Americans should recoil from the president’s praise for a violent assault on a reporter doing his Constitutionally protected job."

The Montana Senate race is personal for Trump, as he is making it his mission to unseat two-term Democratic senator Jon Tester, who is in a close race against Matt Rosendale, the current state auditor. The president has visited Montana three times for this purpose, with the midterm elections being dubbed "an election of Kavanaugh, the caravan, law and order, and common sense" by Trump. Despite Trump's efforts, Tester maintains a slight lead in the highly expensive political contest.

On August 20, a net pen holding 305,000 Atlantic salmon at a Cooke Aquaculture fish farm near Cypress Island in Washington state collapsed, leading to a massive escape of the fish. The Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife (WDFW) is urging the public to help catch as many of the fish as possible, with no limit on size or number. The fish are approximately 10 pounds each, and it is unknown how many escaped. Cooke Aquaculture, the company that owns the fish farm, claims that the escape was caused by "exceptionally high tides and currents coinciding with this week’s solar eclipse." However, tide tables show that the tides around Cypress Island were not abnormally high on the day of the spill.

The escape of the Atlantic salmon is causing concern among fishermen, environmental groups, and native tribes, who fear that the non-native fish could out-compete native chinook salmon and steelhead for food and spawning grounds. Kurt Beardslee, director of the Wild Fish Conservancy Northwest, called the event an "environmental nightmare." The Atlantic salmon bring with them pollution, virus, and parasite amplification, which could harm Pacific salmon and the waters of Washington.

Cooke Aquaculture is also proposing a larger Atlantic salmon net pen in the Strait of Juan de Fuca, which has been met with controversy. Lummi fishers are incensed at the Atlantic salmon intruding in their home waters of native Washington Pacific salmon. "It's a devastation," said Ellie Kinley, whose family has fished Puget Sound for generations. "We don't want those fish preying on our baby salmon. And we don't want them getting up in the rivers."

The WDFW is urging recreational fishers to get as many of the Atlantic salmon as possible. A valid fishing license is needed, but the fish don't need to be recorded on fish tickets and there are no bag limits. Buyers may also legally buy the Atlantics from commercial and tribal fishers. Warren, of the WDFW, said the fish were placed in the pens in May 2016 and treated for yellow mouth, a bacterial infection, in July 2016. He said the fish that escaped are believed to be healthy and disease-free.

Penalties for the escape are being evaluated, Warren said. Phone calls to Cooke Aquaculture, a Canadian company with salmon farms on three continents, were not returned. The company purchased the Cypress Island salmon farm last year. The incident has sparked protests and calls for stricter regulations on salmon farming in the region.

The world's cheapest smartphone, the Freedom 251, is set to be delivered to customers, despite initial skepticism and a police investigation. The Noida-based startup Ringing Bells, which manufactures the device, has faced doubts and allegations since its announcement in February. The company received over seven crore registrations before its payment gateway crashed within three days.

Ringing Bells Founder and CEO Mohit Goel has stated that the company is ready to deliver nearly two lakh Freedom 251 handsets, with deliveries starting from June 30. Goel also plans to open a second phase of registrations for the device after the first 200,000 units are shipped.

The Freedom 251 features a 4-inch, dual-SIM display, 1.3GHz quad-core processor, 1GB of RAM, 8GB of internal memory, and supports external memory cards of up to 32GB. It runs on Android 5.1 (Lollipop) and has an 8MP primary camera with flash, a 3.2MP front camera for selfies, and a 1,800 mAh battery.

Despite taking a loss of Rs 140-150 per unit, Goel hopes to make a profit on volumes. He believes the device will help bridge the gap between metros and rural areas, aligning with the government's "Digital India" and "Make in India" initiatives.

Ringing Bells is also planning to launch a 32-inch HD LED television, called "Freedom," in the first week of July. The television will be available for less than Rs 10,000, making it the cheapest in India.

Critics have expressed concerns over the device's authenticity, as some experts claim no phone can be manufactured for less than Rs 2,000. However, the company maintains that it has developed the device with government support.

It remains to be seen whether the Freedom 251 is an elaborate scam or a genuine attempt to provide affordable technology to the masses. With deliveries set to begin soon, consumers will soon find out if the device lives up to its promise.

Chris Watts, a 33-year-old man from Colorado, was sentenced to five life sentences without the possibility of parole for the murder of his pregnant wife, Shanann Watts, 34, and their two daughters, Bella, 4, and Celeste, 3. The murders occurred on August 13, 2018, and the bodies were found at a secluded site where Watts worked.

In the weeks leading up to the murders, Shanann saw Watts becoming cold and distant. She had canceled a party where she was to reveal the gender of her unborn child. The couple had been experiencing marital problems, with Watts going on dates with a mistress in Colorado while Shanann was away in North Carolina with the children.

Arguments between Watts and Shanann intensified when he reunited with the family in North Carolina in late July and early August. By the time they returned to Colorado, Shanann revealed to friends that her husband told her he didn't want the baby.

On August 8, Shanann wrote to her husband, "I don't know how you fell out of love with me in 5.5 weeks, or if this has been going on for a long time, but you don't plan another baby if you're not in love." Watts responded, "I'm not just staying because of the kids. They are my light and that will not change. I didn't fall out of love in 5 weeks, that's impossible. I don't want to erase 8 years just like that."

A friend reported Shanann missing on August 13, saying she wasn't responding to messages. Police found no one home at the Watts residence. Watts, after returning from work, told police that he had informed his wife early that morning that he wanted a separation. They had not argued, but they were both upset and crying, he told police. He told police that she'd indicated she was leaving for an unnamed friend's house.

On August 15, Watts submitted to a polygraph test and was found to be lying. When confronted about the deception, he admitted to killing his wife while sticking to the claim that she killed the girls. He admitted to putting the girls in the oil tanks.

Investigators found evidence of Watts' affair with Nichol Kessinger, a coworker, through phone records. Kessinger told investigators that Watts used a credit card to pay for their dinner at The Lazy Dog Sports Bar and Grill in Erie on the night of the murders, which was a lie. Watts had told police that he ate dinner with friends at the restaurant after a Colorado Rockies game.

Shanann's body was found in a shallow grave, wrapped in a fitted sheet, and the bodies of Bella and Celeste were found in commercial oil tanks at a company where Watts had worked. Watts had strangled his wife and suffocated the children.

The newly released documents include a police investigator's analysis of data from Chris Watts' and Shanann Watts' phones. The messages show increasing strain as Shanann's summer trip in North Carolina progressed. Some excerpts from the documents:

* July 10: Shanann writes to Chris, "You OK? It's like you don't want to talk l kept trying to talk and I had to dig it out of you?"
* July 24: Shanann remarks that Chris has been slow to respond to her. "Thought something happened. But you don't care about others feelings... Or think about others feelings."
* July 29: After a 14-minute phone conversation, Shanann writes, "lt would have been nice for my husband to show interest in how the girls and I are, and the baby. l'm done with begging for you to talk."
* August 5: Shanann messages Chris, "l don't know how you fell out of love with me in 5.5 weeks, or if this has been going on for a long time, but you don't plan another baby if you're not in love. Kids don't deserve a broken family ... You show up and I have to practically ask for a kiss in airport."
* August 6: Shanann writes to Chris, "Your only response last night was 'l don't want to lose the kids!' 'You used me to just have a 'boy!' Only reason you wanted another kid?! I can't handle this and you are ok with it. Why didn't you just tell me you were done?l? Why get me pregnant?!?"

Watts pleaded guilty to first-degree murder and other charges on November 6, 2018, and was sentenced on November 19, 2018.

The French presidential election held on May 7, 2017, resulted in a clear victory for centrist Emmanuel Macron, who defeated the far-right Marine Le Pen. The election was closely watched by leaders across the world, as France is a key member of the European Union (EU) and a close ally of Germany.

The EU leaders breathed a sigh of relief as Le Pen, who is fiercely anti-Europe, was defeated. German Chancellor Angela Merkel and European Commission President Jean-Claude Juncker congratulated Macron, with Merkel saying that his victory was a victory for a strong and united Europe and for French-German friendship. EU Council President Donald Tusk also offered his congratulations, saying the French had chosen "liberty, equality and fraternity" and "said no to the tyranny of fake news."

One of Macron's new responsibilities as French president will be negotiating the terms of Britain's exit from the EU along with the bloc's other leaders. British Prime Minister Theresa May called Macron to congratulate him and discuss Brexit, with May reiterating that the UK wants a strong partnership with a secure and prosperous EU once it leaves.

US President Donald Trump also congratulated Macron on Twitter, saying he looked forward to working with him. However, Trump's ideologically similarities with Le Pen and his earlier praise of the National Front leader over her security policy raised questions about the relationship between the two leaders.

Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau also congratulated Macron, saying he looked forward to working closely with him on a progressive agenda to promote international security, increase collaboration in science and technology, and create good, middle-class jobs on both sides of the Atlantic.

Brazil's President Michel Temer and Australia's prime minister also congratulated Macron, with Temer saying that Brazil and France will continue to work together for democracy, human rights, development, integration, and peace.

Macron's first public gesture as president was to deliberately walk under spotlights across the Louvre's Napoleon courtyard to Beethoven's Ode to Joy, the European anthem. This was a carefully coordinated reference to the style of the late Socialist president François Mitterrand, who presented himself as a kind of republican, elected monarch.

Macron, who will take office within days, will have a significant challenge ahead of him. He is taking over a country exhausted by decades of mass unemployment, impatient with a stagnant economy, still living under a state of emergency, facing a constant terrorist threat, and at war abroad. The election has highlighted a significant divide between rich and poor, between thriving, diverse cities and the far away de-industrialized peripheral areas and countryside.

Macron has promised to bring a youthful "revolution" to French politics but also to return to the historic tradition of a strong leader who can "embody the nation." He believes that ever since King Louis XVI's head was chopped off in the revolution, France has been constantly trying to compensate for the lack of a true leader figure who could personify France. Macron, a centrist political novice, who had never before run for election and until three years ago was unknown, believes he can fill the role of republican guide of the nation.

Macron's first moves as president will be to cut and streamline France's strict labor laws in favor of businesses, loosen red tape for small businesses, and cut class sizes in primary schools in disadvantaged areas. However, labor law changes were forced through by decree under Hollande and saw months of street demonstrations in 2016. Navigating the hangover from that social confrontation will be his first major challenge.

Macron knows better than most that the first days of a French presidency can make or break an entire mandate. He was deputy chief of staff to the Socialist president Hollande, whose lack of preparation and dithering in the early days led to an unpopularity from which he was never able to recover. Macron is also aware of ill omens. He was on the newly elected Hollande's plane to Berlin to see Angela Merkel when it was hit by lightning – a metaphor for a tepid diplomatic relationship that did not fully recover.

Macron will make his first foreign leader visit to Merkel quickly. He is also expected to make an early trip to see French troops in Mali to signal that French international military engagement will continue.

One of Macron's most-repeated promises has been "efficiency" of government. He wants to introduce new ethics rules for politicians, including an initiative against nepotism after the corruption investigations of the right-wing candidate François Fillon and the investigations of Marine Le Pen's party funding during the presidential campaign. He also wants quickly to loosen red tape for small businesses and cut class sizes in primary schools in disadvantaged areas.

However, exactly how he will deliver his manifesto pledges depends on whom he appoints as prime minister and whether his fledgling "neither right or left" political movement En Marche! (On the Move!) can win a majority in the parliamentary elections in June. Without a majority, Macron's hands will be tied. The next six weeks of parliamentary campaigning will be crucial.

There has never been so much secrecy surrounding who will be appointed French prime minister. Because the centrist Macron, who comes from no political party, needs to strike a balance between supporters from the left and right, he has kept quiet about who he will pick. He has said only that the prime minister must be "strong" and politically experienced. Speculation has ranged from a centrist ex-minister such as François Bayrou to ex-ministers from the political right or left, or the centrist MEP Sylvie Goulard, but it could also be an appointment from civil society. His 15-minister government will have a male-female balance, one-third of whom will be new to politics.

"We need to do away with this political class, which is all too often made of men over 50 who never had a proper job," Macron has said, promising that his 577 parliamentary candidates will be half women and half political newcomers.

Former Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice warned against feeling reassured by the expected defeat of far-right candidate Marine Le Pen in the French presidential election. Rice argued that the rise of populism, nativism, and a tinge of isolationism around the world is having an impact on politics, even if the candidates aren't winning. In a surprising turn of events, President Donald Trump announced on July 26, 2017, via Twitter that transgender individuals would no longer be allowed to serve in any capacity in the U.S. military. The announcement caused immediate concerns among transgender service members and their advocates. However, the U.S. military has yet to implement any changes to the current policy, as Defense Secretary Jim Mattis has not received any direction from the President to do so.

In a memo to all military service chiefs, commanders, and enlisted military leaders, Gen. Joseph Dunford, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, stated that there would be no modifications to the current policy for the time being. He also emphasized that all personnel would continue to be treated with respect and that the military would remain focused on its assigned missions.

The Dunford statement suggests that Mattis was not given any presidential direction on changing the transgender policy. Mattis has been on vacation this week and has been publicly silent on the matter. His spokesmen declined to comment on the issue on Thursday. On Wednesday, they said the Pentagon would work with the White House and provide revised guidance to the military "in the near future."

Dunford himself was not aware that Trump was going to announce the ban, according to a U.S. official who spoke on condition of anonymity. The announcement caught the Pentagon flat-footed and unable to explain what it called Trump's "guidance."

Trump's announcement appears to halt a decades-long trend toward more inclusive policies on military service, including the repeal in 2010 of a ban on gays serving openly. President Bill Clinton began the push to allow gays to serve in 1993, and President Barack Obama's Pentagon chief, Ash Carter, announced in December 2015 that all military positions would be open to women. Liberalizing policy on transgender troops was the next step.

Just last week, when asked about the transgender issue at a Senate hearing, Gen. Paul Selva, vice chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, said, "I am an advocate of every qualified person who can meet the physical standards to serve in our uniformed services to be able to do so."

Transgender people have been able to serve openly in the military since 2016, when Carter ended the ban. Since October 1, transgender troops have been able to receive medical care and start changing their gender identifications in the Pentagon's personnel system. Carter also gave the services until July 1 to develop policies to allow people already identifying as transgender to join the military if they meet normal standards and have been stable in their identified genders for 18 months.

On June 30, Mattis extended the July 1 deadline to next January 1, saying the services should study the impact on the "readiness and lethality of our forces."

White House press secretary Sarah Huckabee Sanders said Trump had made "a military decision." She said it was his judgment that allowing transgender service "erodes military readiness and unit cohesion." Sanders said the "president's national security team was part of this consultation" and that Trump "informed" Mattis of his decision immediately after he made it on Tuesday.

Criticism for Trump's action was immediate and strong from both political parties. Sen. John McCain, an Arizona Republican and Vietnam War hero, said Trump was simply wrong. "Any American who meets current medical and readiness standards should be allowed to continue serving," he said. "There is no reason to force service members who are able to fight, train, and deploy to leave the military -- regardless of their gender identity."

Not everyone at the Capitol agreed. Rep. Duncan Hunter, a member of the House Armed Services Committee, said, "It's about time that a decision is made to restore the warrior culture and allow the U.S. military to get back to business."

Transgender people already in uniform were concerned about what comes next. Rudy Akbarian, 26, who is in the military but did not want to identify his branch, said, "Everybody is hurt, everybody is scared."
