On Saturday, two men skiing in Alaska's Rainbow Mountains were caught in an avalanche, resulting in the death of 35-year-old Eric Peterson from Delta Junction. The surviving skier, 63-year-old Michael Hopper from Fairbanks, was reported to have spent several hours digging himself out from the snow to seek help. The body of Peterson has not been recovered yet, and his family has been notified.

The incident occurred near the Black Rapids Lodge, which is owned by Hopper. The lodge often holds an avalanche safety course. Hopper was found by a motorist, Kimberly McRoberts, who saw his headlamp near the road and provided him with a ride.

Responding to the scene were Alaska State Troopers, military members from Black Rapids, Fort Greely Fire Department, and Rural Delta Fire and Rescue. The area where the avalanche occurred is reported to be unstable and deteriorating due to additional heavy snowfall. The authorities plan to recover Peterson's body once the weather and conditions permit.

This is an ongoing story, and updates can be found on KTUU.com and Channel 2 newscasts.

The report by Human Rights Watch reveals that in 2012, only 3% of U.S. drug defendants in federal cases chose to go to trial instead of pleading guilty. The small number is attributed to the significant power wielded by federal prosecutors who threaten defendants with steep prison sentences or stack charges to increase their time behind bars. The report argues that prosecutors essentially force defendants to plead guilty due to the threat of mandatory minimum sentences.

In 1980, the percentage of federal drug defendants who pleaded guilty was slightly more than 60%, and it has risen steadily since then, largely due to the advent of mandatory-minimum sentencing laws in the mid-80s. These laws require judges to impose harsh, predetermined sentences on people convicted of drug distribution and, in some circumstances, possession. Prosecutors can offer defendants smaller sentences as part of a deal, making it more attractive for them to plead guilty.

The report found that defendants who take their case to trial face prison sentences on average 11 years longer than those who plead guilty. In all, a whopping 97% of defendants plead guilty. The issue is significant because about half of the people in U.S. prisons got there after being charged with and convicted of drug offenses.

The report uncovered dozens of cases where defendants were sent to prison for nearly a half-century for first-time drug offenses. In one such case, Mary Beth Looney refused a plea deal that would have sent her to prison for 17 years for dealing methamphetamines and having guns in her house. Prosecutors added more charges against her, ultimately resulting in a sentence of more than 45 years behind bars.

The Justice Department responded by stating that it is critical to ensure the criminal justice system operates fairly in every case, and their charging policies reflect that goal. However, the report found some cases where the Justice Department appeared to disregard this policy.

The report calls for Congress to restore discretion to federal judges by getting rid of mandatory minimums or giving judges more power to depart from sentencing guidelines based on the facts in an individual case. The Senate Judiciary Committee will consider some of these options when the Senate returns from recess next week. The report also suggests that Attorney General Eric Holder should bar prosecutors from threatening longer sentences because defendants in drug cases refuse to plead guilty.

Researchers from the Czech Republic have found that people can predict the intelligence of men by looking at their faces, but not women. The study, published in the journal PLoS One, found that faces perceived as highly intelligent are longer, with a wider distance between the eyes, a larger nose, a slight upturn to the corners of the mouth, and a sharper, pointing, less rounded chin. By contrast, the perception of lower intelligence is associated with broader, more rounded faces with eyes closer to each other, a shorter nose, declining corners of the mouth, and a rounded and massive chin. However, the researchers found no correlation between these facial traits and actual IQ scores. The study also found that people can accurately judge intelligence by looking at faces of men, but not women, and that this may be due to the fact that attractiveness clouds the judgement or that women are judged according to their attractiveness. The researchers say this could be due to the fact that cues of higher intelligence are sexually dimorphic and are thus apparent only in men's faces, or that the strong halo effect of attractiveness may prevent an accurate assessment of the intelligence of women. The study suggests that a clear mental image of what an intelligent-looking face should look like exists for both men and women within the community of human raters.

The Jamaican bobsled team, making a return to the Winter Olympics after a 12-year absence, is accompanied by a catchy reggae tune titled "The Bobsled Song." Composed by Sidney Mills and Jon Notard, the song is designed to sync perfectly with the twists and turns of the Olympic bobsled track in Sochi, Russia. The song's lyrics and chorus follow the course of the 1,500-meter track with its 17 turns and 125.5-meter vertical drop. The Jamaican team, considered a long shot to win a medal, qualified for the two-man bobsled competition without racing in any World Cup events but accumulating enough points in lower-tier races in North America. The team's run to the Calgary Games in 1988 was depicted in the film "Cool Runnings." Fans can download the song at BobsledSong.com and follow updates via Twitter @JAMBOBSLED.

Derrick Henry, the Alabama running back and Yulee native, is expected to enter the 2016 NFL Draft after the Heisman Trophy ceremony on Saturday. His draft position is a topic of debate, with concerns about his workload, running style, scheme fit, and potential injury susceptibility. Dan Hatman, a former scout for Philadelphia and the New York Giants and Jets and current director of The Scouting Academy, evaluated Henry and found him to be a better fit for an offense that concentrates on a zone blocking system. Hatman also noted Henry's impressive balance, good vision, and patience, but expressed concerns about his lateral agility and the number of carries he has had in college. Henry's draft stock could also be impacted by how many NFL teams will enter the draft feeling they're set at running back. Despite the concerns, Henry is not complaining about the work and is eager to make plays.

The small community of Sutherland Springs, Texas, is in mourning after a gunman opened fire at the First Baptist Church during Sunday morning services, killing at least 26 people and wounding 20 others. The shooter, identified as Devin Patrick Kelley, was later found dead in his vehicle. The victims ranged in age from 5 to 72 years old. The shooting has devastated the community, which is described as a place where "everyone knows everyone." The church is both a religious center for the town and a provider of community services. The suspect was seen at a gas station across the street from the church before the shooting, and a local resident used his own rifle to engage the shooter, who then fled the church and was later chased and killed by law enforcement. The community is holding vigils and offering support to the victims and their families.

The Navy has its first female candidates for two elite special operations roles previously closed to women, including a prospective SEAL and a special warfare combatant crewman. The candidates' identities remain undisclosed due to security concerns. The news comes over 18 months after the Pentagon allowed women to serve in front-line combat positions. The path ahead for these candidates is challenging, as they must complete the same rigorous training as men, without any allowances for physical differences. The training is physically and mentally demanding, with high attrition rates. It may take months or years before the first woman graduates from these elite Navy positions. Additionally, the Navy's elite operations have also welcomed a transgender individual. The first female candidates represent a significant milestone for the Navy, as women were previously excluded from the SEALs and SWCC community. This development also marks a step forward for military special operations, as no female soldier has made it through the selection process for any other Army special operations element.

The report discusses the growing influence of creationism in South Korea, where efforts to remove references to evolution from high school textbooks have been successful. The Society for Textbook Revise (STR) led a petition to remove examples of evolution, including the evolution of the horse and the Archaeopteryx, from textbooks, claiming victory after the Ministry of Education, Science and Technology (MEST) announced that textbook publishers would revise editions to exclude these examples. Biologists were alarmed as they were not consulted in the process.

The STR is an offshoot of the Korea Association for Creation Research (KACR), which seeks to provide evidence in support of the creation myth described in the Book of Genesis. Creation science has gained influence in South Korea, with the KACR scoring a hit with a successful exhibition at Seoul Land, one of the country's leading amusement parks. The STR aims to delete the "error" of evolution from textbooks to "correct" students' views of the world, citing recent discoveries that Archaeopteryx is one of many feathered dinosaurs, and not necessarily an ancestor of all birds, as evidence.

The roots of the South Korean antipathy to evolution are unclear, although it is suggested that they are partly due to strong Christianity in the country. Nearly one-third of South Koreans don't believe in evolution, with some claiming insufficient scientific evidence, others citing religious beliefs, and others stating they don't understand the theory. In response, Dayk Jang, an evolutionary scientist at Seoul National University, is organizing a group of experts, including evolutionary biologists and theologians who believe in evolution, to counter the STR's campaign by working to improve the teaching of evolution in the classroom and in broader public life.

The report also mentions that in the United States, efforts to limit the teaching of evolution have made headway in a couple of states, but the successes are modest compared to those in South Korea. The report concludes that the STR's victory in South Korea is a significant setback for the teaching of evolution and that efforts are needed to counter creationist campaigns in both countries.

In Tennessee, police are investigating a potential connection between the abduction of 20-year-old nursing student Holly Bobo in Parsons and a similar attack on Heather Sullivan, a resident of Centerville. Sullivan was approached by a man outside her home in January, who grabbed her arm before being scared off. Bobo was taken away by a man in camouflage clothing from her home on April 13. Both incidents occurred near wooded areas. Mark Gwyn, director of the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation, has not ruled out a connection between the two cases. An $80,000 reward has been offered for information regarding Bobo's case, with her family continuing to hope for her safe return. Meanwhile, searches have been conducted in the woods near Bobo's home, and a blood sample found nearby has been tested, but the results have not been disclosed. Bobo's mother, Karen Bobo, made a tearful plea for her daughter's safe return.

The Nielsen Company's Women of Tomorrow Study, which surveyed 6,500 women across 21 countries, found that Indian women are the most stressed, with 87% reporting feeling stressed most of the time and 82% claiming they have no time to relax. Mexican and Russian women also reported high levels of stress, with 74% and 69% respectively. Despite the stress, Indian women are the most likely to spend disposable income on themselves, with 96% planning to buy clothes and 77% planning to spend on health and beauty products. Women in developing economies tend to spend more on clothes, health and beauty items, groceries, and education for their children, while women in developed economies dedicate more of their cash to vacations, savings, and paying off debt. The survey also found that women in emerging markets are more optimistic about their daughters' future opportunities, with 80% believing their daughters will have greater financial stability and 83% believing they will have more educational opportunities. Women around the world are more prolific users of social networking than men, and marketers should use social media strategies to connect with women, as they follow brands more than men. The survey, conducted from February to April, covered nearly 6,500 women in 21 countries, including India, Mexico, Russia, China, Thailand, South Africa, Nigeria, Malaysia, Brazil, the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, Italy, France, Germany, Spain, Sweden, Japan, Australia, and South Korea.

McDonald's has launched its nationwide all-day breakfast, but with some limitations. The McGriddle sandwiches, bagel sandwiches, cinnamon melts, "Big Breakfast" platters, Egg White Delight, and steak, egg, and cheese McMuffin are not available on the all-day menu. However, in most markets, customers can order sausage burrito, "Fruit ‘N Yogurt" parfait, "Fruit & Maple" oatmeal, hash browns, hotcakes, hotcakes with sausage, and sausage McMuffin. In markets offering McMuffins, the egg McMuffin, sausage McMuffin with egg, and sausage McMuffin are available. In markets offering biscuits, customers can order bacon, egg, and cheese biscuit, sausage biscuit with egg, and sausage biscuit. The all-day breakfast menu varies by location, but the deliciousness remains the same.

The body of Tamerlan Tsarnaev, one of the Boston Marathon bombers, has been claimed by an uncle and is now at a funeral home in Massachusetts. However, before burial, Tsarnaev will undergo a second autopsy at the request of his relatives. The funeral home is facing challenges in finding a burial site due to fears of reprisals from the public. Tsarnaev died on April 19 after a shootout with police, following the bombing of the Boston Marathon on April 15, which killed three and injured over 260. Dzhokhar Tsarnaev, his younger brother, is being held and charged with using a weapon of mass destruction.

Investigators have found explosives residue in the apartment Tsarnaev shared with his family, and believe the marathon was not the original target. Instead, the brothers had planned to attack the city's Independence Day celebration. The FBI is also investigating whether the brothers received assistance from or learned from terror groups. Three of Tsarnaev's friends have been charged with conspiring to discard potentially incriminating items and making false statements to investigators.

Separately, the National Rifle Association's Executive Vice President Wayne LaPierre criticized the Boston police for disarming residents during the manhunt for Dzhokhar Tsarnaev, stating that "good guys with guns" could have stopped the terrorists.

The marathon bombings have sparked a debate on the role of law enforcement, cooperation among agencies, and the potential for self-radicalization among individuals not part of a massive conspiracy or network. An independent government review is underway to examine whether intelligence, law enforcement, and homeland security agencies could have done more in their investigation of Tamerlan Tsarnaev in recent years.

The Occupy Oakland general strike on Wednesday, November 2nd, 2011, drew thousands of protesters for rallies and marches. The event turned chaotic early Thursday after protesters took over a vacant building and police moved in, firing tear gas and flashbang grenades.

On the night of the strike, protesters blocked the entrance to the Port of Oakland, preventing trucks and other vehicles from entering. Scuffles between protesters and truckers occurred, with one protester hitting a truck with a sign. Most trucks were turning around and going back the other way, but one big rig was having trouble turning around due to the narrow street.

As the night progressed, the protest had mostly ended by 3:30 a.m., with only a handful of protesters remaining near the police line. The police were also beginning to leave.

Earlier in the day, the protesters had gathered at Frank Ogawa Plaza and marched on banks in the city. The march was peaceful, with no arrests made, despite several incidents of vandalism around the downtown area. The protesters' goal was to send a message to the 1% and show support for the 99%.

The event was a test of the 1% and a warning to them that the protesters did not need them and they needed the protesters. The event was also a show of solidarity with Scott Olsen, a former marine who was seriously injured by a police projectile during a previous protest. Olsen was aware of the strike and showed support for it on Facebook.

The Oakland Police Department tried to move its command center from the area, while the Teamsters union helped direct protesters to entrances. No injuries had been reported to the city as of a 5 p.m. news conference held by city leaders, but the Port was asking for protesters to allow port workers safe passage home.

The total crowd at 5 p.m. was estimated at between 4,500 and 5,000 people, with about 3,000 marching peacefully to the Port.
