Michael David Elliot, a convicted murderer serving five life sentences for four murders in 1993, escaped from the Ionia Correctional Facility in Michigan on Sunday and was captured in Indiana on Monday evening. Elliot allegedly stole four vehicles during his 24-hour run from the law, leading to a chase in LaPorte County, Indiana, where he was eventually apprehended.

The escape occurred around 7 p.m. on Sunday, but jail workers did not notice Elliot was missing until a routine prisoner check at 9 p.m. Elliot left through the sally port, a secured garage where prisoners are brought into the facility, and got through a hole in the fencing system. He then made a three-and-a-half mile trek into Ionia where he carjacked a woman, police said. The two then drove to the Elkhart, Ind. area.

The woman escaped at a gas station there and he fled in her Jeep Liberty. That SUV was found early Monday morning in Shipshewana, Ind. LaPorte County, where Elliot was arrested, is west of Shipshewana. Elliot was arraigned Tuesday in Indiana on auto theft charges.

Authorities are still investigating the circumstances surrounding Elliot's escape, with Michigan Gov. Rick Snyder thanking the law enforcement agencies that aided in the search and capture of Elliot. Elliot was described as polite and emotionless during his arrest, and looked tired, like he had not slept in days.

Elliot was convicted of four murders in 1993, and was serving five life sentences in the Ionia Correctional Facility. In the early morning of Aug. 8, 1993, Elliot broke into a home in Bentley Township, north of Midland, killed four people then set the house on fire. Charles and Paul Treece, and Tammy LaCross were with Elliot when the murders were committed. Charles Treece was also convicted of four counts of first-degree murder, and is also serving life in prison at the Alger Correctional Facility in Munising in the Upper Peninsula.

LaCross, who was 16 at the time and is victim Vickie Currie’s daughter, and Paul Treece both testified against Elliot. Under the terms of plea agreements, they pleaded guilty to robbery and felony firearm charges. In 2005, Elliot filed a motion for release, saying that there was new evidence in his case — namely a 1994 letter from Charles Treece that attested to Elliot’s innocence. A state court denied his request. Elliot maintains he is innocent, according to the court documents.

In the New Hampshire Republican primary, Donald Trump finished first, while Ohio Governor John Kasich presented himself as a compassionate alternative and a potential source of momentum for the upcoming primary states. Kasich, a moderate conservative, described his campaign as a battle of heart and mind, and he criticized the Democratic candidates, particularly Bernie Sanders, who won the New Hampshire primary on the Democratic side. Sanders, in his victory speech, declared that his win was a result of an enthusiastic and aroused electorate and that he would continue his campaign to bring real change. Hillary Clinton, who lost the primary, vowed to fight for every vote in every state and to continue her campaign to make a difference in people's lives. On the Republican side, Trump, despite finishing second in the Iowa caucuses, showed no signs of humility and instead boasted about winning and making America great again. He also took jabs at Bernie Sanders and ignored Hillary Clinton in his victory speech.

In a sharp escalation of partisan tensions over the confirmation of Supreme Court nominee Brett Kavanaugh, President Trump attacked one of his accusers, Deborah Ramirez, in harsh and stark language on Tuesday. Trump dismissed Ramirez's account of Kavanaugh exposing himself to her at a party while they were both students at Yale University, calling it a "con game" played by Democrats. Trump accused Ramirez of being drunk and having gaps in her memory, and questioned the credibility of her allegations.

The president's charged rhetoric came as Republicans closed ranks around Kavanaugh, with Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell expressing confidence about Kavanaugh's prospects and dismissing the allegations as politically motivated. The full Senate could vote on Kavanaugh's confirmation as early as next Tuesday, with the high court set to begin its new term on Monday.

Kavanaugh has strongly denied the allegations from both Ramirez and Christine Blasey Ford, who accused him of sexual assault when they were high school students in Maryland. Top panel staffers held a call with Kavanaugh on Tuesday to interview him about the allegation outlined in the New Yorker, and he again denied the allegation in the staff interview, according to a panel spokesman.

In a move to avoid a repeat of the 1991 hearing where an all-male panel's questioning of Anita Hill about her allegations of sexual impropriety against Supreme Court nominee Clarence Thomas angered female voters, Republicans hired a female lawyer from outside the panel to lead the questioning of Ford and Kavanaugh at Thursday's hearing. The committee's chairman, Sen. Charles E. Grassley, confirmed that Arizona prosecutor Rachel Mitchell would do the questioning.

Senate Democrats plan to ask questions of Kavanaugh and Ford, and the Democratic panel members met midday Tuesday to strategize about the hearing. Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer criticized McConnell and Senate Republicans for their handling of the allegations, saying they were not treating the accusations with respect and fairness.

A third accuser could come forward this week, as lawyer Michael Avenatti has said he is representing a woman with accusations about Kavanaugh's behavior in high school. The White House is open to testimony from Ramirez, but press secretary Sarah Huckabee Sanders stressed that the confirmation process needs to come to a close. The New Yorker reported that Ramirez was reluctant to characterize Kavanaugh's role in the alleged incident with certainty, but after six days of assessing her memories, she said she felt confident enough to say that she remembers Kavanaugh had exposed himself at a drunken dormitory party, thrust his penis in her face, and caused her to touch it without her consent as she pushed him away.

The preliminary report from the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) regarding a fatal plane crash in East Haven, Connecticut on August 9th has been released. The crash resulted in the deaths of four individuals, including pilot William Henningsgaard and his 17-year-old son, Maxwell, as well as 13-year-old Sade Brantley and her 1-year-old sister, Madisyn Mitchell, who were in a house that was struck.

A witness reported seeing the plane, a multi-engine, propeller-driven aircraft, inverted and traveling at a high rate of speed before the crash. Another witness living two houses away from the crash scene reported seeing the plane descending at a 90-degree angle, right-side down, into the houses.

The plane had taken off from Teterboro Airport in New Jersey and was scheduled to land at Tweed-New Haven Airport. Two minutes before the crash, the pilot acknowledged that he could see the airport. The last radar target was at 11:20 a.m., approximately .7 miles north of the runway.

Upon arrival at the crash site, investigators found the front half of the plane, including the cockpit, left engine, and front two-thirds of the fuselage in the basement. The right wing struck another house, and the right engine and propeller struck the ground between the two houses. The wind at the time of the crash was reported as 12 knots, gusting to 19 knots, with a visibility of nine miles and an overcast ceiling at 900 feet.

The NTSB is continuing its investigation into the cause of the crash. Cleanup at the crash site is ongoing, and once completed, the homes will be demolished. A fundraiser was held at two Dunkin Donuts restaurants to support the affected families.

The article discusses the ongoing debate between Jimmy Kimmel, a late-night talk show host, and Senator Bill Cassidy over the Graham-Cassidy health care bill. Kimmel has been critical of the bill, arguing that it fails to meet the "Jimmy Kimmel test" he co-authored with Cassidy, which requires coverage for individuals with pre-existing conditions. Cassidy has countered that Kimmel does not understand the nuances of the legislation.

Experts say that the bill could potentially lead to insurers hiking premiums for patients with pre-existing conditions and could roll back the Affordable Care Act's Medicaid expansion. The bill has been criticized by various health organizations, including the American Diabetes Association, American Medical Association, and American Heart Association.

President Trump has expressed support for the bill, stating that it includes protections for patients with pre-existing conditions. However, experts say that the bill does not guarantee those protections and could lead to significant reductions in coverage for millions of Americans.

Some conservatives have disputed the claim that the bill would lead to coverage cuts, citing the possibility of state flexibility and lower premiums bringing more uninsured Americans into the market. The Congressional Budget Office has stated that it will not be able to provide an analysis of the bill's impact for several weeks, long after the September 30 expiration of the reconciliation bill that allows Republicans to pass the measure with a simple majority.

The debate between Kimmel and Cassidy has garnered significant attention, with Kimmel tripling down on his condemnation of the bill during his monologue on Thursday. Kimmel has argued that the bill is not in the best interests of Americans, particularly those with pre-existing conditions. Cassidy has responded by stating that Kimmel does not understand the legislation.

The article concludes by stating that while Kimmel may not be an expert on health policy, his personal story and large audience have made him a prominent voice in the health care debate. However, it is important for people to seek out more informed opinions on the matter.

A former University of Illinois graduate student, Brendt Christensen, faces new charges and potential death penalty for the kidnapping and alleged murder of a visiting scholar from China, Yingying Zhang, who went missing in June. The federal grand jury indictment alleges that Christensen kidnapped Zhang in a manner that was "especially heinous, cruel, or depraved," involving torture or serious physical abuse, and was the result of substantial planning and premeditation.

In addition to the kidnapping charge, Christensen is also charged with two counts of making false statements to FBI agents regarding his whereabouts and actions on the day Zhang disappeared. If convicted on the kidnapping charge, Christensen could face the death penalty, although the decision on whether to seek it will be made at a later date by U.S. Attorney General Jeff Sessions. If the death penalty is not sought, a conviction would result in mandatory life without parole.

Christensen, who is being held without bond, is tentatively set to go to trial on February 27 before U.S. District Court Judge Colin Bruce. His lawyer, Robert Tucker, had no comment when reached by telephone on Tuesday.

The investigation into Zhang's disappearance rattled the University of Illinois campus and sent shockwaves throughout China. Prosecutors allege that Zhang, who began her research appointment in April, was on her way to sign a lease when she was abducted by Christensen. Surveillance footage captured the exchange, and police determined that Christensen's car was the one seen in the footage.

Christensen initially told the FBI he was home all day playing video games on the day Zhang disappeared, but when questioned again three days later, he changed his story, claiming he offered Zhang a ride because she said she was late to an appointment. However, police also found visits to a sadomasochism fetish website on Christensen's phone, as well as discussion threads on kidnapping fantasies.

The FBI also conducted audio surveillance on Christensen, recording him pointing out people in the crowd at a campus walk and vigil in Zhang's honor and describing his "ideal victim." Other surveillance tapes allegedly recorded Christensen admitting to having kidnapped Zhang and describing how she fought back as he held her against her will. The source of the recordings has not been revealed.

Zhang's family remains in the Urbana area and intends to stay until she is found. Attorney Steve Beckett, who represents Zhang's family, said the superseding indictment "is not unexpected."

The U.S. intelligence community has issued a statement confirming that the attack on the U.S. consulate in Libya on September 11 was a deliberate and organized terrorist attack, contradicting earlier claims that it was a spontaneous protest. The statement comes as the Obama administration faces criticism for shifting accounts of the attack, which resulted in the death of U.S. Ambassador Christopher Stevens and three other Americans. The attack was carried out by extremists linked to Al-Qaeda, according to the intelligence community, but it is unclear whether any group or person exercised overall command and control of the attack. The statement from the Director of National Intelligence (DNI) reflects an evolution in the information emerging from investigations into the attack, but it does not yet answer the question at the heart of a growing political controversy: whether the assault was a premeditated attack that the administration should have known about. Some Republican critics have implied that the Obama administration knew that the attack was preplanned by terrorist groups but hid that fact to avoid exposing security failures. White House officials say that isn't the case and that they have conveyed what facts they knew at the time. The U.S. has ramped up its probe, with the CIA sending operatives to Libya to assist with the investigation. The attack posed an unexpected challenge to President Barack Obama's foreign policy record just weeks before the November election. The DNI's statement is an effort to explain that early reports are often wrong or incomplete, and that the intelligence community continues to work around the clock to gather details and understand exactly what happened in Benghazi. The crime scene in Benghazi has posed security problems for the U.S. investigators, but federal agents are using intelligence and analyzing intercepts, and some are doing interviews in Tripoli. The attack has led to increased reporting on Libyan terror groups, with counterterrorism-related U.S. intelligence reports on Libya increasing at least fivefold in the days following the attack.

Sofia Vergara and Joe Manganiello, popular celebrities, are engaged, according to Page Six. The engagement took place during Christmas vacation in Hawaii, where Manganiello, known for his role in "True Blood," proposed to Vergara, famous for her role in "Modern Family." Vergara has been seen sporting a large diamond ring on her left hand, and the couple has been publicly together since June, having been introduced at the White House Correspondents Dinner in May.

Manganiello had previously expressed his admiration for Vergara, calling her his "dream girl." The couple celebrated Manganiello's 38th birthday on Saturday, with Vergara posting a birthday message on Twitter and Instagram.

Nick Loeb, Vergara's ex-fiance, has expressed his happiness for Vergara and Manganiello. Loeb and Vergara ended their engagement in May, but two months later, Us Weekly revealed their relationship. The couple spent their engagement week at the luxurious St. Regis Princeville Resort in Kauai, according to sources.

The engagement was a family affair, with both families present for the proposal on Christmas day. The ring, described as giant and very sparkly, has been a topic of conversation among onlookers. The couple seems to be very happy and deeply in love, according to sources.

U.S. Senator Barbara Boxer, a longtime ally of San Diego Mayor Bob Filner, has called for his resignation in a personal and professional letter, citing the numerous sexual harassment allegations against him. Boxer expressed her disappointment and concern over Filner's behavior towards women, particularly those who are survivors of sexual assault. The letter comes as Filner is undergoing behavioral modification therapy earlier than anticipated, and is expected to return to City Hall on August 19th. The call for Filner's resignation is now unanimous, as all nine City Council members have demanded his departure. The latest development comes after two former military personnel, both victims of sexual assault during their service, accused Filner of making crude advances at a conference designed to help women who have suffered sexual assault. The allegations are being investigated by local, state, and federal agencies. Filner's political support continues to crater as he faces numerous calls for his resignation.

Skye McCole Bartusiak, the child actress who gained prominence for her role as Mel Gibson's youngest daughter in the 2000 film "The Patriot," passed away on Saturday at the age of 21. Bartusiak's mother reported that she died in her sleep at their Texas home, although the cause of death remains unknown.

Bartusiak's acting career began at the tender age of 6, with her first major role in "The Cider House Rules" in 1999. She went on to appear in several films, including "Don't Say a Word" opposite Michael Douglas in 2001. Bartusiak also made a mark on television, featuring in popular shows such as "24," "Lost," and "House M.D."

In recent months, Bartusiak had been preparing to produce and direct her first feature film. Tragically, her boyfriend found her unresponsive in her garage apartment at their Houston home. Bartusiak's mother believes she may have suffered an epileptic seizure and choked, as the actress had been experiencing such seizures since infancy, although they had subsided for a few years until their recent return.

Bartusiak's mother spent Sunday morning reminiscing through photos of her daughter, which include images with Presidents George W. and George H.W. Bush, Mel Gibson, Dennis Hopper, and Michael Douglas. "The girl has lived such an amazing life," she said.

Johnny Strange, a renowned adventurer from Malibu, tragically passed away at the age of 23 following a wingsuit BASE jumping accident in the Swiss Alps on Thursday. Strange took off from Mt. Gitschen around noon, but crashed a few seconds later, according to Swiss police. The incident occurred amidst reports of strong winds on the mountain that day.

Strange had recently discussed his trip to Switzerland on KROQ-FM’s Kevin and Bean show, where he also filmed himself wingsuit flying. The video showcases Strange soaring through the sky, traversing over rocky peaks, and parachuting to break his fall. This was his last video posted on YouTube, and his last Instagram photo depicted him flying over a tree-topped mountainside with the caption, "Which tree should we bring home for Christmas?"

Gigi Hadid, a fellow Malibu High School alumnus, mourned Strange, describing him as having an adventurous spirit. Strange was known for his daredevil stunts, including wingsuit BASE jumping, a risky sport that involves leaping from mountains, ledges, and buildings while wearing a wingsuit to extend flight range and time.

The dangers of wingsuit BASE jumping were highlighted by the deaths of rock climbers Dean Potter and Graham Hunt, who leaped off Taft Point at Yosemite National Park in May and died with their parachutes failing to deploy. Potter had addressed the dangers in a blog post, expressing his concerns despite feeling safe during the activity.

Strange acknowledged the risks of wingsuit BASE jumping on his social media accounts and expressed condolences for fellow jumpers who had lost their lives. At 17, Strange became the youngest person to climb the "seven summits," the world's highest mountains in seven continents.

Donald Trump, a former presidential candidate, is set to moderate a Republican presidential debate hosted by Newsmax and airing on Ion Television on December 27 in Iowa. The debate, which will not be limited to a specific topic, is scheduled just a week before the Iowa caucuses. Trump's involvement is significant as he carries influence with the conservative base, particularly the Tea Party wing, due to his bombastic style and controversial statements. Newsmax, which has a broad reach into the conservative base, invited several candidates to the debate, but their responses are yet to be confirmed. Trump's role as a moderator is expected to be one of the more memorable moments in a primary season that has already been marked by unusual spectacle. Trump's influence and media presence, despite past flirtations with presidential campaigns that ultimately did not materialize, make him a powerful draw for news media attention.

In a significant development, Mexican President Enrique Peña Nieto has reiterated his refusal to fund the construction of a border wall with the United States, following Donald Trump's signing of executive orders that include plans for border barrier construction. Peña Nieto, who is scheduled to meet Trump on January 31, did not cancel the trip but left the decision open, causing confusion among many in Mexico.

Trump's executive order aims to build a wall along the nearly 2,000-mile US-Mexico border, with the cost estimated to range from $12 billion to $38 billion. Trump has famously stated that Mexico would pay for the wall, but Mexican officials have categorically rejected this claim, stating that it is "unacceptable."

The border wall is a significant part of Trump's campaign promises, and the executive order marks a step towards implementing this promise. However, the order leaves many questions unanswered, such as the exact type of wall to be built, the cost, and the payment method.

The likely effectiveness of the planned wall is fiercely disputed. Research shows that immigrants are more law-abiding than non-immigrants, and more Mexican immigrants have returned to Mexico from the US since the end of the 2007-08 financial crisis, according to the Pew Research Center.

Peña Nieto has consistently rejected Trump's suggestion that Mexico will pay for the border wall and promised to put Mexico first in any negotiations. However, analysts suggest that the president has few strong options in confronting an American administration considered the most hostile to Mexico since the Mexican-American war of the 1840s.

Peña Nieto's personal popularity ratings currently languish at 12%, the lowest in history. The president has encountered sustained criticism for failing to come up with a decisive strategy to deal with Trump's combative policies.

Trump's executive order to build a wall came on the same day that Mexico's foreign minister Luis Videgary and economy minister Ildefonso Guajardo met with senior Trump administration officials. The meeting was intended to discuss various issues, including the future of NAFTA, which facilitates more than $500bn annually in cross-border trade.

Mexican officials have expressed hopes of salvaging NAFTA, but Guajardo has stated that Mexico would consider walking away from the deal if necessary. Canadian officials have also mused about abandoning Mexico to forge a bilateral deal with the US, leaving Mexico's increasingly export-oriented economy in a bind.

In response to Trump's executive order, Vicente Fox, a former Mexican president, tweeted, "Mexico is not going to pay for that fucking wall." Trump's border wall bashing may backfire if the peso plunge forces poor migrants north, potentially exacerbating the situation.

Peña Nieto has promised to impose conditions on any negotiation with the US, including addressing issues such as smuggled guns streaming across the border, arming drug cartels, and Mexico’s efforts to detain and deport migrants who transit its territory in attempts to reach the US. However, the president is playing a weak hand, while his approval rating of just 12% is hampering his attempts at fomenting unity in a time of crisis.

Lady Gaga's album "Born This Way" debuted at No. 1 on the Billboard 200 chart with 1.11 million copies sold in its first week, marking the highest sales week since 2005. This is Gaga's first No. 1 album, surpassing her previous best, "The Fame," which peaked at No. 2. The album's impressive sales were partly attributed to a promotional offer by Amazon, which sold the album for 99 cents on two separate days, leading to an estimated 440,000 downloads. The last album to sell more copies in a week was 50 Cent's "The Massacre" in 2005. This is the 17th album to sell a million in a week since SoundScan began tracking sales data in 1991. Gaga is only the fifth woman to achieve a million-plus week, with Britney Spears' "Oops! I Did It Again" holding the record for the highest sales week for a woman. The album's digital downloads totaled 662,000, representing 60% of the set's overall first week sales, making it the biggest week for a digital album in SoundScan history.

The alleged mastermind behind the online drug marketplace known as Silk Road, Ross William Ulbricht, was arrested at the Glen Park library branch in San Francisco on Tuesday. Ulbricht, a 29-year-old Libertarian engineer, is accused of being "Dread Pirate Roberts," the anonymous mastermind behind Silk Road, which facilitated the sale of heroin, cocaine, and other drugs.

Ulbricht collected tens of millions of dollars in commissions, according to federal prosecutors, who also accused him of narcotics trafficking, money laundering, and attempting to murder a witness. The FBI said Ulbricht ran Silk Road from San Francisco, where he had been living for the past year.

The charges were the result of an investigation during which law-enforcement officials made more than 100 undercover purchases of drugs from Silk Road vendors from 10 countries. The site itself didn't sell drugs, but connected sellers with buyers, who would generally ship items through the mail.

Ulbricht has in the past railed against government control. After studying solar cells as a graduate student in Pennsylvania, he wrote on his LinkedIn profile that his goals had changed. "The most widespread and systemic use of force is amongst institutions and governments, so this is my current point of effort," he said. "I am creating an economic simulation to give people a first-hand experience of what it would be like to live in a world without the systemic use of force."

That simulation, the government alleged, is Silk Road. Federal authorities had seized the website by the time Ulbricht appeared Wednesday in U.S. District Court in San Francisco, where he was remanded into custody pending a hearing Friday. His attorney declined to comment.

Ulbricht allegedly sought to use violence to protect his domain. The Maryland grand jury indictment said a federal agent began communicating with Ulbricht in April 2012 while posing as a drug smuggler. Then in January, prosecutors said, Ulbricht paid the agent $80,000 to torture and kill a Silk Road employee who had stolen Bitcoins and had been arrested, prompting fears he would become a government witness.

In February, the agent sent staged photographs of the employee being tortured and a picture of the purported dead body, prosecutors said. Another try came in March, when Ulbricht offered $150,000 to a Silk Road user "to execute a murder-for-hire of another Silk Road user, who was threatening to release the identities of thousands of users of the site" unless he was given $500,000.

Ulbricht was again given a picture of the purportedly dead victim, a resident of British Columbia, but there were no reports of anyone having been killed there, the FBI said. "Your problem has been taken care of," the reported hit man wrote in a message to Ulbricht, authorities said.

Ulbricht "has acted as a law unto himself in deciding how to deal with problems affecting Silk Road, and that he has been willing to pursue violent means when he deems that the problem calls for it," Tarbell wrote.

Authorities said they identified Ulbricht by tracing his online activity. They said that in June he was living with a friend on Hickory Street in San Francisco's Hayes Valley, just 500 feet from an Internet cafe on Laguna Street "from which someone logged into a server used to administer the Silk Road website." By July, he had moved to 15th Street in San Francisco, where U.S. Department of Homeland Security agents visited him to see why a package for him that they had intercepted contained nine fake identification documents, all with his picture on it, authorities said.

Ulbricht refused to discuss the counterfeit papers, the affidavit said, but "volunteered that 'hypothetically' anyone could go onto a website named 'Silk Road' on 'Tor' and purchase any drugs or fake identity documents the person wanted."

The Silk Road site had many of the trappings of popular online retail sites, like user comments, which sought to ward off shady dealers and undercover cops. It featured wares like "amphetamine paste" and "high quality #4 heroin." One commenter wrote after making a purchase that he "had to snort almost triple the amount of this new stuff to get where I was with the old."

Over the past two years, Silk Road had been used by "several thousand drug dealers and other unlawful vendors" to sell "hundreds of kilograms" of illegal drugs, generating the Bitcoin equivalent of $1.2 billion in sales and $80 million in commissions, Tarbell wrote. At one point, Ulbricht hid behind the username "altoid" to marvel about Silk Road, describing it as an "anonymous Amazon.com."

Sen. Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., who in 2011 asked federal agents to take down the site after it began to get media attention, applauded the arrest. "Sayonara to Silk Road," Schumer said. "The country is safer now that this open market for lawbreaking has been shuttered."

The study, published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, analyzed body-worn camera footage from traffic stops in Oakland, California, to determine if police officers speak more respectfully to white community members than to black ones. The researchers developed computational linguistic methods to automatically measure the respect level of officers' language towards community members. The study found that officers spoke with less respect towards black community members, even after controlling for factors such as officer race, infraction severity, stop location, and stop outcome. The findings suggest that common, everyday interactions between police and the communities they serve have important implications for procedural justice and the building of police-community trust. The study also highlights the potential of body-worn camera footage as a rich source of data for studying and potentially improving police-community relations. The research was approved by the Stanford University Institutional Review Board and was conducted in collaboration with the Oakland Police Department.

The incident occurred on February 27, 1859, when United States Congressman Daniel Sickles shot and killed Philip Barton Key, U.S. attorney and son of the author of the "Star-Spangled Banner," in broad daylight near the White House. Sickles had received an anonymous letter detailing an affair between Key and his wife, Teresa, and upon investigating, he found evidence of their trysts. On the day of the murder, Sickles confronted Key and shot him three times. Sickles turned himself in and confessed to the crime, but he successfully pleaded temporary insanity as his defense, becoming the first American to do so.

The trial was highly publicized, with Sickles gaining support from President James Buchanan and many members of Congress. The court of public opinion also sided with Sickles, viewing the murder as justifiable given the immorality of Key's actions. The jury found Sickles not guilty, and he was hailed as a hero by some.

However, Sickles's life was marked by controversy and scandal. He was known for his womanizing and was eventually ostracized by society. His successful insanity plea lived on, earning the nicknames "Twinkie defense" and "abuse excuse." In 1984, the Insanity Defense Reform Act was passed in response to the John Hinckley Jr. case, shifting the burden of proof from the prosecution to the defense.

Daniel Sickles finished his last term in Congress in 1860 and went on to serve as a brigadier general and major general during the Civil War. He was later appointed ambassador to Spain and allegedly became the deposed Queen of Spain's paramour. Sickles's life was marked by audacious beginnings, willful behavior, and a penchant for grand gestures. He was a rogue who rose through the political machine at Tammany Hall and was known for his good looks, dashing manner, and ability to win over men and women. However, his compulsive womanizing ultimately led to his downfall.

The National Liberation Front of Corsica (FLNC), a separatist group that has been seeking independence for the island since 1976, has announced an end to its 40-year armed struggle against France. The group, known for bombings, robberies, and assaults, stated that it has started the process of demilitarization and will focus on conventional political channels to further its ambitions.

The decision comes after several recent advances via conventional means, such as a bill limiting land and property purchases to long-term residents, aimed at curbing real estate inflation on the island. The FLNC believes these measures trace the outlines of a political solution and mark a shift from combat and resistance to the construction of a true Corsican political power.

This development follows a similar move by Eta, the Basque separatist organization in Spain, which agreed to decommission weapons in February. The FLNC's communiqué, confirmed as authentic by a local journalist, stated that the group comprises over 100 members and still enjoys support among many of Corsica's 320,000 residents.

Corsica, the birthplace of Napoleon Bonaparte, has been under French control since the 1700s and is a popular tourist destination today. The FLNC's decision signals a significant shift in the long-standing conflict on the island, with thousands of attacks carried out in Corsica and the French mainland since the separatist movement was founded.

Twin sisters, aged 29, from Australia, made a suicide pact and shot each other at a gun range in Colorado. One sister died, and the other is in stable condition. The incident occurred at the Family Shooting Center inside Cherry Creek State Park. The sisters were on cultural visas and had traveled to the US and Canada frequently. The exact motive behind the suicide pact remains unknown, and the surviving sister has not revealed any details during an emotional interview with investigators. The Sheriff's Department is withholding the names of the sisters until U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement confirms the identity of the deceased. This incident marks at least the seventh suicide involving rented guns at US shooting ranges this year, and the third at the Family Shooting Center since 2004.

Adele's highly anticipated album, '21', was released yesterday, revealing a heartbroken Adele following a painful breakup. The album, which serves as a form of "cheap therapy" for the singer, is a collection of deeply personal songs inspired by her past relationship. Adele's soulful performance in tracks like 'Someone Like You' and 'Rolling in the Deep' showcases her raw emotion and candidness, making her talent stand out without the need for bells and whistles. The album is a testament to Adele's resilience and ability to turn personal heartache into powerful music.

In addition, Adele discusses her newfound inspiration in American musical traditions such as country and bluegrass, hinting at future explorations in these genres. The album has been well-received, with fans praising Adele for her vulnerability and emotional depth. The album, while a product of heartbreak, offers hope to fans going through similar experiences.

Kim Cattrall, known for her role as Samantha Jones in Sex and the City, has publicly stated that she is not friends with her co-stars Sarah Jessica Parker, Kristin Davis, and Cynthia Nixon. In an interview with Piers Morgan, Cattrall claimed that they have always maintained a professional relationship and that there is a clear line between their personal and professional lives.

Recent speculation about a third Sex and the City film was halted due to Cattrall's alleged "outrageous demands," a claim that Cattrall has vehemently denied. She asserted that she never asked for any money or projects and finds the label of a diva to be absurd.

Sources have suggested that Cattrall's demands, including the studio buying her films in development and giving her a TV deal, were the reasons for the cancellation of the film less than a week before shooting was scheduled to begin.

During the interview, Cattrall also discussed her decision not to have children, citing her busy schedule on Sex and the City as the primary reason. She expressed a sense of maternal instinct but ultimately chose to mentor young actresses instead.

Cattrall has blamed Sarah Jessica Parker for the negative press she has received, stating that Parker could have been nicer. However, she also expressed disappointment with the other cast members for not reaching out to her. Cattrall described the relationship as "toxic."

The potential for a third Sex and the City film, which fans had been eagerly anticipating, has now officially been declared "over" by Sarah Jessica Parker. The full interview with Cattrall will air in the UK on Monday night.

LulzSec, a notorious hacker group known for its high-profile cyber attacks, has announced its retirement after a 50-day spree of hacking corporate and government targets. In its final release, LulzSec dumped a vast amount of data including technical documents from AOL and AT&T, account details for over 550,000 users of Battlefield Heroes, user details for Hackforums.net and NATO online bookshop, evidence of hacking the US Navy website, IP numbers of internal corporate networks, email login details for private investigators, and "silly routers" with passwords set to 'root' or 'admin'. The group's statement suggests a planned 50-day cruise, but it's unclear if this was the plan all along or if the group is retreating due to potential backlash from law enforcement. LulzSec's final release can be found at http://thepiratebay.org/torrent/6495523/50_Days_of_Lulz.

Senator Rand Paul of Kentucky is seeking legislation to allow him to run for both the U.S. Senate and the presidency in 2016, aiming to hedge his political bets. The current state law prohibits a candidate's name from appearing on a ballot more than once, which would typically force a candidate to choose between the two offices. However, Senate Majority Leader Damon Thayer is working on clarifying this law, believing it to be unconstitutional if interpreted to bar simultaneous Senate and presidential candidacy.

If successful, Paul could potentially win the GOP presidential nomination and run in the general election for the presidency and Senate re-election. If he wins both, he would relinquish his Senate seat. Alternatively, if he loses the presidential election but wins the Senate re-election, he would serve a second term as a U.S. senator from Kentucky.

Since his election in 2010, Paul has advocated for term limits in Congress, allowing members to serve a maximum of 12 years in each chamber. His fellow Kentucky Republican, Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell, faces a challenge from the political right in his own party, and if he loses, Paul would become the senior U.S. senator from Kentucky and likely the recognized leader of his party in the state.

The bill's passage is not guaranteed, as a veteran Republican Party operative in Kentucky has reportedly stated that the Democratic-controlled House of Representatives would not allow it to pass. The bill's filing window expires this Wednesday. Paul has not officially announced his intention to seek higher office.

A Tennessee high school student, Emily Gipson, posted an anti-bullying video on YouTube, titled "Welcome to Lebanon High School," which has garnered nearly 600,000 views. The video, inspired by a classmate's suicide in October, criticizes the school's culture and administration's response to bullying. Gipson was given a two-day in-school suspension for the video, with school administrators citing a lack of permission to record the video in a classroom as the reason for her punishment. However, Gipson disputes this claim, stating that she had two coaches' permission.

In the video, Gipson criticizes her peers' reaction to the Stop It app the school had put out in response to the death, and she also targets the school administration for not addressing bullying effectively. She questions the school's culture, stating that creativity is discouraged, and bullies are not punished. Gipson's grandfather and guardian, Kenneth Gipson, expressed pride in his granddaughter for expressing herself and bringing attention to a sensitive and needed subject.

The school's principal, Scott Walters, said he took issue with the video being recorded in a classroom without a teacher's permission and that it hurt his and teachers' feelings. However, he also acknowledged that he can appreciate the perspective of the video and that people could learn from Gipson's viewpoint. Walters has received feedback from parents and students who didn't agree with the video, but he also said people could learn from Gipson's viewpoint.

Following her suspension, Gipson posted another spoken-word poem on YouTube, titled "Have I Made a Difference Yet?" urging teenagers like her to speak up against bullying. Gipson believes that the video has brought attention to a national problem and that bullying is an issue in today's schools. The school has not commented on the video's message or its impact on the school community.

The article discusses the disparity in workers' compensation benefits for identical injuries between different states in the US. The story focuses on two men, Jeremy Lewis and Josh Potter, who both lost their left arms in industrial accidents, but received vastly different compensation due to the state they lived in.

Lewis, who lived and worked in Alabama, received only $45,000 in workers' compensation, while Potter, who lived and worked in Georgia, was awarded benefits that could surpass $740,000 over his lifetime. The reason for this disparity is that Alabama has the nation's lowest workers' comp benefits for amputations, while Georgia is far more generous.

The article goes on to explain that the amount of compensation workers receive for traumatic injuries varies dramatically from state to state, with some states even putting a value on the loss of a testicle. The benefits are determined by a "schedule of benefits" that divides up the body like an Angus beef chart, with workers awarded a portion of their wages up to the state maximum for the specified number of weeks assigned to each body part.

The article also highlights the impact of these benefits on the lives of injured workers. Lewis, for example, lost his house, three brand new vehicles, and was left with only $33,500 after attorney's fees and costs, while Potter has been able to maintain some semblance of his former life with the $285 a week he receives in benefits.

The article concludes by noting that the amounts of compensation are often the result of political expediency, sometimes based on bargains struck decades ago. The rollback in protections for injured workers nationwide has forced injured workers' families and taxpayers to subsidize the lost income and medical care costs generated by these conditions.

Overall, the article highlights the need for a more uniform and fair workers' compensation system across the US, as the current system leaves injured workers in vastly different situations depending on the state they live in.

In this summary, we will discuss two separate issues related to Wells Fargo: the bank's plan to offer premium checking accounts for Latino immigrants and a series of complaints from customers and employees regarding the bank's sales practices.

Firstly, Wells Fargo announced a new initiative to provide premium checking accounts for Latino immigrants, allowing them to send money across the border at no charge. The accounts could be opened with a minimum deposit of $50, but customers were expected to have at least $25,000 on deposit within three months or face a $30 monthly charge.

Secondly, Siham El-Dahan, a former Wells Fargo employee, claimed that she was fired in retaliation for speaking out about her managers' alleged mistreatment of employees. El-Dahan stated that her managers played favorites, denied required breaks, and regularly threatened employees about meeting sales quotas. In response, employees reportedly opened bogus accounts for customers who did not want them. When El-Dahan asked to be transferred to another branch, she was referred back to her managers. She believes she was fired due to her complaints, as the stated reason was a customer she signed up for a loan defaulting.

Additionally, Frank Ahn, a convenience store owner, reported problems with unwanted accounts being opened in his name despite his repeated protests. The issues started four years ago, with the opening of two accounts, followed by persistent attempts by bank employees to open more accounts he didn't need. Despite numerous phone calls and branch visits, Ahn was unable to have all the improper fees reversed or the accounts canceled, leading to a total of ten accounts. Ahn felt that the ordeal made him less productive and expressed sympathy for immigrants who might not have the English skills to handle such issues.

Wells Fargo declined to comment on both El-Dahan's and Ahn's stories. This summary highlights concerns about the bank's sales practices and the impact on both employees and customers.

Saddam Hussain, a marine engineer from Jamshedpur in Jharkhand, is struggling to find employment due to his namesake, the former Iraqi dictator Saddam Hussein. After graduating from Tamil Nadu's Noorul Islam University in 2014, Saddam has been rejected by multinational shipping companies 40 times, despite ranking second in his batch. The reason for the rejections is the fear of complications from encounters with immigration officials across international borders due to his name.

Saddam initially tried to change his name to Sajid and obtained new documents, but his woes did not end there. Prospective employers ask for his educational certificates, but his university has refused to change the name until he gets his Class 10 and 12 exam certificates changed first. Saddam approached the Central Board of Secondary Education (CBSE) for a name change, but the authorities have not acted yet.

Driven to desperation, Saddam moved the Jharkhand high court with a plea to direct the CBSE to change his name. The court has set a hearing date for May 5. Saddam remains fond of his grandfather, who gave him the name, but feels he is paying for his folly.

The issue of a namesake causing problems is not unique to Saddam. In Iraq, many Saddam Husseins have faced similar issues, with some being fired from their jobs, captured by militias, or subjected to verbal abuse. The name Saddam Hussein, once a symbol of power and authority, has become a burden for many.

The story was first published on March 21, 2017, and it highlights the challenges faced by individuals with names that are associated with controversial figures. The case of Saddam Hussain serves as a reminder of the impact that a name can have on an individual's life and career.

The article discusses Emmis Digital's unique approach to hiring interns, which involved a social media competition dubbed the "Intern Games." Over 25 college students applied for a single unpaid internship position at Emmis Digital's River North office. The top 10 candidates were interviewed, and the field was narrowed down to three finalists: Kelsey Halverson, Jake Bouvy, and Katie.

Each finalist was tasked with driving social media engagement by encouraging their friends, family, and followers to follow Emmis Digital pages and create videos explaining why they were the best candidate. For two weeks, the three finalists competed under the hashtags #TeamJake, #TeamKelsey, and #TeamKatie.

Jake Bouvy, a marketing major at Indiana University, and Kelsey Halverson, a journalism major at Iowa State, emerged as the top contenders. Bouvy's slick video to a hip-hop beat showcasing his technical skills and social media success promoted indie music videos online, while Halverson's social media efforts drove more traffic and Facebook "likes" for Emmis.

In the end, both Bouvy and Halverson were declared winners of the social media contest and offered unpaid internships. Emmis Digital's Katlyn Hayes, who created the Intern Games, explained that the decision was made due to the candidates' complementary skills, creating what she called "a super intern."

The article also discusses the growing trend of employers using social media to engage with potential employees before they even ask them to fill out an application. National Public Radio (NPR) has created hiring managers out of all its employees, allowing prospective hires a better understanding of the company culture. NPR has also created a dedicated Twitter handle, @NPRjobs, which has become one of their top sources of hiring.

The article concludes by emphasizing that in the social media age, employers are no longer just looking for words on a piece of paper, but rather the best talent in 140 characters or less. The choice between using blue or black ink on an application has been replaced by the choice of six- or 15-second video platforms. Internships remain competitive, but the article suggests that the best candidates are those who can effectively showcase their skills through social media.

The Malaysian Airlines Flight 370, a Boeing 777, disappeared without a trace three days ago while en route from Kuala Lumpur to Beijing. The plane vanished somewhere between Malaysia and Vietnam, and search efforts involving 10 countries have been ongoing, but with no success so far.

Two men, who apparently boarded the plane with stolen passports, have become a focus for investigators. Their identities and reasons for being on the flight are yet to be revealed. The FBI is running their thumbprints through a database after receiving them from Malaysian officials. The use of stolen passports follows a pattern similar to human smuggling rings, but it's unclear if it's related to the plane's disappearance.

The search area has grown significantly, now covering hundreds of miles in the Gulf of Thailand. Investigators are weighing various possibilities, including terrorism, but haven't ruled anything out. Family members of passengers are being told to prepare for the worst, but some are holding onto hope due to the lack of answers.

The stolen passports add to the mystery, as they were reported stolen in Thailand and are listed in INTERPOL's databases. Thai authorities are investigating the passport thefts. The true identities of the men who used the stolen passports are yet to be confirmed, and there are concerns about the possibility of terrorism.

Search and rescue officials are expanding the search area and are investigating a report of debris found south of Hong Kong, but it's unlikely to be confirmed until Tuesday. The lack of any emergency signal and the growing search area make the search more challenging. Underwater search experts have warned that crucial time is passing as the search continues.

In a historic first, Chicago experienced no snow on the ground in January and February, a record that has raised concerns about climate change. The National Weather Service recorded this milestone at O'Hare International Airport, although small amounts of snow that melted later in the day were not included. The weather service has been keeping data on snow on the ground for 146 years.

The record near-snowless start was overshadowed by severe storms moving through the state on Tuesday, with forecasts of large hail, winds, localized flooding, and tornadoes. A tornado hit Ottowa on Tuesday evening, resulting in one fatality. More stormy weather is expected for the week, including possible snow.

Warm weather has been beneficial for many, with lower heating bills, fewer weather-related accidents, increased shopping, and additional construction. However, it has also posed risks for fruit growers, trees, insects, and migrating bird species.

Chicago's least amount of snow in a January was in 1928 with 0.2 inches. This January had 0.5 inches. This February is tied for the least amount of snow with 1987 and 1998, with all of them having just a trace of snow. Some experts predicted another "snowpocalypse" this winter, but warmer-than-average temperatures were predicted due to the warm summer and autumn in 2016.

The record-breaking temperatures have drawn Chicagoans outdoors, and the city experienced its first significant snowfall since Stella on March 14, with 7.7 inches of snow. This March snow event is on par with the heaviest of the season in Chicago, which was 7.8 inches Dec. 10-11.

In this summary, Queen Elizabeth II delivered her annual pre-recorded Christmas message to the nation, emphasizing the importance of family and friendship. The message was recorded on December 9, before Prince Philip was hospitalized for a heart procedure. The royal family, minus Prince Philip, celebrated Christmas at St. Mary Magdalene Church on the Queen's Sandringham estate in Norfolk. Notable attendees included Prince William, Kate Middleton, Prince Harry, Prince Charles, and Camilla, Duchess of Cornwall, among others. The Queen's granddaughter, Zara Phillips, and her husband, Mike Tindall, were also present. After the service, children presented the Queen with bouquets of flowers, and she handed them to her granddaughters, Princesses Beatrice and Eugenie. The Queen's Christmas message, focusing on family and community, will be broadcast later. Prince Philip is recovering in the hospital and is expected to receive visits from family members after lunch.

In a daring heist, thieves have stolen 300 bottles of fine wines worth €250,000 (£230,500) from a private cellar in a fashionable Paris neighborhood near the Luxembourg gardens and the French Senate. The thieves reportedly used a secret pathway in the Paris Catacombs, a vast underground tunnel network, to access the cellar. This network, which stretches for several miles beneath the city, houses approximately six million human remains.

The Catacombs were once mines but were converted into ossuaries in the late 18th century to address the overflow of bodies in Paris's cemeteries. The Catacombs are known for their confusing structure, lack of light, and the presence of skulls and rib cages along the walls. While only a tiny fraction of the Catacombs is accessible to tourists, many Parisians, known as 'Cataphiles,' like to explore the restricted areas at night.

The theft is believed to be the work of well-informed thieves who likely conducted extensive research and planning to navigate the Catacombs and drill a hole through the cellar wall. The Paris police are investigating the case, and the thieves remain at large. This incident highlights the allure and danger of the Paris Catacombs, a unique and intriguing part of the city's history.

In Pittsfield, Massachusetts, two men, Joseph E. Van Wert and Randy W. Lambach, are facing charges for allegedly running a citywide prostitution ring involving multiple women, some of whom may have been as young as 15. The investigation began in the spring of 2017 after an increase in prostitution complaints. Most of the activity was centered around specific streets, and many of the women were recruited by a man named "Randy." Randy would photograph the women and post advertisements online seeking clients for sexual services.

Lambach, who is believed to have run the prostitution ring for several years, would set up meetings and rates with prospective clients. He would transport the women to and from specific locations and collect a significant portion of their earnings, sometimes paying them in drugs instead of cash. Some of the women he recruited were formerly his foster children.

Van Wert allowed some of the meetings to take place in his third-floor apartment at a senior living facility in exchange for drugs and cash. Police arrested Van Wert and Lambach last week, and both have pleaded not guilty to their charges. The investigation is ongoing, and additional charges may be coming. The Pittsfield Police Department, along with several other law enforcement agencies, are assisting with the investigation.

The woman accused of killing her twin sister by driving their SUV off a cliff in Hawaii, Alexandria Duval, is fighting her extradition from New York to face a murder charge. Duval was arrested in Albany, NY, after being tracked down by authorities. The sisters were involved in a fatal crash in May, where their vehicle plunged off a cliff in Hawaii. The sisters were embroiled in a fight over the steering wheel at the time of the accident. Duval's attorney described the crash as a tragic accident, but authorities believe it was deliberate. Duval was initially arrested and jailed in Hawaii, but was later released due to lack of probable cause. However, a grand jury in Hawaii indicted her on a second-degree murder charge in late October, and a warrant was issued for her arrest. Duval is currently being held in a New York jail and is scheduled for an extradition hearing on December 16. The case made national headlines, and Duval's attorney has stated that she will not waive her right to an extradition hearing. The twins were originally from the Utica area.

A 21-year-old Army National Guard combat medic, Semantha Bunce, was seriously injured in a shootout at her east Charlotte home on Tuesday. The incident occurred when intruders broke into her home, and Bunce exchanged gunfire with them, sustaining multiple gunshot wounds. Her baby was unharmed during the incident. Reco Latur Dawkins Jr., a 23-year-old man, has been charged with attempted murder, felony breaking and entering, and conspiracy in connection with the shooting. Dawkins turned himself in to the Charlotte-Mecklenburg police's violent criminal apprehension team on Sunday morning.

Bunce is a member of the U.S. Army's 105th Engineer Battalion, based in Raeford. Her husband, Paul Bunce III, believes that her training as a combat medic helped her stay mentally focused and calm during the shooting. The case has made national headlines, and a Go Fund Me site has been established to help pay for Bunce's utility bills, child care, travel expenses, home repairs, medical bills, and missed wages. Paul Bunce's employer, MAA, has also established a fund on YouCaring to support the family.

Dawkins has a criminal history dating back to his teenage years, with several charges of breaking and entering on his record. He was convicted of breaking and entering in 2010 and sentenced to three years of probation. The police are still investigating the incident and have not confirmed whether they are looking for any other suspects in connection with the shooting.

Neighbors reported hearing gunshots and described the incident as a shocking event. The community has come together to support the family, with some neighbors taking turns driving around the neighborhood to keep an eye out for any suspicious activity. The police have not released a description of the shooters, and the investigation is still ongoing.

A tragic incident occurred in Cincinnati on Tuesday morning when a father, mistaking his 14-year-old son for an intruder, fatally shot him in the neck at their home in the 1200 block of Blanchard Ave, East Price Hill. The father, whose name has not been disclosed, had dropped his son, Georta Mack, off at school but the boy returned home. After hearing a noise in the basement, the father, who had a gun, was startled by the son and accidentally shot him. The father called 911 and the boy was taken to Cincinnati Children's Hospital Medical Center, where he was pronounced dead shortly after 8:15 a.m. Neighbors expressed their shock and grief, describing Georta as a good kid who often helped with yard work. Police are investigating the incident and interviewing the father, who has been cooperative. Cincinnati Police Chief Eliot Isaac called the shooting a "terrible, terrible tragedy" and emphasized the importance of gun responsibility and awareness in the home. The case is being discussed with the Hamilton County Prosecutor's office, but it is unknown if the father will be charged.

In the aftermath of the Baltimore riots, a video went viral showing a mother, Toya Graham, confronting her son who was participating in the protests. Graham, a single mother of six, was seen repeatedly smacking her son and shouting at him, expressing her concern that he could end up like Freddie Gray, a 25-year-old man who died mysteriously in police custody, sparking the protests.

Graham told CBS News that she launched into action after spotting her 16-year-old son Michael amid the protesters, wearing a hoodie and mask. She said her son knew he was in trouble and even considered running, but Graham's stern approach made him wince.

Graham denounced the vandalism and violence against police officers, stating that rioting was not the way to seek justice for Freddie Gray. She hopes the incident will serve as a teachable moment for her son, and she believes more mothers monitoring their sons could have prevented some of the violence.

Commissioner Anthony Batts of the Baltimore Police Department praised Graham's actions, stating that he wished more parents took charge of their children during such incidents. The riots resulted in at least 20 police officers being injured, one person being critically hurt in a fire, and 235 arrests, including 34 juveniles. The streets were calmer on Tuesday with a 10 p.m. to 5 a.m. curfew in effect and the National Guard deployed.

British Prime Minister Theresa May survived a no-confidence vote from her Conservative party on Wednesday, but more than a third of her lawmakers said she was no longer the right leader to implement Britain's exit from the European Union. The vote came after May cancelled a parliamentary vote on her Brexit deal, designed to maintain close future ties with the bloc, after it became clear she would lose it badly. Eurosceptic critics of the deal within her own party triggered the no-confidence vote in her leadership. After two hours of voting, Graham Brady, chairman of the 1922 Committee of Conservative backbenchers, said 200 Conservative lawmakers had voted in support of May as leader, and 117 against, indicating her party was bitterly divided over the direction of Brexit. Supporters said the result showed the party should now get behind her. But hardline Brexit supporters who triggered the vote because they saw her deal as a betrayal of the 2016 referendum said she should now quit. The outcome will shape Britain's $2.8 trillion economy, have far-reaching consequences for the unity of the kingdom and determine whether London keeps its place as one of the top two global financial centres. The Brexit deal, which was struck after two years of negotiations, has been plunged into crisis by parliamentary opposition to the divorce deal, opening up possibilities including a delay to Brexit or even another referendum on membership.

The Mo Ibrahim Prize for African Leadership, a prestigious $5 million award for good governance, has not been awarded this year as no candidate met all the criteria. The prize, which includes a $200,000 annual stipend for life, is given to democratically elected leaders who have governed well, raised living standards, and voluntarily left office. Last year's winner was Cape Verde President Pedro Verona Pires, who was recognized for his fight against Portuguese colonialism, introduction of multi-party politics, and improvement of living standards.

The prize was established in 2007 by Sudan-born telecoms entrepreneur Mo Ibrahim to encourage good governance in Africa. Ibrahim emphasized that the prize is not given out for positive messages but for exceptional leadership. The two other winners since the prize's inception were Botswana's President Festus Mogae and Mozambique's Joaquim Chissano.

In a separate development, the Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences was awarded to two American economists, Alvin Roth and Lloyd Shapley, for their research into market design. Their work focuses on how to fairly and efficiently match people with things, such as employers, schools, or donated kidneys. Their research led to systems used by various organizations, including school districts in New York City and Boston, hospitals for organ matching, and a program for assigning medical-school graduates to hospitals for residency programs.

The Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences was established in 1968 by the Swedish central bank in Alfred Nobel's memory and has been handed out with the other Nobel prizes since then. Each award is worth 8 million Swedish kronor, or about $1.2 million.

The estranged wife of acclaimed concert pianist Vadym Kholodenko, Sofya Tsygankova, has been ruled mentally incompetent to stand trial for allegedly killing the couple's two young daughters. Tsygankova, who is 32 and charged with two counts of capital murder of a person under age 10, will be committed to a state mental health facility for 120 days of treatment. The hope is that she will regain a reasonable degree of rational understanding and be able to face justice upon her release.

Tsygankova has pleaded not guilty to charges of killing daughters Nika, 5, and Michaela, 1, at their Benbrook, Texas home. The incident occurred on March 17, when Kholodenko arrived at his wife's home to pick up the girls for preschool and found Tsyganova covered in blood with cuts on her wrists and the two children dead in their beds.

Kholodenko, a Ukrainian musician who won the gold medal at the 14th Van Cliburn International Piano Competition in 2013, resumed playing concerts a month after his daughters were killed. He expressed his grief and asked for support from his fans.

Investigations revealed that Tsygankova had visited a state mental health facility a day before the children's bodies were found. Inside the home, police found an empty prescription bottle of quetiapine, an antipsychotic drug used to treat mental illnesses such as bipolar disorder and schizophrenia.

Steve Weidner, a school janitor at Alan Shephard Elementary School in Bourbonnais, IL, received an unexpected display of admiration from students on June 2. For over 15 years, Weidner, affectionately known as "Mr. Steve," has been a beloved figure at the school, known for his care and concern for the students.

While students were signing each other's yearbooks on the playground, they formed a line to get Weidner's signature. The line was so long that it wound around the playground, with so many students wanting his autograph that a chair was provided for him. The school reported that Weidner was touched and amazed by the show of affection from the students.

The heartwarming moment was shared on Reddit, where it quickly gained popularity, amassing thousands of upvotes and comments. Although the associated WARC files from the crawl are not currently available to the general public, the event highlights the strong bond between Weidner and the students at Alan Shephard Elementary School.

The University of Texas at Austin has released a comprehensive report on training campus police to handle sexual assault cases more effectively. The report, titled "Blueprint for Campus Police," was drafted by UT Austin's Institute on Domestic Violence and Sexual Assault and will be incorporated into training for over 600 officers across all eight of the university's academic institutions.

The report offers specific guidelines for officers from the moment they first interact with victims, emphasizing empathy and understanding that victims of sexual assault often behave differently than victims of other crimes due to trauma. The training is especially necessary because of the prevalence of sexual assault, with one study finding that more than 18% of female undergraduates at UT Austin had been sexually assaulted since arriving on campus.

The report addresses common rape myths and concepts such as victim blaming, encouraging officers to adopt policies that are "victim-centered, science-based, and trauma-informed." It also acknowledges that trauma victims often omit, exaggerate, or make up information when trying to make sense of what happened to them or to fill gaps in memory.

The report comes as the university is facing a lawsuit from a male student who is seeking to stop his expulsion over allegations of sexual assault. The student, who is one semester away from earning a degree in physics, denies the allegations and claims he has not been afforded his Constitutional due process rights.

The lawsuit alleges that the student met two girls at a house party near campus, went to one of their apartments, and had consensual sex with one of them. However, the alleged victim later claimed she was unconscious during the sex and was upset her friend had left her alone in her apartment with the student.

The university launched a Title IX investigation into the events, despite the alleged victim not being a student at the university. The student told campus Title IX officials he believed he had consent from the victim because "she was talking dirty, she was enjoying it." However, the campus Title IX investigators found that the student had sexually assaulted another student and recommended his expulsion.

The student's attorney argues that there was gender bias by investigators against the student in violation of Title IX, and that the hearing he has been afforded has such strict rules on presenting evidence that it hampers his due process rights under state law. The lawsuit also claims that the university's "definition and application of the term 'consent' in the context of sexual assault disciplinary actions is so broad that the University may expel a student without proving that there were any objective indicators of non-consent from the alleged victim."

The report on training campus police to handle sexual assault cases is intended to address the unique challenges of investigating sexual assault and to ensure that victims are treated with empathy and respect. However, the lawsuit against the university highlights the ongoing challenges of ensuring due process for students who are accused of sexual assault.

A growing number of former NFL players, including Jamal Anderson, Chris Doleman, and O.J. Santiago, have joined over 1,500 others in suing the NFL, alleging that the league hid the dangers of concussions. The lawsuit, filed in Atlanta, asserts that the NFL failed to take necessary steps to protect players from head injuries and misled players about the risks associated with concussions. The NFL has denied these allegations, stating that player safety is a priority. The lawsuit cites recent scientific studies linking concussions to chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), a neurodegenerative disease causing Alzheimer's-like symptoms. Former Green Bay Packer Dorsey Levens, who filed a similar suit in 2011, stated that players were unaware of the long-term ramifications of concussions during his playing days. The Boston University's Center for Traumatic Encephalopathy is attempting to examine the brain of Junior Seau, who died by suicide, to determine if he suffered from CTE. If Seau is found to have CTE, it could significantly impact the perception of football and its impact on players.

In this summary, a 21-year-old woman named Alexandra Nicole Laird from Pleasant Grove, Alabama, has been indicted for endangering her newborn baby girl, who was born addicted to heroin and spent a month in an Intensive Care Unit due to withdrawals. Laird admitted to using heroin one to two times a week during her pregnancy. She has been free on bond since her initial arrest in May 2015 but is now back in jail due to a new child endangerment charge, as she is pregnant again.

The grand jury indicted Laird on April 15, 2015, and she faces a Class B felony for chemical endangerment of a child. Laird's first child is not in her custody, and Pleasant Grove police Lt. Danny Reid expressed concern about the potential long-term effects on the child. Laird also faces an unrelated drug possession charge from a traffic stop less than two months after her daughter's birth.

In a separate development, President Barack Obama signed a law aimed at protecting drug-dependent newborns and assisting their parents. The Comprehensive Addiction and Recovery Act emphasizes drug treatment and overdose prevention to combat the nation's heroin and opioid drug epidemic. However, Obama expressed disappointment that the legislation did not provide sufficient resources for addiction treatment.

The law requires states to follow a 2003 law that was often ignored, calling for hospitals and social services to report, track, and assist drug-dependent newborns and their families. Reuters found that only nine states were following this requirement, and many drug-dependent babies were not being reported as required by law. The law promises a non-punitive approach, including "safe care plans" aimed at keeping newborns at home with their parents, who will receive additional help.

Laird's case underscores the need for such legislation, as her actions have put her children at risk. The new law is a step forward in addressing the nation's opioid epidemic and providing support for vulnerable families. However, more funding is needed to fully address the issue.

India's top court has declared adultery as unconstitutional and struck down a 158-year-old colonial-era law that treated women as male property. The law made it a crime for a man to have a sexual relationship with a married woman without her husband's consent. The court ruled that the law was archaic, arbitrary, and discriminatory against women, depriving them of agency.

The case was brought by an Indian businessman living in Italy who challenged the law, arguing that it discriminated against men and women and treated women like objects. The government opposed the petition, insisting that adultery should remain a criminal offense to uphold the sanctity of marriages.

The court's decision is one of several socially progressive rulings this session, including the decriminalization of homosexuality and a case about whether women in their menstruating years can be restricted from entering Kerala state's Sabarimala temple.

Critics have called the law "staggeringly sexist," "'crudely anti-woman," and "'violative of the right to equality." Some have argued that the law should have been made gender-neutral instead of being struck down. The ruling has been welcomed by women's rights activists, who say it is a step towards gender equality in India.

Adultery is considered illegal in 21 American states, as well as in Islamic countries such as Iran, Saudi Arabia, Afghanistan, Pakistan, Bangladesh, and Somalia. Taiwan and Indonesia also punish adultery with prison sentences. However, in the UK, adultery is not a criminal offense and is one of the main reasons given for divorce.

The succession of high-profile cases provides a notable send-off for Chief Justice Dipak Misra, who has been the subject of public complaints from his fellow judges over his handling of politically sensitive cases. The Delhi high court is currently examining another law that makes an exception for sexual assault if the perpetrator and victim are married. The government and several men's rights groups have filed petitions against scrapping the marriage exception.

Karuna Nundy, a supreme court lawyer leading the case to overturn the marital rape law, said Thursday's judgment bolstered her argument. "Both laws based on the doctrine of a man owning his wife, the wife being property," she said. Nundy said the court had shown in recent judgments that it now believed "sexually autonomy is not forfeited at the marital door."
