Like the decision to legalize homosexual acts, some advocates against the adultery law characterized Thursday's decision as an act of decolonizing the country's Raj-era criminal code. Rekha Sharma, the head of India's National Commission for Women, said, "It was an outdated law, which should have been removed long back. This is a law from British era. Although the British had done away with it long back, we were still stuck with it."

The court has been more willing to affirm British-era legislation when it comes to restricting speech, in recent years endorsing imperial laws against criminal defamation and creating (but later dropping) a rule that Indians must stand while the national anthem is played in movie theatres. Gautam Bhatia, a Delhi-based lawyer and legal scholar, said, "I wouldn't yet call it a progressive era in the court. He said in cases such as the adultery or homosexuality rulings, the court was dispensing with laws that had clearly fallen behind social mores. "These are the low-hanging fruit," he said.

Thursday's decision was decried by some prominent feminists, including Swati Maliwal, Delhi's commissioner for women. She said the adultery law should have become gender-neutral because it could be a deterrent against men abandoning their families, in a society where women wield little power, especially in poorer or deeply patriarchal areas of the country. "Thousands of women approach the commission, many from disadvantaged backgrounds, saying their husbands are acting in an adulterous manner and have left them without support to look after the children," Maliwal said. "At least with this law a woman can get a sense of justice, and the men have a kind of fear that when they enter a relationship, it has some sanctity that they have to live with."

Lawyers for the central government had opposed scrapping the adultery law, arguing that diluting sanctions against infidelity would "result in laxity of the marital bonds." The law had survived three previous legal challenges, the most recent in 1988. The succession of high-profile cases provides a notable send-off for Misra, an at times controversial chief justice who has been the subject of public complaints from his fellow judges over his handling of politically sensitive cases.

The Nettleton School District in Mississippi has announced it will no longer use race in school elections, following an outcry over a policy that alternated class officer positions between white and black students. The policy, in place for 30 years, was intended to ensure minority representation, but has been criticized for promoting racial segregation and excluding students of mixed race. Brandy Springer, a mother of four mixed-race children, was shocked when she learned her daughter couldn't run for class reporter because she wasn't the right race. The school district acknowledged the outdated nature of the policy, stating that it "acknowledges and embraces the fact that we are growing in ethnic diversity and that the classifications of Caucasian and African-American no longer reflect our entire student body." Springer's plight sparked a call for a Justice Department investigation by the NAACP and widespread criticism online. The school district has since reversed its policy.

President Donald Trump announced on May 8, 2018, that the United States is withdrawing from the Iran nuclear deal, a landmark pact signed in 2015. The deal aimed to halt Iran's pursuit of nuclear weapons and allow international checks on its facilities in exchange for the rollback of sanctions that had crippled its economy. Trump's decision signals a dramatic reversal of U.S. policy and raises concerns that Iran might resume its nuclear weapons program.

Trump stated that the current agreement is "decaying and rotten" and that the U.S. will withdraw from it. He also announced that the highest level of sanctions would be imposed, affecting not only Iran but also other countries doing business with it. The Treasury Department stated that a series of primary and secondary sanctions, affecting American and foreign partners of Iran, would go back into effect after wind-down periods specified by law.

The Iran nuclear deal was widely seen as the biggest foreign policy accomplishment of President Barack Obama's administration. Trump has long been a critic of the agreement, calling it the "worst deal ever." His decision to withdraw from the deal raises two important questions for the Trump administration and the international community: whether Iran will respond by resuming its quest for nuclear weapons, and whether reneging on the Iran pact might affect North Korea's willingness to cut a denuclearization deal of its own with the president.

U.S. Secretary of State Mike Pompeo was in the air on his way to North Korea during the announcement, and Trump said. Critics of Tuesday's move said Trump is giving North Korea little reason to trust him. Former President Obama called Trump's actions "misguided" and harmful to America's standing in the world, stating that in a democracy, there will always be changes in policies and priorities from one administration to the next, but the consistent flouting of agreements that our country is a party to risks eroding America's credibility, and puts us at odds with the world's major powers.

French President Emanuel Macron, who spoke with Trump Tuesday morning before the announcement, tweeted his "regret" over the president's decision. "The nuclear non-proliferation regime is at stake," he wrote. The withdrawal of the U.S. leaves a big hole at the negotiating table after Trump had sought over the past six months to force a new deal by threatening to scrap the existing one.

Some in the administration and outside it were hopeful that Trump's declaration would create pressure on Iran and America's partners in that deal — Britain, France, Germany, Russia, and China — to negotiate a new agreement in which Iran abandons its ballistic missile development, funding of terrorist groups, stated quest to destroy Israel, and cyber-attacks on the U.S. and its allies. That group included some American critics of Trump's move, including members of his own party, who expressed hope that the U.S. would be a part of a renegotiated agreement in the coming months.

For his part, Iranian President Hassan Rouhani said Tuesday that his country would remain engaged with the other signatories to the original deal. It is difficult to say exactly how Trump’s maneuver is likely to play out over time. The U.S. sanctions are complex, and only part of the international picture. Moreover, the reactions of each country involved in the original deal are difficult to predict precisely — including that of Iran itself: Even if Tehran doesn’t kick-start its nuclear weapons program, its leaders could banish inspectors.

In the meantime, foreign countries and companies will be risking their ability to do business in the U.S. if they continue to buy Iranian oil. Iran initially came to the negotiating table because of the pain caused by economic sanctions imposed by Congress, a series of U.S. presidents, several foreign nations, and the United Nations. Proponents of the deal say that it has worked — that Iran has kept its promises to halt the nuclear weapons program and to allow international vetting of its energy capabilities. However, Trump campaigned on rewriting the pact, and in a speech to the U.N. last year, called it a major "embarrassment" and "one of the worst and most one-sided transactions the United States has ever entered into." Until Tuesday, though, he had taken a more measured approach to the deal. Last October, in declining to certify that Iran had lived up to its end of the bargain, Trump kicked a decision on whether to re-impose U.S. sanctions to Congress — which did not act. Trump pushed the call to Congress, even though he always has had the power to re-impose sanctions through executive action and perhaps because he knew it was unlikely Congress would be capable of agreeing to anything. Back then, his national security adviser was H.R. McMaster, who was considered a moderate on Iran. Now, though — with leading Iran critic John Bolton newly installed in McMaster's old role — Trump has decided to take on Tehran, a decision that has worried America's European allies. Trump's announcement did draw a positive response from some, including many congressional Republicans and the Saudi government — whose U.S. ambassador tweeted that it "fully supports the measures" — and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who gave a much-publicized presentation late last month in which he accused Iran of violating the deal because it hadn't shared pre-existing plans for nuclear weapons with the international community. In his remarks Tuesday, Trump pointed to thousands of documents detailing the program that Israeli intelligence operatives had spirited from Iran. In a televised address following Trump's speech, Netanyahu praised the president for his "courageous leadership."

The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) has frozen its grant programs, according to sources within the agency. EPA staff have been instructed to halt all grants, including funding for research, redevelopment of former industrial sites, air quality monitoring, and education, among other things. The freeze is reportedly in response to the transition to the Trump administration, but it's unclear whether it's indefinite or temporary.

The EPA has also imposed tight controls on external communication, including press releases, blog posts, social media, and content on the agency's website. An email sent to staff on Monday stated that these restrictions are effective immediately and will remain in place until further direction is received from the new administration's transition team.

The freeze could have a significant impact on programs across the country, as EPA grants are distributed at varying intervals and frequency. The Trump administration has appointed Myron Ebell, a fierce EPA critic, to oversee the transition work at the agency. The administration's moves have been described as "extreme and troubling" by a former Obama administration EPA official.

The move by the EPA is part of a broader trend of communication restrictions within the Trump administration. Staffers at several other federal agencies, including the Department of Agriculture and Health and Human Services, have also been told to shut down external communication for the time being.

President Trump has signed an executive order formally withdrawing the U.S. from the Trans-Pacific Partnership trade deal, instituted a federal hiring freeze, and reinstated the "Mexico City policy." It's unclear whether the EPA grant freeze is related to the hiring freeze.

The EPA awards over $4 billion in funding for grants and other assistance agreements each year. For now, it appears that funding is on hold, casting a cloud of uncertainty over the scientists, state and local officials, universities, and Native American tribes that often benefit from the grants. The agency has stated that it is continuing to award environmental program grants and state revolving loan fund grants to the states and tribes, and is working to quickly address issues related to other categories of grants.

The Wall Street Journal has been accused of misrepresenting and attacking the multiple cases brought by former New York Attorney General Eliot Spitzer against AIG and its former chairman and CEO, Hank Greenberg. The cases involve allegations of fraudulent reinsurance contracts and Greenberg's removal as CEO by his own board after his refusal to answer questions about his involvement. Five people were convicted in 2008 for their role in these frauds, and AIG settled the case with Spitzer's office in 2006 by restating its financial results and paying a fine of $1.6 billion.

Spitzer also brought cases against Marsh & McLennan for various financial and business crimes. Two of the cases against employees of the company were dismissed after the defendants had been convicted, but the judge found that certain evidence that should have been turned over to the defense was not. Marsh as a company paid an $850 million fine to resolve the claims and brought in new leadership.

Spitzer's column on Slate.com advocating prosecution of corporate wrongdoers and defending his own enforcement activity against Marsh and AIG has led to two libel lawsuits seeking $90 million by former Marsh executives, who contend that they were defamed by the column. Spitzer has declined to comment on the lawsuits.

The cases against Greenberg and AIG have been both proper and successful, according to Spitzer, and have been necessary to the vindication of justice and ethics in the marketplace. Spitzer also criticizes the mindset of some corporate leaders who continue to deny the need for government intervention to address irresponsible behavior in the marketplace. He cites the example of Steve Schwarzman, the founder and CEO of Blackstone, who compared the attempt to tax private equity fees to Hitler's invasion of Poland.

In conclusion, the Wall Street Journal has been accused of misrepresenting the cases brought by Eliot Spitzer against AIG and Marsh & McLennan, and Spitzer has been hit with two libel lawsuits seeking $90 million by former Marsh executives over a column posted on Slate.com. Spitzer continues to advocate for government intervention to address irresponsible behavior in the marketplace and criticizes the mindset of some corporate leaders who deny the need for such intervention.

Three California men, including a sheriff's deputy, were arrested in York County, Pennsylvania, following a major drug bust last week. The bust involved the seizure of 247 pounds of marijuana, valued at approximately $2 million, along with $11,000 in cash during a traffic stop in West Manheim Township. The deputy, Christopher Heath, was on vacation and had his badge and service weapon on him at the time of his arrest. The trio, who have been charged with drug-related offenses, are currently out on bail. The arrest was part of an ongoing investigation based on tips into law enforcement and was not a routine traffic stop. The investigation is ongoing, and the men could face additional charges due to the interstate transportation of the drugs. The seized marijuana had a sophisticated packaging and had a street retail value in excess of $2 million. The arrest was made with the assistance of local police and involved several law enforcement agencies. Joe Jackson, the patriarch and early manager of the Jackson family, died at the age of 89 on June 27, 2018, after a battle with cancer. Born in 1928, Joe married Katherine in 1949 and together they had 11 children, including pop stars Michael and Janet Jackson, and the sibling singing group, The Jackson 5.

As a manager, Joe launched the career of the Jackson 5 out of Gary, Indiana, in the 1960s. The group signed with Berry Gordy's Motown Records, and in 1970, their first four singles topped the Billboard Hot 100, making them the first act to achieve this feat.

Joe's health had been declining, and on June 21, his son Jermaine tweeted about his father's health, stating that he was not dying, but rather "dying" was a harsh word chosen by headline writers. However, on June 24, a more ominous update was posted on Joe's Twitter page, and Paris Jackson, Michael's daughter, tweeted that the account was taking advantage of the situation.

Daughter Janet Jackson spoke of her father on June 22 at the Radio Disney Music Awards in Hollywood, where she was honored with the Impact Award, now known as the Janet Jackson Award. She praised her father for driving her to be the best that she can.

Joe suffered a stroke while visiting Brazil in 2015 and was again hospitalized after a car accident in Las Vegas in 2017. Despite being known for his iron-fisted management of his children, Joe was honored as Best Entertainment Manager of All Time by the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2002.

Throughout his life, Joe was criticized for being a harsh taskmaster, but he defended his methods, stating that he was strict because he wanted the best for his family. Joe is survived by his wife, Katherine, and their 10 children. His death was met with tributes from his grandchildren and other family members.

Sally Jewell, the CEO of Recreational Equipment Inc., was confirmed by the Senate as the new U.S. Interior Secretary in a bipartisan vote of 87-11. Jewell, a former petroleum engineer and commercial banker, pledged to balance the conflicting demands of using federal land for recreation, conservation, mining, and forestry. Her nomination was supported by environmental groups such as the Sierra Club, but Republican senators questioned her ties to environmental groups that opposed oil and coal use near national parks or on government lands. Jewell will replace Ken Salazar at the Interior Department, which manages national parks and 500 million acres of mineral-rich land, and oversees development of offshore resources. The department also provides services to 566 federally recognized Indian tribes. Jewell, an accomplished mountain climber, expert skier, and longtime bicycle commuter, pledged to resign her post at REI once confirmed by the Senate. The Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee approved Jewell with a bipartisan 19-3 vote last month.

The article from CNN discusses a new study that challenges the long-held theory about the decline of the Easter Island civilization, known for its iconic stone statues. The study, published in the Journal of Pacific Archaeology, suggests that the society that created the statues was more sophisticated and collaborative than previously believed.

The researchers used a unique method to study the society by analyzing the chemical composition of stone tools used to carve the statues. The analysis revealed that the tools were made from a single quarry, indicating a high level of collaboration among the islanders.

Easter Island, located 2,300 miles off the coast of Chile, was settled by Polynesian seafarers around 900 years ago. The population grew, and they carved full-body statues, known as moai, to represent important ancestors. The sheer size and number of the statues indicate a complex, sophisticated society.

The study's findings contradict the popular narrative that the islanders destroyed their own society through infighting and over-exploitation of resources. Instead, the researchers believe that the society was cooperative, with chiefs, priests, and guilds of workers who fished, farmed, and made the moai.

The study's authors urge caution, as they believe that this is just the beginning of understanding the complex history of Easter Island. They encourage further research to shed more light on the moai carving process and the interactions between the Rapa Nui people.

The study's findings have wider-reaching implications, as they provide insights into how societies function and how human behavior shapes the world. According to Laure Dussubieux, a study co-author, "What happens in this world is a cycle, what happened in the past will happen again. Most people don't live on a small island, but what we learn about people's interactions in the past is very important for us now because what shapes our world is how we interact."

Alan Rickman, renowned for his iconic role as Professor Severus Snape in the Harry Potter series, knew his character's true allegiance even before the first films were made, despite Snape being portrayed as a villain throughout the series. J.K. Rowling had informed Rickman that Snape was secretly working for Dumbledore, and he had to keep this knowledge hidden from the film directors and journalists. Fans of Harry Potter, who often had a love-hate relationship with Snape, can watch a YouTube video that compiles all of Snape's most important moments into a 14-minute emotional rollercoaster. The video includes key scenes such as Snape's feelings for Harry's mother Lily and his eventual actions, including the death of Dumbledore.

Rickman's life was celebrated through a series of photos, showcasing his career in films such as 'Alice in Wonderland', 'Galaxy Quest', and 'Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows'. His impact on the film industry and the Harry Potter series will continue to be felt.

The link between height and cancer risk has been further substantiated in a new study, suggesting that taller individuals have a higher risk of developing cancer due to having more cells in their bodies. For every 10cm over the average height, a person's risk for cancer increases by 10%. This research, published in the Proceedings of the Royal Society B, also found that taller people are at a much higher risk of melanoma, and women specifically have greater odds of developing thyroid cancer.

The study, led by Leonard Nunney, an evolutionary biologist at the University of California, Riverside, examined data from massive cancer databases to explore the relationship between the number of cells in a person's body and their cancer risk. The findings align with previous studies, revealing that for every 10 centimeters over the average height, the risk of developing any cancer increases by around 10%.

Taller people, such as basketball players, have approximately twice the risk of cancer compared to shorter individuals. However, it's essential to note that this doesn't mean tall people should panic, as they cannot change their height. Instead, Professor Nunney advises that extremely tall individuals should be aware of the increased risk and seek medical attention if they have concerns.

The study also found that environmental effects can mask height effects for certain cancer types, such as stomach, mouth, and cervical cancer. The high risk of thyroid cancer in taller women remains a mystery, as the research did not provide a clear explanation for this anomaly.

The link between height and cancer risk is thought to be due to the increased number of cells, which provides more opportunities for dangerous mutations to occur. Additionally, taller people have slightly higher levels of insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) in their blood, which encourages cell division and growth. This could potentially account for the extra cancer risk in taller individuals.

On the flip side, having no IGF-1 appears to bestow anti-cancer qualities, as a remote population of dwarf people in Ecuador with a mutation in the growth hormone receptor preventing the release of IGF-1 does not seem to have any cancer.

The research emphasizes that height is not the only factor determining cancer risk. Everyone, regardless of their height, can reduce their cancer odds by eating well, exercising, staying away from smoking, and being careful in the sun. Smoking, for instance, is a far greater risk than being tall.

In the aftermath of Hurricane Harvey, which made landfall in Texas as a Category 4 hurricane on August 25, 2017, Houston and other parts of southeast Texas are experiencing widespread flooding. The storm has caused significant damage, with thousands of people being rescued from flooded homes and neighborhoods. The National Weather Service predicts that the storm will linger for several more days, with an additional 15 to 25 inches of rainfall expected along the upper Texas coast and southwest Louisiana through Friday. The service also warns of the possibility of 50 inches of total rainfall in some areas, exceeding previous Texas records.

Flooding has been reported in numerous communities in Texas, including Houston, La Grange, and Dickinson. In Houston, many families have shared harrowing accounts of their close calls with the floodwaters. Maya Wadler, a 17-year-old resident, described the moment she was rescued from her home around 4 a.m. on Sunday. She said the water "bubbled up from the doors, seeped in from the windows" and that everywhere she turned, there was a new flowing puddle. She was eventually helped onto a dump truck driven by rescue workers and said she was sitting in the corner holding her father tightly, fearing for their safety.

The Coast Guard has been conducting rescue operations, with Lt. Mike Hart reporting that they have received upwards of 1,000 calls per hour and have rescued over 3,000 people since the storm. Houston Mayor Sylvester Turner reported that over 3,000 people have been rescued in Houston alone since the storm flooded the city. Four people have died as a result of the storm, with five other deaths suspected to be storm-related.

The storm has caused significant damage to infrastructure, with many roads and bridges being washed out or flooded. The average annual rainfall in Houston is 50 inches, and the city has already seen 25 inches of rain in two days, with another 25 inches possible by Saturday. Several cities, including Katy, Alvin, Friendswood, League City, Pasadena, Pearland, Seabrook, and Webster, have instituted curfews. The Houston Independent School District has canceled school for the week for its 215,000 students.

President Trump has pledged "rapid action from Congress" to provide disaster relief funding to the areas affected by Harvey. He also said he believes Congress will act fast to provide the funding. Trump is scheduled to visit Texas on Tuesday.

The storm has been described as a "landmark event" by FEMA Administrator Brock Long, who said that Harvey will likely require one of the largest recovery housing efforts the nation has ever seen. The storm is expected to surpass 2008's Hurricane Ike and 2001's Tropical Storm Allison, two of the most destructive storms to hit the Gulf Coast in recent memory. Millions of people from Corpus Christi to New Orleans are under flood watches and warnings as Harvey's storm bands repeatedly pummel the same areas.

The storm's slow-moving nature has fueled the rain and flooding, with Houston's William P. Hobby Airport recording more than a foot of rain on Saturday and 11 inches of rain on Sunday, the two wettest days recorded since 1930. Even when the rain is gone, dangers will persist, said National Weather Service Director Louis Uccellini, because "the flooding will be very slow to recede."

The Pentagon is identifying resources, including trucks, aircraft, and troops, that can be dispatched for hurricane relief if the request comes, and Governor Greg Abbott has activated the entire Texas National Guard, roughly 12,000 Guardsmen. The Army Corps of Engineers has begun releasing water from the Addicks and Barker dams in west Houston to prevent dam and levee failures. Residents living along the Brazos River in Fort Bend County have been ordered to evacuate after the National Weather Service predicted river levels of 56.1 feet, nearly 2 feet above the record during flooding last year.

The storm has also caused significant damage to the energy sector, with several oil refineries along the Gulf Coast being shut down. The U.S. government has authorized the release of up to 4.5 million barrels of oil from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve to help alleviate potential fuel shortages. The NFL has moved the Houston Texans' preseason game against the Dallas Cowboys from Houston to the Cowboys' home stadium in Arlington, Texas. The MLB's Astros and the University of Houston and University of Texas football teams, as well as Louisiana State University, which has a game scheduled for Saturday in Houston, are all monitoring the storm before deciding if they will play.

The Honda Accord has been identified as the most stolen and recovered vehicle in the United States for the fifth consecutive year, according to a report by LoJack. In 2013, $121 million worth of stolen vehicles equipped with LoJack were recovered, with the most expensive vehicle being a 2011 Porsche Panamera valued at $103,400. The National Insurance Crime Bureau (NICB) also reported similar findings, indicating that the Honda Accord was the most stolen car for the fifth year in a row.

The popularity of the Honda Accord among thieves is attributed to its high demand due to its reliability, making it a lucrative target for professional thieves. The interchangeability of car parts across multiple model years also increases the value of stolen Accords, as thieves can sell them for parts up to three times the vehicle's value.

LoJack's top 10 list of most stolen and recovered LoJack-equipped vehicle models in 2013 was also topped by the Honda Accord. The National Crime Information Center's report for 2012 also indicated the Honda Accord as the most stolen car.

Honda, in response, stated that the Accord's popularity is due to its long-standing popularity in the US and its reputation for quality, reliability, and durability. The company also mentioned that it equips its new vehicles with the latest security devices, including the Immobilizer Theft-Deterrent System.

Other vehicles on LoJack's list of most stolen cars include the Honda Civic, Toyota Camry, Toyota Corolla, Chevy Silverado, Acura Integra, Cadillac Escalade, Ford F350, Nissan Altima, and Chevy Tahoe.

In Southern China, authorities have agreed to a rare compromise with villagers in Wukan, Guangdong province, following a nearly two-week standoff over land seizures. The standoff escalated after the death of a village negotiator, Xue Jinbo, in police custody, leading to protests and planned marches. A senior official met with a village representative, and villagers reported that some demands had been met, including the release of three other detained village leaders and the return of Xue's body. The villagers, who claim their land was sold to developers without proper compensation, have agreed to halt further protests, but have threatened to return to the streets if promises are not kept. The situation in Wukan has garnered attention due to its scale, and it comes amidst a series of labor disputes and protests over land grabs in China. A separate protest erupted in Haimen, also in Guangdong province, over local government plans to build a power plant.

In Loudoun County, Virginia, over 200 students who took the SAT exam on May 2 can now avoid a re-take, as the missing tests were found on Monday at Broad Run High School. Initially, it was believed that the tests were lost by UPS, but it was later discovered that the sealed box containing the answer sheets was found on the bottom shelf of a cart in the school's shipping area.

The school had been searching for the tests for about a month. The box was initially locked in the Guidance Office at Broad Run, but was moved to the shipping area at 9:07 a.m., where it was intended to be shipped to Educational Testing Services (ETS). However, a mix-up occurred when the boxes were moved from the school's guidance office to the shipping area on May 4, and the box with the answers somehow ended up on another cart.

An ETS representative was at the school when the tests were found and will take the box to an ETS facility in Princeton, New Jersey. The school will conduct an investigation into the loss of the tests and review its handling of test deliveries. The students were initially given the option to retake the test in June, but they will now be spared from having to do so.

In a study published in the Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory and Cognition, researchers from Colorado College found that the belief of having a good night's sleep can significantly improve cognitive abilities, even if the sleep was not actually restful. The study, led by Christina Draganich and Professor Kristi Erdal, involved 164 students who were told a new technique would measure their sleep patterns. The participants were randomly divided into two groups, one being told they had above-average sleep quality and the other below-average.

Both groups were given a five-minute talk on the importance of sleep for cognitive function and were shown a simulation of a machine measuring their brainwave frequency. The students in the "above-average" sleep quality group were informed they spent 28.7% of their sleep time in REM, while those in the "below-average" group were told they spent only 16.2%.

The students who believed they had a good night's sleep performed significantly better in a cognitive exercise called the Paced Auditory Serial Addition Test, which measures the ability to listen and process information. The authors of the study refer to this phenomenon as "placebo sleep," suggesting that the mindset regarding one's sleep can influence cognitive states positively and negatively.

On March 10, 2014, Steve Douglass and Dean Muskett, along with a group of fellow photographers, were at Amarillo International Airport in Texas when they spotted the contrails of three high-flying, unidentified aircraft. Initially, they believed the planes were B-2 bombers, but upon reviewing their photos, they noticed that the aircraft had a different shape, with a smooth backside rather than the distinctive "W"-shaped back of a B-2.

An inquiry to Whiteman Air Force Base ruled out the possibility that a flight of three B-2s was flying over Texas on that day. Aviation experts, including Bill Sweetman and the AW&ST team, have since investigated the mystery aircraft sighting, concluding that the photos show something real, although it does not resemble the X-47B drone.

The mystery aircraft appears to be larger than the Navy's new killer drone, and some speculate that the moment may have arrived to reveal it to potential resurgent enemies, such as Russia, as a show of force, similar to the F-117 reveal 30 years earlier. The images have prompted interest in the industry, with editors at Aviation Week reporting that they appear to be "something real." Douglass has reached out to Whiteman Air Force Base for confirmation but has not received a response.

On Wednesday, April 18, 2018, Cuba will witness a historic political transition as President Raul Castro, aged 86, steps down and hands over the office to a younger successor, marking the first time in nearly six decades that someone outside the Castro family will occupy the country's highest government office. The transition will take place over two days, with the Cuban National Assembly electing a new president on Wednesday and announcing the replacement the following day.

The National Assembly, known for its unanimous votes, will select leaders of the legislature before voting for the president and other members of the Council of State, Cuba's highest government body. State media will broadcast the significant moments of the session live. The vote will be counted by the National Electoral Commission and announced on Thursday.

The favorite to replace Castro is First Vice President Miguel Diaz-Canel Bermudez, aged 57. Although Cuba's constitution allows for any member of the 605-seat legislature to be elected as head of the council of state, Diaz-Canel's low-profile image has changed slightly this year as state media highlighted his public appearances.

Diaz-Canel gained prominence as the top Communist Party official in central Villa Clara province, where he was known as a hard-working, modest-living technocrat dedicated to improving public services. He became higher education minister in 2009 before moving into the vice presidency.

In a leaked video from a Communist Party meeting last year, Diaz-Canel expressed orthodox positions, including shutting down some independent media and labeling certain European embassies as outposts of foreign subversion. However, he has also defended academics and bloggers who became targets of hardliners, leading some to describe him as a potential advocate for greater openness in a system intolerant of virtually any criticism or dissent.

The transition comes as Cuba faces economic stagnation, an aging population, and increasing disenchantment among younger generations. Raul Castro is stepping down as president to ensure that new leaders can maintain the government's grip on power. He will remain head of the Communist Party, designated by the constitution as "the superior guiding force of society and the state."

Cubans have mixed feelings about the transition. While some appreciate the need for rejuvenation, particularly in the economy, others express concerns about the potential for capitalism and the preservation of equality among citizens. The new president will face the challenge of balancing these concerns while addressing the country's economic issues.

The legislative session and the transition of power were accompanied by a media campaign emphasizing the continuity of Cuba's single-party politics and socialist economy. State media assured Cubans that no fundamental changes were occurring, despite the new faces at the top. The new national leadership is expected to be officially announced on the anniversary of the defeat of U.S.-backed invaders at the Bay of Pigs in 1961.

Samuel Shaffer, a self-proclaimed cult leader and former prophet of the doomsday cult group The Knights of the Crystal Blade, was sentenced to 15 years to life in prison for felony sodomy on a child in Sanpete County on Wednesday. Shaffer had previously been sentenced to 25 years to life in prison for first-degree felony rape of a child and one second-degree felony count of child abuse in Iron County. The sentences will run concurrently, requiring Shaffer to serve a minimum of 26 years in prison.

The investigation into Shaffer and his cult began in December 2017 after his ex-wife reported that John Alvin Coltharp, another cult member, had taken their four children and fled after losing custody in divorce proceedings. An Amber Alert was issued for Coltharp's daughters. Two of the girls were found in a single-wide trailer, while the other two were found in empty 50-gallon water drums.

Shaffer initially refused to tell authorities the whereabouts of the remaining two girls but eventually did. The girls were found in "poor health with signs of dehydration and acting lethargic" in the trailer. All four girls were transported by ambulance to the Cedar City hospital where they received emergency medical care.

Coltharp pleaded guilty on June 13 to charges of child sodomy and child bigamy and is scheduled to be sentenced on August 8. On June 8, a third man was identified as an alleged follower of the doomsday group and charged with child sexual abuse.

Shaffer's attorney, Troy Sundquist, could not be immediately reached for comment on whether he plans to appeal the sentencing. The cult believes in doomsday prophecies and practices polygamy. Shaffer had told detectives that he was married to the 8-year-old daughter of John Coltharp, while Coltharp had said he was married to Shaffer’s 7-year-old daughter.

An 82-year-old man named Masafumi Nagasaki, who lived as a castaway on a deserted island in Japan for nearly three decades, has been removed from his home after becoming the longest-lasting voluntary castaway alive. Known as the "naked hermit," Nagasaki arrived on Sotobanari Island in 1989 and lived a life in solitude until he was discovered in 2012.

Nagasaki spent decades on the island without modern conveniences such as phones, lighters, fresh water, or many clothes. He braved typhoons and biting mosquitoes in the buff and found friends in strange places, such as turtles and their eggs.

Nagasaki's only wish was to die on the island he called home for the last three decades. He told Reuters in 2012 that he wanted to die surrounded by nature and that he had chosen the island as his place of death.

It is unclear how Nagasaki ended up on Sotobanari Island. He was a photographer before escaping civilization, but he does not want to talk about his past. He even ran his own hostess club in Niigata, a port city in Japan's main island.

Nagasaki said he was working in a factory in Osaka when one day a colleague told him about a mysterious archipelago. He was "horrified" by the amount of pollution he saw in the sea below and "exploded." So the self-confessed "city man with no outdoor experience" packed his bags and found his remote island hideaway. He thought he would stay perhaps two years max, but ended up clocking almost 30 years.

Nagasaki spent his first few years on the island clothed but when a typhoon swept through and destroyed his few belongings, he realized "wearing clothes here was completely out of place for me" and began to live life commando. He told Reuters in 2012 that walking around naked felt right and that if he put on clothes, he would feel completely out of place.

Fast forward to April 2018 and authorities have removed the 82-year-old and returned him back to civilization. It is unclear why he was removed, but Alvaro Cerezo, who documents island castaways, said that since being removed, Nagasaki is now living in the nearest city to the island, Ishigaki, 60 kilometers away in a government house.

For more information about Masafumi Nagasaki, visit nagasaki.docastaway.com. For more information on Alvaro Cerezo and Docastaway, visit docastaway.com.

On September 27, 2014, Mount Ontake, Japan's second-highest active volcano, erupted without warning, causing a mass tragedy. The eruption occurred during a beautiful fall day, attracting hundreds of hikers, including children, to the mountain. The blast spewed large amounts of ash and stones, trapping many hikers and causing injuries.

As of Monday, at least 36 people are feared dead, with 12 confirmed deaths and 63 injuries reported. Eight people are still missing, but it is possible that some of them may be among the deceased. The search for victims was halted on Monday due to fears of toxic gases.

Rescuers found five more bodies on Monday near a shrine at the summit, bringing the total number of bodies found to 17. The exact cause of death for all victims remains unclear, with possibilities including toxic gases, suffocating ash, falling rocks, or other causes.

Rescue efforts were particularly challenging due to the thick layer of ash covering the mountain, as well as the strong smell of sulfur at the peak. Helicopters were used to airlift laden stretchers from the summit, but the search was eventually abandoned due to the toxic fumes.

Japan is one of the world's most seismically active nations, and this is Japan's first fatal volcanic eruption since 1991. The last major eruption of Mount Ontake was in 1979. Hikers reported no warning of the eruption, and experts have noted that it was difficult to predict due to a lack of other changes in the mountain and the nature of the steam-driven explosion.

The eruption did not affect the restart of the Sendai nuclear plant in southwestern Japan, an area of active volcanic sites. The Meteorological Agency, which monitors volcanic activity, is expected to reconsider its surveillance system in light of the tragedy.

On October 28, 2015, a shooting occurred at the Washington Square Mall in Indianapolis, resulting in three injuries. The incident took place around 6:30 p.m. near the Target store. According to Indianapolis Metropolitan Police Deputy Chief of Operations Brian Mahone, the suspect and the intended victim knew each other and had some sort of dispute. The suspect, who is still at large, approached the victim and shot him, with two other bystanders also being injured by ricochet fire.

The victims, two men and a woman, all young adults, were transported to hospitals. One of the male victims was initially in serious condition but is now expected to survive, while the other two did not have life-threatening injuries. The suspect has not been apprehended, and police are hoping the victims can help identify him.

Witnesses described a chaotic scene inside the mall, with people screaming and parents trying to find their children. Joshua Matthews, who was in the mall with his three-year-old son, picked up his son and started running when the gunfire began. Matthews saw at least two of the victims fall to the ground.

The mall's property manager, Adrian T. Lewis Sr., issued a statement confirming the shooting and expressing sympathy for the victims and their families. The mall is cooperating with the police investigation and has a highly-trained staff prepared to respond to emergencies.

Police are urging anyone with information about the shooting or possible suspect to call Crime Stoppers at 262-TIPS or text "INDYCS" plus tip information to 274637 (CRIMES). All tips are considered anonymous.

Bob Tracey, a SEPTA worker in suburban Philadelphia, found a bag containing $15,200 in cash in March 2016 and immediately turned it over to the police. Upper Darby Police Superintendent Michael Chitwood was impressed by Tracey's honesty and believed the money should go to him if no one claimed it. After a year-long legal battle, a judge ordered the money returned to Tracey on Monday. The delay was due to bureaucratic procedures, and it's unclear why Tracey's legal battle dragged on for six months. The bag also contained drug paraphernalia, making it unlikely that the real owners would come forward.

In a separate incident, nine people were shot at a North Philadelphia party, with Michael Chitwood, Upper Darby superintendent of police, commenting that such an incident would be considered a mass shooting in Bensalem. Stephanie Farr, a Daily News reporter, covered the story. It's unclear if any updates have been made regarding the investigation into the shooting.

The historic summit between U.S. President Donald Trump and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un took place on June 12, 2018, in Singapore. The two leaders met for a one-on-one meeting, joined only by interpreters, and later had a larger meeting with their respective aides. Trump described the one-on-one meeting as "very, very good" and said he and Kim have an "excellent relationship." Kim said it was not easy to get to the summit but they overcame the obstacles.

The two leaders shared a historic handshake and were expected to meet alone for about 45 minutes, with only a pair of interpreters in the room. This decision raised concerns about the risk of holding such a monumental meeting with barely anyone to bear witness. After the intimate huddle, they were scheduled to hold a larger meeting and working lunch.

Trump arrived on Singapore's Sentosa Island for the summit and was flanked by his chief of staff, Secretary of State, and national security adviser. Kim also arrived on Sentosa Island for the meeting. The summit was aimed at settling a standoff over Pyongyang's nuclear arsenal.

Trump predicted that he and Kim would have "a terrific relationship" and said he'll know within minutes whether a deal can be made. Kim said it was a significant moment for the two countries and that he was looking forward to a successful and outcome-oriented meeting.

Trump earlier defended his decision to meet with Kim, tweeting that North Korea has already released three detainees and that missile tests have halted. Critics have argued that Kim has notched a win by getting a sit-down with the U.S. president.

Former NBA star Dennis Rodman arrived in Singapore hours before the summit, but he was not expected to play an official role in the diplomatic negotiations. Trump is also expected to visit U.S. military bases in Guam and Hawaii on his return from the summit.

The White House said that the talks with North Korea are moving "more quickly than expected," and Trump now plans to depart Singapore on Tuesday evening ahead of schedule. The summit presented a test of Kim's willingness to agree to deal his nuclear weapons away for "protections" from the United States. The joint statement signed by Trump and Kim pledged to work toward complete denuclearization of the Korean Peninsula, but provided few details of how that might work.

An embarrassing scandal involving 11 Secret Service agents and five American service members in Colombia has been revealed, just hours before President Obama's arrival for an international summit. The agents, who were part of an advance team assigned to secure a local hotel, were accused of taking advantage of Colombia's policy of legal prostitution. The scandal began when an agent refused to pay a prostitute, leading to a dispute that was reported to local police and the U.S. Embassy. The Secret Service immediately launched an investigation, and at least one supervisor was among those involved. The agents were staying at the beachfront Hotel Caribe, where guests reported seeing them drinking heavily during their weeklong stay. The incident threatened to overshadow President Obama's visit to the summit, but he has not yet addressed the matter. The agents have been recalled to Washington, and their careers are reportedly over. The military members involved have been confined to their quarters in Colombia and ordered not to have contact with others. The Secret Service did not elaborate on the allegations, but the Associated Press confirmed that they involved prostitutes. The White House said Obama has full confidence in the Secret Service, but the incident has been a distraction for the media.

The Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences, responsible for awarding the Oscars, has taken significant steps to address criticism regarding its lack of diversity. In response to concerns about an overwhelmingly older, male, and white membership, the Academy has extended unprecedented invitations to 683 film industry professionals, with nearly half being women and 41% being people of color.

The list of invited directors includes a diverse range of international heavyweights, Hollywood mainstays, and up-and-comers, such as Catherine Breillat, Park Chan-wook, Lucrecia Martel, and the Wachowskis. The list of acting invitees features a mix of established actors like Idris Elba, Kate Beckinsale, and Michael B. Jordan, as well as up-and-coming talents like Regina King, Eva Mendes, and Ice Cube.

This move comes following the hashtag #OscarsSoWhite, initiated by April Reign in 2015, which highlighted the Academy's lack of diversity. The Academy has pledged to double the number of women and people of color in its ranks by 2020, and Wednesday's invitation list marks the first step towards achieving this goal. The list includes three Wayans brothers and a variety of other professionals in the film industry. This move is aimed at addressing the ongoing diversity problem in the film industry and promoting a more inclusive environment.
