Larry Villarin, a 62-year-old Californian, is America's oldest male sexual surrogate. He works one-on-one with clients to help them work through sexual dysfunction. Over the past 35 years, Larry has worked with a diverse range of clients, including disabled individuals, abuse survivors, and people from strict religious backgrounds, as well as millionaires, geniuses, and 40-year-old virgins. Most clients pair his hands-on therapy with trips to a psychologist to prepare for real-life intimacy.

Larry's job involves navigating emotional complexities, such as what happens when a client falls in love with him or how to gently address body hang-ups and deeply internalized anxieties. In one case, he helped a 35-year-old woman who had never kissed a man or seen one naked due to a car accident that left her blind in one eye and filled with self-doubt. Through sessions, she learned to trust Larry and eventually opened up to intimacy.

Larry's work is far less sexy than it might seem. During their first session, clients unload their emotional baggage and set therapy goals. No sexual touching is allowed. If all goes well, they'll move to hand stroking and a face caressing. Later, he'll try a blindfolded "trust walk" to help clients get "out of their heads."

Larry claims that birthdays are the number-one reason women come to see him. Late-in-life virgins, turning 30 or 40, see the date looming and want to take the plunge. Emotional blocks can turn physical for some women, and Larry has helped clients with conditions like vaginismus, which causes the vaginal canal to tighten involuntarily, preventing sex.

Although trust is crucial to Larry's work, he maintains an emotional distance to avoid complications. Some clients have fallen in love with him, which can push him into a tricky ethical gray area. To avoid this, Larry has set boundaries, such as building a "therapy room" instead of allowing sessions in his own bedroom.

The job is full of ethical landmines, and paying for sex is illegal in the U.S. IPSA skirts prostitution law by not acknowledging intercourse as part of the practice. Despite the risks, Larry sees his work as primarily therapeutic or socially instructive, helping clients overcome emotional barriers and improve their lives.

In the wake of Tunisian President Zine El Abidine Ben Ali's departure, the country experienced widespread looting and destruction of properties belonging to the Trabelsi family, the wife of the former president and her extended family. The Trabelsis were widely perceived as the ultimate symbol of corruption and excess, with Leila Ben Ali, a former hairdresser, and her siblings operating like a mafia, extorting money, demanding stakes in businesses, and dividing up concessions among themselves. Their control over Tunisia's economy was vast, with interests in banks, airlines, car dealerships, Internet providers, radio and television stations, industry, and big retailers.

The public's anger was directed more towards the Trabelsis than at Ben Ali and his authoritarian regime. Within a day of Ben Ali's departure, many of their sumptuous villas and businesses were pillaged and burned, and some reports suggested that one family member was killed by an angry mob. A Tunis Air pilot who refused to take off with five fleeing family members on board became a national hero.

The economic fallout of the Trabelsis' web of corruption and influence-mongering was palpable, with "Tunisian investors...forgoing new investments, keeping domestic investment rates low and unemployment high." A lack of jobs in this highly educated nation fueled the month of popular protests that toppled Ben Ali. The uprising began in December after a despairing university graduate set himself on fire and died because police confiscated his goods.

The co-author of a book on Leila Trabelsi, "La Regente de Carthage," says the Trabelsis played an "absolutely capital" role in the fall of the regime. The arrest of 33 members of the family has been announced, and an investigation into corrupt practices and enrichment by members of the ousted regime has been launched. Switzerland has also taken measures to freeze the bank accounts and other assets of both Ben Ali and Ivory Coast's Laurent Gbagbo.

In the remote Tunisian outpost of Tataouine, thousands of Libyans fleeing their country's civil war have found refuge, with hundreds of Tunisians opening their homes to these newcomers since April. Despite Tunisia's own challenges following its own revolution, the generosity of its people has been remarkable, housing over 2,500 Libyan refugees in their homes. The Tunisian government has also kept the country's borders open, with an estimated 276,000 people, most of them foreign workers, fleeing Libya for Tunisia. The incursion of Libyan forces into Tunisian territory in early May sparked outrage, but was quickly resolved. Meanwhile, the situation in Misrata, Libya's biggest rebel enclave, has worsened, with rebels accusing Gaddafi's forces of using larger rockets, causing greater destruction. The rebels have called on NATO to halt the bombardment of the city. The conflict in Libya has led to international rifts, with critics arguing that NATO bombing is an attempt to overthrow the government.

On Tuesday, a man identified as James Dirk Crudup, 41, who is homeless, was apprehended by the Secret Service after jumping the White House fence. The incident was broadcast live on CNN, showing armed officers ordering the man to lie down, handcuffing him, and securing a backpack thrown over the fence. The Secret Service stated that Crudup would be charged with unlawful entry and contempt of court due to past incidents, as he had been previously ordered to stay away from the White House. The incident caused a temporary lockdown, but there was no immediate information on whether the intruder posed a security threat. In an unusual twist, a 6-year-old girl reached the White House lawn on Sunday night by going through the fence, and was escorted out by the Secret Service.

Jurgen Klinsmann, the coach of the United States men's soccer team, had a memorable dining experience with President Obama, Chancellor Angela Merkel, Nobel laureates, and astronauts at a gala in Berlin. However, his team's recent losses in two consecutive matches led to criticism in the media, damaging their chances of qualifying for the 2018 World Cup. Despite this, Klinsmann defended his record as coach, expressing confidence and comfort in his position.

On Monday, U.S. Soccer, the federation overseeing the sport in the U.S., announced that Klinsmann had been fired. The decision was made following a meeting with two of the federation's top executives at a hotel in the Los Angeles area. U.S. Soccer did not immediately name Klinsmann's replacement, but it is expected that Bruce Arena, a veteran coach from Major League Soccer who led the national team from 1998 to 2006, will take over through the end of the current World Cup cycle.

U.S. Soccer President Sunil Gulati stated that while they are confident in the team's quality players, the form and growth of the team up to this point necessitated a change in direction. Gulati is expected to elaborate on the reasoning behind Klinsmann's dismissal during a conference call with the media on Tuesday afternoon.

In a series of interviews, Mitt Romney's foreign policy advisers defended his criticism of President Obama, stating that the ongoing protests in the Middle East would not have occurred under a Romney presidency. Richard Williamson, a top Romney foreign policy adviser, argued that the assassination of an American ambassador since Jimmy Carter's presidency would not have happened under Romney's leadership. Williamson also criticized Obama for a lack of American resolve and inability to protect American property in Egypt, Libya, and Yemen.

The Romney campaign's aggressive approach on foreign policy has thrust the issue to the forefront of the presidential campaign, following criticism of Romney's handling of the situation overseas. However, criticism from Republicans over Romney's response quieted on Thursday, with influential voices in the party's foreign policy establishment rallying to Romney's defense.

Obama faced criticism for saying that he did not consider Egypt an ally, a comment that his administration struggled to explain. Administration officials tried to parse Obama's statement without appearing to contradict him, stating that the term "ally" refers to countries with which the United States has a mutual defense treaty. However, the United States has designated Egypt as a "major non-NATO ally" since 1989, bestowing approval, weapons sales, and defense cooperation prohibited to non-treaty nations.

At campaign stops in Nevada and Colorado, Obama avoided mentioning Romney and instead paid tribute to those who lost their lives in Libya, promising to track down their killers. The Obama campaign responded by noting that the protests this week were triggered by the video, not by U.S. policy, and that the video likely would still have been produced if Romney had been president. They also noted that there have been attacks on Americans under every president in recent history, including Presidents Ronald Reagan and George W. Bush.

Romney himself struck a more measured tone and tried to refocus on his core economic argument on the campaign trail. He did not mention Obama by name, but suggested that the president was a weak commander in chief and unreliable guardian of American strength abroad. Romney's policy advisers laid out steps that a President Romney would have taken in the Middle East that they said Obama has not done, including having a vision for the future of the Middle East and supporting those who have been shortchanged by the administration.

The Romney campaign hopes to force a broader debate about America's role in the world and to argue that while Obama has been successful in fighting terrorism, his foreign policies have resulted in waning U.S. influence abroad. However, Obama consistently outpolls Romney on foreign policy and earned high marks for the killing of al-Qaeda leader Osama bin Laden.

The sharpest foreign policy difference between the two candidates is on Iran. Romney has said he would not allow Iran to enrich uranium, suggesting he would enforce a series of United Nations Security Council resolutions demanding that Iran "suspend" its production of all nuclear fuel. However, Iran was in violation of that demand through most of Bush's second term, and suffered fewer economic consequences than it has under Obama, who has imposed the first sanctions against Iran's oil revenues.

On Egypt, Romney's campaign has attacked a statement issued by the American Embassy in Cairo hours before protests began there, stating that "you don't issue a conciliatory statement that says we don't support freedom of speech." The statement did condemn a virulent anti-Muslim video that set off the violence, but it also included references to both the importance of free speech and religious tolerance.

In a shooting rampage at a shopping center in Arizona, four bystanders prevented further casualties by disarming the gunman, who was later identified as 22-year-old Jared Loughner. The attack resulted in six deaths, including a federal judge and a 9-year-old girl, and wounded 14, including Representative Gabrielle Giffords, who was the target of the attack. The gunman was armed with a 9-millimeter Glock semi-automatic, which he obtained last November. Patricia Maisch, one of the bystanders, is being hailed as a hero for wrestling away a fresh magazine of bullets as the gunman tried to reload. Maisch, along with Bill Badger, Roger Salzgeber, and Joseph Zamudio, helped to stop the shooter and prevent further carnage. Federal prosecutors have charged Loughner with attempting to assassinate a member of Congress, killing an employee of the federal government, and attempting to kill a federal employee. The investigation is ongoing, and additional charges may be filed. Sheriff Clarence Dupnik, who has received attention for his remarks attacking the amount of "vitriol" in political rhetoric, repeated his view that such rhetoric may contribute to violence and criticized Arizona's gun laws.

The Internet Archive is working on a project to preserve web pages as they are created and archive pages that are referenced, aiming to fix broken links on the web. This is done by replacing broken links with archived versions of the pages or providing a companion link to the original intended content. In a separate incident, a substitute teacher at Brookland-Cayce High School in Lexington, South Carolina, was arrested for being drunk on school premises. The teacher, Judith Elizabeth Richards-Gartee, is not an employee of the school district but works for Kelly Services, a company contracted to provide substitute teachers. The school district removed Richards-Gartee from the classroom and reported the incident to law enforcement, who have filed criminal charges. Richards-Gartee was also found in possession of an open container of alcohol and was taken to the hospital. The Lexington County Sheriff's Department has since released no further information regarding the incident.

James Gandolfini, the acclaimed actor best known for his role as Tony Soprano on HBO's groundbreaking series The Sopranos, has passed away at the age of 51. The cause of death is believed to be a heart attack, which occurred while he was on vacation in Rome.

Gandolfini played Tony Soprano for six seasons from 1999-2007, winning three Emmys for best actor in a drama series. The show was a critical and commercial success, luring millions of subscribers to HBO.

At the time of his death, Gandolfini was working on the HBO limited series Criminal Justice, in which he played a downtrodden jailhouse attorney. He also had a role in the upcoming crime drama Animal Rescue, set for release in 2014.

In addition to his work on The Sopranos, Gandolfini had a notable film career, appearing in movies such as The Man Who Wasn’t There, The Taking of Pelham 1 2 3, Welcome to the Rileys, Killing Them Softly, Not Fade Away, Zero Dark Thirty, and The Incredible Burt Wonderstone.

Before his breakout role on The Sopranos, Gandolfini often appeared as a heavy in films such as True Romance, Get Shorty, and Crimson Tide. He was born in Westwood, New Jersey, and graduated from Rutgers University.

Gandolfini is survived by his wife of four years, Deborah Lin, his teenage son from a previous marriage, and two sisters. HBO released a statement saying, "We're all in shock and feeling immeasurable sadness at the loss of a beloved member of our family."

The Sopranos creator David Chase called Gandolfini "a genius" and "one of the greatest actors of this or any time." Chris Albrecht, who greenlit the series at HBO, said, "Jimmy was the spiritual core of our Sopranos family, and I am stunned at this devastating loss."

Gandolfini's death has been met with an outpouring of tributes from his colleagues in the entertainment industry. Edie Falco, who played his TV wife on The Sopranos, said, "I'm truly crushed at the passing of my friend Jim Gandolfini. He was a man of tremendous depth and sensitivity, with a kindness and generosity beyond words." Lorraine Bracco, who played his therapist on the show, said, "We lost a giant today. I am utterly heartbroken."

Gandolfini's passing has left a significant void in the entertainment industry, and he will be deeply missed by his fans and colleagues.

In a historic summit in Singapore, U.S. President Donald Trump and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un signed a document committing to work towards peace. The meeting, which lasted nearly four hours, was described as going better than expected by President Trump. The leaders exchanged mutual compliments, shared a handshake, and had a lunch consisting of a prawn cocktail.

The summit aimed to bring about Pyongyang's nuclear disarmament, a significant step towards easing tensions on the Korean peninsula. Kim, one of the world's most reclusive leaders, made an evening tour of Singapore's waterfront before the summit.

U.S. Secretary of State Mike Pompeo injected a note of caution, stating it remained to be seen whether Kim was sincere about his willingness to denuclearize. Officials from both countries held last-minute talks to lay the groundwork for the meeting.

The summit was a significant milestone, as it was almost unthinkable just months ago when the two leaders were exchanging insults and threats. The meeting could potentially lead to the dismantling of North Korea's nuclear program, which threatens the United States.

Pompeo emphasized that North Korea would need to move towards complete, verifiable, and irreversible denuclearization. However, North Korea has shown little appetite for surrendering nuclear weapons, which it considers vital to the survival of Kim's dynastic rule.

Sanctions on North Korea would remain in place until denuclearization had occurred, Pompeo said. "If diplomacy does not move in the right direction... those measures will increase."

The White House later stated that discussions with North Korea had moved "more quickly than expected," and Trump would leave Singapore on Tuesday night, earlier than originally scheduled. Kim is due to leave on Tuesday afternoon.

Kim made a rare public appearance on Monday evening, waving and smiling to onlookers. The summit marks a significant shift in Kim's image, moving away from his previous international pariah status.

Former U.S. National Basketball Association star Dennis Rodman arrived in Singapore for the summit, expressing excitement about being part of the event.

The summit is a significant step towards peace and potential denuclearization on the Korean peninsula. However, skepticism remains among experts about Kim's commitment to complete denuclearization. The process could be doomed if the two sides fail to reach a common understanding of denuclearization.

France's National Assembly approved a controversial bill on Tuesday, allowing same-sex couples the same spousal and adoption rights as heterosexual couples, marking President François Hollande's first major social reform. The legislation, which redefines marriage as a contract between two people, was backed by 329 deputies and opposed by 229. The bill will now go to the Senate, expected to approve it, making France the 12th country to legalize same-sex marriage. The move has been met with opposition from the Catholic Church and social conservatives, who have organized large protests, with another rally planned for March. The bill also faced resistance over the issue of medically assisted procreation for lesbians, which will be debated later in the year. The bill's passage comes as the UK also moves towards legalizing same-sex marriage, with the US and Australia divided on the issue.

In the aftermath of Christina Grimmie's tragic death, her family, friends, and fans have shown an overwhelming outpouring of love and support. Grimmie's father, Bud, expressed his gratitude for the memorials, donations, and tributes from fans and the media and entertainment industry. Brian Teefey, Grimmie's manager, created a GoFundMe page to assist the family in their time of need. Adam Levine, Grimmie's coach on The Voice, offered to pay for her funeral expenses. Grimmie was shot and killed by a deranged fan on June 10 after a concert. The GoFundMe page has raised over $100,000 to help with funeral expenses. Marcus Grimmie, Christina's brother, expressed his gratitude for the support and shared his grief on social media.

Harrison Ford, the renowned actor known for his roles in "Star Wars" and "Indiana Jones," was injured after crash-landing a vintage World War II plane on a golf course in Venice, California on March 5, 2015. The incident occurred shortly after takeoff from the Santa Monica Airport. Ford, an experienced pilot, was hospitalized and expected to undergo surgery for his injuries, which were reported to be non-life-threatening. His family stated that he was in stable condition.

Witnesses reported seeing the plane clip a tree before crash-landing, and emergency services responded quickly, ensuring no other injuries were sustained. Dr. Sanjay Khurana, a spinal surgeon on the golf course, bravely assisted Ford despite the potential danger of a fuel leak.

Ford's career in Hollywood spans over six decades, with his iconic roles in "Star Wars" and the "Indiana Jones" series. He continues to star in blockbuster hits and has signed on for future films. The cause of the plane crash is currently unknown. This incident serves as a reminder of Ford's passion for aviation, as he often pilots planes and helicopters for leisure and search and rescue missions.

The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has issued a warning letter to 23andMe, a popular genetic-testing company, ordering them to halt sales of their Personal Genome Service (PGS). The FDA states that the company has failed to provide the necessary scientific data to prove that the test works as advertised, and that the potential health consequences of false positive or negative assessments could lead to unnecessary or ineffective treatments. The FDA has been working with 23andMe since 2009 to help them comply with regulatory requirements, but the company has yet to provide the required information. The FDA is concerned about the lack of context and interpretation provided to consumers, and the potential for misleading results. The move by the FDA highlights the contentious debate over the government's role in regulating direct-to-consumer genetic testing. 23andMe has confirmed that they have received the FDA's warning letter and are committed to addressing their concerns. The company has 15 days to detail how they will go forward, or else they could face other regulatory actions such as civil fines or injunctions. The FDA's move towards regulating genetic tests marketed directly to consumers has been ongoing since 2010, and the agency is working to create a regulatory structure that will govern such tests in the future.

In this summary, an Egyptian man named Taymour el-Sobky was sentenced to three years in prison with hard labor for making derogatory comments about married women on a television show in December. El-Sobky claimed that 30% of married Egyptian women have a readiness for "immorality" and are prone to cheating on their husbands. The comments sparked a public outcry, leading to his arrest and subsequent trial. The court found that his comments harmed public peace and damaged public interest. El-Sobky can still appeal the sentence.

This incident has raised concerns about freedom of speech in Egypt, as it follows a series of sentences against artists, writers, and intellectuals for violating public modesty or defaming religious symbols. Prominent rights lawyer Gamal Eid stated that el-Sobki's case shares similar attributes with the expulsion of Tawfiq Okasha from parliament earlier this month for meeting Israel's ambassador to Egypt. Eid believes that these cases demonstrate how "it is not the law, but it is pressure and public opinion, and rallying around someone, that acquits or incriminates him."

The cases are seen as an example of the state's inconsistent application of the law and the increasing harassment and threats against individuals with no connection to politics or activism. The sentencing of el-Sobky and other high-profile figures has caused concern within Egypt's artistic and intellectual community, who fear for the future of free speech and creativity in the country.

The investigation into the death of 19-year-old Kenneka Jenkins, who was found dead in a hotel freezer in Rosemont, Illinois, has been closed by authorities, who have determined it to be accidental. However, lawyers for Jenkins' mother have expressed concerns about graphic police photographs released as part of the case, which they say "raise more questions than answers."

The photographs, which were posted on the Rosemont police website, show Jenkins' body in the hotel freezer where she was found. According to a police report, her shirt was pulled up, exposing her breasts. Lawyers for Jenkins' mother have described the photos as "graphic and disturbing" and "of a personal, private and indecent nature."

Jenkins was found dead in a hotel freezer on September 10, about 21 hours after she went missing following a party she attended in a ninth-floor room. According to police reports, she was found on her side, face down, with her left arm underneath her, her right shoe off, and a small cut on her right foot.

The police investigation into Jenkins' death generated 135 reports and involved interviews with 44 people, including 30 who were confirmed to have been in the hotel room at some point during the night of the party. Authorities also viewed dozens of hours of surveillance video, conducted five photo line-ups, performed forensic analyses on four cellphones, and submitted three search warrants and four preservation of evidence warrants.

The Cook County Medical Examiner's office had already classified Jenkins' death as accidental and caused by hypothermia, with alcohol intoxication listed as a contributing factor. The police statement said the "death and circumstances surrounding are especially sad."

In announcing the closure of the case, Rosemont police outlined the scope of their investigation and said they found no evidence that Jenkins was the victim of foul play, contrary to the many conspiracy theories that have sprouted on social media. The police statement added that there was no evidence that Jenkins was forced to drink alcohol or consume any narcotics while at the hotel.

The police also said that the hotel room where the party took place was booked with a fraudulent credit card and that they believe they have identified two perpetrators who booked the room. The case involving the fraudulent booking is still ongoing.

The release of the photographs and other documents related to the case has sparked controversy and raised questions from Jenkins' family and their lawyers. It remains to be seen whether the release of the information will put an end to the speculation and conspiracy theories surrounding Jenkins' death.

In a series of unusual incidents, two passengers caused disruptions on separate Indian flights. On September 24, a drunk passenger attempted to enter the cockpit of an IndiGo Airlines flight from Mumbai to Kolkata, claiming he needed to charge his phone. The unruly passenger was offloaded and handed over to police for questioning, but was later released without charge.

In another incident on September 22, a passenger on a GoAir flight from New Delhi to Patna attempted to open a plane door, apparently mistaking it for the toilet. The man, believed to be a first-time flyer, was handed over to police after the plane landed safely in Patna.

In yet another incident last week, more than 30 passengers on a Jaipur-bound flight were hospitalized due to nose bleeds, headaches, and ear pain after the cabin crew forgot to pressurize the cabin.

These incidents highlight the importance of adhering to standard operating procedures and the potential consequences of disregarding safety protocols on commercial flights.

The United States Olympic Committee (USOC) has initiated a hearing that could lead to the dissolution of USA Gymnastics, the national governing body for the sport, due to its handling of the sexual abuse scandal involving former national team doctor Lawrence G. Nassar. The USOC filed a complaint 16 days ago, seeking to remove USA Gymnastics' recognition as a national body following the abuse of hundreds of female athletes. USA Gymnastics has chosen not to relinquish its status, instead questioning the USOC's hearing process.

The hearing will be chaired by a USOC board member and will have representatives from the NGB and athlete advisory councils. USA Gymnastics will have the opportunity to present evidence and legal arguments regarding the allegations. After the hearing, a report will be issued, and the USOC's board of directors will make the final decision.

The process could take several weeks to a few months. USA Gymnastics will continue to operate as usual during the revocation process. If it is stripped of its NGB status, the USOC would take control of the elite programs until a new NGB is identified. USA Gymnastics could continue to exist, but its members would likely migrate to a new group.

The USOC has revoked NGB status or cut off funding only three times, with taekwondo, team handball, and modern pentathlon. However, the USOC had no choice but to intervene with USA Gymnastics due to its repeated missteps in dealing with the Larry Nassar scandal. Nassar, the longtime team physician for USA Gymnastics and Michigan State, is serving an effective life sentence after pleading guilty to child pornography and sexual abuse charges.

USA Gymnastics has been through three CEOs since 2016, with the latest, Mary Bono, lasting only five days due to heavy criticism from gymnasts about her fitness to lead and the message her hiring sent to survivors. The federation is also mired in mediation with survivors, has lost all major sponsors, and held its national championships without a title sponsor in August.

The final straw for the USOC was USA Gymnastics' recent discovery of medical records from the Karolyi ranch that two executives had told Congress were nowhere to be found. Penny, who ordered the removal of the records, was indicted in Walker County, Texas, in September on a count of tampering with evidence.

USA Gymnastics has defended itself by saying its board inherited "an organization in crisis" when it was seated in June and is taking steps to reform. However, the moves might have come too late.

"Creed," the seventh installment in the Rocky series, is a refreshing departure from the trailers' promised brutal boxing melodrama. Instead, it delivers an excellent sequel that introduces new characters while paying homage to the enduring appeal of its predecessors. The film follows the themes and gambits of classic fight films, but it is far from a paint-by-numbers imitation.

The plot revolves around Adonis Johnson Creed, the out-of-wedlock, essentially abandoned child of the late champ Apollo Creed. Adonis, played by Michael B. Jordan, aspires to climb up the ranks to the top of the professional totem pole in boxing. He must learn how to protect his fragile soul on his way to the championship.

Adonis' mentor is Rocky Balboa, who returns to his archetypal role in a touching, deeply felt performance by Sylvester Stallone. Rocky, now 69, is no longer the main character but definitely a main character. He has the adorable, hangdog demeanor of an aged pet bulldog, making him the ideal sidekick for Adonis in this mismatched buddy picture.

Stallone's performance as Rocky is sly, pushing away the tough guy iconography of Rocky and revealing the man. Tessa Thompson plays Adonis' girlfriend, reaching just as deep as the nightclub singer who demands 100 percent honesty from him at all times.

The story builds through a trio of key fight scenes, one three-minute barrage composed with no visible cuts as if the camera is realistically capturing a real brawl. The film is morally sound beginning to end, with Adonis' title fight triggering giddy heights of cathartic glee, but the stirring finale comes as Stallone and Jordan slowly mount the steps of the Philadelphia Museum of Art, an image that leaves you undecided whether to cheer or get out your handkerchief.

Overall, "Creed" is a cornball, formulaic, and wonderfully delicious film that unabashedly manipulates audiences without guile, jerks tears, piles on hardships, and smooths out conflicts on its way to a wholesome, uplifting finale. It is a great team effort by Stallone and Jordan, with Stallone getting by more on an affable regular guy persona than talent. The film is rated PG-13 for violence, language, and some sensuality.

Tiger Woods is planning to return to the PGA tour in the Spring, following his completion of rehab for sexual addiction. He is currently undergoing treatment at Pine Grove Behavioral Health and Addiction Services in Hattiesburg, Mississippi, and is aiming to show everyone that he intends to change. His wife Elin has not visited him during his rehab, and there is speculation about the future of their marriage. Tiger has been linked to at least 14 women during his marriage, with his most recent affair being with Rachel Uchitel. He has not been seen in public since driving into a fire hydrant and tree in the early morning hours after Thanksgiving.

The Hart family, consisting of Jennifer and Sarah Hart and their six adopted children, were on a road trip from Oregon to California when their vehicle plunged off a cliff on March 26, 2018, killing five people and leaving three children missing. Investigators have determined that the family traveled south from Newport, Oregon on US-101 until they reached Highway 1 in Legget, California. They stayed in the Fort Bragg area until around 9 p.m. on March 25, and Jennifer Hart was spotted at a Safeway in Fort Bragg at 8:05 a.m. on March 25. The family's route goes cold after this point, and a possible sighting of Jennifer Hart in a surveillance video from Fort Bragg is being investigated. The three missing children are still presumed to be in the vehicle at the time of the crash. The crash is believed to have been intentional, as there were no skid marks at the top of the cliff and the vehicle's software data suggests that the driver accelerated off the cliff. Sarah Hart had a domestic assault conviction in Minnesota in 2011, and a former friend of the family reported to Oregon welfare officials in 2013 that the children were being deprived of food as punishment. The search for the three missing children is ongoing.

The story highlights two brothers, Tamerlan and Dzhokar Tsarnaev, who came to America with their family to start a new life. Tamerlan, 26, was a talented boxer who represented New England as a heavyweight in the National Golden Gloves boxing tournament and aspired to make it on an Olympic team. Dzhokar, 19, graduated from Cambridge Rindge & Latin School and was awarded a $2,500 scholarship. He was also an athlete, a wrestler, and was named student athlete of the month.

However, something went wrong, and the brothers became the suspects behind the Boston Marathon bombings that occurred on April 15, 2013. The bombings killed three people and wounded at least 170. The brothers were the target of a massive manhunt, and Tamerlan was shot and killed by police early Friday, while Dzhokar was taken into custody Friday night.

The story also includes photographs of the aftermath of the bombings, the manhunt for the suspects, and the arrest of Dzhokar. It also includes interviews with people who knew the brothers, including their aunt, who described them as nice, friendly, and quiet. The story also mentions that the FBI interviewed Tamerlan in early 2011 following a tip from a foreign government that he was a follower of radical Islam and was preparing to leave the United States to join underground organizations. However, the FBI statement said that their investigation did not find any terrorism activity at the time.

The story also includes a timeline of events, starting with the brothers' arrival in America and ending with their arrest. It also mentions that the brothers' family is ethnic Chechens, whose small republic's attempts at independence following the collapse of the Soviet Union were brutally crushed by Moscow. Both brothers were born in the Central Asian state of Kyrgyzstan, and Dzhokhar was a naturalized U.S. citizen.

The story also mentions that the FBI is scouring government data banks to determine if spy and police agencies missed potential clues that might have alerted them to the two brothers. It also mentions that investigators are trying to determine whether the brothers had any confederates either inside the United States or overseas.

Overall, the story provides a comprehensive summary of the Boston Marathon bombings, the manhunt for the suspects, and the background of the brothers involved. It also includes photographs and interviews with people who knew the brothers, as well as information about the FBI's investigation into the bombings.

The study published in the BMJ suggests that a round of golf can confer longevity benefits just as robust as a 100-mile bike ride. The research is based on the mortality records of 9,889 athletes who competed in the Olympic Games between 1896 and 1936. The study found that engaging in cycling and rowing (high cardiovascular intensity) had no added survival benefit compared with playing golf or cricket (low cardiovascular intensity).

The study adds to a small but growing body of research suggesting that years-long doses of extreme exercise, measured by amount or intensity, may be unproductive, if not counterproductive. The research suggests that the well-established longevity benefits of exercise may cease to accrue or may even diminish beyond a point, for instance, 20 miles a week of running.

The study found that athletes from disciplines with a high risk of bodily collision and high levels of physical contact had higher mortality than other Olympians later in life. However, the research is too preliminary and controversial to trigger warnings against marathons and triathlons. The study's authors suggest that high-intensity exercise can cause micro traumata that accumulate over time, leading to damage and aging.

The study was conducted by a vitality-and-aging department at Leiden University Medical Centre in Leiden, Netherlands. The authors of the study are R Zwiers, F W A Zantvoord, F M Engelaer, D van Bodegom, F J G van der Ouderaa, R G J Westendorp, and F Engelaer. The study was published in the Christmas edition of BMJ.

The Eta Aquarid meteor shower, caused by Earth's collision with debris from Halley's Comet, will be visible from May 5 to May 6. The radiant, where meteors appear to emerge from, rises along with the constellation Aquarius in the early morning hours. Viewers with clear skies and minimal light pollution can expect to see between 10 to 20 meteors per hour. The morning of May 5 is predicted to have slightly more meteors visible. If weather conditions are unfavorable, viewers can watch a live show hosted by the Slooh Community Observatory. The shower is known for producing "persistent trains" - colorful, glowing streaks that can last from a few seconds to several minutes after the meteor has disappeared. These are believed to be caused by the exceptional speed of the meteoroids, which ionize air molecules or chemically react with ozone and oxygen to produce the glow. The Slooh show begins at 8 p.m. EDT on May 5. The meteor shower will peak on May 5 and end around May 28.

During the third night of the Democratic National Convention, President Barack Obama surprised attendees with a friendly kiss on the mouth to Jill Biden, the wife of his running mate, Joe Biden. This unexpected moment sparked discussions about the various ways an accidental kiss can unfold, ranging from a potential romantic advance to a humorous situation with a close friend or family member.

In some cases, an accidental kiss with a crush might lead to further advancements or create confusion. On the other hand, if the kiss is with an inappropriate person, such as a boss or family member, it may require a firm apology or denial.

President Obama has a history of using kisses to win over potential adversaries and reward friends, particularly women. One notable instance was his kiss with Diane Sawyer during an ABC News interview. Obama's affectionate nature towards powerful women has also been evident in his interactions with Hillary Clinton and Carla Bruni, the French first lady.

Recently, a lack of a customary kiss between Obama and Carla Bruni during a NATO summit in Strasbourg, France, caused a stir in the media. Despite the initial handshake, the two eventually shared a polite double kiss at a later dinner.

Michelle Obama's fashion choices during the summit also attracted attention, as she wore a magenta dress by Thakoon, a significant price upgrade from her previous J. Crew ensembles. In comparison, Carla Bruni opted for a simple grey Dior coat.

In summary, the unexpected kiss between Barack Obama and Jill Biden during the Democratic National Convention has sparked discussions about the various ways an accidental kiss can unfold, while also highlighting the President's affectionate nature towards powerful women and Michelle Obama's fashionable choices during the NATO summit.

A former Dallas police officer, Amber Guyger, has been indicted on a murder charge for the shooting death of Botham Shem Jean, an unarmed black man, in his own apartment on September 6th. Guyger initially claimed she entered Jean's apartment, thinking it was her own, and shot him in self-defense. The indictment comes two months after the shooting incident, which sparked protests in Dallas.

Guyger was originally charged with manslaughter but was indicted on a more serious murder charge. District Attorney Faith Johnson stated that the grand jury presented the evidence and explained the law, leading to the murder charge. Johnson explained that murder constitutes someone intentionally and knowingly committing a crime, while manslaughter involves recklessly doing something.

Guyger's attorney, Robert Rogers, expressed disappointment but not surprise at the indictment. He stated that Guyger believed she was acting in self-defense and is confident that a jury will find her not guilty. Dallas Police Chief U. Reneè Hall stated that the department continues to feel anguish about the event and has developed a framework for policy change, including restructuring the Citizen Review Board, revamping implicit bias training, and seeking input from employee advisory and community advisory boards.

Jean's family, represented by attorney S. Lee Merritt, stated that the grand jury decision is a step towards justice. Allison Jean, Jean's mother, expressed satisfaction with the murder indictment and stated that her son did not deserve to be killed. The family has also filed a lawsuit against Guyger and the city, alleging excessive force and a pattern of police violence against minorities.

The indictment is a significant development in the case, as it represents a higher level of accountability for police officers who use deadly force. The case will now move forward to trial, and it is expected to take more than a year before Guyger appears in court. The Lawyers' Committee for Civil Rights Under Law stated that the indictment is an important reminder that police derive their authority from the people and must be held accountable when they fail to exercise it lawfully.

Coca-Cola has ventured into the alcoholic beverage market for the first time by launching a lemon-flavored alcopop in Japan. This move marks a significant shift in the company's 125-year history. The new product, which ranges from 3% to 8% alcohol, is modeled after the popular Chu-Hi drinks in Japan, known for their fruit flavors and popularity among young women. The drinks are not currently planned to be sold outside of Japan.

The launch of these new drinks comes as Coca-Cola aims to tap into new markets and consumer bases. Chu-Hi drinks, an abbreviation for shochu highball, have been marketed as an alternative to beer and have proven particularly popular among female drinkers. Local companies like Suntory, Asahi, and Kirin currently dominate the sector for canned Chu-Hi drinks, with strong citrus flavors like grapefruit and lemon being the most popular.

The new Coca-Cola drinks were met with curiosity at a sampling event in Fukuoka, with some attendees expressing surprise at the company's foray into Japanese-style alcohol. The launch of these new drinks recalls the boom of alcopop drinks in Europe and the UK during the 1990s, with brands like Smirnoff Ice and Bacardi Breezer becoming popular, although these drinks were controversial due to concerns they encouraged young people to drink more alcohol due to their soft drink-like taste. Coca-Cola has not yet announced any plans to bring the new drinks range to markets outside of Japan.

The United Nations annual climate change summit in Cancun, Mexico, concluded with the adoption of a set of agreements that lay the groundwork for future negotiations. The deal, which took four years of negotiations to reach, should lead to less deforestation, the transfer of technology to developing countries, and the establishment of a yearly fund, potentially worth up to $100bn, to help countries adapt to climate change. The deal, however, falls short of a global treaty and pushes many of the most important decisions to future negotiations.

The agreement was hailed as restoring faith in the multilateral UN process but will not reduce temperatures as much as scientists say is needed. The deal was reached after more than 190 countries attempted to agree on the best way to cut carbon emissions, with the last attempt in Copenhagen ending in chaos. The Cancun deal commits all countries to keeping temperature rise below 2C (3.6F) by reducing emissions. Rich countries have agreed to consider an extension of the Kyoto Protocol while poor countries will sign up to emission cuts for the first time.

There are also a series of key decisions on setting up a green fund to help poor countries cope with climate change and halting deforestation. The deal was greeted with strong reservations by environment groups, with some calling it a slap in the face of those who suffer from climate change. Critics argue that the agreement does not go far enough to reduce emissions and could still lead to a temperature rise of 5C.

The debate over the agreement was heated, with Bolivia claiming it was tantamount to genocide because cuts are not tough enough to stop dangerous global warming. However, after repeated attempts to achieve consensus, the UN decision was taken without the agreement of the South American country. The deal was finally adopted after intense pressure from the chair of the talks and other countries.

The Mexican presidency was roundly praised for its handling of the negotiations, with many praising its efforts to maintain transparency and inclusiveness. The deal will be further worked out as climate change negotiations begin in 2011, and there will be a push to produce a legally binding treaty at the annual conference in Durban, South Africa, next year.

Researchers have discovered that the colorful and varied faces of Guenon monkeys, a group of over 25 species native to Central and West Africa, have evolved as a means to avoid crossbreeding. The study, published in the journal Nature Communications, used human facial recognition technology to identify and compare Guenon features, finding that their looks have evolved to become more distinctive from their close relatives. This is the best evidence to date of visual signs acting as a barrier to breeding across species.

Guenons often travel, feed, and sleep together, increasing the likelihood of mating with each other. Their faces feature differently colored eyebrow patches, ear tufts, nose spots, and mouth patches. In the 1980s, Oxford zoologist Jonathan Kingdon suggested that the variety of facial appearances was due to the need to identify their own species and avoid mating with others. However, he failed to find firm evidence for his theory.

The researchers, from New York University and Exeter University, wanted to test Kingdon's explanation by using modern identification methods. They spent 18 months photographing 22 species of Guenons in zoos in the US and UK and in a wildlife sanctuary in Nigeria. Primates' features were distinguished and compared with other species using a computer program developed for human face recognition (known as the eigenface technique).

The results showed that the face patterns of Guenon species have evolved to become more visually distinctive from other Guenons, especially those they come into contact with and are at risk of crossbreeding with. The researchers believe this is the strongest evidence to date for a role of visual signals in the key evolutionary processes by which species are formed and maintained.

The team is now carrying out more research to find out whether Guenons are more distinctive from those species they now live beside or those they were living with at the time their species emerged. The study provides insights into the evolution of species and the role of visual signals in maintaining species boundaries.

The latest ABC News/Washington Post poll indicates a challenging political landscape for both President Barack Obama and potential Republican candidates, particularly former Massachusetts Governor Mitt Romney and former Alaska Governor Sarah Palin.

Romney is currently in a statistical tie with Obama, running evenly with him among all Americans and leading him among registered voters. However, Obama still leads other potential Republican opponents, with Palin trailing Obama by 17 points among all adults and 15 points among registered voters.

Despite her advancement in GOP primary preference, Palin faces significant challenges. Sixty-four percent of Americans say they will not vote for her for president, and 63% describe her as unqualified for the job. Even within her own party, 41% of Republicans rule out voting for her, and 39% see her as unqualified.

The poll also reveals a lack of enthusiasm for the Republican field, with fewer than half of Republicans and Republican-leaning independents describing themselves as satisfied with their choice of candidates for the nomination. This is significantly lower than the level of satisfaction in June 2007.

The risks to Obama are underscored by the ABC News Frustration Index, which stands at 68, similar to what it was going into the 2010 midterm elections. The index correlates strongly with House re-election rates and presidential prospects alike.

The index peaked at 80 in 2008, when the Democrats regained the White House, and at 73 in summer 1992, shortly before the first President Bush lost re-election. The index was 67 last fall, when the GOP regained the House and scored major inroads in the Senate.

The index today is a relatively mild 50 among Democrats, but a boiling 80 among Republicans – and close to it, 72, among independents, the quintessential swing voters in national elections.

The poll also highlights potential risks for Romney, particularly from the health care plan he signed into law as governor of Massachusetts in 2006. A majority of leaned Republicans oppose that plan, and while a mere 3% support it strongly, 25% describe themselves as strong opponents.

Palin, for her part, does slightly better with white evangelical Republicans than with non-evangelicals, but Romney edges Palin among conservative potential GOP voters, and runs evenly with her among supporters of the Tea Party political movement.

In head-to-head matchups with Obama, Palin trails by 17 percentage points, the worst of the six possible candidates tested. The president leads Gingrich and former Utah governor Jon Huntsman Jr. by 10 points. He runs 11 points ahead of former Minnesota governor Tim Pawlenty and 13 points ahead of Rep. Michele Bachmann (Minn.).

Romney owes his relatively good standing against the president to support from independents. He and Obama garner roughly equal percentages from those in their own parties. But independents split for Romney 50% to 43%.

Overall, the poll suggests a pessimistic mood in the country this spring as higher gasoline prices, sliding home values, and a disappointing employment picture have raised fresh concerns about the pace of the economic recovery. Nearly six in 10 Americans say the economy has not started to recover, regardless of what official statistics may say, and most of those who say it has improved rate the recovery as weak.

The survey was conducted June 2-5, 2011, among a random national sample of 1,002 adults, including landline and cell-phone-only respondents. Results for the full sample have a 3.5-point error margin.

The head of the Senate Intelligence Committee, Senator Dianne Feinstein, has accused the CIA of improperly searching a stand-alone computer network established for Congress, potentially violating several laws and constitutional principles. The dispute centers around the CIA's investigation into allegations of CIA abuse in a Bush-era detention and interrogation program.

Feinstein claimed that the CIA searched the network in January, raising concerns about an agreement made with the committee regarding the monitoring of their use of CIA computers. The CIA, however, denies spying on the Senate Intelligence Committee.

The controversy has led to calls for an independent probe, with Senator John McCain suggesting that such a move may be necessary. The White House, meanwhile, has expressed confidence in CIA Director John Brennan.

Feinstein has demanded an apology and acknowledgment that the CIA's actions were wrong, but has not received one. She has also referred the matter to the Justice Department for possible criminal prosecution.

The dispute has blown wide open a dispute that has simmered behind the scenes in recent weeks, with Feinstein confirming that committee investigators had obtained documents detailing the interrogation policy, but the source of these documents remains unclear.

Feinstein's speech has been praised for its clarity and importance by fellow senators, with Senator Patrick J. Leahy calling it one of the best speeches he'd ever heard and Senate Majority Leader Harry M. Reid crediting Feinstein for speaking out and defending the separation of powers.

The study published in the International Journal of Obesity reveals that adults consume nearly 92% of the food they put on their plates, with minor variations depending on distractions and whether the meal is a snack or a meal. The study, led by Brian Wansink, director of the Cornell Food and Brand Lab, was conducted with Katherine Abowd Johnson from the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health. The study found that the urge to clean one's plate is not exclusive to the United States, as the results were consistent across several countries, including Canada, France, Taiwan, South Korea, Finland, and the Netherlands.

Interestingly, children were found to eat only about 60% of what they served, possibly due to uncertainty about whether they would like a particular food. The study also found that people who eat healthier foods, such as fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and lean meat or dairy, consume more (91.2%) than those who eat less healthful foods (80.6%).

The study aimed to fill a gap in research on portion size and its connection to the epidemic of overweight and obesity. By analyzing 14 studies, the researchers found that people are likely to consume almost all of what they serve themselves, which can help individuals be more mindful of appropriate portion size. Wansink suggests that next time one serves oneself, one should consider how much one wants to eat.

The document discusses the controversial decision by the Trump administration to ease penalties on Chinese telecommunications giant ZTE, which was banned for violating sanctions against Iran and North Korea. The deal, which involves a significant fine and management changes, has been met with criticism from top senators, including Chuck Schumer and Marco Rubio, who argue that ZTE is a notorious intellectual property thief and should not be rewarded for its behavior.

The article highlights ZTE's history of intellectual property theft, citing over 126 patent infringement lawsuits in the US alone in the last five years, and additional lawsuits in other countries. ZTE is accused of thumbing its nose at traditional rules of fair play in intellectual property matters, commonly engaging in delay, misrepresentation, and hold out when dealing with patent owners.

The article also discusses ZTE's treatment of San Francisco-based Via Licensing Corp, a patent pool operator, and how ZTE quit the patent pool in 2017 without paying for its use of other members' patents. Via and its member companies are still trying to get ZTE to pay for its use of their intellectual property.

The deal with ZTE is seen as a concession to China by the Trump administration, and has been met with resistance in Congress. U.S. intelligence and law enforcement agencies have serious concerns that ZTE and other Chinese telecommunications firms use their equipment to gather intelligence on US citizens. The U.S. Department of Defense has also stopped selling ZTE's mobile phones and modems in stores on its military bases, citing potential security risks.

The deal is expected to be announced by Commerce Secretary Wilbur Ross in the coming days, and is part of a broader effort to prevent a trade war between the US and China. ZTE needs US components for its mobile phones and network equipment, and US companies provide an estimated 25-30% of components in ZTE's equipment. The deal is expected to lift the ban on ZTE buying US products, which has crippled the company and caused it to lose over $3 billion since the ban was imposed in April.

In a landmark decision, an Ontario Court judge has found animal activist Anita Krajnc not guilty of mischief for giving water to pigs outside a slaughterhouse. The case, which attracted international attention, had been ongoing for two years and was seen as a rallying point for animal rights activists. Krajnc, the founder of Toronto Pig Save, was charged after she poured water into the openings of a metal trailer outside Fearman's Pork Inc. in Burlington, Ont., in June 2015.

The trial included five days of testimony, and if convicted, Krajnc could have been fined and sent to jail for six months. However, Justice David Harris dismissed the charge, stating that Krajnc did not obstruct the "lawful use" of property. He noted that the pigs had made it to their final destination despite Krajnc's actions, and that the slaughterhouse had never refused to accept a load of pigs for that reason.

Krajnc's lawyers argued that pigs are persons and not property, and drew comparisons between her actions and those of historical figures such as Mahatma Gandhi and Nelson Mandela. However, Harris rejected these comparisons, stating that under Canadian law, pigs are considered property, not persons.

Farm groups expressed their disappointment with the decision, stating that it could embolden animal rights activists and spark further confrontations between the two groups. Krajnc and her supporters marked the decision with a vegan lunch at the courthouse before heading to a nearby slaughterhouse to hold an afternoon vigil.

This is not the end of Krajnc's legal woes, as she is also charged with obstructing police after a truck rollover near Fearman's in October. Her next appearance on that charge is May 17 in Milton court.

The Islamic State (ISIS) group has launched a new media arm, the Zora Foundation, which targets women supporting Islamist fighters by providing guidelines on how to be "good wives of jihad". The organization's slogan is "preparing for the honor of jihad", and it has already gained over 2,000 followers on social media.

Zora's material, all in Arabic, has been shared by ISIS supporters across social media. The latest post from the al-Zora Media Twitter account was a recipe shared with the introduction: "To the victorious supporters [of jihad] and the beloved muhajiraat [for example, women who go to Syria], may Allah bless their efforts and reward them accordingly, we dedicate this first recipe to the heroes on the front line."

Charlie Winter, a researcher at the Quilliam Foundation, said that Zora is aimed at those preparing to go out and support the group, while also acting as a facility for the women already out there. He added that he hasn't seen anything like this before, and that there will probably be forums doing similar things online, but this is the first time he's come across an actual media organization giving guidance to women on their role.

The emergence of ISIS can be traced back to 2000, when Abu Musab al-Zarqawi formed an al-Qaeda splinter group in Iraq, al-Qa’eda in Iraq. Its brutality from the beginning alienated Iraqis and many al-Qaeda leaders. In 2014, ISIS declared itself the Caliphate, calling itself Islamic State (IS), and captured Mosul, Iraq’s second largest city, Tal Afar, just 93 miles from the Syrian border, and the central Iraqi city of Tikrit. These advances sent shockwaves around the world.

ISIS has also been involved in brutal executions and violent atrocities, training regimes for fighters, and threats to the West as the US-led coalition air strikes continue. The group has raised its flag in key cities and has been responsible for the murder of several Western hostages.

ISIS has also been profiting from cross-border trade with Turkey, with Turkish traders of everything from energy drinks to cement benefiting from the conflict. While Turkey imposed financial sanctions on Assad three years ago, the trade is legal and shows up in Turkish customs data. Transporters enter a no-man's land where state control is absent and they pay whoever controls the crossing.

Overall, the emergence of the Zora Foundation and its focus on women supporting ISIS highlights the group's continued efforts to recruit and maintain support, despite its brutal tactics and violent actions. The group's new media arm is just one of many ways in which ISIS is using social media to spread its message and recruit new followers.

McDonald's has reintroduced its Mighty Wings after a price reduction of 40% due to poor sales last year. The bone-in chicken wings, which were originally priced at $1 per wing, are now sold in packs of 5 for $3, making them approximately 60 cents each. This price reduction is aimed at making the wings more competitive in the market.

McDonald's initially faced challenges with Mighty Wings due to consumer resistance to the high price and the spiciness of the wings. However, the company has not changed the recipe, but there is now more awareness about the wings' spicy kick.

The reduced price is a strategic move to clear excess inventory accumulated at the end of 2013, when Mighty Wings were launched nationally. The new price reduces operating margins on wings by about 10 percentage points, but McDonald's is willing to take a slight loss to sell the excess inventory.

The national advertising campaign for Mighty Wings began this week, and while it's too early to write off the product, its success depends on whether the new price will drive sales. Scott Hume, founder of the BurgerBusiness.com blog, suggests that if Mighty Wings sell well at the new price, they will likely continue, but if not, McDonald's may reconsider offering wings in the future.

The article from the Daily Mail discusses the raid on Osama Bin Laden's compound in Abbottabad, Pakistan, where Bin Laden was killed by U.S. Navy SEALs. Three of Bin Laden's wives and several of his children were taken into custody by Pakistani intelligence forces after the raid. However, there is speculation that one of Bin Laden's sons, Hamza, who has been dubbed the "Crown Prince of Terror," may have escaped during the raid. This information came from Pakistani security officials during the interrogation of Bin Laden's wives. Another son, Khalid, was confirmed dead by the U.S. military. The article also discusses the details of the U.S. special forces team that was sent to find Bin Laden, including the president's insistence that the task-force had to be large enough to fight off hostile Pakistani soldiers if necessary. The article also mentions that Hamza has been implicated in the murder of Pakistani leader Benazir Bhutto and has appeared in Bin Laden's propaganda videos.

The study reveals that Mars once had a massive ancient ocean covering nearly half of its northern hemisphere, making it a more promising place for alien life. The ocean, which covered a fifth of the planet's surface and was a mile deep in places, held 20 million cubic kilometers of water. This evidence adds to the emerging picture of Mars as a warm and wet world in its youth, with streams, winding river deltas, and long-standing lakes.

The infrared maps show that water near the Martian ice caps is enriched with deuterium, indicating that Mars must have lost a vast amount of water in the past, equivalent to more than six times that now locked up in the planet's frozen ice caps. The scientists calculate that the amount of water was enough to create a global ocean that covered the entire surface of Mars to a depth of 137 meters.

The ocean lasted for millions of years but over time, the Martian atmosphere thinned, causing more ocean water to waft into space. The planet lost much of its insulation too, causing the ocean to recede and eventually freeze. Today, only 13% of the ocean remains, locked up in the Martian polar caps.

The study radically rewrites what many scientists believed only a decade ago, as flowing water was widely considered to have been a more erratic presence on Mars, gushing forth only rarely, and never forming long-standing seas and oceans. The search for life on Mars will ramp up in 2018 when the European Space Agency sends its Exomars rover to the red planet, looking for chemical signatures of life.

In Iran, the morality police have intensified a crackdown on the sale of Barbie dolls, viewing them as a threat to Islamic values due to perceived Western cultural influences. The dolls, manufactured by U.S. company Mattel Inc, were first declared un-Islamic in 1996. Despite earlier bans, they were openly sold in Tehran shops until recently, when shopkeepers were ordered to hide them behind other toys to avoid closure.

The Iranian government's efforts to combat Western cultural influences date back to the Islamic revolution in 1979, which saw the enforcement of Islamic dress codes, bans on Western music, and restrictions on foreign satellite television.

In a further move against the West, Iranian media reported that toy versions of the U.S. spy drone captured by Iran in December will soon be available for sale. The models, which will be one eightieth the size of the original aircraft, are set to be mass-produced in various colors and sold on the Iranian market for around $4. However, the Iranian government has rejected a formal request from the U.S. administration to return the drone, considering its incursion into Iranian airspace as an invasion and a hostile act.

In summary, Iran's morality police are enforcing a ban on Barbie dolls, citing their perceived threat to Islamic values. Meanwhile, Iranian companies are planning to sell toy versions of the U.S. spy drone captured by Iran, and the Iranian government has rejected a U.S. request to return the drone. These actions reflect the ongoing tension between Iran and the West.

The United States is reconsidering its support for Israel at the United Nations following Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's comments during the Israeli election that appeared to reject a two-state solution for Israel and Palestine. Netanyahu, in an interview with MSNBC, affirmed his support for a two-state solution but stated that circumstances must change for it to be achievable. White House Press Secretary Josh Earnest characterized Netanyahu's comments as a "cynical Election Day tactic" and hinted that the US may support a UN Security Council resolution laying down the principles for a two-state solution or a Palestinian bid to join the UN as a full member. The Israeli-US Strategic Partnership Act, which passed the House of Representatives last December, identified a two-state solution as a US goal to resolve the conflict with the Palestinians. Netanyahu also faced criticism for comments made during the election urging his supporters to counteract the effect of Arab voters, which Earnest said "erode at the values that are critical to the bond between our two countries." Despite this, Netanyahu stated that there is an "unbreakable bond" between the US and Israel and downplayed strains in his personal relationship with President Barack Obama. The White House has stated that it will be carefully watching the actions of Netanyahu, his party, and his coalition moving forward.

A newly discovered sketchbook of post-Impressionist artist Vincent Van Gogh, containing works never before released to the public, will be published by French publisher Seuil in November. The sketches, titled "Vincent Van Gogh, Le Brouillard d'Arles" (The Fog of Arles), are described as "stunning, dazzling" by Seuil officials. Details about the origin and discovery of the sketches are scarce, with the publisher promising to reveal more at a press conference in Paris in mid-November. The sketches have generated excitement and anticipation, with expectations running high for their release.

The second-born giant panda cub born to Mei Xiang at the Smithsonian National Zoo in Washington, D.C., died on August 26, 2015. The smaller cub, born five hours after its twin on August 22, went into cardiac arrest and could not be revived despite extreme efforts by the dedicated zoo staff. The larger cub, born first, appears to be strong and healthy and is with its mother. The zoo's chief veterinarian, Donald Neiffer, said that despite the loss, they remain optimistic about the future of the surviving panda. A necropsy will be performed to determine the exact cause of the cub's death. Mei Xiang, who was artificially inseminated in April, has had a history of losing cubs, with one stillborn in 2013 and another dying in 2012 after six days. She has two other surviving cubs, born in 2013 and 2005.

On Saturday, Algerian troops ended a four-day siege at a natural gas plant in the Sahara, where militants had taken foreign and local workers hostage. The siege resulted in at least 81 deaths, with many bodies found so badly disfigured that it was unclear whether they were hostages or militants. The Algerian government said at least 32 extremists and 23 hostages were killed during the assault. However, on Sunday, Algerian bomb squads found 25 more bodies, raising the overall death toll.

The crisis began on Wednesday when militants attacked two buses carrying foreign workers to the remote site in south-eastern Algeria. The militants then took Algerians and expatriates hostage at the complex, which was quickly surrounded by the Algerian army. The leader of the hostage-takers was a veteran fighter from Niger, named as Abdul Rahman al-Nigeri by the Mauritanian news agency ANI, which had been in contact with the militants.

The militants initially said the operation was payback for French military intervention in neighboring Mali, where al-Qaida-linked rebels are on the march, but later they said it was two months in the planning, long before France sent in troops. The dead were known to include American, Filipino, and French workers. Algerian authorities said 685 of their citizens, the backbone of the workforce, escaped without saying how many may have died. More than two dozen foreigners were unaccounted for.

The Algerian government has been criticized for its tough response to the crisis, favoring military action over negotiation. The Masked Brigade, which claimed responsibility for the attack in the name of al-Qaida, demanded the release of 100 prisoners held by the Algerian government in exchange for the hostages. However, the Algerian government refused to negotiate with the militants.

The crisis has raised concerns about the threat of terrorism in North Africa and other parts of the world. US President Barack Obama's senior adviser, David Plouffe, said that al-Qaida and al-Qaida-affiliated groups remain a threat and that the US is determined to help other countries destroy those networks. French Foreign Minister Laurent Fabius said that the terrorists were to blame for the hostages' deaths.

The Vatican is investigating a leak of Pope Francis' much-anticipated environmental encyclical, "Laudato Si" (Be Praised), which was published early by Italian newsweekly L'Espresso. The Vatican called the document a draft, but it covered many of the same points as Francis' recent statements. L'Espresso's veteran Vatican correspondent, Sandro Magister, was suspended indefinitely for the publication, with Magister claiming that his editor, not he, obtained the document. The encyclical addresses global warming, calling for a change in human behavior to save the planet and prevent the poor from suffering the effects of industrial degradation. Some speculate that the leak was aimed at undermining the official launch of the encyclical, which features a Catholic cardinal, an Orthodox theologian, an atheist scientist, and an economist discussing its contents. The Vatican has a history of leaked documents, with the last major scandal occurring in 2012, resulting in the pope's butler being put on trial for stealing private papers. The Vatican City State updated its criminal code to include penalties for leaking Vatican documents or publishing news from them. Sandro Magister is a well-respected vaticanista, known for his accuracy and insight into the Vatican's inner workings. He has a history of predicting papal policies and has been credited with accurately predicting Pope Benedict XVI's skeptical approach to Islam. Reading the mind of a pope is a risky business, but Magister is known for his ability to discern the influences within the Vatican.

In Poland, a controversial raid on the offices of news magazine Wprost, aimed at finding leaked tapes that embarrassed the government, has sparked controversy and concerns over journalistic confidentiality. The tapes, which were published earlier this week, allegedly contain a private conversation between Poland's top banker and a minister, discussing political matters that are deemed inappropriate under Polish law as the central bank must remain independent of politics.

The raid, led by a prosecutor and state security agents, was broadcast live on several TV channels. The editor of Wprost claimed that physical force was used in an attempt to seize his laptop. The justice minister, Marek Biernacki, has criticized the raid, stating that it raised legitimate concerns and could be considered as "too far-reaching".

The leaked recordings have put Prime Minister Donald Tusk under severe pressure, with Tusk backing the involved parties and calling the recordings an attempt at a coup d'etat. The emergence of the tapes and the government's handling of the situation has led to discussions of a snap election.

The tapes also raise questions about who made the recordings and why they surfaced now, at a time of significant shifts in regional security. Potential suspects include political enemies, disgruntled security operatives, or Russian agents. The businessman who provided the tapes to Wprost has not been identified.

The conversation in the tapes is critical to understanding the comments made, as it reflects the earlier frustration of Poland's top officials about the United States' interest in deepening its commitment to regional security. However, Russia's annexation of Crimea turned that attitude around, as shown by President Obama's warm reception in Warsaw this month.

Colgate Total® toothpaste, a trusted brand for oral health for over 20 years, is uniquely formulated with triclosan, an antibacterial ingredient, to combat harmful plaque germs that cause common oral health issues. With over 90 clinical studies and involving over 20,000 people, the efficacy and safety of Colgate Total® are well-established.

Clinical studies have shown that Colgate Total® reduces the germs that cause gum disease, providing 12-hour protection against plaque germs that can lead to gingivitis, a common issue affecting 75% of American adults. If left unchecked, gingivitis can progress to periodontitis, a more serious stage of infection that can result in tooth and bone loss.

The FDA has acknowledged the benefits of triclosan in Colgate Total® toothpaste, stating that it is effective in preventing gingivitis. The Cochrane Oral Health Group, in a review of oral health benefits of triclosan/copolymer, the active antibacterial system in Colgate Total® toothpaste, found that after six or more months of use, it provided a 22% reduction in plaque and gingivitis, a 41% reduction in plaque severity, and a 48% reduction in gum bleeding compared to traditional fluoride toothpaste.

Colgate Total® is the only toothpaste that provides both antibacterial protection and direct anti-inflammatory action, emphasizing the importance of good oral health and its connection to overall health. The FDA's final rule, issued in 2013, prohibits the marketing of antibacterial soaps and body washes containing triclosan and triclocarban, but Colgate Total® toothpaste continues to be available.

However, the FDA has raised concerns about the long-term use of triclosan in consumer products, citing potential hormonal effects and the development of bacterial resistance to antibiotics. The FDA and the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) are collaborating to review the effects of triclosan from different perspectives.

In conclusion, Colgate Total® toothpaste, with its unique formulation and extensive clinical support, continues to be a trusted choice for maintaining healthy teeth and gums. While concerns about triclosan exist, the benefits of Colgate Total® toothpaste in preventing oral health problems outweigh these concerns for many users.

In this summary, two significant issues related to security and violence are highlighted, one involving the White House and the other concerning the National Football League (NFL).

Firstly, following a security breach at the White House, Rep. Peter King has called for a full investigation and potential congressional hearings. A man was able to jump the White House fence and enter the North Portico doors, despite the first family not being present at the time. Rep. King, a member of the House Homeland Security Committee, deemed this incident inexcusable, especially given the current heightened security concerns and the potential for complex assassination plots.

Secondly, Sen. Dianne Feinstein has urged the NFL to adopt a zero-tolerance policy for domestic abuse, following the arrest of 49ers defensive lineman Ray McDonald. Despite still being in the team's lineup for a Sunday game, Sen. Feinstein expressed shock and determination to address the issue. She emphasized the growth in violence in the league and called for suspensions for arrested players and termination upon conviction. Sen. Feinstein, a former mayor of San Francisco and long-time 49ers fan, acknowledged the league's past glory but stressed the need for the NFL to set an example for society and uphold the values of right and wrong.

Both incidents have sparked calls for action and investigations, with Rep. King focusing on White House security and Sen. Feinstein advocating for a stricter stance against domestic abuse in the NFL.

The Sodomite Suppression Act, a ballot initiative in California proposed by attorney Matt McLaughlin, calls for the execution of gay individuals and the imprisonment of those advocating for gay rights to minors. Despite its unconstitutional nature and lack of chance for collecting the necessary signatures, California Attorney General Kamala Harris is required by law to allow the measure to circulate for signatures.
