A new study suggests that a toxin produced by the bacterium Clostridium perfringens, responsible for a million cases of food poisoning in the U.S. each year, could potentially trigger multiple sclerosis (MS), an inflammatory disease affecting 400,000 Americans. Researchers at Weill Cornell Medical College in New York found that the toxin, called epsilon, targets the cells associated with MS and kills the brain's myelin-producing cells, similar to the damage seen in MS lesions. The study adds to a growing body of evidence linking epsilon toxin with MS, and if further studies confirm these findings, a vaccine or drug that neutralizes the toxin's ability to trigger MS could potentially stop or prevent the disease. However, experts urge caution and more research is needed to explore the link between epsilon toxin and MS.

In Los Angeles, an 11-year-old boy named Yonatan Daniel Aguilar was found dead in a small closet in his family's home, weighing only 34 pounds. Court documents obtained by the Los Angeles Times suggest that Yonatan had been hidden away in the closet for three years, often sedated with liquid sleep medication to keep him quiet.

Investigators believe that even Yonatan's stepfather, who lived in the home, was unaware of his presence. His mother, Veronica Aguilar, had previously managed to convince teachers, counselors, coaches, medical staff, and social workers that Yonatan was safe in her home, despite reports of possible child abuse.

Four years before his death, when Yonatan stopped attending school, his mother told people he had gone to live in an institution in Mexico. However, court documents indicate that Yonatan's three siblings and his mother were the only ones in on the secret.

Officials with the county Department of Children and Family Services (DCFS) had responded to six reports of possible abuse or neglect involving the family from 2009 to 2012 and marked the boy's risk of abuse "high" four times. However, they had no further contact after allegations of abuse were deemed inconclusive or unfounded, and no formal case was opened.

On August 22, 2016, Aguilar led her stepfather, Jose Pinzon, to the closet where Yonatan's emaciated body was found. Pinzon then ran to a nearby 7-Eleven and called the police. Aguilar is now charged with murder and child abuse causing death and remains jailed on $2 million bail.

On March 29, 2016, a man named Seif al-Din Mustafa hijacked an EgyptAir flight from Alexandria to Cairo and forced it to land in Larnaca, Cyprus. The hijacking was believed to be motivated by a personal dispute between Mustafa and his ex-wife who lives in Cyprus. Mustafa, described as mentally disturbed, used a fake suicide belt to hijack the plane and demanded to speak with his ex-wife upon landing.

Authorities in Egypt have requested Mustafa's extradition under a 1996 bilateral extradition treaty. He has been remanded in custody in Cyprus for eight days and faces charges including air piracy, kidnapping, and threatening behavior. Mustafa did not speak at his court appearance but gave a victory sign as he was driven away by police.

The hijacking incident lasted over six hours, during which almost all passengers and crew were freed unharmed. One crew member climbed out of a cockpit window minutes before Mustafa surrendered. Cypriot Foreign Minister Ioannis Kasoulides said Mustafa initially asked to speak with his Cypriot ex-wife, who was brought to the airport by police, before making a series of "incoherent" demands.

The incident has raised concerns about Egyptian airport security, particularly in light of the downing of a Russian plane over Sinai in October 2015. Egyptian authorities have stressed that their security measures were not to blame and praised the EgyptAir flight crew for their handling of the situation.

A photograph showing a British man posing with the hijacker inside the plane has been widely circulated. Ben Innes told the Sun newspaper he was trying to get a better look at Mustafa's belt. Egyptian press has expressed concern that the incident will affect tourism in Egypt.

Mustafa is set to appear in court on Wednesday where authorities will ask that he be held on a number of unspecified charges. Egyptian authorities have questioned Mustafa's relatives and have released surveillance video showing him being thoroughly searched at the Alexandria airport. Aviation expert Philip Baum praised the EgyptAir crew for their handling of the situation.

Florida has surpassed New York to become the third-most populous state in the United States, according to the U.S. Census Bureau's annual report released on Tuesday. With an estimated population of 19.9 million residents, Florida has overtaken New York's 19.7 million residents. Florida's population grew by 293,000 over the year, while New York's population expanded by only 51,000 residents.

The report shows that the U.S. population increased by three-quarters of a percent between July 1, 2013, and July 1, 2014, to 318.9 million residents. Forty-four states and the District of Columbia added population over the last year, while six states, including Illinois, West Virginia, Connecticut, New Mexico, Alaska, and Vermont, lost population. Puerto Rico experienced the largest population decline, with a 1.3 percent decrease or 47,000 residents.

The fastest-growing states were mostly in the West and the South, with the exception of North Dakota, where an energy boom is attracting new residents. Texas added the most residents, with 451,000, followed by California, Florida, and Georgia, all of which saw their populations grow by six figures. For the first time in its history, Georgia surpassed the 10 million resident mark.

Florida likely reached the milestone of surpassing New York's population sometime last spring, but it wasn't official until the Census said so. An Associated Press analysis earlier this year showed that ex-New Yorkers represented about 1 in 10 new Florida residents, while migrants from other countries made up about a quarter of Florida's new residents. California and Texas remain the largest and second-largest states, with populations of 38.8 million and 27 million residents, respectively. The other states rounding out the 10 largest in the nation are Illinois, Pennsylvania, Ohio, Georgia, North Carolina, and Michigan. Six states saw population declines, with North Dakota being the fastest-growing state.

On January 29, 2015, a 19-year-old man armed with a fake gun stormed into the headquarters of Dutch national broadcaster NOS in Hilversum, demanding airtime. The man, who claimed to be from a "hackers' collective," was arrested without a struggle after a brief standoff with police. The incident caused the broadcaster to be off-air for around an hour. The man threatened that bombs would go off at several locations around the Netherlands if his demand wasn't met, but police found no explosives during a search of the building. The suspect, from the small town of Pijnacker near The Hague, is being held on suspicion of making a threat, weapons possession, and taking a hostage. His name was not released by the prosecutor. The motive for the incident is still under investigation, and there was no immediate indication that it was related to Islamic extremism. The broadcaster later reported that the man had a silencer on the pistol and threatened a security guard, forcing him to take him upstairs to the editorial offices. The headquarters had beefed up security in the aftermath of the attack on satirical newspaper Charlie Hebdo that left 12 people dead in Paris. The media park in Hilversum, home to many Dutch broadcasters, has been tightly guarded for years, since populist Dutch politician Pim Fortuyn was gunned down in a parking lot there in 2002.

In Lumberton, North Carolina, a 3-week-old baby was recovered after a man mistook a doll in a stolen truck for an unresponsive infant, leading to the vehicle's recovery. The incident occurred on Monday when a woman reported her pickup truck stolen, along with her 3-week-old baby, while she was taking two other children inside a house.

The police issued an alert, and the truck and baby were abandoned in a nearby parking lot minutes later. A man walking past the truck noticed a window was down and saw a doll inside, believing it to be an unresponsive child. He called 911, and deputies from the Robeson County Sheriff's Office arrived and found the infant, unharmed, in the child-restraint seat.

No arrests have been made as of Tuesday, and police are looking for two suspects. The quick response of the man who saw the doll and the Sheriff's Office was credited for reuniting the mother and her child. Anyone with information is asked to contact Lumberton police Detective Deana Locklear.

On July 1, U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) at Los Angeles International Airport intercepted a shipment of 67 giant African snails, a highly invasive species that poses a threat to agriculture, the environment, and public health. The snails, weighing nearly 2 pounds each and measuring about 6 inches in length, arrived from Lagos, Nigeria, in two plastic baskets with paperwork stating they were for human consumption.

The mollusks, known as Archachatina marginata or giant African land snails, can consume over 500 types of plants and even eat the stucco and paint off houses if fruits and vegetables are not available. They can also carry several parasites harmful to humans, including one that can lead to meningitis.

CBP officials took preventative measures to quarantine the snails and sent specimens to a local U.S. Department of Agriculture lab for further examination. Experts identified the creatures, which can grow up to 8 inches in length and live up to 10 years in the wild, as the giant African snails.

After identification, the entire collection was turned over to the USDA, which disposed of the snails through incineration. This incident highlights the efforts of CBP agriculture specialists in protecting the nation's agriculture from the introduction of threatening foreign pests, plants, and diseases.

Tennessee Senator Stacey Campfield, known for his controversial statements, posted a joke about pressure cookers being used as weapons on his blog, a week after the Boston Marathon bombings that killed three people. The post, titled "Here comes Feinstein again," depicted a pressure cooker labeled as an "Assault Pressure Cooker" with features similar to military-style assault weapons. Campfield defended the post, stating that people need to "lighten up" and that it's insensitive to target gun rights after the Sandy Hook shooting.

The post sparked criticism, and Campfield responded by questioning the lack of outrage from the left over gun control after the Sandy Hook shooting. He further added that he was exposing a double standard. Campfield has a history of controversial statements, including dropping a bill linking a student's academic performance to their family's welfare benefits, threatening to cut funds for the University of Tennessee for promoting sex education, and proposing a law preventing students from being taught about homosexuality due to the higher HIV rate in the homosexual community.

In Flint, Michigan, two dogs have recently tested positive for lead toxicity, marking the state's first such cases involving dogs in five years. State Veterinarian Dr. James Averill confirmed the cases, which occurred in October 2015 and January 2016, but declined to disclose further details, citing confidentiality. Both dogs are still alive, and their tests were conducted in Genesee County, where high levels of lead in the tap water system have been a major crisis.

Officials continue to advise against drinking unfiltered tap water for both humans and pets. Averill suggests pet owners in Genesee County get their water tested, use filtered water for their pets, and avoid giving them unfiltered tap water. He also advises pet owners to watch for any deviations from their pets' normal behavior, as these could be signs of lead poisoning.

The state has not released details about the dogs' symptoms, weight, or age. However, Averill mentioned that mental dullness, possibly arthritis, and general malaise could be potential symptoms. He also emphasized the importance of seeking veterinary care if pets are not their normal selves.

The state provides reportable disease/condition case information down to the county level, but specifics about individual cases are kept confidential due to the Animal Industry Act of 1988. The "vast majority" of tests for lead in dogs have been negative, according to Averill, but he encourages pet owners to see their veterinarian if they notice their pets acting unusually.

If a veterinarian determines a dog may have lead toxicity, the lab testing is provided free of charge. However, symptoms can vary widely, making it challenging to diagnose. Dr. Michael Merrithew, a veterinarian near Flint, and Dr. Lawrence Ehrman, a veterinarian in Flint Township, both report not having seen any recent cases they'd attribute to lead, but they are monitoring for symptoms.

Averill suggests pet owners in Flint bathe their pets in tap water but only give them filtered or bottled water to drink. For those without immediate access to bottled or filtered water, melting snow could be a safer alternative to straight Flint water.

The first comprehensive map of the world's hidden groundwater has been published, providing insights into the planet's most exploited and precious natural resource. The study, led by Dr. Tom Gleeson of the University of Victoria, estimates that less than six percent of groundwater in the upper two kilometers of the Earth's landmass is renewable within a human lifetime.

The study, published in Nature Geoscience, estimates a total volume of nearly 23 million cubic kilometers of groundwater, with 0.35 million cubic kilometers being younger than 50 years old. Old groundwater, found deeper and often used for agriculture and industry, can contain harmful substances like arsenic and uranium, while modern groundwater, closer to the surface and more vulnerable to climate change and contamination, is a more renewable resource.

The study's maps show most modern groundwater in tropical and mountain regions, with significant deposits in the Amazon Basin, the Congo, Indonesia, and North and Central America. The least amount of modern groundwater is found in more arid regions such as the Sahara.

The study provides valuable information for water managers, policy developers, and scientists to better manage groundwater resources sustainably. The next step is to analyze the volumes of groundwater in relation to how much is being used and depleted.

Funding for the study came from the Natural Sciences and Research Council, Canadian Institute for Advanced Research, US National Science Foundation, and the American Geophysical Union. The full study can be found at http://nature.com/articles/doi:10.1038/ngeo2590. Media contacts are Dr. Tom Gleeson and Suzanne Ahearne of the University of Victoria.

The family of Ryder Johnson, a 20-year-old man from Lafayette, Colorado, is offering a $100,000 reward for information leading to his whereabouts. Johnson went missing on January 17, 2016, after finishing his shift at Eldora Mountain Resort near Nederland. His car was found later that night parked at 5800 Gross Dam Road in southwest Boulder County, but no signs of Johnson were found during extensive searches of the area.

Boulder County Sheriff's Office has stated that there have been no new leads in the case and no confirmed sightings. Johnson's parents are offering the reward for information that finds Johnson or has information that could lead to an arrest if foul play was involved in his disappearance. The reward is being funded by donations from friends and family, and the deadline to claim the reward is January 17, 2017, marking the one-year anniversary of his disappearance.

Investigators have not been able to rule out foul play, but it is likely that Johnson disappeared on his own volition. Searches have been conducted using drones, boats, and rescue crews, and family members have organized various searches of the area. Johnson is described as a white male standing 5 feet 10 inches tall, weighing 155 pounds with brown hair and brown eyes. He was last known to be wearing a red and black coat with an Eldora ski jacket and black pants.

In a separate incident, a severed foot found in a boot at the base of Eldora Mountain Resort in June does not belong to Johnson. The boot is a Rugged Outback men’s Apex Leather waterproof boot, size 13, for the left foot. Anyone with information about Johnson's whereabouts is asked to call the sheriff's office at 303-441-4444.

In July 1992, Morrad Ghonim, then 19, lost his wife Vicki in a shooting incident that occurred at a park in La Mirada, California. The investigation into Vicki's murder went cold until nearly two decades later when a breakthrough led investigators to a drug dealer, Leon Martinez, who claimed Ghonim had hired him to stage a robbery and kill Vicki.

Ghonim and Vicki had taken their 6-month-old son to Creek Park, a special place for the couple who often sneaked away from school to spend time together. According to Ghonim, they heard catcalls from a group of people, which he believed were gang members. Vicki responded, and Ghonim felt a bad feeling, ushering his family towards their car. They heard gunfire, but Ghonim never got a look at the shooter.

Police collected a clump of clothes from the park, including a sweatshirt that a witness recognized as one worn by a man jogging nearby after the shooting. However, detectives could never determine whose items they belonged to. Ghonim eventually remarried and had five children, including Vicki's son, whom he raised with his new wife.

In 2015, Ghonim was extradited from Antigua and charged with hiring Martinez to kill his wife. During the trial, Martinez testified that Ghonim had asked him if he knew anyone who would kill for money after they had met through a mutual acquaintance and Ghonim had bought crack cocaine from him. Martinez admitted to shooting Vicki and said Ghonim wanted it to look like a robbery.

The defense argued that the case relied on the credibility of a convicted killer and Ghonim's ex-wife, who stood to gain from Ghonim's conviction. They also pointed out inconsistencies in Martinez's testimony and questioned the motive and access to money for a teenager like Ghonim. However, the judge ruled there was enough evidence to try Ghonim, and he was ordered to return to court for arraignment.

In a subsequent trial, a jury found Ghonim guilty of first-degree murder, and he was sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of parole. The prosecution had not yet decided whether to seek the death penalty.

Junot Díaz, the Pulitzer Prize-winning author of "The Brief Wondrous Life of Oscar Wao," has denied allegations of inappropriate behavior with women, including a claim he once "forcibly kissed" writer Zinzi Clemmons. In an interview at the offices of Liberty Square Group, a Boston communications firm representing him, Díaz said he was "distressed," "confused," and "panicked" by the accusations but insisted he had not bullied the women or been sexually inappropriate.

The case may be rewriting the narrative of the #MeToo movement, as Díaz has kept his teaching job at MIT and his editing position at Boston Review following separate investigations that found the accusations lacked "the kind of severity that animated the #MeToo movement."

Díaz, whose fiction is full of male characters behaving badly toward women, now finds himself trying to draw distinctions between the artist and his art, between sexual misconduct and consensual relationships gone wrong. He said, "There is a line between being a bad boyfriend and having a lot of regret, and predatory behavior."

The Dominican-American writer has been a literary darling since his first book, "Drown," became a national bestseller in the mid-1990s. With stories that dwell on the legacy of trauma and characters steeped in cultural misogyny and racism, Díaz has long evoked strong feelings, but never more than in recent weeks, when the complaints of several female writers riveted — and divided — the literary establishment.

So far, Díaz has been spared, largely because the deluge of #MeToo stories his accusers predicted hasn't come. Also, some of the allegations have withered under scrutiny. An exchange recalled by one woman as "a blast of misogynist rage and public humiliation" sounded, to others, like an author being defensive about his work. And Clemmons, who accused Díaz of forcibly kissing her in a stairwell, has refused to say whether it was on the lips.

Díaz's allies have decried the rush to judge him, while his accusers view him as the misogynist who got away. They stand by their allegations, saying a broad array of behaviors should be addressed as part of the #MeToo movement.

The case has deeply divided writers, editors, and academics, who have sparred in thoughtful open letters published in the Chronicle of Higher Education and in a barbed back-and-forth on social media. Both sides say they have been harassed by spiteful trolls.

Díaz arrived at the interview with names and contact information of friends, colleagues, former students, and even ex-girlfriends who could attest to his character. Among them was psychologist Wendy Walsh, who dated Díaz on and off for four years and still holds him in high regard. She views Díaz as a champion of women of color and credits him with encouraging her biracial daughter to attend an Ivy League college. Walsh, who also happens to be one of the first women to allege sexual harassment by former Fox News anchor Bill O'Reilly, said Díaz was never abusive, though she acknowledged flaws, likening him to the inveterate cheater in his books.

The second public complaint about Díaz arose from a conversation about Yunior, the philandering narrator of Díaz's 2012 short-story collection, "This is How You Lose Her." Carmen Maria Machado, who was then an unpublished writer, asked Díaz about Yunior during the author's visit to the University of Iowa. Machado tweeted that Díaz became "enraged" and veered into "bullying and misogyny." Díaz denied being verbally abusive to Machado, and said he feels vindicated by a recording of the event that has since surfaced online, revealing him to be defensive, but not raising his voice. Machado, a National Book Award finalist for her story collection, "Her Body and Other Parties," stands by her account.

Monica Byrne was the third writer who spoke out about Díaz, detailing a 2014 dinner party dispute she characterized on Twitter as a "verbal sexual assault." In an interview, Byrne said the conversation concerned the statistical disparity between male and female authors who get published and reviewed. Byrne told Díaz that The New Yorker had rejected an excerpt of her novel and questioned whether that was evidence of gender bias. Díaz, who appears regularly in The New Yorker, responded by saying something like: "I don't know if you know how statistics work, but that's like saying if you haven't been raped then nobody's been raped," Byrne said. Byrne considered the comment "completely bizarre, disproportionate, and violent." Díaz recalled it merely as a "messy conversation." Byrne — like other accusers — contends there are additional women who have not spoken out, but she will not disclose their names. She said she's compiling a list that includes secondhand stories and published accounts, like that of a man who tweeted about Díaz belittling his manuscript in a writing workshop. Asked whether such an account from a writing workshop describes a sexual abuser or a jerk, Byrne responded: "What is the difference?" "Me Too covers a huge spectrum of behaviors as problematic and as specifically misogynist," said Byrne.

MIT, where Díaz has taught creative writing since 2003, conducted an investigation, contacting all current students who'd taken a class with Díaz and speaking to staff and faculty dating back to 2003. In addition, the university combed the comments on students' teacher evaluations for any hint of impropriety. There were none, the school said, and on a 7-point scale, Díaz received an average overall rating of 6.82. MIT concluded the inquiry saying it had "not found or received information that would lead us to take any action to restrict Professor Díaz in his role as an MIT faculty member." Boston Review, where Díaz has been fiction editor for 15 years, likewise decided to keep the author on its masthead after a "careful review of the public complaints" and interviews with "women writers of color" revealed no reason to remove him. An investigation by the Pulitzer Prize board, of which Díaz is a member, is still ongoing.

An Alabama man, Keith Maddox, has been arrested and charged with reckless endangerment after videos of him threatening bicyclists went viral. In the videos, Maddox expressed frustration about sharing the road with bicyclists, using aggressive language and even suggesting he might run them off the road. The videos were discovered by cycling enthusiast groups who alerted the Calhoun County Sheriff's office. Maddox was released on a $3,000 bond after his arrest. On his Facebook page, Maddox apologized for his actions, stating that they were in poor taste and that he never intended to harm anyone. He also expressed a desire for road users to be aware of bicyclists and for everyone to share the road. A compilation of the videos Maddox posted can be found online.

The article discusses a new study that suggests children living near the Fukushima nuclear disaster site have a higher rate of thyroid cancer than children elsewhere, with rates being 20 to 50 times higher than the norm. The study, led by Toshihide Tsuda of Okayama University, is based on a large public health survey conducted in Japan's Fukushima prefecture following the 2011 nuclear accident. The study found 137 cases of thyroid cancer among the 370,000 children in Fukushima prefecture, a number that rose by 25 from a year earlier.

The study has been published in the November issue of Epidemiology, and the data comes from tests overseen by Fukushima Medical University. The authors of the study contend that the higher rate of thyroid cancer undermines the government's position that more cases have been discovered in the area only because of stringent monitoring.

However, scientists are divided on the conclusions of the study. Scott Davis, professor at the Department of Epidemiology in the Seattle-based School of Public Health, agrees with the findings of the World Health Organization and UNSCEAR, both of which have carried out reviews on Fukushima and predicted cancer rates will remain stable, with no rises being discernable as radiation-caused. David J. Brenner, professor of radiation biophysics at Columbia University Medical Center, takes a different view, stating that the higher thyroid cancer rate in Fukushima is "not due to screening. It's real."

The study's conclusions have implications for compensation and other policies, as many people who live in areas deemed safe by the government have fled fearing sickness, especially for their children. An area extending about 20 kilometers (12 miles) from the nuclear plant has been declared an exclusion zone, and decommissioning the plant is expected to take decades.

The study has limitations, including the lack of individual-level data to estimate actual radiation doses. Andrew F. Olshan, professor at the Department of Epidemiology at the University of North Carolina, noted that research on what follows a catastrophe is complex and difficult. "Dr. Tsuda's study had limitations including assessment of individual radiation dose levels to the thyroid and the ability to fully assess the impact of screening on the excess cases detected," he said. "Nonetheless, this study is critical to initiate additional investigations of possible health effects, for governmental planning, and increasing public awareness."

The article also includes personal stories of individuals affected by the disaster, including Noriko Matsumoto, a nurse who fled Tokyo with her daughter after the disaster due to concerns about radiation exposure. Matsumoto's daughter developed nosebleeds and rashes, and Matsumoto believes radiation is behind her daughter's sickness.

In conclusion, the study suggests that children living near the Fukushima nuclear disaster site have a higher rate of thyroid cancer than children elsewhere, with rates being 20 to 50 times higher than the norm. However, scientists are divided on the conclusions of the study, with some agreeing with the government's position that the higher rate is due to stringent monitoring, while others believe the higher rate is real. The study has implications for compensation and other policies, as many people have fled areas deemed safe by the government out of fear of sickness.

The World Cup in South Africa is being marked by the widespread use of vuvuzelas, plastic horns that create a loud, continuous drone. While some find the noise annoying, particularly during television broadcasts, organizers have decided not to ban them. FIFA president Sepp Blatter, who has two vuvuzelas himself, believes they are part of the local culture and should not be banned. England defender Jamie Carragher, who played in the England-USA match, said the noise did not bother him, and even some players who have complained about the noise, such as Portugal's Cristiano Ronaldo, have acknowledged that they will have to get used to them. The England Supporters' Band, which has not missed an England game since 1996, also supports the use of vuvuzelas. Organizers have said they will continue to monitor the use of vuvuzelas and may ban them if there are grounds to do so, but have also urged fans not to use them during national anthems or as weapons. Despite some complaints from broadcasters and viewers, FIFA has previously refused to ban vuvuzelas, citing their role in creating the unique African atmosphere of the tournament.

In Philadelphia, a 36-year-old woman with special needs was found chained to a bed in the basement of a house on Linton Street in the Olney section. The woman was discovered during a police investigation into an ongoing neighborhood dispute. Regina Bennett, 46, was arrested for threats and assault against a neighbor. As officers were leaving the location, they learned a child was living there, although there weren't any visible signs. Upon further investigation, police found the woman in unsuitable conditions and charged Bennett with aggravated assault, kidnapping for ransom, and neglect of care. Neighbors described Bennett as having two different personalities, with a history of run-ins with neighbors. This incident bears resemblance to a previous case in Southwest Philadelphia where a disabled man was held captive for his Social Security checks. No attorney for Bennett could be located.

In a separate incident, a 63-year-old deaf and mute man was found locked in the basement of a Southwest Philadelphia home, allegedly abused by 56-year-old Dwayne Young for months. The family described Young as an acquaintance, and police arrested him after finding the victim. The victim was held against his will after being abducted off the street in April, and his social security checks were cashed by the suspect. This case is similar to another, unrelated case involving Linda Weston where police allege Weston kidnapped and assaulted her mentally disabled victims in a Tacony basement to profit from her victims’ social security benefits. Young remains in jail with his bail set at $1,000,000.

A 29-year-old man named Joseph Adam White from Hartstown, Pennsylvania, was arrested after admitting during a polygraph pretest for a state trooper position that he had sex with an underage girl in 2011. The incident occurred during White's police cadet lie detector exam at the Meadville barracks. The girl, now 19, was interviewed, and the police corroborated the information, leading to White's arrest on Thursday for four counts of unlawful sexual contact with a minor and 10 counts of corruption of minors. Online court records do not list an attorney for White, and he does not have a listed phone number. The man will not be pursuing a career as a state trooper.

The Duke and Duchess of Cambridge, Prince William and Kate Middleton, have released a new family portrait featuring their son, Prince George, ahead of their upcoming tour to New Zealand and Australia. The photo, taken by photographer Jason Bell, shows the family of three at their London residence, Kensington Palace, with George wearing a light blue jumper and focusing his attention on their pet dog, Lupo. The family will embark on their tour from April 7 to 25, but it's unclear which of their engagements Prince George will be present at. This is the third official release of photos of Prince George and the first since his christening last October. The tour will mark George's first official overseas visit, echoing the Prince and Princess of Wales's visit to Australia and New Zealand in 1983, when they took William, then aged nine months, with them. The tour will include visits to various cities, military bases, and commemorative ceremonies for World War I, as well as cultural events such as a yacht race and rugby matches. The couple's 11-member entourage includes their new nanny, Maria Teresa Turrion Borrallo, and a hairdresser. This is the third joint official trip abroad for the duke and duchess, following their visits to Canada and the US in 2011 and their South Pacific tour in 2012.

Archaeologists in the UK have discovered a medieval well, believed to be dedicated to Saint Anne, the mother of the Virgin Mary. The well, known as St. Anne's Well, was found buried on private land near Liverpool and was initially identified by photographs taken in 1983.

The well, which is more like a shallow spring used for bathing, was likely a late Medieval foundation, as the cult of St. Anne did not become widespread in England until after the end of the 14th century. During the Medieval Period, healing wells were popular in Britain, and St. Anne was commonly attributed to them, although other saints were also honored.

The well, which is approximately 1.2 meters deep, would have seen pilgrims stepping into the water to wash away sins or seek healing. A small three-roomed structure was built around the well, and two monks were responsible for its caretaking. The well's popularity attracted a significant number of pilgrims, necessitating the construction of the structure and the full-time care of the monks.

According to legend, the well was cursed during the 16th century. The story goes that a neighboring landowner, Hugh Darcy, had a dispute with one of the monks, Father Delwaney, over the well's size, and Delwaney cursed Darcy after a heated argument. Moments later, Delwaney fell over dead. Darcy experienced a series of unfortunate events for the next year, including the death of his son and financial troubles. Eventually, Darcy was found dead near the well, although the circumstances of his death are unclear.

The researchers suspect that religious pilgrims continued to bathe in the well's waters up until the 19th century, after which it was abandoned and ploughed over. Now that it has been unearthed, the team plans to add wood around the water to prevent it from getting covered up again or damaged, and will work with local farmers to ensure the site is maintained. The team's work has yet to appear in a peer-reviewed journal, but they hope to share the details of their work with the public and the scientific community upon further analysis. If all goes well, one of the longest-lasting holy wells in the UK will be revived, and hopefully, it will be curse-free.

Michael Phelps, the most decorated Olympian in history, is set to participate in his fifth Olympic Games, a record among male swimmers for the United States. At 31 years old, Phelps will compete in three individual races - the 200-meter butterfly, 200-meter individual medley, and 100-meter butterfly - as well as multiple relays at the 2016 Summer Games in Rio. Given his first-place finishes in each discipline at the U.S. team trials in Omaha, it is expected that Phelps will add to his impressive collection of 22 medals, including 18 golds.

Phelps and his teammate Ryan Lochte, who turns 32 on Aug. 3, have repeatedly proven themselves to be outliers in a sport where youth typically reigns supreme. Should either win gold in a solo race in Brazil, they would become the oldest to win individual Olympic gold, surpassing Dutch swimmer Inge de Bruijn.

Looking back at Phelps' previous Olympic appearances, his debut was at the 2000 Sydney Games, where he made history as the youngest U.S. male to swim in the Olympics since 1932. In 2004, at the age of 19, Phelps set world records in four different events and qualified in all of them at the Olympic trials. His performance in Athens was one of the greatest in Olympic swimming history, earning him seven gold medals and two bronze.

In 2008, Phelps broke his own records and won eight gold medals in Beijing, setting world records in seven of his races. However, his quest for eight golds was briefly derailed in London in 2012, where he placed fourth in his first final, the 400-meter IM. Despite this setback, Phelps went on to win four more golds and six medals overall, becoming the most decorated Olympian of all time.

Now, Phelps is preparing for a record-setting fifth Olympic Games. The Opening Ceremony will be held on Aug. 5 at the Maracanã Stadium in Rio de Janeiro, and Phelps has been chosen as Team USA's flag bearer. In a press conference, Phelps expressed his honor and pride in representing the U.S. and his desire to make his family proud, rather than focusing solely on medals. The 2016 Olympic Games will mark the first time they are held in South America.

On Monday, a 27-year-old man identified as Akayed Ullah, an immigrant from Bangladesh, detonated a homemade pipe bomb strapped to his body in a crowded Manhattan subway passage. The attack occurred around 7:20 a.m. in an underground passageway from the subway station at 42nd Street and Eighth Avenue to a nearby station at Seventh Avenue. The pipe bomb was affixed with Velcro and zip ties. The attack caused minor injuries to three commuters and left Ullah with burns and cuts to his hands and abdomen.

Ullah told investigators that he was inspired by propaganda from the Islamic State terror group. The FBI and the New York Police Department are investigating, and charges in federal court are expected to be filed against Ullah soon. The bomb was intended to detonate at that spot in the tunnel, where Ullah had connected a small battery to a set of Christmas lights in the pipe bomb.

The incident rekindled public debates about terrorism, public safety, and immigration. President Trump stated that the incident was another example of why the United States needs to curb immigration. Ullah came to the United States on a type of visa for relatives of people already living legally in the country.

The explosion brought Monday's morning commute in crowded Times Square to a standstill, and a massive police response locked down the area while authorities searched for other bombs. The attack occurred just weeks after a man driving a truck plowed through pedestrians and bicyclists on a path along Manhattan’s West Side, killing eight people and wounding a dozen others.

Akayed Ullah seemed to be an ordinary member of a Bangladeshi enclave in Brooklyn. He often prayed at a mosque in an unassuming brownstone in the Kensington section of the borough, where a few thousand of his countrymen reside. Like many immigrants in New York, he made his living driving for a car service. However, on Monday morning, he strapped a pipe bomb to his body and set out to detonate it in a Times Square subway station.

Verizon Wireless has announced a new "Share Everything" plan, set to roll out on June 28, which allows customers to share a common bucket of data, similar to voice minutes and text messages under a family plan. The new plan offers unlimited voice and text messages, but comes at a higher price for individuals, particularly those who do not use much data.

Under the new plan, individuals with minimum voice options will see plan rates jump from as low as $69.99 (450 minutes and 2GB of data) to the lowest smartphone option of $90 for just 1GB of data. However, families who want multiple devices all with data will save quite a bit, with a family of five dropping to $270 for five lines with a shared pool of 4GB, including unlimited talk and text.

The new shared data plans come with monthly line access fees of $40 for a smartphone, $30 for a basic feature phone, $20 for USB sticks, notebooks, and netbooks, and $10 for tablets. These plans also include WiFi hotspot functionality.

The new plan is geared towards families, particularly those in which a few members do not use as much data, at the expense of individuals. Some people may be okay with giving up their old grandfathered unlimited data plans, but many are unhappy with the change.

The new plan is also likely to be followed by AT&T, which could be bad news for individuals on that carrier. Some analysts believe that in a world where incentives for families favor concentrating around a single provider, the biggest providers like Verizon and AT&T will win.

Overall, the new plan offers convenience for families, but comes at a high price for individuals who do not use much data. Some people may be willing to pay the higher price for the convenience of a shared data plan, but many are unhappy with the change. It remains to be seen how the new plan will be received by customers and how it will impact the wireless industry.

Two bills aimed at tightening North Dakota's abortion laws have been passed by the Senate and are now awaiting the governor's signature. If signed into law, these bills would establish some of the most restrictive abortion regulations in the nation.

House Bill 1305 makes it a Class A misdemeanor for physicians to perform abortions based on gender or genetic abnormalities. House Bill 1456 requires a physician to determine the presence of a detectable heartbeat before performing an abortion, with violations resulting in a Class C felony. If enacted, HB1456 would institute the earliest abortion restriction in the country, as heartbeats can be detected as early as six weeks after conception.

The debate surrounding these bills was heated, with emotional appeals and personal stories shared by senators. Opponents argue that the bills infringe upon women's rights and federal law, which protects abortions up to 24 weeks. The potential six-week mark is stricter than the 12-week limit set by a bill passed by the Arkansas Legislature. A federal court recently overturned an Idaho law banning abortions after 20 weeks.

HB1305 was divided into two parts during the debate, with one section removing the reference to genetic abnormalities. Supporters of the bill argue that it aims to prevent sex-selective abortions and those based on genetic abnormalities, which they believe is a step towards eugenics. Opponents, however, view the comparison to China as "silly" and criticize the Legislature for attempting to govern women's bodies.

If signed by Governor Jack Dalrymple, these bills would make North Dakota the first state to ban abortions based on genetic defects like Down syndrome. The American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) and other national abortion rights groups have condemned the measures, warning that they would likely be deemed unconstitutional by federal courts. If enacted, these bills could lead to a costly legal battle over the Supreme Court's 1973 Roe v. Wade decision that legalized abortion.

Vanity Fair is set to publish a controversial article about Gwyneth Paltrow, despite the actress's efforts to prevent it. The magazine's editor-in-chief, Graydon Carter, confirmed the story, stating that it will be written by a talented writer and will be published. In May, Paltrow reportedly emailed her celebrity friends asking them not to cooperate with the author of the piece and to never work with Vanity Fair again. Carter's confirmation of the article comes after a New York Times report in September claimed that Paltrow was feuding with the magazine. The article is expected to reveal the true Paltrow, and Carter's determination to publish it has reportedly increased since Paltrow's email went public. Carter defended his magazine's coverage of Hollywood, stating that it is part of their job to have tension with their subjects. He also expressed frustration with the rise of reality TV celebrities like the Kardashians, stating that they will disappear in ten minutes. Paltrow, who has had five Vanity Fair covers and numerous appearances in the magazine, may find Los Angeles very different and difficult, according to Carter.

The U.S. job market showed resilience in February, with employers adding 242,000 jobs, according to the Labor Department. This rebound follows a modest slowdown in hiring in January. The unemployment rate remained steady at 4.9%, and the labor-force participation rate increased to its highest level in a year, with over half a million people joining the labor force.

However, average hourly wages decreased by 0.1%, and the number of hours worked per week dropped to a two-year low of 34.4 hours. Economists had forecast the addition of 195,000 jobs for February, and the unemployment rate was expected to remain at 4.9%.

The hiring surge has been driven by sectors such as construction, retail, and healthcare, which have offset layoffs in manufacturing and fossil fuel industries. Despite global economic challenges, including a slowdown in China, declining oil prices, and a stronger dollar, U.S. consumers have continued to fuel economic growth through increased spending on autos, housing, and meals out.

The Federal Reserve is closely monitoring the jobs report as a key indicator of the economy's health. The central bank is considering whether to raise interest rates again amid global risks that could impact broader economic growth. However, investors have dismissed the likelihood of another rate hike at the upcoming Fed meeting.

NBC has terminated an employee for distributing an old "Today Show" clip featuring hosts Katie Couric, Bryant Gumbel, and Elizabeth Vargas discussing the Internet and email addresses in 1994. The clip, which went viral last week, features Gumbel expressing confusion about the Internet and its symbols, and Couric attempting to explain it. NBC confirmed the employee violated company standards by distributing various materials without permission, emphasizing that the firing was not solely due to the clip's release. Former Norwegian Prime Minister Kjell Magne Bondevik experienced a lengthy questioning and detention at Dulles Airport on Tuesday, following a visit to Iran in 2014. Bondevik, who served as prime minister twice between 1997-2005, was traveling to the United States to attend the National Prayer Breakfast.

Upon arrival, customs agents noticed his visit to Iran in his passport and held him for approximately an hour. Despite his diplomatic passport and status as a former prime minister of a U.S. ally, Bondevik was placed in a room with travelers from the Middle East and Africa facing extra scrutiny. He was eventually questioned for about 20 minutes regarding his trip to Iran.

Bondevik's detention was not related to President Trump's controversial travel ban, but rather a 2015 law signed by President Obama aimed at protecting the U.S. from terrorists. The law places extra restrictions on citizens from 38 countries, including Norway, who have visited Iran, Iraq, Sudan, Syria, Libya, Somalia, or Yemen since March 2011.

Bondevik's office was informed by the U.S. Embassy in Oslo prior to his trip that his passport and a separate electronic travel authorization (ESTA) would be sufficient for entry into the United States. However, he was still subjected to additional questioning and detention.

Bondevik expressed concern about the U.S.'s treatment of international leaders and the potential impact on the country's reputation. He also expressed concern about the Trump administration's tactics, stating that they treat entire ethnic groups in a way that is reminiscent of authoritarian leaders.

In response to Bondevik's detention, a spokesperson for U.S. Customs and Border Protection stated that they are prohibited by law from discussing specifics of any individual's admissibility review. The Norwegian Embassy in D.C. was contacted after the incident and reported that things were sorted out.

This incident occurred as protests and worldwide condemnation continue over President Trump's travel ban, which temporarily bans all travelers from seven Muslim-majority countries and suspends the U.S. refugee resettlement program for 120 days. The ban has caused chaos at airports across the U.S. and has been met with resistance from many individuals and organizations.

In a unique small claims court case in Madeira Beach, Florida, a judge ruled that a black Labrador retriever mix named Elario should be shared between two neighbors, David Somerville and Tina Marie Walker, due to their significant bond with the dog. The 4-year-old Elario, who means joy, was adopted by Walker in 2016, but Somerville, a Vietnam War veteran recovering from lung cancer, had been taking care of him and covering the vet bills. The judge ordered a custody arrangement similar to divorced parents, with a detailed pickup schedule.

The story began when Walker asked Somerville for a ride to the Pinellas County Animal Services shelter, where she found Elario. She started bringing him to Somerville's apartment, and they grew close. However, a rift formed between the neighbors, with different versions of the events leading to the court case.

Walker claims she started taking Elario to Somerville's apartment when she adopted him, but a disagreement arose when Walker went on vacation and left Elario with Somerville. Somerville, on the other hand, claims the animosity began when he wanted Elario's microchip printed with his name.

The judge's ruling has resulted in a shared custody arrangement for Elario, a decision that reflects the strong bond he has formed with both neighbors. Despite the legal battle, both parties continue to express their love for the dog.

A grand jury has indicted Ariel Castro, the suspected kidnapper and murderer, on 977 new criminal charges, extending his imprisonment period from 2002 to the end of his decade-long captivity of Amanda Berry, Gina DeJesus, and Michelle Knight. The new indictment includes 512 counts of kidnapping, 446 counts of rape, seven counts of gross sexual imposition, six counts of felonious assault, three counts of child endangerment, and one count of possessing criminal tools. It also includes two counts of aggravated murder, stemming from claims that Castro beat and tortured one of the women into miscarrying a child.

Although the prosecutor, Timothy J. McGinty, can seek the death penalty for aggravated murder if it is coupled with a kidnapping charge, he has not called for it in this case. The prosecutor's office is still evaluating whether to pursue the death penalty, and the defense attorneys have expressed hope for a resolution that minimizes additional trauma for the women.

The trial is scheduled to begin on August 5, and the women have received over $1 million in donations to a fund set up on their behalf. The women recently released a YouTube video thanking supporters and conveying an image of recovery. Castro, who is being held in Cuyahoga County Jail, has appeared in court with shackles on his wrists and ankles, and his head bowed.

The UFO memorial in Sheffield, Massachusetts, which marks a 1969 UFO sighting, has been ordered to be moved again due to its location on a town right-of-way easement. The memorial, which was installed in 2015, was initially moved a few weeks later when it was discovered it was on town land. Thom Reed, one of the four people who had a close encounter near the bridge on Sept. 1, 1969, is objecting to the move and is threatening legal action. The memorial was purchased with donations from community members and UFO enthusiasts. The town administrator, Rhonda LaBombard, stated that the town has bylaws and allowing one place to put something up could lead to others doing the same. The memorial is a 6-foot tall, white, concrete block bearing a plaque from Governor Charlie Baker's office and the Massachusetts seal. It is flanked by a bench donated by Reed and the International UFO Museum Research Center in Roswell, N.M., as well as two black light posts. The event was reported on by WSBS radio and was deemed an "off-world incident ... historically significant and true" by the Great Barrington Historical Society in 2015. The 1969 sighting has been the subject of several television shows and documentaries. Reed, who lives in Kentucky, is the most vocal about the incident and has worked with town officials to find the memorial's current placement. UFO enthusiasts may take legal action to prevent the memorial's removal.

The article discusses the ongoing debate over the primary and caucus dates for the 2012 Republican presidential nomination. Mitt Romney's campaign has pushed for an earlier date for the Nevada caucuses, which were recently moved to January 14 from February 18, to strengthen Romney's position as the frontrunner. However, New Hampshire Secretary of State Bill Gardner has threatened to move the state's primary to as early as December 6, which could potentially diminish the importance of New Hampshire in the electoral process and harm Romney's chances of winning the nomination.

Romney's rivals, such as Gov. Rick Perry and Herman Cain, could cite the difficulty of competing in New Hampshire on a compressed schedule, and the media might be happy to play along. An earlier date would also leave a four-week gap between New Hampshire and the Iowa caucuses, which could cause momentum to be lost.

However, if Nevada moves its caucus date to Tuesday, January 17, New Hampshire could slot in on January 10, giving a January calendar that resembles the one in 2008. This would be beneficial for Romney's campaign, as a loss in Iowa would not be as damaging, and a win in New Hampshire would allow his campaign to recover from any loss in momentum.

Bill Gardner, who has control over setting the nation's first primary date, has shown no interest in negotiating and has infuriated other early state chairs and the Republican National Committee. Gardner's decision to move the primary up could alter the entire nature of the campaign, giving an advantage to Romney, who is ahead in local polls. The article concludes by stating that a lot hinges on Gardner's decision, which took on new importance after Florida moved its primary to January 31 and South Carolina and Nevada moved up their dates in response.

The In Other Words community, a feminist bookstore in Portland, Oregon, has severed ties with the popular TV show Portlandia, which frequently filmed at their location for six seasons. The decision was made in response to a particular episode that left the store in disarray, mistreated staff, and negatively impacted neighboring businesses. The show's content is also seen as diametrically opposed to the bookstore's politics and vision.

The bookstore received minimal financial gain from being on the show, as the flat fee paid did not cover the profits lost during filming or the additional business lost by neighbors. The show's segments featuring the bookstore are criticized for being trans-antagonistic and trans-misogynist, with jokes deemed harmful and unfunny, particularly in light of the increasing violence against transgender individuals, especially Black trans women.

The lack of racial diversity on Portlandia, despite Portland's multicultural population, is also a point of contention. The show's portrayal of Portland's gentrification is seen as trivializing a serious issue that leads to mass displacement of communities. The production crew's request to remove the Black Lives Matter sign from the window during filming further highlights the disconnect between the show and the bookstore's values.

The current board, staff, and volunteers at In Other Words were not involved in the initial decision to allow Portlandia to film at the bookstore. They stand behind their decision to discontinue the relationship with the show and have displayed a "Fuck Portlandia" sign in their window. The community encourages donations to support their work as a hub for Portland's social justice community and welcomes volunteers.

In the central Indian state of Chhattisgarh, eight women have died and 69 have been hospitalized following a mass sterilization drive, according to local medical officials. The surgeries, which were conducted in six hours, were performed by a doctor who used infected instruments and exceeded the daily limit of 30 sterilizations. The doctor, R.K. Gupta, has been suspended and a criminal investigation is underway. The incident has been labeled as a case of negligence by the state's chief minister, Raman Singh.

The sterilization drive was part of India's efforts to control population growth, with India having the world's third-highest female sterilization rate. Women often suffer most from such population control measures, with one-day sterilization drives being commonplace in India. The deaths in Chhattisgarh are a culmination of no accountability in the system and poor hygiene conditions, according to Kerry McBroom, director of the Reproductive Rights Initiative at the Human Rights Law Network.

The deaths were due to infection causing septic shock, according to Amar Singh Thakur, chief health officer for Bilaspur district. Four women are still in critical condition, while eight died on Monday and two passed away on Tuesday. Prime Minister Narendra Modi has asked Chhattisgarh's leader to ensure a thorough investigation and action on the "unfortunate tragedy."

Sterilizations in India are voluntary, with couples choosing between a tubectomy or vasectomy. From April 2010 to March 2013, the government paid about 510 million rupees ($8 million) for 15,264 deaths or failed surgeries. Women are offered as little as 600 rupees ($10) in compensation for participating in the procedure, which usually takes about 15 minutes and is done under local anesthesia.

Activists blame sterilization quotas for leading health authorities to pressure patients into surgery rather than advising them on other forms of contraception. The state has suspended four government doctors, including the surgeon who performed the operations and the district's chief medical officer. The state will also give compensation payments of about $6,600 to each of the victims' families.

The incident in Chhattisgarh highlights the coercive environment that has existed for several decades in India's family planning program, with district health workers threatened with salary cuts or dismissals if local targets aren't met. The state's surgeons are discussing whether to continue the state's sterilization schedule, with a target of 180,000 for the year ending in March set by the central government.

The Episcopal Church, a major Protestant denomination in the United States, has approved rituals for same-sex marriage ceremonies, making it the third mainline Protestant denomination to do so. The decision was made during the Episcopal Church's 78th General Convention in Salt Lake City, following a week of debate. The House of Deputies, the voting body of clergy and lay participants, voted 184-23 to approve the new liturgy, and 173 to 27 to approve a change to the church's canon, redefining marriage as being between two persons instead of a man and a woman.

The Episcopal Church's move comes after the Supreme Court's decision in June to legalize same-sex marriage in all 50 states, and a shift in public support for the change. The Episcopalians now join the Presbyterian Church (USA) and the United Church of Christ in offering such rituals to same-sex couples.

The Episcopal Church has a history of supporting gay rights, having voted in 1976 that gays and lesbians were "a full and equal claim with all other persons upon the love, acceptance, and pastoral concern and care of the church." In 2003, the Episcopal Church elected its first openly gay bishop, a move that triggered a major schism. The church has lost 12 percent of its membership over the past nine years.

Beginning November 29, congregations will be authorized to use a rite called "The Witnessing and Blessing of a Lifelong Covenant," which is designed without reference to gender. The use of the liturgies would be subject to the permission of a diocese's bishop, and any cleric can refuse to marry any couple for any reason, according to the voted resolution.

The church's actions have caused controversy, with some arguing that it goes against biblical principles. The Archbishop of Canterbury, Justin Welby, stated that the move would cause distress for some and have ramifications for the Anglican Communion as a whole. The Episcopal Church is the U.S. wing of the Anglican Communion, an 80 million-member global fellowship of churches.

The vote eliminates gender-specific language from church laws on marriage, so that same-sex couples could have religious weddings. The changes were approved 173-27. The convention also approved a gender-neutral prayer service for marriage on a 184-23 vote. The measures take effect the first Sunday of Advent, Nov. 29.

The document highlights significant legal victories for women's movements globally, celebrating the 100th anniversary of International Women's Day. In 2010, women played crucial roles in extending employee protections for domestic workers worldwide and were instrumental in the revolutions in Tunisia and Egypt. The Global Fund for Women showcased the Top 10 wins for women's movements, including strengthening abortion rights and legalizing same-sex marriage.

The document also discusses the challenge in determining the "worst countries for women," with various factors such as humanitarian issues, educational attainment, health statistics, cultural biases, and economic conditions considered. The U.N. Development Program's Gender Inequality Index is presented as a modern metric for understanding gender relations globally, with perfect equality being zero and perfect inequality being 1.

According to the 2008 Gender Inequality Index, Yemen had the highest (worst) score, 0.853, followed by the Congo (0.814), Nigeria (0.807), Mali (0.799), and Afghanistan (0.797). The Netherlands had the lowest (best) score, 0.174, while the United States scored 0.400, placing it behind Croatia and Lithuania but ahead of Estonia. The document underscores the ongoing challenges faced by women in various countries, despite the advancements in women's rights.
