In a series of interviews, several high-ranking officials have criticized President Barack Obama's handling of international crises, particularly in Iraq and Syria. Senator Dianne Feinstein, chairwoman of the Senate Intelligence Committee, expressed concern over Obama's cautious approach to the growing threat from Islamic militants, specifically the Islamic State of Iraq and the Levant (ISIL). Feinstein agreed with an op-ed by Republican Senators John McCain and Lindsey Graham, calling for an immediate military plan to confront ISIL.

ISIL's goal, according to Feinstein, is to take Baghdad and attack the American Embassy. Though Obama was criticized last week for not having a strategy for dealing with ISIL, Feinstein stated that the Pentagon and State Department have been planning for some time. However, she expressed hope that these plans will coalesce into a strategy that a coalition of allies can use to confront the militant group.

Feinstein did praise Obama for including the new Iraqi government in the planning, stating that he is trying to give the Iraqi government an opportunity to offer an alternative to Sunni people in the country.

Representative Mike Rogers, chairman of the House Intelligence Committee, also criticized Obama's foreign policy, stating that his "don't-do-stupid-stuff" approach isn't working and that the White House's response to multiple international crises is causing problems for allies. Rogers called for a stronger response to provocations from Russia and China and to the terrorist threat from Islamic militants in Syria and Iraq.

Senator John McCain called for "additional U.S. troops" to help in the fight against ISIL, but he said those troops should continue playing a support role and not be directly involved in combat. McCain urged the Obama administration to provide more weapons to Kurdish fighters in Iraq and to expand the U.S. military airstrikes in Iraq to Syria.

Representative Dutch Ruppersberger, the top Democrat on the House Intelligence Committee, defended Obama's much-criticized Thursday remark that when it comes to taking on ISIL in Syria, "We don’t have a strategy yet." Ruppersberger stated that the Obama administration is working to develop a plan and that "when the time is right, we will do what we have to do."

In response to criticism, President Obama has stated that he is committed to defeating ISIL and that he will take action when necessary. However, he has emphasized the need for a comprehensive strategy that includes diplomatic, military, and economic components. The ongoing criticism from both Democrats and Republicans suggests that finding such a strategy will be a challenging task.

In Texas, a woman named Michelle O'Brien is recovering after a trip to the beach turned into a life-threatening scare. She stepped on an oyster, which exposed her to Vibrio Vulnificus, a flesh-eating bacteria. The bacteria attacked her immune system and could have destroyed her foot, hand, or any open wound. She spent five days in the hospital, mostly in the ICU, and is thankful for the second chance she has been given. Most cases of the bacteria happen between May and October, and Michelle warns that the bacteria is not just on oysters, but also in the water.

In a separate incident, a Georgia couple, Lenny and Joann Buck, were on their 24th wedding anniversary at the beach in Baldwin County. Lenny contracted Vibrio Vulnificus after eating raw oysters at an Orange Beach restaurant. He has been at South Baldwin Regional Medical Center for the past 13 days and faces his 6th surgery. He won't be able to walk for at least four months.

Vibrio Vulnificus thrives in warm, saltwater and can enter the body through open wounds or by eating contaminated shellfish. The bacteria can be particularly dangerous to people with pre-existing medical conditions or compromised immune systems.

In Florida, 32 people have been sickened by the illness, with symptoms including vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, skin lesions, fever, chills, and a decline in blood pressure. Ten people have died from the flesh-eating bacteria in Florida over the past few years. Health officials advise caution, especially for those with weakened immune systems. Despite the danger, they do not advise cancelling vacations to the beach.

The arrival of a makeshift table in Madrid's Puerta del Sol square marked the beginning of a significant protest movement in Spain, known as los indignados (the indignant ones). Thousands of protesters, frustrated with the government's economic policies and high youth unemployment, have occupied city squares across Spain, defying a government ban on political protests ahead of local elections.

The movement, inspired by the Arab Spring, demands jobs, better living standards, a fairer democracy, and changes to the government's austerity plans. Protesters have set up tents, mattresses, and a canteen in the square, showcasing their organizational prowess. The crowd is diverse, with people of all ages and backgrounds participating.

The protests began six days ago in Madrid's Puerta del Sol as a spontaneous sit-in by young Spaniards frustrated at 45% youth unemployment. The crowd camping out in the square has grown, and the protest has spread to other cities across the country. The protesters' demands, pasted up all over Puerta del Sol, are impossible to ignore.

The Spanish government has expressed some sympathy for the protesters but is expected to fare poorly in the upcoming elections. The protesters have vowed to remain in the square, defying the government's ban on political protests on the day before elections. The movement's future remains uncertain, but it has already made a significant impact on Spanish politics.

Adam Mayes, a 35-year-old man, has been added to the FBI's Top Ten Most Wanted Fugitives list, accused of killing a mother and her oldest daughter to kidnap two younger girls. Mayes is believed to be armed and on the run with the kidnapped girls, who were last seen on April 27. The FBI, Tennessee Bureau of Investigation, and U.S. Marshals Service have offered a combined reward of $71,000 for information leading to Mayes' whereabouts and the safe return of the girls.

Mayes and his wife, Teresa, are both charged with first-degree murder and especially aggravated kidnapping. Teresa confessed to police that she witnessed Adam kill JoAnn Bain in the garage of the Bain's Tennessee home and kill Adrienne Bain in the house itself. The bodies of mother and daughter were found earlier this week in the backyard of Mayes' home.

Teresa and Mary Mayes, Adam's mother, were arrested and charged on Tuesday. Mary is charged with conspiracy to commit especially aggravated kidnapping. Both women confessed to police that Teresa helped transport the children and bodies from Mississippi.

Adam Mayes was last seen on April 30, in surveillance video from a grocery market in Guntown, Miss., where he lives. Police have also found a trailer Mayes rented from Guntown that contained personal items belonging to the two young girls. The FBI believes Mayes may have changed his appearance and the appearances of the two girls since they were last seen.

The kidnapping has sparked a massive manhunt, with authorities warning that Mayes may pose a significant danger to the two young girls. A prayer vigil was held for the missing mother and her three daughters in Bolivar, Tenn. on Tuesday.

In a recent event in New Hampshire, Republican presidential candidate Rick Perry delivered a speech that was described as unusually expressive. A video montage of the speech, which highlights the giddiest and strangest moments, has been circulating online, raising concerns about Perry's manner during the speech. The video, posted on YouTube by an account named CharlieJohnson1986, has sparked discussions about Perry's performance, with some describing it as different. Initially, Perry's spokesman declined to comment, but later stated that Perry was passionate about the issues he discussed. The video has been edited to make Perry appear unprofessional, but it does capture elements of his speech that were widely remarked upon by those who attended the event. The video can be found online, with the strange moments starting around 2:20.

In a Reuters/Ipsos national tracking poll released on Wednesday, a majority of Americans, 56%, felt that Democratic presidential candidate Hillary Clinton performed better than Donald Trump in the first presidential debate on Monday. However, the poll did not show an immediate boost in Clinton's support among likely voters. After the debate, both candidates claimed victory, with Trump stating that he won every online poll and Clinton's campaign spokesman claiming that she clearly won the debate as Trump was unprepared, unhinged, and incoherent.

The poll found that 34% of likely voters felt that the debate improved Clinton's chances of winning the White House, while 16% said the debate benefited Trump. Among those who watched the debate, Clinton led Trump 44% to 39%. The poll also showed that Clinton's support among likely voters remained stable, with 42% supporting Clinton and 38% supporting Trump, a lead that Clinton has maintained over the past few weeks.

The poll has a credibility interval of 3 percentage points for the entire sample and the sample of likely voters, and a credibility interval of 4 percentage points for the likely voters who watched the debate. The poll is conducted every day in English in all 50 states, and it often detects trends in sentiment before most other polls.

National opinion polls have differed this year in how they measure support for Clinton and Trump, with some polls including only likely voters and others including all registered voters. Polling aggregators have shown that Clinton's lead over Trump has been shrinking this month to about 2 percentage points.

The article titled "Worse Comes to Worst: Bananas and Panama Disease—When Plant and Pathogen Clones Meet" published in PLOS Pathogens on November 19, 2015, discusses the global threat posed by the Fusarium oxysporum f.sp. cubense (Foc) fungus, the causal agent of Panama disease, to Cavendish bananas.

The banana is the most popular fruit globally, with 85% of its production destined for local markets and only 15% entering international trade. Bananas originated in the Indo-Malayan archipelago and evolved from two seeded diploid Musa species. Over time, a few clones developed into global commodities, with Cavendish bananas being the most prominent.

Panama disease was first reported in Australia in 1876 and in Costa Rica and Panama in 1890. The disease caused major epidemics in the 1900s, linking its most prone geographical area to its colloquial name. In 1910, the soil-borne fungus Foc was identified as the causal agent.

Foc belongs to the F. oxysporum species complex and has a polyphyletic origin. Traditionally, phenotyping has identified three Foc races, but Foc lineages show a remarkable dichotomy, referred to as types or clades. High-resolution genotyping-by-sequencing analyses using DArTseq revealed that 24 Foc strains split into two distinct clades, with VCG01213 containing all TR4 isolates that cause the current Panama disease epidemic in Cavendish bananas.

The current epidemic in Cavendish bananas, colloquially called Tropical Race 4 (TR4), threatens not only the export trade but also regional food provision and local economies. TR4 is a single pathogen clone that has spread across Southeast Asia, Australia, Africa, the Middle East, and the Indian subcontinent. Comparison of re-sequencing data of TR4 isolates from different geographical locations shows a very low level of single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), suggesting that the temporal and spatial dispersal of TR4 is due to a single clone.

The researchers at Wageningen University have demonstrated that the same clone of the Fusarium fungus is infecting Cavendish bananas in several countries dotted across the globe. The results from the research highlight that the quarantine measures and information provided around the globe apparently have not had the desired effect.

To stop further spreading, the team is working with a large number of partners in different locations across the globe to develop short-term solutions for Panama disease management. Long-term solutions, particularly host resistance, can only be developed in strong multidisciplinary alliances with various partners and industry.

In conclusion, the current Panama disease epidemic caused by Tropical Race 4 (TR4) poses a significant threat to global banana production, particularly due to the massive monoculture of susceptible Cavendish bananas. The research highlights the need for global awareness and quarantine campaigns to protect banana production from another pandemic that particularly affects vulnerable, small-holder farmers.

The 1994 Honda Accord was the most stolen car in the United States for the fourth consecutive year in 2012, according to the National Insurance Crime Bureau (NICB). The Honda Civic (1998) and Ford F-150 pickup (2006) followed in second and third place, respectively. The NICB attributes the high theft rate of the 1994 Accord to its lack of security features and popularity. The report also notes an increase in thefts of later-model vehicles due to thieves' ability to illegally obtain replacement key codes. Despite the rise in thefts of newer vehicles, overall vehicle thefts are decreasing, with thefts not being this low since 1967. The NICB encourages motorists to follow their "layered approach" to auto theft prevention, which includes common sense measures like locking cars and using warning and tracking devices.

The Guadalupe-Nipomo Dunes Center in California is hosting a special event on June 12, 2020, to unveil a sphinx excavated from the set of the 1923 silent film "The Ten Commandments." The sphinx is the centerpiece of a new permanent exhibit, funded by the Santa Barbara Foundation, and will be available for viewing before it opens to the public. The event is a 1920s-themed gala, with tickets available for $25 per person, and proceeds will benefit the fund to revamp nature education exhibits in the Dunes Center.

The gala will feature jazz music, 1920s-inspired fare, cocktails, and a chance to mingle with the archaeologists who excavated the set of "The Ten Commandments." There will also be a silent auction of the first giclée in Steve Thomas' "See America" series, which features a sphinx from "The Ten Commandments" perched near the ocean in the Guadalupe-Nipomo Dunes.

In addition to the gala, there will be a Brunch With the Sphinx on Saturday, June 13, featuring a light self-serve breakfast. Tickets for the brunch are also available on the Dunes Center's website.

The sphinx was left over from the filming of "The Ten Commandments," which was filmed in the Guadalupe-Nipomo Dunes in 1923. The film's director, Cecil B. DeMille, constructed 100-foot-tall gates, four 35-foot pharaoh statues, and 21 sphinxes for the film, but left the gigantic set out in the dunes for unknown reasons.

The sphinx was recently removed from the dunes as part of a $120,000 excavation project and will be on display at the Guadalupe-Nipomo Dunes Center starting Saturday, June 13. The exhibit will also feature customized artwork, a separate sphinx head from a 2012 excavation, and artifacts such as tobacco tins, bottles, and photos from DeMille's film set.

The Guadalupe-Nipomo Dunes Center is open Wednesday through Sunday, 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. For more information about purchasing the sphinx poster, visit www.justlookinggallery.com. Tickets to the Roaring '20s Gala Unveiling can be purchased at www.dunescenter.org.

An Indiana couple, Michael Barnes, 19, and Toni Wilson, 22, have been charged with child neglect and criminal recklessness with a deadly weapon after a video on Barnes' phone showed a one-year-old baby playing with a handgun. The video, obtained by authorities, shows the baby putting the gun in her mouth and making sounds like it was firing, while Barnes and Wilson encouraged her to play with the weapon. The gun was a .40 caliber handgun, contrary to Wilson's claim that it was a pellet gun.

Barnes was initially arrested on Thursday for trying to sell a handgun to an undercover officer, and during a follow-up investigation, the disturbing video was discovered on his phone. Wilson was arrested at her home on Friday after investigators confronted her about the video.

The 12-month-old girl in the video and one-month-old twins in the home were placed in emergency care. Barnes faces additional charges in connection with the thwarted gun sale, while both he and Wilson face charges related to the child neglect incident. It is unclear if they have obtained attorneys or how they intend to plead.

Aubrey Plaza unexpectedly stormed the stage during Will Ferrell's acceptance of the Comedic Genius Golden Popcorn at the 2013 MTV Movie Awards. The incident was unplanned, as Plaza was not initially part of the act. She attempted to wrestle the statue from Ferrell, drawing comparisons to Kanye West's interruption of Taylor Swift's speech at the 2009 MTV Video Music Awards. Social media reactions were positive, with many suggesting that Plaza and Ferrell should work together more often. The 2013 MTV Movie Awards concluded, with coverage continuing for red-carpet photos, winners list, and exclusive movie premieres. Twitter users were reminded that they can control their location settings when tweeting.

In early April 2011, journalist James Foley was captured on a Libyan battlefield and imprisoned in Tripoli. He was released 45 days later following an international campaign led by his friends and family. During his imprisonment, Foley converted to Islam and adopted the name Abu Hamza, according to Jejoen Bontinck, a teenage convert to Islam who shared a cell with Foley during the summer of 2013. Foley's conversion was also confirmed by three other recently released hostages and his former employer.

Among other Western prisoners, Peter Kassig, who took the name Abdul-Rahman, also converted during their captivity. Most of the foreigners converted under duress, but Foley was said to have been genuinely captivated by Islam. When guards brought an English version of the Quran, Foley spent hours engrossed in the text, while others just pretended to be Muslims.

Foley's first set of guards, from the Nusra Front, viewed his professed Islamic faith with suspicion. However, the second group holding him seemed moved by it, and the abuse stopped. Unlike the Syrian prisoners, who were chained to radiators, Foley and John Cantlie were able to move freely inside their cell.

The authenticity of Foley's conversion has been questioned, with concerns about whether it was genuine or a survival tactic. Meanwhile, Pope Francis spoke about martyrdom during a homily at St. Martha's House in the Vatican, reflecting on the persecution and murder of Christians around the world, including those who are martyred for their faith in the present day.

The study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences reveals that plants make up the largest proportion of life on Earth, accounting for 80% of all carbon stored in living organisms. Bacteria are the second most abundant, followed by fungi and animals. Humans, despite their large population, only account for 0.06% of the world's biomass, but their impact since the beginning of civilization has been significant. Humans and their livestock outweigh wild mammals by more than 20-fold, and domesticated fowl surpass all other birds. The study was conducted by quantitative biologists who spent three years combing the scientific literature to determine the biomass of each creature. The ultimate goal of the study was to discover the most abundant protein on the planet, but they are still working on that question. The study highlights the disproportionate impact humans have on the planet, particularly in terms of their dietary choices, which have a significant effect on the habitats of animals, plants, and other organisms. The researchers hope that the findings will encourage people to consider the environmental impact of their choices. The study is the first comprehensive estimate of the weight of every class of living creature and overturns some long-held assumptions about the distribution of life on Earth. The study was led by Prof. Ron Milo of the Weizmann Institute of Science in Israel.

Pete Seeger, a folk music legend who passed away at the age of 94, was known for penning "Turn, Turn, Turn" and popularizing "This Land is Your Land." However, there are several lesser-known facts about Seeger. He adapted and popularized "We Shall Overcome," wrote "If I Had a Hammer," and opposed McCarthyism, marching beside Martin Luther King Jr. and leading environmental campaigns. Seeger continued to perform into his 90s and was a mentor to many musicians, including Bruce Springsteen, Joan Baez, and Arlo Guthrie. Seeger was once a member of the Communist Party, and was convicted of contempt of Congress for refusing to testify about his past membership. Despite this, he continued to protest and was blacklisted by commercial TV networks until 1967. Seeger's influence on American music and activism is still felt today, and he will be remembered as a pioneer of folk music and a champion of social justice.

On Wednesday, a 42-year-old British man, Michael Cohen, lost parts of both legs in a great white shark attack at Fish Hoek beach in Cape Town, South Africa. The incident occurred around lunchtime, with witnesses reporting that Cohen was about 50 yards from the shore when he was attacked. His friends managed to pull him out of the water, and he was later airlifted to Constantia Hospital for surgery.

The attack occurred despite shark warning flags flying on the beach and a siren that usually warns of predators not functioning due to a power cut. Witnesses reported seeing three large great whites in the area 90 minutes before the attack and on previous days. Shark spotters, employed by the local council, confirmed that Cohen was a regular swimmer at the beach and had been warned about the presence of sharks in the past.

Tracy Sassen, a surfer from Clovelly, was one of the witnesses who saw the attack. She described seeing a burst of water and then seeing people pulling Cohen out of the water. Kathy Geldenhuis, a local resident, held the drips as paramedics worked on Cohen, who was wearing a diabetic tag.

Monwabisi Sikweyiya, one of the shark spotters, helped drag Cohen from the water and used his own clothes as tourniquets. Sikweyiya confirmed that Cohen was a regular swimmer at the beach and had ignored warnings about the presence of sharks.

Cohen, who is single, is a British citizen born in Canada and is thought to have lived in Chiswick, west London, at some point. Last month, another British man, Ian Redmond from Lancashire, was killed by a shark while swimming off the Seychelles.

Following the attack, the beach and three nearby beaches were closed as a precaution until further notice. The shark was still in Fish Hoek Bay in the afternoon and was being monitored by the spotters.

President Obama signed an executive order aimed at narrowing the wage gap between men and women, forcing federal contractors to allow employees to discuss their salaries and disclose more information about their earnings. The order is part of a broader effort to increase turnout among female voters and address the persistent problem of pay inequity. The order prohibits federal contractors from retaliating against workers who discuss their salaries and requires them to file data with the federal government showing how they compensate employees, including by sex and race. The order affects only federal contractors and does not protect female employees in the private sector. The administration is disappointed that Republicans in Congress have opposed another bill, the Paycheck Fairness Act, which includes reforms like the ones that Obama is applying to federal contractors. The wage gap between men and women continues to be a significant issue, with women earning 77 cents for every dollar men earn, on average. Even the most conservative estimates suggest that women earn 5 to 12 percent less for doing similar jobs as men. The White House is not immune to inequalities, with an analysis showing that the median salary for female White House staffers is 12 percent lower than that for male staffers. The administration prioritizes hiring women and diverse talent at all levels and has made an effort to advance women through the ranks within the White House. The order is intended to address the "pay secrecy" that often keeps workers from seeking more equitable compensation and could spur companies to take voluntary measures to equalize salaries. Opponents argue that the order is a political ploy and cuts flexibility in the workplace for working mothers.

Title: Twitter Introduces Location Feature for Tweets and Billboard Newsletters Offer Daily Music News

Twitter has recently introduced a new feature that allows users to add their city or precise location to their Tweets, either from the web or via third-party applications. This feature can enhance the geographical context of the tweets, making them more relevant and engaging for the local audience. Users have the option to delete their Tweet location history at any time.

In other news, Billboard has launched a new service that delivers daily music news directly to your inbox through Billboard Newsletters. This service aims to keep music enthusiasts updated on the latest trends, releases, and events in the music industry. By subscribing, users can stay informed about their favorite artists, genres, and industry news, making it a valuable resource for music lovers and professionals alike.

In summary, Twitter's new location feature offers users the ability to add location details to their tweets, while Billboard Newsletters provide daily music news updates for music enthusiasts.

Paul McCartney, the iconic songwriter and former Beatle, has filed a lawsuit against Sony/ATV Music Publishing, seeking to regain copyright ownership of a catalog of songs he co-authored with John Lennon during their time in The Beatles. The lawsuit, filed in a U.S. District Court in New York, aims to confirm McCartney's ownership of songs such as "Yesterday," "Hey Jude," and "The Long and Winding Road."

McCartney is leveraging the termination provisions of the 1976 Copyright Act, which allows authors to reclaim the rights to their works after a set period of time. The works at issue include some of The Beatles' best-known songs, including "Love Me Do," "P.S. I Love You," "Thank You Girl," "Bad to Me," "I Want to Hold Your Hand," and "All You Need Is Love."

McCartney began serving termination notices in October 2008, and the terminations will become effective in 2018. The lawsuit notes that Sony/ATV gave no indication to McCartney that they contested the efficacy of his termination notices for years, but the publisher did challenge termination notices made by Duran Duran in a lawsuit filed in the United Kingdom.

The lawsuit claims that Sony/ATV executives indicated they would try to use the Duran Duran decision against McCartney. McCartney's legal team is seeking assurances that the publisher will not take legal action against him to cloud his title to The Beatles' works.

Sony/ATV has issued a statement maintaining that it "has the highest respect for Sir Paul McCartney with whom we have enjoyed a long and mutually rewarding relationship with respect to the treasured Lennon & McCartney song catalog." However, the publisher believes the lawsuit is unnecessary and premature.

The lawsuit is an attempt to protect McCartney from a legal strategy Sony/ATV used in U.K. courts in December to hold off an attempt by Duran Duran to reclaim its publishing. The publisher bought Michael Jackson's share of the company for $750 million last year.

In a recent interview on "60 Minutes," Mitt Romney reiterated his stance on taxes, stating that he wants to maintain the current progressivity in the tax code and not reduce taxes for high-income individuals. However, this stance contradicts his previous promises of significant tax cuts for the wealthy without increasing the deficit or raising taxes on the middle class.

The Tax Policy Center, a nonpartisan tax research organization, has declared that Romney's tax plan is "not mathematically possible" under the current tax breaks and deductions. Romney's campaign initially dismissed the Tax Policy Center's findings, but later studies by right-leaning economists and outlets suggested that Romney's tax plan could work under unrealistic assumptions.

One such study, conducted by economist Martin Feldstein, shows that Romney's tax plan could be revenue-neutral if tax deductions and exemptions for high-income earners are limited, but this would result in a significant tax increase for people making between $100,000 and $250,000 to pay for the tax cuts for the wealthy. However, Romney has defined middle-income earners as those making $200,000 to $250,000, and has stated that households making more than $100,000 are not middle-income.

Romney has been promoting this study as evidence that his tax plan can work, but he has been caught in a contradiction when asked if $100,000 is middle-income, to which he responded that middle-income is $200,000 to $250,000 and less. This contradiction highlights the fact that Romney's tax plan, even under the most favorable assumptions, would require tax increases on the people he defines as the middle class.

Romney's economic plan is largely substance-free, focusing on the same goals as previous Republican administrations, such as weaker environmental protection and lower taxes on the wealthy. However, there is no evidence to suggest that returning to Bush-era policies would cure the ongoing economic slump, which began during the Bush administration. Romney has also denounced the Federal Reserve's efforts to step up and address the economic downturn.

Romney has based his campaign on the premise that he can become president simply by not being Barack Obama, and he has declared that his election would spark an economic boom through increased optimism. However, there is no evidence to support this claim, and Romney's economic plan lacks specifics to address the ongoing economic slump. Romney's stance on taxes, combined with his lack of a substantive economic plan, raises concerns about his ability to lead an economic recovery.

The Fort Lee lane closure scandal, also known as the George Washington Bridge lane closure scandal or Bridgegate, is a political scandal in which a staff member and political appointees of New Jersey Governor Chris Christie, a Republican, colluded to create traffic jams in Fort Lee, New Jersey, by closing lanes at the main toll plaza for the upper level of the George Washington Bridge. The problems began on Monday, September 9, 2013, when two of three toll lanes for a local street entrance were closed during morning rush hour. Local officials, emergency services, and the public were not notified of the lane closures, which Fort Lee declared a threat to public safety. The resulting back-ups and gridlock on local streets ended only when the two lanes were reopened on Friday, September 13, 2013, by an order from Port Authority Executive Director Patrick Foye. He said that the "hasty and ill-informed decision" could have endangered lives and violated federal and state laws.

As testimony in the George Washington Bridge lane-closing trial continues past its first week, New Jersey Governor Chris Christie faces a new problem: a citizen's criminal complaint filed against him in Fort Lee Municipal Court. Brian Thompson reports. (Published Thursday, Sep 29, 2016)

David Wildstein has pleaded guilty in the scheme to tie up traffic at the bridge, and ex-Christie staffers Bridget Kelly and Bill Baroni face fraud, conspiracy, and civil rights charges in the case. Christie has repeatedly denied knowing anything about the scheme until long after it was carried out.

Bergen County activist Bill Brennan told NBC 4 New York that he filed the complaint of official misconduct in the second degree on Wednesday. A court official confirmed the filing. Brennan said the case has cost taxpayers tens of millions of dollars and added of the main players in the case: "When listening to the nonchalant manner in which these people are discussing, the magnitude of the pettiness, is just absurd."

Brennan said his criminal complaint of the governor was over the government's star witness David Wildstein's accusation that the governor knew by midweek about the lane shutdowns for political retaliation against Fort Lee's mayor, as well as the governor's subsequent failure to seek criminal prosecution of his staffers once he found out.

Witness: Christie Knew About GWB Lane Closures
A former official at the Port Authority says Governor Christie knew the GWB lane closures were happening. Brian Thompson reports. (Published Tuesday, Sept. 27, 2016)

The governor is on record repeatedly, and as late as Tuesday, denying he was told about the closures the week of the shutdown.

The citizen's complaint was sent to the Superior Court in Hackensack, per state law, according to the court official in Fort Lee. According to a legal expert, if a superior court judge determines a probable cause, the case would go to a county prosecutor, and then if that office moves forward, to a grand jury.

The Los Angeles police have accused actor Michael Jace, known for his role in "The Shield," of fatally shooting his wife, April Jace, at their Hyde Park home on Monday night. April Jace, a financial aid employee at Biola University, was reportedly shot multiple times after returning home from picking up their sons from baseball practice. The motive for the shooting is believed to be domestic violence, with law enforcement sources citing past accusations of domestic violence against Michael Jace dating back nearly two decades.

In court documents from his divorce with his previous wife, Jennifer Bitterman, Michael Jace was described as temperamental and unreliable. Bitterman alleged that he threatened to kill her if they went to "war" over his visitation rights of their son. She also described a violent incident she witnessed between the couple, where Michael Jace allegedly choked and hit Bitterman and slammed her against the wall while their son screamed in his crib.

Neighbors in Hyde Park, where the shooting occurred, described the couple as loving and friendly, with no signs of violence. However, the financial stress Michael Jace was under may have played a role in the incident. In a significant development, the Supreme Court heard oral arguments on Wednesday for the Defense of Marriage Act (DOMA), a law that denies federal benefits to legally married same-sex couples. The court's deliberations came after two days of hearings on the constitutionality of California's Proposition 8 ban on gay marriage.

Justice Anthony M. Kennedy, considered the pivotal justice on the issue, expressed concerns about the federal Defense of Marriage Act (DOMA) potentially intruding on the traditional role of state governments in defining marriage. He argued that the law's recognition of marriages only between a man and a woman ignores states that have legalized same-sex marriage.

Kennedy also highlighted the impact of the more than 1,100 references to marriage contained in federal laws and regulations on citizens' daily lives, creating a "real risk of running in conflict with what has always been thought to be the essence of the state police power, which is to regulate marriage, divorce, custody."

Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg raised questions about the law's withholding of benefits such as tax advantages, Social Security benefits, and leave to care for a spouse, stating, "What kind of marriage is it?"

The court's liberal justices seemed more supportive of gay rights and same-sex marriage, while conservatives appeared more tolerant of government action to protect "traditional marriage." During the arguments, Chief Justice John G. Roberts Jr. was skeptical of the idea that gay people lack political power in government actions.

Roberts also questioned the Obama administration's decision to enforce DOMA until the Supreme Court decides its fate, stating, "I don't see why he doesn't have the courage of his convictions to stop enforcing the law."

The arguments revealed an expected divide on the court, with liberal justices more supportive of gay rights and same-sex marriage and conservatives more tolerant of government action to protect traditional marriage. The case, brought by 83-year-old Edith Windsor, who married her partner of more than 40 years in Canada in 2007, could lead to a decision on DOMA by the end of June.

The hearings took place amid growing support among Americans for gay marriage but division among the 50 states. Nine states recognize it, while 30 states have constitutional amendments banning it, and others are in-between. DOMA limits the definition of marriage as between a man and a woman, permitting benefits such as Social Security survivor payments and federal tax deductions only for married, opposite-sex couples, not for legally married same-sex couples.

President Bill Clinton signed DOMA into law in 1996, but earlier this month, he called for the law to be overturned. The atmosphere outside the courthouse was more subdued than on Tuesday, with a largely pro-gay marriage crowd of several hundred holding signs and waving American flags. Hundreds more waited patiently in line for a chance at the handful of seats in the courtroom allocated to the public.

The DOMA case is about whether Windsor, who was married to a woman, should get the federal estate tax deduction available to heterosexuals when their spouses pass away. Windsor's marriage to Thea Spyer was recognized under New York law, but not under DOMA. When Spyer died in 2009, Windsor was forced to pay federal estate tax because the federal government would not recognize her marriage. She later sued the government, seeking a $363,000 tax refund.

Windsor's lawyers argue that the federal government has no role in defining marriage, which is traditionally left to the states. Lower courts have ruled in her favor. The roughly 133,000 gay couples nationwide, married in one of the nine states where it is legal, are not recognized as married by the federal government, Windsor's supporters say. Various groups are calling for DOMA to be struck down.

The Obama administration has agreed with Windsor that the section of law that defines marriage violates the U.S. Constitution's guarantee of equal protection under the law. The Justice Department has thus declined to defend the statute, leaving a legal group acting on behalf of the Republican-dominated U.S. House of Representatives, known as the Bipartisan Legal Advisory Group, as the party defending the federal law.

The hearings on DOMA and Proposition 8 are expected to result in rulings by the end of June. The outcomes could have significant implications for the recognition and treatment of same-sex marriages in the United States.

The Hubble Space Telescope has discovered a bizarre object in the asteroid belt, named P/2013 P5, which appears to have six comet-like tails of dust. The object, which measures up to 240 meters wide, has been ejecting dust periodically for at least five months. Scientists believe that the asteroid's rotation rate increased to the point where its surface started flying apart, causing dust to slide towards the equator, shatter, and fall off, forming the tails. The tails are believed to be formed by a series of impulsive dust-ejection events, and radiation pressure from the sun is thought to have spun the asteroid up. This phenomenon, known as the YORP effect, heats up the sun-facing side of an asteroid, causing it to spin faster, and could explain the strange spoke features of P/2013 P5. Follow-up observations are needed to confirm whether the dust leaves the asteroid in the equatorial plane, which would provide strong evidence for a rotational breakup. This discovery could indicate that rotational breakup is a common phenomenon in the asteroid belt and could be the main way small asteroids die.

Greece is on the brink of a major vote on Sunday that will shape the future of its economy and Europe's monetary union. The country has been in a financial crisis since 2009, and in 2010, it received a bailout from European governments and the International Monetary Fund (IMF). However, the bailout failed to fix the problem, and Greece is once again in trouble.

In 2015, a new government led by Alexis Tsipras came to power and sought to renegotiate the terms of the bailout. The government wanted to restore some of the spending cuts, reverse some of the revenue hikes, and receive outright forgiveness of some of the debt. The creditors, including the IMF, the European Central Bank (ECB), and the European Commission, disagreed with the Greek government's requests.

The IMF loan that came due on June 29 was important because it was a key payment to the IMF, and Greece defaulted on it. This has made Greece an international pariah, and the IMF will continue to seek repayment. The ECB decided last weekend that it could no longer keep accepting additional collateral from Greek banks, which means no more extraordinary lending will be extended. This has caused Greece to close its banks and impose limits on cash withdrawals.

If Greece votes "yes" in the referendum, it is possible that the existing government (likely reorganized) will be able to reopen the banks and conclude a deal. However, if the public votes "no," there will be a sharp recession over the next few months, and the Tsipras government is unlikely to survive. If the post-Tsipras government opts to proceed with the default, it is unclear how long it will take for the economy to stabilize.

The Greek crisis has the potential to spread to other countries in Europe, especially if people believe that their governments may also default on debt. The ECB is likely to be able to head off this problem, but the political contagion is harder to assess.

In conclusion, Greece is facing a major economic crisis, and the outcome of the referendum on Sunday will determine the country's future. If the public votes "yes," it is possible that a deal can be reached, but if they vote "no," there will be a sharp recession. The crisis has the potential to spread to other countries in Europe, and the IMF will continue to seek repayment from Greece.

Two lawsuits were filed in federal court on Thursday, aiming to shut down Colorado's regulated marijuana industry. The suits, initiated by the anti-drug group Safe Streets and three other plaintiffs, target Colorado lawmakers and participants in the state's commercial marijuana industry. The plaintiffs argue that Colorado's recreational marijuana laws violate federal law, which considers marijuana illegal, and are seeking damages due to alleged injuries brought on by legalization.

The lawsuits name various marijuana businesses, their owners, and several parties who have provided banking, insurance, and accounting services to these businesses as defendants. The suits also name a construction company that allegedly agreed to transport water to a marijuana grow. The plaintiffs are members of Safe Streets, a Washington, D.C.-based group dedicated to combating crime and drugs.

The suits argue that under the U.S. Constitution's supremacy clause, Colorado's legalization of recreational marijuana is unconstitutional, as marijuana remains illegal at the federal level. The plaintiffs are asking federal courts to order Colorado lawmakers to comply with federal law, cease issuing licenses to marijuana businesses, and shutter the entire industry in the state.

Colorado state Rep. Jonathan Singer (D), a vocal supporter of the state's marijuana laws, described the lawsuit as a "bad idea" and a "waste of time." He pointed out that Colorado voters strongly approved Amendment 64, legalizing recreational marijuana in the state, in 2012, and the first retail marijuana shops opened their doors on Jan. 1, 2014. Since then, the marijuana industry has grown to a value of around $700 million, and the state has taken in about $60 million in taxes and fees, some of which is going toward school construction and renovation.

Singer also highlighted that employment numbers are up, crime rates are down in Denver, highway fatalities are at near-historic lows, and marijuana use among teens has not grown more widespread under the new laws. However, there have been some worrying episodes since the new laws went into effect, such as two tragic and high-profile fatalities in Denver linked to marijuana use.

In response, state lawmakers and the marijuana industry have worked to refine the laws over time. Today, more than a year since sales began, Colorado voters still don't appear to regret ending prohibition of the drug. The lawsuits mark the second time in a matter of months that someone has targeted Colorado's marijuana laws with litigation. The state has yet to officially respond to the previous lawsuit filed by Nebraska and Oklahoma in the U.S. Supreme Court.

Liliane's memory of the day Yohanna disappeared is vivid. She recalls giving a taxi driver the destination and leaving her daughter with her then-boyfriend while she went out of town for work. When she returned, her boyfriend told her that Yohanna was with his mother, who offered to babysit so he could visit Liliane. However, when they returned to Montreal together, he told her his mother lived in Boston. When Liliane flew to Boston to get her baby, he told her Yohanna had drowned and was buried.

The case went cold, and Liliane's boyfriend, Aaron Lewis Guay, was deported due to lacking the proper papers to stay in Quebec. No charges were laid, but he was told not to return. The case was reopened in 1994, and Guay was charged with kidnapping, but he denied everything, and a judge ruled there was not enough evidence to proceed.

Through the years, Liliane has pursued leads and experienced both hope and disappointment. In 2005, a U.S. woman contacted the Missing Children's Network, but DNA tests revealed she was not Liliane's daughter. However, two weeks before the 35th anniversary of Yohanna's disappearance, Liliane received a private message on Facebook from a woman living in the United States. The woman asked how she could get in touch with the investigators in charge of Yohanna's case and inquired about a Y-shaped birthmark on Yohanna's index finger, which the woman claimed to have. Liliane confirmed the birthmark, and the woman told her she might be Liliane's daughter.

Local police are now communicating with American authorities so the woman can have DNA tests performed to confirm her identity. Liliane remains hopeful but cautious, reminding herself not to get her hopes too high until the results are in. The article concludes with a request for anyone with information concerning Yohanna's whereabouts to contact the Missing Children’s Network.

Two lawyers, Thomas Bowers and Reggie London, have been hired to investigate the police treatment of Ahmed Mohamed, a 14-year-old teenager from Irving, Texas, who gained national attention after being arrested for bringing a homemade clock to school that was mistaken for a bomb. Ahmed's family has accused the authorities of humiliating him and causing him emotional distress. The lawyers plan to have a medical professional examine Ahmed and investigate the actions of the city and school district. Thomas Bowers, who previously represented a former stripper in a lawsuit against Cowboys owner Jerry Jones, will work on the case with Reggie London, who typically handles criminal defense cases. The lawyers have contracted with Ahmed's father and are considering legal options to retrieve the boy's clock from the Irving Police Department. On Christmas Day 2017, thousands of lottery players in South Carolina believed they had struck luck with winning tickets for the Holiday Cash Add-A-Play game. Between 5:51 p.m. and 7:53 p.m., gas stations and convenience stores across the state issued tens of thousands of winning tickets, worth up to $500 each. However, due to a computer glitch, these tickets were produced in error, causing approximately 71,000 winning plays.

The South Carolina Education Lottery (SCEL) blamed its former computer gaming vendor, Intralot, for the error, stating that the company failed to run adequate quality assurance testing prior to deploying the game. The glitch caused machines to repeatedly print tickets depicting nine tree symbols, resulting in the biggest prize.

After a five-month analysis, the SCEL announced that it would not be delivering more than $30 million in prizes to players who bought tickets during the brief window. Instead, players would be reimbursed only for the cost of each lottery ticket: $1 for each claim that is mailed in.

The SCEL asked players to mail the original Holiday Cash Add-A-Play tickets to the P.O. Box 11039, Columbia, SC 29211-1039, along with their name and return address. The lottery will refund the purchase price for each returned ticket and reimburse the player for postage up to the amount of first-class USPS postage for the ticket(s) submitted.

The cost of the error-filled tickets would have totaled approximately $35 million, but the SCEL is out about $1.7 million—the sum players were able to cash-in before the mistake was discovered on Christmas Day. Two lawsuits have been filed against the state lottery and Intralot on behalf of people who have been denied prize money.

The SCEL reported record ticket sales in the most recent fiscal year (2016-2017) totaling $1.64 billion and issued more than $1 billion in prizes. Nearly $5 billion has been allocated to education programs throughout the state since the start of the lottery in 2002.

The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) Administrator Scott Pruitt has defended his frequent first-class flights at taxpayer expense, citing security concerns and unpleasant interactions with other travelers. Pruitt spoke about his flight costs on Tuesday in New Hampshire, following a first-class flight to meet with the state's Republican governor and tour a toxic waste site. Pruitt told the New Hampshire Union Leader that he had some "incidents" on flights shortly after his appointment by President Donald Trump last year.

Pruitt said that the security decisions were made by others and that he was not involved in the decision to fly first class. He confirmed to the newspaper that he had flown first class from Washington to Boston before continuing on to New Hampshire. Pruitt's ticket cost six times what EPA paid for his aides seated in coach.

The Associated Press reported in July and again in December that spending on commercial airline tickets purchased for Pruitt indicated he was flying in premium-class seats. EPA's press office has repeatedly refused to comment on whether Pruitt was flying first class.

Federal regulations allow government travelers to fly business class or first class when no cheaper options are "reasonably available" or if there are exceptional security circumstances. However, past federal audits have found that those rules have been routinely violated by high-ranking government officials under both Republican and Democratic administrations.

The use of luxury air travel by members of Trump's Cabinet has been under scrutiny for months, after the resignation of Health and Human Services Secretary Tom Price in September following media reports he spent at least $400,000 in taxpayer funds on private jets for himself and his staff.

A report released Wednesday by the inspector general at the Department of Veterans Affairs found that Secretary David Shulkin and his staff made "false representations" to justify his wife accompanying him at taxpayer expense on an 11-day European trip that mixed business and sightseeing.

Records show Pruitt has taken at least four flights on non-commercial aircraft, costing more than $58,000. EPA has said all of those flights were necessary and pre-approved by ethics lawyers.

EPA spokesman Jahan Wilcox did not immediately respond Wednesday to questions about whether Pruitt had been granted similar waivers allowing him to fly premium class or about the past security incidents to which Pruitt referred.

Pruitt's frequent government-funded travel, which records show has often included weekend layovers in his home state of Oklahoma, is currently under review by EPA's internal watchdog. The office of EPA Inspector General Arthur Elkins said Wednesday it expects to release the results of its investigation by summer.

Meanwhile, the White House's budget proposal for EPA released earlier this week seeks to cut $3.7 million, or 9 percent, in funding for Elkins' office. His spokeswoman, Jennifer Kaplan, said that would impair the ability of the inspector general to perform investigations like the one into Pruitt's spending.

"Without sufficient resources, we would not be able to take on many discretionary audits and investigations that the OIG believes yield considerable value and return on investment," Kaplan said.

In Uttar Pradesh's Kushinagar district, six newly-wed brides from both Hindu and Muslim communities have protested against their in-laws due to the lack of toilets in their households. In response, Sulabh International, a non-profit organization focused on sanitation, has agreed to construct toilets in the affected households at no cost.

The brides' action has been praised as bold and extraordinary by Sulabh International's founder, Bindeshwar Pathak, who believes it reflects a changing mindset among women regarding the importance of toilets. Pathak also highlighted the issue of lack of toilets in rural areas, particularly affecting women, and its associated costs, which amount to nearly $54 billion annually in India due to hygiene-related illnesses, loss of productivity, and other issues.

Pathak pointed out that a bride from UP's Maharajganj district, Priyanka Bharti, was previously honored for her efforts in constructing a toilet in her in-laws' house. Bharti now works as a Sulabh motivator and has appeared in a sanitation advertisement alongside a Bollywood actress.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi has also addressed the issue, urging parliamentarians and the corporate sector to help build separate toilets for girls in schools. Modi's speech marked the first time a prime minister has mentioned the issue of toilets for girls in India's history.

The lack of toilets in rural India, particularly in villages like Khesiya, poses numerous challenges for women, including exposure to the risk of attack and the need to wait for darkness to attend to their needs. In his Independence Day speech, Modi vowed to end open defecation in the 21st century, acknowledging the numerous problems women face due to this issue.

San Francisco City Attorney Dennis Herrera is facing a legal challenge from Monster Beverage Corp, as the company attempts to halt Herrera's investigation into the marketing of its highly caffeinated energy drinks to minors. In a lawsuit filed in U.S. District Court in Los Angeles, Monster claims that Herrera's actions would violate constitutional rights and impose undue burdens on interstate commerce.

Herrera has been investigating Monster Energy drinks since October under California's unfair competition law, targeting marketing claims that the drinks are completely safe and that consumers can never get too much of a good thing. In March, Herrera joined a group of 18 doctors from medical centers across the country in calling for the U.S. Food and Drug Administration to regulate caffeine levels in energy drinks, citing health risks, particularly for youths.

Under current FDA standards, caffeine in sodas can register no higher than about 71 milligrams per 12-oz. serving. Energy drinks often have between 100 and 300 milligrams of caffeine per 8-oz. serving and are often sold in larger quantities per can.

Monster markets to children as young as 6 years old, according to Herrera's office, which produced screen shots from the beverage company's "Monster Army" website listing an 11-year-old as a "Monster Army Major" and a 6-year-old as a "Reserve." The company maintains that its product has less than half the caffeine of a Starbucks coffee. However, Herrera's office argues that Starbucks does not market sweet, highly caffeinated drinks to young people.

Herrera has vowed to aggressively fight Monster's lawsuit, stating that the company is claiming an unfettered right to continue marketing its products to children and youth, despite the evidence of serious health risks.

Microsoft's new version of Windows, Windows 8, is a significant shift for the company, marking a move towards mobile machines from the traditional personal computer. The operating system, which is being released as a consumer preview on Wednesday, is designed to be an excellent touchscreen operating system, offering a more intuitive and user-friendly interface compared to Apple's iPad.

However, Windows 8 also has a split personality, as it is optimized for touchscreens while still intended to run on laptops and desktops. The new OS features two completely different interfaces: the Desktop, which is the traditional Windows interface, and Metro, a new interface inspired by Microsoft's Windows Phone. The Metro interface is the gateway to Windows' new interface and is the first thing users will see when turning on a Windows 8 PC.

The Metro interface is easy to use and offers several advantages over the traditional Windows model, particularly for touchscreen devices. However, it is also the most radical transformation in Windows' history, and users may find it disorienting, especially when using it on a big-screen PC rather than a tablet.

One of the key differences between the Metro and traditional Windows interfaces is that Metro only runs specially designed apps, which are only available through Microsoft's built-in Windows Store. This change is designed to make apps easier to install and reduce the prevalence of malware. Traditional Windows programs can still be downloaded, but they will run in the Desktop view.

Overall, Windows 8 offers a significant upgrade to an aging OS, but it remains to be seen whether Windows' adherents will consider it too much change, too fast. The new interface offers several advantages over the traditional Windows model, particularly for touchscreen devices, but users may find it disorienting, especially when using it on a big-screen PC.

A recent study published in the journal Obesity Facts suggests that body weight tends to be highest on Mondays and lowest on Fridays due to weekend behaviors such as increased calorie intake and decreased physical activity. The study, which analyzed data from 80 adults, found that those who successfully lost weight had lower weights during the week, with their lowest weight generally recorded on Friday. The study's authors propose that meal sizes and calorie intake tend to increase while physical activity tends to decrease during weekends, and that allowing yourself a few indulgences over the weekend may help you stick with eating better and managing your weight over the long term. The study also found that successful weight losers were allowing themselves some serious dietary leniency over the weekend, which may have contributed to their weight loss success. The study's authors suggest that if you like to regularly weigh yourself, it's best to compare the same day of the week, and that allowing yourself a few indulgences over the weekend may help you lose weight long-term as long as you can compensate during the week. The study was conducted by Anna-Leena Orsama and colleagues from the VTT Technical Research Center of Finland.

On July 17, Ashley Wright, a 23-year-old resident of Pensacola, Florida, was arrested for child abuse, petty theft, and resisting an officer. The incident occurred at the Santa Rosa Mall in Mary Esther, where Wright allegedly shoplifted clothing worth $261 from Dillard's.

When a deputy approached her car, Wright refused to exit and, holding her three-month-old daughter as a shield, threatened the officer, saying, "You will have to shoot through the baby to get me!" During the ensuing struggle, Wright threw her infant daughter at the deputy, who managed to avoid harming the baby.

Wright was eventually apprehended but not without a struggle. She was found to be bleeding after tripping and hitting her head on the ground. Wright, who had consumed a few beers, claimed her actions were due to her needing school clothes for her children. However, the stolen items were adult clothing, not children's garments.

Wright remains in the county jail, awaiting a $7000 bond. The baby was not injured during the incident. The incident has raised concerns about the use of children as shields in such situations and the potential risks to the children involved.

The Internet Archive is working on a project to archive web pages as they are created and preserve links to the archived versions of pages that are changed or removed from the web. This initiative aims to fix broken links on the internet.

Meanwhile, researchers have discovered the remains of a Swedish warship, the Mars, that sank in the Baltic Sea in 1564 during the Northern Seven Years’ War. The ship, which contained hundreds of soldiers, exploded in the Baltic Sea, and its remains were discovered near the Swedish island of Öland in 2011.

The latest discoveries from the wreckage were revealed during a press conference in Öland. Researchers found more skeletal parts, large guns, a hand grenade, and a grapnel, which is a unique find and can shed new light on Medieval and Early Modern naval warfare. Divers also found remains of possible arms and armour, including helmets and swords.

The Mars sank due to a gunpowder explosion at the front of the ship, but it had been under attack by Danish and Lübeckian warships before the explosion. Researchers have documented a change in Swedish tactics from a focus on close quarter combat to long-distance fighting, as indicated by large cannons up to 4.8 meters long.

The wreckage provides a snapshot of a moment in time and captures a piece of military and political history. It is an international history as the Seven Years’ War was fought across national boundaries. The exploration of Mars was carried out by researchers from the Marine Research Institute MARIS at Södertörn University in Sweden, and divers from the diving organization GUE, Västervik Museum, Ocean Discovery, and MMT.

The Internet Archive's project aims to preserve the internet's history by archiving web pages and fixing broken links. The Mars warship's remains provide a unique insight into Medieval and Early Modern naval warfare and offer a snapshot of a moment in time during the Northern Seven Years’ War.

FBI Agent Chase Bishop, based in the Washington Field Office, has been charged with second-degree assault following an incident at a Denver nightclub on June 2. Bishop, who was off-duty and on vacation, is accused of accidentally firing his gun while performing a backflip at the Mile High Spirits bar. The incident resulted in a bystander, Thomas Reddington, being shot in the leg.

Bishop turned himself in to the Denver Sheriff Department on Tuesday and was booked into jail. The Denver District Attorney's office stated that additional charges may be pending, depending on the results of alcohol and drug tests, which are still awaited to determine Bishop's blood alcohol content at the time of the incident.

The FBI is conducting an internal investigation into the incident, with potential outcomes including termination, suspension, or reprimand. The victim, Reddington, is considering a lawsuit against the FBI. Bishop is scheduled to be advised of the charge in Denver District Court on Wednesday.

The Domain crawl of the Luxembourg web domain (.lu) was conducted by the Internet Archive on behalf of the National Library of Luxembourg in June and July of 2017.

Meanwhile, in Detroit, a homeless man named Abe Hagenston, also known as "Honest Abe," has been panhandling for donations, including credit and debit cards, using a card reader attached to his cell phone. He has been living under the 8 Mile overpass on I-75 for seven years. Despite the relatively mild winter, Hagenston expressed his need for snow for snow removal work and to buy new eyeglasses.

Hagenston and a group of fellow homeless individuals have organized themselves like a union to panhandle in shifts. He also uses the extra time to make donations more efficient by accepting various credit cards through Square.com. Square readers attach to credit cards and turn a smartphone into a card reader.

The exact number of homeless individuals in Detroit is unknown, but last year's count included an estimate of 2,700. This year's count is not yet ready. Volunteers spent the night counting the homeless and offering warmth and shelter, but some chose to remain on the streets.

Hagenston has also created a website where people can make contributions to a collection of homeless individuals, hire them for odd jobs, or report fake panhandlers. He aims to use his situation to help others and turn it into something beneficial. Hagenston has been homeless for ten years and hopes to find a way to rebuild his life.

On November 28, approximately 100 Occupy Philly protesters remained at City Hall, defying a deadline set by Mayor Nutter to vacate the premises. Despite the deadline, no eviction took place, and city officials refrained from speculating about future actions. Protesters, many of whom were homeless, chanted slogans and railed against corporate greed while serving food and water. Police looked on calmly, with no plans to evict anyone, according to Chief Inspector Joseph Sullivan. The city needs to erect fencing for renovation work at Dilworth Plaza, including the addition of a winter ice rink. Over the last few days, some tents had been taken down, and two protesters, Darrin Annussek and William Tuttle, were preparing to move to the Occupy site in Washington. Annussek believed Nutter had exaggerated health and safety concerns to justify denying the protesters a new location. Ellen Rogovinhart, a supporter, hoped the city would not use force to evict the protesters, as had occurred in other cities. The LAPD early Monday declared an unlawful assembly on the streets surrounding City Hall and ordered Occupy L.A. protesters to disperse or face arrest. Police officers were present, but no arrests had been made as of the article's publication. The Los Angeles encampment, which had grown to approximately 400 tents and 700 to 800 people, was one of the largest on the West Coast aligned with the national Occupy Wall Street movement. The mayor had given protesters until just after midnight to remove their tents and leave or face a forcible removal, setting the stage for a potential showdown. However, police commanders later said they would permit the Occupy LA encampment to stay until at least daybreak, and it was thought unlikely that the camp would be forced to shut down on Monday.

On May 28, a series of flood advisories and warnings were issued across various counties in Colorado, including Grand, Jackson, Rio Blanco, Mesa, Eagle, Routt, Larimer, Weld, and Mesa County. The most significant incident occurred on Grand Mesa, where three residents from Collbran and Mesa areas are missing after a mudslide estimated to be 2 miles wide, 4 miles long, and 250 feet deep. The slide occurred along Salt Creek Road, near Vega State Park, and was reported to sound like a freight train. The area is remote, with no cellphone service, and rescue crews are on the scene. Officials are discouraging people from entering the area, and a roadblock has been established outside the mudslide perimeter for safety. The incident is ongoing, and further updates are expected on May 29.

The G7 summit in Quebec, Canada, is expected to be marked by tension and confrontation between U.S. President Donald Trump and his allies over trade and foreign policy disputes. Trump's protectionist tariffs on steel and aluminum imports, his decision to exit the Iran nuclear accord, and his retreat from global efforts to combat climate change have led to a rift between the U.S. and its allies.

Trump's reception in Canada is set to be a far cry from the friendly visit of President Ronald Reagan three decades ago. Trump and Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau have been publicly feuding over the tariffs on Canada's metals industries, with Trudeau calling them "insulting." Trump has also threatened to impose tariffs on Canadian dairy products, claiming a 270% tariff on U.S. dairy products.

French President Emmanuel Macron has suggested that Trump might not sign the final summit statement on G7 priorities, stating that "the American president may not mind being isolated, but neither do we mind signing a 6-country agreement if need be." Macron has also tweeted that the EU trade surplus with the U.S. is $151 Billion, and Canada keeps U.S. farmers and others out.

Trump has offered his own digs, tweeting that Macron and Trudeau are charging the U.S. massive tariffs and creating non-monetary barriers. Trump has also threatened to leave the summit early, stating that he will travel directly to Singapore from Canada in anticipation of his upcoming meeting with North Korea's leader Kim Jong Un.

Trudeau has charged that he finds the tariffs "insulting" and that such tactics are hardly how two close allies and trading partners that fought side-by-side in World War II, Korea, and Afghanistan should treat one another. The Trump administration has also clashed with Canada over his insistence that the 24-year-old North American Free Trade Agreement involving the United States, Canada, and Mexico be written to better serve the U.S.

Given the conflicts between Washington and its allies, the most likely outcome of the G7 talks is "polite acrimony." The United States has experienced tense relations with its allies before, but Trump's moves have taken the hostility to new heights. Experts suggest that this is the first time the U.S. government is seen as truly acting in bad faith, in treating allies as a threat, in treating trade as negative, and in fundamentally undermining the system that it built.

Canada and other U.S. allies are retaliating with tariffs on U.S. exports, and Trump has mused about wanting to split up NAFTA and negotiating separate trade deals with Canada and Mexico in what Ujczo sees as a divide-and-conquer strategy. The summit threatens to mark the outer limit of international patience for the avowed nationalistic Trump, as leaders who had sought to cajole and "bromance" the president are embracing more hard-nosed tactics.

The 70th annual Cannes Film Festival concluded on Sunday with the Palme d'Or award going to Swedish director Ruben Ostlund's satire, The Square. The film, a follow-up to Ostlund's 2014 hit Force Majeure, explores Swedish art, commerce, politics, and national identity. The Grand Prix was awarded to 120 Beats per Minute by Robin Campillo, a film about the French gay rights struggle focusing on ACT UP–Paris.

Sofia Coppola became only the second woman to win the best director prize for her film The Beguiled, starring Nicole Kidman and Colin Farrell. Coppola was not present to receive her award, but Maren Ade accepted on her behalf and thanked director Jane Campion for being a role model. Nicole Kidman was honored with a special prize for the festival's 70th anniversary, and Joaquin Phoenix was awarded the best actor prize for Lynne Ramsay's You Were Never Really Here. Diane Kruger received the best actress award for her work in In the Fade, her first German-language starring role.

In her speech, Kruger dedicated her award to victims of terror. "Those trying to pick up the pieces and go on after having lost everything, please know you are not alone," she said. Loveless, helmed by Russian writer-director Andrey Zvyagintsev, took the jury prize.

The Palme d'Or for short film was given to A Gentle Night from Chinese director Qiu Yang. A special mention for short film was awarded to Teppo Airaksinen for Katto. The Camera d’Or, given to the best first film that played in the festival regardless of section, went to Leonor Serraille for Jeune Femme (Montparnasse-Bienvenüe).

The jury included president Pedro Almodovar and members Will Smith, Jessica Chastain, Fan Bingbing, Agnès Jaoui, Park Chan-wook, Maren Ade, Paolo Sorrentino, and Gabriel Yared. The festival faced controversy this year due to the inclusion of Netflix films in competition, with Almodovar stating beforehand that he didn't want the Palme to go to a movie that isn't shown on big screens. As a result, Cannes announced that starting next year, streaming-only films will not be eligible for the Palme d'Or.

A federal criminal investigation has been initiated into the deadly duck boat sinking on Table Rock Lake in Missouri, which resulted in the deaths of 17 people. The investigation targets the captains of two Ride the Ducks boats, Kenneth Scott McKee and Barry King, and Ripley Entertainment, the company that operates the tourist rides. The captains are accused of operating the vessels in a manner that endangered lives, while Ripley Entertainment is under investigation for potential criminal liability. The U.S. Attorneys' manual defines a "target" as a person with substantial evidence linking them to the commission of a crime, and a "subject" as a person whose conduct is within the scope of the investigation. The National Transportation Safety Board is also conducting an investigation into the cause of the sinking. The first 911 call about the sinking came 14 minutes after the boat entered the water, and the National Weather Service had issued a severe thunderstorm warning with winds of up to 60 mph. The Coast Guard notified the U.S. Attorney's Office that its preliminary probable cause determination was that the sinking resulted from the misconduct, negligence, or inattention to duties of the captain of the vessel, which is a violation of federal criminal law. The federal investigation is being conducted in addition to a separate criminal probe by the Missouri attorney general. Several lawsuits have been filed on behalf of passengers who died and a survivor, alleging that Ripley Entertainment disregarded known dangers and made the conscious decision to begin the excursion on the water in volatile weather. The court documents filed Wednesday cite a federal law regarding negligence or misconduct when operating a vessel, with potential penalties of fines or imprisonment. Ripley Entertainment has stated that it is cooperating fully with federal and state authorities.

A holiday potluck invitation sent to approximately 25,000 Utah state employees on Friday caused a massive reply-all chain, leading to thousands of emails flooding state employees' inboxes. The initial email was sent by an unidentified individual from an unspecified department. The reply-all responses included curt, angry, and confused messages, as well as requests to be removed from the email thread. The chain clogged up phones and computers for several hours, with the thousands of polite responses only amplifying the crescendo of emails. Utah Lt. Gov. Spencer Cox humorously referred to the incident as an "emergency" on Twitter. By 11:10 a.m., the flood of emails seemed to have abated, according to a public information officer for the Utah Division of Emergency Management. This incident is reminiscent of a similar reply-all chain that occurred between Reuters' 33,000 employees a few years ago.
